payload.page_title: Dependency Failure Resilience Playbook (Enterprise Onboarding)

sections.body:
Purpose

This playbook documents a standardized approach for identifying, preventing, and remediating failures caused by third-party or internal dependency outages during enterprise onboarding and early go-live. It focuses on the technical mitigations, telemetry assertions, and communication patterns Customer Success (CS), SRE, and Platform teams should follow when dependencies degrade or fail.

Scope

- Applies to enterprise onboarding windows, canary rollouts, and first-72-hour post-go-live stability runs.
- Covers external partners (cloud provider APIs, SCM, identity providers, SaaS connectors) and internal services we rely on (ingress-gateway, fanout-proxy, telemetry-gatekeeper, embedding-indexer, kvcache, model-router).
- Does NOT cover purely customer-side outages (e.g., customer DB down) except where we coordinate cutover.

Owners and RACI

- Primary owner: Customer Success (Onboarding) — Ava Chen
- Technical owner (SRE escalation): Eng SRE — Diego Morales
- Platform mitigations and config changes: Eng Platform — Priya Natarajan
- Observability contract owner: Eng DevEx — Samir Gupta
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Detection: Eng SRE (R), Eng DevEx (C), CS (I)
2) Triage/Customer comms: CS (R), Eng SRE (A)
3) Mitigation (routing/fallback): Eng Platform (R/A)
4) Postmortem & action items: Eng SRE (R), CS (C)

Pre-Go-Live Dependency Map Checklist (must be completed before go-live gate)

1. Dependency inventory: maintain a single table with service name, owner, SLA (external), API endpoints, auth method, and last verified test run.
2. Telemetry assertions: add at least three assertion checks for each dependency (latency, error rate, presence of expected metrics).
3. Fallback compatibility: confirm an alternate path exists for each critical dependency (e.g., cached read, degraded feature, queued processing).
4. Runbook verification: ensure a runbook paragraph exists for each item with detection signal and mitigation steps.
5. Communication template: verify customer comms and internal incident templates are available and signed-off.

Dependency Resilience Matrix (example table)

| Dependency | Criticality | SLO tie | Failure modes | Primary detection signal | Immediate mitigation | Owner |
|-----------|-------------|---------|---------------|--------------------------|----------------------|-------|
| ingress-gateway | P0 | 99.9% availability | TLS handshake failures, 502 spikes | 5xx rate > 0.5% over 5m, TLS errors spike | Reroute to standby gateway, enable traffic-shaping to slow new sessions | Eng Platform (Priya) |
| telemetry-gatekeeper | P0 | Inference telemetry 1h TTL | Missing spans, dropped metrics | Missing ingestion heartbeat for 2m, sample rate drop | Fallback to passive buffering sidecar; enable synchronous flush | Eng DevEx (Samir) |
| fanout-proxy | P1 | 99% throughput | Queue growth, per-tenant blocking | Queue depth > 80% capacity for 3m | Enable per-tenant throttles, route low-priority tenants to degraded path | Eng Platform |
| external-idp (SCIM) | P2 | External SLA 99.5% | 429/403 from idp | auth failures or 429s > 1% | Switch to cached user mapping; pause provisioning jobs | Customer Success |
| embedding-indexer (internal) | P1 | Indexing SLA 95% | Index lag, OOM | indexing-lag > 10m | Apply incremental backfill window, drop non-critical batches | Eng Serving Runtime |
| model-router | P0 | Serving SLA 99.95% | Model load failures, KV cache misses | model load errors, cache miss rate > 15% | Switch to compatible quantized variant, enable cache warmup | Eng Serving Runtime |

Operational Runbook (detection -> mitigation -> validate)

1. Detection (first 5 minutes)
   - Watchers: SRE alerting channels receive automated signals (PagerDuty, Slack #sre-ops).
   - Initial checks: run ./tools/check-dependency-health --service <name> to confirm alarm.

2. Triage (5–20 minutes)
   - Assign a triage lead (SRE) and a customer liaison (CS).
   - Confirm blast radius: run tenant impact query (example):

     curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $MONITOR_API" "https://telemetry-api.prod/tenant-impact?service=fanout-proxy&window=10m" | jq .

   - If impact > threshold (defined below) escalate to on-call Eng Platform.

3. Immediate mitigations (20–60 minutes)
   - If ingress-gateway is degraded: flip to standby gateway with the CLI:

     rwdctl gateway failover --from ingress-gw-us-west-2 --to ingress-gw-us-east-1 --reason "onboarding surge"

   - If telemetry-gatekeeper ingestion is missing: enable buffering and start a fast-backfill:

     kubectl -n telemetry apply -f buffering-sidecar-override.yaml
     ./tools/backfill-telemetry --start $(date -u -d '15 minutes ago' +%s) --end $(date -u +%s)

   - If model-router fails to load a quantized variant: re-route traffic to fallback model:

     rwdctl model route --from model:prod:v2 --to model:prod:quantized-v1 --percent 100 --force

4. Validate (after 60 minutes)
   - Confirm telemetry asserts: all dependency assertions pass for 10 consecutive minutes.
   - Confirm SLO posture re-evaluated for impacted tenants and document customer-facing impact.

Escalation thresholds (examples)

- Severity P0: Any customer-facing error rate causing >1% 5xx across the tenant fleet or single large tenant with >0.5% 5xx for 10m. PagerDuty P0, incident bridge, executive notify.
- Severity P1: Throughput drops causing queue growth beyond 50% for >15m. PagerDuty P1; CS alerts impacted customers.
- Severity P2: Auxiliary systems (SCIM, billing connector) errors causing background job failures. Email + Slack notify; CS to log and monitor.

Customer Communication templates

- Initial acknowledgement (under 15 minutes):
  "We’ve detected a degradation affecting [feature/service]. Our engineering team is triaging. We will provide an update within 30 minutes and a root-cause timeline within 4 hours.

  Impact: [brief impact].
  Mitigation: [what we’re doing].
  Contact: your CS rep, [name], + link to status page."

- Mitigation update (30–90 minutes):
  "Summary: We identified [dependency] as the primary cause. We’ve applied [mitigation] which restored service for X% of requests. Engineers continue to monitor and will follow up with next steps by [time]."

Telemetry Assertions (examples to add to onboarding checks)

1. Ingestion heartbeat: telemetry-gatekeeper.heartbeat == true in last 1m
2. Model load success rate: model-router.load_success_rate >= 99.9% over 5m
3. KV cache hit ratio: kvcache.hit_ratio >= 85% over 10m

Add these to the onboarding synthetic suite; example JSON snippet for assertion:

{
  "assertion_name": "kvcache_hit_ratio_onboarding",
  "expr": "avg(kvcache_hit_ratio{env=\"prod\",stage=\"onboarding\"}) > 0.85",
  "window": "10m",
  "owner": "eng-serving-runtime"
}

Canary Failure Simulation (run prior to go-live)

1. Simulate partial dependency failure: throttle upstream responses to 50% for 10 minutes using traffic-shaper job.
2. Verify that fallback paths engage within target time (<= 30s) and degraded responses are metric-tagged.
3. Run customer communication dry-run: ask CS to publish the initial acknowledgement and verify internal observers see it.

Post-Incident Walkthrough and Action Items (within 72h)

- Convene triage + CS + platform; capture timeline and mitigation chronology.
- Generate action items: code fix, observability gaps, config changes, customer compensation if SLA breach. Assign owners and target dates.
- Update dependency map and onboarding checklist with any missed validations.

Common Failure Mode Playbooks (short form)

- Telemetry ingestion drop
  1) Buffer sidecar enablement
  2) Backfill telemetry for the gap window
  3) Postmortem: add assertion and test to synthetic suite

- External SCIM throttling
  1) Pause provisioning
  2) Switch to cached identity mapping for auth flows
  3) Retry queue with exponential backoff and jitter

- KV cache cold start leading to latency spike
  1) Warm cache using sample keyset: ./tools/warm-kvcache --tenant <tenant-id> --keys-file warm-keys.json
  2) If warmfail, route to model variant with smaller memory footprint

Appendix: Useful commands and references

- rwdctl status dependencies --tenant <id> --since 15m\- shows dependency health summary\-
- ./tools/check-dependency-health --service telemetry-gatekeeper --verbose\- detailed probe for the service\-
- Example buffering-sidecar-override.yaml (snippet):

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: telemetry-buffer-override
data:
  buffer.max_bytes: "50000000"
  flush.interval_s: "10"

Appendix: Postmortem checklist template (to attach to incident)

- Incident title and severity
- Detection time, mitigation applied, time to recovery
- Impacted tenants (list) and customer-facing communication timeline
- Root cause and contributing factors
- Concrete action items (owner, due date, verification test)

FAQ (short)

Q: When should CS ask for credits or SLA remedies?
A: Follow the existing SLA reconciliation playbook — if the incident breaches the contracted uptime or per-tenant SLO defined in the contract, CS should initiate the billing remediation flow after the postmortem is complete.

Q: Can we always failover to another region?
A: Not always. Region-based failover is a last-resort for data residency or private deployment customers. Follow the regional failover checklist and confirm customer consent where required.

Related pages and references

- Onboarding failure mode scenarios (linked internally)
- Canary simulation playbook (Eng SRE)
- SLA remediation and billing process

This playbook is intended to be a living document. Update the dependency matrix and telemetry assertions after every simulation and postmortem.

payload.page_title: ingress-gateway-client-cert-rotation-and-ssl-ops-playbook-2026

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes the safe, auditable process for rotating TLS certificates and client (mutual TLS) certificates used by enterprise ingress gateways during onboarding and later maintenance windows. It covers hosted/Dedicated/Private deployment patterns, impacts to customers, verification steps, rollback guidance, monitoring queries, and automation snippets. Intended readers: Customer Success engineers, SREs, Onboarding engineers, and Enterprise security contacts.

Scope and intent

- Scope: ingress gateways (edge load balancers, ingress-controller layer, API gateway proxies) and their associated client certs used for tenant mTLS or upstream service authentication.
- Intent: minimize customer downtime and avoid failed requests during cert rotation while preserving auditability for regulated customers.

When to use this playbook

1. Scheduled certificate rotation (regular maintenance cycle).
2. Emergency rotation because of suspected key compromise.
3. Changing CA (e.g., moving from customer-supplied certs to managed PKI or vice versa).

Roles & ownership

- Owner: Customer Success (Onboarding pillar) — primary operator for customer-facing coordination.
- Technical lead: SRE/Infra on-call — executes gateway changes and validation.
- Security reviewer: Security team — approves key-handling and rotation plan.
- Customer contact: Named enterprise security or platform engineer.

Prerequisites

1. Confirm tenancy: tenant name, gateway endpoint(s), IP allowlists, and whether tenant uses mTLS.
2. Confirm backup and rollback access: ops runbook access, ability to re-deploy a previous ingress config, and secret-store access (Vault/KMS).
3. Confirm TTL and expiry of current certs: obtain certificate chain and expiry dates.
4. Slack/Email channel and scheduled maintenance window agreed with customer.

Certificate inventory table (example)

| Component | Current Cert Common Name | Expires | Provider | Affects mTLS? | Stored location |
| - | - | - | - | - | - |
| ingress.company.example | ingress.company.example | 2026-09-15 | Managed ACME | No | vault/prod/ingress/cert |
| tenant-xyz-client | client-xyz.company | 2026-05-20 | Customer-supplied | Yes | vault/tenants/xyz/client-cert |

Rotation schedule and SLAs

- Preferred maintenance window: customer low-traffic window (UTC), typically 02:00–04:00 local.
- SLO for rotation: no customer-facing errors > 3 minutes attributable to cert handshake failure per rotation.
- Maximum tolerated error rate spike: 5% for up to 10 minutes; notify on escalation.

High-level procedure (summary)

1. Pre-check and customer communication.
2. Provision new certs and upload to secret store in parallel.
3. Stage new certs behind feature-flag / secondary listener where supported.
4. Switch traffic gradually (canary) to new cert configuration.
5. Run validation tests (connectivity, HTTP/2, WebSocket, mTLS client auth).
6. Monitor metrics and rollback if failures exceed thresholds.
7. Finalize and rotate CRLs/OCSP entries if applicable.
8. Post-rotation audit and customer sign-off.

Detailed procedure (step-by-step)

1) Pre-checks (T-72h to T-1h)
- Verify contact list and maintenance window in calendar.
- Export current certificate details: openssl commands below.
  - Command: openssl s_client -connect ingress.company.example:443 -showcerts | openssl x509 -noout -text
- Confirm secret-store write permissions and backups: vault kv get/put examples.
- Confirm observability dashboards are operating and linked to the incident Slack channel.

2) Prepare new certificates (T-48h to T-2h)
- If customer-managed PKI: obtain signed cert and intermediate CA chain from customer. Validate chain:
  - openssl verify -CAfile chain.pem new-cert.pem
- If platform-managed: request issuance via PKI service (give CSR, SANs). Keep private key in KMS/Vault.
- Store cert and key in secret store path with versioned metadata: vault kv put secret/prod/ingress/cert cert=@cert.pem key=@key.pem version=rot2026-08-03

3) Stage and dry-run (T-1h)
- Deploy to a staging listener or a secondary port when supported. Example Kubernetes snippet for an ingress patch (dry-run):

  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: tenant-xyz-ingress-stage
    annotations:
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
  spec:
    tls:
    - hosts:
      - ingress.company.example
      secretName: tenant-xyz-new-tls
  EOF

- Validate that the controller accepted the cert: kubectl describe secret tenant-xyz-new-tls -n ingress-system

4) Canary traffic switch (T=0)
- If load-balancer supports weight-based routing, route 10% traffic to listeners using new cert for first 2 minutes, then 50% for 5 minutes, then 100% if healthy.
- If weight-based routing is not supported, perform gateway-by-gateway switch where possible (region-by-region).

5) Validation and smoke tests (immediately after switch)
- Connectivity: curl -v --resolve "ingress.company.example:443:PUBLIC_IP" https://ingress.company.example/healthz
- TLS handshake and cert chain check: openssl s_client -connect ingress.company.example:443 -showcerts
- mTLS validation (if applicable):
  - curl --cert client.pem --key client.key -v https://ingress.company.example:secured-endpoint
- WebSocket test: wscat -c wss://ingress.company.example/socket-endpoint
- API contract tests: run tenant synthetic suite (script path: /ops/synthetics/run_tenant_tests.sh tenant-xyz)

6) Monitoring and thresholds (live)
- Primary metrics to watch: TLS handshake failures, 4xx/5xx rate, request latency P95, active connections.
- Example PromQL queries (replace labels per environment):
  - tls_handshake_failures = sum(rate(nginx_tls_handshake_errors_total[1m])) by (instance)
  - p95_latency = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance))
- Alerting thresholds during rotation: if tls_handshake_failures > 10/min OR p95_latency increases by > 150% compared to baseline -> trigger rollback.

7) Rollback procedure (if thresholds exceeded)
- Immediately revert listener configuration to the previous secret reference.
- If a staged deployment used weight routing, shift weight back to 100% old cert.
- Redeploy previous ingress config: kubectl apply -f backup/ingress-tenant-xyz-pre-rotation.yaml
- Notify customer and open an incident in PagerDuty with tags: cert-rotation, rollback, tenant-xyz.

8) Finalization and cleanup (T+30m to T+24h)
- Remove staging secrets after 24h and annotate rotation metadata: vault kv put secret/prod/ingress/cert metadata=rotated-2026-08-03 by=Maya
- If client certs were rotated, ensure CRLs/OCSP pointers are updated in customer-facing docs.
- Produce audit log entry and send to customer: include rotation time, actors, cert fingerprints (SHA256), and verification results.

Example automation snippets

- Verify certificate fingerprint (SHA256):
  - openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 -in cert.pem
- Simple Vault upload script (bash):
  - #!/bin/bash
    set -euo pipefail
    VAULT_PATH="secret/prod/ingress/cert"
    vault kv put $VAULT_PATH cert=@cert.pem key=@key.pem rotation_id="$1"

Testing checklist (must pass)

- [ ] TLS chain validates to trusted root on public internet.
- [ ] No 4xx/5xx spike in synthetic checks for 15 minutes post-cutover.
- [ ] mTLS clients (if present) can authenticate and receive 200 OK for known endpoints.
- [ ] WebSocket and streaming endpoints maintain connectivity.
- [ ] Dashboard metrics show handshake failures at baseline.

Customer communication templates

- Pre-maintenance notice (72h): short email with window, expected impact (briefly), rollback commitments, and primary contact.
- Live update (during): Slack messages to agreed channel with percent complete and validation status.
- Post-maintenance report: attachment with audit details and signature of ops lead.

Post-rotation audit sample content

- Rotation ID: rot-2026-08-03-tenant-xyz
- Performed by: maya.chen@redwood.ai
- Certificate SHA256: ABCD:...
- Validation script results: all checks passed (attach logs)

Common failure modes & mitigations

1. Missing intermediate certificates -> Ensure chain.pem provided and validated; add to secret store as bundle.
2. Clock skew causing validation failure -> Check NTP status on ingress hosts.
3. Client does not trust new CA -> Coordinate with customer to update trust store; provide CA bundle and installation instructions.
4. Secret-store permission errors -> Rollback and escalate to Infra IAM team; avoid direct secret re-issue without approval.

Appendices

A. Example PromQL alerts to create temporarily during rotation:
- alert: TLSHandshakeSpike
  expr: increase(nginx_tls_handshake_errors_total[5m]) > 5
  for: 1m
  labels: {severity: "critical", phase: "rotation"}

B. Example notification snippet (Slack):
- "Rotation rot-2026-08-03-tenant-xyz: 50% traffic on new cert, running validation tests. No errors observed in first 5m."

C. Rollback ownership matrix

| Step | Owner | Contact | Expected time to revert |
| - | - | - | - |
| revert listener ref | SRE | srepair-oncall@redwood.ai | 3 minutes |
| redeploy ingress | Infra | infra-deploy@redwood.ai | 10 minutes |
| customer notification | Customer Success | maya.chen@redwood.ai | Immediate |

References

- TLS termination standards: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/tls-termination-standards-2025
- Vault secret naming conventions: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/vault-secret-guidelines-2024

Change log

- 2026-02-12: Drafted by Maya Chen.
- 2026-05-05: Security review and mTLS section expanded (Priya Kapoor).
- 2026-08-03: Minor edits and published with automation snippets (Daniel Ortiz).

Contact

- Primary operator: Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.ai)
- SRE on-call: srepair-oncall@redwood.ai
- Security reviewer: security@redwood.ai

End of playbook

payload.page_title: Enterprise cutover dry-run simulation and QBR blueprint

sections.body:
Purpose and scope

This playbook defines a repeatable dry-run simulation for enterprise tenant cutovers and a companion synthetic QBR (Quarterly Business Review) blueprint. It is intended for Customer Success, Solutions, and SRE teams running pre-cutover validations and for post-cutover QBRs that validate fidelity, costs, and operational readiness. Use this document for: planning rehearsals, validating telemetry, executing controlled cutovers, and producing a synthetic QBR package for stakeholders.

Key objectives

- Validate end-to-end telemetry, alerting, and cost-attribution for a tenant migration/cutover.
- Exercise rollback and failback procedures in a low-risk simulation.
- Produce a reproducible synthetic QBR artifact showing availability, inference economics, and quality metrics.
- Ensure cross-team coordination and clearly assigned owners for cutover day.

Primary owners and roles

- Cutover Lead: Customer Success (primary contact for the tenant) — owner: Priya Kapoor
- Technical Lead: Solutions Engineering (cutover commands and tenant config) — owner: Diego Morales
- SRE Lead: Eng-SRE (monitoring, runbook steps, capacity) — owner: Chen Wang
- Observability Owner: Eng-Platform (dashboards and traces) — owner: Alyssa Kim
- Security Gatekeeper: Security & Compliance (network and ACL approvals) — owner: Maria Jensen

Preconditions and environment

- Target tenant in staging with production-like data subset.
- Telemetry forwarding enabled (metrics -> MetricsCluster.prod, traces -> TracingCluster.redwood).
- Access: all owners have temporary escalation access in the access control system.
- Canary model version pinned to v2.3.1-quant (or the version planned for production).

SLOs and pass/fail thresholds for the dry-run

| Metric | Pass threshold (staging) | Warning threshold | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| P50 latency (inference) | < 60ms | 60–120ms | Measured token-start to token-end for typical 64-token request |
| P95 latency (inference) | < 160ms | 160–300ms | If above warning, reduce batching or increase pool size |
| Error rate (5m window) | < 0.1% | 0.1%–0.5% | Includes 5xx and model-internal decode failures |
| Availability (5m) | >= 99.9% | 99.5%–99.9% | Successful streaming connection and final token received |
| Token cost delta (baseline) | <= +10% | +10%–+25% | Compare to baseline tenant cost for identical synthetic workload |
| KV cache hit ratio | >= 70% | 50%–70% | Important for chat-style workloads |

Pre-run checklist (minimum)

1. Confirm schedule with tenant stakeholders and all owners (48h notice).
2. Provision staging capacity that mirrors target production config (GPU type, batch size, pool size).
3. Export and pin synthetic prompt set (see "Synthetic test plan") and upload to the Eval Harness under ID: cutover-dryrun-<tenant>-2026-01.
4. Verify telemetry pipelines: sample metrics present in dashboards within 2 minutes of synthetic traffic start.
5. Validate ACLs and network paths for private tenants (VPN, peering, firewall rules).
6. Prepare rollback script and acceptance criteria (stored in tenant playbook repo).

Synthetic test plan (what to run)

- Duration: 45m baseline -> 15m scale-up -> 30m soak -> 10m failover test -> 15m rollback validation.
- Traffic mix: 60% chat-completion (avg 120 tokens), 30% embeddings (batch=16), 10% rerank.
- Burst profile: simulate 3x traffic for 2 minutes at minute 30 to validate autoscaling and queueing.
- Data masks: replace all PII in prompts; use pseudonymization preset.

Example synthetic runner command

curl -X POST https://staging-api.redwood.ai/v1/simulate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${SIM_KEY}' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"suite_id":"cutover-dryrun-tenant42","duration_min":105,"mix":{"chat":0.6,"embeddings":0.3,"rerank":0.1}}'

Monitoring and alerts to validate live

- Dashboards: Tenant Overview, Model Pool Health, Token Economics, Streaming Errors.
- Critical alerts (must be ON): high-error-rate (5m > 0.5%), p95-latency-breach (5m > 300ms), queue-length (> 500 requests), billing-anomaly (> +20% compared to baseline).
- Tracing: sample 1% of requests with full flamegraph recording for the 15m scale-up window.

Dry-run timeline and responsibilities (example runbook)

1) T-60m: Preflight check (Cutover Lead)
   - Confirm all stakeholders present on the run channel (#cs-cutover-tenant42-run).
   - SRE verifies pool capacity and autoscaler status.
2) T-30m: Baseline traffic start (Synthetic runner)
   - Observe baseline metrics; collect initial QBR snapshot.
3) T-15m: Scale-up simulation
   - Trigger 3x burst for 2 minutes. Solutions verifies request routing and fallback paths.
4) T+0m: Soak window (15–30m)
   - Monitor KV cache hit ratio, model decoding errors, and memory usage.
5) T+30m: Failover exercise
   - Simulate primary region degradation: route 50% of requests to fallback region; validate graceful degradation (no more than 2x latency increase).
6) T+45m: Rollback and data integrity check
   - Execute rollback script: revert routing to original variant and validate session continuity for 95% of synthetic sessions.
7) T+60m: Post-run debrief and artifact snapshot
   - Capture dashboards, traces, alert logs, and cost estimate.

Rollback and emergency procedures

- If error-rate > 1% sustained for 5m: abort scale-up and roll back model variant to previous stable version (v2.3.0). Owner: Solutions Engineering.
- If availability < 99% for 10m: escalate to SRE on-call and initiate tenant short-circuit to a safety pool (see runbook ID: safepool-switch-2025).
- If billing spike exceeds +40% within 1h: pause synthetic runner and open finance notification.

Post-run deliverables (artifact checklist)

- Synthetic QBR PDF (auto-generated): includes availability graphs, latency percentiles, cost delta, and quality regressions (NLG BLEU/ROUGE-like scores where applicable).
- Runbook incident log: timeline with commands executed and owner notes.
- Telemetry package: zipped Grafana dashboard JSON, 5m sampled traces, metric export (Prometheus textfile).
- Action items: prioritized list and owner assignment.

Synthetic QBR blueprint (sections to include)

1. Executive summary (1 page): high-level status, go/no-go recommendation, top risks.
2. Availability and latency (2 pages): p50/p95/p99 + short narrative on tail behaviour.
3. Inference economics (1–2 pages): token cost vs baseline, caching effect, suggestions for batching/quantization.
4. Quality and regression checks (1 page): sample prompts, reference outputs, regression flagging rules.
5. Operational readiness (1 page): runbook gaps, alert tuning, and capacity recommendations.
6. Action plan and owners (1 page): 30/60/90 day remediation items.

Template metrics to include in the QBR (minimum)

- Uptime (7d window)
- P50/P95/P99 latency (end-to-end)
- Error rate (5m and 60m windows)
- Token consumption and cost delta vs baseline (7d)
- KV cache hit ratio (soak window)
- Number of rollbacks / failovers during run
- Top 5 error signatures and sample traces

Common failure modes discovered in past dry-runs

- Misconfigured telemetry forwarding (missing tag: tenant_id) -> dashboards show no per-tenant split. Fix: validate metric labels before run.
- Autoscaler cooldown too long -> inability to scale during bursts. Fix: lower cooldown to 30s for cutover pool.
- Private-network ACL missing outbound to MetricsCluster -> missing metrics. Fix: preflight network test.

Appendices

A. Command snippets

- Rollback model variant (CLI):
  redwoodctl tenant update --tenant tenant42 --model v2.3.0 --force

- Switch to safepool (SRE):
  redwoodctl pool route --tenant tenant42 --target safepool-standby --reason "dry-run failover"

B. Dashboards to snapshot (IDs)
- tenant-overview-42, model-pool-health, token-econ-tenant42, streaming-errors-42

C. Contact list (on-call and escalation)
- CS: Priya Kapoor +1 (pager)
- Solutions: Diego Morales +1
- SRE: Chen Wang (primary), oncall@redwood.ai

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: Created by Priya Kapoor (initial draft).
- 2025-12-05: Added failover exercise and cost checks (reviewer: Diego Morales).
- 2026-01-18: Published: refined QBR template and included command snippets (reviewers: Chen Wang, Alyssa Kim).

End of document.

payload.page_title: tenant-chaos-gaming-and-resilience-onboarding-playbook-2026

sections.body: This playbook defines the tenant-level chaos gaming and synthetic-resilience program used during enterprise onboarding and the first 90 days post-cutover. It standardizes simulated failure scenarios, telemetry assertions, success criteria, and escalation steps to validate that a new tenant meets Redwood Inference stability, performance, and cost-safety requirements prior to and immediately after canary-to-100% rollouts.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Purpose: Reduce production surprises by exercising realistic failure modes against a customer’s dedicated or private deployment in a controlled, observable way.
- Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants (VPC/on-prem) being onboarded or undergoing major model/capacity cutovers. Does not replace load testing performed by SRE for platform-wide capacity.
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
- Availability SLO: 99.95% for API success rate (5xx and client-facing errors excluded per contract).
- Median latency target: <120ms for small-gen calls (<128 tokens) during canary windows.
- Cost safety guardrail: 2x expected cost spike tolerance during orchestrated synthetic tests; anything beyond triggers immediate throttling.
sections.heading: Service-level targets (tenant SLOs)

sections.body:
- Playbook owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel)
- Runtime escalation owner: Eng SRE (Miguel Ramos)
- Dedicated/private deployment owner: Eng Private Deployments (Jordan Lee)
- Customer POC: (fill per customer onboarding sheet)
sections.heading: Owners and contacts

sections.body:
1. Tenant must be deployed to a non-prod or canary tenant slice with identical routing, or to a production tenant with explicit consent and an agreed blast radius.
2. Observability contract validated: metrics, traces, and logs forwarded to Redwood telemetry cluster and customer-observability link.
3. Canary token/key configured and QA test suite green.
4. Rollback and safe-failover plans approved by customer and SRE.
sections.heading: Prerequisites (before running a game day)

sections.body:
- Schedule and obtain approvals from customer, SRE, and account team (minimum 72 hours notice).
- Configure synthetic load generator (see examples below) and ensure isolation of test traffic via label/filter.
- Snapshot current tenant config and telemetry baseline (last 24h).
- Confirm cost cap and automatic throttles are active.
- Run a brief smoke test of observability dashboards and alerting rules.
sections.heading: Game day checklist (pre-execution)

sections.body:
1) KV-cache corruption simulation
   - Intent: Ensure graceful detection and refetch behavior for prefix cache invalidation.
   - Method: Inject cache-miss pattern by toggling a feature flag in the canary runtime to disable cached lookup for 60s.
   - Success criteria: Error budget unaffected; latency increase <50% for affected requests; automated PK cache warm-up completes within 120s.

2) Model-variant fallback under load
   - Intent: Validate model fallback routing if primary quantized model fails or is cyclically unavailable.
   - Method: Simulate model-worker OOM by marking worker pool unhealthy via the orchestration API.
   - Success criteria: Requests routed to fallback variant within 10s; tail latency spike limited to 2x baseline for under 5 minutes.

3) Sudden traffic surge from one tenant (ingress storm)
   - Intent: Confirm tenant fairshare and quota protector sidecar behavior.
   - Method: Generate a 10x RPS spike for 5 minutes using synthetic generator.
   - Success criteria: No cross-tenant degradation; affected tenant receives throttling with appropriate 429s and customer-notification webhook triggers.

4) Telemetry pipeline delay and partial loss
   - Intent: Ensure offline buffering and alerting are robust when telemetry forwarding lags.
   - Method: Introduce deliberate forwarding latency in the staging observability forwarder for 3 minutes.
   - Success criteria: Alerts that depend on telemetry use alternative guard signals (health check pings); post-mortem shows no blind spots longer than 5 minutes.
sections.heading: Synthetic scenarios (recommended list)

sections.body:
1. Kickoff: Confirm attendees and intent. Document start time in the incident timeline channel.
2. Baseline sampling: Start 5m metric sampling to baseline key telemetry (request_rate, error_rate, p50/p95 latency, cost_per_minute).
3. Scenario run: Execute scenario steps as defined. One scenario per 15–30 minute window.
4. Observability watch: SRE and CS watch dashboards for SLO violations. Assign a single comms owner.
5. Containment: If a hard threshold is crossed (see thresholds table), immediately stop the synthetic generator and trigger rollback if needed.
6. Cooldown: 15–30 minutes post-scenario for caches and queues to settle. Collect logs and traces.
7. Post-checks: Run validation tests (sanity generations, embedding consistency checks).

Thresholds and automated actions (table represented in plain text):

- If 5xx rate > 0.5% for >2 minutes -> Automated throttle and page SRE (Pager).
- If median latency > 3x baseline for >5 minutes -> Pause canary rollouts and create severity-3 incident.
- If cost rate > 3x baseline sustained >10 minutes -> Trigger cost-protector webhook and notify finance-safety.

Telemetry assertions (examples to add to the telemetry contract):

- request.success_rate >= 99.5% (rolling 10m)
- model.fallback.count <= 5 per 10m window during synthetic tests
- cache.hit_ratio >= 70% post-warmup (rolling 5m)
- ingress.rps <= documented expectation for the tenant + 10% burst allowance
sections.heading: Execution play (numbered runbook)

sections.body:
- Error rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m]))
- Median latency: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) by (le))
sections.heading: Observability queries (examples)

sections.body:
- k6 (simple RPS spike)
  - Command: k6 run --vus 0 --iteration-duration 5m --rps 200 spike-script.js
  - Note: Use request headers to tag traffic: {\"X-Tenant-Test\":\"chaos-game-2026\"}

- locust (ramp test):
  - Command: locust -f locustfile.py --headless -u 500 -r 50 --run-time 10m --host=https://tenant.example
sections.heading: Synthetic load generator examples

sections.body:
1. Stop synthetic generators immediately.
2. If degradation is tenant-isolated and within cost guardrails, hold and let cooldown complete.
3. If cross-tenant impact or severity thresholds exceeded, perform automatic fairshare enforcement and execute configured rollback (model pin to previous stable version).
sections.heading: Rollback and safe-failover steps

sections.body:
- Short RCAs for any threshold breach (published within 3 business days).
- Telemetry snapshot and comparison to baseline (attach to the onboarding ticket).
- Action items with owners and target completion dates (tracked in JIRA).
sections.heading: Post-game day analysis (deliverables)

sections.body:
- Add game day results to the QBR packet: include pass/fail per scenario, regression deltas for p95, and cost delta.
- Recommend final tenant readiness vote (Accept / Accept with mitigations / Reject) during the commercial go/no-go.

Appendix A — Example alerting rule YAML (snippet):

alert: TenantHigh5xx
expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:

  runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-process"

Appendix B — Tracing play snippet:

- When a scenario runs, add a trace tag: chaos.game=tenant-onboard-<ID> so Perf and Trace teams can filter.

Appendix C — Postmortem template fields to include:

- Timeline of actions (UTC)
- What failed vs expected
- Root cause and contributing factors
- Immediate mitigations and permanent fixes
- Customer impact and communications

A: Only with explicit customer written consent and a pre-negotiated blast radius. Use a dedicated canary slice where possible.

Q: Who authorizes rollbacks?

payload.page_title: Onboarding Experiments and Fidelity-Cost Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook defines an experiment-driven approach for onboarding new developer customers to Redwood Inference with an explicit mapping between fidelity profiles, cost signals, and SLA entitlements. The goal is to minimize developer friction while making unit economics predictable and measurable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Audience
- Product managers and go-to-market leads running onboarding pilots
- Solutions engineers and customer success teams executing migrations
- Platform engineers implementing fidelity policy controls and telemetry

Scope and intent
- Defines a set of onboarding experiment cohorts (A/B/C) tied to fidelity presets and priced trial credits.
- Establishes measurable criteria to graduate customers between fidelity tiers.
- Provides rollout steps, required product hooks, billing implications, and rollback guidance.

Definitions
- Fidelity profile: A named bundle of runtime characteristics (model variant, quantization level, batching limits, streaming vs chunked responses).
- Onboarding credit: Time-limited usage credit applied to a tenant to cover trial costs.
- Entitlement SLA: Explicit latency and availability guarantees associated with a pricing tier.

High-level approach
1) Create 3 onboarding cohorts:
   - Cohort A (Exploratory): High-fidelity default model, minimal batching, extended latency budget (200ms p50 target), 1,000 onboarding credits.
   - Cohort B (Balanced): Mid-fidelity variant (int8 or mixed precision), moderate batching, standard latency budget (120ms p50), 2,500 onboarding credits.
   - Cohort C (Economy): Quantized variant with aggressive batching and prefix-caching, tight cost limits, relaxed p50 latency (220ms), 5,000 onboarding credits to demonstrate cost savings.

2) Instrument: Telemetry hooks for per-request fidelity tags, credit burn-rate, per-route latency distribution, and quality regressions tied to shadow-eval prompt sets.

3) Gate graduation: Customers must meet usage and quality thresholds in their cohort for N days before automatic promotion. Promotion is governed by the Fidelity Promotion Rule (FPR) below.

Fidelity Promotion Rule (FPR)
- Inputs (measured over the last 7 days): 1) Daily active tokens >= 10k, 2) Regression rate against shadow prompts <= 1.2x baseline, 3) Average credit burn per 1k tokens within cohort budget.
- If all inputs satisfied for 7/7 days -> promote to next fidelity tier.
- If regression spikes > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive days -> immediate rollback to prior tier and open a fidelity incident.

Required product hooks (implementation checklist)
- Tenant metadata: onboarding_cohort, onboarding_start, onboarding_credits_remaining (API + Console).
- Runtime: fidelity_tag header on inference requests; ability to map fidelity_tag to model variant and quantization profile.
- Billing: trial credit ledger entries and reporting APIs for credit burn by route/model.
- Observability: dashboard showing cohort distribution, credit velocity, p50/p95 latency, shadow-eval regression trend.
- Admin tooling: manual override for promotion/rollback and audit log with who/when/why.

Experiment matrix (example)
(Represented here as a text table; implement as dashboard table in Console)
| Cohort | Model Variant | Quant | Batch Size | p50 Target | Trial Credits | Expected unit cost delta vs baseline |
| Cohort A | redwood-xl-v2 | fp16 | 1-2 | 200ms | 1k | +45% |
| Cohort B | redwood-xl-v2-mix | int8-mix | 4-8 | 120ms | 2.5k | +5% |
| Cohort C | redwood-xl-quant | int8-q | 16-64 | 220ms | 5k | -60% |

Pricing and packaging implications
- Trial credits should be delivered as non-billable ledger items that expire at onboarding_end + 30 days.
- Credits consumed beyond trial convert to regular billing at the tenant's chosen pricing tier.
- Cohort-specific uplift: if customer is kept at Cohort A after trial, charge a 10% fidelity surcharge to reflect higher unit cost; conversely, Cohort C conversion includes a 5% low-fidelity discount.

Quick decision table
- If customer requires regulated private deployment (VPC / on-prem): default to Cohort B unless explicit cost-savings mandate -> run Cohort C only after security review.
- If the customer reports quality complaints within first 72 hours: escalate to CSM; consider one-time temporary credit and possible immediate promotion to higher fidelity for diagnosis.

PRD requirements (minimal viable set for Q4 onboarding pilots)
- PRD-1: New tenant fields (onboarding_cohort, onboarding_expires_at, onboarding_credits) exposed in Accounts API and Console.
- PRD-2: Fidelity tags in inference API with mapping stored in Variant Catalog.
- PRD-3: Credit burn reporting pipeline with hourly aggregation and tenant-level export.
- PRD-4: Shadow-eval integration that runs 1% of requests through shadow variants and surface regression alerts to the Console.
- PRD-5: Console cohort visualization and manual override controls with audit trail.

Design constraints and non-goals
- We will not perform per-request model switching beyond fidelity_tag during onboarding; staged promotion happens at tenant-level only.
- We will avoid introducing new pricing SKUs during pilot; use credit accounting + simple surcharges/discounts.

Telemetry and SLOs
- Required telemetry spans: fidelity_tag, model_variant, quant_profile, tokens_in, tokens_out, request_latency_ms, shadow_eval_result (pass/fail), credit_delta.
- SLOs for onboarding pilot: 99.5% of cohort B requests must meet p50 latency <= 120ms; 99% for p95 <= 400ms.

Rollout plan and milestones
- Week 0 (prep): implement tenant metadata + variant-mapping.
- Week 2 (alpha): enable Cohort C for 5 internal customers and run synthetic traffic for 72 hours.
- Week 4 (beta): invite 10 developer customers via self-serve onboarding flow. Monitor credit burn and quality regressions.
- Week 8 (pilot review): analyze cohort-level economics, surface pitch for formal pricing adjustments.
- Week 12 (expand): enable automated graduation rules and add cohort-aware default in Console templates.

KPIs and success criteria
- Onboarding-to-paid conversion rate >= 18% within 60 days (target for pilot customers).
- Average cost per 1k tokens for converted customers not > 25% of projections for Cohort B baseline.
- Shadow-eval regression alert rate < 1% for promoted tenants.

Rollback and incident playbook
1) Detection: regression alert triggers on-call, CSM informed.
2) Immediate action: flip tenant to prior fidelity_tag, revoke promotion, and issue one-time debugging credits.
3) Postmortem: include shadow-eval logs, sample prompts, token-level traces, and time-series of latency and burn rate.

Billing and finance checklist
- Finance must approve the credit-expense budget for the pilot and receive weekly burn rate updates.
- Define an accounting tag for onboarding credits to separate promotional cost center.

Console UX notes (developer-facing)
- Onboarding banner in Console with cohort, credits remaining, expected upgrade path, and a one-click request to speak with SE (optional).
- Visual timeline showing days until automatic promotion or expiry.

Sample API mapping snippet (tenant metadata update)
{ "tenant_id": "acct_12345", "onboarding_cohort": "cohort_b", "onboarding_credits": 2500, "onboarding_expires_at": "2028-09-02T00:00:00Z" }

Owners and contact points
- Product lead: Maya Chen (owner)
- Engineering lead (hooks & telemetry): Priya Nair
- Solutions & CSM: Diego Alvarez
- Finance contact: Lena Rodriguez

Appendix: example console dashboard panels to build
1) Cohort distribution heatmap by tenant size and industry.
2) Credit velocity timeseries (daily & hourly) with anomaly detection.
3) Shadow-eval regression table with sample failing prompts and links to recordings.

Open questions and recommended experiments
- Should promotions be rate-limited to avoid capacity spikes? Recommendation: stagger promotions by rolling window (max 5% of tenants per hour).
- What is the optimal trial credit sizing per industry? Recommendation: run a 3-month A/B test with stratified sampling by ARR and expected daily tokens.

Change log
- 2028-08-03: Draft authored.
- 2028-09-15: Added PRD checklist and finance gating steps after stakeholder review.

Related artifacts and links
- Variant Catalog (internal): /engineering/serving-runtime/variant-catalog
- Shadow-eval harness design: /applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/shadow-eval-spec

End of document

payload.page_title: Tenant egress fallback and fair-share throttling playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes the operational procedures, validation tests, and escalation steps for tenant egress fallback and fair-share throttling for Dedicated and Private tenants. It targets customer-success, SRE, and platform engineers responsible for onboarding enterprise customers with unpredictable burst traffic or constrained egress capacity.

Goals

- Ensure predictability for tenant traffic when outbound (egress) capacity is constrained.
- Maintain latency SLOs for high-priority tenants while applying fair-share policies to noisy neighbors.
- Provide a deterministic automated fallback that preserves availability and preserves customer data guarantees.

When to use this playbook
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Pre-production validation for Dedicated/Private tenant cutovers.
2) Go-live where tenant traffic patterns are unknown or have burst risk.
3) Incidents where egress link saturation, pod/instance ejects, or third-party API throttles cause increased latency or errors.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Customer Success (Onboarding team) — Amira Patel
- Operational owner: Eng SRE — Diego Morales
- Runtime/Platform owner: Eng Platform — Priya Natarajan
- Pager: #sre-oncall (primary), #cs-help (secondary)
- Escalation: If pager not acknowledged in 15m, escalate to SRE L2 and Customer Success Manager.

Scope and constraints

- Applies to tenants on Dedicated capacity and Private VPC deployments.
- Not for Hosted (shared) tenants unless explicitly configured with fair-share proxies.
- Does not modify customer data retention or encryption policies.

Prerequisites and config artifacts

- Tenant capacity profile created in Capacity Service (capacity-service v2): tenant_id, target_rps, burst_rps, expected_seq_len.
- Ingress and egress proxies must expose the following metrics to metrics-ingest: ingress.rps, egress.bandwidth.bytes, proxy.queue_length, request.latency.p50/p95/p99.
- Fair-share controller enabled in tenant_proxy.conf with the following knobs: max_tokens_per_second, priority_weight, weight_decay_window_ms.
- Sufficient observability: synthetic journey for tenant with end-to-end p50/p95 thresholds.

Validation tests (pre-go-live)

Execute the validation harness below in a staging environment that mirrors production network topology. Document all results in the onboarding ticket.

1) Baseline characterization
- Inject steady traffic at target_rps for 10 minutes. Verify p95 latency < tenant_p95_slo and error rate < 0.1%.
- Required metrics: ingress.rps, egress.bytes/s, kvcache.hit_rate.

2) Burst resilience check
- Ramp all tenant test clients from target_rps to burst_rps over 60s. Observe fallback behavior. Expected outcome: lower-priority tenants receive graceful rate-limiting; high-priority tenants retain >= 85% of baseline throughput.

3) Egress saturation simulation
- Throttle external egress (eg simulate 40% link loss). Verify that fallback to local cache and degraded-mode responses occur: response codes 200 (degraded ok) or 503 (if hard fail) per policy. Verify circuit-breaker triggers at configured thresholds.

4) Fair-share fairness validation
- Run 10 tenants simultaneously with varied priority_weight values. Measure delivered RPS per tenant and verify proportional share within +/- 10% of configured weights.

Pre-Go-Live checklist (must pass all items)

- [ ] Capacity profile uploaded and approved.
- [ ] Tenant proxy config reviewed and committed to config repo (reviewer: Eng Platform).
- [ ] Synthetic journey created and scheduled for tenant.
- [ ] Alerting rules created: high egress utilization (>85%), proxy queue_length > 50, fair-share-imbalance > 15%.
- [ ] Backstop fallback policy documented in the customer runbook (customer-facing).

Go-Live steps (recommended timebox: 60–90 minutes)

1) Golden path smoke (0–10m)
- Verify ingress/routing is pointing to Dedicated/Private capacity.
- Run 2 quick synthetic requests and validate correlation IDs flow through logs.

2) Canary ramp (10–30m)
- Start with 5% of traffic routed to new tenant environment. Monitor p50/p95, error rate, and proxy queue.
- If p95 increases > 25% baseline or error rate > 0.5%, abort canary and roll back routing.

3) Gradual ramp (30–60m)
- Increase traffic by 20% every 10 minutes, monitoring fairness and egress usage.
- Confirm fair-share controller is distributing capacity proportionally.

4) Full cutover and verification (60–90m)
- Update routing to 100%. Keep enhanced monitoring for 6 hours. Document any anomalies.

Degraded-mode behavior and automatic fallback

- Soft-fallback: When proxy queue_length > 75 or egress_bandwidth >= 90% for > 30s, the system applies fair-share throttling and enables degraded responses for non-critical endpoints (e.g., background embeddings refresh).
- Hard-fallback: If requests.latency.p99 > 3x SLO for > 2 minutes, or error rate > 2% for > 5 minutes, fail open to read-only cached responses and notify SRE.
- Customer notification: For hard-fallbacks, Customer Success must send a templated notification within 30 minutes describing impact and mitigation steps.

Automated remediation actions (ordered)

1) Activate fair-share throttling profile (fast path).
2) Evict low-priority background requests for 60s.
3) Route new tenant traffic to lower-cost region if cross-region fallback policy exists and region latency delta < 50ms.
4) Provision burst capacity (manual escalation to capacity team if autoscale cannot allocate).

Telemetry, alerts, and SLOs to configure

- Metrics to send to metrics-ingest: tenant.{id}.ingress_rps, tenant.{id}.egress_bps, tenant.{id}.delivered_rps, tenant.{id}.throttle_rate, tenant.{id}.priority_share_pct.
- Core alerts (severity mapping):
  - P0: egress_bandwidth >= 95% for > 3m (pager)
  - P1: proxy.queue_length >= 75 for > 2m (page + slack)
  - P2: fair-share-imbalance > 20% for > 10m (slack only)
- Suggested SLOs (tenant-level):
  - Availability: 99.95% (excluding scheduled maintenance)
  - Latency p95: tenant-specific (recommended default 300ms)
  - Throttling transparency: any throttled request must return `X-Redwood-Throttle: true` header and include an advisory in response body where applicable.

Escalation matrix and playbook actions

1) First responder (SRE oncall) — Triage, perform automated remediation steps 1–3.
2) If unresolved after 15 minutes — SRE L2 and Customer Success notified; open incident channel and begin stakeholder comms.
3) If unresolved after 60 minutes — Eng Platform and Capacity team pager.
4) If unresolved after 3 hours — Executive escalation and formal incident postmortem.

Incident comms template (short)

Subject: [Incident] Tenant {tenant_id} - Egress congestion detected\\nBody:
- Impact: Elevated latency and partial degradation for tenant {tenant_id}.
- Timeline: {start_time} UTC
- Mitigation: Applied fair-share throttling and evicted background requests; routing adjusted.
- Next steps: Capacity team provisioning in progress; monitoring in place.

Post-incident items and QBR inputs

- Document the root cause, timeline, and mitigation in the incident ticket.
- Recommend capacity or architectural changes: e.g., increase egress pool by N GPUs or enable region-fallback by default.
- Add the incident to the next QBR with the following artifacts: synthetic journey traces, request/response samples with correlation IDs, and fairness delta graphs.

Testing scenarios matrix (examples)

| Scenario | Goal | Expected outcome | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Single-tenant burst | Verify high-priority preserved | High-priority tenant keeps >=85% throughput | Run for 30m
| Multi-tenant simultaneous burst | Validate fair-share | Proportional throughput within +/-10% | Use 10 tenants
| Egress link failure | Validate degraded-mode | Cached responses + advisory header | Simulate packet loss at edge

Appendix: sample tenant_proxy.conf snippet

Recovery and rollback guidance

- Long-term remediation: Schedule capacity expansion, add egress caching layer for large-response endpoints, or adjust tenant priority weights for steady-state fairness.

Document history and change log

Related pages and references

- Dedicated tenant cutover safety-net playbook — see related_pages for link.
- Synthetic health suite implementation guide (health-and-qbr).
- Eng SRE capacity profiling guide for tenant planning.

End of playbook

sections.body:
TITLE: Adaptive Request Prioritization and Fairness — Enterprise Onboarding Playbook

SUMMARY
This playbook describes the recommended configuration, validation, and operational handoff for enabling tenant-aware request prioritization and fairness controls during enterprise onboarding. It is intended for Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, and Platform SREs working with Dedicated or Private tenants who require predictable latency and cost isolation while preserving fair access across internal user groups.

AUDIENCE
- Customer Success Managers (CSMs)
- Solutions Engineers (SEs)
- Platform SRE / Infra Onboarding Engineers
- Tenant Engineering Leads

SCOPE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Functional goals and acceptance SLOs for prioritization and fairness.
2) Configuration templates for ingress priority maps and quota-snooze windows.
3) Onboarding validation tests and telemetry queries.
4) Runbook for common failure modes and escalation flow.
5) Handoff checklist and post-go-live QBR signals.

OUT-OF-SCOPE
- Low-level kernel tuning for GPU runtime (see eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling).
- Billing reconciliation and invoicing (see finance-and-legal/procurement).

GOALS & ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Latency SLO: 95th percentile tail latency for gold-tier requests <= 180 ms under steady-state load (customer-defined).
- Isolation: Background batch/ingest traffic must not cause >10% degradation on gold-tier p95 latency.
- Fairness: No single API key or tenant-owner group should exceed 40% of overall capacity for more than 10 minutes without being auto-rate-limited or flagged.
- Observability: Dashboards and alerting must be present and validated before handoff.

KEY CONCEPTS
- Priority buckets: gold | silver | bronze — map to service-level CPU/GPU lanes and admission controls.
- Fairness window: sliding 5–15 minute window used to compute dominant share and trigger automated throttles.
- Snooze policy: temporary, scheduled relaxation of limits to allow business-critical bursts (e.g., monthly reports) with explicit expiry.

ROLES & RESPONSIBILITIES
- Customer Success (owner): validate business intent, drive acceptance, coordinate stakeholders.
- Solutions Engineering (owner): produce tenant configuration, run pre-go-live simulations, produce the validation report.
- Platform SRE (owner): apply ingress policies, verify router behavior, enable telemetry & alerting.
- Customer Engineering (owner): provide representative workload, participate in game-day.

CONFIGURATION REFERENCE (EXAMPLE)
1) Ingress priority map (YAML):

--- yaml
sections.heading: This document covers

sections.body:
tenant_id: tenant-acme-123
priority_map:
  - matcher: "/v1/generate*"
    default: gold
    overrides:
      - api_key_prefix: "acme-analytics-"
        priority: silver
      - route_header: "X-Batch-Job: true"
        priority: bronze
fairness_policy:
  enabled: true
  window_minutes: 10
  max_share_percent: 40
snooze_windows:
  - name: "monthly-reporting"
    start: "2026-06-15T02:00:00Z"
    duration_minutes: 90
    allowed_priorities: [gold, silver]
---

2) Admission control snippet (JSON) for router plugin:

{
  "plugin": "adaptive-admission",
  "config": {
    "base_concurrency": 8,
    "burst_tokens": 16,
    "fairshare_window_sec": 600,
    "dominant_share_threshold_pct": 40
  }
}

VALIDATION & TESTING CHECKLIST (pre-go-live)
1) Synthetic workload replay:
   - Run 30-minute mixed workload (60% chat, 30% embeddings, 10% batch) at 120% of expected baseline traffic.
   - Verify gold p95 <= configured SLO and bronze traffic is degraded gracefully.
2) Dominant-share stress test:
   - Simulate a single API key consuming 60% of capacity for 20 minutes — confirm automated throttle triggers at 40% threshold and alert fires.
3) Snooze test:
   - Apply snooze window for 90 minutes and verify elevated concurrency is allowed during the window and removed after expiry.
4) Failure injection:
   - Cause an ingress service restart and confirm fairshare bookkeeping recovers within 2 windows.

TELEMETRY & DASHBOARDS
sections.heading: tenant-priority-map.yaml

sections.body:
- Metrics (Prometheus naming conventions):
  - ingress_requests_total{tenant,priority,route}
  - ingress_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant,priority}
  - admission_rejected_total{tenant,reason}
  - dominant_share_percent{tenant}
- Alerts (examples):
  - alert: GoldP95LatencyBreach
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(ingress_latency_seconds_bucket{priority="gold"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.18
    for: 5m
  - alert: DominantShareExceeded
    expr: max_over_time(dominant_share_percent[10m]) > 40
    for: 2m
- Dashboard panels to include:
  - Tenant capacity map (by priority lanes)
  - Dominant share trend and top-10 API keys
  - Admission rejects and reasons by route

GAME-DAY AND PRE-GO-LIVE RUN
1) Schedule a 90-minute game day with the customer and internal SRE/SEs.
2) Run the synthetic scenario; customer verifies UX and latency targets.
3) Exercise escalation flow (send a simulated dominant-share alert, perform manual throttle and policy rollback).
4) Capture runbook actions and update the confluence page with any deviations.

COMMON FAILURE MODES & RUNBOOK ACTIONS
1) Symptom: Gold p95 spikes but total ingress QPS is normal.
   - Probable cause: priority lane starvation due to misrouted bronze traffic.
   - Steps:
     1. Check ingress_requests_total by priority.
     2. If bronze >> expected, temporarily set bronze concurrency to 1 and watch gold p95.
     3. If resolved, roll back and apply more specific route matchers.
2) Symptom: Dominant-share throttle not triggering on heavy single-key usage.
   - Probable cause: Fairshare bookkeeping lag or misconfigured window.
   - Steps:
     1. Inspect dominant_share_percent metric for the API key.
     2. Confirm fairshare_window_sec in plugin config.
     3. If lagging, restart the bookkeeping worker with the trace flag enabled; engage eng-serving-runtime on-call if persistent.
3) Symptom: Snooze window did not expire.
   - Steps:
     1. Verify the scheduled task processed the expiry event (check /var/log/snooze-service).
     2. If the task failed, manually remove snooze and notify customer of corrective action.

ESCALATION PATHS
- Tier 1 (CSM/SE): initial troubleshooting and customer comms.
- Tier 2 (Platform SRE): policy verification, telemetry deep-dive, temporary policy changes.
- Tier 3 (Runtime Eng): kernel/runtime intervention, fairshare bookkeeping bugs, urgent fixes.
sections.heading: Minimum telemetry required before handoff

sections.body:
- Platform SRE on-call: pages -> #sre-oncall -> 10 min response target.
- Runtime Eng on-call: pages -> #runtime-oncall -> 15 min response target.

HANDOFF & DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS
Before final handoff to Customer Success (long-term support):
- Completed validation report (attach synthetic run logs).
- Dashboard URL and playbook link.
- Confirmed alert routing to customer and Redwood Slack channel.
- Signed acceptance: CSM, SE, and Tenant Engineering Lead.

POST-GO-LIVE QBR SIGNALS (30/90/180 day)
- Usage concentration: fraction of traffic coming from top-3 API keys — target < 60%.
- SLO breaches per month for priority lanes.
- Number of manual snooze windows and business justification.
- Cost delta attributed to prioritization changes (included in QBR template).

CHANGE CONTROL & ROLL-BACK
- All changes to priority maps or admission control config must go through the change management process (policies-and-process/change-management).
- Rollback procedure: revert to previous config via the platform config-store with a tagged release and monitor metrics for 20 minutes.

APPENDIX A — SAMPLE PROMQL QUERIES
- Gold p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(ingress_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant="tenant-acme-123",priority="gold"}[5m])) by (le))
- Dominant share for API key k: max_over_time( dominant_share_percent{tenant="tenant-acme-123",api_key="k"}[10m])

APPENDIX B — CONTACTS & OWNERSHIP
- Playbook author: Priya Raman (CSM) — priya@redwood.ai
- Platform SRE owner: Marcus Lee — sre-platform@redwood.ai
- Runtime eng escalation: Sofia Martínez — runtime-oncall@redwood.ai

REVISION HISTORY
- 2026-02-15: Draft created by Priya Raman.
- 2026-03-10: Added synthetic validation templates and PromQL examples (Marcus Lee).
- 2026-05-03: Finalized snooze schema and game-day checklist (published).

payload.page_title: Onboarding Handback and First-90-Days Operational Guide

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the technical handback process and the operational expectations for the first 90 days after an enterprise customer goes live on Redwood Inference (hosted or Dedicated). It is intended for CSMs, Solutions Engineering (SE), Onboarding Engineers, and the L2 oncall team.

Scope

- Applies to enterprise customers with Dedicated or Private deployments and enterprise-level Hosted integrations that require an SE handover.
- Covers: handoff checklist, SLA matrix, runbook entries for common post-go-live issues, escalation steps, monitoring baseline, and QBR readiness checklist for the first 90 days.

Goals and success metrics (first 90 days)

- Availability SLO: 99.95% per calendar month for production inference endpoints.
- Latency SLO: P95 request-to-first-token < 300 ms for short-text generation workloads (<= 256 tokens) on Dedicated pools.
- Error budget: < 0.05% failed requests (5xx) attributable to Redwood services. Customer-side errors (4xx) excluded.
- Onboarding health: 80% of customer-defined success criteria met by day 30, 95% by day 90.
- QBR readiness: onboarding artifacts, traffic profile, cost trends, and open action items delivered two weeks before the 90-day review.

Handback checklist (must be completed before formal handoff)

1) Contractual & access items (owner: CSM)
   1. Confirm customer account and billing profile in Finance (billing contact verified).
   2. Verify list of whitelisted IPs, VPC peering, or VPN endpoints (for Dedicated/Private).
   3. Confirm KMS/HSM key rotation schedule and access for logs/audit.

2) Technical verification (owner: SE / Onboarding Engineer)
   1. Baseline performance test completed: runbench report attached and passing acceptance criteria (attach: runbench-<customer>-v1.json).
   2. Model versions pinned and documented (model-id, quantization profile if any).
   3. Ingress/egress networking validated: HTTPS termination, MTU checks, and route tables.
   4. Observability hooks installed: metrics, ingest for traces, and token-level cost tagging enabled.

3) Operational readiness (owner: Oncall + CSM)
   1. Oncall runbooks created for the customer under team wiki (link to runbook entry).
   2. Alerting thresholds verified (see SLA matrix below).
   3. Access matrix for customer ops and Redwood SRE/SE is finalized (least privilege).

Operational SLA matrix (reference thresholds and owners)

| Area | SLO / Threshold | Primary owner | Escalation target |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Endpoint availability | 99.95% monthly | Customer Success (CSM) / SE | SRE oncall within 30m |
| P95 latency (<=256 tokens) | < 300 ms (Dedicated) | SE / Runtime team | Runtime oncall within 60m |
| Error rate (5xx) | < 0.05% | Runtime team | SRE within 30m |
| Cold-start median | < 1200 ms | Runtime team | Engineering within 2h |
| Cost anomaly | < 25% deviation vs forecast | Finance + CSM | Growth/RevOps notified 1 business day |

Note: thresholds above are targets agreed during onboarding and may be tuned per-contract. All alerts should map to the customer-specific alerting policy in PagerDuty and Slack channel.

Escalation & handoff timeline (high level)

- Day 0 (Go-live): SE oncall and CSM present. Monitor first 24 hours for errors and latency regressions.
- Day 1–7: Daily sync between CSM, SE, and SRE for the first-week incidents and visibility.
- Day 8–30: Bi-weekly operational check-ins, performance tuning (batching/KV cache config), and cost review.
- Day 31–90: Weekly check-ins until SLA stability and customer success criteria are met; prepare QBR artifacts by day 75.

Handoff procedure (detailed, numbered)

1. Pre-handoff readiness demo (SE + customer): run the baseline load test (recommended: k6 or locust harness) and demonstrate acceptance criteria.
2. Fill the Onboarding Runbook template: include endpoints, model pins, route policies, alerting, and contact matrix.
3. Create customer-specific monitoring dashboard: tokens-per-minute, p95 latency, 5xx rate, cost-by-route. Share read-only link with customer.
4. Add the customer to the SRE PagerDuty rotation as a secondary for the first 30 days.
5. Formal handoff meeting: CSM presents business context, SE presents technical state, SRE presents monitoring/alerts. Capture action items in Jira and assign owners.

Post-handoff runbook excerpts (copy these into the customer runbook)

- Immediate checks when an alert fires:
  - Step 1: Verify if alert is customer-generated (4xx) vs platform (5xx) by checking trace id and edge logs.
  - Step 2: If platform (5xx), run diagnostic command: curl -v -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://api.redwood.example/v1/engines/<engine-id>/health || cat /var/log/runtime/errors.log (SE only).
  - Step 3: Check KV cache hit rate and batching stats from /metrics endpoint (prometheus name: redwood_runtime_kv_cache_hit_ratio). Thresholds: < 60% indicates mis-priming.
  - Step 4: Escalate per matrix (see table above) and create a postmortem if the incident causes > 30m downtime affecting > 10% of requests.

Common post-go-live issues and mitigations

- High P95 latency after deployment:
  - Likely causes: non-optimal batching, model quantization fallback, and warmup not run.
  - Mitigation steps: confirm batching policy in route config, enable prefix/KV cache for repeated prompts, trigger a lightweight warmup job: POST /internal/warmup {"engine":"<engine-id>","samples":10}.

- Increased token spend vs forecast:
  - Likely causes: prompt inflation, unexpected retries, or high token-per-request usage.
  - Mitigation steps: enable token-limit policy on the route, add request logging with sampling to capture outlier prompts, review SDK integration to verify retries/backoff.

- Frequent 429s (rate limit) during ramp:
  - Likely causes: client-side concurrency and missing client-side rate limiting.
  - Mitigation: apply client-side leaky-bucket throttling; coordinate with SE to provision burst capacity for first 48 hours.

Monitoring & instrumentation checklist (must be visible in the first 24 hours)

- Dashboards: Tokens/minute, per-route cost, p95 latency, 5xx rate, KV cache hit ratio.
- Traces: sample 1% of requests with full request/response payload for the first 7 days. Ensure PII redaction enabled.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with request_id, trace_id, route, model_id. Retention: 90 days by default for enterprise customers.

CLI and example snippets

- Fetch engine health:
  - Example: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.example/v1/engines/my-prod-engine/health

- Warmup job (cURL example):
  - curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"engine":"my-prod-engine","samples":["Hello","Summarize: short text"],"concurrency":2}' https://api.redwood.example/internal/warmup

- Sample route config (JSON fragment to include in onboarding runbook):
  - {
      "route_name": "customer-a-default",
      "engine": "my-prod-engine",
      "batching": { "max_batch_tokens": 1024, "max_batch_size": 32 },
      "cache": { "prefix_cache": true, "kv_profile": "high-hit" },
      "slo_tags": ["enterprise-2026"],
      "rate_limits": { "requests_per_minute": 1200 }
    }

QBR readiness checklist (to deliver by day 75)

- Usage trends and cost breakdown (token-level) for day 0–75.
- Performance baseline vs current (p50/p95/p99).
- Open incidents and remediation items.
- Proposed optimization roadmap (batching/cache/quantizaton) with estimated cost impact.

Owner & contacts

- Onboarding SE: name & email (populate in runbook).
- Customer Success Manager: name & email (populate in runbook).
- Runtime Oncall: rotas listed in Ops PagerDuty.

Appendix: Acceptance test checklist (sample commands)

1. Latency smoke test (10 concurrent requests): run k6 script; expected p95 < configured threshold.
2. Fault injection: simulate a dropped node and verify automatic fallback to other capacity pools within 60s.
3. Cost smoke test: replay representative traffic for 1 hour and measure tokens-per-minute vs forecast.

Notes and links

- Attach: baseline runbench JSON, onboarding runbook template, SLA addendum (if different from platform defaults).
- For security-sensitive customers, coordinate with Security & Compliance for audit logging and evidence packages.

If you have questions about any step, ping #cs-onboarding or open a ticket in the Onboarding queue.

payload.page_title: Onboarding Risk Scenarios and Service Contract Matrix

sections.body:
Purpose

This page catalogs prioritized onboarding risk scenarios for enterprise customers, maps each scenario to the supporting contractual commitments (SLA tier, remediation windows, credits), and provides step-by-step simulation and test scripts teams should run during the onboarding phase. The document is intended for Customer Success (CS), Solutions Engineering, SRE, and Legal when negotiating operational terms.

Scope and audience

- Scope: Enterprise onboarding (provisioning of Dedicated or Private deployments and first 90 days after cutover).
- Audience: CS, Solutions Engineering, SRE, Account Management, Legal.

Quick summary of intent

- Standardize which failure modes we simulate during onboarding and who owns remediation.
- Ensure contractual language maps cleanly to operational playbooks (SLO -> test -> remediation -> credit calculation).
- Provide reproducible test scripts and acceptance criteria so cutovers are repeatable and auditable.

Executive risk matrix (high-level)

| Risk category | Impact to customer | Likely root causes | Primary owner | Escalation path |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Provisioning failure (tenant never provisioned) | High - prevents go-live | IAM misconfig, cloud quotas, terraform drift | Solutions Eng | CS -> Infra SRE -> Eng Platform -> Legal (if contract delay) |
| Capacity surge (unexpected traffic growth) | High - latency/SLO breaches | Under-provisioning, misconfigured autoscale policy | SRE | CS -> SRE -> Product Ops |
| Model degradation / accuracy regression | High - incorrect outputs | Model version mismatch, data drift, prompt change | CS & Applied ML | CS -> Applied ML -> Model Onboarding |
| Network isolation / peering failure (Private) | High - customer unable to route | Firewall rules, VPC peering misconfig | Eng Private Deployments | CS -> Eng Private -> Networking |
| KV cache inconsistency / data staleness | Medium - decreased perf / cost | Cache invalidation bug, TTL misconfig | Eng Serving Runtime | CS -> Serving Runtime -> SRE |
| Billing / quota misattribution | Medium - unexpected charges | Metering bug, attribution config | Finance & Billing | CS -> Finance -> Billing Eng |
| Security gate delay (audit/compliance) | High - regulatory hold | Missing evidence, KMS/HSM integration issues | Security & Compliance | CS -> Security -> Legal |

Risk-to-contract matrix (operational clauses)

Below is a standard mapping we use when reviewing contract language during onboarding. Use this table to validate a customer's Master Services Agreement (MSA) or SOW.

| Risk scenario | Minimum SLA tier offered | Expected SLOs / windows | Standard remediation window | Credit / Remedy | Required acceptance tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Provisioning failure | Enterprise | Provision within 8 business hours for Dedicated; 5 business days for Private on-prem installer | 24 hours initial response, 72 hours remediation plan | Service credit: 10% monthly for >72h outage | Runbook: full terraform apply dry-run; API health probe; audit of resource creation records |
| Capacity surge causing sustained 95th p99 latency breaches | Priority | 95th percentile latency < 200ms for typical gen calls; availability > 99.5% | 1 hour mitigation window, 24h root cause | Auto-scaling burst allowance; credit based on duration beyond mitigation window | Load test at 2x anticipated peak, validate autoscale triggers, fallbacks to cheaper model variant |
| Model quality regression after model upgrade | Enterprise | Quality regression tolerance defined in SOW (e.g., <3% metric drop for primary eval set) | Rollback within 2 hours to previous variant | Remediation: rollback + model QA; credit if unremediated >24h | Canary eval set run (example scripts below); automated acceptance criteria pass |
| Network peering failure (Private) | Enterprise | Connectivity established and verified during cutover | 4 hours to identify, 48 hours to remediate peering in specialist cases | On a case-by-case basis; telepresence and scheduled maintenance windows documented | Packet path test, traceroutes, private endpoint handshake confirmation
