payload.page_title: Go-Live Protocols: Cross-Org Communications & Escalation

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the cross-organizational go-live protocol used by Redwood Inference for enterprise tenant cutovers. It focuses on communications, stakeholder coordination, and an escalation ladder tailored for high-risk or high-visibility customers. Use this runbook as the canonical checklist for the 72 hours before, during, and 72 hours after a cutover where multiple teams (Customer Success, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Product, and Sales) must be coordinated.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private deployment go-lives and tenant migrations with SLA commitments (any customer with an enterprise contract or > $50k monthly spend).
- Out of scope: self-serve trial accounts, routine model-only updates without routing changes.

Goals and SLOs to Protect
-------------------------
- Availability SLA target to protect during cutover: 99.9% (monthly) for production routes.
- Immediate remediation thresholds (trigger escalation):
  - Error rate spike: sustained >5% errors for 5 minutes across tenant endpoints.
  - Latency spike: P95 latency >2000ms for 10 minutes.
  - Token cost anomaly: >200% of projected token spend in 30 minutes.
  - KV cache miss-rate >30% sustained for 15 minutes (for cache-sensitive workloads).

Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-1 hours)
-------------------------------
1. Confirm stakeholders and channels
   - Primary CSM (Customer Success Manager): name + mobile number.
   - Tech lead (Customer): contact + escalation path.
   - Solution Engineer (SE): responsible for ingress, API contract verification.
   - Oncall SRE/Platform owner: PagerDuty schedule and runbook owner.
   - Slack channels: #cs-<customer>-go-live (private channel), #oncall-redwood, #se-ops.
2. Telemetry sanity checks — must pass before proceeding:
   - Synthetic journey (happy path) passes end-to-end: <customer> -> Redwood API -> response < 1s.
   - PromQL checks: error_rate/instance < 0.005 for 10m; p95_latency_query < 1500ms.
3. Canary plan and acceptance criteria
   - Canary traffic: route 1% of production for 30 minutes with zero critical errors.
   - Acceptance: no P0/P1 incidents during canary and no regression in model quality metrics (if applicable).
4. Whitelist and firewall confirmations
   - Verify ingress IP ranges, customer egress rules, and TLS client certs.

During Cutover (T0 to +4 hours) — Immediate Checklist
----------------------------------------------------
- Primary communications protocol:
  - All updates posted to #cs-<customer>-go-live every 10 minutes during the first hour, then every 30 minutes until stable.
  - The CSM posts customer-facing status updates; technical details posted to private channel only.
- Live monitoring dashboard (owner: Oncall SRE):
  - Tenant-specific dashboard showing throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, KV cache hits, token consumption.
- Escalation triggers (first responder must escalate within 5 minutes if triggered):
  1) P0: service unavailable for customer routes — immediate page to P1 oncall and notify Engineering Director.
  2) P1: sustained SLO breach (see thresholds above) — page SE and PM, start RCA and mitigation steps.
  3) P2: model quality regression detected — notify Applied ML and SE; consider traffic switch to verified model snapshot.

Escalation Ladder (contact order and responsibilities)
----------------------------------------------------
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------
- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------
1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
   - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}'
   - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
   - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
   - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------
- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
  - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------
- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
  - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
  - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------
- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------
- CSM: customer comms and executive escalation.
- SE: onboarding technical lead, API contract signoff, whitelist verification.
- Oncall SRE: monitoring, mitigation, and platform config changes in emergencies.
- Product/Applied ML: model quality regressions and rollbacks.
- Finance Ops: post-cutover cost anomalies and quota adjustments.

Appendix A — Playbook Checklist (copyable)
-----------------------------------------
- [ ] Confirm private channel and all stakeholder contacts pinned
- [ ] Telemetry smoke test passed (synthetic happy path)
- [ ] Canary plan scheduled and accepted by SE and SRE
- [ ] Firewall/whitelist config validated by Network team
- [ ] PagerDuty rotations confirmed and escalation contacts available
- [ ] Customer-facing status template approved by CSM
- [ ] Post-cutover QBR slot scheduled with customer (within 30 days)

Appendix B — Links and References
--------------------------------
- Tenant cutover checklist (internal): /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- Incident comms templates: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-communication-templates
- PagerDuty runbook: https://pagerduty.com/orgs/redwood-incidents (private)

Appendix C — Escalation Contact Quickview
----------------------------------------
- Oncall SRE: pagerduty (PD ID: PD12345), Slack: @oncall-sre, mobile: +1-555-0102
- SE on duty: Slack: @se-ops, mobile: +1-555-0148
- CSM (Primary): Priya Patel, Slack: @priya.cs, mobile: +1-555-0190

Revision History
----------------
- 2027-02-10: Created by Priya Patel.
- 2027-03-02: Reviewed and clarified rollback steps; added expense reconciliation task (Marisol Gomez).

Notes and governance
--------------------
Keep this page updated after every enterprise go-live. If the customer contract contains additional communication obligations (e.g., weekly executive summaries), add them to the post-cutover tasks and pin them in the customer channel.

payload.page_title: Reducing Alert Fatigue and Clear Oncall Ownership: A Customer-Facing Incident Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines how Redwood’s Customer Success, Support, and Platform teams should coordinate to reduce alert noise, establish unambiguous oncall ownership, and manage customer-visible incidents with minimal customer disruption. It is focused on enterprise tenants (Dedicated/Private) but also applies to hosted API incidents where customer impact is suspected.

Goals
- Reduce actionable pager noise by >=50% for customer-impacting alerts within three months of adoption.
- Ensure every alert has a single owning team and a documented remediation runbook or a suppression policy.
- Provide clear steps for customer-safe remediation and communications to minimize churn and SLA exposure.

Scope
- Included: alerts generated by Redwood control plane, tenant routing/proxy, model serving (inference failures), quota and billing anomalies, and integration connectors that impact request processing.
- Excluded: internal CI/CD job failures (owned by eng-infra) and local developer tooling alerts.

Definitions
- Noise: alerts that repeatedly fire without leading to a meaningful action within the past 30 days.
- Actionable Alert: an alert with a documented owner, severity, and a runbook that is executed at least once when it fires.
- Customer-facing Incident: an event where customer SLOs (availability/latency) are materially impacted, or billing/data integrity is at risk.

Roles & Ownership
- First Responder (Support/Platform): The oncall person who owns initial triage within 15 minutes. Responsibilities: validate, gather impact, open incident if needed, begin mitigation.
- Engineering Owner (Runtime/Infra/Product): Team responsible for full remediation and post-incident follow-up. Must be staffed for major incidents.
- Customer Success Lead (CS): Primary communicator to customer stakeholders and coordinates internal communications for ERs/SEVs.
- Incident Commander (IC): Assigned for Sev2+/Sev1 incidents. Coordinates cross-team tasks and manages escalation.

Alert Classification Matrix
(Use this table to assign ownership and expected response time)

| Category | Example alert | Owner | Response SLA | Customer impact | Auto-suppress allowed? | Severity |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Platform Availability | control-plane-400-errors > 5% over 5m | eng-platform | 5m | High | No | Sev1 |
| Model Degradation | p95_token_latency_increase > 2x baseline | eng-serving-runtime | 15m | Moderate/High | No | Sev2 |
| Tenant Quota Hit | tenant_x_rate_limit_429s > 10/min | support | 15m | Moderate | Yes (1m suppression) | Sev2 |
| Telemetry Drop | metrics-forwarder_lag > 120s | eng-infra | 30m | Low/Moderate | Yes (grouped) | Sev3 |
| Billing Anomaly | invoice_delta > $5k unexpected | finance-legal & support | 60m | High (customer) | No | Sev1 |

Triage & Escalation Procedure (first 30 minutes)
1. First Responder acknowledges alert within Response SLA.
2. Determine if alert is symptomatic or root: check runbook tags: symptomatic -> follow immediate mitigations; root -> route to Engineering Owner.
3. If multiple alerts correlate (same tenant or upstream), mark incident and assign IC.
4. IC coordinates: set incident priority, notify CS Lead, open incident bridge, document initial timeline.
5. If customer-visible, CS Lead drafts initial comms template (internal + external) and posts a holding message to the customer’s designated channel within 30 minutes of incident start.

Runbook Patterns (examples)
- Symptomatic mitigation (fast path):
  - Example: tenant_x_rate_limit_429s
    - Action: enable short suppression (1m) for duplicate alerts; find offending tenant key; apply temporary burst-limit increase for that tenant via admin API:
      - curl -X POST https://admin.redwood/api/v1/tenants/{tenant}/burst-adjust
        -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN'
        -d '{"burst_window": 60, "max_burst": 500}'
    - Verify: run `curl https://telemetry.redwood/api/tenant/{tenant}/metrics | jq .rates` and ensure 429s drop below threshold for 5 consecutive minutes.

- Root cause engagement (slow path):
  - Example: p95_token_latency_increase > 2x baseline
    - Action: collect traces (tracer query examples below), review recent deployments, check GPU health and KV cache hit rate.
    - PromQL snippet to attach with incident: `increase(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="runtime",quantile="0.95"}[5m])`
    - Escalate to eng-serving-runtime and provide packet of: tenant list, timestamps, top traces, and pre/post deploy diffs.

Alert Reduction Playbook (how to reduce noise)
1. Ownership mapping: every alert must have the `owner_team` label and a single Slack/Pager contact. No alert without owner is considered noise.
2. Suppress identical alerts for the same tenant for a configurable debounce window (default 1 minute) unless it evidences growing error rates.
3. Dedup & group by root cause: implement correlation rules in the alert router (grouping-key: tenant|service|error-code).
4. Use adaptive thresholds based on rolling windows and baseline seasonality instead of static fixed thresholds.
5. Implement an alert lifecycle: open -> acknowledged -> resolved -> closed. Alerts that bounce back without remediation are automatically escalated to IC.
6. Maintain a suppression whitelist for noisy 3rd-party integrations with documented mitigation steps.

Key Metrics to Track
- Pager burn rate: number of paged alerts per oncall shift (target < 8 actionable pages/shift).
- Alert to incident conversion: percent of alerts that become incidents (target < 10%).
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) and mean time to remediate (MTTR) by alert class.
- Noise ratio: alerts suppressed / total alerts (target > 30% but balanced).
- Customer-impacting incidents per quarter (trend must be non-increasing).

Customer Communication Templates
- Holding message (30m):
  - Subject: We’re investigating a service disruption affecting {tenant-name}
  - Body: We are aware of increased errors for your requests and our teams are investigating. We will provide an update within 1 hour. Reference: {incident-link}
- Update cadence: 30m until root cause identified, 60m after that while in mitigation, then hourly as needed.
- Post-incident summary: include timeline, root cause, customer impact (tokens/requests affected), remediation steps taken, and scheduled follow-ups.

Escalation Matrix (customer-impacting)
- Sev1 (platform down for tenant or billing integrity risk): escalate to IC, eng-platform lead, CS Director, and Legal/Finance on call. Pager -> immediate bridge.
- Sev2 (degraded inference quality/latency impacting SLAs): Support first responder -> eng-serving-runtime -> CS Lead -> scheduled customer update.
- Sev3 (telemetry or low-impact errors): owner team handles within standard SLAs; escalate on repeated bounce.

Implementation Checklist (for Support & Platform)
- [ ] Annotate all alerts with owner_team, severity, and runbook link.
- [ ] Configure the alert router: suppression windows, grouping keys, and dedupe rules.
- [ ] Add Slack channel / PagerDuty escalation bindings per team.
- [ ] Create customer comms templates and CS contact list per enterprise tenant.
- [ ] Create dashboards: Alert noise panel, top firing rules, MTTA/MTTR trends, per-tenant alert volume.

Sample Alert Definitions (examples for runtime engineers)
- p95 latency spike (Prometheus):
  - ALERT RuntimeHighP95Latency
  - IF histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance)) > 2.0
  - FOR 3m
  - LABELS { severity="page", owner_team="eng-serving-runtime" }

- Tenant error rate (example rule):
  - ALERT TenantHighErrorRate
  - IF increase(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",tenant=~".+"}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
  - LABELS { severity="page", owner_team="support" }

Oncall Handover & Fatigue Reduction Practices
- Handover notes: outgoing oncall must leave the top 3 active alerts, any muted rules, and follow-ups in the team Handoff doc.
- Scheduled quiet windows: non-urgent noisy alerts may be auto-muted during scheduled low-traffic maintenance windows if documented and approved by CS.
- Rotation length: prefer 7-day rotations for platform teams and 3-4 day rotations for support to balance knowledge and burnout. Review quarterly.
- Pager triage cap: any engineer receiving >12 pages in a day must have their load reviewed by manager; consider temporary rotation pause.

Post-Incident & Continuous Improvement
- Post-Incident Tasks (within 72 hours):
  1. Full RCA and timeline (eng owner).
  2. Action items assigned with owner and due date.
  3. Alert audit: any alert that fired and did not lead to remediation must be suppressed or reclassified.
  4. Customer-facing summary drafted and approved by CS Lead and Legal (if PII/financial impact).
- Quarterly Alert Review: each team publishes an alert inventory and noise metrics; operations council reviews and approves suppression/threshold changes.

Playbook for Customer-Facing Degraded Performance (quick checklist)
1. Validate incident and measure customer impact (requests, latency, error rate).
2. If impact confirmed, IC open and CS Lead notified.
3. Apply symptomatic mitigations (traffic shaping, fallback models, tenant routing to warm capacity).
4. If mitigation succeeds, prepare customer rollback and update comms.
5. If mitigation fails, escalate to engineering and determine rollback or multi-tenant fallback.

Appendices
A. Useful Queries and Tools
- Traces: `trace-search --tenant {tenant} --from {iso-ts} --to {iso-ts}`
- Top error sample: `curl https://telemetry.redwood/api/errors?tenant={t}&window=10m | jq .top`
- Alert router health check: `kubectl -n observability exec router-0 -- /bin/healthcheck`

B. Contacts
- Support Pager: #support-pager (Slack) and PagerDuty escalation policy: Redwood-Support-Escalation
- Eng Platform oncall: eng-platform-oncall@redwood.internal
- CS Director: cs-director@redwood.internal

C. Change History
- 2026-03-01: Created by Asha Murthy (published).
- 2026-06-10: Added sample PromQL and tenant mitigation API examples (reviewer: Benji Park).
- 2026-10-12: Expanded metrics section and added rotation guidance (reviewer: Lena Hoffmann).

If you are implementing these changes, coordinate with Observability (eng-platform) and Support for a staged rollout. For assistance, tag @cs-ops in #ops-requests.

payload.page_title: Jira Field Guidelines + SLA Timers (SUP Tickets)

sections.body: This page defines the **required Jira fields, priority/severity rules, SLA timer usage, and linking/closure standards** for customer-facing Support tickets in the **SUP** project.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Reduce time-to-triage and time-to-mitigation with consistent, searchable ticket data.
- Ensure Support **SLAs** are tracked consistently (first response + update cadence) and align with Engineering on-call practices.
- Make escalations auditable: every page/bridge/incident should be linkable from the SUP ticket.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to all SUP tickets (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).
- Applies to Support + CS when creating/updating SUP tickets.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Replacing incident process (#incidents + incident commander). Use SUP as the **customer-impact record** and handoff anchor.

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
1) **One SUP ticket per customer issue** (even if Engineering work spans multiple teams). Link out to Linear/GitHub as needed.
2) Every SUP must have:
   - **Priority (P0–P4)**
   - **Incident Severity mapping (Sev0–Sev3)** when escalated
   - **Customer/org**, **tier**, **region**, **model**, and **request IDs** (or explicit note that none are available)
   - **SLA timers set** (first response + next update due)
3) If a Slack bridge exists, the ticket must include a **Slack link**, and the Slack bridge must include the **SUP link**.
4) When closing a ticket, write resolution notes so the next on-call can answer: **what happened, what we changed, what the customer should do next**.

---
sections.heading: Golden rules (read first)

sections.body:
Fill these at creation or during initial triage. Missing fields are the #1 cause of delays.

**Customer & routing**
- **Customer / Org**: Company name and (if applicable) workspace/org identifier.
- **Customer tier** (`customer_tier`): `self_serve` | `dedicated` | `private` | `enterprise`
- **Product area** (`product_area`): Hosted API | Dedicated | Private | Console | Optimize | SDK | Billing
- **Environment** (`environment`): prod | staging | private cluster (name)

**Technical context**
- **Region** (`region`): e.g., `us-east`, `eu-west` (or `N/A` for Private/on-prem where region is not applicable)
- **Model** (`model`): exact model ID + version if known (e.g., `rw-llama-70b@2026-01-31`) or `unknown`
- **SDK + version** (`sdk`): python/ts/go + version, or `HTTP` if direct REST
- **Request IDs** (`request_ids`): at least 1–3 IDs for failing requests (preferred). If unavailable, include timestamp window + client IP hash if provided.
- **Symptoms** (`symptoms`): short, customer-observable description (errors, timeouts, truncation, latency)

**Impact & comms**
- **Impact summary** (`impact_summary`): what’s broken + who is affected + since when.
- **Customer-facing comms owner** (`comms_owner`): Support owner (and CSM for enterprise)
- **Slack link** (`slack_thread_or_channel`): link to Slack thread/bridge if used

**Escalation tracking (when applicable)**
- **Escalation status** (`escalation_status`): Not escalated | Monitoring | Eng engaged | Incident declared | Mitigated | Resolved
- **Incident link** (`incident_channel` / `incident_id`): if moved to #incidents, link the incident channel + incident record if one exists
- **Engineering tracking link(s)** (`linear_link`, `github_pr_link`): links created during escalation

---
sections.heading: Required fields (SUP)

sections.body: Support uses **P0–P4** to manage urgency and SLA behavior. Engineering incident response uses **Sev0–Sev3**.
sections.heading: Priority (Support) vs Severity (Incident)

sections.body: - See: *Severity Matrix and Escalation Triggers*
sections.heading: Use the published rubric as the source of truth

sections.body:
**P0 — Critical, active customer outage**
- Production down or near-down for customer(s), no viable workaround.
- Examples: auth outage, widespread 5xx, total inability to stream across a region.

**P1 — Major degradation or high-risk incident**
- Severe performance degradation, partial outage, or failure affecting key flows; workaround may exist but is risky/complex.

**P2 — Significant issue with acceptable workaround**
- Material impact but customers can proceed via documented workaround, or impact is limited in scope.

**P3 — Minor issue / “how-to” with some urgency**
- Small subset affected; minimal business impact.

**P4 — General question / request / non-urgent**
sections.heading: Quick selection guidance (Support Priority)

sections.body:
- Assign **Sev** only when escalation/incident process is engaged (or imminent).
- If you set a Sev, also set: `escalation_status`, Slack link, and the on-call/team engaged.

**Rule of thumb:** If you are paging on-call or moving to #incidents, you should have a Sev mapping.

---
sections.heading: When to assign Incident Severity

sections.body:
1) **`first_response_due_at`**
- The deadline for the *first human response* to the customer.
- This is based on **customer tier** and the SLA policy.

2) **`sla_due_at`**
- The deadline for the *next required customer update* (update cadence timer).
- Reset this after every meaningful customer update.
sections.heading: We track two time-based fields on SUP tickets

sections.body: - See: *SLA Policy by Customer Tier*
sections.heading: Reference policy

sections.body:
- Set both timers at ticket creation (or immediately during initial triage).
- Update `sla_due_at` every time you send a customer update (email, support portal response, or agreed Slack Connect update).
- If you are waiting on the customer, set ticket status to **Waiting on Customer** and follow the “pause” guidance below.
sections.heading: SLA timer rules

sections.body:
- Only move to **Waiting on Customer** when we have asked a clear question AND provided the next step the customer can take.
- Add a public comment stating what is needed (e.g., request IDs, timestamps, region).
- **Do not silently stop updates** for P0/P1 tickets. If impact persists and we’re actively mitigating, keep updates on the agreed cadence.

(If your Jira configuration supports SLA pausing, the automation will pause update timers in Waiting on Customer. If it does not, explicitly set `sla_due_at` to a reasonable follow-up checkpoint and note the expectation in the ticket.)

---
sections.heading: To avoid SLA confusion

sections.body:
1. Set **Priority (P0–P4)**.
2. Confirm **tier, region, model, SDK version, request IDs**.
3. Set **`first_response_due_at`** and **`sla_due_at`**.
4. Respond to customer with acknowledgment + request for missing diagnostics.
5. Add labels:
   - `hosted` / `dedicated` / `private`
   - `streaming` / `quota` / `autoscaling` / `audit-logs` / `sso` etc.
sections.heading: 1) Intake (first 10 minutes)

sections.body:
- Use the *Support Triage Intake Checklist*.
- Link dashboards/runbooks in internal comments.
- If the issue matches a known issue, add `known_issue_link` and use the macro.
sections.heading: 2) Triage (first 30–60 minutes)

sections.body:
1. Create (or join) a Slack bridge per *Slack Bridge and Incident Channel Conventions*.
2. Fill:
   - `slack_thread_or_channel`
   - `escalation_status = Eng engaged`
   - incident fields if moved to #incidents
3. Page the correct team via the escalation directory (do not “drive-by DM”).
4. In the ticket, add an internal comment with:
   - Why we escalated (trigger)
   - What we’ve tried
   - What we need from Engineering (specific ask)
sections.heading: When escalating

sections.body:
- Keep `sla_due_at` aligned to the customer update cadence.
- For mitigations, document:
  - What changed (config knob, region failover, retry guidance)
  - Customer action required
  - Any risk/rollback plan
sections.heading: 4) Mitigation / Monitoring

sections.body:
- Issue is fixed and verified, OR
- Workaround is documented + customer confirms acceptable outcome, OR
- Customer confirms they no longer need help.
sections.heading: Close only when one of the following is true

sections.body:
- Add a final customer-facing summary.
- Complete the **Resolution Notes** section (template below).
- Link any related Engineering follow-ups (Linear/GitHub) and known-issues article.

---
sections.heading: Before closing

sections.body:
- Always link the Slack artifact used for coordination:
  - Single thread: paste permalink in `slack_thread_or_channel`
  - Bridge channel: paste channel link + pin the SUP link in the channel
sections.heading: Slack

sections.body:
- If escalation becomes an incident:
  - Link the #incidents channel in the SUP ticket
  - Add the incident identifier (if your incident tooling generates one)
  - Keep customer updates aligned with the incident comms owner
sections.heading: Incidents

sections.body:
- Link at least one of:
  - Linear issue (bug/task)
  - GitHub PR
- In the SUP ticket, add a one-line “why it matters” translation (customer impact) so Engineering doesn’t have to parse the ticket.
sections.heading: Engineering work

sections.body:
- If there is a known issue article:
  - Add the link in `known_issue_link`
  - Use consistent language in customer updates (copy/paste-ready)
- If you discover a repeatable issue without an article:
  - Flag it with label `known-issue-candidate`
  - Add a short draft workaround in an internal comment

---
sections.heading: Knowledge base / known issues

sections.body:
Add a final internal section called **Resolution Notes** with the following structure. This is mandatory for P0–P2.

**Resolution Notes (template)**
- **What the customer saw (symptoms):**
- **Customer impact:** (scope, region, tier, timeframe)
- **Root cause (known/likely/unknown):** (be explicit about confidence)
- **Mitigation applied:** (what we changed; include config values if safe)
- **Customer action required:** (if any)
- **Verification:** (how we confirmed recovery; include dashboards/logs at a high level)
- **Follow-ups:** (Linear/GitHub links; doc updates; monitoring gaps)
- **Prevent recurrence:** (if applicable)
sections.heading: Resolution notes standards (required)

sections.body:
- Write so someone outside the original thread can understand in <2 minutes.
- Avoid customer-sensitive details in broadly visible fields; if needed, put sensitive artifacts in restricted locations and reference them.

---
sections.heading: Quality bar

sections.body:
- Use the region where the request was served (customer’s configured region), not the customer HQ.
- If multi-region: list all affected regions and note primary.
sections.heading: `region`

sections.body:
- Prefer the exact model ID + pinned version.
- If the issue may involve fallback, explicitly note “fallback suspected” and link relevant routing metrics if available.
sections.heading: `model`

sections.body:
- Minimum: 1 request ID per failure mode.
- For streaming issues: include both the initial request ID and any reconnect request IDs if client retries.
sections.heading: `request_ids`

sections.body:
- Do not “upgrade to P0” just because the customer is loud. Use the rubric + impact.
- Do upgrade to P0/P1 when there is broad/regional impact even if the first ticket is from a single customer.
sections.heading: `priority`

sections.body:
Good: “~35% of streaming requests reset mid-generation in us-east for Hosted API customers since 14:05 UTC; affected customers report truncated outputs; no workaround confirmed yet.”
Bad: “Streaming is broken.”

---
sections.heading: `impact_summary`

sections.body:
(Exact automation names may vary, but expected behaviors are below.)

- On ticket creation in SUP:
  - Prompt for required fields (tier, region, model, request IDs)
  - Set placeholder SLA timers if not set (must be corrected by triager)
- On Priority change:
  - Update escalation prompts (e.g., “Create bridge for P0/P1”)
  - Remind to set/update `sla_due_at`
- On transition to Waiting on Customer:
  - Prompt for a clear customer ask and next follow-up checkpoint
- On transition to Resolved/Closed:
  - Validate Resolution Notes present for P0–P2

If you see the automation misbehaving or blocking legitimate cases, file an internal request and tag **Dylan Brooks** (Jira automation owner).

---
sections.heading: Automation expectations (what Jira will do)

sections.body:
- Priority: P0
- Tier: enterprise
- Region: us-east
- Model: rw-llama-70b@2026-01-31
- Request IDs: 3 sample IDs from customer
- Slack: bridge channel link
- SLA:
  - `first_response_due_at`: set per enterprise policy
  - `sla_due_at`: set to next scheduled customer update (per cadence)
- Resolution Notes:
  - Includes mitigation (client-side reconnect guidance), verification (error rate drop), and Engineering follow-up PR link.
sections.heading: Example A: P0 streaming resets (Hosted)

sections.body:
- Priority: P2
- Tier: self_serve
- Request IDs: sample ID + header captures
- Known issue link: rate-limit/headers workaround
- SLA: first response + update checkpoint
- Resolution Notes:
  - Clarifies headers vs quota enforcement and points to corrected SDK configuration.

---
sections.heading: Example B: 429 confusion after SDK upgrade (Hosted)

sections.body:
- Do not paste customer secrets (API keys, full payloads with proprietary prompts) in Jira.
- For logs, request IDs are preferred. If payload samples are required, redact and confirm customer consent.
- If you must store sensitive artifacts, use restricted storage and reference location/owner in the ticket.

---
sections.heading: Compliance and confidentiality

sections.body:
- 2026-02-18: Clarified Waiting on Customer guidance and added mandatory Resolution Notes fields for P0–P2.
- 2026-02-12: Added `first_response_due_at` + `sla_due_at` definitions and reset rules.
- 2026-02-06: Initial publication for escalation playbook refresh.

payload.page_title: SOP: intake and coordination for customer-managed audit log export requests

sections.body: This SOP describes how Customer Success (CS) and Support intake, scope, and coordinate **customer-managed audit log export** requests across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- A customer asks to export Redwood audit logs to their cloud storage or SIEM pipeline.
- A security questionnaire requires audit log delivery details and customer wants automated export.
sections.heading: When to use

sections.body:
- Customer company
- Deployment mode: Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- Regions in use
- Desired sink: S3 | GCS | Azure Blob
- Destination details:
  - bucket/container name
  - prefix
  - destination region
- Identity method:
  - AWS assume-role / IRSA
  - GCP workload identity
  - Azure workload identity
- Retention intent (customer-owned)
- Operational contact + escalation contact
- Target date (if tied to an audit)
sections.heading: Collect the following in the internal-support Jira ticket

sections.body:
- Project: internal-support
- Issue type: Support Request
- Priority guidance:
  - P2 for standard requests
  - P1 if tied to a customer audit deadline within 14 days
  - P0 only if this blocks a live incident response obligation
sections.heading: 1) Create the internal-support Jira ticket

sections.body:
- Assign Security reviewer and request approval per the Security controls page.
- Attach destination policy snippets and encryption confirmation.
sections.heading: 2) Security approval

sections.body:
- cross-region export is requested
- customer requests additional PII fields beyond standard audit schema

sections.heading: Escalate to Legal/Privacy if

sections.body:
- Hosted: route to Eng Platform oncall / platform ops
- Dedicated: route to Eng Infra

sections.heading: After approvals

sections.body: Subject: Audit log export enablement – next steps
sections.heading: Customer communication template (email)

sections.body:
- Thanks for the request. We can enable automated export of Redwood platform audit logs to your [S3/GCS/Azure] destination.
- Please confirm you have created the destination bucket/container and enabled encryption at rest.
- Please provide the workload identity / role configuration using the attached template.
- Once received and approved, we will enable export and ask you to confirm objects are landing under the agreed prefix.

sections.body:

sections.body:

- Dedicated runbook

payload.page_title: Silent Degradation Detection and Automated Remediation Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines how Redwood detects 'silent degradations' (performance or quality regressions that do not immediately trigger customer-facing errors) and how we automatically remediate or escalate them. It centralizes detection signals, automated mitigation actions, ownership, and customer communication templates.

Scope: Applies to hosted API, Dedicated, and Private tenants for production inference pipelines. Focus areas: inference quality drift (semantic regressions), behind-the-scenes latency/cost regressions, and resource contention that degrades tail latency without complete failures.

Principles

- Detect early using behavioral signals instead of waiting for incident thresholds.
- Prefer automated safe remediation (circuit breakers, model fallback, synthetic rollbacks) when available.
- Keep customers informed for any automated action that modifies their request routing, model variant, or cost profile.

Key Definitions

- Silent Degradation: Degradation in availability, latency tail, unit cost, or model output fidelity that does not meet an immediate SLA but will materially affect customer experience over time (e.g., 15% increase in 95th percentile latency sustained for 30 minutes while error rate remains <1%).
- Mitigation Ladder: Ordered set of remediation steps ranked by low customer-impact and safety-first (observability -> soft mitigation -> hard mitigation -> human escalation).
- Synthetic Journey: End-to-end customer request simulation that verifies correctness, latency, and token cost against a baseline.

Signals and Detection Rules

1) Telemetry signals (primary):
   - p95 latency increase: >20% over rolling 60-min baseline for a customer segment.
   - Median tokens-per-generation increase: >30% vs. expected prompt distribution.
   - Inference unit cost variance: >25% sustained for 30 minutes.
   - Model-quality drift: decrease in internal eval accuracy/QA score by >5% on control prompt-set.
   - Synthetic journey failure rate: >3% failed assertions in last 10 runs.

2) Composite alerts (trigger when 2+ signals occur within a 30-minute window):
   - Example: p95 latency + tokens increase -> composite degradation alert.

3) Noise control and suppression:
   - Require minimum sample size (50 requests) in 30-minute window to avoid noisy triggers.
   - Apply anomaly detection smoothing: use robust median-of-means to ignore one-off spikes.

Mitigation Ladder (Automated-first flow)

Stage 0 — Observability escalation (automatic, no customer impact):
- Enrich alert with correlating dimensions: region, model_variant, tenant_id, pod_id, request_path.
- Run synthetic journey (fast) against the same variant and region.
- Snapshot KV cache hit ratio and batch size distribution.
- Notify oncall via Slack channel #ops-customer-alerts with prefilled context.

Stage 1 — Soft mitigations (safe, reversible):
1. Adaptive single-tenant batching loosen: reduce max batch wait time from config (default 25 ms -> 10 ms) to reduce tail latency for latency-sensitive customers.
   - Command: curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/tenants/{tenant}/config -d '{"batch_wait_ms":10}'
2. Prefix-KV cache warmup disable/enable toggle: temporarily disable prefix cache prefetch for affected tenant to prevent thrash.
3. Reduce quantization aggressiveness for the specific model_variant (if supported) to restore tail latency at expense of small cost increase.
- Automation: playbook automation runs these incrementally with health checks after each change (10-minute stabilization window).

Stage 2 — Hard mitigations (automated but higher-impact):
1. Model-fallback to higher-latency but more stable variant (e.g., redwood-model-v2.small -> redwood-model-v2.base).
   - Route policy change: set "fallback=true" for affected tenant and route for 15 minutes.
2. Cross-region failover for regional capacity anomalies (only for customers with cross-region enabled).
3. Temporary request-throttling or per-tenant fairshare enforcement to protect shared capacity.
- Automation: require 3 confirmation checks (composite signal persists across 3 consecutive 10-minute windows) before applying.

Stage 3 — Human-in-the-loop and customer-impacting actions:
- Paging to SRE and Customer Success for coordinated action.
- Consider scheduled model rollback (if recent model rollout is correlated).
- Initiate coordinated customer communication and QBR action items.

Escalation matrix and Ownership

- Primary owner: SRE (eng-sre) — responsible for automated runbook maintenance and operations targeting.
- Secondary owner: Customer Success — responsible for customer notification and follow-up.
- Tertiary owner: Runtime/Serving team — responsible for fixing systemic regressions (kernel changes, batching logic).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Sev-3 (Degradation): p95 latency up 20%, small customer impact. Action: Stages 0-1 automated. Notify CS.
- Sev-2 (Significant Degradation): p95 up 50% or synthetic failures >10%. Action: Stages 0-2 automated plus SRE paging.
- Sev-1 (Critical): sustained degradation causing customer SLA breach or data loss. Action: Full incident runbook; immediate human response and customer-wide comms.

Customer Communication Templates

- Auto-notify (low impact): "We detected increased latency affecting your tenant in region X. We've applied temporary mitigations and are monitoring. No action required on your side. Status: investigating."
- Escalated notification (when model-fallback or throttling applied): "To prevent downstream impact we temporarily routed requests to a stable model variant. Expected impact: small quality delta for 15–60 minutes. We will notify when normal routing is restored."

Implementation details and examples

1) Synthetic Journey definition (YAML example):
| name: conversational-check
| frequency_minutes: 5
| tenant_scope: control
| steps:
|   - send_prompt: "Summarize: The market yesterday..."
|   - assert_latency_lt_ms: 350
|   - assert_tokens_lt: 300
|   - compute_quality_score: baseline_eval.json

2) Example alert rule (pseudo):
- name: silent-degradation-composite
  condition: (p95_latency > 1.2 * rolling_p95) AND (median_tokens > 1.3 * rolling_median_tokens)
  min_samples: 50
  window: 30m
  action: trigger_auto_mitigation_workflow

3) Sample automation flow (CLI snippets):
- Run synthetic journey:
  curl -X POST $SYNTH_API/run -d '{"journey":"conversational-check","region":"us-west-2"}'
- Apply batching config tweak:
  curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/tenants/tenant-123/config -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"batch_wait_ms":10}'
- Apply model-fallback (atomic):
  curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/routing -d '{"tenant":"tenant-123","route_override":{"model":"redwood-model-v2.base","duration_min":15}}'

Safety checks and guardrails

- Automatic changes must be bounded: no single automated change should increase tenant costs >20% without human approval.
- Any automated model-fallback that alters output fidelity requires CS notification and an opt-out flag for customers who have strict fidelity SLAs.
- All automated actions must be logged with request-level correlation IDs and rollback timers.

Testing and validation

- Nightly synthetic runs against Canary tenants to validate auto-remediation code paths.
- Game-day quarterly validation: simulate silent degrations (increase latency, reduce KV cache hits) and verify automation triggers and rollbacks.
- Regression validation in PRs that modify batching/kv/quantization code paths: include synthetic journey baseline runs in CI.

Runbook: Step-by-step response (when automation triggers)

1. T=0: Composite alert triggers -> run automated diagnostic snapshot (observability enrichment).
2. T=0–10m: Orchestrator runs synthetic journey and posts results to incident channel.
3. T=10–25m: Automation applies Stage 1 mitigations sequentially with 10-minute stabilize checks.
4. T=25–60m: If composite persists, automation promotes to Stage 2 mitigations; SRE is paged.
5. T>60m: If unresolved, escalate to incident playbook (oncall rotation, CS outreach, exec notification if >2 customers impacted).

Operational metrics to track

- Mean time to detect (MTTD) for silent degradations.
- % of degradations mitigated fully by automation (no human involvement).
- False positive rate of composite alerts.
- Average cost delta introduced by automated actions.
- Customer satisfaction delta post-remediation (tracked in QBR).

QBR inputs and Recommended Reporting

For Quarterly Business Reviews (CS + Customer): provide:
- Incidents summary that used this playbook (count, mitigation type, customer impact).
- MTTD/MTTR and how many were fully automated.
- Any recurring root causes and action items (e.g., batching kernel bug, KV cache cold-start).
- Cost vs. quality tradeoffs observed and recommended model/quantization profile changes.

Appendices

A. Sample JSON payload for alert enrichment:
{
  "alert_id":"sd-20260702-001",
  "tenant":"tenant-123",
  "signals":["p95_latency","tokens_increase"],
  "region":"us-west-2",
  "snapshot_time":"2026-07-02T14:35:00Z"
}

B. Quick checklist for Customer Success when notified:
1. Confirm automated action applied and duration.
2. Validate customer critical flows (support request or synthetic) if requested.
3. Proactively schedule a short postmortem if customer observes visible impact.
4. Log follow-up items in customer QBR agenda.

C. Related runbooks and pages:
- Tenant synthetic suite onboarding guide (link in related_pages).
- SLO taxonomy and burn-rate thresholds (eng-sre).

Document maintenance

- Owner: SRE (primary) — review every 3 months or after any major automation incident.
- Reviewer cadence: CS/Runtime/Observability teams to review changes prior to publication.
- Change log: Record brief entries below with date and author.

payload.page_title: Tenant Configuration Drift Detection and Safe Rollback Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines the detection surface, alerting thresholds, triage rules, and safe automated rollback procedures for tenant configuration drift across Redwood Private and Dedicated deployments. It is intended for Customer Success engineers, SREs, and On‑Prem deployment engineers responsible for tenant stability during onboarding and post‑go‑live operations.

Goals and acceptance criteria

- Detect configuration drift that can materially affect inference correctness, throughput, or security (examples below) within 15 minutes of occurrence.
- Provide an automated, auditable safe-rollback path that returns the tenant to a verified last-known-good state within 60 minutes for P1/P2 incidents, with human-in-the-loop gating for production-critical changes.
- Ensure rollback preserves data integrity and produces clear post-action telemetry for QBR review.

Scope and definitions

- Configuration drift: any divergence between the expected, committed tenant config (control plane) and the live runtime state that affects routing, model selection, RBAC, volume mounts, or network policies. Examples: unexpected ingress rule changes, KV cache eviction policy flips, altered model pinning, quantization profile swap, unintended scaling min/max changes.
- Last-known-good (LKG): an immutable snapshot of tenant configuration and service checksums created after a successful canary and synthetic acceptance gate. Stored in the tenant-config-bucket (S3/GCS equivalent) with key format: tenant/<tenant-id>/lkg/<YYYYMMDDHHMM>.
- Drift severity levels:
  - S1 (Critical): RTT/throughput regressions causing customer-visible SLA breaches, or security-relevant changes (RBAC, egress firewall).
  - S2 (High): Model mismatch or quantization change causing output-quality regressions or token-cost spikes.
  - S3 (Medium): Non-critical tuning changes (batch sizes, non-critical autoscale tweaks).

Signals and telemetry sources
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- control-plane-config-checksum: periodic (5m) checksum comparison between tenant LKG and live config.
- ingress-route-ttl-mismatch: delta between expected ingress certificates/routes and live (1m sampling).
- runtime-model-manifest-diff: difference between model version pinned in control plane and model manifest reported by the runtime.
- kvcache-hit-rate-drop: > 40% drop vs baseline over 10m window.
- token-cost-surge: > 2x baseline 30m token spend without corresponding throughput growth.
- customer-reported-llm-regression: triaged from support channel with trace id.

Alerting and on‑call routing

- All S1 alerts -> Pager rotation: Customer Success SRE oncall -> eng-sre escalation if not acknowledged within 5m. Pager payload must include: tenant-id, signal, timestamp, LKG pointer, recent commit id, recommended rollback action.
- S2 alerts -> routed to Customer Success Queue and owner of the tenant’s onboarding cohort; escalate to Product ML for model regressions.
- S3 alerts -> routed to CSops runbook queue for scheduled reconciliation.

Automated detection pipelines (implementation notes)

1) Config checksum worker (k8s Job)
- Runs every 5 minutes per tenant.
- Compares canonical LKG YAML against /runtime/state/config via agent API.
- Emits config-drift-{tenant} metric with tags {drift_keys, delta_size}.

2) Behavioral delta detector (streaming job)
- Combines kvcache/latency/cost signals using a weighted anomaly model (weights maintained in infra config).
- Triggers a synthesized alert with a reason code (e.g., MODEL_PIN_MISMATCH) and recommended play: [inform, soft-rollback, hard-rollback].

3) Audit and snapshotter
- On any detected config change, immediately create a snapshot in tenant-config-bucket with a unique id and set lifecycle tags: {detected_by:checksum, severity}.

Triage matrix and decision flow (short)

1. Alert received with severity Sx.
2. Run automated triage script (cs-triage --tenant <id> --alert <id>) which returns: delta_scope (network/runtime/model), lkg_candidate (snapshot id), confidence_score.
3. If S1 or confidence_score > 0.85 AND delta_scope ∈ {network, model, rbac}: recommend automated rollback to LKG candidate with a safety hold of 5 minutes for human approval in production.
4. If S2 and confidence_score between 0.6–0.85: create a canary rollback in a single pod/replica and run synthetic tests for 3 minutes.
5. If S3 or confidence_score < 0.6: schedule non-urgent reconciliation and notify tenant steward.

Safe rollback mechanics

- Preconditions:
  - LKG snapshot exists and has passed synthetic acceptance (metadata flag: accepted=true).
  - No active maintenance window with rollback suppression flag.
  - Recent backups of critical tenant artifacts present within last 24h (verify via backup-manifest list).

- High-level rollback steps (automated path):
  1. Lock writes to tenant control-plane (control-plane:acquire-lock --tenant <id> --reason rollback).
  2. Create immutable incident record (incident-store create --tenant <id> --type rollback --ref <alert-id>).
  3. Apply LKG patch to runtime via agent (agent apply --tenant <id> --snapshot <lkg-id> --mode dry-run) and validate (agent validate --checks smoke,models,ingress).
  4. If validation passes, agent apply --mode live.
  5. Run post-rollback synthetic suite (synthetic-run --tenant <id> --tests smoke,latency,kvcache) for 10 minutes and collect telemetry.
  6. If post-suite passes and no new S1 signals registered for 15 minutes, release control-plane lock and close incident with notes.
  7. If failure in any step, escalate to SRE and preserve evidence bundle (logs, snapshots, traces).

- Commands (examples):
  - Check LKG list:
    aws s3 ls s3://tenant-config-bucket/tenant/1234/lkg/ --human-readable
  - Trigger dry-run apply:
    cs-agent apply --tenant 1234 --snapshot lkg-202602100730 --mode dry-run --output json
  - Promote snapshot to live:
    cs-agent apply --tenant 1234 --snapshot lkg-202602100730 --mode live --reason "auto-rollback:S1-drift"

Human-in-the-loop gating rules

- Production tenants with committed contract > $50k MRR: require explicit CS Director approval for any automated rollback that changes network/RBAC or causes a service restart of more than 2 minutes. This approval can be provided via the UI or via signed CLI token (one-time use).
- Staging/non-critical tenants: automated rollback can proceed after a 5-minute pause with on-call notification.

Safeguards and post-rollback governance

- Immutable incident record and snapshot IDs are attached to the tenant’s QBR artifacts.
- Every automated rollback triggers a post-incident RCA template to be populated by the owner within 3 business days.
- For model regressions that triggered rollback, record: model id, quantization profile, kernel/md5 checksums, and prompt-set failure rate. Attach to the model-onboarding queue for evaluation.

Testing and maintenance cadence

- Monthly: dry-run rollbacks for a randomly selected 3% of tenants in non-prod to ensure snapshot integrity.
- Quarterly: tabletop exercise between CS, SRE, and Runtime teams; verify LKG restore procedures under simulated production load.
- After any production rollback: follow-up 2-week monitoring window with elevated sampling of customer telemetry and weekly update to the account owner.

Runbook appendix (quick reference)

- Immediate play (S1):
  1. Acknowledge alert.
  2. Run cs-triage --tenant <id> --alert <id>.
  3. If recommended: cs-agent apply --tenant <id> --snapshot <lkg-id> --mode dry-run.
  4. Validate; then cs-agent apply --mode live.
  5. Post-rollback: synthetic-run and notify account owner.

- Canary rollback (S2):
  1. Create canary flag: cs-agent apply --tenant <id> --snapshot <lkg-id> --mode canary --replicas 1
  2. Run canary tests for 3–10 minutes.
  3. If pass, promote to live. If fail, revert canary and escalate.

- Evidence collection checklist:
  - incident id, alert id, timestamps
  - pre- and post-config checksums
  - agent logs (last 1h) and runtime metrics (last 24h)
  - snapshot id and verification results

Roles and responsibilities

- Customer Success (CS) Engineer: first responder for S1/S2, communicates status to customer, coordinates approvals for production gating.
- CSops: owns automation tooling, snapshot lifecycle, and audit records.
- Eng-SRE: escalation owner for failed automated rollbacks or unknown runtime anomalies.
- Product ML: consulted for model-output regressions and model pinning decisions.

Related artifacts and links

- tenant-config-bucket LKG policy: s3://tenant-config-bucket/README
- cs-triage CLI reference: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/cs-triage-cli.md
- Synthetic suite definition: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/health-and-qbr/synthetic-acceptance-gates-2025

Revision history

- 2026-02-10: Initial authoring by Aisha Rahman.
- 2026-03-05: Updated gating rules for high-value tenants and added canary timing guidance.

payload.page_title: QBR telemetry storyboard and action plan

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a repeatable "telemetry storyboard" and actionable runbook for Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with enterprise customers. The intent is to provide a concise narrative that links telemetry signals to customer outcomes, surface prioritized actions, and assign owners with deadlines. The storyboard helps Customer Success Managers (CSMs), Solutions Engineers (SEs), and Product leads present a coherent operational story to executive and engineering stakeholders.

Audience

- CSMs and SEs preparing QBRs for enterprise accounts
- Customer engineering and platform teams that consume telemetry
- Product and Engineering stakeholders responsible for post-QBR follow-up

Goals

1. Convert raw telemetry into a 5–7 minute operational narrative for executives.
2. Produce a prioritized action plan with owners, deadlines, and acceptance criteria.
3. Reduce time-to-resolution for top customer risks by 40% quarter-over-quarter.

Required data sources
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Ingress/egress request volume (per-tenant, per-route)
- Per-request latency percentiles (P50/P90/P99) by model and sequence length
- Token-level cost and token usage by model variant
- Error rates and error class distribution (4xx vs 5xx, model fallbacks)
- Model-quality regressions from evaluation harness (monthly prompt set scores)
- Cache hit ratio (prefix / KV cache) and cache utilization trends
- Capacity allocation and reservations for Dedicated tenants
- Recent incidents and customer-impacting config changes
sections.heading: Collect the following telemetry ahead of every QBR

sections.body:
| Data source | Owner | Required fields | Freshness | Retention | Query template |
|-------------|-------|-----------------|-----------|----------|----------------|
| Request logs | ingress-team | tenant_id, route, timestamp, latency_ms, model | 5m | 90d | SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id=... |
| Error stream | platform-observability | tenant_id, error_code, request_id, stack | 1m | 180d | SELECT count(*) ... |
| Cost ledger | billing | tenant_id, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd | 1d | 365d | SELECT SUM(cost_usd) ... |

Storyboard format

Use this short template to craft the QBR narrative. The final narrative should fit in a single slide or the first 5 minutes of the review.

1) Executive one-liner (30s):
- Current state in one sentence (health + trend + top ask). Example: "Tenant X had steady throughput in Q1 with a 12% P99 latency increase driven by larger context workloads; proposed action is to enable adaptive batching and a canary of the quantized v2 model."

2) One visual (60s):
- A single chart that ties user-visible latency or error spikes to a root cause signal (e.g., sudden increase in long-sequence requests, cache degradation, or a model rollout). Prefer overlays: request size distribution + P99 latency + cache-hit ratio.

3) Risk & impact (60s):
- Top 3 customer risks (e.g., sustained P99 > 2s on interactive routes, >10% traffic fallback to slower variants, monthly cost delta > 20% budget).
- For each risk: expected business impact and estimated cost/time to remediate.

4) Proposed actions (90s):
- Short-term (<= 2 weeks): tactical mitigations with owners and acceptance criteria.
- Medium-term (<= 3 months): config or model changes with canary plan.
- Long-term (>= 3 months): architecture or product requests (e.g., dedicated capacity increase, region expansion).

Pre-QBR checklist (to be completed 7 business days before meeting)

1. Validate data freshness from all required sources and confirm queries run without errors.
2. Create the single-chart visual and attach raw query results.
3. Run the evaluation harness on the customer prompt sample and note any regressions.
4. Confirm assigned owners and preliminary remediation estimates.
5. Send an executive summary (one-pager) to customer 3 business days before QBR.

During-QBR playbook (facilitator: CSM)

1. Opening (3 minutes): executive one-liner and agenda.
2. Data narrative (6–8 minutes): present the storyboard visual and explain causal links. Keep technical detail for the appendix.
3. Action negotiation (7–10 minutes): propose short- and medium-term actions, capture customer preferences and constraints.
4. Commitment & next steps (2–3 minutes): confirm owners, deadlines, and success criteria; schedule follow-up checkpoint within 2 weeks.

Action runbook (post-QBR)

Every action is tracked as a ticket in the customer success tracker (preferred backends: Jira project REDWOOD-CUST or internal tracker). For each action, fill in the ticket template below:

- Title: short description (e.g., "Enable adaptive batching for tenant X on route /chat")
- Owner: person/team
- Priority: P0/P1/P2
- Acceptance criteria: precise metric change and timeframe (e.g., "P99 latency reduction from 2.1s -> <=1.2s within 7 days")
- Test plan / Canary: route traffic fraction, monitoring queries, rollback trigger conditions
- ETA and dependency list

Action ticket example: priority P1, owner: infra-performance, acceptance criteria: 20% token cost reduction on inference-heavy routes measured over 72h, canary 5% of production traffic, automatic rollback if error rate > 0.5% above baseline.

Alert-to-action mapping (quick lookup)

- P99 latency spike & correlated increase in long-context requests -> Action: enable batching with max batch latency 40ms + increase KV cache TTL by 30% (Owner: serving-runtime).
- Sudden fallback to smaller model variant -> Action: investigate model-serving capacity and rollback recent deploys; if capacity constrained, route traffic to regional spare pool (Owner: infra-sre).
- Regressions in eval harness score (->3 points on customer prompt set) -> Action: open model-quality incident, pause canary rollout, and schedule rollback (Owner: applied-ml).

Example queries and dashboard snippets

- Example Prometheus/SQL pseudo query for P99 by route:
  SELECT route, percentile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p99_latency
  FROM request_logs
  WHERE tenant_id = 'TENANT_X' AND timestamp > now() - interval '7 days'
  GROUP BY route

- Cache hit ratio:
  SELECT SUM(cache_hits) / NULLIF(SUM(cache_hits + cache_misses),0) AS hit_ratio FROM kvcache_metrics WHERE tenant_id='TENANT_X' AND timestamp > now() - interval '14 days'

Post-QBR cadence and SLA for action closure

- Short-term actions (<=2 weeks): SLA = 14 calendar days from QBR date to implement or to produce a mitigation plan.
- Medium-term actions (<=3 months): Progressive checkpoints at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks.
- If any action exceeds SLA without customer-agreed extension, escalate to Customer Success Manager Director and Product PM.

Ownership and escalation path

- CSM: primary facilitator and owner of customer comms and ticket backlog.
- SE (solutions engineer): technical owner for on-calls to implement canaries and run tests.
- Infra/SRE: owner for capacity, routing, and network fixes.
- Applied ML/Product: owner for model-quality actions and rollbacks.
sections.heading: Data contract table (example)

sections.body:
1) Owner -> CSM
2) CSM -> SE Lead or Infra SRE on-call (if technical unblock needed)
3) CSM -> Customer Success Manager Director -> Product PM -> Head of Engineering (if cross-team commitments required)

Templates and attachments (appendix)

- Executive one-pager template (copy/paste):
  Title: QBR Executive Brief – Tenant X
  One-liner (30s): <fill>
  Visual: attach chart file
  Top 3 risks: list
  Top 3 actions: owner, ETA, acceptance criteria

- Ticket template (copy/paste):
  Summary: <short text>
  Description: <context + query links + raw results>
  Acceptance criteria: <quantified metric>
  Canary plan: <traffic % and rollback triggers>
  Attachments: <links to dashboard + raw CSVs>

Appendix: common pitfalls and mitigations

- Pitfall: Telemetry freshness mismatch. Mitigation: Run sanity queries and include raw CSVs in QBR packet; push a data contract alert to platform-observability.
- Pitfall: Overfitting to noisy P99 spikes. Mitigation: Require correlated signal (request size, cache drop, or deployment event) before actioning high-cost remediations.
- Pitfall: Customer acceptance criteria too vague. Mitigation: Convert criteria to measured SLO deltas and require a 72h verification window.

Related pages and templates

- Use the QBR operational checklist as the pre-QBR timeline: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/health-and-qbr/qbr-template-and-operational-checklist-2026
- For telemetry contract examples see: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/tenant-telemetry-contracts

Change history

- 2026-02-15: Created by Priya Menon.
- 2026-03-10: Clarified SLA table and added alert-to-action mapping (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Maya Chen).

Contact

For questions about the storyboard or to request a custom template for a specific customer, contact the Customer Success Enablement team at cs-enablement@redwood.ai.

payload.page_title: Kernel Priority Calibration Lab Notebook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This lab notebook documents a sequence of controlled experiments to calibrate kernel-level priorities and credit assignments in the Redwood serving runtime. The objective is to produce a repeatable mapping from request traffic characteristics to scheduler priority/weight settings that meet our latency SLOs while minimizing cost and token-level variance.

Purpose and scope
------------------
- Purpose: Establish a defensible, observable calibration process for kernel priority settings used by kernel-manager and scheduler-coordinator.
- Scope: Experiments span the dedicated GPU pool (gpool-rt-prod-sim), the local experiment cluster (lab-gpu-01..04), and the shadow-routing infrastructure used by the performance lab. This notebook does NOT change production configuration; it defines candidate settings for canary rollout.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
Over the last 18 months we've observed recurring p95 tail spikes for small interactive chat workloads when mixed with long-running batch generations. Investigation shows credit starvation and kernel handoff delays in the dispatcher + kernel pipeline. This calibration aims to:
1) Quantify how per-request weight, kernel quantum size, and preemption granularity affect latency distribution.
2) Generate recommended rule sets for the priority expression language used by kernel-manager.
3) Provide an audit trail and artifacts (traces, kernel-profiles, sample payloads) for sign-off prior to rollout.

Key concepts and definitions
---------------------------
- Kernel: GPU execution unit as exposed by kernel-agent (e.g., attn-kernel-v2).
- Priority weight: numeric weight applied by scheduler-coordinator when allocating slot quantum.
- Quantum: minimal GPU time-slice unit in microseconds (default 2000us in lab).
- Preemption point: safe boundary (KV cache alignment) where kernels can be interrupted.

Testbed and baseline configuration
----------------------------------
- Hardware: 4 x A100-80GB (lab-gpu-01..04), NVLink disabled for determinism in early runs.
- Software: runtime v3.14.2 (branch: experiment/kernel-calibration), kernel-agent v2.7.0, dispatch-service v1.22.
- Telemetry: traces via trace-proxy -> jaeger-lab, metrics to prometheus-lab, payload capture persisted to s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04.
- Baseline SLOs used in lab: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 120ms for short-chat profile; throughput target 400 reqs/s for medium packing.

Experiment matrix (summary)
---------------------------
| Run | Priority profile | Quantum (us) | Preempt? | Workload mix | Note |
|-----|------------------|--------------:|:--------:|---------------|------|
| A   | default (1,1,1)  | 2000         | no       | 80% short /20% long | baseline
| B   | favor-short (3,1,0.5) | 2000  | yes      | 80% short /20% long | test preemptive handoff
| C   | weight-linear (2,1,1) | 1000   | yes      | 50/50 mixed        | smaller quantum
| D   | conservative (1,1,0.25) | 4000 | no      | 20% short /80% long | test long-run impact
| E   | dynamic-adaptive* (see rule) | 2000 | yes | synthetic burst traces | adaptive weight function

(See "Experiment logs" below for raw outputs and links to traces.)

Calibration procedure (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
1. Prepare lab cluster: reboot lab-gpu nodes, disable NVLink, ensure kernel-agent v2.7.0 running.
2. Load baseline model: llama-compat-13b-int8 (tag: lab-2026-02) to isolate kernel behavior from model variance.
3. Deploy traffic generator (tg-runner) with recorded production short-chat and long-burst corpora. Command:

   ./tg-runner --target lab-gateway:8443 --corpus corpora/short-chat.json --rps 320 --duration 900 --tag run-A

4. Apply priority profile via kernel-manager CLI (example):

   rwd-kernelctl set-profile --profile-name favor-short --rules "priority(expression='request.shape == \"short\" ? 3 : 1', preempt=true, quantum_us=2000)"

5. Collect telemetry: Ensure sampling via experiment-telemetry job. Key artifacts:
   - jaeger traces: trace-id prefix "calib-2026-04-A"
   - prometheus metrics: histogram rwd_kernel_latency_{quantile}
   - captured payloads: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/run-A/

6. Run 1-hour trial, then a 6-hour steady-state for stability measurement.
7. Post-process: run analysis notebook /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb to compute p50/p95, fairness index, and variance.

Telemetry and measurement definitions
-----------------------------------
- Latency decomposition: request_total = frontend_queue + dispatch_delay + kernel_wait + kernel_exec + post_process. Each is traced and tagged.
- Fairness Index (FI): normalized Jain's index on per-cohort latency at p95 (goal >= 0.85).
- Kernel Utilization: GPU active seconds / wall-time (target 0.6-0.85 depending on workload).
- SLO thresholds: alert if burst p95 > 2x target or FI < 0.7.

Example priority rule table (recommended canonical format)
--------------------------------------------------------
| name | expression | weight | preempt | quantum_us | notes |
|------|------------|-------:|:-------:|-----------:|-------|
| favor-short | request.shape == "short" AND model.family == "llama-compat" | 3 | true | 2000 | Good for interactive agents
| default | true | 1 | true | 2000 | Fallback
| background-batch | request.type == "batch" | 0.5 | false | 4000 | Allow large runs but deprioritize

Sample kernel-manager JSON profile (apply via rwd-kernelctl)
-----------------------------------------------------------
{
  "profile_name": "favor-short",
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "short-interactive",
      "expr": "request.shape == \"short\" and request.max_tokens < 512",
      "weight": 3.0,
      "preempt": true,
      "quantum_us": 2000
    },
    {
      "id": "batch-low",
      "expr": "request.type == \"batch\"",
      "weight": 0.5,
      "preempt": false,
      "quantum_us": 4000
    }
  ]
}

(When saving this document into kernel-manager, remember to redact any sensitive model keys.)

Experiment logs (high level)
---------------------------
- Run A (2026-04-20): baseline run, observed p95=138ms (exceeded target). Notes: dispatcher queueing prominent. Trace set: calib-2026-04-A.*
- Run B (2026-04-22): favor-short, preemption enabled, p95=86ms, FI=0.82. Short requests improved; tails reduced but long jobs saw increased runtime by 6%.
- Run C (2026-05-03): smaller quantum (1000us) reduced tail by 12% but increased kernel dispatch overhead (extra context switches). Kernel exec variance up 8%.
- Run D (2026-05-18): conservative quantum for long jobs reduced throughput by 14% with negligible improvements to short p95.
- Run E (2026-09-07): dynamic-adaptive rule using recent-ten-second-load reduced peak p95 by 20% in burst scenarios; needs further stability testing.

Decision rules and acceptance criteria
------------------------------------
Use the following rule to accept a candidate profile into canary:
1. Candidate must achieve p95 <= 1.1 * lab SLO for three independent 6-hour runs under synthetic production-mix.
2. FI >= 0.8 across cohorts for the same runs.
3. GPU utilization not below baseline by more than 10% (to avoid wasteful idle capacity).
4. No increase in observed model inference errors (model failure rate <= baseline + 0.1%).

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)
----------------------------
- [ ] Create canary plan: targeted to dedicated pool canary-nodes (2 nodes).
- [ ] Prepare automatic rollback policy in control-plane: revert-to-profile=default if p95 > threshold for 15m.
- [ ] Create dashboard: /dashboards/kernel-calibration-canary with alert rules (p95, FI, top-kernel-waits).
- [ ] Run security review for config file storage (CI secrets redaction).
- [ ] Schedule 48h passive monitoring window with oncall coverage.

Troubleshooting checklist
-------------------------
- If p95 regresses after profile apply:
  1) Re-run short deterministic microbenchmarks (script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh).
  2) Collect full jaeger traces with full payload sampling for 30m.
  3) If kernel wait dominates >60% of tail, revert profile and open ticket on #sre-runtime.

Observed side-effects and mitigation notes
----------------------------------------
- Smaller quantum increases context-switch overhead. Mitigation: only use quantum <= 1000us for sub-100ms expected executions.
- Aggressive preemption can increase cache thrash for models with large KV caches; avoid preemption for models with >60M KV footprint.

Open experiments (next steps)
---------------------------
- Evaluate adaptive-weight learning that uses online p95 feedback loop with conservative damping.
- Test hardware-tiered profiles (fast-gpu vs econ-gpu) for cross-pool routing decisions.
- Validate interaction with quantization-profiles: int8 kernels show different preemption sensitivity.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Document owner: Maya Chen (serving-runtime / kernel-experiments).
- Primary contacts: Arjun Kapoor (scheduler), Lena Ortiz (telemetry), Diego Morales (SRE).
- Escalation: oncall-runtime -> #oncall-runtime -> PagerDuty escalation as per runbook.

Artifacts and storage locations
-----------------------------
- Traces: jaeger-lab (query tag calib-2026-04-*)
- Metrics: prometheus-lab (job=rwd-runtime-lab)
- Artifacts: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/
- Analysis notebooks: /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb (gitlab: infra/perf-lab)

Change log (notable entries)
---------------------------
- 2026-04-15 (Maya Chen): created notebook and executed Runs A-B.
- 2026-05-03 (Maya Chen): added Run C results and small-quantum guidance.
- 2026-09-07 (Maya Chen): added adaptive profile (Run E) summary and acceptance criteria.
- 2026-11-02 (Maya Chen): consolidated logs, added rollout checklist and decision rules for canary sign-off.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Apply JSON profile: rwd-kernelctl apply --file favor-short.json --target lab-kman-01
- Query p95 from prometheus-lab (example):
  curl -s "http://prom-lab:9090/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(rwd_kernel_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))" | jq

- Microbenchmark script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  for i in $(seq 1 100); do
    rwd-client --model llama-compat-13b-int8 --prompt "hello" --max-tokens 64 >/dev/null;
  done

Related reading
--------------
- Scheduler observability contract and simulated injector (see related pages).
- Telemetry feedback & kernel autotune playbook.

Notes on document conventions
----------------------------
- This notebook is intentionally structured as a lab-first artifact: preserves time-stamped experiment runs, raw artifact locations, and decision rationale.
- When moving candidate profiles into production, create a dedicated ADR referencing this notebook and link to the canonical profile artifacts in /infra/configs/kernel-profiles/ with immutable tags.

End of notebook.
