payload.page_title: QBR KPI inference-to-business-metrics mapping playbook

sections.body:
How to translate Redwood inference telemetry and model signals into customer business KPIs for QBRs. Includes a repeatable mapping matrix, telemetry queries, slide checklist, and escalation points to keep QBR conversations actionable.
Overview

This playbook describes a repeatable process for mapping low-level inference telemetry (latency, p50/p95/p99, token usage, model variant switches, error rates, and cost-per-1000-tokens) to customer-facing business KPIs (conversion, time-to-answer, cost per active user, SLA adherence). The goal is to produce concise, business-oriented QBR slides that clearly identify risks, opportunities, and recommended actions.

When to use

- Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with product/ops stakeholders.
- Post-cutover stabilization reviews (weeks 1–6).
- Any time a model rollout or pricing change materially affects customer costs or latency.

Audience

- Customer success leads (owner)
- Customer engineering / integration contacts
- Internal product and platform stakeholders

Roles and responsibilities

1. Customer Success (CS) owner: assemble data, narrative, and slides; own action items.
2. Observability engineer: provide verified telemetry queries and raw data extracts.
3. Solutions engineer: validate mapping assumptions with customer integration details.
4. Finance/RevOps (if cost material): validate cost-per-unit computations.

Mapping matrix (example)

Use this matrix to convert telemetry signals into one-line business impacts. Replace values with customer-specific thresholds during prep.

| Inference telemetry signal | Typical threshold | Business KPI impacted | One-line interpretation for customer |
|---------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------------------------|
| p95 latency (in ms) | > 1200 ms | Time-to-answer / conversion | Increased answer time — potential drop in conversions for interactive flows |
| Token churn per session | +20% vs baseline | Cost per active user | Higher token usage → higher monthly bill per seat |
| Model fallback rate (%) | > 3% | Feature availability / SLA | Frequent fallbacks to cheaper variant → degraded feature fidelity |
| Streaming disconnects per 10k sessions | > 5 | User experience (dropouts) | Session truncation risk; affects retention during long sessions |
| Error rate (5xx) | > 0.5% | SLA and incident risk | Elevated errors → SLA may be breached; remediation required |
| Embedding latency (p99) | > 300 ms | Search relevance and UX | Indexing/search slowdown → query throughput/latency regressions |

Step-by-step prep for the QBR (2-week cadence before meeting)

1. Week -2: CS owner requests telemetry dumps from observability team for the past 90 days and a delta window of last 14 days. Define baseline period (customer’s historical median).
2. Week -2: Solutions engineer confirms model variants and expected tokenization differences for known flows. Document any recent prompt or prompt-template changes.
3. Week -10 days: Observability engineer runs production queries (examples below) and validates sampling. Attach raw CSVs to the QBR folder.
4. Week -7 days: CS owner drafts 6-slide narrative: headline, current-state metrics (business KPI), top 3 technical signals, root cause hypotheses, proposed actions, and ask.
5. Week -4 days: Circulate draft to reviewers (product, finance, customer-eng).
6. Week -1 day: Finalize slides and run internal dry-run with internal stakeholders.

Queries and telemetry snippets (examples)

Note: adapt to your telemetry stack (Prometheus, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Datadog). Below are pseudocode/SQL patterns.

- P95 latency (per route):
  SELECT route, PERCENTILE(latency_ms, 95) as p95_latency, date
  FROM inference_latency
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>' AND date >= DATE_SUB(current_date, INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  GROUP BY route, date

- Token churn per session (session-level token delta):
  SELECT session_id, SUM(output_tokens + input_tokens) as tokens, date
  FROM token_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY session_id, date

- Model fallback rate:
  SELECT date, SUM(fallbacks)/SUM(requests) as fallback_rate
  FROM request_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY date

Sample business narratives (write these as slide headlines)

- Headline (Good): "Stable inference latency; conversion unchanged; opportunities to reduce token churn by 12% via prompt templates."
- Headline (Risk): "p95 latency increased 45% in last 14 days — predicted 2–4% drop in trial-to-conversion for interactive chat flows."
- Headline (Cost): "Token churn up 30% after model upgrade: estimated $12k/mo incremental spend; recommended stop-gap: roll back or enable aggressive prefix caching."

Slide checklist for QBR

- One-line executive summary (impact + ask)
- Top-level business KPI(s) with trend lines (90d and 14d)
- Top 3 technical signals mapped to KPIs (with thresholds annotated)
- Root-cause hypotheses with confidence levels and data references
- Action plan with owners, ETA, and expected KPI delta (e.g., reduce p95 by 200 ms → recover 1.5% conversions)
- Financial impact estimate (if > $5k / month)
- Risk and rollback criteria for any recommended changes

Post-QBR follow-up and measurement

1. Create a triage ticket in CS board with: summary, telemetry links, owners, and success criteria.
2. Tag the ticket with labels: qbr-action, telemetry, cost-impact.
3. Observability engineer adds a synthetic test to the customer’s synthetic suite to verify the remediation.
4. Re-check the mapped KPIs at 7 and 30 days; report back as a short one-slide update.

Escalation thresholds (customer-facing)

- Immediate (page): p95 latency > 2x target and > 2 seconds for core interactive route.
- High (email & Slack CC): fallback rate > 10% sustained for 1 hour and impacting top route.
- Medium (ticket + weekly sync): token cost delta > 25% month-over-month and projected spend > $5k.

Operational tips and guardrails

- Use model variant tags in telemetry to attribute cost/quality to each variant.
- Normalize token cost calculations by customer-specific pricing tiers and reserved commit adjustments.
- Avoid attributing conversion regressions to model performance unless you can show temporal alignment and user cohort parity.

Appendix: sample mapping CSV (columns to include)

- timestamp, route, model_variant, requests, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, errors_5xx, tokens_in, tokens_out, fallbacks, synthetic_check_pass, notes

Related resources and links

- QBR template and operational checklist (link to internal page)
- Telemetry cost attribution connector guide (link to internal page)

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: Customer Success (Nina Park) — review quarterly.
- Observability owner: Eng Platform (Arjun Mehta) — provide telemetry within 10 business days of request.

Change log

- 2026-02-12 — Draft and initial internal review.
- 2026-04-01 — Added fallback rate thresholds and sample SQL patterns.
- 2026-05-10 — Finalized slide checklist and added escalation thresholds.

payload.page_title: Automated QBRs and Tenant Synthetic Healthchecks Playbook

sections.body:
Runbook and implementation guide for automating quarterly business reviews (QBRs) with tenant-level synthetic healthchecks and escalation triggers. Covers probe design, onboarding checklist, alert thresholds, automated report generation, and customer communication templates.
Overview:
This playbook defines a production-ready approach to combine tenant-scoped synthetic healthchecks with automated QBR generation for enterprise customers. The goal is to surface service regressions early, quantify inference economics for customer stakeholders, and reduce manual effort for Customer Success (CS) and Support teams during QBR cadence or incident follow-ups.

Use cases:
- Ongoing tenant stability monitoring with SLA-aligned synthetic probes.
- Auto-generated QBR starter packs (latency/cost/quality metrics) for CS to curate.
- Early drift detection for model outputs and routing fallbacks.
- Customer-facing incident summaries synthesized from probe history.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Customer Success: owns QBR cadence, stakeholder invites, and narrative.
- Observability/Platform: maintains probe templates, probe scheduling service, and data exports.
- Support: triages alerts that cross severity thresholds and coordinates remediation.

High-level architecture:
1) Probe engine (service: telemetry-probes) runs tenant-scoped synthetic requests at configured frequencies.
2) Telemetry ingestion stores probe results in metrics DB (prometheus long-term + clickhouse for traces).
3) QBR generator (service: qbr-orchestrator) pulls aggregated metrics, runs evaluation suites (sample prompts/evals), and renders a QBR bundle (PDF + CSV + slide deck).
4) CS UI integration surfaces the latest QBR bundle in the account dashboard and creates a draft calendar invite.

Design principles for probes:
- Lightweight and deterministic: synthetic payloads should be small and reproducible across runs.
- Representative workload: each probe should map to a customer workload archetype (e.g., short-chat, long-context-generation, embedding-query).
- Isolated side-effects: probes must use a read-only instrumented model version or a dedicated probe model variant to avoid affecting production KV caches and billing.
- Per-tenant scoping: include tenant_id, routing tag, and pinned model version in probe metadata.

Probe catalog (recommended minimal set):
- latency-short: 100ms target P95, frequency: 1m, description: 16-token prompt generation.
- latency-long: 500ms target P95, frequency: 5m, description: 2048-token continuation sampling.
- embedding-query: frequency: 10m, description: 512-dim embedding for a canonical phrase.
- correctness-check: frequency: 30m, description: run eval on 10 curated prompts, compute pass-rate.
- kvcache-hit-rate: frequency: 5m, description: run prefix queries to estimate cache warmness.

Configuration table (example):
| probe_name | frequency | target_slo | sample_payload | model_variant | probe_account_role |
| latency-short | 1m | P95 < 120 ms | {"prompt": "Hello"} | pinned-v1 | probe-only-key |
| correctness-check | 30m | pass_rate >= 95% | 10-prompts.json | eval-pinned | probe-only-key |

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step):
1. CS Owner creates the tenant probe profile in the Onboarding Hub with: tenant_id, contact list, pinned_model, preferred-region, business-hours window.
2. Platform provisions a probe-only API key scoped to tenant probe profile (TTL: 365d, rotation: automated quarterly).
3. Platform maps the tenant profile to the probe execution schedule and deploys probes into the tenant's routing group.
4. Run a 48-hour smoke window: validate probes produce results, check for false positives, and confirm cost estimate.
5. CS reviews the initial auto-QBR draft produced after 48 hours and adjusts which metrics are surfaced to stakeholders.
6. Mark onboarding complete once stabilization (no critical alerts) for 7 days is met.

Alerting and escalation matrix:
- Severity P0 (Immediate action): any probe indicating total unavailability for > 5 minutes across multiple model variants or region failover.
  - Trigger: probe engine stops receiving responses (HTTP 5xx or timeouts) across >=3 consecutive probes.
  - Notification: PagerDuty P0 to oncall SRE + CS lead + account executive.
  - Customer comms: immediate incident banner and dedicated Slack/phone bridge.

- Severity P1 (High): probe correctness-check pass_rate drops >= 10 percentage points below baseline OR P95 latency exceeds SLO for 30 minutes.
  - Trigger: rolling 30-minute window breach.
  - Notification: Support oncall, CS Owner, Platform engineer assigned.
  - Customer comms: templated email within 60 minutes and QBR note.

- Severity P2 (Medium): intermittent latency spikes or embedding variance above threshold affecting < 5% of probes.
  - Trigger: sporadic single-probe anomalies.
  - Notification: Support ticket auto-created, CS Owner notified next business day if unresolved.

Alert thresholds (recommended):
- Availability: <= 99.9% -> Severity P0 if outage confirmed.
- Latency: tenant P95 > configured_slo * 1.25 -> Severity P1 after 30m sustained.
- Correctness: pass_rate drop >= 10% absolute or sliding window drop >= 3% per 24h -> Severity P1.

Automated QBR generation templates and fields:
- QBR bundle includes: executive summary, availability & latency trends, inference economics, embedding stability, probed eval pass rates, incident timeline (last quarter), recommended actions, and appendix (raw CSVs, probe configs).
- Example CLI to generate a one-off bundle on demand:
  - curl -X POST "https://internal-api.redwood.local/qbr/generate" -H "Authorization: Bearer PROBE_KEY" -d '{"tenant_id":"acct-123", "range":"90d", "include_evals": true}'
- Output: a zip with files: qbr-summary.pdf, metrics.csv, top-alerts.json, slide-deck.pptx.

Customer communication templates (short):
- Incident banner (templates/incident-banner.md):
  - Title: Service Degradation – [Short description]
  - Body: We are investigating increased latency affecting some requests for your account. Our engineers are working on a fix. We will post updates on this page and via your designated Slack channel.

- Post-incident summary (templates/post-incident-summary.md):
  - Title: Incident summary: [date] – [short title]
  - Sections: timeline, root cause, customer impact, mitigation steps taken, follow-up actions with ETA and owners.

False positives and calibration guidance:
- Initial two-week period: set probe sensitivity to conservative (wider thresholds) to avoid alert fatigue.
- Keep a rolling baseline window of 28 days for latency and correctness baselines.
- Label probes as diagnostic vs. business-critical; only business-critical probes trigger P1/P0 paths.

QBR cadence and automation schedule:
- Weekly: automated micro-report (1-page) emailed to CS Owner with rolling 7-day highlights.
- Monthly: draft QBR bundle auto-created and placed in CS draft folder for review.
- Quarterly: finalized QBR generated 7 days prior to customer meeting and attached to the calendar invite.

Sample metrics to include in QBR (minimum):
- Tenant availability (90d), error rate (4xx/5xx), P50/P95/P99 latency by route, per-token cost trends, embedding cosine drift, eval pass rates (trend), top 5 incidents with MTTR.

Operational playbook for escalations (numbered runbook):
1. Triage: Support receives alert -> create ticket with tags: tenant_id, probe_name, severity, link to recent probe traces.
2. Initial Diagnosis (15 min): Support verifies probe metadata and reproduces using probe-only-key. If reproduced, escalate to Platform engineer.
3. Mitigation (30-90 min): If mitigation is available (fallback to alternate model variant, restart worker pool, clear KV cache for that tenant), perform action and document steps.
4. Customer Communication (within 60 min for P1/P0): CS drafts and sends templated update; update incident banner.
5. Postmortem: For any P1/P0, create a postmortem within 72 hours and include probe history snippets and QBR implications.

Instrumentation and data retention:
- Probe raw payloads: retained 14 days.
- Aggregated metrics & rollups: retained 540 days for QBR trend analysis.
- Eval sample outputs (for correctness-check): stored in encrypted blob store with tenant access controls, retained 90 days by default.

Privacy and compliance notes:
- Probes must avoid sending any customer-sensitive real data. Use synthetic canonical text or pseudonymized samples.
- For regulated tenants requiring Private deployment, probes must run inside the tenant's VPC or with on-prem probe runner.

FAQ (short):
Q: Will synthetic probes increase my bill?
A: Probes are billed at a minimal rate and can be scoped to a probe-only billing key. We include an estimated monthly cost in the onboarding smoke window.

Q: Can a probe cause false cache warming?
A: Probes use probe-only model variants when possible. If probes must exercise the same model path as production, include metadata so KV cache metrics can be filtered out of customer billing.

Related pages and templates:
- Onboarding Hub -> Probe Profiles (internal link: /confluence/xxxxx)
- templates/post-incident-summary.md (internal templates repo)
- qbr-orchestrator README (github: internal/qbr-orchestrator)

Appendix: Example probe JSON (for latency-short)
{
  "probe_name": "latency-short",
  "tenant_id": "acct-123",
  "frequency": "60s",
  "payload": { "prompt": "Summarize: Redwood Inference" },
  "expected_p95": "120ms",
  "model_variant": "pinned-v1"
}

Contact points:
- Customer Success: cs-leads@redwood.ai
- Platform / Observability: observability@redwood.ai
- Support: support@redwood.ai

Document history:
- 2025-11-12: Created by Aisha Patel
- 2025-12-02: Added probe catalog and onboarding checklist (reviewers: Marco Rivera)
- 2026-02-18: Updated alerting thresholds and automation schedule after pilot (reviewers: Evelyn Chen, Samir Desai)

payload.page_title: Governed Inference QBR: Metrics & Evaluation Framework

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document describes a repeatable, governed framework for quarter‑by‑quarter customer QBRs focused on inference health, LLM evaluation, and operational signals. The goal is to give Customer Success (CS), Engineering, and Product a shared set of metrics, evaluation artifacts, dashboards, and playbooks so QBR conversations are evidence‑driven and actionable.

Audience
- Customer Success Managers (CSMs) and Customer Reliability Engineers (CREs)
- Product owners responsible for model and feature roadmaps
- Engineering owners for serving runtime and telemetry pipelines

Scope
- Hosted and Dedicated customers; guidance includes private deployment considerations where telemetry may be delayed or sampled.
- Metrics span cost, latency, availability, quality (evaluations), and request patterns that drive economics.

Key Outcomes for a QBR using this framework
1) Shared indicator set with one golden dashboard per customer.
2) Actionable health classifications (Green/Amber/Red) with recommended runbook steps.
3) A reproducible evaluation snapshot (prompt set, baseline model, scoring summary).

Governed Metric Set (minimum required)
| Metric | Purpose | Owner | Frequency | Threshold (Amber) | Threshold (Red) | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| P50 P95 token latency (inference) | Customer perceived responsiveness | infra-serving | daily | P95 > 350ms | P95 > 700ms | Break out by route/model variant |
| Request success rate (2xx/total) | Availability signal | sre | 10m | < 99.5% | < 98.0% | Include 5xx and 429 rates separately |
| Tokens per USD (cost efficiency) | Cost economics | finance/cs | weekly | 10% degradation vs baseline | 25% degradation | Compute per-route and model family |
| Eval pass rate (gold prompt suite) | Quality regression detector | cs/product | per-release | delta < 2% | delta > 5% | See Eval snapshot section below |
| Embedding similarity drift | Semantic regressions in retrieval | product | daily | cosine drop > 0.02 | cosine drop > 0.05 | Compare to rolling 30d baseline |
| Prefix cache hit rate | Cost/latency optimization | infra | hourly | < 60% | < 40% | Indicative of prompt variability |

Data sources and instrumentation
- Golden dashboards must be composed from: API access logs, model runtime metrics (GPU tail latencies, queue lengths), cost attribution (token-level billing), and evaluation harness outputs.
- For Private deployments: collect the same artifacts via the customer telemetry agent; if sampling is required, include sampling multiplier metadata in the dashboard.

Evaluation snapshot (what to store for each QBR)
- Baseline model name and exact version (e.g., redwood/gptx-rlhf@2026-01-20)
- Prompt set: canonical list of N=150 prompts representing high-impact flows (attach as CSV).
- Scoring rubric: automated metrics (exact match/F1, BLEU for structured data, embedding cosine for semantic retrieval) and human annotations for top 10 failure cases.
- Eval summary: pass rate, false negative rate, top 5 failure prompts with short transcripts.

Example evaluation artifact (CSV header)
prompt_id,prompt_text,expected_label,model_version,automated_score,human_flag,notes

Dashboard templates and sections (minimum panes)
1) Executive summary: SLO status, cost delta, top 3 risks.
2) Latency & availability: heatmaps by region/model, P50/P95/P99.
3) Cost breakdown: tokens, embeddings, per-route unit economics.
4) Quality & evals: pass rate trend, per-prompt failure list.
5) Usage patterns: spikes, client SDK versions, burst sources.
6) Action items & owners.

Suggested SQL/BigQuery examples
- 7‑day P95 token latency per model\
```
SELECT model_name, APPROX_QUANTILES(token_latency_ms, 100)[OFFSET(95)] AS p95_latency_ms
FROM `redwood_prod.api_logs`
WHERE event_time BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
GROUP BY model_name;
```

- Eval pass rate per release tag\
```
SELECT release_tag, COUNTIF(pass) / COUNT(1) AS pass_rate
FROM `redwood_prod.evals.results`
WHERE eval_suite = 'qbr-golden-150' AND event_date BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
GROUP BY release_tag
ORDER BY event_date DESC;
```

Health classification and recommended QBR actions
- Green: All core SLOs met. Action: continue trend monitoring; highlight positive optimizations.
- Amber: One or more SLOs breached at Amber. Action: open a short remediation ticket and schedule a 72‑hour stabilization plan (see Remediation Runbook).
- Red: Critical SLO or quality regression. Action: immediate incident coordination with CS, SRE, and Product; consider temporary model rollback or rate limiting.

Remediation Runbook (72‑hour stabilization)
1) Triage (within 1 hour): Confirm metric source; capture log window and sampling. Owner: CRE.
2) Containment (within 4 hours): If quality regression, pin production traffic to previous model version or enable fallback routing. If latency/capacity, enable burst capacity or autoscale policy. Owner: infra-serving oncall.
3) Mitigation (24 hours): Apply prompt-level mitigations (truncate inputs, enforce early-cache keys), adjust batching policy, or temporarily increase compute commit. Owner: engineering and CS.
4) Recovery verification (48–72 hours): Re-run golden evals, monitor pass rate and latency trend, and validate cost impact. Owner: CS + infra.
5) Post‑mortem and QBR action item creation.

Ownership and cadence
- CSM (primary): prepares customer narrative, highlights business impact, and tracks action items.
- CRE (telemetry & triage): provides data pulls, golden dashboard, and supports oncall during the quarter.
- Product (quality owner): curates the prompt suite and reviews eval rubric.
- SRE/Infra: provides availability/latency context and executes runtime mitigations.

QBR Preparation checklist (2 weeks before meeting)
1) Verify data completeness for the quarter (CSM + CRE). 2) Run the golden eval suite and attach results to QBR deck. 3) Confirm proposed action items and owners. 4) Smoke test the dashboard links and include reproducible queries. 5) Share pre-read with customer 3 business days before QBR.

Example action triggers (automated)
- Auto-create ticket when eval pass rate drops by >3% vs rolling 14d baseline.
- Create cost alert when tokens per USD drop by >15% month-over-month on a customer route.
- Auto-assign CRE when prefix cache hit rate < 40% for >6 hours.

Appendix: Template subject lines and pre-reads
- Email subject: "[QBR] Inference Health & Action Items — Q1 2026 — <Customer Name>"
- Pre-read attachment list: golden_eval_summary.csv, dashboard_links.md, cost_snapshot.pdf, proposed_actions.xlsx

Related standards and links
- See: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/instrumentation-standards
- See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes/model-versioning-policy

Contact and escalation
- Primary CS contact: <assigned CSM>
- CRE oncall rota: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations
- Emergency escalation: follow enterprise escalation playbook (link in related_pages).

Revision history
- 2025-11-03: Initial draft (Aisha Khan)
- 2026-01-12: Added automated triggers and SQL examples (Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-02-08: Finalized remediation runbook and private deployment notes (Priya Nair)

payload.page_title: Onboarding Stability Sprint: Post-Go-Live Retro & Repair Sprint

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the "Onboarding Stability Sprint": a focused 7–10 day cross-functional activity that runs immediately after an enterprise customer’s first live traffic cutover. The goal is to close early reliability gaps, stabilize cost/latency profiles, and deliver a structured retro that feeds QBR metrics and long-term remediation tickets.

Why this exists
----------------
Many go-lives appear successful on day-0 but surface repeated, low-severity reliability and cost issues over weeks (burst throttles, KV cache misses, cold-starts for rare routes). The Stability Sprint is a bounded, repeatable process to:
- Reduce mean time to remediation for non-critical but high-frequency issues
- Align engineering, SRE, product, and customer success on priority fixes
- Produce measurable outcomes for the customer’s first QBR and SLA review

Audience
--------
- Customer Success (primary owner)
- SRE and Runtime Engineering (operational remediation)
- Integrations and Solutions Engineering
- Product Manager for the customer
- Customer engineering contacts (participation as required)

Scope and success criteria
-------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Stability: Reduce 95th/99th latency and error spikes for tenant routes observed in the first 72 hours
2) Cost alignment: Identify top 3 per-token cost drivers and produce short-term mitigations (batching changes, latency/cost routing)
3) Observability gaps: Add or refine telemetry assertions used for QBRs
4) Process: Triage and convert urgent fixes into tracked engineering work with owners and ETA
sections.heading: Inbound scope (what we cover during the sprint)

sections.body:
- Pass: 3 of the 4 inbound scope goals completed and customer signs off on readiness for QBR metrics collection
- Partial: 1–2 goals completed with clear remediation plan and committed ship dates
- Fail: fewer than 1 goal completed and no committed remediation plan

Sprint cadence and timeline (example 7-day sprint)
-------------------------------------------------
Day 0 (cutover evening)
- Customer Success runs the cutover acceptance checklist and starts the sprint document
- SRE enables increased short-term telemetry retention for the tenant (72h high-fidelity window)

Day 1: Triage & quick wins
- Morning: 60–90 minute cross-functional triage meeting (see Meeting agenda below)
- Identify top 5 signals (errors, 99p latency routes, token-cost anomalies) and assign owners
- Implement 1–2 quick fixes (e.g., route pinning, temporary rate caps, client-side batching guidance)

Day 2–4: Focused repair work
- Parallel squads work queued tickets: instrumentation gaps, caching adjustments, configuration tuning
- Daily 30-minute sync for blockers and status updates

Day 5: Validation and hardening
- Run synthetic journeys (customer-specific) against fixed routes for 24–48h validation window
- Confirm telemetry assertions and cost telemetry alignment

Day 6–7: Retro and QBR prep
- Draft the sprint retro artifacts, remediation backlog, ownership matrix, and QBR-ready dashboard snapshots
- Customer Success coordinates a 60-minute stakeholder retro and produces a 1-page QBR summary

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Customer Success (CS): sprint owner; coordinates meetings, customer comms, and sign-off
- SRE Lead: owns incident-style triage and operational changes (routing, SLAs, infra tweaks)
- Runtime Eng: implements kernel/runtime/quantization configuration changes that affect latency/cost
- Integrations/SE: assists with client-side SDK guidance and validates contract changes
- Product: prioritizes cross-cutting product changes into roadmap if necessary

Triage meeting agenda (60–90 minutes)
------------------------------------
1) Quick status & customer impact summary (CS) — 5m
2) Top signals review (observability owner) — 10m
3) Action items and owners for quick fixes — 20m
4) Risk heatmap and decide if escalation to priority path required — 10m
5) Communication plan for customer (who says what and when) — 10m
6) Schedule re-checks and define success criteria — remaining time

Telemetry and synthetic checks (examples)
--------------------------------------
sections.heading: Success criteria (pass/fail)

sections.body:
- 99th latency per route (ms)
- Error rate by tenant and route (5m/1h windows)
- KV cache miss ratio and effective hit amplification
- Per-request token cost variance (7d baseline comparison)
- Streaming connection resets & gRPC idle stream resets

Example telemetry assertion (JSON snippet used by the synthetic runner):
{
  "assertion_name": "tenant-99p-latency-under-400ms",
  "metric": "route.latency.99p",
  "tenant_id": "TENANT-1234",
  "threshold_ms": "400",
  "window_mins": "60"
}

Observability checklist (table)
------------------------------
| Item | Owner | Minimum requirement | Why it matters |
|------|-------|---------------------|----------------|
| 99p latency per-route | SRE | 5m resolution | Detect tail latency spikes |
| Token cost breakdown | Finance/CS | per-route / per-model | Surface cost drivers |
| KV cache hit rate | Runtime Eng | 1m resolution | Affects downstream latency & cost |
| Streaming resets | Integrations | 5m resolution | Client compatibility and stability |

Quick remediation patterns (common fixes)
-----------------------------------------
- Route-level pinning to a stable model variant for 24–72 hours
- Apply temporary soft rate-limits to bursty tenant endpoints (CS+SRE approved)
- Enable aggressive prefix caching for high-reuse prompt families
- Adjust batching window for low-latency interactive routes to reduce token churn
- Short-term increase in dedicated capacity (if contract allows) for traffic hot-paths

Escalation ladder for issues discovered during the sprint
------------------------------------------------------
1) Sprint triage owners (first responders) — 30m SLA for acknowledgement
2) SRE lead + Runtime Eng — 2h SLA to propose temporary mitigations
3) On-call manager / Eng Director — 4h SLA to approve emergency capacity or cross-region failover
4) Exec stakeholder & customer leadership — notify if >8h unresolved customer-impacting degradation

Communication templates (customer-facing)
----------------------------------------
Subject: Post-go-live stability sprint: initial findings
Hi <Customer Name> team,

Thank you again for your cutover last night. We’ve initiated a 7-day stability sprint to ensure the experience meets your SLAs. Initial observations: increased 99p latency on conversational route ‘chat/v1-consumer’, and an elevated token cost variance on the re-ranking route. We will: (1) pin the route to a stable model variant within 2 hours, (2) deploy a temporary rate cap on low-impact endpoints, and (3) share a daily 09:30 PST update for the next 72 hours.

If you prefer a different cadence or immediate technical deep-dive, please let us know.

Best,
Customer Success (Aisha Patel)

Retro template (to capture outcomes)
----------------------------------
- What went well (bullet list)
- What surprised us
- Highest impact fixes delivered (with ticket IDs)
- Outstanding risks and owners
- Recommended product/roadmap changes
- QBR metrics to include for next meeting

QBR integration and artifacts to produce
-------------------------------------
- 1-page sprint summary with: top-5 signals, fixes delivered, outstanding items, and customer sign-off
- QBR dashboard snapshot with: 99p latency trend, per-route cost, error-rate trend, synthetic journey pass-rate
- Remediation backlog grouped by priority and owner with ETA

Post-sprint handoff checklist
----------------------------
1) Ensure all temporary mitigations have explicit TTLs and owners (no open temporary configs)
2) Create corresponding tickets in the product/engineering backlog with linked JIRA IDs
3) Schedule follow-up check at 30 and 90 days post-cutover to validate long-term stability
4) Attach synthetic run artifacts and telemetry snapshots to the account record

Runbook snippets and commands
----------------------------
Example: temporarily pin a route to a model variant via the admin CLI:

bash
redwoodctl route update --tenant TENANT-1234 --route chat/v1-consumer --pin model:openlite-v2-quant --ttl 72h

Example: query 99p latency via metrics CLI (Prometheus-compatible):

bash
redwoodctl metrics query "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(route_request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"TENANT-1234\"}[5m])) by (le, route))"

Appendix: typical remediation effort sizing
------------------------------------------
- Quick fixes: 1–4 engineer-hours (routing, config changes)
- Instrumentation gaps: 1–3 engineer-days (add metrics/assertions)
- Runtime changes requiring deploys: 3–10 engineer-days (may span releases)
- Product/roadmap work: tracked as epics (multi-sprint)

Appendix: decision log (example entries)
--------------------------------------
- 2026-11-05: Sprint framework ratified by CS and SRE leadership — A. Patel
- 2026-12-10: Added per-route cost telemetry requirement — M. Chen
- 2027-02-12: Expanded communication templates and telemetry assertions (Ravi Kumar)

Related documents and where to store artifacts
--------------------------------------------
- Store sprint artifacts (telemetry snapshots, synthetic runs) in the customer record folder: s3://redwood-enterprise-artifacts/<tenant-id>/stability-sprints/<date>/
- Link JIRA epics to the customer account in the CRM and include sprint summary PDF.

Notes and caveats
-----------------
- The Stability Sprint is not a replacement for emergency incident response. If a P0 occurs, follow the standard incident process and pause the sprint cadence in favor of incident postmortem flows.
- Customer opt-in: this sprint is part of our enterprise onboarding offering and should be presented as recommended but may be opted out by customers under special circumstances.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-11-05: Created (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-12-10: Added cost telemetry requirements (Michael Chen)
- 2027-02-12: Expanded communication templates and telemetry assertions (Ravi Kumar)

payload.page_title: Enterprise cost anomaly detection and action playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines detection, triage, and remediation steps for enterprise billing and inference-cost anomalies observed against Redwood-hosted or Dedicated/Private deployments. It is intended for Customer Success (CS), Support Engineers (L2/L3), and the Cost Ops oncall. Use this document when automated alerts or customer reports indicate unexpected token spend, embedding usage spikes, or model-switch-related cost regressions.

Goals
- Detect large-cost deviations early (target: detect >20% day-over-day spend delta within 60 minutes).
- Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for cost anomalies to < 4 hours for Class A incidents.
- Preserve customer trust with clear comms and remediation options (credits, rate-limits, rollbacks).

Scope
- Applies to Hosted API calls, Dedicated capacity customers, and Redwood Private control plane billing events.
- Does NOT cover non-inference billing (e.g., storage-only charges) — see Finance billing runbook.

When to use this playbook
- Alert conditions met from the Cost Anomaly detector (see "Detection sources" below).
- Customer reports a cost spike or unexpected raft of usage in support ticket or QBR review.
- Rollout of a new model/quantization profile resulting in large unit-cost changes.

Detection sources (inputs)
1) Cost Anomaly Detector (CAD) — primary signal
   - Triggers when a 1-hour spend exceeds 3x the 7-day moving average OR a 24h spend delta > 50% vs prior 7-day average.
   - Enrichment: customer_id, project_id, model_variant, region, pipeline_id, request_bucket (chat/generation/embeddings).
2) Token-level telemetry from Ingest Pipeline
   - High tokens-per-request rate or sudden increase in long-context tokens (>5k tokens) causes per-token unit cost blowups.
3) SDK / Integration Alerts
   - Client-side exponential retries or misconfigured batching can flood endpoints; detected via >200 TPS sustained for 5 minutes above normal.
4) Manual customer report or finance billing anomaly

Alert thresholds and classification
- Class A (Critical): Customer spend projection >$10k over expected next 24h OR sustained x10 spike in per-minute spend.
- Class B (Major): 200%–1000% hourly spike OR unexplained 3–10x token-rate increase.
- Class C (Minor): <200% hour spike or localized to a single non-critical project.

Immediate actions (first 60 minutes)
1) Acknowledge and owner assignment
   - CS owner creates/update ticket, tags #cost-ops, assigns L2 engineer.
   - Communicate ETA to customer: initial update in 30 minutes, hourly thereafter.
2) Triage checklist (parallel):
   - Verify CAD alert details and enrichment fields.
   - Pull billing projection run for affected customer_id (Finance dashboard: /dash/billing/customer/{customer_id}).
   - Query request telemetry for last 2 hours: model_variant, route, client_ip, sdk_version, request_size distribution.

Runbook: triage and remediation steps (detailed)
1) Validate scope and confirm impact
   - Execute sample query (SQL-like) in Telemetry Explorer:

      SELECT timestamp, model_variant, route, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate
      FROM inference_requests
      WHERE customer_id = 'CUST_12345'
      AND timestamp >= now() - interval '2 hours'
      ORDER BY timestamp DESC

   - Identify top 5 request signatures by cost_estimate.
2) Identify root cause vectors (check each):
   - Model change: recent rollout, canary -> check rollout timeline and revisions in Rollouts console.
   - Prompt explosion: repeated retries or user prompts that append context in loop.
   - Integration bug: SDK infinite loop or retry storm. Check client sdk_version and recent deploys.
   - Config mismatch: batch_size or max_tokens configured incorrectly for embedding pipelines.
   - Billing/config mismatch for Dedicated/Private: check reserved capacity vs burst mapping.
3) Immediate mitigations (choose minimal customer-impact step first):
   - Apply per-route temporary rate limit (example CLI):

      redwoodctl routes set-rate-limit --customer CUST_12345 --route "/v1/generate" --rps 10 --duration 2h

   - Enable auto-throttle on offending model (console toggle) to cap tokens per request at 2,048.
   - For Critical incidents, perform on-path fallback to a lower-cost variant (same quality tier):

      redwoodctl rollout promote --customer CUST_12345 --from modelX-v3 --to modelX-v2 --immediate

   - If a dedicated customer is misrouting to hosted endpoints, update routing policy and notify infra.
4) Cost protection and credits
   - For confirmed platform side issues, CS to propose a temporary credit (finance approval required for >$5k). Use credit template: /templates/credits/cost-protection.

Escalation matrix and ownership
- L2 Support: initial triage, run Telemetry Explorer queries, implement temporary rate-limits (Primary owner).
- CS Manager: customer comms and approval for service-level mitigations.
- Cost Ops (oncall): model-switch suggestions, immediate rollback authority for Hosted.
- SRE / Infra: network or Dedicated routing and capacity issues.
- Finance: approve credits >$5k or contractual adjustments.

Escalation steps by severity
- Class A: escalate to Cost Ops and SRE within 30 minutes. Daily executive summary to be prepared for customers with >$50k impact.
- Class B: escalate to Cost Ops within 2 hours. CS manager to own customer comms.
- Class C: L2 to resolve; document findings in ticket.

Communication templates
- Initial ack (30 min):
  "Thanks for flagging this — we've opened ticket #TKT-XXXXX and an engineer is investigating. We'll follow up within 60 minutes with initial findings and next steps."
- Follow-up (after triage): include root-cause summary, mitigations applied, expected impact, and next milestone.
- Post-incident summary: structured RCA, cost impact table, and recommended prevention actions for QBR.

Prevention controls and long-term fixes
- Alert tuning: reduce CAD false positives by refining model-variant baselines and segmenting quotas by route type.
- SDK safe-guards: ship SDK 2.1.0+ with client-side batching guardrails and exponential-backoff caps.
- Template rate-limits: recommend conservative default per-route rate-limits for new customers (10 rps per route per project).
- Automated rollback policies: enable canary auto-rollback when unit-cost increases >200% after rollout.

QBR and reporting guidance
- Metrics to include in QBR slides:
  - 7-day and 30-day cost trend, normalized by monthly active routes.
  - Number of cost anomalies, MTTR, and total cost delta recovered.
  - Top 3 root causes observed and prevention status.
- Recommended cadence: include a Cost Risk slide in monthly QBR for all customers with >$10k monthly spend.

Operational dashboards and canned queries (Appendix)
- Dashboard names/locations:
  - Cost Anomaly Center: /dash/ops/cost-anomalies (primary)
  - Customer Billing Snapshot: /dash/billing/customer/{customer_id}
  - Token Distribution Explorer: /dash/telemetry/token-dist

- Example time-series alert (PromQL-like pseudo):
  - cost_rate_by_customer[1h] > 3 * avg_over_time(cost_rate_by_customer[7d])

Post-incident actions (within 72 hours)
1) Root Cause Analysis (RCA) doc: owner = L2 engineer. Include timeline, query outputs, config diffs, and mitigation rationale.
2) Permanent remediation: schedule engineering ticket for SDK fix, rate-limit defaults, or rollout policy change.
3) Customer-facing summary and credit reconciliation (if applicable).
4) Update detection rules and dashboards to reduce recurrence.

Appendix: example SLAs and thresholds
| Metric | Warning threshold | Critical threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Hourly spend vs 7-day MA | > 50% | > 300% | Cost Anomaly detector / Cost Ops |
| Sustained TPS (5m) vs baseline | > 2x | > 10x | Telemetry / SRE |
| Token size per request | > 2,048 tokens | > 10,000 tokens | Runtime / Serving team |

Appendix: quick-reference CLI snippets
- Temporarily limit route:
  redwoodctl routes set-rate-limit --customer CUST_12345 --route "/v1/embed" --rps 20 --duration 4h
- Promote rollback:
  redwoodctl rollout rollback --customer CUST_12345 --model modelY --to-revision modelY-v12

Related resources
- Cost Anomaly detector design doc: /confluence/eng-platform/roadmap/cost-anomaly-detector-2025
- Billing and credits policy: /confluence/finance-and-legal/billing/credits-policy-2024
- SDK batching guidance: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides/safe-batching-v2

Ownership and contacts
- CS owner (playbook custodian): Maya Alvarez (maya@redwood.example.com)
- Cost Ops oncall: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-schedule
- Finance approver: Angela Boyd (angela@redwood.example.com)

Change log
- 2026-01-10: Created (M. Alvarez)
- 2026-02-15: Added CLI snippets and clarified credit thresholds (E. Cole)

End of document

payload.page_title: Customer Onboarding: SLO–Contract Mapping and QBR Calibration

sections.body: This playbook defines a repeatable process for translating enterprise contract commitments (SLA / SLO clauses) into operational SLOs, telemetry contracts, alert thresholds, and the Quarterly Business Review (QBR) calibration agenda. It is intended for Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, and EngOps stakeholders responsible for onboarding enterprise customers with Dedicated or Private deployments.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Ensure every contractual SLA/SLO has an unambiguous operational mapping to metrics and alerts.
- Produce a calibrated QBR agenda that highlights contractual compliance, trends, and actionable remediation steps.
- Reduce post-go-live churn caused by misaligned expectations between contract language and telemetry.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Scope: Redwood-hosted Dedicated and Private deployments; multi-tenant customers with contractual SLOs; QBRs for customers > $100k ARR.
- Audience: CSMs, SEs, EngOps, SRE liaison, customer technical leads.
sections.heading: Scope and Audience

sections.body:
1) Signed Service Agreement with SLO/SLA clauses and penalties.
2) Customer onboarded to telemetry forwarding (metrics + traces + logs) or Redwood-managed telemetry ingestion setup.
3) Assigned Redwood owners: CSM, SE, EngOps engineer, and Onsite/Customer success contact.
sections.heading: Prerequisites (Before using this playbook)

sections.body:
- SLA: Legal commitment in contract (uptime, response time guarantees).
- SLO: Operational objective measured by telemetry (e.g., p99 inference latency <= X ms).
- Error budget: Allowable window for SLO misses over evaluation period.
- Telemetry contract: The list of metrics, tags/labels, traces, and logs the customer and Redwood agree to exchange and retain.

1) One-page mapping template (mandatory)
Populate the following table and attach to the customer onboarding packet. Use concrete metric names and queries.

| Contract clause (verbatim) | Operational SLO (human) | Metric name | Aggregation/window | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| "API availability 99.95% monthly" | API availability >= 99.95% per calendar month | system.uptime.redwood-api | availability/month | < 99.95% -> P2 oncall + notify CSM | EngOps (api-team) |
| "Median latency under 120ms" | request.latency.p50 <= 120ms (rolling 7d) | request.latency.p50.redwood-api | p50/7d rolling | > 120ms for 30m -> P2 | Runtime Observability |
| "99th percentile inference latency < 2s" | inference.p99 < 2000ms (1h) | model.inference.latency.p99 | p99/1h | > 2000ms for 15m -> P1 | Serving Runtime |

Notes on the template: enter exact MQL/PromQL/SQL snippets in the Metric name field if available and store them in the customer telemetry folder.

2) Telemetry contract checklist (must be executed during provisioning)
- Metrics: availability, request.latencies (p50/p90/p95/p99), error rates, kvcache.hit_ratio, batch.size distribution, concurrency per tenant, token_count_per_request.
- Traces: end-to-end request traces spanning API gateway -> routing -> model runtime, with a correlation id (trace.customer_request_id).
- Logs: structured error logs with error.code, error.stage. Include sampling policy for debug-level logs for high-volume customers.
- Retention: default 90 days for metrics, 365 days for aggregations (QBR-ready), 30 days for full raw traces. Any deviation must be explicitly approved and added to the contract appendix.

3) QBR calibration agenda (recommended 60–75 minutes)
1. Executive summary (5m): usage, ARR impact, top 3 wins/risks.
2. SLO compliance snapshot (10m): last 90 days, error budget burn, recent misses. Attach the one-page SLO mapping.
3. Inference economics (10m): tokens/day, avg cost per 1k tokens, trends vs previous QBR, recommendation for batching/quantization if cost drift > 12%.
4. Reliability and incidents (10m): top incidents, actions completed, remaining mitigations.
5. Capacity and scaling plan (10m): autoscale behavior, reserved capacity headroom, burst strategy.
6. Roadmap alignment (10m): product features that affect customer (e.g., new caching, kernel upgrades), expected impact and rollback plan.
7. Action items and owner sign-off (10m): explicit owners and due dates.

Deliverables for the QBR: updated SLO table (signed off by customer and EngOps), runbook excerpts for any outstanding mitigations, and a 3-point action plan with owners and ETA.

4) Alert and incident escalation mapping (short matrix)
Use this matrix to set alert severity and who is paged. Insert these rows into the customer-specific alerting policy in PagerDuty/Opsgenie.

| Symptom | Metric/Query example | Severity | Page | Escalation path | Customer notification tier |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| High 99th inference latency | model.inference.latency.p99 > 2000ms (15m) | P1 | Serving-runtime oncall | 15m -> SRE lead -> Eng RTE | Notify CSM (1h) if sustained 30m |
| API availability drop | availability < 99.95% (1h) | P2 | EngOps oncall | 30m -> infra lead | Notify CSM (1h) and AE |
| Elevated error rate | request.errors.rate > 0.5% (rolling 10m) | P2 | Runtime Observability | 30m -> SE triage | Initial email to customer technical contact |

5) Example telemetry queries and alert rules (copy-paste)
- PromQL:
  - request.latency.p99: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, job))
  - availability: 100 * sum(up{service=\"redwood-api\"}) / count(up{service=\"redwood-api\"})
- Example alert (pseudo-YAML):
  - alert: HighInferenceP99
    expr: model_inference_latency_p99{tenant_id=\"{{tenant}}\"} > 2.0
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: P1
    annotations:
      summary: \"{{tenant}}: inference p99 > 2s\"

6) Contractual reporting appendix (what to include in monthly/quarterly compliance reports)
- Monthly uptime statement (ISO-8601 month window) with calculation method.
- SLO evaluation windows and raw data snapshots (CSV of time buckets for the quarter).
- Incident summaries mapped to SLO impacts (time lost, segments affected).
- Any compensations/credits calculation with detailed math and applied time windows.

7) Calibration and dispute process (step-by-step)
1. Detection: Customer or Redwood flags an SLO miss in QBR or via support channel.
2. Evidence collection (3 business days): EngOps exports raw telemetry, traces, and logs for the evaluation window. Owner: EngOps.
3. Analysis (5 business days): Runtime and SE analyze root cause and propose whether the miss is operational (Redwood responsibility) or customer-caused (network, tenant misuse).
4. Reconciliation (2 business days): Finance and Legal calculate credits if applicable.
5. Remediation and closure (ongoing): Implement runbook fixes, monitoring changes, and calendar follow-up in next QBR.

8) Runbook excerpts (examples to add to customer runbook)
- Safe degrade: automatically route to lower-capacity model variant when p99 > 2s for 10m (fallback policy ID: fallback-model-2025).
- Emergency quiesce: reduce non-essential batch jobs and dev-tier traffic during major capacity incidents.
- KV cache warmup: after model rollout, run cache-warmup script for top N prefixes (script path: /opt/ops/cache-warmup.sh).

9) Ownership and sign-off checklist (onboarding gate)
- CSM: Confirm SLO mapping table reviewed with customer.
- SE: Validate telemetry queries and access.
- EngOps: Configure alerts and retention settings.
- SRE liaison: Approve escalation matrix and on-call routing.
- Customer: Sign-off on one-page SLO mapping and QBR cadence.

10) Templates and attachments (references)
- One-page SLO mapping template (CSV).
- QBR slide template (PPTX).
- Example PromQL/SQL snippets (TEXT).
- Sample incident-to-SLO impact worksheet (XLSX).

payload.page_title: Post-Go-Live Performance & Cost Ops Playbook

sections.body: Operational playbook for the first 90 days after enterprise customer go-live focused on latency, throughput, and cost optimization. Includes baselining steps, tuning levers, triage matrix, escalation contacts, and QBR-ready metrics.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This playbook helps Customer Success (CS), Site Reliability (SRE), and the customer engineering teams stabilize performance and unit economics after an enterprise go-live on Redwood Inference. It is intended for the first 90 days but is reusable for periodic performance reviews.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Ensure production P95 latency and error rate meet contractual targets.
- Reduce per-token compute cost where possible without degrading quality.
- Establish reliable escalation paths and observable dashboards for stakeholder reporting.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Post-go-live in the first 90 days (high-priority).
- Before QBRs to prepare performance and cost slides.
- During performance regressions or unexpected cost spikes.
sections.heading: When to use this document

sections.body:
- P95 latency (in-region, 512 token context): target <= 300 ms; alert >= 450 ms.
- Request error rate: target <= 0.1%; alert >= 0.5% over 5m.
- KV cache hit ratio: target >= 60%; action < 40%.
- Tokens/sec per GPU (steady-state throughput): baseline target 120k tokens/s for dedicated gpus (varies by model).
- Cost per 1k tokens (hosted): target depends on committed tier; track delta vs baseline.

Baseline measurement (Day 0–7):
1) Collect workload samples: 5–10 representative request traces covering short, medium, and long contexts (example: 32, 512, 2048 tokens).
2) Run synthetic load with production prompt mixes (use small blast tests then ramp):
   - Script: curl -X POST 'https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"model":"rwd-4b","input":"<sample>"}'
3) Capture metrics: P50/P95/P99 latencies, CPU/GPU utilization, batching distribution, KV cache hit ratio, tail queue length, and cost estimate.
4) Record baseline table (example layout):

| Context | P50 (ms) | P95 (ms) | KV hit % | tokens/s | cost/1k tokens | Notes |
|---------|----------|----------|---------:|---------:|---------------:|-------|
| 32      | 45       | 120      | 78%      | 140k     | $0.38          | fast RPS paths |
| 512     | 120      | 280      | 62%      | 120k     | $0.60          | typical convo |
| 2048    | 320      | 670      | 35%      | 80k      | $1.10          | long-context heavy |
sections.heading: Key metrics & SLOs (example targets)

sections.body:
- Caching: implement/review prefix and KV cache settings first. Small prompts benefit most; aim to improve KV hit ratio via client-side prefixing or shared conversation keys.
- Batching: increase batch sizes for non-latency-critical routes. Target average tokens per batch > 256 where possible.
- Model variant routing: use a lower-cost quantized variant for background tasks; keep high-fidelity model for critical routes.
- Quantization profiles: enable 4-bit quantization on compatible models after validation on a small eval prompt set.
- Sequence length caps: enforce sensible max_input_tokens and max_completion_tokens per route.
- Rate-limiting & prioritization: route user-facing low-latency requests to low-latency pools; batch background jobs.
- Autoscaling and reservation: adjust Dedicated pool size and burst policy to match steady-state traffic and predictable peaks.

Operational runbook: triage matrix (fast path):
1) Symptom: increased P95 latency (> alert threshold)
   - Check 0–5m: Query Redwood Console dashboard for model-specific P95, queue length, and GPU utilization.
     - If queue length high & GPU utilization < 90% -> likely batching inefficiency (increase batch window or batchable traffic).
     - If GPU utilization > 95% and sustained -> request capacity (auto-scale or open Dedicated change) or enable model variant fallback.
     - If KV hit ratio dropped > 20% -> investigate prompt prefixing change or new user behavior.
   - Remediation steps: temporarily enable cheaper model variant for non-critical traffic, increase autoscaler target, or throttle background jobs.

2) Symptom: sharp cost spike (daily cost > 30% of baseline)
   - Check: per-route token consumption, embeddings vs generation mix, continuous vs batch jobs.
   - Remediation: disable noisy background routes, enable caching for embeddings, review quantization profile.

3) Symptom: elevated error rate (>= 0.5%)
   - Check: 5xx vs 4xx breakdown, auth failures, malformed payloads, model health.
   - Remediation: rollback recent client or server changes, restart serving pool, open bug with engineering if model runtime errors are recurring.
sections.heading: Tuning levers (ordered by recommended risk profile)

sections.body:
- Tier 1 CS (oncall): assigned CSM (customer success manager) — contact via Slack #cs-oncall and PagerDuty.
- Tier 2 SRE: eng-sre oncall rotation — page via PagerDuty with subject 'Post-Go-Live Performance Incident: <customer>'.
- Tier 3 Runtime Eng: runtime-owner@example.redwood.com — escalate when GPU-level faults, kernel OOMs, or profiling indicates runtime bug.
- Enterprise escalation: VP Customer Success and CTO if SLA breach is imminent.

Provide these fields in the PagerDuty page: incident_type, customer_name, cluster_id, model, observed_p95, baseline_p95, KV_hit, cost_delta, recent_deploy_commit.
sections.heading: Escalation path (contact chain)

sections.body:
- Apply route config override to reduce max_context_tokens to a safe cap.
- Switch traffic on a route to 'variant-low-cost' for X% of requests (canary 10% -> 50% -> 100%).
- Increase autoscaler min_replicas for the dedicated pool by N (N=1–3 depending on pool size).
sections.heading: Pre-approved mitigation actions (CS can execute)

sections.body:
1) Validate change in staging with production-weighted traces.
2) Start 10% traffic for 15 minutes, monitor P95 and error rate.
3) If metrics stable, move to 50% for 15 minutes.
4) Full rollout if stable; otherwise rollback immediately and notify stakeholders.
sections.heading: Canary rollback and rollout checklist

sections.body:
- Query recent P95 by route (example with Console API):
  curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 'https://console.redwood.example/api/v1/metrics?route_id=<route>&window=5m&metric=p95'
- KV cache diagnostic extractor (pseudo):
  rwd-kv-inspect --cluster cluster-a --route <route> --last 1h --output csv
- Cost delta report (daily cron):
  /bin/bash generate-cost-delta.sh --customer <customer> --since 2026-02-01
sections.heading: Automated scripts & queries (examples)

sections.body:
- Executive summary: availability, response times vs SLA, cost trend, top actions taken.
- Technical appendix: baseline vs current tables for P50/P95/P99, KV hit ratio, tokens/s, autoscaler events.
- Action items & owners: e.g., enable quantization profile by 2026-03-01 (owner: customer eng), validate prompts for cacheability (owner: CSM).
sections.heading: QBR & reporting templates (what to include)

sections.body:
- Day 0–7: Baseline collection and dashboard creation (owner: CSM + CS eng).
- Day 8–30: Implement low-risk levers (caching, batching config) and measure impact (owner: CS eng).
- Day 31–60: Trial quantization on a small test set and review quality metrics (owner: CS eng + Applied ML).
- Day 61–90: Finalize model routing policy and submit recommendations for Dedicated sizing adjustments (owner: SRE + CS).
sections.heading: Checklist for first 90 days (owner assignments)

sections.body:
- For any incident causing SLA degradation, complete postmortem within 7 days and include: timeline, root cause, mitigations, customer impact, and follow-up actions.
- Store postmortems at /confluence/customer-success-and-support/postmortems/ and link to related QBR slides.

Appendix A — Example route configuration snippet (YAML-style):

route_id: convo-fast
model: rwd-4b
max_input_tokens: 1024
max_completion_tokens: 256
batching:
  enabled: true
  max_wait_ms: 25
  target_tokens_per_batch: 512
cache:
  prefix_cache: true
  kv_cache_policy: LRU
  ttl_seconds: 3600
variant_fallbacks:

payload.page_title: LatticeBridge Support — QBR Account Brief (2026 Q1)

sections.body:
LatticeBridge Support is evaluating Redwood Dedicated to replace their in-house retrieval + Lambda-based reranker in order to increase top-5 answer precision and reduce per-query infrastructure cost for ticket deflection and agent assist. In Q1, the team completed a Dedicated POC on a 1M-document subset and validated latency targets for their NA interactive path, with measurable top-5 precision lift over their current Elastic + bespoke reranker baseline. Primary open items are finalizing VPC peering architecture approval, confirming data residency language, and aligning on a commercial model for burst traffic (light deflection checks) vs sustained full rerank traffic.
POC moved from planning to completed benchmark phase (Dedicated POC executed on 1M-doc subset).
Close date slipped from 2026-04 to 2026-05 due to security review queueing and VPC peering design iterations.
Cold-start KV cache SLA concern narrowed: now focused on predictable warmup time after deploy/scale events rather than per-request cache misses.
Cost modeling updated to separate 'light deflection checks' from 'full rerank + generation' paths; customer accepted blended cost framing for QBR.
Increase top-5 accuracy/precision enough to materially improve ticket deflection and reduce agent handling time.
Meet NA interactive latency: p95 retrieval + rerank under 200ms; soft p99 under 350ms.
Provide a transparent unit-cost model with a target blended average below $0.025 per full rerank query at scale, and a low-cost path for high-QPS deflection checks.
Satisfy security requirements: SSO (SAML), audit logs to their SIEM, KMS integration, SOC 2, and clear data residency commitments.
Customer currently runs Elastic for hybrid search with an internal retrieval layer and a Lambda-based reranker. The engineering team is experienced with Elastic and FAISS-like pipelines and is sensitive to vendor lock-in and portability. Their knowledge corpus includes tickets, KB articles, and community posts; average document size is ~3KB with steady growth.
Knowledge index is ~12M documents today with expected growth of ~2M/year. Peak ingest can reach ~50k docs/day during major releases. Query traffic is split into two main paths: (1) lightweight ticket-deflection checks at high burst (historically discussed as up to ~5k QPS), and (2) full rerank + generation at lower sustained volumes (historically discussed as ~600 QPS). Updated Q1 discussions emphasized that burst deflection checks and sustained full rerank workloads will be priced and capacity-planned separately.
Latency SLOs (NA interactive): p50 < 40ms, p95 < 200ms, soft p99 < 350ms for retrieval + rerank.
Throughput planning: support bursty light-check traffic and sustained full rerank workloads without tail-latency regression.
Cost targets: blended average target remains <$0.025 for full rerank queries; light deflection checks should remain materially lower cost than full rerank.
Top-5 candidate quality is the primary KPI; customer previously cited a desired 12–15% improvement as a material operational win.
Reranker must allow configurable feature inputs (e.g., BM25 score, vector distance, recency, ticket metadata).
Prefer a CPU-friendly fast path with an optional heavier path for complex queries; must support A/B testing and automated rollback.
2-week Dedicated POC executed on a 1M-document subset. Benchmarked retrieval + rerank latency under representative NA load profiles and tested reranker configurations (CPU-first with GPU fallback for heavier rerank). Evaluated quality uplift against their baseline using a labeled query set provided during onsite benchmark preparation.
Latency: met NA p95 target for retrieval + rerank on the tested 1M subset under the agreed harness; tail behavior improved after cache warmup tuning.
Quality: achieved target top-5 precision lift versus baseline on the provided evaluation set (validated with customer scoring methodology).
Ops: customer requested additional documentation on KV cache warmup/eviction behavior and explicit rollback procedures tied to SLO degradation.
Customer-reported success criteria alignment: p95 retrieval+rerank under 200ms on the POC harness; top-5 precision lift at or above the agreed threshold; cost estimate within acceptable variance of the commercial quote.
Notes on methodology: customer emphasized production-like traffic mix and requested that we separate metrics for 'light deflection check' vs 'full rerank' paths in future tests.
Security sign-off on VPC peering architecture (network flow diagram and ingress/egress controls requested).
Data residency language confirmation for NA-hosted workloads and any operational telemetry retention.
Commercial: finalize burst traffic policy and any overage model for deflection-check spikes.
Perception risk: engineering skepticism around portability; needs a crisp story for export/migration strategy and operational transparency.
Security kickoff completed in Q1. SOC 2 package and security FAQ provided. Customer requests remaining: finalized network flow diagram for Dedicated in their VPC peering model, confirmation of audit log forwarding format and integration guidance, and data residency guarantees. SSO (SAML) remains required for Console access. KMS integration is expected for encryption key control and rotation alignment with their internal policy.
Deliver final VPC peering architecture diagram and complete security review responses (target: early April).
Provide KV cache warmup/eviction documentation and an explicit rollback runbook tied to p95/p99 regression thresholds.
Run a short follow-up validation test focused on burst deflection checks (tail latency + cost) using the customer’s latest traffic assumptions.
Commercial: finalize order form with Dedicated capacity plan and an agreed burst policy; align procurement timeline to a May close.
Head of Product: "If we can get top-5 accuracy up 12–15% and keep p95 under 200ms, this is a material win for ops."
Security team: "We need the network flows and data residency language to match what we present internally—then we can clear the architecture."
2026-01-18 — Technical deep-dive with SE (Diego): vector store costs, KV cache behavior, and reranker architecture.
2026-02-18 — Exec demo (Avery + Diego): reviewed latency SLOs and fallback policy; customer requested a Dedicated POC.
2026-02-25 — Security kickoff (Renee): shared SOC2 materials; customer requested VPC architecture diagram and residency details.
2026-03-01 — Onsite benchmarks requested: customer submitted sample traces and test corpus.
2026-03-14 — POC benchmark readout: reviewed latency/quality outcomes and identified follow-up documentation items.
Keep the narrative anchored on measurable outcomes: quality lift + latency compliance + predictable cost model.
Be proactive on portability concerns: provide export strategy and clear boundaries of managed components.
Treat KV cache predictability as an SLO-adjacent requirement; document warmup expectations after deploys/scale events.

payload.page_title: QBR Transition: Technical and Commercial Handoff Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines a standardized cross-functional process for transitioning an enterprise customer from post-provisioning operations into a regular QBR (Quarterly Business Review) cadence. It focuses on a two-track handoff: (1) Technical handoff into steady-state SRE/Customer Success operations, and (2) Commercial handoff into Customer Success/Account teams for QBRs and renewed commercial commitments. The goal is to reduce post-go-live friction, ensure telemetry and SLO alignment, and provide a repeatable checklist for both technical and commercial stakeholders.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to enterprise customers after successful go-live and the first 14 days of stability verification.
- Intended for customers using Hosted API, Dedicated, or Private deployments.
- Covers telemetry gating, runbook ownership transfer, QBR readiness criteria, and obligations for escalation.
sections.heading: Scope and Intent

sections.body:
1. After the 72-hour and 14-day stability sweeps complete and the customer is marked "operational" in the cutover checklist.
2. When the customer is expected to enter the first revenue-bearing QBR cycle or when an SLA/commercial review is requested.

Pre-handoff (Technical) Checklist - must be completed before commercial handoff:
1) Telemetry and Dashboards
   - Confirm tenant-specific dashboards exist in Grafana/Looker: "Tenant Overview", "Token Economics", "Model Quality Trends", "Latency & Errors".
   - Confirm synthetic journeys (happy path + edge cases) are running and passing for 14 consecutive days.
2) SLO and Alerting
   - SLOs validated: availability P99 >= 99.5% (for Dedicated) or SLA baseline met per contract.
   - Alert definitions and on-call rotation ownership documented and tested.
3) Security & Compliance Gates
   - Network controls (VPC peering, firewall rules) verified and recorded.
   - Logs retention and access review completed with security contact.
4) Operational Runbooks and Playbooks
   - Tenant runbook created: include common triage steps, known quirks, and rollback criteria.
   - Escalation contacts confirmed and smoke-test call executed.
5) Cost and Quota Protections
   - Billing alerts and quota caps configured; cost-protection webhook validated.
sections.heading: When to use this playbook

sections.body:
- Customer Success (CS): drive commercial handoff, coordinate QBR agenda, own account-level risks.
- SRE/Platform: own technical stabilization, SLO validation, and on-call readiness.
- Solutions Engineering (SE): provide architecture decisions, post-cutover optimizations, and model migration notes.
- Customer: confirm business objectives, authorized stakeholders for QBRs, and acceptance of operational telemetry.
sections.heading: Roles and Responsibilities

sections.body:
- Synthetic success rate >= 99% over 14d for primary flows.
- Observed token throughput within 20% of projected ramp for 7d or documented variance with mitigating plan.
- No P1 incidents in last 7d and P2 incidents trend stable or decreasing.
sections.heading: Telemetry Gating Criteria (hard gates)

sections.body:
1. Finalize and publish tenant runbook to internal wiki; tag SRE on the page and mark as "owned".
2. Export tenant dashboards to the account folder and assign CS read-only links.
3. Run a joint smoke test between SRE, CS, and the customer that simulates these failure modes: model fallback, region failover, quota limit triggered.
4. Confirm on-call rotation contains a named owner for the tenant and verify escalation path to engineering.
5. Record the handoff meeting minutes with action items and owners in the ticketing system.

Commercial Handoff Checklist (concurrent with or after technical handoff):
- Confirm QBR cadence (quarterly by default) and primary agenda items: availability, cost/perf, model quality, roadmap alignment, risk and escalations.
- Prepare the Customer Health one-pager: activation metrics, synthetic pass rate, spend vs. forecast, open action items.
- Deliver a short technical appendix for the QBR: current model hosted, quantization profile, recent rollouts, and performance baselines.
- Agree on success metrics for the next quarter and an escalation SLA (response targets and review triggers).
sections.heading: Technical Handoff Steps (numbered)

sections.body:
- Abort a commercial handoff if any hard telemetry gate fails (synthetic < 99% over 7d) or a P1 incident was recorded in the last 72h.
- Rollback model/route changes if model quality regression is above the agreed threshold: labeled false-positive rate increase > 4% or a decrease in mean quality score > 6 points on the evaluation harness.
sections.heading: Abort and Rollback Criteria (explicit stop conditions)

sections.body:
- Daily health digest for the first 14 days following handoff (email + Slack) summarizing synthetic pass rate, error budget burn, and cost delta.
- Trigger a Technical QBR (mini-review) if cost delta exceeds 25% of forecast or if SLO burn is > 30% in a 7d window.
- Add an item to the next QBR if any major action item remains open at handoff.
sections.heading: Post-handoff Verification and QBR Triggers

sections.body:
1) Executive summary (5m) - health and key asks
2) Operational review (15m) - availability, latency, incidents, SLO burn
3) Cost and capacity (10m) - spend trends, quota requests, committed units
4) Model quality (15m) - eval results, prompt regressions, A/B experiments
5) Roadmap and asks (10m) - upcoming migrations, dedicated capacity requests
6) Action items and owners (5m)

Sample alert thresholds and recommended dashboards (appendix table):
| Area | Metric | Threshold | Owner |
| Tenant Availability | P99 request latency | > 800 ms for 5m | SRE |
| Synthetic Journeys | Failure rate | > 1% over 15m | CS + SRE |
| Cost | Daily spend delta | > 25% above forecast | FinOps/CS |
| Model Quality | Eval pass delta | Drop > 4 points | SE/Research |
