payload.page_title: Enterprise priority: 429 / quota / overload behavior (Support guide)

sections.body:
This page is a Support/CS reference for explaining **429** responses after the **Hot-route capacity protection** rollout. It covers:
- What customers may see (payload + headers)
- How to distinguish **quota** vs **rate-limit** vs **overload shedding/admission control**
- Recommended customer-side retry/backoff behavior
- When and how to escalate (and what data to collect)

This doc is written for Support and TAMs. For implementation details, see the Platform design/ADR pages linked in Related pages.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body: Beginning with the enterprise priority rollout, Redwood enforces **tier-aware capacity protection** on a set of “protected routes” (commonly: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`).
sections.heading: What changed (customer-visible)

sections.body:
- **More predictable 429s** for best-effort/self-serve traffic during regional pressure.
- **Enterprise traffic preserved** longer (priority routing + per-tier budgets), but enterprise requests can still receive 429s when:
  - the account’s own limits are reached, or
  - the route is in sustained overload and the enterprise budget is exhausted.
- **New reason codes** and additional headers to explain why the request was rejected.
sections.heading: Customers may observe

sections.body:
- 429 is **not** a “generic outage” signal. It is a deliberate backpressure mechanism to protect overall fleet health and enterprise SLOs.
- 429 responses are **safe to retry** when the reason indicates transient pressure, using the guidance below.

---
sections.heading: Important framing for customers

sections.body:
- `error.type`: `rate_limit_exceeded` or `quota_exceeded` or `overloaded`
- `error.code`: a stable machine-readable reason code (see table below)
- `error.message`: human-readable summary
- `error.request_id`: request identifier (also returned in response headers)

If a customer claims the payload is missing or inconsistent, ask for:
- raw response body
- full response headers
- SDK version / client library
sections.heading: Most clients will receive an error payload shaped like

sections.body:
Support should request and record these headers when present:
- `x-redwood-request-id`: request ID used for internal tracing
- `retry-after`: seconds to wait before retry (only set for some transient reasons)
- `x-redwood-retry-after-ms`: millisecond retry hint (preferred when present)
- `x-redwood-limit-scope`: `account` | `api_key` | `route` (where enforcement applies)
- `x-redwood-limit-policy`: policy identifier (internal-friendly string; customer can share as opaque)
- `x-redwood-429-reason`: short reason token (maps to reason codes below)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-limit`: numeric limit (requests per window) when applicable
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining`: remaining requests in current window (when applicable)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-reset`: epoch time or seconds-until-reset (when applicable)
sections.heading: Standard headers (may vary by route)

sections.body:
- Some enterprise customers will only see a subset of limit headers depending on contract configuration and route group settings.
- Absence of headers is not automatically a bug; it can indicate a rejection occurred upstream of quota evaluation (e.g., admission control).

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: Use the following table to classify the issue and advise the customer.
sections.heading: Reason codes (how to interpret 429s)

sections.body:
These are expected when a customer exceeds their configured limits.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hard quota exceeded | quota_exceeded | quota_window_exhausted | Customer has consumed their quota for the current window. | Do not retry immediately. Wait until reset. Consider limit increase request. |
| Rate limit exceeded | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_account | Customer exceeded account-level request rate. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Reduce concurrency / smooth bursts. |
| Route-group rate limit | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_route_group | Customer exceeded a per-route or route-group cap. | Same as above; ask them to spread load or request a higher burst allowance. |
| Token / compute guardrail | rate_limit_exceeded | token_budget_exceeded | Customer exceeded a token/compute budget (if enabled for contract). | Reduce max_tokens / request size; smooth traffic; discuss contract sizing. |
sections.heading: A) Quota- and rate-limit-driven 429s (customer-specific)

sections.body:
These indicate transient capacity protection behavior.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Admission control (best-effort shed) | overloaded | shed_best_effort | Fleet/route is under pressure; best-effort traffic is being throttled first. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Prefer queueing client-side. |
| Admission control (enterprise budget exhausted) | overloaded | shed_enterprise_budget | Protected route is overloaded and enterprise budget is fully utilized. | Retry using Retry-After if present; reduce concurrency; contact Support if sustained. |
| Regional capacity constraint | overloaded | region_capacity | Selected region is capacity constrained; request rejected to prevent tail latency cascade. | Retry with backoff; if multi-region is enabled, allow client failover. |
| Policy evaluation deny | overloaded | policy_deny_overload | Policy engine denied admission due to active overload rule (e.g., queue depth trigger). | Treat as transient. Retry with backoff. Provide request IDs for investigation if frequent. |
sections.heading: B) Overload protection / admission control 429s (fleet pressure)

sections.body:
- For enterprise accounts: “This is protective backpressure to preserve latency/availability for protected routes. It can occur during unusual bursts or regional pressure.”
- For self-serve/best-effort: “During peak pressure, the platform prioritizes higher-SLA traffic; your requests may be throttled earlier.”

---
sections.heading: Support positioning

sections.body: Provide the following general guidance (tailor to the customer’s stack):
sections.heading: Recommended customer retry & backoff guidance

sections.body:
- Retry 429s when:
  - `error.type = overloaded` (most cases)
  - `error.type = rate_limit_exceeded`
- Do NOT aggressively retry when:
  - `error.type = quota_exceeded` and the response includes a reset hint (wait until reset)
sections.heading: When to retry

sections.body:
- Use **exponential backoff with full jitter**.
- Start with 250–500ms base delay.
- Cap max delay at 10–30s.
- Add client-side request queueing to avoid stampedes.
- Respect `retry-after` and/or `x-redwood-retry-after-ms` when present (prefer the ms header).
sections.heading: How to retry (recommended algorithm)

sections.body:
1) if `retry-after` present → sleep for that duration (+ small jitter) then retry
2) else backoff = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
3) stop after a reasonable max attempts (typically 5–8) and surface a retriable error to the application
sections.heading: Suggested pseudocode guidance to share (language-agnostic)

sections.body:
- Implement a per-route concurrency limiter (token bucket / semaphore)
- Smooth bursty workloads (batching where possible)
- Avoid synchronized retries across many workers (jitter)
sections.heading: Customers with high parallelism should

sections.body:
- For non-streaming requests, retries are generally safe.
- For streaming requests, see “Streaming semantics” below.

---
sections.heading: Idempotency guidance

sections.body: Some customers report “inconsistent termination” on streaming responses during load shedding.
sections.heading: Streaming semantics during shedding (common ticket driver)

sections.body:
- If a request is rejected **before** streaming begins, they should receive a normal 429 with reason + headers.
- If a request is accepted and then terminated due to downstream pressure, behavior depends on the transport:
  - Customers should treat early stream termination as retriable if they did not receive a completed response.
  - Advise customers to log the `x-redwood-request-id` and last event received.
sections.heading: Support guidance

sections.body:
- customers see a successful HTTP status but the stream ends without an explicit termination signal and without consistent client-visible error handling, or
- the customer provides multiple request IDs showing premature termination correlated with new overload reasons.

---
sections.heading: Escalate if

sections.body:
Request the following in the initial reply to reduce ping-pong:
1) Affected route(s): e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`
2) Region/endpoint base URL (if multi-region)
3) Time window (with timezone) and approximate request rate
4) Sample `x-redwood-request-id` values (3–10 IDs)
5) Full 429 response headers + body (raw)
6) Whether they are using streaming
7) Their current retry policy (backoff, max attempts, concurrency)
8) Whether it’s isolated to a single API key or all keys in the account

Internal-only (if available to TAM/CS): contract tier (Hosted API vs Dedicated), priority class, and any approved exceptions.

---
sections.heading: What Support should ask for (intake checklist)

sections.body:
- Enterprise customer reports sustained 429s on a protected route for **>10 minutes** AND:
  - reason indicates overload protection (`overloaded/*`), OR
  - they claim traffic is within contracted limits but still seeing 429s
- Enterprise customer reports p95/p99 latency degradation plus 429 spikes (possible mis-tuned thresholds)
sections.heading: Enterprise impact thresholds

sections.body:
- `x-redwood-limit-policy` changes unexpectedly after rollout / config migration
- A single tenant is denied while peers are not, and headers indicate route-group limits that don’t match the contract
sections.heading: Suspected misconfiguration

sections.body:
- Missing/incorrect reason codes across multiple requests
- `retry-after` values that are clearly wrong (e.g., negative, extremely large, inconsistent with window)
- Streaming termination inconsistencies correlated with overload events
sections.heading: Possible platform bug

sections.body:
- Customer requests details about other tenants, fleet state, or priority policy internals beyond what we disclose. Route via TAM/CS + Security as needed.

---
sections.heading: Security / access concerns

sections.body:
1) Create/attach a ticket in the Support queue and tag: `overload-protection` + `enterprise`.
2) Post in `#incidents` (if active event suspected) or `#eng-sre` with:
   - customer/account
   - affected routes/regions
   - timeframe
   - reason codes + sample request IDs
   - whether Retry-After was present and followed
3) Link the relevant dashboards (SRE on-call will pull). If you have access, include:
   - enterprise route SLO dashboard
   - overload protection shed-rate panel
   - admission control trigger annotations

If immediate paging is warranted, follow the runbook: “Overload protection and admission control” (Related pages).

---
sections.heading: Escalation process (internal)

sections.body:
Use this when responding to customers (edit for their tier/route):

“HTTP 429 indicates the request was throttled or temporarily rejected to protect latency and availability. For protected enterprise routes, Redwood prioritizes higher-SLA traffic under peak load to prevent fleet-wide degradation. Please implement exponential backoff with jitter and respect any Retry-After headers. If you share a few request IDs and the full response headers/body, we can confirm whether the 429s are due to your configured limits (quota/rate) or transient overload protection.”

---
sections.heading: Approved external explanation (copy/paste)

sections.body:
**Q: Is a 429 an outage?**
A: Not necessarily. For many overload cases, it’s intentional backpressure to avoid tail latency/5xx cascading failures.

**Q: Can enterprise customers still get 429s?**
A: Yes—if they exceed their contracted limits, or in rare cases when a protected route’s enterprise budget is fully consumed during sustained overload.

**Q: Should customers increase retry aggressiveness to “push through”?**
A: No. Aggressive retries worsen overload. Encourage backoff + jitter + client-side queueing.

**Q: Customer says they stayed under their “RPM” but still got 429.**
A: Ask for headers and request IDs. They may be hitting a route-group limit, a token/compute guardrail, or experiencing transient admission control without Retry-After being honored.

---
sections.heading: FAQ (Support)

sections.body:
- 2026-02-06: Added streaming termination guidance + escalation triggers for inconsistent SSE termination.
- 2026-01-23: Updated reason-code table to include `shed_enterprise_budget` and `region_capacity`.
- 2026-01-09: Initial publication for Support enablement ahead of GA rollout.

payload.page_title: LexicoHealth: Embedding dimension mismatch causing rerank errors/timeouts (Known issue + workarounds)

sections.body:
h1. Summary
LexicoHealth experienced production errors and latency regressions on reranking shortly after a model catalog change that promoted a 1024-d embedding model. The immediate symptom was a vector length mismatch between query and candidate embeddings (512 vs 1024), leading to HTTP 4xx/5xx responses and tail latency timeouts on the rerank route.

This page documents the customer-facing symptoms, confirmed root cause, and the supported workarounds. It also summarizes the longer-term preventive work tracked in INT-1123.

h1. Customer + environment
* Customer: LexicoHealth (Enterprise)
* Environment: Redwood Hosted API, dedicated tenant
* Regions observed: us-west (primary), eu-west (failover)
* Affected endpoints:
** POST /v1/embeddings/encode
** POST /v1/rerank
* Models involved:
** open-embed-512-v1 (legacy 512-d)
** open-embed-1024-v2 (newer 1024-d)
** open-embed-default (alias)

h1. Symptoms
* Rerank requests returning errors and timeouts:
** Common message: "reranker: candidate vector length 512 != query vector length 1024"
** Increased 500/504 rate during peak traffic
* Increased latency on rerank calls (median +2–6s in the reported window) due to retries and error-path work
* Batch or async jobs failing validation when mixing stored 512-d vectors with newly generated 1024-d vectors

h1. What changed (high level)
On 2026-03-09, the model catalog was updated such that *open-embed-1024-v2* became the global default for content embeddings. LexicoHealth was relying on the alias *open-embed-default* to resolve to the legacy 512-d model (consistent with their existing stored embeddings and reranker expectations).

h1. Root cause (confirmed)
A catalog migration/promotion flow failed to persist tenant-specific alias overrides for a subset of tenants. For LexicoHealth, this caused *open-embed-default* to resolve to *open-embed-1024-v2* unexpectedly.

The reranker currently performs strict dimensionality checks and does not support automatic compatibility negotiation when provided embeddings from mixed dimensions. When it encounters a mismatch it:
* rejects the request or takes an expensive error-path that can include retries
* increases tail latency and contributes to timeouts under load

h1. Timeline (UTC)
* 2026-03-09 ~15:00: Customer-impacting behavior begins after catalog promotion
* 2026-03-10: Support escalation; SRE investigation identifies tenant alias drift
* 2026-03-10: Temporary routing override applied to force 512-d for LexicoHealth
* 2026-03-11: Hotfix prepared and rolled out to restore alias persistence
* 2026-03-13: Verification completed across affected tenants; monitoring continued
* 2026-03-20: This knowledge base entry updated with validated workaround steps and prevention plan

h1. Workarounds (supported)
h2. Workaround A (recommended): Pin embeddings model explicitly
Pin the embeddings model at the project/policy level so that calls using "open-embed-default" (or calls that omit a model) do not silently move dimensions.

*When to use:* customer has existing stored embeddings (512-d) and wants stable behavior.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Generate a new embedding and confirm vector length is 512.
* Submit rerank requests where both query and candidates are produced with the pinned model; confirm no mismatch errors.

h2. Workaround B: Regenerate embeddings to 1024-d (migration path)
If the customer intends to move to *open-embed-1024-v2*, the customer must ensure dimensional consistency:
* Re-embed the corpus to 1024-d
* Ensure the reranking pipeline uses 1024-d consistently (query + candidates)

*Important:* This is a customer-managed migration and may require reindexing/vector-store rebuild depending on their stack.

h2. Workaround C (temporary): Tenant-level routing override
Support/SRE can apply a tenant-level override to force the embeddings alias resolution.

*When to use:* emergency mitigation while the customer pins configuration or while waiting for catalog fixes to propagate.

h1. Current status (as of last_updated)
* The tenant alias persistence hotfix has been deployed and validated for LexicoHealth.
* For LexicoHealth, *open-embed-default* is confirmed to resolve to *open-embed-512-v1*.
* Global catalog default remains *open-embed-1024-v2* for new projects unless explicitly pinned.

h1. Prevention + follow-ups
sections.heading: Verification

sections.body:
* INT-1123: Implement a backward-compatible embedding adapter strategy in reranker (no silent conversions; clear behavior with explicit controls)
* Add catalog migration validation:
** Pre-deploy checks to confirm tenant alias overrides are preserved
** Post-deploy auditing + alerting on alias drift (per-tenant resolution diffs)
* Improve observability:
** Metrics for reranker dimension mismatch rejections
** Dashboards correlating catalog version changes to rerank error rates and tail latency

h1. Support playbook (for similar tickets)
* Triage questions:
** Are query embeddings and candidate embeddings generated by the same model version and dimension?
** Is the customer using an alias (e.g., open-embed-default) instead of an explicit model?
** Did the customer recently store embeddings that might now be mixed-dimension?
* Fast checks:
** Ask for one embedding sample output length from /v1/embeddings/encode
** Ask for the rerank error message (dimension mismatch is the key signature)
* Recommended response:
** Advise explicit model pinning
** If the customer needs to migrate to 1024-d, provide guidance on re-embedding and reindexing
** Escalate to SRE only if alias drift is suspected or overrides are required

h1. Notes specific to LexicoHealth
* LexicoHealth reported partial mitigation after pinning due to in-flight jobs created before the override propagated; restarting workers and re-running queued batches resolved remaining failures.
* If LexicoHealth opts into 1024-d in the future, coordinate a planned migration window to avoid mixed-dimension corpora.
sections.heading: The following improvements are planned/tracked

payload.page_title: Known Issue: Timeouts with Structured Output (JSON Schema) on Hosted API

sections.body:
Some customers have observed intermittent timeouts when using the Hosted API structured output feature with JSON Schema constraints. The same prompts may succeed when structured output is disabled or when using tool-calling output.

This is typically caused by long-tail latency in the constrained decoding path, especially when schemas are large or contain combinators (e.g., anyOf/oneOf) and deeply nested arrays.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Product: Hosted API
- Endpoint: /v1/chat/completions
- Feature: structured output (JSON Schema)
- Regions: primarily us-east (reports), potential in other regions depending on workload
sections.heading: Affected surface

sections.body:
The following customer reports have been validated by Support/Engineering:
- Kestrel Labs (enterprise)  SUP-4812
- Northwind Analytics (POC)  reported via CS email; correlated request IDs req_1f3b8c0c, req_6aa2d19e, req_09a3f7d1
sections.heading: Known impacted customers

sections.body:
- Client-side request timeout (commonly 60s)
- Gateway timeout (HTTP 504) in some cases
- Long tail latency with structured_output=true
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
1) Reduce max_output_tokens to bound constrained decoding time.
2) Simplify schema:
   - Avoid anyOf/oneOf where possible
   - Keep schemas flatter; limit deeply nested arrays
   - Prefer enums/regex sparingly
3) Consider tool-calling output for complex branching structures.
4) If enterprise traffic is repeatedly hitting gateway timeouts, coordinate with SRE/Runtime for region- and tier-specific timeout tuning.
sections.heading: Workarounds / mitigations

sections.body:
- Mitigation deployed in us-east for enterprise tier: increased internal structured-output step timeout (45s -> 75s) to reduce gateway timeouts.
- Follow-up engineering work: add metrics for schema complexity and constrained decoding wall time; evaluate guardrails for schema size/structure.
sections.heading: Current status

sections.body:
- Jira: SUP-4812
- Slack: #support thread on structured output timeouts
sections.heading: Internal references

sections.body: When communicating externally, avoid implying a platform-wide outage. Describe as a known issue affecting requests with large/complex schemas, and provide the workarounds above.
sections.heading: Customer-facing guidance

payload.page_title: Hosted API overload errors: support guidance, retry/backoff, and escalation

sections.body: This page helps Support/CS respond to customer reports of new “overload protection” errors (circuit breakers + load shedding) on Redwood Hosted API.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Explain what the customer is seeing (stable semantics vs ambiguous timeouts/5xx).
- Provide canonical retry/backoff guidance to prevent retry storms.
- Show how to interpret correlation IDs so Engineering can quickly trace requests.
- Define escalation criteria and the minimum information to collect.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.
sections.heading: What changed (customer-facing)

sections.body:
- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.
sections.heading: Customers may now see

sections.body:
- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.
sections.heading: These responses

sections.body:
1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see “How to recognize” below).
2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).
3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).
4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).
5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see “When to escalate”).
sections.heading: Quick triage checklist (Support)

sections.body:
- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.
sections.heading: Common HTTP statuses

sections.body:
- **Retry-After**: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., `Retry-After: 2`).
- **x-redwood-request-id**: unique ID for a single request attempt.
- **x-redwood-correlation-id**: groups related attempts across services (gateway → routing → runtime). Some clients/logs only show one of these; either is helpful.

If the response is 429/503 *and* includes a Redwood overload error code in the JSON body, treat it as overload protection.
sections.heading: Expected headers (may vary by route)

sections.body: Overload errors are additive and JSON-compatible with existing response parsing.
sections.heading: Error payload: what customers see

sections.body:
- `error.type`: `overload_error` (or `rate_limit_error` in some cases)
- `error.code`: stable machine code
- `error.message`: human-readable
- `error.request_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-request-id` where available
- `error.correlation_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-correlation-id` where available
sections.heading: Typical shape (example)
Example snippet (illustrative only)

sections.body:
Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |
sections.heading: Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers

sections.body:
- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.
- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.
- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.
- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.
sections.heading: Golden rules

sections.body:
If `Retry-After` is present:
- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.

If `Retry-After` is missing:
- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with ±20–40% jitter.
sections.heading: Recommended algorithm (support-approved)

sections.body:
- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10–20 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.
- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10–20%).
sections.heading: Bounds

sections.body:
Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.
- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.
sections.heading: Streaming-specific guidance

sections.body:
- “Just retry in a tight loop.”
- “Retry immediately with the same concurrency.”
- “Spin up many parallel retries to get through.”
sections.heading: What NOT to recommend

sections.body:
1) `x-redwood-correlation-id` (best for cross-service tracing)
2) `x-redwood-request-id` (single request attempt)
3) Timestamp + region + model + route if IDs are not available
sections.heading: Ask the customer for (in order of preference)

sections.body:
- Response headers in their HTTP client.
- SDK exception fields (Python/TypeScript SDKs surface request IDs; newer versions surface correlation IDs when present).
- Their application logs if they log response headers.
sections.heading: Where customers can find them

sections.body:
- Paste the ID(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.
- Capture:
  - the **error.code**
  - the **route** (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, embeddings endpoint)
  - the **region** (requested + served)
  - whether **Retry-After** was present and its value

If Support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the IDs and all details in the escalation template below.
sections.heading: How Support should use them internally

sections.body: “Not necessarily. These errors indicate Redwood is protecting service reliability during temporary saturation in a specific region/model. We reject early with clear retry guidance to avoid timeouts and degraded performance. Please follow the Retry-After header and exponential backoff. If the issue persists beyond a short window, share correlation IDs and we’ll investigate.”
sections.heading: Approved response

sections.body: “503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It’s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.”
sections.heading: Approved response

sections.body:
- If they have **fallback routing configured** (Dedicated/enterprise Hosted tiers or configured routing policies), yes—recommend they enable/verify it.
- Otherwise, advise them to implement client-side fallback only if they can validate output compatibility and safety.
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body:
- Confirm whether they are hitting **429** (likely limit-related) vs **503** (regional/model saturation).
- If 429 is persistent at normal traffic levels, route to CS for capacity/tier discussion.
- If 503 is persistent, treat as reliability issue and escalate to Eng.
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body:
1) **Retry-After header missing on some overload responses**
- Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After.
- Workaround: Recommend exponential backoff with jitter as above.
- Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs.

2) **Fallback model not triggering as expected**
- Symptom: Customer has configured fallback but still sees repeated 503 without failover.
- Workaround: Customer can temporarily specify an alternate model/region explicitly (if acceptable) while we investigate.
- Action: Escalate; include tenant ID, configured fallback policy (what they intended), and correlation IDs.

3) **Customer interprets 503 as “platform outage”**
- Guidance: Use the approved response language; direct them to Retry-After and backoff guidance.
sections.heading: Known issues (Support-facing)

sections.body:
- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.
- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.
- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.
- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).
- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.
- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.
sections.heading: Escalate immediately if any of the following are true

sections.body:
Subject: Hosted API overload errors – customer impact

- Customer / tenant:
- Tier: (Self-serve Hosted / Enterprise Hosted / Dedicated)
- Primary route(s): (e.g., /v1/chat/completions)
- Model(s):
- Region(s): requested / observed
- Time window (with timezone):
- Error HTTP status: 429 / 503
- Error code(s) from body:
- Retry-After present? value(s):
- x-redwood-correlation-id(s):
- x-redwood-request-id(s):
- Customer retry behavior (describe):
- Business impact: (prod down / degraded / batch delay)
- Attachments: sample responses (headers + body), client logs
sections.heading: Escalation template (copy/paste)

sections.body:
- Overload dashboards: shed rate, breaker-open rate, queue depth, saturation signals by region/model.
- Incident channels: #eng-oncall, #incidents (look for breaker announcements).
- Runbook: “Hosted overload / circuit breaker runbook” (linked above).
sections.heading: Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)

sections.body:
- 2025-11-10: Initial publication for overload error rollout (Support readiness).
- 2025-12-05: Updated retry guidance; clarified correlation IDs and escalation thresholds.

payload.page_title: GPU preemption / scheduling stalls: detection, fast-reconcile workaround, and customer-facing guidance

sections.body:
H1: Summary

This page documents a recurring class of incidents observed in Dedicated deployments where GPU preemption or scheduling congestion produces multi-minute 'stalls' (request backpressure and token-generation latency spikes). It provides: a detection recipe, a recommended fast-reconcile workaround to restore tenant throughput quickly, customer-facing guidance for status updates, and long-term mitigation options.

H2: Impact

- Affected surface: Dedicated GPU tenants and burst workers; can also affect Private (on-prem) clusters with shared GPU pools.
- Symptom: streaming responses stall for 30s–300s, in-flight KV-cache misses, increased queueing latency, and elevated 5xx rates for generation endpoints.
- Business impact: degradation of latency SLOs (p95 token latency), customer-visible timeouts, and elevated support tickets during busy schedule windows.

H2: Root cause (common patterns)

1. Node-level preemption / pod eviction events when lower-priority pods are force-evicted to accommodate higher-priority workloads (spot reclaim, autoscaler-driven bin-packing).
2. Kube-scheduler congestion when many large-GPU requests are pending simultaneously and bin-packing heuristics thrash.
3. GPU driver or MIG state mis-synchronization after frequent container restarts causing pods to hang in 'RuntimeCreate' or 'ContainerCreating' for extended periods.

H2: Detection (what to watch for)

- Alert signals (examples):
  - sudden rise in kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total for inference pods
  - large increase in kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason{reason=~".*Preempted|Evicted.*"}
  - sustained abnormally-high generation token-latency p95 > x ms (see SLO thresholds)
  - GPU utilization dips while queue length for inference requests stays high

- Example PromQL queries:
  - Pod eviction spikes (5m):
    increase(kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Failed"}[5m]) by (node)
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: Workaround: Dedicated autoscaling oscillation (latency spikes + replica churn)

sections.body:
Dedicated GPU pools can occasionally enter an **autoscaling oscillation** pattern (rapid scale up/down or repeated rescheduling) that drives **latency spikes**, intermittent **5xx/timeout errors**, and unstable throughput. This article describes how Support/CS can identify the pattern quickly, apply safe short-term mitigations, and determine when to involve SRE/capacity.

This is a *workaround / operational guidance* article. Engineering follow-up for long-term guardrails is tracked in **ENG-4829**.

---
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- **Product/Tier:** Redwood Dedicated
- **Common triggers:** sudden traffic shape change (burst or step-down), spiky token/sec, large variation in prompt length, or a new workload with higher concurrency.
- **Not typically applicable:** Hosted API (different fleet autoscaling), Private (customer-managed cluster autoscaling; similar symptoms but different knobs/ownership).

---
sections.heading: Applies to

sections.body:
- **Latency spikes** (p95/p99 jumps) coincident with scaling events
- **Intermittent timeouts** or gateway **5xx** during scale transitions
- Throughput that “breathes” (fast for a few minutes, then slow), despite stable request volume
- “Warmup” behavior that never settles (replicas keep changing)
sections.heading: Customers may report one or more of

sections.body:
- Frequent “capacity changing” notes in internal dashboards
- Increased queueing / batching delay even when average load looks acceptable
- Elevated retry rates (customer-side) amplifying load

---
sections.heading: Support-side signals you may see

sections.body:
We use “oscillation” to describe any of these patterns over a short window (typically 15–60 minutes):
1) **Replica thrash:** replica count toggles up/down repeatedly (e.g., 6→10→7→11→8…)
2) **Scale-down too aggressively:** scales down quickly after a burst, then immediately scales back up
3) **Placement churn:** replicas are recreated/restarted frequently (less common; usually infrastructure/placement pressure)
sections.heading: What oscillation looks like (pattern definitions)

sections.body:
- If the pool performs **>3 scale actions in 30 minutes** *and* customer latency is materially impacted, treat as oscillation.

---
sections.heading: Practical rule of thumb

sections.body: Use the Dedicated customer’s canonical pool dashboards (Support-safe “quick view” links may be pinned in runbooks; if you don’t have them, ask SRE on-call for the pool’s dashboard link).
sections.heading: How to confirm (dashboards + key metrics)

sections.body:
Before you interpret graphs, confirm:
- Customer/org name
- Dedicated pool name / cluster identifier
- Region (e.g., us-east, eu-west)
- Affected endpoint(s): chat, completions, embeddings, rerank
sections.heading: 1) Confirm the customer + pool + region

sections.body:
In the same time range, review:
- **Replica count** (or “active workers”)
- **Scale events** (up/down)
- **p95/p99 latency**
- **Request rate / tokens per second**
- **Queue depth / scheduling delay**
sections.heading: 2) Look for correlation between scaling and latency

sections.body: - p95 latency spikes align with *scale-down* events or repeated scale actions.
sections.heading: Strong indicator

sections.body: Oscillation often occurs when the autoscaler chases a noisy signal.
sections.heading: 3) Check utilization targets vs actual behavior

sections.body:
- **GPU utilization** (avg and distribution)
- **KV cache / memory pressure** indicators (if available)
- **Concurrency per replica** (if available)
sections.heading: Review

sections.body:
- GPU utilization swings widely (e.g., 20%→90%→30%) while replica count flips.
- Queue depth spikes immediately after a scale-down.

---
sections.heading: Red flags

sections.body:
- **Scale-down cooldown too short** (system scales down before load stabilizes)
- **Min replicas too low** for the customer’s baseline concurrency (causes repeated warmups)
- **Bursty traffic + short averaging window** on the scaling signal
- **Large prompt-length variance** leading to periodic saturation even with stable RPS
- **Client retries** on timeouts increasing effective load (retry storms)
- **Config mismatch**: max replicas too low for burst, causing alternating saturation/relief

---
sections.heading: Common contributing causes (non-exhaustive)

sections.body: These mitigations are intended to reduce customer impact quickly. Apply in order. If you do not have permissions to change scaling config, escalate to SRE/Capacity with the exact requested changes.
sections.heading: Safe short-term mitigations (Support/CS playbook)

sections.body:
**Goal:** avoid scaling down into an unstable baseline.
- Increase **min replicas** to the smallest value that keeps p95 latency stable during steady-state.
- If the customer has a predictable baseline load, set min replicas to cover that baseline without scaling.
sections.heading: Mitigation A: Stabilize by increasing minimum capacity

sections.body: - Prefer a conservative increase (e.g., +1–2 replicas at a time) and observe for 10–15 minutes.
sections.heading: Operational guidance

sections.body:
**Goal:** prevent rapid downscaling that forces repeated warmups and queue spikes.
- Increase **scale-down cooldown** (or “downscale stabilization window”).
- If supported, increase **downscale step size** conservatism (scale down fewer replicas per action).
sections.heading: Mitigation B: Slow down scale-down behavior

sections.body: - Scale-down cooldown: **15–30 minutes** (depending on workload burstiness)
sections.heading: Suggested starting point (typical)

sections.body: **Goal:** prevent client retries from compounding load.
sections.heading: Mitigation C: Reduce retry amplification (customer guidance)

sections.body:
- Exponential backoff with jitter
- Cap retries (e.g., 2–3 attempts)
- Ensure streaming reconnect logic is idempotent where applicable

Only provide retry guidance that’s consistent with the SDK/docs guidance; link to the relevant troubleshooting page if available.
sections.heading: Recommend

sections.body:
- Raise **max replicas** temporarily (if contractually permitted) or enable burst capacity (Dedicated feature dependent)
- Coordinate with **Capacity/SRE** for approval and scheduling constraints

---
sections.heading: If the issue is triggered by predictable bursts

sections.body:
Exact field names vary by pool generation and internal tooling, but the concepts map cleanly.

| Knob | What it controls | Typical symptom when mis-set | Typical mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| min_replicas | Baseline capacity floor | Frequent downscales cause warmup + latency spikes | Increase min_replicas |
| max_replicas | Upper bound of scaling | Pool saturates during bursts, then oscillates | Increase max_replicas (or add burst) |
| scale_down_cooldown / stabilization_window | How soon we allow scale-down after scale-up | Rapid up/down flapping | Increase cooldown |
| target_utilization (GPU or throughput) | The autoscaler target signal | Noisy scaling decisions | Adjust target or smoothing window (SRE-owned) |
| scale_step (up/down) | How many replicas per action | Overshoots leading to reverse correction | Reduce downscale step |
| metric_window / smoothing | Averaging window for metrics | Autoscaler chases noise | Increase smoothing (SRE-owned) |
sections.heading: Configuration knobs (what they do)

sections.body:
- Support/CS should **not** commit to specific numeric changes without SRE confirmation unless the customer has a pre-approved configuration playbook. When in doubt, propose the *direction* (raise min replicas; increase cooldown) and ask SRE to confirm final values.

---
sections.heading: Ownership note

sections.body:
- Customer is experiencing **sustained high latency** (e.g., p95 > 2x baseline) for **>15 minutes**
- **Error rates** (5xx/timeouts) are elevated and correlated with scaling actions
- Oscillation continues after Mitigation A + B (baseline + cooldown adjustments)
- The customer is a high-severity case (per Support Priority/Severity rubric) or contract requires rapid update cadence
- You suspect capacity constraints (max replicas reached, GPU allocation warnings, placement failures)
sections.heading: Escalate immediately if any of the following are true

sections.body:
- Pool repeatedly hits **max replicas** and still queues requests
- The proposed stabilization requires raising min/max above current reserved capacity

---
sections.heading: Capacity-specific triggers

sections.body:
Post this in the Slack bridge / page to SRE on-call.

**Dedicated autoscaling oscillation escalation**
- Customer/org:
- Pool/cluster:
- Region:
- Time window (with timezone):
- Symptoms: (latency spike, timeouts/5xx, throughput drop)
- Current replica range observed:
- # of scale events in last 30 min:
- Dashboards: (links)
- Recent changes: (traffic burst? config change? deploy?)
- What we tried: (min_replicas change? cooldown change? customer retry guidance?)
- Impact: (approx RPS / tokens/sec affected, # endpoints affected)
- Support ticket: (SUP-xxxx)
sections.heading: What to include in the escalation (copy/paste template)

sections.body:
- Screenshot(s) of replica count + latency overlay
- Any placement/restart errors if visible

---
sections.heading: Attach

sections.body:
Use this as guidance; adapt to the customer tier SLA and do not promise timelines you cannot meet.

**Acknowledgement:**
“We’re seeing scaling activity on your Dedicated capacity that can cause short periods of elevated latency. We’re working to stabilize the pool by adjusting scaling behavior and baseline capacity, and we’ll keep you updated as we validate the effect.”

**Mitigation update:**
“We applied changes to reduce scaling churn (increasing baseline capacity and slowing scale-down). You may see improved latency over the next 10–15 minutes as the pool stabilizes. If you continue to see timeouts or latency above your baseline, please share a few recent request IDs and timestamps so we can correlate in our telemetry.”

**If capacity changes are required:**
“To fully stabilize under your current burst pattern, we may need to adjust reserved/burst capacity. We’re coordinating with our on-call reliability and capacity teams and will confirm next steps shortly.”

---
sections.heading: Customer-facing wording (approved-safe)

sections.body:
- If this issue becomes recurring for a specific customer workload, propose a **Dedicated scaling profile** tuned for their traffic shape (requires SRE + Platform coordination).
- Engineering work to add stability guardrails and reduce oscillation risk is tracked in **ENG-4829**.

---
sections.heading: Notes / follow-ups

sections.body:
- 2026-02-14: Added explicit escalation template + clarified suggested cooldown range; linked engineering follow-up (ENG-4829).
- 2026-02-06: Initial publication from known-issues sprint (Dedicated autoscaling oscillation).

payload.page_title: Prescriptive Telemetry Handoff & Operational Roles for Enterprise Onboarding

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines a prescriptive, role-based telemetry handoff used during enterprise onboarding at Redwood Inference. It focuses on what signals must be collected, minimal quality requirements for those signals, ownership of dashboards and alerts, and an operational escalation ladder that meshes Customer Success (CSM), Integration Engineering, and SRE responsibilities. Use this document as the canonical handoff checklist before signoff on the production acceptance gate.

Scope
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers during the final 2 weeks of onboarding and first 30 days of production.
- Covers: request/response traces, per-tenant cost telemetry, model inference metrics, ingress/egress latency, error-classification, and synthetic health checks.
- Does not replace security/compliance artifacts (use the enterprise-deployment-compliance-evidence playbook for that).

Goals
1. Ensure telemetry provides sufficient context for rapid incident TTR (time-to-repair).
2. Prevent noisy alerts while surfacing customer-impacting anomalies.
3. Establish clear owner for each telemetry artifact to be handed to the customer operations contact.

Required Roles & Responsibilities
- Customer Success Manager (CSM): primary contact for business-level escalations, coordinates QBR artifacts.
- Integration Engineer (IE): owns onboarding of telemetry exporters, verifies schema conformance, and performs initial dashboard walk-through.
- SRE / Site Reliability: owns alert rules, runbooks, and escalation endpoints; responsible for uptime SLO enforcement.
- Customer Ops/Platform Engineer: recipient of the handoff; validates telemetry ingestion and runbook mapping on their side.

Ownership Matrix (text-table)
| Artifact | Primary Owner | Secondary Owner | Acceptance Criteria |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Ingress latency (p50/p95/p99) per-tenant | SRE | IE | p95 < 200ms for interactive tenants; dashboard populated for 30d of test traffic |
| Token cost by model & tenant (hourly) | Finance-ops (CS) | SRE | Hourly granularity, cost-tagging matches billing account |
| Model output quality (evals/feature-set) | IE | Customer Success | Prompt set coverage >= 80% of critical flows |
| Error classification (4xx vs 5xx vs model-misbehavior) | SRE | IE | Errors grouped and sampled with 1:100 sampling for traces |
| Synthetic journey (end-to-end) | IE | Customer Ops | Synthetic every 1m, depl. region coverage, alerts on 3 consecutive failures |

Telemetry Contract (required fields)
- Required metric labels: tenant_id, model_name, route, region, request_id, sampling_rate.
- Required trace context: trace_id, parent_span_id, request_id, backend_node.
- Metric retention for onboarding: 90 days at 1m granularity, 13 months at 1h for billing alignment.

Onboarding Handoff Checklist (step-by-step)
1. Integration Engineer deploys telemetry exporter and shares example payloads in JSON. Example payload snippet:
```json
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-123",
  "model_name": "gptx-14b-q4",
  "latency_ms": 134,
  "p99_estimate": 210,
  "request_id": "r-7d6c4",
  "region": "us-west-2"
}
```
2. SRE verifies metrics in Redwood internal metrics cluster and confirms retention policy.
3. IE and Customer Ops complete dashboard walk-through: top-tokens trend, cost burn, and failure heatmap.
4. Runbooks attached and smoke-tested (see "Runbook Tests" section).
5. Final signoff: CSM confirms business acceptance and schedules the first QBR cadence.

Alert Thresholds & SLO Mapping
- Production SLOs (enterprise tier): Availability 99.95% (per-tenant), P99 inference latency < 350ms for up to 64-token responses.
- Initial onboarding alert thresholds (conservative to reduce noise):
  - Synthetic journey failure: 3 failures in 5 minutes -> Pager to IE oncall.
  - P95 latency deviation > 2x baseline for 10m -> Pager to SRE.
  - Hourly cost anomaly > +60% vs rolling 7-day median -> Alert to CSM & Finance-ops.

Runbook Tests (acceptance scenarios)
- Test A: Simulate KV cache miss storm and verify KV cache miss-rate metric rises and a specific runbook step (scale read replicas) succeeds.
- Test B: Induce model swap (canary -> full) and validate fallback policy triggers and customer route fails over to compatibility model.
- Test C: Inject 5xx error rate and validate triage classification and alert routing (CSM notified, IE paged if persistent).

Escalation Ladder (operational flow)
1. Detect: Oncall receives alert, triages using dashboard + recent traces.
2. Contain: If customer-facing, enable temporary traffic shaping/fairshare and notify CSM.
3. Remediate: Execute runbook steps; if unknown, escalate to Engineering on-call with labeled artifact (trace + minimal repro).
4. Postmortem: If P1 outage or persistent regression, SRE owns RCA within 72 hours and CSM prepares customer-facing summary for QBR.

Integration Checklist for Customer (action items)
- Provide service account with read-only access to exported metrics and traces.
- Validate tenant_id mapping and confirm billing_account tag.
- Run synthetic suite provided by IE for 48h and report anomalies.
- Confirm on-call contact list and escalation phone numbers.

QBR & Ongoing Health Handover
- After 30 days of production, handoff artifacts for the QBR should include: cost delta by model, top 5 failure modes, synthetic pass rate, and any closed RCA actions.
- CSM schedules QBR and invites IE + SRE for the technical deep-dive.

Templates & Attachments (inlined)
- Dashboard template IDs: dashboard.enterprise-onboard.tokens (ID: db-4421), dashboard.enterprise-onboard.errors (ID: db-4422).
- Runbook snippet: "Scale GPU pool -> verify KV cache warmup -> validate p95 latency <= baseline".

Acceptance & Signoff
- Acceptance signoff requires: telemetry checks green (all required artifacts present), 48h synthetic stability, and runbook smoke tests passed. Signoff by IE, SRE, and CSM.

Related pages and references
- See also: enterprise-onboarding/post-provisioning-stability-checklist-2026 for provisioning steps; model-migration-cutover-governance-telemetry-sla-carveouts-2027 for model upgrade notes.

Notes & Rationale
- This playbook biases for explicit telemetry contracts to reduce time-to-diagnosis across organizational boundaries. We prefer short, testable acceptance criteria rather than vague assurances.

Revision history
- 2026-02-10: Initial draft by Avery Chen.
- 2026-02-18: Added synthetic acceptance guidance (reviewer: Priya Nair).
- 2026-03-04: Finalized thresholds and signoff criteria (reviewer: Luis Martinez).

For questions or to schedule a handoff walkthrough, contact the author or the Customer Success tooling mailbox: customer-success-tooling@redwood.ai.

payload.page_title: Secure telemetry sampling and unblinding playbook for enterprise onboarding

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines the recommended configuration and the operational steps for secure, privacy-preserving telemetry sampling and the tightly controlled unblinding process during enterprise onboarding and subsequent QBR investigations. It is intended for Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), Security Engineers, and Observability Onboarding Owners.

Scope
- Applies to all enterprise tenants using Dedicated or Private deployments and hosted customers requiring selective telemetry sharing.
- Covers sampling rules, storage retention for sampled records, pseudonymization and re-identification (unblinding) request flow, audit logging, and QBR data export patterns.
- Does NOT replace legal data-subpoena processes; follow Legal for formal data disclosures.

Key goals
- Minimize telemetry volume while preserving signal for SLOs and QBR metrics.
- Protect tenant PII with deterministic pseudonymization by default.
- Provide a short, auditable emergency unblinding path governed by least privilege.

Important services and topics referenced
- telemetry-gateway (edge ingestion service)
- ingest-proxy (tenant routing and token mapping)
- qbr-telemetry-pipeline (aggregation + retention)
- redwood-observability (internal dashboards)
- telemetry-audit-log (WORM log for unblinding approvals)
- kafka topic: telemetry-sampled-events
- tenant-mapper (maps tenant IDs to anonymized IDs)

Baseline sampling policy (recommended defaults)
- Latency slices: 100% for errors, 10% for tail requests (>= 95th percentile), 0.5% for p50–p90 generation tokens.
- Security/PII signals: drop or mask PII fields at ingest unless explicitly allowed by customer agreement.
- Session-based sampling: consistent per-session sampling using deterministic hash of session-id + tenant-salt to avoid double-sampling.
- Max global sample budget: 5 requests/sec per 10k active users for hosted plans; dedicated plans may negotiate higher budgets.

Example sampling config (YAML snippet)
sampling_policy: |
  version: 1
  default: "p0"
  policies:
    - name: errors
      match: "response.status >= 500 or response.error == true"
      rate: 1.0
    - name: tail-latency
      match: "response.latency_ms >= 300"
      rate: 0.10
    - name: regular-requests
      match: "response.latency_ms < 300"
      rate: 0.005
  session_consistent: true
  pseudonymize: true

Onboard step-by-step checklist (CSE)
1) Pre-provisioning (before ingress enabled)
   - Confirm customer telemetry policy in contract (retention, allowed fields, residency).
   - Assign tenant-salt and enter into tenant-mapper.
   - Create onboarding ticket in JIRA: project CS-ONBOARD and attach telemetry contract clause.

2) Initial configuration (first 48 hours)
   - Apply baseline sampling_policy to the tenant in the telemetry-gateway. CLI example:
     $ rwctl telemetry apply --tenant TENANT_ID --file sampling_policy.yaml
   - Verify ingest-proxy tag rules: ensure token scope contains telemetry:read:sampled and telemetry:admin false for non-admin tokens.
   - Deploy tenant dashboard in redwood-observability with p50/p90/p99 and sampled-events stream.

3) Validation (days 2–7)
   - Run a synthetic workload (see Synthetic probes below) to validate sampling match-rate within +/- 15% of expected.
   - Confirm pseudonymization fields are not reversible without unblinding protocol (see Audit requirements).

4) QBR and steady state
   - Present sampled-data summaries in the customer QBR. For deep investigations, escalate to the unblinding request flow with legal and security approval.

Synthetic probes (validation harness)
- Use the onboarding synthetic runner: onboarding-sim v2.1
- Run with tenant-salt attached and assert: sampled_count / total_requests ≈ configured_rate +/- 15% over 10k requests.
- Command example:
  $ onboarding-sim --tenant TENANT_ID --requests 10000 --check-sampling --expected-rate 0.005

Unblinding request flow (for investigative use)
Purpose: enable re-identification of pseudonymized telemetry for a narrowly scoped investigation (security incident or contractual investigation).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Formal request ticket in Jira CS-UNBLIND-REQ with: tenant ID, scope, time window, justification, and approved approvers (cust success lead + security reviewer + legal reviewer).
- Customer written consent if contract requires (attach to ticket).
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.body:
1) Create Jira request and tag approvers. Template fields must include exact query and minimal time window.
2) Security reviewer validates scope and confirms logs required.
3) Legal confirms whether customer consent or subpoena is needed.
4) If approved, Security triggers the unblinding job via rwctl:
   $ rwctl telemetry unblind --ticket CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234 --tenant TENANT_ID --query "SELECT * FROM telemetry_sam WHERE session_hash = 'abc'" --audit true
5) telemetry-audit-log records the operator, approvers, timestamp, and HSM-signature.
6) Unblinded data is exported to a secure S3 bucket (customer-specific, access-expiring 24 hours) and an access event is recorded in the telemetry-audit-log.
7) Post-unblinding: CSE and Security perform a 3-day review to confirm no overexposure; results attached to the Jira ticket.

Access controls and technical guarantees
- Pseudonymization method: HMAC-SHA256(session_id + tenant_salt) truncated to 16 bytes stored as session_hash. Keys rotated quarterly.
- Unblinding keys stored in KMS/HSM with require-multi-party-approval (2 of 3 approvers).
- telemetry-audit-log is WORM and retained for at least 7 years for compliance customers.
- Only named roles: telemetry-admin, security-investigator, legal-auditor can initiate unblinding; role grants must be requested via IAM-REQ.

SLOs and telemetry health metrics we report to customers
- Sampling accuracy: sample-rate drift < 20% week-over-week.
- Sample ingestion latency: sampled events available in qbr-telemetry-pipeline within 30s of ingestion (95% of events).
- Unblinding turnaround for approved requests: target 4 business hours for emergency requests, 48 business hours for standard requests.

Common troubleshooting and known issues
- Symptom: sample rate appears at 0% for a tenant
  - Check ingest-proxy token scope and tenant-salt presence.
  - Verify that sampling_policy was applied: rwctl telemetry get --tenant TENANT_ID
- Symptom: unblinding job fails with KMS permission error
  - Ensure 2-of-3 approver signature present in telemetry-audit-log. Check KMS access policy for telemetry-service-account.
- Symptom: sampled events missing PII fields (expected) but QBR requires redacted user email for correlation
  - Use the unblinding flow with explicit customer consent; do not modify sampling policy to include PII unless contractually allowed.

Audit and reporting for QBRs
- For each QBR, provide an attachable PDF containing:
  - Sampling policy used during the quarter (YAML).
  - Aggregated sample counts (by latency slice, error vs success).
  - List of any unblinding requests and their Jira ticket IDs (redacted when required by customer).
- Maintain a quarterly internal memo summarizing sample-rate stability and any incidents related to telemetry exposure.

Rollbacks and emergency safeties
- If a sampling policy change causes unintended exposure, immediately:
  1) Revert to previous policy: rwctl telemetry revert --tenant TENANT_ID --to-revision REV_ID
  2) Open incident channel #telemetry-emergency and add Security and CSE owner.
  3) Notify legal if exposure involves PII.

Ownership and contacts
- Customer Success (primary): Maya Chen (author) — escalation contact: cs-oncall@redwood.ai
- Security (approval & investigation): Aisha Patel — security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Observability (dashboards & pipeline): Luca Romano — observability@redwood.ai
- Platform (ops): Diego Alvarez — infra-oncall@redwood.ai

Appendix: example audit log entry (text)
{timestamp: 2026-03-09T14:20:12Z, ticket: CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234, operator: "diego.alvarez", approvers: ["aisha.patel","priya.nambiar"], hsm_sig: "SIG_BASE64", scope: "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z..2026-03-01T02:00:00Z", export_location: "s3://redwood-secure/tenants/TENANT_ID/unblind-CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234.csv"}

payload.page_title: Edge Telemetry Validation and Onboarding Playbook for Enterprise Tenants

sections.body:
Overview:
This playbook defines the recommended validation, onboarding workflow, and operational handoff for enterprise customers connecting edge or client-side telemetry (web SDKs, mobile SDKs, edge ingestion proxies) into Redwood’s telemetry pipeline. It focuses on minimizing false positives in alerts, ensuring SLO alignment, and providing clear escalation and rollback steps for integration engineers and customer success teams.

Scope:
- Applies to enterprise tenants connecting production telemetry for: request traces, sampling events, client-side metrics (latency, token counts), and structured request metadata (tenant_id, route, model_version).
- Covers both SaaS-hosted customers and Dedicated/Private tenants where telemetry is proxied through a sidecar.
- Excludes proprietary third-party observability adapters (see related pages for adapter guides).

Owner and contact information:
- Playbook owner: Maya Chen (Customer Reliability Lead) — maya@redwood.com
- Primary oncall for telemetry ingestion: telemetry-oncall@redwood.com
- Engineering consult: eng-observability@redwood.com
- Customer Success (CS) handoff alias: cs-ops@redwood.com

Goals and acceptance criteria (must be green before handback):
1) Events accepted and parsed without >1% schema failures over 10,000 test events.
2) Ingress latency for validated events <200ms p95 to telemetry-gatekeeper in the customer region.
3) No more than 0.05% increase in global alert noise attributable to new tenant in the first 72 hours.
4) SLOs for tenant-specific dashboards created and reviewed with customer stakeholders.

Key services and components (names used in commands below):
- ingress-gateway (edge ingress HTTP/2 endpoints)
- telemetry-gatekeeper (validation and rate-limiting service)
- tenant-metrics-proxy (tenant-aware proxy that scrubs PII)
- observability-collector (aggregator -> timeseries/long-term storage)

Prerequisites from customer before starting:
- A test API key generated with telemetry:write scope and tenant_id provided.
- Network allowlist for Redwood ingress IPs (list provided by CS).
- A short test dataset (500–2,000 synthetic events) mapped to expected client SDK shapes.
- Designated technical contact and test window (2 hours).

Validation checklist (pre-cutover):
- 1) Schema validation tests
  - Use the test harness to run the sample suite against telemetry-gatekeeper. Expected result: schema_failures = 0 (or <= 1% of events).
  - Example curl payload (JSON):
    curl -X POST https://ingress-gateway.redwood.example/v1/events \n      -H "Authorization: Bearer <TEST_KEY>" \n      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n      -d '{"tenant_id":"acme-corp","event_type":"generation_request","timestamp":"2026-03-04T15:23:10Z","request":{"model":"redwood-llm-v1","prompt_len":312,"tokens":138},"client":{"sdk":"js", "sdk_version":"2.1.0","session_id":"s-123"}}'

- 2) Ingress & validation latency
  - Run 500 events at 5 rps from customer side during test window. Measure time-to-ack from ingress-gateway to telemetry-gatekeeper.
  - Acceptable: p95 < 200ms; if p95 between 200–400ms tag for follow-up optimization.

- 3) Rate-limit and quota checks
  - Confirm tenant quotas in telemetry-gatekeeper: default_quota limits and burst settings.
  - Example admin check (internal CLI):
    rwdctl telemetry quotas get --tenant acme-corp --env prod
    Expected sample output: "daily_quota: 5,000,000; burst_rate: 2000r/s; overage_action: throttle"

- 4) PII scrubbing and allowed fields
  - Confirm tenant-metrics-proxy scrubbing rules. Provide sample event with PII fields and verify removal.

- 5) Dashboard and SLI creation
  - Create tenant-level dashboard: latency_by_route, schema_failure_rate, event_ingest_rate, error_rate.
  - Define SLIs and target thresholds with customer: 
    - Event delivery success = 99.9% over 7d
    - Schema-failure-rate <= 0.5% (initial target)

Step-by-step onboarding procedure:
1. Preparation (CS + Eng alignment, 2–5 business days)
   a) CS collects prerequisites and creates an onboarding ticket in JIRA: ONB-<TENANT>-<YYYYMMDD>.
   b) Assign owners: CS lead, Observability Eng reviewer, Network Engineer for allowlist.
   c) Schedule 2-hour integration window and share IP allowlist and test key.

2. Dry-run validation (1–2 hours, non-production)
   a) Customer pushes 500 synthetic events.
   b) Run schema validation harness: 
      telemetry-harness run --target https://ingress-gateway.redwood.example --key <TEST_KEY> --events sample-set.json
   c) CS and Eng review harness report. If schema_failures >1%: iterate on mapping and retry.

3. Canary (low-volume production-like, 3–24 hours)
   a) Allow 1–5% of production traffic (or 10 rps, whichever is lower) routed to telemetry-gatekeeper.
   b) Monitor dashboards and alert noise for 24 hours.
   c) If alert noise increases >0.05% attributable to tenant, reduce canary volume and troubleshoot.

4. Full cutover (after canary and SLA signoff)
   a) CS issues a go/no-go and schedules final cutover with customer.
   b) Switch traffic and monitor p95 latency, success rate, schema failures at 1, 6, 24, 72 hour marks.

5. Handback and documentation (post-cutover, within 5 business days)
   a) Compile onboarding report and attach to JIRA ticket.
   b) Create tenant-specific dashboard folder and grant read access to customer stakeholders.
   c) Update runbook snippets and signal any config changes to infra as a change request.

Quick verification queries (Grafana/PromQL examples):
- Schema failure rate (last 24h):
  sum(rate(telemetry_schema_failures_total{tenant="acme-corp"}[24h])) / sum(rate(telemetry_events_received_total{tenant="acme-corp"}[24h]))

- Ingest latency p95 (last 1h):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(telemetry_ingest_latency_bucket{tenant="acme-corp"}[1h])) by (le))

Common failure modes and remediations:
- High schema_failure_rate (>1%)
  - Likely cause: SDK version mismatch or missing required fields.
  - Action: Ask customer to upgrade SDK or apply a mapping shim. Use telemetry-harness to generate failing samples and share stack traces.

- Sudden alert noise spike after cutover
  - Likely cause: low-cardinality fields or missing tenant scoping in metric labels.
  - Action: Re-scope metrics, add tenant label, and apply cardinality limits. Open change request to tenant-metrics-proxy.

- p95 ingest latency elevated
  - Likely cause: network peering or region mismatch.
  - Action: Check egress/ingress peering stats, validate region header, and consider routing via closer edge node.

Escalation matrix (when to page whom):
- Severity P0 (ingest down for tenant or >5% request failures for 15m):
  - Page: telemetry-oncall -> engage Observability Eng -> CS Lead -> Exec oncall if >60m.
- Severity P1 (schema failures >5% sustained for 30m or major alert noise increase):
  - Notify: eng-observability, cs-ops; Schedule 30-minute war room.
- Severity P2 (latency p95 >1s for 1 hour):
  - Triage with Network Eng and Observability Eng; schedule 2-hour fix window.

Rollback and safety net steps:
- Immediate rollback: update ingress routing to drop or re-route tenant traffic to a staging collector:
  rwdctl routing set --tenant acme-corp --target staging-collector --reason "emergency-rollback"
- Quarantine mode: enable quota throttle and scrubbers at telemetry-gatekeeper:
  rwdctl telemetry quarantine --tenant acme-corp --duration 30m --action throttle

Post-onboarding checklist (within 7 days):
- Confirm SLI/SLA targets in contract are instrumented and visible in QBR dashboards.
- Conduct a short post-mortem if any P1/P0 events occurred during onboarding.
- Move ticket to "Completed" and ensure knowledge transfer session recorded and stored in onboarding folder.

Operational guidance and best practices:
- Prefer SDK version parity: require customers to run a supported SDK (listed in SDK compatibility matrix).
- Low-cardinality labels only: advise customers to avoid user_id/session_id as primary metric labels; send as trace attribute instead.
- Use sampling for high-volume client events and send full traces for problematic sessions only.

Appendix A — Example minimal event schema (required fields):
{
  "tenant_id": "string",
  "event_type": "string",
  "timestamp": "ISO8601",
  "request": { "model": "string", "tokens": "int" },
  "client": { "sdk": "string", "sdk_version": "string" }
}

Appendix B — Helpful CLI tools and contacts:
- telemetry-harness: repo internal at git@redwood:observability/telemetry-harness.git
- rwdctl (internal CLI) for telemetry and routing changes
- For compliance-sensitive telemetry (PII concerns), involve privacy@redwood.com before canary

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12: Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-02-10: Added canary acceptance thresholds and quarantine CLI commands (reviewer: Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-03-04: Updated SLI targets and added Grafana queries (reviewer: Priya Nambiar)

End of playbook.

payload.page_title: Sensitive Data Retention & Pseudonymization Playbook — Enterprise Onboarding

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes the recommended end-to-end handling of customer-sensitive data for enterprise customers during onboarding and recurring operations. It focuses on: retention policy mapping, pseudonymization approaches we support across deployment modes (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private), request and audit flows, verification steps for handback, and escalation paths for data incidents. Follow this playbook when a customer requires contractual controls over retention, deletion, or partial pseudonymization for compliance (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, sector regulations).

When to use this playbook
- New enterprise customers whose contract or security questionnaire includes data retention/deletion obligations.
- Customers requesting pseudonymization or reversible tokenization for specific data classes.
- During migrations or cutovers where data residency or retention windows change.

Owner & SLA targets
- Document owner: Customer Success (Samantha Lee)
- Technical owner: Platform Security (Diego Alvarez)
- Oncall escalation: Security oncall (rotation – see Security runbook)
- Target SLAs for requests originating from the customer security contact:
  1) Acknowledgement: within 4 business hours.
  2) Technical plan (for retention/pseudonymization changes): 48 business hours.
  3) Completed reversible pseudonymization request (up to 5M records): 7 business days.
  4) Full deletion requests (hosted metadata + cached keys): 48 hours for Hosted; 5 business days for Dedicated; customer-managed in Private (support assists with playbook).

Data classification matrix
| Customer data class | Typical location | Recommended treatment | Retention default | Notes |
|---------------------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------|-------|
| PII (names, emails) | Request body, logs (redacted) | Pseudonymize + encrypted at rest | 365 days (configurable) | PII in logs must be redacted at ingestion
| Generated text (user prompts + responses) | Model input/output, cache zones | Respect customer policy: retain or delete on request | 180 days default | KV cache TTL configurable per customer
| Auth tokens & API keys | Secrets store / KMS | Never stored in plain form; rotate per policy | 90 days | Redwood does not index plaintext tokens
| Audit logs & traces | Observability backend | Aggregated and low-cardinality retention | 365 days | High-frequency logs sampled to meet cost SLOs

Architectural options and implications
- Hosted API: Redwood controls retention/keys; fastest path for contractual deletion. Provide retention profile in contract (standard/short/strict).
- Dedicated: Redwood-managed infra for customer; we operate deletion tools but must coordinate with Reserved Capacity Ops. Deletion time windows are longer due to bulk processing.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): Customer controls primary data plane; Redwood provides step-by-step scripts and verification checks for data erasure.

Selection guidelines
1) If customer requires sub-48-hour deletion, recommend Hosted with strict retention profile.
2) If customer requires on-prem isolation but needs Redwood assistance for migration, document reversible pseudonymization approach during handoff.

Operational request flow (high level)
1. Customer raises a retention/pseudonymization/deletion request through their designated CS contact or Support portal (ticket).
2. CS triages: confirm customer identity, scope (IDs, time window, data classes), and desired outcome (delete vs pseudonymize vs export).
3. CS opens a JIRA (tag: data-retention) and attaches signed authorization if required by contract.
4. Platform Security reviews and approves technical plan.
5. Ops executes plan in sandbox then prod.
6. Verification report produced and shared with customer; ticket closed after sign-off.

Detailed runbook: delete request example (Hosted)
1) Intake & validation
   - Required fields from customer: customer_id, record_ids OR retention window (ISO8601), contact email, signed auth (if contract requires).
   - Validate ticket owner against contract SSO groups.
2) Prepare rollback-safe snapshot (if requested by customer)
   - For Hosted, take a filtered snapshot of metadata only (no secrets) and store in retention vault for 30 days unless customer declines.
3) Execute pseudonymization or deletion
   - Use the data management tool (internal CLI: redwood-datactl) with dry-run first.
   - Sample command (dry-run):
     redwood-datactl delete --customer 12345 --window 2024-01-01:2024-12-31 --dry-run
   - Production run:
     redwood-datactl delete --customer 12345 --window 2024-01-01:2024-12-31 --confirm --audit=case-789
4) KV cache considerations
   - Invalidate affected KV cache prefixes and trigger background eviction if large.
   - Confirm no long-lived prefixes remain for pseudonymized records.
5) Post-process & verification
   - Run verification query to confirm zero results for scoped identifiers.
   - Generate signed verification report including run ids, hashes of affected record ids, and operator audit trail.

Escalation ladder (data handling incidents)
1) Customer Success Engineer (first responder) — <cs-oncall>@redwood.com — 4h SLA for acknowledgement.
2) Platform Security — sec-oncall@redwood.com — 2 business-hour escalation for suspected exposure.
3) Dedicated Ops Lead — ops-dedicated@redwood.com — for capacity/throughput constraints impacting deletion windows.
4) VP Customer Success — vp-cs@redwood.com — for contractual disputes or regulatory notices.

Verification checklist (required before closing ticket)
- [ ] Authorization verified and attached to ticket.
- [ ] Dry-run executed and approved by Platform Security.
- [ ] Production run complete; job IDs and timestamps recorded.
- [ ] KV cache invalidated and redis/edge eviction confirmed.
- [ ] Verification report generated and signed.
- [ ] Customer acknowledgment received or 7-day silent acceptance elapsed.

Sample pseudonymization approach (reversible tokenization)
- Tokenization step: replace sensitive fields with reversible token stored in a customer-scoped, envelope-encrypted store (KMS-wrapped).
- Token format example (JSON):
  {
    \"token\": \"tok_3G6aZ...\",
    \"method\": \"aes-gcm-kms\",
    \"kms_key_id\": \"projects/redwood/locations/global/keyRings/enterprise/cryptoKeys/ent-2025\"
  }
- Controls: token access requires explicit ACL entry and MUST be logged to audit trail.

Example API request for deletion (customer-facing support assist)
- Customer can initiate a scoped export or deletion via the Support portal or API (if enabled in contract). Example curl (support agent acting on behalf):
  curl -X POST \"https://api.redwood.ai/v1/admin/customers/12345/actions/delete\" \
    -H \"Authorization: Bearer ADMIN_TOKEN\" \
    -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
    -d '{\"scope\": {\"from\":\"2025-01-01\",\"to\":\"2025-06-30\"}, \"data_classes\":[\"generated_text\",\"pii\"], \"signed_auth\":\"<base64-pdf>\"}'

Telemetry & observability requirements
- Every retention/pseudonymization job MUST emit the following fields to the data-management metrics stream:
  - job_id, customer_id, operator, job_type (delete/pseudonymize/export), affected_count, start_ts, end_ts, outcome (success/partial/failure), verification_hash
- Alerting thresholds: failure rate > 3% across jobs in 24h window triggers an Ops incident.

Legal & compliance artifacts (required per enterprise contract)
- Signed Data Processing Addendum (DPA) with retention table
- Signed scope authorization for each deletion request (if outside DPA windows)
- Verification report (PDF) with audit hashes and operator signatures

Common failure modes & workarounds
- Large-volume deletion timeouts: schedule batched deletes during low-traffic windows and use background streaming deletions.
- Stale KV cache keys: force eviction and increment cache prefix version for affected customer.
- Missing authorization: route to CS Legal for expedited approval after identity proofing.

FAQ
Q: Can Redwood restore deleted data after a customer deletes?
A: For Hosted and Dedicated, Redwood maintains an optional short-lived snapshot only if customer requests a rollback window; otherwise deletion is irreversible after verification report. For Private, restoration depends on customer backups.

Appendix A — Example verification report outline
- Header: customer_id, case_id, operator, date
- Scope: retention window, data classes
- Execution summary: job_id, nodes used, duration, affected_count
- Hash table: list of hashed identifiers confirming deletion (salted hashing scheme)
- Signatures: operator and Platform Security approver

Change log
- 2025-11-12: Created by Samantha Lee.
- 2025-12-20: Added KV cache eviction guidance (review Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-01-28: Tightened SLA language and added telemetry fields (review Michael Chen).

Related links and references
- Redwood Console: Data Retention UI (internal link)
- Security runbook: data-exposure-incident-playbook
- Product docs: retention-profiles-reference
