payload.page_title: Telemetry Sampling & Privacy‑Balanced Onboarding Guide

sections.body:
Purpose
This document explains a repeatable onboarding pattern for enterprise customers that need high-fidelity observability while honoring privacy constraints and cost budgets. It is intended for Customer Success engineers, SREs, and partner integration teams who run Redwood inference workloads in hosted, dedicated, or private environments.

Scope
- Applies to telemetry collected from production inference traffic: logs, traces, token-level telemetry, request/response payloads, and derived metrics.
- Covers sampling strategies, privacy filtering, acceptance criteria, telemetry assertions, and rollback triggers.
- Does not replace legal or Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA); engage Security/Legal for regulated customers.

Goals
1. Ensure minimum observability to meet tenant SLOs and onboarding acceptance tests.
2. Minimize PII exposure and customer privacy risk by design.
3. Keep telemetry cost predictable and within customer / internal budget.
4. Provide clear operational runbook for escalation and rollback.

Key Terms
- High‑fidelity sample (HFS): full request/response payload, token-level timing, and traces.
- Metric-only sample (MOS): aggregated metrics and sampled traces but no payload.
- Privacy‑filtered: payloads with PII redacted or pseudonymized.

Recommended sampling matrix
Use this matrix to pick an initial sampling configuration based on customer tier and regulatory needs. Adjust during the onboarding runway.

| Customer tier | Default initial sampling | Privacy posture | Typical rate (requests/day) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Enterprise (regulated) | MOS + privacy-filtered HFS for canary | High: pseudonymize, redact | 0.1% HFS, 100% MOS | Use for PCI/PHI customers; review with Security |
| Enterprise (standard) | MOS + 1% HFS | Medium: redaction of known PII types | 1% HFS, 100% MOS | Good balance for SLAs + debugging |
| Growth/PLG | MOS | Low: redaction by default | 0% HFS, 100% MOS | Cost-conscious; escalate to HFS on incidents |

Guidelines for choosing sampling algorithm
- Deterministic reservoir sampling keyed by tenant_id + day for reproducibility.
- Priority-based sampling: elevate failed requests, high latency, or behavioral anomalies to HFS.
- Adaptive sampling: increase HFS during canary windows or after model upgrade events.

Privacy and PII handling
1. Default policy: redact known PII (SSNs, credit card numbers, unstructured PHI) from payloads before any HFS storage.
2. Use ephemeral pseudonymization when customer consents to richer telemetry. Store mapping in customer-managed KMS-backed vaults when required.
3. Tokenization logs: never store raw user-provided sequences for customers that opt out of raw telemetry. Use hashed prefixes for correlation.
4. Provide customers a telemetry expectations doc with clear opt-in/opt-out steps and retention windows.

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step)
1. Pre-onboarding: legal & security signoff for telemetry posture. Record consent level in tenant profile.
2. Define SLOs and acceptance criteria with customer (latency P50/P95, error rate, freshness of embeddings).
3. Baseline run: enable MOS for 7 days to collect metrics and establish normal ranges.
4. Canary window (7–14 days): enable priority-based 1% HFS for a small subset (0.5–2% traffic) and validate instrumentation.
5. Privacy validation: run redaction/pseudonymization tests against synthetic PHI fixtures.
6. Cost projection: run a 48‑hour HFS burst to estimate billing impact; record in tenant pricing sheet.
7. Go/No‑Go gates: must pass telemetry assertions (see below), security review, and cost approval.
8. Post‑go live: keep MOS enabled and scheduled HFS bursts for weekly quality checks.

Telemetry assertions (automated checks to run during acceptance)
- Coverage: 95% of routed requests produce metric envelopes and traces (MOS).
- Correlation: 100% of HFS samples have trace IDs that map to MOS metrics within 30s.
- Privacy: no raw PII found in HFS payloads for tenants with privacy opt-out. Run regex-based and ML-based detectors.
- Freshness: derived metrics and cost-attribution tags are visible in Redwood Console within 5m of ingestion.

Example sampling configuration (YAML)
```yaml
telemetry:
  sampling_strategy: priority_adaptive
  default_metric_sample: 1.0         # 100% MOS (metrics + minimal traces)
  high_fidelity:
    rate: 0.01                        # 1% HFS for canary by default
    triggers: [error, latency_p95_exceed, manual_tag]
  privacy:
    redaction_profile: standard-2026
    pseudonymization: optional
  retention_days: 30
  owner: cs-integration-engineering@redwood.com
```

Example HFS JSON snippet (privacy‑guarded)
```json
{
  "request_id": "r-123456",
  "tenant_id": "t-abc",
  "trace_id": "trace-987",
  "payload": "<redacted>",
  "tokens_observed": 42,
  "latency_ms": 86,
  "sample_type": "HFS",
  "privacy_flags": ["pseudonymized"]
}
```

Operational playbook for incidents during onboarding
1. Detection: telemetry assertion failure alerts to CS/SRE channel.
2. Immediate action: reduce HFS rate to 0% for affected tenant, keep MOS at 100%.
3. Triage: run tool-assisted PII scan on most recent HFS window. If PII is found, follow the Sensitive Data Exposure Escalation (notify Security and Legal, preserve evidence, start customer notification timeline within 48h).
4. Recovery: re‑deploy privacy filter rule updates, run synthetic validation tests, and permit incremental HFS re‑enablement (start at 0.01%).
5. RCA: produce a short incident summary for the customer and an internal postmortem with action items and owners.

Escalation contacts and ownership
- Primary: CS Integration Lead — Aisha Patel (cs-integration@redwood.com)
- Secondary: Observability SRE — Liam Chen (sre-observability@redwood.com)
- Privacy Escalation: Security Analyst — Marcos Rivera (security-telemetry@redwood.com)

QBR & Health check integration
- Include telemetry baseline graphs in the go‑live QBR packet: MOS coverage, HFS sampling rate, privacy incidents (0 expected), and telemetry cost delta vs baseline.
- Suggested QBR cadence in first 90 days: weekly health reports for first month, biweekly for month 2–3, then monthly.
- Actionable metrics for QBRs: metric coverage %, median trace latency, number of HFS samples flagged for privacy review, and monthly telemetry spend by tag.

Documentation & APIs to use
- Telemetry Schema (internal): /docs/telemetry/schema-v2 (request via platform docs portal).
- Sampling control API (example): POST /admin/v1/telemetry/{tenant_id}/sampling
- Redaction rules repository: git://redwood/telemetry/redaction-rules  (access controlled)

Testing and validation matrix
- Unit tests: redaction rules must pass fixture suite for 200+ synthetic PII patterns.
- Integration tests: ensure MOS envelopes correlate with HFS samples across trace boundaries.
- Load test: run 48h of MOS + scheduled 1% HFS at production RPS; validate cost projection within 20% of estimate.

Common pitfalls & mitigations
- Overindexing on HFS early: keeps costs and privacy risk high. Mitigation: use MOS + targeted HFS triggers.
- Insufficient correlation keys: require tenant_id and request_hash in all envelopes.
- Drift in telemetry schema: enforce schema validations at ingest with automatic alerting.

Appendix: sample onboarding checklist (one‑page)
1) Legal/Security telemetry posture OK — checkbox
2) MOS enabled and baseline collected (7 days) — date: ________
3) Canary HFS configuration set (rate: __%) — window start: ________
4) PII redaction verification passed — tester: ________
5) Cost projection uploaded to tenant sheet — owner: ________
6) Go/No‑Go decision: ________ (CS lead, SRE, Customer)

Revision history
- 2026-03-15: Draft authored by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-06-10: Added adaptive sampling guidance and YAML example (reviewers: Liam Chen).
- 2026-08-02: Finalized privacy escalation flow and QBR integration notes (published).

Questions or feedback? Open a ticket to #cs-integration or email cs-integration@redwood.com.

payload.page_title: Quota Protector Webhook Integration and Reconciliation Guide

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This integration guide describes the Quota Protector webhook used by Redwood Inference to reliably surface customer quota events and automate protective credits and throttling adjustments during anomalous billing or rate-limit events. The document explains the webhook contract, delivery guarantees, recommended reconciliation workflow for enterprise customers, on-call runbooks for mismatches, and examples for implementing a receiver and reconciliation worker in third-party billing systems.

Goals
- Reduce false-positive quota rejections for enterprise customers during bursty or partial-failure conditions.
- Provide deterministic reconciliation steps to reconcile token usage vs. billing records within a 72-hour window.
- Support automated protective credits (temporary credits) and safe rollback actions with auditability.

When to use this integration
- Enterprise customers with reserved or committed capacity (Dedicated or Private) that need automated protective measures when perceived usage spikes or system anomalies occur.
- Partners who want proactive notifications and a standard reconciliation API for invoicing systems.

Prerequisites
- Customer must have a configured webhook receiver endpoint reachable from Redwood (HTTPS/TLS).
- Shared secret (HMAC-SHA256) provisioning via the console or SRE onboarding link.
- Access to your billing system’s ingestion pipeline (batch or streaming) for reconciliation.

Webhook contract (delivery semantics)
1) Event types (payload field event_type):
   - quota.alert: short-lived alert when usage approaches a quota threshold (INFO).
   - quota.protective_action: Redwood applied a temporary protective credit or soft-throttle (ACTION).
   - quota.reconcile_request: Redwood requests reconciliation for an identified discrepancy (RECONCILE).
   - quota.reconcile_result: Customer posts back reconciliation outcome (RESULT).
2) Delivery guarantees:
   - Redwood will attempt delivery with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours.
   - Events are delivered at-least-once; receivers must be idempotent (see Idempotency section).
   - Quota.reconcile_request is guaranteed to be emitted once per discrepancy case.
3) Security:
   - Each HTTP request includes X-Redwood-Timestamp and X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256 of body + timestamp with shared secret).
   - Request body is application/json and UTF-8 encoded.

Example payloads
- quota.protective_action (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "e7d1f2b8-9c7a-4a4b-8a6d-2f4a1a6c9b1e",
  "event_type": "quota.protective_action",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T21:03:12Z",
  "action": "temporary_credit",
  "amount_tokens": 250000,
  "reason": "ingestion spike during redesploy",
  "correlation_id": "ops-rollback-20260218-1",
  "metadata": {"affected_routes": ["/v1/generate"], "instance_pool": "dedicated-prod-3"}
}
```
- quota.reconcile_request (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "r2a9b4c5-44f6-4c9b-95d6-0b9f3a2c3d7b",
  "event_type": "quota.reconcile_request",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T22:00:00Z",
  "window_start": "2026-02-18T20:00:00Z",
  "window_end": "2026-02-18T21:00:00Z",
  "reported_usage_tokens": 1200000,
  "observed_usage_tokens": 980000,
  "suggested_action": "credit_25000_tokens_or_manual_review",
  "details_url": "https://console.redwood.com/tenants/enterprise-42/recon/r2a9b4c5"
}
```

Idempotency and receiver best practices
- Use event_id as the primary idempotency key. Store event_id and processing result for 90 days.
- Design reconciliation handlers to accept repeated reconcile_request events and only create a single case per unique correlation_id.
- Return standard HTTP codes: 200 for success, 202 for accepted (async processing), 4xx for client errors, 5xx for transient failures. Redwood will retry on 5xx and network errors.

Sample receiver flow (recommended)
1) Verify signature and timestamp within +/- 5 minutes. Reject otherwise with 401.
2) Check local dedupe store by event_id; if found, return 200 with existing outcome.
3) For quota.protective_action: apply temporary internal protective credit and create an internal ticket with priority=high if action==temporary_credit.
4) For quota.reconcile_request: enqueue a reconciliation job that performs matching between reported_usage_tokens and your billing records for the provided window. Post a quota.reconcile_result when complete.

Reconciliation worker design
- Match level: ingestion-level (per request ID) if available; fallback to route-level aggregation by minute.
- Tolerance band: accept discrepancies <= 2.5% as noise; >2.5% and <=10% trigger automated protective credit up to suggested_action. >10% escalates to human review.
- Audit trail: include the Redwood event_id, your reconciliation_job_id, and links to raw records.

Automated protective credits and accounting flow
1) On reconcile_request that falls into the automated band, your system should:
   - Create a refundable credit entry tied to the tenant and reconciliation_job_id.
   - Post quota.reconcile_result with fields (event_id, job_id, outcome: auto_credit_applied, credit_amount_tokens, note).
2) Finance integration: reconcile refundable credit entries weekly against Redwood billing exports.
3) Auto-expiry: credits applied as protective must be stamped with expiry (default 30 days) and a reconciliation flag to convert to permanent credit only after human approval.

SLOs and monitoring
- Delivery SLOs: Redwood aims for 99.5% successful initial delivery (non-5xx) across webhook endpoints.
- Customer receiver SLOs: process reconcile_request within 8 hours or reply with 202+job_id to indicate longer processing windows.
- Alerting: customers should alert if more than 5 reconcile_request events are queued for >24 hours for a single tenant.

On-call runbook: unresolved reconciliation mismatch
1) Redwood emits quota.reconcile_request with suggested_action. Customer system posts back quota.reconcile_result. If no result after 24 hours, do:
   a) Check delivery logs (Redwood Console -> Integrations -> Webhooks -> Delivery).
   b) Confirm webhook receiver health (CPU, request queue depth, TLS cert validity).
   c) If receiver healthy but processing stuck, escalate to internal billing ops: create ticket with tags [recon-stuck, tenant:<tenant_id>] and assign to billing-ops on-call.
2) If the reconcile_result indicates disagreement (customer refutes observed usage), run a manual audit:
   a) Export raw request logs from Redwood for the window (Console -> Tenants -> Export Usage).
   b) Crosswalk timestamps and request IDs. If discrepancies persist, open a joint investigation with Redwood SRE via the enterprise support channel.
3) If finance disputes remain after 7 days, follow the contractual dispute process (see related_pages billing-credit-policy).

Troubleshooting common errors
- 401 Unauthorized: bad HMAC signature or clock skew. Verify shared secret and sync NTP.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity: missing required fields (event_id, event_type, tenant_id, timestamp). Confirm JSON schema.
- Repeated duplicates: confirm dedupe store retention and idempotency key correctness.
- Large backlog: increase worker parallelism and consider accepting 202 with job_id for long-running reconciliation.

Implementation examples and helper scripts
- Minimal Node.js receiver skeleton (pseudocode)
```js
const express = require('express');
app.post('/webhooks/rdw', verifySignatureMiddleware, async (req, res) => {
  const event = req.body;
  if (await alreadyProcessed(event.event_id)) return res.status(200).send({status:'duplicate'});
  enqueueReconcile(event).then(jobId => res.status(202).send({job_id: jobId}));
});
```

Operational recommendations for enterprise customers
- Keep a rolling 7-day window of raw request logs for quick manual audits.
- Configure alert thresholds on per-tenant queue depth and reconcile_request age.
- Regularly rotate webhook secrets and use mutual TLS for sensitive integrations.

Privacy and audit considerations
- Webhook payloads may contain tenant identifiers and usage aggregates. Do not log PII.
- All reconciliation actions must be recorded with who/what/when for billing audit trails.

Appendix: field reference
- event_id: UUID v4, unique per event.
- correlation_id: opaque string that groups related protective actions / reconcile flows.
- reported_usage_tokens: integer, tokens Redwood observed.
- observed_usage_tokens: integer, any computed alternate observation.
- suggested_action: free-text suggestion (credit_x_tokens | manual_review).

Contact and ownership
- Integration owner: Customer Success (Elena Park) — elena.park@redwood.com
- Escalation path: first-line CSM -> Billing Ops -> Redwood SRE (via enterprise Slack channel #eng-support-enterprise).

Revision history
- 2026-01-12: Created initial draft (Elena Park).
- 2026-02-20: Clarified idempotency and added tolerance bands for automated credits (reviewers: Marcus Li, Priya Nair).

Related artifacts and links
- Console integration page: https://console.redwood.com/docs/integrations/webhooks
- Billing export schema: https://console.redwood.com/docs/finance/billing-export-schema

payload.page_title: Batched Webhook Contracts for Large Payloads and Backpressure Handling

sections.body:
Summary:

This integration guide defines the contract, operational controls, and recommended implementation patterns for integrating customer endpoints that receive batched webhooks containing large payloads. It is intended for platform engineers, integration engineers on customer teams, and Customer Success engineers who coordinate go-lives. The goal is to minimize dropped traffic, bound memory/CPU cost at the receiver, and ensure predictable retry/backpressure behavior across Redwood hosted and Dedicated/Private environments.

Audience:
- Customer Success (CS) and Solutions Engineers
- Integration/Platform Engineers at customer organizations
- Redwood SREs responsible for ingress proxies and client libraries

Why this exists:
- Customers frequently need batched delivery to reduce per-request overhead for high-throughput use cases (e.g., embedding sync, event batches, document uploads).
- Large payloads (>256 KB) amplify failure modes: slow receivers, head-of-line blocking, and unexpected client memory spikes.
- Without an explicit contract, different clients interpret retries/backoff differently leading to cascading load and downtime.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: webhook-style delivery (HTTP/HTTPS) from Redwood integration proxies to customer-owned endpoints used during onboarding and production flows.
- Not covered: pure streaming (gRPC) integrations or in-band synchronous inference responses. See streaming-webhook guide for streaming semantics.

Key definitions (used in this guide):
- Batch: a single HTTP POST containing an array of records/events/documents.
- Payload size: total bytes of the request body, after compression if compression negotiation is used.
- Delivery window: time period within which Redwood will attempt retries before handing the message to dead-letter or escalation flows.
- Backpressure token: short-lived header (X-RWBP-Token) issued by the receiver to indicate temporary capacity constraints.

Contract: request and response expectations

Required request headers:
- Content-Type: application/json
- X-RW-Tenant: <tenant-id> (mandatory for Dedicated/Private routing)
- X-RW-Batch-Count: <integer> (number of items in this batch)
- X-RW-Batch-Bytes: <integer> (uncompressed size in bytes)
- X-RW-Id: <uuid> (idempotency key for the batch)
- Accept-Encoding: gzip (supported, optional)

Recommended (optional) headers:
- X-RW-Prefetch: <estimated-items-ahead> (used by receivers to tune prefetch/buffers)

Response codes and semantics:
- 200 OK: Full acceptance. Redwood considers batch delivered; no retries. Body may contain a JSON acknowledgment mapping ids to per-item statuses (see per-item ack format below).
- 202 Accepted: Receiver accepted batch for asynchronous processing. Redwood treats as success (no retry).
- 429 Too Many Requests: Receiver is asking the sender to slow down. Must include Retry-After (seconds) header or X-RW-Backoff (ms). Redwood will respect Retry-After and fall back to exponential backoff.
- 503 Service Unavailable: Temporary capacity problem. Must include Retry-After or X-RW-Backoff. Redwood will attempt retry according to configured retry window and failover policies.
- 4xx (other): Permanent client errors (e.g., malformed payload). Redwood will surface to customer and not retry.
- 5xx: Transient server error. Redwood will perform retries and escalate per escalation policy if persistent.

Per-item acknowledgment format (optional body on 200):
- If receiver wants to indicate partial acceptance, return 200 with JSON: { "id_statuses": [{"id": "<item-id>", "status": "accepted|rejected|retry", "reason": "optional human text" } ] }
- Redwood will retry only items marked "retry" or missing from id_statuses when configured for fine-grained retries. Coarse-grained integrations should return full 200/202 and avoid partial acceptance.

Payload sizing and batching constraints (default recommended):
| Threshold | Value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Recommended max batch items | 200 | Prevent large CPU/JSON parse spikes on receivers |
| Recommended max batch bytes (uncompressed) | 8,388,608 (8 MB) | Soft recommendation; verify with customer during onboarding |
| Hard max batch bytes (policy) | 16,777,216 (16 MB) | Redwood will reject >16MB with 413 Payload Too Large unless negotiated |
| Preferred per-item size for stability | < 512 KB | Items larger than this should be split or uploaded separately

Negotiating larger payloads: multipart upload handshake
- For sustained use-cases requiring items >512KB or batches >8MB, customers should implement a two-phase handshake:
  1) Receiver responds with 202 and X-RW-Upload-Url: pre-signed URL for multipart upload (S3 or Azure blob allowed).
  2) Redwood will upload large blobs to the provided URL and then POST a trimmed batch with references (blob ids/URLs) instead of inlining payloads.
- Handshake failures should be returned as 4xx/5xx accordingly; Redwood will retry the batch flow but not the individual large-blob uploads unless the receiver accepts them.

Backpressure and flow control mechanism
- Short-term backpressure: receiver returns 429 or 503 with Retry-After in seconds or X-RW-Backoff in milliseconds. Redwood will:
  - Respect Retry-After and pause pushes to that endpoint for the duration plus jitter.
  - Gradually ramp down parallel connections (min connection limit = 1, not 0) then attempt slow probe requests.
- Token-based capacity signaling (recommended):
  - Receiver may issue an X-RWBP-Token header in responses (value valid for 30s). When set, Redwood reduces concurrency to the level encoded in the token metadata (opaque to Redwood). Tokens are advisory and used to coordinate multi-proxy setups.
- Long-term flow control: If an endpoint repeatedly signals backpressure (more than N times within M minutes), Redwood will move the tenant to an adaptive-fanout queue and notify the CS owner for remediation.

Retry policy (default, overridable by customer contract)
1) Immediate retries: on 5xx up to 2 immediate attempts, 200ms apart.
2) Exponential backoff: initial 1s, multiplier 2, max interval 60s. Total retry window default 15 minutes for individual batches.
3) For TTL-sensitive messages (configurable flag in integration manifest), total retry window reduced to 90 seconds.
4) After exhausting retry window, Redwood will:
  - Move batch to tenant-specific dead-letter queue (DLQ) for inspection, AND
  - Trigger CS escalation per the escalation matrix below.

Observability contract: metrics and traces the receiver must expose/emit during onboarding
- Required telemetry for onboarding:
  - DeliverySuccessRate (per tenant, per endpoint)
  - AvgProcessingLatency (p50/p95) measured from initial receipt to 202/200 response
  - CurrentQueueDepth or PendingJobs (if asynchronous processing)
- Redwood will correlate traces using the X-RW-Id and a trace header X-RW-Trace-Id (if present). Customers should log/emit the trace id in request processing logs.

Integration test checklist (onboarding preflight)
1) Basic handshake: Redwood POSTs a batch of 10 small items, endpoint returns 200.
2) Partial acceptance: return per-item ack and verify Redwood retries only expected items.
3) Backpressure simulation: return 429 with Retry-After=30 and confirm Redwood respects the pause.
4) Large payload: send a single 1.5 MB item and verify multipart handshake path completes.
5) Rate flood: simulate burst of 500 batches in 60s and confirm receiver CPU/heap remains within expected bounds.
6) Observability: confirm DeliverySuccessRate and AvgProcessingLatency are visible in both Redwood console and customer dashboards.

Operational runbook and escalation matrix
- Owners:
  - Redwood CS Integration Lead: Maya Chen (primary)
  - Redwood SRE Oncall: eng-sre team (pager)
  - Customer Engineering POC: named during onboarding
- Escalation steps (automated and manual):
  1) Automated: If DeliverySuccessRate < 95% for 5 consecutive minutes, send automated alert and open a P1 incident in Redwood PagerDuty.
  2) CS outreach: CS Integration Lead pages customer POC and opens joint debugging session.
  3) Platform mitigation: SRE may route affected tenant to a buffered DLQ/fanout layer, temporarily reducing direct push traffic.
  4) Executive: If outage extends beyond 2 hours and impacts SLA, CS and Sales notify customer execs and prepare credit/mitigation plan.

Rollout/canary guidance for customers
- Start with a small tenant sample of 1–5% of traffic.
- Enforce a hard peek-limit: max 1 connection and 1 batch/second during initial 24h.
- Gradually increase by doubling traffic every 24 hours while monitoring AvgProcessingLatency and server heap usage.

Examples and code snippets
- Example POST body (compact):
{
  "batch_id": "4c2b8a56-...",
  "items": [ {"id": "i1", "payload": "..."}, {"id": "i2", "payload": "..."} ]
}

- Example 429 response (recommended headers):
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
X-RW-Backoff: 30000
Content-Type: application/json
{ "message": "temporarily overloaded, try after 30s" }

- Example partial ack 200 body:
{ "id_statuses": [{"id": "i1", "status": "accepted"}, {"id": "i2", "status": "retry", "reason": "transient db lock"}] }

FAQ (short)
- Q: What if my endpoint cannot handle batches but can handle many small requests?
  A: Negotiate smaller batch sizes (items <= 20, bytes <= 256KB) and increase concurrency at the receiver side. We can configure Redwood to send more parallel requests instead of large batches.
- Q: Do you support mutual TLS?
  A: Yes. During Dedicated/Private onboarding, mutual TLS and pinned certificates are supported. See onboarding checklist to exchange certs.
- Q: What happens to items lost after retries?
  A: Items that exhaust retries land in a tenant DLQ and are available to the customer for inspection and re-ingestion. The CS team will coordinate DLQ access.

Appendix: configuration knobs (examples to share with customer)
- inbound.max_batch_bytes = 8388608
- inbound.max_items_per_batch = 200
- delivery.retry_window_seconds = 900
- delivery.immediate_retries = 2
- delivery.initial_backoff_ms = 1000

Related reading:
- Streaming webhook retry and deduplication guide (streaming-webhook-retry-and-deduplication-guide-2026)
- Tenant onboarding acceptance testing checklist (enterprise-onboarding/tenant-onboarding-acceptance-testing-and-telemetry-assertions-2027)

Ownership & contacts:
- Document author: Maya Chen (Customer Success Integration Lead)
- CS reviewer: Jonas Meyer
- SRE reviewer: Priya Rao

Change log:
- 2027-09-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2027-11-03: Added multipart upload handshake section after customer pilot.
- 2028-01-10: Finalized backpressure token recommendation and rollout guidance.

This guide should be applied during Dedicated and Private tenant onboarding by default and offered as an integration option for Hosted customers with high-throughput ingestion patterns. For implementation help, contact the CS Integration Lead or open a ticket routed to the integration squad.

payload.page_title: Telemetry-driven SLA Calibration and Handoff for Enterprise Onboarding

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents a telemetry-first approach to calibrating Service Level Agreements (SLAs) during enterprise customer onboarding, and the formal handoff from Customer Success (CS) to Production Operations / SRE. It is intended for CS leads, integration engineers, and production operations owners responsible for ensuring predictable inference economics and availability for new enterprise tenants.

Scope

- Applies to Hosted API and Dedicated (reserved-capacity) onboarding flows.
- Focuses on availability, tail latency, error rate, and cost signal alignment during the first 90 days post-provisioning.
- Does not replace contractual SLA language — this is an operational calibration & handoff procedure that maps telemetry to escalation and runbook actions.

Goals

1. Produce tenant-specific SLA targets informed by observed workload in the onboarding runway.
2. Define a deterministic, auditable handoff checklist from CS to SRE/Platform.
3. Ensure alerting and dashboards are in place with ownership and documented mitigation steps.

When to use this playbook

- Customer goes through enterprise onboarding and reaches the cutover/workload validation stage (typically week 2–6).
- Customer requests contract-level SLA profiling or has bespoke latency/cost targets.
- Early-production anomalies (cost spikes, tail latency regressions) require structured root-cause and adjustment of targets.

Roles and responsibilities

- Customer Success (CS) Lead: coordinates telemetry collection, customer communication, and initial run validation.
- Integration Engineer: implements telemetry tags, sample logs, and assists with synthetic tests.
- SRE / Production Ops Owner: configures final alerts, owns post-handoff incident response.
- Solutions Architect: recommends batching/quantization/routing changes when needed.

Key telemetry signals and mappings

- request_p95_latency_ms: primary latency indicator mapped to "SLO latency".
- request_p99_latency_ms: tail latency; escalation threshold mapping to incident response.
- request_error_rate_5m: 5-minute rolling error rate; triggers severity-2 at >=1%.
- tokens_per_second_per_tenant: throughput / cost proxy; used for cost-forecasting alerts.
- cache_hit_ratio_prefix: KV cache effectiveness; low values (>20% drop) trigger cache-investigation playbook.
- infra_utilization_gpu_pct: system-level signal — sustained >85% indicates capacity saturation.

Example mapping table (text table)

Metric | Observed threshold (onboarding) | Operational mapping
------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------
request_p95_latency_ms | <= 250 ms (interactive apps) | Meet latency target: OK to hand off
request_p99_latency_ms | <= 800 ms | If >800ms for 3 consecutive days -> SRE review
request_error_rate_5m | < 0.1% | 0.1%–1% -> CS triage; >1% -> Page SRE
tokens_per_second_per_tenant | baseline from week-1 synthetic | Forecast cost and reserve capacity
cache_hit_ratio_prefix | > 70% | If drops by >20 percentage points -> investigate cache warming
infra_utilization_gpu_pct | < 65% | >85% sustained -> consider dedicated capacity / autoscale

Telemetry collection and tagging checklist (integration engineer)

1. Ensure all tenant-bound inference requests include tenant_id, route_id, model_variant, and flow_tags in telemetry headers and logs. Example JSON envelope:

```
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-fin-001",
  "route_id": "chat-infer-v1",
  "model": "redwood-open-7b-q4",
  "flow_tags": ["interactive","high-priority"]
}
```

2. Emit per-request timing spans: client_enqueue, server_queue, decode_start, decode_end.
3. Emit token counts (prompt_tokens, completion_tokens) per request for cost attribution.
4. Instrument synthetic canary tests (see Synthetic test matrix below).

Synthetic test matrix (recommended)

- Warmup sequence: run 50 short inference requests (seq_len 32) to populate KV cache.
- Mixed load test: 10-minute run with 70% short (seq_len 32) + 30% long (seq_len 1024) at target TPS.
- Tail test: specific long-context requests (seq_len 4096) to confirm tail latency SLOs.

SLA calibration procedure (step-by-step)

1. Week-1 baseline (CS + integration engineer)
   - Run warmup and mixed synthetic tests at projected production TPS.
   - Collect 7 days of production-adjacent telemetry while customer runs in shadow/validation mode.
   - Compute baseline metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5m error rate, tokens/day, cache_hit_ratio.

2. Draft SLA targets (CS + solutions architect)
   - Use baseline metrics to propose tenant SLA bands: allow SLOs to be anchored to observed p95/p99 plus safety margin. Example: SLA_p95 = observed_p95 * 1.25 but capped to contract upper bound.
   - Document expected tail behavior for long-context requests and map to separate long-tail SLO (e.g., p99_long_seq).

3. Customer review and sign-off (CS + customer stakeholders)
   - Present telemetry summary, forecasted unit cost, and proposed SLOs in a short QBR-style deck.
   - Obtain explicit sign-off on targets or agreed-upon phase plan (e.g., Stage 1: soft SLOs for 30 days, Stage 2: hardened SLOs).

4. Handoff prep (CS + SRE) — minimum 48 hours before formal handoff
   - Ensure alert rules are implemented and tested in staging (see Monitoring queries).
   - Create tenant-specific dashboards and add to the SRE dashboard group.
   - Confirm on-call rotation and escalation contacts: primary SRE, secondary, CS on-call.

5. Formal handoff (SRE accepts ownership)
   - SRE runs synthetic verification and confirms alerts.
   - SRE documents runbook updates and acknowledges ownership in the handoff checklist.
   - CS schedules a 30-day checkpoint post-handoff for QBR alignment.

Acceptance criteria for handoff

- Required: 14 days of telemetry matching baseline behavior (no regressions >15% in p95 or error rate).
- Required: Tenant dashboard and 3 alerts configured (latency, error_rate, infra_utilization).
- Required: SRE runbook added to central runbook repo and owner acknowledged.
- Optional: Cost guardrails and quota caps configured if customer requires budget protection.

Monitoring queries (examples)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- p95 latency (ms):
```
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m])) by (le))
```
- error rate (5m percent):
```
(sum(rate(request_errors_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) / (sum(rate(requests_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) * 100
```
- GPU utilization (avg 1m):
```
avg by (instance) (rate(gpu_utilization_percent_total[1m]))
```
- cache hit ratio (5m):
```
(sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) / (sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m])) + sum(rate(kv_cache_misses_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) * 100
```

Alerting thresholds (starter recommendations)

- Severity-1 (page): request_error_rate_5m > 3% for 5 minutes OR request_p99_latency_ms > 2000ms for 2 minutes.
- Severity-2 (notify + Slack): request_error_rate_5m between 1% and 3% for 10 minutes OR request_p95_latency_ms exceeds SLA_target by 30% for 10 minutes.
- Cost anomaly: tokens_per_hour increases by >150% relative to 7-day rolling average -> create investigation ticket.

Runbook excerpts (actions)

- On page (S1):
  1) Acknowledge page and add immediate note in incident tracker.
 2) Check tenant-specific dashboard for recent deploys, model variant, and queue depth.
 3) If infra_utilization_gpu_pct > 90% -> execute short-term scaling (burst or add capacity) and inform CS.
 4) If error spikes correlate with a specific model_variant -> fall back to last known-good variant using routing policy.

- On notify (S2):
  1) Post summary in tenant Slack channel and CC CS lead.
 2) Increase sampling of traces for affected route.
 3) Schedule triage within standard SRE response window (4 business hours).

Customer communications templates

- Pre-handoff sign-off confirmation (email):

Subject: [Action Required] SLA Calibration Summary & Handoff for {{tenant_name}}

Hi {{customer_contact}},

We completed 14 days of telemetry collection and synthetic validation for your environment. Attached is a short report with observed p95/p99 latency, error rates, and a cost forecast. Proposed operational SLAs: p95 <= {{SLA_p95}} ms; p99 <= {{SLA_p99}} ms; error rate < {{SLA_error}}%.

Please reply with approval or suggested changes. Once approved, we will schedule a formal handoff to our production ops team and enable tenant alerts.

Best,
{{cs_lead}}

Maintenance and post-handoff governance

- 30-day checkpoint: CS + SRE review telemetry and customer satisfaction.
- Quarterly reviews: incorporate QBR metrics and proposal for model/quantization changes that improve economics.
- Regression policy: any regression in p95 or error rate >20% post-handoff triggers an immediate joint triage and potential short-term rollback.

Operational notes and caveats

- Tail-sensitive workloads: for workloads that include sporadic long-context requests, maintain separate long-tail SLOs and make that explicit in the contract appendix.
- Warm caches: onboarded tenants that rely on prefix caching should expect a warm-up period; factor into SLA negotiation.

Appendix: Example dashboard widgets to include

- Tenant Overview: p50/p95/p99 latency trends (24h/7d), request rate, error rate.
- Cost attribution: tokens_per_hour, tokens_by_model, estimated $/hour.
- Capacity: GPU utilization, avg queue depth, instance count.
- Diagnostic traces: sample trace links for recent errors or high-latency requests.

Appendix: Quick CLI snippets for integration engineers

- Query recent tenant logs (example):
```
rdw logs query --tenant acme-fin-001 --from "-6h" --filter "route:chat-infer-v1" --limit 500
```
- Trigger synthetic test:
```
rdw synth run --tenant acme-fin-001 --test mixed-load --duration 10m --concurrency 10
```

Document maintenance and ownership

- Owner: Priya Shah (Customer Success) — maintain telemetry templates and sign-off checklist.
- Secondary owner: Miguel Torres (SRE) — owns alert rules and dashboard templates.
- Review cadence: biannual or when onboarding process changes materially.

Notes and references

- See related runbooks: tenant-stability-predictive-signals-runbook-2026.json for predictive signal definitions.
- See eng-platform dashboards for dashboard JSON templates.

End of document

payload.page_title: Adaptive ingress connection warmup for bursty tenants

sections.body:
Overview

This guide describes the recommended adaptive connection warmup pattern for customers that exhibit highly bursty traffic at onboarding or after a policy change. The goal is to reduce 502/503 spikes, prevent ingress-proxy CPU spikes, and ensure steady, observable ramping of backend capacity for Dedicated and Private tenants. This is intended for Customer Success (CS), Solutions Engineering, and Eng-Infra/SRE teams who coordinate on new tenant cutovers, scale tests, or major product rollouts.

When to use this guide

- New enterprise customers expected to go from test traffic to production burst (e.g., sudden nightly batch, scheduled marketing sends, or unpredictable chatbots).
- Customers migrating to Dedicated instances where tenant-specific warmup helps autoscaler behavior.
- Known bursty workloads that previously caused connection churn, increased 5xxs, or token-processing backlog.

Goals and SLO alignment

- Keep ingress-level 5xx rate <= 0.2% during ramp windows.
- Ensure 95th percentile request latency at ingress proxy < 350 ms for short sequences during warmup (customer baseline may differ).
- Avoid cold-start-style resource contention that causes model-serving GPU preemption or long queueing.

Owner and stakeholders

- Primary owner: Customer Success (CS) - Onboarding & Escalations (owner: Priya Raman).
- Engineering partners: Eng-Infra (networking/ingress), Eng-Serving-Runtime (kernel/batching), Eng-SRE (autoscaling, capacity).
- Customer contacts: Solutions Engineer and Customer Platform/DevOps representative.

High-level approach

1) Classification: identify the tenant’s traffic profile (burst amplitude, events/s, average tokens per request).
2) Adaptive warmup policy: implement progressive connection and request rate increases using client-side and edge-side pacing.
3) Observability & gating: evaluate health via real-time dashboards and synthetic probes during each step.
4) Containment & rollback: automated throttles and failback paths if error thresholds exceed safe limits.

Pre-cutover checklist (CS + SE)

- Confirm tenant capacity profile: expected peak RPS, average token length, concurrency budget.
- Assign SRE on-call for the cutover window and notify Eng-Infra 24h ahead.
- Create a temporary warmup policy in the tenant config namespace (see examples below).
- Schedule synthetic traffic harness run and baseline snapshot 2 hours before cutover.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
This YAML snippet demonstrates an ingress-side warmup policy applied via the edge-sidecar config. Replace placeholder values with tenant-specific parameters.

---
apiVersion: redwood.io/v1
kind: WarmupPolicy
metadata:
  tenant: tenant-acme-inc
spec:
  initial_connection_limit: 20              # initial half-open connections allowed
  connection_ramp: [20, 50, 150, 500]      # connections by step
  step_duration_sec: 600                   # 10 minutes per step
  request_rate_cps: [5, 20, 80, 300]       # requests per second per connection pool
  health_gate:
    max_5xx_rate_pct: 0.2
    max_ingress_cpu_pct: 70
    max_queue_latency_ms: 500
  backoff_policy:
    on_threshold_breach: scale_down_step
    cooldown_sec: 300
---

Client-side recommendations

- Encourage the customer to use exponential backoff with jitter for retries (max 3 attempts) and a capped concurrency.
- Provide a lightweight reference client that respects server-supplied warmup tokens and per-connection rate hints. Example HTTP header: X-Redwood-Warmup-Window: step=2;allowed-cps=20.

Step-by-step warmup playbook

1) Step 0 — Preparation (T-120 to T-10 minutes)
   - Validate tenant config and warmup policy presence.
   - Start synthetic probe job hitting representative endpoints at low CPS (2–5 cps).
   - Take baseline telemetry snapshot (ingress 50/95/99 latencies, 5xx rates, edge CPU).

2) Step 1 — Initial connections (T=0 to +10 minutes)
   - Allow initial_connection_limit connections and enforce request_rate_cps[0].
   - Observe for anomalous 5xx increase or client retransmissions.
   - If health_gate breached: trigger backoff (see Containment).

3) Step 2 — Moderate ramp (+10 to +20 minutes)
   - Increase connection limit to connection_ramp[1] and CPS to request_rate_cps[1].
   - Validate KV cache hit ratios and runtime queue depths (should be trending down).

4) Step 3 — High ramp (+20 to +30 minutes)
   - Increase to connection_ramp[2] / request_rate_cps[2].
   - Confirm model-serving worker pools are scaling and GPU utilization <= 85%.

5) Step 4 — Full throughput (+30 to +40 minutes)
   - Allow final ramp step and monitor for steady-state metrics.
   - Mark warmup complete in tenant metadata and remove step header guidance to clients.

Containment and rollback

- Automated containment: edge-sidecar evaluates health_gate every 30s. If any metric breaches: reduce to previous stable step and set cooldown for cooldown_sec.
- Manual rollback: SRE can immediately flip tenant to safe-mode (hard throttle to 10 cps and single connection pool) and open an incident with CS and Eng-Serving-Runtime.

- Emergency isolation: If ingress proxy becomes unhealthy across nodes (ingress CPU > 90% for 2 minutes or 5xx rate > 2% for 1 minute), execute tenant isolation script: /ops/isolate-tenant --tenant tenant-acme-inc --mode drop-new-conns. Notify customer.

Observability and dashboards

Essential charts to have on the warmup dashboard (CS + SRE):
- Ingress: 5xx rate (1m/5m), 50/95/99 latency, connection counts, active streams.
- Edge-sidecar: per-tenant connection pools, queue depth, average request processing time.
- Serving runtime: request queue latency, GPU utilization, batching efficiency, KV cache hit ratio.
- Synthetic probes: success rate, median latency, token throughput.

Suggested Grafana queries (examples)

- 5xx rate: sum(rate(requests_total{status=~"5..",tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m]))
- Ingress connections: sum(ingress_connections{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"})
- Queue latency histogram: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_processing_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[5m])) by (le))

Verification checklist (post-warmup)

- Latency: 95th percentile request latency below target (customer-specific, default 350 ms).
- Error rate: 5xx rate < 0.2% sustained for 30 minutes.
- Throughput: achieved >= 90% of projected peak RPS without queue growth.
- Resource: GPU utilization stable and not sustained > 88% for > 10 minutes.
- Client: client observed fewer than 1 retry per 1,000 requests.

Communication templates

- Pre-cutover email to tenant: short checklist, warmup window, expected behavior, contact on-call.
- Post-cutover summary: snapshot of key metrics, anomalies, and next steps.

Escalation path (if warmup fails)

1) CS Lead -> SRE on-call (pager) -> Eng-Serving-Runtime -> Eng-Infra networking lead.
2) If there is immediate customer impact (customer-reported errors affecting revenue), open a P1 and follow incident runbook.

Sample run-command for emergency isolation
sections.heading: Example policy (edge-side)

sections.body:
redwood-ops tenant isolate --tenant tenant-acme-inc --conns 10 --reason "warmup breach"

FAQs and edge cases

Q: Customer uses third-party proxies that pre-open connections.
A: Recommend brokered warmup token returned via header; proxy teams must honor X-Redwood-Warmup to avoid pre-filling connection pools. If impossible, schedule longer step_duration_sec and smaller per-step ramp.

Q: Warmup causes autoscaler thrash (scale up and immediate scale down).
A: Increase scale stabilization window in the tenant autoscaler policy and rely on edge warmup to smooth the observed load.

Q: Token-based workloads vs. many short requests.
A: For token-heavy requests, prioritize KV cache priming: run representative synthetic requests that mirror real token lengths during the earlier warmup steps.

Appendix: quick links and scripts

- Tenants: /ops/tenants/{tenant-id} (view/add warmup policy)
- Warmup script: /scripts/warmup-injector --tenant tenant-acme-inc --pattern ramped --duration 40m
- Isolation runbook: /runbooks/tenant-isolation.md

Change log

- 2026-04-12: Initial draft and CS-Infra alignment.
- 2026-05-03: Added backoff policy examples, dashboard queries, and isolation script commands.

Contact

For questions or to request a custom warmup policy, contact the CS Onboarding lead (Priya Raman) or Eng-Infra (pager).

payload.page_title: Ingress Observability Bakeoff and Telemetry Declaration for Enterprise Cutovers

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the standardized bakeoff and telemetry declaration process used during enterprise tenant cutovers and large customer integrations. The goal is to validate ingress observability, telemetry completeness, and SLA readiness before a production flip. This reduces incident churn, shortens the stabilization window, and provides a clear pass/fail decision path for the cutover gate.

Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private launch cutovers and any Hosted onboarding with >1M monthly tokens or complex network topologies (VPC peering, private link, or regional egress controls). Not intended for small self-serve trials.

Audience: Customer Success Engineers, Solutions Engineers, Platform Oncall, Customer SRE, and Product Integration owners.

Summary of changes vs. previous practice:
- Formalizes a measurable bakeoff with explicit SLO thresholds and telemetry schema declaration.
- Introduces a compact "Telemetry Declaration" template that customers and Redwood must sign off on before canary.
- Defines ownership and escalation paths for failed observability checks to prevent ambiguous handoffs.

Roles & Responsibilities

- Customer Success (CSE): coordinates schedule, invites stakeholders, captures acceptance artifact.
- Solutions Engineering (SE): runs ingress tests, verifies request/response parity and header-level telemetry.
- Customer SRE / Network: validates network routing, TLS, and client certificate behavior.
- Platform Oncall: validates server-side traces, span naming, and alerts.
- Product Integration Owner: final sign-off for functional equivalence and rollout readiness.

Pre-bakeoff checklist (minimum required)

1) Provisioning and access
- Tenant configuration deployed (route table, DNS entries, certs, API keys).
- Red-team access account for SE & Platform Oncall active.
- Signed Telemetry Declaration draft (see template).

2) Baseline telemetry verified
- Metrics exposed: ingress_rps, ingress_error_rate, request_latency_p50/p95, token_count_per_request.
- Traces created for request start/end and model invocation with parent/child spans.
- Logs include request_id, tenant_id, route, and sampling flag.

3) Alerting and dashboards
- Canary dashboard created with the tenant tag.
- Alerts configured: ErrorRate >= 2% sustained for 5m, p95 latency > 2s for 10m, Token cost delta +30% vs baseline for 1h (optional).

Bakeoff procedure (90–120 minute window recommended)

Preparation (30m)
1. Confirm windows and invites; ensure stakeholders available for rapid decisions.
2. Seed simulated workload: run the standard ingress load generator for the workload class (examples in appendix).
3. Snapshot baseline: capture current dashboards, traces, and logs as the "pre-bakeoff" reference.

Phase A — Functional validation (20m)
1. Run 200–500 requests across core routes with representative payloads (short, medium, long).
2. Verify request/response parity for 100% of sampled requests (no silent truncation, correct streaming delim).
3. Validate header propagation: X-Request-Id, X-Tenant-Id, X-Region, X-Trace-Parent.
4. Record sample traces (3 successful, 1 with synthetic error) and attach to the bakeoff notes.

Phase B — Observability validation (30m)
1. Metrics: Confirm ingestion to Redwood telemetry or customer telemetry endpoint within 60s for meter points below.
2. Traces: Open a trace in APM and confirm model invocation spans contain span attributes: model.name, model.version, kv_cache_hit (true|false), quantized (true|false).
3. Logs: Search last 500 log lines for request_id mapping to trace_id.
4. Dashboard: Canary dashboard shows ingresses tagged by tenant and route.

Phase C — Stress and edge-cases (20–40m)
1. Burst test: 3x expected peak RPS for 60s to validate aggregation and sampling behavior.
2. Partial failure: Induce an artificial model timeout for 30s and confirm fallback policy is visible in traces and fallback_count metric increases.
3. Token and billing sample: Send a mixture of short/long prompts and compare per-request token metadata to billing token counters.

Acceptance criteria (pass/fail)

Pass requires ALL of the following: (explicit numeric thresholds)
- End-to-end request success rate >= 98% during functional validation.
- Observability latency: metrics ingestion lag <= 60s 95% of the time.
- Traces sampled and linkable: >= 95% of sampled request IDs must map to at least one trace with a model invocation span.
- Header propagation: 100% of sampled requests must contain X-Request-Id and X-Tenant-Id in both logs and inbound request headers.
- Alerts: No unacknowledged critical alerts fired during the bakeoff window (SRE may temporarily mute non-actionable alerts with approval).

Fail conditions (examples)
- Metrics ingestion lag > 120s or >5% metric points lost.
- Traces missing model invocation attributes in >=10% of sampled traces.
- Token accounting divergence >15% vs expected (requires immediate triage).

Telemetry Declaration Template (customer + Redwood sign-off)

Provide the following fields and confirm agreement before canary. Use the minimal JSON snippet below as the canonical declaration that will be attached to the cutover ticket.

--- JSON snippet (single-line friendly) ---
{ "tenant_id": "<tenant-id>", "telemetry_target": "redwood:observability-prod OR customer:apm-endpoint", "metrics": ["ingress_rps","ingress_error_rate","request_latency_p95","token_count_per_request"], "traces_required": true, "log_fields_required": ["request_id","tenant_id","route","status_code"], "ingestion_slo_seconds": 60 }
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- telemetry_target: specify if telemetry should be forwarded to Redwood ingestion or to a customer-managed APM. If customer-managed, include endpoint and auth in related secure doc.
- traces_required: if false, bakeoff must be approved only for low-risk features; default is true.

Telemetry mapping recommendations

Metric name -> Redwood canonical mapping
- ingress_rps -> telemetry.ingress.rps
- ingress_error_rate -> telemetry.ingress.errors.percentage
- request_latency_p95 -> telemetry.ingress.latency.p95_ms
- token_count_per_request -> telemetry.billing.tokens_per_req

Span attribute recommendations
- model.name (string)
- model.version (string)
- model.invocation_time_ms (number)
- kv_cache_hit (boolean)
- quantized (boolean)
- request.priority (string)

Rollout decision matrix (example)

- Green: All acceptance criteria met -> Proceed to canary (10% traffic) and schedule 2-hour monitoring block.
- Yellow: One non-critical observability gap (e.g., missing optional span attribute) -> Defer canary until quick remediation or allow canary under compensating control (shorter canary, increased sampling). Must be approved by Platform Oncall and CSE.
- Red: Any metric or trace lag failures, token accounting divergence >15%, or missing header propagation -> Halt cutover and open a joint incident with SRE and SE.

Post-bakeoff artifacts (deliverable attachments)

- Bakeoff summary note (1–2 pages).
- Exported sample traces (3–10 traces) with trace IDs.
- Canary dashboard snapshot (PNG).
- Signed Telemetry Declaration JSON (attached to ticket).

Escalation & contact matrix

- First 15m: On-call Platform Engineer (pager) + SE lead slack channel (#se-platform-integration).
- 15–60m: Customer SRE + CSE primary.
- >60m or critical failure: Engineering Incident Lead and Product Integration Owner notified; declare joint incident with runbook id: OB-INGRESS-2028.

Appendix A — Example commands and snippets
sections.heading: Notes on fields

sections.body: curl -s -D - -H "X-Request-Id: test-req-123" -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-prod-42" https://tenant.example.redwood.ai/v1/generate | jq '.
sections.heading: Curl header propagation verification

sections.body: record: tenant_request_latency_p95_ms = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=~"tenant-prod-.*"}[5m])) by (le, tenant))
sections.heading: Record per-tenant p95 in ms

sections.body:
trace_id = search_traces("attributes.request_id:test-req-123")

Appendix B — Workload generator reference

- Use the ingress-load-tool repo (internal): se-tools/ingress-load-generator. Recommended profile: "enterprise-chat-mixed" (50% short, 30% medium, 20% long).
- Command: ./loadgen --profile enterprise-chat-mixed --tenants tenant-prod-42 --rps 50 --duration 300

Governance and versioning

This document is the canonical bakeoff procedure for enterprise ingress observability. Any deviations must be recorded on the cutover ticket and approved by Customer Success and Platform Oncall. Changes to the Telemetry Declaration template must be reviewed by the Observability Standards working group.

Related documentation and links

- Onboarding post-provisioning stability checklist (internal)
- Observability fallback circuit and customer escalation protocol

Document history

- 2027-11-15: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2027-12-06: Added stress test and token accounting checks after SE field feedback.
- 2028-01-10: Revised telemetry SLO to 60s ingestion lag and formalized Telemetry Declaration template.

Contact for questions: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) or #customer-success-integrations on Slack.

payload.page_title: edge-telemetry-sidecar-onboarding-and-fidelity-guardrails-2026

sections.body:
Overview

This guide describes the recommended onboarding flow, configuration guardrails, and troubleshooting ladder for deploying the Redwood Edge Telemetry Sidecar in enterprise Dedicated and Private deployments. The sidecar provides low-latency, filtered observability from customer ingress points to Redwood's telemetry pipeline while protecting PII, maintaining metric fidelity, and ensuring bounded resource impact on tenant gateways.

Who should use this guide

- Customer Success and Solutions Engineers onboarding dedicated/private tenants with custom ingress.
- Customer Platform Engineers responsible for sidecar installation and runtime validation.
- Observability/Telemetry Engineers verifying contract compliance and SLOs.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals: ensure telemetry completeness for critical signals, protect sensitive data at the edge, limit sidecar CPU/memory to avoid contention, provide clear rollback and escalation paths.
- Non-goals: full ingestion pipeline design; this guide assumes the customer's telemetry will route to Redwood's ingestion endpoints or a validated forwarder.

Key terms

- Sidecar: the telemetry agent deployed alongside an ingress/gateway service (Kubernetes DaemonSet / per-pod sidecar).
- Fidelity: percent of expected events/metrics retained after filtering and scrubbing.
- Contract: the documented set of events/metrics/logs the customer and Redwood agree to collect.

Quickstart checklist (high level)

1) Preflight: sign the Observability Contract SOW and verify CIDR allowlist.
2) Install sidecar in a staging namespace with sample traffic.
3) Validate signature TLS and auth with Redwood ingestion.
4) Run fidelity tests (see Validation section).
5) Approve production rollout, enable sampling/PII scrubbing rules, and monitor SLOs for 72 hours.

Required artifacts from customer before install

- Ingress topology diagram (service names, pods, expected peak RPS).
- Sample event/metric schema or example payloads.
- Accepted sampling targets and privacy constraints (fields to redact).
- Network egress rules (outbound to Redwood ingestion endpoints).

Sidecar configuration guardrails

The following guardrails are mandatory for Dedicated and Private environments unless an explicit exception is approved by Security and Compliance. Each item includes a rationale and recommended default.

- TLS-only transport to Redwood (rationale: prevent eavesdropping). Default: enforce mTLS, TLS 1.2+ with cert pinning.
- Max CPU per sidecar: 0.25 cores (rationale: avoid noisy neighbor on gateway pod). Default: request=100m, limit=250m.
- Max memory per sidecar: 256Mi (rationale: KV cache and buffers). Default: request=128Mi, limit=256Mi.
- Bounded local buffer: 10MB per sidecar, backpressure to client after buffer reach (rationale: avoid OOM and loss during downstream outages).
- PII redaction pipeline: apply schema-driven scrubbing before any logs/attributes leave the sidecar (rationale: regulatory compliance).
- Default sampling: 100% for error/latency traces, 10% for standard request traces, configurable per-route.
- Schema validation: drop fields that fail schema contract and emit a validation_error metric.

Example sidecar config snippet (kubernetes manifest fragment)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: telemetry-sidecar-config
data:
  sidecar.yaml: |
    transport:
      endpoint: https://telemetry-ingest.redwood.example
      tls: { enable: true, mTLS: true }
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
      limits:   { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
    buffer:
      max_bytes: 10485760
    sampling:
      default_trace_rate: 0.10
      error_trace_rate: 1.0
    pii_scrub_rules:
      - path: $.request.user.email
        action: redaction
      - path: $.request.body.credit_card
        action: drop

Validation and acceptance tests (executable steps)

1) Connectivity and auth (owner: customer-platform / Redwood Oncall)
   - curl -v --cert client.crt --key client.key https://telemetry-ingest.redwood.example/health should return 200.
2) TLS verification (owner: customer-platform)
   - Check peer certificate CN matches expected.
3) Resource containment (owner: customer-platform)
   - Deploy load generator with 50% of expected peak RPS for 10 minutes. Confirm sidecar resource usage <= configured limits.
4) Fidelity smoke tests (owner: customer-success)
   - Send 1,000 synthetic requests with seeded IDs. Confirm at least 995 IDs (>=99.5%) are observed in Redwood ingestion indexing within 30s.
   - For error conditions (50 injected 5xx responses), confirm all error traces arrive (100% capture).
5) PII scrubbing test (owner: customer-security)
   - Send payloads including known PII fields. Verify those fields are redacted/dropped in the ingested payloads.
6) Backpressure behavior (owner: eng-sre)
   - Simulate downstream outage by blocking egress; confirm sidecar exposes an http 429 to upstream when buffer > 80% and recovers when egress is restored.

SLOs and acceptance criteria

- Telemetry completeness: 99.5% of contract-required events are delivered to Redwood ingestion within 30s (measured per hour).
- Ingest latency: 95th percentile <= 2s from event emission to ingestion acknowledgment.
- Sidecar CPU: < 60% of configured limit under normal peak.
- PII leakage incidents: 0 per 90-day window.

Monitoring and dashboards

Required metrics to publish to the tenant's dashboard (suggested panel names):

- sidecar.event_delivery.success_rate (panel: "Telemetry Delivery Rate")
- sidecar.buffer.usage_bytes (panel: "Sidecar Buffer")
- sidecar.tls.handshake_failures (panel: "TLS Failures")
- sidecar.pii.redaction.count (panel: "PII Redactions")
- sidecar.validation.error_rate (panel: "Schema Validation Errors")

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- P0: sidecar.event_delivery.success_rate < 95% for 5m — page on-call SRE and Customer Success.
- P1: sidecar.buffer.usage_bytes > 80% for 10m — create incident and notify customer platform.
- P2: sidecar.tls.handshake_failures > 5 per minute for 5m — notify security and review cert rotation.

Rollback and canary strategy

- Canary Deployment: 1% of production pods for 30m, validate SLOs, increase to 10% for 1h, then 30% for 2h before full rollout.
- Fast rollback criteria (automated): any P0 alert or buffer > 95% for 5m should trigger an automated rollback to prior sidecar image config.
- Manual rollback: Customer Success must coordinate with customer platform and SRE; use documented runbook: "kubectl rollout undo" command and confirm traffic stability for 15 minutes.

Troubleshooting ladder (ordered)

1) Symptom: No telemetry received from tenant
   - Check sidecar pod status (kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=telemetry-sidecar).
   - Review sidecar logs for TLS errors and auth failures.
   - Confirm egress firewall rules include telemetry ingestion endpoints.

2) Symptom: High validation_error metrics
   - Compare incoming payloads to agreed contract. If contract has changed, route to Solutions for schema versioning.
   - If unexpected fields appear frequently, add transformation rule in sidecar config and patch via ConfigMap.

3) Symptom: PII observed in Redwood ingestion
   - Immediately circuit the pipeline: switch sidecar to fail-closed mode (drop all logs) and open an incident (see Escalation matrix).
   - Collect impacted sample messages and perform forensics with Security.
   - Temporary mitigation: enable additional regex-based scrub rules applied server-side until sidecar rule can be patched.

Escalation matrix (who to call)

- First contact: Customer Success Engineer (CSE) assigned to account — slack: #cse-<customer>-oncall
- If unresolved in 15 minutes: Observability Engineer (obs-eng) — slack: #obs-oncall
- If PII or regulatory exposure suspected: Security Incident Response — pager: sec-incident-pager and notify legal.
- If sidecar resource exhaustion threatens production: SRE pager.

Post-deployment ops and QBR inputs

For the first QBR after onboarding, Customer Success should prepare the following artifacts:

- Telemetry fidelity report (30/60/90-day buckets) showing delivery rate, latency, and redaction counts.
- Incident log summarizing any sidecar-related alerts, root cause, and mitigations.
- Resource utilization trend across the tenant's gateway fleet.
- Proposed optimizations (e.g., tune sampling or move heavy traces to async export).

Ownership and contacts

- Customer Success (primary owner for onboarding): Marcus Li (marcus@redwood.example)
- Observability Engineering (validation & dashboards): Priya Kapoor (priya@redwood.example)
- Security (PII rules & incident): Eleanor Chen (eleanor@redwood.example)
- SRE (rollouts & performance): Diego Marquez (diego@redwood.example)

Appendix A: Example fidelity test harness (shell)

  id="test-$(date +%s)-$i"
  curl -s -X POST https://tenant-ingress.example/endpoint -d \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"payload\\\":\\\"ping\\\"}\" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' &
done

payload.page_title: Observability Privacy Filter and Keyed Telemetry Onboarding Playbook

sections.body: This playbook describes the recommended process for onboarding enterprise customers to Redwood's keyed telemetry pipeline with a privacy-filtering layer ("Observability Privacy Filter") between customer data sources and Redwood observability systems. It is intended to ensure compliance with customer privacy constraints, minimize PII leakage, and preserve the fidelity required for SLO/QBR reporting and cost accounting.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers integrating their application telemetry (request traces, token-level cost attributions, custom metrics) into Redwood observability.
- Covers contract schema negotiation, filter configuration, implementation patterns, validation, rollout, and post-onboarding handoff to customer ops and Redwood CS.
- Does not replace legal data processing agreements; coordinate with Security & Legal for restricted data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs) onboarding telemetry
- Integration engineers on the customer side
- Platform/SRE teams validating ingestion and SLOs
- Account teams preparing QBR telemetry bundles
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Keyed telemetry: telemetry records that include a tenant identifier (key) for attribution and routing.
- Observability Privacy Filter (OPF): a configurable filter service deployed at the customer edge or as a Redwood-managed middleware that redacts/replaces sensitive attributes while preserving routing keys and aggregates.
- Telemetry Contract: a schema agreement between customer and Redwood that defines field names, types, retention hints, and sensitivity labels.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) Signed Data Processing Addendum (DPA) and any sector-specific addenda (finance, healthcare).
2) Approved telemetry contract draft and agreed retention windows.
3) Network ingress configured: IP allowlist, TLS certificates, and, if Private, VPC peering details.
4) Access to a staging project/tenant in Redwood with synthetic traffic capability.
5) Contact list: CSE, customer integration lead, customer security lead, Redwood SRE reviewer.
sections.heading: Prerequisites (customer & Redwood)

sections.body:
- Customer Success (owner): run onboarding, validate acceptance tests, and deliver QBR reporting templates.
- Customer Integration Lead (owner): implement client-side emitters and local filters.
- Security & Legal (reviewer): sign-off on privacy filter rules and DPA terms.
- Platform/SRE (reviewer): confirm ingestion capacity and SLO measurement hooks.

Step-by-step onboarding checklist (recommended timeline: 4–8 business days):
1) Kickoff (Day 0):
   - Introductions and objectives; share this playbook and telemetry contract template.
   - Confirm DPA status and desired retention/region constraints.
2) Contract negotiation (Day 0–2):
   - Exchange telemetry contract JSON schema (example below).
   - Mark sensitive fields with sensitivity labels: PUBLIC | CONFIDENTIAL | PII.
3) Filtering strategy workshop (Day 1–3):
   - Decide where OPF will run: customer-side agent (recommended for Private) or Redwood-managed ingress.
   - Choose operators: redact, hash (HMAC-SHA256 with tenant salt), truncate, pseudonymize.
4) Staging implementation (Day 2–4):
   - Customer deploys emitters to staging; OPF applied to traffic.
   - CSE runs acceptance suite including token-counting, latency sampling, and synthetic loads.
5) Validation and telemetry QA (Day 3–5):
   - Verify key preservation for routing and aggregation.
   - Assert no PII in fields labeled PII via automated scans (see validation commands).
6) SLO mapping and QBR dataset selection (Day 4–6):
   - Map telemetry fields to SLOs (latency, error-rate, token-cost).
   - Define QBR metrics and retention windows for executive dashboards.
7) Production go/no-go and rollout plan (Day 5–7):
   - Agree on canary % pattern, throttling/queue limits, and fallback to raw ingest for debugging windows.
8) Production rollout (Day 6–8):
   - Apply OPF to production canary; monitor for missing keys or metric gaps.
   - Gradual ramp with checkpoints at 10%, 50%, 100%.
9) Post-go monitoring and tuning (Week 1):
   - Monitor telemetry completeness, SLO drift, and cost attribution accuracy.
   - Tune filter rules to restore necessary fields if over-redaction occurs.
10) Handoff and QBR preparation (Week 1–2):
   - Deliver a QBR telemetry bundle and runbook for customer ops.
sections.heading: Roles and Ownership

sections.body:
| field_name | type | example | sensitivity | retention_hint | notes |
| request_id | string | "req_01a7..." | PUBLIC | 7d | routing key for traces |
| tenant_id | string | "tenant:acme" | CONFIDENTIAL | 30d | must be preserved (hashed if required) |
| user_email | string | "alice@acme.com" | PII | 30d | must be redacted or pseudonymized unless DPA allows |
| prompt_tokens | integer | 12 | PUBLIC | 90d | used for cost attribution |
| response_tokens | integer | 64 | PUBLIC | 90d | used for cost attribution |
| model_id | string | "redwood/gptx-4b-q" | PUBLIC | 365d | model attribution for cost and debugging |
sections.heading: Telemetry contract (example snippet)
Telemetry contract JSON (recommended format)

sections.body:
- redact: remove the field entirely from emitted telemetry. Use when customer policy prohibits storage.
- hash: HMAC-SHA256 with tenant-specific salt; preserves grouping but hides original value.
- pseudonymize: generate stable pseudo-id via keyed PRF; can be reversible only under strict legal control.
- aggregate: replace detailed values with buckets (e.g., token counts -> 0-32,33-64,...).
sections.heading: Filtering operators (recommended patterns)

sections.body:
- Run the Redwood telemetry linter: rwd-telemetry-lint --schema telemetry_contract.json --sample sample_payloads/
- PII scan (simple grep approach for email): grep -E "[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Za-z]{2,}" logs/ingested/ || echo "PII-free"
- Request count verification: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://staging-redwood/api/telemetry/tenant/<tenant_id>/counts
sections.heading: Validation commands and test harness (staging)

sections.body:
- Latency p50/p95 per model_id -> SLO 99.5% p95 < 350ms
- Token-cost attribution: daily delta per tenant -> used in finops QBR
- Ingest completeness: 99% of requests must include request_id and tenant_id
sections.heading: SLO and QBR mapping (example)

sections.body:
1) Missing tenant_id after filter applied:
   - Symptom: Billing and routing gaps, alerts for missing-key ingestion spikes.
   - Cause: Filter misconfiguration replaced rather than hashed/preserved.
   - Remediation: Re-deploy OPF with tenant-preserve rule; run re-ingestion for the window if allowed.
2) Over-redaction causing SLO regression:
   - Symptom: Missing model_id or token counts; SLO dashboards show gaps.
   - Cause: Aggressive redact rules or wildcard match in OPF.
   - Remediation: Narrow rule scope, enable aggregated fallback (buckets) to preserve SLO signals.
3) Unexpected PII in ingestion:
   - Symptom: Automatic DLP scan flags stored records.
   - Cause: New emitters added fields that bypass the agreed contract.
   - Remediation: Freeze producer schema, run full scan, and engage Security & Legal per DPA.

Known issues and workarounds (current as of last_updated):
- Issue: HMAC salted hashing drift when tenant salt rotated causes broken grouping. Workaround: use versioned salt identifiers in emitted record and schedule a rehash job for recent windows.
- Issue: High-cardinality keys (full user_email hashed) inflates cardinality of metrics and increases cost. Workaround: pseudonymize to coarse buckets for analytics and preserve hashed emails only for reverse-lookup windows under strict access control.
- Issue: Edge OPF running on CPU-constrained appliances causes 200ms spike during peak ingest. Workaround: enable per-route sampling (1%) for detailed traces and send aggregated summaries for high-volume routes.
sections.heading: Troubleshooting and common failure modes

sections.body:
- No PII present in fields labeled PII in the agreed contract for production data (automated DLP scan).
- Ingest completeness >= 99% for required keys (tenant_id, request_id) across canary period.
- Token-cost attribution within 2% of staging baseline.
- SRE sign-off on ingestion capacity and fallback plan.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (must pass before handoff)

sections.body:
- Telemetry contract JSON and final OPF rule-set
- Staging and production verification runbooks (commands and dashboards)
- QBR telemetry bundle and dashboard snapshot with sample queries
- Short operational runbook for rehash/rotation and emergency debug window steps

Appendix A: Example OPF rule (yaml)
- name: redact_user_email
  match: "event.user_email"
  action: "redact"
  reason: "Customer requested no email storage"
- name: hash_tenant_id
  match: "event.tenant_id"
  action: "hash:hmac-sha256:tenant-salt-v1"
  reason: "Preserve grouping without storing raw id"

Appendix B: Escalation path for data policy incidents:
1) CSE opens internal incident in PagerDuty with tag "telemetry-data-policy".
2) Notify Security & Legal immediately and place a temporary ingest halt if data exposure suspected.
3) Execute the containment checklist (snapshot, freeze schema changes, begin audit log collection).
4) If confirmed, follow DPA breach notification timelines; coordinate customer communications via Account team.
sections.heading: Handoff artifacts to provide to customer after onboarding

sections.body:
- Primary CSE: Leila Moreno (leila@redwood.example)
- Platform/SRE reviewer: Ethan Park (ethan@redwood.example)
- Security & Legal contact: Rima Gupta (rima@redwood.example)
sections.heading: Contact and support matrix

sections.body:
- Owner: Customer Success (telemetry onboarding squad)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or on major stream changes

End of document.
