payload.page_title: Office Plant Care and Desk Jungle Guidelines

sections.body: This page documents lightweight, community-driven guidelines for caring for office plants and maintaining a pleasant desk-plant ecosystem. It is intended to keep shared spaces tidy, reduce plant mortality, and provide simple escalation paths for issues. These guidelines are informal and may be superseded by facility vendor contracts or building policies.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Applies to all plants in shared spaces (kitchen, conference rooms, lounge) and to potted plants kept at individual desks when they interact with shared facilities (water stations, plant shelves).
- Excludes customer office gardens and third-party contracted plant maintenance.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1. Low-effort, resilient plants preferred: choose hardier species for communal areas (e.g., pothos, snake plant, ZZ plant).
2. Shared responsibility: facilities owns ordering and large maintenance; community volunteers do day-to-day checks.
3. Non-judgmental culture: if a plant is wilting, flag it; no shaming.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
- Facilities (Facilities Manager): owns budget, vendor coordination, pest escalation, and the monthly supplies reorder.
- Desk Jungle Stewards (rotating volunteers): 1-2 people per floor who perform weekly checks and watering for shared-planter zones.
- Individual Employees: responsible for personal desk plants (follow desk guidelines below).
sections.heading: Roles & Responsibilities

sections.body:
1. Monday: Steward inspects shared planters, notes soil moisture, and rotates plants if shade distribution is uneven.
2. Wednesday: Quick misting for humidity-sensitive plants (only in winter months).
3. Friday: Tidy loose soil, remove dead leaves, and record any pest signs in the shared Plant Log (Google Sheet link in related pages).
sections.heading: Weekly Care Schedule (recommended)

sections.body:
- Pot size: keep to 4–8 inch pots for desks; larger pots belong in floor planters.
- Watering: use a tray to prevent accidental spills; water at desk only in non-sensitive equipment areas.
- Lighting: if a plant requires bright light, place near windows; avoid blocking walkways.
- Allergies: pick hypoallergenic species when possible or keep plants contained inside cubicle boundaries.
sections.heading: Desk Jungle Guidelines (for personal plants)

sections.body:
- Labeling: all shared planter pots should have a small waterproof label with plant name and last-watering date.
- Rotation: every three months facilities will rotate plants to refresh displays and prevent one area bearing all sun/heat exposure.
sections.heading: Shared Planters & Conference Rooms

sections.body:
- Facilities will maintain a basic kit: peat-free potting mix, small pruning shears, plant food (low-dose), trays, and labels.
- To request supplies: submit a ticket in #facilities-requests Slack channel or file a help ticket (link in related pages). For emergency replacement (pests, floods), contact Facilities Manager directly.
sections.heading: Supplies & Ordering

sections.body:
- Immediate action: isolate affected plant, take photos, and post to the Plant Log with time/date and steward name.
- Quarantine window: keep suspected plants isolated for 7–10 days; do not compost onsite without Facilities approval.
- Escalation: if pests persist or spread to multiple planters, Facilities will engage vendor or building management for treatment.
sections.heading: Pests & Health Issues

sections.body: - Temporary decorations (e.g., pot toppers, small plaques) allowed but must be removed within 48 hours after the event. No open flames or food-based decorations in shared planters.
sections.heading: Event Use & Decorations

sections.body: - If a plant in a shared zone is being mistreated or over-cared (e.g., overwatered), leave a polite note on the shared Plant Log. If unresolved after one week, escalate to the Facilities Manager who will mediate.
sections.heading: Conflict Resolution

sections.body:
- Q: Can I rehome my unhealthy desk plant into a shared planter?
  A: No — rehoming must be approved by a Steward after assessment to avoid introducing pests or disease.
- Q: Who pays for a replacement plant I broke?
  A: Personal desk plants are the owner’s responsibility; accidental damage to shared planters should be reported and may be covered by the facilities petty fund depending on circumstances.

payload.page_title: Misc Office Ops and Runtime Quirks

sections.body:
Overview:

This page is a deliberately miscellaneous collection of operational notes, small runbook fragments, and a handful of office logistics items that surfaced during on-call rotations and weekly runtime syncs. It is not a canonical architecture doc; treat items here as context-rich noise that may be useful when triaging odd runtime behaviours or planning small infrastructural housekeeping.

Purpose:
- Capture small, non-actionable observations about serving-runtime quirks.
- Keep a short checklist for low-cost office operations (vending, supplies) so on-call folks can avoid interruptions.
- Surface minor suggestions that don't yet warrant a full ADR or Confluence page.

Quick summary of notable runtime quirks (engineering context):
1) Occasional small-object GC pauses seen when background maintenance jobs overlap with burst traffic windows. Hypothesis: Python-based admin tasks touching model caches cause incremental memory pressure and CPU spikes on control-plane nodes.
2) Batching spikes when request size distribution shifts (more short queries than expected) leading to suboptimal packing. Temporary mitigation: reduce max-wait-ms in the inference router for affected prefix.
3) KV cache fragmentation after rolling restarts in mixed-quantization pools; increase measured tail latency by ~10–15ms for cold prefix workloads.

Actionable suggestions (short):
- For short-term GC pauses: schedule heavy control-plane jobs (snapshot, compliance exports) outside peak hours (US morning).
- For batching variance: add histogram metrics for request token-length by route to auto-detect distribution shifts.
- For KV fragmentation: include a lightweight post-rolling-check that validates KV consistency and warms the top N prefixes.

Office ops (non-technical but useful for continuity):
- Vending machine: restock request process: slack #facilities with photo, item list, and preferred vendor. Typical turnaround ~3 business days.
- Printer toner: shared_drives/engineering/_temp_uploads/toner-orders is the interim order sheet (legacy).

Runbook fragment: diagnosing a small spike in tail latency (<= 1 hour incident)
1) Check the Console SLO dashboard for the route and time range, confirm affected percentiles (p50/p90/p99).
2) Query recent deploys and rolling restarts: grep deploy logs for the service tag; correlate to control-plane maintenance jobs.
3) Inspect batching metrics: batching_queue_time_ms, batch_fill_ratio, and avg_tokens_per_request. If batch_fill_ratio < 0.6 and batch_size smaller than expected, consider temporarily lowering max-wait-ms on router.
4) Check KV cache hit rate and last_warm_timestamp for model variants. If hit rate < 85% and last warm < 2 hours, trigger a targeted warm-up (script: scripts/warm_prefixes.sh --top 50).
5) If CPU steal or I/O wait is high on nodes, check noisy-neighbor signals and recent dedicated capacity autoscaling events.

Small configuration table (example thresholds used by on-call)
- SLO target (route default): 95% requests <= 120ms, p99 <= 500ms
- Alert thresholds: p95 > 200ms for 5m OR p99 > 600ms for 1m
- Batching: default max-wait-ms = 12, max-batch-tokens = 4096
- KV cache warm threshold: < 85% hit triggers warm-up

Checklist for adding trivial housekeeping items to this page:
1) Add item with a short title and one-paragraph rationale.
2) If the item is clearly actionable in < 1 hour, move to eng-sre action list and assign.
3) If the item is long-form, draft an ADR and link from here.

Ownership and escalation:
- Maintainer: eng-serving-runtime on-call rotation (primary contact via PagerDuty).
- Triage owner for office ops items: facilities@redwood-inference (use internal alias).
- For anything tagged security or legal, escalate to security-and-compliance and stop; do not document sensitive details here.

Related artifacts and links:
- Deploy checklist: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/deploy-checklist
- Incident playbook: confluence/eng-sre/incident-response
- Warm-up script (repo): github/redwood/tools/warm-prefixes (note: small helper script, may be moved)

Notes and miscellaneous noise (explicitly informal):
- Coffee machine cycles correlate poorly with sprint deadlines but this is anecdotal.
- We keep a small spare HDMI->DP dongle in the engineering kitchenette labeled "borrow me." Return within 48 hours.
- If you find a half-eaten sandwich near the NUC rack, please notify facilities and remove before it attracts pests.

Revision history and authorship:
- 2023-11-15: Initial draft, Maya Chen.
- 2024-06-20: Added KV fragmentation notes, Lucas Patel.
- 2024-07-03: Minor edits and office ops checklist, Aisha Kapoor.

If something in this page looks like it should be a formal runbook, ADR, or incident postmortem, please create the canonical page and link it from here. This page intentionally accumulates small, cross-cutting notes that often get lost in ephemeral channels.

payload.page_title: Oddball Office Procedures: Handling Miscellaneous Situations

sections.body:
This page documents a set of intentionally lightweight and occasionally whimsical procedures for small, real-world oddities that have occurred at Redwood Inference offices. The purpose is pragmatic: provide a repeatable, low-friction decision path for front-desk staff, people-ops, and any engineer who volunteers to handle the strange but non-critical situations that crop up.

These are not policies with legal force; they are pragmatic guidance and a place to capture low-risk defaults so we avoid ad-hoc escalation. Treat this page as an informal supplement to Office Guidelines.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- The issue is non-safety-critical (no bodily harm, fire, major property damage).
- The situation is awkward, unexpected, and not covered by standard HR or security playbooks.
- You need a quick, sensible default to avoid micro-escalations (e.g., who takes custody of a found office cactus).
sections.heading: When to use this page

sections.body:
1. Found items: keys, umbrellas, electronics
   - Put in the labeled "Found" basket at reception with date and finder initials.
   - Photograph item and post a single-line thread in #office-lost-and-found (photo + approximate location + date).
   - After 30 days unclaimed: donate (clothing) or recycle securely (storage devices) per IT disposal guidance.

2. A plant that clearly belongs to no one (the Rogue Plant)
   - Move it to the communal window bench and label with a sticky note: "Rogue Plant — survivor program."
   - If it’s thriving after 60 days and no owner identified, people-ops will adopt into the office green roster and assign a caretaker volunteer.

3. Persistent smell in the breakroom (non-emergency)
   - Ventilate windows/doors, check trash and forgotten food, log incident in the facilities queue.
   - If smell persists after two checks, escalate to facilities manager and note the date/time and area.

4. Small animal or insect guest (non-dangerous)
   - Safely trap or guide outside using a cup and paper or request facilities assistance.
   - For bees/wasps/large pests: do not attempt removal; contact facilities immediately.
sections.heading: Common scenarios and recommended handling (quick-reference)

sections.body:
1. Secure item and take a clear photo.
2. Label with date, finder initials, and a one-line description.
3. Place in reception "Found" basket or the secure bin for electronics.
4. Post notice in #office-lost-and-found with photo and location.
5. Record a 1-line note in the Facilities ticket system (ticket title: Found item — <short desc>).
6. After 30 days, follow disposal rules aligned to item type (electronics -> IT disposal; clothing -> donation).
sections.heading: Step-by-step playbook: "Rogue Office Item"

sections.body:
| Item type | Short-term home | 30-day outcome | Responsible owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Clothing | Found basket (closet shelf) | Donate | People-Ops |
| Keys / Wallets | Locked reception drawer | Security hold + attempt owner contact | Facilities |
| Electronics (phones, USB) | Secure bin (keyed) | IT erase / recycle | IT Ops |
| Houseplants | Communal bench | Assign caretaker or rehome | People-Ops |
sections.heading: Table: Disposal guidelines (quick)

sections.body:
- Slack post (short): "Found a [item] near <location> at <time>. Photo attached. Putting it in reception. Please DM if it’s yours."
- Reception note (sticky): "Found: <item>. Date: <YYYY-MM-DD>. Finder: <initials>."
sections.heading: Communication templates

sections.body:
- Default owner for first 30 days: Reception / Facilities.
- If item appears high-value or clearly sensitive (e.g., labeled drives, encrypted devices): immediate escalation to IT and Security. Do not power on unknown devices.
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:

- Past oddities that inspired this doc: a potted fern relocation, an unclaimed umbrella stash after a heavy rain day, and a mysterious jar of pickles left in a fridge (resolved by donation).

payload.page_title: Office plant care and decor guidelines

sections.body: This page documents the recommended care, placement, and procurement guidelines for office plants and low-effort decor in Redwood Inference offices. The goal is to maintain a safe, healthy workplace, reduce allergens and pest risk, and ensure plants support wellbeing and culture without creating maintenance burden.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Applies to all shared indoor office spaces, meeting rooms, and communal areas in Redwood-managed offices.
- Does not cover employee personal desk plants (see "Personal desk plants" section).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Low-maintenance: prioritize species that tolerate office lighting and intermittent watering.
- Safety-first: avoid plants with known toxic sap or excessive shedding in high-traffic areas.
- Inclusive: accommodate allergies and scent sensitivities; avoid highly fragrant plants in shared spaces.
- Aesthetic coherence: plants and decor should be neutral and consistent with brand colors where practical.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1) Morning quick-check (mon-fri): inspect high-traffic common area plants for wilting, standing water, or pests.
2) Watering: follow the plant-specific schedule (see table below); avoid overwatering. Use saucers to prevent leaks.
3) Clean leaves monthly: wipe dust buildup to keep plants healthy and improve air quality.
4) Report issues: log major problems in #facilities with a photo and location.
sections.heading: Daily care checklist (facilities team)

sections.body:
- Snake plant (Sansevieria): water every 4–6 weeks. Low light tolerant.
- ZZ plant (Zamioculcas zamiifolia): water every 4–6 weeks. Very low maintenance.
- Pothos/Devil's ivy: water every 10–14 days; trim vines if they encroach on walkways.
- Spider plant: water every 10–14 days; prefers bright, indirect light.
- Peace lily: water every 7–10 days; avoid placement where pollen may bother coworkers.
- Succulents/Cacti: water every 3–6 weeks depending on season.
sections.heading: Watering schedule by plant type (general guidance)

sections.body:
- Do not place plants where they block egress, fire extinguishers, electrical panels, or sensors.
- Avoid hanging plants directly over desks where drips could occur.
- Ensure pots have trays; mopping and carpet damage incidents have previously come from unchecked overflow.
- Do not place heavily-shedding plants in meeting rooms or near shared keyboards and equipment.
- Plants with known mild-to-high toxicity (e.g., philodendron, oleander) are not allowed in common areas.
sections.heading: Placement and safety guidelines

sections.body:
- Allowed but must be maintained by the owner. If a plant becomes a nuisance (pests, mold, water damage) facilities may request removal.
- Use a waterproof tray and keep a small saucer under the pot.
- Notify facilities in case of spider/ant/pest sightings so coordinated treatment can occur.
sections.heading: Personal desk plants (employee-owned)

sections.body:
- To request a new plant or replacement, file a request in the Facilities request form (link in sidebar) with: proposed location, desired plant type (if known), and any accessibility concerns.
- Facilities maintains a small budget for replacements. For larger decorative refreshes, submit a ticket to People Ops with proposed spend and rationale.
- Preferred vendors: local nurseries and the approved vendor list (see Facilities vendor doc).
sections.heading: Procurement and requests

sections.body:
- Pots and stands should be neutral (matte blacks, grays, natural wood) unless coordinated as part of a themed refresh.
- No scented candles or oil diffusers in shared areas.
- Avoid porous pots that retain moisture directly against furniture; use trays and felt pads under stands.
sections.heading: Decor guidelines (small items accompanying plants)

sections.body:
- Facilities: weekly checklists, monthly leaf-clean, quarterly plant health review.
- People Ops: budget approvals, large refresh planning, and accommodation handling for allergies/sensitivities.
- Teams may volunteer to sponsor plants in their area (signup through People Ops); volunteer teams are responsible for basic watering on a shared rota.
sections.heading: Maintenance cadence and ownership

sections.body:
- If pests (aphids, spider mites) are detected, quarantine the plant and notify #facilities immediately. Do not attempt over-the-counter pesticide sprays without coordination.
- For allergy complaints, People Ops will identify nearby plants and offer relocation/removal options. We prioritize non-confrontational resolutions and temporary workarounds (e.g., moving desks).
sections.heading: Pest and allergy procedures

sections.body:
- If an individual requires a scent-free or plant-free workspace for medical reasons, People Ops will provide reasonable accommodation, including relocation or desk shields if needed.

sections.body: Title: Office Art & Plant Guidelines
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This page documents lightweight guidelines for installing office art, plants, and temporary desk decorations at Redwood Inference offices. It is intended to balance aesthetic expression with safety, accessibility, and shared workspace norms. These notes are informal and maintained by People Ops.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
1. Safety first: no obstructing egress, fire alarms, or emergency equipment. Avoid tripping hazards.

payload.page_title: Cafeteria Beanbag and Ambient Noise Guidelines

sections.body:
Summary

This page documents a lightweight, experimental set of guidelines for beanbag seating and ambient noise considerations in Redwood Inference shared spaces (cafeteria, lounge, and overflow areas). The goal is pragmatic: improve employee comfort and informal collaboration while keeping operational burden low.

Scope

- Applies to: cafeteria, adjacent lounge, satellite huddle areas on main campus and leased offices.
- Does NOT apply to: focus rooms, phone booths, secure rooms, or private customer meeting rooms.

Guiding principles

1. Respect for teammates: conserve shared spaces for implicit consent — assume people nearby prefer moderate noise levels.
2. Minimal ops: prefer low-maintenance furniture and sensors; avoid complex approvals for small purchases.
3. Data-informed: measure and iterate; use a simple decibel sampling process before large rollouts.

Furniture guidelines (beanbags and soft seating)

- Quantity: limit beanbag count per room to 6 units or 25% of casual seating, whichever is smaller.
- Placement: require at least 1.5m clear circulation path; do not block egress or access to kitchen equipment.
- Materials: choose wipeable, flame-retardant covers rated for commercial use.
- Procurement checklist (sample):
  1. Model spec and SKU
  2. Flame retardant certificate (pdf)
  3. Supplier lead time and return policy
  4. Estimated cost per unit
  5. Maintenance plan (wipe schedule)

Ambient noise guidance

- Target levels: daylight cafeteria 45-55 dB typical; lunchtime peaks allowed up to 65 dB for short periods.
- Quiet windows: designate 11:30-12:30 on Tuesdays as a quiet-lunch pilot in one lounge for two quarters and evaluate.

Quick decibel sampling procedure

1. Tools: smartphone with a basic dB meter app (note: consumer apps vary).
2. Sampling: take 6 samples across a 30-minute window during a target time (e.g., Wednesday 12:00-12:30).
3. Record: document median and max values. Store sample note on the facilities ticket with a short comment.

Example CLI-style sample (for reference in case teams use a measurement device):
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
Operational checklist for pilot rollout (one-month pilot)

1. Facilities ops to order up to 4 beanbags for Pilot Location A.
2. People Ops to publish the pilot notice and expectations (quiet windows, cleanup).
3. Facilities to execute sampling on week 1 and week 4 and upload notes.
4. Survey: send a 3-question pulse survey after week 4 (comfort, noise impact, cleanup).

Safety, maintenance, and waste

- Cleaning: wipeable covers weekly; deep-clean monthly.
- Disposal: follow office recycling guidelines; avoid foam landfill where programs exist.

Decision and escalation

- If complaints > 10% of local headcount in pilot area, pause and review.
- Escalation owner: Facilities Lead (email: facilities@example.com).

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: People Ops (Aisha Khan).
- Review cadence: pilot review at month 1, full review at month 3.

Related artifacts and references

- See: Office space guidelines (Confluence) for building rules and safety.
- See: Facilities procurement template (Drive) for ordering checklist.

Attachments and sample forms

- Procurement sample checklist (attach to ticket)
- Decibel sampling notes (CSV)

Notes and known limitations

- This is intentionally lightweight and experimental. It is not a binding policy for client-facing meeting rooms or regulated spaces. If a space is used for interviews or customer meetings, revert to formal meeting-room standards.

payload.page_title: fine-grained-causal-profiling-for-multi-kernel-paths-2026

sections.body: This playbook describes a repeatable, low-risk process for performing fine-grained causal profiling across multi-kernel execution paths in the Redwood serving runtime. It targets cases where a single inference request may exercise multiple kernels (attention variants, fused matmuls, quantized vs FP16 paths) and where attribution of end-to-end latency or tail spikes to a specific kernel, combination of kernels, or scheduling interaction is uncertain.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Serving runtime engineers
- Oncall SREs investigating tail latency
- Profiling / performance owners evaluating kernel rollouts
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) Produce a causal hypothesis ("kernel X caused tail at 99.9p") with an associated confidence score and required evidence.
2) Generate a minimal, reproducible profiling experiment that isolates the suspected kernel path and quantifies its impact on: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU occupancy, SM stall time, and memory bandwidth.
3) Provide clear remediation guidance (rollforward/rollback, kernel knobs, scheduling policy changes).
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- New kernel variant rollout shows unexpected tail increase in canary or production shadowing.
- Mixed workload exposes previously unseen interference between kernels (e.g., sparse attention + fused softmax).
- Quantization rollout correlated with higher variance across cohorts.
sections.heading: When to use

sections.body:
- Access to trace IDs for affected requests and the consolidated trace store (trace-id -> kernel sequence).
- Profiling lab with the same accelerator family and driver stack as production.
- Baseline microbenchmarks for each kernel variant (available in /benchmarks/kernel-microbenchmarks).
- SLO targets and alert thresholds (example: p99 <= 1200ms for chat.route-alpha).
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.body:
1) Triage and hypothesis formation
   a. Collect representative request traces for the incident window (use trace exporter: rwd-trace-export --start <ts> --end <ts> --label incident-42).
   b. Build a candidate list of kernels observed in the slow traces, ordered by aggregated kernel time.
   c. For each candidate kernel, capture: kernel name, variant tag, callsite (model shard id), observed kernel time distribution, and upstream queue wait time.

2) Causal probing via selective shadowing
   a. Create a shadow cohort in the profiling lab that replays the same trace corpus but forces a single kernel variant at a time (kernel override injection).
   b. Run 500–2000 replayed requests across varying concurrency shapes (1, 4, 16) and collect full-device perf counters (SM utilization, L2 read/write, DRAM BW).
   c. Compare distributions and compute delta metrics: delta_p99_ms, delta_occ_pct, delta_L2_miss_rate.

3) Interference experiments (pairwise)
   a. If multiple kernels are plausible, run pairwise interleaving experiments (A-only, B-only, A+B co-scheduled) to detect emergent interactions.
   b. Capture cross-correlation of latency with GPU scheduler backpressure signals and kernel start time jitter.

4) Controlled perturbations and causal inference scoring
   a. Apply small, safe perturbations: tensor packing/unpacking flags, reducing the kernel launch grid size by 10%, or enabling a single safety-fallback path.
   b. Use the following scoring rubric to assign confidence: EvidenceScore = 0.5*(delta_p99_normalized) + 0.3*(occupancy_change_normalized) + 0.2*(repro_rate). Normalization bounds are defined in the Appendix.

5) Remediation play
   a. If EvidenceScore >= 0.7: prepare an emergency canary rollback for the kernel variant with a one-hour monitor window.
   b. If 0.4 <= EvidenceScore < 0.7: open a kernel regression ticket, schedule a non-disruptive A/B test with shadow routing for 48 hours.
   c. If EvidenceScore < 0.4: capture experiment artifacts, label the hypothesis as low confidence, and schedule deeper instrumentation (see Appendix).
sections.heading: Procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Full request trace with kernel sequence and timestamps (trace store id).
- Kernel-level histograms (start_time, duration, queue_wait).
- Device perf counters sampled at 10ms granularity: SM_util, warp_occ, DRAM_bw, L2_rd/wr, tensor_core_ops.
- Scheduler telemetry: slot assignment, preemption events, admission decisions.
- Execution environment: driver version, CUDA/cuDNN/ROCm versions, kernel build flags.
sections.heading: Observability checklist (data to collect)

sections.body:
- Start a deterministic replay with kernel override:
  rwd-replay --trace-corpus traces/incident-42.tar.gz --kernel-override attention:v2 --concurrency 8 --sample-rate 1.0 --out /tmp/replay-output

- Collect perf counters with rwd-prof (example):
  rwd-prof --pid <replay-pid> --counters SM_UTIL,DRAM_BW,L2_MISS --interval_ms 10 --out profiling/case-42.json

- Example kernel-override YAML used by the replay harness:
  overrides:
    - kernel: attention
      variant: v2
      force: true
sections.heading: Safe lab commands and snippets

sections.body:
1) replay-output/log.json
2) profiling/case-42.json (perf counters)
3) delta-report.csv (p50/p95/p99 deltas, occupancy deltas)
4) experimental-runbook.md (chosen remediation path)
sections.heading: Expected artifacts (attach to incident)

sections.body:
| EvidenceScore | Action | Rollout scope | Monitoring window | Owner |
|---------------|--------|---------------|-------------------|-------|
| >= 0.7 | Emergency rollback | Canary -> Prod stop | 1 hour | Kernel-owner |
| 0.4–0.7 | Targeted A/B | 5% traffic shadow | 48 hours | Runtime-release |
| < 0.4 | Deeper instrumentation | Lab only | N/A | Profiling team |

Appendix A — Normalization constants and thresholds:
- delta_p99_normalized = min(1.0, observed_delta_p99_ms / 300)  # 300ms maps to 1.0 for scoring
- occupancy_change_normalized = min(1.0, abs(delta_occ_pct) / 40)  # 40% occupancy swing maps to 1.0
- repro_rate = fraction of lab runs that reproduce > 90th percentile effect (0..1)

Appendix B — When to escalate to security/compliance:
- If the repro experiment required production customer data to trigger: mark confidentiality=restricted and notify security for data handling clearance.
- If remediation requires hotpatching customer-facing codepaths, open Change Management with at least one reviewer from Platform Security.

Appendix C — Recommended hooks to add for future incidents (owner: runtime-observability):
- Add kernel-variant tag to trace root and ensure sampling retains tag for 48 hours post-deploy.
- Emit per-kernel occupancy delta metrics to metrics store: runtime.kernel.occupancy.delta{kernel_variant}.
- Add an automated replay job that can reconstruct the top-100 slow traces for any 24h window.

payload.page_title: Asymmetric Kernel Fidelity Profiling  Guidelines and Experiment Matrix

sections.body:
This playbook documents a repeatable approach to profile and evaluate asymmetric kernel variants used by the runtime: kernels that offer different fidelity or approximation levels (full-precision, quantized, approx-attention, mixed-kernel offloads). It provides an experiment matrix, instrumentation checklist, and interpretation guidance so kernel rollouts keep application-level quality and SLOs intact.
Applies to runtime kernel families used in production inference (attention, matmul, kv-cache ops). Focuses on profiling permutations where a request may fall back between kernel fidelity levels and on measuring the operational cost of transitions.
Detect fidelity regressions at prompt-set level; quantify latency and p99 tail per-kernel and per-sequence-length; validate graceful fallback behavior and measure reconfiguration costs; provide a go/no-go decision matrix for kernel rollout aligned with SLO thresholds.
High-fidelity kernel: reference kernel prioritized for output quality (FP16/FP32). Economical kernel: optimized for cost/throughput (quantized, approximate) with potential quality delta. Fallback oscillation: repeated switching between kernels that causes latency spikes or quality divergence.
Owned by eng-serving-runtime (profiling lead) with review from kernel maintainers and SRE. Required infra: profiling cluster with representative GPUs (A100/H100 and a low-cost pool like A10G), workload-replay service, and tracing hooks enabled. Provide access to artifact storage, a dashboard template (Grafana id: runtime.kernel.fidelity.profile), and the applied-ml-evals harness.
Kernel-level timers per dispatch; request timeline markers (request_receive, model_load, kv_attach, kernel_dispatch(N), kernel_complete(N), response_stream_start); memory copy accounting between device regions; fidelity flag telemetry attached to kernel_dispatch events; quality trace linking prompt_id -> candidate_hash -> golden_eval_id.
Stratified sampling by sequence length cohorts: short (<=64), medium (65-512), long (>512). SLO-aware sampling: increase sample rate during tail events and for high-sensitivity customers. Telemetry cost cap: profiling telemetry should not exceed 6% of production inference compute on the profiling cluster.
1) Baseline characterization: reference kernels only; canonical prompt-set; metrics: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, memory, energy, quality. 2) Single kernel substitution: replace one operator kernel with economical variant; run per cohort and measure quality drift and latency delta. 3) Mixed-mode (fallback) replay: enable runtime fallback policy and inject capacity events; track fallback frequency, transition time, oscillations. 4) Session-boundary stress: simulate long chat sessions to measure cache conversion/regeneration costs. 5) Canary with adversarial corpus: include prompts sensitive to approximation; run human eval gates for semantic regressions.
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --cohort short,medium,long --kernel-policy ref_only --out results/baseline
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --cohort short,medium,long --kernel-policy economical_attention --out results/attn_sub
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --policy fallthrough --inject-load 0.7 --out results/fallback

Profiling-exporter config (YAML): trace_filters: include: [kernel_dispatch, kernel_complete, request_receive, kv_attach] tags: [kernel_variant, seq_len, tenant_id] sample_rate: 0.01 cohorts: [short, medium, long]
p50 delta (economical vs baseline) <= +10% for short/medium cohorts. p99 delta <= +15% for any cohort; above requires mitigation. Quality regression threshold: task-specific metric drop <= 1.5% absolute; for generative metrics use human review gate if >0.6% change. Fallback frequency expected <= 2% normal; >5% indicates misconfiguration. Transition cost target: <= 20ms avg; >100ms needs action.
Tail latency increase + low fallback rate -> suspect slow kernel micro-latency. Tail increase + high fallback rate -> policy thrashing or oscillation. Quality drop without latency improvement -> algorithmic regression in economical kernel. Memory spikes during switch -> examine device copy accounting and slab allocators; evaluate lazy-conversion or state-compat modes.
Narrow rollout with sequence-length gating; increase hysteresis in kernel selection policy; soft-fallback to non-critical routes or lower-tier tenants; convert state lazily (conversion-on-read) to reduce upfront cost.
Experiment: economical_attention substitution; Date & cluster: <date> / profiling-h100-1; Workloads: dev-corpus-v3 cohorts; Key metrics: p50 +X%, p99 +Y%, quality delta -Z, fallback freq P%. Decision: example - proceed to canary with seq_len <= 256 gating and 1% traffic.
1) Create experiment ticket (JIRA epic: KERNEL-PROF-<ID>) with replay parameters and dashboard link. 2) Run baseline and upload trace tarball to artifact store (s3://redwood-profiling/<id>/). 3) Run candidate kernels until minimum sample (n>=5000 requests per cohort) or 6 hours. 4) Review automated report and trigger human evals for quality delta >0.3%. 5) If pass, approve staged canary: 0.1% -> 1% -> 5% with rollback gates. 6) Post-canary: 72-hour continuous monitoring focused on p99 and fallback frequency.
If p99 jumps: run trace-inspector --filter kernel_variant=approx-attn and inspect long kernel_dispatch events. If memory conversion dominates: capture nvprof and compare device copy bytes pre/post-switch. For quality diffs: run quality-diff --golden golden_id --candidate candidate_id --metrics ll,accuracy and schedule human review.
Slack: #runtime-profiling. Pager: eng-sre oncall for incidents during canary. Kernel regressions: assign to kernel-team@redwood.internal with trace tarball and report.
2025-11-15: Created initial playbook and experiment matrix. (Asha Patel)
2026-01-20: Added canary gating thresholds and sample CLI snippets; clarified transition-cost threshold. (Asha Patel)

payload.page_title: Model chaining profiling and batch shaping playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents the recommended approach for profiling, benchmarking, and operationalizing multi-model request chains ("model chaining") in the Redwood serving runtime. Model chaining occurs when a single API request triggers sequential or conditional invocations across multiple model variants or pipelines (for example: classifier -> reranker -> generator). These patterns are increasingly common in production flows (routing, tool-calling, multimodal pre- and post-processing) and expose unique scheduling, caching, and batching interactions that require targeted profiling and shaping to meet latency and cost SLOs.

Audience
- Runtime engineers who implement scheduler/kernel changes
- Performance engineers owning microbenchmarks and end-to-end SLOs
- Oncall SREs and platform owners responsible for incident triage
- Solutions engineers validating customer workloads that chain models

Goals
- Provide a repeatable procedure to attribute latency and cost across a chained execution path.
- Offer batch-shaping and warmup recommendations that preserve p95 SLOs while minimizing per-token cost.
- Define benchmark scenarios and acceptance thresholds to gate releases that impact chained workloads.

When to use this playbook
- Adding a new chained pipeline to production
- Observed p95 regressions correlated with multi-model invocations
- Rolling out kernel or scheduler changes that affect batching/eviction logic

Key concepts and terms
- Link: one hop in the chain (e.g., token-classifier).
- Chain: ordered list of links that execute per request.
- Interlink latency: time window between link completion and next link start. Includes network, marshalling, and scheduling delay.
- Batch shaping: runtime techniques to control how requests in a chain are aggregated into kernel batches.
- Prefetch/warmstart: proactive loading of KV cache or kernels prior to link execution to reduce cold latency.

Observability checklist
- Per-link latency histogram (p50/p95/p99) with distinction of kernel vs scheduling vs marshalling time.
- Interlink gap histogram and correlation with kernel admission events.
- Kernel occupancy and batch size distribution per link.
- KV cache hit ratio per model link and warmup success rate.
- Cost per request and per-token cost tagged with chain-id and feature flags.

Suggested metrics (examples)
- chain.request.count (tags: chain_id, customer_tier)
- chain.latency.p95 (tags: chain_id, link_index)
- kernel.batch.size (tags: kernel_variant, link_index)
- kvcache.prefetch.success_rate (tags: chain_id, model)

Profiling procedure (step-by-step)
1) Identify representative chains
   - For the workload under investigation, extract the top 10 chain shapes by request volume and by p95 contribution. Use tracing to enumerate link types and their average token lengths.

2) Baseline capture (shadow/topology snapshot)
   - Capture a 10-minute tracing window in shadow mode with full span collection and kernel annotations. Use the replay harness to export the trace as a synthetic corpus.
   - Command example:
     ./tools/trace-export --service=ingress --filter=chain_id:checkout_v2 --out=checkout_v2.trace

3) Microprofile each link in isolation
   - Replay links individually against the same model-variant to collect kernel-level latency and batch distributions. Use the microbenchmark agent with kernel annotation turned on.
   - Command example:
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --link=2 --annotate-kernel --concurrency=50 --duration=60s --out=link2-profile.json

4) End-to-end chain replay with controlled shaping knobs
   - Re-run the synthetic chain while toggling shaping knobs: contiguous-batching, interlink-throttle, slot-reservation, kv-prefetch. Capture per-link breakdowns.
   - Command example:
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --shaping='slot_reserve=2;interlink_throttle=50ms;kv_prefetch=on' --duration=600s --out=chain-run-1.json

5) Attribution and root cause analysis
   - For each chain run, compute: per-link kernel median/p95, interlink gap median/p95, batch-size vs latency correlation, and cost per request.
   - If p95 regressions are kernel-localized, open a kernel performance investigation. If regressions are due to interlink scheduling gaps, follow the Scheduler tuning steps below.

Batch shaping strategies (patterns and trade-offs)
- Tight slicing: enforce small, bounded batch slice per link to guarantee lower tail latency at higher per-token cost. Use when tail SLO is high priority.
- Opportunistic coalescing: allow larger batches across links when background load is stable to improve cost efficiency but monitor p95 drift.
- Slot reservation for sequential links: reserve N kernel slots across link boundaries for a chain to prevent preemption and eviction mid-chain. Useful for long KV warmup sequences.
- Interlink throttle: impose a minimal delay between links to allow the scheduler to co-locate subsequent link work into an opportunistic batch. Useful when immediate re-invocation results in wasted small batches.
- Adaptive prefetch: trigger KV/model prefetch for the next link when the probability of continuation exceeds a threshold. Tune by observing prefetch hit success and added upstream latency.

Configuration examples
- YAML example for batch shaper (runtime config):

| key | type | description | example |
|-----|------|-------------|---------|
| shaping.mode | string | One of: tight, opportunistic, reserved | reserved |
| slot_reservations | int | Number of kernel slots to reserve per chain | 2 |
| interlink_throttle_ms | int | Milliseconds to delay between link transitions | 30 |
| kv_prefetch_enabled | bool | Enable prefetching for next-link models | true |
| prefetch_confidence_threshold | float | Trigger threshold (0-1) for prefetch | 0.65 |
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
shaping:
  mode: reserved
  slot_reservations: 2
  interlink_throttle_ms: 30
  kv_prefetch_enabled: true
  prefetch_confidence_threshold: 0.65

Kernel scheduling tuning checklist
- Ensure link affinity: tag chains with affinity labels so the scheduler prefers the same GPU/NUMA domain for adjacent links.
- Verify slot-reservation accounting: aggregated reserved slots should not exceed node capacity. The admission controller must expose a rejection metric for reservation overcommit.
- Prioritize prefetch I/O: prefetch requests should be admitted with lower admission latency guarantees to reduce cold-link penalties.
- Backpressure integration: interlink backpressure should surface as a chain-level signal to the admission controller.

Benchmarking suite additions (how to add chain tests)
1) Add synthetic corpus: export representative chain traces (see Baseline capture) to the corpus repo under benchmarks/chains/.
2) Define chain SLO matrix: for each chain define p50/p95/p99 thresholds and cost-per-request gates.
3) Add CI job: a nightly chain-run that executes the chains under variable background noise profiles and validates against the SLO matrix.

Sample SLO matrix (example)
| chain_id | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | cost/request (tokens) |
|----------|----------:|---------:|----------------------:|
| checkout_v2 | 60 | 220 | 1.8 |
| multimodal-qa | 120 | 420 | 3.6 |
| routing-fallback | 30 | 150 | 0.6 |

Release gating guidance
- Any change to kernel batching, admission controller, or slot-reservation logic must include a chained-workload benchmark in the release candidate validation matrix.
- Required artifacts: chain-run results (clean vs noisy), annotated traces showing per-link kernel attribution, and cost delta analysis.

Known issues (current)
- CHAIN-2321: Intermittent double-prefetch for conditional chains. Symptom: elevated upstream latency and duplicate KV reads. Mitigation: disable prefetch by setting prefetch_confidence_threshold to 0.9 for affected chain.
- CHAIN-2456: Slot reservation can starve small-batch tails under extreme node pressure. Symptom: increased rejection metric admission.slot_reservation_reject_count. Mitigation: reduce slot_reservations or enable opportunistic mode.
- CHAIN-2510: Tracing overhead at 100% span sampling increases measured interlink gap by ~8–12ms. Symptom: observed increase in chain latencies during full-trace captures. Mitigation: use 10% long-span sampling with synthetic replay for detailed kernel probes.

Runbook: p95 chain latency degradation
1) Triage
   - Check chain.latency.p95 and per-link histograms for the last 30m. Identify whether the p95 shift is isolated to a single link or distributed.
2) If single-link kernel regression
   - Open kernel perf ticket and roll kernel variant to previous stable using the kernel rollback playbook.
3) If interlink gap increase
   - Inspect admission.slot_reservation_reject_count and kernel.batch.size distributions. Temporarily enable reserved mode with slot_reservations=1 for the chain and measure impact.
4) If due to cold KV cache
   - Trigger a controlled warmup using the synthetic replay harness in warmup-only mode:
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --warmup-only --repeat=500
5) Communication
   - Post an incident note on #runtime-alerts and notify owners: runtime-performance@redwood.com. Include the annotated per-link trace and recent commit IDs.

Operational ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: runtime-performance (team alias)
- Kernel lead: Marcus Chen
- Profiling/benchmarks steward: Priya Desai
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre rota (follow oncall directory)

Appendix: quick command reference
- Export chain trace: ./tools/trace-export --service=ingress --filter=chain_id:<chain> --out=<name>.trace
- Microprofile link: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --link=<n> --annotate-kernel --concurrency=<n>
- Full chain replay with shaping: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --shaping='<k=v;...>' --duration=600s
- Warmup replay: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --warmup-only --repeat=<n>

Related pages
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026 (for fallback policy interaction)
- kernel-and-scheduling/slot-reservation-protocol-and-deferred-warmstart-manual-2026 (reservation economics)
- profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026 (prefetch tuning)

Document change log
- 2025-09-10: Created by Elena Alvarez.
- 2026-01-18: Added slot reservation best-practices and SLO matrix examples (reviewer: Marcus Chen).
- 2026-03-01: Documented CHAIN-2510 tracing overhead observation and updated runbook steps.

payload.page_title: microprobe-operator-manifest-and-sampling-economics-playbook

sections.body:
Title: Microprobe Operator Manifest and Sampling Economics Playbook

Summary
-------
This playbook defines the Microprobe Operator (MPO): a lightweight runtime component and operational pattern for high-signal, low-cost instrumentation inside the Redwood serving runtime. The MPO is intended for short-duration probes that diagnose kernel-level behavior, KV-cache warmup characteristics, and burst-tail latency without blowing observability budgets or perturbing production scheduling.

Purpose and scope
------------------
- Purpose: Provide a repeatable contract and operational playbook for introducing, tuning, and retiring microprobes across the runtime surface.
- Scope: In-process and sidecar probes that run on serving nodes (GPU hosts and inference routers). Not intended for deep kernel modifications or external end-to-end tracing frameworks.
- Audience: runtime engineers, profiler owners, oncall SREs, and experimenters.

Ownership and stakeholders
-------------------------
- MPO owner: runtime-profiling team (team contact: @priya).
- Observability integration: telemetry-adapters team (reviewer: Daniel Wu).
- Scheduling/Kernel impact review: kernel-scheduler team (reviewer: Marco Alvarez).
- Release gate: must pass profiling lab acceptance criteria (see Benchmarks section).

Design principles
------------------
1. Non-invasive: probes must avoid long-lived locks or changes to scheduler behavior.
2. Budgeted: every probe is assigned a fixed cost budget (CPU ms, bytes emitted, average frequency).
3. Lightweight sampling: prefer probabilistic micro-sampling over continuous tracing.
4. Amortize work: aggregate telemetry at the operator boundary and send compacted summaries.
5. Kill-switchable: MPOs must honor a single operator-level remote flag for immediate global disablement.

Microprobe operator architecture
-------------------------------
- Components:
  - Controller (central): issues probe manifests and budgets via ConfigStore.
  - Agent (node-level MPO): receives manifests, enforces local budgets, collects samples, and emits compressed summaries.
  - Exporter: adapts compressed summaries to the telemetry pipeline and decides real-time vs batched ingestion.

Probe types
-----------
1. Touch probes: measure cold-start wall time of model shard activation (100-200ms probe).
2. Kernel rendezvous probes: sample kernel launch latencies and kernel queue lengths during busy windows.
3. KV-cache sweep probes: light samplers that touch a small prefix/slot distribution to estimate hit rates.
4. Tail request microtraces: capture 1-in-N full traces for requests above a latency threshold.

Budgeting and economics (mandatory fields)
-----------------------------------------
Each probe manifest contains a table of required budget fields. Operators must supply limits before activation.

Table: Probe budget schema (CSV-like)
probe_id,owner,probe_type,cpu_budget_ms_per_min,node_emit_bytes_per_min,max_sample_rate_per_min,ttl_minutes,backoff_policy
mp-touch-01,priya,touch,200,50000,20,60,exponential
mp-kernel-queue-01,marco,kernel-rendezvous,500,120000,10,30,linear
mp-kv-sweep-01,analytics,kv-sweep,150,30000,30,120,exponential
mp-tailtrace-rare-01,sre,tail-trace,1000,500000,2,1440,manual

Sampling policy and heuristics
-----------------------------
- Default mode: budgeted probabilistic sampling. Node agent maintains a leaky-bucket counter per-probe.
- Threshold triggers: probes may be promoted to higher fidelity if a health rule fires (e.g., rising tail latency > 99th percentile threshold).
- Reservoir caps: maximum number of retained microtraces kept in memory (default 32 per node).
- Backoff behaviors: exponential backoff when emission errors > 5% for 2 consecutive minutes.

Operational lifecycle (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
1. Draft manifest: profiling owner prepares probe manifest with budgets and rationale.
2. Risk review: submit to kernel-scheduler and telemetry-adapters for capacity and perturbation review.
3. Canary rollout (week-long): enable MPO at 1% of serving fleet with debug-level local sampling, validate no scheduler jitter.
4. Acceptance: run the profiling-lab acceptance checklist and cost simulation (see Benchmarks).
5. Production rollout: ramp to target fraction with progressive budget tightening.
6. Retention and sunset: every probe must include a sunset_date or a quarterly review ticket.

Deployment checklist
---------------------
- Manifest fields populated: probe_id, owner, budgets, safe-mode flag, TTL.
- Canary matrix defined: which clusters, node classes, and models.
- Observability: metrics defined (probe_success_rate, emit_errors, budget_utilization).
- Kill-switch validated end-to-end.

Runbook: probe-overload incident (short)
---------------------------------------
1. Symptoms:
   - sudden spike in exporter queue length or telemetry pipeline backpressure metrics.
   - increased scheduler soft-evictions during probe windows.
2. Immediate actions:
   1. Trigger MPO global kill-switch via ConfigStore.
   2. Identify offending probe_id using controller logs and budget_utilization panel.
   3. Notify probe owner and kernel-scheduler oncall.
3. Recovery:
   - After kill, verify exporter queues drain and scheduler quota stabilizes for 10 minutes.
   - If safe, re-enable in canary with 10x tighter budget and monitoring.

Benchmarks and acceptance criteria
----------------------------------
- CPU overhead: < 0.5% average CPU across probes in steady state (measured on target node class).
- Telemetry volume: < 1.5% of total telemetry bytes for active probes in aggregate.
- Perturbation: no measurable increase (>1%) in 95th percentile latency for the canary cohort.
- Safety: killing MPO must restore baseline within 2 minutes.

Measurement harness (how to verify)
----------------------------------
1. Use the profiling harness: ./tools/probe-harness --manifest <manifest.yaml> --simulate-workload <trace.json>
2. Collect metrics from MPO dashboards: probe_success_rate, budget_utilization, exporter_queue_ms.
3. Run A/B: mirror 10% of traffic to a shadow node with MPO enabled and compare latency histograms.

Configuration examples
----------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
---
probe_id: mp-kv-sweep-01
owner: analytics
probe_type: kv-sweep
cpu_budget_ms_per_min: 150
node_emit_bytes_per_min: 30000
max_sample_rate_per_min: 30
ttl_minutes: 120
backoff_policy: exponential
kill_switch_flag: /config/probes/enabled
telemetry_targets: ["compact-summary", "rare-full-trace"]
---

CLI examples (agent)
--------------------
- List active manifests: rwd-mpoctl list --env prod --cluster west-gpu
- Force kill: rwd-mpoctl kill mp-kv-sweep-01 --reason "emitter-backpressure"
- Drain and archive: rwd-mpoctl drain mp-tailtrace-rare-01 --archive-to s3://redwood-probe-archives/

Telemetry contract (what MPO emits)
------------------------------------
- Compact summary (default): gzipped protobuf containing aggregated counters, 95/99 latency summaries, small histograms.
- Rare full trace: sampled full trace with kernel IDs and microsecond timestamps (reserved for tail traces).
- Emission envelope must include probe_id, sample_timestamp, node_id, and budget_consumed.

Retrospective and changelog
---------------------------
- 2024-03-15: Initial draft and prototype.
- 2025-07-02: Added global kill-switch and exporter backpressure heuristics.
- 2026-02-10: Finalized budget schema and acceptance benchmarks; moved to published.

Related artifacts and references
-------------------------------
- Profiling lab acceptance checklist: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
- Observability adapter design: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/observability-adapter-sidecar-design-manual-2026
- Kernel scheduler risk matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025

Appendix: safe experiment template (copy-paste)
------------------------------------------------
1) Experiment name: <owner>-<probe_id>-<date>
2) Hypothesis: short 1–2 sentence statement.
3) Canaries: cluster / node-class list and expected ramp.
4) Budget table: include CPU and bytes.
5) Success criteria: latency windows, telemetry quota, no-sd.
6) Rollback plan: immediate kill-switch + postmortem owner.

Notes and cautions
------------------
- Microprobes are powerful but can create subtle feedback with the scheduler; always use the lab harness before production rollout.
- Never increase sample rates in production without kernel-scheduler signoff when running on preemptible node classes.

Contact
-------
For questions, reach out to Priya Menon (pri@redwood.ai) or the runtime-profiling Slack channel (#runtime-profiling).

payload.page_title: Variance-driven Sampling and Cost-Latency Correlation Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines an operational pattern for using variance-driven sampling of runtime telemetries to detect and triage episodes where cost per inference increases without a corresponding improvement in quality, or where latency and cost diverge across model variants and request shapes. It describes instrumentation signals, adaptive sampling algorithms, alert thresholds, an investigation checklist, and recommended mitigations for common root causes (batching, KV cache misses, kernel fallbacks, and topology shifts).

Goals
-----
- Detect sustained or transient incidents where per-token cost increases by > 15% at p95 or where p99 latency regresses > 20% relative to baseline.
- Reduce alert noise by focusing on high-variance cohorts (request shapes, model versions, customer tiers).
- Provide a repeatable triage procedure that links telemetry to kernel-level causes and cost drivers.
- Recommend automated mitigations (sampling rate changes, fallback model routing, cache warmups) and manual runbook steps.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Audience: Runtime SREs, Serving Runtime Engineers, Performance Engineers.
- In-scope: Host-level and request-level telemetry, kernel selection traces, KV cache hit/miss streams, batching metrics, model variant rollouts.
- Out-of-scope: Model quality evaluation (use eval-harness), billing reconciliation (use finance tooling).

Key signals to collect
----------------------
1. Per-request fields (high-cardinality):
   - request_id, route, model_version, sequence_length, input_tokens, output_tokens, customer_tier
   - observed_latency_ms (end-to-end), kernel_latency_ms, queue_time_ms, batch_size_at_exec
   - kvcache_lookup_count, kvcache_miss_count, quantization_variant
2. Host & kernel telemetry (low-cardinality):
   - gpu_util_pct, sm_occupancy, memory_bytes_used, kernel_name, kernel_duration_ms
3. Cost proxies:
   - per-token_cpu_cycles_estimate, gpu_kernel_time_ms, amortized_gpu_seconds_per_call
4. Sampling metadata: sampling_bucket, sampling_score, sample_decision_reason

Design: variance-driven sampling
--------------------------------
Rationale: Static uniform sampling underweights rare but high-cost request cohorts (large seq len, model rollouts). The variance-driven sampler adapts sampling probabilities to prioritize cohorts with high observed variance in cost and latency so investigations capture explanatory examples with fewer total samples.

Algorithm (overview)
1. Define cohort key = hash(route, model_version, sequence_length_bin, customer_tier).
2. Maintain rolling window (W = 30m default) for each cohort with sample_count N and sample variance S^2 of cost-per-token and p95 latency.
3. Compute score = alpha * normalized(S_cost) + beta * normalized(S_latency) + gamma * recent_regression_indicator. (alpha=0.5, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1 default).
4. Map score -> sampling probability p = min(p_max, base_p * (1 + score)). Defaults: base_p=0.01, p_max=0.5.
5. Persist sampled traces to the central profiling sink for kernel traceback and storage.

Implementation notes
--------------------
- Use probabilistic reservoir per cohort to bound memory.
- Normalize variances using robust scaling (median absolute deviation) to avoid outlier blowup.
- Ensure sampling decisions are deterministic per request_id + sampling_window to prevent double-sampling across retries.
- Emit sampler telemetry: sampling_rate_by_cohort, missed_samples_due_to_quota, reservoir_overflow_count.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)
----------------------------------------
| parameter | description | recommended value | rationale |
|-----------|-------------|-------------------|-----------|
| W | rolling window length | "30m" | captures transient episodes without excessive state |
| base_p | baseline sampling probability | "0.01" | keeps storage costs low |
| p_max | sampling cap | "0.5" | ensures hot cohorts don't overwhelm storage |
| alpha,beta,gamma | score weights | "0.5,0.4,0.1" | weight cost more than latency |
| sequence_length_bins | bins for cohorting | "[<=32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+]" | separates short vs long requests |
| reservoir_size | per-cohort reservoir | "500" | memory bound per cohort |

Operational alerts and thresholds
--------------------------------
- Alert: "HighCostVarianceByCohort"
  - Trigger: cohort sampling variance in per-token cost increases > 15% and sampled p95 cost-per-token increases > 10% over baseline for W.
  - Severity: P2.
  - Pager: SRE on-call.

- Alert: "Cost-Latency Divergence"
  - Trigger: cohort where cost-per-token increases > 15% but p50 latency unchanged and kernel_latency_ms increased by > 30%
  - Severity: P3.

- Alert: "Sampling-Reservoir-Pressure"
  - Trigger: reservoir_overflow_count > 0 for > 5m.
  - Action: autoscale sampler or reduce base_p.

Investigation checklist (triage steps)
-------------------------------------
1. Validate alert and gather context: cohort key, time window, sample_count, top 10 sampled trace ids.
2. Compare with baseline: run cohort in benchmarking harness (use synthetic request replay) with identical model_version and input shape.
3. Examine kernel traces for sampled IDs: look for kernel_name fallback (ex: aten_attention_non_fused -> fused_attention) and increased kernel_duration_ms.
4. Check KV cache signals: high kvcache_miss_count correlating with increased model_compute_time implies cache warmup or shard misrouting.
5. Inspect batch dynamics: high variance in batch_size_at_exec can cause head-of-line latency spikes leading to inefficient kernel launches.
6. Cross-check recent rollouts and routing rules (route table changes, firmware/drivers, GPU topology reassignments).
7. If hardware-level (SM occupancy low, GPU underutilized) correlate with small batch sizes or poor kernel packing.

Mitigation playbook (ordered)
----------------------------
1. Short-term (automated):
   - If sampling indicates KV cache coldness: enable on-demand prefix caching for affected customer_tier or trigger a background warmup job (see Runbook: dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup).
   - If kernel fallback detected: route 10% of traffic to the previous model_variant until kernel mapper patch is deployed.
   - If reservoir pressure: reduce base_p by 2x for non-critical tiers.
2. Mid-term (manual, < 2 hours):
   - Increase batch window tolerance for the affected pool (increase batching latency SLO by 10–25% while monitoring error budget).
   - Rebalance KV cache shards to co-locate hot keys with serving shards.
3. Long-term (postmortem & dev work):
   - Add kernel fusion/optimization or adjust kernel-mapper heuristics to prefer fused kernels for the cohort shapes.
   - Add dedicated capacity for high-cost cohorts (Dedicated pool reservation) or surface cost-aware routing rules.

Playbook run example (commands)
-------------------------------
1) Query recent sampled traces via telemetry CLI:

```
redwood telemetry query --dataset=runtime_samples --filter "cohort=route:chat,model:v2,seq_bin:513+" --range "-45m" --limit 200 --output json > sampled_traces.json
```

2) Run local replay for top samples against bench harness:

```
bench-runner replay --input sampled_traces.json --model v2 --profile kernel-trace --out replay_results.json
```

3) Extract kernel summary:

```
jq -r '.traces[] | {trace_id, kernel_summary}' replay_results.json | less
```

Integration with benchmarking & release process
------------------------------------------------
- Any model or kernel mapper change that increases sample variance for any cohort by > 10% must be added as a checkpoint in the pre-release gating pipeline.
- Include a variance report (automated) in release notes: histogram of per-cohort sampling_score deltas versus baseline, top 3 regressing cohorts, and mitigation flags.

Example incident root cause matrix (quick reference)
--------------------------------------------------
| symptom | common root cause | first-check | short-term mitigation |
|--------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| sudden p99 latency spikes for long-seq requests | kernel fallback to generic attention kernel | kernel_name in sampled trace | route to fallback-safe variant, roll back mapper change |
| increased per-token cost, stable latency | KV cache percent misses | kvcache_miss_count by cohort | enable cache warmup, rebalance shards |
| higher variance in cost across replicas | GPU topology change or firmware regression | recent node agent rollout | pin affected nodes out of pool, escalate to infra |

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Sampler service owner: eng-serving-runtime/perf-team.
- On-call: runtime-SRE rotation (see SLOs page).
- Sampling retention: sampled traces stored for 90 days in the profiling sink by default.

Metrics to report in QBRs
-----------------------
- median sampling_score across top 100 cohorts
- fraction of alerts triaged to kernel vs cache vs batching causes
- storage cost per 10k samples
- mean time to mitigative action (MTMA) for HighCostVarianceByCohort alerts

Appendix: recommended telemetry schema snippet
--------------------------------------------
(Illustrative example; actual schema enforced by telemetry ingestion service)
```
{
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "timestamp": "ISO8601",
  "route": "chat",
  "model_version": "v2",
  "sequence_length": 640,
  "sequence_length_bin": "513+",
  "input_tokens": 512,
  "output_tokens": 128,
  "observed_latency_ms": 422.1,
  "kernel_latency_ms": 391.3,
  "batch_size_at_exec": 4,
  "kvcache_lookup_count": 512,
  "kvcache_miss_count": 128,
  "kernel_name": "fused_attention_v3",
  "gpu_util_pct": 78.2,
  "sm_occupancy": 0.62,
  "sampling_bucket": "high_variance",
  "sampling_score": 3.4
}
```

Related reading
---------------
- Runtime: Dynamic KV cache resilience and warmup playbook (link above)
- Benchmarking: Mixed workload SLO simulation suite (link above)
- Profiling: Continuous runtime profiling strategy (internal)

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-11-03: Created by Maya Chen (initial design and defaults).
- 2026-01-12: Updated defaults for base_p and reservoir_size after pilot.
- 2026-02-14: Added mitigation step for kernel fallback routing and expanded alert definitions.

Contact
-------
For questions or to request an experiment slot for high-cost cohorts, contact eng-serving-runtime/perf-team or email maya.chen@redwood.com.

payload.page_title: developer-sandbox-benchmarking-playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook describes the developer-local runtime sandbox and associated benchmarking + profiling workflows used to reproduce key production behaviors without requiring full cluster access. The sandbox is intentionally lightweight and deterministic: it models the runtime dispatch, a KV cache shim, a kernel-proxy for scheduling experiments, and easy-to-run microbenchmarks. Use this guide to iterate on kernel scheduler patches, evaluate batching strategies, and validate optimization hypotheses before graduating changes to the full perf suite.

Scope
- Reproduce request lifecycle: API -> dispatcher -> kernel-proxy -> model executor (mock or quantized engine).
- Run microbenchmarks that mimic production prompt shapes (short, medium, long) and multi-turn chat traces.
- Exercise scheduling policies (fair-share, priority-driven, cooperative preemption) in a reproducible environment.
- Capture perf traces (CPU/GPU timelines), kernel occupancy, and per-token cost estimates.
- Limitations: does not emulate multi-tenant noisy neighbors at scale, and GPU topology is single-node only. See Known Differences section.

Prerequisites
1) Linux workstation with Docker 20.10+ or a macOS machine with Docker Desktop and a supported GPU passthrough (optional).
2) tools/runtime-sandbox repo checked out (internal): git clone git@repo.internal:redwood/tools/runtime-sandbox.git
3) Python 3.10+, pipenv or virtualenv for running harness scripts.

Sandbox Components (what runs locally)
- runtime-dispatcher-lite: lightweight HTTP front-end that accepts Redwood API-style requests and translates compute work into a scheduling request.
- kvcached-shim: in-memory KV cache with controllable hit-rate to simulate warm/cold sessions.
- kernel-proxy: process that implements a subset of production kernel selection + queuing logic; pluggable policies: simple_fifo, fair_share, priority_shepherd.
- model-mock: tunable latency stub or a real local quantized engine (GGML/onnxruntime path) for end-to-end verification.

Quickstart: run the sandbox (example)
1) Start the sandbox (default ports: 8080 dispatcher, 9090 proxy):
```bash
cd tools/runtime-sandbox
./scripts/start_sandbox.sh --workers 4 --policy priority_shepherd --kv-hit-rate 0.2
```
2) Run a short prompt microbenchmark (50 token generation, batch size 8):
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py --endpoint http://localhost:8080/generate --prompt-file examples/short_prompts.txt --batch-size 8 --tokens 50 --samples 100
```
3) Collect traces and open local report:
```bash
./scripts/collect_traces.sh --out=artifacts/run-$(date +%s)
open artifacts/run-*/index.html  # (Linux: xdg-open)
```

Benchmark Catalog (recommended microbenchmarks)
- short_prompt_50: 50 tokens, mean prompt length 12 tokens, simulates chat replies and low-latency assistant responses.
- medium_prompt_200: 200 tokens, mean prompt length 80 tokens, represents longer instruction completions.
- long_prompt_1024: 1024 tokens, stress test for KV cache and kernel memory usage.
- multi_turn_continuation: sequence of 4 calls with KV cache warmup between calls.
- mixed_priority_mixture: concurrent clients with priority labels (gold/silver/free) to exercise preemption.

Example benchmark command (mixed workload)
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_mixed.sh \
  --clients 40 --gold-share 0.1 --silver-share 0.3 --policy fair_share \
  --duration 300 --output artifacts/mixed-$(date +%s).json
```

Kernel Scheduling Experiments
We expose the following knobs in kernel-proxy to emulate production scheduling behavior:
- batch_window_ms: how long to wait to form a batch before dispatch. Typical test values: 1, 4, 8, 16 ms.
- max_batch_tokens: maximum token budget allowed for a single batch.
- preempt_granularity: slice size used for cooperative preemption (in tokens).
- priority_weight: mapping table for gold/silver/free request weight.

Experiment template (compare batch_window_ms)
1) Start sandbox with identical worker count and model-mock latency profile.
2) Run short_prompt_50 with batch_window_ms set to 1, 4, 8, 16. Each run: 3 warmup minutes + 10 minute sampling.
3) Metrics to record: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), mean batch size, dispatch queue depth.
4) Success criteria: for short_prompt_50, p95 <= 120ms and throughput drop <= 5% relative to baseline.

Profiling and Tracing Guidance
- Enable kernel telemetry: set env RUNTIME_TELEMETRY=1 in start_sandbox.sh to capture per-kernel timings and memory high-water marks.
- GPU traces: when running with a local GPU engine, enable CUPTI tracing via ./scripts/start_gpu_tracing.sh. For CPU-only runs, use perf and flamegraphs.
- Annotate traces with request provenance: the dispatcher attaches request_id and priority_tag to every scheduling event. Include these when uploading traces to the central trace collector.

Trace artifact format and required fields
When you upload a trace for triage, include the following in the artifact zip:
- run_metadata.json (fields: run_id, start_ts, policy, worker_count, kv_hit_rate, model_path)
- kernel_timings.csv (columns: timestamp, kernel_name, duration_ms, occupancy_pct, allocated_bytes)
- batch_events.ndjson (one line per batch event: request_ids[], batch_size, policy, outcome)
- system_monitor.log (CPU, GPU, memory samples at 1s resolution)

Example run_metadata.json (literal snippet)
```json
{
  "run_id": "local-20260210-001",
  "policy": "priority_shepherd",
  "worker_count": 4,
  "kv_hit_rate": 0.2,
  "model_path": "local-ggml/7b-q4_0.bin"
}
```

Runbook: triage workflow for an unexpected latency regression
1) Reproduce locally using the same artifact and policy. If you cannot reproduce, escalate to runtime-sre with full artifact.
2) Run `./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py` with `--diagnostic=true` to produce kernel_timings and batch_events.
3) Check batch size distribution and batch wait times. If mean batch_size drops by >25% vs baseline, suspect batching regressions.
4) Inspect kernel_timings.csv for spikes in a specific kernel. If a single kernel shows >50% increase in median duration, flag as kernel regression and attach minimal repro to a kernel-owner PR.
5) If GPU memory HWM increased significantly, run the memory-fragmentation diagnostic script: `./scripts/gpu_memory_frag_diag.sh`.
6) Document findings in the triage template and update the related run in the benchmarking dashboard.

Known Differences vs Production
- Multi-node routing and remote shard topology are not modeled; cross-node latencies and NUMA effects may be missing.
- The sandbox runs a single GPU device; device-local scheduling differences and inter-GPU NVLink behaviors are not captured.
- Autoscaling and burst capacity behavior is not exercised.
- Real tenant-induced KV-cache conflicts are out of scope.

Best Practices for Developers
- Start with model-mock for rapid iterations; only switch to a local quantized engine (GGML/ONNX) when validating memory and kernel changes.
- Keep run_metadata for every experiment. It is the single source of truth when comparing runs.
- Use stable random seeds when benchmarking (pass --seed <n>) to reduce variance.
- Run at least 3 independent samples for each configuration and report median with IQR.

Onboarding Checklist (for new runtime contributors)
1) Read this playbook and the runtime profiling guidelines page.
2) Run the short_prompt_50 microbenchmark and verify baseline numbers (p95 <= 120ms on a dev workstation with model-mock).
3) Submit one small change (e.g., tweak batch_window_ms) and show the before/after artifacts in a PR.
4) Request review from kernel owners and runtime-sre for approval.

Troubleshooting common errors
- `Connection refused` on kernel-proxy: ensure the proxy is up (docker ps) and ports 9090/9091 are free.
- `Empty batches` warnings: check dispatcher logs; increase batch_window_ms by 2ms for noise-sensitive environments.
- `OOM on model-mock`: reduce model size or run with --simulated-memory=true flag.

Document changelog
- 2024-09-15: Initial draft and quickstart (Asha Patel).
- 2025-06-02: Added mixed_priority_mixture benchmark and new priority_weight knob (Marco Rivera).
- 2026-02-10: Added trace artifact schema and updated triage runbook (Elena Kim).

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-observability (Asha Patel)
- Runtime kernel owners: Marco Rivera (kernel mapper), Linh Tran (preemption infra)
- Escalation: runtime-sre on-call (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)

Appendix: example minimal policy YAML for kernel-proxy
```yaml
policy: priority_shepherd
params:
  batch_window_ms: 4
  max_batch_tokens: 2048
  preempt_granularity: 32
  priority_weight:
    gold: 3
    silver: 2
    free: 1
```

If you have questions about extending the sandbox or integrating additional telemetry hooks, reach out to the runtime-observability channel on Slack and attach run artifacts.
