payload.page_title: Trace augmentation and kernel causal linkage protocol

sections.body: This document defines the Trace Augmentation and Kernel Causal Linkage Protocol (TACKL): a standardized pipeline and set of annotations for enriching runtime traces so that kernel-level events, scheduler decisions, and high-level request metadata can be correlated deterministically for attribution, triage, and experiment analysis. TACKL is intended to reduce mean-time-to-detect for performance regressions, support causal attribution of tail latency to kernel events, and provide a repeatable lab protocol for validating fixes.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to all runtime components that emit execution traces and kernel telemetry: dispatcher, scheduler, kernel plugins, KV cache, and the GPU dispatcher layer.
- Covers production sampling, deterministic augmentation in canary environments, and the lab replay pipeline.
- Not intended to replace end-to-end distributed tracing standards (Zipkin/Jaeger) but to extend them with kernel-specific causal markers and deterministic linkage.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- trace_id: Global request identifier propagated across layers.
- causal_span: A span annotated with a causal tag pointing to a kernel decision or event.
- kernel_anchor: A short opaque token (8-char) representing a kernel-level event group (e.g., preemption, handoff, slow-kernel).
- decision_provenance: Compact encoded tuple showing scheduler policy, priority bucket, and timestamp.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- Link >= 95% of sampled request traces to a kernel_anchor when a kernel event influenced latency > 5ms.
- Reduce investigation time for kernel-related tail latency incidents by 40% within 3 months of roll-out.
- Provide reproducible lab replays where kernel anchors map to the same sequence of kernel events in the sandbox.
sections.heading: Goals and success criteria

sections.body:
1) Instrumentation contract:
   - All services in the runtime must propagate trace_id and include a 3-field augmentation header when emitting kernel-facing requests: kernel-anchor (nullable), decision-provenance, and preface-timestamp (RFC3339).
   - Kernel modules emit event batches to the augmentation-forwarder with fields: kernel_anchor, event_type, local_timestamp_ns, metrics={latency_ns, occupancy_pct, memory_bytes}.

2) Augmentation-forwarder responsibilities:
   - Deduplicate and fold kernel events into the canonical trace stream.
   - Attach a compact event-sig (sha1 hex truncated to 12) to the trace as causal_span.signature.
   - Promote kernel_anchor to trace-level if any event in the batch exceeds configured thresholds.

3) Sampling and retention policy:
   - Default production sampling rate: 1% of requests.
   - Tail-path selective sampling: sample all requests that enter the >99th percentile latency or hit SLA fallback paths.
   - Full diagnostic retention window for augmented traces: 30 days for incidents, 7 days for general sampling.
sections.heading: Protocol overview

sections.body:
- emitter (service) -> runtime-proxy -> kernel (events) + augmentation-forwarder -> trace-assembler -> observability-store
- The forwarder runs an enrichment worker that uses a lookback table of recent scheduler decisions to attach decision_provenance to event batches.

Attribution model (heuristic + causal tagging):
- Primary attribution heuristic: when kernel_anchor exists and event latency contribution > 5ms, mark causal_span.primary = true and increment kernel_blame_score by normalized latency percent contribution.
- Secondary attribution: if multiple anchors overlap, compute weighted attribution by (kernel_event_latency * occupancy_factor) and emit a sorted list of suspected causes.
- Confidence estimate: each attribution emits a confidence tag (high|medium|low) based on event coverage and correlation score.
sections.heading: Trace augmentation pipeline (components and flow)

sections.body:
1) Create a deterministic replay corpus using request-surface-replay tool with URI and tokenized prompt corpus. Example CLI:
   $ ri-replay --corpus requests.jsonl --seed 42 --output replay.sig
2) Enable full trace augmentation in the sandbox cluster and set sampling=100% for the replay namespace.
3) Record kernel anchors during the run and export augmentation bundles with:
   $ augmentation-export --run-id <id> --format ndjson --output augment.ndjson
4) Validate linkage: run the causal-link-checker to ensure each trace_id in augment.ndjson maps to at most one dominant kernel_anchor.
   $ causal-link-checker augment.ndjson --threshold-ms 5
5) Compare kernel event sequences between baseline and candidate kernels using event-sig diffs and produce a report.

Investigation runbook (when you see persistent tail latency):
1) Triage: identify representative traces from the 99.9th percentile from the observability-store (filter by model, seq_len, tenant).
2) Confirm augmentation: verify trace has kernel_anchor and causal_span.signature present. If not, increase sampling for the affected route and re-run.
3) Attribution: consult the attribution table (dashboard) to see top kernel anchors and their kernel_blame_score.
4) Reproduce: run the replay protocol in a sandbox pinned to the same kernel build and scheduler policy.
5) Hypothesis & patch: use the kernel anchor mapping to propose either a scheduler param change (see table below) or a kernel fallback patch.
6) Canary: deploy patch to a canary pool with 5% traffic and augmentation sampling=100% for 1 hour. Monitor kernel_blame_score and SLO.
7) Rollback criteria: if canary SLO breach > 2x baseline or kernel_blame_score worsens by >20%, rollback immediately.

Operational controls, dashboards, and alerts:
- Dashboard widgets to create: Top kernel_anchors by blame_score, kernel_anchor time series, per-route augmentation coverage, and attribution confidence distribution.
- Alerts:
  - alert_kernel_anchor_spike: trigger when kernel_anchor frequency increases > 3x baseline in 15m window.
  - alert_unlinked_tail_traces: trigger when >30% of 99.9th percentile traces are missing kernel_anchor.
  - alert_attribution_confidence_drop: trigger when average confidence for top causes drops below 60% for 30m.
sections.heading: Experiment lab and replay protocol (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- anchor spike: 3x baseline for 15 minutes.
- unlinked tail traces: 30% missing link in 1 hour.

Scheduler parameter table (common knobs to try during hypothesis patching):
| parameter | range | effect | suggested safe delta |
| priority_bias | -1.0..1.0 | shifts scheduler preference between latency-sensitive and economic throughput | +/-0.1 |
| preempt_window_ms | 0..200 | window that allows cooperative preemption to occur | -10ms to +20ms |
| kv_prefetch_budget | 0..10 | number of concurrent prefetch slots per shard | +/-1 |
| evict_grace_ms | 0..500 | extra grace for soft-evictions to complete | +50ms |

Example augmentation JSON snippet emitted by augmenter (ndjson line):
{"trace_id":"t-3f7c8a","kernel_anchor":"KA9b2f1d","causal_span":{"signature":"c1a9d3b7f2aa"},"decision_provenance":"sched=v2|bucket=high|ts=2026-02-02T15:04:05Z","events":[{"type":"slow-kernel","latency_ns":8200000,"occupancy":0.86}]}
sections.heading: Threshold suggestions

sections.body:
- The augmentation-forwarder is a best-effort component: it must not increase request tail latency. If augmentation queue lag exceeds 100ms, the forwarder will switch to async best-effort mode and emit a telemetry event.
- Avoid storing PII in augmented traces; strip user prompt content unless requested and approved under a support ticket.
- Encryption: augmented bundles at rest must be encrypted with the default KMS key for observability assets.
sections.heading: Implementation notes and safety

sections.body:
- Primary owners: Runtime Observability team (owner: Priya Nayar).
- Secondary owners: Scheduler team (reviewer: Ethan Blake), Kernel team (reviewer: Mariana Soto).
- Rollout plan:
  1. Implement forwarder prototype in sandbox (Q4 2025).
  2. Internal lab validation and 100% sampling replay (Jan 2026).
  3. Canary in production with 1% sampling (Feb 2026).
  4. Full rollout with dashboards and runbook training (Mar 2026).

Appendix A — common failure modes and mitigations:
- Missing trace propagation: ensure all HTTP/gRPC libraries include trace_id header and are upgraded to runtime 3.4+. Mitigation: emergency patch to inject trace_id at proxy layer.
- Forwarder overload: backpressure to kernel emitter and fall back to async ingestion. Monitor forwarder_queue_length > 2000 as critical.
- False positive anchors: refine anchor generation by tightening event grouping windows and requiring two corroborating signals (occupancy and latency).

payload.page_title: Latency fingerprinting and kernel-sensitivity index: measurement and runbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page documents the Latency Fingerprinting methodology and the Kernel-Sensitivity Index (KSI) used by the serving runtime team to:
- Quantify per-kernel impact on P50/P95/P99 for representative text-generation workloads.
- Rank kernels by sensitivity so scheduling and preemption policies can be tuned without risking regressions.
- Provide a reproducible investigation runbook for tail-latency incidents attributed to kernel scheduling or kernel-level regressions.

Audience
--------
Primary: runtime engineers, SREs, performance QA, and release engineers. Secondary: product managers and infra owners who need a traceable cost/latency signal when evaluating kernel rollouts or quantization changes.

Why this matters
-----------------
We observe intermittent tail spikes that correlate with kernel version rollouts and heterogeneous job mixes. High-level SLOs are: P95 < 250ms, P99 < 800ms for short-sequence interactive routes; P50 < 30ms for control-plane fast-paths. Without a per-kernel sensitivity metric, rollouts rely on opaque aggregate telemetry and longer canary windows. KSI accelerates detection and points to a minimal remediation surface.

Definitions
-----------
- Latency fingerprint: a compact profile (histogram summary + contextual tags) describing how a specific workload shape (sequence length distribution, prompt tokenization class, decoding mode) maps to the latency curve observed on a given kernel build.
- Kernel-Sensitivity Index (KSI): a scalar in [-1.0, +1.0] representing the normalized change in tail latency attributable to a kernel compared with a baseline kernel. Positive KSI means the kernel increases latency.
- Workload shape: a tuple of {model_variant, avg_sequence_length, decoding_mode, batch_size_distribution}.

Measurement approach (high level)
--------------------------------
1) Select representative workload shapes from the operational workload catalog (see runtime-sandboxing lab manual). Each shape must include a seed prompt set (N=512) sampled from production anonymized traffic.
2) Run A/B microbenchmarks with deterministic seeds: baseline kernel (K0) vs candidate kernel (K1). Use traffic replay harness with request timing jitter to reflect production concurrency.
3) Collect per-request timing, kernel-name tag, compile flags, GPU occupancy, kernel queue depth, and full trace ids.
4) Compute the latency fingerprint (histogram quantiles plus conditional breakdowns) and the KSI per-shape.
5) Validate significance with bootstrap sampling (95% CI).

Detailed measurement protocol
-----------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Access to performance lab fleet with matching GPU family and driver version.
- Canary traffic replay harness (repo: infra/rl-replay) checked out at commit referenced in related_pages.
- Profiling agent v2.3+ installed (service: runtime-profiler).

Commands (example)
1) Install profiling agent and start harness:

$ git clone https://repo.internal/redwood/infra/rl-replay.git
$ cd rl-replay && ./setup.sh --gpu-family ampere --driver 555.40
$ ./replay --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --concurrency 128 --pacing jittered --profile --out /tmp/replay-output.json

2) Run candidate vs baseline pair with pinned kernel metadata:

$ ./replay --kernel-tag K0 --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --run-id baseline-2026-02-01 --profile --out baseline.json
$ ./replay --kernel-tag K1 --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --run-id candidate-2026-02-01 --profile --out candidate.json

3) Compute latency fingerprint and KSI (python tool):

$ pytools/latency_fingerprint/compute_ksi.py --baseline baseline.json --candidate candidate.json --out ksi_report.json

What the KSI output looks like
----------------------------
- ksi_report.json (example fields, abbreviated):
  - work_shape: "gpt-7b,avg_seq=64,topk=40"
  - ksi_value: "0.23"
  - p95_baseline: "312ms"
  - p95_candidate: "384ms"
  - p99_baseline: "820ms"
  - p99_candidate: "1102ms"
  - bootstrap_ci: "[0.18, 0.29]"
  - significant: "true"

Interpreting KSI
----------------
- KSI > +0.1: kernel is considered high-risk for the shape (investigate and block wide rollouts).
- +0.02 <= KSI <= +0.1: caution — prefer canary gating and extended sampling windows.
- -0.02 <= KSI <= +0.02: neutral — no action required beyond normal canary.
- KSI < -0.02: improvement — note in release notes and consider prioritized rollout.

Kernel-sensitivity matrix (example ASCII table)
------------------------------------------------
Each row is a workload shape; each column is a kernel candidate. Values are KSI (rounded).

| workload \t| kernel_K0 \t| kernel_K1 \t| kernel_K2 \t|
| short-chat \t| 0.00 \t| 0.23 \t| -0.04 \t|
| long-summarize \t| 0.00 \t| 0.07 \t| 0.12 \t|
| embeddings-batch \t| 0.00 \t| -0.02 \t| 0.01 \t|

This matrix is stored in the performance dashboard under: dashboards/ksi/matrix-latest (grafana).

Runbook: Investigate a kernel-attributed tail-latency incident
-------------------------------------------------------------
If an alert fires that correlates to a kernel rollout (alert name: kernel-sensitivity-p99-spike):
1) Triage: capture alert context, affected routes, and kernel-tag from the release event.
   - Owner: oncall-runtime (pager duty: runtime-team)
   - Initial data: timeframe, route(s), kernel-tag, % of traffic using kernel-tag.
2) Pull latency fingerprints for the top 3 affected shapes from the last 24h (dashboard query).
3) Run a quick A/B with the exact baseline and candidate on a staging replica using the seed prompts for the affected routes (10 minutes).
4) If KSI > +0.1 and bootstrap CI excludes 0: escalate to Kernel Rollout WG and block rollout. Create an issue: infra/kernel-rollout-blocker with the KSI report attached.
5) If KSI in (+0.02, +0.1): set temporary rate limit on the candidate kernel in the scheduler (see command below) and increase sampling to 4x for next 4 hours.
6) If neutral: continue monitoring and annotate release notes with the verification run id.
7) Record mitigations and postmortem if incident SLI impact exceeds threshold (sla-impact > 1 hour or customer-facing SLO breaches).

Commands to throttle candidate kernel in scheduler (example)
----------------------------------------------------------
- CLI (schedulerctl) to reduce slot weight for kernel-tag K1:

$ schedulerctl set-weight --kernel K1 --weight 0.2 --reason "ksi-quick-mitigation-2026-02-01"

- Revert:
$ schedulerctl set-weight --kernel K1 --weight 1.0 --reason "revert-ksi-mitigation"

Telemetry and observability contract
-----------------------------------
Every replay and production request must carry these trace tags:
- runtime.kernel_tag
- runtime.kernel_build_id
- runtime.kernel_variant (e.g., fp16-quant, int8-sym)
- runtime.kv_hit (true|false)
- runtime.queue_depth (integer)

Dashboards and alerts to check
-----------------------------
- dashboards/ksi/summary: KSI trend per kernel and workload shape.
- dashboards/latency/route-breakdown: per-route P50/P95/P99.
- alerting/kernel-sensitivity-p99-spike: triggers when KSI-based p99 delta > 150ms and traffic fraction > 5%.
- alerting/kernel-regression-ci-failure: flags if canary KSI exceeds +0.05 over three successive daily runs.

Guidance for release engineers
------------------------------
- Add KSI reports to the kernel candidate artifact in the release bundle under /artifacts/ksi/*.json.
- Require a KSI sign-off (responsible: perf-lead) for kernels with KSI > +0.02 on any production shape before global rollout.
- Use staged rollouts with weight 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with KSI checks at each gate.

Limitations and known caveats
----------------------------
- Small sample sizes for rare workload shapes inflate CI; prefer combining shapes with the same kernel hotpath.
- KSI attribution is sensitive to queueing effects; ensure queue depth tags are stable across A/B runs.
- Driver or compiler-level nondeterminism (JIT variability) can create noise — repeat runs and follow up with kernel-level deterministic tracing.

Maintenance and ownership
-------------------------
- Owner team: serving-runtime/perf (primary), eng-sre (secondary).
- Dashboard owner: telemetry-team.
- Review cadence: quarterly. Update this doc when the profiling agent or replay harness changes major versions (major semver).

Appendix: Quick checks and YAML example for CI gating
-----------------------------------------------------

If you have questions or need a dedicated pairing session to walk through the replay harness, ping the perf channel (#perf-runtime) or reach out to the doc reviewers listed above.

payload.page_title: Kernel Determinism Investigation and Replay Protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents a structured protocol for investigating non-deterministic latency or correctness regressions that appear to originate from kernel execution or kernel-selection behavior in the serving runtime. It provides a hypothesis-driven replay workflow, the required data artifacts, checklist of signals to inspect, and a reproducible sandbox procedure for iterating on kernel-level fixes. The intent is to reduce mean time to root cause for kernels that produce intermittent slow paths or divergent outputs across retries.

Scope

- Applies to runtime versions 2023.11 and later and to kernels managed by the kernel mapper (kmux).
- Focuses on issues where the same request input produces different execution characteristics (latency, kernel choice, memory usage) across retries or across replicas.
- Excludes: pure network/transit issues (see eng-sre incident runbooks), and model-level randomness that is expected by design (e.g., sampling).

Definitions

- Determinism failure: the same complete request (headers, model version, prompt, session KV state) produces different kernel selection, resource consumption, or tail latency without legitimate reason.
- Replay corpus: a saved set of requests + runtime context used to deterministically re-run workload in a sandbox.
- Kernel trace: annotated timeline of kernel lifecycle events (select, load, handshake, exec_begin, exec_end, evict).

When to use this playbook

- Tail latency spikes that correlate with kernel-change events in traces (kernel_swap, kernel_fallback).
- Flaky regression test failures in the throughput bench that cannot be reproduced by simple load replay.
- Divergent telemetry across cold and warm runs where KV cache and kernel-choice paths differ.

Prerequisites and permissions

- Access to the runtime profiling cluster and ability to create sandbox sandboxes (incubation clusters) — request via infra-ticket-jenkins with tag "profiling-sandbox".
- Read access to kernel binary registry and kernel metadata (kmux/catalog service).
- Tools: local replay harness (repo: infra/replay-harness), trace-analyzer (repo: infra/trace-tools), a copy of the production request-sampler export (stored in /artifacts/profiles/year-month).

High-level workflow (quick view)

1) Triage: capture representative requests and runtime traces.
2) Isolate: build a minimal replay corpus that reproduces divergence.
3) Replay: run deterministic replay under the sandbox with full kernel telemetry enabled.
4) Hypothesize: enumerate kernel-level causes and validate by controlled experiments.
5) Patch & validate: deploy kernel fix to canary and run regression suite.

Detailed procedure

1) Triage and initial capture

- Collect the request payloads and full trace IDs for 10-100 affected requests. Include: request headers, model name+commit, session_id, router route, and exact timestamp. Example required metadata JSON (single-line):

  {"request_id":"<id>","model":"redwood-open-7b-v2","seq_len":128,"route":"text.generate","trace_id":"abcd-1234"}

- Pull the trace events using trace-analyzer:

  trace-analyzer export --trace-id abcd-1234 --out /tmp/trace-abcd.json

- Identify kernel events: search for event types select_kernel, kernel_load, kernel_exec_begin, kernel_exec_end, kernel_evict. Record kernel binary hash, node id, and slot_id.

2) Build a deterministic replay corpus

- For each request record: full body, headers, KV cache snapshot (if available), and the exact model variant string (e.g., redwood-open-7b-v2@2025-11-03-rc2).
- Prefer requests that: previously triggered both fast and slow outcomes; have identical inputs; and show kernel-choice flip in traces.
- Store corpus under: /artifacts/replay-corpora/kernel-determinism/<run-id>/corpus.jsonl . Each line is a JSON object with flat fields.

3) Configure sandbox for deterministic replay

- Provision a sandbox cluster with identical software ABI and kernel catalog. Use the infra playbook to pin: runtime image (sha256), kmux catalog revision, and kernel binaries revision.
- Enable deterministic runtime flags in /etc/runtime/conf.d/replay.toml:

  [replay]
  enforce_kv_snapshot = true
  disable_dynamic_kernel_prefetch = true
  seed_kernel_mapper = "fixed"

- Start the sandbox runtime with kernel telemetry level = 5 and trace sampling = 100%.

4) Run replay and capture outputs

- Command (example):

  replay-harness run --corpus /artifacts/replay-corpora/kernel-determinism/<run-id>/corpus.jsonl --target http://sandbox-runtime:8080 --concurrency 4 --repeat 3 --write-traces /tmp/replay-traces

- For each replay iteration, collect: latency percentile distribution, kernel trace files, kernel binary checksums, and any divergence in model output tokens.

5) Hypothesis generation and controlled experiments

- Common hypothesis patterns to test: 
  - Kernel handshake race: two concurrent requests caused a different kernel to be selected due to a timing window.
  - Eviction-induced cold path: aggressive eviction policy allowed a kernel to be reloaded on hot path causing startup overhead.
  - Kernel compatibility fallback: kmux selected a binary variant with different quantization profile under memory pressure.
  - Kernel threading/SM occupancy variance: same kernel executed at different GPU occupancy causing execution time variability.

- For each hypothesis, design a minimal controlled change and re-run the replay:
  1. Handshake race: serialize kernel selection with a 10ms mutex and observe if flip disappears.
  2. Eviction: increase kernel hot-cache TTL to 300s during replay.
  3. Compatibility fallback: pin kernel selection to the primary binary (force_kmux_binary = <hash>).
  4. Occupancy: pin GPU affinity to single SM mask to measure per-kernel exec time variance.

6) Observability signals and acceptance thresholds

- Signals to inspect (table described in text):
  - metric: kernel_select_rate_change -> acceptable: <= 2x baseline during repro
  - metric: exec_time_p95 (per-kernel) -> acceptable: p95 within 10% of baseline for stable kernels
  - event: kernel_fallback_count -> acceptable: 0 for deterministic-corpus runs
  - log: handshake_timeout -> acceptable: none

- If any signal exceeds the threshold, mark the hypothesis as plausible and escalate to kernel-owner.

7) Patch, canary, and regression suite

- If a kernel binary or kernel-selection policy change is required:
  - Build a kernel binary with debug symbols and a short-lived toggle flag.
  - Canaries: deploy to a single sandbox shard and run the full replay corpus 10x.
  - Regression: add a synthetic test to the microbench that replays the failing corpus and assert median+p95 latency and kernel_fallback_count == 0.

8) Postmortem artefacts and documentation

- Required artifacts for closure: replay corpus, raw traces, diff of kernel catalog, patch PR, canary run logs, and regression test entry. Attach these in the incident ticket and link to this playbook.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: runtime-kernel-team (pager: oncall-kernel).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre (for sandbox provisioning and capacity).
- Escalation path: kernel oncall -> runtime tech lead -> infra reliability director. Use the standard oncall escalation timeline (15/45/90 minutes).

Example artifacts

- Minimal trace extract (abbreviated):
  {
    "trace_id":"abcd-1234",
    "events":[
      {"ts":1678891200123, "type":"select_kernel", "binary":"khash:aa11"},
      {"ts":1678891200150, "type":"kernel_load", "node":"gpu-17"},
      {"ts":1678891200450, "type":"kernel_exec_begin", "slot":3},
      {"ts":1678891200788, "type":"kernel_exec_end", "duration_ms":338}
    ]
  }

- Sample replay harness command for deterministic pinning:
  replay-harness run --pin-binary aa11 --concurrency 1 --repeat 5 --write-traces /tmp/fixed

Runbook checklist (quick reference)

- [ ] Collect 10 representative traces and request payloads.
- [ ] Build deterministic replay corpus and upload to artifacts storage.
- [ ] Provision sandbox with pinned runtime + kernels.
- [ ] Run replay with telemetry = 100% and collect kernel traces.
- [ ] Validate hypothesis with at least one controlled experiment.
- [ ] Patch and run canary + regression tests.
- [ ] Document artifacts and close incident with owners tagged.

Appendix A: Common pitfalls

- Missing KV snapshot: If KV cache snapshot is not available, some nondeterminism will persist. Always prefer requests tied to explicit KV snapshots.
- Environment mismatch: small differences in CUDA/driver versions can produce different SM scheduling behaviour — ensure sandbox matches production drivers at the ABI level.
- Over-interpreting noise: small p50/p75 changes are expected under load; focus on p95/p99 and binary selection flips.

Appendix B: Where to find helpers

- replay-harness: git@github.com:redwood/infra/replay-harness
- trace-analyzer: git@github.com:redwood/infra/trace-tools
- artifacts storage: s3://redwood-internal/profiles/

Appendix C: Change log

- 2024-03-20: Initial draft (M. Chen).
- 2025-08-09: Added controlled experiment recipes and runbook checklist (E. Rivera).
- 2026-02-11: Updated sandbox pinning flags and observability thresholds (L. Sørensen).

payload.page_title: KV-prefetch audit and experiment guide

sections.body:
Overview
This document is a pragmatic audit + experiment playbook for evaluating and iterating on KV-cache prefetch strategies in the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates instrumentation, test-corpus design, hypothesis-driven experiments, safety gates, and clear remediation steps to validate that a prefetch change improves throughput or cost without regressing latency or output fidelity.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers (kernel and scheduler owners)
- Performance and profiling teams
- SREs running capacity and incident drills
- Release engineers validating runtime rollouts

Goals
1) Provide a repeatable audit checklist to assess existing prefetch behaviour and its observability gaps.
2) Define experiment templates (canary, A/B, ramp) with required telemetry, sample sizes, and SLO-aligned success criteria.
3) Offer rollout and rollback runbook steps with specific threshold values and playbook actions.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: KV prefetch heuristics, warmup policies, prefetch batch sizing, prefetch prioritisation across tenants/model variants, and their impact on kernel scheduling and KV cache hit/miss behavior.
- Non-goals: Changes to model serialization or offline model compile pipeline (handled elsewhere). This guide does not substitute for security or compliance sign-off for customer-sensitive telemetry.

Background and terminology
- KV prefetch: pro-active population of a model's key-value cache before predicted use (e.g., during warmstart or after canary shadowing).
- Warmstart: placement of a model variant onto a GPU with pre-warmed KV state for a target user session.
- Prefetch window: sequence-length- and token-count-derived horizon for which we request early KV population.
- Shadow traffic: mirrored request streams used for dry-run experiments.

Observability contract (what to collect)
Collect these signals for all experiments. Instrumentation must be enabled at service, runtime-shard, and kernel levels.
- Metrics (per-second or histogram as noted):
  - kvcache.prefetch.requests_total (counter)
  - kvcache.prefetch.success_ratio (gauge) = success / attempts per minute
  - kvcache.hit_ratio_by_prefix_length (histogram buckets by prefix tokens)
  - kvcache.prefetch_latency_p50/p95 (histogram ms)
  - kernel.queue_wait_ms (histogram) labeled by priority bucket
  - runtime.topology.eviction_rate (counter per shard)
  - gpu.memory.oversubscription_events (counter)
  - request.latency.p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end including network + kernel)
  - request.tail_slo_breaches (counter) where tail SLO := requests > configured target (e.g., 95th > 120ms)
  - cost.per_token.estimated (derived using token counts + kernel accounting)
- Traces: request span with children: prefetch.call, prefetch.cache_write, kernel.exec, kv_lookup; include tags: model_id, variant_tag, session_id, shard_id, kernel_id, tenant_id, prefetch_hint_id.
- Logs: structured event for prefetch decisions: {"decision":"prefetch|skip","reason":"prefix-match|heuristic|manual","estimated_tokens":N,"evicted":true|false,"latency_ms":N} as newline-delimited JSON to the observability pipeline.

Audit checklist (baseline assessment)
1) Baseline traffic capture
   - Capture at least 72 hours of representative production traffic or use a validated synthetic corpus (see Test corpus section).
   - Ensure sampling includes peak hour and low-hour slices.
2) Reproduceability of prefetch events
   - Verify prefetch events are traceable to requests in shadow logs. Correlate prefetch_hint_id across traces.
3) Telemetry completeness
   - Confirm all metrics and traces listed in Observability contract are present. If any are missing, add target instrumentation and replay a synthetic subset to validate.
4) Heatmaps and correlation checks
   - Build the following diagnostics:
     - heatmap: prefix_length -> prefetch_success_rate
     - scatter: per-request prefetch_latency vs request_latency
     - timeline: eviction_rate vs memory_pressure
5) Failure mode inventory
   - Enumerate cases found in logs (e.g., prefetch eviction within 2s, prefetch causing kernel queueing). Classify severity and likely root causes.

Test corpus recommendations
- Canonical corpora: use a mix of (a) production-scrubbed request traces, (b) replayable synthetic sessions (session bundles), and (c) jittered-edge sequences to exercise long prefixes.
- Session bundle format (JSONL, one session per line):
  {"session_id":"s-123","model":"vicuna-13b-q4","turns":["Hello","Summarize: ...","Followup: ..."],"timestamps":[...]}
- Size guidance: minimum 5000 sessions covering 10k prefix variations for a statistically meaningful p95 comparison in canary windows.

Experiment designs
All experiments must be hypothesis-driven and limited in blast radius. Follow the experiment checklist below.

A) Shadow (no impact) hypothesis test
- Goal: Validate prefetch hit-rate and false-positive eviction costs without affecting production latency.
- Method: Mirror 1:1 traffic to a shadow runtime with the new prefetch strategy. Do not route responses.
- Duration: 48–72 hours or until 10k prefetch decisions observed.
- Required metrics: kvcache.prefetch.success_ratio, eviction_rate, prefetch_latency.
- Success criteria: improvement in prefetch.success_ratio by >=5% or reduction in cold-start kernel execs by >=10% with no increase in eviction_rate > 2% over baseline.

B) Canary small ramp (impactful but controlled)
- Goal: Measure end-to-end latency and kernel queue impact under production conditions.
- Method: Route 1% of traffic to canary pool with the new prefetch strategy. Use canary tags and separate metrics.
- Observation windows: 1 minute, 15 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours.
- Safety gates (auto-rollback triggers):
  - request.tail_slo_breaches increases by >20% relative to baseline in a 15-minute window -> immediate rollback.
  - kernel.queue_wait_ms.p95 increases by >30% sustained for 10 minutes -> immediate pause and manual review.
  - gpu.memory.oversubscription_events > 0 (new events) in canary -> pause.
- Success criteria: no SLO breach increase; p95 request latency change within +/- 5% and prefetch.success_ratio improved or neutral.

C) A/B experiment with fidelity measurement
- Goal: Measure fidelity / model output drift when prefetching influences KV state timing (rare but possible).
- Method: 50/50 split where identical prompts are sent to control (no change) and candidate (new prefetch). Collect deterministic evaluation prompts and human-eval random sample.
- Fidelity metrics: BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity on deterministic prompts, plus small human quality cohort (n=200) to detect hallucination/regression.
- Success criteria: embedding cosine similarity > 0.995 on deterministic prompts and no statistically significant decrease in human-score (alpha=0.05).

Telemetry and sample size calculations
- Latency experiments: to detect a 5% p95 change with 90% power typically needs O(20k) p95 samples per group; for canaries prefer longer duration instead of increasing blast radius.
- Hit-rate experiments: to detect a 5% absolute increase in hit rate with alpha=0.05/power=0.8, ~thousands of prefetch events are required depending on baseline rate; use exact binomial test calculator.

Experiment orchestration and dashboards
- Dashboards: create canary-specific dashboards with the prefixed label canary=kv-prefetch-vX. Panels: prefetch.success_ratio, request.p95, kernel.queue_wait_ms.p95, eviction_rate, memory_pressure, tail_slo_breaches; include shaded baseline band.
- Alerts: temporary canary alerts that auto-resolve after ramp is complete.

Rollout and rollback runbook (step-by-step)
1) Preflight (1–3 days before canary)
   - Verify instrumentation and dashboards are green.
   - Run shadow test and ensure metrics are recorded.
   - Prepare rollback image and clear owner contact list.
2) Canary 1% (0–2 hours)
   - Deploy config to canary pool. Monitor 1m and 15m windows.
   - If any auto-rollback trigger fires, execute rollback playbook (step 5).
3) Ramp to 5% (2–12 hours)
   - After 6 hours of stable signals, increment to 5%. Continue monitoring 1m/15m/1h/6h windows.
4) Ramp to 20% (12–48 hours)
   - Confirm A/B fidelity checks pass on deterministic prompts.
5) Full roll (48–72 hours)
   - Only after 72 hours with no gate violations and cost analysis favorable, schedule full rollout.
6) Rollback procedure (when triggered)
   - Step A: Pause canary routing (set weight=0).
   - Step B: Revert runtime config to previous prefetch policy image.
   - Step C: Collect postmortem trace dump, capture 2-hour window around trigger for RCA.
   - Step D: Open incident with severity classification and tag owners.

Common failure modes and mitigations
- Failure: Increased kernel queueing due to premature prefetch floods.
  - Mitigation: Add rate limiter on prefetch.requests per shard per second; add backpressure signal from kernel.queue_wait_ms.
- Failure: Prefetch evicts hot state for other tenants.
  - Mitigation: Implement tenant-aware prefetch budgeting and soft reservations.
- Failure: Memory oversubscription from prefetch writes.
  - Mitigation: Pre-allocate lightweight shadow stores and throttle writes when memory_pressure > 70%.

Debugging checklist (fast triage)
1) Correlate prefetch decision trace with kernel.exec and eviction events (trace id).
2) If prefetch_latency_p95 > 100ms, inspect network path and serialization overhead.
3) If eviction_rate spikes after prefetch, check memory per shard, recent model swaps, and estimate of prefetch window size.
4) Re-run small synthetic session set in debug pool with verbose logging on canary image.

Example config snippets
- Prefetch policy YAML (example):
```yaml
prefetch_policy:
  name: horizon-predictor-v2
  enabled: true
  max_concurrent_per_shard: 8
  token_horizon: 64
  priority: low
  tenant_budget_percent: 5
  eviction_backoff_seconds: 30
  metrics_emit_interval_s: 10
```
- CLI commands (examples)
  - Capture shadow stream (devbox):
    rdxctl kvcapture --model vicuna-13b-q4 --window 72h --out /tmp/vicuna-shadow.jsonl
  - Deploy canary config:
    rdxctl deploy-config --pool canary-kv-prefetch-v2 --config ./prefetch-policy.yaml --tag kv-prefetch-v2
  - Pause canary routing:
    rdxctl set-weight --pool canary-kv-prefetch-v2 --weight 0

Post-experiment analysis and documentation checklist
- Produce a short experiment report that includes: hypothesis, traffic windows used, sample sizes, raw metrics time-series, heatmaps, global and per-tenant impact, cost delta estimate, and recommended next action (rollback, tweak, full rollout).
- Archive experiment artifacts: traces, dashboards, config version, and sample sessions used for reproducibility.
- If fidelity regressions observed, escalate to model onboarding and research for root-cause and mitigation.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: Runtime performance team (runtime-perf@redwood.com).

payload.page_title: Hybrid sample + replay profiling playbook (workload reconstruction)

sections.body: This playbook describes our hybrid profiling approach: low-overhead statistical sampling in production combined with controlled full-trace capture (replay-ready) for targeted sessions. The goal is to reconstruct representative requests (inputs, model variant, KV cache state) for offline replay, root-cause subtle performance regressions, and validate mitigations in a staging replay cluster.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Continuous sampling answers "what's happening" at scale with minimal overhead (0.5–1% CPU/RU).
- Full-trace capture (trace-on-demand) captures exact execution paths (kernels invoked, kernel timings, batch composition, KV cache hits) for a small subset of sessions to enable deterministic replay and perf validation.
- We combine both approaches to reduce signal-to-noise, limit storage costs, and produce actionable repros for runtime/kernel scheduling regressions.
sections.heading: Context and motivation

sections.body:
1. Tail-latency regressions that don't surface in microbenchmarks.
2. Kernel scheduling anomalies (priority inversion, starvation) suspected from sampled traces.
3. Regression triage after a rollout (canary or gradual) where sampled metrics indicate increasing variance.
sections.heading: When to use this playbook

sections.body:
- Playbook owner: eng-serving-runtime profiling team (primary: Asha Menon).
- Response SLA for initiating a replay capture after an alert: 2 business days.
- Repro attempt and initial report: 5 business days.
sections.heading: Owner and SLAs

sections.body:
1. Analyze continuous sample telemetry and identify candidate sessions.
2. If available, attach matching trace-on-demand session(s). If not, enable trace-on-demand for the relevant traffic slice for a limited window.
3. Export inputs and KV cache deltas to the replay bucket.
4. Reconstruct request in replay environment and run deterministic workload.
5. Compare kernel timeline and resource occupancy between production sample and replay.
6. Iterate with kernel scheduling or batching config changes; rerun replay.
sections.heading: High-level steps (overview)

sections.body:
A. Selecting candidate sessions from samples:
1. Query the profiler sampling index for windows where P99 latency deviates > 20% from baseline for the model and route.
2. Filter sessions by: model_version, route_tag, tenant_id, and sequence_length bucket.
3. For each session, compute a "replay_score" = weight(latency) + weight(kernel_variance) + weight(kvcache_miss_rate). Use thresholds: scores > 0.7 mark as high-priority.

B. Enabling trace-on-demand safely:
- Window: 5–15 minutes for initial capture.
- Rate cap: max 1 trace/min per node; global cap 50 traces per hour across cluster.
- Use route-level sampling policy: tag routes to limit to affected customer/experiment.
- Commands:
  - Enable:
    TOGGLE_CMD=$(redwoodctl profiling trace enable --route my-route --window 10m --cap 50)
  - Disable:
    redwoodctl profiling trace disable --route my-route

C. What to capture in a trace (mandatory fields):
- request_id, model_version, prompt_hash, tokenized_input (safe-hashed), full kernel invocation timeline (per-kernel name, start_ns, duration_ns), batch_id, batch_composition (other request IDs in same batch), GPU index, device memory map, KV cache delta (keys evicted/inserted) as changelog, and environment tags (node, runtime-build).
sections.heading: Detailed procedures

sections.body:
| artifact | storage path | retention | rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sampled-metrics (aggregates) | s3://profiling/samples/yyyy/ | 90 days | rollups for alerting and SLO backfills |
| trace-on-demand raw | s3://profiling/traces/yyyy/ | 30 days | full replays are costly; short TTL |
| replay-recons | s3://profiling/replays/yyyy/ | 180 days | preserve repros tied to releases |
| kvcache-deltas | s3://profiling/kvcache-deltas/yyyy/ | 90 days | needed to reconstruct warmstart state |
sections.heading: Storage and retention policy (table)

sections.body:
1. Match runtime binary and kernel versions: use artifact tag from trace (runtime_build: tag).
2. Provision GPU nodes with identical or superset topology. For known NUMA-sensitive regressions, match node SKU and affinity masks.
3. Configure model weights path and quantization profile as recorded.
4. Seed KV cache from kvcache-deltas: apply changelog in order to an empty cache.
5. Configure batch scheduler to accept the recorded batch composition and arrival timings (use synthetic inter-arrival to reproduce burst/coalescing).
sections.heading: Replay environment setup checklist

sections.body:
- Export traces for replay run:
  redwoodctl profiling export --trace-id 1234abcd --out /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz
- Initialize replay environment:
  replayctl init --bundle /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz --runtime-tag release-2026-01-15
- Apply KV cache deltas:
  replayctl kvcache apply --bundle /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz --target replay-node-1
sections.heading: Reconstruction commands (examples)

sections.body: replayctl run --trace-id 1234abcd --repeat 3 --compare-baseline /tmp/prod_timeline.json --output /tmp/replay_result.json
sections.heading: Deterministic replay run (example)

sections.body:
- Kernel timeline (per-step) and per-kernel duration distribution.
- GPU occupancy and SM utilization trace.
- CPU-to-GPU transfer timings (host staging times).
- Batch composition mismatch report (if scheduler coalesced requests differently).
- KV cache hit/miss timeline before and after warmstart.
sections.heading: Validation and artifacts to collect from replay runs

sections.body:
- If replay kernel timeline matches production within 5% but latency differs > 15% -> investigate host-level interference (noisy neighbor) and network jitter.
- If kernel variance differs > 20% -> likely scheduling non-determinism or different concurrency mix in production. Check batch-size distribution over 1 hour window.
- If KV cache miss delta explains > 30% of token processing time -> treat as cache warmup issue and consider extending cache TTL for route.
sections.heading: Alert thresholds and triage heuristics

sections.body:
1. Validate runtime and kernel versions are identical. If mismatch, recreate replay with correct binary.
2. Re-run replay on node with isolated CPU/GPU (pinning) to rule out host noise.
3. Toggle kernel scheduling knobs: kernel_credit_limit, preemption_window_ms, eager_batching_enable. Use incremental changes and single-variable experiments.
4. If scheduling changes affect latency positively in replay, run small canary rollout with those knobs for 1% traffic and monitor sampled P95/P99.
sections.heading: Mitigations and runbook actions (ordered)

sections.body: - Any kernel-level knob change must include an automatic rollback policy: revert if P99 increases > 10% or error rate increases > 0.5% within 30 minutes.
sections.heading: Safe rollback guidance

sections.body:
-----BEGIN CONFIG-----
profiling:
  sampling:
    default_rate: 0.005  # 0.5% of requests
    stratified_by: [model_version, sequence_length_bucket, route_tag]
  trace_on_demand:
    enabled: false
    global_cap_per_hour: 50
    per_node_rate_limit: 1/min
  artifacts:
    traces_bucket: s3://profiling/traces/{{YYYY}}/{{MM}}/{{DD}}
    replay_bucket: s3://profiling/replays/
-----END CONFIG-----
sections.heading: Example profiler config (YAML)

sections.body:
- Never store full prompt text for customer requests. Store tokenized inputs with reversible hashing disabled; keep a prompt_hash and only store cleartext for synthetic/internal test traces.
- Access to replay artifacts is restricted to eng-serving-runtime and incident response SSO groups. All exports are logged to audit.
sections.heading: Security and privacy notes

sections.body:
- profiler.sampled.latency.p99 (by model_version, route_tag)
- profiler.trace.count (successful captures)
- profiler.kvcache.hit_rate
- runtime.kernel.duration.per_kernel (heatmap)
- replay.compare.delta_ms (post-replay comparison)
sections.heading: Telemetry keys and dashboards to consult

sections.body:
- If a replay produced a fixable action, attach the replay_result.json and a short remediation summary to the incident ticket and update the related kernel ADR if the fix changes scheduling guarantees.

Appendix: common troubleshooting nuggets
- If replay shows identical kernel durations but production is higher, instrument node-level cgroups & host IO (disk/NIC) — often a transient IO spike can amplify token latencies.
- For quantization-induced variance, compare matrix-multiplication microbenchmarks between prod and replay nodes; numerical noise can change control flow in rare models.
sections.heading: Postmortem and documentation updates

sections.body:
- Primary profiling lead: asha.menon@redwood.ai
- Runtime kernel SME: diego.ramirez@redwood.ai
- On-call SRE for replay infra: infra-oncall@redwood.ai
sections.heading: Contacts

sections.body:

- 2026-02-18: Added retention table and replay commands (review feedback).
- 2026-02-28: Finalized thresholds and published.

payload.page_title: Runtime adaptive probing and safe experimentation manual

sections.body:
Summary
This document describes a structured, low-risk approach for running adaptive probes and safe experiments against the serving runtime. The goal is to let engineers validate kernel scheduling, prefetch, KV-cache, and fallback changes in production-adjacent conditions while protecting customer SLOs and cost budgets. It covers experiment design, traffic shaping, observability checks, escalation criteria, and rollback procedures.

Why we need this
- The runtime surface changes frequently (kernels, scheduler heuristics, prefetch hints). Small regressions can cause outsized tail-latency or cost spikes.
- Full canaries are slow and expensive; controlled probes let teams exercise code paths with minimal impact.
- We need an explicit safety envelope and operator checklist to avoid cross-tenant mistakes.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: kernel scheduling variants, kv-prefetch hints, admission-controller tuning, preemption and slice sizes, and experimental kernel flags.
- Non-goals: model-level quality evaluation (handled by eval-harness), long-running traffic migration (handled by deployment runbooks).

Key definitions
1) Probe: a short-lived, small-percentage traffic injection targeted at a cohort (by route/model/tenant).
2) Staging fidelity: running probe traffic through a shadow path and measuring fidelity metrics versus production path.
3) Safe window: pre-defined SLO headroom and alert thresholds that must hold for a probe to run.

Operational guardrails (must be met before any probe)
- Service-level prechecks (automated):
  - Global token success rate >= 99.9% over 1h
  - 95th-tail P99 latency for the baseline route below route_SLO * 0.9 for 30m
  - Node GPU utilization under 70% cluster-wide for 15m
- Isolation requirements: target cohort must be scoped to <= 2% of global QPS or explicitly to a small test tenant.
- Cost cap: probe should not increase per-token GPU energy by more than 12% compared to baseline in the first 10m of collection.

Design a probe (checklist)
1) Hypothesis: clear, short statement (e.g., "reduce P99 by 10% for short-sequence requests by enabling slice preemption").
2) Metrics to observe: latency quantiles (P50/P95/P99/P999), success rate, kernel queue depth, gputop power, per-token cost estimate, KV cache hit rate, and fidelity delta (if applicable).
3) Cohort selection: pick either (a) synthetic test tenant, (b) low-risk customer cohort (explicitly consented), or (c) shadow path only.
4) Duration and ramp: start 5 minutes at 0.5% ramping to 2% over 10 minutes. Maximum probe duration by default is 60 minutes unless approved.
5) Rollout gates: automated checks and human signoff thresholds listed below.

Automated gates (must be green to continue)
- Latency: P99 <= baseline_P99 * 1.08 for the first 15 minutes, and <= baseline_P99 * 1.05 for the following 30 minutes.
- Error surface: request errors + internal 5xx must not exceed baseline_error_rate + 0.02%.
- Kernel failures: no kernel soft-failures or watchdog resets in the target shards.
- Observability fidelity: traces and kernel-level spans must be present for >= 95% of sampled requests.

Human approval gates
- Tier 1: engineering owner may approve probes that affect <= 0.5% traffic for non-critical routes.
- Tier 2: eng-platform lead + SRE approval required for probes affecting 0.5%–2% or probes that change eviction/admission policy.
- Tier 3: executive-level approval + security signoff for probes that cross tenants without prior consent or change secrets/PKI.

Instrumentation and metrics to collect
- Runtime metrics (per-request): request_id, route_id, model_variant, kernel_id, dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_exec_ms, gpubusy_pct, kv_hit, bytes_sent.
- Aggregates: P50/P90/P95/P99/P999 latency, mean QPS, retry rate, per-token GPU ms, energy estimator.
- Tracing: end-to-end trace including route classification, scheduler decision, kernel selection event, and fallback events.
- Cost signal: approximate per-request cloud cost and per-token GPU seconds (used for cost-gating).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- "sum(rate(kernel_exec_ms_sum{kernel=\"exp-scheduler-v2\",route=\"chat.short\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kernel_exec_ms_count{kernel=\"exp-scheduler-v2\",route=\"chat.short\"}[5m]))"
- Use this to compare average kernel execution time between baseline and probe cohorts.

Traffic shaping and routing configuration (sample YAML)
| Field | Meaning | Example |
|---|---:|---|
| cohort_selector | route or tenant selector for probe | route: chat.short, tenant: test-tenant |
| initial_weight | starting traffic percent | 0.5% |
| max_weight | max allowed traffic percent | 2% |
| ramp_minutes | minutes to reach max_weight | 10 |
| duration_minutes | total probe runtime | 60 |
| observability_backends | list of tracing/metrics exports | "otel, prometheus,kinesis" |
sections.heading: Example observability query (PromQL-like pseudo)

sections.body:
---
probe:
  name: "slice-preempt-probe-2025-11"
  cohort_selector:
    route: "chat.short"
    tenant: "canary-ops"
  initial_weight: 0.5
  max_weight: 2.0
  ramp_minutes: 10
  duration_minutes: 60
  flags:
    scheduler_variant: "preempt-slice-v2"
  observability_backends: ["otel","prometheus"]
---

Safe experiment types (ranking by risk)
- Level 1 (lowest): Shadow-only fidelity probes (no production path impact).
- Level 2: Synthetic tenant or consented low-traffic tenant with strict automated gates.
- Level 3: Real traffic micro-probes (0.5%–2%) that exercise kernel handoffs or preemption.
- Level 4 (highest risk): Degraded-routing or multi-tenant admission experiments (requires executive review).

Runbook: step-by-step for executing a Level 3 probe
1) Preflight (T-30 to T-5 minutes):
   a) Run cluster health checks: kubectl get nodes, GPU utilization dashboard snapshot, and baseline latency snapshot.
   b) Create probe config and submit to the routing operator in dry-run mode.
   c) Notify the oncall SRE and the owning product/eng team.
2) Start (T0):
   a) Apply probe with initial_weight.
   b) Verify traces are present and that the probe cohort is sampling correctly.
3) Automated monitoring (T0+0–15m):
   a) Watch automated gates; abort if any gate trips.
   b) Post short update to the experiment channel with key metrics (P95/P99, error rate, kernel failures).
4) Ramp (T0+15m–T0+30m):
   a) If gates remain green, allow the operator to ramp to max_weight.
   b) Continue 1m cadence metric posts for the first 30m, then 5m cadence.
5) Stability window (final 30m):
   a) Confirm no divergence in cost and latency signals; run additional synthetic probe queries that exercise edge kernels.
6) Wind-down and analysis (Tfinal):
   a) Remove probe config and confirm traffic returns to baseline.
   b) Run a postmortem-style checklist: did any gate trip? Were kernel anomalies observed? Was per-token cost affected?
   c) If green, prepare experiment notes and schedule follow-up A/B or canary runs.

Abort and rollback criteria (automated or manual)
- Immediate abort if: P999 > baseline_P999 * 1.25, or kernel watchdog resets observed, or error rate increase > 0.1% absolute.
- Soft abort (move to 0.1% for 10m): if P99 > baseline_P99 * 1.15 or per-token energy estimate > baseline * 1.20.
- Manual rollback: any unexplained tail-latency regressions or customer complaints referenced by route.

Post-experiment analysis template
- Experiment id: <uuid>
- Hypothesis: text
- Duration and total QPS impacted
- Quantitative results: table with latencies, errors, cost delta, kv_hit diff, kernel fail counts
- Tracing excerpts: top 3 correlated trace patterns
- Root cause hypothesis (if regression observed)
- Next steps: revert change / iterate kernel / run longer canary / close experiment

Ownership and escalation
- Experiment owner: the engineer who proposed the change (required).
- Secondary owner: runtime-sre pager.
- Escalation chain: owner -> runtime-sre -> eng-platform lead -> VP of Eng if customers affected.

Tooling and automation suggestions (short roadmap)
- Lightweight probe operator CLI that enforces automated gates and posts to experiment channel.
- Observability dashboard template: side-by-side baseline vs probe cohort with auto-highlighted deltas.
- Synthetic micro-workload generator that can be targeted at kernel edge-cases (short sequences, long-context, mixed-batch).

Appendix A: Example CLI flow
sections.heading: YAML snippet (for the routing operator)

sections.body: redwoodctl probe create --file slice-preempt-probe-2025.yaml --dry-run
sections.heading: create probe (dry-run)

sections.body: redwoodctl probe apply --file slice-preempt-probe-2025.yaml
sections.heading: start probe

sections.body: redwoodctl probe status --id probe-1234 --watch
sections.heading: query probe status

sections.body:
redwoodctl probe abort --id probe-1234 --reason "P99 regression"

Appendix B: Example metric dashboard panels to include
- Baseline vs probe P99 overlay (5m rollup)
- Per-shard kernel queue depth heatmap
- Kernel error and watchdog event timeline
- Per-token GPU-ms and estimated per-request cost
- KV cache hit-rate and hot-key skewness

Appendix C: Safe defaults (can be overridden with approvals)
- Default max_weight: 2%
- Default duration: 60 minutes
- Default abort thresholds: P99 > baseline * 1.15, error_rate + 0.05%

Related resources and references
- Runtime experiment feedback loop protocol (link above)
- SLO catalog (internal) for route-specific baselines
- Kernel telemetry schema (internal)

Change log
- 2025-03-14: Initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-06-11: Added cost gating and synthetic micro-workload guidance (reviewers Marco Fernandez, Liang Zhao).
- 2025-11-02: Tightened automated gates and clarified abort semantics after a correlated regression incident.

Contact
For questions or to request an exception to the guardrails, open an issue in the eng-serving-runtime experiments board and @ the runtime-sre rotation.

payload.page_title: Predictive Bundling & SLA Credit Algorithm Playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook defines the predictive bundling model and SLA crediting algorithm used to (1) recommend bundled credit products for tenants, (2) apply automated SLA credits when latency or availability SLOs are missed, and (3) simulate the downstream financial impact of different bundling strategies. The goal is to enable predictable customer billing while preserving fairness and operational incentives across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes.

Key objectives:
- Provide a transparent, auditable algorithm for SLA credit calculations tied to measurable telemetry signals.
- Surface predictive bundle recommendations that balance expected token consumption, latency SLOs, and cost-to-serve.
- Offer a simulation harness (offline and lightweight online mode) to estimate revenue and credit exposure before packaging changes.

Scope:
- Applies to all Hosted API customers and Dedicated plans that opt-in to usage-bundles. Private deployments may use the same algorithm as a reference but must explicitly opt into centralized billing behavior.
- Covers per-route and per-tenant SLOs for latency (p50/p95/p99) and availability (error budget burn).
- Excludes paper credits/goodwill adjustments which remain a manual CS workflow.

Definitions and primitives:
- Unit: a billing unit equivalent to 1,000 embedding tokens or 1,000 generation tokens depending on product SKU.
- Bundle: named package with N units + SLO promise (e.g., "Baseline-50k-20ms") and an associated monthly price and credit terms.
- Credit pool: per-tenant ledger where automatically applied SLA credits are deposited and visible on invoices.
- Exposure: estimated future credit liability (USD) under current observed SLO miss rates.

Algorithm overview (high-level):
1) Consumption forecast: estimate next-period token usage per tenant using exponential smoothing + feature adjustments (seasonality, recent growth spikes, marketing campaigns).
2) Cost projection: map forecasted consumption to expected cost-to-serve using model variant and quantization profile mapping (SKU->cost-per-unit matrix).
3) Bundle scoring: for candidate bundles compute a score = utility(consumption_coverage, cost_savings, latency_hedge) - risk(exposure, SLA-violation-rate).
4) SLA credit mechanism: when observed SLOs in a billing window fall below threshold, compute credit = min(max_credit_cap, severity_weight * usage_fraction * bundle_price).
5) Simulation: run monte-carlo scenarios for the next 12 billing windows and produce an expected credit liability distribution.

Telemetry inputs and sources:
- Primary signals: route latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), 5xx/4xx rates, sustained error budget burn (30-day), token counts by sku and route, model variant mapping, quantization profile labels.
- Data sources: Console telemetry: /metrics/latency-hist, /metrics/error-rate, billing ingestion: /billing/token-usage, runtime mapping: /service/variant-map.

Config table (algorithm knobs):
| config_key | description | default | allowed_values | owner |
|------------|-------------|---------|----------------|-------|
| forecast.window_days | lookback window for consumption forecast | 28 | 7-90 | product-data |
| forecast.alpha | smoothing factor for exponential smoothing | 0.25 | 0.01-0.5 | product-data |
| bundle.max_credit_ratio | max fraction of bundle price that can be auto-credited per billing period | 0.2 | 0.0-1.0 | pricing |
| sla.p95_threshold_ms | maximum p95 latency allowed for covered routes | 200 | 50-2000 | runtime-product |
| risk.exposure_decay_days | window over which past SLA misses decay for exposure calc | 90 | 30-365 | finance |
| scoring.weight_latency | relative importance of latency hedge in bundle score | 1.0 | 0.0-3.0 | product |
| scoring.weight_cost_savings | relative importance of cost savings in bundle score | 1.0 | 0.0-3.0 | product |
| simulation.scenario_count | monte-carlo scenario count | 2000 | 100-10000 | product-data |

SLA credit formula (detailed):
- Inputs: observed_miss_rate (fraction of requests in billing window that exceeded threshold), average_usage_in_window (units), bundle_price, severity_factor (0.5/1.0/1.5 for minor/major/critical).
- Raw credit = observed_miss_rate * average_usage_in_window * (bundle_price / bundle_capacity_units) * severity_factor.
- Credit applied = min(Raw credit, bundle_price * bundle.max_credit_ratio, tenant.credit_pool_balance + manual_adjustment_cap).
- Example: tenant T on a 50k-unit bundle at $12/month, observed_miss_rate = 0.06 over the month, average_usage_in_window = 30k units, severity_factor=1.0 => Raw credit = 0.06 * 30k * (12/50k) = $0.0432 * 30k? (See worked example below.)

Worked numeric example (simplified):
- Bundle: 50,000 units, price = $12/month. bundle_price per unit = $12 / 50,000 = $0.00024/unit.
- Tenant usage in window: 30,000 units. observed_miss_rate = 6% (0.06). severity_factor = 1.0.
- Raw credit = 0.06 * 30,000 * 0.00024 = 0.06 * 7.2 = $0.432.
- Assuming bundle.max_credit_ratio = 0.2 => max_credit = $12 * 0.2 = $2.40. Applied credit = min(0.432, 2.40) = $0.432.

Rollout and operational runbook (step-by-step):
1) Staging validation (product-data): run the prediction and simulation harness against last 12 months for a representative tenant cohort (20 tenants spanning small/medium/large). Validate prediction MAPE < 20% on usage and exposure estimate within 15% of observed credit payouts.
2) Canary pricing experiment (growth): publish opt-in bundles to 5% of newly onboarded tenants for one billing cycle. Monitor: credit payouts, change in churn intent, average ticket volume to CS.
3) Production enablement (pricing + finance): enable predictive bundling recommendation in Console for all self-serve tenants. Provide opt-out toggle.
4) Auto-credit enforcement (billing): enable automatic SLA crediting for bundles for tenants who explicitly accept terms. For those who do not accept, flag credits as "pending" for manual CS review.
5) Post-launch audits (quarterly): finance and audit run reconciliation comparing simulated exposure to realized credits and adjust scoring knobs if divergence > 20%.

Monitoring and success criteria:
- Primary metrics: monthly auto-credit payout (USD), credit frequency (percent of subscriptions receiving >0 credit), MAPE of consumption forecast, change in average per-unit realized price.
- SLOs for the algorithm: forecast_mape < 25% (target), applied_credit_false_positive_rate < 1% (customers disputing automatic credits), model_stability (no >10% score swings week-to-week for identical inputs).

Audit and dispute process:
- All automatic credits must generate a structured invoice line item and an audit record in /audits/sla-credits with keys: tenant_id, window_start, window_end, raw_credit_calc, applied_credit, reason_code, operator_override (if any).
- Disputes: CS agent receives an automated ticket if customer disputes > $5 or requests an explanation. The ticket must include the Monte-Carlo scenario snapshot for the billing window and the raw telemetry used for the calculation.

Implementation notes and pseudo-code snippet:
```
# Simplified pseudo-code for monthly credit calc
for tenant in billing_window.tenants:
  forecast = Forecast(tenant.usage_history, window=forecast.window_days, alpha=forecast.alpha)
  bundle = RecommendBundle(forecast, tenant.route_profile, scoring_weights)
  observed_miss_rate = ComputeMissRate(tenant.latency_histograms, sla.p95_threshold_ms)
  raw_credit = observed_miss_rate * tenant.avg_usage * (bundle.price / bundle.capacity_units) * SeverityFactor(tenant.incident_severity)
  applied_credit = min(raw_credit, bundle.price * bundle.max_credit_ratio)
  AuditLog(tenant, raw_credit, applied_credit, bundle.id)
  if tenant.accepts_auto_credit:
    ApplyCreditToInvoice(tenant, applied_credit)
  else:
    CreatePendingCredit(tenant, applied_credit)
```

Security and compliance considerations:
- Credit computation and simulated exposures are financial artifacts. Access to the simulation harness results and raw telemetry must be RBAC-controlled (roles: pricing-analyst, finance-auditor, cs-manager).
- Logs used for audits must be retained for 2 years to satisfy revenue recognition and potential disputes.

Open questions and future work:
- Should we allow negative credits (upsell penalties) when usage exceeds forecast by >200% and latency remains within SLO? (Finance requested a guardrail discussion.)
- Integrate model-based anomaly detection to tag consumption spikes that are non-billable (testing, bot traffic).
- Evaluate replacing exponential smoothing with a hierarchical time-series model for large enterprise tenants.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product: Nina Rao (playbook owner)
- Product-data / Forecasting: Lukas Meyer
- Pricing and Finance: Priya Desai
- Runtime / Telemetry: Marcus Lin
- Customer Success escalation: Talia Brooks

Appendices:
- Appendix A: Timeline for rollout (Gantt summary)
  - Week 0-4: Data integration and simulation validation
  - Week 5-8: Canary experiment with opt-in tenants
  - Week 9-12: Console UI exposure and opt-out paths
  - Week 13: Production enablement and audit window

- Appendix B: Simulation output sample (CSV columns): tenant_id, scenario_id, month, simulated_credit_usd, percentile(5/50/95), forecast_units, observed_miss_rate

- Appendix C: References and related pages
  - Pricing playbooks and previous bundles: /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/preemptible-capacity-crediting-guidelines-2026-07-19
  - Consumption simulation toolkit: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/consumption-sim-harness

If you plan to implement changes to knobs in the live system, create a PR against infra-configs and include a simulation snapshot comparing baseline vs proposed within the PR description.

payload.page_title: Scheduler integration and end-to-end profiling playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents an end-to-end procedure for integrating scheduler-level signals with kernel and runtime profiling to diagnose performance regressions, validate scheduler changes, and produce deterministic benchmarking artifacts. It covers required telemetry, experiment templates, step-by-step collection recipes, analysis heuristics, SLO checks, and incident/runbook guidance. The intended audience is runtime engineers, scheduler authors, SREs, and performance QA.

Scope and goals

- Scope: production and staging runtime clusters, kernel scheduler variants (e.g., preemptive handoff, admission-controller tweaks), and profiling pipelines that touch GPU/CPU kernel execution, KV cache behavior, and request multiplexing.
- Goals:
  - Provide a repeatable profiling and benchmarking workflow that links scheduler decisions -> kernel execution metrics -> end-to-end latency distribution.
  - Define minimal telemetry contract and collection commands so experiments are comparable across hardware and model variants.
  - Produce artifacts for regression triage (trace bundles, synthetic replay, and a short summary report).

When to use this playbook

1. After a scheduler change (policy or implementation) that touches admission, preemption, or batch slicing.
2. When a P95/P99 latency regression is observed after release.
3. Prior to a canary rollout of a scheduler or kernel change.
4. During capacity planning or hardware-fit experiments.

High-level architecture impact

- Scheduler decisions should carry a deterministic context token (scheduler_decision_id) that is injected into request provenance and all downstream traces.
- The decision token must propagate to kernel dispatch layers, runtime traces, and exporter annotations. This allows trace correlation across layers without manual mapping.
- Telemetry producer components: request-gateway, admission-controller, kernel-dispatcher, kvcache-shard, and kernel-runner.

Minimal telemetry contract (required fields)

Each sampled trace must include the following fields (as tags/fields):
- trace_id (string)
- request_id (string)
- scheduler_decision_id (string)
- cohort (string) — e.g., canary|control|baseline|experiment
- model_variant (string)
- kernel_variant (string)
- gpu_id / cpu_node (string)
- seq_len (int)
- token_count (int)
- enqueue_time, dispatch_time, kernel_start_time, kernel_end_time, response_write_time (ISO timestamps)
- batch_size (int)
- admission_reason (string) — e.g., immediate, queued, preempted, hedged
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- kernel_exec_ms (histogram) - kernel execution duration per request
- enqueue_ms, queue_wait_ms (histogram)
- kvcache_hit_rate (gauge) per tenant/cohort
- kernel_retry_count (counter)
- scheduler_action_counts{action} (counter)

Collection and tooling prerequisites

- Tracing: Jaeger-compatible traces with 100% decision token sampling for scheduled experiments.
- Kernel traces: nsys (NVIDIA Nsight) or ROCm tracing for AMD, plus lightweight per-kernel timing exposed via runtime counters.
- Profiler builds: builds instrumented for timeline annotations (build tag: prof/annotated-2026*).
- Replay harness: request-surface-replayer v2.1 or later.
- Central artifact store: s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/{experiment}/{date}/

Standard experiment template (single file: experiment.yaml)
sections.heading: Suggested additional metrics (histograms / counters)

sections.body:
experiment_name: scheduler-hand-off-microburst-2026-02-01
description: Measure tail-latency impact of preemptive handoff under microburst traffic for llama-13b-quant
cohorts:
  - control: scheduler:stable, kernel:baseline, cohort:control
  - experiment: scheduler:preemptive-hand-off-v3, kernel:baseline, cohort:experiment
traffic_profile: microburst-1s-on-9s-off
model_variant: llama-13b-quant
sequence_distribution: p(<=64)=0.7, p(65-256)=0.25, p(256+)=0.05
collect_traces: true
trace_sample_rate: 1.0
artifact_bucket: s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/scheduler-hand-off-microburst-2026-02-01/

Step-by-step collection recipe (canonical)

1) Prepare baseline: pin control cohort to scheduler:stable and kernel:baseline. Verify canary isolation (no cross-cohort mixing).
2) Start the replay harness against staging cluster with the defined traffic_profile. Use request-surface-replayer with injected request_id and scheduler_decision_id:
sections.heading: Example experiment metadata (YAML)

sections.body:
request-surface-replayer --experiment experiment.yaml --outdir /tmp/exp-run --inject-decision-token

3) Start system-level collectors (run on all nodes hosting kernel-runner processes):
- Start nsys for GPU: sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys-${NODE}.qdrep --sample=cpu,gpu --trace=nvtx --duration=600s --capture=all
- Start cpu perf or eBPF sampler: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -o /tmp/perf-${NODE}.data sleep 600
- Start lightweight runtime exporter: curl -X POST http://localhost:9001/debug/trace/start?out=/tmp/trace-${NODE}.ndjson

4) Start distributed trace capture (Jaeger) with 100% sampling for the experiment cohort.
5) Run the replay for configured duration (recommended 10–30 minutes for microburst experiments).
6) After run completes, collect artifacts from nodes and upload to experiment artifact bucket following naming convention: {experiment}/{cohort}/{node}/{timestamp}/trace.qdrep, perf.data, runtime-trace.ndjson, jaeger-trace.json

Analysis heuristics (quick triage)

- Correlate scheduler_decision_id with kernel_exec_ms from kernel traces. Create a pivot table: scheduler_action -> median kernel_exec_ms, p95 kernel_exec_ms, mean queue_wait_ms.
- Look for cohorts where kernel_start_time is significantly delayed relative to dispatch_time (>10 ms baseline depending on model shape).
- If kernel_exec_ms variance grows with batch_size, inspect batch-slicing/handoff logs for cross-tenant batching.
- If eBPF/perf shows system-level scheduling preemption spikes coincident with high p99, search for SIGSTOP/SIGCONT patterns or GPU watchdog resets.

Automated checks and SLO gates

Before a scheduler change is promoted to production, these automated checks must pass in staging:
- Regression-free on p50/p95/p99 for baseline workload within 5%/8%/12% respectively.
- Kernel retry rate increase < 2% absolute.
- kvcache_hit_rate delta < 1% (unless expected).
- No increase in scheduler_action_counts{preempt} > 3x baseline without documented rationale.

Alerting rules (sample)

- alert: SchedulerTailLatencyRegression
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_exec_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, cohort)) > 1.12 * baseline_p99
  for: 10m
  labels: {severity: page}

- alert: KernelRetrySpike
  expr: increase(kernel_retry_count[5m]) > 100 && increase(kernel_retry_count[5m]) / increase(request_count[5m]) > 0.02
  for: 5m
  labels: {severity: ticket}

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)

- [ ] Experiment YAML committed to repo and pinned to artifact bucket.
- [ ] Tracing + kernel trace infrastructure smoke-tested.
- [ ] Baseline run completed and artifact snapshot stored.
- [ ] Owners & oncall notified (Slack #serving-runtime with experiment tag).
- [ ] Canary policy configured (5% of traffic for 30 minutes -> 25% for 1h -> 100% with rollback).
- [ ] SLO gates configured in deployment pipeline.

Runbook: triage flow for observed tail-latency regression

1) Verify alert source and cohort. If cohort != canary and no rollout in progress, page oncall.
2) Fetch experiment artifact bundle and open the summary report (artifact/{experiment}/summary.json). Key fields: delta_p99, median_queue_wait_ms, kernel_retry_rate.
3) Cross-correlate scheduler_decision_id for top 10 slow traces and inspect kernel qdrep slices at those timestamps.
4) Check node-level telemetry: GPU utilization, nvlink errors, dmesg, OOM/killer events, and GPU watchdog messages.
5) If traces show kernel_start_time delayed but steady kernel_exec_ms, suspect admission latency or queueing; escalate to scheduler owner.
6) If kernel_exec_ms inflated and kernels show >1.5x expected occupancy drift, open a kernel regression issue and attach qdrep.
7) If system-level indicators show GPU thermal throttling, coordinate with SRE to move canary to alternate hardware.

Known issues and mitigations (short catalog)

- mis-attributed-decision-token: Some legacy gateway versions drop scheduler_decision_id when requests are proxied through legacy route. Mitigation: enforce gateway version >= 2025.11 and run injector sidecar for older routes.
- perf-sampling-sparsity-on-high-throughput: perf recorder under-samples when node CPU is saturated; mitigation: reduce sampling frequency and increase test duration for stability.
- nsys-file-size-bloat: long runs generate large qdrep files; mitigation: use time-windowed capture and aggregate smaller windows with qdrep-concat.

Release notes (summary of recent changes relevant to this playbook)

- 2026-01-10: scheduler:preemptive-hand-off-v3 landed. The new policy reduces starvation but introduced additional preempt events; this playbook includes a specific experiment template to quantify the latency impact under microbursts.
- 2025-12-03: runtime:annotated-prof builds published; these include NVTX span annotations for scheduler_decision_id and batch lineage. Use these builds for kernel-level correlation.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owners: Serving Runtime - Scheduling subteam (owner alias: runtime-scheduler@redwood.com).
- SRE escalation: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com.
- Performance lab contact: perf-lab@redwood.com.

Artifact naming and retention policy

- Naming: {experiment}/{cohort}/{node}/{YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS}/{artifact}.{ext}
- Retention: experiments used for production rollouts retained for 365 days. Debug/ephemeral experiments may be retained for 30 days. Critical regression runs (P99 delta > 10%) archived indefinitely.

Appendix A — useful commands and snippets
sections.heading: run from perf workstation

sections.body: sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/qdrep --capture=nvtx,cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu,gpu --duration=60s --trace=nvtx --quiet
sections.heading: Collecting a short GPU slice with nsys

sections.body: nsys stats --report gputimeline --format json /tmp/qdrep.qdrep > /tmp/qdrep.timeline.json
sections.heading: Extracting timeline to JSON (local)

sections.body:
jq -c '.[] | select(.tags.scheduler_decision_id != null) | {trace_id: .trace_id, decision: .tags.scheduler_decision_id, kernel_ms: .metrics.kernel_exec_ms}' jaeger-trace.json | python -c 'import sys, json; data=[json.loads(l) for l in sys.stdin]; print(len(data))'

Experiment result template (copy into artifact summary.json)

- experiment: string
- cohort: string
- p50_control, p95_control, p99_control: ms
- p50_experiment, p95_experiment, p99_experiment: ms
- delta_p99_percent: float
- kernel_retry_rate_control, kernel_retry_rate_experiment: float
- notes: string (root cause hypothesis)

Related documentation

- Kernel scheduling handbook (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/runtime-scheduler-decision-fabric-and-telemetry-playbook-2024
- KV cache and session lifecycle: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024

Feedback and continuous improvement

- Add new experiment templates to this page and tag with the date.
- After each canary, the owner must add a short summary to the experiment artifact and tag whether the SLO gate passed.

Document history

- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Asha Kapoor)
- 2025-12-15: added known issues and retention policy (review by Daniel Park)
- 2026-02-03: clarified telemetry contract and added rollout checklist (review by Marta Gutierrez)
