sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This runbook defines an observability-first approach to enterprise onboarding for Redwood Inference customers. It standardizes the telemetry contract, synthetic acceptance checks, escalation paths, and QBR handoff artifacts used during a customer go-live and the first 90 days of production.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private deployments and to Hosted customers with enterprise SLAs.
- Covers telemetry-onboarding, pre-cutover validation, day-0 to day-14 stabilization, and QBR handoff.

Owners and Primary Contacts
- Customer Success (owner): Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.com)
- SRE / Platform escalation: Arjun Patel (arjun.patel@redwood.com)
- Serving Runtime SME: Sofia Martinez (sofia.martinez@redwood.com)
- Account Executive (commercial): Liam O'Connor (liam.oconnor@redwood.com)

Acceptance gates (must pass before route to production)
1) Telemetry contract validation (required)
   - Metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, token_consumption_total, kvcache_hit_ratio, active_connections_by_tenant
   - Traces: 95% of generation requests produce a trace with span for model-select and runtime-exec
   - Logs: structured request_id on all runtime logs with severity mapping (INFO/WARN/ERROR)

2) Synthetic scenario pass (3 independent runs)
   - Latency synthetic: 95th percentile end-to-end generation under 2.5s for the workload profile
   - Accuracy synthetic: pre-agreed prompt set map-of-outputs >= customer baseline (see "synthetic-prompt-set" artifact)
   - Failover synthetic: simulate a model-variant fallback and verify successful completion within 3s of fallback trigger

3) Cost and quota sanity check
   - Token burn projection for first 30 days within agreed threshold +/- 30%
   - Adaptive-rate-limiter integrated and returning 429s with observability tags when saturating

Telemetry contract: implementation checklist
- Instrumentation owners must ensure metrics emit at the tenant/request granularity. Required labels: tenant_id, region, model_name, route
- Preferred exporters: Prometheus (metrics), OpenTelemetry (traces), JSONL to S3 for long-term logs.
- Retention: 90d metrics, 30d traces, 365d logs (customer may opt for shorter).

Prometheus example queries (copy into onboarding dashboard)
- Total requests by tenant (30m): rate(request_count{tenant_id=~"TENANT_ID.*"}[30m])
- 95th percentile latency (10m): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[10m])) by (le))
- KV cache hit ratio: sum(rate(kvcache_hit_total[5m])) by (tenant_id) / sum(rate(kvcache_lookup_total[5m])) by (tenant_id)

Synthetic health checks and dashboard layout
- Dashboard sections: Overview, Latency & Throughput, Token Economics, Failure Modes, Instance Health, Rollout & Canary Status
- Widgets to include: p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, request rate by tenant, token burn by route, cache hit ratio trend, recent errors table (parsed with error codes), live traces sample panel

Pre-cutover procedure (Day -3 to 0)
1) Day -3: Telemetry smoke test
   - Verify data arriving in Grafana and alerting pipeline.
   - Run the baseline synthetic suite; document results in the onboarding ticket.
2) Day -2: Load profile run
   - Ramp to expected steady-state TPS for 30 minutes, then peak to 2x for 15 minutes.
   - Confirm autoscaling/queueing behaves as expected, confirm no token anomalies.
3) Day -1: Canary rollout
   - 1% of traffic routed to the new tenant config. Monitor the canary for 60 minutes.
   - Check for errors, latency, and cost deltas. If any SLO breach detected, abort and roll back.
4) Day 0: Full cutover
   - Schedule 60 minute maintenance window. Notify stakeholders (email template provided below).
   - Enable full route, run post-cutover synthetic suite after 15 minutes, and validate telemetry contract.

Stability operations (Day 0–14)
- Daily cadence: 09:30 PST standup (CS + SRE + Runtime) for first 7 days, then every-other-day till day 14.
- Check list for standup:
  - Any SLO alerts fired in last 24h? (yes/no, link to alerts)
  - Token burn variance > 20%?
  - Customer reported LLM output quality regressions?
  - Any escalations initiated?

Escalation matrix and SLAs
- P1: Production-wide outage for customer's tenant (affects > 90% requests)
   - First response: SRE on-call (15m), followed by CS lead (30m)
   - Escalation: Paging to Engineering runtime leads at 60m, exec-brief within 2h
- P2: Severe degradation (p95 > target or error rate > 5%) for a single route
   - First response: CS + SRE (30m), resolution target 4h
- P3: Functional bug with workaround (non-blocking)
   - Response: Assigned support engineer within 8 business hours

Escalation contact table (use internal contact channel first, then email if needed):
- SRE on-call: PagerDuty roster (use paging code "RI-SRE-CUST")
- Platform lead: arjun.patel@redwood.com
- Runtime SME: sofia.martinez@redwood.com
- CS Lead: maya.chen@redwood.com

Communication and customer comms templates
- Pre-cutover notification (email):
  Subject: [Redwood] Scheduled go-live window for <tenant_name> on <date>
  Body: Short summary, expected window, primary contacts, rollback criteria, monitoring link (dashboard URL).

- Incident update template (customer-facing):
  1) What happened (concise)
  2) Impacted customers/tenants
  3) Mitigation steps taken
  4) ETA for resolution or next update

Rollback and safe-fail procedures
- Automatic rollback trigger conditions (examples):
  - p95 latency increase > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes
  - error rate > 5% sustained for > 5 minutes
  - token burn projection exceeds agreed cap by > 50% within next 24 hours
- Rollback steps:
  1) Use routing control to switch traffic back to previous deployment (CLI example):
     redwood route set --tenant <TENANT_ID> --route <ROUTE> --target previous
  2) Re-enable canary at 5% and rerun synthetic
  3) Open a post-rollback ticket and schedule a root-cause analysis (RCA) meeting

Postmortem and RCA handoff criteria
- Trigger an RCA when any of the following occur:
  - P1 incident
  - P2 incident that required > 4 hours to resolve
  - Any customer quiet-go-live rollback within first 14 days
- RCA ownership: SRE + Runtime + CS representative. Deliverable: written RCA (timeline, root cause, corrective actions) within 5 business days.

QBR handoff and artifacts (first QBR after go-live)
- Dashboard snapshot exported with:
  - Latency/Throughput trends since go-live
  - Token economics and cost delta vs projection
  - Error and degradation timeline with RCA links
  - Synthetic suite pass/fail history and prompt-set differences
- Customer Success playbook for the QBR:
  1) Review contract SLOs and whether we met them
  2) Share operational highlights and any outstanding risks
  3) Agree on quality/regression plan (if any)

Runbook annexes (copy into onboarding folder)
- Synthetic prompt set template: synthetic-prompt-set-v1.json
- Grafana dashboard JSON: onboarding-dashboard-template.json
- Prometheus alert rules: onboarding-alerts-rules.yml

Troubleshooting checklist (quick steps during an incident)
1) Identify affected tenants and routes: run request_count PromQL filter by tenant_id.
2) Check instance health and oom/killed events on nodes serving tenant.
3) Inspect traces to find whether slowdown occurred in model selection or runtime execution.
4) If KV cache hit ratio dropped significantly, flush affected prefix cache and monitor.
5) If error codes 5xx dominate, scale burst pool or reroute to fallback variant.

FAQ
- Q: What if synthetic checks pass but customers report poor output quality?
  A: Open a quality triage ticket and escalate to Applied ML; attach failing prompts and model version. Consider A/B rolling back to prior model variant.

References and links
- Onboarding dashboard template: //grafana.redwood/internal/dashboards/onboarding-dashboard-template
- Telemetry contract spec (internal): /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/telemetry-contract-spec
- Canary playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/canary-rollout-playbook

Revision history
- 2026-11-02: Created by Maya Chen
- 2027-01-12: Added synthetic failover scenario (reviewer Sofia Martinez)
- 2027-02-14: Added PromQL examples and expanded escalation matrix (reviewers Arjun Patel, Liam O'Connor)

payload.page_title: Runtime fidelity sprint handbook: profiling, kernel interactions, and rollback protocols

sections.body:
Overview

This handbook describes the goals, lab protocol, measurement artifacts, and safe rollback procedures for a 'fidelity sprint' — a focused engineering sprint whose objective is to change or validate runtime fidelity (model variant, quantization, kernel variant, batching policy, or routing policy) without regressing customer-facing SLOs or quality metrics. It is intended for engineers, SREs, and applied ML practitioners who run experiments across the serving runtime.

Why a fidelity sprint?
- Reduce regressions: small behavioral changes in kernels, quantization, or batching can introduce subtle regressions in output quality or latency distribution.
- Reproducibility: define a repeatable lab protocol for new kernel rollouts and quantization profiles.
- Operational safety: codify rollback and guardrails that preserve availability and cost targets.

Scope
- Applies to changes that affect inference fidelity or execution internals: kernel variants, quantized weights/ops, KV-cache prefetch hints, scheduler admission policies, batching heuristics, and model-variant routing.
- Does NOT cover: API surface changes, control-plane-only feature flips, or customer-facing configuration changes that don't change execution fidelity.

Owners and stakeholders
- Sprint lead: owner of the change (name + pager) — typically a runtime or applied-ML engineer.
- QA / Evals: applied-ml team responsible for the prompt-suite and regression gates.
- Oncall SRE: responsible for rollout monitoring and rapid rollback steps.
- Product owner: for business risk decisions when rolling out to Dedicated/Private customers.

SLOs and acceptance criteria
- Latency SLOs: 99th percentile tail latency increase <= 10% relative to baseline for the same workload mix.
- Error budget: no more than 5% additional errors (5xx or runtime timeouts) during canary windows.
- Quality gate: prompt-eval pass-rate delta <= 0.5% absolute (for high-sensitivity tasks) or <= 2% for low-sensitivity tasks.
- Cost delta: per-token cost increase <= 5% (unless explicitly approved).

Labs and environment matrix (table)
- The lab matrix documents target hardware, kernel variants, and fidelity settings we exercise:

| Environment | GPU type | Kernel variant | Model variant | Typical sequence lengths | Notes |
|-------------|----------|----------------|---------------|-------------------------|-------|
| local-lab-rt | A100 80GB | v2-lowlat | fp16 | 32-128 | dev-only, limited concurrency |
| perf-lab-1 | A100S | v2-default | int8-q | 16-256 | synthetic replay of production traces |
| canary-region | T4/GPU | v2-explicit-prefetch | fp16 | 8-512 | small % of real traffic |
| dedicated-staging | H100 | v3-kernel-tiling | int8-q | 64-1024 | reserved for enterprise smoke tests |

Prerequisites (checklist)
1) Baseline capture: collect a 24-hour production trace and compute baseline SLOs and per-route token distribution.
2) Eval prompt set: ensure there is a labeled prompt set for at least three sensitivity tiers (high/medium/low).
3) Telemetry hooks: feature flags, kernel parameter tags, and tracing for kernel decisions must be enabled.
4) Canary plan: percentage targets, ramp schedule, and alert thresholds declared in the sprint ticket.

Experiment procedure (numbered steps)
1. Prepare artifacts\   a. Build the kernel/quantization artifact and tag with semver: kernel:vX.Y.Z-fidelity-sprint\   b. Generate a benchmark spec (JSON) that includes: route list, concurrency shape, sequence-length distribution, and sample prompt corpus. Example: {"routes": ["chat_v1","completion_short"], "concurrency": "Poisson(8)", "sample_corpus": "gs://redwood-evals/fidelity-sprint/"}
2. Run lab smoke tests (local-lab-rt)\   a. Execute unit-level smoke with trace replay: ./scripts/replay_trace.sh --trace=24h-baseline --kernel=kernel:vX.Y.Z\   b. Validate memory, no OOMs, and kernel logs for warnings.
3. Microbenchmark suite (perf-lab-1)\   a. Run throughput and tail-latency suite: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec fidelity_bench.json --out /tmp/bench-results.json\   b. Record: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU UTIL, kernel occupancy.
4. Offline quality evals\   a. Run the labeled prompt-set through both baseline and candidate artifacts: eval-runner --baseline s3://... --candidate s3://... --metrics rouge,bert-score,exact_match\   b. Produce a delta report and flag prompts with >X% change for manual review.
5. Canary rollout\   a. Start with 0.5% traffic in canary-region for 30 minutes. Monitor SLO and eval signal.\   b. If green, ramp to 2% for 2 hours, then to 10% for 4 hours.\   c. During each window, run shadow-mirroring to capture full outputs for offline eval.
6. Production ramp and final validation\   a. Only after meeting acceptance criteria for two independent canary windows do we proceed to full region or Dedicated rollout.\\n
Monitoring and telemetry (what to watch)
- Latency heatmap per route and per-sequence-length bin.
- Kernel decision rate: % of requests using new kernel vs fallback.
- Error types: kernel-timeout, OOM, scheduler-rejected, model-internal-errors.
- Output divergence fingerprints: fingerprint ID match rate between baseline and candidate outputs (approximate hash equality).
- Cost signals: per-route GPU time, kernel time breakdown, and billing samples.

Alert thresholds (sample)
- p99 latency increase > 12% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- error-rate increase > 5% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- eval-pass-rate drop > 1% absolute for high-sensitivity prompts (manual review) -> escalate to product + applied-ml

Rollback procedure (runbook)
1) Automated rollback trigger \   - If any P1 alert above fires during canary, the system must automatically flip routing to baseline kernel variant for the affected cohort.
2) Manual rollback steps (if automation unavailable)\   a. Oncall runs: curl -XPOST https://controlplane.internal/api/rollout/rollback -d '{"target":"kernel:vX.Y.Z","reason":"p99-latency"}'\   b. Confirm traffic reverts using: k get routes --selector fidelity-sprint=true -o wide\   c. Validate telemetry: confirm p99 returns to baseline within 3x of mean reversion time (typically 2 minutes).
3) Post-rollback actions\   a. Create a hotfix ticket, attach all trace artifacts and eval failure cases.\   b. Hold a 2-hour warroom with applied-ml and kernel-owner to triage.\\n
Quality analysis guidelines
- For each flagged prompt, capture: input, baseline output, candidate output, token-level alignments, and logits (where available).
- Use the scoring rubric: 1=identical, 2=minor wording difference (acceptable), 3=meaningful semantic change (requires escalation), 4=hallucination/regression (blocker).
- Tag each prompt with sensitivity and business impact.

Kernel scheduling interplay notes (short guide)
- Batching tradeoffs: larger batches improve throughput but increase latency tail for short-sequence requests. During fidelity sprints focus on sequence-length-aware batching (max_batch_size per-seqlen-bin).\- Preemption: enable preemption for priority traffic to avoid head-of-line latency for interactive routes. Validate preemption counters don't inflate kernel switch rate by >3x.\- KV-cache prefetching: for long chat sessions, prefetching reduces token latency but increases memory pressure. Add memory headroom checks and a soft cap of 80% GPU memory for prefetch cache.

Benchmarks and artifact naming convention
- Bench artifact names: fidelity-bench.{kernel_tag}.{model_tag}.{gpu}.{date}.json\- Always store raw traces, aggregated metrics, and the prompt-evaluation delta report in: gs://redwood-bench/fidelity-sprints/{sprint_id}/

Reporting and post-mortem
- After the sprint complete (success or rollback), the sprint lead must produce a 1-page summary with: baseline vs candidate summary table, failure cases, root cause hypothesis, and recommended next steps. Attach raw artifacts and the canary ramp timeline.

Appendices
A) Example benchmark spec (JSON)\\{
  "sprint_id": "fs-2026-07-23",
  "routes": ["chat_v1"],
  "shapes": [{"concurrency":10, "seq_len":64}],
  "duration_minutes": 60
}\\n
B) Quick commands\- Collect runtime traces: ./tools/capture_runtime_trace --duration 60 --out /tmp/trace.json\- Run bench: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec /tmp/fidelity_bench.json --kernel kernel:vX.Y.Z --out /tmp/results.json\- Trigger rollback (manual): ./scripts/rollback_kernel.sh --target kernel:baseline

C) FAQ\- Q: Can we skip shadow-mirroring during canary?\   A: No — shadow outputs are the primary artifact for post-rollout quality analysis.\- Q: Who signs off a Dedicated customer rollout?\   A: Product + Customer Success + Security (if private deployment).

Document maintenance
- Owner: Maya Chen (runtime). Update cadence: before every major kernel release or every 6 months.
- Record of changes: last major revision consolidated monitoring thresholds (2026-11-30).

Related links
- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025\- Rollout orchestration: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026

payload.page_title: Runtime experiment lab protocols and kernel fuzz suite 2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This page documents the Runtime Experiment Lab protocols and the Kernel Fuzz Suite (KFS): a repeatable, auditable set of experiments and tooling we use to exercise scheduling, kernel selection, and execution edge cases in the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to find latent correctness bugs and fidelity regressions, validate mitigation strategies, and produce reproducible artifacts for profiling and remediation teams.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all internal runtime kernel builds and scheduler releases before a canary rollout.
- Targets GPU and accelerator execution layers, batch slicing, KV-cache prefetch pathways, and scheduler handoff code paths.
- Not intended for customer-facing load testing or production-scale benchmarking (see the benchmarking catalog).

Owning team and contacts
-----------------------
- Primary owner: Eng - Serving Runtime (runtime-experiments@redwood.example.com)
- Experiment custodian (lab ops): Aisha Patel
- Observability liaison: Marco Nguyen
- Security reviewer: Lin Chen
- Slack channel: #runtime-lab

Motivation and success criteria
-------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Many kernel regressions are non-deterministic and appear only under complex interleavings of scheduling and batching.
- Automated fuzzing can expose correctness issues (bad memory accesses, kernel crashes), API contract regressions (inference fidelity changes), and performance cliffs.
- Success criteria for a release candidate: zero reproducible kernel crashes, fidelity drift within defined bounds, and no unexplained tail-latency increases after exercising the KFS and protocol suite.

High-level testbed architecture
-------------------------------
sections.heading: Why we run a fuzzing/testbed program

sections.body:
- Lab controller: lightweight service that orchestrates experiments, collects artifacts, and uploads to the experiment bucket (s3://redwood-runtime-lab).
- Isolated runner cluster: ephemeral fleet of instances with representative accelerator types (A100/RTX/Custom). Each runner is instrumented with the profiler agent and secure collector.
- Kernel harness: small shim that loads the runtime binary, injects test inputs, and toggles kernel-selection flags.
- Fuzzer engine: mutated input generator + workload orchestrator (see KFS modules).
- Observability stack: traces (X-Ray/Jaeger), perf kernels, GPU telemetry (SM utilization, memory histograms), aggregated into the runtime-lab dashboard.

Kernel Fuzz Suite (KFS) components
----------------------------------
- Input mutation engine (IM): generates permutations of sequence lengths, prompt/prefix shapes, and KV-cache states.
- Scheduling combinator (SC): composes concurrency shapes and priority mixes (e.g., 80% background low-priority long seq, 20% high-priority short seq bursts).
- Kernel toggler (KT): flips kernel selection heuristics and quantization code paths at runtime to test fallback logic.
- State snapshotter (SS): captures kernel inputs, memory maps, and KV cache deltas for deterministic replay.
- Crash triage agent (CTA): automatic symbolication and core extraction; posts to lab bug queue with attachments.

Representative KFS testcases (examples)
--------------------------------------
1) Mixed-fidelity handoff: 500 low-priority requests with sequence=512 interleaved with high-priority requests sequence=64 every 30ms. Kernel toggles to half-precision for background path.
2) KV-cache eviction race: two tenants share a shard; induce eviction threshold crossing while prefetcher runs.
3) Preemption + batch-slice race: synthetic workloads that induce cooperative preemption, followed by load spike to trigger slice reassembly logic.
4) Cross-kernel migration: on-the-fly switch from optimized attention kernel A to fallback kernel B with KV merge.

Experiment protocol (must be followed exactly)
--------------------------------------------
Preconditions: runner images are built from the release candidate branch, instrumentation flags enabled, and lab controller at v1.4.

1. Reserve lab quota: create a lab ticket in the tracker and tag the candidate.
2. Provision ephemeral runners using the lab controller: `labctl provision --flavor=a100-small --count=4 --tag=rc-1234`
3. Upload the release candidate binary to s3 and sign the artifact: `aws s3 cp build/runtime-rc-1234.tar.gz s3://redwood-runtime-lab/rc-1234/`
4. Start baseline sweep: run KFS quick-check suite (5m smoke) to assert no immediate crashes. `labctl run-suite --suite=kfs-quick --rc=rc-1234`
5. Run targeted fuzz campaigns (per schedule): `labctl run-fuzz --campaign=kv-eviction-race --duration=2h --seed=42`
6. After each campaign: collect traces, snapshots, and profiler outputs. `labctl collect --rc=rc-1234 --campaign=kv-eviction-race --out=rc-1234/kv-eviction-race/`
7. If CTA reports a crash, do an immediate stop of related runners and tag the issue number in the lab ticket; escalate to the on-call kernel owner.
8. Repro attempt: use the included deterministic replay harness with snapshot produced by SS.
9. Postmortem: if crash is reproducible, run the minimal failing-case isolation and attach a replay artifact to the bug.

Metrics and observability requirements
------------------------------------
Minimum telemetry captured for every experiment run (stored alongside artifacts):
- Trace ID and flame graph (string id).
- Kernel name/variant and selection signal sequence.
- Per-request latency histogram (p50/p90/p99).
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory usage, PCIe transfer rates.
- Host metrics: CPU steal, context-switch rate.
- Fidelity checksums: deterministic output hash for fixed prompts, and token-by-token diffs when applicable.
sections.heading: Components and their roles

sections.body:
| Metric | Threshold | Action |
|-------|----------:|--------|
| Crash rate | > 0 reproducible crashes | Block and triage immediately |
| P99 latency regression | > 25% over baseline | Notify perf-oncall and schedule deeper profiling |
| Fidelity drift | > 0.5% token mismatch rate for control prompts | Hold rollout and open quality regression ticket |
| Memory growth | sustained >20% over 30 minutes | Investigate leak; attach allocator traces |

Repro and isolation checklist
-----------------------------
- If a crash is observed: collect CTA bundle, mark the runner-safe image, and run `labctl replay --snapshot <id> --deterministic` to attempt reproduction.
- If non-deterministic: increase chaos seed variety and run for 24 hours with varied seeds; collect top 5 distinct stack traces.
- For fidelity issues: run the fidelity harness comparing outputs across kernel variants and quantization profiles; attach a token-diff report.

Failure modes and triage playbook (summary)
-----------------------------------------
- Kernel crash on launch: check linked libraries and driver mismatch; confirm CUDA/cuDNN versions. If mismatch, mark as infra regression and revert platform driver upgrade.
- Silent output corruption: run checksum comparisons with golden inputs, then enable per-layer logging and binary search across kernel patches.
- Tail latency spike correlated to batch reassembly: inspect scheduler traces for preemption windows and slice queuing; attach timeline view.

Security and isolation constraints
--------------------------------
- All experiment artifacts live in ACL-protected S3 bucket with lab-only read/write.
- Runners must run in an isolated VPC with NAT disabled for external test runs; allow egress for observability only via lab collector.
- No customer data may be used in experiments; anonymized synthetic corpora are provided in s3://redwood-runtime-lab/corpora/

Artifacts and retention policy
----------------------------
- Crash bundles: retained for 90 days.
- Deterministic snapshots and replay artifacts: retained for 180 days.
- Aggregated telemetry and dashboards: retained per observability policy (default 365 days).

Automation and gating for release flows
-------------------------------------
- Example CI gating rule (pseudocode):
```
if (kfs_smoke.pass && no_reproducible_crashes && fidelity_ok) {
  allow_canary=true
} else {
  block_release=true
}
```
- KFS runs are executed as part of the release pipeline (post-build, pre-canary). Full campaign runs are nightly for main branch and on-demand for RCs.

Integrations and tooling snippets
--------------------------------
- Start a campaign: `labctl run-campaign --name kernel-migration-smoke --rc rc-1234 --profile heavy-preempt`
- Fetch artifacts: `aws s3 sync s3://redwood-runtime-lab/rc-1234/kernel-migration-smoke/ ./artifacts/`
- Replay with deterministic harness: `python replay_harness.py --snapshot s3://.../snapshot-id --binary runtime-rc-1234.tar.gz`

Reporting and communication
-------------------------
- On any reproducible crash: automatically create a ticket in the kernel tracker with CTA attachments and link to the lab ticket.
- Weekly lab digest: lab-ops publishes a summary of top findings to #runtime-lab and the Engineering PagerDuty stakeholders.

Runbook: immediate steps for on-call (short)
--------------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge lab ticket and check CTA bundle.
2. If crash reproduces locally, annotate with minimal repro and assign to kernel-owner.
3. If not reproducible, request longer campaign with seed sweep and attach new artifact.
4. Coordinate with observability for deeper sampling if needed.

Appendix A: Sample fidelity harness output (token diff)
----------------------------------------------------
{
  "prompt_id": "golden-001",
  "baseline_hash": "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e",
  "variant_hash": "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e",
  "token_mismatches": []
}

Appendix B: Common labctl commands
----------------------------------
- `labctl provision --flavor=<flavor> --count=<n> --tag=<tag>`
- `labctl run-suite --suite=<name> --rc=<rc>`
- `labctl collect --rc=<rc> --campaign=<name> --out=<path>`
- `labctl replay --snapshot <id> --deterministic`

Related pages and next steps
---------------------------
- Link the experiment findings to the release notes for the RC and to the performance regression huntbook when appropriate.
- Next planned enhancements: integrate fuzzing signals into the kernel autotuner and add differential fuzzing between quantized and full-precision paths.

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-10: Created (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-01-24: Added CTA automation instructions and thresholds (Marco Nguyen).
- 2026-02-03: Clarified retention policy and added sample CI gating snippet (Aisha Patel).

payload.page_title: Runtime Observability Sleuthing and Probing Toolkit

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the toolkit, operational patterns, and safe procedures used by runtime engineers to perform rapid sleuthing (hypothesis-driven triage) and non-disruptive probing of the serving runtime in production and pre-production environments. The guidance balances signal fidelity with cost and safety constraints and provides concrete probe recipes, a sampling governor configuration, escalation paths, and ownership.

Summary / intent
- Goal: reduce mean-time-to-detect and mean-time-to-resolve for latency, fidelity, and kernel-related regressions while containing overhead to a safe telemetry budget.
- Audience: runtime oncall, profiling team, SRE, and feature owners who need to instrument kernels/scheduler and run targeted experiments.
- Non-goal: exhaustive academic profiling — this is a pragmatic, ops-first playbook for production-safe investigation.

Signal taxonomy (quick reference)
1) Traces: end-to-end request streams with kernel handoffs annotated. Use for causal chain reconstruction and tail-latency attribution.
2) Microprobes: high-frequency short-duration kernel timings (GPU dispatch, memcpy, kernel enqueue latency). Use for kernel regressions and scheduler jitter.
3) Counters & gauges: queue lengths, admission tokens, KV-cache hit rates, busy GPU percent, slot credits. Use for capacity and trend analysis.
4) Synthetic samples: replayed request surface (shadow) to reproduce behavior without impacting live traffic.

Sleuthing checklist (initial 10-minute triage)
1. Confirm symptom and scope: aggregate error/latency dashboards, which tenants/routes affected, and start time.
2. Correlate with deployments and config changes (canary rollouts, kernel changes, model swaps) using the deployment timeline.
3. Check kernel and scheduler health streams: kernel-failure-rate, kernel-queueing-latency, enqueue-to-start gap.
4. Validate resource & thermal indicators: GPU utilization, power capping events, PCIe/NVLink errors.
5. If the above are inconclusive, enable targeted microprobes (see Probe recipes).

Safe probing principles
- Principle 1: Budget first. Probes must respect the tracing budget (default 0.05% of total request CPU and < 1% of GPU extra work for a cohort).
- Principle 2: Non-blocking. Probes should not alter scheduling or kernel behaviour — use passive sampling and read-only metrics where possible.
- Principle 3: Scoped rollouts. Apply probes to a single small cohort (shadow or 0.5–2% of production tenants) and observe for 30–90 minutes before scaling.
- Principle 4: Fail-open. Add circuit-breaker guardrails: if P99 latency increases by > 10% or error rates double in the probed cohort, automatically disable the probing flag.

Probe recipes (practical, copy-paste)
1) Microprobe: kernel enqueue-to-start distribution - Purpose: detect scheduling stalls and handoff jitter - Target: one node in the affected pod group or a dedicated canary - Steps:
   1. Create feature flag "microprobe.enq_start" with cohort 0.5%.
   2. Configure runtime to emit microprobe events with 200ns timestamp resolution for each kernel enqueue and dispatch.
   3. Sampling: 1-in-N request sampling with N = 250 by default (adjust down to 50 for an active canary).
   4. Collect for 30 minutes and generate a heatmap of enqueue->start latency by kernel type.
   5. If enqueue->start P99 > 3x baseline, escalate and increase sampling to 1-in-25 for one node for 10 minutes.

2) Trace enrichment: correlated trace + KV-cache delta - Purpose: connect cache warmup/fidelity issues to end-to-end latency - Steps:
   1. Enable trace-enrichment flag for the affected route.
   2. For sampled traces, attach KV-cache hit/miss sequence and cache size at request start.
   3. Use the trace-joiner job to merge microprobe events with trace spans post-collection.
   4. Run the synthesized trace analysis to find patterns where cache miss bursts precede tail latency.

3) Shadow replay burst: safe synthetic stress - Purpose: reproduce a peaky failure surface without saturating live capacity - Steps:
   1. Mirror 0.5% of production traffic to a shadow cluster with strict admission caps (20% of node CPU/GPU used by shadow).
   2. Run the same request ordering but pause prefixes at the scheduler to test pre-emption and kernel churn.
   3. Capture both runtime-level telemetry and kernel microprobes.

Sampling governor and config (copy into config manifest)
| key | default | unit | meaning | safe bounds |
| sampling.global_rate | 0.0005 | fraction | fraction of total requests traced | 1e-6 .. 0.01 |
| sampling.microprobe_strategy | periodic | string | selection approach: periodic | periodic|adaptive|fingerprint |
| sampling.max_additional_cpu_pct | 0.05 | fraction | extra CPU budget for probes | 0.0 .. 0.1 |
| sampling.node_quota | 100 | items/s | per-node microprobe quota | 10 .. 1000 |

Example YAML snippet

sampling:
  global_rate: 0.0005          # 0.05% of requests
  microprobe_strategy: adaptive
  max_additional_cpu_pct: 0.05
  node_quota: 100

Telemetry retention & cost controls
- Keep high-resolution microprobe traces for 7 days by default. Aggregate rollups (histograms, heatmaps) are preserved for 90 days.
- If monthly trace ingestion exceeds 120% of budget, automatic downsampling triggers: reduce global_rate by 2x and notify owners.

Investigation playbook (step-by-step, 60–120 minutes)
1. Kickoff: capture hypothesis and assign a lead (Slack #runtime-oncall).
2. Snapshot: export dashboards, last 6 hours of traces, deployment timeline, and kernel-change list.
3. Execute targeted probes: enable "microprobe.enq_start" at cohort 0.5% and trace-enrich for the route.
4. Collect: wait 30–60 minutes or until 5–10k sampled events.
5. Analyze: run enqueue histograms, span waterfall visualizations, and correlate with KV-cache deltas.
6. Decide: if a kernel or scheduler regression identified, escalate to Kernel Team and open an investigation ticket with priority P1/P2 depending on impact.
7. Remediate & validate: apply rollback or hotfix, reduce probe cohort to 0.1% and observe for 60 minutes.

Escalation & ownership
- First responder: runtime-oncall (rotation).
- Profiler lead: assigned profiling-engineer on call (see team roster).
- Kernel owner: Kernel Team (kernel@redwood.ai).
- SLA triggers:
  - P99 latency increase > 25% across > 3 routes -> P0 incident page and cross-team warroom.
  - Reproducible regression localized to kernel variant -> open Kernel Team ticket and link telemetry snapshots.

Operational safety automations (what we enable)
- Automatic guardrail: probe circuit-breaker reacts to cohort latency signal and disables sampled flags.
- Budget monitor: monthly telemetry budget check with automated rate adjustments.
- Canary escalation: if a canary probe shows adverse change, the system auto-rolls to previous kernel variant for that canary.

Query and CLI examples
- Collect traces from timeframe (example CLI):
  rwi trace fetch --from 2026-02-10T02:00Z --to 2026-02-10T03:30Z --route /v1/generate --output traces.json

- Example microprobe event (JSON line):
  {"ts":1623345623123456789,"node":"node-15","kernel":"matmul_v2","phase":"enqueue","lat_ns":215}

- Join traces and microprobes (post-processing):
  python tools/join_traces_microprobes.py --traces traces.json --microprobes mp.json --out joined.json

Safety checklist before enabling a probe in production
1. Confirm owner and oncall contact listed.
2. Confirm cohort size, node quotas, and budget allowance in telemetry dashboard.
3. Define failure thresholds and circuit-breaker settings.
4. Add experiment to the experiment registry with start/stop times and intended metric signals.

Related pages and templates
- Runtime profiling playbook (template) — use the experiment template to register runs.
- Kernel rollout checklist — follow before toggling kernel variants.
- Incident runbook: runtime incident playbook (link to runbooks directory).

Appendix: quick heuristics
- If P99 enqueue->start spikes but raw kernel durations remain stable, suspect scheduler contention or admission-tokens scarcity.
- If kernel durations increase across the board, prioritize kernel variant rollback and test on replayed synthetic traffic.
- If only certain models/routes show degradation, focus on KV-cache and model-variant selection metrics.

Contacts & maintenance
- Doc owner: Marina Alvarez (marina@redwood.ai) — update cadence: quarterly or after any major telemetry change.
- Reviewers: Ethan Brooks, Priya Nair.

Change log
- 2025-11-02: created (initial cookbook).
- 2026-02-15: added sampling governor table, YAML examples, and automated safety checklist.

payload.page_title: Kernel Interaction Correlation Lab and Investigation Checklist

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a repeatable lab and step-by-step investigation checklist for diagnosing subtle kernel-level interaction issues in the serving runtime (contention, preemption races, KV cache coherence artifacts, and cross-kernel priority inversion). The intent is to provide a reproducible experimental harness, required telemetry fields, and a prioritized checklist on-call and SRE engineers can follow.

Audience: runtime SREs, performance engineers, kernel engineers, and on-call rotation members.

Scope and when to use this guide
- Use this playbook when: tail latency spikes (>99th percentile increases by >2x), unexplained GPU scheduler stalls, intermittent model-switch oscillations, or when a regression appears only under mixed-concurrency workloads.
- Out of scope: hardware-level power faults (use hardware incident runbook), application-level correctness bugs in the model code.

Background and rationale
- Modern inference workloads combine continuous batching, KV cache, and multiple kernel variants. Subtle interactions (e.g., a long-running kernel holding a tensor memory lock while preemption is attempted) can manifest as short-lived but high-impact latency spikes. These interactions are difficult to identify from high-level traces; causal correlation across runtime, kernel scheduler, and GPU dispatch telemetry is required.

Telemetry and signal catalog (required)
- Request-level signals:
  - request_id (string)
  - route/model (string)
  - timestamp_queued_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_enqueue_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_start_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_end_ms (int)
  - cpu_thread (string)
  - kernel_variant (string)
  - batch_id (string)
  - kv_cache_hit_ratio (float)
  - tokens_generated (int)

- Kernel/dispatcher signals:
  - gpu_dispatch_time_ms
  - gpu_complete_time_ms
  - kernel_preempt_attempts (int)
  - kernel_preempt_duration_ms
  - occupancy_percent
  - tensor_memory_alloc_bytes
  - kernel_wait_queue_len

- System signals:
  - node_cpu_load_1m
  - node_gpu_temp_celsius
  - nvlink_retry_count
  - iommu_faults
  - cgroup_preempt_events

Quick reference thresholds (operational defaults)
- 99th percentile latency increase: alert if > 2x baseline for 5m window.
- Kernel preempt attempts: alert if > 10 attempts/min on a node.
- GPU occupancy: alert if > 95% for sustained 2m while tail latency increases.

Investigation checklist (ordered, prescriptive)
1) Triage and collect artifacts (first 10 minutes)
   - Capture high-level traces: request traces for the afflicted timeframe (trace ID or request_id).
   - Export kernel-level telemetry: gpu_dispatch_time_ms, kernel_variant per batch, preempt counters.
   - Snapshot node-level metrics: top process GPU memory, nvtop snapshot, nvidia-smi dmon 1s for 30s.
   - Preserve scheduler logs and admission controller decision logs for the period.

2) Fast correlation (10–30 minutes)
   - Correlate request trace timestamps with kernel start/end timestamps. Look for requests with long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start (queueing at CPU/dispatcher).
   - Identify whether affected requests share model/version or batch shape. If yes, candidate a model-specific kernel variant.
   - Query: Prometheus example
     - promql: |
       increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[5m])

   - Quick grep on dispatcher logs for spike patterns: grep -E "preempt|handoff|wait_queue" /var/log/runtime/dispatcher.log | sed -n '1,200p'

3) Kernel-level deep-dive (30–120 minutes)\   - Reconstruct kernel timeline using kernel_trace_id map to request_ids.
   - If preemption attempts are present, examine preempt_duration_ms distribution. Long durations indicate stalled preempt handlers or unexpected GPU stall.
   - Run a focused microbenchmark: replay a small synthetic trace containing the same batch sizes and sequence lengths. Use the lab harness described below.

4) Hypothesis-driven fault injection (1–3 hours)
   - Hypothesis examples:
     - H1: A kernel variant with large scratch memory occasionally triggers a slow tensor allocation path causing long preempt durations.
     - H2: KV cache hot-skip path causes serialization on a shared mutex while kernel handoff waits, causing queue buildup.
   - For H1: deploy a canary variant with reduced scratch growth (quantized variant) and run shadow traffic. Observe preempt and tail latency.
   - For H2: run mutex contention stress test: deliberately increase concurrent KV hits on same keyspace and observe kernel_wait_queue_len.

5) Mitigation and rollback (if confirmed)
   - Immediate mitigations:
     - Route affected traffic to fallback kernel variant or smaller model variant.
     - Temporarily reduce max_concurrency for the node to shed potential long-running kernels.
   - Rollback checklist:
     - Validate fallback route maintains 95th/99th latency SLOs for a 10-minute observation window.
     - If stable, start a staged rollout of the stable kernel variant with 10/30/60 minute ramp steps.

Lab experiment protocol (reproducible)
- Goal: reproduce tail-latency spike deterministically in the lab, isolate kernel interaction sequence, and test mitigations.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Lab cluster with identical GPU family and runtime build (container image tag).
- Corpus of requests: select real traffic sample (anonymized) with 1k requests covering observed sequence length distribution.
- Harness repo: git@internal:redwood/runtime-labs.git, branch: telemetry-repro-2024
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.body:
1. Environment setup\   - Deploy runtime image: docker run --rm -e RUNTIME_TAG=telemetry-repro-2024 redwood/runtime:telemetry-repro-2024\   - Ensure profiling sidecar enabled (ENV: ENABLE_PROFILE=1) and lightweight BPF tracing agent running (rbpf-agent).
2. Load injection\   - Use lab injector: ./injector --corpus=corpus/sample-telemetry-corpus.json --qps=target --concurrency=target --shape=traffic-shape.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro\   - Example: ./injector --corpus=sample.json --qps=120 --concurrency=64 --shape=mixed-burst.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro
3. Collect artifacts automatically\   - run: ./collect-artifacts --since "2024-07-15T00:00:00Z" --out ./artifacts/test-repro.tar.gz\   - Artifacts: traces/*.json, kernel_telemetry.csv, dispatcher.log, nvidia-dmon.log, rbpf-traces/*.perf
4. Repeatability notes\   - Run at least 5 iterations per configuration; seed injector with deterministic random seed.

Observability playbook: queries and examples\- Prometheus examples:
  - Tail latency spike detection (5m): |
    (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
  - Kernel preempt heatmap: |
    sum by (node, kernel_variant) (increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[15m]))

- Trace join example (SQL-ish pseudocode for internal trace store): |
  SELECT r.request_id, r.route, t.kernel_variant, t.start_ms, t.end_ms
  FROM requests r JOIN kernel_spans t ON r.trace_id = t.trace_id
  WHERE r.timestamp BETWEEN '2024-07-15T10:00:00Z' AND '2024-07-15T10:10:00Z'
  ORDER BY t.start_ms DESC

Kernel-level capture snippets
- BPF tracer snippet (example): |
  sudo rbpf-agent --attach=nv_dispatch --out /tmp/rbpf-attach.log --fields pid,tgid,dispatch_timestamp,kernel_name,stack_id

- nvidia-smi sampling (30s high-fidelity window): |
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1000 -o TD > nvidia-dmon.log &

- Minimal script to extract slow kernel spans (bash): |
  awk -F',' '$6 - $5 > 50 {print $0}' kernel_telemetry.csv | head -n 200

Fault injection template (Caution: only run in lab or staging)
- Introduce artificial allocation latency at the runtime allocator path to emulate slow scratch growth:
  - Use LD_PRELOAD wrapper which sleeps on gpu_alloc path once every N allocations.
  - Invocation YAML snippet: |
    fault_injection:
      type: allocator-sleep
      sleep_ms: 25
      every_n: 1000

Acceptance criteria for mitigations
- Measured improvement: 99th latency returns to within 1.2x baseline and kernel_preempt_attempts drop by >= 60% in 15-minute window.
- No increase in error rate or model output degradation (compare eval prompts used in shadow traffic).

Runbook ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-sre@redwood.com (rotation: oncall-runtime).
- Secondary: kernel-team@redwood.com.
- Pager escalation: if mitigation not effective within 30 minutes, escalate to oncall-eng-lead and open a Sev-2 incident.

Post-incident hygiene
1. Tag all artifacts and traces with incident id: INC-YYYYMMDD-XXX.
2. Record principal hypothesis and final resolution in the incident doc.
3. Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite (benchmarks/interaction-regressions) if the issue was root-caused to a kernel variant.

Appendix: example artifact file formats
- kernel_telemetry.csv (columns): timestamp_ms, node, gpu_id, batch_id, kernel_variant, start_ms, end_ms, preempt_attempts, preempt_duration_ms, tensor_alloc_bytes
- dispatcher.log entries: timestamp iso8601 | node | event | details

Appendix: common failure patterns (cheat sheet)
- Pattern: "enqueue drift" — long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start; likely dispatcher saturation or priority inversion.
- Pattern: "preempt tail" — repeated preempt attempts with long preempt_duration_ms; likely kernel stall or driver-level hang.
- Pattern: "kv hotlock" — KV cache hit correlation with dispatcher mutex contention; look for high kv_cache_hit_ratio and mutex wait traces.

Related pages and artifacts
- Add links to the final artifacts tarball in the incident doc and tag the change with the runtime build that was running.

Maintenance and cadence
- This playbook is reviewed quarterly by the profiling team. Add new signal fields when the runtime or kernel telemetry schema changes.

Contact and feedback
- For clarifications or to propose changes to the checklist, open a pull request against runtime-labs/docs/kernel-interaction-checklist.md or ping Priya Nair on Slack (#runtime-profiling).

End of document

payload.page_title: Event-sourced Observability: Correlation & Triage Runbook

sections.body: This runbook defines the event-sourced observability model we use to correlate distributed runtime signals (traces, metrics, logs, kernel events) and perform fast, reproducible triage of inference incidents. It documents the canonical event envelope, enrichment rules, minimal required fields, triage playflow, example queries, and rollout checklist for instrumenting new runtime components.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Provide a single cross-team contract for events produced by runtime components (dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator, model-swaps).
- Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for performance regressions and correctness incidents by standardizing correlation keys and triage steps.
- Ensure low-cost, high-utility telemetry: bounding event size, pre-aggregation guidelines, and sampling rules.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Use this runbook for any incident that involves latency spikes, tail latency regressions, memory pressure OOMs, soft degradation, or model swap oscillations.
- Not intended for application-layer logic bugs (customer prompt-level bugs) unless they cause runtime-level resource anomalies.
sections.heading: Scope and when to use

sections.body:
Every runtime event MUST be an immutable envelope with the following fields (minimum set):
- event_id: globally unique id (uuid4)
- ts_iso: ISO8601 timestamp in UTC
- origin_service: short name (e.g., dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator)
- host_id: node identifier (k8s node / instance id)
- shard_id: runtime shard or device id when applicable (e.g., gpu-0)
- request_id: upstream request trace id if present, otherwise generated
- route_tag: customer or route identifier (when applicable)
- phase: high-level phase (ingest, scheduling, dispatch, kernel_exec, postprocessing)
- level: INFO/WARN/ERROR
- payload: structured JSON blob with event-specific fields (see examples)
sections.heading: Event model (canonical envelope)

sections.body:
| field       | type   | example                        | notes |
|-------------|--------|--------------------------------|-------|
| event_id    | string | 9f8b6aab-...                   | uuid4 |
| ts_iso      | string | 2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z       | UTC |
| origin_service | string | kernel                      | short service name |
| host_id     | string | i-0a1b2c3d4e5f                 | k8s node id or instance |
| shard_id    | string | gpu-0                         | device/shard context |
| request_id  | string | req-4b123                      | correlates to client request |
| route_tag   | string | prod-chat-1                   | optional but highly recommended |
| phase       | string | kernel_exec                   | one of the canonical phases |
| level       | string | WARN                          | log level |
| payload     | object | {"lat_ms": 4.2}              | event-specific details |
sections.heading: Minimal telemetry fields table (copyable)

sections.body:
{
  "event_id": "9f8b6aab-1234-4cde-8a7b-0abcde123456",
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z",
  "origin_service": "kernel",
  "host_id": "node-42",
  "shard_id": "gpu-0",
  "request_id": "req-4b123",
  "route_tag": "prod-chat-1",
  "phase": "kernel_exec",
  "level": "INFO",
  "payload": {
    "lat_ms": 12.4,
    "seq_len": 256,
    "kv_hit": true,
    "kernel_variant": "vectored-tc"
  }
}
sections.heading: Event envelope example (JSON)

sections.body:
1) Attach stable host_id and shard_id at process startup. Fail open: if shard unknown, set "shard_id": "unknown".
2) Propagate request_id from surface API through the dispatcher to the kernel; if absent, synthesize and mark with a "synthesized_request_id" boolean in payload.
3) Route tagging: upstream routers should add route_tag; if missing, call-site should derive route from model_id or team config.
4) Add deployment metadata (commit hash, kernel build id) to host-level heartbeat events produced every 5 minutes.
sections.heading: Enrichment rules (construction time)

sections.body:
- Full tracing is expensive. Apply progressive sampling: 100% sampling for ERROR events, 10% for WARN, and reservoir sampling for INFO subject to label-based overrides (e.g., always sample requests tagged as "perf-eval").
- For high-volume kernels, emit aggregated rollup events per minute per shard with the fields: ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q1,q50,q95,q99,invocations,total_tokens. Use these for fast dashboards and cost-aware alerts.
sections.heading: Sampling and retention guidance

sections.body:
1) Detect: alert triggers (e.g., p99 latency > SLO threshold on a route) should create an incident ticket with a link to the minute rollup and sample traces.
2) Initial burst analysis (5 min): run the minute rollup query filtered by route_tag -> check p50/p95/p99 delta, invocation count, token distribution.
3) Correlate with host-level signals: filter events by ts range and examine host heartbeats for thermal/power anomalies, collector reports for kernel build mismatch, and allocator warnings.
4) Expand to kernel-level events: pull kernel_exec events for the suspect shards and examine payload fields (lat_ms, seq_len, kernel_variant, tensor_core_util). Look for step changes in kernel_variant mix or sudden rise in seq_len.
5) Cross-check kvcache: look for kvcache miss spikes in the same time window using payload.kv_hit==false and kvcache warmup events. A kvcache miss storm often explains latency spikes.
6) If no kernel resource anomaly, inspect dispatcher and admission controller events for queue depth, preemption, or credit exhaustion.
7) If root cause unclear, collect a deterministic trace sample: set temporary sampling override to 100% for the offending route_tag for 2 minutes and capture full traces.
8) Containment: based on root cause, apply one of the quick mitigations (see Quick mitigations below), open a rollback or canary pause if needed, and annotate incident ticket with event ids of representative traces.
sections.heading: Triage playflow (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Increase per-route concurrency cap by +20% for 2 min via routing console (when admission controller is too restrictive).
- Temporarily pin route to a lower-fidelity model-variant to avoid kernel stalls.
- Evict cold kvcache on a small percentage of nodes to re-balance warm cache.
- Throttle low-priority background workloads on nodes reporting thermal or memory pressure.
sections.heading: Quick mitigations (common)
Example KQL/SQL queries (schematic)

sections.body:
- Reproduce local microbench with same kernel_variant and seq_len distribution.
- Compare kernel build id from host heartbeat to the canary fleet build id.
- Run a synthetic traffic replay using the request surface replay harness with identical token distribution.
- If memory pressure suspected, capture allocator diagnostic snapshot (see allocator-runbook).

Runbook for kernel regression rollback decision: (decision matrix)
- Severity: P0 (customer impacting or SLO breach > 1 hour): immediate rollback to last known good kernel_variant and schedule hotfix release.
- Severity: P1 (intermittent SLO breach < 1 hour): throttle traffic via routing and open detailed profiling ticket.
- Severity: P2: schedule follow-up experiment and kernel bisect.

Ownership, SLAs and notifications:
- Primary owner for this contract: Serving Runtime Observability (oncall): runtime-observability@redwood.ai.
- Oncall response SLA: acknowledge within 15 minutes for P0/P1, start triage within 30 minutes.
- Postmortem requirement: detailed incident postmortem for any event that caused > 1 hour SLO breach or > 5% customer error increase.

Rollout checklist for instrumenting a new component into the contract:
1) Add the canonical envelope producer to the component library with local validation.
2) Emit host-level heartbeat and attach deployment metadata.
3) Unit test event envelope, including synthesized request_id path.
4) Stage sampling rules and verify ingestion at low volume to the ingest cluster.
5) Add dashboard tiles: per-minute rollup, p95/p99 heatmap, kvcache-hit-rate, kernel_variant mix.
6) Run a 48-hour shadow run with sample-rate parity and measure telemetry cost.
sections.heading: Investigation checklist (runnable)

sections.body:
- Collect live kernel traces: rtr-collect --shard gpu-0 --since 2026-02-14T18:00Z --limit 200 --output /tmp/traces.ndjson
- Query rollups: rtql "SELECT * FROM runtime_rollups WHERE route_tag='prod-chat-1' AND ts_minute >= '2026-02-14T17:00'"

Appendix: Known anti-patterns and gotchas:
- Relying solely on p95 can hide p99 regressions that are caused by rare long sequences; always check p99 and the seq_len distribution.
- Missing request_id propagation from the gateway makes correlation much slower; instrument synthetic propagation in test harnesses.
- Overly aggressive INFO sampling can starve postmortem investigators of the causal chain.
sections.heading: Debugging utilities and commands (examples)

sections.body:
- Causal latency attribution playbook (see related_pages)
- Runtime rollup schema (runtime_rollup_schema.md)
- Allocator diagnostic runbook (allocator-runbook)
sections.heading: References and related docs

sections.body:
- Document owner: Aisha Patel (aisha.patel@redwood.ai)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major incident.
sections.heading: Contact and maintenance

sections.body:
- 2025-11-04: Created initial draft.
- 2026-01-10: Added sampling guidance and rollup schema.
- 2026-02-15: Finalized triage playflow and decision matrix.

payload.page_title: Kernel observability SLAs and profiling cadence

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines a pragmatic, operationally focused observability SLA for the serving runtime kernel layer and specifies a profiling cadence and playbook for keeping kernel regressions visible and remediable. The goal is to ensure kernel-level performance signals (latency, dispatch/backpressure, memory pressure, and kernel success rates) are actionable by oncall and engineering, tied to benchmarking experiments, and budgeted within profiling cost constraints.

Why this matters

- Kernel regressions are the root cause of the majority of hard-to-diagnose tail-latency incidents.
- Observability at the kernel boundary is expensive; we need a cost-aware sampling strategy and a clear schedule so telemetry budgets are predictable.
- Tying profiling to the benchmarking suite and release gates reduces the chance of regressing a deployment unnoticed.

Scope

This document covers the manifest, SLOs, sampling & tracing cadence, profiling runbook, integration points with the benchmarking suite and release process, and known limitations. It applies to:

- The inference runtime kernel components (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel executor, KV cache interface).
- Host-level telemetry produced by kernel shim and GPU-side counters that we ingest via the kernel agent.

Key definitions

- Kernel sample: a single end-to-end kernel execution record (dispatch -> kernel launch -> completion) including timestamps, kernel variant id, request classification, memory footprint, and outcome code.
- Observability SLA: the target for alertable metrics derived from kernel samples (e.g., kernel_p99_duration, kernel_error_rate).
- Profiling window: an intentional time-bounded full-capture session used for deep analysis (trace-level).

Observability SLA (metrics and thresholds)

Table: metric | alert threshold | target (SLO) | runbook severity
- kernel_p95_execution_ms | > 80ms sustained 5m | SLO: p95 < 60ms over 24h | Sev2
- kernel_p99_execution_ms | > 200ms sustained 5m | SLO: p99 < 150ms over 24h | Sev1
- kernel_error_rate (non-transient) | > 0.5% over 10m | SLO: < 0.2% | Sev1
- kernel_dispatch_queue_depth | > 200 for 1m | SLO: median < 50 | Sev2
- kernel_memory_pressure_evictions_per_min | > 1/min | SLO: < 0.1/min | Sev2

Notes: thresholds are intentionally tighter than product-level SLA to detect regressions earlier. Alerting rules are configured in Monitoring (Grafana/Prometheus) under team "runtime-kernel-observability". Alerts map to runbook escalation in the Runbooks section.

Sampling policy and retention budget

- Continuous aggregated metrics: emitted for all kernels (high-cardinality fields are hashed). Retained for 90 days.
- Detailed traces (span-level, per-request kernels): sampled using hybrid sampling: deterministic sampling for top 1% traffic cohorts by token volume + probabilistic reservoir sampling (0.5% of all requests) to ensure long-tail visibility.
- Profiling windows (full capture): scheduled 3 times per week in production canaries and once weekly in a matched staging shard. Each profiling window is limited to 15 minutes per shard to keep cost bounded.
- Retention: full-trace artifacts retained for 30 days (aligned with the incident review window) and archived to cold storage (GCS) for 12 months for cross-release comparisons.

Profiling cadence (recommended schedule)

1) Daily lightweight probes (continuous):
   - Metric rollups + micro-histogram snapshots every minute.
   - Purpose: detect immediate shifts in medians and p95.

2) Weekly focused traces:
   - 2x profiling windows (15m each) in staging matched to production traffic shape.
   - Run: guided by the benchmark suite scenarios (see integration).

3) Release gating profiling:
   - For any kernel or scheduler change that lands in main and is tagged for canary, run a release profiling session (two 15m windows) in canary. Must pass the profiling gate (no new anomalies at p99 and no unexplained error-rate increase).

4) On-demand deep captures:
   - Triggered from an incident or a scheduled experiment. Can be 30–120 minutes, must be pre-approved by runtime leadership if > 30 minutes due to cost.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Preconditions: you are oncall or the owner of a flagged release. Have access to the profiling orchestration tool (profilingctl) and the benchmark runner.

1) Validate the alert: confirm Prometheus/Grafana alert and cross-check with product-level SLOs.
2) Correlate: use the request-tagged rollups to identify cohorts (model variant, seq_length_bucket, priority_class).
3) If tail signals are present, promote a profiling window targeting the affected shard(s) for 15 minutes (profilingctl start-window --shard <id> --duration 15m --cohort <tag>).
4) Collect kernel samples and GPU-side counters. Verify the sample set exceeds the minimum capture size (>= 200 kernel samples for statistical validity).
5) Run the local analysis pipeline (profile-analyze) to generate: hotspot table, costly-kernel-variants, and cross-correlation with dispatcher queue depth.

- Hotspot table: top 10 kernel variants by p99 increase vs baseline.
- Costly-kernel-variants: kernel ids with a >2x increase in per-invocation GPU time.

6) Triage: if a single kernel variant explains >40% of the p99 shift, open an RFC and page the kernel owner. If no single variant emerges, escalate to sysinfra and kernel scheduling owners to look for admission/queueing interactions.

7) Mitigation options (short-term):
   - Rollback kernel patch; or
   - Switch offending cohort to a fallback model variant; or
   - Temporarily increase admission control for the priority class to shed non-critical traffic.

8) Postmortem: capture the artifact id of the profiling capture and link it to the incident ticket. Run a follow-up benchmark against the microbench suite to validate proposed fixes.

Integration with benchmarking suite

- The profiling orchestration integrates with the benchmarking suite via a shared experiment manifest. Each profiling window can be replayed against the benchmark harness to produce a reproducible microbench against the exact kernel variants observed.
- Benchmark experiments to run after a profiling session:
  - sequence-length-scaling scenario at 4 concurrency points
  - KV-cache-warmup profile to emulate long-session traffic
  - scheduler-priority-noise injection to validate admission controls

Release gating and automation

- Any release that touches: kernel code, scheduler, admission controller, or the dispatcher must include a profiling gate. The CI pipeline will schedule a canary profiling window automatically and fail the gate if:
  - kernel_p99_execution_ms increases by > 10% vs canary baseline; or
  - kernel_error_rate increases by > 0.05 percentage points.

Runbooks (high level)

- Sev1: (p99 spike or error rate)
  1) Page runtime-oncall and kernel-owner.
  2) Run profiling window (15m) targeted at canary shard(s).
  3) If profiling confirms a single kernel variant: apply emergency rollback and re-run profiling.
  4) If not, invoke admission-control escalation to shed traffic and restore SLOs.

- Sev2: (p95 or queue depth)
  1) Perform correlation and schedule a 15m profiling window.
  2) Tune admission control thresholds for the affected priority class.
  3) Schedule a follow-up benchmark to validate tuning.

Known limitations and gotchas

- Sampling bias: deterministic sampling of top cohorts improves reproducibility but can miss rare degradations in low-volume tenants. Use on-demand deep captures for those.
- GPU counters missing on legacy accelerator drivers: in those cases we fallback to host-side timing and increase sampling rate for statistical confidence.
- Profiling cost: full-trace windows are expensive; long captures require leadership sign-off. Abuse of on-demand windows has previously consumed >30% of monthly profiling budget — we now require ticketing and attach artifact ids.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Kernel observability ownership: runtime-observability@redwood.com (primary: Marcus Alvarez).
- Scheduler & kernel owners: see TEAM-OWNERS index in the runtime-team wiki.
- Oncall rota: runtime-oncall (primary) and kernel-secondary (secondary).

Appendix: handy commands and queries

- Start a short profiling window (CLI): profilingctl start-window --shard canary-3 --duration 15m --note "p99-burst-investigation"
- Generate a hotspot report: profile-analyze --capture-id <id> --output hotspots.csv
- Grafana query for kernel p99: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_execution_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, variant))
- Baseline comparison job: bench-runner --manifest capture-<id>.json --replay --compare baseline-2024-11-01.json

References and related pages

- Runtime profiling guidelines (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmark suite catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025
- Release gating policy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

Change log

- 2024-01-12: initial draft and schedule proposal.
- 2024-06-01: tightened sampling policy; added deterministic cohort capture.
- 2025-11-03: increased profiling window retention and clarified release gating thresholds.

payload.page_title: GPU memory fragmentation diagnostics and remediation playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook defines a concrete, repeatable process for diagnosing and remediating GPU memory fragmentation observed in Redwood serving hosts. It consolidates telemetry to capture, commands and tooling to run during a live incident, thresholds we consider actionable, short-term mitigations to restore capacity, and long-term fixes to avoid recurrence.

Why this matters:
- Fragmentation can cause apparent out-of-memory (OOM) or allocation failures even when aggregate free memory looks sufficient.
- For inference workloads with persistent KV caches, allocator metadata, and mixed allocation sizes (small tensors, large KV pages), fragmentation reduces usable contiguous memory and increases tail latency / request rejection.
- Fast triage reduces customer impact and avoids unnecessary instance reprovisioning.

Scope / Audience:
- Applies to Redwood Dedicated and Private runtime nodes running CUDA-based inference backends (PyTorch/TVM/Rust CUDA runtime).
- Intended for oncall SREs, runtime engineers, and platform-hosting engineers.

Symptoms that point to fragmentation (not just peak usage):
1) Allocation failures or repeated cudaMalloc retries while nvidia-smi reports >20% free memory.
2) Rapid oscillation of free memory without matching process exit/creation events.
3) Frequent small free segments reported by allocator introspection (see "Telemetry to collect").
4) Successful large allocations after contiguous-space freeing (restart/evict/cache-trim).

Telemetry to collect (must be available on all runtime nodes):
- NVML / nvidia-smi samples (1s granularity if possible): memory.total, memory.used, memory.free, utilization.gpu, process PIDs and memory per process.
  - Command: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,memory.free,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 1
- CUDA allocator metrics (if enabled via runtime): per-process: allocated_bytes, reserved_bytes, allocation_failures, peak_reserved.
  - For PyTorch: TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=enabled_stat=true or custom allocator hooks.
- CUDA malloc-async / mempool stats: free_count, reserved_count, largest_free_block_size (if runtime exposes).
- Host-level memory churn and OOM events: dmesg for oom-killer, system journal for process SIGKILL.
- GPU per-process mmap-style allocations: nv-hostengine / Nsight info or driver logs.
- Runtime-level KV cache metrics: shard_reserved_bytes, shard_active_bytes, eviction_count.
- Traces / flamegraphs around allocation calls during suspect windows.

Derived metrics and dashboard panels we recommend:
- Fragmentation ratio = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free_block / memory.free). (If largest_contiguous is unavailable, approximate using max single free chunk observed via allocator telemetry.)
- Allocation failure rate / minute per process.
- Average and P95 contiguous_free_block_size over 5m windows.
- % of memory held by long-lived allocations (> 10m).
- Eviction frequency and time-to-evict for KV cache.
- Requests rejected due to mem budget exceeded.

Actionable thresholds (initial defaults, tune per fleet):
- Fragmentation ratio > 0.6 for more than 2 minutes => investigate.
- Allocation failure rate > 3/min for any process => immediate mitigation.
- Largest_contiguous_free_block < model_max_allocation_size * 1.1 => urgent.

Immediate triage steps (ordered, meant for live incidents):
1) Confirm symptom: correlate API error logs (cuda OOM, allocation failed) with GPU telemetry timestamps.
2) Capture snapshot (do not reboot until snapshot taken):
   - sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv -f /tmp/gpu-proc-snapshot.csv
   - sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -f /tmp/gpu-snapshot.csv
   - Collect runtime allocator stats (endpoint /debug/alloc-stats or environment hooks).
   - If possible, run nsight systems quick snapshot: nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda --output=/tmp/nsys-snapshot
3) Identify long-lived owners: sort per-process used_memory and cross-reference process start times. If a single process holds a lot of small allocations, open a ticket for that service to examine pooling settings.
4) Apply safe short-term mitigations (pick in descending order of non-disruptiveness):
   - Trigger runtime cache trimming API for the affected shard(s). Example: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:9001/admin/cache/trim?target=20%
   - If allocator supports trimming (cudaMallocAsync pools), call the pool release function (approx: CUDA API cudaMemPoolTrim).
   - Reduce per-request cache prefetch length or per-request tensor pre-allocation via feature flags.
   - As last resort for single-host recovery: gracefully restart the offending process (preferred) rather than full host reboot. Use graceful drain/replica failover steps documented in the service's runbook.
5) If mitigations restore contiguous memory, keep the node in investigational mode: increase logging, take several post-mitigation snapshots.

If live mitigations fail (escalation path):
- If multiple nodes show fragmentation simultaneously, escalate to runtime+infra owners immediately.
- Reprovision with hot-swap of capacity: put node into drain in autoscaler, migrate traffic, then reboot host to reclaim whole GPU state. Reboot is last resort and requires labeling for postmortem.

Root cause analysis checklist (post-incident):
- Which allocator was in use (cudaMalloc, cudaMallocAsync, cub::DeviceMemoryPool, PyTorch caching allocator)?
- Were there mixed allocation sizes or a burst of very small allocations (tens to hundreds of KB)?
- Were there pinned host allocations interfering with DMA?
- Is there a mismatch between tensor pooling parameters (max_split_size_mb) and typical tensor sizes for this workload?
- Did kernel scheduling (concurrent kernels) leave many small allocations resident?
- Was quantization or model shard fragmentation causing many small mapping allocations (memcpy/backing pages)?

Long-term remediation patterns and engineering changes:
1) Enable allocator-level stats by default in canary fleets and add fragment metrics to runtime telemetry.
2) Switch heavy-allocation workloads to cudaMallocAsync + explicit mempool trimming where supported.
3) Tune TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF settings for services with many small tensors. Example: export TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:32,garbage_collection_threshold:0.7
4) Introduce periodic background consolidation: low-priority background job that releases cached pools when utilization is low.
5) Add a shard-aware allocator: prefer coalesced large allocations for KV cache pages and compact small per-request allocations into batch arenas.
6) Add preflight allocation check: ensure largest_contiguous_free_block >= model_peak_allocation before scheduling a heavy request (fail fast/route to fallback).
7) Improve admission control: route requests that need large contiguous allocation to nodes with verified contiguous capacity.

Recommended config snippets and examples:
- PyTorch allocator stats enable (env):
  export TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=enable_stat=true,max_split_size_mb:32

- Example pool trim via CUDA (pseudocode):
  // runtime exposes admin endpoint calling into CUDA mempool API
  cudaMemPoolTrim(memPool, bytesToTrim);

- Grafana / Prometheus query examples (PromQL-like pseudo):
  - frag_ratio = 1 - (gpu_largest_contig_free_bytes / gpu_free_bytes)
  - allocation_failures_per_min = increase(cuda_allocation_failures_total[1m])
  - p95_largest_free = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (gpu_largest_free_block_size_bytes_bucket))

Ownership and SLAs for mitigations:
- First responder: runtime oncall (SRE) — initial triage and snapshot collection within 5 minutes of alert.
- Runtime engineering: implement short-term mitigations and coordinate safe process restarts within 30 minutes.
- Platform infra: if host reboot required, schedule and annotate, and complete within 60 minutes with approval.
- Post-incident RCA: assigned to runtime engineering, deliverable within 7 business days with action items.

Playbook for reproducibility tests (QA / dev):
1) Create a synthetic workload that alternates many small allocations with sporadic large allocations to mimic KV + request tensors.
2) Run on a canary node with allocator statistics enabled and measure fragmentation growth.
3) Test mitigations: trimming, adjusting max_split_size_mb, and using cudaMallocAsync. Measure time to recover and allocation failure counts.
4) Record results and add to the regression test harness (link in related pages).

Postmortem template fields to fill if fragmentation caused production impact:
- Incident start/end timestamps
- Symptoms observed and evidence (logs, snapshots)
- Short-term mitigations applied and timestamps
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence supporting it
- Long-term actions planned and owners

Appendix: quick commands and notes
- Snapshot GPU processes: sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv
- Continuous NVML sampling: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -l 1 > /tmp/gpu-sample.csv &
- Nsight quick trace: nsys profile --trace=cuda --output=/tmp/trace -t 10s <workload-cmd>
- PyTorch: print(torch.cuda.memory_stats()) and torch.cuda.memory_reserved()/memory_allocated() endpoints.

Notes and tradeoffs:
- Reboots clear fragmentation but hide underlying leaks/anti-patterns. Prefer tracing and allocator changes over reboot as the primary fix.
- Enabling allocator stats has a small perf overhead; start with a 1% canary population before fleet-wide rollout.
- Some hardware/driver combos expose more allocator metadata (e.g., newer CUDA runtimes). Maintain a compatibility matrix in the runtime wiki.

Contacts and escalation list:
- runtime-oncall@redwood.internal (primary)
- eng-serving-runtime@redwood.internal (engineering owners)
- infra-pool-management@redwood.internal (capacity and host reboots)

Document provenance and change log:
- 2026-01-18: initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-14: reviewed and published; added PromQL examples and explicit thresholds (reviewers: Marco Nguyen, Lena Hoffmann, Diego Alvarez).
