payload.page_title: Occupancy and Concurrency Audit Playbook for Serving Runtime

sections.body: This playbook describes a repeatable audit process to assess and remediate GPU occupancy and request concurrency issues in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for on-call engineers, performance engineers, and SREs responsible for multi-tenant inference pools and kernel scheduler tuning. The goal is to detect pathological occupancy/concurrency patterns early, quantify their impact on latency/cost, and prescribe targeted mitigations.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Low GPU occupancy (SM utilization) or poor warp efficiency increases per-token cost and can drastically raise tail latency for short requests.
- Excessive concurrency without appropriate kernel crediting can cause kernel contention, eviction churn, and KV-cache thrash.
- Multi-tenant pools and dynamic batching increase the surface area for occupancy anomalies; automated audits help prevent regressions when we change kernel mappers, quantization profiles, or shard placement rules.
sections.heading: Why this matters

sections.body:
- Scope: GPUs used by Redwood-hosted runtime (heterogeneous pools), Dedicated clusters on RDW, and Private deployment models where we operate the inference stack.
- Audience: runtime performance team, serving runtime owners, SRE, release engineers.
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body:
- SM Occupancy: fraction of Streaming Multiprocessor compute capacity active. Monitored with nvidia-smi dmon/ DCGM metric: gpu_sm_active and nvprof metrics like sm_efficiency.
- Warp Efficiency: fraction of executed threads performing useful work (warp_execution_efficiency).
- GPU Active Time / Kernel Time: total kernel execution time versus idle/wait time.
- CUDA Stream Utilization: concurrency of CUDA streams per process (useful for kernel overlap).
- Kernel Queue Length: number of enqueued kernels waiting execution per GPU.
- Token-per-second per-GPU and per-request token latency: application-visible metrics correlated with kernel metrics.
sections.heading: Key concepts and metrics (short primer)

sections.body:
- Avg SM Occupancy: target 30%–80% depending on model size. Small models (<=4B) should aim for >45% with batching; large models (>=70B) may be 20%–40% due to register pressure.
- Warp Efficiency: target >70%; investigate below 60%.
- Kernel Queue Length (p95): <= 8 for latency SLOs; if >16, treat as congestion.
- Kernel Preemption Events: zero preferred; any spike should be investigated.
sections.heading: Acceptance thresholds (operational guidance)

sections.body:
- Scheduled audit: weekly automated run across production pools.
- Release-triggered audit: run after kernel mapper, quantization, or scheduler changes.
- Incident-triggered audit: triggered by sustained SLO degradation (p95 latency increase >20% or error spike).
sections.heading: Audit cadence and triggers

sections.body:
1) DCGM / Prometheus exporter snapshots for each GPU: sm_efficiency, sm_active, gpu_util, mem_used, sm_clock, power.
2) Kernel-level traces (perfetto / CUPTI) sampled for 60s across representative nodes.
3) Per-request runtime traces (trace-id keyed) including batch size, sequence length, model variant, and scheduling priority.
4) Kernel queue metrics and kernel metadata (kernel name, duration, per-kernel average latency).
5) KV-cache hit/miss rates and warmup time per request shard.
6) System-level metrics: NUMA statistics, PCIe throughput, nvlink/ nvlink errors.
sections.heading: Automated data collection (what to gather)

sections.body:
1. Kick off collection:
   - Run the automated collector job (prod-audit-collector) for the target pool. CLI:

   ```bash
   ./tools/profiler/run-audit --pool gpu-pool-2 --duration 60s --out /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.json
   ```

   - Ensure collector captures DCGM metrics at 250ms granularity and samples 1 CUPTI trace per physical GPU.

2. Baseline correlation (automated):
   - Run the baseline comparator tool to correlate p95 latency and per-GPU sm_efficiency. Example:

   ```bash
   ./tools/perf/compare-baseline --current /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.json --baseline s3://perf-baselines/gpu-pool-2/2026-01-01.json
   ```

   - Output: CSV with columns (metric, current_p50, current_p95, baseline_p95, relative_change).

3. High-level triage (manual):
   - Open the generated dashboard link from the collector output. Inspect: SM occupancy heatmap, kernel queue length timeseries, per-model aggregated warp efficiency.
   - If p95 latency correlates with occupancy drop (sm_efficiency falls while kernel queue increases), flag as kernel contention.

4. Deep dive: kernel-level analysis:
   - Identify top 5 kernels by total time in the trace. Use the kernel map to attribute kernels to model layers (attention, MLP, softmax).
   - For each kernel, inspect duration distribution, occupancy-dependent latency (plot duration vs active warps).
   - Look for kernels with large variance or heavy tail (p99 > 4x median). Those are primary candidates for micro-optimization or fallback tuning.

5. Concurrency accounting check:
   - Verify kernel-credit accounting logs to ensure per-request credit consumption matches runtime expectations. Query:

   ```promql
   sum by (pool) (increase(kernel_credit_consumed_total[5m]))
   ```

   - If observed concurrency > configured_max_concurrency by >20%, investigate admission control or credit leak bugs.

6. KV-cache correlation:
   - Join per-request latency with KV-cache hit rate. A simultaneous drop in hit-rate and SM occupancy often indicates aggressive eviction policies during high concurrency.

7. NUMA/PCIe check:
   - If occupancy low but GPU util high and kernel times are fragmented, inspect NUMA binding and transfer stalls. Use `numactl --hardware` and `perf record` to validate.
sections.heading: How to run an audit (step-by-step)

sections.body:
1) Apply immediate throttling: reduce admission concurrency for the affected model/pool by 20% (fast rollback).
2) Switch to a compatible lower-parallel kernel variant (runtime supports alternative kernel variants labeled fast-path, conservative).
3) Increase batching window for short-sequence workloads for 30s to evaluate impact.
4) Adjust kernel mapper hints to prefer fewer concurrent small kernels on the same GPU (see kernel mapper tuning snippet below).
sections.heading: Automated remediation recommendations (ordered)

sections.body:
- purpose: prefer sequential execution for kernels with low occupancy and high variance
- config keys (YAML):

  kernel_mapper:
    prioritize_small_kernel_serialization: true
    small_kernel_threshold_ms: 1.5
    concurrency_grouping_window_ms: 12
    backpressure_on_queue_length: 10
sections.heading: Kernel mapper tuning example (config snippet)

sections.body:
- SM occupancy heatmap: avg(sm_efficiency) by (gpu_id) over 5m
- Kernel queue alarm: (max_over_time(kernel_queue_length[5m]) > 12)
- Warp inefficiency alert (event): increase(warp_stall_cycles_total[5m]) / increase(instruction_issued_total[5m]) > 0.35
- Correlation panel: overlay p95(request_latency) with 1 - avg(sm_efficiency) (both normalized) to surface inverse relationships.
sections.heading: Metrics and dashboard recipes (Grafana/PromQL examples)

sections.body:
- Symptom: sudden p95 spike for short-text generation where throughput hasn't changed.
  Triage: run audit collector for 60s; find that kernel queue length jumped and sm_efficiency dropped to 18% on two GPUs.
  Remediation: throttle concurrency for model route, apply kernel mapper change to serialize small kernels. Result: p95 restored within 3 minutes.

- Symptom: slow cold-start for mini-batches after rollout of a quantized kernel.
  Triage: KV-cache miss surge and multiple small kernels with long tail.
  Remediation: revert to previous kernel variant for the model, schedule controlled rollout with traffic shadowing.

Decision criteria matrix (when to change runtime configs vs when to open a kernel engineering ticket):

- Quick config change (runtime): if issue is resolved by admission control, mapper hint flips, or batch-window adjustments and change reduces p95 by >15% in canary.
- Kernel engineering ticket: if top kernel p99 > 3x median and variance does not change with concurrency reduction or mapper hints, escalate to kernel team with trace bundle.
sections.heading: Incident play examples (short)

sections.body:
- Primary: serving-runtime-performance@redwood.internal (team lead: Priya Natarajan).
- Kernel engineering: kernel-core@redwood.internal (owner: Diego Morales).
- Oncall escalation: page SRE oncall if SLO breached after the second remediation step.
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation paths

sections.body:
- audit collector JSON and generated dashboard link
- top-5 kernel trace bundle (CUPTI/Perfetto) with timestamped ranges
- per-request trace subset (10–100 representative trace ids) with correlated KV-cache and scheduler decisions
sections.heading: Artifacts to attach to the audit ticket

sections.body:
1) Immediately revert the admission control change via runtime CLI: `runtimectl set-concurrency --pool <pool> --value <previous>`
2) Revert kernel mapper config using config rollback tag in S3 and trigger a config reload: `runtimectl reload-config --tag <previous-tag>`
3) If kernel variant was replaced, rotate traffic back to previous variant and monitor p95 for 10 minutes.

Checklist for a good audit report (what we expect in the ticket):

- Executive summary (one paragraph): impact, affected pools/models, summary of root cause.
- Data appendix: top graphs and a CSV of key metrics.
- Remediation applied and measurable effect (before/after numbers).
- Recommendations (short-term / long-term).
- Owner and ETA for follow-up (if kernel ticket created).
sections.heading: Rollback playbook (if remediation regresses production)

sections.body:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025

Appendix: Useful commands and example outputs

- DCGM sample query (JSON):

```bash
dcgmi dmon -e 250 -s 60 -o /tmp/dcgmi-gpu-pool-2.json
```

- Example PromQL for kernel queue p95:

```promql
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_queue_length_bucket[5m])) by (le, gpu))
```

- CUPTI/Perfetto capture invocation (example):

```bash
perfetto --txt -c /etc/perfetto/prod-gpu-capture.cfg --out /tmp/perfetto-gpu-$(date +%s).trace
```
sections.heading: Related pages

sections.body:
- 2025-11-10: Document created (initial draft).
- 2026-01-15: Added kernel mapper tuning snippet and PromQL recipes.
- 2026-02-02: Hardened remediation ordering and clarified ownership/escalation.
sections.heading: Change log

sections.body:
- Integrate audit collector with auto-remediation playbooks (low-risk throttles) once we have robust canary testing.
- Add ML-driven anomaly detection for warp efficiency drop that triggers a lightweight sampler trace.
sections.heading: Notes and future work

sections.body:

- Diego Morales (kernel engineering) — diego@redwood.internal

payload.page_title: Debugging kernel selection and launch config (profiling playbook)

sections.body: This page is the standard playbook for debugging **kernel selection** (v1 and v2) and **GPU launch configuration** in Redwood Serving Runtime.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Capturing kernel selection traces (telemetry + local dumps)
- Reproducing a mis-selection locally with the same inputs
- Comparing candidate kernels apples-to-apples
- Interpreting common GPU/perf counters for prefill vs decode
- Recognizing common failure signatures and the fastest mitigations

**Non-goals:** deep kernel implementation details or architectural rationale (see the design + ADR).

---
sections.heading: It covers

sections.body:
- p95/p99 latency regression after enabling Kernel Auto-Selection v2
- Throughput instability on mixed workloads (short + long prompts)
- Unexpected fallback to a slower “generic” kernel
- GPU-SKU-specific regressions (A100 vs H100 vs L40S, MIG vs non-MIG)
- Suspected nondeterminism (same request → different kernel choice)

---
sections.heading: Use this when you see any of the following

sections.body:
- **Prefill:** processing the prompt/context (usually GEMM-heavy; long-context sensitive)
- **Decode:** token-by-token generation (latency sensitive; typically attention-heavy)
- **Seq bucket:** selector’s coarse regime classification (prefill/decode characteristics + token ranges)
- **Candidate kernels:** kernel implementations compatible with the request + model + GPU SKU
- **Launch config:** CUDA kernel launch parameters and runtime execution path configuration (e.g., split-K, CTA shape, persistent kernels, etc.)

---
sections.heading: Glossary (runtime terms)

sections.body:
1) Identify **what changed**
   - Runtime version (e.g., 1.21 canary)
   - Selector version (v1 vs v2)
   - Driver/CUDA version
   - GPU SKU (including MIG)
   - Model version / quantization profile

2) Pull a single representative **trace**
   - Capture selection telemetry for the request(s)
   - Confirm chosen kernel, seq bucket, and fallback reason (if any)

3) Sanity check feature extraction
   - model_family correct?
   - prefill_tokens/decode_tokens estimates correct?
   - gpu_sku normalized correctly?

4) Compare with a forced kernel baseline
   - Force “known-good” kernel on same GPU SKU
   - Check prefill vs decode deltas; confirm regression is in the suspected phase

5) If customer-impacting
   - Apply runbook mitigation (disable v2 by model/GPU/region or pin kernel)
   - Then continue root-cause analysis offline

---
sections.heading: Quick-start triage checklist (10–15 minutes)

sections.body:
For any debugging thread / ticket, include:
- **Model**: name + version hash (or Redwood model revision)
- **GPU**: sku (normalized), MIG mode (if present), driver + CUDA
- **Workload**: prompt tokens, max output tokens, streaming on/off, typical concurrency
- **Selector**: v1/v2 enabled, allowlist/denylist state, forced kernel overrides
- **Evidence**: 1–3 trace IDs and a short time window to query dashboards
sections.heading: Data you should collect (minimum)

sections.body:
- Nsight Systems (.nsys-rep) for one request
- Nsight Compute report for the dominant kernel (prefill or decode)

---
sections.heading: Recommended extras

sections.body: Kernel selection emits a per-request event (sampled) when telemetry is enabled.
sections.heading: A) Using production telemetry (preferred)

sections.body:
- selector_version (v1 or v2)
- model, model_family
- gpu_sku, driver_version, cuda_version
- prefill_tokens, decode_tokens_est
- seq_bucket
- candidates (compact list)
- chosen_kernel
- fallback_reason (if any)
- decision_hash / determinism_fingerprint

**Recommended query pattern (Hosted/Dedicated):**
- Filter by model + gpu_sku + seq_bucket
- Compare selection distribution before/after the regression window
- Correlate with p95/p99 latency by the same dimensions
sections.heading: What to look for in the event payload

sections.body:
- Sampling is intentionally low by default to control overhead and cardinality.
- If you need more coverage during a canary, coordinate with SRE/Observability to temporarily increase sampling for a narrow allowlist (model + region).
sections.heading: Sampling note

sections.body:
Use the runtime CLI flags to dump the selector’s decision record.

**Common flags (runtime 1.21+):**
- `--kernel-select.v2=0|1` (enable/disable v2)
- `--kernel-select.dump=/path/selector_dump.jsonl` (writes JSONL)
- `--kernel-select.sample-rate=0.0..1.0` (local only; do not use 1.0 in prod)
- `--kernel.force=<kernel_id>` (force a kernel; bypass selection)
- `--kernel-select.dump-candidates=1` (include candidate set; larger output)
- `--kernel-select.determinism-check=1` (assert stable decision_hash for repeated runs)

**Example: dump selection for a single run**
1. Start runtime locally with dumping enabled:
   - `rw-runtime serve --model llama-3.1-70b --kernel-select.v2=1 --kernel-select.dump=/tmp/sel.jsonl --kernel-select.sample-rate=1.0`
2. Send one request (use your normal client or `curl`).
3. Inspect `/tmp/sel.jsonl` and verify:
   - seq_bucket matches expectations
   - chosen_kernel is in candidates
   - fallback_reason is empty

**Expected dump line (shape, example fields):**
- `timestamp`
- `request_id`
- `model`
- `model_family`
- `gpu_sku`
- `driver_version`
- `cuda_version`
- `prefill_tokens`
- `decode_tokens_est`
- `seq_bucket`
- `candidates`
- `chosen_kernel`
- `fallback_reason`
- `selector_version`
- `decision_hash`

(Exact field names can change; treat this as the conceptual contract.)

---
sections.heading: B) Local dump (repro and deep debugging)

sections.body: Goal: reproduce the same decision with the same inputs, then iterate quickly.
sections.heading: Reproducing a mis-selection locally

sections.body:
To avoid false leads, match:
- GPU SKU (and MIG mode)
- Driver + CUDA
- Runtime build (commit hash)
- Model revision and quantization settings
sections.heading: Step 1: Pin the environment

sections.body:
- Prefer the same architecture (e.g., H100 SXM vs H100 PCIe still differs; document it)
- Do not draw firm conclusions from cross-SKU comparisons without a controlled benchmark
sections.heading: If you cannot match GPU SKU exactly

sections.body:
- Use the request payload captured in logs/traces (prompt, params, max_tokens, sampling settings)
- Ensure tokenization is identical (same tokenizer/model revision)
sections.heading: Recommended approach

sections.body:
- Disable unrelated variability (temperature=0, top_p=1) when isolating perf/selection
- Warm the model (at least 10–20 requests) before measuring
sections.heading: Practical tips

sections.body:
Run the same request N times (N=20 is usually sufficient) with:
- `--kernel-select.determinism-check=1`

If the decision_hash changes across runs, skip ahead to **Failure signatures → Nondeterministic selection**.

---
sections.heading: Step 3: Verify determinism

sections.body: Selection regressions are often “real” but can be misattributed due to measurement mistakes.
sections.heading: Comparing kernels (A/B) correctly

sections.body:
1) Choose a workload profile
- Short: prefill ~256–1k tokens, decode ~64–256
- Long-context: prefill 8k–32k tokens, decode small/medium
- Mixed: alternating short and long requests (to stress cache/batching)

2) Compare two conditions on the same host/GPU
- Condition A: selector v2 normal
- Condition B: `--kernel.force=<known_good>` OR selector v1

3) Measure:
- End-to-end latency (p50/p95/p99)
- Prefill time and decode time (if you have phase breakdown)
- Throughput (tokens/sec) at a fixed concurrency
sections.heading: Baseline method

sections.body:
- Keep concurrency and batcher settings fixed.
- Ensure compilation/warmup is not included (or include it consistently in both conditions).
- Watch for “silent” changes: different quantization path, different attention backend, different KV cache policy.
sections.heading: Guardrails

sections.body:
If you suspect selector overhead or frequent kernel switches:
- Use the selector dump to confirm how often the chosen kernel changes for similar requests.
- Measure CPU-side selector time (if exposed) and confirm it is not on the critical path.

---
sections.heading: Identifying kernel switch overhead

sections.body:
- **Nsight Systems (nsys):** timeline, kernel launch frequency, CPU/GPU overlap
- **Nsight Compute (ncu):** kernel-level metrics (occupancy, memory throughput, tensor core utilization)
sections.heading: Tools

sections.body:
- Memory bandwidth saturation + poor L2 hit rate
- Excessive attention-related workspace allocations
- Reduced tensor core utilization (e.g., due to shape mismatch or fallback kernel)
sections.heading: Typical indicators

sections.body:
- Are we using the expected “long-context prefill” kernel variant?
- Did we accidentally select a kernel optimized for decode (small seq) for a large prefill?
- Is the launch config appropriate for the sequence length and head dimension?
sections.heading: What to check

sections.body:
- Increased kernel launch count (too many small kernels)
- Lower occupancy due to small problem sizes or poor scheduling
- Higher CPU overhead per token (scheduling/selector/telemetry)
sections.heading: Typical indicators

sections.body:
- Are we selecting a decode-optimized kernel for short seq?
- Is continuous batching behavior consistent (same batch sizes)?
- Any sign that telemetry sampling is too high (CPU spikes)?

---
sections.heading: What to check

sections.body:
- p50 unchanged, p99 worse
- Only affects large prefill (8k+ tokens)
- Selection traces show a “short/mid” seq bucket for long prompts or an unexpected kernel
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Seq bucket misclassification at bucket boundaries
- Incorrect prefill token estimation (tokenizer mismatch, truncation, or streaming config)
- Missing long-context kernel for the GPU SKU → fallback to generic
sections.heading: Likely causes

sections.body:
1) Confirm `prefill_tokens` and `seq_bucket` in the trace.
2) Force the known-good long-context kernel; verify p99 recovers.
3) If confirmed: add a temporary denylist rule for (model_family, gpu_sku, seq_bucket) and follow the rollback runbook.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- Same instance type shows different sku strings across environments
- Selection differs unexpectedly between “same” GPU hosts
- Fallback_reason mentions “no compatible kernel for SKU”
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- SKU normalization mismatch (cloud naming vs PCI IDs)
- MIG partitions reported as distinct SKUs without mapping
sections.heading: Likely causes

sections.body:
1) Capture raw GPU identifiers (from runtime startup logs).
2) Confirm normalized `gpu_sku` in selection traces.
3) If normalization is wrong, stop: comparisons are invalid until normalized.
4) Workaround: pin kernel or disable v2 on that SKU until mapping is corrected.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- chosen_kernel is a generic or “safe” kernel
- fallback_reason indicates denylist hit or missing kernel
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Known-bad kernel/SKU combo is denied
- Kernel not built/registered for this runtime build + CUDA
- Driver/CUDA guardrail disables a kernel path
sections.heading: Likely causes

sections.body:
1) Read fallback_reason; do not guess.
2) Check known-issues page for that SKU/driver.
3) Validate the kernel registry for the runtime build.
4) If it’s a new driver combo: treat as unsafe until validated; keep fallback.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- decision_hash changes across repeated runs
- kernel choice flips between two candidates without config changes
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Unordered candidate iteration (map/set ordering)
- Floating-point scoring instability (if any scoring exists)
- Hidden dynamic inputs (e.g., scheduler hint updates mid-run)
sections.heading: Likely causes

sections.body:
1) Enable determinism check flag locally.
2) Ensure scheduler hints are fixed for the test (or disable hints input).
3) Capture dumps for multiple runs and diff `candidates` ordering.
4) If confirmed: block rollout for the affected path; determinism is a hard requirement.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- CPU usage increases, minor but broad latency regressions
- Metrics ingestion/backends show increased series counts
- Alerts fire for “metric cardinality” changes
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Sampling too high
- Candidate sets emitted too verbosely
- High-cardinality tags (e.g., request_id) accidentally included
sections.heading: Likely causes

sections.body:
1) Reduce sampling immediately; keep only the dimensions required by the standard.
2) Confirm dashboards still work with reduced detail.
3) Coordinate with Observability for query/panel updates.

---
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
1) **Validate** the regression is real
   - Same GPU SKU, same model rev, same concurrency

2) **Get a trace**
   - Confirm chosen kernel, candidates, seq bucket, fallback reason

3) **Reproduce locally**
   - Dump selector decisions and verify determinism

4) **A/B**
   - Selector v2 vs forced known-good kernel (or v1)

5) **Profile**
   - nsys: timeline and kernel launch patterns
   - ncu: dominant kernel metrics

6) **Mitigate** (if needed)
   - Disable v2 for (model/GPU/region) or pin kernel via runbook

7) **Close the loop**
   - Add/update known issue entry
   - If a rule threshold changes, add a regression test case (long-context boundary)

---
sections.heading: Recommended debugging workflow (end-to-end)

sections.body:
- If regression impacts Hosted canary or Dedicated pools: page **Runtime Oncall** and coordinate with **SRE** for rollback authority.
- Kernel selection logic issues: **Yuki Sato** (owner), **Hiro Tanaka** (kernels lead)
- Tail latency / observability issues: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Allison Grant**
- Perf suite additions / reproductions: **Marcus Reed**, **Claire Dubois**, **Sahana Iyer**

---
sections.heading: Escalation and ownership

sections.body:
- For a fixed (model, gpu_sku, seq_bucket), chosen_kernel distribution is stable over time.
- p95/p99 deltas are within rollout budgets, with no long-context outliers.
- decision_hash is stable (deterministic) given identical inputs.
- Telemetry provides enough context to explain every fallback without additional logging.

---
sections.heading: Appendix: What “good” looks like

sections.body:
- Runtime version / commit:
- Environment (Hosted/Dedicated/Private):
- Model + revision:
- GPU SKU + MIG + driver/CUDA:
- Selector: v1/v2, allowlist/denylist state, forced kernel?
- Workload: prefill tokens, decode tokens, concurrency, streaming:
- Trace IDs (1–3):
- Observed: (p95/p99 change, throughput change)
- Expected:
- Selection details: chosen_kernel, candidates, seq_bucket, fallback_reason:
- Mitigation applied (if any):
sections.heading: Copy/paste into a ticket

payload.page_title: edge-case-kernel-flake-hunting-and-bisect-playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook documents a pragmatic, reproducible process for identifying, diagnosing, and safely remediating intermittent ("flake") regressions originating in the serving runtime kernel or scheduler layers. It emphasizes low-risk bisecting, deterministic trace capture, and guarded rollouts with automated rollback hooks. This is intended for runtime oncall, kernel engineers, and performance SREs.

Why this is necessary:
- Flaky kernel behavior (slow kernels that sometimes spike, rare preemption races, transient memory corruption, or sporadic NVLink stalls) is one of the highest-impact sources of nondeterministic tail latency and customer-facing errors.
- These issues are often subtle and require a structured approach: isolate scope, reproduce at scale, collect causal telemetry, and perform a controlled binary/config bisect.

Scope and ownership:
- Applies to: kernel modules, kernel-level scheduler adapters, dispatcher, and low-level kernel-to-accelerator handoffs.
- Owners: kernel-and-scheduling team (primary), eng-serving-runtime oncall (secondary), runtime-observability (telemetry).

Alerting and signal triage (first 15 minutes):
1) Triage signals to confirm flakiness vs. sustained regression:
   - Check tail-latency dashboards and the request heatmap for cohort spikes.
   - Look for correlated spikes in kernel-duration, kernel-restarts, and GPU-queue-depth metrics.
2) Apply quick filters to rule out environmental noise:
   - Node-level thermal throttling (node.thermal.throttle > 0).
   - Cloud spot eviction or host reboots in the same time window.
3) If signal persists, declare a "flake investigation" and assign a lead.

Reproduction checklist (ordered):
1) Narrow to a small reproducible workload. Prefer a request-corpus of 10–100 requests that historically triggered spikes.
2) Create a dedicated test cohort on a shadow fleet segment with identical runtime flags.
3) Use the lightweight stress harness (see commands below) to replay requests with controlled concurrency and seed for randomness.
4) If unreproducible on shadow, collect a multi-hour capture from production ring buffer (dependency: telemetry retention > 6h).

Commands and utilities (examples):
- Start deterministic replay harness (local):
  ./tools/replay_harness --corpus=/data/corpora/flaky-trigger.json --concurrency=8 --seed=1234 --duration=600

- Kernel trace collector (node):
  sudo /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-trace-capture --duration 120 --filters="kernel_id=kv_shard|scheduler" --out=/tmp/trace-$(date +%s).tar.gz

- Lightweight GPU queue snapshot:
  /opt/runtime/bin/gpu-queue-snapshot --gpu 0 --samples 100 --out /tmp/queue.json

Deterministic bisect protocol (binary/config):
Goal: identify the smallest change (git revision or config knob) that converts sporadic behavior into deterministic failure.
Preconditions: a reproducible harness that fails at least 10% of attempts under baseline.

Steps:
1) Create a minimal experiment matrix with these axes: kernel binary (N revisions), scheduler config (3–5 knob permutations), quantization/precision path (fp16/int8/quantized fallback).
2) Start with binary-only bisect: if recent kernel commits exist in the window, perform a binary bisection across commits using the harness.
   - Use git-bisect-style automation integrated with CI: see /infra/ci/kernel-bisect-runner.
   - Run 30 harness iterations per candidate revision; record pass/fail rate.
3) If binary bisect is inconclusive, move to config bisect: toggle single knobs per iteration (batch slicing, preemption-window-ms, async-handoff-enable).
4) For nondeterministic outcomes, apply statistical stopping rules: stop when 95% confidence that candidate is different from baseline (binomial test with alpha=0.05).

Telemetry to collect for each candidate run (minimum):
- kernel.duration_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- kernel.context-switches (per-shard)
- kernel.preempt-mismatch-count
- gpu.dispatch-latency_ms
- kvcache.hit-rate
- node.thermal.throttle
- process.core-dumps (if present)

Trace artifact cataloging (naming and meta):
- Use standardized artifact names for trace uploads: flake-{ticket}-{host}-{rev}-{ts}.tgz
- Attach a JSON meta file with keys: "rev", "config", "workload_signature", "seed", "pass_rate", "owner". Example file contents (one-line JSON):
  {"rev":"abc123","config":"preempt=25,async_handoff=on","workload_signature":"chat:short-avg-32","seed":"1234","pass_rate":"0.2","owner":"aisha"}

Causal analysis workflow (after candidate identified):
1) Correlate kernel trace events with scheduler logs and GPU queue snapshots to find temporal overlap windows.
2) Graph event waterfall using the trace-annotator tool:
   ./tools/trace-annotator --input trace.tgz --events kernel.schedule,kernel.preempt,gpu.dispatch --out annotated.html
3) Look for these common failure modes:
   - Preemption races where a higher priority job preempts but leaves stale kernel metadata.
   - Asynchronous handoff timeouts where a kernel path assumes GPU-side state that was evicted.
   - Tiny window allocator exhaustion leading to occasionally failed allocations.

Risk-controlled remediation checklist (patch or config rollout):
1) If fix is a configuration toggle, prefer staged rollout via the rollout-controller with 5% -> 25% -> 100% steps and automated rollback on error budget breach (>2x baseline p99). 2) If fix requires binary change, publish a canary build to dedicated canary pool with the same workload as reproduce harness. Observe for 24h under 2x traffic.
3) Ensure oncall runbooks and quick-rollback artifacts are present before a larger rollout.
4) For kernel patches touching allocator or preemption code, schedule code review and run the special verification suite (see table below).

Verification test matrix (run before full rollout):
| Test suite | Purpose | Min iterations |
|---|---|---|
| deterministic-replay | reproduce failure mode | 100 |
| thermal-stress | rule out thermal interaction | 20 |
| multi-tenant-noise | surface contention issues | 50 |
| long-tail-latency | measure p99 stability over 12h | 1 (12h run) |

Escalation and postmortem policy:
- If the fix increases incidents or fails canary: revert the change immediately and open an incident ticket.
- Required postmortem for any customer-facing outage or >4h degradation: include timeline, bisect artifacts, root cause hypothesis, and action items.

Instrumentation and platform changes recommended after a frequent flake (owner = runtime-observability):
- Add a lightweight deterministic request tagging header so traces from reproduce runs are trivially filterable.
- Increase trace sampler for failing cohorts to 100% for the first 24 hours after detection.
- Add a synthetic monitor that runs the reproduce harness every 6 hours and emits a pass/fail metric.

Quick reference: common commands and locations
- Replay harness: /opt/runtime/tooling/replay_harness
- Trace uploads (S3): s3://redwood-runtime/flake-traces/
- Bisect runner: infra/ci/kernel-bisect-runner (internal CI job)

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Primary: kernel-and-scheduling@redwood.com (pager), lead: Owen Patel
- Observability: runtime-observability@redwood.com, lead: Hannah Lee
- Oncall: eng-serving-runtime-oncall rotation (see rota)

Appendix A — Statistical stopping rule (short):
- Model each harness run as Bernoulli trial (success = no spike). When comparing baseline pass-rate p0 and candidate pass-rate p1, stop when p-value (two-sided) < 0.05 and effect size >= 10 percentage points, or after 200 trials. Use Fisher exact/binomial test depending on counts.

Appendix B — Example incident timeline (abridged):
1) 2026-01-22 03:08 UTC: tail-latency p99 spikes from 120ms -> 420ms (detected by synthetic).
2) 03:12: declare flake investigation, assign lead.
3) 03:28: reproduce locally with deterministic harness (seed 742).
4) 05:10: binary bisect identifies commit abc123 as candidate (pass rate drop 78% -> 22%).
5) 06:30: roll forward small config toggle to canary (5%). Observability shows immediate improvement; schedule full rollout after verification.

Related pages and artifacts:
- See the reproduction corpus index: /data/corpora/flake-corpus-index.csv
- Trace annotator docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/tools/trace-annotator-docs

Revision history:
- 2024-11-05: initial draft by Aisha Kapoor
- 2025-06-18: added statistical stopping rule and artifact naming standard
- 2026-02-10: updated verification matrix and expanded telemetry list
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)

sections.body:
This playbook describes how to reproduce a perf-suite result and capture the artifacts needed to attribute changes (runtime, scheduler, kernels, environment). It is intended for:
- Investigating perf-canary regressions (PR-level, nightly, or release-branch).
- Explaining deltas between baseline runs (Q1 2026 “golden” anchor) and candidate changes.
- Producing consistent traces/logs that can be shared across Runtime, Kernels, and SRE.

This page focuses on *how to profile* (traces, kernel timelines, scheduler logs) rather than *what workloads to run*. For workload definitions and required metrics, see the baseline plan and representative suite pages.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
For any investigated run, attach or link the following artifacts (even if you also have dashboards):
1) Run manifest JSON (per ADR-0172) with *all* environment capture enabled.
2) Results JSON/CSV (p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, throughput, plus variance statistics if available).
3) Scheduler log bundle:
   - Queue wait time distribution
   - Batch assembly time distribution
   - Batch size histogram
   - Load-shed/drop counters (if any)
   - Correlation IDs / request IDs for trace alignment
4) Kernel selection debug dump (sampled) with fallback reasons (if any).
5) Nsight Systems (nsys) trace for at least one representative interval.
6) Optional but recommended: Nsight Compute (ncu) capture for the top 1–3 kernels (only when kernel-level regression is suspected).

---
sections.heading: What “good” looks like (minimum artifact set)

sections.body:
To avoid “apples to oranges,” ensure the profiling run uses the same boundaries as the perf suite metrics:
- **TTFT (Time To First Token)**: measured at the server boundary: request admitted → first token emitted to server streaming layer. Excludes client read/parse time.
- **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**: measured at the server boundary for decode tokens only. Excludes prefill; excludes client overhead.
- **Throughput**: server-side tokens/sec or requests/sec depending on endpoint mode.

If you must deviate (e.g., reproducing a customer report with client-side timings), label the run explicitly as “client-inclusive” and do not compare to baseline dashboards without adjustment.

---
sections.heading: Measurement boundaries (so traces match reported metrics)

sections.body:
Before profiling, confirm the baseline anchor for comparison:
- Runtime git SHA / tag (baseline)
- Benchmark harness version
- Model revision (weights + tokenizer)
- Scheduler profile and kernel-selection ruleset
- Region and GPU SKU

If you are unsure which build is the Q1 baseline anchor, check the baseline freeze thread and the baseline run tracker.
sections.heading: A. Confirm you are targeting the same baseline anchor

sections.body:
These steps are required for “baseline-comparable” profiling runs:
1) Use a dedicated benchmarking node (no co-tenancy).
2) Lock GPU application clocks where permitted by fleet policy.
3) Pin CPU governor to performance.
4) Ensure consistent container image and driver/CUDA versions.
5) Run standardized warmup (see below).

If any variance-reduction step cannot be applied, mark the run as “non-baseline-comparable” in the run label and expect higher noise.
sections.heading: B. Reduce variance (required for attribution)

sections.body:
Warmup reduces first-run variance from model load, JIT/compilation caches, allocator behavior, and KV cache initialization.
- Warmup duration: 3–5 minutes per (model, GPU, workload mode)
- Warmup workload: same request shape as the measured workload, but with lower concurrency
- Discard warmup metrics; only analyze traces taken after warmup completes

---
sections.heading: C. Warmup standard (required)

sections.body: Consistent naming is required so engineers can drill down from dashboard → manifest → traces.
sections.heading: Run labeling and naming conventions

sections.body:
Use the following run_id format (single line, no spaces):
`perfq1_2026/<workload>/<model>/<region>/<gpu>/<runtime_sha>/<harness_ver>/<timestamp_utc>/<run_variant>`
sections.heading: Run ID format

sections.body:
- `perfq1_2026/chat_streaming/llama3_1_70b/us-east/h100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T21-14-08Z/cold_cache`
- `perfq1_2026/long_prefill/qwen2_5_72b/eu-west/a100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T23-40-51Z/warm_cache`
sections.heading: Examples

sections.body:
Include at least these tags as part of the run_variant suffix:
- `cold_cache` or `warm_cache` (we report both; do not mix)
- `baseline_comparable` or `non_baseline_comparable`
sections.heading: Required run_variant tags

sections.body:
- `kernel_pin_<name>` (if pinning a kernel)
- `scheduler_override_<name>` (if changing scheduler knobs)
- `client_inclusive` (only if using client-side TTFT)

---
sections.heading: Optional tags (use when relevant)

sections.body: > The exact CLI flags may vary by harness version; the intent is to capture the same artifact set. If a flag below doesn’t exist in your harness build, file an issue in benchmark-lab and note it in the run summary.
sections.heading: Step-by-step: reproduce a perf suite run with profiling enabled

sections.body:
1. Start from the manifest used by the baseline run (from dashboards or the run tracker).
2. Copy it and increment `manifest_version` only if required by schema changes.
3. Verify these fields are present and accurate:
   - Model identifier + revision
   - Hardware: GPU SKU, GPU count, MIG settings (if any)
   - Region/zone
   - Runtime build SHA + build type
   - Driver/CUDA/Triton versions
   - Scheduler profile name + knobs
   - Kernel selection ruleset version
   - Workload seed and distribution parameters
   - Cache mode (cold/warm)

**Output:** `run_manifest.json`
sections.heading: 1) Create (or locate) the canonical manifest

sections.body:
- GPU info (nvidia-smi dump)
- Driver/CUDA versions
- Container image digest
- Host kernel version
- CPU model, NUMA topology summary
- Power/clock settings (if available)

**Sanity check:** ensure the manifest “env” section is populated before you proceed. Missing env capture is a common reason runs can’t be compared later.
sections.heading: Enable full environment capture in the harness

sections.body:
Run warmup using the same workload generator but with reduced concurrency.
- Confirm warmup completes without errors (no OOM, no load-shed unless expected).
- Confirm steady-state GPU utilization.

**Output:** warmup logs (attach if investigating stability issues).
sections.heading: 3) Run standardized warmup

sections.body:
- Scheduler instrumentation enabled (queue wait, batch assembly time, batch size distributions).
- Kernel selection debug dump enabled (sampled is fine; 1–5% sampling is typical).

**Outputs:**
- `results.json` (metrics)
- `scheduler_metrics.jsonl` or equivalent
- `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`
sections.heading: Run the measured workload with

sections.body:
Capture nsys for a representative steady-state window. Recommendations:
- Trace window: 30–90 seconds during steady state.
- Capture CUDA + NVTX ranges.
- Minimize trace overhead: avoid tracing the full run unless necessary.
sections.heading: 5) Capture an Nsight Systems (nsys) trace (required for attribution)

sections.body:
- If you control the runtime build, ensure key phases emit NVTX ranges:
  - request admitted
  - queue wait
  - batch assembly
  - prefill
  - decode
  - stream flush
- If ranges are missing, still capture the trace; file an issue for missing NVTX markers.

**Output:** `trace.nsys-rep` (or equivalent).
sections.heading: Operational guidance

sections.body:
- A regression correlates with a kernel selection change, or
- nsys shows kernel time dominated by one/few kernels, or
- Kernel-level variance is suspected (e.g., new fused attention path).
sections.heading: Use ncu only when

sections.body:
- Profile a single process and short window to keep overhead manageable.
- Focus on top kernels by time; avoid broad “collect everything” profiles.

**Output:** `kernel_profile.ncu-rep` (or equivalent).
sections.heading: Guidelines

sections.body:
For every run you investigate, create a short run summary (Confluence comment, Slack triage thread, or ticket) that includes:
- run_id
- manifest link
- results link
- trace links
- “what changed” hypothesis
- whether the run is baseline-comparable

---
sections.heading: 7) Upload artifacts and link them in the run summary

sections.body: Attach links (preferred) rather than pasting raw files into Confluence.
sections.heading: Artifact checklist and where to find them

sections.body:
- Run manifest: `run_manifest.json`
- Results: `results.json` (or results CSV exported by harness)
- Scheduler logs: `scheduler_metrics.jsonl`
- Kernel selection dump: `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`
- Nsight Systems trace: `trace.nsys-rep`
sections.heading: Required artifacts

sections.body:
- Full runtime logs for the measured window (with correlation IDs)
- GPU clock/thermal readings during the run
- Harness configuration file used to launch

---
sections.heading: Recommended context

sections.body:
When investigating TTFT p99 or TPOT p99 changes, align the following:
1) Pick a set of request IDs from the tail (p99 cohort) in the results export.
2) Locate those request IDs in scheduler logs:
   - Identify whether tail comes from queue wait, batch assembly, prefill, decode, or stream flush.
3) In the nsys trace, confirm:
   - GPU busy/idle patterns during the tail interval
   - Kernel timeline changes (different kernels, different durations)
   - CPU-side stalls that correlate with queue wait or dispatch
4) Cross-check kernel selection dump:
   - Ensure the expected kernel regime is selected for the sequence length bins
   - Investigate fallback reasons (often the root cause of step-function regressions)
sections.heading: How to align traces with reported metrics

sections.body:
- **Higher TTFT p99 with stable throughput:** often queueing/backpressure or batch-assembly changes.
- **Higher TPOT with stable TTFT:** often decode kernel changes, KV cache behavior, or reduced overlap.
- **Lower throughput with higher TTFT:** often saturation, contention, or poor batching efficiency.

---
sections.heading: Common interpretations

sections.body: - Server-side metrics look stable, but external client TTFT inflates.
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Confirm you’re using server-boundary TTFT.
- Ensure streaming pacing is server-driven in the harness (avoid client read throttling).
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body: - Repeated runs differ by more than the regression threshold; p99 swings without code changes.
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Verify clock locking and isolation.
- Increase sample size.
- Ensure warmup was performed.
- Check for node-level noise: thermal throttling, background jobs, noisy neighbor.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body: - Step-function slowdown at particular sequence lengths.
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Inspect kernel selection dump for fallback reasons.
- Compare to the kernel selection matrix for expected regimes.
- Consider pinning the baseline kernel temporarily for diagnosis; label run_variant accordingly.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body: - Elevated drop counters, timeouts, or long queue wait.
sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body:
- Confirm concurrency targets match workload spec.
- Validate backpressure thresholds (baseline vs overridden).
- Use scheduler metrics to determine whether overload is admission control vs batch assembly.

---
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
Open a Linear issue (or escalate to perf triage) when any of the following are true:
- Regression is reproducible in baseline-comparable conditions.
- Kernel selection changed unexpectedly vs matrix.
- Scheduler metrics show a clear regime shift (queue wait, batch size collapse) not explained by workload.
- Trace indicates a new stall in a known critical path (prefill/decode overlap, KV cache operations).
sections.heading: When to open a ticket vs continue debugging

sections.body:
- run_id(s)
- baseline comparison run_id(s)
- links to manifest/results/traces
- suspected component owner (scheduler/kernels/runtime infra)

---
sections.heading: Include in the ticket

sections.body:
- Benchmark harness & methodology: Rina Kobayashi, Claire Dubois
- Scheduler instrumentation: Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel selection & kernel timelines: Hiro Tanaka
- SRE benchmarking fleet stability: Sean Gallagher

If you encounter missing instrumentation (NVTX ranges absent, logs not emitted, schema fields missing), file an issue against the appropriate repo and link it in the run summary so the next investigation is faster.
sections.heading: Primary owners

payload.page_title: Known issue: Tensor-parallel hangs under sustained load

sections.body: Tensor-parallel (TP) replicas can intermittently **hang (no forward progress)** under sustained, mixed workloads (prefill + decode, long-context, bursty concurrency). This typically presents as **streaming responses stalling** and eventually **request timeouts**. In the worst case, one or more GPUs appear “wedged” until the replica is drained/restarted.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Observable symptoms and common signatures
- Affected configurations (models, TP sizes, hardware)
- How to detect and confirm a TP stall
- Recommended mitigations (operational + config)
- Fix status by runtime version and feature flags

> If you are actively in an incident: jump to **Immediate mitigations** and then follow **Triage**.

---
sections.heading: This page documents

sections.body:
- **Customer impact:** Streaming completions stall; end-users see long hangs then timeouts. Enterprise Dedicated accounts are most affected due to higher sustained concurrency.
- **Operational impact:** Autoscaler thrash (p99 latency spikes trigger scale-up; wedged replicas never recover), elevated error rates, Sev1 potential.
- **Cost impact:** Stalled replicas waste GPU capacity and increase retry/duplicate compute.

---
sections.heading: Impact / why we care

sections.body:
- Streaming response starts and then stops emitting tokens mid-decode.
- Requests remain in-flight until client timeout (commonly 60–300s depending on route).
- Retry storms (client SDK retries or application-level retries) amplify load.
sections.heading: External (API / client-facing)

sections.body:
- **No tokens produced** while GPU utilization may remain non-zero or drop unexpectedly.
- One TP rank appears stuck while others continue to enqueue work (or also stop).
- NCCL may not throw an explicit error; hangs can be “silent” without async error handling.
sections.heading: Internal (replica-level)

sections.body:
We currently bucket stalls into these high-level signatures (see `runtime.tp_stall_reason` below):
1. **collective_wait**: rank waiting for NCCL collective completion.
2. **collective_mismatch**: collective ordering divergence across ranks (often manifests as silent wait).
3. **scheduler_starvation**: collectives not scheduled fairly under prefill-heavy batching.
4. **stream_sync_gap**: CUDA stream/event ordering issue around NCCL boundary.
5. **kv_compaction_divergence**: KV cache compaction/fragmentation causes rank-side divergence.
6. **cancelled_stream_deadlock**: client disconnect/cancellation leaves ranks in inconsistent step state.

---
sections.heading: Common failure signatures (taxonomy)

sections.body: This issue has been observed most reliably under the following conditions.
sections.heading: Affected configurations

sections.body:
- Mixed prompt lengths (high variance) + streaming decode
- Long context (8k–32k) + high concurrent requests
- Bursty arrival patterns (spikes causing deep scheduler queues)
- Prefill-heavy traffic interleaved with ongoing decodes
sections.heading: Workload characteristics

sections.body:
- **Dedicated:** most common due to steady saturation and strict p99 expectations.
- **Hosted:** seen in a smaller number of high-throughput routes during peak bursts.
sections.heading: Deployment modes

sections.body:
| Category | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Large dense, long-context | Llama-70B class, Qwen-72B class | Higher risk when TP=4/8 and context > 8k |
| MoE models | Mixtral 8x7B class | Sensitive to scheduling/fairness under mixed prefill/decode |
| Any model with aggressive batching | Any high-throughput route | Risk increases with deep queues and long prefill batches |
sections.heading: Models and TP sizes (most affected)

sections.body:
| Hardware | Topologies seen | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A100 80GB | NVLink intra-node | Most reproductions and customer reports |
| H100 80GB | NVLink intra-node | Also observed; typically at higher throughput |
| PCIe-only multi-GPU | Mixed | Less common in production; higher sensitivity to comms latency |
sections.heading: Hardware / topology

sections.body:
- Observed most often on **runtime 1.18.x** in the presence of CUDA graph capture + mixed workloads.
- Some signatures also present on early **1.19.0 canaries** prior to watchdog + ordering hardening.

---
sections.heading: Runtime versions

sections.body: - See: **TP stall and timeout dashboard** (Confluence: `tp-stall-and-timeout-dashboard`).
sections.heading: Dashboards

sections.body:
> Metric names reflect the current standards agreed with SRE; older versions may differ.

1) **Per-rank heartbeat**
- `runtime_tp_rank_heartbeat_seconds{replica_id, tp_rank, model, cluster}`
- Signal: heartbeats stop updating for one or more ranks.
- Rule of thumb: **gap > 10s** during active traffic is suspicious; **gap > 30s** is a likely stall.

2) **Stall reason counters**
- `runtime_tp_stall_reason_total{reason, model, tp_size, cluster}`
- Watch for spikes in `collective_wait`, `scheduler_starvation`, `cancelled_stream_deadlock`.

3) **In-flight collective counters**
- `runtime_nccl_inflight_collectives{replica_id, tp_rank, collective}`
- Signal: counter remains >0 with no progress (and heartbeat gap).

4) **Scheduler pressure indicators**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{replica_id, queue}`
- `runtime_scheduler_prefill_decode_ratio{replica_id}`
- Signal: queue depth grows while decode throughput collapses.

5) **Customer-visible indicators**
- `gateway_request_timeout_total{route, model}`
- `gateway_streaming_disconnect_total{route, model}`
- `request_p99_latency_ms{route, model}`
sections.heading: Key metrics (authoritative)

sections.body:
Look for structured fields (availability depends on runtime version):
- `tp_stall_detected=true`
- `tp_rank=<int>` and `tp_size=<int>`
- `stall_reason=<enum>`
- `inflight_collectives=<int>`
- `last_progress_ms=<int>`
sections.heading: Logs (what to grep)

sections.body: Use only for time-boxed windows due to verbosity/perf impact. Coordinate with SRE (see INT: enable extra NCCL debug logging).
sections.heading: NCCL debug (use with care)

sections.body:
- `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1`
- `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN`
- `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL`

Do NOT leave `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` enabled broadly on production Dedicated clusters.

---
sections.heading: Suggested minimal settings for targeted capture

sections.body: These mitigations prioritize restoring service and preventing global GPU wedging.
sections.heading: Immediate mitigations (incident-safe)

sections.body:
- Drain the affected replica(s) at the orchestrator level (preferred) rather than waiting for recovery.
- If multiple replicas show heartbeat gaps, drain in a staggered fashion to avoid full capacity loss.
sections.heading: 1) Drain/replace suspect replicas

sections.body:
Recommended temporary caps (starting point; adjust per model/hardware):
- Reduce `tp.max_concurrency_per_replica` by **30–50%**
- Reduce `max_batch_prefill_tokens` (or equivalent) by **25–40%**
- Prefer limiting **prefill batch growth** over decode to preserve streaming responsiveness
sections.heading: 2) Reduce concurrency and/or batch size (fastest risk reduction)

sections.body:
Depending on runtime version and flags, consider:
- Disable CUDA graphs for TP decode on affected routes:
  - `runtime.tp.cuda_graphs_decode.enabled=false`
- Enable conservative stream/event synchronization around NCCL:
  - `runtime.tp.nccl_stream_sync_hardening=on`
sections.heading: 3) Disable high-risk execution paths (if available)

sections.body:
If the watchdog feature is available in your runtime build, enabling it can prevent indefinite hangs:
- `runtime.tp_watchdog.enabled=true`
- `runtime.tp_watchdog.timeout_ms=<workload-specific>` (see below)

> Watchdog enables **controlled abort + replica drain** semantics instead of indefinite waits. This will increase error counts during true stalls but improves overall availability.
sections.heading: 4) Enable watchdog + safe abort (where supported)

sections.body:
- If stall signals are present, enable overload protection to **reject/redirect new requests** away from the wedged replica pool.
- Prefer fallback to a compatible model variant/region if configured for Dedicated/Hosted.

---
sections.heading: 5) Load shedding / routing fallback (platform-level)

sections.body: For clusters with frequent TP stall history, keep these guardrails enabled until runtime 1.19.2+ is fully deployed.
sections.heading: Recommended default mitigations (non-incident)

sections.body:
| Guardrail | Recommendation | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency cap | Set conservative `tp.max_concurrency_per_replica` | Reduces scheduler pressure and mixed-step divergence risk |
| Prefill batch cap | Limit `max_batch_prefill_tokens` | Prevents prefill-heavy batches from starving collectives/decodes |
| Async error handling | `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1` | Surfaces errors sooner; reduces silent waits |
| Stream sync hardening | Enable if perf impact acceptable | Avoids event/stream ordering gaps around collectives |
| Watchdog | Enable with staged rollout | Converts indefinite hang into bounded failure + recovery |
sections.heading: Configuration guardrails

sections.body:
Use model/workload-specific defaults; avoid overly aggressive thresholds that create false positives under long-context.
- Small/medium (≤13B dense): start at **8–12s**
- Large dense (≥70B) TP=4/8: start at **15–25s**
- Long-context (≥16k): start at **25–40s**
sections.heading: Watchdog timeout guidance

sections.body:
1) Canary one cluster/route
2) Validate stall detection + error rate impact
3) Expand to Dedicated
4) Expand to Hosted

---
sections.heading: Always stage changes

sections.body:
Follow the detailed steps in the playbook (Confluence: `tp-stall-triage-playbook`). Quick checklist:

1) **Confirm customer symptom**
- Streaming stuck mid-response, elevated timeouts, p99 jump.

2) **Check TP heartbeat gaps**
- Identify impacted `replica_id` and `tp_rank`.

3) **Correlate with in-flight collectives**
- `runtime_nccl_inflight_collectives` stuck >0 indicates comms boundary involvement.

4) **Check scheduler pressure**
- Queue depth rising while throughput drops suggests scheduler starvation component.

5) **Search logs for stall reason**
- Confirm `stall_reason` and `last_progress_ms`.

6) **Mitigate**
- Drain replica(s) and apply caps/flags.

7) **Capture artifacts** (only if safe)
- Minimal NCCL WARN logs
- Trace IDs for representative stuck requests
- Replica runtime logs around the stall window

---
sections.heading: Triage checklist (confirming a TP hang)

sections.body: This is an active reliability initiative tracked in Linear: **ENG-4821**.
sections.heading: Fix status / roadmap

sections.body:
| Area | Status | References |
|---|---|---|
| Heartbeat + stall reason tagging | Landed | PR-21834; dashboard panels in observability pack PR-412 |
| Scheduler fairness / collective ordering guardrails | Landed | PR-21841; mitigates `scheduler_starvation` and ordering divergence |
| NCCL stream/event sync hardening | Landed (feature-flagged) | PR-21853; evaluate perf impact per model |
| Watchdog + safe abort + replica drain | Landed (feature-flagged) | PR-21860; ADR-0127 defines semantics |
| KV cache compaction safety | Landed | PR-21866; targets `kv_compaction_divergence` |
| Cancelled streaming deadlock fix | Landed | PR-21890; targets disconnect-triggered stalls |
| Improved NCCL error surfacing | In rollout | PR-21912; improves customer-facing diagnostics |
| Load shed on TP stall signal | In rollout | PR-21875 |
sections.heading: Fixes delivered / in-flight

sections.body:
| Runtime version | Guidance |
|---|---|
| ≤ 1.18.7 | Higher risk. Keep concurrency/prefill caps. Prefer disabling CUDA graphs for TP decode on affected routes. Drain-on-stall is primary recovery. |
| 1.19.0–1.19.1 | Use only with watchdog and stream sync hardening flags in canary first. Validate stall reasons and noise. |
| 1.19.2+ | Target stable baseline for Dedicated + high-throughput Hosted. Keep monitoring; reduce guardrails only after 2+ weeks without stall alerts on target workloads. |
sections.heading: Version guidance (operational)

sections.body:
- Dedicated-first rollout with explicit go/no-go gates: see Linear **ENG-4829**.
- Canary success metrics:

payload.page_title: On‑Call Rapid Investigation Cheatsheet — Serving Runtime

sections.body:
Purpose

This one-page cheatsheet is designed for first responders on the serving-runtime oncall rotation. It emphasizes fast, high-confidence checks to determine whether a user-visible degradation is: 1) a routing/capacity incident, 2) a kernel or accelerator-level regression, 3) a model/quantization quality issue, or 4) a networking/storage problem. Use this as the initial investigation path to minimize mean time to mitigation (MTTM).

When to use

- Any alert with SLO impact: 95th/99th token latency breach, error rate spike > 1% absolute, or token cost anomaly.
- Customer-reported failures affecting multiple tenants or a Dedicated pool.
- Sudden increase in timeouts, streaming truncations, or model-variant fallbacks.

Quick triage checklist (1–10 minutes)

1) Validate user-facing signal
   - Confirm whether the symptom is global or cohort-specific (hosted vs Dedicated vs Private).
   - Check primary dashboards: "Routes SLO Overview" and "Token Latency by Model Variant" for immediate spikes.

2) Confirm impact scope
   - Isolated to one region? One model? One capacity pool?
   - Look at per-route and per-tenant panels. If only one tenant -> follow customer escalation playbook.

3) Surface network and infra alarms
   - Fast check on infra alerts: node reboots, GPU watchdogs, NVLink errors, cloud network flaps.
   - If there are node-level alerts, mark as likely infra and contact infra-sre.

4) Kernel / scheduling symptoms
   - Identify: concurrent kernel queue growth, long queue times, repeated preemption events.
   - If kernel queue depth correlates with latency, apply admission-control throttle (see Temporary Mitigation).

5) Model & quantization fallbacks
   - Check model swap events and fallback logs: "model_swap_reason" and "quantize_fallback" tags in traces.
   - Correlate recent deployments/rollouts to timing of incident.

6) Caching and KV warmup
   - Look for high miss rates on KV cache and cold-start traces. If a mass warmup is in progress, expect transient latency as caches populate.

Immediate data sources (quick links)

- Observability dashboards: /dashboards/runtime/routes-slo-overview, /dashboards/runtime/kernel-queue, /dashboards/runtime/kvcache-hitrate
- Tracing: Jaeger/Tempo -> Search by trace tags: service=runtime, event=dispatch|kernel|evict, model=<name>
- Logs: central-log (fluentd) queries: "level>=WARN AND (kernel OR eviction OR model_swap)" within last 15m
- Metric queries (Graphite/Prometheus):
  - runtime_dispatch_queue_length{pool="<pool>"}
  - kernel_execution_time_seconds{kernel="attention"}
  - kvcache_hit_rate{shard="*"}
  - per_route_error_rate{route="<route>"}

Fast instrumentation queries (copy-paste)

- Prometheus: max_over_time(runtime_dispatch_queue_length[5m]) > 100 -> indicates queue saturation
- Prometheus: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_execution_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le,kernel))
- Fluentd (CLI): 
  curl -s "https://logs.redwood.internal/query?q=level%3D%3DWARN%20AND%20(kernel%20OR%20evict%20OR%20model_swap)&from=-15m" | jq -r '.results[] | .message'

Temporary mitigations (safe, quick)

- Canary route diversion: divert 50% of traffic from affected route to the stable model-variant for 10m. Use console -> Routing -> Temporary divert.
- Admission throttles: apply soft admission limit on the afflicted pool to target queue depth <= 50. Command (operator CLI):
  rwdctl pool throttle set --pool-id <pool> --max-queue 50 --reason "oncall-mitigation"
- Increase autoscale burst for Dedicated pool (if allowed by contract) to blunt sudden throughput surges.
- Retry policy tweak: temporarily set per-request client retry to linear backoff 200ms x 3 to reduce concurrent pressure.

When to escalate

- Escalate to Eng-SRE within 10 minutes if any of: GPU watchdogs present, node OOMs, NVLink bit errors, or >2% sustained 5m SLO breach.
- Escalate to Serving Runtime Kernel team if kernel queue growth remains after admission throttles or if kernel execution time 99th increases by >2x.
- Escalate to Model Onboarding if model fallback/quality regressions coincide with a new model rollout.

Escalation contacts (fast list)

- Eng-SRE Pager: +1-555-0100 (pager) / #eng-sre-oncall
- Serving Runtime Kernel team: @kernel-oncall (Slack) / email kernel-oncall@redwood.ai
- Model Onboarding: @model-oncall / model-oncall@redwood.ai

Investigation play (30–90 minutes)

1) Capture canonical traces: use sampling label "oncall-rapid" and capture 200 traces across affected routes.
2) Run head-to-head microbenchmarks for suspect model-variant on a sandbox node to reproduce elevated kernel exec times. Use the local perf harness:
   ./perf/harness/run_bench --model <model> --sequence 512 --batch 1 --profile
3) If KV miss rate high: run kvcache-prefetch for top 10 prefixes for the route:
   rwdctl kvcache prefetch --route <route> --prefix-file top_prefixes.txt
4) If networking suspected: correlate pod/node network metrics (qdisc drops, retransmits) and cross-check cloud VPC flow logs.

Post-incident steps (ownership and timeline)

- Owner: first responder creates incident ticket and assigns to kernel or infra with summary, key traces, metric snapshots, and mitigation steps taken.
- Within 48 hours: postmortem draft with timeline, root cause hypothesis, and proposed corrective actions.
- Within 7 days: implement one low-effort fix (config, throttle change, or alert tuning).

Quick reference table: SLO thresholds and first responder targets

| Signal | SLO | First-responder target | Typical owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 95th token latency (global) | <= 400ms | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 30m | Eng-SRE / Runtime |
| 99th token latency (route) | <= 800ms | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 60m | Runtime Kernel |
| Error rate (per-route) | <= 0.5% | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 30m | Runtime / CS |
| KV cache hit-rate | >= 95% | Identify warmup in 10m | Runtime Ops |

Appendix: Useful snippets and dashboards

- Example trace tags to search:
  - span.tags: {"runtime.phase": "dispatch"}, {"kernel.name":"matmul"}, {"model.variant":"v2-quant"}
- Console actions (UI):
  1. Routing -> Route Health -> Open incident divert
  2. Pools -> Select pool -> Throttles & Autoscale -> Apply temporary change
- Local helper scripts (location): /ops/oncall-scripts/fast_summaries.sh

FAQ / gotchas

- "Why did admission throttle not reduce latency?" -> If kernel execution is the dominant contributor (not queueing), throttling won't help; check kernel_execution_time.
- "We see many model_swap events but no deploys" -> Check quantization autoswitch policy and per-tenant override config.

Owners and maintenance

- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Oncall rotation (team wiki -> rotation calendar).
- Document maintainer: Aisha Patel (serving-runtime-observability team). Please update this cheatsheet after any change to Route SLOs, dispatch instrumentation, or oncall runbook.

Revision history

- 2023-11-15: Initial draft (A. Patel).
- 2024-06-18: Added KV-prefetch quick step and Prometheus queries (D. Morales).
- 2024-12-05: Updated escalation thresholds and automation commands (P. Shah).
