payload.page_title: Runtime experiment registry and reproducibility protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the canonical registry, metadata contract, and execution protocol for all runtime-level experiments at Redwood Inference. It covers experiment registration, required metadata, how to capture and store traces, profiling and benchmarking steps, kernel-scheduler configuration checkpoints, runbook hooks for anomalies, and a release-note template for experiments that affect production runtime behavior.

Why this exists

Teams run many experiments that touch the serving runtime: new kernel rollouts, scheduler-policy changes, KV-cache warmup heuristics, quantization variants, and fallback routing alterations. Without a single registry and reproducible protocol we lose provenance, can’t compare results reliably, and risk unsafe rollouts. This doc is the operational contract for reproducible runtime experimentation.

Scope

- Applies to all experiments that change behavior of services under sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime (runtime-router, kernel-dispatcher, kv-cache, prefetcher, admission-controller).
- Includes lab runs, canary rollouts, and production toggle experiments.
- Excludes purely model-only experiments (those belong to applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding).

Definitions and identifiers

- Experiment ID: EXP-YYYY-NNN (e.g., EXP-2025-042). Unique across the registry.
- Artifact snapshot: git commit + container image digest (sha256).
- Kernel version: runtime kernel semantic tag (e.g., k-2.4.1-hotfix).
- Trace bundle: compressed trace file containing request-level events (trace.jsonl.gz).

Required metadata for registry entry

Every experiment must be registered before execution in the experiments table in the Registry service. Minimum fields:

| Field | Example | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| experiment_id | EXP-2025-042 | Assigned by registry UI/CLI |
| owner | eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team | Team and primary oncall |
| hypothesis | "Reduce p95 by < 10% for short-text gen by enabling kernel-waveform v2" | One-line hypothesis |
| artifacts | repo:infra@abcdef, image:runtime:v2025.09@sha256:... | List of artifact snapshots |
| kernel_version | k-2.4.1-hotfix | Kernel and kernel-extensions |
| quant_flags | q4_0, fp16-cache | Quantization flags used |
| traffic_shape | short-gen:60%, long-gen:40% | Traffic mix for synthetic runs |
| seed_traces | s3://exp-bundles/EXP-2025-042/traces/seed-20250912.jsonl.gz | Location of trace bundle |
| benchmark_suite | evbench-v3 | Name of benchmark harness used |
| rollout_plan | canary-5%-24h -> 25%-48h -> 100% | Rollout steps (if planned) |
| sros | runtime-p95:120ms, runtime-p99:450ms, cpu-util:80% | Target SLOs for the experiment |

Registering an experiment

1. Create registry entry via /internal/experiments API or the Registry UI.
2. Attach artifact snapshots and upload seed trace bundle to S3 using cli:infra exp upload-trace --id EXP-XXXX --file traces/seed.jsonl.gz.
3. Add reviewers and link related playbooks (runbooks or chaos scenarios).

Execution protocol (lab run)

1. Reserve a lab-cluster via infra-tag: runtime-lab-XX for the exact kernel and image.
2. Replay seed traces using the Benchmark Harness (evbench-v3):
   - CLI: evbench run --suite evbench-v3 --trace s3://... --concurrency 8 --out s3://exp-results/EXP-2025-042/
3. Collect traces and profiles:
   - runtime-trace-collector --output /tmp/traces --sample 100%
   - perf-kernel-capture --kernel k-2.4.1-hotfix --out /tmp/kernel-profiles
4. Perform profiling: capture GPU counters, kernel dispatch latencies, KV-cache hit breakdowns.
5. Run the standard benchmark matrix: cold-start (10 retries), warm-start (1000 requests), microbursts (10x peak QPS for 10s).

Kernel-scheduler checkpoint and configuration snapshot

Before making scheduler changes, save a checkpoint record that includes:
- Scheduler policy YAML (scheduler-policy.yaml)
- Priority buckets and token rates
- Admission-controller thresholds (tokens per-second)
- Kernel credit accounting config

Store the checkpoint alongside the experiment under s3://runtime-checkpoints/EXP-YYYY-NNN/. Example snippet (scheduler-policy.yaml):

```yaml
priority_buckets:
  - name: interactive
    weight: 100
    token_rate: 200
  - name: batch
    weight: 20
    token_rate: 20
admission:
  max_concurrent: 250
  preemption_enabled: true
```

Observability checklist (required for canary/production experiments)

- p50/p95/p99 latency dashboards for impacted routes
- Kernel dispatch histogram by request_size and model_variant
- KV-cache hit ratio and warmup curve
- Error budget burn rate alert (notify eng-sre)
- Trace correlation ID consistent between runtime-router and kernel-dispatcher

Runbook hooks and anomaly handling
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- latency p95 > target by > 25% for 10m OR
- error-rate > 0.5% absolute increase OR
- kernel crash rate > 0.1%
sections.heading: If any of the following occur during a canary

sections.body:
1. Pause rollout and scale down canary traffic to 0% (automatic via admission-controller).
2. Trigger experiment incident: tag EXP-XXXX in incident channel #runtime-incidents.
3. Collect last 1h traces and kernel profiles: infra collect-exp-bundle --id EXP-XXXX --window 60m.
4. Engage oncall (owner listed in metadata) and follow the Incident Triage runbook.

Profiling playbook distilled steps

1. Start a controlled replay with sample rate 100% for 1k requests.
2. Capture: compact traces, nvprof counters, kernel-dispatch latency, scheduler token queues.
3. Annotate traces with kernel_version, scheduler-policy hash, and artifact digest.
4. Run causal-attribution script: tools/causal-attrib --before before.tar.gz --after after.tar.gz --out analysis.json

Benchmark mapping and acceptance criteria

- Map each experiment to at least one benchmark in the central suite (evbench-v3, microburst, tail-latency).
- Acceptance: p95 must not regress > 5% for the primary route; p99 regressions require a manual review and explicit approval.

Known-issues capture and linking

When an experiment surfaces a reproducible issue, create an issue entry in the runtime known-issues board and add the following tags: experiment_id, kernel_version, severity (sev1-3). Example known-issue entry fields: [issue_id, experiment_id, summary, repro_steps, traces, owner, mitigation]. Always link the known-issue id back to the experiment registry entry.

Release notes template for experiments that progress to production

- Title: EXP-YYYY-NNN: <short description>
- Summary: one paragraph
- Impacted services: runtime-router, kernel-dispatcher, kv-cache
- SLO deltas observed in canary: p95 before -> after
- Rollout plan: (same as registry)
- Revert instructions: kubectl rollout undo ...; admission-controller rollback command: infra rollback-exp --id EXP-YYYY-NNN
- Contact: owner (email) and oncall rotation

Retention and provenance

- All experiment artifacts (registry entry, traces, kernel checkpoints, profiles) are retained for 540 days in s3://exp-retention/ by default.
- Ownership: the owner field on registry entry is responsible for clean-up and long-term follow-up.

Appendix: quick CLI reference

- Register: infra exp create --id EXP-2025-042 --owner eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team --hypothesis "..."
- Upload trace: infra exp upload-trace --id EXP-2025-042 --file seed.jsonl.gz
- Start lab run: infra exp run --id EXP-2025-042 --cluster runtime-lab-03 --suite evbench-v3
- Collect bundle: infra exp collect-bundle --id EXP-2025-042 --out s3://exp-results/EXP-2025-042/bundle.tar.gz

Owners and points of contact

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team (Aisha Patel)
- SRE: Diane Chen
- Applied ML liaison: Omar Haddad

If you plan an experiment that touches kernel scheduling, profiling, or rollout mechanics, register it here first and follow this protocol end-to-end. This ensures we preserve reproducibility, reduce blast radius, and make results comparable across runs.
sections.heading: Then

payload.page_title: Execution Cohort Playbook and Experiment Journal

sections.body:
Purpose
-----
This document describes the "execution cohort" concept we use to group similar inference requests for improved latency predictability and cost efficiency. It combines architecture notes, scheduling policy pseudocode, a profiling playbook for cohort-related regressions, a benchmarking experiment design, a release checklist, a curated known-issues list, and incident runbooks.

Audience
--------
- Runtime engineers implementing or tuning the scheduler and kernel selection.
- SREs owning runtime availability and alerting.
- Applied ML engineers designing workload-fit experiments.

Goals and success criteria
--------------------------
- Reduce P99 tail latency variance for small/interactive models by >= 20% versus baseline.
- Maintain per-tenant throughput within 10% of historical baseline while reducing per-token cost.
- Provide deterministic, reproducible experiment artifacts for every scheduling change.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
- In scope: cohort creation heuristics, scheduling policy, kernel dispatch interaction, profiling and benchmark plans, runbook steps for cohort incidents.
- Not in scope: model quantization strategy, private-deployment network setup (see eng-private-deployments docs).

Architecture overview (text diagram)
-----------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- runtime-cohort-manager (component that classifies incoming requests into cohorts)
- kernel-dispatcher (maps scheduled slots to GPU kernels/queues)
- kv-cache-proxy (shared KV cache service for prefix reuse)
- scheduler-ledger (global admission controller and capacity accounting)
- telemetry-ingest (traces, events, metrics pipeline)
sections.heading: Key services and components involved

sections.body:
client -> ingress-router -> runtime-cohort-manager --+--> scheduler-ledger --> kernel-dispatcher --> GPU
                                                       |\
                                                       +--> kv-cache-proxy (hot prefix reuse)
sections.heading: Simple ASCII diagram

sections.body:
- Cohorts are immutable for the lifetime of a request. Classification is cheap and stable (hash + lightweight fingerprint).
- Scheduler decisions are made at cohort granularity (batching, priority, slot reservation).
- The kernel-dispatcher uses cohort metadata to select optimized kernels and execution paths (e.g., fused-attention, reduced-precision path).

Cohort definition and metadata fields
------------------------------------
Each cohort record contains flat fields used by multiple subsystems:
- cohort_id (string)
- workload_family (string, e.g., "chat-short", "embedding-long")
- model_variant (string)
- target_slo_ms (numeric as string, e.g., "120")
- prefer_low_latency (true/false as string)
- suggested_batching (string, e.g., "auto|max_tokens:64|min_batch:1")
- kv_cache_key_hint (short string)
- owner (team/email)

Cohort lifecycle
----------------
1. Classification: runtime-cohort-manager computes fingerprint and assigns cohort_id.
2. Admission: scheduler-ledger evaluates slot credits and admission rules.
3. Dispatch: kernel-dispatcher picks the kernel path and queue.
4. Post-process: telemetry-ingest tags traces with cohort_id and quality signals.

Priority and fairness policy (plain-language)
-------------------------------------------
- Priority is a function of (SLO attainment delta, observed tail risk, tenant SLAs).
- Fairness is enforced by token-based credit accounting in scheduler-ledger.
- Emergency preemption rules: high-priority control-plane traffic and SLA-protected cohorts can preempt best-effort cohorts up to a configured cap (default 15% of active slots).

Scheduling policy pseudocode
----------------------------
// Simplified view used in design discussions
function admit_request(request):
  cohort = classify(request)
  credits = ledger.peek_credits(cohort.owner)
  if credits < cohort.min_credit_threshold:
    if cohort.prefer_low_latency == "true":
      // try fast-path hedging up to X times
      return try_fast_path_hedge(request, cohort)
    else:
      return queue_in_backlog(request, cohort)
  // apply latency headroom check
  estimated_latency = kernel_dispatcher.estimate_latency(cohort, request.tokens)
  if estimated_latency <= cohort.target_slo_ms * 1.2:
    ledger.consume(credits, estimate_cost(request))
    return schedule_on_queue(request, cohort.preferred_queue)
  else:
    return fallback_to_variant_or_degrade(request)

Key tunables (table)
--------------------
- min_credit_threshold: smallest credit bucket to allow admission (default "5").
- hedging_max_attempts: max hedges for low-latency cohorts (default "2").
- preemption_cap_pct: percentage of slots reclaimable for SLAs (default "15").
- kv_prefetch_window_ms: how far ahead to warm prefix cache (default "200").

Profiling playbook for cohort regressions
---------------------------------------
When a cohort shows increased tail latency or error rate, follow these steps:
1. Capture a deterministic traffic sample (10k requests) by inserting a traffic mirror rule for cohort_id.
2. Run lightweight traces: set telemetry-ingest sampling to 100% for cohort_id for 1 minute.
3. Collect kernel-level timelines: use kernel-trace-tool "ktctl sample --cohort <id> --duration 60s --out /tmp/kt.json".
4. Correlate traces with ledger events: ledger.trace_id -> kernel-trace -> application trace.
5. If KV cache miss rate > 30% for the cohort, run kv-cache-warmup script and re-evaluate.
6. If kernel queuing time accounts for >50% of tail latency, escalate to kernel team with attached kt.json and sampled traces.

Profiling commands and quick checks
----------------------------------
- Check admission backlog: curl -s http://scheduler-ledger.local/metrics | jq '.backlog_by_cohort["<cohort_id>"]'
- Kernel queue times: ktctl histogram --cohort <id> --metric queue_ms
- KV cache hit ratio: curl http://kv-cache-proxy/metrics | grep cohort_<id>_hit_ratio

Benchmarking experiment design (template)
---------------------------------------
Objective: evaluate impact of cohort-aware scheduling on tail latency and cost.
sections.heading: Design intent

sections.body:
- Variables: batch_size {1,4,8}, concurrency_shape {steady, bursty-10s, spiky-1s}, model_variant {v1, v1-quant}
- Metrics: P50, P95, P99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec, tokens/cost, cohort_kv_hit_ratio, queue_time_ms.
sections.heading: Experiment matrix (examples)

sections.body:
```yaml
workload_name: chat-short-burst-test
model: gptx-chat-v1
cohort_label: chat-short
duration_s: 900
phases:
  - name: warmup
    qps: 50
    duration_s: 120
  - name: burst
    qps: 1200
    duration_s: 30
  - name: steady
    qps: 200
    duration_s: 660
request_shape:
  avg_tokens: 48
  seed_variability: high
batch_policy:
  enabled: true
  max_batch_tokens: 256
  max_batch_requests: 8
```
sections.heading: Sample YAML workload config

sections.body:
- Mirror production ingress for the cohort (shadow-mode)
- Collect kernel-trace logs (ktctl) and telemetry traces for entire run
- Snapshot scheduler-ledger state before/after test
- Record cost estimate via runtime-cost-sim tool

Release checklist for scheduler/cohort changes
--------------------------------------------
1. Update unit tests for scheduler policy language and cohort classification.
2. Run local microbenchmarks (microbench-suite) and record baseline artifacts.
3. Create canary branch with new policy and schedule canary deployment across 1% of requests for 24 hours.
4. Monitor KPIs: P95, P99, queue_time_ms, kernel_queue_depth, error_rate.
5. If regressions are detected, revert using feature-flag rollback or scale down new variants.
6. Post-mortem experiment: reproduce with synthetic workload within 72 hours.

Known issues (curated)
---------------------
1) Cohort oscillation under mixed bursty traffic
- Symptom: cohort membership toggles for identical request fingerprints leading to cache fragmentation.
- Probable root cause: fingerprint window too short (default 30s).
- Mitigation: increase fingerprint stability window to 5 minutes for high-throughput cohorts; schedule a follow-up stability test.

2) Hedging-created duplicate kernel load
- Symptom: hedged fast-path attempts increase GPU occupancy and raise queue times for best-effort cohorts.
- Root cause: lack of cross-cohort hedging circuit-breaker.
- Mitigation: enforce global_hedge_inflight limit and introduce per-node hedging accounting.

3) KV prefetch storm on rollout
- Symptom: massive KV warmups when a variant is rolled out, causing transient I/O saturation.
- Root cause: naive prefetch for all cohorts on deploy.
- Mitigation: stagger kv_prefetch_window and use probabilistic prefetch sampling (10% initially).

4) Scheduler-ledger stale view after partial-network-partition
- Symptom: admission decisions based on outdated credits causing over-admission.
- Root cause: optimistic-local-ledger without timely reconciliation.
- Mitigation: enable short reconciliation heartbeat (default 2s) and fall back to conservative admission if heartbeat missed > 3x.

Runbook: Cohort starvation incident
----------------------------------
Trigger: alert "cohort_p99_latency > 2x target for 5 minutes" or backlog growth > 5000 requests.
Immediate steps (0–5 minutes):
1. Pager to oncall runtime engineer.
2. Run quick health checks:
   - curl http://scheduler-ledger.local/health
   - ktctl histogram --cohort <id> --metric queue_ms --last 5m
3. If kernel queue_ms > 300ms and backlog growing, scale temporary admission down: curl -XPOST http://scheduler-ledger.local/actuate "{\"action\":\"throttle_cohort\",\"cohort\":\"<id>\",\"pct\":\"50\"}"
4. If KV miss ratio > 40%, trigger kv-cache warmup and allocate one prefetch worker: kvprefetchctl start --cohort <id> --workers 1
5. If situation persists beyond 15 minutes, revert recent scheduler changes (feature flag) and roll back canary.
sections.heading: Benchmark collection checklist

sections.body:
- Run profiling playbook and attach artifacts to incident ticket.
- Schedule a postmortem and update cohort stability parameters.

Telemetry and dashboards (recommended)
-------------------------------------
Essential metrics (metric names follow internal conventions):
- cohort.<cohort_id>.p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms
- cohort.<cohort_id>.queue_time_ms
- cohort.<cohort_id>.kv_hit_ratio
- scheduler.ledger.backlog_by_cohort
- kernel.queue_depth, kernel.exec_time_ms_histogram
- runtime.coalesced_batch_size_by_cohort

Suggested alert thresholds (example)
- cohort.<id>.p99_ms > target_slo_ms * 2 for 5m -> P1
- cohort.<id>.kv_hit_ratio < 0.5 for 10m -> P2
- scheduler.ledger.backlog_by_cohort > 1000 -> P1

Experiment journal template (copy into new experiment ticket)
------------------------------------------------------------
- experiment_id: (auto)
- lead: name/email
- hypothesis: short sentence
- cohort_ids: list
- config_snapshot: (link to S3 / artifact)
- benchmark_matrix: (variables & ranges)
- start_time / end_time
- raw_artifacts: list of links (ktctl, traces, ledger snapshots)
- outcome: pass/fail/observations
- followups: actionable items

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- runtime-cohort-manager: @runtime-team (primary)
- kernel-dispatcher: @kernels-team (secondary)
- scheduler-ledger: @sre-runtime
- telemetry and traces: @observability

Appendix: quick reference commands
---------------------------------
- classify example: curl -XPOST http://runtime-cohort-manager/classify -d '{"request": "..."}'
- ledger peek: curl http://scheduler-ledger.local/credits?owner=<team>
- start a focused trace: tracectl start --filter cohort_id=<id> --duration 60s
- canary rollback: ffctl disable feature.scheduler_new_policy

Notes and change history
------------------------
- 2026-02-15: Created by Aisha Khatri.
- 2026-03-01: Added hedging limits and incident runbook; reviewers Marcus Li, Sofia Alvarez, Dmitri Petrov.

Related reading
---------------

payload.page_title: Request Classification and Observability Contracts for Runtime Routing

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the request classification model and the corresponding observability contract used across the serving runtime. The goal is to produce deterministic routing decisions, consistent SLO mapping, and standardized telemetry that enables rapid triage and automated policy enforcement (e.g., cost-aware routing, fallback decisions, and quality guards). This is an engineering-facing spec intended for runtime, router, and telemetry consumers.

Scope

- Applies to all inbound inference requests processed by Redwood public and dedicated runtimes.
- Covers: request tagging, workload classes, priority heuristics, routing attributes, required telemetry fields, and common debugging workflows.
- Excludes: IAM/auth schemes, billing pipeline (except for reference label mapping), and model content inspection for privacy.

Why this matters

Inconsistent request semantics produce noisy SLO attribution, incorrect capacity decisions, and inaccurate cost signals. Aligning on a single classification scheme reduces variance in routing outcomes and enables reusable dashboards, alert rules, and automated remediation.

Definitions

1) Workload class: A short label describing the expected performance and quality envelope for the request. Examples: "realtime", "interactive", "batch", "embedding-internal", "low_priority_scrape".
2) Priority: Discrete integer (0..9) used by schedulers to shape kernel allocation and preemption policies. 0 is highest priority (system-critical).
3) Route intent: High-level objective for the request (e.g., "low_latency", "low_cost", "high_quality").
4) Fingerprint: Stable hash of request properties used to group similar requests across telemetry and cache keying.

Contract: Required request attributes

Every request that enters a runtime path must include at minimum the following envelope attributes. If missing, the router will fill with conservative defaults and emit a visibility warning (see Debugging section).

- request_id: UUID v4
- client_id: team or org identifier
- model: model name or alias (string)
- model_version: semver-like or sha tag
- workload_class: one of (realtime, interactive, batch, embedding, maintenance)
- priority: integer 0..9
- route_intent: one of (low_latency, low_cost, high_quality, degrade_gracefully)
- sequence_hint: expected token count (optional but recommended for long-form workloads)
- fingerprint: hex encoded sha1 of canonicalized attributes (see fingerprinting rules)
- provenance: origin (api, console, sdk, internal)
- ttl_ms: optional time-to-live for queued work

Fingerprinting rules (stable, language-agnostic)

1) Canonicalization order: client_id, model, model_version, workload_class, route_intent, sequence_hint (empty values omitted).
2) Normalization: lowercase strings, trim whitespace, replace multiple spaces with single space.
3) Hashing: sha1(canonical_string) and hex-encode.
4) Example canonical string: "acme:bert:2026-01-02:interactive:low_latency:512" -> fingerprint: "e6f3..."

Workload class semantics and SLO mapping

- realtime: Target p95 latency <= 120ms; used for websockets, streaming endpoints. Priority default 3.
- interactive: Target p95 latency <= 350ms; used for chat-like UX. Priority default 4.
- batch: No strict latency SLO; throughput and cost are primary. Priority default 7.
- embedding: Target p95 latency <= 300ms for dedicated embedding endpoints. Priority default 5.
- maintenance: For scheduled background tasks; can be preempted aggressively. Priority default 9.

Routing policy precedence (ordered)

1) Explicit route bindings (customer-specified pin)
2) SLO-driven routing (map workload_class -> compatible model variants)
3) Cost policy (if route_intent == low_cost)
4) Capacity availability fallback (regional/variant fallthrough)
5) Canary/rollout overrides (if in canary window and route matches)

Telemetry contract (required fields for ingestion)

Telemetry must be emitted at three points: router-in (accept), runtime-start, runtime-complete. Each emission is a JSON line with the following flat keys. All keys are strings unless noted. Timestamp fields are ISO8601 UTC.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- ts_iso: timestamp
- event_type: router-in | runtime-start | runtime-complete
- request_id
- fingerprint
- client_id
- model
- model_version
- workload_class
- priority (stringified int)
- route_intent
- selected_variant (the variant/kind chosen or "none")
- region
- node_id (when available)
- seq_len_hint (if present)
sections.heading: Required fields (all events)

sections.body:
- latency_ms (integer)
- tokens_out (integer)
- tokens_in (integer)
- error_code (empty if success)
- preempted (true|false)
- cost_estimate_usd (string)
sections.heading: Additional fields (runtime-complete)

sections.body:
router-in:
{
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-12T20:34:12.123Z",
  "event_type": "router-in",
  "request_id": "4a1f...",
  "fingerprint": "e6f3...",
  "client_id": "acme",
  "model": "gpt-redwood-3b",
  "model_version": "v2026-02-01",
  "workload_class": "interactive",
  "priority": "4",
  "route_intent": "low_latency",
  "selected_variant": "gpu-v1",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "node_id": "node-42"
}

runtime-complete:
{
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-12T20:34:12.501Z",
  "event_type": "runtime-complete",
  "request_id": "4a1f...",
  "fingerprint": "e6f3...",
  "latency_ms": 378,
  "tokens_out": 120,
  "tokens_in": 24,
  "error_code": "",
  "preempted": "false",
  "cost_estimate_usd": "0.0032"
}

Derived metrics and dashboards (minimum set)

- p50/p95/p99 latency per workload_class x model_variant
- success_rate (1 - error_rate) per priority bucket
- preemption_rate per client_id and workload_class
- cost_per_1k_tokens by model_variant and region
- queue_depth and wait_time distributions for batch queues

Alerting guidelines

- Latency SLO breach: if p95(realtime) > 120ms for 10m with volume > 10 req/s -> P1 page and trigger fallback routing to low-latency variants.
- Unexpected preemption spike: preemption_rate increase by 5x relative to 1h baseline -> P2 investigate kernel fairness and priority inversion.
- Fingerprint drift: sudden >40% increase in unique fingerprints for a client in 30m -> P2 check client SDK changes or bot traffic.

Debugging checklist (fast path)

1) Confirm router-in event exists for request_id. If absent, check ingress hooks and SDK instrumentation.
2) Validate fingerprint consistency across router-in and runtime-complete. Mismatches indicate canonicalization bugs.
3) If high latency, query node_id and run quick diagnostics: gpu utilization, kernel queue length, eviction_count.
4) For preemptions, inspect kernel-scheduler logs and priority queues for inversion traces.
5) If cost unexpectedly high, check selected_variant and route_intent; ensure quantized variant was eligible.

Common misconfigurations and remediations

- Missing sequence_hint: For long-form interactive tasks, omission causes kernel to select conservative unbatched path. Remediation: Upgrade SDK to v1.8+ or set default seq_len_hint on the route.
- Incorrect workload_class mapping from SDK: Use migration script provided in tools/routing-migrate.sh.
- Fingerprinting version skew: Ensure all SDKs use fingerprint spec v2.0 (see appendix) or enable compatibility header "Fingerprint-Version: v1".

Operational playbook: automated remediation examples

1) Auto-fallback on SLO breach:
   - Trigger: p95(realtime) > 120ms for 10m
   - Action: Router attaches tag "fallback_low_latency" and re-routes new requests to cached low-latency variants for 5m.
   - Postmortem: Create alert ticket and run throughput simulation against captured traces.

2) Auto-throttle noisy client:
   - Trigger: unique_fingerprints_per_minute(client_id) > threshold AND error_rate > 1%
   - Action: Inject rate-limit header, shadow route to cost-tiered variant, notify account owner.

Appendix A: Configuration examples

YAML: route binding example

routes:
  - name: acme-realtime
    client_id: acme
    workload_class: realtime
    default_priority: 3
    allowed_variants: ["gpu-v1", "gpu-small-v2"]
    route_intent: low_latency
    fallback_order: ["gpu-small-v2", "cpu-quantized"]

CLI snippet: emit a router-in test event

$ ./tools/emit-test-telemetry --type router-in --request-id 0000-1111 --client acme --model gpt-redwood-3b --workload interactive

Appendix B: Fingerprint compatibility table

| SDK version | fingerprint spec | notes |
|-------------|------------------|-------|
| 1.x         | v1               | legacy: canonicalization omitted sequence_hint |
| 2.0         | v2               | current: canonicalization includes sequence_hint and route_intent |
| 2.1+        | v2               | adds optional deterministic client-salt header |

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: runtime-routing team (primary), telemetry-shared (secondary)
- Rollout: SDK + router integration to be staged across canary -> region-wide over 6 weeks.
- Migration windows: SDKs older than 2.0 will be supported with compatibility headers for 90 days.

Open items and future work

- Formalize a bounded vocabulary for route_intent to support programmatic policy synthesis.
- Investigate compact binary telemetry envelope for high-throughput short events.

Related reading

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

Document revision history

- 2025-11-12: created by Aisha Patel
- 2026-01-18: added preemption alert thresholds (Daniel Kwon)
- 2026-02-15: clarified fingerprinting canonicalization and telemetry example formats (Marco Ruiz)

payload.page_title: Scheduler Shadowplay and Telemetry Convergence Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook defines the 'Scheduler Shadowplay' experiment pattern and a telemetry convergence protocol for validating scheduler and kernel-scheduling changes against production-like traffic. It combines parallel (shadow) scheduling runs, targeted profiling, and a gated quality checklist so teams can iterate on scheduling policies without risking customer SLAs.

Why this exists
- Scheduler changes (admission, preemption, kernel hints) can introduce subtle latency and fidelity regressions that are hard to detect with unit tests or synthetic microbenchmarks.
- Shadowing real traffic through a non-authoritative (shadow) scheduler lets us compare end-to-end observables while keeping live traffic untouched.
- Telemetry convergence defines statistical checks and gating rules so rollouts proceed only when measurable signals align with safety thresholds.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to changes in: scheduler policy DSL, kernel selection heuristics, priority mapping, preemption thresholds, and admission controllers.
- Assumes: shadow scheduler can be run in parallel to production pods (no write-side-effects), tracing headers are propagated (trace-id/kvcache-hash), and a profiling instrumentation sidecar is available.

Owners and contacts
- Playbook owner: eng-serving-runtime Scheduling Guild (primary: Maya Chen)
- On-call escalation: runtime-sre team (pager: #runtime-sre)
- Reviewers: listed in metadata above

High-level pattern
1) Prepare shadow environment
   - Deploy a shadow scheduler instance that consumes mirrored decision requests. Shadow scheduler MUST NOT affect traffic (read-only decision path).
   - Ensure shadow pods have the same kernel build (or explicitly labeled if testing kernel changes).
2) Collect baseline
   - Run shadowplay with baseline scheduler to establish reference telemetry for 48h (recommended) or one production peak cycle.
3) Deploy candidate scheduler
   - Switch shadow cluster to candidate scheduler and run for an identical period.
4) Telemetry convergence checks and gating
   - Compute delta metrics (candidate vs baseline) and run statistical tests.
5) Profiling and targeted instrumentation
   - On any significant divergence, run focused profiler sessions using the profiling sidecar.
6) Decision and rollout
   - If all gates pass, proceed to canary with controlled traffic. If not, collect diagnostics and iterate.

Metric and signal catalog
- Latency: p50/p90/p95/p99 for request end-to-end (ms). Primary gating metric: p95.
- Errors: 4xx/5xx within runtime, kernel faults, NVLink reprobes.
- Kernel switch count: average kernel flips per request (should not increase >10%).
- KVCache hit ratio: prefix/KV cache hit % (should not degrade >1.5ppt for high-fidelity cohorts).
- Token throughput: tokens/sec aggregated per shard.
- Resource signals: GPU SM occupancy, memory allocs/sec, swap activity (on-host), CPU steal.
- Cost proxy: normalized per-token GPU utilization estimate.

Gating thresholds (default)
- p95 latency: candidate <= baseline + 10 ms OR no statistically-significant increase (p-value > 0.05 for Mann-Whitney U test)
- Error rate: candidate <= baseline + 0.1% (absolute)
- KVCache hit: no decrease greater than 1.5 percentage points for workloads with >10% cacheable prefixes
- Throughput: candidate >= 95% of baseline under matched load
- Cost delta: normalized per-token cost increase <= 8% (ops must approve >8%)
- Stability: no kernel panics, watchdog resets, or GPU timeout events during the shadow period

Statistical procedures
- Use paired comparisons where possible: align requests by trace-id to compute per-request deltas and run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test for latency deltas.
- For non-paired aggregated signals, use bootstrap confidence intervals (95%) to judge convergence.
- Require at least N=10k matched requests for meaningful p95 comparisons; otherwise extend the shadow window.

Data sources and dashboards
- Primary time-series: runtime.metrics.{latency,end_to_end}_p95, runtime.errors.count, runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio, kernel.switch_rate, gpu.utilization_pct
- Traces: trace.span.runtime_request -> annotate with scheduler.variant and kernel.hints (tag names: scheduler.variant, kernel.tag, shadow.play_id)
- Dedicated dashboards: "Scheduler Shadowplay Convergence" (Grafana) and "Scheduler Shadowplay Diff" (Heatmap). Ensure diff dashboard shows per-cohort comparisons.

Runbook: immediate remediation flow (if candidate fails during shadow)
1) Abort: stop candidate shadow traffic and revert shadow scheduler to baseline.
2) Snapshot: capture a 10-minute high-fidelity profile (pprof + GPU traces) and save a trace sample set with trace-ids.
3) Notify: post summary to #runtime-ops including key deltas and linking the snapshot.
4) Triage: schedule a focused investigation within 4 business hours with scheduling, kernel, and SRE.
5) Rollback plan: candidate must remain off the production decision path until the issue is resolved and a new shadow run passes gates.

Profiling playbook (when divergence detected)
- Step 1: Reproduce in controlled shadow window with load-sculpting tool (load-sculptor-cli).
  Example: load-sculptor-cli replay --corpus=samples/peak-1H --concurrency=120 --trace-ids=./trace-seed.json
- Step 2: Enable sidecar collection: set env SHADOW_PROFILING=enabled and increase trace sampling to 100% for 5 minutes.
- Step 3: Capture: GPU traces (nsys), kernel timeline (ktrace), and runtime CPU flamegraphs.
- Step 4: Annotate: tag traces with reason tags (e.g., preemption-regression, kernel-selection) and add kernel hint dumps.
- Step 5: Analyze: correlate p95 latency spikes with kernel switch counts and NVLink activity. Use causality checklist below.

Causality checklist (common root causes)
- Kernel hint mismatch: candidate suggested a heavier kernel path for mid-length sequences.
- Increased kernel churn: frequent kernel switches per request due to sequence length fragmentation.
- Admission backpressure: new admission thresholds caused head-of-line blocking at dispatcher.
- KV cache coldspots: candidate ordering increases cold-start requests for popular prefixes.
- Resource contention: increased SM occupancy leading to longer kernel enqueue latencies.

Example scheduler policy snippet (YAML)
- name: test-candidate-policy
  admission:
    max_slots_per_shard: 48
    queue_timeout_ms: 120
  preemption:
    enabled: true
    debt_threshold_ms: 5
  kernel_hints:
    prefer_quantized: true
    max_kernel_switches_per_request: 2
  priority_synthesis:
    economic_weight: 0.7
    fidelity_weight: 0.3

CLI example: start a shadow run (ops)
1) Create play:
   rwd ctl shadow create --name=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --source=mirror-prod --target=shadow-cluster-03 --duration=48h --note="candidate kernel: v2-opt-hint"
2) Switch policy:
   rwd ctl shadow set-policy --play=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --policy-file=policies/test-candidate-policy.yaml
3) Watch progress:
   rwd ctl shadow status --play=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --format=wide

Acceptance checklist before promoting candidate to canary
- All gating thresholds satisfied for target cohorts for a minimum of 48 hours (or one peak cycle).
- Telemetry pipelines show <5% missing trace propagation during the shadow window.
- No kernel-level faults or GPU watchdog events recorded.
- Profiling artifacts and a short investigation note uploaded to the shadowplay artifact bucket: s3://redwood-shadowplay/artifacts/{play_id}/
- Approval from runtime-sre and Scheduling Guild leads.

Rollout matrix (recommended)
- Shadow -> Canary 1 (5% traffic, 4h) -> Canary 2 (20% traffic, 12h) -> Gradual ramp to 100% over 72h if no regressions.
- If canary shows divergence, follow rollback immediate remediation flow above.

Operational tips and anti-patterns
- Tip: Align shadow windows to production peak hours for more representative load.
- Tip: Use cohort labels (e.g., small-seq, long-seq, embeddings-heavy) to avoid signal dilution.
- Anti-pattern: Short (15–30 minute) shadow runs; these often miss tail behaviour.
- Anti-pattern: Ignoring KV cache observables; many scheduler changes shift ordering and indirectly alter cache hit rates.

Appendix A — Example diff report fields
- total_matched_requests
- p95_baseline_ms, p95_candidate_ms, p95_delta_ms, p95_pvalue
- errors_baseline, errors_candidate, errors_delta_pct
- kvcache_hit_baseline_pct, kvcache_hit_candidate_pct, kvcache_delta_pp
- gpu_util_baseline, gpu_util_candidate, util_delta_pp
- artifact_link (S3)

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick hits
- If p95 increases but kernel switch count unchanged: look for NVLink queueing or host CPU starvation.
- If KV hits drop: verify request ordering and any implicit batching changes.
- If errors spike with no latency change: prioritize investigating kernel-level assertions and runtime error wrapping.

References and related docs
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (link in metadata)
- Profiling: causal latency attribution playbook (link in metadata)
- Runtime runbooks: eviction, warmstart, and graceful degradation playbooks

Change log
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2026-03-22: Added statistical procedure guidance and default gating thresholds (reviewers: Priya Nair)
- 2026-06-30: Expanded profiling playbook and added CLI examples; set publication status to published

End of document

payload.page_title: Cross-Layer Execution Audit & Escalation Playbook

sections.body:
Purpose
This playbook defines a repeatable cross-layer audit and escalation process for execution anomalies that cross scheduler, kernel, runtime, and networking boundaries. It is intended for oncall engineers and runtime owners who need to triage incidents impacting latency, correctness, or cost SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments managed by the runtime.
- Covers anomalies that cannot be diagnosed from a single layer (for example: a spike in p95 latency that coincides with increased kernel queue depth and model variant swaps).
- Does not replace single-service runbooks; it coordinates them.

Summary of responsibilities
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (primary).
- Secondary: kernel-scheduler team.
- Tertiary: infra/networking team (for cross-host or NVLink issues).
- Communication: SRE/incident commander if SLO impact > 30 minutes or customer escalation.

Key SLOs & alert thresholds (reference)
- p95 request latency (inference): 150 ms (alert at 200 ms sustained for 5m).
- error rate (5xx): 0.5% (alert at 1% sustained for 5m).
- GPU kernel queue depth: baseline varies by family, critical if > 90th historical quantile and rising.
- KV-cache warmness: < 80% warm triggers quality-check pipeline.

High-level investigation flow (quick checklist)
1. Confirm scope and impact
   - Confirm if the issue is global, per-region, or per-tenant. Use:
     - Dashboard: "Per-region latency by model"
     - PromQL: sum by(region) (increase(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\"}[5m]))
2. Capture short-term forensic snapshot (first 10 minutes)
   - Collect traces, scheduler telemetry, kernel metrics, and node-level system stats.
   - Commands:
     - redwoodctl trace fetch --start "-15m" --filter "service:runtime" --limit 1000 > /tmp/trace-snapshot.json
     - redwoodctl telemetry slice --metric kernel.queue_depth --start "-15m" --end "now" --out /tmp/kqueue.json
     - kubectl top node --heapster > /tmp/node-top.txt
3. Correlate signals across layers
   - Match trace IDs across: API gateway -> request router -> runtime dispatcher -> kernel trace.
   - Look for common request attributes (model, sequence length, prompt size, routing policy).
4. Run quick hypotheses (examples)
   - Hypothesis A: a bad model variant rollout increased token compute. Verify: sudden rise in tokens-per-request and kernel time per token.
     - Query: rate(runtime_tokens_processed_total[1m]) by(model_variant)
   - Hypothesis B: NVLink degradation increased cross-host transfer time. Verify: network egress/intra-node bandwidth and per-GPU pci errors.
     - Query: increase(node_network_transmit_bytes_total[5m]) and dmesg /var/log/kern.log for NVLink errors.
   - Hypothesis C: Scheduler starvation from a noisy tenant. Verify: kernel slot accounting and priority debt.
     - Query: runtime_scheduler_priority_debt_seconds{tenant=~".*"}

Detailed collection recipes (what to collect and where)
- Trace artifacts (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/traces): JSON traces from redwoodctl, full headers for 10 representative requests (p95/p99).
- Kernel telemetry (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/kernel): kernel.latency.histogram, kernel.queue_depth, kernel.context_switches, kernel.kv_prefetch_hits.
- Scheduler logs (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/scheduler): admission decisions, preempt events, slot allocations for last 30 minutes. Sample collector:
  - redwoodctl scheduler dump --since "-30m" --format json > /incident/$INC_ID/scheduler_dump.json
- Node diagnostics (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/nodes): nvidia-smi topo, nvlink status, gpu temperatures, dmesg. Commands:
  - nvidia-smi topo --matrix > /incident/$INC_ID/gpu-topo.txt
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /incident/$INC_ID/gpu-sample.csv & (stop after capture window)

PromQL / Metrics recipes (copy-paste)
- P95 latency (approx): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))
- Kernel queue depth by shard: sum(rate(kernel_queue_depth_total[1m])) by (shard_id)
- Preempt events: increase(runtime_preempt_events_total[5m])
- KV-cache hit ratio: sum(runtime_kvcache_hits_total) / sum(runtime_kvcache_requests_total)

Escalation matrix and decision rules
- Tier 1 (oncall): can resolve in 30–60 minutes with runbook actions (restart kernel shard, adjust admission knobs).
- Tier 2 (kernel-scheduler): escalate if root cause points to kernel regressions, fairness policy violation, or kernel-level resource leaks.
- Tier 3 (infra/hardware): escalate for NVLink, host-level memory pressure, or cloud provider networking incidents.
- Emergency (exec + customer success): if customer-facing SLA breach > 1 hour or sensitive customer data impacted.

Safe remediation actions (ordered, low-risk -> high-risk)
1. Reroute to a healthy model variant or region via routing policy (no restart).
2. Adjust admission controller temporary thresholds: reduce burst admission for noisy tenants.
   - Example: redwoodctl admission set --tenant noisy-tenant --max-burst 0.5
3. Restart a kernel shard (graceful): follow runtime shard restart checklist (drain, snapshot KV-cache if needed, warm start).
   - Command: redwoodctl shard restart --shard-id shard-17 --graceful
4. Rollback recent kernel patch (Tier 2 involvement).
5. Full node recycle (Tier 3) for hardware-linked anomalies.

Post-incident tasks (within 24–72 hours)
- Runbook update: add the exact reproduction steps and any new queries that were useful.
- Regression test: add a synthetic test to the benchmark suite covering the failing scenario (e.g., long-context small-batch tails).
- RCA: owner writes a concise RCA and assigns follow-up tickets with owners and SLA for fixes.
- SLA customer comms: coordinate with Customer Success for affected accounts.

Example incident timeline (template)
- 00:00 — Alert triggers: p95 > 200 ms for 12m.
- 00:03 — Oncall collects traces and kernel telemetry snapshot.
- 00:12 — Correlation found: model-variant v2 rollout coincident with token/time-per-token increase.
- 00:18 — Remediation: rollback model-variant and reduce admission for v2.
- 00:25 — Latency returns to baseline.
- 00:55 — Postmortem scheduled; artifacts uploaded to /incidents/INC-1234.

Quality gates and bench additions (for product/bench team)
- Add a benchmark that mirrors the incident: sequence-length distribution, per-tenant concurrency, and small-batch microbursts.
- Add kernel-level fuzz tests for queue-depth edgecases.

Templates and copyable snippets
- Incident folder naming: /incidents/INC-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-tag>
- Redaction checklist before sharing logs externally: remove Authorization headers, PII from prompts, customer IDs.

Ownership matrix (who does what)
- Oncall (serving-runtime): initial triage, trace collection, safe remediations.
- Kernel-scheduler: kernel telemetry interpretation, kernel rollbacks, scheduler policy updates.
- Infra: hardware health, NVLink, node-level diagnostics.
- Bench/product: add regression tests and synthetic workloads to prevent reoccurrence.

Appendix A — Useful queries and sample JSON
- Example PromQL for noisy-tenant detection: topk(10, sum by(tenant) (rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])))
- Example trace-filter (redwoodctl syntax): redwoodctl trace fetch --filter 'span.service:\"kernel\" AND error:true' --start '-30m'
- Example minimal trace JSON snippet: {
  \"trace_id\": \"abcd1234\",
  \"spans\": [
    {
      \"id\": \"s1\",
      \"service\": \"api-gateway\",
      \"duration_ms\": 12
    },
    {
      \"id\": \"s2\",
      \"service\": \"runtime-dispatch\",
      \"duration_ms\": 85
    },
    {
      \"id\": \"s3\",
      \"service\": \"kernel\",
      \"duration_ms\": 320
    }
  ]
}

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Ava Martinez.
- 2026-02-10: Updated with PromQL recipes and escalation matrix (reviewers: Samuel Kim, Priya Desai, Luca Romano).

Related runbooks and playbooks
- See runbooks: runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers, adaptive-fidelity-decision-log, kernel-continuity-state-reconciliation for layer-specific actions.

Contact and oncall roster
- serving-runtime oncall rotation page: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/oncall (link internal).
- Kernel-scheduler primary: @sam.kim, secondary: @luca.romano.

End of document

payload.page_title: Runtime Sandboxing Experiment Lab Manual

sections.body:
Overview

This manual describes the lab-grade sandboxing environment used by the runtime team to run invasive performance experiments, kernel-scheduler patches, and mixed-workload benchmarks without risking production stability. It documents the sandbox architecture, isolation model, step-by-step experiment runbook, profiling and telemetry requirements, benchmark invocation patterns, known issues encountered during experiments, and incident runbooks specific to lab activities.

Goals

- Create a reproducible, auditable environment for risky runtime changes.
- Ensure experiments are isolated from production control planes and do not leak telemetry or credentials.
- Provide a standard profiling and benchmarking workflow so results are comparable across runs.
- Capture failure modes and required mitigation steps.

Audience

- Runtime engineers doing kernel and scheduler work.
- Performance engineers running comparative benchmarks.
- SREs supporting lab infrastructure.

High-level sandbox architecture

Components

- lab-gateway: Lightweight ingress that routes experiment traffic and enforces quotas.
- kernel-orchestrator: Service that deploys custom kernel/kernelspecs into lab nodes.
- sandbox-runner: Per-node agent that configures cgroups, MIG partitions and GPU modes, and applies kernel module overrides.
- kvcache-sim: A synthetic KV cache used to emulate prefix / session caching behavior.
- telemetry-proxy: Collects and stamps telemetry for lab runs, marks data with lab_run_id, and writes to the lab telemetry bucket.

Isolation model

- Network: Lab runs live in the lab VPC (vpc-lab-1). No cross-VPC peering with prod. All egress is via nat-lab with explicit allow lists.
- Compute: Nodes are labeled "lab:true" and exist in a separate autoscaling group. Node OS images include the debug kernel and a signed kernel module whitelist.
- GPU: Two isolation modes supported: NVIDIA MPS per-experiment (for multi-process concurrency experiments) and MIG partitions (for perf isolation). sandbox-runner toggles these per experiment.
- Storage and secrets: Lab runs use ephemeral PVCs. Secrets are provided by the lab KMS with a short TTL and are not replicated to production KMS.

Kernel-scheduling considerations for lab experiments

- Scheduler variants: The lab supports several scheduler builds under kernel-orchestrator: baseline, preemptive-slice, adaptive-slice, and priority-decoupled. Each build is tagged and has a known compatibility matrix for driver and CUDA versions.
- Mapping priorities to runtime classes: Use the experiment configuration to map Redwood priority classes to kernel priorities. For example: "interactive" -> SCHED_RR with 10ms quantum; "batch" -> SCHED_DEADLINE with ED=50ms/1s.
- Fairness accounting: When testing cooperative preemption, enable kernel credit accounting (lab flag: enable_credit_accounting=true) to observe queue-smear effects.

Experiment environment provisioning

1) Request sandbox allocation

- Open RFC in the experiments tracker with: title, hypothesis, required node types, GPU mode, expected run time, and roll-back criteria. Example: "RFC: preemptive-slice latency reduction vs baseline".
- On approval, run the allocation script: ./scripts/request-lab --project runtime --nodes 4 --gputype a100 --duration 8h --labels preemptive-test

2) Provisioning checklist (automated but must be validated)

- Confirm nodes in ASG have label lab:true.
- Confirm kernel-orchestrator has deployed the requested kernel tag.
- Verify sandbox-runner applied requested GPU mode: kubectl get nodes -l lab=true -o json | jq '.items[].metadata.annotations.gpu_mode'
- Ensure telemetry-proxy is configured with lab_run_id and bucket path.

Step-by-step experiment runbook

1. Prepare experiment config (YAML)

- Minimal example (save as experiment-config.yaml):

experiment_name: preemptive-slice-compare-2026
environment: staging-sim
node_selectors:
  - lab:true
kernel_tag: preemptive-slice-v3
gpu_mode: MIG-1g.5gb
workload_profiles:
  - name: interactive
    qps: 120
    seq_length_p95: 320
  - name: batch
    qps: 2
    seq_length_p95: 2048
measurement_windows_s: 300
telemetry_bucket: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123

2. Start with a short smoke run (10 min)

- Validate functional correctness, all services respond, and telemetry tags are present.
- Commands: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --smoke

3. Full run

- Start bench: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --duration 3600 --trace-sampling 0.1
- Monitor: kubectl top nodes -l lab=true; ./observability/quick-check --run-id=experiment-123

4. Collect artifacts

- Kernel traces: /var/log/lab/experiments/experiment-123/kernel-trace.tar.gz
- Flamegraphs: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/flamegraphs/
- Perf counters (per-node): s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/perf/
- Telemetry manifest: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/manifest.json

Profiling playbook (lab-specific)

- Sampling strategy: Start with probabilistic sampling at 10% for p50/p95 slices and 100% sampling for all p99+ traces during the first 5 minutes and then drop to 1% for the remainder. This accelerates root-cause collection without overloading telemetry.
- Metrics to capture: per-request wall_time, kernel_queue_time, kv_cache_hit, gpu_busy_time, gpu_memory_alloc, context_switches/sec, scheduler_runqueue_length.
- Tracing hooks: Ensure runtime-gateway and kernel-orchestrator include lab_run_id and experiment_name in trace root spans.
- Perf tooling: Use perf + Nsight CLI for A100 profiling. Example: sudo perf record -a -g -- sleep 300; perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

Benchmarking suite invocation

- Use the canonical runner that wraps the microbenchmark harness.
- Example command: ./bench-suite/run --profile latency --shards 4 --concurrency 64 --model redwood-v0.9-quant --seed 42 --out s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/bench

- Config table (CSV-like text)

config_key,description,default,lab_override
shards,number of client shards,4,4
concurrency,total outstanding requests per shard,32,64
sequence_distribution,which lengths to sample,prod-like,tail-enhanced
model_variant,model binary to run,baseline,preemptive-slice-v3

Data hygiene and retention

- All lab telemetry must be tagged with lab_run_id and have a retention of 90 days by default. If an experiment is deemed sensitive, adjust confidentiality to 'restricted' and contact security.
- Do not import lab telemetry into production dashboards. To compare to production, export aggregated metrics only (no traces, no raw kernel profiles).

Release notes for this manual (v1.2)

- 2026-01-12: v1.0 initial release documenting the sandbox architecture and minimal runbook.
- 2026-01-25: v1.1 added kernel scheduling mappings and new perf counter list.
- 2026-02-03: v1.2 added MIG / MPS guidance and bench-suite invocation examples.

Known issues and mitigations (lab-specific)

- GPU driver mismatch causing node panic: Always pin driver version to node image and verify with ./scripts/verify-driver.sh. Mitigation: cordon and reprovision node with driver-consistent AMI.
- Telemetry proxy dropping spans at >2k RPS: Reduce trace sampling or scale telemetry-proxy (HPA target cpu 70%).
- kvcache-sim inconsistent TTL behavior under heavy load: Increase kvcache-sim replica_count to at least 3 and enable read-through logging.

Incident runbooks for lab activities

1) Node panic during experiment

- Step 1: Pause experiment: ./lab-runner pause --run-id=experiment-123
- Step 2: Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node-id> && kubectl describe node <node-id> | tee /tmp/node-diagnostics.txt
- Step 3: Capture kernel oops: sudo journalctl -k -b -1 > /tmp/kernel-oops.txt; attach to incident.
- Step 4: Reprovision using: ./scripts/reprovision-node --node <node-id> --ami ami-lab-debug-20260101

2) Telemetry corruption detected

- Verify manifest integrity: aws s3 cp s3://lab-telemetry/.../manifest.json - | jq .status
- If manifest shows missing files, escalate to telemetry team (owner: telemetry-eng@redwood.com) and mark run as partial.

Safety and approvals

- Any experiment that modifies kernel scheduling semantics that could change tenant isolation must have a security review and an SRE sign-off. Use the experiment-approval workflow in the tracker and attach the signed checklist.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: runtime-experiments@redwood.com (team: Runtime Performance)
- On-call for lab infra: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com (pager duty)
- Telemetry owner: telemetry-eng@redwood.com

Appendix: quick reference commands

- Request nodes: ./scripts/request-lab --nodes 4 --duration 8h
- Start bench: ./bench-suite/run --profile latency --out <s3path>
- Smoke run: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --smoke
- Collect kernel trace: sudo tar czf /var/log/lab/experiments/<run>/kernel-trace.tar.gz /sys/kernel/debug/tracing

Document history and contributors

- Written by: Maya Alvarez (runtime-experiments)
- Contributors: Arjun Patel, Sofia Lin, Liam O'Connor

Feedback

- Add comments on this page or open an issue in the experiments tracker with the label "lab-manual".

payload.page_title: Runtime Integration Gateway & Operator Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This page documents the design, operational contract, and runbooks for the Runtime Integration Gateway (RIG) and the Operator component used by Redwood’s serving runtime. The RIG is the control plane facade that mediates decisions between the API surface, routing layer, and the kernel scheduler. The Operator is the local agent that implements prefetch/eviction hints, capacity decisions, and safety checks on a per-host basis. Together they enable consistent fallback behavior, cache coordination, and safe kernel handoffs across deployments (hosted, dedicated, private).

Scope

- Cross-cutting: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling hints, profiling instrumentation, benchmark protocols, evacuation/eviction runbooks, and release guidance.
- Intended audience: runtime engineers, SREs, oncall, platform/ops teams, and partners owning Private deployments.

Design overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Preserve latency SLOs while maximizing throughput and cache hit ratios.
- Provide safe, observable prefetch and eviction signals to kernels without exposing internal kernel details.
- Offer a deterministic handshake for model swap, graceful degradation, and fast rollback.
sections.heading: Key goals

sections.body:
1) Runtime Integration Gateway (RIG): global control plane component that synthesizes routing policy, historical telemetry, and fidelity budgets to produce per-tenant hints (prefetch score, target warmup priority, eviction budget).
2) Operator agent: host-local agent that receives hints and enforces them via kernel scheduler APIs and kvcache controls.
3) Kernel Scheduler: GPU-local execution layer that exposes a narrow set of safe primitives (reserve_slot, prefetch_token, soft_evict, priority_boost).

Behavioral contract (high level)

- Hints are advisory: Operator must never trigger kernel state transitions that break in-flight requests. All transitions are atomic and checkpointed.
- Backpressure loop: if Operator observes a >10% SLO degradation coincident with hint enforcement, it must throttle hint application and report a delta to RIG.
- Revisioning: every hint includes a version token; kernels reject stale tokens.

Kernel scheduling integration patterns
sections.heading: Core components

sections.body:
| Primitive | Inputs | Expected behavior | Safety checks |
|---|---:|---|---|
| reserve_slot | model_id, seq_len_est, ttl | Reserve a logical GPU slot for expected new sequence starts. Not a physical allocation. | Reject if host soft-oom or thermal throttling active. |
| prefetch_token | kv_key, priority, expected_live_ms | Start asynchronous KV prefetch and stage to warm cache. | Limit bytes prefetched per-second by host budget. |
| soft_evict | kv_key, reason | Mark entry for eviction; kernel may defer until safe window. | Respect in-flight references; must not kick out active session entries. |
| priority_boost | tenant_id, boost_level | Raise kernel scheduling priority for specific tenant's packets. | Must honor fairness quotas and not exceed token budget. |
sections.heading: Recommended primitive semantics (stable API)

sections.body:
- Use request timeline annotations (trace_id + event_ids) when translating prefetch into kernel operations to permit traceability.
- All kernel APIs return an op_result and telemetry tag; Operators should emit both as structured logs.

Profiling & observability guidance
sections.heading: Integration notes

sections.body:
- Hint lifecycle traces: RIG:hint:generate -> Operator:hint:apply -> Kernel:hint:ack.
- Prefetch stats: bytes_initiated, bytes_completed, success_rate, tail_latency_p95/p99.
- Eviction surface: evict_attempts, evict_success, delayed_eviction_count, in_flight_blocker_reasons.
sections.heading: Required telemetry flows (minimum)

sections.body:
- 100% of hint lifecycle events must be annotated and sampled at 10% for full trace capture.
- Stratified sampling: always capture 100% when SLO > breach_threshold or when evictions coincide with model-swaps.
sections.heading: Sampling policy

sections.body:
1) Identify symptom: increased generation tail latency or token error rate.
2) Correlate with hint application windows (RIG/Operator traces).
3) If evictions increased: pull kvcache-backed references and examine in-flight reference counts.
4) If prefetch failures: check network I/O metric (prefetch throughput) and per-host prefetch budget exhaustion.
5) Deploy a controlled canary: disable prefetch for a single tenant cohort and compare SLA slices; report delta to RIG.

Benchmarking protocol (how to validate changes safely)

- Objective: measure delta in per-token cost, tail latency, and cache hit ratio after any change to hint heuristics or Operator enforcement.
- Minimum benchmark matrix:
  - Workloads: short-chat (mean seq_len 32), long-chat (mean seq_len 512), embedding-bulk (batch-size 128), mixed-burst (poisson arrivals lambda=200).
  - Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens-per-second, cache_hit_rate, kernel_preemption_count, host_cpu_percent, GPU_util.
  - Duration: each profile run = 2h steady-state after 20m warmup. Repeat 3x and report median.
sections.heading: Profiling playbook excerpt (investigation steps)

sections.body:
- Synthesize traffic: ./benchctl --profile mixed-burst --tenant test-tenant --duration 02:00 --seed 42
- Collect traces: benchctl collect --trace-filter "RIG:hint* OR Operator:hint*" --out bench-2026-02-collect.json

Release & rollout guidance

- All Operator changes must pass a green gate on the benchmark matrix above with no >5% regression in p95 for the short-chat workload across three replicate runs.
- Rollout strategy: staged canary by affinity cohort (10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%) with automated rollback on >3s sustained p95 regression or 2x increase in eviction-induced request failures.
- Release note template: include exact benchmark artifact links, canary cohort ids, and throttling parameters.

Known issues (current summary)

| ID | Symptom | Impact | Workaround | Owner |
| KVO-2025-11 | Prefetch storms on model swap causing network saturation | Elevated tail latency for embedding workloads | Stagger prefetch by 2s buckets via RIG hint windowing | eng-serving-runtime |
| OP-2025-07 | Operator sometimes double-applies soft_evict after transient disconnect | Elevated evict_attempts and unnecessary cache churn | Blacklist consecutive soft_evicts within 500ms per-kv | kernel-team |
| THERM-2025-02 | Thermal-induced GPU throttles reject reserve_slot calls | Rejection leads to rapid fallback to lower-capacity kernels | Preemptively lower prefetch budget when thermal_throttle > 0 | infra-sre |

Eviction & prefetch runbook (operational playbook)

When customers report latency regressions possibly tied to prefetch/eviction:
1) Triage: capture traces across RIG, Operator, and kernel for the suspect timeframe.
2) Check host budgets: run `rigctl host-status --host <node>` and inspect prefetch_budget and eviction_backlog.
3) If prefetch_budget_pressure > 80%: temporarily reduce RIG prefetch window for the affected cohort: `rigctl hint-update --cohort <id> --prefetch-window-ms 200`
4) If eviction churn > 100/min: enable soft-eviction-mitigation mode on Operator: `operatorctl set soft-evict-delay 1200` (ms).
5) If step 3–4 restore SLOs: schedule a follow-up bench run and root-cause analysis. If not, escalate to oncall kernel-team.

Escalation matrix

- Oncall runtime (pager): Triage and apply immediate mitigations.
- Kernel team (pager): For kernel API misbehavior or invariant violations.
- Infra SRE: For network, thermal, or host-level resource saturation.

Ownership and maintenance

- RIG control plane: eng-serving-runtime/core-routing (primary).
- Operator agent: eng-serving-runtime/operator (primary); kernel-team (secondary for API changes).
- Bench harness and artifact storage: benchmarking-team.

Appendix: sample Operator config (yaml)

```yaml
operator:
  prefetch:
    enabled: true
    max_bytes_per_sec: 250000000 # 250MB/s
    per_tenant_limit: 50MB
  eviction:
    soft_evict_delay_ms: 1000
    max_concurrent_evictions: 16
  safety:
    slo_throttle_threshold_pct: 10
    telemetry_sampling_pct: 10
```

FAQ and change log

- Q: Why are hints advisory not mandatory?
  A: Kernels have richer context about in-flight requests and memory graphs; advisory model preserves safety and prevents hard failures.
sections.heading: Bench commands (example)

sections.body:
- 2024-11-12 initial draft and prototype Operator integration.
- 2025-04-03 added prefetch budget enforcement and hint versioning.
- 2026-02-18 added canary gating rules and expanded benchmark matrix.

Related reading

- See runtime-execution-safety-matrix-2026 for safety invariants.
- See kvcache-epoch-synchronization-and-repair-procedures-2026 for epoch reconciliation procedures.

If you implement or modify the Operator or RIG, update this playbook and attach benchmark artifacts to the release notes before rolling past 30% canary.

payload.page_title: Experiment Governance and Release Gates Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines governance, metric gates, and operational procedures for running experiments that change the serving runtime surface: kernel selection, scheduling policies, KV cache heuristics, quantization rollouts, and runtime admission controllers. It consolidates requirements from runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, and release runbooks into a single actionable checklist for engineers and release managers.

Purpose and audience

- Purpose: Ensure safe, measurable, and auditable runtime experiments with clear release gates and rollback criteria.
- Audience: Runtime engineers, SREs, release managers, experiment owners, and applied ML engineers validating model-serving changes.

Scope

Applies to any change that touches the serving runtime execution path including but not limited to:
1) New or updated kernel implementations or kernel hints.
2) Scheduler policy changes (priority, preemption, admission).
3) Prefetch/KV cache algorithm changes or cache layout.
4) Quantization profile rollouts and mixed-fidelity execution.
5) Changes to batching logic and slotting/credit accounting.

Key concepts and decision model

- Risk tiering: Every experiment must be classified into Low / Medium / High risk. Classification factors: blast radius (cross-tenant potential), SLO sensitivity, frequency of affect, and revert complexity.
- Canonical metrics: latency P50/P95/P99, errors per 1000 requests, kernel-failure-rate, token-cost (per-1000 tokens), tail-kernel-duration, queue-depth distribution, successful-prefetch-rate, and fidelity-regression-score (from eval harness).
- Gate types: Canary gating (traffic slice + duration), Shadow gating (mirrored traffic), Microbench gating (isolated bench harness), and Staged rollout (percent-based ramp).

Experiment lifecycle and checklist

1) Proposal and classification (owner creates an experiment RFC with: description, affected services, implementation plan, risk tier, feature flag path, and target metrics).

2) Automated prechecks (CI):
   - Linting and static safety checks on kernel code.
   - Unit tests and deterministic scheduler simulation pass.
   - Performance microbench: baseline vs candidate on representative model snapshot (script provided below).

3) Offline evaluation:
   - Run the candidate through the benchmarking harness with the same request surface as prod for 1M synthetic tokens or 24h of replay, whichever is earlier.
   - Record per-token cost and throughput delta.
   - Run the fidelity suite (prompt set) and capture quality signals: F1, BLEU (if applicable), and our fidelity-regression-score.

4) Canary plan:
   - Canary size: start at 0.5% traffic for High risk, 1% for Medium, 5% for Low.
   - Canary duration: minimum 4 hours and until at least 10k live tokens have been served.
   - Observability hooks: enable detailed tracing (kernel spans), increase sampling of tail traces to 100% for canary cohort.

5) Gate evaluation:
   - Pass conditions (all must hold):
     a) Latency: P95 no worse than +10% relative to baseline and P99 no worse than +15% (configurable by risk tier).
     b) Errors: error-rate increase <= +0.05 errors/1k requests.
     c) Kernel reliability: kernel-failure-rate < 0.01% and no escalation events in runtime watchdog.
     d) Cost: per-token cost delta <= +8% for throughput-optimized rollouts.
     e) Fidelity: fidelity-regression-score <= 0.5 points drop (or owner-provided SLA).
     f) Observability: required traces and metrics flowing and not sampling-masked.

   - Fail conditions (any triggers immediate rollback):
     a) P99 latency regression > +25% or P95 > +40% for High risk experiments.
     b) Error-rate increase > +0.2 errors/1k.
     c) Any kernel panic/watchdog node hang.
     d) Model-quality regressions above threshold defined in the RFC.

6) Staged rollout and primary release:
   - Ramp schedule: exponential ramp doubling every 6–12 hours with metric-level check at each step.
   - Final gate: full cluster performance benchmark on a representative mixed-workload shadow for 6 hours with no critical threshold breaches.

Rollback and incident interaction

- If a fail condition is observed, the oncall or experiment owner must:
  1) Flip the feature flag to revert candidate.
  2) Notify SRE and runtime owners in #runtime-incidents with a short post including metrics and trace links.
  3) Open a postmortem stub (template below) within 24 hours.

- For partial degradations (e.g., localized node issues), consider throttling the rollout, isolating faulty topology (node affinity), and running targeted kernel telemetry collection rather than full rollback.

Telemetry and required signals
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- metric.runtime.latency.{p50,p95,p99}.percentile (per-model and per-route)
- metric.runtime.errors.perk (errors per 1k requests)
- metric.kernel.failure_rate
- metric.kvcache.hit_rate
- trace.kernel.span with attributes: kernel.name, kernel.variant, seq_len, request_id
- metric.token.cost.per_1000
- sample.trace.tail (100% for canary cohort)

Profiling and targeted investigation steps

When a threshold is near a gate limit, follow this profiling recipe:
1) Reproduce with microbench harness: use the candidate build and the 'production-replay-corpus' with:
   ./bench/run_microbench --build=canary --model=gpt-compat --tokens=200000 --concurrency=32 --kvcache=true

2) Attach kernel tracer and collect 1k tail traces:
   - Enable kernel debug span: curl -X POST $OBS_API/trace-config -d '{"sampling": "100%", "filters": ["kernel.span.tail"] }'
   - Use kernel-timeline tool: kernel-timeline --input traces.json --group-by kernel.name --percentiles 50,95,99

3) Heap/fragmentation and GPU diagnostics: run the GPU memory profiler and the allocator snapshotter:
   - gpu-prof --pid $RUNTIME_PID --duration 60s > gpu-snapshot.json
   - allocator-dump > alloc-$(date +%s).json

4) Scheduler contended path: replay the canary trace with the scheduler-sim binary to observe admission drops and preemption events:
   scheduler-sim --replay traces.json --policy candidate.json --output sim-report.json

Benchmarking harness and pass/fail example YAML
sections.heading: Minimum telemetry the experiment must produce

sections.body:
---
job: runtime-microbench
build: canary
model: llama-13b
corpus: production-replay-corpus
tokens: 1000000
concurrency_profiles: [burst, steady, poisson]
measurements:
  - latency_p95
  - p99_tail_latency
  - tokens_per_sec
  - kernel_fallbacks
pass_criteria:
  latency_p95: "<= baseline * 1.10"
  p99_tail_latency: "<= baseline * 1.15"
  tokens_per_sec: ">= baseline * 0.95"
  kernel_fallbacks: "<= 0.005%"
---

Release orchestration and roles

- Experiment owner: authors RFC, tracks the gate, owns rollback.
- Runtime SRE: configures canary traffic split, escalates to infra on hardware issues.
- Observability owner: ensures traces/metrics are enabled and dashboards available.
- Release manager: signs off on staged roll when canary gates pass.

Template: RFC/Canary plan (text fields to include)

- Title
- Summary and motivation
- Affected paths (services, kernels, schedulers)
- Risk tier and justification
- Telemetry required (list)
- Microbench baseline results (attach artifact link)
- Canary size & ramp schedule
- Pass/fail gates (numeric thresholds)
- Rollback plan and estimated revert time
- Post-rollout monitoring window

Known issues catalogue excerpt (how to document and label)

When filing a known issue for an experiment, include these labels in the ticket: [runtime, kernel, experiment-{id}, sla-impact-{low|medium|high}]. Use the following template in the ticket body:
- Observed behaviour
- First-seen timestamp and canary ID
- Affected topology/nodes
- Reproducer steps (ideally microbench command)
- Attached traces and trace IDs
- Immediate mitigation taken

Postmortem and continuous improvement

- Create a concise postmortem that includes timeline, root cause hypothesis, remediation, and preventative actions. Tag the experiment RFC and link the microbench artifacts and dashboards.
- Quarterly review: the runtime team will review all High and Medium risk experiments for pattern detection (SLO regressions, kernel instability patterns) and update the gate thresholds or CI microbench profiles accordingly.

Appendices

A. Example quick rollback CLI
- Toggle feature flag: curl -X POST $FF_API/flags/candidate-kernel -d '{"state":"off"}'
- Evict canary session cohort: ./runtime-admin evict --cohort canary-2026-01-18

B. Postmortem stub (plain text)
- Title:
- Summary (1–2 sentences):
- Timeline:
- Impact (SLOs breached, customer-visible):
- Root cause:
- Remediation and follow-ups:
- Owner:

C. Observability dashboard checklist
- Canary overview tile (p50/p95/p99 over time)
- Kernel variant heatmap (counts and failures)
- KV cache hit-rate and eviction rate by prefix length
- Token-cost and throughput by model and route

D. Escalation contacts (roles)
- Runtime oncall: @runtime-oncall (rotation)
- Kernel lead: Diego Martinez (diego@redwood.com)
- SRE lead: Ava Chen (ava@redwood.com)
- Observability lead: Rohit Singh (rohit@redwood.com)

E. Related documents
- Runtime decision graph and behaviour catalog (internal)
- Continuous profiling strategy (internal)
- Microbench harness README (repo link)

If you are preparing an experiment and need a quick sanity review, ping #runtime-experiments and attach the RFC link and the benchmark artifact URL.
