payload.page_title: runtime-failure-scenario-simulator-and-capture-format-2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the Runtime Failure Scenario Simulator (RFSS): a deterministic, configurable simulator and a compact capture format for recording real production requests and environment signals so we can reliably reproduce and reason about failures, regressions, and scheduling anomalies in the serving runtime. RFSS is intended for engineering teams working on kernel scheduling, shard placement, eviction, and KV-cache warmup logic.

Motivation
----------
We frequently observe complex multitenant failures and regressions that are hard to reproduce in a lab because:
- Production request mixes, ordering, and interleaving matter (prefix caching, KV hits).
- Heterogeneous GPU topology and eviction interactions vary by tenant co-location.
- Timing-sensitive scheduler decisions (preemption, handoff) only manifest at specific concurrency shapes.

RFSS gives a small, portable way to:
1) Capture a faithful snapshot of request traces + environment signals (compact capture format).
2) Re-run the captured workload in a simulator that models kernel queueing, KV-cache state, and tenant credit accounting.
3) Produce deterministic diagnostics (latency decomposition, kernel timeline, eviction traces) to accelerate triage and root cause analysis.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Multitenant inference request captures (HTTP/gRPC metadata + token-level lengths + decision traces).
- Runtime signals required for scheduling decisions (queue depths, current kernel credits, per-shard memory headroom).
- Deterministic simulator that approximates kernel dispatch latencies, backpressure, and preemption effects.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Full-cycle GPU microarchitectural simulation (we rely on parametric latency models derived from microbenchmarks).
- Privacy-sensitive payload retention (customer prompt text is redacted by default; refer to Data Handling section).

Design overview
---------------
- Capture layer (edge-side hook): lightweight capture that samples requests and enriches them with provenance: tenant_id, model_variant, seq_len, request_timestamp, and scheduler-decision-snapshot (priority, affinity, quota_token_balance).
- Compact capture format (.rfscap): newline-delimited JSON records with a header describing environment parameters and a sequence of request events. Each event contains token counts and pointers to anonymized prompt hashes if full text is not stored.
- Simulator core: event-driven discrete-time simulator with components: KernelQueue, KVCacheModel, ShardTopology, AdmissionController. Each component exposes a minimal state API to load snapshot values and emit time-annotated events.
- Output artifacts: kernel-timeline.tsv, eviction-log.ndjson, latency-decomposition.txt, deterministic replay log (.rfsreplay).

Capture format (compact, human-reviewable)
----------------------------------------
Top-level header (single JSON object, required):
| key | description | example |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| version | capture schema version | "1.0" |
| cluster_profile | named cluster profile used during capture | "gpc-prod-eu" |
| seed_time | UTC timestamp of capture start | "2026-02-10T12:05:23Z" |
| topology_snapshot | short token summarizing shard mapping | "shardmap-v12" |

Each subsequent line is a JSON event record. Example event fields:
- ts: absolute timestamp (ms since epoch)
- req_id: opaque id
- tenant: tenant short id (redacted)
- model: model id and variant
- seq_len: user token length (int)
- kv_hint: small set of cache keys touched (list of short strings)
- scheduler_snapshot: {priority, aff_group, credit_balance} (stringified map)
- probe_meta: optional performance probes captured at edge (latency_ms)

Note: because JSON objects in the capture events must be single-line, the format is NDJSON-style with escape conventions.

Simulator components and models
-------------------------------
1) KernelQueue
- Model: token-based service time model: service_time_ms = kernel_base_ms + per_token_ms * seq_len * kernel_multiplier(model_family).
- Admission: takes scheduler priority and kernel credits into account. If credits insufficient, sim emits "deferred" event and queues.

2) KVCacheModel
- Tracks warm/cold key sets per shard. Cache hit reduces per_token_ms by a hit_reduction_factor. Eviction follows LRU with configurable bucket sizes.

3) ShardTopology
- Abstracts the mapping of requests to physical shards and NUMA domains. Topology file is loaded from the capture header and supports simulating NUMA-induced transfer penalties.

4) AdmissionController / Scheduler
- Implements the same priority/credit semantics as production: token-bucket crediting, preemption thresholds, and cooperative yielding. The simulator exposes knobs: preemption_grace_ms, max_inflight_per_tenant, kernel_credit_decay_window_ms.

Operational runbook: capture -> reproduce -> triage
--------------------------------------------------
1) When to capture:
- Any persistent latency regression (>2x p99 observed vs baseline) or kernel-related error spikes (GPU watchdog, kernel OOM).
- Every failed canary during runtime rollout.

2) Capture procedure (engineer-facing):
1. From the incident page, request capture slot and mark timeframe.
2. Enable RFSS capture for 5–20 minutes with sample rate conservatively set (default 1:1000) or higher for targeted tenants.
   - CLI: rfsctl capture start --profile gpc-prod-eu --duration 600 --sample-rate 0.01 --tenants=T123,T456
3. Wait capture window, then stop and securely upload to the sandbox bucket: rfsctl capture stop --upload s3://redwood-sandbox/rfscaps/2026-02-10/
4. Create a simulator job: rfsctl simulate --cap s3://.../capture.rfscap --profile lab-simulator-small --seed 12345 --output s3://.../replays/

3) Reproduce steps:
1. Run simulator in deterministic mode using the capture header seed.
2. Compare simulator output artifacts to production traces (latency histograms, kernel-timeline).
3. If mismatch beyond tolerance, iterate by adjusting cluster_profile parameters (kernel_base_ms, per_token_ms, numav_penalty_ms).

4) Triage checklist (results-driven):
- If the simulator reproduces the regression: extract the earliest divergent event and trace back to scheduler_snapshot differences.
- If simulator shows eviction storms, flag "eviction-correlated-latency" and assign to kernel-scheduler oncall.
- If simulator fails to reproduce any backlog but production had tail latencies, escalate to SRE for topology-level investigation (nvlink issues, node-level watchdogs).

Example config table (simulator knobs)
| knob | default | description | safe-range |
|------|---------|-------------|-----------|
| kernel_base_ms | "0.4" | base kernel dispatch overhead in ms | "0.1 - 2.0" |
| per_token_ms | "0.03" | additional per-token work in ms | "0.01 - 0.1" |
| hit_reduction_factor | "0.55" | multiplier applied when KV cache hits | "0.3 - 0.95" |
| preemption_grace_ms | "8" | delay before preemptible tasks are yielded | "1 - 50" |

Data handling and privacy
-------------------------
- By default, prompt_text is omitted. Captures contain prompt_hash and short tokenized fingerprint. Teams may request full text for escalations; access requires security approval and an audit entry.
- Captures are TTL'd to 90 days in the sandbox and archived only with explicit owner approval.

Acceptance criteria for a good capture
-------------------------------------
- Contains at least 10k request events across affected tenants or 1 hour of contiguous traffic, whichever is smaller.
- Includes topology_snapshot that matches the production cluster profile used in the incident.
- Sampled scheduler_snapshot fields are present for >95% of events.

Integration and tooling roadmap (next 12 months)
------------------------------------------------
- Q2: Add automated diff tool that highlights scheduler_snapshot deltas aligned with latency spikes.
- Q3: Expose a web UI to playback kernel-timeline and zoom to eviction hot spots.
- Q4: Add a lightweight on-host collector that records fine-grained NVLink/temperature signals to improve NUMA modeling.

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Owner: Kernel & Scheduler team (primary), Observability team (secondary).
- Oncall routing: kernel-scheduler oncall receives alerts when simulator reproduces an "eviction storm" label.
- Expected turnaround: 48 business hours from new capture uploaded to a first diagnostic pass.

Appendix A: Example capture event (single-line NDJSON)
{"ts":164+000, "req_id":"r-9f3b", "tenant":"T123", "model":"redwood-7b.q4", "seq_len":234, "kv_hint":["k:lice-23"], "scheduler_snapshot":"p=high;aff=zone-a;credits=12", "probe_meta":{"edge_latency_ms":3}}

Appendix B: Troubleshooting notes
- If simulation fails with inconsistent kernel_base_ms, run the microbenchmark harness to recalibrate the model: tools/kernel-microbench --profile gpc-prod-eu --out calib.json
- For persistent mismatches with production, add a focused production-run with "shadow-mode" simulation to capture unresolved variables.

Contact and further reading
-------------------------
- RFC: runtime-replay-and-capture-rfc-2025 (internal link)
- Owners: Asha Natarajan (kernel & scheduling), Liam Chen (observability)
- Slack channel: #rfs-sim

payload.page_title: Observability Adapter Sidecar: Design Manual and Onboarding Guide

sections.body:
Overview

This document describes the design, operational contracts, and onboarding checklist for the Observability Adapter Sidecar (OAS)—a lightweight per-node sidecar that attaches to serving runtime processes and provides production-safe, low-overhead instrumentation for per-request fidelity signals, adaptive sampling, and enriched traces. It is intended for runtime engineers, profiling owners, and SREs who will operate and extend the OAS.

Goals

- Provide a stable, low-latency mechanism for enriching requests with fidelity metadata (kernel hints, kv-cache hit/miss, quantization variant).
- Support adaptive, policy-driven sampling that balances observability coverage with cost and privacy constraints.
- Decouple heavy signal processing from the hot runtime path via asynchronous sinks and backpressure-aware queues.
- Offer clear contracts so runtime teams can consume telemetry without coupling to probe implementations.

Scope and Non-Goals

- In scope: sidecar API contract, sampling controller protocol, configuration schema, rollout checklist, security constraints, and troubleshooting playbook.
- Not in scope: changes to kernel scheduling heuristics, evaluation algorithms for model quality, or storage-side analytics pipelines (those are handled by telemetry-backend teams).

Design Principles

1. Non-blocking hot path: sidecar must not add synchronous latency to inference token emission or RPC response paths.
2. Bounded memory & predictable cost: local queues have strict bounds; policies exist to drop or aggregate when saturated.
3. Policy-driven behavior: sampling and enrichment governed by remote policy controller with health-fallback to cached defaults.
4. Minimal privileges: run with least privilege; network egress only to approved telemetry endpoints.
5. Observable and debuggable: expose health, queue-length, and sampling-rate metrics for immediate SLO correlation.

Architecture (text diagram)

- Serving process (runtime) <--> Local IPC socket (unix/grpc) <--> Observability Adapter Sidecar (OAS)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Ingress listener: small sync layer to accept lightweight event envelopes (<= 1KB) over unix socket.
  - Adaptive sampler: local policy engine + short-lived remote policy cache (refresh TTL 30s).
  - Local aggregator & aggregator worker pool: batch events and flush asynchronously to sink.
  - Backpressure manager: implements admission/drop + p99 tail guard for sync APIs.
  - Telemetry sink: pluggable output (http/gRPC to telemetry backend, local file for debug).

Component Contracts

1) Ingress contract
- Envelope format: JSON lines or protobuf-lite. Required fields: request_id, model_variant, shard_id, event_ts_iso, event_type, token_count, kernel_hint (optional), kvcache_status (hit/miss/partial), extra_tags (map).
- Max envelope size: 1024 bytes. Larger events must be truncated and flagged.

2) Sampling controller contract
- Policy model: simple JSON with rules (matchers on route/model/metadata) and actions (sample_rate 0.0-1.0, aggregate:true/false, redact_fields:list).
- Local behavior: if controller unreachable, fall back to baked-in policy at start-up and operate in degraded mode.

3) Sink contract
- Accept batched payloads via HTTP POST application/json with Authorization: Telemetry-Key header.
- Retry policy: exponential backoff capped at 5 retries, then drop and increment metric oas.sink.drop_count.

Configuration (example YAML)

-- oas-config.yaml --
listen:
  unix_socket: "/var/run/oas.sock"
  max_concurrent_ingress: 64
sampler:
  policy_url: "https://telemetry-policy.internal/api/v1/policy"
  refresh_interval_seconds: 30
  default_policy:
    - matcher: "route == '/v1/completions' and model_variant =~ '.*-quant'"
      action:
        sample_rate: 0.05
        aggregate: false
queue:
  max_items: 20000
  max_bytes: 50MB
sink:
  url: "https://telemetry-ingest.internal/v1/ingest"
  auth_header: "Telemetry-Key: ${OAS_KEY}"
  batch_max_size: 100
  flush_interval_ms: 200
security:
  allowed_egress_hosts: ["telemetry-ingest.internal"]
  run_as_user: "oas-agent"
  restrict_capabilities: true

Operational Signals and Metrics (as a text table)

Metric name | Type | SLI indication | Alert threshold
oas.health | gauge | service up | health == 0 for 3m
oas.queue.length | gauge | admission pressure | queue.length > 80% for 5m
oas.sampler.effective_rate | gauge | observability coverage | effective_rate < configured - 10%
oas.sink.latency_p50/p95 | histogram | sink performance | p95 > 5s
oas.sink.drop_count | counter | data loss | drop_count increase > 100/min

Deployment and Rollout Checklist (numbered)

1. Pre-flight validation:
   a. Verify unix socket permissions and SELinux/AppArmor policy.
   b. Confirm OAS container resource limits: CPU 200m, mem 128Mi to start.
   c. Validate policy endpoint reachable from canary nodes.
2. Canary (5% nodes):
   a. Enable OAS in 'observe-only' mode (sample_rate=0, aggregate=true) and flow to debug sink.
   b. Check oas.queue.length and oas.sink.latency_p95 for regressions.
   c. Confirm no increase in serving p99 latency beyond 1%.
3. Progressive ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 72h observing signals; adjust sample rates if sink latency increases.
4. Enable adaptive sampling live with conservative initial policies (global sample_rate <= 0.02).

Validation Tests (quick list)

- Latency regression: run synthetic replay with representative token distributions and ensure p99 latency delta < 2%.
- Failure injection: block sink and verify OAS backpressure behavior and that serving continues with bounded memory.
- Policy mismatch: deploy an invalid policy payload and confirm OAS rejects it and reverts to cached default.

Troubleshooting Runbook (step-by-step)

1. Symptom: increased serving p99 at peak.
   - Check oas.queue.length and oas.sink.p95. If both spike, scale sink or reduce sample_rate.
2. Symptom: oas.health == 0 on node.
   - Examine sidecar logs /var/log/oas/*.log for startup failures, permission errors, or TLS issues.
   - If crashloop, isolate with strace and check for blocked socket binds.
3. Symptom: high oas.sink.drop_count.
   - Verify telemetry backend auth and rate limits. Rotate keys if auth failures are observed.
4. Symptom: privacy violation flag from telemetry-backend.
   - Immediately enable redact_fields in policy and trigger a 'flush-and-scrub' protocol (contact telemetry-backend runbook).

Security and Data Protection

- PII redaction: sidecar must support policy-driven redaction of fields and should never transmit raw user_prompt unless expressly allowed by customer config.
- Egress controls: OAS must respect allowed_egress_hosts and refuse any unexpected DNS resolutions.
- Keys & secrets: use instance-level KMS-wrapped keys, not environment-injected plaintext secrets.
- Auditing: emit audit events for every policy change and policy fetch with timestamp and signature verification.

Extension Points for Runtime Teams

- Kernel hint schemas: runtime owners can add new kernel_hint keys but must submit a schema bump PR to runtime-telemetry contract repo and add mapping to the downstream ingest pipeline.
- Aggregation plugins: teams can propose a custom aggregator (e.g., histogram summarizer) that implements the aggregator gRPC signature. These plugins must pass the plugin-safety CI suite.

Onboarding Checklist for New Runtime Projects

- Implement a small adapter client that serializes envelopes to the unix socket. Example snippet:

curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/oas.sock -X POST http://localhost/enqueue -d '{"request_id":"r1","model_variant":"redwood-7b","event_ts_iso":"2026-03-01T12:00:00Z","event_type":"response","token_count":24}'

- Add OAS sidecar to your Pod spec with resource limits and a readiness probe:

containers:
  - name: oas-agent
    image: registry.internal/infra/oas:2026-02-01
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "200m"
        memory: "128Mi"
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command: ["/usr/bin/oasctl","health"]
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10

Ownership and SLAs

- Primary owner: runtime-observability team (pager: oncall-runtime-obsv).
- Support escalation: send to infra-sre@redwood.ai and telemetry-backend oncall if sink outages exceed 5 minutes.
- Operational SLO: OAS health >= 99.5% monthly and effective sampling coverage within 10% of policy target.

Change Management and Policy Review

- All policy schema changes must be reviewed by telemetry-backend and privacy team.
- Major behavioral changes (e.g., switching to synchronous enrichments) require a canary plan and sign-off from runtime performance sig.

Appendix: Example Sampling Policy JSON

{
  "version": "1",
  "rules": [
    {"matcher": "model_variant =~ '.*-quant'","action": {"sample_rate": 0.02,"aggregate": false}},
    {"matcher": "route == '/v1/chat' and tenant in ['enterprise-a']","action": {"sample_rate": 0.2,"aggregate": false}},
    {"matcher": "default","action": {"sample_rate": 0.005,"aggregate": true}}
  ]
}

Frequently Asked Questions (short)

Q: Will enabling OAS slow down my model?
A: When configured per the rollout checklist, OAS is bounded to add <1% p99 latency. If you observe larger regressions, check queue saturation and sampler policies.

Q: How do I add a new telemetry field?
A: File a schema PR to the telemetry-contracts repo, include a migration plan for existing ingestion pipelines, and coordinate with telemetry-backend for parsers.

Related pages and next steps

- Implement the client adapter template in runtime-examples repo and submit for review.
- Coordinate with telemetry-backend to register your model_variant mapping.

Document history

- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Patel.
- 2026-02-10: Added rollout checklist and sink contract after SOC review.
- 2026-03-01: Final edits and published.

payload.page_title: Runtime Instrumentation Catalog and Incident Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the canonical runtime instrumentation catalog for the serving runtime, the metric and trace contracts teams must follow, and an investigation playbook for the most common performance incidents. It merges runtime architecture signal expectations, kernel scheduler hooks, profiling runbooks, and how the benchmarking suite should be used to validate instrumentation changes.

Scope and audience
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, profiling engineers, and release owners who change execution, kernels, or observability.
- Scope: production and canary environments for Redwood Inference hosting and Dedicated clusters. Does not cover client SDK metrics.

Key goals
- Provide a small, stable set of metric and trace contracts that are cheap to collect and sufficient for SLO ownership.
- Standardize kernel-level signals that scheduler engineers must expose to telemetry.
- Offer a reproducible profiling and benchmarking workflow for validating changes to instrumentation and scheduler behavior.
- Provide step-by-step incident triage for tail latency and kernel hang patterns.

Metric and trace contract catalog (single-table view)
Note: this table is the ground truth for dashboards, SLOs, alerts, and benchmarking assertions. Keep stable names; rename only via ADR and release notes.

| Service | Metric name | Interpretation | Owner | SLI window | SLO | Alert threshold |
| Serving Runtime | runtime.request.p95_ms | p95 end-to-end runtime request latency excluding queue time | runtime-observability | 5m | p95 < 120 ms | p95 > 250 ms for 3m |
| Serving Runtime | runtime.kvcache.hit_rate | fraction of token-level KV cache hits | runtime-cache | 1h | > 0.75 across traffic | drop > 0.15 relative to baseline in 15m |
| Kernel Dispatcher | kernel.dispatch.utilization | GPU kernel dispatch utilization (0-1) | kernel-scheduler | 5m | 0.35-0.85 is healthy | sustained > 0.95 or < 0.15 for 10m |
| Kernel Dispatcher | kernel.preempt.count | number of cooperative preemptions per minute | kernel-scheduler | 1h | < 5/min averaged | > 20/min in 10m |
| Network | grpc.connection.reuse_rate | fraction of reused connections | infra-network | 1h | > 0.8 | drop below 0.5 for 30m |

Instrumentation guidance and conventions
- Metric naming: dot-separated domain.prefix.metric. Use lower case and underscores only for labels.
- Units: always append units in metric descriptions (ms, bytes, percent). Avoid unitless counters unless absolute counts.
- Cardinality: labels are limited to runtime, model_family, model_variant, region. Do not introduce free-form user identifiers.
- Sampling: traces default to 0.5% in production; increase to 2% on canaries. For kernel events, use deterministic sampling for error paths and probabilistic sampling for happy-path events.
- Baggage and spans: top-level span name must be request_id. Span tags: model, sequence_length, route.

Kernel scheduler signals and hooks
- Exposed signals: kernel.dispatch.start, kernel.dispatch.end, kernel.kernel_hint (quantization_level, preferred_slice), kernel.kvcache.prefetch_hits, kernel.handoff.reason.
- Hook semantics: kernel.dispatch.start must be emitted before any GPU work. kernel.dispatch.end must include kernel.wall_ms and kernel.tokens_produced. kernel.handoff.reason must be one of: preemption, eviction, migration, thermal_throttle.
- Backpressure indicator: runtime.queue.depth_by_priority. Use this with kernel.dispatch.utilization to compute admission decisions.

Profiling playbook: when and how to profile
1) Trigger conditions
   - Regression alert fires for runtime.request.p95_ms or kernel.dispatch.utilization anomalies.
   - Release candidate that introduces kernel or scheduler code.
2) Safe sampling plan
   - Start with live sample at 0.5% using tracing agent. Collect 10k requests or 1 hour minimum.
   - For kernel-level deep samples, schedule a controlled profiling job on canaries with overlay traffic at 10% of production QPS.
3) Commands and artifacts to collect
   - tcpdump and connection logs around the incident window (if networking suspected).
   - Kernel traces: enable kernel hook logging level 3 and collect 60s of GPU metrics via nvidia-smi or platform agent.
   - Use the profiling harness: ./tools/profiler/run_sampled_capture --trace-rate 0.01 --duration 3600 --tag regression-YYYYMMDD
4) Analysis checklist
   - Decompose latency by span: pre-queue, queue, kernel dispatch, post-process. If kernel dispatch dominates, open kernel investigation.
   - Correlate kvcache.hit_rate drops with sequence length changes.
   - Look for sudden increases in kernel.preempt.count or kernel.handoff.reason=thermal_throttle.

Benchmarking suite integration
- Purpose: validate that instrumentation changes do not skew SLOs or increase overhead beyond threshold.
- Baseline rules: every PR that changes metric emission or adds tags must run the microbenchmark suite that asserts per-token CPU overhead < 1.2x baseline and p95 latency variance < 5%.
- Synthetic corpus: use workload lanes defined in workloads/catalog.yaml where lanes include short-chat, long-infer, embedding-batch. Always run short-chat and long-infer.
- Representative test matrix: model families (small, medium, large), sequence lengths (32, 256, 1024), batch shapes (1x1, 8x8).

Release notes snippet (example for instrumentation changes)
- v2.4.0-instrumentation: Added kernel.handoff.reason field and reduced default trace sampling to 0.5% in prod. Backwards compatibility: dashboards continue to read runtime.request.p95_ms. Migration: update any alert rules that used deprecated tag "kernel_phase".

Known issues and guidance
- Issue: transient kvcache hit_rate drop on warm startups. Workaround: enable kvcache.warmup_hint for canaries to prefetch top 10k prefixes.
- Issue: occasional nvlink interconnect flapping shows as kernel.dispatch.utilization oscillation. Guidance: treat as infra/networking incident and escalate to infra-network team.
- Issue: high preemption counts after scheduler changes. If kernel.preempt.count > 20/min, rollback scheduler commit or apply temporary admission controller to reduce concurrency by 30%.

Incident triage playbook: high tail latency (p95 spike)
Step 0: Declare incident if p95 > 250 ms for 3 consecutive minutes and SLO burn expected. Notify oncall and post to channel #runtime-incident.
Step 1: Immediately check top-line signals
   - runtime.request.p95_ms, runtime.request.error_rate, kernel.dispatch.utilization, runtime.queue.depth_by_priority
Step 2: Narrow to span that increased
   - Use trace sample drilldown to find whether queue or kernel dispatch increased. If queue increased, jump to Step 4. If kernel dispatch increased, go to Step 3.
Step 3: Kernel investigation
   - Check kernel.preempt.count, kernel.handoff.reason, kernel.kernel_hint distributions.
   - If preemptions are high, run a canary with reduced concurrency. If handoffs show thermal_throttle, open hardware ops ticket.
Step 4: Queue and admission control
   - Inspect request arrival rate and admission controller logs.
   - If backpressure misconfiguration suspected, apply emergency admission policy: reject low-priority routes and reduce max tokens per request by 20%.
Step 5: Mitigation and rollback
   - If a recent deploy is implicated, follow the runtime deployment circuit breaker and rollback matrix. If not, apply temporary circuit breakers and schedule deeper profiling.
Step 6: Postmortem
   - Fill incident template: impact, root cause hypothesis, timeline, remediation, monitoring changes, action items. Assign a 2-week follow-up for regression test addition.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary oncall: runtime SRE rotation. Secondary: kernel-scheduler rotation. Tertiary: infra-network oncall.
- Pager duty runbook link: docs/pagerduty-runtime (internal link).

Related pages and anchors
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration (architecture contract)
- kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector (scheduler test harness)
- profiling-playbook/controlled-kernel-perturbation-playbook (kernel perturbation lab)

Appendix: common CLI snippets
- Quick latency decomposition using trace sampler: curl -X POST https://canary-api.internal/trace/decompose -d '{ request_id: R123 }'
- Start a controlled profiling capture on canary: ./tools/profiler/start_capture --env canary --tag perf-capture --duration 300

Document maintenance
- This document is the central catalog for metric and kernel signal contracts. Any change to names, units, or cardinality requires an ADR and a release-note entry.
- Owner: runtime-observability. Review cadence: quarterly or ahead of any major scheduler release.

payload.page_title: Execution Telemetry Quorum and Sampling Policy

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the Execution Telemetry Quorum and Sampling Policy for Redwood's serving runtime. It explains the signals we collect, the quorum rules used to trigger high-fidelity capture, the sampling knobs available to runtime operators and SREs, and operational playbooks for incidents and benchmarks. The goal is to balance diagnostic fidelity for production incidents and regressions with telemetry cost and privacy constraints.

Why this matters

- Full-fidelity traces for all requests are prohibitively expensive (bandwidth, storage, ingestion cost).
- Certain failures and regressions only manifest under narrow execution cohorts; a simple uniform sampler reduces reproducibility.
- Kernel-level scheduling signals, KV-cache deltas, and cross-device handoff traces are high-value for root-cause analysis but high-cost to capture.
- We need a deterministic, auditable policy that: preserves SLO observability, limits cost, enables postmortem reproducibility, and supports controlled ramping during experiments.

Scope and definitions

- Execution telemetry: structured traces, kernel scheduling events, per-kernel latency histograms, KV cache hit/miss traces, device-to-device handoff events, and request provenance metadata.
- Quorum: a multi-signal predicate that determines whether a specific request execution should be elevated to high-fidelity capture.
- Sampling knob types: uniform, cohort-based, adaptive, and quorum-triggered.

Quorum signals (used in predicates)

1) SLO breach candidate: request latency > 95th percentile for route/model for the last 15 minutes.
2) Kernel anomaly: per-kernel execution time > kernel_baseline * 3 (fast local baseline).
3) Cross-tenant contention signal: GPU kernel preemption or eviction events observed within request lifetime.
4) KV cache warmup failure: expected cached prefix missing for an established session (session age > 1 minute).
5) Error family match: any 5xx or structured runtime error matching the incident regex list.

Quorum policy (default production)

- Elevate to high-fidelity capture when any two distinct quorum signals are true for the same request OR when a single critical signal is flagged (Error family match or GPU preemption).
- High-fidelity capture includes: complete kernel event stream, full per-token scheduler decisions, gpu telemetry slice, request input/output payloads (redacted), and KV cache deltas.

Sampling tiers and retention

- Baseline (always-on): lightweight request metrics and sparse trace IDs (1% uniform). Retention: 90 days aggregated metrics, 7 days indexed traces.
- Diagnostic (cohort-based): 5% of traffic per high-risk route (see table below) or cohort sampling determined by route annotations. Retention: 30 days indexed traces.
- Quorum-captured (elevated): retained for 90 days in compressed archive with access controls; access requires incident ticket and approval.

Operational table: sampling defaults by route profile

- low-latency-read: uniform 0.5% (embeddings, short completions).
- interactive-chat: uniform 1%, cohort 3% for power users.
- long-generation: uniform 2%, cohort 10% for pinned beta customers.
- batch-embedding-job: uniform 0.2%, cohort capture via job-id sampling 1%.

(Operators can override per-customer using route config in Redwood Console; see "How to override" below.)

Cost/benchmark impact guidance

- Turning on kernel-level event capture increases per-request telemetry payload by ~8–12KB and ingestion CPU by ~1.4x in our benchmarks. Expect storage 10x for full request-level captures vs. aggregated metrics.
- Benchmarks run with high-fidelity capture enabled should use the "telemetry-isolated" flag to prevent polluted baseline comparisons. See the CLI section below.

Implementation notes (runtime hooks)

- Kernel scheduler hooks: place a light-weight hook at kernel dispatch entry to emit a 64-byte token with request id and scheduling decision. Hooks must be non-blocking and batch-emitted at 50ms intervals.
- KV cache tracing: emit a compact diff (keys touched, miss/hit) with session id and hashed prefix. Do not include raw prompt text unless redaction pass is applied.
- Device handoff: emit handshake events with device ids, estimated queue depth, and kernel queue latency.

Sample quorum predicate (YAML)

quorum:
  version: 1
  rules:
    - id: slo_and_kernel
      description: "Latency spike + kernel abnormality"
      predicates:
        - signal: slo_breach_candidate
        - signal: kernel_anomaly
      require: 2
    - id: critical_error
      description: "Immediate capture on critical errors"
      predicates:
        - signal: error_family_match
      require: 1

How to override sampling in Console (step-by-step)

1) Navigate to Console > Runtime > Routes and select the route.
2) Click "Telemetry" tab.
3) Edit Sampling Profile: choose baseline/cohort/quorum-enabled.
4) Optional: attach a temporary experiment tag (telemetry.debug=true, expiry in 24h). Changes are audited and emitted as config diff to S3: s3://redwood-runtime-configs/telemetry-overrides.
5) Monitor cost impact: Console shows estimated daily ingestion delta before committing.

Runbook: incident capture and access flow (for SREs)

1) Triage: determine whether the incident is reproducible and whether quorum predicates would have captured examples.
2) If not captured, flip a cohort override for the affected route with a 10x cohort multiplier for 30 minutes. Use the CLI: redwood telemetry override --route <route> --multiplier 10 --duration 30m --reason "incident PID-<id>".
3) Collect captures: link to S3 tarball in the incident ticket. Retain copy in incident workspace (encrypted).
4) Postmortem: annotate the captured traces with kernel snapshot id, runtime version, and scheduler policy.

CLI examples
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: redwood telemetry override --route /v1/generate--chat --set quorum_enabled=true --duration 20m --owner sre-team
sections.heading: Enable ephemeral high-fidelity capture for route

sections.body:
redwood bench run --workload long-gen --telemetry-isolated=true --output ./bench-results

Privacy and redaction rules

- Request payloads are redacted by default: only prompt hashes and token counts are stored. Full text is captured only when: (a) customer consent is present, OR (b) explicit legal/incident approval is granted.
- PII redaction pipeline: apply token-level redaction that replaces probable PII tokens with <REDACTED_STRING> and emits confidence score.

Testing and rollout plan for changes to quorum policy

1) Developer preview: enable policy in the sandbox runtime (tag: telemetry-sandbox) for 1 week with 100% traffic in sandbox. Verify schema, CPU overhead <= +15%.
2) Canary: rollout 1% of production routes with telemetry-isolated benchmark. Monitor ingestion and per-token cost delta for 48h.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over rolling four-day windows. SRE gate: ingestion cost increase must be <= 30% of forecasted budget per stage.

Release notes (policy v1.2)

- 2026-01-18: v1.2 released. Key changes: added "cross-tenant contention" quorum signal, tightened default cohort rates for long-generation routes, introduced telemetry-isolated flag for benchmarks.

Known issues and mitigations

- #KT-1823: occasional race in kernel hook emission can drop the first scheduling token under high concurrency. Mitigation: bump batch flush window from 25ms to 50ms and retry on missing kernel snapshot.
- #KV-991: session-id collisions in high-throughput job batching caused misattribution in KV diffs. Mitigation: switch session-id generator to 128-bit random uuid and add job-id namespace.

Ownership and escalation

- Ownership: Observability Platform (owner) + Serving Runtime (maintainer). Primary contacts: observability@redwood.ai, runtime-oncall@redwood.ai.
- Escalation: if telemetry ingestion > 2x forecast, page Observability Platform lead and SRE. Use incident channel #telemetry-ops.

Appendix: schema snippets and sample JSON trace (compact)

- Compact trace example (fields explained):
{
  "trace_id": "abcd-1234",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "model": "rw-open-7b",
  "events": ["kernel_dispatch:ts:...","kv_cache_delta:...","handoff:..."],
  "meta": "schema_v1"
}

- Telemetry cost estimator quick lookup (Console): per-100k requests estimated delta with kernel_capture=on: +$1,200/day (region=us-west-2, as of 2026-01).

Related documentation

- Runtime tracing contract (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025.json
- Benchmarks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025.json

Contact and feedback

For questions or to propose changes to the policy, open a PR against the telemetry-policy repo in Git (gitlab.redwood.internal/git/telemetry-policy) and ping Eleanor Chen and Marco Ruiz for review.

Revision log

- 2025-09-15: Initial draft (Eleanor Chen)
- 2025-11-02: Added cohort default table and CLI examples (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-01-20: Formalized quorum signals and published v1.2 release notes (Marco Ruiz)

payload.page_title: Runtime integration service contracts and debugging cookbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This document specifies the operational contracts between the Redwood serving runtime and the wider platform (API surface, console, Dedicated/Private control planes, and developer tooling) and provides a pragmatic debugging cookbook for the most common oncall scenarios. The goal is to reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) by standardizing observability signals, log schemas, escalation steps, and safe remediation patterns for kernel and scheduler changes, profiling runs, and benchmark integrations.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: runtime engineers, platform engineers, SREs, SDK and developer-experience owners, and solutions engineers running Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Scope: request lifecycle contracts, kernel scheduling signals, profiling/playbook guidance, benchmark integration points, runbook steps for 3 common incidents, and a release/rollout checklist for kernel or runtime changes.

1) Service contract (request lifecycle)

Short summary: every inbound request into the runtime must carry a minimal set of headers and context for observability, routing, and cost accounting. The runtime must emit canonical telemetry during the five canonical phases: ingress, scheduling, kernel execution, KV/cache interactions, and egress.

Required request headers/context (in order of importance):
1. X-Request-Id: unique 128-bit hex string (UUID4 accepted).
2. X-Customer-Id: numeric tenant id or anonymous-token for hosted flows.
3. X-Route-Id: API route or model route identifier (string).
4. X-Desired-SLO-ms: integer SLO target (ms) to drive admission and priority decisions.
5. X-Experiment-Id (optional): A/B/canary identifier for rollout correlation.

Telemetry emission contract (every request):
- Ingress span: tags {request_id, customer_id, route_id, desired_slo_ms, payload_tokens} emitted at reception.
- Scheduling events: queue_enqueue, queue_dequeue, scheduling_decision (reason=priority/affinity/overloaded).
- Kernel span(s): per-kernel traces with attributes {kernel_variant, shard_id, sequence_length, effective_batch_size, kernel_latency_ms}.
- KV/cache events: kvcache_lookup, kvcache_hit/miss (include key pattern categories e.g., prompt-prefix/hash).
- Egress span: final status code, response_tokens, total_token_ms, tail_lat_ms.

2) Observability contract (metrics, logs, traces)

SLOs and key metrics to be exported to the metrics platform (Prometheus/OTLP):
- runtime_request_success_rate (1m, 5m windows) per route_id; SLO target 99.95% for hosted-critical routes.
- runtime_p50_latency_ms, runtime_p95_latency_ms, runtime_p99_latency_ms per (route_id, kernel_variant).
- runtime_queue_depth and runtime_enqueue_rate per scheduling pool (labels: pool_name, priority_level).
- kernel_cpu_utilization_percent, kernel_gpu_utilization_percent per shard.
- kvcache_hit_ratio and kvcache_eviction_rate per shard.
- kernel_oom_count and kernel_memory_pressure_events.

Suggested PromQL queries (store as saved queries):
- P95 latency for route r: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route_id="r"}[5m])) by (le)))
- KVCACHE MISS STORM: increase in miss rate: increase(kvcache_lookup_total{shard="*"}[5m]) - increase(kvcache_hit_total{shard="*"}[5m]) > 1000

Logging schema (single-line JSON log each major event):
| timestamp | level | component | request_id | event | payload | details |
Example log (kernel span start):
{
  "ts":"2026-03-02T15:24:18.123Z",
  "level":"INFO",
  "component":"kernel-runtime",
  "request_id":"8f7a4b2e-1c6b-4a2d-b9d3-4f2c7a1a9f2e",
  "event":"kernel_start",
  "kernel_variant":"kv-quant-int8-v2",
  "shard_id":"shard-21",
  "sequence_length":1024,
  "effective_batch_size":6
}

Tracing contract: every request must be traceable end-to-end with a 128-bit trace id and per-span attributes matching the telemetry contract above. Span names should be stable: ingress, schedule, kernel:<variant>, kvcache:<op>, egress.

3) Kernel and scheduler change rollout checklist (safe rollout and rollback)

Pre-rollout (dev->canary):
- Benchmarks: run microbenchmark suite for candidate kernel against baseline using the stable-run harness (sample config block below).
- Static checks: kernel binary signature, schema validation for kernel hints, and deterministic unit tests for small sequences.
- Canary matrix: select 2% traffic across 3 route shapes (short chat, long-form synthesis, embedding).

Canary config sample (YAML):
---
canary: true
traffic_fraction: 0.02
routes: ["chat-short","text-gen-long","embeddings-avg"]
monitoring: ["p95_latency","error_rate","kvcache_hit_ratio"]
thresholds:
  p95_latency_increase_pct: 15
  error_rate_increase_pct: 0.1
---

Rollout steps (numbered):
1. Start canary with traffic_fraction and attach shadow-mirroring to baseline for fidelity checks.
2. Observe for 30 minutes minimum; validate p95, error rate, kvcache metrics.
3. If anomalies detected beyond thresholds, abort and roll back using the canary_abort endpoint.
4. If stable, ramp to 25% for 2 hours, then to 75% for 6 hours before global.
5. Post-rollout: run a fidelity evaluation against 100 golden prompts and verify token-level output similarity >= 98.5%.

Rollback quick commands:
- redwoodctl runtime canary abort --id <canary_id>
- redwoodctl runtime kernel rollback --variant <baseline_variant> --force

4) Profiling and benchmarking playbook (high level)

Profiling cadence and instrumentation:
- Continuous lightweight sampling: 1% of requests are sampled for full traces and kernel-level microtraces (sufficient for trend detection).
- Full profiling runs for a target route should be scheduled weekly for high-traffic routes and on-demand for incident triage. Use the profiling pipeline with an export window of 72h.
- Budget: keep continuous sampling overhead under 2% CPU/GPU cycle impact.

Benchmark harness integration (developer instructions):
1. Create a scenario YAML describing request surface (percent short/long, concurrency, token distribution). Example:
   - name: long-form-synthesis
     qps: 15
     sequence_length: 1024
     concurrency: 64

2. Run harness against candidate kernels:
   ./bench-runner --scenario scenarios/long-form-synthesis.yaml --kernel kv-quant-int8-v2 --duration 30m --out results/kv-int8-march2026.json

3. Generate comparison report (bench-compare):
   bench-compare --baseline results/baseline.json --candidate results/kv-int8-march2026.json --metrics p95,p99,cost_per_token

Expected pass criteria (example):
- end-to-end p95 <= baseline.p95 * 1.12 for long sequences
- cost_per_token <= baseline.cost_per_token * 0.95 (if claim is cost-reducing)
- no kernel_oom events during 30m run

5) Troubleshooting cookbook (three prioritized incidents)

A. Scenario: sudden spike in p99 tail latency on a model route
Symptoms: p50 stable, p95 up 8%, p99 up 3x, queue_depth rising, kernel_latency_ms shows long tail for kernel_variant kv-quant-int8-v2.

Step-by-step response:
1. Identify affected route and time window (Prometheus query: increase(runtime_request_duration_seconds_count{route_id="<r>"}[10m]) and p99 series).
2. Check scheduling queue for backpressure: runtime_queue_depth{pool_name!~"default"} and recent scheduling_decision events.
3. Inspect kernel spans for tailing latency: filter traces where kernel_variant==kv-quant-int8-v2 and span.duration > 500ms.
4. If kernel spans are long and present across many shards, mark kernel variant as degraded and route to fallback using routing policy: set route override to baseline kernel (redwoodctl route update --route <r> --kernel <baseline>).
5. Kick off a controlled kernel rollback per checklist.
6. After mitigation, capture a reproducible trace (use shadow traffic replay) and file an issue with trace id + top 5 offending spans.

B. Scenario: KVCACHE miss storm after model swap
Symptoms: sudden tail latency and increased GPU utilization; kvcache_hit_ratio drops from ~0.82 to <0.1; high eviction_rate observed.

Steps:
1. Confirm model swap event/time via deployment events store.
2. Run kvcache lookup logs: grep for kvcache_miss events in the window and sample keys.
3. If miss pattern indicates prefix variance, run prefix-hash audit (script: tools/kvcache/prefix-audit.py --trace <trace-id>) to identify mismatched prompt normalization.
4. If prompt normalization is the root cause, roll forward with normalization patch or enable kvcache_warmup mode for affected shards: redwoodctl kvcache warmup --shard <shard-id> --seed-corpus 10k --rate 200/s.
5. If eviction_rate is high due to memory pressure, temporarily increase kvcache capacity for the shard (config change), and schedule a full warmup run.

C. Scenario: intermittent kernel OOMs on heterogenous GPU pool
Symptoms: kernel_oom_count increments scattered, node-level OOM events in node_exporter, some dispatch failures and SIGKILL.

Steps:
1. Identify offending nodes: query kernel_oom_count by node and cross-check node memory pressure metrics.
2. Isolate workload: taint node or cordon it from scheduling to stop new kernels landing: kubectl cordon <node>; redwoodctl runtime drain --node <node> --mode cordon-no-evict
3. Retrieve kernel logs and coredumps for analysis (redwoodctl runtime collect-diagnostics --node <node> --since 1h).
4. If reproducible with specific kernel_variant and sequence_length, schedule immediate rollback of that variant and run a patch: kernel memory request increase or limit tuning.
5. Reintroduce node once validation passes; monitor kernel_oom_count for 2h.

6) Incident handoff and ticketing template

When an incident is triaged and a mitigation applied, create an internal ticket with the following fields (ticket template):
- Title: short summary (route/kernel/incident-type)
- Severity: Sev1/Sev2/Sev3
- Start time / detection time
- Detection signal & link (prometheus/trace id)
- Mitigation applied (commands, canary id, rollback id)
- Root-cause hypothesis
- Owner for RCA and ETA for fix

7) Runbook for oncall rotation owners (quick actions)

Immediate triage checklist (first 15 minutes):
- Confirm scope and blast radius (routes/customers).
- Capture a reproducible trace id and attach to the incident ticket.
- If SLO impact > 0.05% breach projected, escalate to senior SRE and paging policy.
- Execute mitigation (route override, kernel rollback, or kvcache warmup) and note command history.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall engineer -> runtime-sre lead (pagess) -> runtime eng manager -> product security if customer data affected.

8) Known issues (current catalogue)

- KV-prefetch warmup not idempotent for normalized prompts (INC-2026-0423): symptom is duplicate warmup entries and poor hit stabilization. Mitigation: run warmup with dedupe flag (tools/kvcache/warmup --dedupe). Owner: runtime-cache team.
- Intermittent scheduler preemption hang on GPUs with mixed tensor cores (TICKET-2026-0311): transient preemption leads to long kernel tails; mitigation: apply scheduling fallback to partitioned pool. Owner: scheduler team.
- GRPC connection churn under high multiplex (BUG-2025-2117): affects connection reuse and increases enqueue latency; mitigation: increase per-process connection pool and enable keepalive tuning. Owner: grpc-proxy team.

9) Release notes template for runtime/kernels (to be included in release notes channel)

- Summary: one-sentence summary of change.
- Risk: low/medium/high (reasons).
- Canary plan: traffic fractions, routes in canary.
- Observability: metrics to watch (p95, error_rate, kvcache_hit_ratio, kernel_oom_count).
- Rollback plan and commands.

10) Developer integration checklist (for SDKs and console)

- Ensure SDKs propagate required headers (X-Request-Id, X-Customer-Id, X-Desired-SLO-ms).
- Provide developers a debug helper in SDK (redwood.sdk.debug.capture_trace(request_id)) to attach annotated logs.
- Console must surface route-level canary controls and saved metric views (p95, p99, error_rate) for each canary.

Appendix A — Example configs and commands

1) Example bench-runner command to run mixed workload:
./bench-runner --scenario scenarios/mixed-prod-shape.yaml --kernel kv-quant-int8-v2 --duration 45m --concurrency 128 --out /tmp/kv-int8-run.json

2) redwoodctl quick debug commands:
- redwoodctl runtime traces get --request-id <id> --format json
- redwoodctl runtime metrics snapshot --route <route> --window 15m --out snapshot.json

3) Minimal trace correlation in logs (recommended):
Log line must include: request_id, trace_id, shard_id, kernel_variant, step. Example: "req=%s tid=%s shard=%s kernel=%s step=schedule"

Appendix B — Ownership and SLAs

- Runtime SRE: primary pager for runtime incidents; SLA to acknowledge Sev1 within 5 minutes.
- Kernel & Scheduler team: responsible for kernel rollouts, 24-hour patch turnaround for regressions in canary.
- Developer experience: ensure SDKs carry headers and provide debug helpers.

Appendix C — Where to look next (related docs)

- See runtime-architecture playbooks for deep dive on fallback orchestration.
- See profiler-runner readme for trace collection and analysis steps.

If you have an improvement to this cookbook or an additional triage scenario to include, add a PR to the team-wiki folder or ping @Priya on Slack.

payload.page_title: Runtime plugin safety and deployment checklist

sections.body:
Overview
-------

Purpose: This page documents a prescriptive checklist, gating criteria, and automated tests required to safely introduce runtime plugins (kernel adapters, scheduler plugins, or sidecar instrumentations) into Redwood's inference runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, kernel authors, and release owners.

Scope: applies to any code that executes inside the serving runtime process or modifies kernel scheduling behavior, including:
- third-party kernel drivers or accelerator adapters
- custom scheduler plugins and admission controllers
- observability sidecars that inject telemetry or sampling hooks
- experimental serialization/deserialization modules that touch request/response flows

Goals
-----
- Minimize production blast radius for plugin rollouts.
- Ensure deterministic performance and memory behaviour under peaky traffic.
- Guarantee observability and fast rollback on regressions.
- Provide reproducible benchmarking and profiling steps for acceptance gates.

Key risks and failure modes
-------------------------
- Non-deterministic kernel latency growth (tail latency spikes).
- Memory fragmentation or soft-ooms from plugin state leaks.
- Priority inversion introduced by scheduler hooks.
- Telemetry amplification causing control-plane overload.
- Silent semantic changes to model inputs/outputs (format drift).

Pre-deployment checklist (must pass all gates)
--------------------------------------------
1) Code & static safety
   - PR has clear README describing purpose, public interfaces, and intended failure modes.
   - Static analysis run: no unsafe deserialization, no unbounded allocations without guardrails.
   - Third-party dependencies reviewed for license and CVEs (security team sign-off for >= moderate).

2) Unit and integration tests
   - Unit coverage >= 80% for new code paths.
   - Integration tests exercise: request lifecycle (begin, KV cache lookup, kernel dispatch, response), error injection (timeouts, kernel failure), and graceful degradation.
   - Fuzz harness enabled for parser/serializer plugins.

3) Performance and resource budgets
   - Microbenchmarks added to the repo with the submitter-provided baseline and expected overhead.
   - Memory budget defined: max RSS delta <= 5% on steady-state synthetic workload; peak transient <= 15% with GC/eviction verified.
   - Max per-request added latency budget: p50 <= 1ms, p95 <= 5ms (defaults; product/route owners may tighten).

4) Profiling & observability hooks
   - Traces: plugin exposes span(s) with standardized tags: plugin.name, plugin.version, request.id, kernel.variant.
   - Metrics: must emit per-plugin counters for invocations, errors, and duration histogram (Prometheus format).
   - Logs: structured JSON logs with level, timestamp, request.id, and short context.

5) Canary and rollout plan
   - Canary matrix prepared (traffic slices, model variants, sequence lengths).
   - Rollout strategy defined: staged percentages 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows.
   - Automatic rollback rules enumerated (see SLO gates below).

6) Security and data handling
   - No write access to persistent customer data outside defined KV caches unless explicitly approved.
   - KMS/HSM integration validated if plugin requests keys.

Acceptance gating: telemetry & SLOs
--------------------------------
The plugin rollout must satisfy these gating rules during every canary window:
- Error rate: plugin-specific error_rate <= baseline_error_rate + 0.2% absolute AND service-level errors not increased.
- Latency regressions: p95 latency of route using plugin must not exceed baseline p95 + 10% or +50ms (whichever smaller).
- Resource signals: node memory pressure and GPU memory delta stable (no increase in OS OOM kills).
- Kernel health: no increase in kernel queue length > 2x baseline sustained > 5 minutes.
- Observability completeness: 99% of requests must include plugin spans and metric emission.

If any gate fails, the automated rollout must immediately revert to the previous release and file an incident.

Canary and rollout step-by-step procedure
---------------------------------------
1) Pre-canary (run in staging):
   - Deploy plugin build to staging runtime cluster.
   - Run synthetic benchmark plan: 30m steady-state, 5m microburst at 10x, and 10k unique prompt corpus replay.
   - Validate telemetry completeness and that integration tests pass on the canary lab.

2) Canary 1% (production shadow+1%):
   - Route 1% of production traffic through the plugin-managed path; mirror requests to comparison path.
   - Monitor gates for 30 minutes.
   - If green, promote to 5%. If not, rollback and open triage.

3) Canary 5% and 25%:
   - At each stage, run targeted microbenchmarks for the active model variants and sequence length distributions.
   - Run the profiling playbook (see Profiling section).

4) Full rollout:
   - Once at 100% for 60 minutes with no gate violations, mark feature as GA.

Profiling and benchmarking playbook (quick reference)
---------------------------------------------------
- Tools: perfbench (internal), microtrace (span collector), nvprof/nvtx (for accelerator plugins), pprof (CPU), jemalloc statistics.
- Synthetic load: use the inference-workload-replay tool with the golden corpus of route-specific prompts. Example command:
  ./inference-workload-replay --route my-route --duration 30m --qps 250 --seq-distribution seq-dist.json --compare baseline-build:12345

- Kernel-level profiling: run a 10-minute mixed workload and collect nvtx ranges labelled plugin:entry and plugin:exit. Example nvprof invocation:
  NVPROF_LOGFILE=nvlog.json nvprof --profile-child-processes --export-profile nvprofile.nvprof -- ./runtime --plugin path/to/plugin.so

- Memory and allocator checks:
  - Capture jemalloc stats pre/post using: curl localhost:9100/allocator/stats | jq '.'
  - Ensure active fragment count delta < 3% for steady-state runs.

- Tracing validation: verify every request has plugin span and that duration histogram aligns with microbenchmarks. Use microtrace query:
  microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=MY_PLUGIN" --stats p50,p95,p99

Test matrix (text table)
----------------------
Route | Model variant | Seq lengths | QPS profile | Required checks
------|---------------|------------|------------|----------------
search-low | base-merged | [8,32] | 200 | latency p95, mem delta, spans
chat-long | llama-xl | [64,512] | 50 | p95, kvcache correctness, distributional checks
batch-embed | embedder-v2 | [1,1] | 800 | throughput, batching overhead, histogram stability

Rollback and incident triage playbook
-----------------------------------
1) If automatic rollback triggered:
   - Oncall patches route to prior build and escalates to runtime-oncall and plugin owner.
   - Collect artifacts: traces (microtrace TTL 7d), nvprof logs, jemalloc dumps, kernel queue length logs, and pod-level logs.

2) Triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
   - Reproduce failure in canary lab with identical traffic profile.
   - Check for memory leaks: run 15-minute soak with heap snapshot.
   - Confirm whether failure is semantic (input/output differences) or performance (latency/memory).

3) Post-incident:
   - Fill incident template with root cause hypothesis, mitigation, test to prevent regressions, and owner for follow-up.
   - Schedule a 2-hour postmortem within 72 hours if customer impact occurred.

Operational runbook extracts (for oncall)
---------------------------------------
- Quick checks when alerted:
  1) Query: Prometheus - plugin:errors_total{plugin=\"MY_PLUGIN\"} by (instance) over 10m.
     Alert threshold: > 1% of total requests.
  2) Kernel queue depth: runtime_kernel_queue_length{instance} > 2x baseline for 5m.
  3) Memory: node_memory_available_bytes and container_memory_rss_bytes trend.
  4) Trace sampling: microtrace sample rate and presence of plugin spans; if missing, fail closed (treat as regression).

Ownership, signoff and documentation requirements
------------------------------------------------
- Code owner: must be an engineering team with 24/7 oncall coverage.
- Release owner: a named engineer responsible for canary monitoring and rollback.
- Documentation: README, deployment manifest, schema for metrics and spans, and example benchmark artifacts must be committed to the plugin repo.

Appendix A: sample deployment fragment (Kubernetes)
-------------------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: runtime-plugin-myplugin
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        runtime.redwood.com/plugin-name: "myplugin"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/runtime:canary-2028-01-10
        args: ["--plugin", "/opt/plugins/myplugin.so", "--plugin-metrics-prefix", "plugin_myplugin_"]
      - name: plugin-sidecar
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/plugin-sidecar:1.0.0
        env:
        - name: PLUGIN_MODE
          value: "sandboxed"

Appendix B: sample validation script (bash snippet)
-------------------------------------------------
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
sections.heading: Overview

./inference-workload-replay --route search-low --duration 5m --qps 100 || { echo 'replay failed'; exit 1; }
microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=myplugin" --stats p95 || { echo 'tracing missing'; exit 1; }

Appendix C: FAQ
---------------
Q: What qualifies as a plugin vs an integration?
A: Plugins execute inside the runtime or affect scheduling. Integrations that run externally (e.g. separate microservices) are treated as normal service integrations and follow a different checklist.

Q: How do I request higher latency budgets for experimental features?
A: Submit a feature request to the runtime-product channel with workload benchmarks and target routes. Product must approve any SLO changes before canary.

Contacts
--------
- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai
- Runtime product manager: elena.park@redwood.ai
- Security review: security-reviews@redwood.ai

Related documents
-----------------
- Kernel scheduler contract and telemetry spec (see related pages).
- Profiling playbook for nvprof and microtrace.

Change log
----------
- 2028-01-12: Created (Asha Verma).
- 2028-02-20: Added automated gating criteria and sample Kubernetes fragment (reviewers: Marco Diaz, Elena Park).

payload.page_title: Cross-layer Observability & Diagnostics Playbook — Burst and Degradation Incidents

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a cross-layer, repeatable approach for detecting, diagnosing, and mitigating short-duration bursts and progressive degradation in the Serving Runtime. It bridges runtime architecture, kernel scheduling signals, profiling playbooks, and benchmarking checks so oncall and runtime engineers can quickly restore SLOs and reduce mean time to innocence (MTTI).

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated runtime clusters and the operator-facing control-plane paths (Dispatcher, SlotAllocator, KernelRunner, KVCache, and Runtime Router).
- Audience: Serving runtime oncall, runtime engineers, release owners, and performance SREs.

Goals and SLO references
------------------------
- Primary detection SLOs: 95th token-latency < 100ms, 99th token-latency < 300ms for default small-model profile. (See per-model SLO sheet.)
- Operational goals: initial triage within 5 minutes, mitigation (fallback or ramp) within 15 minutes, restore to within 10% of baseline P95 within 60 minutes.

How this playbook fits with other docs
-------------------------------------
This is an operational layer that references: profiling playbooks for telemetry sampling, kernel-scheduler design docs for decision points, benchmarking suite for reproducible load, and existing runbooks for fallback and warmstart. Use this playbook when alerts indicate sudden tail-latency or progressive throughput drop.

Key concepts and system components
----------------------------------
- Dispatcher: user-facing ingress that performs request classification and route affinity. Primary source of request-level traces.
- SlotAllocator: assigns execution slots (cohort/priority) used by the scheduler. Tracks queue lengths and admission metrics.
- KernelRunner: GPU process pool executing kernels. Emits kernel_latency_hist, kernel_qps, kernel_error_rate, and kernel_memory_pressure.
- KVCache: per-session prefix cache. Key signals: hit_rate, eviction_rate, and warmup_latency.
- Runtime Router / Graceful Fallback: orchestrates model variant fallbacks and cross-region routing.

Signal catalog and quick thresholds
----------------------------------
(Use these to prioritize initial checks.)

| Signal (metric)                      | Type         | Quick threshold (when to escalate) |
|--------------------------------------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| dispatch.request_p95_ms              | latency      | > baseline * 1.2 or > 200ms       |
| kernel_latency_p95_ms                | latency      | > 1.5x baseline                   |
| kernel_queue_depth                   | gauge        | > 80% of max slots                |
| slot_allocator.queue_wait_time_p95   | latency      | > 50ms                            |
| kvcache.hit_rate                     | ratio        | drop > 15 percentage points       |
| grpc.reconnect_rate                  | rate         | sustained > 5/min                 |
| node_gpu_utilization                 | utilization  | > 95% (thermal risk)              |
| infra.network_rtt_p95                | latency      | > baseline + 20ms                 |

Note: baseline is the rolling 7-day median for the service and model profile.

Triage checklist (first 5 minutes)
----------------------------------
1) Validate alert and scope
   - Confirm alert: check Alerting UI + trace sample in the last 2 minutes.
   - Determine scope: single node, single pool, entire region, or global. Use the Dispatcher topology view.
2) Quick telemetry pull
   - Pull P95/P99 for dispatch.*, kernel_*, kvcache.* and slot_allocator.* for last 30m vs 3h.
   - Commands (on the runbook box):
     ```bash
     rmetric query --service=dispatcher --metrics="dispatch.request_p95_ms,dispatch.request_p99_ms" --range=30m
     rmetric query --pool=kernerrunner --metrics="kernel_latency_p95_ms,kernel_queue_depth" --range=30m
     rlog fetch --trace-id $(rmetric top-traces --service=dispatcher --limit=1) --follow=1m
     ```
3) Fast isolation heuristics
   - If kernel_queue_depth high and kernel_latency rising: likely kernel scheduling or admission.
   - If kvcache.hit_rate collapsed and kernel P95 is higher: consider cache warmup cascade.
   - If node_gpu_utilization is low but kernel queue depth is high: investigate scheduler admission/NUMA balance.

Isolation procedures (15–30 minutes)
-----------------------------------
A. Kernel scheduling checks
   - Check scheduler decision log: `rkctl scheduler inspect --pool <pool> --window 10m`
   - Look for recent policy changes (priority weights, admission caps). If there was a rollout in the last hour, rollback to the previous scheduler config.
   - Check GPU mismatch signals: `rkctl node inspect --node <id>` -> note nvlink errors, thermal events.
B. Admission and backpressure
   - Validate admission thresholds: `SlotAllocator.admit_rate` vs observed arrival rate.
   - If admission is overly conservative, temporarily increase soft-cap by +10% and monitor.
   - If admission is broken, flip to the safe fallback profile: `rkctl route set-fallback --route <route> --profile reduced-memory`
C. KV cache warmup cascade
   - If kvcache.eviction_rate spiked, trigger a targeted prefetch job for the affected sessions:
     ```yaml
     apiVersion: redwood.io/v1
     kind: KVPatchJob
     spec:
       model: <model-name>
       sessions: [session-ids-file]
       concurrency: 4
     ```

Mitigation patterns (approved temporary actions)
------------------------------------------------
- Short term (minutes): route to warm fallback model variant in-region; increase admission soft-cap by 5–10%; reduce batch size target to lower per-call kernel time.
- Medium term (hours): evict peaky low-util priority cohorts; initiate rolling restart of KernelRunner pool if drivers show instability; apply kernel restart mitigation which drains pending short calls first.
- Long term (post-incident): schedule simulation in the benchmarking suite to reproduce the burst, add synthetic traffic signature to the mixed-workload SLO test, and create a scheduler policy change with canary and rollout plan.

Diagnostic playbook for kernel-level regressions
------------------------------------------------
1) Reproduce with a targeted microbenchmark
   - Use the perf harness: `bench-run --profile kernel-latency --model <model> --sequence 256 --concurrency 8 --duration 5m`
   - Collect kernel traces: `kerntrace collect --pool <pool> --out /tmp/kerntrace.pb`
2) Compare kernel signature to baseline
   - Run diff against golden: `kerntrace diff /tmp/kerntrace.pb gs://benchmarks/kernel-gold/<model>.pb`
3) If reproducible, tag as kernel-regression and create a hotfix branch with kernel config rollback. Include the diff and perf artifacts in the PR.

Benchmarks and quick acceptance tests
------------------------------------
Use the standard benchmarking suite to validate mitigations before full rollout. Minimum test matrix:
- Mixed workload replay (30m): baseline QPS, 30% long sequences, 20% high-concurrency short sequences.
- Kernel microbench: 1–8 batch sizes, sequence 16/128/512.
- Admission and fallback test: inject synthetic saturating arrival and assert fallback triggers within 10s.

Sample benchmark run (CLI)
```bash
benchctl run --suite mixed-workload --tag incident-capture-$(date +%s) --params "qps=500,duration=30m,seqmix=0.3:512,0.5:128,0.2:16"
benchctl collect --artifact incident-capture-1234 --to gs://bench-results/incident-capture-1234
```

Release notes and change correlation
-----------------------------------
- Always check the Deployment Log (release-control) for any scheduler or kernel config changes in the 60 minutes before incident start.
- Use the release correlation query: `rctl releases list --since 1h --component scheduler,kernerrunner,kvcache`
- If a canary rollout is present, pause or rollback the canary immediately and re-evaluate.

Known issues to consider (fast checks)
------------------------------------
- NVLINK flapping on a subset of nodes causes intermittent kernel stalls (workaround: cordon nodes with nvlink_errors > 0 and drain after cooldown).
- Kernel memory fragmentation causing soft OOMs under interleaved batches (mitigation: apply compacting GC in 2.3.1-hotfix and restart KernelRunner).
- GRPC connection recycling leading to small head-of-line stalls at the Dispatcher (workaround: increase connection pool size temporarily).

Runbook appendices and artifacts to collect
-------------------------------------------
Collect these during the incident and attach to the postmortem:
- Top 20 traces (dispatch) during incident window.
- kernel_trace.pb files for affected KernelRunner nodes.
- SlotAllocator decision log for the interval.
- Bench artifacts if a reproduction was run (benchctl outputs).
- Release correlation snapshot (release-control export).

Post-incident actions (owner: runtime-performance squad)
-------------------------------------------------------
1) Assign postmortem owner within 24h.
2) Reproduce incident in bench lab with identical traffic signature within 72h.
3) Create follow-up tickets: scheduler policy change, kernel tuning, KVCache prefetch improvements, or infra remediation (if hardware).
4) Add a synthetic SLO probe to the mixed-workload suite for future detection.

Operational contacts and escalation
----------------------------------
- Oncall (runtime): #runtime-oncall Slack, Pager schedule in PagerDuty
- Kernel squadra: kern-team@redwood.com
- Infra hardware: infra-hw@redwood.com

Maintenance checklist (for release owners)
-----------------------------------------
- Before rolling scheduler changes: run the canary matrix (3% traffic) for 60 minutes against mixed workload.
- Attach bench artifacts and kernel diffs to the PR.
- Notify SRE and runtime performance reviewers 24h prior to rollout.

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Aisha Kapoor)
- 2026-01-18: added KVCache warmup cascade procedures and benchmark commands (reviewers: Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-03-01: expanded kernel-level diagnostics and known issues section; published (reviewers: Evelyn Park, Daniel Kim)

Related resources and links
-------------------------
- Dispatcher traces dashboard: /dashboards/dispatcher/traces
- Mixed-workload bench suite: /tools/benchctl/doc
- Scheduler policy language reference: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Kernel tracing guide: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kernel-observability-sla-profiling-cadence-2024

If you have questions or need a walkthrough, ping the runtime-performance squad in #runtime-performance and request a live lab replication session.
