payload.page_title: Async KVCache Prefetch and Adaptive Kernel Selection Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook describes the design, operational controls, profiling guidance, benchmarking recipes, and incident runbooks for the asynchronous KV cache (KVCache) prefetcher and the adaptive kernel selection subsystem. The document explains how the prefetching pipeline integrates with the request classifier and kernel selector to reduce token-era latency for long-context and multi-shot workloads while preserving cost and fairness SLOs.

Why this exists
- Root cause: Tail latency often originates from sequential KV loads and conservative kernel choices for requests with uncommon sequence profiles.
- Goal: Reduce P95/P99 generation latency by prefetching KV segments and selecting kernels tuned to the observed request pattern without increasing average GPU occupancy or costs by more than 8%.

Scope
- Included: Async prefetch coordinator, request classification heuristics, kernel selection policy, metrics and alert thresholds, profiling steps, benchmarking recipes, rollout and rollback steps.
- Excluded: Model architecture changes, quantization profiles (see quantization-profiles directory), network-level transport changes.

High-level architecture (text diagram)
- Ingress -> Request Classifier -> Routing & Prefetch Coordinator -> Kernel Selector -> GPU Dispatcher -> KVCache (per-shard) -> Runtime Executor
- Feedback loop: Runtime Telemetry -> Adaptive Policy Engine -> Prefetch & Kernel Policy Store

Components and responsibilities
1) Request Classifier
- Tag requests at ingress with a sequence profile: typical length distribution, presence of tool/function calls, streaming flag, and priority class. Uses lightweight sampling models (logistic model trained on historical traces).
- Responsible for assigning a prefetch hint (none, soft-prefetch, eager-prefetch) and candidate kernel families (A/B) for the Kernel Selector.
2) Prefetch Coordinator
- Receives hints and maintains per-session prefetch state. Issues non-blocking KV reads to co-locate likely KV pages before the request reaches the hot kernel path.
- Uses backpressure-aware dispatch: prefetch requests are priority-0 and are throttled by an adaptive token bucket per-GPU to maintain tail SLOs.
3) Kernel Selector
- Maintains a policy table indexed by (model-variant, sequence-profile, priority). Each entry contains candidate kernels with expected latency & cost vectors.
- Uses a bandit-style experiment framework for online exploration (epsilon-greedy by default) with decay windows tied to model version rollouts.
4) Adaptive Policy Engine
- Periodically (5m) retrains lightweight policies from telemetry. Generates updated thresholds for prefetch aggressiveness and kernel switching.

Key design tradeoffs and safeguards
- Safety first: Kernel switches are allowed only if the candidate improves expected latency without exceeding a configured cost delta (default +8%).
- Backpressure integration: Prefetch-level throttles yield immediately under GPU memory pressure or when per-GPU kernel saturation > 85%.
- Gradual exploration window: exploration rate is capped to avoid noisy regressions in canaries.

Operational metrics and dashboards (minimum required)
- Prefetch hit rate (per model, per region): percent of requests where prefetched KV page satisfied first KV fetch.
- Prefetch to primary fetch latency delta (ms).
- Kernel selection distribution: percent usage of each kernel family by model-version.
- P50/P95/P99 generation latency (token complete) by kernel family and sequence-profile.
- GPU occupancy and queue length by kernel family.
- Cost-per-token delta by kernel family.

SLO guardrails (observable thresholds)
- P95 generation latency: target 120ms, alert if >160ms sustained for 3m.
- Prefetch hit rate: target >= 70% on long-context workloads, warning if <50%.
- Kernel-induced cost delta: warn at >+8% sustained 30m, page at >+12%.

Profiling playbook (how to investigate quality/latency regressions)
1) Initial triage
- Verify if latency spike correlates with: recent kernel rollout, prefetch policy change, model-version rollout, or GPU pool capacity event.
- Query traces: filter by request classifier tag and kernel family.
2) Reproduce with developer sandbox
- Use the sandbox driver with the same sequence-profile and batch shape. Run microbenchmarks with and without prefetch: ./bench_driver --model vX --profile long-context --prefetch on/off --kernel A/B.
3) Telemetry collection
- Capture a full trace set for 5 minutes: kernel dispatch times, KVCache miss/hit events, per-token latency, and GPU occupancy. Use the runtime trace sampler: rt-sample --duration 300 --labels kvcache,prefetch,kernelselect.
4) Root-cause patterns and fixes
- High KV miss & low prefetch hit -> increase conservative prefetch window and examine classifier false negative rate.
- Kernel family P99 regressed -> disable exploration flag for that family; roll back canary.
- GPU memory pressure during prefetch -> reduce per-GPU prefetch tokens or restrict eager-prefetch to dedicated pools.

Benchmarking suite (recipes and canonical configs)
- Objective: quantify cost/latency tradeoffs for prefetch aggressiveness and kernel families across representative profiles.
- Canonical workload set: short-chat (avg len 30), long-instruction (avg len 512), multi-shot session (avg len 800 with KV locality).
- Benchmark config table (text):
  - Test name: long-kv-prefetch-scan
    concurrency: 200
    seq_profile: long-instruction
    prefetch: eager
    kernels: [A-optimized, B-latency]
    duration: 30m
  - Test name: mixed-plg-burst
    concurrency: 500
    seq_profile: mixed
    prefetch: soft
    kernels: [A-optimized]
    duration: 60m
- Key result artifacts to capture: per-token latency histograms, GPU occupancy heatmaps, prefetch hit/miss timelines, and cost-per-token estimations. Store outputs as parquet with schema: trace_id, timestamp, model_version, kernel_family, cpu_ms, gpu_ms, kvcache_event, cost_units.

Release and rollout plan
1) Local QA: unit tests + microbench suite.
2) Canary: enable soft-prefetch + adaptive kernel selection in a 1% canary pool with exploration rate 1%. Monitor the following for 30m: P95 latency, prefetch hit rate, kernel cost delta.
3) Staged expansion: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> global. At each stage the policy engine must show no adverse impact on SLOs for 30m before advancing.
4) Automatic rollback triggers: sustained P95 regression > 20% or prefetch hit rate drop > 30% vs baseline for 15m.

Runbook snippets (incident steps)
- Symptom: sudden P99 spike for long-context model
1) Check recent policy changes: /ops/deploy-log or policy-store update id.
2) Query prefetch hit rate and kernel distribution for the last 10m.
3) If prefetch hit rate dropped > 40%: immediately flip prefetch to conservative mode for the affected model-version: rt-cfg set prefetch.policy conservative --model vX --scope pool:us-east-1-canary
4) If a kernel family shows P99 > baseline by >50%: reroute to fallback kernel family: rt-route set --model vX --kernel-family B --scope pool:us-east-1-canary
5) Engage runtime-oncall and kernel-owner (see ownership section).

- Symptom: elevated GPU memory pressure correlated with prefetch activity
1) Reduce per-GPU prefetch tokens: rt-cfg set prefetch.tokens 4 --scope pool:eu-west-1
2) If memory pressure persists, disable eager-prefetch globally for the affected pool: rt-cfg set prefetch.enabled false --scope pool:eu-west-1
3) Schedule a postmortem and attach sampled traces.

Observability and tracing guidance
- Span instrumentation: add spans for prefetch.issue, prefetch.wait, kvcache.load, kernel.select, kernel.dispatch.
- Sampling: keep deterministic sampling for requests in canary pools and stratified random sampling across sequence profiles (target 1% global, 10% for canaries).
- Annotation: annotate spans with request_classifier tag, prefetch_hint, kernel_family, and kvcache_page_id.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owners: Serving Runtime - Kernel and KV team (team slack: #runtime-kv-kernel)
- Secondary: Eng-SRE for capacity events (#eng-sre)
- Pager duties: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai

Open issues and known limitations
- Prefetch heuristics still misclassify some nested tool-calling sessions; leads to wasted KV reads in low-locality sessions. Tracking work item: RUNTIME-1126.
- Kernel exploration can oscillate under non-stationary traffic patterns; mitigation: add per-model decay windows (WIP: RUNTIME-1183).

Appendices
A) CLI snippets
- Re-run microbench: ./bench_driver --model vX --profile long-context --prefetch eager --kernel-family A --out results.parquet
- Toggle conservative prefetch: rt-cfg set prefetch.policy conservative --model vX
B) Suggested alert definitions (PromQL-like, text form)
- prefetch_hit_rate < 0.5 for 10m -> severity: warning
- p95_generation_latency{model="vX",kernel_family!="fallback"} > 160ms for 3m -> severity: page

C) Related experiments and artifacts
- Experiment: kernel-A vs kernel-B bandit logs (s3://redwood-experiments/kernelselect/bandit/2025-11)

Document history
- 2025-07-15: Initial authoring (Anya Patel)
- 2025-11-02: Added benchmarking recipes and rollout thresholds (reviewers: Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-02-03: Clarified GPU backpressure behavior and added CLI snippets (reviewers: Priya Shah, Evan Chao)

End of document
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: cross-layer-failure-taxonomy-and-healing-playbook-2028

sections.body: This document defines a cross-layer failure taxonomy for the Redwood serving runtime and prescribes a prioritized set of automated and manual healing patterns. It ties failure classes to observable signals, SLO impact estimates, kernel-scheduler interactions, and a validation protocol (simulation + benchmarks) to verify healing effectiveness. The goal is to reduce MTTI (mean time to impact resolution) and minimize customer-visible SLA violations while retaining explainability for operators and on-call engineers.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Systems covered: serving runtime (scheduler, kernel plugins, KV cache, model swapping path, request multiplexer), GPU nodes, and control-plane routing that affects inference.
- Not covered: provisioning infra (cloud provider account-level failures), storage backend outages unrelated to KV cache persistence.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1) Failure mode: a discrete class of root cause (e.g., kernel starvation, KV cache thrash, model swap oscillation).
2) Signal: an observable metric or event correlated with a failure mode (e.g., per-gpu-run-queue-latency, kernel-backpressure-count).
3) Healing pattern: an automated or manual mitigation action (e.g., graceful model downgrade, preempt-and-slice, kernel rollback).
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
- Hardware Degradation:
  - Examples: NVLink flapping, thermal throttling, ECC corrections escalations leading to GPU driver resets.
  - Typical signals: thermal_temperature_gpu > 85C sustained, nvlink_error_rate > baseline, driver-restart events, unexpected GPU offline.
  - Immediate impact: abrupt token latency spikes, increased tail latency, node removal from pool.

- Kernel-level Regression / Latency Inflation:
  - Examples: new kernel release with suboptimal tiling for medium sequence length; per-kernel code-path takes 2x cycles for specific ops.
  - Signals: kernel_duration_p50/p95 increase for impacted kernel id, kernel-inflight-queued, kernel-error-ratio.
  - Interaction: scheduler may increase backpressure, leading to higher queueing latency across tenants.

- Scheduler Misconfiguration or Policy Conflict:
  - Examples: aggressive fairness policy resulting in starvation of high-priority SLOs; priority inversion with ephemeral plugins.
  - Signals: queue-depth-by-priority, delayed-scheduler-invocations, starvation-duration>threshold.

- KV cache evictions & cold-start storms:
  - Examples: bulk tenant requests after model swap cause cache churn and repeated warmups.
  - Signals: kvcache-hit-rate drop, warmup-requests-per-minute spike, per-request-additional-latency-with-warmup.

- Model-variant oscillation / continuous fallback churn:
  - Examples: routing policy repeatedly swaps between quantized and full-float model variants under marginal quality regressions.
  - Signals: model-switch-count, transient-quality-regression-alerts, per-session-inconsistency.

- Control-plane routing instability:
  - Examples: region-level routing flaps, misapplied rollout policy, bad canary rules.
  - Signals: route-change-events, sudden shift in capacity-utilization across regions, <route>-fallback-invoked.
sections.heading: Cross-layer failure taxonomy (compact)

sections.body:
- Sev 1 (customer-impacting steady): sustained 50% increase in tail-99 latency, >5% error rate for >5 minutes.
- Sev 2 (degraded but partially functional): 20–50% tail-99 increase, transient errors affecting <5% of requests.
- Sev 3 (anomalous but within SLO): localized kernel latency bump, single-node thermal throttling with graceful failover.
sections.heading: Severity matrix and SLO correlation (short)

sections.body:
- infra.*: gpu_temp_celsius, nvlink_errors, driver_restarts, node_oom_kills
- kernel.*: kernel_exec_time_ms{kernel_id}, kernel_error_count, kernel-inflight
- scheduler.*: queue_depth{priority}, time_to_schedule_ms, preemptions_per_minute
- kvcache.*: hit_rate, warmup_ops_per_minute, eviction_rate
- model.*: model_swap_count, variant_latency_ms, quality_regression_delta
- request.*: per_request_tail_latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, request_error_rate
sections.heading: Observable signals catalog (recommended)

sections.body:
1) Protective throttling and admission control (safe):
   - When queue_depth{all} > Q_HI and p99_latency > L_HI, trigger per-tenant admission-shed at 5–20% increments with exponential backoff.
   - Purpose: immediately reduce queuing amplification and allow kernels to drain.

2) Kernel safety-net rollback (safe with guardrails):
   - Trigger conditions: kernel_exec_time_p95 exceeds baseline * 1.6 AND kernel_error_increase > X.
   - Action: flip the kernel feature-flag to the previous stable kernel variant on affected shard group; increment kernel-rollback-counter; notify runtime-ops.
   - Validation: quick microbenchmark run (10s, sample requests) against canary path to confirm p95 return.

3) Model variant staged fallback (safe for quality):
   - Trigger: model_latency_multiplier > 1.5 OR kvcache-hit-rate < 0.2 for > 30s.
   - Action: route new requests to a fallback variant (quantized or smaller context) using session-preserving redirect; enable quality-guardrail sampling for first 100 requests.

4) KV cache conservative mode & priming (safe):
   - Action steps: reduce cache target size for new sessions, enable proactive priming background job for top-N prefixes, temporarily exempt high-SLA tenants from eviction until priming completes.

5) Node isolation & graceful eviction (higher disruption):
   - If node-level GPU errors or thermal thresholds persist, mark node in draining state; initiate graceful eviction of live sessions with session-transfer when supported; prevent new allocations for 5 minutes; coordinate with fleet-autorepair.

6) Scheduler quick-slice preemption (experimental):
   - Use when kernel-backed stalls cause broad queueing but kernels still launch. Create short preemption slices (50–100ms) to interleave low-latency tenants. Only enabled under controlled flags and rollouts.
sections.heading: Automated healing patterns (ordered by safety)

sections.body:
- Do not perform model-variant fallback if quality-monitoring signals show >2% quality degradation in last 30s.
- Kernel rollback requires at least one successful microbenchmark verification and should record an audit event with a trace id.
- Admission-shed must be tenant-scoped and rate-limited; global sheds are an emergency-only action.
sections.heading: Decision heuristics and guardrails

sections.body:
1) Initial detection (0–5 minutes):
   - Pull SLO dashboard for affected route/model.
   - Check node health (gpu_temp_celsius, driver_restarts), kernel errors, and scheduler queue depths.
2) Quick containment (5–15 minutes):
   - If spike is noise, observe for additional 5 minutes.
   - If persistent, enable tenant-scoped admission-shed at 10% and monitor p99.
3) If kernel regression suspected (15–30 minutes):
   - Trigger kernel-rollback play (via runtime admin cli): runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group <id> --cause "p95-regression-<id>"
   - Run microbenchmark: bench-tool --target sh://<shard> --template warmup_short --duration 10s
4) If KV cache storm (15–45 minutes):
   - Apply kvcache-conservative-mode for affected shards: runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards <list> --mode conservative
   - Kick off priming job: priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --window 10m
5) Escalate to runtime-core if cross-shard rollback needed or if node isolation fails.
sections.heading: Manual triage and runbook (for on-call)

sections.body:
- Preemption semantics: preemption should avoid inflight KV mutations; prefer slice boundaries at request or token boundaries where possible.
- Batching trade-offs: increased batching increases throughput but amplifies kernel regressions across tenants; include batch-size hysteresis in scheduler policy to quickly reduce batch size on p95 inflation.
- Priority inversion detection: monitor latency deltas by priority band; automated alert if p95_low_priority improves while p95_high_priority worsens beyond threshold.

Simulation & validation recipe (must-run for any new healing policy):
1) Test harness: use the operational workload simulator with a blended-client-corpus (from request-surface-replay) and inject fault primitives (thermal_increase, kernel_slowdown_x2, kvcache-eviction-spike).
2) Benchmarks to run:
   - pre/post p95/p99 delta test (steady state 5m window)
   - tail amplification ratio under 5% error injection
   - model-quality-sampling to validate fallback fidelity (1000 sampled completions compared via eval-set).
3) Success criteria: automated healing must reduce p99 to <=1.2x baseline within 120s for Sev2 and within 300s for Sev1 while quality regression remains within policy bounds.
4) Regression checks: ensure no >0.5% increased error surface for unrelated tenants during tests.

Operational playbook for release validation (Autonomous Recovery v1):
- Feature description: Autonomous Recovery v1 implements kernel-rollback, kvcache-conservative-mode, and tenant-scoped admission-shed as coordinated automated responses.
- Staged rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 3 days with automated rollback on predefined SLO regressions.
- Acceptance tests for each stage: run the simulation recipe for 15m and confirm success criteria.
- Rollback criteria: p99 latency regression > 1.5x baseline OR quality-sampling failure > 2% in two consecutive windows.
sections.heading: Kernel scheduling interactions (guidance)

sections.body:
- Add a healing-events stream: healing_event{type, target, trigger, actor, trace_id}.
- Annotate request traces with healing_hint when fallback/rollback applied.
- Add a dashboard: "Healing Effectiveness" showing time-to-heal histograms, success-rate by type, and per-tenant impact.
sections.heading: Telemetry and observability additions required

sections.body:
- If rollback didn't reduce p95: verify microbenchmark runner executed against same shard; confirm kernel-side metrics were ingested.
- If admission-shed did not apply: confirm policy sync to edge routing; check policy-eval-latency.
- If kvcache priming thrashed memory: inspect priming job concurrency and rate-limit to avoid OOM.
sections.heading: Troubleshooting checklist (fast)

sections.body:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: runtime-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary: eng-sre (pager: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com).
- Escalation path: on-call -> runtime-core -> infra-platform lead -> engineering director.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets:
- Rollback kernel:
  runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group sg-17 --kernel-id k-2027-11 --reason "p95_regression_20270302"
- Set kvcache conservative mode:
  runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards sg-17,sg-18 --mode conservative --ttl 10m
- Start priming job:
  priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --sample-size 500 --shard sg-17

Appendix B — Minimal YAML policy sample (human-readable):
  healingPolicies:
    - name: kernel-safety-net-v1
      conditions:
        - metric: kernel_exec_time_p95
          comparator: ">"
        - threshold: 1.6
      actions:
        - type: rollback-kernel
          cooldown: 120s
sections.heading: Ownership & escalation

sections.body:
- Runtime incident orchestration and capacity decision matrix (internal)
- Kernel safety net and rollback playbook
- Runtime observability data model and tracebook
sections.heading: References and related pages

sections.body:
- 2026-11-15: doc created (Maya Chen)
- 2027-01-18: added simulation recipe and success criteria (Rafael Ortiz)
- 2027-03-02: updated rollout acceptance tests and telemetry requirements (Priya Kapoor)

payload.page_title: Cross-layer Experiment Matrix and Validation Checklist

sections.body: This document is a consolidated experiment matrix and validation checklist for cross-layer runtime experiments that touch kernel scheduling, KV-cache behavior, profiling instrumentation, and benchmark acceptance. It's intended for engineiners running controlled experiments that may affect SLOs and cost. Use this as the canonical checklist and runbook for planning, executing, and validating experiments that modify scheduler policies, kernel variants, or observation sampling rates.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: experiments affecting serving runtime execution path, kernel selection, batching, KV cache prefetch, and telemetry sampling.
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance researchers, release engineers.
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body:
1) Scheduling policy changes
  - Example: priority-driven crediting -> opportunistic slot coalescing
  - Impact areas: tail latency, fairness, kernel queue depth, eviction rate
2) Kernel variant rollouts
  - Example: fast-attention-v2 vs safe-attention-v1 (reduced memory, different numeric stability)
  - Impact: per-token CPU/GPU time, p99 latency, EPS (errors per second)
3) KV-cache behavior and prefetch tuning
  - Example: asynchronous prefetch enabled/disabled, prefetch window size
  - Impact: cold-starts, token generation latency, cache warmup time
4) Telemetry and sampling changes
  - Example: full traces -> sampled traces with adaptive enrichment
  - Impact: signal fidelity, profiling cost, root-cause analysis windows
5) Quantization/Kernel-precision changes
  - Example: fp16 -> int8 with calibration profile B
  - Impact: model quality regressions, kernel numerical edgecases
sections.heading: High-level experiment categories (matrix)

sections.body:
- Define hypothesis in a single sentence. Example: "Opportunistic slot coalescing reduces average batch overhead by >= 8% without increasing p99 latency by > 5%."
- Identify owners and reviewer: owner (runtime-team), reviewer (profiling-team lead).
- Identify target canary cohort: (e.g., internal-dev, 5% routed to experimental pool).
- Required approvals: SLO-risk review (eng-sre), data-privacy signoff (if traces contain customer content).
- Safety gates: circuit-breaker thresholds (see table).
sections.heading: Experiment planning checklist (pre-run)

sections.body:
- p50 latency: no increase > 15%
- p95 latency: no increase > 10%
- p99 latency: no increase > 5%
- Error rate: no absolute increase > 0.05% or > 2x baseline (whichever smaller)
- Observability signal: successful trace capture >= 60% of warm requests
sections.heading: Safety gate thresholds (example)

sections.body:
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 measured at token-level and end-to-end request-level
- Throughput: tokens/sec per GPU, requests/sec per slot
- Cost: per-token GPU time, energy proxy (W*ms) if available
- Correctness: model output diffs measured with eval prompt set (small fidelity harness)
- Resource signals: GPU SM util, memory alloc/peak, NVLink error rate
- Scheduler signals: queue depth, kernel startup time, preemption occurrences
- KV cache signals: hit rate, eviction churn, warmup time
sections.heading: Validation matrix (what to measure)

sections.body:
1) Baseline capture: run 30-minute stable baseline with mirrored production trace. Collect: kernel traces, CPU/GPU counters, KV-cache logs, end-to-end latencies.
2) Change capture: enable experimental flag for 5% traffic with traffic mirror. Capture same signals and tag traces with experiment id.
3) Sampling strategy: use stratified sampling across sequence-length buckets: 0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024. Target at least 1000 traces per bucket.
4) Trace enrichment: attach kernel-id, scheduler-decision, kvcache-cohort, slot-id, and model-variant tags to each trace.
5) Differential analysis: compute delta per metric per bucket and generate a hypothesis test (bootstrap CI).
sections.heading: Profiling playbook (short form)

sections.body: - Use the canonical workload generator (redwood-bench 1.4) with the following profile file for acceptance tests. Always run bench in shadow-mode first (no live routing).
sections.heading: Benchmarking protocol (operational)

sections.body:
redwood-bench run --profile profiles/mixed-dialogue-2026.yaml --duration 30m --target-gpus 4 --mirror=true --tag exp-crosslayer-{{experiment_id}}

Example profile snippet (profiles/mixed-dialogue-2026.yaml):
---
name: mixed-dialogue-2026
sequence-distribution:
  short: 0.55
  medium: 0.30
  long: 0.15
concurrency: 120
  # simulated clients sending variable-length turn-taking dialogues
sections.heading: Sample bench invocation

sections.body:
- Stable p95 throughput within -5% / +6% of baseline for the same cost tier
- p99 latency no worse than baseline + 4%
- No numerical exceptions or OOMs across 1,000 long traces
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (bench)

sections.body:
- Prefer per-tenant credit buckets for Dedicated pools where business SLAs exist.
- Use opportunistic slot coalescing only if average sequence length > 128 in target workload.
- Avoid naive preemption on kernels marked as non-interruptible. Instead, use cooperative-yield signals.
- When testing new kernel variants, run the kernel under a synthetic microbench of 1-10 token sequences and 512-token sequences to surface divergences.

Runbook: experimental canary rollout (step-by-step):
1) Preflight (local): run bench shadow run and confirm metrics stable.
2) Canary 1 (internal-dev): route 0% -> 1% -> 5% over 30-minute windows. Monitor safety gates.
3) Canary 2 (internal-paid): route 10% for 2 hours. If metrics exceed thresholds, roll back to 0% and capture traces.
4) Controlled ramp: 10% -> 25% -> 50% over 24h windows with periodic smoke checks.
5) Full rollout: schedule during low-traffic maintenance window. Keep 30% rollback capacity for first 24h.
6) Post-mortem checklist: collect diffs, update experiment registry entry, and schedule follow-up regression tests if any signal exceeded warning thresholds.
sections.heading: Kernel scheduling guidance (operational rules)

sections.body:
- First responder: experiment owner (runtime team engineer).
- SRE on-call: Pager duty group "runtime-sre".
- If p99 latency threshold breached for > 15 minutes: escalate to on-call manager + product impact channel.
- If numerical regressions observed (BLEU/Rouge/embedding drift) above tolerance: involve applied-ml team and freeze rollout.

Appendix A — sample runtime feature flag YAML (deploy-time):
---
feature_flag:
  name: opportunistic_slot_coalesce
  enabled: false  # set true in canary
  rollout:
    strategy: gradual
    steps: [1,5,10,25,50,100]
  metrics_watch: [latency_p99, error_rate, kvcache_hit_rate]

Appendix B — common troubleshooting commands:
- Collect live traces for a slot: redwood-cli traces fetch --slot-id <slot> --from <time> --to <time> --format ndjson
- Dump scheduler queue state: kubectl exec -n runtime svc/scheduler -- schedulerctl queue-dump --output json | jq '.top10'
- Revert feature flag: redwood-cli flags set opportunistic_slot_coalesce --enabled=false --reason "slo-rollback"

Appendix C — minimal regression gating tests (CI):
- integration/e2e/fidelity-check: run 200 eval prompts generating at least 95% semantic similarity according to eval-harness v2.1
- perf/pipeline/smoke: run 30s microbench verifying kernel warmup time < 15ms on target hardware
- telemetry/sampling-check: confirm trace coverage >= configured target for each seq-length bucket
sections.heading: Escalation and ownership

sections.body:
- We prioritize conservative latency SLOs during canaries; cost improvements that cause small tail regressions should be debated with product if they affect user experience.
- The matrix enforces that any experiment that touches both kernel selection and KV-cache must include both microbench and end-to-end corpus fidelity tests.
sections.heading: Notes and rationale

sections.body:
- 2026-02-11: initial draft (Priya N.)
- 2026-03-16: added acceptance criteria and bench profile examples (Marcus P.)
- 2026-05-03: expanded profiling sampling guidance and escalation steps (Leah Z.)
sections.heading: Change log

sections.body:
- See runtime-decision-delegation-and-observer-patterns-2026 for observer tagging conventions.
- See causal-latency-attribution playbook for detailed statistical test recipes.

If you plan to run an experiment, create an entry in the experiments registry and assign the fields: hypothesis, owner, expected-safety-gates, mirror-run-id, and bench-tag. Attach the mirroring trace dataset to the registry entry before starting the canary.
sections.heading: Related references

payload.page_title: Kernel Health Index and Oncall Investigation Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This page defines the Kernel Health Index (KHI) — a composite signal used to detect regressions and degradation in the serving runtime’s kernel layer — and provides a step-by-step oncall investigation and remediation playbook. The KHI aggregates kernel-level telemetry (latency, error rates, kernel queue lengths, preemption events, and GPU memory pressure) into a single, interpretable score per scheduler cohort. The goal is early, actionable detection with minimal false positives and clear escalation steps.

Why we need KHI:
- Kernels are a frequent choke point for tail latency and cross-tenant interference.
- Single-signal alerts (e.g., p50 token latency) are noisy when mixed workloads or rolling deploys are active.
- KHI provides a stable, cohort-scoped index that surfaces meaningful kernel-level change while preserving correlation to user-visible SLOs.

Scope and ownership:
- Scope: GPU kernel operations and the scheduler/handoff surface inside the runtime (kernel invocation, queueing, preemption, kernel handoff errors, kernel timeouts).
- Owning team: eng-serving-runtime (runtime kernel and scheduling subteams).
- Oncall escalation: runtime oncall -> kernel scheduling rotate -> runtime performance owners.

KHI definition (high level):
- KHI is a normalized, weighted sum of standardized component signals for a cohort and 1-minute window:
  - Latency sensitive kernel tail (K_tail): percentile-based tail of kernel execution time (e.g., 99th percentile of measured kernel time).
  - Kernel error spike score (K_err): count of kernel-level errors (failed launches, launch timeouts) normalized by request volume.
  - Queue pressure index (K_q): average queue length / slot capacity ratio in scheduler queues.
  - Preemption churn (K_preempt): count of preemption events per minute normalized by active kernels.
  - Memory pressure index (K_mem): fraction of kernels that triggered OOM/soft-OOM or elevated allocation/reclaim events.

- Simplified score formula (illustrative):
  KHI = 100 * (0.35*norm(K_tail) + 0.25*norm(K_err) + 0.15*norm(K_q) + 0.15*norm(K_preempt) + 0.10*norm(K_mem))
  where norm(x) maps the raw metric to [0,1] using cohort-specific baseline percentiles (historical 7d median + MAD).

Interpretation buckets:
- KHI < 15: healthy. No action required.
- 15 <= KHI < 40: watch. Add to daily telemetry digest and correlate with SLO deltas.
- 40 <= KHI < 70: alert to oncall. Start triage checklist.
- KHI >= 70: high-priority incident. Execute mitigation matrix and page kernel scheduling owners.

PromQL and query recipes (examples):
- 99th percentile kernel exec time per cohort (example):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_exec_duration_seconds_bucket{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) by (le, cohort))

- Kernel error spike (5m):
  sum(rate(kernel_launch_errors_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m]))

- Queue pressure (1m avg):
  avg_over_time(scheduler_queue_length{queue=~"kernel-.*",cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m]) / scheduler_queue_capacity{cohort="web-embeddings"}

- Preemption churn (1m):
  sum(rate(kernel_preemptions_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m])) / max(1, sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m])))

- Memory pressure (ratio):
  sum(rate(kernel_memory_pressure_events_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m]))

Alerting rules (recommended thresholds):
- KHI Alert (page): KHI >= 40 for 2m sustained OR KHI delta >= 25 in 5m. Severity: P2 (first responder), escalate to P1 if sustained > 10m or correlated SLO breach.
- Kernel error rate guide: kernel_launch_error_rate > 0.005 (0.5%) sustained 5m -> generate paging alert.
- Queue pressure guide: scheduler_queue_length / capacity > 0.7 for 3m -> fire warning; >0.9 -> page.

Oncall investigation checklist (ordered):
1) Confirm alert and scope
   - Look at KHI time series and cohort tag. Is the spike localized to one cohort or global?
   - Check related SLO dashboards (token latency, request success rate) for correlation.
2) Immediately gather fast artifacts (first 2 minutes)
   - grep or use trace UI to collect 5–20 traces that hit altered kernels.
   - Snapshot kernel metrics: kernel_exec_duration_seconds, kernel_launch_errors_total, scheduler_queue_length, kernel_preemptions_total, kernel_memory_pressure_events_total.
   - Capture top-10 affected hosts/pods and GPU IDs.
3) Triage for common fault classes (parallelizable):
   - Regression in kernel binary/driver: check recent kernel-related rollouts or kernel-variant canaries in the last 30m. Command: git rev-list --since="30 minutes ago" -- kernel/
   - Resource exhaustion: look at node GPU memory util and host-level OOM logs. CLI examples: kubectl top pod -n runtime | sort -k3 -nr; ssh to host and check nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv
   - Scheduler misconfiguration: check admission-controller and credit buckets for cohort. Query admission metrics and recent config pushes.
   - Hot-path kernel slowdown due to sequence length change: correlate request sequence_length histogram to kernel latency.
4) Apply fast mitigations (choose applicable, run one at a time):
   - Route affected cohort to safe model variant or lower fidelity model to reduce kernel load. (Console route change; follow routing rollback checklist.)
   - Increase scheduler slots or temporarily widen admission (if SLO permits).
   - Abort rollout: revert recent kernel or kernel-config change via canary rollback.
   - Evict noisy tenant(s) if cross-tenant noise is identified (follow eviction authority policy).
5) If mitigations fail, page kernel scheduling owner and SRE with incident severity.

Post-incident diagnostics and writeup (10 steps):
1) Capture full 1h/24h metric windows and annotate the KHI spike and mitigations applied.
2) Replay sample traces with throttling reproduction harness (use the replay-runbook below).
3) Run targeted microbenchmarks against suspected kernels (see section: microbenchmark recipes).
4) Check for correlated infra events (network blips, cloud NPU maintenance notices, host reboots).
5) Extract kernel flame graphs and differential profiles against a pre-incident baseline.
6) If a new kernel variant is implicated, run the compatibility test matrix and kernel-safety smoke tests.
7) Update KHI normalizers if the baseline has shifted legitimately due to new model mix.
8) Produce a short incident summary with root cause, corrective actions, and preventive work.
9) Link a follow-up ticket with owners and target dates for any code/config change.
10) Verify remediation by validating KHI and SLOs for 48–72 hours.

Microbenchmark recipes (quick):
- Controlled invocation: run the kernel microbench driver with varying sequence lengths and batch shapes to reproduce tail behavior. Example command: 
  ./kernel_microbench --model=decoder_v2 --batch-shape=1x64x512 --sequence=1024 --repeat=200

- Kernel launch stress: synthetic parallel launch script to exercise launch paths. 
  python tools/parallel_launch.py --workers=128 --ops=2000 --cohort=web-embeddings

Observability changes to implement (backlog):
- Add KHI cohort breakdown to the daily perf digest email and Console uptime dashboard.
- Store 7d sliding baseline histograms per cohort to make normalization robust to diurnal patterns.
- Introduce automatic root-cause candidate ranking: link top correlated signals and host/pod lists in alert payload.

Known limitations and caveats:
- KHI can be biased during large deployments or A/B experiments; always annotate major rollouts and use rollouts tag to mute alerts during coordination windows.
- The normalization function requires 7d stable baseline; newly onboarded cohorts with <24h data should use default baseline.
- Cross-tier routing events can create transient KHI spikes; correlate routing events to avoid unnecessary paging.

Example incident timeline (short):
- 09:02 KHI crosses 40 for cohort web-embeddings.
- 09:03 Oncall investigation started; top 5 hosts show GPU memory pressure.
- 09:05 Route impacted cohort to quantized variant; KHI falls to 22 within 6 minutes.
- 09:30 Root cause identified: canary kernel variant introduced a memory growth regression.
- Postmortem: canary gate tightened; new safety test added to microbenchmark suite.

Appendix A — Sample alert payload (suggested fields):
- alert_name: kernel_health_index_high
- cohort: web-embeddings
- khi_value: 73
- khi_delta_5m: 38
- top_metrics: {k_tail: 0.99, k_err: 0.007, k_q: 0.85, k_preempt: 0.12, k_mem: 0.22}
- top_hosts: [ip-10-1-12-3, ip-10-1-13-9]
- recent_rollouts: [kernel-variant-1.7.2, scheduler-config-2026-11-12]

Appendix B — Example canary mute policy (operational):
- During a scheduled kernel canary (window: 30m), KHI alerts are muted if canary_rollout_tag=true AND KHI increase is restricted to canary cohort only. Non-canary cohort impact always pages.

Appendix C — Links and references:
- Runtime telemetry data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Scheduler admission matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-admission-matrix-and-signal-negotiation-manual-2026
- Microbenchmark suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025

If you are oncall and unsure, follow the checklist under 'Confirm alert and scope' and escalate immediately. This playbook will be iterated on after each incident and quarterly review by the kernel scheduling team.

payload.page_title: Runtime Execution Safety Matrix and Contraction Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the Runtime Execution Safety Matrix (RESM) — a prescriptive mapping from runtime signals to safe, deterministic mitigation actions — plus an operational playbook for 'execution contraction' (the controlled reduction of runtime concurrency and feature surface during incidents). RESM complements existing runbooks by codifying exact thresholds, owners, and automated vs manual actions for kernel scheduling, KV-cache, and model-variant routing subsystems.

Why this exists

- Reduce ambiguity during incidents where multiple subsystems degrade (e.g., kernel queuing + NVLink error flurries).
- Provide deterministic, tested contraction paths to preserve customer-facing SLOs while minimizing cost and blast radius.
- Standardize telemetry-to-action mappings so oncall, SRE, and runtime engineers share a single source of truth.

Scope and audience

- Audience: runtime engineers, SRE, oncall, release engineers, and incident commanders.
- Scope: serving runtime control plane, kernel scheduler, KV-cache layer, routing/fallback, and the integration points with autoscaler and Dedicated capacity. Not a replacement for low-level kernel docs — it references them.

Key concepts

1) Execution contraction

A controlled sequence of runtime state degradations designed to reduce resource pressure while preserving critical (customer-facing) traffic. Contraction is implemented by:
- narrowing concurrency windows (reduce max inflight requests per shard),
- tightening admission control (shortening queue depth),
- reducing model fidelity (switching to quantized / smaller variants),
- disabling non-critical features (structured output validation, large-context caching prefetch).

2) Safety matrix entries

Each entry maps: observable signal -> threshold -> categorical severity -> automated action -> oncall notification -> rollback condition.

Execution contracts (examples)

- Contract: "CPU-bound preemption storm"
  - Signal: kernel preemption failures (metric: kernel.preempt.fail.count)
  - Threshold: >= 20 failures / 30s on > 30% of shards
  - Severity: high
  - Automated action: apply kernel conservative mapper (priority: low), reduce concurrency target on affected shards to 40%
  - Notification: page oncall-sre@redwood (pagerduty) and post Slack #runtime-incidents
  - Rollback: kernel.preempt.fail.count < 2 / 5m AND p95 latency back within 120% of baseline

- Contract: "KV-cache storm (cold misses)"
  - Signal: kvcache.miss.rate > 0.85 for 10m AND kvcache.warmup.rate < 1.0
  - Severity: medium
  - Automated action: enable prefix-preservation mode, pause aggressive eviction heuristics, and increase prefetch window to 1.2x for identified tenant cohorts
  - Notification: post to #kvcache-observability; create triage ticket with runbook tag
  - Rollback: kvcache.miss.rate < 0.2 for 15m

Safety matrix table (text format)

| ID | Signal | Threshold | Severity | Automated Action | Owner | Metric to monitor |
|----|--------|-----------|----------|------------------|-------|------------------|
| RESM-01 | kernel.preempt.fail.count | >=20/30s on >30% shards | High | Conservative kernel mapper + concurrency reduce to 40% | kernel-team | p95_latency, kernel.preempt.fail.count |
| RESM-07 | kvcache.miss.rate | >0.85 for 10m | Medium | Prefix-preserve + pause eviction | storage-team | kvcache.miss.rate, kvcache.warmup.rate |
| RESM-12 | model.variant.switch.rate | >5/min across region | Low | Disable warm model swap; route to pinned stable variant | routing-team | model.swap.errors, route-err-rate |

Operational playbook: contraction flow (step-by-step)

1) Detect and classify
   - Automated monitors evaluate RESM entries every 30s (see monitoring rule bundles/resm-checks).
   - If an entry crosses 'automated' threshold, the automation enters a 'pre-commit' hold state for 20s to gather corroborating signals.

2) Execute minimal-impact mitigations (automated)
   - Apply the action in the Safety Matrix. Automation will:
     - run the scheduler control API: curl -X POST $SCHED_API/apply -d '{"shard": "shard-id", "concurrency_target": 0.4, "mapper_profile": "conservative"}'
     - set KV cache policy via admin cli: redwood-kvctl set-policy --shard shard-id --policy prefix-preserve --evict-pause true
   - Automation annotates rollback conditions and creates a short-lived incident (auto:RESM-<id>-auto).

3) Observe for 5–10 minutes
   - If rollup metrics improve to safe bounds, automation marks the incident resolved and records actions in incident index.
   - If still degraded or new signals appear, escalate to manual intervention.

4) Manual contraction and customer impact staging (human)
   - Oncall follows the manual contraction checklist below.
   - If customer-visible latency or error SLOs are at risk, initiate a canary traffic shift to Dedicated or fallback model region.

Manual contraction checklist (for oncall)

1. Verify correlated signals: kernel traces, NVLink errors, dispatch queue depths.
2. Lock the change window in the control plane (set change_window: locked).
3. Reduce global concurrency cap in 10% increments (max three steps). Command: redwood-runtimectl set-global-concurrency --pct 80
4. Pin critical customers to stable variants: redwood-routingctl pin --tenant-tenants=LIST --variant=stable-v1
5. Disable non-critical features: redwood-configctl toggle --feature structured-output-validation --off
6. Re-assess for 15 minutes between steps; document each action in the incident timeline.

Kernel scheduling interactions

- Priority mapping: RESM triggers may bump top-level request priorities for system-critical flows (health checks, control-plane requests). Use priority level 0 (highest) through 9 (lowest).
- Admission control: The scheduler supports dynamic queue depth per priority bucket. During contraction we prefer to reduce low-priority queue depths first.
- Cooperative preemption: On detected compute starvation, activate cooperative preemption window (default 200ms). This is a temporary measure to reduce tail latency but increases preemption overhead; used only when RESM-01 or RESM-03 active.

Profiling and instrumentation guidance

- Sampling policy: increase kernel-trace sampling from 0.5% -> 5% for affected shards during contraction. Use the profiling agent: redwood-profctl set-sampling --shard shard-id --rate 0.05
- Tag traces with RESM id: ensure every automated action attaches header X-RESM-ID: RESM-01 so traces can be filtered.
- Repro artifacts: collect a 10s GPGPU timeline, scheduler trace, and KV-cache histogram. Store under /artifacts/incidents/<incident-id>/ for postmortems.

Benchmarking matrix for contraction validation

- Validate contraction sequences on the staging bench using these controlled profiles before enabling automation:
  - Profile A: 90% short requests (<= 32 tokens), 10% long (>=1024 tokens). Target p95 latency 110% of production baseline.
  - Profile B: Mixed tenant concurrency with hotspot (10% tenants produce 60% load). Ensure eviction strategies do not thrash.
  - Failure injection: simulated NVLink flaps and kernel-preempt spikes. Automation must not raise error-rate above 0.5% for 5 minutes.

Release and rollout checklist for RESM automation

1. Unit and integration tests for each matrix entry (simulate signals and assert actions).
2. Run staged stress experiments on the bench (Profile A/B) for 48h.
3. Canary the automation to 2% of traffic for 24h with observability hooks.
4. Monitor key metrics for 72h and gather canary feedback.
5. Full rollout with 1-hour watch window and a designated rollback owner.

Operational metrics and SLOs referenced by RESM

- p95 latency (short seq): 120ms (SLO target), p99: 300ms (SLO target for hosted API).
- Error rate (5xx on inference path): <0.2% (SLA-sensitive).
- Kernel preemption failure: baseline <1 / 30s across fleet.
- KV-cache miss rate: baseline <0.15 for warmed cohorts.

Post-incident and continuous improvement

- Incident owners must attach a RESM review note to postmortems (template: RESM-review.md) capturing: why automated action triggered, what worked, false positives, and suggestions.
- Quarterly: kernel and scheduler teams run contraction drills (game days) with 1% production traffic mirrored to bench.

Appendix: sample configs and commands

- Scheduler apply (JSON payload):

  curl -X POST $SCHED_API/apply -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '\n  {\n    "targets": ["shard-id-1","shard-id-2"],\n    "changes": {"concurrency_target": 0.4, "mapper_profile": "conservative"},\n    "annotation": "RESM-01 auto mitigation"\n  }'\n
- KV policy (CLI):

  redwood-kvctl set-policy --shard shard-id-1 --policy prefix-preserve --evict-pause true --note "RESM-07 auto"\n
- Profiling (increase sampling):

  redwood-profctl set-sampling --shard shard-id-1 --rate 0.05 --attach-header "X-RESM-ID:RESM-07"\n
- Example configuration table (text):

| config_key | default | RESM override | notes |
|-----------|---------|---------------|-------|
| scheduler.concurrency_global | 1.0 | 0.8,0.6,0.4 | Reduced in three steps during manual contraction |
| kvcache.eviction_aggression | 1.0 | 0.0 | Pause during prefix-preserve mode |
| profiling.sampling_rate | 0.005 | 0.05 | Increased for affected shards during investigation |
| kernel.mapper_profile | balanced | conservative | conservative reduces speculative work and preemption |

Contact and ownership

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-safety subgroup) — Aisha Patel (author)
- Kernel team contact: Marcus Liu
- KV/Storage contact: Priya Kannan
- Oncall escalation: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations/ (internal link)

Change log

- 2026-01-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2026-02-18: Added KV-cache storm guidance and automated action payloads.
- 2026-03-01: Formalized rollback conditions and canary checklist (published).

payload.page_title: runtime-contributor-onboarding-lab-guide-2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This lab-style guide is intended to onboard new contributors and rotating engineers into the serving runtime team. It consolidates the minimum safe workflow for making experimental changes, running targeted profiling and benchmarks, exercising scheduler/kernels in sandboxes, and shipping small iterate-able improvements with maintained SLOs. The guide is written for engineers with prior Linux and Python experience; no prior kernel-development experience is required.

Audience
--------
- New members of eng-serving-runtime (runtime, kernel, scheduler, and tooling subteams)
- Rotating SREs and performance engineers who will run experiments or triage incidents

Why this exists
----------------
- Reduce time-to-meaningful-contribution while minimizing risk to production pools
- Establish reproducible experiments and artifact capture for each change
- Ensure every contributor follows the same safety, observability, and rollback gates

Prerequisites (local and cloud)
------------------------------
1. GitHub account with repo access: request via infra-oncall ticket if missing.
2. Bastion + kubectl access to dev clusters: dev-serving-1 and dev-serving-2.
3. GPU-enabled dev nodes (tag: runtime-lab) provisioned by infra.
4. Python 3.10 environment with dev dependencies: pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
5. Familiarity with the following playbooks: the runtime profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contract, and the canary-run matrix (links in "Related pages" above).

Quick environment setup (copy-paste)
-----------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U pip setuptools
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
sections.heading: Create virtualenv and install

sections.body:
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config
kubectl config use-context dev-serving-1
sections.heading: Configure kube context and dev cluster port-forwarding

sections.body:
kubectl -n runtime port-forward svc/dispatcher 8080:8080 &

Local sandbox: starting a single-shard runtime for experiments\-----------------------------------------------------------
We maintain a lightweight developer runtime image that mirrors production behavior but restricts capacity. Use this to iterate fast:
sections.heading: port-forward dispatcher for local profiling UI

sections.body:
kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/sandbox-single-shard.yaml
kubectl -n runtime rollout status deploy/sandbox-runtime --timeout=120s

Once the sandbox is up, you can push model binaries to the sandbox bucket and point the runtime at them for kernel experiments.

Experiment lifecycle (minimum viable experiment)
------------------------------------------------
1) Hypothesis & test plan (commit to a small MD file under experiments/): include the expected metric delta and the signal source (trace, histogram, microbenchmark).
2) Local reproduction: run an isolated microbenchmark against sandbox using workload-replay tool.
3) Capture artifacts: profiling traces, kernel counters, target traces, and the synthetic corpus used. Attach artifacts to the experiment PR.
4) Peer review: request at least one reviewer from the kernel or runtime team depending on the change.
5) Canary run: run change in canary pool with trace sampling enabled and compare SLOs.
6) Rollout gate evaluation: use the rollout checklist (section below).
7) Roll forward or rollback based on gate results.

Profiling quick-start (what to collect and why)
------------------------------------------------
- Flame traces (CPU path) — to attribute host scheduling cost.
- GPU kernel timeline (nsight/metric export) — to find stalls or serialization.
- Kernel dispatch histograms (per-kernel latency P50/P90/P99).
- KV cache hit/miss counters and session lifecycle traces.
- Request and token level latency breakdown (dispatcher, kernel queue, kernel run).

Collecting a trace (example commands)
------------------------------------
sections.heading: start a single-node sandbox (local dev box must be in dev cluster)

sections.body: replay --config experiments/basic-replay.yaml --duration 300 --trace-out artifacts/trace-$(date +%s).zip
sections.heading: run the replay harness for 5 minutes and collect traces

sections.body:
ssh gpu-dev-node-1 sudo /opt/runtime/bin/pull-counters --out artifacts/counters-$(date +%s).json

Benchmarks: recommended suite and how to run
-------------------------------------------
We maintain a curated benchmark suite that mirrors common customer workloads. Benchmarks are separated into three categories: micro (kernel-level), meso (single-model end-to-end on a shard), and e2e (multi-tenant dispatcher+shard).

Running a microbenchmark (example)
1. Build kernel hint artifact: make -C runtime/kernel artifacts/bench_hint.o
2. Run microbench: python tools/microbench.py --kernel bench_hint.o --iters 1000 --out artifacts/micro-$(date +%s).json

Running the meso benchmark (dispatcher + single shard)
1. kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/bench-meso.yaml
2. python tools/bench_driver.py --scenario meso-latency --duration 600 --sample-rate 100

SLOs and safety gates for experiments
------------------------------------
- Baseline SLOs (applies to all experiments unless otherwise noted):
  - P99 end-to-end latency (single-token): <= 250ms on dev shards
  - P95 inference latency (per request): <= 180ms
  - Error rate (HTTP 5xx): <= 0.05% in canary
  - Kernel regressions: no increase > 5% P99 kernel-run-time vs baseline for the same sequence-length distribution

Gate checklist (before canary)
1. Unit tests and microbench suite pass locally.
2. Profiling artifacts attached to PR.
3. Performance regression test (meso benchmark) within threshold.
4. Observability: trace sampling enabled and dashboards updated.
5. Rollout plan with timeboxed canary and rollback TTL.

Canary run matrix (example)
--------------------------
- Canary group A: 1 shard, 10% production trace sampling, 12-hour run, synthetic and shadow traffic.
- Canary group B: 2 shards, real production traffic at 1%, 24-hour run, enhanced telemetry.

Rollback triggers (automated/manual)
------------------------------------
- Automated: error rate exceeds 0.1% OR P99 latency regresses by > 10% sustained for 5 minutes.
- Manual: on-call or owning engineer observes customer-visible degradation or fidelity regression.

Making kernel changes: additional cautions
------------------------------------------
- Kernel patches must include deterministic microbench and counter-driven rationale.
- Avoid changes that alter kernel ABI or input serialization without explicit compat notes.
- Include a fallback path (config flag) to switch back to previous kernel implementation at runtime.

Example CI job for kernel change (YAML snippet)
------------------------------------------------
ci-jobs:
  kernel-change-check:
    steps:
      - name: run-unit-tests
        run: make test
      - name: run-microbench
        run: python tools/microbench.py --iters 200 --out artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: upload-artifacts
        run: ./tools/ci/upload-artifacts artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: auto-profile-compare
        run: python tools/ci/compare_profiles.py --baseline s3://bench-baselines/kernel-p99.json --candidate artifacts/ci-micro.json
\nPost-merge observability and ownership
--------------------------------------
- Ownership: the author owns the change for a 72-hour burn-in period. The oncall takes secondary watches.
- Dashboards: add a dashboard panel named feature/<pr-number> to the Runtime Canary folder.
- Alerts: for short-lived experiments use an alert muting policy; create a tagging rule to ensure faster triage.

Runbook snippets and playbook links
----------------------------------
- If kernel stall is suspected: follow the "kernel-stability-siege-testing" playbook (see Related pages) and collect GPU timelines, host traces, and allocator stats.
- For cross-tenant noise: consult the "multi-tenant-affinity-noise-mitigation" benchmark procedures.

Checklist for turning an experiment into a permanent change
----------------------------------------------------------
1. Confirm that artifacts, benchmarks, and canary runs are reproducible and archived.
2. Update runtime feature flags or configuration schema.
3. Add automated microbench to CI with the new baseline.
4. Document the change in release notes and link to experiment artifacts.
5. Schedule a follow-up verification run after 30 days.

Roles & responsibilities (table)
--------------------------------
| Role | Responsibility | Escalation |
|---|---|---|
| Author | Write experiment plan, implement change, run local CI | Team lead |
| Reviewer | Validate benchmarks and safety gates | Senior runtime engineer |
| Oncall | Monitor canary, trigger rollback if thresholds hit | SRE lead |
| Bench steward | Maintain benchmark baselines and runner infra | Performance lead |

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
------------------------------------
- Pitfall: running benchmarks with mismatched sequence-length distributions.
  Remedy: verify input corpus stats with tools/corpus_stats.py and attach results.
- Pitfall: forgetting to enable trace sampling in canary.
  Remedy: use the canary template from infra/canary-templates/canary-config.yaml.
- Pitfall: not including a fallback flag for kernel ABIs.
  Remedy: always add a runtime toggle and document expected behavior.

Appendix A: Useful commands and tooling paths
--------------------------------------------
- replay: tools/replay/README.md
- microbench: tools/microbench.py
- profiler UI: http://localhost:8080 (port-forward to dispatcher)
- trace archive convention: experiments/<pr-number>/artifacts/<timestamp>.zip

Appendix B: On-call contacts and escalation matrix
--------------------------------------------------
- Runtime oncall (primary): #eng-runtime-oncall Slack
- Performance lead: lena@redwood.ai
- Kernel lead: theo@redwood.ai

Related pages
-------------
See the profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contracts, and the benchmarking suite for deeper reference material. This page is the operational glue that explains how to safely move through the change lifecycle from idea to production.

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-18: Initial draft by Aisha Romero.
- 2026-04-12: Added canary matrix and CI YAML by Theo Martinez.
- 2026-09-10: Clarified SLO thresholds and added rollout checklist by Aisha Romero.

payload.page_title: Fidelity budgeting and runtime cost governor manual

sections.body:
Overview
========
This document defines the Fidelity Budgeting model and the Runtime Cost Governor (RCG) — a declarative control plane that enforces per-tenant/route fidelity budgets at serving time. The goal of the RCG is to keep customer-visible SLOs within targets while bounding per-token and per-request spend across mixed workloads.

Intended audience
- Runtime and scheduler engineers
- Product owners for Dedicated/Private customers
- SRE and capacity-planning teams
- Benchmark and profiling engineers

Why this exists
- Inference cost is variable by model variant, sequence length, batching shape and kernel choices.
- We need a single, auditable mechanism to trade fidelity for cost under pressure (autoscale, thermal events, capacity constraints).
- RCG ties scheduling signals, kernel hints, and quantization/variant routing decisions to a budget and provides a deterministic downgrade strategy.

Principles
- Predictability: budget enforcement must be explainable and reproducible.
- Observability: every fidelity decision must be logged with provenance (trigger, score, pre/post metrics).
- Minimize user impact: preservation of critical tokens and short requests is prioritized over long/low-priority generation.
- Fast rollback: policy changes must be reversible within a single canary window.

Key concepts and terminology
- Fidelity budget: numeric allowance per time window (tokens or token-equivalents) that a tenant/route can spend.
- Fidelity credit: per-request currency derived from model variant cost and sequence projection.
- Degradation ladder: ordered list of fidelity actions (e.g., small-quantize -> shorter-prefix-cache -> model-variant -> response-truncation).
- Governor evaluation window: default 30s sliding window for budget accounting.

Metrics, signals and SLOs
- Primary SLOs: 99th-pct tail latency <= 250ms (interactive tier), ERR_RATE <= 0.5%
- Budget signals: token_consumed, credit_burn_rate, on_gpu_slots, queue_depth, kernel_wait_time_ms
- Observability artifacts: fidelity_decision events (json), pre/post latency histograms, regression score (quality delta vs baseline prompts).

Architecture overview
- Inputs: request classifier (priority, route), model catalog pricing table (tokens / cost), runtime telemetry (slot usage, kernel queue), profiling hints (sequence length distribution).
- Decision engine: lightweight policy evaluator that produces an ordered list of degradation actions and an urgency score.
- Enforcers: scheduler (admission control and slot assignment), kernel adapter (per-request kernel flags), router (model variant routing), kvcache layer (prefix eviction hints).
- Audit sink: fidelity-decision store and metrics exporter.

Budgeting controls and policy primitives
- static_budget: fixed tokens per-minute (example: 1e6 tokens/min)
- proportional_budget: fraction of cluster budget for shared pools (0.02 = 2%)
- emergency_buffer: reserved credits only used when latency or error budgets are breached

Simple policy example (YAML)
--------------------------
policy_name: interactive-default
owner: team-runtime
window_seconds: 30
budget_type: token_quota
budget_amount: 50000
degradation_ladder:
  - action: prefer-quantized-variant
    min_quality_delta: -0.02
  - action: reduce-max-output-tokens
    reduction_percent: 25
  - action: route-to-small-variant
    acceptable_loss: -0.05
priority_overrides:
  - route: /chat/completion
    min_reserve: 2000

Scheduler integration
- Admission checks use the RCG decision as a prefilter. If a tenant is above budget, admission returns PROBATION with a recommended action list.
- Scheduler applies soft-slot labels (e.g., fidelity=low) to place downgraded requests on consolidation pools to reduce interference.
- Kernel hints are conveyed via request metadata: {kernel_hint: "prefetch_off,quantize_a2"}.

Profiling & benchmarking guidance
- For each candidate policy change run:
  1) Local microbenchmark with synthetic sequences (short, medium, long) to measure latency and kernel divergence.
  2) Shadow traffic pass (1 hour minimum) to observe real distribution effects.
  3) Quality regression suite (prompt set) measuring ROUGE/BLEU and model-specific evals.
- Required artifacts to land a policy: before/after cost-per-token, latency p50/p95/p99, quality regressions per prompt set, and fidelity_decision trace samples.

Operational runbook: budget breach (quick triage)
1) Detection
  - Alert: fidelity_budget_burn_rate > 120% for 1 minute or fidelity_decision_failure_count > 5/min
2) Immediate actions (first 5 minutes)
  - Escalate to runtime-oncall and set channel #runtime-fidelity with incident tag.
  - Switch policy to safe-mode: static_budget=nominal/4, enforce-first-ladder-only.
  - Create shadow traces for 5 minutes: set header X-Trace-Fidelity-Detail=true.
3) Investigation (5–30 minutes)
  - Check recent deployments: kernel or scheduler changes in the last 30 minutes (kubectl/CI links).
  - Correlate with capacity metrics: GPU_utilization, kernel_wait_time_ms, queue_depth.
  - Run profiling job: sample 2% of traffic for deep trace (use trace-capture CLI below).
4) Mitigation (30–120 minutes)
  - If degraded by thermal or hardware: move high-priority tenants to reserved pools.
  - If caused by regression: revert policy or kernel flag and roll forward safe-mode config.
  - If intentional load spike: negotiate temporary budget increase with product (document in audit).
5) Postmortem requirements
  - Within 48 hours: publish summary, root cause, timeline, and any policy code changes.

Trace capture CLI (example)
- - -
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
runtctl trace capture --tenant acme --events fidelity_decision --limit 10000 --out /tmp/acme-fidelity-trace.ndjson

Policy rollout checklist
1) Author policy with rationale and expected cost delta.
2) Unit tests for policy parser and fallback actions.
3) Local benchmark (p50/p99, cost delta).
4) Canary deploy (1% traffic, 30m), monitor fidelity_decisions and latency SLOs.
5) 10% shadow for 2 hours, examine quality regressions.
6) Gradual 20% -> 50% -> 100% steps with automated rollback thresholds (p99 latency +10% or error_rate > 0.2%).

Example governance matrix (text table)
- Name: interactive-default | Owner: team-runtime | Window: 30s | Budget: 50k tokens
- Rollout gate: p99_latency_delta <= +10ms & quality_regression <= 1%

Telemetry and audit
- fidelity_decision schema (logged): request_id, tenant_id, route, budget_window_start, budget_remaining, chosen_action, reason_code, decision_score, timestamp
- Export to: metrics (Prom), events (kafka topic: fidelity-decisions), long-term store for 90d.

Ownership & contacts
- Policy author: Ava Chen (runtime@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler integration owner: Marcus Patel
- Oncall for fidelity incidents: runtime-oncall rotation (oncall@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — configuration samples
- Governor config (JSON snippet):
{
  "policy_name":"interactive-default",
  "window_seconds":30,
  "budget_amount":50000,
  "degradation_ladder":["prefer-quantized-variant","reduce-max-output-tokens","route-to-small-variant"]
}

Appendix B — quality regression example
- For the "prefer-quantized-variant" action we allow a maximum QA score delta of -0.03 as measured on the interactive-quality prompt set. If measured delta exceeds threshold during canary, the canary aborts.

Related work and references
- See runtime-architecture predictive-prefetch doc for sequence projection inputs.
- See benchmarking suite docs for how to generate the required before/after artifacts.

Change log
- 2025-01-15: created (A. Chen)
- 2025-06-12: added emergency_buffer section and scheduler hints (M. Patel)
- 2025-10-02: clarified rollout gates and updated trace capture CLI (L. Ortiz)

End of document
