payload.page_title: Telemetry rollup and sampling strategies for the serving runtime

sections.body: This document describes the telemetry aggregation (rollup) and sampling strategies used by the Redwood serving runtime. It gives concrete rollup policies, sampling heuristics for traces/requests, cardinality guidance, example ingestion configurations (Prometheus/OTLP/agent), and migration/runbook steps to reduce telemetry cost while preserving SLO-aligned visibility.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Keep operational dashboards and SLO alerting robust while lowering metric cardinality and storage costs.
- Standardize rollup windows and aggregation keys across runtime services to make cross-service joins reliable.
- Provide deterministic sampling rules for traces and high-frequency events so debugging remains possible for class-of-failures.
- Preserve fine-grained telemetry for canaries and high-priority customers (Dedicated/Private) while applying stronger rollups for best-effort workloads.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: - Observability engineers, runtime/infrastructure owners, SREs, and oncall responders.
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) SLO-driven fidelity: choose retention and granularity so that any alertable SLO has the required percentile and time-window fidelity. If a 10-minute p99 is an SLO target, ensure that rollups keep 1s/10s resolution-derived p99 for the relevant signal.
2) Limit cardinality at the ingestion layer: drop or hash low-value tags before series creation. Use label allowlists per metric.
3) Separate control-plane vs data-plane telemetry: control-plane operations (deploys, rollouts) keep full labels; high-volume data-plane metrics use coarser keys.
4) Deterministic sampling: sampling decisions should be stable (based on deterministic hash of request id / customer id) when possible so traces for a customer are consistent across retries and fallbacks.
sections.heading: Principles and tradeoffs

sections.body:
- Metric prefix: runtime_<component>_<metric> (e.g., runtime_shard_kernel_latency_seconds).
- Canonical tags (allowlist order of importance): service, model, model_variant, region, shard, priority_tier, customer_tier.
- Non-canonical / scrubbed tags: request_id, user_prompt_digest (hashed), raw_input_size (binned: small/medium/large).
sections.heading: Metric naming and canonical tags

sections.body:
- 15s raw ingestion retention: 7 days (default for critical metrics tied to SLO).
- 1m rollups: 30 days.
- 5m rollups: 90 days.
- 1h rollups (aggregated summaries): 1 year.
Notes: For Dedicated/Private customer lanes, maintain 15s raw for 30 days when contract requires longer retention.
sections.heading: Rollup windows and retention (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- Counters: standard delta aggregation.
- Gauges: last-sample aggregation for rollup window, plus min/max.
- Histograms: keep exemplars where available; rollup histograms by merging buckets using consistent bucket boundaries. Avoid dynamic buckets per-instance.
- Summaries: discouraged for cross-host rollups; prefer histogram-based approach for pXX calculations.
sections.heading: Aggregation semantics

sections.body:
1) Enforce label allowlists at the ingestion client (agent): only forward tags in canonical list.
2) Hash low-entropy user identifiers when they must be retained, and annotate the metric with hashed_id_bucket (e.g., hashed_customer_bucket=0..1023).
3) Use per-metric label limits: if unique label values exceed 1000 in a 5m window, trigger autoscrub mode for that metric and remove the offending label.
4) Example denylist: full_text, prompt_blob, kvcache_key.
sections.heading: Cardinality control and label strategies

sections.body:
- Default sampling: 1% deterministic trace sampling (by stable hash of request_id) for production best-effort workloads.
- Priority sampling: 100% for errors (HTTP 5xx, internal error flags), timeouts, and requests contributing to tail-latency (e.g., if token-generation time > 2x median).
- Canary and customer lanes: 100% traces for canary clusters and Dedicated customer_tier requests.
- Adaptive spike sampling: when trace storage budget exceeded for the minute, reduce best-effort sampling to preserve error+tail capture. Implementations should lower non-error sampling stochastically but keep deterministic sampling for a fixed seed segment.
sections.heading: Sampling rules (traces and request spans)

sections.body:
- Rollup policy (YAML):
  rollup_policy_version: v1
  metrics:
    - name: runtime_kernel_latency_seconds
      rollup_windows: [15s, 1m, 5m, 1h]
      labels_allowed: [service, model, model_variant, region, priority_tier]
      cardinality_limit: 2000
    - name: runtime_requests_total
      rollup_windows: [15s, 1m, 5m]
      labels_allowed: [service, region, shard, customer_tier]
      cardinality_limit: 1000
  trace_sampling:
    default_rate: 0.01
    priorities:
      - condition: error_or_status_5xx
        rate: 1.0
      - condition: customer_tier == "dedicated"
        rate: 1.0
      - condition: canary == true
        rate: 1.0
sections.heading: Example agent configuration (OTel/Prometheus hybrid)

sections.body:
- p50/p95/p99 from histogram (Prometheus):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_kernel_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service, model, model_variant))
- request rate (per-region):
  sum(rate(runtime_requests_total[1m])) by (region)
sections.heading: PromQL and query examples (for dashboards/alerts)

sections.body:
- Inference latency SLO (small_seq): objective: p99 < 150ms over 10m window.
  Signal: runtime_kernel_latency_seconds histogram filtered by model_variant=small_seq.
  Required retention: 15s raw or 1m rollup that preserves histogram buckets.
- Request success SLO: 99.95% success over 1h.
  Signal: 1 - (sum(increase(runtime_requests_total{status!~"2.."}[1h])) / sum(increase(runtime_requests_total[1h])))
sections.heading: SLO mapping examples (how metrics map to SLOs)

sections.body:
- P99 latency breach: when 99th percentile > target for 3 of 5 consecutive 1m windows -> P0 alert.
- Error-rate spike: when error rate increases 3x baseline or > 0.5% absolute for 15m -> P1.
sections.heading: Alert thresholds (examples)

sections.body:
- Service overview: throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rate, autocost estimates.
- Kernel health: per-shard GPU utilization, kernel queue length, average kernel execution time.
- KV cache impact: cache hit ratio, warmup rate, cache-size-by-shard.
- Customer-tier slices: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private.

Runbook excerpt: handling a sudden cost spike from metric churn
1) Detect: Alert triggers for cardinality explosion (metric series growth > 15%/min).
2) Triage: Identify metric and offending label via series cardinality query (example query: topk(10, increase(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_total[5m]))).
3) Mitigate: Apply ingress label drop rule for the offending metric (agent config push): remove label or replace with hashed bucket.
4) Validate: Confirm series count stabilizes and dashboard panels return to expected series counts.
5) Postmortem: Create incident note with root cause and owner, adjust label allowlist or client instrumentation accordingly.
sections.heading: Dashboards and slices to maintain

sections.body:
- Backfill approach: do not backfill histograms by merging old dynamic-bucket histograms; instead regenerate from raw request logs where necessary.
- Rolling agent update: deploy rollup/allowlist changes via the config service in a canary->region->global rollout with feature flag to revert.
- Coordinate with telemetry-cost team for major label changes (expected cost delta estimation required) before global rollout.
sections.heading: Compatibility and migration guidance

sections.body:
- Use 5k series per node as a budgeting heuristic for standard best-effort nodes.
- Estimate trace storage: 1% sample of 10k rps with average 10 spans/request -> ~1MM spans/day; use compression and exemplar policies to reduce long-term retention.

Ownership, escalation, and contacts:
- Ownership: Observability team owns ingestion pipelines and rollup infra. Runtime infra (serving-runtime) owns metric naming and client-side allowlist.
- Oncall: Observability rotation for ingestion issues; runtime SRE rotation for metric correctness and SLO alerts.
- Contacts: obs-oncall@redwood.ai, runtime-sre@redwood.ai.
sections.heading: Cost estimation guidelines

sections.body:
- (Action) Define per-model bucket schemas for histograms to avoid bucket mismatches during rollup. Owner: Priya Nair. Target: 2026-04-01.
- (Action) Implement adaptive sample-rate controller that lowers sample rate during ingestion spikes but preserves deterministic sampling for hashed buckets. Owner: Jordan Li. Target: 2026-06-15.
- (Research) Evaluate compressed histogram encodings (t-digest / HDR) for long-term retention cost savings.

Appendix: quick CLI examples
- Force an ingress allowlist update (example):
  curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/v1/rollup-policies \\n    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \\n    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\n    -d '{"policy_name": "reduce-cardinality-2026-02", "updates": [{"metric": "runtime_requests_total", "drop_labels": ["raw_prompt"]}]}'

- Check current top series by growth:
  promql: topk(20, increase(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_total[5m]))
sections.heading: Open action items and future work

sections.body:
- Related: runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026 (data model and tracebook)
- Related: production-rollout-tuning-checklist-2026 (rollout steps for infra changes)
sections.heading: References

sections.body:
- 2024-11-12: initial draft
- 2025-03-10: added deterministic sampling rules and cost heuristics
- 2026-02-18: finalized rollup windows and added runbook steps
sections.heading: Document history

payload.page_title: Scheduler Health Oracle and Self‑Heal Procedures

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook defines the Scheduler Health Oracle (SHO) — an auditable, real‑time decision layer that monitors kernel/scheduler health, synthesizes signals across layers, and executes pre‑approved self‑heal actions. The goal is to reduce noisy oncall interrupts for transient kernel noise while providing rapid, reversible remediation for deterministic faults that threaten SLOs.

Audience:
- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers
- Kernel and scheduler owners
- Runtime observability and automation engineers

Why SHO: problem statement
- Scheduler-level regressions (priority inversion, admission spikes, kernel starvation) often manifest across multiple signals with non-obvious causality.
- Manual triage is slow; highly-automated remediation must be conservative, observable, and reversible.
- The SHO provides a standard decision contract and safe remediation actions so teams can opt-in with clear guardrails.

High-level design
1) Signal ingestion: aggregated telemetry from dispatcher, kernel-profiles, KVCache, GPU telemetry, and network layer.
2) Feature synthesis: rolling-error rates, kernel latency percentiles, credit-accounting deltas, slot utilization, and memory pressure indices.
3) Heuristic and ML tiers: short ruleset-based checks for high-confidence faults + an optional ML model to identify correlated multi-signal anomalies.
4) Policy engine: maps detected failure modes to approved remediation actions with associated confidence thresholds.
5) Actuation/blocking: dry-run, non-blocking notification, or automatic remediation. All actions are logged to the incident trace and can be rolled back automatically or manually.

Detection signals and thresholds (baseline)
- kernel_cpu_latency_p50/p95/p99 (per-kernel): p95 > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive 1m buckets => medium severity
- scheduler_queue_depth: sustained > 85% of configured capacity for 2m => medium
- kernel_preemptions_rate: increase > 3x baseline => high
- slot_evictions_per_min: > 10/min for a node cohort => medium
- kvcache_warmup_failures: 5 failures within 5m => low
- gpu_thermal_throttle: any non-transient throttle event logged by NVML => high
- cross-signal rule: if p99 latency increase + scheduler_queue_depth spike + kernel_preemptions_rate rise => immediate canary rollback action at confidence >= 0.8

Policy mapping examples
- High-confidence GPU thermal throttle (NVML): immediate isolate node (cordon + drain policy) => action: schedule node cordon, redirect new requests, start evacuation.
- Kernel preemption storm (rule-based): lower background priority cohort for 2m, enable cooperative preemption mode => action: toggle scheduler param preempt_coop=true for affected cohort.
- Latency increase with KV cache misses: enable KV prefetch hints + increase warm pool size by +10% for 10m.
- Admission overload (queue depth): enable temporary token-based backpressure: set admission.max_inflight to 70% of baseline for 5m.

Runbook: automated remediation decision flow
1. Detection: SHO raises an event with reason_code and confidence score.
2. Verification: SHO attempts a secondary verification sampler (shadow query of kernel health; targeted microtraces) — 30s.
3. Mode selection: 
a) Confidence >= 0.9 and matches high-impact rule => automatic remediation with full audit.
b) Confidence between 0.6 and 0.9 => gated remediation: perform non-blocking action (e.g., param tweak plus page to oncall) and run 5m watch.
c) Confidence < 0.6 => create incident page and alert, no actuation.
4. Actuation: perform action using orchestration API (see Actuation API spec snippet below).
5. Observe: track remediation effect via pre and post windows (1m, 5m, 10m).
6. Rollback: if metrics do not improve or regress further, automatically revert parameter and mark as failed remediation.
7. Postmortem: automatically create an incident skeleton and assign to the owning team if confidence >= 0.6 and an action was taken.

Actuation API: example cURL and YAML policy (safe defaults)
- cURL (sample):

curl -X POST https://orchestrator.internal/api/v1/actuate 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SHO_TOKEN' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d '{"action":"tweak_scheduler_param","target":"cohort:gpu-rt-*-west","params":{"preempt_coop":"true","duration":"300s"},"correlation_id":"sho-20261102-1234"}'

- Policy YAML (human-editable):

policy_id: sho_default_2026
description: Conservative remediation policies for scheduler-level faults
rules:
  - id: cordon_on_gpu_thermal
    selectors: ["gpu_thermal_throttle==true"]
    confidence_threshold: 0.9
    action:
      name: cordon_node
      params: {drain_timeout: 120, evac_cohort: gpu-rt-*}
  - id: coop_preempt_during_preempt_storm
    selectors: ["kernel_preemptions_rate>3x"]
    confidence_threshold: 0.8
    action:
      name: tweak_scheduler_param
      params: {preempt_coop: true, duration: 300}

Observability and dashboards
- SHO Dashboard (Grafana):
  - Primary row: composite SHO confidence time-series, active remediations, last_revert_time.
  - Signal heatmap: per-cluster kernel p99, queue depth, preemption_rate.
  - Action audit log: rendered list of actuations with correlation_id and link to incident page.

- Tracing: all SHO decisions attach a correlation_id (sho-<date>-<seq>) to traces. Use the tracing explorer to filter traces by correlation_id.

Oncall playbook (quick steps)
1. Page received with action_id and correlation_id. Immediately check SHO dashboard link; confirm whether the action was automatic or gated.
2. If an automatic action executed: verify the pre/post metric windows.
   - If improvement within 2 windows (5/10m) -> mark incident as mitigated and start RCA.
   - If no improvement -> press the "revert" button in the SHO UI; revert executes immediate rollback and creates a hotfix ticket.
3. If it was a gated action: follow the remediation recommendation, but use the orchestrator-console to perform a controlled manual action instead of automatic.
4. If GPU node cordoned: confirm evacuation succeeded and note impacted customers; follow customer notification template (appendix).
5. After action: run short hypothesis test (see Appendix B) and annotate the incident with the traced signals used by SHO.

Safety and guardrails
- All automated actuations are rate-limited: max 2 concurrent cluster-wide automated actions per 10m.
- Any actuation that affects routing (fallback to variant models, cross-region shift) requires emergency-owner approval and cannot be automatically initiated.
- A signed audit entry with operator and source (SHO vs manual) must exist for all actuations.
- All policy changes must pass a canary in the staging fleet for 48h before being promoted to production.

Testing the SHO in staging (step-by-step)
1. Deploy SHO snapshot to staging cluster with policy sho_staging_2026.
2. Seed synthetic traffic with a controlled preemption spike using the stress-injector: 
   ./tools/stress-injector --target cohort=gpu-rt-staging --preempt-rate=5x --duration=120s
3. Verify SHO detected event and logged dry-run actuation.
4. Promote to gated mode and validate that a param tweak was recommended but not auto-applied.
5. Promote to auto-mode for non-destructive actions (e.g., increasing warm pool size) only after 48h.

Operational telemetry to collect (minimum)
- sho.decisions.count (by outcome: dryrun, gated, auto, revert)
- sho.decision_confidence.histogram
- sho.action_latency_ms (time between decision and actuation)
- kernel.latency.p99 (per-kernel, per-cohort)
- scheduler.queue_depth.percentile (1m, 5m)
- orchestrator.action_success_rate and revert_rate

Post-incident process and RCA guidance
- If SHO action was involved in mitigation, the RCA must include: decision rationale, confidence score, pre/post graphs, and audit correlation_id.
- Use the RCA template: Summary, Timeline, Hypothesis, Evidence (graphs/traces), Root cause, Mitigation, Long-term fix, Owner, ETA.

Appendix A: Example incident annotations (paste into incident page)
- sho:correlation_id: sho-20261102-1234
- sho:policy: sho_default_2026
- sho:decision: coop_preempt_during_preempt_storm
- sho:confidence: 0.87
- pre-window: kernel.p99=48ms -> post-window: 22ms

Appendix B: Hypothesis quick-tests
1. Isolate: reproduce the kernel preemption spike in staging with identical workload shapes.
2. Swap: reroute a small traffic cohort to an alternate scheduler variant and measure p99 delta.
3. Harden: apply the param tweak in a canary cohort and run a 1-hour stress profile.

Appendix C: Customer notification template (if nodes evacuated)
- Subject: Temporary capacity change in <region> (date/time)
- Body: We detected elevated thermal events affecting a subset of nodes and routed traffic to healthy capacity. No data exposure is suspected. We are monitoring and will update when all nodes are rejoined.

Appendix D: Common CLI commands and quick checks
- sho-status: show active SHO decisions
  $ shoctl status --cluster=us-west --format=table
- list recent actuations
  $ shoctl actions --since=1h --limit=50 --cluster=us-west
- revert an action manually
  $ shoctl revert --action-id=act-20261102-9876 --reason="no improvement"

payload.page_title: Observability Injection and Kernel Validation Harness

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This page describes the Observability Injection and Kernel Validation Harness (OIKVH): a lightweight, repeatable framework to verify kernel-level execution correctness, safety, and observability contracts under realistic telemetry perturbations. The goal is to detect regressions that only surface when tracing sampling, sidecar proxies, or SDK instrumentation are enabled in production and to ensure kernel safety nets (fallbacks, handshakes, hedging) continue to meet SLO-preservation guarantees.

Goals
-----
- Provide an automated harness to exercise kernels and scheduler paths with controlled observability perturbations (sampling, added latency, dropped events).
- Validate observability contracts: trace spans, correlation IDs, kernel IDs, and event sequencing required by debuggers and autotuners.
- Assert that runtime SLOs (P50, P95, P99 token latency, and error budget consumption) remain within tolerance under injected noise.
- Surface silent failures caused by instrumentation (e.g., excessive serialization time, blocking I/O) before rollouts.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
Real regressions have been observed where tracing sidecars or extended span annotations introduced CPU/GPU stall contention or increased critical-path latency in specific kernels. Those regressions are intermittent and correlate with specific sampling rates and SDK backpressure behavior. The OIKVH complements existing microbenchmarks by exercising full request lifecycles under observability stressors and validating both functional outcomes and telemetry integrity.

Design overview
---------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Workload generator: replays synthetic and recorded traces with sequence-length and token-branching distributions.
2) Kernel driver: invokes runtime kernel entry points (attention, kv-cache operations, kernel handshakes) with deterministic seeds and controlled input shapes.
3) Observability injector: programmatically modifies sampling rates, span size, annotation payloads, and simulates sidecar delays or event drops.
4) Assertion engine: collects runtime metrics, traces, logs, and performs deterministic checks for ordering, missing spans, SLO regressions and resource anomalies.

Harness components and interfaces
--------------------------------
- harnessctl: CLI to configure and launch experiments.
- harness-agent: small in-process shim that can toggle SDK behavior (sync vs async logging, sample rate) at runtime.
- replay-corpus: directory of sampled request traces and generated synthetic workloads.
- assertion-library: a set of reusable checks (latency budgets, kernel-signal presence, KV cache warmup checks).

Operational diagram (text)
-------------------------
1. harnessctl launches a controller (k8s job or local process).
2. Controller schedules N parallel kernel drivers against a test runtime cluster or a mocked harness runtime image.
3. Observability injector instruments the runtime via harness-agent and network proxies to inject delays or drop events.
4. Assertion engine gathers metrics via Prometheus, traces via Jaeger/OTLP collector, and logs from stdout.

Key test scenarios
------------------
|| Scenario || Perturbation || Acceptance criteria || Owner ||
|| Span amplification || Add 2x span annotations per token (500B payload) || No more than +7% P95 token latency; no missing kernel handshake spans; no increase >3% in GPU stall time || runtime-kernel-team ||
|| Sampling skew || Vary sampling rate from 100% -> 0.1% during steady traffic || Reconstruction of request lineage must succeed for at least 95% of sampled traces; SLO change <5% || observability-team ||
|| Sidecar headroom loss || Sidecar adds 10–250ms per span on a configurable fraction of calls || System remains within degradation budget and fallback policy triggers correctly when latency > 200ms || infra-team ||
|| SDK sync-blocking || Toggle agent to synchronous flush on process-critical path for 1 minute || No kernel-level timeouts or watchdog escalations; error rate delta <0.5% || sdk-team ||

Example harness configuration (YAML)
----------------------------------
```yaml
experiment_name: observability-span-amplification
duration: 15m
parallel_clients: 48
replay_corpus: gs://redwood-test-corpus/kernels/seq-len-tail
observability_injection:
  span_amplification:
    enabled: true
    extra_annotation_size_bytes: 512
    fraction_of_requests: 0.25
  sidecar_delay:
    enabled: true
    p99_delay_ms: 120
assertions:
  - type: latency_budget
    p95_ms: 70
  - type: span_presence
    required_spans:
      - kernel.handshake
      - kernel.eviction
```

Running the harness (CLI examples)
---------------------------------
- Dry run locally (fast validation):
  ```bash
  harnessctl plan --config=./observability-span-amplification.yaml --dry-run
  ```
- Full experiment against staging cluster (k8s):
  ```bash
  harnessctl apply --config=./observability-span-amplification.yaml --namespace=staging-runtime
  harnessctl watch --experiment observability-span-amplification
  ```
- Tail assertion output:
  ```bash
  harnessctl logs --experiment observability-span-amplification --assertion-stream
  ```

Assertion engine: common checks
-------------------------------
- Latency budgets: P50/P95/P99 token and request latency thresholds.
- Span integrity: presence of kernel.* spans, consistent correlation_id propagation, and incremental sequence numbers for kernel events.
- Telemetry volume sanity: ensure instrumentation doesn't increase Prometheus scrape cardinality >10x for the run.
- Resource counters: GPU SM utilization, memory stall counters, and kernel execution time histograms.
- Detected anomalies: signature for KV-cache warmup regressions, cold-start variance, and kernel handshake timeouts.

Automated gating and rollout policy
----------------------------------
1. Every kernel or scheduler change must be validated with the OIKVH in known-good staging and with 3 targeted experiments: baseline (no injection), moderate injection (10–20% request fraction), and heavy injection (50% fraction).
2. Gating criteria: all assertions pass or are explained by a documented change. Failures must open a ticket in the runtime backlog and block rollout.
3. For critical kernels (attention, kv-cache, dispatcher), require a k-change postmortem for any P95 increase >10% under moderate injection.

Telemetry assertions and dashboard queries
----------------------------------------
The assertion engine publishes a results bundle (JSON) and a short summary to the harness dashboard. Example PromQL checks the P95 token latency:
```promql
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
```
Check for missing kernel.handshake spans using trace counts: ensure trace_count(kernel.handshake) / requests_sampled > 0.9 for sampled requests.

Failure modes and mitigation guidance
-----------------------------------
- Symptom: P95 increases only when tracing enabled.
  Action: Reduce tracing payloads, switch SDK to async flush, rerun harness to isolate span that correlates.
- Symptom: Prometheus scrape cardinality explosion.
  Action: Revert instrumentation that creates high-cardinality labels; add label aggregation; schedule a follow-up microbenchmark.
- Symptom: Kernel handshake missing under head-of-line injection.
  Action: Increase kernel handshake timeout and add a non-blocking hedging path; validate with targeted harness test.

Ownership and lifecycle
-----------------------
- Primary owner: runtime-kernel-team (oncall: runtime-kernel-oncall).
- Observability integration and support: observability-team.
- SDK shim maintenance: client-sdks team.
- Quarterly: run the full corpus across latest staging image and publish an experiment digest to the Runtime QA channel.

Runbook: quick steps for a failed experiment
------------------------------------------
1. Inspect harnessctl logs and the assertion output. Identify the first failed assertion timestamp.
2. Correlate with Prometheus and tracing timeslices.
3. If impact is limited to instrumentation metrics (cardinality/latency) and kernel functional metrics are unaffected, open a follow-up with sdk-team and mark experiment as ‘investigated – non-blocking’.
4. If kernel SLOs are violated, page runtime-kernel-oncall, capture a diagnostic packet (harnessctl gather --since <ts>), and escalate per incident runbook.

Appendix: example minimal assertion JSON output
----------------------------------------------
```json
{
  "experiment": "observability-span-amplification",
  "result": "failed",
  "failed_assertions": [
    {"id": "latency_p95_token", "observed_ms": 78, "threshold_ms": 70},
    {"id": "span_presence_kernel_handshake", "missing_pct": 12}
  ],
  "attachments": ["s3://redwood-test-artifacts/harness/2026-11-07/exp-1234.tgz"]
}
```
Appendix: quick checklist before a kernel rollout
-------------------------------------------------
- [ ] Run OIKVH baseline, moderate, and heavy injection experiments.
- [ ] Confirm no assertion regressions or file tickets for each failure.
- [ ] Publish experiment digest and reviewers’ signoff.
- [ ] Include instrumentation delta summary in release notes.

References and related pages
---------------------------
- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Kernel handshake patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026
- Canary and SLA gate matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

If you are implementing or extending the harness, contact the runtime-kernel-team channel and add your experiment to the replay-corpus index (gs://redwood-test-corpus/index.yaml).

payload.page_title: KV Cache Compaction Improvements — Design Doc (Runtime 1.22)

sections.body:
h1. Overview
This document proposes KV cache compaction + tier-aware eviction for Redwood’s serving runtime to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) during sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* A measurable definition of *fragmentation* for the KV arena
* A compaction mechanism (incremental, budgeted) integrated with the scheduler
* A safe eviction strategy (tier-aware LRU + pinned-session handling)
* Feature flags / kill-switches for staged rollout and rapid disable
* Observability standards (metrics + tracing) and rollout guardrails

h2. Context and problem statement
The runtime maintains a GPU-resident KV cache for active sequences (and optionally cached prefixes). Under mixed prompt lengths and high churn, long-lived allocations + frequent frees can create holes in the allocator arena. Over time, the allocator may fail to find contiguous blocks for new KV pages, causing:
* Increased allocator overhead (free-list scanning, defragment bookkeeping)
* Opportunistic evictions at high pressure moments
* Copy/relocation work occurring at inopportune times
* Worst case: OOM/forced request shedding or large p99 latency spikes
sections.heading: The design adds

sections.body:
* Bursty chat traffic (many short sessions, some long sessions)
* Mixed decode lengths, long-running streams, and frequent cancellations
* Dedicated pools with high utilization and limited headroom

h2. Goals
* Reduce memory fragmentation in the KV arena without harming steady-state throughput.
* Reduce tail latency under burst traffic (p95/p99) and mixed length distributions.
* Add an eviction policy that is safe (correctness), observable (metrics), and configurable (tier/model/profile).
* Provide guardrails: compaction budgets/limits, backpressure integration, and kill-switches.

h2. Non-goals (initial release)
* Customer-facing configuration UI in Console (flags/config only).
* Major kernel rewrites unrelated to KV movement (minimal copy/pack kernels allowed).
* Changing the semantic contract of KV residency (i.e., no “approximate” KV).

h2. Stakeholders / owners
* Tech lead (KV): Omar El-Sayed
* Allocator/compaction: Samir Qureshi
* Scheduler integration: Sofia Ivanova
* Architecture/correctness: Noah Patel
* Observability standards: Allison Grant
* SRE guardrails/rollout: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
* Kernels (if needed): Hiro Tanaka, Grace Kim, Yuki Sato

h1. Current KV allocation model (as of runtime 1.21)
h2. High-level model
* KV is stored in a GPU “arena” split into fixed-size pages (per layer, per head layout), allocated per sequence.
* A sequence holds a list of pages per layer (or a compact per-seq structure pointing into per-layer slabs, depending on model profile).
* Allocation is primarily driven at two points:
  # Prefill: reserve initial KV pages proportional to prompt length
  # Decode: allocate more pages as tokens append
* Free occurs when:
  * Sequence completes
  * Sequence is cancelled
  * Sequence is evicted due to memory pressure

h2. Allocator details (simplified)
* Arena is sized per GPU and model profile (varies by hosted tier / dedicated pool).
* Free space is tracked in a free-list keyed by contiguous ranges of pages.
* Allocation uses “first-fit”/“best-fit-ish” heuristics tuned for speed.
* Coalescing occurs on free where adjacent ranges are merged.

h2. Why fragmentation happens
Fragmentation emerges because allocation requests are not uniform:
* Mixed sequence lengths: some sequences grow slowly, others rapidly
* Long-lived sessions: hold pages for long time, forcing new allocations to fit around them
* High churn: frees create holes that are too small for subsequent requests
* Cancellation edge cases: mid-decode cancellation can free non-uniformly across layers, increasing small holes

Net result: free space exists but is split into many small ranges, increasing allocator overhead and raising the probability of forced eviction or OOM when new contiguous ranges are needed.

h1. Definitions and fragmentation measurement
We standardize the following key terms (see metrics standard page for canonical names):

h2. Key terms
* *Arena bytes*: total bytes managed by KV allocator for a model profile.
* *Free bytes*: total bytes currently free.
* *Largest free span*: the largest contiguous free range.
* *Fragmentation ratio*: 1 - (largest_free_span_bytes / free_bytes), with 0 meaning perfectly contiguous free space.
sections.heading: We see the most pronounced issues in

sections.body:
* We compute this per device and per model profile (and, where feasible, per pool).
* We also track “free spans count” (count of free ranges) as a secondary indicator.

h2. Health thresholds (initial)
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
* Warn: fragmentation_ratio > 0.55 AND free_bytes > 2 GB
* Critical: fragmentation_ratio > 0.70 AND free_bytes > 1 GB

Rationale: fragmentation is only actionable if meaningful free space exists; otherwise pressure is “real” and eviction may be required.

h1. Proposed design
sections.heading: These are starting points and will be tuned via canary

sections.body:
* Compaction: relocate KV pages to reduce fragmentation, performed incrementally with budgets.
* Eviction: tier-aware eviction when pressure is high and compaction cannot recover sufficient contiguous space quickly.

The compaction mechanism is integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls and to allow backpressure/guardrails.

h2. Design principles
* Correctness first: relocation must preserve per-seq KV content and ordering.
* Budgeted work: bound compaction by *time* and/or *bytes moved* per scheduling cycle.
* Avoid tail spikes: do not perform large relocation inside latency-sensitive decode inner loops.
* Observable: export metrics + tracing spans to correlate compaction/eviction with tail latency.
* Safe-by-default: feature flags + kill-switch + staged rollout.

h1. Compaction mechanism
h2. What we compact
We compact at the granularity of allocator “pages” (or blocks) used for KV storage. Compaction moves live pages to earlier (lower) addresses in the arena to create larger contiguous free spans.

We do not attempt to change the logical layout of KV within a page; we only relocate pages and update indirections.

h2. Preconditions / invariants
sections.heading: We propose a two-part approach

sections.body:
* A sequence’s KV pointer table must not point to freed/moved pages.
* Reads during decode must see a consistent view of the KV pointers.
* Cancellation/free racing with relocation must not leak pages or double-free.
sections.heading: During relocation we must preserve

sections.body:
* A per-sequence “relocation lock” (logical lock in scheduler state; not a heavy mutex).
* A relocation state machine (see kv-cache-memory-layout-overview page).
* A two-phase commit for relocation:
  1) Copy live page(s) to new location
  2) Atomically swap pointer(s)
  3) Release old page(s) back to free-list

h2. Incremental compaction (primary)
Incremental compaction runs as a small step each scheduler cycle, bounded by budgets.
sections.heading: We enforce these with

sections.body:
1) Determine if compaction should run:
   * fragmentation_ratio above threshold
   * free_bytes above minimum actionable free
   * allocator under “pressure soon” or “pressure now” signals (see integration)
2) Choose relocation candidates:
   * Prefer sequences with pages scattered across many spans
   * Prefer low-priority tiers first (Hosted Free/Dev > Hosted Pro > Dedicated)
   * Avoid sequences marked as pinned or “latency critical”
3) Choose destination:
   * Allocate a contiguous target span near the “front” of the arena
   * If no contiguous destination exists, compaction step becomes no-op
4) Copy pages:
   * Use GPU memcpy/pack kernel as appropriate
   * Update indirections
5) Update allocator metadata and emit metrics
sections.heading: Algorithm sketch

sections.body:
* bytes_moved_budget_per_tick (default varies by tier)
* time_budget_per_tick_ms (hard cap)

A step stops when any budget is exhausted or when scheduler enters a latency-critical boundary.

h2. Background compaction (secondary; optional)
We support an optional background compaction worker thread that can perform additional relocation when:
* The scheduler indicates the system is in a low-utilization window
* Or when a pool is in “stabilize” mode after a burst

This worker is strictly lower priority than request processing and must also respect global budgets. Initial rollout will keep background compaction disabled by default; incremental compaction is the primary mechanism.

h2. Compaction triggers
sections.heading: Budgets

sections.body:
* fragmentation_ratio > trigger_threshold
* free_span_count > span_count_threshold
* allocator_failures_recent > 0 (failed allocations that required fallback/eviction)
* tail_latency_guardrail engaged (SRE signal; see guardrails doc)
sections.heading: We trigger compaction when any of the following are true

sections.body:
* Trigger on threshold_high; stop when below threshold_low.

h2. Candidate selection and fairness
We maintain a small priority queue of candidate sequences. Each sequence is scored by:
* scatter_score (number of spans touched)
* bytes_to_compact (estimated)
* tier_weight (lower tiers more eligible)
* pinned_penalty (pinned sequences typically ineligible)
sections.heading: We also include hysteresis to avoid oscillation

sections.body:
* No single sequence can consume > X% of a tick budget.
* Round-robin across candidates to avoid starvation.

h2. Kernel requirements
Most moves can use device-to-device memcpy. For some layouts (paged KV with interleaved head dimension), we may need a lightweight pack kernel to maintain alignment/coalescing.
sections.heading: We also enforce fairness

sections.body:
* Start with memcpy for page-aligned moves.
* Add pack kernel only if benchmarks show significant regression due to misalignment or if page strides require transformation.

h1. Eviction policy
Compaction reduces fragmentation but cannot create memory out of thin air. When true memory pressure exists (or compaction cannot quickly produce a contiguous span), we must evict.

h2. Policy summary
sections.heading: Initial plan

sections.body:
* Evict whole sequences (freeing all KV pages for that sequence).
* Prefer evicting:
  * Lower-tier traffic first (e.g., Hosted Free/Dev)
  * Older/idle sequences (LRU by last_token_timestamp)
  * Sequences not marked pinned

We do not evict partial layers or partial KV for a sequence in the initial release.

h2. Pinned sessions and correctness
sections.heading: We implement tier-aware LRU eviction at the sequence level

sections.body:
* Dedicated customer pinned sessions (contractual / product requirements)
* Internal canary/test sessions
sections.heading: Some sessions are pinned

sections.body:
* emergency_oom_mode is enabled (explicit, off by default)
* and SRE oncall flips the kill-switch policy (see runbook)

h2. Prefix cache interaction
sections.heading: Pinned sessions are ineligible for eviction unless

sections.body:
* Prefix cache entries are separately tracked and are more evictable than active sequences.
* Under pressure we evict prefix cache entries before evicting active sequences.
* Compaction does not move prefix cache entries in v1 unless they share the same arena; if shared, they participate as low-priority candidates.

h2. Customer-facing behavior
sections.heading: If prefix caching is enabled for a model profile

sections.body:
* Request error (e.g., RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED) or retryable overload signal depending on caller type
* Or graceful degradation if routing can retry on a different replica/region (when enabled)

We will not silently drop tokens.

h1. Scheduler integration
The scheduler is the control point to ensure compaction does not cause tail latency spikes.

h2. Integration points
sections.heading: Eviction of an active sequence manifests as

sections.body:
* End of prefill phase: safe window to do small relocation steps
* Decode boundary between token steps: only if budget is tiny and queue depth is low
* After completion/cancellation processing: coalesce + small compaction step

h2. Budget enforcement
Budgets are enforced by the scheduler, not solely within allocator code:
* The scheduler provides a per-tick budget context:
  * time_budget_ms
  * bytes_budget
  * max_sequences_to_touch
* The allocator/compactor must check the context and return early.

This is intentional to keep latency control centralized and consistent with other runtime maintenance tasks.

h2. Backpressure and overload signals
sections.heading: We integrate compaction into scheduler phases

sections.body:
* Prefer shedding new work over doing heavy compaction.
* Compaction should enter “stabilize” mode:
  * perform minimal work required to prevent allocator failure
  * rely on eviction if needed
sections.heading: When overload is detected

sections.body:
* queue_depth_high
* decode_utilization_high
* p99_latency_rising
* allocator_failures_recent

h2. Safety: cancellation and concurrent events
Cancellation can race with relocation. We handle with:
* Sequence state transitions guarded by scheduler state machine.
* Relocation “epoch” per sequence:
  * cancellation waits for relocation swap to complete or aborts relocation at a safe point
* Allocator operations must be idempotent for the old page free after pointer swap.

We will add targeted stress tests for cancellation during relocation (see validation plan).

h1. Configuration and feature flags
All controls are runtime config flags (no Console UI in v1).

h2. Feature flags (names are internal; subject to config registry constraints)
* runtime.kv_compaction.enabled (default: off initially)
* runtime.kv_compaction.mode = off | incremental | incremental_plus_background
* runtime.kv_compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio_high (default: 0.70)
* runtime.kv_compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio_low (default: 0.55)
* runtime.kv_compaction.min_actionable_free_bytes (default: 2GiB hosted; 1GiB dedicated)
* runtime.kv_compaction.bytes_budget_per_tick (default: hosted 128MiB; dedicated 256MiB)
* runtime.kv_compaction.time_budget_per_tick_ms (default: hosted 0.35ms; dedicated 0.50ms)
* runtime.kv_compaction.max_sequences_per_tick (default: 2)
sections.heading: Signals

sections.body:
* runtime.kv_eviction.enabled (default: on; existing behavior refined)
* runtime.kv_eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru_v1
* runtime.kv_eviction.allow_evict_pinned (default: off)
* runtime.kv_eviction.prefer_prefix_cache_first (default: on)
sections.heading: Eviction

sections.body:
* runtime.kv_compaction.kill_switch (default: false)
  * When true: disables compaction immediately and blocks new relocation steps.

h2. Tier defaults (proposal)
* Hosted Free/Dev:
  * compaction enabled after canary
  * smaller budgets to minimize latency risk
  * aggressive eviction permitted (non-pinned only)
* Hosted Pro:
  * compaction enabled after hosted subset validation
  * slightly higher budgets
* Dedicated:
  * compaction enabled last
  * higher budgets allowed, but stronger guardrails on eviction (pinned sessions common)

Final defaults will be set after benchmark + canary results (see experiment tracker).

h1. Observability
sections.heading: Kill-switch

sections.body:
* Metrics
* Tracing spans
* Dashboards and alerts (SRE-owned)

h2. Metrics (high level)
sections.heading: We add

sections.body:
* kv_allocator_fragmentation_ratio
* kv_allocator_free_bytes
* kv_allocator_largest_free_span_bytes
* kv_allocator_free_span_count
* kv_allocator_allocation_failures_total
sections.heading: Allocator health

sections.body:
* kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total
* kv_compaction_time_ms_total
* kv_compaction_steps_total
* kv_compaction_aborted_steps_total
sections.heading: Compaction activity
Eviction

sections.body:
* Export exemplars linking compaction spans to latency traces.

h2. Tracing
sections.heading: Correlations

sections.body:
* compaction_step
* relocation_copy
* relocation_pointer_swap
* eviction_selection
* eviction_execute
sections.heading: We add spans around

sections.body:
* model_profile
* gpu_id
* bytes_moved
* sequences_touched
* fragmentation_ratio_before/after (sampled)

h1. Performance and correctness validation
h2. Benchmark plan
We extend the benchmark suite with scenarios designed to induce fragmentation:
* Mixed prompt lengths (p50 short, p90 long)
* High churn (frequent cancellations)
* Long-lived decode sessions (streaming)
* Bursty arrival patterns (traffic spikes)
sections.heading: Each span includes attributes

sections.body:
* p50/p95/p99 latency (prefill and decode)
* throughput (tokens/s/GPU)
* fragmentation_ratio time series
* compaction_bytes_moved and overhead
* eviction rate
sections.heading: KPIs

sections.body:
* No more than 1–2% steady-state throughput regression at equivalent load.
* p99 tail latency improvement in burst/mixed-length scenarios, or at minimum elimination of the worst spikes.
* Compaction overhead stays within budget, with no sustained scheduler stalls.

h2. Correctness and stress tests
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (initial)

sections.body:
* Cancellation during relocation (including repeated cancel/retry)
* Concurrent completion + eviction
* Long-running sessions with intermittent backpressure
* Adversarial patterns: alternating small/large allocations to maximize fragmentation

h2. Failure modes and mitigations
* Decode stalls due to heavy compaction:
  * Mitigation: strict scheduler-enforced budgets, disable background compaction by default
* Copy overhead increases GPU utilization:
  * Mitigation: limit bytes moved; tune thresholds; add pack kernel only if needed
* Pointer swap race leading to incorrect KV:
  * Mitigation: relocation state machine + invariants + stress tests + tracing
* Increased evictions:
  * Mitigation: compaction first when actionable; tier-aware eviction; prefix cache evicted first

h1. Rollout plan
We will follow staged rollout with explicit guardrails and rollback triggers.

h2. Stage 0 — Internal dev & perf lab
* Enable compaction in controlled benchmarks and staging clusters.
* Validate metrics dashboards and trace exemplars.
* Validate cancellation stress tests.
sections.heading: Add/extend tests

sections.body:
* Benchmarks meet acceptance criteria.
* No correctness regressions.

h2. Stage 1 — Internal canary (small %)
* Enable on a small internal canary pool.
* Watch:
  * p99 decode latency
  * allocator_failures
  * bytes_moved/time_ms per tick
  * eviction spikes
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
* p99 sustained regression beyond guardrail for > N minutes
* allocator_failures increase significantly
* suspected correctness issue (immediate disable)

h2. Stage 2 — Hosted subset (tier-limited)
* Enable for a subset of Hosted (starting Free/Dev, then Pro).
* Tight budgets; aggressive monitoring.

h2. Stage 3 — Dedicated pools (opt-in, then default)
* Start with one dedicated pool with known burst issues.
* Allow per-customer override via config registry.

h2. Communications
* Runtime release note (Runtime 1.22) includes:
  * What changed
  * What metrics to monitor
  * How to disable (oncall)
* Support/CS enablement:
  * How to interpret p99 improvements and eviction errors

h1. Rollback / kill-switch plan
sections.heading: Rollback criteria

sections.body:
* runtime.kv_compaction.kill_switch = true
* runtime.kv_compaction.enabled = false
sections.heading: Oncall/SRE can disable compaction within minutes via

sections.body:
* No new relocation steps start.
* In-progress relocation steps complete or safely abort at a barrier.
* Allocator continues without compaction (existing behavior).

If eviction policy changes contribute to incidents, we can revert eviction policy to previous behavior via:
* runtime.kv_eviction.policy = legacy

h1. Alternatives considered
* Full stop-the-world defragmentation:
  * Rejected due to unacceptable tail latency impact.
* Pure eviction-only strategy:
  * Rejected because it increases customer-visible errors and is avoidable when free space exists but is fragmented.
* Changing to a completely different allocator (buddy allocator / slab by size classes):
  * Deferred; more invasive, higher migration risk.

h1. Open questions
* Do we need a pack kernel for specific KV layouts (e.g., interleaved heads) to avoid alignment regressions?
* What is the best default fragmentation trigger per model profile (7B vs 70B) given very different KV footprints?
* Should we expose compaction controls in Console for Dedicated customers in a later release?
* How should we treat cross-replica routing retries when an active sequence is evicted (product behavior vs pure infra behavior)?

h1. Appendix: Pseudocode (illustrative)
sections.heading: Expected behavior on disable

sections.body:
1) if !enabled or kill_switch: return
2) if fragmentation_ratio < low_threshold: return
3) budget = scheduler.get_compaction_budget()
4) candidates = allocator.select_candidates(max_sequences_per_tick)
5) for seq in candidates:
   a) if budget.exhausted(): break
   b) if seq.pinned: continue
   c) plan = allocator.plan_relocation(seq)
   d) if plan.none: continue
   e) bytes_moved = relocate(plan, budget)
   f) allocator.commit(plan)
   g) emit metrics
sections.heading: Compaction step (simplified)

sections.body:
1) if allocation fails or free_bytes < min_free_bytes:
2) evict prefix cache entries first (if enabled)
3) if still pressure:
4) select seq by tier-aware LRU, excluding pinned
5) evict seq, emit reason and tier

---
sections.heading: Eviction (simplified)

sections.body:
* 2026-01-23: Initial draft (O. El-Sayed)
* 2026-02-02: Added scheduler budgeting section + trigger hysteresis (S. Ivanova)
* 2026-02-09: Updated metrics list + tracing attributes (A. Grant)
* 2026-02-16: Added tier defaults + rollback criteria aligned with SRE guardrails (S. Gallagher)

payload.page_title: Scheduler Resource Tagging and Precedence Manifest

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the resource-tagging and precedence manifest used by Redwood's scheduler to make deterministic decisions about kernel assignment, admission control, and graceful degradation. Resource tags let higher layers add lightweight metadata to requests (workload characteristics, cost-sensitivity, fidelity budget, retry semantics) that the scheduler uses together with telemetry to make per-request placement and preemption choices.

Goals
- Make scheduling decisions predictable and auditable by standardizing tags and precedence rules.
- Expose controllable levers to product and platform teams to express cost vs fidelity tradeoffs.
- Ensure backward compatibility: untagged requests follow current best-effort policies.
- Provide operator runbooks and profiling guidance for tag-driven regressions.

Scope and Non-Goals
- Scope: runtime admission controller, scheduler policy layer, kernel hinting, and observability fields.
- Non-Goals: model selection logic, API surface changes for customers (tags are internal to Redwood and derived from routing policies or per-tenant config).

Key Concepts and Terminology
- Resource Tag: structured label attached to a request at the service boundary. Tags are short key:value tokens.
- Precedence Manifest: ordered rule set that maps tag combinations to scheduling actions (admit, queue-with-sla, degrade-mode, preemptible).
- Degradation Mode: a policy action that reduces fidelity (quantized model variant, prefix cache usage, early cutoff).
- Kernel Hint: annotation passed to kernel mapper that influences kernel selection (e.g., preferred kernel family or tight latency bound).

Design Principles
1) Keep tags small and typed: allow exactly the tag keys documented in the manifest.
2) Deterministic precedence: rules are evaluated top-to-bottom; earlier rule wins.
3) Least-privilege impact: tags can only reduce resource footprint or request priority, never increase allocation.
4) Observability-first: every evaluation emits a traceable event containing the matched rule id and rationale.

Resource Tag Schema (canonical keys)
- fidelity: {high, standard, economical}  # fidelity budget for the request
- cost_sensitivity: {low, medium, high}  # willingness to use expensive kernels or CPU fallback
- latency_class: {interactive, best_effort, batch}  # latency tolerance
- preemptible: {true, false}  # candidate for preemption under pressure
- cache_hint: {kv_prefetch, prefix_cache_ok, no_cache}  # cache preferences
- isolation: {tenant_dedicated, tenant_shared}  # tenancy isolation; impacts shard placement

Example Tagging Table (ascii)
| Tag key | Purpose | Default | Notes |
| fidelity | fidelity budget | standard | high=use highest-quality model variant if latency allows |
| cost_sensitivity | operator cost tolerance | medium | low=prefer quantized kernels and batching |
| latency_class | scheduling latency target | interactive | impacts admission timeout |
| preemptible | preemption candidacy | false | true allows background eviction under pressure |

Precedence Manifest (human-readable sample)
1) rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
   match: fidelity=high AND latency_class=interactive AND isolation=tenant_dedicated
   action: admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false
   rationale: SLA-backed dedicated tenant traffic must be prioritized; kernel hint prefers kernels tuned for short sequences

2) rule_id: P-02-econ-background
   match: fidelity=economical OR cost_sensitivity=high OR preemptible=true
   action: queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true
   rationale: background tasks should use cost-optimized paths and accept higher latency

3) rule_id: P-03-standard-shared
   match: isolation=tenant_shared AND latency_class=interactive
   action: admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=true

4) rule_id: P-99-default
   match: catch-all
   action: best-effort admit, kernel_hint=balanced

Manifest Format and Storage
- Manifest is stored as a versioned YAML in the control plane: /manifests/scheduler/resource-precedence/{version}.yaml
- Each manifest publishes: id, created_by, created_at, rules[], validation_hash.
- Validation: control plane runs static validation on update (no contradictory rules, explicit default rule present).

YAML Example (extracted)
---
version: v1.2
created_by: scheduler-team
created_at: 2026-02-01
rules:
  - id: P-01-critical-interactive
    match: "fidelity == 'high' && latency_class == 'interactive' && isolation == 'tenant_dedicated'"
    action: "admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false"
  - id: P-02-econ-background
    match: "fidelity == 'economical' || cost_sensitivity == 'high' || preemptible == 'true'"
    action: "queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true"
---

Runtime Evaluation Flow (per-request)
1) Request enters ingress; routing layer attaches derived tags (from customer config, route labels, or system defaults).
2) Admission controller fetches latest precedence manifest and evaluates rules top-to-bottom.
3) Matched action produces an Admission Decision object containing: target kernel_hint, admission_bucket, preemptible flag, degradation plan id.
4) Admission decision is persisted as an event and attached to the request trace for auditing.
5) Kernel mapper consumes kernel_hint and schedules kernel execution; preemption decisions are handled by the quota controller.

Observability and Telemetry Changes
- New telemetry fields to include in traces/metrics: precedent_rule_id, admission_decision, computed_slot_cost_estimate, kernel_hint, preemptible_flag.
- Exported metrics: precedence_rule_match_count{rule_id}, precedence_rule_latency_ms{rule_id}.
- Alerting: sudden shift in matches to P-02-econ-background for a high-SLA tenant triggers an incident.

Profiling and Benchmarking Guidance
- Profiling playbook change: when benchmarking slot consumption, record matched precedence_rule_id for each trace. Use this to correlate rule effects on tail latency.
- New microbench: tag-sensitivity-stressor. Procedure:
  1) Generate synthetic traffic with identical payloads but differing tag sets (high vs economical).
  2) Measure kernel selection distribution, per-token latency, and per-request cost.
  3) Validate that economical tags reduce per-token cost by >= 20% vs standard baseline for same model family.

Operator Runbook: Precedence Regression (critical)
- Symptom: production latency spike coinciding with increased matches to P-02-econ-background for interactive routes.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Query traces for precedence_rule_match_count where rule_id==P-02-econ-background over last 15m.
     CLI: rquery metrics precedence_rule_match_count --filter "rule_id=P-02-econ-background" --range 15m
  2) Identify affected tenant_ids from traces with tag isolation=tenant_shared and latency_class=interactive.
  3) Roll back manifest to previous version: control-plane-cli manifest rollback --name resource-precedence --to-version v1.1
  4) If rollback not possible, apply emergency override: control-plane-cli manifest patch --set "rules[0].action='admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=false'"
  5) Post-incident: run profiling microbench and annotate the root cause in the incident ticket.

Release Notes (short entry)
- 2026-06-15: Introduced Resource Tagging & Precedence Manifest v1.2.0.
  - Adds fidelity/cost_sensitivity/latency_class tags.
  - Default manifest contains deterministic precedence and observability hooks.
  - Telemetry fields added: precedent_rule_id, kernel_hint.

Backward Compatibility and Migration
- Untagged traffic is matched by P-99-default and behaves like existing scheduler logic.
- Migration plan for Dedicated customers: gradually attach isolation=tenant_dedicated at routing-layer; this unlocks lower-latency kernels and disables preemption.

Security and Privacy Considerations
- Tags contain no PII and are generated by routing logic or internal policy.
- Manifest changes are restricted to scheduler-admin role with audit logging enabled.

Known Limitations and Issues
- K-101: Under multi-tenant noise, the "queue-with-sla(200ms)" action can lead to unpredictable slot entanglement. Mitigation: add explicit per-tenant queue caps in next manifest.
- K-102: Kernel_hint favors quantized kernels for economical tags; regression found on short-sequence chat where quantized kernel introduces hallucination regressions under specific logits threshold. Tracking ticket: SCHED-4793.

Testing and Validation Checklist for Manifest Changes
1) Static validation: lint manifest, ensure default rule present.
2) Unit tests: rule matching semantics, short-circuit precedence ordering tests.
3) Integration canary: deploy to canary pool for non-critical tenants for 48h.
4) Benchmark gate: run tag-sensitivity-stressor and verify cost/latency deltas against baseline.
5) Beta rollout: enable for 10% traffic of new tenants, monitor precedence_rule_match_count and tail latency.

Operational Metrics to Monitor After Rollout
- precedence_rule_match_count by rule_id (trend and sudden shifts)
- admission_decision_latencies P50/P90/P99
- kernel_selection_entropy (higher indicates varied kernel churn)
- per-tenant preemptions per-minute

Owner and Contact
- Primary owner: eng-serving-scheduler team (oncall alias: eng-serving-scheduler@redwood.ai)
- Document steward: Asha Patel (asha.patel@redwood.ai)

Appendix A: Example Trace Snippet (annotated)
- trace_id: 0001
- tags: fidelity=high, latency_class=interactive, isolation=tenant_dedicated
- precedence_rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
- admission_decision: admit_prefetch; kernel_hint=low-latency; preemptible=false
- kernel_selected: kernel-family-v2-lowlatency

Appendix B: FAQ
Q: Can customers influence tags?
A: Not directly. Tags are derived from routing rules and customer's plan mapping (dedicated vs shared, SLAs), and from internal cost-sensitivity mappings.

Q: Will tags slow down admission?
A: Tag matching is optimized and cached per route; additional latency is under 200us in canary measurements.

Document History
- 2026-02-10: Draft created by Asha Patel
- 2026-03-05: Internal review and telemetry additions by Miguel Ortega
- 2026-06-15: Published (v1.2) with schedule-team approved changes

End of Document

payload.page_title: Hybrid accelerator integration and fidelity guidelines

sections.body:
Summary
This document defines the integration contract, quality/fidelity guidelines, and operational runbook for bringing hybrid accelerator resources (on-host GPUs + third‑party accelerators such as NPUs/DPUs/TPUs via remote attach) into Redwood’s serving runtime. It covers compatibility decisions, kernel-scheduling boundaries, profiling and benchmark requirements, preflight checks, rollout criteria, and rollback gates. The goal is to enable safe, measurable performance improvements while preserving inference fidelity and SLOs.

Scope and audience
- Scope: hybrid accelerator attachments that extend the runtime’s kernel execution layer (e.g., hardware with different numeric formats or reduced FP precision, remote-attached inference ASICs).
- Audience: runtime engineers, kernel scheduling owners, platform SREs, profiling engineers, and release engineers who validate new accelerator integrations.

Goals and design principles
1) Safety-first: no automatic traffic routing to a new accelerator variant without passing fidelity & stability gates.
2) Observable fidelity: every accelerator variant must emit a fidelity profile and regression signals tied to canonical prompt sets.
3) Isolated scheduling: scheduler must treat hybrid accelerator pools as distinct resource classes with explicit mapping rules.
4) Deterministic fallbacks: runtime must be able to fall back to a verified CPU/GPU kernel variant with bounded latency and output drift.

Definitions
- Accelerator variant: a compiled kernel implementation or model quantization that executes on a particular accelerator type/version.
- Fidelity profile: per-model/per-prompt metrics comparing outputs vs a golden baseline (semantic similarity, token-level divergence, hallucination indicators).
- Degradation event: fidelity drop or p95 latency breach after activation.

Compatibility matrix (example)
| Accelerator class | Min firmware | Supported quant formats | Expected max seq_len | Verified models (examples) | Notes |
|-------------------|--------------:|------------------------|----------------------:|---------------------------|-------|
| Remote NPU v1     | 2025-04-12    | int8, int8-with-scale   | 2048                 | Llama-2-13B, MPT-7B      | supports KV cache via proxy, 1.8x throughput gain |
| On-host A100-48GB | n/a           | fp16, bf16, int8        | 4096                 | Llama-2-70B              | native CUDA kernels, priority pinning required |
| ThirdParty-TPU    | 2024-12-01    | bfloat16                | 4096                 | Flan-T5-large            | network-attached, higher cold-start penalty |

Pre-integration checklist (must be completed before any staged traffic)
- [ ] Hardware and firmware versions recorded in the accelerator registry.
- [ ] Provider compatibility tested with the kernel mapper test harness.
- [ ] Baseline golden outputs produced using the canonical baseline environment (host-GPU fp16) for each target model and prompt set.
- [ ] Fidelity profile generation job configured and passing (see ‘Profiling and fidelity tests’).
- [ ] Scheduler policy authored: pool label, admission control thresholds, priority groups.
- [ ] Monitoring & alerting configured: fidelity-alert (>=3% semantic drop), latency-alert (p95 breach > configured SLOs).
- [ ] Rollout and rollback playbook drafted with owners identified.

Scheduler integration guidelines
- Resource classification: hybrid accelerators must be mapped to one of three scheduler resource classes: dedicated-accel, shared-accel, network-accel. Code-level tags: accel.class = {dedicated,shared,network}.
- Admission control signals: each pool exposes available_credits, max_concurrency, and warm_ratio (fraction of warmed KV sessions). Inject these into the request admission flow.
- Kernel hints: kernels must advertise fallback_compat set (list of compatible kernel variants) and deterministic_fallback_cost (approx ms). The scheduler consults fallback_compat before routing.
- Priority synthesis: combine request priority, SLO sensitivity, and customer tier to produce a scheduling key. For hybrid pool admission require: request_priority >= pool_min_priority and warm_ratio >= pool_min_warm.

Profiling and fidelity tests (playbook)
1) Canonical prompt set generation
   - Use the internal prompt-set-builder to produce 3 prompt cohorts: short-chat (<=128 tokens), multi-turn (3 turns, average 400 tokens), long-context (>=2048 tokens).
   - Save the seed corpus and store the job ID in the release ticket.

2) Golden baseline collection
   - Command (example):
     run-benchmark --model Llama-2-13B --backend host-gpu-fp16 --prompts prompts/llama13b-canonical.json --out baseline/llama13b-host-fp16.json

3) Accelerator run and raw trace capture
   - Command (example):
     run-benchmark --model Llama-2-13B --backend remote-npu-v1 --prompts prompts/llama13b-canonical.json --trace raw-traces/npu-v1/

4) Automated fidelity metrics job
   - Compare outputs with baseline and compute: ROUGE-L, BLEURT, token-level KL, and a semantic-similarity embedding score (cosine).
   - Thresholds (example):
     - Embedding cosine >= 0.92 vs baseline for short-chat cohort
     - BLEURT delta <= -0.03 for multi-turn cohort
     - No hallucination rate increase > 0.5% (see hallucination-detector v2)

5) Statistical significance and A/B harness
   - Run paired A/B for n >= 500 samples per cohort. If metrics are borderline, collect n >= 2000.

Benchmarking suite requirements
- Microbenchmarks: per-kernel latency histogram for 1..4096 sequence lengths, token throughput (tokens/s) under 1, 4, 16 concurrent sessions.
- End-to-end benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 for representative routes (completion, chat, embeddings).
- Cost model: estimate cost-per-token based on observed util and amortized kernel credits. Provide delta vs baseline.
- Energy estimate: if hardware monitoring available, include watt-seconds/token.

Release validation matrix
| Check | Pass criteria | Owner |
|-------|---------------|-------|
| Functional smoke | No errors on 100 sample requests | Release engineer |
| Fidelity | Embedding cosine >= 0.92 AND BLEURT delta within threshold | Profiling owner |
| Latency SLO | p95 <= configured SLO (route specific) | SRE |
| Stability | No OOMs, no kernel crashes for 24h soak | Kernel owner |
| Observability | Traces, metrics, and traces contain accel tags | Observability team |

Runbook: activate new accelerator pool (staged rollout)
1) Canary: enable pool for internal/beta customers only (5% of traffic). Monitor fidelity and latency in 1m buckets for 2 hours.
2) Expand: move to 20% if no alerts. Validate via A/B test comparing golden baseline metrics.
3) Ramp: move to 50% over 6-12 hours if rolling windows show steady state.
4) Full switch: 100% only after 48h of production stability and business sign-off.

Rollback gates and automated safety breakers
- Fidelity-alert: configured to trigger if embedding cosine drops by >= 0.03 on rolling 30-minute window across the canonical prompt set. Immediate automated action: pause routing to the accelerator pool and shift to fallback kernel for affected models.
- Latency SLO breach: if p95 breaches SLO for 3 consecutive 5-minute windows, reduce accelerator pool traffic by 50% automatically and notify SRE on-call.
- Crash circuit: 3 kernel crashes within 10 minutes triggers full evacuation and disables pool.

Investigation playbook (if degradation observed)
1) Capture failing requests using trace IDs from the fidelity job and store full KV state.
2) Re-run failing inputs locally against: baseline, accelerator variant, and deterministic fallback to compare token-by-token diffs. Use internal tool: fidelity-inspect --baseline baseline.json --variant variant.json --output diffs/
3) Check kernel telemetry: kernel-latency-distribution, kernel-mem-residency, and hardware-err logs.
4) If hardware fault suspected, quarantine node and escalate to hardware vendor with collected traces and firmware versions.

Kernel developer checklist for accelerator-targeted kernels
- Export deterministic_fallback_cost and fallback_compat metadata.
- Provide a regression harness (Docker image) that reproduces microbenchmark and includes a mock KV cache.
- Ensure deterministic seeding for ops that rely on RNG or beam search.
- Provide a smoke vector of at least 200 canonical prompts with expected output hashes.

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum required panels)
- Accelerator pool health: uptime, crash_count, avg_warm_ratio
- Fidelity rollup: embedding_cosine_rolling_30m, BLEURT_delta_30m, hallucination_rate_24h
- Cost & throughput: tokens/s, util_percent, estimated_cost_per_1M_tokens
- Observability traces: sample request traces with accel.* tags and kernel version metadata

Contacts and ownership
- Kernel integration owner: Priya Nambiar (pri@redwood.example.com)
- Scheduler policy owner: Ethan Morales (ethan@redwood.example.com)
- Profiling and fidelity owner: Sofia Chen (sofia@redwood.example.com)
- On-call SRE escalation channel: #sre-accelerator (pager: SRE on-call rotation)

Appendix A — Example scheduler policy snippet (YAML)
policy_name: \"npu-v1-weighted-pool\"
pool_label: \"remote-npu-v1\"
accel:
  class: network-accel
  max_concurrency: 64
  warm_ratio_threshold: 0.6
admission:
  min_priority: 20
  fallback_compat: [\"host-gpu-fp16\",\"on-host-a100-int8\"]

Appendix B — Common failure signatures and first actions
- High token-drop: look for quantization saturation (check kernel counter: q_saturation_rate). Action: reduce batch size and fall back.
- KV mismatch after warmstart: indicates proxy state desync. Action: flush session and force cold restart with warm hint disabled.
- Increased hallucination: compare hallucination_anchors and run hallucination-detector; run A/B with baseline.

Document maintenance and cadence
- This page is reviewed quarterly by the kernel integration guild.
- Any production incident that involves a hybrid accelerator must attach an incident note and suggested updates to this doc.

Related resources
- Kernel mapper test harness (internal repo)
- Fidelity evaluator job spec (link in related_pages)
- Scheduler policy language reference

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Created (Priya Nambiar)
- 2026-02-18: Added automated safety breaker thresholds and YAML policy example (Priya Nambiar)
