payload.page_title: Paged KV: Compact Sweep + Granular Pin Coordinator Rollout Guide

sections.body: This page describes how to safely roll out (and roll back) the paged-KV compact sweep reclamation pass and the granular pin coordinator in production. These changes reduce fragmentation and pin-induced allocator stalls, improving 99p latency under mixed workloads. The guide includes recommended configs, feature gates, dashboards, canary procedure, and known failure modes.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
Long-lived pins and coarse reclamation can cause tail-latency spikes and fragmentation in the paged KV backend. The compact sweep pass opportunistically coalesces sparse blocks; the granular pin coordinator tracks mini-span pins inside blocks to avoid head-of-line blocking during eviction/reuse contention.

This guide is a production-facing update to the implementation that landed in redwood#91534. Since the PR merged, rollout controls, metric names, and default gating have been updated based on perf-canary and two real-world regressions (see “Known issues & mitigations”).
sections.heading: Background

sections.body:
- Runs opportunistically when the allocator reports sufficient slack.
- Moves live mini-spans into denser blocks and releases empty blocks back to the global pool.
- Adds bounded background CPU work to reduce fragmentation and improve reuse.
sections.heading: Compact sweep

sections.body:
- Exposes per-mini-span pin tokens.
- Fast-path acquisition via atomic bitmap/refcount; fallback path uses a short wait strategy before parking.
- Integrates with eviction scoring (frecency + pin density) to prefer reclaim candidates with fewer pinned spans.
sections.heading: Granular pin coordinator

sections.body: The original PR introduced a scheduler gate named `kv.background_pin_lane`. During rollout hardening (Dec 2025–Jan 2026), we standardized flags and changed defaults.
sections.heading: Feature gates and current defaults

sections.body:
1) Scheduler background lane for long pins
- Old key (deprecated): `kv.background_pin_lane`
- New key: `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled`
- Current default: true in canary, false in general production unless explicitly enabled by service config (see “Rollout procedure”).

2) Compact sweep enablement
- Key: `kv.compact_sweep.enabled`
- Current default: true for paged-KV enabled services.

3) Compact sweep aggressiveness
- Keys: `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio`, `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct`, `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run`
- Notes: `max_move_bytes_per_run` was added after perf-canary feedback to cap worst-case relocation bursts.
sections.heading: Gates

sections.body: Use these as baseline values. Adjust per cluster based on workload mix and SLO sensitivity.
sections.heading: Recommended configuration (2026-02)

sections.body:
- `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true`
- `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio=0.18`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct=1.0`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run=268435456`  (256 MiB)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false`
sections.heading: Baseline (safe)

sections.body:
- `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true`
- `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio=0.12`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct=2.0`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run=536870912`  (512 MiB)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=true`
sections.heading: Performance-optimized (after canary success)

sections.body: Metric names were normalized after the PR. If your dashboard uses older names, update it.
sections.heading: Key metrics (current names)

sections.body:
- `kv.compact_sweep.runs_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.coalesced_blocks_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.moved_bytes_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.run_duration_ms`
- `kv.compact_sweep.throttled_total` (incremented when CPU budget or move cap prevents additional work)
sections.heading: Compact sweep

sections.body:
- `kv.pin_coordinator.active_tokens`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` (histogram)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.waiters`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.fallback_path_total`
sections.heading: Pin coordinator

sections.body:
- `kv.paged_allocator.fragmentation_index` (0..1)
- `kv.paged_allocator.free_ratio`
- `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` (histogram)
sections.heading: Allocator / fragmentation

sections.body:
- `scheduler.background_lane.queue_depth`
- `scheduler.background_lane.run_latency_ms`
sections.heading: Scheduler lane (when enabled)

sections.body:
- Traces: `compactSweep()` spans include tags `moved_bytes`, `coalesced_blocks`, `throttled`.
- Pin acquisition traces include tags `fast_path=true|false`, `wait_ms`.
- Log sampling: keep at <= 0.1% for pin wait warnings; otherwise high-QPS services can flood.
sections.heading: Traces / logs

sections.body:
- Serving 99p/99.9p latency
- OOM / RSS growth rate
- Token cost or GPU utilization (service-dependent)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99
- `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` p99
sections.heading: SLO signals to watch during canary

sections.body:
- You are on a runtime build that includes the post-merge config normalization (>= runtime v1.19.3).
- You have dashboards updated to the metric names above.
- You can revert flags without redeploy (dynamic config or config-map reload).
sections.heading: 0) Preconditions

sections.body:
1. Set `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true` (if not already).
2. Start with baseline settings:
   - `min_free_ratio=0.18`, `max_cpu_pct=1.0`, `max_move_bytes_per_run=256MiB`.
3. Run for 24 hours.
4. Success criteria:
   - Fragmentation index drops by >= 20% relative to baseline over comparable traffic.
   - No sustained increase in tail latency (> 2% at p99) and no elevated eviction stall p99.
sections.heading: 1) Canary: enable compact sweep only (recommended order)

sections.body:
1. Set `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`.
2. Keep `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false` initially.
3. Run for 24 hours.
4. Success criteria:
   - Reduction in `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` p99 (target: 10–25% depending on workload).
   - `kv.pin_coordinator.fallback_path_total` stable or decreasing after warm-up.
sections.heading: 2) Canary: enable granular pin coordinator (if not already default)

sections.body:
1. Set `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=true`.
2. Run for 24–72 hours.
3. Success criteria:
   - No throughput regression on continuous batching.
   - Background lane queue depth remains bounded (no persistent growth).
sections.heading: 3) Canary: enable background lane for long pins (optional)

sections.body:
- Ramp 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% by cluster, holding at least 12 hours per step.
- Use the same step schedule for enabling background lane.
sections.heading: 4) Ramp-up

sections.body:
If any of the following occurs, rollback the most recent step first:
- Sustained p99 latency increase > 5% for 30 minutes.
- OOM events increase or RSS growth accelerates unexpectedly.
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99 increases > 2x baseline.
sections.heading: Rollback procedure

sections.body:
1) Disable background lane: `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false`
2) If still bad, disable pin coordinator: `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=false`
3) If still bad (rare), disable compact sweep: `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=false`
sections.heading: Rollback order

sections.body: - Disabling compact sweep may increase fragmentation over hours; plan for a follow-up defragmentation window if needed.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
The original microbench numbers in redwood#91534 remain directionally correct, but production outcomes vary by workload.

Observed ranges in canary (Nov 2025–Feb 2026):
- 99p latency: 12–25% improvement for short-sequence / mixed hot-cold traffic; minimal change for long-context dominated traffic.
- Fragmentation index: 25–45% reduction after 6–24 hours of steady traffic.
- Token cost: 3–7% improvement where eviction/reuse contention was a limiter.
sections.heading: Expected performance impact (field data)

sections.body:
1) Burst relocation causing short CPU spikes
- Symptom: `kv.compact_sweep.run_duration_ms` and host CPU jump, correlated with small latency blips.
- Mitigation: lower `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct` or `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run`.

2) High contention pin waits under pathological micro-span churn
- Symptom: `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99 increases and `fallback_path_total` climbs.
- Mitigation: ensure background lane is disabled initially; if enabling, confirm background lane queue depth stays bounded. Consider raising allocator free ratio target (service-specific).

3) Config key mismatch after standardization
- Symptom: changes to `kv.background_pin_lane` have no effect.
- Mitigation: migrate to `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled`. The old key is ignored in runtime >= v1.19.3.
sections.heading: Known issues & mitigations

sections.body:
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime (Kernel & Scheduling)
- Escalation: #eng-serving-runtime-oncall
- Related work items: ENG-7342, ENG-7460
sections.heading: Ownership & support

sections.body:
- [ ] Confirm `kv.paged_allocator.free_ratio` is stable after enabling compact sweep.
- [ ] Confirm fragmentation index trends downward over a full diurnal cycle.
- [ ] Confirm eviction stalls p99 is not worse than baseline.
- [ ] Confirm pin coordinator wait latency p99 is stable.
- [ ] If background lane enabled, confirm scheduler queue depth is bounded.
sections.heading: Appendix: quick validation checklist

payload.page_title: Deterministic Scheduler Simulation & Verification Manual

sections.body:
Summary

This document specifies the deterministic scheduler simulation and verification manual used to assert functional and latency determinism for the runtime scheduler. It defines the simulation harness, reproducible test vectors, verification metrics, and an operational rollout plan for scheduler changes that must preserve determinism guarantees when enabled.

Goals

- Provide a repeatable simulation harness that deterministically replays request surfaces, resource events, and kernel execution ordering.
- Define acceptance tests and metrics for determinism regressions (bit-level or behavioral).
- Give a practical verification and rollout procedure for scheduler code changes, including fuzzing, shadow validation, and staged canaries.
- Document common sources of non-determinism and mitigations.

Scope and Audience

Intended for runtime engineers, scheduler maintainers, test-infra owners, and oncall. This applies to core scheduler components: admission controller, slot allocator, preemption/cooperative handoff, kernel mapper, and the admission backpressure loop. It does not replace performance benchmarking (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite).

Background and Rationale

The scheduler influences tail latency and correctness of prefix/KV cache warmup, eviction decisions, and kernel assignment. Small non-deterministic changes can produce variable SLO regressions that are hard to triage in production. Enforcing deterministic behavior in simulation lets us:

- Isolate regressions to code diffs quickly.
- Reproduce field incidents in a lab without noisy environmental factors.
- Provide stronger invariants for rollback gates.

Key definitions

- Deterministic run: A simulation run that, given the same seed and input trace, produces the same discrete decision sequence (admit/reject/slot-id/kernel-id/preempt events), and the same timeline of observable scheduling events.
- Pseudo-deterministic run: Same high-level sequence but differing low-level timings within acceptable epsilon (used for GPU kernel jitter tolerant checks).

Design overview

1) Deterministic scheduler mode: a test-only compilation flag that enforces ordered processing in places where production uses best-effort parallelism. When enabled:
   - Single-threaded logical decision loop with explicit event queue ordering.
   - RNG seeded from test vector header.
   - Kernel hinting decisions resolved using stable tie-breaker rules (e.g., sort by tenant-id then request-id).

2) Simulation harness (scheduler-sim):
   - Accepts input corpus: request traces, hardware event streams (thermal/power/capacity changes), and injected noise profiles.
   - Produces deterministic traces, event logs, and a decision diff artifact for golden comparison.

3) Trace format and seed model:
   - Each trace file is a newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) where each record includes: timestamp_ns, request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, sequence_length, token_count, client_priority, and optional kernel_hint. A header line includes a 64-bit seed and metadata.

Simulation harness architecture

- Injector: replays request events into the scheduler sim at virtual timestamps.
- VirtualClock: drives timers deterministically (no reliance on host OS clock).
- KernelSimulator: models kernel execution duration deterministically from kernel profile lookup table (see profiling corpus).
- SchedulerCore: the deterministic decision engine (admission, slot allocation, preemption resolution).
- Snapshotter: records deterministic state checkpoints (admission queues, slot maps, kvcache indexes) at configured intervals.

Test corpora and sources

- Production traces: anonymized and sampled workload traces from shadow-mirroring (sanitized).
- Synthetic fuzz corpus: generated request shapes stressing edge cases: bulk-preempt, microbursts, long-seq streaming, 50/50 tiny+long tokens.
- Kernel latency profiles: extracted from profiling-playbook lab runs; stored as stable fixture and used to compute KernelSimulator durations.

Verification metrics

| Metric | Type | Pass threshold | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Decision sequence equality | binary | exact match | Byte-for-byte sequence of decision events vs golden |
| Event timeline delta | numeric (ns) | <= 100us cumulative drift | Allows limited microtiming drift when using pseudo-deterministic mode |
| Divergence onset latency | numeric (ms) | > 5000ms for long traces | Where first divergence occurs; higher is better |
| Stateful snapshot hash equality | binary | exact match | Hash of serialized scheduler snapshot at checkpoints |
| Non-deterministic source counter | numeric | 0 new sources | Number of code paths flagged as non-deterministic since last accepted run |

Procedure: local verification (developer flow)

1) Run unit-level deterministic scheduler mode: BUILD=deterministic make scheduler-sim
2) Pick a canonical trace: tools/sim/select_trace --name=canary-compact-2025.ndjson
3) Execute: ./bin/scheduler-sim --trace=canary-compact-2025.ndjson --seed=0x5a3f1c9b --snapshot-interval=500ms --output=out/
4) Validate outputs: tools/sim/verify_golden --candidate out/decision.ndjson --golden golden/canary-compact-2025.decision.ndjson
5) On mismatch: run bisect-mode (see troubleshooting) to find diffing commit range.

Procedure: CI verification gates

1) On pull request that touches scheduler code, CI triggers deterministic-sim job with 3 canonical traces (fast, mixed, long-tail).
2) CI compares decision sequence equality and snapshot-hash equality.
3) If CI fails: require explicit reviewer signoff and an exemption note in the PR if the change is expected to be non-deterministic (rare).

Fuzzing and stress verification

- Differential fuzzing harness: runs the same trace under deterministic and production-parallel modes and compares high-level invariants (no deadlock, admission fairness, memory usage bounds).
- Randomized seed sweep: run N=256 seeds for each fuzz-input and record any divergence. Seeds that cause divergence must be captured and promoted as a reproducible minimal test case.
- Adversarial microbursts: synthetic traces with 100x baseline concurrency spikes to test slot starvation and preemption fairness.

Sources of non-determinism and mitigations

1) Parallel reduction order (GPU-side): enforce canonical ordering by adding an ordering step in kernel mapper during verification builds.
2) Network IO arrival jitter: use VirtualClock and deterministic injector instead of wall-time in sim.
3) Thread scheduling in C++ worker pools: deterministic mode uses a single logical decision thread; production differences caught by differential fuzz harness.
4) RNG without seed: all RNG usage must accept an explicit seeded RNG from harness. Add linter rule: no std::random_device without injection.
5) External system calls that return ordered-but-non-deterministic values: wrap and stub in sim.

Simulation configuration reference (YAML example)

sim-config.yaml:
  seed: 0x5a3f1c9b
  traces:
    - name: canary-compact-2025
      file: traces/canary-compact-2025.ndjson
  snapshot_interval_ms: 500
  kernel_profile: profiling/amd-a10x-kernel-profile.v1.json
  checkpoint_hash_algo: blake2b
  tolerances:
    timeline_drift_ns: 100000

CLI examples and helper commands

- Build deterministic sim: BUILD=deterministic bazel build //runtime/scheduler:scheduler-sim
- Run single trace: ./bazel-bin/runtime/scheduler/scheduler-sim --config=sim-config.yaml
- Verify candidate: ./tools/sim/verify_golden --candidate out/decision.ndjson --golden golden/canary-compact-2025.decision.ndjson
- Snapshot compare: ./tools/sim/compare_snapshot --a out/snap-00010.blob --b golden/snap-00010.blob

Rollout and production safety checklist

1) Developer verification: local deterministic sim + fuzz sweep (N=32 seeds).
2) CI: deterministic-sim gate with full snapshot-hash equality.
3) Shadow stage: deploy scheduler change behind feature-flag with 0% traffic but shadow mirroring to collect decision diffs for 24h.
4) Canary stage: enable change for a single low-traffic cluster (1% traffic) with active snapshot comparison and telemetry logging.
5) Sweep stage: increase to 10% traffic in 24h if no diffs or SLO impact.
6) Full rollout: 100% across regions after 72h of stable metrics and no deterministic divergence reports.

Rollback triggers (immediate)

- Decision sequence mismatch observed in canary vs golden.
- Tail-latency P99 increase > 20% sustained > 30 minutes.
- Memory growth rate change > 2x in scheduler process over baseline.

Observability and telemetry requirements

- Emit deterministic-run-id in trace logs (header) so diffs can be joined with production request ids.
- Snapshot-hash telemetry exported every snapshot interval to a centralized store.
- Divergence event must include: trace-id, seed, first-divergence-offset, scheduler-version, kernel-profiles-used.

Ownership and contacts

- Scheduler core owners: @ashapatel (primary), @marcov (secondary).
- Test-infra owner: @sofianguyen.
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood.com (follow runbooks/runtime-oncall-rapid-investigation-cheatsheet-2023.json).

Troubleshooting and bisecting

1) If verify_golden fails with a single commit range: run tools/sim/bisect --commit-range <A>..<B> --trace canary-compact-2025.ndjson --seed <seed>
2) To diagnose non-deterministic root cause: enable snapshotter at higher frequency and compare earliest snapshot divergence.
3) If divergence only in production-parallel mode but not deterministic sim, run differential fuzzer with thread-interleaving injection.

Appendix A: Minimal reproducer checklist

- Extract minimal trace (tools/sim/minify_trace) that still reproduces divergence.
- Reduce kernel profile set to smallest matching set.
- Lock build id and include uname and toolchain info in the reproducer bundle.

Appendix B: Audit checklist for PR reviewers

1) Does the change introduce unseeded RNG usage? (FAIL if yes without justification)
2) Are new parallel regions accompanied by a deterministic-mode implementation or a test that tolerates non-determinism?
3) Are stable tie-breakers used where ordering matters?
4) Is there a new golden or updated trace added to sim-corpus if behavior intentionally changes?

References

- Profiling corpus and kernel fixtures: ../profiling-playbook/kernel-hint-propagation-profiling-pipeline-2026.json
- Scheduler observability injector: ../kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026.json
- CI gating spec: ../runtime-architecture/release-readiness-integrated-checklist-technical-gate-2024.json

Revision history

- 2025-11-03: Drafted by Asha Patel.
- 2025-12-20: Added fuzz sweep guidance and YAML config examples (reviewer: Marco Villanueva).
- 2026-02-14: Finalized rollout checklist and telemetry requirements (published).

payload.page_title: Kernel ABI & Quantization Kernel Compatibility Guidelines

sections.body:
Summary

This document describes the compatibility matrix and operational guidelines for kernel ABIs and quantization-optimized kernels used by the Redwood serving runtime. It covers version mapping, supported GPU microarchitectures, recommended fallback strategies, preflight tests, safe rollout and rollback procedures, and required telemetry for forensic analysis. The goal is to make kernel selection predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments and to reduce upgrade risk for private (VPC / on-prem) customers.

Scope

- Kernel ABIs exposed by the runtime (cuda/cudnn/cuBLAS, ROCm, oneAPI-compatible kernels)
- Quantization-aware kernels (int8, int4, dynamic-float16 paths) and heuristics that select them
- Compatibility across accelerator generations (NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper, Ada; AMD CDNA2/CDNA3; Intel Gaudi/ARC where applicable)
- Runtime-level rollback and canary test procedures for private deployments

Audience

This is intended for: runtime engineers, kernel maintainers, private-deploy field operators, SREs, and solutions engineers who run customer rollouts.

1) High-level compatibility principles

- ABI-first: prefer stable runtime ABI targets (e.g., CUDA 11.x vs 12.x). Kernel optimizations should be feature-gated, not ABI-breaking.
- Architecture-aware selection: kernels must declare supported architectures (e.g., sm_80, sm_90, gfx110x) and a minimum driver/firmware requirement.
- Graceful fallback: for any quantized kernel that fails validation, the runtime must fall back to the next-safe kernel (e.g., int8 -> fp16 -> fp32) while preserving request semantics.
- Telemetry and evidence preservation: every kernel switch must emit structured telemetry (see "Telemetry requirements" section) to support post-incident forensics.

2) Kernel compatibility table (summary)

| Kernel type | Typical ABI / Driver req | Supported HW (examples) | Quant modes | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|-------------|-------|
| high-throughput-mha-optim (CUDA) | CUDA 12.1+, driver 535+ | NVIDIA Ada (RTX 40x0/ GH200 variants), Hopper (H100) | fp16, bf16 | Uses Tensor Cores; requires cuBLAS/cuDNN GPU kernels; prefers workspace memory >= 8 MB |
| int8-mha-fastpath | CUDA 12.1+, driver 540+ | NVIDIA Hopper (H100) with int8 tensor cores | int8 | Only for models validated to <1% quality delta; must be feature gated per-customer |
| rocm-mha-optimized | ROCm 5.6+ | AMD CDNA2 (Instinct MI100), CDNA3 | fp16, bf16 | Requires ROCm kernel packages; falls back to CPU-hosted fp32 path if missing |
| oneapi-bf16-path | oneAPI 2023.4+ | Intel Gaudi/ARC experimental | bf16 | API experimental; enabled only in internal QA and by explicit customer opt-in |

(Full machine-readable matrix is stored in the kernel registry: /internal/registries/kernel-compat-2026.csv)

3) Preflight checks (private deployments)

Before enabling a new kernel set on a private deployment, run the checklist below. These steps must be automated and recorded in the release ticket.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. Inventory: collect accelerator model, driver version, firmware revision and OS kernel (uname -a) from every node.
2. Sizing: ensure ephemeral workspace and pinned GPU memory meet kernel requirements (example: 8 MB workspace recommended for mha-optim).
3. Driver validation: verify drivers meet minimum versions listed in the compatibility table.
4. Artifact attestation: verify kernel artifacts signatures using the internal signing key (see CLI snippet).
5. Unit kernel smoke: run the kernel smoke harness (tools/kernel-smoke-runner) on a representative node.
6. Regression eval: run a small, deterministic prompt set against the canary cluster (N=1k tokens) and check quality regressions (absolute delta thresholds per model).
7. Telemetry gating: ensure telemetry hooks are deployed and forwarding to the evidence sink.
sections.heading: Preflight checklist (ordered)

sections.body: $ sudo /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-inventory --output json > gpu-inventory.json
sections.heading: retrieve GPU inventory (Linux)

sections.body:
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-verify --artifact /opt/kernels/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz --trusted-keys /etc/redwood/trusted-keys.pem

4) Canary rollout plan (safe pattern for private/VPC deployments)

Principles: small blast radius, automatic quality gates, rollback hooks, and customer notification where required.
sections.heading: verify kernel artifact signature

sections.body:
1. Create a canary pool: reserve 2–4 nodes (must be isolated from production tenant traffic).
2. Apply kernel bundle to canary nodes and restart runtime components using the operator's safe-restart hook.
3. Run functional smoke and deterministic evals. Must pass model-level quality gates:
   - Top-level service SLOs (p95 latency, error rate) must remain within 10% of baseline.
   - Quality regression per-model must be <= configured delta (default 0.8% absolute token-level difference).
4. Run load-validation: replay recorded production traces at 1x and 2x QPS for 30 minutes. Monitor CPU/GPU utilization and latency tails.
5. If all gates pass, promote kernel bundle to a staged subset (10% of production nodes) and run the same checks for 2 hours.
6. Gradually increase to 50% and then 100% using automated health checks.

If any gate fails, follow the rollback procedure immediately. Notify the customer and create a postmortem if customer-affecting.

5) Rollback procedure (operator-safe)

Goals: restore previous stable kernel, preserve forensic evidence, avoid data loss.
sections.heading: Step-by-step canary plan

sections.body:
1. Abort ongoing promotions using the operator: /opt/redwood/bin/operator promote --abort <bundle-id>
2. Mark the canary nodes read-only for new model swaps: /opt/redwood/bin/node-ralm --set read-only
3. Revert kernel artifacts to the last-known-good bundle: /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-apply --bundle-id <last-good>
4. Restart runtime components with --preserve-kv to avoid KV cache loss when possible.
5. Run validation smoke and replay a 10-minute production trace.
6. Collect forensic evidence: kernel logs, telemetry spans, driver stack traces. Package them with the rollback ticket.
sections.heading: Immediate rollback steps

sections.body:
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-apply --bundle-id rwbundle-2026-09-12 --force && sudo systemctl restart redwood-runtime --preserve-kv

6) Forensic telemetry and required traces

Minimum telemetry emitted on kernel switch events (every value must be present):
- event_type: KERNEL_SWITCH
- timestamp_utc
- node_id
- bundle_id
- previous_kernel_id
- new_kernel_id
- driver_version
- firmware_revision
- validation_signatures (artifact sig id)
- smoke_results: pass/fail and short hash of the test output
- quality_eval_summary: per-model numeric deltas

Retention: for private deployments, preserve full forensic packages for 90 days (customer contract permitting). Evidence bundles must be stored in the customer-specific evidence bucket with immutability flags when requested by compliance.

7) Quality gating configuration (suggested defaults)

- latency_p95_increase_threshold: 10%
- error_rate_absolute_threshold: 0.5%
- per_model_quality_delta: 0.8% absolute token-level difference
- smoke_harness_timeout: 300s

8) Known incompatibility patterns & mitigation recipes

Pattern: int8 kernel yields subtle hallucination drift on long prompts.
Mitigation: restrict int8 to short-sequence inference or enable per-model calibration. If a customer requires long-context fidelity, prefer bf16 or fp16 kernels.

Pattern: ROCm kernel fails on nodes with older firmware microcode.
Mitigation: require firmware >= vendor-specified minimum; if not possible, mark nodes as non-candidate for this bundle.

9) Customer-facing configuration knobs (private deploys)

Operators can expose the following flags to customers during onboarding (document in the customer-runbook template):
- enable_experimental_kernels: boolean (default false)
- per_model_quantization_profile: URL to customer-approved profile
- max_latency_slo: integer (ms) to allow tuning fallback aggressiveness

10) Post-incident checklist and postmortem template

1. Preserve evidence bundle and copy to secure forensic store.
2. Populate postmortem with timeline, root cause hypotheses, and customer impact.
3. Run replays using isolated sandbox and test candidate fixes.
4. Share corrective action plan with stakeholders and schedule follow-up.

Appendix A — Kernel artifact signing and verification

- All kernel bundles must be signed by the release pipeline using the Redwood release key. Artifacts without a valid signature are rejected by the operator.
- Signing command (CI):
$ gpg --batch --yes --armor --sign --detach-sign --local-user redwood-release-key artifacts/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz

- Verification (operator):
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-verify --artifact artifacts/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz --trusted-keys /etc/redwood/trusted-keys.pem

Appendix B — Minimal test matrix (smoke harness samples)

| Test name | Purpose | Expected result | Run time |
|-----------|---------|-----------------|----------|
| kernel-basic-launch | Validate kernel loads and exports expected symbols | success, no segfault | 30s |
| inkernel-inference | Basic generate for short prompt (N=3 tokens) | exact output hash match | 45s |
| stress-multi-stream | 8 concurrent streams for 60s | p95 latency < configured threshold | 60s |

Appendix C — Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: kernels team (eng-serving-runtime) — Mateo Alvarez
- Secondary: SRE on-call for serving runtime
- Escalation: if rollback required and customer impact > 10% of SLO, page Director of Platform (on-call list) and notify Customer Success lead for the affected account.

Related documents and artifacts

- Kernel compatibility registry: /internal/registries/kernel-compat-2026.csv
- Kernel smoke harness: git@internal:redwood/tools/kernel-smoke-runner.git
- Artifact signing key rotation policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/crypto-agile-key-rotation-2026

Change log

- 2026-02-15: Created (initial draft)
- 2026-06-01: Added canary rollout timings and telemetry fields (Priya Rangan)
- 2026-08-12: Clarified rollback commands and preserved-kv restart semantics (Janelle Park)

payload.page_title: Eviction–Kernel Coordination Protocol and Signal Handbook

sections.body:
A practical handbook describing the protocol and operational guidance for coordinating memory eviction (KV cache, model weights/shards) with kernel scheduling signals to prevent tail-latency spirals and preserve throughput SLOs.
Overview
========
This document defines the Eviction–Kernel Coordination Protocol (EKCP), a lightweight control plane and operational playbook that synchronizes cache/shard eviction decisions with kernel scheduling hints and backpressure signals emitted by the serving runtime. The goal is to avoid reactive thrashing (concurrent eviction + heavy kernel activation) and reduce tail latency regressions when the system rehydrates caches or migrates shards under load.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: KV cache eviction, session/sequence eviction, model shard migration, and kernel activation scheduling in the serving runtime.
- Excludes: higher-level routing policies (tiered fallback routing) and customer-side session management.

Why this matters
----------------
During mixed workloads we observed sequences of events that amplify tail latency:
1) Memory pressure triggers mass eviction of KV cache and/or lightweight session state.
2) Immediately after eviction, the scheduler admits high-priority requests that require cache rehydration and heavy kernel execution.
3) Kernel queue saturation and memory reallocation cause long-tail latencies and increased error rates.

EKCP provides a modest coordination layer of signals and policies to:
- Stagger and rate-limit rehydration work.
- Prefer low-fidelity fallbacks until caches are warmed.
- Prioritize small, cheap inference requests during warmup windows.

Design principles
-----------------
- Backwards-compatible: Defaults are conservative; behavior toggled via config flags per cluster/pool.
- Signal minimal: Only a few semantic signals to avoid high cardinality.
- Observability-first: Emit clear metrics and traces for every decision.
- Experiment-friendly: Feature flags + canary ramp plan included.

Protocol summary (high level)
----------------------------
EKCP uses three coordinated signal channels between eviction manager and kernel scheduler:
- EvictionIntent: emitted when a tenant/pool plans mass eviction (soft signal).
- WarmupWindow: a timeboxed period after eviction where rehydration is rate-limited and scheduler favors cheap kernels.
- RehydrationProgress: incremental reports of cache warm percentage (0-100) and shard residency counts.

State machine (per-pool)
------------------------
States: IDLE -> EVICTING -> WARMUP -> NORMAL
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) IDLE -> EVICTING: EvictionIntent(true) issued when free_memory < threshold_low and reclaim_plan applies.
2) EVICTING -> WARMUP: Once eviction completes, WarmupWindow opens for N seconds (configurable).
3) WARMUP -> NORMAL: When RehydrationProgress >= warmup_target OR warmup timeout expires.
4) Any state -> IDLE: Manual override or pool drain event.

Message formats (examples)
-------------------------
All messages are lightweight JSON blobs carried over the internal control plane (gRPC or internal pub/sub). Example payloads:
sections.heading: Transitions

sections.body:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "initiator": "eviction-manager:v2",
  "reason": "memory-pressure",
  "estimated_evicted_mb": 15360,
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:08Z"
}
sections.heading: EvictionIntent example

sections.body:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "warmup_seconds": 45,
  "priority_policy": "favor-l2-small-requests",
  "rehydration_target_percent": 30,
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:18Z"
}
sections.heading: WarmupWindow example

sections.body:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "cache_percent": 22,
  "shard_residency": {"model-A": 3, "model-B": 7},
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:42Z"
}

Operational policy parameters (recommended defaults)
--------------------------------------------------
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| memory_threshold_low | 0.15 | Fraction free memory that triggers soft eviction |
| warmup_seconds_default | 30 | Default warmup window length |
| warmup_rehydrate_target | 25 | Percent of important cache that should be present to exit warmup |
| rehydrate_slowdown_factor | 0.6 | Rate limiter: reduce parallel rehydration tasks by this factor during warmup |
| allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup | false | Whether to allow heavy kernels during warmup |

Scheduler integration points
----------------------------
The kernel scheduler consumes EKCP signals and implements the following behaviors while warmup is active:
- Admission shaping: lower concurrency for kernels requiring > X MB scratch or > Y streams.
- Kernel hinting: prefer quantized or small-batch kernels for a configured percent of early requests.
- Soft-fallback: route to cheaper model variant (if available) for non-critical requests until warmup passes.

Observability contract
----------------------
sections.heading: RehydrationProgress example

sections.body:
- trace/span with event tags: pool_id, state, initiator, reason, warmup_seconds
- metrics (per-pool): ekcp_evictions_total (counter), ekcp_warmup_seconds (histogram), ekcp_rehydrate_percent (gauge), ekcp_warmup_blocked_requests_total (counter)
- logs: structured JSON logs with correlation_id for cross-service debugging

Suggested dashboard widgets
---------------------------
- Warmup windows active (count) by pool (heatmap)
- 95p/99p latency vs EKCP state time series (line)
- Rehydration percent vs throughput (scatter)
- Eviction triggers trend (bar)

Runbook: triage when tail latencies spike after evictions
---------------------------------------------------------
1) Verify recent EKCP events: query ekcp_evictions_total and ekcp_warmup_seconds for pool in question.
2) Check RehydrationProgress: if cache_percent < warmup_rehydrate_target, warmup is ongoing. Decide if you should extend warmup.
3) Examine kernel queue depth and GPU occupancy. If occupancy > 90% and warmup is active: reduce admission for heavy kernels.
4) Apply quick mitigations (ordered):
   a) Increase warmup_seconds for the pool by +30s.
   b) Enable allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup=false (if toggled).
   c) Temporarily divert non-critical traffic to cheaper variant or fallback region.
   d) If kernel queue remains saturated, scale up ephemeral burst capacity (if available).
5) Post-incident: run a targeted replay of representative requests to validate recovery and update the eviction threshold if repeated.

Benchmarking and validation protocol
-----------------------------------
Goal: ensure EKCP reduces 99p latency regressions without materially reducing 50p latency or throughput.
sections.heading: Every EKCP event must produce

sections.body:
1) Baseline capture: capture normal steady-state for 30m, record latency distribution and cache hit ratio.
2) Controlled eviction injection: simulate 2x the memory pressure to trigger eviction and observe behavior with EKCP OFF.
3) EKCP ON: repeat the eviction injection with EKCP enabled.
4) Compare: 99p latency, throughput, cache rehydration time, and error rates.
5) Run stress matrix across tenant mixes (pure chat, embeddings-heavy, mixed short-long sequence).

Sample synthetic driver commands
-------------------------------
sections.heading: Procedure

sections.body: redwood-testctl simulate-eviction --pool gpu-pool-23 --pressure 1.5 --duration 90
sections.heading: Start a warmup-aware eviction test

sections.body:
redwood-metrics query "ekcp_rehydrate_percent{pool_id=\"gpu-pool-23\"}" --since 5m

Rollout plan (canary -> regional -> global)
------------------------------------------
1) Feature flagged, default disabled. Enable EKCP in 1 canary pool (non-critical workloads). Run for 48 hours.
2) If canary is stable, enable for backup pools for 7 days.
3) Enable in 20% of production pools for 72 hours.
4) Gradually roll to 100% with continuous monitoring of 95/99p latency and throughput.

Testing checklist before global rollout
--------------------------------------
- Unit tests for state transitions and message validation.
- Integration tests with a stubbed scheduler and eviction manager.
- End-to-end replay testbench with synthetic traffic.
- Observability verification (metrics, traces, logs).

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling team (oncall: #runtime-scheduling).
- Secondary: Kernel Performance team (oncall: #kernel-perf).
- Escalation: Eng SRE lead (pager).

Troubleshooting examples (short)
-------------------------------
Symptom: Warmup window never completes and cache_percent stalls at 1-5%
Likely cause: Rehydration tasks are being rate-limited too aggressively or blocked by admission shaping.
sections.heading: Observe samples and metrics

sections.body:
- Inspect rehydrate_slowdown_factor and temporarily set to 1.0
- Temporarily increase warmup_seconds to allow background rehydration workers to catch up
- Check for kernel hot-path saturation and enable additional background worker slots

Appendix A: Example cluster config snippet
-----------------------------------------
sections.heading: Remediation steps

sections.body:
ekcp_config:
  enabled: true
  memory_threshold_low: 0.12
  warmup_seconds_default: 45
  warmup_rehydrate_target: 30
  rehydrate_slowdown_factor: 0.7
  priority_policy: "favor-l2-small-requests"
  allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup: false

Appendix B: Telemetry queries (promql examples)
----------------------------------------------
sections.heading: ekcp config for a GPU pool (YAML)

sections.body: sum(ekcp_warmup_seconds_count) by (pool_id)
sections.heading: warmup windows currently active

sections.body:
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool_id, ekcp_state))

Change log
----------
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft.
- 2026-04-02: Added RehydrationProgress payload and warmup_rehydrate_target param.
- 2026-07-02: Published after canary; updated default parameters and troubleshooting steps.

Related reading
---------------
- NUMA-aware shard placement and eviction playbook (see related_pages).
- Scheduler admission shaping guidelines (internal kernel scheduling doc).

Notes and future work
---------------------
- Explore probabilistic warmup targets based on request shape prediction.
- Add cross-pool coordination to avoid simultaneous warmups in colocated pools.

End of document

payload.page_title: Ephemeral Plugin Priority Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook describes the recommended priority arbitration, telemetry, and operational patterns for ephemeral plugins and extension runtimes that run inside the serving runtime process or as proxied microservices. Ephemeral plugins (feature adapters, custom prerun hooks, third-party tokenizers) can introduce variable latency and resource pressure; this document defines guardrails to preserve SLOs, avoid priority inversion, and safely degrade plugin behavior under strain.

Context and motivation:
- Ephemeral plugins are lightweight processes or in-process extensions loaded per-request or per-session to modify prompts, validate outputs, or call external enrichment services.
- Because they are often developed independently (customer-provided or third-party), they are a frequent source of tail-latency and unpredictable kernel-choice interactions (e.g., plugins that increase sequence length causing kernel breakpoints).
- The goal is to allow extensibility while maintaining the serving runtime's latency SLOs and cost bounds.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood Inference runtime versions that support the extension-plugin API (v2+) and the priority arbitration shim.
- Covers both in-process ephemeral plugins and proxied plugin backends.
- Does not cover persistent background services nor compile-time kernel changes.

Ownership and contacts:
- Runtime scheduling and plugin safety: eng-serving-runtime (primary)
- Observability and alerts: eng-platform (secondary)
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre (see runbook section)

Key principles:
1) Demand-fence early: classify plugin calls as potentially latency-sensitive and treat them as early-stage resource candidates (before kernel selection).
2) Fail fast and degrade predictably: define conservative time budgets and safe fallbacks for all plugin categories.
3) Telemetry-driven policy: use rolling telemetry windows (p95/p99) to automatically adjust priority weights and enable graceful shedding.
4) Quantization- and kernel-aware: plugin-induced sequence or token changes must be signalled to the kernel mapper so the scheduler can choose kernels that avoid long-tail regressions.

Plugin classification and default budgets:
- Type A: Latency-critical (e.g., token filters used in the final decode loop) — default budget 20ms.
- Type B: Inline enrichment (e.g., prompt expansion, metadata injection) — default budget 75ms.
- Type C: Non-blocking analytics or telemetry enrichment — default budget 250ms (execute as background or sampled paths).

Configuration table (example, YAML-style fields shown as a table):
| field | description | default |
|---|---|---|
| plugin.class | One of [A, B, C] | B |
| plugin.max_latency_ms | Max allowed wall time per invocation | 75 |
| plugin.priority_weight | Relative weight for scheduler | 100 |
| plugin.cpu_isolate | Whether plugin requires vCPU isolation | false |
| plugin.kv_cache_hint | Hint if plugin extends sequence length | none |
| plugin.fallback_mode | "skip" | "skip" |

Example runtime policy snippet (textual example):
- policy:
  - match: request.extension == "token-augment" AND request.model.family == "redwood-*/gpt"
    action:
      plugin.class: B
      plugin.max_latency_ms: 50
      plugin.priority_weight: 80
      plugin.fallback_mode: skip

Telemetry signals to collect (mandatory):
- plugin.invocations.count (per-plugin)
- plugin.latency.p50/p95/p99 (per-plugin, rolling 1m/5m/1h)
- plugin.error.rate (HTTP 5xx, timeouts, exceptions)
- kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin (histogram)
- request.tail-latency.delta when plugin enabled vs disabled (sampled)

Policy automation rules (examples):
1) Auto-shed: If plugin.latency.p99 > 3 * plugin.max_latency_ms for 2 consecutive 5m windows AND plugin.error.rate > 2%, mark plugin as deferred for new requests and set fallback_mode to "skip".
2) Down-weight: If total system CPU utilization > 85% and plugin.p95 > 2x baseline, reduce plugin.priority_weight by 50% for 10 minutes.
3) Kernel hint propagation: If kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin histogram shows >5% of requests crossing a kernel break point, add a routing hint to use long-seq-optimized kernels for requests that match this plugin pattern.

Graceful degradation patterns:
- Skip mode: Plugin is not executed; log event and add telemetry tag plugin.skipped=true.
- Async mode: Return immediately and enqueue best-effort enrichment; annotate response with enrichment.pending=true.
- Throttle mode: Rate-limit plugin invocations per tenant to a configured RPS.

Runbook: Immediate mitigation steps for plugin-related latency incidents
1) Detect: Pager triggers when global request.p99 increases > 25% and plugin-tagged requests show disproportionate delta (plugin.delta.p99 > 30ms).
2) Triage: Query telemetry for plugin.latency.p99 (1m,5m,1h) and kernel.sequence-length.post_plugin histogram.
3) Short-lived mitigation (1–10 minutes):
   a) Toggle plugin.fallback_mode to skip for the offending plugin across the fleet (or per-region).
   b) Apply rate-limits to plugin invocations at the gateway: curl -X PATCH https://controlplane/api/plugins/{id}/policy -d '{"max_rps": 10}'
4) Stabilize (10–60 minutes):
   a) If sequence-length growth caused kernel breakpoints, route affected traffic to long-seq-optimized model variants or reserve dedicated kernel slots.
   b) If CPU pressure is root cause, reduce plugin.priority_weight globally by 50% and enable async mode for non-critical classes.
5) Postmortem: Add findings to incident report, update plugin onboarding checklist with discovered failure modes.

Canary and rollout guidance for new ephemeral plugins:
- Local dev: run the plugin in the sandboxed runtime with --sample-rate=1% and collect latency histograms for at least 1000 requests.
- Canary stage: Deploy to 2% of production traffic with full telemetry and automatic abort if plugin.latency.p99 > 2x baseline or error.rate > 1% for 10 minutes.
- Gradual ramp: 2% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100% with manual review at each step.

Example alerting thresholds (suggested):
- Severity: P1 (page oncall): plugin.latency.p99 (5m) > 3x configured max_latency_ms AND plugin.error.rate > 2%
- Severity: P2 (notify team): plugin.latency.p95 (5m) > 2x configured max_latency_ms
- Severity: P3: plugin.error.rate (1h) > 0.5%

Developer onboarding checklist for plugin authors:
1) Declare plugin.class and max_latency_ms in manifest.yaml.
2) Provide a compatibility shim for sequence-length hints when the plugin mutates token counts.
3) Add unit tests that simulate slow external backends and assert fallback behavior.
4) Include telemetry tags: plugin.name, plugin.version, plugin.owner.
5) Run local sandbox suite (>=1k synthetic requests) and upload profiling output to the runtime profiling dashboard.

Operational notes and caveats:
- Quantized kernels may amplify tail effects if plugins introduce additional tokens; always validate plugin behavior with the quantized model variants used in production.
- In-process plugins bypass some OS-level isolation; prefer proxied plugins for untrusted third-party code.
- Priority weights are relative; ensure tenant-level fairness rules are enforced downstream of weight changes to avoid starvation.

Appendix: Example plugin manifest (manifest.yaml)
---
name: redwood-token-augment
version: 0.6.2
owner: team-extensibility
plugin.class: B
max_latency_ms: 50
priority_weight: 80
kv_cache_hint: increases_by_up_to: 32
fallback_mode: skip
---

Appendix: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
- Is the plugin running in-process or proxied? Proxied reduces blast radius.
- Are kernel hints emitted? If not, enable sequence-length-post-plugin sampling.
- Does disabling the plugin reduce tail latency? If yes, follow runbook mitigation and schedule a full regression test.

Related work and references:
- See scheduler policy language and warmstart docs for how priority_weight is translated into kernel slot allocation.
- See runtime telemetry sampling guide for how to collect and store plugin histograms.

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft and internal trial with two customer plugins.
- 2026-02-10: Added automation rules and example manifests after canary evaluation.

payload.page_title: Token-Aware Scheduler: Telemetry, Safety Checks, and Fallback Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents the Token-Aware Scheduler (TAS) telemetry contract, production safety checks, and step-by-step fallback and mitigation procedures used by the serving runtime. TAS is the scheduler layer that considers request token counts, sequence-length distributions, and per-request SLO budgets when assigning kernels and shaping batching windows. The goal of this document is to make the scheduler-to-runtime observable, auditable, and safe for rapid rollouts without surprising regressions in tail latency or model fidelity.

Goals and scope

- Define the telemetry signals required by the scheduler and runtime for token-aware decisions.
- Enumerate deterministic safety checks and thresholds for automatic fallback or throttling.
- Provide an operational runbook for incidents caused by token-shape variability, kernel mismatches, or batching anomalies.
- Give test-and-rollout recipes for canarying TAS versions and new kernel handoff behaviors.
- Scope: applies to hosted and dedicated clusters running v2 scheduler runtime API. Does not prescribe cloud-provider specific autoscaling settings.

Actors and ownership

- Owner (operational): eng-serving-runtime/scheduler-team (engineering)
- Primary oncall: runtime-sre
- Secondary: inference-platform-team
- Reviewer group: perf-eng, observability

Key concepts and definitions

- Request token shape: observed pair {prompt_tokens, completion_budget} used to pick batching window and kernel hints.
- Kernel hint: metadata tag passed to runtime indicating preferred execution variant (float16/quantized/sharded-attn variant).
- Batching window: the time horizon TAS holds requests to form a batch; adaptive to token shape and SLO.
- Fidelity clamp: policy that gracefully reduces model variant (e.g., smaller model or lower precision) to preserve SLOs.

Required telemetry (contract)

All signals must be emitted at request decision time and at kernel completion. These are structured as key/value tags in the trace and as metrics in Prometheus/OTel.

- request.id (string)
- request.arrival_ts (epoch-ms)
- request.token_estimate (int)
- request.completion_budget_tokens (int)
- request.priority_tier (string) — {critical, standard, best_effort}
- scheduler.decision_ts (epoch-ms)
- scheduler.batch_id (string|null)
- scheduler.chosen_batching_window_ms (int)
- scheduler.kernel_hint (string) — e.g., "kv-sharded-ep10-q4",
- scheduler.predicted_latency_ms (int)
- scheduler.predicted_cost_micros (int)
- runtime.kernel_start_ts (epoch-ms)
- runtime.kernel_end_ts (epoch-ms)
- runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate (float)
- runtime.actual_tokens_emitted (int)
- runtime.memory_pressure_level (low|medium|high)
- runtime.fidelity_action (none|quantize|model-fallback|rate-limit)

Metric families (Prometheus)

- tas.request_token_distribution{tenant,model} histogram (buckets by 1,8,32,128,512,2048)
- tas.batch_size{pool,model} gauge
- tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio histogram
- runtime.kernel_handshake_failures counter (labels: reason)
- runtime.fidelity_actions_total counter (labels: action,reason)
- tas.batch_window_ms gauge

Safety thresholds and deterministic rules

The scheduler enforces these safety constraints before committing a request to a batch and emitting the kernel_hint.

1) Kernel compatibility gate
- If runtime reports kernel_handshake_failures > 5 in last 1m for chosen kernel_hint, mark hint as degraded and pick next compatible variant. If no variant available, fallback to model-fallback.

2) Token-window SLO guard
- If scheduler.predicted_latency_ms > SLO_target * 0.9 for the request.priority_tier, reduce batching_window_ms by 50% for the next 30s for that tenant-model pair.

3) Memory-pressure guard
- If runtime.memory_pressure_level==high on the target node, route new requests to alternative pool or trigger fidelity_action: quantize for best_effort only.

4) KV cache instability guard
- If runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate drops >20% vs baseline over 2 minutes, disable long-prefix batching for affected model for 5 minutes.

Fallback and mitigation actions (ordered by severity)

- Soft fallback (no fidelity change): reduce batching_window_ms, increase preemption priority for critical requests, spin up additional execution slots.
- Quantization fallback: switch kernel_hint to a quantized execution path (q4/q8) if the model variant has been validated for the tenant. Label action in telemetry: fidelity_action=quantize.
- Model fallback: route to a smaller/compatible model variant. Must attach a quality-warning header to downstream callers for auditing.
- Rate-limit fallback: for best_effort tier only, apply 429 with retry-after and emit runtime.fidelity_action=rate-limit.

Runbook: Incident response for elevated tail latency attributed to token-shaped bursts

Initial detection
1) Alert threshold: tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio > 1.4 for p99 over 5m for a tenant.
2) Pager triggers to runtime-sre oncall.

Triage steps (oncall)
1) Pull recent traces for sample request.id showing predicted latency and actual kernel durations.
2) Check scheduler.batch_window_ms and tas.batch_size trends.
3) Query runtime.memory_pressure_level and kernel_handshake_failures for 10m window.
4) If kv_cache_hit_rate dropped: identify whether a model rollout or cache eviction happened.

Immediate mitigations
1) If kernel_handshake_failures > 5: temporarily blacklist faulty kernel_hint (CLI below) and restart canary kernel pool.
2) If memory_pressure_level==high: trigger eviction policy, and if unavoidable, set tenant policy to quantize for next 10m.
3) If batch_window_ms is large and predicted latency is underestimated: reduce batch_window_ms by 40% for affected tenant-model via dynamic policy API.

CLI commands and examples

- Blacklist kernel hint (safely):
  rdsctl scheduler blacklist-kernel --kernel "kv-sharded-ep10-q4" --reason "handshake-failures" --duration 10m

- Set tenant-model dynamic policy (reduce batching):
  rdsctl scheduler set-policy --tenant acme-corp --model t-rxl-3b --batch-window-ms 25 --reason "tail-latency-mitigation"

- Force quantized fallback for best_effort:
  rdsctl runtime set-fidelity --tenant acme-corp --model t-rxl-3b --action quantize --duration 15m

Validation checklist (post-mitigation)

- Confirm tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio returns <1.1 at p99 for 10m window.
- Confirm runtime.fidelity_actions_total increments are expected and labeled properly.
- Run 1000 synthetic requests matching the original token shape via loadsculptor and compare responses for quality regressions (automated evaluation harness).
- Confirm related customer-facing routes show no 5xx spikes.

Canary and rollout recipe for new TAS kernel handoff behavior

1) Unit + integration tests: scheduler decision simulator with synthesized token-shaped workloads.
2) Private canary: enable on 1% of traffic with strict shadow tracing enabled (emit scheduler.* telemetry but route to stable path).
3) Observability gates for promotion (all must pass):
   - p99 latency difference <+5% vs baseline
   - kernel_handshake_failures == 0 sustained for 60 minutes
   - fidelity_action model-fallback count == 0
4) Progressive rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows and auto-rollback on gate failure.

Testing guidance and bench harness

- Use load profiles that mirror long-tail token shapes: create corpora with 1%, 5%, 20%, 50% tails at 512+ tokens.
- Run A/B fidelity checks using our eval harness repository: refer to related_pages below.
- Synthetic chaos: inject kernel handshake failures and KV cache eviction events while running the bench to validate deterministic fallbacks.

Operational notes and best practices

- Prefer proactive KV cache warming for models with long-prefix reuse; TAS will prefer longer batching windows only after hit rate >70%.
- Annotate model variants with compatibility matrix: kernel capabilities, max_sequence_length, quantization validated flags.
- Maintain an "execution-compatibility" manifest per model in the model-onboarding catalog so TAS can enumerate fallbacks deterministically.

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026

Appendix: quick policy YAML example

policies:
  - tenant: "acme-corp"
    model: "t-rxl-3b"
    batch_window_ms: 40
    kernel_hints_priority:
      - "kv-sharded-ep10-q4"
      - "kv-sharded-ep10-fp16"
    emergency_fallbacks:
      - action: "quantize"
        allowed_for_tiers: ["best_effort"]
      - action: "model-fallback"
        allowed_for_tiers: ["standard","best_effort"]

Contact and escalation

- Oncall: runtime-sre Slack (#runtime-oncall)
- Pager duty: runtime-sre primary
- Engineering owners: scheduler-team@redwood.com

Document history

- 2027-11-15: Created by Aisha Park
- 2027-12-10: Added canary recipe and metric gates (reviewers: Diego Marquez)
- 2028-01-22: Updated telemetry contract with new kernel_handshake_failures counter (reviewers: Evelyn Chen)

payload.page_title: Sharded Attention Execution Guidelines

sections.body: This guide describes recommended execution patterns, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling steps, benchmark integration notes, and operational runbook actions for sharded-attention execution in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for engineers who implement or tune shard-aware kernels, SREs triaging performance regressions, and platform owners running the benchmarking suite.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a compact, actionable checklist to achieve predictable latency and throughput for sharded attention workloads.
- Describe scheduling primitives and policy knobs the runtime exposes and when to use them.
- Outline profiling and benchmark procedures that produce reproducible performance artifacts.
- Document triage/runbook steps for common regressions and known mitigations.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: Sharded attention (tensor-parallel splits across KV shards) is used for large-decoder models and some encoder-decoder variants to scale state and computation. In our fleet, sharded attention adds interaction points with: GPU memory placement, KV cache routing, communication schedules (all-reduce / reduce-scatter), and kernel selection (FP16 vs int8 mixed paths). Mistuned scheduling or batching can produce amplified tail latency and cross-request interference.
sections.heading: Context and background

sections.body:
- Logical components:
  - Request router: assigns incoming requests to shard groups based on model-version and shard topology.
  - Execution orchestrator: slices requests into micro-batches for compute kernels and coordinates cross-shard comms.
  - Kernel mapper: selects kernel variant based on seq_len distribution, quantization profile, and available comm topology.
  - KV cache manager: handles prefix cache hits, partial cache reuse and eviction across shards.

- Dataflow sketch:
  1) Request arrives -> route to shard-group leader
  2) Orchestrator computes micro-batch plan (batch size, slice offsets)
  3) KV indices resolved; cross-shard comm plan computed
  4) Kernels invoked on each shard with coordinated comm primitives
sections.heading: Architecture overview (high level)

sections.body:
- Priority lanes: per-tenant/per-route numeric priority (0..7). Use lanes to isolate high-SLO customers from best-effort workloads.
- Deadline-aware slicing: requests with tight latency budgets can be sliced into smaller micro-batches that avoid queueing behind large batches. Config knob: scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled (boolean) and scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices (int).
- Backpressure thresholds: two soft thresholds (queue_soft_ms, queue_hard_ms). If queue latency exceeds queue_soft_ms the scheduler reduces auto-batched slice sizes by 25% until below threshold. If queue_hard_ms is exceeded the request is re-routed to fallback model variant.
- Affinity constraints: pin hot shard leaders to NIC/GPU pairs to reduce cross-host comm overhead for latency-sensitive flows. affinity.policy can be set to host-local | spread | packed.
sections.heading: Key scheduling primitives and policies

sections.body:
- Inputs considered: seq_len distribution (p50/p95/p99), effective micro-batch size, quantization profile, active comm topology.
- Heuristic examples:
  - If p95_seq_len < 64 and micro-batch >= 8 -> choose fused-attention-kernel-v2 for stable throughput.
  - If quant_profile == int8 and there are frequent prefix-cache-hits -> prefer int8-kernel-with-cache-optimized-path to reduce decode overhead.
  - If all-reduce latency > 120us -> choose locality-optimized kernels that favor reduce-scatter + overlap-compute.
sections.heading: Kernel selection heuristics (how mapper picks kernels)

sections.body:
1) Reproduce on staging with the same model-version and shard-topology. Record the exact git commit / runtime image.
2) Capture end-to-end traces for 5k requests across representative traffic: use agent tracing (trace level = debug) and kernel-level telemetry. Commands:
   - rwinfctl trace start --model my-model:2026-02-01 --duration 10m --level debug --out /tmp/trace-$(date +%s).zip
   - nvprof (for local reproduce) or perf on host; capture GPU kernel timelines.
3) Produce flamegraphs for the orchestrator and per-GPU kernel timelines. Tools and scripts: scripts/perf/trace_to_flame.sh /tmp/trace.zip > /tmp/flame.svg
4) Validate comm microbench: run inter-shard all-reduce ping-pairs to measure baseline latency (expected < 80us in colocated racks).
5) Compare metric deltas vs baseline: p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, GPU occupancy, SM utilization, PCIe bandwidth.
6) Run focused microbench with synthetic seq_len slices to isolate kernel selection boundaries. Use the benchmarking harness:
   - benchctl run --workload sharded-attn-sweep --model my-model --seq-lens 8,32,128 --micro-batch-sizes 1,4,8 --out ./bench-results.json
7) If kernel hotpath spans >20% of observed latency and comms are under budget, open a kernel ticket and include reproducible microbench steps (see "Ownership and escalation").
sections.heading: Profiling and investigation playbook (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Canonical workloads: sharded-attn-sweep (sweeps seq lens and micro-batches), long-prefix (emulates long prefix reuse), mixed-traffic (production mix weighted by route).
- Metrics to publish per run (JSON fields required): run_id, model_version, shard_topology, seq_len_p50/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec_mean, tail_latency_ms_p99, gpu_utilization_mean, comm_latency_us_mean.
- Acceptance criteria for a candidate kernel change: tokens_per_sec >= baseline * 1.02 OR tail_latency_p99 <= baseline * 0.98, with no increase in memory-footprint > 5%.
- Artifact retention: keep raw traces and kernel timelines for at least 90 days for any benchmark that triggers a perf regression alert.
sections.heading: Benchmarking suite notes (integration and expectations)

sections.body:
Incident: sudden p99 spike for sharded models across a rack
  1) Check scheduler queue depth and queue_soft_ms/queue_hard_ms events in the last 30 minutes.
  2) Validate inter-shard all-reduce latency from telemetry. If > 150us, escalate to networking and check NIC interrupts/traffic shaping.
  3) If comms healthy, inspect kernel selection logs for unexpected switch to slow kernel variant (kernel_mapper.log).
  4) Hot mitigation: enable priority lane for affected routes (rwctl route update <route> --priority 1) and reduce batch windows for that node group (set scheduler.batch_window_ms = 3).
  5) If mitigation fails, failover affected routes to fallback model variant with local (non-sharded) execution: route->fallback:model:local-encoder-compat.

Incident: long running fragmentation / OOMs on shard GPUs
  1) Run host-diagnostics to capture GPU memory fragmentation metrics.
  2) If fragmentation ratio > 0.65, schedule a rolling drain of the host, trigger unified-allocator defrag (adminctl allocator defrag --target gpu0).
  3) If OOM persists, reduce per-shard KV cache retention for that model (kvcache.retention_ms = 600000).

Known issues and current mitigations (as of runtime v3.4.x):
- Issue: intermittent 10–20% p99 degradation when sequence-length distribution shifts suddenly toward long prefixes.
  - Mitigation: enable adaptive_kernel_mapper.seq_len_smoothing to avoid thrashing kernel selection.
- Issue: all-reduce tail latency anomalies correlated with kernel preemption on mixed workloads.
  - Mitigation: set affinity.policy=packed for latency-critical routes and move large-batch offline traffic to dedicated nodes.
- Issue: int8 cache-path regressions when cache eviction patterns align with quantized tile boundaries.
  - Mitigation: use fallback quantization profile int8-stable for models with >10% prefix reuse until kernel patch is released.

Release notes snapshot (runtime v3.4.2):
- Improved locality-optimized kernels for 8x shard topologies; expected comm latency reduction ~18% for colocated racks.
- Added deadline_slicing scheduler knob and two new telemetry counters: scheduler.slice_count and scheduler.slice_drop_rate.
- Fixed memory leak in fused-attention-kernel-v1 when micro-batch size == 1.
sections.heading: Operational runbook snippets (common incidents)

sections.body:
- Kernel mapper and scheduling primitives: Runtime Core team (team lead: Miguel Santos).
- Benchmarks and profiling harness: Bench Team (owner: Sofia Ramos).
- SRE operational playbooks: Platform Reliability (lead: Liam O'Connor).
- Escalation path: On-call runtime engineer -> Runtime Core -> Networking -> Kernel dev. Use the incident-runbook channel for urgent comms.
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:
1) Implement kernel and add feature flag kernel.<name>.enabled=false by default.
2) Add unit-level microbench in bench/harness (sharded-attn-sweep).
3) Run full benchmark matrix on staging and publish artifacts to /bench-artifacts/<run_id>.
4) Open a PR with documentation entry in this guide and a migration note for operators.
5) Iterate on heuristics and land default enablement only after 2 successful benchmark runs with artifacts reviewed by Bench Team.
sections.heading: Adding a new kernel variant (developer checklist)

sections.body:
- Kernel mapper design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026
- Shard topology reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024
- Benchmarking harness README: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026

Appendix: Quick config table (YAML-like example)
| key | example value | description |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled | true | enable slicing for tight-latency routes |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices | 6 | max micro-slices per request |
| scheduler.batch_window_ms | 6 | how long to wait for auto-batching (ms) |
| affinity.policy | host-local | affinity placement policy (host-local|spread|packed) |
| kvcache.retention_ms | 600000 | default per-model KV cache retention |

If you make changes to this doc, update the related_pages list and add the bench run_id that validates the change.
sections.heading: References and links

payload.page_title: Tenant-aware Kernel Ladder: Architecture, Profiling, and Runbook

sections.body: This handbook documents the tenant-aware kernel ladder: a runtime subsystem that adaptively promotes and demotes kernel configurations per-tenant to meet latency SLOs while optimizing GPU utilization and cost. It combines architecture rationale, kernel scheduling rules, profiling playbook, benchmarking plan, rollout checklist, and an incident runbook.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, on-call, and performance engineers.
- Scope: design and operational procedure for the kernel ladder (promotion/demotion, telemetry signals, safety guards, and rollback).
- Non-goals: hardware provisioning, global autoscaler policies, and model architecture changes.

1) High-level design
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
- Kernel ladder is a discrete set of kernel profiles (K0..K4) that trade throughput/cost for worst-case latency. Each profile is a precompiled kernel bundle + scheduler hints (batch slice size, preemption score, qcache warmup).
- Per-tenant control plane maps tenant -> ladder policy. Policy attributes: base_profile, min_profile, max_profile, promotion_cooldown_s, demotion_cooldown_s, telemetry_weights.
- Runtime components:
  - Ladder controller (per-node): watches incoming telemetry and per-tenant session state, emits profile-change intents.
  - Kernel activation agent (per-GPU): applies profile bundles and issues kernel handshake; ensures safe rollback if activation fails.
  - Quota crediter: ensures profile changes respect slot accounting and kernel credits.
  - Telemetry exporter: publishes promotion/demotion events and rationale to metrics and traces.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Request -> Request-classifier -> Tenant policy lookup -> Ladder controller -> Kernel activation agent -> GPU dispatcher -> Kernel execution -> Telemetry sink

2) Policy model and scheduling rules
sections.heading: Architecture diagram (text)

sections.body:
| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| base_profile | string | default kernel profile for tenant | K1 |
| min_profile | string | lower bound allowed | K0 |
| max_profile | string | upper bound allowed | K3 |
| promotion_metric | string | telemetry metric used for upshift | tail_latency_99ms |
| promotion_threshold | string | threshold to trigger promotion | 150ms |
| demotion_metric | string | metric used for downshift | avg_tokens_per_second |
| promotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between promotions | 60 |
| demotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between demotions | 300 |
sections.heading: Policy fields (table)

sections.body:
- Prefer non-disruptive profile changes: when possible, move only new allocations to the higher profile and let existing sessions finish (soft promotion).
- Hard promotion: if tail latency > promotion_threshold for 3 consecutive 1-min windows, force immediate kernel swap for hot sessions with warm-up prefetch.
- Demotion: only demote when sustained over a 10-minute window and GPU utilization headroom > 25%.
- Safety: at most 20% of a node's kernels can be in an experimental (K4) profile concurrently.

3) Telemetry & SLOs
Canonical metrics (exported to metrics namespace rwd.runtime.ladder):
- tenant.tail_latency_99_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.avg_latency_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.token_throughput_tps (gauge)
- node.gpu_utilization_pct (gauge)
- ladder.promotion_events_total (counter)
- ladder.failed_activations_total (counter)
sections.heading: Scheduling rules (short)

sections.body:
- Enterprise interactive: p99 latency <= 180ms for requests <= 256 tokens, availability >= 99.95%.
- Standard API customers: p99 latency <= 300ms, availability >= 99.9%.
- Background batch: p99 latency <= 2s, availability >= 99.5%.
sections.heading: SLO guidance (example tenant class)

sections.body:
- Pager (SEV2): tenant.tail_latency_99_ms > 250ms sustained for 5m AND ladder.promotion_events_total increased by > 30% in 10m.
- Ops (SEV3): ladder.failed_activations_total > 5 in 10m on a single node.

4) Profiling playbook (how to collect targeted signals)
Objective: gather representative traces and microprofiles to decide ladder step definitions and promotion thresholds.
sections.heading: Alert thresholds (examples)

sections.body:
1. Identify representative tenants: choose 3 tenants per SLA class (interactive, standard, batch).
2. Use sampled tracing at 1% of requests for 24h with request context "ladder-prof"; capture kernel dispatch timings, batch shapes, KV cache hit ratio, and prefetch latencies.
3. Run microbenchmarks on candidate kernel bundles: run 10k synthetic short requests (32–64 tokens) and long requests (512 tokens) across K0..K4. Collect p50/p95/p99 and memory working set.
4. Create a ladder-definition artifact (YAML) for each tenant class. Example:

---
tenant_class: interactive
ladder_steps:
  - id: K0
    description: minimal-latency (low-batch, high-priority, small kernels)
    expected_p99_ms: 120
    cost_factor: 1.8
  - id: K1
    description: balanced
    expected_p99_ms: 160
    cost_factor: 1.0
  - id: K2
    description: throughput-optimized
    expected_p99_ms: 260
    cost_factor: 0.6
---

5. Validate ladder offline using the workload replay harness in benchmarking suite (see section 5).

5) Benchmarking plan and acceptance criteria
- Bench harness: use the operational-workload-simulator with recorded traces. For each ladder candidate, measure: node throughput, tail latency, GPU idling, kernel switching time, and cost-per-token estimate.
- Acceptance criteria (release gating):
  - p99 latency improvement for promoted tenants >= 25% vs base_profile under matched load, AND
  - Cost uplift per-token <= 40% for interactive tenants (for enterprise customers with higher SLOs), OR
  - No more than 5% increase in node-level tail latency for mixed-tenant workloads.

6) Release & rollout checklist
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- Generate ladder YAML artifacts and commit to repo rwd/ladder-defs.
- Run full bench harness and attach results to release ticket.
- Code review and canary gate: enable ladder in canary region with traffic fraction 0.5% for 2 hours.
sections.heading: Pre-flight

sections.body:
1. 0.5% traffic - 2h - check metrics and failed_activations_total.
2. 2% traffic - 4h - validate p99 and GPU utilization headroom.
3. 10% traffic - 6h - watch cross-tenant tail latencies.
4. 50% traffic - 24h - if stable, escalate to 100%.
sections.heading: Gradual rollout

sections.body:
- Any single-node ladder.failed_activations_total > 10 in 5m -> immediate rollback of ladder on that node.
- Cross-tenant node p99 latency regressions > 15% sustained for 15m -> rollback to previous kernel bundle set.

7) Operational runbook (on-call playbook for SEV2/SEV3)
When triggered: detect via alert or manual observation.
A. Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
1. Check ladder.failed_activations_total and node.gpu_utilization_pct graphs.
2. Identify affected tenants and node(s) via trace ids and metrics.
3. If failed_activations_total spikes on a node: ssh to node and inspect /var/log/rwd/kernel-activation.log for handshake errors; run `rwdctl kernel status --node $NODE`.

B. Mitigation steps (10-30 minutes):
1. Soft demote affected tenant(s): `rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K1 --mode soft`.
2. If kernel activation handshake fails repeatedly, drain node from scheduler and trigger a rolling restart of kernel agent: `rwdctl node cordon $NODE && rwdctl agent restart kernel-agent --node $NODE`.
3. If cross-tenant p99 regressions: temporarily enable global conservative policy: `rwdctl ladder set-global --max_profile K1` (admin only).

C. Post-incident actions (30m+):
1. Collect the following artifacts and attach to incident ticket: kernel-activation.log, last 30m of ladder telemetry, sample traces (ladder-prof), bench-run summary.
2. Open a performance regression ticket if ladder caused regressions, assign to kernel-scheduling team.

8) Known limitations and issues
- Kernel activation latency: some legacy kernels require a cold handshake that can take 120–250ms. Workaround: prefer soft promotions and warm-prefetch for affected models.
- Cache-skew edge-case: per-tenant promotions may create KV cache fragmentation; mitigation: periodic KV compaction job (daily) and prefetch heuristics.
- Rollout oscillation: naive promotion/demotion based solely on p99 can oscillate. The ladder uses cooldown windows and hysteresis, but complex multi-tenant bursts may still cause flapping. Future fix: add predictive smoothing using short-term AR models.
sections.heading: Rollback criteria (automated)

sections.body:
| id | symptom | workaround | owner |
| KLD-101 | failed kernel handshake on A100p 2.0 nodes | cordon node and restart kernel-agent | kernel-scheduling team |
| KLD-112 | tenant p99 spike after hard promotion | revert tenant to previous profile and soft-warm | SRE/perf |
| KLD-117 | KV cache fragmentation for >1000 active tenants | run kv-compact and limit concurrent promotions | runtime-infra |

9) Postmortem and metrics to track after rollout
- Reduction in tenant-tail-p99 per SLA class
- ladder.promotion_events_total/k (normalized) vs failed_activations_total
- Node-level avg GPU-ptime (time kernels are active) and idle fraction
- Cost per token estimates before/after ladder

10) Ownership, contacts and escalation
- Primary maintainers: kernel-scheduling (team alias: team-kernel-sched@redwood.com)
- On-call rotation: kernel-scheduling SRE and runtime-platform SRE (see oncall roster link: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-roster)
- Pager escalation: SEV2 -> oncall SRE, then engineering manager.
sections.heading: Known issues table (brief)

sections.body:
- rwd/ladder-defs repository (internal)
- Benchmark runs: /artifacts/bench/ladders/2026-01 (links attached to release ticket)
- Related pages: predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration-2026, delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
- Check a tenant's current profile:
  rwdctl ladder get --tenant $TID
- Force soft promotion for debugging:
  rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K2 --mode soft --reason "debug/latency-test"
- Dump last activation logs for node:
  sudo journalctl -u rwd-kernel-activation -n 500 | tee ~/activation-tail.log
sections.heading: References and artifacts

sections.body:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Ava Martinez).
- 2026-02-10: Add acceptance gating criteria and bench harness steps (Daniel Cho).
- 2026-03-02: Update rollout steps and rollback automation triggers (Marcus Flynn).
