payload.page_title: Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack (H100/B200/L40S) — Project Overview

sections.body:
Redwood Inference will deliver a **hardware tuning profiles pack** for the serving runtime focused on **kernel + scheduler performance** across the current and near-future NVIDIA fleet: **H100, B200, L40S**.

The pack consists of **curated, versioned runtime configuration profiles** that are:
- **Safe-by-default** (guardrails, compatibility checks, sane fallbacks)
- **Measurable** (benchmarked against a workload matrix with tracked deltas)
- **Operationally rollout-friendly** (canaries, regression gates, rollback semantics)
- **Consistent across deployment modes** (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)

This page defines the project goals, non-goals, target SKUs, success metrics, ownership, and the milestone plan.

---
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
As our model catalog expands and fleet heterogeneity increases, performance issues increasingly come from **serving configuration mismatch** rather than model quality. Today, “best settings” are often:
- discovered ad-hoc,
- embedded in code defaults,
- inconsistently applied across pools/regions,
- and hard to rollback when they regress tail latency.

This pack operationalizes “Redwood-verified performance profiles” as a repeatable, versioned artifact.

---
sections.heading: Why we’re doing this

sections.body:
1) **Ship a versioned profile pack** for H100, L40S (GA) and B200 (experimental/gated) with clear intended workload envelopes.
2) Provide a **profile schema + loader** that supports:
   - hardware detection and normalization (SKU string variance),
   - explicit compatibility with runtime releases,
   - a deterministic override/precedence order,
   - and validation/guardrails (reject unsafe combos; fallback safely).
3) Improve production economics while protecting user experience:
   - raise tokens/sec and reduce cost per 1M tokens,
   - maintain or improve p50 latency,
   - and cap p95 regressions via guardrails + canary gates.
4) Make changes **easy to observe and debug**:
   - expose selected profile + override source in metrics/logs,
   - provide a “dump effective config” mechanism for oncall and Support.
5) Establish a **benchmark and regression framework**:
   - representative workload matrix,
   - standardized reporting artifacts,
   - pre-merge and post-deploy perf-canary gates.

---
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Writing entirely **new kernels** from scratch (we tune selection and toggles; we don’t build net-new kernel families in this initiative).
- Major public API changes to Redwood API/SDKs.
- Customer-by-customer bespoke tuning as part of the pack release (handled via Solutions/Support follow-ups; the pack is for standard supported presets).
- Guaranteeing contractual performance/SLO improvements (docs will describe **expected behavior** and known trade-offs, not guarantees).

---
sections.heading: Non-goals (initial release)

sections.body: We are targeting the following NVIDIA SKUs across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Profiles must account for common fleet variance (HBM size, PCIe vs SXM, clocks, MIG/partitioning, multi-GPU nodes).
sections.heading: Target hardware SKUs

sections.body:
- Primary production workhorse for latency-sensitive + throughput workloads.
- Profile family: **balanced** default + optional throughput-first mode (guardrailed).
sections.heading: H100 (GA)

sections.body:
- Cost-sensitive workloads; more stringent memory constraints.
- Profile emphasizes KV cache budgeting, OOM prevention, and stable batching.
sections.heading: L40S (GA)

sections.body:
- Early enablement with limited fleet access.
- Profile is gated behind an explicit feature flag and strict stack/version checks.
- Must include a clear fallback plan (H100-compatible behavior where applicable, or “disable profile” to runtime defaults).

---
sections.heading: B200 (Experimental, gated)

sections.body:
Profiles are allowed to set knobs in these categories (final supported keys are defined in the schema doc):

1) **Kernel selection + execution toggles**
- Sequence-length bucket heuristics
- Attention/kernel selection toggles
- Quantization-friendly execution path toggles (when compatible)

2) **Scheduling + batching presets**
- Continuous batching settings
- Prefill vs decode fairness and backpressure
- Queue limits and admission control
- Streaming vs non-streaming handling (where runtime supports separate policies)

3) **Memory + KV cache behavior**
- KV cache budgeting and caps
- Fragmentation-aware behavior (where available)
- Safe defaults for long-context workload buckets

4) **Collectives / NCCL / multi-GPU (where applicable)**
- Conservative tuning only; must be safe across topology variance

5) **CPU-side runtime settings**
- Threading/concurrency settings that materially affect scheduling and end-to-end latency

---
sections.heading: Scope: what a profile can tune

sections.body: We measure success via benchmark deltas on the workload matrix and production signals during canary rollouts.
sections.heading: Success metrics

sections.body:
| Metric | How it’s measured | Success target (pack v1) |
|---|---|---|
| **Throughput (tokens/sec)** | per model + workload bucket; steady-state | +5–15% in targeted buckets, with explicit notes where neutral |
| **Latency p50** | end-to-end request latency; streaming includes TTFT + per-token | No regression in p50; ideally modest improvement in high-concurrency |
| **Latency p95** | end-to-end tail latency | Guardrails: p95 should not regress >3–5% in “balanced” profiles; throughput-first may allow limited regression with explicit labeling |
| **Cost per 1M tokens** | GPU-time-derived unit cost proxy (bench) + production allocation | Downward trend proportional to throughput gains; documented per SKU |
sections.heading: Primary metrics (bench + canary)

sections.body:
- OOM / allocation failure rate (must not increase; L40S specifically must improve under long-context workloads)
- Retry rate / fallbacks triggered (should remain stable; increased fallbacks indicate unsafe tuning)
- Error budget consumption during canary pools
- Profile selection correctness (rate of “unknown SKU” and fallback-to-default)
- Config drift: “effective config” should match expected profile + overrides
sections.heading: Secondary metrics (safety + operability)

sections.body:
- Profiles are versioned and shipped per the distribution ADR.
- Schema validation prevents invalid/unsafe configs from starting.
- Perf-canary gates exist for each SKU profile with noise-reduced thresholds.
- Rollout runbook is complete and has been exercised at least once in a controlled canary.
- Expected-behavior docs are published for H100/L40S and experimental guidance for B200.

---
sections.heading: “Definition of done” for the pack

sections.body:
- **Program lead:** Talia Benson
- **Executive sponsor (Runtime):** Mateo Alvarez
sections.heading: Program and executive sponsorship

sections.body:
- **Kernel tuning:** Hiro Tanaka (lead), Grace Kim, Yuki Sato, Isabella Rossi
- **Scheduling/batching:** Sofia Ivanova (lead), Lena Fischer, Marcus Reed
- **Runtime architecture / regression strategy:** Noah Patel
- **KV cache / memory behavior:** Omar El-Sayed, Samir Qureshi
- **Schema + guardrails:** Ethan Park
- **Loader + rollout primitives:** Benji Okafor, Diego Santos, Quentin Harris
sections.heading: Engineering owners

sections.body:
- **Benchmark methodology:** Claire Dubois
- **Benchmark harness:** Rina Kobayashi
- **Perf regression detection tooling:** Kira Volkov
- **Infra/fleet rollout sponsor:** Irene Choi; with Vanessa Ortiz, Keiko Yamamoto, Nina Petrova
- **SRE sponsor:** Neha Kapoor; rollout + oncall coordination via Sean Gallagher
- **Dashboards / canary gates:** Aisha Bello, Allison Grant
sections.heading: Perf + infra + reliability

sections.body:
- **Applied ML sponsor:** Dr. Maya Srinivasan
- Reviewers: Arjun Desai, Jonas Weber

---
sections.heading: Applied ML review

sections.body:
Dates are illustrative and shift with fleet access (especially for B200).

1) **Kickoff + requirements (Week 1)**
- Confirm target SKUs and known fleet variance.
- Define “safe-by-default” constraints and acceptance metrics.
- Align on doc language: “expected behavior” vs guarantees.

2) **Baselines (Weeks 1–2)**
- Lock benchmark suite inputs and workload matrix.
- Collect baseline curves per GPU SKU (and key instance variants where relevant).

3) **Schema + implementation (Weeks 2–5)**
- Profile schema, inheritance/versioning, and validation.
- Loader + hardware detection and normalization.
- Implement initial presets and safe fallback behavior.

4) **Validation + staged canary rollout (Weeks 5–8)**
- Add/adjust perf-canary gates; reduce flake/noise.
- Stage rollout by region/pool; observe production metrics.
- Triage regressions; add targeted fixes and regression tests.

5) **Documentation + release (Weeks 7–10)**
- Publish reference pages per SKU: knobs, deltas, workload envelope, trade-offs.
- Ship rollout runbook and oncall playbook; training for SRE/CS.
- Release checklist and sign-offs.

---
sections.heading: Milestone plan (8–10 weeks)

sections.body:
All rollouts must be reversible quickly at the pool/region level.

1) **Pre-merge gates**
- Microbench sanity checks (kernel selection changes)
- Workload-matrix subset for fast signal
- Schema/override precedence integration tests

2) **Post-deploy canaries**
- Enable profile pack in a small canary pool per SKU
- Monitor latency (p50/p95), throughput, errors, OOMs
- Require dashboards to segment by selected profile + override source

3) **Staged expansion**
- Expand by region/pool tiers
- Avoid simultaneous multi-SKU changes unless explicitly approved

4) **Rollback semantics**
- Disable the profile at the pool/region level (revert to runtime defaults or previous profile version)
- For B200, keep the profile gated (opt-in) until stability is proven

(Operational steps and thresholds live in the rollout runbook.)

---
sections.heading: Rollout strategy (high level)

sections.body:
1) **Tail latency regressions from throughput tuning**
- Mitigation: balanced vs throughput-first modes; explicit guardrails; p95 canary gates; fairness/backpressure limits.

2) **Hardware variance (HBM size, PCIe/SXM, MIG, multi-GPU)**
- Mitigation: conservative defaults; detection normalization; compatibility rules; safe fallback when detection is ambiguous.

3) **B200 limited access + evolving stack requirements**
- Mitigation: experimental gating; strict driver/CUDA checks; pool-scoped enablement; explicit disable plan.

4) **Perf-canary noise/flakiness**
- Mitigation: runner stability work, robust aggregation, threshold tuning, and “investigate” vs “block” severity tiers.

5) **Config drift between runtime defaults and profile pack**
- Mitigation: normalize defaults; log effective config; enforce precedence tests; document override order.

---
sections.heading: Key risks and mitigations

sections.body:
- Canonical design docs:
  - Profile schema and compatibility rules
  - Distribution + override-order ADR
- Operational docs:
  - Rollout runbook
  - Perf-canary gates and dashboards
  - Known issues and mitigations
- Per-SKU reference:
  - H100 tuned profile reference
  - L40S tuned profile reference
  - B200 tuned profile reference (experimental)

For questions or changes to scope/targets, contact **Talia Benson** (program), **Hiro Tanaka** (kernels), or **Sofia Ivanova** (scheduling).
sections.heading: Communication + where to look

payload.page_title: Model-aware Request Shaper — Design and Operations

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the design, operational procedures, and observability requirements for the Model-aware Request Shaper (MARS): a cross-layer runtime component that adapts admission, batching, and kernel hints based on the target model variant, request class, and active fidelity constraints.

MARS is intended to reduce SLA violations and improve unit cost by making shaping decisions informed by model characteristics (sequence length distribution, KV cache friendliness, quantization profile) rather than treating all requests uniformly. This page covers: design goals, architecture diagrams, scheduler interactions, telemetry and profiling playbook, benchmark procedure, rollout checklist, runbook for common incidents, configuration reference, and ownership.

Goals and non-goals
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Reduce 95th/99th token-latency SLO violations for multi-model fleets by coordinating batching and kernel selection per model variant.
- Preserve strict fairness across tenants while enabling cost-aware prioritization for Reserved/Dedicated pools.
- Provide actionable telemetry and knobs for on-call and SRE to react to model-specific regressions quickly.
- Allow per-customer/model feature flags (prefetching, aggressive batching, relaxed latency window) and safe fallbacks.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- MARS does not replace global admission controllers that enforce account-level rate limits; it augments them with model-aware signals.
- MARS does not attempt to change model weights or quantization at runtime; it surfaces suggestions to the Optimize team only.

High-level architecture

(ASCII diagram)

Client -> API Gateway -> Router -> MARS -> Admission Controller -> Scheduler -> Kernel Executor
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Model Hint Registry: Stores per-model metadata (expected token distribution, hot prefix likelihood, kv-cache sensitivity, preferred kernel families). Populated from model-onboarding pipeline and updated by profiling jobs.
- Request Classifier: Lightweight classifier that attaches a request signature (model_id, prompt-length-bucket, customer-tier, op_type) to each request. Runs in the front-line router.
- Shaping Policy Engine (MARS Core): Evaluates policies to decide shaping actions: permit/queue/reject, batch slicing keys, kernel hints, kv-prefetch directives, and expected tail-fallthrough rules. Uses declarative policy profiles authored by scheduler team.
- Telemetry Enricher: Adds model-aware fields to traces and metrics (model.variant, hint_version, predicted_sequence_bucket, chosen_kernel_hint).
- Feedback Loop: Periodic job that reconcilies actual latency/cost vs predicted and updates Model Hint Registry (signal back to Profiling Playbooks).

Policy model and examples

Policies are expressed in our scheduler policy DSL (see scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles) and are composed of conditions and actions. Example policies (pseudo-DSL):

1) Low-latency small prompt policy:
when model.family == "redwood-compat-tiny" and prompt_bucket in [0-64]:
  - set kernel_hint = "fast-small-ctx"
  - max_batch_size = 16
  - admission_priority = "interactive"

2) Cost-sensitive long-seq policy for batch windows:
when model.quant_profile == "int4" and median_length > 256:
  - enable_kv_prefetch(true)
  - set_kernel_hint = "concat-friendly"
  - target_batch_latency_ms = 120
  - admission_priority = "best-effort"

Scheduler interactions and kernel handshake

MARS communicates intent to the scheduler and kernel executor via:
- Kernel hint header: structured token the scheduler maps to kernel families (sharded vs fused attention, prepacked weights).
- Batch-slice key: chosen to optimize packing (e.g., same prompt_bucket + kv-cache affinity).
- Preferred prefetch directive: instruct kernel to pre-issue KV cache lookups or to use lazy prefetch.

The scheduler must validate kernel hints against the current kernel compatibility matrix. If a hint is incompatible with the node (e.g., missing kernel plugin), the scheduler will either map to a nearest compatible hint or follow the MARS-declared fallback priority list.

KV cache coordination

MARS can request coordinated KV prefetch windows for long-running sessions. Coordination rules:
- Prefetch is gated by per-node memory watermarks (see config table below).
- Prefetch concurrent limit default: 4 per-GPU.
- When prefetch window is enabled, MARS will mark the request as heavy; admission priority may be lowered unless the customer tier is Reserved.

Telemetry and profiling playbook (operational)

Purpose: ensure model-aware shaping decisions are observable and profile their impact on latency, cost, and fidelity.

1) Enrichment fields (required):
- model.id, model.variant
- request.predicted_seq_bucket (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024)
- kernel_hint, hint_version
- batch_slice_id, batch_size_actual
- kv_prefetch_enabled (bool), kv_prefetch_duration_ms
- scheduling_latency_ms, kernel_enqueue_ms, kernel_exec_ms

2) Key dashboards and alerts:
- Model-level SLO rollup: 95th/99th token-latency per model.variant. Alert if 95th > SLO*1.1 for 5m.
- Hint-compatibility mismatch: rate of rejected/translated kernel hints > 0.5% over 10m.
- Prefetch OOM signal: memory.watermark_eviction_count > 0 in window. Critical alert.
- Batch-slice starvation: fraction of requests assigned to native batch < 90% for an active model.

3) Profiling procedure (when suspect model-level regression):
- Step 1: mirror 1% of production traffic for the target model into the profiling cluster (shadow-run) with same MARS policy.
- Step 2: collect 1,000 representative requests per prompt_bucket for 30 minutes.
- Step 3: run kernel-level microbenchmarks for the exact kernel_hint variants observed (use microbenchmark-suite).
- Step 4: analyze traces to attribute latency to scheduling vs kernel vs serialization (use causal-latency-attribution playbook).
- Step 5: propose policy adjustment (e.g., reduce target_batch_latency_ms, change kernel_hint) and run A/B shadow test for 24 hours.

Benchmark protocol for validating MARS effects

Objective: quantify cost/latency/fidelity tradeoffs introduced by MARS policies.
sections.heading: Components

sections.body:
- Use the operational workload simulator (service: workload-synth) and a corpus of request templates grouped by prompt_bucket and op_type.
- Baseline: scheduler with model-agnostic shaper (current mainline).
- Treatment: scheduler + MARS with policy profile X.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, per-token GPU utilization, per-request cost estimate, kernel queue time distribution.
sections.heading: Benchmark setup

sections.body:
1) seed the model hint registry with profile X.
2) run 60-minute steady-state at target QPS for mid-tier pool.
3) collect traces and aggregate.
4) compute relative delta and run statistical significance (t-test) per metric.
sections.heading: Run script (short)

sections.body:
- p95 delta <= -10% (reduced) or <= +2% (acceptable increase) AND per-request cost delta <= -5% OR there is a documented product tradeoff.

Configuration reference (example table)

| key | default | description | notes |
|-----|---------|-------------|-------|
| mars.max_prefetch_per_gpu | 4 | Max concurrent kv-prefetch per GPU | Soft limit enforced by scheduler |
| mars.max_batch_latency_ms | 150 | Maximum batch formation latency target | Lower improves latency, raises cost |
| mars.policy_reload_interval_s | 60 | How often MARS refreshes policy and hints | Use 60s in prod |
| mars.hint_fallback_ttl_s | 300 | Time to trust a mapped fallback hint | Set to 5m to allow smooth conversions |
| mars.prefetch_memory_watermark_pct | 0.7 | Node-level watermark to allow prefetch | 0.7 recommended |

Operational runbook (common incidents)

Incident: Elevated model p99 for model.variant A after policy rollout
1) Immediately open a remediation incident and tag "mars-incident".
2) Check alert dashboard: confirm p95/p99 increase and affected prompt_buckets.
3) Abort rollout: set policy flag to previous version via policy rollback API:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" \
     https://internal-control-plane/api/mars/policy/rollback
   Confirm policy reload succeeded (logs in /var/log/mars/reloader.log).
4) Run profiling replay for 15 minutes using captured requests for each affected bucket.
5) If kernel_hint mismatch rate non-zero: check kernel plugin health on nodes (svc: kernel-plugin-manager).
6) If kv-prefetch caused OOMs: drain prefetch windows by toggling mars.max_prefetch_per_gpu=0, then roll forward with reduced prefetch.
7) Postmortem scope: include hypothesis, root cause (policy misclassification/kernal incompatible/misprofiled), timeline, and mitigations.

Incident: Hint-compatibility spike (translated-to-fallback count rising)
- Check Model Hint Registry: ensure hint_version is the same across front-line routers. If not, force reload:
  kubectl rollout restart deployment/mars-reloader -n runtime
- If nodes lack plugin: schedule kernel-plugin-manager restart on affected node pool.

Rollout checklist (safe rollout matrix)

- Canary: deploy policy to 0.5% traffic for model variant; monitor 1h.
- Shadow: mirror 1% traffic to a MARS-enabled staging cluster and compare traces for 24h.
- Gradual increase: 0.5 -> 1 -> 5 -> 20 -> 100% with 1h holds and automated rollback if p95 > SLO*1.1.
- Post-rollout validation: run benchmark protocol for 60m.

Ownership and contacts

- MARS Core Owner: Maya Patel (eng-serving-runtime).
- Scheduler integration: Daniel Chen (kernel-and-scheduling).
- Profiling and lab: Sofia Martinez (applied-ml-and-evals).
- On-call: runtime-sre rotation (link to oncall page).

Appendix: sample policy JSON (examples)

{
  "policy_name": "interactive-small-ctx-v1",
  "conditions": ["model.family == 'rwd-tiny'", "prompt_bucket == '0-64'"],
  "actions": {
    "kernel_hint": "fast-small-ctx",
    "max_batch_size": "16",
    "target_batch_latency_ms": "30",
    "admission_priority": "interactive"
  }
}

Notes and future work

- Integrate MARS with Optimize to allow policy suggestions based on cost budgets.
- Explore per-tenant adaptive learning of target_batch_latency using automatic feedback.
- Work with Private Deployments team to expose a restricted subset of MARS policies for self-hosted customers.

Related resources

- scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles (internal)
- runtime-microbenchmark-suite and kernel-hinting-matrix
- profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2026.json

Revision history

- 2026-02-14: Created (Maya Patel)
- 2026-04-07: Added telemetry enrichment and runbook sections (Daniel Chen)
- 2026-06-01: Tuned rollout thresholds and benchmark acceptance criteria (Sofia Martinez)
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria

payload.page_title: Kernel admission matrix and signal negotiation manual

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the kernel admission matrix and the signal negotiation protocol used between the runtime request router, the scheduler, and kernel instances. It provides a prescriptive matrix of signals and thresholds, sample policy YAML for the admission broker, instrumentation guidance, an operational runbook for admission-related incidents, and a rollout checklist for changes to the admission logic.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: runtime engineers, scheduler owners, SREs, and reliability-focused product engineers.
- Scope: admission decision inputs and outputs, signal definitions, negotiation rounds, safety gates for degradation, and testing/rollout steps.

Goals:
- Make admission decisions deterministic and auditable across heterogeneous GPU pools.
- Preserve latency SLOs by prioritizing low-latency cohorts while allowing controlled degradation for best-effort traffic.
- Provide a safe negotiation protocol that avoids oscillation when kernel availability fluctuates.

Key concepts:
1) Admission broker: a small, deterministic service colocated with the request router responsible for converting traffic intent into kernel "slot" requests.
2) Signals: typed metrics used in negotiation (see table below).
3) Negotiation round: a single exchange in which the broker proposes a slot profile and kernel replies with an acceptance, partial-accept, or reject.
4) Slot profile: an immutable descriptor (model variant, max_seq_len, prioritization_token, quality_tier) used to match kernel capabilities.

Signals and metrics (definitions):
- runtime.admit.latency_ms: time taken by the admission broker to respond to router before handoff.
- kernel.acceptance_rate: fraction of proposals accepted by kernels per 1m window.
- scheduler.queue_depth: number of pending kernel requests.
- kernel.available_slots: sum of free execution slots across matched kernels.
- fidelity.headroom_pct: estimated percentage of quality headroom remaining if requested batch is admitted.
- kvcache.warmth_score: heuristic (0.0-1.0) of prefix cache locality expected for the request.

Admission decision matrix (human-readable table):
| Traffic class | Min SLO p50 (ms) | Max allowed queue_depth | Min kernel.available_slots | kvcache.warmth_score min | Default action |
|---------------|------------------:|------------------------:|--------------------------:|------------------------:|----------------|
| interactive (high) | 50 | 10 | 4 | 0.6 | accept-or-hedge
| standard | 150 | 40 | 2 | 0.4 | accept-if-available-else-queue
| background | 500 | 200 | 0 | 0.0 | best-effort / defer or quantized variant

Interpretation notes:
- queue_depth and available_slots are averaged with an EWMA alpha=0.33 over 10s.
- fidelity.headroom_pct is estimated from the latest quality model and is used to decide whether a cheaper quantized kernel can be used.

Policy example (admission-broker.yaml):
```yaml
version: v1
policies:
  - name: interactive-strict
    traffic_class: interactive
    max_queue_depth: 10
    min_available_slots: 4
    allowed_variants: [gpu-full, gpu-quantized-8bit]
    fallback_sequence: [gpu-full, gpu-quantized-8bit, cpu-approx]
    gating:
      - metric: fidelity.headroom_pct
        operator: ">="
        value: 0.25
      - metric: kvcache.warmth_score
        operator: ">="
        value: 0.6
  - name: background-queueable
    traffic_class: background
    max_queue_depth: 200
    min_available_slots: 0
    allowed_variants: [gpu-quantized-8bit, cpu-approx]
    fallback_sequence: [gpu-quantized-8bit, cpu-approx]
```

Negotiation protocol (sequence):
1) Router -> Broker: send request envelope with traffic_class, model_id, seq_len, prompt_hash, provenance.
2) Broker -> Candidate kernels: issue propose(slot_profile) with TTL=250ms for interactive and 1s for background.
3) Kernel -> Broker: respond accept | partial-accept(capacity=N) | reject(reason). Include kernel.acceptance_rate in response header.
4) Broker: pick best fit; if partial-accept, issue hedged-proposals to fallback kernels.
5) Router: on accept, proxy request to kernel with a short-circuit shadow to fallback path for observability.

Safety gates and anti-oscillation rules:
- Hysteresis windows: any admission change that increases allowed queue_depth or relaxes fidelity must be held for 30s before acceptance.
- Rate-limit admission changes to 1 update per 10s per shard.
- If kernel.acceptance_rate < 0.2 for 60s, automatically trigger fallback to lower-fidelity variants and alert SRE.

Instrumentation and telemetry contract (required metrics):
- runtime.admission.e2e_time_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- runtime.admission.rejections.count (by reason)
- kernel.accept_response_latency_ms
- kernel.acceptance_rate (1m, 5m rollups)
- scheduler.queue_depth (per shard)
- kernel.available_slots (per variant)
- admission.negotiation_rounds.count
- fidelity.degradation_events.count

Recommended dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboard: "Admission health" showing p95 admit latency, acceptance_rate heatmap, queue_depth by traffic class, and trending of fidelity_degradations.
- Alerts:
  - P0: p95 runtime.admission.e2e_time_ms > 400ms for >3m or kernel.acceptance_rate < 0.15 for 2m.
  - P1: sudden increase (>3x) in admission.rejections.count within 5m.

Operational runbook: admission failures
1) Symptom: spikes in "admission.e2e_time_ms" or mass rejections for interactive traffic.
2) Immediate checks (run these in order):
   a) Check broker process health: curl http://broker.local/healthz (expect 200).
   b) Query metrics: `kubectl get --namespace=runtime -l app=admission-broker -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'` then `kubectl port-forward svc/admission-broker 8080:8080` and `curl localhost:8080/metrics | grep admission`.
   c) Inspect kernel pool: `rctl kernel list --variant=gpu-full --shard=<shard>` and verify kernel.available_slots > policy.min_available_slots.
   d) Check scheduler queue depth: `promql "sum(scheduler_queue_depth) by (shard)"` in Grafana Explore.
3) Remediation steps (ordered):
   1) If broker CPU is saturated: scale broker replicas by +2 and pin to dedicated node pool.
   2) If kernel.acceptance_rate is low: mark problematic kernel nodes unschedulable and drain for further investigation: `rctl kernel drain <kernel-id> --reason=acceptance-drop`
   3) If queue_depth is high: temporarily shift background traffic to rate-limited route: `rctl route update background --throttle=0.2`
   4) If fidelity.headroom_pct low for interactive: enable forced fallback variant for interactive for 5 minutes: `rctl policy set interactive-strict --force-variant=gpu-quantized-8bit --ttl=300s`
4) Post-incident: run the admission regression harness (see Testing section) and file an incident with tags: `admission, kernel, degradation`

Testing and rollout checklist:
- Unit tests for policy parser with synthetic signals.
- Integration test: simulate 3 negotiation rounds with mixed kernel responses; assert router receives accept within TTL 99% of the time in synthetic load.
- Shadow rollout: enable new negotiation logic in 10% of routers for 48h and compare fidelity.degradation_events.count and admit latency.
- Canary: 2% live traffic gating for 2h, then 10% for 4h, then 50% for 4h, monitor p95 admit latency and kernel.acceptance_rate.

Admission regression harness (how to run):
- Repo: infra/runtime-admission/tests/harness
- Command: `make run-harness ENV=staging PROFILE=interactive THREADS=200 DURATION=10m`
- Outputs: CSV of admission.latency, accept_rate, fallback_usage.

Configuration and example knobs (table):
| Field | Type | Default | Recommended change window |
|-------|------|--------:|--------------------------:|
| max_queue_depth | integer | 40 | immediate (tweak small steps) |
| min_available_slots | integer | 2 | 30s hysteresis |
| negotiation_ttl_ms | integer | 250 | testing only |
| admission_hysteresis_s | integer | 30 | config change must observe for 30s |

Troubleshooting scenar os (short):
- Symptom: oscillation between full-fidelity and quantized kernels.
  Action: increase hysteresis window to 60s, enable smoothing on fidelity.headroom_pct to 30s EWMA.
- Symptom: headroom reports high but users see poor quality.
  Action: run fidelity-sample-set against the quantized variant and verify objective metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity).

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: runtime-scheduler team (oncall alias: #oncall-runtime-scheduler)
- Secondary owner: kernel-team (oncall alias: #oncall-kernel)
- Pager rule: any P0 alert must page runtime-scheduler oncall immediately and create an incident in PagerDuty.

References and related artifacts:
- Link: /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/request-surface-replay-and-synthetic-corpus-builder-2025 (replay corpus format)
- Link: /eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2026 (observability method)

Appendix: diagram (text):
- "Broker negotiation flow": a sequence diagram where Router -> Broker (envelope) -> Kernel candidates; kernels respond; Broker decides; Router proxies. Include correlation IDs for every exchange and attach them to tracing span `admission.negotiation.span`.

Change history:
- 2026-01-12: created by Jordan Kim (initial draft).
- 2026-02-20: added hysteresis rules and telemetry contract (Elena Rossi reviewer).
- 2026-03-02: finalized remediation steps and rollout checklist (Marcus Lee reviewer).

payload.page_title: Kernel Auto-Selection v2 — Design

sections.body:
h1. Kernel Auto-Selection v2 — Design

*Owner:* Yuki Sato (Runtime Kernels)
*Design leads:* Hiro Tanaka (Kernels), Noah Patel (Architecture/perf correctness)
*Primary stakeholders:* Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling), Lena Fischer (Workload regime characterization), Omar El-Sayed (tail-latency/observability), Marcus Reed (perf validation), Ethan Park (control-plane gates)

h2. 1) Summary
Kernel auto-selection v2 ("selector v2") updates the Serving Runtime kernel selection logic to be explicitly keyed on:
1) *Model family/architecture* (e.g., Llama-family vs Mistral-family vs Qwen-family vs Gemma-family)
2) *Sequence length regime* (prefill/decode characteristics and buckets)
3) *GPU type/SKU* (A100/H100/L40S + variants, incl. MIG where applicable)

The intent is to reduce *p95/p99 latency* and improve *throughput stability* across heterogeneous fleets while preserving:
- Correctness (no numerical/caching correctness regressions)
- Determinism (same inputs -> same selection decision)
- Operational safety (fast rollback + overrides)

Selector v2 ships behind feature gates, with allowlist/denylist controls by model + GPU SKU + region.

h2. 2) Motivation / Problem Statement
Selector v1 has grown organically and primarily selects kernels using a limited feature set (mostly model size + a coarse prefill/decode heuristic). This has resulted in:
- Mis-selections in long-context workloads (tail latency spikes when a kernel is optimal for short prompts but degrades for large prefill)
- SKU sensitivity (kernels that are stable on H100 may regress on L40S; some A100 variants differ in optimal kernel choice)
- Hard-to-debug incidents (selection decisions are not sufficiently observable per request; hard to reproduce in staging)
- Rollout friction (lack of targeted controls increases blast radius)

Selector v2 makes feature extraction explicit, selection rules auditable, and fallbacks guaranteed.

h2. 3) Goals and Non-Goals
h3. Goals
- *Performance:* reduce p95/p99 latency and reduce variance in decode throughput across mixed workloads.
- *Stability:* prevent tail latency spikes from long-context misclassification.
- *Safety:* safe fallbacks when a kernel is unavailable, unstable, or unsupported for a given GPU SKU / driver / model.
- *Determinism & replayability:* selection decisions must be reproducible and stable given identical inputs and config.
- *Observability:* emit per-request selection decision telemetry with bounded overhead.
- *Operational controls:* feature-gated rollout and hot-reloadable allow/deny lists.

h3. Non-Goals
- Learning-based kernel selection (out of scope for v2; see ADR-017 for rationale).
- Changing the scheduler policy itself (selector consumes scheduler hints; scheduling remains authoritative for batching/placement).
- Automatic kernel compilation at request time (selector only chooses among registered kernels / precompiled variants).

h2. 4) Current Behavior (Selector v1)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Inputs: model identifier, estimated prefill length, estimated max output tokens, some runtime flags.
- Behavior:
  - Picks one attention kernel family (e.g., flash-attn vs baseline) and a small set of fused ops if enabled.
  - Performs minimal hardware branching ("H100" vs "other") and relies on defaults for most SKUs.
  - Has implicit fallbacks spread across multiple call sites.
- Gaps:
  - No explicit model-family classification; model variants can land in the wrong bucket.
  - Coarse seq-length logic (short/long threshold) does not handle mixed workloads.
  - Limited per-request traceability.

h2. 5) Proposed Approach (Selector v2)
Selector v2 is a *rule-based* decision engine with:
- A normalized feature vector extracted from request + model metadata + hardware metadata.
- A kernel registry mapping (model_family, gpu_sku, seq_bucket, op_set) -> candidate kernels.
- A deterministic decision procedure that produces:
  - chosen_kernel_set (attention + fused ops package)
  - fallback_reason (if not using preferred kernel)
  - selection_version (for audit/replay)

h3. 5.1 High-level architecture placement
Selection occurs at *plan construction* time (before execution), after:
- model is resolved (including version pin)
- hardware runtime reports GPU properties
- scheduler provides optional workload hints
sections.heading: Selector v1 (simplified)

sections.body:
(model_id, model_revision, gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, seq_bucket, selector_config_hash)

h2. 6) Inputs and Feature Signals
h3. 6.1 Model family / architecture classification
sections.heading: Selection result is cached (bounded) by

sections.body:
- model_family: {llama, mistral, qwen, gemma, other}
- architecture_tags: list (e.g., rope_variant, gqa/mqa, kv_head_count, hidden_size bucket)
sections.heading: We introduce a model-family classifier that produces

sections.body:
- model manifest (preferred)
- runtime introspection of model config (fallback)
sections.heading: Primary sources

sections.body:
- Classification must be deterministic and stable across model aliases.
- For unknown models, family=other and we default to conservative kernels.

h3. 6.2 Sequence length regime and buckets
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- prefill_tokens_est (prompt length)
- decode_tokens_est (expected output / max_tokens)
- optional scheduler_hint: observed_workload_seq_histogram

Define seq_bucket (initial):
- S: prefill <= 256
- M: 257–2048
- L: 2049–8192
- XL: > 8192

Additionally define workload_mode:
- prefill_heavy (prefill dominates)
- decode_heavy (decode dominates)
- mixed/unknown
sections.heading: We bucket requests using a combination of

sections.body:
- If prefill_tokens_est is missing/unknown, bucket="unknown" and select a safe baseline kernel.

h3. 6.3 GPU SKU normalization
We normalize GPU identity into gpu_sku_norm and capability tags:
- gpu_family: {a100, h100, l40s, other}
- sm_version: e.g., 80, 90
- hbm_gb (rounded bucket)
- mig_profile (if MIG enabled; otherwise "none")
- driver_norm + cuda_norm (coarse versions for known-unstable blocks)
sections.heading: Guardrail

sections.body:
- Treat A100 40GB vs 80GB as same family but different hbm bucket for memory-sensitive kernels.
- For MIG: include profile string (e.g., "1g.10gb") to avoid selecting kernels requiring larger shared resources.

h2. 7) Kernel Registry and Candidate Generation
h3. 7.1 Registry structure
The registry provides candidates per (op, model_family, gpu_sku_norm, seq_bucket):
- attention_kernels: ordered list
- kv_cache_kernels: ordered list
- fused_ops_package: ordered list
sections.heading: Normalization rules (initial)
Each candidate has metadata

sections.body:
1) Filter kernels by hard constraints (support + version blocks).
2) Sort by preference order (rule-based, per GPU family and seq bucket).
3) Return candidate list + rationale.

h2. 8) Decision Logic
Selector v2 is deterministic and rule-based. At a high level:

*Step A — Extract features*
- model_family, architecture_tags
- seq_bucket, workload_mode
- gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, cuda_norm

*Step B — Build candidates*
- For attention: preferred list for (model_family, gpu_family, seq_bucket)
- Apply denylist blocks (kernel_id, gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, model_id)

*Step C — Choose*
- Choose the first candidate that passes constraints and is not blocked.
- If none pass, fall back to baseline.

*Step D — Emit selection record*
- selected_attention_kernel_id
- selected_fused_ops_package_id
- candidate_ids (possibly sampled)
- feature vector (redacted/hashed where needed)
- selection_version + config_hash

h3. 8.1 Example rule sketch (illustrative)
- If gpu_family=h100 and seq_bucket in {S,M} and model_family in {llama,mistral,qwen}:
  - prefer attention=flashattn_v2_sm90
- If seq_bucket in {L,XL}:
  - prefer attention=paged_attn_smXX_longctx (if supported) else flashattn_v2 with longctx parameters
- If gpu_family=l40s:
  - prefer attention=flashattn_v2_sm89_tuned (if stable) else baseline_attn

(Concrete kernel IDs and tuning parameters are maintained in the registry; the selector references them by stable ID.)

h2. 9) Fallback Hierarchy (Safety First)
We formalize a single fallback hierarchy to remove implicit, distributed fallbacks.

h3. 9.1 Fallback precedence
If preferred kernel is unavailable/blocked/unsupported, fall back in this order:
1) Same kernel family, conservative parameters (e.g., disable aggressive tiling)
2) Alternate high-performance kernel validated for SKU (e.g., flash-attn -> paged-attn or vice versa, per registry)
3) Baseline attention implementation (reference path) with conservative fused ops disabled
4) Emergency safe mode: baseline attention + disable non-essential fusions + force safe KV cache behavior

h3. 9.2 Reasons for fallback (telemetry enum)
- KERNEL_NOT_REGISTERED
- KERNEL_BLOCKED_BY_DENYLIST
- GPU_UNSUPPORTED
- DRIVER_BLOCKED
- SEQ_BUCKET_UNSUPPORTED
- MODEL_TAG_UNSUPPORTED
- VALIDATION_GATE_NOT_PASSED (e.g., kernel marked canary-only)

h3. 9.3 Guarantee
Selector v2 must always produce a valid executable plan if the runtime supports the model at all. If the model is unsupported, fail early with an explicit error (do not loop through kernels).

h2. 10) Determinism Guarantees
Determinism is a hard requirement for debugging and for Dedicated/Private customers.

h3. 10.1 Deterministic selection definition
sections.heading: For each op category

sections.body:
- model_id + model_revision
- request-derived features (prefill_tokens_est, decode_tokens_est) and scheduler hints (if enabled)
- normalized hardware identity (gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, cuda_norm)
- selector_config (including allow/deny lists)

…the selector must return the same selection result.

h3. 10.2 Guardrails to enforce determinism
- Feature extraction must be pure (no time-based or random inputs).
- Candidate ordering must be stable and not depend on hash-map iteration.
- All config inputs used for selection must be captured in selector_config_hash.
- If scheduler hints are used, the hint must be a stable, serialized snapshot value (not a moving pointer).

h3. 10.3 Replay
We define a “selection replay record” that can be captured (sampled) and replayed locally:
- feature vector
- kernel registry snapshot version
- selector_config_hash
- resulting kernel IDs

h2. 11) Observability and Telemetry
h3. 11.1 Required per-request fields (sampled)
- selector_version (e.g., "v2")
- selection_config_hash
- model_id, model_family
- gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, cuda_norm
- seq_bucket, workload_mode
- selected_attention_kernel_id
- fallback_reason (if any)

h3. 11.2 Optional fields (more aggressively sampled)
- candidate_kernel_ids
- candidate_filter_reasons (top-N)
- selection_latency_us (selector evaluation overhead)

h3. 11.3 Sampling and overhead
- Default sampling: 0.1% per route/model, with ability to increase temporarily during canary/debug.
- Hard cap: do not exceed 1% by default in Hosted; Dedicated/Private adjustable via config.
- Selector evaluation time budget: p50 < 50µs, p99 < 200µs on control path (excludes registry load).

h2. 12) Configuration, Feature Gates, and Overrides
h3. 12.1 Feature gate
- Flag: runtime.kernel_selector.v2.enabled
- Scope: {global, region, pool, model}
- Evaluation order: model override > pool > region > global

h3. 12.2 Allowlist / denylist
- Allowlist: enable v2 only for specified model families/models during rollout.
- Denylist: block specific (kernel_id, gpu_sku_norm, driver_norm, model_id) combinations.
- Hot reload: supported with bounded propagation time (target < 2 minutes) and explicit audit log.

h3. 12.3 Manual pinning (debug/emergency)
- CLI/runtime flag: --force_attention_kernel=<kernel_id>
- CLI/runtime flag: --dump_kernel_selection
sections.heading: Given the same

sections.body:
- bypass the selector for the pinned op
- still validate hard constraints (fail fast if truly incompatible)

h2. 13) Performance / Correctness Validation Plan (Design-level)
See benchmark matrix page for full coverage. At a design level, v2 requires:
- Microbench: selector overhead and kernel switch overhead bounds
- Macrobench: end-to-end p95/p99 latency and throughput across:
  - model families: Llama/Mistral/Qwen/Gemma
  - seq buckets: S/M/L/XL with mixed distributions
  - GPU SKUs: A100/H100/L40S (+ common variants)

Pass/fail gates (initial, subject to SRE review):
- No correctness regressions (golden output + KV cache invariants)
- Error rate not worse than v1 (p99 + absolute threshold)
- p99 latency regression budget: <= 1% overall; any per-bucket regression > 3% requires explicit signoff + denylist or rule adjustment

h2. 14) Risks and Mitigations
- *Risk: long-context misclassification leads to tail spikes.*
  - Mitigation: conservative thresholds; XL bucket forced safe kernels; add explicit longctx guardrail; canary focused on long-context routes.

- *Risk: GPU SKU normalization misses a variant (e.g., cloud naming mismatch).*
  - Mitigation: normalization unit tests with known SKU strings; log raw GPU name in debug traces; default to safe kernels on unknown SKU.

- *Risk: telemetry cardinality blow-up.*
  - Mitigation: stable normalized GPU strings; sample candidate lists; limit tag dimensions; review with Observability team.

- *Risk: nondeterminism due to scheduler hints.*
  - Mitigation: treat hints as optional; require snapshot serialization; fallback to request-derived estimates.

h2. 15) Open Questions
1) *Seq bucket thresholds:* Are the S/M/L/XL thresholds appropriate across our customer mix, especially for summarization and RAG workloads?
2) *Mixed workload handling:* Should we bias selection toward prefill-heavy safety when scheduler hints indicate a long-tail of XL prompts?
3) *MIG support policy:* Do we treat MIG as a first-class sku_sublabel in all environments or disallow v2 by default on MIG until coverage improves?
4) *Driver/CUDA blocks:* What is the minimal safe set of driver_norm blocks at launch (avoid overblocking and losing perf gains)?
5) *Registry ownership and update cadence:* Who owns the steady-state updates of kernel preference ordering (Kernels vs Perf/Evals vs Release Eng), and how do we gate changes?
6) *Cache key stability:* Are we comfortable with caching decisions by (seq_bucket) only, or do we need additional bucketing by decode_tokens_est for certain kernels?

h2. 16) Appendix: Pseudocode (selector)
{code}
function select_kernels_v2(request, model, hw, scheduler_hint, config):
  feats = extract_features(request, model, hw, scheduler_hint)
  cfg_hash = hash(config.selector_rules, config.allowlist, config.denylist)

  candidates = registry.get_candidates(
      model_family=feats.model_family,
      gpu_sku=feats.gpu_sku_norm,
      seq_bucket=feats.seq_bucket)

  candidates = apply_denylist(candidates, feats, config.denylist)

  for k in candidates.attention:
    if supports(k, feats) and passes_gates(k, config):
      selected = k
      reason = "NONE"
      break

  if selected is null:
    selected = registry.get_baseline_attention()
    reason = "FALLBACK_BASELINE"

  emit_telemetry_sampled(feats, selected, candidates, reason, cfg_hash)
  return selected
{code}

h2. 17) Changelog
- 2026-01-14: Initial draft (Yuki Sato)
- 2026-02-03: Added explicit determinism + replay requirements (Noah Patel review)
- 2026-02-12: Added SKU normalization rules + MIG notes (Isabella Rossi input)
- 2026-02-21: Updated fallback reason taxonomy + telemetry sampling guidance (Omar El-Sayed, Allison Grant)

payload.page_title: Traffic Mirroring End-to-End Benchmark Protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the canonical end-to-end (E2E) benchmark protocol for measuring runtime performance using traffic mirroring. Traffic mirroring benchmarks run real production traffic in read-only mode against candidate runtime builds, model variants, or kernel scheduling configurations. The goals are to:

- Obtain representative latency and correctness signals with minimal production risk.
- Compare candidate changes to a baseline across cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Produce reproducible artifacts suitable for release gating and perf regression detection.

Scope

Applies to: eng-serving-runtime teams running hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This protocol is intended for:
- New kernel scheduling releases
- Runtime build changes that touch request routing or batching
- Model-variant rollout validation (e.g., quantized vs float variants)
- Autoscaling/slotting policy experiments

Excludes: experiments that mutate customer-visible state or alter traffic semantics (see safety checklist).

Key Concepts

- Mirrored traffic: a copy of production requests sent concurrently to the candidate system without forwarding responses back to the user.
- Shadow target: an isolated cluster or pool that processes mirrored traffic for measurement and logging.
- Replay-safe: traffic transformed to remove sensitive PII and non-idempotent operations.

Roles and Ownership

- Benchmark Owner: person who schedules and signs off the run (example: Priya Shah).
- Runtime Owner: service-level owner of the candidate runtime build.
- Observability Owner: responsible for ensuring required dashboards and traces are available.
- SRE Approval: SRE must sign off for any run that exceeds baseline resource consumption thresholds.

SLOs and Acceptance Criteria

Baseline: production cluster A (stable). Candidate: cluster B (mirrored). Acceptance requires:
- P50 latency delta <= +10% compared to baseline under same load shape.
- P95 latency delta <= +15%.
- P99 tail-latency delta <= +25% OR absolute p99 < 3000ms (whichever is stricter for the workload).
- Throughput: candidate must sustain 95% of baseline sustained QPS without queue growth.
- Error rate (5xx): candidate <= baseline + 0.1 percentage points.
- Semantic parity: for deterministic workloads, token-level equality >= 98%. For non-deterministic outputs, use embed-similarity thresholds (cosine >= 0.985).

Safety Checklist (must be completed before any mirror run)

1) Sanitize inputs: remove Authorization headers and any customer PII using the request-sanitizer pipeline.
2) Ensure the candidate is strictly read-only: no upstream writes, no metrics emitted to billing systems.
3) Mirror traffic rate scaling: start at 1% of production QPS and increase only after SRE approval.
4) Resource isolation: shadow target must have separate autoscaling group / node-pool and no shared persistent storage with prod.
5) Alerting: create temporary alert suppressions to avoid noisy page storms and ensure critical alerts still page.

Procedure: Run Plan

1) Prepare candidate build and environment:
   - Deploy candidate runtime to shadow cluster B with identical network topology and model pins.
   - Ensure KV cache behavior is reset unless intentionally testing cache warmup.
   - Tag build with bench-run/<YYYYMMDD>/<run-id> for trace correlation.

2) Configure mirroring:
   - Use the traffic-mirror service (internal) to configure rule: mirror-rule:<service>-<route>-<run-id>.
   - Example rule config (YAML):

     mirror_rule:
       name: chat-completions-shadow-2027-01
       source: prod-gateway
       match: path_prefix: "/v1/chat/completions"
       sampler: fixed_rate
       rate: 0.01
       sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
       targets: ["shadow-cluster-b"]

   - CLI to apply (internal):
     $ traffic-mirror apply --from prod-gateway --to shadow-cluster-b --path-prefix /v1/chat/completions --rate 0.01 --sanitizer request-sanitizer-v2 --name chat-completions-shadow-<run-id>

3) Warmup and ramping:
   - Start with 0.1% mirror rate for 10 minutes to validate pipeline. Confirm no errors and resource headroom.
   - Ramp to target mirror rate (commonly 1% or 5% depending on risk classification) in exponentially increasing steps (0.5%, 1%, 2%). Each step: hold for 5–15 minutes and observe metrics.

4) Data collection windows:
   - Short-run benchmarking: 30–60 minutes. Use when kernel or kernel-parameter changes are small.
   - Long-run benchmarking: 6–24 hours. Use for model-variant comparisons or autoscaling policy changes.
   - Capture request/response timeline traces, kernel metrics, GPU utilization, per-token latency histograms, KV cache hit rates, and queue length series.

5) Instrumentation and required telemetry
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- request.timeline: trace spans for gateway->router->runtime->kernel->executor
- runtime.latency_ms: p50/p95/p99 histograms by route and model
- kernel.queue_length: 1s resolution time-series per GPU slot
- kernel.dispatch_time_ms: per-request quantiles
- gpu.utilization_pct: per-GPU
- kvcache.hit_rate: rolling 1m and 5m
- embed-similarity: sample of 200 request pairs comparing baseline vs candidate outputs

Tagging: all metrics must include bench.run_id and bench.build_tag dimensions.

Artifacts to persist

- Raw traces: stored in obs.test-bench/traces/<run-id> (retention 90d)
- Aggregated histograms: obs.test-bench/histograms/<run-id>.json
- Representative sample of requests and candidate responses (sanitized): s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/samples.jsonl.gz
- Perf report: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/report.html (generated by bench-reporting tool)

Analysis and Reporting

1) Automated report generation:
   - After the run finishes the bench-orchestrator will produce a summary report containing latency deltas, resource deltas (GPU-hours used), and semantic similarity.
   - The report includes waterfall diagnostics for slow tail requests and a heatmap of queue growth over time.

2) Manual triage checklist:
   - If p99 delta > acceptance, run failure mode triage: inspect kernel dispatch traces, check for blocking allocations, and examine kernel-runloop starvation.
   - Compare kvcache.hit_rate trends: a sudden drop suggests cache population mismatch or differing shard keys.
   - Check for dispatcher backpressure events and kernel preemption counts.

3) Release gating:
   - Candidate passes if all acceptance criteria are met and no new critical incidents were generated during the run.
   - For marginal cases, run a focused replay of suspect requests with increased sampling (100–500x) to amplify differences for debugging.

Troubleshooting and Common Failure Modes

- Symptom: Elevated p95 with normal GPU utilization
  Action: Inspect kernel.queue_length and dispatch_time_ms for contention; verify batch-slicing thresholds and preemption windows.

- Symptom: Higher error rate on candidate
  Action: Check sanitizer pipeline for malformed transformed requests; validate model version pins; look for OOMs in runtime logs.

- Symptom: Semantic drift (embed-similarity drop)
  Action: Confirm identical tokenizer and model quantization parameters; check for off-by-one sequence padding differences.

- Symptom: Large cost delta with similar latency
  Action: Analyze per-token GPU cycles using kernel-cycle counters; check for degenerate scheduling producing small, inefficient kernels (e.g., repeated tiny-attention launches).

Operational Controls and Cost Limits

- Default mirror rate cap for non-critical patches: 1% of prod QPS.
- For kernel/platform team experiments that intentionally stress resources, a waiver must be obtained from SRE and Finance for temporary increased cloud spend (submit bench-cost-waiver/<run-id>).

Automation recipes and scripts

- bench-orchestrator job spec (short):
  - name: mirror-bench-<run-id>
  - baseline_cluster: prod-a
  - candidate_cluster: shadow-b
  - routes: ["/v1/chat/completions"]
  - mirror_rate: 0.01
  - sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
  - artifact_bucket: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>

- Example invocation:
  $ bench-orchestrator run --spec ./specs/mirror-bench-<run-id>.yaml --notify @eng-runtime --tag bench.run_id=<run-id>

Postmortem and Artifact Retention

- All run artifacts are retained for 90 days by default. Stakeholders must archive essential artifacts to the release retro bucket for multi-year retention if used for compliance.
- Any unexpected production-facing incident correlated to a mirroring run triggers a full incident review and possible rollback of mirror permissions.

Notes on Privacy and Compliance

- The request-sanitizer pipeline must run in-line before the mirror emitter. It should: strip auth tokens, normalize or redact PII fields, and replace customer ids with stable pseudonyms.
- For customers with restricted data residency, mirroring is disabled unless an explicit contractual exception is documented.

Appendix A: Example artifact schema (samples.jsonl line)

{
  "bench.run_id": "<run-id>",
  "timestamp": "2026-12-08T14:22:12Z",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "sanitized_input": "{...}",
  "baseline_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 120, "tokens": 48},
  "candidate_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 160, "tokens": 48},
  "embed_similarity": 0.992
}

Appendix B: Quick checklist for small patch owners

1) Run preflight unit perf tests in sandbox.
2) Schedule 30min mirror at 0.5% and validate no increased error rate.
3) Expand to 1% for 60min and evaluate report.
4) If candidate is clean, request staging rollout.

References

- Traffic mirror service README (internal): /tools/traffic-mirror/README
- Bench-orchestrator docs: /tools/bench-orchestrator/guide
- Request sanitizer config templates: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/request-sanitizer-templates

Contact

For questions or help running a mirror benchmark, ping #eng-runtime-perf or email perf@redwood.example.com.

payload.page_title: Runtime Scheduler Decision Fabric and Telemetry Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the "Decision Fabric" concept for the runtime scheduler: a structured set of decision points, the telemetry signals required to make those decisions, and a practical playbook for evaluating, rolling out, and debugging scheduler policy changes. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and owners of scheduling policy components.

Goals

- Make scheduling decisions auditable and reproducible.
- Ensure telemetry is sufficient to explain why any request took the path it did.
- Provide safe rollout and rollback steps for scheduler changes.
- Define incident triage and escalation steps when scheduling misbehavior impacts SLOs.

Scope

Covers: kernel scheduling policy decision points, admission controllers, priority tags, preemption windows, kernel selection hints, and the telemetry & alerts that validate these decisions.
Does not cover: low-level GPU kernel source code changes or vendor driver instrumentation (those belong to kernel-and-scheduling code docs).

1. Decision Fabric: concepts and nodes

The Decision Fabric is a logical DAG of discrete decision nodes that operate on enriched request context and produce actions or routing hints. Nodes are micro-decision units intended to be small and testable. Example nodes:

- Request Classification: maps incoming request attributes to a class (e.g., interactive, batch, background).
- Admission Gate: enforces concurrency & slot availability budget for class and tenant.
- Priority Arbiter: resolves conflicts between competing requests (SLA, customer tier, emerging emergency).
- Kernel Selector: picks the kernel variant and quantization profile.
- Prefetch/KV Hint: decides whether to fetch KV cache for a session.
- Fallback Router: chooses alternate model variant/region on capacity or error.

Each node emits a standardized Decision Event (see Telemetry section). Nodes are composed into runtime pipelines.

2. Decision Event schema (telemetry contract)

All scheduler decision nodes MUST emit a Decision Event at the moment a decision is made. This makes decisions traceable end-to-end. The near-term schema (text representation):

Example Decision Event (single-line JSON text for logs; the runtime also emits structured proto for the tracing pipeline):
{
  "request_id": "string",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-15T14:12:03Z",
  "node": "PriorityArbiter:v2",
  "input_signals": ["tenancy_tier:standard","seq_len_estimate:32","recent_error_rate:0.002"],
  "decision": "grant:slot-id=slot-42, kernel_hint=gptq-4bit-fp16",
  "reason_codes": ["tenancy_quota_ok","latency_target_50ms"],
  "latency_ms": 0.42,
  "cost_weight": 1.0
}

- Note: Events should be JSON-encoded when landing in structured logging systems; they must also exist as compact binary in the tracing pipeline for high-cardinality sampling.

Required fields (text form): request_id, timestamp (ISO8601), node (string), decision (string), reason_codes (list), latency_ms (number), cost_weight (number), input_signals (list).
Optional but recommended: model_version, kernel_revision, tenant_id, route, sampled_trace_id.

3. Minimal telemetry to support common investigations

To triage scheduling issues within 5–15 minutes, the following telemetry streams are required:

- Decision Events (high cardinality, sampled): ~1 per decision; sample strategy below.
- Request Timeline Trace (distributed trace spanning API -> admission -> kernel dispatch).
- Per-kernel execution metrics: queue_time_ms, kernel_exec_ms, retry_count.
- Admission & slot pool stats: available_slots, inflight_by_tier, eviction_count.
- Request classification histogram: seq_len, token_budget, request_surface_type.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
| Stream | Sampling | Hot retention | Cold retention |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|Decision Events|100% for tier=enterprise; 5% for standard/free|7d|180d|
|Request Traces|100% for p99+ tail traces, 1% baseline|14d|90d|
|Kernel exec metrics|Aggregate per-min buckets 100%|30d|365d|

4. Reason-coding taxonomy (short list)

Decision nodes should attach reason codes. We maintain a canonical set to avoid free-form strings. Examples:

- quota_exhausted
- latency_slo_risk
- high_seq_len
- emergency_preemption
- kernel_incompatible
- kvcache_miss
- model_swap_fallback

5. Playbook: safe rollout of scheduler changes

This is the sequential process you must follow when deploying a scheduler policy change (e.g., new PriorityArbiter logic, admission thresholds, kernel selector rules):

1) Design review and unit tests
- Create an ADR (link to decision record). Include decision fabric impact map (which nodes change).
- Unit tests: determinism tests for decision nodes and reason_code coverage matrix.

2) Local and integration testing
- Run deterministic replay of representative request corpus (use the operational workload simulator) and compare Decision Event diffs.
- Validate no new reason codes introduced unintentionally.

3) Canary rollout (safety gates)
- Canary cohort: 0.5% baseline requests or a narrow tenant set of non-critical accounts.
- Observability checks (automated):
  - p50/p95 request latency for canary <= baseline + 5%
  - decision_event.reason_code change rate <= 2x baseline for any single reason code
  - admission.rejection_rate <= baseline + 0.1% absolute
  - kernel_exec_ms median unchanged or improved

4) Gradual ramp and policy checks
- Ramp to 5% after 30m if canary signals pass for 15m rolling windows.
- Run the differential tracer extractor to verify decision path similarity (expectation: >95% of canary decisions match legacy for non-experimental paths).

5) Full rollout and post-mortem observation
- After 24 hours at 100% observe metrics for 72 hours.
- If any SLO regressions occur, trigger automatic rollback and open a postmortem.

6. Incident triage checklist (scheduling-related)

When customers observe increased latency or error rates that trace to scheduler behavior:

1. Confirm alert and scope: check SLO dashboards for elevated p99 and per-route errors.
2. Correlate with Decision Event spike: query decision_event.node aggregated by reason_code in last 15m.
3. Inspect admission pool state: available_slots, pool_eviction_count, queue_time_ms.
4. Query kernel health: dispatch_fail_rate, nvlink_errors, watchdog_restarts.
5. If decision nodes show a sudden change in reason_code distribution (e.g., quota_exhausted spikes), identify the upstream change (policy, config, traffic surge).
6. If root cause is policy regression, execute rollback (see Rollback snippet).
sections.heading: Suggested retention and sampling

sections.body:
redwood-schedctl rollback --bundle-id=rb-2026-0007 --reason="p99-latency-regression"

Wait for slot metrics and decision_event reason_code to normalize, then annotate the incident.

7. Debug recipes and quick checks

- "Why did my request get preempted?"
  1) Search Decision Events by request_id -> look at PriorityArbiter and Admission Gate nodes.
  2) Check reason_codes: if emergency_preemption present, check active incident tags and owner.

- "Why was kernel_variant X chosen?"
  1) Inspect KernelSelector decision event; cross-check input_signals for sequence length and model_version.
  2) Look at kernel_revision compatibility table (see table below).
sections.heading: Roll back to last stable policy bundle

sections.body:
| kernel_revision | model_family | quant_profile | notes |
| kv1.4 | gpt-j | 8bit | legacy; higher latency for long seqs |
| gq-2025-4b | llama-family | gptq-4bit-fp16 | low cost; prefer for background tasks |
| vbench-rc2 | opt | int8 | experimental; disable for enterprise tenants |

8. Metric and alert definitions (examples)

- sched.decision.rate (counter): decision events per second. Alert: sustained drop >30% over 5m -> scheduler stall investigation.
- sched.admission.rejection_rate (gauge %): Alert if >0.5% absolute above baseline for 10m.
- sched.kernel.queue_time_p99 (ms): Alert if >250ms for 5m.
- sched.reasoncode.quotas_exhausted.rate (counter): Alert if sudden spike (>5x expected) during deployment windows.

9. Sampling and storage plan for Decision Events
sections.heading: Kernel compatibility table (text)

sections.body:
1) High-fidelity path (tracing infra) stores sampled full traces and Decision Events for a narrow sample of requests and all p99 tail traces.
2) Low-cost aggregated path stores per-minute aggregated counters and histograms for long-term analytics.
sections.heading: We recommend a two-path approach

sections.body:
- sample_by_tier: {enterprise: 100%, standard: 5%, free: 1%}
- tail_capture: p99+ of request_latency || error_rate -> force sample.

10. Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: runtime-scheduler team (oncall rota: runtime-scheduler@pagerduty).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre (for capacity, node-level issues).
- Incident severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: customer-facing outage (SLO > 30m breach) -> notify exec-oncall, start incident bridge.
  - Sev-2: p99 latency spikes without complete outage (SRE & scheduler oncall).

11. Compatibility and migration notes

- When changing reason codes or Decision Event schema, include a compatibility shim for 60 days. Update the schema registry and add transformers in the analytics pipeline.

12. Appendix: example decision event query patterns

- Find the decision path for a request id (pseudo-SQL):
  SELECT * FROM decision_events WHERE request_id = 'req-123' ORDER BY timestamp ASC;

- Aggregate reason code rate by node:
  SELECT node, reason_code, count(*) FROM decision_events WHERE timestamp > now() - interval '15m' GROUP BY node, reason_code ORDER BY count DESC;

13. Change log

- 2024-09-12: initial draft by Riley Chen.
- 2025-03-02: added kernel compatibility table and rollout gates (Aisha Patel review).
- 2026-01-15: updated Decision Event schema and sampling defaults (Marco Silva).

Related material and references

- Scheduler policy language spec (see related pages).
- Request classification and telemetry contract (team-wiki).

Contact

For questions or to request changes to the decision fabric, open a PR against the runtime-scheduler repo and add runtime-scheduler@team as reviewers.

payload.page_title: Admission Insight and Decision Telemetry for Scheduler

sections.body: This page documents the admission and decision-level telemetry requirements for Redwood's kernel scheduler admission controller. It defines the health signatures we rely on for proactive alerting, the canonical decision trace payloads emitted by the scheduler, guidance for downstream consumers (SRE, monitoring, and profiling pipelines), and an operational runbook for incidents that start with admission anomalies.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Make admission behavior observable, debuggable, and auditable without heavy sampling.
- Provide deterministic signals for automated scaling and QoS fallbacks.
- Standardize the decision payload so cross-team tooling (benchmarks, profilers, incident triage) can reason about admission outcomes.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: Applies to: kernel admission controller (admission-layer that decides whether a request is accepted, queued, shed, or routed to fallback), prioritization hooks, and admission-related sidecars that mediate kernel selection. Does not include: detailed kernel internal telemetry (see profiling playbooks) or application-layer traces.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Owner: Kernel Scheduling Team (oncall: kernel-scheduling@redwood.com)
- SLOs for telemetry availability: 99.9% of admission decision events delivered to the trace/telemetry bus within 30s.
- Required retention: 90 days for aggregated metrics; 7 days for full decision traces (default).

Signals and Metrics (what to emit)
1) Admission Counters (per pool, per priority):
- admitted_total: counter of accepted requests
- queued_total: counter of requests placed into the admission queue
- shed_total: counter of requests rejected due to admission policy (backpressure/cost-governor)
- fallback_routed_total: counter of requests routed to lower-fidelity model variant or region

2) Latency Distributions:
- admission_latency_ms: histogram of time spent in admission decision (ms). Important percentiles: p50, p95, p99, p999.

3) Decision Quality Signals:
- kv_prefetch_miss_rate: fraction of requests where the admission decision triggered a KV-prefetch because candidate placement lacked warmed cache
- kernel_mismatch_rate: fraction of admissions where selected kernel was replaced by fallback before execution (indicates race or topology mismatch)

4) Resource Pressure Correlates (per node/pool):
- gpu_memory_pressure_pct: sampled as gauge
- dispatch_credit_deficit: gauge tracking pending credit shortfall that affected admission decisions

5) Decision Trace Payload (one JSON event per decision):
- Fields (canonical):
  - event_id (string): stable UUID for decision event
  - ts (ISO8601 string): time decision completed
  - tenant_id (string): opaque tenant identifier (hashed)
  - request_id (string): request correlation id
  - pool_id (string): scheduler pool or capacity unit
  - intent (string): e.g., text_generation|embedding|chat|rerank
  - priority (string): e.g., realtime|batch|background
  - decision (string): accept|queue|reject|route_fallback|defer
  - reason_codes (list[string]): machine-parsable reasons: e.g., ["memory_limit","slot_saturation","policy_quota"]
  - chosen_kernel (string|null): kernel identifier requested
  - effective_kernel (string|null): kernel actually scheduled (if different)
  - kvcache_state (string): warm|cold|partial
  - estimated_cost_units (number as string): pre-decision estimate of compute units consumed
  - admission_latency_ms (number as string)
  - upstream_routing_hint (string|null): e.g., region/alt-model
  - preemptible (bool as string): "true"|"false"
  - annotations (list[string]): freeform, but limited length

Note: because Confluence JSON schema here requires flat types, the representation above is a spec; emitted traces follow this exact key set. All numeric values are emitted as numbers in telemetry producers; logging pipelines will transform to strings for indexing where necessary.

Alerting and Health Signatures
High-signal alerts (severity: P0/P1):
- Admission rejection spike: shed_total / (admitted_total + queued_total) > 5% sustained for 2m in a customer-facing pool -> P1
- Admission latency growth: p99 admission_latency_ms increases > 3x baseline (baseline = rolling 24h p99) for >5m -> P1
- Kernel flipstorm: kernel_mismatch_rate > 1% sustained for 10m -> P1 (indicates routing or topology bug)
- Decision trace backlog: telemetry queue depth > 1M events or delivery latency > 2m -> P1
Lower-signal alerts (severity: P2):
- kv_prefetch_miss_rate increased by > 2x baseline for 15m -> P2 (may indicate cold start wave)
- dispatch_credit_deficit per pool > threshold -> P2 (operator action may be required)
sections.heading: Owner and SLAs

sections.body:
| Alert name | Query sketch | Threshold | Oncall |
| Admission rejection surge | rate(shed_total[2m]) / rate(admitted_total[2m] + queued_total[2m]) | > 0.05 | kernel-scheduling |
| Admission latency p99 rise | p99_over_window(admission_latency_ms, 5m) / p99_baseline(24h) | > 3x | kernel-scheduling |

Downstream Consumers and Use Cases
- SRE dashboards: per-customer admission heatmap, queue depth, and rejection ratios.
- Auto-scaling controller: uses admitted_total, queued_total, and dispatch_credit_deficit to decide burst capacity vs. preemptible fallbacks.
- Profiling & perf lab: decision traces are sampled (adaptive) and sent to the profiler to reproduce admission-to-kernel mapping regressions.
- Billing correlation: estimated_cost_units used to flag unexpectedly large requests.

Trace Sampling Policy
- Deterministic sampling: keep 1 in 1000 decisions per pool always (for long tail analysis).
- Adaptive tail-sampling: if admission_latency_ms > p99_baseline * 2 or decision==reject or kernel_mismatch, mark for full capture.
- Anonymization: all user-provided tokens must be scrubbed before final trace storage using the standard PII redaction pipeline.

Runbook: Admission Anomaly (triage flow)
1) Detection: Pager triggers for admission rejection surge or p99 latency growth.
2) Initial scoring (5 min): check related metrics: gpu_memory_pressure_pct, dispatch_credit_deficit, kernel_mismatch_rate.
3) Correlate with recent deploys: check canary flags and kernel rollout tags (CI/CD).
4) Fetch decision traces: pull decision_trace events for the affected pool (last 15m). Commands:
- cli: rtel telemetry query --pool <pool_id> --since 15m --filter decision!=accept --output json | jq .
- dashboard: Admission -> Pool -> "Decision Traces" (time range)
5) If kernel_mismatch_rate high -> rollback kernel rollout or toggle routing to safe kernel variant.
6) If memory pressure -> trigger eviction playbook (link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook-2026).
7) If dispatch_credit_deficit -> increase pool burst quota or enable preemptible routing for low-priority classes.
8) Post-incident: attach decision trace artifacts to the incident and run a 72h regression watch.

Implementation Notes and Instrumentation Examples
- Emit decision events synchronously to the local agent (lightweight UDP forwarder) and batch to the telemetry bus. Use backpressure strategy: if telemetry channel is congested, still accept requests but mark decision.trace_sampled=false and increment shed_telemetry_backpressure counter.
sections.heading: Alert definition table (example)

sections.body:
```go
type DecisionEvent struct {
  EventID string
  TS string
  TenantID string
  RequestID string
  PoolID string
  Intent string
  Priority string
  Decision string
  ReasonCodes []string
  ChosenKernel string
  EffectiveKernel string
  KVCacheState string
  EstimatedCostUnits float64
  AdmissionLatencyMs float64
  UpstreamRoutingHint string
  Preemptible bool
  Annotations []string
}

func emitDecision(e DecisionEvent) error {
  // light validation, then enqueue to local forwarder
  payload, _ := json.Marshal(e)
  localAgent.Enqueue(payload)
}
```

Telemetry Elasticity and Cost Considerations
- Full decision traces are expensive. Default policy: 99.9% of decisions reduce to counters/metrics; full JSON trace capture limited by sampling policy above.
- Provide an opt-in "forensic capture" mode for support tickets (time limited, customer-scoped). Forensic captures require approval and generate a special marker in the trace header.

Backwards Compatibility and Migration
- New fields must be optional. The ingestion pipeline tolerates missing keys. Consumers should prefer name-based lookup, not positional parsing.
- Migration plan for any field rename: maintain alias mapping in the telemetry ingest layer for 90 days and emit both keys for the transition period.

References and Links
- Kernel policy language: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Memory pressure runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook-2026
- Profiling playbook (decision-to-kernel mapping): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026

Appendix: Quick queries
- Rejection ratio (PromQL sketch): sum(rate(shed_total[2m])) / (sum(rate(admitted_total[2m])) + sum(rate(queued_total[2m])))
- Kernel mismatch rate: sum(rate(kernel_mismatch_count[5m])) / sum(rate(admitted_total[5m]))

Contact and escalation
- Kernel Scheduling oncall: kernel-scheduling@redwood.com
- Telemetry infra: telemetry-platform@redwood.com

sections.body:

- 2026-02-15 — Added sampling policy, alert thresholds, and runbook actions (Ethan Walker)
