payload.page_title: Hotpath Runtime Compendium: Scheduler, Profiling, and Benchmarking

sections.body: This page consolidates our operational guidance for the serving runtime hotpath: architecture notes, kernel scheduling strategies, a step-by-step profiling playbook, our benchmarking suite workflow, release / rollout checklist for runtime changes, and common runbook actions for incidents. It is intended for runtime engineers, oncall SREs, and performance-focused ML engineers.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to the Redwood serving runtime (hosted + dedicated pools) for transformer-style text models (causal / encoder-decoder).
- Covers latency-sensitive request flows (inference hotpath) from request ingress to token emission.
- Assumes familiarity with basic GPU tooling (nvidia-smi, nsight, nvprof alternatives) and our observability stack (Prometheus / Grafana / Jaeger).

1) Hotpath architecture (concise)
sections.heading: Scope and assumptions

sections.body:
- Ingress: API gateway -> rate-limit / auth -> request router
- Router: policy engine (route by latency tier, model variant, region) -> dispatcher
- Dispatcher: request admission + slot allocator -> worker pool (CPU warmup, KV cache lookup)
- Worker: process request (tokenize -> forward cache lookup -> kernel invocation -> emit tokens)
- Kernel layer: per-model kernel selector chooses optimized operator kernels based on sequence length, dtype, and hardware capability.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- request-router-service (team: eng-platform) - routing logic and policy config
- hotpath-dispatcher (team: eng-serving-runtime) - admission, batching, backpressure
- worker-runtime (team: eng-serving-runtime) - kernel invocation, KV cache, async emission
- kernel-selector (team: eng-serving-runtime) - maps model profiles -> kernel bundle
sections.heading: Key components and ownership

sections.body:
- tail P99 latency (1-token step): 120ms for "low-latency" tier models
- request success rate (no internal error): 99.95% monthly
- GPU utilization target per-pool: 65-85% (avoid sustained 95%+)

2) Kernel scheduling and batching patterns
sections.heading: SLOs to enforce (examples)

sections.body:
- Maximize throughput and GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs for low-latency tiers.
- Graceful degradation: when under pressure, reduce batch size and fallback to smaller kernel or quantized variant.
sections.heading: Design goals

sections.body:
- Admission control: token-budget based admission (requests carry a token budget calculated from expected tokens * model profile).
- Continuous batching: sliding-window batching with max batch size and batch-hold windows tuned per-model.
- Slotting: reserve a fraction of GPU slots (5-15%) for preemptible low-latency tickets.
- Preemption: long batch jobs (cost-optimized queues) can yield to latency tickets with checkpointed KV cache snapshots.
sections.heading: Policies implemented in runtime

sections.body:
1. If context length <= short_seq_threshold -> use small-seq fused kernels (fast path).
2. If dtype == int8/4 && accuracy-profile ok -> use quantized kernels.
3. If requested streaming == true -> prefer kernels that support incremental KV updates with minimal kernel launch overhead.
4. When GPU SM occupancy low -> consider larger GEMM epilog kernels that increase occupancy at expense of some latency.
sections.heading: Kernel selection heuristics (high-level)

sections.body:
- max_batch_size: 32
- batch_hold_ms: 6  # max time to wait for additional requests
- slot_reserve_percent: 10
- preemption_timeout_ms: 45
- short_seq_threshold: 64

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Goal: gather targeted traces that isolate kernel latencies, memory traffic, and scheduler behavior for a failing SLA or performance regression.
sections.heading: Operator-level scheduling knobs (config examples)

sections.body:
- Reproduce on staging with same model version and quantization profile.
- Ensure GPU MIG / VM shape matches production (if applicable).
- Clear KV cache between runs unless reproducing cached behavior.
- Note current config: model_profile_id, kernel_bundle_id, dispatcher_config_id.

B) Collection commands (examples)
- Lightweight traces (first-pass):
  - Collect runtime spans: curl -sS "http://staging-metrics:4317/trace?span=hotpath" > /tmp/hotpath-spans.json
  - Prometheus scrape: curl -sS "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=hotpath_token_latency_ms"
- GPU-level sampling (10s sampling to avoid noise):
  - ncu --target-processes all --set full --duration 10 --output ./ncu-hotpath-10s ./bin/worker-runtime --run-case PROFILE
- NVTX markers: ensure run compiled with NVTX_ENABLED=1. Use nvtxRangePushA / Pop around scheduling and kernel launches.
- Kernel timeline: nsight systems capture for 15s: nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output=hotpath-nsys-15s ./bin/worker-runtime --run-case PROFILE
sections.heading: A) Pre-collection checklist

sections.body:
- Frequent short kernels with large launch overheads: indicates high kernel-launch overhead; consider kernel fusion or batched dispatch.
- Long device-to-device memcpy around KV cache: indicates suboptimal KV layout or host-GPU path.
- Underfilled GPU SM occupancy during large GEMM: verify tensor shapes and autoshape padding.
- Kernel thrashing: frequent context switches between kernels tied to many tiny batches.

D) Example NVTX strategy (C++ pseudocode)
- nvtxRangePushA("dispatch:admit"); admit(); nvtxRangePop();
- nvtxRangePushA("kernel:attention_fused"); launch_attention(); nvtxRangePop();
sections.heading: C) What to look for in traces

sections.body:
- Attach: nsys output, ncu summary, traces (jaeger/spans), Prometheus graphs (p50/p95/p99), GPU metrics (util, mem BW, SM occupancy).
- Summarize: top 3 suspects, recommended mitigations (config + code change), regression delta vs baseline.

4) Benchmarking suite and reproducibility
sections.heading: E) Reporting checklist

sections.body:
- redwood-runtime-bench (harness): generates synthetic and replayed traffic (replay from production traces redwood-replay-format).
- model-profile catalog: canonical input shapes, token distributions, quantization settings.
- harness runner: supports --latency-only, --throughput-saturation, --profile-kernels.
sections.heading: Suite components

sections.body:
1. Latency test (single-tenant, concurrency=1): command example:
   redwood-runtime-bench --model-id gptx-lite-6B --mode latency --samples 200 --seed 42 --output results/latency-gptx-6b.json
2. Throughput saturation (find max tokens/sec while keeping p99 <= target):
   redwood-runtime-bench --model-id gptx-lite-6B --mode throughput --target-p99 150 --max-concurrency 128 --auto-scale
3. Cold-start memory profile (cold worker startup):
   redwood-runtime-bench --model-id gptx-lite-6B --mode cold-start --iterations 50
sections.heading: Standard benchmarks (run on a reserved pool)

sections.body:
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies (per-token and per-request)
- tokens/sec and GPU utilization (per-GPU and pool-level)
- memory high-water marks and swap counts (if any)
- kernel-level breakdown: top 10 kernels by total time
sections.heading: Metrics to record (minimum)

sections.body:
- Use deterministic seeds and fixed tokenizer versions.
- Record: hardware image, driver version, cuDNN / CUDA versions, kernel bundle hash, model artifact hash.
- Store benchmark run metadata in artifacts: artifacts/<benchmark-id>/metadata.json

5) Release notes and rollout checklist for runtime changes

When releasing a kernel change, scheduler tweak, or dispatcher patch follow this minimal checklist:
1. PREP: create RFC and target metrics (p99 latency change allowed, throughput delta).
2. LAB: run full benchmark suite on a staging pool; attach results to PR.
3. CANARY: deploy to 1-3% of traffic in non-critical region, enable detailed traces.
4. OBSERVE: watch the canary for 24h (or 3x the peak window), key metrics: errors, p99, GPU util, slot starvation events.
5. ROLLOUT: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 1h stabilization windows; rollback if p99 increased by > 15% or error rate increased > 0.05%.
sections.heading: Reproducibility notes

sections.body:
- pause deployments: kubectl -n runtime scale deploy worker-runtime --replicas=0 (canary pods removed)
- redirect new traffic to previous model kernel bundle via kernel-selector override: curl -X POST "$ROUTER_API/override" -d '{"model":"gptx-lite-6B","kernel_bundle":"bundle:v23.11"}'
- if auto-scaling groups are affected, scale down new pool and scale up previous pool.

6) Known issues (brief catalog & mitigations)

- Issue: Kernel-launch jitter causing P99 spikes
  - Symptoms: many 1–3ms kernels visible, high scheduler queueing, P99 oscillation with low throughput.
  - Mitigation: enable kernel fusion for short sequences or increase batch_hold_ms by +2ms; short-term, add 5% slot reserve for low-latency traffic.

- Issue: KV cache thrash on long-context workloads
  - Symptoms: excessive device-host memcpy, cache miss storms, higher latency for streaming requests.
  - Mitigation: increase KV shard count and use pinned memory for KV mapping; tune cache eviction policy to LRU-approx with time decay.

- Issue: GPU memory OOM during mixed-concurrency bursts
  - Symptoms: OOM errors, worker restarts, degraded throughput.
  - Mitigation: enforce per-request memory budgets and backpressure; enable soft-eviction that offloads least-recent tokens to host fallback store.

7) Runtime runbooks (stepped procedures)

A) High P99 incident (triage)
1. Confirm alert (Grafana) and collect time window + request ids.
2. Check recent deploys: git tag / image digest for worker-runtime and kernel-bundle.
3. Run lightweight profiling (2–5s ncu sample) on a canary node to see kernel breakdown.
4. If kernel-launch jitter suspected, switch to fallback kernel-bundle:
   curl -X POST "$ROUTER_API/override" -d '{"model":"<model>","kernel_bundle":"<fallback>"}'
5. If KV thrash suspected, temporarily raise cache-hit padding (eviction_lifetime_ms += 50).
6. Notify stakeholders via incident channel with status and mitigation actions.

B) GPU OOM recovery
1. Identify OOMing worker (kubectl logs -n runtime <pod>).
2. Mark node unschedulable and cordon (kubectl cordon <node>).
3. Drain non-critical pods and restart the worker-runtime with reduced concurrency profile: set env WORKER_MAX_CONCURRENCY=2.
4. Verify memory stabilizes for 15 minutes, then gradually restore concurrency.
5. Root cause follow-up: collect heap + device mem snapshots for forensics.

8) Appendices

A) Example dispatcher config (YAML)
---
dispatcher_config_id: hotpath-smallseq-2026
max_batch_size: 24
batch_hold_ms: 6
slot_reserve_percent: 10
preemption_timeout_ms: 45
short_seq_threshold: 64
---

B) Kernel mapping table (abbreviated)
| Sequence len | Dtype | Kernel bundle | Notes |
|-------------:|:-----:|:-------------:|:------|
|  <=32        | fp16  | kbundle:fast-fused-v1 | fused-attn + qkv merge |
|  33-128      | fp16  | kbundle:balanced-v2   | occupancy vs latency trade |
|  >128        | fp16  | kbundle:large-batched | padded GEMM for occupancy |
|  any         | int8  | kbundle:quant-v1      | accuracy-tested quant ops |

C) Useful CLI snippets
- Check pool GPU status: kubectl -n runtime exec -it pool-manager -- /bin/pool-status --pool hotpath-smallseq
- Trigger a local benchmark: redwood-runtime-bench --model-id example-7b --mode latency --samples 100

D) Contact / escalation matrix
- Primary oncall (serving-runtime): @diego (Slack: #oncall-serving-runtime)
- Secondary: @priya (Slack)
- Escalation to eng-sre: page SRE pager if incident impact > 30 minutes or P99 > target by 2x.

payload.page_title: Adaptive Fidelity Decision Log & Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This document captures the decision rationale and operational playbook for adaptive-fidelity behavior in the serving runtime. It is intended for oncall engineers, runtime operators, and product owners who must make or review changes to fidelity-orchestration policies (quality <-> cost <-> latency tradeoffs) and eviction/topology actions during normal operations and incidents.

Why this exists:
- Adaptive fidelity (also known as fidelity orchestration) is the runtime component that reduces model or execution fidelity to preserve SLOs (latency/availability) during capacity pressure or incident scenarios.
- Without a documented decision trail and safe runbook, fidelity changes risk causing silent quality regressions or customer-impacting rollbacks.

Scope and systems referenced:
- fidelity-orchestrator (service): policy engine that issues fidelity-advice (quantize, half-precision, variant-switch, reduce-beam) and hard actions (route-to-variant, throttle, shed).
- runtime-orchestrator: accepts fidelity advice and performs routing/eviction as well as kv-cache coordination.
- scheduler-gw / kernel-shepherd: component responsible for admission control and kernel selection.
- eviction-operator: cross-node component that enacts shard-level evictions and reports consistency fences.

Decision log (chronological highlights):
1) 2025-07-21 — Adopted a two-tier fidelity policy: advisory (soft) and enforced (hard). Rationale: allow safe observability and gradual rollouts. Owner: Runtimes team.
2) 2025-11-03 — Introduced "fidelity-budget" per tenant to bound economic impact during long incidents. Rationale: protect high-value tenants from repeated large-quality shifts. Owner: Finance+Runtimes.
3) 2026-01-10 — Default policy change: prefer model-variant-switch to kernel-level quantization for burst-induced latency SLO preservation. Rationale: empirical regressions in long-form generation when live-quantizing. Owner: Applied ML + Runtimes.

Operational guarantees and SLO mappings:
- Safety boundary: any enforced fidelity change must be logged and include a validated rollback path (automated or documented manual steps).
- Quality SLO: per-model baseline eval_score (internal eval harness metric). Hard guard: enforced fidelity must not reduce eval_score by > 3 percentage points without explicit stakeholder signoff.
- Latency SLOs (examples):
  - short-response 95th pctl <= 120ms (route preference: low-latency variants)
  - completion 99th pctl <= 1s for <512 tokens on dedicated pools
- Cost guardrails: fidelity-budget throttle at 30% monthly overspend triggers notification and limits further enforced fidelity changes.

Playbook: when fidelity-orchestrator recommends a change (automated or manual)
1) Triage and context (owner: oncall/runtime):
   - Confirm trigger: kernel queue length > Q_HIGH (default 4x baseline) OR node-eviction-in-flight OR NVTHERMAL alert.
   - Pull recent traces: runtime-orchestrator/traces/<request_id> and fidelity-orchestrator/decision/<decision_id>.
   - Check related KPIs: 95p latency, kernel-queue-depth, model-kvcache-hit-rate.

2) Advisory mode (first 10 minutes):
   - Apply advisory-only advice in fidelity-orchestrator (no enforced routing).
   - Create a short-lived traffic mirror (shadow) to the advised variant for perf/quality verification. Use CLI:
     rdxctl fidelity advise --tenant $TENANT --policy burst-preserve-latency --mode advisory --duration 10m
   - Observe: latency, token-cost delta, eval-score proxy (short sample prompt set).

3) Enforce-only after verification (manual or automated conditional):
   - If advisory mirror shows latency improvement >= 30% on key cohorts and eval-score proxy degradation <= 1.5 points, proceed to a staged enforce:
     a) Canary group (1% traffic) for 5 minutes
     b) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 30 minutes if KPIs healthy
   - rdxctl fidelity enforce --tenant $TENANT --policy model-variant-switch --canary 1% --rollback-window 30m

4) Rollback and emergency revert:
   - Automated rollback conditions (runtime-orchestrator): 95p latency increases by > 20% vs baseline OR error-rate spike > 5x
   - Manual rollback steps (oncall):
     1. rdxctl fidelity rollback --decision <decision_id>
     2. Validate KV-consistency: rdxctl kvcache check --shard <shard_id> and wait for fence=clear (max 2m).
     3. If kvcache fence fails, escalate to eviction-operator owners and follow "KV recovery and rehydration" runbook (link below).

Safety checklist before any enforced policy is applied:
- Owner and reviewer listed in fidelity decision record (email + ticket).
- Corresponding canary health dashboards created: latency, error-rate, cost-per-token, eval-proxy.
- Rollback automation verified and tested in the last 72h (smoke).

Runbook: emergency fidelity hard-stop (when incident requires immediate preservation of availability)
- Trigger: simultaneous NVTHERMAL + kernel-watchdog + 95p latency > SLO and burst length > 10s.
- Action (immediate):
  1) Oncall executes: rdxctl fidelity emergency-hold --global --reason "thermal+queue"
  2) runtime-orchestrator will immediately switch affected routing to pre-approved low-fidelity variants (predefined set) and disable new long-running kernels.
  3) Notify impacted tenants via incident channel and open incident ticket with tag runtime-fidelity-emergency.
  4) Begin 15-minute observation window. If stability returns, begin staged re-enable per "Playbook" above.

KV cache and eviction coordination notes:
- Eviction ordering: eviction-operator must ensure kvcache fence idempotency: eviction-operator -> runtime-orchestrator: POST /eviction/start -> include fence_id -> runtime-orchestrator acknowledges -> proceed.
- If an enforced fidelity change requires variant swap with incompatible KV layout, follow this sequence:
  1) Advisory mirror (no kvcache writes)
  2) Quiesce writes to kvcache shard: rdxctl kvcache drain --shard <id> --timeout 60s
  3) Perform variant swap and warmstart new kernels
  4) Rehydrate cache via background replay (rate-limited)

Example policy config (JSON snippet to be used in fidelity-orchestrator):
{
  "policy_id": "burst-preserve-latency-v2",
  "triggers": {
    "kernel_queue_multiplier": 3.5,
    "node_cpu_usage": 0.85
  },
  "actions": [
    {
      "type": "model_variant_switch",
      "variants": ["variant-latency-1", "variant-latency-2"],
      "scope": "tenant"
    }
  ],
  "guards": {
    "max_eval_drop_pct": 3.0,
    "cost_budget_pct": 30
  }
}

Smoke tests (pre-deploy validation):
- Synthetic microburst: simulate 10s 10x traffic spike against staging clusters with fidelity-budget=unbounded and ensure auto-advisory path runs without errors.
- KV compatibility test: run variant-swap + cache-drain + rehydrate sequence in a local 3-node staging cluster. Verify no dropped requests and latency within 2x baseline.
- Canary rollback test: force an error-rate spike and verify the automated rollback completes within the configured rollback-window.

Dashboards and alerts (minimum set):
- fidelity-orchestrator/decisions (counts by type, avg latency benefit, avg eval-proxy delta)
- runtime-orchestrator/95p-latency-by-tenant (alert: > SLO*1.25 for 5m)
- kvcache/eviction-fence-failures (alert: >0 in 10m)
- scheduler-gw/kernel-queue-depth (warning: > baseline*3)

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owners: Runtimes team (oncall rotation: runtimes-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary owners: Applied ML (quality regressions), SRE (eviction/cluster stability), Finance (fidelity budget overrun).
- Escalation path: oncall -> service-owner -> SRE lead -> VP Eng. Use incident tag: runtime-fidelity.

Post-incident analysis and required artifacts:
- Decision record update: add reason, traces, metrics and signed-off owner within 48 hours.
- Eval-run: run the canonical eval set for affected models (mark baseline vs post-change) and store results in /evals/fidelity/<decision_id>.
- Experiment: if an enforced policy was used, create an experiment ticket to test alternate mitigations (e.g., latency-aware batching) within 14 days.

Appendix A — Quick CLI cheatsheet:
- Advise (advisory-only): rdxctl fidelity advise --tenant $TENANT --policy $POLICY --duration 10m
- Enforce with canary: rdxctl fidelity enforce --tenant $TENANT --policy $POLICY --canary 1% --rollback-window 30m
- Rollback: rdxctl fidelity rollback --decision <decision_id>
- KV drain: rdxctl kvcache drain --shard <shard_id> --timeout 60s

Appendix B — Example staging test matrix (table):
- Test | Goal | Pass criteria
- Synthetic microburst | ensure advisory path triggers | advisory decision recorded, no errors
- Variant-swap + rehydrate | KV compatibility during swap | no requests dropped, cache warm within 10m
- Canary rollback | verify rollback automation | rollback completes within 2x rollback-window

References:
- Runtime decision delegation patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-delegation-and-observer-patterns-2026
- KV cache lifecycle: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024
- Fidelity containment experiment notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/fidelity-containment-and-cost-feedback-playbook-2026

Last reviewed: 2026-03-10 by Jonah Kim and María Torres.

payload.page_title: Slow Kernel Detection and Hotfix Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes detection, automated containment, and manual hotfix procedures for incidents where a GPU kernel (or small set of kernels) regress in latency or CPU/GPU time and produce sustained throughput degradation. It focuses on actionable detection signals, escalation thresholds, immediate mitigations to protect SLAs, and validated release steps for kernel hotfixes.

Scope

- Applies to production inference runtime kernels (attention, fused-matmul, kv-cache ops, rotary/rope ops) across hosted and dedicated clusters.
- Does NOT cover hardware faults (power/thermal fails) or driver-level crashes — those are handled by infrastructure runbooks.

Ownership and contacts

- Incident owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall (primary).
- Kernel lead: @Maya Chen (runtime-kernels).
- Escalation: runtime-arch-sre@redwood.internal.

When to use this playbook
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Kernel latency spike or variance is correlated with increased end-to-end p95/p99 serving latency for >5 minutes.
2) Throughput drop or request queuing increases by >30% while GPU utilization is not saturated.
3) Automated regression detection (see Alerting rules) fires.

Detection signals and telemetry
sections.heading: Use this playbook when

sections.body:
- kernel.exec_time_ms (histogram per kernel): sudden shift in median or tail.
- kernel.cpu_time_ms and kernel.gpu_time_ms: divergence indicates scheduling/serialization issues.
- runtime.request_queue_depth: sustained increase suggests backpressure.
- gpu_utilization_pct: if <85% while queue depth grows => kernel stalls/serialization.
- kernel.retry_count / kernel_ejection_count: raised ejection counts.
sections.heading: Primary metrics to monitor (examples)

sections.body:
- name: KernelTailLatencyExceeded
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[2m])) by (le,kernel)) > 12
  for: 4m

- name: KernelVarianceSpike
  expr: (quantile_over_time(0.95, kernel_exec_time_ms[10m]) / quantile_over_time(0.5, kernel_exec_time_ms[10m])) > 4
  for: 3m

- name: QueueGrowthWithLowUtil
  expr: (increase(runtime_request_queue_depth[5m]) > 30) and (avg_over_time(gpu_utilization_pct[5m]) < 85)
  for: 5m

Investigation timeline (first 30 minutes)

1) Triage (0–5m):
   - Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and tag with incident channel.
   - Attach the alert graph and note the affected model(s)/cluster(s).

2) Quick checks (5–12m):
   - Confirm whether regression is per-kernel or broad: query kernel.exec_time_ms grouped by kernel_name and host.
   - Check recent releases or kernel rollouts in the last 60 minutes.
   - Inspect kernel ejection logs and driver warnings.

3) Decide containment (12–20m):
   - If kernel impact is limited to a subset of workers, use targeted quarantine (see Automated mitigations).
   - If impact is global or affects control-plane operations, follow full degradation playbook and notify product & CS.

Automated mitigations (safe by default)

We prefer automated, reversible actions to avoid manual intervention during noisy transient spikes. Typical automated mitigations:

- Kernel quarantine: mark kernel variant as degraded and route traffic to next-compatible variant (e.g., fallback quantized kernel or older kernel build).
- Per-host kernel disable: use runtime-agent to toggle kernel blacklist on affected hosts.
- Graceful request shed: temporarily reduce concurrency for affected hosts and redirect to healthy pools.
sections.heading: Suggested alert rules (promQL-like pseudocode)

sections.body:
redwood-runtimectl quarantine-kernel --kernel-name fused_attn_v2 --reason "p95 regression 2026-02-28" --scope hosts=pool-3b
redwood-runtimectl set-concurrency --host host-12 --max-concurrency 2
sections.heading: Example internal CLI commands

sections.body:
| Impact pattern | Immediate action | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Single-host / single-kernel | Kernel quarantine + local restart | Limits blast radius |
| Multi-host same kernel | Route to fallback variant + scale healthy pool | Prevents large SLA violations |
| Global performance regression | Activate degradation SLOs and roll back recent kernel rollout | Protect customer-facing SLAs |

Manual hotfix procedure (if automation insufficient)

1) Create incident branch and patch:
   - Branch from release-tag: git checkout -b hotfix/kernel-<id>-<date> release/<tag>
   - Add guard-logging (timestamps + kernel id) and revert recent non-essential optimizations if needed.

2) Build and smoke test in staging:
   - Build: make -C runtime kernels && ./tools/build-kernel --name hotfix-kernel --ccache
   - Unit smoke: ./tools/smoke-runner --kernel hotfix-kernel --profile micro-latency
   - Perf microbench: ./bench/kernel-bench --kernel hotfix-kernel --seq-lens 8,64,512 --shots 200

3) Canaried rollout (targeted pattern):
   - Canary to 2–3 hosts with mirrored traffic for 10m.
   - Metrics to watch during canary: p50/p95 kernel.exec_time_ms, request_queue_depth, gpu_utilization, error_rate.
   - Canary acceptance criteria: no >5% regression vs baseline on p50 and <3% change in p95.

4) Gradual ramp: 20% -> 50% -> 100% or by host pools depending on topology. Evaluate at each step for 10–15 minutes.

Rollback criteria and steps

Rollback if any of the following occurs during canary or ramp:
- p95 increases by >10% relative to the pre-incident baseline.
- request queue depth increases by >2x.
- error rate (5xx) increases above SLO thresholds.
sections.heading: Containment decision matrix (summary)

sections.body:
1) Immediately set routing to previous kernel variant using runtime controller.
2) Drain canary hosts and reboot agent if necessary: systemctl restart runtime-agent on canary hosts.
3) Mark hotfix branch for postmortem and revert patch in mainline if necessary.

Verification checklist after rollback/hotfix

- Verify kernel.exec_time_ms histograms have returned to baseline over 30 minutes.
- Validate no increase in request_retries or request_timeouts.
- Confirm logs show no new driver warnings.
- Close incident with updates to relevant oncall and product teams.

Post-incident follow-up

- Owner prepares postmortem within 72 hours: root cause, timeline, mitigations, action items.
- If kernel regression was caused by a code change, add mandatory microbench in CI for the offending kernel with 95th percentile assertions.
- Schedule a retro with kernel authors and SRE to adjust thresholds or automation if false positives/negatives caused disruption.

Testing and benchmark additions

When a kernel shows instability add these tests to the CI pipeline:
- Deterministic microbenchmark for sequence lengths: 8, 32, 128, 512 (200 iterations each).
- Telemetry spike test: inject synthetic jitter and assert no >2x increase in hardware stall markers.
- Multi-host soak test: run 60-minute concurrent-run against a mirrored traffic profile.

Quick reference commands

- Query per-kernel tail latency (internal monitoring):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MONITOR_TOKEN" "https://monitoring.internal/api/query?q=kernel_exec_time_ms%7Bcluster%3D%5C\"prod%5C\"%7D"

- Quarantine kernel: redwood-runtimectl quarantine-kernel --kernel-name <kernel> --scope hosts=<pool>
- Re-enable kernel: redwood-runtimectl unquarantine-kernel --kernel-name <kernel>
- Canary rollout: redwood-runtimectl deploy-kernel --image hotfix-kernel:canary --hosts host-12,host-13

Appendix: recommended thresholds (editable)

| Setting | Default value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| p95_kernel_latency_alert_ms | 12 | Trigger for KernelTailLatencyExceeded rule |
| kernel_variance_ratio_alert | 4 | Ratio of p95/p50 over 10m window |
| queue_growth_pct_alert | 30 | Percent growth over 5 minutes |
| canary_observe_window | 10m | Observation window for canary acceptance |

Related artifacts and links

- Kernel perf harness: git:/repo/runtime/kernels/bench/
- Quarantine controller docs: /eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/quarantine-controller-2025
- Incident tracker template: /oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

Revision history

- 2026-01-15: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-10: Added automated mitigation examples and CLI snippets.
- 2026-02-28: Finalized thresholds and canary acceptance criteria (published).

payload.page_title: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype — rollout runbook

sections.body:
This runbook describes how to safely enable and ramp the mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware scheduling) in production pools.

Primary goal: reduce user-visible p95 tail latency (TTFT and end-to-end) under mixed prompt-length distributions without materially regressing throughput or fairness.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Preconditions and required sign-offs
- Feature flag enablement and safe parameter ramps
- Monitoring checklist and known-bad signals
- Rollback procedure
- Owner rotation and escalation

---
sections.heading: This runbook covers

sections.body: Applies to runtime version(s) that include the prototype scheduler (currently: runtime-1.18+ candidate builds where the feature flag is present).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Hosted API: a single canary region/pool first (typically us-east)
- Dedicated: a small, opt-in subset of Dedicated GPU pools with mixed-workload symptoms
sections.heading: In-scope deployment targets

sections.body:
- Multi-tenant QoS tier productization
- Broad admission-control redesign (only minimal coupling to existing backpressure)

---
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Short vs long class**: request classification based on prompt/context length and/or predicted prefill cost.
- **Two-queue dispatch**: separate queues for short/long with a policy bias toward short while guaranteeing progress for long.
- **Aging/starvation prevention**: long requests accrue priority with time-in-queue, preventing indefinite delay.
- **Token budgets**: per-iteration limits (especially for long-prefill dominance) to avoid tail amplification.

---
sections.heading: Definitions (quick)

sections.body:
- Rollout driver / on-point: **Rafael Mendes (SRE/Canary Ops)**
- Runtime scheduling on-call / implementation: **Marcus Reed** (backup: **Omar El-Sayed**)
- Scheduler policy TL: **Lena Fischer**
- SRE sponsor / guardrails: **Sean Gallagher**
- Observability: **Allison Grant** (backup: **Logan Wright**)
- Release coordination: **Connor O'Brien**
sections.heading: Primary owners (during canary windows)

sections.body:
Escalate immediately to #incidents and page SRE on-call if any rollback trigger fires (see “Rollback triggers”).

If symptoms are contained and do not breach rollback triggers:
1) Ping #eng-runtime with dashboard links + parameter snapshot
2) If suspect instrumentation or dashboard integrity: ping #eng-sre and @Allison Grant
3) If suspect kernel thrash/selection instability: ping kernel on-call and @Yuki Sato
sections.heading: Escalation rules

sections.body:
- Coordination: #eng-runtime, #eng-sre, #eng-releases
- Incidents: #incidents

---
sections.heading: Comms channels

sections.body:
- Feature flag is present and off by default in target pools.
- Config validation bounds are deployed (prevents unsafe parameter values).
- Per-class metrics are emitting in the target environment.
sections.heading: 1) Code + config readiness

sections.body:
- Dashboard for class metrics is live and verified in the target region/pool.
- Tail latency guardrails (allowed drift) are agreed for the canary window.
- Rollback procedure is tested (dry-run) in staging.
sections.heading: 2) SRE guardrails and dashboards ready

sections.body:
- Baseline measurements captured for at least 24h (or one full traffic cycle) with flag OFF:
  - p50/p95/p99 TTFT
  - p50/p95 end-to-end latency
  - throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec)
  - error rates (timeouts, cancellations)
  - queue time distribution
- Perf-canary nightly job is green for mixed workload scenarios (or explicitly waived with justification).
sections.heading: 3) Canaries and baseline established

sections.body:
- Runtime Scheduling EM (Sofia Ivanova) approves the canary enablement.
- SRE sponsor (Sean Gallagher) approves guardrails + rollback triggers.
- Release coordinator (Connor O'Brien) acknowledges the ramp window and comms plan.

---
sections.heading: 4) Approvals

sections.body: - `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled`
sections.heading: Feature flag name

sections.body:
- Can be enabled per pool.
- Should NOT be enabled globally during prototype.
sections.heading: Flag scope

sections.body:
These are the minimum knobs expected to be exposed for safe ramps. Exact names may differ slightly by runtime build; verify in runtime config docs for the current release.

1) Classification
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.mode`: `tokens` | `prefill_cost`
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.short_prompt_tokens_threshold`: e.g., 256
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.long_context_tokens_threshold`: e.g., 2048 (optional override)

2) Dispatch policy
- `scheduler.mixed.dispatch.short_weight`: bias for short queue selection (e.g., 3)
- `scheduler.mixed.dispatch.long_weight`: baseline for long queue (e.g., 1)
- `scheduler.mixed.aging.enabled`: true/false
- `scheduler.mixed.aging.half_life_ms`: e.g., 2000–6000ms

3) Token budgets / guardrails
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.enabled`: true/false
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long`: e.g., 4096–8192
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long`: e.g., 1024–2048
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_skew_ratio_short_to_long`: e.g., 6.0 (prevents starving long)

4) Safety bounds
- `scheduler.mixed.safety.burst_cap_short_queue`: e.g., 2–4 iterations of preferential short dispatch before forcing a long opportunity
- `scheduler.mixed.safety.max_queue_wait_ms_long`: e.g., 15000 (if exceeded, the system should prioritize long)

---
sections.heading: Core knobs (prototype)

sections.body:
- Ramp in two dimensions separately:
  1) Enable flag for a very small traffic slice (or a small pool subset)
  2) Increase policy bias/weights gradually (do not jump to aggressive settings)
- Prefer parameter changes over code changes during canary.
- Keep rollback simple: flip the flag OFF first; only then consider reverting config.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1) **Stage 0: Baseline** (flag OFF)
   - Duration: 24h
   - Output: baseline dashboard snapshot + notes on known mix (% long contexts)

2) **Stage 1: Enable with conservative params**
   - Scope: 1 canary pool (or lowest viable slice)
   - Duration: 2–4h
   - Goal: validate correctness + no regressions, confirm metrics

3) **Stage 2: Increase bias modestly**
   - Duration: 4–8h
   - Goal: observe p95 improvement for short class without long starvation

4) **Stage 3: Overnight soak**
   - Duration: 12–24h
   - Goal: cover diurnal mix changes, capacity shifts, and autoscaling events

5) **Stage 4: Expand scope**
   - Add one more pool OR increase slice in same region
   - Only after meeting success criteria + no near-miss rollbacks
sections.heading: Standard ramp plan (Hosted API canary)

sections.body:
Dedicated pools may have workload-specific sensitivity. Use opt-in pools with active mixed-workload pain. Keep initial enablement to a single pool and do not overlap with customer-side releases when possible.

---
sections.heading: Dedicated ramp plan

sections.body: Use these as starting points; do not treat as universal defaults.
sections.heading: Parameter presets (starting points)

sections.body:
- short_weight=2, long_weight=1
- aging.enabled=true, aging.half_life_ms=6000
- budget.enabled=true
- max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long=4096
- max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long=1024
- short_prompt_tokens_threshold=256
- burst_cap_short_queue=2
sections.heading: Preset A (Conservative)

sections.body:
- short_weight=3, long_weight=1
- aging.enabled=true, aging.half_life_ms=4000
- budget.enabled=true
- max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long=8192
- max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long=2048
- short_prompt_tokens_threshold=256
- burst_cap_short_queue=3
sections.heading: Preset B (Balanced)

sections.body:
- Start with Preset A for first enablement in a new environment.
- Move to Preset B only after confirming long-class queue wait and starvation counters remain stable.

---
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body:
1. Confirm change window and on-point coverage.
   - Rollout driver + runtime scheduling + SRE on-call available for the full ramp.
2. Verify target pools and current runtime version.
   - Ensure runtime build includes mixed scheduler flag + metrics.
3. Validate dashboards are live and correct (no missing labels).
   - Queue depth by class
   - Time-in-queue by class
   - TTFT p50/p95 by class
   - End-to-end p95 by route/model
   - Starvation counters
4. Capture baseline snapshot links (flag OFF):
   - 30m window and 6h window
5. Confirm rollback path:
   - Who flips the flag
   - Where to flip it
   - How to confirm it propagated
sections.heading: A) Pre-flight checklist (T-60 to T-15)

sections.body:
1. Apply Preset A (Conservative) to the target pool(s).
2. Enable the feature flag for the target pool(s):
   - Set `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled = true`
3. Confirm propagation:
   - Within 5–10 minutes, verify per-class metrics show non-zero dispatch share in both classes.
   - Confirm the scheduler reports the active policy in runtime logs (expected once per process start or config reload).
sections.heading: B) Enablement (Stage 1)

sections.body:
1. If stable after 30–60 minutes (no rollback triggers), adjust toward Preset B:
   - Increase `short_weight` by +1 (max one adjustment per hour).
   - Optionally reduce `aging.half_life_ms` by 10–25% to improve long progress.
2. After each change, wait a full observation window:
   - Minimum: 30 minutes
   - Preferred: 60–120 minutes if traffic is bursty
3. Do not change classification thresholds and weights in the same step.
sections.heading: C) Ramp (Stage 2/3)

sections.body:
- At least one full soak period (overnight preferred)
- Documented results vs baseline
- No starvation incidents and no near-miss rollback triggers

---
sections.heading: Only expand scope after

sections.body: Monitor the following at minimum.
sections.heading: Monitoring checklist (what to watch)

sections.body:
- Short-class TTFT p95 (primary)
- Overall TTFT p95/p99 (guardrail)
- End-to-end latency p95 by route/model
- Long-class latency p95 (guardrail; should not drift beyond allowed limits)
sections.heading: Latency

sections.body:
- Queue depth by class
- Time-in-queue p95 by class
- Long-class max time-in-queue (watch for creeping ceilings)
sections.heading: Queueing

sections.body:
- Starvation counters (long)
- Dispatch share short vs long (should remain within configured skew bounds)
sections.heading: Fairness / starvation

sections.body:
- Tokens/sec per GPU
- Requests/sec
- GPU utilization stability (watch for oscillation)
sections.heading: Throughput and utilization

sections.body:
- Timeouts (client and server)
- Cancellations / aborted requests
- OOM / KV-cache allocation errors

---
sections.heading: Errors

sections.body: Any of the following should trigger a pause and likely rollback, depending on severity and duration.
sections.heading: Known-bad signals (stop-the-line indicators)

sections.body:
- Sustained p99 TTFT regression > SRE guardrail for the region/pool (per SRE doc).
- Any evidence of long-class starvation:
  - Starvation counters increasing steadily for >5 minutes, OR
  - Long-class time-in-queue max exceeding `scheduler.mixed.safety.max_queue_wait_ms_long` for >10 minutes.
- Error-rate spike attributable to scheduler change (timeouts/cancellations) beyond normal variance.
- Kernel selection instability / thrash that causes visible jitter:
  - Rapid oscillation in kernel choice correlated with latency spikes
  - GPU utilization seesawing with no capacity change
sections.heading: Immediate rollback triggers (do not wait)

sections.body:
- Overall throughput regression > ~3–5% sustained (unless explicitly accepted in the canary plan).
- Long-class p95 increases materially even if short-class improves.
- Queue depth growth without matching traffic increases (possible scheduling dead zone).

---
sections.heading: Investigate and consider rollback

sections.body: Rollback should be fast, reversible, and documented. Prefer flipping the flag OFF before modifying multiple parameters.
sections.heading: Rollback procedure

sections.body:
1) Announce rollback in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre with:
- Pool/region
- Time window
- Dashboard links
- Current parameter snapshot

2) Disable feature flag:
- Set `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled = false` for the target pool(s).

3) Confirm rollback took effect:
- Within 5–10 minutes:
  - Dispatch share by class should collapse to baseline behavior (class metrics may remain but should show no policy bias).
  - TTFT should begin trending back toward baseline.

4) If latency does not recover:
- Check for confounders: capacity events, autoscaling, upstream traffic changes, model rollout.
- If required, revert the config knobs to baseline defaults (last known good).

5) Create follow-up action items:
- File a runtime bug for the observed failure mode, include parameter snapshot and reproduction hints.
- If starvation-related, link to the regression test coverage and validate it ran.
sections.heading: Rollback steps

sections.body:
- If rollback was triggered by guardrails, treat as a canary failure: do not re-enable in that pool until a fix or parameter revision is reviewed by Scheduling TL + SRE sponsor.

---
sections.heading: Post-rollback notes

sections.body: Likely cause: overly aggressive short bias or insufficient aging.
sections.heading: Symptom: short improves, long gets “stuck”

sections.body:
- Verify starvation counters and long time-in-queue.
- Increase long opportunities:
  - Reduce `short_weight` by 1, OR
  - Increase aging aggressiveness (lower `aging.half_life_ms`), OR
  - Reduce `burst_cap_short_queue`.
- If already near limits or unclear, rollback.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body: Likely cause: kernel auto-selection instability when mixing sequence lengths or token budgets causing batch composition oscillations.
sections.heading: Symptom: TTFT jitter / sawtooth patterns

sections.body:
- Check kernel selection logs/metrics for oscillation.
- Temporarily increase long token budget caps (avoid too-tight budget that fragments work) OR return to Preset A.
- If jitter causes p95 regression beyond guardrail, rollback and engage kernel team.
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body: This can be an acceptable trade-off only if explicitly aligned to the canary success criteria.
sections.heading: Symptom: throughput drops but latency improves

sections.body:
- Quantify: tokens/sec delta and cost impact.
- Check whether the token budgets are too conservative (causing under-filled batches).
- If throughput regression is sustained and > agreed bounds, rollback.

---
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
During each stage, the rollout driver must capture:
- Pool(s), region(s), runtime version
- Parameter snapshot (before/after)
- Start/end timestamps for each stage
- Dashboard links: baseline vs canary windows
- Any incidents/near-misses and actions taken

Store links in the Linear initiative (ENG-2417) and update the results summary page if outcomes are meaningful.

---
sections.heading: Documentation requirements (during rollout)

sections.body:
NOTE: Field names may differ by build; use runtime config schema for your release.

```
sections.heading: Appendix A: Example configuration snippet (illustrative)

sections.body:
runtime:
  scheduler:
    mixed_workload:
      enabled: true
      classification:
        mode: tokens
        short_prompt_tokens_threshold: 256
      dispatch:
        short_weight: 2
        long_weight: 1
      aging:
        enabled: true
        half_life_ms: 6000
      budget:
        enabled: true
        max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long: 4096
        max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long: 1024
      safety:
        burst_cap_short_queue: 2
        max_queue_wait_ms_long: 15000
```

---
sections.heading: pool: hosted-us-east-canary

sections.body:
- Short-class TTFT p95 improved or neutral
- Overall p95/p99 within SRE drift guardrails
- No rising starvation counters
- Long-class max time-in-queue stable and below cap
- Errors within normal variance
- Throughput within acceptable bounds

NO-GO / Rollback if any trigger is met (see “Known-bad signals”).
sections.heading: GO if all are true for the prior observation window

payload.page_title: Serving runtime hotfix procedure (Hosted API)

sections.body:
This runbook describes how to execute an emergency hotfix or emergency rollback for the *Hosted API serving runtime*. It is optimized for speed while preserving safety (blast-radius control, verification, rollback readiness).

**Applies to:** runtime pods (model-server), runtime scheduler, runtime sidecars, runtime config/feature flags, and kernel selection/quant profiles when delivered via runtime image/config.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- If there is active customer impact: declare an incident (Sev1/Sev2) and use the incident channel for coordination.
- Confirm EPC approvals per the Emergency production change policy.
- Identify the rollout target: region(s), tier(s), and route(s). Default is: one region canary first.
sections.heading: Preconditions

sections.body:
- Hosted API: request success rate (2xx/4xx/5xx) by region
- Runtime: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency and time-to-first-token
- Runtime: crash-loop rate / container restarts
- GPU fleet: utilization + queue depth
- Error taxonomy: top runtime error codes (oom, kv_cache_eviction, stream_disconnect)
sections.heading: Required dashboards (open before changing anything)

sections.body:
1. If regression started after a known deploy and rollback is available: **rollback** is preferred.
2. If rollback is not available or doesnt address the issue: apply a **mitigation** (feature flag off, reduce max tokens, adjust batch limits).
3. If issue is correctness/security: prefer **hotfix** with minimal diff and targeted rollout.
sections.heading: Decision tree (hotfix vs rollback vs mitigation)

sections.body:
1. Identify last known good runtime version (tag) from: release notes, deploy history, or the incident timeline.
2. Validate rollback artifacts exist: image tag present in registry and deployment tool can reference it.
3. Roll back in this order:
   1) One canary cell in us-east
   2) Full us-east
   3) One canary cell in eu-west
   4) Full eu-west
4. Verification after each step (must pass before proceeding):
   - 5xx rate returns to baseline
   - p95 latency improves or is flat (no >10% regression)
   - restarts trending down
   - no new error signature dominates
5. Post in incident channel: what changed, where, and observed effect.
sections.heading: Step-by-step: emergency rollback

sections.body:
1. Reduce scope: minimal code/config change that addresses the issue. Avoid refactors.
2. Build + publish hotfix artifact per Release Engineering checklist (emergency path).
3. Deploy sequence:
   - Canary: 1 cell / 1 region / 10 minutes minimum observation
   - Expand: 25% of region
   - Expand: 100% of region
   - Repeat for next region
4. Monitoring gates (stop/rollback if any occurs):
   - error rate +0.3% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
   - p95 latency +15% sustained for 10 minutes
   - restart rate doubles for 10 minutes
   - GPU OOM events increase >20%
5. Record the following in the EPC record: version/tag, flags changed, cells/regions impacted, approvals, and verification evidence.
sections.heading: Step-by-step: emergency hotfix

sections.body:
- Disable experimental scheduler features: `RW_SCHED_EXPERIMENTAL=0`
- Reduce max batch tokens: `RW_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS`
- Reduce max concurrent streams per pod
- Force conservative kernel selection (turn off fused attention for impacted arch)
- Temporarily lower max output tokens for affected routes
sections.heading: Common mitigations (preferable to code changes when possible)

sections.body:
Immediately rollback if any of the following are observed and attributed to the change:
- elevated 5xx correlated with rollout expansion
- widespread stream disconnects increase
- crash-loop / OOM increases
- customer escalations spike tied to the rollout region
sections.heading: Rollback triggers (hard)

sections.body:
- If the mitigation is visible (rate limits, reduced max tokens), coordinate with Support/CS and post status update when required.
- Avoid promising exact recovery times; provide next update cadence.
sections.heading: Customer comms reminders

sections.body:
- GitHub PR + merge SHA (or rollback tag)
- Deploy command / job link
- Dashboards used for verification
sections.heading: Appendix: What to link in the incident timeline

payload.page_title: SIGTERM Connection Drain and Graceful Shutdown Playbook

sections.body:
Purpose
-------
This playbook describes the operational procedure, runtime integrations, and verification steps for performing graceful shutdowns of inference runtime workers in response to SIGTERM (or equivalent orchestration signals). It covers: connection draining, inflight request completion, kernel-scheduler handoff, KV cache persistence, observability checks, and rollback. The goal is to avoid user-facing 5xx/timeout spikes and to preserve SLOs for p99 latency and error rate during deployments and preemptions.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: runtime worker processes (redwood-runtime-worker), shard proxies (kv-shard-proxy), and the request-router service.
- Deployment modes: Hosted API, Dedicated nodes, and Private single-tenant installs (behavior differs slightly; see "Mode differences" below).

Ownership and Contacts
---------------------
- Runbook owner: Runtime Operations (runtime-ops@redwood.internal)
- Primary on-call: eng-sre/runtime team (page: /oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process)
- Escalation: Runtime Lead — Arjun Patel, and Kernel Scheduling Lead — Lina Gomez

Key SLOs to preserve during shutdown
----------------------------------
- p99 request latency for text-generation endpoints: 300ms target degradation window
- 5xx error rate: < 0.5% global increase tolerated during drain windows
- Maximum queue length per worker: 8 (if exceeded, router will re-route)

Principles
----------
- Prefer draining over immediate process kill. Allow inflight generation to finish up to a configurable soft timeout (default 10s).
- Prevent new requests: stop accepting new upstream connections and signal the router to stop routing new sessions to the instance.
- Give kernel scheduler and batcher time to flush batched work and spill KV cache if storing to shared cache is necessary.
- Instrument every step with metrics and trace spans so SREs can verify correctness automatically.

Sequence: Graceful Shutdown (recommended)
----------------------------------------
1) Orchestrator signals SIGTERM to redwood-runtime-worker. This may be from k8s (preStop), autoscaler, or a manual kill.
2) Worker transitions to DRAINING state and publishes event: runtime.instance.drain_start (tags: instance_id, node_pool, model).
3) Worker removes itself from service-discovery / load-balancer via Router API: POST /router/v1/instances/{id}/set-drain with payload {"drain": true, "soft_timeout_ms": 10000}.
4) Router ceases assigning new requests. Any sessions already routed continue until completion. Router emits router.instance.eviction and begins rebalancing.
5) Kernel scheduler is notified to finish current kernel runs but avoid scheduling new batches for this worker. Scheduler sets kernel-credit to 0 for new kernels on that worker.
6) If a batch is currently running, the runtime allows up to soft_timeout_ms for completion. If batch overruns, the batcher signals preemption checkpoints: write KV cache to ephemeral storage (if configured) and surface incomplete token count in traces.
7) After inflight work completes or the soft timeout expires, worker flushes KV cache shards that are configured for warm-start persistence. Use CLI: /usr/local/bin/rw-kv-flush --shard <id> --dest /mnt/ephemeral/kvcache/<id>.
8) Worker publishes runtime.instance.drain_complete and transitions to SHUTTING_DOWN.
9) Perform final telemetry flush: flush traces, metrics, and event logs to central collector (otel-collector:4317).
10) Worker exits with code 0. Orchestrator can then terminate the VM or detach the GPU.

Abort path (forced kill)
-----------------------
- If a SIGKILL or 30s post-SIGTERM timeout occurs, worker must attempt one last telemetry flush. The forced-kill event runtime.instance.forced_kill must be emitted with reason and inflight_count.
- The router should detect dropped connections and increment a router.eviction.dropped counter; automated mitigation routes traffic to fallback model variants within 2s.

Mode differences
----------------
- Hosted API (multi-tenant): router enforces aggressive re-routing. soft_timeout_ms default=10s
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): more lenient soft timeout, default=30s, because throttling downstream is under customer contract.
- Private (on-prem): operator-configurable; document recommends aligning to Dedicated defaults unless operator constraints require shorter windows.

Kernel-scheduler interactions and knobs to tune
-----------------------------------------------
- kernel_credit_window: how many kernel launches are permitted during the drain window. Set to 0 to prevent new launches.
- batcher_drain_mode: when true, batcher stops aggregating new requests into kernels destined for this worker.
- preempt_checkpoint_interval_ms: interval for writing a consistent preemption checkpoint inside long-running kernels (recommended 500ms for generation workloads > 2s).
- Example config YAML snippet (runtime config):

  ---
  runtime:
    shutdown:
      soft_timeout_ms: 10000
      flush_kv: true
      preempt_checkpoint_interval_ms: 500
    scheduler:
      kernel_credit_window: 0
      batcher_drain_mode: true
  ---

Observability and verification checklist (pre- and post-shutdown)
----------------------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Verify instance has active sessions: gauge runtime.sessions.active > 0. If none, immediate shutdown OK.
- Emit drain_start event and confirm router acknowledgement (router.instance.ack_drain == true).
- Record current p99 latency baseline for the model.
sections.heading: Pre-shutdown (automated)

sections.body:
- Monitor: runtime.inflight.count, runtime.kernel.active_batches, kvcache.flush.latency_ms.
- Traces: Ensure spans include drain_start and drain_complete and that root span duration <= soft_timeout_ms + 2s.
- Alerts to watch: router.eviction.dropped > 0 persist for > 10s (trigger paged alert).
sections.heading: During shutdown

sections.body:
1) Run a canary traffic test that sends 50 requests distributed across same model and compares p99 latency to baseline. Pass criteria: p99 <= baseline + 20%.
2) Confirm no unexplained 5xx spike: metrics.delta(api.errors.5xx) < 0.5%
3) Check telemetry logs for runtime.instance.forced_kill — if present, trigger a postmortem.

Runbook: manual operator procedure (fast path)
-------------------------------------------
1) On-call receives alert about scheduled maintenance or faulty node.
2) SSH to controller and note instance id: curl -s http://metadata.internal/instance-id
3) Trigger drain via Router API: curl -X POST "https://router.internal/api/v1/instances/<id>/action" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"action":"drain","soft_timeout_ms":10000}'
4) Wait for runtime.instance.drain_complete event (timeout: 60s). If not complete, inspect runtime logs: journalctl -u redwood-runtime-worker -n 200
5) If kernel batch stuck > soft_timeout_ms: request kernel-team to inspect live kernel stacks: /usr/local/bin/rw-kernel-dump --pid <pid> > /tmp/kernel-dump.txt
6) If unable to recover, trigger failover: tag instance as unhealthy in service-discovery and scale up replacement nodes via autoscaler.
7) After replacement nodes are up and passing smoke tests, decommission old instance.

Testing and validation matrix
---------------------------
- Unit tests: runtime integration tests simulate SIGTERM and validate sequence transitions.
- Integration tests: run on staging release lanes with variable latency models including long-running generation (20–60s) and check KV flush artifacts land in expected S3 prefix s3://staging-runtime-kv/<instance>/
- Chaos tests: scheduled preemptions injected at random phases of kernel execution (see: benchmarking-and-perf-suite/synthetic-chaos-stress-profiles-2026)

Dashboards and Alerts
---------------------
sections.heading: Post-shutdown verification (automated smoke)

sections.body:
- Instance Drain Overview: shows runtime.instance.* events, inflight counts, kernel active batches, kv flush latency, and router ack status.
- Eviction Impact Dashboard: p99 delta vs baseline, error rate delta, dropped connection count.
sections.heading: Recommended dashboards

sections.body:
- router.eviction.dropped > 10 in 60s AND p99 delta > 25%
- runtime.instance.forced_kill > 0
- kvcache.flush.latency_ms > 5000

Post-incident analysis (if forced_kill observed)
--------------------------------------------
- Owner: Runtime incident responder. Timeline to collect: kernel dumps, router routing table at time of event, traces with drain tags, and orchestrator event stream (k8s events or cloud provider preemption log).
- Metrics to include: inflight_count, active_batches, kernel_wait_time_histogram, and router.retry_count.
- Output: short-form incident report with root cause, mitigation, and action items (file to /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/incident-review/).

Compatibility notes and caveats
-----------------------------
- Some older models that rely on pinned KV state may need longer soft_timeouts; consult model-onboarding docs before changing defaults.
- In air-gapped Private installs, ensure the KV flush destination is reachable (NFS or operator-provided S3-compatible store).
- Draining behavior for GPU co-located processes: if multiple runtime workers share a GPU, prefer in-place workload migration with kernel scheduler support rather than draining all workers simultaneously.

Appendix: Helpful CLI snippets
----------------------------
- Trigger router drain (example):
  curl -X POST "https://router.internal/api/v1/instances/<id>/action" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"action":"drain","soft_timeout_ms":10000}'

- Check last drain events for instance:
  curl -s "https://events.internal/query?instance_id=<id>&event=runtime.instance.drain_*" | jq '.'

- KV flush (example):
  /usr/local/bin/rw-kv-flush --shard 4 --dest s3://runtime-kv-backups/staging/<id> --sync

- Kernel dump (debug only):
  /usr/local/bin/rw-kernel-dump --pid $(pgrep -f redwood-runtime-worker) > /tmp/kernel-$(date +%s).dump

References
----------
- Runtime architecture overview: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- Kernel scheduler contracts: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/runtime-priority-decoupling-and-preemptive-shepherding-2026
- Eviction and eviction strategies: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/gpu-affinity-and-eviction-strategies-2026
- Chaos and stress profiles: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/synthetic-chaos-stress-profiles-2026

Change log
----------
- 2024-11-01: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2025-01-10: Added kernel-scheduler knobs and CLI examples (reviewer: Lina Gomez).
- 2025-02-20: Finalized mode-specific defaults and added postmortem checklist.
sections.heading: Suggested alerts (pager for PRD-impacting metrics)

payload.page_title: Adaptive Request Shaper and Priority Synthesis - Runtime Guide

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the Adaptive Request Shaper and Priority Synthesis subsystem: a runtime-layer component that shapes incoming inference traffic, synthesizes per-request priority scores, and coordinates with kernel scheduling and batching to meet latency SLOs while minimizing cost. It covers high-level architecture, scheduling interactions, telemetry and profiling guidance, integration with the benchmarking suite, release and rollout checklist, and an operational runbook.

Why this exists

- Problem: production LLM workloads exhibit widely varying sequence lengths, cold prefixes, and priority semantics (interactive vs background). Static admission controls either waste GPU cycles or violate latency SLOs.
- Goal: provide a predictable, transparent shaping layer that maps business intents (user-facing vs background, deadline, cost-sensitivity) to runtime actions (admit, delay, throttle, reroute) and exposes deterministic knobs for SRE/product to tune.

Scope and non-goals

- In-scope: admission control, token-budget-aware shaping, deadline-aware batching hints, priority score synthesis and annotation, integration points to kernel scheduler and batcher, relevant telemetry and dashboards.
- Out-of-scope: model optimizer internals, KV cache replication, network-level routing across regions (handled by Smart Routing).

Design overview

1) Request API annotations
- New optional fields the API accepts (internal header or SDK metadata):
  - priority_hint: {"interactive"|"standard"|"background"}
  - deadline_ms: integer (soft deadline relative to request arrival)
  - cost_sensitivity: {"low"|"medium"|"high"} (guides quantization/cache preference)
  - work_token_budget: integer (max tokens allowed for request)

2) Priority synthesizer
- Consumes API annotations, historical per-identity tail-latency distribution, and a local cost estimator to compute a normalized priority_score in [0.0, 1.0].
- Score semantics: closer to 1.0 = higher admission and preference for low-latency kernels and smaller batches. Scores are deterministic given inputs for reproducibility in benchmarking.

3) Adaptive shaper / admission controller
- Core responsibilities:
  - Admit immediately to active queue (fast-path)
  - Place in delay queue with per-client backoff (soft-hold)
  - Reject with structured error or reroute to cheaper model variant (fallback mapper)
  - Annotate requests with batch hints (min_batch_size, max_wait_ms) for the batcher
- Local policy uses dynamic thresholds computed from target SLO utilization and observed kernel queue lengths.

4) Scheduler interaction points
- Kernel scheduler accepts requests annotated with priority_score and batch hints. The scheduler maps high priority requests onto preemptible GPU lanes or hot-shard contexts; lower priority requests are eligible for cooperative preemption.

5) Cost estimator
- Lightweight model that provides per-request expected token-cost given current quantization profile and KV cache hit probability. Used in priority synthesis when cost_sensitivity is set.

Configuration (defaults and critical knobs)

Configuration table (values represent recommended defaults for hosted tier):

| parameter | default | description | operational range | unit |
|-----------|---------|-------------|-------------------|------|
| global_target_p99_ms | 200 | target p99 latency for interactive route | 50-1000 | ms |
| fastpath_queue_depth | 256 | max parallel requests admitted to fast-path | 64-2048 | requests |
| delay_queue_base_ms | 30 | base delay for soft-hold queue | 10-200 | ms |
| priority_decay_half_life_s | 120 | half-life for historical tail influence | 30-600 | s |
| min_batch_hint | 1 | minimum suggested batch size to batcher | 1-16 | tokens/requests |
| max_batch_wait_ms | 30 | maximum batch wait the shaper suggests | 5-200 | ms |
| cost_weight | 0.3 | weight on cost_sensitivity in score calc | 0.0-1.0 | fractional |
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
shaper:
  enabled: true
  global_target_p99_ms: 200
  fastpath_queue_depth: 256
  delay_queue_base_ms: 30
  priority_decay_half_life_s: 120
  cost_weight: 0.3
sections.heading: Example runtime config (YAML fragment)

sections.body:
- Toggle shaper on a node pool: rwdctl runtime shaper set --nodepool=pred-hosts --enabled=false
- Inspect queues: rwdctl runtime shaper stats --node=runtime-23
- Force a request to background priority (test): rwdctl runtime simulate --priority=background --seq-len=512

Telemetry and dashboards
sections.heading: CLI snippets (admin)

sections.body:
- shaper.request_admitted_total{route,priority_hint} (counter)
- shaper.request_delayed_total{route,delay_bucket} (counter)
- shaper.request_rejected_total{reason} (counter)
- shaper.priority_score_distribution (histogram)
- shaper.estimated_cost_hist (histogram)
- shaper.delay_queue_depth (gauge)
- shaper.fastpath_queue_depth (gauge)
- shaper.slo_breach_by_priority (counter)
sections.heading: Essential metrics (all exported with request tagging)

sections.body:
- Per-route priority breakdown (pie + timeseries)
- Delay-queue depth vs p99 latency (scatter)
- Cost-sensitivity impacts: cost per token vs p99 by priority group

Profiling and evaluation guidance

1) Micro-profiling the shaper itself
- Goal: ensure shaper logic adds <1ms median overhead in critical path.
- Procedure:
  1. Use runtime-profiling harness: rwd-bench profile --module=shaper --workload=interactive-1000 --samples=5000
  2. Measure: CPU time per request, lock contention, GC pauses.
  3. If median >1ms, capture flamegraph and file an issue with kernel-and-scheduling.

2) End-to-end profiling (shaper + scheduler + batcher)
- Run the mixed workload suite (see benchmarking integration below) and compare:
  - Baseline: shaper disabled, default scheduler
  - Candidate: shaper enabled with current thresholds
- Key traces to collect: kernel queue latency, batch sizes, preemption events, tail-latency percentiles per priority.

Benchmarking suite integration

- Add a dedicated scenario to the mixed_workload_slo_simulation_suite named shaper_mixed_priority_v1. Scenario characteristics:
  - 60/30/10 split interactive/standard/background
  - Sequence length distribution: {short: 45%, medium: 35%, long: 20%}
  - Inter-arrival CV (coefficient of variation): 1.2
- Success criteria:
  - interactive p99 <= global_target_p99_ms
  - cost per 1k tokens reduced or unchanged vs baseline
  - no >2% increase in rejected requests from synthetic product tests

Release and rollout checklist

- Unit and integration tests covering synth logic and boundary conditions.
- Staging run: 12h continuous run against mixed_workload_shaper with telemetry pushed to staging dashboards.
- Canary: enable shaper for 5% of traffic for 24 hours in a single region. Monitor:
  - shaper.slo_breach_by_priority (must not exceed historical by more than 0.5%)
  - user-visible error rate (SLOs); rollback if >3x baseline for >5 minutes
- Gradual expansion: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with automated health gating.

Operational runbook (page on-call should follow)
sections.heading: Suggested dashboards

sections.body:
1) shaper.delay_queue_depth > fastpath_queue_depth for > 5m AND interactive p99 rising > 20% -> page oncall_runtime_primary
2) shaper.request_rejected_total unexpectedly increases by > 1% of traffic in 10m -> page runtime-owner.
sections.heading: Alerts that should page (examples)

sections.body:
1) Check the shaper dashboard: queue depths, p99 by priority, priority_score_distribution.
2) If interactive p99 is high and delay queue deep: scale up fastpath_queue_depth or temporarily disable shaper for affected route: rwdctl runtime shaper set --route=search --enabled=false
3) If rejections rise: inspect reject reasons (capacity vs policy). If policy misconfiguration suspected, apply rollback: rwdctl runtime shaper rollback --config-version=previous
4) If CPU saturation on shaper process observed: escalate to eng-platform to allocate additional CPU or isolate the shaper to a dedicated control-plane CPU pool.

Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: Priority oscillation with bursty clients
  - Symptom: requests flip rapidly between fast-path and delay queue, causing spiky preemption.
  - Mitigation: increase priority_decay_half_life_s to 300s or apply per-client smoothing.

- Issue: Overly aggressive cost-driven demotion for long-sequence requests
  - Symptom: long-running generation tasks get rerouted to fallback model and produce degraded outputs.
  - Mitigation: cap cost influence for sequences with deadline_ms set; use a separate routing profile.

- Issue: Telemetry gaps after autoscaler events
  - Symptom: delay_queue_depth and priority distributions reset after scale-down events.
  - Mitigation: ensure shaper state persists in the shard metadata store (config flag: persist_shaper_state = true).

Implementation notes and file locations

- Core service: rwd-shaper-service (repo: infra/rwd-shaper)
- Priority synthesizer library: infra/rwd-shaper/pkg/priority (unit tested)
- Cost model: infra/estimators/request-cost (offline training harness in perf/estimators)
- Kernel hooks: runtime/kernel-adapter/shaper-integration.md

Related pages

- /eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/priority-driven-kernel-scheduler-spec-2026
- /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026

Appendix: example scoring function (pseudo)

priority_score = clamp(\
  w_annot * annotated_score + w_history * historical_score + w_cost * (1 - normalized_estimated_cost), 0.0, 1.0\)
sections.heading: On-call initial steps

sections.body:
- annotated_score maps priority_hint: interactive=1.0, standard=0.6, background=0.2
- historical_score derived from empirical tail-latency (higher if client historically meets SLO)
- normalized_estimated_cost is cost estimate normalized to [0,1]
- weights (w_annot, w_history, w_cost) are tunable; default = (0.5, 0.2, 0.3)

Contact and ownership

- Primary owner: Nikhil Rao (eng-serving-runtime)
- Secondary: Leah Patel (eng-sre)
- Slack channel: #rwd-runtime-shaper

Document history

- 2025-11-02: Draft created (N. Rao)
- 2025-12-15: Added profiling checklist and telemetry (L. Patel)
- 2026-02-10: Updated rollout gating and known-issues (M. Diaz)

End of document
