payload.page_title: Eviction Rewind and State Reconstruction Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
========
This playbook documents the procedure to recover from kvcache eviction events that cause request-level state divergence or incomplete KV reconstruction during model swaps, preemption, or kernel handoffs. It covers triage, automated rewind and state reconstruction action sequences, verification checks, rollback criteria, and safety tests. The intended audience is oncall SREs, serving-runtime engineers, and incident responders.

Why this matters
-----------------
- Eviction-induced state gaps can lead to incorrect completions, user-facing hallucinations, or repeated model fallbacks.
- Fast, deterministic reconstruction preserves SLOs and avoids large-scale reroutes to lower-fidelity fallback models.
- This playbook provides a safe, repeatable sequence to reconstruct per-session KV state and safely resume traffic.

When to run this playbook
-------------------------
Run this playbook when one or more of the following are observed:
- Sudden spike in kvcache_reconstruction_failures (> 10/min sustained for 5 minutes)
- Increase in tail latency correlated with eviction_rate or kernel_handoff_rate
- Model swap incidents where > 0.5% of sessions show token regression or repeated left-pad artifacts
- Automated canary signals mark warmup_failure=true during rollout

Impact and SLOs
---------------
- Target: recover affected sessions and restore p95 inference latency within 10 minutes of start of remediation.
- Acceptable interim error budget consumption: up to 2x normal error budget for the affected service for a single incident.
- Escalate to incident commander if reconstruction extends beyond 30 minutes or if reconstruction failures exceed 1% of total affected sessions.

Ownership and permissions
-------------------------
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime (runtime-sre)
- Secondary owner: Kernel Scheduling Team (kernel-scheduler)
- Required permissions: ability to trigger kvcache reconstruction jobs, pause model-swap-agent rollouts, and modify scheduler admission controls.
- Contacts: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai, kernel-scheduler@redwood.ai, runtime-release@redwood.ai

Pre-incident checklist (quick)
-----------------------------
- Confirm current SLA window and active deployments.
- Check if any maintenance or known rollouts are in progress (model-swap-agent, kernel rollouts).
- Ensure a recent snapshot of kvcache index exists (last 24h).
- Open a dedicated incident channel and note affected clusters/regions.

Immediate triage (first 10 minutes)
-----------------------------------
1) Tag and isolate: Identify affected shard sets and tag them in the incident channel. Use the runtime incident tool:  `rtctl shards list --filter=\"eviction_rate>0.1\"`
2) Confirm metric correlations: Dashboard: Runtime / KVCACHE / Reconstruction. Check metrics: eviction_rate, kvcache_reconstruction_failures, kvcache_warmup_seconds, kernel_handoff_rate, p95_latency.
3) Stop compounding actions: Pause any model-swap-agent rollouts for affected model-versions: `rtctl rollout pause --model vX --clusters shard-a,shard-b`.
4) Reduce admission pressure: Temporarily tighten admission control to reduce new sessions to affected shards: `schedulerctl admission set --target 60% --scope shard-a`

Automated reconstruction flow (recommended)
------------------------------------------
Use the automated reconstruction pipeline (recon-runner) to attempt fast rewind and state rebuild before manual steps. Steps it performs:
- Fetch latest durable prefix snapshots from persistent-store (S3 / object-store).
- Rehydrate session KV caches using checkpointed KV deltas.
- Replay last N tokens from request logs (N default 32) into warmed kernel contexts to re-establish KV validity.
- Validate by running synthetic trace assertions.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- `recon-runner start --shards shard-a,shard-b --max-parallel 4 --replay-window 32 --dry-run=false`

Manual reconstruction procedure (if automated runner fails)
---------------------------------------------------------
1) Stop accepting new traffic to affected shards: `schedulerctl drain --shard shard-a --mode immediate`
2) Snapshot live kernel state (if available): `rtctl kernel snapshot --shard shard-a --out /tmp/shard-a-snap.tgz`
3) Extract last-request logs for affected sessions: `logql query \"{service=\"runtime-gpu-proxy\", shard=\"shard-a\"} | json | last(5000)\" > /tmp/shard-a-requests.ndjson`
4) Run replay tool in isolated reconstruction cluster (no external traffic):
   a) `replay-tool --input /tmp/shard-a-requests.ndjson --model-model-path gs://models/vX --kv-checkpoint gs://kvcache/snapshots/shard-a/latest --replay-window 64 --out /tmp/shard-a-replay-results.json`
   b) Inspect replay failures: `jq '.failures | length' /tmp/shard-a-replay-results.json`
5) Apply KV deltas to in-memory cache with controlled rate-limiter: `kvcachectl apply-deltas --shard shard-a --source /tmp/deltas --rate 1000/s`
6) Re-enable traffic with traffic shaping: `schedulerctl admission set --target 30% --ramp 10m --scope shard-a`

Verification checks (post-reconstruction)
----------------------------------------
- Metric convergence: kvcache_reconstruction_failures -> 0/min; kvcache_hit_rate >= previous baseline - 2% within 15 minutes.
- Synthetic assertion: run 100 representative prompts (from canary prompt-set) against reconstructed shards and assert token-by-token parity >= 99.5% (or within acceptable fidelity reg thresholds).
- Latency: p95 within 10% of baseline for reconstructed shards.
- Error logs: no new kernel panics or repeated model-fallback events for 30 minutes.

Rollback and fallback policy
---------------------------
sections.heading: Command to start automated run on a shard set

sections.body:
- Immediately revert model swap (if the swap caused the state divergence) using: `rtctl rollout revert --model vX --to vX-previous --scope shard-a`
- If revert is not possible, route affected traffic to a hardened fallback pool (fallback-tier-2) with conservative admission limits.
- Mark incident as "stalled reconstruction" and escalate to runtime product and kernel-scheduler leads.

Post-incident actions (within 72 hours)
--------------------------------------
- Run a formal postmortem with causal timeline, including kernel handoff signals and eviction bursts.
- Bake-in new canary checks if missing: add warmup_failure assertion to canary pipeline.
- Create a blocker ticket for any persistent root cause (e.g., persistent NVMe contention, faulty eviction heuristics).

Testing and canary protocol for recon changes
--------------------------------------------
1) Unit tests for recon-runner with synthetic KV deltas and deterministic replay.
2) Integration test: deploy recon-runner in canary A (single shard) with traffic mirror of 2% for 2 hours. Assert: warmup_success=true, reconstruction_latency < 300s.
3) Rollout: gradual - 5% clusters -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback on warmup failure.

Telemetry and dashboards to consult
----------------------------------
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Eviction Rate (eviction_rate)
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Reconstruction Failures (kvcache_reconstruction_failures)
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Warmup Duration (kvcache_warmup_seconds)
- Runtime / Kernel / Handoff Rate (kernel_handoff_rate)
- APIGW / Inference / p95 latency (p95_inference_latency)
- Runtime / Synthetic / Canary Fidelity (canary_token_parity)

Diagnostic commands and snippets
-------------------------------
- List active recon jobs: `reconctl list --status active`
- Tail kernel logs for shard: `kubectl -n runtime logs -l shard=shard-a -c kernel --since=20m | grep -i eviction`
- Inspect last kvcache checkpoint manifest: `gsutil cat gs://kvcache/snapshots/shard-a/manifest.json | jq`

Config table (important params)
------------------------------
Parameter | Default | Purpose / Impact
--------- | ------- | ------------------
replay_window | 32 | Number of tokens replayed to reconstruct KV. Increasing improves fidelity but increases time.
max_parallel_recon | 4 | Maximum parallel reconstruction jobs per region. Higher value speeds recovery but raises load.
apply_delta_rate | 1000/s | Rate at which KV deltas are applied to in-memory kvcache to avoid memory spikes.
snapshot_ttl | 24h | How long persistent snapshots are kept. Longer TTL increases recovery surface but costs storage.
warmup_assertion_threshold | 0.995 | Minimum token parity to consider reconstruction successful.

Example reconstruction config (YAML)
-----------------------------------
reconstruction:
  shards: ["shard-a", "shard-b"]
  replay_window: 64
  max_parallel_recon: 2
  apply_delta_rate: 750/s
  synthetic_canary_set: "canary-recon-v2"
  notify_on: ["success","failure"]

Safety notes and caveats
------------------------
- Never apply deltas across model-version boundaries unless the model architecture and tokenizer are compatible. Cross-version KV application will produce corruption.
- If kernel snapshot feature is unavailable for a shard, prefer routing traffic away rather than performing blind reconstruction.
- Reconstruction may surface latent bugs in quantization path; watch for sudden increase in soft-errors from kernel telemetry.

Appendix: quick checklist (one-pager)
------------------------------------
1) Pause rollouts and tag shards.
2) Run recon-runner (dry-run first if time permits).
3) If recon-runner fails, drain shard and run replay-tool in isolated cluster.
4) Apply KV deltas with rate-limiter and re-enable traffic with ramp.
5) Verify fidelity with canary prompt-set and metrics.
6) Revert or fallback if fidelity/latency unacceptable.

Related links and artifacts
--------------------------
- Kernel signal handbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/eviction-coordinate-protocol-and-kernel-signal-handbook-2026
- Reconstruction automation repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/recon-runner
- Canary prompt sets: gs://runtime-canaries/canary-recon-v2/prompts.ndjson

Document history
----------------
- 2026-01-15: Created by Sophie Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-04-08: Added automated recon-runner section and YAML config (Marco Alvarez).
- 2026-07-02: Updated verification thresholds and telemetry lists (Dmitri Sokolov).

payload.page_title: Serving Runtime Hotfix Runbook (Emergency Patch Release)

sections.body:
h2. When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when a serving-runtime change must be shipped quickly to mitigate an active incident (typically Sev-1). This covers code change, build, validation, and handoff to rollout owners.

h2. Preconditions
* Emergency change approvals recorded per /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* Incident channel exists (or a dedicated Slack thread) with IC identified
* A rollback plan exists (previous runtime image tag + restart procedure)

h2. Step 1 — Cut a hotfix branch
1. Create branch naming: hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>
2. Cherry-pick the minimum fix commit(s) only.
3. Update CHANGELOG entry under 'Runtime Hotfixes'.

h2. Step 2 — Create PR and get emergency reviews
1. Open GitHub PR targeting release branch (preferred) or main if release branch is not available.
2. Required reviewers: runtime on-call + SRE on-call (or IC).
3. Include in PR description: incident link, hypothesis, risk, rollback, rollout owners.

h2. Step 3 — Build + sign artifacts
Follow /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/hotfix-build-and-signing. Minimum artifacts:
* runtime container image (multi-arch if applicable)
* SBOM (CycloneDX)
* provenance attestation

h2. Step 4 — Validate the fix
*Minimum* validation required even in an incident:
* Unit tests for affected module
* One perf-canary run for representative model (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B)
* One stress test at the incident-triggering pattern (sequence length + concurrency)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Error rate improves or eliminates the triggering error
* p95 latency does not regress > 10% compared to previous runtime image for the same workload
* No increase in OOM or GPU reset counters

h2. Step 5 — Prepare rollout notes
In the incident channel, post:
* New runtime image tag
* Expected impact during rollout (restarts, brief connection resets)
* Canary target (Hosted region or Dedicated cluster)
* Rollback criteria (metrics + customer symptom)

h2. Step 6 — Handoff to rollout owners
* Hosted: hand off to Platform/SRE per /eng-platform/runbooks/hosted-rollout-and-rollback-procedure
* Dedicated: hand off to Infra + CSEM per /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/dedicated-cluster-hotfix-rollout-notes

h2. Rollback reminder
If rollback triggers are met, roll back immediately; do not wait for a full incident update cadence. Announce rollback in incident channel and update status page wording to reflect mitigation change.

h2. Appendix — Common pitfalls
* Fix includes unrelated refactors (reject; keep minimal).
* No canary defined (must be explicitly waived by IC).
* Artifact unsigned or missing SBOM (must not ship).

payload.page_title: Runtime hotpatch and quick redeploy playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook captures step-by-step guidance for applying small, targeted hotpatches to the serving runtime (kernel or scheduling components) and for performing a fast emergency redeploy when a hotpatch is not possible or has failed. It targets oncall engineers and runtime SREs who must restore service within the next 15–60 minutes while preserving customer SLOs and minimizing blast radius.

When to use this playbook

- Critical kernel or scheduler bug causing elevated 99th-percentile latency or hard errors (5xx) for >1 minute and automatic mitigations have not restored SLOs.
- Memory corruption or a known safe patch exists that can be applied without a full image build.
- Emergency patch path is documented in the kernel safety-net and approved by the runtime owner.
- If the issue is a broader configuration, refer to the deployment circuit-breakers playbook instead.

Owners and escalation

- Primary: runtime-oncall (pager duty) — first responder.
- Secondary: runtime-sre (pager) — 10 minutes escalation if unresolved.
- Tertiary:serving-runtime-eng (email/Slack) — for cross-team rollout coordination.

Required checks before hotpatching (preflight)

1) Confirm actual customer impact:
   - Check per-route 99th latency spikes and 5xx rate in the last 5 minutes.
   - Verify error budgets: if < 10% remaining for the hour, proceed with caution.

2) Validate trace and kernel signal presence:
   - Look up last 100 traces that hit the failing path (trace tag: runtime.kernel.failure=true).
   - Confirm root cause candidate aligns with a supported hotpatch (see Acceptable Hotpatch Types table below).

3) Confirm rollback path and canary target nodes are available:
   - Identify a canary cohort of 5–10% of nodes in the affected pool (minimum 3 nodes).
   - Ensure at least one warm spare pool is ready for immediate slot migration.

Acceptable Hotpatch Types (short table)

| Hotpatch Type | Allowed when | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| JIT config tweak (no binary change) | Fixes runtime flags or scheduler thresholds | Low |
| Lua/JS actuator script swap | Script corrects route matching / backoff | Low–medium |
| Binary function-level hotfix (approved diff) | Small critical logic change with signed patch | Medium |
| Kernel microservice restart with staged image | When binary replacement is required but can be canaried | Medium–high |

Note: Full binary rebuilds that change kernel ABI are NOT eligible for hotpatch and require a standard canary image rollout.

Hotpatch procedure (fast path) — target time 15–25 minutes

1) Announce intent (1 minute)
   - Post to #runtime-incidents with: incident id, short description, target nodes, and expected time window.

2) Quiesce auxiliary load (2 minutes)
   - Use the admission controller to shift non-critical burst traffic:
     redwoodctl route-weight --scope affected --weight 0.1 --duration 5m
   - Enable temporary cache bypass for debug traces:
     redwoodctl debug cache-bypass --routes debug-* --on

3) Apply the hotpatch to canary cohort (3–5 minutes)
   - For config/script changes: push via the config service:
     curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/v1/hotpatch -d '{"patch":"<base64>"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
   - For signed binary microfix: use the runtime hotpatch signer:
     redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --patch-file /tmp/patch.bin --signature /tmp/patch.sig
   - Confirm deployment status:
     redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort canary --wait 60s

4) Observe telemetry for 10 minutes (minimum)
   - Dashboards to watch: per-node 99th latency, per-route 5xx rate, kernel-exception-rate.
   - Run smoke query:
     curl -sS https://svc-internal/health-check -H 'x-test-trace: hotpatch-canary' | jq .status

5) If stable -> progressive expand (10–20 minutes)
   - Expand cohort in steps: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%, with 5–10 minute observation windows between steps.
   - Use automated rollout:
     redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval 5m --steps 10,30,60,100 --cohort affected

Emergency redeploy procedure (when hotpatch fails or not allowed) — target time 30–60 minutes

1) Abort any in-flight hotpatch and mark canary as failed:
   - redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --abort --reason "hotpatch failed"

2) Prepare a fast redeploy image (prebuilt emergency image recommended)
   - If a prebuilt emergency image exists, tag it as emergency:
     redwoodctl image tag --image-id img-2026-11-09-emergency --tag emergency-<incident-id>
   - If not, build minimal image with the exact production ABI and only the required fix. Use the fast-build profile:
     ./build-image --profile fast --include runtime:hotfix-module --tag emergency-<incident-id>

3) Canary redeploy to the canary cohort (5–10 minutes)
   - Deploy the emergency image to the canary cohort:
     redwoodctl deploy --image emergency-<incident-id> --cohort canary --max-concurrency 3
   - Attach observability hooks: trace-sampling=100%, metric-enrichment=hotpatch-incident.<id>

4) Automated smoke and runbook checks (10–15 minutes)
   - Run the smoke suite against the canary:
     redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort canary --tests core-latency,kv-consistency,session-stability --timeout 600s
   - Verify no increase in memory RSS, no new 5xx, and no kernel panics.

5) Expand or rollback (progressive)
   - Follow the same progressive expansion steps as the hotpatch procedure.
   - If at any point the 99th latency or 5xx rates regress above pre-incident thresholds, trigger rollback immediately.

Rollback and containment

- To rollback a hotpatch to the previous known-good state:
  redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort affected --rollback-to stable-<timestamp> --force-checks
- To rollback a redeploy:
  redwoodctl deploy --image stable-image-<timestamp> --cohort affected --force
- Containment steps if rollback is not possible quickly:
  1) Shift traffic away from affected pool using route weights.
  2) Attach fallback routing:
     redwoodctl routing fallback --policy model-variant --target variant-stable --duration 30m

Telemetry and post-incident tasks

- During the operation ensure the following metrics are captured at 10s granularity for at least 30 minutes: per-node cpu/gpu utilization, per-node memory RSS, kernel-exception-rate, per-route 99p latency, per-route 5xx rate, kvcache-hitratio.
- Create an incident bridge note with timeline and include command transcripts.
- Postmortem: owner is runtime-sre; draft within 72 hours; public summary to go-to-market within 7 days if customer-facing.

Command reference (common commands)

- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --patch-file <file> --signature <sig>
- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --abort --reason <text>
- redwoodctl deploy --image <image-tag> --cohort <cohort> --max-concurrency <n>
- redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval <min> --steps <csv> --cohort <cohort>
- redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort <cohort> --tests <list> --timeout <s>
- redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort <cohort> --wait <s>

Safety thresholds (must abort and rollback if any triggered)

- Per-route 5xx rate increases by >200% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Per-route 99p latency increases by >50% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Any kernel panic or OOM observed on >1% of nodes in cohort.

Configuration snippets and examples

- Example emergency rollout policy (YAML):

  apiVersion: redwood/v1
  kind: RolloutPolicy
  metadata:
    name: emergency-fast-expansion
  spec:
    strategy: progressive
    steps: [10, 30, 60, 100]
    intervalMinutes: 5
    maxConcurrency: 5
    safetyChecks:
      - metric: kernel-panic-count
        threshold: 1
        windowSeconds: 60

- Example smoke test list (JSON array):

  ["core-latency","kv-consistency","session-stability","model-fidelity-basic"]

Post-incident hygiene checklist

1) Record the exact patch artifact and commit hash used.
2) Create a test matrix entry that reproduces the failure in the sandbox.
3) Schedule a controlled rebuild and standard canary for the patch (no emergency tags) within 72 hours.
4) Update the kernel hotpatch whitelist if the hotpatch type will be reused.
5) Update runbook: add any missing steps or commands discovered during the incident.

Appendices

A. Quick diagnostics commands
- tail -n 200 /var/log/runtime/kernel.log | grep -i panic
- redwoodctl metrics query "avg(99p_latency) by route" --from -10m
- redwoodctl traces query --tag runtime.kernel.failure --limit 100

B. Canary cohort sizing guidance
- For small pools (< 100 nodes) use minimum 3-node canary.
- For large pools (> 1000 nodes) prefer 5–10% but cap canary at 200 nodes.

C. Links and references
- Kernel safety and rollback playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-safety-net-and-rollback-playbook-2027
- Deployment circuit breakers: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- Canary matrix and validation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

If you are the oncall taking this action: add your name to the incident timeline and ping runtime-sre for audit and postmortem ownership.

payload.page_title: Cold-start Quality Degradation Detection and Recovery Runbook

sections.body: This runbook describes how to detect, triage, and recover from quality degradations that are correlated with cold-start events in the runtime (examples: increased hallucination rate, lower QA pass rate, deterministic prompt-prefix regressions after model swap, or output truncation tied to KV cache misses). It is focused on production incidents where client-facing correctness metrics drop following service restarts, model swaps, autoscaler-driven scale-ups, or routing to undersized warm pools.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments running the Redwood serving runtime. Applicable to model swaps, node restarts, autoscaling events, or any scenario where a high proportion of requests experience cold execution (empty KV/embedding caches, unprimed kernels).
- Intent: detect regressions quickly, preserve customer-facing SLOs, and restore previous-quality behavior with minimal disruption. This runbook prioritizes safe, reversible actions and clarifies ownership.
sections.heading: Scope and intent

sections.body:
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (eng-serving-runtime team)
- Escalation: runtime-sre lead, model-onboarding owner, customer-success for impacted customers
sections.heading: Who owns this runbook

sections.body:
1) Behavioral quality metrics (primary):
   - QA pass rate on synthetic prompt-sets (rolling 5m and 1h buckets). Alert if 1h pass rate drops >20% relative to 6h baseline.
   - Hallucination indicator: fraction of responses matching negative heuristics (nonsense score, repeated tokens). Alert if >5% of responses exceed hallucination threshold and correlated with cold-start tags.
2) Telemetry and execution signals (correlated with cold-start):
   - KV cache miss rate: per-shard and per-model KV miss rate spike (Prometheus: runtime_kvcache_miss_rate). Alert if >= 80% of requests for a cohort are cold for >10min.
   - Prefix latency spike: token-latency for first N tokens (token_index <= 32) up by >2x baseline.
   - Model swap events: recent model variant switch or kernel rollouts (eventlog entries).
3) Sampling-based checks (low-volume but high fidelity):
   - Shadow evaluation: sample requests shadowed to previous model/variant; if shadowed outputs differ on correctness checks by >15% relative to live, flag as regression.
sections.heading: Key signals to monitor (detection)

sections.body:
- Automated alerts to page oncall when any primary signal triggers. Alerts should include:
  - affected model(s)/variant(s) and cohort IDs
  - recent autoscaler/node events in last 10 min
  - KV cache miss heatmap and per-shard error rate
  - attached sample of 10 failed responses (anonymized)
sections.heading: Detection playbook (automated alerts and triage)

sections.body:
1) Validate alert: confirm metric anomalies using PromQL and sampling endpoints. Quick PromQL queries:
   - QA pass rate: sum(rate(eval_qa_pass_total[5m])) / sum(rate(eval_requests_total[5m]))
   - KV cold fraction: increase(runtime_kvcache_miss_rate[10m]) > 0.2
2) Correlate with infra events: check cluster events, node restarts, pod reschedules, and model rollout timestamps (kubectl get events, /ops/eventlog).
3) Isolate scope: check whether issue affects single model variant, model family, single region, or all customers. Use per-route and per-token tagging.
4) Collect traces & dumps: capture 30s full trace for a failing request pattern (trace-id), and export kernel telemetry and KV warmup state for the affected shard(s). CLI snippets below.

Immediate mitigations (order of preference — safer first):
1) Route traffic to warm pool or previously healthy variant:
   - Use routing policy to send impacted percentage to warm pool while keeping the rest on primary for canary validation.
   - Command (control plane): redwood route update --model <model> --variant prev-stable --percent 30 --reason "cold-start-quality-rollback"
2) Force KV prefill for high-impact cohorts: schedule an immediate prefill job for affected keys (see prefill command below). Prefill avoids cold KV misses that often trigger hallucination in long-context models.
   - Prefill CLI: redwood runtime prefill-kv --shard <shard-id> --keys-file /tmp/prefill-keys.json --priority high
3) Temporarily widen quality SLO to reduce batching/fusion: reduce concurrency and batching for the affected variant to reduce kernel cold micro-behavior that affects output shape.
   - config patch (example YAML snippet):
     batcher:
       max_batch_tokens: 4096
       target_latency_ms: 50
       enable_prefill: false
4) Rollback model variant if the degradation coincides with a recent variant rollout and automated canary validation fails. Rollback is disruptive; prefer routing to warm pool when customer impact is partial.
sections.heading: Initial triage (oncall checklist)

sections.body:
- Capture a full trace (oncall machine with access):
  curl -sS "https://obs-api.redwood.internal/trace/collect?model=<model>&window=30s&sample=1" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBS_KEY" > /tmp/trace.json
- Export KV state for shard:
  redwood infra kvcache dump --shard <shard-id> --output /tmp/kvcache-shard-123.dump
- Run batch of synthetic QA prompts against previous-stable variant:
  redwood eval run --model <model>:prev-stable --prompt-file qa-failure-sample.json --concurrency 5 --out /tmp/eval-prev.json

Operational controls (threshold table — editable):
- This table lists the default thresholds used by the detection engine. Operate conservatively and update only after post-incident review.

| signal | alert threshold | severity | default action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1h QA pass drop vs baseline | >20% absolute drop | Sev2 | page oncall; run shadow eval |
| KV cold fraction (cohort) | >80% cold requests for 10m | Sev1 | route to warm pool; prefill KV |
| Prefix token latency change | >2x for token_idx < 32 | Sev2 | decrease batch size; reduce concurrency |
| Shadow-vs-live correctness delta | >15% | Sev1 | immediate rollback or route to prev-variant |

Note: The table above should be managed in the runtime-config repo (config/runtime/coldstart-detection.yaml). Sample YAML fields:

signal_thresholds:
  qa_pass_drop_pct: 20
  kvcold_fraction_threshold: 0.8
  prefix_latency_multiplier: 2.0
  shadow_delta_pct: 15
sections.heading: Commands & data-collection recipes

sections.body:
1) If KV cold fraction is main driver: run prefill job, validate reduced KV miss rate, then gradually increase traffic to variant.
2) If model swap is root cause and prior variant performs better on shadow eval: route 100% to previous variant and open a rollback change in the deployment tracker.
3) If the issue is due to kernel rollout or scheduling change: pause the kernel rollout, set scheduler to conservative profile, and engage kernel owner to examine kernel changes.
4) If widespread and unknown: enable temporary degradation mode that firms up safety heuristics (shorten response length, add conservative decoding params like top_p=0.8) while engineers investigate.
sections.heading: Recovery playbook (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Create a postmortem within 72 hours with: timeline, contributing causes, sampling artifacts, KV dump, traces, rollout IDs, and remediation owner.
- Update the thresholds table if alert was noisy or too lax.
- Add targeted integration tests to the benchmark suite: shadow-evaluation scenarios that mimic the failed cohort shape.
- Schedule a follow-up: kernel scheduling replay across recorded traces to reproduce the behavior in the lab.
sections.heading: Post-incident actions (postmortem checklist)

sections.body:
- Sev1 (customer-impacting correctness): page oncall immediately, 15 min ack, 1 hour mitigation or rollback.
- Sev2 (degraded QA but limited subset): page oncall, 30 min ack, mitigation within 4 hours.
sections.heading: Runbook escalation matrix and SLA

sections.body:
- Small cohorts (low traffic) produce noisy QA signals; require a minimum sampling floor of 200 requests/hour before auto-alerting.
- Not every KV miss spike implies hallucination — cross-check with decoding entropy and repeated token heuristics.
- Prefill can be expensive. Use prioritized prefill for high-value cohorts only.
sections.heading: Known gotchas and heuristics

sections.body: - Case: Model-variant X rollout (2025-08-13) produced a 35% QA pass drop for long-context summarization requests. Root cause: optimistic kernel fusion that skipped boundary prefetch for windowed attention. Recovery: immediate rollback to prev-stable, patch to prefetch check in kernel 2.1. Patch released with canary and shadow checks.
sections.heading: Examples and case studies (short)

sections.body:
- Prefill job operator docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/prefill-job-operator-manual
- Cold-start warmup patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025
- Observability data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

Appendix: quick checklist card (for oncall)
1) Verify alert artifacts and sample 10 failing traces.
2) Check KV cold fraction and prefill if >80%
3) Shadow-eval prev-stable variant (5m)
4) Route traffic to warm pool or prev-stable variant (30% -> 100% if good)
5) If kernel rollout correlated, pause rollout and contact kernel owner
6) Open postmortem and attach kvcache dump + traces
sections.heading: References and links

sections.body:
- serving-runtime oncall: #oncall-serving-runtime (Slack)
- runtime-sre lead: diego.alvarez@redwood.ai
- kernel owners: kernel-team@redwood.ai
- model-onboarding: models@redwood.ai
sections.heading: Contact list

sections.body:
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime runbooks guild (rotate quarterly)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev1 incident tied to cold-start quality

End of document.

payload.page_title: Runtime incident orchestration and capacity decision matrix

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook defines an operational decision matrix and step-by-step orchestration patterns for runtime incidents that span capacity, kernel scheduling regressions, model-fidelity degradation, and mixed-workload stress. It codifies: when to scale, when to switch model variants, which kernel tuning recipes to attempt, how to trigger targeted profiling and benchmarking, and rollback rules for safe recovery.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all production serving clusters running the Redwood serving runtime (hosted + dedicated pools).
- Relevant for incidents impacting latency SLOs, error rate regressions, GPU capacity saturation, and kernel scheduling anomalies.
- Not for control-plane-only incidents (see incident-process/control-plane-runbook).

Goals and SLOs referenced:
- Tier-1 latency SLO: 95th percentile request latency <= 250ms for short-chat shape (<=128 tokens).
- Tier-1 availability SLO: 99.95% per-customer route over 30d window.
- Escalation thresholds used in decision matrix:
  - Latency P95 increase > 25% sustained for 5m -> on-call notification.
  - Error rate > 0.5% or traffic-received drop > 10% for two consecutive 1m buckets -> immediate pager.
  - GPU utilization > 92% with persistent queue growth > 2s average -> capacity triage.

On-call owners and contacts:
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (rotation: eng-serving-runtime-team).
- Kernel scheduling SME: Marco Alvarez (pager for kernel-critical).
- Model/onboarding SME: Priya Natarajan.
- SRE lead for pool scaling: Chen Li.

Decision matrix (quick):
- Symptom: Latency spike, short shape, single model variant
  - If P95 up < 40% and GPU util < 85%: enable per-request kernel hedging (fast path) and increase batching window by 5ms.
  - If P95 up >= 40% or tail outliers concentrated on specific kernel: escalate to kernel SME -> apply hotfix kernel credit adjustments (recipe K-1).
  - If GPU util > 90% and queue growth: trigger autoscale policy (scale up reserved capacity) and enable model variant fallback (lower-fidelity quantized model).

- Symptom: Elevated error rate with GRPC status 14 / UNAVAILABLE
  - Check GRPC connection pool metrics and per-node fd usage. If fd exhaustion -> restart affected dispatcher process after draining new connections (graceful restart). If restart fails -> cordon node and shift traffic with delta-routing to healthy pools.

- Symptom: Progressive cost or throughput regression after an internal kernel rollout
  - Immediately flip kernel rollout flag to previous stable kernel using feature-flag API (see Commands). If rollback not possible, shift canary allocation to fallback pool and throttle nonessential background batches.

Runbook steps (first 15 minutes):
1) Triage: gather the top-3 metrics in a single view: per-pool GPU util, request queue depth, P95 latency by model, error rate by status code. Use the 'incident-quick' dashboard.
2) Annotate timeline: add tags (kernel_rollout, model_swap, autoscaling_event) to correlate with deploys.
3) Apply immediate mitigations (choose only one primary):
   - Increase admission controller token bucket by +10% (fast local change).
   - If kernel suspicion: enable kernel hedging for short shapes on affected pool.
   - If capacity pressure: issue scale up (temporary burst).
4) Trigger targeted profiler capture for affected nodes (5m sample) and start parallel benchmarking job with a synthetic replay of the failing request shape.
5) Notify stakeholders in #runtime-incidents and create a Jira incident with tags and initial hypothesis.

Commands and sample ops snippets (CLI):
- Annotate incident and add a tag:
  rtxctl incident annotate --id INCIDENT-1234 --tag kernel_rollout

- Enable kernel hedging for pool 'pool-west-1-g1':
  rtxctl pool update pool-west-1-g1 --kernel-hedging true --hedge-threshold-ms 6

- Trigger short burst autoscale (30m):
  rtxctl autoscale request --pool pool-west-1-g1 --delta 4 --duration 30m --reason "incident-burst"

- Rollback kernel rollout (feature flag):
  rtxctl flags set kernel.runtime_variant=stable-20260115 --env prod --target pool-west-*
Kernel scheduling tuning recipes (ordered, safe->aggressive):
- K-1 (safe): reduce cooperative_batch_slice from 16ms -> 12ms, enable per-priority admission shaping. Use for P95 regressions without memory pressure.
- K-2 (moderate): enable preemption-aware batch slicing; lower max_batch_tokens by 10% for latency-sensitive classes. Requires canary for 5–10% traffic.
- K-3 (aggressive): evict low-priority KV cache entries and enable immediate slot preemption for priority class 0. Use only when latency impact is severe and CPU/GPU memory headroom < 8%.

Profiling checklist (what to capture):
- Kernel timeline trace (collect 5m window) including per-kernel occupancy, active threads, and stall-time.
- Full request trace with trace_id and kernel-hints annotated.
- Sampled host metrics: cgroup memory, GPU SM utilization, nvlink counters, PCIe error counts.
- Replay benchmark: synthetic corpus focusing on 3 representative shapes (short-chat <=128 tokens, mid 512 tokens, long 2048 tokens).

Benchmark triggers and gating:
- Run the per-pool benchmark suite whenever:
  - Kernel change enters canary (must pass per-token-latency regression < 3% on synthetic suite).
  - Model quantization profile is updated.
  - Autoscaler configuration is modified.
- Pass criteria: P50/P95/P99 within acceptable envelopes. Envelopes defined in the 'benchmark-envelopes' config in the docs.

Rollback and canary matrix:
- For kernel changes: three-stage rollout.
  - Stage 1 (Canary): 1% traffic for 30m with continuous latency monitoring and shadow tracing.
  - Stage 2 (Ramp): 10% traffic for 1h if canary passes.
  - Stage 3 (Full): 100% after 24h stable signal.
- Immediate rollback rule: any of the following during Canary/Ramp -> rollback to previous variant:
  - P95 increase > 12% vs baseline AND error rate increase > 0.2% absolute.
  - GPU queue growth > 1.5s sustained for 10m.

Escalation and post-incident analysis:
- If mitigation doesn't restore SLOs within 30m, escalate to Level-2 with SRE lead and Kernel SME. Prepare binary artifacts: kernel trace + profiling tarball + benchmark replay output for 72h ingestion.
- Post-incident runbook items (within 3 business days):
  1) Create postmortem with timelines, hypothesis, and RCA.
  2) Add a regression test to the perf-suite covering the failing shape.
  3) Schedule a kernel rollout policy change if root cause was policy misconfiguration.

Ownership and long-term actions:
- Immediate ownership during incident: serving-runtime oncall.
- Follow-up ownership: eng-serving-runtime (primary) with kernel-scheduling team as secondary.
- Long-term projects to reduce recurrence: improved synthetic workload coverage, deterministic kernel stress tests, and expanded K-2 canary automation.

Tables / quick reference (text table):
- Decision matrix excerpt:
  Symptom | Primary action | Owner | Safe window
  Latency P95 +25% | Enable kernel hedging / increase batching slightly | Oncall | 5-30m
  Queue growth +2s | Trigger autoscale burst + lower-fidelity fallback | SRE lead | 10-60m
  Kernel canary regress | Rollback kernel flag -> run targeted replay | Kernel SME | Immediate

Example config snippets (admission controller YAML):
- Example: adjust admission tokens
  ---
  admission:
    default_tokens: 1000
    token_bucket_refill_ms: 1000
    per_route_overrides:
      - route: "/v1/chat"
        tokens: 1200

Notes and caveats:
- Avoid applying multiple aggressive kernel recipes simultaneously. Always prefer staged changes and monitor.
- Profiling captures are disk and network heavy; prefer sampling at 10% for clusters with >100 nodes.
- When invoking an autoscale burst, annotate the change with incident id and reason to ensure cost reconciliation.

Related artifacts and dashboards:
- incident-quick dashboard (link internal)
- kernel-trace-aggregator service logs (service: kernel-trace-agg)
- perf-suite replay job id pattern: perf-replay-<incident-id>-<shape>

Revision history and references:
- Drafted 2026-02-03 by Evan Park. Reviewed by Priya Natarajan and Marco Alvarez. Published 2026-03-01.
- See also: runtime-architecture execution stitching doc and runtime-deployment circuit-breakers playbook for additional fallback policies.

Appendix: rapid checklist (one-liner for pager recipient):
1) Confirm SLO symptom and affected pool. 2) Choose one immediate mitigation (admission/hedge/scale). 3) Capture 5m profiler & start replay. 4) If kernel suspect, rollback kernel flag. 5) Escalate if unresolved at 30m.

End of document.
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: Runbook: Runtime keycache index corruption causing GPU OOMs (runtime-2.4.x hotfix)

sections.body:
This runbook covers detection, mitigation, and rollout steps for a class of incidents where long-running sessions experience sustained GPU memory growth, degraded tail latency, and eventual GPU OOMs due to keycache index inconsistency after journal compaction.

This page supersedes the emergency notes in ENG-424242 by consolidating the confirmed root cause, the runtime-2.4.x hotfix behavior, and operational procedures for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
Over multiple escalations (Hosted + Dedicated), customers reported sudden GPU OOMs coinciding with:
- Sustained GPU memory growth on long-running sessions
- Increased p95/p99 latency
- Spikes in keycache journal compaction time
- Repeated key index resync events

In affected cases, stale index entries prevented proper eviction. Under fragmentation, the GPU allocator entered a stall pattern (increased reserve/retry loops), leading to runaway reservation for a subset of sessions and eventual OOM.
sections.heading: Summary (what happened)

sections.body:
The initial hypothesis (dangling pointers in the merge path) was partially correct but incomplete.

**Confirmed cause (runtime-2.4.0 through runtime-2.4.1):**
A race condition in the keycache journal compaction + snapshot merge path where concurrent eviction and a compaction commit could publish a partially-updated index view. The index version could advance while a subset of segments still referenced pre-compaction offsets, producing a mixed-generation index.

**Why it showed up “cross-environment”:**
Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments manifested at different thresholds because:
- Workload mixes differed (long-tail autoregressive vs. short requests)
- Memory pressure differed (fragmentation tolerance varies by GPU SKU and co-tenant load)
- Some environments had higher compaction frequency due to key churn

**Secondary amplifiers:**
- Long-tail autoregressive requests with large KV footprints avoid typical short-circuit evictions.
- Fragmentation increases allocator compaction overhead; once stalls begin, handle cleanup lags, increasing pressure further.
sections.heading: Confirmed root cause (updated)

sections.body:
- High severity when it triggers: request failures due to OOM, degraded throughput, and sometimes traffic migration.
- Hosted: multi-tenant transient throttles and elevated retries.
- Dedicated/Private: prolonged degradation possible if nodes are not restarted or upgraded.
sections.heading: Blast radius / customer impact

sections.body:
1) Rapidly increasing GPU memory (allocated or reserved) without matching throughput
2) Keycache index resync loops and/or elevated compaction latency
3) GPU allocator stall metrics increasing (reserve failures, retry loops)
4) OOMs on long-running sessions that do not reproduce on fresh pods
sections.heading: Use this runbook when you observe any combination of

sections.body:
- Memory fragmentation / arena metrics: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/mem-frag-ENG-424242
- GPU OOM heatmap: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/gpu-oom-heatmap
sections.heading: Primary dashboards

sections.body:
- runtime.keycache.journal_compaction_duration_ms (p95, max)
- runtime.keycache.index_resync_count
- runtime.keycache.eviction_failures
- runtime.gpu.allocator_stall_ms (p95)
- runtime.gpu.memory_reserved_bytes vs runtime.gpu.memory_allocated_bytes (gap indicates fragmentation/reservation pressure)
- runtime.session.handle_leaks (if available)
sections.heading: Key metrics to watch (names may differ slightly by cluster)

sections.body:
1. Confirm scope
   - Is it a single model deployment, a region, or multi-region?
   - Identify whether issues correlate with long-running sessions.

2. Confirm symptoms
   - Check OOM logs and allocator stall metrics.
   - Check for index resync spikes and compaction spikes.

3. Identify runtime version
   - Versions at highest risk: runtime-2.4.0, runtime-2.4.1.
   - Hotfix versions: runtime-2.4.2-hotfix (preferred) and runtime-2.4.1-hotfix (intermediate, if already deployed).

4. Decide immediate mitigation
   - If active OOMs: apply emergency mitigations first (below), then proceed to rollout/upgrade.
sections.heading: Triage checklist (15 minutes)

sections.body:
- Temporarily lower max session TTL (if supported by the serving config) and/or reduce max context length for affected endpoints.
- Preferably target only the affected model deployment(s) to minimize customer impact.
sections.heading: Mitigation A: Reduce long-lived session pressure

sections.body:
If the deployment supports runtime flags, enable safe eviction mode to reduce the probability of publishing mixed-generation index views during pressure.

Set one of the following flags (depending on environment tooling):
- KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=1
- RUNTIME_KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=true
sections.heading: Mitigation B: Force safe eviction mode (runtime flag)

sections.body:
- Safe eviction can reduce throughput by ~2–6% on KV-heavy workloads; treat as temporary.
- If OOMs persist after enabling, proceed to Mitigation C and upgrade.
sections.heading: Operational notes

sections.body: If allocator stalls are already severe, a rolling restart can restore service while you prepare the hotfix rollout.
sections.heading: Mitigation C: Controlled restart / pod recycling

sections.body:
- Hosted: follow standard regional rolling restart policy; keep capacity headroom.
- Dedicated/Private: coordinate with Customer Success; do not restart all nodes simultaneously.
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body:
**runtime-2.4.2-hotfix** (preferred)
- Adds index generation fencing and atomic publish semantics for compaction merges.
- Introduces stricter validation around index segment boundaries.
- Adds a bounded emergency reclaim path to break allocator stall loops.
sections.heading: Recommended fix version

sections.body: - runtime-2.4.1-hotfix reduces incidence via linearized merge fencing, but does not fully eliminate mixed-generation edge cases under extreme churn. Upgrade to runtime-2.4.2-hotfix as soon as feasible.
sections.heading: Notes on earlier hotfix

sections.body:
- New metric: runtime.keycache.index_generation_conflict_count (should remain near zero)
- Additional log lines when safe eviction is triggered under fragmentation
- Emergency reclaim triggers only when stall thresholds are exceeded; it is rate-limited
sections.heading: What the hotfix changes (operator-facing)

sections.body:
1. Stage
   - Deploy runtime-2.4.2-hotfix to staging.
   - Run replay workload for at least 6 hours (24 hours preferred if incident pressure is low).

2. Canary
   - Start at 5–10% traffic in a low-risk region (historically eu-west-1 was used).
   - Monitor for at least 12 hours; extend to 48 hours if the incident is ongoing or signals are noisy.

3. Regional expansion
   - Increase to 25% then 50% in the canary region.
   - Expand to one additional region.

4. Global
   - Proceed to full rollout once key signals stabilize (see Success Criteria below).
sections.heading: Hosted rollout (canary → regional → global)

sections.body: - If index_generation_conflict_count increases or OOM rate worsens, roll back to prior stable runtime and enable KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=1 until a corrected build is deployed.
sections.heading: Rollback plan

sections.body:
1. Confirm maintenance window with Customer Success.
2. Upgrade one node first (or one pool) and run a 2–4 hour soak test.
3. Upgrade remaining nodes in rolling fashion.
4. Leave safe eviction enabled for 24 hours post-upgrade if the customer runs KV-heavy workloads, then disable if stable.
sections.heading: Dedicated/Private rollout

sections.body:
- No OOM regressions on historical replay traces or during soak.
- allocator stall metrics decrease materially (target: ≥25% reduction from incident baseline).
- Memory fragmentation improves (arena free-percentiles improve by ~20% within 24 hours on representative load).
- Index resync count returns to baseline; generation conflicts remain ~0.
- Impacted customers confirm restored baseline throughput.
sections.heading: Success criteria (what “fixed” looks like)

sections.body:
1) OOMs persist after hotfix rollout
- Verify the running version actually updated.
- Check if workload exceeds expected KV limits; consider tightening context/TTL.
- Enable safe eviction mode temporarily.
- Escalate to Serving Runtime on-call with:
  - Region(s), model deployment(s)
  - Runtime version(s)
  - 2–4 hour window of dashboards
  - Representative request traces (redacted)

2) Throughput regression after enabling safe eviction
- Disable safe eviction after hotfix deployment and 24 hours of stability.
- If throughput remains degraded, check for unrelated GPU fragmentation drivers (driver version changes, co-tenancy shifts, model swaps).
sections.heading: Failure modes and what to do

sections.body:
- For active incidents: publish a brief customer-facing status update noting mitigations in progress and an ETA for a runtime hotfix.
- For Dedicated/Private: provide a maintenance window and a rollback plan.
- After full rollout: share a short incident summary and confirm monitoring improvements.
sections.heading: Communications guidance

sections.body:
- Primary incident tracking: linear://ENG-424242
- Hotpatch PRs:
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892 (initial fencing + tests)
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1894 (instrumentation + allocator guardrails)
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1901 (index generation atomic publish + validation)
- Dashboards:
  - https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/mem-frag-ENG-424242
  - https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/gpu-oom-heatmap
sections.heading: References

sections.body:
- 2026-03-12: Initial runbook drafted from ENG-424242 investigation.
- 2026-03-16: Added canary and rollback procedure; documented safe eviction flag.
- 2026-03-22: Updated root cause to confirmed mixed-generation index publish; updated recommended version to runtime-2.4.2-hotfix; added generation conflict metric guidance.

payload.page_title: Serving Runtime Patch Rollback & Dependency Compatibility Runbook (2026)

sections.body: This runbook standardizes how we review, roll out, and (if necessary) roll back patches that touch Serving Runtime request routing, batching, configuration parsing, or client-compatibility behavior. It is intended for on-call engineers, patch authors, and reviewers.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Batching router and queueing logic
- Legacy config parsing and request header parsing
- Dependency upgrades that can affect wire formats, caching formats, or client interoperability
- Observability/metrics naming changes that can break dashboards or alerting

Out of scope: database schema migrations owned by other teams (follow the owning team’s migration runbook), unless the runtime change includes an embedded migration step.
sections.heading: Applies to changes in

sections.body: A recurring high-risk pattern is a small router or parser change that is logically correct but fails under concurrency or with older clients. Typical symptoms include intermittent 5xx spikes during high concurrency runs and unexpected 4xx responses when optional client headers are missing.
sections.heading: Background / Common Risk Profile

sections.body:
- Change touched split-batching fast-path and legacy config parsing.
- Older clients did not send a new optional header; initial implementation returned 415 for some request shapes.
- Staging saw intermittent 502s during batching boundary transitions due to a race in router queue-length calculation.
sections.heading: Recent example category (tracked under INF-2293)

sections.body:
- "Old client": any client version that predates the optional header behavior (see Client Compatibility Contracts page).
- "Compatibility shim": minimal patch that restores old behavior when the optional header is absent or malformed.
- "Canary": small traffic slice routed to a dedicated pool or deployment for early detection.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- Confirm unit tests cover the header-absent case with safe defaults.
  - Required cases: no-header, bad-header, extra-field/unknown value.
  - If the parser previously accepted missing header, it must continue to do so unless there is an approved deprecation.
- Confirm the API/contract is updated if behavior changes.
  - If behavior is conditional on header presence/absence, document it explicitly and include a deprecation timeline.
sections.heading: 1) Compatibility behavior

sections.body:
- Integration test required for split-batching + old-client compatibility.
  - Must run in CI (may be tagged as slow), and must include a mixed workload where a subset of requests omit the optional header.
  - Current standard: 30 minutes minimum for the long-run stability test on the canary build.
- Ensure the change does not introduce new flakiness.
  - If it does, address flakiness before merge or add a temporary feature flag + follow-up ticket.
sections.heading: 2) Tests and CI gating

sections.body:
- Validate metric naming backwards compatibility.
  - Do not rename existing metrics without providing a migration plan and updating dashboards.
  - If new metrics are added, ensure they are clearly scoped and labeled.
sections.heading: 3) Observability and metrics

sections.body:
- Verify no changes to tokenization, KV cache format, or any persisted on-disk format.
  - If any format change is unavoidable, block until a versioned migration strategy is defined.
- Verify no new DB migrations or schema changes.
  - If present, ensure rollback is explicitly documented and ownership is confirmed.
sections.heading: 4) Dependencies and formats

sections.body:
- Prefer a feature flag for behavior changes.
  - Requirement (2026 standard): any router behavior change that could affect latency/5xx must be behind a flag or must have a documented safe fallback.
sections.heading: 5) Rollout controls

sections.body: - Spikes of 502/503 during batching boundary transitions under high concurrency.
sections.heading: Symptom

sections.body:
- Router queue-length calculation is atomic/consistent.
- Boundary update logic does not produce transient invalid state.
sections.heading: What to validate

sections.body: - Some internal clients return 415/400 when the optional header is missing.
sections.heading: Symptom

sections.body:
- Missing header defaults to the prior safe behavior.
- Malformed header fails gracefully (ideally warning + fallback) unless explicitly a hard error.
sections.heading: What to validate

sections.body: - Dashboards missing data; alerts silent/noisy due to renamed metrics.
sections.heading: Symptom

sections.body:
- Existing metric names remain stable.
- Any additions include a dashboard update plan.
sections.heading: What to validate

sections.body:
1) Start runtime with staging-like config and reduced batching thresholds.
2) Run load script with mixed client population (at least 50% old-client simulation that omits the optional header).
   - Recommended: scripts/loaders/split_batch_test.py
3) Inspect logs for batching boundary update events and correlate with any 5xx.
4) If latency jumps, enable router/queue debug logs and collect a CPU profile.
sections.heading: Local repro

sections.body:
1) Deploy to staging pool with debug logging enabled for the router component only.
2) Run the same mixed client load for at least 20 minutes.
3) Confirm:
   - No header-related warnings at steady state.
   - No sustained 5xx above baseline.
sections.heading: Staging validation

sections.body:
1) Deploy to canary pool.
2) Start at 5% traffic for 12 hours.
   - If the change is high-risk (router/batching logic), extend to 24 hours.
3) Monitor:
   - Error budget burn and 5xx rate (page if >1% over a 5-minute window)
   - p50/p99 latency, especially tail latency on hot routes
   - Any increase in 4xx related to parsing/headers
4) If stable, promote incrementally (e.g., 25% -> 50% -> 100%).
sections.heading: Canary Rollout Plan (Standard)

sections.body: - Small canaries can hide statistically significant regressions; if traffic is low, extend duration rather than increasing percentage too quickly.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- Revert the merge commit and redeploy.
  - Command guidance: use a standard git revert of the merge SHA and deploy hotfix to canary, then production.
- Communicate in #sre-oncall and #serving-runtime if the rollback is due to customer-visible impact.
  - Open an incident channel if >1% error rate over 5 minutes or if tail latency breaches SLO.
sections.heading: Fast path (preferred)

sections.body:
- Deploy a compatibility shim:
  - Accept missing optional header and fall back to old behavior.
  - Keep the shim minimal and well-tested.
- Promote shim via canary first.
sections.heading: If revert is blocked by dependent PRs

sections.body:
Initiate rollback if any of the following holds during canary:
- 5xx > 1% for 5 minutes and attributable to the change
- p99 latency regression > 15% sustained for 15 minutes on critical routes
- Any new systematic 4xx for old-client population (header missing/malformed)
sections.heading: Rollback decision thresholds (operational)

sections.body:
- Backport only the minimal safe subset.
  - Typical backport contents: parser default behavior + compatibility tests + feature flag plumbing.
  - Avoid backporting batching optimizations unless explicitly approved by release owner.
- Current stable target (as of last update): release/2026-03-stable.
- Label backports with: backport/stable and link to the original PR.
sections.heading: Backport Guidance (Stable Branch)

sections.body:
- Verify p50/p90/p99 latencies per route.
- Run a small synthetic workload:
  - 100 requests/sec
  - at least 40% old-client simulation (no optional header)
  - confirm zero parsing-related 4xx/5xx
- Check logs for header-related warnings.
  - Target: zero occurrences of "unknown-client-header" (or equivalent warning string for the current parser).
sections.heading: After canary promotion (and again after full rollout)

sections.body:
- Does the optional header default to a safe value in all call sites?
- Is conditional behavior documented in the client compatibility contract?
- Is there a feature flag (or equivalent rollout control) for risky behavior changes?
- Are metrics backwards compatible, and is there a dashboard migration plan if needed?
- Are before/after performance numbers provided (p50/p99 under representative load)?
sections.heading: PR Review Talking Points (Copy/Paste)

sections.body:
- Create a short blameless postmortem within 2 business days.
- Add a regression test that would have caught the issue.
- Update this runbook if the rollback path was unclear or slow.
sections.heading: If a rollback occurs

sections.body:
- Runbook owner: Eng Serving Runtime
- Primary maintainer: Evan Blake
- Canary monitoring rotation: Serving Runtime on-call (coordinate with SRE for paging thresholds)
sections.heading: Ownership

payload.page_title: End-to-End Latency Decomposition and Kernel Hinting Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook describes a standard, repeatable process for decomposing end-to-end inference latency into measurable components and using those signals to drive kernel hinting changes in the runtime. It combines observability queries, targeted profiling, an action checklist, and a safe rollout procedure for kernel-hint configuration updates. The goal is to reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions while preserving throughput and fairness across tenants.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated serving clusters running the Redwood serving runtime.
- Targets interactive text-generation and chat workloads (typical seq_len 16–2048).
- Focuses on per-request latency; does not replace per-token cost optimization playbooks.

When to use this playbook:
1) Sudden increase in p95 or p99 latency for a model route.
2) Regressions observed after a kernel rollout, quantization change, or autoscaler tuning.
3) Persistent tail latency despite normal kernel telemetry.

Owner and escalation path:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall team (primary: @runtime-oncall).
- Secondary owner: Serving Runtime Kernel SIG (rotation: kernel-sig@redwood).
- Escalation: If changes affect >2x latency or traffic outage, escalate to SRE Pager and Product (use internal pager flow).

Key concepts and definitions:
- E2E latency: measured at edge proxy from request start to final byte.
- Scheduling latency: time spent waiting in runtime scheduler queue before kernel dispatch.
- Kernel execution latency: GPU kernel time (inclusive of kernel launch and completion).
- KV prefetch / warmup time: additional per-shard I/O or KV cache population time that occurs before kernel execution.
- Serialization / networking: edge, reverse-proxy, and inter-node serialization + network transfer time.

Observability checklist (quick diagnostic):
1) Open the route dashboard (Grafana): route.latency.p95, route.latency.p99, route.success_rate.
2) Split E2E into spans: proxy_span, scheduler_queue_span, kernel_exec_span, kv_warmup_span. Grafana panels exist with these derived metrics.
3) Run a time-range query (last 15m and last 6h) to check whether the tail event is transient or sustained.

Useful PromQL and sample queries:
- p95 E2E: quantile_over_time(0.95, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
- Avg scheduling queue time: avg_over_time(runtime_scheduler_queue_seconds_sum[5m]) / avg_over_time(runtime_scheduler_queue_seconds_count[5m])
- Kernel execution 99th: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_exec_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel_name))
- KV warmup rate spike: increase(kv_warmup_ops_total[5m]) / increase(runtime_request_total[5m])

Initial triage steps (ordered):
1) Confirm signal: validate the alerting query and look for correlated error spikes (grpc errors, resource saturation).
2) Isolate scope: is the regression single-route, model-variant, or cluster-wide? Filter by route, model_id, shard_id.
3) Compare to kernel telemetry: check kernel_exec_seconds histogram and per-kernel concurrency.
4) Check scheduler telemetry: per-priority queue lengths, wait-time distributions, and preemption events.
5) Inspect GPU host metrics: GPU utilization, memory pressure, nvlink error counters, PCIe throughput.
6) If kernel_exec latency is stable but queue times increased -> suspect scheduler/backpressure or KV warmup.
7) If kernel_exec latency increased -> suspect kernel regressions, new kernel rollout, instruction set mismatch, or memory thrashing.

Profiling playbook (when deeper analysis needed):
1) Capture a targeted trace using the runtime trace-sampler for the affected route (sample rate 100% for a 2 minute window):
   - CLI: redwood-runtime trace capture --route <route> --duration 120s --out /tmp/trace.json
2) Run offline trace decomposition tool (trace-decompose) to split timings by span and annotate kernel traces with CUDA timestamps.
   - Example: trace-decompose /tmp/trace.json --output /tmp/decomposed.csv
3) If kernel exec is dominant -> collect CUPTI and kernel-level samples on the node (coordinate with infra oncall).
4) If KV warmup is dominant -> enable kvcache debug logs at INFO for the route for 10 minutes and gather sample logs.

Kernel hinting: intent and mechanics
- Kernel hinting lets the high-level scheduler bias scheduling decisions for a request: e.g., prefer fused attention kernels, prefetch KV cache, or mark as latency-sensitive so it bypasses large-batch queues.
- Hint sources: static model profile, dynamic telemetry rule, manual override via rollout. Hints are attached to request metadata and consumed by the scheduler and kernel mapper.

Example kernel-hint configuration (YAML snippet):
```
kernel_hint_profiles:
  - id: short-chat-low-latency
    match:
      max_seq_len: 256
      model_family: "redwood-chat"
    hints:
      prefer_kernel: "fused_attn_v3"
      priority: high
      kvcache_prefetch: true
      prefetch_window_ms: 50
```

Interpreting hint effects:
- prefer_kernel: if the preferred kernel is available on the node, scheduler will route to matching nodes first.
- priority: routes the request into a priority queue; high-priority queues are policed to preserve SLOs.
- kvcache_prefetch and prefetch_window_ms: cause asynchronous KV prefetch before kernel dispatch to reduce warmup latency.

Safety constraints for hint changes (must be followed):
- Any new hint profile must have an automated canary with traffic fraction <= 2% for 24 hours and p95/p99 compared to baseline before rollforward.
- Run an A/B test with traffic mirroring for at least 2 hours and collect per-token tokenization parity checks.
- Ensure hint profiles are scoped by route or tenant to avoid cross-tenant performance impact.

Rollout procedure for kernel-hint adjustments (step-by-step):
1) Create a kernel-hint PR in infra-configs with: rationale, telemetry baselines, YAML snippet, and rollback plan.
2) Apply to canary pool (label: canary-hint) at 1% traffic. Observe for 1 hour.
3) If no regressions: increase to 2% for 24 hours while running differential metrics and trace capture.
4) Run targeted load tests from benchmarking suite: replicate production p95 with synthetic load to validate scaling behavior.
5) If stable: increase to 10% for 2 hours, then 50% for 2 hours, then full rollout.
6) On any regression, immediately rollback by removing the canary hint profile; trigger postmortem.

Playbook for common symptoms and recommended actions:
- Symptom: p99 latency increase but kernel_exec stable -> Action: investigate scheduler queueing. Consider creating a temporary priority hint for affected routes or enabling limited prefetch to avoid queue spike.
- Symptom: kernel_exec p99 spike on specific kernel -> Action: pin route to alternative kernel (prefer_kernel override) or revert recent kernel rollout. Collect CUPTI traces.
- Symptom: KV warmup spikes on cold-starts -> Action: increase prefetch_window_ms for small window; evaluate pre-warm policies in autoscaler.
- Symptom: NVLink or PCIe-related variance -> Action: move traffic away from affected nodes via decommission flag; open infra ticket for hardware investigation.

Observability artifacts to collect when filing an incident:
- Route ID, model ID, user-visible error/latency windows, p50/p95/p99 baseline and during incident.
- 2–5 representative decomposed traces (decomposed.csv) and corresponding raw trace.json.
- Kernel histograms and queue length time-series for the incident window.
- Node-level GPU metrics and recent kernel-rollout history.

Postmortem guidance and experiment tracking:
- Any hint-profile change that affects latency by >10% p95 or p99 requires a short postmortem (owner: author of the config PR).
- Track experiments in the runtime experiment dashboard with traffic fractions, start/end times, and success criteria.

Appendix A — Example Grafana panels and what they show:
- Scheduler queue heatmap: shows per-priority queue depth over time (useful for burst/backpressure).
- Kernel selection vector: fraction of requests using preferred kernel vs fallback kernels.
- KV prefetch hit rate: percent of requests that served from warm KV.

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick commands:
- Tail runtime logs for route: kubectl logs -l route=<route> -c runtime --tail=500
- Capture traces: redwood-runtime trace capture --route <route> --duration 120s --out /tmp/trace.json
- Apply hint config locally (dry-run): infra-configctl apply --file hint.yaml --dry-run

Related pages and references:
- Benchmarking playbooks for synthetic p95 simulation (see related pages).
- Kernel mapping and policy language specification (kernel mapper docs in kernel-and-scheduling).

Notes and rationale:
- Kernel hinting is a surgical lever: it should be used to rescue latency-sensitive routes where global kernel changes would harm throughput-critical workloads. The playbook prioritizes measurement, small canaries, and observability to avoid cross-tenant regressions.

Change history:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-03: Added canary percentages and PromQL examples (reviewed by Diego Martinez).

payload.page_title: Emergency rollback: Serving Runtime (Hosted + Dedicated)

sections.body:
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes how to perform an *emergency rollback* of the Serving Runtime release across *Hosted* and *Dedicated* fleets. It focuses on restoring SLOs safely and quickly while preserving evidence for later analysis.

h1. When to rollback (triggers)
Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:
* p95 *time-to-first-token (TTFT)* regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
* error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
* canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly
* repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build

*If unsure*: declare an incident and page Runtime + SRE (see incident process) and start preparing rollback steps in parallel.

h1. Preconditions
* An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely (see SEV process page).
* Runtime oncall has identified *candidate rollback target* (prior runtime release tag).
* Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback (see CI/CD rollback doc).

h1. Ownership and roles
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence.
* Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target.
* Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling.
* SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

h1. Rollback decision checklist
Before executing rollback, capture in the incident channel:
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: h1. Step-by-step procedure
sections.heading: Confirm the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod)

sections.body:
* If a rollout is in progress, *pause* it immediately (do not continue canary expansion).
* Ensure no automated progressive delivery job will re-advance the rollout.
sections.heading: 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression

sections.body:
Follow the CI/CD rollback doc to pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then:
* Roll back in this order:
  # non-critical region (if any still on canary only)
  # remaining canary cohort
  # all regions currently on the bad release
* After each region completes, verify:
  * 5xx rate normalizes
  * GPU utilization returns to expected
  * TTFT and token/s recover to baseline
sections.heading: 2) Hosted rollback (global fleets)

sections.body:
* Dashboard: "Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health"
* Metrics to watch: request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count
sections.heading: Hosted verification queries (Console)

sections.body:
Dedicated rollbacks must consider customer-specific change windows and comms. In emergencies, proceed under the emergency change policy.
* Identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants:
  * Check "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" dashboard
  * Confirm whether each tenant is on the bad release
* Execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure.
* For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals (see comms guide).
sections.heading: 3) Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)

sections.body:
* Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated)
* Confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear
* Ensure autoscaling stabilizes (watch for over-provisioning due to the regression)

h1. Guardrails and common failure modes
* If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess (may be traffic pattern or model mix).
* If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback (requires IC approval).
* Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases; if you must re-roll forward, document the reason and require runtime lead approval.

h1. Required artifacts (for later review)
sections.heading: 4) Post-rollback validation

sections.body:
* CI/CD job link(s) for rollback
* Affected regions / clusters
* Metrics screenshots or dashboard permalinks
* Any customer comms sent

h1. References
* SEV process for runtime regressions (incident roles, paging, timelines)
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure (exact CI/CD steps)
* Emergency change policy (approvals and documentation)
* Customer/status comms guide (templates and approval chain)
