payload.page_title: KV-cache shard skew and quantization interaction: investigation, mitigation, and runbook

sections.body: This document captures an investigation into a recurring class of production incidents where uneven KV-cache (prefix/KV) distribution across shard workers combined with aggressive post-training quantization (8-bit asymmetric) produced high tail latency and occasional OOMs. It includes root-cause evidence, detection queries, a short-term mitigation runbook, recommended scheduler and quantization configuration changes, and a checklist for long-term fixes and testing.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Affects: hosted and dedicated serving pools using split-shard KV routing + quantized model families (q8_a and q8_b).
- Symptom window: intermittent p99/p999 spikes (200–800ms over baseline), spikes concentrated during synthetic-batched workloads and long-context chat sessions (>= 2048 tokens).
- Frequency: 3 incidents between 2025-09 and 2025-11 in US-east-1 GPU pools; reproduction locally with shard skew simulator.
- Business impact: API error rate increased 1.4–2.3x during events; customers on Dedicated saw throughput degradation prompting support escalations.
sections.heading: Scope and impact

sections.body:
1) Shard assignment heuristic allowed up to 2.5x more active KV-entries on certain workers for common long-prefix prompts, causing memory pressure and slower KV lookups.
2) Quantized kernels (8-bit asymmetric) for recent model variants introduce nonuniform per-layer memory layout that increases temporary workspace allocation variance per token. When combined with prefetching, this exacerbated peak memory use.
3) Kernel scheduler prioritized throughput over memory headroom during steady-state autoscaling; under high skew this led to transient OOM kills and a cascade of request retries that amplified tail latencies.
sections.heading: Key findings (short form)

sections.body:
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard (gauge) — alert if max_shard / median_shard > 1.6 for 5m
- kv_cache_hit_rate (percent) — warn if < 92% for 10m on a model route
- gpu_mem_headroom_pct (gauge) — critical if any device < 12% for 1m
- request_latency_ms{route} p99 and p999 — critical if p999 > baseline_p999 * 3 for 5m
- kernel_scheduler_pending_queue_length — warn if > 1000 for 2m
sections.heading: Relevant metrics and alerting thresholds

sections.body:
- Shard skew ratio:
  max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})
- GPU headroom percentage (device-level):
  100 * (1 - (avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_used_bytes[1m]) / avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_total_bytes[1m])))
sections.heading: PromQL examples (Grafana)

sections.body:
- Kernel traces showing repeated cudaMalloc failure -> fallback path for q8 kernels (attached as trace IDs: trc-20251004-42, trc-20251021-08).
- Heap dumps from affected workers demonstrating 60–80% of incremental allocations were temporary layer workspaces tied to the quantized fused-kernel (dump ids: heap-20251004-a, heap-20251102-b).
- Repro script: scripts/kv-skew-sim/runner.py (internal repo: infra/sim) — reproduces p99 spike by driving long-prefix variety and forcing unbalanced shard assignment.

Immediate mitigation (short-term runbook) — use during incidents:
1) Detect: confirm shard_skew_ratio PromQL > 1.6 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct any device < 12% or p999 > baseline*2.
2) Quarantine affected model route: add a temp-route override to route requests to a non-quantized fallback model (e.g., model-xv2-fp16) via the routing control plane.
3) Throttle synthetic-heavy customers: apply per-client rate limit for 10m windows on routes causing skew.
4) Rebalance shards: trigger targeted shard-respin for the worker pool (CLI):
   - rcli shard rebalance --pool us-east-1-prod --strategy uniform --drain=true --concurrency=2
5) If OOM persists, scale up a hotfix worker-sized pool with higher-memory instances:
   - terraform: apply -var='pool_size=4' -target=module.hotfix-us-east1
6) Monitor: ensure kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio returns < 1.2 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct > 18% before resuming normal routing.
sections.heading: Investigation artifacts (evidence)

sections.body:
- Check shard skew quickly (kubectl + prom):
  kubectl -n serving exec -it svc/prom-query -- curl -sG 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode 'query=max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})' | jq
- Force scheduler to prefer memory headroom (onbox flag):
  echo 'MEMORY_FIRST=1' > /etc/redwood/runtime_flags.d/priority.conf && systemctl restart redwood-runtime-scheduler.service
sections.heading: Commands and ops snippets

sections.body:
- Allocation pattern: the quantized fused attention kernel uses dynamic temporaries sized to sequence length and per-layer hidden-size alignment. Some hardware-specific kernel variants pad workspace to 64-byte boundaries; combined with our allocator metadata this produced a 20–40% bloat versus FP16 kernels under long sequences.
- Shard topology and assignment: the greedy prefix hash used for low-latency routing did not incorporate current KV cache size or recent allocation footprint. That optimization favored route-affinity but ignored memory balance.
- Scheduler policy: the priority-driven scheduler groups tasks into batches by estimated token cost but uses static headroom thresholds. In skewed scenarios it allowed many high-cost requests to land on a single worker because affinity minimization lowered request hop cost metric.
sections.heading: Root-cause analysis (detailed)

sections.body:
- Option A — Always prefer FP16 fallback for long-context (>2048) requests: reduces cost/throughput but increases latency per token slightly for some model families.
- Option B — Update shard assignment to be headroom-aware: requires global KV size propagation (adds 200–400ms route lookup overhead unless cached).
- Option C — Kernel change: adjust quantized kernels to pre-reserve workspace conservatively, reducing dynamic allocation churn (engineering cost high, long lead time).
Recommendation: Combine B + short-term A during rollout. B provides the most sustainable operational improvement with tolerable lookup overhead if we cache single-key headroom info in the routing plane.
sections.heading: Design decisions and trade-offs considered

sections.body:
- Immediate (SRE / eng-serving-runtime) — Implement a headroom-aware shard assignment flag and enable in canary pool (owner: Ravi Patel) — ETA: 2026-03-10.
- Near-term (runtime team) — Add memory-first scheduler mode toggles and expose on control-plane flags (owner: Aisha Kumar) — ETA: 2026-04-01.
- Medium (kernel team) — Rework q8 fused-kernel workspace allocation to use pooled temporaries and deterministic preallocation (owner: Lena Schwartz) — ETA: 2026-07-15.
sections.heading: Planned short-to-medium term fixes (owners and ETA)

sections.body:
1) Add a new scenario to the perf-suite: long-context mixed-prefix workload with intentional skew (workload id: long-prefix-skew-2026). Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99/p999 latency, tokens/sec, retry rate, GPU util, mem headroom.
2) Unit tests for shard assignment: simulate 10k concurrent prefixes and assert skew ratio < 1.3 under headroom-aware policy.
3) Kernel perf run: compare q8_old vs q8_pooled on sequence lengths 512/1024/2048 measuring workspace allocations (nvprof traces).
4) Canary rollout: enable headroom-aware routing in dedicated canary pool of 5 workers for 72h; if p999 regressions occur > 10% abort.
sections.heading: Testing and benchmarking plan (how we will validate)

sections.body:
- Canary p999 latency does not increase by more than 10% relative to baseline for the same traffic mix.
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio <= 1.3 sustained for 24h.
- No device reports gpu_mem_headroom_pct < 10% for more than 1 minute.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria for rollout

sections.body:
- When rebalancing, prefer graceful drain (drain=true) to avoid losing KV in-flight; allow 60s for KV transfer per shard.
- Avoid enabling both memory-first scheduler and aggressive batching in the same pool simultaneously—conflicting objectives can hurt throughput.
- Document temporary route fallbacks in the routing change log with the incident tag (inc-20251004-kv-skew).
sections.heading: Operational notes and playbook tips

sections.body:
- Add integration tests in infra/sim for skewed KV distributions and quantized kernel stress.
- Add end-to-end benchmark in perf-suite with automated alerting hook comparing new runs to historical baselines.
- Update the Runtime Scheduler config schema (runtime-configs/scheduler_v2.yaml):
  # example excerpt
  scheduler_mode: \"memory_first|throughput_first\"
  memory_headroom_threshold_pct: 18
  shard_assignment_cache_ttl_ms: 250
  headroom_propagation: true

Appendix A — Example alert runbook (short):
1) Pager triggers: SRE oncall receives p999 alert for route X.
2) Triage: confirm shard_skew_ratio > 1.6 and check pool memory headroom.
3) Action: apply temporary route override to FP16 fallback and trigger shard rebalance.
4) Post-incident: run heap-dump collector on affected workers and upload to s3 with tag inc-YYYYMMDD-kvskew.

Appendix B — Experimental notes from local reproducer:
- On an AWS p4d-like instance: sequence length 4096 + q8 kernel -> temporary allocations peaked at 64MB per layer; reducing per-layer workspace alignment to 32 bytes reduced peak by ~18%.

If you make changes to scheduler flags or shard assignment heuristics, add a short design note in eng-serving-runtime/decision-records and tag reviewers: Aisha Kumar, Lena Schwartz, Ravi Patel.

payload.page_title: Hardware tuning profiles: known issues and mitigations (living)

sections.body:
This page is a living list of issues we have observed (or can reliably reproduce) when enabling the **hardware tuning profiles pack** for the serving runtime (H100, B200, L40S). Each issue includes:
- Symptoms you can validate quickly (what customers/oncall will see)
- How to detect (metrics/log signatures)
- Immediate mitigation steps (safe toggles/flags)
- Longer-term fix status (when known)

This is *not* an incident log. It is intended to reduce time-to-triage during rollouts and prevent repeated regressions.

**Primary audience:** Runtime oncall, SRE, Infra rollout owners, Support/Solutions.

**Owner:** Serving Runtime (Scheduling + Kernels). Operational upkeep coordinated by SRE.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
1) Identify the deployment + pool + GPU SKU (H100/B200/L40S) and confirm whether a profile is selected.
2) Check if the symptom matches one of the patterns below.
3) Apply the mitigation in the order listed (prefer “revert to baseline/default profile” over ad-hoc knob edits).
4) If mitigation requires disabling profiles for a pool/region, follow the rollout runbook and record the toggle + time window.

**Fast checks (recommended order):**
- Runtime startup logs: profile version + compatibility matrix (runtime version vs profile pack)
- Metrics: `runtime_profile_selected{sku,profile}` and `runtime_profile_override_source{source}`
- Tail latency: p95/p99 by route/model, segmented by profile
- OOM/restart rate and GPU memory headroom

---
sections.heading: How to use this page during an incident

sections.body: These are the mitigations referenced throughout the issue list.
sections.heading: Common mitigations (safe-by-default toggles)

sections.body:
- **Use when:** unknown regression, ambiguous GPU detection, widespread tail-latency increase.
- **Effect:** runtime falls back to built-in baseline defaults.
- **Notes:** Use per-pool override first; avoid global unless impact is broad.
sections.heading: A) Disable profile selection (force baseline)

sections.body:
- **Use when:** throughput-first mode causes tail latency or streaming instability.
- **Effect:** keeps profile benefits while restoring fairness/backpressure.
sections.heading: B) Force a specific profile mode (e.g., H100 balanced)

sections.body:
- **Use when:** tail latency spikes, request queue growth, streaming stutter.
- **Effect:** reduces queueing delay at the cost of throughput.
sections.heading: C) Reduce batching / tighten queue limits

sections.body:
- **Use when:** OOMs, frequent restarts, memory fragmentation, long-context workloads.
- **Effect:** caps memory reserved for KV cache; may reduce max concurrency for long contexts.
sections.heading: D) Constrain KV cache budget

sections.body:
- **Use when:** any regression in B200 pools; if driver/CUDA mismatch suspected.
- **Effect:** revert to H100-like baseline or “generic” safe config.

(Exact flag/env/Helm key names vary by deployment mode; see the rollout runbook and the profile schema doc for current canonical names.)

---
sections.heading: E) Disable experimental B200 profile

sections.body:
**Applies to:** H100 (primarily), sometimes B200 when experimental mode is enabled.

**Symptom(s):**
- p95/p99 latency increases (often 20–60%) while average tokens/sec improves.
- Queue depth increases; “time-to-first-token” (TTFT) regresses most.
- Customers report “slow start” on long prompts, especially during load spikes.

**Likely trigger:**
- Workload skewed to long prefill (e.g., large context ingestion, retrieval-heavy prompts, tool-call scaffolding) combined with high concurrency.

**How to detect:**
- Segment by request type: prefill vs decode (if available).
- Look for disproportionate increase in TTFT and “prefill queue wait time.”
- `scheduler_fairness_adjustments_total` trending up (if instrumented) alongside tail latency.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch pool to **balanced** mode profile (B).
2) Tighten max queue depth / reduce batching (C).
3) If still regressing: disable profiles for the pool (A) and proceed with rollback criteria.

**Status / notes:**
- A similar tail-latency regression was previously fixed in the prefill/decode fairness logic; if this appears after a profile pack update, treat as a candidate regression and compare to prior profile pack version.

---
sections.heading: KI-PP-001: Long-prefill-heavy workloads regress tail latency under throughput-first scheduler presets

sections.body:
**Applies to:** H100, L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Benchmarks pass; real traffic shows intermittent streaming stalls (“chunky” streaming) and elevated partial-response retries.
- p50 steady; p95 spikes correlate with peak concurrency.

**Likely trigger:**
- Real prompts include tool-calling patterns, high variance in output length, or client-side disconnects; these stress backpressure/streaming buffers.

**How to detect:**
- Increase in `stream_send_blocked_seconds` (or equivalent), and `client_disconnects_total` correlated with latency spikes.
- Elevated `request_retries_total{reason="upstream_timeout"}` on streaming routes.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce max in-flight streams per worker / tighten backpressure settings (C).
2) Prefer balanced mode (B) for streaming-heavy pools.
3) If stability issues persist, rollback profiles for the pool (A) and file an issue to expand workload matrix coverage.

**Status / notes:**
- Treat as a “workload matrix gap” if it passes canary but fails in prod; update the workload matrix with a representative streaming mix.

---
sections.heading: KI-PP-002: “Too-clean” benchmark prompt mix hides streaming instability

sections.body:
**Applies to:** L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Sudden OOMs during prefill on long contexts; pods restart.
- GPU memory headroom oscillates; fragmentation increases over time.
- p95 latency spikes preceding OOMs (retries and warm-up effects).

**Likely trigger:**
- L40S has tighter memory constraints; aggressive KV cache budgeting that is safe on H100 can be unsafe on L40S.

**How to detect:**
- `gpu_oom_events_total` increases.
- `gpu_memory_free_bytes` trends downward across hours even at similar QPS (fragmentation pattern).
- Runtime logs mention KV cache allocation failure or emergency eviction.

**Mitigation:**
1) Enforce L40S profile with explicit KV cache budget constraints (D).
2) Reduce max batch size and/or max queued requests (C).
3) If OOMs continue: disable profiles (A) and set conservative runtime memory defaults until re-validated.

**Status / notes:**
- If you see “creeping” fragmentation, capture an hourly memory snapshot and attach to the tracking ticket; this typically indicates a reuse/allocator behavior mismatch for this workload.

---
sections.heading: KI-MEM-001: L40S OOMs under long-context + high concurrency due to KV cache over-reservation

sections.body:
**Applies to:** L40S (most common), occasionally H100 in high churn traffic.

**Symptom(s):**
- Tokens/sec gradually declines over time; p50 stable but p95 creeps.
- No explicit OOMs; instead, more frequent small allocations and cache thrash.

**Likely trigger:**
- High variance in sequence lengths and frequent cancellations time-slice allocations differently than the benchmark harness.

**How to detect:**
- `kv_cache_evictions_total` increases without QPS growth.
- `gpu_memory_fragmentation_ratio` (if available) increases.
- Elevated `cuda_malloc_retry_total` / allocator warning logs.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce KV cache target utilization (D).
2) Prefer settings that reduce churn: cap max concurrent long-context requests (C + D).
3) If impact is severe: roll pool and disable profiles (A) pending deeper allocator analysis.

**Status / notes:**
- Often shows up only on specific traffic mixes; request a traffic replay / prompt distribution sample (sanitized) to reproduce.

---
sections.heading: KI-MEM-002: Memory fragmentation leading to degraded throughput after several hours (allocator behavior)

sections.body:
**Applies to:** H100; can affect B200 if heuristics borrowed.

**Symptom(s):**
- TTFT regresses for short prompts (e.g., <256 tokens input) while long prompts improve.
- Overall throughput may appear neutral, but UX impact is high for chat-like workloads.

**Likely trigger:**
- Heuristic bucket boundaries (sequence length bins) don’t match the real distribution; “short” bucket gets a kernel optimized for different occupancy characteristics.

**How to detect:**
- Segment TTFT by prompt length buckets.
- Compare `kernel_selected{bucket=...}` distribution pre/post profile.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch to balanced mode or the “general” kernel selection preset for that SKU (B).
2) If available, enable adaptive kernel selection rather than pinned selection for short buckets.
3) If no safe option: disable profiles (A) for the affected pool.

**Status / notes:**
- When filing a follow-up, include bucket histograms (input/output length) and the kernel selection stats.

---
sections.heading: KI-KRN-001: Kernel auto-selection chooses a suboptimal path for short sequences, causing TTFT regression

sections.body:
**Applies to:** All SKUs; most common in mixed fleet environments and during provider expansion.

**Symptom(s):**
- Runtime selects “generic” profile unexpectedly, or selects the wrong SKU profile.
- Performance deviates from expectations; in worst cases, stability issues if an incompatible toggle is applied.

**Likely trigger:**
- GPU model strings differ across drivers/providers/instance types (e.g., formatting or suffix variations).

**How to detect:**
- Startup log shows `gpu_sku_raw` and `gpu_sku_normalized` mismatch; profile selection metric shows fallback.
- Increased rate of `profile_selection_ambiguous_total`.

**Mitigation:**
1) Force explicit SKU/profile via pool override (B) until detection is fixed.
2) If forced override is not possible: disable profiles (A) and run with baseline.
3) File an Infra ticket with the raw strings and node types involved; add to normalization allowlist.

**Status / notes:**
- This should be treated as a correctness issue, not “just performance.” Incorrect profile selection can invalidate canary results.

---
sections.heading: KI-KRN-002: Kernel mismatch when GPU SKU string detection is ambiguous (provider-specific strings)

sections.body:
**Applies to:** H100, L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Requests time out upstream; runtime appears healthy but queue depth spikes.
- p99 latency spikes; retries increase; effective throughput drops.

**Likely trigger:**
- Profile queue limits allow too much buffering relative to gateway/client timeouts; burst traffic fills queue faster than it drains.

**How to detect:**
- `request_queue_depth` increases; `gateway_timeouts_total` increases.
- `queue_wait_ms` becomes dominant contributor to latency.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce queue limits and tighten backpressure (C).
2) Align per-route timeout budgets with expected max queue wait.
3) If customer impact persists, rollback profile for pool (A) and re-validate burst behavior.

**Status / notes:**
- Prefer smaller queues and more explicit load shedding for customer-visible endpoints; large queues hide overload until timeouts cascade.

---
sections.heading: KI-SCH-001: Queue growth + timeouts during burst traffic due to queue limit mismatch with upstream timeouts

sections.body:
**Applies to:** Dedicated H100 pools with mixed tenant traffic.

**Symptom(s):**
- One tenant’s long-context or high-output requests dominate batching windows.
- Other tenants see tail-latency regressions and inconsistent TTFT.

**Likely trigger:**
- Batching parameters optimized for aggregate throughput without sufficient per-tenant fairness constraints.

**How to detect:**
- Latency segmented by tenant spikes for “small” tenants during another tenant’s traffic burst.
- Batch composition metrics show high skew.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch pool to balanced profile mode (B).
2) Apply stricter per-tenant concurrency limits (if configured via routing/gateway).
3) If needed, split tenants to separate pools (operational action) and re-run perf validation.

**Status / notes:**
- Treat as a product/SLA concern; do not “optimize away” fairness unless the pool is explicitly single-tenant.

---
sections.heading: KI-SCH-002: Multi-tenant interference in Dedicated pools when throughput-first batching is enabled

sections.body:
**Applies to:** B200 only (experimental gated).

**Symptom(s):**
- Profile not applied even when enabled; runtime logs show version guardrails tripping.
- In some cases: increased error rate, sporadic kernel launch failures.

**Likely trigger:**
- B200 profile requires minimum driver/CUDA stack; partial fleet upgrades lead to mixed compatibility.

**How to detect:**
- Startup logs show “incompatible stack” warning and selected fallback.
- `profile_compatibility_violation_total{sku="B200"}` increases.

**Mitigation:**
1) Disable experimental B200 profile for the pool (E).
2) Verify driver/CUDA versions match the B200 bring-up checklist; upgrade fleet before re-enabling.
3) Re-enable only with canary gating and a rollback plan.

**Status / notes:**
- Default posture for B200 remains “gated + explicit enablement.” Treat any enabling as a staged change with extra SRE oversight.

---
sections.heading: KI-B2K-001: Driver/CUDA mismatch causes silent fallback or instability

sections.body:
**Applies to:** B200 (experimental) in specific pools/regions.

**Symptom(s):**
- Immediate p95 regression post-enable; canary gate triggers or customer reports.

**How to detect:**
- Perf canary gate breach for B200 pools; increased tail latency segmented by region.

**Mitigation:**
1) Disable experimental B200 profile for the impacted pool/region (E).
2) Leave other regions unchanged until root cause is understood.
3) Capture: node type, NCCL/topology characteristics (if multi-GPU), and driver stack details.

**Status / notes:**
- Regional differences (network topology, firmware, provider) can invalidate assumptions. Ensure each region has baseline curves.

---
sections.heading: KI-B2K-002: Cross-region regression requiring pool-level disable (known precedent)

sections.body:
When escalating to Runtime (Scheduling/Kernels) or Infra, include:
- Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), region, pool name, GPU SKU, MIG status (if any)
- Runtime version + profile pack version
- Selected profile and override source (fleet default vs per-pool vs per-deployment vs manual)
- Before/after comparison window and traffic level (QPS, concurrency)
- Workload characteristics: prompt length distribution, output length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming share
- Key metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, TTFT, tokens/sec, queue wait, OOM/restart rate
- Relevant logs: startup compatibility matrix, kernel selection summary, allocator warnings

---
sections.heading: Observability: what to capture when filing a follow-up

sections.body:
- Add a new entry when: (a) reproducible in perf suite, (b) observed in prod and confirmed profile-related, or (c) known hazard with a clear mitigation.
- Retire an entry only when the mitigation is no longer needed *and* the fix is present in the supported runtime/profile versions.
- Keep entries terse and operational. Link deeper analysis to the relevant PR/ADR/ticket.

**Maintainer rotation:** Kira Thompson (Docs/Runbooks) with quarterly review by Noah Patel (Runtime architecture) and Aisha Bello (SRE dashboards).

---
sections.heading: Update process (for maintainers)

sections.body:
- 2026-02-20: Added B200 compatibility and regional disable guidance; expanded observability capture checklist.
- 2026-01-14: Added kernel auto-selection TTFT regression pattern and detection steps.
- 2025-12-09: Added L40S KV cache budgeting/OOM patterns and recommended guardrails.
- 2025-11-26: Initial publication (bootstrap list from rollout triage and perf suite findings).

payload.page_title: gRPC connection reuse and pipeline regeneration: root causes, triage, and mitigations

sections.body:
Summary

This page documents a recurring class of production issues we tag as \"gRPC connection reuse / pipeline regeneration events\" that affect the serving runtime's frontproxy -> worker (dispatcher/gpu-proxy) communication path. The problem manifests as sudden latency spikes, increased CPU on frontproxy, and a transient drop in request throughput for a subset of tenants. These incidents have been observed across heterogeneous pools (A100 and H100) and correlate with high client churn, long tail responses, or server-initiated stream resets.

Goals

- Provide a clear symptom checklist and deterministic triage workflow.
- Identify short-term mitigations and longer-term remediation patterns.
- Standardize monitoring, tests, and release guidance to prevent regressions.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to gRPC multiplexed HTTP/2 connections used by frontproxy and internal GPU-side proxies.
- Does not cover public API client SDKs (separate doc).
- Assumes HTTP/2 flow control, stream reset (RST_STREAM), and GOAWAY semantics are in play.

Observed symptoms (production signature)

1) Sudden P50->P99 latency divergence for affected route(s). P99 increases by 3x+ while median increases modestly.
2) Frontproxy CPU climbs to >75% in the cluster pool while worker GPU utilization remains stable.
3) Error burst of grpc.StatusCode.UNAVAILABLE and INTERNAL with message fragments like \"RST_STREAM\" or \"REFUSED_STREAM\".
4) Connection-level metrics show spike in active connection churn (connections/sec) and TCP retransmits.
5) Streaks of reorders in request ids in the trace logs due to stream reassignments.

Root cause taxonomy (how this happens)

- A: Client churn + stream reuse exhaustion: large number of short-lived clients exhausts MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS and triggers RST_STREAM or REFUSED_STREAM; frontproxy retries rebuild pipelines to other worker connections causing in-flight reorder and temporary head-of-line blocking.
- B: Server-side keepalive and GOAWAY miscoordination: worker-side GOAWAY to drain leads frontproxy to open new connections while in-flight streams are aborted due to aggressive RST semantics.
- C: Middlebox path MTU or TLS renegotiation causing short disconnects: connection rekeying or PMTU events cause transport resets and pipeline re-creation.
- D: Backpressure-induced stall: GPU-side request processing stalls (long decode/attention spike) causing HTTP/2 flow-control window exhaustion; frontproxy treats stall as connection failure and rebuilds session.

Immediate triage checklist (ordered)

1) Identify affected routes and tenants. Query the request log aggregator for spikes in grpc UNAVAILABLE/INTERNAL for last 15m.
   - Kibana query: service:frontproxy AND grpc.code:(UNAVAILABLE OR INTERNAL) AND @timestamp:[now-15m TO now] AND route:<ROUTE>
2) Check frontproxy connection churn: connections_opened_per_min and connections_closed_per_min for frontproxy pool.
   - Grafana panel: frontproxy.connections_opened_rate / frontproxy.connections_closed_rate
3) Inspect trace spans for RST_STREAM, REFUSED_STREAM, and GOAWAY markers. Correlate trace ids across frontproxy -> worker hops.
4) Validate server keepalive and window sizes in worker logs. Look for GOAWAY frames with last_stream_id < current_stream_id.
5) CPU vs GPU utilization: if frontproxy CPU high but GPU healthy, likely pipeline rebuild churn.
6) Confirm whether error pattern follows a config change or deploy within the last 30 min.

Short-term mitigations (operational playbook)

- Apply an emergency rate limit per-source IP for the affected route to reduce churn. Example: edge-bind limit 150 rps per ephemeral client for the route.
- Temporarily increase MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS and flow-control window on frontproxy-worker connection endpoints (config knobs below). Note: increasing streams increases memory and per-connection CPU.
- Disable aggressive keepalive or delayed GOAWAY on the worker to allow graceful stream completion.
- If the issue correlates with a recent kernel or runtime patch, rollback using the runtime rollback matrix.

Permanent fixes and engineering changes

- Connection leasing: implement short-lived connection leases that reduce per-client connection churn while enforcing per-lease stream accounting. This avoids opening new TCP/TLS connections for every client burst.
- Adaptive MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS: runtime-side controller that increases allowed streams when measured per-connection CPU overhead is low and decreases during overloads.
- Improved GOAWAY semantics: coordinate GOAWAY issuance with stream-level graceful window to avoid aborting in-flight streams.
- Flow-control heuristic: detect in-flight compute stalls (GPU-side stalls > threshold) and advertise smaller initial windows so frontproxy spreads streams across more connections rather than piling onto a blocked connection.
- Health-aware routing: extend the smart routing policy to avoid using worker connections with elevated stall signals; prefer routing new streams to underutilized connections.

Config knobs and recommended safe ranges

| config_key | default | recommended emergency | tradeoffs |
|------------|---------|------------------------|-----------|
| grpc.max_concurrent_streams | 100 | 200 | higher concurrency reduces connection churn but increases memory/CPU per-connection |
| grpc.initial_window_size | 65535 | 65535 | very large windows can worsen head-of-line blocking when stalls occur |
| grpc.stream_idle_timeout_ms | 60000 | 120000 | longer idle avoids premature RST from transient spikes but delays resource reclamation |
| worker.goaway_grace_ms | 500 | 2000 | larger grace means fewer aborted streams during drain at the cost of slower rollouts |

Note: the table above is presented as text in this page; apply changes during low risk windows or use canary first.

Monitoring and alerting recipes

- New composite alert: GRPC_PIPELINE_REGEN_HIGH
  - Trigger: frontproxy.connections_opened_rate > 5x baseline AND frontproxy.grpc_unavailable_rate > 3x baseline in 3m window.
  - Severity: P2 when affecting <5% tenants, P1 when >5% tenants or SLO breaches.
  - Runbook link: this page.

- Dashboards to add:
  - Connection churn per route (heatmap)
  - Stream reset reason breakdown (REFUSED_STREAM / RST_STREAM / GOAWAY) by worker pool
  - Average outstanding streams per connection and avg stream lifetime

Reproduction procedure (dev sandbox)

1) Test harness: grpc-client-spammer (internal tool). Start with N=500 concurrent short-lived clients sending 1-2 requests and terminating.
2) Vary MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS to 20, 50, 100 and observe when REFUSED_STREAM increases.
3) Introduce artificial GPU-side stalls by injecting a sleep in the decoder path for a subset of requests and observe frontproxy behavior.
4) Capture tcpdump and http2 frame logs to confirm GOAWAY and RST frames.

Fix rollout guidance and canary strategy

- Any change to grpc.max_concurrent_streams or worker.goaway_grace_ms must be canaried: apply to 5% of worker nodes for 2 hours under production-like synthetic traffic.
- For code changes (connection leasing, adaptive controller): feature-flag and side-by-side deployment with telemetry gates. Telemetry gates must include stream-reset rate, per-connection CPU, and P99 latency for canary tenants.

Testing checklist for PRs and releases

- Unit tests for new state machines (lease lifecycle, goaway-coordination).
- Integration test: simulated churn harness with deterministic verification of no stream loss above threshold.
- Load test: scaled to 300k streams/min with mixed short/long sessions showing <=3% REFUSED/RST under steady state.
- Chaos test: inject GOAWAY and RST under load and assert graceful completion percent >= 95%.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: runtime-networking (oncall: @runtime-networking-oncall).
- Secondary owner: frontproxy-team.
- SLT escalation: runtime-eng-manager@example.redwood.com

Post-incident analysis template

1) Incident timeline: collect timestamps for first error spike, detection, mitigation, and recovery.
2) Affected tenants: list tenant ids and approximate request volume during window.
3) Root cause evidence: trace screenshots, tcpdump snippets, worker logs with GOAWAY/RST frame dumps.
4) Remediation actions taken and time to implement.
5) Follow-ups and code patches assigned with owners and ETA.

Appendix: example diagnostic commands and snippets

- grpc tranlogs: curl -s \"https://logs.internal/api/search?q=grpc.code:REFUSED_STREAM%20AND%20service:frontproxy&from=now-15m\"
- tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/conn-regen.pcap host <worker_ip> and port 443
- http2 frame log extract (dev tool): ./http2-frame-dump --file /tmp/conn-regen.pcap --filter 'GOAWAY|RST_STREAM'
- quick config bump (kubectl patch): kubectl -n runtime patch configmap frontproxy-config --type merge -p '{\"data\":{\"grpc.max_concurrent_streams\":\"200\"}}'

Revision history

- 2025-04-10: Created by Sofia Martinez.
- 2025-05-02: Expanded mitigation list and added monitoring alert recipe (Ravi Menon).

References

- HTTP/2 GOAWAY semantics: RFC 7540 section 6.8
- Internal: frontproxy connection metrics schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

If you see an ongoing incident matching the symptom checklist, follow the triage checklist first and notify runtime-networking. For long-term work, file a tracking ticket in the runtime backlog with label \"grpc-pipeline-regen\" and link to this doc.
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: CUDA sparse-attention degradation under burst load (investigation & mitigations)

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This page documents a recurring production degradation mode observed in inference fleets running CUDA-accelerated sparse-attention kernels under short, high-intensity request bursts. Symptoms include elevated 99th/99.9th percentile token latency, sudden KV-cache thrashing, and transient GPU SM saturation that persists longer than the burst window. We describe detection signals, reproducible steps, short-term mitigations (runbook), and the engineering plan for a permanent fix.

Background
----------
We onboarded a custom sparse-attention kernel (sparse-cuda-v2) in Q4 2025 to reduce memory pressure and token compute for long-context models. In low-to-moderate steady-state traffic the kernel performs as expected. Over the last two months, multiple SRE and runtime teams observed repeated incidents where microbursts (50–300 concurrent short requests, <200 tokens) cause a 3–6x jump in tail latency and an increase in dropped streaming connections.

Scope and impact
----------------
- Affects: heterogeneous GPU pool types using sparse-cuda-v2 kernel (A100 and H100 variants tested).
- Percent of fleet observed: ~12% of nodes in west-2 region over Jan–Feb 2026.
- Customer impact: elevated tail latency for hosted API routes using these model variants; some enterprise customers observed timeouts against strict 500ms SLOs.

Observed symptoms & measurements
--------------------------------
- 99.9th token latency increases from baseline ~420ms to 1.8s during incidents.
- GPU SM util jumps to sustained 95–100% for 2–8s after a burst.
- Average batch size drops (due to preemption/priority shuffling) while in-flight kernels show increased warp serialization.
- KV-cache churn rate metric (kvcache.churn_rate) spikes by 5–12x.

Repro recipe (lab)
------------------
1. Use a test driver to send 250 concurrent 80-token requests over a 1s window to the model variant with sparse-cuda-v2. Example:

   sh ./tools/loadgen/run_burst.sh --concurrency 250 --tokens 80 --duration 1s --host inference-west-2.internal --model my-sparse-model:v2

2. Collect GPU traces (nsys) on a target node and record the kernel timeline:

   nsys profile --stats=true --output burst-profile %PID%

3. Capture runtime traces and KV metrics via the runtime tracer:

   curl -sS http://localhost:9080/debug/trace > /tmp/trace.json

4. Confirm the same signature: tail-latency spike aligned to a burst window and sustained SM saturation.

Telemetry & detection rules
--------------------------
We recommend the following production detectors to triage quickly. Add to alerts and dashboards where missing.

Table: Detection thresholds (text table)
Metric | Alert threshold | Recommended action
kvcache.churn_rate | > 8x baseline (5m) | Route to SRE, enable burst-mitigation runbook
gpu.sm_utilization | > 90% (1m sustained) combined with tail latency | Auto-scale eligible pool/shift traffic
model.tail_latency.99.9 | > 1200ms (5m) | Trigger rolling routing policy to fallback model-variant
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
ALERT SparseAttentionBurst
IF increase(kvcache_churn_rate_total[2m]) > 8
AND avg_over_time(gpu_sm_utilization[1m]) > 0.9
FOR 2m
LABELS {severity="page", team="runtime"}
ANNOTATIONS {summary="Sparse-attention burst signature: kvcache churn + gpu saturation"}

Immediate mitigations (runbook)
------------------------------
These steps are for on-call SREs to contain customer impact quickly. Follow the numbered procedure.

Runbook: emergency containment (SRE)
1) Identify affected nodes: query fleet telemetry for nodes with matching model variant and sm_utilization > 90%.
   - CLI: curl -sS http://telemetry-api.internal/query?query="gpu_sm_utilization>0.9 and model_variant=\"sparse-cuda-v2\""
2) Temporarily shift traffic for the impacted routing key to the dense fallback model-variant (dense-cuda-v1) via the routing API:
   - curl -X POST https://routing.internal/v1/route-shift -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","from_variant":"sparse-cuda-v2","to_variant":"dense-cuda-v1","percent":100}'
3) If shifting traffic is not possible, enable per-node burst backpressure by setting admission_controller.max_burst_inflight=50 on the node agent and trigger a graceful drain:
   - kubectl patch daemonset runtime-node-agent -n runtime --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"50"}]'
4) If nodes remain saturated, scale the pool by +20% capacity or enable emergency autoscale for the dedicated pool.
5) After mitigation, collect traces and attach to the incident ticket. Note any repro artifacts and timestamps.

Short-term engineering remediation (2–4 weeks)
----------------------------------------------
- Hotfix A (config): Reduce the eager thread concurrency in sparse-cuda-v2 kernel launcher when per-GPU concurrent requests exceed 96. Configuration patch: set kernel_launch.max_worker_threads = 64 for burst conditions. This reduces thread oversubscription and warp serialization.
- Hotfix B (runtime): Add a rapid cool-down slot for KV-cache eviction to avoid over-eviction during bursts: kvcache.eviction_cooldown_ms = 5000.
- Monitoring: Add per-kernel warp-serialization counters and expose them through kernel telemetry.

Long-term engineering plan (Q2–Q3)
----------------------------------
1) Kernel rewrite: introduce cooperative micro-scheduling within sparse kernel so that kernel work yields when global stream stalls are detected (non-blocking cooperative yield). Goal: reduce post-burst SM hang time by >50%.
2) Admission-controller enhancement: predictive admission controller that uses short-term traffic forecasts (burst detector) to apply temporary batching policies and pre-warm KV-cache for hot keys.
3) Scheduler: extend GPU scheduler to prefer batch-consolidation over preemptive micro-batching when the burst is predicted to finish within X seconds (configurable X).
4) Regression tests: add a burst-sculpting synthetic test to the benchmarking suite that asserts tail latency and kvcache churn bounds.

Root cause hypothesis
---------------------
Our working hypothesis is a compound interaction: a) the sparse kernel's internal thread-launch strategy aggressively spans SM warps to improve utilization under steady-state; b) during a microburst the host enqueues many small kernel launches causing kernel serialization and increased register pressure; c) combined with aggressive KV-cache eviction policy, the runtime thrashes cache and prolongs kernel busy signals, leading to sustained SM saturation beyond the burst window.

Data to collect for RCA
-----------------------
- nsys timeline and kernel launch parameters (grid, block, shared mem) for affected windows.
- kvcache.events (evict, fetch, miss) with per-key provenance.
- per-kernel warp-serialization and occupancy metrics.
- host-side thread pool statistics and kernel launch latencies.

Acceptance criteria for a permanent fix
--------------------------------------
- Tail latency 99.9th reduced to <= 750ms under the same synthetic burst profile.
- kvcache.churn_rate under bursts reduced to <= 2x baseline.
- No regression in steady-state throughput (within 5% of current).

Open action items and owners
---------------------------
- SRE: add detection alert and dashboard — Miguel Torres (owner) — due 2026-03-05
- Runtime: implement eviction_cooldown and config gate — Chen Li (owner) — due 2026-03-12
- Kernel: prototype cooperative-yield in sparse-cuda-v3 — Rina Sato (owner) — due 2026-04-02
- Bench: add burst-sculpting test to perf-suite — Priya Bhandari (owner) — due 2026-03-22

Related artifacts and logs (examples)
------------------------------------
- Example kernel launch line from nsys:
  Kernel: sparse_attention_v2 grid=(128,1,1) block=(256,1,1) shared=64KB regs=64
- Sample kvcache event: {timestamp: 2026-02-04T16:03:12.123Z, node: gpu-12, key: "sess:abcd1234:prefix", event: "evict", reason: "memory_pressure", age_ms: 12}

Operational notes and follow-ups
-------------------------------
- When shifting routes to a dense variant, watch for memory pressure on dense nodes; do not exceed 70% memory utilization per GPU.
- Add a scheduled run of the lab repro every week to catch regressions.
- Document kernel-exported telemetry fields in the telemetry contract docs before v3 rollout.

Appendix: quick detection checklist (for on-call)
------------------------------------------------
1. Check alerts: SparseAttentionBurst firing?
2. Inspect gpu.sm_utilization and model.tail_latency.99.9 aligned to burst timeframe.
3. If confirmed, run mitigation runbook steps 1–4.
4. Attach traces and escalate to Runtime oncall if Hotfix A/B needed.

If you have additional logs or repro traces, attach them to the incident ticket and ping #runtime-incidents with the ticket link.

-- Priya Bhandari, Runtime Performance Engineering

payload.page_title: transient-model-switch-oscillation-incident-and-mitigation-2026

sections.body: This document describes a recurrent production phenomenon we observed in Q4 2025–Q1 2026 that we have labeled 'Transient Model Switch Oscillation' (T-MSO). Symptoms include a rapid sequence of model routing changes for the same logical request stream, causing repeated KV-cache invalidations, throughput collapse, and elevated tail latency for 20–40s bursts. The behavior was visible across multiple tenants and both Hosted and Dedicated modes.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Audience: runtime engineers, oncall SREs, platform reliability, and product teams coordinating model rollout policies.
- Purpose: document root cause analysis, reproduction steps, mitigation and long-term fixes, and monitoring/alerting recipes.
sections.heading: Purpose and audience

sections.body:
1) First escalations: 2025-11-12 — intermittent customer reports of long tail latencies (95th–99.9th spike) during midday traffic.
2) Pattern recognition: 2025-11–2026-01 — telemetry showed recurring multi-second oscillations coincident with model rollout events and autoscaling bursts.
3) Root-cause CVE to product: production incidents impacted 3 high-throughput tenants (2 enterprise, 1 AI-startup).
4) Severity: P2 on affected tenants; burst loss of throughput and 2x token-cost increase due to repeated re-warmups.
sections.heading: Incident timeline and impact

sections.body:
- Per-request traces show routing decisions flip between Model-A (quantized) and Model-A-v2 (float) multiple times during a single conversation session.
- KV cache miss-rate spikes from baseline ~5% to ~70% for affected sessions.
- Kernel scheduling shows alternating allocation of shard ownership across NUMA nodes leading to extra cross-node memcpy and dispatch delays.
- Autoscaler logs show a short-lived scale-up then immediate scale-down (<45s) before traffic stabilizes.
sections.heading: Observed symptoms (signals)

sections.body:
1) Route-policy hysteresis gap: the routing policy that chooses model variants had insufficient hysteresis for transient capacity signals. It used a simple threshold on per-model GPU utilization and a last-eviction timestamp without multi-sample confirmation.
2) Fast autoscale + conservative warmup policy: autoscaler reacted to short spikes by adding nodes; warmup and placement logic attempted to place the preferred model variant on newly provisioned nodes without synchronized cache warming.
3) Fallback policy collision: the fallback mechanism to switch to a cheaper variant when capacity is constrained did not lock per-session routing decisions. Multiple concurrent components (router, fallback controller, and per-tenant policy agent) raced to reconcile the model id.
4) Model-version affinity: model variants shared the same model family id but had incompatible KV cache representations (different quantization metadata), which forced cache invalidations when a session switched variants.

Put together, a short traffic spike would trigger autoscale -> router attempted to move traffic to new nodes -> fallback policy evaluated capacity and flipped model variant -> per-session routing did not persist a decision -> router flipped variant again when observed latency on new nodes rose -> oscillation continued until traffic dropped or a manual kill-switch engaged.

Reproduction steps (sanitized, deterministic):

1) Environment: use a staging cluster with two-node initial pool (GPU A1, GPU A2) and the same autoscaler policy used in production (scale-step: +1, cool-down 30s).
2) Models: upload Model-A (8-bit quantized) and Model-A-v2 (fp16) with distinct model_variant_ids and the same model_family tag. Ensure model_variant metadata has different cache_schema fields.
3) Traffic generator: run sustained baseline QPS 120 with short spikes: every 90s inject 30s burst of 600 QPS.
4) Observe: within 1–3 burst cycles, routing flips per-session multiple times, KV cache miss-rate spikes, and tail latency increases.

Temporary mitigations (applied Nov 2025–Jan 2026):

- Hysteresis increase: increased routing decision confirmation window from 3s to 45s (multisample policy). Deployed as a stop-gap to reduce flip frequency.
- Per-session sticky routing: introduced sticky-routing flag for at-most-once routing decisions for session TTL = 120s to keep sessions bound to the same model_variant_id while warming caches.
- Autoscaler hold: added a 60s 'placement-quarantine' after scale-up during which routing avoids moving sessions to newly provisioned nodes for that tenant.
- Fallback locking: implemented an optimistic lock in fallback controller; fallback changes now require acquiring per-session key for the TTL duration.

These mitigations reduced oscillation frequency by ~90% in canaries and restored tail latency to acceptable SLOs for affected tenants.
sections.heading: Contributing factors (combined)

sections.body:
1) Stronger routing contract (owner: runtime-routing team). Timeline: Q2 2026.
- Implement a small state-machine per-session: {PreferredVariant, FallbackVariant, Transitioning} with explicit TTL, and expose it to router + fallback controller via a single authoritative store (Redis cluster/sharded snapshot).
- Ensure routing decisions are idempotent and can be reconciled from traces.

2) Cache schema compatibility registry (owner: model-onboarding). Timeline: Q2–Q3 2026.
- During model onboarding, compute a compatibility signature for KV cache schema. Reject variant pairings that are incompatible unless a migration plan is provided.

3) Autoscaler grace API (owner: eng-sre + autoscaler). Timeline: Q3 2026.
- Autoscaler should expose placement state for new nodes and allow the routing layer to query 'ready_for_session_migration' boolean.
- Add 'soft-add' option where capacity bookkeeping increases but routing waits until warmup script returns success.

4) Observability: enhanced traces and derived metrics (owner: telemetry team). Timeline: Q2 2026.
- New tracing span: routing.decision.{evaluate|commit} with tags model.family, model.variant, decision.ttl, decision.reason.
- Telemetry to emit 'session_routing_flip' event with sample of request ids.
sections.heading: Permanent fixes and design proposals (owner & timeline)

sections.body:
- Immediate alert (P95 spike correlated with session-flip rate):
  Condition: p95_latency(service:inference) > 2x baseline AND rate(session_routing_flip) > 5/min for 5m.
  Pager: oncall-runtime primary.

- PromQL example (sample):
  # session flip rate per tenant
  sum(rate(session_routing_flip_total[1m])) by (tenant_id)

- Grafana dashboard panels to add:
  - per-tenant routing flip heatmap (time vs tenant)
  - KV-cache miss-rate and miss-to-hit ratio overlayed with routing flips
  - autoscaler events timeline aligned with routing.decision spans
sections.heading: Monitoring and alerting recipes (immediate and long-term)

sections.body:
1) When alerted, run quick triage (5m):
  a) Query session_routing_flip_total for affected tenant.
  b) Check autoscaler events: list recent scale-up/scale-down events.
  c) Identify if fallback controller applied variant change events (via event log).
2) Mitigate (10–20m):
  a) If flip rate is high and autoscaler churn is observed, activate 'routing-hysteresis-override' for tenant to 120s via console.
  b) If particular model variants are involved, mark the newer variant as 'do-not-route' until canary is analyzed.
  c) If on Dedicated, coordinate with SRE to hold node termination/scale-down.
3) Post-incident (24–72h):
  a) Capture traces and attach to the incident with key spans highlighted.
  b) Run the deterministic reproduction in staging and file a follow-up ticket to implement missing design fix.

payload.page_title: OpenAI-compat streaming truncation (missing [DONE]) - suspected gateway idle timeout

sections.body:
We are tracking intermittent truncation of SSE streams on the OpenAI-compatible route (`/v1/chat/completions` with `stream=true`). The observed symptom is that clients receive some token events and then the connection closes without the terminal `[DONE]` event. Clients often see HTTP 200 with partial content.

This has been reported by multiple customers and correlates with a spike in client disconnect telemetry in **eu-west** (INC-2025-02-13-STREAM).
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body: The OpenAI-compat streaming stack can exhibit brief upstream quiet periods (no tokens emitted) during generation. When the upstream is quiet long enough, the API gateway/proxy may trigger a read/idle timeout and close the downstream connection, which appears to the client as a truncated SSE stream.
sections.heading: Root cause hypothesis

sections.body:
- OpenAI-compat uses HTTP/1.1 SSE with chunked transfer; some intermediaries are sensitive to idle gaps
- Current `proxy_read_timeout` for this route in eu-west is lower than we expect for long generations
- We do not currently emit heartbeat comments when the upstream is quiet
sections.heading: Contributing factors we suspect

sections.body:
Emit an SSE comment line periodically when upstream is quiet to keep the connection active. Example payload (comment):
`: heartbeat

`
sections.heading: 1) SSE heartbeat comments

sections.body:
- heartbeat interval: 5s
- only when no downstream bytes have been sent in the interval
sections.heading: Proposed settings

sections.body: Increase read timeout for OpenAI-compat streaming route in eu-west. (Coordinate with Eng Platform; see confluence://eng-platform/runbooks/api-gateway-timeouts.)
sections.heading: 2) Gateway timeout tuning

sections.body:
- Treat missing `[DONE]` as a failure and retry
- Capture `x-request-id`, region, and last SSE event for investigation

payload.page_title: GPU watchdog: intermittent node hang investigation and mitigation

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document captures the investigative findings, short-term mitigations, and long-term remediation plan for a class of intermittent GPU node hangs observed in the production serving fleet during Q4 2025. The pattern is characterized by a kernel-space watchdog firing followed by an immediate kubelet restart and a multi-minute node unavailable window. This page is intended for SRE and runtime engineers who perform triage and for release owners planning a preventative rollout.

Scope
-----
- Affects: a subset of dedicated and private pools running NVIDIA A100 and A10X nodes with GPU driver versions 535.x and specific firmware revisions.
- Services impacted: runtime-gateway, shard-manager, schedulerd, model-evictor; customer-visible effect: elevated 99th-percentile latency and transient 5xx errors while node is flapping.
- Not affected: small CPU-only pools and older driver versions 520.x (no incidents observed).

Observed impact and SLO implications
----------------------------------
- Symptom window: node enters 'NotReady' for 90–420s after watchdog trigger.
- Typical customer impact: short-lived burst of 504/502 for in-flight sessions; streaming connections drop and must reconnect.
- SLOs affected: request-level latency (p99) and success rate (error budget burn correlated with pool size). Example: a single A100 node hang in a 16-node pool caused a 0.9% availability regression for the pool over 8 minutes during a production rollout.

Symptoms / How this shows up in tooling
--------------------------------------
- Kubernetes: repeated kubelet restarts on the node; pod re-scheduling patterns look like a flock of pods moving simultaneously.
- Node logs: dmesg entries with lines similar to: "NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:xx:00): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus" followed by kernel watchdog stack traces.
- Driver logs: /var/log/nvidia-installer.log often contains firmware timeout entries prior to the hang.
- Metrics: sudden drop in node_gpu_utilization, spike in node_restarts_total, and increased request queueing on shard-manager.

First-response checklist (for oncall)
-------------------------------------
1. Identify affected node(s): kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=<pool-name> -o wide and check for 'NotReady' / kubelet AGE.
2. Collect kernel and driver logs: scp or run remote tail of /var/log/messages, dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log.
3. Capture GPU metrics snapshot: grafana -> GPU pool -> export time range covering the event (5m before to 10m after).
4. Evacuate traffic from the node (if still reachable): kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force <node>.
5. If the node is unresponsive at SSH level and remains in NotReady > 10m, escalate to infra for host power-cycle.
6. Add an incident note with affected customer IDs and the pool name.

Quick mitigation options (short-term)
------------------------------------
- Automatic circuit-breaker: enable node-level automatic failing of scheduling for nodes with kubelet_restart_count > 1 within 10m. This prevents repeated placement on unstable nodes.
- Scheduler policy tweak: reduce concurrent long-lived streaming sessions per node by 20% to lower surface area during known risk windows (e.g., during driver upgrades).
- Runtime fallback: configure shard-manager to keep a warm standby routing for hot sessions to avoid full reconnects when a node goes NotReady.

Detection queries and alerts (examples)
--------------------------------------
- PromQL to detect surges of kubelet restarts across a pool:
  sum by (pool) (increase(node_kubelet_restart_total{job="node-exporter"}[15m])) > 2
- PromQL to flag GPU firmware errors in driver metrics (if exposed):
  increase(nvidia_driver_errors_total{type="firmware_timeout"}[10m]) > 0
- Alert rule guidance: fire P1 if >2 nodes in a dedicated pool restart within 30m; fire P2 if a single node restart correlates with >10% p99 latency regression for the pool.

Repro steps (safest non-prod reproduction)
-----------------------------------------
1. Create a staging pool matching production node image, driver, and firmware (tagged 'staging-a100-watchdog').
2. Deploy a synthetic workload that pins the GPU: run a continuous 75%+ utilization workload for 30+ minutes (the benchmark-runner container is available in images/runtime/synthetic-gpu-burner:stable).
3. Run a targeted firmware stress test by toggling ECC on/off and running memory-fill patterns (do not run on prod).
4. Monitor dmesg and nvidia-smi -q for early signs of timeouts. If reproduced, collect full system trace using sosreport and nv-hostengine debug toggles.

Root cause analysis (summary)
----------------------------
After correlating multiple incidents we determined two contributing factors:
- A race condition in the kernel-level GPU driver interaction when heavy sustained SM utilization coincided with an asynchronous firmware housekeeping task. This occasionally produced a GPU 'fall off bus' (Xid 79) and subsequent watchdog path triggering.
- The host kernel watchdog configuration and kubelet restart policy resulted in an aggressive and non-idempotent restart behavior that extended the outage window. Specifically, the kubelet triggered a systemd restart of the node agent rather than isolating the GPU device and allowing a graceful driver reset.

Permanent remediation plan (high level)
--------------------------------------
1. Driver and firmware upgrade: collaborate with Nvidia to obtain a driver build that fixes the observed race (target window: Q1 2026). Test on staging pool.
2. Kubelet and systemd policy changes: modify kubelet restart thresholds and add a device-level isolation handler that attempts a driver reset (nvidia-smi --reset) before full kubelet restart.
3. Runtime-level safeguards: extend shard-manager's warm-standby and session-mirroring so customer sessions can continue on alternate nodes without full reconnect requirements.
4. Automated canaries: add continuous canaries exercising firmware housekeeping with health checks that simulate long-lived streaming connections.
5. Fleet rollout plan: phased kernel/driver rollout with canary pools (5% -> 20% -> 60% -> 100%) and a two-hour observation window per phase. Abort criteria: any increase in node_restarts_total or Xid-related driver errors.

Suggested kernel and kubelet config snippet (for change PR)
----------------------------------------------------------
- systemd override for kubelet.service (/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-restart.conf):

```
[Service]
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
StartLimitIntervalSec=600
StartLimitBurst=5
```

- kubelet startup flag suggestion (kubelet.yaml):
```
--eviction-hard=memory.available<100Mi,nodefs.available<5%
--pod-infra-container-image=our-registry/pause:1.8
--feature-gates=DeviceShutdown=true
```

Operational runbook: step-by-step (for engineers)
------------------------------------------------
1. Triage: Confirm the node identity and time range using kubectl and Grafana. Attach initial incident ticket and severity.
2. Isolate: cordon & drain the node if the node is reachable. If pods are stuck evacuating (Evicted -> Terminating for >5m), proceed to node power-cycle with infra.
3. Collect: run the following collection script (example):
```
#!/bin/bash
NODENAME=$1
ssh root@${NODENAME} 'mkdir -p /tmp/incident-logs && dmesg > /tmp/incident-logs/dmesg.txt && journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager > /tmp/incident-logs/kubelet.log && nvidia-smi -q > /tmp/incident-logs/nvidia-smi.txt && tar czf /tmp/incident-logs.tgz -C /tmp incident-logs && cat /tmp/incident-logs.tgz | base64'
```
Paste the base64 blob into the incident ticket for offline analysis.
4. Mitigate: if driver logs show Xid 79 sequence, attempt graceful driver reset:
```
ssh root@<node> 'nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i 0 || nvidia-smi --reset -i 0'
```
If reset fails, escalate to infra for power cycle.
5. Restore: after node recovers, uncordon and monitor pod rescheduling. Ensure no duplicate Xid errors post-restore.

Post-incident timeline and notes
------------------------------
- 2025-10-21 03:12 UTC: first large occurrence during model-rack throughput test; 3 nodes in pool-a100-2 restarted within 12 minutes.
- 2025-10-22 18:40 UTC: full collection from staging reproduction and initial vendor contact opened (Case #NV-2025-117).
- 2025-11-05 09:00 UTC: vendor sent patched driver candidate for internal validation.
- 2025-12-07 14:15 UTC: candidate driver passed synthetic stress canaries in staging; phased rollout scheduled.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: Linnea Sorensen (runtime reliability)
- Secondary owner: Arjun Patel (gpu-fleet)
- SRE on-call: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations
- Vendor liaison: Maya Li (NV driver program)

Tests and validation matrix
--------------------------
| Test | Target env | Pass criteria | Notes |
| Smoke GPU stress | staging-a100-watchdog | No Xid 79 observed in 6 hours | Run 75% sustained util workload |
| Long-term soak | canary pool (5 nodes) | 0 node_restarts_total in 72 hours | Real traffic mirror |
| Kubelet restart policy | canary nodes | Node recovers within <90s w/o full kubelet restart | Validate with induced device error |

Follow-ups and engineering tickets
----------------------------------
- RUNTIME-1234: Add nvidia-driver sanity-check and auto-disable node on first Xid-79 event.
- RUNTIME-1278: Implement device-level reset handler in kubelet wrapper.
- INFRA-2042: Coordinate firmware upgrade window and backout plan.
- OBS-1210: Add new Grafana dashboard panel for Xid error rate and per-pool electron counts.

Appendix: example logs (sanitized)
----------------------------------
- dmesg excerpt:
```
[ 1234.567890] NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:65:00): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus.
[ 1234.567921] NVRM: Xid (0000:65:00): PID 4412: Name: python
[ 1234.567947] kernel: watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#2 stuck for 22s!
```

- kubectl event pattern: multiple pods show following:
```
Warning  NodeNotReady  2m   kubelet, ip-10-0-1-23  Node ip-10-0-1-23 status is now: NodeNotReady
```

Document maintenance
--------------------
- This page will be updated as vendor fixes are validated and rollout completes.
- Next review scheduled: 2026-04-01.

Related reading
---------------
- Kernel watchdog design notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024
- Kubelet restart and systemd behavior: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/sigterm-connection-drain-and-graceful-shutdown-playbook-2025
