payload.page_title: Coordinated Execution: Benchmarks & Sampling Protocol

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines a coordinated execution benchmark and sampling protocol for validating scheduler and kernel interactions across mixed inference workloads. It complements existing per-component tests by providing a reproducible end-to-end measurement harness, standardized metrics, and a lightweight on-call triage flow for anomalies that arise during benchmark runs.

Goals
-----
- Provide an experiment protocol that produces stable, comparable signals for: latency P50/P95/P99, token throughput, per-token GPU time, kernel-switch rate, and KV-cache hit/miss impact.
- Standardize sampling, tracing, and aggregation so regression hunts can compare like-for-like across runtime versions and hardware shapes.
- Offer step-by-step runbook sections for running, interpreting, and responding to benchmark anomalies.

Scope and Non-Goals
-------------------
- Scope: multi-tenant mixed inference profiles (chat + single-turn generation + long-context summarization), scheduler interaction patterns (admission, preemption, handoff), and sampling-based profiling to attribute tail latency to kernel or network layers.
- Non-goals: this is not a replacement for microbenchmarks (kernel unit tests) nor for customer-specific capacity planning; it should be used as a cross-cutting integration verification and regression detector.

Overview of the Protocol
------------------------
1. Define workload cohorts: head (short chat, 8–64 tokens), mid (generation, 64–512 tokens), tail (long-context, 512–4k tokens). Each cohort has an associated QPS target and entropy profile.
2. Synthesize request surface: use the workload corpus generator (see Appendix) to produce deterministic request sequences for each cohort.
3. Run a staged experiment matrix across hardware shapes and kernel build variants. For each cell collect: end-to-end traces (sampled), kernel-level traces (per-dispatch timestamps), and telemetry counters (scheduler signals, admission events, eviction events).
4. Apply the sampling and aggregation rules below to produce a canonical report.

Workload Cohort Definitions
- Head: 100ms target latency, 8–64 tokens, QPS per-cohort: 100–300.
- Mid: 200–500ms target, 64–512 tokens, QPS: 10–50.
- Tail: 500ms–5s target, 512–4k tokens, QPS: 0.5–5.

Key Metrics (aggregation rules)
- Latency: P50/P90/P95/P99 measured end-to-end and kernel-only. Kernel-only = sum(kernel execution windows on device).
- Token throughput: tokens/sec measured per-cohort and aggregated weighted by customer-weighted token shares.
- Kernel-switch rate: number of kernel handoffs per request (normalize by sequence length).
- KV-cache hit ratio and miss latency contribution: report absolute and delta vs baseline.
- Preemption/eviction rate: events per 1k requests.

Sampling & Tracing Rules
------------------------
- Deterministic seed: All synthetic corpora must be generated with a fixed RNG seed per experiment id. Record the seed in the run metadata.
- Stratified sampling: sample 1 in N end-to-end requests per cohort to capture full trace data. N is chosen so that overhead < 2% CPU and <1% GPU time: default N=100 for head, 50 for mid, 10 for tail.
- Kernel-level sampling: enable fine-grained kernel timestamps for 1 in 500 kernel invocations (circular buffer). These traces should be uploaded as compressed artifacts for offline attribution.
- Trace metadata requirements: every trace must include request id, cohort tag, sequence length, model variant id, kernel-variant tag, scheduler-policy snapshot, and node/hardware id.

Telemetry Signals to Collect
- Scheduler: admission decisions, slot allocation, priority buckets, preemption timestamp, backpressure signals.
- Kernel: kernel_id, kernel_variant, start_ts, end_ts, device_mem_used, thread_block_count.
- Network / RPC: inbound queue time, serialization time, outbound flush latency.
- KV-cache: shard_id, hit/miss, fetch_latency, warmup_state.

Experiment Matrix Example (table)
| Dimension          | Values / Notes                      | Default selection |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------|
| Hardware shape    | A100x8, A100x4, L40x8, H100x8        | A100x8            |
| Model variant     | fp16, int8-quant, trimmed-ctx       | fp16              |
| Scheduler policy  | latency-first, economic-governor    | latency-first     |
| Load pattern      | steady, poisson-burst, diurnal-saw  | steady            |
| Cohort mix        | 70/25/5 head/mid/tail               | 70/25/5           |

Pass/Fail Criteria (example thresholds)
- Kernel P99 regression: fail if kernel-only P99 increases > 15% vs baseline.
- End-to-end P99: fail if > 25% increase OR absolute > 2s for mid cohort.
- KV-cache miss contribution: fail if miss-induced latency increases > 30ms average.

Investigation & Triage Runbook
------------------------------
1. Validate inputs: confirm RNG seed, cohort mix, and hardware cell match the experiment matrix.
2. Compare traces: aggregate top-3 root cause candidates by per-request kernel-only latency contribution.
3. Check scheduler signals: are admission delays or preemptions elevated? Check admission queue length and priority inversion counters.
4. Inspect kernel histogram: look for new long-tail modes indicating kernel stalls or thermal throttling.
5. Inspect device metrics: GPU SM utilization, PCIe transfer spikes, and nvlink error counters.
6. If kernel-only latency is unchanged but end-to-end regresses, inspect RPC and serialization metrics and network egress congestion.
7. Run targeted microbenchmarks: isolate suspect kernel variant on controlled single-tenant run to confirm reproducer.
8. If reproducer found, create an issue with: run id, seed, failing metrics, top traces (compressed), and suggested hypothesis.

Quick Mitigations (operational)
- Swap scheduler policy to economic-governor for degraded tail pressure scenarios.
- Pin cohort-heavy customers to isolation pool (dedicated capacity) if noisy neighbor observed.
- Temporarily enable kernel hedging for long tail requests (config toggle, see Runtime Flags table).

Runtime Flags & Configuration Table
| Flag name                         | Purpose                                      | Recommended value |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| runtime.benchmark.sample_rate    | stratified sampling divisor (per-cohort)     | head:100,mid:50,tail:10 |
| runtime.kernel.trace_window      | kernel-level trace buffer (entries)          | 500               |
| runtime.scheduler.policy         | active scheduler profile                     | latency-first     |
| runtime.kv.prefetch_threshold    | tokens ahead to prefetch                     | 64                |

Release Checklist (when using this protocol for a CVE/regression gate)
- Update canonical baseline artifact (store in artifact repo with run id).
- Run full experiment matrix across two hardware shapes.
- Ensure telemetry upload succeeded and artifacts are checksumed.
- Attach report + top 10 worst traces to PR and tag on-call owners.

Ownership and Contact
---------------------
- Owner: serving-runtime benchmarking team (oncall alias: eng-runtime-bench@redwood.example.com).
- Escalation: if evidence of hardware degradation, escalate to eng-infra GPU fleet team (pager: eng-gpu-fleet).

Appendix A — Example benchmark config (YAML)
```
experiment_id: coordinated-exec-2026-02
seed: 452318
cohort_mix:
  head: 70
  mid: 25
  tail: 5
hardware: A100x8
scheduler_policy: latency-first
sampling:
  head: 1/100
  mid: 1/50
  tail: 1/10
tracing:
  kernel_sample_divisor: 500
  artifacts_retention_days: 14
```

Appendix B — CLI snippets
- Start a run: redwood-bench run --config path/to/config.yaml --out /tmp/run-artifacts --note "perf-tuning-experiment"
- Upload artifacts: redwood-bench upload /tmp/run-artifacts --repo experiments/coord-exec
- Create quick report: redwood-bench report /tmp/run-artifacts --format html > /tmp/report.html

Appendix C — Example failure report template
- Run id: <run id>
- Baseline id: <baseline id>
- Delta metrics: {end_to_end_p99: +X%, kernel_only_p99: +Y%}
- Top 5 traces (compressed path): /artifacts/<run>/trace-1.gz ...
- Hypothesis: <short description>
- Next steps: <list>

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-03: created by Aisha Gupta (initial draft).
- 2026-01-12: added stratified sampling defaults and kernel sampling buffer guidance (reviewer: Marco Alvarez).
- 2026-02-10: clarified triage steps and added runtime flags table (reviewer: Nina Park).
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: TP Stress Suite Spec (Multi-GPU Tensor Parallel Reliability + Performance)

sections.body: This document specifies the **TP Stress Suite**: a set of repeatable workloads and pass/fail criteria used to detect **multi-GPU tensor-parallel (TP)** regressions in Redwood’s serving runtime. The suite targets known failure modes under sustained load (mixed prefill/decode, long context, bursty concurrency, cancellation, memory/KV pressure) that have historically produced **request hangs, GPU stalls, and downstream timeouts**.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
1) **CI smoke + gating** (fast, minimal hardware): catches obvious deadlocks and correctness-breaking changes.
2) **Perf lab + perf-canary** (representative GPUs, longer burn): catches probabilistic stalls, p99 latency inflation, and throughput regressions.
sections.heading: The suite runs in two modes

sections.body:
- Detect and prevent re-introduction of TP hangs/timeouts (primary).
- Provide early, actionable signals that localize stalls to **compute vs NCCL/collectives vs scheduler starvation**.
- Establish stable, versioned workload definitions (distributions, seeds, thresholds) to make results comparable over time.
- Integrate with existing Redwood pipelines:
  - benchmark-lab repro harness
  - perf-canary scenarios
  - runtime release gating and canary dashboards
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Model quality/evals (we use fixed prompts purely as workload generators).
- Exhaustive hardware coverage (we prioritize the fleet/hot paths; full coverage remains a lab responsibility).
- Replacing microbenchmarks; this suite complements kernel-level microbench tests.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- **Replica**: one runtime instance serving requests.
- **TP degree (TP=2/4/8)**: number of GPUs participating in one replica’s model partition.
- **Prefill**: prompt processing; **decode**: token-by-token generation.
- **Hang**: request fails to complete without explicit error; typically presents as streaming stuck, stalled NCCL, or scheduler deadlock.
- **Stall detector**: runtime metric indicating lack of progress (heartbeat gap, collective in-flight growth, queue depth growth without completion).
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body: The suite is composed of **scenario groups**, each with a workload generator and pass/fail criteria.
sections.heading: Suite Overview

sections.body:
1) **Mixed Prefill/Decode (Streaming)**
2) **Long Context + Heavy Prefill**
3) **Bursty Concurrency + Backpressure**
4) **Cancellation / Client Disconnect**
5) **KV Cache Pressure + Compaction Edges**
sections.heading: Scenario Groups (required)

sections.body:
6) **Replica churn during sustained load** (drain/restart while traffic continues)
7) **Fault injection** (forced collective timeout to validate watchdog + abort semantics)
sections.heading: Scenario Groups (optional / phased)

sections.body:
- Deterministic by default via **seeded randomness**.
- Pluggable distributions for prompt length, output length, think-time, and request interarrival.
- Supports streaming and non-streaming requests.
- Emits structured artifacts:
  - request timeline summary
  - per-rank progress markers
  - runtime metrics snapshot references (Prometheus query links)
  - trace sample IDs (if enabled)
sections.heading: All generators share these properties

sections.body:
- **Model + TP config**: model identifier, quantization profile if relevant, TP degree.
- **Traffic config**: concurrency targets, arrival distribution, duration.
- **Request config**: distributions of prompt lengths and max_new_tokens, streaming on/off.
- **Failure hooks**: cancellation rate, replica restart events, memory pressure toggles.
- **Success criteria**: thresholds and required signals.
sections.heading: Each scenario defines

sections.body:
- **Prompt length distribution (tokens)**: mixture of short + medium + long
  - 60%: 128–512 (uniform)
  - 30%: 1,024–4,096 (log-uniform)
  - 10%: 8,192–16,384 (log-uniform; only on long-context-capable models)
- **Max new tokens distribution**:
  - 70%: 64–256 (uniform)
  - 25%: 256–1,024 (log-uniform)
  - 5%: 1,024–2,048 (log-uniform; decode stress)
- **Interarrival**:
  - CI mode: fixed-rate to keep variance low.
  - Perf mode: Poisson arrivals with occasional burst windows.
sections.heading: Unless overridden per scenario

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Reproduce starvation and ordering issues caused by prefill-heavy batches interleaving with streaming decode steps.

**Config (baseline):**
- TP: 4
- Duration: 20 minutes (perf), 5 minutes (CI)
- Concurrency target: 24 in-flight requests per replica (perf), 8 (CI)
- Streaming: enabled
- Prompt length: standard distribution
- Max new tokens: skewed toward short/medium (to keep decode churn high)

**Additional knobs:**
- Decode step budget: enforce continuous decode iterations (avoid all-prefill phases).
- Prefill burst windows: 30s windows with 2x arrival rate every 5 minutes.

**Pass/fail:**
- **Hard fail** if any request exceeds timeout:
  - CI: > 120s wall time
  - Perf: > 300s wall time
- **Hard fail** if stall detectors trigger:
  - per-rank heartbeat gap > 30s (CI) / > 60s (perf)
  - in-flight collective counter monotonic growth without completion for > 30s
- **Soft fail** (regression) if:
  - p99 end-to-end latency increases > 15% vs pinned baseline for same hardware/profile
  - decode tokens/sec decreases > 10% (throughput regression)
sections.heading: 1) Mixed Prefill/Decode (Streaming)

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Catch long-context issues that amplify NCCL ordering sensitivity and scheduler backpressure, and stress KV allocation paths.

**Config (baseline):**
- TP: 4 (required), TP: 8 (lab-only where supported)
- Duration: 30 minutes (perf), 8 minutes (CI)
- Concurrency: 8 (perf), 2 (CI)
- Streaming: disabled by default (focus on prefill correctness); optional streaming variant
- Prompt lengths:
  - 50%: 8k–16k
  - 40%: 16k–32k (only for models configured for 32k)
  - 10%: 32k–64k (lab-only)
- Max new tokens: 64–256

**Pass/fail:**
- **Hard fail** on any hang / stall detector trigger.
- **Hard fail** if OOM occurs when below expected headroom thresholds (see “Memory expectations”).
- **Soft fail** if prefill latency p95 increases > 20% vs baseline.
sections.heading: 2) Long Context + Heavy Prefill

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Validate scheduler fairness and load-shedding hooks; ensure we don’t wedge replicas during sudden spikes.

**Config:**
- TP: 4
- Duration: 20 minutes perf, 5 minutes CI
- Baseline arrival: maintain 50% of steady-state throughput target
- Burst: 3x arrivals for 20s, every 2 minutes
- Concurrency cap: set to production-like default; verify we reject/queue correctly

**Pass/fail:**
- **Hard fail** on hang.
- **Hard fail** if queue depth grows without completion for > 60s.
- **Soft fail** if burst recovery time (p95 latency returning to within 10% of baseline) > 90s.
sections.heading: 3) Bursty Concurrency + Backpressure

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Catch deadlocks caused by cancellation paths leaving collectives waiting or ranks diverging.

**Config:**
- TP: 4
- Duration: 15 minutes perf, 5 minutes CI
- Streaming: enabled
- Cancellation rate: 2% of requests cancel mid-decode; 1% cancel during prefill
- Cancellation timing: random uniform over request lifetime, seeded

**Pass/fail:**
- **Hard fail** if any cancellation causes:
  - replica wedging (no progress on subsequent requests)
  - watchdog abort storm (excess aborts) exceeding rate limit
- **Soft fail** if cancellation increases error rate > 1% above baseline (excluding intentional cancellations).
sections.heading: 4) Cancellation / Client Disconnect

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Exercise fragmentation/compaction interactions with TP and ensure no rank divergence under memory pressure.

**Config:**
- TP: 4
- Duration: 25 minutes perf, 8 minutes CI
- Workload: long-ish prompts + moderate decode to keep KV resident
- Enable KV compaction feature flag(s) per current default
- Memory pressure: keep steady-state at ~80–90% of KV budget through concurrency and sequence choices

**Pass/fail:**
- **Hard fail** if:
  - ranks diverge (detected via per-rank progress mismatch / collective mismatch signals)
  - deadlock or stall detector triggers
- **Soft fail** if compaction causes p99 latency increase > 20% without corresponding throughput gain.
sections.heading: 5) KV Cache Pressure + Compaction Edges

sections.body: The suite is defined to be portable; execution targets depend on mode.
sections.heading: Hardware + Runtime Matrix

sections.body:
- Minimum: TP=2 or TP=4 on a single node, single replica.
- GPU class: smallest available multi-GPU CI runner (team-owned pool).
- Duration constraints: scenarios truncated; focus is hang detection.
sections.heading: CI (gating) targets

sections.body:
- A100 80GB (TP=4) (primary)
- H100 80GB (TP=4) (primary)
- L40S (TP=2/4 where used in hosted tiers) (secondary)
sections.heading: Run nightly (or per-release) across representative fleet

sections.body:
- driver/CUDA version
- NCCL version
- runtime build SHA
- model + quantization profile
sections.heading: Each hardware run records

sections.body:
- Request metrics:
  - request_count, success/error rate
  - end-to-end latency p50/p95/p99
  - streaming: time-to-first-token (TTFT) p50/p95/p99
  - decode tokens/sec and prefill tokens/sec
- TP progress / stall metrics:
  - per-rank heartbeat timestamp and gap
  - in-flight collective counters (by type if available)
  - scheduler queue depth and starvation indicators
  - stall reason code counts (compute/comms/scheduler/memory/unknown)
- Resource metrics:
  - GPU SM utilization, HBM usage, PCIe/NVLink (where available)
  - NCCL error counters / timeouts
sections.heading: Each run MUST emit or link to

sections.body: - sampled spans must include rank IDs and collective counters for correlation.
sections.heading: If traces are enabled in perf mode

sections.body:
A scenario run is **FAIL** if any of the following occur:
- Any request exceeds the scenario timeout (CI: 120s; perf: 300s unless scenario overrides).
- Any stall detector triggers above configured thresholds.
- Any replica enters a non-recovering state (no completions for > 60s under active load).
- Any NCCL error is surfaced (except explicitly-injected fault tests).

A run is a **REGRESSION (non-gating)** if:
- p99 latency regression > 15% vs pinned baseline for that scenario/hardware.
- throughput regression > 10% (tokens/sec) vs baseline.
sections.heading: Pass/Fail Criteria (Global)

sections.body:
- release branch baseline for canary
- last green main build for CI
sections.heading: Baseline comparisons should be pinned to

sections.body:
- Scenarios should be configured to avoid OOM under expected headroom.
- If OOM occurs, the run is considered FAIL unless:
  - the scenario explicitly configures “expected OOM” (not currently used), or
  - the model/profile/hardware combination is marked unsupported in the scenario registry.
sections.heading: Memory Expectations

sections.body:
- Scenario definitions live as versioned configs in the perf-canary and benchmark-lab repos.
- The runtime repo owns:
  - metric names/labels stability guarantees
  - stall detector semantics and thresholds (feature-flagged where necessary)
sections.heading: Repository / config ownership

sections.body:
- Trigger: on changes touching TP scheduling, NCCL/collectives boundary, KV compaction, cancellation paths, watchdog/abort.
- Execution:
  - run a reduced set: Scenario 1 + Scenario 4 (mandatory), plus one of (Scenario 2 or 5) depending on changed area.
  - total runtime target: <= 20 minutes.
- Outputs:
  - junit-style summary + links to logs
  - Prometheus snapshot link (if available)
  - failure bundle with last 2 minutes of per-rank logs
sections.heading: CI Integration (gating)

sections.body:
- Full suite with standard durations.
- Stored artifacts:
  - scenario run metadata (hardware/software/sha)
  - aggregated metrics
  - sampled traces (if enabled)
  - NCCL debug logs only when “debug window” is explicitly enabled via run parameter
sections.heading: Perf Lab Integration (nightly)

sections.body:
- Dedicated-first rollout: run on Dedicated canary clusters prior to broad Hosted enablement.
- Gating checklist ties to runtime release ticket:
  - all TP scenarios green on target hardware
  - no new stall reason spikes
  - abort/watchdog rates within limits
sections.heading: Perf-canary Integration (release)

sections.body:
- NCCL debug logging is **off by default**. Enable only via explicit “debug window” parameter to avoid performance and data volume issues.
- Logs must avoid customer prompt contents; use synthetic prompts only.
- For any FAIL:
  - capture rank-local logs and runtime structured error codes
  - include the stall reason code summary and last-known progress markers
sections.heading: Operational Safety and Logging

sections.body:
- model identifier
- TP degree
- scenario config name
- run mode: ci | perf
- duration override (optional)
sections.heading: Required inputs

sections.body:
1) Select hardware pool and reserve node(s).
2) Deploy runtime build SHA to a single replica with TP enabled.
3) Start scenario generator with seed pinned; record run ID.
4) Monitor dashboards for heartbeat gaps and queue depth.
5) On completion, publish summary + compare to baseline.
6) If FAIL, file/associate a Linear issue and attach failure bundle.
sections.heading: Standard run procedure

sections.body:
- Primary owner: **Marcus Reed** (perf/regression coverage)
- Scenario definitions: **Rina Kobayashi** (repro harness + perf canary)
- CI wiring: **Sahana Iyer** (GPU regression coverage)
- SRE alert alignment: **Aisha Bello**, **Rafael Mendes**
sections.heading: Ownership and Change Control

sections.body:
- metric names/labels
- stall detector thresholds
- pass/fail thresholds
- scenario distributions
must be reviewed by at least one of:
- Scheduling lead (Sofia Ivanova) for scheduler-related scenarios
- Kernel lead (Hiro Tanaka) for NCCL/stream-sync scenarios
- SRE reviewer (Rafael Mendes or Aisha Bello) for alertability implications
sections.heading: Any change to

sections.body:
Use as starting defaults; tune per model/hardware.

- Mixed Prefill/Decode (Streaming):
  - p99 latency regression: 15%
  - tokens/sec regression: 10%
  - heartbeat gap fail: 60s (perf)

- Long Context + Heavy Prefill:
  - prefill p95 regression: 20%
  - heartbeat gap fail: 60s (perf)

- Bursty Concurrency:
  - recovery time > 90s -> soft fail

- Cancellation:
  - replica wedge -> hard fail
sections.heading: Appendix: Recommended Baseline Threshold Table

sections.body:
When failing, include one tag in the run summary (best effort):
- collective_ordering_mismatch
- stream_wait_deadlock
- scheduler_starvation_decode
- kv_compaction_rank_divergence
- cancellation_collective_wait
- watchdog_abort_spike
- unknown_progress_stall

payload.page_title: Service Fidelity Spotlight — End-to-end Benchmark & Kernel Impact Mapping Protocol

sections.body:
Overview

This page defines a repeatable, cross-team protocol for spotlighting service-level fidelity changes (quality vs. cost/latency) and mapping those changes to kernel scheduling and runtime subsystems. Use this protocol when onboarding a new model variant, validating a quantization rollout, or investigating regressions in production SLOs. The goal: produce a minimal, reproducible benchmark and instrumentation bundle that ties observable customer impact to kernel-level signals and actionable runbook steps.

Scope

- Applies to: runtime-dispatcher, kernel-scheduler, kvcache-store, gpu-dispatcher, request-multiplexer, and model-variant-adapter.
- Not covered: client-side SDK behavior, non-inference storage tiers, or billing pipelines (except where cost-per-token is measured).

Success Criteria

- A reproducible benchmark (input corpus + harness) that reproduces the customer-visible regression within ±5% on p95 latency and token-efficiency.
- Mapped kernel signals (GPU occupancy, kernel-duration histogram, warp-stall rate, memory-copy latency) correlated with at least one service-level metric.
- A short remediation runbook with owner and rollback clause that can be executed within a 2-hour operational window.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
| Metric | Level | Target window | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| p95 request latency (inference path) | service | 60s | end-to-end, excluding client network |
| p99 tail latency | service | 60s | critical for SLO signoff |
| tokens/sec per-GPU | infra | 60s | aggregated by gpu-dispatcher |
| kernel duration (histogram) | kernel | 10s | per-kernel id, percentile buckets |
| GPU occupancy | kernel | 10s | % of active warps/SMs |
| KV cache hit ratio | service | 60s | per-session prefix reuse |
| end-to-end quality delta | application | corpus-run | BLEU/ROUGE/LL-judge score per prompt set |

Bench harness and corpus

1) Choose a narrow corpus that represents the failing surface: typically 200–1000 prompts drawn from production replay (anonymized) or curated prompt set.
2) Define a deterministic run profile: request concurrency, sequence length distribution, and per-request stop tokens.
3) Use the benchmark harness located at infra/bench/harness (team artifact) with the following example invocation:
sections.heading: Quick summary of metrics to capture (minimum)

sections.body:
./bench/harness \
  --target http://localhost:8080/v1/generate \
  --corpus ./corpora/fidelity-spotlight/replica-2026.jsonl \
  --concurrency 16 \
  --seqlen-dist ./seqlen/prod-trimmed.yaml \
  --collect-kernel-traces /tmp/kernels.trace \
  --tag "fidelity-spotlight-$(date +%Y%m%d)"

Instrumentation checklist (kernel -> service mapping)

- Enable per-kernel tracing: kernel-scheduler must be started with KERNEL_TRACE=1 and trace export to a path with timestamps in nanoseconds.
- Correlate each request id with kernel trace id via the request-provenance header. Ensure request-provenance is present in the harness.
- Capture GPU metrics (SM utilisation, memory bandwidth, PCIe latency) using gpu-exporter at 5s resolution for the run.
- Collect runtime-level traces (request timeline) with trace level=INFO and the following fields: request_id, model_variant, sequence_length, kvcache_hit, chosen_kernel_hint, gpu_node.

Causal kernel-impact mapping procedure (numbered step playbook)

1. Baseline run: execute the bench harness against the previously certified model variant and collect all signals. Label artifact as baseline-<tag>.
2. Test run: execute the harness against the candidate model/quantization/kernel-change. Label artifact as candidate-<tag>.
3. Compute deltas for service metrics (p95/p99, tokens/sec, error-rate, quality delta). If deltas are <= threshold (p95 delta < 7%, quality delta within guardrail), proceed to step 7.
4. If regression observed, run kernel-signal diffing: align kernel traces by request_provenance and compute per-kernel-duration deltas and stall-rates.
5. Identify top-3 kernel IDs with largest duration increase and check associated inputs (sequence length, batch size, kvcache-hit). If top kernels map to attention or fused-matmul kernels, flag possible memory layout or schedule regressions.
6. Cross-check scheduling signals: examine scheduler decisions for these requests — preemption events, slice boundaries, and co-scheduled kernel sets. If scheduler consistently inserts extra preemption/slice boundaries for candidate, add scheduling hypothesis to incident doc.
7. Re-run targeted microbenchmarks for suspect kernels (single-kernel isolations) with 5–10% input perturbations to confirm sensitivity. Document command used and raw kernel profiles.
8. Produce remediation plan: configuration tweak (kernel-flag or scheduler param), model pin, or rollback. Include risk assessment and estimated cost impact.

Example kernel-focused profile snippet (text excerpt)

--- kernel-deltas.txt ---
kernel_id | baseline_p95_ms | candidate_p95_ms | delta_ms | suspected-cause
K_ATT_012 | 3.4 | 6.7 | +3.3 | attention-fused-layout-regression
K_FGEMM_03 | 1.1 | 1.3 | +0.2 | higher batch-padding (sequence skew)
K_COPY_00 | 0.05 | 0.8 | +0.75 | unexpected host->gpu memcpy (eviction)
--- end ---

Profiling playbook excerpts (how to capture good traces)

- Prefer stratified-capture: sample 1 in N requests for full kernel trace but collect light-weight metrics for all (tokens/sec, kv-hit). N depends on cost budget; default N=5.
- For tail investigations, use targeted 100% tracing on a small cohort of requests that hit the fault surface.
- Always correlate traces with the benchmark tag and git SHA of runtime to enable fast bisects.

Benchmark analysis checklist (deliverable items)

- Repro artifacts: corpus, harness args, kernel traces, gpu-exporter TSV, runtime log bundle, and model SHA.
- A concise findings table (1–2 pages) answering: What regressed? Which kernels changed? Which scheduler behavior changed? What is the recommended remediation?
- Estimated rollback cost and performance delta if remediation is applied.

Release notes & labelling template (short)

When a kernel or scheduler change is promoted to canary or prod, include the following in the release note:

- Change ID: release/kernel-<X> or release/scheduler-<Y>
- Short description: what the change modifies
- Risk summary: p95 impact observed in lab runs (absolute and percent), top kernels affected
- Canary checklist: yes/no (list of required traces and metrics)
- Rollout gates: automatic rollback threshold (p99 increase > 15% or BLEU drop > 2 points)

Known-issues cataloging format (how to add an entry)

When you discover a novel kernel or scheduling-related issue, create an entry in the known-issues catalog with these flattened fields (one-line examples):

- id: KERNEL-2026-0123
- title: unexpected memcpy on model swap causing p99 spikes
- symptom: intermittent p99 spikes when model-variant-adapter performs hot-swap after session affinity change
- kernel_evidence: kernel COPY_00 duration increased by 10x for affected requests
- workarounds: reduce per-node max-connections to avoid hot-swap batching; disable aggressive prefetcher
- owner: Evan Ross

Runbook snippet (emergency mitigation for kernel regressions)

1. Triage: confirm alerts (p99 spike and tokens/sec drop) and fetch latest bench harness run tag.
2. Validate: run a short 5–10 minute harness with request-provenance set to 'triage-<incident>' against a replica canary pool.
3. If kernel duration anomaly reproduced, scale down candidate pool and route traffic to baseline variant (mechanism: runtime-routing annotate route/variant with fallback=true).
4. If routing not available, execute rapid rollback to previous runtime image via k8s rollout undo for runtime-dispatcher.
5. Collect post-mitigation traces and attach to incident ticket.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall team (pager: #infra-oncall).
- Kernel/scheduler engineering owner: Liang Zhou (pager: @liang).
- Escalation path: owner -> eng-sre -> platform-ops -> exec on-call (document chain in incident ticket).

Appendix: useful commands and small configs

payload.page_title: Sequence Length Scaling and Kernel Breakpoints — characterization and operational playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents an empirical characterization of how sequence length distribution interacts with kernel selection and scheduling in the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates the benchmark design, observed kernel breakpoints, profiling steps, and an operational runbook for diagnosing and mitigating performance cliffs that appear when request token lengths cross specific thresholds. The goal is to provide a reproducible approach for teams to:

- quantify per-model breakpoints where the runtime swaps execution kernels or changes memory strategy,
- map those breakpoints to tail and p50 latency regressions under realistic traffic mixes, and
- provide a low-friction remediation path (config, routing, and rollout guidance).

Why this matters

Sequence length interacts with many runtime subsystems: attention kernel selection, KV-cache allocation, beam/decoder loop scheduling, and cross-GPU shard placement. Small shifts in length distribution (e.g., 64 -> 96 tokens) can cause:

- kernel fallback to slower attention implementations,
- increased temporary GPU memory pressure that triggers spilling or allocator pathologies,
- larger per-request batching mismatches that break latency SLOs, and
- degraded model quantization code-paths (fp16->int8 fallback) on older kernels.

This doc summarizes controlled experiments and provides playbooks to identify and mitigate these effects in production.

Principles and definitions

1) Breakpoint: a sequence length value at which the runtime changes kernel, memory allocation pattern, or scheduling policy.
2) Hot path kernel: the primary highly-optimized kernel chosen for the majority of requests below the first breakpoint.
3) Slow path kernel: fallback kernel or non-optimized path taken above a breakpoint.
4) Effective length: request length + expected generated tokens when the runtime preallocates KV or scratch.

Experiment summary (high level)

- Workload: 10k synthetic prompts per model, sampled across prompt templates used by product teams (short chat, multi-turn context, doc summary). Generation budgets: 16, 64, 128 tokens.
- Models: two LLaMA-family variants (7B, 13B), a non-sharded 70B, and a trimmed 3B quantized.
- Hardware: A100-40GB (single-GPU runs), A100-80GB (single and 2-way sharded), H100-80GB (single-GPU), and RTX-6000 for legacy stack tests.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel name (telemetry tag), GPU mem high-water, scheduler queue depth, batch composition, and KV-cache hit/miss rate.

Key observed breakpoints (example)

| Model | Observed breakpoints (tokens) | Typical effect | Notes |
|-------|-------------------------------:|----------------|-------|
| 3B-quant | 96, 256 | 96 triggers slower attention kernel (vectorized->scalar), 256 triggers allocator spilling | quantization path causes extra memory copies on GPU_Legacy drivers |
| 7B-sharded | 64, 192 | 64->192 increases per-shard KV footprint; above 192 scheduler switches to larger slice size causing +40% p95 | shard placement tuning recommended |
| 13B | 80 | kernel switch to tiled attention; p99 spikes for small batch sizes | tiling increases kernel launch overhead |
| 70B | 64, 128 | 64 increases async memcpy contention; 128 often requires 2-shard execution which changes network RTTs | check NCCL tuning |

Benchmark methodology (repro steps)

1) Environment setup
   - Use the perf harness in tools/runtime-bench. Ensure CUDA visible devices set and driver/harness versions recorded.
   - Commands (example):

     ```bash
     export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
     git checkout main && bazel build //tools/runtime-bench:bench_runner
     ./bazel-bin/tools/runtime-bench/bench_runner \\n       --model-path gs://redwood-models/llama-7b --run-config configs/bench/seqscale-2026.yaml \
       --target-rt a100-40gb --iterations 10000 --seed 42
     ```

2) Sequence sweep
   - Sweep effective lengths: [8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 128, 160, 192, 256] with fixed gen budget where applicable.
   - For each length record: kernel_name, batch_size, queue_wait_ms, gpu_mem_mb, p50/p95/p99 latency.

3) Mixed traffic test
   - Construct realistic traffic mix from product telemetry (ratios e.g., 70% short-chat (<=64), 20% medium (65-160), 10% long).
   - Run under target concurrency and measure tail latencies and KV cache hit rate.

4) Repeat across hardware and driver versions to separate hardware/compiler effects.

Telemetry tags to capture

- kernel.name
- kernel.variant
- scheduler.queue_depth
- batch.composition
- kvcache.size
- alloc.high_water_mb
- api.request_effective_length
- model.shard_count

Analysis guide

- Identify the first length where kernel.name changes for >1% of requests; call that L1.
- Plot p95/p99 by length and overlay kernel.name. Breakpoints appear where latency changes sharply with correlated kernel switch.
- Correlate alloc.high_water_mb with p99 spikes: if mem rises by >10% at a breakpoint, consider quantization/alloc path investigation.

Operational playbook (triage + remediation)

1) Detect
   - Alerting: create an alert when model.route p99 latency increases by >25% vs 7d baseline and kernel.name for >5% of requests is a known slow path. Use telemetry query:

     ```sql
     SELECT kernel_name, count(*) FROM runtime.events
     WHERE model_name = 'llama-7b' AND ts > now() - interval '5m'
     GROUP BY kernel_name ORDER BY count DESC
     ```

2) Triage steps (ordered)
   - Confirm whether p99 increase maps to shift in request length distribution (compare api.request_effective_length histograms).
   - Check scheduler.queue_depth and batch.composition to rule out batch skew.
   - Verify KV-cache hit rate; a sudden drop can inflate effective length due to upstream re-fetching.
   - Inspect GPU alloc.high_water_mb for leaking/spill behavior.

3) Immediate mitigation (fast path)
   - If kernel switch caused regression and a faster compatible kernel exists for longer lengths, enable temporary model override to force that kernel for this model/route (use route-level config). Example: set runtime.override_kernel = "attention-tiled-opt-v2" for routes matching /chat/* .
   - If KV-cache is the issue, enable short-term per-route prefix-caching or reduce prefix size to avoid crossing the breakpoint.

4) Medium-term remediations
   - Add a routing rule: split traffic by predicted effective length (<=L1 vs >L1) and route long requests to a node pool with larger GPUs or a kernel-optimized pool.
   - Adjust autoscaler warm targets for nodes that serve long sequences to avoid cold-shard placement during bursts.
   - Work with runtime team to prioritize kernel optimization (see section below).

5) Postmortem items
   - Add failing prompt examples to the model’s regression set and schedule quantized-kernel compatibility test in nightly perf suite.
   - Update per-model sequence breakpoints table in team wiki and annotate deployment manifests with expected L1/L2.

Kernel scheduling and compilation action items

- For each runtime kernel variant, maintain a short compatibility matrix: supported sequence ranges, preferred hardware, and quantization compatibility.
- Where a kernel has a small but expensive launch overhead (tiling kernels), include a warm-start micro-benchmark in the perf suite to measure amortized cost vs per-request overhead.
- Add compiler flag matrix to CI for kernels that use vendor-provided fused ops — this prevents unexpected fallbacks when new drivers are rolled.

Profiler playbook (how to collect actionable traces)

1) Light-weight trace (2–5 mins under live traffic)
   - Capture telemetry tags listed above at 5s granularity.
   - Export top-3 kernel_name occurrences with latency percentiles.

2) Full GPU profile (for repro)
   - Use NVIDIA Nsight Systems and measure kernel launches, memcpy, and occupancy. Command example:

     ```bash
     nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn --sample=timer --output seq-breakpoint-7b \\n       -- ./bazel-bin/tools/runtime-bench/bench_runner --model llama-7b --length 96 --iterations 1000
     ```

3) Kernel-level microprofile
   - Capture kernel-level flamegraphs and symbolized traces. Correlate with allocator calls to find allocation hotspots that precede kernel fallback.

Configuration table (suggested thresholds and overrides)

| Config key | Recommended default | When to change | Owner |
|------------|---------------------|----------------|-------|
| runtime.seq_breakpoint_override[model] | unset | When production L1 causes SLO breach and fast kernel is known | runtime-kernel-team |
| runtime.route_length_routing.enabled | true | For routes with >10% long requests | infra-ops |
| runtime.kvcache.max_prefix_tokens | 256 | Reduce if crossing L1 frequently | modeling |
| autoscaler.warm_target_long_seq | 2 nodes | Increase when long requests cause shard cold starts | srescaling |

Notes on experiments that produced these values

- All experiments were run with GPU driver 535.xx and CUDA 11.8 unless noted. On H100 with CUDA 12.x some breakpoints shifted by ±8 tokens due to different kernel tiling defaults.
- Quantized models showed more frequent kernel fallbacks on legacy drivers; driver upgrades removed one observed breakpoint in the 3B-quant tests.

Runbook snippets (quick commands)

- Force route-level kernel override:

  ```bash
  redwoodctl routes update --route /chat/llama-7b --set runtime.override_kernel=attention-tiled-opt-v2
  ```

- Add temporary length split rule (route annotations):

  ```yaml
  routes:
    - name: chat-short
      match: /chat/*
      predicate: "api.request_effective_length <= 64"
      pool: short-seq-pool
    - name: chat-long
      match: /chat/*
      predicate: "api.request_effective_length > 64"
      pool: long-seq-pool
  ```

Knowledge transfer and next steps

- Owners: runtime-kernel-team (kernel optimization and flags), infra-ops (routing and pools), modeling (prefix sizing guidance).
- Add a nightly test to the benchmarking suite: seqscale-nightly that runs the sequence sweep for all production models and records L1/L2 breakpoints to a central table.
- Track kernel regressions as part of release gating for runtime releases; a change that introduces a new breakpoint must have a documented mitigation and perf test.

Appendix A — reproducible artifacts and results

- Benchmark configs: gs://redwood-perf/seqscale-2026/{llama-3b,7b,13b,70b}.yaml
- Raw telemetry snapshot (airgapped): s3://redwood-archives/perf/seqscale-2026/summary.tar.gz
- Notebooks: internal link to notebooks showing plotting routines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/seqscale-visualizations

Appendix B — known caveats

- Breakpoints are sensitive to driver and compiler versions; do not copy absolute token values between clusters without running the sweep.
- Mixed-batch workloads can mask breakpoints due to amortized kernel launch costs; both isolated and mixed tests are required.
- Some models employ decoding-time length conditioning that changes effective length distribution; ensure input generation in benchmarks replicates production preprocessors.

If you have questions, want the raw experiment logs, or need help adding a model to the nightly sweep, ping the runtime-kernel-team in #runtime-kernel and assign a short task in the infra-ops backlog.

payload.page_title: model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This document defines a practical matrix and operational playbook for selecting model variants at routing time to balance per-request latency, unit cost, and end-to-end quality. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and product owners who operate the routing and fallback layers of the serving runtime.

Goals
- Provide a compact, auditable representation (the Variant Selection Matrix) that maps request classes to candidate model variants and their tradeoffs.
- Define telemetry and SLOs required to validate selection choices in production.
- Provide rollout and rollback playbooks for changing variant mappings.
- Give examples of automation hooks (autoscaler, router) that consume the matrix.

Intended audience and ownership
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (routing subgroup)
- Secondary: eng-sre, eng-platform, product (API performance)

Key definitions
- Model variant: a served artifact, e.g., llama-2-13b-q4_0, redwood-clarity-3-small-int8, or gptx-16k-fast. Includes quantization/precision, max-seq, and kernel-profile tags.
- Request class: a classification computed at the edge or ingress that captures latency sensitivity, token budget, and quality requirement (e.g., chat-low-latency, batch-embed, long-seq-generation).
- Unit cost: a normalized per-token cost metric that includes GPU time, memory amortization, and software overhead (expressed in microcost units).
- Latency budget: 95th percentile target for end-to-end generation for the request class.

The Variant Selection Matrix (VSM)
- The VSM is a table (stored as a JSON/YAML in the config store) mapping request_class -> ordered list of candidate variants with annotations. The router evaluates candidates in order and will fall back according to configured policies.

Example matrix (ASCII table excerpt)
+----------------------+-----------------------------+----------------+----------------+----------------------+
| request_class        | candidate_variant           | est_latency_ms | est_unit_cost   | quality_delta_pts    |
+----------------------+-----------------------------+----------------+----------------+----------------------+
| chat-low-latency     | redwood-clarity-3-small-i8  | 120            | 1.0            | -0.5                |
|                      | llama-2-13b-q4_0            | 230            | 0.75           | +0.4                |
|                      | redwood-clarity-3-medium-i8 | 180            | 1.3            | +0.7                |
+----------------------+-----------------------------+----------------+----------------+----------------------+
| batch-embed          | embed-compact-512           | 60             | 0.12           | N/A                 |
|                      | embed-accurate-1536         | 220            | 0.45           | +2.1                |
+----------------------+-----------------------------+----------------+----------------+----------------------+

Notes on table fields
- est_latency_ms: median token-generation time under representative load on dedicated pool. Populate from benchmarking suite.
- est_unit_cost: normalized units; derived from per-GPU time and amortized infra cost.
- quality_delta_pts: expected performance change on key evals (positive means better). Put ‘N/A’ for metrics not applicable.

How the router consumes the VSM
1) At request ingress, compute request_class (deterministic classification using prompt heuristics and headers).
2) Query config store for VSM entry for that class.
3) Evaluate candidate variants in order; for each candidate:
   - Check capacity availability in target pool (via allocator API).
   - Validate current observed 95p latency for the variant vs. request_class latency budget (from recent telemetry window).
   - If variant passes both, route request and annotate trace with variant_id, decision_reason=primary.
4) If no candidate passes, consult the fallback policy: either queue (short delay), route to best-effort low-cost variant, or proxy to Hosted API with higher SLA.

SLOs and telemetry required
- Per-variant 95p token-latency per request_class. Tag with variant and request_class.
- Per-variant per-1m throughput and active sessions.
- Per-variant quality regressions: daily evals on representative prompt sets, and online quality signals (e.g., rerank disagreement, human QA hits).
- Cost burn rate per-variant aggregated to product/unit.
- Decision coverage: fraction of requests classified and matched in VSM (target > 99%).

Benchmarking inputs and methodology
- Use the microbenchmark harness from benchmarking-and-perf-suite to produce: median/95p per-token latency under 1, 5, 10, 20 concurrent streams; memory footprint; kernel occupancy profiles.
- For quality deltas, run the curated eval suites from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks with at least 3 random seeds; report mean and 95% CI.
- Unit cost computed as: (GPU-ms * gpu_price + infra_overhead) / tokens_generated. Keep calculation script in /ops/costing/vsm_cost_calc.py and reference in the matrix metadata.

Rollout and change playbook (stepwise)
1) Author a matrix change PR: update YAML in config repo with rationale, benchmarking snapshots, and expected impact.
2) Automated preflight: run smoke simulations with sample workload in canary cluster (script: infra/tools/vsm_simulator.sh).
3) Canary deploy: enable new mapping for 1% traffic, observe these metrics for 2 hours: 95p latency, error rate, quality_signal, and cost burn.
4) Ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with 30–60 minute hold windows.
5) If any SLO regresses beyond thresholds (95p latency +20% absolute or quality delta <-1.0 on eval), rollback to previous matrix and open a production incident.

Rollback and incident triggers
- Immediate rollback triggers: error rate > 0.5% absolute increase, OOM or GPU watch-dog nodes thrown, or quality alerts (manual QA or automated threshold).
- Soft triggers: cost burn > expected by 30% for sustained 4h; treat as investigation item, may not trigger rollback automatically.

Operational knobs exposed to oncall
- emergency_variant_overrides: per-customer or per-route pin to a specific variant.
- degraded_mode: route all low-priority request_classes to minimal-cost variants.
- admission_timeout_ms: how long router will attempt to match before falling back.
- sampling_ratio: fraction of routed requests to sample for quality telemetry.

Example VSM YAML snippet (consumed by router)
---
request_classes:
  chat-low-latency:
    latency_budget_ms: 200
    candidates:
      - variant: redwood-clarity-3-small-i8
        note: fast-default
      - variant: redwood-clarity-3-medium-i8
        note: higher-quality
      - variant: llama-2-13b-q4_0
        note: cost-optimum
  batch-embed:
    latency_budget_ms: 1000
    candidates:
      - variant: embed-compact-512
      - variant: embed-accurate-1536
...

Telemetry example queries (Prometheus / SQL)
- 95p latency by variant/request_class: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, variant, request_class))
- Cost burn per variant (1h): sum(rate(gpu_ms_total[1h])) by (variant) * price_index

Testing and validation matrix (pre-merge checklist)
- [ ] Benchmarks attached for each candidate (median/95p and memory).
- [ ] Quality deltas for key evals are provided and annotated.
- [ ] Canary simulation passed with 0 incidents in automated run.
- [ ] Runtime telemetry schema updated if new tags were introduced.

Known interactions and gotchas
- Kernel scheduling differences: low-precision quantized variants may have lower per-token latency but produce worse occupancy for mixed-length sequences, causing 95p surprises under bursty workloads. When adding such variants, force-run occupancy microbenchmarks.
- KV cache fragmentation: switching variants with incompatible KV key formats will cause cold cache penalties. Matrix entries should include kv_compatibility tags.
- Cross-tenant memory eviction: heavy variants on shared pools can cause noisy-neighbor effects. Prefer dedicated pools or pool-quotas for heavy variants.

Release notes and auditability
- Every matrix change must be submitted as a PR and the PR description must contain: benchmark artifacts, telemetry snapshot (last 7d), and risk assessment. The config repo auto-tags changes and writes an audit entry to the change-log stream.

Related runbooks and pages
- See runtime runbooks for: emergency_variant_override, kvcache-consistency, and graceful-fallback-runbook. Links: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024
- See benchmarking suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026

Appendix A: Short decision record
- Decision: Model selection should prioritize latency budget for low-latency request_classes and cost for batch/throughput request_classes.
- Rationale: Product teams require predictable tail latency for chat experiences; batch embedding customers are more price-sensitive.
- Owner: routing subgroup (eng-serving-runtime)

Appendix B: Example incident timeline (summary)
1) 2025-01-17 03:12 UTC: Canary roll from 5% to 20% for chat-low-latency mapping to llama-2-13b-q4_0.
2) 03:28 UTC: 95p latency for chat-low-latency increased from 190ms -> 320ms.
3) 03:30 UTC: Automated rollback to previous matrix (clarity small-i8). Incident created: IR-2025-0117-variant-latency.
4) Postmortem: kernel occupancy for llama-2-13b-q4_0 at target concurrency was 40% vs. expected 72%; microbenchmarks had been run at lower concurrency.

Appendix C: Suggested experiments
- A/B traffic split experiments where 0.5% of requests are shadowed to a new variant and offline-quality is measured before enabling live traffic.
- Pressure testing: run burst tests with 10x typical concurrency to evaluate 95p degradation modes.

Contacts and escalation
- Routing subgroup oncall: #runtime-routing-oncall (Slack)
- SRE pager: eng-sre-pager@redwood.ai
- Document owner: Ava Martinez (ava.martinez@redwood.ai)

Document history
- 2024-11-15: Created by Ava Martinez
- 2025-03-02: Reviewed and published (minor clarifications and added rollback thresholds)

payload.page_title: Canary SLA Oracle and Benchmark Gate Specification

sections.body: Title: Canary SLA Oracle and Benchmark Gate Specification
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This document defines the design, operational contract, and runbook for the Canary SLA Oracle — a deterministic decision service that evaluates canary releases against a defined set of benchmark gates before permitting progressive rollout. The specification ties release tooling to the benchmarking suite and runtime observability so releases are gated by both fidelity (quality) and operational SLOs (latency, error budget, cost).
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a repeatable, auditable gate for canary decisions that combines synthetic benchmark signals with live canary telemetry.
- Reduce false positives/negatives by using weighted evidence and time-windowed aggregation.
- Ensure fast feedback for small canaries while remaining robust for larger traffic ramps.
- Emit human-readable verdicts and machine-readable artifacts for automation (ok/reject/conditional).
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: This spec covers: Canary SLA Oracle behaviour, benchmark gate definitions, data ingestion and enrichment, verdict calculation, tie-breaking, and required observability hooks. It does NOT specify UI/console layouts; those are product deliverables.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Canary: A controlled subset deployment of a new runtime component, kernel, or model variant.
- Benchmark Gate: A single pass/fail criterion computed from benchmark or telemetry data (e.g., P99 <= 80ms).
- Oracle Verdicts: {ok, reject, conditional, inconclusive}.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) Ingests two data streams in parallel: static benchmark results from the perf-suite and live telemetry from the canary shard(s).
2) Normalizes metrics to canonical units (ms, tokens/sec, error-rate) and tags by route/model/tenant.
3) Runs gate evaluators and a weighted aggregator to compute a single verdict.
4) Emits a signed artifact (JSON) with detailed gate evidence, confidence score, and rollback recommendations.
sections.heading: Architecture overview

sections.body:
| Gate name | Input source | Unit | Default threshold | Failure mode | Notes |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| latency_p99_path | live telemetry | ms | <= 120 | reject | path is route-specific P99 over 5m window |
| latency_median_change | perf vs baseline | % | <= +10% | conditional | small regressions allowed with review |
| tail_error_rate | live telemetry | errors/1000 | <= 1.0 | reject | counts 5xx and model-failure errors |
| quality_similarity | perf-suite eval | cosine | >= 0.92 | reject | embedding/response-similarity check against baseline |
| cost_per_token_delta | perf-suite and billing | % | <= +15% | conditional | flags large regressions in unit cost |
sections.heading: Gate taxonomy and thresholds (default)

sections.body:
- Each gate produces an evidence object: {gate, status, measured, threshold, weight, rationale}.
- We compute a score S = sum(weight_i * score_i) / sum(weight_i) where score_i = 1 for pass, 0 for fail, 0.5 for conditional.
- Default weights: latency_p99_path=3, latency_median_change=1.5, tail_error_rate=4, quality_similarity=5, cost_per_token_delta=1.
- Verdict mapping: S >= 0.85 => ok; 0.6 <= S < 0.85 => conditional; S < 0.6 => reject; insufficient/conflicting data => inconclusive.
sections.heading: Aggregation and weighting

sections.body:
- Live telemetry: rolling windows of 1m, 5m, 15m; primary decision window is 5m with 15m as confirmation.
- Perf-suite results: treated as single-snapshot evidence with decay function: weight *= e^{-age/48h}.
- Minimum sample floor: for latency/error gates require >= 500 requests in the 5m window or verdict is marked inconclusive.
sections.heading: Time windows and sampling

sections.body:
- Normalize percentiles using the runtime's histogram export (OpenMetrics). Convert to ms and apply route-specific knobs (see section on route sensitivity).
- Enrich with: model_variant_id, kernel_commit, instance_type, region, traffic_mix (proportion of streaming/chat/embedding).
sections.heading: Data enrichment and canonicalization

sections.body:
- If aggregation yields inconclusive or conditional, the policy allows a human approver to escalate with justification. The Oracle will surface the top three signals that would flip the verdict if they changed.
- Overrides are auditable: approver id, timestamp, justification, and a TTL for the override (default 1 hour).

Runbook: Canary release flow (operators):
1) Author triggers a canary via the release tool with expected traffic fraction and perf-suite job id.
2) Perf-suite runs pre-release benchmarks (synthetic SLOs) and uploads results to the benchmark-store.
3) Release tool marks canary as active; the Oracle begins ingesting live telemetry automatically.
4) Oracle evaluates gates at T+5m and emits initial verdict artifact to the release tool and logs.
5) If verdict == ok => auto-progress to next stage per release policy.
6) If verdict == conditional => hold, notify on-call and product reviewer with evidence bundle.
7) If verdict == reject => trigger automatic rollback policy and create incident for postmortem.
8) If verdict == inconclusive => extend canary for an additional 10m or require perf-suite re-run with larger synthetic load.
sections.heading: Tie-breaking and human override

sections.body:
- Alert: Oracle failure (ingest/compute) => P1 oncall.
- Alert: inconclusive rate > 10% across canaries in last 24h => investigate metric sparsity or perf-suite health.
- Gauges to expose: current_score, gate_pass_rate, evidence_age_seconds, min_sample_count.
- Dashboards: Canary Health (per-release), Gate Violations (heatmap by route), Evidence Drift (time series of quality_similarity).
sections.heading: Operational alerts and observability hooks

sections.body:
```
{
  "release_id": "r-2026-0104",
  "canary_shard": "canary-eu-7",
  "verdict": "conditional",
  "score": "0.72",
  "evidence": [
    {"gate":"latency_p99_path","status":"pass","measured":"95ms","threshold":"120ms","weight":"3"},
    {"gate":"quality_similarity","status":"fail","measured":"0.88","threshold":"0.92","weight":"5"}
  ],
  "timestamp": "2026-06-10T16:12:03Z",
  "artifact_signature": "sha256:..."
}
```

(That JSON is illustrative; the real artifact must be signed and include schema_version.)
sections.heading: Example verdict artifact (machine-readable)

sections.body:
- Trigger a canary and attach a perf job:
```
redwoodctl release start --component runtime --sha abcd1234 --canary 0.01 --perf-job perf-2026-06-10-phi
```
- Query Oracle verdict:
```
redwoodctl release verdict --release r-2026-0104 --json
```
sections.heading: Rollout automation examples (CLI snippets)

sections.body:
- Monthly calibration: update default thresholds and weights against a held-out corpus of releases from the last 6 months.
- Backfill experiments: re-run perf-suite on historical images and compute oracle false-positive/false-negative rates; aim for < 5% FP at current thresholds.
sections.heading: Quality and calibration process

sections.body:
- Oracle service owner: eng-serving-runtime - Release Engineering (primary).
- Benchmarking suite ownership: eng-serving-runtime - Perf & Benchmarking team.
- Oncall escalation: runtime oncall rotation.
sections.heading: Ownership and responsibilities

sections.body:
- Unit tests for gate evaluators and weight decay logic.
- Integration tests against simulated telemetry with deterministic verdict expectations.
- Synthetic canary first-run in staging must show correct artifact emission and signed artifact verification.
sections.heading: Testing and release criteria for Oracle service itself

sections.body:
- Small-traffic tenants: floor on sample counts will cause frequent inconclusive verdicts; teams should use larger synthetic perf-suite runs for such customers.
- Cross-region canaries: network variance will affect latency gates; the Oracle applies region-aware baselines but teams must review region-specific thresholds.
- Model-aware quality gates assume availability of a reference embedding; new-model onboarding must include a reference dataset.
sections.heading: Compatibility notes and known limitations

sections.body:
1) Run Oracle in shadow mode for two release cycles and compare with legacy canary decisions.
2) Publish discrepancy report and adjust weights/thresholds.
3) Opt-in small set of services for auto-enforcement for 30 days.
sections.heading: Migration plan for existing gating mechanisms

sections.body:
A. Route sensitivity knobs table:
| Route type | sensitivity multiplier | recommended median threshold change tolerance |
| api:chat | 1.2 | 8% |
| api:generation | 1.0 | 10% |
| api:embedding | 0.8 | 6% |

B. Benchmark artifact schema (subset):
- perf_job_id (string)
- model_variant_id (string)
- date (ISO8601)
- metrics {latency_p50, latency_p95, latency_p99, tokens_per_sec, quality_similarity, cost_per_token}

C. Related runbooks:
- runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 (detailed canary matrix and roll criteria)
- runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 (fallback policies)
