payload.page_title: runtime-topology-stability-index-and-degradation-simulation-2027

sections.body:
Overview
-------
This page defines our Runtime Topology Stability Index (RTSI), the accompanying Degradation Simulation framework, and operational playbooks for using these signals to guide kernel scheduling decisions, profiling campaigns, and benchmark validation. The goal is to provide a reproducible method for quantifying how a runtime topology (sharding, KV cache layout, kernel variants, and scheduler policies) reacts to progressive stress and to capture early warnings before user-visible SLO degradation.

Why this exists
 - We frequently ship scheduler and kernel changes that affect tail latency and fidelity in subtle ways; unit tests and microbenchmarks are insufficient.
 - RTSI provides a single, actionable score tied to observability signals and a simulation harness to stress topologies in controlled ways.
 - The output informs rollout gating: canaries, weighted rollouts, and automated fallback thresholds in the router.

Scope
 - Applies to all Hosted and Dedicated runtime topologies. Private deployments should re-run the simulation with local traffic shapes.
 - Focuses on inference-serving concerns: latency quantiles, error rates, memory pressure, shard-eviction churn, kernel-failure propagation, and KV cache warmup dynamics.

Definitions
 - Topology: placement of model shards, KV cache shards, and scheduler domains across GPUs and nodes.
 - RTSI: scalar 0–100 where 100 is fully stable under synthetic and replayed traffic stress; lower scores indicate increasing instability.
 - Degradation Mode: class of graceful-fallback or failure (e.g., soft-fidelity degradation, eviction storm, kernel stall).

RTSI design and signals
----------------------
RTSI is computed from a weighted aggregation of normalized signals collected during a simulation run:
1) Latency head/tail scores (p50, p95, p99) — directionally prioritized to penalize tail shifts.
2) Error amplification factor — rate of increased 5xx/response-timeouts vs baseline.
3) Eviction churn index — rate of KV/shard evictions per minute and the time-to-warm (cold-hit penalty).
4) Kernel slip events — frequency of kernel slow-path engagements and soft-fallback triggers.
5) Cross-cohort interference — latency correlation coefficient across tenant cohorts.
6) Recovery velocity — time for metrics to return to baseline after load drop or mitigation (seconds).

Weighting and normalization
 - Default weights: tail latency (0.35), error amplification (0.20), eviction churn (0.15), kernel slip (0.15), cohort interference (0.10), recovery velocity (0.05).
 - Signals are normalized to 0..1 where 0 is worst-case observed in historical incidents and 1 is baseline. RTSI = 100 * weighted_sum(normalized_signals).
 - The weight set is configurable per release; changes must be reviewed with SRE and runtime leads.

Degradation Simulation Framework (how to run)
-------------------------------------------
Purpose: execute deterministic experiments combining synthetic bursts and replayed production traces to surface interaction effects across layers (scheduler, kernel, cache).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Access to the simulation harness (git: infra/runtime-sim) and a small cluster configured with the topology under test.
 - An anonymized request trace (see trace-redaction-playbook) or the synthetic suite.
 - Baseline golden metrics for the model/sequence distribution.
sections.heading: Prereqs

sections.body:
1) Checkout infra/runtime-sim@stable and configure experiment.yaml (example below).
2) Start cluster: ./scripts/sim-cluster up --topology topology.json --nodes 4
3) Load baseline: ./scripts/load-baseline --trace traces/golden-corpus.json
4) Run progressive storm: ./scripts/run-storm --burst-factor 3 --duration 600 --cohorts 3
5) Collect artifacts: ./scripts/collect-artifacts --out /tmp/sim-output
6) Compute RTSI: python tools/compute_rtsi.py --input /tmp/sim-output --weights config/weights.yaml

Example experiment.yaml:
| name | value |
| experiment_name | rtsi-sanity-2027 |
| topology_file | topologies/4node-nonuniform.json |
| trace | traces/median-length-100.json |
| burst_pattern | step(1,3,30m) |
| scheduler_profile | econ-priority-governor-v2 |
| kernel_variants | [tf32, int8-fallback] |

Kernel-scheduling interaction checklist
--------------------------------------
When scheduling policy changes are proposed, run the following minimal checklist against RTSI:
1) Local pressure test: simulate single-node degradation and measure eviction churn and kernel slip.
2) Cross-node blast: multi-cohort ramp to expose interference.
3) Fallback exercise: intentionally trigger a kernel slow-path and validate graceful fallback latency bound.
4) Canary schedule: run weighted rollout simulation with 5/25/70 split and verify RTSI delta <= 6 points.

Profiling playbook (collection guidance)
-------------------------------------
sections.heading: Quick run (smoke)

sections.body:
- Latency histograms (per-cohort, per-model) with 1ms bins up to 2s.
 - Kernel telemetry: kernel-id, path (fast/slow), elapsed_ns, occupancy, tensor shapes.
 - KV cache metrics: hits, misses, evictions, warmup-latency per key-range.
 - Node-level: GPU-util, memory_used, page_faults, temperature, nvlink-errors.
 - Scheduler: slot-queue-length, per-priority utilization, preemptions, admission denials.
sections.heading: Signals to collect during simulation runs

sections.body:
- For simulation runs keep full traces and kernel telemetry for 30 days. Aggregates (per-minute) are retained for 90 days.
 - Use stratified sampling for long runs: preserve all p99 contributors and sample head requests at 1% to save storage.

Benchmarking suite integration
-----------------------------
sections.heading: Data retention and sample rates

sections.body:
- Pre-merge checks run a lightweight sim (10m, small cluster) and verify RTSI >= 85 for low-risk backports.
 - Release gates run extended sims (2–6 hours) on release branches; failures (RTSI delta > 10 vs baseline) block signoff.
 - Benchmark artifacts include an artifacts manifest with: topology.json, scheduler_policy.yaml, kernel_build_hash, raw traces, and computed RTSI report.

Release notes and versioning
---------------------------
When a runtime change modifies scheduling or kernels, release notes must include:
 - RTSI baseline and delta observed in extended sim runs.
 - Kernel variant compatibility table and roll-forward/rollback instructions.
 - Recommended canary matrix (percentages, duration, SLOs to watch).
 - Any config toggles to delay rollout (feature flags) and their default state.

Known issues and interpretations
-------------------------------
We surface deterministic patterns that should not be treated as immediate blockers but require follow-up:
 - Eviction ripple: small increases in eviction rate that grow over minutes indicate mis-sized KV partitions. Triage: re-evaluate shard sizing and prefetch hints.
 - Kernel slip noise: intermittent slow-path entries isolated to particular tensor shapes. Triage: add microbench for the shape and consider kernel specialization.
 - Inter-cohort correlated tails: events where a small tenant induces p99 increases across unrelated cohorts — typically scheduler admission quanta or quota shaping misconfig.

Operational runbooks (step-by-step)
---------------------------------
Runbook A: RTSI regression detected during CI
1) Abort the merge and alert runtime-sre@redwood.
2) Attach artifacts manifest and full sim output to the ticket.
3) Triage: run quick delta profiler (scripts/quick-delta) to localize to scheduler/kernel/cache.
4) If kernel suspected, run kernel smoke on microbench harness and isolate commit.
5) If scheduler suspected, revert policy or reduce canary weight and re-run sim.
6) Update the release notice with root cause and mitigation.

Runbook B: Production tail-latency spike suspected to match simulation signature
1) Toggle circuit-breaker: route traffic to fallback model-variant.
2) Open incident, tag with simulation label and link to last successful RTSI run.
3) Run targeted replay for the last 10 minutes using production trace sampler.
4) If RTSI-like signature reproduced, follow kernel rollback path.
5) If not reproduced, escalate to SRE/runtime-engineering for deeper tracing.

Ownership and governance
-----------------------
 - Primary owner: Runtime Architecture (runtime-arch@redwood).
 - SRE for policy: eng-sre (oncall rotation).
 - Profiling and kernel analysis: Performance and Applied ML teams.
 - Changes to RTSI formula or default weights require: runtime-arch + eng-sre + perf signoff.

Appendix A — Example weight file (config/weights.yaml)
---
sections.heading: RTSI is integrated into the acceptance benchmark suite

sections.body:
tail_latency: 0.35
error_amp: 0.20
eviction_churn: 0.15
kernel_slip: 0.15
cohort_interference: 0.10
recovery_velocity: 0.05

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist (fast)
 - p99 spiked but p95 stable: check kernel slip histogram and tail shapes.
 - Eviction count rising: check partition distribution and hot-key lists.
 - One-node pressure causing cross-node tails: investigate slot reservation and NUMA bindings.

Appendix C — Links and artifacts
 - Simulation harness: git.internal.redwood/infra/runtime-sim
 - Trace redaction playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/trace-redaction-playbook
 - RTSI computation script: tools/compute_rtsi.py (runtime-sim repo)

Revision history
----------------
 - 2026-11-15: Initial draft (Priya Desai).
 - 2027-01-18: Added kernel-slip instrumentation guidance (Miles Chen).
 - 2027-03-12: Finalized weights and CI integration checklist (Anika Rao).

payload.page_title: Delta routing and cost-partitioning architecture for request dispatch

sections.body: This document describes the Delta Routing and Cost-Partitioning Architecture: a cross-cutting design that unifies request dispatch, cost attribution, and kernel scheduling signals across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Delta Routing is intended to reduce tenant-visible latency spikes during heterogeneous workload mixes while enabling precise per-route/per-model cost partitioning for billing and autoscaling decisions.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Goals:
  - Provide a deterministic dispatch policy that balances latency SLOs, per-token cost targets, and GPU kernel efficiency for mixed workloads.
  - Enable cost-partitioning signals that feed the billing pipeline and autoscaler without adding >1% p99 latency overhead.
  - Allow graceful degradation: automated fallback to cheaper model variants or cached responses when kernel pressure threatens SLOs.
- Non-goals:
  - Replace local kernel mappers; Delta Routing complements kernel selection but does not reimplement device-level scheduling.
  - Solve cold-start model loading for on-prem packages (handled by deployment bootstrap docs).
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body:
1) Ingress and classification:
  - Incoming request enters the API gateway and is annotated with: model_id, route_id, client_tier, requested_max_tokens, streaming_flag, and idempotency_key when provided.
  - The classifier computes a compact workload fingerprint (sequence_length_percentile, prompt_entropy_estimate, streaming_hint) used to consult local routing caches.

2) Delta Router (service):
  - Stateless microservice running in every region/edge that decides: target-serving-pool, kernel-compatibility-tag, and cost-partition-token.
  - Inputs: runtime telemetry (kernel queue lengths, p50/p95/p99 at pool), model variants matrix (latency/cost profiles), tenant policy (latency SLO, cost cap, allowed fallbacks).
  - Outputs: dispatch_decision = {pool, kernel_tag, priority_bucket, partition_token, fallback_reason (optional)}.

3) Cost Partitioning and Attribution:
  - Cost partition token is a short opaque ID that flows with the request through serving runtime and is appended to usage events.
  - The runtime multiplies per-token resource units by a kernel-efficiency factor (table below) before attributing to partition_token.
  - Partition tokens are rotated per-hour and resolved offline to human-readable cost centers to avoid per-request metadata explosion.

4) Kernel scheduling signal propagation:
  - Delta Router writes (lightweight) scheduling hints to a shared ring buffer consumed by the kernel mapper on the GPU host. Hints include priority_bucket and expected_sequence_quantiles.
  - Kernel mapper uses hints to pick kernel implementations and adjust slice sizes; it remains authoritative for final mapping.
sections.heading: High-level architecture overview

sections.body:
- Priority buckets: real-time (p99 target <= 75 ms), interactive (p99 <= 250 ms), batchable (p99 <= 2s).
- Cost-aware routing rule: if projected cost per 1k tokens > tenant_cost_cap and a compatible quantized variant exists with <= 8% relative quality delta, prefer fallback.
- Kernel pressure fallback: if GPU kernel queue growth rate > 30% and average kernel latency > baseline*1.5, mark pool as degraded and trigger cross-pool redistribution.
sections.heading: Policy heuristics and decision rules

sections.body:
- fp16-optimized-kernel: 1.0
- int8-q4-kernel: 0.62
- grouped-attention-shard-kernel: 0.85
- causal-seq-opt-kernel: 0.94

These factors are tuned from benchmarking runs and updated monthly. The runtime multiplies raw token counts by the selected factor to produce \"resource units\" for billing.
sections.heading: Kernel-efficiency factor table (example)

sections.body:
- Delta Router emits the following metrics per route and per-pool:
  - router.dispatches_total (labels: route_id, pool_id, decision)
  - router.fallbacks_total (labels: fallback_reason, route_id)
  - router.latency_ms_bucketed (p50/p95/p99)
  - router.estimated_resource_units (sum)
- Traces must include the partition_token and a wire-level tracepoint at: ingress -> delta-router -> pool-proxy -> kernel-entry.
- Critical logs: any decision that chooses fallback must log tenant_id, route_id, quality_delta_estimate, and reason.
sections.heading: Telemetry and observability requirements

sections.body:
- When deploying a new routing heuristic or updated efficiency factors, enable a 5% sample of production traffic routed to A (control) and B (candidate) for 48 hours.
- Collect kernel-level spans for sampled requests with the tag sample.delta-routing=true. Store full spans for up to 7 days; aggregated metrics for 90 days.
- Use the local profiling CLI to extract representative traces from a given pool:

  # profile sampler for pool-3 between timestamps
  rwt profile --pool pool-3 --from 2026-02-10T12:00Z --to 2026-02-10T14:00Z --tag sample.delta-routing=true --output traces.ndjson
sections.heading: Profiling playbook / sampling strategy (short form)

sections.body:
- Synthesize three canonical mixes for validation:
  - Mix A (interactive-heavy): 70% short chat (<=64 tokens), 20% medium (64–256), 10% long (>256).
  - Mix B (embedding-and-batch): 50% embedding requests, 30% text generation (batchable), 20% reranking requests.
  - Mix C (burst-churn): repeated high-concurrency hotspots with 1s bursts every 30s to emulate PLG spikes.
- Metrics to record per-run: p50/p95/p99 generation latency, kernel_throughput_tokens_per_sec, gpu_utilization_by_kernel, resource_units_consumed, cold-cache_miss_rate.
- For comparative experiments, keep deploy delta isolated: run A/B for 2M tokens or 24 hours whichever is earlier.

Runbook: pool-degradation and emergency fallback (operator steps):

1) Detection:
  - Pager triggers when router.fallbacks_total for a pool > 5/min for 10 min OR p99 latency for real-time bucket exceeds SLO by >25% for 5 min.
2) Quick Triage (5 min):
  - Check router.dispatches_total to confirm increased dispatches to fallback variants.
  - Query kernel mapper metrics: kernel_queue_length, avg_kernel_latency, memory_pressure.
3) Immediate mitigations (10 min):
  - If kernel queue growth rate > 40%: toggle pool read-only to new requests and redirect traffic to warm standby pool. Command: rwt pool set-accepting --pool pool-x --accepting false
  - If memory pressure detected (swap or OOM events): scale down concurrency slots on the pool and enable aggressive KV-cache eviction: rwt pool tune --pool pool-x --concurrency 0.5 --kvcache-eviction aggressive
4) Recovery actions (30–120 min):
  - Rolling restart of GPU hosts with drain policy: follow SIGTERM drain (see sigterm-connection-drain-and-graceful-shutdown-playbook).
  - Recompute kernel-efficiency factors if a new kernel release was deployed in the previous 72 hours.
5) Postmortem and action items:
  - Create incident with tags: delta-routing, pool-id, fallback. Attach sampled traces and resource-unit time series.
  - Run a benchmark job that replays the incident workload under controlled conditions and propose changes to fallback thresholds.
sections.heading: Benchmarking guidance (workload design)

sections.body: - When releasing updates that affect the router decision logic or efficiency factors, attach the following to the release: 1) a benchmark report comparing resource_units for Mix A/B/C; 2) a toggled rollout plan with 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% gates and automatic rollback on p99 increase >10%; 3) updated profiling sampler config.
sections.heading: Interplay with release process and rollout notes

sections.body:
- Cross-pool affinity churn: if a model has heavy KV-cache affinity to GPU-host A and Delta Router moves a chunk of concurrent sessions to pool B, cold misses will spike. Mitigation: affinity-aware cost of migration is included in projected cost model; prefer delayed migration for long-lived sessions.
- Partition token resolution delay: offline resolution of partition tokens can lag up to 2 hours in heavy billing windows; ensure customer-facing billing UI displays a preliminary estimate with note about reconciliation.
- Quality cliffs on low-bit quantization: automatic fallback uses a conservative 8% quality delta threshold; for sensitive routes (payment, legal) the policy must be set to disallow quantized fallbacks.
sections.heading: Known caveats and edge cases

sections.body:
- Dynamic partition token aggregation windows: can we reduce billing churn by grouping partitions across short-tenure tenants?
- ML-guided decisioning: evaluate whether a learned policy yields materially better resource vs. latency tradeoffs than heuristic routing. Planned experiment Q2 2026.

Appendix: example dataflow (text diagram)

Ingress -> classifier -> Delta Router -> pool proxy -> kernel mapper -> GPU kernels
  |                                      ^
  +-- trace: partition_token -------------+
sections.heading: Open design questions (for future work)

payload.page_title: Runtime Optimization Config Apply Pipeline (Versioned Safe Apply + Rollback)

sections.body:
This page describes how the Serving Runtime fetches, caches, and applies *versioned* Optimization Configs, and how it safely rolls back to a prior known-good version.

Optimization Configs control runtime tuning knobs that materially impact cost/latency/reliability, including:
- Batching heuristics (e.g., continuous batching targets, max batch tokens)
- Caching toggles and KV/prefix cache settings
- Quantization profile selection (where supported per model)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- **Versioned, immutable configs** (apply a specific version ID)
- **Idempotent application** (safe retries, safe duplicate events)
- **Partial rollout safety** (canary/percentage-based apply)
- **One-click rollback** with predictable time-to-mitigate
sections.heading: The runtime must support

sections.body:
- Control plane data model and API details (covered in the Optimization Config Service page)
- Console UX flows (covered in Console & Tooling docs)

---
sections.heading: Non-goals for this document

sections.body:
**Optimization Config Version (OCV):** Immutable record with an ID like `ocv_01J2R...`, created in the control plane.

**Effective config:** The config version that a worker uses for request execution at a given moment.

**Scope:** The target set for a config apply. In runtime terms, scope is resolved to a routing key with dimensions:
- `tenant_id` (or `account_id`)
- `deployment_id` (Hosted/Dedicated)
- `model_id` (and optional `variant_id`)
- `region`

**Apply transaction:** Runtime-local state machine that stages changes and only flips to a new effective config once preconditions are met.

**Checkpoint:** A persisted marker used to ensure safe progress and safe rollback across restarts.

---
sections.heading: Key concepts and terminology

sections.body:
1. Operator (Console/API) creates a new Optimization Config Version.
2. Control plane validates schema + semantic constraints.
3. Control plane starts a staged rollout (e.g., canary 5% → 25% → 100%), gated by SLO and (for quantization) eval signals.
4. Control plane updates the *desired* config version per scope/shard and publishes a change event.
sections.heading: 1) Control plane creates/validates/applies

sections.body:
1. Runtime components (routers and model workers) fetch desired version for the relevant scope and cache it.
2. Workers apply the new version using an idempotent apply transaction.
3. Workers emit metrics tagged with `config_version` and `apply_state`.
4. Control plane observes rollout health and either progresses, pauses, or triggers rollback.
sections.heading: 2) Runtime receives desired version and applies safely

sections.body:
Control Plane (Optimization Config Service + Rollout Controller)
  -> change event (apply/promote/rollback)
  -> Desired Version per scope/shard

Runtime
  Router: resolves scope/shard -> selects worker pool -> forwards requests
  Worker: fetches config version -> validates local compatibility -> apply transaction -> serves with effective config

---
sections.heading: Text diagram

sections.body:
- Resolves request routing keys (tenant/model/region) and applies shard/percentage assignment used by the canary controller.
- Adds response debug headers when enabled:
  - `x-redwood-optimization-config-version: <ocv_id>`
  - `x-redwood-optimization-config-apply-state: stable|applying|rolled_back` (best-effort)
sections.heading: Router / Frontend (request routing)

sections.body:
- Maintains a local cache of config payloads by version.
- Applies config updates using a transaction with checkpoints.
- Guarantees idempotency and safe re-application.
sections.heading: Worker / Model executor

sections.body:
- Subscribes/polls for desired version changes (implementation differs by environment, see below).
- Drives apply transaction and reports apply status.

---
sections.heading: Runtime Config Agent (sidecar thread inside worker process)

sections.body:
- **Desired version** is owned by the control plane (per scope/shard).
- **Config payload** is retrieved by version ID from the Optimization Config Service.
sections.heading: Sources of truth

sections.body:
1. **Version pointer cache (desired version):**
   - Small object: `{scope_key, desired_ocv_id, updated_at}`
   - TTL: 15s (Hosted/Dedicated), configurable in Private
   - Invalidation: change events (when available) + TTL as fallback

2. **Config payload cache (by OCV ID):**
   - Stores the full normalized config payload and a checksum
   - TTL: 10 minutes (payloads are immutable; TTL mostly protects memory)
   - LRU eviction, max size by worker memory budget

3. **Derived settings cache:**
   - Parsed/compiled runtime settings derived from payload (e.g., precomputed batching limits)
   - Evicted alongside payload
sections.heading: Runtime cache layers

sections.body:
- Hosted/Dedicated: runtime receives config change events via internal event stream (best-effort), with polling as fallback.
- Private: polling is always available; event stream is optional depending on installation.

---
sections.heading: Eventing vs polling

sections.body: Workers treat config application as a safe transaction with explicit checkpoints. This prevents mixed or partially applied state within a single worker.
sections.heading: Apply transaction (worker)

sections.body:
- `STABLE(ocv=A)`
- `FETCHING(ocv=B)`
- `STAGING(ocv=B)`
- `COMMITTING(ocv=B)`
- `STABLE(ocv=B)`
- `ROLLING_BACK(from=B,to=A)`

Checkpoints are persisted to local durable storage (host path / ephemeral disk depending on env) so that worker restart resumes safely.
sections.heading: States (persisted)

sections.body:
1. **Detect desired version**
   - If `desired_ocv_id == effective_ocv_id`: no-op
   - If new: transition to `FETCHING`

2. **Fetch config payload by version**
   - GET by `ocv_id` with strong read consistency requirements handled by service
   - Verify checksum and schema version

3. **Local compatibility checks (runtime-level semantic validation)**
   These checks are fast, deterministic, and prevent applying settings that would crash or violate worker invariants. Examples:
   - Quant profile exists for `model_id` and runtime build supports it
   - Batching settings within runtime hard limits (e.g., `max_batch_tokens <= runtime_cap`)
   - Cache toggles are compatible with model architecture (e.g., KV cache required for streaming)

   If checks fail: worker reports `apply_failed` and remains on prior stable version. Control plane gate should halt progression.

4. **Stage changes (no traffic impact yet)**
   - Build derived settings structures
   - Pre-allocate buffers where applicable
   - Prepare cache policy changes (do not invalidate until commit unless required)

5. **Commit (atomic switch of effective config)**
   - Swap effective config pointer to `ocv=B`
   - Apply any required cache invalidation rules
   - Emit `optimization_config_apply_success` with tags

6. **Post-commit stabilization window**
   - Worker monitors immediate internal health signals (e.g., executor errors)
   - If local failures exceed threshold, worker can self-trigger a local rollback to last stable (guardrail; control plane remains source of truth)
sections.heading: Step-by-step

sections.body:
We guarantee atomicity at the **worker level**: a worker either serves entirely with OCV A or OCV B after commit. We do not guarantee cluster-wide atomicity (rollouts are staged by design).

---
sections.heading: Atomicity boundary

sections.body:
The apply pipeline is designed so that repeating any step produces the same outcome:
- Fetching the same immutable version returns identical payload
- Applying a version already applied is a no-op
- A restart resumes from the last checkpoint (does not re-run destructive actions twice)
sections.heading: Idempotency rules

sections.body:
- Duplicate change events
- Polling reads desired version multiple times during rollout
- Worker restart mid-apply
sections.heading: Common retry scenarios

sections.body:
Workers enforce a single-flight apply per `(scope_key, worker_instance)`:
- A per-worker mutex (or async lock) ensures only one apply transaction executes at a time.
- If a rollback request arrives while applying, rollback wins (see Race conditions).

---
sections.heading: Concurrency controls

sections.body: Rollback is implemented as “apply the prior known-good version” and uses the same transaction machinery.
sections.heading: Rollback mechanism

sections.body:
- Control plane changes desired version pointer back to a previous OCV (or to a promoted stable version).
- Control plane emits audit events and a change event.
- Runtime sees desired version revert and applies it.
sections.heading: How rollback is triggered

sections.body:
- Worker follows the apply transaction steps with `desired_ocv_id=A`.
- Cache invalidation is handled carefully:
  - If B enabled aggressive caching and A disables it, we invalidate relevant caches at commit.
  - If B changed batching heuristics only, we avoid full cache clears.
sections.heading: When switching from OCV B back to OCV A

sections.body:
Workers track `last_stable_ocv_id` locally for guardrail rollback. The authoritative “known-good” is owned by the control plane (promotion semantics).

---
sections.heading: “Last known-good” definition

sections.body: A known failure mode is interleaving `apply(B)` and `rollback(A)` leaving a worker in an undefined state.
sections.heading: Concurrent apply and rollback

sections.body:
- Single-flight apply ensures only one transaction runs.
- Desired-version reads are checked at each checkpoint. If desired version changes mid-apply:
  - Abort staging/commit if safe to do so
  - Restart transaction toward latest desired version
- Commit step is guarded by a compare-and-set of `pending_ocv_id` → `effective_ocv_id`.
sections.heading: Mitigations

sections.body:
During canary rollouts, some workers will legitimately run different versions. We must ensure:
- Metrics are always tagged with `config_version` so gates can compare cohorts.
- Router/shard assignment is stable for a request (avoid per-request flapping). We use a deterministic shard function based on `(tenant_id, request_id)` for percentage rollout cohorts.

---
sections.heading: Partial rollout “mixed worker states”

sections.body:
All runtime metrics impacted by optimization settings must include:
- `tenant_id` (or anonymized tenant hash where required)
- `model_id`
- `region`
- `config_version` (effective)
- `rollout_id` (when available)
sections.heading: Required tags

sections.body:
- `runtime_optimization_config_effective_version` (gauge)
- `runtime_optimization_config_apply_success_total` / `_failure_total`
- `runtime_optimization_config_apply_latency_ms` (histogram)
- Request SLO metrics with config tags:
  - `requests_5xx_rate`
  - `request_latency_p95_ms`, `request_latency_p99_ms`
  - `tokens_per_second`, `queue_depth`, `gpu_utilization`
sections.heading: Key metrics emitted by runtime

sections.body:
- `optimization_config.apply.start`
- `optimization_config.apply.commit`
- `optimization_config.apply.fail` (with reason code)
- `optimization_config.rollback.start/commit`
sections.heading: Workers emit structured logs on state transitions

sections.body:
See: `eng-sre/dashboards-and-alerts/optimization-rollout-health-dashboard`.
At minimum, dashboards must support filtering by `config_version` and annotate apply/rollback events.

---
sections.heading: Dashboard expectations

sections.body:
| Failure mode | Symptom | Runtime behavior | Operator expectation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cannot fetch payload | 5xx/timeout to config service | Keep serving with current effective version; retry with backoff | Rollout gate should pause; SRE investigates service health |
| Local compatibility check fails | Worker reports apply failure | Stay on prior stable; emit failure with reason | Fix config or runtime capability; do not progress rollout |
| Crash during apply | Worker restarts | Resume from checkpoint; do not double-apply destructive steps | Apply should eventually converge; rollback remains available |
| Desired version flaps | Multiple changes in short window | Worker applies latest desired; intermediate versions may be skipped | Control plane should enforce cooldowns; Console warns on rapid changes |
| Cache invalidation causes latency spike | p95 increases immediately after commit | Prefer targeted invalidation; allow small transient; emit metric `cache_invalidation_count` | Gate thresholds should account for small transient; rollback if sustained |

---
sections.heading: Failure modes and runtime behavior

sections.body:
- Config fetch and parsing must be off the request critical path.
- Apply operations should not block token generation threads. The Config Agent performs staging and a minimal commit action guarded by a short lock.
- Recommended apply latency targets (per worker):
  - Batching-only changes: p50 < 250ms, p95 < 1s
  - Cache policy changes: p50 < 500ms, p95 < 2s
  - Quant profile switches: model-dependent; typically staged during low traffic and/or requires worker restart in some configurations

---
sections.heading: Performance considerations

sections.body:
- Event stream is enabled; polling is fallback.
- `config_version` may be surfaced in response headers for debugging when account setting `debug_headers=true`.
sections.heading: Hosted + Dedicated

sections.body:
- Polling always works; event stream may be disabled.
- Operators can pin a config version and apply/rollback via installer/Helm/Terraform integration.
- If the private deployment runs with restricted egress, ensure the config service endpoint is available within the private control plane network.

---
sections.heading: Private (VPC/on-prem)

sections.body:
- If you suspect an optimization config regression, follow the runbook: `eng-platform/runbooks/rollback-optimization-config`.
- Runtime team on-call should focus on:
  - Worker apply failures with reason codes
  - Unexpected cache invalidation spikes
  - Any evidence of non-convergence (workers stuck in `STAGING` or oscillating)

---
sections.heading: Operational guidance (runtime-owned)

sections.body:
Runtime reports a normalized reason code to reduce triage time:
- `FETCH_TIMEOUT`
- `FETCH_5XX`
- `SCHEMA_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED`
- `MODEL_NOT_COMPATIBLE`
- `QUANT_PROFILE_NOT_AVAILABLE`
- `BATCHING_LIMIT_EXCEEDS_CAP`
- `CACHE_MODE_UNSUPPORTED`
- `INTERNAL_EXCEPTION`

---
sections.heading: Appendix A: Reason codes for apply failures

sections.body: `{"event":"optimization_config.apply.commit","tenant_id":"tnt_123","model_id":"llama3-70b","region":"us-east-1","from_ocv":"ocv_01J2...A","to_ocv":"ocv_01J2...B","apply_latency_ms":412,"worker_id":"wrk_9f2c"}`
sections.heading: Appendix B: Example log line (structured)

payload.page_title: Granular eviction and adaptive execution patterns for mixed inference workloads

sections.body:
Summary

This document describes the design, operational controls, and runbook for the Granular Eviction and Adaptive Execution Patterns (GEAEP) subsystem in the Redwood serving runtime. GEAEP is a set of runtime techniques that: (1) reduce unnecessary KV-cache evictions, (2) enable per-request execution path selection (fast path vs. accuracy path), and (3) smooth contention across heterogeneous kernel families in the GPU pool. The guidance here is intended for runtime engineers, SREs handling inference incidents, and product teams evaluating cost/latency tradeoffs.

Why this doc exists

- Prior problems addressed: eviction storms during traffic spikes, oscillation between quantized and full-precision kernels, and sudden tail-latency increases for mixed short/long sequences.
- Goals: lower tail latency for short-prefix requests, reduce unnecessary recompute, expose safe knobs for cost-vs-accuracy routing, and provide clear operational steps for triage and rollback.

Design principles

1) Local, demand-driven granularity: evictions and prefetches are controlled per-shard and per-session rather than globally. This avoids thrashing when a single tenant (or bursty bot) requests long sequences.
2) Execution adaptivity: requests carry an execution-hint header that lets the scheduler choose a lightweight kernel (quantized, truncated context, prefix-cached) or the accuracy path (full-precision, full-KV materialization). Default policy is conservative (favor accuracy) unless overridden by explicit cost profile or model-variant rules.
3) Cost-safety guards: automated budget limits and soft-fallbacks prevent runaway cost when adaptivity picks expensive paths.

Key concepts and terminology

- shard-eviction-window: configurable time window used to compute per-shard eviction score.
- per-request execution-hint: request metadata field (execution_hint) with values: fast_path | balanced | accuracy_path.
- eviction-stabilizer: smoothing function that delays eviction decisions when churn is detected.
- kernel-ladder: ordered family of kernels (e.g. q4_8_fast, q8_0_balanced, fp16_full) that the dispatcher may move through for a request.

Configuration reference (example YAML)

runtime_geaep:
  enabled: true
  shard_eviction_window_sec: 60
  eviction_score_threshold: 0.12
  eviction_stabilizer_alpha: 0.6
  execution_hint_defaults:
    short_prefix: fast_path
    long_prefix: balanced
  kernel_ladder:
    - q4_8_fast
    - q8_0_balanced
    - fp16_full
  cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min: 20000
  per_tenant_hard_cap_tokens_per_min: 100000

Explanation of important keys

- eviction_score_threshold: a normalized value [0,1]; shards with score > threshold become candidates for eviction. We tune this to balance memory pressure against recompute cost.
- eviction_stabilizer_alpha: smoothing parameter for exponential moving average used by the stabilizer. Higher = more inertia.
- cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min: safety budget applied to adaptivity decisions; once exhausted, adaptivity falls back to balanced or fast_path depending on flags.

Observability and metrics

Instrument the following metrics (already emitted by ri-runtime v3.8+):
- runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard (gauge, evictions/min)
- runtime.geaep.eviction_candidates (gauge)
- runtime.geaep.prefetch_hits (counter)
- runtime.geaep.execution_path.count{path=fast_path|balanced|accuracy_path} (counter)
- runtime.geaep.kernel_switches.count (counter)
- runtime.kvcache.recompute.tokens_cost (counter)
- runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining (gauge)

Alerting thresholds (suggested)

- P0: runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard > 0.5 for more than 2 minutes AND 99th_latency.service > 800ms for a modeled short-prefix route -> Pager.
- P1: runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining < 10% for 5 minutes -> Page to oncall if impacting cost or SLOs.
- P2: kernel_switches.count rate increases > 5x baseline over 10 minutes with increased tail latencies -> Slack alert to #serving-runtime.

Operational runbook: common incidents

1) Eviction storm (symptoms: sudden spikes in eviction_rate and 99p latency for short requests)

- Owner: serving-runtime oncall.
- Immediate checks:
  1. rictl metrics get runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard --since 15m --top 5
  2. rictl trace find --tag="eviction" --since 10m | head -n 50
  3. Check per-tenant traffic with rictl tenant stats --top 10

- Mitigation steps (fast):
  A. Enable eviction-stabilizer in read-only override: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_stabilizer_override=true --duration=15m
  B. Lower eviction aggressiveness: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_score_threshold=0.20
  C. If issue persists, pin affected shard(s) to no-evict: rictl shard annotate <shard_id> no-evict=true --reason="eviction_storm_mitigate"

- Recovery check: after changes, monitor eviction_rate and short-prefix 99p latency for 10 minutes. If rates drop and latency stabilizes, keep stabilizer enabled and schedule a retrospective.

2) Kernel oscillation (symptoms: frequent kernel_switches, rising GPU queue length, throughput drop)

- Owner: serving-runtime + kernel-team.
- Immediate checks:
  1. runtime.geaep.kernel_switches.count --since 30m by kernel_family
  2. GPU dispatcher queue lengths and occupancy: grafana:GPU/dispatcher/queue_length
  3. Last deploys: ci-cd job checks to see if a kernel rollout coincided with the start time.

- Mitigation steps:
  A. Limit kernel ladder to two levels for the most-affected tenants: rictl config set runtime_geaep.kernel_ladder_override.<tenant_id>='["q8_0_balanced","fp16_full"]' --duration=1h
  B. Throttle adaptivity scoring for the tenant: rictl config set runtime_geaep.adaptivity_alpha_override.<tenant_id>=0.2
  C. If the oscillation started after a kernel rollout, rollback the kernel plugin: rictl kernel rollback <kernel_plugin_name> --to-version <previous-version>

- Recovery check: kernel_switches should fall to baseline and GPU queue length return to normal within 15–30 minutes.

3) Budget exhaustion (symptoms: adaptivity_budget_remaining hits 0 and many requests fall back unexpectedly)

- Owner: serving-runtime + product cost ops.
- Immediate checks:
  1. runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining and per-tenant consumption.
  2. Which routes consumed most tokens: rictl profiling route-consumption --since 1h --top 20

- Mitigation steps:
  A. Temporarily increase cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min for the affected region: rictl config set runtime_geaep.cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min=30000 --region=us-west-2
  B. If spending spike is unexpected, identify and throttle offending route(s) via per-route quotas in the control plane.

Design validation and benchmarking notes

We validated GEAEP on the mixed-workload simulator (see benchmarking suite 'mixed_short_long_2026') with these noteworthy outcomes:
- Short-prefix 99p latency decreased 18–26% when using per-request execution_hint defaulting to fast_path for sequences < 64 tokens.
- Overall token cost increased 4–6% in the balanced test; but with cost-safety budgets enabled, the increase was bounded to under 6%.
- Under synthetic eviction storms, the stabilizer reduced shard-level evictions by 70% at peak.

Configuration rollout checklist

1. Feature flag: geaep.v1 enabled in staging only.
2. Canary: two nodes in us-west-2 with production traffic shadowed (no adaptivity writes). Run for 48 hours.
3. Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 7 days, with SLO gate: short-prefix 99p < 350ms and adaptivity budget utilization < 80%.
4. Post-rollout: schedule 2-week observation period and capture baseline metrics for the next kernel rollout.

Testing and validation tools

- rictl simulate --profile=mixed_short_long --seed=42 --duration=2h --out=./geaep-sim-2027-02
- runtime-bench run --scenario geaep-adaptivity-compare --concurrency 128 --seq-dist short:0.7,long:0.3
- scripts/validate_eviction_stability.py (documentation in repo/runtime/tools/validation.md)

Implementation notes for engineers

- Execution-hint is exposed as an HTTP header X-RI-Execution-Hint and as SDK metadata field execution_hint on the Python/Node SDKs. SDKs will default to balanced when model length is unknown.
- Kernel ladder decisions are made in two stages: (a) soft decision (dispatcher hint) and (b) hard enforcement (kernel plugin selection) at kernel-launch. Both emits traces: trace.tag=">geaep:soft_decision" and ">geaep:kernel_launch".
- Prefetch logic uses a low-priority background queue and will not prefetch across tenant hard-cap boundaries.

Ownership and review cadence

- Author/Primary owner: Aisha Patel (serving-runtime).
- Secondary owner: Jonah Kim (kernel infra).
- Quarterly review: every release cycle (quarterly) the GEAEP config defaults must be reviewed as part of runtime release checklist.

Related artifacts and links

- Simulation results: s3://redwood-inference/benchmarks/geaep/mixed_short_long/2027-02-01/results.csv
- Tooling: repo/runtime/tools/geaep (contains validators and scrubbers)
- Telemetry dashboard: grafana://dashboards/GEAEP-Overview

Appendix: quick commands

- View top eviction shards: rictl metrics get runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard --since 30m --top 10
- Temporarily pin shard to no-evict: rictl shard annotate <shard_id> no-evict=true --duration=30m --reason "triage"
- Adjust threshold: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_score_threshold=0.20 --duration=10m
- Force a kernel ladder override for a tenant: rictl config set runtime_geaep.kernel_ladder_override.<tenant_id>='["q8_0_balanced","fp16_full"]' --duration=1h

If you are a product or solutions engineer reading this and want guidance for choosing the default execution_hint for a customer workload, open a PR on repo/runtime/configs/geaep-defaults.yaml and tag @PriyaSingh for review.

ChangeLog

- 2026-11-15: Initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-12-07: Added budget and alert recommendations after first staging run (reviewers: Jonah Kim).
- 2027-02-03: Clarified kernel ladder enforcement and added rollout checklist (published).
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: KV Cache Memory Layout Overview (Allocator + Compaction)

sections.body:
This page documents the serving runtime’s KV cache memory layout and allocator structures, and describes the compaction-related state machines introduced in runtime 1.22. The goal is to make the KV arena behavior predictable under mixed sequence lengths and bursty churn, while keeping decode throughput stable.

**Audience:** runtime engineers, kernel engineers, SREs debugging tail latency/OOM, and performance engineers updating benchmarks.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- **KV cache:** Per-sequence cached key/value tensors for attention, extended incrementally during decode.
- **Sequence (seq):** A single request stream (chat or completion) tracked by the scheduler.
- **Token position:** Decode step index within a sequence.
- **Page:** Fixed-size allocation unit in the KV arena. Pages are the unit of accounting, relocation, and free-list management.
- **Block:** A logical view of KV storage assigned to a sequence for a contiguous range of token positions; implemented as one or more pages.
- **Arena:** Pre-reserved GPU memory region used for KV pages (per model profile / device).
- **Fragmentation:** Free memory exists but is split across non-adjacent page runs, increasing allocation overhead and increasing the chance of opportunistic eviction/compaction at bad times.

---
sections.heading: Terminology

sections.body:
The KV cache is stored in a GPU-resident arena allocated per device, partitioned into pages.

**Key design constraints:**
1. Allocation must be fast on the decode critical path (O(1) or small constant factors).
2. Relocation (compaction) must be safe during concurrent decode, cancellation, and streaming.
3. The runtime must be able to attribute memory to a seq for eviction decisions and observability.
sections.heading: High-level layout

sections.body:
```
KV Arena (GPU)
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Page 0 | Page 1 | Page 2 | Page 3 | Page 4 | ... | Page N     |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
   ^ used by seq A   ^ free    ^ used by seq B   ^ free

Compaction moves “used” pages to form longer contiguous free runs.
```

---
sections.heading: Diagram (conceptual)

sections.body:
- **Default page size:** 2 MiB (profile-dependent; see configuration section).
- **Alignment:** 256 bytes minimum; page base is aligned to 2 MiB.
- **Rationale:** 2 MiB is a good tradeoff between allocator metadata overhead and relocation granularity; it also plays well with large contiguous copies.
sections.heading: Page size and alignment

sections.body:
A page is a container for KV data plus a small header stored in CPU memory (metadata) and a corresponding lightweight tag stored in GPU memory for debugging/tracing.

**CPU-side page metadata (per page):**
- `page_id` (u32)
- `state` (enum; Free, Allocated, RelocatingSrc, RelocatingDst, Quarantined)
- `owner_seq_id` (u64; 0 for free)
- `owner_layer_range` (small range or profile id)
- `token_span` (start_pos, length)
- `refcount` / `pin_count` (for pinned sessions / in-flight kernels)
- `last_touched_ts` (for eviction heuristics)

**GPU-side tag (optional, debug builds / sampling):**
- `page_id`, `seq_id`, `generation` (to detect stale pointers)
sections.heading: What a page contains

sections.body:
Each sequence maintains a list of blocks describing where its KV lives. Blocks are appended as decode progresses.

**Block fields:**
- `seq_id`
- `start_pos` (token index)
- `length` (tokens)
- `page_run` (start_page, num_pages)
- `layout_profile` (model-specific KV stride and packing)

**Invariant:** For a given seq, blocks are strictly increasing in `start_pos` and non-overlapping.

---
sections.heading: Block view (per sequence)

sections.body:
KV storage is model-profile specific but follows a consistent abstraction:

- KV is stored per layer, per head (or grouped heads), per token position.
- The runtime uses a **layout profile** (resolved at model load) to compute per-token KV bytes and the page fill factor.
sections.heading: KV tensor packing within a page

sections.body:
- `dtype` (fp16/bf16/int8 for quantized KV where supported)
- `head_dim`
- `num_kv_heads`
- `layers_per_arena_group` (some models group layers across arenas)
- `kv_stride_bytes` (bytes per token position per layer-group)
- `pack_mode` (contiguous K then V; or interleaved KV)
sections.heading: A layout profile defines

sections.body:
Given `(page_base, token_pos, layer, kv_head, component)`:
- `offset = token_pos * kv_stride_bytes + layer_offset(layer) + head_offset(kv_head) + component_offset(component)`
- `component` ∈ {K, V}

**Notes:**
- The scheduler treats pages as opaque; only the attention kernels interpret the layout profile.
- Compaction never changes the logical layout; it only moves whole pages (or page runs) and updates block metadata.

---
sections.heading: Addressing function (conceptual)

sections.body:
- **Hosted:** typically one arena per (model, quantization profile, device).
- **Dedicated:** may allocate per pool with higher headroom to reduce eviction pressure.

**Arena fields (CPU):**
- `base_ptr` (GPU VA)
- `page_size_bytes`
- `num_pages`
- `watermarks` (low/high pressure thresholds)
- `feature_flags` (compaction enabled, eviction enabled, debug sampling)
sections.heading: Each GPU device maintains one or more KV arenas

sections.body:
1. **Run-based free list:** tracks contiguous free page runs for fast “best fit within class” allocations.
2. **Bitmap / page state array:** tracks per-page state for correctness checks and fast scanning.

**Allocation path (simplified):**
1. Determine required pages for requested `token_span` growth (rounded up).
2. Attempt to allocate from a free run of sufficient length.
3. If no run available but total free pages is adequate → fragmentation case (signals compaction candidate).
4. If under high pressure and compaction budget exhausted → eviction may be triggered depending on tier/policy.
sections.heading: We maintain two complementary indices

sections.body:
We track fragmentation at the arena level.

**Definitions (used in metrics and guardrails):**
- `free_pages_total`
- `largest_free_run_pages`
- `fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (largest_free_run_pages / max(1, free_pages_total))`
sections.heading: Fragmentation measurement

sections.body:
- 0.0 means all free pages are in one contiguous run.
- Values approaching 1.0 indicate heavy fragmentation.

---
sections.heading: Interpretation

sections.body:
Compaction reduces fragmentation by relocating allocated pages into lower-address regions, consolidating free space into larger contiguous runs.

**Key properties:**
- **Incremental:** bounded by a time/bytes budget to avoid decode stalls.
- **Safe under concurrency:** respects in-flight kernels and cancellation.
- **Observable:** exports bytes moved, time spent, stalls avoided, and correlation exemplars.

Compaction operates at the page granularity (whole pages), not individual tokens.

---
sections.heading: Compaction: design overview

sections.body:
1) **Arena-level compaction controller** (plans work and consumes budget)
2) **Per-page relocation lifecycle** (safe movement and commit)
sections.heading: Compaction is represented by two linked state machines

sections.body:
**States:**
- **Idle:** No compaction planned.
- **Armed:** Fragmentation threshold exceeded; waiting for scheduler phase/budget.
- **Planning:** Identify candidate runs: destination free run (low address) + source allocated pages (high address).
- **Relocating:** Execute relocation steps while budget remains.
- **RebuildingFreeRuns:** Update run lists/bitmaps for newly freed pages.
- **Cooldown:** Brief pause to avoid thrash (hysteresis).
- **Aborted:** Stop due to kill-switch, errors, or pressure changes.

**Transitions (high-level):**
- Idle → Armed when `fragmentation_ratio` > trigger and `free_pages_total` above minimal working set.
- Armed → Planning at scheduler boundary (prefill end, decode batch boundary) when budget granted.
- Relocating → Cooldown when budget consumed or no safe candidates.
- Any → Aborted if kill-switch enabled or correctness guard triggers.
sections.heading: 1) Arena-level compaction controller

sections.body:
Relocation moves a page’s contents from a source page to a destination page.

**States:**
- **Allocated:** Page is owned by a seq.
- **RelocatingSrc:** Source is selected; pinned/refcount checked.
- **RelocatingDst:** Destination reserved and tagged.
- **CopyInFlight:** Copy kernel launched (async).
- **CommitPending:** Await synchronization point where it is safe to update pointers.
- **Committed:** Block metadata updated; destination becomes the new owner.
- **Reclaimable:** Source has no pins; can return to free list.
- **Quarantined:** Used if an error is detected (prevents reuse until inspected).

**Safety rules:**
- A page can only transition to `RelocatingSrc` if `pin_count == 0` (or if pins are from known-safe phases with explicit handoff).
- Commit is performed at a scheduler-managed quiescent point to avoid kernels reading old addresses.
- Cancellation is handled by either (a) finishing relocation then freeing both old metadata and destination if seq ended, or (b) aborting before commit and releasing destination. See bugfix notes in runtime 1.22.1 for edge cases.

---
sections.heading: 2) Per-page relocation lifecycle

sections.body:
Compaction is not allowed to steal unbounded time from decode.

**Budget enforcement** (see ADR: compaction budgeting):
- Budget is granted in **bytes moved** and **wall time** (whichever is hit first).
- The scheduler allocates budget at specific boundaries:
  - After prefill, before entering steady decode batches
  - Between decode micro-batches when queue depth is stable
  - During backpressure handling (optional), to reduce future allocation pressure

**Guideline:** avoid launching compaction copy kernels on the critical path when p99 latency is already elevated unless memory pressure is high.

---
sections.heading: Scheduler integration points

sections.body:
Eviction is separate from compaction but uses the same observability surface.

- Compaction is preferred when total free pages are sufficient but fragmented.
- Eviction is considered when the arena is under pressure (low free pages) or when compaction cannot create a sufficiently large run within budget.

**Tier-aware behavior (summary):**
- Lower-priority tiers are eligible for eviction earlier.
- Pinned sessions (explicit) are protected.
- Prefix-cache pages may be marked preemptible depending on profile.

---
sections.heading: Eviction interaction (tier-aware)

sections.body:
This page documents the “shape” of configuration; exact names may differ by environment.

| Flag / Setting | Default (Hosted) | Default (Dedicated) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `kv.page_size_mib` | 2 | 2 | Profile-dependent; changing requires validation. |
| `kv.compaction.enabled` | true (canary-gated) | true (pool-gated) | Kill-switch overrides. |
| `kv.compaction.fragmentation_trigger` | 0.35 | 0.45 | Dedicated often tolerates more fragmentation due to headroom. |
| `kv.compaction.max_bytes_per_step` | 256MiB | 512MiB | Upper bound per scheduler-granted step. |
| `kv.compaction.max_ms_per_step` | 2ms | 3ms | Target to avoid p99 regressions. |
| `kv.compaction.cooldown_ms` | 50ms | 50ms | Prevent thrashing. |
| `kv.eviction.enabled` | true | true | Policy is tier-aware + LRU by seq. |

**Operational note:** oncall should prefer flipping `kv.compaction.enabled=false` before disabling eviction if correctness is suspected; see runbook for ordering.

---
sections.heading: Configuration (runtime flags)

sections.body:
Metrics and trace spans are mandatory for rollout.

**Core metrics (names standardized elsewhere):**
- `kv_fragmentation_ratio` (gauge)
- `kv_free_pages_total` (gauge)
- `kv_largest_free_run_pages` (gauge)
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_steps_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_aborts_total` (counter)
- `kv_evictions_total{reason,tier}` (counter)

**Tracing:**
- `kv.compaction.plan` span
- `kv.compaction.copy` span (includes bytes, src/dst page ids sampled)
- `kv.compaction.commit` span
- `kv.eviction.select` span

**Required dashboards:**
- Fragmentation ratio over time with p95/p99 latency overlay
- Bytes moved + steps per minute
- Evictions per minute by tier and reason

---
sections.heading: Observability hooks

sections.body:
- A page is owned by at most one seq at a time (`owner_seq_id` is single-valued).
- A block references only pages in `Allocated` or `RelocatingDst` state (during commit).
- No page can be freed while pinned.
- Commit is atomic from the scheduler’s perspective: either the seq sees old pages or new pages, never a partial mix for a given token span.
sections.heading: Invariants

sections.body:
- Quarantine any page involved in a failed relocation until inspected.
- If repeated aborts occur (e.g., >N per minute), automatically reduce compaction aggressiveness and alert.
- If p99 latency increases beyond canary threshold while compaction bytes moved spikes, trigger automated rollback (see SRE guardrails page).

---
sections.heading: Guardrails

sections.body:
**Why move whole pages instead of compacting within a page?**
Page-level movement keeps attention kernels and layout profiles simple and avoids per-token repacking, while still addressing allocator fragmentation (the dominant contributor to tail spikes under churn).

**Does compaction change output quality?**
No. It does not change numeric operations; it only changes where KV resides in GPU memory.

**What’s the most common operational failure mode?**
Aggressive compaction budgets can introduce additional copy work and scheduling interference, showing up as p99 spikes during bursts. The rollout defaults favor stability; tuning should be validated in benchmark-lab and perf-canary.

---
sections.heading: FAQ

sections.body:
- 2026-02-20: Updated state machine definitions; clarified commit/quiescent points; added configuration table defaults by tier.
- 2026-02-03: Added fragmentation ratio definition and allocator index description (run-based + bitmap).
- 2026-01-21: Initial publication for runtime 1.22 compaction rollout docs.

payload.page_title: adaptive-fidelity-orchestration-and-evaluation-checklist-2026

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the Adaptive Fidelity Orchestration pattern we use to balance latency, cost, and output quality in the inference-runtime. It documents the telemetry contract, decision matrix, rollout and evaluation checklist, and emergency rollback procedures used by runtime, scheduling, and ops teams.

Goal

- Enable safe, measurable fidelity degradations (quantization, smaller variants, reduced sampling) to preserve SLOs during pressure events while keeping quality regressions bounded and observable.
- Provide a reproducible evaluation checklist for any fidelity-orchestration rollout or experiment.

Scope

Applies to: hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments using the inference-runtime components: scheduler, kernel-mapper, fallback-router, kv-cache, and telemetry-pipeline. Does NOT include model training or model selection upstream (use model-onboarding docs for that).

Key concepts and vocabulary

- Fidelity action: an operational change that reduces computational work per request (e.g., lower quantization, switch to 8-bit kernel, prune attention heads, reduce beam width, shorten context window).
- Fidelity policy: declarative rules that map runtime signals to fidelity actions. Policies are evaluated in the scheduler and enacted via the fallback-router.
- Fidelity event: telemetry emission when a policy evaluates to a non-default action (see Telemetry Contract).

High-level architecture (text diagram)

inference-api -> request-router -> scheduler -> kernel-mapper -> gpu-dispatcher -> kernels
                                         |
                                         v
                                fallback-router -> model-variant-store
                                         |
                                         v
                                 telemetry-pipeline -> metrics/trace/store

The scheduler consults fidelity policies at decision points (admission, pre-dispatch, warmstart). The fallback-router performs model swaps and quantization-profile changes with KV warm-up hints.

Telemetry contract (mandatory)

Every fidelity action must generate these telemetry events (span-based + metrics):

- execution.fidelity_check (span tag): {policy_id, trigger_signal, evaluated_at, decision}
- execution.fidelity_change (counter): increments when an action is applied (labels: action_type, pool, model_family, rollout_id)
- kernel_selection.hint (gauge): kernel_name selected for request (sampled 1%)
- kernel_latency_ms (histogram): end-to-end kernel latency after action (p50/p95/p99 buckets)
- quality.regression_signal (counter + sample): when offline/online eval detects quality drop > threshold (labels: eval_suite, prompt_set)

Sampling and retention

- Default fidelity_check sampling: 5% (increase to 100% for canaries or error bursts).
- kernel_latency_ms retained for 90 days; fidelity_change events retained 365 days.

Decision matrix (example)

When pool CPU/GPU metrics cross thresholds, follow ordered actions. Each action is additive unless explicitly exclusive in the policy.

| Signal | Threshold | Primary action | Quality guard | Rollback threshold |
|--------|-----------|----------------|---------------|-------------------|
| GPU_util | > 92% over 2m | enable-8bit-kernel | offline eval loss delta < 0.8% | GPU_util < 85% for 5m |
| p95 latency | > target*1.3 | reduce-batch-size (limit concurrency) | p50 latency steady | p95 < target*1.1 |
| queue-depth | > 500 | degrade-fidelity: short-context (truncate 50 tokens) | quality delta < 1.5% | queue-depth < 200 |
| memory_pressure | > 80% | kvcache-evict-older-prefetch | no data loss | memory_pressure < 60% |

Policy format (YAML example)

policy_id: fast_sustain_2026
description: "Reduce compute during sustained high GPU utilization while preserving output quality"
triggers:
  - signal: gpu_util
    operator: ">="
    value: 92
    window: 120s
actions:
  - name: enable_quantized_kernel
    params:
      mode: 8bit
      models: ["gpt-medium-family"]
  - name: kvcache_prefetch_mode
    params: {mode: conservative}
guards:
  - type: offline_eval
    eval_suite: "regression-critical-prompts"

Rollout and evaluation checklist (pre-deployment)

1. Author policy in repo: infra/fidelity-policies/<policy_id>.yaml, include rationale and owner.
2. Unit tests for policy parser and basic simulation of triggers (use fidelity-sim harness).
3. Local simulation: run replay of 24h production trace in sandbox, record cost and eval metrics vs baseline.
4. Canary deploy: select 1% of traffic in one Dedicated pool with 100% telemetry sampling.
5. Run online A/B for 48h: compare key metrics: p95 latency, tokens-per-second, offline eval pass rate.
6. Post-canary review: reviewers must sign off in PR checks and add sign-off tags.
7. Automated gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 48h with health gates at each step.

Health gates (automated)

- p95 latency must not regress > 10% vs baseline for two consecutive windows of 30m.
- quality.regression_signal rate must be <= 0.5x historical rate for the same prompt set for 24h.
- cost-per-token must not increase more than 2% (goal is net decrease).

Emergency rollback procedures

1. Alerting: fidelity-change if rate spikes > 10x baseline for 5m or quality.regression_signal exceeds configured threshold triggers a P1 paging to eng-sre.
2. Automated rollback CLI (useful for oncall):
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwoodctl runtime fidelity suspend --policy fast_sustain_2026 --scope pool:us-west-1-dedicated
redwoodctl runtime fidelity rollback --policy fast_sustain_2026 --to default_profile

3. Manual model swap (if rollback CLI fails): update fallback-router policy to route to model-variant-store:default.

Quality evaluation (offline and online)

- Offline: must run 'regression-critical-prompts' and 'semantic-stability-suite' on 2,000 prompt pairs. Thresholds:
  - semantic-stability delta (BLEU/ROUGE-style proxies) < 0.8%
  - hallucination increase < 0.5% (measured by hallucination-sign detector)
- Online: shadow traffic evaluation with stash/score mode: sample 0.5% of live requests and score against golden answers or human raters.

Owner and contacts

- Policy owner: eng-serving-runtime (Priya N., priya@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler owner: Miguel Santos (miguel@redwood.ai)
- Oncall: eng-sre rotation (see /oncall roster link)

Integrations and operational notes

- Observability: ensure fidelity_change and kernel_latency_ms are exposed as Prometheus metrics and ingested by observability alerting rules.
- Alerts: add a dedicated alert group 'Fidelity Guardrails' with thresholds matching the health gates.
- Audit: every policy change must create an entry in config-audit (timestamp, author, diff).

Acceptance criteria for merging policy PR

- All unit tests pass.
- Canary simulation logs attached and include kernel_latency_ms distributions.
- Reviewer sign-offs from runtime, SRE, and applied-ml teams.
- Rollback playbook references (this doc + runbook link).

Guidance for private deployments

Private deployments often have constrained telemetry. In that case:
- Require 100% local fidelity_check sampling for the canary period.
- Run longer canary windows (72h) before global rollout.
- Default to conservative actions (e.g., reduce-batch-size before quantization) when offline_eval data is limited.

Operational runbook snippets

- To force a specific fidelity action for investigation:
redwoodctl runtime fidelity apply --policy test_investigation --action reduce_context --params '{"tokens":50}' --scope pool:debug-sandbox

- Query recent fidelity events (last 2h):
query-metrics "execution.fidelity_change{pool=\"us-west-1-dedicated\"}" --from now-120m --to now

- Promote a canary policy to global (after sign-off):
1) Ensure automated ramp script is configured in deploy-runner.
2) kubectl apply -f infra/fidelity-policies/fast_sustain_2026.yaml --context=deploy-runner

Appendix: example evaluation table (pass thresholds)

| Evaluation suite | Metric | Baseline | Allowed delta | Pass
|------------------|--------|----------|---------------|------
| regression-critical-prompts | semantic-stability | 0.812 | -0.006 (<=0.8%) | required
| hallucination-smoke | hallucination-rate | 0.045 | +0.0025 (<=0.5%) | required
| latency-sla-proxy | p95 (ms) | 230 | +25 (<=10%) | required

References and related reading

- Runtime telemetry model: ../team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Fidelity containment playbook: ../runbooks/fidelity-containment-and-cost-feedback-playbook-2026
- Kernel autotune playbook: ../profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2025-09-14: initial draft by Priya N.
- 2025-11-02: added offline eval thresholds and canary escalation steps (review: Jordan L.).
- 2026-02-10: formalized telemetry contract and private deployment guidance (review: Zoe K.).

payload.page_title: Lane Gating and Quality Quota Manifest

sections.body:
h1. Lane Gating and Quality Quota Manifest

Short description
This document defines "execution lanes" and the associated quality quota model used by the runtime to enforce per-tenant and per-route fidelity guarantees. It explains interactions with the kernel scheduler, profiling checkpoints, benchmarking guidance, incident runbooks, and rollout controls. The intended audience is runtime architects, scheduler engineers, and oncall SREs.

h2. Overview
Execution lanes are logical channels that group requests by fidelity budget, SLO class, and resource claim characteristics. Lane gating is the policy layer that decides which lane a request is admitted to and what quality (model variant, quantization, prefix-cache usage) may be applied. Quality quotas are time-windowed budgets (tokens/per-minute) that debit based on per-request estimated cost and output fidelity impact.

h2. Key goals
- Maintain 99.95% p50 latency for interactive lanes under normal load.
- Bound cost for bursty tenants via short-term quota windows (default 60s) and long-term smoothing (default 1h).
- Enable graceful fidelity degradation rather than hard rejects during capacity constraints.
- Give operators deterministic knobs to trade latency, quality, and cost.

h2. Definitions
- Execution lane: named string (e.g., "interactive-high", "batch-economy", "slo-critical") with associated admission rules.
- Quality quota: numeric budget assigned per tenant/route that decrements on request admission; refunds or adjustments happen on cancellation/retry.
- Lane lease: ephemeral allocation of kernel credit for a short duration to service a request without additional contention checks.
- Fidelity band: descriptor of allowed model variants / quantization / KV cache usage (e.g., "v1.1-fp16-kvprefetch")

h2. Lane taxonomy (default system lanes)
1. interactive-high
   - SLO: 99% of requests <= 120ms tail-50 across p95 measured at service ingress
   - Fidelity band: high (full model, fp16, no quantized fallback)
   - Admission: low-latency heuristics, warm cache preferred
2. interactive-standard
   - SLO: 99% <= 350ms
   - Fidelity band: standard (quantized variants allowed with quality check)
3. batch-economy
   - SLO: throughput-optimized, 3-5s latency window
   - Fidelity band: aggressive quantization and batching
4. background-guesstimate
   - SLO: best-effort; heavy KV-prefetch and asynchronous recompute allowed

h2. Quality quota math (simplified)
- Each lane has a per-request debit formula: debit = base_cost * length_factor * variant_penalty
- Example coefficients (defaults): base_cost=1.0, length_factor = max(1, tokens/64), variant_penalty = 1.0 for high fidelity, 0.4 for quantized small-weights
- Short window: 60s sliding window; long window: 3600s moving-average
- Refill policy: proportional to subscription tier; burst credit up to 3x refill allowed for sudden spikes (configurable)

h2. Policy examples (YAML-like table)
| lane | short_window_limit | long_window_limit | refill_rate | burst | fidelity_band |
| interactive-high | 1000 | 10000 | 16/s | 3x | full-model:fp16 |
| interactive-standard | 2000 | 20000 | 30/s | 2x | mixed:quantized-primary |
| batch-economy | 50000 | 200000 | 500/s | 1x | quantized-heavy |

h2. Admission flow (high level)
1. Ingress selects initial lane using route metadata and traffic shape.
2. Cost estimation service (estimator) computes expected debit and latency sensitivity score.
3. Lane gating service checks short/long quota; if available, issues a lane lease ticket to the kernel.
4. Kernel scheduler consumes the lane lease, maps to GPU slot, and annotates the request trace with kernel_id and lease_id.
5. On completion, the runtime posts actual metrics back to the quota ledger; ledger adjusts future debits based on realized tokens and quality delta.

h2. Kernel scheduler interactions
- Lane leases are translated into scheduler tickets with a 'soft-reserve' flag. Soft reserves do not preempt guaranteed reservations but speed allocation for time-sensitive lanes.
- The scheduler exposes the following signals used by lane gating:
  - slot_availability_ratio: percentage of GPU SMs free for immediate scheduling
  - kv_cache_hotness_score: expected cache hit probability for request prefix
  - kernel_pressure_index: rolling 30s metric estimating contention
- The kernel supports a 'fidelity-hint' header in the dispatch proto. Allowed values: {best, balanced, economical}. The scheduler may favor compact kernels (faster, less memory) for economical hints.

h2. Telemetry and profiling checkpoints
- Mandatory trace annotations that must be emitted by runtime codepaths:
  - lane.selection (tags: lane_name, debit_est)
  - lane.lease.issue (lease_id, short_window_before, short_window_after)
  - kernel.dispatch (kernel_id, hint, slot_alloc_ms)
  - fidelity.applied (model_variant, quant_bits, kv_prefetch_bytes)
- Profiling playbook: every major lane change requires a two-phase profiling run:
  1. Shadow sampling: 1% of live traffic mirrored to the profiling harness for 2h.
  2. Synthetic ramp: controlled load generator replaying representative request shapes for each lane across three kernel binaries.
- Checkpoint windowing: correlate lane.trace_id across ingress -> gating -> scheduler -> egress. Use TTL-based rollups for cost accounting (recommended TTL: 3h).

h2. Benchmarking guidance
- Benchmarks must include mixed-latency workloads that emulate: short-chat (<=64 tokens), long-infer (>=1024 tokens), and multimodal bursts.
- Use the "lane-mixer" harness to reproduce realistic lane admission pressure. Parameters to sweep:
  - cohort size (1-500 tenants)
  - burstiness (Poisson lambda with bursts from 2x-20x)
  - cache entropy (fraction of unique prefixes)
- Primary metrics to collect: p50/p95/p99 latency per lane, kernel_occupancy, debit-leak (delta between estimated and actual debit).

h2. SLOs and Alerting
- SLO matrix (example):
  - interactive-high: p95 latency <= 200ms; error rate <= 0.1%; debit-overshoot <= 10%
  - interactive-standard: p95 <= 400ms; error rate <= 0.5%; debit-overshoot <= 15%
  - batch-economy: throughput >= target 500 qps; median latency <= 2s
- Alerts:
  - quota-throttle-rate > 1% sustained for 5m -> page oncall-sre
  - kernel-pressure-index > 0.85 -> escalate to runtime-kernel pager
  - debit-estimation-drift > 30% over 15m -> open incident for estimator team

h2. Runbook: lane-imbalance incident (quick steps)
1. Detect: alert fires for lane_throttle_rate > 1% and p95 latency degradation.
2. Triage: check 'lane.lease.issue' traces and ledger short_window_before/after metrics; run quota-dashboard for affected tenant.
3. Short-term mitigation:
   - Temporarily increase refill_rate for critical lanes (CLI: redwood ctl quota override --route <route> --lane interactive-high --delta +50%)
   - Route low-sensitivity traffic to batch-economy using traffic-scripting rules in the routing layer
4. Kill-switch: if kernel_pressure_index > 0.95 and eviction does not relieve pressure, toggle conservative-kernel-mode (runtime flag) to false to enable preemptive degraded kernels.
5. Postmortem: collect profiling snapshot, replay with lane-mixer to validate resolution.

h2. Rollout checklist for lane policy changes
- Local unit tests for quota math and refill behavior
- Shadow deploy gating logic with 2% traffic for 24h
- Run synthetic benchmark with lane-mixer for 6h and compare debit drift
- Stage rollout to one region, monitor SLOs for 48h
- Full rollout with automated canary rollback if p95 increases by >10% or debit-overshoot > 25%

h2. Ownership and contacts
- Owner team: engineering (runtime scheduling)
- Primary owner: Avery Chen (avery.chen@redwood.ai)
- Reviewers: Priya Raman, Carlos Mendez, Linh Tran
- Escalation: runtime-kernel pager (pager duty: #runtime-kernel)

h2. Related pages
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/lane-mixer-harness-manual-2026

h2. Labels
execution-lanes, lane-gating, quota, scheduler, profiling, benchmarking, runbook

h2. Confidentiality: internal

h2. Change log
- 2025-09-10: Draft created by Avery Chen
- 2026-11-02: Clarified debit math, added kernel_pressure_index alert thresholds (Avery Chen)
