payload.page_title: Fidelity Orchestrator — telemetry contract and runbook

sections.body:
SUMMARY
-------
This document defines the Fidelity Orchestrator: a small, horizontally scalable control plane that uses live telemetry to decide kernel selection, execution fidelity, and degradation policies for inference requests. It contains the architecture overview, required telemetry contract (metrics/events), a deterministic decision flow, operational runbook for incidents, rollout checklists, and example policy snippets. The goal is predictable SLO adherence (latency/cost/quality) while enabling safe, measurable degradation across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

AUDIENCE
--------
- Runtime engineers (owners, oncall)
- Kernel/scheduler team
- SRE and Observability
- Product owners for latency/cost tradeoffs

PROBLEM STATEMENT
-----------------
The runtime must route requests to optimal kernel variants and execution fidelities (full precision / quantized / reduced context / cached) without violating SLOs. Decisions must be based on standardized telemetry so they are auditable, testable, and reversible. Historically we saw oscillation when metrics lacked determinism and when fallback policies were underspecified.

COMPONENTS
----------
- fidelity-orchestrator (service name): stateless control plane exposing a gRPC decision API (/v1/decide) and an HTTP health endpoint.
- telemetry-ingest: stream aggregator that normalizes kernel and queue metrics and writes to the telemetry stream used by the orchestrator.
- decision-cache: fast in-memory cache (per-node) to keep recent decision results for identical signatures (TTL 30s).
- policy-store: versioned policy repository (Git-backed) with JSON policy files and canary rollout capability.

ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW
---------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Request arrives at request-router with attributes: model_id, route, token_budget, interactive_flag, tenant_tier, seq_len_estimate.
2) Router forwards request to serving-runtime and asks fidelity-orchestrator: decide(request_signature, current_node_telemetry).
3) Orchestrator evaluates the policy with the telemetry snapshot and returns kernel_hint, exec_fidelity, fallback_chain.
4) Serving runtime applies hint and continues; decision cached locally for matching signatures.

CONTRACT: REQUIRED METRICS & EVENTS
-----------------------------------
All producing services must emit the following keys (metric names are canonical):

- kernel_latency_p50, kernel_latency_p95, kernel_latency_p99 (ms) — per kernel variant, 10s sliding window
- kernel_qps (rps) — per kernel variant
- kvcache_hit_ratio — per model-shard, 1m window
- request_queue_depth — per node, per queue-class
- outstanding_tokens_per_session — gauge
- token_cost_estimate_per_model (nanos) — model-level estimate for cost accounting
- recently_throttled (bool/event) — indicates prior admission throttles in last 30s
- node_cpu_pct, node_gpu_mem_free_mb — node health indicators
- model_quality_regressions (event) — evaluation flag from Optimize that can block aggressive quantization
sections.heading: Flow (simplified)

sections.body:
- Aggregation window: 10s for kernel latencies, 1m for kvcache and qps.
- Max ingestion lag: 5s — orchestrator must tolerate up to 10s stale snapshots but should annotate decisions with snapshot_age.
- Cardinality: metrics must include labels: model_id, kernel_variant, zone, tenant_tier.

DECISION RULES (simplified)
---------------------------
1) If request.interactive_flag == true and token_budget >= baseline_min_tokens (default 16) then prefer low-latency kernels if kernel_latency_p99 < interactive_p99_target (default 150ms) AND node_gpu_mem_free_mb > eviction_threshold (default 800MB).
2) If kvcache_hit_ratio > 0.6 and a cached_execution_variant exists, prefer cached path to reduce per-token cost (tie-breaker: if kernel_qps < kernel_qps_limit).
3) If model_quality_regressions flagged within 24h for model_id, block all aggressive quantization and enforce exec_fidelity == full_precision until cleared.
4) If request is from enterprise tenant_tier and SLA_priority == high, enforce fallback_chain that includes at least 1 alternate region.
5) If node health indicates thermal or memory pressure (node_gpu_mem_free_mb < 400MB OR node_cpu_pct > 90%), select degraded_fidelity (reduce batch-size, smaller kernel, or quantized variant) and set degrade_reason tag.

POLICY EXPRESSIONS
------------------
Policies are stored in policy-store as JSON. Example (illustrative):

{
  "id": "policy/interactive-default/v1",
  "conditions": [
    {"name": "is_interactive", "expr": "request.interactive_flag == true"},
    {"name": "p99_ok", "expr": "telemetry.kernel_latency_p99 < 150"}
  ],
  "action": {"kernel_hint": "kernel-lowlatency-v2", "exec_fidelity": "balanced"},
  "fallback": ["kernel-lowlatency-v1","kernel-quantized-v3"]
}

(The orchestrator enforces a schema; policies that fail validation are rejected by the CI gate.)

TRACE & ANNOTATION CONTRACT
---------------------------
Each decision call must annotate tracing/decision provenance for debugging:
- decision_id (uuid)
- snapshot_age_ms
- telemetry_keys_used (list)
- policy_id
- score_explain (short text: why chosen)

OPERATIONAL SLOS
----------------
- decision_api_p99_latency < 30ms (measured at request-router to orchestrator round-trip)
- decision_service_uptime: 99.95% monthly
- decision_cache_hit_rate >= 40% for common interactive signatures

RUNBOOK: INCIDENTS & MITIGATION
--------------------------------
sections.heading: Telemetry delivery semantics

sections.body:
- Alert A1: decision_api_p99_latency > 50ms for 5m (SEV-2)
- Alert A2: unexpected_jump_in_degradation_rate > 5% in 10m (SEV-1 when > 20% tenant-impact)
- Alert A3: policy-validation-failures during rollout > 1 per deploy (SEV-2)
sections.heading: Detection (automated alerts)

sections.body:
1) Pager to runtime-oncall and kernel-owner (see ownership table below).
2) Run: curl -sS http://fidelity-orchestrator.prod/_health | jq .; check last_reloaded_policy and decision_latency_ms.
3) If decision latency is high: switch router to bypass-orchestrator mode (router flag: --bypass-fidelity). This will pick safe defaults and fall back to serving runtime local heuristics. See section "Bypass mode".
4) If excessive degradation is due to policy change (identified by last_reloaded_policy matching recent commit), rollback policy via policy-store: git revert <policy-commit> and POST /v1/policies/reload.
5) If telemetry missing/stale: restart telemetry-ingest service and inspect ingestion lag (kafka consumer offset). Command: kubectl -n observability logs deploy/telemetry-ingest -c consumer | tail -n 200.
6) Post-incident: create an incident report with traces (decision_id list), affected tenants, and action items.

Bypass mode (safe default, fallthrough)
--------------------------------------
- Behavior: router skips orchestrator and uses serving-runtime heuristics:
  - default_kernel: kernel-lowlatency-safe-v1
  - exec_fidelity: balanced
  - quota_enforcement: unchanged
- Safe rollout: bypass is temporary and logged with reason. Router automatically re-enables orchestrator if decision API healthy for 3 consecutive 10s windows.

OWNERSHIP & CONTACTS
--------------------
- Fidelity Orchestrator service owner: runtime-control-plane (team alias)
- Primary oncall rotation: runtime-sre
- Kernel owner (low-latency kernels): kernel-scheduling team
- Observability: telemetry-platform

CONFIG TABLE (key, default, description)
---------------------------------------
| key | default | description |
| decision_api_timeout_ms | 25 | gRPC client timeout for router -> orchestrator |
| decision_cache_ttl_s | 30 | TTL for local decision cache |
| interactive_p99_target_ms | 150 | interactive p99 latency SLO |
| kvcache_cached_variant_cutoff | 0.6 | min kvcache_hit_ratio to prefer cached path |
| policy_canary_pct | 5 | percent traffic to canary during policy rollout |

ROLLOUT & CHANGE MANAGEMENT
---------------------------
- Policy changes must be checked into policy-store with a PR and two approvers: one from kernel-scheduling and one from runtime-sre.
- Canary rollout: set policy_canary_pct and gradually increase per the automated canary job. Metric gates:
  - no increase in tenant_error_rate > 0.1%
  - decision_api_p99_latency within 10% of baseline
  - degradation_rate < configured baseline + 2%
- Full promotion requires a successful 1h canary with gates passing and manual approval.

BENCHMARK & TESTING PLAN
------------------------
- Unit: mock telemetry harness with synthetic latency and kvcache hit injections.
- Integration: replay of production request signatures in the sandbox using the request-surface-replay tool (see related pages).
- Load test: run mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite against policy variations to measure decision_api_p99 and downstream kernel tail behavior.

SAMPLE POLICY (YAML snippet)
---------------------------
apiVersion: v1
kind: OrchestratorPolicy
metadata:
  id: interactive-default/v1
  author: marin.patel@redwood.ai
spec:
  match:
    interactive: true
  gates:
    - telemetry.kernel_latency_p99 < 150
    - telemetry.node_gpu_mem_free_mb > 800
  action:
    kernel_hint: kernel-lowlatency-v2
    exec_fidelity: balanced

DEBUGGING CHECKLIST
-------------------
1) Inspect decision trace for the request_id: curl "http://tracing.prod/decisions/{decision_id}".
2) Check telemetry snapshot age attached to the decision. If > 10s, prioritize fixing telemetry-ingest.
3) Validate policy against schema: ./tools/policy-validate policy.json
4) Reproduce locally using the sandbox replay tool: ./bin/replay --policy interactive-default/v1 --sample 1000

POST-INCIDENT ACTIONS
---------------------
- Create a corrective PR for missing metric instrumentation.
- Add a unit test to policy CI for any edge-case that caused oscillation.
- Adjust canary gates to include the newly-observed signal if missing.

APPENDIX: EXAMPLE TRACE ANNOTATION (JSON)
----------------------------------------
{
  "decision_id": "uuid-xxxx",
  "policy_id": "policy/interactive-default/v1",
  "snapshot_age_ms": 4200,
  "telemetry_keys_used": ["kernel_latency_p99","kvcache_hit_ratio","node_gpu_mem_free_mb"],
  "score_explain": "selected lowlatency kernel: p99 120ms < 150ms and mem ok"
}

RELATED DOCUMENTS
-----------------
- runtime-execution-cascades-and-soft-fail-synthesis-2028.json (cascading behavior description)
- runtime-observability-data-model-and-traceback-2026.json (telemetry schema and trace links)
- preflight-runtime-certification-and-integration-playbook-2025.json (integration tests and CI gates)

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
---------------
Contributors: Avery Brooks, Diego Alvarez, Sofia Chen, runtime-sre oncall

LAST REVIEW NOTES
-----------------
- 2026-02-03: Added explicit snapshot_age handling and canary gate thresholds (Marin Patel)
- 2025-12-01: Initial draft and CI policy schema examples (Avery Brooks)

payload.page_title: Runtime Execution Quilt: Cross-layer Handoff Patterns and Kernel Contract Reference

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the Execution Quilt concept — a cross-layer catalog of handoff patterns between the request dispatcher, runtime scheduler, kernel selector, and KV cache. It also specifies the kernel contract (inputs, expected invariants, telemetry tags), profiling recipes aligned to each handoff pattern, benchmark integration points, a short release note for the first quilted rollout, and an operator runbook for handoff regressions.

Audience: runtime engineers, scheduler authors, profiler/benchmark owners, oncall, and SRE.

Goals
- Provide a minimal, verifiable contract that kernel implementations must satisfy to be considered compatible with runtime handoffs.
- Enumerate canonical handoff patterns and the expected telemetry envelopes for each (latency slices, tail percentiles, cost counters).
- Prescribe profiling and benchmark steps that map a detected regression to a handoff pattern and candidate kernel faults.
- Offer an operational runbook to identify, triage, and mitigate cross-layer handoff regressions.

Design principles
1) Explicit contracts: each handoff point publishes a small JSON contract blob that contains preconditions and postconditions (see Kernel Contract section).
2) Observability-first: every handoff emits an immutable trace span with standardized tags (see Telemetry section).
3) Small surface area for kernel authors: the contract exposes only deterministic input buffers and a handful of guarded side effects.
4) Incremental rollout: new kernel variants must pass shadow-mode handoffs and a fidelity gate in the benchmark suite before canary.

Kernel Contract (reference)
- contract_id: string (human-readable, e.g., "kv-prefetch-v1")
- inputs: list of input descriptors (type, max_size_tokens, alignment)
- invariants: list of assertions the kernel must preserve (e.g., deterministic kv-cache lookups, no cross-tenant side effects)
- outputs: envelope description (token stream framing, checksum, optional compressed payload)
- error modes: canonical error codes and recommended fallbacks
- telemetry_tags: mandatory tags to be attached to the handoff span
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```
{
  "contract_id": "streaming-attn-compact-v1",
  "inputs": ["kv_snapshot:base64","request_tokens:int[]","session_metadata:map"],
  "invariants": ["kv_snapshot_timestamp <= request_timestamp","no_gpu_buffer_pinning_across_sessions"],
  "outputs": ["token_chunks","final_checksum"],
  "error_modes": ["E_KV_MISS","E_KERNEL_TIMEOUT","E_CONSISTENCY"],
  "telemetry_tags": ["kernel.variant","handshake.duration_ms","kvcache.hits"]
}
```

Handoff patterns (catalog)
1) Fast-path local-kv-prefetch: Dispatcher requests a KV prefetch; kernel must accept a snapshot and return a confirmation handshake within 2ms median. Telemetry: kvcache.prefetch_ms, kvcache.prefetch_size. Fallthrough: on prefetch timeout, runtime proceeds without prefetch and marks the span tag prefetch.fallback=true.

2) Streaming-attention with slice hedging: Kernel consumes slices and emits partial tokens. The scheduler may hedged-dispatch the same request to an alternative kernel if slice latency exceeds threshold. Telemetry: slice.count, hedge.invocations, hedge.vs_primary_latency_ms.

3) Cross-tenant memory reclamation handoff: Kernel indicates an ephemeral memory pressure hint; scheduler coordinates a cooperative eviction and emits sustained backpressure signals. Telemetry: pressure.level, eviction.duration_ms.

4) Quantized-fallback handshake: Kernel advertises quantized_profile id and expected precision; if quality checks fail at output verification stage, runtime triggers a graceful fallback to a higher-precision kernel. Telemetry: quant.profile, verification.fail_count.

Telemetry & Tagging standard
Every handoff must emit a single span named "handoff.<contract_id>" with these tags:
- kernel.variant (string)
- kernel.commit (short sha)
- handoff.duration_ms (integer)
- handoff.stage (one of: prefetch, accept, execute, finalize)
- kvcache.hits (integer)
- request.surface_id (string)
- fidelity.score (float, optional)

Profiling playbook mapped to handoff patterns
- When to use: run this playbook whenever a latency or fidelity regression is localized to the post-dispatch horizon (i.e., after request routing and admission).
- Tools: native tracer (TRACE-RT), kernel microprofiler (kmprof), sampling proxy (shadow-agent), replay harness (req-replay).

Profiling steps (ordered)
1) Reproduce in shadow: enable shadow-mode for the suspect kernel and collect full traces for N=500 requests sampled from the offending cohort.
2) Isolate handoff spans: filter traces for spans named "handoff.*" and sort by handoff.duration_ms 95th percentile.
3) Run kmprof on the top 20 slow handoff traces to collect per-instruction latency and GPU stall regions.
4) Correlate with scheduler telemetry: pull scheduler slot allocations and preemption events for the same time window.
5) Differential trace: replay the same request on a known-good kernel variant and produce a diff report.
6) If kernel microprobes point to memory-copy hot loops, instrument kernel with optional pinned-buffer mode and rerun.

Profiling example command set
- Enable shadow traces: ./opsctl handoff-shadow enable --contract streaming-attn-compact-v1 --duration 2h
- Extract handoff spans: tracer-cli query --span-filter "name:handoff.* AND tag:surface_id=chat_v1" --p95 --out handoff_p95.json
- Run kmprof (GPU): kmprof record --trace-file handoff_p95.json --out kmprof_top20.kmp

Benchmark integration points
- Add a handoff-focused benchmark to the microbenchmark suite (bench/handshake) that exercises: prefetch, slice hedging, quantized fallback, and memory pressure signals.
- Performance matrix: for each kernel variant, report median p50/p95 handoff.duration_ms, handshake success rate, and end-to-end delta vs baseline.
sections.heading: Example (JSON contract blob)

sections.body:
| kernel_variant | p50_handoff_ms | p95_handoff_ms | handshake_success_pct | e2e_delta_ms |
|----------------|----------------|----------------|-----------------------|-------------:|
| streaming-attn-compact-v1 | 1.2 | 6.8 | 99.5 | +3 |
| streaming-attn-compact-v2 | 0.9 | 5.3 | 99.7 | +1 |

Release notes (excerpt): Execution Quilt rollout v0.9.3
- 2026-11-12: Introduced kernel contract enforcement at admission time and new handoff telemetry tags.
- 2026-11-19: Added bench/handshake microbenchmark to CI and a canary gate requiring <10% p95 increase across candidate shards.
- Rollout notes: v0.9.3 was deployed to 10% of traffic for dedicated pools; two regressions (one in quantized-fallback path, one due to ephemeral nvlink contention) were caught by the handoff p95 gate and rolled back before canary expansion.

Runbook: handoff regression triage (operator steps)
1) Detect: alert threshold = 2x baseline p95_handoff_ms for a surface for >=10 minutes.
2) Contain: shift new requests for the surface to fallback route (runtime config: route.fidelity=stable) and enable hedged dispatch disabled for the surface.
3) Collect: run the profiling steps above for 30-60 minutes and upload kmprof artifacts to /artifacts/handoff-regressions/<incident-id>.
4) Mitigate: pin the surface to the previous kernel by contract_id using opsctl: ./opsctl kernel-pin set --surface chat_v1 --contract streaming-attn-compact-v1 --until 2026-11-30
5) Postmortem: publish incident page with root cause, timeframe, and a remediation plan.

Known issues (current list)
- NI-2026-115: Intermittent handshake delay when large kv_snapshot (>4MB serialized) is provided to compact kernels. Workaround: enable incremental-kv-prefetch on large sessions.
- NI-2026-127: Hedge count mismatch between dispatcher and kernel under extreme queueing (observed at >95th percentile load). Mitigation: tune hedge.max_attempts to 1 for vulnerable surfaces.

Open mitigations and action items
1) Introduce an incremental prefetch protocol to split large snapshots; owner: kernel-team; ETA: 2027-01-15.
2) Add handoff p99 to the bench/handshake matrix; owner: perf-suite; ETA: 2026-12-31.
3) Formalize a test harness that simulates NVLink fluctuations and measures handshake success rate; owner: infra-performance; ETA: 2027-02-01.

Operational ownership and links
- Runtime architecture owner: Evelyn Park (evelyn.park@redwood.ai)
- Kernel validation & contract owner: Diego Morales (diego.morales@redwood.ai)
- Benchmark suite owner: Priya Nambiar (priya.nambiar@redwood.ai)

Related pages
- See: runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026 for routing and fallback mappings.
- See: kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026 for prefetch sizing guidance.

Appendix A — Quick-check list for kernel authors (pre-submit)
1) Include a contract_id and attach a small example contract JSON in your PR.
2) Add mandatory telemetry tags to your kernel code paths.
3) Run bench/handshake locally and ensure p95_handoff_ms <= baseline * 1.10.
4) Provide a graceful fallback path (documented error codes).

Appendix B — Short glossary
- Handoff: the deterministic exchange between runtime layers when control for a request transitions to a kernel or other execution unit.
- Contract: immutable descriptor of expected inputs, invariants, outputs, and telemetry for a kernel.
- Hedge: a speculative duplicate dispatch intended to reduce tail latency.

Document history
- 2026-11-02: Initial draft (Amira Chen)
- 2026-11-12: Added release notes and bench integration (reviewers: Diego Morales)
- 2026-12-15: Finalized runbook steps and known issues (published)

payload.page_title: Adaptive KV Coordinator and Eviction Contract

sections.body:
Overview

This document specifies the runtime contract for the Adaptive KV Coordinator (AKC), the eviction policy interface, and the safety guarantees that downstream services (shard-manager, runtime-executor, request-router) rely on. It is intended for runtime engineers, infra SREs, model-serving owners, and private deployment integrators.

Goals

- Define a minimal, implementation-agnostic API for KV cache coordination across shards and variants.
- Provide deterministic eviction semantics under constrained memory pressure to avoid cross-variant nondeterminism.
- Specify telemetry, SLOs, and runtime knobs required for safe rollouts and private deployments.
- Outline a migration path and rollback plan for changing eviction strategies.

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: in-memory KV caches used for model KV caches (attention cache, prefix cache) and request-level prefix caches managed by runtime nodes. Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Non-goal: application-level caching (customer caches outside the runtime) and long-term persistent caches.

Design principles

1. Deterministic eviction ordering. Eviction must be stable given the same sequence of allocation and access signals.
2. Isolated fairness. No tenant or model variant may cause starvation of unrelated workloads on the same GPU node.
3. Observability-first. Every eviction decision emits structured telemetry with reason codes and causal attribution.
4. Configurable conservatism. Default policy is conservative; aggressive policies must be gated and tested.

Contract: API surface

AKC exposes the following endpoints and message types (gRPC/HTTP):

- Allocate(request): request { tenant_id, variant_id, shard_id, bytes_requested, priority_hint } -> response { grant_bytes, lease_id, expiration_ts }
- Touch(lease_id, key_hash, usage_weight): updates last_access and weight for eviction ranking
- Release(lease_id, key_hash): explicit release when caller invalidates a prefix
- EvictionPlan(shard_id): returns ordered list of candidate keys and reason codes (soft/urgent)
- SetPolicy(policy_name, policy_config_yaml): operator API to set node-local policy
- ReportMetrics(summary): push interface for periodic aggregated telemetry

All endpoints must accept and return a deterministic request_id header for trace correlation. The Allocate response must return a stable lease_id that encodes shard and sequencing metadata (opaque to callers but stable for tracing).

Eviction semantics and reason codes

Eviction decisions carry one of the following reason codes (exact strings):

- memory_pressure_soft: invoked when usage > 70% of configured node cache budget
- memory_pressure_urgent: invoked when usage > 95% and soft eviction failed to reduce memory
- tenant_quota_exceeded: tenant has passed its soft quota and lower-priority keys are eligible
- stale_ttl: key TTL expired according to AKC-soft-lease semantics
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
rank = alpha * lru_score + beta * (1/usage_weight) + gamma * tenant_priority_rank

Default constants: alpha=0.6, beta=0.3, gamma=0.1. Policy configs may tune constants within safe ranges documented later.

Safety and determinism guarantees

1. Given identical sequences of Allocate/Touch/Release and identical policy configs, the eviction order must be identical across restarts within a shard. Implementations must persist minimal sequence markers (e.g., per-shard monotonic counters) to ensure ordering is reproducible during graceful restart.
2. During a split/merge of shards, AKC emits a planned migration manifest with: old_shard_id -> [new_shard_ids], keys_moved_estimate, expected_live_leases. Migration must be annotated with a migration_id and planned_cutover_ts.
3. Rollbacks: Any policy change applied via SetPolicy must support an automatic rollback if the per-minute eviction_rate increases by > 3x and tail_latency_spike > 1.5x within a 15-minute window.

Telemetry requirements (minimum)

Every node running AKC must export these metrics at 10s granularity:

- akc.evictions.count (labels: reason, shard_id, tenant_id)
- akc.allocations.granted_bytes_total (labels: shard_id, tenant_id)
- akc.leases.active_count (labels: shard_id)
- akc.eviction_rate_per_minute (shard_id)
- akc.tail_rehydration_latency_p95 (shard_id)

Structured logs for each eviction event must include: event_ts, shard_id, tenant_id, variant_id, key_hash_prefix, reason, rank_score, pre_eviction_memory_usage, post_eviction_memory_usage, trace_id. Logs must be JSON-lines and sparse-sampled at 1% for full detail and 100% for reason=memory_pressure_urgent.

SLOs and thresholds

- Rehydration latency: 95th percentile rehydration latency for evicted keys should be < 120ms for hosted; < 250ms for dedicated; < 350ms for private baseline.
- Eviction impact: < 0.5% increase in model output error rate (measured by the eval harness) attributable to eviction-driven rehydration per rolling hour window.
- Eviction rate: soft evictions should not exceed 1% of allocations per minute under normal traffic (95th)

Operator controls and safe rollout checklist

1. Staged rollout: apply policy changes to non-prod, small canary pool (1% nodes), medium canary (10%), ramp to 50% with a 24hr observation window, then 100% with 72hr monitoring.
2. Monitor: akc.evictions.count, tail_rehydration_latency_p95, model-quality-regression alerts, and per-tenant error budgets.
3. Abort criteria: any of the following triggers automatic rollback and operator paging:
   a. tail_rehydration_latency_p95 > configured_threshold for two consecutive windows
   b. eviction_rate_per_minute increases > 3x baseline AND model-quality-regression alert fires
   c. tenant_quota_exceeded events affecting > 5% of tenants in 30 minutes
4. Post-rollback diagnostics: collect snapshot of eviction logs, in-memory lease map, and allocation histogram; create postmortem within 48 hours.

Policy configuration example (YAML)

policy_name: conservative_default
nodescope: node-local
constants:
  alpha: 0.6
  beta: 0.3
  gamma: 0.1
soft_threshold_pct: 70
urgent_threshold_pct: 95
tenant_quota_policies:
  default_soft_quota_bytes: 1073741824 # 1GiB
  tenant_priority_overrides: {}

Implementation guidance and pitfalls

- Do persist only compact sequence markers for determinism; avoid full key persistence (heavy).
- Prefer lease-based short expirations to hard deletes to allow reconstructable state during recovery.
- Beware of clock skews when computing expiration_ts; use monotonic counters combined with wall-clock epoch.
- During preemption (GPU eviction), AKC must admit a transient fudge window: grace_window_ms = 5000 where leases remain valid but marked at risk.

Migration and versioning plan

1. Versioned policy schemas: store policy schema version in policy_config_yaml and reject SetPolicy requests with unknown schema_version unless force flag is set.
2. Two-phase migration for major changes: (a) deploy code with both vN and vN+1 algorithm active behind feature flag; (b) run canary traffic comparing deterministic eviction ordering; (c) flip flag when stability metrics pass.

Checklist for private/on-prem deployments

- Ensure admin exposes SetPolicy over authenticated channel (mTLS + role-based check).
- Default thresholds relaxed: soft_threshold_pct=80, urgent_threshold_pct=98.
- Require customers to opt in to automatic rollback agent or provide an operator contact list.

Open questions and future work

- Explore cross-node cooperative eviction for hot-key de-duplication when model variants share large prefixes.
- Evaluate ML-driven ranking that replaces the alpha/beta/gamma linear model while retaining determinism guarantees.

Appendix: quick CLI examples
sections.heading: Priority ranking formula (default conservative)

sections.body: $ akcctl allocate --tenant t123 --variant v2 --shard s4 --bytes 4194304 --priority hint=interactive
sections.heading: Request 4MiB lease

sections.body: $ akcctl eviction-plan --shard s4 | jq .
sections.heading: Inspect eviction plan for shard s4

sections.body:
$ akcctl set-policy --policy-file conservative.yaml --schema-version 1

Owners and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-kernel team)
- Secondary: eng-infra (gpu-fleet team)
- Pager: runtime-sre rota (oncall page)

payload.page_title: Execution Stability Certification Protocol

sections.body:
Overview

This document specifies the Execution Stability Certification Protocol (ESCP): a repeatable, automated acceptance process that a runtime feature or kernel rollout must pass before being enabled for canary or production traffic. The goal is to provide deterministic gates for latency, error-rate, resource-safety, and downgrade behaviour across model variants and quantization profiles.

Goals

- Provide a short, reproducible certification path for runtime features and kernel variants.
- Ensure rollouts preserve customer-facing SLOs and do not materially increase operator toil.
- Capture behavioural contracts for fallbacks, KV cache consistency, and preemption semantics.

Scope

- Applies to: kernel releases, scheduler policy changes, KV cache algorithm changes, preemption/hothand-off logic, quantization rollout candidates.
- Excludes: experimental lab-only kernels flagged "sandbox" (see Appendix C for sandbox tagging conventions).

Acceptance criteria (table)

| Class | Metric | Gate | Measurement window |
|-------|--------|------|--------------------|
| Latency | runtime.request_latency.p95 | <= 2x baseline or absolute 1200ms (whichever lower) | 1h steady-state under canonical load |
| Error rate | runtime.request_error_rate | <= baseline + 0.1% absolute | 1h |
| Kernel stalls | kernel.hang_count | 0 detected events per 24h projected | measured during stress and 1h soak |
| KV cache correctness | kvcache.consistency_failures | 0 | end-to-end replay with golden trace |
| Resource safety | gpu.memory_exceed_events | 0 | stress profiling run |
| Degradation fidelity | degrade.fidelity_drop | no more than 5% of requests fall to lower fidelity erroneously | 2h soak |

Certification stages (high level)

1. Pre-cert: unit and integration tests; smoke benchmark on microbenchmark suite.
2. Local soak: run on single-node lab with synthetic traffic matching target cohort (sequence length distribution, token mix). Validate p50/p95 and basic telemetry.
3. Stress test: fault-injection and resource-constrained runs (OOM, NVLink flakiness, network jitter). Run soak >= 2h and track kernel stall signals.
4. Shadow canary: mirror 1–5% production traffic (no write-path) for 24h; compare divergence metrics.
5. Canary rollout: progressive, 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automatic rollback on gating violations.

Test harness and commands

- Harness: runtime-certify (internal test harness). Key flags:
  - --trace-corpus <path>   (replay corpus of real requests)
  - --kernel-variant <name>
  - --model-profile <json>
  - --soak-duration <minutes>
  - --stress-injector (enable fault injection)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: $ runtime-certify --trace-corpus traces/q2-webchat-8k.json --kernel-variant maelstrom-v2 --model-profile profiles/longform-8k.json --soak-duration 120 --stress-injector
sections.heading: Example run

sections.body:
model_profile:
  name: longform-8k
  avg_sequence_length: "3700"
  spike_percentile_95: "7800"
  concurrency_shape: "poisson"
  kvcache_enabled: "true"

Observability gating (signals to stream to gating engine)

- Latency: runtime.request_latency.{p50,p95,p99}
- Error: runtime.request_error_rate
- Kernel: kernel.queue_depth, kernel.active_waves, kernel.hang_count
- Memory: gpu.memory_usage_pct, gpu.vram_alloc_failures
- KV cache: kvcache.hits, kvcache.misses, kvcache.consistency_failures
- Fidelity: degrade.fidelity_drop, degrade.unexpected_falls

Gating thresholds are codified in the certification engine. Any threshold exceedance triggers an automated abort and alerts on-call.

Rollback and mitigation checklist

1. Immediately route traffic away using tiered-fallback routing to fallback-kernel (configured in routing manifest).
2. If stall pattern observed, trigger kernel-snapshot and collect live-traces: /ops/tools/collect-kernel-snapshot --target <node>
3. If KV inconsistency detected, snapshot replicas, pause rollouts, and engage DB team for trace reconciliation.
4. For memory pressure, disable the variant and escalate to infra; append nodes to dedicated-gpu-pool for burst capacity.

Ownership and contacts

- Certification owner: Sofia Patel (runtime stability, @sophiap)
- Kernel engineering: Marco Chen (@mchen)
- Scheduler team lead: Priya Iyer (@priya)
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood-inference.com

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)

- [ ] Automated tests green for kernel and scheduler policy
- [ ] Benchmark harness: 90th percentile runtime against baseline measured and stored in bench-db
- [ ] Telemetry mappings reviewed and mapped to gating engine
- [ ] Runbook updated with new signal names and escalation steps
- [ ] Reviewers signoff

Operational runbook excerpt (for oncall)

1. Observe: check runtime.request_latency.p95 and kernel.hang_count; if either spikes beyond gate, mark deployment paused.
2. Collect: runtime-certify --collect-trace --deployment <id>
3. Mitigate: enable fallback route, reduce concurrency admission using admission-controller set --target-concurrency <n>
4. Escalate: if KV failures present, page storage@redwood-inference with tag "kv-inconsistency" and attach trace id.

Appendix A — Example benchmark scenario (table)

| Scenario | Concurrency | Avg seq len | Warm cache | Ramp |
|---------|-------------:|------------:|-----------:|-----|
| baseline | 50 | 300 | yes | 10m |
| peak-test | 200 | 2,500 | mixed | 30m |

Appendix B — Known pitfalls and mitigations

- Non-deterministic quantized kernels: ensure bitwise-compatibility tests run for 1000 traces; if divergence > 0.2% fail.
- NVLink transient throttling: include network jitter injector in stress tests; add compensating retry logic in dispatcher.
- Replay corpus bias: rotate corpora monthly and sample by traffic cohorts to avoid overfitting to a single client pattern.

Appendix C — Tagging and metadata for sandbox kernels

- sandbox:true (disallowed for certification)
- stability_level: experimental|beta|stable
- required_metadata: changelist-id, kernel-binary-hash, compatible-model-ids

Related artifacts

- Bench DB: bench-db.prod.redwood (benchmarks are stored as time-series snapshots)
- Certification engine repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/cert-engine
- Telemetry mapping spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/observability-adapter-sidecar-design-manual-2026

Document history

- 2026-03-10: created by Sofia Patel
- 2026-05-02: stress-injector section added (reviewers: Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-07-12: expanded failure modes and rollback checklist

payload.page_title: Accelerator ABI and Driver Graceful Degradation ADR

sections.body:
Summary

This ADR defines the Accelerator ABI (application binary interface) and the runtime-side driver graceful-degradation policy for heterogeneous accelerator fleets (GPU, TPU-like ASICs, and vendor-provided inference accelerators). The goal is a small, well-specified handshake and capability set that: 1) allows the runtime to negotiate performance/precision tradeoffs with device drivers; 2) exposes a deterministic degradation path when an accelerator cannot satisfy requested guarantees; and 3) provides operational signals for capacity, thermal, and error states so higher layers (routing, fallback) can make policy decisions.

Context and motivation

Redwood's serving runtime runs across mixed hardware: cloud GPUs with different memory/compute, vendor inference chips with quantization-aware runtimes, and experimental on-prem ASICs for Private deployments. Historically each driver exposed a different surface (promises about sequence-length limits, supported quantization, KV cache semantics), which led to fragile fallbacks and silent quality regressions. Operations has observed incidents where a node reported "healthy" but silently served half-precision tensors, creating subtle hallucination regressions in downstream evals. We need a minimal ABI and a deterministic downgrade model so the orchestration and routing layers can react before customer-visible quality drops.

Decision (what we are adopting)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Accelerator ABI (driver runtime surface)
- A JSON capability manifest returned during driver handshake with these required fields: vendor, model, memory_bytes, peak_fp32_throughput, supported_precisions (list), max_sequence_length, kv_cache_model (none|keyseg|segmented), supported_quant_modes (list), fail_modes (list of canonical failure codes).
- A gRPC control channel for health + telemetry that emits structured events: THERMAL_WARNING, MEMORY_PRESSURE, DRIVER_DEGRADATION(start/end), ARTIFACT_ERRORS. Events include numeric fields (temp_celsius, available_bytes, eviction_count).
- Deterministic downgrade functions exposed by drivers: get_degradation_path(requested_precision) -> ordered list of fallback precisions and a max-acceptable-seq-length for each step.

2) Graceful-degradation policy (runtime orchestration expectations)
- If a driver indicates DRIVER_DEGRADATION or memory pressure that will affect >P% of requests in next T seconds, the runtime must:
  a) Mark node as "degrading" and emit a metric (accelerator.node.degradation{reason}).
  b) For new requests, consult degradation path and either re-route to compatible node, fall back to a quantized variant, or invoke a lower-fidelity model per client policy.
  c) For in-flight requests, attempt best-effort KV-preserving re-execution (see runbook) but avoid silent precision demotion unless explicitly allowed by the tenant's model policy.

Rationale

- Small manifest + events provide actionable signals without locking in per-vendor RPCs.
- Centralizing downgrade logic in drivers avoids guessing behavior and ensures the runtime can reason about end-to-end effects (e.g., seq length vs precision tradeoff).
- Separating "allowed by tenant policy" from automatic demotion prevents silent regressions for customers with strict fidelity requirements.

Alternatives considered

1) Do nothing / keep vendor-specific surfaces
   - Pros: no immediate engineering cost
   - Cons: repeated incidents, unpredictable fallbacks, poor observability for quality regressions (rejected).

2) Full feature-rich driver RPC (rich schema for every kernel)
   - Pros: maximum expressivity
   - Cons: long vendor integration time, brittle across versions (rejected).

3) Runtime-only heuristic demotion (runtime interprets raw metrics and decides)
   - Pros: driver-agnostic
   - Cons: wrong assumptions across devices; drivers have the ground truth (rejected).

Implementation specification

1) Manifest schema (JSON example)
{
  "vendor": "string",
  "device_model": "string",
  "memory_bytes": 68719476736,
  "peak_fp32_throughput": 12000.0,
  "supported_precisions": ["fp32","fp16","int8*"],
  "max_sequence_length": 4096,
  "kv_cache_model": "segmented",
  "supported_quant_modes": ["static8","dynamic8","awq"],
  "fail_modes": ["OOM","THERMAL","DRIVER_FAULT"]
}

2) Control channel: gRPC proto (summary)
- Service: AcceleratorControl
- RPCs: GetManifest(), StreamEvents(stream Event) -> ack, SetThrottle(level) -> ack
- Event structure: {timestamp_ms, node_id, code, numeric_map, text}

3) Degradation API (driver-side function)
- get_degradation_path(requested_precision: string, requested_sequence: int) -> list of {precision, max_sequence_length, estimated_throughput_ratio}

Operational runbook (short)
sections.heading: We adopt a two-part contract

sections.body:
1) Event THERMAL_WARNING with temp_celsius > 85 for 30s -> put node into read-only drain and notify SRE.
2) DRIVER_DEGRADATION with predicted_available_bytes < requested_memory -> mark degrading, reduce offerable concurrency by 50% and trigger rescheduling.
sections.heading: Triggers and immediate actions

sections.body:
1) For transient thermal events: verify cooling system, evict long-running ephemeral jobs, restart driver process if required.
2) For persistent artifact errors: collect driver logs / dmesg, escalate to vendor with manifest and event stream.

Routing & API implications

- API layer must include these fields in the request envelope: preferred_fidelity (strict|best-effort|cost-optimized) and allow_demote boolean.
- Default tenant policy: preferred_fidelity=best-effort, allow_demote=false. Allowing demote requires explicit opt-in by the customer and is surfaced in Console settings.

Testing and acceptance criteria

- Unit: manifest parsing, event handling, degradation-path evaluation.
- Integration: simulate driver events (thermal, OOM) in testbed and assert runtime re-routes or rejects per tenant policy.
- Quality regression: run prompt-suite CI (refer to prompt-suite-ci-contract-testing-guidelines) before and after simulated demotion; metrics: BLEU/ROUGE analogs and hallucination rate must not regress beyond tenant thresholds.

Metrics to monitor

- accelerator.node.degradation.count by code
- accelerator.request.demoted.count by tenant and model
- end_to_end_quality_regressions.per_model (linked to evals)
- routing_fallbacks.per_minute

Rollout plan

1) Stage 0: Spec review and vendor alignment (2 weeks).
2) Stage 1: Driver shim implementation for two vendor drivers and testbed integration (6 weeks).
3) Stage 2: Runtime support (handshake, event processing, routing changes) in canary (4 weeks).
4) Stage 3: Tenant opt-in on Dedicated and Private (2 weeks).
5) Stage 4: Full launch for Hosted (after 8 weeks of canary stability).

Owners and contacts

- Design author: Michael Chen (runtime team)
- Driver integration lead: Nadia Alvarez (kernel & drivers)
- SRE contact: Priya Singh
- Product liaison: Daniel Romero

Open questions and future work

- How to represent approximate numeric fidelity (e.g., AWQ variants with mixed blocks)? We propose a small extension to the manifest to include per-layer fidelity profiles in a later ADR.
- Should the runtime be allowed to force demotion for system safety (e.g., to avoid cascading OOMs)? Current decision: only when "system_safety" flag present in tenant policy (requires legal/product sign-off).

Appendix A: Example degradation path table

| requested_precision | step | fallback_precision | max_seq | throughput_ratio | notes |
|---------------------|------|--------------------|---------|------------------|-------|
| fp32                | 0    | fp32               | 4096    | 1.0              | native |
| fp32                | 1    | fp16               | 4096    | 0.65             | reduced numerical headroom |
| fp32                | 2    | int8               | 2048    | 0.35             | quantized; requires calibration |

Appendix B: Example tenant request headers (JSON)
{
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "model": "redwood-base-13b",
  "preferred_fidelity": "best-effort",
  "allow_demote": false
}

Related documents

- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026.json
- architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026.json

Revision history

- 2026-02-18: Drafted by Michael Chen.
- 2026-03-05: Reviewed with drivers team; updated event schema and rollout plan.

payload.page_title: Graceful Fidelity Staircase and Degradation Modes

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the "graceful fidelity staircase": a deliberate, observable sequence of degradation steps the serving runtime may take when capacity, latency, or cost constraints demand reduced resource usage or model fidelity. The staircase is intended to preserve availability and SLOs while minimizing user-visible quality regressions.

Goals
- Provide a single, auditable decision model for runtime-initiated fidelity changes.
- Make each degradation step reversible and safely testable in canaries.
- Tie telemetry signals and SLO thresholds to explicit rollback and escalation actions.
- Standardize operator runbooks and automation hooks for fidelity-layer transitions.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private runtime deployments managed by Redwood inference runtime components (inference-router, batch-coordinator, kernel-proxy, kv-cache-daemon).
- Non-goal: this doc does not prescribe model-specific prompt transforms or application-level fallbacks (those belong to application owners).

Fidelity layers (catalog)

The runtime uses discrete layers (L0..L4) ordered from highest fidelity (L0) to lowest (L4). Each layer is described with expected quality impact, components affected, SLO target adjustment, and typical triggers.

| Layer | Short name | Effect on quality | Components impacted | Typical trigger | Estimated cost delta |
|-------|------------|-------------------|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| L0 | Full fidelity | No change in model output or decoding | Serving runtime: normal routing, full KV cache, quantization disabled | Healthy cluster, nominal load | 0% |
| L1 | Cache-prefill | Slightly faster responses for repeated prefixes; minimal quality change | kv-cache-daemon more aggressively serves prefixes; prefix prefetch enabled | Temporary tail-latency spikes | -5% |
| L2 | Batching+subscription | Minor increase in p50 latency and slight beam diversity loss | batch-coordinator increases target batch size; elastic batching active | Moderate sustained load, cost optimization window | -12% |
| L3 | Quantized runtime | Small quality regressions for some prompts; large cost savings | kernel-proxy switches to 4/8-bit kernels, evap pruning of KV | Cost-driven or capacity-constrained (70%+ GPU utilization) | -35% |
| L4 | Model-variant fallback | Noticeable fidelity change (smaller model variant) | inference-router routes to smaller variants or distilled models | Emergency capacity shortages or region outage | -60% |

Operational rules and decision graph

- The runtime evaluates the decision graph every 15s. Inputs: cluster utilization (GPU/CPU/mem), tail latency (p99), error rate, reserve capacity fraction, and cost budget signal.
- Hard SLO breaches (p99 > SLO*1.5 for >2m) trigger immediate protective steps: stop accepting new long-context requests and escalate to oncall.
- Soft pressure (sustained util > 65% for 10m) enters the staircase starting at L1 and progresses no more than one layer per 5m unless an emergency threshold is crossed.
- Rollback policy: a layer transition is reversed if KPIs (p99, error rate, avg tokens/sec) return to within safe margins for 3 consecutive evaluation windows (3x15s).

Mapping to runtime components (concrete)

- inference-router: implements routing rules and model-variant switching. Config keys: router.fidelity_stepback.enabled, router.max_fallback_percent.
- batch-coordinator: controls target_batch_size and dynamic_batch_window. Config keys: batch.target_size_hint, batch.max_latency_ms.
- kernel-proxy: holds kernel selection table and quantization profiles. Config keys: kernel.q_profile, kernel.fallback_sequence.
- kv-cache-daemon: controls prefix caching TTL and prefetch heuristics. Config keys: kv.prefix_ttl_ms, kv.prefetch_enabled.

Example config fragment (YAML)

fidelity_staircase:
  evaluation_interval_s: 15
  max_progress_per_window: 1
  layers:
    - { name: L1, action: kv.prefetch:true, priority: 10 }
    - { name: L2, action: batch.target_size_hint:32, priority: 20 }
    - { name: L3, action: kernel.q_profile:4bit, priority: 30 }
    - { name: L4, action: router.model_variant:compact-v2, priority: 40 }

Note: YAML above is a human-readable excerpt. The runtime operator objects accept the same keys under runtime.feature_flags.fidelity_staircase in the configuration API.

SLOs, thresholds and concrete numeric examples

- Global request SLO (example): p99_gen_latency <= 750ms, availability >= 99.95%.
- Emergency thresholds (example): p99_gen_latency > 2250ms for 2 minutes => escalate and advance staircase by 2 layers (skip L1).
- Cost window trigger: projected token-cost > budget_weekly * 1.12 => evaluate L3/L4 if utilization > 70%.

Escalation and human-in-the-loop steps

1) Automated action: runtime advances staircase layer (or applies targeted action). All changes are annotated in the decision-trace log with correlation ID and owner (automation).
2) Pager: if p99 remains > SLO*1.2 after 3 minutes, send page to inference-oncall with tag "fidelity-change".
3) Oncall procedure: follow the Runtime Fidelity Triage (see Runbook section). If human rollback is required, use the operator CLI: redwood-runtime fidelity rollback --correlation-id <id>.

Runbook: Runtime Fidelity Triage (for oncall)

1. Observe: open /dashboards/runtime/fidelity-overview, filter by model and region. Confirm the active layer and recent layer transitions.
2. Verify signals: GPUs (utilization), host memory, p99, error rate, KV hit ratio.
3. If layer was automated and KPIs improved: monitor for 15 minutes and allow automatic rollback.
4. If KPIs worsen or error rate increases > 3% absolute after a layer transition: immediately roll back one layer and page the runtime-owner.
5. If rollback fails or cannot restore SLOs: trigger incident and escalate to platform-incident channel.

Example CLI snippets
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: redwood-runtime status --model my-chat --region us-west-2 --fields fidelity,correlation_id
sections.heading: show current fidelity status

sections.body: redwood-runtime fidelity rollback --correlation-id 2026-06-10-abc123 --reason "rollback test"
sections.heading: force rollback

sections.body:
redwood-runtime canary create --target cluster:canary-usw --override kernel.q_profile=4bit --duration 30m

Telemetry, alerts and annotation conventions

- Decision-trace: every automated fidelity decision emits a decision-trace event (trace_id: string) with fields: from_layer, to_layer, reason, metrics_snapshot, triggered_by (auto/manual).
- Alert: fidelity-layer-progression-excessive fires when more than 3 layer changes happen within 10 minutes for the same model/region. Severity: P2.
- Dashboards: fidelity_overview (per-tenant), fidelity_latency_heatmap (cross model).

Playbook for reproducing and validating quality impact

1) Record baseline: capture 1000 representative requests from production (anonymized) using request-proxy replay.
2) Run A/B replay: replay corpus to L0 and L3 in the sandbox runtime and collect response diffs.
3) Metrics to compute: token-wise similarity (BLEU/ROUGE not ideal for chat; use embedding-similarity with cosine threshold), function-call fidelity, hallucination rate on a curated prompt set.
4) Quality gate: if embedding-similarity mean < 0.92 or hallucination increase > 1.5x, mark L3 as requiring additional tuning (quant profile or reduced batch size).

Safety and rollout checklist (pre-canary)

- Add unit tests for decision-graph transitions (simulate triggers).
- Create traffic mirroring rule for canary.
- Ensure canary cluster has at least 2x expected memory headroom for quantized kernels.
- Create evaluation prompt set and automated comparator job.

Ownership and contacts

- Runtime fidelity automation owner: Maya Chen (runtime-core).
- Kernel & quantization contact: Arjun Patel (runtime-kernel).
- Oncall channel: #oncall-runtime, Incident runbook link: /oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/runtime-fidelity-incident-template.

Appendix: short glossary

- Fidelity staircase: ordered set of runtime degradation actions applied to reduce resource usage or preserve availability.
- Decision-trace: structured event emitted for every automated fidelity decision.

Appendix: minimal experiment matrix (CSV-ready)

scenario,layer,metric,baseline,target
baseline,L0,p99,600,<=750
sustained-load,L2,p99,700,<=900
quantized,L3,embedding_mean,0.95,>=0.92
model-fallback,L4,availability,99.99,>=99.9

References and related reading

- See runtime-architecture/observability-driven-runtime-refinement-playbook-2027 for telemetry signal definitions.
- See kernel-and-scheduling/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026 for quant-specific guidance.

Document history

- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-03-02: Added CLI examples and escalation thresholds (Arjun Patel review).
- 2026-06-10: Finalized rollback policy and canary checklist (Sofia Alvarez review).

payload.page_title: Deterministic Inference Mode: Reproducibility Spec & Runbook

sections.body: This page defines the "Deterministic Inference Mode" (DIM): a configuration and operational contract that provides reproducible token output and execution traces across repeated inference runs for a pinned model variant and configuration. DIM is intended for debugging, eval reproducibility, and regression investigation where bit-for-bit repeatability (within documented tolerances) is required.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a single switchable runtime mode (global or per-route) that reduces nondeterminism sources across scheduler, kernels, and model IO.
- Enumerate required kernel/runtime properties and configuration knobs to enable reproducible outputs for common models (decoder-only, encoder-decoder, multimodal pipelines).
- Provide an operator runbook for enabling DIM in canary and production, including telemetry, verification tests, and rollback criteria.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- DIM is not a substitute for formal cryptographic determinism across heterogeneous hardware families (we document hardware compatibility and limits).
- DIM does not freeze model weights; model version pinning remains required for reproducibility.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Deterministic Inference Mode (DIM): a set of runtime and kernel settings plus input seeding rules intended to make repeated calls with identical inputs and model version produce the same token sequence and internal trace signatures.
- Trace signature: a compact hash synthesized from key telemetry points (request_id, model_version, RNG seeds, kernel checksums, kvcache identifiers) used to quickly validate run equivalence.
- Tolerance window: allowed floating-point numerical variance range (default 1e-6 relative) documented per-model class.
sections.heading: Definitions and scope

sections.body:
| Requirement | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| RNG seed pinning exposed per-request | Async subgraph operators and sampling must consume a deterministic seed | runtime-team |
| Kernel numerics mode (fast/precise) | Choose consistent fused-kernel behavior; disable nondeterministic fusions | kernel-team |
| Threading affinity deterministic scheduling | Prevent race-order variability in parallel matmuls | scheduler-team |
| KV cache stable eviction ordering | Eviction order must be deterministic to avoid cache-dependent outputs | runtime-team |
| Quantization deterministic paths | If quantized kernels differ in numeric ordering, document and pin variant | perf-team |
sections.heading: Requirements (operator and engineering)

sections.body:
runtime.flags:
  deterministic_inference: true
  rng_seed_mode: request_provided # alternatives: time_based, zero_padded
  kernel_numerics: precise
  disable_async_kernel_prefetch: true
  kvcache_eviction_policy: lru_stable_order
  max_concurrent_threads: 1  # can be relaxed per-hardware after validation
sections.heading: Operational configuration (example YAML)

sections.body:
{
  "route": "/debug/replay",
  "model": "gptx-7b-v2",
  "runtime_override": {
    "deterministic_inference": true,
    "rng_seed": 8675309
  }
}

Enabling DIM (canary -> rollout) — operator runbook (short):
1) Prepare a deterministic test corpus: 500 short, 200 medium, 50 long prompts covering sampling+greedy, top-k/top-p, and streaming. Include explicit instruction permutations for temperature-based sampling.
2) Provision a canary pool: single-node pool of same GPU SKU used in target fleet. Pin kernel bundle to previously validated release.
3) Deploy runtime flags with deterministic_inference=true and rng_seed_mode=request_provided.
4) Run the corpus three times with identical request payloads and collect: token sequences, trace signatures, kernel checksums, and per-request telemetry.
5) Verification step: Token sequences must match exactly for all three runs; trace signature must be identical. If mismatch, abort and collect full traces for kernel-team.
6) Gradual scale: expand canary to 10 nodes, repeat corpus. Increase concurrency to target SLO while monitoring divergence.
7) If stable for 48 hours and regression-free against baseline outputs, schedule 10% production traffic routing with DIM flag. Observe for 7 days.
8) Full rollout: staged 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% (minimum 24–72 hour holds depending on traffic shape).
sections.heading: Per-route override example (HTTP/Route JSON)

sections.body:
- Determinism unit test harness: replay single-batch with pinned seeds on CPU and GPU golden kernel; assert tokens and checksums equal.
- Nightly cross-hardware matrix: run 100-corpus tests across supported GPU families and report divergence rates.
- Fuzz-sampling profile: random sampling seeds should never collapse into nondeterministic behavior for greedy decode.
sections.heading: Verification & automated tests (CI)

sections.body:
- New telemetry keys (telemetry names):
  - dim.enabled (boolean)
  - dim.rng_seed (int/string)
  - dim.trace_signature (string)
  - dim.kernel_checksum (string)
  - dim.kvcache_epoch (int)
  - dim.repro_status (enum: ok|mismatch|tolerance_exceeded)
- Logs: on mismatch, write compact failure event with request_id, route, seed, kernel_checksum, top-3 divergent tokens and stack trace. Tag event with priority P0 for oncall.
- Dashboards: Determinism health panel (count of mismatches per hour), top offending routes, distribution by model and hardware SKU.
sections.heading: Telemetry and observability requirements

sections.body:
- Repro mismatch rate must be < 0.01% across canary corpus at target concurrency.
- Tolerance_exceeded events allowed only for documented model classes (e.g., very large multimodal pipelines) and must be listed in the known limitations section.
sections.heading: SLOs and acceptance criteria (canary gating)

sections.body: 1) Symptom: Repro status=mismatch, kernel_checksum differs.
sections.heading: Common failure modes and triage steps

sections.body:
- Compare kernel version and bundle checksums between runs (kernel-team).
   - Run single-step microtrace to isolate matmul/softmax layer causing divergence.
   - If fused/unfused kernel flip is observed, pin kernel_numerics to 'precise' and re-run.
2) Symptom: Repro mismatch only under high concurrency.
sections.heading: Triage

sections.body:
- Reduce max_concurrent_threads to baseline. If stable, incrementally increase and identify concurrency threshold.
   - Capture thread-affinity and kernel launch order traces; escalate to scheduler-team.
3) Symptom: Determinism fails with quantized model variant.
sections.heading: Triage

sections.body:
- Verify quantized-kernel deterministic flag; if not available, run inference with full-precision hotpath and compare.
   - Add quantization path to nightly cross-hardware matrix for ownership and acceptance.

Kernel and scheduler requirements checklist (for kernel-team):
- Deterministic kernel launch ordering when DIM=true.
- Deterministic reduction primitive (no atomic non-associative reductions that depend on launch order).
- Deterministic RNG consumer contract for dropout, sampling logits, and any augmentations.
- Stable fused-kernel commit with checksumable artifact.
sections.heading: Triage

sections.body:
- NVIDIA A100 (CUDA 11.x): Supported with kernels compiled with --deterministic-flags.
- NVIDIA H100 (CUDA 12.x): Supported, but requires kernel precision flag 'precise' (see notes).
- AMD MI250: Partial support — some fused kernels not yet deterministic; see limitation list.
- CPU fallback: Supported but slower; useful for debugging golden traces.
sections.heading: Compatibility matrix (high-level)

sections.body:
- DIM cannot guarantee bit-exact results across different hardware families. We provide per-hardware checksums and recommend golden-hash comparisons instead of raw bit-for-bit expectation.
- Some third-party ops (custom attention blocks) may not expose deterministic variants. These must be wrapped and versioned before DIM rollout.
sections.heading: Known limitations (short)

sections.body:
- Automatic rollback if repro mismatch rate exceeds 0.05% over a 1-hour sliding window during rollout.
- Manual rollback criteria: any P0 customer-facing incident tied to DIM changes, unexplained SLO degradation, or a memory/cpu thermal spike correlated with DIM changes.
sections.heading: Backout and rollback criteria

sections.body:
- Run deterministic harness (local):
  ./bin/runtime-debug --model gptx-7b-v2 --route /debug/replay --seed 42 --runs 3 --collect-traces --out reprun.log
- Extract trace signature from log (python):
  python tools/trace_tools.py --extract-signature reprun.log --out sig.json
- Compare kernelsums between two nodes (remote):
  ssh ops@node1 'cat /var/lib/runtime/kernelsums' > node1.txt
  ssh ops@node2 'cat /var/lib/runtime/kernelsums' > node2.txt
  diff node1.txt node2.txt || echo "kernel mismatch"
sections.heading: Example debugging commands and utilities

sections.body:
- Merge gate requires passing the determinism unit test suite.
- Release pipeline emits 'determinism-compatibility-report' artifact that gets stored with release metadata.
sections.heading: Quality gates and CI sensors

sections.body:
- Primary owner: runtime-team (incidents: oncall-runtime@redwood.ai)
- Kernel regressions: kernel-team (kernel-owners@redwood.ai)
- Hardware compatibility: infra-gpu (infra-gpu@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — Repro trace signature format (human-readable):
- trace_signature = sha256(concat(request_id, model_version, rng_seed, kernel_checksum, kvcache_epoch))
- kernel_checksum = sha256(binary-kernel-bundle || compile-options || git-commit)

Appendix B — Test matrix (abbreviated):
- CPU x FP32: baseline regression tests (golden)
- A100 x FP16 fused: primary validated target
- H100 x BF16 fused: validated with tolerance window 1e-5
- MI250 x FP16: exploratory; documented differences allowed
sections.heading: Owner and escalation

sections.body: - This spec is owned by Aisha Raman (runtime-team). For clarifications, add reviewers or raise a ticket in #runtime-determinism on Slack.
sections.heading: Contact and follow-ups

sections.body:

payload.page_title: Execution Scenario Orchestrator: Spec and Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the Execution Scenario Orchestrator (ESO), a cross-cutting component that composes, schedules, and replays representative end-to-end inference scenarios against the runtime. ESO is intended to:

- Provide a reproducible, versioned way to define complex multi-tenant workloads (prefixes, kv-cache warmup, mixed sequence lengths, burst patterns).
- Integrate with kernel scheduler hooks so scenario fidelity is preserved when testing scheduler changes.
- Produce traceable profiling artifacts consumable by the benchmarking suite and the profiling playbook.

Scope and audience: engineers owning runtime architecture, kernel-and-scheduling, profiling, and SREs running performance experiments or incident triage.

Design goals

1) Determinism and provenance: every scenario is a small, self-contained script with a hashable manifest and metadata (model version, quantization profile, hardware fingerprint).
2) Scheduler-aware playback: the orchestrator can attach scheduler context (priority, tenant-id, kernel-hint) to each request so the runtime executes the scenario as intended.
3) Observability-first: scenario runs automatically capture structured traces, kernel attributions, and per-token cost deltas and upload to the central perf store.
4) Lightweight chaos vectors: the orchestrator supports controlled perturbations (evictions, forced preemption, simulated NVLink degradation) to surface degradation modes.

Component overview

- Scenario DSL (YAML): declarative description of request series, injected events, and expected assertions.
- Runner: controller that materializes requests and submits them to a chosen endpoint (local sandbox, canary cluster, full production mirror).
- Scheduler Adapter: library that translates DSL affinity/priority fields into scheduler annotations and kernel hints.
- Collector: post-run artifact collector (traces, kernel telemetry, raw responses, golden diffs) with upload to perf-bucket.

Scenario DSL (conceptual example)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
manifest_version: "1.0"
name: "multi-tenant-burst-warmup"
model: "llama-13b-q4f16"
hardware_fingerprint: "g4dn-8nvlink-2026-03"
sequence_profile: "mix-small-medium-long"
timeline:
  - t: 0
    action: "warmup"
    params: "prefix_file=warmup-prompts.txt,concurrency=4"
  - t: 30
    action: "burst"
    params: "clients=120,shape=50%short-30%med-20%long,priority=production"
  - t: 90
    action: "evict"
    params: "tenant=tenant-42,reason=memory-pressure"
assertions:
  - type: "median-latency-below"
    value_ms: "200"
  - type: "tail-99-latency-below"
    value_ms: "800"

Scheduler integration

The Scheduler Adapter exposes three annotations consumed by the kernel mapper: kernel_hint (preferred kernel variant), priority_class (production/canary/batch), and affinity_token (NUMA/slot placement hint). When the runner submits requests it attaches these fields as HTTP headers (X-ESO-Kernel-Hint, X-ESO-Priority, X-ESO-Affinity) to preserve signal across transport layers.
sections.heading: A minimal scenario manifest in YAML. Fields must remain flat (no nested objects with unknown keys) for deterministic hashing.

sections.body:
curl -X POST https://runtime-canary.internal/api/v1/generate
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
 -H 'X-ESO-Kernel-Hint: grouped-attn-v2'
 -H 'X-ESO-Priority: production'
 -H 'X-ESO-Affinity: numa-0:slot-3'
 -d '{"prompt":"Summarize ..."}'

Profiling playbook integration

When an ESO run completes the Collector creates a run package and triggers the profiling playbook pipelines:

1) Minimal trace upload: we include per-request trace IDs and compact kernel-attribution CSVs.
2) Sampling policy: for runs > 10k requests, we apply stratified sampling by sequence length and priority class.
3) Correlation loop: perf store populates the run record with scheduler decision traces so the profiler can compute causal latency deltas associated with kernel selection.

Benchmarks and synthetic load harness

ESO can emit two modes of workload: synthetic (generated tokens for microbenchmarks) and recorded-replay (playback of production request surface with anonymization). The benchmarking suite consumes scenario manifests to run SLO-driven experiments.

SLO-driven experiment matrix (example)

| parameter | example values | notes |
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| concurrency | 1, 8, 64, 256 | cluster-dependent cap |
| sequence mix | 60/30/10 (s/m/l) | affects kernel crossing points |
| kv-cache state | cold, warm, hot | warmimplies prefix-caching |
| priority distribution | 90/10 prod/batch | scheduler stress test |

Runtime runbook: Replaying a production slowdown

Purpose: step-by-step guide to reproduce a reported production slowdown using ESO.

1) Triage and capture: collect the incident ID and the example request IDs from the status page.
2) Assemble a scenario: create a manifest that replays the failing requests (redacting PII), include the observed client headers and priority classes.
3) Select target: use a canary cluster that mirrors the production scheduler version and kernel set.
4) Run with tracing enabled: set environment variable ESO_TRACE_LEVEL=debug and run the runner with --collect-kernel-csv.
4a) If the slowdown reproduces, immediately tag the run with incident:<id> and notify SRE channel.
5) If the slowdown does not reproduce, run a higher-fidelity replay using recorded-replay mode with full affinity and session cookies (use only in secure sandbox).

Investigation checklist (what to look for)

- Kernel attribution spikes: sudden shift from grouped-attn-v2 to scalar-attn-fallback during medium sequences.
- Preemption events: scheduler logs containing "evict" + matching trace IDs.
- GPU metrics: duty-cycle drop, NVLink error counters, and sudden memory compaction events.
- KV-cache miss rate increase after eviction window.

Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: affinity headers not propagated by edge proxy in old canaries.
  Mitigation: upgrade proxy config to preserve X-ESO-* headers; work-around: include scheduler hints in body metadata.
- Issue: reproducibility variance when running on different NVLink topologies.
  Mitigation: include hardware_fingerprint in the manifest and pin to identical pool for replay.
- Issue: large recorded-replay runs can saturate perf-store ingest.
  Mitigation: use bucketed uploads and the incremental-collector option.

Release notes (summary of changes that introduced ESO)

- 2026-01-12: initial beta of ESO runner and DSL, supports warmup/burst/evict actions.
- 2026-06-03: Scheduler Adapter v1 added kernel_hint mapping and header propagation.
- 2026-09-22: Collector incremental upload and stratified-sampling policies added to reduce perf-store load.

Operational requirements and configs
sections.heading: Example headers (curl)

sections.body:
| key | type | default | description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| eso.runner.target | string | "canary" | target cluster: sandbox|canary|prod |
| eso.collector.sample_rate | float | "0.1" | fraction of requests to keep in full trace (0.0-1.0) |
| eso.scheduler.propagate_headers | bool | "true" | ensure X-ESO-* headers are forwarded by gateways |
| eso.archive.bucket | string | "gs://perf-bucket/eso-runs" | destination for run artifacts |

Security and privacy notes

- Recorded payloads must be redacted. The runner supports an anonymizer plugin that hashes or drops PII fields before uploading.
- Access controls: only members of runtime QA or SRE may run recorded-replay against production-mirrors. ESO enforces RBAC via OAuth groups.

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: runtime-infra team (primary), profiling team (secondary). Contacts: Marta Alvarez (runtime-infra), Kofi Mensah (profiling).
- Rollout stages: alpha (sandbox-only) -> beta (canary clusters, opt-in) -> GA (policy: default available to oncall).
- Acceptance criteria for GA: deterministic replay of previously recorded incidents in 90% of cases (same kernel selection and equivalent per-token latency within 15%).

Appendix: Example full scenario manifest and runner commands
sections.heading: Config keys (example table)

sections.body:
manifest_version: "1.0"
name: "incident-2026-299-replay"
model: "vicuna-7b-q2"
hardware_fingerprint: "a100-mig-4g-2026-05"
sequence_profile: "60%short-30%med-10%long"
timeline:
  - t: 0
    action: "replay-requests"
    params: "file=incident-2026-299-requests.ndjson,concurrency=32,priority=production"
  - t: 45
    action: "chaos"
    params: "type=evict,tenant=default,duration=5s"
sections.heading: scenario.yaml

sections.body:
eso-runner --manifest scenario.yaml --target canary --trace-level debug --collect-kernel-csv --upload-bucket gs://perf-bucket/eso-runs/incident-2026-299

Support matrix and troubleshooting quick tips

- If kernel CSVs are empty: confirm X-ESO-Kernel-Hint header propagation and ESO_TRACE_LEVEL.
- If reproductions differ by >20% latency: pin hardware_fingerprint and verify NVLink topology.
- If perf-store upload fails: retry with --incremental-collector and check bucket ACLs.

Document change log

- 2026-02-14 (Marta Alvarez): created initial draft.
- 2026-06-10 (Kofi Mensah): added scheduler adapter header spec.
- 2026-09-22 (Jade Patel): updated sampling policy and release notes.

Related artifacts and references

- Kernel mapper annotation contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Profiling integration guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2027
- Perf store upload API: internal PRD #4571

End of document.
