payload.page_title: Cache Hit-Rate Dashboards Spec (Prefix + KV Cache Telemetry)

sections.body:
This page defines the **Grafana dashboard set** and **alert rules** for the new prefix/KV cache telemetry emitted by the serving runtime. It is intended to support:
- **SRE oncall** triage for regressions (hit-rate drops, eviction pressure, telemetry gaps)
- **Runtime/Platform** debugging (miss reason attribution, request-shape sensitivity)
- **Product/Optimize** validation (is caching effective enough to recommend changes?)
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- **Filters and breakdowns** that match how Redwood operates (model/route/deployment/region/request shape)
- **Cardinality controls** (avoid per-tenant explosions; use allowlisted route/model identifiers)
- **Operational readiness** (panels that distinguish real behavior changes vs missing telemetry)

---
sections.heading: This spec is deliberately opinionated about

sections.body:
- SRE/Observability (primary)
- Runtime (cache + scheduler)
- Platform/Telemetry (tagging, ingestion, sampling)
- Support/CS (secondary; for customer investigations)
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) **“Why did cost/token jump?”** → correlate hit-rate drop with miss reasons (e.g., version_mismatch, policy_disabled) and eviction pressure.
2) **“Is caching working for this workload?”** → inspect reuse depth by prompt-length buckets and wasted prefill.
3) **“Is this a real regression or a telemetry issue?”** → check telemetry health panels and ingestion drop indicators.
4) **“Where should we tune knobs?”** → identify top routes/models with low hit-rate but high reuse opportunity, and whether memory pressure is limiting.

---
sections.heading: Use-cases

sections.body:
We ship three dashboards under: **Platform → Runtime Cache Telemetry**

1) **Cache Overview (SRE)**
- Goal: fast detection and triage across prod
- Default scope: prod, all regions, top models

2) **Cache Deep Dive (Runtime/Platform)**
- Goal: explain *why* (miss reasons, request-shape buckets, partial reuse)
- Default scope: single model + region, drill into route

3) **Cache Telemetry Health**
- Goal: detect pipeline breaks, label drops, sampling/rate-limit misconfig
- Default scope: prod, all regions
sections.heading: Dashboard set (Grafana)

sections.body:
- Support consistent variable names (see below)
- Avoid “Top N by tenant_id” style queries
- Prefer **recording rules** for expensive aggregations

---
sections.heading: Each dashboard must

sections.body:
- Runtime emits counters/histograms/gauges to **Prometheus** (via OTel collector).
- Grafana queries Prometheus.
sections.heading: Metric source

sections.body:
- `env` (e.g., prod, staging)
- `region` (cloud region, e.g., us-east-1)
- `deployment_mode` (hosted | dedicated | private)
- `model` (allowlisted stable model identifier, e.g., llama3.1-70b)
- `model_version` (allowlisted version string; not raw commit hash)
sections.heading: Required labels (must be present on all cache metrics)

sections.body:
- `route` (allowlisted route identifier; never raw customer-provided names)
- `route_tier` (shared | premium | internal)
- `prompt_len_bucket` (bucketed; e.g., 0-256, 257-512, 513-1024, 1025-2048, 2049+)
- `request_shape` (bucketed; e.g., chat_streaming, chat_non_streaming, completions)
- `miss_reason` (stable enum)
sections.heading: Optional labels (only on some metrics; use with care)

sections.body:
- No raw prompts, no per-request IDs, no per-tenant IDs as metric labels.

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
All dashboards must expose the same variables to make screenshots/runbooks reusable.

**Variables**
| Variable | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` | dropdown | prod | include staging for rollout validation |
| `deployment_mode` | dropdown | all | hosted/dedicated/private |
| `region` | multi-select | all | keep “all” as default |
| `model` | multi-select | top 10 by traffic | allowlisted model IDs |
| `model_version` | multi-select | all | used mainly in Deep Dive |
| `route` | multi-select | none | only in Deep Dive; allowlisted |
| `request_shape` | dropdown | all | chat_streaming is critical |
| `prompt_len_bucket` | dropdown | all | only shown on bucketed panels |
| `window` | dropdown | 5m | allowed: 1m/5m/15m |

**Default time range**
- Overview: last 6h (with quick picks 1h/24h/7d)
- Deep Dive: last 1h (with quick picks 15m/6h)
- Telemetry Health: last 24h

---
sections.heading: Global dashboard variables (Grafana templating)

sections.body: This spec uses the following canonical concepts (exact metric names may evolve; dashboards should use the recording rules where provided).
sections.heading: Metric conventions referenced by this spec

sections.body:
- **Prefix cache hit-rate**: fraction of prefill tokens served from prefix cache (token-weighted), plus request-weighted view.
- **KV cache reuse effectiveness**: how much previously computed KV was reused during decode/prefill for multi-turn and repeated prompts.
- **Miss reasons** (stable enum):
  - `capacity` (insufficient cache capacity / allocation failed)
  - `ttl_expired`
  - `policy_disabled` (caching disabled by config/route)
  - `hash_mismatch` (canonicalization mismatch)
  - `version_mismatch` (model_version incompatibility)
  - `unknown`
- **Eviction pressure**: gauges/counters that explain drops in hit-rate.
- **Wasted prefill**: prefill tokens that did not lead to subsequent reuse due to misses/evictions (token-weighted).
sections.heading: Core concepts

sections.body:
To keep Grafana responsive and reduce PromQL repetition, the telemetry pipeline should expose recording rules similar to:
- `:cache_prefix_hit_rate_tokens_5m` (token-weighted)
- `:cache_prefix_hit_rate_requests_5m` (request-weighted)
- `:cache_kv_reuse_rate_tokens_5m`
- `:cache_wasted_prefill_rate_tokens_5m`
- `:cache_eviction_rate_5m`
- `:cache_memory_pressure_5m` (smoothed gauge)

If recording rules are not available in an environment, dashboards may use direct PromQL, but must be reviewed by Telemetry (owner: Nadia Rahman) before shipping.

---
sections.heading: Recommended recording rules (dashboards should prefer these)

sections.body: **Purpose:** quickly answer “is caching healthy?” and “where is it broken?”
sections.heading: Dashboard 1: Cache Overview (SRE)

sections.body:
1) **Prefix cache hit-rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by `deployment_mode` (stacked optional)
- Filters: env/region/model
- Notes: token-weighted is the best cost proxy.

2) **Prefix cache hit-rate (request-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by `deployment_mode`
- Notes: catches cases where a small set of long prompts masks broader regressions.

3) **KV cache reuse rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by model

4) **Wasted prefill rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by deployment_mode
- Interpretation: rising wasted prefill alongside stable hit-rate often indicates eviction thrash or locality issues.
sections.heading: Row A — Executive summary

sections.body:
5) **Hit-rate heatmap by region**
- Viz: heatmap/table
- Dimensions: `region` x `model`
- Display: last 30m avg, plus delta vs previous 30m

6) **Top regressions (route/model)**
- Viz: table
- Columns: model, route, current hit-rate, week baseline, delta, traffic (req/s), wasted prefill
- Guardrails:
  - Only show routes in allowlist
  - Require minimum traffic threshold (e.g., > 1 req/s over 30m) to reduce noise
sections.heading: Row B — Where is it happening?

sections.body:
7) **Miss reasons (prefix cache) — distribution**
- Viz: stacked area
- Breakdown: `miss_reason`
- Scope: aggregated (no route by default)

8) **Eviction rate and memory pressure**
- Viz: dual-axis time series
- Metrics: eviction_count rate + memory pressure gauge

9) **Version mismatch misses (early warning)**
- Viz: time series
- Filters: model + model_version (optional)
- Notes: spikes often correlate with rollouts; should be caught quickly.
sections.heading: Row C — Why is it happening?

sections.body:
10) **Cache telemetry ingestion volume**
- Viz: time series
- Metric: total cache metric samples ingested / dropped
- Notes: used to distinguish real hit-rate drop vs ingestion label-drop.

11) **“Zero hit-rate” detector**
- Viz: stat panel
- Logic: flags if hit counters are flatline while request traffic is non-zero.

---
sections.heading: Row D — Telemetry sanity (quick checks)

sections.body: **Purpose:** explain root cause with high-signal breakdowns without cardinality blowups.
sections.heading: Dashboard 2: Cache Deep Dive (Runtime/Platform)

sections.body:
1) **Traffic and token volume**
- Viz: time series
- Panels:
  - request rate
  - prefill tokens/sec
  - decode tokens/sec
- Notes: always interpret hit-rate changes in context of traffic mix.

2) **Prompt length distribution**
- Viz: histogram/stacked bar
- Dimension: `prompt_len_bucket`

3) **Request shape mix**
- Viz: stacked bar
- Dimension: `request_shape`
sections.heading: Row A — Scope and workload shape

sections.body:
4) **Prefix hit-rate by prompt_len_bucket**
- Viz: multi-series line
- Breakdown: `prompt_len_bucket`
- Notes: regression isolated to long prompts usually points to capacity/eviction pressure.

5) **Prefix reuse depth (reused tokens) distribution**
- Viz: heatmap
- Dimension: reuse_depth_bucket (if available) vs time
- Notes: validates canonicalization and multi-turn reuse.

6) **Partial hit semantics (optional panel)**
- Viz: stacked series
- Display: full-hit vs partial-hit vs miss (token-weighted)
- Notes: if partial-hit rises while full-hit drops, check prompt canonicalization drift.
sections.heading: Row B — Prefix cache effectiveness

sections.body:
7) **KV reuse rate by request_shape**
- Viz: multi-series line
- Breakdown: request_shape
- Notes: chat_streaming often behaves differently; look for retry artifacts.

8) **Batched prefill attribution guard panel**
- Viz: stat + sparkline
- Purpose: detect anomalies consistent with continuous batching misattribution.
sections.heading: Row C — KV cache effectiveness

sections.body:
9) **Miss reasons by route (top 10 routes only)**
- Viz: table
- Columns: route, miss_reason (top), miss share, hit-rate, wasted prefill
- Guardrails:
  - hard limit to 10 routes
  - minimum traffic threshold

10) **Miss reasons over time (selected route)**
- Viz: stacked area
- Filters: route
sections.heading: Row D — Miss reason attribution

sections.body:
11) **Evictions by reason**
- Viz: stacked area
- Breakdown: eviction_reason (if available) or “evicted_total” only

12) **Cache memory utilization**
- Viz: time series
- Metrics: bytes used, bytes max, utilization %
- Notes: show per cache type (prefix vs kv) where applicable.

13) **Pressure vs hit-rate correlation**
- Viz: scatter plot
- X: memory pressure / utilization
- Y: hit-rate
- Group: prompt_len_bucket
- Notes: should only be used with sufficient sample count.
sections.heading: Row E — Eviction and memory

sections.body:
14) **Wasted prefill rate by miss_reason**
- Viz: stacked area
- Notes: a large wasted prefill share attributed to `hash_mismatch` suggests canonicalization opportunity.

15) **Wasted prefill per request (p50/p95)**
- Viz: time series
- Notes: spikes often precede cost incidents.

---
sections.heading: Row F — Wasted prefill analysis

sections.body: **Purpose:** ensure telemetry is present, correctly tagged, and within sampling/rate-limit expectations.
sections.heading: Dashboard 3: Cache Telemetry Health

sections.body:
1) **Samples ingested vs dropped (cache metrics)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: drop_reason (cardinality_guard, rate_limit, malformed)

2) **Label presence completeness**
- Viz: table
- Rows: required labels (env/region/deployment_mode/model/model_version)
- Columns: % series missing label over last 1h

3) **Series cardinality (cache metrics)**
- Viz: time series + stat
- Thresholds: warn at 80% of budget; critical at 95%

4) **Counter reset detector**
- Viz: stat
- Purpose: identify restarts misinterpreted as behavior changes.

5) **Trace annotation volume (if enabled)**
- Viz: time series
- Notes: ensure spans are sampled and not exploding.

---
sections.heading: Panels

sections.body: Alerts are *guardrails*, not customer SLAs. Prefer **ticket** over **page** unless there is strong evidence of customer impact.
sections.heading: Alerting spec (Prometheus alert rules)

sections.body:
1) **Cache hit-rate sudden drop (token-weighted) — global**
- Condition: hit-rate down > X% relative to 7d baseline for 15m, and traffic above minimum
- Action: page
- Notes: baseline comparison should be workload-aware (exclude low traffic).

2) **Telemetry missing / ingestion drop**
- Condition: request traffic present but cache hit/miss counters flatline OR drop rate above threshold for 10m
- Action: page
- Runbook: Cache Telemetry Pipeline Incident Runbook

3) **Eviction pressure critical**
- Condition: utilization > 95% for 15m AND eviction rate elevated
- Action: page
- Notes: include region/model in alert labels; avoid route in alert labels.
sections.heading: Paging alerts (SRE oncall)

sections.body:
4) **Version mismatch miss spike**
- Condition: version_mismatch miss share > threshold for 30m
- Action: ticket to Runtime + Release Eng

5) **Hash mismatch elevated (canonicalization opportunity)**
- Action: ticket to Product/Optimize and Runtime

6) **Wasted prefill elevated**
- Action: ticket; attach Deep Dive dashboard link with model/region pre-filled.
sections.heading: Ticket-only alerts

sections.body:
- env, region, deployment_mode, model (optional), severity
Avoid route/model_version unless strictly necessary; use annotations to include “top offenders” as text.

---
sections.heading: Alerts must include only

sections.body:
- Cache Telemetry Pipeline Incident Runbook
- Cache Telemetry Validation Checklist
- Cache Efficiency SLO Proposal

For Overview panels, each heatmap/table row should link to Deep Dive with variables pre-populated (region/model, optionally route).

---
sections.heading: All dashboards must include pinned links (top of page)

sections.body:
- **Workload mix changes** can move hit-rate without any regression. Always check prompt_len_bucket and request_shape mix before escalating.
- **Streaming retries** can distort counters if regression is reintroduced; use the Deep Dive “retry/streaming sanity” panels.
- **Batched prefill** can misattribute hits; the Deep Dive guard panel is required until we have 2+ stable releases.
- If you see **hit-rate = 0%** but traffic is healthy, check Telemetry Health for label drops and cardinality guards.

---
sections.heading: Operational notes and pitfalls

sections.body:
Dashboards are considered “shippable” when:
- Overview loads in < 10s on prod for last 6h
- Deep Dive loads in < 15s with a single model + region selected
- No panel requires adding a high-cardinality label (tenant_id, raw route names, prompt hashes)
- At least one successful oncall drill: identify (a) real hit-rate regression and (b) ingestion label-drop incident using dashboards alone

---
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (for this spec)

sections.body:
- Dashboard owner: **Allison Grant (Observability)**
- Alert owner/approver: **Sean Gallagher (SRE)**
- Metrics schema owner: **Nadia Rahman (Telemetry)**
- Runtime subject-matter reviewers: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Sofia Ivanova**

Change policy: any changes that add labels, expand breakdown dimensions, or introduce new expensive queries require review from Telemetry + SRE.
sections.heading: Ownership

payload.page_title: Kernel Selection Architecture Overview (Serving Runtime)

sections.body:
Kernel selection is the Serving Runtime subsystem responsible for choosing the concrete GPU implementation (“kernel plan”) for a request, given:
- Model identity and architecture/family
- Workload regime (prefill vs decode characteristics; sequence length buckets)
- Hardware target (GPU SKU, driver/CUDA capability, MIG partitioning)
- Runtime feature flags (quantization profile, attention variant, KV-cache layout)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Where selection happens in the execution pipeline
2) Interfaces to Scheduler and Compilation Cache
3) How decisions are cached, serialized, and made replayable/deterministic

This is an architectural overview. For the v2 decision logic and fallback policy, see ADR-017 and the v2 design doc.

---
sections.heading: This page describes

sections.body:
- Ensure **correctness-first** selection: only choose kernels that are compatible with the request + target hardware.
- Maintain **determinism and replayability**: identical inputs must yield identical selection (modulo explicitly versioned policy changes).
- Reduce tail latency by selecting optimized kernels per SKU and per seq-length regime.
- Keep selection overhead low (bounded CPU time, bounded telemetry overhead).
- Provide operational controls: allow/deny lists, feature gates, and forced overrides.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Training or learning a model-based selector (out of scope for v2; we use explicit policy rules).
- Deciding cluster placement (region/pool routing is handled by control plane and scheduling layers).

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body: Kernel selection runs inside the per-request runtime execution path after model resolution and before compilation/execution.
sections.heading: High-level execution pipeline (where selection occurs)

sections.body:
1. **Front Door / API Adapter**
   - Validates request, resolves model alias → `model_id` + `model_version`.
   - Normalizes request options (max_tokens, streaming, tool/function calling toggles) into `RequestOptions`.

2. **Scheduler / Batcher**
   - Assigns request to a worker process on a GPU.
   - Produces lightweight workload hints (e.g., observed prefill/decode distribution for the batch queue).

3. **Kernel Selector** (this subsystem)
   - Extracts features (`SelectorFeatures`) from request + model metadata + GPU metadata + scheduler hints.
   - Applies feature gate + allow/deny rules.
   - Generates candidate kernels and selects a `KernelPlan`.
   - Emits selection telemetry (sampled).

4. **Compilation Cache + Launcher**
   - Checks compilation cache for compiled artifacts matching `KernelPlan`.
   - Compiles if missing (within guardrails), then launches the selected kernel.

5. **Execution + Metrics**
   - Executes prefill/decode.
   - Reports latency breakdown, kernel identifiers, and errors.

Selection occurs at step 3, and is designed to be:
- **Pure** with respect to its inputs (no hidden dependence on time or ambient process state)
- **Versioned** via policy version IDs and runtime build version

---
sections.heading: Request flow (text diagram)

sections.body:
**Owner:** Runtime Kernels + Runtime Architecture

**Responsibilities:**
- Feature extraction and normalization
- Candidate generation
- Rule evaluation and scoring (v2)
- Fallback selection
- Decision caching and serialization
- Telemetry emission hooks

**Does not own:**
- GPU placement / pool selection (control plane + scheduler)
- Compilation artifact generation logic (compiler backend owns compilation; selector only keys it)
sections.heading: Kernel Selector module

sections.body: A registry of kernel implementations and their compatibility constraints.
sections.heading: Kernel Registry

sections.body:
- `kernel_id` (stable string)
- Model family/architecture compatibility (e.g., llama-like, mistral-like)
- Capability requirements (SM version, CUDA capability flags)
- Supported quantization profiles
- Known-bad deny rules (SKU/driver specific)
sections.heading: Registry entries are keyed by

sections.body:
- Built-in runtime defaults
- Hot-reloadable config overlays (for emergency deny/pin)
sections.heading: Registry is loaded from

sections.body:
Selector produces a `CompilationKey` / `PlanKey` used by compilation caching.

Compilation cache uses `CompilationKey` to:
- Lookup a compiled artifact (in-process memory + on-node disk cache)
- Avoid recompiles across requests
sections.heading: Compilation Cache interface

sections.body:
- If `CompilationKey` is identical, compiled artifacts should be reusable.
- If a choice changes any codegen-relevant parameter, it must reflect in `CompilationKey`.
sections.heading: Selector guarantees

sections.body: Scheduler provides *optional* hints that improve stability for mixed workloads.
sections.heading: Scheduler hints interface

sections.body:
- Estimated `prefill_tokens` and `decode_tokens` for the in-flight batch
- Observed queue regime classification (short prompts vs long-context dominated)
- Batching parameters currently in effect (max batch size, continuous batching mode)

Selector treats hints as inputs to selection, but the hint schema is:
- Explicitly versioned (`hints_schema_version`)
- Safe to omit (selector must fall back to request-derived features)

---
sections.heading: Examples of hints

sections.body:
SelectorFeatures is the normalized set of signals used for decision-making.

At a minimum, v2 uses:
- `model_family` (e.g., llama-like, mistral-like, qwen-like, gemma-like)
- `model_id`, `model_version`
- `seq_bucket` (see below)
- `gpu_sku_normalized` (see below)
- `sm_version` / `compute_capability`
- `driver_version` and `cuda_runtime_version` (guardrails)
- `quant_profile` (fp16/bf16/int8/int4 where applicable)
sections.heading: SelectorFeatures (normalized inputs)

sections.body: Selection uses coarse buckets to reduce decision noise while capturing the main performance regimes.
sections.heading: Sequence bucket definition

sections.body:
- `S`: prefill ≤ 512 and expected decode ≤ 128
- `M`: prefill 513–2048 or decode 129–512
- `L`: prefill 2049–8192 or decode 513–2048
- `XL`: prefill > 8192 or decode > 2048 (long-context / long generation)
sections.heading: Current buckets (subject to policy updates)

sections.body:
- Buckets are computed from request limits + scheduler hints (when present).
- For streaming requests, decode bucket should be based on expected decode tokens (max_tokens) but may be clamped to historical workload hints.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: We normalize cloud instance naming, PCI IDs, and MIG partitioning into a stable SKU string.
sections.heading: GPU SKU normalization

sections.body:
- `nvidia-a100-80gb` (covers common PCI IDs; memory size retained)
- `nvidia-h100-80gb-sxm`
- `nvidia-l40s-48gb`
- `nvidia-a100-40gb-mig-1g.5gb` (MIG partitions include slice info)

Normalization is performed once per process at GPU init and passed as immutable metadata to the selector.

---
sections.heading: Examples

sections.body: KernelPlan is the selector’s output. It is a structured record that must fully describe the execution choice.
sections.heading: KernelPlan

sections.body:
- `selected_kernel_id`
- `policy_version` (e.g., `kasv2-2026-02-18`)
- `fallback_reason` (empty if primary rule matched; otherwise explicit)
- `compilation_key` (string; stable serialization)
- `execution_toggles` (e.g., attention variant, KV-cache layout)
sections.heading: KernelPlan includes

sections.body:
- Log/trace fields
- A stable “plan key” string for caching
- A replay record for deterministic tests

---
sections.heading: The plan must be serializable into

sections.body: To keep overhead low and avoid repeated policy evaluation, we use a two-level cache.
sections.heading: Decision caching (what is cached and where)

sections.body:
- **Scope:** per worker process
- **Key:** `DecisionCacheKey`
- **Value:** `KernelPlan` (including compilation_key)
- **Eviction:** bounded LRU (default 5k entries) + TTL (default 30 minutes)
sections.heading: Level 1: In-process Decision Cache (L1)

sections.body:
- `model_version`
- `model_family`
- `gpu_sku_normalized`
- `seq_bucket`
- `quant_profile`
- `driver_version_major_minor` (coarsened)
- `policy_version`
sections.heading: Recommended key fields

sections.body:
- This captures stable performance regimes and avoids per-request recomputation.
- Including `policy_version` prevents stale cache reuse across policy updates.
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body:
Compilation caching is separate from decision caching.

- Decision cache returns a `KernelPlan` quickly.
- Compilation cache ensures the chosen plan maps to a compiled artifact.

Important: do **not** conflate “same decision” with “compiled exists”. A KernelPlan can be cached even if compilation misses occur; compilation cache handles that separately.

---
sections.heading: Level 2: Compilation Cache (L2)

sections.body: Determinism is a hard requirement for kernel selection.
sections.heading: Serialization & determinism

sections.body:
- Selection must be a pure function of explicitly provided inputs.
- Any policy changes must be represented by a versioned `policy_version`.
- Any non-deterministic ordering (e.g., iterating hash maps) is forbidden in candidate ordering and rule evaluation.
sections.heading: Determinism rules

sections.body: For sampled requests (and for forced-debug runs), we serialize a compact SelectionRecord.
sections.heading: SelectionRecord (replay + debugging)

sections.body:
- `selector_version` (runtime build + module version)
- `policy_version`
- `decision_cache_key`
- `selected_kernel_id`
- `candidate_kernel_ids` (ordered)
- `model_id`, `model_version`, `model_family`
- `seq_bucket`
- `gpu_sku_normalized`, `sm_version`, `driver_version`, `cuda_runtime_version`
- `allow_deny_outcome` (e.g., allowed by model allowlist; denied by SKU rule)
- `fallback_reason` (if any)
sections.heading: SelectionRecord fields (minimum)

sections.body:
- Trace span attributes on the request root span (sampled)
- Structured logs in `runtime-kernel-selection` log stream (sampled)
- Optional per-request dump when `--kernel_selection_dump=1` is enabled (debug-only)
sections.heading: Storage locations

sections.body:
- `decision_cache_key`
- `compilation_key`
sections.heading: We require stable string encoding for

sections.body:
- Use `key=value` segments joined by `|` in a fixed order.
- No whitespace.
- No high-cardinality freeform fields.
sections.heading: Encoding guidance

sections.body:
`policy=kasv2-2026-02-18|model=llama-3.1-70b@2026-02-01|gpu=nvidia-h100-80gb-sxm|seq=XL|quant=bf16|drv=550.54`

---
sections.heading: Example (illustrative)

sections.body: Kernel selection behavior can be modified at runtime via control-plane-provided gates and local debug flags.
sections.heading: Interfaces to rollout gates and overrides

sections.body:
- Gate name: `kernel_selection_v2`
- Scope: environment/region/pool + model allowlist
- Evaluation point: **before** selector applies v2 rules
sections.heading: Feature gates

sections.body: - Selector falls back to v1 selection or a conservative default plan (per policy).
sections.heading: If gate is disabled

sections.body:
- Deny specific `kernel_id` on a `gpu_sku_normalized` (and optionally driver/CUDA)
- Deny v2 entirely for a `model_version`
- Pin a kernel for a model+SKU+seq_bucket for fast mitigation
sections.heading: Support for emergency and proactive safety

sections.body:
1. Local debug flags (on-call / reproduction only)
2. Control plane hotfix rules (deny/pin)
3. Built-in denylist guardrails (known unstable combos)
4. v2 normal policy
5. v1 fallback policy
6. Conservative baseline kernel (last resort)

---
sections.heading: Override precedence (highest to lowest)

sections.body: The selector emits the following telemetry (subject to sampling and cardinality controls):
sections.heading: Observability hooks (what we emit)

sections.body:
- `kernel_selection_decisions_total{policy_version, model_family, gpu_sku, seq_bucket, selected_kernel_id}` (sampled or aggregated)
- `kernel_selection_fallbacks_total{reason, gpu_sku, model_family}`
- `kernel_selection_eval_ms` (CPU overhead)
- `kernel_selection_cache_hit_ratio` (L1 decision cache)
sections.heading: Metrics

sections.body:
- Span event: `kernel_selection` on request root span
- Attributes include `selected_kernel_id`, `policy_version`, `seq_bucket`, `gpu_sku_normalized`, and `fallback_reason`
sections.heading: Traces

sections.body: - Structured log line in `runtime-kernel-selection` stream for sampled requests
sections.heading: Logs

sections.body:
- No prompt text, no customer identifiers.
- Model identifiers are internal version IDs; customer-provided model aliases must be resolved before logging.

---
sections.heading: PII/Sensitive data note

sections.body: Kernel selection has explicit fallback behavior to avoid correctness issues and to bound tail latency.
sections.heading: Failure modes and fallback behavior

sections.body:
- Kernel missing for a SKU (registry mismatch)
- Known unstable kernel+driver combination (guardrail deny)
- Seq bucket misclassification leading to long-context regressions
- Compilation failure for a selected plan
sections.heading: Common failure modes

sections.body:
- Prefer a known-safe kernel with acceptable perf over an unverified optimized kernel.
- Treat compilation failure as a signal to fall back to the next candidate (bounded retries) before failing the request.
- Emit explicit telemetry on fallback reason.

For the authoritative fallback hierarchy, see ADR-017.

---
sections.heading: Fallback principles

sections.body: Dedicated and Private deployments often have constrained SKU sets and driver policies.
sections.heading: Operational notes (Dedicated / Private)

sections.body:
- Pre-register and validate kernel registry entries per allowed SKU set.
- Keep a minimal emergency override file that can:
  - Disable v2 per model
  - Pin a known-good kernel
  - Deny known-bad kernel+SKU combos
- Ensure selection telemetry sampling is tuned to avoid excessive cardinality in smaller clusters.

---
sections.heading: Recommended practices

sections.body:
The following names are representative; refer to the runbook for exact flags per runtime version.

- `--enable_kernel_selection_v2=true|false`
- `--kernel_selection_policy_version=<id>` (debug only; production uses release-default)
- `--kernel_selection_force_kernel_id=<kernel_id>` (debug only)
- `--kernel_selection_dump=1` (writes SelectionRecord to local logs)
- `--kernel_selection_decision_cache_size=<n>`
- `--kernel_selection_telemetry_sample_rate=<0..1>`

---
sections.heading: Appendix: configuration and debug controls (runtime)

sections.body:
- Architecture/perf correctness: Noah Patel
- Selector logic: Yuki Sato
- Kernel registry + implementations: Hiro Tanaka, Grace Kim
- Scheduler hints integration: Sofia Ivanova
- Tail latency and observability: Omar El-Sayed
- Control-plane rollout gates: Ethan Park

For on-call actions, see: Kernel Selection v2 Override and Rollback Runbook.
sections.heading: Owners

payload.page_title: Runtime backpressure and saturation signals (export + semantics)

sections.body:
This page defines the runtime-level backpressure and saturation signals used by Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding. It documents:
- What signals the serving runtime emits (queues, throughput, KV cache, memory pressure, fragmentation proxies).
- Exact semantics and units.
- Export pipeline (metric types, sampling, aggregation, and cardinality constraints).
- How upstream systems should interpret the signals without creating feedback loops.

This is a reference for Runtime, SRE, Gateway/Control Plane, Smart Routing, and Observability.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
**In scope**
- Signals emitted by the GPU-serving runtime at admission/scheduling boundaries.
- Metrics intended for near-real-time overload decisions (seconds).
- Metrics intended for dashboards/alerting (minutes).

**Non-goals**
- Per-request tracing details (handled by tracing pipeline).
- Model-quality or output correctness signals.
- Fine-grained per-GPU/per-process troubleshooting metrics with high cardinality (those live in restricted debug endpoints and are not used for load shedding).

---
sections.heading: Scope and non-goals

sections.body:
At a high level, the runtime splits work into:
1) **Admission**: request accepted by runtime process (after gateway/routing). Some requests may be queued locally before scheduling.
2) **Prefill**: prompt encoding + KV cache population.
3) **Decode**: incremental token generation using the KV cache.
4) **Streaming**: tokens flushed to the upstream response stream.
sections.heading: Runtime architecture context (where backpressure happens)

sections.body:
- **Runtime admission**: applies concurrency caps and queue limits (soft/hard), returning overload signals upstream when exceeded.
- **Scheduler**: dynamically reduces effective concurrency when saturation is detected (e.g., memory pressure, KV cache exhaustion), and can mark the instance as “degraded” for routing.
sections.heading: The runtime enforces backpressure at two points

sections.body:
- Prompt-length variance (prefill heavy vs decode heavy workloads)
- Streaming-induced tail amplification
- Noisy-neighbor patterns (single tenant sending long prompts / high max_tokens)

---
sections.heading: The signals below are designed to be robust under

sections.body:
1) **Queueing saturation**: backlog is growing and/or wait time is increasing.
2) **Compute saturation**: tokens/sec is at or near sustainable peak; marginal load increases latency sharply.
3) **Memory / KV cache saturation**: KV cache capacity or allocation efficiency is limiting throughput; OOM risk increases.
4) **Health degradation**: dependency or internal faults (allocator errors, repeated CUDA errors) impacting capacity.

Upstream policies should prefer **early, stable signals** (queue depth + queue wait) over late symptoms (timeouts).

---
sections.heading: We classify runtime saturation into four categories

sections.body:
- Primary export: **Prometheus** (scraped) and mirrored into our metrics backend.
- Secondary export: **OpenTelemetry metrics** for long-term correlation (not used in admission decisions).
sections.heading: Metric transport

sections.body:
- “Breaker-grade” metrics update every **1s** (rolling window) where feasible.
- Most gauges/counters are exported at **5s** resolution.
- Percentiles (e.g., queue wait p95) are computed using runtime-side histograms and exported as Prometheus histograms.
sections.heading: Resolution and update cadence

sections.body:
- No per-request IDs.
- No per-customer dimensions.
- Labels are limited to: `region`, `cluster`, `runtime_pool`, `model_family`, `route_class` (small finite sets).
- Optional label `model` is only allowed when the catalog size is bounded in that pool; otherwise prefer `model_family`.

**Important:** If a team needs high-cardinality breakdowns for a live incident, use the restricted debug endpoint (see “Debug-only signals”), not Prometheus.

---
sections.heading: To avoid metric blowups

sections.body:
These are the primary early-warning signals.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{stage="prefill"}` (gauge, requests)
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{stage="decode"}` (gauge, requests)

**Semantics**
- Number of requests currently waiting to be scheduled for the given stage.
- Excludes requests actively running on GPU.

**Interpretation**
- Sustained non-zero decode queue depth correlates strongly with rising p95 latency for streaming workloads.
- Prefill queue depth spikes are common during bursty long-prompt traffic; use queue *wait* to differentiate transient bursts vs persistent saturation.
sections.heading: 1) Scheduler queue depth (prefill / decode)

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="prefill"}` (histogram)
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="decode"}` (histogram)

**Semantics**
- Time from enqueue → start of GPU execution for that stage.

**Interpretation**
- Queue depth without wait time can be misleading (e.g., many tiny tasks).
- For overload decisions, queue wait p95 is preferred.
sections.heading: 2) Scheduler queue wait time

sections.body:
We export both “actual tokens/sec” and “saturation ratio” relative to a calibrated baseline.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_tokens_generated_total` (counter, tokens)
- `runtime_token_throughput_tps` (gauge, tokens/sec; runtime-computed over rolling 10s window)
- `runtime_compute_saturation_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–2.0)

**Semantics**
- `runtime_token_throughput_tps` is derived from the counter and a stable rolling window.
- `runtime_compute_saturation_ratio` is `observed_tps / sustainable_tps_baseline`.
  - The baseline is pool+model_family specific and shipped via config; it is periodically recalibrated from load tests.

**Interpretation**
- Ratio > 0.95 sustained indicates compute saturation; additional load should be shed/queued.
- Ratio < 0.7 with high queue depth indicates another bottleneck (often memory/KV pressure or fragmentation).
sections.heading: 3) Effective tokens/sec and saturation ratio

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_inflight_requests{stage="prefill"}` (gauge)
- `runtime_inflight_requests{stage="decode"}` (gauge)
- `runtime_admission_concurrency_limit` (gauge)

**Semantics**
- Stage-specific active work running on GPU.
- `runtime_admission_concurrency_limit` is the current effective cap (may be lowered by degradation mode).

**Interpretation**
- Use with queue signals to reason about whether we are “maxed out” or blocked.

---
sections.heading: 4) In-flight requests and concurrency

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_kv_cache_bytes_used` (gauge)
- `runtime_kv_cache_bytes_capacity` (gauge)
- `runtime_kv_cache_utilization_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–1.0)

**Semantics**
- Capacity is the configured KV cache arena size for the pool.
- Used bytes include active sequences plus reserved blocks for in-flight batching.

**Interpretation**
- Sustained utilization > 0.9 correlates with admission stalls and/or forced evictions.
- Under KV pressure, prefill may look healthy while decode queue wait grows (decode needs KV residency longer).
sections.heading: 5) KV cache utilization (pool level)

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total` (counter)
- `runtime_kv_cache_reclaim_failures_total` (counter)

**Semantics**
- Evictions occur when the runtime must reclaim KV blocks earlier than ideal to admit new work.
- Reclaim failures indicate allocator could not free sufficient contiguous blocks (often fragmentation-related).

**Interpretation**
- Rising eviction rate during steady traffic is a strong signal for load shedding or reduced max_tokens caps.
sections.heading: 6) KV cache eviction / reclamation pressure

sections.body:
We avoid exporting raw per-GPU memory usage by device ID (cardinality and privacy concerns). We export pool-level aggregates.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_gpu_memory_bytes_used` (gauge, pool aggregate)
- `runtime_gpu_memory_bytes_total` (gauge, pool aggregate)
- `runtime_gpu_memory_headroom_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–1.0)

**Semantics**
- Aggregate across devices in the pool (sum used / sum total).
- Includes model weights + runtime allocations + KV cache arena.

**Interpretation**
- Headroom ratio < 0.05 sustained is a high OOM risk zone. Admission should become conservative.

---
sections.heading: 7) GPU memory headroom and allocator pressure

sections.body: We cannot reliably export “true fragmentation” across allocators/hardware, so we use two proxies that correlate with allocator churn and inability to satisfy large allocations.
sections.heading: Memory fragmentation proxies (practical, export-safe)

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_allocator_allocation_failures_total{class="kv"|"workspace"|"other"}` (counter)
- `runtime_allocator_retry_total{class="kv"|"workspace"|"other"}` (counter)

**Semantics**
- Allocation failures count unsuccessful attempts that required fallback (e.g., GC/reclaim) before succeeding or erroring.
- Retries count attempts that succeeded after one or more reclaim cycles.

**Interpretation**
- A rising retry rate typically precedes latency spikes.
- Allocation failures that bubble up as request errors must be classified as runtime capacity degradation and should trigger aggressive shedding.
sections.heading: 8) Allocation failure and retry counters

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_allocator_largest_free_block_bytes_bucket` (histogram)

**Semantics**
- Runtime periodically samples the allocator and records the approximate largest allocatable contiguous block.
- Exported as a histogram to avoid per-instance variability dominating the signal.

**Interpretation**
- Falling largest-free-block distribution while total free memory remains stable indicates fragmentation (or pinned allocations).

---
sections.heading: 9) “Largest free block” approximation (bucketed)

sections.body:
**Metrics**
- `runtime_overload_state{state="ok"|"degraded"|"overloaded"}` (gauge; 1 for current state)
- `runtime_overload_reason{reason="queue"|"compute"|"kv"|"memory"|"dependency"|"unknown"}` (gauge; 1 for current dominant reason)

**Semantics**
- State is computed in runtime from a weighted ruleset (see below).
- Reason is best-effort; it is used primarily for dashboards and oncall triage.

**Interpretation**
- Upstream circuit breakers should treat `overloaded` as a “hard stop” indicator for new admissions in that pool/region.
- `degraded` indicates we should prefer feature reduction (caps) and cautious admission rather than blanket shed.
sections.heading: 10) Runtime overload state and reason

sections.body:
- Enter `degraded` when (any):
  - decode queue wait p95 > 250ms for 30s
  - compute saturation ratio > 0.95 for 30s
  - KV utilization > 0.92 for 30s
  - allocator retry rate > 1/s for 30s
- Enter `overloaded` when (any):
  - decode queue wait p95 > 750ms for 20s
  - GPU headroom ratio < 0.03 for 10s
  - allocation failures increasing AND error rate in runtime > 0.5% for 60s
- Exit criteria require the signal to remain below threshold for a longer interval (typically 60–120s) to avoid flapping.

**Note:** These thresholds are defaults; policy engine can override per pool/model_family with guardrails.

---
sections.heading: The runtime computes state with conservative hysteresis

sections.body:
- Per-GPU device utilization, memory, and kernel timings
- Per-model exact TPS baselines
- Per-batch sizes and microbatch timings
sections.heading: For deep performance work we also maintain

sections.body:
- `runtime-admin` endpoint (restricted network + RBAC)
- Short-lived “incident capture” bundles

Do not build automated shedding rules on debug-only signals.

---
sections.heading: These are available via

sections.body:
Recommended order of evaluation (fast to compute, stable):
1) Runtime `runtime_overload_state` (overloaded → reject early)
2) decode queue wait p95 and queue depth (protect p95/p99)
3) KV utilization + eviction rate (protect memory stability)
4) compute saturation ratio (protect throughput)
sections.heading: Gateway / admission control

sections.body:
- Prefer consistent, explicit overload errors over timeouts.
- Avoid retry storms: only shed with stable Retry-After contracts (see ADR-014 for semantics).
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body:
- Use `overloaded` state to avoid routing new traffic into an already-saturated pool.
- Use `degraded` as a hint to prefer alternate pools/regions for latency-sensitive tiers.
- Do not rapidly oscillate between regions based on 1–5s spikes; require sustained state changes (>= 30s) or use the routing system’s built-in damping.
sections.heading: Smart routing

sections.body:
- Alerts should be based on *sustained* signals and correlated with customer-visible impact metrics (5xx/timeouts/latency), not on single gauges.

---
sections.heading: SRE dashboards and alerts

sections.body:
**Decode queue wait p95 by region**
- `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, region) (rate(runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="decode"}[5m])))`

**KV utilization ratio (pool aggregate)**
- `avg by (region, runtime_pool) (runtime_kv_cache_utilization_ratio)`

**Compute saturation ratio (p95 across instances approximated by max)**
- `max by (region, runtime_pool) (runtime_compute_saturation_ratio)`

**Allocator retries rate**
- `sum by (region, runtime_pool) (rate(runtime_allocator_retry_total[5m]))`

---
sections.heading: Example PromQL snippets (for dashboards)

sections.body:
1) **Queue depth without queue wait is ambiguous.** Always pair them.
2) **Prefill vs decode bottlenecks differ.** A prefill-heavy burst may not require shedding if decode remains stable.
3) **KV pressure can masquerade as compute saturation.** When KV utilization is high, throughput may drop while GPUs look “busy.”
4) **Sampling noise:** 1s gauges will be spiky. Use 30–60s windows for state changes.
5) **Metric delays:** scrape + pipeline delays are typically 2–10s. Runtime state gauges help reduce dependency on downstream aggregation.

---
sections.heading: Operational notes and pitfalls

sections.body:
- metric names, labels, or types
- runtime_overload_state ruleset thresholds
- sampling cadence

…must include:
- A backwards-compatibility plan (add new metrics; deprecate old after 2 releases)
- Updates to overload dashboards and any policy-engine mappings
- SRE sign-off if used for paging or automated load shedding

---
sections.heading: Any changes to

sections.body:
- Runtime scheduling + backpressure: **Sofia Ivanova**, **Lena Fischer**
- Saturation signals implementation: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Julian Moore**
- Telemetry pipeline coordination: **Logan Wright**
- Oncall consumers (dashboards/alerts): **Rafael Mendes**, **Aisha Bello**
sections.heading: Owners

payload.page_title: Runtime Observability and Self-Heal Orchestration Manual

sections.body:
Overview
========

This document describes the observability-driven self-healing orchestration layer that sits above the serving runtime. It defines telemetry contracts, the priority-rebalancer and automatic fallback controllers, validation/benchmarking harnesses, and an operational runbook for investigation and rollback. The goal is to keep customer-facing SLOs intact while enabling safe automated remediation of common degradation patterns (kernel stalls, KV cache thrash, NUMA imbalance, and soft OOMs).

Why this exists
---------------

Redwood’s runtime is highly-optimized but operates in multi-tenant, bursty environments. Human intervention is slow for tail-latency regressions and kernel regressions that require quick mitigation. The self-heal orchestrator reduces MTTI/MTTR by safely applying corrective actions (routing, shedding, kernel rollback, re-quantization, and temporary QoS changes) under tight observability contracts.

Scope
-----
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Telemetry signals and minimal observability contract
- Recovery actions and safety gates for each failure class
- Priority-rebalancer logic and knobs
- Profiling & benchmark validation recipe for automated remediations
- Incident runbook with checklists, CLI commands and escalation path
- Known limitations and migration notes

Architecture (text diagram)
-------------------------

Serving runtime node(s)  <-->  Telemetry collector (trace/metrics/logs)  <-->  Orchestrator (policy engine + decision log)  <-->  Remediation drivers (router, KV manager, kernel-toggle controller)

Components and responsibilities
--------------------------------

1) Telemetry collector (observability-adapter)
- Aggregates kernel-level traces (kernel_id, kernel_latency_p50/p95/p99), per-request token counts, KV cache hit-rate by prefix, allocator pressure, and GPU thermal/power events.
- Exposes an ingest API (protobuf over gRPC) with 10s aggregation windows by default.

2) Policy engine (self-heal-orch)
- Consumes summarized telemetry; evaluates policies (SLA preservation, unit-cost guardrails).
- Emits decisions as append-only decision logs (immutable), with a decision_id, rationale, and safety checks.

3) Remediation drivers
- Router: adjusts routing weights across model variants/regions.
- KV manager: toggles aggressive prefetching and evictions; issues warmup hints.
- Kernel controller: enables/disables kernel variants or rolls back kernel bundles per-node.

Telemetry contract (must be implemented by services sending signals)
------------------------------------------------------------------

Required metrics (names are canonical; agents must map to these names):
- runtime.request.latency.p50, p95, p99 (ms)
- kernel.exec.latency.p50, p95, p99 (ms) per kernel_id
- kvcache.hit_rate (0..1) per tenant and prefix-class
- allocator.free_bytes and allocator.fragmentation_pct per host
- gpu.utilization_pct, gpu.power_watts, gpu.temperature_c
- trace.sample: end-to-end trace with tags: kernel_id, tenant_id, model_variant, request_surface, slot_id

Ingestion SLA and retention
- Ingestion latency: <= 15s for 10s aggregates for production clusters.
- Minimum retention for decisioning: 1h of high-resolution traces and 14d of aggregated metrics.

Policy & decision safety gates
-----------------------------

Every automatic remediation must satisfy three gates before action:
1) Evidence gate: at least two independent signals (latency spike + kernel exec tail) above threshold for >= 3 evaluation windows.
2) Impact gate: simulation/estimate that remediation preserves SLO for at least 90% of active requests.
3) Rollback gate: a precomputed rollback path exists and has been smoke-validated in staging within the last 7 days.

Priority rebalancer algorithm (summary)
--------------------------------------

Purpose: dynamically rebalance kernel priority credits across concurrent workloads to prevent priority inversion and kernel starvation.
sections.heading: This manual covers

sections.body:
- queue_length_by_priority (short, mid, long)
- kernel_exec_latency_p95_by_priority
- token_rate_by_priority
- slot_utilization and free_memory_estimate
sections.heading: Inputs

sections.body:
```
if kernel_exec_latency_p95_by_priority['short'] > SLO_short * 1.4 and slot_utilization < 0.8:
    transfer_credit(from='background', to='short', amount=min(credit_pool*0.2, deficit_estimate))
elif allocator.fragmentation_pct > 70%:
    throttle_background_jobs(pressure=0.3)
else:
    decay_transfers()
```

Knobs and configuration table
------------------------------

| param_name | default | range | description |
|-----------|---------:|------:|------------|
| evaluation_window_s | "10" | "5..60" | Aggregation window for decision inputs (seconds). |
| evidence_confirmation_windows | "3" | "1..10" | Number of windows required to confirm an event. |
| max_credit_transfer_pct | "0.2" | "0..0.5" | Maximum fraction of credit pool transferable in one decision. |
| emergency_fallback_timeout_s | "30" | "10..300" | Time to wait for a successful rollback before expanding mitigations. |

Profiling and benchmark validation recipe
----------------------------------------

Automated mitigation must be validated using a deterministic synthetic workload prior to roll-to-prod. Use the runtime-benchmark harness (see config snippet below).
sections.heading: Core heuristic (pseudocode)

sections.body:
```
benchmark_job:
  name: "self_heal_validation_burst_short_priority"
  traffic_profile:
    - shape: "sudden_burst"
      duration_s: 120
      qps: 800
  request_surface: "short-chat"
  sample_tracing: 100%
```
sections.heading: YAML example (benchmark job for validation)

sections.body:
- No P99 regression > 10% vs baseline for the primary route.
- Fallback actions reduce P99 by >= 20% in degraded scenarios within 45s.
- No data-loss or request duplication observed in trace reconciliation (trace IDs monotonic).

Runbook: Incident triage and automated remediation checklist
-----------------------------------------------------------

1) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   1.1 Check SLO dashboard: runtime.request.latency.p99 and kernel.exec.latency.p99.
   1.2 Correlate with recent decision log entries: `self-heal/decisions` feed.
   1.3 Snapshot a 2-minute trace sample for the impacted tenant(s).

2) Confirm pattern (10-20 minutes)
   2.1 Ensure evidence gate satisfied: at least two signals across 3 windows.
   2.2 If evidence gate not satisfied, escalate to oncall and increase sampling to 100% for 5 minutes.

3) Execute remediation (automation preferred)
   3.1 For kernel tail regressions: trigger kernel rollback for impacted nodes via kernel controller: `redwoodctl kernel rollback --nodes <node-list> --bundle <bundle-id>`
   3.2 For KV cache thrash: change eviction policy to `freq=aggressive` and issue prefetch hints: `redwoodctl kv adjust --prefix <prefix> --policy aggressive`
   3.3 For NUMA-induced latency: enforce numa-affinity hint on new allocations: `redwoodctl host set-affinity --host <host> --policy strict`

4) Observe and validate (20-45 minutes)
   4.1 Ensure remediation decision recorded and visible in decision-log with decision_id.
   4.2 Validate P95/P99 trends and check no cascading failures.
   4.3 If remediation fails to reduce P99 within emergency_fallback_timeout_s (default 30s), expand to next mitigation step (e.g., route to fallback variant).

5) Post-incident (within 24h)
   5.1 Open a post-incident review with decision-log export and kernel trace bundles attached.
   5.2 Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite that reproduces the trigger pattern.

Quick CLI commands
-------------------
- View recent decisions: `redwoodctl decision tail --since 10m`
- Force a manual decision abort: `redwoodctl decision abort --decision-id <id>`
- Increase telemetry sampling: `redwoodctl telemetry sampling set --scope tenant:<t> --rate 100`
- Rollback kernel bundle: `redwoodctl kernel rollback --nodes <nodes> --bundle <bundle>`

Benchmarking suite integration points
------------------------------------

- The orchestrator integrates with the benchmark suite via a webhook that runs validation jobs when a remediation policy is created/updated.
- Validation must run on a staging fleet that mirrors production heterogeneity (GPU types, slot sizes, and NUMA topologies).
- Reports are stored in the benchmark-results bucket under `self-heal-validations/` with JSON results and trace artifacts.

Release notes (summary of notable changes)
------------------------------------------
- 2026-01-18: v0.9 release — initial production rollout of self-heal orchestrator with evidence & rollback gates.
- 2026-02-08: v1.0 release — added priority-rebalancer, KV manager driver, and admission gate improvements.
- 2026-03-02: v1.1 patch — tightened evidence confirmation windows default from 5 -> 3 windows and fixed decision-log truncation bug.

Known issues and mitigations
---------------------------
- Issue: rare false positives when short-lived network stalls cause spurious kernel p99 spikes.
  Mitigation: evidence gate requires multiple signals and decision engine now cross-checks host-level network err_count.
- Issue: rollback path sometimes fails when staging rollback has drifted from prod kernel metadata.
  Mitigation: staging bake jobs now run nightly and verify bundle checksums; policy engine rejects auto-remediation if last staging verification is older than 7 days.

Operational ownership and SLAs
-----------------------------
- Owner: Serving Runtime SRE (oncall roster: runtime-sre@redwood.internal)
- Escalation: runtime-sre -> Runtime Platform lead -> Eng oncall (pager) -> CTO (for customer-impacting incidents)
- Operational goal: automated mitigations should resolve 70% of transient P99 spikes within 60s in non-critical tenants.

Privacy and safety considerations
--------------------------------
- Decision logs are treated as internal telemetry; do not be exported to customer logs.
- Any remediation that may route customer traffic across regions requires prior legal review (see `security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions`).

Appendix A — Decision log schema (flattened example)
---------------------------------------------------
- decision_id: string
- created_at: ISO8601 timestamp
- trigger_signals: comma-separated list
- rationale: short string
- action: short string (e.g., kernel_rollback, adjust_kv)
- impacted_nodes: comma-separated list
- rollback_action: short string
- safeties_checked: comma-separated list

Appendix B — Smoke-validation checklist for kernel rollback
----------------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm kernel bundle checksum in staging: `redwoodctl kernel verify-staging --bundle <bundle>`
2) Run microburst validation (see YAML above) against the staging mirror.
3) Ensure no more than 1% increase in token-drop-rate and zero duplication in traces.
4) Mark bundle as staged: `redwoodctl kernel mark-staged --bundle <bundle>`

References and links
--------------------
- Runtime decision graph: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Incident orchestration matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-incident-orchestration-and-capacity-decision-matrix-2026
- Benchmarking protocols: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026

If you are implementing or modifying policies, add unit tests for both the evidence gate logic and the rollback gate, and request an architecture review from the runtime-sre team before enabling in production.

payload.page_title: Edge Consumption Affinity & Local Cache Playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook explains the product intent, design trade-offs, and rollout plan for enabling consumption affinity and local cache behavior for edge and near-edge Redwood deployments. The goal is to improve tail-latency for conversational and short-sequence workloads while reducing per-token compute cost through coordinated local caching and affinity routing. This is a product-facing reference for PMs, solutions engineers, and partner integrators.

Key principles:

1) Latency first for interactive workloads: preserve 95th/99th tail latency SLOs for conversational routes (target 95th < 120ms for short prompts in edge regions).
2) Cost-aware fallthroughs: local cache hits reduce GPU token cost; misses should gracefully route to cost-optimized hosted variants without impacting correctness SLA.
3) Consistency and privacy: cached prefixes must honor tenant isolation and retention policies (KMS-backed encryption for private deployments).
4) Observability and rollbackability: every affinity policy must log decision reasons and expose observability hooks for SLO regressions and cost impact.

Scope and components:

- Consumption Affinity Service (CAS): a lightweight control-plane microservice that computes a per-tenant affinity score for edge vs. central serving, based on recent traffic patterns, per-route SLOs, and capacity signals.
- Local Prefetch Proxy (LPP): an optional customer-side (or VPC) proxy that maintains a local prefix/KV cache and prefetches hot model context (embedding vectors and KV segments) from upstream replicas.
- Affinity Router: runtime policy embedded in the gateway which consults CAS to decide request routing: local -> dedicated edge pool -> hosted fallback.
- Cache Coordination Protocol: a compact protocol (HTTP/2+ gRPC) for cache eviction hints, prefetch requests, and lease-based ownership of cached segments.

SLOs and thresholds (product defaults):

- Interactive conversational (short prompts, <256 tokens): 95th latency target = 120ms, 99th = 300ms.
- Cache hit target: 60% steady-state for routes with affinity enabled within first 72 hours after warmup.
- Cost impact guardrail: no single-tenant affinity policy may increase monthly token-related spend by >5% without explicit approval.

Customer-facing behaviors and configs:

Table: default per-route config (text table)

Name | Default | Description
-----|---------|---------
affinity_enabled | true | Whether CAS can set affinity for this route
prefetch_window | 90s | Lookback window for prefetch heuristics
min_traffic_for_affinity | 100 req/day | Minimum traffic to qualify for persistent affinity
cache_ttl | 6h | Default lease/TLL for prefetched KV segments
fallback_model_tier | standard | Model tier used when local misses occur

How affinity decisions work (high level):

1. Route registers with CAS with route metadata (SLO, expected seq length distribution, tenant id).
2. CAS ingests traffic telemetry (per-route QPS, recent cache hit rate, tail latency) and computes an affinity score (0.0-1.0) based on configured weights: latency_weight (0.5), hit_rate_weight (0.3), cost_delta_weight (0.2).
3. If score > 0.7 and capacity is available in edge pool, CAS marks route as Affinity=LOCAL and issues prefetch hints to LPP.
4. Affinity Router enforces a small percentage of canary bypasses (2%) to validate quality against hosted baseline.

Operational runbook (for product and SRE):

Pre-deployment checklist:
- Confirm tenant encryption keys available (KMS).
- Verify edge pool capacity >= expected steady-state QPS for routes marked local.
- Enable affinity in staging and validate hit-rate >= 40% after warmup.

Incident handling (high level):
1. Symptom: sudden drop in cache hit-rate or spike in tail latency in an edge region.
2. Page oncall SRE and tag the route in CAS UI.
3. Actions: (a) revert route affinity to FALLBACK for affected tenants; (b) invalidate suspicious LPP caches by issuing eviction hints; (c) collect KV cache diagnostic bundle from LPP (see diagnostics API).
4. Postmortem: update prefetch heuristics or raise min_traffic_for_affinity if instability is workload-driven.

Rollout plan (Q4 2026 -> Q1 2027):

- Phase 0 (pilot): select 3 enterprise customers with strict latency needs and low privacy constraints. Deploy LPP and enable Affinity in a single edge region. Collect metrics for 4 weeks.
- Phase 1 (early access): open to more customers with an opt-in flag in Console; expose per-route configuration controls and cost-impact simulator.
- Phase 2 (general availability): enable automatic affinity suggestions for qualifying routes and add self-serve toggle in Console with default safe thresholds.

Pricing and packaging implications:

- Affinity-enabled routes will qualify for a reduced token charge on local cache hits (example: 40% discount on per-token compute metric for hits), implemented as a post-processing credit applied to invoices.
- Dedicated edge pools used for affinity will be eligible for reserved-capacity pricing; product must surface guidance on commit sizing (recommended 30% headroom).
- Premium support add-on: affinity stabilization SLA (four-week warmup assistance and weekly health check-ins).

Console and API examples:

- Sample API: enable affinity on route via Redwood API (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/routes/route-123/affinity \n  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
  -d '{"affinity_enabled": true, "min_traffic_for_affinity": 200, "cache_ttl_seconds": 14400}'

- Affinity decision query (gRPC snippet concept):
// affinity_service.getAffinity(route_id, tenant_id) -> {score: 0.82, reason: ["low_tail_latency", "high_local_hit_rate"]}

Monitoring and telemetry requirements:

- Telemetry events to emit: affinity_evaluation, cache_prefetch_hint, cache_hit, cache_miss, affinity_enforcement_event.
- Dashboards: per-region affinity hit-rate, per-route tail-latency vs. baseline, monthly cost delta for affinity-enabled tenants.
- Alerts: cache_hit_rate < 40% sustained for 30m, or tail_latency_95th increase > 30% vs baseline.

Security and compliance notes:

- All cache contents must be encrypted at rest using customer KMS keys for Private deployments.
- Prefetch requests must carry tenant scoping headers and be rate-limited (default 10 prefetches/sec per tenant).
- For regulated customers, affinity can be restricted to dedicated private edge pools only.

Decision log (why we chose this approach):

- Alternatives considered: purely central caching, full-model replication to every edge, and client-side only caching.
- Tradeoffs: model replication provides best latency but unacceptable cost and variant proliferation; client-only caching lacks coordination and instrumentation. Consumption Affinity + coordinated prefetch gives a practical middle ground with measurable cost and latency improvements.

Open questions and follow-ups:

- Quantify warmup curve behavior across multi-tenant noisy neighbors and update prefetch heuristics accordingly.
- Define SLO for prefetch bandwidth costs and establish billing for heavy prefetch consumers.
- Evaluate stronger consistency modes (read-through vs. lease-based) for high-security customers.

Ownership and contacts:

- Product lead: Sofia Park (product)
- Engineering owner: Lars Becker (eng-serving-runtime)
- SRE lead: Ethan Cole (eng-sre)
- Solutions & Partnerships: Maya Singh (customer-success)

Appendix: example prefetch heuristics pseudocode

// simplified scoring for whether to prefetch a prefix
function should_prefetch(route_metrics) {
  score = 0
  if (route_metrics.qps > 5) score += 0.4
  if (route_metrics.recent_cache_hits > 0.5) score += 0.3
  if (route_metrics.tail_latency > baseline * 1.2) score += 0.3
  return score > 0.6
}

Diagnostic CLI (LPP) to collect cache bundle:

redwood-lpp collect-cache-bundle --route route-123 --output /tmp/route-123-cache-bundle.tgz

References:
- Local prefetch proxy PRD (internal): requirements/local-prefetch-proxy-prd-2028-10-04
- Hybrid cache coordinator design: design-specs/hybrid-cache-coordinator-design-spec-2029-06-15

This playbook will be updated iteratively as pilot data arrives and heuristics are tuned. For feature requests or questions, contact the owners listed above.

payload.page_title: Escape Hatch: Congestion Decompression & Kernel Handshake Manual

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's official "escape hatch" strategy for handling sustained congestion and kernel saturation: a coordinated congestion decomposition and kernel-handshake protocol that (1) reduces tail-latency exposure, (2) preserves critical SLOs by controlled fidelity degradation, and (3) provides a clear operator runbook for diagnosing and recovering from congestion events. The guidance spans runtime architecture trade-offs, scheduler/kernel interactions, profiling checks, benchmark validation, release notes for v0.14 of the handshake protocol, and a known-issues appendix.

Why this exists

- Congestion is multi-dimensional: CPU/host networking, GPU kernel throughput, KV cache pressure, and admission-controller throttles interact and can amplify tail latency.
- Previous ad-hoc mitigations (global queue cuts, blunt shedding) risked client-visible errors or large quality regressions.
- This manual codifies a minimal, observable, and reversible path — the "escape hatch" — that runtime and operations can use without full-scale rollback.

Scope and owners

- Scope: Serving runtime (request orchestration, scheduler/kernel admission, KV cache warmup), telemetry contracts between runtime and scheduler, operator runbook.
- Owners: runtime-scheduler (primary), kernel-engineering (secondary), eng-sre (oncall runbook), observability (telemetry contract).

Key concepts (short)

- Congestion decomposition: Break an incident into orthogonal stressors (kernel queueing, KV miss storm, network slope) and treat each with targeted mitigations.
- Kernel handshake: A lightweight per-request negotiation between dispatcher and kernel to confirm admission and a fidelity/priority token.
- Escape hatch stages: 1) Soft-cohort shaping, 2) Priority-aware fidelity staircasing, 3) Kernel offload (batch-eviction + fallback model), 4) Emergency rejection (last resort).

Architecture overview

1) Dispatcher -> Scheduler -> Kernel handshake flow

- Dispatcher issues a pre-admit probe to scheduler with metadata: model_id, sequence_length_est, client_priority_tier, kv_prefetch_hint, trace_id.
- Scheduler responds with a handshake token: {admitted: bool, expected_wait_ms: int, fidelity_profile: string, kernel_slot_hint: id, trace_flags}.
- Dispatcher attaches token to the request and routes to the claimed kernel node. Kernel validates the token (nonce + timestamp) before binding resources.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Avoids blind offload: kernels only begin expensive work once token validated.
- Enables admission-time decisions (expected wait) surfaced to callers and observability.

2) Congestion decomposition surface points

- Kernel queueing: long kernel start latency despite short network and dispatch times.
- KV cache miss storm: many cold sessions with repeated kv-prefetches causing memory pressure and eviction churn.
- Dispatcher/multiplex contention: overloaded event loop or slow gRPC channels.
- Network backpressure: transient NIC saturation or cross-AZ variance.

Telemetry contract (required signals)

- Required per-request fields (exported to traces/metrics): pre_admit_ts, handshake_issue_ts, handshake_response_ts, kernel_bind_ts, kernel_start_ts, kernel_complete_ts, kv_miss_count, admitted_fidelity_profile, kernel_slot_id, tv_cpu_ms, gpu_busy_ms.
- Aggregates/alerts: 95/99/99.9 kernel_bind_time; kv_miss_ratio over 2-minute windows; admission_reject_rate; per-model fidelity-downgrade-rate.

Escape hatch stages (detailed)

Stage 0 — Detection
- Triggers (any one): 99.9 kernel_bind_time > 500ms for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows OR kv_miss_ratio > 0.25 AND error_rate increase > 0.5%.
- Action: escalate to oncall, annotate traces with incident_id, and enable enhanced sampling for affected models.

Stage 1 — Soft-cohort shaping (fast, reversible)
- Goal: Reduce inflow rate using priority-aware shaping and client-visible hints.
- Steps: 1) Scheduler flips cohort-shaped admission (80% of low priority requests are moved to a rate-limited queue). 2) Emit a 429-with-hint response that instructs SDK to backoff + optionally switch to smaller max_tokens.
- Expected impact: 20–40% kernel queue reduction within 30s.

Stage 2 — Priority-aware fidelity staircasing (controlled quality tradeoff)
- Goal: Reduce per-token kernel work for non-critical requests.
- Steps: 1) For affected kernels, inject fidelity_profile override via handshake token (e.g., quantized-8b-fast, llm-lite-summary). 2) Scheduler ensures canary A/B percentages for fidelity change (default 5% -> 25% -> 50% per 2-minute steps). 3) Monitor quality regressions using sentinel prompt set evaluation (see profiling section).
- Rollback: automatic if quality alert > threshold or error rate increases.

Stage 3 — Kernel offload and fallback routing
- Goal: Preserve SLOs by moving some load off saturated kernels to compatible fallback variants (smaller model, different GPU class, CPU-based short-run).
- Steps: 1) Router consults fallback_matrix for model compatibility. 2) For in-flight requests with long expected wait, router reissues handshake to fallback kernel with incremental fidelity. 3) Upgrade path: when capacity returns, tokens expire and dispatcher resumes original routing.

Stage 4 — Emergency rejection (last resort)
- Goal: Prevent catastrophic cascade and maintain control plane stability.
- Steps: 1) Admission controller returns structured rejection with exact reason code and safe duration. 2) Operators run immediate remediation (kernel drain, node reboot, capacity surge via Dedicated burst policy).

Operator runbook (step-by-step)

1) Triage (first 5 minutes)
- Open incident and tag affected models.
- Run quick decomposition checklist: check kernel_bind_time, kv_miss_ratio, dispatch loop latency, NIC metrics.
- If kernel_bind_time is primary, apply Stage 1. If kv_miss_ratio is primary, apply Stage 1 and enable KV-prefetch backoff.

2) Apply Stage 2 (if Stage 1 insufficient)
- Use admin CLI to apply fidelity overrides for model X in zone Y:

- CLI example:
  rwdctl runtime handshake override --model xlarge-1 --zone us-west-2 --profile quant8-fast --fraction 0.25 --reason "incident-<id>"

3) Escalate to kernel-engineering if kernel_busy_ms continues > 90% for > 5 minutes. Provide trace ids and sample payloads.

4) Recovery & validation
- Monitor sentinel prompt set regression suite (see Profiling checks below).
- Gradually remove overrides once 95/99 kernel_bind_time back within SLO for 10 consecutive 1-minute windows.

Profiling & benchmark verification

- Purpose: ensure any fidelity changes do not create unacceptable quality regressions, and that kernel handshake yields expected latency improvements.

1) Sentinel prompt set (operational)
- A curated set of 200 prompts per model capturing worst-case sequence lengths, KV dependence, and multi-turn. Run with fidelity variants and compare: exact match rate, BLEU-like similarity, and latency distribution.
- Baseline run command (local harness):
  python perf_harness.py --model xlarge-1 --profile quant8-fast --concurrency 50 --duration 5m --tracing

2) Microbenchmarks for handshake overhead
- Expectation: pre-admit handshake roundtrip adds <= 2ms median and <= 10ms p99.
- Test procedure: run a short synthetic workload with handshake enabled and disabled; measure kernel_bind_time delta.

3) End-to-end shadow test
- Mirror 2% of production traffic to a sandbox fleet with handshake and fidelity staircasing enabled. Observe divergence metrics over 30 minutes and ensure error delta < 0.2%.

Release notes (protocol v0.14)

- New: per-request handshake token with nonce/timestamp and fidelity_profile field.
- New: scheduler sampling flag handshake_verbose that enables extra telemetry for incident triage.
- Change: default pre-admit threshold lowered from 200ms to 150ms for high-priority tiers.
- Fix: race between token expiry and kernel_bind that could cause stale admissions under high-clock-skew.

Known issues (short appendix)

- ISSUE-1134: KV prefetch backoff sometimes over-throttles cold-start interactive sessions. Workaround: increase per-account warmup budget for 5 minutes.
- ISSUE-1187: Handshake round-trip may exceed 10ms for cross-AZ dispatch in certain AZ pairings due to suboptimal route selection; mitigation: prefer intra-AZ routing for handshake where available.
- ISSUE-1210: Some third-party SDKs ignore 429-with-hint and aggressively retry causing repeated admission attempts. Mitigation: server responds with Retry-After and stream-close flag; recommend SDK update.

Operational checklists (cheat-sheet)

- Detection: run `rwdctl metrics query --metric kernel_bind_p99 --window 5m --model <model>`
- Apply soft shaping: `rwdctl runtime admission shape --model <model> --cohort low --rate-limit 20rps`
- Apply fidelity override: `rwdctl runtime handshake override --model <model> --profile quant8-fast --fraction 0.25`
- Validate sentinel suite: `python perf_harness.py --model <model> --profile <profile> --sanity`

Post-incident follow-up (RCA template)

- Description: short summary of what triggered the escape hatch and which stage was used.
- Root cause decomposition: kernel-binding vs kv-miss vs dispatch.
- Evidence: traces, metrics, CLI actions taken, timestamps.
- Remediation: code change, scheduler tuning, capacity adjustment.
- Preventative experiments: shadow runs, benchmark expansion.

Appendix: JSON handshake token example

{
  "token": "rwd-tn-1234abcd",
  "admitted": true,
  "expected_wait_ms": 48,
  "fidelity_profile": "quant8-fast",
  "kernel_slot_hint": "k-az3-7",
  "issued_at": "2026-10-03T15:12:22Z",
  "nonce": "f3b9a2",
  "sign": "sha256:..."
}

Appendix: Quick signal glossary

- kernel_bind_time: time between handshake_response_ts and kernel_bind_ts.
- kv_miss_ratio: fraction of requests that encountered at least one KV miss in the warmup window.
- admitted_fidelity_profile: the effective fidelity the kernel will run.

Related pages and references

- See runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog for incident classification.
- See runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook for integrated rollback patterns.

Revision history

- 2026-02-15 (A. Menon): initial draft describing handshake concept and stage flow.
- 2026-04-30 (D. Chen): added telemetry contract and CLI examples.
- 2026-10-03 (A. Menon): published; added sentinel profiling suite and v0.14 release notes.
