payload.page_title: Demand Signal Fusion and Burst Resilience Manual

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a practical approach for fusing heterogeneous demand signals (telemetry, request semantics, tenant profiles) to make deterministic, explainable decisions during traffic bursts. It pairs decision heuristics with concrete alert rules, scaling actions, and integration examples for our operational tooling (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Capacity Orchestrator). The goal is to preserve customer-facing SLOs while minimizing cost and churn during transient and sustained traffic events.

Scope

- Audience: SREs, oncall, runtime engineers, product owners for latency-sensitive endpoints.
- Systems covered: inference-gateway, batching-service, model-warm-pool, admission-controller, capacity-orchestrator.
- Not covered: billing reconciliation, legal/customer communications (see customer-success).

Definitions

- Demand signal: any metric or event that correlates with upcoming or current request load (examples below).
- Burst: a >3x baseline increase in RPS or token-rate sustained for >30s and <30m.
- Surge: burst that continues >30m.
- Headroom: available capacity reservable for latency-sensitive tenants without violating SLOs.

Key telemetry & signals to fuse

1) Ingress signals (real-time):
   - rps_total, rps_per_route, token_rate
   - queue_depth (per route / per pod)
   - request_duration_p50/p95/p99

2) Backend resource signals:
   - gpu_utilization, gpu_memory_pressure, host_load_1m
   - model_kv_cache_hit_rate, model_warm_pool_free_slots

3) System events & semantic signals:
   - model_variant_fallbacks (counts)
   - tenant_priority_header (high/standard/low)
   - large-batch-job-submitted (boolean/event)

4) External signals (optional):
   - scheduled-marketing-campaigns (calendar feed)
   - infra-degradation (cloud provider health API)

Fusion heuristics (high level)

- Short-window aggregation: compute 15s rolling window aggregates for RPS/token_rate and 60s for queue_depth and GPU metrics.
- Priority-weighting: multiply tenant-specified priority weight (2.0 high, 1.0 standard, 0.5 low) when calculating effective demand.
- Signal consensus: escalate to SRE action if >=2 independent signals cross thresholds (ingress + backend or ingress + model_kv cache drop).
- Burst classification:
  - transient: burst duration < 30s — prefer local admission and soft-throttling.
  - sustained-burst: 30s–30m — prefer warm-pool expansion and non-disruptive routing.
  - surge: >30m — engage reserved capacity and formal capacity reallocation.

Decision matrix (example)

| Observed condition (consensus) | Immediate action (automated) | Escalation threshold | Oncall action | Rationale |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 3x RPS spike, queue_depth < 50, GPU utilization < 60% | Increase concurrent batch window by +20% on low-prio routes | N/A | Monitor | Use batching to accept transient increase without new capacity |
| 5x RPS, queue_depth > 200, kv_cache_hit_rate < 70% | Trigger warm-pool: +2 warm GPUs; mark low-prio tenants degraded | 90s sustained | Page SRE | Warm pool reduces cold starts and stabilizes latency |
| Backend GPU mem pressure > 85% and p99 latency rising | Evict background batch jobs; enable shed-on-low-priority=true | immediate | Page SRE | Maintain SLOs for high-priority tenants |
| Surge > 30m with sustained error budget burn > 5% | Activate reserved capacity swap (capacity-orchestrator) | sustained 30m | Page + Alert customer-facing comms owner | Ensure durable capacity; coordinate with sales/CS |

Concrete thresholds (recommended starting point)

- rps spike factor: 3.0 (burst), 5.0 (critical)
- queue_depth critical: 200 requests total across cluster
- kv_cache_hit_rate warning: < 80% ; critical: < 70%
- gpu_utilization critical: > 90% for >120s
- model_warm_pool_free_slots low: < 10% of pool size

Prometheus alert examples

1) Burst-detection rule (15s window):

ALERT BurstDetected
IF increase(requests_total[15s]) / avg(requests_total[5m]) > 3
FOR 15s
LABELS { severity = "warning", category = "demand" }
ANNOTATIONS { summary = "Detected 15s RPS spike >3x baseline" }

2) KV cache degradation alert:

ALERT KVCacheDegradation
IF avg_over_time(model_kv_cache_hit_rate[1m]) < 0.75
FOR 30s
LABELS { severity = "critical", category = "model" }
ANNOTATIONS { summary = "KV cache hit rate below 75%" }

Operational tooling integrations

- Capacity Orchestrator (CO): define policies for warm-pool expansion, reserved-capacity swaps, and preemptible eviction. Example policy snippet YAML (CO):

policy_name: burst-warmup
min_warm_gpus: 2
max_warm_gpus: 8
scale_step: 2
scale_cooldown: 90 # seconds
triggers:
  - metric: kv_cache_hit_rate
    operator: lt
    value: 0.75
    window: 60s
  - metric: queue_depth
    operator: gt
    value: 150
    window: 30s

- Admission Controller: add a soft throttle knob that reduces allowed concurrency for low-priority tenants by a configurable fraction. Example CLI to simulate:

# reduce low-priority concurrency by 50%
./admctl set-tenant-guardrail --tenant-group low --concurrency-factor 0.5 --reason "burst response"

Runbook: immediate triage for an ongoing burst (15–90s window)

1) Verify the signals: check the four categories above and confirm consensus (at least two). Quick checklist:
   - Grafana dashboard: rps_total, queue_depth, p99 latency, gpu_utilization, kv_cache_hit_rate.
   - Prometheus alerts firing: BurstDetected OR KVCacheDegradation.
2) Apply non-disruptive mitigations (automated preferred):
   - Increase batching concurrency on low-priority routes (automated via API)
   - Trigger warm-pool expansion by policy: CO API -> apply policy "burst-warmup"
3) If latency still rising after scale_step with 60s cooldown, escalate to SRE (page) and mark affected tenants with degraded_status=true in topology db.
2) Document actions in incident tracker ticket and tag: demand-fusion-burst.

Runbook: sustained surge (30m+)

1) Confirm sustained signals and error budget burn. Calculate projected error budget depletion using current burn rate.
2) Initiate reserved capacity swap: call CO runbook: swap reserved for inference-gateway.
3) Coordinate with Product & CS for messaging if any high-priority customers may be impacted.
4) Kick off an incident review with a hypothesis: root cause = demand mismatch vs provisioning; include signal fusion artifact.

Post-incident review checklist (required for any burst that caused SLO degradation):

- Attach the fused-signal log (see logging spec below) to the postmortem.
- Validate that decision matrix mapping matched observed outcome or document deviations.
- Update thresholds if false positives/negatives contributed to delay.
- Schedule a 2-week follow-up to run a controlled surge replay in staging.

Fused-signal logging spec (single-line JSON per event)

- Fields (flat key set): timestamp, window_start, window_end, rps_total, rps_factor_vs_baseline, queue_depth, gpu_util, kv_cache_hit_rate, warm_pool_free_slots, consensus_signals, action_taken, action_origin, action_id

Example (single-line JSON stored in log-index):
{ "timestamp":"2026-12-03T14:12:05Z", "window_start":"2026-12-03T14:11:50Z", "window_end":"2026-12-03T14:12:05Z", "rps_total":"4200", "rps_factor_vs_baseline":"3.6", "queue_depth":"240", "gpu_util":"88", "kv_cache_hit_rate":"0.68", "warm_pool_free_slots":"1", "consensus_signals":"[ingress,model]", "action_taken":"warm-pool-scale+2,evict-background-jobs", "action_origin":"automated-policy:burst-warmup", "action_id":"co-20261203-001" }

Tooling validation & test harnesses

- Synthetic replay: use the burst-replay tool to re-ingest recorded ingress traces with modulated RPS and tenant-priority weights. Command example:

burst-replay --trace-id 2026-11-30-bigtth --rps-multiplier 4 --tenant-weight high:1.5,low:0.5 --duration 5m

- Canary test: before applying new thresholds in production, run a canary in a shadow cluster that mirrors 2% of traffic and verify fused-signal decisions for at least 3 synthetic bursts.

Ownership & SLA alignment

- Owners: SRE runtime (primary), Serving Runtime (secondary), Capacity Orchestrator team (policy maintenance).
- SLO implications: ensure that actions preserve p99 latency SLO for high-priority tenants 99.95% monthly. If preserved only via degradation of low-priority tenants, record that as controlled remediation.

Change control & rollout guidance

- All threshold changes require: unit tests in alerting harness, a canary run (2% traffic mirror) for 72 hours, and a post-canonical runbook review with SRE lead.
- Emergency tweak path: oncall SRE can bypass canary if >5% error budget at 24h projection; document the reason in the incident ticket.

Appendix: quick reference commands

- Force warm pool expansion (CO):
  curl -XPOST https://co.internal/api/v1/policies/burst-warmup/trigger -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CO_TOKEN'

- Evict background batch jobs:
  ./batchctl evict --label background=true --max-evict 5

- Read fused-signal logs for time range:
  es-query "index=fused-signals AND @timestamp:[2026-12-03T14:00 TO 2026-12-03T15:00]"

Change log

- 2026-11-12: Initial draft and policy sketches (created).
- 2026-12-10: Added Prometheus rules and logging spec (review by Asha Patel).
- 2027-01-09: Published with CO policy YAML and runbook refinements (finalized).

Related resources

- Capacity playbooks: ../capacity-planning/demand-profile-curation-and-headroom-policy-2026.json
- SLO governance: ../slo-and-error-budgets/slo-provenance-and-incident-evidence-catalog-2025.json
- CO policy docs: ../operational-tooling/capacity-orchestrator-and-slo-reconciliation-cookbook-2026.json

Contacts

- Oncall SRE rotation: #sre-oncall Slack channel
- Capacity Orchestrator pager: CO-pager (ops-genie)
- Document owner: Daniel Kim (daniel.kim@redwood.com)

payload.page_title: SLO Shadowing and Capacity Canary Framework

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose
This page documents the SLO Shadowing and Capacity Canary Framework: a lightweight, repeatable pattern SREs and service owners can use to validate SLO behavior, verify capacity plans, and exercise graceful-degradation paths before wide rollouts. The framework bridges correctness (SLO observability) and capacity safety (canarying load on a controlled pool).

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference services and multi-tenant routing layers (hosted API, Dedicated pools).
- Primary focus: production-similar traffic replay, progressive capacity ramping, and SLO metric shadow evaluation.
- Not intended for full security/compliance certification or long-term load testing (use dedicated performance harness).

Key principles
- Shadow, don’t disturb: shadowed SLO evaluation must not affect real traffic paths or budgets.
- Small, measurable steps: ramp canaries using discrete capacity increments (5% -> 20% -> 50%).
- Observability-first: each canary must have a dashboard and pre-defined stop/rollback criteria.
- Actionable alerts: SLO guardrails convert directly to runbook steps.

Terminology
- Shadow SLO: running the SLO evaluation logic in parallel against a mirrored stream of requests to measure expected behavior without influencing live routing decisions.
- Capacity Canary: a controlled experiment that routes a proportion of real or synthetic traffic to a target deployment to validate capacity behavior.
- Capacity Bridge: temporary autoscale and routing configuration applied during canaries to ensure controlled resource allocation.

Architecture (textual diagram)
1) Traffic Replay / Traffic Forker -> 2) Shadow Evaluator (stateless service) \u2014> metrics (SLO success, latency P50/P95/P99, token cost)

                                          +-> 3) Canary Pool (isolated nodes) -> realtime metrics (GPU utilisation, queue length)

Components and responsibilities
- Traffic Forker: duplicates a sample of incoming production requests to the shadow stream. Responsible: service owner.
- Shadow Evaluator: computes SLO checks (latency, error classification, output sanity). Responsible: eng-platform / observability.
- Canary Orchestrator: applies Capacity Bridge, controls percentage routing, and records experiment metadata (owner, start/stop, commit). Responsible: eng-sre.
- Metric Collector / Analyzer: composite dashboards and automated stop triggers. Responsible: observability team.

SLOs evaluated in shadowing
- Latency SLO: p95 < 1200ms for short-text generation routes; p99 < 2500ms for long contexts.
- Correctness SLO (syntactic): 99.5% pass rate on structural output checks (valid JSON, schema conformance).
- Error SLO: < 0.5% 5xx rate across evaluated routes.
- Cost guardrail: 95th token-cost-per-request must not exceed baseline by > 25% during canary.

Pre-run checklist (must be green before starting)
1) Owner and experiment name recorded in the Canary Orchestrator.
2) Observability dashboards instantiated with baseline comparisons.
3) Canary pool capacity allocated (minimum 3 nodes for redundancy).
4) Alerting hooks configured: stop/rollback thresholds for each SLO metric.
5) Synthetic traffic blocks validated and alignment with sampled production traffic verified.

Canary run procedure (step-by-step)
1) Initialize: tag experiment and capture baseline metrics (last 24h).
2) Shadow-only validation (0% real routing): run shadow evaluator on real-time fork; verify SLO differences <= 2x acceptable drift.
3) Synthetic soak (5% equivalent load): use replay generator to apply 5% of peak qps to canary pool with Capacity Bridge protections in place. Observe for 30 minutes.
4) Progressive ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% (30-minute holds or until steady-state). At each step evaluate:
   - latency p95/p99 delta vs baseline
   - error rate and error classification (model timeout, OOM, networking)
   - queue length and GPU util
   - cost per token delta
5) Stop/rollback criteria (automatic):
   - latency p99 > baseline p99 * 2 for two consecutive windows (5m)
   - 5xx rate > 1% sustained for 10m
   - GPU queue length > 2x steady baseline or OOMs observed
   - cost-per-token exceeds guardrail for 3 consecutive evaluation windows
6) If all checks pass at 50% hold, schedule full rollout gating (hand-off to deployment and product QA).

Incident and post-failure runbook (short)
- If automated rollback triggers:
  1) Canary Orchestrator drains canary pool and re-routes traffic back to baseline nodes.
  2) SRE runbook: collect trace slices for failed window, capture kernel/scheduler logs, dump KV cache metrics.
  3) Annotate experiment with failure reason tags (latency, OOM, model-regression).
  4) Open a triage issue in the SLO regression board and assign to owner.

Data and metrics to collect
- request_id, route, tenant_id (hashed for privacy), request_size_tokens, response_tokens, model_variant, backend_node, start_ts, end_ts, result_code, error_class
- resource metrics: gpu_util_pct, gpu_mem_used_mb, preemption_events, queue_depth, docker_restart_count
- derived SLO metrics: success_rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, token_cost_per_request

Example stop-condition PromQL snippets (examples for observability team)
- p99 latency spike (5m rolling):
  avg_over_time(service_latency_p99[5m]) > (baseline_p99 * 2)
- elevated 5xx rate (10m):
  increase(http_server_errors_total{code~"5.."}[10m]) / increase(http_requests_total[10m]) > 0.01

Safety engineering: Capacity Bridge configuration (sample table)
| config_key | recommended_value | rationale |
|-----------|-------------------:|----------|
| min_nodes | "3" | maintain redundancy during canary |
| reserve_cpu_pct | "20" | headroom for autoscaler spikes |
| reserve_gpu_mem_mb | "1024" | avoid OOM boundary conditions |
| probe_interval_s | "30" | quick detection of regressions |

Ownership and governance
- Canary orchestration owner: eng-sre / capacity-sig.
- Shadow evaluator maintenance: observability team.
- Service owners must sign off on final rollouts and confirm acceptable correctness thresholds.
- Quarterly review: every team runs at least one SLO shadow + capacity canary for high-impact routes.

Operational tooling snippets
- Start a named canary with the orchestrator CLI:
  rdo canary start --name "chatv2-slo-shadow-2026-01" --service "chatv2" --pool "canary-gpu-n1" --ramp "5,20,50" --hold-min 30
- Query shadowed SLO output (example JSON):
  {
    \"experiment\": \"chatv2-slo-shadow-2026-01\",
    \"p95_latency_ms\": \"890\",
    \"p99_latency_ms\": \"1320\",
    \"error_rate\": \"0.21%\"
  }

Rollout gating checklist (pre-decision)
- Shadow SLO drift within expected bounds (owner confirmation).
- Canary pool metrics stable for one canary hold period.
- Cost impact acceptable to finance guardrail.
- Post-canary signoff: service owner + eng-sre + observability.

Postmortem template for canary failures (condensed)
- Title, experiment id, owner, start/stop times
- Observed symptoms and metric deltas (attach dashboard snapshots)
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (kernel logs, model regression diffs)
- Action items (short/medium/long-term) with owners and ETA
- Test plan to validate fix (including shadow re-run)

Appendix: small examples and heuristics
- Use a hashed tenant_id when collecting telemetry for customer-sensitive services.
- For models with long runtimes (>= 10s), length-aware SLO windows (p95 over 1h) are recommended.
- If canary detects model quality regressions, run A/B evaluation harness against curated prompt set before any scaling decisions.

Related resources
- Link: SLO rollout readiness checklist (internal)
- Link: Observability SLO pipeline design

Revision history
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft (Evelyn Chen).
- 2025-11-03: Added Capacity Bridge config and automated stop criteria (Marcus Li).
- 2026-01-15: Clarified shadow-only validation step and updated PromQL examples (Aisha Patel).

payload.page_title: Token Evidence Sampling and SLO Assertion Runbook

sections.body:
Overview

This runbook describes Redwood Inference’s standardized approach to token-level evidence sampling, SLO assertion at token granularity, and operational playbooks for investigating SLO regressions that are driven by inference workload characteristics (sequence length variability, quantization noise, cache-hit patterns). The goal is to enable high-fidelity SLO debugging without overwhelming telemetry storage and to provide a deterministic triage path when token-level signals are required for incident review or postmortem evidence.

Intended audience
- SREs owning model-serving SLOs and telemetry
- Runtime engineers implementing sampling hooks
- Observability/infra engineers operating metrics/trace pipelines
- Incident commanders (ICs) during degradation events

When to use this runbook
- P95/P99 latency, and token-error SLOs show unexplained drift
- Regression alerts that correlate with longer sequence length or higher KV-cache-miss rates
- Post-incident evidence requests from customers or compliance that require token-level context

Definitions and goals
- Token evidence: a compact per-request artifact capturing sequence length, per-token latencies (aggregated), model-variant id, quantization profile tag, KV-cache hit flag, and a short prompt-hash.
- Assertion window: time window used to evaluate an SLO (examples: 1h rolling, 7d rolling).
- Target SLOs for model-serving (examples; your service may vary):
  - Availability: successful responses >= 99.95 over 7d
  - Latency p99 (end-to-end): <= 400 ms for short-context (<=128 tokens) requests
  - Token-level processing latency p99: <= 8 ms/token

Telemetry strategy and sampling tiers
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Baseline aggregate metrics (always-on)
- What: per-route counters and histograms (requests, errors, latency buckets, token-rate histograms, cache hit ratio).
- Retention: 90d for histograms and 365d for aggregated daily summaries.
- Purpose: produce SLO dashboards and alerts without token evidence.

2) Adaptive token sampling (targeted, 0.1%–5% global depending on load)
- Trigger conditions:
  - Rolling burn-rate > 0.5 (medium) OR
  - p99 latency breach on short-context route OR
  - Canary traffic during rollouts (all canary traffic sampled at 100%)
- What: per-request token evidence blob (compact JSON with per-token latency deciles, sequence length, model_variant, quant_profile, cache_flags, prompt-hash).
- Target global overhead: 0.5% of requests normal; adjustable by route and priority.
- Retention: 14d full token blobs; 180d summarized token deciles only.

3) Forensic capture (on-demand, 100% for targeted tenant/route during incident)
- Activated by an SRE runbook step or incident commander.
- What: full token traces including token-level logits snapshots for up to 1k tokens, request/response payloads (subject to privacy rules).
- Retention: 30d or as directed by incident/legal. Requires approval from Security for customer-sensitive data.

Sampling configuration examples
- Global adaptive sampling policy (YAML):

sampling_policy: |
  version: 2
  default_rate: 0.005                # 0.5% baseline
  triggers:
    - name: slo_burn_medium
      condition: burn_rate > 0.5
      rate: 0.02                    # 2% while burning
    - name: short_context_p99_breach
      condition: route_context == \"short\" AND latency_p99 > 400
      rate: 0.05
    - name: canary_all
      condition: traffic_tag == \"canary\"
      rate: 1.0
  max_storage_gb_per_day: 80

- Runtime toggle (CLI):
  rwoodctl telemetry sampling set --service model-runtime --policy-file /etc/telemetry/adaptive-sampling.yaml

Metric names and labels (canonical)
- inference.requests.count{route, tenant, model_variant}
- inference.responses.success{route, tenant} (boolean)
- inference.latency.ms.histogram{route,tenant,context_size_bucket}
- inference.token.latency.ms.quantiles{model_variant,quant_profile}  # token-level summaries
- inference.kv.cache_hit_ratio{model_variant,route}  # 0..1
- inference.token_evidence.captured{route,tenant,sampling_tier}

Alerting and SLO assertion examples
- Alert for p99 latency:
  - Expression (Grafana/PromQL-like):
    sum_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(inference.latency.ms.histogram[5m]))[1h:]) / ignoring() > 400
  - Initial IC action: check token sampling rate, routing failures, and cache-hit ratios. If adaptive sampling active, examine token evidence for last 1h.

- Burn-rate escalation thresholds and actions:
  1) burn_rate > 1.0 (critical): trigger high-priority incident, enable forensic capture for affected tenants, notify product and customer success.
  2) 0.5 < burn_rate <= 1.0 (warning): increase adaptive sampling rate to 5% for affected routes for 30 minutes and evaluate root-cause.

Runbook: step-by-step triage (p99 latency breach)
1) Initial evidence collection (0–5 minutes)
  - Verify alert source and timespan.
  - Confirm current sampling_policy: rwoodctl telemetry sampling get --service model-runtime
  - Pull aggregate metrics for the route: cpu, memory, qps, latency histograms, kv cache ratio.
  - If burn_rate > 0.5, set adaptive sampling rate to 2x default for 30m: rwoodctl telemetry sampling patch --route <route> --rate 0.02 --duration 30m
\2) Inspect token evidence (5–20 minutes)\  - Query recent token evidence blobs:
    ES query example: POST /_search?q=route:<route> AND @timestamp:[now-1h TO now]&size=100
  - Look for: sudden shift in median sequence length, percentile token latency skew (p95/p99 token latency increases), high cache-miss rate per request.
  - If token evidence shows consistent model_variant change, check rollout/traffic-routing config.
\3) Short fixes (20–60 minutes)\  - If a new model variant causes degradation: rollback to previous stable model and monitor.
    - rwoodctl model rollout rollback --route <route> --to-version <previous>
  - If cache-miss increase: restart KV-cache workers for the model shard (see KV-cache runbook) and monitor cache-hit metrics.
  - If quantization profile mismatch: pin requests to non-quantized variant and notify model-onboarding.
\4) Forensic (if needed)\  - If evidence insufficient, escalate to forensic capture: IC opens an incident board and requests Security approval if request payloads contain PII.
  - Enable forensic capture for tenant X: rwoodctl telemetry capture start --route <route> --tenant <tenant> --duration 2h --level forensic
\5) Post-incident evidence package and postmortem (post-incident)
  - Export token-evidence samples (CSV + summarized deciles) and attach to the incident.
  - Correlate with deployment timeline, autoscaler events, and cross-region routing decisions.
  - Make a concrete remediation: sampling tuning, SLO adjustment, model rollback, autoscaler tuning, or failover rules.

Privacy and retention controls
- Token evidence may contain prompt hashes only; do not store full prompt or response payloads except under forensic capture with explicit approval.
- Redact or hash any PII before indexing. The telemetry pipeline will run the redaction filter prior to storage:
  - redaction.enabled: true
  - redaction.rules: [prompt_hashing, ip_masking]

Ownership and SLAs for evidence requests
- Telemetry engineering team owns sampling platform.
- On-call SREs own immediate triage and enabling adaptive sampling during incidents.
- Forensic capture approvals are coordinated with Security and Legal for customer-sensitive requests.
- Evidence request SLA: 48 business hours for a signed customer evidence package (longer if legal review required).

Operational caveats and trade-offs
- Sampling biases: adaptive triggers can over-sample failing tenants. Always verify global and per-tenant sampling rates before drawing conclusions.
- Storage budget: keep global max_storage_gb_per_day and enforce alerting when > 80% capacity.
- Performance impact: token evidence capture should add <5% p95 latency; run regular performance benchmarks when changing capture format.

Dashboards and queries to inspect
- Dashboard: \"Token Evidence Health\" (Panels)
  - Global sampling rate over time
  - token.latency.deciles by model_variant and quant_profile
  - Cache-hit ratio and token-evidence capture events timeline
  - Forensic capture active flags per-tenant
\\- Example Elasticsearch aggregation for token p95 by model_variant (pseudo-DSL):
  {
    \"size\":0,
    \"aggs\":{
      \"by_variant\":{
        \"terms\":{\"field\":\"model_variant\"},
        \"aggs\":{
          \"p95_token_latency\":{
            \"percentiles\":{\"field\":\"token_latency_ms\",\"percents\":[95]}
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }

Change control and rollout guidance
- Any sampling policy change that modifies default_rate or max_storage must be reviewed by Observability and SRE leads.
- Roll out changes to sampling_policy gradually via canary: enable new policy for low-traffic route for 24h, validate storage/latency impact, then expand.

Known limitations
- Token evidence is not a substitute for model internals debugging (logits/time-sliced internals). Use forensic capture in those cases.
- Long-tail (rare) requests may still be missed by sampling; tune adaptive triggers accordingly.

Appendix A: Example token evidence blob (compact)
{
  \"request_id\": \"r-34a7\",
  \"timestamp\": \"2026-07-14T13:24:12Z\",
  \"route\": \"chat-short\",
  \"model_variant\": \"gptx-13b-q4\",
  \"quant_profile\": \"q4_8bit\",
  \"sequence_length\": 96,
  \"token_latency_deciles_ms\": [1.0,1.2,1.3,1.4,1.7,2.1,3.8,5.4,7.6,12.0],
  \"kv_cache_hit\": false,
  \"prompt_hash\": \"sha256:ab12...\"
}

Appendix B: Escalation contacts
- Telemetry engineering (pager): #telemetry-oncall
- Model runtime oncall: #model-runtime-oncall
- Security (approval for forensic): security-approvals@redwood.ai

Revision history
- 2025-11-02: Initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2026-01-12: Added adaptive-trigger rules and CLI examples (review Marcus Nguyen)
- 2026-07-14: Updated retention policy and forensic approval workflow (review Priya Kapoor)

payload.page_title: SLO-Capacity Escalation Synthesis Handbook

sections.body:
Overview

This handbook defines a synthesis process that ties SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, incident review standards, operational tooling, and on-call runbooks into a single escalation and remediation workflow. The goal is to provide clear, repeatable decision paths so teams can: preserve customer-facing availability, protect error-budget-funded experiments, and objectively reconcile capacity needs after SLO events.

Audience

- SREs and service owners responsible for SLOs and capacity
- On-call engineers and rotation leads
- Product and platform managers involved in SLO tradeoffs
- Observability/telemetry engineers who build tooling to automate this workflow

Summary of approach

1) Detect: automated SLO/error-budget signals from telemetry pipeline (see "Telemetry inputs").
2) Classify: map the signal to a severity and category (latency tail, availability drop, error spike, capacity saturation).
3) Escalate: invoke runbook actions per severity tier (informational -> advisory -> mandatory mitigation).
4) Contain: protective throttles, model fallbacks, or capacity soft-preemption as described in containment patterns.
5) Remediate: short-term mitigations then capacity/provisioning actions.
6) Review: incident review focused on SLO attribution and capacity reconciliation templates.

Key definitions

- SLO: Service Level Objective as measured at the customer-facing API. Expressed as the primary metric + target (e.g., p99 latency < 450ms, availability >= 99.95%).
- Error budget: Remaining allowed violations for a rolling window (typically 28 days).
- Capacity headroom: Reserved compute/GPU/IO margin kept to absorb bursts (expressed as percent of provisioned capacity).
- Escalation tier: A discrete level mapped to SLO impact, e.g., Tier 0 (informational) through Tier 3 (emergency).

Telemetry inputs

- SLO metrics: per-tenant, per-route latency quantiles (p50,p95,p99), availability, and error-rate.
- Capacity telemetry: node utilization (GPU memory, GPU SM utilization, host CPU, network egress), warm model pool occupancy, queue length, prewarm success rates.
- Cost signals: token-per-second billing delta (for hosted tiers) to detect runaway cost patterns.
- Auxiliary signals: KV cache hit rate, batching efficiency, cold-start frequency.

Classification matrix (high level)

| Symptom | Primary cause buckets | Escalation tier | Immediate action |
|---|---|---:|---|
| sustained p99 latency > target for 10m | model slowdown / memory pressure / backpressure | Tier 2 | Disable low-priority tenancies, raise warm-pool target |
| availability drop >=0.5% in 5m | control-plane or infra outage | Tier 3 | Failover region, route to fallback model variant |
| error-rate spike x10 above baseline | model regression / input encoding | Tier 2 | Disable newest model variant, revert rollout |
| GPU OOMs on serving hosts | memory leak / quantization mismatch | Tier 3 | Evict warm-pools, trigger OOM mitigation runbook |

Escalation playbook (step-by-step)

1) Alerting: Alerts are generated by the SLO observability pipeline (alerting rules live in ops/alerts repo). Each alert payload must include: service_id, route, tenant_id (if affected), metric, window, value, and computed tier.

2) Triage (5 minutes): On-call engineer performs quick triage: correlate with deployment timeline, confirm metric sanity (no ingestion gaps), and run canned telemetry queries. Use the CLI helper:

```
# quick SLO triage
ri telem query --service $SERVICE --range 10m --metrics p99,errors,cpu,gpu_mem
```

3) Mitigate (15–30 minutes): If Tier 2 or above, run mitigations from the containment catalog:

- Route-level: apply token-priority reshaping (limit low-priority traffic).
- Model-level: switch to a smaller, validated variant (automated canary rollback).
- Node-level: add temporary burst capacity from elastic reservoir pool.

CLI example to switch model variant:

```
ri deploy promote --service $SERVICE --to-variant small-v1 --reason "emergency fallback"
```

4) Capacity actions (30–90 minutes): When telemetry indicates sustained resource saturation:

- Approve burst allocation from capacity escrow (requires two approvals: oncall lead + capacity steward).
- Trigger autoscale policy override to add nodes with soft-preemption flags.
- If cloud quotas block scale, escalate to cloud-ops via the capacity escalation channel with the provisioning template below.

Provisioning template (use in cloud-ops ticket):

---
service: $SERVICE
requested_by: $ONCALL
justification: "SLO protection - p99 > target for 20m"
required_resources:
  - gpu_type: a100-80gb
    count: 6
    preemptible: true
    reason: "burst capacity"
impact_window: 4h
rollback_plan: "scale down by 50% after stabilization"
---

5) Communication (immediate): If Tier 3, notify Customer Success + Product + Security (if customer-sensitive). Use the incident notification template in the communications folder.

Containment patterns (catalog excerpt)

- Token priority lanes: assign traffic priority scores to requests and drop/shape the bottom tier under saturation.
- Model fallbacks: maintain a verified fallback variant per model family; automate traffic weight shift.
- KV prefix caching: enable cross-tenant prefix caching for deterministic prompts to reduce compute.
- Queue shedding: short-circuit long-running requests and respond with 429 + retry-after when queues exceed threshold.

Runbook templates (for service owners)

Title: <service name> - SLO Escalation Runbook\Owner: <team>\SLOs: list primary SLOs + error budget window\Contact: oncall rotation pager and secondary\Telemetry queries: ready-made queries for p99, errors, GPU mem, warm-pool occupancy\Mitigation matrix: ordered actions by tier with runbook commands and required approvers\Post-incident steps: incident review link, capacity reconciliation ticket template\nSample runbook snippet (text):

1. If p99 > target for 10 minutes -> run `ri runbook start containment --id <runbook-id>`\2. If GPU mem > 90% for 5m -> evict low-priority pools and open capacity ticket\3. If error budget < 10% -> stop non-critical experiments and notify product

Incident review standards (SLO-focused)

Every incident that consumes >5% of an error budget or causes a Tier 3 must follow the SRE incident review template:

- Timeline: include SLO metrics (windows before/after), deploys, and capacity changes\- Attribution: assign primary cause (service bug / infra / external dependency / config)\- Impact quantification: tokens/requests affected, customers impacted, estimated cost delta\- Corrective actions: short-term mitigations and long-term capacity changes (e.g., increase warm-pool size by N)\- Regression test: include a synthetic test added to the SLO harness to prevent recurrence

Deliverables from the review

- RCA document (link in the review ticket)\- Capacity reconciliation ticket with exact resource deltas and FAT (fix acceptance tests)\- SLO baseline re-evaluation (if target or measurement method needs adjustment)\- Postmortem sign-off by owner, SRE lead, and product manager

Tooling integration checklist

- Alerts emit normalized labels: service_id, route, tenant_id, escalation_tier, evidence_links\- Ticket automation: critical alerts auto-open an incident ticket with prepopulated runbook checklist\- Approvals: capacity-escrow approvals are wired to the corporate approver workflow with audit logs\- Telemetry queries embedded into alerts (so responders can click through to pre-filtered dashboards)

SLO burn detector (algorithm overview)

We use a weighted burn detector that flags non-linear spend of error budget. Core idea: compute expected burn rate given elapsed window and compare to observed burn rate. If observed >= 2x expected for 30m -> generate Tier 2 alert. Pseudocode:

```
window_days = 28
elapsed_days = days_since(window_start)
allowed_violations = window_days - target_fraction*(window_days)
expected_burn_rate = allowed_violations / window_days
observed_burn_rate = observed_violations / elapsed_days
if observed_burn_rate > expected_burn_rate * 2 and sustained(30m):
  raise_alert(tier=2, reason="accelerating error budget burn")
```

SLO and capacity reconciliation workflow (post-incident)

1) Within 24 hours: owner files capacity reconciliation ticket including exact resource deltas and justification.\2) Within 72 hours: infra schedules capacity adjustments or releases escrowed capacity.\3) Within 2 weeks: team runs a validated load test (shadow traffic or synthetic canary) to verify changes.

Decision log example (table)

| Decision | Date | Owner | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approve 6 A100 burst for inference pool | 2025-11-13 | Capacity Steward - Marcus Liu | Approved - 4h provisioning; scaled back 50% after 3h |

Ownership and escalation contacts

- Primary owner: service team (service-config owner)\- SRE escalation lead: pager on rotation (listed in oncall roster)\- Capacity steward: Marcus Liu (capacity@redwood.com)\- Observability owner: Eleni Novak

Operational playbook examples

- Routine: monthly SLO health review meeting. Agenda: SLO trend, error-budget spend, capacity forecast and planned experiments.
- Runbook rehearsal: quarterly tabletop where teams run through a Tier 2 scenario with shadow traffic.
- Chaos insertion: targeted, SLO-scoped chaos experiments in staging to validate graceful degradation paths.

Appendices

A. Quick CLI snippets
```
# Open capacity ticket
ri capacity open --service $SERVICE --reason "p99 over target" --resources a100:6 --duration 4h

# Query error budget status
ri slo status --service $SERVICE --window 28d
```

B. Example alert payload (JSON)
```
{
  "service_id": "inference-core",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "tenant_id": "public-xyz",
  "metric": "p99_latency",
  "window": "10m",
  "value": "520ms",
  "escalation_tier": 2,
  "evidence_links": ["/dashboards/…"]
}
```

C. Runbook review checklist

- Is the trigger threshold well-defined and observable?
- Are mitigation steps ordered and executable by the on-call engineer?
- Do mitigation steps include owner and approval requirements?
- Is there a clear capacity reconciliation path and deadline?
- Was the follow-up test added to the SLO harness?

How to adopt this handbook

1) Teams should mirror the runbook template into their service repos and wire the CLI commands to their automation.
2) Observability engineers should ensure alerts publish normalized labels and evidence links.
3) Capacity stewards must register escrow pools and approval delegates.

Contacts, links and references

- Capacity stewardship: Marcus Liu - capacity@redwood.com\- Observability: Eleni Novak - observability@redwood.com\- Incident review template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/post-incident-evidence-retention-and-deep-dive-playbook-2024\- Alerts repo: git@github.com:redwood/ops-alerts

Revision history

- 2025-11-12 - created by Ava Martinez\- 2026-02-08 - expanded capacity templates and added CLI snippets (reviewers: Ravi Patel, Eleni Novak)

payload.page_title: Tiered Error Amortization and Priority Reshaping Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes how Redwood SREs should amortize transient customer-facing errors across service tiers and reshape request priorities when capacity constraints threaten SLOs. The goal is to maximize overall service availability for high-value traffic while preserving a clear audit trail and post-incident evidence for error-budget reconciliation.

Scope: Applies to all multi-tenant inference control-plane services and the following serving stacks: 'realtime-router', 'batch-ingester', 'kv-cache-proxy', and 'priority-broker'. This playbook is relevant during: sustained error-budget burn, cross-cluster capacity incidents, and observed SLO regressions that correlate with priority imbalance.

Key principles
- Preserve correctness and security: prioritization must never change authz/auditing decisions.
- Deterministic, reversible actions: all automated changes create an audit event and are reversible by runbook steps.
- Favor graceful degradation: steer lower-priority work to delay or adaptive retries before hard rejection.
- Maintain customer transparency: notify affected tenants per Escalation & Communication section.

Definitions and service tiers
- Critical tier (Tier 0): control plane endpoints, authentication, billing webhook delivery. Target SLO: 99.99% availability.
- High tier (Tier 1): paid/enterprise realtime inference routes and reserved-dedicated endpoints. Target SLO: 99.9% availability.
- Standard tier (Tier 2): self-serve free/PLG realtime and standard embedding endpoints. Target SLO: 99.5% availability.
- Bulk tier (Tier 3): asynchronous batch jobs, long-running retraining/embedding jobs, non-timebound background work. Target SLO: 99.0% availability.

Signals and telemetry (what to watch)
- Metrics (prometheus names):
  - redwood_slo_error_rate_30d (by service, tier)
  - redwood_error_budget_remaining (percentage)
  - redwood_burn_rate_5m (rate multiple)
  - redwood_request_queue_latency_seconds_bucket (p99, p999)
  - p99_latency_ms (by model-variant)
  - token_consumption_rate_per_minute (tokens/min)
  - cluster_gpu_utilization_percent and node_cpu_utilization_percent
  - priority_queue_length and token_priority_score_distribution
- Alerts (example thresholds):
  1) Priority-Burn Warnings: error_budget_remaining < 15% for Tier 1 OR burn_rate_5m > 4x => notify SRE on-call (SEV4).
  2) Sustained Tier degradation: Tier 1 p99_latency_ms > 800ms for > 5m AND error_budget_remaining < 5% => SEV2 pre-incident engagement.
  3) Critical service impact: Tier 0 availability < 99.97% for 2m => SEV1 immediate escalation.

Decision matrix (high level)
- If Tier 0 impacted: take immediate protective actions (section: Immediate mitigations).
- Else if Tier 1 burn_rate > 4x and error_budget_remaining < 10%: trigger priority reshaping (automated policy + manual verification).
- Else if Tier 2 burn_rate > 6x: schedule deferred batch draining and rate limits to reduce tail latency.
- If cluster GPU utilization > 92% and queue latency p99 rising: enable token-priority shedding based on token_priority_score threshold.

Immediate mitigations (on-call play)
1) Triage and confirm scope (5 minutes): identify impacted services, tiers, model variants, and tenant subsets via dashboards: 'SLO Overview', 'Priority Ledger', 'Cluster Health'.
2) Apply protective canary routing (10 minutes): route all Tier 1 traffic to reserved-capacity pool 'dedicated-reserve-a' if available. Command:
   - kubectl annotate svc realtime-router action=route-to:dedicated-reserve-a --overwrite
3) If dedicated reserve unavailable, enable short-term conservative throttles on Tier 3 endpoints:
   - CLI example (priority-broker):
     priority-broker throttle set --tier=3 --qps=20 --reason="capacity-hedge"
4) If latency continues to climb, enable automated priority reshaper in 'traffic-shepherd' to slow or delay token-heavy requests from Tier 2/3 by adding adaptive retry-backoff headers for clients.

Priority reshaping flow (automated + manual)
- Preconditions: automated policy only eligible when error_budget_remaining < 10% for impacted tier AND operator approval flag set in 'ops-certified' vault.
- Automated steps (tooling: priority-orchestrator v2):
  1) Compute token_priority_score for each active tenant (weighted by paid status, recent SLA, and recent error budget contribution).
  2) Apply soft caps: reduce allowed concurrency by 30% for tenants with token_priority_score < 0.25.
  3) Reallocate freed concurrency to Tier 1 via 'burst-absorber' request pools with 60s lease TTL.
  4) Emit audit events to 'sre-audit-log' and notify #sre-ops channel with delta.
- Manual override: SRE lead may escalate an individual tenant by invoking:
  - priority-orchestrator override grant --tenant-id <tenant-id> --reason "sales-approved-emergency" --expires-in 3600s

Capacity planning tie-ins
- Use the 'capacity-debt ledger' to track long-term artifacts from priority shedding events. Every shedding event must create a capacity-debt item with: owner, estimated tokens delayed, expected recovery window, and follow-up remediation (e.g., scale-up, model quantization, or tenant cost-optimization).
- Quarterly exercises: run a capacity reconstitution drill that simulates a 30% reduction in available GPU capacity for 1 hour. Verify that priority reshaper + canary routing maintain Tier 1 SLOs with no more than one SEV2.

Runbook: step-by-step for a Tier 1 sustained burn (typical SEV2 scenario)
1) Confirm: validate burn signals across 3 independent telemetry sources (prometheus, edge logs, priority broker checkpoints).
2) Notify: post to status page draft and #sre-ops; include affected tenant list and preliminary ETA.
3) Protective routing: route Tier 1 traffic to dedicated-reserve pool as described above.
4) Reduce lower-priority concurrency: enact priority-orchestrator policy id 'amortize-2026-01' to reduce Tier 2 concurrency by 40%.
5) Observe for 10 minutes and check p99 and error_budget_remaining.
6) Engage product (if >30 customer impact) to coordinate temporary feature flags that reduce token use (e.g., smaller context window or response length caps).
7) If mitigation fails after 20 minutes, initiate cross-cluster failover using 'cluster-shuttle' procedure (see related_pages).
8) Record event and create capacity-debt entry.

Operational tooling (what exists and what to use)
- Priority-Orchestrator v2: policy engine for per-tenant concurrency and token budgets. Has CLI and REST control plane.
- Traffic-Shepherd: adaptive retry/backpressure service that can inject Retry-After and adjust backoff headers.
- Burst-Absorber pools: ephemeral pool allocation for short bursts; config in configmap 'burst-pools' in namespace redwood-system.
- Token-Priority Ledger (postgres): stores tenant priority scores and override history. Table schema referenced in runbook docs.
- SRE-Audit-Log (ELK): all automated changes are indexed under index 'sre-audit-v2'.

Telemetry dashboard checklist
- SLO Overview (single-pane): error_budget_remaining by tier, burn_rate_5m, p99_latency, p999_latency.
- Priority Health: token_priority_score distribution, top-30 tenants by token consumption.
- Cluster Stress: gpu_utilization, pod_eviction_rate, enqueue_time histogram.
- Audit Trail: last 100 priority-orchestrator events.

Escalation & communication templates
- Quick status post (internal #sre-ops): "[INCIDENT] Tier 1 error-budget burn: p99=850ms, error_budget_remaining=6% (5m burn_rate=7x). Active mitigations: route->dedicated-reserve-a, enacted policy amortize-2026-01. Action owner: Aisha Patel. Next update in 10m."
- Customer-facing: short note for affected customers specifying impacted tiers, mitigations, and expected recovery window created by CS lead.

Incident review and evidence standards (post-incident)
- Required artifacts: SLO signal timeline (1m granularity), priority-orchestrator event log, cluster telemetry (node-level), a sample of 5 affected request traces (edge-id + priority tag), and capacity-debt entries.
- Review template: summary, timeline, root cause, mitigation steps, owners, follow-up action items with due dates. Link to standard postmortem checklist and retro cadence.

De-escalation and recovery
- Criteria for rollback of priority-shedding: p99_latency_ms for impacted tier < 400ms for 15 consecutive minutes AND error_budget_remaining > 20%.
- Safe ramp-down: restore concurrency in 3 increments (25%, 50%, 100%) with 5 minute observation windows and automated rollback on regression.

Follow-up and capacity remediation (SRE/Infra/Product tasks)
- Short-term (within 7 days): apply temporary model-level caps, add top-10 heavy tenants to reserved pools, schedule targeted customer outreach for opt-in dedicated capacity.
- Medium-term (30–90 days): tune autoscaling policies, increase dedicated-reserve sizes, and roll optimization suggestions from Redwood Optimize (quantization / caching).
- Long-term: incorporate amortization scenarios into capacity forecasts and update the capacity-debt ledger with remediation plans and budget owner.

Testing and runbook exercises
- Monthly tabletop: SRE + Product + CS run scenario 'amortize-surge-2026' following this playbook. Objectives: ensure operator familiarity, validate dashboards, and measure mean time to safe restore.
- Chaos test: once per quarter, run a controlled GPU capacity loss experiment in staging with the priority reshaper enabled. Verify no Tier 0 regression and Tier 1 SLOs preserved.

Ownership and contacts
- Playbook owner: SRE Reliability Guild (primary contact: Aisha Patel).
- Tooling owners: priority-orchestrator (Miguel Santos), traffic-shepherd (Lena Korhonen), burst-absorber (Infra Capacity team).

Appendix A — example configs and commands
- priority-orchestrator policy snippet (YAML):
  policy: amortize-2026-01
  eligibility:
    min_error_budget_remaining: 0.0
    max_error_budget_remaining: 10.0
    min_tier: 1
  actions:
    - reduce_concurrency_by: 30
      target_tiers: [2,3]
    - reallocate_to_pool: dedicated-reserve-a

- CLI examples:
  - Check error budget: curl -s "https://observability.internal/api/v1/error_budget?service=realtime-router&window=30d" | jq .
  - Enact policy: priority-orchestrator apply --policy amortize-2026-01 --dry-run=false --requester=a.patel@redwood.ai

Change history
- 2026-02-15: Created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-03-01: Reviewed and published; added test/chaos guidance and tightened rollback criteria (Miguel Santos, Lena Korhonen).

Related documents and references
- capacity-debt ledger (internal): link to capacity-debt dashboard
- SLO playbook index: /eng-sre/runbooks/slo-provenance-and-incident-evidence-catalog-2025.json
- Priority broker design doc: /eng-sre/operational-tooling/priority-broker-design-notes-2025

End of document

payload.page_title: SLO CI gates and test harness for inference rollouts

sections.body: This document specifies the SLO-driven continuous integration (CI) gates and the reusable test harness used to validate inference service rollouts. The goal is to ensure every code or model rollout that can affect production inference SLOs is automatically checked against a repeatable set of behavioural and telemetry assertions before being promoted to canary or stable channels.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Prevent regressions in SLOs (latency, availability, correctness) from being deployed to production.
- Standardize a minimal CI gate set that is lightweight to run but representative of production traffic profiles.
- Provide a shared test harness (YAML + helper library) that teams can include in their repo or pipeline.
- Ensure CI failures produce actionable artifacts for oncall and owners.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to code, configuration, and model-version changes that touch the inference path: runtime, kernel selection, batcher, KV cache, quantization config, routing policy, and model weights.
- Does NOT replace load/stress tests and long-running chaos exercises; those remain in the capacity and resilience test schedules. CI gates are a precondition for rollout.
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- SLO assertion: a deterministic testable predicate over telemetry (for example, p95 < 120ms for 95% of requests in synthetic run).
- Gate types: unit-style smoke checks, micro-synthetic run (short inference harness), and telemetry assertions (post-run checks against metrics produced by the harness).
- Harness run: a containerized job that executes N synthetic requests using the candidate artifact and records traces/metrics to the CI telemetry sink.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
1) Latency budget: p50/p95/p99 measured against the synthetic traffic mix. Minimum acceptance: p50 <= baseline_p50 * 1.10, p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.15, p99 <= baseline_p99 * 1.25.
2) Availability: >= 99.5% of requests must return a 2xx within the timeout. Timeout = baseline_timeout + 50ms.
3) Correctness smoke: A deterministic prompt set (10-30 examples depending on model class) must produce expected structured responses (exact-match or canonical similarity threshold).
4) KV cache/consistency check: For multi-turn prompt seeds, the KV cache hit-rate should not drop below baseline - 5%.
5) Resource OOM/exception guard: No OOM or memory/CPU throttling events recorded in the harness container logs.
sections.heading: Minimum required SLO assertions (CI-level)

sections.body:
- Gate A (fast smoke, <= 60s): 10 requests, single short completion prompt, checks: availability, 1 correctness canonical case, no OOM.
- Gate B (micro-synthetic, 3–5 minutes): 1 representative traffic mix (100 requests: 60 short, 30 medium, 10 long), checks: latency p50/p95/p99 vs baseline ratios, KV cache sanity, trace sampling.
- Gate C (telemetry assertion, post-job): ingest metrics produced by harness to CI evaluation function, run statistical check versus baseline, and produce evidence bundle (traces, profiler outputs).
sections.heading: CI gate matrix (example)

sections.body:
- All projects must store a small baseline artifact in the models/ or config/ directory (JSON) that contains: baseline_p50, baseline_p95, baseline_p99, baseline_timeout, baseline_kv_hit_rate, and canonical_prompt_set_id. Baseline updates must be approved via the SLO baseline change process.
- CI jobs MUST push metrics via the standard CI telemetry API (endpoint: telemetry.ci.internal/v1/submit). The payload should include latency histogram, success/failure counters, KV hit counts, and sampled traces (trace IDs + span summary).
sections.heading: Baseline and observability requirements

sections.body:
jobs:
  slo_ci_gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Build candidate container
        run: |
          docker build -t $CANDIDATE_IMAGE .
      - name: Run SLO harness (Gate B)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -e CI=true -e TELEMETRY_SINK=$TELEMETRY_SINK $CANDIDATE_IMAGE \\n            python -m redwood_ci_harness.run --profile=inference-micro --out=/tmp/harness-output.json
      - name: Evaluate SLO assertions
        run: |
          python tools/slo_evaluator.py --input /tmp/harness-output.json --baseline baseline.json --report /tmp/slo-report.json || (cat /tmp/slo-report.json; exit 2)
      - name: Upload evidence bundle
        if: failure() || success()
        run: |
          curl -X POST $TELEMETRY_SINK/bundles -F "file=@/tmp/harness-output.json" -F "report=@/tmp/slo-report.json"
sections.heading: Example CI job (GitHub Actions-like YAML snippet)

sections.body:
1) Immediate triage: The pipeline owner (author of the MR) receives automated notification with link to evidence bundle. If pipeline is part of an automated canary pipeline, the canary is blocked.
2) Reproduce locally: Follow reproducer steps in the evidence bundle to run harness locally. Collect docker logs, traces, and profiling artifacts.
3) If latency regression: run targeted profiler against the candidate container (CPU/GPU counters, kernel usage) and compare to baseline profiler snapshot.
4) If correctness regression: run expanded canonical prompt set (50–100 examples) and produce an example diff file.
5) If OOM or infra exception: escalate to infra-oncall and attach container logs and kubernetes events.
6) If telemetry shows KV drop or cache regression: escalate to model-serving runtime owner; include policy and rollout history (quantization, kernel changes).
7) Decide: revert candidate, patch + re-run CI, or approve an exception. Exceptions must be recorded in the SLO exception ledger with justification and a compensating mitigation plan.

Evidence and artifact guidance (what CI must save on gate failure):
- harness-output.json (structured metrics & sampled traces)
- slo-report.json (assertion results and diffs)
- container logs (last 5000 lines)
- profiler snapshot (when enabled)
- minimal reproducer script with env vars and input prompts
sections.heading: Failure modes and runbook (when CI gate fails)

sections.body:
- Use two-sided relative change checks with Welch's t-test for latency means when N >= 50. For small runs, use conservative multiplicative thresholds (see minimum required SLO assertions).
- CI must run each micro-synthetic harness 3 times if results are borderline (one metric outside threshold by less than 5%) and aggregate results. If 2/3 runs exceed threshold, gate fails.
sections.heading: Statistical checking and false-positive mitigation

sections.body:
- Reuse the redwood_ci_harness Python package (internal pip) to avoid duplication. The package exposes: run_profile(name), push_metrics(sink), collect_traces(path).
- Keep canonical prompt sets in an agreed directory path: tests/ci/canonical_prompts/{model_family}/{set_id}.json
- Provide an approved baseline.json adjacent to baseline config. Baseline changes must include a changelog entry and reference to an A/B experiment if applicable.
sections.heading: Integration patterns for teams

sections.body:
- SRE operational-tooling team owns the harness library, telemetry schema, and CI gate evaluation code.
- Product/Model teams own canonical prompt sets and baseline values for their model families.
- Each repo must have an oncall contact in CODEOWNERS and a SLO-backer listed in the baseline.json.
sections.heading: Ownership and governance

sections.body:
1) Install redwood_ci_harness and include a job template in pipeline config.
2) Commit baseline.json with owner fields.
3) Add canonical_prompt_set (10–30 examples) to tests/ci/.
4) Add the evaluation step that posts evidence bundles to CI telemetry sink.
5) Run a first full gate on a PR and validate the artifacts are viewable by SRE.
sections.heading: Rollout checklist for enabling these gates on a repo

sections.body:
- Reduction in production SLO regressions caused by code/model rollouts by 40% in the first 6 months after adoption.
- Mean time to detect (pre-deploy) of regressions approaches 0 (detected in CI immediately).
- False-positive gate rate < 3% across all repos using the harness.

Appendix A — Example assertion JSON (harness-output.json simplified):
{
  "meta": { "run_id": "ci-2026-02-01-abc123", "profile": "inference-micro" },
  "latency_histogram": "(histro data omitted)",
  "p50": "78",
  "p95": "140",
  "p99": "320",
  "success_rate": "0.995",
  "kv_hit_rate": "0.82"
}

Appendix B — Common questions:
Q: How heavy should the micro-synthetic run be?
A: Keep it below 5 minutes in CI to keep feedback fast. Most teams converge on 100–300 requests depending on model latency. Use sampling to represent real mix.

Q: What if production traffic differs materially from CI synthetic mixes?
A: CI gates protect against obvious regressions; production-only skew must be covered by canary traffic profiling, chaos tests, and staging jobs that mirror production load.

payload.page_title: multi-tenant-capacity-fairshare-and-backfill-runbook-2026

sections.body:
SUMMARY
This runbook defines the operational model, procedures, and automation for fair-share capacity allocation and backfill in Redwood's multi-tenant inference fleet. It describes how SLOs and error budgets drive routing, admission control, and emergency backfill when burst demand collides with constrained capacity. The goal is to keep customer-facing SLOs stable while maximizing utilization and minimizing customer impact.

SCOPE AND AUDIENCE
- Scope: Redwood Hosted and Dedicated clusters that run the inference serving runtime (service names: agents-gateway, inference-router, serving-pool-manager, batch-cache). Excludes Private (on-prem) deployments where customer-specific policies apply.
- Audience: SREs, Platform engineers, Product owners for tiering/SLAs, Solutions Engineers for large customers.

KEY DEFINITIONS
- Tenant: a billing/customer boundary.
- SLO (per-tenant): target availability/latency objective that the tenant purchased or was assigned by default.
- Error budget: the allowed budget of errors (or latency violations) for an SLO over a rolling window (typically 30d).
- Fair-share weight: numeric weight assigned to each tenant used for proportional capacity allocation during contention.
- Backfill: short-term use of idle capacity reserved for other tenants but made available when nobody from the owning tenant uses it.

SLOS AND ERROR BUDGETS (Operational Model)
1) Canonical SLO types we monitor per-tenant:
   - Request success rate (5xx / total) — default target: 99.95% (platinum), 99.9% (gold), 99.5% (standard).
   - 95th percentile tail latency (token-response) — default targets: 200ms (platinum), 350ms (gold), 600ms (standard).
2) Error budget window: 30d rolling for latency & availability.
3) Error budget accounting: both routed and fallback responses count; synthetic probes (healthcheck) are excluded.
4) Error budget consumption (EBC) triggers:
   - EBC > 25% (amber): notify customer success and add to watchlist.
   - EBC > 50% (red): ramp-down non-critical batch jobs and reduce backfill for that tenant to 0%.
   - EBC > 80% (critical): enable protective routing (constrain burst tickets to minimal weights) and notify SRE on-call.

FAIR-SHARE CAPACITY ALLOCATION PRINCIPLES
- Baseline reservation: Platinum and Gold customers receive guaranteed reservation capacity defined in their contract. Standard customers are best-effort and rely on fair-share.
- Weighted fairness: When contention occurs, available capacity is apportioned by normalized fair-share weight W_t for each tenant t. Example: W_platinum=4, W_gold=2, W_standard=1.
- Minimum carve-outs: 10% of overall serving capacity is reserved for safety-critical system traffic (control-plane and monitoring) and cannot be backfilled.
- Backfill rules: idle reserved capacity is offered as backfill to other tenants subject to their current EBC and per-tenant backfill caps. Backfill can be revoked within 10s of owner's traffic resumption.

AUTOMATED POLICY FLOW (High-level)
1) Telemetry collector computes per-tenant utilization and EBC every 30s.
2) admission-controller consults policy engine and decides to: accept, queue, shed, or route-to-degraded-model.
3) router applies per-tenant weight + dynamic throttling token bucket.
4) If reserved owner resumes traffic, an immediate reclaim event reduces backfill traffic via a gradual drain (max 10s).

OPERATIONAL RUNBOOK (Step-by-step during capacity contention)
1) Detection: Alert "multi-tenant-capacity-pressure" fires when cluster utilization > 92% and 3+ tenants have > 10% above baseline traffic for 2 min. Pager: SRE on-call (severity P2).
2) Initial response (SRE on-call):
   a) Open triage channel: #sre-capacity (private incident thread).
   b) Run quick diagnostic:
      - CLI: rwi cluster-metrics --cluster=<id> --window=5m --format=table
      - Query: SELECT tenant, cpu_alloc, cpu_used, ebc FROM telemetry.tenant_summary WHERE window='5m';
   c) Identify top-3 contributing tenants and their EBC.
3) Mitigation actions (in order):
   - If any tenant is above critical EBC (>80%): immediately restrict its backfill to 0% via:
      curl -X POST "https://platform-api/config/tenant/<tenant-id>/backfill" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN" -d '{"backfill":0}'
   - Apply proportional throttle to non-reserved tenants per weights:
      PUT /router/throttle {"strategy":"weighted","weights": {"tenantA":4,"tenantB":2}}
   - If latency SLOs for platinum customers degrade > 20%: preempt best-effort batch jobs by setting job admission to "paused":
      kubectl patch cronjob backfill-worker -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' -n backfill
4) Communicate: post incident update to #customer-impact and notify affected CSMs with template (see Appendix B).
5) Recovery: once cluster utilization < 70% and EBCs fall by 50% from peak, revert throttles and resume paused batch jobs with a 5-minute ramp.

PREVENTATIVE CAPACITY PLANNING (Cadence & Exercises)
- Weekly: Run fair-share simulation job (job name: capacity-fairshare-sim) that replays 30 days of production tenant traces and reports expected SLO miss rates. Owners: capacity-planning team.
- Monthly: Capacity review with product and sales to reconcile reservations vs committed usage. Deliverables: capacity plan and forecast (90/95/99 percentile).
- Quarterly: Chaos test that simulates a top-customer spike (x10) to validate reclaim + backfill revocation within 10s. Documented test runbook: chaos/fairshare-spike-2026.md.

INCIDENT REVIEW AND POSTMORTEM STANDARDS (When multi-tenant contention causes SLO regressions)
- Trigger: Any incident where a platinum SLO is violated for > 10 minutes or an unplanned outage affecting > 5% of tenants.
- Postmortem template: include timeline, root cause analysis, contributing factors (policy mismatch, incorrect weights, autoscaler misconfig), impact matrix (tenants affected, duration, data lost if any), and remediation owners with due dates.
- Required artifacts: telemetry dump (30m windows), router configuration snapshot, capacity-sim outputs for the incident time window.
- RCA expectations: provide action items that are either engineering changes, policy updates, or process changes. One short-term mitigation must be defined and owned.

OPERATIONAL TOOLING AND AUTOMATION
- Policy Engine (service: policy-evaluator): stores per-tenant weights, backfill caps, and emergency rules. Config is in S3 at s3://platform-config/policies/fairshare/{env}.yaml.
- Router control API: supports dynamic throttle updates. Endpoint: /api/v1/router/controls. Auth: service account with router-admin role.
- Telemetry pipeline: transporter -> timeseries db (Influx) -> scheduler for simulations. Use the built-in emulators locally via: `make dev-telemetry`.
- Playbooks as code: All mitigation actions are codified in the automation repo (repo: infra/fairshare-ops). PRs updating runbook actions must include an integration test that uses the simulator.

KPIS, DASHBOARDS, AND ALERTS
- Dashboards: FAIRSHARE > per-tenant utilization, EBC heatmap, backfill usage, reserved reclaim events.
- Alerts: multi-tenant-capacity-pressure (P2), tenant-critical-EBC (P1 for platinum), backfill-reclaim-failure (P1).
- SLA metrics for on-call: mean reclaim latency (target <10s), successful throttle revert rate (>99%).

OWNERSHIP, ESCALATION, AND COMMUNICATIONS
- Primary Owner: eng-sre capacity team (oncall alias: eng-sre-capacity@redwood.ai).
- Secondary: infra-platform (for autoscaler issues), product-ops (for tiering disputes).
- Escalation path: SRE on-call -> capacity lead -> Head of SRE -> CTO (for customer-impacting multi-hour incidents).
- Customer comms cadence: initial ack within 30 min, status updates every 60 min until resolved, postmortem within 72 hours.

APPENDIX A — SAMPLE POLICY YAML
| tenant_id | weight | reserved_cpus | backfill_cap_pct | tier |
|-----------|--------|---------------|------------------|------|
| tenant-platinum-123 | "4" | "64" | "10" | platinum |
| tenant-gold-456 | "2" | "16" | "20" | gold |
| tenant-standard-789 | "1" | "0" | "100" | standard |

Example (s3://platform-config/policies/fairshare/prod.yaml):

---
tenants:
  - id: tenant-platinum-123
    weight: 4
    reserved_cpus: 64
    backfill_cap_pct: 10
    tier: platinum
  - id: tenant-gold-456
    weight: 2
    reserved_cpus: 16
    backfill_cap_pct: 20
    tier: gold

APPENDIX B — CUSTOMER NOTIFICATION TEMPLATE (Use for >50% EBC)
Subject: Redwood — Temporary impact to inference performance
Hi <CSM / Customer>,
We detected temporary capacity pressure affecting inference latency for some requests. We have applied controlled throttling and reduced non-critical batch work to protect your SLOs. Current status: active mitigation. Next update: in 60 minutes.
If you require a higher-availability posture, please contact your Solutions Engineer to discuss upgraded reservations.

DOCUMENT CHANGE LOG
- 2025-11-03: Created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2025-12-15: Added simulation cadence and YAML examples (reviewer: Diego Morales).
- 2026-02-20: Finalized reclaim latencies and communications cadence (reviewers: Lina Zhou, Marcus Reed).

FOR QUESTIONS OR UPDATES
Contact: eng-sre-capacity@redwood.ai or open PR in infra/fairshare-ops repo.

payload.page_title: Evaluator Sidecar Integration and Telemetry Contract

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the integration pattern, API/telemetry contract, and operational playbook for the "evaluator sidecar" — a lightweight process that runs alongside production model endpoints (hosted, dedicated, or private) to:

- capture representative probes
- run local/eager evaluations against candidate model variants
- emit standardized telemetry and quality signals
- drive local fallback and quantization-aware routing decisions

The sidecar architecture reduces time-to-detect quality regressions, improves locality of eval data, and enables private deployments to run meaningful evals without shipping raw customer data off-cluster.

Scope
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) architecture and responsibilities of the evaluator sidecar
2) event and telemetry schema (fields, cardinality, retention semantics)
3) SDK / HTTP contract for probe submission and evaluator responses
4) onboarding checklist for model owners and platform engineers
5) guardrails for quantized and KV-cache-sensitive models
6) regression triage fast path and runbook

Out of scope: long-term offline evaluation pipelines (handled by eval-harness batch runners) and human-in-the-loop labeling workflows (refer to the annotation charter).

Architecture and responsibilities

- Sidecar placement: deployed as a co-located container/process in the same pod/VM as the model serving process for low-latency access to model metrics and KV cache.
- Responsibilities:
  - Ingest a sample stream (shadow or sampled production traffic) and run lightweight probes.
  - Run targeted evals (syntactic checks, safety sentinels, coherence slices) within a fixed CPU/RAM budget.
  - Emit standardized telemetry events to the local agent/collector and the central eval ingestion endpoint.
  - Apply local fallback policies (e.g., disable quantized variant for failing slices) if configured.
  - Maintain a small rolling cache of probe inputs/responses (retention config; default 48 hours).

Telemetry contract (schema)

All telemetry events MUST be emitted as JSON objects matching the fields below. Event types: probe_request, probe_result, evaluator_health, fallback_action, quant_metric. Agents must attach a consistent trace_id for cross-correlation.
sections.heading: This page covers

sections.body:
| field | type | description | example | cardinality | retention |
|------|------|-------------|---------|-------------|-----------|
| event_type | string | One of probe_request/result/health/fallback/quant_metric | probe_result | low | 90d |
| timestamp_utc | string (ISO8601) | Event time in UTC | 2026-01-05T14:23:11Z | high | 90d |
| service_name | string | Redwood service identifier (e.g., text-gen-v1) | text-gen-v1 | low | 90d |
| model_variant | string | Model id + flavor (e.g., llama2-70b-q8) | llama2-70b-q8 | medium | 90d |
| slice_id | string | Canonical slice tag for the probe (see slice registry) | coherence-longcontext | medium | 180d |
| trace_id | string | Correlation id shared across events | abc123-xyz | high | 90d |
| probe_latency_ms | number | End-to-end latency for the probe | 124 | high | 90d |
| token_count | number | Token count produced | 48 | high | 90d |
| quality_score | number | Aggregated numeric quality score (0-100) | 82.4 | medium | 180d |
| fail_reasons | list[string] | Short codes for detected failures | ["hallucination_linked_entity"] | low | 180d |
| kv_cache_hit | boolean | Whether reply used KV cache | true | medium | 90d |
| quant_mode | string | "fp16" | "q8" | low | 90d |
sections.heading: Telemetry table (human-readable)

sections.body:
- probe_request: emitted when a probe is scheduled. Minimal payload (trace_id, slice_id, model_variant, probe_prompt_hash). Retain 7d by default.
- probe_result: emitted after the probe runs. Must include quality_score, fail_reasons (if any), and token_count. Retain 180d for auditable slices.
- evaluator_health: periodic heartbeat; includes cpu_percent, mem_mb, probe_queue_length. Retain 90d.
- fallback_action: emitted when sidecar triggers a local policy (e.g., roll back to fp16). Must include justification and TTL. Retain 180d.
- quant_metric: specialized metric for quantization degradations (coherence_delta, ngram_overlap). Retain 180d.

API / SDK contract

The sidecar exposes two endpoints on localhost for the serving process to interact with:

1) POST /v1/sidecar/probe - schedule an immediate probe\Request body (JSON):
{
  "trace_id": "string",
  "slice_id": "string",
  "prompt": "string",
  "max_tokens": 256,
  "meta": {"tenant_id": "string", "request_origin": "shadow"}
}

Response: 202 Accepted (queued) or 400 with validation errors.

2) GET /v1/sidecar/probe/{trace_id} - fetch latest probe_result by trace_id\Response body (JSON):
{
  "trace_id": "string",
  "status": "completed|failed|queued",
  "quality_score": 82.4,
  "fail_reasons": ["safety_trigger_anchor"],
  "raw_response": "string",
  "meta": {"quant_mode": "q8", "kv_cache_hit": true}
}

Implementation note: the HTTP contract must be resilient to partial failures and provide idempotent probe scheduling. The SDK wrappers (py/ts) used by platform engineers should translate local fallbacks into service-level observability events.

Resource and performance budgets

- Sidecar CPU cap: default 0.25 cores per endpoint (configurable by tier).
- Memory cap: default 256MB.
- Probe time budget: 2500ms wallclock for non-blocking probes; 90% probes must complete under 2s.
- Allowed synchronous probes (blocking the main request) must be explicitly opt-in and have a 500ms budget.

Onboarding checklist (model owners)

1) Register slices: Add commonly used slices for your model to the slice registry with owners and annotation rules. (See slice-registry template link.)
2) Define quality metrics: provide at least 3 numeric metrics (coherence, safety_pass_rate, factual_precision) and thresholds for soft/alarm/fail states.
3) Provide fallback policy: default behavior on sidecar detection (no-op, fail-open, fail-closed, quant-disable).
4) Supply probe prompts: 20 canonical probes per slice and 50 synthetic edge probes for long-tail stress testing.
5) Validate resource footprint: run the sidecar profiling harness (script below) and confirm CPU/mem requirements.
sections.heading: Event semantics and retention

sections.body:
Quantization and KV-cache guardrails

Quantized models and KV cache interactions are frequent sources of regressions. The sidecar enforces a set of safety checks before a quantized variant is marked healthy:
- coherence_delta < 6.0 (percent point drop) over a sliding 72-hour window for core slices.
- ngram_overlap >= 0.78 against fp16 baseline for instruction-following slices.
- embedding_similarity variance < 0.03 for retrieval-augmented slices.

If checks fail, sidecar MAY emit a fallback_action to disable the quantized variant locally and mark a ticket with owner_team. Fallback actions must include: justification_code, measured_delta, recommended_action, and TTL.

Quality guardrail wiring

- Soft alarms: quality_score between warning and fail thresholds; generate eval-ticket assigned to model owner with P2 priority.
- Fail alarms: quality_score below fail threshold or safety sentinel triggered; generate immediate incident with oncall. Trigger automatic canary rollback if within a canary window.

Regression triage fast path

When a production regression is detected via sidecar telemetry, follow the fast path:
1) Acknowledge alarm and capture relevant probe_result events (trace_ids).
2) Run automated bisect: compare recent promotion artifacts (model_variant commit, quant profile, kernel version) against last known-good baseline.
3) If bisect identifies candidate cause, apply short-circuit: temporarily disable quant mode or revert to previous variant for 30 minutes.
4) Create a triage Slack thread with #eval-regressions, include diagnostics bundle (probe_results, telemetry snippets, model config diff).
5) If root cause not identified in 60 minutes, escalate to SRE/platform lead and open an incident per incident process.
sections.heading: Run local evaluator sidecar profile against model socket\$ ./tools/sidecar-profile.sh --endpoint localhost:8080 --samples 100 --budget-ms 2500

sections.body:
- 10 probe_result events spanning before/after regression\- model_variant manifest (commit, quant profile id)\- kernel/runtime version\- cpu/mem utilization and sidecar health events

Runbook steps (operator-friendly)

1) Identify: filter telemetry for event_type=probe_result and quality_score < fail_threshold for the affected model_variant.
2) Isolate: if kv_cache_hit correlates with failures, temporarily flush local cache and re-run probes.
3) Mitigate: if quant_metric indicates coherent degradation, trigger fallback_action to disable quant mode.
4) Restore: after fix, run 200 synthetic probes for core slices and monitor rolling quality_score for 2 hours before re-enabling quant mode.

Ownership and SLAs

- Model owner: responsible for slice definitions, probe set maintenance, and quality thresholds. SLA: respond to P1 eval incidents within 30 minutes.
- Eval platform team: owns sidecar binaries, central ingestion, and alerting pipeline. SLA: sidecar heartbeat coverage >= 99.5% across active endpoints.
- SRE: owns operational rollbacks and capacity adjustments. SLA: execute rollback within 15 minutes of approved fallback action.

Appendices

Appendix A — Example probe_result JSON (storage event)
{
  "event_type": "probe_result",
  "timestamp_utc": "2026-01-05T14:23:11Z",
  "service_name": "text-gen-v1",
  "model_variant": "llama2-70b-q8",
  "slice_id": "coherence-longcontext",
  "trace_id": "abc123-xyz",
  "probe_latency_ms": 124,
  "token_count": 48,
  "quality_score": 72.1,
  "fail_reasons": ["coherence_drop", "ngram_mismatch"],
  "kv_cache_hit": false,
  "quant_mode": "q8"
}

Appendix B — Quick links and references
- Slice registry template: /applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/slice-registry-template
- Eval-harness runner: /applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/synthetic-workload-profiles-and-stress-protocol-2026
- Quant profile catalog: /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/quant-profile-synthesis-and-safety-playbook-2024

Change log
- 2025-03-12 (Marco Chen) initial draft
- 2025-09-18 (Aisha Patel) added quant guardrail thresholds and retention semantics
- 2026-01-05 (Priya Singh) tightened probe budget and updated SLAs
