payload.page_title: Tenant SLO contracting matrix and onboarding checklist

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the canonical SLO-to-capacity contract matrix used when onboarding new tenants to Redwood’s inference platform, plus the operational onboarding checklist runbook. The goal is to provide a repeatable negotiation and verification process that ties customer-visible SLOs to concrete capacity commitments, error-budget policies, and telemetry gates.

Scope
- Applies to hosted and dedicated tenants being onboarded by Platform/Customer Success.
- Covers initial SLO definition, capacity reservation, error-budget policy, monitoring/alerting configuration, and acceptance tests.
- Not a replacement for legal terms. This is the operational contract used by SRE / Platform to translate commercial commitments into runbookable controls.

Key definitions
- Tenant: a customer account (org) on Redwood.
- SLO: objective measured from production telemetry (availability, p99 latency, and quality where applicable).
- Error budget: allowed breach budget for a rolling 30d window unless otherwise agreed.
- Reserved headroom: pre-provisioned capacity (GPU slots / token-headroom) held for a tenant for burst absorption.

1) SLO — Capacity contract matrix (example)

| SLO name | Metric source | Quantile / target | Error budget (30d) | Reserved headroom | Escalation tier | On-call SLA |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| API availability | platform/ingress.healthy_ratio | >= 99.95% | 0.05% | 0.5 x baseline qps | Tier 1 (P0) | 1 hour |
| Text gen p99 (200 tokens) | runtime/latency_p99{model=\"rwd-gpt-4b\"} | <= 250ms | N/A (latency SLO) | 0.25 x baseline qps | Tier 1 | 1 hour |
| Embedding 95th | runtime/embedding_p95 | <= 180ms | N/A | 0.2 x baseline qps | Tier 2 | 4 hours |
| Quality regression (eval set) | quality/eval_score{promptset=\"tenant-A\"} | >= 0.92 | automatic rollback on -0.03 | N/A | Tier 2 | 4 hours |

Notes: Reserved headroom is expressed as a proportion of baseline (steady-state) QPS agreed during commercial onboarding. Baseline QPS is measured during the shadowing phase (see checklist).

2) Contract negotiation rules (operational policy)
- Default SLO template: availability 99.95% (30d), p99 latency targets per workload class, and quality gates for model-driven features.
- If a customer requires stronger SLOs, Platform must: (a) capture incremental reserved capacity required, (b) route financial uplift to Sales/Finance, and (c) enter a capacity-commitment ticket.
- Where the customer cannot pay for headroom, negotiate a reduced availability tier and add automatic fallback policies (cheaper quantized model or lower context).

3) Onboarding checklist (step-by-step runbook)
Preconditions: signed TA/contract, tenant account created, billing verified. Owner: Platform Engineer + Customer Success.

1. Discovery sync (owner: Solutions Engineer)
   - Collect workload profile: baseline QPS, peak QPS, distribution (gen/embedding), typical prompt lengths, and 99/95 token lengths.
   - Identify critical routes (e.g., chat vs. background embeddings) and data-sensitivity requirements.
2. Baseline shadowing (owner: Platform)
   - Deploy tenant in shadow mode for 72 hours. Capture: runtime service-level metrics, peak/median sequence lengths, and KV/cache hit distribution.
   - Prometheus query to capture baseline QPS:
     sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[5m]))
   - Record steady-state QPS = 95th percentile of 5m-aggregated QPS from shadow window.
3. Populate contract matrix (owner: SRE)
   - Fill the matrix above with measured baseline and proposed reserved headroom. Save to the tenant record: /tenants/TENANT_X/contract-matrix.
4. Capacity reservation (owner: Capacity Manager)
   - If reserved headroom > 0, create a capacity allocation ticket and mark required GPU type, memory, and quantization profile. Example allocation: 2x A100-80GB equivalent for steady-state 150 qps embedding workload.
   - Set autoscaler min = reserved headroom floor, max = negotiated burst ceiling.
5. Monitoring & alerting (owner: Observability)
   - Create per-tenant dashboards and alerts wired to SLOs. Example alert: \"tenant-TENANT_X-p99-latency\" fires when p99 > target for 10m and consumes > 10% of error budget.
   - Example PromQL for p99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[5m])) by (le))
6. Error-budget policy config (owner: SRE)
   - Configure the error-budget engine with: window=30d, burn_rate_alert=4x (auto throttle), emergency_throttle_threshold=0.9 of headroom.
   - Set automated responses: if burn_rate > 8x for 1h -> open incident, if burn_rate > 4x for 6h -> throttle lower-priority routes.
7. Acceptance testing (owner: SRE + QA)
   - Run synthetic traffic at 1.2x baseline for 1 hour, verify SLOs hold and reserved headroom absorbs 100% of burst.
   - Run quality regression harness against tenant prompt-set (must pass configured quality gates).
8. Cutover and handoff (owner: Customer Success)
   - Move tenant traffic to production route with gradual ramp (10% -> 50% -> 100%) over 4 hours, monitor SLOs and error budget consumption.
   - Post-cutover 48h checkpoint: confirm metrics and sign-off.

4) Error-budget governance and automated controls
- Error-budget levels: green (>75% remaining), yellow (25–75%), red (<25%).
- Automated actions by level:
  - Yellow: notify tenant SRE contact and enable caching optimizations (prefix caching) and increased batching windows for non-latency-critical routes.
  - Red: start priority throttling (non-critical routes), enable model fallback to a cheaper variant, and, if configured, pause low-priority background jobs.
- Burn rate policies (examples):
  - If burn_rate > 4 for 6h -> SRE-runbook business-review and throttle non-critical traffic.
  - If burn_rate > 8 for 1h -> trigger P0 playbook and possible emergency capacity allocation.

5) Capacity proof & preflight (acceptance tests)
- Synthetic load harness steps:
  1) Replay 1x baseline (30m) to verify steady-state.
  2) Apply 1.5x burst (15m) to validate headroom absorption.
  3) Apply 2.0x extreme burst (5m) to observe graceful degradation behaviour.
- Required checks before production cutover:
  - Dashboard exam: no sustained alerts for 15m.
  - Error-budget status: must be green or yellow, not red.
  - Quality gate: pass.

6) Incident handling & post-incident requirements (tenant-specific)
- If tenant breaches SLOs beyond configured error-budget, follow standard incident process but include contract-specific attachments: the tenant contract matrix, reserved headroom allocation ticket, and the shadowing baseline report.
- Post-incident deliverables (owner: SRE):
  - For severity P0: 72-hour incident evidence packet and 10-day remediation plan.
  - For P1 with contract exposure: include capacity adjustment proposal and financial impact estimate.

7) Operational tooling integrations (how we implement controls)
- Capacity orchestration: Capacity Orchestrator service (capacity-orch) — create allocation via API:
  curl -X POST https://capacity-orch.internal/api/v1/allocations
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
    -d '{"tenant":"TENANT_X","gpu_type":"A100-80","reserved_slots":2,"min_replicas":2}'
- Error-budget engine: eb-engine — configure per-tenant policy with CLI:
  ebctl set-policy --tenant TENANT_X --window 30d --burn-alert 4 --emergency-throttle 0.9
- Monitoring: dashboards stored in grafana/dashboards/tenants/TENANT_X.json; alerts via alertmanager with route tenant-TENANT_X.

8) Roles & responsibilities (short)
- Platform: owns onboarding execution and capacity reservation tickets.
- SRE: owns contract matrix validation, error-budget policy, and acceptance tests.
- Observability: dashboards and alerting.
- Customer Success: coordinates cutover and sign-off.
- Sales/Finance: negotiates capacity uplift and pricing tied to reserved headroom.

9) Audit & review cadence
- Quarterly contract review between Platform, SRE, and Customer Success for high-value tenants. Items reviewed: baseline drift, error-budget consumption trends, model quality regressions, and recommended capacity adjustments.
- Annual capacity re-certification for on-prem/dedicated tenants (hardware footprint and quantization profile).

Appendix A — Example PromQL queries
- Baseline QPS (5m rate): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[5m]))
- p99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[5m])) by (le))
- 30d availability (synthetic canary):
  sum_over_time(canary_success_total{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[30d:1d]) / sum_over_time(canary_total{tenant_id=\"TENANT_X\"}[30d:1d])

Appendix B — Example acceptance checklist (condensed)
- [ ] Shadowing window completed (72h)
- [ ] Contract matrix saved to tenant record
- [ ] Capacity reservation ticket created & approved
- [ ] Dashboards & alerts configured
- [ ] Error-budget engine policy enabled
- [ ] Synthetic acceptance tests passed
- [ ] Quality gate passed
- [ ] Cutover ramp completed and 48h checkpoint passed

payload.page_title: GPU workload characterization and pool-tiling guidelines

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This document captures an operationally-actionable approach for classifying GPU workloads, estimating pool sizes, and applying a pool-tiling (micro-pool) strategy to improve throughput, latency predictability, and cost-efficiency across Redwood's multi-tenant GPU fleet. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who make capacity and scheduling decisions.

Goals
-----
- Provide a repeatable workload characterization methodology using sampled traces and eval job profiles.
- Define pool-tiling (micro-pool) patterns and when to apply them (latency-sensitive vs batch).
- Give concrete Terraform module knobs, Prometheus queries, and autoscaler settings for implementing tiled pools.
- Describe an operational playbook for pool lifecycle (create, scale, drain, retire) with rollback steps.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- GPU-backed inference and eval batches run in hosted and dedicated modes.
- Both fractional GPU multiplexed jobs (mps/containers) and whole-card allocations.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Model quantization guidance (see quantization-profiles).
- Low-level kernel selection or model-specific optimization (see serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling).

Definitions
-----------
- Tile: a small, functionally-homogeneous GPU pool (e.g., 2 x A100:80GB cards in a single AZ) with a fixed scheduling policy.
- Workload class: label for job characteristics (latency-sensitive, throughput-batch, eval, CI-eval, spot-burst).
- Tail-latency SLO: 95th/99th percentile latency requirement for a workload class.
- Effective GPU-seconds: a unit for capacity planning (tokens * average-seq-length * cost-factor).

Measurement methodology
-----------------------
1. Data sources:
   - Request traces: sample of production RPCs from gateway (1% sample over 7 days).
   - Job metadata: cluster job logs and scheduler labels (job_type, model_family, seq_len_est).
   - Prometheus metrics: per-node nvidia_smi metrics, runtime token / step throughput, and per-request latency histograms.

2. Minimum dataset to characterize a workload class:
   - 1000 requests or 3 days of traffic (whichever is larger).
   - Distribution of request sizes (tokens), arrival process (poisson vs bursty), and concurrency per tenant.

3. Core metrics to compute:
   - P50/P95/P99 latency by model and route.
   - Average tokens-per-request and variance.
   - CPU / host memory / GPU utilization percentiles.
   - KV cache hit fraction (for chat-like workloads).

Standard Prometheus queries (examples)
------------------------------------
- 95th token generation latency for model X:
  sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{model="m-x",route=~".*"}[5m])) by (le) | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum_rate...)
- Average GPU utilization across tile:
  avg_over_time(nvidia_smi_utilization_gpu[5m])

Note: adapt exact label names to the cluster exporter. Use the dashboard template at /eng-infra/dashboards/gpu-tile-overview to visualize.

Workload classification matrix (example)
--------------------------------------
- Latency-sensitive inference (LSI): p95 <= 200ms, token mean <= 128, good KV hit (>60%)
- Interactive chat (IC): p95 <= 500ms, stateful, KV hit variable, high concurrency spikes
- Throughput batch (TB): throughput-optimized, best-effort latency (p95 unconstrained), long sequences
- CI/Eval (CI): scheduled, high GPU-seconds, tolerant to preemption
- Spot-burst (SB): intermittent bursts, fallback tolerant

Pool-tiling patterns and when to use them
----------------------------------------
1. Single-sku latency tile (LSI tile)
   - Composition: homogeneous high-memory GPU (e.g., A100-80GB), strict colocated NVLink disabled for multi-tenant safety.
   - Scheduler: strict preemption protection, minimal packing, conservative overcommit (0.6 CPU per GPU thread).
   - Use when: per-request latency SLO is priority and KV cache locality matters.

2. Fractional-multiplex tile (High-density tile)
   - Composition: GPUs with high multiprocessor utilization allowed (mps/container multiplexing).
   - Scheduler: bin-packing allowed, enable fractional-GPU runtime profile, eviction grace period = 90s.
   - Use when: throughput batch / CI-eval jobs dominate and demand is elastic.

3. Spot-burst tile (Economy tile)
   - Composition: cheaper spot instances and mixed-sku.
   - Scheduler: aggressive preemption allowed, automatic fallback routing to LSI tile if critical route.
   - Use when: non-critical evals, background retraining, and scheduled jobs.

Sizing guidance and formulae
---------------------------
1. Baseline capacity estimate (per workload class)
   - Required GPU-seconds per day = sum_over_jobs(average_tokens * token_cost_coefficient * requests_per_day)
   - Convert to number_of_cards = ceil((GPU-seconds-per-day) / (day_seconds * card_throughput_factor * utilization_target))

2. Tile sizing rules
   - Keep tiles small: 4–16 cards per tile is recommended for isolation and easier rolling upgrades.
   - For latency classes, bias toward more tiles with fewer cards (e.g., 6 cards/tile) to reduce blast radius.

Terraform module knobs (example table)
-------------------------------------
The table below lists common vars to expose in our gpu-pool module. Adapt names to module in sources/confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac.

| var_name | description | recommended default | notes |
| pool_name | logical name for the tile | "lsi-tile-<region>-v1" | include workload_class tag |
| gpu_sku | GPU instance type | "a100-80gb" | select homogeneous sku |
| desired_cards | target number of physical cards | "6" | integer |
| min_cards | autoscaler min | "2" | safety floor |
| max_cards | autoscaler max | "24" | upper bound |
| preemptible_ok | allow spot / preemptible nodes | "false" | true for spot tiles |
| eviction_grace_seconds | drain wait before force-evict | "120" | tune per workload |

Scheduling policy (decision flow)
--------------------------------
1. Classify incoming request/job: attach label workload_class.
2. Lookup tile candidates that accept that class. Prefer exact tile match.
3. If no tile has capacity and workload_class is latency-sensitive:
   - Check fallback routing policy: attempt warm spare in dedicated LSI tile.
   - If still no capacity: enqueue short-circuit throttle and return 429 with backoff header.
4. For CI/Batch: schedule to any high-density tile with sufficient card quota.

Autoscaler parameters and heuristics
----------------------------------
- Scale-up trigger: sustained (>2m) tile-level GPU utilization > 70% and queue length > 2.
- Scale-down trigger: sustained (<10m) tile-level GPU utilization < 25% and queue length == 0.
- Cooldown windows: 2m upstream and 10m downstream for scale-down to avoid oscillation.
- Safety caps: never grow > 2x in a single scaling step for a tile.

Operational lifecycle: create -> warm -> active -> drain -> retire
---------------------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
1. Open infra change request with module parameters and cost estimate.
2. Terraform apply with preview and approval.
sections.heading: Create

sections.body:
1. Deploy tile in a non-production AZ initially.
2. Run synthetic traffic generator (see /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/ephemeral-gpu-pools-for-ci-and-eval-runs.json) to validate latency and throughput.
sections.heading: Warm

sections.body: 1. Shift traffic via traffic-router flags. Monitor tile dashboards for p95/p99 and util.
sections.heading: Active

sections.body:
1. Toggle tile label accept_new_workloads=false.
2. Set eviction_grace_seconds to configured value.
3. Monitor for active sessions; for stateful chats, wait for idle window (default 15m).
4. Force-evict only after grace + safety wait with manager approval.
sections.heading: Drain (safe retire)

sections.body:
1. Terraform destroy with state backup.
2. Update capacity plan and run cost reconciliation.

Runbook: emergency scale and failover (quick steps)
------------------------------------------------
- Symptom: p95 increase > 2x for LSI routes and tile GPU util > 95%
1. Identify tile with highest p95 via dashboard.
2. Temporarily re-route 20% of LSI traffic to a cold spare LSI tile using traffic-router.
3. If no spare tile: enable expedited scale policy (allow 1.5x immediate scale) and notify oncall.
4. If issue persists > 15m, throttle non-critical tenants and turn on token-based rate-limiting per tenant.
5. Post-incident: run root-cause triage and update workload classification if pattern recurs.

Monitoring and alerts (recommended thresholds)
--------------------------------------------
- Tile p95 latency > SLO * 1.5 for 5m -> P0 alert to oncall.
- Tile GPU util > 92% for 3m and queue > 5 -> P1 to infra-runner.
- Eviction rate on tile > 1% of running sessions per 10m -> P2; investigate preemption dynamics.

CI/CD and testing guidance
-------------------------
- Use ephemeral tiles for validation of new autoscaler or scheduling changes. Reuse pipeline in /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/canary-gpu-provisioning-safety-net-pipeline.json.
- Add integration tests that assert: tile creation/destruction via Terraform, traffic-router flag changes, safe drain behavior.
- Backward compatibility: do not rename tile tags consumed by traffic-router; instead add new tags and deprecate old names for one release cycle.

Cost estimation example
-----------------------
- Input: 1M requests/day, avg_tokens=200, token_cost_coefficient=0.002 GPU-seconds/token -> GPU-seconds = 400,000
- Card throughput factor (A100-80): 0.9 -> day_seconds=86400 -> cards = ceil(400k / (86400*0.9*0.6)) = ceil(400k / 46656) = 9 cards
- Add 20% buffer for headroom and failover -> 11 cards -> split into 2 tiles of 6 and 5.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Tile owner: infra-gpu-ops@redwood.dev (primary), infra-sre (secondary).
- Change approvals: infra lead + cost-control.
- Escalation path: oncall -> infra-ops -> eng-sre -> CTO for >4h unresolved production degradation.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Terraform plan (example):
  cd infra/modules/gpu-pool && terraform init && terraform plan -var-file=overrides.tfvars
- Simulate traffic (loadgen):
  python tools/gpu_loadgen.py --model m-x --qps 50 --duration 600
- Force drain with grace:
  curl -XPOST "https://infra-api.internal/tiles/lsi-nyc-v2/drain?grace=300" -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

Related documents and dashboards
-------------------------------
- /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-placement-slo-driven-provisioning-playbook.json
- /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/ephemeral-gpu-pools-for-ci-and-eval-runs.json
- Dashboard: /eng-infra/dashboards/gpu-tile-overview

Change log
----------
- 2024-10-15: Initial draft and experimentation notes (Maya Patel).
- 2024-12-10: Added autoscaler heuristics and Terraform knobs (Ethan Roberts).
- 2025-02-02: Published with sizing formulas and emergency runbook (Lena Kowalski).

payload.page_title: Anticipatory SLO Drift and Capacity Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines a structured, anticipatory approach to detecting SLO drift early, preserving error budgets, and synthesizing short-term capacity hedges for Redwood Inference multi-tenant inference services. It combines telemetry-based detection, automated mitigation policies, manual runbook steps, and post-action verification to keep customer-facing SLOs within tolerance while minimizing cost and operational blast radius.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Services covered: inference-api, batch-embeddings, realtime-chat, routing-proxy.
- Applies to: latency and availability SLOs, burst headroom planning, tenant isolation/priority actions.
- Not covered: long-term capacity procurement, contract-level SLA negotiations (see finance/legal).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1) Detect SLO drift (trend-based and distributional) before error budget depletion.
2) Provide an ordered set of automated and manual mitigations to preserve error budgets with minimal customer-visible degradation.
3) Create capacity hedges (short duration) using elastic pools, pre-warmed models, and tenant prioritization.
4) Ensure clear ownership, observable outcomes, and fast rollback.
sections.heading: Objectives

sections.body:
- SLO drift: a sustained shift in SLO metrics (p90/p99 latency, availability) relative to baseline trend over the last 24–72 hours.
- Anticipatory action: mitigation taken while error budget remains > 0 but trending to depletion within horizon T (default T = 6 hours).
- Hedged capacity: short-lived capacity reserved from burst pool or spare GPU fleet to reduce tail pressure.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
- Primary owner: service steward (service manifest: owners field). For inference-api this is @steward-inference.
- SRE on-call: triage alerts, execute automated policy escalations, coordinate with service owner.
- Platform/Capacity team: approve and enact reserved-capacity allocations (>2h).
- Product/customer-success: communicate customer-impacting actions when degradation expected >15 minutes.

Detection: telemetry signals and queries
- Inputs (minimum telemetry): request latency histogram (per-route), success/error rate, queue length, GPU utilization, model-kv-cache-hit, request-sizes, tenant-priority label.
- Detection rules (examples):
  * Trend rule: if p99 latency has increased by >25% vs rolling-7d baseline for 2 consecutive 15m buckets and error budget burn rate > 2x expected, generate SLO-drift alert with severity MEDIUM.
  * Distributional rule: if p95–p99 spread widens by >2x and tail instance count > 0.5% of traffic, alert TAIL-EXPANSION.
  * Burn-rate horizon rule: compute time_to_depletion = current_error_budget / recent_burn_rate; if time_to_depletion < T (default 6h) fire PRE-EMPTIVE mitigation trigger.
sections.heading: Ownership and on-call responsibilities

sections.body:
- p99 latency trend: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="inference-api"}[5m])) by (le))
- burn rate (windowed): (increase(error_budget_consumed_total[10m]) / 600) / error_budget_size

Alerting classification and channels
- Severity: P2 (anticipatory) | P1 (imminent depletion or customer-affecting).
- Notifications: PagerDuty for P1, Slack #sre-triage for P2 with clear runbook links. Include time_to_depletion, top affected tenants, and recommended mitigations in alert payload.

Triage and decision matrix (high-level)
1) Confirm: validate telemetry (duplicate queries, check for ingestion gaps).
2) Scope: identify affected routes, models, tenants, and geographic regions.
3) Classify: drift type = capacity-constrained | model-regression | traffic-shift | infra-degradation.
4) Select mitigation tier using the matrix below.
sections.heading: PromQL (examples)

sections.body:
- Tier 0: Non-disruptive (automated, low-cost)
  * Enable prefix/KV cache warmers for top models for 10–30 minutes.
  * Increase batching size cap (if latency SLO allows) by +1 for configurable endpoints.
  * Apply adaptive sampling (reduce low-priority tenant sampling) to throttle non-critical requests.
- Tier 1: Short-lived hedges (elastic, pre-authorized)
  * Provision hedged GPUs from burst pool (max 1h by default) using rwt capacity.alloc --pool burst --count N --expiry 1h
  * Activate pre-warmed model replicas (scale up replica count for affected model variants).
- Tier 2: Priority actions and graceful degradation
  * Apply tenant-priority routing: shift best-effort tenants to degraded model variant (quantized or smaller model).
  * Route critical routes to dedicated capacity lanes (reserved instances) via routing policy update.
- Tier 3: Emergency containment (requires manager approval if >30m)
  * Service-level admission control: reject or queue requests above per-tenant thresholds.
  * Canary rollback of recent model/version changes.
  * Cross-region failover if local region capacity exhausted.

Automated policies and guardrails
- Burn-rate autopilot: when time_to_depletion < 6h, automatically perform Tier 0 actions and notify on-call. Escalate to Tier 1 if post-action burn rate reduction < 30% within 10 minutes.
- Auto-hedge budget: platform maintains a configurable burst budget per org; automatic hedges must not exceed 20% of monthly burst budget without manual approval.
- Safety checks before automated scaling:
  * validate binary instrument signals (no ingestion gaps),
  * ensure model-variant compatibility for fallback routing,
  * allocate GPUs in same region unless cross-region failover configured.

Runbook: ordered steps for SRE on-call (quick checklist)
1) Acknowledge alert. Pin the SLO drift alert channel and open service dashboard.
2) Run validation queries (copy/paste):
   - Check p99 trend: (PromQL provided above).
   - Top-ten tenants by error-budget-burn: topk(10, sum(increase(error_budget_consumed_total[10m])) by (tenant_id))
3) If automated Tier 0 actions not applied, trigger them via: rwt actions run --playbook anticipatory-cache-warm --service inference-api
4) If time_to_depletion < 6h and Tier 0 ineffective, request hedged capacity: rwt capacity.request --pool burst --region {region} --count X --duration 1h --reason "SLO drift hedge"
5) If Tier 2 required, coordinate with product/customer-success before tenant-impacting routing changes. Use Slack bridge and update status page if customer-visible.
6) Record all actions taken in incident channel and in the event timeline (timestamps, commands, owner).
sections.heading: Mitigation tiers (ordered by preferability)

sections.body:
| Symptom | First action | Escalate to | Typical rollback |
|---|---|---|---|
| p99 up 25% but error budget healthy | Tier 0 cache/batching | SRE lead | revert batching to previous cap |
| Burn-rate horizon < 6h | Auto-tier0 then request hedge | Platform Capacity | deallocate burst pool GPUs |
| p99 up after model rollout | Canary rollback | Model owner + SRE | rollback to previous model tag |

Post-action verification checklist
- Verify burn-rate decreased by >= 30% within 10 minutes of action.
- Validate tail latency percentiles (p95/p99) returned to baseline within 30 minutes.
- Confirm no telemetry ingestion gaps and no secondary regressions (errors, queue growth).
- If hedged GPUs allocated, ensure utilization >30% within 10 minutes, otherwise deallocate to avoid waste.

Communication and coordination
- If action is non-customer-visible (Tier 0/1), update Slack SRE channel and append a short note in #service-status.
- If impact > 5% of tenants or > 15 minutes, trigger customer-success and prepare a proactive message (template in customer-success/integration-guides).
- For cross-team actions (model rollback, routing changes) include owners in the alert thread and record approvals.

Post-incident and follow-up tasks
- Create a short incident RFC if error budget consumption > 25% of monthly: include hypothesis, actions taken, and timelines.
- Run an SLO drift root-cause analysis (RCA) within 3 business days: was drift caused by traffic shift, model change, resource contention, or telemetry corruption?
- If root cause tied to capacity sizing, add demand profile adjustments to next quarter capacity plan.

Appendix A — Example commands and snippets
- Request hedged capacity (example):
  rwt capacity.request --pool burst --region us-west-2 --count 4 --duration 1h --tags "slo_hedge,inference-api" --reason "Anticipatory hedge for p99 surge"
- Pre-warm cache job example (K8s job yaml snippet described):
  kubectl apply -f prewarm-job-inference-api.yaml --namespace inference-warmers
- Quick Prometheus sanity check: curl -sS "http://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=up" | jq .

Appendix B — Tunable parameters (default values)
| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| anticipatory_horizon_hours | "6" | Time horizon to compute time_to_depletion |
| auto_hedge_max_duration_minutes | "60" | Max automatic burst pool allocation without manual approval |
| burn_rate_reduction_threshold_pct | "30" | Required reduction to consider action effective |
| hedged_gpu_util_threshold_pct | "30" | Minimum utilization to keep hedged capacity allocated |
sections.heading: Decision matrix (simple table)

sections.body:
- See capacity-procurement and burst-pool-runbook for long-lived allocations.
- See model-onboarding standards for pre-warming and cache compatibility.

sections.body:
- 2025-11-12 created by Jordan Li (initial draft).
- 2025-12-08 updated: added PromQL examples and automated policy thresholds (reviewers: Asha Patel).
- 2026-02-14 updated: refined decision matrix, added hedged GPU utilization rules (reviewers: Luis Moreno, Priya Singh).
sections.heading: Document change log

sections.body:
- SRE on-call rotation: #sre-oncall (PagerDuty).
- Platform capacity: platform-capacity@redwood.com.
- Service steward: see service manifest in repo infra/service-manifests/inference-api.yaml.

payload.page_title: Demand-to-Headroom Rationale and SLO Mapping Manual

sections.body: This manual defines a reproducible, auditable process to map product demand and SLOs to headroom targets and capacity provisioning decisions. It codifies the reasoning used by SRE and Capacity teams when we: (1) translate observed and forecasted request profiles into headroom buckets, (2) budget error‑budget consumption, and (3) create emergency and rolling contingency plans.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a single-source decision flow for demand→headroom→capacity mapping.
- Make tradeoffs explicit (latency SLO vs cost vs warmup risk).
- Ensure repeatable calculations and guardrails for oncall and capacity stewards.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to all public-facing inference endpoints, dedicated GPU pools, and important internal control-plane services.
- Not intended for ephemeral dev/test environments.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Demand: measured inbound request rate (RPS) and distribution of sequence lengths / token counts per request.
- Headroom: reserved extra capacity above steady-state baseline to absorb short-term bursts (expressed as % of baseline or absolute GPUs/instances).
- Safety factor: multiplicative buffer to account for telemetry noise, estimation error, and model warmup.
- Error budget policy: SLO-linked tolerances used to decide throttle/fallback thresholds and capacity escalations.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
1) Tie headroom to SLO risk, not purely to cost. Critical, low-latency routes (p50 < 100ms) get more conservative headroom.
2) Use distribution-aware metrics (p50/p95/p99 + arrival burstiness) rather than single averages.
3) Keep fast path for canary and rollback: canary traffic should never consume >10% of headroom.
4) Prefer elastic burst capacity with pre-warm pools where cold start cost materially hurts latency.
sections.heading: Principles we follow

sections.body:
- 90d historical RPS histogram by 1s granularity and 5m aggregates.
- Token distribution per request (mean, median, 95th).
- Tail latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99) across model variants.
- Warmup cost (ms tokens to reach steady throughput) per model.
- Current autoscale policies, min/max instances, and provisioning lag.
- Oncall error budget burn rate (tokens and SLO violations) for last 7d and 30d.
sections.heading: Required telemetry and inputs (pre-flight checklist)

sections.body:
1) Baseline identification (owner: service steward)
   1.1 Pull steady-state baseline RPS = 95th-percentile of 5‑minute windows over the last 14 days.
   1.2 Baseline tokens/sec = baseline RPS * median tokens/request.

2) Burst profile characterization (owner: SRE capacity analyst)
   2.1 Compute short-window spike factor = max 1s RPS over last 7d / baseline RPS.
   2.2 Compute sustained surge factor = 10m rolling max / baseline RPS.
   2.3 Label burstiness: {spiky, sustained, mixed} using thresholds (spiky if short-window spike factor > 4 and sustained surge factor < 2).

3) Headroom target selection (owner: capacity planning)
   3.1 For each route, pick base headroom by criticality:
       - Critical low-latency (SLO p99 < 250ms): headroom = max(20%, short-window spike factor - 1)
       - Core throughput (batch/embedding heavy): headroom = max(15%, sustained surge factor - 1)
       - Best-effort background: headroom = 5–10%
   3.2 Add safety factor: +5% for multi-tenant unknowns, +10% if telemetry fidelity < 72h retention.

4) Translate headroom to capacity units (owner: infra provisioning)
   4.1 Estimate tokens/sec per GPU for target model variant and quantization profile (see kernel profiles table below).
   4.2 Required GPUs = ceil((baseline tokens/sec * (1 + headroom)) / tokens/sec_per_gpu)
   4.3 If autoscale lag > 2m, provision warm pool = min(2 GPUs, floor(Required GPUs * 0.2))

payload.page_title: Global GPU capacity calendar and drain coordination

sections.body:
Purpose
-------
This document defines the Global GPU Capacity Calendar and the operational runbook for scheduling, coordinating, and executing node drains and capacity maintenance across Redwood’s multi-region GPU fleet. It standardizes preflight checks, IaC/CI gating, drain sequencing, and post-maintenance verification to minimize customer impact and maintain SLOs.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all production GPU pools (hosted &dedicated) that serve inference traffic: `gpu-allocator`, `capacity-sentry`, `burst-orchestrator`
- Regions: us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1
- Changes covered: kernel upgrades, driver updates, instance image rotation, topology changes, and bulk node retirements

Definitions & stakeholders
------------------------
- Maintenance window: scheduled 2-hour block reserved for non-emergency drains
- Drain lead: oncall eng-infra engineer responsible for coordination during a window
- Rollout owner: service or team owning the change (e.g., runtime, kernel team)
- Stakeholders: Runtime team, SRE, Capacity planning, Customer Success (for enterprise tenants)

Maintenance cadence & global calendar (operational policy)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Safe weekly windows per region (default):
  - US: Tue 02:00–04:00 UTC, Thu 03:00–05:00 UTC
  - EU: Wed 01:00–03:00 UTC
  - APAC: Mon 22:00–00:00 UTC
- Major batch operations (>=10% pool): coordinate 14 days prior, limit to 1 window/week/region
- Emergency windows: ad-hoc; must follow emergency drain protocol below

Maintenance risk matrix (SLO / capacity guidance)
-----------------------------------------------
| Change size | Expected capacity impact | Preflight target | Rollback threshold |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Small (<2% of pool) | Negligible | smoke tests green | auto-rollback on >1% error increase |
| Medium (2–10%) | Minor | full canary traffic for 30m | manual rollback if p95 latency spikes >20% |
| Large (>10%) | Risk of SLO violations | staged rollout + capacity reserve | abort and restore capacity if errors >5% for 15m |

Preflight checklist (runbook)
----------------------------
1. Announce window in #infra-maintenance and to affected customers 72/48/24 hours out.
2. Verify capacity runway: `capacity-sentry` target reserve >= 20% for large changes, >=10% for medium.
3. Terraform plan & diff approved: run `terraform plan -var-file=env.tfvars` and attach plan to change ticket.
4. CI/CD health gates: all dependent CI pipelines pass for the last successful image and the candidate image.
5. Canary provisioning: spin canary pool with new image/config (1–2 instances); run end-to-end suite for 30 minutes.
6. Monitoring baseline snapshot: capture current metrics (p50/p95 latency, 5xx rate, KV cache hit ratio).

Terraform / IaC patterns for safe drains
--------------------------------------
- Use blue/green-friendly node group naming and immutable image promotion. Example snippet for terraform variables and strategy:

```hcl
variable "gpu_node_pool_strategy" {
  description = "rolling | bluegreen"
  default     = "bluegreen"
}

module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v2.3"
  name   = "gpu-pool-${var.region}-${var.stage}"
  strategy = var.gpu_node_pool_strategy
  desired_capacity = var.desired_capacity
}
```

- Flags to include in CI/CD: `--approve-canary`, `--constrain-drain-concurrency=3`, `--dry-run`
- Locking: use remote-state seat reservation `seat_reservation=true` before applying large-scale changes

CI/CD gating & automation (how changes are promoted)
--------------------------------------------------
- Pipeline stages: plan -> canary-apply -> canary-smoke -> gradual-rollout -> verification -> finalize-apply
- Gating checks (automated):
  - `kube-smoke` pass against canary nodes (latency, qps, error-rate)
  - `alloc-check` ensures `gpu-allocator` has available slots >= requested concurrency
  - `batch-sim` simulates burst traffic for 10 minutes against canary fleet
- Human approval required for Medium/Large changes after canary-smoke

Drain coordination runbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------------
1. Ownership & communication
   - Drain lead confirms roster and primary backup. Post start time in #infra-maintenance.
2. Verify preflight: confirm checklist items 1–6 are green.
3. Reserve capacity: temporarily increase warm-pool by % reserve if needed: `rwdctl capacity set --pool ${POOL} --reserve 20%`
4. Begin staged drains (concurrency limit = 3 unless emergency):
   a. Select node subset (label `maintenance=true`)
   b. For each node:
      i. `kubectl cordon <node>`
      ii. `rwdctl drain-node --node <node> --grace-period 120s --wait-for-active-sessions=false`
      iii. Monitor `runtime.request_latency` and `service.5xx_rate` for 5m before moving to next node
5. If any metric breach occurs (see thresholds): pause rollout, scale up warm-pool, or trigger rollback.
6. Post-drain validation: run end-to-end smoke tests, confirm KV cache warm ratio >= 90% for top 10 tenants.
7. Finalize: update terraform state for drained instance group, close maintenance ticket, and publish summary.

Automated rollback & emergency mitigation
---------------------------------------
- Abort conditions (example):
  - sustained p95 latency increase >20% for 15m
  - 5xx rate increase >2% absolute for 10m
  - Pod OOM or executor restarts >3x within 15m
- Immediate actions:
  1. Halt further drains: `rwdctl rollouts pause --project infra`
  2. Restore capacity via warm-pool or fallback to lower-cost model variant: `rwdctl capacity override --pool ${POOL} --type burst`
  3. If required, reverse node changes by reattaching previous instance image via Terraform (see rollback CLI snippet):

```bash
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
TF_VAR_ami=ami-previous terraform apply -var "force_replace=true" -auto-approve
```

Post-maintenance verification checklist
-------------------------------------
- All nodes in pool show `Ready` and expected kernel/drivers.
- Telemetry: p50/p95 back to baseline ±5%, 5xx at pre-maintenance levels.
- KV cache hit ratio restored to target for top tenants.
- Billing/scheduling sanity: no sustained cost increase >3% over baseline.
- Release notes: short summary posted to #infra-maintenance and ticket closed with links to telemetry graphs.

Monitoring & dashboards to watch
-------------------------------
- Dashboards: `GPU Fleet Overview`, `Capacity Sentry`, `KV Cache Heatmap`, `Per-tenant Latency`
- Critical alerts: `gpu_pool_capacity_below_reserve`, `allocator_p95_surge`, `node_drain_failures_rate`
- SRE runbook for paging: page on-call SRE when any critical alert persists for >10 minutes during window.

Ownership & escalation
----------------------
- Drain lead (oncall) is primary during window.
- If rollback >15 minutes to execute or ambiguity in root cause, escalate to the runtime owner and SRE lead.
- For customer-impacting regressions, notify Customer Success immediately and begin enterprise incident process.

Change log (summary of recent updates)
------------------------------------
- 2024-09-12: Initial draft published.
- 2024-11-04: Added terraform seat-reservation pattern and canary gate `batch-sim`.
- 2025-02-07: Updated global calendar and adjusted rollback thresholds for large changes.

Appendices
----------
A. Example `rwdctl` commands
```
sections.heading: restore previous image by forcing terraform apply with previous AMI variable

sections.body: rwdctl capacity get --pool gpu-prod-usw2
sections.heading: check pool reserve

sections.body: rwdctl capacity set --pool gpu-prod-usw2 --reserve 20%
sections.heading: set reserve

sections.body:
rwdctl drain-node --node ip-10-0-5-23 --grace-period 120s --wait-for-active-sessions=false
```

B. Contact matrix
- Runtime lead: runtime-team@redwood.ai
- SRE oncall: pagerduty-sre
- Capacity planning: capacity@redwood.ai

If you have feedback or see gaps in this runbook, open a PR against this page and notify the reviewers listed in the metadata.

payload.page_title: Capacity stewardship cadence and SLO portfolio alignment

sections.body:
Overview

This document prescribes a repeatable cross-functional cadence for capacity stewardship that ensures the SLO portfolio is aligned with real capacity supply and business priorities. It focuses on continuous reconciliation of SLOs, error budgets, and multi-tenant capacity allocation (headroom) so teams can make predictable trade-offs between cost, latency, and availability.

Goals

- Maintain >=95% confidence that committed SLOs are achievable given current capacity commitments and forecasted demand.
- Detect and remediate SLO drift and error-budget consumption early (target detection within 24 hours of significant change).
- Provide a predictable, auditable cadence for capacity reallocation and non-disruptive migration of tenant traffic.

Scope and audience

This is intended for SREs, product/platform owners, and service stewards responsible for inference-serving and multi-tenant routing. Applies to hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments where central capacity governance is required.

Key concepts and definitions

- SLO portfolio: the set of active SLOs (latency, availability, correctness) across services that are eligible for central capacity stewardship.
- Error budget: remaining fraction of SLO slack for a lookback window (typically 30d); used as the operational currency for throttles/rollouts.
- Headroom: reserved capacity buffer (expressed in GPU-minutes or RPS-calc) to absorb short-term demand spikes without violating SLOs.
- Stewardship window: the recurrent meeting where stewards reconcile portfolio health and allocate headroom (see Cadence).

Stewardship cadence (calendar)

1) Daily: Automated health pass (SRE automation)
- What runs: portfolio telemetry pipeline computes a daily "Stewardship Snapshot" by 06:00 UTC.
- Outputs: list of services with >5% 24h jump in burn-rate, tail-latency regressions beyond configured thresholds, and any new error budget alarms.
- Owners: telemetry pipeline (sre-observability) writes to #sre-capacity-alerts and issues an automatic ticket for services crossing critical thresholds.

2) Weekly: Triage & short-term allocation (SRE + product stewards)
- Objective: triage items surfaced by daily snapshots and perform one-week capacity trades.
- Attendees: SRE oncall steward, product steward(s), runtime performance owner.
- Agenda (30 minutes): review top-5 consuming services, approve emergency capacity grants (max 15% of pool), schedule deeper investigations.
- Output: annotated authorization in the capacity ledger and an action ticket with owner and SLAs for remediation.

3) Monthly: Capacity reconciliation and forecasting (SRE platform + finance)
- Objective: reconcile observed headroom usage vs. forecast, adjust reserve targets, and identify upcoming model rollouts that require provisioning.
- Inputs: 30d telemetry, 90d forecast from product teams, reserved capacity utilization metrics.
- Deliverables: updated headroom target per pool, prioritized provisioning request list, finance impact estimate.

4) Quarterly: SLO portfolio review and admission policy refresh (cross-functional)
- Objective: review SLOs for business alignment, retire/modify low-value SLOs, and update admission rules for new tenants.
- Attendees: SRE leads, product managers, platform engineering, customer success for at-risk enterprise tenants.
- Deliverables: SLO change proposals, revised admission thresholds, and rollout plan for any SLO changes.

Decision matrix: When to grant capacity vs. require optimization

- Emergency grant (auto-approved at weekly triage): services with >50% 24h burn rate increase attributable to traffic (not regressions). Grant limit: 15% pool capacity for 72 hours.
- Short-term grant (requires steward sign-off): for planned campaigns or model experiments lasting <=14 days. Grant limit: up to 30% pool with documented rollback plan.
- No grant / require optimization: services with persistent error-budget burn due to non-traffic regressions (code/quantization). Action: require remediation and capacity-neutral rollout.

SLO and error-budget thresholds (recommended baseline)

| Tier | Typical SLO | Error-budget policy | Headroom target (pool %) | Escalation window |
|------|-------------|---------------------|--------------------------|------------------|
| Platinum | 99.95% availability / p99 latency SLA | Auto-grant only for verified region incidents; reserve 20% headroom | 25 | 1h |
| Gold | 99.9% / p95 latency target | Weekly steward approval for short grants; finance notification above 10% cost delta | 15 | 4h |
| Standard | 99.5% / median latency | Must optimize before capacity increase; can request experiments | 8 | 24h |

(Represent table in Confluence as above; values are guidance and must be adapted per pool.)

Operational signals and alert thresholds

- Burn-rate anomaly: relative change > 5x baseline burn-rate over 6h -> severity P2 alert.
- Tail-latency delta: p99 latency regression > 20% over 12h -> P2.
- Error budget remaining < 30% -> P3 advisory; <10% -> P1 immediate review.
- Headroom utilization > 80% -> P1 capacity planning alert.

Sample telemetry queries

- Prometheus (tail latency):
  sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-runtime",le="1.0"}[5m])) by (service) / sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_count{job="inference-runtime"}[5m])) by (service)

- BigQuery (error budget burn):
  SELECT service, SUM(tokens) as tokens_consumed, SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'ok' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as errors
  FROM `redwood-prod.telemetry.tokens_v2`
  WHERE event_time BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  GROUP BY service

Ownership and roles

- Steward (primary): maintains the capacity ledger, chairs weekly triage, approves short grants.
- Service steward (per-service): responsible for remediation, SLO proposals, and forecasting.
- Capacity platform: implements grants, runs autoscaling, and enforces quota guards.
- Finance liaison: validates cost impact for quarterly provisioning.

Runbook excerpts: emergency headroom exhaustion

1) Trigger: headroom utilization > 90% for two consecutive 15m windows or error budget < 5%.
2) Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
   - Declare "Capacity Alert" in incident tooling and notify #sre-capacity-ops.
   - Identify top 3 services by allocation using the capacity ledger query.
   - Execute automated soft-throttle on non-critical tenants (pre-authorized lists).
3) Next actions (15-60 minutes):
   - Approve emergency grant (if traffic-driven and within limits) or escalate to oncall SRE lead.
   - If grant not approved, activate degraded routing policy (route to smaller models, reduce max tokens).
4) Post-incident (within 72 hours):
   - Produce a stewardship post-incident note: cause, mitigation, capacity changes, and recommendations for future prevention.

Templates and artifacts

- Capacity ledger entry (example fields): service, pool, requested-gpu-minutes, rationale, approved-by, expiry, rollback-plan.
- Stewardship Snapshot (automated): service, burn_rate_30d, burn_rate_24h, headroom_pct, error_budget_remaining, p99_latency_change.
- Monthly reconciliation template: forecast delta table, finance impact, provisioning plan.

Practical guidance and anti-patterns

- Prefer optimization before buying capacity: a 10% tail-latency reduction often yields more headroom than a 10% capacity add.
- Do not use error budget as permanent capacity justification. Recurrent high burn rates require root cause fixes and potential SLO re-evaluation.
- Avoid manual, undocumented temporary grants. All grants must be logged in the ledger with expiry.

Related policies and pages

- See service-onboarding-runway-and-slo-admission-playbook for admission criteria and templates.
- See slo-rollout-readiness-and-capacity-checklist for pre-deployment checks.

Appendix: common CLI commands and queries

- Create a ledger entry (example):
  curl -X POST https://capacity-api.internal/v1/ledger -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"service":"vision-infer","pool":"dedicated-east","requested_gpu_min":3600,"expiry":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z"}'

- Check headroom by pool (Prometheus example):
  sum(avg_over_time(gpu_utilization{pool="dedicated-east"}[1h])) by (pool)

Feedback and iteration

This cadence is expected to evolve. Submit suggested changes via the stewardship RFC process (label: capacity-rfc). For initial adoption, we recommend a 90-day pilot on one dedicated pool to validate thresholds and tooling integration.

Owners

- Primary owner: Amina Patel (SRE capacity lead)
- Secondary owner: Diego Morales (Platform SRE)

payload.page_title: tenant-throttling-simulator-and-parameterization-guide-2026

sections.body:
Summary:
This guide describes the Tenant Throttling Simulator (TTS): a reproducible experiment harness for exploring throttling and eviction policy parameterizations across multitenant inference workloads. TTS is intended for platform engineers who must make data-driven choices for tenant rate limits, priority slices, and eviction heuristics that balance SLO attainment, fairness, and cost.

Problem statement and motivation:
- At scale, small changes to per-tenant throttles or eviction thresholds can produce large, non-linear effects on latency SLOs and tail cost.
- We lack a repeatable way to run parameter sweeps that combine realistic arrival patterns, KV cache statefulness, and cross-region failover scenarios.
- The simulator gives operators a way to (a) quantify SLO vs cost tradeoffs, (b) stress-test fairness under skewed tenant distributions, and (c) generate rollout safe-ranges for production configuration.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: platform operators, SREs, runtime engineers, and product owners who own tenant-level economics.
- Scope: local and cluster-scale simulation of request routing, batching, KV-prefix cache hit-rate dynamics, and admission control. Not in scope: full model inference latency micro-benchmarks (those belong in eng-serving-runtime).

High-level architecture (textual diagram):
- Driver (experiment runner): orchestrates scenarios and parameter sweeps.
- Synthetic workload generator: tenant arrival distributions, request size histogram, interactive vs batch mix.
- Runtime model: simplified per-GPU queuing model + batch formation + kv-prefix cache layer + eviction/admission logic.
- Metrics collector: computes SLO attainment, p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens-per-second, and cost proxy.
- Analyzer: generates heatmaps, Pareto frontiers, and recommended parameter ranges.

Key concepts and knobs:
- tenant_throttle (rpm): per-tenant request-per-minute soft cap applied before batching.
- priority_slice: integer tier (0..N) controlling burst credits and admission precedence.
- eviction_policy: {LRU, LFU, TTL-weighted, recency+size} for KV prefix cache.
- admission_margin: float [0.0, 1.0], portion of capacity reserved for SLO-critical traffic.
- batch_window_ms: batching delay budget used to assemble batches (affects throughput vs latency).

Representative experiment matrix (table):
| Experiment ID | tenant skew | tenant_throttle | priority_slice distribution | eviction_policy | admission_margin | notes |
| E-101 | even (N=200) | 30 rpm | {gold:5%,silver:15%,bronze:80%} | LRU | 0.1 | baseline |
| E-203 | skewed (90/10) | 10 rpm for tail | {gold:2%,silver:8%,bronze:90%} | TTL-weighted | 0.25 | high-skew stress |
| E-311 | enterprise burst | 200 rpm burst | {gold:50%,silver:30%,bronze:20%} | recency+size | 0.0 | burst credit sizing |

Inputs required for a run:
- tenant manifest (CSV): tenant_id, class (gold/silver/bronze), baseline_rps, burst_profile_id
- arrival profile (JSON): Poisson/zipf parameters, diurnal window, synthetic outage window
- runtime config (YAML): admission_margin, batch_window_ms, throttle_map, eviction_policy params

Quick start (local):
1) Clone the simulator repository (private/internal): git clone git@redwood:platform/tenant-throttling-sim.git && cd tenant-throttling-sim
2) Create a scenario: cp scenarios/example-scenario.yaml scenarios/your-test.yaml and edit tenant counts and skew
3) Run a single-point experiment: ./bin/run_experiment --scenario scenarios/your-test.yaml --out results/exp-your-test.json
4) Produce a dashboard-style summary (local): ./bin/analyze --input results/exp-your-test.json --format html --out results/exp-your-test.html

Parallel parameter sweep (cluster):
- The driver supports Kubernetes Job fanout: use k8s template jobs/sim-job.yaml and a param generator to map sweep dimensions to jobs.
- Tip: limit parallelism to 40 jobs to avoid overloading shared telemetry backends during analysis.

Interpreting outputs and recommended thresholds:
- SLO attainment: primary metric is p95 latency <= configured SLO for SLO-critical tenant classes. If p95 breach > 5% of time windows, mark config as risky.
- Fairness score: normalized ratio of p95 between gold and bronze (target < 2.0 to avoid extreme disparity).
- Cost-proxy: tokens-per-second / effective_gpu_utilization. Use increase over baseline to estimate incremental cost.

Decision matrix (example):
- If SLO attainment for gold < 99.5% and fairness score > 2.5 -> increase admission_margin by +0.1 and reduce batch_window_ms by 10ms.
- If cost-proxy increases > 15% but SLOs remain good -> consider tightening throttle for bronze by 10% and increasing eviction aggressiveness.
- If KV cache hit-rate < 40% for high-volume tenants -> prefer recency+size eviction and increase cache hot-shard allocation.

Production rollout runbook (safe rollout pattern):
1) Canary: apply new parameter set to a small isolated shard (1% of traffic) for 24h. Monitor p50/p95/p99, token-cost, and error rates.
2) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% over 3–7 days with automated abort if p95 breach > 2% in any window.
3) Fallback: pre-provision and keep previous config snapshot; automated fallback job will restore previous admission_margin and throttle_map if rollback triggered.
4) Post-rollout review: publish experiment artifacts and a short findings note to the runbook.

Operational alerting guidance (dashboards and alerts):
- Create a synthetic SLO monitor for representative tenants per class; alert when p95(SLO-class) breaches target for 3 consecutive windows of 1 minute.
- Cost drift alert: when cost-proxy delta > 12% sustained for 30 minutes.
- Fairness regression alert: when fairness score change > 0.5 in 1 hour.

Experiment reproducibility checklist:
- Commit scenario YAML and driver version (git SHA) into artifacts directory.
- Include seed values for RNGs to ensure identical arrival traces.
- Archive any telemetry dumps required for offline replay.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: mixing synthetic and production traces without normalization -> Mitigation: use normalization layer that rescales arrival rates to match target qps.
- Pitfall: ignoring KV cache warmup -> Mitigation: run warmup phase for at least 2x median TTL before measurement window.
- Pitfall: telemetry overload during large sweeps -> Mitigation: aggregate at driver and emit summarized metrics rather than full traces.

Ownership, responsibilities and SLAs:
- Owner: Platform/Serving Capacity team (primary), Eng-SRE (secondary). Contact: platform-eng@redwood.internal
- SLA for experiment infrastructure: driver availability 99.9% during business hours.

Retrospective and continuous improvement notes (how to use results):
- Store the Pareto frontier (SLO vs cost) from each major sweep in the experiment catalog.
- Quarterly review: re-run E-101 baseline against latest traffic shapes; identify drift in recommended admission_margin.

Appendix: sample runtime-config YAML snippet:
```yaml
admission_margin: 0.15
batch_window_ms: 30
throttle_map:
  gold: 60
  silver: 30
  bronze: 10
eviction_policy:
  name: recency+size
  max_entry_size_kb: 64
  recency_weight: 0.7
  size_weight: 0.3
```

Appendix: example CLI invocation for cluster sweep (k8s):
- python tools/param_sweeper.py --param admission_margin:0.0,0.1,0.2 --param eviction_policy:name:LRU,recency+size --parallel 20 --out s3://redwood-experiments/2026-ttsim/

Notes and references:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: it links simulator outputs to rollout steps and alerting. For microbenchmarking guidance see eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling.
- If you use this harness for customer-impacting changes (tenant-visible throttles or burst credits), include Security and Compliance in the review cycle.

Contact and feedback:
- Open an RFC (platform/experiments) if you want new knobs added to the simulator. For urgent help during rollouts, ping #platform-ops on Slack or email platform-eng@redwood.internal.

payload.page_title: Service Criticality and Capacity Prioritization Guidelines

sections.body:
Summary
This guideline defines how Redwood SRE assesses service criticality, allocates capacity, and enforces error-budget-driven prioritization. It combines SLO policy, capacity hedging, incident escalation priorities, and operational tooling patterns into a single decision framework for on-call teams and product owners. Use this document to: determine capacity pre-commitments, run surge prioritization, and decide which services receive emergency capacity in constrained scenarios.

Context and goals
- Objective: ensure customer-facing and revenue-significant features meet latency and availability commitments while minimizing waste across the GPU fleet and reserved pools.
- Scope: applies to all services that serve production inference traffic (hosted API, dedicated, private control plane) and platform dependencies that affect SLOs (routing, auth, billing).
- Not in scope: internal dev/test workloads, ephemeral CI jobs (see infra-standards for CI quotas).

Definitions
1) Service criticality tier (used for prioritization decisions)
   - Tier A (critical): Revenue-facing APIs and model endpoints used by >1M monthly requests or with enterprise SLAs. Examples: /v1/generate, dedicated inference gateways.
   - Tier B (important): Features with user-facing impact but lower revenue sensitivity or lower scale (e.g., internal embeddings used by search).
   - Tier C (non-critical): Experimental features, analytics-only jobs, internal tooling.

2) SLO constructs
   - Availability SLO: % of successful responses within defined HTTP code set and within latency target.
   - Latency SLO: p99 / p95 token latency measured on production traffic after warm caches.
   - Error budget: 1 - SLO over a rolling window (typically 30 days). Error budget burn = observed violations / budget.

Service criticality table (summary view)
| Column | Description | Sample threshold |
|-------|-------------|------------------|
| Tier | Criticality label | A / B / C |
| Ownership | Primary product and SRE owner | product: embeddings; sre: team-gamma |
| Core SLOs | Primary SLOs that drive capacity decisions | availability 99.95% / latency p99 < 300ms |
| Capacity policy | Pre-commit / hedging strategy | reserved 4x baseline for Tier A |

Policy: How capacity commitments are decided
- Baseline RPS calculation: for each service, compute 7-day median RPS and 95th percentile of hourly peaks. Baseline = max(7-day median, 95th-peak * 0.6).
- Headroom multiplier by tier: Tier A = 4.0, Tier B = 2.0, Tier C = 1.2. These are applied to baseline to determine reserved capacity on Dedicated pools or autoscaler targets in hosted regions.
- Cost-optimization review cadence: quarterly for Tier A and B, biannual for Tier C. Reviews must include model quantization plans and caching strategies.

Error budget prioritization (decision ladder)
When error budget is burning, apply the following prioritized actions in order (do not skip earlier steps unless explicitly approved by SRE lead):
1) Throttle non-critical background traffic (Tier C) via rate-limiters and global traffic shaping.
2) Enable aggressive prefix/KV cache usage and bypass model cold starts where possible.
3) Engage model-variant fallback (quantized / smaller models) for non-enterprise customers.
4) If error budget remains negative for >6 hours, open emergency capacity arbitration and consider reassigning reserved nodes from Tier C services.
5) For sustained critical burns (>24 hours), trigger product escalation: reduce feature flags for non-SLA customers and notify sales/customer-success for impacted enterprise tenants.

Runbook: Capacity emergency triage (ordered steps)
1) Identify the scope: runredwood query:
   redwoodctl metrics query --service <service> --range 60m --metrics requests,errors,latency
2) Check SLO dashboard: Grafana link (dash:prod/service-slo) and error-budget burn graph.
3) If burn rate > 3x expected and p99 latency > 2x target, notify on-call and create incident with impact level P1/P2.
4) Apply short-term mitigations:
   a) Route non-enterprise traffic to fallback region: redwoodctl route set --service <s> --region fallback-west --filter "!enterprise"
   b) Scale up dedicated pool: redwoodctl capacity allocate --pool dedicated-g1 --count +2 --reason "emergency hedging"
   c) Update autoscaler policy to more aggressive scaling: kubectl apply -f autoscaler-emergency.yaml
5) Re-evaluate every 15 minutes until error budget burn rate reduces below threshold.

Incident review and capacity ownership checklist
- Evidence to collect (during incident): timeline of scaling events, autoscaler logs, GPU utilization heatmaps, kernel-level stalls, model KV cache hit rates, and routing traces.
- Minimum metadata to attach to post-incident review: owner, rollback window, capacity decisions, and cost delta for emergency capacity.
- Review cadence: incidents impacting Tier A SLOs require a blameless postmortem within 72 hours and a capacity remediation plan in the first retro.

Operational tooling recommendations
- Metrics and dashboards: Prometheus + Cortex for long retention, Grafana dashboards per-service with the following panels: requests, pct-iles latency, error-rate, CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, kv-cache-hit.
- Alerts (recommended thresholds):
   - service_slo_error_budget_burn_rate > 1.0 for 1h -> SEV3
   - p99_latency > p99_target * 1.5 for 30m -> SEV2
   - gpu_utilization > 88% for 10m and queue_length > 50 -> SEV2
   - routing_5xx_rate > 0.5% for 10m -> SEV2
- Integrations: PagerDuty for on-call, Slack incident channel automation, and runbook links embedded in alerts. Use the internal tool redwood-alerts to attach runbook pointers automatically.

Capacity prioritization algorithm (for automated arbitration)
- Input signals: SLO priority score (weighted by tier and enterprise impact), current error budget remaining, cost per vGPU-hour, and region redundancy margin.
- Simplified scoring formula (example):
   priority_score = (tier_weight * SLO_score) + (enterprise_weight * enterprise_qps_share) - (cost_weight * vgpu_cost)
   where tier_weight: A=100, B=60, C=20; enterprise_weight is proportion of requests from paid customers; cost_weight normalizes to dollars/hour.
- Use-case: when total demand exceeds capacity by X% (configurable), automated arbiter will: 1) reallocate up to configured soft-reserve from Tier C with lowest score, 2) apply throttles to flagged low-priority routes, 3) propose manual approval to allocate paid reserved nodes.

Capacity change governance and audit trail
- Any manual reallocation of reserved capacity must be recorded in the capacity-change ledger (redwoodctl capacity log --record) with the following fields: service, from_pool, to_pool, node_count, rationale, approver.
- Audit retention: capacity logs retained 13 months. Capacity changes tied to incidents are included in postmortem artifacts.

Pre-deployment checklist for new services (capacity & SLO readiness)
1) Define primary SLOs (availability and latency) and target error budget.
2) Provide 14-day synthetic traffic profile or representative replay.
3) Declare criticality tier and justify from product owner.
4) Estimate baseline RPS and recommended headroom.
5) Register service on capacity dashboard and set initial autoscaler policies.

Example artifacts and snippets
- Sample autoscaler override (YAML):
  apiVersion: autoscaling.redwood.io/v1
  kind: InferenceAutoscaler
  metadata:
    name: embeddings-autoscaler
  spec:
    minReplicas: 3
    maxReplicas: 30
    scalePolicy:
      cpu: 0.7
      queueLength: 20
    emergencyOverrides:
      p99Latency: 300ms
      enabled: true

- Capacity query example (CLI):
  redwoodctl capacity plan --service embeddings --window 7d --percentile 95 --output json

Ownership and escalation paths
- Primary owner: SRE team assigned in service metadata (sre-owner label).
- Secondary owner: Product manager or engineering manager for the owning team.
- Capacity triage contact list: on-call, capacity-allocator, infra-ops. If on-call is unreachable escalate to SRE lead and product director.

Audit and continuous improvement
- Quarterly exercises: simulate 10–30% sudden cross-region traffic spikes and validate arbitration behavior. Record lessons and refine headroom multipliers.
- Monthly SLO sprint: product and SRE run a 2-week review of service-level regressions and capacity rebalancing proposals.

Appendix: quick links and runbooks
- SLO dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/prod/service-slo
- Capacity ledger: https://internal.redwood/capacity/ledger
- Runbooks:
  - Service degradation (link): /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/service-degradation-and-fallbacks-runbook-2026
  - Emergency autoscale steps: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/slo-driven-autoscale-hybrid-inference-runbook-2026

Contact and feedback
If you have questions about applying this guideline to a specific product, email sre-policy@redwood.ai or open an RFC in the eng-sre team wiki.

Change log
- 2025-11-03: Initial draft authored by Nora Patel.
- 2026-02-10: Added automated arbitration scoring and CLI snippets; reviewed by Ethan Brooks and Maya Singh.

payload.page_title: Elastic reservoir capacity runbook for bursty inference workloads

sections.body: This runbook documents the Elastic Reservoir pattern we operate across the inference fleet to absorb short, high-amplitude traffic bursts without violating customer-facing SLOs. The pattern is designed for inference workloads (text generation, chat, embeddings) that have unpredictable burstiness due to external events (campaigns, viral features) and internal retry storms. The document explains detection signals, hedging policies (error budget-aware), automated mitigation actions, and manual escalation steps for SREs on-call.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Maintain primary latency SLOs (P50/P90/P99) and availability SLOs for multi-tenant hosted API and Dedicated pools during short bursts (2–30 minutes).
- Prevent full-tenant evictions where possible; prefer graceful degradation (rate-limited tail, prompt-preserving routing).
- Limit cost by using short-duration reservoir capacity and prioritized tenant admission.
- Apply uniformly to: hosted inference API (front-end gateway + model-serving clusters), dedicated pools, and cross-region failover targets.
sections.heading: Goals and scope

sections.body:
- Reservoir capacity: transient pool of spare GPU instances or pre-warmed model workers assigned to absorb burst demand for up to B minutes.
- Hedging window: sliding time window used for short-term capacity estimation (default: 5 minutes).
- Emergency throttle: prioritized request shedder that enforces token-level and request-level limits to protect SLOs.
- SLO burn signal: percentage of error budget consumed in last X minutes (default X=60). High-burn triggers become part of decision rules.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
| Metric | Target | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| API availability (success rate) | 99.95% / 30d | Applies to hosted API token-scoped traffic |
| Latency P95 (generation) | < 350ms | Measured at edge for short responses (<=128 tokens) |
| Latency P99 (generation) | < 1200ms | Tail target guiding throttles and fallback |
sections.heading: Service-level targets (example baseline)

sections.body:
- Primary signals (real-time):
  - Request rate per tenant / cluster (qps, tokens/s) sampled at 10s granularity.
  - Serving queue length and worker CPU/GPU utilization per model-variant.
  - Token processing latency histogram (P50/P90/P99) per route.
  - SLO burn rate: short-window error-budget consumption (5m, 1h).
  - Admission gateway rejections and 429 spikes.
- Secondary signals (supporting):
  - Upstream API key metadata (campaign tag, known marketing campaigns) from customer headers.
  - Recent config changes / rollouts in the last 60 minutes.
sections.heading: Telemetry & detection signals

sections.body:
1) Detection: trigger when all of the following hold for hedging window (default 5m):
   - cluster-wide incoming token rate > baseline + 3 sigma (60m baseline), AND
   - model-serving queue depth > configured threshold for > 2 sampling intervals, AND
   - SLO burn rate for impacted tenant or cluster < 50% (we favor mitigation without exhausting budgets).
2) Pre-check: verify reservoir free capacity > 1 worker equivalent. If yes, allocate; otherwise proceed to controlled throttle.
3) Allocation: spin up reservoir workers (see "Runbook actions"), route a fraction of new requests to reservoir with probabilistic admission to avoid cache stampede.
4) Observability: create an ephemeral incident timeline entry and tag traces for the affected tenants/models. Notify on-call via existing pager channel and create an ephemeral Slack channel with auto-archive in 8 hours.

Runbook actions (automated + manual):
- Automated actions (system-initiated):
  1. Reservoir allocation: call internal actuator to attach N worker pods (N = min(ceil(delta_qps / worker_capacity), configured_max_burst)). Example CLI: redwoodctl reservoir allocate --cluster model-eu-1 --workers 6 --reason "burst-hedge"
  2. Localized routing: enable reservoir routing policy for target model-variants (route header X-Reservoir: true).
  3. Soft-throttle low-priority tokens: apply token-priority map, demote best-effort traffic to 10% of baseline.
  4. Activate degraded fast-path: switch generation mode to lower-memory quantized kernel on non-critical variants when latency tail is rising.
- Manual SRE checklist (if auto actions fail or SLOs continue to degrade):
  1. Confirm telemetry (dashboards: Reservoir Overview, Token QPS per tenant, P99 heatmap).
  2. Run reservoir status: redwoodctl reservoir status --cluster <cluster> (verify worker readiness).
  3. If allocation failed due to quota, escalate to capacity-oncall (pager ID: capacity-team) and request temporary quota increase for 30–120 minutes.
  4. If tenant-specific burst: coordinate with customer success to enable tenant-side rate limits or move tenant to dedicated queue.
  5. If cross-region fallback is required: follow cross-region failover playbook (step-by-step below).
sections.heading: Automatic decision policy (priority order)

sections.body:
1) Validate that warm standby region has compatible model variant and quantization profile.
2) If standby capacity >= required workers, update routing policy to mirror 20% of traffic and monitor for 5 minutes.
3) Gradually increase mirrored traffic in 20% increments while observing P99.
4) If mirror test passes for 15 minutes, perform full shift with TTL-based DNS fallback and global edge reconfiguration.
sections.heading: Cross-region fallback (summary)

sections.body:
- Priority levels (high -> low): system-critical (control-plane), premium customers, standard tenants, best-effort tenants.
- Eviction order: best-effort -> standard non-paying -> standard paying under negotiated SLAs -> premium (last). Evictions should be explicit (owner notified) and tracked in the eviction ledger for 90 days.
- Throttle knobs: request-rate cap, token-rate cap, request concurrency cap. Provide examples: redwoodctl throttle set --tenant <id> --token-rate 500 --concurrency 8 --duration 15m
sections.heading: Throttle & eviction policy (prioritization)

sections.body:
- Never consume reservoir capacity for more than 20% of a tenant's monthly error budget without manual approval.
- If cluster SLO burn exceeds 70% in 1h window, halt automatic reservoir expansion and switch to conservative throttles + incident postmortem.
- Maintain a rolling list of emergency quotas for busy periods; each emergency quota must be approved by capacity-team lead and recorded.
sections.heading: SLO-aware hedging guardrails

sections.body:
1) If the hedging event lasted > 10 minutes or caused > 1% SLO degradation, open a post-incident review (PIR) using the standard template.
2) Required artifacts for PIR: 10s QPS series, worker allocation timeline, traces for 100 sample slow tokens, reservoir allocator logs, admission gateway decisions, related customer contact history.
3) Tag PIR with mitigation decisions and any manual overrides (quota increases, manual evictions).
sections.heading: Post-incident actions and evidence collection

sections.body:
- Reservoir Overview (grafana): cluster, allocated_reservoir_workers, reservoir_fill_ratio, average_recovery_time
- Hedging Health (grafana): short-window burn, priority throttle rate, cross-region mirror success rate
- Traces: trace-service (filter tag: event:reservoir-hedge)
- CLI tooling: redwoodctl (reservoir allocate/status/release), admissionctl (throttle, priority-map), quotactl (request temporary quota)
sections.heading: Operational tooling & dashboards referenced

sections.body:
- Runbook owner: Priya Raman (serving-runtime team).
- Capacity policy owner: Capacity Oncall / eng-sre.
- Review cadence: quarterly review and after any reservoir-triggered PIR.
- Test plan: monthly chaos drill (inject synthetic burst at 1.5x typical high percentile for 10m) to verify end-to-end allocation and routing.
sections.heading: Maintenance and runbook ownership

sections.body:
- Mean time to reservoir attach (goal < 60s).
- Fraction of bursts absorbed without tenant eviction (> 90%).
- Average SLO burn delta during hedging events (goal < 5% additional burn).
- False-positive hedges (events where reservoir allocated but not materially used) target < 15%.
sections.heading: Metrics to track for continuous improvement

sections.body:
- Allocate reservoir (example):
  redwoodctl reservoir allocate --cluster model-us-west-2 --workers 4 --reason "auto-hedge"
- Check status:
  redwoodctl reservoir status --cluster model-us-west-2 --json
- Example admission throttle JSON (used by admissionctl):
  {
    "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
    "token_rate": 1000,
    "concurrency": 12,
    "expires_at": "2026-11-03T12:45:00Z"
  }
sections.heading: Runbook appendix (example commands and JSON snippets)

sections.body:
- 2025-07-12: Initial authoring (Priya Raman).
- 2026-02-09: Add SLO guardrail to cap reservoir consumption per tenant (Lucas Nguyen).
- 2026-11-03: Expand cross-region mirror procedure and add false-positive KPI (Mariana Costa).
sections.heading: Change log

sections.body:
- Service-onboarding and SLO admission playbook (service-onboarding-runway-and-slo-admission-playbook-2026)
- Capacity observability and recovery playbook (capacity-observability-and-recovery-playbook-2026)
- Cross-region failover execution and verification playbook
