payload.page_title: Zero-Data-Loss Private Deploy Upgrade Playbook (SRE Runbook)

sections.body:
This runbook describes a tested, operator-focused process to perform upgrades to Private (VPC / on-prem) deployments with an explicit goal: zero data loss for runtime state (KV caches, tenant snapshots, model artifacts) and minimal customer-visible disruption. It combines atomic state checkpointing, staged model activation, transactional KMS-friendly key rotation, and automated verification gates.

This 2031 revision reflects changes in tooling (snapshot v4.x), updated latency gates, and a stricter definition of “wave success” after several 2030 incident learnings.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: Tenant-facing runtime components in private deployments (inference runtime, KV cache, model store, control-plane agents, local telemetry collectors).
- Not in scope: physical firmware upgrades for HW (see onprem-packaging docs) and customer-managed load balancer changes.
- Audience: SREs, field operators, deployment engineers, and delivery leads executing upgrades in customer environments.
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body:
- Operator access to customer control plane and operator-run SSH bastion or management VPN.
- Backups of model artifacts and KV state accessible in immutable object store (S3 compatible).
- Snapshot tooling version >= 4.1.0 installed on operator workstation (replaces 3.x).
- KMS integration supports offline wrapping/unwrapping, key versions, and dual-primary “grace” windows (see KMS rotation appendix).
- Pre-approved maintenance window in calendar and customer acceptance of canary flow.
- NOTE: Starting 2031-01, “strong” KV snapshots are mandatory for tenant-critical namespaces (see KV notes).
sections.heading: Prerequisites and assumptions

sections.body:
1) Validate and baseline: collect telemetry and pre-upgrade evidence.
2) Cold checkpoints: produce consistent, point-in-time snapshots of tenant runtime state.
3) Canary upgrade: upgrade control plane + 1–3 tenants with staged runtime activation and smoke tests.
4) Gradual roll: expand tenant upgrades in bounded waves with automated validation gates.
5) Switch-over: final atomic activation for remaining tenants with KV rehydrate and verification.
6) Fortify and evidence: preserve upgrade artifacts and run post-upgrade acceptance tests.
sections.heading: High-level strategy (phases)

sections.body:
- No loss of KV keys between pre-checkpoint and post-activation (0 missing keys; 0 unexpected new keys in protected namespaces).
- Latency and tail-p99 meet SLOs for canary tenants (< 140ms p50, < 450ms p99) OR match pre-upgrade baseline within configured delta (default: +10% p50, +15% p99).
- Error budget change < 3% during the wave (tightened from 5%).
- All smoke evaluation prompt-sets show no regressions beyond configured threshold.
- Snapshot restore drill remains viable: restore test of at least one tenant snapshot to a staging runtime must succeed during T-24h baseline window.
sections.heading: Success criteria (per wave)

sections.body:
A. Baseline collection (T-24h to T-1h)
  1. Run auto-benchmark agent:
     `rwoodctl telemetry baseline --tenants all --duration 1h --out baseline.json`
  2. Export list of active tenants and outstanding long-lived KV sessions:
     `rwoodctl tenants list --format csv`
  3. Verify object-store snapshot health and retention window >= 96h (updated from 72h).
  4. Create pre-upgrade evidence bundle (sha256) and upload to evidence bucket.
  5. Validate KMS health and key-version visibility from the customer environment:
     `rwoodctl kms status --out kms-status.json`

B. Cold checkpoint (T-2h)
  1. Quiesce write-heavy routes: add temporary rate-limit rule for tenant hotpaths.
  2. Trigger KV checkpoint:
     `rwoodctl kv snapshot create --consistency strong --label pre-upgrade-2031-01-10`
  3. Verify snapshot completion and checksum.
  4. Export a short read-only witness token for customers that require audit proof.
  5. (New) Record snapshot manifest ID returned by snapshot v4.x (required for restore concurrency control).

C. Canary wave (T)
  1. Select 1–3 low-risk tenants (non-critical, representative workload).
  2. Upgrade control plane components (control-plane agents, operator-tools): follow package manifest install and smoke test commands in order.
  3. For each canary tenant: perform in-place runtime upgrade with staged model activation:
     - Upload new model variant to model-store with staging label `staged-<version>`
     - Start runtime in `dual-binary` mode: accept both old/new model loads but route 95% traffic to old version for 20m (reduced from 30m if gates are clean).
     - Run synthetic workload and compare outputs to golden prompt-set (automation command):
       `rwoodctl eval run --tenant TENANT_ID --prompt-set ./canary-prompts.json`
  4. If checks pass (no regressions, latency within gate), increase traffic to new model 50% for 10m, then 100%.
  5. Monitor telemetry for 60 minutes after 100% cutover before proceeding.

D. Wave expansion and throttling rules
  - Waves are timeboxed to 90 minutes each (updated from 2 hours) to reduce blast radius and improve operator focus.
  - A wave fails if any of:
    - KV drift > 0 keys in protected namespaces (auth/session/rate-limit)
    - Error rate spike > 35% over baseline for > 10 minutes (tightened)
    - P99 latency exceeds gate for > 15 minutes
    - Any KMS unwrap failure affecting model-store or snapshot envelope (now an automatic stop)
  - On failure: execute rollback for that wave (see Rollback procedures).
sections.heading: Detailed checklist and operator steps

sections.body:
1. Immediate rollback trigger conditions: KV inconsistency detected, persistent tail latency degradation, KMS unwrap/rewrap failures, or customer emergency request.
2. Per-wave rollback steps:
   - Reapply older model label and switch runtime routing:
     `rwoodctl runtime route set --tenant TENANT_ID --model-label previous --force`
   - If model routing cannot be reverted within 5 minutes, trigger KV snapshot restore from `pre-upgrade` snapshot and restart runtime processes (see KV restore command below).
   - (New) If KMS rotation Phase 2 has started, pause rotation and keep old key version active; do not delete or disable any key versions.
3. Full rollback (global):
   - Pause all waves and open incident bridge (see related runbook).
   - Restore object-store model artifacts from `pre-upgrade` evidence bundle.
   - Restore KV for affected tenants:
     `rwoodctl kv snapshot restore --snapshot pre-upgrade-2031-01-10 --tenants TENANT_LIST`
   - Run full smoke regression and hold traffic behind circuit-breaker until verified.
sections.heading: Rollback procedures (per-wave and final)

sections.body:
- Create snapshot:
  `rwoodctl kv snapshot create --consistency strong --label pre-upgrade-2031-01-10 --out /tmp/snap.json`
- Restore snapshot (v4.x supports adaptive concurrency; start conservative):
  `rwoodctl kv snapshot restore --snapshot /tmp/snap.json --concurrency 2 --confirm`
- Start dual-binary runtime:
  `rwood-runtime --mode dual --old-bin /opt/runtime/v1 --new-bin /opt/runtime/v2 --health-probe /health`
- Model staging upload:
  `rwoodctl model upload --file model-1.q8 --label staged-2031-01-10`
sections.heading: Commands and examples

sections.body:
- Always use strong-consistency checkpoints for tenant-critical KV namespaces (session tokens, auth grants, rate-limiter counters).
- Snapshot v4.x: strong-consistency snapshots may take longer but provide deterministic manifest + checksum. Plan wave timing accordingly.
- Ephemeral caches (in-memory LRU) are allowed to be warm-started; do not rely on them for correctness.
- Use the kvcmp tool to assert key-level equality for a small sample:
  `kvcmp --from snapA --to runtime --sample 1000`
sections.heading: KV and cache consistency notes

sections.body:
- When upgrading components that touch key-wrapping (model-store encryption, snapshot envelopes), perform a two-phase key rotation:
  Phase 1: Add new key version as a secondary wrapping key and re-encrypt non-critical artifacts asynchronously.
  Phase 2: After successful canary and wave 1, promote new key version to primary and rewrap remaining artifacts.
- 2031 update: maintain a 14-day grace window where both old and new key versions remain enabled for unwrap operations in customer environments that may lag configuration propagation.
- Do not delete old key versions until full forensic evidence is archived and customer confirms successful acceptance.
sections.heading: KMS rotation and key versioning during upgrade

sections.body:
| Step | Check | Command / Tool |
|------|-------|----------------|
| Pre-snapshot | Active worker count and mem pressure | `rwoodctl metrics get --worker-count` |
| Post-snapshot | Snapshot checksum matches runtime expected | `rwoodctl kv snapshot verify --snapshot /tmp/snap.json` |
| Canary outputs | Prompt-set semantic similarity >= 0.93 vs baseline (tightened) | `rwoodctl eval similarity --a baseline.json --b canary.json` |
| Post-activation | No increase in 5xx errors for 30m | `rwoodctl alerts query --metric 5xx --window 30m` |
| Post-activation | KMS unwrap error count == 0 for 30m | `rwoodctl alerts query --metric kms_unwrap_errors --window 30m` |
sections.heading: Verification matrix (minimum checks per tenant)

sections.body:
- Waves continue only after automated gate + human sign-off from SRE on-call for restricted/private deployments.
- For large tenants (> $X revenue) also require delivery lead and customer success sign-off.
- For small tenants, automated gates suffice unless customer opted into manual approval.
sections.heading: Roll-forward gates and sign-off

sections.body:
- If snapshot fails due to network timeouts: increase object-store multipart timeout and retry with concurrency 1–2.
- If model load fails with OOM: reduce max_concurrent_requests on runtime and throttle traffic; escalate to runtime team with `#runtime-ops` bridge.
- If KMS unwrap fails for a tenant: fetch secondary wrapping key and attempt offline unwrap; if unsuccessful, open high-priority support SR with KMS vendor and stop rollout.
- If post-upgrade P99 regresses but correctness is intact: hold at current wave, roll back only affected tenants, and collect heap/CPU profiles before proceeding.
sections.heading: Troubleshooting quick hits

sections.body:
- Retain evidence bundle (snapshots, checksums, logs, eval outputs) for minimum 180 days for restricted upgrades (updated from 90 days).
- Run full evaluation harness across representative prompt-sets at 1h, 6h, 24h post-upgrade.
- Update deployment manifest and chronic record in upgrade ledger:
  `rwoodctl ledger append --entry upgrade-2031-01-10 --artifact evidence-bucket/pre-upgrade-2031-01-10`
sections.heading: Post-upgrade monitoring and evidence preservation

sections.body:
- Upgrade owner (primary): SRE On-Call (per rota)
- Runbook owner: Arjun Patel (eng-sre)
- Private deploy engineering liaison: Sofia Martinez
- Runtime/Kernel escalation: Li Wei
- Customer Success liaison: Maya Thompson

Appendix A — Sample manifest diff (text):
- runtime_image: v3.1.2 -> v3.2.0
- model_store_schema: 2030-08 -> 2031-01 (staged label defaults + stricter checksum enforcement)
- kv_snapshot_tool: 4.0.2 -> 4.1.0 (manifest IDs + improved verify)

Appendix B — Forensic checklist (mandatory for restricted upgrades):
- SHA256 of all snapshots and model artifacts
- Snapshot manifest IDs and restore logs (including concurrency settings)
- System logs from control-plane agents (window T-1h to T+2h)
- Eval outputs and similarity scores for canary tenants
- KMS key versions and rotation event log (including grace-window config)
sections.heading: Owner and escalation matrix

sections.body:
- 2029-02-15: Created by Sofia Martinez (initial draft)
- 2029-03-02: Added KMS rotation guidance and hardened rollback gates (reviewers: Arjun Patel, Li Wei)
- 2031-01-10: Migrated into eng-sre runbooks; tightened wave gates, retention policy, and updated snapshot tooling requirements (owner: Arjun Patel)
- 2031-02-05: Updated latency/error gates and added mandatory KMS unwrap checks; clarified v4.x snapshot manifest handling (reviewers: Priya Nair, Maya Thompson)
sections.heading: Change history

sections.body:
- See `kv-cache-migrations-and-runtime-state-migration-playbook-2025` for deep dive on snapshot internals.
- See `private-deploy-evidence-preservation-and-forensic-playbook-2026` for compliance evidence retention guidelines.
- See `private-deploy-upgrade-incident-bridge-guide-2030` for incident coordination.
sections.heading: Related reading and references

sections.body: - For immediate assistance during an upgrade, open the `#private-deploy-upgrades` channel and tag `@ops-oncall` and `@sre-oncall`.

payload.page_title: SLO Commitment Negotiation and Delegation Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook defines a repeatable process for negotiating SLO commitments with product teams, delegating SLO stewardship, and converting commitments into capacity reservations and error-budget guardrails. It emphasizes pragmatic tradeoffs (latency vs cost vs availability) and formal handoffs to ensure measurable accountability.

Goals
- Produce SLO agreements that are measurable, testable, and pair with concrete capacity commitments.
- Reduce negotiation friction and speed up safe rollouts.
- Ensure error-budget actions and capacity changes are enacted automatically where possible, or with clear human approval steps.

Scope
Applies to: model-serving services, inference frontends, embedding pipelines, and any tenant-facing inference subsystem. Excludes internal-only batch analytics (handled by infra-cost team).

Definitions
- SLI: Service Level Indicator (e.g., p99 latency excluding cold starts; 99.9% inference success).
- SLO: Service Level Objective (target value for an SLI over a rolling window).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO over the evaluation window (commonly 28 days).
- Steward: individual responsible for SLO health, runbook updates, and coordination.

SLO Taxonomy and Examples
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Latency SLOs (user-facing): p50/p95/p99 tail per route, measured at ingress after auth.
- Availability SLOs (success rate): 5xx+4xx-excluding-rate-limited / total requests.
- Correctness SLOs (quality): task-specific metric, e.g., regression against verified prompt set (for core models).
- Cost-awareness indicators: tokens-per-request and mean GPU-ms per request (inform capacity reservations).

Example baseline commitments (starting point for negotiations):
- Hosted-generation-default: p95 <= 350ms, success >= 99.5% (28d), error budget 0.5%.
- Large-context-chat: p95 <= 800ms, success >= 99.0% (28d), error budget 1.0%.
- Embeddings-batch: p95 <= 1200ms, success >= 99.8% (28d), error budget 0.2%.
(These are examples — negotiate per-tenant when needed.)

Negotiation Process (Step-by-step)
1) Preparation (Product Owner + SRE Steward)
   - Gather: expected QPS, request size distribution (tokens), critical routes, SLA requirements, geographic constraints.
   - Run the capacity estimator tool (see Appendix) with 14-day traffic forecast.
   - Prepare a recommended SLO and a conservative capacity reservation (GPU hours + burst allowance).
2) First-pass negotiation (cross-functional meeting)
   - Present tradeoffs: lower latency requires higher reserved capacity or higher cost. Show cost delta estimates.
   - Propose two-tier options: Standard (lower cost, higher error budget) and Premium (lower latency, dedicated capacity).
   - Capture non-functional constraints: data residency, private deployment needs.
3) Draft SLO contract (SRE drafts)
   - SLO statement (metric, window, target), monitoring sources, alerting thresholds, runbook reference, steward assignment, capacity reservation ID.
   - Attach rollback and phased rollout plan (canary percentages and step durations).
4) Sign-off and storage
   - Product PO and SRE steward sign off in the confluence contract page. The contract is versioned and stored under the product’s folder.
5) Implementation
   - Create capacity reservation ticket in Capacity Tracking board with exact machine types, commit windows, and autoscale policies.
   - Wire alerts and dashboards (see Telemetry section).
6) Operationalization
   - Configure error-budget controller thresholds (auto-throttle at 50% consumed, escalation window at 75%).
   - Schedule monthly review in SLO standing meeting.

Delegation and Stewardship Matrix
- Product Owner: defines feature-level criticality and approves SLO tradeoffs.
- SRE Steward: owns SLO definition, alerting, runbook updates, and capacity negotiations.
- Platform Capacity Manager: implements reservation, cost tracking, and shares forecasting.
- Oncall (Service): executes runbook steps and coordinates incident escalation.

Capacity Commitment Flow (mapping SLO -> resources)
1) Telemetry-derived baseline (7d): compute mean and 95th token lengths, QPS distribution per route.
2) Model profile lookup: tokens-to-GPU-ms conversion from benchmarking matrix.
3) Safety margin: apply 30% headroom default (tunable per tenant).
4) Reservation plan: CPU/GPU count, node types, local NVMe needs, and network egress estimate.
5) Autoscale policy: minimum reserved fraction and burstable ceiling with graceful fallbacks to smaller models.

Capacity Negotiation Template (summary for execs)
- Proposed SLO: p95 latency <= 350ms, success >= 99.5% (28d)
- Expected steady QPS: 120
- Mean tokens per request: 180
- Profiled GPU-ms/request: 42ms (A100-40GB equivalent)
- Reserve: 6 GPUs (NVIDIA A100 equiv) + 30% headroom
- Estimated monthly cost delta: $XXk
- Action: approve reservation or accept Standard tier with p95 <= 550ms and shared capacity

Telemetry and Evidence (what to wire)
- Essential SLIs: ingress_p95_latency_ms, request_success_rate, tokens_per_request, gpu_ms_per_request
- Dashboards: 28d rolling SLO summary, per-route latency heatmap, error-budget burn-down chart.
- Alerts:
  - SLO-warning: error_budget_remaining < 50% over 24h -> Pager (severity: low) to SRE steward
  - SLO-escalation: error_budget_remaining < 25% over 6h -> Pager (severity: high) + product PO notification
  - Immediate-degradation: request_success_rate drops below target - 0.5% absolute -> Pager to oncall (severity: critical)
- Evidence collection: link to saved traces, a slice example (tenant, route, time range), and pre-populated playback queries.

Runbook: SLO Depletion and Mitigation Procedure
1) Triage (oncall)
   - Verify telemetry: confirm SLI alert, check burn rate, and scope (tenant vs global).
   - Execute quick containment: throttle non-critical routes, divert to cached responses, or reduce model context length.
2) Temporary capacity actions
   - If autoscale available: increase replica count up to the burst ceiling.
   - If reservation needed: request pre-approved burst tokens (see Capacity board fast-path).
3) Degradation plan (when capacity cannot be added)
   - Apply graceful degradation policy: route lower-priority tenants to lower-cost model variant; enable token cap per request.
4) Communication
   - Post to status page with clear user-facing impact, ETA, and mitigation actions.
   - Notify sales/customer-success for affected enterprise customers.
5) Post-incident
   - Create incident ticket, collect slices and artifacts, and run the incident-review checklist (see Incident Review Standards).

Incident Review Standards (brief)
- Trigger: any event that consumes >50% of error budget in 24h or any P0 outage.
- Required deliverables: timeline, evidence, root cause hypothesis, mitigation record, and remediation plan with owners and deadlines.
- Blameless facilitation: SRE steward runs the review within 5 business days.

Operational Tooling Recommendations
- Capacity estimator: runcapacity --service <name> --window 14d --safety 0.3 (returns GPU-hours + suggested node types).
- Error-budget controller: configure with the following thresholds in the orchestration UI: warning=0.5, escalate=0.25, hard-stop=0.05.
- Dashboard snippets (Grafana/Panel IDs included as text): panel ids: latency-overview-034, errorbudget-burn-121, per-route-heat-507.

Rollout and Canary Guidelines
- Canary cadence: 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100% with at least 30 minutes at each stage and SLO checks.
- Abort criteria: any canary stage that increases error burn rate by >3x baseline or produces >0.5% absolute drop in success rate.

Templates & Examples
- Contract excerpt:
  SLO: ingress_p95_latency_ms <= 350ms (28d); Measurement point: ingress-proxy v2; Steward: <name>
  Capacity reservation: reservation-2025-ACCT-42; Node type: a100-40gb; Min replicas: 3; Burst ceiling: 9

- Example alert query (PromQL-like pseudocode):
  1 - (sum(successful_requests) by (service) / sum(total_requests) by (service))
  Use rolling_window = 28d and compare to contract target.

Appendix: Practical checks before sign-off
- Confirm telemetry sources (traces, metrics, logs) are producing for the full retention period.
- Run synthetic canary to validate p95 under a 1.5x expected load.
- Confirm policy for emergency preemptive scaling and customer communication.

Ownership and maintenance
- SRE stewards must review active SLOs quarterly, and trigger a negotiation if traffic patterns shift >25% or if cost exceeds projections by >15%.
- Archive retired SLO contracts after 2 years; keep a read-only audit trail.

Contact points
- Oncall rotations: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response
- Capacity board: #capacity-tracking (internal)

Revision history
- 2025-03-18: initial draft by Maya Patel
- 2025-09-02: added auto-throttle recommendations and canary abort criteria (reviewers: Ethan Rivera)
- 2026-01-12: expanded telemetry and capacity template (reviewers: Priya Nambiar, Liam O'Connor)

payload.page_title: SDK telemetry surge response and SLA playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents the developer-facing runbook for SDK telemetry surges that threaten customer-facing SLAs. It is intended for SDK owners, developer experience (DevX) oncall, and eng-sre responders. The focus is on fast containment, root-cause isolation, graceful degradation patterns supported by the SDK, and follow-up remediation.

Goals and scope
- Contain telemetry-volume incidents that can: inflate costs, back-pressure the telemetry pipeline, or cause API latency regressions.
- Protect public inference SLOs (p90 latency <= 250ms for small-gen routes; p99 <= 2s for chat surfaces) and telemetry-integration SLAs (ingest latency <= 10s for 99% of events).
- Cover all SDKs (python, js, go, java) and both hosted and private customers where SDKs forward diagnostics to Redwood telemetry endpoints.

When to use this document
1) A spike in telemetry events attributed to a particular SDK version, customer, or route.
2) Rapid cost increases from telemetry egress or storage.
3) Ingest pipeline back-pressure causing increased user-visible latency or errors.

Primary contacts and responsibilities
- SDK Owner (primary): triage, reproduce, ship hotfix or mitigation.
- DevX Oncall (secondary): coordinate customer communications, temporary gating, and telemetry feature flags.
- Eng-SRE (supporting): scale ingest, apply rate limits, and adjust retention/compaction policies.
- Product (FYI): customer impact assessment and postmortem.

Telem metrics to watch (dashboards)
- sdk.telemetry.events_per_minute (by sdk_version, tenant_id, route)
- sdk.telemetry.event_size_bytes_p95
- ingestion.pipeline.backpressure_ratio
- api.request.p99_latency_by_route
- billing.telemetry_estimated_monthly_cost_by_tenant

Alerting thresholds (default)
| Alert name | Trigger | Severity | Pager | Notes |
|------------|---------|----------|-------|-------|
| Telemetry Surge (tenant) | events_per_minute > 20k for 5m for single tenant | P1 | eng-sre | immediate containment required |
| SDK Error Flood | sdk.client.errors > 0.5% of requests for 10m | P2 | devx-oncall | likely rollout/regression |
| Ingest Backpressure | backpressure_ratio > 0.2 for 2m | P1 | eng-sre | ingress scaling or throttling |
| Telemetry Cost Spike | estimated_cost_growth > 150% week-over-week | P3 | finance-legal (notify) | billing review |

Pre-flight checks (before mitigation)
1. Confirm the spike is real: cross-check ingestion logs, raw S3/segments with dashboard aggregates.
2. Identify scope: tenant_id, sdk_version, route pattern, and region.
3. Check deploys: recent SDK releases, client-side feature flags, or server-side rollout windows in last 72h.
4. Determine impact to user-facing SLOs (p90/p99 latency and error rate).

Immediate containment steps (0–30 minutes)
1. Create a dedicated incident channel and tag stakeholders (use the standard #inc-telemetry channel).
2. If a single tenant is responsible: apply tenant-scoped telemetry rate limit via ingress policy (commands below).
3. If a single SDK version is responsible: set the server-side safety gate for that version to disable forwarding of optional diagnostics (see feature-flag procedures).
4. If ingestion is overloaded: enable transient compaction (drop non-critical sampling events) on the ingestion cluster.
5. If user-facing latency is rising: activate adaptive request shaping in the runtime to prioritize production traffic and defer optional telemetry flushes.

Commands and snippets
- Apply tenant rate limit (k8s ingress policy CLI example):
  kubectl exec -n telemetry ingress-controller -- /bin/sh -c '\n  telemetryctl rate-limit apply --tenant={{TENANT_ID}} --limit=1000rpm --window=60s --reason="surge-mitigation"\n  '

- Flip SDK telemetry gate for version (feature-flag service):
  curl -X POST https://flags.redwood.internal/api/v1/flags/disable \n    -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${FF_TOKEN}' \n    -d '{"flag":"sdk-telemetry-forward","selector":{"sdk_version":"1.4.2"},"duration":"2h","reason":"surge-mitigation"}'

- Ingestion compaction toggle (CLI):
  ingestctl compaction enable --policy=drop-noncritical --cluster=ingest-prod --duration=60m --note="auto-mitigate-surge"

Graceful SDK-side degradations (recommended patterns)
- Sampling and reservoir sizing: SDKs must implement adaptive sampling that reduces non-essential event sampling to <= 0.1% under a surge signal.
- Batching thresholds: increase batch_size to reduce per-event overhead during high-throughput windows.
- Backoff & buffer caps: SDKs should place an upper limit on buffered events (default 5MB) and return immediate non-blocking drops when buffer is exceeded in 'best-effort' mode.
- Local persistence policy: for private deployments, route telemetry to local buffer and only ship critical alerts until ingest stabilizes.

Investigation steps (30–180 minutes)
1. Narrow to a root cause: client bug, bad input pattern (e.g., infinite loop emitting events), misconfiguration, or coordinated customer test.
2. Reproduce in staging using the same sdk_version and tenant traffic shape. Use the incident replay harness: \n  - tools/replay/run.sh --tenant {{TENANT_ID}} --pattern "high-event-rate" --duration 10m
3. Inspect recent commits and changelogs for the SDK repo: look for changes in telemetry format, default sampling, or retry logic.
4. If the source is client-side malfunctioning customers: prepare targeted rollback instructions or a compatibility patch.

Communication playbook
- Immediately: post a public incident banner in the status page indicating degraded telemetry ingestion with an ETA for the next update (15–30 minutes).
- Within 1 hour: notify affected customers with tenant-scoped messages. Provide mitigation steps (client-side toggle, recommended temporary SDK version).
- Post-resolution: publish a postmortem documenting cause, impact, timeline, and remediation steps within 72 hours.

Post-incident remediation and hardening
- Patch the SDK: release a non-breaking patch that restores sampling defaults or fixes any infinite-loop condition. Use the SDK semver policy and include migration notes.
- Telemetry schema and validation: add stricter schema checks at ingestion to reject obviously malformed events and count them separately to avoid backpressure.
- Add per-tenant cost alerting: automate monthly cost projection alerts for sudden telemetry spending.
- Improve SDK canary gating: require a 48-hour dark canary for telemetry-related changes that modify defaults or format.

Proposed SLO changes and thresholds to consider
| SLO | Current | Proposed change | Rationale |
|-----|---------|-----------------|----------|
| Telemetry ingest latency | 99th <= 10s | keep | Maintain rapid processing for debugging data |
| SDK telemetry event size p95 | 1.2kB | reduce target to <= 1kB | limit per-event bytes to control costs |
| Tenant telemetry rate soft-limit | 10k rpm | add adaptive soft-limit with automatic notification at 5k rpm | early warning and graceful slowdown |

Telemetry schema (recommended minimal fields)
{\n  "event_id": "uuid-v4",\n  "timestamp": "ISO8601",\n  "tenant_id": "string",\n  "sdk_version": "semver",\n  "route": "string",\n  "event_type": "enum(usage,diagnostic,error,heartbeat)",\n  "payload_size": "int",\n  "sampling_rate": "float"\n}

Troubleshooting matrix
- Symptom: sudden 10x increase from single tenant
  - Likely cause: customer load test or runaway client loop
  - Immediate action: tenant rate-limit -> notify customer -> request mitigation or apply tenant rollback
- Symptom: telemetry size spikes with stable event rate
  - Likely cause: changed payload schema or richer attachments
  - Immediate action: identify SDK version -> rollback schema change -> temporary drop attachments at ingress
- Symptom: multi-tenant gradual rise across versions
  - Likely cause: product rollout increasing verbose diagnostics
  - Immediate action: evaluate rollout plan, enable global sampling, and coordinate with product for opt-in reduction

Runbook for SDK owners (checklist)
1. Reproduce locally and in staging.
2. Prepare a patch or configuration change.
3. Draft customer-facing instructions.
4. Coordinate with eng-sre to lift temporary ingress limits.
5. Schedule postmortem and follow-up work.

Monitoring & observability improvements (actionable items)
- Add tenant-level attribution to the telemetry cost dashboard.
- Create a lightweight probe that validates telemetry schema for new SDK releases automatically during CI.
- Implement a rolling synthetic test that emits representative telemetry from each SDK platform every 4 hours to detect regressions early.

Appendix: links and references
- Incident template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-template
- Telemetry API spec: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-telemetry-telemetry-schema-2026
- Feature flag service docs: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/feature-flags

Revision history
- 2027-02-15: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2027-03-01: Updated containment command examples and added ingress compaction procedure (Marco Rivera).

payload.page_title: Tenant SLO Migration: Safe Drain and Eviction Procedure

sections.body:
Overview:
This runbook describes the safe, observable procedure for migrating tenant SLO contracts between backend pools and performing controlled tenant drain/eviction when required. It covers preconditions, capacity hedging, error-budget handoffs, automated tooling, canary steps, rollback criteria, and post-migration incident review standards. Intended audience: SRE oncall, platform engineers, and solutions engineers executing tenant migrations or emergency evictions.

Why this exists:
- Migrations and controlled evictions are high-risk operations: they impact SLOs, customer experience, and billing.
- We must preserve SLO commitments (latency and availability) while ensuring fair capacity distribution across tenants.
- This runbook codifies operational policy to minimize surprises and enable rapid, evidence-driven postmortems.

Key definitions and SLO expectations:
- Tenant SLO Contract: a tuple of availability SLO, latency SLO (p50/p95/p99), and any throughput or SLA clauses (e.g., burst allowances).
- Default migration safety thresholds: availability >= 99.95% (30d), p95 latency <= 250ms for interactive endpoints, error budget consumption <= 30% in last 7d prior to migration.
- Hedging capacity: temporary excess capacity allocated to the target pool to absorb migration bursts (recommended 10–25% of migrating tenant's peak RPS).

Pre-migration checklist (must be completed before starting):
1) Ownership and approvals:
   - Confirm migration owner (platform engineer) and secondary oncall.
   - Confirm business owner approval for any scheduled evictions.
2) SLO and error budget validation:
   - Verify tenant error budget consumption: should be <= 30% over last 7d. If >30%, raise to "migration with caution" state and require senior SRE signoff.
   - Confirm SLO contract version tags for source and target pools.
3) Capacity and routing readiness:
   - Ensure target pool has hedging capacity: target_pool.available_gpu_slots >= migrating_peak_rps * hedging_multiplier (default 1.15).
   - Validate autoscaler cooldowns and burst policies are tuned for migration window.
4) Telemetry and alerting:
   - Create temporary synthetic canaries for the tenant (3 endpoints, 1rps each) and configure dashboard with p50/p95/p99, error rate, queue depth, and KV cache hit rate.
   - Ensure alert thresholds are active: p95 > 400ms or availability drop > 0.1% triggers immediate rollback.
5) Rollback plan and comms:
   - Document rollback steps, required IAM principals, CLI commands, and expected timeline (target < 10 minutes to rollback full traffic).
   - Notify stakeholders and set status in #platform-ops and incident channel.

Automated tooling and commands (examples):
- Dry-run migration plan (shows capacity delta and routing plan):
  $ rlctl migration plan --tenant my-tenant --from pool-a --to pool-b --dry-run

- Start phased drain (phase size = 10% by default):
  $ rlctl migration start --tenant my-tenant --to pool-b --phase-size 10 --monitor true

- Force immediate rollback:
  $ rlctl migration rollback --tenant my-tenant --to pool-a --force --reason "p95 spike"

Phased migration procedure (recommended):
1) Phase 0 (Canary verification):
   - Route 1% of traffic (or 10 RPS, whichever smaller) to the target pool.
   - Observe telemetry for 15 minutes. Key checks: p95, error rate, queue backlog, model KV miss rate.
   - Pass criteria: no p95 spike > 2x baseline, error rate <= baseline + 0.05%.
2) Phase 1..N (gradual ramp):
   - Increase routed traffic in increments of 10% with a 10–15 minute observation window per phase.
   - If any threshold breach occurs, pause and investigate; consider 5% rollback if effect is localized.
3) Finalization:
   - After 100% traffic is shifted and stable for 30 minutes, mark migration complete and remove temporary canaries.

Emergency eviction procedure (when tenant is exceeding safety thresholds or causing cross-tenant degradation):
1) Trigger criteria (any of):
   - Tenant consumes > 60% of cluster memory/GPU for > 10 minutes and is not throttled by quotas.
   - Tenant error budget consumption => 100% within 24h and causing repeated retries/fallbacks across hosts.
   - Tenant-caused degradation returns cross-tenant p95 increases > 15% on core services.
2) Eviction steps (fast path):
   - Notify stakeholders and set channel status.
   - Quarantine new admissions: update ingress policy to return 429 for non-admin control-plane clients.
   - Begin eviction: $ rlctl tenant evict --tenant my-tenant --mode graceful --grace-period 120
   - If graceful eviction fails to reduce load within 5 minutes, escalate to force eviction: $ rlctl tenant evict --tenant my-tenant --mode force
3) Post-eviction diagnostics:
   - Collect per-host logs, kernel metrics, GPU utilization, and scheduler decisions for the 30 minutes preceding eviction.
   - Capture model runtime stack traces and KV cache eviction stats.

Rollback criteria (immediate rollback triggers):
- p95 latency on target pool > 3x baseline for > 5 minutes.
- Availability drop > 0.25% absolute across tenant or >0.1% across aggregate customer-facing endpoints.
- Error rate spikes > 0.5% absolute from baseline.
- Sudden increase in queue depth or persistent GC/OOM signals on target hosts.

SLO-awareness in incident review and postmortem standards:
- Any migration or eviction that resulted in SLO breaches requires a structured incident review with the following minimum evidence: migration plan, telemetry dashboards, rlctl logs, alert timeline, and mitigation actions.
- Postmortem must include: root cause hypothesis, detection latency, error-budget delta, capacity delta, an action owner for each remediation item, and a follow-up timeline (max 30 days).
- Severity determination: if customer-facing availability drops > 0.5% or >3 tenants impacted for > 30 minutes, classify as Sev2 and notify executive oncall.

Capacity planning and debt mitigation guidance:
- Maintain a "migration buffer" of 15% available capacity in each region for scheduled tenant migrations.
- For long-running draining of large tenants (> 2k RPS), schedule during low-traffic windows and pre-warm target pools (warm replicas, primed KV caches).
- Track migration-related capacity debt in the SRE backlog and prioritize optimizations that reduce cache cold-starts and first-token latency.

Telemetry and dashboards to monitor during operations:
- Tenant migration dashboard (default panels): routed-traffic %, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, request queue depth, KV cache hit rate, host GPU utilization, autoscaler actions, ingress rejects (429s).
- Alerting matrix (examples):
  | Signal | Threshold | Action |
  |--------|-----------|--------|
  | p95 latency | > 400ms (tenant) | Pause migration, investigate model runtime |
  | Error rate | > baseline + 0.5% | Rollback 10% traffic, open incident |
  | Host GPU load | > 90% sustained 5m | Add temporary capacity, migrate other low-priority tenants |
Operational responsibilities and ownership:
- Migration owner: executes runbook and holds the migration lock until finalization.
- Oncall SRE: monitoring, immediate rollback authority if thresholds breach.
- Platform engineering: responsible for rlctl automation and capacity provisioning.
- Solutions engineering: communicates customer impacts and billing reconciliations.

After-action and continuous improvement:
1) Immediate (within 24h): create incident record and collect required evidence.
2) Short-term (within 7d): perform blameless postmortem, identify 3 concrete mitigations (automation, telemetry, capacity).
3) Long-term (30d): schedule follow-up work into SRE roadmap; update migration automation if it required manual intervention.

Appendix A — Example migration YAML (used by rlctl):
---
migration_request:
  tenant: "my-tenant"
  from_pool: "pool-a"
  to_pool: "pool-b"
  phase_size_percent: 10
  canary_rps: 5
  hedging_multiplier: 1.15
  max_rollout_minutes: 180
  rollback_on:
    p95_multiplier: 3.0
    availability_drop_absolute: 0.0025
    error_rate_absolute: 0.005
---

Appendix B — Quick checklist (one-page) to paste in incident channel:
- Migration owner and backup named
- SLO check: last 7d error budget <= 30%
- Hedging capacity validated (>= 1.15x)
- Canary endpoints created and verified
- Alerts active for p95, error rate, host load
- Rollback CLI tested and ready

Contact and escalation matrix:
- Platform oncall: #sre-oncall (pager)
- Platform lead: Marco Ruiz (marco@redwood.ai)
- Solutions: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai)

Document history:
- 2025-11-15: Created by Elena Morozova
- 2026-03-02: Revised hedging defaults and added eviction fast-path steps

Related policies and templates:
- Service capacity governance handbook (eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025)
- Eviction and tenant isolation policy (security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions/tenant-isolation-policy)

End of document.

payload.page_title: Oncall Triage & Communication Canvas

sections.body:
Summary

This runbook describes a structured canvas for oncall triage, incident communication, and rapid containment for inference workloads. It focuses on: SLO and error-budget-aware decisions, capacity and routing checks, stakeholder communication templates, evidence packaging for post-incident review, and short playbooks to move from alert to recovery. The document is intended for SREs, oncall engineers, incident commanders, and on-call responders for Redwood Inference.

Goals

- Reduce time-to-detect and time-to-ack by standardizing triage checkpoints.
- Make burn-rate-driven decisions deterministic (when to pause low-priority tenants, when to enable burst pools).
- Provide clear, reusable communication artifacts for internal and customer-facing updates.
- Ensure evidence collected is sufficient for RCA and SLO impact assessment.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to model serving, routing, and capacity-related incidents (including quantized-serving latency regressions, OOM cascades, KV cache corruption, and burst overloads).
- Assumes access to: Redwood Console (model telemetry), Grafana dashboards, PagerDuty, Slack (#incidents, #sre-war-room), and the evidence-store (S3 bucket with access audit).

Key roles and responsibilities

1) PagerDuty responder (first ACK): triage initial signal, run steps 1–4 in the triage checklist.
2) Incident Commander (IC): coordinates comms, decides severity, invokes runbook actions (routing, throttling, tenant isolation).
3) Service Owner / Model Steward: provides model-specific context (expected latency profile, recent rollouts).
4) Communications lead: prepares status updates and customer notices if needed.
5) Evidence steward: packages traces, sample tokens, and Grafana snapshots for postmortem.

SLO and error-budget decision ladder

- Baseline SLOs:
  - Latency p95 <= 120 ms for hosted text-generation endpoints.
  - Availability >= 99.9% (monthly).
  - Embedding throughput p90 >= X (normalized to 1k tokens/s per shard).

- Error budget burn thresholds (for a single service tenant-aggregated view):
  1. Normal (< 10% burn in 24h): standard triage, monitor.
  2. Elevated (10%–50% burn in 24h): notify Product, enable higher-fidelity tracing on affected routes, prepare to throttle low-priority tenants.
  3. Critical (> 50% burn in 24h OR predicted to exhaust within 6h): IC declares Severity 1/2 depending on customer impact; take protective measures (evict non-op staff traffic, warm up dedicated pools, enable canary rollback).

NOTE: Burn calculations are tenant-weighted by committed capacity for Dedicated customers; hosted customers are weighted by usage. Use the error-budget API endpoint: curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" https://console.redwood.ai/api/v1/errorbudgets?tenant=$TENANT-ID

Triage checklist (first 12 minutes)

1) Acknowledge and classify
   - Acknowledge PagerDuty alert within 2 minutes.
   - Classify: latency | error rate | OOM | memory leak | cold-start regressions | routing/fallbacks.
2) Quick impact sweep (2–6 minutes)
   - Check Grafana: p50/p95/p99 latency panels for the affected model and aggregate.
   - Query request rate and queue depth on the serving tier (example PromQL):
     sum(rate(requests_total{service=\"runtime\",model=~\".*\"}[1m])) by (model)
   - Verify whether KV cache hit ratio dropped: kv_cache_hits / kv_cache_requests.
3) Hit isolation knobs (6–10 minutes)
   - If queue depth > 3x baseline AND latency p95 increased > 2x, apply tenant throttles per the throttling matrix below.
   - If OOMs observed on quantized pods: enable mem-slim mode (routing flag) and remove larger batch sizes from the router.
4) Evidence snapshot and initial comms (10–12 minutes)
   - Post to #incidents: short summary (one-line), impact, IC, next update cadence. Use template below.
   - Save Grafana snapshots and a representative 1-minute packet capture from the router.

Throttling matrix (safe defaults)

| Condition | Immediate action | Owner | Rollback condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Queue depth > 3x + p95 > 2x | Apply tenant soft-throttle: 70% of baseline rate | IC / runtime-ops | p95 < 1.2x and queue depth < 1.5x |
| Error rate spike > 5% absolute | Route to fallback model variant (lower-cost, higher-stability) | Model Steward | error rate < 1% for 10m |
| Memory reclaim loop / repeated OOMs | Evict speculative batchers and pin to lower-batch profile | SRE | no OOMs for 30m and memory pressure normalizes |

Routing and fallback steps

- When activating fallback routes:
  1. Update routing policy in the router service: routerctl set-policy --route <route> --policy fallback-variant.
  2. Validate via canary: send 50 synthetic requests using the canary harness.
  3. If canary success (error rate delta < 0.5% and latency delta < +20ms), promote the fallback and increase traffic in 10% increments every 5 minutes.

Communication templates

- Initial incident post (Slack #incidents):
  [INCIDENT] <short-id> — <one-line summary>
  Impact: <services/customers affected>
  IC: <name> | Severity: <S1/S2/S3>
  Next update: <ETA in minutes>

- External customer facing (email / support):
  Subject: Redwood Inference — Service disruption affecting <feature>
  Body: We are investigating increased latency for <model/service>. Our engineering team has identified the impact and is actively mitigating. Current ETA for next update: <time>. We will follow up with root cause and customer impact in the post-incident summary.

Evidence checklist for post-incident review

- Required evidence items (submit to evidence-store under incidents/<short-id>/):
  - Grafana snapshots (latency, error-rate, queue-depth) covering 30 minutes before to 30 minutes after alert.
  - Router request logs (sampled) for affected models (include token-level IDs, not raw customer data).
  - A 10-second heap/profile dump if memory issues suspected.
  - Error traces from Sentry with tags for model and route.
  - Error budget delta export (CSV) for the affected tenants.
  - Command history (kubectl/routerctl/ops scripts) used during mitigation.

Post-incident review (quick template)

- Timeline: concisely list timestamps for detection, ack, mitigation, resolution, customer communication.
- Impact summary: affected customers, SLOs impacted, total error-budget consumed.
- Root-cause hypothesis and supporting evidence.
- Corrective actions and owners (tag owner_team and due date).
- Severity classification sanity check and whether escalation was correct.
- Lessons learned: what to automate next, dashboard/pager adjustments.

Automations and tooling guidance

- Use the incident generator to rehearse: python tools/incident_replay.py --scenario latency_spike --duration 10m --tenant sample-tenant.
- For evidence capture, rely on the runbook helper: runbook-helper capture --incident <id> --folders grafana,routerlogs,sentry --compress. The helper will return a signed URL for the evidence bundle.
- Alert tuning guidance: prefer two-stage alerts (warning then critical) with the following thresholds:
  - Latency-warning: p95 > 90ms sustained for 5m.
  - Latency-critical: p95 > 200ms for 3m OR p99 > 500ms for 1m.

Capacity playbook shortcuts (when capacity is the suspected cause)

1) Check headroom in dedicated pools: HEADROOM = provisioned_capacity - in_use_capacity. If HEADROOM < 15% for > 10m, trigger dedicated-reserve flow.
2) Rapid warm pool: instruct capacity-orchestrator to spin up n+2 shards for the affected model: capacityctl warm --model <id> --count 2.
3) Redistribute traffic: enable regional routing preference to unaffected region if latency and egress rules permit.

Oncall drills and checklists (weekly cadence)

- Weekly micro-drill: 30-minute scenario run using incident_replay. Rotate IC role among SREs.
- Monthly table-top: review latest three incidents, validate evidence bundles and action item closure.

Runbook change control

- Any change to throttling matrix, error-budget ladder, or alert thresholds requires:
  1. Draft PR in docs repo with changes.
  2. Two reviewer approvals from eng-sre.
  3. One rehearsal in staging using incident_replay.

Appendices

A) Quick CLI snippets
- Fetch error budget for tenant:
  curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" https://console.redwood.ai/api/v1/errorbudgets?tenant=$TENANT-ID | jq
- Snapshot Grafana panel (example):
  grafana-cli snapshots create --panel-id 42 --from \"now-30m\" --to \"now\" --org 1
- Trigger soft throttle:
  routerctl throttle --tenant $TENANT-ID --rate 0.7

B) Evidence file naming convention
- incidents/<short-id>/grafana-<panel>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMM>.png
- incidents/<short-id>/routerlogs-sample-<YYYYMMDD-HHMM>.ndjson
- incidents/<short-id>/heapdump-<pod>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMM>.tar.gz

C) Escalation contact matrix

| Severity | PagerDuty | Escalate to | Customer comms owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | paging-sre | Eng Director oncall, CTO | Head of Customer Success |
| S2 | paging-sre | Eng Manager oncall, Product TPM | Support Ops Lead |
| S3 | email | Service Owner | Support Team |

D) Change history
- 2025-04-10: Initial published by Asha Kapoor.
- 2025-10-02: Added throttle matrix and error-budget ladder; reviewer: Miguel Torres.
- 2026-01-15: Added capacity shortcuts and evidence helper CLI; reviewer: Priya Nair.

If you are oncall and this playbook is used to resolve an incident, file a short blameless retro within 72 hours and attach the evidence bundle link to the post-incident review page.

End of document.
