payload.page_title: third-party-dependency-resilience-and-quarantine-runbook-2026

sections.body:
Summary
This runbook describes how Redwood SRE handles reliability and capacity impacts caused by third-party dependencies (external model registries, cloud storage, telemetry ingest pipelines, downstream partner APIs, and managed database services). It defines SLO mapping for dependent systems, error-budget policy when third-party issues surface, capacity and timeout guardrails, and a standardized quarantine workflow to contain and recover from dependency-induced degradation.

Scope
- Applies to platform-facing services (Redwood API, Dedicated routing, Console ingestion, KV cache sync) that call or rely on external services.
- Not intended for purely internal downstream jobs that do not affect customer-facing SLOs (those have separate runbooks).

Definitions
- Dependent service: any external service (SaaS, managed cloud service, external partner API) that Redwood calls synchronously or asynchronously.
- Dependency SLO: the expected reliability contract we map a dependency to for the purposes of capacity/error-budgeting.
- Quarantine: an emergency state where traffic to a particular dependency is isolated, routed to fallback, or rate-limited to prevent system-wide failure.

Why this matters
Third-party outages frequently look like internal latency spikes, queue growth, or cascading OOMs. Without fast quarantine and well-defined fallbacks, a single degraded dependency can consume headroom and burn error budget across multiple services. This runbook reduces blast radius and preserves customer-facing SLOs.

Dependency SLO mapping (examples)
| Redwood surface | Observable metric | Mapped dependency SLO | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Redwood API token generation | 99th p50 latency | 99.5% requests < 200 ms for token validation | auth provider latency via third party impacts token handshakes |
| Embedding pipeline | end-to-end success rate | 99.0% success for trained model-hosting calls | embedding failures degrade PLG onboarding UX |
| Console telemetry ingestion | ingestion success rate | 99.5% for daily batches | backpressure can cause size-based retention loss |

Error budget & containment policy
1) Assign an operational dependency severity when an incident is detected:
   - D1 (critical): dependency is failing and causing customer-visible SLO breaches or >X headroom consumption (see threshold table).
   - D2 (major): intermittent failures or latency that increases error budget burn but still under customer-visible threshold.
   - D3 (minor): low-rate anomalies; monitor.
2) On D1/D2 classification, SRE must:
   - Trigger quarantine evaluation within 10 minutes.
   - Reduce traffic to dependency by 50–90% depending on fallback maturity.
3) Error-budget crediting: when a dependency is confirmed out-of-scope (third-party incident), the owning SRE team may apply a proportional error-budget exemption to customer SLOs after post-incident review. The decision template is in the Post-incident section.

Thresholds & decision matrix
| Symptom | Immediate trigger | Quarantine action |
|---|---:|---|
| Upstream HTTP 5xx > 5% of requests for 3m | D1 | Route to cached responses or fast-failure mode (50–90% reduction) |
| P95 latency x2 baseline for 10m | D2 | Lower concurrency and enable circuit breaker (50% reduction) |
| Queue depth growth > 4x normal | D2 | Backpressure producers, enable sampling |

Capacity planning considerations for dependencies
- Reserve headroom: maintain a dependency-hedge pool equal to 15% of steady-state request capacity for at least the top 20% tenants by qps. This pool is used for graceful degradation fallback routes.
- Warm-up and shadowing: before integrating a new dependency, shadow traffic at 5–10% for 48–72 hours across typical tails and token lengths. Record tail latencies and cold-start variance.
- Throttles and rate windows: cap per-tenant concurrent calls to external dependencies (default 5) with exponential backoff and jitter. Document overrides in tenant profile for Dedicated customers.

Runbook: Immediate actions (first 30 minutes)
1) Detect: confirm alerts for dependency anomalies (5xx/latency/queue). Open an incident Slack channel and tag #sre-oncall.
2) Triage: identify the dependency, ingress path, and affected tenant scope. Use telemetry dashboards: dependency-tracing -> recent traces -> top causes.
3) Short-circuit: if D1, execute quarantine play (see CLI and examples). Steps:
   - Toggle circuit breaker: POST /api/control/circuit-breakers {"dependency":"<name>","state":"open"}
   - Apply traffic reroute: update routing rule to point to fallback pool, using the routing control API.
   - Update status page: note degraded external dependency.
4) Communicate: notify product and customer success with initial impact estimate and mitigation steps.

Runbook: triage and mitigation flow (30m–4h)
1) Root cause hypothesis: correlate deployment events, configuration changes, cert expiries, and cloud provider incidents.
2) Scale or reduce: if the dependency is slow but available, reduce internal concurrency and increase client-side timeouts to avoid build-up.
3) Engage partner: open support ticket with dependency provider using provided run template (include traces, request IDs, and sample curl commands). Keep ticket ID in incident channel.
4) Iterate: if fallback reduces customer impact and error budget consumption drops, keep quarantine until root cause confirmed or a workaround is in place.

Quarantine & rollback procedures
- Quarantine types:
   - Traffic redirection to internal cache or noop handler.
   - Fast fail (immediate 503 with explanatory payload).
   - Sampling (reduce to steady 1–5% for diagnostic calls).
- Rollback criteria:
   - Dependency's 5xx < baseline + 1% for 30 minutes and P95 latency back within 1.5x baseline.
   - Telemetry indicates no queue buildup and CPU/mem across affected services stable.
- Stepwise rollback: 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 15-minute intervals with monitoring at each step.

Tooling & telemetry requirements
- Required dashboards: dependency-health (per-dependency), headroom-consumption, queue-lengths, tail-latency by tenant.
- Traces: span tags must include dependency.name, dependency.request_id, and tenant.id.
- Synthetic tests: run per-minute lightweight health checks (smithy probes) for each external endpoint; maintain 7-day rolling baseline.
- Automation: quarantine actions must be scriptable via control-plane API and exposed to incident CLI: redwoodctl quarantine <dependency> --mode=fast-fail --percent=75

Ownership & escalation matrix
- Primary: runtime-infrastructure (pager rotation).
- Secondary: platform-integration (day rotation).
- Tertiary: on-call for product-engineering when feature flags or recent rollouts are implicated.
- Escalate to engineering director when incident > 3 hours and > 10% customers impacted.

Post-incident review & evidence checklist
- Confirm timeline: alert -> quarantine -> mitigation -> rollback.
- Attach artifacts: alert graphs, trace snippets, routing change diff, control-plane API commands used, dependency provider ticket IDs.
- Root-cause hypothesis: was it an external outage, capacity mismatch, config error, or cert/permission issue?
- Policy decision: determine whether customer SLOs receive an exemption or partial credit. Include the proportionality rationale.
- Remediation actions (owner + due date): e.g., increase headroom hedge to 20% (runtime-infra, 2025-07-15), add extra synthetic checks for dependency X (platform-integration, 2025-06-30).

Appendix A — sample quarantine CLI usage
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwoodctl quarantine model-registry-prod --mode fast-fail --percent 80 --reason "external 5xx spike"

Appendix B — minimal JSON payload for control-plane circuit-breaker API
{
  "dependency": "model-registry-prod",
  "action": "open",
  "percent": "80",
  "initiator": "sre-oncall@redwood.com",
  "comment": "Fast-fail due to sustained 5xx > 5%"
}

Appendix C — Quarantine decision checklist (short)
1) Confirm customer-facing SLO impact and estimate error-budget burn.
2) Verify fallback available (cache, local model, noop).
3) Execute quarantine and monitor for 15 minutes.
4) Keep stakeholder comms updated every 30 minutes.
5) Prepare rollback plan before full restoration.

Contact & references
- Incident comms template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/incident-communication-template-2024.json
- Control-plane API spec: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/control-plane-api-spec.json
- SLO policy reference: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-lifecycle-capacity-debt-remediation-playbook-2026.json

Revision history
- 2024-11-12: Created by Maya Thompson.
- 2025-06-03: Added automation examples and tightened threshold table (reviewers: Diego, Priya, Liam).

payload.page_title: SLO rollback confidence scoring and automated rollback playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines a reproducible, telemetry-driven approach to compute a rollback confidence score for canary and production rollouts. The goal is to standardize automated rollback decisions and make manual rollback actions consistent across model-serving, runtime, and routing incidents.

Intended audience
- SRE oncall engineers
- Model-serving and runtime owners
- Platform reliability engineers

Scope and goals
- Provide a defensible numeric "rollback confidence score" (0–100) that aggregates multiple SLO signals.
- Define actionable thresholds and automated steps tied to score ranges.
- Ensure safe guards to avoid noisy/false rollbacks (debounce windows, quorum of signals).
- Provide a simulation procedure for testing rollbacks against historical incidents.

Key definitions
- Rollback confidence score: composite score indicating confidence that a rollout is violating SLOs and requires rollback.
- Primary SLOs: request success rate (SLO-error), tail latency (P99), token error-rate for generation models.
- Secondary signals: queue length, KV cache miss rate, out-of-memory (OOM) errors, GPU saturations, host-level CPU steal.

High-level decision model
1. Collect real-time signals with fixed short windows (30s, 5m, 15m).
2. Compute per-signal anomaly confidence (0–100) using baseline deviation and recent trend.
3. Weight signals into an aggregate rollback confidence score.
4. Apply hysteresis and safety checks (minimum canary duration, traffic floor, operator overrides).
5. Map score bands to automated or human actions.

Telemetry signals and example thresholds
- request_error_rate_5m (primary): unacceptable if >1.5x SLO threshold AND absolute >0.5%
- latency_p99_5m (primary): unacceptable if >1.6x baseline P99 AND >200ms above baseline for critical routes
- token_failure_rate_5m (primary, generation): unacceptable if >0.3% AND trend increasing 3 consecutive windows
- kv_cache_miss_rate_5m (secondary): concerning if >40% increase from baseline
- queue_length_30s (secondary): concerning if >75th percentile of historical peak for this canary size
- oom_events_5m (secondary): any non-zero OOMs are severe and should be elevated

Example weight table (used by aggregator)
| Signal                     | Role      | Weight |
|---------------------------|-----------|--------|
| request_error_rate_5m     | primary   | 35     |
| latency_p99_5m            | primary   | 30     |
| token_failure_rate_5m     | primary   | 20     |
| oom_events_5m             | secondary | 10     |
| kv_cache_miss_rate_5m     | secondary | 3      |
| queue_length_30s          | secondary | 2      |

Scoring algorithm (text)
- For each signal, compute an anomaly confidence in 0–100. This can be a scaled z-score or percentile-of-baseline method.
- Multiply each signal confidence by its configured weight.
- Sum weighted confidences and normalize to 0–100 by dividing by total weights.
- Apply exponential decay for older evidence so short transient spikes do not dominate.

Example scoring pseudo-code (Python snippet)
```python
import math

def scale_confidence(deviation, baseline_std):
    # deviation in units of baseline stdev -> scaled to 0..100
    z = deviation / (baseline_std + 1e-6)
    return max(0, min(100, 50 * math.tanh(z / 2)))

WEIGHTS = {
    'request_error_rate_5m': 35,
    'latency_p99_5m': 30,
    'token_failure_rate_5m': 20,
    'oom_events_5m': 10,
    'kv_cache_miss_rate_5m': 3,
    'queue_length_30s': 2,
}

def aggregate_score(anomaly_confidences):
    total_weight = sum(WEIGHTS.values())
    weighted = sum(WEIGHTS[s] * anomaly_confidences.get(s, 0) for s in WEIGHTS)
    return weighted / total_weight
```

Prometheus/PromQL examples (operational)
- request error rate (5m rolling):
```
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-server",status!~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-server"}[5m]))
```
- p99 latency (5m) for route /generate:
```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="model-server",route="/generate"}[5m])) by (le))
```

Aggregation and automation mapping
- Score < 30: monitor only. No automated action. Alert to oncall with informational priority.
- Score 30–55: elevated alert (P2). Initiate increased sampling, snapshot traces, and extend canary duration by +50% (if canary).
- Score 55–75: P1 alert. Trigger automatic traffic cutback to 25% of canary traffic, create rollback-prep ticket, and notify model owner.
- Score >= 75: automated rollback (if allowed by policy). Steps: shift traffic to previous stable variant, trigger post-rollback validation probes, escalate to incident commander.

Safety and cooldown rules
- Require at least 5 minutes of continuous score above threshold before automated action.
- Require two independent primary signals (e.g., error rate and p99) to be above their primary thresholds for auto-rollback.
- If canary traffic < 5% of production, do not auto-rollback (false positives are more likely); escalate to manual.
- Respect manual "no-auto-rollback" label set by release owner in rollout metadata.

Automated rollback sequence (safe path)
1. Record pre-action snapshot: metrics 15m, current canary tasks, model hash, rotation config.
2. Reduce canary traffic to 25% and hold for 2 minutes while sampling traces.
3. If score remains >=75 after hold, initiate traffic cut to 0% and route to fallback variant.
4. Trigger verification probes (smoke tests, golden prompt set).
5. Post-rollback audits: automatic evidence bundle is attached to rollback ticket.

Manual rollback checklist (for oncall)
- Confirm metric baselines are valid (no ingestion gaps).
- Check correlating infra alerts (OOM, node reboots).
- Review traces for systemic errors vs single-tenant failures.
- Execute controlled rollback using the platform console or CLI and observe probe results.
- Document reason, duration, and impacted tenants in the rollback ticket.

Runbook step-by-step: oncall response
1. Triage alert with playbook tag "rollback-confidence": gather top-5 signals and compute score.
2. If score <55: continue monitoring, run additional diagnostics (trace capture, slow queries).
3. If score 55–75: contact model owner and prepare rollback artifacts; follow escalation timeline (15 min).
4. If score >=75: verify safety checks and execute automated rollback if policy allows; otherwise escalate to incident commander.
5. After rollback, monitor SLOs for 60 minutes and capture evidence for incident review.

Simulation and validation harness
- Maintain a simulation pipeline that replays historical telemetry for synthetic rollouts. The harness should be able to:
  - Inject signal noise and baseline shifts
  - Run scoring algorithm against replayed telemetry
  - Verify that actions would have been correct (true positive / false positive analysis)
- Recommended test cases: slow drift (latency increase over 30m), spike failure (error rate spike for 2–10m), infra-only failure (OOM without error-rate increase).

Dashboards, alerts, and evidence bundles
- Dashboards: rollback confidence score (time series), per-signal confidences, recent automated actions, canary metadata panel.
- Alerts: attach score and top-3 contributing signals to alert body. Include links to traces and the last snapshot.
- Evidence bundle: JSON payload containing timestamped metrics, top traces (max 5), deployment metadata, and the computed score timeline (30m).

Testing and deployment guidance
- All changes to weights or thresholds must be gated by a canary experiment and a 2-week review window.
- Use the simulation harness to test proposed changes; require minimum 10k synthetic runs for statistical confidence.
- Version control: scoring configuration must be stored in Git (repo: infra/sre/rollback-config) and tagged per release.

Ownership and review cadence
- Owner: SRE Runtime Reliability (primary) with Model Onboarding team as secondary.
- Quarterly review: validate weights, thresholds, and false-positive rates.
- Post-incident: if an automated rollback occurred, include scoring telemetry in incident RCA and adjust weights as necessary.

Appendix: sample evidence extraction query (SQL-like)
- Extract the top contributing signals for a 30-minute window:
```
SELECT signal, avg(value) as avg_val, stddev(value) as sd_val
FROM telemetry_metrics
WHERE service = 'model-server' AND timestamp >= now() - interval '30 minutes'
GROUP BY signal
ORDER BY avg_val DESC
LIMIT 10;
```
Appendix: quick CLI snippets
- Force compute score for current canary (example):
```
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "score": 82,
  "top_contributors": ["request_error_rate_5m", "latency_p99_5m"]
}
```
Change log
- 2026-11-15: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2027-01-20: Added simulation harness requirements and refined weights after tabletop exercise.
- 2027-02-10: Adopted final safety/cooldown rules and published.

Related reading
- See runbooks for "canary rollout checklist" and "multi-model rollback hedging" for complementary procedures.

Contact
- For questions or exceptions, contact the SRE Runtime Reliability rotation (sre-runtime@redwood.ai).

payload.page_title: SLO Regression Detection and Mitigation Playbook

sections.body:
Purpose
This playbook describes how Redwood's SRE team detects, classifies, and mitigates SLO regressions across serving, routing, and model-backed features. It is intended for on-call engineers, on-call leads, and service owners.

Scope
- Services: all inference-facing services, routing layers, caching/KV subsystems, and the control plane pieces that affect SLOs (auth, rate-limiting, billing).
- SLO types: latency P50/P95/P99, availability (success rate), request-level correctness checks (synthetic prompt checks), and queueing/backpressure targets.
- Exclusions: long-term quality regressions due to model drift (handled by Applied ML).

Summary of responsibilities
- On-call engineer: triage alerts, execute immediate mitigations, and populate incident record.
- Service owner: coordinate follow-up, approve rollbacks, and lead post-incident review.
- Observability team: review and tune detector thresholds quarterly.

Detection: signals and correlated telemetry
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) SLO burn rate alert (default: burn_rate > 10 sustained for 3m) — triggers P1.
2) Sustained P95 latency > configured target + 30% for 5m.
3) Error rate (5xx or model-failure codes) > baseline + 0.5% absolute for 2m.
4) Synthetic probe failures: Canary prompt failure rate > 2% for 10m.
5) Queue depth/backlog increase > 2x typical 95th for 5m.
6) Cross-service spike in client retries or dropped requests.
sections.heading: Primary signals (automatic detectors)

sections.body:
- Infrastructure: GPU utilization, host OOMs, node reboots.
- Network: inter-region latency spikes, packet loss on egress.
- Config changes / rollouts: deployment events, model variant toggles, routing policy changes.

Example detector implementation (PromQL + comments)
- SLO burn rate:
  sum(rate(error_count[5m])) / sum(rate(success_count[5m]))
  // Adopt per-SLO labels: service, slo_name, region. Create alerts when burn_rate > 10 for 3m.
- Latency regression (P95):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[2m])) by (le, service))
  // Compare to slo_target: if p95 > slo_target*1.3 for 5m -> alert.
- Synthetic probe example (pseudo):
  probe_failures_ratio = probe_failed_total / probe_total

Alerting policy conventions
- Severity mapping: P1 (service impact, immediate mitigation required), P2 (degraded but tolerable, mitigation within 1 hour), P3 (non-critical, follow-up ticket).
- Pager rules: P1 pages SRE on-call and service owner; P2 pages on-call only.
- Auto-silencing: if a P1 is triggered and an active mitigation ticket exists with a documented mitigation strategy, suppress duplicate alerts for 10m.
sections.heading: Secondary signals (recommended correlations)

sections.body:
1) Validate alert: open observability dashboard for service, check burn-rate, P95, error-class breakdown.
2) Check recent deploys/rollouts: kubernetes events, CI deploy IDs, model rollout logs (last 30m).
3) Run quick smoke tests from two regions (curl or SDK): record request IDs and latencies.
4) Identify whether issue maps to: serving runtime, model quality, routing/caching, infra (node/GPUs), or external dependencies.
5) Classify incident type: Capacity, Regression, Degradation, Dependency, or Configuration.

Immediate mitigations (choose applicable steps; aim to restore SLO quickly):
A) Capacity-driven regressions
   - Increase target pool size (hot path): trigger autoscale policy override to +30% for 15m.
   - Add capacity: spin up pre-provisioned GPU nodes (runbook CLI: redwood infra capacity scale --service <svc> --delta 4 --reason "SLO burn")
   - Reduce concurrency per worker: temporarily lower max concurrent requests to favor latency.
B) Serving/runtime regressions
   - Toggle to a lower-latency model variant or quantized profile via routing policy. Command: redwood route set-variant --service <svc> --variant <fallback> --rollback-window 30m.
   - Rollback the last runtime change: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<svc> --to-revision=<prev>
C) Model-quality or prompt regressions
   - Cutover synthetic traffic to previous model version; enable canary-only rollback for full traffic after 5m validation.
   - Throttle user-facing traffic by 10–30% using rate-limiters to reduce noise while rollback is validated.
D) Configuration or dependency failures
   - Revert config changes via config-store and redeploy. Keep config-change id in incident notes.
   - Route around the dependency: change to a cached response or local stub if available.

Containment checklist (for on-call to mark in incident record)
- [ ] Primary SLO impact confirmed
- [ ] Mitigation action taken (describe)
- [ ] Traffic reduction / capacity change executed (times & commands)
- [ ] Customer-facing status page updated if impact > 10 minutes
- [ ] Pager rotation and owner notified

Escalation and decision gates
- If burn rate remains > 5 for 30 minutes despite mitigations -> escalate to SRE lead and product on-call.
- If mitigation may cause user-visible degradation (rate-limits, rollbacks), notify customer-success for enterprise customers within 15 minutes.
- Use change freeze exception channel to allow urgent rollbacks outside normal release window.

Recovery and follow-up actions
- Short-term (within 24h): implement resilient routing fallback, increase synthetic probe cadence to 1m, and create follow-up ticket with RCA owner.
- Medium-term (3–14 days): capacity adjustments, permanent routing policy changes, or runtime fixes (kernel or batching modifications) tracked on JIRA.
- Long-term (30–90 days): postmortem with action items, quality/regression guardrails added to model onboarding, and SLO target review.

Runbook: Example commands and snippets
- Check P95 by service (CLI wrapper): redwood obs query "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[2m])) by (le,service))" --service <svc>
- Scale dedicated pool (example): redwood infra capacity scale --pool redwood-dedicated-pool --add-gpus 4 --ttl 30m --ticket <incident-id>
- Route to fallback variant (example JSON patch):
  { "service": "translate", "route": { "primary": "gptx-3-120b", "fallbacks": ["gptx-3-60b-quantized"] } }

Monitoring hygiene and tuning cadence
- Quarterly review: detector thresholds, burn-rate sensitivity, and synthetic probe coverage.
- Monthly: observe false-positive rate for SLO alerts; aim to keep false-positive rate < 20%.
- After every incident: update playbook steps and detector queries within 5 business days.

Incident review and evidence standards (post-incident)
- Evidence to collect before retro: timeline of alerts, CI/CD deploy IDs, model rollout IDs, sampled request IDs and traces, host-level metrics, and synthetic probe logs.
- Postmortem template: impact summary, detection timeline, root cause analysis (with evidence), action items (owner + due date), and verification criteria.
- Severity-based retention: P1 and P2 incidents -> mandatory 90-day readout; P3 -> optional.

SLO & error-budget policy examples (table)
| SLO name | Target | Burn-rate threshold (P1) | Escalation |
| inference-availability | 99.95% monthly | burn_rate > 8 | SRE + service owner |
| inference-p95-latency | 500ms global | p95 > 650ms for 5m | SRE on-call |
| embedding-success-rate | 99.9% | error delta > 0.2% | SRE + applied-ml |

Retention of artifacts and follow-up verification
- Store incident artifacts in /incidents/<incident-id>/, include dashboards snapshots, trace links, and command history.
- Verification: owner marks action item complete only after associated SLO is observed back to target for a minimum of 72h (unless action specifically limited to a different window).

Ownership and contact matrix (table)
| Area | Primary on-call | Secondary | Pager |
| Serving runtime | runtime-oncall@example.redwood.com | runtime-senior@example.redwood.com | #sre-runtime |
| Model routing | routing-oncall@example.redwood.com | routing-engineer@example.redwood.com | #sre-routing |
| Capacity | capacity-oncall@example.redwood.com | infra-lead@example.redwood.com | #sre-capacity |

Related automation and tooling tasks (actionable items)
- Add a synthetic probe per top 20 customer prompts and ensure per-region coverage.
- Build a quick rollback playbook for common model toggles (CLI + telemetry guardrails).
- Implement an incident CLI wrapper that captures deployment/model IDs automatically when an alert fires.

Appendix: Example Prometheus alert rule (YAML snippet)
- name: SLOBurnRateHigh
  expr: |
    sum(increase(slo_error_count[5m])) / sum(increase(slo_request_count[5m])) > 0.10
  for: 3m
  labels:
    severity: P1
  annotations:
    summary: "High SLO burn rate for {{ $labels.service }}"
    runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/slo-regression-detection-and-mitigation-playbook-2025"

Appendix: Post-incident verification checklist (short)
1) All action items have owners and due dates.
2) Synthetic probes show traffic parity for 72h.
3) SLOs are stable at target for 72h post-fix.
4) Retro draft posted within 5 business days.

Revision history
- 2025-02-14: Created by Ravi Patel (initial playbook).
- 2025-09-07: Added synthetic probe cadence and capacity override CLI.
- 2026-01-12: Clarified burn-rate thresholds and added escalation gates.

For questions or clarifications, contact the SRE documentation owner: runtime-docs@example.redwood.com
sections.heading: Triage play (first 10 minutes)

payload.page_title: Runbook: Backup/Restore Smoke Test (On-Call) — Redwood Private

sections.body: This runbook describes the periodic smoke test SRE performs to ensure Redwood Private backup artifacts are usable and that a restore into a staging environment is repeatable.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Weekly (or per-customer requirement) integrity checks of the most recent control-plane backup.
- Scheduled restore drills into a dedicated staging cluster.
- Alerting and paging guidance when checks/drills fail.
sections.heading: This runbook is used for

sections.body:
- Validate the **latest control-plane backup** exists, can be decrypted, and passes integrity checks.
- Perform a **restore drill into staging** using the supported installer workflow.
- Run post-restore validation (health, API checks, basic tenancy/config verification).
- Record drill duration and outcomes; trigger paging/escalation per policy.
sections.heading: In scope (smoke test)

sections.body:
- Full region-loss DR execution (see DR plans).
- Cluster-level recovery (e.g., etcd rebuild) unless the restore drill indicates cluster corruption.
- Customer-specific, bespoke workflows not supported by the toolkit.
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Backup artifact**: Encrypted tarball + manifest (format per ADR-027). Stored in configured backend (S3/NFS/GCS).
- **Restore drill**: Restore artifact into a clean staging namespace/cluster and validate readiness.
- **RPO/RTO (targets)**: See matrix page; this runbook focuses on verifying we can meet targets in supported reference setups.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body: - SRE on-call (this runbook)
sections.heading: Primary

sections.body:
- Control plane restore/ordering issues: **Ethan Park** (Control Plane Eng), **Benji Okafor**
- Backup artifact format / migrations: **Michael Nguyen**
- KMS/encryption failures: **Hanae Suzuki**, **Marcus Lin**
- Release/bundle signing issues (on-prem/offline tooling): **Connor O'Brien**, **Sahana Iyer**
- Observability/dashboard gaps: **Allison Grant**, **Sergio Costa**
sections.heading: Escalate to

sections.body:
- #eng-oncall (coordination)
- #eng-sre (triage)
- #eng-platform (control plane)
- #eng-security (KMS/crypto)
- #eng-releases (signing/packaging)
sections.heading: Slack channels (internal)

sections.body:
- Access to staging K8s cluster(s) used for drills (kubeconfig + RBAC).
- Access to the backup storage backend (read-only is sufficient for integrity checks; restore requires read).
- KMS permissions (decrypt) for the backup key used by staging.
- The Redwood Private installer CLI version pinned for staging drills (see “Version alignment”).
sections.heading: You will need

sections.body:
- kubectl
- helm
- installer CLI (examples use `rw-private`)
- jq
sections.heading: Required tooling

sections.body:
- Integrity check: **daily** (automated) + **weekly** (manual spot-check by SRE)
- Restore drill: **weekly** for Redwood-managed staging; **monthly** for release branches or when requested by enterprise accounts

If a staging restore drill is currently automated, use this runbook for manual execution and for triage when automation fails.
sections.heading: Recommended default cadence

sections.body:
- The same or explicitly compatible **backup format version** supported by the installer.
- A staging deployment version that is within the supported compatibility window.
sections.heading: Restore drills must use

sections.body:
- If the installer reports “incompatible backup version”, do **not** attempt ad-hoc patching. File an escalation ticket and block the drill as “tooling regression”.

---
sections.heading: Policy

sections.body:
1) Determine the environment and backup backend for staging drills.
   - Common: S3 bucket + prefix (e.g., `s3://rw-private-backups-staging/control-plane/`)

2) List the most recent backup and capture:
- Backup ID (timestamp or UUID)
- Manifest path
- Artifact blob path
sections.heading: A1. Identify the latest backup artifact

sections.body: - `aws s3 ls s3://rw-private-backups-staging/control-plane/ --recursive | tail -50`
sections.heading: Example (S3)

sections.body:
- backup_id
- created_at
- platform_version
- backup_format_version
- components included
- encryption metadata (provider, key reference)
- checksums for artifact(s)
sections.heading: The manifest should include at minimum

sections.body:
- Download manifest locally:
  - `aws s3 cp s3://.../backup-<ID>.manifest.json ./`
- Validate fields:
  - `jq -e '.backup_id and .backup_format_version and .checksums and .encryption' backup-<ID>.manifest.json`
sections.heading: Example

sections.body:
- Download encrypted artifact locally (or stream):
  - `aws s3 cp s3://.../backup-<ID>.enc.tar ./`
- Verify checksum matches manifest:
  - `sha256sum backup-<ID>.enc.tar`
  - Compare to `.checksums["backup-<ID>.enc.tar"].sha256` (field name may vary by version)
sections.heading: Checksum verification

sections.body:
- Manifest parses.
- All required fields present.
- Artifact sha256 matches.
sections.heading: Pass criteria

sections.body: - Missing manifest, invalid JSON, mismatched checksums, or missing encryption metadata.
sections.heading: Fail criteria

sections.body:
Goal: ensure we can decrypt with the configured KMS key and that the decrypted stream is structurally sound.

Run a non-destructive decrypt test using the installer CLI (preferred) because it validates expected headers/format.
sections.heading: A3. Validate decryptability (KMS / envelope encryption)

sections.body:
- `rw-private backup verify --manifest ./backup-<ID>.manifest.json --artifact ./backup-<ID>.enc.tar --output ./verify-report.json`

If verify supports a “decrypt-only” mode:
- `rw-private backup verify --manifest ... --artifact ... --mode decrypt-only`
sections.heading: Example

sections.body: - Verify exits 0 and report indicates “decrypt_ok=true” and “checks_ok=true”.
sections.heading: Pass criteria

sections.body:
- KMS AccessDenied / missing grants
- Wrong region/key ARN
- KMS throttling/outage (retry logic may mask; inspect report)
- Clock skew causing token expiry (if using short-lived credentials)
sections.heading: Common failure modes

sections.body:
- Last backup timestamp <= expected interval (e.g., 24h).
- Retention policy is respected (no unexpected deletion).
sections.heading: Check

sections.body:
- STAGING: last_success_age > 48h => investigate (non-page)
- PROD: last_success_age > 24h or 2 consecutive failures => page per policy below
sections.heading: Recommended thresholds

sections.body:
- Backup ID
- created_at
- verify-report.json (attach to ticket if failures)

---
sections.heading: Record

sections.body:
- Dedicated staging cluster, or
- Dedicated staging namespace with clear isolation and an approved restore workflow.

Do NOT run restores in production.
sections.heading: Only run restore drills in

sections.body:
- Announce in #eng-oncall: “Starting Private restore drill in staging, ETA 60–90 min.”
- Confirm no conflicting maintenance windows.
sections.heading: Before starting

sections.body:
Option 1 (preferred): clean staging cluster
- Provision a fresh cluster using the standard staging Terraform/cluster template.

Option 2: clean namespace in shared staging cluster
- Create namespace:
  - `kubectl create ns rw-restore-drill-<YYYYMMDD>`
- Ensure required CRDs are installed cluster-wide (common failure: missing CRDs).
sections.heading: Choose one

sections.body:
- `kubectl get nodes`
- `kubectl -n <ns> get pods`
- Confirm storage class, ingress controller, cert-manager (if required by staging profile).
sections.heading: Pre-flight checks

sections.body:
- Identify the expected platform version from the backup manifest:
  - `jq -r '.platform_version' backup-<ID>.manifest.json`
- Use the matching/compatible installer build.
sections.heading: B2. Ensure the correct installer and charts

sections.body: - Ensure chart version matches the installer expectations.
sections.heading: If staging uses a Helm-based install

sections.body: Preferred flow uses the installer restore workflow which enforces ordering and produces a validation report.
sections.heading: B3. Run restore apply

sections.body:
- `rw-private restore apply \
    --manifest s3://rw-private-backups-staging/control-plane/backup-<ID>.manifest.json \
    --artifact s3://rw-private-backups-staging/control-plane/backup-<ID>.enc.tar \
    --kube-context <staging-context> \
    --namespace rw-restore-drill-<YYYYMMDD> \
    --wait \
    --report-out ./restore-report-<YYYYMMDD>.json`

If artifacts must be imported locally (restricted egress/air-gapped-like staging):
- `rw-private backup export --manifest s3://... --artifact s3://... --out ./bundle/`
- `rw-private restore apply --manifest ./bundle/... --artifact ./bundle/... ...`
sections.heading: Example (conceptual)

sections.body:
- Restore exits 0.
- Report indicates:
  - preflight_ok=true
  - restore_steps_ok=true
  - postchecks_ok=true
sections.heading: Pass criteria

sections.body:
- Incompatible backup format version
- Repeated missing CRDs/ordering failures that indicate a broken release artifact
- KMS decrypt failures (unless confirmed transient and retriable)
sections.heading: Hard stop criteria (abort restore and escalate)

sections.body:
1) Core pods healthy
- `kubectl -n <ns> get pods`
- No CrashLoopBackOff; no pending pods due to PVC issues.

2) Control plane API health
- If an internal health endpoint exists, hit it via port-forward:
  - `kubectl -n <ns> port-forward svc/rw-control-plane 8080:80`
  - `curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz`

3) Backup status endpoint surfaces last-success (if enabled)
- Verify endpoint responds and shows a plausible last_success timestamp.

4) Configuration restore sanity
Validate that a known staging tenant/config object is present (use the standard staging test tenant if configured):
- Routing policy exists
- Model pins/versions restored (if part of control plane state)
- Secrets are NOT expected to be restored as raw material if policy is “references only” (confirm expected behavior)

5) Basic functional smoke
- Run the standard “Private smoke test” job if available.
- At minimum: create a no-op request to a staging inference endpoint if wiring exists (this can be a stub depending on staging topology).
sections.heading: Run the following checks (minimum set)

sections.body:
- Duration from restore start to “all checks green”
- Any manual interventions required
sections.heading: Record

sections.body:
- Save reports to the runbook folder / attach to ticket.
- Delete namespace:
  - `kubectl delete ns rw-restore-drill-<YYYYMMDD>`
sections.heading: If using a temporary namespace

sections.body:
- Decide whether to keep it for additional validation or tear down per cost policy.

---
sections.heading: If using a dedicated cluster

sections.body:
Dashboards/alerts should be based on structured metrics emitted by backup/restore tooling, including:
- backup_job_success (0/1)
- backup_job_duration_seconds
- backup_bytes_written
- backup_last_success_timestamp
- restore_drill_success (0/1)
- restore_drill_duration_seconds

sections.heading: Signals (expected)

sections.body:
- Page SRE on-call when:
  1) **Two consecutive scheduled backups fail** for any production Private deployment we operate, OR
  2) **backup_last_success_age > 24h**, OR
  3) Integrity verification fails (checksum mismatch or decrypt failure)

Staging (quality signal, usually non-customer-impact):
- Create a ticket and notify #eng-sre when:
  - restore drill fails once
- Page only when:
  - restore drill fails **2 weeks in a row**, OR
  - failure indicates a release regression likely to affect customers (e.g., incompatible backup version, systematic CRD ordering bug)
sections.heading: Production (customer-impact risk)

sections.body: - If backups are intentionally paused, silence alerts with an expiration and a linked change record.
sections.heading: Silencing / maintenance windows

- Environment (prod/staging), cluster identifier, region
- Backup ID, manifest path, artifact path
- Installer version and chart version used

- Top 50 lines of relevant logs (KMS errors, RBAC denies, missing resource types)

---

sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.body: - #eng-security, Hanae Suzuki / Marcus Lin

payload.page_title: SLO design, triage, and cost-aware mitigation playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook defines a pragmatic, quantitatively driven process for SLO design, on-call triage, and cost-aware mitigation when error budgets burn. It is intended for platform and service owners responsible for model-serving, API gateways, and batch inference endpoints. The goal is to keep user-facing availability and latency within commitments while minimizing unnecessary capacity and cost increases.

Scope

- Applies to customer-facing Redwood services and multi-tenant model endpoints.
- Covers SLOs for availability, API p50/p95 latency, and per-request correctness signals where applicable.
- Integrates with capacity planning, incident response, and release rollouts.

Definitions

- SLO (Service Level Objective): Target for a reliability metric over a rolling window.
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; the allowable fraction of bad events in the window.
- Burn rate: Speed at which the error budget is consumed relative to the budgeted allowance.
- Mitigation ladder: Ordered set of actions that trade cost, latency, and feature availability to recover SLOs.

Principles for SLO design

1. Measure customer impact: Prefer user-visible metrics (e.g., request success, model output validity).
2. Multi-dimensional SLOs: Use an availability SLO + at least one quality or latency SLO for model-inference services.
3. Observability-first: Instrument request-level metadata (route, model-version, tenant-id, sequence-length).
4. Align windows with business cycles: 30d rolling is default, 7d for high-churn features or experiments.
5. Be explicit about exemptions: scheduled maintenance, controlled experiments, and canary rollouts must be excluded via audit-tagging.

SLO examples (recommended defaults)

| Metric | SLO | Window | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| API availability (200 HTTP success) | 99.95% | 30d | Critical production endpoints |
| Generation latency (p95) | < 450ms | 30d | Latency-sensitive product flows |
| Quality regression (eval testset pass rate) | >= 98% | 7d | Detect model-output regressions early |

Error budget burn policy (high level)

- Normal burn: < 2x expected rate — monitor and alert to oncall Slack channel.
- Elevated burn: 2–5x — open a SEV-lite ticket, owner investigates top contributors by route/model/tenant.
- Critical burn: > 5x or projected budget exhaustion in < 24h — trigger mitigation ladder and optionally page SRE primary.

Operational tooling and telemetry requirements

All services must emit the following per-request fields to the observability pipeline:
- timestamp, request_id, route, model_variant, tenant_id (or anon-tenant), tokens_generated, server_latency_ms, response_code, error_class, eval_flags
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- SLO summary: current burn rate, days-to-exhaustion, 30d/7d windows.
- Top contributors: by route, model_variant, tenant_id, and sequence-length bucket.
- Cost signal overlay: estimated GPU-minutes and request-cost per route.

Runbook: High error-budget burn (triage + mitigation)

1) Detection
   - Alert thresholds: burn-rate > 2 for 30m or more for SEV-lite; burn-rate > 5 for 5m for SEV.
   - Pager flow: SEV-lite -> Slack incident channel; SEV -> page SRE primary and product owner.

2) Triage (first 20 minutes)
   - Identify top 3 contributors using the SLO dashboard query: sort by budget impact.
   - For each contributor, capture: affected routes, model_variant, tenant impact %, recent deploys, and infra events.
   - Quick hypothesis checklist (yes/no): recent rollout? memory pressure? inference timeouts? model-quality drift? network flaps?

3) Mitigation ladder (apply in order until SLO immediate risk subsides)
   1. Redirect: Route non-critical traffic to a lower-cost or cached model variant.
   2. Graceful degradation: Disable non-essential features (e.g., embeddings-on-write, heavy post-processing).
   3. Prefix cache: Serve cached responses for repeat prompts where cache-safe.
   4. Autoscale policy shift: Temporarily increase throughput on dedicated pools for critical tenants (short window, auto-revert).
   5. Rate-limit/Backpressure: Apply fair-share throttles with tenant-class weighting.
   6. Emergency fallback model: Switch traffic to a smaller, fully-quantized model variant with known correctness profile.
   7. Capacity add (last resort): Provision extra GPUs with explicit cost approval flow.

Note: each mitigation must include an expected SLO improvement estimate and cost delta. Document choices in the incident timeline.

Runbook: Capacity pressure (latency-induced errors)

1) Detection signals:
   - p95 or p99 latency spike correlated with GPU_utilization >= 85% for > 10m.
   - Queue depth increases, request_timeouts increment.

2) Rapid steps (first 30 minutes):
   - Activate autoscaling policy to add warm nodes if available.
   - Temporarily increase batching_thresholds for latency-tolerant routes.
   - If multi-tenant contention is suspected: engage fairshare throttle to cap noisy tenants at configured max_rps.

3) Longer-term actions:
   - Run capacity replay of the traffic window to estimate headroom needed for 95th percentile load.
   - If sustained, schedule commit in capacity plan with cost sizing and expected time-to-ship.

Cost-aware mitigation ladder (detailed guidance)

- Small impact, short duration: Prefer caching and throttles.
- Medium impact, moderate duration: Prefer emergency fallback model and temporary autoscale (with cost cap).
- Large impact, long duration: Prefer route-level rate limiting and negotiated capacity for affected enterprise tenants (contractual SLA intervention).
sections.heading: Dashboards (required)

sections.body:
- Use when error-class indicates model runtime failures or when quantized variant maintains acceptable eval pass rate (>95% on guardrail tests).
- Announce in incident channel, start canary at 1% traffic for 5 minutes, then 10% for 10 minutes, monitor correctness signals continuously.

Incident review and follow-up requirements

- Every critical burn (projected budget exhaust < 24h or paging) must produce an Incident Review doc within 5 business days.
- Incident review must include: timeline, root cause hypothesis, metrics to validate, remediation actions (owner + due date), and a regression test covering the failure mode.
- If mitigation included capacity adds or cost incursions, finance must be notified and charge codes recorded.

Acceptance tests and CI gates for SLO regressions

- Pre-rollout: any model or infra change that touches request path must run SLO-safety checks in CI: synthetic workload that validates p95 latency and error rate against a baseline.
- Post-rollout: automated canary traffic with SLO assertions for first 60 minutes. Canary must be auto-rollback if burn-rate > 3 for 10 minutes.

SLO config example (YAML)

service: inference-public-api
slos:
  - name: availability
    metric: http_success_rate
    target: 0.9995
    window: 30d
  - name: gen-latency-p95
    metric: server_latency_ms_p95
    target: 450
    window: 30d
error_budget_policy:
  normal_burn_threshold: 2.0
  elevated_burn_threshold: 5.0
  page_on_threshold: 5.0

Ownership and run conditions

- SLI owner: service team (primary).
- SLO steward: platform SRE (secondary).
- Oncall responsibilities: rotate between service and platform SREs for escalation; service team owns long-term remediation and postmortem actions.

Related dashboards and queries

- slo:current-burn-rate (Grafana)
- slo:top-burn-by-route (Looker/Grafana)
- infra:gpu-utilization-by-cluster

Appendix A — Example triage checklist (copyable)

1. Confirm alert validity and window.
2. Run top contributors query.
3. Check recent deploys (+git sha).
4. Inspect infra events (node terminations, AZ network errors).
5. Check model regressions using eval-testset (last 24h).
6. Decide mitigation and record expected improvement and cost.
7. Apply mitigation, observe for 10m.
8. If mitigated: create ticket for permanent fix; if not: escalate to SEV and follow incident review process.

Appendix B — Decision matrix (short form)

| Symptom | Likely cause | First mitigation | Cost profile |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Latency p95 up with GPU util high | Insufficient capacity | Increase batch/scale or fairshare | Medium-High |
| Error-rate spike with model timeouts | Model runtime regression | Emergency fallback model | Low-Medium |
| Availability drop for single tenant | Noisy neighbor | Fairshare throttle | Low |

Appendix C — Contact and escalation

- Platform SRE rotation: #sre-oncall (Slack)
- Incident commander escalation: page -> email template in PagerDuty integration
- Finance contact for emergency capacity: finance-ops@redwood.ai

Document maintenance

- Owner should review annually or after any major SLO incident.
- Significant changes require at least two reviewers from SRE and Product.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Distributed Backpressure & Capacity Triage Runbook

sections.body:
Overview:
This runbook defines the operational play for diagnosing and remediating distributed request-level overloads using backpressure, traffic shaping, and short-term capacity triage. It covers how to: detect when SLOs and error budgets are under pressure, apply automated and manual backpressure controls, scale safely, and ensure graceful degradation while minimizing customer impact.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to: Redwood inference serving tier (proxy/router, model-backend pods, KV cache layer, and GPU serving pool).
- Assumes metrics (Prometheus), tracing (Jaeger), logs (Elastic), and dashboards (Grafana) are available and up-to-date.
- Assumes access to autoscaler (k8s HPA/CustomAutoscaler), traffic router (Traefik/Envoy), and feature flags/traffic-control UI (Operations Console).

Key SLOs & Error Budgets (examples):
| SLO name | Target | Measurement window | Alert trigger | Error budget action |
|----------|--------:|-------------------:|---------------|--------------------|
| API availability (global) | 99.95% | 30d | < 99.9% last 6h | Tier-1 escalation + emergency capacity |
| Generation latency (P95, text-gen) | < 300ms | 7d | P95 > 450ms for 15m | Apply fast-path backpressure, reduce batch sizes |
| Request error rate (5xx) | < 0.5% | 30d | > 1% for 10m | Failover to canary model variants |
| Embeddings throughput (tokens/s) | N/A (throughput SLO) | 7d | Sustained 85% capacity utilization | Scale capacity / enable burst pool |

Monitoring & alerting (what to look for):
- Alerts: availability, elevated 5xx, saturation (cpu/gpu/mem), queue length, request latency spikes, autoscaler errors, prefix-cache hitrate drop.
- Dashboards: "Serving - Global Overview", "Per-model latency & errors", "GPU Utilization & Queues", "Ingress request queues & backpressure signals".

Pre-incident checklist (done by oncall within first 5m):
1) Acknowledge alerts in PagerDuty and mark coordinator.
2) Confirm scope: identify impacted services, regions, and models.
3) Capture baseline: current SLO windows, error-budget burn rate, and traffic trends (last 60m).
4) Check active deploys/rollouts in the last 60 minutes.
5) Verify autoscaler and scheduler health.

Immediate triage steps (0–15 minutes):
1) Identify whether issue is traffic surge vs. infrastructure failure:
   - Traffic surge indicators: sudden increase in ingress rate, client-side burst patterns, queue growth across replicas.
   - Infra failure indicators: nodes lost, OOM/killed pods, kernel-level errors, increased 5xx with unchanged ingress.
2) If infra failure, follow the standard node/pod remediation runbook and notify SRE infra leads.
3) If traffic surge or mixed: apply backpressure and traffic shaping (see Backpressure Controls).
4) Throttle non-critical routes: use rate-limit rules at the router for least-critical routes (e.g., batched bulk clients, non-real-time pipelines).
5) Shift traffic to lower-cost-safe models or smaller sequence-length variants when possible (model-fallback).

Backpressure controls (ordered by speed/safety):
| Control | Scope | Typical effect | When to use |
|---------|-------|---------------|-------------|
| Router-level rate limits | Ingress route | Immediate drop/429 to clients | Large external client floods |
| Client-side Retry-Control header | Specific client token | Reduces retries, buys time | Misbehaving SDKs or aggressive retries |
| Prefix / KV cache warm-up | Model backends | Reduce repeated compute for hot prefixes | Sudden repeated prompts causing recompute |
| Per-model concurrency cap | Backend pods | Limits active decodes per GPU | Protects GPU memory/throughput under overload |
| Queue depth signal to autoscaler | Internal | Triggers faster scale up | When autoscaler lagging behind demand |

Applying backpressure (runbook actions):
1) Router rate-limit: add a temporary rate-limit rule with a 5–15 minute TTL for the offending route. Example Envoy command (Ops Console):
   - Set: limit-by:origin, requests_per_minute: 1000 (adjust per route)
2) Set per-model concurrency cap via the Control Plane API:
   - curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/models/{model}/concurrency -d '{"max_concurrency": 4}'
3) Toggle client retry-control header override for known SDK versions via feature flag: ops/featureflags:set retry_control_override=true
4) If clients are internal, contact integration owners to reduce client-side concurrency immediately.

Capacity triage and safe scaling:
- Goal: scale quickly enough to stop SLO burn without overshooting and causing instability/queue storms.
1) Check current autoscaler state and pending scaling events: kubectl get hpa && describe hpa {serving-hpa}.
2) If autoscaler is stuck (OOMKilled pods, insufficient nodes), scale cluster capacity (add nodes) via cloud autoscaling group or request temporary burst pool (Dedicated burst).
3) If safe: perform a manual, staged scale-up of serving replicas by +25% steps with 2–4 minute stabilization windows, validating latency and queue depth after each step.
4) If GPU node provisioning latency is high (> 10m), enable temporary CPU-based fallbacks for small models or use lower-precision quantized variants as an intermediate mitigation.

Traffic shaping and routing strategies:
- Prefer weighted routing to fallback models over hard-blocking when possible to preserve degraded functionality.
- Use canary circuit-breakers for new routes. Example Grafana/Alert procedure: create evaluation rule to automatically shift 10% traffic away if P95 > threshold for 10m.

Safe rollback and failover considerations:
- If a recent rollout correlates with the onset, immediately pause/cancel the rollout and rollback if errors continue.
- Do not perform large config rollbacks while the system is under autoscaling churn unless they are the confirmed cause.

Communications and escalation (first 30m):
1) Post incident status to #incidents and the customer status page if public impact is expected.
2) Notify product/support owners for customers in the affected cohort.
3) If error budget breach is likely, page SRE manager and the product SLO owner.

Post-incident tasks and incident review template (owners and deadlines):
- Short incident summary (by oncall) — due within 24h.
- Timeline & evidence (traces, graphs, commands executed) — due within 48h.
- Root cause hypothesis and corrective actions — 72h.
- Action item owners + due dates — tracked in JIRA; follow-up review in next SRE weekly.

Incident review checklist (to include in postmortem):
1) Was backpressure applied? What controls and when?
2) Did capacity autoscaling respond? Times and deltas.
3) Were model fallbacks or quantized variants used? Effectiveness measured.
4) Customer impact classification and whether SLOs were missed.
5) Recommendations to prevent recurrence (tooling, thresholds, playbook updates).

Operational tooling & queries (quick references):
- Prometheus: current ingress rate (total_requests per 10s), P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le)).
- Check GPU queue depth: sum(serving_pending_tasks) by (node,model).
- Identify hot prefixes: topk(20, sum(rate(reqs_total[5m])) by (prompt_hash)).
- Example kubectl checks:
  - kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide
  - kubectl describe hpa serving-backend

Ownership and runbook maintenance:
- Runbook owner: Maya Chen (SRE – Serving).
- Review cadence: quarterly, or after any incident that used this runbook. Update the runbook within 7 days after each major incident.

Appendix: sample incident timeline entry (format):
- 2026-02-09T14:03Z — Alert: P95 text-gen latency > 450ms (15m).
- 14:07 — Router rate-limit applied to /v1/generate for API key X (5m TTL).
- 14:12 — Per-model concurrency cap set to 6 for model-abc.
- 14:20 — Manual scale-up +25% (3 -> 4 replicas). P95 reduced to 320ms.
- 15:40 — Autoscaler caught up; rollback rate-limit at 15:45.

References and related materials:
- See: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/predictive-slo-driven-capacity-playbook-2026.json
- See: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/error-budget-orchestration-traffic-throttle-playbook-2026.json

End of document.

payload.page_title: Runtime Interlock & Kernel Safety: Operator Manual

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This manual documents the runtime interlock and kernel safety mechanisms used by Redwood's serving runtime and provides operator procedures for diagnosing, mitigating, and recovering from incidents that involve kernel scheduling, cross-kernel handoffs, and fidelity-preserving fallback. It combines high-level architecture context with prescriptive runbooks, profiling/benchmarking steps, and rollout guidance.

Audience: Oncall SREs, runtime engineers, release engineers, and third-party accelerator integrators.

Summary: The runtime interlock is a thin coordination layer that mediates kernel lifecycle operations (start/stop/slice/handoff) and enforces safety invariants (memory isolation, KV cache consistency, credit accounting). Kernel scheduling safety modes (Strict, Graceful, Soft) define how preemption, eviction, and fallback behave under pressure. This doc explains operator-visible signals, safe mitigation pathways, and how to run targeted perf/quality experiments before/after changes.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner_team: engineering (serving-runtime squad)
- Pager duty: serving-runtime-oncall
- Escalation list: runtime-tech-lead@redwood.ai, infra-sre-lead@redwood.ai, product-reliability@redwood.ai

SLOs and Safety Thresholds

Table: Key SLOs and operational thresholds
| Signal | SLO / Threshold | Action if exceeded | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P50 request latency (short seq) | < 50ms | Monitor; no action | runtime-observability |
| P99 tail latency | < 600ms | Investigate kernel queueing; run preemption audit | oncall |
| Kernel backlog depth | < 120 queued slots | Activate graceful mode; migrate cohorts | runtime-op |
| Total GPU mem usage per node | < 92% | Evict opportunistic cohorts | capacity-planning |
| KV cache miss rate | < 8% | Trigger KV warmup policy | model-serving |
| Kernel soft-failure rate | < 0.1% | Auto-retry; if >1% escalate | oncall |

Design and Architecture Notes

- Interlock role: The interlock sits between the dispatcher and kernel manager. It validates admission, attaches safety tokens (credit, cohort id), and annotates each slot with fidelity and rollback metadata. It also emits the canonical decision trace for later repro.
- Kernel safety assertions: each kernel exposes a safety contract: {memory_budget, allowed_quant_modes, preemptibility, kv_consistency_hint}. The interlock verifies contracts before scheduling.
- Scheduling surfaces: admission controller, slot allocator, kernel handoff API, eviction coordinator. Each has a small set of operator-visible flags exposed via /api/internal/admin and metrics with _safety suffix.

Kernel Scheduling Safety Modes

1) Strict Mode (default for Dedicated):
- No preemption for in-flight requests; admission rejects if not enough contiguous memory.
- Use when tenant requires deterministic latency and no fidelity changes.
- Operator actions: preserve, do not evict, raise capacity request if backlog sustained.

2) Graceful Mode (default for Hosted burst):
- Allows cooperative preemption: kernels complete current micro-batch then yield.
- Eviction results in fallback to a pinned model variant (quantized or smaller).
- Operator actions: monitor fallback rate, check quality regression dashboards.

3) Soft Mode (default for low-cost tiers):
- Aggressive eviction + immediate hedged routing to cheaper variants.
- Best-effort KV cache preservation; higher miss rate tolerated.
- Operator actions: tune economic governor thresholds and watch token-level cost signals.

Operator Runbooks (high-level decision tree)

Incident triage summary: For latency spikes or kernel failures follow the numbered steps below. Treat production degradation as in_priority until resolved.

1) Identify scope:
  a) Run: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ADMIN_TOKEN}" https://admin.internal/runtime/signals?window=5m | jq .summary
  b) Check metrics: kernel_backlog, kernel_miss_rate, gpu_mem_util, kv_miss_rate, fallback_rate.

2) Rapid mitigation (first 3 minutes):
  a) If gpu_mem_util > 95% on nodes and kernel_backlog > 150: set scheduler to Graceful for affected cluster:
     - CLI: rwctl scheduler set-mode --cluster prod-eu-1 --mode graceful --reason "emergency memory pressure"
  b) If kernel soft-failure rate spikes: increase kernel retry multiplier to 3x and open incident.
  c) If P99 latency > target and fallback_rate rising: temporarily raise admission threshold for opportunistic cohorts to 0 to reduce noise.

3) Containment (3–30 minutes):
  - Trigger KV-cache aggressive warmup on hot cohorts: rwctl kvcache warmup --cohort <cohort-id> --target-size 80%
  - Rebalance heavy cohorts to nodes with spare GPU availability: rwctl cluster rebalance --source <node> --dest <node-list>
  - If a kernel binary is suspected: roll a canary rollback to previous kernel version in a small cohort. See Rollback steps below.

4) Recovery and postmortem preparation (30–120 minutes):
  - Restore scheduler to previous mode once backlog reduced and mem utilization below 88%.
  - Save decision traces: /var/log/runtime/decision-traces/<inc-id>.ndjson and attach to ticket.
  - Annotate incident with kernel metrics, trace ids, and any manual interventions.

Escalation Criteria

- If fallback_rate > 3% sustained for 15 minutes -> page runtime-tech-lead.
- If node GPU mem remains > 95% for 20 minutes after mitigations -> page infra-sre-lead.
- If kernel panic or node reboot occurs -> follow hardware incident playbook (eng-infra).

Profiling and Benchmarking Procedures

Purpose: Provide repeatable steps to profile a kernel interaction and validate safety changes.

1) Controlled profiling with shadow traffic
  - Prepare a mirrored workload with 1% traffic (shadow channel) and tag with experiment id. Use the shadow harness described in the benchmarking-suite (see related pages).
  - Commands:
     - Start mirror: rwctl mirror start --source-route /v1/generate --rate 1% --label safety-test-<id>
     - Enable kernel tracing: rwctl trace enable --kernel <kernel-id> --sample-rate 100% --out /tmp/trace-<id>.json

2) Kernel microbench
  - Run the microbenchmark runner on an isolated node with identical kernel parameters:
    - ./bench/kernel_runner --kernel-revision <rev> --seq-len 64 --batch-shapes "[1,2,4,8]" --samples 2000 --out perf-<id>.csv
  - Capture CPU/GPU counters using perf/NVTX: nvprof or nvidia-smi dmon and the telemetry bridge.

3) Observability checklist
  - Ensure traces include: admission_decision, kernel_hint, kv_prefetch_hint, preemption_window, fidelity_tag.
  - Confirm parity between shadow and production decision traces for a sample of requests.

4) Quality gate
  - Run prompt-set evaluation: take 500 sampled prompts spanning short/long/interactive flows and compare outputs across candidate kernels. Gate criteria: median ROUGE-L difference < 0.6 and hallucination signal delta < 0.8 (per eval harness).

Release/Cutover Checklist for Kernel or Interlock Changes

1) Preflight
  - Verify unit tests and scheduler simulator pass in CI.
  - Create a benchmark artifact with microbenchmark CSVs and a decision-trace sample. Attach to PR.
  - Author a short rollout plan with canary cohort ids and rollback criteria.

2) Canary (internal)
  - Canary cohort size: 1–2% traffic in mirrored mode for 30 minutes. Monitor kernel soft-failure, fallback_rate, kv_miss_rate, P99 latency.
  - Required signoff: runtime lead, bench team, and model-onboarding reviewer.

3) Gradual ramp
  - Ramp using traffic slices: 5% -> 15% -> 40% -> 100% with 30–60 minute steady windows.
  - At each ramp step validate: no >10% increase in fallback_rate, no >2x increase in kernel soft-failures, P99 within SLO.

4) Rollback
  - Immediate rollback command: rwctl kernel rollback --target <kernel-id> --to-rev <rev> --force-restart 0
  - If rollback does not reduce failures, switch scheduler to Strict and divert traffic to a known-good region.

Known Issues (operator-facing)

- Large-model eviction oscillation (INC-2026-034): Under mixed short/long workloads some cohorts constantly oscillate between eviction and warmstart, increasing tail latency. Mitigation: enable epoch-based eviction window and increase KV warmup weight for affected cohorts.
- Heterogeneous quant-mode mismatch (KERNEL-QUANT-12): Some kernels compile with a quant-mode that causes higher tensor-conversion overhead under small batch shapes. Workaround: pin quant-mode=dynamic for small-batch kernels till patch.
- Tracer overhead under 100% sampling (TRACE-OVERHEAD-07): Enabling 100% kernel tracing on busy nodes can itself increase latency. Use 10% stratified sampling for live traffic; reserve 100% for isolated profiling nodes.

Appendix: Operator Commands and Policy Snippets

Example scheduler policy (YAML)
|---
cluster: prod-eu-1
policy:
  admission:
    max_backlog: 120
    reserve_quota: 6
  eviction:
    mode: graceful
    epoch_window: 28s
  fidelity_governor:
    soft_threshold: 0.03
    hard_threshold: 0.08
|---

CLI quick reference
- rwctl scheduler set-mode --cluster <cluster> --mode <strict|graceful|soft> --reason "<text>"
- rwctl kvcache warmup --cohort <id> --target-size <percent>
- rwctl trace enable --kernel <id> --sample-rate <0-100> --out <file>
- rwctl kernel rollback --target <kernel-id> --to-rev <rev> --force-restart <0|1>

Decision-trace example (NDJSON line)
{"ts":"2026-02-18T12:34:56Z","req_id":"r-abc123","decision":{"admit":true,"kernel":"k-42","fidelity_tag":"q8-dyn","kv_hint":true}}

Operator tips and heuristics

- Before changing admission thresholds, always run the admission simulator with a shadow workload for at least 15 minutes.
- When investigating KV miss spikes, correlate with model-onboarding events; new model versions often have cold KV footprints.
- Use node annotations to mark hardware pressure and avoid automatic rebalancing for nodes undergoing infra maintenance.

Post-incident artifacts to collect

1) Kernel trace files (/tmp/trace-*.json)
2) Decision traces for the incident window (/var/log/runtime/decision-traces/<inc-id>.ndjson)
3) Perf CSVs and NVTX exports from the microbench run
4) Rollout and change history (PR ids, CI artifacts)

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Mariana Chen.
- 2026-01-10: Added profiling checklist and quality gate requirements (reviewer: Omar Singh).
- 2026-02-18: Expanded runbook decision tree, updated thresholds based on Q4 load tests (reviewer: Lena Morales).

Contact and feedback

For corrections or follow-ups, open a doc request in the runtime-docs channel or send mail to runtime-docs@redwood.ai.
