payload.page_title: Incident Ownership Mapping + Remediation SLA Matrix (v1)

sections.body: This page defines the **primary ownership mapping** for each incident type/subtype in the v1 taxonomy, plus **remediation SLAs** (time-to-mitigate and time-to-fix expectations) by **severity** and **customer tier** (Hosted / Dedicated / Private).
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Make ownership **unambiguous** during live incidents (one accountable team per incident).
- Enable consistent paging/escalation and reporting by type/owner.
- Set realistic but improvement-driving remediation expectations.

**Applies to:** customer-impacting incidents and high-severity internal incidents that materially threaten reliability.

---
sections.heading: The intent is to

sections.body:
- **Primary owner:** the single team accountable for mitigation and driving the incident to resolution (may delegate tasks but retains accountability).
- **Secondary owner:** team likely needed for mitigation/fix; consulted early; may lead specific workstreams.
- **Consulted:** subject-matter experts who may be needed depending on symptoms.
- **Time-to-mitigate (TTM):** time from **incident declared** (Sev assigned) to a mitigation that restores service to within agreed SLO/SLA guardrails (or to “degraded but stable” per policy).
- **Time-to-fix (TTF):** time from **incident declared** to a durable fix (merged + deployed or config updated) that prevents recurrence of the same failure mode.

**Severity scale (v1):**
- **Sev0:** complete outage / widespread critical customer impact; no viable workaround.
- **Sev1:** major degradation (sustained 5xx/latency/streaming failures) affecting many customers or a top-tier Dedicated/Private tenant.
- **Sev2:** partial degradation or limited-scope impact; mitigations exist; some customers affected.
- **Sev3:** minor impact / near-miss / internal-only reliability risk.

---
sections.heading: Definitions (used throughout)

sections.body:
1) **SRE is always paged for Sev0/Sev1** (IC + comms + coordination), regardless of incident type.
2) The **Primary owner on-call** is paged immediately once incident_type is set (or once the IC is confident on a likely type).
3) If incident_type is **Unknown/Unclassified** after 10 minutes:
   - IC pages **SRE + Platform Control Plane on-call** (default triage), then updates type as soon as evidence emerges.
4) **Multi-cause incidents:** pick a **single primary incident_type** based on the *first-order driver of customer impact* (see taxonomy decision tree). Record other drivers as **contributing systems** in the incident record/postmortem.
5) **Security triggers:** if auth failures look suspicious (credential stuffing, impossible travel, token anomalies) or audit findings require, **dual-track** with Security Ops (see security alignment page).
6) **Cloud provider / force majeure events:** still classify and mitigate, but SLA breach evaluation may be paused per the carve-outs section below.

**Escalation path (when primary owner cannot mitigate quickly):**
- **T+15 min (Sev0/1):** page secondary owner(s) if not already engaged.
- **T+30 min (Sev0/1):** page engineering manager (EM) for primary owner.
- **T+60 min (Sev0) / T+90 min (Sev1):** page director for primary owner; engage executive sponsor (SRE) if cross-org blockers persist.

---
sections.heading: Escalation and paging rules (global)

sections.body:
- Team names align to current rotations and Slack channels.
- “Service boundary” indicates the system most likely to contain the change/fix.
- Owner mapping is implemented in control plane config (versioned + auditable) and consumed by incident-bot.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
| Incident type (v1) | Subtype (v1) | Primary owner (team) | Secondary owner(s) | Consulted | Primary service boundary | Primary Slack | Pager rotation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Availability / 5xx | Request 5xx spike (non-overload) | Platform Control Plane | Serving Runtime, Smart Routing | SRE, Observability | api-gateway, request-router, admission-control | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Availability / 5xx | Overload / admission control | Infrastructure/Fleet | Smart Routing | SRE, Observability, Runtime | fleet-manager, rate-limiters, batcher | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Availability / 5xx | Dependency outage (DB/KV/queue) | Platform Control Plane | SRE | Observability | control-plane-db, config-store | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Latency regression | Global p95/p99 latency regression | Serving Runtime | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE, Observability | runtime-scheduler, kernel-selector, batching | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Latency regression | Model rollout regression | Serving Runtime | SRE | Product, Observability | model-registry, rollout-controller | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Latency regression | Network path / cross-region latency | Infrastructure/Fleet | Private Deployments/Networking | SRE | edge-ingress, peering, region-network | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Streaming | Stream disconnect spike | Platform Control Plane | Infrastructure/Fleet | Runtime, Support | streaming-gateway, websockets/sse layer | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Streaming | Partial tokens / stalled stream | Serving Runtime | Platform Control Plane | Observability | runtime-streamer, token-emitter | #eng-runtime-oncall | serving-runtime |
| Routing / fallback | Incorrect fallback policy execution | Smart Routing | Platform Control Plane | SRE, Observability | policy-engine, router | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Routing / fallback | Fallback loop / thrash | Smart Routing | Infrastructure/Fleet | Runtime, SRE | router, health-checker | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Routing / fallback | Region selection bug | Smart Routing | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE | router, region-selector | #eng-routing-oncall | smart-routing |
| Capacity / fleet | Regional GPU shortage | Infrastructure/Fleet | Smart Routing | SRE, Support/CS | fleet-manager, provisioning | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Capacity / fleet | Provisioning lag / autoscaler failure | Infrastructure/Fleet | Platform Control Plane | SRE | autoscaler, capacity-planner | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Capacity / fleet | Dedicated tenant saturation | Infrastructure/Fleet | Support/CS | SRE, Product Dedicated | dedicated-scheduler, tenant-quotas | #eng-infra-oncall | infra-fleet |
| Control plane | Config write failures | Platform Control Plane | SRE | Observability, Support | control-plane-api, config-store | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Control plane | Rollout/registry outage | Platform Control Plane | Serving Runtime | SRE | model-registry, rollout-controller | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Auth / RBAC | Token issuance/validation failures | Security Ops | Platform Control Plane | SRE, Support | auth-service, api-gateway authn | #security-ops-oncall | security-ops |
| Auth / RBAC | RBAC/permission misconfig | Platform Control Plane | Security Ops | Support/CS | rbac-service, org-policy | #eng-platform-oncall | platform-control-plane |
| Telemetry / observability | Metrics ingestion outage | Observability | SRE | Platform, Runtime | metrics-pipeline, collectors | #eng-observability-oncall | observability |
| Telemetry / observability | Logging/tracing blind spot | Observability | Platform Control Plane | SRE | log-pipeline, trace-collector | #eng-observability-oncall | observability |
| Private deployments | Connectivity (DNS/TLS/VPN/peering) | Private Deployments/Networking | Infrastructure/Fleet | SRE, Support | private-gateway, customer-vpc-connect | #eng-private-oncall | private-networking |
| Private deployments | Customer config / upgrade regression | Private Deployments/Networking | Platform Control Plane | Support, SRE | private-agent, upgrade-controller | #eng-private-oncall | private-networking |
sections.heading: Top-level incident types → ownership

sections.body:
**Overload vs routing:**
- If the *trigger* is lack of GPU capacity / saturation / provisioning lag → **Capacity/Fleet primary**.
- If the *trigger* is incorrect policy, routing loop, or wrong fallback execution even with healthy capacity → **Smart Routing primary**.
- If both present, choose the type that best explains the *first-order* customer impact and list the other as contributing.

**Streaming disconnects:**
- If disconnects correlate with gateway errors, websocket/SSE resets, or ingress churn → **Platform Control Plane primary**.
- If streams are established but stall mid-generation with runtime errors/oom/kv-cache thrash → **Serving Runtime primary**.

**Auth anomalies:**
- If it’s clearly a production bug (token validation library change, cert rotation mistake) → still classify under **Auth/RBAC**, but **Security Ops primary** unless Security explicitly delegates to Platform.

---
sections.heading: Ownership notes for common disputed boundaries

sections.body: These are **internal remediation SLAs** used for operational discipline and reporting. Customer-facing SLA/credit terms remain governed by contracts and published policies.
sections.heading: Remediation SLA matrix (v1)

sections.body:
- **Hosted:** optimize for fast mitigation; durable fixes follow normal change management unless Sev0/1.
- **Dedicated:** stronger expectation for mitigation + fix because customers have reserved capacity and explicit commitments.
- **Private:** mitigation may require customer participation; our SLA focuses on *our* response/mitigation within Redwood-managed components and clear handoffs.
sections.heading: SLA philosophy by tier

sections.body:
TTM and TTF are measured from the time the incident is declared with a severity.

| Severity | Hosted TTM | Hosted TTF | Dedicated TTM | Dedicated TTF | Private TTM | Private TTF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sev0 | 30 min | 72 hours | 20 min | 48 hours | 30 min | 5 business days |
| Sev1 | 60 min | 5 business days | 45 min | 3 business days | 60 min | 10 business days |
| Sev2 | 4 hours | 10 business days | 3 hours | 7 business days | 4 hours | 15 business days |
| Sev3 | 2 business days | 30 days | 2 business days | 21 days | 3 business days | 45 days |

**Interpretation notes:**
- **TTM** = “service restored” or “degraded but stable” per incident commander + SRE sign-off.
- **TTF** requires a tracked change (PR/config) and deployment (or customer-delivered upgrade for Private, if the fix is on their side; see carve-outs).
- If a durable fix requires a longer roadmap change, the TTF can be met by delivering a **risk-reducing fix** (guardrail, rollback, safer default) plus a committed follow-up milestone.
sections.heading: Default remediation SLAs by severity and tier

sections.body:
Some incident types have different practical fix timelines. Use these overrides when applicable.

| Incident type | Subtype | Override applies to | Dedicated/Hosted/Private | TTF override | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Control plane | Config write failures | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 3 business days | Config integrity bugs typically require code + migration; prioritize hotfix lane. |
| Telemetry / observability | Metrics ingestion outage | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 7 business days | Durable fix often includes capacity + pipeline changes; ensure interim mitigations (sampling, backpressure) are in place. |
| Private deployments | Connectivity (DNS/TLS/VPN/peering) | Sev0–Sev2 | Private | 10 business days | May require customer networking changes; our obligation is fast triage + clear “next action owner”. |
| Capacity / fleet | Regional GPU shortage | Sev0–Sev2 | Hosted/Dedicated | 10 business days | Durable fix may be procurement/provider constrained; require documented mitigation plan + capacity forecast update. |

**Who approves overrides:** SRE on-call for live incidents; post-incident, SRE program lead (Rafael Mendes) for reporting consistency.

---
sections.heading: Type-specific adjustments (overrides)

sections.body:
- SLA clocks start when the incident is **declared** with severity (Sev0–Sev3) in incident-bot.
- If the incident is initially declared as Sev2 and later upgraded to Sev0/1, the SLA clock for that severity starts at the **upgrade time** (we retain the original for audit).
sections.heading: When the clock starts

sections.body:
- **TTM stops** when mitigation is in place and validated via dashboards/metrics (or customer confirmation where metrics are unavailable).
- **TTF stops** when the fix is deployed (or config change is rolled out) and a verification check is complete.
sections.heading: When the clock stops

sections.body:
Timers may be paused only with an explicit reason recorded in incident-bot:
- **Cloud provider outage / region-wide event** that is the dominant cause.
- **Customer-caused incident** (e.g., invalid client behavior, misconfigured private networking) once confirmed.
- **Force majeure** events.

**Pauses require:** SRE approval (Sev0/1) and a post-incident note describing evidence.
sections.heading: Pausing timers (allowed but audited)

sections.body:
- Any projected TTM breach for **Sev0/Sev1** triggers:
  - Immediate page to primary owner EM at **T-10 min** to breach.
  - Escalation to director at breach time if not already engaged.
- Any actual breach triggers:
  - A postmortem requirement (Sev0/Sev1 always; Sev2 if breach is customer-impacting).
  - A follow-up ticket tagged **reliability-sla-breach** with owner + due date.

---
sections.heading: Breach escalation

sections.body:
1) Declare incident + set severity.
2) Classify **incident_type/subtype** using the decision tree.
3) Confirm **Primary owner** from mapping (incident-bot will resolve after selection).
4) Page primary owner on-call; add secondary owners if the boundary is unclear.
5) Track TTM and TTF targets in the incident channel topic (incident-bot prints due times).
6) If classification changes, update incident_type and record the reason.

---
sections.heading: How to use this during an incident (operator checklist)

sections.body:
- Symptoms: 429s + queue depth + GPU utilization pinned.
- Classification: **Capacity / fleet → Dedicated tenant saturation**.
- Primary owner: **Infrastructure/Fleet**.
- Secondary: **Support/CS** (customer comms + burst expectations).
- SLA (Dedicated Sev1 typical): **TTM 45 min, TTF 3 business days**.
sections.heading: Example A: Dedicated tenant sees 429s during burst

sections.body:
- Symptoms: websocket resets, elevated gateway errors, runtime healthy.
- Classification: **Streaming → Stream disconnect spike**.
- Primary owner: **Platform Control Plane**.
- SLA (Hosted Sev1 typical): **TTM 60 min, TTF 5 business days**.
sections.heading: Example B: Global spike in streaming disconnects after gateway deploy

sections.body:
- Symptoms: token validation failures, anomalous IP patterns.
- Classification: **Auth / RBAC → Token issuance/validation failures**.
- Primary owner: **Security Ops** (dual-track security incident if warranted).

---
sections.heading: Example C: Auth failures with suspicious pattern

sections.body:
- **2026-02-12:** Clarified overload vs routing primary-owner rule; added TTF override for regional GPU shortage; added timer pause requirements.
- **2026-01-24:** Added Private connectivity subtype details and clarified customer handoff expectations.
- **2026-01-10:** Initial v1 published.

payload.page_title: SRE Resilience Playbook: SLOs, Capacity, and Runbooks

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook centralizes Redwood Inference’s SRE practices for SLO definition and enforcement, error-budget policy, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, and canonical runbooks. It is the working reference for on-call engineers, SRE project leads, and platform product owners.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood-hosted inference endpoints (text-generation, chat, embeddings) and associated control-plane services (model catalog, routing).
- Includes both production and Dedicated clusters unless explicitly noted.

Key contacts and ownership
- SRE lead: Marcus Chen (marcus.chen@redwood.com)
- Platform product owner: Priya Nambiar (priya.nambiar@redwood.com)
- Oncall rotations: eng-sre oncall (pagerduty: redwood-sre-prod)

1) SLOs and SLIs (definitions and examples)

Principles for SLOs
- User-centric: measure what customers experience (availability, latency, correctness).
- Observable: SLIs must be expressed as queries against production metrics or traces.
- Economical: SLO targets balance user satisfaction and cost (error budget allocation).
- Actionable: SLOs must have clear escalation and remediation playbooks.

SLO catalog (summary)
| Service area | SLI | SLO (rolling 30d) | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Public text-generation API (/v1/generate) | Successful responses (HTTP 2xx within timeout) | 99.95% availability | 7-day error budget burn > 10% => page | API Platform Team (owner: priya.nambiar@redwood.com) |
| Embeddings API (/v1/embeddings) | Median embedding latency (end-to-end user-visible) | P95 < 200ms | P95 > 300ms for 1 hour => page | Vector Team (owner: diego.alvarez@redwood.com) |
| Control plane (model catalog + routing) | API error rate (5xx) | 99.9% availability | 24h rolling error > 0.1% => slack alert | Platform Core (owner: marcus.chen@redwood.com) |
| Dedicated customer control plane | Provisioning success rate | 99% | Any failed provisioning >= 1% in 24h => page | Private Deployments team |

SLI examples (Prometheus/Observability)
- Availability SLI (generation):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-server", route="/v1/generate"}[30d])) - sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-server", route="/v1/generate", status=~"5..|4.."}[30d]))
  divided by total requests (use exact query in dashboard).
- Latency SLI (P95):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api-server", route="/v1/generate"}[5m])) by (le))

2) Error budget policy and actions

Error budget windows and cadence
- Primary window: rolling 30-day window used for business reporting and quarterly planning.
- Short-term window: rolling 7-day for operational alerts and automated mitigation.

Burn thresholds and automated responses
- Warning: 10% of 30-day budget burned in 7 days. -> Slack alert to #sre-alerts, runbook owner notified, follow-up in 24h.
- Action: 25% burned in 7 days -> PagerDuty page to oncall. Oncall must: (1) assess active incidents, (2) recommend traffic shaping/rollback, (3) notify platform PO.
- Emergency: 50%+ burned in 7 days -> Exec-level escalation, trigger cross-functional incident command (IC) for customer-impact mitigation, freeze non-critical rollouts until budget stabilizes.

Error budget use cases and conservations
- Product features that intentionally degrade latency (e.g., low-cost quantized model) must explicitly reserve error budget in the launch plan and be approved by SRE PO.
- Dedicated customers consuming > 20% of cluster capacity require a separate SLO conversation and a contract-defined SLA.

3) Capacity planning and headroom policy

Targets
- Cluster utilization targets (production inference clusters): sustained CPU/GPU utilization at 55%–65% for cost efficiency.
- Headroom reserve: maintain nominal 30% capacity spare headroom across all clusters to handle burst traffic and failover.
- Autoscaling: autoscaler triggers to keep p95 latency within SLO while maintaining at least 10% instant scaling headroom.

Forecasting process (quarterly)
1. Collect telemetry: monthly QPS, peak-QPS, model mix (tokens/sec), average sequence length, batch efficiency.
2. Convert to GPU-seconds required using benchmark table (see Capacity Calculation example below).
3. Add safety multiplier (1.3 for production).
4. Divide by GPU-hours available per machine to estimate node counts.
5. Validate with runbook-based load tests (canary with 10% of production traffic).

Capacity Calculation example (table)
| Workload | Peak QPS | Avg seq len | Tokens/sec | GPU-seconds/day | GPU nodes (A100 80GB equiv) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Gen-api (prod-east) | 1,200 | 128 | 153,600 | 13,000 | 12 |
| Embeddings (prod-west) | 4,500 | 32 | 144,000 | 9,500 | 9 |

Operational runway and procurements
- Procurement lead times: GPUs and cloud commitments require at least 8 weeks planning for normal growth, 16+ weeks for specialized procurement.
- Reserved vs spot mix: baseline reserved capacity for 70% of predicted sustained demand, spot or burst for remaining headroom.

4) Reliability initiatives (projects and OKRs)

Current initiatives (2025-Q1/Q2)
- Continuous Batching Improvements (owner: Anika Bose) — Goal: improve average tokens/sec by 18% in production; deliverable: new batching scheduler + canary.
- KV-cache persistent snapshotting (owner: Diego Alvarez) — reduce cold-start latency for long-context models by 40% in dedicated clusters.
- Model fallback policy engine (owner: Marcus Chen) — automated routing to compatible quantized variants when primary model capacity is constrained.

Initiative governance
- Each initiative must publish: scope, success metrics (quantitative), rollout plan, rollback criteria, and error-budget reservation.
- Quarterly reliability review with SRE, Platform, and Product to prioritize top 3 initiatives where reliability ROI is highest.

5) Incident review standards and postmortem template

Incident severity model
- Sev0 (Critical): multi-region outage impacting >50% of production traffic or sustained customer-facing data loss. Immediate IC.
- Sev1 (Major): single-region outage with significant latency or >5% customer error rate for 30+ minutes.
- Sev2 (Minor): localized degradation, partial functionality loss, or operator-only impact.

Postmortem timeline and structure (must be blameless)
- Postmortem draft: within 72 hours of incident mitigation.
- Final postmortem: within 14 days including remediation tickets and owners.
- Required sections: Summary, Timeline (UTC), Impact (customers/metrics), Root cause, Contributing factors, Detection and mitigation, Corrective actions, Follow-ups (tickets with owners), and Lessons learned.

Severity to RCA SLA mapping
- Sev0: RCA and remediation plan within 3 business days.
- Sev1: RCA within 7 business days.
- Sev2: RCA within 21 days.

Blameless language guidance
- Use neutral phrasing: e.g., "a service failed to scale due to missing autoscaler constraint" versus blaming an individual.
- Focus on systemic fixes: tests, alerts, documentation, runbook improvements.

6) Operational tooling and dashboards

Canonical dashboards and alerts
- Production API Health (Grafana): availability, p95/p99 latency, error rate by route. Dashboard ID: grafana-prod-api-01.
- Capacity Planner (Looker Studio): rolling 12-week forecast, per-cluster utilization and headroom.
- Error Budget Manager (internal service): shows current burn, projected burn curves, suggested mitigations. Endpoint: https://internal.redwood.com/error-budget

Alerting guardrails
- Pager duty for action-level alerts (oncall); Slack for informative/warning alerts.
- No alert should fire for more than 5% of incidents as repetitive noise. If it does, review and re-tune thresholds.

Developer tools and self-service
- Infra-as-code modules (Terraform): module names: tf-redwood/gke-inference, tf-redwood/gpu-autoscaler. Repo: git@github.com:redwood/infrastructure.git.
- SRE runbook CLI: rdb-runbook (internal tool) e.g., rdb-runbook run api-high-latency --dry-run.
- Canary harness: load-gen scripts and example config under /ops/canary-load-tests.

7) Runbooks (canonical)

A. Runbook: API high-latency (oncall checklist)
1. Confirm alert: open Grafana "Production API Health" panel and check p95/p99 and error rate.
2. Verify scope: is it single-region or multi-region? Check region label in metrics.
3. Check recent deploys: git commits in the last 60 minutes (git log --since='60 minutes' origin/main). If a suspected deployment, rollback via CI:
   - CI rollback: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" https://ci.redwood.com/api/v1/rollback -d '{"service":"api-server","to":"previous"}'
4. Identify resource pressure: check node GPU utilization (kubectl top pods -n inference) and autoscaler events (kubectl get events -n inference --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp).
5. Apply mitigation: scale replicas (kubectl scale deployment api-server --replicas=XX -n inference) or enable traffic shaping to reduce non-critical routes.
6. If error budget burn > 25% in 7d, escalate to PD and trigger cross-team IC.
7. Post-incident: if a human action fixed the issue, add an automated check or alert to detect the condition preemptively.

B. Runbook: GPU OOM / node eviction
1. Detect: nodename and pod metric show OOM kills (kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Failed).
2. Quarantine node: cordon node (kubectl cordon <node>) and drain if necessary (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data).
3. Collect diagnostics: journalctl -u nvidia-driver, /var/log/syslog, dmesg; save to S3: aws s3 cp /tmp/node-<node>-diag.tgz s3://redwood-diagnostics/$INCIDENT_ID/
4. Restart scheduler or redeploy model instances with lower batch size; update model config through admin panel to reduce memory per-worker.
5. File ticket to infra team for hardware replacement if driver/kernel issue is confirmed.

8) Playbook maintenance and ownership
- Document owner (this page): Marcus Chen. Maintain cadence: update after any Sev1/Sev0 event or quarterly.
- Reviewers: SRE leads, Platform PO, and Security when changes touch access controls.
- Labels and lifecycle: tag runbooks with a last-verified date in the page header.

Appendix: Templates and links
- Postmortem template: /confluence/templates/postmortem-template.md
- Capacity forecast spreadsheet: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/forecast-template.xlsx
- Error budget API: internal endpoint and documentation: https://internal.redwood.com/docs/error-budget-api

Change log
- 2024-09-15: Initial draft (Marcus Chen).
- 2024-11-02: Added capacity forecasting example and headroom policy (Anika Bose review).
- 2025-03-04: Updated error budget thresholds, added GPU OOM runbook steps and initiative list (Priya Nambiar).

If you are oncall and unsure, page redwood-sre-prod and reference this playbook in your incident channel.

payload.page_title: SLO Entropy Scan and Capacity Annealing Playbook (2026)

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook defines the SLO Entropy Scan and Capacity Annealing processes used by SRE to detect latent SLO fragility, proactively rebalance capacity, and reduce unexpected error-budget burn. It combines a periodic 'entropy' analysis of SLO signal instability with an automated annealing workflow that simulates controlled load, validates fallbacks, and adjusts capacity / throttles.

Scope:

- Applies to Redwood public inference endpoints and multi-tenant Dedicated clusters.
- Intended for services with hard latency SLOs (p99 latency, request success rate) and token-based billing impact.
- Not a replacement for incident runbooks; this playbook is a proactive reliability initiative with an associated drill cadence.

Why an entropy-driven approach?

SLOs can be stable on average while hiding discontinuous failure modes caused by workload shifts, model rollouts, or quantization changes. Entropy = an operational metric of SLO signal volatility across dimensions (latency, error-rate, tail token count). High entropy predicts future SLO regression and enables targeted capacity annealing before significant error-budget consumption.

Definitions:

- Entropy Scan: a periodic analytics job that measures day-over-day and week-over-week volatility in SLO telemetry across tenants and routes.
- Capacity Annealing: a controlled procedure to rehearse degraded states and then 'cool' the system via capacity reconfiguration or traffic shaping to return to steady-state with validated mitigations.
- SLO shard: a logical subset of traffic (route/model/tenant) that is tracked as a distinct SLO.

Roles & Responsibility:

- SRE (owner): run scans, approve annealing windows, execute automated anneal jobs, and verify post-runbook KPIs. Owner: eng-sre/team-alpha.
- Runtime Team: implement and validate fallbacks, KV/prefix cache warming, and model variant routing.
- Product/Model Onboarding: provide expected token distributions and rollout plans for new models.
- Oncall: respond to high-severity alerts triggered during annealing drills.

SLO Design Matrix (example):

| SLO Dimension | Metric | Target | Window | Entropy Threshold (alert) | Owner |
|--------------|--------|--------|--------|---------------------------|-------|
| Latency (P99) | request_latency_ms | 250ms | 30d rolling | 3x baseline MAD across 7d | runtime-team |
| Success Rate | success_rate | 99.5% | 30d rolling | >0.5% step-change week-over-week | eng-sre |
| Embedding Freshness | embedding_recompute_ratio | 95% | 14d | >6% variance | infra |
(NOTE: replace example values per-service in the SLO registry.)

Error Budget Policy (condensed):

1) Error budget windows are 30 days by default unless contractual SLAs require otherwise.
2) If a 7-day projected burn-rate > 5x baseline, schedule a mandatory annealing window within 72 hours.
3) If an emergency incident consumes >50% of the remaining budget in <24 hours, raise a P1 and engage product + runtime for rollback.

Entropy Scan Procedure (weekly automated job):

1) Data sources: SLO metrics from metrics-store (prometheus-aggregation), token-level traces from token-evidence pipeline, and model-serving traces (kv-hit/miss rates).
2) Compute per-route entropy: for each shard compute coefficient-of-variation and median absolute deviation (MAD) over 7d and 30d windows and aggregate into an entropy score.

CLI / example queries:

- PromQL (latency volatility):
  - quantile_over_time(0.99, request_latency_ms[7d])
  - stddev_over_time( request_latency_ms[7d] ) / avg_over_time(request_latency_ms[7d])

- Token evidence sampling (SQL):
  - SELECT model, route, COUNT(*) AS tokens, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) FROM token_evidence WHERE ts >= now() - interval '7 days' GROUP BY model, route;

3) Output: CSV with columns {shard, entropy_score, recent_burn_rate, kv_miss_rate, top-ten error messages}. Upload to reliability-dashboard and notify #sre-ops when any shard crosses entropy threshold.

Capacity Annealing Workflow (high level):

Purpose: validate graceful degradation and tune capacity allocation before an incident.

Preconditions:
- Anneal windows are scheduled during low traffic (per-customer blackout windows respected).
- At least one oncall and one runtime engineer are present and reachable.
- Backout plan defined in the runbook (rollback commands / config flags).

Steps (sequence):
1) Authorization: SRE lead approves the anneal job in the reliability dashboard.
2) Canary baseline: capture live baseline traces (10 minutes) and snapshot per-shard SLO metrics.
3) Controlled perturbation: incrementally increase synthetic load or selectively disable cache layers per the anneal plan. Perturbation steps are staged (10%, 25%, 50%, 75% of the targeted stress) with a 5–10 minute observation window between steps.
4) Fallback validation: at each stage verify fallbacks trigger as designed (model-variant routing, quantized fallback, prefix cache warm). Record exact artifact ids and KV-cache heatmaps.
5) Anneal decision gate: if p99 latency rises above 2x SLO or success_rate drops below 90% for >3 minutes, pause and execute immediate cooldown (traffic cutback + template rollback).
6) Cooldown & reconfiguration: apply capacity increases, re-route low-priority tenants, or enable rate-limiting profiles.
7) Post-anneal validation: run smoke canaries and synthetic queries for 15 minutes, then publish anneal report.

Automated commands (examples):

- Start anneal job: curl -X POST https://reliability.redwood.internal/api/v1/anneal -d '{"shard":"nlp-gen-prod", "Plan":"cache-disable-stage"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${SRE_TOKEN}'
- Emergency rollback: rctl apply -f rollback-template.yaml --target shards=nlp-gen-prod

Incident Decomposition & Evidence Packaging Standard:

When entropy scan or anneal uncovers a regression requiring incident review, follow these standards for evidence packaging:

Required artifacts (packaged as a single .tar.gz):
- timeline.json (ordered events with UTC timestamps)
- metrics-snapshot.csv (30d baseline + 72h surrounding window)
- token-evidence-sample.json (50 representative tokens with redacted customer ids)
- anneal-runbook-log.txt (if anneal executed)
- tracer-level traces (.zip) for affected services
- configuration snapshot: routing.yaml, autoscaler-state.json

Evidence labeling rules:
- Timestamps must be ISO8601 UTC.
- Customer-identifying fields must be hashed or removed.
- Each artifact must include an "ingested_by" header with SRE run-id.

Operational Tooling & Integrations:

- Reliability Dashboard: reliability.redwood.internal (SRE-owned) displays entropy heatmap, anneal schedule, and per-shard SLOs.
- Alerts:
  - ALERT_SLO_ENTROPY_HIGH (pagerduty) — severity P2, threshold: entropy_score > 0.8 AND projected burn > 3x.
  - ALERT_ANNEAL_FAILURE (slack + p1 pagerduty) — fired when automated anneal step fails to validate fallback.
- ChatOps: /run anneal <shard> starts a preflight check; approved runs post updates to #sre-anneals.
- Telemetry: token_evidence pipeline stores samples in evidence-store (S3), indexed by run-id.

Drill Cadence & Governance:

- Weekly entropy scans run automatically.
- Monthly annealing drills: rotate through top-10 high-risk shards (based on entropy + business criticality).
- Quarterly tabletop with product, model-onboarding, and runtime to review anneal reports and update SLOs.

KPIs & Success Criteria:

- Reduction in 30-day unplanned error-budget burns by 30% within 3 months of adopting annealing.
- Mean-time-to-detect for SLO regressions improved to <30 minutes for shards with entropy alerts.
- 90% of annealing drills complete without triggering emergency rollback.

Runbook Template (text):

- Title:
- Shard name:
- Owner(s):
- Precondition checklist: (1) schedule, (2) oncall notified, (3) rollback ready
- Perturbation plan: (staging steps, durations)
- Metrics to capture: (p99, p90, success_rate, kv_miss_rate)
- Stop criteria: (explicit thresholds)
- Rollback steps: (ordered commands)
- Post-run validation: (smoke queries, traces)

Threshold table (recommended defaults):

| Signal | Warn threshold | Stop threshold | Action |
|--------|----------------|----------------|--------|
| Entropy score | 0.6 | 0.8 | schedule anneal / immediate alert |
| p99 latency uplift | 1.5x baseline | 2.0x baseline | pause anneal, rollback |
| success_rate drop | 0.5% absolute | 2% absolute | traffic cutback, emergency rollback |
Post-Run Report (deliverable):

- executive summary (1 paragraph)
- timeline of events (minute resolution)
- artifacts attached (list of packaged files)
- conclusions and recommended next steps (config changes, SLO tuning, model rollback)
- owners and follow-ups with target dates

Playbook Examples (short):

Example A — High entropy on route /v1/generate:
1) Entropy scan flags /v1/generate with entropy_score=0.72 and projected burn-rate=4x.
2) SRE schedules anneal in 48 hours, notifies product and customer success.
3) Anneal executes with cache-disable stage; fallback to quantized flow validated at 25% perturbation; at 50% perturbation p99 crosses stop threshold, anneal paused and cooldown applied.
4) Post-run: increase cache warmup, add 5% reserved capacity to shard, update SLO runbook.

Example B — Rapid burst causing token-level errors:
1) Token evidence shows top error 'kv-miss-timeout' correlated with a model rollout.
2) Immediate short-term mitigation: enable per-token throttling profile and route new model traffic to dedicated pool.
3) Longer-term: update onboarding checklist to include pre-warm KV caches and an anneal rehearsal before rollout.

Checklist before closing an anneal-related incident review:
- [ ] Evidence package uploaded and validated
- [ ] Post-anneal smoke tests passed 15m after cooldown
- [ ] Action items assigned with owners and due dates
- [ ] SLO registry updated if target changes required

References & related pages:

- SLO registry (internal): /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/slo-attribute-matrix-and-capacity-mapping-manual-2025
- Anneal scheduler API docs: reliability.redwood.internal/api/docs/anneal
- Token evidence pipeline: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/token-evidence-sampling-and-slo-assertion-runbook-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-01-20: created by Evelyn Chen
- 2026-02-12: added CLI examples and evidence packaging rules (review: Amir Khatri)
- 2026-03-01: clarified anneal stop criteria and KPI targets (review: Maya Alvarez)

payload.page_title: canary-rehearsal-and-escalation-exercise-playbook-2026

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook codifies a recurring, cross-team canary rehearsal and escalation tabletop exercise designed to validate: SLO behavior during partial rollouts, automated and manual rollback paths, paging and escalation flows, and end-to-end telemetry (synthetic and production). The goal is to surface gaps in runbooks, alerting, and team coordination before a real incident. Exercises should be scheduled quarterly for each high-impact service and after major changes to routing, autoscaling, or rollout tooling.

Scope

- Services: model-serving frontends, request-router (smart-router), autoscaler, cache layer (prefix/KV), billing-rate-limiters.
- Failure modes simulated: degraded tail latency, model-variant regression, cache-priming failure, burst-induced overload, and partial config rollouts.
- Not in scope: full data-plane outages requiring cloud provider escalation; these are covered by separate disaster recovery drills.

Objectives

1. Verify canary traffic routing and metrics capture for the nominated SLOs within 5 minutes of cutover.
2. Confirm automatic fallback triggers (model-variant fallback or routing to older commit) work as designed.
3. Validate human escalation and paging flows to oncall, product owner, and infra leads.
4. Exercise capacity hedging: ability to increase dedicated capacity or route to burst pool within 15 minutes.
5. Capture improvement actions and update runbooks within 48 business hours.

Prerequisites

- Exercise owner assigned and communicated to participating teams 7 days prior.
- Canary configuration saved as a named spec (e.g., canary-specs/rehearsal/<service>/<date>).
- Synthetic traffic harness configured and smoke tests passing.
- Telemetry dashboard snapshot and alert policies baselined.
- Test tenant(s) or token-scoped traffic that will not be billed/charged.

Roles & Responsibilities

- Exercise Lead: schedules, coordinates, runs the tabletop, collects artifacts (1 person).
- Service Owner: responsible for executing canary cut, monitoring, and rollback (team lead for the service).
- Oncall Engineer: primary responder for the canary window.
- Platform/Autoscaler Engineer: executes capacity actions (scale-up, burst pool attach).
- Product Safety / Trust: reviews customer-impact considerations where applicable.
- Scribe: records timeline, screenshots, and action items.

Exercise Types (pick one per rehearsal)

A. Performance Degradation (tail latency regression)
- Inject: increase request size or force quantized-path fallback to simulate slow tokens.
- Validate: SLA and P99 latency rise observed on the canary slice; alerts fire.

B. Behavioral Regression (quality drift)
- Inject: swap in a model variant with a synthetic prompt set that yields measurable metric delta (e.g., top-1 rerank score).
- Validate: quality monitors flag regression; routing fallback or rollback is exercised.

C. Capacity Surge (burst)
- Inject: ramp synthetic requests to 5x baseline for 8 minutes targeted at canary slice.
- Validate: autoscaler behavior, graceful degradation policies, and fair-share throttles.

D. Telemetry Loss (observability failure)
- Inject: disable a telemetry collector for the canary slice.
- Validate: alerting on missing telemetry, alternative evidence sources, and documentation of the telemetry gap.

Step-by-step Playbook

1) Pre-day (7–1 days before)
   - Publish exercise plan, list of participants, and expected blast radius.
   - Register canary spec as: `canary-specs/rehearsal/<service>/<YYYYMMDD>-<owner>`
   - Validate synthetic harness: `scripts/harness/run_smoke.sh --spec canary-specs/...`
   - Snapshot dashboards: save as `dashshots/<service>/<YYYYMMDD>`

2) Day-of (T=0)
   - 00:00 — Kickoff call (15 minutes) for objectives, abort criteria, and roles.
   - 00:15 — Apply canary routing: `rtrctl cutover --spec canary-specs/... --weight 10%`
   - 00:20 — Start synthetic traffic for chosen exercise type.
   - 00:25 — Scribe captures initial telemetry and dashboard links.

3) Observation window (T+5 to T+30 minutes)
   - Monitor SLOs: latency, error-rate, and customer-impact indicators.
   - If automated fallback conditions met, verify actions and record timestamps.
   - If rollout not safe, follow rollback procedure (see step 5).

4) Escalation path (triggered by defined thresholds)
   - Threshold examples: P99 latency > 2500ms on canary or error-rate increase > 3x baseline for 5 minutes.
   - Primary oncall page —> Platform lead if unresolved within 10 minutes —> Eng director if unresolved within 30 minutes.
   - Use Pager shorthand: `pager duty: page-oncall --service <svc>`

5) Rollback and Containment
   - Automated rollback: confirm that the router executes the fallback within configured SLA. Record `fallback_timestamp`.
   - Manual rollback command example: `rtrctl rollback --spec canary-specs/... --to-tag v<previous>`
   - Validate system recovery: confirm metrics return to baseline for 3 consecutive minutes.

6) Wrap-up (T+60 to T+120)
   - Capture timeline, console logs, and dashboard snapshots.
   - Collect participant notes and raw screenshots into the exercise folder: `gs://redwood-exercises/<service>/<date>/`
   - Raise action tickets for observed gaps with severity, owner, and due date (max 48 business hours to triage).

Telemetry & Validation Checklist (table)

- SLOs to monitor:
  - Availability SLO: 99.9% (expected impact < 0.01% of total traffic during canary).
  - Latency SLO: P99 < 1200ms for production; canary threshold set to 2500ms for early detection.
  - Error-rate SLO: 0.1% baseline; alert at 0.3% sustained for 5 minutes.

- Dashboards and Alerts to snapshot:
  - Canary slice latency/chart (P50/P90/P99)
  - Model-quality regression chart (eval score deltas)
  - Autoscaler event stream and node attach logs
  - Request-router routing table and fallback events

Escalation Matrix (succinct)

1. Oncall engineer (first 10 minutes): ACK page, attempt quick mitigation (traffic drain, increase concurrency limit).
2. Platform lead (10-30 minutes): perform capacity attach or policy update (burst pool attach).
3. Service owner and product (30-60 minutes): authorize broader rollback or customer comms.
4. Exec oncall / Director (>60 minutes): coordinate incident declaration and support SRE in postmortem.

Runbook Checklist (pre-populated for each rehearsal)

- [ ] Canary spec committed to repo with descriptive name.
- [ ] Synthetic harness validated within test tenant.
- [ ] Dashboard snapshots created and linked.
- [ ] Alerting policies and escalation contacts verified.
- [ ] Abort criteria communicated and accepted by attendees.

Post-exercise Actions & Governance

- Immediate (within 48 business hours): triage all action items; update runbook with at least one code/config fix or documentation change.
- Medium (2 weeks): implement monitoring improvements or escalation automations agreed in the exercise.
- Quarterly: incorporate lessons into SRE onboarding training and run the exercise with a fresh set of engineers.

Artifacts to capture

- Timeline CSV with event timestamps.
- Dashboard snapshots and raw metrics export (Prometheus export or telemetry dump).
- Synthetic harness logs and request traces (trace IDs).
- Action ticket list with owners and SLAs.

Templates

- Post-exercise summary (example):

  Title: Canary Rehearsal — <service> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
  Lead: <name>
  Type: <Performance|Behavioral|Capacity|Telemetry>
  Summary: Short 3-4 sentence narrative of what happened.
  Timeline: Bullet of timestamps and events.
  Impact: Which SLOs were affected and how.
  Actions: ActionID, brief description, owner, due date.

Appendix: Common CLI snippets / examples

- Apply canary (example):
```
rtrctl cutover --spec canary-specs/rehearsal/modelsrv/20260201-mchen --weight 10 --dry-run=false
```

- Rollback (example):
```
rtrctl rollback --service modelsrv --from canary-20260201 --to v20260129 --comment "rehearsal rollback"
```

- Attach burst pool (example):
```
platformctl attach-burst --service modelsrv --pool burst-pool-1 --reason "rehearsal: capacity surge test"
```

- Export dashboards (example): `dashctl export --id <dash-id> --range "-1h" --out gs://...`

Appendix: Abort Criteria (examples)

- Any production customer impact detected outside the test tokens or test tenants.
- Data exfiltration or unexpected access to PII lists is observed.
- Observable billing meter increase affecting customer accounts.

Ownership & Review cadence

- Owner: Eng-SRE Reliability Initiatives (rotation: Maya Chen -> Arjun Patel -> Lucia Gomez).
- Review: Annual review plus a mandatory review after any relevant incident or large rollout.

Related pages and references

- Canary rollout automation checklist — internal link (see related_pages above).
- SLO alerting policy reference: `/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-alerting-policy-2025`

Contact

- For questions or to request an exercise: `eng-sre-reliability@redwood.ai`

End of playbook

payload.page_title: SLO Steward Rotation and Capacity Handoff Manual

sections.body:
Overview:

This document defines the SLO Steward rotation pattern, a formal capacity handoff protocol, and the associated artifacts required to safely transfer operational responsibility for service SLOs and error budgets between teams. It bridges oncall practices, capacity planning, and SRE reliability initiatives so that ownership transitions preserve headroom, evidence context, and recovery plans.

Why this matters:
- SLOs and error budgets are operational contracts; ad-hoc handoffs cause missed mitigation windows and incorrect throttling decisions.
- Inference workloads are bursty and heterogeneous; capacity state and quantization/instance profiles must be explicitly communicated.
- A predictable stewarding process reduces escalations, accelerates recovery, and preserves customer trust.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to all model-serving and multi-tenant inference services (hosted, dedicated, private) managed by eng-sre and runtime teams.
- Covers regular rotation (shift changes), planned handoffs for maintenance/change windows, and emergency ownership transfers during incidents.
- Does not replace per-service runbooks; it references them and prescribes required artifacts for handoff.

Definitions:
- SLO Steward: the oncall or designated engineer responsible for SLO health, error-budget decisions, and capacity handoffs for a given service window.
- Capacity Headroom: the measurable spare token-processing capacity based on GPU pool sizing + warm pools. Expressed as percent of provisioned throughput.
- Error Budget Reserve: the currently available budget (in % of allowed SLI violation) allocated for planned experiments or absorbable incidents.
- Handoff Artifact: required context items (see checklist) shared at rotation or handover time.

Required artifacts for every handoff (Handoff Checklist):
1) Current SLO status snapshot (quantile latencies, availability, daily burn rate)
2) Error budget remaining and 7d trend
3) Capacity headroom (%), largest tenants consuming capacity, and recent allocation changes
4) Open mitigations and active throttles/fallbacks (routes, model fallbacks)
5) Recent synthetic canary failures and their ticket/PR links
6) Known upcoming events (deploys, batch jobs, scheduled migrations)
7) Contact list: owner, escalation chain, support rotation for dependent services
8) Runbook links and reproduction harness commands

Handoff schedule and cadence table (example):
| Frequency | Who initiates | Minimum handoff window | Ownership record | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Daily rotation | Outgoing steward | 10 minutes | Slack message + Handoff doc | Include last 1-hour telemetry snapshot |
| Pre-maintenance | Change owner | 30 minutes | Jira change + capacity check | Tag oncall and capacity-orch channel |
| Emergency transfer | Incident commander | Immediate | Incident channel + evidence bundle | Follow emergency transfer steps below |

Operational tooling integrations:
- PagerDuty escalation profile: "SLO-Stewards" (priority -> pager)
- Slack channels: #sre-stewards, #capacity-orchestration, #model-serve-incidents
- Capacity Orchestrator (cap-orch) API endpoints used in handoffs: GET /v1/headroom, POST /v1/evict, POST /v1/eviction-preview
- Telemetry dashboards: per-model SLI dashboard (latency p50/p95/p99), error-budget burn rate chart, tenant-heatmap

Standard handoff procedure (regular rotation):
1) Outgoing steward populates the Handoff Checklist document (template below) and posts to #sre-stewards.
2) Outgoing shares a 10-minute verbal summary with incoming steward: current SLO state, active mitigations, and capacity pressures.
3) Incoming verifies live dashboards and runs the quick verification commands (examples below).
4) If incoming detects a discrepancy > 10% headroom variance or >20% error budget change from the snapshot, escalate to the service owner and delay handoff.
5) Record the handoff in the rotation log with timestamp and artifacts attached (link to checklist).

Emergency ownership transfer (incident-driven):
1) Incident commander declares transfer and assigns new SLO Steward in the incident channel.
2) Outgoing steward pushes an evidence bundle (last 1 hour traces, top 5 slow traces, eviction events) to the incident docket.
3) Incoming steward runs the incident triage checklist and confirms control planes for throttling and fallback are available.
4) If capacity change is required, call cap-orch emergency API and update incident timeline.

Quick verification commands (examples):
- Verify headroom: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://cap-orch.internal/v1/headroom?service=model-serving | jq .headroom_percent
- Error budget snapshot: curl -s https://slo-metrics.internal/api/v1/snapshot?service=model-serving | jq .error_budget_remaining
- Canary status: kubectl -n serve get pods -l app=canary -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.phase}'

Thresholds and decision matrix:
| Signal | Threshold | Immediate action | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Headroom <= 15% | <= 15% provisioned | Initiate emergency capacity request; enable throttling | SLO Steward + CapOps |
| Error budget burnrate > 2x baseline | 2x sustained for 1 hour | Pause risky experiments; escalate to incident command | SLO Steward |
| P99 latency increase > 40% | relative to 7d median | Verify deployment, check hot cache, run warm-pool refill | Runtime team |
| Canary failures >= 3 in 15m | 3 failures | Halt rollout; rollback candidate | Platform owner |

Handover message template (Slack):
"Handoff: model-serving | Outgoing: @aisha | Incoming: @marco | SLO: availability 99.95% | Headroom: 22% | ErrorBudget: 68% | Active mitigations: throttling to tiered lanes; canary paused | See docs: <link>"

Evidence and archival policy:
- Attach handoff checklist and 1-hour evidence snapshot to the daily rotation log. Retain rotation logs for 90 days.
- Incident-driven transfers: append evidence bundle to incident record; retention per incident policy (1 year for Sev2+, 90 days for Sev3+).
- For audits: export CSV of rotation logs and handoff artifacts on quarterly cadence.

Training and rollout:
- All stewards must complete a 1.5-hour training: overview, simulator lab, emergency transfer drill.
- New rotation members shadow outgoing stewards for two full rotations before independent handoffs.
- Bi-annual tabletop: run a cross-team capacity handoff exercise and record metrics (handoff time, missed signals).

Post-handoff review and KPIs:
- KPIs to track: average handoff duration, % of handoffs with complete checklist, incidents arising within 2 hours of handoff, mean time to stabilization after emergency transfer.
- Review cadence: SRE leadership reviews KPIs monthly; improvements are tracked as reliability initiatives.

Appendix A — Handoff checklist template (copyable):
- Service: 
- Steward outgoing: 
- Steward incoming: 
- Timestamp: 
- SLO snapshot (p50/p95/p99 latency, availability): 
- Error budget remaining (current, 7d trend): 
- Capacity headroom (% and top 5 tenants): 
- Active mitigations and where configured (route ids): 
- Recent deploys and canary status: 
- Open tickets/PRs relevant to runtime: 
- Links: dashboards, runbooks, incident channel 

Appendix B — Example: planned maintenance handoff checklist excerpt:
- Scheduled maintenance window: 2024-06-23 22:00–23:00 UTC
- Expected cap reduction: 18% while nodes reboot
- Pre-approved reserve: +10% burst allocation requested via cap-orch ticket #CO-442
- Mitigation plan: pre-warm caches, enable fallback small-model variant, notify customers with high-traffic flag

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary: SLO Steward (oncall)
- Secondary: Runtime owner (team runtime)
- Tertiary: ENG-SRE Lead (pager)

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-sre (stewardship working group)
- Review cadence: annually or after any handoff-related incident resulting in customer impact
- Change process: PR to this page with at least two reviewers from SRE + Runtime

Contact and resources:
- Slack: #sre-stewards (operational), #capacity-orchestration (capacity ops)
- PagerDuty: SLO-Stewards escalation policy
- Templates: /docs/rotation-templates/handoff-checklist.md

End of document.

payload.page_title: Capacity Conservator Handbook: SLO Allocation Patterns and Stewardship

sections.body:
Summary:
This handbook defines the Capacity Conservator role, standard SLO allocation patterns, error budget stewardship procedures, and capacity reconciliation practices for model-serving and API services. It consolidates guidance for on-call, SRE owners, and product teams to ensure predictable availability while preserving runway for feature velocity and cost optimization.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce ambiguity about how SLOs and capacity commitments are negotiated, provisioned, and reconciled across multi-tenant inference workloads.
- Scope: Redwood-hosted inference services, Dedicated clusters, and Private deployments where Redwood provides operational guidance. Does not change formal SLO contracts for customers (see pricing-and-packaging).

Key definitions:
- SLO (Service Level Objective): Target percent for an observable (e.g., p99 latency < 300ms, availability 99.95%).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; tracked as burn rate over sliding windows (1h, 24h, 7d).
- Capacity Conservator: Primary SRE responsible for capacity stewardship for a set of services or model families.
- Stewardship window: Standard review cadence for allocations (weekly small, monthly major).

Roles and responsibilities:
1) Capacity Conservator (SRE)
   - Owns SLO allocation ledger and capacity forecasts for assigned tenants.
   - Chairs weekly stewardship sync with product/eng stakeholders.
   - Initiates pre-emptive throttles or tenant rebalancing when forecasted burn indicates >50% risk to SLOs in next 24h.
2) Service Owner (product/eng)
   - Proposes SLO targets, priority classes, and canary/rollback plans.
   - Provides workload profiles (token distribution, seq_len histogram, concurrency patterns).
3) Platform Capacity Planner
   - Maintains cluster sizing models, cost estimates, and provisioning pipelines.

SLO Allocation Patterns (templates):
- Conservative (production-critical):
  - Availability: 99.99%
  - Error budget: 52 minutes/month
  - Default priority: P0
  - Allocation rule: Dedicated pool or strict fairshare with guaranteed min throughput.
- Balanced (high-volume product features):
  - Availability: 99.95%
  - Error budget: ~4.38 hours/month
  - Default priority: P1
  - Allocation rule: Elastic fairshare with burst credit up to 150% for short windows.
- Economical (background/async batch jobs / low-latency-tolerant):
  - Availability: 99.5%
  - Error budget: ~3.65 days/month
  - Default priority: P2
  - Allocation rule: Spot-backed capacity or preemptible nodes with lower admission priority.

Capacity allocation decision flow (summary):
1) Service owner submits Allocation Request (JIRA template) with workload telemetry and desired SLO tier.
2) Capacity Conservator runs the Allocation Simulator (see tooling) and returns recommended reserve (vGPU units) and throttle policies.
3) If recommended reserve increases monthly commit > 20% vs baseline, escalate to Platform Capacity Planner for procurement lead time.
4) Approve -> schedule provisioning window -> update SLO ledger and dashboards.

Allocation decision checklist (for conservators):
- Confirm recent 4-week traffic histogram and 95th / 99th percentiles for sequence length and tokens per request.
- Validate model variant and quantization (FP16, int8) assumptions that affect per-token CPU/GPU cost.
- Ensure KV cache hit-rate assumptions are specified.
- Evaluate cross-tenant correlated surge risk (region outages, marketing events).
- Record acceptance criteria for success (latency p95/p99, throughput targets).

Error budget stewardship (operational rules):
- Burn rate tiers and automated signals:
  - Normal: burn_rate <= 1.0 over 24h -> no action.
  - Elevated: burn_rate 1.0-3.0 over 1h -> Capacity Conservator notified; begin mitigation planning.
  - Critical: burn_rate > 3.0 over 1h or projected > 2.0 over 24h -> auto-invoke throttles per priority policy and schedule incident review.
- Automatic mitigations (high-level):
  1) Soft admission controls: reduce lower-priority tenant concurrency by 20%.
  2) Prefetch/caching rehydration for common prefixes.
  3) Route new traffic to compatible cheaper model variants (fast-fallback policy).
  4) Expand autoscale group (if headroom available) with emergency capacity tag.
- Manual mitigations:
  - Negotiated temporary SLO relaxation clauses: only by Platform + Product sign-off during major incidents.

Operational tooling and telemetry contract:
- Required dashboards:
  - SLO ledger: per-service SLO, current burn (1h/24h/7d), priority class.
  - Capacity posture: cluster headroom %, upcoming scale events, spot eviction risk.
  - Tenant heatmap: per-tenant token/sec and tail-latency exposure.
- Alerting thresholds (Prometheus-style examples):
  - SRE Alert: slo_burn_rate{window="1h"} > 3 -> SEV2 -> paged to oncall.
  - Capacity Alert: cluster_free_gpu_percent < 10 and provisionable == false -> SEV1 -> mandatory page.
  - Throttle Alert: tenant_throttle_rate > 5% -> SEV3 -> notification to owner.

Example Prometheus rule (text):
- record: slo:burrn_rate_1h
  expr: increase(slo_burn[1h]) / 3600

Example alert (text):
- alert: SLOBurnCritical
  expr: slo:burrn_rate_1h > 3
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Critical SLO burn rate >3x for {{ $labels.service }}"

Incident review standards (SLO/capacity lens):
- Evidence collection checklist for SLO incidents:
  1) Timeline of burn rate and traffic spikes (1h/24h windows).
  2) Top 10 tenants by token volume during window.
  3) Model variants and num_gpus in-use; scheduler logs for preemptions.
  4) Autoscaler decision logs and provisioning latency.
  5) Any rollout or config changes in the last 72h.
- Post-incident remediation categories:
  - Capacity: add guardrail (min-reserve, autoscale tuning) or reclassify priority.
  - Operational: improve alerts, fix telemetry gaps.
  - Product: negotiate tenant behavior change or request feature-level smoothing.
- SLO incident timeline artifact: include a 1-page summary with top 3 root causes, required next steps, owners, and target remediation date.

Runbook excerpts (actionable steps for on-call):
1) If SLOBurnCritical fires:
   a) Acknowledge and attach initial notes in incident tracker.
   b) Run `capacity-sim assess --service ${SERVICE} --window 1h` to get projected runway.
   c) If projection < 6h and cluster_free_gpu_percent < 15%: execute failover plan (see step d).
   d) Failover plan: `reroute --from ${SERVICE} --to ${FALLBACK_SERVICE} --ratio 0.25` then iterate until burn stabilizes.
2) If cluster_free_gpu_percent < 5%:
   a) Check pending node provisioning: `kubectl get nodes -l redwood/emergency-capacity=true`
   b) If none, open procurement trigger (automated ticket) and apply temporary throttles to P2 tenants per priority table.

Priority table (short):
- P0: platform-critical, 30% headroom guaranteed, preempt not allowed.
- P1: customer-facing, 10% headroom guaranteed, preempt allowed only for P0.
- P2: best-effort, subject to preemption and throttles during elevated burn.

Capacity reconciliation and monthly stewardship ritual:
- Monthly ritual steps (owner: Capacity Conservator):
  1) Pull actual usage and compare to forecast for each service and tenant.
  2) Identify variance > 15% and flag for optimization or re-provisioning.
  3) Run cost/perf simulation for recommended changes and present in monthly stewardship board (template attached).
  4) Approve or schedule changes with Platform Capacity Planner.

Controls for Dedicated and Private deployments:
- Dedicated: recommend explicit reserve lanes and an isolation test before onboard. Record reserved slot sizes and emergency add procedures.
- Private: provide a runbook template to customers describing how Redwood stewards error budget signals and what actions Redwood can take under support contract (e.g., advisory only vs active throttle).

Templates and CLI snippets (appendix):
- Allocation Request JIRA fields (text list): service, owner, desired_slo_tier, historical_token_profile_link, kv_cache_hit_rate, model_variant, quantization_profile, proposed_commit_change, acceptance_criteria.
- Example CLI: `redwood-capacity request --service search-infer --slo-tier Balanced --expected-qps 1200 --duration 30d`

Related pages and artifacts:
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-onboarding-runway-and-slo-admission-playbook-2026
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025

Revision history:
- 2026-01-10: Created by Samira Chen (draft).
- 2026-02-05: Added automated mitigation rules and Prometheus examples (reviewers: Diego Morales).
- 2026-03-01: Published after stewardship board feedback and added Dedicated/Private controls.

Contact and ownership:
- Primary contact: samira.chen@redwood.ai
- Oncall alias for capacity conservators: oncall-capacity@redwood.ai

Appendix: Quick decision flow for emergency throttle (one-liner):
- If projected error budget runway < 6h -> reduce P2 concurrency by 30% -> re-evaluate after 5 minutes -> escalate to SEV1 if no improvement.
