payload.page_title: service-lifecycle-operational-blueprint-2025

sections.body:
Summary:
This blueprint describes a single, structured operational flow that SREs and service owners follow from service onboarding through steady-state operations to decommissioning. It standardizes SLO definitions, error-budget governance, capacity planning, runbook templates, incident evidence requirements, and the set of tooling integrations we rely on for inference-serving workloads. The intent is to reduce ambiguity when services (particularly model-serving endpoints) transition between teams and to make reliability economics explicit.

1) Purpose and scope
- Purpose: ensure consistent, auditable practices for defining and operating SLO-backed services across Redwood Inference (hosted, dedicated, and private modes).
- Scope: applies to any production-facing service that contributes to customer-visible inference latency/availability or billing (e.g., text generation APIs, embedding endpoints, reranking jobs, batch exporters). Excludes purely internal support tools unless they have a customer SLA.

2) High-level lifecycle stages
- Onboard (define owners, SLOs, traffic profile, initial capacity)
- Harden (run synthetic canaries, set telemetry, runbook authoring, pre-prod load tests)
- Operate (monitoring, error-budget governance, capacity management, monthly reviews)
- Evolve (rollouts, A/B experiments, model-variant pinning, quantization changes)
- Decommission (drain traffic, archive evidence, remove capacity allocations)

3) Roles & ownership
- Service Owner: product/engineer responsible for correctness and customer impact (primary contact for SLO changes).
- SRE Steward: long-lived on-call and capacity steward; maintains runbooks and headroom calculations.
- Platform Owner: maintains infra primitives (Autoscaler, Cache, Model Warm Pools).
- Incident Reviewer: designated SRE who leads post-incident evidence validation.

4) SLO and error-budget standards (required fields)
Each service must publish an SLO document with these fields before production traffic is allowed:
- SLO name (short)
- Objective (e.g. 99.9% success within 300ms P95 or 99.5% availability windowed monthly)
- Measurement signal(s) and query definitions (PromQL/Cortex query or SLO Ledger metric id)
- Time window for SLO evaluation (30d rolling, 7d canary window)
- Error budget unit (tokens/minute, percentage of requests, % latency violations)
- Owners and escalation path
- Related runbook id(s)

Required thresholds and governance:
- Initial production threshold: all new model-serving routes default to a 99.9% availability SLO (30d) and 99th-percentile latency SLOs aligned to product-class (interactive: P99 < 450ms; async/embeddings: P95 < 2500ms).
- Error-budget burn policy (example):
  - Green: burn rate < 1.0 -> normal ops
  - Yellow: burn rate 1.0–3.0 -> SRE Steward review within 6 hours, disable risky releases/canaries
  - Red: burn rate > 3.0 or cumulative budget > 50% used in 24h -> immediate mitigation: auto-throttle non-critical tenants, open incident ticket, schedule postmortem if recovery not in 2 hours

SLO measurement examples (text for copying into SLO doc):
- Availability: sum(status == 200)/count(all requests) over 30d rolling 
- Latency violation rate: count(latency_ms > target)/count(all requests) over 30d rolling
Include exact PromQL or SLO Ledger query and a synthetic canary mapping for each SLO.

5) Capacity planning & headroom methodology
Objective: express required capacity in three frames: baseline (steady-state), headroom (buffer for +99th percentile bursts), and emergency buffer (graceful degradation lane).
Steps: 
1. Collect 14–30 days of request profile: tokens/sec distribution, sequence length histogram, tenant-weighted percentiles.
2. Convert workload to GPU inference units using our internal cost model:
   - baseline_gpu = ceil(mean(tokens_per_sec * cost_factor) / gpu_throughput_profile)
   - headroom_gpu = ceil(baseline_gpu * headroom_multiplier) where headroom_multiplier defaults to 1.5 for multi-tenant hosted routes and 1.25 for dedicated lanes.
3. Add graceful-degradation capacity: reserve 10–20% of baseline_gpu (or 1 hot spare GPU for small services) to enable controlled fallback (lower-precision model, longer tail latency).
4. Autoscaling policy template (minimum):
   - min_replicas = baseline_gpu
   - target_utilization = 65% (tokens-per-second based)
   - cooldown_scale_up = 30s; cooldown_scale_down = 5m
5. Capacity review cadence: initial review at deploy, monthly headroom review, and after any significant model change (quantization, new tokenizer) or customer onboarding >10% traffic.

Capacity artifacts to attach to service page:
- Traffic profile CSV (tokens_s distribution)
- Cost model input sheet (gpu cost per token by sequence length)
- Simulated canary runs (k6/locust configs)

6) Runbook template (mandatory sections)
Every service runbook must include the following clearly labeled sections:
- Title & owners (service owner, SRE steward, escalation contacts)
- Symptoms (what triggers runbook)
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered, human-readable)
- Automated mitigations (throttle policies, failover routes, circuit breaker commands)
- Verification checklist (queries to validate recovery, expected metrics)
- Post-incident evidence template (attach logs, trace ids, token-sampling, SLO Ledger export)
- Rollback & rollback verification steps
- Links to dashboards, alert runbooks, and relevant RFCs

Example quick mitigation (short form):
1) Identify spike source: run query 'topk(10, sum by(tenant)(requests_total) )'
2) If tenant spike present: enable token-priority cap for tenant via Traffic Sculptor CLI: 'tsctl cap tenant <id> 0.3'
3) If P99 latency > threshold and GPU utilization > 95%: scale up warm pool: 'ci-scale warm-pool --service <service> --add 2'

7) Incident review and evidence standards
Purpose: guarantee reproducible, structured post-incident reviews that feed capacity, SLO, and product decisions.
Required evidence collected within 24h of incident:
- Incident timeline (machine timestamps, author)
- SLO Ledger snapshot and burn-rate graph for the incident window
- Relevant traces (Jaeger ids) and sampled request payloads (redacted) covering pre-failure and recovery windows
- Model-serving internal metrics: kv-cache hit rates, batch sizes, kernel-fallbacks, OOM counts, device temperature anomalies
- Autoscaler and scheduler events (scale decisions, eviction logs)
- Any config changes (git hash) and rollout IDs active at time of incident
Post-incident artifacts must be attached to the review doc and preserved for 90 days. The Incident Reviewer scores the evidence completeness: 3 (complete), 2 (partial), 1 (insufficient). Score <3 triggers an evidence-gap action item.

8) Operational tooling & integrations (standard stack)
- Observability: Prometheus + Cortex, Grafana (dashboards), Loki for logs, Jaeger for traces. Export SLOs to SLO Ledger for governance.
- Capacity orchestration: Capacity Orchestrator (internal), Warm-Pool controller, and Autoscaler service (ci-autoscale).
- Traffic control: Traffic Sculptor (priority caps, tenant shaping), Throttle Manager.
- Evidence collection: Incident Evidence Collector (samples requests, stores in S3 with KMS encryption).
- Experimentation: Canary Runner (k6 integration) and Shadow Mirroring pipeline.
Integration checklist for a new service: instrument metrics + labels (service, model_version, tenant), create Grafana dashboard, add SLO Ledger entry, wire up Evidence Collector sampling policy.

9) SRE governance & meeting rhythm
- Onboarding review: must occur prior to production(approval by SRE Steward and Platform Owner).
- Monthly SLO health sync: product + SRE to inspect burn patterns and upcoming capacity events.
- Quarterly capacity forecast: SRE, finance, product to align on committed capacity for Dedicated customers.
- Post-incident review: within 5 working days; corrective actions scheduled and tracked to closure.

10) Rollout & Decommission checklist
Rollout (must be followed for any model or infra change impacting latency/availability):
1. Create canary with 1–5% traffic and 7d observability window.
2. Run synthetic canaries for 24–72h with representative prompts (include edge-case prompt-set).
3. Validate SLOs in canary window and run headroom simulation.
4. Stage rollout increments (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with automated gate checks on burn rate and latency.
5. Record rollout id, config hash, and recovery commands in runbook.

Decommission:
1. Notify stakeholders 30 days prior (or per contractual SLA if Dedicated).
2. Drain traffic: set routing weight to 0 over at least 48 hours.
3. Archive SLO and evidence artifacts (90-day retention) and update capacity ledger.
4. Release reserved GPU capacity and mark for finance reconciliation.

Appendix: sample SLO table (text)
| metric | objective | window | owner | measurement_query |
| availability | 99.9% | 30d | @service-owner | sum(success)/sum(requests) |
| latency_p95 | P95 < 350ms | 30d | @service-owner | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(latency_bucket[30d])) by (le)) |

CLI snippets and quick copies:
- Add SLO entry (SLO Ledger): 'sloctl create --service <svc> --name availability --objective 99.9 --window 30d --query "sum(status==200)/count()"'
- Throttle tenant: 'tsctl cap tenant <tenant-id> --pct 20'
- Warm pool scale: 'ci-scale warm-pool --service <svc> --add 2 --reason "headroom for traffic spike"'

Concluding guidance:
This blueprint is prescriptive where risk is customer-facing (SLO definition, evidence collection, capacity headroom) and advisory where teams need flexibility (autoscaler tuning, exact headroom multiplier). Service Owners should treat this doc as the single source of truth for lifecycle decisions and attach the required artifacts to the service Confluence page.

Change log:
- 2025-02-10 created by Maya Chen
- 2025-09-07 added warm-pool guidance and headroom multipliers (review: Evan Brooks)
- 2026-01-12 updated incident evidence retention to 90 days and clarified burn-rate thresholds (review: Priya Nair)

payload.page_title: Service Stability: Financial Friction & Capacity Trading Manual

sections.body:
Overview

This manual defines the operational and financial mechanism we use to reconcile SLO-driven error budgets, cross-team capacity needs, and short-term capacity trading. The goal is to reduce friction for business-driven launches while protecting global availability and preserving fair allocation across tenants and services.

Who should read this
- SREs owning model-serving SLOs
- Product/feature owners planning launches
- Capacity planners and finance partners
- Service owners who may request temporary headroom

Key terms
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g. 99.5% p99 latency for text-generation).
- Error budget: allowable SLO budget (1 - SLO) consumed by poor performance.
- Capacity credit: a time-bounded token issued to a team permitting additional headroom above nominal allocation.
- Trading window: the period (default 72 hours) during which capacity credits can be used.

Principles
1) Safety first: SLO preservation is the overriding constraint; no trade may push a dependent SLO below its emergency threshold without explicit authorization.
2) Measurable economics: every capacity trade must be accompanied by an estimate of marginal cost (GPU-hour equivalent) and expected customer value.
3) Short-term flexibility: support temporary, revocable capacity expansions (credits) rather than permanent reallocation for launches.
4) Auditability: all trades are logged, reconciled weekly with finance, and visible on the SRE capacity dashboard.

Operational model summary
- Capacity credits are issued by the Capacity Steward (CS) team and are denominated in "token-headroom units" (THU). 1 THU approximates 1 vGPU-hour on our standard inference instance.
- Credits expire after the trading window and do not convert to long-term allocation without formal capacity onboarding.
- Trades may be requested via the CLI or the Capacity Portal; automated approval flows exist for low-risk requests (below threshold) and manual approvals for higher-risk requests.

SLO thresholds and gating rules (summary table)
| SLO target | Soft burn threshold | Hard gate threshold | Action when crossed | Responsible party |
|------------|---------------------|---------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| p99 latency <= 200ms | 30% error budget burn in 1 hour | 60% burn in 30 minutes | Soft gate (reduce batch size, enable fallback variant) | Oncall SRE + Service Owner |
| availability >= 99.9% | 20% error budget burn in 24h | 50% burn in 1h | Immediate rollback, capacity escrow activation | Oncall SRE + CS Team |
| embedding throughput >= 10k qps | sustained queue length > 2x baseline | queue growth > 10%/min | Throttle non-critical tenants, invoke capacity trading | Oncall SRE |

Note: The full threshold matrix is available on the SRE dashboard and is parameterized per service.

Pre-deploy economic checklist (feature owners must provide)
1) Expected incremental burst (THU) and duration.
2) Estimated marginal cost ($/THU) and business justification (expected revenue/retention uplift).
3) Rollout plan: canary size, ramp cadence, observability queries (see telemetry section).
4) Fallback plan and rollback criteria mapped to SLO thresholds.

Requesting capacity credits (example procedure)
1) Open a capacity request via: redwood-capacity request --service my-service --amount 240THU --window 72h --reason "Black Friday promotion" --owner @product-team
2) Automated checks run: cross-SLO impact simulation, thermal headroom check, and marginal cost estimate.
3) If request < 500THU and no dependent SLO simulated impact > 5%, the system issues provisional credits and notifies CS.
4) For larger requests or flagged simulations, CS schedules a 30-minute triage.

Approval decision matrix (abbreviated)
- Auto-approve: request <= 500THU AND no dependent SLO risk > 5%
- CS review: 500THU < request <= 2,000THU OR dependent SLO risk between 5–15%
- Exec review: request > 2,000THU OR dependent SLO risk > 15%

Deployment gating runbook (step-by-step)
1) Preflight (T-24h): Ensure capacity credits are active, canary plan uploaded, and telemetry queries exist. Notify oncall.
2) Canary (T-0): Start with 1% traffic. Observe p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, queue depth, and token-level cost.
3) Canary decision (T+10m window): If soft thresholds exceeded, pause rollout and remediate (increase cache, lower batch size). If hard thresholds exceeded, rollback to previous model/version immediately.
4) Ramp phases: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with 15–30 minute observation windows. Each ramp requires a green light in the dashboard.
5) Post-rollout (T+24h): Reconcile THU usage and file post-deploy evidence (see Post-deploy reconciliation).

Rollback and mitigation playbook (fast actions)
- Immediate rollback: execute redwood-deploy rollback --service my-service --to-tag stable-20260210
- Activate fallback variant: set model-routing weight to 0.25 for new model: redwood-routing set-weight --service my-service --model new-model:0.25 --model stable-model:0.75
- Lease emergency headroom: CS can issue emergency credits (up to 200THU) with exec notification; these are time-limited to 4 hours.

Telemetry & dashboards (what to monitor)
- latency.p99.% (service.my-service.latency.p99)
- request.error_rate (service.my-service.errors.total / requests.total)
- queue.depth (service.my-service.request_queue.depth)
- token_cost.per_minute (finance.service.token_cost.min)
- capacity.thu_consumed (capacity.service.thu_conso)
- dependent_slo.impact_estimate (simulation.run.latest)

Alerting rules (examples)
- PAG (P1): p99 > SLO and error budget burn > 60% in 30m -> PAGER (sre-oncall + product oncall)
- PAGE (P2): sustained soft-burn (30% in 1h) -> channel #sre-deployments + page if escalation conditions met

Audit & reconciliation (weekly cadence)
1) Every Monday CS publishes capacity ledger for the week: issued credits, consumed THU, refunded/expired credits, and marginal cost tallies.
2) Finance and Product reconcile expected marginal cost vs actual; discrepancies > 20% trigger a postmortem and a new cost estimate requirement for future trades.
3) SRE publishes list of removed trades (reversed due to SLO impact) and corrective actions.

Post-deploy evidence template (attach to capacity request)
- Start/End timestamps for the rollout
- THU allocated and THU consumed (by tag)
- Canary metrics snapshot (p50, p95, p99, error rate)
- Any mitigation actions taken and timestamps
- Final decision (complete / partial rollback / rollback) and justification

Example capacity trade request (JSON payload example for API)
{
  "service": "my-service",
  "amount_thu": "240",
  "window_hours": "72",
  "justification": "Seasonal campaign - expected 4x baseline for 12 hours",
  "owner": "product-team@redwood.com"
}

(Submit via POST /api/v1/capacity/trades with API key scope=capacity:request)

Failure modes & mitigations
- Unbounded consumption: implement token bucket throttles tied to THU, auto-throttle non-critical tenants.
- Simulation underestimates dependent impact: apply conservative multipliers and require manual signoff for repeated underestimates.
- Disputed chargebacks: escalate to financial reconciliation committee; freeze future auto-approvals for offending product teams until resolved.

Ownership & escalation paths
- Capacity Steward (CS) Team: issues credits, maintains ledger, performs weekly reconciliation. Contact: cs-team@redwood.com
- SRE Oncall: operational lead during deployment windows and incident response. Contact: #sre-oncall
- Product Launch Owner: provides business justification and ROI estimates.

Appendix A: Example CLI commands
- Request credits: redwood-capacity request --service my-service --amount 240 --window 72 --reason "marketing surge"
- Check credits: redwood-capacity status --service my-service
- Revoke credits: redwood-capacity revoke --id TR-20260301-42 --force

Appendix B: Recommended dashboard queries
- Canary snapshot: rate(api.requests{service="my-service",route="/v1/generate"}) by (quantile)
- Burn rate query: sum(increase(error_budget_burn[1h])) / error_budget_total

Appendix C: Example scenarios
- Small launch (<=500THU): Use auto-approval, standard canary. Post-deploy reconciliation required within 48 hours.
- Large launch (>2000THU): CS + SRE + Finance tabletop prior to issuance. Post-launch cost variance threshold set to 10% for immediate remediation.

Document change log
- 2025-11-20: Created by Priya Ramanathan (initial draft).
- 2026-01-12: Added automated approval thresholds and CLI examples (reviewer: Ethan Park).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized gating thresholds and reconciliation cadence (reviewers: Maya Singh, Liam O'Connor).

Related artifacts
- SRE capacity dashboard (internal link)
- Capacity API spec (internal link: /confluence/engineering/api/capacity-spec)

End of document

payload.page_title: Chaos Exercises and Failure Hypothesis Library (SRE Program 2026)

sections.body: This page documents Redwood Inference's formal chaos engineering program for 2026, including a curated Failure Hypothesis Library (FHL), exercise cadence, success criteria tied to SLOs and error budgets, safety guardrails, tooling references, and a lightweight post-exercise review template aligned with our incident review standards. The goal is to proactively validate resilience assumptions, reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), and surface capacity and operational gaps before customer impact.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Validate critical SLOs and verify graceful degradation strategies under realistic failure modes.
- Exercise cross-team runbook execution and automation paths (serving runtime, autoscaler, routing).
- Identify capacity bottlenecks and quantify error-budget burn under controlled conditions.
- Produce reproducible artifacts (metrics, traces, runbook notes) for continuous improvement and follow-up work.
sections.heading: Objectives

sections.body:
- Quarterly full-service game days (company-wide, ~72-hour window for preparation and follow-up).
- Monthly targeted micro-chaos tests (single-service or infra component, low blast radius).
- Ad-hoc pre-release or pre-migration exercises for major changes (e.g., new autoscaler, kernel update, quantization rollout).
sections.heading: Scope and frequency

sections.body:
- Every exercise must declare one or more target SLOs it is intended to probe (examples below).
- Error-budget impact is simulated and measured; exercises are stopped if projected burn rate exceeds the emergency threshold (see Safety Guardrails).
- Key SLO examples we use as anchors:
  - Hosted API availability: 99.95% monthly (goal).
  - 99th-token-latency (p99) for generation endpoint: < 1200ms for short contexts (<= 512 tokens).
  - Embeddings throughput SLO: 95% of requests <= 100ms p95 under baseline load.
  - Latency SLOs are expressed per-route and per-model; exercises must list which route(s)/model(s) are affected.

Failure Hypothesis Library (FHL) — canonical entries:
(Use this table as the source of truth for game-day scenarios. Choose 1–3 hypotheses per exercise.)

| ID | Hypothesis | Target services / systems | Primary metrics to monitor | Expected customer-visible effect | Failure mode controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FHL-01 | Partial GPU node pool failure during peak traffic | Serving runtime (gpu-pool-west), load balancer, autoscaler | request success rate, p95 latency, GPU utilization, queue depth | Increased latency; queued requests; degraded throughput for pinned model versions | Immediate rollback to pinned fallback model; scale up reserved capacity; abort test on >2% sling in availability |
| FHL-02 | Persistent KV-cache corruption leading to incorrect prefixes | KV cache service, prefix cache layer, reranking | output-quality regression metrics, error rate, cache hit ratio | Silent quality regressions causing higher downstream corrections | Disable cache and fall back to cold inference path; test data validation hooks |
| FHL-03 | Control plane latency (DB read/write) causing rollout delays | Deployment API, control-plane DB, plan-apply queue | API latency, deployment success rate, autoscaler lag | Rollouts pause/fail; can cause cascade if automated rollouts backlog | Rate-limit control-plane operations; applied automation circuit breaker |
| FHL-04 | Cross-region network partition between US and EU regions | VPC peering, smart routing service | cross-region request rate, fallback routing activations, error budget burn | Regional traffic surge, increased cross-region egress costs, possible customer SLA impact | Force-routing to local region; enable degraded feature set for restricted customers |
| FHL-05 | Model quantization path regression under long contexts | Runtime quantized kernels, model variant selection | p99 latency, generation correctness (eval prompts), memory pressure | Higher hallucination / truncated responses for long context users | Auto-fallback to full-precision variant; abort if quality delta > threshold |
(Test authors should add new hypotheses to the FHL with clear owner, reproducibility steps, and required preconditions.)

Exercise lifecycle (preparation → execution → review):
1) Proposal (2–3 weeks before):
   - Define hypothesis IDs from FHL, target SLOs, blast radius, test schedule, detection metrics, and abort conditions.
   - Register on the Chaos Calendar (internal calendar) and notify affected teams.
   - Pre-authorize capacity reserves (if test needs additional burst capacity).
2) Pre-flight checklist (72 hours before):
   - Verify metric dashboards and runbook links are available.
   - Confirm on-call coverage and communication channel (Slack #chaos-exercises).
   - Create one-click kill switches and API toggles for the test.
3) Execution window (≤ 4 hours for targeted tests; ≤ 6 hours for full-service micro-games):
   - Monitor SLO and error-budget dashboards continuously.
   - Keep an operations lead (OL) and a safety officer (SO) assigned.
4) Abort and rollback: follow abort conditions strictly (see Safety Guardrails).
5) Post-exercise review (within 5 business days):
   - Complete the Post-Exercise Report and action items in JIRA.
   - Add reproducible scripts and artifacts to the FHL entry.
sections.heading: Alignment with SLOs and error budgets

sections.body:
- Exercise owner: drafts hypothesis, runs the test, collects artifacts. (Typically Reliability or Platform team engineer).
- Operations lead (OL): monitors KPIs during the test and triggers rollback if thresholds are exceeded.
- Safety officer (SO): has unilateral authority to abort exercises immediately.
- Observability owner: ensures dashboards and traces are collecting the required signals.
- Product/customer success liaison: assesses customer-impact risk and communicates external messaging if necessary.
sections.heading: Roles & responsibilities

sections.body:
- Abort on: projected monthly error-budget burn rate > 25% (based on observed short-window burn extrapolation), or SLO breach > 5% absolute for critical routes for > 10 minutes.
- No experiments against customer-managed private deployments unless explicit customer approval and a signed change request.
- All experiments must have an accessible kill switch (Slack command + automation runbook).
- Low-blast defaults: start with canary subset (1% traffic) and ramp only with explicit OL approval.

Metrics, dashboards and alerting (operational tooling):
- Required dashboards for every exercise: SLO burn dashboard, request success + error classification, latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), resource utilization (GPU/CPU/Memory), autoscaler events, deployment events.
- Alerting hooks: automated alert when rolling 5m error rate implies >10% of monthly error-budget burn if sustained.
- Tracing: include a correlation id header (X-Game-Day-ID) on all injected traffic to filter traces and logs.
sections.heading: Safety guardrails (mandatory)

sections.body:
- Example abort command (via Ops CLI):
  rwn ops abort-game --id GAME-2026-013 --reason "p99 latency > safety-threshold"
- Example scale-up automation (Kubernetes/GPU autoscaler):
  kubectl patch hpa serving-gpu-pool-west -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":10}}' --namespace serving
- Playbook snippet to fallback a model route to a smaller variant:
  1. Pause traffic routing: curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/route/pause -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","reason":"game-day rollback"}'
  2. Update route to fallback model: PATCH /api/route/{id} body {"model":"redwood-fast-quant-v1"}
  3. Verify success rate and p95 latency, then unpause.

Evidence and post-exercise review template (aligns with incident review standards):
- Title: [GAME-ID] — short hypothesis summary
- Owner: name and team
- Start / stop timestamps (UTC)
- Hypothesis IDs from FHL
- SLOs and metrics targeted (explicit numeric goals)
- Raw artifacts: dashboards links, traces, logs, experiment scripts, correlated request ids
- Outcome: pass / partial / fail (with measuring criteria)
- Root causes (if any issues surfaced) and contributing factors
- Action items (JIRA links) with owners and due dates
- Follow-up test plan (if partial or fail)
sections.heading: Runbook integration and automation examples

sections.body:
- Metric extraction query examples (Prometheus/ClickHouse/Tempo): include example queries in the exercise doc.
- Experiment scripts (bash/python) stored in repo: infra/chaos/2026/<game-id>/.
- Screenshot checklist for dashboards to capture at t=0, t=mid, t=end.
sections.heading: Templates and artifacts to attach

sections.body:
- In-house automation runner (rwn-chaos) — preferred for low-blast experiments; integrates with Redwood control plane and kill switches.
- Gremlin / Litmus — approved for deep-failure injection on infra-layer only.
- Grafana / Prometheus / ClickHouse / Tempo for metrics and traces.
- ChatOps integration (Slack) for one-click abort and status updates.
sections.heading: Tooling (recommended & supported)

sections.body:
- If an exercise requires reserved capacity changes, coordinate with Capacity Planning and Finance for temporary credits.
- Run a pre-test capacity simulation that projects autoscaler behavior and expected token throughput. Capture these projections in the proposal.
sections.heading: Capacity and cost considerations

sections.body:
- Running large-blast experiments without a designated SO.
- Not pre-registering rollback paths or lacking a kill switch.
- Focusing purely on latency without validating output quality (for inference services both are critical).

Success criteria and KPIs for the chaos program (quarterly review):
- Number of documented hypotheses exercised per quarter >= 6.
- Mean time to abort (MTTA) for tests with issues < 2 minutes (target).

payload.page_title: Incident Playbook: Tiered Recovery & Capacity Fallback Matrix

sections.body: This playbook defines a compact, decision-oriented approach to handling SLO violations, capacity stress, and progressive recovery for Redwood's inference platform. It combines: a) a clear SLO/error-budget taxonomy, b) an executable capacity fallback matrix, c) incident escalation and retrospective triggers, and d) operational tooling integrations for automation and observability.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Services covered: serving-runtime, model-router, ingress-gateway, kv-cache, telemetry-pipeline, capacity-orchestrator.
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private fleets where Redwood controls autoscaling and routing.
- Excludes non-LLM control plane services (billing pipeline, payroll).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Keep p99 token latency and availability SLOs within targets while minimizing cost and user-facing failures.
- Provide deterministic, auditable actions for progressive degradation and recovery.
- Ensure incident review requirements scale with severity and SLO impact.
sections.heading: Objectives

sections.body:
- Critical SLOs:
  - Availability: 99.95% (monthly) for control-plane endpoints, 99.9% for tenant inference endpoints (tier-dependent).
  - p99 generation latency: <= 500ms for small models, <= 1200ms for long-context models as defined per model-profile.
- Error budget windows: rolling 30d for availability; rolling 7d for latency-sensitive production routes.
- Burn-rate levels (7d window):
  - Green: burn_rate <= 1x (no automated mitigation)
  - Amber: 1x < burn_rate <= 4x (automated mitigations triggered)
  - Red: burn_rate > 4x (escalation to oncall + capacity fallback)
sections.heading: SLO & Error Budget Taxonomy (quick reference)

sections.body:
- Inputs evaluated every 60s by capacity-orchestrator: current burn rate, cluster utilization, queue length, p95/p99 latency delta, model compatibility set.

| Tier | Trigger condition | Automated actions (order) | Human action | Notes |
|------|-------------------|--------------------------|--------------|-------|
| Tier 0 (Normal) | burn_rate in Green; utilization < 70% | None (observe) | N/A | Normal ops. |
| Tier 1 (Moderate) | Amber burn_rate OR utilization 70-85% | 1) Activate prefix KV cache eviction policy; 2) Enable request coalescing for identical prompts; 3) Increase per-replica concurrency (if safe) | Notify oncall channel; assess traffic profile | Apply conservative cost caps. |
| Tier 2 (High) | Red burn_rate OR utilization 85-95% OR sustained p99 > target *1.2 | 1) Route new low-priority tenants to cheaper model-variants; 2) Autoscale add warm-pool nodes (best-effort preemptible + reserved); 3) Throttle background rerank/embeddings jobs; 4) Increase batching window to 50ms | Pager to SRE primary; run capacity checklist | Metric gating prevents cascading. |
| Tier 3 (Critical) | utilization > 95% OR catastrophic model-serving failure | 1) Global routing fallback to smaller model family for public routes; 2) Reject new long-context requests with 413 + client hint; 3) Emergency divert to dedicated spare-region; 4) Trigger purchase/burst contract (if configured) | Full incident war room; exec notify | Trigger incident review with highest severity. |
sections.heading: Tiered Capacity Fallback Matrix (decision table)

sections.body:
1) Telemetry detects burn_rate > 1x for 15m -> mark Amber.
2) Amber sustained 30m or all model partitions show latency delta -> apply Tier 1 automated actions.
3) If Amber escalates to Red or utilization thresholds hit -> apply Tier 2.
4) For catastrophic component failure (node-pool OOM, kernel failure) -> immediate Tier 3.
sections.heading: Decision flow (condensed)

sections.body:
- telemetry-pipeline: emits s.lo_burn, p95/p99, queue_depth, per-tenant request rates to metrics cluster.
- capacity-orchestrator: reads metrics and posts decisions to router/api for routing/scale changes.
- error-budget-orchestrator: owns burn-rate calculation and triggers webhooks.
- runbook-runner: executes pre-approved actions (cache toggles, reroute, throttle) as idempotent jobs.
sections.heading: Operational Tooling Integrations (implementation)

sections.body:
{
  "event": "capacity_fallback",
  "service": "serving-runtime",
  "tier": "2",
  "reason": "burn_rate:5.3,util:88%",
  "actions": ["route-low-priority-to-variant:small-v2", "scale:warm_pool:+8"]
}

Runbook: Tier 2 recovery checklist (executable steps):
1) Confirm alert details (metrics window, affected partitions, top-10 tenants by QPS).
2) Execute automated fallback (runbook-runner job idempotent-run-<ts>).
3) Validate that p95 improved within 5 minutes. If not:
   a) Rollback increased batching; b) Verify KV cache hit-rate; c) Check per-model memory pressure logs (/var/log/serving/*).
4) Inform product owners and SRE lead with impact summary.
5) If Tier 2 persists 30m -> escalate to Tier 3 and open incident channel.
sections.heading: Sample automation webhook payload (JSON)

sections.body:
- Sev3 (Tier 1): Document incident summary and mitigation within 72 hours; no formal postmortem required unless customer impact > 1% of tenant base.
- Sev2 (Tier 2): Full postmortem required; include timeline, contributing factors, runbook gaps, and a remediation plan with owner and ETA.
- Sev1 (Tier 3): Immediate incident review within 48 hours; executive summary within 24 hours; full postmortem and blameless RCA with mitigation tickets entered in backlog within 7 days.
sections.heading: Incident Severity & Postmortem Requirements

sections.body:
- Required artifacts for postmortem: metrics dashboards (60m window pre/post), service logs filtered by trace-id, capacity-orchestrator decision log, error-budget-orchestrator webhook history, runbook-runner job records, and customer-facing status updates.
- Postmortem template fields: summary, impact, root cause analysis, timeline, detection & mitigation, why-not/why-did-not-mitigate, corrective actions, validation plan.
- Evidence retention: attach telemetry snapshots (raw) and logs to the postmortem page; store in confluence attachments for 90 days minimum.
sections.heading: Incident Review Standards (evidence checklist)

sections.body:
- Headroom policy: maintain 20% free capacity headroom at monthly 99th percentile traffic.
- Warm pools: maintain warm pool equal to 10% of steady-state replicas per region. Warm pool should be heterogenous across instance families to avoid simultaneous preemption.
- Autoscale limits: per-cluster max_scale set by cost tier; critical customers may have dedicated quotas.
- Preemption strategy: preemptible nodes used for background embeddings/low-priority traffic only; blocklist critical routes.
sections.heading: Capacity Planning Guidance (practical knobs)

sections.body:
- New model rollouts require a canary at 5% traffic for 24h and SLO observability. If canary impacts error budget burn > 2x baseline -> automatic rollback to previous version.
- Traffic shaping config stored in git (config repo: infra/traffic-shaping). Changes must pass CI sim tests.
sections.heading: Quality Gates & Rollouts

sections.body:
- Force-enable request coalescing for model family small-v2:
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane/api/v1/ops/coalesce -d '{"model_family":"small-v2","enable":true}'

- Trigger warm pool scale:
  rdctl cluster scale --region us-west2 --pool warm --delta 8 --reason "autofallback-tier2"
sections.heading: Playbook examples (CLI snippets)

sections.body:
- Detection & instrumentation: Observability team (primary), SRE (secondary).
- Automated fallback policies: SRE platform (primary), Serving runtime (secondary).
- Incident reviews & postmortems: SRE (primary), Product & Model Ops (reviewers).
sections.heading: Ownership & RACI (short)

sections.body:
- Runbooks and the capacity matrix are reviewed quarterly during the SRE reliability sync.
- Any automated action that performs a write to control-plane must have a two-person approval and an undo action defined.
sections.heading: Runbook Maintenance & Governance

sections.body:
- Quarterly chaos drills must include one scenario that validates the Tier 2 -> Tier 3 escalation path.
- Maintain a small suite of synthetic prompts per traffic class to measure p99 across model variants; baseline daily and surface regressions in the reliability dashboard.

Appendix A: Example metrics thresholds (for reference):
- p95 latency delta threshold: 1.15x baseline.
- queue_depth threshold per-replica: 250 concurrent in-flight tokens.
- KV cache hit-rate target: >= 75% under steady state.
- acceptable background job throttle: up to 90% reduction for low-priority embeddings.

Appendix B: Contact list (oncall rota):
- SRE primary: @sre-primary (pager duty)
- SRE secondary: @sre-secondary
- Platform lead: Marcus Lee
- Observability owner: Aisha Khan

For questions or proposed edits, open a pull request in infra/runbooks and tag the SRE reliability sync team.

payload.page_title: Scheduled Launch Capacity Safeguard & Post-Event Incident Template

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the SRE runbook and post-event incident template for scheduled, high-impact launches (marketing campaigns, partner integrations, large customer migrations). It covers pre-launch SLO/error-budget gating, capacity booking and reservations, operational tooling to validate run readiness, live-day safeguards and escalation paths, and a structured post-event incident review that combines reliability and business impact analysis. Use this when a launch is expected to increase QPS, unique session length, or bursty embedding/chat workloads > 5x baseline for more than 30 minutes.

Goals
-----
- Protect tiered SLOs while maximizing launch throughput and customer experience.
- Provide a repeatable pre-launch checklist that ties capacity pledges to error budget impact.
- Define live-day operational controls and automated throttles to prevent prolonged SLO burn.
- Standardize post-event incident reviews to capture capacity-forensics, model-quality regressions, and customer impact.

Scope and applicability
----------------------
- Applies to any coordinated external launch that will materially change request profile for hosted/Dedicated/private tenants.
- Not intended for routine deployments (< 10% traffic change) or internal A/B experiments below canary threshold.
- Cross-functional stakeholders: Product launch owner, Platform PM, SRE oncall, Model owner, Customer Success.

Pre-launch: decision criteria and gating
--------------------------------------
1) Risk assessment (owner: Product launch owner)
   - Expected peak multiplier (QPS): <value> (example: 6x baseline)
   - Session length shift: median token count change (e.g., +40%)
   - % traffic to new model variant / unvalidated prompt sets
   - Business-critical SLAs during launch window (e.g., 99.9% p50 latency; 99.5% p99)

2) Error-budget gating (owner: SRE lead)
   - For the service(s) affected, compute projected error budget burn over launch window using historical traffic and synthetic canaries.
   - Gating rule: proceed only if projected burn keeps the monthly error-budget consumption <= 60% unless an approved risk waiver is recorded.

3) Capacity reservation and verification (owner: Capacity/Infra)
   - Reserve headroom: min(reserved_gpu_tokens, projected_peak_tokens * 1.25).
   - Reserve a warm-pool of model hot-pools: N warm instances per region (recommended: baseline_hotpool * 0.5 rounded up).
   - Test plan: run synthetic workload with 1.0x, 2.5x, and expected_peak multiplier for at least 15m each and capture latency, KV cache hit rates, GPU memory pressure.

Example capacity reservation request (JSON)
| payload |
{
  "tenant": "marketing-campaign-aug25",
  "start": "2025-08-25T10:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-08-25T14:00:00Z",
  "peak_qps_estimate": "12000",
  "model_profile": "gpt-4x-infer-8k-quant",
  "hot_pool_instances": "12",
  "reserve_reason": "Public launch - campaign"
}

Operational tooling readiness checklist (owner: Platform/Tooling)
- Canary pipelines validated and toggles wired to traffic router (feature flags and routing policies).
- Telemetry retention for launch window: increase sampling to 100% for p95/p99 latency, error types, and tokenized model outputs for 24h post-launch.
- Synthetic canary jobs scheduled and healthy: canary-id, last-success timestamp.
- Automated throttle guard configured: error_budget_controller and traffic_shepherding policy attached to tenant.
- Model shadowing enabled where feasible: mirror 10–20% of traffic to new variant for quality checks without user-facing exposure.

Live-day runbook (owner: SRE oncall / Launch coordinator)
1) T-minus 60m: final readiness check
   - Confirm capacity reservations are active and warm pools at target.
   - Confirm datadog/telemetry dashboards show expected synthetic baseline.
2) T-minus 15m: enable expanded sampling and reduced aggregation windows (1m).
3) Launch start: staged ramp strategy (owner: Traffic Ops)
   - Stage 0 (0–5m): 5% traffic to new route. Verify latency p50/p95 and error-rate.
   - Stage 1 (5–20m): escalate to 25% if no SLO regression and error budget controller reports < 10% incremental burn.
   - Stage 2 (20–60m): escalate to 60–80% depending on business target.
   - Full ramp after 60m if all indicators green.
4) Real-time decision thresholds (automated & manual)
   - Auto-abort if p99 latency > baseline_p99 * 3 OR 5xx rate > baseline_5xx * 4 sustained for 3m.
   - Soft throttle if projected error budget burn rate exceeds 15% of remaining monthly budget within a 30m window.
   - Manual rollback if model-quality alerts detect >3% semantic regression on held prompt set or if customer-impacting errors observed for >10m.
5) Runbook escalation matrix
   - Pager: SRE oncall -> Platform lead -> Model owner -> Product launch owner.
   - Slack channel: #launches-live (pinned runbook link and incident playbook).

Telemetry and alerting specifics (owner: Observability)
- Required metrics (per-route and per-model): qps, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, token consumption, KV cache hit ratio, GPU memory pressure, scheduling latency.
- Alert types and thresholds:
| Metric | Alert | Priority | Action |
| p99 latency | p99 > baseline*2 for 5m | P1 | Auto-throttle + page SRE |
| 5xx rate | 5xx rate > baseline*3 for 3m | P1 | Auto-abort route + page SRE |
| error-budget-burn-rate | projected > 25% remaining in 1h | P2 | Throttle recommendations to traffic ops |
| model-quality-regression | semantic-score drop > 2% vs baseline set | P1 | Mirror traffic to fallback, page model owner |

Automated tooling snippets
- Example CLI to create a temporary traffic gate:
  redwood traffic create-gate --tenant marketing-campaign-aug25 --rule "percent=0.05,condition=metrics.p99<2000" --expires "2025-08-25T11:00:00Z"

- Example alert rule (YAML):
alert: Launch_P99_Throttling
expr: rate_latency_p99{route="marketing-campaign"}[5m] > baseline_p99 * 2
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: critical
annotations:
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/scheduled-launch-capacity-safeguard-and-postmortem-template-2025"

Live forensic capture guidance
- When an alert fires during a launch, immediately enable launch-mode traces for the affected route for at least 30m.
- Capture the following artifacts into the incident evidence bucket:
  - telemetry snapshot (1m resolution) for 30m before and after alert
  - sampled request/response payloads (redacted) for model-quality triage
  - GPU host metrics timeseries and scheduler logs
  - traffic router decisions (which nodes served which tokens)

Post-event incident review: template and required deliverables (owner: SRE/Incident Lead)
1) Executive summary (required)
   - One-paragraph summary: what happened, impact to customers, duration, and resolution.
2) Timeline of key events (required)
   - Structured timeline with timestamps, actor (automation or human), and decision.
3) Data and metrics appendix (required)
   - Include time-series charts and a table of key KPIs: baseline vs observed (QPS, p50/p95/p99, error-rate, token consumption, error budget consumed during window).
   - Example KPI table:
| KPI | Baseline | Peak during launch | % delta |
| QPS | 2,000 | 12,000 | 500% |
| p99 latency | 800ms | 2,400ms | 200% |
| monthly error budget used | 15% | +18% during window | n/a |
4) Root cause hypothesis and validation steps (required)
   - Enumerate hypotheses and evidence supporting or refuting each.
5) Operational actions taken (required)
   - Describe throttles, rollbacks, and config changes performed, with timestamps.
6) Business impact and follow-up (required)
   - Customer tickets created, credits issued, and cost delta for extra capacity.
7) Postmortem remediation plan (required)
   - Owners, priority, expected completion dates, and verification criteria.
   - Example remediation items: optimize KV cache warm-up to reduce cold-start p99 by 30% (owner: runtime team, due: 2025-09-30).
8) Lessons learned for future launches (required)
   - Concrete changes to the pre-launch checklist or tooling.

SLO & capacity change recommendations after a launch
- If launch burned >60% of monthly error budget, schedule a retrospective to reassess monthly SLOs and tenant admission policies.
- Consider temporary SLO relaxations with explicit customer communication only when: business critical and after approval by product + SRE director.
- Update capacity projection model inputs with real observed peak multiplier, session length shift, and quantized-model memory usage.

Ownership matrix (table)
| Role | Responsible | Contact / Pager |
| Product launch owner | Defines business targets and tolerances | product+launch@redwood.ai |
| SRE lead | Error-budget gating, runbook authority | sre-lead@redwood.ai |
| Capacity/Infra | Reservations and hot-pool ops | infra-capacity@redwood.ai |
| Observability | Dashboards, alerts, forensic snapshots | observability@redwood.ai |
| Model owner | Quality regression triage and rollback | model-owner@redwood.ai |

Approval and waiver process
- If pre-launch error-budget gating fails, a waiver may be requested with: justification, compensating controls, and explicit rollback criteria. Approval required from SRE director and Product VP. Record waiver in the launch ticket and link to this playbook.

Runbook maintenance and periodic exercises
- Runbook owner: SRE lead (review cadence: quarterly).
- Mandatory tabletop exercise: run a simulated launch twice per year with synthetic traffic and at least one cross-functional incident drill reproducing an auto-abort scenario.

Appendix: sample postmortem checklist (quick reference)
1) Link incident page and capture evidence artifacts.
2) Produce executive summary and timeline within 48 hours.
3) Complete remediation plan with owners within 7 days.
4) Publish postmortem and schedule follow-up verification within 30 days.

References and related pages
- Capacity reservation API (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/capacity-reservations-api
- Model quality evaluation guide: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails/model-quality-evals

Change history
- 2025-03-18: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-08-26: Added live forensic capture guidance and example CLI by Liam Chen.
- 2026-01-12: Minor edits to auto-abort thresholds and sampling recommendations by Sofia Martinez.

payload.page_title: Resilience Engineering Playbook: Model Inference Lifecycle

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook codifies how Redwood’s SRE and runtime teams operate across the model inference lifecycle to preserve customer-facing SLOs while managing cost and capacity. It ties SLO definitions and error budget policy to capacity planning, incident review standards, operational tooling, and concrete runbooks for common failure modes in model-serving (latency spikes, KV cache thrash, OOM cascades, multi-tenant headroom exhaustion).

Purpose and scope

- Purpose: Provide a single, actionable reference that converts SLOs and error budgets into deterministic operational behavior across detection, triage, remediation, and post-incident learning.
- Scope: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private (customer-managed) deployments for inference runtime. Focus is on production inference services (text generation, chat, embeddings).
- Out of scope: model training pipelines, data labeling workflows, and product UX changes.

Audience

- Primary: SREs, runtime engineers, oncall engineers, incident commanders.
- Secondary: Product owners, capacity planners, solutions engineers, security reviewers.

Key definitions

- SLO: The measurable objective we protect. Example: token-level latency p95 <= 350ms for text-generation API (regional).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; tracked as burn percentage over a rolling 28-day window unless otherwise specified.
- Headroom: Allocated margin above baseline expected utilization used for safe bursts and graceful degradation.
- Burn rate: Rate at which the error budget is consumed vs expected.

SLOs and error budget policy (operational rules)

1) Canonical SLOs (per-model-class, per-region):
   - Availability SLO (request success rate): 99.95% monthly (primary API route).
   - Latency SLOs (generation): p50 <= 50 ms, p95 <= 350 ms, p99 <= 900 ms (short requests, <= 512 tokens).
   - Embedding throughput SLO: 99% of embedding requests served within 200ms for batch size <= 4.

2) Measurement windows and backing metrics:
   - Primary window: rolling 28 days for contractual SLOs, 7 days for fast operational indicators.
   - Metrics: success_rate, latency_p50/p95/p99, token_throughput, cpu_gpu_utilization, kv_cache_hit_rate, queue_depth.

3) Error budget burn policy (automated responses):
   - Low burn (0–10% of budget consumed/week): normal ops.
   - Moderate burn (10–40%/week): investigate trends, run additional traffic mirroring for suspected regressions, increase sampling of slow traces.
   - High burn (40–100%/week): engage oncall escalation, freeze risky rollouts, reduce non-essential background jobs, enable pre-configured capacity hedges.
   - Critical burn (>100% in 24h or >80% week-to-date): declare SLO incident and execute emergency capacity borrowing and graceful degradation policies.

4) Rollout constraints tied to budget: Any candidate runtime change that would risk increasing weekly burn by >10% requires gating via canary with traffic shadowing and rollback window of 60 minutes at the first confirmed p95 regression.

Capacity planning and headroom policy

- Forecast cadence: weekly demand profile refresh for 4-week runway; quarterly capacity planning for 12-month procurement needs.
- Headroom targets (multi-tenant pools): maintain 25% reserved compute headroom for burst absorption for tier-1 customers, 15% for tier-2. Adjust by historic burst factor per model family.
- Elastic reservoir: hold a small pool of ephemeral capacity controlled by SRE for emergency scaling (default reserve = 5% of active fleet per region).
- Preemption and soft-eviction rules:
   1. Non-critical batch jobs (indexing, offline evals) are preempted first.
   2. Dedicated+Private tenant SLAs honored — only hosted best-effort workloads preempted.
   3. When sustained CPU/GPU utilization > 85% for > 10 minutes, trigger autoscale candidate and notify oncall.

Reliability initiatives and exercises

- Quarterly chaos scenarios focusing on: cross-region failover, model hotpatch rollback, KV cache cold-start, and multi-tenant noisy neighbor.
- Pre-release resilience checklist for new model onboarding: warm-pool verification, KV cache sizing, deterministic latency budget tests, and synthetic workload run.
- Resilience radar: maintain a public team board of top-10 failure modes with mitigation status and owners.

Incident review standards and evidence requirements

- Post-incident timeline: initial incident report within 2 hours, draft post-incident review (PIR) within 72 hours, final PIR and action items tracked within 14 days.
- Required evidence for an incident review (minimum):
  - Full timeline of events with UTC timestamps.
  - Alert rules that fired, metric dashboards snapshot (pre/post), and trace samples for slow requests.
  - Heap/GC logs, GPU memory charts, CVM autoscaler events if involved.
  - Runbook steps taken and who executed them.
  - Root-cause hypothesis, confidence level, and planned mitigations.
- PIR structure (template):
  1) Summary and impact (customers, SLO delta).
  2) Timeline.
  3) Root cause & evidence.
  4) Corrective actions (short-term & long-term).
  5) Action owners and due dates.
  6) Post-deployment verification plan.

Operational tooling and automation patterns

- Tooling inventory (recommended):
  - Telemetry: Prometheus (metrics), Tempo (traces), Loki (logs).
  - Alerting: Alertmanager with SLO-linked routing.
  - Runbook automation: Runbook-runner + annotated playbooks in Confluence.
  - Capacity & autoscale control plane: Fleet-orchestrator (internal service), with debounce and safety gates.
  - Canary/shadowing: Traffic-mirroring service integrated with observability.

- Automation patterns to reduce toil:
  1. SLO-driven auto-throttles: when p95 latency > threshold for 5m and error budget burn accelerating, automatically lower non-critical concurrency by 30%.
  2. One-click rollback: policy that ties canary samples to an automated rollback pipeline if latency regressions exceed defined thresholds.
  3. Evidence snapshot automation: on alert, capture dashboard snapshots + trace samples, attach to incident channel.

Runbooks (quick reference)

A) Hotpath triage: sudden latency spike for text-generation route (priority oncall)

1) Initial verification (0–5 minutes):
   - Confirm alert: check Alertmanager and p95 metric.
   - Get impact snapshot: number of affected tokens/minute, per-region spread, any customer escalations.
   - Post status to incident channel with short summary and assign IC.

2) Rapid containment (5–20 minutes):
   - If CPU/GPU utilization > 90%: enable emergency capacity pool (invoke fleet-orchestrator: /api/v1/reserve?pool=emergency&percent=5).
   - If KV cache hit rate dropped > 20%: increase cache size or fall back to cold-path mode with aggressive batching.
   - If model variant rollout ongoing: pause rollout and divert traffic to previous stable variant.

3) Root cause probing (20–60 minutes):
   - Capture representative trace for slow request.
   - Check kernel-level OOMs, CUDA errors in GPU logs, and RPC latency between inference pods and KV store.
   - Run canary traffic to validate mitigation before scaled rollback.

4) Recover and verify (60+ minutes):
   - Confirm p95 back within SLO for two consecutive 5-minute windows.
   - Begin post-incident evidence collection and set PIR timeline.

B) Coldpath remediation: progressive error-rate increase in embedding route (oncall + platform)

1) Verify incidence and scope: compare baseline embedding throughput, queue length, and worker crash logs.
2) Reduce ingestion rate (traffic shaping) for low-priority tenants via rate-limiter service.
3) Redeploy embedding worker with increased batch buffer size and monitor queue drain.

Escalation matrix and ownership

- Tier 1 oncall: initial triage, containment, and short-term mitigations.
- Tier 2: runtime engineers for kernel/quantization issues, model owners for model-level regression investigations.
- SRE Pager lead: incident command if error budget critical or customer-impacting.

Post-incident actions and SLO feedback loop

- For any incident that consumes > 25% of the monthly error budget: require a follow-up capacity plan that includes headroom changes or autoscale parameter adjustments.
- Action item categories: observability gaps, capacity changes, code/regression fixes, runbook updates, and guardrail improvements. Each action must have an owner and a visible target date in the team board.

Sample alert thresholds and response mapping (reference)

| Alert name | Trigger (duration) | Immediate response | Owner |
| Token-latency-p95-high | p95 > 350ms (5m) | Hotpath triage | Oncall Tier 1 |
| Success-rate-drop | success_rate < 99.90% (10m) | Start incident, engage SRE lead | Pager Lead |
| KV-cache-cold | kv_cache_hit_rate < 60% (10m) | Increase cache; enable cold-path | Runtime Team |
| GPU-mem-OOM | OOM count > 1 node (2m) | Isolate node; reassign pods | Infra/SRE |

Autoscaler sample policy (JSON snippet)

payload.page_title: Service Dependency SLO Federation Guide

sections.body: This guide defines a practical model for federating SLOs, error budgets, and capacity decisions across service dependency graphs. It describes how owner teams should map downstream SLOs to upstream commitments, implement propagation rules, and run coordinated incident reviews when cross-service error budgets are consumed. The goal is predictable customer experience, fair capacity allocation, and clear oncall responsibilities during multi-service degradation.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- SREs and service owners responsible for production SLOs and capacity planning
- Platform/product engineers designing cross-service SLAs
- Incident commanders coordinating multi-team responses
sections.heading: Intended audience

sections.body:
- Goals:
  1) Provide a repeatable, automatable process to compute and enforce propagated SLO obligations when a dependent service degrades.
  2) Ensure error budget transparency so consumer teams can make reliable routing and fallback choices.
  3) Enable capacity decisions (reserve, scale, shed) that respect both upstream and downstream priorities.
- Non-goals:
  - This guide does not define customer-facing legal SLAs (commercial contracts live in finance-and-legal).
  - It does not replace per-service SLO design; it augments SLOs with dependency-aware policies.
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body:
- Provider service: a service that offers functionality consumed by one or more consumer services.
- Consumer service: a service that depends on providers to deliver its SLOs.
- Federated SLO: the effective commitment a provider offers to a particular consumer, derived from the provider's global SLO but adjusted by capacity, tenancy, and priority.
- Error budget anchoring: the policy that determines how a consumer's error budget burn is attributed to provider failures versus local issues.
sections.heading: Scope and definitions

sections.body:
- Principle 1: Single source of truth for SLO status — provider must publish a machine-readable SLO status endpoint and per-consumer adjusted commitments.
- Principle 2: Minimally invasive propagation — avoid over-committing providers by limiting propagated obligations to what capacity and tenancy allow.
- Principle 3: Observable attribution — burn attribution must be auditable in post-incident reviews.
- Principle 4: Fairness and tiering — prioritize mission-critical tenants with explicit quotas and documented trade-offs.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1) Each provider maintains:
   - Global SLOs (availability, p99 latency, correctness where applicable).
   - Tenant slice config: reservations, limits, and soft-guarantee tiers (gold/silver/bulk).
   - A published "federation manifest" (JSON) listing per-consumer adjusted SLOs and capacity windows.
2) Each consumer references provider manifests during admission and can implement fallback/graded degradation based on the manifest.
3) Automation periodically reconciles manifests and computes propagated budgets at a rolling 24h, 7d, and 28d granularity.
sections.heading: SLO mapping and federation model (high level)

sections.body:
manifest_version: v1
provider: payments-service
published_at: 2026-09-01T08:00:00Z
consumer_slices:
  - consumer: checkout-api
    tier: gold
    adjusted_slos:
      availability: "99.95% / 28d"
      p99_latency: "250ms / 28d"
  - consumer: analytics-ingest
    tier: silver
    adjusted_slos:
      availability: "99.5% / 28d"
      p99_latency: "500ms / 28d"

Note: manifests must be machine-readable JSON in our implementation; YAML above is for human readability.
sections.heading: Example federation manifest (illustrative YAML block)

sections.body:
- When provider global SLO burn exceeds 20% for the rolling 28-day window, provider must flag all consumer manifests with a degradation tag and a projected additional burn estimate.
- Consumers may use the presence of a degradation tag to trigger local fallbacks or routing to alternate providers.
- If a provider's 28d burn > 50% and projections indicate continued burn, consumers must initiate emergency throttles for non-critical traffic according to their own tiering policy.
sections.heading: Propagation rules (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- Provider teams should expose three capacity knobs:
  a) Reservation capacity: guaranteed token count for a tenant tier (measured in qps or GPU minutes).
  b) Elastic headroom: capacity available for burst but preemptible.
  c) Grace pool: small shared buffer for black-swan events.
- Admission controller responsibilities (implementation checklist):
  1) Read provider manifest at admission time.
  2) Verify reservation/elastic headroom availability for requested QPS/keys.
  3) Apply conservative smoothing to avoid headroom exhaustion (e.g., 80% overcommit cap).
  4) Emit admission telemetry tagging requests with resolved slice, reservation id, and manifest version.

Runbook: consumer-side degradation response (quick play):
1) Detection:
   - Alert: consumer p99 latency > configured threshold for 10m AND error rate increase > 3x baseline.
   - Check provider manifest status endpoint for degradation tag and projected burn.
2) Triage:
   - Confirm whether errors are attributable to provider (use correlated traces and dependency tags).
   - If provider manifests degradation, escalate to provider oncall per oncall handoff table.
3) Mitigation:
   - If consumer is gold: enable degraded-mode that retries with exponential backoff and reduced payloads; enable alternate provider routing if available.
   - If consumer is silver/bulk: begin shedding non-essential endpoints and throttle background jobs.
4) Communicate:
   - Post to incident bridge with manifest snapshot and admission telemetry window.
   - Update customer facing status page if customer-impacting.
5) Recovery and roll-forward:
   - Monitor provider manifest for cleared degradation tag and confirm error budget recovery projections before restoring full traffic.

Provider-side runbook: admission and emergency eviction template:
1) Pre-incident:
   - Maintain current manifests and publish every 4h or after capacity changes.
   - Run daily reconciliation job that checks reservations vs observed consumption.
2) Emergency path when headroom < 5%:
   - Throttle elastic slices in priority order: bulk -> silver -> gold-protected until headroom stabilizes.
   - If throttling still insufficient, activate graceful degradation routes (e.g., degrade quality of responses, turn off non-essential features).
3) Incident closure:
   - Publish a manifest revision showing restored capacities and add event tags for forensics.
sections.heading: Capacity allocation and admission controls

sections.body:
- Scope determination: identify the set of consumers impacted by provider burn and map error-budget attribution for each (percent of consumer burn attributable to provider vs local issues).
- Evidence artifacts (required):
  - Provider manifest snapshots for the incident window (machine-readable).
  - Admission telemetry (sampled request traces labeled with slice/reservation id).
  - Capacity telemetry: reservations vs observed usage, GPU/machine level metrics, headroom events.
  - Error budget delta timeline for provider and top 10 consumers.
- Review cadence: for any incident where aggregated cross-consumer burn > 5% of provider 28d budget, run a federated postmortem with provider, top-affected consumers, and product representatives.
- Postmortem outputs required:
  1) Root cause with reproducible hypothesis and evidence links.
  2) Clear action owners for manifest changes, capacity adjustments, and platform automation improvements.
  3) SLO recalibration recommendations if original SLOs were misaligned with observed behavior.

Operational tooling: required telemetry and dashboards (minimum viable):
- Provider manifests: searchable index (time-travel capability) and current state API.
- Cross-service SLO matrix dashboard: rows=consumers, cols=provider adjusted SLOs, colored by current burn rate.
- Admission trace explorer: sample traces with slice/reservation id and manifest version.
- Error budget scatter: consumer vs provider attribution over rolling 7d window.
- Automation hooks: webhooks when provider burn crosses thresholds (20%, 50%) to automatically create incident bridges and notify consumers.
sections.heading: Incident review standards for federated incidents

sections.body:
- metric_name | description | cardinality | retention
- provider_slo_burn_percent | provider rolling burn percent (28d) | per-provider | 90d
- manifest_version | manifest id | per-provider | 365d
- admission_slice_id | id for reservation slice | per-request sampled | 14d
- per_consumer_attributed_burn | percent of consumer burn attributed to provider | per-consumer per-provider | 90d
sections.heading: Telemetry schema (compact table)

sections.body:
- manifest publish (curl):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $PUBLISH_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://manifests.internal.redwood/api/v1/publish -d @manifest.json

- quick reconciliation (psuedo-command):
  reconcile-manifests --since 24h --emit-alert-if-headroom-lt=0.05 --output=reports/$(date +%F)-reconcile.json
sections.heading: Automation examples (snippets)

sections.body:
- For a provider serving diverse tenants, reserve capacity to cover 80% of steady-state demand for gold slices, 60% for silver, and share remaining headroom as elastic.
- Map error budget burn to $cost impact: compute expected token costs during projected burn windows; use this to prioritize reserved purchases or temporary cloud pool increases.
- Run quarterly capacity drills that simulate 2x traffic from top-3 consumers and verify admission and throttling automation.
sections.heading: Capacity planning guidance and SLO budgeting heuristics

sections.body:
- Provider team must:
  - Publish initial federation manifest and implement manifest endpoint (owner: provider-sre).
  - Wire admission controller to read manifests and emit admission telemetry (owner: platform-team).
  - Add manifest time-travel to observability index (owner: observability).
- Consumer team must:
  - Integrate manifest consumption into admission flow and implement graceful degradation strategies (owner: consumer-sre).
  - Add manifest snapshot to incident runbooks and postmortem evidence (owner: consumer-sre).
- Rollout steps (recommended):
  1) Pilot with 2 provider-consumer pairs for 4 weeks.
  2) Run tabletop exercises simulating manifest-driven throttles.
  3) Enable automated webhooks for 20% burn threshold.
  4) Expand to top-20 services over next quarter.
sections.heading: Ownership and rollout checklist

sections.body:
- Q: What if a provider refuses to publish manifests?
  A: Escalate to platform leadership; until manifest support exists, consumers must use conservative local fallbacks and treat provider as best-effort.
- Q: How do we handle multi-hop dependencies?
  A: Propagate manifests transitively but limit transitive adjustments to a single hop for operational simplicity; deeper transitive impacts must be handled during incident reviews.

Template: minimal manifest JSON (single-line for copy/paste):
{"manifest_version":"v1","provider":"example-service","published_at":"2026-11-02T12:00:00Z","consumer_slices":[{"consumer":"example-consumer","tier":"gold","adjusted_slos":{"availability":"99.95%/28d","p99_latency":"200ms/28d"}}]}

Appendix: links and references:
- See: eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025 for capacity policy foundations.
- See: eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025 for telemetry pipeline requirements.

This guide is expected to evolve; submit improvements via the SRE documentation PR process and reference the related_pages above for coordination.

payload.page_title: Regional Failover Automation Upgrade — Program Overview (Reliability Program 2026)

sections.body:
Redwood Inference is upgrading its regional failover automation as part of the 2026 Reliability Program (SLO maturity, incident reduction, and graceful degradation).

Today, region failover is a mix of manual steps and partially automated routing policies. Trigger signals are frequently noisy (false positives), slow to confirm true regional impairment, and hard to validate safely. During real incidents, this increases customer-visible errors, creates capacity cascades, and increases on-call cognitive load.

This initiative standardizes trigger signal hierarchy, adds deterministic policy evaluation and rollback guardrails, improves observability, and validates the end-to-end system via controlled failover tests (“game days”) for Hosted API and Dedicated.

---
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
When a region is impaired (network reachability, elevated 5xx, tail latency blowups, or capacity exhaustion), customers experience:
- Elevated error rate (timeouts/5xx) and increased tail latency
- Streaming disconnects/retries during redirects
- Slower time-to-mitigate due to manual verification and decisioning
- Secondary impact from overload/thundering herd when traffic shifts unevenly
sections.heading: Customer impact we are addressing

sections.body:
1) **Noisy triggers and inconsistent prioritization**
- Multiple signal sources exist (gateway, runtime, network, fleet capacity), but the decision logic is inconsistent across routes and environments.
- Alerts are not always correlated to a regional impairment; local service issues can look like regional failures.

2) **Detection is slow and hard to validate**
- On-call often needs to validate impairment manually across dashboards.
- There is no reliable “region health” aggregation service acting as a single source of truth.

3) **Automation guardrails are incomplete**
- Partial automation can flip routing policies without consistent anti-flap protections.
- Rollback semantics are not standardized; oscillation risk increases under intermittent impairment.

4) **Limited game day coverage**
- Testing is ad hoc and not repeatable.
- There is no consistent, measurable success criteria (failover time, error budget burn, overload behavior).

---
sections.heading: Current-state gaps

sections.body:
- **Reduce customer-visible impact** during regional impairments by shrinking detection + failover time and preventing cascading overload.
- **Standardize failover trigger hierarchy** and rollback behavior across Hosted API and Dedicated.
- **Prove reliability via controlled tests** with repeatable, low-blast-radius game days in staging and production.
- **Improve observability** so on-call can distinguish region-level impairment vs. service-level/local failures in minutes.
sections.heading: Primary goals

sections.body:
These are program-level targets; exact thresholds are defined in the SLO doc and alert specs.
- **Time to detect (TTD):** reduce by 50% vs. baseline for regional impairment scenarios
- **Time to fail over (TTFO):** achieve consistent automated failover within a defined window for validated impairments (target range: low single-digit minutes, dependent on DNS/traffic steering constraints)
- **Availability outcome:** reduce multi-region availability error budget burn during regional incidents
- **False positives:** materially reduce paging/automation actions caused by non-regional issues (track “automation action rate” vs. confirmed incidents)
- **No oscillation:** enforce anti-flap limits (max policy flips per tenant per hour; hold-down timers) with auditability

---
sections.heading: Success metrics (initial targets)

sections.body:
- Multi-cloud migration or changing cloud providers
- Rewriting the core serving runtime
- Changing customer contracts/SLA language (tracked separately)
- Fully bespoke automation for Private deployments (we will provide guidance and recommended patterns)

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Hosted API + Dedicated: multi-region routing and policy evaluation
- Region health aggregation (reachability, latency/error burn, capacity, network reachability) with caching/TTL
- Failover automation controller with deterministic evaluation, dry-run mode, approval hooks (where required), and rollback guardrails
- Circuit breakers/load shedding behavior during failover to avoid thundering herd
- Dashboards, alerts, and on-call runbooks
- Incident-bot/status comms support (annotations, summaries, operator-friendly audit trails)
- Controlled failover tests in staging and production with explicit success criteria and rollback conditions
sections.heading: In-scope

sections.body:
- Private deployments: documentation + recommended patterns, explicit boundaries on what Redwood supports

---
sections.heading: Adjacent / partial

sections.body:
- **Executive sponsor:** Neha Kapoor (VP Infrastructure & Reliability)
- **Reliability program lead:** Sean Gallagher (Director SRE)
- **Delivery lead:** Rafael Mendes (SRE Manager)
- **Architecture lead:** Miles Thornton (Staff SRE)
sections.heading: Program leadership

sections.body:

- **Routing policy tech lead:** Ravi Menon

sections.heading: Core engineering partners

sections.body:
- Product (Console messaging + customer expectations): Nikhil Sharma (Hosted), Lauren Bishop (Dedicated)
- Support/CS comms and escalations: Dev Patel (Support escalation owner)

---
sections.heading: Cross-functional

sections.body:
1) **Signal pipeline** collects regional signals:
- Network reachability (synthetic probes + provider symptoms)
- Error-rate burn (5xx/timeout burn against SLO)
- Tail latency burn (p95/p99 burn vs SLO thresholds)
- Capacity headroom + backpressure signals (fleet)

2) **Region Health Service** aggregates signals into a consistent regional health view:
- Normalizes inputs, applies TTL/jitter, emits “region health state” and evidence

3) **Policy Engine** evaluates deterministic trigger hierarchy:
- Applies signal priority, corroboration rules, dampening, and hold-down timers

4) **Failover Controller** executes safe routing changes (or recommends via dry-run):
- Produces a decision and optionally executes policy flips
- Enforces per-tenant safety limits and anti-flap
- Emits structured audit events and annotations

5) **Data plane safeguards** reduce amplification during failover:
- Gateway circuit breaker tuning, retries/timeouts, standardized overload responses (Retry-After)
- Streaming reconnect behavior improvements on redirect

---
sections.heading: High-level architecture (described)

sections.body:
- On-call receives signal(s) (often noisy)
- Manual cross-check across dashboards and provider status
- Manual or semi-automated routing policy changes
- Ad hoc rollback and post-event validation
sections.heading: Current-state (simplified)

sections.body:
- Signals corroborate; region health summarizes impairment state with evidence
- Policy engine evaluates deterministic trigger hierarchy
- Controller runs in **dry-run** by default (initial rollout), posting recommended actions + confidence/evidence
- With guardrails satisfied (and optional approvals), controller executes automated failover
- Anti-flap + rollback semantics prevent oscillation
- Audit log + dashboard annotations provide a clear timeline

---
sections.heading: Target-state workflow (simplified)

sections.body:
The authoritative policy is defined in ADR-042; the summary below exists to align stakeholders.

**Principle:** Prefer signals that indicate true inability to serve traffic over symptoms that could be local or transient.
sections.heading: Trigger hierarchy (program-level)

sections.body:
1) **Reachability loss** (authoritative; cross-region probes + edge reachability)
2) **5xx/timeout burn rate** (SLO burn; corroborated)
3) **Tail latency burn** (p95/p99; corroborated)
4) **Capacity exhaustion / headroom collapse** (used for gating failover and for pre-failover load shedding)
sections.heading: Proposed priority order (summary)

sections.body:
- Dampening windows to avoid reacting to brief blips
- Hold-down timers to avoid oscillation
- Corroboration requirement for symptom-based triggers
- Per-tenant blast-radius constraints and max flips per hour

---
sections.heading: Guardrails (summary)

sections.body:
The authoritative policy is defined in ADR-043; summary below:
- Rollback is not simply “signals look better.”
- Rollback requires passing a stability window and respecting hold-down timers.
- Automation must record an audit event for every recommend/execute/rollback action, including evidence signals.
- Anti-flap rate limits apply to both failover and rollback.

---
sections.heading: Rollback semantics (program-level)

sections.body:
The goal is to make ownership boundaries explicit so incidents do not stall on “who owns the knob.”

| Area | Component / Service | Primary owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signals | perf-canary cross-region probes | Victor Alvarez (Network) | Publishes reachability + latency probes to ingestion stream |
| Signals | fleet headroom / capacity metrics | Vanessa Ortiz (Fleet/Capacity) | Defines headroom thresholds used for routing gates |
| Aggregation | Region Health Service | Ethan Park (Control Plane) | Source of truth for regional health state; TTL + jitter |
| Decisioning | Routing policy engine | Ravi Menon (Routing) / Jordan Lee (Policy engine) | Deterministic evaluation, hierarchy, corroboration, timers |
| Execution | Failover automation controller | Miles Thornton (SRE) / Benji Okafor (Guardrails) | Dry-run, approvals, audit trail, anti-flap, per-tenant limits |
| Data plane | API gateway circuit breakers | Peter Holtz (Overload) | Retries/timeouts, overload responses (Retry-After) |
| Data plane | Streaming redirect/reconnect behavior | Vikram Singh (Data plane) | Idempotency and reconnect guidance |
| Observability | Dashboards/alerts | Allison Grant / Sergio Costa | Burn-rate alerts, failover panels, annotations |
| Tooling | incident-bot summaries | Devon Price | Automated summaries + links posted to incident channels |
| Ops | Runbooks + paging hygiene | Tomáš Novák | Ensures on-call procedures match automation behavior |

---

sections.body: This is a planning view; execution is tracked in Linear (ENG-2411 umbrella).

sections.body:

sections.heading: Phase 5 — Rollout + hardening (Weeks 10–12+)
