payload.page_title: SLOs + Oncall Escalation & Capacity Trigger Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines how SRE measures and enforces service-level objectives (SLOs), links SLO consumption to oncall escalation, and defines capacity triggers that must surface to product and infra teams. It contains concrete burn-rate thresholds, alert-to-action mappings, capacity-forecast triggers, and reproducible escalation templates (PagerDuty, Slack, email). Use this as the canonical reference for SRE-led operational responses related to SLO and capacity risk.

Scope

- Applies to all customer-facing Redwood services in the Hosted and Dedicated fleets (examples: ingest-api, model-router, generation-service, embeddings-service).
- Not intended for internal tooling without customer impact (see internal tooling runbooks).

Definitions

- SLO: The measurable target for a service (e.g., availability, latency).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (time or request-weighted over a rolling window).
- Burn rate: Ratio of error budget used per unit time relative to the nominal rate.
- Alert: A signal from monitoring indicating metric degradation.
- Page: Phone/SMS/Push using PagerDuty (critical paging).

Baseline SLOs (examples)

- ingest-api: Availability SLO 99.9% (monthly rolling window). Monthly error budget ≈ 0.1% of minutes (~43.2 minutes for a 30-day month).
- model-router: P95 response latency SLO < 300ms (30-day window, request-weighted).
- generation-service: Availability SLO 99.5% (monthly) for non-billing customers, 99.9% for enterprise SLA customers.

Measurement & Instrumentation Requirements

- SLO signal sources: production Prometheus/Grafana metrics for request_success_count and request_total; synthetic transactions for end-to-end availability; tracing-derived latency histograms.
- SLO calculation frequency: 1 minute rollup, stored as 1-minute SLO windows and aggregated to 1h/24h/30d views.
- Recording rule examples (PromQL):
  - availability_ratio = sum(rate(request_success_count[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total[5m]))
  - p95_latency_ms = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) * 1000
- Dashboarding: Every SLO must have a dedicated Grafana panel (30d, 7d, 1d) and an SLO summary panel with error budget remaining.

Error Budget Burn Policy (Actions mapped to burn rate)

- Low burn (burn rate < 2): Monitor, auto-triage if there is a correlated alert. No paging.
- Elevated (2 <= burn rate < 5 for > 30m): SRE oncall receives an informational notification (PagerDuty non-critical, Slack #incidents-monitoring). Owner review required within 30 minutes.
- Critical (burn rate >= 5 for > 15m): Trigger a critical page to SRE primary and service owner. Immediate mitigation required (see runbook).
- Sustained depletion (error budget consumed >= 50% in < 24h): Schedule a short-term remediation meeting (within 4 hours) with product and infra stakeholders; consider temporary traffic shaping or feature throttles.
- Exhausted (0% remaining): Enterprise SLA customers: automatic failover to backup model variant or Dedicated capacity slot if configured; notify customer-facing teams and initiate postmortem. For non-SLA: reduce non-critical features, enable lower-cost fallbacks per routing policy.

Burn rate detection rules (examples)

- Burn rate calculation: (error_budget_used in last 1h) / (error_budget_allowed_per_hour).
- Prometheus alert snippets (illustrative):
  - name: ErrorBudgetCritical
    expr: (sum(increase(request_failed_total[1h])) / sum(increase(request_total[1h]))) / (1 - SLO_target) > 5
    for: 15m
  - name: ErrorBudgetElevated
    expr: (sum(increase(request_failed_total[30m])) / sum(increase(request_total[30m]))) / (1 - SLO_target) > 2
    for: 30m

Oncall Integration and Escalation Flow

1) Detection
  - Metric alert or synthetic ping fails; alert routes to the service-specific Grafana/Atlas alerting rule.
2) Triage (automated)
  - Alert enrichment adds recent deploys, active incidents, and top error traces (via tracing link).
  - The alert runbook is attached to the PagerDuty incident.
3) Preliminary human triage (SRE first responder)
  - Verify signal validity (check for noisy exporters, pagination/rollups).
  - If false positive, close and annotate the alert.
  - If valid, execute the service-specific SLO runbook steps (see Runbook section).
4) Escalation
  - If critical burn threshold reached, page SRE primary + service owner.
  - After 10 minutes with no acknowledgement, escalate to SRE secondary and engineering manager.
  - After 30 minutes, page on-call for product and infra leads.

PagerDuty page template (critical)

- Title: [CRITICAL] {service} SLO burn-rate {burn_rate}x — {short symptom}
- Body:
  Service: {service}
  SLO: {slo_name} ({slo_target})
  Current burn rate: {burn_rate} (over {window})
  Error budget remaining: {percent}%
  Top alert: {alert_name}
  Immediate ask: Join {#incidents-{service}} or dial {conference_link} and follow runbook: {runbook_link}
  Links: Grafana panel | Traces | Recent deploys | Capacity dashboard

Slack escalation template (when alert is non-critical)

- Channel: #incidents-{service} (or #incidents-monitoring for cross-service)
- Message: :warning: {service} elevated SLO burn ({burn_rate}x). Please review dashboard: {grafana_link}. If you are oncall owner, ping @sre-oncall.

Runbook: High SLO Burn (quick checklist)

1) Identify failure mode:
  - Check recent deploys: git rev, image tag, helm release (CI/CD UI link).
  - Query top error codes and request paths (PromQL / traces).
  - Check external dependencies (upstream models, third-party APIs).
2) Triage mitigation (pick first available):
  - Rollback recent deploy to last-known-good (if deploy correlates with onset).
  - Increase capacity (scale replica count or spin a dedicated capacity slot for enterprise tenants).
  - Apply traffic shaping: reduce non-critical feature rollout percentages, apply rate-limits to noisy clients.
  - Enable cached responses / prefix-KV cache warmup for repetitive tokens.
3) Post-mitigation verification:
  - Observe error rate drop for 15 minutes and confirm burn rate has fallen below 2x before de-escalating.
4) Document actions in the PagerDuty incident and mark for postmortem if error budget > 50% consumed or customer impact occurred.

Capacity Triggers and Forecasting

- Daily capacity health check: SRE runs an automated job that reports per-service utilization (GPU vCPU, active model sessions, memory, queue length) and projects 7/30-day consumption based on trailing 7-day load.
- Thresholds that must create immediate tickets:
  - Expected 7-day demand growth > 80% of available spare capacity for a model family.
  - Queue length > 2x median and P95 latency for that queue crosses SLO by > 30%.
  - Sustained CPU/GPU utilization > 85% for > 6 hours for Dedicated pools.
- Decision actions when thresholds hit:
  - <2 weeks runway: open an urgent capacity request to Infra (cc product, sales if enterprise customers impacted).
  - <72 hours runway: execute rapid provisioning play (activate burst capacity, spin reserved nodes in cloud, or move lower-priority workloads to deferred buckets).

Capacity request template (ticket fields)

- Service: {service}
- Model family: {model}
- Reason: {sudden spike | sustained growth | scheduled event}
- Current utilization: {gpu%, vcpu%}
- Runway: {hours/days}
- Proposed mitigation: {burst, reserve, throttle}
- Owners: {service_owner, infra_owner}

Operational Tooling & Integrations

- PagerDuty: primary paging channel; SRE policy configured for burn-rate alerts and capacity runouts.
- Grafana: SLO dashboards with alert links and runbook attachments.
- BigQuery / DataLake: long-term SLO history and incident annotation store (used for retros).
- Slack: #incidents-{service}, #sre-ops, #capacity-planning; automated postings include links to dashboards and playbooks.
- Runbook storage: Confluence canonical page link included in all alerts; service runbooks must be kept under /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/{service_name}-runbook.

Incident Review & Postmortem Standards (minimum requirements)

- When required: Any incident where error budget > 50% consumed, outage > 15 minutes for customers, or enterprise SLA customers affected.
- Template must include: timeline (UTC), detection method, root cause analysis, action items (owner + due date), mea culpa communications, and a clear signal-to-prevent recurrence (test/monitoring/deployment change).
- Severity classification: Sev1 (customer-facing outage), Sev2 (partial impact / high degradation), Sev3 (minor). Each Sev1/Sev2 must have a postmortem published within 7 business days.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Assemble timeline from automated logs/traces (UTC).
2) Run RCA: code/regression, capacity, dependency, config, data, external.
3) Identify permanent fixes and add tests/alerts to prevent regression.
4) Assign owners and target dates (no more than 4 weeks for high priority fixes).

Ownership and RACI (summary)

- SRE: metrics, burn-rate alerts, first-line mitigation, capacity forecasts.
- Service Owner (product/engineering): fix root cause, roll forward or rollback decisions, remediation code changes.
- Infra: provisioning, cluster-level scaling, reserve capacity operations.
- Customer Success / Sales: customer comms for SLA-impacting incidents.

Appendix A — Useful PromQL snippets

- Error rate over 1h: sum(increase(request_failed_total[1h])) / sum(increase(request_total[1h]))
- Error budget remaining (approx): 1 - avg_over_time(error_rate[30d]) / (1 - slo_target)

Appendix B — Quick links and contacts

- SLO dashboards: {grafana-slo-home}
- Capacity dashboard: {grafana-capacity}
- PagerDuty SRE escalation policy: {pagerduty-policy-link}
- Oncall rotation: {sre-oncall-rotation}
- Contact list: SRE leads (Maya Chen), Infra lead (Arjun Patel), Product ops (Lena Morales)

Change log

- 2025-11-02: Created by Maya Chen (initial published playbook).
- 2025-12-12: Added capacity-runway thresholds and ticket template (reviewers: Arjun Patel).
- 2026-01-15: Updated burn-rate thresholds and automated paging policy; clarified enterprise SLA failover steps (reviewers: Lena Morales, Diego Alvarez).

End of document

payload.page_title: Release Notes: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds + Predictive Mode

sections.body:
h1. Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds + Predictive Mode (GA)

*Release date:* 2025-09-12

This release adds customer-configurable autoscaling guardrails for *Redwood Dedicated* deployments (hard *min/max capacity bounds*) and an optional *Predictive* mode that pre-scales for known traffic ramps while preserving safety invariants and auditability.

h2. What changed

h3. 1) Customer-configurable autoscaling bounds (hard enforcement)

You can now set *hard* per-deployment capacity bounds:

* *Min capacity* (baseline): autoscaler will not scale below this value.
* *Max capacity* (ceiling): autoscaler will not scale above this value.

Bounds are enforced in the autoscaler loop via deterministic clamping:

* We compute *requested desired capacity* (from reactive + optional predictive inputs).
* We compute *bounded desired capacity* = clamp(requested_desired, min, max).
* We persist/emit a reasoned decision record (requested vs bounded and why).

h3. 2) Predictive mode (optional, bounded, with reactive override)

When enabled, Predictive mode biases scale decisions using forecasted demand signals (e.g., time-of-day patterns and historical workload characteristics). Predictive mode is designed as a *bias*, not a replacement:

* Reactive signals (queue depth / saturation) can override prediction when prediction is wrong.
* All outcomes are still constrained by min/max bounds.
* If forecasts are stale/unavailable, the autoscaler falls back to reactive behavior.

h3. 3) Safety, stability, and failure-mode handling

This release includes additional guardrails to reduce oscillation and prevent unsafe downscales:

* Scale cooldowns + dampening (anti-oscillation)
* Minimum step sizing for scale changes (where applicable)
* Safe handling of missing/invalid predictive inputs (no scale-to-zero behavior)
* Improved behavior and surfacing when *min capacity cannot be met* due to region capacity shortages

h3. 4) Observability + auditability

New metrics, logs, dashboards, and alerts make scaling behavior explainable and supportable:

* Desired vs bounded capacity time series
* Bound-hit counters (min-hit and max-hit)
* Predictive error metrics (prediction vs actual demand, forecast staleness)
* Scale event timeline with reasons (reactive vs predictive vs bounded)
* Audit events for config changes (who/when/what) and scaling decisions (requested, bounded, why)

h2. Availability

* *Applies to:* Redwood Dedicated deployments
* *Rollout stage:* GA for eligible Dedicated accounts
* *Default behavior:* No behavior change for existing Dedicated deployments unless the feature is enabled for the account and a scaling policy is configured.

h2. How to enable

h3. Prerequisites

* Account must be allowlisted / feature-flag enabled for autoscaling policy configuration (Dedicated).
* The deployment must be using the Dedicated autoscaler (standard for Dedicated fleets).

h3. Enable in Console

1. Navigate to *Dedicated* → select deployment → *Scaling policy*.
2. Configure:
   a. *Min capacity* (baseline)
   b. *Max capacity* (ceiling)
   c. Optional: *Cooldowns* (if exposed for your account)
3. Optional: toggle *Predictive mode*.
4. Save. The control plane validates constraints (e.g., min ≤ max) and records an audit log event.

h3. Enable via API / IaC

* API: Update the deployment scaling policy via the Control Plane scaling policy endpoints.
* Terraform: Set min/max and predictive mode in the Redwood Dedicated modules (where available for your account).

For exact field names and examples, refer to the design spec (see Links).

h2. Semantics and precedence (important)

* Bounds are *hard* and always applied to the final desired capacity.
* Predictive mode can increase/decrease the requested desired capacity, but cannot violate bounds.
* Reactive signals can override prediction when the system is saturating or queueing, but cannot violate bounds.
* All decisions are deterministic and recorded with both requested and bounded values.

For the normative specification, see: *ADR: Autoscaling bounds precedence and safety invariants*.

h2. Migration notes

h3. Existing Dedicated deployments

* No changes are applied automatically.
* If you set bounds, ensure the *min capacity* is consistent with your baseline SLO needs and regional capacity availability.
* If you enable Predictive mode, start with conservative bounds and review prediction error and bound-hit metrics during the first week.

h3. Recommended rollout for a customer deployment

1. Set *max capacity* first (budget/safety ceiling) while keeping min at current baseline.
2. Observe bound-hit rate and queue depth for 2–3 business days.
3. Adjust min upward only if you need stronger baseline latency protection.
4. Enable Predictive mode (optional) and validate:
   * p95 latency during ramps
   * queue depth trends
   * prediction staleness / error

h2. Operational impact and support guidance

h3. What on-call should expect

* New alerts for max-bound saturation (often correlated with queue buildup).
* New degraded state when min cannot be met due to regional shortage.
* New audit log entries for policy changes and autoscaler decisions.

h3. Common scenarios

* *Customer hits max bound and sees queueing:* This is expected behavior. The system will not exceed max. Work with CS/TAM to evaluate raising max, optimizing throughput (batching/quantization), or adding burst capacity options.
* *Customer expects predictive to “fix” max-bound queueing:* Predictive mode cannot violate max. It can only pre-scale within the ceiling.
* *Customer sees oscillation after enabling predictive:* Use cooldown/dampening defaults; validate forecast staleness; consider disabling predictive temporarily and returning to reactive-only.

h2. Known limitations (as of this release)

* Predictive mode effectiveness depends on sufficient history and stable ramp patterns.
* Timezone/schedule mismatches can reduce forecast quality; verify deployment region/timezone alignment in customer configuration.
* Predictive mode does not perform cross-region placement optimization (out of scope for this release).

h2. Links

* PRD: Dedicated autoscaling bounds + predictive mode
* Design spec: Autoscaling policy schema and Console UX
* ADR: Bounds precedence and safety invariants
* Dashboard spec: Autoscaling bounds observability dashboard
* SLO/alerting updates: Dedicated autoscaling indicators and paging thresholds
* Runbook: Dedicated autoscaler troubleshooting

h2. Owners / escalation

* *Product (Dedicated):* Lauren Bishop
* *Fleet autoscaler:* Vanessa Ortiz / Keiko Yamamoto
* *Control plane policy:* Ethan Park
* *SRE readiness:* Rafael Mendes
* *Observability:* Allison Grant / Sergio Costa

For customer escalations, coordinate via Customer Success (Rachel Kim / Dev Patel) and reference the dashboards + runbook above.

payload.page_title: Dedicated Burst Capacity: SLOs, Error Budgets, and Alerting Policy

sections.body:
This page defines Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budgets, and alerting policy for **Dedicated Burst Capacity**.

The guiding principle is: **burst must never regress baseline Dedicated reliability for non-bursting tenants**. Bursting is a paid add-on and may be denied; denial is not, by itself, a breach as long as denial behavior is consistent with documented limits and the platform remains reliable.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- What we protect (non-burst tenants first)
- What we measure (SLIs and metric sources)
- When we page (and when we ticket)
- Rollout gates for beta/GA by region and hardware class
sections.heading: This document is normative for

sections.body:
- Dedicated requests served from reserved capacity (baseline)
- Dedicated requests served using burst pools (burst path)
- Admission controller behavior and routing integration
- Fleet safety caps and global circuit breaker behavior
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- Hosted API SLOs
- Cross-region burst (not supported in initial release)
- Customer-specific burst pools (initial release uses Redwood-managed shared pools)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Baseline (reserved) capacity:** Tenant’s contracted Dedicated GPUs.
- **Burst capacity:** Temporary additional capacity drawn from a shared, region+hardware-class burst pool.
- **Burst-eligible request:** A request that exceeds baseline concurrency/throughput at the time of evaluation and is allowed to attempt burst by tenant config.
- **Admission decision:** Deterministic allow/deny (or allow-with-constraints) computed by the Burst Admission Controller.
- **Denial:** Admission controller returns a burst denial reason code; routing must apply configured fallback/backpressure policy.
- **Neighbor impact:** Observable degradation (latency, error rate, tail amplification) in *non-burst* tenants correlated with burst activity.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- **Gateway/Routing metrics** (authoritative for request-level success and end-to-end latency)
- **Serving runtime metrics** (GPU saturation, queue depth, tail latency contributors)
- **Burst Admission Controller metrics** (decision latency, decision outcomes, telemetry freshness)
sections.heading: We use the following SLI sources

sections.body:
- Time windows: **28-day** SLO window for error budget accounting (unless otherwise stated).
- Latency measurements are **end-to-end at the Redwood gateway** (request received to first token for streaming; request received to full response for non-streaming).
- Success is defined as HTTP **2xx** for completed requests. Controlled overload/denial responses are tracked separately.
sections.heading: Global conventions

sections.body: Burst capacity must not cause a material regression to non-burst tenants. This is the primary rollout gate.
sections.heading: SLO 0 (Non-negotiable): Protect non-burst Dedicated tenants

sections.body:
- **Population:** Dedicated tenants/requests *not* using burst capacity for the request.
- **SLI:** `successful_requests / total_requests` (2xx / all)
- **SLO:** **99.90%** success over 28 days
- **Error budget:** 0.10% of requests over 28 days
sections.heading: SLO 0A: Non-burst request success rate

sections.body:
This is a *regression* SLO (guardrail) rather than a classic absolute latency SLO, because absolute lat targets vary by model and customer workload.
- **Population:** Dedicated tenants/requests not using burst capacity
- **SLI:** `p95_latency_ms_nonburst` and `p99_latency_ms_nonburst`
- **Guardrail:** During burst-enabled operation in a region+hardware class, relative increase must stay within:
  - **p95:** <= **+8%** vs trailing 7-day baseline (same day-of-week/time bucket)
  - **p99:** <= **+12%** vs trailing 7-day baseline
- **Accounting window:** evaluated continuously; also summarized daily for rollout gate
sections.heading: SLO 0B: Non-burst tail latency stability (regression guardrail)

sections.body:
- The baseline is computed from periods where burst feature flag is OFF (or effective burst usage is ~0) and then continuously updated.
- This guardrail is enforced via the **SLO regression gate** (see Rollout Gates).
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: Burst is an add-on with expected denials when customers hit caps or pools saturate. We still protect correctness and platform behavior.
sections.heading: SLO 1: Dedicated burst path reliability (best-effort, deny allowed)

sections.body:
- **Population:** Requests that were admitted for burst (decision=ALLOW) and routed to burst pool capacity
- **SLI:** `2xx / total_admitted_burst_requests`
- **SLO:** **99.50%** over 28 days
- **Error budget:** 0.50%
sections.heading: SLO 1A: Burst request completion success rate (when admitted)

sections.body:
- This measures serving reliability once we decided to burst.
- Failures include 5xx, upstream timeouts, and serving runtime errors.
sections.heading: Interpretation

sections.body:
- **Population:** All burst-eligible requests calling admission controller
- **SLI:** `p99(admission_decision_latency_ms)`
- **SLO:** **p99 <= 25ms** (per 30-day view; operationally alert on shorter windows)
sections.heading: SLO 1B: Admission decision latency

sections.body: - Admission checks must not add significant overhead to the hot path.
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body: We treat denials as acceptable when they are **consistent, explainable, and bounded**.
sections.heading: SLO 2: Denial correctness and customer supportability

sections.body:
- **Population:** Burst-eligible requests denied by admission
- **SLI:** `% of denials with a populated, valid denial_reason_code`
- **SLO:** **99.99%**
sections.heading: SLO 2A: Denial reason code coverage

sections.body:
- **Population:** Admission controller requests
- **SLI:** `(5xx + timeouts) / total_admission_requests`
- **SLO:** **99.95%** success (i.e., <= 0.05% errors)
sections.heading: SLO 2B: Unexplained admission errors

sections.body: - Admission controller errors are not “denials”; they are a reliability issue. Routing must fail safe (see Failure Policy).
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
1) If tenant is within baseline capacity signals: route as non-burst.
2) If request requires burst to proceed: respond with controlled backpressure (429/503 with `burst_denied_reason=ADMISSION_UNAVAILABLE`) OR route to configured fallback model/capacity if contractually allowed.
sections.heading: Fail-safe behavior is

sections.body: - Admission controller must not become a single point of cascading failure.
sections.heading: Operational requirement

sections.body:
- Deny burst with explicit reasons (e.g., `POOL_SATURATED`, `TENANT_CAP_REACHED`, `FLEET_SAFETY_CAP`) rather than allowing queue growth that impacts neighbors.
- Trigger circuit breakers before non-burst latency regresses.
sections.heading: Expected behavior under saturation

sections.body:
Telemetry lag can lead to unfair denials or over-admission. We enforce:
- Hard upper bound on telemetry staleness used for admission decisions.
- Conservative fallback policy when staleness exceeds threshold.
sections.heading: Telemetry lag

sections.body: We use multi-window burn rate alerting for error-budget SLOs and threshold alerts for guardrails.
sections.heading: Alerting policy

sections.body:
**Page (SEV2/SEV3 depending on impact) when:**
- Non-burst success SLO burn rate indicates likely breach within 24h
- Non-burst latency regression guardrail exceeds threshold for sustained window
- Admission controller errors/latency exceed thresholds and impact request path
- Global circuit breaker engages unexpectedly or flaps

**Create ticket (no page) when:**
- Denial rates increase but remain within expected caps (customer-config-driven)
- A single tenant hits its cap repeatedly (route to CS for enablement/tuning)
- Dashboards show gradual pool saturation trend without immediate SLO risk
sections.heading: Paging vs ticketing

sections.body:
- SLO: 99.90% (SLO 0A)
- Alerts:
  - **Fast burn:** 2% budget/hour (approx), triggers when `burn_rate_1h > 14` AND `burn_rate_6h > 7`
  - **Slow burn:** triggers when `burn_rate_6h > 2` AND `burn_rate_24h > 1`
- Routing: page **SRE on-call** and **Dedicated Platform secondary**
sections.heading: A1: Non-burst success rate burn (PAGE)

sections.body:
- Trigger when either:
  - p95 regression > +8% for **20 of 30 minutes**, OR
  - p99 regression > +12% for **15 of 30 minutes**
- Required annotations:
  - region, hardware_class, top contributing pools, current burst utilization
- Automated action (where enabled): **reduce burst caps by 50%** and/or engage circuit breaker for the impacted region+class if regression persists >30 min.
sections.heading: A2: Non-burst latency regression guardrail (PAGE)

sections.body:
- Trigger when `(timeouts+5xx)/total_admission_requests > 0.20%` for 10 minutes
- Or when p99 decision latency > 75ms for 10 minutes
- Rationale: admission instability can cascade into user-facing 429/503 and false denials.
sections.heading: A3: Admission controller availability (PAGE)

sections.body: - Trigger when global or regional circuit breaker state changes > 3 times in 30 minutes OR engages outside a planned test window.
sections.heading: A4: Circuit breaker engaged or flapping (PAGE)

sections.body:
- Trigger when burst pool utilization > 85% for 60 minutes OR queue depth trend indicates reaching 90% in next 2 hours.
- Owner: Fleet/Infrastructure (capacity) with SRE as watcher.
sections.heading: A5: Burst pool saturation early warning (TICKET)

sections.body:
- Trigger when `denial_reason=UNKNOWN` > 0.01% OR a new denial reason appears without doc update.
- Owner: Platform Control Plane.
sections.heading: A6: Denial reason anomaly (TICKET)

sections.body: Rollout is staged by **region + hardware class** and is controlled by feature flags.
sections.heading: Error budget gates for rollout

sections.body:
Before enabling burst in a region+hardware class:
- Admission controller p99 latency <= 25ms in staging and in at least one production region.
- Dashboards and alert routes validated (see `Burst Capacity Dashboards`).
- Runbook reviewed and on-call trained.
sections.heading: Gate 1: Pre-enable (required)

sections.body:
- No active A1/A2/A3 pages in the last 72 hours for the target region+class.
- Non-burst success rate (SLO 0A) error budget burn rate < 1.0 (steady state) over trailing 7 days.
- Latency regression guardrail baseline computed and validated.
sections.heading: Allowed when

sections.body:
Allowed when ALL are true for trailing 14 days in the target region+class:
- SLO 0A: burn rate < 1.0 (no projected breach)
- SLO 0B: p95 and p99 regression within guardrails; no sustained excursions > 30 minutes
- SLO 1A: admitted burst success >= 99.5%
- No unresolved SEV2+ incidents attributable to bursting
sections.heading: Gate 3: GA expansion (wider tenant set)

sections.body:
Burst must be automatically reduced/disabled (region+class) when:
- A2 triggers and persists > 30 minutes after automated cap reduction, OR
- A1 fast burn triggers twice within 24 hours with correlated burst utilization, OR
- Admission controller error rate > 1% for 15 minutes.
sections.heading: Automatic rollback / disable criteria

sections.body:
1) Reduce max burst ratio (policy)
2) Reduce per-tenant cap
3) Engage regional circuit breaker (deny all burst)
4) Disable feature flag for region+class
sections.heading: Rollback action order

sections.body:
- Burst is **best-effort** and may be denied due to:
  - tenant cap reached
  - pool saturation
  - cooldown/fairness enforcement
  - fleet safety cap / circuit breaker
- Baseline Dedicated performance remains protected; burst does not change baseline SLA.
- We provide transparent denial reason codes and usage reporting to support customer debugging.
sections.heading: Customer-visible expectations (what we promise)

sections.body:
Canonical metric families (names may be suffixed by service namespace):
- `redwood_burst_admission_requests_total{decision, denial_reason, region, hardware_class, tenant_tier}`
- `redwood_burst_admission_latency_ms_bucket{region, hardware_class}`
- `redwood_burst_telemetry_staleness_ms{region, hardware_class}`
- `redwood_burst_pool_utilization_ratio{region, hardware_class, pool}`
- `redwood_burst_pool_queue_depth{region, hardware_class, pool}`
- `redwood_gateway_requests_total{tenant, deployment_mode="dedicated", path}`
- `redwood_gateway_request_latency_ms_bucket{tenant, deployment_mode="dedicated", burst="true|false"}`
sections.heading: Metrics (reference)

sections.body:
- Do not label by request_id or model_revision.
- Tenant labels must use stable `tenant_id` and/or `tenant_tier`, with sampling for high-volume queries where needed.
sections.heading: Cardinality requirements

sections.body:
- Primary on-call for pages A1–A4: **SRE**
- Secondary responders:
  - Admission controller: Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park / Benji Okafor rotation)
  - Guardrails/autoscaling: Infra Guardrails (Keiko Yamamoto rotation)
  - Pool capacity/procurement: Fleet (Vanessa Ortiz rotation)
  - Routing/fallback correctness: Smart Routing (Mina Haddad rotation)
sections.heading: Operational ownership and escalation

sections.body:
- If non-burst regression is observed, prioritize **mitigation (disable burst)** over root cause.
- If customer escalations cite “unexpected denials,” validate config, caps, and denial reason distribution before treating as incident.
sections.heading: Escalation guidance

sections.body:
- Burst pool overload mitigation: `confluence://eng-sre/runbooks/burst-pool-overload-mitigation-runbook`
- Admission controller service doc: `confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/burst-admission-controller-service`
- Dashboards catalog: `confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/burst-capacity-dashboards`

payload.page_title: Support SLA vs Engineering SLO Mapping (Paging Thresholds + Customer Impact)

sections.body:
This page is the reference for how Support SLAs (first response + update cadence) should map to Engineering SLOs (availability/latency) and how paging thresholds should relate to *customer impact*.

This is **not** a contractual SLA document. For contract language and tier-specific coverage windows, refer to: **Customer Success & Support → SLA policy by customer tier**.

**Goals**
- Prevent mismatches where Support promises a cadence that Engineering on-call cannot meet.
- Ensure paging triggers correlate to real customer impact (not only internal “red” alerts).
- Standardize language between Support (Jira priorities P0–P4) and Engineering incident severity (Sev0–Sev3).

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
**Support SLA (operational):** Response/update targets used by Support/CS for incident comms and ticket handling. These are constrained by coverage windows and the current incident process.

**Engineering SLO:** Reliability objectives for production services (e.g., request success rate, latency). SLOs drive error budgets and alerting policies.

**Customer impact:** A combination of (a) number of customers affected, (b) tier (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; Enterprise vs self-serve), and (c) degradation type (hard outage vs partial degradation vs “sharp edges”).

**Burn rate alerts:** Alerts that fire when error budget is being consumed quickly (fast burn) or steadily (slow burn). Burn rate is a more reliable paging signal than single-point thresholds.

**Time-to-triage (TTT):** Time from Support intake to a qualified owner engaged with enough context to act.

**Time-to-mitigation (TTM):** Time from detection/escalation to a customer-visible mitigation (rollback, routing change, scaling, workaround, etc.).

---
sections.heading: Definitions (shared language)

sections.body:
The exact targets may vary by region/model and are recorded in the SLO registry. The table below describes the *common SLO classes* and how they should inform Support expectations.

| SLO class | Primary metric (examples) | What customers feel | Typical mitigations | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| API availability | Request success rate (2xx/3xx), 5xx rate, auth failure rate | Outage, elevated errors, failed requests | Rollback, capacity shift, routing/fallback, dependency remediation | Availability issues generally justify rapid paging when widespread. |
| API latency | p95/p99 end-to-end latency; queue time; time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming | Slow responses, timeouts, UI/app slowness | Scaling, routing, batching controls, rollback, dependency tuning | Latency can be as severe as errors for synchronous apps; focus on duration + breadth. |
| Streaming health | Stream disconnect rate, truncated streams, reconnect loops | “Partial success” but bad UX; repeated retries | Gateway config adjustments, region shift, client guidance | Often appears as “works sometimes”; Support should collect request IDs + client details. |
| Control plane availability (Console/SSO/config) | Login success rate, token exchange, config API availability | Can’t log in, can’t manage keys/routes | Auth/SSO fixes, control plane rollback | Customer impact can be business-critical even if inference plane is healthy. |
| Async pipelines (e.g., audit logs) | Delivery lag (p95/p99), backlog depth, drop rate | Missing/late logs; compliance workflows blocked | Backlog drain, pipeline scaling, temporary export guidance | Typically not “Sev0” unless contractual/compliance deadlines are at risk. |

---
sections.heading: Engineering SLOs (what we optimize for)

sections.body:
Support SLAs are defined per tier. This mapping focuses on *how to adjust comms* based on Engineering signals and incident posture.

**Key principle:** When Engineering SLO burn indicates a fast-moving incident, Support update cadence should increase and escalation should occur even if an individual ticket is still gathering details.

The tiered SLAs (first response and update cadence) live in: **SLA policy by customer tier**. Support should follow that page for targets; this page clarifies *when to trigger paging and/or raise incident severity*.

---
sections.heading: Support SLAs (how we communicate)

sections.body:
1) **Support cadence must follow incident posture.**
   - If the issue qualifies as an incident (Sev0/Sev1), comms cadence is driven by the incident commander (IC) and comms owner, and Support should align rather than invent a parallel cadence.

2) **Page based on customer impact + burn rate, not “noise.”**
   - A single noisy host or one customer’s unusual traffic pattern should not page SRE without evidence of broader risk.
   - Conversely, a multi-customer degradation with high burn rate should page quickly even if absolute error % seems “small.”

3) **Prioritize actions that reduce TTM for the most customers.**
   - For Hosted: routing/fallback and regional traffic shifts are often the fastest mitigations.
   - For Dedicated: capacity and autoscaling controls are common mitigations.
   - For Private: diagnostics bundle + safe rollback paths reduce time-to-resolution.

4) **Support and Engineering severity must match.**
   - Support P0/P1 should not map to an Engineering Sev2 unless there is a clear reason (e.g., single-customer, self-inflicted, or no platform fault).

---
sections.heading: Mapping principles (Support SLA ↔ Engineering SLO)

sections.body: This section defines recommended paging triggers for SRE/on-call. It is intentionally framed as **policy guidance**, not a rigid rule. Use judgment and document exceptions.
sections.heading: Paging thresholds: tying SLOs to customer impact

sections.body:
Page SRE/on-call when *any* of the following is true:
- **Fast-burn SLO alert** fires for Hosted inference in a production region.
- **Multi-customer availability incident**: sustained elevated 5xx/auth failures affecting more than one customer or a material share of traffic in a region.
- **Region-level latency degradation**: sustained p95/p99 latency increase causing customer timeouts or meaningful throughput loss.
- **Streaming health regression**: elevated stream disconnect/truncation rate across multiple customers or across a region.
sections.heading: A. Default paging triggers (broad customer impact)

sections.body:
Page the owning on-call (SRE or Platform/Private Deployments per escalation matrix) when:
- **Dedicated:** customer’s reserved capacity is not meeting contracted throughput/latency expectations due to platform-side causes (autoscaling instability, GPU pool churn, cluster issues), especially if customer cannot mitigate by retry/backoff.
- **Private:** upgrade/install failures blocking production usage or compliance obligations, or widespread control plane failures (SSO, key management, audit logs) with documented evidence.
sections.heading: B. Tier-weighted paging (Dedicated / Private)

sections.body:
A single enterprise customer can still justify paging when one or more is true:
- The issue blocks a critical workflow (e.g., production launch, compliance deadline) and there is no safe workaround.
- The ticket meets Support P0 criteria and there is evidence the platform is at fault.
- The ticket is likely an early signal of a broader incident (e.g., correlated in time with deploys, region signals, or similar symptoms in other tickets).

---
sections.heading: C. Single-customer escalation (high criticality)

sections.body:
Engineering alerting should align to error budget policy. Support should understand what these alerts imply about urgency.

**Fast burn (page):** indicates we are on track to violate the SLO quickly (minutes to an hour). Support should treat this as P0/P1 depending on breadth.

**Slow burn (page during supported hours; consider after-hours based on tier/impact):** indicates sustained degradation that will consume significant budget over several hours.

**Example (conceptual):**
- Fast burn: consuming ~2% of monthly error budget in 1 hour
- Slow burn: consuming ~5% of monthly error budget in 6 hours
sections.heading: Recommended alert posture (burn-rate oriented)

sections.body:
- If Engineering declares Sev0/Sev1, **Support update cadence** should match the incident comms plan and be explicitly stated in customer emails.
- If a slow burn is detected but customers are not yet reporting, Support should prepare macros and proactively monitor incoming tickets.

---
sections.heading: Support guidance

sections.body:
Use this table during triage and when deciding to page.

| Support priority | Typical customer impact | Engineering signals to look for | Paging expectation | Support comms expectation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | Hard outage / widespread inability to use product; severe revenue or compliance risk | Fast-burn availability alert; broad 5xx/auth failures; region down; major routing failure | Page immediately; start Slack bridge; move to #incidents when criteria met | Acknowledge fast; frequent updates; align with IC; avoid speculation; share mitigations/workarounds when validated |
| P1 | Major degradation; partial outage; many customers affected or one enterprise blocked | Elevated latency/timeouts; streaming disconnect spike; slow-burn turning into fast-burn | Page quickly if sustained; otherwise engage on-call via escalation path | Set update cadence explicitly; include what we’re measuring and next checkpoint |
| P2 | Limited degradation; workaround exists; smaller blast radius | Localized metrics; no burn-rate alerts; isolated region/model | Do not page by default; escalate via owning team queue; page if trend worsens | Provide workaround; define “when to escalate” conditions; request required diagnostics |
| P3 | Minor issue; product question; no service risk | No abnormal metrics | No paging | Macro-driven response; doc links |
| P4 | Informational / enhancement request | N/A | No paging | Route to product/feedback |
sections.heading: Mapping table: Support priority → Engineering signals → paging + comms

sections.body:
- A P1 that is clearly caused by customer misconfiguration should not be escalated as an Engineering incident, but Support should still help the customer quickly.
- If Support is uncertain whether impact is broad, treat as **P1 with a short investigation window** (e.g., 15–30 minutes) and page if evidence suggests multi-customer impact.

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
On-call efficiency depends on Support providing consistent context. Before paging, collect what you can without blocking escalation.

**Minimum required context (copy/paste):**
- Product/tier: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (+ region)
- API surface: chat/generate/embeddings/rerank/console/audit logs
- Model + version (and whether pinned)
- Time window (UTC) + first observed time
- Request IDs / trace IDs (at least 3 examples)
- Error codes/messages or latency percentiles as observed by customer
- Any recent customer-side changes (SDK version, proxy changes, retries)
- Any observed mitigations tried (retries/backoff, region switch, smaller batches)

If the issue is streaming-related, include:
- Transport details (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2; proxy/CDN; keepalive settings)
- Client language/SDK version
- Whether failures correlate with long generations or specific token counts

---
sections.heading: Symptom-driven guidance: what to collect before paging

sections.body:
- Support should **stop using generic SLA language** and instead use the incident cadence (e.g., “next update in 30 minutes”).
- Support should link the bridge channel + incident ID in Jira (SUP ticket) and keep comms consistent with the status page guidance.
sections.heading: 1) When Engineering declares an incident

sections.body:
- Use P1/P2 and set an explicit checkpoint: “We are investigating and will update you by <time>.”
- If Engineering signals show burn-rate risk increasing, escalate to incident posture.
sections.heading: 2) When there is degradation but no incident declared (yet)

sections.body:
- Treat as a new investigation unless clearly tied to known residual impact.
- Collect fresh request IDs and confirm region/model.

---
sections.heading: 3) When an incident is resolved but customer symptoms persist

sections.body:
- If metrics show stable availability but ticket volume spikes and headers appear inconsistent, treat as **P2** (workaround + investigation).
- Page only if there is evidence of platform-side enforcement misclassification affecting multiple customers.
- Support should link the relevant known-issue article and capture header samples.
sections.heading: Example A: Elevated 429s / quota confusion

sections.body:
- If multiple customers report stream disconnects and streaming-health metrics spike, treat as **P1 → page quickly**.
- If only one customer reports and no metrics show impact, treat as **P2 with a short investigation window**; page if additional evidence appears.
sections.heading: Example B: Streaming resets in a single region

sections.body:
- If lag exceeds documented expectations and affects enterprise compliance workflows, treat as **P1** (even if inference plane is healthy).
- Page Platform/SRE depending on ownership; align comms to expected delivery windows and provide temporary export/retry guidance if validated.

---
sections.heading: Example C: Audit log delivery lag

sections.body:
- Follow the **Escalation paths and contacts** directory for who to page by product area.
- Support should not bypass the incident process. If the situation warrants an incident, use the prescribed bridge conventions and move to #incidents per policy.

---
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation alignment

sections.body:
Support comms, Slack bridges, and status page updates must be consistent. Refer to **Customer incident comms alignment** for:
- What qualifies for a status event
- Approval workflow
- How to avoid conflicting ETAs or overly specific root-cause claims

---
sections.heading: Status page vs Support comms

sections.body:
If Support SLAs repeatedly fail to match what Engineering can operationally deliver:
1) File a ticket against this policy owner (SRE) and the SLA policy owner (Customer Success).
2) Include examples of mismatches (ticket IDs + timestamps + on-call notes).
3) Propose one of:
   - Adjust SLA wording/cadence for a tier
   - Adjust paging thresholds / alert routing
   - Add a known-issue workaround article + macros

**Owner:** SRE (Sean Gallagher) in partnership with Support Ops (Dev Patel).

---
sections.heading: Change management

sections.body:
- Link: SUP ticket ↔ Slack bridge ↔ incident channel ↔ relevant dashboards.
- Use one “current state” comment that is continuously updated (timestamped) rather than multiple conflicting notes.
- When a workaround is provided, label it explicitly as **temporary** and include “when to escalate” criteria.
sections.heading: Appendix: Practical guidance for on-call friendly Support tickets

payload.page_title: Planned Change: SLO / Error Budget Impact Review Requirements

sections.body: This document defines the minimum SRE review steps for planned changes that may impact availability, latency, or throughput SLOs for any production environment (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
SRE review is required for any change that is classified Medium/High/Critical risk under the Production Change Management Policy, or any change that:
- Requires disabling alerts
- Requires a maintenance window
- Has a credible risk of increased 5xx, latency regression, or capacity shortfall
sections.heading: When this review is required

sections.body:
- Confirm current 30-day error budget remaining for impacted services/tenants.
- If error budget remaining is below 25%, attach an explicit risk acceptance from Engineering + SRE lead.
sections.heading: 1) Current SLO state

sections.body:
- Confirm GPU and request capacity headroom for the expected window.
- Confirm no overlapping capacity events (region maintenance, fleet migrations, known shortages).
sections.heading: 2) Capacity + saturation

sections.body:
- Identify the “watch list” metrics for the change window (at minimum: 5xx rate, P95 latency, saturation/queue depth, restarts/OOM, and synthetic checks).
- Confirm alerts are enabled and routed to an active on-call.
sections.heading: 3) Monitoring coverage

sections.body:
- Validate that rollback can be executed within the defined “time-to-restore” target for the customer (or platform).
- Identify the decision point for rollback (e.g., after control-plane or after data-plane).
sections.heading: 4) Rollback feasibility

sections.body:
- Confirm no concurrent high-risk changes affecting the same customer/region.
- If overlap exists, record mitigation or reschedule.
sections.heading: 5) Change overlap

sections.body:
- Error budget is healthy or risk acceptance is documented
- Monitoring is ready and on-call coverage confirmed
- Rollback plan is concrete and feasible
- Customer comms plan exists when customer-visible
sections.heading: SRE will recommend GO only if

sections.body:
- [ ] Error budget screenshot/link
- [ ] Capacity headroom note (GPU + queue)
- [ ] Alert routing confirmation
- [ ] Rollback time estimate + decision point
- [ ] List of services/routes impacted
sections.heading: Minimum evidence checklist (copy/paste into change record)

payload.page_title: PRD: Auto-rollback on SLO breach integration (Rollouts + SLO Monitors)

sections.body:
Redwood’s rollout controller supports canary, A/B testing, and staged model deployments. Today, mitigation for rollout-induced latency and error regressions is largely manual, relying on on-call detection and intervention. This PRD defines an integrated capability that automatically pauses or rolls back a rollout when SLO monitors detect sustained breaches, scoped to the exact rollout dimensions (route/service, model version, region, customer tier).

This feature is a core reliability differentiator for Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments: it reduces time-to-mitigation and helps prevent SLA violations during aggressive iteration.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Automatically mitigate rollout regressions by pausing/rolling back when SLOs breach with high confidence.
2) Provide clear auditability: “what happened, why, and what did the controller do?”
3) Provide safe, configurable policy controls with guardrails to prevent oscillation and false positives.
4) Make behavior predictable for SRE and service owners via standard metrics, dashboards, alerts, and runbooks.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Multi-region failover orchestration beyond rollback/pause (explicitly out of scope).
- Quality/eval-based rollback signals (handled under eval guardrails; to be added later as an additional signal class).
- Replacing existing incident response processes; this is an auto-mitigation rail that integrates with them.
sections.heading: Non-goals (MVP)

sections.body:
- Reduce MTTR for rollout-induced latency/error incidents.
- Avoid paging storms and flappy behavior; ensure minimum-sample gating and debounce.
- Ensure monitors are present, fresh, and correctly scoped; detect and alert on missing/stale monitors.
- Have runbook-ready events that show scope, breach evidence, and action taken.
sections.heading: SRE / Observability

sections.body:
- Roll out model versions safely with confidence that regressions will be contained.
- Configure policies per route/model/tier with templates and safe defaults.
- Understand “why did we rollback/pause?” directly in Console with links to relevant dashboards.
- Override/suppress automation when needed (e.g., known telemetry outage), with justification recorded.
sections.heading: Platform / Service Owners (Hosted API, Dedicated control plane services, Console services)

sections.body: - Provide clear customer-facing explanations and evidence during escalations (audit trail + screenshots/links).
sections.heading: Product / Support (secondary)

sections.body: Rollouts can change latency, error rates, or saturation dynamics (e.g., batching/quantization changes, kernel regressions, routing changes). When issues occur, manual detection and mitigation can take minutes to tens of minutes. For higher tiers and latency-sensitive customers, this can burn error budgets and risk SLA violations.
sections.heading: Problem statement

sections.body:
- True regression during canary step (p95/p99 latency increase, 5xx spike).
- Monitor gaps (missing, stale, wrong labels) causing false negatives.
- Telemetry lag/partial outage causing false positives (e.g., missing data interpreted as breach).
- Oscillation: repeated pause/rollback/retry cycles.
sections.heading: Common failure modes we must handle

sections.body:
- **Rollout**: a controlled shift of traffic from baseline model version to candidate version via steps (canary, staged %, or A/B).
- **Scope**: dimensions that identify the rollout target, at minimum: {service/route, model, model_version, region, customer_tier}. Some services also include {workspace/customer_id} for dedicated/private.
- **SLO monitors**: pre-defined latency/error/saturation monitors that can be queried for burn-rate/breach state over fast and slow windows.
- **Auto action**: a controller-initiated action: Pause rollout / Rollback to last known-good / Shift traffic back to baseline (A/B) / No-op (evaluate only).
sections.heading: Definitions / terminology

sections.body: The rollout controller must be able to evaluate SLO breach signals for the precise rollout scope.
sections.heading: R1. Monitor subscription & scoping

sections.body:
- Identify the set of eligible monitors for the rollout scope:
  - Latency: p95 and/or p99 by route
  - Error rate: 5xx (and optionally 429/timeout where designated)
  - Saturation: GPU queue depth / request backlog / throttling (where available)
- Support scoping at minimum by: route/service, model_version, region, customer_tier.
- If a rollout step changes traffic split, evaluation must continue to use the candidate’s scoped metrics (not global service aggregates).
sections.heading: Functional requirements

sections.body:
- For a staged rollout on one route in us-east-1 (self-serve tier), the evaluator queries monitors that match that exact scope.
- Scope is visible in the audit event and Console UI.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria

sections.body: We will use burn-rate based evaluation with dual windows and debounce/holdoff (see ADR-0127).
sections.heading: R2. Breach evaluation semantics

sections.body:
- Dual-window confirmation (fast + slow):
  - Fast window: 5m (detect sharp regressions quickly)
  - Slow window: 30m (confirm sustained impact)
- Minimum sample sizes to avoid low-traffic false positives.
- Debounce/holdoff to avoid flapping during transient spikes.
- Explicit handling for monitor staleness/missing data.
sections.heading: MVP semantics

sections.body:
- **BREACH_CONFIRMED**: conditions met (dual-window + min sample) -> eligible for auto action.
- **BREACH_SUSPECTED**: partial conditions met (e.g., fast window only) -> may pause depending on policy.
- **NO_BREACH**: normal.
- **INSUFFICIENT_DATA**: sample size below threshold.
- **MONITOR_STALE / MONITOR_MISSING**: cannot safely evaluate.
sections.heading: Breach outcomes

sections.body: The system must support distinct actions depending on rollout type and policy.
sections.heading: R3. Actions and rollout state transitions

sections.body:
1) **Pause rollout**
- Freeze traffic split at current step.
- Mark rollout as PAUSED_AUTO with reason.

2) **Rollback rollout (revert to last known-good)**
- For canary/staged: shift traffic back to baseline model version.
- Must be safe and rate-limited (step-down strategy) and idempotent.
- Mark rollout as ROLLED_BACK_AUTO with reason.

3) **Shift traffic back to baseline (A/B)**
- For A/B tests: set candidate traffic to 0% (or safe minimum) and return to baseline.
- Mark as AB_BASELINE_RESTORED_AUTO.

4) **Suppress action (evaluate only)**
- Record that a breach was observed but action was suppressed due to configured suppression windows or manual overrides.
sections.heading: Supported actions (MVP)

sections.body:
- RUNNING
- PAUSED_MANUAL
- PAUSED_AUTO (new)
- ROLLED_BACK_MANUAL
- ROLLED_BACK_AUTO (new)
- COMPLETED
- FAILED (system failure, e.g., rollback executor error)
sections.heading: Rollout states (user-visible)

sections.body:
- Auto actions must be single-flight and idempotent.
- If rollback fails, mark rollout FAILED and page/notify per alert policy.
sections.heading: State transition notes

sections.body:
Every evaluation that triggers an action must produce an audit trail record following ADR-0128.

MVP audit fields (user-facing summary in Console; full event in logs/event stream):
- rollout_id, rollout_type, current_step
- scope: route/service, model, candidate_version, baseline_version, region, customer_tier
- decision: action_taken (pause/rollback/restore/suppress), decision_time
- monitors evaluated: monitor_ids + type (latency/error/saturation)
- evidence summary:
  - windows (fast/slow)
  - burn-rate state / breach boolean
  - sample sizes
  - data freshness timestamps
- policy: policy_id + policy_version + configured thresholds
- suppression: any suppression reason (manual override, incident hold, telemetry outage flag)
- correlation_id(s) for dashboards/logs
sections.heading: R4. Auditability and Console visibility

sections.body:
- Rollout timeline includes auto actions inline with clear labels.
- Event detail panel includes:
  - “Why did we act?” narrative (generated summary)
  - Link(s) to Grafana dashboard filtered by rollout_id and scope
  - “What changed?” baseline vs candidate versions
  - Admin-only controls to suppress/retry (if permissioned)
sections.heading: Console UX requirements

sections.body:
- Per-rollout override (highest precedence)
- Per-service/route default
- Global safe defaults (fallback)
sections.heading: Policy must be configurable at

sections.body:
- Provide templates (e.g., “Conservative”, “Balanced”, “Aggressive”) with tier-specific defaults.
- Inline warnings when configs are unsafe (e.g., no min sample, too short windows, rollback on insufficient data).
- Preview of “effective policy” (computed final config after inheritance).
- Display what monitors must exist for the selected scope; show readiness status.
sections.heading: UX principles

sections.body:
- Enabled: true/false
- Signals enabled: latency_p95, latency_p99, error_rate_5xx (saturation optional per service readiness)
- Thresholds:
  - latency regression (relative and/or absolute)
  - error rate threshold
- Evaluation:
  - fast_window, slow_window
  - min_requests_fast, min_requests_slow
  - debounce_seconds, holdoff_seconds
- Action policy:
  - on_confirmed_breach: rollback | pause
  - on_suspected_breach: pause | notify_only | none
- Suppression:
  - suppression_window_minutes after action
  - admin suppression toggle + required justification
sections.heading: Configuration fields (MVP)

sections.body: Defaults are tiered to match SLA expectations and typical traffic patterns. These are starting points; SRE may tune based on incident history.
sections.heading: R6. Default thresholds (proposed)

sections.body:
- Latency thresholds are defined as relative regression vs baseline for the same scope.
- “Error rate” refers to 5xx / total requests for the scoped route.
- If service has very low traffic, min sample gating will prevent actions.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
| Tier | Signals (default) | Confirmed breach action | Suspected breach action | Fast/Slow windows | Min req (fast/slow) | Latency regression threshold | Error rate threshold | Debounce/Holdoff | Suppression window |
|------|-------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Self-serve (Hosted) | p95 + 5xx | Pause | Notify-only | 5m / 30m | 300 / 2,000 | p95 +20% OR +60ms (whichever higher) | >1.0% for 5m AND >0.5% for 30m | 120s / 300s | 30m |
| Dedicated | p95 + p99 + 5xx | Rollback | Pause | 5m / 30m | 200 / 1,200 | p95 +15% OR +40ms; p99 +20% OR +80ms | >0.5% for 5m AND >0.25% for 30m | 120s / 300s | 45m |
| Private (VPC/on-prem) | p95 + p99 + 5xx | Rollback | Pause | 5m / 30m | 100 / 600 | p95 +10% OR +30ms; p99 +15% OR +60ms | >0.25% for 5m AND >0.10% for 30m | 180s / 600s | 60m |
sections.heading: Proposed defaults table (MVP)

sections.body:
- Never rollback on INSUFFICIENT_DATA, MONITOR_MISSING, or MONITOR_STALE.
- If only fast window breaches (suspected), default is pause (or notify-only for self-serve).

Open question (PM/SRE): do we want p99 enabled by default for self-serve, or only for Dedicated/Private initially to reduce noise?
sections.heading: Guardrails on defaults

sections.body: The system must reduce the chance of false positives and oscillation.
sections.heading: R7. Safety guardrails

sections.body:
1) **Minimum sample gating**: no action unless request counts exceed thresholds for both windows.
2) **Dual-window confirmation**: confirmed breach requires both windows to meet criteria (configurable, but bounded by safe limits).
3) **Debounce/holdoff**:
   - Debounce: require breach state to persist for N seconds before acting.
   - Holdoff: after an action, do not evaluate/act again for a cooldown period.
4) **Suppression during known incidents**:
   - Allow a global “known incident” suppress flag (managed by SRE) to stop auto actions during telemetry/monitoring outages.
5) **Rate-limited rollback execution**:
   - Traffic shifts must be incremental (step-down) with safeguards.
6) **Missing/stale monitors behavior**:
   - Default to fail-open for rollout progress (do not automatically rollback), but emit an alert/notification and block “enable auto rollback” readiness (release gate).
sections.heading: Guardrails (MVP)

sections.body: We must ship standard metrics and dashboards.
sections.heading: R8. Observability requirements
MVP metrics (conceptual)

sections.body:
- “Auto action triggered” alert (notify; page only if rollback fails or repeat failures occur).
- “Monitor missing/stale for enabled policy” alert (notify owner; gate enablement).
- Dashboard panels for:
  - auto actions over time
  - top routes by auto actions
  - suppression reasons
  - stale/missing monitor counts
sections.heading: Dashboards and alerts

sections.body:
- Admin-only overrides (suppress/unsuppress/retry) must be permissioned via RBAC.
- Every override requires justification and is audited.
- Ensure audit events contain no customer prompt content. Only operational metadata and monitor references.
sections.heading: R9. Permissions and security

sections.body:
1) As an SRE on-call, when a canary rollout causes p95 latency to increase sharply, I want the rollout to auto-pause or rollback within minutes so customer impact is minimized.
2) As a platform engineer, I want to configure a rollout policy template for my route and see clear warnings if my thresholds are unsafe.
3) As a service owner, I want to view a rollout timeline and click into an auto-rollback event to see monitor evidence and links to the dashboard.
4) As an SRE, I want alerts if monitors are missing/stale for routes that have auto-rollback enabled.
5) As an admin, I want to suppress automation during a telemetry incident for 2 hours, with justification captured, and later re-enable it.
sections.heading: User stories

sections.body:
- Toggle: “Auto-mitigation on SLO breach” (enabled/disabled)
- Template dropdown: Conservative / Balanced / Aggressive (tier-aware)
- Editable fields: signals, thresholds, windows, min sample, action mapping
- Inline validation with safe bounds (e.g., minimum slow window, minimum min_requests)
- Effective policy preview (read-only summary)
sections.heading: Rollout Policy Editor (new section)

sections.body:
- Timeline events show: “Auto-paused due to latency SLO burn (p95)” or “Auto-rolled back due to 5xx breach”
- Event detail panel:
  - Scope chips (route/model/version/region/tier)
  - Decision summary + timestamp
  - Evidence summary (fast + slow window status, sample sizes)
  - Links: “Open dashboard (filtered)” and “View monitor definitions”
  - Admin actions (if permissioned): suppress for X minutes; re-attempt rollout step (if supported)
sections.heading: Rollout Detail: Audit timeline

sections.body:
- Rollout controller hooks (state machine integration)
- SLO monitor provider / slo-toolkit burn-rate endpoint supporting rollout scoping
- Policy engine schema + validation + inheritance
- Observability pack: dashboards + alert rules
- Incident-bot / Slack notifications for auto actions
- RBAC updates for override endpoints
sections.heading: Dependencies

sections.body:
- Confirm evaluation semantics (ADR-0127) and audit schema (ADR-0128)
- Finalize tier defaults and safe bounds with SRE
- Identify initial internal canary services/routes
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Support pause on confirmed breach for canary/staged rollouts
- Audit trail events emitted; Console timeline view available behind flag
- Basic dashboards and notifications
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- E2E test: inject synthetic latency and 5xx, verify auto pause, audit event, dashboard links
- No observed flapping in simulation suite
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Enable rollback actions for Dedicated/Private tiers (and selected internal routes)
- Add idempotency/locking and safe traffic shift strategy
- Add suppression + admin override
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Game day scenarios passed:
  - latency spike
  - 5xx burst
  - monitor staleness
  - telemetry lag
- Runbook published and on-call training completed
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Enable behind feature flag by environment and region
- Start with internal production route(s), then expand to dedicated customers with high operational maturity
- Self-serve enablement later, defaulting to pause (not rollback) to reduce risk
sections.heading: Phase 3: Production enablement (1–2 weeks, staged)

sections.body:
- Auto actions causing >1 significant false positive per day for enabled routes
- Any safety issue in rollback executor (double execution, incorrect scope, unsafe shift)
- Monitor health instability (staleness across >10% of enabled scopes)
sections.heading: Backout criteria

sections.body:
- Reduce MTTR for rollout-induced latency/error incidents by 50% (median) for enabled routes.
- Reduce number of SLA-impacting incidents attributable to rollouts by 25% over a quarter (for cohorts with feature enabled).
sections.heading: Primary

sections.body:
- Time-to-auto-mitigation (TTA) under 5 minutes for confirmed fast+slow breaches.
- < 1 false-positive auto rollback per 30 rollout-days (Dedicated/Private cohorts).
- Monitor readiness: >95% of enabled routes have fresh, correctly-scoped monitors.
- Operator satisfaction: SRE survey indicates audit trail is sufficient for triage without digging into raw logs (target: 4/5).
sections.heading: Secondary

sections.body:
- Risk: False positives due to telemetry lag or low traffic.
  - Mitigation: min sample gating, dual-window confirmation, staleness detection, debounce.
- Risk: Oscillation during intermittent regressions.
  - Mitigation: holdoff + suppression window; require manual confirmation to retry after repeated actions (future enhancement).
- Risk: Missing monitors prevent automation.
  - Mitigation: readiness checks and release gates; alert owners; document monitor requirements.
- Risk: Rollback executor safety (partial failures, double-execute).
  - Mitigation: idempotency keys, locking, step-down traffic shifts, comprehensive E2E tests.
sections.heading: Risks and mitigations

sections.body:

2) What is the default for “suspected breach” action in Dedicated/Private: pause vs immediate rollback for error spikes?

4) What is the policy for suppressing automation during a declared incident: global toggle only, or per-service?
5) Should “monitor missing/stale” block rollouts (fail-closed) for certain tiers, or remain notify-only in MVP?

payload.page_title: Change Freeze and Risk Assessment (SLO/Error Budget Aware)

sections.body:
h1. Summary
This page defines when Redwood enforces change freezes or heightened risk review based on live reliability posture (SLO compliance and error budget burn). These rules apply to production changes for Hosted API and Console.

h1. Why this exists
When services are degraded, deployments often increase customer impact and make diagnosis harder. Error-budget-aware change control prioritizes stability while preserving a clear path for urgent fixes.

h1. Inputs used for decision
* SLO compliance for the last 7 and 28 days
* Error budget remaining for the active SLO period
* Current incident status (active Sev 0/1/2)

h1. Change control states
|| State || Trigger || Allowed changes || Required approvals ||
| Green | No active Sev0/1 and \u2265 60% error budget remaining | Normal changes allowed | Peer + service owner (plus security/SRE if applicable) |
| Yellow | \u003c 60% and \u2265 25% error budget remaining OR sustained alerting for \u003e 30 minutes | Changes allowed with heightened review | Peer + service owner + SRE on-call approval |
| Red | \u003c 25% error budget remaining OR active Sev0/1 OR repeated rollbacks in last 24h | Freeze on non-essential changes | Only incident-related mitigations and fixes | IC + service owner + SRE on-call approval |

h1. How to run a risk assessment (required for Yellow/Red)
1. Identify affected SLOs (latency, availability) and current burn rate.
2. Describe expected impact window and blast radius (services/regions).
3. Confirm rollback can be executed in \u003c 10 minutes.
4. Confirm monitoring coverage for the changed surface area.
5. Decide canary strategy (region vs % traffic).

h1. Change freeze declaration and communication
* SRE on-call or IC declares freeze in #eng-oncall and #eng-releases.
* If customer-impacting degradation exists, coordinate messaging with the status page owner (see Planned Maintenance and Change Communications).

h1. Exemptions
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Incident mitigation and urgent security fixes
* Changes required to stop data loss or billing corruption

All exemptions must be documented in the change record with approving SRE/IC.

h1. Related pages
* Production Change Management Standard (v2)
* Prod Deployment Gates: Hosted API and Console
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook

payload.page_title: Runtime workload signatures and SLO derivation playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a repeatable process for converting observed runtime workload signatures into defensible Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and cost-sensitivity profiles for Redwood inference services. It ties together sampling, profiling, experiment design, and SLO derivation so teams can make consistent, evidence-based SLOs for new routes, model variants, and capacity plans.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all inference-facing HTTP/streaming routes and internal RPCs that contribute to model-serving latency or cost. Excludes: purely offline batch jobs (see eng-infra runbooks) and human-in-the-loop lab experiments.

Definitions
-----------
- Workload signature: a compact description of request shape and distribution (sequence length percentiles, batching patterns, KV cache hit ratio, request concurrency, special flags like streaming or tool-calls).
- Cost-sensitivity: the change in per-request GPU/time cost when a workload attribute shifts (e.g., +10 tokens => +X ms / +Y token-cost).
- SLO bucket: a named target (e.g., P95 latency 120ms for interactive, P99 500ms for high-throughput) tailored for a workload class.

Key Principles
--------------
- Evidence-first: SLOs must be justified by sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments.
- Workload-driven segmentation: avoid one-size-fits-all SLOs; segment by signature clusters that materially change cost/latency.
- Cost-aware guardrails: every SLO must include an associated cost-sensitivity statement used for tradeoff decisions (e.g., whether to enable larger batch sizes or fallback to cheaper model variants).
- Operational observability: each derived SLO must have dashboards, automated alerts, and an attached experiment plan for periodic revalidation.

Procedure: Derive SLOs from workload signatures (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------------------------------
1. Collect signatures (1–2 weeks):
   - Instrument route to emit compact signature blobs at sampling rate 1–5% (configurable per traffic volume). Required fields: route_id, timestamp, seq_len, input_tokens, output_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag, client_tier, model_variant_hint.
   - Example signature JSON (emit to telemetry):

   {
     "route_id": "generate-chat",
     "timestamp": "2025-10-28T14:12:33Z",
     "seq_len": 1024,
     "input_tokens": 128,
     "output_tokens": 256,
     "kv_cache_hit": 0.62,
     "streaming_flag": false,
     "client_tier": "standard"
   }

2. Cluster signatures (offline job):
   - Run k-means / hierarchical clustering on normalized features: seq_len, total_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag (binary), concurrency_hint. Aim for 3–6 clusters per route unless variance indicates more.
   - Save cluster centroids and representative percentiles (p50/p90/p99) for each numeric field.

3. Profile representative clusters (controlled experiments):
   - For each cluster, replay 10k representative requests against target model variants and runtime configurations (batch sizes, quantization profiles, kernel paths). Collect: p50/p90/p99 latencies, tail latency (p999), token throughput, GPU utilization, memory pressure, failure rate.
   - Record cost-per-request estimate (energy + GPU time + amortized infra) using the internal cost-modeler.

4. Construct candidate SLO buckets:
   - Use profiling results to propose SLOs that are achievable with a 95% confidence margin given current infra. Example logic: set P95 latency target to profiling p90 + 15% buffer; set error-rate target to observed mean + 3σ but not exceeding 1%.

5. Attach cost-sensitivity and fallback policy:
   - For each SLO, include a table showing how latency and cost change when you: increase batch_by, enable quantization Q4/Q5, or downgrade to smaller model variant.
   - Define automatic fallback thresholds (e.g., if queue length > 200 and P95 approaching target, route 20% to cheaper variant).

6. Review and publish with runbook:
   - Include owners (service, infra, SRE), approval from product for user-facing impact, and security sign-off when signatures include user data.

7. Deploy SLO and monitor:
   - Create dashboards that show per-cluster SLI trends, cost-per-1000-requests, and deviation from target. Configure alerts: SLO_red (p95 > target for 10m), SLO_yellow (p95 > 90% of target for 15m), cost_alert (cost growth > 20% week-over-week for the cluster).

Representative table: sample SLO derivation for a chat-gen route
----------------------------------------------------------------
| Cluster | Centroid seq_len (p90) | Profiling p95 | Proposed SLO (p95) | Cost/request | Fallback action |
|---------|------------------------:|-------------:|-------------------:|-------------:|-----------------|
| Short-turn | 64 | 80 ms | 95 ms | $0.0009 | no fallback, optimize batching |
| Normal | 256 | 160 ms | 190 ms | $0.0021 | enable burst batching or route 10% to smaller model |
| Long-turn | 1024 | 420 ms | 500 ms | $0.0065 | enable quantization Q4 + degrade non-critical tools |

(When converting to Confluence markup, render as a table with exact values and links to profiling runs.)

Cost-sensitivity matrix (example)
--------------------------------
- Changing batch_size from 1 -> 8 on `Normal` cluster: +20% p95, -30% cost/request.
- Enabling Q4 quantization on `Long-turn`: +12% p95, -45% cost/request, memory drop 18%.

Operational playbook snippets
---------------------------
- When an SLO_red fires (p95 > target for 10m):
  1. Pager to oncall (SRE) and service owner.
  2. Run the quick triage checklist: confirm signature cluster involved, verify ongoing experiment/rollout, check GPU node saturation and preemption events.
  3. If saturation: trigger temporary priority decay policy and increase fallthrough to cheaper variant per SLO fallback policy.
  4. Post-incident: schedule a 2-hour root-cause session and update SLO derivation if recurring.

Best practices and guidance
---------------------------
- Prefer cluster-specific SLIs rather than global route-level; combine for a user-facing composite only when necessary.
- Maintain an experiment repository: every profiling run must have a reproducible seed, input corpus, model hash, and runtime flags.
- Re-derive SLAs quarterly or when a model variant, kernel path, or major infra change is shipped.
- Use conservative buffers for user-facing production routes (15–25%) and tighter buffers for internal tooling (5–10%).

Example: small CLI to extract centroids from signatures (pseudo)
------------------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
python tools/signature_agg.py
  --input s3://redwood-telemetry/signatures/generate-chat/2025-10/
  --sample-rate 0.02
  --cluster 4
  --output /tmp/generate-chat-centroids.json

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Owner: runtime-performance@redwood (primary service owner)
- SRE: oncall-sre@redwood for alerts and incident response
- Review cadence: annual architecture review and post-major-release revalidation.
- Metrics steward: product-analytics for cost attribution and SLA reporting.

References and related pages
----------------------------
- service-profiling-experiment-matrix-and-slo-extrapolation-2026 (profiling matrix and test harness)
- runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026 (kernel selection tradeoffs)
- infra-standards/resource-qos-and-profiling-playbook-2024 (node qos and resource tagging)

Appendix: template for SLO record (to be copied into the SLO catalog)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
- route_id: string
- cluster_id: string
- cluster_signature_examples: list of example signature ids
- derived_SLOs: list of {metric: p95 latency, target_ms: number, buffer_pct: number}
- cost_sensitivity: list of {action: quantize/batch/downgrade, delta_cost_pct: number, delta_latency_pct: number}
- profiling_run_ids: list of run ids
- owners: list of emails
- rollback_plan: short text

Contact
-------
For questions or to request a signature sampling rollout, contact runtime-performance@redwood or open a ticket in the Performance channel.
