payload.page_title: Consolidated Fidelity Governance Blueprint

sections.body:
Overview

This blueprint defines a consolidated governance and commercialization approach for output "fidelity" across Redwood’s product surface (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private, and Optimize). It describes principles, roles, product requirements, design constraints, a cross-functional rollout roadmap, pricing/packaging implications, telemetry and quality gates, and a phased release and experiment plan. This doc is intended for PMs, product engineering, applied ML, finance, and sales leadership.

Goals and motivation

1. Make fidelity a first-class product primitive: expose clear levers (fidelity tiers, fallback variants, quantization switches, latency tiers) that customers can reason about and adopt.
2. Align SLAs, pricing, and operational controls so fidelity transitions are predictable for customers and profitable for Redwood.
3. Provide governance that prevents quality regressions while enabling rapid experimentation (A/B, canary) across customers.

Scope

- Surface areas: Hosted API, Redwood Dedicated, Redwood Private, Redwood Optimize advisor and conductor.
- Fidelity controls included: model variant selection, token-budgeting, quantization profiles, batching/caching fidelity knobs, streaming fidelity negotiation.
- Not in scope: model training fidelity, open-source-model licensing constraints (handled by model-onboarding).

Principles

- Observable: every fidelity change must be instrumented with cost, latency, and quality metrics mapped to prompt-sets.
- Reversible and safe: rollouts must include automatic rollback triggers tied to loss/quality regressions or cost thresholds.
- Commercially explicit: customers know which fidelity tier maps to consumption rates and pricing credits.
- Unified: same governance primitives across hosted, dedicated, and private where feasible.

Governance model (high level)

- Product Council (monthly): PMs from Hosting, Dedicated, Optimize + Applied ML + Finance + Sales. Approves fidelity tier definitions, pricing deltas, and major rollout windows. Owner: product.
- Technical Review Board (bi-weekly): engineering leads from serving runtime, infra, and SRE review operational constraints, rollout automation, and safety checks. Owner: engineering.
- Experiment Review: ad-hoc sign-off for cross-customer experiments that affect fidelity defaults or fallback policies. Owner: applied ML.

Roles & responsibilities

- Product (owner): define tier definitions, customer-facing UX/Docs, commercial mapping.
- Applied ML: quality metrics, prompt-set maintenance, acceptance gates for quantized/low-fidelity variants.
- Eng (Serving Runtime): implement fallback/negotiation hooks, rollout flags, performance profiles.
- Eng (SRE/Platform): SLOs, alerts, capacity planning for staged rollouts.
- Finance & GTM: pricing CAD/negotiation guidance, revenue/regression modeling for tier changes.

Key SLOs and thresholds

- Fidelity-guarded quality SLOs:
  - Regression signal: average rouge-like fidelity score delta across canonical prompt-sets <= 2% per rollout window.
  - Latency SLO by tier: P95 <= 300ms (premium), P95 <= 700ms (standard), P95 <= 1.5s (economy).
  - Availability SLO: 99.9% for hosted premium endpoints; 99.5% for economy.
- Cost signal thresholds (relative to baseline variant): upgrade if cost delta <= +12% for equivalent quality; fallback/rollback if delta >= +30% or if customer spend predictability is violated.

Product requirements (PRD-style)

1) Fidelity Tier Definition API & UX
- Expose named tiers: premium, standard, economy, and adaptive. Each tier includes: model variant set, max tokens-per-request, quantization profile, batching policy, fallback policy.
- UI: per-route fidelity selector in Console with clear cost delta and latency estimate.
- API: per-request header and route-level default for fidelity.

2) Rollout/Experiment Framework
- Canary targets: tenant-level targeting, % traffic, and duration parameters.
- Automatic rollback triggers: quality delta > threshold, cost delta breach, or error-rate increase > 2x baseline.
- Data capture: aligned eval captures (input, reference, model output hash) stored to secure retention.

3) Billing & Commercial Mapping
- Each fidelity tier maps to a multiplier applied to base token consumption (e.g., premium x1.0, standard x0.85, economy x0.6). Multipliers must be configurable per contract.
- Credits reconciliation: fidelity downgrades/upgrades across billing periods must be prorated.

4) Observability & Quality Gates
- Per-route fidelity dashboards: token-cost, p50/p95 latency, quality delta vs baseline prompt-sets, fallback counts.
- Alerting: fidelity-regression PagerDuty channel with severity tiers (SEV3: early warning; SEV2: rollback recommended; SEV1: automatic rollback executed).

Design constraints and non-goals

- Design for multi-tenant safety: avoid noisy-neighbor effects from aggressive batching when a tenant is in premium tier.
- Where runtime differences between Dedicated and Hosted make exact parity impossible, define explicit compatibility matrices and documented fallback behavior.
- Non-goal: providing per-customer bespoke fidelity models outside variant marketplace (handled by enterprise professional services).

Operational rollout plan (phases)

Phase 0 — Preparation (Q4 2026)
- Finalize tier definitions and acceptance prompt-set.
- Implement telemetry panels and acceptance pipelines.
- Finance to define pricing multipliers and crediting logic for internal simulation.

Phase 1 — Internal dogfood (4 weeks)
- Run platform internal tenants on new fidelity tiers. Collect metrics and tune rollback thresholds.
- Owner: product + applied ML.

Phase 2 — Opt-in customers (8–12 weeks)
- Invite 10–15 customers across sizes and verticals to opt-in. Run A/B experiments with controlled traffic percentages.
- Sales/GTM to provide commercial opt-in credits during experimentation.

Phase 3 — Gradual default exposure (6 months)
- Make adaptive tier available as default for new developer accounts with explicit consent and pricing disclosures.
- Expand tier availability across Dedicated clusters where capacity profiles match performance targets.

Phase 4 — Global rollout and pricing general availability
- G/A documentation, billing primitives, and long-term contracts update.

Pricing and packaging implications (table)

| Tier | Price multiplier | Typical latency band (P95) | Recommended use-cases |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Premium | x1.00 | <= 300ms | Production-critical low-latency transactional flows |
| Standard | x0.85 | <= 700ms | Most SaaS features, chat and content generation |
| Economy | x0.6 | <= 1.5s | Bulk generation, offline batch, high-throughput pipelines |
| Adaptive | variable | negotiated | Hybrid workloads — runtime chooses variant based on SLOs and cost targets |

(Implementation detail: multipliers are stored as per-customer configuration keys and applied at charge-time; for Dedicated contracts, multipliers can be overridden by contract SKU).

Observability and telemetry plan

- Required metrics: fidelity_tier, variant_id, request_id, customer_id, prompt_hash, quality_score_delta, tokens_consumed, latency_ms, fallback_triggered.
- Dashboards: per-tenant / global aggregation with retention 90 days by default (extended retention as paid add-on).
- Alert rules: quality_delta > 2.0 percentage points across canonical prompt-set (rolling 6h) -> SEV3; 4.0pp -> SEV2; 6.0pp and ongoing -> SEV1 + auto-rollback.

Quality evaluation and acceptance tests

- Canonical prompt-sets: curated per-vertical with ~500 prompts for primary languages supported. Maintained by applied ML with quarterly refresh.
- Acceptance run: every quantized or low-fidelity variant must pass nightly batch evaluation with acceptance thresholds defined per tier.

Developer and customer UX

- Console: fidelity selector, cost preview, latency estimate, sample outputs from chosen tier.
- API: headers to request fidelity overrides, plus per-response metadata identifying active variant and fallback reasons.
- Docs: migration guide and cheat sheet for choosing tiers.

Release notes and communications

- Release note draft for Phase 2 opt-in, Phase 3 default exposure, and Phase 4 GA. Each note includes: what changed, expected customer impact, rollback plan, and contact channels.
- GTM playbook: messaging templates for sales and success, opt-in crediting mechanics, and escalation contacts.

Open questions / decisions required

1. Exact multiplier values for per-tenant negotiated contracts (Finance input).
2. Retention policy for fidelity evaluation captures in regulated/customer-sensitive contexts (Legal & Security).
3. Compatibility and expectation matrix for on-prem/private deployments where hardware variability may require different fidelity defaults.

Appendix A — Example API snippets

- Request header to request a tier:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "X-Redwood-Fidelity: standard" -d '{"input":"Summarize the following..."}'

- Response metadata sample:
{"variant_id":"gpt-like-q3-std","fidelity_tier":"standard","fallback":"none","tokens":174}

Appendix B — Rollout checklist (owner: product)

1. Acceptance prompt-set verified and signal dashboards green.
2. Billing multipliers configured in staging and validated with simulated invoices.
3. Canary automation configured (traffic targeting and rollback hooks).
4. GTM materials and support runbook published.
5. Legal & security sign-off on capture retention.

Summary

This consolidated governance blueprint balances product velocity with commercial discipline and safety. It creates a repeatable playbook for introducing fidelity as a measurable, monetizable product primitive while protecting customers from regressions. Next steps: finalize multiplier ranges (Finance), lock acceptance prompt-set (Applied ML), and begin Phase 0 workstreams in Q4 2026.
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: SLO definitions for rollout safety (auto-pause/auto-rollback signals)

sections.body:
This document defines which Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are eligible to act as *safety signals* for Redwood rollouts (canary, A/B, staged model deployments) and provides recommended thresholds by customer tier.

These SLOs are consumed by the rollout controller’s SLO evaluator to decide whether to **pause** a rollout or **rollback** traffic to the last known-good baseline.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Hosted API routes (multi-tenant)
- Dedicated capacity routes
- Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments where Redwood operates/observes the serving plane
sections.heading: Applies to

sections.body:
- Quality/regression eval signals (handled by eval/guardrails)
- Multi-region failover (beyond rollback/pause)
sections.heading: Out of scope for initial release

sections.body:
- **Rollout scope**: the specific tuple the evaluator queries against: *(service/route, model version, region, customer tier)*.
- **Baseline**: currently promoted/last-known-good model version and configuration for the same scope.
- **Fast burn / slow burn**: two windows used for SLO evaluation (e.g., 5m and 30m) to catch acute regressions and sustained degradation.
sections.heading: Terminology

sections.body: The rollout controller MAY use the following signals to drive auto actions.
sections.heading: Eligible SLO signal types

sections.body:
- **p95 latency** (primary) for user-perceived responsiveness
- **p99 latency** (secondary) to capture tail amplification during batching/cache changes
sections.heading: Eligible metrics

sections.body:
- Always enabled for interactive/chat generation routes
- Recommended for embeddings and rerank routes where latency variance is meaningful
sections.heading: When to use

sections.body:
- Latency must be scoped to the rollout’s traffic slice (canary/A/B cohort) where possible.
- Latency SLOs must exclude known client-side timeouts and network edge artifacts when those are not actionable by the serving plane.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- **5xx rate** (server errors)
- **non-2xx rate** for specific routes where 429/408 are treated as reliability-impacting (must be explicitly documented per service)
sections.heading: Eligible metrics

sections.body:
- Use **5xx** as the default error signal.
- Include **429** only for tiers where rate limiting is considered a platform regression (rare; must be approved by SRE).
sections.heading: Default eligible definition for rollout safety

sections.body:
Saturation is an eligible signal only if it is *strongly correlated* with imminent latency/error regressions and can be measured reliably at the rollout scope.

Eligible saturation signals (choose at most 1–2 per service to avoid noise):
- **GPU utilization** sustained above threshold (per pool) with corresponding queueing
- **Scheduler queue time / request queue depth** (preferred if available)
- **KV cache eviction rate** or cache miss amplification (runtime-specific; use only when mature)

Saturation signals SHOULD be configured as **pause-only** for MVP unless a service has demonstrated that saturation reliably predicts a user-visible breach.
sections.heading: 3) Saturation / capacity risk signals

sections.body:
- Single-host/node health checks (too noisy; handled by infra autoscaling/repair)
- Debug counters without stable semantics (e.g., “internal warnings”)
- Business metrics (conversion, engagement)
- Unscoped global SLOs that cannot be attributed to the rollout slice (risk of rolling back due to unrelated incidents)
sections.heading: The following MUST NOT be used to trigger auto rollback

sections.body: These are *starting points* intended to be safe and to bias toward preventing widespread customer impact. Services may deviate with SRE approval.
sections.heading: Recommended default thresholds by tier

sections.body:
- Fast burn window: **5 minutes**
- Slow burn window: **30 minutes**
- Decision requires: **fast OR slow window** to be in breach, subject to debounce and minimum samples (see below)
sections.heading: Default evaluation windows

sections.body:
- Latency: at least **N=300 requests** in the fast window OR **N=1,500 requests** in the slow window (per rollout slice)
- Error-rate: at least **N=200 requests** in the fast window OR **N=1,000 requests** in the slow window

If sample sizes are below minimum, the evaluator records **INSUFFICIENT_DATA** and does not auto-rollback.
sections.heading: Auto actions MUST be sample-gated to reduce false positives

sections.body:
The thresholds below are for *incremental regression* during a rollout. They are expressed as either an absolute SLO threshold or a relative regression against baseline.

**How to interpret:**
- Prefer **relative-to-baseline** thresholds when a strong baseline exists for that exact scope.
- Fall back to **absolute** thresholds when baseline is missing or unstable.

| Tier | Latency (p95) | Latency (p99) | Error rate (5xx) | Saturation (pause-only) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted (self-serve) | Breach if p95 > max( baseline * 1.25, baseline + 150ms ) for 5m OR 30m | Breach if p99 > max( baseline * 1.30, baseline + 250ms ) | Breach if 5xx > max( baseline + 0.5pp, 1.0% ) | Queue depth > 2x baseline OR queue time p95 > 100ms |
| Dedicated | Breach if p95 > max( baseline * 1.20, baseline + 100ms ) | Breach if p99 > max( baseline * 1.25, baseline + 200ms ) | Breach if 5xx > max( baseline + 0.3pp, 0.5% ) | Sustained pool saturation (e.g., scheduler queue time p95 > 75ms) |
| Private (managed) | Breach if p95 > max( baseline * 1.15, baseline + 75ms ) | Breach if p99 > max( baseline * 1.20, baseline + 150ms ) | Breach if 5xx > max( baseline + 0.2pp, 0.3% ) | Per-customer saturation signals; must be validated per deployment |

pp = percentage points.
sections.heading: Threshold table (recommended)

sections.body:
- Latency regression multiplier MUST be between **1.05x and 2.00x**
- Absolute latency deltas MUST be between **+25ms and +2,000ms**
- Error-rate absolute thresholds MUST be between **0.1% and 10%**
- Fast window MUST be between **2m and 10m**; slow window between **15m and 60m**

(See ADR-0127 for rationale; these are enforced by policy validation.)
sections.heading: To prevent unsafe configurations

sections.body:
- **Latency breach**: rollback for Dedicated/Private; pause-first for Hosted unless breach is severe (see below)
- **Error-rate breach**: rollback for all tiers (errors typically indicate correctness/outage)
- **Saturation breach**: pause-only by default
sections.heading: Default actions by signal

sections.body: Because Hosted is multi-tenant, we bias toward avoiding rollback oscillation that can create additional load.
sections.heading: Severity escalation (Hosted safety)

sections.body: - If p95 breach is > **1.50x baseline** AND sample size requirements are met, the evaluator may choose **rollback** (otherwise pause).
sections.heading: Hosted severity rule

sections.body:
- Baseline must be the last promoted version for the same rollout scope.
- Baseline must have at least **24 hours of stable traffic** OR pass a “stable baseline” heuristic:
  - No known active incident tags for the scope
  - Monitor data freshness within limits
  - Request volume above minimum

If baseline is unavailable, evaluator uses absolute thresholds and logs **BASELINE_MISSING**.
sections.heading: Relative comparisons depend on a valid baseline

sections.body: Auto actions MUST NOT be driven by stale or missing telemetry.
sections.heading: Monitor freshness and missing data

sections.body:
- Monitor data points must be no older than **2 minutes** for the fast window
- No older than **5 minutes** for the slow window
sections.heading: Freshness requirements

sections.body:
- Evaluator records **MONITOR_STALE** or **MONITOR_MISSING**
- Default behavior: **fail open** (do not rollback) and **pause** only if policy explicitly allows “pause on missing data”

Rationale: missing data is often caused by telemetry issues; rolling back during telemetry outages can hide the root cause and increase instability.
sections.heading: If stale or missing

sections.body:
1) Define the route-level SLOs (latency + error-rate) in the SLO toolkit with the required labels for rollout scope.
2) Ensure dashboards exist for:
   - Baseline vs canary latency and error-rate
   - Monitor freshness/staleness
   - Auto-action outcomes
3) Run a staging simulation (synthetic latency injection + synthetic 5xx) and confirm:
   - Pause triggers on mild regressions
   - Rollback triggers on severe error-rate regressions
   - Audit trail includes monitor IDs, decision trace, and metric snapshot link
4) Enable the policy template for the lowest-risk tier first (typically Hosted internal routes), then expand.
sections.heading: To enable rollout-safety SLOs for a new service or route

sections.body:
- Latency p95 (required)
- Error-rate 5xx (required)
- Latency p99 (recommended for generation/chat)
- Saturation (optional; pause-only)
sections.heading: Minimum required SLO set

sections.body:
- KV cache behavior
- Batching effectiveness
- Token distribution shifts
- Quantization and kernel selection
sections.heading: Model rollouts frequently change tail latency due to

sections.body:
- Prefer p99 monitoring for generation models with long outputs.
- When introducing new batching/kv-cache strategies, temporarily tighten saturation pause thresholds to stop harmful rollouts early.
- If a model is known to change latency distribution (e.g., longer outputs), consider setting thresholds relative to **time-to-first-token (TTFT)** and **time-per-output-token** where available, but only if those monitors are stable and scoped.
sections.heading: Recommendations

sections.body:
- Default action is **pause-first** for latency to reduce flapping across multi-tenant pools.
- Rollback is appropriate for error-rate or severe latency regressions.
sections.heading: Hosted (self-serve)

sections.body:
- Rollbacks are safer because traffic patterns are more stable and capacity is isolated.
- We expect stricter thresholds and faster rollback.
sections.heading: Dedicated

sections.body:
- Deployment environments vary; absolute thresholds should be validated per customer.
- Ensure local monitor collection is reliable before enabling auto rollback.
sections.heading: Private

sections.body:
- SRE owns default thresholds and eligible-signal definitions.
- Service owners own service-specific overrides and must document why they differ.
sections.heading: Ownership and change process

sections.body:
- Updates to this page require review by **Observability Standards (Allison Grant)** and **SLO dashboards/alerts (Aisha Bello)**.
- Changes to enforcement/guardrails must be recorded in an ADR.
sections.heading: Change control

sections.body:
- p95 baseline: 650ms
- Threshold: max(650ms*1.25=812ms, 650+150=800ms) => 812ms
- If p95 over 5m is 900ms with N=1,000 requests: pause; if 1.50x baseline (975ms) exceeded, rollback may be selected.
sections.heading: Example 1: Hosted chat route (pause-first)

sections.body:
- Baseline 5xx: 0.05%
- Threshold: max(baseline+0.3pp=0.35%, 0.5%) => 0.5%
- If 5xx over 5m is 2% with N=5,000 requests: rollback.
sections.heading: Example 2: Dedicated embeddings route (rollback on error spike)

sections.body:
- Queue time p95 exceeds 100ms for 10 minutes
- Action: pause rollout (do not rollback solely on saturation unless explicitly configured and validated)

---
For operational procedures (triage, overrides, suppression), see the runbook: Auto-rollback on SLO breach.
sections.heading: Example 3: Saturation pause only

payload.page_title: Post-Incident Action Triage and Continuous Remediation Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines a standardized, SLO-driven process for triaging post-incident actions and executing continuous remediation across Redwood Inference services. It focuses on converting incident findings into prioritized, time-boxed work items tied to SLOs, capacity commitments, and automated validation using our operational tooling. The goal is to reduce repeat incidents, lower SLO regression risk, and shorten mean time to fix for systemic causes.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to incidents with customer-facing impact (Pages SEV-2/SEV-1) and any SLO breach event detected by the SLO observability pipeline.
- Covers immediate action triage, remediation planning, rollouts, validation, and runbook/tooling updates.
- Not a replacement for the incident commander or postmortem — this is the actionable remediation workflow that starts at the end of the incident timeline.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- SLO-first prioritization: Actions are prioritized by their expected reduction in SLO burn and customer impact, not by ease of implementation.
- Time-boxed remediation: Every remediation is assigned a remediation class (hot, fast, normal) with target SLAs.
- Evidence-driven verification: Automated, reproducible checks must validate each remediation before and after rollout.
- Continuous improvement: Runbooks and tooling are updated as part of the remediation and are included in the completion criteria.
sections.heading: Key principles

sections.body:
- Incident owner / service owner: Ensures the produced action list is accurate and assigned.
- Remediation owner: Implements the fix, drives rollout and validation.
- SLO steward (SRE): Scores each action against SLO impact and approves prioritization.
- QA / Canary owner: Builds canary tests and validation jobs in the observability pipeline.
- Product stakeholder: Confirms business risk/priority when remediation conflicts with roadmap.
sections.heading: Roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
1) Hot (P0): Immediate engineering change required; target remediation window = 72 hours. Examples: misconfiguration causing sustained SLO breach, runaway process consuming KV cache.
2) Fast (P1): High-reduction action; target window = 30 days. Examples: model quantization profile regression identified; autoscaling rule mis-tuning.
3) Normal (P2): Improvements with clear benefit but lower urgency; target window = 90 days. Examples: telemetry gaps, non-critical refactors.
sections.heading: Remediation classification and SLAs

sections.body:
1. Populate the Post-Incident Remediation Board (Jira project: SRE-REM) within 24 hours of incident close. Use the template `SRE-REM - Remediation Template`.
2. For each action, the remediation owner provides: summary, technical cause, estimated effort (T-shirt size), mitigation steps, validation criteria, and rollback plan.
3. SLO steward runs the SLO impact scoring worksheet and assigns an SLO impact score (0-10).
4. Prioritize backlog by:
   - SLO impact score (desc)
   - Customer exposure (desc)
   - Cross-service blast radius
   - Implementation effort (asc)
5. Assign remediation classification (Hot/Fast/Normal) and set target completion date.
sections.heading: Triage procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- 8-10: Immediate SLO breach or recurring >50% daily burn
- 5-7: Noticeable burn, intermittent customer impact, potential to escalate
- 1-4: Low immediate risk; candidate for batching with other tasks
sections.heading: SLO impact scoring quick reference (worksheet excerpt)

sections.body:
- Title (short)
- Severity class (Hot/Fast/Normal)
- SLO impact score
- Affected services/components
- Detailed technical summary
- Proposed change (PR/infra change/service config)
- Validation plan (canary + synthetic checks)
- Rollback plan and guardrails
- Estimated effort and owners
- Link to incident postmortem

Validation and automated checks (required before marking remediation complete):
- Canary job in CI/CD that mimics incident traffic profile (minimum 2 repeats).
- Pre/post metric snapshots for SLOs and error budget burn rate. Include: p50/p95/p99 latency, success rate, token-level rejection rates.
- Synthetic test run showing no regression for the relevant prompt sets (if applicable).
- Telemetry ingestion sanity: logs, traces, and sampling for the change must be available for 14 days.
sections.heading: Action ticket template (required fields)

sections.body:
| Check | Owner | Pass condition | Evidence required |
|--|--|--|--|
| Canary passes under incident-profile load | QA/Canary owner | 0 failures for 1 hour | Canary run ID, logs |
| Latency p99 <= SLO threshold | SRE | p99 <= 1200ms for model-generation svc | Metric snapshot link |
| Error budget burn halts | SRE | Burn rate reduced by >= 60% | Burn-rate graphs |
| No increase in downstream errors | Service owner | Downstream 5xx under baseline | Traces + logs |
sections.heading: Example validation checklist (table-like)

sections.body:
- All Hot remediations require: canary (10% route), feature-flagged rollout, and automated rollback at 5% error-rate delta or 2x burn-rate.
- Fast remediations require a staged rollout (canary -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 24-hour hold windows and metric checks.
- Normal remediations follow a regular deployment cadence but must include synthetic validation post-deploy.
sections.heading: Rollout and gating policy

sections.body:
- Update the affected runbook with a reproducible reproduction section and new remediation steps.
- Add a diagnostic checklist to the runbook that is no longer >3 manual steps without an automated check.
- If the remediation introduced new observability, add dashboards and alerts to the SRE Dashboard catalog.
sections.heading: Runbook and tooling updates (completion criteria)

sections.body:
- If remediation touches autoscaling or capacity configuration, include a capacity rehearsal step: simulate expected traffic for 30 minutes at projected peak and validate scaling events.
- Reserve a temporary capacity pool for Hot remediations that require burst testing. Open a capacity request ticket to infra with the tag `sre-capacity-test` and provide expected GPU/CPU and duration.

Incident review linkages and metrics to track post-remediation:
- Time to remediation (TTRem): time between incident close and remediation completion. Target medians: Hot <= 7 days, Fast <= 45 days, Normal <= 120 days.
- Remediation effectiveness: % of remediations that prevent recurrence within 90 days. Target: >= 85%.
- Runbook coverage: % of incidents where runbook was updated as part of remediation. Target: >= 95%.
- Mean validation automation: percent of remediations with automated validation pipelines. Target: >= 90%.
sections.heading: Capacity and provisioning considerations

sections.body:
1. If remediation target date will be missed, remediation owner must file an `SRE-REM` update and notify SLO steward within 48 hours with a mitigation plan.
2. If product or legal constraints block a remediation, tag the ticket with `blocked-by-policy` and route to Product or Legal for decision within 5 business days.
3. Arbitration: SRE lead + Product manager + Infra lead decide priority tradeoffs for any Hot remediations that compete for capacity or runway. Decision recorded on the remediation ticket.
sections.heading: Escalation and arbitration process

sections.body:
- Jira template: `SRE-REM - Remediation Template` (fields are enforced via Jira schema).
- CI job: `remediation-canary-test` (parameters: service, profile, run-id).
- Observability job: `slo-impact-snapshot` (outputs a JSON artifact attached to ticket). Example CLI:
```
$ infra-cli remediation-canary --service model-gen --profile incident-2026-01 --duration 60m --notify SRE
$ observability-cli slo-impact-snapshot --service model-gen --since incident-start --until now --out artifact://sre/12345.json
```

Post-mortem to remediation handoff checklist (immediate tasks after incident close):
- Confirm incident entry in postmortem repo and link (owner).
- Create SRE-REM board entries for all actionable items (owner).
- SLO steward assigns impact scores (within 48 hours).
- Initial prioritization meeting (weekly SRE triage) adds Hot items to the next sprint if not already scheduled.
sections.heading: Playbook templates and automation hooks (examples)

sections.body:
- Weekly SRE remediation triage meeting: review Hot items, stalled tickets, and capacity conflicts. Attendees: SRE leads, service owners, product liaisons.
- Monthly metrics review: TTRem, effectiveness, and tooling coverage to Engineering leadership.
- Quarterly remediation audit: random sample of remediations audited for evidence, validation artifacts, and runbook updates.

Appendix A — Ticket lifecycle sample (narrative):
- Incident closes on 2026-01-10; postmortem authored and links 4 technical findings. By 2026-01-11, SRE-REM board has 6 tickets. Two items classified Hot (misconfigured autoscaler, missing KV cache TTL), both assigned and given 72-hour windows. By 2026-01-14 both have canary validation passing and are rolled to 100% with no regression. Evidence artifacts are attached and runbooks updated.

Appendix B — Example SLO impact statement (to include in ticket):
"This remediation addresses an autoscaler misconfiguration that caused sustained p99 latency breaches for the model-generation service, burning ~65% of the daily error budget during the incident window. Implementing the corrected scaling policy is expected to reduce p99 latency by 35-50% under current traffic profiles and eliminate the observed error-budget spike."
sections.heading: Reporting and governance cadence

sections.body:
- Link to SLO observability pipeline (internal): /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025
- Remediation board: Jira project SRE-REM
- Postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/postmortem-template
sections.heading: Related pages and artifacts

sections.body:
- 2026-01-15: created by Anika Shah
- 2026-02-10: clarified validation checklist and added capacity rehearsal requirement (Ravi Patel)
sections.heading: Change history

sections.body: - For questions about this playbook, contact the SRE guild (sre-guild@redwood-inference.internal) or the author.
sections.heading: Contact

payload.page_title: SLO Root-Cause Translation and Remediation Workshop Template

sections.body: This page provides a reproducible workshop template for translating an SLO failure or concerning error‑budget trend into concrete capacity and remediation actions. Use this template as part of the post‑incident or monthly SLO review cadence to ensure fixes are (a) scoped with measurable acceptance criteria, (b) costed for capacity impact, and (c) assigned clear owners and timelines.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- After any incident where an SLO (latency, availability, quality) was breached or came within 10% of burning the monthly budget.
- During periodic SLO health reviews when an error‑budget trend shows regression for 2+ weeks across key tenants.
- Pre‑deployment reviews for large model/infra changes that risk SLO consumption.
sections.heading: Intent and when to use

sections.body:
1) Incident Facilitator (SRE lead) — runs the workshop, keeps time, enforces scope.
2) Service Owner (feature/product owner) — provides user impact context and acceptance criteria.
3) Runtime/Infra Engineer — explains runtime telemetry, capacity headroom, and constraints.
4) Observability Engineer — provides query examples, dashboards, and instrumentation gaps.
5) Applied ML / Model Owner (when quality/LLM regressions) — explains prompt/quality regressions and eval results.
6) Finance/Cost Engineering (optional) — reviews cost impact for proposed remediations.
sections.heading: Participants (roles and responsibilities)

sections.body:
- Incident timeline & evidence clip (owner: Incident Lead): timestamped API traces, example tokens, stack traces.
- SLO definition and current burn (owner: Service Owner): metric definition, SLI query, threshold, rolling window.
- Capacity + topology snapshot (owner: Runtime Engineer): pool sizes, GPU types, headroom, recent scale events.
- Sample traffic replay and representative prompt set (owner: Applied ML or QA): 50–500 sample requests prioritized by customer impact.
- Cost delta estimate template pre-filled (owner: Finance/Cost Eng): cost per vGPU/hour, estimated hours for fix, and maintenance overhead.

Workshop agenda (90–120 minutes):
1) 0–10m: Goals & success criteria — facilitator defines what "done" means (e.g., <1% monthly SLO burn within 30 days, or rollback plan + canary for new model).
2) 10–30m: Alignment on facts — short readouts of timeline, SLO metric, capacity snapshot, and sample failing traces.
3) 30–60m: Root‑cause translation exercise — map observed symptoms to probable failure modes using the RCA matrix below.
4) 60–90m: Remediation ideation & selection — generate candidate remediations, cost, risk, and quickness-to-rollout. Prioritize with ICE (Impact, Confidence, Effort) scoring.
5) 90–110m: Action assignment and acceptance criteria — owners, timelines, verification checks, rollback triggers.
6) 110–120m: Publish notes & required follow-ups (doc owners, testing windows, QBR inclusion).
sections.heading: Pre-Workshop artifacts to gather (owner and checklist)

sections.body:
- Symptom: latency p99 spike during morning peak
  - Possible root causes: sudden tail‑latency due to co‑tenant eviction; model cold starts; KV cache thrashing on large context.
  - Evidence to validate: per‑token compute time vs. queuing time; pod restart events; model load times.

- Symptom: sustained error‑budget burn for embeddings endpoint
  - Possible root causes: model degradation after quantization change; traffic shift to heavy embedding clients; upstream payload format changes.
  - Evidence: quality eval diffs; request size distribution; recent rollout tags.
sections.heading: RCA translation matrix (example)

sections.body:
- Configure runtime shims (fastest): e.g., prefer smaller model variant for cheap tenants, enforce max input tokens, apply per‑token admission controls.
- Observability fixes (low cost, high leverage): increase SLI granularity (region, tenant), add synthetic canaries, instrument model variant labels.
- Capacity changes (medium time/cost): add hot replica pool, increase reserved GPU counts for a specific tenant, tune autoscaler thresholds.
- Model changes (higher risk/cost): rollback quantized variant, re‑train prompt anchoring, apply small parameter fine‑tune.
- Traffic shaping (operational & customer coordination): token quotas, rate limits, burst credits with finance approval.
sections.heading: Candidate remediation categories (with examples)

sections.body:
- Columns: Candidate, Expected impact (SLO delta), Confidence, Estimated hours to implement, Revert risk, Cost delta/month, Owner.
- Fill example row: Prefer-small-model-by-tenant | -2% SLO burn | 0.8 | 8h to implement | low | +$400/month | Runtime Team
sections.heading: Decision table (use during remediation selection)

sections.body:
- Impact: 0–10 (SLO reduction estimate translated to points)
- Confidence: 0–10 (evidence strength)
- Effort: 0–10 (implementation time in relative points, lower is better)
- ICE score = (Impact * Confidence) / max(1, Effort)

Verification & acceptance criteria templates (copy into ticket):
- Success metric: “After rollout, observed monthly p99 latency reduced to <= X ms or monthly error‑budget burn < Y% over a 30‑day rolling window.”
- Test plan: synthetic replay of 1M tokens with 95th percentile latency target measured; tenant samples in prod shadow for 72 hours.
- Rollback triggers: sustained SLO regression > 25% of pre‑fix within 24h or error rate spike > 2x baseline.
sections.heading: ICE prioritization quick formula (workshop)

sections.body:
- SLI (Prometheus) example for p95 latency on text-generation endpoints:
  - prometheus: rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate",le!="+Inf"}[5m])
- Error budget burn rate (pseudo PromQL):
  - increase(api_errors_total{service="generation"}[30d]) / increase(api_requests_total{service="generation"}[30d])
- Hot pool utilization (Kubernetes metrics):
  - avg_over_time(gpu_utilization{pool="hot"}[1h])
- Synthetic canary script example (bash):
  - #!/usr/bin/env bash
    for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
      curl -sS -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"canary test"}' >/dev/null
    done

Ticket + runbook creation checklist (copy to JIRA ticket):
- Summary: concise problem statement
- Root cause hypothesis: up to 3 bullet points
- Proposed action(s) and ICE score
- Owner + due date
- Verification steps and rollback criteria (copy acceptance template)
- Cost estimate and approval (if > $1,000/month)
- Link to sample failing traces and synthetic replay inputs
sections.heading: Instrumentation & queries (examples)

sections.body:
- Any remediation that changes fleet capacity requires a preapproved maintenance window and cost signoff if monthly delta > $1k.
- Remediations with uncertain impact (Confidence < 0.5) must be canaried for 72 hours before global roll.
- If multiple teams propose conflicting capacity actions, SRE prioritizes by ICE and customer impact; escalate to SRE management if unresolved after 3 business days.
sections.heading: Follow-up governance rules

sections.body:
- Root cause: quantized model variant increased token decoding tail; evidence: per‑step kernel time increased for last 128 tokens.
- Chosen remediation: revert to previous quantization profile for production traffic and create a canary with 5% traffic to the new quantized profile with 7‑day evaluation (owner: Runtime; due: 2026‑03‑02).
- Verification: synthetic replay with 500k tokens shows p99 latency improvement from 1.9s to 1.2s; reward: accepted.
sections.heading: Example outcomes from a workshop (fictional)

sections.body:
- RCA note template: "Observed, Impact, Hypotheses (1..n), Evidence, Tests to run, Chosen fix, Owner, ETA"
- Action item tracker CSV header: "id,summary,owner,impact,confidence,effort,ice_score,eta,status,verification_link"
sections.heading: Templates and artifacts (copyable)

- eng-sre/runbooks/slo-evolution-capacity-simulations-runbook-2025
- eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025
- eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/oom-cascade-and-memory-throttling-runbook-2026
sections.heading: Related runbooks/pages to consult in the workshop

sections.body:
- Save workshop notes into the service's incident folder and add a monthly check to confirm actions progressed.
- SRE Lead will schedule a 30‑day post‑implementation review to evaluate whether the remediation met acceptance criteria.

Appendix: quick PromQL snippets and example dashboard widgets (copy into Grafana)
- Rolling error budget remaining (30d):
  - 1 - (increase(api_errors_total[30d]) / increase(api_requests_total[30d]))
- Per‑tenant p99 latency heatmap query suggestion: use label_replace to collapse tenant tags beyond top N.

payload.page_title: Quantized Model Memory Leak Forensics + SLO Impact Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This playbook defines a standard, operationalized investigation and mitigation path for memory leaks observed in quantized model serving stacks. It ties the technical forensic steps to SLO impact assessment, error-budget remediation, and capacity decisions. Use this when serving instances running quantized models (INT8/4/LLM quantization variants) exhibit progressive memory growth, OOM cascades, or unexplained eviction behavior.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Redwood Inference internal serving clusters and private deployments where quantized kernels (qint8/q4 variants) are used.
- Covers detection, immediate mitigation, evidence capture, root-cause forensics, SLO impact estimation, and post-incident remediation.
- Not a replacement for the OOM cascade runbook (link above); this document focuses on leak patterns that are slow-burning and correlated with quantized-mode memory paths.

Summary of intent
------------------
- Rapidly stabilize customer-facing SLOs (p95 latency, availability) while preserving forensic evidence.
- Collect minimal viable artifacts to reproduce and attribute leaks to code, kernel, model, or workload patterns.
- Provide a repeatable SLO-impact template so product and SRE can agree on credits/remediation.

Signals that trigger this playbook
--------------------------------
- Sustained monotonic increase in per-container RSS (>= 5% upward trend over 30m) for quantized-serving pods.
- Repeated node-level swap activity or kernel OOM events tied to inference processes.
- Elevated OOM kill rate for model-serving processes without concurrent CPU/IO spikes.
- P95/P99 latency regressions with correlated allocation-growth metrics (kv-cache residency anomalies).
- Alerts: qserv.memory-growth-alert, qserv.swap-activity-warning, qserv-oom-trend-signal.

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Primary: eng-sre-model-serving oncall (pager: #sre-model-serving).
- Secondary: eng-serving-runtime team (owners: runtime-kernel-leads).
- Escalation timeline: 0–10m stabilize, 10–45m evidence collection, 45–120m mitigation & capacity decisions.

Immediate stabilization (first 0–10 minutes)
--------------------------------------------
1. Mark incident and notify affected stakeholders: SRE, Runtime, Customer Success for impacted tenants.
2. Toggle conservative autoscale policy: set autoscale.max_replicas = current_replicas + 1 and autoscale.scale_cooldown = 300s.
3. Enable per-tenant token-priority throttling for noisy tenants (if enabled): apply policy: priority_level = 0 for background jobs.
4. If OOMs are ongoing, move traffic off affected nodes: cordon node(s) and use drift-safe drain (--graceful 120s).
5. If immediate rollback candidate exists (kernel patch or quantization fallback), follow canary rollback procedure: roll back 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 15m observation windows.

Evidence collection (10–45 minutes) — minimal reproducible set
-----------------------------------------------------------
Collect artifacts in order of decreasing volatility. Preserve timestamps and correlate to SLO telemetry.
- Process snapshots: `pstree -paw` and `pmap -x <PID>` for inference workers.
- Heap/allocator traces: run jemalloc profiling snapshot (if enabled): `MALLOC_CONF=prof:true,lg_prof_interval:22` and `jeprof` capture.
- Kernel dmesg and /var/log/kern.log (capture last 1h): `journalctl --since "1 hour ago" -u qserv`
- Runtime internal counters: kv-cache hits/misses, kv-cache checksum drift, per-request KV-residency (expose via /debug/metrics).
- GPU memory accounting (if hybrid host/GPU leak suspected): `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,used_memory --format=csv` and `rocm-smi --showdrm` as applicable.
- Environment: `pip freeze` for deployed runtime image, quantization lib versions, and /etc/ld.so.cache listing.
- Core dumps: enable temporary core collection: `sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern=/var/crash/qserv-%e.%p.core` and capture compress+hash.
- Container runtime traces: `ctr logs`, `docker inspect`, and `runc exec --log`.

Evidence checklist (mark during incident)
---------------------------------------
- [ ] Process memory growth graph (30m window) for affected containers
- [ ] Kernel OOM/kill events matched to pids
- [ ] jemalloc/allocator profile snapshot keyed to timestamp
- [ ] Quantization kernel version and symbol map
- [ ] Sample request payload(s) that reproduce the growth (anonymized)
- [ ] GPU memory trace if applicable
- [ ] Core dump(s) or tcmalloc/heap profile files uploaded to incident storage

Forensics deep dive (45–240 minutes)
------------------------------------
1. Reproduce locally in isolated canary: spin a canary cluster with identical runtime image, model shard, and quantization flags. Replay captured sample requests (use replay harness described below).
2. If leak reproduces, increment debug levels to trace allocations with symbolized stacks. Use `gdb` on a live pid if safe, or `perf record -g` for offline analysis.
3. Compare allocator profiles across quantized vs. non-quantized variants to isolate kernel vs. runtime allocator differences.
4. Correlate KV-cache eviction patterns with memory growth — are cached prefixes not being released due to a reference counting bug?
5. Validate third-party kernel/wasm/FP16 libs: check known CVEs and prior bug reports.

Telemetry and queries (examples)
-------------------------------
- Per-pod memory growth: PromQL: rate(container_memory_usage_bytes{job=\"qserv\"}[5m]) > 0 and increase(container_memory_usage_bytes{job=\"qserv\"}[30m]) > (0.05 * avg_over_time(container_memory_usage_bytes{job=\"qserv\"}[30m]))
- OOM kill spikes: increase(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason=\"OOMKilled\"}[10m]) > 0
- Allocation hotspots: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (source_file) (increase(allocator_alloc_ns_bucket[15m])))

Replay harness (how to reproduce safely)
--------------------------------------
1. Use the incident replay cluster (namespace: replay-<incident_id>) with isolated quota and no production traffic.
2. Replay requests using the capture: `replay-cli --source s3://incidents/<id>/trace.json --concurrency 1 --rate 50/s --target qserv-canary:8080`
3. Run heap/jemalloc profiling concurrently and stream profiles to incident S3.

SLO impact assessment template
-----------------------------
- Affected SLOs: list (example: text-generation p95 latency, embedder availability 99.9)
- Window: <start_ts> to <end_ts>
- Measured breach: metric, observed value, SLO threshold, breach duration
- Error-budget consumption: estimated tokens/requests impacted and % of monthly budget consumed
- Customer-impact summary: tenant IDs, request classes, any credit/refund recommendations

Capacity & error budget decisions (playbook rules)
-------------------------------------------------
- If incident causes <= 1% monthly error-budget consumption and is contained within 3h, document remediation and continue normal SLO governance.
- If > 1% but <= 5% and mitigation requires capacity headroom > 10%, initiate temporary capacity carveout: reserve burst pool with preemptible capacity and update SLO ticketing.
- If > 5% or multi-tenant widespread, invoke emergency capacity protocol and prioritize critical tenants per tenant-priority-matrix.

Mitigation options (ranked)
--------------------------
1. Software workaround: enable quantization-fallback flag (runtime will load float16 kernel path) for affected model versions. Rollout via canary.
2. Hotpatch: apply small allocator-fix if available following the emergency hotpatch checklist.
3. Traffic shaping: strip long-response/chain requests with advisory header X-Redwood-Degrade: true.
4. Capacity: spin dedicated warm-pool nodes with larger headroom, prefer nodes with increased host memory ratio.

Post-incident remediation (48–90 days cycle)
-------------------------------------------
- Short term (0–7d): merge temporary rollback or flag as permanent with test coverage.
- Medium term (7–30d): add synthetic canaries that exercise edge-case quantized paths and run daily memory-regression checks.
- Long term (30–90d): schedule allocator/quantization kernel code review, fuzzing harness for prefix eviction logic, and a SLA review with Product for model owners.

Incident review responsibilities and artifacts to attach
-----------------------------------------------------
- Incident lead: SRE oncall — produce TL;DR and timeline within 24h.
- Runtime owner: provide kernel-level analysis and patch plan.
- Attachments: all artifacts from Evidence checklist, replay traces, reproduction guide, and SLO impact template.

Runbook commands and helpers (copyable snippets)
------------------------------------------------
- Capture processes: `kubectl -n <ns> exec -it <pod> -- pmap -x 1 > /tmp/pmap-$(date +%s).txt`
- Enable temporary jemalloc prof: `kubectl -n <ns> exec <pod> -- env MALLOC_CONF=prof:true jeprof -d /tmp/profiles`
- Create replay namespace: `kubectl create ns replay-<incident_id> && kubectl apply -f replay-quota.yaml -n replay-<incident_id>`

Configuration table (critical thresholds)
----------------------------------------
| Signal | Threshold | Action |
| container_memory_delta_30m | > 5% | Trigger qserv.memory-growth-alert and start forensic snapshotting |
| kube_oom_kills_10m | > 1 | Cordon node, begin immediate traffic shift |
| p95_latency_increase_15m | > 20% | Enable token-priority throttling for noisy tenants |

(When adding thresholds, notify observability owners to validate noise sensitivity and false-positive rates.)

Prevention checklist (for platform roadmap)
-----------------------------------------
- Add memory-leak unit tests for quantized kernels in CI and nightly leak-detection job.
- Expand canary matrix to include mixed-quantization request shapes (long prefix + multi-tool calls).
- Bake allocator-coverage into runtime fuzzing for prefix reference cycles.
- Maintain a compatibility map of quantization library versions to kernel symbols.

Appendix: common root causes observed historically
------------------------------------------------
- Reference-counting regression in kv-cache when using compressed representation.
- jemalloc arena fragmentation with long-lived small allocations from quantized kernel.
- Third-party quantization library holding persistent GPU host-side buffers.
- Lazy deserialization bug: repeated small allocations that are never freed due to exception paths.

Links and related runbooks
-------------------------
- OOM cascade and memory throttling runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/oom-cascade-and-memory-throttling-runbook-2026
- Forensic telemetry snapshot policy: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/forensic-telemetry-snapshotting-and-slo-evidence-retention-policy-2023
- SLO impact and error-budget guidance: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-oncall-escalation-and-capacity-triggers-2026

Contacts and oncall rotations
----------------------------
- SRE model-serving rotation: @sre-model-serving (primary)
- Runtime kernel leads: Marco Silva, Priya Reddy
- Observability owner: Aisha Kapoor

Change log
----------
- 2026-02-14 created by Claire Nguyen (initial draft)
- 2026-03-02 reviewed and published after tabletop rehearsal (minor clarifications to evidence checklist)

payload.page_title: Incident Review: Tool-call argument JSON malformed in streaming (us-east)

sections.body: On 2025-02-12, a configuration canary in us-east introduced malformed JSON in tool/function calling arguments for a small subset of streaming requests. At least one dedicated customer escalation (HelioPay) reported strict JSON parsing failures.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Symptom: `tool_calls[].arguments` contained trailing commas or invalid escaping
- Primary impact: customer tool router failed to deserialize arguments; resulted in request retries and error spikes
- Affected: streaming-enabled tool calls with arguments spanning multiple deltas
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- External: customer escalation via Support (SUP-1842)
- Internal: increased 5xx rate in a dedicated tenant route; no automated alert existed for JSON validity
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 2025-02-10 23:00: canary enabled `tool_args_delta_coalesce_v2` in us-east
- 2025-02-12 15:10: customer escalation reported malformed JSON
- 2025-02-12 16:05: rollback of `tool_args_delta_coalesce_v2` completed
- 2025-02-13 09:00: CS published workaround guidance
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: The streaming delta coalescer appended separators when joining tool-call argument fragments and did not correctly handle the end-of-object boundary when a fragment ended with a comma token. This produced an extra comma immediately before `}` in rare chunk boundary cases.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- Rolled back the canary flag in us-east
- Provided customer workaround guidance (disable streaming for tool calls; validate + retry)
sections.heading: Mitigation

sections.body:
1. Add end-of-tool-call JSON validation in the serializer path
2. Add metric: `tool_args_json_valid_rate` per region/model
3. Add alert when valid rate < 99.9% for 15 minutes
sections.heading: Corrective actions

sections.body:
- Jira: SUP-1842
- Slack: #support ts=1739293321

payload.page_title: SLO Saturation Incident Evidence Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook describes the standardized evidence collection and containment sequence for incidents where one or more SLOs are saturating (sustained burn or sudden spike) and error budget exhaustion is imminent or has occurred. It is intended for oncall SREs, service owners, and post-incident reviewers.

Scope:
- Applies to production inference endpoints for Redwood API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Primary focus: availability (failed requests), correctness (model-level regressions tied to routing/variants), and latency SLOs for serving runtime.
- Excludes incidents that are purely infra provisioning (e.g., provider console outage) unless they cause downstream SLO saturation.

Goals:
1. Capture authoritative telemetry and evidence within the first 30 minutes.
2. Preserve replayable artifacts for post-incident analysis.
3. Provide a decision matrix for immediate mitigation (throttles, graceful degradation, variant fallback).
4. Produce an evidence bundle suitable for a blameless incident review within 72 hours.

Owner & Escalation:
- Primary owner: service oncall (model-serving-team).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre incident commander.
- Escalation to Product & Solutions Engineering when customer-facing SLA breach is likely.

Key Signals (Immediate checks) - first 5 minutes:
- Error budget consumption rate: check monthly and rolling-24h usage. Expected normal burn < 2% per day for high-tier SLOs.
- Latency quantiles: 50th/95th/99th for token-generated paths and embedding pipelines.
- Request success rate (HTTP 2xx vs 5xx/4xx) per route/model.
- Model variant mix: current routing percentages and any recent rollout.
- Autoscaler events: recent scale-ups/scale-downs, failure to scale, and preemption logs.

Evidence Collection Checklist (strict order) - collect within 30 minutes:
1) Snapshot SLO status dashboard:
   - Export SLO dashboard (PNG + CSV) and attach to incident.
2) Telemetry snapshots (time-window = start-30m to start+30m):
   - Prometheus queries (PromQL) export for: request_rate, error_rate, latency_quantiles, kv_cache_hit_ratio, active_gpu_pools, model_memory_pressure.
   - Example query (PromQL):
     ```
     sum(rate(redwood_api_request_total{route=~"/v1/(generate|chat|embed).*"}[5m])) by (route,model)
     ```
   - Export as CSV and raw metrics JSON.
3) Token-level traces and spans:
   - Pull representative traces for both successful and failing requests (trace IDs).
   - Key fields: model_version, routing_decision, kernel_variant, batch_id, KV_cache_hit, gpu_id.
4) Request/response samples (redact PII):
   - Save 20 request pairs that match the failure mode across different tenants/keys.
   - Use sampling: top failed routes and random good requests for baseline.
5) Autoscaler and cluster events log (k8s events, instance lifecycle):
   - Export events for pods/nodes in affected clusters.
6) Scheduler and runtime diagnostics:
   - Runtime OOMs, CUDA OOMs, CUDA meminfo snapshot, kernel selection warnings.
7) Model artifact metadata:
   - Model hash, quantization profile, tokenizer version, pinned variant.
8) Routing policy snapshots and recent changes:
   - Rollout config, canary weight history, and policy fallback rules.
9) Customer-facing tickets and alerts correlation:
   - Link customer incidents, support tickets, and external status page activity.
10) Resource-level counters: GPU utilization, vCPU, host network drops, disk pressure.

Containment Playbook (initial triage steps - 0 to 30 minutes)
1) Stabilize telemetry and communication (0-5m):
   - Create incident channel (Slack + PagerDuty record).
   - Post high-level symptom: affected routes, SLOs impacted, rough ETA for next update (T+10m).
2) Apply safe degradations (5-15m):
   - If latency SLOs breach and error budget burn is high: enable model-variant fallback to smaller quantized variant (pre-approved variants only).
   - If availability is the issue: enable rate-limiting ingress (per-token priority first), route low-priority tenants to degraded mode (embedding-only circuit).
   - If autoscaler failing: manually scale warmed pools (reserve-hot-pool) to absorb burst if capacity budget permits.
3) Temporary routing and throttling (15-30m):
   - Apply policy: throttle tokens per-key to configured thresholds (see table below).
   - Enable prefix/KV cache fast-path for eligible requests.

Mitigation Decision Matrix
- Table: Metric | Trigger | Immediate action | Risk
  - "Error rate > 0.8% for 10m" | Triggers canary rollback to last healthy variant | Rollback split traffic to previous model | Low (if canary recent)
  - "99th latency > 2x SLO for 5m" | Route to lower-latency quantized variant | Enable variant fallback or increase batching window | Medium (quality impact)
  - "Error budget burn > 50% in 24h" | Activate admission control for non-critical tenants | Apply token-level throttles and customer priority gates | Medium-High

Admission Control & Throttles (configuration table)
- default_per_key_tps: 10 (tokens/s)
- burst_capacity: 50 tokens
- priority_levels: [system, enterprise, standard, free]
- preempt_policy: preempt lower priority when headroom < 15%

For oncall: CLI snippets and queries to run
- Export top failing routes (Prometheus):
  ```
  topk(20, sum(rate(redwood_api_error_total[5m])) by (route,model))
  ```
- Get per-tenant error budget usage (example SQL against billing_evidence):
  ```
  SELECT tenant_id, sum(errors) as errors, sum(tokens) as tokens, errors/tokens as error_rate FROM inference_usage WHERE ts >= now() - interval '1 day' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY error_rate DESC LIMIT 50;
  ```
- Snapshot traces for a sample trace id:
  ```
  curl -sS "https://traces.internal.redwood/v1/trace/{TRACE_ID}" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TRACE_DUMP_TOKEN" > /tmp/trace-{TRACE_ID}.json
  ```

Evidence Bundle (what to attach to ticket)
- SLO dashboard PNG and CSV
- Prometheus exported CSVs and raw JSON for queries above
- 20 request samples (redacted) and 5 representative trace files
- Autoscaler events export and k8s events, with timestamps
- Runtime logs from affected pod(s) (last 1 hour)
- Model artifact metadata and routing config snapshot

Post-incident actions (72 hours)
1) Incident timeline and causation hypothesis: use evidence bundle to fill template.
2) Fix backlog: rank remediation items into Immediate (hotfix), Near-term (2–4 weeks), and Long-term (quarterly).
3) SLO adjustments: if incident caused by a model rollout, pause rollouts until canary checks expanded; update canary criteria (e.g., include 99th-by-model metrics).
4) Capacity & budget changes: recommend headroom increases or revised autoscaler thresholds if capacity more frequently saturates.
5) Runbook updates: capture any missing telemetry or automation that would speed containment next time.

Forensic artifacts and storage policy
- Store evidence bundle in incident evidence bucket: s3://redwood-incident-evidence/{incident-id}/. Retain for 1 year unless legal holds apply.
- All artifacts must be immutable (versioned) and checksummed.

Checklists for the postmortem (template fields)
- Title, incident id, severity, owner, start/stop times.
- SLOs impacted (exact numerics and windows).
- Evidence snapshot references (S3 paths).
- Root cause hypothesis and confidence level.
- Action items with assignees and ETA.

Related runbooks and references
- SLO escalation thresholds and oncall triggers: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-oncall-escalation-and-capacity-triggers-2026
- Capacity governance: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025
- Runtime OOM handling: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/oom-cascade-and-memory-throttling-runbook-2026

Appendix A — Example evidence timeline (text table)
- T+0m: Pager triggers, create channel, collect SLO snapshot
- T+5m: Top failing routes and top tenants exported
- T+10m: Traces and 20 request samples collected
- T+20m: Autoscaler and k8s events exported, runtime mem snapshots taken
- T+30m: Containment actions applied (throttle / fallback) and update posted

Appendix B — Safe fallback variant policy (excerpt)
- Only variants marked `fallback: true` in model-catalog are eligible for automated fallback.
- Fallback change must preserve token accounting and comply with enterprise customer pinning.

Notes on privacy and redaction
- All request/response samples must have PII removed before attaching to evidence. Use the redwood-internal redact tool: `redwood redact --file requests.ndjson --out requests.redacted.ndjson`.

Revision history:
- 2026-11-03: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft)
- 2027-01-18: Published after review by Ravi Singh and Elena Park (added admission-control table and evidence storage policy)

Contact: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) — for clarifications and suggested improvements.

payload.page_title: Automated Customer Incident Reporting and SLO Impact Generator

sections.body:
Summary:

This document defines the design, operational runbook, verification checks, and customer-facing templates for Redwood's Automated Customer Incident Reporting and SLO Impact Generator (ACIR-SIG). ACIR-SIG produces standardized, auditable customer incident summaries within a defined SLA window after an incident is classified as customer-impacting. The system computes SLO impact automatically from telemetry and timeline evidence, assembles a concise narrative, and supports automated delivery to customers (via Console, email, or support ticket) with human-in-the-loop gating.

Goals and scope:
- Goal: Reduce time-to-customer-summary while preserving accuracy, traceability, and blameless language.
- Scope: infra and inference incidents that affect production API responses (latency, availability, errors). Excludes: billing, account-level policy, or non-production incidents.
- Output: structured incident summary (human-readable + machine JSON payload) and an SLO impact statement.

Ownership and roles:
1) SRE oncall: responsible for verification and approval when gating is required.
2) Incident commander (IC): final sign-off for any customer report that contains mitigation details or security-sensitive statements.
3) Customer Success (CS): decides routing and cadence for customer notifications and escalations.
4) Reporting service (service-owner: ops-tooling): implements ACIR-SIG automation and maintains templates.

Key constraints and principles:
- Always calculate SLO impact from the canonical SLO aggregator (slo-aggregate-service) and telemetry (tracing, api-metrics, regional-health). Do not use local approximations.
- Maintain a human-in-the-loop for incidents where the automated confidence < 92% (see confidence rules).
- Use standardized, blameless language and give measurable impact (requests affected, time windows, and computed %SLO burn).
- Store evidence pointers (trace IDs, query snippets, dashboards) in the report payload for audits and follow-ups.

SLO impact computation (algorithm):
- Inputs:
  - timeseries of successful requests S(t) and total requests T(t) at 1s aggregation or the highest fidelity available.
  - policy: SLO target (e.g., availability 99.9% over 30d) and SLO window used for customer-facing burn calculation (typically rolling-30d).
  - incident window [t_start, t_end] defined by timeline service.
- Steps:
  1) Compute baseline SLO compliance before the incident: baseline_compliance = sum_{t < t_start}(S(t))/sum_{t < t_start}(T(t)) over a baseline period (default 24h).
  2) Compute incident compliance: incident_compliance = sum_{t in [t_start,t_end]}(S(t))/sum_{t in [t_start,t_end]}(T(t)).
  3) Convert to SLO burn for the rolling window:
     - delta_unavailability = max(0, target - incident_compliance) * (duration_of_window_weight)
     - approximate SLO%_burn = (sum_{window} expected_bad_seconds_from_incident) / (total_window_seconds * (1 - target)) * 100
- Simplified formula (used by ACIR-SIG for short reports):
  SLO_burn_percent = round(100 * ((target - incident_compliance) * incident_duration_seconds) / (rolling_window_seconds * (1 - target)), 2)
- Example:
  - target = 99.9% (0.999), rolling_window_seconds = 30*24*3600 = 2,592,000s, incident duration = 900s, incident_compliance = 0.95.
  - SLO_burn_percent = 100 * ((0.999 - 0.95) * 900) / (2,592,000 * (1 - 0.999)) = 100 * (0.049 * 900) / (2,592,000 * 0.001) = 100 * 44.1 / 2592 = 1.70% (rounded).

Confidence scoring and gating rules:
- Confidence inputs (scored 0–100):
  - telemetry_coverage (percentage of requests covered by high-fidelity metrics): weight 40
  - timeline_agreement (percent overlap between automated detection and timeline boundaries): weight 20
  - anomaly_correlation (correlation of errors/latency with topology/event): weight 20
  - evidence_linkage (presence of traces/logs matching top error signatures): weight 20
- Final confidence = weighted_sum(components).
- Gating thresholds:
  - confidence >= 92: auto-generate and auto-send short customer summary (no mitigation detail) after 2h post-incident verification window.
  - 75 <= confidence < 92: auto-generate draft; require SRE oncall verification and IC approval.
  - confidence < 75: do not generate automated customer content; produce internal report only.

Automated customer summary template (short):
- Title: (Service) Incident Summary — (YYYY-MM-DD) — (region)
- One-line impact: During (time window), customers experienced increased (errors/latency/availability) affecting approximately N requests (~X% of requests) in (region).
- What happened: brief description of root cause or leading hypothesis (automated, with confidence).
- What we did: mitigation steps taken and timeframe.
- SLO impact: SLO_burn_percent for rolling window and absolute requests affected.
- Links & evidence: dashboard links, trace IDs, support ticket link for follow-up.
- Next steps: planned remediation and expected ETA when available.

Full machine payload (JSON) — example snippet for automation (ACIR-SIG sends this to CS or support):
{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-1234",
  "service": "inference-api",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "window": "2026-08-14T15:12:00Z/2026-08-14T15:27:00Z",
  "requests_affected": "18234",
  "approx_pct_requests": "3.6",
  "slo_burn_pct": "1.7",
  "confidence": "94",
  "evidence": ["dash://api-availability/overview", "trace://abc123"],
  "narrative": "A partial control-plane configuration regression caused router miss-paths leading to elevated 5xxs for 15 minutes. Mitigation: rollback of config at T+6."
}

Automation architecture (high level):
- Inputs:
  - slo-aggregate-service (canonical SLO metrics)
  - telemetry-mesh (metrics/traces/logs)
  - timeline-service (incident boundaries and annotations)
  - incident-bus (events from PagerDuty/ops)
- Components:
  - generator-worker: computes SLO burn and assembles payloads.
  - confidence-evaluator: calculates confidence and determines gating.
  - draft-store: stores auto-drafts for human review (if needed).
  - delivery-orchestrator: posts to Console, creates CS ticket, or sends email.
- Safety layers:
  - rate limiter: ensures only one auto-customer report per incident, and no more than one per hour for the same customer group.
  - redaction module: strips PII or security-sensitive fields per policy.
  - audit logger: immutable storage of generated payloads and final send event (retention policy defined below).

Runbook: step-by-step operator flow when a draft is generated and human gate required:
1) Alert: oncall receives automated draft notification (Slack + Console).
2) Quick checks (5–10 min): verify top evidence links, ensure traces contain indicative errors, confirm region and affected customers.
3) Approve or reject: Approve via Console button to publish; reject sends back to draft with reason.
4) If approved, CS will receive the published summary and follow-up engagement steps are initiated automatically.
5) If rejected, SRE tags draft with notes and sets auto-resend window to 2h.

Manual override and safety escalation:
- IC can hold customer notifications for up to 24h for incidents involving legal, compliance, or high-sensitivity customers.
- If an automated summary is already sent and later found inaccurate, publish a correction using the same payload schema and include a clear correction header.

Verification checklist (pre-send):
- [ ] Evidence pointers present (>=2 of {dashboard, trace, logs})
- [ ] SLO computation cross-checked by slo-aggregate-service snapshot
- [ ] PII redaction module passed (redaction=false means pass)
- [ ] Confidence >= configured threshold for auto-send or IC approval obtained
- [ ] Delivery channel contact list validated for affected customer segments

Operational observability and metrics for ACIR-SIG itself:
- Metric: acir.reports.generated (count) — label by outcome: auto_sent/draft/rejected/corrected
- Metric: acir.processing.latency (ms) — time from incident-closed to draft ready
- Metric: acir.confidence.distribution — histogram of confidence scores
- Alert: if acir.processing.latency P95 > 45min for 3 hours => paging to ops-tooling

Retention and audit policy:
- Generated payloads and evidence pointers retained for 365 days in immutable audit store.
- Access to full payloads limited by RBAC: engineering/incident-review and CS lead roles, security/legal by approval.

Security and privacy notes:
- Redaction rules are centrally controlled: do not include customer payloads, secrets, or raw logs in customer-facing narrative. Evidence pointers are allowed but must not embed credentials.
- For incidents involving regulated customers, default confidentiality escalates to 'restricted' and a manual IC approval is required before any outgoing message.

Testing and validation cadence:
- Quarterly TT (tabletop) exercises: validate automated outputs against mock incidents.
- Monthly synthetic incidents: run ACIR-SIG in shadow mode to measure drift in confidence and SLO calculation correctness.

Rollout and migration plan for first production release:
1) Phase 1 (shadow): 2 months, run in draft-only mode for a subset (20%) of incidence types.
2) Phase 2 (co-pilot): human-in-the-loop gating required for all drafts; telemetry and metrics validated.
3) Phase 3 (autorelease): enable auto-send for confidence >= 92; monitor metrics and enable roll-back flag for first 30 days.

Appendix A — Example customer-facing short summary (final):
Service: Redwood Inference — Hosted API
Date: 2026-08-14
Impact window: 15:12–15:27 UTC
Summary: Between 15:12–15:27 UTC customers in us-west-2 experienced elevated 5xx errors affecting approximately 18k requests (~3.6% of normal request volume). We rolled back a recent control-plane configuration change at 15:18 which restored normal routing by 15:18:30 and fully recovered by 15:27.
SLO impact: Estimated to consume 1.7% of the 30-day availability budget for Hosted API (99.9% target).
Links: Dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/incident-1234 Trace: trace://abc123 Ticket: https://support.redwood.ai/t/INC-2026-1234
Next steps: Root cause analysis in progress; RCA will be published within 72 hours.

Appendix B — Quick references:
- SLO aggregation playground: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/slo-aggregate-playground
- Incident timeline canonicalization: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/incident-hypothesis-repro-environment-spec-2024
- PII redaction policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-management/redaction-policy

Questions or feedback: reach out to the ops-tooling owners (ops-tooling@redwood.ai) or file improvements via the Console suggestions flow.

Change log:
- 2026-01-10: Initial draft (Priya Natarajan)
- 2026-04-02: Added confidence scoring schema and gating thresholds (Jonah Meyer)
- 2026-08-15: Added rollout plan, retention table, and expanded examples (Sofia Alvarez)

payload.page_title: incident-forensics-evidence-handoff-procedure-2026

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This document defines the standard procedure for collecting, preserving, and handing off forensic evidence after a major service incident at Redwood Inference. It focuses on: SLO/error-budget impact artifacts, capacity and topology evidence, telemetry and trace capture, and chain-of-custody/audit steps so evidence is admissible for post-incident analysis, legal requests, and reliability initiatives. This is an operational runbook intended to be executed by SRE oncall and the incident commander.

Scope
-----
- Services covered: inference-gateway, model-router, kv-cache, request-proxy, batch-ingest
- Incident severity: Sev1 / Sev2 that triggers a full post-incident review (PIR) or legal/data requests
- Evidence types: logs, traces, metrics, profiling snapshots, model artifacts, autoscale events, cloud provider capacity events, routing and rollout state

Owner & Contacts
------------------
- Primary owner: SRE Incident Forensics Squad (contact on-call: #sre-oncall)
- Service owners: listed in service-catalog page (see related_pages below)
- Legal / Privacy escalation: security@redwood.com (required for any PII exposure)

Why this matters
------------------
- Ensures consistent SLO impact measurement for runbook improvements and error-budget accounting.
- Preserves evidence needed for capacity planning exercises and reliability initiatives.
- Provides auditable chain of custody for internal/external compliance reviews.

Pre-incident / Prerequisites
---------------------------
1) Ensure incident ID and canonical artifact bucket are created at incident start: INCIDENT_ID format rdx-YYYYMMDD-NNN (runbook automation does this).
2) Ensure oncall has access to s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/ and temporary encryption key via KMS alias: alias/incident-enc.
3) Ensure automation token (read-only) for telemetry APIs is available in vault path secret/incidents/automation-token.

Immediate collection checklist (first 2 hours)
--------------------------------------------
1) Create artifact path and initial manifest (owner: incident commander)
   - s3 path: s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/rdx-20260301-001/ (replace with INCIDENT_ID)
   - Create manifest file manifest-<INCIDENT_ID>.yaml with metadata (who, why, timestamp).
2) Capture SLO and error-budget snapshot (owner: SRE oncall)
   - Query SLO service: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://slo.internal.redwood/api/v1/snapshot?service=inference-gateway&window=30d > slo-snapshot.json
   - Rationale: this snapshot is the baseline for post-incident error-budget burn calculations.
3) Export last 48 hours of metrics at 10s resolution for affected services (owner: metrics-worker)
   - prometheus snapshot example:
     curl -sG "https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/export" --data-urlencode "query=up{job=\"inference-gateway\"}" --data-urlencode "start=$(date -d '48 hours ago' +%s)" --data-urlencode "end=$(date +%s)" > metrics-inference-gateway-48h.json
4) Capture traces and spans for the incident window (owner: tracing-team)
   - run: otel-collector export with filter service.name in (inference-gateway, model-router) and timeframe = incident_window
   - store as traces-<INCIDENT_ID>.ndjson\n5) Snapshot routing and rollout state (owner: platform-team)
   - kubectl get rollout -n redwood --all-namespaces -o yaml > rollout-state-<INCIDENT_ID>.yaml
   - capture model-router config: curl https://config-store.internal/v1/model-router/config > model-router-config.json\n6) Preserve autoscaler and capacity events (owner: cloud-ops)
   - cloud events: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=ec2.amazonaws.com --start-time "$START" --end-time "$END" > cloud-events.json

Chain-of-custody & Audit Log (must be completed before handoff)
----------------------------------------------------------------
- Every action that reads/writes the artifact path must be recorded in the manifest with: actor, timestamp, action, reason, and request-id. Example CSV row appended to manifest-audit.csv:
  timestamp,actor,action,artifact,request_id,notes
  2026-03-01T14:23:45Z,priya.desai,upload,metrics-inference-gateway-48h.json,req-32f4c,initial snapshot
- Access policy: artifacts are encrypted with KMS alias/incident-enc; temporary read grants are given via the incidents IAM role (arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/incident-worker-<INCIDENT_ID>).
- Do not delete or modify original artifacts. If modification is necessary (e.g., PII redaction), store a copy with clear suffix "-redacted" and log the reason.

Evidence retention and TTLs
--------------------------
- Retention defaults (unless legal hold):
  - Logs and metrics: 90 days
  - Traces/spans: 30 days (but incident exports saved for 365 days)
  - Raw GPU/scheduler profiles: 365 days
  - Model artifacts used in inference: 365 days or as required by model registry policy
- To request extended retention, create ticket in INC-RETENTION with justification and legal approval.

Detailed collection commands (copy-paste ready)
------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: aws s3api put-object --bucket redwood-incident-artifacts --key rdx-20260301-001/ --acl bucket-owner-full-control
sections.heading: Create incident path (incident commander)

sections.body: kubectl get pods -n inference -l app=inference-gateway -o name | xargs -I {} kubectl logs {} -n inference --since=24h > /tmp/inference-gateway-logs-24h.log

sections.body:
