sections.heading: Tar and upload

sections.body:
- Prefer local redaction and then upload both original encrypted locally and redacted copy with explicit audit entries.
- Redaction example (python):
python - <<'PY'
import re,sys,json
with open('metrics-inference-gateway-48h.json') as f:
    data=f.read()
red=re.sub(r'([A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Za-z]{2,})','[REDACTED_EMAIL]',data)
with open('metrics-inference-gateway-48h-redacted.json','w') as f:
    f.write(red)
PY

Roles & responsibilities
-------------------------
- Incident Commander: create incident artifact path, ensure manifest exists, verify chain-of-custody.
- SRE Oncall: collect SLO snapshot, metrics, top-level logs, and coordinate with tracing-team.
- Tracing-team: export spans and root-cause traces for the incident window.
- Cloud-ops: collect cloud provider capacity events, autoscaler logs, and VM lifecycle events.
- Platform-team: capture routing and rollout state.
- Legal/Security: approve redaction and extended retention requests.

Post-incident handoff checklist (within 48 hours)
------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm manifest completeness (all artifacts listed and checksum-verified).
   - Example: sha256sum metrics-inference-gateway-48h.json >> manifest-checksums.txt
2) Attach PIR ticket and summary to artifact path (owner: incident commander).
3) Grant read-only access to reviewers (SRE reviewers, service-owner, product, and legal if needed). Use IAM role with duration 8 hours as default.
4) Schedule the post-incident review (PIR) within 7 business days. Attach required artifacts.

Evidence checklist table
------------------------
| Artifact name                         | Required by | Retain (days) | Owner            | Notes |
|---------------------------------------|-------------|---------------|------------------|-------|
| manifest-<INCIDENT_ID>.yaml           | All         | 365           | incident-commander| Metadata + audit CSV |
| slo-snapshot.json                     | SLO        | 365           | SRE oncall       | timestamped snapshot |
| metrics-*-48h.json                    | Capacity   | 90            | metrics-team     | 10s resolution recommended |
| traces-<INCIDENT_ID>.ndjson           | RC root-cause | 365         | tracing-team     | export with sampling preserved |
| rollout-state-<INCIDENT_ID>.yaml      | Platform   | 365           | platform-team    | includes model routing state |
| cloud-events.json                     | Capacity   | 365           | cloud-ops        | autoscale and termination events |
| gpu-profiles-<INCIDENT_ID>.tar.gz     | Perf       | 365           | infra-perf       | scheduler + nvprof outputs |
\nSLO & error-budget notes (how artifacts are used)
---------------------------------------------------
- The SLO snapshot and metrics exports are the canonical inputs to the Error Budget Burn worksheet. The SRE oncall must tag the incident with the SLOs impacted (e.g., inference-gateway: availability 99.95%, latency p99 < 120ms).
- If a retro requires measuring partial-period SLO impact, use slo-snapshot.json and metrics to compute weighted burn. Keep calculation artifacts (notebooks) in the artifact path.

Integration with reliability initiatives and capacity planning
-----------------------------------------------------------
- Use captured capacity events and metrics to populate capacity-runbook templates for recurring incidents. Example: if autoscaler thrash coincides with p95 latency spikes, create a follow-up reliability initiative ticket tagged reliability:autoscale-thrash.
- Attach exported traces to the reliability initiative card to tie causal traces to corrective work (e.g., scale-policy-tuning).

Automation & tooling recommendations
-----------------------------------
- Use incidentctl (internal CLI) to create incident artifact path and template manifest automatically:
  incidentctl create --id rdx-20260301-001 --services inference-gateway,model-router --owner priya.desai
- Incorporate a Lambda function that verifies manifest checksums nightly for active incidents and alerts if any artifact is missing.
- Add a Prometheus alert rule to fire when artifact export jobs fail more than 3 times in 1 hour: rule name: IncidentArtifactExportFailure.

Example manifest (manifest-<INCIDENT_ID>.yaml)
------------------------------------------------
incident_id: rdx-20260301-001
created_by: priya.desai
created_at: 2026-03-01T14:20:00Z
services: [inference-gateway, model-router]
artifacts:
  - name: slo-snapshot.json
    path: s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/rdx-20260301-001/slo-snapshot.json
    sha256: <sha256sum>
  - name: metrics-inference-gateway-48h.json
    path: s3://...
    sha256: <sha256sum>
audit_log: s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/rdx-20260301-001/manifest-audit.csv

Related pages
--------------
- /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/slo-design-triage-cost-aware-mitigation-2026 (SLO triage patterns)
- /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025 (capacity governance)
- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/rollout-and-traffic-shift-playbook (traffic shift guidance)
\nAppendix: common troubleshooting snippets
-----------------------------------------
- Check autoscaler pod restarts
  kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cluster-autoscaler -o wide
- Extract top 100 slowest traces by latency (using internal trace search API):
  curl -sG https://tracing.internal/api/search --data-urlencode "service=inference-gateway" --data-urlencode "sort=-duration" --data-urlencode "limit=100" > top-100-slow-traces.json

Document change history
-----------------------

- 2026-03-01: Published after review by Liam O'Connor, Mei Zhang, Carlos Alvarez

End of document

payload.page_title: Blameless Timeline and Evidence Standards for Incident Reviews

sections.body: This page prescribes standardized, blameless requirements for incident timelines and evidence collection for all Redwood production incidents. The goal is to ensure consistent-quality post-incident reviews, preserve high-fidelity artifacts for RCA, and enable repeatable automation.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to all incidents involving production-facing services (hosted API, dedicated model pools, and console).
- Includes incidents that meet the Incident Classification threshold (P1/P2) or that consume >25% of a relevant service's monthly error budget.
- Excludes internal non-production experiments unless they impact customer-facing metrics.

Why a timeline + evidence standard?
- Consistency: reviewers must be able to reconstruct a timeline without ad-hoc requests.
- Speed: clear evidence manifests accelerate RCA and mitigation playbooks.
- Auditability: compliance and enterprise customers require reproducible investigation artifacts.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- redwood-api-prod (text-generation): availability SLO = 99.95% monthly; error budget = 0.05%.
- embeddings-service-prod: p99 latency SLO = 600ms; error budget triggers when p99 > 600ms for 6 hours.
- model-routing: request-failure-rate SLO = 0.3% per week.
sections.heading: High-level SLO alignment (examples)

sections.body:
1) Immediate (0–1h):
   - Create an incident page in Confluence using the incident template. Fill incident-start time, affected services, classification (P1/P2/etc.), and oncall roster.
   - Create/attach an evidence manifest (see below) to the page.
   - Notify SRE oncall and engineering owners via PagerDuty/Slack channel.
2) Short term (1–24h):
   - Document observed symptoms, customer impact (estimate of requests affected, error budget burn percentage), and mitigation steps taken in the incident page.
   - Attach initial logs/trace links and key metric dashboards.
3) Medium term (24–72h):
   - Draft the incident narrative and preliminary timeline (minute-level events where available).
   - Collect and preserve immutable artifacts for final review.
4) Postmortem (72h–7d):
   - Publish a full postmortem with RCA, action items, and acceptance criteria.
   - Assign owners and due dates for every action.
   - If incident impacted enterprise customers, notify Customer Success and Legal; escalate per the enterprise incident runbook.

Evidence manifest (required fields)
- incident_id: Confluence page id (or incident slug)
- incident_start_utc: ISO8601 timestamp
- affected_services: list of service names (e.g., redwood-api-prod, kv-cache, model-worker-gpu)
- observed_metrics: list of metric names and snapshot links (e.g., api.errors.rate -> https://grafana/redwood/api/errors)
- trace_links: list of trace/trace-group URLs (e.g., https://tracing.redwood/trace/abcd1234)
- logs_query: saved query or file (e.g., logging:/projects/redwood/prod/search?q=ERROR%20Rate)
- config_hashes: git commit SHAs or config snapshot links for service(s) involved
- core_dumps/archive: storage path if applicable (e.g., s3://redwood-incidents/2025-02-14/coredump.tgz)
- screenshots/dashboards: image links or attachments
- retained_artifact_ttl: retention window in days (default 365)

(Example manifest JSON fragment — include on incident page):
{
  "incident_id": "inc-2025-02-13-redwood-api-502",
  "incident_start_utc": "2025-02-13T03:42:00Z",
  "affected_services": ["redwood-api-prod", "model-cache"],
  "observed_metrics": ["grafana://dash/redwood/api/errors"],
  "trace_links": ["https://tracing.redwood/trace/abcd1234"],
  "logs_query": "logging:/projects/redwood/prod?q=service:redwood-api AND status>=500"
}

Minimum evidence checklist (attach at time of page creation):
- Snapshot of primary dashboards (PNG or dashboard link).
- At least one high-level trace that crosses the customer request path.
- Representative log slice: 5–10 contiguous minutes that show errors or latency spikes.
- Relevant config version commit SHA(s).
- Screenshot of PagerDuty/alerting trigger with timestamp.
- Error budget burn estimate (percent and absolute units).

Ownership and roles (who does what)
- Incident commander (IC): coordinates response and ensures evidence manifest is updated in 0–1h. Owner: rotating SRE oncall.
- Service owner(s): provide config SHAs and validate the timeline. Owner: service engineering manager.
- Postmortem author: drafts narrative and action items within 72h. Owner: designated author (can be IC or service owner).
- RCA reviewer(s): at least one SRE + one service owner.

Postmortem deliverables and acceptance criteria
- Complete timeline (minute-resolution if available).
- Clear causal chain linking root cause to impact (noting contributing factors).
- Action items with owners, due dates, and a test or validation step.
- Evidence manifest attached and verified (link checks succeed).
- Severity and customer impact stated with mitigation rationale.

Review cadence and meeting agenda
- Within 7 days: run a blameless review meeting (max 60 minutes):
  1) Quick recap and impact (5m)
  2) Timeline walk-through (15m)
  3) Root cause and contributing factors (15m)
  4) Action items and acceptance criteria (15m)
  5) Open questions and follow ups (10m)
- Invitees: SRE oncall, service owner, product representative, security/legal if sensitive.

Retention and compliance
- Default artifact retention = 365 days.
- For incidents involving customer data or regulated workloads, extend retention per legal guidance and mark page confidentiality = restricted.
- Audit snapshot: keep the evidence manifest and references immutable (export to S3/archive bucket) before editing the incident page for legal auditability.

Automation and tooling recommendations
- Incident creation: use the "incident-create" CLI to scaffold the page and evidence manifest. Example:
  curl -X POST https://infra-api.redwood/internal/incidents \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $INFRATOKEN' \
    -d '{"service":"redwood-api-prod","start":"2025-02-13T03:42:00Z","classification":"P1"}'
- Logs: prefer saved queries (logging:/...) rather than raw downloads to keep context.
- Traces: create a span-group link and attach to manifest.
- Dashboard snapshots: use grafana API to export PNGs and attach to Confluence page automatically.

Escalation matrix example (error budget driven)
- If incident causes >10% of monthly error budget to burn within 1 hour -> auto-escalate to SRE manager + product owner.
- If incident duration >4 hours and customer impact persists -> signaled page to exec SRE and CS lead.

Quality gates for closure
- All action items have owners and testable acceptance criteria.
- Evidence manifest verified and links reachable.
- CI tests (where applicable) added to prevent recurrence.
- Postmortem annotated with lessons learned and linked to related runbooks or playbooks.

Appendix A — Common queries and snippets
- Grafana snapshot (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" \
       https://grafana.redwood/api/snapshots --data "{\"dashboard\":{...}}"
- Tracing quick link (example): https://tracing.redwood/trace?service=redwood-api&from=2025-02-13T03:30:00Z&to=2025-02-13T04:00:00Z
- Logs example (Stackdriver-like):
  gcloud logging read 'resource.labels.project_id="redwood-prod" AND severity>=ERROR' --start-time="2025-02-13T03:30:00Z" --end-time="2025-02-13T04:00:00Z" > errors.json

Appendix B — Template: quick incident evidence checklist (to paste into incident page)
- incident_id:
- incident_start_utc:
- affected_services:
- dashboards_attached:
- trace_links:
- logs_query_or_file:
- config_shas:
- retained_artifact_ttl:

payload.page_title: Forensic SLO Attribution and Evidence Cookbook

sections.body:
Overview

This cookbook is a concise, operational reference for fast, repeatable SLO attribution and evidence collection during incident reviews. It codifies a defensible chain of reasoning from raw telemetry to a remediation action (capacity or configuration) and a post-incident improvement. Use this for live incident forensics and for evidence packages attached to postmortems.

Scope

- Applies to inference services and supporting control-plane components (routing, model cache, admission).
- Focus areas: latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99), availability SLOs (error rate), token/throughput headroom, and quantized-serving memory pressure.
- Excludes: billing disputes, pure product UX issues, and non-service human errors (these should reference the appropriate product or people-ops process).

Roles and ownership

- Oncall Engineer (owner): gather live evidence, run queries, and produce the initial attribution hypothesis.
- SRE Lead (reviewer): validate attribution steps and decide immediate mitigations (throttle, failover, capacity surge).
- Runtime Team: provide model-serving kernel traces and memory profiles.
- Telemetry/Observability Team: assist with any missing metrics, retention queries, or archived traces.

Definitions (quick)

- Primary SLO: the customer-facing metric we measure (e.g., inference p99 latency <= 350ms).
- Error budget burn: how much of the budget was consumed in the incident window.
- Attribution hypothesis: ranked list of likely causes that explain telemetry.

Procedure: Fast SLO attribution (15–45 mins)

1) Prepare evidence snapshot
   - Capture a reproducible time window (start/end) where the SLO deviation occurs. Record timezone and data retention IDs.
   - Snapshot: alert trigger timestamp, synthetic canary failures, deployment markers, autoscaler events, and control-plane logs.

2) High-level sanity checks (5 mins)
   - Confirm scope: Is this global or single-region? Use region tag on requests.
   - Check correlated alerts: CPU/GPU utilization, OOM events, provisioning failures, and network errors.

3) Telemetry triage (10–20 mins)
   - Query SLO signal by tenant and route. Example PromQL (replace labels):
     - sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{le=\"0.35\", route=~\".*\"}[5m])) by (route, tenant)
     - increase(error_count_total[10m]) / increase(request_count_total[10m])
   - Verify tail latency pattern: is p99 rising while p50 stable? That indicates queuing, cold-cache, or rare OOMs.

4) Evidence linkage (10–25 mins)
   - Link each candidate cause to at least two independent signals. Preferred signal types: metrics -> logs, traces -> kernel counters, and autoscaler events -> capacity alarms.
   - Example evidence table (copy into PM):
     | Candidate cause | Metric signal | Log/trace evidence | Confidence | Suggested immediate action |
     |-----------------|---------------|--------------------|------------|----------------------------|
     | Model hot-shutdown during GC | GPU_util spikes; node_restarts | kubelet logs: container restarted | high | Evict and replace node, failover to dedicated pool |
     | Demand microburst (tenant) | request_rate spike; queue_length rise | ingress logs: large client bursts | medium | Temporary throttling for offending tenant |
     | Cold KV cache misses | p99 increase only for long-tail keys | span traces show cache_miss path | medium | Warm cache for hot prefixes; enable prefix caching |

5) Decide mitigation (owner + SRE lead)
   - Follow decision heuristics: prefer non-disruptive mitigations first (circuit breakers, tenant throttles, model variant fallback) when confidence is medium. Use capacity surge or node replacement for high confidence infrastructure faults.
   - Document CET (Confidence, Effort, Time-to-restore) for each mitigation. Example: Confidence=high, Effort=low, TTR=3m for tenant throttle.

6) Create evidence package for postmortem
   - Minimum package: time window, PromQL queries executed, raw alert payloads, representative trace IDs, kernel logs, autoscaler events, and a one-paragraph attribution. Attach to the incident ticket.

SLO attribution heuristics (quick reference)

- Tail-only latency regression: look first at queuing (backpressure metrics), cache miss rates, and preemption/eviction events.
- Uniform latency shift across percentiles: likely upstream routing change, network degradation, or instance-wide CPU/GPU saturation.
- Error rate spike with no latency change: likely application-level errors (model runtime exceptions) or misrouted validation traffic.
- Correlated increases in token counts per-request: suspect prompt inflation or client-side changes.

Evidence collection checklist (copyable)

- [ ] Alert definition and raw payload (timestamped)
- [ ] SLO time series snapshot (CSV/PNG) for 1h before/after
- [ ] Representative request IDs and trace IDs (3–10 samples)
- [ ] Node/GPU memory and kernel logs for the window
- [ ] Autoscaler and provisioning events (scale-up/scale-down)
- [ ] Deployment manifests and commit SHA of any recent deploys
- [ ] Tenant ID and client headers for suspect traffic
- [ ] Any applied mitigations and timestamps

Example queries & snippets

- PromQL: p99 latency by model\
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(inference_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))

- SQL (request samples):
  SELECT request_id, tenant_id, route, tokens_in, tokens_out, created_at
    FROM request_samples
    WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2023-11-09T20:00:00Z' AND '2023-11-09T21:00:00Z'
    AND model = 'gptx-13b'
    LIMIT 200;

- Kernel trace grep example:
  sudo journalctl -u runtime-service --since '2023-11-09T20:00:00' | grep -i oom

- Quick script to package traces (pseudo):
  1. export TRACES=(trace1 trace2 trace3)
  2. for t in ${TRACES[@]}; do curator download-trace $t --out /tmp/evidence/$INCIDENT_ID; done

Decision matrix: when to throttle vs. scale vs. failover

- Throttle tenant: if evidence shows isolated tenant burst and throttling reduces queue_length in <2m.
- Scale (elastic): if cluster utilization > 85% for >10m across multiple nodes and autoscaler failed to provision.
- Failover to baseline model variant: if model-specific memory OOMs or degraded kernel performance with no infra change.

Post-incident improvements (examples)

- Add synthetic canary that exercises long-tail prefixes when we identify cold-cache regressions.
- Create tenant-level rate limiters and customer-safety throttle routes for high-risk tenants.
- Add kernel-level OOM counters to the SLO dashboard when model quantization changes.

Practice guidance and tabletop use

- Run a quarterly 2-hour tabletop using a recorded evidence package: verify we can reconstruct the attribution in <60 mins and that mitigation decisions follow documented heuristics.
- Maintain a short playbook of 3 frequently used PromQL queries in the oncall rota.

Appendix: repository links and templates

- Incident evidence template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/templates/evidence-package-template
- SLO dashboard canonical panels: /grafana/d/rlw/inference-slo-board
- Postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/templates/postmortem-template

Contact and escalation

- For missing telemetry: observability@redwood.com
- For runtime kernel traces: runtime-team@redwood.com
- For capacity procurement during an outage: infra-capacity@redwood.com

Notes

This cookbook is intentionally lightweight — the goal is reproducible evidence that supports a clear remediation action. Keep attachments small (representative traces rather than full archives) and document how to re-run any key queries used for attribution.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Controlled failover test regression (us-east → eu-west) – transient 5xx + tail latency

sections.body:
On **2026-01-15**, during a **planned controlled regional failover test** (Hosted API and a limited Dedicated slice) from **us-east** to **eu-west**, we introduced a **customer-visible regression**. A sequence of noisy regional-impairment signals and insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails caused repeated routing policy changes (“flip/rollback”) and a transient overload condition in the target region.

**Customer impact:**
- **Hosted API:** elevated 5xx/timeouts and tail latency for a subset of routes while traffic re-converged.
- **Dedicated:** minimal direct impact due to scoped tenants, but some control-plane operations (drain workflow status) were delayed.
- **Streaming:** some clients experienced disconnects on redirect and did not recover cleanly without application-level retries.

**Why this postmortem exists:** This was an intentional test. The regression was not catastrophic, but it was **customer-visible** and exposed gaps in our automation safety model. The goal is to make sure controlled testing improves reliability without creating new incidents.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- **Incident type:** Planned test causing unplanned customer-visible regression
- **Severity:** SEV-2 (customer-visible errors for a limited subset; short duration; mitigated quickly)
- **Services impacted:** Hosted API (gateway + smart routing), failover automation controller, region health evaluation pipeline
- **Regions:** us-east (source), eu-west (target)
sections.heading: Severity and scope

sections.body:
- Transient **HTTP 5xx** and **gateway timeouts** during the flip/rollback window.
- Elevated **p95/p99 latency** for successful requests during the same interval.
- Some **streaming sessions** dropped when redirected cross-region; a subset of clients did not resume streaming until they retried from the application.
sections.heading: Customer impact (what users experienced)

sections.body: - We did not publish an external status page incident because this was a planned test with limited blast radius; however, **Support received inbound tickets** from customers who noticed errors during the window. Support response guidance was issued in-channel and via SUP-25310.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
> Times are approximate; see dashboard annotations and incident-bot thread for exact event markers.

- **16:55** – Pre-flight checks complete (SRE + Routing + Infra). Dry-run output reviewed; “go” granted.
- **17:00** – Controlled failover test begins. Routing policy automation enabled for the scoped routes/tenants.
- **17:02** – Region health aggregator reports degraded reachability for us-east based on synthetic probe failures.
- **17:03** – Failover controller recommends and executes a policy flip to prefer eu-west (within the scoped policy).
- **17:04–17:08** – eu-west sees request surge; latency rises. Gateway retries amplify load; some 5xx/timeouts observed.
- **17:06** – A second reachability signal changes state; controller interprets as recovery + triggers rollback logic sooner than expected.
- **17:07–17:10** – Flip/rollback oscillation observed (multiple policy updates within minutes). Error rate and p99 spike.
- **17:10** – On-call disables automation for the scoped policy; routing stabilized manually.
- **17:14** – Error rates return to baseline; latency recovers as retries subside.
- **17:25** – Post-test validation begins; Support notified with customer-facing explanation.
- **18:10** – Initial retro notes captured; action item tracker created.
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body:
**Detection:**
- We detected the regression via:
  - SRE dashboards for failover signals (5xx burn + tail latency burn)
  - Routing policy flip counters (unexpected rate)
  - Support ping that a customer saw transient errors (correlated to test window)

**Response:**
- Disabled failover automation for the scoped policy (feature flag / controller disable).
- Reduced gateway retry pressure using existing runtime/gateway knobs (temporary tuning) while traffic re-stabilized.
- Confirmed eu-west capacity headroom and verified no persistent impairment.
- Coordinated comms with Support: acknowledged planned test, explained transient errors, offered retry guidance.
sections.heading: Detection and response

sections.body:
The regression was caused by **policy oscillation** (flip/rollback) triggered by **noisy reachability signals**, combined with insufficient guardrails that allowed multiple routing policy changes in a short period. The oscillation produced a traffic pattern that:
1) **increased cross-region redirects**, and
2) **amplified retries** at the gateway/client level,
leading to transient overload and elevated error rates in the target region.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- **Reachability probes produced false positives** (brief, correlated failures) that were treated as authoritative without adequate corroboration.
- **Hold-down and anti-flap timers were too permissive** for the observed signal volatility.
- **Rollback semantics were correct per implementation**, but not aligned with our intended ADR-level behavior (we rolled back too quickly and re-triggered failover immediately).
sections.heading: Key technical drivers

sections.body:
- Reachability was treated as “high priority,” but we lacked a strict requirement for corroboration (e.g., simultaneous 5xx burn or control-plane health degradation) before acting.
- Probe failures were short-lived and likely influenced by transient provider/network behavior; the region health pipeline did not dampen enough.
sections.heading: 1) Trigger noise and insufficient corroboration

sections.body:
- Policy flip rate limiting (per policy/per tenant) was not strict enough for production-like behavior.
- The controller was allowed to both:
  - fail over on a high-priority signal transition, and
  - roll back on early recovery indication,
  without a sufficiently long “stabilization” window.
sections.heading: 2) Rollback gaps / anti-flap guardrails

sections.body:
- Gateway retry budgets and client retry behavior interacted poorly with redirects and timeouts.
- During oscillation, some requests were retried across regions, increasing load at the exact time the target region was receiving new traffic.
sections.heading: 3) Retry amplification during routing changes

sections.body:
- We had dashboards, but lacked consistent **automation-driven annotations** (start/stop, flip, rollback, reason) visible across all relevant panels.
- Signal evaluation logs were not easily searchable by policy + decision id, slowing triage.
sections.heading: 4) Observability gaps during the test

sections.body:
- Blast radius controls worked: the test scope limited impact to a subset of routes/tenants.
- On-call and engineering coordination was fast; disabling automation stabilized the system quickly.
- The team captured decision points and signal state changes in real time, enabling clear follow-up.
sections.heading: What went well

sections.body:
- The automation acted faster than our operational ability to confirm whether the impairment was real.
- We did not have a single “confidence score” view combining signal corroboration, dampening state, and decision rationale.
- Support was notified quickly, but we did not proactively message a small set of known sensitive accounts before running the test (we relied on the planned-test guidance rather than a targeted heads-up).
sections.heading: What didn’t go well

sections.body:
- eu-west had enough headroom that the overload was short-lived.
- The oscillation stayed within a few minutes; a longer duration could have caused a larger SLO burn and broader customer impact.
sections.heading: Where we got lucky

sections.body:
- Disabled automation for the scoped policy upon observing oscillation.
- Manual stabilization of routing preference and verification of regional health.
- Support response guidance provided for inbound tickets about transient errors.
sections.heading: Immediate remediation (completed during/after the event)

sections.body: > This section is the contract: what we will change so a controlled test does not regress customer experience again.
sections.heading: Corrective and preventive actions (CPAs)

sections.body:
1) **Corroboration requirements**
   - Require at least one corroborating signal for reachability-based failover in production scopes (e.g., 5xx burn OR control-plane health OR sustained probe failure above threshold).
   - Owner: **Ravi Menon** (Routing policy)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

2) **Dampening + hold-down tuning**
   - Increase minimum sustain time for reachability impairment and increase recovery hold-down.
   - Add jitter/TTL protections on health reads to avoid stampedes.
   - Owner: **Victor Alvarez** (Network) + **Jordan Lee** (Policy engine)
   - Target: **2026-02-21**
sections.heading: A. Trigger signal pipeline hardening

sections.body:
3) **Rate limiting for policy flips**
   - Enforce max flips per hour per policy and per tenant tier, with hard stop + paging if exceeded.
   - Owner: **Benji Okafor** (Guardrails)
   - Target: **2026-02-21**

4) **Rollback semantics aligned to ADR-043**
   - Ensure rollback cannot immediately re-open the same decision loop; require stable window before re-evaluating for failover.
   - Produce an auditable “decision id” for each state transition.
   - Owner: **Jordan Lee** (Policy engine) + **Ethan Park** (Control plane)
   - Target: **2026-03-01**

5) **Approval hooks for production game days**
   - Require on-call acknowledgment before executing an automated flip in production during controlled tests until we meet success criteria in two consecutive game days.
   - Owner: **Rafael Mendes** (SRE) + **Ethan Park** (Control plane)
   - Target: **2026-02-10**
sections.heading: B. Rollback/anti-flap guardrails

sections.body:
6) **Gateway retry budget + redirect guidance**
   - Cap retries during active failover events; prefer fast-fail with standardized Retry-After for overload.
   - Update SDK/docs guidance for idempotent retries and streaming reconnect.
   - Owner: **Peter Holtz** (Gateway) + **Vikram Singh** (Data plane)
   - Target: **2026-03-08**

7) **Streaming reconnect hardening**
   - Ensure redirect responses carry enough info for safe client reconnection; improve idempotency guidance.
   - Owner: **Vikram Singh**
   - Target: **2026-02-28**
sections.heading: C. Retry/load-shedding behavior

sections.body:
8) **Automation-driven annotations**
   - Add consistent dashboard annotations for: test start/end, flip, rollback, reason, decision id, policy id.
   - Owner: **Allison Grant** + **Sergio Costa**
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

9) **Audit log retention + supportability**
   - Persist failover audit events (recommended/executed/rolled back) with searchable keys: tenant tier, route, policy id, decision id.
   - Owner: **Devon Price** (Tooling) + **Allison Grant** (Observability)
   - Target: **2026-03-01**
sections.heading: D. Observability and auditing

sections.body:
10) **Go/no-go criteria update**
   - Add explicit “anti-flap guardrails enabled + validated in staging” to go/no-go checklist.
   - Owner: **Talia Benson** (Program) + **Tomáš Novák** (Runbooks)
   - Target: **2026-02-07**

11) **Customer comms targeting**
   - For production tests, proactively notify a small set of enterprise accounts with strict HA expectations if their traffic might be in scope, even when blast radius is limited.
   - Owner: **Dev Patel** (Support escalation) + **Lauren Bishop** (Dedicated PM)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**
sections.heading: E. Process changes for future controlled tests

sections.body:
For two consecutive production game days with scoped blast radius:
- No more than **one** routing policy transition per policy (flip only; rollback only if explicitly invoked by on-call).
- No customer-visible 5xx increase above agreed threshold for scoped tenants.
- p99 latency in target region remains within defined tolerance band during convergence.
- Audit events and dashboard annotations allow reconstruction of the decision timeline within 10 minutes.
sections.heading: Success criteria (for declaring this class of regression “fixed”)

sections.body:
- “Reachability > 5xx burn” is correct only if reachability is truly authoritative; without corroboration, it can be the noisiest signal.
- Rollback is not inherently safe; rollback without stabilization can create a control loop that is worse than staying failed over.
- Controlled tests must be treated like real incidents operationally: annotations, clear decision authority, and customer comms preparedness.
sections.heading: Appendix A: Key lessons

sections.body:
- Should we treat reachability as authoritative only when multiple independent vantage points fail, or when combined with provider status signals?
- For Hosted API streaming, do we want a first-class “resume token” pattern to reduce user impact during redirects?
- What is the right default DNS/traffic-steering posture for faster failover without amplifying transient network noise?
sections.heading: Appendix B: Open questions

sections.body:
- Primary owner for follow-through: **Rafael Mendes (SRE delivery lead)**
- Architecture owner: **Miles Thornton (Failover architecture lead)**
sections.heading: Owner

sections.body: - This postmortem is complete. Action items are tracked in **ENG-2426** and linked sub-issues. Updates should be reflected here if any CPA materially changes scope or target dates.
sections.heading: Status

payload.page_title: post-incident-slo-capacity-mapping-template-2026

sections.body:
Summary:
This document is a practical template and decision guide for post-incident reviews that explicitly maps SLOs, error budget consumption, and capacity signals to incident severity, remediation priorities, and follow-up actions. It is intended for SREs, oncall engineers, and service owners who run post-incident reviews (PIRs). Use this template to standardize evidence collection, causal analysis, and capacity-driven remediation work accepted into the reliability backlog.

Scope and audience:
- Covers incidents that impact core Redwood inference services (runtime, routing, KV cache, autoscaler, ingress) and adjacent control plane components that affect customer-facing SLOs.
- Not intended for purely business-side issues (billing portal outages) unless they cause measurable user-facing SLO regressions.
- Primary audience: SRE oncall, service owners, platform reliability leads, and incident reviewers.

Why this exists:
- We observed inconsistent mapping from error-budget consumption to concrete post-incident work. That led to either under-emphasis of high-impact capacity issues or over-commitment of development resources for low-impact degradations. This template enforces a reproducible mapping: evidence -> SLO impact -> capacity signal -> prioritized remediation.

Quick reference: 
- Severity mapping (high-level):
  1) Sev1: >5% global user-visible error-rate increase sustained >5m OR >=25% of customers experiencing P50 latency >2x baseline OR catastrophic capacity collapse (node pool down)
  2) Sev2: measurable SLO breach window or cumulative error-budget burn >2% in 1 hour for a tier-1 model/service
  3) Sev3: transient spikes, config rollbacks, or non-customer-facing degradations with localized impact

- Post-incident timeboxes: PIR within 72 hours, follow-up plan within 14 days, remediation backlog item or cancel decision within 30 days.

Incident metadata (fill at start of PIR):
- Incident ID: (e.g., INC-2026-0718-23)
- Primary service(s): (e.g., serving-runtime-gpu, request-router)
- Initial severity: (Sev1/Sev2/Sev3)
- Start time / End time / Duration
- Oncall rotation and primary responder
- Summary (1–2 sentences)

Evidence checklist (required attachments):
- Telemetry: SLO dashboards, error-rate timeseries, latency P50/P95/P99 for affected tenants (CSV or screenshot)
- Capacity signals: node-usage, GPU memory pressure, queue length, scheduler wait times, eviction counts
- Autoscaler logs: scale decisions, timestamped metrics for scaling triggers
- Deployment events: rollouts, image hashes, config changes, feature-flag changes
- Traces: representative distributed traces for failed requests (trace IDs)
- Service logs: filtered logs around incident window (include sampling keys / tenant IDs)
- Postmortem evidence archive link: (Confluence / GCS / internal artifact storage)

SLO / Error budget mapping table (copy into the PIR):
| SLO name | Target | Observed window | Deviation | Error budget consumed | Tenant impact (est) | Comment |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| inference-generation-availability | 99.95% (30d) | 99.40% (1h) | -0.55% | 40% of hourly budget | 18% of active tenants had 5+ failures | autoscaler delayed recovery under load |
| embedding-p99-latency | <120ms | 310ms (5m) | +190ms | N/A (latency SLO) | All tenants below baseline SL tier | quantized-serving tails increased |

Decision criteria (how severity & follow-up are derived):
1) If error-budget lost in rolling 1h >= 20% for a tier-1 SLO -> escalate to Sev1 review and schedule emergency remediation planning.
2) If capacity signals show sustained GPU memory pressure >85% for >10m correlated with SLO degradation -> prioritize capacity engineering (slot increase, scheduler tuning, or model-pin rollback).
3) If incident caused by deployment config -> owner must provide rollback, canary gating improvements, and at least one automation test in CI.
4) If multiple tenants impacted but error-budget loss <5% -> classify as Sev2 and prioritize mitigations that prevent recurrence (alert tuning, circuit-breakers).

RCA template (structured, short answers):
- Problem statement (one sentence):
- Impacted SLO(s) and customer-visible effect: 
- Root cause hypothesis (what failed at the system boundary):
- Evidence supporting hypothesis (list items with links):
- Contributing factors (ranked): 1) , 2) , 3)
- Why automation/manual steps failed (if applicable):
- Immediate mitigations taken and timestamps:
- Long-term remediation proposals (3 options with cost/effort and owner):

Capacity signal catalog (mapping common signals to actions):
- GPU memory pressure >85% (sustained 10m):
  - Likely causes: model state growth, KV cache leak, incorrect batch sizing, hot-tenant pressure
  - Immediate action: trigger tenant throttling for heavy tenants, enable graceful degradation for non-critical models, add emergency nodes (if pool has spare capacity)
  - Follow-up: model-level quota, autoscaler tuning, KV cache TTL snapshotting
- Scheduler queue length >1000 requests / 30s:
  - Likely causes: ingress spike, downstream dependency slow, autoscaler cold start delay
  - Immediate action: enable backpressure / shed best-effort routes, route traffic to fallback region/model, signal autoscaler with pre-warm policy
  - Follow-up: implement request-level pre-warming and ramping policy in the autoscaler config
- Node eviction count >0.5%/hr:
  - Likely causes: OOM, driver crash, ephemeral storage saturation
  - Immediate action: remove faulty AMIs, drain pool, alert kernel/drivers team
  - Follow-up: kernel upgrade plan and crash-dump automation

Incident-to-backlog decision matrix (use during PIR closure):
- Tier A remediation (must do within 14d): 1) Direct root cause fix that prevents recurrence of Sev1-like capacity collapse; 2) Fix when error-budget consumption >25% and >1% customers impacted.
- Tier B remediation (plan within 30d, implement within 90d): performance tuning, alerting gaps, runbook updates.
- Tier C remediation (deferred): non-critical documentation, minor telemetry increases.

Concrete runbook changes to consider (check at PIR):
- Add capacity signals to the oncall dashboard: GPU memory heatmap, per-tenant qps, scheduler backlog by model-size.
- Create an automated playbook for emergency node pool add/remove that an oncall can trigger from the Slack/CICD bot with RBAC controls.
- Add synthetic canaries that exercise long-tail quantized paths and gating thresholds before each major rollout.

Execution checklist for PIR facilitator (numbered procedure):
1) Validate required evidence is attached. If telemetry is missing, escalate to telemetry owner and kick off a 48h evidence collection window.
2) Present SLO mapping table and a one-slide timeline of events.
3) Confirm root cause hypothesis and mark "hypothesis confidence" (low/medium/high).
4) Decide remediation tier and owner. For Tier A assign a primary and secondary engineer with expected deliverable and deadline.
5) Add remediation to reliability backlog board and tag with incident ID and SLO impacted.
6) Re-run post-incident synthetic checks and confirm recovery for affected tenants.
7) Publish PIR summary to stakeholders and archive evidence.

Follow-up triggers and automation hooks (examples):
- If same SLO is implicated in 3 incidents within 90 days -> create a reliability initiative ticket and require dedicated capacity experiments.
- If autoscaler back-pressure is activated twice in a week for same model -> require pre-warming policy change and owner-level retrospective.
- Automation: a nightly job will re-evaluate incident SLO tables and flag stale remediations older than 30d to the reliability lead.

Example CLI and query snippets (for evidence collection):
- Query recent errors for a tenant: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://telemetry.internal/api/errors?tenant_id=TENANT123&from=2026-10-01T10:00Z&to=2026-10-01T12:00Z"
- PromQL: avg_over_time(request_latency_ms_p95{service="inference"}[10m]) > 200
- K8s: kubectl top pods --namespace serving | sort -rk 3 | head -n 20

Ownership and escalation contacts (examples):
- SRE oncall rotation: #sre-oncall in Slack (primary contact during incident)
- Serving runtime lead: Marco Ruiz (marco@redwood.ai)
- Autoscaler owner: Elena Kim (elena@redwood.ai)
- Telemetry owner: Derrick Wang (derrick@redwood.ai)

Retention & evidence storage policy:
- Store all incident artifacts in GCS under gs://redwood-incidents/YYYY/MM/INC-ID/ with an index.json listing attachments.
- Evidence retention: 540 days for Sev1/Sev2, 180 days for Sev3.

Appendix: sample outcome summary (to publish)
- Short summary: (1–2 sentences) state impact and fix.
- Timeline highlights: bullet list with timestamps and actions.
- Root cause and contributing factors: 2–3 bullets.
- Remediation plan and owners: list with due dates.
- Business impact estimate: lost requests, customer support tickets, revenue exposure (if known).

References and related reading:
- SLO escalation and capacity triggers (link internal)
- Autoscaler design spec (link internal)
- Incident evidence standards (link internal)

Notes and versioning:
- This template v1.0 created 2026-07-06 by Aisha Patel. Last updated 2026-10-02 to clarify capacity triggers and retention policy.
- Changes: added nightly job automation trigger and expanded capacity signal catalog.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Tiered SLO Grace Period and Capacity Broker Runbook

sections.body:
Overview

This runbook describes Redwood Inference’s policy and operational play for applying short-term, tiered SLO grace windows and an automated Capacity Broker when services approach or exceed error-budget and capacity friction thresholds. The intent is to preserve customer-facing availability while preserving long-term SLO discipline and ownership.

Scope

Applies to: all user-facing model-serving services (hosted API, dedicated frontends, and routing proxies).
Excludes: internal-only tooling (CI jobs, analytics pipelines) unless they directly affect production request surfaces.

Why this exists

As traffic patterns fluctuate (batch jobs, large model rollouts, experiments) SLO violations can cascade. A short, structured grace period plus a Capacity Broker that orchestrates temporary prioritized capacity and traffic shaping reduces the blast radius and buys time to remediate root cause, while keeping customers’ critical requests online.

Key concepts

- Tiered SLO Grace Window: a conservative, time-boxed pause on automated punitive actions for specific SLO classes to allow controlled mitigation steps. Three tiers: P0 (no grace), P1 (10–30 min), P2 (1–4 hours).
- Capacity Broker: a control-plane component that enforces routing priorities, temporary capacity reservations, priority queuing, and preemption policies across GPU pools and regions.
- Error-Budget States: Normal, At-Risk, Exhausted — driven by rolling 7d SLO burn and 24h acceleration signal.

Ownership and roles

- SRE Oncall: executes runbook, communicates, triggers Capacity Broker if required.
- Service Owner: leads investigation and remediation; coordinates rollouts and model fallbacks.
- Platform Engineering: owns Capacity Broker automation and capacity policy templates.
- Product/Support: customer comms for impacted paid customers.

Trigger signals and thresholds
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- 7d rolling availability burn rate > 60% of error budget -> At-Risk
- 24h burn acceleration (burn rate last 2h / average previous 24h) > 3x -> Immediate review
- P50 latency > SLO * 1.5 for 5 minutes AND P95 latency > SLO * 1.25 -> traffic shaping candidate
- GPU utilization > 85% in a region + queue depth growth > 25% in 10 minutes -> capacity broker invocation candidate

Decision matrix (human-readable)

| Condition | Immediate action | Grace Tier | Broker action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| P0 service outage (total unavailability) | Pager to SRE & SE | N/A | Emergency preemption and multi-region failover |
| Error budget exhausted for business-critical route | Notify owners + evaluate fallback | P0 | Reserve capacity from low-priority pools, elevate queue priority |
| Burst causing elevated latency but partial success | Monitor + advisory | P1 (10–30m) | Prioritized queuing, temporary burst pool attach |
| Sustained slow burn trending to exhaustion | Prep mitigations | P2 (1–4h) | Schedule capacity transfers and scheduled throttle windows |

Runbook — step-by-step

1) Detection & Triage (SRE Oncall)
   - Confirm alerts and correlated telemetry (SLO dashboard, per-route latency, GPU pool utilization, queue depth).
   - Run quick queries:
     - curl -s https://telemetry.redwood.internal/api/now?service=<svc>&window=2m | jq '.slo.burn'
     - kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=<svc> -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}'
   - Classify impact (P0/P1/P2) and choose Grace Tier.

2) Initial containment (0–15 minutes)
   - If P0: trigger emergency fallback (route to replica region or model variant) and escalate to SEs.
   - If P1/P2: enable Tiered Grace Window for the affected route using the SLO policy API:

     POST /platform/slo-policy/activate
     {
       "service": "<svc>",
       "grace_tier": "P1",
       "duration_minutes": 20,
       "reason": "traffic_burst_{YYYYMMDDHHmm}"
     }

   - The policy API will: (a) pause automatic punitive throttles for the route, (b) emit an auditable event, (c) notify Platform Engineering.

3) Capacity Broker invocation (15–60 minutes)
   - If capacity signals persist, call Capacity Broker CLI to create a temporary reservation:

     redwood-capacity broker reserve --service <svc> --priority high --gpu-kind a100-80gb --region us-west1 --minutes 120 --preemptible-allowed true

   - Broker will attempt these actions in order (configurable):
     1. Attach burst pool (pre-warmed GPUs).
     2. Rebalance less-critical tenant jobs to other regions/pools.
     3. Elevate request queue priority for the service.
     4. If all else fails, preempt non-critical low-priority pods with 15m termination window.

4) Traffic shaping and graceful degradation (concurrent)
   - Apply per-route soft-fallbacks: shorter generation length limits, episodic response sampling, explicit 429 retry-after headers for low-priority customers. Example config snippet:

     routes:
       - name: /v1/generate
         priority_profile: high
         fallback: "+short_gen,partial_response"
         throttle_policy: \"adaptive\"

   - Notify customer-facing teams for targeted comms if paid customers are impacted.

5) Escalation and remediation (60–240 minutes)
   - Service owner performs root cause (model regression, kernel contention, infra failure).
   - If remediation requires rollback or model pinning, follow the Model Rollout rollback checklist (link in related_pages).
   - If Capacity Broker reservation is insufficient, schedule emergency capacity reallocation with Platform Engineering.

6) Grace end and enforcement (post-window)
   - At Grace expiration, the policy controller will automatically: re-enable throttles, decrement temporary reservations, and publish a compliance event.
   - If the service remains in an unhealthy state, move to enforcement: automatic rate limits and customer-facing throttles are restored.

Automation, observability and telemetry requirements

Minimum telemetry items (must be present for broker to act automatically):
- Per-route 1m and 5m SLO burn, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error classification (4xx/5xx/model-failures).
- GPU pool utilization and per-node queue depth.
- Capacity Broker action logs (audit trail).
- Grace policy events with start/end timestamps and operator id.

SLO policy schema (example YAML)

- service: com.redwood.svc.generate
  slo_set:
    - name: availability
      target: 99.5
      window_days: 7
  grace_policies:
    - tier: P1
      duration_minutes: 20
      allowed_actions: [reserve_capacity, elevate_priority, suspend_backpressure]

Safety and guardrails

- Grace windows are explicit and auditable. No manual, indefinite grace. Max single grace for a route: 4 hours in a 30-day window.
- Capacity Broker must respect multi-tenant fairness labels: reserved capacity is isolated to the extent that it cannot starve critical system services.
- All preemption must respect a 15-minute drain window and Post-Preempt hooks must trigger automated requeue or job resumption logic.

Customer communication play

- If paid customers are in the impacted cohort, Customer Support & AE are notified at the At-Risk threshold.
- Draft notice template (50–200 chars):
  \"We are experiencing elevated latency for <svc> and have applied short-term mitigations to preserve availability. We will follow up with impact and timeline.\"

Post-incident review and continuous improvement

- For any invocation of the Capacity Broker that lasted > 30 minutes or involved preemption, require a focused incident review within 5 business days.
- Incident review must cover:
  - Why the grace was needed (root cause summary).
  - Broker actions executed and time-to-attach/reserve.
  - Cost impact estimate (reserved minutes, preemptions).
  - Suggested permanent fixes (capacity increases, model quantization, query shape changes).

Metrics to track (SRE program)

- Number of grace activations per service per month (target <= 2 for business-critical routes).
- Mean time to attach capacity (target < 10 minutes for pre-warmed pools).
- Post-grace violation rate (percent of grace windows followed by enforcement within 24h).
- Cost delta attributable to broker actions (monthly).

Operational checklist (quick reference)

- Confirm alert -> classify P-tier -> activate grace policy -> call capacity broker -> apply traffic shaping -> track uptime and burn -> expire grace and re-evaluate -> open review if >30m.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets
sections.heading: Primary signals (examples)

sections.body: curl -X POST https://platform.redwood.internal/v1/broker/reserve -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"service":"com.redwood.svc.generate","gpu_kind":"a100-80gb","minutes":120,"priority":"high"}'
sections.heading: Reserve capacity (programmatic)

sections.body:
redwood-capacity broker cancel --id <reservation-id>

Appendix B — Audit event example (JSON string for logs)

{
  "event_type": "grace_policy.activate",
  "service": "com.redwood.svc.generate",
  "tier": "P1",
  "start_ts": "2027-02-15T02:13:00Z",
  "initiated_by": "oncall-aisha@redwood.internal",
  "reason": "scheduled-batch-burst"
}

Related resources

- Capacity Broker design doc (platform/architecture)
- Per-service SLO dashboard (dashboards -> service-name -> slo)
- Model Rollout and Pinning runbook

Change log

- 2026-11-03: initial draft and internal review.
- 2027-02-15: formalized broker CLI commands, tightened max grace caps, added audit schema.

Contact

SRE rotation: sre-oncall@redwood.internal
Platform eng lead: platform-ops@redwood.internal

payload.page_title: SRE Evidence Capture and Incident Chronicle

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines a standardized, minimal-yet-sufficient evidence capture format (the Incident Chronicle) and an operational procedure for collecting, preserving, and auditing telemetry and artifacts during SRE incidents. The goal is to enable fast, accurate triage, reproducible forensics, and reliable post-incident analysis while minimizing oncall cognitive load.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all model-serving and inference control-plane incidents with SLO impact >= 1% burn in a 1-hour window or any customer-impacting outage.
- Intended audience: oncall SREs, responders, incident commanders, service owners, and postmortem authors.
- Not a replacement for existing runbooks; this prescribes evidence primitives and a lean chronicle artifact to attach to incident reviews.

Key principles
--------------
- Timeliness: capture essential artifacts in the first 10 minutes.
- Determinism: evidence should be reproducible where possible (commands, timestamps, node IDs).
- Completeness: preserve provenance (who captured what, why).
- Least privilege: redact secrets automatically; sensitive artifacts get restricted access.

Incident Chronicle (artifact) - canonical fields
------------------------------------------------
Provide a single, small JSON or Markdown document (the Chronicle) attached to the incident ticket (JIRA/ServiceNow). The Chronicle is purposely compact. Required fields:

1) incident_id: human-readable incident identifier (e.g., INF-2026-0423)
2) timeline_start_utc: ISO-8601 timestamp when responder first observed problem
3) observed_signals: short bullet list of primary alerts/metrics (name and short metric sample)
4) impact_summary: one-sentence customer and SLO impact statement
5) initial_hypothesis: short sentence (e.g., "KV cache saturation on model-pool-a")
6) captured_artifacts: list of artifact keys (log segments, traces, dump paths)
7) capture_commands: exact commands used to collect artifacts (copy with args)
8) owner_oncall: name and pager handle of primary oncall
9) evidence_bucket: storage path with expiration policy
10) preservation_flags: list of retention/permission overrides (if any)
11) final_state: closed|mitigated|ongoing
12) chronicle_version: schema version (e.g., v1)

Example Chronicle snippet (Markdown form)
---------------------------------------
incident_id: INF-2026-0423
timeline_start_utc: 2026-02-12T15:07:00Z
observed_signals:
- generation-latency.p95 = 3.6s (baseline 0.7s)
- error-rate.tokenize = 0.9% (baseline 0.01%)
impact_summary: Canary traffic experiencing sustained tail latency causing canary SLO to burn 12% in 30m
initial_hypothesis: model hotstart OOM thrash in quantized serving path
captured_artifacts:
- /evidence/INF-2026-0423/host-12/systemd-journal-15m.log
- traces/INF-2026-0423/trace-3f2a.json
- snapshot/redis-keys-2026-02-12T15-12.json
capture_commands:
- ssh ec2-user@host-12 'sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since "2026-02-12 14:55" > /tmp/journal-15m.log'
- rtracer fetch --trace-id 3f2a --to /evidence/INF-2026-0423/trace-3f2a.json
owner_oncall: Aisha Patel (@aisha-oncall)
evidence_bucket: s3://redwood-evidence/INF-2026-0423/ (retention=90d)
preservation_flags: [keep, legal-hold=false]
final_state: mitigated
chronicle_version: v1

Evidence capture primitives (what to collect first)
--------------------------------------------------
Collect in priority order. If automation is available, rely on it but always attach the Chronicle.
1) Alert context and relevant Grafana panel snapshot (p95/p99, heatmap if available)
2) Traces for the offending request(s) (3 top traces by latency or error)
3) Short log slices (15 minutes before, during, 5 minutes after) for implicated hosts
4) Runtime memory snapshots (if safe) or memory pressure metrics (RSS, OOM count)
5) Scheduler/Kubernetes pod events and deployments in last 30 minutes
6) Cache/KV metrics and recent eviction counts
7) Inference runtime metrics: batch sizes, queue depth, token issuance rate
8) Config/feature flags changed in the last 24 hours (via config history)
9) Sample input triggering the issue (redacted for PII)

Roles & responsibilities
------------------------
- First Responder: generate Chronicle, collect top-3 artifacts, mark timeline_start_utc.
- Incident Commander: validate Chronicle, assign acquisition of any long-lived artifacts (heap dumps) and request retention overrides.
- Evidence Steward (SRE runbook role): ensure artifacts are uploaded to evidence_bucket, set ACLs, and record preservation_flags.
- Service Owner: provide domain context and confirm final_state before postmortem kick-off.

Step-by-step rapid capture procedure (first 10 minutes)
----------------------------------------------------
1) Create incident ticket and set severity tag.
2) Populate Chronicle required fields (incident_id, timeline_start_utc, observed_signals, owner_oncall).
3) Run automated proof-capture (if enabled): `rundoc capture --incident $INCIDENT_ID --profile rapid` (captures graphs and traces).
4) If automation unavailable, run the manual minimal commands below and paste into capture_commands.
5) Upload artifacts to evidence_bucket and attach Chronicle link to ticket.
6) Set preservation_flags if legal or escalated customer involvement is detected.

Manual minimal capture commands (copy/paste)
-------------------------------------------
- grafana snapshot: curl -X POST "https://grafana.internal/api/snapshots" -d '{\"dashboard\": \"$DASH_ID\"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
- traces: rtracer fetch --service runtime --limit 3 --from=2026-02-12T15:00 --to=2026-02-12T15:15 > /tmp/top-traces.json
- logs: ssh $HOST 'sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since "$(date --utc --date='15 minutes ago' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"' > /tmp/runtime-logs-15m.log
- pod events: kubectl -n inference get events --field-selector lastTimestamp>=$(date -d '15 minutes ago' -Iseconds)

Retention, access control, and redaction policy
------------------------------------------------
- Default evidence retention: 90 days.
- Preservation flags allow 1-year or legal-hold: Evidence Steward escalates to Security/Legal.
- Sensitive artifacts (PII, customer-provided prompts) must be redacted before storing; automation will detect common PII patterns and mark artifact as restricted.
- ACLs: oncall SREs + service owner + evidence-steward have read access by default; Legal/IR can be added with request.

Audit and post-incident obligations
----------------------------------
- Within 48 hours: attach Chronicle to postmortem draft and list captured_artifacts with checksums.
- Within 7 days: Evidence Steward validates retention settings and documents any preservation_flags.
- For incidents that trigger external communications, redact and produce an external-friendly evidence summary separate from the Chronicle.
- Periodic audit: quarterly run to ensure evidence buckets have correct ACLs and retention policies.

Operational tooling integration checklist
--------------------------------------
- Ensure `rundoc capture --profile rapid` exists in the toolchain and is callable from the oncall workstation.
- Integrate with PagerDuty: create incident and automatically populate incident_id and owner_oncall into Chronicle template.
- Provide a Confluence template macro to attach Chronicle to the incident page.
- Build a Lambda that enforces evidence_bucket encryption and retention on object creation.

Appendix A — Incident Chronicle checklist (quick)
------------------------------------------------
- [ ] Incident ticket created and severity set
- [ ] Chronicle created with initial_hypothesis
- [ ] Top-3 traces captured and uploaded
- [ ] 15m logs from implicated hosts captured
- [ ] Grafana snapshot attached
- [ ] Evidence bucket path recorded in Chronicle
- [ ] Preservation flags set if needed

Appendix B — Example annotated capture_commands (for copy/paste)
---------------------------------------------------------------
ssh ec2-user@host-12 'sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since "2026-02-12 14:55" > /tmp/journal-15m.log && aws s3 cp /tmp/journal-15m.log s3://redwood-evidence/INF-2026-0423/host-12-journal-15m.log'
rtracer fetch --trace-filter 'span.service:runtime and span.duration>1000' --limit 3 --to s3://redwood-evidence/INF-2026-0423/top-traces.json

Change history
--------------
- 2025-11-03: Initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2025-12-10: Added evidence stewardship role and retention defaults (Diego Morales)
- 2026-02-14: Schema v1 locked; added automated capture CLI references (Claire Nguyen)

Related artifacts and links
-------------------------
- Incident evidence retention policy: confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/evidence-retention-policy-2024
- Trace ingestion and rtracer CLI: confluence/eng-platform/operational-tooling/trace-ingest-and-tools
- SLO burn thresholds and alerting rules: confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-oncall-escalation-and-capacity-triggers-2026

Contact
-------
For questions about the Chronicle schema or to request automation integration, contact the Evidence Steward mailbox: evidence-steward@redwood.ai or @evidence-steward on Slack.

payload.page_title: Eval-driven Quality SLO & Error Budget Triage Runbook

sections.body:
Overview

This runbook defines how Redwood SREs and Model Owners operationalize quality SLOs that are driven by recurring evals (acceptance test suites, regression suites and monitoring prompts). It ties eval outputs to an error budget, describes telemetry and alerting, and provides a step-by-step triage and mitigation procedure for quality regressions that impact customers.

Scope

- Applies to any production inference service and model variant that has a defined Quality SLO (examples: /v1/generate text models, embedding models, and rerank endpoints).
- Covers measurement, alerting, incident triage, containment, rollback, and post-incident review for quality regressions (not pure infra outages).

Definitions

- Quality SLO: A service-level objective expressed as the acceptable rate of passing a curated eval test-suite over a rolling window (e.g., 99% pass rate over 28d).
- Eval Job: A scheduled job that runs a deterministic set of prompts/cases against a production model to produce metrics (pass_rate, f1, rouge, latency).
- Error Budget (quality): The complement of the SLO (e.g., SLO=99% -> budget=1% over the SLO window). Burning the budget indicates degraded quality.
- Regression Alert: An automated alert triggered when the rolling pass_rate drops below the alert threshold (usually SLO - delta).

Principles

- Ground SLOs in deterministic evals: production traffic sampling is useful for signal, but SLOs and error budgets are measured from the curated eval harness to be repeatable and auditable.
- Fast containment, slow blame: prioritize rollback/mitigation over root cause attribution.
- Link SLO burn to operational playbooks: burn should trigger staged mitigations (canary rollback, deploy freeze, throttling).

SLO design guidance (recommended defaults)

1) Metric: eval.pass_rate (fraction of eval cases classified as PASS on the golden/acceptance suite).
2) Window: rolling 28-day for contractual SLOs; 7-day for short-lived experimental SLOs.
3) Target: 99.0% for GA models; 99.8% for critical enterprise tenants (customer-specific SLOs live in Dedicated contracts).
4) Alert thresholds:
   - Warning: pass_rate <= SLO - 0.25% (7-day window)
   - Incident: pass_rate <= SLO - 0.75% (24-hour window)
5) Error budget: budget = 1 - SLO (example: 1.0% for 99% SLO). Track burn-rate as budget_used / budget_size over the SLO window.

Example SLO table

| Model | Eval Suite | Window | SLO | Error Budget | Criticality | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| text-clarity-v2 | clarity-acceptance-v1 | 28d | 99.0% | 1.0% | high | @ml-service-steward |
| embed-semantic-v1 | embed-stability-v1 | 7d | 98.5% | 1.5% | medium | @embedding-team |

Telemetry and dashboards

- Eval-runner -> telemetry pipeline produces metrics: eval.pass_rate, eval.mean_f1, eval.case_breakdown[failing_case_id], eval.job_run_duration.
- Dashboards: Quality SLO Overview (per-model, per-tenant), Case Heatmap (failing prompts by tag), Error Budget Burn Chart (28d view).
- Alerting: PagerDuty for Incident alerts (quality-incident), Slack channel #sre-quality for warning alerts.

Alert rules (examples)

1) Incident alert (firing):
   - condition: eval.pass_rate (24h) < SLO - 0.75%
   - severity: P1
   - notify: pd-sre-quality (escalation policy), #sre-quality, model-owner oncall

2) Warning alert (non-pagerduty):
   - condition: eval.pass_rate (7d) < SLO - 0.25%
   - severity: P3
   - notify: #sre-quality, mailbox-model-owners

Runbook: Quality SLO Breach (Incident triage steps)

This section defines a rapid, ordered checklist to contain model-quality incidents. Ownership: the oncall SRE + oncall model steward.

1) Acknowledge and classify (0-10m):
   - Acknowledge PagerDuty alert.
   - Record initial facts in the incident doc: model name, variant, eval suite name, current pass_rate, window and immediate burn rate.

2) Scope and blast radius (10-30m):
   - Check production traffic signals: Is customer-facing error rate or user complaints increasing? (metrics: api.error_rate, api.latency, customer-telemetry).
   - Check tenant-level SLOs (if multi-tenant): identify impacted tenants and their contractual criticality.

3) Triage with eval evidence (15-45m):
   - Open latest eval-job artifact (link from dashboard). Inspect failing_case_ids and clusters.
   - Run the failing eval cases manually against the production endpoint and the previous stable model (if available) to confirm regression. Use the eval harness:

     $ eval-runner run --suite clarity-acceptance-v1 --model text-clarity-v2 --output /tmp/run-123.json

   - Compare outputs using the eval-compare tool:

     $ eval-compare /tmp/run-123.json /tmp/previous-stable-run.json --report short

4) Containment and mitigation (30-90m): (choose the least disruptive effective action)
   - If regression reproduces and is customer-impacting, prioritize rollback to last known-good model variant.
     - Rollback command (example):

       $ rctl deploy rollback --service inference-text --model-variant text-clarity-v1 --reason "quality SLO breach"

   - If rollback is not possible or slow, apply policy-driven routing to divert traffic to Dedicated/backup variants:

       $ rctl routing set --service inference-text --policy "prefer: text-clarity-v1; fallback: text-clarity-v2-readonly"

   - For noisy single-case failures, consider adding short-term case-level patches (score thresholds, prompt fixes) with signoff from model owners. Document these as temporary mitigations.

5) Verify recovery (30-120m):
   - Confirm eval.pass_rate returns above the incident threshold and that customer signals normalize.
   - If rollback occurred, confirm histograms for other metrics (latency, error rate) remain within SLOs.

6) Communicate and runbook closure (within 24h):
   - Post an incident summary to #sre-quality and to the product owner with the initial timeline, actions taken, and immediate impact.
   - If error budget was exhausted or materially reduced for a tenant, partner with Customer Success to coordinate credits/communication per the crediting policy.

Post-incident review and standards

- If incident led to > 25% of error budget consumed in a 28d window OR customer facing impact > P2, perform a formal incident review within 5 business days. Required artifacts: incident timeline, eval artifacts, model diffs, deployment changelog, and mitigation commands executed.
- Use the template: "Incident -> Eval Regression Review" and include a replayable test harness (CI job) that reproduces the failing eval cases.
- Action items must be tracked in the SLO remediation board and assigned to owners with due dates.

Operational tooling and automation suggestions

- Eval-runner: schedule nightly runs (staggered across regions) that push artifacts to object storage and emit metrics to the telemetry pipeline.
- Auto-triage job: on incident alert, create a triage ticket with links to last 3 eval runs, diffs and top N failing cases.
- Rollback safe-guard: require two-step authorization for model rollouts to production (oncall SRE + model steward) with an audit log.

Rollout & canary checklist (pre-deploy)

- Pre-deploy: run the full acceptance suite and a seeded traffic replay against the canary.
- Canary-window: run 24–72h with daily eval checks and 95th percentile of pass_rate >= production SLO.
- Stop-deploy criteria: any single-day drop > 0.5% against SLO or any reproducible customer complaint correlated to the canary.

Appendix A — Alert payload examples

- PagerDuty payload (simplified):

  {
    "title": "Quality SLO breach: text-clarity-v2 (eval.pass_rate=98.1%)",
    "service": "sre-quality",
    "details": "pass_rate 24h=98.1% (SLO=99.0%) — failing cases: [case-42, case-117] — run_id: 2025-02-10T03:12Z"
  }

Appendix B — Example eval job YAML

- eval job spec (example):

  name: clarity-acceptance-v1
  schedule: "0 03 * * *"  # UTC daily at 03:00
  suite: clarity-cases-2024-11
  model: text-clarity-v2
  thresholds:
    pass_rate: 0.99
    mean_f1: 0.90

Appendix C — Ownership and contacts

- Oncall SRE: see PD rotation (team: sre-rotation, channel: #sre-oncall)
- Model Steward: check service OWNERS file under repo infra/services/inference-text/OWNERS
- Customer Success escalation: cs-enterprise@redwood.ai

References and related pages

- Eval harness spec: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/runbook
- Model onboarding & acceptance criteria: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/acceptance-guidelines
- SLO policy and crediting: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-crediting-policy-2024

Change history

- 2024-11-15: initial draft by Morgan Li.
- 2025-02-10: published, added automated triage job steps and canary window guidance.
