payload.page_title: client-request-shaping-and-local-fallback-playbook-2026

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents practical, production-ready patterns for client-side request shaping and local fallback when calling the Redwood inference API from application servers and client SDKs. It focuses on minimizing cost and tail latency while preserving correctness and observability. The guidance is intended for SDK authors, backend engineers integrating Redwood APIs, and platform teams building resilient bridges to the Redwood runtime.

Goals

- Reduce 95th/99th percentile request latency through client-side shaping and speculative strategies.
- Lower per-token compute cost via token-aware batching and prefix caching.
- Provide robust local fallback behavior to keep user-facing flows available when network or backend degradations occur.
- Preserve telemetry continuity so downstream incident and cost analysis is accurate.

Scope and audience

- In-scope: SDKs (server and browser-safe shims), service-side adapters, edge proxies, and application integration patterns.
- Out-of-scope: deep server-side model serving internals and on-prem packaging for customers (covered under eng-private-deployments).

Key concepts and terminology

- Request shaping: client-side pre-processing to group, truncate, or transform calls to maximize batching and reduce tokens.
- Token-aware batching: grouping requests by prompt length budget and model variant to form optimal batches.
- Local fallback: strategies executed on the client when Redwood endpoints are degraded (cached responses, smaller model variants, or degraded UX).
- Speculative concurrency: launching multiple candidate requests and using the first acceptable response to reduce tail latency.

Patterns and recipes

1) Token-aware batching (recommended for server SDKs)

- When to use: high QPS, many short prompts (<= 128 tokens), or workloads with many small concurrent requests (chat widgets, autosuggest).
- How it works: group incoming requests into buckets by model, instruction-type, and expected token length. Dispatch a batch when either (a) batch token budget is reached, or (b) max wait (e.g. 15 ms) elapses.

Minimal config (example):

- bucket_key: model_name + instruction_tag
- max_batch_tokens: 16_384
- max_batch_size: 64 requests
- max_wait_ms: 15

Operational notes:

- Choose max_wait_ms to balance throughput and tail latency; 10–25 ms is typical for low-latency services.
- Monitor batch token utilization: aim for 60–85% to avoid wasted compute while keeping SLOs.

2) Prefix/KV caching (client-local & shared caches)

- Use case: assistants and multi-turn chat where many prompts share prefixes or system messages.
- Implementation options:
  - SDK-level in-memory KV cache for a single worker process.
  - Shared Redis/memcached cache for pool-based backends (store serialized prefix KV state).

Cache keys and TTLs:

- key: sha256(model + conversation_id + last_committed_prompt_hash)
- ttl: 5–30 minutes depending on concurrency and conversation stickiness

Data hygiene:

- Ensure cached KV blobs are encrypted at rest when stored in shared caches.
- Invalidate cache on policy or system prompt changes (explicit cache-bust header).

3) Local fallback strategies (graded)

Design fallbacks in tiers from least to most invasive. Choose combinations per route.

- Tier A: Local synthetic reply (best-effort message: "We're having trouble processing your request. Try again in a moment.") – preserves UX but loses LLM fidelity.
- Tier B: Cached golden responses for known prompts (embeddings + retrieval of top-N canonical responses).
- Tier C: Route to smaller/cheaper embedded model (on-device or local microservice) with a post-filter step.
- Tier D: Fallback to read-only user experience (e.g., show last saved state).

Policy and UX guidance:

- Prefer Tier B/C for user-facing critical paths where stale but coherent output is acceptable.
- Always surface that content may be degraded (UI banner or toast).

4) Speculative concurrency (latency-first flows)

- Pattern: for latency-sensitive endpoints, issue two parallel requests: one to the primary production model and another to a smaller low-latency model. Use the first response that passes a basic acceptance filter (non-empty, not obscene, size threshold).
- Cost tradeoff: increases compute cost but can drastically cut P99 latency. Limit speculative requests to important routes (search, assist, autosuggest) and to <5% of total QPS by sampling.

Instrumentation and telemetry (must-haves)

All SDKs and adapters must emit the following telemetry fields on each logical request:

- request_id (UUID)
- client_sdk (name + version)
- model_requested and model_served (string)
- batch_size and batch_token_count (integers)
- shaping_strategy (none | small-batch | full-batch | speculative)
- fallback_action (none | cached | synthetic | reduced_model)
- latency_ms and network_time_ms
- acceptance_result (accepted | rejected_by_filter)

Exporters and traces:

- Span boundaries: client-shaping, outbound-call, cache-lookup, speculative-merge, response-validation.
- Tag the trace with route and SLO tier (e.g., route:search, slo:interactive-100ms).

SLOs and thresholds (suggested)

- P50 latency: 50–100 ms for interactive routes (including client shaping).
- P95 latency: <= 200 ms.
- P99 latency: <= 400 ms (use speculative concurrency to reduce spikes).
- Batch token utilization: target 60–85%.

Quickstart: adding token-aware batching to a Node server SDK

1) Install the batching adapter (example CLI):

npm install @redwood/batch-adapter@latest

2) Minimal adapter config (YAML snippet)

adapter:
  model: redwood-gen-1
  max_batch_tokens: 16384
  max_wait_ms: 15
  acceptance_filter:
    min_tokens: 4

3) Pseudocode (server):

- onIncomingRequest(req):
  - compute bucket_key from model + intent
  - enqueue request into bucket pool
  - when bucket triggers, assemble batch payload, attach request_ids, and call Redwood API
  - fanout responses back to individual waiting requests

Troubleshooting and canonical fixes (top support issues)

Issue: Burst of small requests causing high tail latency and cost
- Symptom: Many 1–2 token prompts under high concurrency, high P99, inefficient GPU utilization.
- Fix: Enable token-aware batching, set min_batch_size or min_batch_tokens to avoid dispatching tiny batches. Add jitter to request arrival times (micro-delay 5–10ms).

Issue: Cache poisoning or stale KV responses
- Symptom: Users receive outdated context or system messages after a rollout.
- Fix: Implement cache-bust on system prompt rollouts; version cache keys using system_prompt_version. Add short TTLs during rollout windows.

Issue: Fallback responses look incoherent or harmful
- Symptom: Local fallback returning content that fails safety checks or confuses users.
- Fix: Add the same safety filter used in production as a lightweight post-filter. For cached golden responses, maintain a small set of QA assertions (regex checks, length bounds, presence of required fields).

Operational playbook: rolling out shaping+fallback

1) Stage in canary environment with 1–2% of traffic routed through shaping adapter. Monitor: batch_utilization, per-request latency, and acceptance rates.
2) Run A/B for fallback UX: compare completion rate and CSAT for degraded flow vs. blocking.
3) Gradually increase to 25% then 100% while validating telemetry correlation.

Production checklist before wide rollout

- SDK emits required telemetry fields and traces.
- Batch adapter has circuit-breaker metrics and configurable thresholds.
- Safety and acceptance filters are present and tested.
- All cache keys are versioned and encrypted for shared caches.
- Rollback plan: disable shaping router and revert to direct calls; ensure canary is small so rollback is immediate.

Ownership and contact points

- Pattern owner: SDK Reliability Team (sre-sdk@redwood.ai)
- Observability: Eng Platform (telemetry@redwood.ai)
- Security review: AppSec (appsec@redwood.ai)

Related resources

- Local request/response playback quickstart (see related_pages)
- SDK batching & streaming canonical fixes (see related_pages)

Appendix: example acceptance filter pseudocode

function acceptanceFilter(response) {
  if (!response || response.trim().length === 0) return false;
  if (response.includes('<PROHIBITED_PHRASE>')) return false;
  if (response.split('
').length > 50 && route === 'interactive') return false;
  return true;
}

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-01-15: Added speculative concurrency guidance and telemetry fields (reviewers: Alvarez, Nair).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized production checklist and rollout guidance; marked published.

payload.page_title: Marketplace inference value casebook: seller growth & trust use-cases

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This casebook equips sales and solutions engineers with a compact, repeatable story for marketplace customers (two‑sided platforms: buyers + sellers). It bundles positioning, competitive context, sample pricing scenarios, a one‑page pitch outline, a short customer case study, and a prospect-focused Security FAQ. Use this when: discovery surfaces seller-side personalization, automated moderation, fraud detection, or onboarding automation as top priorities.

Audience: GTM (AEs, SEs, AMs), solutions architects, and customer engineering.

Key thesis

- Marketplaces scale when seller activation, trust, and buyer-seller matching improve simultaneously.
- Inference controls the economics: latency and per-call cost directly affect throughput (conversions) and margin.
- Redwood’s differentiated offering: predictable SLO-backed serving, cost-aware controls (batching/quantization), and deployment flexibility (hosted/dedicated/private) reduces risk for platform teams.

Why marketplaces care (concise outcomes)

- Faster seller onboarding -> higher activation: automated intake + personalized recommendations reduce time-to-first-listing.
- Higher buyer conversion from personalized search/rank -> small latency wins compound to large revenue lifts.
- Trust & safety at scale -> automated moderation + reranking saves manual review costs and reduces fraud exposure.
- Unit economics clarity -> predictable per-transaction inference costs enable margin modelling for marketplace take rates.

Positioning and messaging (battle-tested lines)

Top-line positioning for pitches (3 variants depending on buyer):
- For Product/Marketplace PMs: "Make seller activation 2x faster while keeping latency under 150ms for search personalization — with predictable, auditable inference costs."
- For Engineering/Platform: "Replace brittle self-hosted inference pipelines with a single runtime that gives deterministic p99 latency, autoscaling, and can failover to cheaper model variants automatically."
- For Security/Legal: "Run inference where you need it: hosted for speed, dedicated for isolation, or Private/VPC for audited data paths and KMS integration."
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
"Redwood Inference helps marketplaces serve personalized results and seller automation with production-grade latency and cost controls. We give engineering teams predictable SLOs, built-in fallbacks, and the deployment options needed for regulated markets — so you can grow transactions without hidden inference costs."

Competitive brief (snapshot)

Objective: Provide a quick comparative frame for common objections. Keep this to one slide in a pitch.

Competitors compared: generic cloud managed endpoints, open-source self-hosted stacks, and single-vendor LLM API platforms.

| Capability | Redwood Inference | Cloud-managed endpoints | Self-hosted open stack | Single-vendor LLM API |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Predictable p99 latency (SLO) | Yes — SLA tiers | Varies | Depends on infra | Varies by model |
| Cost controls (batching/quantization) | Built-in, recommendations + Optimize toolkit | Manual tuning | Requires infra & infra-engineering | Limited |
| Private/VPC / On‑prem option | Yes (private control plane + on‑prem) | Limited | Yes (but heavy ops) | Rare |
| Rollouts + automatic fallback | Canary/A-B + model-variant fallback | Limited | Needs orchestration | Limited |
| Observability (token-level cost breakdown) | Yes | Basic | Custom | Limited |
| Time-to-production for new models | Days | Days–weeks | Weeks–months | Days |

Key rebuttals and scripts

- Objection: "We can host models ourselves, cheaper."
  Script: "Hosting looks cheaper until you add the engineering hours for kernel tuning, KV cache correctness, autoscaling for tail latency, and incident response. Redwood buys down that operational effort and gives you predictable economics you can model against transactions."

- Objection: "We can just use a public LLM API for prototypes."
  Script: "Public APIs are great for prototypes. For marketplaces, you need deterministic latency, data controls, and transparent per-token economics at scale — especially when inference cost becomes a meaningful line item in your unit economics."

Pricing guidance and example scenarios
sections.heading: Three-line elevator pitch (use in outreach)

sections.body:
- Anchor to business metrics (e.g., lift in activation rate, conversion, or reviews processed) not tokens.
- Use a blended model for pilots: hosted API at usage-tiered rates -> move to Dedicated when sustained throughput increases predictability.
- Show the math: per‑transaction inference cost * transactions = monthly inference spend; provide suggestions to reduce unit cost (quantization, caching, lower-capacity variant for background jobs).

Representative pricing scenarios (simplified, for conversation only)

Assumptions: average inference call = 350 tokens (generation + context), marketplace handles 2M inference calls/month for personalization and onboarding automation.

Scenario A — Hosted (fast pilot):
- Price: $0.0008 per generate token (example anchor for sales) + $0.0003 per embed token for embedding calls.
- Monthly estimate: 2M calls * 350 tokens * $0.0008 = $560,000/month.
- Mitigations: Enable prefix caching for templates (expected 30% token reduction), use cheaper model for non-latency-sensitive workloads (reduce to $0.0004/token).
- Adjusted estimate: 560k * 0.7 * 0.5 = ~$196,000/month (pilot-optimized).

Scenario B — Dedicated (predictable throughput):
- Reserved capacity contract with committed monthly spend (example): $85k/month for a pool that comfortably serves 2M calls with p99 < 200ms.
- Added benefits: data isolation, predictable latency, lower unit cost when compared to peak-hosted pricing.

Scenario C — Private (regulatory / enterprise):
- Platform fee + support + infra requirement. Typical starts at $150k/year platform fee + infra costs; break-even often occurs when you require audited data paths and ~>X throughput where infra costs are internalized.

How to run a short pilot (3-week plan)

1. Week 0: Discovery & success metrics (activation lift %, p99 latency target, allowed cost per conversion). Owner: AE + SE.
2. Week 1: Pilot setup — decide hosted vs dedicated evaluation lane, small dataset onboarding, key prompts / templates. Owner: SE.
3. Week 2: Integration & monitoring — token-level cost dashboard, early quality evaluation (sample prompt sets), baseline A/B test. Owner: Customer Eng + SE.
4. Week 3: Demo results & conversion plan — show measured lift and economics, propose committed pricing or dedicated sizing. Owner: AE + AM.

Pitch deck outline (single-page / 5-slide quick deck)

Slide 1: Problem — friction in seller activation, moderation backlog, and conversion leakage. Include 1–2 data points.
Slide 2: Redwood solution — low-latency inference with cost controls and deployment flexibility.
Slide 3: Customer outcome — sample metrics (activation time down 40%, manual reviews down 70%).
Slide 4: Pricing & deployment options — hosted pilot estimate, Dedicated example, Private summary.
Slide 5: Next steps & pilot checklist (3-week plan).

One-page battlecard (talking points for SEs)

- Opening: "We help marketplaces keep search under 150ms p99 while reducing per-conversion inference spend."
- Tech advantage: runtime tuned for KV caching and continuous batching; automatic model fallback.
- Business angle: predictable inference spend that can be directly modeled into take-rate economics.
- Risk mitigation: private control plane for regulated sellers + KMS integration for per-tenant encryption keys.

Customer case study (anonymized composite): Marketly (fictional composite built from similar wins)

Context: Mid-market two-sided marketplace focusing on niche home services. Pain: Low seller activation and manual moderation backlog of 12k content items/month.
Approach: Pilot used hosted API for onboarding automation and an embeddings + rerank flow for search personalization. Implemented caching for onboarding templates and a dedicated low-cost model for background classification.
sections.heading: Principles to convey during pricing conversations

sections.body:
- Time-to-first-active-seller reduced from 6 days to 1.8 days (70% improvement).
- Buyer search conversions improved by 14% (A/B test).
- Manual moderation workload reduced 62%, saving 0.6 FTE in triage labor (~$40k/year).
- After evaluation, Marketly moved high‑sensitivity workloads to Dedicated capacity with a 30% lower unit cost vs peak-hosted.

Security FAQ for marketplace prospects (short answers to accelerate conversations)

Q: Can we keep PII off Redwood logs?
A: Yes. We support customer-controlled request filtering and tokenization at the SDK layer and provide options to redact/omit PII before it reaches the control plane. For Private deployments, data stays in your VPC.

Q: How do you handle keys and encryption?
A: KMS integrations available (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM for Private customers. We support per-tenant encryption keys and key rotation policies.

Q: Is inference audited? Can we get request traces?
A: Yes. Audit logs include request metadata (no raw prompt bodies unless explicitly enabled). We provide configurable retention windows and can deliver exports for compliance reviews.

Q: What controls exist to prevent model drift or regressions?
A: Redwood Optimize integrates with evaluation harnesses and can run continuous evals on chosen prompt sets. Rollouts are gated with canaries, A/B, and automatic rollback on quality regressions.

Q: How is data residency handled?
A: Deployments can be region-locked. Hosted customers can select cloud-region endpoints; Dedicated/Private deployments allow full control over data residency.

Q: Can we run safe content filters and custom classifiers locally?
A: Yes. You can deploy dedicated classifiers to a private pool for sensitive moderation, or use mixed strategy: public-hosted for low-risk, private for escalations.

Operational targets & SLOs to propose in deals

- Latency: p50 < 40ms, p95 < 120ms, p99 < 250ms (hosted tier sample)
- Availability: 99.9% for hosted API; SLA-backed higher tiers for Dedicated
- Cost variance guardrails: monthly unit-cost drift alert if spend-per-conversion changes > 15% quarter-over-quarter

Rollout checklist for SEs (go-to-production)

1. Agree success metrics and thresholds (conversion delta, latency SLO, allowed cost per active seller).
2. Establish data governance: what user data flows through inference, PII handling, retention windows.
3. Choose pilot deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated) and map infra requirements.
4. Instrument token-level cost dashboards and tracing.
5. Run initial A/B test for personalization or onboarding flow.
6. Evaluate results, propose Dedicated sizing or Private deployment if needed.

Appendix: Quick technical configuration table

| Item | Recommended config for Marketplace personalization pilot |
|---|---|
| Model family | Medium-latency open LLM or moderate-cost generation model |
| Max sequence length | 1024 tokens (truncate non-critical history) |
| Caching | Prefix + KV cache enabled for templates; TTL 24–72 hours |
| Batch size | Runtime auto-batching enabled; target latency budget p95 <= 120ms |
| Monitoring | Token-level cost, latency histograms, model-quality evals daily |
| Security | KMS integration, audit logs enabled, redact PII at ingestion |

Notes and recommended collateral

- Attach: 1-page pricing worksheet (customize during discovery).
- Attach: lightweight A/B test plan template (conversion metrics, sample size calculator).
- Attach: short demo script for SEs (walkthrough of latency and cost dashboards).

Contact & next steps

- Primary SE contact: Lina Chen (lina@redwood.ai)
- GTM deal lead template: include a pilot success spreadsheet and request Dedicated sizing session if pilot exceeds 1.5M calls/month.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Consolidated consumption scenarios and commercial packaging

sections.body: This document consolidates representative customer consumption scenarios and maps them to commercial packaging options for Redwood Inference. It blends product requirements, pricing archetypes, onboarding flows, and launch checklist items into a single reference intended for Product, GTM, and Sales Engineering. The goal is to provide clear mappings from real-world workload patterns to recommended tiers, credit models, and migration steps so that customers receive predictable economics and predictable SLOs.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Product managers and pricing owners
- Sales engineering and solutions architects
- GTM and account teams
- Finance and revenue operations
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Define 6 canonical consumption scenarios derived from field patterns.
- Map each scenario to 2–3 commercial packaging options (hosted, dedicated commit, hybrid credits).
- Provide sample pricing bands and per-unit economics for standard instance sizes.
- Specify PRD-level requirements for telemetry, billing metering hooks, and onboarding automation.
- Deliver a rollout and migration plan for early adopter customers.
sections.heading: Scope and aims

sections.body:
1) Intermittent query bursts (startups, low-traffic prototypes)
   - Characteristics: <100QPS spikes of short chat interactions, heavy short-lived concurrency, token distribution skewed toward short prompts (<128 tokens).
   - Primary concerns: cost predictability, self-serve onboarding friction, instant throttle/guardrails.

2) Steady high-throughput batch generation (analytics, nightly jobs)
   - Characteristics: large daily token volume, predictable windows for heavy load, tolerant of higher latency but wants low per-token cost.
   - Primary concerns: reserved capacity efficiency, batch/throughput discounts, offline prefetching.

3) Low-latency conversational product (consumer-facing chat)
   - Characteristics: strict p95 latency targets (<150ms for token stream), sustained medium QPS, high retention of KV cache across sessions.
   - Primary concerns: dedicated SLOs, KV cache affinity, failover behavior, stream reliability.

4) Regulated/private data (healthcare/finance)
   - Characteristics: private deployment or VPC, audit logs, region-bound residency, strict encryption and KMS controls.
   - Primary concerns: on-prem/private pricing, support SLAs, audit and compliance add-ons.

5) Embeddings-heavy similarity/retrieval ops
   - Characteristics: high volume of small embedding requests, long-term storage TTL for vectors, occasional re-index windows.
   - Primary concerns: per-embedding unit pricing, retention tiering, hybrid cache near-data.

6) Mixed-fidelity pipelines (multimodel pipelines)
   - Characteristics: orchestrated flows that use low-cost models for retrieval/generation and high-fidelity models for finalization.
   - Primary concerns: routing rules, cross-model pass-through costs, fidelity budget caps.
sections.heading: Canonical consumption scenarios (high-level)

sections.body:
- Packaging model A: Self-serve hosted credits
  - Description: pay-as-you-go token & embedding credits, immediate signup, conservative quotas.
  - Fit: Intermittent bursts, small embedding workloads, prototypes.

- Packaging model B: Reserved commit (Dedicated Lite / Dedicated Pro)
  - Description: monthly/annual GPU capacity commitments with discounted per-token rates and priority routing.
  - Fit: Batch generation, low-latency conversational products, high consistent throughput.

- Packaging model C: Hybrid credits + SLO overlay
  - Description: mixture of on-demand credits and reserved pools with explicit SLOs and overflow pricing for bursts.
  - Fit: Mixed-fidelity pipelines, customers requiring elasticity but predictable economics.

- Packaging model D: Private deployment license + support
  - Description: Private control plane or VPC deployment, platform fee, per-node pricing, optional on-prem bundle.
  - Fit: Regulated industries and enterprise customers requiring isolation.
sections.heading: Packaging options and mapping matrix

sections.body:
- Intermittent query bursts -> Model A (Self-serve credits) OR Model C for growth path
- Steady high-throughput batch -> Model B (Reserved commit) with batch-optimized rate cards
- Low-latency conversational -> Model B (Dedicated Pro) + SLO add-on
- Regulated/private data -> Model D (Private) + Compliance package pricing
- Embeddings-heavy -> Model A (for small users) or Model B with embeddings unit discounts
- Mixed-fidelity pipelines -> Model C (Hybrid) with explicit routing credit rules
sections.heading: Sample commercial mapping (short)

sections.body:
| Package | Typical commit | Effective per-1k-token rate* | Embedding unit | Notes |
|---------|----------------|-----------------------------|----------------|-------|
| Self-serve credits | No commit | $0.035 | $0.003 per embed | High elasticity, list pricing

* Effective per-1k-token rates are examples for standard sequence length distributions; final econs depend on quantization and batching.

sections.body:
- Metering: Emit per-request metering events including model_id, route_id, token_in, token_out, fidelity_flag, and routing_decision. Owner: Product/Telemetry. Target: instrumented in initial GA.
- Billing hooks: Billing buffer that consumes metering events with 10s SLA to ledger. Support both eventstream and batch ingest. Owner: Finance + Platform.

payload.page_title: Hybrid Deployment Packages and Consumption Guidelines

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines a set of hybrid deployment packages (hosted+demanded dedicated capacity+private overlay) and the recommended consumption/pricing guidelines for engineering, sales, and finance. It covers package definitions, billing primitives, quota semantics, migration/upgrade flows, acceptance criteria, and rollout milestones. The goal is to provide predictable economics for customers that mix Hosted API traffic with Reserved/Dedicated and Private nodes while preserving latency SLAs and predictable unit economics for Redwood.

Intended audience
------------------
- Product managers and pricing owners
- Solutions engineers and sales
- Billing & finance
- Infra and runtime engineering (capacity and runtime teams)
- Customer success / account teams for enterprise adoption

Motivation and background
-------------------------
Large customers routinely require a mixture of: (A) occasional burst traffic routed through Hosted API, (B) reserved Dedicated pools for baseline throughput, and (C) a Private deployment for sensitive data/regions. Today our SKU model treats these as separate product silos which complicates quoting and causes friction on migration paths. A hybrid packaging model aligns incentives, simplifies quoting, and enables smoother onboarding to Dedicated/Private while retaining predictable unit economics.

High-level goals
------------------
1. Provide 3 composable packages (Baseline, Burst, Private Overlay) that map to customer deployment patterns.
2. Ensure unit economics are preserved: per-token or per-embedding price floor for hosted traffic, committed-rate pricing for Dedicated, and flat subscription for Private control plane.
3. Define clear quota and failover semantics when customers exceed reserved capacity.
4. Provide migration and rollback procedures that minimize service disruption and billing disputes.
5. Ship with billing primitives that allow proration, usage breakouts by route/model, and credits for cache/quantization savings.

Package definitions (summary table)
----------------------------------
| Package name | Primary intent | Billing primitives | Included guarantees | Typical customer fit |
|-------------|----------------|--------------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Baseline | Host most traffic via Hosted API; low friction | per-token pricing, rate limits, monthly invoice | 99.9% control-plane SLA, 95th percentile latency targets | Startups, mid-market teams |
| Reserved (Dedicated Commit) | Predictable throughput and isolation | monthly commit ($/vGPU-hour) + overage at discounted rate | Dedicated pool with throughput SLOs, priority capacity | High-throughput SaaS, regulated workloads |
| Private Overlay | Private control plane + optional on-prem agents | subscription + per-node license | VPC/VPN support, audit logs, custom KMS | Enterprise with compliance requirements |

Billing primitives and formulas
-------------------------------
- Hosted unit price: P_hosted ($ per 1k tokens)
- Reserved commit price: P_commit ($ per vGPU-hour committed)
- Reserved overage price: P_overage (discounted per-token or per-vGPU-hour beyond commit)
- Private subscription: S_private (flat monthly) + N_node * L_node (per-node license)

Example blended cost calculation (monthly)
1. Customer commits to 500 vGPU-hours at $X per vGPU-hour (Reserved baseline).
2. Expected monthly hosted traffic: 200M tokens @ P_hosted.
3. Observed cache savings: 12% of token cost (credited).
4. Overage (burst) consumed: 120 vGPU-hours charged at P_overage.
Total = (500 * P_commit) + (200M/1k * P_hosted * (1 - 0.12)) + (120 * P_overage) + S_private (if applicable).

Quota semantics and failover rules
----------------------------------
1. Baseline traffic is charged against Hosted quota first.
2. If customer has an active Reserved commit and the routing policy is set to "prefer-dedicated", traffic is routed to Dedicated until commit capacity is consumed.
3. When dedicated commit is exhausted within a billing period:
   a. If auto-burst enabled -> traffic continues to be served via Dedicated at P_overage up to configured burst cap.
   b. If auto-burst disabled -> traffic is routed to Hosted and invoiced at P_hosted.
4. Private Overlay customers may opt to enforce strict isolation (no failover to Hosted) or allow graceful fallback to Dedicated/Hosted depending on contract.

Configuration options (customer-facing)
--------------------------------------
- routing.preference: ["prefer-dedicated", "prefer-hosted", "isolate-private"]
- auto_burst: [true|false]
- burst_cap_hours: integer (max vGPU-hours per billing period)
- cache_credit_enabled: [true|false]

API/CLI example (billing config)
--------------------------------
```json
{
  "account_id": "acct_123",
  "billing_package": "hybrid-500-reserved",
  "routing": {
    "preference": "prefer-dedicated",
    "auto_burst": true,
    "burst_cap_hours": 200
  },
  "private_overlay": {
    "enabled": false
  }
}
```

Key product requirements (PRD-style acceptance items)
------------------------------------------------------
1. Billing: Backend emits line-items that break down costs by primitive (hosted_tokens, reserved_commit_hours, reserved_overage_hours, private_subscription). Line-items must be queryable via the Billing API.
2. Quota & routing: Control plane must evaluate routing.preference and route to runtime pools accordingly with deterministic tie-breakers.
3. Observability: Console must show per-route token counts, commit consumption live, cache credits applied, and projected month-end overage estimate.
4. Invoicing: Support proration for mid-period changes to commit size and immediate reconciliation for credits.
5. Contract language: Support isolation clauses where Private Overlay customers can opt-out of cross-surface failover.
6. Tests & safeguards: Synthetic load tests that validate billing alignment to observed commit consumption within 2% for 95% of test scenarios.

Design notes and engineering implications
----------------------------------------
- Runtime routing hooks: Add routing decision API to router that accepts a BillingProfile and routing.preference to make deterministic routing decisions.
- Metering: Route-level metering tags (route_id, model_variant, surface) must be included in every emitted metric/trace for billing aggregation.
- Cache credits: Implement a monthly ledger that converts observed cache/quantization savings into a negative line-item applied against hosted token usage.
- Capacity model: SRE must provide capacity guidelines to guarantee that a 20% overcommit buffer exists for Dedicated pools with auto-burst enabled.

Roadmap & milestones
---------------------
1. Q1 2027 (alpha): API primitives, billing line-item prototype, routing.preference flag, internal-only console view.
2. Q2 2027 (beta): Console UI for commit consumption, proration, auto-burst controls, basic invoice breakout.
3. Q3 2027 (general availability): Sales quoting flow, private overlay contract templates, GA billing export formats (CSV + BI connectors).

Rollout and sales enablement checklist
-------------------------------------
1. Complete billing contract templates and legal sign-off. (Owner: Finance & Legal)
2. Build quoting calculator and SFDC product packages. (Owner: GTM/Product)
3. Run two pilot customers for Reserved+Hosted hybrid (3 month pilots). (Owner: Solutions Eng)
4. Publish migration guides and training for Customer Success. (Owner: Customer Success & Docs)

Migration & upgrade flow (high level)
-------------------------------------
1. Discovery: Assess current usage patterns and recommend hybrid package via estimator.
2. Pilot commit: Customer purchases a small Reserved commit (30–90 days). Configure routing.preference to prefer-dedicated.
3. Observe: Monitor commit consumption; enable auto-burst for controlled ramp.
4. Scale: Increase commit or enable Private Overlay depending on compliance needs.
5. Rollback: If SLA or cost regression occurs, disable prefer-dedicated and route back to Hosted within 15 minutes.

Operational playbook (when commit consumption unexpected)
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Alert: Billing forecast shows projected commit exhaustion in <48 hours.
2. Action: Notify customer success and account owner; suggest increasing commit or enabling temporary burst cap.
3. If customer is private-isolate-true: Engage SRE & Solutions Eng to plan capacity.
4. Reconciliation: Apply cache credits/discounts if behavior was traced to config mismatch.

Acceptance criteria
--------------------
- Console displays live commit consumption within 60s latency of ingestion.
- Billing exports include route-level breakdowns and cache credit line-items.
- Pilot customers report no more than 1% increase in latency after switching to prefer-dedicated routing.

Ownership and stakeholders
--------------------------
- Product (packaging & pricing): Maya Chen
- Billing & Finance: Priya Nair
- Runtime & Routing API: Daniel Kim (eng-serving-runtime)
- SRE / Capacity: Elena Rossi
- Sales & Solutions Eng: Arjun Patel
- Legal & Contracts: Thomas Weaver

Appendix A — Example customer scenarios
---------------------------------------
Scenario A: SaaS company with spiky traffic
- Needs: predictable monthly cost with ability to burst during launches.
- Recommended: Reserved 300 vGPU-hours commit + auto_burst=true, burst_cap_hours=150.
- Expected: ~30% unit cost reduction vs pure-hosted at scale.

Scenario B: Regulated enterprise migrating from on-prem model
- Needs: Private control plane + governed fallback to Redwood Dedicated in region.
- Recommended: Private Overlay subscription + a 100 vGPU-hours Dedicated commit for baseline.

Appendix B — Example billing line-item CSV schema
--------------------------------------------------
| invoice_id | account_id | period_start | period_end | line_type | quantity | unit | unit_price | amount | tags |
|------------|------------|--------------|------------|-----------|----------|------|------------|--------|------|
Example line_types: hosted_tokens, reserved_commit_hours, reserved_overage_hours, private_subscription, cache_credit

Appendix C — Quick CLI to preview cost (internal tool)
-------------------------------------------------------
$ redwood-cost-estimator --account acct_123 --commit-hours 500 --expected-tokens 200000000 --cache-savings 0.12
Estimated monthly: $XX,XXX (breakdown: commit=$YY,YYY hosted(after credits)=$ZZ,ZZZ overage=$A,AAA)

Notes and open questions
-------------------------
- Should we expose per-model quantization discounts as explicit line-items or fold them into cache credits? Tradeoff: visibility vs complexity.
- Pricing: finalize P_overage and burst caps with Finance to ensure margin targets are met for 95th percentile usage patterns.
- Compliance: Private Overlay customers may require dedicated billing accounts; confirm with Payments team.

Next steps
----------
1. Align with Billing & Finance on P_commit and P_overage floors by 2026-12-10.
2. Implement routing.preference flag and prototype metering tags (engineering spike) by 2027-01-15.
3. Schedule first pilot customer onboarding for Q1 2027.

References
----------
- Deployment surface and consumption implications (internal): /confluence/product-docs/product-overview/deployment-surface-consumption-pricing-implications-2026
- Token bundle & enterprise metering: /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/token-bundle-flex-enterprise-metering-2026-08-20

payload.page_title: stream-duration-discount-framework-and-contract-templates

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: Define a standardized pricing framework and contract templates for duration-based discounts on long-running streaming and session-oriented inference workloads. This doc codifies eligibility, discount tiers, contract language, billing hooks, telemetry requirements, and a rollout/playbook for sales, finance, and customer success.

Background

Redwood has observed two commercial patterns where duration-sensitive discounts are necessary: (1) customers with sustained, predictable streaming sessions (e.g., call transcription, conversational agents with long sessions) and (2) high-throughput background ingestion pipelines that keep a small number of long-lived connections to the runtime. Current per-token pricing underestimates the economic benefit of reserving capacity and amortizing KV-cache and batching gains across long sessions. This framework provides clear, auditable rules for offering discounts while protecting unit economics.

Goals

- Make discounting predictable and automatable for sales and finance.
- Tie discounts to measurable signals (session duration, average active connections, KV cache hit, and run-time occupancy).
- Ensure discounts preserve SLO alignment and avoid gaming.
- Provide readily usable legal language and billing hook implementations for engineering.

Discount framework summary
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Session duration (SD): wall-clock time an active session is maintained (in minutes).
- Discount window: the period for which we evaluate SD (rolling 30 days).
- Stability signal: percentage of sessions that exceed a customer-defined threshold.
sections.heading: Key concepts

sections.body:
1) Account-level opt-in to duration program (sales checkbox / contract clause).
2) Median SD over a 30-day window >= 15 minutes.
3) At least 500 sessions (or equivalent 7-day sustained concurrently active minutes > 20k) in the evaluation window.
4) No significant QoS regressions during the previous 90 days (SLO breach rate < 1% for token latency and error budget > 10%).

Discount table (applies to per-token host charges and session warm-capacity add-on; discounts expressed as % off baseline list pricing)

| Median SD (minutes) | Stability signal (percent sessions > threshold) | Discount % | Notes |
|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------|------------|-------|
| 15 - 29             | >= 70                                           | 7%         | Entry tier for short long sessions |
| 30 - 59             | >= 75                                           | 12%        | Moderate benefit to amortize KV cache |
| 60 - 239            | >= 80                                           | 20%        | High amortization and batching benefits |
| >= 240              | >= 85                                           | 30%        | Exceptional long-lived workloads; review required |

Tiered add-ons and caps

- Maximum discount cap per-account: 40% across all bundled credits and discounts.
- Discounts apply only to hosted per-usage compute line items; reserved/dedicated SKU discounts negotiated separately via Dedicated contracts.
- Discounts are additive with volume credits up to cap; additive rules described in Appendix A.

Contract template language (sales/legal)

Insert the following clause in the commercial SOW or Order Form when enabling duration discounts:

"Duration-Based Consumption Discount. Customer may elect to enroll in Redwood's Duration-Based Consumption Discount Program (\"Program\") for eligible streaming and session workloads. Eligibility will be assessed monthly against the metrics and thresholds defined in Redwood's Stream Duration Discount Framework (internal doc ref). When eligible, Customer will receive the applicable percentage discount to the list price for qualifying compute usage for the upcoming billing cycle. Redwood reserves the right to suspend or modify discount eligibility if the Customer's SLO breach rate exceeds 1% in a trailing 90-day window, or if telemetry indicates sustained unmetered behavior. Details on measurement, dispute resolution, and termination of discounts are provided in Appendix B."

Billing hook implementation (engineering)

The billing system needs a deterministic hook that evaluates eligibility at account-month boundary and applies discount line-item for the next billing period. Pseudocode (for billing scheduler):

```
// Run nightly; evaluate for account A
metrics = fetchSessionMetrics(account = A, window=30d)
median_sd = metrics.median_session_duration_minutes
stability = metrics.percent_sessions_over_threshold(15)
sessions_count = metrics.session_count
slo_breach = fetchSloBreachRate(account = A, window=90d)
if (opt_in && median_sd >= 15 && sessions_count >= 500 && slo_breach < 0.01 && stability >= required) {
  discount_pct = lookupDiscount(median_sd, stability)
  createDiscountLineItem(account=A, percent=discount_pct, effective_from=nextBillingCycle)
} else {
  ensureNoActiveDurationDiscount(account=A)
}
```

Billing schema example (JSON line-item)

```
{
  "account_id": "acct_123",
  "period_start": "2027-06-01",
  "period_end": "2027-07-01",
  "line_items": [
    {
      "sku": "hosted-inference-v4-compute",
      "units": 1234567,
      "unit_price": 0.000012,
      "discounts": [ { "type": "duration", "percent": 0.20, "reason": "median_sd=72" } ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Telemetry and metrics requirements

Engineering/telemetry must emit the following signals for each account:

- session_start, session_end, session_id, user_agent, model_variant, kv_cache_hit_rate (per-session), tokens_generated, average_token_latency_ms.
- Derived signals to compute: median_session_duration_minutes, percent_sessions_over_threshold(15m/30m/60m), 30-day rolling session_count, per-account SLO breach rate.

Minimum retention: 90 days for eligibility history; 365 days for audit and dispute resolution. Telemetry must be accessible to billing systems via the internal metrics API (metric names: rw.session.duration_median, rw.session.stability_pct, rw.account.slo_breach_rate).

Anti-gaming and guardrails

To avoid artificial extension of sessions to capture discounts:

- Sessions that are idle (no tokens generated for > 5 minutes) should be excluded unless explicitly marked as \"interactive still-active\" by the customer through a documented API flag.
- Requests to artificially extend sessions (heartbeat-only traffic) will be flagged if kv_cache_hit_rate < 0.1 and token generation rate = 0 for > 80% of the extended window; flagged accounts are suspended from discounts pending review.
- Telemetry anomaly detection must run weekly to detect deviations and surface to customer-success for possible manual review.

Rollout plan (phased)

1) Pilot (Q3 2027) — invite 8 customers (mix of chatbots, contact centers, transcription pipelines) to validate measurement signals, billing hooks, and contract language.
2) Beta (Q4 2027) — open to self-serve opt-in for accounts meeting volume minima with automated billing line-items; limit to 200 accounts for capacity monitoring.
3) GA (Q1 2028) — general availability with UI flags in Console, pricing calculator updates, and public docs.

Operational playbook (CS / Finance / Support)

- Sales: Use the duration discount checkbox on SOW; attach Appendix A additive-credit table if customer negotiates multiple discounts.
- Finance: Verify discount line-item generation for pilot accounts weekly; reconcile with invoices.
- Support/CS: On flagged accounts run the session replay tool and provide remediation or guidance.
- Legal: Use the contract template and escalate any changes to the Program clause.

SLO considerations and risk assessment

- Because discounts are tied to long sessions, we must ensure capacity planning accounts for a higher proportion of sticky connections. Add 12% headroom in warm-pool sizing for accounts on the Program during Beta.
- If long sessions increase KV cache churn, measure per-account cost delta; failure to maintain expected amortization should trigger discount review.

Appendix A — Additive discount decision matrix

- Volume credits (V) + Duration discount (D) apply additively up to cap: Effective discount = min(V + D, account_cap).
- Example: V=10%, D=20%, cap=40% => effective = 30%.

Appendix B — Dispute and audit process (summary)

1) Customer may dispute eligibility within 30 days of invoice.
2) Finance will rerun telemetry calculation for disputed billing cycle within 10 business days.
3) If error found, pro-rated credit is issued and discount eligibility corrected.

Appendix C — Example onboarding checklist for Sales Engineers

- Validate telemetry availability: rw.session.duration_median and rw.account.slo_breach_rate populated for the account.
- Run the session-sample-replay on 3 representative long sessions.
- Estimate cost delta and expected amortization benefit (attach short memo to SOW).

Ownership and contacts

- Product: Leah Patel (PRD and launch owner).
- Revenue Operations: Marcus Chen (billing integration).
- Engineering: Diego Martinez (billing hooks and telemetry).
- Legal: Nora Svensson (contract language).

Document change log

- 2027-05-04 — Draft created by Leah Patel.
- 2027-05-20 — Added billing hook pseudocode and contract language (reviewers: Diego Martinez, Aisha Raman).
- 2027-06-01 — Published after pilot-scope approval; added anti-gaming rules and rollout plan.

References

- See: /product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/predictive-bundling-and-sla-credit-algorithm-playbook-2027-06-18
- See: /product-docs/product-overview/session-resilience-onboarding-and-fallback-playbook-2025-08-21

payload.page_title: Fidelity Degradation Insurance and SLA Pricing Guidance

sections.body: This guidance defines an approach for pricing, packaging, and contracting an add-on insurance product that compensates customers when runtime-driven fidelity degradations occur (short-duration quality or capability reductions due to capacity, cost, or preemptible resource constraints). The document explains the insurance product concept, SLA mappings, credit calculations, example pricing bands, recommended commercial wording, implementation milestones, telemetry and audit requirements, and customer-facing communication templates.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Purpose: Provide a repeatable commercial framework that lets Redwood offer predictable remediation (credits/compensation) to customers for measurable fidelity degradations while protecting platform economics and incentivizing sensible usage patterns.
- Scope: Hosted and Dedicated deployment modes initially; Private deployments considered but require separate legal/KMS/audit controls and are out-of-scope for the 1.0 launch. This guidance covers pricing heuristics, credit mechanics, observability signals, and a rollout roadmap.
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
As customers adopt adaptive fidelity (quantization, model fallbacks, degraded sampling) to manage costs, they request contractual assurances for correctness-sensitive workloads (e.g., legal summarization, billing reconciliation, compliance triage). Traditional uptime SLAs do not capture output quality reductions that are short-lived and controlled by runtime heuristics. The fidelity insurance product is designed to:

1) Translate measurable quality regressions into compensable credit events.
2) Maintain incentives for customers to use adaptive fidelity tools (e.g., fallback variants, cache-first routing).
3) Limit financial open-ended exposure for Redwood via defined caps and tiered pricing.
sections.heading: Background and rationale

sections.body:
- Fidelity Degradation Event (FDE): A measurable, runtime-detected change in model output fidelity for a specific route or customer that is caused by platform-driven routing, fallback, preemption, or quantization changes (not customer prompt changes).
- Fidelity Window: Time-bounded period (default 5 minutes) over which degraded outputs are observed and aggregated for event detection.
- Severity Grade: Classification of FDEs (minor, moderate, major) based on delta in quality metric (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity/eval-set pass-rate) and customer route importance.
- Insurance Credit: Monetary or usage credit applied to customer account as remediation.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
- Minor (severity = minor): Observable 5–10% drop in eval-set pass-rate or >0.85 embedding-similarity delta; credit = 5% of route spend during fidelity window (cap 2x monthly).
- Moderate (severity = moderate): Observable 10–30% drop or embedding-similarity delta >0.70; credit = 15% of route spend during window (cap 5x monthly).
- Major (severity = major): >30% drop or embedding-similarity delta <0.70 for critical routes; credit = 40% of route spend during window (cap 10x monthly).

Note: Route spend = billable tokens/embedding units consumed on the affected route(s) during the fidelity window. These mappings are the baseline and can be tuned during pilot.
sections.heading: SLA and credit mapping (high-level)

sections.body:
We propose three packaging options for customers: Basic, Advanced, and Enterprise. Pricing below assumes a per-month subscription fee + usage band multiplier. All prices are illustrative and require commercial review.

1) Basic (self-serve)
- Monthly fee: $250
- Included coverage cap: up to 2x monthly credits (cumulative).
- Per-incident deductible: $250 equivalent or 2% of monthly spend (whichever higher).
- Suitable for dev/test or low-criticality routes.

2) Advanced (SMB / production)
- Monthly fee: $1,500
- Included coverage cap: up to 5x monthly credits.
- Per-incident deductible: $1,000 or 1.5% of monthly spend.
- SLA: 99.9% fidelity-window monitoring coverage and quarterly joint reviews.

3) Enterprise (custom)
- Monthly fee: custom (starting at $8,000)
- Included coverage cap: negotiable, typical 10x monthly credits with overage caps.
- Deductible: negotiable; typically waived for customers >$100k monthly spend.
- Includes priority remediation, audit trail exports, and per-contract severity thresholds.
sections.heading: Pricing bands and packaging

sections.body:
- Maximum annual exposure per customer is capped at min(25% of annual committed spend, $2M) unless explicitly approved by Finance.
- Credits are applied as usage credits first, with cash refunds processed only for exceptional cases and require finance approval.
- Multiple overlapping events within the same fidelity window are de-duplicated and combined into a single incident for crediting.

Observability, telemetry, and detection rules (implementation):

1) Signals required for detection:
- Per-route eval-set pass-rate (rolling window metrics at 1m resolution)
- Embedding similarity baseline and rolling delta per tenant
- Model variant change log (which runtime variant served each request)
- Prefix cache-hit ratio and rate of fallback decisions
- Token-level latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) to correlate load-driven degradations

2) Detection algorithm (prototype outline):
- Maintain a per-route baseline computed over trailing 30d excluding known maintenance windows.
- For each 1m window compute delta = (baseline_pass_rate - current_pass_rate).
- Apply anomaly suppression for windows with <1000 tokens or <10 eval probes.
- Map delta to severity grade using thresholds defined in SLA mapping.
- Generate FDE incident and attach evidence payload (sampled request ids, variant ids, metric slices).

3) Audit & evidence retention:
- Evidence for credited incidents must be retained for 365 days.
- Provide an exportable incident package (JSON or CSV) to customers under Enterprise.
sections.heading: Commercial guardrails and caps

sections.body:
1) Fidelity Insurance Addendum (snippet):
"The Provider operates an insurance product that credits Customer accounts for Fidelity Degradation Events attributable to the Provider's runtime decisions. Fidelity Degradation Events are defined in the attached Schedules and are subject to detection rules, deductibles, caps, and exclusions. Credits are applied in accordance with the Provider's published guidance and the customer's selected subscription tier."

2) Exclusions (examples):
- Customer-caused prompt changes or test harnesses.
- Known maintenance windows and scheduled capacity transitions.
- Degradations resulting from third-party model provider outages (unless Redwood controls the model hosting).
sections.heading: Contract language (recommended clauses)

sections.body:
- Incident generates a provisional credit estimate in Console > Incidents > Fidelity Insurance.
- Customer receives an email notification with a link to the provisional incident package and an appeal window of 7 calendar days.
- If the customer appeals, a Technical Review is kicked off (triage SLA = 5 business days).
- After the appeal window closes or review completes, credit is applied as a usage offset in the next billing cycle.
sections.heading: Billing mechanics and UI flows

sections.body:
- 0–90 days (Pilot):
  1) Build detection pipeline prototype (per-route baselines, 1m ingest).
  2) Implement provisional incident UI and export package.
  3) Pilot with 3–5 power customers (mixed Hosted/Dedicated).
  4) Validate severity thresholds and credit math against historical incidents.

- 90–180 days (MVP):
  1) Integrate crediting into billing system (usage credits ledger).
  2) Launch Basic and Advanced packaging tiers on Console.
  3) Add audit retention and automated export for Enterprise.
  4) Create sales enablement, legal addendum templates, and partner training.

- 180–365 days (Scale):
  1) Expand to Private deployments (requires legal & security review).
  2) Add predictive pre-notifications for customers approaching deductible thresholds.
  3) Iterate pricing bands based on loss analytics and customer feedback.
sections.heading: Implementation roadmap and milestones (90/180/365)

sections.body:
- Product adoption: % of customers with production routes who purchase insurance within 6 months of availability (target 8% for Advanced tier in year 1).
- False positive rate: proportion of provisional incidents successfully appealed (target <8%).
- Finance impact: annualized credit exposure as % of ARR (target <=1.2% at launch).
- Customer satisfaction: NPS change for customers using the product (target +6 points).
sections.heading: Metrics and success criteria

sections.body:
1) Detection -> Auto-triage (system assigns severity) -> Provisional credit estimate published.
2) Customer notified with evidence packet.
3) Customer may accept or appeal.
4) Technical Review (if appealed): 2 engineers (Platform + Applied-ML) validate evidence and return decision within 5 business days.
4) Billing applies credit; Finance logs the adjustment.
sections.heading: Operational runbook (incident lifecycle)

sections.body:
- Risk: Overcrediting due to noisy detection.
  Mitigation: Conservative thresholds during pilot, appeal window, and human review for Moderate/Major incidents.
- Risk: Adverse selection (customers purchase insurance only for high-risk routes).
  Mitigation: Deductible and pricing bands encourage broad coverage; negotiated enterprise caps.
- Risk: Legal exposure for Private deployments.
  Mitigation: Separate contract track and additional contract controls before availability.
sections.heading: Risks and mitigations

sections.body:
- Deductible math for high-volume tenants and wholesale exceptions.
- Whether credits are limited to usage offsets or whether cash refunds are permitted as a standard option.
- Final severity thresholds and metric selection (embedding similarity vs. eval pass-rate) for multilingual workloads.

Appendix A — Example detection pseudocode (prototype):

```
sections.heading: Open decisions (needs leadership/legal/finance signoff)

sections.body:
for route in routes:
    baseline = compute_baseline(route, lookback_days=30)
    for window in windows(route, size=1m):
        if window.tokens < 1000: continue
        pass_rate = eval_probe_pass_rate(route, window)
        delta = baseline.pass_rate - pass_rate
        if delta > grade_thresholds.minor:
            create_fde(route, window, delta)
```

Appendix B — Example console notification copy:

Subject: Provisional Fidelity Insurance Incident for [route-name] (ID: FDE-2029-0810-03)

Hello [Customer Contact],

We detected a temporary fidelity degradation on route [route-name] between 2029-08-10T11:32Z and 2029-08-10T11:37Z. A provisional credit of $1,220 has been calculated and will be applied to your account after the 7-day appeal period unless you request a technical review. View incident details: [link].

Next steps: Accept or request a review within 7 days.
sections.heading: pseudo-python: sliding-window baseline and detection

sections.body:
- Product (owner): lead the pilot, coordinate legal/finance, define tier pricing finalization.
- Applied ML: design and validate detection metrics and thresholds.
- Platform/Serving Runtime: surface variant-level logs, route tagging, and ensure sample retention.
- Finance: implement usage-credit ledger and exposure reporting.
- Legal: prepare addendum templates and finalize exclusions.

This is a restricted, pre-release commercial playbook. For pilot nominations and feedback, contact: asha.patel@redwoodinference.com.
