payload.page_title: Response Consistency SLA and Customer Migration Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the Response Consistency SLA framework (RCSLA), the policy and technical controls we will expose to customers to guarantee deterministic response characteristics, and a step-by-step migration playbook for moving customers from existing fidelity/packaging models to RCSLA-backed offerings. It combines product requirements, operational runbook tasks, pricing guidance, and customer communications designed for a staged rollout across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Goals:
- Provide clear, measurable guarantees for response consistency (latency stability, token fidelity, and determinism).
- Minimize customer disruption when migrating to the RCSLA model.
- Align pricing and billing incentives to operational cost while preserving quality.
- Create repeatable testing and validation steps so that SRE, Support, and Solutions teams can certify migrations.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: Redwood-hosted API, Redwood Dedicated, and Redwood Private (VPC) deployments.
- Audience: Product managers, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Customer Success, Sales, and Engineering teams executing migrations.

Background and motivation:
Historically, customers chose among fidelity packages that traded cost for output variability. As customers scale, product owners require contractual guarantees about response behavior (e.g., p95 latency windows, determinism for idem-potent pipelines, bounded quality drift for quantization rolls). RCSLA formalizes these guarantees into: a) measurable SLOs, b) operator-visible controls (batching, cache pinning, kernel selection), and c) migration patterns with minimal risk.

Terminology (short):
- Response Consistency: Combined property of latency stability, repeatability (determinism for same prompt + seed), and fidelity (no regression beyond defined thresholds).
- Determinism: Same input and model variant produce identical token sequence every run (when enabled).
- Fidelity Budget: Numeric allowance for acceptable delta in evaluation metrics (e.g., exact-match, ROUGE-L) when applying performance/quantization changes.
- RCSLA Tier: One of Platinum / Gold / Standard that maps to specific SLOs and billing terms.

RCSLA Tiers (summary):
We will expose three primary Response Consistency tiers. Each tier defines: latency window (p95), determinism guarantee, fidelity budget, and operational commitments (planned maintenance windows, rollback SLAs).

ASCII table:
Tier | p95 latency (tokens=128) | Determinism | Fidelity budget (eval delta) | Planned maintenance notice
-----|-------------------------|-------------|----------------------------|--------------------------
Platinum | <= 75 ms | optional determinism opt-in, 99.99% | max -0.3% EM / -0.6 ROUGE-L | 72 hours notice + can request blackout
Gold     | <= 150 ms | probabilistic stable outputs (99.5% token-match) | max -1.0% EM / -1.2 ROUGE-L | 48 hours notice
Standard | <= 300 ms | no determinism guarantee | max -3.0% EM / -3.5 ROUGE-L | 24 hours notice

SLOs and thresholds (service-level specifics):
- Latency: p95 measured at Redwood edge for standard request shape (prompt=80 tokens, gen=128 tokens). Use the Redwood Console metric path: metrics.request.latency.p95 per-tenant per-route. SLO burn is tracked hourly.
- Error budget: 0.1% monthly for Platinum, 0.5% monthly for Gold, 1% monthly for Standard. Error budget sources include server errors (5xx), timeout, and degraded fidelity rollbacks.
- Fidelity regression guard: Any model release that increases regression beyond tier's fidelity budget triggers automatic canary rollback by the runtime.

Service controls exposed to customers:
- determinism=true|false (API flag) — available on Platinum only; under the hood this sets RNG seeding and disables nondeterministic kernels.
- consistency_hint: {low, medium, high} — used by automatic batching and kernel selection to trade cost vs. stability.
- fidelity_tolerance: numeric percentage for custom fidelity governance at tenant level (Gold+).
Example API snippet (JSON):
{
  "model": "rwd-neo-XXL-v2",
  "prompt": "<customer prompt>",
  "determinism": true,
  "consistency_hint": "high",
  "max_tokens": 128
}

Migration playbook (high level, repeatable for each customer):
Pre-migration planning (Solutions Eng + Customer Success):
1) Gather telemetry: collect 14-day baseline for latency distribution, token costs, and quality metrics using customer-provided prompt-set (min 200 examples). Use Redwood Optimize instrumentation to produce baseline report.
2) Tier recommendation: propose RCSLA tier aligned to customer's SLO needs and economics (include cost delta and expected token savings).
3) Contract changes: attach RCSLA addendum to customer contract (legal to approve blackout terms).
4) Migration window: agree on target window and rollback criteria.

Migration execution (SRE + Runtime + Solutions):
1) Canary stage (3–7 days): enable deterministic mode for 1% of traffic (Platinum candidates) or high consistency_hint for Gold trials. Monitor: latency.p95, fidelity metrics, customer-observed deltas.
2) Validation gates: after 72 hours, pass if: latency within tier target, fidelity regression <= budget, error rate within error budget.
3) Broad rollout: increment to 10%, 25%, 50%, 100% in 24–72 hour increments depending on telemetry stability. Each step requires automated gate checks.
4) Post-rollout watch: 14-day high-sensitivity monitoring window where SRE and Solutions actively monitor dashboards and remain on-call for escalations.

Rollback procedure (automated + manual):
- Automatic rollback: runtime triggers if fidelity regression > 2x budget OR error budget consumed > 50% in an hour.
- Manual rollback: Solutions Eng can trigger tenant-level rollback via Admin Console: set determinism=false and revert model variant to the pinned version. CLI example: rwd-admin rollback --tenant <id> --reason "fidelity-exceed"

Testing & validation checklist (before signoff):
- Unit tests for determinism toggle (seeded repeat runs produce identical token streams).
- Integration test: full request path (ingress -> runtime -> telemetry -> console) with synthetic load for 200rps sustained.
- Eval harness: run customer prompt-set on control and candidate stacks and compute the exact-match and ROUGE-L deltas.
- End-to-end customer verification: Solutions Eng coordinates an acceptance test suite with the customer; acceptance requires <=tier fidelity delta and p95 target.

Billing and pricing impact:
- Pricing model: RCSLA is a premium add-on with a per-token uplift and commitment discount tiered by Platinum/Gold/Standard.
- Chargeable items: determinism opt-in (flat monthly surcharge for instance isolation), consistency compute premium (per-token %), and dedicated SLO credit for Platinum (annual subscription).
- Example pricing matrix (illustrative):
Tier | base token uplift | determinism surcharge | typical uplift range
Platinum | +25% | +$2,500/month | +30–45% total
Gold     | +12% | n/a | +12–18% total
Standard | +0%  | n/a | baseline pricing
- Billing events: when a tenant is rolled to a higher tier mid-billing-cycle, prorated charges are applied and visible in the Console billing preview. Finance to confirm in billing-ops runbook.

Operational runbook (SRE focus):
- Dashboards to create: per-tenant RCSLA overview (latency p50/p95, fidelity delta, error budget remaining), aggregated tier health, canary watchlist.
- Alerts:
  - RCSLA.Platinum.LatencySpike when p95 > 90ms for 10m (severity P2).
  - RCSLA.Fidelity.Alert when canary fidelity delta exceeds budget for two consecutive 10m windows (severity P1).
  - RCSLA.Rollback.Executed when runtime triggers an automated rollback (inform on-call and Solutions Eng).
- On-call play: initial responder reinspects canary nodes, verifies kernel selection logs and quantization flags, escalates to runtime team if rollback triggered.

Customer communication templates (brief):
- Pre-migration notice: 72-hr email that summarizes expected behavior, blackout windows, rollback plan, and contact details.
- Post-migration status: 14-day summary with measured deltas and cost impact.
(Templates appended as Appendix A).

Rollout schedule (recommended):
Phase 0 (Nov 2029): internal pilot with 3 internal customers (Dedicated + Hosted).
Phase 1 (Dec 2029 - Jan 2030): invite-only customers (PLG enterprise pilots) — limit 10 customers.
Phase 2 (Feb 2030 - Apr 2030): general availability for new customers; migration paths open for existing customers via Solutions Eng engagements.

Success metrics and KPIs:
- Adoption: % of top 50 customers enrolled in RCSLA within 6 months. Target 40%.
- Quality: aggregate fidelity regression < 0.6% across all migrations.
- Economics: realized per-token cost delta improvement of >= 10% for customers that applied recommended consistency_hint changes.
- Reliability: automated rollback rate < 2% of migrations.

Ownership & contacts:
- Product owner: Priya Kapoor (product@redwood.ai)
- Runtime lead: Rakesh Nair (runtime@redwood.ai)
- SRE on-call: see on-call roster in eng-sre/team-wiki.
- Solutions Eng: Marta Li (se@redwood.ai)
- Finance lead (billing impact): Hannah Schultz (finance-legal@redwood.ai)

Appendices:
A) Email templates (short):
- Pre-migration subject: "[Redwood] Upcoming migration: Response Consistency SLA trial for <tenant>"
  Body: Hi <contact>, we plan to enable the RCSLA <tier> for your tenant on <date>. Expected impact: p95 -> <target>, determinism: <on/off>. See migration plan attached.

B) CLI commands and admin checklist:
- Generate baseline report: rwd-cli optimize baseline --tenant <id> --prompt-set prompts.json --out baseline-report.json
- Enable determinism (admin): rwd-admin set-tenant-flag --tenant <id> --flag determinism=true --actor <owner>
- Rollback tenant: rwd-admin rollback --tenant <id> --reason "fidelity-exceed"

C) Evaluation metrics to capture: exact_match, rouge_l, perplexity_delta, token_cost_usd, p95_latency_ms.

D) Related pages and reference links:
- Serving economics decision guide: [internal link] (see related_pages)
- Fidelity packages migration playbook (legacy): [internal link]

Revision history:
- 2029-11-01: created by Priya Kapoor (draft)
- 2029-11-08: added canary gating rules and API flag examples (reviewers: Marta Li)
- 2029-11-15: published after signoff from Runtime, SRE, and Finance

Notes and open questions:
- Legal: finalize contract addendum wording for Platinum blackout and SLA credits.
- Billing integration: Finance must add prorated tier change capability to billing pipeline before GA.
- Determinism compute cost model: runtime team to estimate GPU delta for enabling determinism on large models (due 2029-12-01).

End of document.
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: PRD: RBAC v2 (Enterprise Controls)

sections.body:
RBAC v2 is Redwood Inference’s next-generation authorization layer designed for regulated enterprise workloads across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. RBAC v2 provides least-privilege access control with deny-by-default enforcement, consistent permissions across product surfaces, scoped role bindings (org/project/environment/cluster), and auditability of authorization decisions for SOC2 evidence and enterprise security questionnaires.

This PRD defines: (1) the customer problem and target personas, (2) functional requirements for the platform, API Gateway, control plane, and Console, (3) success metrics and guardrails, and (4) a phased release plan with migration and compatibility constraints.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
Redwood’s existing authorization model (RBAC v1 and/or mixed service-local checks) is insufficient for enterprise buyers who require:
- Least-privilege access control (separation of duties, minimal default permissions).
- Provable enforcement (consistent permission checks across Gateway, control plane services, and Console).
- Clear auditability (who attempted what, on which scoped resources, what policy was evaluated, and why it was allowed/denied).
- Operational usability (role templates, permission search/viewer, and actionable denial guidance).

In practice, current gaps show up as:
- Inconsistent enforcement across endpoints (Gateway vs service checks; unannotated endpoints).
- Coarse roles that over-grant and fail separation of duties.
- Limited ability to scope permissions (e.g., operator needs access to a specific environment/cluster, not the whole org).
- Permission-denied errors that are hard to troubleshoot (no clear reason, no "why denied" guidance, incomplete audit context).
sections.heading: Problem statement

sections.body:
1) Canonical permission model
- Define a consistent, versioned permission catalog covering sensitive actions across Hosted API, Console, control plane, Dedicated, and Private operations.
- Establish a stable naming convention and deprecation/versioning policy.

2) Deny-by-default enforcement
- Ensure all security-relevant requests are evaluated against RBAC v2 policies.
- Prevent bypasses due to missing annotations/middleware.

3) Enterprise-grade scoping
- Support role bindings scoped to org, project, environment, and (for Private) cluster.
- Provide clear semantics for how scopes apply to resources and actions.

4) Auditability and evidence
- Log authorization decisions with context (subject/action/resource/scope/policy version/decision/denial reason).
- Produce evidence-friendly artifacts: permission inventory, role matrix, coverage reports, and audit samples.

5) Operator and admin UX
- Provide role templates and a role/permission viewer.
- Provide "why was I denied?" guidance, with safe exposure controls.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- A general-purpose customer-configurable ABAC/policy language (custom rule scripting).
- Re-architecting authentication/identity beyond integration points (SSO remains; RBAC is authorization).
- Perfectly eliminating all legacy roles immediately (migration requires compatibility and staged rollout).
sections.heading: Non-goals (v2)

sections.body:
- Enterprise customers in regulated industries (financial services, healthcare, insurance) requiring strict access controls and audit log export to SIEM.
- Deployment modes:
  - Hosted API + Console
  - Dedicated capacity
  - Private deployments (VPC and on-prem), including installer/admin bootstrap flows
sections.heading: Target customers and deployment modes

sections.body:
- Define least-privilege roles and separation of duties.
- Manage users, groups, and role assignments.
- Validate audit logs and support internal audits.
- Respond to incidents and coordinate emergency access.
sections.heading: Responsibilities

sections.body:
- Hard to grant read-only/auditor access without over-granting.
- Limited transparency into what a role actually allows.
- Insufficient audit context to prove authorization decisions.
sections.heading: Pain points today

sections.body:
- Can assign standard templates (Security Admin, Auditor, Deployment Operator) with minimal changes.
- Can scope access to specific projects/environments.
- Can export audit logs to SIEM with allow/deny decision context.
sections.heading: What success looks like

sections.body:
- Operate model serving and routing policies safely.
- Manage deployments, capacity, and environment-specific configurations.
- Troubleshoot production issues quickly.
sections.heading: Responsibilities

sections.body:
- Either lacks access to needed operational actions or is granted broad admin.
- Permission errors lack actionable detail.
- Unclear which actions are allowed in which environments.
sections.heading: Pain points today

sections.body:
- Can do day-to-day operations (routing, rollouts, capacity changes) scoped to an environment/cluster.
- Denied actions include a clear next step (request role / contact admin), and admins can debug quickly.
sections.heading: What success looks like

sections.body: - Help enterprise customers configure roles, troubleshoot 403s, and validate controls during security reviews.
sections.heading: Responsibilities

sections.body:
- Clear documentation, stable templates, and an internal playbook.
- Quick triage of denial spikes during migration (feature flags, dashboards, logs).
sections.heading: What success looks like

sections.body:
1) Onboarding (enterprise)
- Customer enables SSO and provisions initial org admins.
- Customer applies role templates (Security Admin, Auditor, Operator) and binds them to IdP groups.

2) Scoped operations
- Operator updates a routing policy in Environment: “prod-us-east” within Project: “payments”.
- Authorization must evaluate with environment scope and record the decision.

3) Audit readiness
- Auditor exports audit logs for last 30 days with decision context and filters by project/environment.
- Logs are SIEM-compatible and include policy version identifiers.

4) Migration safety
- Existing customers upgrade without breaking existing workflows.
- Dual-read mode detects and flags discrepancies between v1 and v2 decisions.

5) Emergency access (break-glass)
- Time-bound elevation with approval, high-visibility logging, and post-use review.
sections.heading: Key user journeys

sections.body:
REQ-1.1 Permissions
- The system MUST have a canonical, versioned permission catalog.
- Permissions MUST be granular enough to support separation of duties across:
  - Org/user/role management
  - API key creation/rotation/revocation
  - Secret management and integrations (KMS/HSM references, credential rotation)
  - Routing policy changes (including fallbacks and region routing)
  - Model pinning/version rollouts/canaries
  - Data retention/residency configuration
  - Private deployment administrative operations (installer bootstrap, cluster config changes)
  - Audit log export and configuration

REQ-1.2 Roles
- The system MUST support named roles as collections of permissions.
- The system SHOULD support both:
  - Built-in role templates (managed by Redwood policy bundle)
  - Custom roles (customer-defined) with explicit permission selection

REQ-1.3 Role bindings and scopes
- The system MUST support binding principals (users, service accounts, IdP groups) to roles at the following scopes:
  - Org
  - Project
  - Environment
  - Cluster (Private deployments)
- Scope inheritance MUST be defined and documented (e.g., org-level binding applies to all projects/environments unless overridden by deny rules).
- Scopes MUST be representable in audit logs and denial reasons.

REQ-1.4 Deny-by-default
- Any request requiring authorization MUST be denied unless an allow decision is computed.
- The evaluation MUST be deterministic for a given policy version and subject context.
sections.heading: 1) RBAC v2 primitives and semantics

sections.body:
REQ-2.1 Standard enforcement points
- The platform MUST enforce authorization consistently across:
  - API Gateway (first-line check)
  - Control plane services (defense-in-depth; must not trust gateway alone)
  - Console backend endpoints
- Endpoint metadata MUST include required permission(s) and resource/scope mapping.

REQ-2.2 Coverage guardrails
- The build/release process SHOULD fail if security-relevant endpoints are missing permission annotations.
- The team MUST maintain a coverage report for endpoints/jobs mapped to permissions.

REQ-2.3 Error semantics
- Denied requests MUST return a standardized error response.
- The response MUST be safe by default (no sensitive policy details to non-admins).
- The response SHOULD include:
  - A stable denial reason code
  - A human-readable message
  - A request id / trace id
- For authorized admins (or in explicitly enabled debug mode), the response MAY include:
  - Missing permission(s)
  - Evaluated scope
  - Policy version id
sections.heading: 2) Enforcement and API behavior

sections.body:
REQ-3.1 Role templates
- Console MUST provide a set of built-in role templates appropriate for enterprise use.
- Console MUST explain intended usage and scope for each template.

REQ-3.2 Role and permission viewer
- Console MUST allow searching and viewing permissions by name, description, and product area.
- Console MUST show which permissions are included in a role and where that role is bound.

REQ-3.3 Role assignment flows
- Console MUST allow binding roles to users/groups at org/project/environment scope.
- Console SHOULD support bulk assignment and import/mapping patterns for IdP groups.

REQ-3.4 "Why denied" guidance
- Console MUST display a user-friendly permission-denied state with next steps.
- Console SHOULD provide an admin-only view explaining the denial reason code, missing permission, and evaluated scope.
sections.heading: 3) Console UX requirements (admin tooling)

sections.body:
REQ-4.1 AuthZ decision logging
- The audit log pipeline MUST include authorization decision context for relevant events and explicit authorization checks:
  - Subject identity (user/service account), org id, and authn method (SSO/API key)
  - Action/permission
  - Resource identifiers and scope
  - Policy version id (and policy bundle version if applicable)
  - Decision: allow/deny
  - Denial reason code (if deny)
  - Request id / trace id

REQ-4.2 Export and retention
- Audit log export MUST include the above fields and map cleanly to common SIEM schemas.
- The system SHOULD support filtering by scope (project/environment) for enterprise use cases.
sections.heading: 4) Audit logging and SIEM export

sections.body:
REQ-5.1 Compatibility
- During migration, the system MUST avoid breaking existing customers’ access.
- The system MUST support a staged rollout using feature flags.

REQ-5.2 Dual-read / discrepancy detection
- The platform SHOULD support dual-read mode (evaluate v1 and v2) to detect mismatches.
- Mismatches MUST be observable (metrics + logs) and triageable.

REQ-5.3 Default mappings
- The system MUST provide default role mappings from legacy roles to RBAC v2 templates.
- The system SHOULD provide a safe path for customers to customize roles post-migration.
sections.heading: 5) Migration and backwards compatibility

sections.body:
REQ-6.1 Time-bound elevation
- Break-glass elevation MUST be time-bound and require explicit approval.
- Break-glass actions MUST be highly visible in audit logs.

REQ-6.2 Monitoring and alerting
- Break-glass usage MUST trigger alerts to SecOps.
- The system SHOULD require post-use review and documentation.
sections.heading: 6) Break-glass controls (enterprise + internal)

sections.body:
REQ-7.1 Latency budget
- Authorization evaluation MUST add minimal overhead and avoid cross-region dependencies where possible.
- The system SHOULD use safe caching scoped to subject/policy version and invalidated on role/policy changes.

REQ-7.2 Availability
- Authorization failures MUST fail closed by default.
- Any break-glass exemption path MUST be explicitly controlled and auditable.

REQ-7.3 Regression prevention
- The platform MUST maintain integration tests covering critical sensitive actions (e.g., key rotation, role changes, routing edits).
sections.heading: 7) Performance, reliability, and safety

sections.body:
- Customer-defined deny rules and policy conditions beyond RBAC (ABAC-like conditions).
- Fine-grained data-plane authorization for prompt/content access (separate initiative).
- Delegated administration patterns beyond role bindings (e.g., approval workflows for specific actions).
sections.heading: Out-of-scope / future considerations

sections.body:
- Canonical permission registry + inventory coverage baseline
- Gateway middleware deny-by-default with standardized errors
- Control plane endpoint annotations + enforcement
- Built-in role templates + minimal Console role assignment flows
- Audit logging schema extension + SIEM export support for authz fields
- Feature flags + dual-read mode + rollback plan
sections.heading: MVP (must ship for enterprise pilots)

sections.body:
- Full custom role editor UX with advanced permission search and diffs
- Expanded scope UI (cluster-level workflows for Private)
- Admin debug tooling improvements (policy evaluation traces)
- Coverage gates broadened to additional services/jobs
sections.heading: Follow-on (post-pilot)

sections.body:
Product outcomes
- Enterprise security reviews: reduce time-to-approve for RBAC/audit sections (measured via Sales/SE feedback) by 30%.
- Supportability: reduce RBAC-related support tickets per pilot account after week 2 by 50%.

Technical metrics
- Authorization coverage: 100% of designated “sensitive endpoints” annotated and enforced in gateway + service.
- Deny rate monitoring: baseline deny rate established; alert on sudden spikes (e.g., >2x week-over-week) during rollout.
- Latency impact: P95 incremental authz evaluation overhead <= 5 ms for Hosted control plane requests (measured at gateway), and <= 10 ms for Private deployments with local control plane.
- Audit completeness: >= 99.9% of authz decisions for covered actions have decision context fields populated.

Security/compliance metrics
- Evidence readiness: permission catalog, role matrix, enforcement standard, and audit log samples packaged for SOC2 and customer questionnaires.
- Break-glass: 100% of break-glass events include approval record + post-use review within 5 business days.
sections.heading: Success metrics

sections.body:
- Dashboard: authz allow/deny counts by permission, scope, deployment mode, and customer tier.
- Dashboard: discrepancy rate (dual-read mismatches) by endpoint/permission.
- Dashboard: authz evaluation latency (gateway + service), cache hit rate, and error rate.
- Logs: structured denial reason codes and request ids to support rapid triage.
sections.heading: Analytics, logging, and dashboards

sections.body:
- Permission registry/policy bundle repo (role templates generated from YAML; versioned artifacts).
- API Gateway middleware + endpoint annotation framework.
- Control plane service adoption (org/users/roles, routing, model pinning/rollout, audit export).
- Audit log pipeline + exporter (SIEM mappings).
- Console UX and backend endpoints for role management.
- Private installer bootstrap for initial admin bindings and IdP group mapping guidance.
sections.heading: Dependencies

sections.body:
Risk: Migration causes denial spikes for existing admins/operators.
- Mitigation: feature-flag rollout, dual-read comparison, explicit default mappings, and a rollback plan.

Risk: Missing annotations lead to bypasses or inconsistent enforcement.
- Mitigation: coverage gating in CI, centralized permission registry, and defense-in-depth checks in services.

Risk: Debug information leaks sensitive policy details.
- Mitigation: admin-only debug headers, strict gating, safe error defaults, and audit logging of debug usage.

Risk: Cache staleness leads to incorrect allow decisions.
- Mitigation: cache keying by policy version, short TTLs, invalidation on role changes, and metrics/alerts for anomalies.
sections.heading: Risks and mitigations

sections.body:
Phase 0 — Discovery & inventory (Weeks 0–4)
- Produce permission inventory and sensitivity tiers.
- Identify endpoints/jobs lacking consistent checks.
- Align naming conventions and scope semantics.

Phase 1 — Design finalization (Weeks 3–8)
- Finalize RBAC v2 primitives, scope model, and evaluation flow.
- Finalize audit log decision fields and denial reason codes.
- Publish enforcement standards and endpoint annotation requirements.

Phase 2 — Implementation (Weeks 6–16)
- Land gateway middleware deny-by-default.
- Annotate + enforce control plane endpoints; add coverage tests.
- Implement policy evaluator client with safe caching.
- Implement audit log schema changes + SIEM export mapping.
- Console MVP: role templates, assignments, permission viewer/search.

Phase 3 — Pilot rollout & validation (Weeks 12–24)
- Internal dogfood with IT/admin workflows.
- Enterprise pilots (Private + Dedicated) behind feature flags.
- Monitor deny rates, latency, mismatch rates; iterate on role templates.
- Publish customer-facing guidance and support playbooks.

Phase 4 — GA and deprecation (Post-pilot)
- Default-enable RBAC v2 for new enterprise orgs.
- Expand GA to all customers after stability and documentation thresholds.
- Begin deprecating legacy RBAC v1 roles/paths with a published timeline.
sections.heading: Phased release plan

sections.body:
- Scope inheritance and precedence: how do we resolve org-level grants vs narrower-scoped bindings (and future deny rules)?
- Project vs environment boundaries for key actions (routing policy edits, model rollouts) across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
- Minimum viable custom roles for MVP: do we require custom roles at pilot, or templates-only plus API support?
- Which denial reason codes are safe to expose to end users vs admins, and how do we gate that exposure?
sections.heading: Open questions

sections.body:
- Permission inventory published and referenced by engineering; at least the “enterprise-sensitive” set mapped to permissions.
- Gateway and service checks are active for the sensitive set with deny-by-default.
- Audit logs include authz decision context fields for covered actions and are exported to SIEM correctly.
- Console provides role templates and role bindings at org/project/environment scopes.
- Feature flags, dashboards, and rollback plan are in place and tested.
- Documentation: customer guidance + internal runbooks + support triage steps are published.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (for MVP pilot readiness)

payload.page_title: Interactive Cost & Fidelity Sandbox — PRD and Launch Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This document defines the Product Requirements and launch playbook for the Interactive Cost & Fidelity Sandbox (ICFS), a developer-facing environment that lets engineering and product teams run realistic, query-level simulations of Redwood inference consumption to evaluate cost, latency, and quality tradeoffs before committing to a deployment or capacity plan. ICFS unifies: a lightweight local runtime, a cloud-backed simulation harness, fidelity profiles, and telemetry-driven cost modeling into a single interactive UX and programmatic API.

Motivation
----------
Teams building LLM features need fast, reproducible answers to questions like:
- What is the per-10k-token cost for conversational workloads at our expected distribution of prompt lengths and response lengths?
- How does quantization (Q4, Q8) affect output quality on our prompt set?
- Which batching and KV cache configuration meets our 200ms P50 latency target while minimizing cost?

Existing tools produce static estimates or require heavy manual traffic replay. ICFS provides a repeatable, interactive way for developers, SREs, and solutions engineers to run scenario experiments against the same fidelity and telemetry models Redwood uses in production.

Goals (what success looks like)
--------------------------------
1. Developers can generate an end-to-end consumption estimate (cost, latency, model-variant mix, and quality delta) for a supplied prompt set within 2 minutes.
2. The scenario simulation matches production billing signals within +/- 7% for token-based routes and within +/- 10% for embedding-heavy workloads for standard fidelity profiles.
3. Provide a web-based interactive UX and a programmatic API (OpenAPI) that supports: sampling, deterministic traffic replay, and sensitivity analysis for batching, KV cache hit rates, and quantization.
4. Integration with Redwood Console telemetry so simulations can be saved, shared, and used to suggest Dedicated sizing recommendations (initial alpha).

Non-goals
---------
- ICFS will not be used as a production traffic proxy or gateway. It is strictly for simulation and estimation.
- The first public release will not support every third-party model adapter; we will ship with the top 6 model families used by Redwood customers.

Stakeholders and ownership
---------------------------
- Product lead: Leah Moreno (owner)
- Eng lead: Ravi Kapur (eng-serving-runtime)
- UX/Design: Dana Li (eng-developer-experience)
- Applied ML / Evaluations: Omar Ruiz
- SRE & Capacity: Priya Sinha
- Sales & Solutions enablement: Marcus Holt

User personas
-------------
- Individual engineer: quick back-of-envelope estimates for feature design.
- ML platform engineer: sizing Dedicated pools and choosing quantization policies.
- Solutions engineer: create shareable scenarios for customer onboarding and purchase conversations.

High-level feature set (MVP)
----------------------------
1. Interactive UI: scenario builder with source prompt upload (CSV/JSONL), selection of model variants, fidelity profiles, and target SLA (latency P50/P95).
2. Programmatic API: simulate endpoint that accepts a prompt set, configuration JSON, and returns: per-token cost estimate, latency distribution, token breakdown (input/output), and a quality delta score for user-supplied evals.
3. Local runtime shim: Docker image + lightweight CLI that can (optionally) replay traffic locally using a small model or the Redwood lightweight kernel for offline experiments.
4. Fidelity profiles: presets (high, standard, cost-optimized, quantized-q4) with exact parameter definitions (attention kernels, KV caching assumptions, float vs quantized memory footprint).
5. Telemetry mapping: simulation outputs include the same telemetry labels used in Console (route, model_variant, tenant_id) to allow upload & comparison.
6. Shareable scenario artifacts: human-readable summary, JSON export, permalink into Console for stakeholders with appropriate RBAC.

Functional requirements (detailed)
----------------------------------
FR-1: Scenario ingestion
- Accept CSV/JSONL with fields: id, prompt, expected_response_length_hint (optional), metadata (optional).
- Validate schema and sample distribution (report basic statistics: token length histogram, top n prompt types).

FR-2: Simulator core
- Simulate per-request tokenization, prefix KV hit (configurable hit rate), batching policy, and model kernel selection.
- Use production-derived latency models per model_variant and GPU class.
- Produce per-request traces including: tokens_in, tokens_out, kernel_path, simulated_latency_ms, and cost_usd.

FR-3: Quality delta evaluation
- Accept an eval harness (small labeled set) and compute a quality delta for each fidelity profile using BLEU/ROUGE or a user-specified metric.
- Return aggregated quality delta and per-example diffs (truncated) for manual review.

FR-4: API and UX results
- Provide results via interactive UI and a JSON API. API responses must include summary and a per-percentile latency and cost table.
- API must be authenticated via Redwood API keys and honor tenant scoping when used in cloud mode.

FR-5: Export and Console sync
- Allow scenario export as a JSON artifact and optional upload to Console workspace. Linking should preserve scenario metadata and attach telemetry tags.

Non-functional requirements
----------------------------
NFR-1: Accuracy targets
- Cost estimates within +/-7% of production for token routes across standard fidelity profiles.
- Latency percentiles within +/-12% for P50/P95 when using the same model_variant and hardware class.

NFR-2: Performance and scale
- Cloud simulation cluster must support 200 concurrent scenarios (each up to 10k prompts) without queueing beyond 3 minutes.

NFR-3: Security and privacy
- Uploaded prompts are treated as customer data, stored encrypted at rest when stored more than 24 hours.
- Provide an option to auto-delete artifacts after scenario completion.

API contract (example)
---------------------
sections.heading: Overview
Request (POST /v1/simulate)
Response (200)

sections.body:
| field | type | description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| route | string | customer-defined route name |
| model_variant | string | model variant used in simulation |
| scenario_id | string | ICFS scenario GUID |
| fidelity_profile | string | preset name |
| sim_latency_ms | number | simulated end-to-end latency |
| sim_cost_usd | number | simulated cost per request |

Quality scoring notes
---------------------
- The baseline release will support BLEU and ROUGE and a Redwood internal embedding-similarity delta for semantic drift.
- Scoring must be configurable to allow customers to supply their own scorer function in the harness (lambda or local script in the local runtime mode).

UX flows and wireframe notes
---------------------------
1. Onboarding: quick wizard to upload prompts, pick target fidelity profile, select model variants, and pick summary metrics to produce.
2. Run: progress bar with early preview: after 10% of prompts simulated the UI shows a provisional estimate.
3. Compare: side-by-side fidelity profile comparison with toggles for batching and KV cache assumptions.
4. Share: generate permalink with access control and option to attach to a Console project.

Pricing & packaging guidance (alpha recommendations)
--------------------------------------------------
- Beta access will be free for self-serve tenants up to 5 scenarios/month.
- For scale usage we will meter scenarios as a blend: compute-time (per-sim-minute) + storage for saved artifacts. Example rate: $0.10 / sim-minute + $0.02 / GB-month for artifacts beyond 30 days.
- Enterprise customers with Dedicated contracts: include 1,000 sim-minutes/month as part of the SLA bundle and custom pricing for on-prem sandbox appliances.

Launch & rollout plan (90 days)
------------------------------
Phase 1 (30 days): internal alpha
- Deliver core simulator, local runtime, and internal UI.
- Run 20 internal scenario validations against production telemetry and adjust latency/cost models.
- Success gate: accuracy within targets on 3 sample tenants.

Phase 2 (30 days): closed beta
- Invite select customers and Solutions engineers.
- Add Console integration for scenario save/share.
- Collect feature requests and telemetry comparison artifacts.

Phase 3 (30 days): public beta
- Self-serve onboarding, documentation, and SDKs.
- Release pricing and create playbook for Sales.

Release notes template (for each public release)
------------------------------------------------
- New fidelity profiles added (list)
- Accuracy model updates and calibration notes
- API changes (contract, new fields)
- Known limitations and recommended workarounds

Operational runbooks & support
------------------------------
- Runbook: ICFS service health page, SLOs, common alerts (simulation-queue-depth > 30, model-latency-drift > 20% vs baseline).
- Support playbook: how to convert a scenario into a Dedicated sizing recommendation and handoff to SRE for capacity reservation.

Open risks and mitigations
-------------------------
1. Drift between simulator models and production kernel behavior (risk): mitigate with continuous calibration job that re-benchmarks kernels monthly.
2. PII in prompt uploads (risk): mitigate via auto-redaction option and strict retention defaults.
3. Overreliance by customers (risk): label estimates as guidance and include confidence interval and calibration scores on all outputs.

Next steps / immediate action items (owner: Leah)
------------------------------------------------
1. Finalize fidelity profile definitions with Applied ML (due: 2026-03-01).
2. Build initial latency/cost model skeleton and validate against two production tenants (due: 2026-04-01).
3. UX wireframes and CLI UX (due: 2026-04-08).
4. Prepare closed beta customer list and Solutions enablement kit (due: 2026-04-15).

Appendix: example scenario summary
--------------------------------
Scenario: "Customer X conversational helpdesk"
- Prompts: 5,432 JSONL objects, median prompt tokens = 28, median expected response tokens = 46.
- Selected model variants: redwood-v3-small, redwood-v3-medium-quant-q4
- Results (simulated): estimated monthly cost (100k queries/day): $8,420; p50 latency = 198ms; quality delta vs baseline = -1.4% (semantic similarity).

Contact and governance
----------------------
Product owner: Leah Moreno (leah.moreno@redwood.ai)
Eng lead: Ravi Kapur (ravi.kapur@redwood.ai)
Security review: schedule with Security & Compliance before public beta.

payload.page_title: Conversational buffering: cost-aware capacity model PRD

sections.body:
Overview

This PRD describes Conversational Buffering: a cost-aware capacity model and runtime contract for managing short-term conversational state buffering, prioritized request shaping, and dynamic capacity allocation for low-latency chat workloads. The feature targets Redwood Hosted and Dedicated runtimes with the long-term intention to support Private deployments (VPC) via the same control-plane semantics.

Context and motivation

Conversational applications commonly issue many small, high-frequency requests (token-limited exchanges, keep-alive pings, short-system-utterance updates). These requests have tight latency requirements but are costly to serve when treated as full, independent inference calls. Current approaches either: (a) force customers to provision excess Dedicated capacity to maintain latency SLOs for bursty small-requests, or (b) accept higher cost per request on Hosted by not employing batching or buffering.

Conversational Buffering introduces an opt-in runtime capability that: (1) groups small conversational operations into short-lived buffers, (2) provides configurable cost-prioritization tiers and SLAs for buffered vs immediate execution, and (3) exposes a consumption and capacity model so customers can reason about economics (billing), SLOs, and compatibility with existing routing/fallback policies.

Goals

- Reduce per-request cost for small conversational exchanges by 30–60% at equivalent latency SLOs for typical chat workloads.
- Maintain P50 latency within 100ms and P95 within customer-configurable thresholds for 'immediate' tier requests.
- Provide clear billing semantics and capacity accounting so customers can trade cost for eventual consistency in conversational state.
- Integrate with Redwood routing and fallback policies (latency-tiered routing, model-variant fallthrough).

Non-goals

- This PRD does not change model-level fidelity or introduce new quantization schemes.
- Not proposing changes to token billing unit definitions; buffering impacts how work is scheduled and metered but token accounting stays consistent with the billing surface.

Key concepts

- Buffer window: a short time window (configurable 10–500 ms) during which small requests for a given conversation id are coalesced into a single inference operation where possible.
- Priority tiers: immediate, standard-buffered, delayed-buffered. Immediate bypasses buffering; standard-buffered aims to preserve interactive feel; delayed-buffered trades latency for higher batching efficiency.
- Buffer budget: per-tenant and per-route budget controlling how many buffered operations are allowed concurrently.
- Capacity crediting: consumed compute for buffered work is debited from a separate budgeting bucket when configured; unused buffering credits do not expire within a short retention period.

Success metrics (initial targets)

- Hosted: mean cost per small conversational request reduced by 40% for tier 'standard-buffered' in synthetic chat workload.
- Dedicated: equivalent throughput per GPU increases by 20% for small-request dominated workloads when standard-buffering is enabled.
- Customer impact: 90% of beta customers report acceptable UX (no perceived stutter) after tuning buffer window <= 150ms.

User stories

1) As an e-commerce chat product owner, I want the chat runtime to aggregate typing and short clarification updates so my inference costs drop while users see immediate responses for critical messages.
2) As a platform engineer, I want to set different buffering budgets and SLOs per-route so support and billing-sensitive routes keep strict latency while general conversational routes save cost.
3) As a CTO, I want predictable billing and a simulated cost/latency estimator before enabling buffering in production.

Functional requirements

1. API and config surface
   - New per-route configuration flags: buffering.enabled (bool), buffering.window_ms (int), buffering.priority (enum: immediate, standard, delayed), buffering.budget_id (string).
   - Admin CLI / Console support: enable/disable buffering per-tenant, per-route; view buffer queue lengths and budget consumption.

2. Runtime behavior
   - If buffering.enabled and request.size_tokens <= 64 and request.conversation_id present, attempt coalescing within buffering.window_ms.
   - Coalescing semantics: merge prefix tokens and KV cache where safe; preserve per-request metadata and respond with per-request deltas.
   - Immediate-tier requests must not be buffered; standard-tier may be buffered up to tenant buffer budget.

3. Capacity accounting and billing
   - Metering: buffered operation counts as a single inference operation for compute usage when coalesced; per-request token billing is prorated to original requests.
   - Expose buffer_credit usage in telemetry and billing exports.

4. Observability and alerts
   - Real-time metrics: buffer_coalesce_rate, buffer_drain_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), buffer_reject_rate (budget saturation), buffer_billed_compute_wh.
   - Alerts: buffer_reject_rate > 1% sustained for 5m (pager), buffer_drain_p95 > route.slo.buffered_p95 for 10m (page).

5. Safety and correctness
   - Ensure function/tool-calls and streaming responses are not inappropriately merged. Streaming messages must still be delivered immediately; buffering only applies to non-streamed short requests.
   - Maintain idempotency guarantees and preserve per-request headers/metadata.

Non-functional requirements

- Latency SLOs: immediate-tier P50 <= 100ms, P95 <= 250ms. Standard-buffered P50 <= 120ms, P95 <= 350ms (configurable).
- Throughput: runtime must support 10k concurrent buffered conversations per Dedicated GPU (beta target).
- Consistency: buffer windows must be weakly ordered per-conversation id.

Capacity model and billing examples

We define three accounting units: request_tokens (R), coalesced_ops (C), buffer_credits (B).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
| Scenario                            | Requests | Avg tokens/request | Coalesced ops | Billing model                             | Notes |
|-------------------------------------|----------|--------------------:|--------------:|-------------------------------------------|-------|
| 1: 5 rapid 10-token edits (no buffer)| 5        | 10                 | 5             | 5 * token billing                          | baseline |
| 2: same with standard-buffering     | 5        | 10                 | 1 or 2        | coalesced_ops * model_compute + prorated tokens | cost reduced if coalesced |

Operational examples

- If standard-buffering has window_ms=100 and three small requests arrive at t=0, t=30, t=90 for same conversation_id, runtime will attempt a single inference at t=100 combining the prefix and deltas.
- If immediate-tier request arrives at t=50, it bypasses buffering and is sent immediately; buffered inference still produces a response containing the earlier requests.

Telemetry and console UX

Console must show: per-route buffer window, current buffer queue size, live coalescing rate, cost-savings estimate (approx %), buffer budget remaining. Billing CSV export column additions: buffer_credits_used, coalesced_ops, uncoalesced_small_ops.

Rollout plan

1. Alpha (internal) - 4 weeks: implement runtime coalescing prototype for Hosted dev environment, expose telemetry only.
2. Beta (selected customers) - 8 weeks: per-route config in Console, billing export proof-of-concept, invite 5–10 customers with small-request workloads.
3. GA (public) - 6–8 weeks post-beta: finalize billing contract, full Console UX, Dedicated support, and private deployment docs.

Migration and compatibility

- Default state: buffering.enabled = false. Customers must opt-in per-route.
- Provide a simulator tool in Console allowing customers to replay historical request traces to estimate cost and latency impact.

Risk analysis and mitigations

- Risk: Poor UX due to over-aggressive buffering causing perceived input lag. Mitigation: conservative default window (100 ms), immediate-tier override, per-route SLOs, and simulator.
- Risk: Billing confusion. Mitigation: clear telemetry columns, billing preview exports during beta, and explicit contract language in pricing docs.
- Risk: Incorrect coalescing leading to semantic changes. Mitigation: strict safeguards (no coalescing for streaming, function calls, or requests with interactive tool invocations) and unit tests for merging logic.

Ownership and next steps

- Product owner: Marco Chen.
- Engineering lead: Priya Kapoor (serving-runtime).
- Observability owner: Daniel Ortiz (eng-platform).
sections.heading: Example table (ASCII)

sections.body:
1) Schedule 1-week spike for runtime merge semantics and KV cache compatibility (owner: Priya).
2) Design Console mockups and billing export columns (owner: Product design).
3) Build simulator prototype that replays traces against buffering algorithm (owner: eng-dx).

References and related pages

- Adaptive KV cache spec: product-docs/design-specs/adaptive-kv-cache-consistency-and-rollback-spec-2027-06-03.json
- Predictive retry and regional failover PRD: product-docs/requirements/prd-predictive-retry-and-regional-failover-2025-09-30.json
- Cost-simulator SDK PRD (use for integration): product-docs/requirements/prd-cost-simulator-and-visibility-ux-sdk-2026-08-01.json

Appendix: CLI examples (beta)

payload.page_title: PRD (2025): Cohort-driven evaluation harness, graduated A/B gates, and staged failover for Optimize

sections.body:
This PRD defines a production-ready evaluation harness for Optimize that:
1) uses cohort-driven and sentinel prompt sampling,
2) gates A/B rollouts with statistical + business thresholds, and
3) implements a staged rollback/failover policy that escalates from automated throttles to cohort-level reverts to full rollback.

The goal is to reduce undetected regressions while keeping rollout velocity high for model and configuration updates.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
We have recurring incidents where model/config rollouts pass coarse checks but produce regressions in specific customer cohorts or long-tail prompts. Current canaries are per-model and global; they miss cohort-specific quality regressions and provide coarse binary pass/fail decisions.

Optimize needs a more granular, actionable evaluation contract that ties observable signals to deterministic remediation steps and human-in-the-loop (HIL) triage when necessary.
sections.heading: Background / Problem

sections.body:
- Detect cohort-specific degradation with >90% recall for regressions causing >5% change in a business-impact metric.
- Prevent silent regressions via sentinel prompt detection and progressive gating across traffic slices.
- Reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) to under 20 minutes for high-severity regressions via deterministic rollback actions.
- Enable safe rapid rollouts with objective pass criteria at each stage.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Improve underlying model training processes (this is a serving/eval policy change).
- Replace manual post-deploy human QA for complex policy/regulatory cases.
- Provide full auto-rollback for noisy low-signal metrics without human review.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
Cohorts are deterministically assigned at request time using request metadata + customer/account attributes. The v1 taxonomy is:
- Persona: developer, analyst, support-agent
- Region: NA, EU, APAC
- Flow: latency-sensitive, long-context, tool-calling, regulatory
- Customer tier: top-enterprise, enterprise, growth, self-serve
sections.heading: Cohorts (v1 taxonomy)

sections.body:
- EU-regulated flows (all tiers)
- Top-10 enterprise customers (account list maintained by Customer Success; synced daily)
sections.heading: Finalized list for v1

sections.body:
1) Sentinel prompt library
- Maintain a versioned library of sentinel prompts organized by cohort (persona/region/flow/tier).
- Include safety sentinels, reliability sentinels (tool-calling), and business-value sentinels (retention-sensitive / conversion proxies).

2) Cohort labeling and bucketing
- Deterministic bucketing at request time with a stable cohort key.
- Cohort labels must be available in evaluation events and rollout decisions.

3) Evaluation pipeline
- Compute per-cohort metrics in near-real-time with a maximum 3 minute lag (updated from 5 minutes based on SRE sizing and on-call usability).
- Support both online sampling (production traffic) and controlled replay (sentinel runs).

4) Graduated A/B gates in Console
- Gate rule configuration includes: minimum sample size, minimum detectable effect (MDE), alpha/beta, max allowed regression, and sustained-duration requirements.
- Default statistical method updated: sequential testing is the default for low-to-mid traffic cohorts; fixed-horizon remains available.

5) Staged rollback / failover engine
- Actions include: throttling new variant traffic, cohort-level divert to previous stable variant, full rollback.
- Each action is tied to explicit triggers and produces an auditable event in the release timeline.

6) Human-in-the-loop (HIL)
- HIL holds are required for blocked cohorts past 5% ramp.
- HIL is required for ambiguous composite detector states.
- Reviewer SLO: 30 minutes for P1 releases.

7) Surfacing and alerts
- Expose evaluation results and runbook links in Console release UI.
- Alert integration for Slack + PagerDuty with cohort breakdown and recommended action.
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
- Sentinel library: >= 650 prompts covering at least 10 predefined cohorts, versioned and attributable (updated from 500/8 based on Evals team coverage plan).
- Per-cohort metrics computed and stored with <= 3 minute latency.
- Gate config defaults:
  - alpha = 0.05
  - beta = 0.2
  - sequential mode enabled by default for cohorts with < 50k daily requests
- Minimum sample size calculator present in UI and enforced for gate validity.
- Automated rollback triggers implemented (updated thresholds after SRE + Evals calibration in staging):
  - (a) Immediate throttle if any safety sentinel shows > 0.3% absolute regression sustained for 5 minutes.
  - (b) Automatic cohort-level divert to previous stable variant if composite quality score drops > 3% sustained for 10 minutes in that cohort.
  - (c) Full rollback if business KPI regression > 4% sustained for 10 minutes (updated from 5% for 5 minutes to reduce false negatives while avoiding brief KPI noise).
- Console includes a playbook link for each trigger with owner, checklist, and comms templates.
- End-to-end test harness can simulate cohorts and verify gating/rollback behavior in staging.
sections.heading: Acceptance Criteria

sections.body:
Phases and traffic slices (updated ramp plan to reduce step-size risk for large enterprise cohorts):
- Phase 0: Staging validation with synthetic traffic (2 weeks)
- Phase 1: Internal canary (0.5%) for 48 hours
- Phase 2: Beta customers (2%) for 72 hours
- Phase 3: Gradual ramp (10% for 24 hours, 25% for 24 hours, then 100% if gates pass)
sections.heading: Rollout Strategy

sections.body:
- Each phase requires passing cohort-specific gates.
- If any cohort fails a gate, apply automated action per remediation playbook and pause the release pending investigation.
- Blocked cohorts cannot ramp beyond 5% without explicit HIL approval in Console.
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
- Binary signals (e.g., sentinel hit rate): two-sided proportion test.
- Continuous scores (e.g., composite quality): Welch’s t-test.
- Default alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.2.
sections.heading: Defaults

sections.body: For cohorts with limited traffic, use sequential analysis with alpha spending (Pocock-style boundary) to allow earlier decisions while controlling Type I error.
sections.heading: Sequential testing (default for low-to-mid traffic cohorts)

sections.body: Console enforces a minimum sample size requirement. The UI provides an MDE and n estimator and records the assumed baseline used for the calculation.
sections.heading: Sample size and MDE

sections.body:
- Level 1 (Transient noise)
  - Auto-throttle new release traffic by 30% immediately.
  - If signals persist for 10 minutes, increase throttle to 50%.
  - Notify on-call; continue observation for 15 minutes.
- Level 2 (Cohort regression)
  - Divert failed cohort traffic to previous stable variant.
  - Create a P1 investigation ticket and open a dedicated War Room channel.
  - Require an explicit “resume” action with notes in Console.
- Level 3 (Business KPI impact)
  - Immediate full rollback of the release.
  - Notify via status page + account reps; schedule postmortem within 48 hours.
- Human-in-the-loop
  - For ambiguous composite detector states or blocked cohort ramps, move the release to HOLD.
  - Reviewers have a 30 minute SLO to approve/deny for P1 releases.
sections.heading: Remediation Playbook

sections.body:
- Sentinel hit rate per cohort.
- Composite quality score per cohort (weighted accuracy proxy + hallucination penalty + latency penalty).
- Business KPIs: conversion rate, retention signal (as provided by customer integrations).
- Infrastructure: token cost variance, GPU latency P95, request error rate.
- Anomaly detectors: distribution drift (embedding distance) and abrupt change in output length.
sections.heading: Monitoring Signals

sections.body:
- Release details page
  - Add a “Cohorts” tab: per-cohort metrics, sentinel breakdown, sample viewer.
  - Add a “Gates” panel: pass/fail status, confidence intervals, and sustained-duration progress.
- Gate configuration
  - Configure alpha/beta, fixed vs sequential mode, MDE, sustained-duration requirements, and mapped remediation actions.
- Notifications
  - Slack + PagerDuty wiring integrated into the release flow with cohort-aware routing.
sections.heading: Console / UI Changes

sections.body:
- Storage for per-request metadata and evaluation events; retention updated to 180 days (from 90) to support quarter-over-quarter regressions and enterprise audit requests.
- Streaming pipeline to route sampled requests to evaluation workers (implementation depends on platform standard; initial deployment uses Kafka as in SRE sizing).
- Evaluation workers to run controlled prompts and compute metrics; require autoscaling profile and quotas.
- Dashboard endpoints and Console API to surface near-real-time cohort results.
sections.heading: Data & Infra

sections.body:
- 2025-11-05: PRD created
- 2025-11-12: Design review & cohort taxonomy finalized
- 2025-11-20: API contract for gates approved
- 2025-11-28: Staging harness deployed
- 2025-12-06: Internal canary start
- 2025-12-12: Beta customers start (updated from earlier plan to allow extra staging burn-in)
- 2025-12-18: Target GA (updated from 2025-12-15 based on ramp plan and blocked cohort review bandwidth)
sections.heading: Timeline (updated)

sections.body:
- Aisha Patel — PM (owner)
- Marco Li — Engineering (release engineering)
- Rina Gomez — Head of Evals
- Victor Chen — Console UX
- Sanjay Rao — SRE
- Priya Desai — Customer Success
sections.heading: Stakeholders

sections.body:
- What is the acceptable latency tradeoff for running sentinel prompts synchronously vs async for latency-sensitive flows?
- After-hours escalation owner for Level 2 cohort regressions (proposal: SRE primary with Evals secondary).
- Should Console surface raw model outputs for sampled requests, or only aggregated signals (compliance implications; default proposal: aggregated-only, with restricted break-glass access for on-call)?
sections.heading: Open Questions

sections.body:
- 2025-11-20: Initial PRD moved to in-review in Linear pending sign-off on alpha/beta defaults and blocked cohorts.
- 2025-12-03: Updated (a) evaluation lag target to <= 3 minutes, (b) sentinel library target to 650 prompts / 10 cohorts, (c) ramp steps to 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100%, (d) rollback thresholds for safety and KPI signals, and (e) retention to 180 days.

payload.page_title: per-route-slo-creditization-and-billing-prd-2027-09-15

sections.body:
Overview

This PRD defines the Per-Route SLO Creditization feature: a metering and billing model that maps customer-defined SLOs and route-level policies to fractional credit allocations. The goal is to let engineering teams and finance owners tie SLAs (latency, availability, error budget) directly to a customer’s committed consumption bundle so that billing reflects the cost of meeting higher SLOs without forcing coarse-grained reserved capacity purchases.

Motivation and background

Problem: Customers currently choose between broad reserved capacity (Dedicated) or pay-as-you-go hosted pricing. There is no first-class way to express that route / model X requires 99.9% latency SLO at 50 RPS while route Y is best-effort and can be served by cheaper fallbacks. This leads to overprovisioning, unpredictable bills, and inefficient routing decisions.

Opportunity: Introduce a per-route creditization layer that: 1) allows customers to attach SLO profiles to routes, 2) translates SLO strictness to a fractional credit multiplier, 3) surfaces consumption and projected spend by route, and 4) integrates with billing to charge at SLO-adjusted rates.

Goals (measurable)

- Reduce over-reservation-related spend for customers by enabling route-level SLO differentiation; target 15% unit cost reduction for customers who adopt per-route creditization within 6 months of rollout.
- Provide precise billing visibility: expose per-route spend estimates in Console with <5% error compared to actual invoice for first 90 days.
- Maintain platform reliability: feature must not increase 99th percentile request latency by >2% on control clusters.

Non-goals

- This PRD does not introduce entirely new pricing tiers; it introduces a metering layer and billing multiplier that maps to existing bundles.

User personas and primary user stories

- Platform Engineer (FinOps): "I want to assign SLO-backed credit weights to API routes so that cost maps to importance."
- Product Manager: "I want per-route spend dashboards and forecasts to decide which routes to prioritize for optimization."
- Account Manager: "I want to justify a Dedicated upsell by showing a route is consistently above its soft SLO multiplier."

Functional requirements

1) Route SLO profiles: UI + API to create SLO profiles with fields: name, latency_slo_ms (p50/p95/p99), availability_slo_pct, error_budget_pct, fallback_priority (low|medium|high), and modifier_tags (list).

2) Credit multiplier mapping: system must translate SLO profile to a credit multiplier in range [0.5, 4.0]. Mapping is configurable via a server-side table: stricter latency, higher availability -> larger multiplier. Default mapping must be documented and overridable via enterprise config.

3) Route assignment: customers can attach an SLO profile to any ingestion route or model variant via Console, REST API, or Infrastructure-as-Code (example CLI shown below). Assignment must support bulk operations and labels.

4) Real-time metering: serving runtime must emit per-request metering events that include route_id, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, error_flag, and applied_multiplier. Events are consumed by billing pipeline to compute SLO-adjusted consumption.

5) Console visibility: Cost Explorer and route dashboards must show: raw token consumption, applied multiplier, adjusted credits consumed, 30d rolling spend estimate, and forecast at current traffic.

6) Billing integration: Billing pipeline must accept adjusted credits and produce invoices mapping adjusted credits to existing per-credit price. Accounting must preserve raw consumption for audits.

7) Compatibility & fallback: If incident or region fallback triggers a downgrade to a cheaper variant, the applied multiplier must reflect the active SLO (and may be reduced per config). All fallback events must be logged and included in the allocated credit calculations for transparency.

8) Auditability: Every change to SLO profiles and route assignments must be tracked in an immutable audit log (who, when, previous_values).

Non-functional requirements

- Performance: emitting metering events must add <1ms median overhead and not increase 99th percentile latency by more than 2% on benchmarked paths.
- Scalability: Support 50K routes per tenant and 10k events/sec aggregated ingestion for metering without loss.
- Security: SLO profile management requires role-based access control: manage_slo_profiles permission.

API & CLI examples

1) Create SLO profile (HTTP JSON payload):
{
  "profile_name": "checkout-critical-99p9",
  "latency_slo_ms": {"p50": 30, "p95": 150, "p99": 500},
  "availability_slo_pct": 99.9,
  "error_budget_pct": 0.1,
  "fallback_priority": "high",
  "modifier_tags": ["checkout","payments"]
}

2) Assign SLO to route (CLI):
redwood route assign --route-id r_7f3a --slo-profile checkout-critical-99p9 --apply-to model:variant:v1

Billing mapping (described table)

The following is the canonical mapping table the billing pipeline will use (stored as config in billing-service). Values are illustrative and can be tuned in rollout:

| SLO Bucket | Multiplier | Rationale |
|------------|------------|-----------|
| best-effort | 0.5 | low latency/availability requirements; allow large batching and cold variants |
| standard | 1.0 | baseline; same as existing PAYG rate |
| assured | 1.8 | higher availability and tighter p95/p99; requires more reserved capacity or higher-precedence routing |
| critical | 4.0 | strict 99.9-99.99 targets and dedicated resource guarantees |

Acceptance criteria

- API/Console: Create/update/delete profile flows work with end-to-end tests.
- Metering: Serving runtime emits events with applied_multiplier and events can be consumed by billing pipeline in staging with end-to-end checksum parity against simulated traffic.
- Console: Per-route cost view shows adjusted credits and matches billing pipeline within 5% in staging over a 7-day window.
- Load: Feature works under 10k events/sec for a tenant in performance tests.
- Security: RBAC enforced with unit tests and access logs enabled.

Monitoring & SLOs for the feature itself

- Event delivery success rate to billing pipeline: target 99.95% over rolling 7d. Alert at <99.9%.
- Applied multiplier correctness: audit test that 1000 sampled events per day have correct multiplier mapping; alert on >0.5% discrepancy.
- Console sync latency: per-route dashboard should show updated 1-minute aggregation within 90s of ingestion; alert at 3m.

Rollout plan and migration path

1) Alpha (internal): Enable for Redwood internal tenants only. Validate end-to-end billing parity using synthetic traffic. Duration: 4 weeks.
2) Beta (opt-in customers): Invite 5 customers across SMB/Enterprise with active FinOps contacts. Provide support runbooks and weekly syncs. Duration: 8–12 weeks.
3) Public launch (GA): Gradual ramp across all hosted customers using feature flag. Default SLO multiplier mapping remains conservative. Announce via Console banner and migration guide.

Migration considerations

- Default behavior: Routes without an SLO profile will continue to be billed as 'standard' (multiplier=1.0).
- Historical invoicing: We will not retroactively apply multipliers to prior consumption.
- Enterprise overrides: Enterprise customers can opt for a custom multiplier mapping; this requires contractual amendments and will be handled via Sales/Finance.

Operational playbooks (summary)

- High failure rate in event delivery: Fail open flag -> continue billing from raw tokens and generate reconciliation report for the tenant.
- Discrepancy >5% between Console and Billing: Trigger automated reconciliation job and notify billing ops; throttle route-level multipliers until resolved.

Ownership and stakeholders

- Product (owner): Asha Patel (this doc).
- Eng infra: Liam Chen (billing pipeline), Priya Nair (serving runtime metering).
- Finance/Billing: Maya Rodriguez.
- Sales/AM: Ethan Park (customer communication and enterprise overrides).

Open questions and decisions needed

1) Multiplier range and bucket boundaries: proposal above is starting point but require Finance sign-off.
2) Handling of cross-tenant routed traffic in multi-tenant clusters: requires SRE input for costing.
3) Discounts and promotions: how do existing token credits interact with adjusted credits? Require legal and finance to confirm.

Appendix: related configs and storage

- SLO profiles stored in config-store with versioning; each change creates an immutable profile version (profile_vX).
- Metering event schema: json-lines with fields [tenant_id, route_id, profile_version, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, timestamp, applied_multiplier].
- Billing pipeline schema will store both raw_tokens and adjusted_credits for auditability.

Next steps

- Alignment session with Finance to finalize multiplier table (agenda: revenue impact model, sample accounts).
- Prototype: 4-week eng spike to implement metering emission and billing-service support.
- Draft Console UX flows and developer API docs for review.

payload.page_title: PRD: Quantization & Fidelity Experimentation Lab

sections.body: This PRD defines the Quantization & Fidelity Experimentation Lab (the Lab): a reproducible, service-backed environment for running targeted fidelity experiments when introducing quantized model variants, pruning, or other cost-saving serving techniques. The Lab's outputs are deterministic experiment artifacts, decision signals (pass/fail/gated), and standardized reports used by Product, Applied ML, and Serving Runtime to decide rollouts and fallback strategies.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a single source of truth for fidelity impact of any automated compression or quantization profile across representative tenant workloads.
- Produce machine-readable experiment results (quality deltas, latency/cost deltas, statistical significance) and a human-readable report with recommended rollout gating (allow, canary, block).
- Support experiment types: full-model quantization, per-layer mixed-precision, activation pruning, low-rank adapters, and forced KV-cache eviction behaviors.
- Integrate with the Optimize and Serving Runtime rollout pipelines to automatically recommend safe rollouts and guardrail thresholds.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- The Lab will not itself perform live production A/B rollouts. It produces evidence and artifacts consumed by the rollout systems.
- The Lab does not replace long-term model quality monitoring (that remains in Console/Optimize).
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- 90% of candidate quantization profiles produce a deterministic Lab report within 48 hours of submission (on standard profiles).
- >=75% reduction in manual evaluation time for quantization-related rollouts (measured via engineering survey).
- Fallbacks triggered by Lab-approved rollback policies reduce customer-seen quality regressions by >60% vs ad-hoc rollouts.
sections.heading: Success metrics (first 6 months)

sections.body:
- Product (owner): Ivy Chen (product lead) — defines acceptance criteria and experimental matrix templates.
- Applied ML (owner): Rafael Ortega — curates evaluation sets and quality metrics per workload/domain.
- Eng: Serving Runtime (owner): Arjun Malhotra — provides runtime hooks and cost/latency telemetry, implements automated rollout integration.
- Eng: DevEx — SDK/CLI for experiment submission and artifacts retrieval.
sections.heading: Stakeholders and owners

sections.body:
1) As an Applied ML engineer, I want to submit a quantization profile and a list of evaluation prompt sets and receive a standardized fidelity report (metrics, significance, artifact links) so I can recommend rollout policy.
2) As a Product manager, I want a summary dashboard showing pass/fail across customer segments, so I can prioritize safe rollouts.
3) As an SRE, I want experiment artifacts to include traceable request IDs and telemetry so I can audit regressions that reach production.
sections.heading: User stories

sections.body:
- Accept experiment definitions as YAML or JSON via SDK/REST and return a job id.
- Run experiments against: canonical test harness (deterministic RNG seeds), a configurable subset of model variants (float32, int8, 4-bit mixed), and a set of workload slices (chat, code, long-form completion, embeddings).
- Capture and persist: per-example outputs, token-level latencies, resource utilization (GPU RAM, kernels used), and per-example quality scores.
- Produce a structured report containing: aggregated metrics (mean, median, p99), delta vs baseline, 95% confidence intervals, A/B test p-values, and an automated pass/fail recommendation based on policy.
sections.heading: Experiment runner requirements (functional)

sections.body:
- Turnaround: typical small experiments complete within 24 - 48 hours; pilot-level experiments (large prompt sets) within 5 days.
- Reproducibility: experiments run with immutable seeds, pinned model binaries, and environment hashes.
- Multi-tenant safety: experiments run in an isolated namespace, with no customer data used unless explicitly authorized and scrubbed.
sections.heading: Experiment runner requirements (non-functional)

sections.body:
- Primary metrics per workload:
  - Chat/Completion: semantic similarity (embedding cosine) vs baseline, normalized F1 when applicable, and response length parity. Gate: mean embedding cosine drop <= 0.012 AND 99th-percentile semantic delta <= 0.02.
  - Code generation: pass@k and compilation success rate. Gate: pass@1 drop <= 1.5 percentage points and compile-failure delta <= 0.5pp.
  - Embeddings: mean cosine similarity drop <= 0.015; downstream retrieval MAP drop <= 0.8%.
  - Latency/Cost: p50 latency must not increase more than 8% for the target serving configuration; cost/unit must be reduced by >= 12% to be considered.
- Automated pass/fail decision algorithm:
  1. Compute per-workload deltas and CIs.
  2. If any primary metric breaches gate thresholds -> FAIL.
  3. If primary metrics pass but secondary metrics (edge-case slices) show regressions above 95th-percentile thresholds -> WARN (manual review).
  4. Produce recommendation: allow | canary (10% traffic) | block.
sections.heading: Quality metrics and gating logic

sections.body:
---
  experiment_name: "int4-mixed-prune-v2"
  model_variant: "redwood-open-7b-v2"
  baseline_variant: "redwood-open-7b-fp16"
  profiles:
    - name: "int4-mixed"
      quantization: "mixed-int4"
      per_layer_overrides: ["attn-16:8", "mlp-5:4"]
  workload_slices:
    - name: "customer-chat-small"
      sample_set: "canonical/chat-1000"
      metrics: ["embed_cosine","mean_length","toxicity_rate"]
  eval_repeat: 3
  rng_seed: 41321
sections.heading: Experiment definition schema (example YAML)

sections.body:
- Events captured: experiment.submitted, experiment.started, example.{id}.inference.start, example.{id}.inference.end, experiment.completed, experiment.report.generated.
- Telemetry must include: job_id, model_variant, profile_hash, seed, environment_hash, worker_version, and timestamps.
- Artifacts stored: raw outputs (per example), normalized metric table (CSV), aggregated report (JSON and human-readable markdown), and an immutable experiment metadata file.
sections.heading: Telemetry and artifact requirements

sections.body:
- No customer PII may be used in Lab experiments unless explicitly consented and processed in a restricted workspace.
- When customer data is approved, the Lab will apply automated scrubbing per the Data Management policy: remove names, tokens matching credit-card patterns, and PII heuristics.
sections.heading: Data handling and PII policy

sections.body:
- Rollout Integration: Lab will call the Rollout Recommendation API with pass/canary/block and attach experiment artifact links. Serving Runtime will annotate model variants with experiment ids.
- Console: Add a new page type "Experiment Report" where product and applied-ml can browse experiments, filter by model, and export PDFs.
- CLI: redwood-lab submit --file experiment.yaml -> returns job id; redwood-lab report --id JOB -> downloads artifacts.
sections.heading: Integration points and automation

sections.body:
- Baseline test cluster: 8x A100(80GB) equivalent nodes for parallel small experiments; ability to burst to 32 nodes for large sweeps.
- Storage: lifecycle retention of experiment artifacts: 90 days hot, 1 year cold archive.
- RBAC: roles: lab-admin, lab-runner, lab-viewer. lab-runner may execute jobs but cannot delete artifacts.
sections.heading: Operational requirements and infra sizing

sections.body:

Summary: Pass with WARN on edge-case legal prompts. p50 latency -3.4%, cost/unit -18.7%
sections.heading: Reporting and human-readable output (example)

sections.body:
| workload | baseline | variant | delta | CI95 | decision |
| chat-1000 | 0.872 | 0.861 | -0.011 | ±0.003 | PASS |
| legal-slice | 0.790 | 0.760 | -0.030 | ±0.010 | WARN |
Notes: The legal-slice regression is concentrated in documents with very long citations (see artifact: /artifacts/12345/legal-edge-cases.csv). Recommend a canary to 5% with automated fallback to fp16 for flagged tenant tags.
sections.heading: Primary metrics table

sections.body:
1. Experiment authorates PRD + attaches Lab report.
2. Applied ML reviews WARNs; if minor, mark canary; if block, require engineer to iterate.
3. If canary approved, schedule a 2-week canary at 5-10% traffic with monitoring alerts configured (quality delta, token-level fraud checks).
4. If canary succeeds (no production quality regression for 14 days), promote to gradual rollout.

Testing, QA, and guardrails:
- Unit tests: experiment runner validation logic, schema conformance.
- Integration tests: end-to-end run against a small synthetic workload with deterministic outputs.
- Chaos test: randomly kill runner nodes; verify retry semantics and artifact integrity.
- Guardrails: experiments that touch PII require approval from Data Governance.
sections.heading: Rollout gating workflow (recommended)

sections.body:
- How to budget the infra cost of large sweep experiments vs. business value? (Mitigation: quota-based submission and cost-credits workflow.)
- Potential overfitting to canonical prompt sets. (Mitigation: require at least one customer representative slice for any production rollout.)
sections.heading: Open questions and risks

sections.body:
- Q1: MVP experiment runner, CLI, and basic report generation; integrate with Rollout Recommendation API.
- Q2: Support for mixed-precision per-layer overrides, artifact retention policy, and Console report UI.
- Q3: Auto-recommendations tied to Optimize insights (cost/latency tradeoff visualizer) and canary orchestration link.
