payload.page_title: PRD: Dedicated Throughput SLO + Tier Guarantees (v1)

sections.body:
Redwood Dedicated is being formalized with a throughput SLO that customers can purchase, monitor, and enforce via standardized tiers. This PRD defines:

- The customer problem and the Dedicated throughput commitment we will offer
- The canonical metric and measurement rules (what counts, what does not)
- Tier taxonomy (Standard / Plus / Premium) with explicit entitlements and exclusions
- Mapping from tier → standardized hardware “shapes” (by region) and packaging guardrails
- Rollout plan, launch criteria, and success metrics

This document is customer-commitment–shaping. Engineering implementation details live in the SRE SLO doc and Infra shape catalog.

---
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
Dedicated demand has shifted from “isolated capacity” to “predictable capacity.” Enterprise and high-volume customers are requesting:

- A written throughput guarantee that can be referenced in procurement/legal
- A clear definition of measurement and exclusions (especially for streaming)
- A reliable escalation path and remedies when Redwood under-delivers

At the same time, we need a commitment model that:

- Is measurable and hard to game
- Can be operationalized at scale across regions and heterogeneous GPUs
- Preserves fleet economics (standard shapes, tier-aware admission control, consistent accounting)

---
sections.heading: Why now

sections.body:
**Problem 1: Unclear expectations.** Customers don’t know whether “Dedicated” implies a guaranteed minimum throughput or simply isolated compute.

**Problem 2: Measurement disputes.** Customers see different tokens/sec numbers depending on their client metrics vs Redwood’s dashboards (streaming and retries are common sources of mismatch).

**Problem 3: Procurement blockers.** Security and legal teams ask for explicit commitments, defined exclusions, and remedies. Without this, deals stall.

**Problem 4: Hard to size.** Customers need a predictable mapping from their workload to a shape and tier, with realistic burst rules.

---
sections.heading: Customer problems (voice of customer)

sections.body:
1. **Define a purchasable throughput SLO** for Dedicated deployments with clear semantics (what is guaranteed, how it is measured, and under what conditions it applies).
2. **Introduce tiered Dedicated packages** (Standard / Plus / Premium) with explicit entitlements:
   - Throughput floor commitment type
   - Burst policy (if any)
   - Failover posture expectations
   - Support response targets and escalation policy
   - Remedy/credit posture (where applicable)
3. **Standardize capacity accounting** by aligning tiers to a limited set of regional hardware shapes and shape-specific performance envelopes.
4. **Operationalize** via dashboards, alerting, and support playbooks to minimize ambiguity and time-to-resolution.

---
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Guaranteeing absolute latency percentiles (latency SLO is a separate initiative; we will still monitor latency and use it as a diagnostic signal).
- Guaranteeing quality (eval/quality regression processes remain separate).
- Guaranteeing throughput across arbitrary customer model mixes within a single deployment without constraints (v1 requires pinned model/version per Dedicated deployment for a committed SLO).
- Offering fully custom shapes or bespoke per-customer performance contracts (exception process only via exec approval).

---
sections.heading: Non-goals (v1)

sections.body:
| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Dedicated Deployment | A customer-isolated inference deployment pinned to a Redwood-provisioned pool and configured via Redwood control plane. |
| Committed Throughput (CT) | The minimum effective output throughput Redwood commits to deliver for a given Dedicated deployment under defined conditions. Measured in output tokens/sec. |
| Burst Throughput | Additional throughput above CT that may be available per tier policy (best-effort or reserved). |
| SLO Window | The measurement interval used to evaluate compliance (rolling windows; see measurement section). |
| Effective Output Tokens | Tokens emitted by the model to the customer (streamed or non-streamed), after correcting for known accounting pitfalls (e.g., double counting on streaming). |
| Supported Model/Version | A model ID + version that Redwood has certified for the given shape and included in the Dedicated shape catalog. |

---
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
For Dedicated deployments on Plus or Premium tier, Redwood commits that the deployment will deliver at least the purchased **Committed Throughput** (output tokens/sec) during Eligible Time, measured by Redwood’s metering, provided the customer operates the deployment within the documented constraints (supported model/version, context limits, and request patterns).

Standard tier includes a published baseline performance profile and operational support, but **does not** include a written throughput SLO commitment or service credits.
sections.heading: Commitment statement (draft)

sections.body:
**Metric name (conceptual):** `dedicated_effective_output_tokens_per_second`

**Unit:** output tokens / second

**Attribution:** per `deployment_id` (not per route), tagged by `model_id`, `model_version`, `region`, and `tier`.

**Rationale:** A per-deployment metric aligns with how Dedicated is purchased and provisioned; tokens/sec is model-agnostic for customer sizing and maps better than requests/sec to variable output lengths.

(See ADR-027 for rationale and rejected alternatives.)

---
sections.heading: Canonical metric

sections.body:
- **Primary evaluation window:** 5-minute rolling windows
- **Compliance target:** ≥ 99.0% of Eligible Windows per calendar month meet or exceed CT
- **Eligibility:** Only windows meeting eligibility conditions count toward the denominator (see exclusions)
sections.heading: Measurement window

sections.body:
1. Sum **effective output tokens** successfully emitted for requests attributed to the deployment in W.
2. Divide by the window duration in seconds.

`throughput_W = effective_output_tokens_W / 300`

A window is **SLO-met** if `throughput_W >= CT`.
sections.heading: For each 5-minute window W

sections.body:
- Streaming responses count output tokens as they are emitted.
- Known double-counting issues must be corrected in Redwood’s canonical metric pipeline (tracked by Eng; fixes required for GA).
sections.heading: Streaming accounting

sections.body:
- Customers may send requests at any concurrency. Redwood will apply tier-aware admission control to preserve fairness and prevent overload collapse.
- If a customer’s request pattern violates documented constraints (e.g., unsupported context, excessive cancellations), impacted windows may be excluded.

---
sections.heading: Client behavior assumptions

sections.body:
Eligible Time is the time during which Redwood is responsible for meeting CT. The following are excluded from SLO evaluation (do not count against the SLO):

1. **Customer-side throttling or insufficient load**
   - The customer does not submit enough load to allow the deployment to reach CT.
   - The customer imposes client-side rate limits or has upstream backpressure.

2. **Unsupported configuration**
   - Model/version not in the supported list for the purchased shape.
   - Customer changes model/version without Redwood-approved process for that tier.
   - Context length or max output exceeds published constraints for the shape/tier.

3. **Warm-up and provisioning transitions**
   - First 30 minutes after initial provisioning or after a Redwood-initiated restart/roll.
   - Autoscaling warm pool activation windows as documented per tier.

4. **Planned maintenance**
   - Announced maintenance windows (with notice per tier policy).

5. **Customer-induced error conditions**
   - Invalid requests, authentication failures, customer timeouts, or request cancellations.

6. **Force majeure / upstream cloud provider regional outages**
   - Only where Redwood cannot reasonably route/fail over within tier entitlement.
sections.heading: Exclusions and “Eligible Time”

sections.body:
- Exclusions must be auditable and visible in internal dashboards.
- For Premium tier, expected failover behavior reduces the scope of exclusions for regional impairment (see tier entitlements).

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
| Tier | Throughput commitment | Burst policy | Failover posture | Support targets | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | No written throughput SLO; published performance envelope | Best-effort burst only (no reservation) | Best-effort within region | P1 response target: 2 business hours | No service credits for throughput |
| Plus | Written CT SLO (99% eligible windows / month) | Limited burst: up to 1.5× CT for short intervals, subject to published limits | Regional redundancy not guaranteed; best-effort failover within region | P1 response target: 1 hour (24×7) | Service credits for verified misses |
| Premium | Written CT SLO (99.5% eligible windows / month) | Reserved burst pool: up to 2× CT within defined policy | Multi-AZ within region + prioritized failover paths; defined incident comms | P1 response target: 15 minutes (24×7) + named escalation | Enhanced credits + RCA commitments |
sections.heading: Summary table

sections.body:
**Standard**
- Includes: Dedicated isolation, standard dashboards, standard oncall triage.
- Positioning: “Dedicated capacity and predictable baseline,” but not a contractual throughput guarantee.

**Plus**
- Includes: Contractual CT, burn-rate alerting internally, customer-visible SLO reporting (monthly summary), defined escalation + credits.
- Requires: model/version pinning and shape adherence.

**Premium**
- Includes: Contractual CT with higher target, reserved burst allocation, stronger failover posture, faster support, incident comms with timelines, RCA for material breaches.
- Requires: stricter change control (maintenance scheduling, model/version changes via controlled rollout).

---
sections.heading: Entitlement details

sections.body: We will sell Dedicated tiers only on a standardized catalog of shapes per region. Shape details (GPU type/count, CPU/RAM, networking, max context guidance, and supported model list) are defined in the Infra shape catalog.
sections.heading: Hardware shapes and packaging constraints (product requirements)

sections.body:
1. **Shape normalization:** Each tier must map to a small number of shapes per region (target ≤ 4 shapes/region for v1).
2. **Model constraints:** A CT commitment is only valid for supported model/version pairs on that shape.
3. **CT ranges by shape:** For quoting, we will publish a **CT floor range** per shape and model class (e.g., “7B/13B class”, “70B class”), derived from benchmark baselines with safety margin.
4. **No silent oversell:** Quoting tooling must prevent CT values that exceed safe sustained throughput at target utilization + headroom policy.
sections.heading: Product requirements

sections.body:
- Shape catalog page (engineering-owned)
- Sales capacity export (quoting-friendly) showing: region availability, lead times, recommended CT bands, and tier eligibility

---
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body:
1. **Dedicated Tier Overview**
   - What is guaranteed by tier
   - Practical examples (how to size; what happens during burst)

2. **Throughput SLO explanation**
   - Metric definition, windowing, and how to interpret dashboards
   - Common causes of apparent under-delivery (client throttles, context drift)

3. **FAQ and examples**
   - Streaming vs non-streaming token accounting
   - Multi-model needs (recommend separate deployments)
   - How credits work (Plus/Premium)

---
sections.heading: Customer-facing documentation requirements

sections.body:
- Canonical per-deployment throughput metric with correct streaming token accounting.
- Tier-aware dashboard views:
  - CT vs achieved throughput
  - Eligible vs excluded windows breakdown
  - Saturation signals (GPU utilization, queue depth, cache hit rate)
sections.heading: Instrumentation and dashboards

sections.body:
- Burn-rate alerts for throughput SLO for Plus/Premium.
- Paging policy must route to SRE with clear runbook links.
sections.heading: Alerting

sections.body:
- Support/CS escalation playbook must define:
  - Initial triage steps
  - How to validate whether it’s an SLO miss vs exclusion
  - When to page Infra vs SRE
  - Customer comms templates

---
sections.heading: Runbooks & escalations

sections.body: This PRD does not set final list prices, but defines packaging rules needed to keep pricing defensible and fleet-manageable.
sections.heading: Pricing and quoting requirements (v1 guardrails)

sections.body:
1. **List price maps tier → shape → region** with a small number of SKUs.
2. **Discount guardrails**
   - Tier-based maximum discount without Deal Desk approval
   - Mandatory Deal Desk triggers for:
     - Non-standard CT requests
     - Non-standard shapes
     - Premium tier with custom failover terms
3. **Burst metering**
   - Meter burst consumption separately from committed throughput for reporting and (if applicable) overage billing.

---
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
- Finalize metric semantics and exclusions
- Validate benchmark baselines and safety margins by shape
- Draft customer-facing language + legal review
sections.heading: Phase 0: Discovery + alignment (2–3 weeks)

sections.body:
- ADR approved
- Draft SLO language reviewed by Legal + CS
- Initial tier entitlement table agreed by Product/Infra/SRE/Finance
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Publish v1 shape catalog per region
- Define CT bands per shape/model class for quoting
- Pricing proposal + margin checks
sections.heading: Phase 1: Tier + shape design + pricing model (3–4 weeks)

sections.body:
- Finance sign-off on pricing floors and utilization/headroom assumptions
- Sales enablement draft complete (cheat sheet + deck)
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Ship instrumentation, SLO evaluator, and dashboards
- Tier-aware routing and admission control guardrails
- Meter burst usage
sections.heading: Phase 2: Implementation (2–4 weeks)

sections.body:
- Streaming accounting correctness verified against test harness
- Burn-rate alerts tuned to acceptable noise
- Escalation playbook in place and oncall trained
sections.heading: Exit criteria (GA blockers)

sections.body:
- Launch to a small set of Dedicated customers (target 3–5) across at least 2 regions
- Weekly review of SLO measurement disputes, exclusions, and operational load
sections.heading: Phase 3: Limited GA (beta customers)

sections.body:
- No unresolved measurement disputes after 2 reporting cycles
- Support handling time within target; no repeated alert noise issues
sections.heading: Exit criteria

sections.body:
- Enable for all new Dedicated deals; migrate existing customers on renewal or via opt-in

---
sections.heading: Phase 4: Broad GA

sections.body:
- ≥ 80% of new Dedicated Plus/Premium deals reference the standardized throughput SLO language with no bespoke addenda.
- Reduce procurement cycle time for enterprise Dedicated deals where “throughput guarantee” is a stated blocker (baseline to be set by Sales Ops).
- CSAT for Dedicated onboarding/sizing improves (target +0.3 over baseline quarter).
sections.heading: Customer outcomes

sections.body:
- For Plus/Premium deployments: ≥ 99% / 99.5% eligible windows meeting CT (by tier target) with < 5% measurement disputes.
- Burn-rate alert noise: < 2 pages/week across all Dedicated SLO alerts after tuning.
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for Premium P1: ≤ 15 minutes.
sections.heading: Reliability and operations

sections.body:
- Attach rate: ≥ 40% of new Dedicated bookings choose Plus or Premium within 2 quarters of GA.
- Gross margin meets tier targets (tracked by Finance): no systematic underpricing due to oversold CT.

---
sections.heading: Business / fleet economics

sections.body:
1. **Model-dependent throughput variance creates disputes**
   - Mitigation: pin supported model/version per deployment for CT; publish CT bands by model class; enforce constraints in control plane.

2. **Streaming token accounting mismatch**
   - Mitigation: canonical pipeline fixes + regression tests; publish clear docs; dashboard should show “effective output tokens” definition.

3. **GPU supply constraints by region**
   - Mitigation: shape catalog is region-specific; quoting tool must show lead times; Premium may require pre-commit scheduling.

4. **Gaming the SLO (e.g., pathological request patterns)**
   - Mitigation: eligibility exclusions for cancellations/timeouts; tier-aware admission control; document supported request patterns.

5. **Operational burden from credits/RCAs**
   - Mitigation: credits only for verified misses; Premium RCAs only for material breaches; automate reporting.

---
sections.heading: Risks and mitigations

sections.body:
1. Should Standard include any written “performance target” language (non-SLO) without remedies, or keep purely best-effort to avoid implied guarantees?
2. Do we want CT in output tokens/sec only, or also provide an optional requests/sec equivalent for certain endpoints?
3. How do we handle customers requiring multi-model routing within one deployment (contractually)?
4. Premium failover: do we commit to intra-region only, or allow cross-region with defined RTO/RPO-style targets?

---
sections.heading: Open questions

sections.body:
Customer buys CT = 2,000 output tokens/sec on a Plus Dedicated deployment.

- In a given 5-minute window, effective output tokens emitted = 630,000.
- Throughput = 630,000 / 300 = 2,100 tokens/sec → window meets SLO.

If the customer only submits enough load to emit 300,000 tokens in the window (1,000 tokens/sec) and dashboards show low queue depth + low GPU utilization, the window is excluded as “insufficient load / customer throttling.”

---
sections.heading: Appendix A: Example SLO evaluation (illustrative)

sections.body: “Committed Throughput is measured as effective output tokens per second for the Dedicated deployment over rolling five-minute windows. Redwood will meet or exceed the Committed Throughput for at least 99.0% (Plus) / 99.5% (Premium) of Eligible Time windows in each calendar month, excluding periods of planned maintenance, initial warm-up after provisioning or restart, unsupported configuration, and customer-side throttling or insufficient traffic.”
sections.heading: Appendix B: Draft customer-facing commitment language (non-legal)

payload.page_title: Unified Capacity Transition PRD: SLO-aligned Consumption and Dedicated Migration

sections.body:
Executive summary:

This document defines the product requirements, design constraints, rollout roadmap, pricing impacts, and release notes for the "Unified Capacity Transition" initiative. The initiative enables customers to move from legacy per-token consumption and ad-hoc reserved capacity models to an SLO-aligned consumption paradigm that unifies Dedicated reservations, hosted usage, and private deployments under a single migration playbook.

Goals:
- Provide a predictable migration path for customers on Dedicated capacity and legacy token billing to SLO-aligned bundles.
- Maintain or improve customer latency SLOs (p50 <= 45ms for short sequences, p95 <= 250ms for chat workloads) during and after migration.
- Prevent revenue regressions and make pricing transparent to customers.
- Reduce operational overhead for account teams via automated migration tooling, billing reconciliations, and clear rollback policies.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not change model internals, kernel selection, or per-model performance optimizations.
- It does not replace existing enterprise contract negotiation workflows; those remain supported.

Stakeholders and ownership:
- Product (owner): Maya Thompson — overall initiative and PRD.
- Eng Platform: Ravi Singh — migration tooling and rollout automation.
- Eng SRE: Lina Gomez — SLO validation, monitoring, and incident readiness.
- Finance: Alisha Verma — pricing modelling and revenue reconciliation.
- Sales/CS: Account teams (named reps) — customer communications and approvals.

Success metrics (90-day post-rollout):
- 85% of migrated customers meet their pre-migration latency SLOs within +/-10% of baseline.
- Migration churn rate <= 2% attributable to performance regressions.
- Average time-to-migrate (from opt-in) <= 14 days for customers with < 200M tokens/month.
- Net new ARR uplift from SLO-aligned bundles >= 10% for migrated cohort within 3 months.

Functional requirements:
1) Migration offer types (API + Console)
- Offer A: "SLO Starter Bundle" — 99th percentile latency SLO not guaranteed; discounted bundle for low-volume customers.
- Offer B: "SLO Standard Bundle" — p95 latency SLO guarantee with transparent overage pricing.
- Offer C: "Dedicated-equivalent Bundle" — reserved capacity equivalence with burst allowance and SLA.

2) Migration UI and API endpoints
- Console: Guided migration wizard (preview, cost estimate, staging run, apply, rollback).
- API: POST /migration/estimate, POST /migration/start, GET /migration/status, POST /migration/rollback.
- API auth: requires account admin role and signed acceptance of new T&Cs.

3) Billing and reconciliation rules
- Billing engine must support dual-metering window for up to 60 days: customers pay both legacy and new bundle for reconciliation, with credits applied automatically.
- Financial holdback: 10% of first-month revenue held in escrow to cover performance crediting if SLOs are missed.

4) Observability and quality guardrails
- Per-account SLO dashboards (latency, error-rate, token consumption, tail-latency breakdown).
- Auto-escalation: if p95 latency degrades > 20% relative to baseline for 6 consecutive hours, flip to mitigation mode (see Runbook).

Non-functional requirements:
- Backwards-compatible APIs: endpoints must not break existing key flows.
- Rollback time target: full rollback under 30 minutes for customers with < 1M QPS-equivalent requests.
- Storage: migration metadata retention for 365 days.
- Data residency: migration operations must honor customer's region and VPC constraints.

Design overview:
- High-level approach: create a "migration orchestration" service that coordinates cost estimates, staged test runs against a canary route, and final cutover. The orchestration service communicates with: billing, routing, runtime control plane, monitoring, and the console.

- Components:
  - Migration Orchestrator (service): tracks state machine (estimate -> staging -> validate -> cutover -> reconcile -> archive).
  - Estimate Engine: runs simulation using historical token traces + model profiles to produce cost and SLO risk assessments.
  - Staging Proxy: routes a configurable percentage of production traffic to the new bundle variant for validation.
  - Billing Reconciler: coordinates dual-metering and credits.
  - SLO Validator: compares live metrics to baseline and flags pass/fail.

API contract examples:
- Estimate request (JSON)
```
POST /v1/migration/estimate
{
  "account_id": "acct_123",
  "lookback_days": 30,
  "models": ["redwood/gemini-13b", "open/guanaco-7b"],
  "target_bundle": "slo-standard"
}
```
- Example estimate response (abridged)
```
{
  "monthly_cost": "USD 12,400",
  "predicted_p95_delta": "+12%",
  "recommended_configuration": {"burst_capacity": "2000 rps", "quantization_profile": "q3"}
}
```

Migration phases and timeline (high level):
- Phase 0 (Prep, 0-2 weeks): product sign-off, legal T&Cs update, pricing modelling finalized, pilot cohort selected.
- Phase 1 (Pilot, 2-8 weeks): 5–10 reference customers, staging runs, end-to-end billing validation.
- Phase 2 (Scale rollout, 8-20 weeks): self-serve console enablement, sales enablement docs, automated reconciliations.
- Phase 3 (General availability, 20+ weeks): GA launch, public docs, migration incentives sunset.

Rollout steps (detailed numbered procedure):
1. Prepare account profile and collect 30-day telemetry snapshot.
2. Run Estimate Engine to generate cost + SLO risk.
3. Present migration plan to customer via Console and Sales.
4. If customer accepts, create staging proxy and route 1–5% traffic for 48 hours.
5. Run automated SLO validation. If pass, increment to 25% for 72 hours.
6. Final cutover window is scheduled; during cutover route 100% traffic and enable Billing Reconciler.
7. Monitor for 72 hours; if any auto-escalation triggers, run rollback (documented in Runbook).
8. After 60-day dual-billing window, finalize reconciliation and archive migration metadata.

Runbook: auto-escalation and rollback (engineer-facing):
- Trigger conditions:
  - p95 latency increase > 20% vs baseline for 6h.
  - Error rate increase > 1% absolute for 1h.
  - Token consumption variance > 30% and billing delta > 15% projected.
- Immediate actions:
  1) On-call SRE receives page with affected account_id and baseline.
  2) Migration Orchestrator toggles staging proxy to previous route.
  3) Billing Reconciler marks account for manual review and applies interim credits.
  4) Post-incident triage within 48 hours and customer-facing status update.

Pricing and packaging implications:
- Principle: preserve transparency and provide a clear economic mapping between token usage and bundle capacity.
- Example pricing tiers (illustrative):
| Bundle | Monthly commit | Included tokens/mo | Burst | SLA | Overages |
|--------|----------------|--------------------|-------|-----|----------|
| Starter | $1,200 | 50M | 500 rps | best-effort | $0.00007/token |
| Standard | $10,000 | 500M | 5k rps | p95 latency SLO | $0.00006/token |
| Dedicated-equivalent | $45,000 | 3B | 20k rps | SLA-backed | negotiated |

- Migration credits and incentives:
  - 30% credit on the first month for pilots.
  - Volume commitment discounts continue to apply post-migration.

Roadmap and milestones (quarterly themes):
- Q2 2027: Pilot cohort execution, Estimate Engine MVP, console wizard alpha.
- Q3 2027: Billing Reconciler beta, expanded pilot, early self-serve flows.
- Q4 2027: Scale rollout, analytics dashboards GA, CS/sales playbooks.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Customers experience tail-latency regressions after bundling.
  - Mitigation: Staging proxy with progressive traffic ramp + canary performance tuning.
- Risk: Billing reconciliation disputes inflate finance workload.
  - Mitigation: Automate credits, provide clear reconciliation reports, finance SLA with account teams.
- Risk: Migration tooling introduces new surface area for incidents.
  - Mitigation: Circuit-breaker patterns, per-account toggles, and 30-day metadata retention for audit.

Developer notes and implementation constraints:
- Orchestrator state machine must be idempotent; design to tolerate at-least-once events.
- Ensure all calls to runtime control plane include reason and correlation_id for audit.
- Migration UI must surface estimated risk categories (Low/Medium/High) and the primary driver (latency, token variance, model mismatch).

Planned release notes (to be included in product release):
- Added migration wizard to Console to transition customers to SLO-aligned bundles.
- New API endpoints: /v1/migration/estimate, /v1/migration/start, /v1/migration/status, /v1/migration/rollback.
- Billing: dual-metering window support and automatic crediting for migration reconciliations.

Appendices:
A. Example migration checklist (for CS and Sales)
1) Confirm customer's legal acceptance and billing contact.
2) Run Estimate and review predicted p95 delta.
3) Schedule staging window and collect required runbooks.
4) Assign SRE on-call for the cutover window.
5) Validate reconciliation report post-60 days.

B. Example CLI snippet to start a migration (internal tooling)
```
redwood migrate start --account acct_123 --bundle slo-standard --staging-percent 5 --contact "cs-rep@example.com"
```

C. Ownership and contacts
- Product owner: Maya Thompson (maya@redwood.ai)

Document history and next steps:

payload.page_title: PRD: Runtime Fidelity Negotiator & Onboarding Simulation Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the Product Requirement and rollout playbook for the Runtime Fidelity Negotiator (RFN): a service and simulation harness that (1) negotiates an appropriate response fidelity (quality/compute tradeoff) per-session or per-route based on customer SLA, latency and cost constraints, and (2) provides a self-serve onboarding simulator that lets customers preview cost/latency tradeoffs against representative traffic before committing to capacity or fidelity tiers.

Background and motivation:
- Customers routinely request predictable latency and cost guarantees while also requiring output quality suitable for their UX. Current options require manual rule authoring or coarse-grained fidelity tiers that are hard to validate before deployment.
- The RFN will reduce friction for hosted-to-dedicated/on-prem migrations by giving an automated negotiation layer and an experimental sandbox for customers to simulate their workloads against fidelity policies and pricing implications.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Provide an API and runtime that returns a fidelity decision within 30ms median for <= 99th%-tile client negotiation latency <= 150ms under 95th percentile load.
2) Onboarding simulator that accurately predicts token-level cost within ±10% compared to production over a representative 24h synthetic replay.
3) Policy primitives that support: per-route SLOs, per-tenant budget caps, adaptive fallback chains and quantization-aware candidate scoring.

Non-goals:
- RFN is not a full billing engine. It surfaces crediting recommendations and signals to billing, but accounting remains in billing service.
- RFN does not replace model evaluation; it relies on model onboarding quality metadata provided by Applied ML.

Personas:
- Platform engineers: want contract-level guarantees and diagnostics during migration.
- Customer SREs: validate that production fidelity choices meet latency/cost targets.
- Product managers & Solutions engineers: design fidelity defaults for product lines.

Success metrics (first 6 months):
- 50 enterprise onboarding simulations completed with error <=10% vs. observed cost.
- 80% of negotiation calls return decision in <=30ms median.
- 30% reduction in initial overprovisioning when customers adopt RFN simulator vs. previous baseline.

Functional requirements:
1) Public negotiation API: POST /v1/fidelity/negotiate
   - Input: route_id, tenant_id, request_profile (tokens_estimate, response_max_tokens), latency_target_ms, cost_budget_usd_per_1k_tokens (optional), sample_prompts (optional, list hash ids)
   - Output: fidelity_decision {variant_id, quantization_profile, expected_latency_ms, expected_cost_per_1k_tokens, confidence_score}
   - Example payload:
```
{
  "route_id":"checkout-chat",
  "tenant_id":"tenant-42",
  "request_profile": {"avg_input_tokens":120, "max_output_tokens":350},
  "latency_target_ms":150,
  "cost_budget_usd_per_1k_tokens":0.12
}
```
   - Negotiation must be idempotent and log a decision event for audit.

2) Policy language v1 (declarative):
   - Allow constraints: latency:<ms>, cost:<usd/1k>, min_quality:<metric:threshold>, allowed_variants:[ids], blacklist_variants:[ids], fallback_chain:ordered list.
   - Must support tenant-level overrides and route-level defaults.

3) Simulator CLI and UI component:
   - CLI: rfnsim run --tenant tenant-42 --profile profile.yaml --duration 24h --out results.json
   - UI: one-click scenario creation from sample prompt sets, output cost/latency histograms and per-variant confusion metrics.

Non-functional requirements:
- Negotiator availability: 99.9% overall, regionally redundant.
- Negotiation latency: median <=30ms, p99 <=150ms under standard load (500 rps regionally).
- Throughput: baseline capacity 1k negotiation QPS per region, autoscaling to 5k QPS.
- Security: requests authenticated with route token, negotiation decisions stored in audit log with tenant-scoped encryption.

Simulation harness and benchmark scenarios:
- Scenario A (Transactional baseline): 95% short requests (avg input 30 tokens, response 50 tokens).
- Scenario B (Conversational long-tail): 60% mid-size (120 input, 300 output), 40% long (500+ tokens).
- Scenario C (Bursty enterprise): diurnal + sudden 10x bursts lasting 2m every 6h.

For each scenario simulator must produce:
- Per-variant latency profile (p50/p95/p99),
- Token-cost projection (USD/1k tokens),
- Fidelity-impact on quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim depending on route),
- Regression delta vs. model baseline.

Pricing & packaging implications (summary table in text):
- Fidelity tier mapping:
  - high-fidelity: 1.0x base cost, recommended for 'must-pass' routes.
  - balanced: 0.65x base cost, default for interactive consumer routes.
  - economy: 0.4x base cost, suitable for low-sensitivity batch tasks.
- Suggested crediting guidance: when RFN selects a lower-fidelity variant as fallback, bill at fallback multiplier but surface an "fidelity credit" of (1 - multiplier) that can be used for migration credits if customer upgrades to a higher SLA within 30 days.

Rollout plan (phases):
1) Internal alpha (4 weeks): runtime prototype + simulator runs against internal traffic. Metrics: negotiation latency, simulator accuracy vs. replay. Owners: Runtime (Marcus Chen), Applied ML (Sofia Martinez).
2) Partner beta (8–12 weeks): 3 pilot customers, dedicated SRE runbooks, billing hook for fidelity credits, explicit opt-in. Collect per-tenant simulation vs. production deltas.
3) GA: public API, console integration, packaged as part of Dedicated onboarding toolkit.

Observability & telemetry (events and dashboards):
- Decision events: fidelity_decision.created (fields: tenant_id, route_id, decision_id, variant_id, expected_cost, expected_latency)
- Simulator events: sim.run.started, sim.run.completed, sim.estimate.delta (estimate vs observed)
- Dashboards: per-tenant fidelity mix, cost-savings estimate, simulator accuracy over time. Alerts: simulator_accuracy_drop (>=15% deviation for 3 successive sims), negotiation_latency_slo_breach (>150ms p99).

Compatibility and fallback behavior:
- If RFN is unavailable, runtime must apply the route default fidelity_decision with a warning metric (runtime.fidelity.fallback_applied).
- RFN decisions are tagged with compatibility flags (requires-kv-cache, supports-quant128, needs-atten-optim) to ensure candidate model variants are compatible with runtime path.

Sample CLI & API examples:
- Negotiation call (curl):
```
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/fidelity/negotiate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ROUTE_TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"route_id":"checkout-chat","tenant_id":"tenant-42","request_profile":{"avg_input_tokens":120,"max_output_tokens":350},"latency_target_ms":150}'
```
- Simulation run example (CLI):
```
rfnsim run --tenant tenant-42 --scenario conversational-longtail --duration 24h --out report.json
```

Operational runbooks (high level):
1) Investigate negotiation latency spike:
   - Check negotiator cluster CPU/GPU (if applicable) and queue depth.
   - Verify policy store (consul/kvs) latency for policy fetch.
   - If p99 >250ms, toggle emergency static default route and scale negotiator ASG + alert SRE.
2) Simulator accuracy drop:
   - Run replay with raw production traces, compare token-count distribution.
   - Validate model variant performance drift flagged by Applied ML.

Ownership, milestones and open decisions:
- Product owner: Aisha Patel. Engineering leads: Marcus Chen (Runtime), Sofia Martinez (Applied ML).
- Milestones:
  - Prototype complete: 2026-09-15 (done)
  - Internal alpha: 2026-10-10
  - Partner beta start: 2026-11-01
  - GA: 2027-01-15
- Open decisions:
  - Final pricing multiplier thresholds for the fidelity credit program (Finance + Go-to-market).
  - Whether simulator will run deterministic sketches or full-token generation sampling by default.

Related pages:
- /product-docs/product-overview/onboarding-and-cost-advisor-playbook-2026-07-28
- /product-docs/design-specs/quantization-cache-fidelity-coordination-spec-2026-11-15
- /eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/kv-cache-and-batching-overview

Appendix: small YAML policy example:
```
policy:
  route: checkout-chat
  constraints:
    latency_ms: 150
    max_cost_usd_per_1k: 0.12
    min_quality: {embedding_sim: 0.86}
  fallbacks:
    - variant: rwd-13b-quant
      multiplier: 0.65
    - variant: rwd-7b-quant-ev
      multiplier: 0.4
```

End of document. For implementation tasks see the linked design tickets and runtime runbook.

payload.page_title: PRD: Guided Onboarding + “First Production Launch” Checklist (Hosted API MVP)

sections.body:
Redwood Inference is shipping a guided onboarding experience centered on an in-product checklist (“First Production Launch”) in the Redwood Console. The checklist makes the critical steps from signup → first successful API call → first production traffic explicit, trackable, and easier to complete.

This PRD covers the Hosted API MVP, including:
- Checklist content and step definitions
- Console entry points and UX expectations (high-level; detailed UX in the linked spec)
- Progress tracking, event instrumentation, and KPI reporting requirements
- Rollout plan, success metrics, and key risks/tradeoffs
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
We consistently see onboarding friction that delays Time To First Success (TTFS) and Time To First Production traffic (TTFP) and generates avoidable Support tickets. Common issues include:
- Auth setup mistakes (401/403 due to wrong key, env var, project scope)
- Surprise rate limits/quota behavior (429s, lack of backoff/retry)
- Streaming disconnect confusion (client handling, timeouts, network intermediaries)
- Confusion from usage dashboard lag (“I made calls but usage is 0”)
- Unclear “production readiness” steps (pin a model, set budgets/alerts, add basic observability)

Today, these steps are distributed across docs, quickstarts, and tribal knowledge. Customers often skip them until something breaks.
sections.heading: Problem statement

sections.body:
1) Reduce TTFS and TTFP for Hosted API self-serve customers.
2) Increase activation and early retention by improving clarity and confidence.
3) Reduce top onboarding-related Support tickets by proactively addressing known failure modes.
sections.heading: Primary goals (MVP)

sections.body:
- Create a reusable checklist framework that can later support Dedicated and Private onboarding with minimal re-architecture.
- Establish a stable, privacy-reviewed event schema and progress-tracking pattern usable by other in-product enablement features.
sections.heading: Secondary goals

sections.body:
- Full in-product guided tours or walkthrough overlays.
- Automated remediation suggestions (e.g., “we detected 401, click to fix”).
- Dedicated and Private deployment onboarding wizards (content may be future-proofed, but not shipped as productized flows in MVP).
sections.heading: Non-goals (MVP)

sections.body:
- Role: Software engineer / ML engineer at startup or SMB
- Motivation: “I need to ship an LLM feature quickly and safely.”
- Key needs: Fast first call, reliable streaming, sensible retries/timeouts, predictable costs.
- Typical failure modes: env var/key confusion, streaming disconnect handling, 429/backoff.
sections.heading: Persona A: Self-serve engineer (PLG)

sections.body:
- Role: Tech lead or platform engineer owning reliability and cost
- Motivation: “I want to go live without surprises (cost spikes, downtime, regressions).”
- Key needs: Model pinning, fallback policy, quotas/budgets, observability hooks.
sections.heading: Persona B: Team lead / platform engineer (production readiness)

sections.body:
- Role: Enterprise engineering or security reviewer
- Motivation: “I need evidence of controls and a repeatable go-live process.”
- Key needs (future): auditability, RBAC, data residency controls, documented checklist state.
- Note: MVP must not block enterprise needs, but will prioritize self-serve Hosted API flow.
sections.heading: Persona C: Enterprise evaluator (later expansion)

sections.body:
1) Console checklist feature
- Entry points in Console (e.g., home/dashboard + project overview).
- Step list with status states: Not started / In progress / Completed / Needs attention.
- Step details panel/drawer with:
  - acceptance criteria
  - deep links to the exact Console page or docs section
  - recommended defaults (timeouts/retries)
  - troubleshooting links for common errors
- State persistence per project/tenant.
- Admin override tools for Support (mark complete/reset) with audit log.

2) Progress tracking service
- Store checklist state and compute completion safely under out-of-order events.
- Expose read APIs for Console.
- Ingest onboarding events (write-only internal API) and apply to step transitions.
- Idempotency requirements for all event ingestion.

3) Event instrumentation + telemetry
- Standardized onboarding event schema v1.
- Server-side event emission at key lifecycle points (gateway/control plane) to avoid reliance on client instrumentation.
- KPI dashboards:
  - TTFS / TTFP distributions
  - funnel by step completion
  - cohort comparisons and rollout monitoring
  - data freshness and event quality checks

4) Docs + quickstart alignment
- A canonical checklist doc page matching the in-product steps.
- Quickstart updates to reflect “production-safe defaults” (timeouts/retries) and match step order.
sections.heading: In-scope (MVP)

sections.body:
- Personalized step ordering by industry or use case.
- In-checklist interactive testing (“run a test call from the Console”).
- Automatic configuration changes (e.g., “enable budgets” directly from checklist step).
sections.heading: Out-of-scope (MVP)

sections.body:
The following is the MVP step set for Hosted API. Step names must remain stable for eventing and analytics; copy can evolve.

1) Create API key
- Why: Enable authenticated requests.
- Completion signal: API key created event.
- Primary deep link: Console → API Keys.

2) Set up environment (env var + base URL)
- Why: Avoid 401/403 and wrong endpoint issues.
- Completion signal (MVP): user confirms step OR first successful auth-validated request event (preferred when feasible).
- Notes: This step should include troubleshooting for common env var/key mistakes.

3) Make your first successful request (non-streaming)
- Why: Establish basic integration.
- Completion signal: first 2xx response from text/chat endpoint for the project.
- Acceptance criteria: response contains model ID and at least 1 output token.

4) Enable streaming (recommended)
- Why: Improve perceived latency and UX.
- Completion signal: first streaming response established (server emits event when stream starts and first token flush occurs).
- Notes: Include guidance for streaming disconnect handling.

5) Configure production-safe client behavior (timeouts + retries/backoff)
- Why: Reduce flaky behavior and support load.
- Completion signal (MVP): user acknowledgement OR SDK-specific “recommended preset” usage signal when available.
- Requirements: Provide language-specific docs (Python/TS/Go) that define recommended defaults.

6) Review usage + understand dashboard lag
- Why: Reduce confusion and billing/usage mismatch tickets.
- Completion signal: first visit to usage dashboard OR user acknowledgement.
- Notes: Explicitly state expected data delay window and where to see real-time request logs (if available).

7) Set quotas/budgets (cost guardrails)
- Why: Avoid cost surprise on go-live.
- Completion signal: quota/budget created OR user acknowledgement for accounts without permissions.
- Acceptance criteria: at least one cost control configured (budget alert or quota cap).

8) Pin a model version (stability)
- Why: Prevent unexpected behavior changes.
- Completion signal: model pinned in project config OR a pinned model ID used consistently in requests for a window (future enhancement).

9) Configure fallback policy (resilience)
- Why: Improve availability and graceful degradation.
- Completion signal (MVP): fallback policy created in Console.
- Notes: If fallback is not available for all tiers, show “Not available on your plan” with guidance.

10) Add basic observability hooks (recommended)
- Why: Faster debugging; reduce support time-to-resolution.
- Completion signal (MVP): user acknowledgement and/or first request containing trace header / request-id propagation (where supported).
- Notes: Link to logging/tracing guidance; keep minimal for MVP.
sections.heading: Checklist: MVP step definitions

sections.body:
- The checklist must be available per project (not only per user) so progress can be shared across a team.
- Checklist state must be durable and resilient to event ordering issues.
- Steps must support:
  - event-driven completion
  - manual completion/acknowledgement (when instrumentation is not reliable or not available)
  - admin override by Support/CS with audit trail
- Step completion must be monotonic by default (no “regressions” from Completed → In progress due to late events).
sections.heading: Functional requirements

sections.body:
- Checklist entry point must be discoverable on first login.
- Each step must provide:
  - clear action
  - single best deep link
  - short explanation of “why it matters”
  - troubleshooting link(s) for known failures
- Accessibility: keyboard navigable, readable at 200% zoom, compliant with internal accessibility standards.
sections.heading: UX requirements (high-level)

sections.body:
- All events must comply with the onboarding event schema v1.
- Events must be PII-free (no prompt text, no user-entered content).
- Events must include stable identifiers for:
  - tenant/org
  - project
  - environment (prod/sandbox if known)
  - SDK / integration surface (when known)
  - region
- Data quality checks:
  - event volume anomalies
  - missing required fields
  - ingestion lag > defined threshold
sections.heading: Telemetry requirements

sections.body:
- Follow the onboarding telemetry data review for retention and regional storage constraints.
- Ensure admin override access is permissioned and auditable.
sections.heading: Security & compliance

sections.body:
1) TTFS (Time to First Success)
- Definition (MVP): time from “tenant created” to first successful (2xx) inference response for the project.
- Exclusions: internal Redwood tenants, automated tests (tagged), retries that never produce a 2xx.
- Segmentation: by cohort (feature flag), SDK language, region, acquisition channel.

2) TTFP (Time to First Production traffic)
- Definition (MVP): time from “tenant created” to first day where the tenant achieves a minimum production threshold (to be finalized in metrics ticket), intended as a proxy for real go-live.
- Proposed proxy (for validation): first occurrence of either:
  - >= N successful requests in a rolling 24h window AND
  - >= M unique end-user sessions (if available) OR sustained traffic over >= X hours
- Note: The exact thresholds require validation against billing/usage data.
sections.heading: North Star metrics

sections.body:
- Step completion rates and drop-off between steps.
- Median time between steps (e.g., API key → first 2xx; first 2xx → streaming).
- % of tenants reaching “production readiness minimum set” (steps 1, 3, 5, 7, 8).
sections.heading: Funnel metrics

sections.body:
- Volume of onboarding-tagged tickets per 100 new tenants.
- Specific ticket reductions targeted:
  - 401/403 “invalid key/env var”
  - 429 “rate limit surprise”
  - “streaming disconnect” confusion
  - “usage dashboard not updating”
sections.heading: Support metrics

sections.body:
- No statistically significant increase in:
  - overall API error rate attributable to new event emission
  - gateway latency due to instrumentation
  - telemetry ingestion lag beyond thresholds
sections.heading: Guardrail metrics

sections.body:
Phase 0: Discovery + baselines (1–2 weeks)
- Finalize event schema and TTFS/TTFP definitions.
- Baseline current TTFS/TTFP and support ticket rates.
- Finalize checklist step names and acceptance criteria.

Phase 1: MVP build + internal dogfood (3–4 weeks)
- Feature-flagged checklist in Console.
- Progress service + event emission in gateway/control plane.
- Initial dashboards and alerts.
- Dogfood cohorts: Redwood internal projects + selected friendly external tenants (opt-in).

Phase 2: Progressive cohort rollout (2–3 weeks)
- Gradually enable for:
  - new self-serve Hosted API signups in 1–2 regions
  - then all new signups
  - then existing tenants (optional, after backfill)
- Monitor KPIs and support ticket rates.
- Iterate on step copy and deep links (no breaking step name changes).
sections.heading: Phases

sections.body:
- Checklist exposure controlled by a server-side feature flag.
- Kill-switch criteria:
  - elevated error rates correlated with event emission
  - data pipeline lag causing misleading progress display
  - severe UI regressions impacting Console performance
sections.heading: Feature flag + kill switch

sections.body:
- Console UI implementation (Console team: Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin)
- Progress tracking service (Platform team; event ordering/idempotency)
- Gateway/control plane event emission (Platform/Telemetry)
- KPI dashboards and alerting (Telemetry/Data)
- Docs and SDK guidance updates (DevEx + SDK team)
sections.heading: Dependencies

sections.body:
- Risk: Over-optimizing for self-serve could miss enterprise needs (auditability, approvals).
- Mitigation: Ensure checklist is project-scoped, shareable, and has an audit log for overrides; keep step definitions stable.
sections.heading: Tradeoff: Self-serve speed vs enterprise rigor

sections.body:
- Risk: MVP may encode assumptions that do not apply to Dedicated/Private.
- Mitigation: Keep checklist framework generic; isolate content per deployment type; avoid hardcoding Hosted-only copy into step logic.
sections.heading: Tradeoff: Hosted-only MVP vs unified (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)

sections.body:
- Risk: Out-of-order events could cause incorrect step state (including regressions).
- Mitigation: Monotonic transitions, idempotency keys, event time vs ingestion time handling, and regression tests.
sections.heading: Risk: Event ordering and idempotency issues

sections.body:
- Risk: SDK adoption varies; client telemetry can be missing.
- Mitigation: Prefer server-side emission; use client hints only when necessary.
sections.heading: Risk: Over-reliance on client-side signals

sections.body:
- Risk: Accidentally logging prompt/user content.
- Mitigation: Schema review, automated payload linting, and security sign-off; strict allowlist of fields.
sections.heading: Risk: Privacy and PII leakage in events

sections.body:
- Risk: Manual acknowledgements can inflate completion without improved outcomes.
- Mitigation: Prefer event-driven completion where possible; use acknowledgements only for steps not reliably inferable; compare cohorts for actual TTFS/TTFP impact.
sections.heading: Risk: “Checklist theater” (users check boxes without real readiness)

sections.body:
1) Final TTFP proxy thresholds (N/M/X) and validation plan against billing/usage data.
2) Which steps must be strictly event-driven vs can be acknowledged in MVP?
3) Exact definition of “first successful request” across endpoints (chat vs completions vs embeddings) for TTFS.
4) How to handle multi-project tenants: is TTFS per first project, or per default project?
5) How to message “not available on your plan” steps (fallback policy, advanced observability) without harming activation.
sections.heading: Open questions

sections.body:
- A new Hosted API tenant can see the checklist in Console (for enabled cohorts) and complete steps with clear links.
- The progress service accurately reflects completion for at least:
  - API key creation
  - first 2xx request
  - first streaming response
- No step regressions observed under out-of-order events (validated by test suite + dogfood).
- TTFS and funnel dashboards populate with cohort filtering, with data freshness alerts.
- Support can view checklist state and perform admin override actions with audit log.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (MVP)

sections.body:
- Program sponsor: Alex Martinez (VP DevEx)
- Product: Nikhil Sharma (Hosted API), Marissa Cole (Console)
- Console engineering: Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin
- Telemetry: Logan Wright (platform), Mei Lin (data), Nadia Rahman (pipeline)
- Design: Tessa Morgan (lead), Kenji Nakamura (implementation)
- Support enablement: Dev Patel
- Security review: Marcus Lin
sections.heading: Appendix: Owners (DRIs)

payload.page_title: Hosted Inference Connectors 1.0 — telemetry and fallback release notes

sections.body:
Overview

This document summarizes the Hosted Inference Connectors 1.0 release (May 2028). Connectors 1.0 adds a lightweight integration layer for third-party proxies and partner gateways, standardized telemetry fields for consumption attribution, and deterministic fallback behavior when model or region variants are unavailable. The release is targeted at customers using the Hosted API with multi-region routing and partners building managed gateways.

Highlights

- Connector framework: a small, versioned HTTP handshake and configuration contract (v1) for integrating external proxies and managed gateways with Redwood’s request router. Connectors surface capability hints (prefix caching, KV-cache sharing, supported model variants) and receive route assignment metadata.
- Telemetry standardization: new top-level fields for consumption provenance, per-request fidelity token, and connector_id for end-to-end crediting and debugging.
- Fallback determinism: routable fallback policies now support deterministic, audit-logged fallback decisions with optional customer-visible reason codes.
- Backwards compatibility: existing clients continue to work with no change; connectors with older handshake versions will be automatically classified and routed to compatibility fallbacks.

Why this matters

- Customers routing through third-party gateways need consistent cost attribution and observability. The new telemetry fields make it possible to reconcile per-customer token usage across partner boundaries.
- Deterministic fallback behavior reduces flakiness for production integrations and simplifies incident triage: operators can reason about why a request was directed to a cheaper variant or to a different region.
- The connector framework creates a stable integration surface for partners without requiring them to run the full Redwood control plane.

Upgrade and compatibility notes

1) No change required for standard Hosted API users. Connectors are an opt-in integration surface for partners and customers using gateway proxies.
2) Connector operators must implement the v1 handshake and add a connector_id token to requests.
3) The telemetry fields are additive; older clients will continue to receive charged-attribution as before but lack connector-specific provenance.

Connector handshake (summary)

- Endpoint: POST /connector-handshake
- Payload (JSON):

```json
{
  "connector_name": "string",
  "connector_version": "string",
  "supported_models": ["string"],
  "capabilities": {"prefix_cache": true, "kv_cache_sharing": false},
  "contact": "ops@example.com"
}
```

- Response: 200 OK with assigned connector_id and accepted routing policies.

New telemetry fields (required when connector_id is present)

| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---:|---|
| connector_id | string | Redwood-assigned ID for the connector integration | conn-57b2 |
| provenance_id | string | Deterministic trace for consumption attribution across hops | prov-20280512-01 |
| fidelity_token | string | Short token representing negotiated fidelity/variant at ingestion time | fid-lowlatency-v2 |
| connector_hop | string | Optional short metadata describing gateway behavior (e.g., "prefetch-enabled") | prefetch-enabled |

Rollout plan

- Opt-in pilot (May 12–June 9): enable connectors for 6 internal partners and 3 beta customers. Collect telemetry, validate cost attribution, and exercise fallback audit logs.
- Gradual enablement (June 10–July 7): expose connector sign-up in Console with an onboarding checklist and monitoring dashboards.
- General availability (July 14): full Console support, SDK docs, and public changelog entry.

Operator runbook: validating connector telemetry

1. Query raw request logs by connector_id:

```
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwood logs query --connector conn-57b2 --from 2028-05-12 --to 2028-05-19
```

2. Reconcile provenance_id across hops: verify provenance_id appears in both gateway and Redwood logs. Missing provenance_id indicates an integration bug that will cause attribution gaps.

3. Check fallback audit stream for unexpected fallthroughs: alert if >0.3% of requests for a connector are falling back to lower-fidelity variants during peak.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| config | recommended | impact | notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| allowed_fallbacks | ["same-model-quantized","regional-variant","lower-fidelity"] | Medium | Order matters: first matching policy is used. |
| max-fallback-depth | 2 | Low | Limits chained fallbacks to prevent oscillation. |
| provenance-ttl-days | 30 | High | How long to retain provenance keys for reconciliation. |
| telemetry-sampling-rate | 1.0 | High | Start with 100% for pilot, reduce after reconciliation assured. |

SLO and telemetry targets

- Connector handshake latency: P99 < 50ms (during normal control-plane load).
- Fallback decision logging latency: < 200ms end-to-end from decision to audit log ingestion.
- Attribution reconciliation: > 99.5% of connector requests must have matching provenance_id in Redwood logs during the pilot.

Known issues and mitigations

- Missing provenance_id: some gateways strip custom headers. Mitigation: provide a lightweight JavaScript shim and Nginx snippet to preserve headers; include in onboarding materials.
- Cost double-counting across partners: rare race condition during rolling connector_id assignment. Mitigation: reconcile counts daily and apply corrective credits; fix in routing service (target patch v1.0.2).
- Older SDK incompatibility: very old SDKs may not attach connector metadata. Customers using SDKs earlier than 2026-11 should upgrade or use the transparent proxy shim.

Developer and partner documentation links

payload.page_title: Hosted Inference v3: Streaming, Batch Fusion, and Fidelity Telemetry — Release Notes

sections.body:
Summary
-------
Hosted Inference v3 (HIF-v3) is a major platform release focused on three customer-facing improvements: stable streaming semantics across modes, Batch Fusion (an adaptive microbatching optimization), and per-request fidelity telemetry for production quality signals. This release targets hosted API customers and is the foundation for Dedicated/Private parity in Q1 2029.

Highlights
----------
- Stable streaming API with exactly-once token ordering guarantees for streamed fragments and improved backpressure handling.
- Batch Fusion: runtime-level microbatcher that merges low-latency single-shot requests into short-lived fused batches to improve GPU utilization without increasing tail latency for latency-sensitive routes.
- Fidelity Telemetry: per-request quality metadata (model_variant, quantization_profile, prompt_hash, eval_flag) surfaced through console and streaming headers for downstream quality monitoring and automated rollback triggers.
- Backwards-compatible client surface: existing REST and SDK calls continue to work; new optional flags enable v3 behaviors.
- Operational improvements: new dashboards (hosted.hif.v3.*) and alerting templates for fidelity regressions.

Compatibility and API diff
------------------------
- Existing endpoints remain available. Two optional query parameters and one response header are added:
  - request_param: streaming_mode=v3 (string; optional) — toggles new streaming engine.
  - request_param: batch_fusion=auto|on|off (string; default=auto) — controls Batch Fusion heuristic.
  - response_header: X-Redwood-Fidelity-Telemetry (JSON blob) — present when fidelity telemetry is enabled for the tenant.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?streaming_mode=v3 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d '{"model":"rw-v3-1b","input":"Summarize the following...","batch_fusion":"auto"}'
sections.heading: Example request (curl)

sections.body:
X-Redwood-Fidelity-Telemetry: {"model_variant":"rw-v3-1b.q4_0","quant_profile":"econ-1","prompt_hash":"a3f2...","eval_flag":"baseline:2028-10-12"}

Behavioral changes and guarantees
--------------------------------
1. Streaming ordering: HIF-v3 guarantees that tokens emitted by the server for a single request maintain strict ordering and are idempotent across reconnects. If a client reconnects mid-stream using the resume_token returned in the initial stream preamble, the runtime will re-stream only the missing suffix.
2. Backpressure: the client SDKs expose a small-buffer consumer that avoids head-of-line blocking for long-running streams. Node/Python SDKs updated in SDK 4.x.
3. Batch Fusion heuristics: default 'auto' mode fuses compatible small requests within a 4–12 ms window depending on workload. Auto-mode aims to improve tokens/s on V100/A100-class instances by ~18–40% on conversational workloads while preserving 99th percentile latency targets for routes configured with latency_slo < 200ms.

SLOs and Performance (hosted tier guidance)
-------------------------------------------
- Median token latency: unchanged; measured per-customer baseline.
- 95th percentile latency impact (expected): +0–15ms for batch-fusion benefitting routes; customers with strict 95th latency SLOs should set batch_fusion=off on those routes.
- Throughput gain: 18–40% tokens/sec for small-request conversational mixes (see performance appendix).
- Fidelity telemetry delivery SLA: metadata header included for >99.9% of streaming/generate responses in hosted control planes.

Upgrade and migration notes
--------------------------
- No forced client upgrade: default server behavior remains legacy-compatible. Tenants should opt-in to streaming_mode=v3 to enable new behavior.
- Recommended steps for production rollout:
  1. Opt-in a single low-traffic route (canary) with streaming_mode=v3 and batch_fusion=auto. Monitor latency and fidelity dashboards for 48–72h.
  2. If 95th latency increases beyond acceptable thresholds, switch batch_fusion=off for that route and open a support ticket.
  3. Enable fidelity telemetry to capture prompt_hash and quant_profile across a representative prompt set. Tie telemetry to existing quality monitors (Eval Runner / QA webhooks).
  4. Gradually expand to more routes and/or set batch_fusion=on where throughput matters more than tail latency (e.g., offline batch generation).

Configuration matrix (recommended defaults)
-----------------------------------------
| Route type | streaming_mode | batch_fusion | recommended | notes |
|------------|----------------|--------------|-------------|-------|
| Low-latency interactive | v3 | off | keep tail latency | Avoid fusion for sub-100ms 95th SLOs |
| Conversational chat | v3 | auto | default | Auto fusion improves throughput while preserving latency for most workloads |
| Bulk generation | legacy | on | maximize throughput | Use batch_fusion=on with larger window for bulk jobs |

Note: the table above is provided as ASCII for Confluence rendering; console shows same options in per-route settings UI.

Observability and telemetry
--------------------------
- New metrics emitted (prefix hosted.hif.v3):
  - hosted.hif.v3.batch_fusion.mean_batch_size
  - hosted.hif.v3.batch_fusion.window_ms
  - hosted.hif.v3.streaming.resume_rate
  - hosted.hif.v3.fidelity.mismatches (counts of eval regression flags)
- Console: per-route Fidelity Panel shows prompt_hash heatmaps, quality regression alerts, and drift timelines.
- Alerting templates: fidelity-regression-high (threshold: fidelity.mismatches > 0.5% over 24h) and batch-fusion-latency-regression (95th latency increase > 20% vs baseline).

Rollout plan and risk mitigation
--------------------------------
- Phased rollout over 6 weeks:
  - Week 0: internal dogfood and integration tests with SDK teams.
  - Weeks 1–2: opt-in canary tenants (low traffic).
  - Weeks 3–4: broaden to self-serve tenants with console toggle.
  - Weeks 5–6: auto-promote to default for conversational routes (metrics permitting).
- Rollback strategy: server-side toggle for streaming_mode and batch_fusion per-tenant and per-route. Escape hatch: global disable for HIF-v3 if systemic issue detected.

Known issues and workarounds
---------------------------
- Intermittent duplicate stream fragments during early canary when network jitter + resume_token mismatch occur. Workaround: client should dedupe by sequence number (SDKs handle this automatically in 4.2.1+).
- Some older SDK versions do not surface the X-Redwood-Fidelity-Telemetry header. Action: upgrade to SDK 4.2.1 or parse telemetry from the console API.

Developer and partner notes
---------------------------
- SDK changes: Node and Python SDKs include a new StreamClient.resume(stream_id, resume_token) helper and a Telemetry.parseHeader(header_str) utility. See SDK changelog for usage examples.
- Partner integrations: marketplace partners who rely on token-level metering should verify billing hooks when fidelity headers are enabled. Contact partner-ops@redwood.ai for an integration checklist.

Appendix A — Performance summary (selected benchmarks)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Conversational mix (50–100 token responses, median request size 32 tokens): A100-hosted pool saw +28% tokens/sec with batch_fusion=auto; 95th latency delta +9ms.
- Single-shot summarization (median 512 tokens): negligible fusion benefit; prefer legacy path.

Appendix B — API examples and JSON schemas
------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Example response header (abbreviated)
Request body example

sections.body:
X-Redwood-Fidelity-Telemetry: {"model_variant":"rw-v3-1b.q4_0","quant_profile":"econ-1","prompt_hash":"a3f2...","eval_flag":"baseline:2028-10-12"}

FAQ
---
Q: Will enabling fidelity telemetry increase request cost?
A: No. Fidelity metadata is a lightweight header and is free at the control-plane level. Some customers may choose to store telemetry in long-term logs (costs depend on retention).

Q: Does Batch Fusion change model outputs?
A: No, Batch Fusion is a scheduling optimization and preserves per-request KV cache isolation and decoding determinism. We include reproducibility checks in the rollout.

Support and contacts
--------------------
- Escalations: support@redwood.ai (include "HIF-v3" in subject).
- Engineering owner: Marisol Vega (product lead), Runtime owner: Ahmed Salim, SDK lead: Priya Nambiar.
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/hif-v3-deployments.json

Change log (selected)
---------------------
- 2028-11-08: Published v1 of release notes; canary rollout scheduled the same day.

End of document

payload.page_title: Developer Sandbox Cost Estimator — Release Notes 1.0

sections.body:
Summary
=======

Release: Developer Sandbox Cost Estimator v1.0
Date: 2026-10-30 (GA) — patch 2026-11-05
Owners: Product (Maya Chen), Eng: dev-tools (Evan Kline), Integrations (Luis Ortega)
Status: GA / gradual rollout to all orgs over two weeks

Intro
-----
This release ships the Developer Sandbox Cost Estimator (DSCE) v1.0: an offline and lightweight online estimator for modeling per-route and per-workload cost and latency at development time. DSCE is designed for engineers to iterate on prompt design, model variant choices, and routing policies without incurring production tokens or warm-capacity consumption.

Key objectives addressed
- Allow developers to get realistic cost+latency estimates for common workloads inside the Developer Sandbox and CLI.
- Provide a stable SDK and an online /v1/cost-estimate API for programmatic integration with onboarding flows and CI checks.
- Reduce onboarding churn and billing surprises during hosted->dedicated migration by surfacing fidelity and quantization trade-offs early.

What’s included in 1.0
- CLI: redwood dsce init / simulate / compare — local-mode and remote-mode (uses low-cost preview instances).
- SDK: Python and TypeScript packages with simulation harness and built-in workload templates (chat, summarization, embedding-heavy).
- Online API: POST /v1/cost-estimate \- JSON input schema and response with per-token breakdowns, KV-cache hit simulation, batching impact, and confidence bands.
- Console UX: "Cost Preview" panel in Developer Playground for sandbox accounts (UI opt-in via the top-right sandbox toggle).
- Telemetry: new events (dsce.simulate.start, dsce.simulate.complete, dsce.api.estimate) and attribution fields to connect estimates to onboarding experiments.
- Guardrails: default SLO for estimator uptime 99.5% (sandbox tier), latency budget 200ms p95 for the online API.

Compatibility & Supported Scenarios
- Works for hosted and dedicated-variant simulations. Private (VPC) customers can run the CLI local-mode using on-prem weights and an agent that simulates capacity knobs (see section "Private deployment notes").
- Models: supports all catalog models plus quantized variants; estimation accuracy is highest for models with verified performance profiles in the catalog.

API reference (summary)
- Endpoint: POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/cost-estimate\- Auth: Bearer token (same scope as developer sandbox: scope dsce:estimate)\- Request (JSON):
  {
    "model": "string (model-id)",
    "input_shape": "{messages:[{role:...}], tokens_avg:int}",
    "workload_profile": "chat|completion|embeddings|reranking",
    "batching": "none|auto|manual",
    "kv_cache_prefix_tokens": "int",
    "quantization": "none|int8|int4",
    "sim_options": "{warmup_steps:int, sample_count:int}"
  }
- Response (JSON summary):
  {
    "estimated_total_tokens": "int",
    "token_cost_usd": "float",
    "inference_cost_usd": "float",
    "estimated_latency_ms_p95": "int",
    "kv_cache_hit_pct": "float",
    "confidence_interval_pct": "float"
  }

Example CLI usage
1) Quick local estimate:
   $ redwood dsce simulate --model redwood-v1 --profile chat --input examples/checkout_flow.json

2) Compare variants:
   $ redwood dsce compare --baseline redwood-v1 --variant redwood-v1-quant --workload chat --output diffs.csv

Accuracy & SLOs
- Target estimator accuracy: within ±10% of real production unit economics for typical dev workloads (chat/completion with median length <512 tokens) on models with catalog-verified profiles.
- Online API latency SLO: p95 < 200ms for sandbox fleet; availability SLO: 99.5%.
- Rate limits: sandbox default 100 rps per org for /v1/cost-estimate; CLI local-mode only constrained by host.

Rollout plan
1) Canary (2026-10-30): 10% of sandbox orgs — telemetry + internal QA.
2) Gradual 50% (2026-11-02): enable CLI remote-mode for beta program orgs and surface UX in Playground for invited users.
3) GA (2026-11-05): enable for all sandbox orgs; default opt-in for new signups.

Migration & adoption guidance
- Developer adoption checklist (recommended):
  1. Add dsce:estimate scope to CI job that runs cost checks on PRs.
  2. Use the compare CLI in a pre-merge job to detect >15% cost regressions.
  3. Link estimation results to performance tests: store dsce outputs as artifact for traceability.

- Customer migration note: Existing consumption-advisor connectors remain the source of truth for billed amounts. DSCE outputs are advisory; customers should continue to validate against warm-capacity and real-run invoices prior to contractual negotiation.

Private deployment notes
- Customers on Private: ship CLI local-mode with an optional on-prem simulator agent. Configure simulator via YAML at /etc/redwood/dsce/simulator.yaml (example below). The agent uses local kernel profiles and does not send data to Redwood public services by default.

Example simulator.yaml (ASCII table representation):
+----------------------+---------------------------+-----------------+
| field                | description               | example value   |
+----------------------+---------------------------+-----------------+
| catalog_profiles_dir  | local path to model proft | /opt/redwood/profiles |
| warmup_steps         | number of internal warmup | 25              |
| sample_count         | Monte Carlo runs          | 50              |
| allow_telemetry      | send non-PII telemetry    | false           |
+----------------------+---------------------------+-----------------+

Known issues & limitations
- Estimator currently underestimates costs for multi-model pipelined workflows by up to 18% when KV cache reuse is large — we plan to address in 1.1 with a cross-model KV coordination model.
- Embedding-heavy batch scenarios with >10k tokens per batch may return wider confidence intervals; increase sample_count in sim_options to tighten bands.

Security & data handling
- Sandbox mode is opt-in and estimator runtime strips PII from sample inputs by default.
- Telemetry events exclude raw prompts; they contain workload fingerprints (hashes) and aggregated metrics. Customers running local-mode can opt out of telemetry in simulator.yaml.

Telemetry & monitoring
- New telemetry events and tags:
  - dsce.simulate.start / dsce.simulate.complete (tags: model_id, workload_profile, org_id)
  - dsce.api.estimate (tags: model_family, quantization, batching_mode)
- Dashboards: Product -> Developer Tools -> DSCE Overview (new) shows estimator accuracy vs production, adoption by org, and CI failure rates for cost regression checks.

Operational runbook (high-level)
1. On alert (estimator_p95_latency > 250ms sustained for 10m): escalate to dev-tools oncall, route to canary rollback group.\2. For accuracy regressions (>20% delta vs production): create incident with severity P2 and notify product.

Component owners & contacts
- Product: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai)
- Eng — Dev Tools: Evan Kline (ekline@redwood.ai)
- Integrations & SDKs: Luis Ortega (lortega@redwood.ai)
- Privacy/Security reviewer: Priya Raman (praman@redwood.ai)

Post-release roadmap (1.1 & 1.2 highlights)
- 1.1 (Q1 2027): multi-model pipeline estimation, tighter KV reuse model, improved embedding batch accuracy.
- 1.2 (Q2 2027): SLO-driven estimator suggestions in Console, merchant-grade SLA for dedicated customers, and a plugins API for custom cost factors.

Links & references
- API spec: /docs/api/cost-estimate
- SDK docs: /docs/sdk/dsce
- Design doc: /confluence/product-docs/design-specs/estimator-simulation-architecture-2026-06-15
- Acceptance tests and sample workloads: git://redwood/internal/dsce/samples

Acknowledgements
Thanks to Eng-dev-tools, Observability, and Privacy teams for shipping DSCE. Please file issues to "redwood/dsce" in the internal issue tracker for bugs and feature requests.

Changelog (high-level)
- 2026-10-30: GA announcement, canary rollout begins.
- 2026-11-02: Gradual rollout to 50% of sandbox orgs, CLI remote-mode enabled for beta partners.
- 2026-11-05: Full GA; Console panel enabled by default for sandboxes.
