payload.page_title: Request Priority & Hinting Protocol Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines a lightweight, backwards-compatible Request Priority & Hinting Protocol (RPHP) for Redwood internal services and external API-facing endpoints. The goal is to give clients safe, machine-readable signals to help the system make scheduling, queuing, and graceful-degradation decisions while preserving observable billing and correctness guarantees.

Motivation

- Services often need to make tradeoffs between latency and cost when capacity is constrained.
- Explicit priority signals from callers improve fairness and reduce tail-latency by letting the runtime schedule work more efficiently.
- Hints reduce inefficient client-side retries and tight coupling between client logic and server-side load-shedding policies.

Goals

1. Minimal impact on existing request schemas (single optional header + optional JSON envelope).
2. Deterministic server behavior based on hint values.
3. Measurable effects (metrics) to evaluate feature adoption and performance impact.
4. Granular client guidance for request composition and retry/backoff.

Protocol summary

- Transport: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC (metadata headers).
- Client hint: X-Redwood-Priority (string) — recommended values: realtime, interactive, standard, bulk, background.
- Optional JSON envelope in request body: "priority_hint" and "max_latency_ms" — used when header-level expressivity is insufficient (e.g., multi-task batch requests).
- Server response headers: X-Redwood-Accepted-Priority, X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms, X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy.

Priority semantics

- realtime: Strict latency SLOs, small token budgets, no batching unless pre-warmed. Use only for single-turn transactional requests.
- interactive: Low latency but tolerant to minor batching (e.g., 10–50ms). Suitable for UI-driven flows and chat messages.
- standard: Default path for most API calls. Balanced latency/cost.
- bulk: High throughput, tolerant to batching and higher latency. Prefer async job endpoints.
- background: Lowest priority; may be queued or deferred indefinitely. Good for maintenance, garbage, or telemetry upload.

Request field table (recommended canonical fields)

| Field | Location | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| X-Redwood-Priority | HTTP header / gRPC metadata | string | One of the recommended values. Fall back to "standard" if absent. |
| priority_hint | JSON body (optional) | string | Same semantics as header when header cannot be set. |
| max_latency_ms | JSON body (optional) | integer | Client-specified upper bound on acceptable latency in ms. Server converts to SLO class for scheduling. |
| preserve_order | JSON body (optional) | boolean | For batch requests; when true, server avoids reordering across items in the same batch. |

Server behavior (must)

1. Defaulting: If no priority provided, treat as "standard".
2. Admission control: When under load, services should consult a priority-aware admission controller that consults current utilization, queue depth, and configured SLO curves.
3. Queueing & scheduling: Maintain separate internal queues per priority class. Implement elastic windowing to avoid starvation: background/bulk drains at a configurable fraction (default 10%) of capacity every minute.
4. Queue-estimate: When queueing a request, include X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms in response headers with a 95th percentile estimate. If the estimate exceeds client max_latency_ms, evaluate fallback immediately.
5. Fallback policy selection: Respond with X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy when falling back (options: retry-with-backoff, accept-async-token, degrade-response, reject-with-retry-after).
6. Invariants: Priority may influence scheduling and batching, but not authorization or tenant-level billing semantics. Priority is advisory; servers must not change access control based on priority.

Client best practices

- Choose the least-permissive priority that meets user experience. Overusing realtime hurts overall system latency.
- Set max_latency_ms for interactive flows to provide a hard bound to the server.
- For multi-item batch requests set preserve_order only when required; otherwise allow server reordering to increase throughput.
- Respect server-provided fallback headers. If server suggests accept-async-token, use the provided async token to poll status rather than retrying immediately.

Operational metrics and dashboards
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- requests_received_total{priority} (counter)
- requests_accepted_total{priority} (counter)
- requests_rejected_total{priority, reason} (counter) e.g., reason=overload, auth, malformed
- queue_estimate_ms_p95{priority} (gauge/histogram)
- average_processing_latency_ms{priority} (histogram)
- fallback_invocations_total{policy, priority} (counter)

Suggested SLOs (example)

- realtime: 99.9% of requests < 50ms server-side latency (excluding network).
- interactive: 99% < 150ms.
- standard: 95% < 500ms.
- bulk/background: No strict latency SLO; require throughput and completion-time monitoring.

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- queue_estimate_ms_p95{interactive} > 500ms for 5m -> page oncall and run overload playbook.
- fallback_invocations_total{reject-with-retry-after} increases > 5x baseline in 15m -> open incident.

Rollout and migration plan

1. Phase 0 — instrumentation only (2 weeks): Accept header, emit metrics but treat all requests as standard for scheduling.
2. Phase 1 — opt-in scheduling (4 weeks): Default behavior unchanged, opt into priority-aware scheduling for selected internal teams. Collect client-side adoption metrics.
3. Phase 2 — gradual enforcement (6 weeks): Honor priority hints for admission control with non-blocking fallbacks. Start returning X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms to callers.
4. Phase 3 — production enforcement (8 weeks): Full scheduling enforcement, background/bulk reservation, and client guidance via SDK defaults.

Migration notes

- Backwards compatibility: Clients that do not send hints must continue to function.
- SDKs: Provide safe defaults in Redwood SDKs (JS, Python, Go). Default to setting X-Redwood-Priority based on callsite helpers (e.g., client.chat.sendInteractive()).
- Canary testing: Use 10% traffic window per region with canary metrics: p95 latency, fallback rate, and error budget burn.

Compatibility and security considerations

- Do not use priority headers for tenant isolation or billing. Treat as non-authoritative.
- Sanitize and rate-limit header size; accept only allowed tokens.
- Logging: redacted in logs; store only enum value. Avoid capturing client-provided free-form strings for privacy.

Ownership and governance

- Policy owner: Runtime Platform team (eng-platform) — responsible for enforcement, metrics, and SDK guidance.
- Specification owner: API Standards working group.
- Review cadence: Annual or when major service changes occur.

Examples and snippets

Example: interactive chat request (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
  -H 'X-Redwood-Priority: interactive'
  -d '{"messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the last policy meeting."}], "max_latency_ms": 200 }'

Server response headers (example)

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Redwood-Accepted-Priority: interactive
X-Redwood-Queue-Estimate-ms: 18
X-Redwood-Fallback-Policy: none

Appendix: sample admission controller pseudocode

1. function admit(request):
2.   p = request.priority or 'standard'
3.   if load > high && p == 'background':
4.     return reject_with_policy('retry-with-backoff', 503)
5.   estimate = queue_estimator.predict(p)
6.   if request.max_latency_ms and estimate > request.max_latency_ms:
7.     return respond_with_policy('accept-async-token')
8.   enqueue(request, queue_for(p))
9.   return accepted

Related pages and references

- API deprecation & versioning playbook (see related_pages)
- Runtime queueing and scheduler architecture (eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture)
- Oncall runbook: overload handling (oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks)

Document revision history

- 2025-09-16: Created by Aisha Martinez.
- 2025-10-02: Initial review feedback incorporated (Jonah Park).
- 2026-01-12: Added metrics and rollout plan (Lucille Nguyen).
- 2026-02-04: Final editorial pass and published.

payload.page_title: Consumption Transition: Quick Reference Decision Matrix and Migration Checklist

sections.body:
Summary

This page is a compact, operational reference for product managers, solutions engineers, and customer success teams leading a customer from Hosted to Dedicated or Edge consumption. It bundles: a decision matrix for choosing migration modes, a pre-migration checklist, cost and latency simulation knobs, a phased rollout plan, and a minimal set of contractual/SLA negotiation talking points. The goal is to reduce cycle time for migration while protecting customer SLAs and Redwood unit economics.

Who this is for
- Solutions engineering (primary)
- Customer success and account executives
- Product/PMs owning onboarding funnels
- SRE/Platform for operational guardrails

Decision matrix (one-page)

Use the table below to quickly classify customers and recommend a default migration pathway. Apply judgment when customers sit on a boundary — escalate to Solutions Eng Lead.

| Customer characteristic | Primary recommended path | Why / key considerations | Minimum SLO targets to require this path |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Low volume PoC (<= 1M tokens/month), developer-led | Remain Hosted (self-serve) | Fastest time-to-value; use dev credits and sandbox | 95th latency < 800ms, error rate < 0.5% |
| Predictable production traffic (1M–50M tokens/mo), data-sensitive | Dedicated (reserved capacity) | Predictable throughput and isolation; contractual SLAs | P95 latency < 350ms, availability 99.9% |
| Regulated workloads or on-prem compliance needs | Private (VPC / On‑prem) | Customer-managed networking/KMS; audit requirements | SLOs agreed per contract; baseline 99.95% availability |
| Burst-heavy, spiky sessions with tight tail latency needs | Dedicated with warm-burst and preemptible fallback | Combine reserved baseline + burst credits | P99 latency target < 800ms for bursts |
| Edge/low-region-variance needs (<50ms regional RT) | Edge light runtime (local cache) + Hybrid routing | Local prefetching + affinity routing | Regional P95 < 120ms |

Pre-migration checklist (operational, step-by-step)

1) Customer discovery & classification
   - Confirm peak tokens/day and tokens distribution by route. Export last 30 days from Console -> Usage -> Route summary.
   - Confirm data residency and retention policy. Capture contract clause requests.

2) Baseline telemetry and regression test bundle
   - Create a shadow-eval prompt set (10–20 prompts) that covers nominal and edge-case behaviors. Add to Shared Evals -> <customer-name>-pre-migration.json.
   - Run 48-hour synthetic traffic replay via consumption-sandbox runner (CLI):
     redwood sandbox run --customer-id <id> --replay-file replay-48h.json --target throughput 120%

3) Capacity planning & SKU proposal
   - Map observed P95 and CPU/GPU utilization to Dedicated SKU templates (see Appendix A). Recommend commit level and warm-burst allowance.

4) Security and compliance baseline
   - Confirm KMS/HSM provider and key rotation timing.
   - Verify audit log export path and retention length (default 90d).

5) Acceptance criteria and rollback window
   - Agree acceptance thresholds (latency, error, quality via shadow-evals) and initial canary duration (default: 72 hours).
   - Define rollback triggers: sustained 15% regression in accuracy on shadow-eval or 2x baseline error rate for 30 minutes.

Cost & latency simulation knobs (how to model choices)

- Batching profile: adjust mean batch size and target latency percentiles. Increasing batch size reduces per-token cost by ~12–25% for conversational workloads with median token length < 64, but increases P95 latency by ~50–200ms depending on the runtime kernel.
- Quantization level: fp16 -> int8 yields ~1.6–2.3x cost reduction; expect quality delta of 0.5–3% depending on model and prompt class (use shadow-evals).
- KV-cache retention: raising session KV lifetime can reduce repeated context costs; model cost reduction depends on prompt reuse.
- Warm-burst vs preemptible: reserved + warm-burst provides predictable P95; preemptible fallback reduces commit cost but requires careful SLO mapping and customer acceptance in contract.

Quick simulation example (CLI + JSON knobs)

1) Create a simulation input file sim-input.json (example):
{
  "monthly_tokens": 20000000,
  "avg_token_length": 45,
  "peak_rps": 120,
  "batch_profile": {"mean": 12, "max": 48},
  "quantization": "int8",
  "kv_retention_hours": 24
}

2) Run the offline estimator (developer sandbox):
   redwood cost-sim --input sim-input.json --region us-west-2 --sku-template dedicated-standard-8

This prints: estimated monthly spend, projected P95 latency, and quality delta vs hosted baseline. Include in proposal.

Phased rollout template (recommended default)

Phase 0: Planning (1–2 weeks) - Align on acceptance criteria, select SKU template, provision Dedicated cluster in customer region, prepare shadow-evals.
Phase 1: Canary (72–96 hours) - Route 2–5% of traffic to Dedicated cluster with continuous shadow-eval; monitor latency, error, and quality.
Phase 2: Ramp (1–2 weeks) - 20% -> 50% -> 100% staged routing; increase autoscaling buffer; re-run cost-sim with observed utilization.
Phase 3: Harden + Handover (1 week) - Finalize runbook, schedule SLO reviews (90d cadence), handover ops to customer success / support engineering.

Rollout monitoring dashboard (must-have metrics)
- P50/P95/P99 latency by route and model variant
- End-to-end error rate (5xx, 4xx) and retries
- Shadow-eval quality delta (loss or score change) with prompt breakdowns
- GPU utilization and queue times for batch windows
- Billing exposure estimate (real-time cost burn vs forecast)

Contract and negotiation quick points
- SLO mapping: propose P95 latency and availability targets tied to credits. Default: 99.9% availability for Dedicated Standard, 99.95% for Enterprise Dedicated with warm-burst.
- Burst credits: define monthly burst pool (tokens) and overage pricing.
- Fallback behavior: document which model variants will be used on preemptible fallback and notify customers of possible small quality deltas.
- Data processing clauses: include explicit language allowing telemetry export for performance debugging (anonymized by default).

Operational runbook snippet (incident triggers & immediate actions)
1) Trigger: P95 latency > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes - Action: Pause routing increments to Dedicated, scale up warm-burst if available, open incident, notify SE and SRE.
2) Trigger: Shadow-eval quality regression > 10% on critical prompt set - Action: Re-route traffic to Hosted fallback, revert to prior variant, open quality incident, engage Research/Applied ML.
3) Trigger: Cost burn > 150% of forecast for 60 minutes - Action: Throttle non-critical routes, alert finance/commercial owner, assess preemptible fallback to control spend.

Ownership and contacts
- Product (Migration playbook owner): Aisha Patel (product)
- Solutions engineering escalation: Marcus Li
- SRE ops lead: Nina O'Connor
- Billing/commercial contact: Sarah Kim

Appendix A: SKU mapping cheatsheet (summary)
| Template | GPU | Typical sustained throughput (tokens/sec) | Suggested commit | Use case |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| dedicated-standard-4 | A10G | 800–1,200 | 2–4k USD / mo | Small to medium production routes |
| dedicated-standard-8 | A10G x2 | 1,600–2,400 | 6–12k USD / mo | Consistent medium workloads |
| dedicated-performance-16 | H100-class | 5,000–10,000 | 20k+ USD / mo | High throughput, low-latency transactional workloads |

Appendix B: Example acceptance criteria (copyable clause)
- Acceptance: During the 72-hour canary, Dedicated P95 latency shall not exceed Hosted baseline by more than 20%, and shadow-eval accuracy shall not degrade by more than 3% on the agreed prompt set. Failure to meet both conditions requires rollback and a joint remediation plan.

Related artifacts (templates and scripts)
- Migration proposal template: /product-docs/templates/migration-proposal-template.docx
- Sandbox runner: redwood-sandbox (internal repo)
- Shadow-eval template: /applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/shadow-eval-template.json

Last updated notes
- 2027-05-03: Added simulation CLI example and refined rollback triggers after two pilot migrations.
- 2026-10-11: Formalized acceptance clause and added SKU mapping ranges.

If you have questions or a migration that doesn't fit these patterns, tag @Aisha Patel on the product-docs Slack channel or open a ticket in the Migration Requests board.

payload.page_title: Developer Workbench: Sandbox Pricing, Onboarding, and Production Migration Brief

sections.body:
Overview

This brief describes the Developer Workbench (internal name: workbench-sandbox) — a hosted sandbox environment that lets engineers iterate with realistic inference traffic while controlling cost and telemetry. The goal is a low-friction path from experimentation to production-grade consumption: predictable pricing, reproducible telemetry, and a clear migration checklist to Dedicated/Private deployments.

Key objectives
- Give engineers a safe, budgeted sandbox that reflects production behavior (latency, KV/cache hits, token shapes).
- Provide transparent cost signals and an expected consumption-to-production delta.
- Automate migration artifacts (prompts, route configs, telemetry mappings) for handoff to platform teams.

Surface and capabilities
- Pre-configured runtime bundles: small, medium, and large sandbox SKUs with throughput backstops and token caps.
- Synthetic workload generator that can replay recorded developer sessions or simulate multi-tenant traffic shapes.
- Inline cost estimator in the console plus CLI: estimates token spend, expected throughput headroom, and warmup delta.
- Telemetry bridge: maps sandbox traces to production telemetry schemas (span names, token-level cost tags, KV cache hit ratios).
- Migration pack export: a zip that includes route definitions, prompt sets, telemetry mapping, and recommended quantization profile.

Pricing and packaging
- Monthly sandbox plan (free-trial + paid tiers):
  - Sandbox-S: $0/month baseline, 50K token cap/month, 10 concurrent sessions limit.
  - Sandbox-M: $199/month, 1M token cap, 50 concurrent sessions, priority queueing.
  - Sandbox-L: $999/month, 10M token cap, 250 concurrent sessions, warm capacity reservation (up to 10% of Dedicated burst pool).
- Overages billed at usage-rate multiplier (1.5x hosted API per-token rate) to keep sandbox cheap but discourage production workloads.
- Migration credit: on first Dedicated contract, up to 25% of paid sandbox months can be credited toward first Dedicated invoice (subject to customer eligibility).

Onboarding flow (developer-facing)
1) Sign up and select Sandbox tier.
2) Choose sample workload or upload recorded session.
3) Run preflight cost estimate and suggested runtime bundle.
4) Iterate on prompts and observe telemetry in the workbench console.
5) Export Migration pack when ready and open an onboarding request to Platform.

Migration checklist for platform handoff (owner: eng-platform)
1) Validate Migration pack artifacts and translate route configs into per-customer manifests.
2) Run synthetic traffic at 1x and 3x of observed sandbox peak to validate autoscaling policies.
3) Attach production SLA and billing contract; mark client allocation in capacity planner.
4) Configure telemetry lineage: ensure sandbox span -> production span mapping exists in tracing pipeline.
5) Execute blue-green rollout and monitor fidelity metrics for 72 hours.

Operational SLOs and guardrails
- Sandbox console availability: 99.9% monthly.
- Preflight estimator accuracy: predicted monthly token spend within ±15% for typical conversational workloads.
- Migration pack exports must succeed within 120s and include all required artifacts.
- Telemetry mapping completeness: >= 95% of sandbox spans must map to a production schema during onboarding checks.

Roadmap highlights (next 12 months)
- Q3 2026: Add configurable per-route fidelity presets and integration with Optimize suggestions.
- Q4 2026: Launch self-service Migration Pack validation checks with synthetic replay.
- Q1 2027: Add private workbench option for VPC-bound customers (onboarding for regulated verticals).

Release notes snapshot (initial GA 2026-04-06)
- Feature: Workbench GA with Sandbox-S/M/L and migration pack export.
- Telemetry: Initial bridge mapping to tracing and kv_hit_ratio metrics.
- Known limitations: Warm-capacity behavior in Sandbox-L is advisory; exact Dedicated warm reservations require formal contract.

Open decisions and risks
- Pricing delta between sandbox and hosted API: tradeoff between cheap experimentation and misuse for production. Proposal ties overages to 1.5x multiplier; monitor usage patterns for 90 days.
- Migration credit eligibility: requires minimum of 3 paid months or controlled pilot; may need exceptions for startups.
- Telemetry fidelity: current mapping covers conversational and request-level traces but lacks full per-token loss telemetry; prioritized for Q4 2026.

Ownership & contacts
- Product lead: Harper Singh (product)
- Engineering owner: Diego Alvarez (eng-platform)
- SRE/ops: Priya Nair (eng-sre)
- Billing/finance contact: Zoe Park (finance-legal)

Appendix: CLI examples
- Estimate command:
  redwood workbench estimate --tier Sandbox-M --trace sample-session.json --out report.json
- Export migration pack:
  redwood workbench export-migration --project my-app --out my-app-migration.zip

Related artifacts and links
- Developer sandbox telemetry mapping matrix (linked in repo: infra/telemetry/sandbox-mapping.csv)
- Migration pack schema (repo: product/workbench/migration-schema.md)

If you are starting a pilot, open a request in the "Workbench Pilot" Jira component and tag the reviewers listed above.

payload.page_title: Conversational SLA Composer and Contract Simulator — Product Brief and Playbook

sections.body: This document describes the Conversational SLA Composer and Contract Simulator (SLA Composer). The SLA Composer is a productized authoring UX and backend simulator that lets sales, solutions engineering, and customers design, preview, and validate SLA-driven consumption contracts for conversational workloads. It couples a declarative contract DSL, a simulation runner (SimRunner), and a telemetry-aware estimator to produce latency, cost, and quality projections for candidate contracts before signing.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Provide a single surface for creating vendor- and tenant-facing SLA contracts for conversational applications (chat, interactive assistants, streaming responses).
- Enable realistic pre-sale simulations matching customer's traffic shape to predict p50/p95 latency distribution, token costs, and fallback frequency.
- Reduce contract churn by surfacing trade-offs (batching, warm capacity, quantization, model variant fallthrough) early.
- Drive consistent commercial packaging by codifying guardrails for minimum economic and reliability thresholds.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- In scope: Authoring UX in Console, contract DSL v1, SimRunner for synthetic traffic playback and scenario slices, estimator for cost & latency, recommended guardrail presets for Hosted / Dedicated / Private.
- Out of scope for v1: full legal contract generation, automated billing integration, marketplace SKU publication.
sections.heading: Scope (what is in/out)

sections.body:
1) SLA Composer UX (console plugin): form-based + YAML editor for advanced users. Generates a Contract YAML using the DSL.
2) Contract DSL v1: fields for routes, SLOs (latency percentiles, availability), fidelity buckets, fallback policies, warm capacity commitments, regional affinity.
3) SimRunner: simulator service that replays customer traffic shapes, applies batching/quantization rules, and models multi-tier fallbacks.
4) Estimator: produces cost, projected token count, and economic confidence bands.
5) Report generator: human-readable SLA preview and machine-readable contract artifact.
sections.heading: High-level components

sections.body:
- Route: logical API path (e.g., /chat/complete, /embed/upsert).
- Fidelity bucket: discrete fidelity profile for responses (high/medium/low quantization + variant).
- Warm capacity: reserved pool expressed in vCPU/GPU-hours or credit-equivalent.
- Fallback frequency: expected % of requests that drop to a lower-cost variant or region under load.
sections.heading: Key concepts and terminology

sections.body:
- Sales: create conservative contract for enterprise prospects, simulate peak-hour load, export contract for SRE review.
- Solutions Engineer: iterate fidelity vs cost trade-offs with customer, validate SLA feasibility on Dedicated.
- Customer Admin: import customer traffic samples and run private simulations in VPC (for Private deployments).
sections.heading: User journeys and primary personas

sections.body:
| id | requirement | acceptance criteria | priority | owner | notes |
| RQ-001 | Contract DSL supports per-route p50/p95 latency & availability | Composer UI shows projection plots and warnings; DSL produces contract YAML | P0 | product/strategy | Must support p95 latency target and p50 baseline |
| RQ-002 | SimRunner must replay traffic shapes and produce latency histogram (p50/p95/p99) | Results reproducible; run for 1M requests within 4h for typical scenario | P0 | eng-platform | Use existing synthetic-runner infra as base |
| RQ-003 | Estimator must output cost estimate with 90% confidence interval | CI calculated from historical variance + model variance | P1 | finance-infra | Integrate with runtime-cost-models service |
| RQ-004 | Support warm capacity commitment presets for Hosted/Dedicated/Private | Presets available in Console and DSL; show cost delta vs on-demand | P1 | product | Presets editable by solutions engineering |
| RQ-005 | Simulator supports modeling fallbacks to compatible variants and regions | Simulator reports fallback frequency and resulting latencies | P0 | eng-serving-runtime | Need variant compatibility matrix input |
sections.heading: Requirements (table)

sections.body:
- As a Sales rep, I want to draft a contract that guarantees p95 <= 350ms for 95% of requests in US-EAST so I can promise an SLA to the prospect.
- As a Solutions Engineer, I want to adjust fidelity buckets and see immediate cost/latency trade-off previews to pick an economically viable configuration.
- As an SRE reviewer, I want a simulation report attached to the contract that includes expected error rates and fallback counts during burst scenarios.
sections.heading: User stories (selected)

sections.body:
1) Console UX allows creating and saving a contract YAML and triggering a simulation.
2) For provided traffic shapes (CSV or JSON trace sample), SimRunner returns latency histograms and cost estimate within 6 hours for 10M effective tokens.
3) Estimator integrates with runtime-cost-models and reports token-level breakdown and warm vs on-demand delta.
4) Generated contract artifact can be exported and consumed by Dedicated provisioning automation (staged API contract).
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (v1)

sections.body:
- Contract DSL: YAML-first with strict schema validation via JSONSchema. Example snippet included in Appendix.
- SimRunner: event-driven replay using existing synthetic-runner with extensions for batch-aware scheduling and KV-prefetch modeling. It will call a local runtime emulator that implements batching/quant behavior to estimate latency rather than making live production calls.
- Estimator: bootstrap from historical telemetry per-model and per-instance family (p95 scaling curves), combine with simulation outputs to produce cost confidence intervals.
- Privacy: for Private deployments, traffic sampling runs in-customer VPC using an ephemeral SimRunner worker; no traces leave the VPC unless customer opts in.
sections.heading: Design notes and technical approach

sections.body:
- Composer UX availability: 99.9% during business hours.
- SimRunner job completion: 95% of jobs complete successfully within target window (6h for 10M tokens).
- Simulation reproducibility: same input + seed -> within 5% variation on p95 latency for stable configs.
sections.heading: Operational SLOs for SLA Composer itself

sections.body:
1) Alpha (Q3 2026): internal-only Console plugin + SimRunner prototype, limited to Sales + SE.
2) Private beta (Q4 2026): enable Private deployment simulation in customer VPCs; collect feedback.
3) Public beta (Q1 2027): full Console flow live in Hosted with standard presets and exports to Dedicated provisioning.
4) GA (Q2 2027): billing hooks, legal artifact export, and partner-facing templates.
sections.heading: Rollout plan and milestones

sections.body:
- Product lead: Priya Natarajan (product) — overall roadmap and business acceptance.
- Tech lead: Luca Martinez (eng-platform) — SimRunner and estimator integration.
- UX: Maya Chen (dev-ex) — Console workflows and reporting.
- Finance integration: Aaron Patel (finance-legal) — cost model calibration and commercial presets.

Telemetry, metrics, and dashboards:
- Per-contract simulation dashboard: latency distributions, fallback heatmaps, token cost breakdown.
- Adoption metrics: contracts created, simulations run, time-to-first-simulation, simulation-to-contract conversion rate.
- Accuracy metrics: historical predicted vs observed p95 error and cost delta; tracked quarterly to recalibrate models.
sections.heading: Ownership and stakeholders

sections.body:
- Private simulations run entirely inside customer network by default. When customer provides traces, we require PII-scrubbing by SE before ingestion unless customer explicitly accepts otherwise.
- Contract artifacts stored encrypted at rest with tenant scoping.
sections.heading: Security and compliance considerations

sections.body:
---
routes:
  - name: chat.complete
    path: /v1/chat/complete
    traffic_shape: { peak_qps: 1200, mean_seq_len: 420, burst_minutes: 10 }
    slos:
      p95_latency_ms: 350
      availability_pct: 99.95
    fidelity_buckets:
      - name: gold
        quant: fp16
        model_variant: rdx-llama-38b-v2
        percent_traffic: 80
      - name: silver
        quant: int8
        model_variant: rdx-llama-7b-q8
        percent_traffic: 20
warm_capacity:
  reserved_gpu_hours_per_day: 12
fallback_policy:
  on_capacity_pressure: route_to: silver, max_fallback_pct: 30
---

Appendix: Simulation CLI example
$ rdx-simrunner run --contract contract.yaml --trace sample_trace.json --seed 42 --out report.json
sections.heading: Example Contract DSL (short snippet)

sections.body:
- Accuracy of estimator for novel models (new model families may lack enough telemetry to produce reliable CI). Mitigation: conservative default multipliers and explicit confidence bands.
- Legal acceptance: simulated guarantees are indicative; we must ensure contract wording delineates simulated projections vs guaranteed contractual obligations. Legal to review before GA.
- Cost of running large-scale simulations can be non-trivial; consider crediting model for customer-initiated sims.
sections.heading: Open questions / risks

sections.body:
- Consumption SLA playbook (internal)
- Dedicated provisioning API and contract schema
- Runtime-cost-models service (telemetry & cost calibration)
sections.heading: Related pages and references

sections.body:
- 30 days: finalize Contract DSL schema and wire up JSONSchema validation; build minimal Console form.
- 60 days: prototype SimRunner job type and validate against three canonical customer traffic shapes.
- 90 days: integrate estimator and produce the first contract preview report for internal review.

payload.page_title: EdgeLite packaging and consumption playbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This playbook describes EdgeLite: a lightweight, opinionated runtime and consumption model designed for developers who need low-latency, low-footprint inference on constrained devices and small edge nodes. EdgeLite is intended as a packaged option for Redwood Private and Dedicated customers who require local inference with predictable economics and incremental feature parity with hosted Redwood API.

Goals and non-goals
------------------
- Goals:
  - Provide a single binary and SDK bundle that enables model-serving at the edge with minimal ops overhead.
  - Offer tiered consumption modes (microbundle, burst, and standby) with transparent unit economics for customers.
  - Maintain graceful fallback to hosted Redwood variants for heavy workloads or degraded local capacity.
- Non-goals:
  - Not intended to match full throughput of Dedicated GPU fleets.
  - Not a replacement for on-prem heavy-duty clusters or the full Private control plane.

Product highlights (what customers get)
-------------------------------------
- EdgeLite runtime: 80–200MB binary with a single-process model shard loader and an optional lightweight proxy for local multi-tenant routing.
- SDKs: Node, Python, and a minimal Rust client for embedded use.
- Consumption modes: microbundle (per-request microcredits), burst-capacity (short prewarm windows billed as bursts), and standby (low-cost keepalive).
- Telemetry: aggregated anonymized telemetry to Redwood Console + local metrics endpoint for Prometheus scraping.
- Security: support for customer-managed KMS integrations and offline signing for package verification.

High-level architecture
-----------------------
1. Control plane (Redwood Private/Dedicated): model catalog, signing keys, entitlements, and consumption accounting.
2. EdgeLite agent: runs on customer node, enforces local entitlements, selects model shard(s), serves requests via local gRPC/HTTP gateway.
3. Local cache + KV store: small LRU-backed key-value cache for KV-caches and prefix reuse.
4. Fallback proxy: routes requests to hosted or dedicated variants based on routing policy and local health.

Design constraints and tradeoffs
-------------------------------
- Memory and binary size constrained to support small ARM x64 instances and Raspberry Pi 4 class hardware.
- Quantized model support assumed (int8/4-bit); full FP16/FP32 is supported only where hardware allows.
- Prefetch vs. prewarm: prefetching model weights on demand minimizes startup cost but increases tail latency; the bundle provides configurable prewarm windows.

Minimum viable feature set (MVP) requirements
--------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. Runtime and packaging:
   - Single, signed binary per supported platform (linux-x86_64, linux-arm64).
   - Model loader that supports sharded weights and delta updates.
   - Local HTTP/gRPC endpoint with the same request surface shape as Redwood API (subset).
2. Security and compliance:
   - Signed artifacts with offline verification.
   - Integration points for customer KMS and audit log export.
3. Consumption and billing:
   - Microbundle metering: per-inference microcredit counters persisted and periodically synced to control plane.
   - Burst windows with configurable duration and cap.
4. Observability:
   - Local Prometheus metrics with standard naming conventions.
   - Periodic encrypted heartbeats to control plane for health and accounting.
5. Failover:
   - Policy-driven fallback to hosted variants with priority and latency thresholds.

Packaging and distribution
-------------------------
- Published artifacts: signed tar.gz packages and Docker images.
- Channels: stable, beta, and nightly.
- Auto-update policy for pinned deployments: optional; default is manual update for Private customers.

Recommended configuration table
-------------------------------
| Setting                     | Recommended value                     | Notes |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------|-------|
| Default prewarm window      | 20s                                   | Balanced start-up latency vs cost |
| Microbundle unit size       | 0.01 USD equivalent per 1K tokens     | Adjustable by customer tier |
| Burst duration max          | 120s                                  | Billed at burst rate per second |
| Standby heartbeat interval  | 300s                                  | Low-cost keepalive for ephemeral nodes |
| Local cache capacity (MB)   | 256                                   | Adjustable; recommend >=128MB for most cases |

Pricing & packaging notes
-------------------------
- EdgeLite introduces two new priceable primitives: microcredits and burst seconds.
  - Microcredits: purchased in bundles (microbundle) or deducted from tenant credit balance. One microcredit approximates 100 tokens on typical quantized models; conversion and modeling must be displayed in Console before purchase.
  - Burst seconds: short prewarm windows purchased as a metered resource; priced per second of active prewarm across a node pool.
- SKU options:
  - EdgeLite Self-Managed: platform binary + metering; billed per microbundle and optional support fee.
  - EdgeLite Managed: includes managed rollout and auto-updates; adds a monthly node management fee.
- Migration discounts: customers migrating from Dedicated to EdgeLite-managed hybrid setups can receive a credit proportional to reserved capacity for the first 6 months.

Developer experience and onboarding
----------------------------------
1. Quickstart path (self-serve):
   - Install CLI, register node with 'redwood-edge register --org <org-id> --node-name <name>'.
   - Pull a verified model 'redwood-edge pull-model --model redwood-v1-mini --shard 0'.
   - Start runtime 'redwood-edge start --config edge-config.yaml'.
   - Send a test request using SDK until a green health check is observed.
2. Templates: pre-built Helm chart for k8s, systemd unit example, Raspberry Pi distro image.
3. SDK ergonomics: maintain parity in request/response fields with hosted API where feasible; clearly document disabled features in EdgeLite (e.g., no long-running streaming beyond burst window).

Operational runbook (incident triage summary)
-------------------------------------------
- Symptom: Node unresponsive to local requests.
  1. Check local systemd logs: journalctl -u redwood-edge.
  2. Verify disk and memory usage (df -h; free -m).
  3. Check local Prometheus metrics endpoint for model-loader error counts (/metrics).
  4. If certificate or signing errors appear, rotate keys via control plane and restart runtime.
- Symptom: Unexpectedly high microcredit usage.
  1. Use local request logs to identify request patterns and prompt lengths.
  2. If traffic spike expected, consider temporary burst enablement or redirect to hosted fallback.

SLOs and acceptance criteria for GA
-----------------------------------
- Functional SLOs:
  - Model load success rate: >= 99.5% across supported nodes during typical prewarm.
  - Local net-tail latency (95th percentile): <= 250ms for single-turn small responses on ARM64 with small quantized variants.
- Operational SLOs:
  - Heartbeat delivery: >= 99% within a 5-minute window per node.
  - Metering sync: per-node billing sync delay <= 10 minutes for 95% of nodes.

Roadmap and milestones
---------------------
- Phase 0 (Q4 2029): internal alpha; core runtime and microcredit accounting.
- Phase 1 (Q1 2030): beta with Node + Python SDKs and two model families supported.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2030): GA, managed offering, pricing published, Console integration for microbundle purchases.
- Phase 3 (H2 2030): support for on-device hardware accelerators and expanded ARM/embedded platforms.

Dependencies and risks
----------------------
- Dependencies:
  - Lightweight quantized model packaging from model-onboarding team.
  - Metering and billing pipeline extension for high-frequency microcredit events.
  - Legal sign-off on node licensing and export controls.
- Principal risks:
  - Underestimating operational complexity for customers managing many small nodes.
  - Metering reconciliation edge cases causing billing disputes.
  - Security posture for devices in hostile networks.

Acceptance checklist for release to GA
-------------------------------------
- [ ] Signed security review and threat model complete.
- [ ] Billing reconciliation tests with synthetic nodes passing for 100k events.
- [ ] Console UI for microbundle purchasing and visualization implemented.
- [ ] Documentation and quickstarts published across SDKs.
- [ ] Support runbook and escalation paths published to customer-success.

Release notes (initial GA blurb)
-------------------------------
EdgeLite GA (v1.0) — 2030-04-15
- Key highlights:
  - Lightweight runtime and SDKs for local inference on modest edge hardware.
  - New consumption primitives: microbundles and burst seconds with integration into Redwood Console.
  - Transparent fallback policies to hosted Redwood variants.

Owners and escalation
--------------------
- Product owner: Lena Park (product)
- Technical lead: Marco Ruiz (eng-serving-runtime)
- Billing integration owner: Keisha O'Connor (finance-legal)
- Support escalation: Customer Success oncall; see support process for playbook IDs.

Appendix: example edge-config.yaml snippet
-----------------------------------------

node_id: "edge-node-42"
model: "redwood-v1-mini"
prewarm_window_seconds: 20
consumption_mode: "microbundle"
microbundle_id: "mb-std-1"
heartbeat_interval_seconds: 300
fallback_policy:
  - condition: "cpu_usage>80% or memory_free<200MB"
    action: "route_to_hosted"

References and links
--------------------
- See related design guidance: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling for model sharding patterns.
- See onboarding templates: eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/edge-lite-helm-chart.

payload.page_title: Fidelity Benchmark Campaign and Pricing Sensitivity Brief

sections.body:
Overview:

This brief defines a cross-functional campaign to: (1) run a structured fidelity benchmarking program across representative developer workloads, (2) measure fidelity vs. unit-cost sensitivity, and (3) generate packaging/pricing guidance and feature rollouts informed by measured economics. The goal is to produce prescriptive recommendations for Optimize/Conductor advisors, onboarding defaults, and pricing experiments for Q3–Q4 2027.

Why this matters:
- Customers trade off cost and result fidelity; we need repeatable, measurable guidance to surface sensible defaults and commercial levers.
- Provides evidence for fidelity-based SKU design, crediting rules, and fallback behaviors.
- Powers product telemetry and UX (Console advisors, preflight checks, cost estimators).

Scope and success criteria:
- Scope: hosted and dedicated serving tiers; text generation and chat; representative embeddings pipelines. Excludes on-prem private packaging and niche multimodal models for this phase.
- Success criteria (30-day):
  1. Complete benchmarking across 6 developer cohorts (see "Cohort Matrix") with quality and cost measurements.
  2. Produce 3 priced fidelity skus (Low/Medium/High) with modeled customer impact curves.
  3. Instrument Console advisor and cost estimator for rollout experiment.

Cohort Matrix (representative workloads):
1) Search reranking (short prompts, high throughput)
2) Conversational assistant (session state; context window 2–8 turns)
3) Document summarization (long context 4k–32k tokens)
4) Code generation (creative-to-deterministic mix)
5) Embeddings for semantic search (batched vectors)
6) Transactional microservices (low-latency constraints)

Measurement plan (what we measure):
- Quality metrics (per cohort): BLEU/ROUGE for summarization, MRR/NDCG for reranking, ROUGE/ROUGE-L for summarization, pass@k for code, embedding cosine recall@k. Also: developer-facing metrics (latency p50/p95), request error rate, token consumption breakdown.
- Economic metrics: cost-per-1M-input-tokens, cost-per-response, normalized cost-per-quality-point.
- Observability: correlation of latency and fidelity mode, KV cache hit rate, batching efficiency, and GPU utilization per profile.

Telemetry and instrumentation (required fields):
Include the following telemetry keys in evaluation runs and production experiments:
- run_id (uuid)
- cohort (string)
- model_variant (string)
- fidelity_mode (low|medium|high|adaptive)
- avg_latency_ms_p50 (number)
- avg_latency_ms_p95 (number)
- tokens_input (int)
- tokens_output (int)
- cost_estimate_cents (number)
- quality_score (float)
- kv_cache_hit_rate (float)
- batch_size_mean (float)
- gpu_util_pct (float)

Example telemetry JSON (for evaluator ingestion):
{
  "run_id": "f8b2c12e-7b2e-4b9a-a6c2-9f6f8e26a2b1",
  "cohort": "conversational-assistant",
  "model_variant": "rw-v3-medium-quant",
  "fidelity_mode": "medium",
  "avg_latency_ms_p50": 85.2,
  "avg_latency_ms_p95": 210.6,
  "tokens_input": 12450,
  "tokens_output": 3200,
  "cost_estimate_cents": 46.2,
  "quality_score": 0.83,
  "kv_cache_hit_rate": 0.42,
  "batch_size_mean": 8.1,
  "gpu_util_pct": 67.3
}

Design constraints and guardrails:
- Fidelity modes must be implementable as composable runtime flags (quantization profile + attention kernel choice + caching policy).
- No fidelity mode should increase p95 latency by >25% for transactional cohort unless explicitly marketed.
- Quality regressions must be detectable by shadow-eval harness with a defined rollback threshold (quality_score drop >= 0.05 normalized points).

Pricing sensitivity model (summary table):
Scenario | Workload | Mode | Mode cost delta | Expected quality delta
--- | --- | --- | ---: | ---:
Baseline (rw-v3-high) | Conversational | High | $0.00 / 1M tokens | quality 1.00
Quantized Medium | Conversational | Medium | -$240 / 1M tokens | quality 0.95
Aggressive Low | Conversational | Low | -$720 / 1M tokens | quality 0.87
Adaptive (slo-aware) | Conversational | Adaptive | -$150 / 1M tokens (estimated) | quality 0.93

Notes: dollar figures are estimated unit economics relative to baseline for GPU amortized costs and do not include margin or infra overhead. Final pricing will fold in network, storage, and Console feature costs.

Decision checkpoints and rollout plan:
1. Benchmarking sprint (2 weeks): run all cohorts through Low/Medium/High modes; collect telemetry and evaluations. Ownership: Applied ML & Evals (lead: Marco Ruiz).
2. Analysis (1 week): compute normalized cost-per-quality and run sensitivity curves; draft SKU proposals. Ownership: Product analytics (Aisha).
3. Pilot pricing experiment (4 weeks): select 4 pilot customers across size/vertical to validate UX and commercial response. Ownership: GTM (Samir Gupta) + Account teams.
4. Console integration (2 weeks parallel): add Advisor card showing recommended fidelity and cost delta with "Apply" flow. Ownership: Eng Developer Experience.
5. Release & A/B (8 weeks): run A/B test comparing current defaults vs. fidelity-sku defaults; track retention, spend churn, quality incidents. Ownership: Go-to-market + Product.

Rollout checklist:
- [ ] Benchmark data ingested into analytics store (schema validated)
- [ ] Shadow-eval alerts wired to regression slack channel (#fidelity-regressions)
- [ ] Console advisor UI implemented with cost-estimate calculator
- [ ] Pricing experiments configured in billing test environment
- [ ] Customer pilot consent and success criteria documented

SLOs and thresholds (per-cohort recommended):
- Transactional microservices: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 150ms, error_rate < 0.1%
- Conversational assistant: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 300ms, quality_score >= 0.88 for Medium mode
- Embeddings: throughput >= 2000 vectors/sec per GPU, recall@10 >= 0.92 for Medium mode

Billing and packaging guidance (draft):
- Introduce three optional fidelity add-ons for Optimize customers: "Fidelity Lite", "Fidelity Standard", "Fidelity Premium". Each maps to Low/Medium/High runtime flags and corresponding credit multipliers.
- Offer a trial period where first 100k tokens of any fidelity change are charged at baseline rates for pilot customers.
- For Dedicated customers, provide a "maintenance credit" for switching to Low mode to encourage trial, applied as a % discount on reserved monthly commit.

Example CLI (developer sandbox):
# run benchmark harness
redwood-cli benchmark run --cohort conversational --model rw-v3 --modes low,medium,high --out /tmp/bench-results.json

# estimate cost for a given prompt set
redwood-cli cost estimate --input /tmp/bench-prompts.json --model-variant rw-v3-medium-quant --fidelity medium

Security, compliance, and data handling:
- Evaluation runs must not include customer PII unless explicitly consented and covered under data-processing addendum (DPA).
- All telemetry used for pricing decisions must be stored in the internal analytics tier with restricted access and audit logs.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product lead: Aisha Patel (product)
- Applied ML & Evals: Marco Ruiz (engineering)
- Pricing & Packaging: Eleanor Chen (finance-product)
- Console UX: Priya Nair (eng-developer-experience)
- GTM pilot coordination: Samir Gupta (go-to-market)

Appendix A — Analysis outputs expected:
- Per-cohort CSVs: (run_id, fidelity_mode, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_cents, quality_score, latency_p50, latency_p95)
- Sensitivity curves: cost-per-quality plots with 90% confidence intervals
- Decision memo: recommended SKU multipliers and pilot customer list

Appendix B — Related references:
- PRD: prd-fidelity-staging-sdk-and-eval-playbook-2026-12-22
- Design: prescriptive-fidelity-advisor-design-2026-08-24
- Prior briefing: fidelity-scaling-advisor-product-brief-2026-10-21

Change log:
- 2027-06-01: Draft created (Aisha Patel)
- 2027-06-08: Added telemetry schema and cohort matrix (Marco Ruiz)
- 2027-06-15: Pricing sensitivity table updated with revised unit cost estimates (Eleanor Chen)

payload.page_title: developer-cost-lab-product-brief-2026-02-08

sections.body:
Overview
========

This product brief describes the Developer Cost Lab: a low-friction, sandboxed environment that bundles a simulated consumption runner, telemetry bridge to Redwood Console, and a lightweight cost-feedback SDK for developer workflows. The Lab is targeted at developer and platform teams who need safe, repeatable experiments to understand unit economics (tokens/embedding/throughput) for different model variants, batching and caching settings, and fidelity policies before committing to Dedicated or Private deployments.

Goals
-----

- Give engineers a fast feedback loop for cost-latency-quality tradeoffs without consuming production credits.
- Surface actional recommendations (batch sizes, kv cache policies, quantization profiles) through Redwood Optimize suggestions.
- Make simulated traffic reproducible and shareable across teams with seeded scenarios and named experiments.
- Integrate telemetry into Redwood Console so that cost signals tie back to the exact sandbox config and prompt set.

Scope and out-of-scope
----------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Playbook and product UX for launching sandbox experiments from the Console and CLI.
- A sandbox runner that can emulate streaming and transactional workloads.
- SDK hooks to capture per-request fidelity toggles and synthetic token counts.
- Integration with Optimize to produce cost-saving recommendations.
sections.heading: In-scope

sections.body:
- Running full Dedicated GPU fleets for the lab (we use capacity-sliced emulator pools and local inference stubs).
- Persistent production-grade billing: sandbox runs consume dedicated credit buckets and do not affect customer invoices.

Why this product
-----------------

Teams frequently under- or over-provision when moving from prototyping to production because they lack reproducible cost-to-performance data. This leads to churn (migrating from Hosted to Dedicated prematurely), poor SLO choices, and surprises during contract negotiations. The Developer Cost Lab reduces risk by making tradeoffs visible and repeatable during onboarding and feature design.

User personas
------------

- Developer (individual contributor): wants a one-click way to simulate N=1000 chat sessions and get a per-utterance cost breakdown.
- ML Engineer / Platform: needs to compare quantization profiles across candidate models and capture quality regression metrics.
- Solutions Engineer / Sales: uses named experiments to demonstrate expected cost at target QPS for a prospective customer.

Key capabilities (high level)
----------------------------

1) Scenario Runner
- Seeded traffic generator supporting: conversational sessions, stateless generation, embeddings batches, and reranking workloads.
- Configurable arrival patterns: constant, poisson, burst (burst profile: amplitude, duration, recurrence).
- Output: synthetic traces formatted for Redwood Console ingestion (span IDs, route, model_variant, synthetic_token_counts).

2) Telemetry Bridge
- Lightweight agent that maps sandbox experiment metadata into Console schemas. Events emitted: experiment.start, run.metrics, experiment.snapshot.
- Cost inference: uses the same per-token unit economics engine as production but applies sandbox credit multipliers (configurable).

3) Developer Cost SDK
- Client-side hooks (Node/Python/Go) for: tagging prompt templates, annotating fidelity toggles, and marking golden prompts for quality capture.
- Local CLI to run sample scenarios and upload results for sharing.

4) Optimize integration
- Automatic recommendations for: batching policy (suggested batch sizes), kv cache prefixing, and quantization profile selection.
- Recommendations include estimated monthly delta (USD) and percentile latency impact.

Minimal success metrics (first 90 days)
---------------------------------------

- 100 distinct experiments created by internal developer teams.
- Average time-to-insight (experiment creation -> cost recommendation) < 10 minutes.
- At least 2 customer pilots convert to Dedicated trials with documented cost regressions prevented.

Requirements (PRD-style)
-------------------------
sections.heading: Out-of-scope

sections.body:
1. FR-1: Experiment lifecycle API (create/list/describe/stop) with immutable experiment snapshot export.
2. FR-2: Scenario DSL that can express: session length distribution, user message length distribution, and multi-stage reranking pipelines.
3. FR-3: Telemetry events must be queryable in Console with filters: experiment_id, model_variant, route, and timestamp range.
4. FR-4: Cost estimator must accept overrides for unit costs (quantized variant price, reserved capacity price) to model Dedicated pricing.
5. FR-5: SDK must capture 'fidelity_tag' semantics and allow developers to opt-in prompt capture for quality regressions.
sections.heading: Functional requirements

sections.body:
- NFR-1: Experiment replay determinism: repeated runs of the same seeded scenario must produce token counts within +/- 3% across runs for the same model configuration.
- NFR-2: Telemetry latency: events from sandbox runner should appear in Console within 60s for 95% of events.
- NFR-3: Sandbox isolation: experiments must only consume from sandbox credits and not affect production quotas.

Design highlights
-----------------

Experiment DSL (example snippet)
- The DSL is YAML-like; example below (shown as plain text):

  scenario_name: small-chat-burst
  workload: conversational
  seeds: 42
  arrival_profile:
    type: burst
    amplitude: 200
    duration_seconds: 30
    recurrence_minutes: 10
  message_length_distribution:
    mean: 42
    p95: 120
  model_variants:
    - name: redwood-ft-lite-q4
      quant_profile: q4_0
    - name: redwood-moderate
      quant_profile: q8_1

Telemetry & Console mapping
- Events emitted include structured fields: experiment_id, run_id, scenario_name, model_variant, batch_size, cache_hit_rate, synthetic_token_count, latency_ms. These are mapped to Console columns for per-experiment dashboards.

Recommendation engine contract
- Input: experiment snapshot + observed metrics. Output: ranked suggestions each with: id, description, expected_cost_delta_percent, expected_p50_latency_delta_ms, confidence_score (0-1).

Pricing/packaging notes
-----------------------

- Sandbox consumption is billed to internal credits. For external pilots we offer a hosted sandbox add-on priced as a monthly seat per-engineer + simulated-credit bucket. Suggested pilot package (beta):
  - 10 seats, 100k simulated tokens/day, priority onboarding support.

- Recommendations must include two price-model projections: Hosted per-token baseline and Dedicated reserved capacity equivalent. This is required for sales/SE playbooks to justify transition decisions.

Roadmap and milestones
----------------------

Q1 2026 (alpha)
- Deliver core scenario runner and local SDKs. Basic Console ingestion for experiment metadata.

Q2 2026 (beta)
- Add Optimize recommendation hook and richer scenario DSL. Implement pilot billing paths and pilot SE playbook.

Q3 2026 (GA)
- Multi-model comparison reports, Dedicated pricing projection support, and per-experiment sharing links in Console.

Rollout steps and runbook excerpt
---------------------------------

1) Internal alpha: enable feature flag for dev and platform teams. Collect feedback (2 weeks).
2) Beta pilot: invite 3 customers (SE-led) to run guided experiments; capture conversion feedback.
3) GA: open to self-serve; surface in onboarding checklist.
sections.heading: Non-functional requirements

sections.body:
- Verify sandbox credit buckets (billing admin).
- Preload recommended prompt sets and golden prompts.
- Confirm Console experiment dashboard shows run metrics within 60s.
- Run a 1-hour burst scenario and validate cost projection divergence between q4 and q8 variants.

Ownership and contact
---------------------

Product lead: Aisha Raman
Eng lead: Diego Morales
Optimize integration owner: Priya Patel
SE pilot coordinator: Samir Gupta

Appendices
----------

A. Example Console query (pseudo-SQL)
  SELECT experiment_id, model_variant, SUM(synthetic_token_count) as tokens, PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p50_latency
  FROM telemetry.events WHERE experiment_id = '<id>' AND timestamp BETWEEN '<start>' AND '<end>' GROUP BY experiment_id, model_variant

B. Suggested experiment naming conventions
- team-feature-scenario-date (e.g., payments-ocr-batch-20260312)

C. Security note
- Sandbox runner will not accept customer data marked as PHI/PII for hosted pilots. All prompt captures must be redacted or flagged and stored with restricted confidentiality.

D. Links and references
- Onboarding playbook: ../product-overview/onboarding-and-cost-advisor-playbook-2026-07-28.json
- Sandbox runner PRD: ../requirements/prd-consumption-sandbox-scenario-runner-2027-04-05.json

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-08: Initial draft (Aisha Raman)
- 2026-03-12: Added Optimize integration details and pricing pilot guidance (reviewers: Diego, Priya, Samir)

payload.page_title: Adaptive KV Eviction Economics: Product Brief & Ops Playbook

sections.body: This document describes the Adaptive KV Eviction Economics initiative: a product and operational playbook to coordinate key-value (KV) cache eviction and retention policies across model variants, tenants, and runtime topologies to reduce end-to-end token cost while preserving latency SLOs and inference quality. It combines a product brief, minimum viable requirements (PRD), high-level design, rollout roadmap, pricing/packaging implications, release notes, and runbook tasks for post-launch operations.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Reduce average token compute cost attributable to redundant KV cache loads by 12–30% for multi-variant serving workloads.
- Preserve 95th percentile latency SLOs for conversational flows (target: p95 <= configured latency tier).
- Provide transparent billing signals and crediting for KV hits to enable commercial packaging (e.g., KV-hit discounts).
- Make eviction policies configurable per-tenant and autopilot-tunable per-workload.
sections.heading: Goals and thesis

sections.body:
- Adaptive eviction policies implemented in the serving runtime and exposed via per-tenant policy objects.
- A cost-aware eviction algorithm combining recency, frequency, and estimated token-cost-savings signal.
- Console UX for policy selection and per-route policy overrides.
- Telemetry and observability (per-tenant KV hit rate, estimated token-savings, policy regressions).
- Billing/credit schema proposals for KV credits and KV-hit discounts.
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- On-prem appliance integration changes beyond policy config API.
- Deep model-level cache insertion hooks (future phase).
sections.heading: Out of scope (phase 1)

sections.body:
- System metric: Mean per-token compute cost drop attributable to KV coordination >= 15% for pilot tenants.
- Performance metric: No more than 2% regression in generation quality (measured by eval prompt set).
- Reliability metric: Incidents attributable to KV eviction policy changes <= 1 per quarter for pilot tenants.
- Adoption metric: 25% of enterprise pilot tenants adopt adaptive policies within 3 months.
sections.heading: Success metrics (first 6 months)

sections.body:
- As an ML platform engineer, I want a default cost-aware eviction policy so my tenant reduces token spend without manual tuning.
- As a product owner, I want per-route overrides so critical flows keep longer KV retention.
- As a billing analyst, I want KV-hit telemetry correlated with billing so I can validate KV credit allocations.

PRD: Requirements (MUST/SHOULD/CAN)

| ID | Priority | Requirement | Acceptance criteria |
|-----|----------|-------------|--------------------|
| R1 | MUST | Runtime supports pluggable eviction module with three built-in policies: LRU, LFU, Cost-Aware TTL | Unit tests, runtime flag to switch policy per-pool and per-tenant, integration test validating eviction outcome on synthetic workloads |
| R2 | MUST | Expose policy object via Control Plane API and Console with schema (ttl, max_entries, cost_prefactor, override_rules) | API docs + example payloads; Console form with validation; e2e apply test |
| R3 | MUST | Emit telemetry: kv.hit_rate, kv.eviction_count, kv.estimated_token_savings (per-route, per-tenant) | Metrics appear in telemetry pipeline; dashboards defined; alerts for sudden drops in hit_rate |
| R4 | SHOULD | Autosuggest policy adjustments based on historical traffic and model variants | MVP: nightly suggestions; UI shows expected savings and confidence score |
| R5 | SHOULD | Billing layer records KV-hit credits for eligible requests | Prototype costing calculation available and validated with finance team |
| R6 | CAN | Provide SDK helpers for local dev (simulating eviction behavior) | Developer docs and small Python helper library |

High-level design

1) Components:
- Control Plane policy store: canonical policy objects per-tenant/route.
- Serving runtime eviction module: pluggable with a Cost-Aware policy.
- Telemetry pipeline: enriched metrics and event tagging.
- Console & API UX: policy editing, suggestions, and rollout controls.
- Billing bridge: computes KV-hit credits and exposes to billing downstream.

2) Cost-Aware eviction algorithm (overview):
- Score each cache entry = alpha * recency_score + beta * frequency_score + gamma * token_cost_savings_estimate.
- token_cost_savings_estimate = expected_future_token_count_saved * model_unit_cost.
- Evict entries with lowest score when capacity exceeded.
- alpha/beta/gamma are tenant-configurable; autosuggest uses historical tracebacks to tune gamma per-variant.

3) Data needed for scoring:
- Per-entry last_access_ts, access_count, average_future_prefix_length (estimated via historical patterns), model_variant_cost_profile.

4) API contract (example):
- PATCH /v1/tenants/{t}/kv-policy
- Payload fields: ttl_seconds, max_entries, policy_type (lru|lfu|cost-aware), cost_prefactor, rules[{route_regex, min_ttl, priority}]

Operational considerations & SLOs

- SLOs:
  - KV pipeline availability: 99.95% monthly.
  - KV-hit telemetry freshness: 30s (90th percentile).
  - p95 inference latency impact after policy change: < +5% compared to baseline.

- Alerts to create:
  - kv.hit_rate drops > 40% for a high-volume tenant within 10 minutes.
  - estimated_token_savings > 2x historical baseline (possible regression in measurement).
  - policy enforcement errors > 1% of requests for a tenant.

- Runbook excerpt (for oncall):
  1. If kv.hit_rate alert fires, identify tenant and recent policy changes.
  2. Rollback tenant policy to previous version via Control Plane API.
  3. If rollback fails, change policy_type to LRU as emergency safe mode.
  4. Notify product and ML teams; run lightweight traffic replay to validate behavior.

Rollout plan & roadmap (quarters)

- Q2 2026: Design, runtime hooks, and API schema; limited unit tests and local dev helpers.
- Q3 2026: Implement LRU/LFU + Cost-Aware prototype; internal dogfood with 3 pilot tenants; initial telemetry dashboards.
- Q4 2026: Console UX, autosuggest MVP, and billing bridge prototype (KV-hit credits).
- Q1 2027: Wider beta, finance validation for KV credits, per-route override polish.
- Q2 2027: General availability with multi-tenant autoscaling constraints and enterprise config controls.

Pricing & packaging implications

- KV-hit credits model (proposal):
  - Define a KV-hit as a cache hit that avoids > X tokens of compute (threshold tunable).
  - KV-hit credit = unit_price_per_token_saved * estimated_tokens_saved * credit_factor.
  - Packaging: include a baseline KV-credit allowance for enterprise Dedicated plans; additional KV-credits purchasable as add-on.

- Commercial impacts to validate with Finance & Sales:
  - How to audit and dispute KV-hit counts.
  - How credits affect refunding and overage calculations.
  - Competitive messaging and support for customers migrating from flat per-token billing.

Release notes (candidate language for product announcements)

Title: Adaptive KV Eviction — Cost-aware cache policies and billing preview\nSummary: Introduces tenant-level adaptive KV eviction policies that reduce token compute spend by prioritizing entries that save the most future compute. Includes API, console controls, telemetry, and a billing preview that implements KV-hit crediting for eligible workloads. Pilot customers can opt in via the Console.

payload.page_title: Fidelity Onboarding: Contracts, SLA Mapping, and Developer Checklist

sections.body:
Summary

This document is a combined product overview, PRD-style requirements list, lightweight design notes, roadmap milestones, pricing implications, and a hands-on developer onboarding checklist for fidelity-related onboarding flows. It provides legal-friendly contract snippets, SLA-to-fidelity mapping rules, and the operational playbook for first 90 days after customer activation. The goal is to standardize how product, sales, and legal align on fidelity entitlements and how developer teams implement client-side negotiation and runtime fallbacks.

Scope

- Audience: Product managers, solutions engineers, contracts/legal, account teams, and developer SDK owners.
- Applies to: Hosted API (Redwood API), Dedicated, and Private deployments where customers negotiate per-route fidelity and SLO entitlements.
- Out of scope: Billing engine implementation details and enterprise legal negotiation templates beyond the sample clauses included.

Key definitions

- Fidelity: The resolution/quality level of an inference response as defined by model variant, quantization profile, token budget, and optional post-processing (reranking, safety filters).
- SLO band: Customer-facing latency/availability target tied to a fidelity band (e.g., High/Medium/Low).
- Entitlement: Contract clause specifying per-route fidelity caps, overage behavior, and fallback permissions.
- Developer preflight: A local or CI step that validates a tenant’s default fidelity settings against a sample prompt set.

Product overview (how this fits together)

1) Contract layer (Sales & Legal): Captures agreed fidelity bands, guaranteed SLOs, and crediting for fallback events.
2) Control plane (Redwood Console): Stores fidelity entitlements per tenant and exposes read-only mapping to SDKs and routing services.
3) Runtime enforcement (Serving runtime): Enforces per-request fidelity caps, applies fallbacks, and emits telemetry for fidelity-related regressions.
4) Developer SDK / Integrator responsibilities: Provide negotiation hooks, graceful fallback UX, and preflight tests to ensure acceptable quality after fidelity changes.

PRD: Requirements (must-have, should-have, optional)

Must-have
1. Contract schema: Standardized JSON schema for storing fidelity entitlements in the control plane (fields: tenant_id, route_id, fidelity_band, max_tokens, quant_profile, fallback_policy, sla_band).
2. SLA mapping table: Clear mapping between fidelity_band and SLO targets that the control plane will honor.
3. SDK negotiation API: Client-side method to request fidelity and receive negotiated fidelity with explicit fallback instructions and human-readable reason codes.
4. Telemetry hooks: Events for fidelity_negotiated, fidelity_fallback, fidelity_degraded, and fidelity_regression flagged with request_id, tenant_id, route_id, and sample prompt hash.
5. Default safe-fallback: If negotiation fails, runtime must fall back to the tenant’s default fidelity for that route.

Should-have
1. Preflight runner: Command-line tool and CI job that runs a small prompt set against a candidate fidelity configuration and produces a pass/fail with sample outputs.
2. Cost estimator: SDK-side estimator to display expected token cost delta when downgrading fidelity.
3. Contract escrow credits: A simple mechanism to put fidelity credits in escrow for customers during staged rollouts.

Optional
1. Auto-negotiation service: Server-side agent that suggests the highest fidelity that meets SLO under current load.
2. Inline quality monitors that run lightweight checks (BLEU/embedding similarity) for selected prompts in real-time.

Design notes and constraints

- Backwards compatibility: The fidelity entitlement schema must be versioned and support a "compatibility_mode" flag for older SDKs.
- Performance: Negotiation path must add <5ms median overhead. If negotiation is unavailable, the SDK should continue with tenant default (no user-visible error).
- Security: Fidelity entitlements are customer-sensitive; control plane endpoints must require tenant-scoped auth and be limited to account admins.
- Observability: Each negotiated request emits tags: fidelity_band, quant_profile, kernel_hint, and final_model_variant. Trace spans should be correlated to token-cost and latency metrics.

SLA mapping (recommended bands)

| Fidelity band | Typical model variant | 95th-latency SLO (ms) | Availability SLO | Notes |
|---------------|----------------------|-----------------------:|-----------------:|-------|
| high          | s-xxl-quant-high     | 120                   | 99.9%            | Full context, no quantization where possible |
| medium        | s-xl-quant-medium     | 220                   | 99.5%            | Quantized weights, reduced sampling beams |
| low           | s-l-quant-low        | 400                   | 99.0%            | Aggressive quantization, prefix-caching encouraged |

(These are recommended defaults; legal SLOs can override.)

Sample contract clauses (developer-friendly language)

1) Entitlement summary clause (recommended):
"The Provider will make available the Tenant’s entitled fidelity band(s) per route as specified in Appendix A. Provider guarantees the Availability SLO per fidelity band. If the Provider must serve a lower fidelity due to capacity constraints, the Provider will credit the Tenant at the rate described in the Credits schedule."

2) Fallback permission snippet:
"Tenant grants Provider the right to serve an alternative fidelity band for up to 5% of monthly requests in the event of capacity constraints or critical incidents, provided Provider notifies Tenant via the Console and credits apply as defined in Section X."

3) Escrow/Credit snippet:
"In the event of fidelity fallback exceeding the contracted allowance, Provider will apply credits equal to the measured delta in token-equivalent cost for affected requests for the billing period."

Developer onboarding checklist (first 90 days)

Day 0–7: Account activation and SDK integration
1. Add tenant credentials to local .env and run SDK preflight: redwood preflight --tenant $TENANT --route default
2. Confirm negotiated fidelity response includes 'fidelity_band' and 'fallback_policy'.
3. Integrate client-side UX for fallback: show 'content may be reduced' message behind feature flag.

Day 8–30: QA, staging, and preflight tests
1. Add the preflight CI job to run against canary route with three sample prompt families (short/long/contextual). Pass threshold: embedding similarity >= 0.88 for high->medium transitions.
2. Validate telemetry shows fidelity_negotiated in traces and that token_cost estimates align within ±10% of observed.

Day 31–90: Rollout and monitoring
1. Canary rollout: 5% traffic with auto-rollback if fidelity_fx_rate > 1% or if median latency > SLO+20%.
2. Run scheduled weekly fidelity regression job: compare top-10 prompts per route for quality drop.
3. Customer success QBR: Include fidelity fallback rate, credits applied, and suggestions for fidelity relocation or dedicated capacity.

Roadmap and milestones (high-level)

- Q2 2026: Entitlement schema v1, SDK negotiation API v1, telemetry events v1.
- Q4 2026: Preflight runner released + CI integration templates, Console fidelity UI (read-only).
- Q2 2027: Auto-negotiation service prototype and contract crediting workflow.
- Q4 2027: Dedicated + Private control-plane federation for tenant-managed fidelity in Private deployments.

Pricing & packaging implications (notes for commercial and pricing teams)

- Fidelity tiers should map to pricing bands. Charging model options: per-token adjusted by fidelity multiplier (e.g., high x1.0, medium x0.8, low x0.5) OR fixed fidelity credits consumed per request.
- Overage credits: Define a simple formula for credit refunds when fallback exceeds allowance (e.g., refund = (contracted_unit_cost - served_unit_cost) * affected_tokens * refund_multiplier).
- Salespack: Offer a fidelity 'guarantee' add-on for enterprise customers with explicit burst capacity and faster escalation SLA.

Release notes (initial feature rollup)

v0.1 (internal release) — 2026-03-01
- Entitlement schema v1 defined.
- SDK negotiation endpoints implemented in beta.
- Telemetry events emitting fidelity_negotiated and fidelity_fallback.

v0.2 (console & tooling) — 2026-11-15
- Preflight runner integrated into developer-templates repo.
- Console read-only view for tenant entitlements.
- Sample contract clauses and commercial guidance published to Sales enablement.

Operational playbook (short)

1. If fidelity_fallback rate > contractual allowance: open a dedicated slack channel with Customer Success, Account Exec, SRE, and Product.
2. Run immediate analysis: top affected routes, time-of-day, upstream capacity signals.
3. Offer temporary credits and put a remediation plan: adjust routing, add dedicated capacity, or schedule model-variant pinning.

Ownership and contacts

- Product lead: Leah Chen (author)
- SDK owner: Marco Geller
- Infra / runtime owner: Reliability team (oncall via #reliability)
- Commercial template steward: Anita Rao

Related artifacts and templates

- preflight-runner README: git+internal://developer-templates/preflight-runner
- entitlement schema spec: /confluence/product-docs/design-specs/fidelity-entitlement-schema-2026-02-20 (TBD)
- sample contract templates: git+internal://commercial/contracts/fidelity-appendix

Next steps / action items

1. Product: finalize entitlement schema v1 and publish JSON schema to the design-specs directory (owner: Leah, due 2026-03-15).
2. SDK: complete negotiation API docs and implement client-side preflight helpers (owner: Marco, due 2026-04-01).
3. Sales/Legal: adopt sample clauses and test with two pilot enterprise customers (owner: Anita, due 2026-06-01).

Appendix: Example entitlement JSON (v1)

{
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "route_id": "search-autocomplete",
  "fidelity_bands": [
    { "band": "high", "max_tokens": "2048", "quant_profile": "none", "sla_band": "gold" },
    { "band": "medium", "max_tokens": "1024", "quant_profile": "q4", "sla_band": "silver" }
  ],
  "fallback_policy": "allow_with_credit"
}

(End of document)
