payload.page_title: Design Spec: Model Version Rollouts (Canonical Plan Template)

sections.body:
h1. Overview
This page defines the canonical rollout plan template for introducing a new LLM model version behind an existing model name (alias) or introducing a new model endpoint that will receive production traffic. It is intended to be copied into a new rollout plan page per change.

h1. When this template is required
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Changing the default version behind a model alias
* Introducing a new version that will receive >0% external customer traffic
* Changing routing policy or fallback behavior in a way that affects customer requests

h1. Rollout plan template (copy/paste)

h2. 1) Summary
* What is changing?
* Why now?
* Expected customer impact (best-case and worst-case)
* Who is on point during rollout (name + Slack channel)

h2. 2) Scope
* Environments: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
* Regions impacted
* Customer tiers or allowlists (if any)
* Request types: chat, completions, embeddings, rerank (as applicable)

h2. 3) Versioning and compatibility
* Model alias (if any)
* New version identifier (e.g., rw-llama-3-70b@2025-10-01)
* Backward compatibility notes (tool calling schema, output formatting, tokenization differences)
* Max context and max output token limits

h2. 4) Success criteria (must be explicit thresholds)
Define pass/fail thresholds for each category and the evaluation window. Minimum required categories:
* Reliability: 5xx rate, timeouts, admission rejects
* Latency: p50/p95 end-to-end and time-to-first-token for streaming
* Cost/efficiency: tokens/sec/GPU, cache hit rate, batch efficiency
* Quality: regression guardrail (eval set delta) and customer-reported issues
sections.heading: Use this template for any of the following

sections.body:
||Metric||Window||Pass threshold||Fail threshold||Owner||
|p95 latency|30 min|<= +5% vs baseline|> +10% vs baseline|SRE oncall|
|5xx rate|30 min|<= +0.05% absolute|> +0.2% absolute|Platform oncall|
|Quality score (internal eval)|per run|>= baseline - 0.3|< baseline - 0.7|Applied ML|

h2. 5) Monitoring and dashboards
* Links to dashboards (by service/model/region)
* Alerts to enable (list)
* Trace/log queries for fast triage
* Who watches what at each ramp step

h2. 6) Rollout strategy
* Canary design: what % first, for how long, and what signals decide next step
* Ramp schedule (with timestamps)
* Controls: per-customer allowlist, per-region traffic caps, concurrency caps
* A/B test plan (if used): experiment id, assignment, evaluation criteria

h2. 7) Rollback and fallback
* Rollback trigger conditions (must map to thresholds)
* Rollback procedure reference (runbook link)
* Fallback policy (automatic): target version(s), ordering, and constraints
* What happens for in-flight requests and streaming responses

h2. 8) Customer communications
* Which customers must be notified (Dedicated/Private, contractually sensitive)
* Channel: email, support ticket, status page, in-product banner
* Timeline: before/at/after rollout
* Message content requirements: change summary, risk, opt-out/pinning path, support contact

h2. 9) Approvals
* Change class (per policy)
* Approvers and timestamps
* Approved change window

h2. 10) Post-rollout validation
* Final KPIs after full ramp
* Customer feedback summary
* Follow-up tasks and owners

h1. Notes
* The plan should be treated as the source of truth during an incident.
* If any section is not applicable, write N/A with a brief justification.
sections.heading: Include a table with thresholds (example)

payload.page_title: Suggestions View (Optimize) — Information Architecture & User Flows (Beta)

sections.body: Define the information architecture (IA) and end-to-end user flows for the **Optimization suggestions (Beta)** experience in the Redwood Console.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Navigation entry points into Suggestions
- The list + details pattern (table + right-side drawer)
- Filtering/sorting patterns
- The end-to-end flow from discovery → understanding → applying config changes (manual + safe rollout)
sections.heading: This spec focuses on

sections.body:
- Quantization recommendations UI (may be referenced but not launched here)
- Auto-apply without user confirmation/rollout controls
- Any savings “guarantee” language

---
sections.heading: Out of scope (Beta)

sections.body:
1. **Actionable**: Always provide a clear next step (deep link + what changes + where it applies).
2. **Trustworthy**: Show assumptions, confidence inputs, staleness, and conservative risk labels.
3. **Comparable**: Enable quick ranking across routes/models (sorting + filters) without losing context.
4. **Safe**: Reinforce that changes should go through rollout controls; avoid “one-click apply” in beta.

---
sections.heading: Product principles (UX)

sections.body:
- **ML/Platform Engineer**: Owns inference configuration, cares about cost/perf tradeoffs and safe rollouts.
- **SRE/On-call**: Wants to avoid regressions; cares about risk clarity, staleness, and rollback paths.
- **Product Engineer** (secondary): Wants quick savings wins but needs guidance and guardrails.
sections.heading: Personas

sections.body:
- Identify top cost-saving opportunities by **route + model**
- Understand “why” and “what could go wrong” (latency/reliability risk)
- Apply changes via the appropriate config surface (batching/caching) with rollout controls

---
sections.heading: Key jobs

sections.body:
- **Optimize → Suggestions (Beta)**
  - Visible only when feature flag is enabled for the org (see “Gating & permissions”).
sections.heading: Left navigation

sections.body:
These should route into the Suggestions view with pre-applied filters:
- **Route details → Cost** panel: “View suggestions for this route”
- **Model deployment/version page**: “View suggestions for this model”
- **Optimize overview** (if present): “Top suggestions” module (beta)
sections.heading: Contextual entry points (deep links)

sections.body:
- `/console/:org/:project/optimize/suggestions`
  - Query params for state:
    - `?route_id=` (optional)
    - `&model_id=` (optional)
    - `&region=` (optional)
    - `&type=` (batching|caching)
    - `&risk=` (low|medium|high)
    - `&confidence=` (low|medium|high)
    - `&sort=` and `&dir=`
    - `&cursor=` (pagination)

Rationale: supports sharable URLs + support debugging without requiring users to repeat filter steps.

---
sections.heading: URL structure (recommended)

sections.body:
- Org-level flag: `optimize_suggestions_beta`
- UI behavior:
  - If not enabled: show an “Access required” state with CTA to request access (links to internal/beta request flow for Redwood-managed accounts).
sections.heading: Feature flag gating

sections.body:
- Permission required to view Suggestions:
  - `optimize:suggestions:read`
- Permission required to follow apply CTAs (config pages may have additional scopes):
  - Example: `inference:config:write` (actual scope may vary by surface)
sections.heading: RBAC

sections.body:
- Suggestions are **project-scoped** by default.
- If the Console supports org-wide views, the Suggestions view must be explicit about scope (“Project: X”) and never mix cross-tenant data.

---
sections.heading: Multi-project/org scoping

sections.body:
- Main content: a table of suggestions (default sorted by “Highest estimated savings/day”).
- Right-side details drawer opens when a row is selected.
- Sticky header contains:
  - Page title + beta badge
  - Filter chips
  - Search (route name / route id)
  - “Last computed” timestamp + staleness indicator
sections.heading: 1) Suggestions list (table)

sections.body:
- Contains:
  - Summary (savings + perf impact + risk)
  - “Why we recommend this” explanation
  - Assumptions + confidence explanation
  - “How to apply” steps + deep links to config surfaces
  - Guardrails / warnings
  - Action footer: “Mark as dismissed” + “Give feedback”
sections.heading: 2) Details drawer (right panel)

sections.body:
- Inline empty states (no telemetry, not eligible, etc.)
- Inline error state (API failure)

---
sections.heading: 3) Secondary panels

sections.body:
1. **Route**
   - Route name + route id (secondary)
   - Optional: environment badge (prod/staging) if available
2. **Model**
   - Model name/version currently pinned for the route (or “Multiple” if route varies)
3. **Suggestion**
   - Type: Batching or Caching
   - Short label, e.g.:
     - “Increase max batch size”
     - “Enable prefix/KV caching”
4. **Est. savings**
   - Primary: `$ / day` (or `$ / month` if user toggles timeframe)
   - Secondary: `%` savings relative to current spend on that route/model
   - Must include tooltip: “Estimated, not guaranteed”
5. **Perf impact (est.)**
   - p50 and p95 latency delta (ms, +/-)
   - If unknown: “—” with tooltip explaining insufficient confidence
6. **Risk**
   - Badge: Low / Medium / High
   - Tooltip copy per risk guidelines page
7. **Confidence**
   - Low / Medium / High (or numeric 0–100 later; beta uses levels)
   - Tooltip: inputs included + what’s missing
8. **Last computed**
   - Timestamp, used to spot staleness
sections.heading: Table columns (beta)

sections.body:
- Keep the list skimmable: prefer short labels and tooltips over long inline explanations.
- Column visibility: on smaller screens, collapse Model + Last computed into secondary row, but keep Savings/Risk visible.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- Clicking a row opens the details drawer.
- Keyboard support:
  - Up/down to move row focus
  - Enter/Space to open drawer
  - Esc to close drawer
- Selected state persists across pagination where possible (by stable suggestion id).

---
sections.heading: Table row behavior

sections.body: - Sort by **Estimated savings ($/day) descending**.
sections.heading: Default sort

sections.body:
- Est. savings ($/day)
- Est. savings (%)
- Risk (Low → High or High → Low; default: show highest savings first)
- Confidence (High → Low)
- p95 latency delta (ascending)
- Last computed (newest first)
sections.heading: Supported sorts (beta)

sections.body:
Filter chips appear beneath the header; selected filters display as removable chips.

1. **Suggestion type**: Batching, Caching (multi-select)
2. **Risk**: Low, Medium, High (multi-select)
3. **Confidence**: Low, Medium, High (multi-select)
4. **Region**: if applicable to the project (multi-select)
5. **Model**: model id/name (single or multi; if too many, use typeahead)
6. **Route**: typeahead search by route name/id
sections.heading: Filters (beta)

sections.body: - **Traffic tier** (e.g., High/Medium/Low QPS) to help large customers focus.
sections.heading: Recommended (if telemetry supports it without confusion)

sections.body:
- Persist filters in URL query params.
- Remember last-used filters per user (local storage) for the project.

---
sections.heading: Filter persistence

sections.body: Drawer sections should follow a consistent order to reduce cognitive load.
sections.heading: Details drawer: content structure

sections.body:
- Route name + route id
- Model name/version
- Suggestion type icon (Batching/Caching)
- Status badges (as applicable):
  - “Stale” (if computed beyond staleness threshold)
  - “Insufficient telemetry” (if partial)
sections.heading: Header (always visible)

sections.body:
- **Estimated savings**
  - `$ / day` and `%`
  - Confidence band if available (beta may show “Range: $X–$Y/day” when estimator provides it)
- **Estimated performance impact**
  - p50 delta, p95 delta
  - If estimator provides only p95, show p95 prominently and p50 as “—”
- **Risk level**
  - Low/Medium/High with 1–2 lines of “why” (not generic)
sections.heading: Section A — Summary (at-a-glance)

sections.body:
- 3–5 bullet explanation grounded in observed telemetry (examples):
  - “High concurrency during peak hours; batching can improve GPU utilization.”
  - “Repeated prompts detected; caching could reduce repeated compute.”
  - “Current cache hit rate is low; enabling prefix caching is expected to increase hit rate by ~X% (est.).”
sections.heading: Section B — Why we recommend this

sections.body:
Must show the inputs used and what might make the estimate wrong.
- Inputs used (examples):
  - request rate window (e.g., last 7 days)
  - sequence length distribution
  - current batching/caching configuration
  - observed cache hit rate (if applicable)
  - token price/cost basis used for estimate
- Confidence explanation:
  - “High” if enough traffic + stable distribution + low variance
  - “Low” if sparse traffic, high variance, or missing cache metrics
sections.heading: Section C — Assumptions & confidence

sections.body:
- Step-by-step guidance:
  1) Review recommended configuration values (show current vs recommended)
  2) Navigate to the relevant config page (deep link)
  3) Apply change using a safe rollout (canary) and monitor latency/error rate
sections.heading: Section D — How to apply (no auto-apply in beta)

sections.body:
- Batching suggestion → “Route config → Batching”
- Caching suggestion → “Route config → Caching”
- If user lacks permissions: show disabled CTA + “Request access” link.
sections.heading: Deep link targets (beta)

sections.body:
- Explicitly call out constraints from guardrails doc (examples):
  - “Low-latency route: avoid increasing batch size beyond X; monitor p95 closely.”
  - “If your prompts include highly dynamic prefixes, caching gains may be limited.”
sections.heading: Section E — Guardrails / warnings

sections.body:
- “Dismiss suggestion” (requires confirmation)
  - Prompt: “Dismiss for this route/model for 30 days” (beta default)
  - Optional reason dropdown (for feedback taxonomy):
    - Not applicable
    - Savings too small
    - Risk too high
    - Estimate seems wrong
    - Already implemented
- “Give feedback” link (opens feedback modal or external form)

---
sections.heading: Section F — Actions

sections.body:
1. User opens **Optimize → Suggestions (Beta)**.
2. User sorts by **Est. savings** (default) and applies filters (e.g., Risk: Low).
3. User clicks a suggestion row; details drawer opens.
4. User reviews:
   - Estimated savings + perf impact
   - Risk explanation
   - Assumptions/confidence
5. User clicks **“Go to config”**.
6. On config page, user updates settings.
7. User applies via rollout controls:
   - Create canary (e.g., 5–10% traffic)
   - Monitor key metrics
   - Increase rollout if stable
8. User returns to Suggestions and marks as “Applied” (beta behavior below).

Beta note on “Applied”:
- We will not automatically detect applied state reliably in beta unless config surfaces expose a canonical signal.
- UX behavior:
  - Provide an **“Mark as applied”** optional action in drawer (records user intent) OR
  - Provide a banner: “After applying, monitor and we’ll refresh estimates in up to N hours.”
- Final decision depends on backend support (see ADR suggestions API contract).
sections.heading: Flow 1 — Discover → Evaluate → Apply

sections.body:
1. User is investigating cost for Route A.
2. User clicks “View suggestions for this route”.
3. Suggestions opens with `route_id=RouteA` filter applied and drawer optionally pre-opened on top suggestion.
4. User proceeds with evaluation/apply.
sections.heading: Flow 2 — From Route page deep link

sections.body:
1. User opens a suggestion.
2. User clicks “Dismiss”.
3. Confirmation modal:
   - Explains dismissal hides suggestion for a period (default 30 days)
   - Optional reason
4. User confirms.
5. Row disappears from default list; can be re-shown via “Include dismissed” toggle (internal-only for beta / support).
sections.heading: Flow 3 — Dismiss

sections.body:
1. User opens Suggestions.
2. System detects missing required signals (e.g., cache metrics not enabled).
3. Show empty state:
   - “We don’t have enough telemetry to generate suggestions yet.”
   - Requirements checklist
   - CTA: “View setup instructions”
4. Once telemetry flows, Suggestions populates.
sections.heading: Flow 4 — Insufficient telemetry

sections.body:
1. User opens drawer and sees savings that conflict with their expectations.
2. User expands “Assumptions & confidence”.
3. User clicks “Give feedback” and selects “Estimate seems wrong”.
4. Feedback captures:
   - Suggestion id
   - Route/model context
   - User-provided note
5. UX confirms: “Thanks — we use this to improve estimator quality. Estimates are not guaranteed.”

---
sections.heading: Flow 5 — Estimate looks wrong (trust recovery)

sections.body: This page references: “Suggestions empty states and onboarding”.
sections.heading: Empty states & error states (link to detailed spec)

sections.body:
- **Feature not enabled**: access required + request access
- **No permission**: RBAC denied message + request access / contact admin
- **No data / insufficient telemetry**: requirements checklist + setup CTA
- **No suggestions available**: neutral empty (“No suggestions right now”) + tips on expanding scope (change time range, check filters)
- **API error**: retry button + “Check status” link (internal) + error id for support

---
sections.heading: Summary of required behaviors

sections.body:
- Always say **“Estimated savings”** and **“Estimated performance impact”**.
- Do not use guarantee language (“will save”, “guaranteed”, “promised”).
- Risk badge tooltips must clarify:
  - Risk refers to **performance/reliability tradeoffs**, not security risk.
- Staleness labels must include a timestamp:
  - “Last computed: 2026-02-20 14:00 UTC”

---
sections.heading: Key microcopy requirements (beta)

sections.body:
- Risk badges must meet contrast requirements; do not rely on color alone (include label text).
- Tooltips must be keyboard accessible.
- Drawer must trap focus when open; Esc closes.
- Table rows must have visible focus states and screen-reader row/column labeling.

---
sections.heading: Accessibility & interaction notes

sections.body:
Event taxonomy is defined elsewhere, but UX must provide the following triggers:
- Page impression (Suggestions view)
- Filter change (type/risk/confidence/model/route)
- Sort change
- Row select / drawer open
- “Go to config” click
- Dismiss initiated + confirmed + reason
- Feedback submitted

UX requirement: ensure that analytics collection does not block rendering; failures should be silent.

---
sections.heading: Analytics (UX instrumentation points)

sections.body:
1. **Applied state**: Do we add “Mark as applied” in beta, or wait until config detection is reliable?
2. **Time window selection**: Should users select 7d/30d windows for estimates on this page, or keep fixed for beta?
3. **Multi-model routes**: How do we represent routes with dynamic model routing? (Show “Multiple” + drawer details?)
4. **Confidence display**: Levels only (Low/Med/High) vs showing a numeric score + inputs.
sections.heading: Open questions (needs final alignment)

sections.body:
- Product decision: Marissa Cole / Aditya Rao
- Feasibility: Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin
- Research validation: George Mbatha

---
sections.heading: Owners

sections.body:
- 2026-02-21: Updated table columns to include “Last computed” and clarified URL query params for supportability.
- 2026-02-10: Added drawer structure and “How to apply” deep link behavior.
- 2026-01-23: Initial IA draft (nav + list/detail pattern).
sections.heading: Change log

payload.page_title: Local Cost Emulator and Developer SDK - Design Spec

sections.body: This design specification describes the Local Cost Emulator (LCE) and accompanying Developer SDK. The LCE is a lightweight, reproducible emulator that lets developers and solutions engineers simulate Redwood Inference consumption scenarios (token counts, streaming vs batched paths, quantization variants, caching hit rates, warmup/coldstart behaviour) on a developer laptop or CI runner without requiring access to a live account. The goal is to give fast, local feedback for cost and latency trade-offs during prompt engineering, model selection, and product integration.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Reduce iteration time for developers who need to evaluate cost/latency implications before running against hosted or dedicated capacity.
- Prevent costly developer mistakes that produce wide-scale unintended consumption (e.g., runaway loops, incorrect sampling settings).
- Provide a consistent baseline for pre-sales and onboarding conversations (estimate impact of fidelity choices).
sections.heading: Why we need this

sections.body:
1. Provide deterministic cost and latency estimates that match production telemetry within a bounded error (target +/- 15% for token cost; +/- 20% for 95th percentile latency for representative workloads).
2. Offer programmatic SDK primitives (Python/Node) that mirror Redwood API surface area for generation, streaming, and embeddings calls used in cost calculations.
3. Support configurable workload profiles: session length distribution, prefix caching rate, batching windows, and quantization variant.
4. Run offline (no cloud calls) with lightweight sample models and precomputed per-variant cost kernels.
sections.heading: Goals (MUST)

sections.body:
- Producing exact latency numbers for specialized hardware (e.g., large multi-GPU setups). LCE provides representative signals, not hardware-level benchmarking.
- Replacing lab-grade performance harnesses and stress testing used by SRE/Runtime teams.
sections.heading: Non-Goals (explicitly out of scope)

sections.body:
- Emulator Core (Rust): deterministic tokenization, cost model evaluator, event-driven session simulator. Exposes a thin FFI to language SDKs.
- Workload Profiles (YAML): composable presets (low-latency chat, high-throughput batch, interactive embeddings) that define request distributions, sequence length histograms, and cache-hit probabilities.
- Cost Kernel Store (JSON): per-model token cost coefficients, per-variant overheads (quantization multipliers, KV cache savings), and precomputed batching efficiency curves.
- Developer SDKs: Python and Node wrappers that expose Redwood-like client APIs (generate(), stream(), embed()) but route calls to the local emulator.
- CLI and CI Integrations: run scenarios, produce CSV/JSON reports, and fail CI gates if cost or latency thresholds are exceeded.
sections.heading: High-level architecture

sections.body:
| field | type | description | sample |
| Profile.name | string | profile identifier | interactive-chat |
| seq_length_p50 | int | median sequence length (tokens) | 128 |
| cache_hit_rate | float | estimated prefix/KV cache hit ratio (0-1) | 0.38 |
| batching_window_ms | int | emulated batching window to approximate runtime batching | 25 |
| model_variant | string | model + quantization label used to select cost kernel | redwood-compat-7b-q4_0 |
sections.heading: Configuration table (examples)

sections.body:
- Token cost = base_token_coeff * generated_tokens * variant_multiplier + per-request_overhead
- Variant multiplier captures quantization and kernel efficiency; derived from lab measurement matrix maintained by Runtime team.
- Batching efficiency curve is a sigmoid approximation: efficiency(batch_size) = 1 - exp(-alpha * batch_size) scaled by sequence composition. The LCE ships with calibrated alpha values for common families.
sections.heading: Cost model details

sections.body:
- LocalClient(profile: str, budget_usd: float = None)
- generate(prompt: str, max_tokens: int, model_variant: str, stream: bool = False) -> dict
- embed(texts: List[str], model_variant: str) -> dict
- run_scenario(scenario_name: str, iterations: int) -> report (JSON)
- audit_report() -> attaches per-call simulated telemetry (tokens_in, tokens_out, estimated_cost, simulated_latency_ms)
sections.heading: Developer SDK surface (public functions)

sections.body:
1. Scenario smoke test: run 'lce run_scenario smoke' as part of PR; fail if estimated cost per 1k requests > budget or median latency > threshold.
2. Regression guard: add a telemetry snapshot to repo; CI verifies that code changes do not increase estimated cost by more than 10% for canonical prompts.
sections.heading: CI integration patterns

sections.body:
1. Initial calibration against 10 canonical workloads using runtime lab traces. Compute multipliers and batching alpha constants.
2. Backtest weekly for first 8 weeks of rollout: compare LCE estimates to production telemetry (token cost and latency buckets) and adjust kernels.
3. Provide a calibration CLI: 'lce calibrate --upload-trace <trace.json>' to propose new kernel coefficients (requires opt-in telemetry upload).
sections.heading: Testing & calibration plan

sections.body:
- LCE runs offline by default and stores no customer secrets. If a customer chooses to calibrate with real traces, the CLI must validate and scrub PII and require an explicit flag.
- Telemetry artifacts collected for calibration are encrypted at rest and retained according to the data retention playbook.
sections.heading: Security and privacy considerations

sections.body:
- 30d: SDK distributed internally; 10 teams have used LCE for at least one integration; calibration pipeline established.
- 60d: Mean absolute error for token cost <= 12% vs production for canonical workloads.
- 90d: LCE integrated into onboarding demo and included in at least 3 sales evaluations; documented CI patterns adopted by SDK teams.
sections.heading: Metrics and success criteria (30/60/90 day)

sections.body:
1. Alpha (internal only): engineering and solutions enablement teams. Collect calibration traces.
2. Beta (wider internal + pilot customers): opt-in for early customers via SDK package; gating requires security review.
3. GA: public release in package manager and included in developer onboarding.
sections.heading: Rollout plan

sections.body:
- Primary owner: Product (Sofia Martinez) — roadmap and prioritization.
- Engineering owner: Runtime tools team (lead: Rajat Singh) — core emulator and cost kernels.
- SDKs: DevDX (lead: Ethan Brooks) — wrappers and onboarding docs.
sections.heading: Ownership and maintenance

sections.body:
- Cost kernels are versioned; reports include kernel_version to ensure reproducible results.
- CI gates should pin kernel_version to avoid noisy diffs; provide an automated 'bump' workflow that re-runs canonical scenarios and annotates PRs.
sections.heading: Backwards compatibility and upgrade notes

sections.body:
1. If calibration delta > 25% across canonical workloads, open an incident tagged 'lce-calibration' and assign to Runtime tools.
2. For reports of large discrepancies from customers, request trace artifacts and run 'lce calibrate' in a secured environment.
sections.heading: Operational runbook (summary)

sections.body:
- Quickstart: local install, run 'interactive-chat' scenario, read report.
- Cookbook: tuning batching_window, simulating coldstart-heavy workloads, interpreting audit_report fields.
- Example CI pipeline snippet (GitHub Actions) and prebuilt canonical scenario JSONs.
sections.heading: Documentation and example artifacts to ship with GA

sections.body:
- Local developer runtime sandbox design spec: /product-docs/design-specs/local-developer-runtime-sandbox-design-spec-2026-02-12.json
- Cost kernel maintenance playbook (Runtime team internal doc)
- Onboarding and cost advisor playbook: /product-docs/product-overview/onboarding-and-cost-advisor-playbook-2026-07-28.json

Appendix: Example scenario YAML
profile: interactive-chat
seq_length_p50: 128
seq_length_p95: 512
cache_hit_rate: 0.40
batching_window_ms: 30
request_rate_rps: 1.2
model_variant: redwood-compat-7b-q4_0
iterations: 250

Notes: This spec focuses on developer velocity and reproducibility rather than lab-grade microbenchmarks. The teams named in Ownership are the intended primary contacts for design review and rollout. For security-sensitive pilot customers, coordinate with Security & Compliance before enabling trace uploads for calibration.
sections.heading: References and related specs

payload.page_title: Real-time Telemetry Cost Normalization — Design Spec

sections.body:
Overview:

This design spec defines the Real-time Telemetry Cost Normalization subsystem — a lightweight, deterministic transformation layer for ingestion telemetry that produces cost-normalized events across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. The goal is to ensure downstream cost analysis, SLO attribution, and fidelity-advisor decisions are comparable across variants, regions, and deployment modes without distorting latency or availability signals.

Motivation and goals:
- Problem: raw telemetry (token counts, VM metrics, GPU kernel timings, sampling differences) varies by runtime, quantization, and batching behavior. Direct aggregation leads to biased cost signals, complicates billing and fidelity-advisor recommendations, and reduces quality of experiments.
- Goals:
  1) Produce a deterministic "normalized cost" value per request/event that maps closely to internal unit economics (USD/token equivalent) and is stable across model variants and runtime optimizations.
  2) Preserve critical SLO signals (p95 latency, error counts, tail-kernel stalls) without smoothing away actionable anomalies.
  3) Be low-latency and lightweight: transformation must operate inline with ingestion (<50ms median added) and be compatible with streaming pipelines.
  4) Enable downstream consumers (billing, Optimize, Console dashboards, fidelity-advisor) to rely on consistent units with documented error bounds.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope:
  - Deterministic mapping rules from event attributes to normalized_cost and normalized_unit (both emitted as part of telemetry envelope).
  - Config-driven variant multipliers (for known quantizations, NVLink differences, and pre-compiled kernels).
  - A small, audited set of heuristics for streaming estimation when full counters are not present (e.g., fallback k-v cache hit estimation).
  - Integration hooks for downstream consumers via schema v2.
- Out of scope:
  - Replacing billing system authoritative sources (billing will continue to use billing pipelines as ground truth; normalized_cost is an analytics/simulator signal).
  - Deep offline model-based cost estimators; this remains a separate research pipeline.

High-level model and outputs:
- Input event (example fields of incoming telemetry envelope):
  - request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, runtime_flags, token_generated, token_prompt, gpu_token_cycles, kv_cache_hits, batch_size, region, timestamp, sampling_rate
- Computed outputs (fields appended):
  - normalized_unit: string (e.g., "norm_token_v1")
  - normalized_cost: float (USD-equivalent per request, rounded to 6 decimal places)
  - normalization_version: string (e.g., "v1.0.0")
  - normalization_flags: comma-separated tokens describing fallbacks applied (e.g., "kv-estimate,quantized-multiplier")

Normalization algorithm (deterministic rule set):
1) Baseline rate lookup: Determine base_usd_per_token for the model_variant and region from a read-only configuration table (see Config section). If model_variant not found, apply fallback_variant mapping.
2) Kernel/cycle adjustment: Convert gpu_token_cycles -> token-equivalent using kernel_efficiency coefficients for the host hardware family. If gpu_token_cycles missing, infer from token_generated * median_cycles_per_token for the model_variant.
3) Batching and amortization: Normalize per-request cost by dividing amortized infra cost of batching: normalized_cost = base_usd_per_token * token_equivalent * batch_amortization_factor(batch_size, runtime_flags). The batch_amortization_factor is >= 0.5 and <= 1.5 by default (configurable).
4) KV cache correction: Reduce token cost when kv_cache_hits > 0 using kv_hit_discount percentage. If kv_cache fields absent, use conservative default (kv_hit_discount = 0.0) and set normalization_flags to include "kv-estimate".
5) Quantization/precision multiplier: Apply model_variant quantization multiplier (e.g., x0.6 for int8-opt, x1.0 for fp16).
6) Edge and Private adjustments: For Private deployments where direct infra metering isn't available, apply a customer-supplied coefficient if present; otherwise, apply region_defaults and emit a warning flag.

Examples (pseudocode):

```
# simplified algorithmic sketch
base = lookup_base(model_variant, region)
cycles = event.gpu_token_cycles or (event.token_generated * median_cycles(model_variant))
kernel_eff = kernel_coeff(host_family)
token_equiv = cycles / kernel_eff
batch_factor = amortization_factor(event.batch_size, event.runtime_flags)
kv_discount = kv_discount_for(model_variant) if event.kv_cache_hits else 0.0
quant_mult = quant_multiplier_for(model_variant)
normalized_cost = base * token_equiv * batch_factor * (1 - kv_discount) * quant_mult
```

Config and tables (must be maintained in repo: telemetry/configs/normalization):
- normalization-base.csv (columns): model_variant,region,base_usd_per_token,fallback_variant,median_cycles_per_token
- kernel-efficiencies.csv: host_family,kernel_coeff
- quantization-multipliers.csv: model_variant,quant_profile,multiplier
- amortization-curves.yaml: batch_size -> amortization_factor (discrete bins, linear interpolation)
- private-deployment-overrides.json (customer_id -> coefficient)

Operational contracts and SLOs:
- Latency overhead: median added processing per event <= 50ms; p95 <= 150ms. Measured in runtime-path synthetic traffic.
- Accuracy bounds: For fully-instrumented events (gpu_token_cycles present), normalized_cost deviation vs billing-simulator must be <= 5% median and <= 15% p95. For partially-instrumented events (fallbacks used), documented error bounds apply: median <= 12%, p95 <= 30%.
- Backfill/compatibility: normalization_version must be present on all events by rollout time. Older events without normalization may be backfilled offline using batch job.

Data schema and telemetry contract:
- Schema: Adopt telemetry schema v2. Add fields normalized_unit, normalized_cost, normalization_version, normalization_flags. All new fields are optional for consumers until T+8 weeks after rollout.
- Retention: Normalized fields are metadata; long-term retention follows existing telemetry retention policies (90 days by default, extended for enterprise accounts as contractually agreed).

Rollout plan and runbook (owner: Metrics Platform, run by Platform + Product):
1) Code and config land in feature branch; unit tests cover deterministic transforms and corner cases (null cycles, missing kv fields, unknown variants).
2) Canary deploy in non-prod: route 1% of synthetic and real traffic in farm.region-a to normalization-service; monitor added latency and cost deviation against offline simulator.
3) Gradual rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 3–7 days per stage if metrics within thresholds.
4) Parallel consumer adoption: Notify Billing, Console, Optimize, and Console-UX teams of schema and semantics. Provide a compatibility window where consumers receive both raw and normalized fields.
5) Backfill: If rollout completes, schedule a backfill job to enrich last 14 days of telemetry for downstream QA.

Rollback criteria (immediate):
- Normalized event stream increases end-to-end p95 latency by > 200ms for consumer pipelines for > 10 minutes.
- Observed normalized_cost deviance > 50% median against the simulator for > 30 minutes.
- Downstream consumers (Billing/Optimize) report unexpected spike in billing projections > 10% within 1 hour.

Observability and dashboards:
- Metrics to publish:
  - normalization_latency_ms: histogram per region/host_family
  - normalized_cost_vs_simulator_delta_pct: gauge per model_variant
  - fallback_rate: percent of events using any fallback (kv-estimate, cycles-infer, private-default)
  - schema_adoption_rate: percent of events with normalization_version present
- Dashboards: Real-time Normalization Overview (global), Variant Quality (sorted by delta_pct), Fallback Heatmap (by tenant and region).

Security and privacy considerations:
- Normalized fields contain no additional customer PII beyond existing telemetry. Customer-specific private-coefficients are stored in encrypted config (KMS).
- Private deployments: if customers opt out of normalization (data sovereignty), the service must emit normalization_version="opt-out" and normalization_flags include "customer-opt-out".

Ownership and next steps:
- Primary owner: Product (Priya Nair) — product requirements and consumer coordination.
- Execution lead: Metrics Platform (Evan Liu) — implementation, testing, rollout.
- Integrations lead: Billing (Diego Morales) and Optimize (Mariana Ruiz).
- Next milestones:
  1) Finalize config tables and commit to telemetry/configs/ by 2026-09-01.
  2) Deliver alpha implementation (non-prod) by 2026-10-01.
  3) Complete canary and consumer validations by 2026-11-05.

Appendix A — Example event before/after (text table):

Before normalization (raw telemetry):
- request_id: r-12345, tenant_id: t-789, model_variant: rw-gpt-large-quant, token_generated: 120, gpu_token_cycles: 360000, batch_size: 1, region: us-west-2

After normalization (added fields):
- normalized_unit: norm_token_v1
- normalized_cost: 0.001824
- normalization_version: v1.0.0
- normalization_flags: quantized-multiplier

Appendix B — Quick operational CLI for running local simulator (example):

```
# run a small simulator against normalization service running locally
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/normalize \n  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n  -d '{"request_id":"r-12345","tenant_id":"t-789","model_variant":"rw-gpt-large-quant","token_generated":120,"gpu_token_cycles":360000,"batch_size":1,"region":"us-west-2"}'
```

Related decisions and references:
- See ADR: telemetry-schema-v2 (link TBD) for field naming choices.
- Related spec: federated-telemetry-cost-aggregation-protocol-ftcap (for cross-account rollups).

Open questions (for review):
1) Should amortization_factor be computed per-tenant during Dedicated commitments to reflect committed warm capacity? (Pros: more accurate; Cons: higher config maintenance).
2) How should we version quantization multipliers when new kernel patches alter cycles-per-token significantly? Proposal: bump normalization_version and keep historical curve mappings.
3) Define a standard consumer contract for "normalized_cost" vs billing values so customers understand this is advisory.

Please review and comment inline.

payload.page_title: Adaptive Fidelity Client Negotiation API - Design Spec

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: Define a stable, forward-compatible API that enables client applications to declare cost- and latency-sensitivity at request time and participate in a runtime negotiation with Redwood Inference to select an execution fidelity profile. This specification covers the API surface, negotiation semantics, default policies, observability hooks, and a rollout plan.

Context: Redwood supports multiple fidelity trade-offs (model variant, quantization, batching behavior, KV cache usage, streaming vs. non-streaming). Today fidelity is determined server-side via routing policies and per-tenant configuration. For certain latency-sensitive or cost-sensitive integrations it is beneficial for clients to express their tolerance and preferred trade-offs per-request. The Adaptive Fidelity Client Negotiation API formalizes that contract while preserving server-side safety and economic controls.

Goals
- Provide a compact request-level contract for expressing cost/latency/quality sensitivity.
- Allow runtime negotiation responses that are deterministic and auditable.
- Enable economical defaults for unauthenticated or legacy clients.
- Integrate cleanly with billing and SLO bookkeeping.

Non-goals
- This spec does not define every fidelity knob (internal kernel selection or micro-quantization configs remain server-only).
- Not intended to replace tenant-level SLA/contract negotiation for Dedicated/Private installs.

Terminology
- Fidelity Profile: a named set of runtime choices (model variant, quantization level, batching class, streaming mode, KV cache policy).
- Cost Sensitivity: client-declared preference on price vs. quality/latency (enum: low|medium|high).
- Latency Constraint: explicit per-request max latency SLO (ms) or a tier (realtime|interactive|background).
- Negotiation Response: server's chosen fidelity profile + metadata & pricing delta.

High-level design
1) Clients supply an optional fidelityHint object on generation/embedding/chat requests. If omitted, server applies tenant defaults.
2) Server evaluates requested constraints against platform policies, capacity, and customer contract.
3) Server returns a negotiation result immediately (synchronous) or a provisional result (when long-running prefetch/compile is needed) and encodes the chosen fidelity in the response header/body.
4) Execution proceeds under the chosen fidelity profile; cost and telemetry attribute to the selected profile.

API contract
- Endpoint: POST /v1/infer (existing) — expanded contract; alternate dedicated endpoint: POST /v1/fidelity-negotiate for preflight checks.
- New request field (optional): fidelityHint (object)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```
{
  "input": "Summarize the quarterly results",
  "model": "redwood-rlhf-13b",
  "fidelityHint": {
    "costSensitivity": "medium",
    "latencyTier": "interactive",
    "minQualityScore": 0.82,
    "preferStreaming": true,
    "acceptableVariants": ["redwood-13b-q8_0", "redwood-13b-q4_0"],
    "fallbackPolicy": "best-effort"
  }
}
```
sections.heading: Example JSON (embedded in request body)

sections.body:
Name | Type | Description | Default
-----|------|-------------|--------
costSensitivity | string | low|medium|high. Controls willingness to accept cheaper variants. | medium
latencyTier | string | realtime|interactive|background. Maps to target p95 latency. | interactive
minQualityScore | number | 0.0-1.0. Client-specified lower bound on model quality (normalized eval metric). | 0.7
preferStreaming | boolean | Prefers streaming tokens as they are produced. May increase cost. | false
acceptableVariants | list[string] | Ordered preference list of model variant ids acceptable to client. | []
fallbackPolicy | string | best-effort|guarantee-min-quality|cost-first. Controls server fallback behavior. | best-effort
sections.heading: Field reference (table)

sections.body:
- fidelityProfile (string): canonical profile id used for execution (e.g., r-13b-q8-batched-realtime).
- effectivePriceMultiplier (number): multiplicative factor applied to base unit price for telemetry/billing.
- expectedP95 (ms): expected p95 latency under selected profile.
- qualityEstimate (0-1): server-side estimate of quality normalized to the requested metric.
- negotiatedFlags: list of server-side applied flags (e.g., kv_cache_disabled, small_batch_mode).
- negotiationTraceId: opaque id used for audit and debugging.
sections.heading: Negotiation response (returned in body and headers)

sections.body:
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
X-RW-Fidelity-Profile: r-13b-q4-smallbatch
X-RW-Negotiation-Trace: trace_20260621_45ab
{
  "fidelityProfile": "r-13b-q4-smallbatch",
  "effectivePriceMultiplier": 0.75,
  "expectedP95": 220,
  "qualityEstimate": 0.78,
  "negotiatedFlags": ["kv_cache_reduced"],
  "negotiationTraceId": "trace_20260621_45ab"
}
```

Authorization and policy enforcement
- Request-level negotiation is allowed only if tenant contract permits per-request modifiers. For Hosted free-tier tenants, negotiation is read-only and returns conservative profiles.
- The platform evaluates requests against: per-tenant quotas, region capacity, active incidents, and model marketplace licensing.
- Admin override: operators can set a global enforcement policy that disables client-specified fallbacks during emergency states.

Negotiation semantics and deterministic behavior
- Determinism: the server must compute the negotiation outcome using deterministic inputs (tenant id, fidelityHint, time-bucket, current capacity watermark). Document deterministic tie-breaking order: 1) explicit acceptableVariants list, 2) costSensitivity, 3) latencyTier, 4) minQualityScore, 5) tenant prefixed overrides.
- Safe-fallback: if no profile satisfies minQualityScore and latencyTier, server returns HTTP 409 with structured error (see Error handling) unless fallbackPolicy == guarantee-min-quality, in which case server attempts higher-cost alternative and returns a pricing delta.

Error handling and client contract states
1) 400 Bad Request: malformed fidelityHint or invalid parameter values.
2) 409 Conflict: cannot satisfy constraints. Body includes suggested adjustments.
3) 412 Precondition Failed: tenant has not enabled negotiation or exceeded negotiation quota.
4) 502/503: platform capacity shortfall; negotiation may suggest queued execution or lower priority batch.

Observability and billing integration
- Telemetry: attach negotiationTraceId to all downstream execution spans and emitted tokens. Emit the following metrics per request: negotiation.duration_ms, negotiation.outcome (chosen_profile), negotiation.cost_multiplier, negotiation.rejections.{reason}.
- Logs: include fidelityHint and negotiation outcome in structured request logs (json) with PII redaction rules.
- Billing: effectivePriceMultiplier is multiplied against existing per-token/embedding unit price. For Dedicated tenants with committed pricing, multiplier may be ignored (documented per-tenant behavior returned in negotiation).

Security and privacy considerations
- Deny-listing: acceptableVariants must not leak internal-only model names to unauthorized tenants. Server should normalize display names in public logs.
- Data residency: negotiation decisions that reference regional capacity must not expose region identifiers beyond allowed tenant scope.

Compatibility and migration path
- Backwards compatibility: if fidelityHint is absent, server behaves exactly as today. New fields are additive.
- SDK changes: SDKs will include a FidelityHint builder helper and validation helpers.
- Migration doc: provide a one-page migration checklist for customers in product-overview (linked).

Rollout plan
1) Phase 0 (internal alpha, 4 weeks): server-side evaluation + simulated negotiation only. No client-facing change.
2) Phase 1 (partner beta, 6 weeks): opt-in toggle for selected Hosted customers. Provide /v1/fidelity-negotiate preflight endpoint.
3) Phase 2 (gradual public rollout, 8 weeks): default-enabled for pay-as-you-go customers with telemetry.
4) Phase 3 (enterprise toggle parity, 4 weeks): integrate with Dedicated/Private feature flags and contract clauses.

Monitoring and SLOs for negotiation service
- Availability: 99.95% for negotiation endpoint (target).
- Freshness: negotiation decisions must complete within 50ms p95 for realtime and 200ms p95 for interactive.
- Correctness: <0.1% of negotiation outcomes will be audited as mismatches between declared and observed quality (via periodic evals).

Operational runbook highlights
- If negotiation.duration_ms p99 > 1s, flip to conservative default profiles and open incident.
- If negotiation.rejections.rate > 0.5% baseline increase, notify product and throttle partner opt-ins.
- Escalation: own by Runtime Reliability -> paged after 15m sustained latency breach.

Appendix: Example negotiation sequences
1) Cheap embedder use-case: fidelityHint {costSensitivity: "high", latencyTier: "background", minQualityScore: 0.6} -> server picks quantized small model, multiplier 0.5.
2) Interactive chat requiring streaming: fidelityHint {costSensitivity: "low", latencyTier: "realtime", preferStreaming: true, minQualityScore: 0.9} -> server may select higher-cost variant, multiplier 1.4, or return 409 if unavailable.

Appendix: Example preflight endpoint (POST /v1/fidelity-negotiate)
Request: same body as /v1/infer but flagged preflight: true. Server returns negotiated profile and "estimatedCostDelta" and does not consume quota or bill.

Ownership and next steps
- Spec owner: Priya Desai (product).
- Primary implementers: Runtime API team (ENG-serving-runtime) and Billing team.
- Action items:
  1. API proto draft (ENG-serving-runtime) — due 2026-06-30.
  2. SDK builders and validators (SDK team) — due 2026-07-10.
  3. Partner beta runbook and legal review (Product + Legal) — due 2026-07-20.

Related documents
- See product-overview: "onboarding-and-cost-advisor-playbook-2026-07-28" for partner onboarding flow.
- See design-specs: "prescriptive-fidelity-advisor-design-2026-08-24" for server-side fidelity recommendations used during negotiation.

Change log
- 2026-06-21: Initial draft (Priya Desai).
- 2026-07-02: Incorporated reviewer feedback on determinism and billing edge-cases (Marcus Li).

End of spec.

payload.page_title: Request Stitching and Session Coalescing Design Spec

sections.body:
A design specification for combining related request fragments into coherent inference sessions ("request stitching") and opportunistically coalescing concurrent tenant sessions onto shared backend resources to reduce per-token cost and KV-cache churn while meeting latency SLOs and tenant isolation constraints.
Overview

This spec defines Request Stitching and Session Coalescing: two coordinated features intended to reduce redundant KV cache warmups, increase effective GPU utilization, and lower per-token costs for multi-request conversational workloads. Request Stitching means merging logically related partial requests (e.g., multi-turn fragments, document-chunked prompts, or streaming deltas) into a single served session when semantics and safety rules allow. Session Coalescing means routing and packing concurrent short-lived or low-fidelity sessions from multiple tenants onto a smaller number of backend model sessions when policy permits.

This document covers goals, constraints, high-level design, API/contract changes, configuration examples, SLO and telemetry requirements, rollout plan, testing and backwards-compatibility considerations, and ownership.

Motivation

- Many customers send bursty conversational traffic composed of short partial updates. Each update causes KV cache overhead and repeated kernel scheduling.
- Cold KV cache population is a top driver of tail latency for LLM conversational workloads and increases per-token GPU time for short requests.
- Dedicated short sessions waste context window compute and reduce packing efficiency.

Goals

1. Reduce average per-token GPU time for conversational workloads by 10–30% for qualifying traffic classes.
2. Maintain per-route p95 latency within existing SLOs (default p95 < 250ms for interactive tiers) for requests eligible for stitching/coalescing.
3. Preserve tenant isolation and auditability; coalescing must never allow cross-tenant data leakage.

Non-goals

- This spec does not change fundamental billing semantics. Billing implications are surfaced as warnings and telemetry; commercial pricing changes are out of scope for the initial technical rollout.
- We will not implement cross-tenant prompt content sharing; session coalescing only shares runtime state when explicitly permitted by policy (see "Affinity & Privacy").

Key concepts and terminology

- Stitchable request: a request identified as semantically mergeable with previous open session fragments by the client or router heuristics (e.g., 'append', 'stream-delta', 'followup').
- Session affinity key: an opaque key used to bind an incoming request to an in-memory model session (can be tenant-level, route-level, or client-provided).
- Coalescing window: a short time window (e.g., 50–500ms) during which compatible short sessions may be co-located onto a single backend session.
Design overview

1) Stitching Model
- API contract: new optional field in generation/chat payload: "stitch_instruction" (enum: none, append, replace, merge_safely) and "stitch_id" (string).
- Server behavior: when stitch_instruction != none and a matching open session (stitch_id) exists, router will route the fragment into the existing session's stream of tokens rather than creating a new KV context.
- Safety checks: compatibility validation includes model family compatibility, pinned model version, request temperature/fidelity thresholds, tokenization alignment check, and per-tenant policy. If validation fails, fallback to normal routing and emit a telemetry event.

2) Session Coalescing Model
- Coalescing is driven by a policy expression attached to tenant entitlements: "allow_coalesce: true|false" and an operational predicate: {max_context_fidelity, max_token_budget, allowed_model_variants}.
- The router maintains short-lived coalesce pools per region and model variant. Eligible sessions are placed into a pool for up to the configured coalescing window. When pool scheduling triggers, the runtime will instantiate as few backend sessions as feasible and map multiple logical sessions into the runtime with strict per-session boundaries enforced at the prompt/result layer.
- Coalescing will not share raw prompt text in-memory across tenants; instead, the runtime uses a multiplexing layer ensuring per-session token isolation in compute kernels and maintaining separate KV namespaces.

3) Affinity & Privacy
- Affinity levels: 
  - tenant_affinity: only same-tenant requests may be coalesced (default for regulated customers).
  - route_affinity: same tenant + same route (stronger isolation).
  - cross_tenant_shared: cross-tenant coalescing allowed only when tenants opt-in and have identical model fidelity constraints.
- Coalescing is disabled automatically for routes with PII classification, high-sensitivity labels, or when KMS-wrapped keys require dedicated HSM-backed sessions.

4) KV and Cache lifecycle changes
- Each logical session maintains a virtual KV namespace id. Backend runtime preserves separate KV keys per logical session to avoid contamination. To reduce duplication, runtime implements "sparse prefix reuse": when two sessions share an identical recent prefix, the kernel re-uses precomputed attention artifacts but still enforces namespace separation.

API changes and examples

- New optional fields for generation/chat API (HTTP/JSON):

  {
    "stitch_id": "string (optional - opaque)",
    "stitch_instruction": "none|append|merge_safely|replace",
    "coalesce_preference": "auto|tenant_affinity|route_affinity|deny",
    "session_ttl_ms": "integer (optional)"
  }

- Example: appending a chunked document: 

  POST /v1/generate
  {
    "model": "rwd-llama-70b-econ-v1",
    "stitch_id": "doc-12345-chunk-1",
    "stitch_instruction": "append",
    "input": "First chunk of a long document..."
  }

Operational configuration table

| Setting | Default | Purpose | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| coalesce_window_ms | 100 | How long router holds eligible sessions to attempt packing | eng-platform |
| max_coalesce_per_backend | 12 | Max logical sessions per backend runtime instance | eng-serving-runtime |
| stitch_validation_timeout_ms | 30 | Timeout in router for compatibility checks | eng-platform |
| tenant_opt_out_label | "no-coalesce" | Tenant label to disable automatic coalescing | customer-success |
SLOs and telemetry

- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for coalesced and non-coalesced paths must be tracked separately. Baseline SLO: coalesced p95 <= non-coalesced p95 + 40ms.
- Cost: track GPU-ms per-token and compare coalesced vs baseline per tenant segment.
- Correctness: monitor stitch-fallback-rate (number of stitch attempts that fell back to normal routing) and stitch-reorder-rate (cases where appending changed logical response ordering). Acceptable initial thresholds: stitch-fallback-rate < 5% and stitch-reorder-rate < 0.05%.
- Security: audit logs for any session coalesce actions, including affinity decision, participating tenant IDs, and decision reason.

Rollout plan

1) Canary (2 weeks): opt-in internal tenants + a small set of low-sensitivity beta customers. Metrics: latency, GPU-ms/token, fallback-rate. Blocker criteria: coalesced p95 worse than baseline p95 by > 60ms for > 10% of requests.
2) Beta (6 weeks): broader self-serve opt-in for customers with normal sensitivity. Provide UI toggle in Console and API flags. Add billing telemetry but no pricing changes.
3) Default-on for host/standard (3 months): flip default to on for non-restricted tenants; provide a 30-day notice and migration guidance.
4) Enterprise mode (parallel): for regulated tenants, provide dedicated per-tenant coalesce pools with tenant_affinity enforced.

Migration and compatibility notes

- Existing clients not sending stitch fields operate unchanged (stitch_instruction defaults to none).
- Customers that currently expect strict per-request billing may observe a small shift in cost-per-token telemetry due to reduced overheads; we will surface this in the Console under "Cost Insights -> Session Coalescing".

Testing matrix

- Unit tests: router decision logic for stitch compatibility, pool placement, TTL expiry.
- Integration: runtime isolation tests validating KV namespace separation under heavy coalesce packing (simulated multi-tenant traffic).
- Perf: synthetic conversational workloads with varying fragment sizes to validate GPU-ms/token improvements and tail latency.
- Security: adversarial mixing tests ensuring no prompt leakage across tenant boundaries.

Instrumentation and dashboards

- New dashboards: 
  - "Session Coalesce Overview" (global coalesce rate, average pool fill, avg coalesce window time)
  - "Tenant Coalesce Health" (per-tenant cost delta, fallback-rate, opt-out status)
  - "Stitch Errors" (reasons: model mismatch, pin mismatch, validation timeout)

Ownership and runbooks

- Owners: 
  - Product: Priya Nair (strategy + customer communication)
  - Eng Platform: Evan Brooks (router/policy)
  - Serving Runtime: Lina Gomez (runtime multiplexing, KV semantics)
- Runbook outlines: failure modes and mitigation. Examples: 
  - If coalesce backend saturates -> throttle new coalesce pools and revert to non-coalesced routing. Notify oncall and adjust coalesce_window_ms down by 50%.
  - If stitch_reorder_rate rises above threshold -> temporarily disable stitching for affected routes and create hotfix that forces strict session ordering.

Open questions (for review)

1. Billing model: should we expose a "coalesce credit" for customers who opt-out but want to pay for dedicated runtime? Recommend cross-team sync with Finance.
2. Deterministic replay: how do we guarantee exact response replay for stitched sessions when a fragment was merged and later trimmed? Proposal: store a lightweight fragment log per logical session for 48 hours.
3. Opt-in UX: should the Console provide per-route default and per-route overrides or a single tenant-level toggle?

Appendix: CLI/Debugging examples

- Inspect router decision for an incoming request:
  $ redwoodctl debug router --request-id=abcd-1234
  Decision: stitch_attempted=true, stitch_id=doc-12345-chunk-1, decision_reason=compatible, pool_id=coalesce-us-west-3-42

- Sample telemetry event (JSON shown for diagnostics):
  {
    "event": "stitch_attempt",
    "request_id": "abcd-1234",
    "stitch_id": "doc-12345-chunk-1",
    "decision": "fallback",
    "reason": "model_mismatch"
  }

Related work and references

- See runtime KV cache lifecycle document for sparse prefix reuse algorithm.
- Prior PRD: Predictive Batching & Cost Optimizer (2026-03-01) for performance baselining.

Summary and next steps

If approved, engineering teams will begin implementation in the router and runtime multiplexing layers per the rollout plan. Product will prepare documentation, migration notes, and Console toggles for customer opt-in. Finance and Sales will be engaged to review billing implications before defaulting this behavior on for any customers.

payload.page_title: SLO to Customer Impact Classifier and Remediation Workflow

sections.body:
Overview

This page defines a reproducible classifier that maps SLO signals to a customer-impact tier and a prescriptive remediation workflow. It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)
- Customer Success (CS) and Support for high-impact incidents

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 200ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Widespread request failures or complete service outage across regions | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

SLO catalog excerpt (example mapping)
| SLO name | Metric | Target | Error-budget window | Default customer-impact tier |
|----------|--------|--------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| request_latency_p95_public | request_latency_p95{route=~"/v1/.*"} | <= 200ms | 30d | 2 |
| api_error_rate_5m | sum(rate(api_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests[5m])) | <= 0.5% | 7d | 1 |
| embedding_throughput_tail | embedding_infer_latency_p99 | < 1.2s | 14d | 3 |
| console_ui_availability | synthetic_check(console_login) | 99.5% monthly | 30d | 3 |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates the following scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Combined score maps to Tier: Score >= 80 -> Tier 1; 60–79 -> Tier 2; 30–59 -> Tier 3; < 30 -> Tier 4.
5) Attach classification to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

Heuristics inputs (examples)
- affected_tenant_ratio: percent of total tenant RPS impacted.
- p95_latency_delta: percent change vs baseline.
- p99_error_spike: absolute increase in error count at p99.
- active_cs_tickets: number of open tickets tagged /inference or /api.

Operational remediations by tier
Tier 1 (Immediate response)
- Page the SRE oncall and SRE lead.
- Open an incident in the incident-management system using template: tag=CUSTOMER_IMPACT_TIER_1.
- Run mitigation playbook: fallback-to-compatible-model-variant (see runbook link).
- If capacity-related: trigger immediate capacity burst policy (see CLI below).
- Notify CS and Product leadership within 15 minutes with templated Slack/Jira.

Tier 2 (High-priority)
- Notify on-call via high-severity Slack alert.
- Execute targeted throttles or tenant fair-share configuration.
- Begin canary rollback of recent model or config changes (if correlated).

Tier 3 (Operational handling)
- Create ticket and schedule on-call investigation within 30–60 minutes.
- Apply mitigations from the runbook: restart worker pool, clear KV cache, or disabled newly-deployed feature flag.

Tier 4 (Monitoring)
- Monitor metrics and let automated remediation run. If unresolved after SLA window (6 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

Sample alert rule (Prometheus-style YAML)
alert: HighAPIErrorRate
expr: |
  sum(rate(api_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
  impact: "possible-customer-impact"
annotations:
  summary: "API error rate >0.5% over 5m"
  runbook: "https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation"

Enrichment query examples (pseudo-SQL / analytics)
- Tenants affected in last 10m: SELECT tenant_id, count(*) FROM requests WHERE status >= 500 AND timestamp > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 50;
- Support ticket correlation: count tickets where created_at >= now()-10m AND tags IN ('api','inference')

Capacity escalation knobs (examples)
| Trigger | Condition | Automated action | Escalation threshold |
|---------|-----------|------------------|----------------------|
| headroom_exhausted | available_gpu_slots < 5% | trigger-burst-alloc --pool=shared-burst | immediate (Tier1) |
| model_warm_pool_empty | warm_pool_size < configured_min | scale-up warm pool by 2 nodes | Tier2 |
| p95_latency_spike | p95 > baseline*1.5 for 10m | enable-prefetch-kv-cache=true | Tier2 |

CLI examples
- Trigger burst capacity (operators only):
  rcmd infra capacity burst apply --pool shared-burst --reason "Tier1 SLO breach" --expires 30m
- Re-route traffic to fallback models:
  rcmd infra routing promote --from model-xyz-v2 --to model-xyz-v1 --weight 100

Communication templates
Slack template (Tier1)
- Channel: #incidents
- Message: :rotating_light: *Tier 1 SLO breach* — request_error_rate_5m at 1.2% impacting ~32% of tenants. IC: @oncall. Mitigation in progress: toggling fallback routing. Please notify CS lead @renee.zhao. Incident link: <INCIDENT_URL>

Jira template fields
- Priority: P0 for Tier1, P1 for Tier2, P2 for Tier3/4
- Components: runtime, routing, capacity, product-feature
- Labels: slo-breach, customer-impact-tier-<n>, automated-enrichment

Post-incident / Error-budget reconciliation
1) Add classification evidence (metrics, tenant list, tickets) to the incident story.
2) Compute error-budget consumption attributable to the incident window.
3) For Tier1/Tier2 incidents: schedule a joint SRE/Product/CS triage within 72 hours. The triage determines whether to take a governance action (e.g., customer credits, temporary throttle, emergency capacity commit).
4) Document remediation plan and assign owners with due dates.

Postmortem checklist (to include in incident review)
- Summary of classifier result and whether the initial tier matched customer reports.
- Timeline of detection -> mitigation -> recovery.
- Root cause and contributing factors including capacity and SLO misconfigurations.
- Action items (owner + due date) and follow-up on error-budget policy.
- Evidence attachments: metrics, logs, enrichment query results.

Automation and operational tooling notes
- The classifier runs in the telemetry enrichment pipeline (owner: telemetry-team). Inputs are Prometheus alerts, request traces, and support ticket API.
- All automated classification decisions must be auditable: store the computed scores and inputs in incident metadata.
- Use feature flags to disable automatic Tier upgrades in sensitive customer accounts.

Ownership and governance
- SLO owner: Each SLO must list a primary owner (SRE or Product) and a secondary owner. Owners are responsible for maintaining mapping in this catalog.
- Classification engine owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com.
- Incident review owner for Tier1/Tier2: SRE lead on rotation.

Runbook links (examples)
- API error mitigation: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation
- Fallback routing: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/fallback-routing-and-rollbacks
- Capacity burst playbook: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/capacity-burst-and-burst-rollback

Change log
- 2026-01-15 — Initial draft published (Priya Natarajan).
- 2026-02-20 — Added capacity knobs and CLI examples (review: Liam O'Connor).
- 2026-03-01 — Finalized communication templates and post-incident checklist (review: Renee Zhao).

Appendix: sample incident evidence payload (JSON snippet)
{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-0115-001",
  "slo": "api_error_rate_5m",
  "computed_scores": { "failure_scope": 78, "severity": 85, "customer_exposure": 60 },
  "mapped_tier": 1,
  "top_affected_tenants": ["tenant-acme", "tenant-vela"],
  "evidence_queries": ["tenant_impact_query_2026-01-15-10m"]
}

If you are an on-call SRE and this workflow appears to misclassify an incident, immediately create a ticket in the SRE backlog and tag the telemetry-owner for a review.

Contact
- Document owner: Priya Natarajan (pri@redwood.com)
- Telemetry owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com
- Incident management: incidents@redwood.com

payload.page_title: Operator Sandbox Hardened Runtime Deploy Guide (VPC & On‑Prem)

sections.body:
Overview

This guide documents the recommended process for deploying Redwood's operator sandbox (a constrained, operator-facing runtime) in hardened private environments. It covers both VPC-backed private deploys and on-prem, air-gapped installations, and focuses on safe field installs, day-2 operational guardrails, upgrade/rollback procedures, and mapping to customer readiness criteria. Target audience: platform/operator engineers and field deployment leads.

Scope and goals

- Scope: operator sandbox runtime (minimal runtime slice used for operator validation, testing, and controlled canary traffic). Includes runtime image layout, agent configuration, and the operator-facing management surface.
- Goals: predictable rollouts, minimal blast radius for experiments, clear telemetry/forensics guarantees, and a tested rollback path that preserves customer evidence for compliance.
- Out of scope: full multi-tenant tenant provisioning, long-term model artifact lifecycle (refer to private-deploy-operator-handshake guide).

Preflight checklist (must be green before starting)

| Item | Minimum requirement | Verification command / note | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Hardware profile | Verified node types (see compatibility matrix) | cat /etc/redwood-hw | Customer infra / Field |
| Network egress | Required endpoints whitelisted (control plane IPs) | curl -sS https://status.redwood.ai/ping | Ops / Customer netops |
| KMS/HSM | Customer KMS reachable and test envelope ok | redwood-cli kms test --key-id=... | Security / Field |
| Time sync | NTP set, max skew < 250ms | chronyc sources ||
| Image signing | Signed images approved by supply chain | cosign verify ... | Platform Security |
| Telemetry contract | Sampling policy agreed; PI filter rules signed | Confirm telemetry contract ID in ticket | Customer success |

Note: If operating air-gapped, the "Network egress" step is replaced by validated offline artifact bundle and a signed manifest (see Air‑gapped artifact delivery below).

High-level deployment strategy

1. Staged operator sandbox: deploy to a small subset of operator VMs (2–3 nodes) in a dedicated operator subnet.
2. Canary traffic: route < 1% of synthetic requests and operator diagnostics traffic to the sandbox.
3. Observability gates: verify metric and trace ingest, KV cache checksum parity, and model-artifact validation.
4. Ramp/abort: use automated gates to either ramp to 20% operator traffic or abort and trigger rollback.

Runtime hardening checklist

- Filesystem: mount runtime directories read-only where possible; writable path constrained to /var/lib/redwood/operator-sandbox.
- Process isolation: run runtime inside an unprivileged container user; drop CAP_SYS_ADMIN and CAP_NET_ADMIN.
- Network egress: restrict to control-plane and approved telemetry endpoints; deny-by-default policy for unknown outbound.
- Secrets handling: KMS envelope-only; no long-lived plaintext keys on disk. Ephemeral session tokens expire <= 10m.
- Image verification: enforce cosign verification step in boot path; abort if verification fails.
- Resource limits: cgroups v2 enforced, mem swap disabled for runtime containers. CPU shares pinned for predictable latency.

Operator sandbox specific config examples

YAML snippet: runtime-config.yaml

---
runtime:
  sandbox: true
  max_workers: 4
  kv_cache_retention_seconds: 300
  telemetry_sampling: 0.05
  kms_provider: customer-kms
  image_signature_policy: "cosign-enforce"
  health_probe_interval_seconds: 15
---

CLI deployment example (VPC)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: redwoodctl bootstrap --env private --control-plane-endpoint https://cp-01.redwood.internal --org-id acme-corp --operator-mode sandbox
sections.heading: bootstrap control-plane handshake (operator)

sections.body:
redwoodctl apply -f runtime-config.yaml --operator-slice sandbox-1

Air‑gapped artifact delivery and verification

1. Customer receives signed artifact bundle (.tar.gz) with manifest.json and cosign signatures.
2. Field operator verifies bundle checksums and signatures locally: sha256sum -c manifest.sha256; cosign verify-blob --signature manifest.sig manifest.json.
3. Import images into local registry: ctr images import ... or docker load ...
4. Populate local artifact index and pin image digests in runtime-config.yaml (do not use mutable tags).

Deployment steps (detailed)

1. Provision operator subnet and reserved nodes (2–3) with required hardware profile. Tag nodes with role=operator-sandbox.
2. Run preflight checklist (above) and create a validation ticket in JIRA with checklist attachments.
3. Push signed runtime images to target registry (or import offline bundle).
4. Bootstrap control-plane handshake: redwoodctl bootstrap ... — obtain operator credentials and verify TLS cert chain.
5. Apply runtime-config.yaml to slice "sandbox-1" with limited resources.
6. Enable metric/trace forwarding with sampling policy 5% and verify ingest (check dashboards: operator-sandbox-health).
7. Start canary synthetic traffic (script included in repo /ops/canary/synthetic-runner).
8. Monitor gates for 30m: latency 95p < 120ms, error rate < 0.5%, KV cache checksum parity = 100%.
9. If gates pass, ramp to 20% operator load and re-evaluate for 60m. If any gate fails, execute rollback procedure.

Automated gate checks (examples)

- latency_95p_operator_sandbox < 120ms for 30m window
- operator_errors_total_rate < 0.5% per minute
- kv_cache_checksum_equivalence == true for all operator nodes
- telemetry_ingest_rate >= expected_sample_rate * nodes

Day‑2 operations runbook (operator slice)

1. Routine checks (daily):
   - Confirm operator-sandbox processes are running: sudo crictl ps | grep redwood-sandbox
   - Check disk usage of writable path: df -h /var/lib/redwood/operator-sandbox
   - Verify clock skew: chronyc tracking
2. Incident triage (high level):
   - If latency regressions observed, switch sandbox traffic to safemode: redwoodctl slice update sandbox-1 --safemode true
   - If persistent errors or KV divergence, quiesce the slice and collect forensic snapshot: redwoodctl collect-snapshot --slice sandbox-1 --output /tmp/snapshot.tgz
   - If disk corruption suspected, mark node for immutable reprovision and fail traffic to replacement.
3. Telemetry sampling and PI scrubbing: ensure telemetry pipeline adheres to agreed PI filters before any external egress. Use redwood-telemetry-validator tool.

Upgrade and rollback procedures

Safe upgrade pattern (stateless first, stateful last):

1. Prepare signed upgrade bundle and update runtime-config with new image digests.
2. Deploy stateless components (ingress, proxy, operator API) to sandbox-1 one replica at a time; validate smoke health checks.
3. Deploy runtime code on one node, run KV cache warm-up and checksum verification.
4. If checks pass, continue rolling update across nodes.

Rollback cookbook (fast abort)

1. If any gate fails during upgrade, run: redwoodctl rollback --slice sandbox-1 --to-image <previous-digest>
2. Immediately create scoped forensic snapshot: redwoodctl collect-snapshot --slice sandbox-1 --reason upgrade-failure --retain 90d
3. Notify customer and security with evidence bundle (signed manifest, logs, checksum report).
4. If previous image is unavailable locally, initiate image pull from validated bucket or customer-provided artifact index.

Forensic and evidence preservation

- Snapshots include: encrypted logs (signed), KV cache digests, image manifest, cosign verification outputs, and telemetry sampling proof.
- Retention policy: sandbox upgrade failure evidence must be retained for 90 days by default for compliance requests.

Customer requirements mapping (quick crosswalk)

- Network whitelists: control-plane endpoints, telemetry endpoints (or offline artifact exchange).
- KMS: ability to perform envelope encryption and sign/verify with customer-managed keys.
- Image supply chain: support for cosign or equivalent signing; offline bundle import.
- Audit: ability to collect and export signed forensic snapshots within SLA.

Minimum customer acceptance test (CAT) checklist

1. Control-plane handshake completes and mutual TLS validated.
2. Signed runtime bundle verified and loaded.
3. Telemetry pipeline receives sampled data and PI scrub verified.
4. Canary synthetic traffic passes gates for 90 minutes.
5. Operator team successfully performs a rollback drill (test rollback) under guidance.

Operational metrics and SLOs (sandbox slice)

- Availability (slice-level): 99.9% per calendar month
- Latency: 95th percentile < 120ms for operator flows under baseline load
- Successful canary gate pass rate (target): 95% of staged canaries complete without rollback

Ownership, escalation, and contacts

- Primary: Operator Field Engineering (owner team) — ops-oncall@redwood.ai
- Security contact: platform-security@redwood.ai
- Customer success lead: assigned per account (check Jira field: customer-owner)

Related pages and artifacts

- Reference: operator-handshake-and-evidence-playbook (internal id: DOC-1422)
- Artifact repo: git@repo.redwood:operator/sandbox-deploy.git
- Telemetry contract template: CON-telemetry-contract-v2

Appendix: useful commands and debug snippets
sections.heading: apply operator runtime manifest

sections.body: sudo crictl ps --label sandbox=true
sections.heading: quick process list

sections.body: redwoodctl kv-checksum --node node-01 > kv-checksum-node-01.txt
sections.heading: collect local KV checksum

sections.body: redwoodctl rollback --slice sandbox-1 --to-image sha256:abcdef1234567890
sections.heading: trigger rollback (example)

sections.body:
cosign verify --key k8s://projects/_/keyRings/myring/cryptoKeys/mykey registry.example.com/redwood/runtime@sha256:abcdef1234

Conformance and audit notes

- All deploys must create a JIRA ticket with the preflight checklist attached.
- Any rollback invoked in production requires a postmortem with evidence bundle attached within 3 business days.

Revision history

- 2026-02-10: Initial draft — Asha Nair
- 2026-04-02: Added air-gapped artifact verification steps — Marco Alvarez
- 2026-07-12: Expanded forensic snapshot and retention guidance — Elena Park
