payload.page_title: Operator Field Autonomy and Observability Contract

sections.body:
Summary:
This contract defines the minimum observability, telemetry, and operator autonomy guarantees for Redwood Private deployments in the field (VPC and on-prem). It is intended for operators, field engineers, solutions engineers, and customer SRE contacts. The goal is to ensure predictable supportability, privacy compliance, and safe operator autonomy while preserving the ability to triage incidents remotely or on-site.

Audience and scope:
- Audience: Field operators, customer SREs, Redwood deployment engineers, security reviewers.
- Scope: All Private mode deployments (VPC and on-prem packaged appliances) delivered after 2025-10-01. Excludes isolated legacy installs with pre-approved exception.

Principles and guarantees:
1) Minimal observability baseline: every installation must export a defined set of metrics, health endpoints, logs, and structured traces to allow Redwood and the customer to validate runtime health and diagnose performance regressions.
2) Operator autonomy: field operators may perform a bounded set of operational actions (start/stop services, rotate local certs, adjust autoscale knobs) defined below. Actions that change cryptographic trust, customer data routing, or model artifacts require coordinated change windows and Redwood approval.
3) Privacy and residency: telemetry must be filtered, sampled, and redacted to meet the customer’s data residency and PII policy. Telemetry that leaves the customer environment must be minimized and tenant-scoped.
4) Fail-safe updates and rollback: all upgrades to telemetry pipelines or observability agents must include canaries, preflight checks, and rollback plans.

Owners and escalation:
- Document owner: eng-private-deployments Observability Squad (primary contact: Asha Menon).
- Field escalation: FieldOps -> SolutionsEng -> Oncall-Redwood-Private -> Security if PII suspected.
- Communication channels: dedicated Slack channel #private-deploy-telemetry, PagerDuty escalation policy: PD-L2 -> PD-L3.

Minimum telemetry contract (table):
Metric/Signal | Unit | Collection frequency | Retention (local) | Export allowed (yes/no) | Purpose
------------- | ---- | -------------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- | -------
runtime.uptime_seconds | seconds | 10s | 90d | yes | basic liveness and uptime SLO
requests.total | count | 5s | 30d | yes | throughput and capacity planning
latency.p50_ms | ms | 5s | 30d | yes | latency SLO monitoring
kv_cache.hit_ratio | ratio | 30s | 14d | no | local performance tuning (sensitive)
model.load_failures | count | 10s | 90d | yes | model rollout health
disk.free_bytes | bytes | 60s | 14d | yes | storage pressure alerts
auth.failures | count | 10s | 30d | no | security-sensitive, only aggregated metrics exported
logs.system | text | streaming | 14d (rotating) | no except summary | debugging; full logs kept locally
trace.requests | spans | sampled | 7d | yes (sampled) | distributed request tracing

Telemetry collection config (examples):
- Prometheus scrape config (field appliance):
  - job_name: redwood-runtime
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['127.0.0.1:9090']
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: ['__address__']
        target_label: 'instance'
- Fluent Bit snapshot config (logs -> local buffer):
  [SERVICE]
    Flush 5
    Log_Level info
  [INPUT]
    Name tail
    Path /var/log/redwood/runtime/*.log
    Tag runtime.*
  [FILTER]
    Name grep
    Match runtime.*
    Regex message (?!.*(SSN|credit_card))
  [OUTPUT]
    Name file
    Match *
    Path /var/lib/redwood/logs/forwarded/%Y-%m-%d.log

Sampling and export policy:
- Default metric export: full for non-PII numerical metrics.
- Log export: only pre-aggregated summaries or alerts may be exported offsite. Raw logs containing potentially sensitive values must remain on local storage and be retrievable under traceable support request with customer consent.
- Trace sampling: default 0.5% global; 100% for error traces (status >= 500) for 30 minutes after an incident detection window.
- Snapshot window: when a critical incident is declared, operators may trigger a 15-minute high-resolution capture (metrics at 1s, traces full, logs forwarded) — requires email or Slack approval from customer contact unless pre-authorized in the contract.

Data handling and privacy safeguards:
- Redaction rules: all log lines MUST be run through the redaction filter that removes email addresses, credit card numbers, and Social Security/ID patterns.
- Local encryption: telemetry at rest must be encrypted using the host KMS (LUKS or cloud KMS-backed) with keys managed by the customer where supported.
- Egress controls: allowlist IPs for telemetry export must be established during onboarding. Any change to allowlist requires a signed change order.
- Data residency: export endpoints must be in the customer-approved region. Global export of tenant-level data is disallowed by default.

Operator autonomy matrix (what field ops can do without Redwood):
- Can: restart runtime services (redwood-runtime.service), clear local non-persistent caches, rotate TLS certs using pre-shared CSR procedure, adjust local autoscaler thresholds within vendor-defined safe ranges, collect local diagnostics bundle.
- Cannot (without coordinated change): replace model artifact repositories, change outbound telemetry allowlist, change KMS key bindings, modify control plane endpoint URLs, adjust privilege escalation or RBAC policies.

Deployment acceptance checklist (numbered):
1) Confirm hardware inventory matches Customer Requirements Minimums and serial numbers registered.
2) Confirm network ACLs and egress allowlist are as documented.
3) Verify Prometheus and Fluent Bit are running and serving /metrics and /health endpoints.
4) Run preflight acceptance tests (see validation queries).
5) Verify telemetry export endpoints are reachable and export handshake succeeds (TLS verification).
6) Validate local encryption at rest and KMS integration.
7) Create and upload initial support bundle to customer-controlled storage; validate retrieval.

Validation queries (examples):
- Prometheus: up{job="redwood-runtime"} == 1
- Alert query: increase(runtime.uptime_seconds[5m]) > 0
- Log sample: grep -E "ERROR|WARN" /var/lib/redwood/logs/recent.log | tail -n 50
- KV cache sanity: curl -s localhost:9091/debug/kv_status | jq '.entries | length'

Upgrade and rollback procedure for observability agents:
1) Author preflight: publish agent version and change log to deployment ticket.
2) Canary: roll to 5% of hosts (or 1 host in single-node installs) and monitor for 30 minutes for: CPU spikes (>20% baseline), missing metrics, or log volume anomalies.
3) Automated tests: run scrape verification and sample trace exports.
4) Gradual roll: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 15 minute observation windows.
5) Rollback: if any canary fails, trigger immediate rollback to previous agent image and collect support bundle with failing host telemetry.
Commands (examples):
- Verify metrics endpoint: curl -fsS http://localhost:9090/metrics | head -n 20
- Collect support bundle: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/collect-support-bundle --out /tmp/bundle.tar.gz --since 1h
- Rollback agent: sudo dpkg -i /var/cache/redwood/agent-1.2.3.deb || sudo apt-get install --reinstall redwood-agent=1.2.2

Operational playbooks (short):
- High CPU/latency during model load:
  1. Check model.load_failures and runtime memory pressure.
  2. If KV cache thrash detected, clear non-persistent cache and schedule model reload with reduced batch size.
  3. If persistent, open ticket with Redwood runtime team and attach support bundle.
- Telemetry export blocked (network):
  1. Verify egress ACLs and DNS resolution.
  2. If outbound is blocked, set local retention to high-resolution buffer; mark incident and schedule assisted export under customer approval.

Acceptance tests and SLOs for observability pipeline:
- Metric availability SLO: 99.9% of expected metric series should be present in Prometheus for each 24h window.
- Alerting latency SLO: critical alerts (node down, model load failure) must generate notification within 30s of detection.
- Support bundle retrieval SLO: support bundle generated and retrievable within 10 minutes of request during business hours.

Templates and example artifacts (appendix):
- Support bundle contents: /var/lib/redwood/logs/*, /etc/redwood/config.yaml, /opt/redwood/state/kv_snapshot.json, prometheus-scrape-logs, system journal tail.
- Example redaction regex: (?: \d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4} )|(?: 4[0-9]{12}(?:[0-9]{3})? )|(?:[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,})

Related pages and references:
- Post-installation telemetry and acceptance checklist (internal)
- Onprem telemetry sampling and privacy playbook (internal)
- Immutable packaging and image signing playbook

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: Created by Asha Menon (initial draft).
- 2026-02-03: Added sampling policy and incident snapshot window (review by Diego Ramirez).
- 2026-09-15: Hardened upgrade canary steps and added SLOs (finalized for GA deployments).

Contact and feedback:
For questions or exceptions, contact eng-private-deployments Observability Squad (obs-owner@redwood.ai) or file a change request in the deployment ticketing tracker.

payload.page_title: VPC Handshake and Operator Blueprint for Private Deploys

sections.body: This playbook defines the VPC "handshake" process and an operator blueprint to safely install, validate, and operate Redwood Private deployments. It combines deployment handoff steps, on-prem packaging checks, day-2 operational guardrails, and a deterministic upgrade/rollback procedure intended for field operators and delivery engineers.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Standardize handoff between Delivery/Install and Customer Ops.
- Ensure a signed, verifiable package and immutable boot path for air-gapped and VPC installs.
- Provide a concise day-2 operator playbook for common incidents, model swaps, and upgrades.
- Define customer-facing requirements and acceptance tests required to proceed to production.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments field-integration (pager: @field-oncall)
- Secondary owner: eng-platform - runtime (email: runtime-ops@redwood.ai)
- Delivery contact: Solutions Eng (assigned per customer)
sections.heading: Owners and contact

sections.body: - Field delivery engineers, SREs operating customer VPCs, customer platform engineers, and account technical leads.
sections.heading: Intended audience

sections.body:
1) Network & routing
   - BGP or static routes in place between customer transit and Redwood egress (if hybrid).
   - Required ports open: 443 (control plane), 9000-9010 TCP (metrics/operational tunnels), 22 only for image signing/verification tasks if operator uses SSH bastion.
2) Identity & secrets
   - Customer KMS reachable and configured for envelope encryption OR HSM module present for air-gapped installs.
   - Service account with least privilege for telemetry uploads (scope: telemetry:write).
3) Hardware & storage
   - GPU nodes: min 2x for HA, recommended 3x per tenant for production.
   - Persistent storage: 1.5x model footprint available for staging + snapshots.
4) Timing
   - Scheduled maintenance window: minimum 2 hours for initial provisioning; upgrades require 30–90 minutes depending on model swap complexity.
sections.heading: Prerequisites (operator checklist)

sections.body:
- Model cache size: recommended 40% of GPU DRAM for L2 caching
- KV cache retention: 3 hours by default, configurable per-tenant
- Batching target latency: 50ms median per-token under normal load
sections.heading: Quick configuration reference (table)

sections.body:
- Customer VPC (private subnets) -> NAT/Egress -> Redwood control plane (mutual TLS)
- Optional: Edge gateway (optional for air-gapped) -> Ops bastion -> On-prem runtime cluster

VPC Handshake: step-by-step operator flow
1) Pre-handshake validation (Delivery):
   a) Delivery engineer runs local preflight script: `redwood-ops preflight --manifest manifest.json` to validate network, DNS, and KMS connectivity.
   b) Gather the following artifacts to send to customer: signed-install-manifest (SHA256), operator-checklist, public key for image signatures.
2) Customer acceptance of manifest:
   a) Customer security lead verifies manifest signature against the provided public key.
   b) Both parties sign the Handoff Acceptance Record (HAR) — a short JSON with timestamps and signer CNs.
3) Secure transfer and attestation:
   a) For managed VPC: exchange ephemeral tokens scoped to the install window (TTL 1 hour).
   b) For air-gapped: deliver signed images and a manifest on removable media with hash evidence; operator performs local verification using `sha256sum` and `gpg --verify`.
4) Bootstrap sequence (operator):
sections.heading: Network topology (text diagram)

sections.body:
1. Import signed image bundle: `redwood-ops image import --signed-bundle bundle.tar.gz`
   2. Verify image signature: failure -> abort and contact Delivery.
   3. Provision control-plane agent: `kubectl apply -f agent-install.yaml` (agent only opens egress to designated endpoints).
   4. Start health-check loop and wait for control-plane registration: `redwood-ops status watch --timeout 600`

Acceptance tests (run by Customer + Delivery):
- Smoke tests (pass/fail):
  1) API connectivity: POST /v1/health -> 200 within 2s
  2) Model load: request cold-load of pinned model -> success within 45s
  3) KV cache warm-path test: repeated prompt sequence returns cached tokens after second call with latency < 30ms
  4) Telemetry & logging: agent logs received by control plane within 60s of event emission
sections.heading: Steps to execute in order

sections.body:
- All images must be signed with a Redwood release key. Operators must verify: `gpg --verify images.sig images.tar.gz` and match SHA256 in manifest.
- Image provenance: include `build-id`, `kgx-version`, `kernel-optim` tag in package metadata.
- Immutable boot: golden-boot image recommended; any divergence requires attestation recorded in ticketing system.
sections.heading: On-prem packaging & verification checklist

sections.body:
- Normal maintenance (daily):
  - Verify agent health: `redwood-ops agent check` (expect status: ready).
  - Confirm telemetry sampling rates: must remain at configured baseline to preserve billing fidelity.
- Model hot-swap (operator-safe path):
  1) Validate new model artifact in staging tenant with 1-2 benchmark traces.
  2) Quiesce traffic for target shard: set routing policy to `drain` for 30s.
  3) Swap model binary with atomic rename + restart worker process.
  4) Health-check and small-traffic canary (5% traffic for 15 minutes).
  5) If regressions observed (quality or latency), perform immediate rollback (see rollback procedure).
- KV cache and shard rebalance: daily low-traffic window preferred; use `cache-evict --grace 60` to avoid cold-start storms.
sections.heading: Day-2 operator blueprint (common flows)

sections.body:
1) Canary upgrade (safe path):
   - Create canary group: select 5% of shards, prefer non-critical customer shards.
   - Deploy new runtime binary + model variant.
   - Monitor metrics for 30 minutes against baseline: p99 latency, error rate, answered tokens, and model quality signals (prompt-set eval).
   - Success criteria: p99 latency regression < +10ms, error rate delta < 0.1%, model quality pass rate > 98% for validation set.
2) Gradual rollout: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 30-minute observation windows.
3) Automated rollback triggers:
   - p99 latency > baseline + 25ms for 3 consecutive observation windows
   - error rate spike > 0.5% absolute
   - Quality regression detected by eval harness (fail fast)
4) Manual rollback steps (operator):
   a) Execute `redwood-ops rollout rollback --deployment <id> --reason \"regression detected\"`
   b) Notify Delivery and open an incident ticket with runbook ID.
   c) Run post-rollback smoke tests and confirm acceptance tests pass.
sections.heading: Upgrade and rollback procedure (deterministic)

sections.body:
1) Detect: alert fires (latency or error rate).
2) Contain: toggle traffic to fallback model variant using `routing policy set --variant fallback`
3) Mitigate: increase autoscale target temporarily, enable prefix caching for affected routes.
4) Remediate: identify root cause, apply hotfix or rollback, schedule postmortem if SLO breach occurred.
sections.heading: Incident runbook (fast triage)

sections.body:
- Customer must provide: VPC contact, KMS endpoint or HSM details, minimal maintenance window, firewall exceptions list, and SLA contact details.
- Acceptance gating: all preflight checks pass, manifest signature validated, acceptance tests pass, and a production runbook handed to customer.
sections.heading: Customer requirements & acceptance matrix (short table)

sections.body:
- Request success rate >= 99.5% (rolling 30d)
- p99 latency <= 120ms for gen endpoints (local-to-region)
- Error budget: 0.5% per month
sections.heading: Operational SLOs (recommended default)

sections.body:
- Handoff Acceptance Record (HAR) JSON
- Image manifest with signature and SHA256 hashes
- Preflight output log (`preflight-<date>.log`)
- Acceptance test results (timestamped)

payload.page_title: Redwood Private: Audit log export to customer-owned object storage (S3/GCS) — design

sections.body:
h1. Overview
Redwood Private customers frequently require that audit logs leave the cluster and land in *customer-owned object storage* (for long retention, centralized SIEM pipelines, and evidence collection). This page defines the intended architecture for exporting Redwood Private audit logs to customer-owned buckets in *AWS S3* and *Google Cloud Storage (GCS)*.

h2. Scope
* In-scope
** Export *audit events* generated by Redwood control plane + runtime components in a Private deployment
** Deliver to customer-owned S3/GCS with least-privilege auth
** Standardized *JSONL* format with deterministic partitioning
** Backpressure handling and on-disk buffering
* Out-of-scope
** Customer’s downstream ingestion (Splunk/Datadog/Chronicle/etc.)
** Hosted API / Dedicated audit log export (separate workstream)

h2. Event sources (initial)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
h2. Exporter architecture
* The in-cluster component is the *audit-log-exporter* deployment (see GitHub PRs in sources/github/audit-log-exporter/).
* Exporter consumes from the internal audit event bus (Kafka in hosted; *NATS JetStream* in Private) and writes batches to object storage.
* Batching defaults: 5s or 5,000 events (whichever first).

h2. Object naming + partitioning
We need predictable paths for compliance searches and customer lifecycle policies.

*Bucket prefix:*
* `redwood-audit/v1/`

*Partition keys:*
* `tenant_id=<tenant>`
* `cluster_id=<cluster>`
* `date=YYYY-MM-DD`

*Final object example:*
* `redwood-audit/v1/tenant_id=t-2f1/cluster_id=prod-usw2/date=2025-02-14/part-000012.jsonl.gz`

h2. Format
* JSON Lines (one event per line)
* gzip compression
* Each event MUST include: `event_id`, `event_time`, `actor_type`, `actor_id`, `action`, `resource_type`, `resource_id`, `result`, `ip`, `user_agent`, `request_id`

Note: This schema is compatible with the evidence requirements doc in the security-and-compliance space.

h2. Auth models
* AWS: AssumeRole via IRSA (EKS) to a customer-provided Role ARN; require an ExternalId
* GCP: Workload Identity Federation; customer provides pool/provider + service account email

We explicitly do *not* support static long-lived access keys.

h2. Failure modes + buffering
* If object storage is unavailable or permissions are misconfigured, exporter should:
** Keep consuming until local disk watermark (default 20Gi)
** Emit warning events into `redwood-private-events`
** After watermark, apply backpressure (pause consumer)
sections.heading: *console-backend* (admin actions, settings changes)

sections.body:
* `audit_exporter_last_success_timestamp`
* `audit_exporter_failed_put_total{reason=...}`
* `audit_exporter_buffer_bytes`

h2. Customer configuration
sections.heading: Operational signals (Prometheus)

sections.body:
{code:yml}
auditLogExport:
  enabled: true
  sink: s3 # or gcs
  bucket: "acme-redwood-audit"
  prefix: "redwood-audit/v1"
  region: "us-west-2"
  kmsKeyId: "arn:aws:kms:..."
  batchSeconds: 5
  compression: "gzip"
{code}

h2. Rollout plan
sections.heading: We expose a single config block in the Private values file

sections.body:

* Do we need Azure Blob support in v1? (Some Private customers asked; see Ava Chen email thread.)
* Do we require server-side encryption always, or allow customer-managed policy-only?

h2. References

* Jira: INT-883 support-driven request
* Slack: #eng-security thread on ExternalId + bucket policy guidance

payload.page_title: VPC Satellite Staging and Operator Packaging Playbook

sections.body: This playbook describes a repeatable, low-risk process for commissioning VPC-connected satellite (edge) nodes that run a Private Redwood runtime, packaging and signing the operator images used for on-prem field installs, and executing a staged rollout with clear day‑2 operational contracts. It is intended for SRE/Platform engineers and operator field teams responsible for multi‑site private deployments and integrates packaging, observability, upgrade, and rollback guidance into a single operational flow.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- New customer requiring geographically distributed VPC satellite nodes (e.g., branch offices, edge sites)
- Customers that require signed operator images and an evidence trail for audits
- Rollouts where minimizing tenant impact and achieving zero data loss are priorities
sections.heading: When to use this playbook

sections.body:
- Document owner: Platform Reliability (owner_team: engineering)
- Runbook contact: SRE Oncall rota (pager: #sre-private-deploy)
- Packaging owner: Build & Image team (lead: Jin Park)
- Field operator lead: Customer Success Ops (lead: Omar Reyes)
sections.heading: Primary owners and contacts

sections.body:
- Target: <150 ms p50 inference latency for pinned small models at 512 tokens (customer SLA dependent)
- Availability SLO: 99.95% for control-plane reachability within region for 30-day windows
- Observability coverage: 100% of traffic routes instrumented; key traces sampled at 5%

Prerequisites checklist (operator + customer):
1) Customer VPC connectivity: BGP/peering configured, CIDR allocation produced, egress rules documented.
2) KMS/HSM access: customer KMS endpoints reachable and service account configured.
3) Hardware & firmware: NVIDIA driver >= 535.x (or vendor equivalent), BIOS firmware matching approved list; GPU thermal policy tested.
4) Image signing policy: build pipeline okta token and signing key present in secure key vault.
5) Telemetry endpoints: telemetry proxy URL, sampling policy, and retention contract defined.
sections.heading: Goals and SLOs for satellite launches

sections.body:
- Phase 1: Canary site (single satellite) — no customer traffic, synthetic load only.
- Phase 2: Pilot sites (2–3 satellites) — limited customer traffic (5–10% modal split).
- Phase 3: Regional roll (N sites) — full traffic gradually shifted via weight-based routing.
Each site runs the same runtime operator but may use model-variant pinning and runtime knobs to match local capacity.
sections.heading: Staging topology and phases

sections.body:
| Phase | Max sites | Traffic share | KV cache policy | Batching multiplier | Fallback model | Rollback trigger |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Canary | 1 | 0% | disabled | 1x | none | control-plane error rate >3% or tail latency >500ms |
| Pilot | 3 | 5–10% | prefix-only | 1–2x | quantized-variant | error budget burn >20% in 12h |
| Regional | variable | incremental to 100% | full | 2–4x | regional-fallback | sustained SLA breach 1h or operator manual stop |
sections.heading: Staged rollout matrix (operator-controlled knobs)

sections.body:
1) Build images in isolated CI pipeline (project: private-packaging).
2) Run image hardening scripts: remove debug bins, validate TLS ciphers, set non-root user.
3) Sign images with customer escrowed signing key using cosign: cosign sign --key k8s-signer.key registry.example.com/redwood/operator:sha256-XYZ.
4) Produce SBOM and attestation artifact (CycloneDX + provenance).
5) Push artifacts to customer approved registry and record digest in the deployment evidence bundle.
Important checks: image digest must match on operator manifest, SBOM must not include unapproved licenses, attestation must include build pipeline run id.
sections.heading: Packaging and image verification (operator build steps)

sections.body:
- Use manifest patches to pin operator image: image: registry.example.com/redwood/operator@sha256:XYZ
- Set rolloutStrategy: "Canary" with maxUnavailable: 1 and progressDeadlineSeconds: 1800
- Enable liveness/readiness probes with backoffLimit 6

Upgrade and rollback procedure (operator-level, step-by-step):
1) Prepare image + evidence bundle and stage in pre-prod registry.
2) Execute dry-run apply to canary site: kubectl apply --server-dry-run -f operator-canary.yaml; validate events.
3) Deploy to Canary with 0% traffic shift. Run smoke tests for 30 minutes (health checks, synthetic inference).
4) Observe metrics for 2 hours: latency, error rate, KV hit ratio, GPU utilization.
5) If pass, advance to Pilot (5–10% traffic) using routing weight change. Monitor 24h.
6) If any metric crosses the rollback trigger, perform immediate rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/operator -n redwood-system --to-revision=<previous>.
7) Collect forensic evidence and create rollback packet: kernel logs, operator events, telemetry windows (T-30m to T+30m).
Notes on safe rollback: avoid simultaneous cache migrations during rollout. If rollforward required, use staged config gate to enable feature flags.

Day‑2 operations and observability contract (operator ↔ customer):
- Logging: control-plane and runtime logs forwarded to customer endpoint with 7d retention by default, 30d optional.
- Metrics: key metrics (rpc_latencies_p50/p95, kv_cache_hits, gpu_mem_free) exported at 10s resolution with 5% trace sampling.
- Alerting thresholds (default recommended):
  - control-plane-http-5xx-rate > 1% sustained 10m -> P1
  - inference-tail-latency95 > 600ms -> P1
  - gpu-temp > 85C for >2m -> P0
  - kv-cache-miss-rate > 40% for 30m -> P2
- Oncall playbook excerpts:
  1) For P1: Activate cross-team incident bridge, flip regional traffic to fallback model, and apply operator safemode (scale to 0 safe pods if necessary).
  2) For P0 (hardware): instruct field operator to perform immediate GPU power cycling and thermal diagnostics per hardware vendor checklist.

Customer readiness checklist (package to deliver to customer before pilot):
- Completed: BGP peering test with RTT < 50ms to control-plane proxy (for regional launches).
- Completed: KMS test with key create/rotate cycle within policy.
- Completed: Signed operator image digest and SBOM delivered with checksum.
- Completed: Telemetry endpoint and sampling policy agreed and firewall exemptions configured.
- Completed: Field operator contact and escalation matrix with 24/7 phone coverage during pilot.
sections.heading: Operator manifest binding example (described)

sections.body:
- Symptom: High tail latency after pilot traffic shift.
  - Likely causes: high KV miss rate, GPU throttling, or ineffective batching.
  - Mitigation: Reduce batching multiplier, enable prefix caching, or shift traffic back to hosted fallback.
- Symptom: Image verification mismatch on customer registry.
  - Mitigation: Re-fetch digest, validate cosign attestation, and re-push signed image; gate operator deployment until digest matches.

Appendix: sample CLI snippets and pseudo-manifests
- Sign image: cosign sign --key /secrets/customer-signer.key registry.customer.example/redwood/operator:1.4.0
- Evidence bundle (example fields): build_id=ci-2026-0423, digest=sha256:XYZ, sbom_url=https://artifact-store/acme/operator/sbom.json
- Routing weight change via control-plane API (curl example): curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \
  https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/route-shift -d '{"satellite_id":"sat-123","weight":5}'
sections.heading: Common failure modes and mitigation recipes

sections.body:

- 2026-02-05: Added SBOM and cosign recommendations (Jin Park).
- 2026-03-02: Finalized rollout matrix and SLOs; security review completed (Leah Kim).

End of playbook. For questions or to schedule a pilot, ping #private-deploys or contact the Platform Reliability lead.

payload.page_title: Operational Hardening and Safe Migration Playbook for Private Deploys

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook describes an engineering-first process for operational hardening and safe workload migration for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem bundles). It combines pre-migration verification, staged rollout guidance, continuous telemetry checks, and a deterministic rollback matrix to minimize customer downtime and data risk during model, runtime, or infra migrations.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: Private deployments delivered via Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) including model swaps, runtime upgrades, kernel/quantization changes, and capacity migration between pools.
- Audience: Field engineers, SREs, deployment engineers, solutions architects, and customer success leads supporting private customers.

Owner and escalation:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments Team (eng-private-deployments).
- Runbook owner: Emma Chen (Runbook maintainer).
- On-call escalation: Private-deploys oncall -> Eng SRE -> Platform Lead.

Success criteria and SLOs for migration activity:
- Migration must not exceed 2x historical 1h error rate at 95th percentile for production traffic during the 30-minute canary window.
- Mean token latency must not regress by more than 15% from baseline across 99th percentile after steady-state (1 hour).
- No data-loss incidents (0 lost requests) and KV/embedding cache semantics preserved.

Prerequisites checklist (must be green before starting):
| Item | Description | Owner | Required state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer readiness call | Confirm maintenance window and rollback authority | Solutions Eng | scheduled/acknowledged |
| Backups | Snapshot model artifacts, KV cache snapshot if stateful | Field Engineer | completed |
| Telemetry hooks | Ensure sampling rules and traces are enabled at 100% for canary nodes | SRE | enabled |
| Capacity reserve | 20% spare GPU headroom in same region or burst pool | Capacity Planner | verified |
| Access | Field engineer has customer admin KMS & SSH keys (if onprem) | Field Engineer | verified |

Pre-migration validation (pre-flight):
1) Inventory and compatibility matrix
- Validate model binary ABI, quantization profile, and kernel compatibility against runtime version using the compatibility-checker tool:
  - CLI: rdx-compat-check --model <MODEL_PATH> --runtime <RUNTIME_TAG> --output summary.json
  - Expected exit 0. Attach summary.json to migration ticket.
2) Smoke harness in staging mirror
- Deploy identical staging shard with 10% representative KV sizes, and run the canonical smoke set (prompt-shard-smoke.json) for 30 minutes.
3) Telemetry assertion baseline
- Collect 1h of baseline telemetry (latency percentiles, error rates, token generation rate) and store in migration-buffer: bucket://redwood-migrations/<customer>/<migration-id>/baseline.json

Staged rollout plan (recommended):
- Phase 0: Dry-run verify (no traffic) — deploy to a single node in the staging cluster and run smoke tests (20–30 minutes).
- Phase 1: Canary (1–3% traffic) — route a small percentage of production traffic to new runtime/model variant for 30 minutes. Use runtime routing policy: ROUTE_POLICY=migration-canary-<id>.
- Phase 2: Ramp (5–25%) — 4 sequential ramps (5, 10, 15, 25%) each with a 15–30 minute observation window.
- Phase 3: Partial production (50%) — if all metrics stable, move to 50% for 30–60 minutes with full end-to-end smoke across customer flows.
- Phase 4: Full cutover (100%) — proceed only after green across all checks for at least 1 hour.

Metric checks and automated abort criteria (each check evaluated continuously during windows):
- Error rate (5xx) must not exceed baseline*2 for canary window or baseline + 1% absolute for larger ramps.
- Latency: P99 token latency regression >15% triggers abort.
- Quality guardrails: Automated evals on canonical prompts must not drop top-1 semantic score by >6 points (or configured customer threshold).
- Resource saturation: GPU memory usage >90% or CPU steal >40% triggers abort and immediate rollback.
- Request failure modes: Increase in KV cache misses >2x baseline -> investigate, hold ramp.

Rollback matrix (deterministic mapping of failure mode -> rollback action):
- Failure: P99 latency regression >15% during any window -> Action: Immediate route revert to prior variant, scale new nodes to 0, alert SRE and field engineer.
- Failure: Error rate >2x baseline in canary -> Action: Pause routing, scale down canary nodes, run 'rdx-dump-logs' and gather stack traces.
- Failure: Quality regression detected on canonical evals -> Action: Stop ramp, close canary, replace candidate model with previous build; if quick fix unavailable, rollback.
- Failure: KMS access error for decryption of model weights -> Action: Revoke new deployment, rollback and coordinate with security/KMS owner.

Immediate rollback commands (examples):
- API rollback (hosted control plane cooperating with private control plane):
  - curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' \n    https://private-control.<customer>.redwood/api/v1/rollouts/<migration-id>/rollback
- On-prem operator (kubectl example):
  - kubectl -n redwood set image deploy/runtime runtime=redwood/runtime:<previous-tag> --record
  - kubectl rollout status deploy/runtime -n redwood --timeout=10m

Post-rollback triage checklist:
1) Capture telemetry from rollback window and retain for 30 days in migration bucket.
2) Open a detailed incident record with root cause hypothesis within 24 hours.
3) Schedule a fix/patch release or adjust config and re-run a scheduled test migration in staging.

Day-2 operational hardening tasks (post-cutover):
- Config hardening: Enforce CIS-like kernel tuning for onprem images (sysctl settings) — include the sample sysctl block below in the node bootstrap:
  - net.core.somaxconn=1024
  - vm.swappiness=10
  - vm.dirty_ratio=15
- Token sampling & traces: Maintain 10% request trace sampling for first 72 hours, then drop to customer agreed sampling (default 1%).
- Log retention: Increase debug-level retention for migration nodes to 168 hours (7 days) and route to customer-owned S3 for audit.

Telemetry and acceptance checks (post-cutover steady-state):
- Validation run (24h): Run full acceptance harness that includes throughput, latency, and guardrail checks.
- Customer smoke test: Coordinate with customer success to validate critical flows using the customer acceptance test suite.
- Drift detection: Run nightly compare of embedding distribution, per-prompt generation length, and tokenization diffs for first 72 hours.

Packaging and artifact concerns:
- Model artifact immutability: Tag artifacts with semantic version + digest (e.g., model-v1.4+sha256:abc123). The runtime only pulls artifacts that match digest.
- Image signing: All runtime images for production use must be signed with internal cosign keys. Verification command example: cosign verify --key /secure/keys/cosign.pub <image>.

Risk matrix (summary):
- High risk: Stateful cache mismatch, KMS decryption errors, embedded token loss during migration. Mitigation: snapshots, dry-run with representative KV sizes, pre-checks for KMS policies.
- Medium risk: Performance regressions due to kernel selection or quantization. Mitigation: compat-checker, small density canaries, telemetry thresholds.
- Low risk: Observability gaps; mitigated by pre-enabling traces and temporary elevated sampling.

Operational play examples (snippets):
- Sample alert policy (Pseudo):
  - alert: Migration_P99_Latency_Regression
    expr: (migration_p99_latency / baseline_p99_latency) > 1.15
    for: 5m
    labels: { severity: page }

- Minimal acceptance smoke curl test:
  - curl -X POST https://private-api.customer.example/v1/generate \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \n    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n    -d '{"model":"<candidate>","prompt":"Hello world","max_tokens":16}'

Related pages and artifacts to attach before starting:
- Link: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-onboarding-and-failover-runbook-2026 (onboarding checklist)
- Link: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/post-installation-telemetry-and-acceptance-checklist-2026 (telemetry norms)
- Artifact: compatibility-checker summary.json

Post-mortem and continuous improvement:
- After any migration that required rollback or exceeded thresholds, run a 72-hour retrospective including: timeline, telemetry snapshots, root cause, corrective actions, and a retro ticket with owner and target fix date.

Appendix A — Quick reference commands:
- rdx-compat-check --model /artifacts/model.tar.gz --runtime runtime:2026-02-01 --output /tmp/compat.json
- rdx-deploy --bundle /artifacts/private-bundle.tar.gz --target canary-node --annotations migration-id=<id>
- rdx-metrics tail --window 30m --filter migration=<id>

Appendix B — Minimal staging smoke suite (file: prompt-shard-smoke.json)
- [
  { "prompt": "Summarize the following text in one sentence:" },
  { "prompt": "Extract the product name from: 'Order 9382: Redwood Tuner'" },
  { "prompt": "Rewrite for clarity: 'Received bad kernel selection leading to slow tokens'" }
]

Contact and support:
- Private Deployments Team Slack: #private-deploys
- On-call pager: +1-650-555-0110 (internal)
- Field sales/customer success contact: see migration ticket metadata

Change log:
- 2026-02-10 — created by Emma Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-04-12 — added deterministic rollback matrix and KMS checks (review by Diego Morales).
- 2026-09-01 — clarified telemetry windows and added example cosign verify step (review by Aisha Patel).

payload.page_title: VPC Peering and Interconnect Design Playbook for Enterprise Private Deploys

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents recommended network topology patterns, routing policies, provisioning steps, validation checks, and operational runbooks for establishing VPC peering, carrier interconnects (Direct Connect / Interconnect), and encrypted transit for Redwood private deployments. It is intended for platform engineers, solutions engineers, and SREs executing enterprise VPC/private control-plane integration work.

Scope: covers cloud VPC peering, dedicated interconnects, transit gateways/hubs, VPN fallback, peering security controls, MTU and path MTU discovery guidance, route propagation and filtering, Terraform examples, acceptance test suites, and day‑2 runbook actions for failover, maintenance, and rollback. Does not cover vendor-specific switch fabric design beyond customer edge considerations.

Key goals
- Provide deterministic latency and predictable bandwidth to the private control plane.
- Ensure isolation between customer data plane and Redwood management/control traffic where required.
- Provide clear rollback and fallback steps that do not require on‑site access.
- Standardize verification and telemetry collection for troubleshooting and billing reconciliation.

High-level topologies (choose one per customer depending on security and SLA)

1) Direct Interconnect + Transit Gateway (Recommended for enterprise)
- Customer uses a carrier or cloud provider direct interconnect (e.g., AWS Direct Connect, GCP Dedicated Interconnect).
- Interconnect terminates at a transit gateway or cloud router in a dedicated backbone account/tenant.
- Transit routes select between private control plane subnets and customer application subnets using route tables and VRFs.
- BGP sessions advertise only approved prefixes; route filtering enforced on both sides.

2) VPC Peering (SMB / Non-sensitive)
- Peer point-to-point between customer VPC and Redwood-hosted VPC.
- No transitive routing; use peering for single-tenant quick integrations.

3) VPN + Failover to Interconnect (Hybrid)
- Primary: Direct Interconnect to transit. Secondary: IPSec VPN over internet with automated health checks and BGP failover.
- Use pre-shared keys rotated by KMS or HSM integration.

Topology selection checklist
- Required throughput and 95th percentile sustained bandwidth. (If >5 Gbps sustained, prefer Direct Interconnect.)
- Regulatory/data residency requirements (if traffic must remain in-customer network, require private physical cross-connect).
- Latency SLOs (target RTT and jitter).
- Planned burst patterns and traffic shaping expectations.

Routing, BGP, and Filtering guidelines
- Use eBGP for interconnects; establish MD5 or TTL protections as supported.
- Advertise only the minimal set of prefixes. Use prefix-lists and AS-path filters.
- Set BGP community tags for route propagation and cost-based preference.
- Default route handling: do NOT advertise 0.0.0.0/0 from customer to Redwood control plane.
- Prefer route leak prevention at the transit gateway: explicit export maps required.

IP addressing and MTU
- Use /24 or larger subnets per AZ for control-plane endpoints to simplify filtering.
- Standard MTU: 1500 for public VPC subnets; 9001 (jumbo) where both sides support it for bulk KV/cache replication and large model artifacts (recommended for interconnects).
- Always validate Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) in acceptance tests.

Security controls and encryption
- Interconnect layer: enforce physical port isolation and VLAN segregation.
- BGP authentication (where supported) and strict community/AS checks.
- Transit encryption: if required by policy, terminate TLS between control-plane components and use end-to-end IPSec tunnels for data-plane paths.
- Key management: integrate with customer KMS/HSM for PSK rotation and TLS certs where requested.
- RBAC: limit who can create peering or route propagation changes. All changes require approval and an automated rollback window.

Provisioning and Terraform snippets
- Provide a minimal Terraform example for AWS Direct Connect + Transit Gateway attachment: (example is illustrative; adapt to account IDs and region)

terraform provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }
resource "aws_dx_connection" "customer_connection" { name = "redwood-cx" bandwidth = "1Gbps" }
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway" "rtg" { description = "redwood-transit" }
resource "aws_dx_gateway" "dg" { name = "redwood-dxg" amazon_side_asn = 64512 }
resource "aws_dx_gateway_association" "dx_to_tgw" { dx_gateway_id = aws_dx_gateway.dg.id transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.rtg.id }
(Replace with provider-specific resources for GCP / Azure; validate local address families and VLAN tags.)

Acceptance tests (automated suite)
- Pre-provisioning validation: verify ASN, VLAN IDs, and advertised tenant prefixes with carrier.
- Connectivity test: establish BGP; verify neighbor state=Established.
  - Command examples:
    - AWS: aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments / aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-peering-attachments
    - On-prem router: show ip bgp summary | grep <remote-as>
- Latency and bandwidth: run iperf3 across peering path at 1m, 95th percentile and 99th percentile windows.
- PMTUD and fragmentation: send varied MTU packets (e.g., ping -M do -s) to validate.
- Route validation: check that only authorized prefixes are present and that no default route leakage exists.
- Encryption validation: validate IPSec SA and TLS ciphers; check cert chain in control-plane TLS endpoints.

Telemetry and observability
- Required metrics to be exported to Redwood monitoring stack and optionally to customer:
  - BGP session state (up/down, flaps)
  - Transit interface RX/TX, drop counts, errors
  - Flow logs for peered VPCs (sampled 1:1000 for billing, increase when debugging)
  - PMTU / ICMP fragmentation counters
- Standard tags: customer_id, deployment_id, region, interconnect_id
- Log retention: 90 days standard; 365 days on request (contracted).

Day-2 runbook: failover and rollback
- Scenario A: Direct interconnect flap
  1) Detect: BGP down alert triggers page and runbook.
  2) Validate: confirm carrier status via carrier portal and transit-cloud console.
  3) Action: if secondary VPN exists and is healthy, promote VPN routes by adjusting route priority (BGP MED/local-preference) and announce via automation.
  4) Notify: post status to customer Slack channel and update incident.
  5) Revert: after carrier confirms fix, withdraw temporary MED and re-enable original route advertisement.

- Scenario B: Route leak detected (unauthorized prefix)
  1) Isolate: immediately advertise more specific null-route (OR community-based blackhole) in transit gateway export map to prevent traffic blackholing other customers.
  2) Audit: collect RIB snapshots from both sides, export flow logs for the offending prefix, escalate to network security and carrier.
  3) Rollback: remove offending advertisement and restore export maps.

Maintenance and upgrade considerations
- Scheduled maintenance must have a 48h notice and a rollback window of at least 2 hours.
- Upgrade steps for transit gateway or cloud router:
  1) Verify control-plane replicas in passive AZ are fully synced and healthy.
  2) Drain existing BGP sessions to a maintenance route target using graceful restart where supported.
  3) Apply software/route-table changes in a canary region (single AZ) and run acceptance tests.
  4) Progressive rollout: 10% of attachments -> 30% -> 100% with automated health gating.
  5) On failure, execute the rollback automation to restore previous route maps and neighbor sessions.

Rollback automation primitives (required for all enterprise deployments)
- Snapshot current route tables and BGP RIB (timestamped JSON) to the configured telemetry bucket.
- Keep IaC and state versioned; use terraform state-locking and store state in a read-only snapshot for rollback agent.
- Run a pre-canned revert plan that: restores prior transit attachments, re-applies prefix-lists, and flips local-preference flags back.

Customer requirements matrix (minimums)
| Requirement | Minimum | Recommended | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Interconnect bandwidth | 500 Mbps | 1 Gbps | For model artifact pulls and KV sync, choose >=1 Gbps for low RTOs |
| ASN | customer-owned ASN or shared with consent | customer-owned ASN | Avoid overlapping private ASNs; use RFC1918-safe planning |
| MTU | 1500 | 9001 (jumbo) | Jumbo recommended for cluster replication traffic |
| BGP session redundancy | 1 | 2+ | Two sessions across diverse edges is required for SLA tier-2 |
| Monitoring export | Flow logs + BGP metrics | Add SNMP and sFlow on request | Agree on retention and access in contract |
(continued)
On‑site vs remote troubleshooting checklist
- On-site: physical cross-connect light check, VLAN tag inspection, patch panel labeling, fiber tester (OTDR) if available.
- Remote: collect BGP RIB, netstat summaries, iperf3 logs, traceroutes with timestamped hops, route table snapshots, flow logs.

Escalation contacts and SLAs
- First responder: Platform NetOps (page escalation) -> 15 minutes response target.
- Engineering escalation: Network SRE -> 1 hour.
- Carrier escalation: use carrier-defined escalation path; have account manager contact in contract.
- SLA targets to include in deployment contract:
  - Interconnect availability: 99.95% (higher tiers negotiable)
  - BGP stability (no flaps >3 per hour) for production routes
  - Mean time to restore (MTTR) for single-edge failure: 30 minutes (with VPN failover)

Appendices
A. Useful commands and checks
- Linux: ip route show; ip -s link; sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n "tcp port 179"
- Router: show ip bgp summary; show bgp neighbors; show interfaces counters
- PMTUD test: ping -M do -s 8972 <remote-ip>
- Bandwidth test: iperf3 -c <remote> -P 8 -t 60

B. Example incident severity decision table
- Sev1: complete control-plane isolation for >5% of customer traffic for >15 minutes.
- Sev2: local edge flaps or steady packet loss >1% affecting <5% traffic.
- Sev3: degraded but stable performance or single route leak isolated to non-critical prefixes.

C. Change request template (must be filled for any interconnect or peering change)
- Change title, owner, start time, duration, rollback plan, verification steps, notification list, impacted prefixes, test commands.

Related docs
- Link to contract appendix for interconnect bandwidth SLAs and billing reconciliation.
- Link to private deploy runbook for control-plane scaling and KV cache replication.

Revision history
- 2026-02-10: Initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-18: Security review and BGP auth additions by Javier Morales.
- 2026-03-01: Added day-2 runbook sections and Terraform example; approved for publication.

payload.page_title: Private Observability Minimum Pack (v1) — Overview

sections.body:
The **Private Observability Minimum Pack** is the baseline, supported observability bundle shipped with **Redwood Private** (VPC and on-prem) installs. It provides a standard set of:
- **Grafana dashboards** (health and performance for control plane + data plane)
- **Prometheus alert rules + recording rules** (golden signals + resource pressure)
- **Structured log collection defaults + export integrations** (sane defaults that work in private environments)
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Customer platform teams can monitor and operate Redwood Private day-2 without bespoke setup.
- Redwood Support/SRE can troubleshoot efficiently using a consistent set of signals.
sections.heading: This pack is designed so that

sections.body:
- Metrics for: control plane services, API gateway, policy/routing, serving runtime pods, installer/upgrade controller, and key integration points (e.g., model registry).
- A curated set of dashboards and alerting that covers the highest-impact failure modes:
  - Availability, latency, error rate
  - Saturation (GPU/CPU/memory), queueing/backpressure
  - Restart loops / crash loops
  - Storage pressure (Prometheus TSDB PVC) and scrape health
- Log pipeline defaults for control plane and runtime logs with redaction-safe guidance.
- Packaging for **online (VPC)** and **offline/air-gapped (on-prem)** installs.
sections.heading: In scope (v1)

sections.body:
- “Premium” observability: long retention defaults, multi-cluster federation, highly customized dashboards, full distributed tracing with customer-specific sampling policies.
- A Redwood-managed SIEM. Instead, we provide supported export paths to common sinks.
sections.heading: Out of scope (v1)

sections.body:
- **Redwood Private (VPC)**: supported
- **Redwood Private (on-prem / air-gapped)**: supported (via offline bundle)
sections.heading: Deployment modes

sections.body:
The pack is validated on reference environments used by Private deployments. As a baseline, Redwood Support expects:
- A supported Kubernetes version per the current Private release notes
- A functional cluster DNS and CNI
- Ability to create PVCs (for Prometheus/Grafana as configured)

If you operate OpenShift or other distros, the pack generally works, but any required SecurityContext/PSA constraints may require customer-side adaptation.
sections.heading: Kubernetes and distro assumptions

sections.body:
The dashboards ship as versioned JSON and are provisioned automatically when the pack is enabled.

**Dashboard set (v1):**
| Dashboard | Primary audience | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Private Runtime Overview | Platform / Oncall | “Are requests succeeding? What’s p95/p99 latency? How many tokens/sec? Is batching helping? Any queue buildup?” |
| Control Plane Health | Platform / Support | “Are core services healthy (gateway, auth integration, policy engine)? Any elevated 5xx or dependency failures?” |
| GPU & Node Resources | Platform / SRE | “Are GPUs saturated? Any GPU memory pressure/OOM? Node CPU/mem pressure?” |
| Prometheus / Scrape Health | Platform | “Are targets being scraped? Any stale series? Is TSDB unhealthy or out of space?” |
| Logging Pipeline Health | Platform | “Is the log collector falling behind? Dropping? Retry/backpressure?” |
sections.heading: 1) Grafana dashboards (minimum supported set)

sections.body:
- Dashboards are designed to be **low-cardinality safe**. We avoid per-request labels and limit high-cardinality breakdowns (e.g., model/route) to aggregated or top-N views.
- Dashboards include “**What to check first**” panels for common incidents.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
Alerts are installed as PrometheusRule resources (when enabled). Recording rules provide stable time series for dashboards and for alert evaluation.

**Alert philosophy**
- Alerts align to Private SLO guidance and are tuned for private cluster realities (varying traffic, customer network policies, constrained resources).
- Severity is standardized:
  - **Sev1 (page)**: likely customer-visible outage or rapid SLO burn
  - **Sev2 (page or urgent ticket)**: high risk of degradation/outage if unaddressed
  - **Sev3 (ticket)**: operational issue, early warning, or configuration drift

**Minimum alert groups (v1):**
| Group | Examples | Default severity |
|---|---|---|
| Availability & Error Rate | API 5xx elevated, gateway upstream failures | Sev1/Sev2 |
| Latency & SLO Burn | p95/p99 latency burn rate, request timeouts | Sev1/Sev2 |
| GPU Saturation & OOM | GPU utilization pinned, GPU memory near limit, OOMKilled inference pods | Sev2 |
| Queueing / Backpressure | queue depth growing, batcher backlog sustained | Sev2/Sev3 |
| Restart Loops | CrashLoopBackOff on critical services | Sev2 |
| Scrape / Telemetry Health | scrape target down, rules failing to evaluate, Prometheus TSDB issues | Sev2/Sev3 |
| Storage Pressure | Prometheus PVC filling quickly, disk space low | Sev2 |
sections.heading: 2) Prometheus alert rules + recording rules

sections.body:
- Each alert includes annotations with:
  - Symptom summary
  - “What to do first” steps
  - Link to the Private day-2 runbook section
sections.heading: Runbook linkage

sections.body:
The minimum pack standardizes **structured logs** and offers supported export patterns suitable for private environments.

**Log sources (v1):**
- Control plane services (API gateway, auth/RBAC integration points, policy/routing service)
- Serving runtime pods
- Installer/upgrade controller

**Structured fields (typical):**
- `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `component`, `namespace`, `pod`, `node`
- `request_id` (generated at gateway)
- `route` (bounded / normalized)
- `model` (bounded / normalized)
- `tenant_id_hash` (when applicable; hashed)
- `status_code`, `latency_ms`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out` (where applicable)

**Redaction and safety**
- The minimum pack is designed to avoid secrets/PII in logs by default.
- Do not enable request/response payload logging in production unless explicitly approved by your security team.
- See: “Private observability and audit log interactions” for retention and redaction guidance.

**Supported export targets (documented patterns):**
- **Loki** (Grafana stack)
- **Elasticsearch/OpenSearch**
- **Splunk HEC**
- **OTLP-compatible endpoint** (where feasible; typically customer-managed collector)
sections.heading: 3) Logs: collection defaults + export options

sections.body:
The minimum pack is shipped as a versioned artifact and wired into both:
- **`redwood-private-installer`** (recommended for most customers)
- **`redwood-helm-charts`** (for teams operating directly via Helm/GitOps)
sections.heading: Installation and enablement

sections.body:
1. During install configuration, set:
   - `observability.minimumPack.enabled=true`
2. Choose one of:
   - **Bring your own Prometheus/Grafana** (recommended if you already run them)
   - **Install reference Prometheus/Grafana** via the provided chart options (sizing required)
3. Choose logging mode:
   - Local collection with retention defaults
   - Export to a supported sink (Loki/ELK/Splunk/OTLP)
4. Run installer preflights:
   - Storage class and PVC provisioning
   - NetworkPolicy reachability for scrape targets
   - Resource requests/limits sanity check
5. Post-install validation:
   - Prometheus scrape health
   - Dashboards provisioned and populated
   - A small set of “canary” alerts appear (not necessarily firing)
sections.heading: A) Enable via Private Installer (recommended)

sections.body:
- `observabilityPack.enabled: true`
- Configure Grafana provisioning (folder, datasource name)
- Configure PrometheusRule installation behavior
- Configure log collector and sink
sections.heading: Enable the pack in your Private values

sections.body: - If you already have cluster-wide Prometheus/Grafana, do not install a second copy unless required. Instead, point the pack to your existing stack and ensure scrape configs include Redwood namespaces.
sections.heading: Operational note

sections.body:
- The minimum pack is versioned and released in lockstep with Redwood Private releases.
- The pack follows semantic versioning **within** the Private release stream:
  - **Patch**: dashboard fixes, threshold tuning, non-breaking alert changes
  - **Minor**: additive dashboards/alerts/metrics, new export options, recording rule additions
  - **Major**: breaking changes to metric names, dashboard schema, or required components (avoided; requires explicit migration guidance)
sections.heading: Pack versioning

sections.body:
- Metric names and labels are treated as an API for customers.
- We aim for backward compatibility across at least one Private minor release.
- If a breaking metric change is unavoidable:
  - We provide a documented migration
  - We include a temporary compatibility recording rule (where possible)
  - We validate upgrade and rollback paths
sections.heading: Compatibility rules

sections.body:
For tickets involving performance, errors, or instability, Redwood Support may request:
- A screenshot/export of the **Runtime Overview** and **Control Plane Health** dashboards for the incident window
- Prometheus “targets” status for Redwood scrape jobs
- Relevant structured logs filtered by `request_id`/time range
- Confirmation of:
  - Observability pack version
  - Private release version
  - Any custom NetworkPolicies or scrape restrictions

If the minimum pack is disabled or significantly modified, Support may ask you to reproduce the issue with the supported defaults to reduce time-to-resolution.
sections.heading: Support boundary (what Redwood Support will ask for)

sections.body:
- High-cardinality breakdowns (per-tenant/per-user) are intentionally not supported in v1 to protect customer Prometheus performance.
- Trace support is limited in v1; use logs + metrics as the primary troubleshooting path.
- Air-gapped installs require that all images and dashboard/rule artifacts come from the offline bundle.
sections.heading: Known limitations and operational notes

sections.body:
1. Prometheus targets show **UP** for Redwood endpoints.
2. Grafana folder **“Redwood Private (Minimum Pack)”** exists and dashboards render.
3. The Runtime Overview shows non-zero traffic after a test request.
4. No continuous rule evaluation errors in Prometheus.
5. Log collector shows stable throughput (no sustained drop/backpressure).
sections.heading: Quick validation checklist (after install/upgrade)

sections.body:
- Product owner: **Vivek Kulkarni** (Private Deployments)
- Engineering owners:
  - Control plane observability: **Ethan Park**
  - Telemetry platform / pack plumbing: **Logan Wright**
  - SRE validation & on-call readiness: **Rafael Mendes**
- Security review: **Marcus Lin**

For day-2 procedures, see the Private Observability Day-2 Runbook.

payload.page_title: VPC Entropy Segmentation and Tenant Shielding Playbook

sections.body: This playbook describes a pragmatic, reproducible approach for reducing cross-tenant interference in VPC-based private deployments using entropy segmentation, tenant shielding, and telemetry contracts. It complements existing network segmentation guidance by focusing on runtime-level request steering, KV-cache partitioning, and telemetry sampling so tenants cannot unintentionally degrade each other or observe noisy neighbor behavior.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Field engineers and operators responsible for private deployments (on-prem and VPC).
- SRE and runtime teams implementing tenant-level guards.
- Solutions engineers validating customer acceptance tests.
sections.heading: Intended audience

sections.body:
- Goals:
  - Ensure tenant noisy-neighbor incidents are detected and mitigated within 2 minutes of onset.
  - Limit tenant-induced 99th-percentile tail latency increase for co-located tenants to <20ms above baseline.
  - Provide a clear telemetry and evidentiary contract for customer audits.
- Non-goals:
  - This playbook does not replace network-level isolation (VPC/NSG rules) — it augments them.
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body:
1) Entropy segmentation (logical request partitioning)
2) Tenant Shield Controller (runtime-side enforcement)
3) Telemetry contract and sampling strategy
4) Operational runbook: detection, mitigation, and rollback
5) Acceptance and SLO verification checklist

1) Entropy segmentation overview
- Concept: split request traffic into deterministic shards based on an entropy key (tenant_id + request_fingerprint). Each shard maps to a bounded set of runtime workers and KV-cache partitions. The goal is to limit blast radius for pathological workloads and to bound working set interference.
- Components: vpc-proxy (edge ingress), shard-mapper service, tenant-shield-controller, runtime-kv-partitioner.
sections.heading: Core components described

sections.body:
- We assume tenants present a tenant_id token in the request header (X-Redwood-Tenant).
- Shards should be sized to keep typical KV working set < 8 GB per shard for current model footprints (adjust per customer HW profile).
- Shard count is configurable per deployment and can be different per tenant tier.
sections.heading: Design constraints and assumptions

sections.body:
- Compute H = siphash(tenant_id || fingerprint)
- shard = H mod N_shards_for_tenant
- N_shards_for_tenant is chosen from tenant profile table (see Acceptance checklist).

2) Tenant Shield Controller (TSC)
- Purpose: enforce runtime limits and apply mitigation rules when a tenant's shard exhibits anomalous resource consumption.
- Key features:
  - Rate-limit enforcement (per-shard and per-tenant)
  - Soft-eviction tokens for bursts (burst_budget with decay)
  - Dynamic KV cache eviction policy (TTL + recency + tenant-cost-weighting)
  - Cross-tenant telemetry fence to prevent cross-tenant KV reads (logical ACL at runtime)
sections.heading: Shard mapping algorithm (summary)

sections.body:
- Normal mode: shard tokens allocated, eviction thresholds at 70% of shard memory budget.
- Degraded mode: when shard memory or CPU > 90% sustained for >30s, TSC throttles new requests to that shard to target 50% CPU within 60s.
- Quarantine mode: for repeated violations (3 triggers in 24h), shard is placed in quarantine and moved to a dedicated fallback pool (lower-cost model variant) with notice to tenant owner.
sections.heading: Operational behaviors

sections.body:
--8<-- start config
tenant_shield_controller:
  global_shard_memory_budget_gb: "8"
  per_tenant_shard_counts:
    free: 2
    standard: 8
    enterprise: 32
  eviction_threshold_pct: 70
  degraded_threshold_pct: 90
  degraded_sustain_seconds: 30
  quarantine_triggers: 3
  quarantine_window_hours: 24
  burst_budget_tokens: 500
  burst_decay_seconds: 300
--8<-- end config

3) Telemetry contract and sampling strategy
- Purpose: deliver sufficient evidence to SLO owners and customers while controlling telemetry volume and respecting privacy.
- Mandatory telemetry fields for every request (ingress): timestamp, tenant_id, shard_id, model_id, route, latency_ms, cpu_ms, mem_mb, kv_hit_bool, token_count. These must be present at 100% sampling for aggregated histograms.
- High-cardinality traces (full request payloads) should be sampled at 0.1% by default for standard tenants, 1% for enterprise (configurable and chargeable).
sections.heading: Example TSC config snippet (YAML)

sections.body:
| Data type | Default sampling | Retention | Rationale |
| Aggregated metrics | 100% (histograms) | 90d | Needed for SLOs and billing accuracy |
| Detailed traces | 0.1% standard / 1% enterprise | 30d | Debugging noisy neighbor incidents |
| KV access logs (per-shard) | 1% | 30d | Investigate cache pollution attacks |
sections.heading: Sampling policy table (text)

sections.body:
- Telemetry must be labeled with tenant_confidentiality_level (public/internal/regulated). Regulated tenants require telemetry to be stored in customer-controlled buckets or excluded from sample exports.
- All telemetry exports must pass through the telemetry-aggregator service and be subject to PII scrubbing hooks.

4) Operational runbook: detection, mitigation, and rollback
Detection: automated detectors running in runtime-observability:
- Detector A (memory-pressure): rolling 10s window where per-shard mem_mb > 90th percentile × 1.5 for 30s.
- Detector B (latency-spike): per-shard p99 latency delta > baseline_p99 × 2 for 60s.
- Detector C (kv-churn): kv_hit_ratio drops > 30% vs baseline over 2 minutes.

When detector fires, the following steps are executed automatically (fast path):
1) Mark shard as degraded in TSC and apply per-shard throttle to ingress (target QPS reduction = 50% or to move p99 under SLO).
2) Snapshot recent telemetry and store in quarantine bucket (tagged with incident ID).
3) Notify oncall via pager with incident playbook link and suggested actions.
sections.heading: Telemetry ingest and labeling requirements

sections.body:
1) Validate detection signal (confirm telemetry snapshot).
2) Identify triggering tenant(s) and determine if the workload is expected (deployments, customer load test, crawler).
3) If unexpected, apply one of the following mitigations in order:
   a) Tighten per-tenant rate-limit policy to safe_qps (calculated: safe_qps = current_qps × 0.6).
   b) Increase shard count for affected tenant (if hardware available) to reduce per-shard working set.
   c) Move shard to fallback pool with quantized/cheaper model variant.
4) If problem persists for >30 minutes, escalate to Product & Customer Success to coordinate a tenant-facing mitigation and possible SLA credits.
sections.heading: Operator checklist (human-in-the-loop)

sections.body:
- If a TSC change causes false positives, the recommended rollback is:
  1) Set TSC.mode=gradual_offline (disables quarantine and degraded enforcement but keeps monitoring).
  2) Revert last TSC release using the canary rollback script (see CLI below).
  3) Re-run telemetry verification for 60 minutes.
sections.heading: Rollback considerations (software changes)

sections.body:
redwood-ops rollback tsc --deployment=tenant-shield-controller --to=release-2026-11-18 --grace=120

5) Acceptance criteria and SLO verification checklist
- Tenant isolation SLOs (applies after playbook enabled):
  - Per-tenant p99 latency overhead vs dedicated baseline <= 20ms  (measured over 1h window).
  - No cross-tenant KV leakage incidents (0 tolerated) in 90 days.
  - Detection-to-mitigation time <= 2 minutes for automated actions.

Acceptance and smoke tests (run in staging with representative tenants):
1) Synthetic noisy-neighbor test: run a workload that generates 200% of expected KV churn on 1 shard and assert that degraded mode triggers and latency for other tenants stays below threshold.
2) Shard-splitting test: increase N_shards_for_tenant and validate KV hit ratio recovers within 5 minutes.
3) Telemetry export test: enable 1% trace sampling for tenant X and confirm trace appears in customer-controlled export bucket (if regulated).
sections.heading: Canary rollback CLI example

sections.body:
- Shard memory utilization (per-tenant heatmap)
- Per-tenant p50/p95/p99 latency (route-level)
- KV hit ratio and churn rate (per-shard)
- Number of degraded/quarantined shards (trend)
- Telemetry sampling rate and export errors

Ownership and run cadence
- Owner: runtime-sre (primary), serving-runtime (secondary), field-ops (customer-facing).
- Oncall: runtime-sre for automated mitigation, field-ops for customer communication.
- Quarterly review: review tenant shield thresholds after any large capacity/quantization changes.
sections.heading: Operational metrics dashboard (recommended panels)

sections.body:
- We employ runtime tenant shielding to protect customer workloads. Shielding may involve routing some requests to fallback model variants or applying short throttles during sustained resource pressure.
- For regulated customers we provide options to increase shard counts, reserve dedicated pool capacity, or require explicit telemetry export controls.

Appendix A — Example incident timeline (text):
- 00:00 Detector A fires (kv-churn). Automatic throttle applied to shard 14 at 00:01. Telemetry snapshot saved. Pager fired to runtime-sre at 00:02. Operator applied shard-split at 00:09 and throttle relaxed at 00:12. Incident closed at 01:00 after 4 consecutive windows of healthy telemetry.

Appendix B — Templates and commands (useful snippets):
- Increase shard count for tenant (operator CLI):
  redwood-ops tenant update-shards --tenant=acme-corp --shards=16 --reason="mitigate-kv-churn"

- Force move shard to fallback pool:
  redwood-ops shard migrate --shard=tenantX-3 --target-pool=fallback-quantized --force --reason="noisy-neighbor"

- Telemetry export check (example jq):
  aws s3 ls s3://redwood-telemetry-exports/tenantX/incident-39485/ | head -n 20
sections.heading: Customer-facing notes (what to tell customers)

sections.body:
- Entropy segmentation reduces but does not eliminate noisy neighbor risk; tenants with extreme burstiness should be offered dedicated pools.
- Shard increases have overhead (re-partitioning warms caches slowly); prefer reactive throttles for short bursts and shard-splits for persistent high working set.
- This playbook requires tenants to include tenant_id in request headers; for legacy integrations we provide a token-mapping proxy but recommend migrating.
sections.heading: Notes and known limitations

sections.body:
- See related runbooks for KV cache migration and rollback in day-2-ops.
- See customer requirements library for minimum HW and network specifications when requesting dedicated pools.
sections.heading: References and related pages

sections.body:
- 2026-06-15: Created by Maya Liu.
- 2026-09-03: Add quarantine mode thresholds and sampling policy adjustments (reviewers Priya Menon, Daniel Ross).
- 2026-12-08: Clarified degraded mode timings and added canary rollback CLI snippet (reviewer Oscar Hernández).
