payload.page_title: Chronological Upgrade Timeline and Customer Notification Protocol

sections.body: This document prescribes a chronological, role-oriented upgrade timeline for private deployments (VPC and on-prem), and the customer-facing notification protocol that must accompany each phase. It is intended for Release Engineering, Field Operations, Solutions Engineering, and Customer Success when coordinating upgrades that may affect tenant SLAs, network topology, or runtime state.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Provide a single, reproducible timeline for upgrades and rollbacks that balances operator safety and customer transparency.
- Define measurable thresholds and automated gates used to trigger rollback decisions.
- Standardize customer communications and escalation templates to reduce confusion during events.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to private deploy upgrades that touch runtime artifacts (model binaries, runtime shards, KV cache format, networking proxies, control plane components).
- Assumes a pre-existing support contract and a named Customer Success owner per upgrade.
- Assumes telemetry and synthetic checks are available (see acceptance checks table).
sections.heading: Scope and assumptions

sections.body:
- Release Lead (RL): coordinates timeline, signs off preflight, primary decision-maker for go/no-go.
- Field Operator (FO): performs the change, runs operator commands, coordinates rollbacks.
- Solutions/SE: verifies customer-specific traffic shaping and runbook coverage.
- Customer Success (CS): triages customer communications and captures acceptance.
- Oncall/Observability (OBS): monitors real-time metrics and runs regression tests after rollout.
sections.heading: Actors and ownership

sections.body:
1) Signed release plan document with risk classification and backout window (RL).
2) Snapshot and evidence: model/artifact hashes, control-plane state snapshot (FO).
3) Telemetry health baselines: 24h baseline of 95p latency, error rate, and KV cache hit-rate (OBS).
4) Customer readiness: written confirmation of maintenance window and support contacts (CS).
5) Rollback artifacts present: previous model image, previous control-plane manifest, and automated rollback job validated in staging (FO).
6) Acceptance tests: smoke script list and synthetic traffic profile validated against baseline (SE).
sections.heading: Preflight checklist (minimum pass to schedule upgrade)

sections.body:
| Check | Frequency | Pass criteria | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 95th latency (token gen) | continuous | <= 1.5x baseline for 30m | OBS |
| Error rate (client-facing 5xx) | continuous | <= baseline + 2% absolute | OBS |
| KV cache miss ratio | every 5m | <= baseline + 10% relative | OBS |
| Token throughput | continuous | within expected throughput envelope | FO/OBS |
| Telemetry ingestion lag | every 1m | < 60s | OBS |

Chronological timeline (recommended template)
Phase A — Planning (T-14d to T-7d):
- T-14d: Release Lead publishes schedule and initial risk assessment. CS notifies customer with a courtesy heads-up.
- T-10d: SE runs customer-specific compatibility checks (networking, KMS/HSM, image allowlist).
- T-7d: Final preflight checklist completed; RL requests formal customer acknowledgement of maintenance window.
sections.heading: Acceptance checks table

sections.body:
Subject: Planned maintenance: Redwood private upgrade scheduled [DATE]
Body (short): We plan a maintenance window on [DATE] targeting component(s): [component list]. Expected customer impact: [none | transient latency | brief unavailability]. Primary CS: [name] — escalation: [email/phone].

Phase B — Pre-deployment (T-2d to T-0):
- T-2d: Run full synthetic acceptance suite against a realistic replay for the target tenant. Save results to artifact store.
- T-1d: Operator dry-run in staging that mirrors operator steps for production (FO).
- T-12h: Final go/no-go sync: RL, FO, OBS, SE, CS. RL records decision outcome in release tracker.
- T-1h: Customer reminder: maintenance start in 1 hour with link to status page and ticket.
sections.heading: Customer notification (Planning)

sections.body:
Subject: Reminder: maintenance window starts in 1 hour — [DATE]
Body (short): Maintenance will begin at [TIME]. No anticipated data loss. If you have high-priority traffic, please notify CS immediately.

Phase C — Deployment (T0 to T+48h):
- T0 (start): FO begins staggered rollout by operator-defined shard. Stagger cadence: 5–10% of tenants or control-plane nodes per batch depending on risk class.
- After each batch:
  - Run smoke acceptance (3–5 min): latency, error rate, kv-consistency.
  - If all checks green, proceed to next batch.
  - If any check fails, pause and escalate. Observe for 10–30 minutes depending on severity.
- Automated gating: CI/CD job will automatically halt rollout if error rate breach occurs and will notify the RL and OBS slack channel.
sections.heading: Customer notification (Reminder)

sections.body:
- 30m stable with all acceptance checks green at batch-level.
- No customer-reported incidents >P2 during staged rollout.
sections.heading: Rollforward success criteria (during Deployment)

sections.body:
- Client-facing 5xx increases by >5 percentage points over baseline across affected tenants for >10 minutes.
- 95th percentile latency >2x baseline for >15 minutes.
- KV cache miss delta >25% leading to sustained throughput degradation >20% for >10 minutes.
- Any data corruption or mismatch detected in model artifact checksums.
sections.heading: Immediate rollback triggers (examples and thresholds)

sections.body:
- If a critical trigger appears within 30 minutes of batch completion: immediate rollback of that batch. FO executes batch backout script.
- If systemic across multiple batches and cannot be isolated: halt rollout and initiate full release rollback (see procedure).

Rollback procedure (operator steps — checklist):
1) Mark release as ROLLBACK in release tracker and notify all stakeholders (RL/CS/OBS/SE).
2) Execute backout job: `rdu operator rollback --release <release-id> --target-batch <id>` (FO).
3) Verify checksum and model artifacts on rolled-back hosts.
4) Re-run smoke acceptance against rolled-back batch.
5) If rollback successful: notify customer with rollback confirmation and follow-up timeline for remediation.
6) Open postmortem ticket and assign to RL for RCA within 72 hours.

Post-deploy observation (T+48h to T+7d):
- T+48h: Full-system synthetic run and customer acceptance validation (SE + CS).
- T+72h: Performance regression sweep; if no regressions, RL moves release to stable and schedules a retrospective.
- T+7d: Close release after final evidence bundle is saved and postmortem (if any) is published.
sections.heading: Rollback decision matrix (simplified)

sections.body:
1) Successful upgrade confirmation:
Subject: Maintenance complete — Upgrade applied to your private deploy [DATE]
Body: The planned upgrade completed at [TIME]. Observability checks show system health within expected ranges (95p latency: [value], error rate: [value]). If you observe issues, open a ticket referencing [release-id].

2) Rollback notification (immediate):
Subject: Action taken: Rollback executed during maintenance [DATE]
Body: We detected [brief reason] and executed a rollback for affected nodes at [TIME]. Impact: [summary]. Next steps: [investigation timeline]. Primary contact: [CS name].

3) Postmortem summary (P3/P2):
Subject: Postmortem: [summary title] — incident summary and remediation
Body: Short timeline, root cause, mitigation steps, and planned preventative actions with owners and ETA.
sections.heading: Customer notification templates (examples)

sections.body:
- Snapshot control plane: `rdu operator snapshot --component control-plane --out /artifacts/$(release-id)-snapshot.tgz`
- Trigger batch rollout: `rdu operator rollout --release <id> --batch-size 10% --wait`
- Force rollback of batch: `rdu operator rollback --release <id> --batch <n> --confirm`
- Evidence upload: `rdu artifacts upload --path /artifacts/<release-id> --tag release-evidence`
sections.heading: Operator runbook snippets (commands and short examples)

sections.body: - For regulated customers, persist: release manifest, operator commands with timestamps, telemetry window (T-24h to T+72h), and signed customer acknowledgement. Retention: 7 years for financial customers; 1 year default otherwise.
sections.heading: Evidence and audit requirements

sections.body:
1) FO attempts mitigation and notifies RL (within 5m of detection).
2) If mitigation fails within 15m, RL declares incident and pages SRE/P0 channel.
3) CS posts to the customer ticket and triggers customer call if impact >P2.
sections.heading: Escalation flow during failures

sections.body:
- Maintenance window confirmed and logged.
- Backup snapshots created and verified.
- Rollback artifacts validated in staging.
- Operator runbooks reviewed and practiced within the last 30 days.
- Observability dashboards and synthetic checks configured and smoke test green.

Appendix A — Example timeline (condensed):
- T-14d: Schedule and risk notice sent.
- T-7d: Final signoff and evidence snapshot.
- T-1d: Dry run completed.
- T-1h: Customer reminder.
- T0: Start staggered batch rollout.
- T+48h: Full-system validation.
- T+7d: Release close and evidence archive.

Appendix B — Quick links and references:
- Upgrade runbook (operator): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/operator-sentinel-escrow-and-durable-rollback-procedures-2026
- Operator cutover checklist: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/operator-cutover-chronicle-and-customer-communication-template-2026
- Evidence retention policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/policy-2025
sections.heading: Checklist for customer-facing readiness before sign-off

sections.body:
- 2024-09-10: Initial draft (Daniel Park)
- 2025-06-03: Added automated gating thresholds and rollback triggers (Leah Kim)
- 2026-01-14: Expanded customer templates and evidence retention details (Omar Ruiz)

End of document.
sections.heading: Revision history

payload.page_title: Redwood Private: Backup and Restore Strategy (Upgrade + Rollback)

sections.body:
This document defines the backup and restore strategy used by **Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem/air-gapped)** during upgrades and rollbacks. The goal is to make upgrades **safe-by-default** by taking a deterministic, auditable backup prior to any irreversible step (notably DB schema migrations), and by providing an operator-friendly restore path when rollback is required.

This strategy is implemented by the **redwood-private-installer** (backup orchestration + state persistence) and supported by Helm hook ordering (pre-upgrade jobs, timeouts, and rollback-safe behavior).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Ensure there is a **known-good restore point** prior to upgrade execution.
- Support both **VPC (cloud)** and **on-prem/air-gapped** deployments with consistent semantics.
- Provide multiple backup mechanisms to match storage backends: **EBS snapshots**, **CSI VolumeSnapshots**, and **logical DB dumps**.
- Enforce **encryption and auditability** requirements suitable for regulated customers.
- Provide a clear **restore verification checklist** to confirm the environment is safe to return to service.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- This is not a full DR/geo-replication design. It focuses on **upgrade/rollback safety** and recovering a single environment to a pre-upgrade state.
- We do not attempt to back up or restore all ephemeral caches (e.g., model KV/prefix caches) beyond best-effort cleanup.

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
The following are required for a “supported” backup/restore posture:
- A backup must be created and verified **immediately prior to upgrade execution** (within the same maintenance window).
- Backups must be **encrypted at rest** using an approved key management method.
- The installer must persist an **Upgrade State Record** linking:
  - the upgrade plan ID
  - target version
  - backup artifact IDs (snapshot IDs and/or dump object URIs)
  - verification results
  - timestamps
- Restore must be possible without pulling new artifacts from the internet (for air-gapped, all required artifacts must already be present in the offline bundle/mirror).

---
sections.heading: Invariants and assumptions

sections.body: Backups are split into **control-plane state**, **Kubernetes object intent**, and **operator/installer state**. We explicitly avoid capturing raw secret material unless the customer selects a secret backend that requires it (see “Secrets and secret backends”).
sections.heading: What we back up

sections.body:
| Component | Why | Backup method | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Control-plane PostgreSQL DB (redwood-control-plane) | Schema migrations are the most common irreversible upgrade step | (Preferred) Volume snapshot of DB PV; (Fallback) logical `pg_dump` | Yes | Snapshot preferred for speed/consistency; dump used for storage backends without snapshots or when PV snapshot fails prechecks |
| Installer state + upgrade state record | Deterministic rollback/restore and audit trail | Copy installer state directory and generated plan/summary to backup destination | Yes | Contains plan ID, step status, artifact checksums, snapshot IDs, and versions |
| Helm release metadata + values | Reproducibility; rollback to known chart configuration | Export `helm get values`, `helm get manifest`, `helm history` | Yes | Stored as text artifacts; does not include decrypted secrets |
| Redwood Private configuration (non-secret) | Restore intended configuration | Export Redwood config CRs/ConfigMaps in allowed namespaces | Yes | Stored as YAML; we exclude large transient objects |
| In-cluster signing keys / TLS materials | Only if customer stores TLS keys inside Kubernetes secrets and opts in | Optional (discouraged) | No | Strongly recommend external secret manager/HSM/KMS-backed storage |
| Audit trail of upgrade | Compliance evidence | Export last N hours of upgrade-related audit events + installer logs | Yes (enterprise) | Also included in support bundle; see “Audit evidence” |
sections.heading: Backup scope (by component)

sections.body:
Included (scoped to Redwood namespaces, e.g. `redwood-system`, `redwood-control-plane`, `redwood-data-plane`):
- ConfigMaps and non-secret CRs that represent **desired state**
- Helm release manifests/values as rendered artifacts
- Custom Resources for Redwood components (where applicable)
sections.heading: Kubernetes objects included/excluded

sections.body:
- `Secret` resources (see below)
- Large ephemeral resources (jobs with logs, transient caches)
- Customer application namespaces outside Redwood-owned namespaces

---
sections.heading: Excluded by default

sections.body:
Backups must be structured so that **secret values are not copied** unless explicitly required. Most Private customers use one of:
- Cloud KMS + external secret store (VPC)
- Vault / HSM / enterprise secret manager (on-prem)
sections.heading: Default stance

sections.body:
- **References** to secret locations (e.g., secret name, external secret path, key alias/ARN, or Vault path), plus validation that those references were reachable during prechecks.
- Kubernetes secret metadata (names/labels) when needed to ensure restore can recreate object stubs.
sections.heading: What we store instead of secrets

sections.body:
If a customer chooses to store TLS private keys or other required secrets exclusively as Kubernetes secrets and does not have an external secret manager, the operator may enable `--include-k8s-secrets` for backup. This is:
- **Restricted** (requires explicit approval in change management for regulated customers)
- Encrypted and access-controlled (see encryption section)

---
sections.heading: If secrets must be included (exception)

sections.body: The installer selects the best available mechanism based on environment detection and prechecks.
sections.heading: Supported backup mechanisms

sections.body:
- StorageClass is backed by EBS
- Snapshot APIs are available and permitted
sections.heading: Used when

sections.body:
- Create EBS snapshots for the DB PV and any other stateful PVs designated as “upgrade-critical”
- Record snapshot IDs in the Upgrade State Record
- Tag snapshots with:
  - `redwood:env_id`, `redwood:cluster_id`, `redwood:private_version`, `redwood:upgrade_plan_id`, `redwood:created_by=installer`
sections.heading: Behavior

sections.body:
- Kubernetes VolumeSnapshot CRDs are installed
- The CSI driver supports snapshots and the snapshot controller is healthy
sections.heading: Used when

sections.body:
- Create `VolumeSnapshot` objects
- Wait for `readyToUse=true` with a bounded timeout
- Record snapshot object names + underlying snapshot handle in the Upgrade State Record
sections.heading: Behavior

sections.body:
- Snapshot mechanisms are unavailable or fail prechecks
- Customer requires a portable DB export
sections.heading: Used when

sections.body:
- Run a Kubernetes Job that performs:
  - `pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges`
  - Optional `pg_dumpall --globals-only` when roles are managed locally
- Upload artifact to destination (S3/object store/file system)
sections.heading: Implementation

sections.body:
- Slower for large DBs; may increase maintenance window
- Restore requires compatible PostgreSQL major version (installer enforces version gate)

---
sections.heading: Caveats

sections.body:
- S3 bucket (customer-managed), with bucket policies limiting access to installer IAM role
- S3 Object Lock (optional) for tamper-evidence (regulated workloads)
sections.heading: VPC (cloud) recommended destinations

sections.body:
- Customer-managed object store (S3-compatible) inside the restricted network
- NFS/SMB file share with restricted ACLs
- Local disk only for staging; not recommended as sole backup destination

The installer writes a “backup manifest” artifact to the destination, alongside logs and exported YAML.

---
sections.heading: On-prem / air-gapped recommended destinations

sections.body:
- Cloud KMS (AWS KMS in VPC deployments)
- Customer-managed keys in an approved HSM/Vault solution (on-prem)
- Envelope encryption (AES-256) with a KEK managed by KMS/HSM
sections.heading: All backup artifacts must be encrypted at rest using one of

sections.body:
- S3 backups must use SSE-KMS with a customer-approved CMK:
  - `x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms`
  - `x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id: <key-arn>`
- EBS snapshots inherit encryption from the source volume when possible; otherwise the installer requires an explicit KMS key.
sections.heading: AWS VPC expectations

sections.body:
- If using an S3-compatible object store, backups must be encrypted either:
  - server-side using the object store’s KMS/HSM integration, or
  - client-side by the installer using envelope encryption
- Keys must never be stored in plaintext on disk. Installer supports loading encryption configuration from:
  - environment variables injected via Kubernetes Secret (reference-only), or
  - a local secure config file protected by OS-level permissions (last resort)
sections.heading: On-prem expectations

sections.body:
- Backups must be readable only by:
  - the installer/operator identity
  - a designated break-glass recovery role
- Backup destinations must be **separate from the cluster** where feasible (to protect against cluster-scoped compromise).

---
sections.heading: Access controls

sections.body:
- Minimum retention for upgrade safety: **7 days**
- Recommended retention for enterprise: **30 days**
sections.heading: Default retention

sections.body:
- EBS/CSI snapshots: default keep **3** most recent pre-upgrade snapshots (configurable)
- Logical dumps: default keep **3** most recent dumps per environment
sections.heading: Snapshot retention

sections.body:
- Cleanup is performed by the installer only when explicitly enabled:
  - `--enable-backup-gc`
- For regulated customers, cleanup is typically delegated to bucket lifecycle policies and/or snapshot retention tooling to meet internal evidence requirements.

---
sections.heading: Cleanup policy

sections.body: Restore is intended to be deterministic and “plan-driven”: operators restore **the backup associated with a specific upgrade plan ID**.
sections.heading: Restore workflow (operator-facing)

sections.body:
- **Rollback during upgrade**: triggered when upgrade fails or when operator chooses to rollback within the maintenance window.
- **Post-upgrade incident restore**: triggered after an upgrade completes but later requires restoring the pre-upgrade state.
sections.heading: Restore entry points

sections.body:
1. **Stop/scale down Redwood workloads** (data plane first, then control plane) to prevent writes during restore.
2. **Restore control-plane DB**:
   - If snapshot-based: restore PV from snapshot and reattach
   - If logical: run `pg_restore` job and verify DB health
3. **Re-apply known-good Kubernetes intent**:
   - Use Helm history/values captured in the backup
   - Pin chart/app versions as recorded in the Upgrade State Record
4. **Bring up control plane** and wait for readiness gates.
5. **Bring up data plane** and validate service health.
sections.heading: High-level steps

sections.body:
- Create backup (pre-upgrade):
  - `redwood-private backup create --reason pre-upgrade --destination s3://<bucket>/<prefix> --kms-key <arn>`
- Verify backup:
  - `redwood-private backup verify --backup-id <id>`
- Restore from backup:
  - `redwood-private restore --backup-id <id> --confirm-impact`

Note: Command names/flags are subject to change; refer to the current installer `--help` output for the installed version.

---
sections.heading: Example installer commands (illustrative)

sections.body: A restore is considered successful only after completing the checks below.
sections.heading: Restore verification checklist

sections.body:
- [ ] PostgreSQL is reachable from control-plane pods and passes readiness checks
- [ ] DB schema version matches the expected pre-upgrade version recorded in the backup manifest
- [ ] Control plane API health endpoint returns OK (internal): `GET /healthz`
- [ ] No crash loops in control-plane namespaces for 15 minutes
- [ ] Audit log shows `restore_started` and `restore_completed` events (enterprise environments)
sections.heading: Control plane verification

sections.body:
- [ ] Data plane controllers are reconciled (no pending rollouts)
- [ ] Canary inference request succeeds against a known small model with a fixed prompt
- [ ] Token streaming works (if enabled)
- [ ] Error rate and latency return to within normal band for the environment (baseline defined by SRE per customer)
sections.heading: Data plane verification

sections.body:
- [ ] RBAC/OIDC connectivity intact (no auth regressions)
- [ ] TLS certificates valid and served correctly
- [ ] No version skew beyond supported range (N-1 ↔ N control plane/data plane constraints)

If any item fails, do not reopen traffic; follow the runbook escalation path.

---
sections.heading: Platform invariants

sections.body:
Before an upgrade proceeds past prechecks, the installer must verify:
- Snapshot jobs completed and snapshot objects are `readyToUse=true`
- Destination is readable and writable with expected encryption settings
- Backup manifest is written and includes:
  - cluster/environment identifiers
  - current Private version and target version
  - snapshot IDs and/or dump object URIs
  - checksums for exported text artifacts
- DB consistency checks (lightweight):
  - ability to run `SELECT 1`
  - migration lock status is clear (no long-running migration locks)

---
sections.heading: Backup verification steps (pre-upgrade)

sections.body:
- **Insufficient storage headroom** for snapshot/dump staging
  - Remediation: expand PV or destination capacity; rerun backup
- **Snapshot controller/CRDs missing** (on-prem)
  - Remediation: install VolumeSnapshot CRDs and controller; or use logical dump
- **KMS permissions denied** (VPC)
  - Remediation: validate IAM role access to CMK and S3 bucket policy
- **Logical dump too slow** for maintenance window
  - Remediation: switch to snapshot; reduce DB size; schedule longer window
sections.heading: Common failures

sections.body:
- If backup creation or verification fails, the upgrade is **blocked**.
- If restore verification fails, the environment remains in “maintenance mode” until operator resolution.

---
sections.heading: Guardrails

sections.body:
For environments with compliance requirements, the following evidence artifacts must be retained alongside the backup:
- Upgrade plan summary (plan ID, steps, versions)
- Precheck report (pass/fail + remediation pointers)
- Backup manifest (IDs, checksums, encryption mode)
- Restore/rollback logs (if invoked)
- Audit log events (minimum fields):
  - `event_type` (upgrade_started, prechecks_failed, backup_completed, rollback_invoked, restore_completed)
  - `actor` (operator identity)
  - `env_id` / `cluster_id`
  - `upgrade_plan_id`
  - `from_version` / `to_version`
  - `backup_id`
  - timestamps

Retention for audit evidence should follow the customer’s policy; Redwood recommends aligning evidence retention to the organization’s change-management retention (commonly 90–365 days).

---
sections.heading: Audit evidence (enterprise/compliance)

sections.body:
The installer writes a human-readable manifest file alongside artifacts:

- File: `backup-manifest.txt`
- Example fields:
  - `backup_id: bkp-2025-06-20T02:14:33Z-7f3a`
  - `env_id: priv-prod-us-east-1-042`
  - `cluster_id: eks-...`
  - `private_version: 1.18.3`
  - `upgrade_plan_id: upgplan-1.19.0-20250620-0210Z`
  - `snapshot_type: ebs`
  - `db_snapshot_ids: snap-0123..., snap-0456...`
  - `helm_values_sha256: ...`
  - `export_bundle_uri: s3://bucket/prefix/bkp-.../exports.tgz`
  - `encryption: sse-kms arn:aws:kms:...`
  - `verification: PASS`

---
sections.heading: Appendix A: Backup manifest (example format)

sections.body:
- Snapshot-based backups typically complete in minutes to tens of minutes (storage dependent).
- Logical dumps scale with DB size; assume roughly **20–60 GB/hour** effective throughput depending on CPU/network and compression.
sections.heading: Appendix B: Sizing guidance

sections.body:
- Destination has at least **2×** expected DB size available for dump-based backups (temporary + final artifact).

---
sections.heading: Operators should ensure

sections.body:
- Primary owner: **Infrastructure Engineering (Private Deployments)**
- Backup/restore implementation owners:
  - Installer orchestration: Release Engineering + Infra
  - Storage backend support (CSI/EBS): Infra
  - Audit signals/dashboards: Observability/SRE

For changes to backup scope, encryption defaults, or retention behavior, request review from Security Engineering and SRE leadership per Private change-management policy.
sections.heading: Owners

payload.page_title: Redwood Private: Upgrade + Rollback Workflow (Overview)

sections.body:
This page describes the end-to-end, operator-facing upgrade workflow for **Redwood Private** deployments (VPC and on-prem/air-gapped). It is intended as a stable overview of:
- Upgrade phases and sequencing between **control plane** and **data plane**
- Safety invariants (what must be true before we proceed)
- Required inputs and artifacts
- Operator UX (CLI-first, with optional Console visibility)
- Rollback entry points and guarantees

This is the canonical workflow referenced by the installer, Helm packaging, Terraform variables, and support/runbooks.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
**Private Control Plane (CP)**
- Private management services (API, auth integration, policy, upgrade coordinator) running in the customer cluster/VPC or on-prem environment.

**Private Data Plane (DP)**
- Inference runtime components and worker pools that serve traffic.

**Installer**
- `redwood-private-installer` (CLI) that performs plan generation, prechecks, backup orchestration, staged execution, and rollback.

**Upgrade plan**
- A versioned, auditable artifact generated before execution. It enumerates stages, steps, dependencies, timeouts, and rollback hooks.

**Supported upgrade path (default)**
- **N-1 → N** (one minor/major hop depending on release train policy). Other jumps may be blocked or require manual approval/steps.

---
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1. **Safe by default:** upgrades do not start until required prechecks pass and backup prerequisites are satisfied.
2. **Deterministic rollback:** clear entry points with known behavior for partial upgrades.
3. **Operator clarity:** failures produce actionable remediation, and the system surfaces exactly which stage/step is blocked.
4. **Auditability:** every run produces persisted artifacts (plan + execution summary) and emits audit events.
5. **Consistency across environments:** VPC and on-prem follow the same phases; air-gapped differs only in artifact sourcing/verification.

---
sections.heading: Goals (what the workflow optimizes for)

sections.body:
- Fully automated multi-hop upgrades across many major versions.
- Automatic remediation of all historical schema edge cases (the plan may require manual intervention for specific migrations).
- Full blue/green replacement as the default mechanism.

---
sections.heading: Non-goals (initial GA)

sections.body:
- **Version compatibility is supported** (policy evaluation passes) for the requested path.
- **Cluster health is good enough** to safely roll workloads (node readiness, scheduling capacity, core components available).
- **Storage headroom meets minimum threshold** for backups + rollouts (see Prechecks spec for exact numbers).
- **Artifact availability is verified** (online registry/chart repo or offline bundle checksum/signature verification).
- **RBAC and auth reachability is validated** (OIDC/SSO endpoints where configured; Kubernetes RBAC for installer SA).
- **Backup prerequisites are satisfied** (encryption/KMS access where required; snapshot capability for selected backend).
- **Operator acknowledges maintenance window** (explicit `--approve` / `--maintenance-window` flag) for steps that can impact availability.
sections.heading: Invariants before execution (hard gates)

sections.body:
- **Control plane upgrades complete before data plane changes**.
- **Schema migrations run exactly once** (idempotent, guarded by locks/timeouts; no best-effort repeats that can corrupt state).
- **Step ordering is respected** (Helm hook ordering + installer stage dependencies).
- **Every step is resumable or roll-backable** (state machine persisted locally and in-cluster).
sections.heading: Invariants during execution

sections.body:
- CP services are healthy and at target version.
- DP workloads are healthy and serving within expected error/latency envelopes.
- Post-upgrade validation passes (connectivity, auth, core APIs, sample inference check where enabled).
- Upgrade summary and audit events are recorded.

---
sections.heading: Invariants to declare success

sections.body:
At minimum, the operator must provide:

1. **Target version**
- Example: `--to 2025.06.0` (exact naming per release train)

2. **Deployment mode + artifact source**
- VPC/online: registry + chart repo endpoints
- On-prem/air-gapped: path to an **upgrade bundle** (manifest + checksums/signatures)

3. **Environment access**
- kubeconfig context or cluster endpoint credentials
- installer service account / RBAC binding (recommended: dedicated SA with least privileges per spec)

4. **Backup configuration**
- Selected backup mode (CSI snapshot, EBS snapshot, logical DB dump as supported)
- Encryption/KMS configuration where applicable
- Retention policy inputs (for environments with strict storage constraints)

5. **Change-management gating (enterprise)**
- Optional but commonly required: `--change-ticket <id>`, `--approver <name/email>`
sections.heading: Required inputs (operator-provided)

sections.body:
- `--upgrade-window "2025-06-22T01:00Z/2h"`
- `--dry-run` (generate plan + prechecks only)
- `--pause-after <stage>` (for manual verification between stages)

---
sections.heading: Optional inputs commonly used

sections.body:
- Plan generation:
  - `redwood-private upgrade plan --from <current> --to <target> [--bundle <path>|--registry <url> ...]`
- Preflight validation:
  - `redwood-private upgrade precheck --plan <plan.json> [--strict]`
- Execute upgrade:
  - `redwood-private upgrade apply --plan <plan.json> --approve`
- Live status:
  - `redwood-private upgrade status [--watch]`
- Rollback:
  - `redwood-private upgrade rollback --to <previous> --from-state <state-dir|cluster> --approve`
- Support bundle (includes upgrade artifacts):
  - `redwood-private support-bundle create --include upgrade --since 24h`
sections.heading: CLI (primary)

sections.body:
- Every command prints:
  - environment identity (cluster name, region/site, deployment id)
  - installer version
  - plan id / execution id
  - next action on failure
sections.heading: Output requirements

sections.body:
Where available, Redwood Console surfaces:
- current CP/DP versions (reported from the environment)
- last upgrade attempt + outcome
- audit trail entries (start/stop, precheck results, backup completion, rollback invoked)

Note: Console is not required to execute upgrades for air-gapped environments.

---
sections.heading: Console (secondary visibility)

sections.body: The workflow is split into phases. Operators typically run them in order; automation may combine them.
sections.heading: Phased workflow (end-to-end)

sections.body:
- Determine current CP/DP versions.
- Identify target version.
- Confirm desired maintenance window and staffing (recommended: at least one operator + one on-call contact).
sections.heading: Phase 0: Identify + scope the upgrade

sections.body:
- Planned upgrade window
- Selected target version
- Change ticket (if required)
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body:
- current state discovery
- compatibility policy evaluation
- artifact manifest (online) or bundle manifest (offline)
sections.heading: The installer generates an upgrade plan from

sections.body:
- stages: `prechecks`, `backup`, `control-plane`, `data-plane`, `postchecks`, `finalize`
- step ordering and dependencies
- timeouts and retry policy
- rollback hooks per stage
sections.heading: The plan includes

sections.body: - `upgrade-plan.json` (persisted locally; optionally uploaded to internal artifact store if enabled)
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body:
- **BLOCK**: must be fixed before continuing
- **WARN**: recorded; operator may proceed with explicit acknowledgment
- **INFO**: informational
sections.heading: Prechecks are executed from the plan and categorized

sections.body:
- Kubernetes cluster health + capacity
- Storage headroom
- DB connectivity + readiness for migrations
- RBAC/auth reachability (OIDC endpoints if configured)
- DNS/TLS sanity (cluster ingress endpoints)
- Artifact reachability/verification (including checksum/signature for offline bundles)
sections.heading: Common prechecks (high level)

sections.body: - `precheck-report.json` + human-readable summary
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body: Backup orchestration runs before any irreversible steps.
sections.heading: Phase 3: Backup (mandatory for rollback guarantees)

sections.body:
- control plane DB (or logical dump depending on backend)
- critical config/state references (including version pins)
- upgrade state metadata (for resumption/rollback)
sections.heading: Backed up at minimum

sections.body:
- backup identifier(s) + verification result
- audit event: `backup_completed` (or `backup_failed`)
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body: This phase upgrades the control plane first, including any migrations needed for the new control plane version.
sections.heading: Phase 4: Upgrade control plane (CP)

sections.body:
- CP upgrade must reach readiness before DP changes.
- Migrations are guarded:
  - idempotent where possible
  - lock timeouts to avoid indefinite blocking
  - explicit failure modes with remediation guidance
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
- CP workloads at target version
- migration status recorded
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body: DP is upgraded only after CP is healthy. The DP rollout is done in a safe order with readiness gates.
sections.heading: Phase 5: Upgrade data plane (DP)

sections.body:
- honor traffic impact controls:
  - rolling updates with max unavailable configured
  - canary where enabled
  - automatic pause on SLO breach (if configured in environment policy)
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
- DP workloads at target version
- DP readiness gates pass
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body:
- CP APIs responding
- DP serving
- key integrations reachable (auth, logging/audit sinks)
- optional sample inference smoke test (recommended in non-air-gapped with test model cache)
sections.heading: Postchecks confirm the environment is stable and consistent

sections.body: - `postcheck-report.json`
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body:
- execution summary
- pointers to backup artifacts
- full step timings
- audit log events
sections.heading: Finalize persists

sections.body:
- `upgrade-summary.json`
- upgrade marked as completed

---
sections.heading: Deliverables

sections.body: The following shows the enforced sequencing and the main gates.
sections.heading: Control plane / data plane sequencing (diagram)

sections.body:
```
Operator
  |
  |  (1) plan
  v
Installer ---------------------------> Generates upgrade-plan.json
  |
  |  (2) precheck
  v
Prechecks ---------------------------> BLOCK/WARN/INFO report
  |
  |  (3) backup
  v
Backups -----------------------------> snapshot/dump + verification
  |
  |  (4) upgrade CP
  v
Control Plane rollout ---------------> CP ready + migrations complete
  |
  |  (5) upgrade DP
  v
Data Plane rollout ------------------> DP ready + serving
  |
  |  (6) postchecks
  v
Validation --------------------------> postcheck report
  |
  |  (7) finalize
  v
Artifacts + Audit -------------------> summary + events
```
sections.heading: High-level flow

sections.body:
```
Stage A: Control plane
  A1. Apply CP Helm release(s)
  A2. Wait for CP readiness gates (API, workers, controllers)
  A3. Run DB migrations (guarded)
  A4. Re-check CP health

Stage B: Data plane
  B1. Apply DP Helm release(s)
  B2. Roll DP workers (respect maxUnavailable)
  B3. Validate DP readiness + basic serving
```

---
sections.heading: Sequencing detail (CP must be stable before DP)

sections.body: Rollback is supported through defined entry points and depends on successful backups.
sections.heading: Rollback overview

sections.body:
- migrations fail and remediation is non-trivial within the maintenance window
- CP is degraded after upgrade and cannot be stabilized quickly
- DP rollout causes sustained serving failures that persist after a pause/rollback of DP-only steps
sections.heading: Rollback is recommended when

sections.body:
- the issue is clearly a transient capacity/network condition and pre-upgrade state is not safer
- the environment has already run forward-only migrations that are explicitly marked non-reversible (these are flagged in the plan)
sections.heading: Rollback is not recommended when

sections.body:
1. **During CP stage** (before migrations complete): revert CP chart to previous version; restore any modified config; validate CP.
2. **After migrations but before DP stage:** rollback is only allowed if the plan marks migrations reversible OR provides an automated restore path.
3. **During DP stage:** rollback DP workloads to previous version; CP stays at upgraded version if compatible (preferred) OR revert both per plan.
4. **After completion:** rollback is supported via the same mechanism but may require downtime depending on restore and cache behavior.
sections.heading: Rollback can be invoked

sections.body:
If the workflow ran through Phase 3 (Backup) successfully and the plan marks the path as rollback-supported:
- We can restore CP state to the last known good snapshot/dump.
- We can revert Helm releases to the previous known good versions.
- We can restore critical config/state needed to restart components.
sections.heading: Rollback guarantees (what we promise)

sections.body:
- Model cache/KV caches are treated as **rebuildable**; rollback focuses on correctness and control-plane state, not preserving cache.
- Some migrations may be forward-only. The plan must clearly label these and require explicit operator acknowledgment before proceeding.

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
Each upgrade attempt produces artifacts (persisted by the installer and included in support bundles):
- upgrade plan (`upgrade-plan.json`)
- precheck report
- backup references + verification report
- execution timeline and step results
- rollback invocation report (if used)
sections.heading: Auditability and artifacts

sections.body:
- `upgrade_started`
- `precheck_passed` / `precheck_failed`
- `backup_completed` / `backup_failed`
- `upgrade_completed` / `upgrade_failed`
- `rollback_invoked` / `rollback_completed` / `rollback_failed`
sections.heading: Audit log events emitted (high level)

sections.body:
- environment id
- operator identity (where available)
- from/to versions
- plan id + execution id
- timestamps

---
sections.heading: Fields that must be included in every audit event

sections.body:
- Run upgrades in a defined maintenance window.
- Ensure a backup target exists and has sufficient retention capacity.
- Ensure on-call coverage and a rollback decision-maker is identified.
- For on-prem/air-gapped: verify bundle signature/checksums *before* the maintenance window.

---
sections.heading: Operational expectations (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- Primary owner: **Private Deployments Engineering**
- Release gating approvals: **Release Engineering (Connor O'Brien)** + **SRE (Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes)**
- Security/compliance review: **Naomi Feldman / Marcus Lin** (audit + backup encryption)
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:
- Follow the "Private upgrade runbook" and page SRE if any of the following occur:
  - migration exceeds timeout and blocks control plane readiness
  - sustained error rate increase during DP rollout
  - rollback attempted and post-rollback health checks fail

---
sections.heading: Escalation during upgrade incidents

sections.body:
- 2025-06-18: Clarified CP/DP sequencing gates; added explicit rollback entry point rules.
- 2025-06-04: Added auditability requirements and artifact list.
- 2025-05-20: Initial published version aligned with upgrade plan + precheck framework.
sections.heading: Change log

payload.page_title: Alpha customers: upgrade notes for Private VPC Terraform modules (design partners)

sections.body:
This page provides **alpha-specific upgrade guidance** for design partners using the **Redwood Private VPC Terraform modules (AWS)**. During alpha, we expect iterative changes to defaults, module interfaces, and validation behavior. This document explains:
- What changes are normal during alpha iterations (and what may be disruptive)
- How to **pin module versions** for stability
- How to **coordinate upgrade windows** with Redwood (SE + Eng)
- A practical **upgrade + rollback playbook** tailored to alpha

This page is intentionally conservative. If anything here conflicts with your organization’s change control, follow your internal process and use the coordination steps below.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Design partner **platform / infra engineers** applying Terraform to provision the Redwood Private VPC footprint
- **Security and networking teams** reviewing endpoint/DNS/logging/IAM changes
- Redwood **Solutions Engineering / Professional Services** running pilots

---
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- AWS only (alpha). Modules live in `redwood-terraform` and are consumed from Git tags.
- Modules cover **foundational networking and security scaffolding** (VPC, subnets, routing/NAT, endpoints, flow logs/log sinks, SG patterns, installer IAM scaffold, optional VPN/DX placeholders).
- The **application/cluster install** is performed separately by the Redwood Private installer/Helm flow.

---
sections.heading: Scope and assumptions

sections.body: Alpha is not a “set and forget” phase. You should expect some churn as we harden defaults across customer environments.
sections.heading: What changes to expect during alpha

sections.body:
These generally show up as in-place updates with low blast radius:
- Additional or expanded **VPC endpoints** (e.g., new endpoint services required by installer preflight)
- Adjustments to **endpoint policy documents** (least-privilege tightening)
- Refinements to **security group rules** (e.g., narrower egress, explicit ports)
- **Flow Logs** configuration tweaks (destination support, retention defaults, log format)
- Output additions (new `outputs.tf` values for installer integration)
- Provider pinning and validation/lint improvements (CI-related)
sections.heading: 1) Changes that are expected and usually safe (typical patch/minor updates)

sections.body:
These can force resource recreation or cause service interruptions if applied casually:
- Subnet / route table shape changes (e.g., AZ mapping, route association refactors)
- NAT gateway strategy changes (count per AZ vs shared) and related route changes
- Private DNS enablement changes for endpoints (can affect image pulls, AWS API resolution)
- Security group posture changes that reduce egress (can break existing egress paths/proxies)
- Logging sink migration (CloudWatch -> S3 or customer-owned bucket requirements)
sections.heading: 2) Changes that may be disruptive (require coordination)

sections.body:
Even during alpha we avoid these unless necessary; if required, Redwood will provide explicit guidance and a migration plan:
- CIDR changes (VPC or subnet CIDRs)
- Renaming or restructuring module resources in a way that causes widespread state churn
- Changes that require re-creating the VPC, private subnets, or core gateways

---
sections.heading: 3) Changes we treat as “breaking” during alpha

sections.body:
We follow semantic versioning, but note the standard alpha caveat:
- **0.x.y** versions may include breaking changes in “minor” bumps.
- We still try to reserve “breaking migrations” for clearly communicated releases and provide upgrade notes.
sections.heading: Semver in alpha (0.x)

sections.body:
- Redwood Support/SE can best help when you are running a **known tagged version** (not an arbitrary commit SHA).
- For design partners, Redwood may request an upgrade to a newer alpha tag to resolve an issue found during pilots.

---
sections.heading: Supportability policy (alpha)

sections.body: Do not consume modules from `main` during alpha. Always pin to an explicit tag.
sections.heading: Pinning module versions (required for design partners)
Example (adjust module paths to match your config)
Pin Terraform and provider versions

sections.body: - Commit `terraform.lock.hcl` to keep provider resolution stable across environments.
sections.heading: Commit lock files

sections.body:
- Keep your pilot `*.tfvars` under source control.
- If Redwood provides an updated example tfvars, treat it as a **diffable artifact**, not a “copy/paste overwrite”.

---
sections.heading: Pin examples and tfvars

sections.body:
- **Default cadence:** no more than **every 2–4 weeks**, unless you are blocked by a known issue.
- **Do not upgrade within 72 hours** of a scheduled go-live / demo unless explicitly agreed.
- **Coordinate first** if your environment has strict egress controls, custom DNS, or centralized networking (shared services VPC, TGW, firewall appliances).

---
sections.heading: Recommended upgrade cadence for design partners

sections.body:
- Any version bump that changes VPC endpoints, private DNS settings, NAT strategy, route tables, or security group posture
- Any change that produces a Terraform plan with **resource recreation** for core network components
sections.heading: Coordinate with Redwood before applying

sections.body:
- Primary: **Markus Klein** (Solutions Engineering lead)
- Engineering escalation: **Irene Choi** (Infra), **Victor Alvarez** (Networking)
- Security review: **Marcus Lin** (Security Eng)
sections.heading: Who to contact

sections.body:
1. Current module tag(s): `vX.Y.Z`
2. Target module tag(s): `vA.B.C`
3. AWS region(s)
4. Connectivity model: Internet egress (NAT), proxy egress, VPN, Direct Connect, TGW, etc.
5. Logging destination: CloudWatch vs S3 (customer-owned bucket?)
6. **Terraform plan output** (sanitized) highlighting:
   - Resources to be replaced
   - Changes to endpoints/private DNS
   - Changes to security group egress
7. Proposed maintenance window + rollback window
sections.heading: Provide the following in your upgrade request

sections.body:
- Confirm whether the change is expected for your topology
- Flag any known issues/limitations for the target tag
- Provide a short validation checklist for post-apply (installer preflight + basic AWS reachability)

---
sections.heading: What Redwood will do

sections.body:
- Ensure you can run `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` from a controlled environment (CI runner or bastion) with stable credentials.
- Confirm no pending manual changes in the AWS console (avoid drift).
- Take note of any “pet” resources attached to the VPC (non-Terraform-managed) that may be impacted.
sections.heading: Step 0 — Pre-flight checks

sections.body:
- Change `ref=vX.Y.Z` -> `ref=vA.B.C`.
- Avoid mixing an upgrade with unrelated refactors.
sections.heading: Step 1 — Update module refs only (no other changes)

sections.body:
- `terraform fmt -check`
- `terraform init -upgrade`
- `terraform validate`
sections.heading: Step 2 — Run validation locally/CI

sections.body:
- `-/+` (replace) actions on: VPC, subnets, NAT gateways, route tables, endpoint resources
- Changes to endpoint `private_dns_enabled`
- Egress changes (0.0.0.0/0 removal, proxy-only egress)
- Flow logs destination and retention changes

If the plan includes replacement of core network resources, stop and coordinate with Redwood before applying.
sections.heading: Pay special attention to

sections.body:
- Apply during an agreed window.
- If you have multiple environments (dev/stage/prod), apply to the least critical environment first.
sections.heading: Step 4 — Apply in a maintenance window

sections.body:
Minimum checks (Redwood and customer teams can run together):
- Confirm VPC endpoints are present for required services (notably ECR API/DKR, STS, CloudWatch Logs as applicable)
- Confirm DNS resolution behavior in private subnets (VPC resolver, endpoint private DNS)
- Confirm nodes/installer runner can reach required AWS APIs without traversing unintended public egress
- Run Redwood installer preflight checks (or equivalent) and confirm no endpoint/DNS warnings
- Confirm flow logs are delivering to the configured sink

---
sections.heading: Step 5 — Post-apply validation

sections.body: Rollback strategy depends on what changed.
sections.heading: Rollback guidance (alpha)

sections.body:
- Revert the module `ref` to the previous tag
- Re-run `terraform init` and `terraform apply`
sections.heading: If changes were primarily additive or in-place

sections.body:
- Replaced subnets / route tables
- Modified NAT strategy (resource recreation)
- Changed private DNS behavior and introduced new resolution paths
sections.heading: Rollback can be complex if the upgrade

sections.body:
- Stop and coordinate with Redwood immediately.
- Do not attempt repeated apply/rollback cycles without a plan; you can thrash routing/endpoint state.
sections.heading: In these cases

sections.body:
- Store Terraform state in a remote backend with versioning (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB locking).
- Ensure CloudTrail/flow logs are active so changes are auditable.

---
sections.heading: State and audit recommendations

sections.body: Symptom: installer or nodes cannot pull images.
sections.heading: Image pull failures (ECR endpoint / private DNS)

sections.body:
- Missing ECR endpoints (API and DKR)
- Endpoint created but **private DNS disabled** when required
- DNS resolver issues in private subnets
sections.heading: Typical causes

sections.body:
- Validate ECR endpoints and private DNS settings.
- Run installer preflight and address endpoint warnings before re-trying.
sections.heading: Action

sections.body: Symptom: core services occasionally fail to resolve AWS/private names.
sections.heading: Intermittent DNS resolution in private subnets

sections.body:
- Conflicting DNS forwarders, custom resolver rules, or split-horizon domains
- Misaligned VPC resolver settings across shared VPC/TGW environments
sections.heading: Typical causes

sections.body:
- Engage customer DNS owners and Redwood to align on resolver path.
- Avoid “quick fixes” that disable private DNS globally; it often creates new failure modes.

---
sections.heading: Action

sections.body:
- Redwood publishes alpha release notes in the Private Deployments space.
- For each pilot, Redwood will maintain a shared “current recommended tag” and known-good config notes.
sections.heading: Change communication and release notes

sections.body:
- Subscribe to release notes updates (or have SE forward the relevant diffs)
- Keep a simple internal changelog: date, version, plan highlights, validation outcome

---
sections.heading: Design partners should

sections.body:
- During your agreed maintenance window, Redwood can provide a live escalation path via your SE.
- If the upgrade impacts connectivity, include your network team on-call.
sections.heading: Support and escalation during upgrades

sections.body:
- Module tag before/after
- Terraform plan snippet showing the unexpected change
- Region/account (or internal alias) and VPC ID
- Endpoint list + private DNS flags (if relevant)
- Installer preflight output (if applicable)

---
sections.heading: Information to include in any escalation

sections.body:
- [ ] Versions pinned to tags (no `main`)
- [ ] Terraform and AWS provider pinned
- [ ] Plan reviewed; no uncoordinated replacements of core network resources
- [ ] Maintenance window scheduled
- [ ] Rollback plan documented
- [ ] Post-apply validation steps agreed (endpoints, DNS, logs, installer preflight)

---
sections.heading: Appendix: Upgrade request checklist (one-pager)

sections.body:
- 2025-07-08: Initial version for design partner pilots.
- 2025-08-02: Clarified version pinning and added coordination requirements for endpoint/DNS changes.
sections.heading: Document history

payload.page_title: Runtime Entropy and Upgrade Safety Playbook for Private Deployments

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines an operator-ready, low-risk procedure for upgrading runtime components and model artifacts in private (VPC and on-prem) deployments while actively managing "runtime entropy"—the divergence between expected runtime state and live system state (config drift, KV cache inconsistencies, quantization/profile mismatches, and asymmetric node configuration). It covers preflight checks, phased rollout steps, automated and manual rollback actions, telemetry/health thresholds, and customer-facing validation required for acceptance.

Scope

- Applies to Redwood Private control plane and runtime stacks (service names: rwd-controlplane, rwd-agent, rwd-runtime, rwd-kvcache).
- Targeted upgrade types: runtime binary (minor/major), model artifact swap (weights/quantization), KV cache schema changes, and packaging (image/firmware) updates.
- Excludes hardware firmware upgrades (see hw-eol-deprecation playbook).

Goals

- Maintain 99.5% request success rate during upgrade windows for production tenants.
- Keep 95th percentile token latency regression within +10% of baseline for 2 hours post-rollout.
- Provide deterministic rollback within 15 minutes for single-service regressions and 60 minutes for multi-service failure modes.

Key definitions

- Runtime entropy: measurable divergence from expected runtime state (config, KV cache, model weights) that increases probability of silent failures or output regression.
- Safe window: period after rollout where metrics are observed against acceptance criteria.

Risk model and primary failure modes

1. KV cache incompatibility: new runtime expects different cache key structure leading to cold starts or wrong outputs.
2. Quantization mismatch: swapped model quantization causes degraded quality/regressions.
3. Partial rollout divergence: mixed-version traffic returns differing outputs and fails eval parity checks.
4. Control plane drift: mis-synced feature flags or routing causing tenant mis-routing.

Preconditions (hard gates before any upgrade)

- Backups and snapshots completed: control plane DB snapshot (rwd-cp-snapshot), KV cache snapshot (where supported) and model artifact registry snapshot.
- Customer acceptance test (CAT) harness uploaded to runbook: basic prompt set (10 prompts) and evaluation script (python) per-customer.
- Capacity buffer: 20% burstable capacity reserved on Dedicated pools or on-prem operator nodes flagged for maintenance.
- Communication: SRE/SE oncall and customer POC notified at least 24 hours prior for >minor upgrades.

Preflight checklist (automated plus manual)

1. Sanity automation (CI-generated): integration smoke passing for rwd-runtime and rwd-agent images (CI tag: release/<tag>).
2. Canary lab: run synthetic load at target QPS for 30m against a canary cluster.
3. KV schema validation: run `rwd-kvctl validate-schema --target release/<tag>` to assert compatibility.
4. Model checksum/parity: `sha256sum model-v<new>.tar.gz` must match checksum in artifact registry.
5. Eval parity: run customer CAT harness and compare embedding/cosine similarity and token-level divergence metrics.

Phased rollout steps (recommended)

Phase 0 — Staging verification (operator):
- Deploy release to staging control plane and runtime.
- Run automated acceptance: unit tests, integration tests, and full CAT harness.
- Confirm monitoring dashboards (rwd-dashboard/staging) show baseline SLOs.

Phase 1 — Small canary (1–3 nodes / 1–5% traffic):
- Route a small percentage of traffic using canary policy `routing.canary=on`.
- Observe live evals (see Telemetry) for at least 45 minutes.
- Run `rwd-ops check-health --tenants sample_tenant_list.txt` and ensure no tenant reports >2% request errors.

Phase 2 — Regional ramp (25% traffic or 2 AZs):
- Increase traffic to 25% in a single region or two availability zones (AZs).
- Run CVR/QA evals: automated reranker and completion-quality tests.
- Observe latency P95 and P99. Abort if thresholds breached.

Phase 3 — Global/All tenants (100%):
- After green light from Phase 2, ramp to 100% using rolling update.
- Keep burst capacity for 60 minutes and SRE on-call paging active.

Monitoring and telemetry (what to watch)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Request success rate (per-tenant): target >= 99.5%. Abort if any tenant drops below 98.0% for 10 consecutive minutes.
- Token-level latency: P95 change <= +10% and P99 change <= +25% relative to baseline. Abort if exceeded for 15m window.
- Model quality regressions: median embedding cosine similarity to baseline lower by >0.03 on CAT harness. Abort.
- Error class spikes: decoder OOM, kernel-failure counts > 5/min system-wide. Abort and roll back.
sections.heading: Primary metrics and thresholds (abort if any triggered)

sections.body:
- Default sampling: 10% full trace + 1% full request payload capture across production tenants.
- For canaries: 100% full trace + 100% payload capture for canary tenant IDs.
- Adaptive sampling: increase to 20% full trace if P95 latency deviates >5%.
- Retention: full samples retained for 7 days; aggregated metrics retained per standard retention policy.

Automated validation hooks (examples)

- Health probe: `curl -fsS http://<node>/healthz` must return 200 and JSON {"status":"ok","kv_synced":true}.
- KV-check: `rwd-kvctl compare --baseline /snapshots/kv_preupgrade --live` returns zero mismatches.
- Model inference parity: run `python scripts/compare_inference.py --old model-vX --new model-vY --prompts cat_prompts.json` and assert token-diff <= 1.2% and embedding-sim >= 0.96.

Abort criteria and automated rollback triggers

- Immediate rollback triggers (automated):
  - kernel-failure rate > 0.5% of requests for 5 minutes.
  - Unexpected KV mismatch count > 50 per minute.
  - Cat harness quality metric breach (see thresholds above).

- Manual abort triggers:
  - Customer POC reports reproducible functional regression.
  - Sustained latency or error trend with no clear mitigation within 30 minutes.

Rollback procedure (fast path for common failures)

1. Freeze rollouts: set `routing.upgrade_pause = true` in control plane flags.
2. Switch traffic back: update routing policy and GradualShift rollback to previous release tag: `rwd-ctl traffic-shift --from release/<new> --to release/<old> --pace 100% --force` (fast path: immediate).
3. Rehydrate KV: if KV incompatibility detected, restore snapshot: `rwd-kvctl restore --snapshot /snapshots/kv_preupgrade --force` and then run `rwd-kvctl warm-cache --target all`.
4. Confirm model artifact swap-back: re-push prior model artifact `rwd-artifact push --file model-v<old>.tar.gz --set-active`.
5. Run sanity checks: `rwd-ops check-health --all` and verify SLOs.
6. Post-rollback communication: immediately notify customers with the templated message below and create an incident in incidenttracker (INC- auto-generated).

Rollback verification checklist

- Control plane health: all components show status "ok".
- KV consistency: zero critical mismatches.
- Model parity: CAT harness within thresholds.
- Latency: P95 returned to baseline within 30 minutes.

Operational runbook scripts and snippets

- Snapshot control plane DB
  - `kubectl exec -n rwd-system rwd-cp-0 -- rwd-cp-tool snapshot create --output /tmp/cp-snap-$(date +%s).tar.gz`
- Warm KV cache (operator helper)
  - `rwd-kvctl warm-cache --tenant-id TENANT_ID --prefetch 1000`
- Quick rollback (one liner)
  - `rwd-ctl rollback --target release/<old> --scope region:us-east-1 --force`

Customer acceptance and fields validation

- Provide customer POC with an acceptance checklist and run CAT harness during Phase 2.
- Required customer signoff items: 1) functional smoke tests pass, 2) latency within acceptance, 3) no dataflow regressions reported.
- Example acceptance email template (send on green):
  - Subject: "[Redwood] Private deployment upgrade complete — validation request"
  - Body: "We completed the staged rollout to your environment. Please run the attached CAT harness (link) and report any anomalies within 48 hours. Contact SE oncall: se-oncall@redwood.ai"

Escalation and ownership

- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments SRE team (oncall alias: rwd-sre-oncall).
- Secondary owner: runtime platform (runtime@redwood.ai).
- SLA/NFR escalation: if rollback exceeds 60 minutes or customer impact affects revenue-bound SLAs, escalate to Director of SRE and Customer Success immediately.

Post-upgrade audit and continuous improvement

- Create a short post-upgrade report within 24 hours: include metrics, anomalies, corrective actions, and retro notes.
- Required fields in report: change-id, release tags, pre/post SLO metrics, canary tenant IDs, CAT harness results.
- If rollback occurred, capture root cause analysis within 72 hours and attach for compliance evidence.

Appendix A — Templates and quick checks

- `rwd-ops check-health` expected output snippet:
  - {"status":"ok", "uptime":3600, "kv_synced":true, "active_release":"release/<tag>"}
- Minimal CAT harness example (python):
  - `python -c "from rwd_eval import Runner; Runner('model-vX').run('prompts.json')"`

Appendix B — Change log

- 2029-01-15: Created by Marco Liu (initial draft).
- 2029-02-10: Expanded telemetry guidance and added adaptive sampling rules (reviewers: Aisha Patel, Claire Nguyen).

Related documents and references

- Incremental stateful upgrade strategy (internal): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/incremental-stateful-upgrade-strategy-2027
- KV cache migration playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/kv-cache-migrations-and-runtime-state-migration-playbook-2025
- Private deploy on-boarding runbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-onboarding-and-failover-runbook-2026

Contact

- For questions and follow-up: Marco Liu <marco@redwood.ai> and rwd-sre-oncall@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: Private (On-Prem) Upgrades & Rollback Guide

sections.body: Standardized, auditable upgrade workflow for Redwood Private on-prem/air-gapped deployments: plan -> prechecks -> backups -> staged rollout -> verification, with deterministic rollback and restore-based recovery when required.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
This page documents the current, supported process for upgrading Redwood Private in on-prem and fully air-gapped environments. It standardizes:
- How we generate and persist a deterministic upgrade plan
- Which preflight checks block vs warn (and how to tune policy)
- Backup/restore approaches across storage backends (CSI snapshots vs logical dumps)
- Rollback semantics, including when rollback requires restore
- Audit evidence and operational verification

This guidance reflects repeated failure modes seen in on-prem upgrades: partial upgrades where Helm state diverges from database state, artifact mismatches in offline mirrors, and inconsistent snapshot capability across clusters.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Customer/on-prem platform engineering teams operating Redwood Private
- Redwood SRE / Support engineers assisting an upgrade window
- Security/compliance stakeholders who require change evidence
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Predictable, staged upgrades (control plane -> data plane) with readiness gates
- Early failure on missing/invalid artifacts (no “surprises” mid-window)
- Clear separation of reversible steps vs restore-required steps
- Evidence: what ran, who initiated it, what artifacts were used, and outcomes
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Blue/green upgrades for on-prem (not currently the default approach)
- Zero-downtime guarantees (some upgrades include brief control plane impact depending on schema changes and cluster capacity)
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body: Redwood Private upgrades are orchestrated by the installer, which wraps Helm in an auditable, stateful workflow.
sections.heading: High-level workflow (plan -> precheck -> backup -> apply -> verify -> (rollback/restore if needed))

sections.body:
> Note: command names may differ in older deployments. As of installer v1.16+, the canonical entrypoint is `redwood-private`.

1) Generate plan (safe to run even if you expect prechecks to block):
- `redwood-private upgrade plan --target <VERSION> --bundle <PATH>`

2) Run prechecks:
- `redwood-private upgrade precheck --plan <PLAN_FILE> --policy <POLICY_FILE>`

3) Execute backups:
- `redwood-private upgrade backup --plan <PLAN_FILE>`

4) Apply staged upgrade:
- `redwood-private upgrade apply --plan <PLAN_FILE> --yes`

5) Verify:
- `redwood-private upgrade verify --plan <PLAN_FILE>`

6) If needed:
- Roll back to a prior stage (only for steps marked reversible):
  - `redwood-private upgrade rollback --plan <PLAN_FILE> --to-stage control-plane`
- Restore from backups (required for steps marked restore-required):
  - `redwood-private upgrade restore --backup-id <ID> --plan <PLAN_FILE>`
sections.heading: Canonical commands

sections.body:
- Current version and target version
- Stages (prechecks, backup, control-plane upgrade, data-plane upgrade, verification)
- Step ordering, dependencies, timeouts
- Rollback metadata per step: reversible vs restore-required vs non-reversible
- Exact artifact references (image digests, chart versions) used for the upgrade
sections.heading: The plan is a versioned artifact that lists

sections.body:
- Default (v1.16+): a dedicated Kubernetes CRD (`UpgradePlan`) plus a local copy on the installer host
- Optional: configmap-only persistence for restricted clusters where CRD installation is not allowed

The goal is that if the installer host dies mid-upgrade, a new host can resume using the persisted state.
sections.heading: Where plan/state is persisted

sections.body: Fully air-gapped clusters must not perform outbound network fetches during upgrade. All dependencies must be vendored into the offline bundle.
sections.heading: Air-gapped / offline bundle delivery and verification

sections.body:
- Container images (or an import manifest for an internal registry mirror)
- Helm charts and vendored chart dependencies
- A manifest with pinned digests
- Checksums for all artifacts
- Signatures for the manifest (required by default as of v1.16+)
sections.heading: A bundle is either a directory or a tarball containing

sections.body:
- Previously: checksums were supported and signatures were optional
- Current: signature verification is enabled by default; checksums remain mandatory
sections.heading: Verification behavior (updated)

sections.body:
- Cosign key-pair verification (recommended for air-gapped)
- Customer re-signing (supported if you repackage artifacts internally)

If verification fails, `upgrade plan` and `upgrade apply` fail early (before backups and before any cluster mutations).
sections.heading: Supported signing modes

sections.body:
Prechecks run before any cluster changes. Each check outputs:
- Status: PASS / WARN / BLOCK
- A short reason (one line)
- Remediation guidance (commands/links)
sections.heading: Preflight checks (block vs warn)

sections.body: Severity is configurable via a policy file so customers can treat certain checks as blocking based on their operational model (e.g., SSO required vs break-glass available).
sections.heading: Severity policy

sections.body:
| Category | Check | Default severity | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Versioning | Unsupported version jump | BLOCK | Multi-hop upgrades are supported per the compatibility matrix; unsupported paths block. |
| Artifacts | Missing artifact(s) or digest mismatch | BLOCK | Prevents mirror/chart skew and “wrong image” upgrades. |
| Kubernetes | Nodes NotReady / DiskPressure | BLOCK | DiskPressure is explicitly blocking. |
| Registry | Internal registry auth/pull test | BLOCK | Detects expired tokens/pull secret issues. |
| DB | DB reachability + basic readiness | BLOCK | Includes connection test and required extensions. |
| Storage | Backup target capacity | BLOCK | Conservative thresholds; tune via policy. |
| Storage | CSI snapshot capability (if snapshot strategy selected) | BLOCK | If snapshots required but unsupported, block. |
| Identity | OIDC/SSO reachability | WARN or BLOCK (policy) | Default WARN if break-glass admin is enabled; otherwise BLOCK. |
| Networking | DNS resolution / latency | WARN | Can be promoted to BLOCK for known-flaky enclaves. |
| Security | TLS certificate validity/expiry window | BLOCK | Prevents mid-upgrade auth/API failures. |
sections.heading: Common checks and default severity

sections.body:
You may store this in your change system to make upgrade behavior auditable:

`upgrade-policy.yaml`
- Set OIDC to BLOCK if operator access depends on SSO.
- Set DNS to BLOCK for enclaves with known DNS instability.
sections.heading: Example policy file (YAML)

sections.body: Backup happens after prechecks pass and before any mutating upgrade steps.
sections.heading: Backup and restore strategy

sections.body:
The installer chooses (or validates) a backup strategy based on cluster capability:
1) CSI snapshots (preferred where supported)
- Best for large DBs and tight maintenance windows
- Fastest restore (snapshot revert)

2) Logical backups (fallback)
- Postgres: `pg_dump`/`pg_restore` (or equivalent for your configured DB)
- Includes export of Redwood CRDs/CRs and installer state
- Restore time scales with DB size; plan accordingly

Mixed environments are common (e.g., Ceph-backed snapshots in one cluster, local PV without snapshots in another). Do not assume snapshot support is uniform.
sections.heading: Strategy selection

sections.body:
- The installer must not dump secret values in cleartext.
- Backups include:
  - Non-secret configuration (CRs/values) required to reconstruct the deployment
  - References/metadata for secrets when an external secrets manager is used
- If Kubernetes Secrets are used, backup inclusion is explicitly controlled by policy and defaults to EXCLUDE secret values.
sections.heading: Secrets handling (clarified)

sections.body: Backups must be encrypted at rest.
sections.heading: Encryption

sections.body:
- Storage-level encryption (customer-managed)
- Installer-level encryption using customer-provided keys
- Passphrase-based encryption as a last resort (documented risk/operational constraints)
sections.heading: Supported models

sections.body: Upgrades are applied in phases to avoid control plane/data plane skew.
sections.heading: Apply phase: staged rollout and readiness gates

sections.body:
1) Control plane
- API, console, controllers
- DB migrations (guarded)
- Wait for readiness gates

2) Data plane
- Serving/runtime components
- Gateways and related deployments
- Wait for readiness gates
sections.heading: Stage ordering (default)

sections.body: Common on-prem failure mode: Helm rollback succeeds, but schema migrations already ran.
sections.heading: Schema migrations (guardrails)

sections.body:
- Migrations run as explicit plan steps with timeouts and clear failure states
- Lock timeout and statement timeout defaults are enforced (configurable)
- Migration steps are tagged as:
  - Reversible (rare)
  - Restore-required (common when schema changes are not backward readable)
sections.heading: Mitigations

sections.body: Rollback is deterministic and driven by the recorded plan execution state.
sections.heading: Rollback semantics: what “rollback” means

sections.body:
- Before migrations: usually reversible via chart/config revert
- After migrations: typically restore-required
sections.heading: Rollback can target the last known-good stage boundary

sections.body:
- Fix-forward: pause, remediate, retry step (only if step is retry-safe)
- Rollback: reverse reversible steps and return to prior compatible state
- Restore: restore DB/config snapshots when the plan marks steps restore-required

The plan must clearly label restore-required steps so operators can decide within a maintenance window.
sections.heading: Fix-forward vs rollback vs restore

sections.body:
- Kubernetes:
  - All Redwood namespaces healthy; no crash loops; no pending critical pods
  - No sustained DiskPressure/MemoryPressure on nodes
- Control plane:
  - API responds; auth path works (SSO or break-glass)
  - Admin actions succeed (list models, list deployments)
- Data plane:
  - Smoke test inference succeeds
  - Latency/error rate within expected bounds
- Observability:
  - Dashboards populate; alerts are not firing persistently
sections.heading: Minimum verification checklist

sections.body:
- Default behavior preserves model cache volumes; the installer will not delete caches during upgrade.
- Cache invalidation occurs only when explicitly required for compatibility and will be called out as a plan risk item.
sections.heading: Model cache handling (updated)

sections.body: On-prem upgrades often require 90+ days retention of change evidence.
sections.heading: Audit evidence and logging

sections.body:
- Plan artifact (human-readable summary + machine-readable plan)
- Precheck report with severities and remediation
- Backup IDs and locations
- Start/stop timestamps and initiator identity
- Apply/rollback/restore events (exportable to SIEM if configured)
sections.heading: Evidence produced by the installer

sections.body:
- Installer logs
- Plan and precheck outputs
- Non-sensitive cluster diagnostics relevant to upgrade
sections.heading: The support bundle may include

sections.body:
1) Run `upgrade plan` and `upgrade precheck` in staging
2) Validate artifact verification in your enclave process (USB drop / mirror)
3) Test your restore path:
   - CSI snapshot restore (if available)
   - Logical backup restore (if snapshots unavailable)
4) Perform a rollback drill tabletop:

   - Confirm operator access path if SSO is degraded
