payload.page_title: staged-quantized-model-rollout-and-forensic-telemetry-playbook

sections.body: This playbook describes a conservative, operator-friendly process for rolling out quantized model variants in private (VPC / on-prem) deployments while capturing forensic telemetry sufficient for root cause analysis and potential regulatory evidence preservation. It covers staged rollout patterns, preflight checks, metric/trace/event contracts, alerting thresholds, and a tested rollback path that preserves artifact provenance and degraded-model evidence.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to model binary changes that modify numeric representation (int8/4/bsr/FP16) and associated runtime flags (KV cache format, kernel selection, weight packing).
- Target platforms: Redwood Private (VPC) and on-prem packaged runtimes managed by operator teams.
- Not in scope: serving-layer protocol changes, control-plane schema migrations (separate upgrade playbook).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1) No more than 1.5x increase in tail latency (P99) vs baseline for quantized model serving under canonical workload.
2) No more than 0.5% degradation in quality signatures for evaluated prompt-sets during rollout window (see Quality Signals section).
3) Maintain forensic telemetry snapshot for any failed rollout for at least 90 days or customer retention window.
4) Zero-customer-data leakage during artifact staging and rollback.
sections.heading: Goals and success criteria

sections.body:
- Primary: Model Operations (modelops@redwood.com), on-call: modelops-rotations (pager duty rule: ModelOps_Push).
- Secondary: Runtime Reliability Team (eng-serving-runtime).
- Escalation matrix: operator -> modelops -> runtime -> security (if evidence indicates data exposure).
sections.heading: Owner and escalation

sections.body:
- Artifact provenance: model build signed and attestation file present (SHA256 + signature).
- Customer contract: private deploy must have approved quantization policy (customer may opt out of certain quant levels).
- Canary environment: isolated tenant with synthetic workload and traffic shadowing enabled.
- Telemetry pipeline: forensic-event topic writable, 14d rolling retention for detailed spans, 90d storage for compressed forensic bundles.
- Backups: KV-cache snapshot and tenant state snapshot (t-0) stored in immutable archive.
sections.heading: Prerequisites and preflight checklist

sections.body:
- Verify artifact signature:
  openssl dgst -sha256 -verify pubkey.pem -signature quantized_model.sig quantized_model.bin
- Generate KV-cache snapshot:
  redwoodctl tenant snapshot --tenant-id=tenant-abc --output=/var/backups/tenant-abc-kv-$(date +%F).tar.gz
- Validate runtime compatibility:
  redwood-runtime-check --image quantized_model.bin --seq-length=1024 --kernels=autoselect
sections.heading: Preflight command snippets (examples)

sections.body:
1) Local operator validation (single-node): smoke test, perf harness at 10qps for 10m.
2) Isolated canary (internal tenant): 0.5% of production traffic, shadow real requests, no direct customer routing. Run 4h minimum and pass quality/latency gates.
3) Incremental production ramp (slope-based): add 1% production traffic every 30 minutes with monitoring gating.
4) Burst window testing: enable 10x synthetic bursts at 2x expected QPS to validate evictions and thermal behavior.
5) Full cutover only after 24h at >=10% traffic with metrics green.
sections.heading: Rollout strategy (stages)

sections.body:
- Latency: P50/P95 remain within 1.2x of baseline; P99 <= 1.5x baseline. (Metric: runtime.infer.latency.{p50,p95,p99})
- Error rate: 5xx rate < 0.1% and stable. (Metric: runtime.request.errors)
- Quality: Prompt-set drift score < 0.5% relative to baseline (see Quality Signals).
- Resource pressure: GPU memory pressure < 85%, thermal throttle events = 0.
- Telemetry completeness: forensic-event publish success rate >= 99.9%.
sections.heading: Gating criteria (automated)

sections.body:
- Per-prompt token perplexity delta and embedding cosine drift on a canonical prompt-set.
- Safety filter hit-rate change vs baseline.
- Deterministic regression checks for templated prompts (yes/no matches).
sections.heading: Quality Signals (examples)

sections.body:
- Trace/span context for every canary inference request including: request_id, tenant_id (hashed), model_variant_id, kernel_path, quant_profile, runtime_flags, shard_node_id, timestamp, sequence_length, kv_cache_hit_ratio.
- Compact artifacts: a 30-minute compressed forensic bundle on failure including: request traces, a 1% sample of request/response pairs (redacted PII), runtime logs from affected nodes, GPU telemetry (power/thermal), kernel failure dumps.
- Evidence tagging: all forensic bundles include a short provenance.json with builder, git-commit, build-timestamp, signature, and operator ID.
sections.heading: Forensic telemetry contract (what to capture)

sections.body:
- Alert A1: P99 latency spike > 1.5x baseline sustained for 5 minutes -> SEV2 to runtime oncall.
- Alert A2: Quality drift > 0.5% on canonical prompt-set measured in canary -> SEV2 to modelops and product.
- Alert A3: Forensic-event publish failure > 0.1% for 10m -> SEV1 (possible telemetry outage).
sections.heading: Alerting (examples)

sections.body:
- The orchestrator exposes staged-flags: model.variant.weight (0-100), model.variant.burst-allow, model.variant-kernel-blacklist.
- A safe-stop webhook halts all percentage ramps and reverts traffic to previous variant if any gating metric trips.
- Recommended operator action on safe-stop: capture forensic bundle, mark rollout as halted in the rollout ledger, notify customers if SLA-affecting.
sections.heading: Rollforward automation and safe stops

sections.body:
1) Prepare artifacts and run preflight commands. Confirm signature and snapshot.
2) Upload quantized artifact to staging registry and set model.metadata.quant_profile = "int8-channelwise-v1".
3) Start a local smoke on a single isolated node: redwoodctl run-smoke --model=quantized:staging --qps=10 --duration=10m.
4) If smoke passes, create canary rollout: redwoodctl start-rollout --model=quantized:staging --target=canary-tenant --initial-weight=0.5
5) Enable forensic capture for canary: redwoodctl telemetry enable --scope=canary-tenant --forensic=true
6) Monitor gating dashboards (Latency / Quality / Telemetry completeness) for 4 hours.
7) If green, ramp to production in controlled steps: for weight in 1 2 5 10 25; do redwoodctl set-rollout-weight --id=<rollout-id> --weight=$weight; wait 30m and validate gates.
8) After hitting 10% and observing 24h stability, complete cutover: redwoodctl finalize-rollout --id=<rollout-id>.
sections.heading: Step-by-step example (operator runbook)

sections.body:
1) Trigger abort: redwoodctl abort-rollout --id=<rollout-id> --reason="gating-failure"
2) Immediately set traffic back to previous variant: redwoodctl set-rollout-weight --id=<rollout-id> --weight=0 --target=previous-variant
3) Preserve forensic bundle: redwoodctl forensic export --rollout-id=<rollout-id> --output=/evidence/<rollout-id>.tar.gz
4) Run artifact sanitization (ensure no customer PII left in sample): redwoodctl evidence redact --input=/evidence/<rollout-id>.tar.gz --policy=pii-strict
5) Document incident in the rollout ledger: redwoodctl rollout-note --id=<rollout-id> --note="Rollback due to P99 latency" --owner=$USER
6) Open postmortem and schedule a gated reattempt only after root cause triage and approval.
sections.heading: Rollback and artifact sanitization steps (on failure)

sections.body:
- Forensic bundles retained 90 days by default; regulated customers may require extended retention — consult legal.
- Access to forensic bundles is RBAC-protected. Any copy outside the platform requires manager-level approval and a signed access justification.
- Immutable artifacts (signed binaries, provenance.json) stored in immutable object store with WORM enabled for the customer retention window.
sections.heading: Data retention and compliance notes

sections.body:
- Functional: templated deterministic requests produce expected tokens for 95% of templates.
- Latency: baseline synthetic p99 within 1.5x across three independent runs.
- Safety: safety classifier false-positive rate within expected bounds.
- Telemetry: forensic bundle contains at least 95% of expected trace/span fields.

Appendix A — Example rollout metadata (JSON snippet):
{
  "rollout_id": "rollout-2026-03-04-quant1",
  "model": "mosaic-qlora-7b",
  "variant": "int8-channelwise-v1",
  "initiated_by": "maya.lopez@redwood.com",
  "start_ts": "2026-03-04T15:20:00Z"
}

Appendix B — Recommended observability query examples:
- P99 latency for model variant: sum(rate(runtime_infer_latency_bucket{le=\"1.0\",model_variant=~\"int8.*\"}[5m])) by (model_variant)
- Quality drift: custom_eval_drift{prompt_set=\"canonical-2026\",model_variant=\"int8-channelwise-v1\"}

Appendix C — Common troubleshooting playbook (short):
- Symptom: sudden P99 spike with no errors.
  - Check GPU memory pressure and kernel recompile logs on nodes in the rollout shard.
  - If kernel OOMs are present, blacklist offending kernel and reattempt with fallback kernel_path.
- Symptom: rising forensic-event publish errors.
  - Validate telemetry broker health, check disk space on telemetry proxy, restart agent with redwoodctl telemetry restart-agent.
- Symptom: deterministic regression on templated prompts.
  - Capture offending request/response pair from forensic bundle, compare float vs quantized decoding, escalate to modelops for re-quantization or bias-correction.
sections.heading: Testing checklist (operator acceptance tests)

sections.body:
- Model artifact supply chain spec (onprem packaging): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/model-artifact-supplychain-and-image-attestation-spec-2026
- KV-cache migration playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/kv-cache-migrations-and-runtime-state-migration-playbook-2025
sections.heading: Related resources and links

sections.body:
- 2026-01-12: Draft by Maya Lopez (initial runbook).
- 2026-02-10: Added telemetry contract and forensic bundle format (review by Ethan Park).
- 2026-03-04: Operationalized gating thresholds and finalized rollback sanitization steps (published).

End of document.

payload.page_title: Hybrid VPC Peering and Split-Tunnel Reference Architecture for Private Deployments

sections.body: This document describes a reference architecture and operational playbook for hybrid private deployments of Redwood Inference that combine direct VPC peering with split-tunnel egress for telemetry and control-plane traffic. The goal is a reproducible pattern that preserves customer network isolation, minimizes cross-VPC egress cost, and provides predictable operational controls for day‑2 operations.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Scope: Private control-plane + data-plane topologies for medium to large customers (10–500 GPUs).
- Audience: Solutions engineering, private deployment SRE, networking, security, and customers' networking teams.
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body:
- Ensure tenant traffic (inference requests & KV cache traffic) remains private within customer VPCs or dedicated peered networks.
- Allow controlled outbound connections for telemetry, control-plane, and staged package updates using split-tunnel proxies.
- Provide explicit failure modes and fallback behaviors for transient peering/route issues.
- Keep observable, auditable routing decisions with standardized metric names and alert thresholds.
sections.heading: Design goals

sections.body:
Customer VPC A (Private Subnet CIDR 10.10.0.0/16)          Redwood Managed Peering VPC (10.20.0.0/16)
  +-------------------+                                       +-------------------------------+
  | Inference Pods    | <--- VPC peering (bi-directional) --> | Dedicated inference pools     |
  | (k8s nodes)       |                                       | (dedicated GPUs)              |
  +-------------------+
         |
         |---> Split-tunnel proxy (Envoy) --(TLS mTLS)--> Telemetry egress (Redwood telemetry collectors)

Notes: Peering is limited to tenant CIDRs and managed peering VPC ranges. Split-tunnel proxy owns per-subnet routing for outbound-only flows (telemetry/control-plane) and marks metrics with egress_tag.
sections.heading: Architecture summary (text diagram)

sections.body:
- Customer VPC routers: enforce CIDR and security group restrictions. Provide static routes to Redwood peered ranges.
- Peering fabric (Redwood): BGP-enabled peering or AWS VPC peering depending on cloud region. Maintains routing ACLs and advertised prefixes per-customer.
- Split-tunnel proxy: lightweight Envoy sidecar or node-level proxy that:
  - routes inference traffic to local k8s services or peered Redwood pools,
  - routes telemetry/control-plane to Redwood collectors via TLS+MTLS,
  - enforces egress allowlist (IP ranges and ports).
- Identity & auth: Mutual TLS for egress; IAM role-based registration for VMs/k8s nodes; KMS integration for customer-encrypted keys.
- Observability: local and remote metrics, traces, and structured audit logs. See Observability section below.
sections.heading: Key components and responsibilities

sections.body:
1) Full peering (default for Dedicated customers):
   - Use AWS VPC peering or cloud-equivalent, full route exchange for tenant CIDRs and Redwood serving subnets.
   - Advantages: low latency, no NAT.
   - Risks: broader blast radius if misconfigured. Restrict via route tables and security groups.
2) Partial peering + split-tunnel (recommended for regulated customers):
   - Peer only the serving subnets; all egress (telemetry/updates) uses split-tunnel proxies that route over outbound TLS to Redwood collectors.
   - Advantages: tighter control over peered prefixes; egress is explicit and auditable.
3) Overlay tunneling (fallback):
   - When direct peering is unavailable, fall back to mTLS-over-HTTPS tunneling for control plane.
   - Advantages: works across restrictive network setups; higher latency and cost.
sections.heading: Routing and peering modes (decision matrix)

sections.body:
| Config key | Example value | Notes |
|------------|---------------|-------|
| tenant_cidr | 10.10.0.0/16 | Customer primary subnet used for inference nodes |
| peering_ranges | 10.20.0.0/24,10.20.1.0/24 | Redwood advertised ranges for serving pools |
| split_proxy_image | redwood/egress-proxy:v1.7.2 | Node-level proxy image; pinned in private deployments |
| egress_allowed_ports | 443, 853 | TLS (443) and DNS-over-TLS (853) for telemetry |
| mTLS_cert_role | redwood:private-deploy | Role used to request mTLS certs from internal CA |
sections.heading: Configuration table (example)

sections.body:
- Minimum open ports on inference subnets:
  - Inbound from peered ranges: TCP 443 (inference API), TCP 10250 (kubelet) only from management ranges.
  - Egress from split-tunnel proxy: TCP 443 to Redwood collectors; UDP 53 or TCP 853 for DNS (depending on operator preference).
- Deny all other inbound traffic by default.
sections.heading: Firewall and ACL guidance

sections.body:
- Network-level SLOs (for private deployments):
  - Peering connectivity: 99.95% monthly availability (measured as BGP adjacency up + route installed).
  - Egress tunnel availability (split-tunnel): 99.9% monthly for active nodes.
  - Token-latency (p95 end-to-end): < 120 ms for local inference when peering healthy. Documented fallbacks when above thresholds are violated.
sections.heading: Operational SLOs and telemetry

sections.body:
- redwood.private.peering.adjacency_status (gauge: 0/1)
- redwood.private.splitproxy.egress_success_count (counter)
- redwood.private.splitproxy.egress_failure_count (counter)
- redwood.private.kvcache.hit_rate (gauge: percent)
- redwood.private.inference.latency_ms.p95 (histogram)
sections.heading: Required metrics (standardized names)

sections.body:
- peering adjacency down for >2 minutes -> P1 alert to private-deploy-sre.
- splitproxy egress_failure_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> P2 alert.
- kvcache.hit_rate drop > 10% relative to baseline for 15m -> P2.

Rollout and validation checklist (pre-deploy -> post-install):
1) Pre-deploy (Network + Security reviews)
   - Confirm customer CIDRs and approved peering_ranges.
   - Exchange and verify public keys for BGP (if using BGP).
   - Validate firewall rules with customer network team.
2) Deploy peering + route entries (automation):
   - Apply peering with limited CIDRs.
   - Configure split-proxy as a DaemonSet (k8s) or systemd service for VMs.
3) Validation tests (automated):
   - Route test: traceroute to serving pool IPs from a sample node. Expect <=3 hops for peered mode.
   - Egress test: curl --resolve to telemetry endpoint via split-proxy and verify TLS mutual auth succeeds.
   - Latency smoke: run perf harness generating 1000 short requests and measure p50/p95.
4) Canary and expansion
   - Start with 5% of nodes in peered route; monitor metrics for 24–72 hours.
   - Gradually expand to 100% with rolling restart preserving KV cache affinity.
sections.heading: Alerting thresholds (examples)

sections.body:
- BGP flap or peering teardown:
  - Detection: redwood.private.peering.adjacency_status -> 0.
  - Mitigation: automatic update of route table to direct inference egress through overlay tunnel; scale up split-proxy instances to handle transient increase in egress.
- Split-proxy certificate expiry
  - Detection: mTLS handshake failures and increased egress_failure_count.
  - Mitigation: automated cert refresh job with 48‑hour renew window; emergency manual rotation steps documented below.
sections.heading: Failure modes and mitigation

sections.body:
1) SSH to control node with privileged key and run:
   - /opt/redwood/pxctl cert rotate --role redwood:private-deploy --force
2) Confirm new cert via: curl -v --cert /etc/redwood/certs/node.crt https://collector.redwood.internal/healthz
3) If rotation fails, enable overlay tunneling and notify customer with expected degraded latency.
sections.heading: Emergency manual rotation steps (condensed)

sections.body:
- Dashboards to create by default for private deployments:
  - Peering overview: adjacency_status, route counts, error events.
  - Split-proxy health: CPU/memory, egress_success/failure, handshake latencies.
  - Inference end-to-end: per-model p50/p95/p99 latency, token consumption, kvcache hit rate.
- Logs: Structured JSON including fields: node_id, tenant_id, egress_tag, request_id, route_path.
- Traces: parent spans for proxy->collector->serving-pool with explicit attributes: net.path, net.latency_ms.
sections.heading: Observability and dashboards

sections.body:
- All egress traffic must be encrypted with mTLS; server certs pinned to Redwood CA.
- KMS-backed key wrap for private keys; HSM integration for FIPS customers available as opt-in.
- Audit logs exported to long-term retention for restricted customers as part of compliance packaging.
sections.heading: Security and compliance notes

sections.body:
- Example split-proxy DaemonSet snippet (k8s YAML, trimmed):
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: DaemonSet
  metadata:
    name: redwood-split-proxy
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: envoy
          image: redwood/egress-proxy:v1.7.2
          env:
            - name: REDWOOD_COLLECTOR
              value: "collector-01.redwood.internal:443"

- Route verification playbook (ansible): ping, traceroute, and TLS handshake checks against known endpoints.
sections.heading: Testing and automation templates (examples)

sections.body:
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (oncall: private-deploy-sre).
- Escalation: eng-sre -> networks -> security.
- Runbook location: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/private-peering-runbook
sections.heading: Ownership and contacts

sections.body:
- Standardize whether BGP will be offered as GA or remain opt-in (tracking: ADR-2026-bgp-service-class).
- Define a default certificate rotation window (proposal: 30 days) and automate via control-plane.

Appendix A — Example commands and verification snippets:
- Check peering routes (AWS CLI example):
  aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=route.destination-cidr-block,Values=10.20.0.0/16"
- TLS handshake test with client cert:
  openssl s_client -connect collector-01.redwood.internal:443 -cert node.crt -key node.key -CAfile redwood-ca.pem

Appendix B — Allowed ports and protocols (quick reference):
| Destination | Source | Ports | Protocol | Purpose |
|------------|--------|-------|----------|---------|
| collector-01.redwood.internal | split-proxy | 443 | TCP/TLS | telemetry, control-plane |
| dns.redwood.internal | split-proxy | 853 | TCP | DNS over TLS |
| peered-serving-pool | inference-node | 443 | TCP | inference API |

Appendix C — Change log:
- 2025-11-12: Document created (Maya Chen).
- 2026-02-05: Added explicit SLOs and emergency rotation steps; tightened egress port guidance (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Priya Nair).

If there are questions about implementation details or customer-specific exceptions, contact the document owners or add a comment to this page.

payload.page_title: Split-horizon edge control-plane routing reference

sections.body:
Summary

This reference describes a split-horizon control-plane and edge routing architecture for Redwood Private deployments. It is targeted at field engineers, network architects, and customer infra teams designing VPC interconnects and on-prem air-gapped bridges. The design balances security (minimal inbound surface area), reliability (regional failover), and operational simplicity for day-2 tasks such as upgrades and telemetry collection.

Goals
- Provide a deterministic routing pattern for control-plane traffic vs. inference data-plane traffic.
- Minimize customer firewall exceptions and required egress flows.
- Define upgrade-safe pathways and rollback steps for control-plane changes.
- Document on-prem packaging constraints that impact routing (e.g., host networking, fabric MTU).

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to Private deployments using: VPC-peered control plane, hybrid control-plane, or air-gapped bridge patterns.
- Assumes customer operates edge routers/firewalls capable of policy-based routing (BGP or static).
- Not a replacement for customer-specific compliance processes; use as a prescriptive reference.

High-level architecture
- Control-plane endpoints: small set of IP ranges (managed by Redwood) used for API registration, config sync, and telemetry ingestion.
- Data-plane (inference) endpoints: per-cluster IP ranges carrying model traffic; typically stays inside customer network or private interconnect.
- Edge routing layer: customer edge router separates next-hops by destination prefix and service tag (CONTROL vs DATA).

ASCII diagram

Customer VPC/On-prem LAN ----[edge router]----+----(private interconnect)---- Redwood Dedicated / Control Plane
                                             |\
                                             +----(internal inference cluster)

Traffic classification and policy
- CONTROL (low bandwidth, high-availability):
  - TCP/HTTPS to Redwood control-plane ranges on 443, 8443 (misc ports documented in onboarding).
  - Uses TLS with client cert or mTLS where configured.
  - Outbound-only from customer edge preferred; inbound NAT only if necessary for legacy management.
- DATA (high bandwidth, low-latency):
  - gRPC or HTTP streaming to internal inference cluster or to a dedicated egress appliance on a private interconnect.
  - Avoid Internet egress for data-plane where possible; use direct VPC peer, private link, or dedicated MPLS.

Recommended VPC design patterns
1) Split-horizon VPC (preferred for regulated customers)
   - Route control-plane egress to Redwood-managed transit via BGP session (advertise only control prefixes).
   - Route data-plane to internal inference subnets; do not advertise these to Redwood.
   - Use security groups / ACLs to restrict control-plane egress to Redwood CIDRs.

2) Bastion relay for air-gapped sites
   - Single-host outbound relay (TLS tunnel) that proxies control-plane traffic and performs attestations.
   - Harden with ephemeral keys and short-lived certs; rotate per-release.

Network configuration snippets
- BGP policy (pseudocode)
```
neighbor 10.0.0.1 remote-as 65001
neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map EXPORT-CONTROL out
route-map EXPORT-CONTROL permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list CONTROL-PREFIXES
```
- Example prefix-list (control prefixes)
```
ip prefix-list CONTROL-PREFIXES permit 198.51.100.0/24
ip prefix-list CONTROL-PREFIXES permit 198.51.101.0/24
```

On-prem packaging and host/network constraints
- Host networking mode: for strict latency SLOs we recommend hostNetwork enabled for inference pods/services; document kernel and NIC driver versions with the customer.
- MTU: ensure uniform MTU across physical path (recommended 9000 for RDMA/GPU clusters).
- Firewall: customers must allow TLS outbound to control prefixes and a small set of TCP ports (443, 8443, 5222 for agent heartbeats where applicable).
- Image signing: on-prem images must be signed and verification performed at the container runtime (we provide cosign keys and verification hooks).

Day-2 operations playbook (edge routing focus)
Preflight checklist (before field handoff)
- Confirm control-plane CIDRs and port list with Redwood onboarding engineer.
- Validate BGP sessions: show ip bgp summary -> established.
- Confirm security group egress rules: only control prefixes allowed.
- Verify TLS trust: client cert or CA installed and test curl to control endpoint.

Common day-2 run actions
- Rotate control-plane credentials:
  1) Generate new client cert via console -> download PEM.
  2) Install on relay or edge appliance, validate with `curl -v https://control.redwood.example/status`.
  3) Decommission old certs after 24 hours of successful metrics.
- Add a maintenance route for cluster migration:
  1) Advertise temporary route to redirect a subset of data-plane traffic to a migration gateway.
  2) Throttle BGP advertisement using community tagging to avoid global impact.

Upgrade and rollback procedure (control-plane changes)
- Upgrade principle: keep control-plane changes isolated from data-plane forwarding. Always validate control-plane connectivity before switching inference binaries.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) PREPARE (owner: field eng)
   - Confirm backups: config export, KV snapshots, certificate backups.
   - Notify stakeholders and schedule maintenance window.
2) STAGED ROLL-OUT (owner: release eng)
   - Deploy control-plane change to Canary relay(s) (1–2 hosts).
   - Monitor health: 5xx rate < 0.5%, control-heartbeat latency < 200ms for 30 minutes.
3) EXPAND (owner: release eng)
   - Gradually update remaining relays in batches of N (N determined by cluster size).
   - Validate data-plane unaffected by control change.
4) VERIFY (owner: field eng)
   - Run acceptance tests (API registration, config sync, real inference requests).

Rollback steps (if canary failure)
1) Revert control-plane release in artifact repository.
2) Re-deploy previous relay image to canary hosts.
3) Revoke any short-lived certs issued during failed rollout.
4) Mitigate customer traffic: if necessary, temporarily withdraw control prefixes from BGP advertisements to force use of fallback relay (documented in related pages).

Incident isolation and diagnostics
- Symptom: control-plane registration failures for multiple hosts
  - Check: edge router outbound ACLs, BGP state, TLS trust chain.
  - Commands: `show ip bgp`, `tcpdump -i eth0 host 198.51.100.5 and port 443`, `curl --cert client.pem https://control.redwood.example/health`
- Symptom: data-plane latency increase post-control-change
  - Check: routing table, MTU mismatch on path, CPU steal on inference nodes.

Customer requirements checklist (copyable table)
- Minimum network requirements:
  - Control-plane egress: 2 x /24 or 4 x /26 dedicated for control endpoints
  - Latency target to control-plane: p50 < 100ms, p95 < 250ms
  - MTU: 9000 recommended; minimum 1500
- Host and packaging:
  - Container runtime: containerd >= 1.6.0 or Docker 20.10 (verified)
  - Kernel: 5.10+ recommended for NIC drivers and NUMA fixes
  - Disk: 2 x NVMe for model cache; encryption at rest enabled
- Security and compliance:
  - KMS/HSM availability for key encryption (customer-managed supported)
  - Firewall rules: outbound TLS to control prefixes; deny unknown inbound to inference nodes

Operational metrics and SLOs (control-plane)
- Availability: control-plane egress must be functional 99.95% during business hours.
- Latency: control-heartbeat p95 < 250ms for healthy operation.
- Error budget: 99.99% of control API calls should return 2xx during normal operation; track with per-tenant metrics.

Ownership and escalation
- Field engineering owner: Marisa Delgado (oncall rotation: eng-private-deployments)
- Release engineering contact: Arun Patel
- Support escalation path: Customer Success -> Field Eng -> SRE -> Executive Escalation (see support playbook link).

Related pages and references
- Secure service mesh reference (recommended when internal service-to-service encryption is required).
- VPC peer and interconnect playbook (detailed BGP templates and cloud provider-specific examples).

Appendix: sample curl test (control-plane)
```
curl --cert ./client.pem --key ./client.key -v https://198.51.100.5:8443/api/v1/agent/status
```

Appendix: quick attestation flow for bastion relay
1) Relay boots with TPM-based attestation.
2) Relay requests ephemeral token from Redwood control-plane via constrained channel.
3) Token used to bootstrap agent and is valid for 5 minutes.

Document history
- 2025-11-18: Created by Marisa Delgado
- 2026-02-10: Expanded day-2 runbook and added rollback guidance (reviewers: Arun, Sofia, Diego)

payload.page_title: Egress isolation and data-shielding patterns for private deployments

sections.body: This reference describes recommended egress isolation and data-shielding patterns for Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments. It bundles architecture patterns, deployment checklist, day‑2 operational controls, upgrade/rollback considerations, and a customer acceptance checklist. The intent is to provide operators and customer engineers a prescriptive, auditable pattern for preventing unauthorized outbound data flow while preserving required external integrations (metrics, licensing, model fetches).
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Prevent uncontrolled outbound connections from runtime hosts or containers.
- Provide a minimal, auditable set of allowed egress endpoints and protocols per-customer.
- Define patterns compatible with both VPC-based and air-gapped on‑prem deployments.
- Cover runtime (agent/sidecar), control plane, telemetry, and packaging considerations.
sections.heading: Goals and scope

sections.body: This doc is targeted at: platform engineers, field engineers performing private installs, security reviewers, and customer network teams.
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- control-plane-api (Redwood-managed, optional Private control plane)
- customer-vpc: private-subnet (runtime instances), management-subnet (operator tooling)
- egress-gateway: proxy+WAF in a hardened subnet (optional NAT for approved destinations)
- telemetry-proxy: TLS-terminated, mTLS to Redwood telemetry ingest endpoints (or customer-owned collector)
- kms/hsm: customer-managed key store reachable via private endpoints
sections.heading: High-level architecture (text diagram)

sections.body:
runtime -> agent-sidecar -> egress-gateway -> (approved external endpoints)
runtime -> agent-sidecar -> private-controlplane-peering -> control-plane-api
sections.heading: Diagram (logical)

sections.body:
1) Default-deny egress at host and network layer
   - Enforce host-level firewall (iptables/nftables) default DROP for outbound, allow only established, loopback, and explicitly permitted destinations.
   - Enforce cloud network controls (Security Groups / NSGs / Network Policies) to restrict outbound where supported.
2) Centralized egress gateway
   - Route all outbound via an egress gateway that performs TLS inspection (when permitted), WAF, and FQDN whitelisting.
   - Gateway provides consistent audit/logging of outbound flows (required for compliance).
3) Split telemetry and control-plane channels
   - Telemetry has a distinct mTLS-authenticated endpoint and allowed egress list.
   - Control-plane traffic uses discrete peering or PrivateLink to avoid traversing public internet.
4) Outbound minimalism and allowlists
   - Only allow minimal DNS, NTP (if required), control-plane, telemetry, package repositories, and licensing endpoints.
   - Use short-lived allowlists that are reviewed quarterly.
5) Fail-closed for sensitive operations
   - If the egress gateway or policy component fails, fail application calls requiring external PII or S3 uploads instead of falling back to public egress.
sections.heading: Key design patterns

sections.body:
- Customer provides: approved egress CIDR/IPs and FQDN list, peering/PrivateLink config, KMS/HSM endpoints, required proxy CA certs and bypass rules, organizational compliance constraints.
- Operator ensures: base OS image hardened, host firewall agent (iptables/nftables or osquery rules), container runtime network policy controller installed (e.g., Cilium/Calico), egress gateway (HA pair) available, telemetry-proxy configured.
sections.heading: Pre-deployment requirements (checklist)

sections.body:
1) Security Group (VPC) egress sample (pseudo):
- Allow outbound to control-plane-api: 10.10.0.0/24:443 (TLS)
- Allow outbound to telemetry-proxy: 10.10.1.0/24:443 (mTLS)
- Allow DNS to resolver(s): 172.16.0.2:53
- Deny all other egress by default

2) iptables host default-deny snippet (Linux):
sections.heading: Network configuration examples (reference snippets)

sections.body:
iptables -F OUTPUT
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
sections.heading: reset

sections.body: iptables -A OUTPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
sections.heading: allow established

sections.body: iptables -A OUTPUT -o lo -j ACCEPT
sections.heading: allow loopback

sections.body: iptables -A OUTPUT -d 10.10.0.0/24 -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
sections.heading: allow control plane

sections.body: iptables -A OUTPUT -d 10.10.1.5 -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
sections.heading: allow telemetry proxy

sections.body:
iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -d 172.16.0.2 -j ACCEPT

3) Kubernetes NetworkPolicy example (allow egress to telemetry proxy):
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-telemetry
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redwood-runtime
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.10.1.0/24
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
sections.heading: allow DNS

sections.body:
1) Validate customer-provided egress allowlist and sign acceptance.
2) Deploy egress-gateway in HA mode in a dedicated subnet with strong ACLs.
3) Provision TLS certs and mTLS identity for telemetry-proxy and agent-sidecars.
4) Apply host firewall baseline (default deny) and test connectivity to control-plane and telemetry endpoints.
5) Configure runtime to use egress-gateway (ip route 0.0.0.0/0 via egress-gateway for runtime hosts).
6) Run acceptance tests (see Acceptance checklist).
7) Cut traffic to egress-gateway and monitor for 24–72 hours before declaring steady state.

Acceptance checklist (customer-facing, must be signed):
- [ ] Control-plane connectivity verified over private peering/PrivateLink (TLS 1.2+).
- [ ] Telemetry events successfully posted to telemetry-proxy (mTLS).
- [ ] No direct outbound flows to public internet observed from runtimes (verify with netflow/sflow).
- [ ] DNS only to allowed resolvers.
- [ ] KMS/HSM reachability via private endpoints confirmed.
- [ ] Egress audit logs captured centrally and retained per customer policy.

Day‑2 operational runbook (high level):
- Monitoring and alerts:
  - Egress-gateway latency: p95 < 50ms for control-plane flows; alert > 150ms sustained 5m.
  - Unexpected outbound flows: alert when > 5 distinct unknown external IPs observed in 1h.
  - Telemetry delivery failure rate: alert when > 1% drop over 5m.
- Log retention and evidence:
  - Egress logs retained for 90 days by default (customer-specific options allowed).
  - Packet sampling enabled at 0.1% for forensic investigations; increase to 1% during incidents.
- Routine operations:
  - Quarterly review of allowed FQDNs and CIDRs.
  - Monthly failover exercise of egress-gateway HA pair.
  - Patch egress gateway and telemetry-proxy with security patches within 7 days of CVE disclosure for critical CVEs.
sections.heading: Deployment procedure (numbered)

sections.body:
- During runtime upgrades that touch networking (CNI, gateway, sidecar):
  - Schedule maintenance window and test in a staging environment that mirrors allowlist rules.
  - Use canary rollout (10% hosts) for CNI/gateway changes for 24h before full roll.
  - Keep previous config as a frozen artifact; rollback by re-applying saved iptables/CNI/gateway configuration.
  - If egress-gateway certificate rotation is required, pre-stage new certs on standby and perform zero-downtime swap using 2-phase reload (drain then swap).
- Evidence preservation for a rollback:
  - Capture current iptables, route table, and gateway config snapshots to object storage with immutable retention for 30 days.
sections.heading: Upgrade and rollback considerations

sections.body:
- Required: private peering / Direct Connect or PrivateLink for control plane.
- Required: egress allowlist (FQDN + CIDR), CA cert bundle for corporate TLS interception if present.
- Recommended: dedicated telemetry collector owned by customer or explicit mTLS credentials.
- Optional: inline TLS inspection (legal-dependent).
sections.heading: Customer requirements matrix (table-style lines)

sections.body:
- Symptom: Runtime cannot reach control plane.
  - Check host routes: ip route show; verify peering routes present.
  - Confirm security group/NSG outbound rules allow 443 to control-plane CIDR.
  - Test: curl -vk --resolve controlplane.example.internal:443:10.10.0.5 https://controlplane.example.internal/healthz
- Symptom: Telemetry backlog after deployment.
  - Verify telemetry-proxy certificate expiration and mTLS identity mapping.
  - Check proxy logs: /var/log/egress-proxy/ and telemetry-proxy errors for 401/403.
sections.heading: Troubleshooting quick hits

sections.body:
- Egress-gateway owner: eng-platform/networking.
- Runtime-side network owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Security contact for compliance questions: security-and-compliance oncall (see internal rota).
- Escalation path: field-engineer -> eng-platform -> eng-sre -> security.
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:
- Deployment templates: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging (image hardening templates)
- Telemetry ingestion patterns: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures/telemetry-ingest-aggregation-patterns-private-deploys-2026
- Operational contracts: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-delivery-and-day2-operational-contracts-2026

Appendix: sample allowlist (minimal)
- control-plane: 10.10.0.0/24:443
- telemetry-proxy: 10.10.1.5:443 (mTLS)
- package-repo (customer mirror): 10.10.2.12:443
- dns: 172.16.0.2:53

If you are implementing this in a regulated environment (PCI/SOC2/HIPAA), set confidentiality to "restricted" and coordinate with security-and-compliance for evidence retention and review cadence.

Document owner: Nina Patel (eng-platform/networking).

payload.page_title: Private deployment compliance evidence and RBAC checklist

sections.body: This playbook defines the minimum RBAC model, audit logging expectations, data residency and retention controls, secure-SDLC gates, incident response evidence collection steps, and compliance-evidence packaging for Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It targets Redwood Private customers and the internal teams (Solutions, SRE, Security, and Customer Success) responsible for onboarding and operating those deployments. The document is scoped to inference control plane and model-serving endpoints, admin consoles, and any data plane components that persist customer-provided prompt/response data.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to all Private deployments managed by Redwood where customer data or keys are resident in customer-managed networks or air-gapped premises.
- Excludes pure-hosted API customers unless an explicit hybrid arrangement is documented.
- Covers: RBAC, audit logging (ingest, retention, redaction), data residency and retention policy mapping, SDLC deployment gates for private packages, incident response evidence collection, and exception handling for control plane access.
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- Principle: Least privilege by default for all entitlements.
- Principle: Immutable, tamper-evident audit trail for all privileged actions with cryptographic integrity where supported.
- SLO: Audit ingestion latency <= 30s for control-plane events (measured at 95th percentile).
- SLO: Audit-collection completeness >= 99.999% for actions that change entitlements or access controls over a rolling 30-day window.
- Retention baseline: 1 year for operational events, 7 years for legal/regulated evidence (configurable per contract and law).
sections.heading: Principles and high-level SLOs

sections.body:
- Onboarding lead: Solutions Eng (owner: aisha.patel@redwood.example)
- RBAC policy custodian: Platform Security (team alias: platform-security@redwood.example)
- Audit collector & retention: Eng SRE (alias: eng-sre@redwood.example)
- Evidence packaging & legal liaison: Security & Compliance (security-compliance@redwood.example)
sections.heading: Ownership and primary contacts

sections.body:
- Roles (recommended minimal set):
  1. deployment-admin — full control over deployment lifecycle, can create/rotate service identities and change network config.
  2. tenant-admin — customer-designated role for per-tenant config (model pinning, usage quotas, data retention overrides).
  3. operator — runtime ops for scaling/backups; cannot change entitlements or customer mappings.
  4. observer-audit — read-only access to logs, metrics, and evidence bundles; no ability to read plaintext customer content.
  5. emergency-signer — timebound JIT role for escalations; must be activated via approval flow and is automatically revoked.

- Checklist for RBAC enforcement in private deployments:
  - All human access must be mapped to SSO identities and short-lived sessions (OIDC/SAML).
  - Service accounts must follow a naming convention: svc/<team>/<purpose>/<deployment-id>.
  - No long-lived credentials stored in plaintext on nodes; require KMS/HSM-backed secrets.
  - JIT access flow: activate emergency-signer with MFA, ticket ID, and 2 approvers. Activation window <= 4 hours and audited.
  - Periodic certification: quarterly entitlement review with evidence exported to evidence-bucket (see Compliance Evidence Workflow).
sections.heading: RBAC model and checklist (private deployment specifics)

sections.body:
- Events to capture (minimum):
  - Authn events: successful/failed logins, MFA challenge results, token issuance/refresh.
  - Authorization events: allow/deny decisions for admin and tenant-admin APIs.
  - Entitlement changes: role grants/revocations, policy updates, JIT activations.
  - Deployment actions: image rollouts, config changes, network policy updates, inbound firewall changes.
  - Data-access alerts: retrievals of persisted customer content flagged as sensitive.

- Required event fields (flat JSON schema snippet shown as example only):
  {
    "timestamp": "2026-01-15T12:34:56Z",
    "event_id": "uuid-v4",
    "actor_id": "user:alice@customer.example",
    "actor_type": "human|service",
    "action": "role.grant",
    "target": "role:tenant-admin",
    "deployment_id": "priv-deploy-123",
    "request_id": "req-xyz",
    "outcome": "success|failure",
    "metadata": "(string blob for low-sensitivity additional context)"
  }

  Note: The snippet above is to be emitted as a single-line JSON event to the configured audit sink. Do NOT include customer PII or raw prompts in the top-level event payload; instead include references (blob IDs) that point to encrypted storage.

- Redaction and sensitivity classification:
  - All prompt/response content marked as Sensitive must be hashed and stored in encrypted blobs with access restricted to tenant-admin only.
  - Audit events MUST NOT include plaintext prompt content.
  - Where plaintext is required for debugging under a legal hold, follow the Legal Hold workflow (see Data Residency & Retention).

Data residency, retention, and legal hold:
- Mapping table (textual representation):
  | Data class | Default residency | Default retention | Legal hold behavior |
  |-----------|------------------:|------------------:|---------------------|
  | Operational logs (non-customer) | Redwood control plane region | 1 year | retained until release |
  | Customer prompts/outputs (sensitive) | Customer VPC / on-prem storage | contract-defined default (30–365 days) | frozen, encrypted, access logged |
  | Audit trail (system events) | Customer-controlled bucket where required; else Redwood immutable store | 1 year operational; extendable to 7+ years | preserved and exported to legal archive |

- Legal hold process (abridged):
  1. Legal issues request hold via security-compliance ticket with case number.
  2. SRE marks related data blobs as immutable and moves to the hold storage class.
  3. All access requires documented justification; access requests are logged and added to the evidence manifest.
sections.heading: Audit logging and evidence requirements

sections.body:
- Pre-release checks (must pass before image can be signed):
  - Static analysis (SAST) and dependency SBOM verification.
  - Container image vulnerability scan (critical CVEs must be remediated or exception documented).
  - Secrets scan: no embedded keys, verified by pipeline verifier.
  - RBAC policy change tests: unit/integ tests that assert no wildcard grants for tenant namespaces.
  - Signed-by: Build must be signed by the CI pipeline key; signature captured in release evidence.

- Release evidence bundle (per private package):
  - Build artifact SHA256, SBOM, signing certificate, vulnerability scan report, RBAC policy diff, and test coverage report.
  - Store bundle in evidence-bucket with manifest: {release_id, signer, timestamp, s3_path} (manifest is a flattened JSON string in evidence index).

Incident response: evidence-first containment for auth/RBAC incidents:
- Trigger conditions: anomalous role grants, repeated failed MFA for privileged accounts, JIT activation without matching ticket, or evidence of audit log tampering.

- Triage & containment runbook (high level):
  1. Detect: SRE/IR platform rules raise pager. Include initial alert data (actor, action, timestamp, request_id).
  2. Isolate: if a service account is implicated, rotate its keys and isolate affected nodes. If a human actor is implicated, revoke active sessions pending certification.
  3. Evidence capture:
     - Snapshot the audit stream window +/- 2 hours to a write-once evidence bucket.
     - Export affected RBAC policy revisions (full diff) and signed releases.
     - Collect network capture metadata and immutable node disk snapshot index (not raw disks).
  4. Legal & Compliance: engage security-compliance and legal for preservation and escalation.
  5. Postmortem: assemble evidence bundle, include timeline, decisions, and retained artifacts.

- Evidence bundle contents (minimum):
  - Incident manifest (flat fields: incident_id, detection_time, lead, business_impact, evidence_paths).
  - Audit event slice (NDJSON file).
  - RBAC policy history (git patch/diff).
  - JIT activation log and approver identities.
  - Any customer-provided consent or legal hold documents.
sections.heading: Secure SDLC gates for private packages and images

sections.body:
- Packaging steps (automated where possible):
  1. Generate manifest with canonical fields (release_id | incident_id | deployment_id | evidence_paths | checksum).
  2. Copy artifacts to evidence-bucket with immutability flag and store a signed index entry in the Evidence Ledger (append-only).
  3. Notify legal via configured webhook and create a sealed export (tar + detached signature).
  4. Retain both an encrypted copy in customer-controlled storage (if contract requires) and a Redwood legal copy under restricted access.

- Access and audit: all evidence access requests require a request ticket, approver chain, and an explicit justification. Access events added to the evidence manifest.

Risk, exceptions, and decision log:
- Exception request template (fields): requester, deployment_id, risk_owner, justification, proposed mitigation, timebox (max 90 days), evidence of impact, approvers.
- Exception review cadence: weekly exceptions triage by Platform Security; high-risk exceptions escalated to SOC and Legal.
- Example risk scenarios and mitigations:
  - Risk: Customer requires plaintext prompts for debugging in their on-prem store.
    Mitigation: Use an ephemeral, access-controlled debug session with MFA + timebound retention + audit slice exported to legal archive.
  - Risk: Audit ingestion delays during heavy load.
    Mitigation: Autoscale collector, buffer to disk with signed sequence numbers, and alert when buffer age > 5 minutes.
sections.heading: Compliance evidence workflow (packaging and handoff)

sections.body:
- Onboarding a new private deployment:
  1. Confirm residency requirements and contract retention windows.
  2. Provision initial RBAC roles and seed tenant-admins.
  3. Validate audit sink connectivity and test event roundtrip.
  4. Run pre-deploy SDLC gates and sign images.
  5. Provide evidence index link in onboarding packet.

- Quarterly audit & certification:
  - Run entitlement export and compare to expected approval graph.
  - Review immutable evidence buckets and verify retention settings.
  - Produce a certification artifact: signed PDF with summary + attached manifest.
sections.heading: Operational checklists (quick actions)

sections.body:
- CLI examples (audit sink health check):
  # Check last ingestion timestamp for deployment
  redwoodctl audit status --deployment priv-deploy-123 --since 1h

- Example manifest (flattened JSON string for index):
  {"manifest_id":"m-20260210-01","deployment_id":"priv-deploy-123","paths":"s3://evidence/priv-deploy-123/m-20260210-01.tar.gz","checksum":"sha256:...","signed_by":"pipeline@redwood.example"}

- Table: Evidence retention decision matrix (text):
  | Artifact | Default retention | Owner | Storage class |
  |---------|------------------:|-------|---------------|
  | Audit NDJSON slices | 1 year | Eng SRE | Immutable hot |
  | RBAC policy history | 7 years | Platform Security | Archive legal |
  | Build artifacts & SBOM | 5 years | Eng Release | Archive |
sections.heading: Appendices and examples

sections.body:
- Created by Aisha Patel (Solutions Eng) 2025-04-15.
- Updated 2026-02-10: clarified legal hold steps and added JIT activation audit requirements.
- Key references: private-deploy-reference-architecture, secure-sdlc/signed-release-gates, security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence/orchestrated-evidence-rbac-integration-playbook-2026.
sections.heading: Change history and references

sections.body:
- For operational issues: eng-sre@redwood.example
- For RBAC/design questions: platform-security@redwood.example
- For legal or evidence escalation: security-compliance@redwood.example

This playbook is intended to be machine-readable where indicated (NDJSON slices and flattened manifests) and also consumable by auditors. If a specific customer contract imposes stricter controls, those override this baseline.

payload.page_title: Structured Offboarding and Transition Playbook

sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This playbook defines a standardized, auditable offboarding and transition process for Redwood Inference employees and contractors. It balances security (timely deprovisioning), continuity (knowledge transfer and role handoff), and people-first exit practices (respectful communication, outplacement resources, and actionable feedback).
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to all full-time employees, contractors, and interns departing Redwood Inference for any reason (resignation, termination, role change, end of contract).
- Includes systems deprovisioning, IP and data controls, knowledge-transfer expectations, manager compliance steps, and reuse/rehire assessment.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Document owner: People Ops (owner: Elena Park).
- Operational steward: HR Operations (primary contact: hr-ops@redwood.ai).
- Escalation: Head of People Ops -> Legal (for compliance questions) -> Security (for suspected data exfiltration).
sections.heading: Owner and escalation

sections.body:
- Account deprovisioning completed within 72 hours of termination; 4 hours for high-risk departures (SLA: 95%).
- Access suspension for voluntary resignation: within 24 hours of first notice if requested by manager for transitions requiring immediate restriction (SLA: 90%).
- Knowledge-transfer artifacts submitted 5 business days prior to last day (target: 80% compliance).
- Exit interview completion rate: >= 80% within 10 business days.
- Time-to-replace tracked per role; offboarding completeness < 5 business days post departure (success metric).

Checklist and timeline (manager + HR responsibilities)

T-30 to T-15 (when notice received or HR informed)
1. Confirm departure details and last working day with employee; log in HRIS.
2. Manager: start role transition plan and identify interim owner(s).
3. HR: schedule an offboarding intake meeting and calendar resignation/termination tasks.
4. Manager + employee: agree on knowledge-transfer deliverables and shadow schedule.

T-14 to T-5
- Employee: prepare Knowledge Transfer (KT) packet (see template below) and update runbooks, repos, and ticket queues.
- Manager: identify recipients of KT, schedule handover sessions.
- Security: review device and data access lists for high-risk access.

T-4 to T-1
- IT: prepare device return instructions and remote wipe schedules; ticket created in ITSM (ticket example: ITSM-12345).
- Finance: finalize expense reimbursements and last payroll items.
- People Ops: schedule exit interview and provide offboarding resource pack (benefits continuation, references, career transition services).

Day 0 (last day)
- Manager: conduct final handoff meeting and confirm KT completion.
- IT/Security: deprovision accounts per the deprovisioning matrix.
- HR: complete separation paperwork and record reason for departure.

Post-departure (T+1 to T+5)
- Verify all hardware received and any access revoked; close open tickets.
- Manager: reassign active work and update hiring intake if replacement required.
- People Ops: send follow-up exit-survey and compile findings.

Knowledge Transfer (KT) packet template (required items)
- Role summary: responsibilities, daily/weekly cadence, key stakeholders and contacts.
- Active projects: status, owners, current blockers, next 3 milestones and expected completion dates.
- Access map: list of repositories, dashboards, service accounts, and permissions needed (owner + help contact).
- Operational runbook snippets: start/stop procedures, incident playbooks, common commands, and known quirks.
- Recommended hires/skills for replacement: profile, must-have skills, and suggested interview prompts.
sections.heading: Key SLAs and success metrics

sections.body:
Owners: @alice (prod), @bob (infra)
Status: In-flight. Next release: 2027-02-18
sections.heading: KT: Payments Model Serving

sections.body:
- rebuild container: ./ci/build.sh --service=payments
 - rotate KV cache before migration: scripts/rotate_kv_cache.sh
Open tickets: RW-4557 (data drift investigation)
```

Security & access controls (deprovisioning matrix)
- Priority 1 (High risk): root/cloud-admin, KMS/HSM keys, production DB admin, access to customer PII. Deprovision within 4 hours of termination.
- Priority 2: Application owners, CI/CD tokens, production deploy keys. Deprovision within 24-72 hours.
- Priority 3: Read-only dashboards, non-sensitive repos. Deprovision per schedule but confirm within 5 business days.

Suggested commands and runbook snippets (IT ops)
- Revoke AWS console access (IAM): aws iam delete-login-profile --user-name <user>
- Disable GitHub access (org-level): gh api -X PATCH /orgs/redwood/memberships/<user> -f role=none
- Device wipe (example): ./tools/wipe-device.sh --serial S123456789

Legal and IP considerations
- Ensure signed Employment Agreements and IP Assignment are recorded in HRIS before final payout.
- For terminations with potential IP concerns, consult Legal before data export or copies are permitted.
- Preserve relevant communications if placed on legal hold; Security & Legal will instruct on scope and retention.

Exit interviews and continuous improvement loop
- People Ops conducts a structured exit interview within 10 business days of departure (phone or video).
- Exit data captured via a standard form: reason for leaving, manager effectiveness, onboarding experience, team dynamics, and suggestions for improvement.
- Quarterly People Ops digest: anonymized exit metrics, themes, and recommended changes to hiring/onboarding processes shared with People Ops leadership and Hiring Managers.
- Example action: if 30% of engineering exits cite unclear role expectations, update job descriptions and the new-hire onboarding checklist within 2 sprints.

Rehire / boomerang policy
- Eligibility window: former employees may be rehired after a minimum 90-day cooling period unless otherwise approved by Head of People Ops.
- Assessment criteria: performance at time of departure, reason for leaving, rehire eligibility flags (e.g., contractual restrictions).
- Rehire path: fast-track interview with manager and People Ops review; previous employment file appended to candidate profile.

Manager obligations and accountability
- Managers must complete the offboarding checklist in Workday (or HRIS) and confirm KT artifacts are available.
- Failure to complete checklist within SLAs will be reported monthly to People Ops and may affect manager performance review calibration.

Reporting and dashboards
- Offboarding dashboard (People Ops/Analytics): offboarding completion rate, mean time to deprovision, KT compliance rate, reason-for-leave heatmap, rehire rate.
- Monthly report cadence: People Ops -> People Leadership (1st Monday of month) with top 3 trends and recommended interventions.

Appendix: templates and forms
- Offboarding checklist (copy to manager): 1) Confirm last day in HRIS; 2) Create KT packet; 3) Schedule knowledge transfer sessions; 4) Request device return; 5) Submit access removal ticket; 6) Complete exit interview scheduling.
- Exit interview standard questions (short list): What prompted your decision? What went well? What didn\u2019t? Suggestions for improvement? Would you consider returning?
- Sample handover email (to stakeholders):

Subject: Handover: [Employee Name] - [Role] - Last day [Date]
Body: Hi team, as [Employee] prepares to leave on [Date], please find the KT packet here: [link]. Primary interim authors: [names]. Outstanding items: ...

Change history and governance
- Version 1.0 (2026-03-15): Initial published playbook.
- Version 1.2 (2026-11-02): Added deprovisioning matrix and SLA targets.
- Version 2.0 (2027-01-10): Introduced boomerang policy and manager accountability clause.

Related resources
- Hiring and onboarding handbook: /confluence/people-ops/hire-onboard-accelerate-playbook-2025
- Internal mobility guidelines: /confluence/people-ops/returnship-and-internal-mobility-guidelines-2028
- Security offboarding runbook: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security

Contact
For questions or help implementing this playbook, contact: hr-ops@redwood.ai or people-ops@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: GPU topology, tenant affinity, and fallback reference

sections.body:
Summary

This reference describes recommended GPU topology patterns, tenant affinity controls, and automated fallback strategies for private (VPC / on-prem) Redwood deployments. The goal is to balance latency SLOs, cost efficiency, and tenant isolation while making operator decisions predictable and auditable. This doc covers: design patterns, configuration matrix, operational runbook, testing & validation, and monitoring/metrics recommended for SREs and operators.

Audience

- Operators running private Redwood control/data planes
- Platform engineers designing tenant placement policies
- Solutions and field engineers responsible for customer failovers and operator handoffs

1. Why GPU topology + tenant affinity matters

Modern inference workloads vary widely by model size, batch profile, and tail-latency sensitivity. Poor placement decisions cause: noisy-neighbor latency spikes, excessive KV-cache churn, higher unit cost from suboptimal packing, and complex forensic evidence during incidents. Explicit topology + affinity rules reduce these risks by:

- Keeping low-latency tenants on homogeneous, small-batched pools
- Co-locating model families that share KV cache semantics
- Pinning tenants with regulatory constraints to dedicated hardware pools

2. Topology patterns (reference)

Pattern A — Latency-isolated pools (recommended for SLO-sensitive tenants)
- Description: Pools sized to provide 95th p99 latency targets with headroom for prefix caching. No heterogeneous GPU packing.
- Typical use: consumer chat, product search reranking, interactive UIs.
- Topology: 4–16 GPUs per pool, identical GPU types (A100s / H100s), local NVMe for model shards.
- Affinity rule: tenant.affinity: strict
- Fallback: synchronous regional fallback to equivalent pool in another AZ; asynchronous model-quantized fallback only if synchronous capacity exhausted.

Pattern B — Cost-optimized mixed pools (recommended for batch/embeddings)
- Description: Heterogeneous GPU packing allowed (mixed memory profiles). Priority on throughput and bin-packing.
- Typical use: high-volume embedding workloads, offline reranking, nightly indexing.
- Topology: 16–64 GPUs per pool, mixed GPU types, centralized model cache with larger KV cache sizes.
- Affinity rule: tenant.affinity: soft
- Fallback: queue-based throttling + degraded-model routing (quantized variants)

Pattern C — Compliance-dedicated pools (recommended for regulated customers)
- Description: Single-tenant or small-tenant pools with strict network & KMS boundaries. Immutable image bootstrapping and signed model artifacts.
- Topology: depends on customer commit; keep odd/even node redundancy for N+1.
- Affinity rule: tenant.affinity: hardware-pinned
- Fallback: operator-initiated cross-tenant fallbacks disabled by default (require approval flow).

3. Affinity and placement knobs (config matrix)

The following table describes the most-used placement knobs and their operator-visible rewrite rules. Operators should expose these as part of the tenant provisioning API.

| Config key | Allowed values | Effect | Default | Owner |
|------------|----------------|--------|---------|-------|
| tenant.affinity | strict | Pin tenant to homogenous pool, deny heterogeneous packing | true | platform |
| | soft | Prefer same pool but allow fallback packing | | |
| | hardware-pinned | Use explicit node list in pool | | |
| placement.memory_margin_pct | 5–40 | Reservation to avoid OOMs when loading quantized weights | 15 | infra |
| placement.max_native_models | integer | Max different model artifacts per GPU before eviction | 1–4 | 2 | runtime |
| fallback.quantized_variant_enabled | true/false | Allow model fallback to quantized variant when capacity insufficient | true | product |
| fallback.synchronous_timeout_ms | 50–2000 | How long to wait for cross-AZ synchronous fallback before invoking async fallback | 300 | 300 | infra |

(Operators: map these keys to API fields: placement.policy, placement.constraints, fallback.policy)

4. Runtime behaviors and examples

- KV cache preservation: when migrating a tenant between pools, the runtime will attempt a KV cache warm transfer for values older than 30s using the routing-service. If warm transfer fails, mark tenant.state:kvc_old and apply cold-start safeguards.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
placement_policy:
  pool_selector: "latency-isolated-us-west2"
  affinity: strict
  memory_margin_pct: 20
  max_native_models: 2
  fallback_policy:
    synchronous_timeout_ms: 500
    allow_quantized_variant: true
sections.heading: Example placement API payload (YAML)

sections.body:
$ redwoodctl placement-preview --tenant T-123 --policy latency-isolated-us-west2
Preview: pool=latency-isolated-us-west2-02, node_affinity=[gpu-3,gpu-4], estimated_p99_latency=95ms

5. Fallback hierarchy and decision tree

Design principle: prefer automated, safe fallbacks that preserve customer SLAs and evidence trails. Fallbacks must be auditable and reversible.
sections.heading: preview placement decision for tenant T-123

sections.body:
1) Synchronous cross-zone routing to an equivalent latency-isolated pool
2) Synchronous cross-region routing (if tenant allows cross-region placement)
3) Degraded model routing (quantized or smaller architecture) with per-tenant quality scoring enabled
4) Queue + backpressure (apply 429 with Retry-After)
5) Operator failover with explicit audit entry and customer notification
sections.heading: Fallback order (runtime)

sections.body:
- If fallback step 1 is used, emit event: fallback.synchronous.az with tags (tenant, src_pool, dst_pool).
- If degraded model routing occurs, include quality_score delta in response metadata: x-rw-quality-delta: -0.07.

6. Operator runbook (day-2 playbook for placement incidents)
sections.heading: Decision tree notes

sections.body:
- spike in runtime.p99 for tenant > 2x baseline for 5 minutes
- runtime.kv_cache.hit_rate drops > 30% after a placement change
- OOM events reported by node exporter for model loader

Immediate steps (0–15 minutes):
1. Run placement preview: redwoodctl placement-preview --tenant <id>
2. Check pool utilization: kubectl top nodes -l pool=<pool>
3. Query routing-service audit: curl -sS http://routing-service.internal/audit?tenant=<id>&window=30m
4. If candidate target pool with spare capacity present, trigger automated migrate: redwoodctl tenant-migrate --tenant <id> --dst-pool <pool> --dry-run=false

Mitigation steps (15–60 minutes):
- If migration fails due to model-artifact limit, increase placement.max_native_models for the tenant and retest.
- If KV cache cold-start would cause user-visible errors, schedule a staged traffic mirror (10% -> 50% -> 100%) while warming caches. Use: redwoodctl traffic-mirror --src <pool> --dst <pool> --percent 10 --duration 10m
sections.heading: Alert symptoms (examples)

sections.body:
- Record incident in the incident tracker with fallback events attached.
- Run forensics: collect node-level traces /tmp/runtime-dumps, routing audit, and tenant response diffs. Place artifacts in S3 evidence: s3://redwood-evidence/<incident-id>/
- Run a placement policy review: was affinity misconfigured? Update placement policy and communicate to platform owners.

7. Testing matrix and validation harness

Every placement policy change must be validated against the following synthetic tests:
- Latency microbench: 1–10 QPS per thread, 128 token prompt, validate p95/p99 budgets
- KV-cache resiliency: simulate 30% model-switch churn and validate hit_rate recovery within 10 minutes
- Affinity violation test: attempt to schedule a hardware-pinned tenant onto mixed pool and assert failure with relevant audit log

Suggested CI job names: placement-unit-tests, placement-integration-chaos, placement-latency-benchmark. Include model artifacts with different quantization levels for realistic validation.

8. Monitoring and SLO implications
sections.heading: Post-incident (within 24 hours)

sections.body:
- runtime.p99.{tenant} (ms)
- runtime.kv_cache.hit_rate.{pool} (percent)
- placement.evictions.{pool} (count / minute)
- fallback.invocations.{type} (count) — types: synchronous_az, synchronous_region, degraded_model, queued, operator

SLO guidance (example decomposition for tenant SLO 99.5% availability, p99 <= 150ms):
- Placement margin: keep spare capacity >= 10% to absorb transient spikes
- KV-cache warming budget: aim to keep warm-transfer success >= 90% for synchronous migrations
- Fallback quality cap: degraded model routing may be invoked no more than 0.5% of requests in steady state without customer approval

9. Audit and compliance controls

- All automated fallback and migration decisions must create an auditable event with: timestamp, operator_id (system or user), src_pool, dst_pool, reason_code, and a checksum of model artifacts moved.
- For compliance pools (Pattern C), operator-initiated cross-tenant action must include a signed approval token and be recorded in the customer evidence bundle.

10. Upgrade & rollback considerations for topo changes

When changing pool topology (e.g., adding heterogeneous GPUs or increasing placement.max_native_models):
1. Rollout to canary pool with synthetic traffic for 48h
2. Monitor key metrics and run KV-cache resiliency tests
3. If rollback required, run operator rollback: redwoodctl topology-rollback --token <rollback-id>
4. Preserve evidence artifacts: keep routing audit and model checksums for at least 90 days for forensics

Appendix A — Common failure modes and mitigations

- Failure: Excessive eviction storms
  Mitigation: reduce placement.max_native_models, increase memory_margin_pct by 5–10, or isolate offending tenant to custom pool.

- Failure: Cross-AZ synchronous fallback flapping
  Mitigation: raise fallback.synchronous_timeout_ms to allow stable handshakes and add backpressure at ingress for brief window.

- Failure: Operator accidentally allows hardware-pinned tenant on mixed pool
  Mitigation: enforce pre-commit validation hook in provisioning pipeline and add automated policy gate in CI.

Appendix B — Example metrics dashboard panels (grafana queries)

- Panel: Tenant latency heatmap
  Query: rate(runtime.p99{tenant=~"$tenant"}[5m])

- Panel: Pool KV cache health
  Query: avg(runtime.kv_cache.hit_rate{pool=~"$pool"}) by (pool)

Contacts and ownership

- Architecture owner: Diego Morales (eng-infra)
- Runtime owner: Marcus Liu (eng-serving-runtime)
- Oncall contact: eng-private-deployments pager rotation

Related reading

- regional-model-fallback-topology-and-dataflow-2028
- tenant-aware-kv-cache-reconciliation-and-model-refresh-playbook-2026

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: Created by Diego Morales
- 2025-12-10: Added operator runbook and metrics per Markus review
- 2026-01-15: Finalized testing matrix and compliance controls
