payload.page_title: Service-meshless tenant shielding patterns for private deployments

sections.body:
Overview
========
This document presents a reference architecture and operational playbook for "service-meshless" tenant shielding in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). The goal is to provide strong tenant isolation, predictable degradation behaviors, and straightforward day-2 ops without introducing a sidecar-based service mesh. This pattern is intended for customers who require minimal runtime modification, low operational overhead, and clear evidence for audits.

Scope
-----
- Applies to private deployments (VPC-connected and on-prem appliances) hosting multiple tenants on a shared control plane and a shared GPU serving tier.
- Focuses on network- and host-level isolation primitives, cryptographic tenant segmentation, and operator workflows for rollout, upgrade, and rollback.
- Not a replacement for zero-trust at the app layer; use in combination with per-tenant TLS, RBAC, and workload-level quotas.

Motivation and tradeoffs
-----------------------
- Why meshless? Avoids per-pod/per-container sidecars that increase memory/CPU and complicate KV cache locality, model hot-swap, and real-time batching.
- Tradeoffs: slightly more complex network policy and host configuration; less protocol-level request observability than a full sidecar mesh. Suitable when predictable latency and GPU locality are critical.

Architecture summary
--------------------
- Control plane and management network remain logically separated from tenant data paths.
- Tenant shielding is implemented with a layered approach:
  1. Network segmentation: per-tenant virtual subnets (VLANs/VRFs or overlay segments) with enforced egress/ingress boundaries.
  2. Host-level enforcement: eBPF-based policy agents and nftables rules for process-level allowance and rate-limiting.
  3. Crypto tenancy: per-tenant TLS certificates / mTLS and per-tenant KMS key prefixes for encryption-at-rest labels.
  4. Orchestration guards: admission-time validators that map tenant identifiers to allowed model catalogs and resource quotas.

Logical dataflow (text description of diagram)
------------------------------------------------
Control-plane (Mgmt VNet) -> Tenant ingress gateway -> Tenant virtual subnet -> Worker hosts (host net + eBPF enforcement) -> GPU serving process (redwood-runtime) -> KV cache / local disk

Configuration table: minimum platform contract
------------------------------------------------
| Component                  | Minimum requirement (per tenant)                               |
|---------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Virtual subnet             | /26 (supports up to 62 tenant endpoints) or VRF per tenant     |
| Control-plane link         | 1 Gbps isolated VPC/VPN, MTU 9000 recommended                  |
| Host kernel               | Linux 5.10+ with eBPF CO-RE support                            |
| KMS                       | Per-tenant key prefixes + rotation API                         |
| Observability retention   | 30 days for tenant-level metrics (default)                     |
| Model artifact storage    | Per-tenant ACLs with signed manifests                          |

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------
- Redwood operator (redwood-ops): configure control-plane networks, supply signed runtime bundles, and operate the management control-plane.
- Customer infra: owns VPC/VPN connections, allocated subnets, and tenant egress firewall ACLs.
- Field engineer (onboarding): runs the initial tenant segmentation playbook and validates telemetry contracts.

Detailed design components
--------------------------
1) Tenant virtual subnets and routing
   - Use cloud VPC segmentation (subnets, VRFs) on public/private clouds. For on-prem, use VLANs + BGP VRF.
   - Routing policy: advertise only the tenant prefix to tenant gateways, do not advertise tenant prefixes in the control plane.
   - BGP communities: set a "redwood-shield" community to prevent accidental export of tenant routes.

2) Host-level enforcement (eBPF agent)
   - Deploy a lightweight eBPF agent (we maintain redwood-ebpf-agent) on every worker host.
   - Responsibilities:
     - Process-to-network mapping (pin runtime processes to tenant IDs)
     - L3/L4 allowlists (reject unknown remote endpoints)
     - Token bucket rate-limits per source/destination tuple for DoS protection (default 1000 req/s burst 200)
   - Advantages: no per-workload sidecars, kernel-enforced policy, low overhead.

3) Cryptographic tenancy and KMS
   - Each tenant receives a unique key prefix and signing certificate.
   - TLS termination occurs at tenant ingress gateway; mTLS between gateway and control-plane endpoints is optional.
   - Key rotation: automated rolling every 90 days; rollback window 30 days.

4) Admission-time enforcement
   - Admission validators are executed in the control plane when customer-provided deployment manifests are accepted.
   - Validators enforce: allowed-model-list, max-gpu-units, allowed-regions, and artifact-signature checks.

Operational playbook: deploy a new tenant (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------------------------
1. Preflight checklist (operator)
   - Confirm tenant CIDR allocation in customer VPC.
   - Verify BGP peering/session (if on-prem) or VPN connectivity.
   - Confirm KMS key prefix provisioned and accessible via IAM.
   - Ensure host eBPF agent is at least v1.4 on target worker pool.
2. Control-plane configuration
   - Create tenant entry in control plane with model catalog ACLs and quota.
   - Upload tenant cert chain and KMS prefix.
3. Network activation
   - Provision tenant subnet and update routing filters (apply redwood-shield BGP community).
   - Apply tenant ingress ACLs on edge gateway.
4. Host binding
   - Tag worker hosts with tenant affinity labels via orchestration tool (example CLI):
     redwoodctl host tag --host=worker-12 --tenant-id=tenant-acme
   - Verify eBPF policy binds the runtime process to the tenant ID.
5. Smoke tests
   - Synthetic inference run at low concurrency (10 qps) for baseline latency.
   - Verify telemetry is flowing: metric names: tenant.requests.total, tenant.latency.p95, tenant.errors.rate.
6. Acceptance
   - Customer and operator agree on SLOs and sign-off in the acceptance checklist.

Day-2 ops: common runbook entries
--------------------------------
- Detecting cross-tenant traffic:
  1. Query host process mappings: redwood-ebpfctl list-processes --host worker-12
  2. Check connection logs: /var/log/redwood/ebpf-connections.log (rotate daily)
- Throttling noisy tenant:
  1. Reduce tenant token bucket with redwood-ebpfctl quota set --tenant tenant-xyz --rate 250
  2. If sustained, move tenant to isolated worker pool: redwoodctl tenant relocate --tenant tenant-xyz --pool isolated-1
- Debugging cold-start spikes:
  - Observe local KV cache misses: metric tenant.kvcache.misses
  - If misses correlated with rollout, scale cache warmers prior to rollout.

Upgrade and rollback
--------------------
Strategy
- All runtime upgrades follow an incremental canary-first pattern with tenant-scope gating.
- No in-place sidecar changes; upgrades target the runtime binary and eBPF agent separately.

Upgrade steps (runtime)
1. Build and sign runtime bundle.
2. Deploy to a canary pool (isolated tenants or internal test tenants).
3. Run synthetic traffic and collect baseline metrics for 24 hours.
4. Gradually expand rollout (10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%) by worker-pool label updates.
5. Monitor: tenant.latency.p95, tenant.errors.rate, runtime.cpu.percent, kvcache.hit_rate.

Rollback criteria
- Immediate rollback if any tenant group shows:
  - p95 latency regression > 30% over baseline for > 10 minutes
  - error rate increase > 1% absolute
  - host-level OOMs or GPU driver failures
- Rollback action: redeploy previous signed bundle to affected pools and validate with smoke tests.

Example network policy (nftables snippet)
-----------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview
nftables fragment for tenant isolation (illustrative)

sections.body:
POST /kms/rotate
payload: {
  "tenant_id": "tenant-abc",
  "rotation_window_days": 90
}

Telemetry contract
------------------
- Metrics (per-tenant tags): tenant.requests.total, tenant.latency.p50/p95/p99, tenant.errors.total, tenant.kvcache.hit_rate, tenant.gpu.utilization
- Logs: connection logs, eBPF policy decision logs (retain 30d), audit trail for KMS operations (retain 365d)
- Traces: sampled 1% by default for tenant inference request paths; increase for troubleshooting.

Acceptance criteria for field handoff
-------------------------------------
- Successful smoke test with < 5% baseline p95 latency variance vs. lab profile.
- No cross-tenant connection logs for 24h in staging after activation.
- Audit evidence for KMS key provision and certificate chain transfer.

Troubleshooting matrix (quick reference)
----------------------------------------
- Symptom: tenant requests intermittently see 503
  - Likely: admission-time ACL rejects or eBPF deny
  - Debug: redwoodctl tenant describe tenant-id; redwood-ebpfctl dump-rules --host
- Symptom: cross-tenant traffic observed
  - Likely: missing BGP community or eBPF agent mismatch
  - Debug: check route tables, run redwood-ebpfctl list-flows
- Symptom: sudden p99 latency spike
  - Likely: GPU thermal or driver issue; check nvidia-smi, dmesg, and runtime logs

Audit and compliance notes
--------------------------
- Keep a signed manifest for each tenant deployment. Manifests must include model checksum, runtime bundle hash, and KMS key ID.
- Evidence artifacts (logs, manifests, KMS history) must be archived to customer-provided storage or an encrypted Redwood audit bucket.

Related reading and references
-------------------------------
- See reference-architectures/edge-gateway-and-airgapped-bridge-architecture-2026 for ingress gateway options.
- See deployment-guides/vpc-entropy-segmentation-and-tenant-shielding-playbook-2026 for operational checklists.

Appendix: sample acceptance checklist
-----------------------------------
- Tenant CIDR allocated and peered: [ ]
- eBPF agent v>=1.4 running on worker pool: [ ]
- KMS key prefix provisioned: [ ]
- Synthetic inference p95 within lab baseline +/-5%: [ ]
- Audit manifest signed and stored: [ ]

Document revision history
-------------------------
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Asha Menon
- 2026-02-03: Added eBPF rate-limiting defaults and rollback criteria (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Marta Kuznetsova)

payload.page_title: Service Subnet Mapping and Multi-tenant Failover Patterns for Private Deployments

sections.body:
Summary:

This page defines recommended network/service-subnet mapping, tenant-isolation models, and automated failover patterns for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It focuses on predictable behavior during capacity pressure, host failure, and upgrades while maintaining tenant isolation, auditability, and minimal customer impact. The guidance applies to: private VPC control-plane + private compute, air-gapped on-prem clusters, and hybrid deployments that use an edge gateway.

Scope:

- Audience: SRE, Field Engineering, Private Deployments PMs, and Solution Architects.
- Applies to: model serving pods/processes (runtime), control-plane components (operator, APIs), telemetry collectors, and sidecar proxies used for egress and sharding.
- Not in scope: internal hosted public API routing logic (see eng-serving-runtime docs).

Goals and constraints:

- Preserve tenant isolation (compute, storage, and network) by default.
- Allow controlled multi-tenant co-location when customers opt-in for capacity efficiency.
- Enable automated failover across availability zones and adjacent VPC regions with deterministic session management for short-running inference and graceful degradation for long-running sessions.
- Minimize blast radius during kernel upgrades, quantization profile changes, and KV cache migrations.

High-level patterns overview:

1) Subnet-based service zoning (recommended default)
   - Allocate three primary subnet classes per deployment: control, compute, and ingress/egress.
   - Control subnet: control-plane APIs, operator, scheduler. Default: private-only, no customer traffic.
   - Compute subnets: isolated per-tenant or shared (see tenant models). Place GPU nodes here.
   - Edge/ingress subnet: ingress gateway, NAT/proxy, and egress enforcement.

2) Tenant isolation models (choose based on risk/cost profile)
   - Dedicated-tenant mode (strong isolation): VLAN/ENI-per-tenant or dedicated compute subnets; recommended for regulated customers.
   - Namespace-tenant mode (balanced): Kubernetes namespaces + network policies + per-tenant routing table entries; recommended default for SMB / mid-market.
   - Shared-tenant mode (cost-optimized): best-effort tenant tagging + per-tenant quotas and software rate limiting; allowed only with explicit customer consent.

3) Failover and graceful degradation patterns
   - Fast-fail route: traffic rerouting to pinned model variant in another zone/region. Used for <150ms queueing SLOs.
   - Slow-fail route: serve shorter completions or cached prefix responses when KV cache cannot be migrated.
   - Admission-control fallback: drop low-priority/non-SLA traffic before high-priority requests during capacity shortage.

Architecture diagram (textual):

[Zone A] --- VPN/Transit --- [Edge GW / Ingress Subnet] --- NAT / egress proxy --- [Compute Subnet (tenantX)]
                          |
                          +-- [Control Subnet: operator, scheduler, telemetry]

Traffic flows:
- External customer requests enter Edge GW, are authenticated by customer-managed IDP (OIDC) or mTLS, then routed to a tenant route table that selects compute pool.
- KV cache and prefix caches are region-local; stateful migration uses orchestrated snapshot + incremental sync.

Detailed configuration tables (examples):

Network allocation (example):
| Component           | CIDR example        | Purpose                          | Notes |
|---------------------|---------------------|----------------------------------|-------|
| Control subnet      | 10.10.0.0/22        | Operator, API control traffic    | No external egress allowed |
| Edge/Ingress subnet | 10.10.4.0/24        | Load balancer, NAT, proxies      | TLS termination at edge | 
| Compute - tenant A  | 10.10.8.0/24        | GPU nodes + runtime processes    | ENI with security groups | 
| Compute - shared    | 10.10.9.0/24        | Workloads tagged shared-rt       | Optional, cost-optimized |

Hardware compatibility snapshot (short):
| Component            | Minimum | Recommended | Notes |
|---------------------|---------|-------------|-------|
| GPU nodes (per-host) | 8xA100 | 8xH100     | H100 preferred for high-throughput batching |
| NVMe local scratch   | 1TB    | 2TB         | KV cache local backing; encryption required |
| Network             | 25GbE  | 100GbE      | 100GbE for cross-host KV sync during migration |

Operational runbook: Steady-state failover (automated)

1. Detection
   - Alert types: NodeDown, HostNetworkPartition, HighQueueLatency (>200ms P90), KV-Sync-Failure.
   - Detection sources: Prometheus alerts (node_exporter, runtime_exporter), control-plane healthcheck events.

2. Automated response (Order of operations)
   1) Mark affected host as DRAINING via orchestrator API: curl -XPOST https://operator.internal/v1/hosts/{host}/drain 
      - Rationale: stop new sessions from landing.
   2) Trigger KV snapshot for hot tenants: POST /v1/kv/snapshot?tenant={id}&priority=high
   3) Schedule cross-zone placement for new sessions: update route table for tenant -> failover pool (prioritized by cost/latency policy).
   4) If drain stalls > 3m, escalate to human on-call (SRE).

3. Rollback (if failover introduced regressions)
   - Criteria to rollback: observed P95 latency increase > 50% vs baseline for 5min or model-quality regression > threshold.
   - Steps:
     1) Pause traffic migration: operator API set migration.enabled=false
     2) Revert tenant routing table to previous state: operator routing import from last-good config snapshot
     3) Restore KV state from pre-failover snapshot (see KV snapshot retention below)

Indexes and retention (telemetry and KV snapshots):
- KV snapshot retention: 3 most recent incremental + 1 full snapshot retained for 72 hours (default), adjustable per-customer.
- Telemetry retention for private deployments: default 30 days for high-cardinality traces, 180 days for aggregated token-cost metrics. Longer retention available as add-on.

Day-2 operations: patching, upgrades, and safe rollout steps

Principles:
- Zero-blast upgrades using canaries and progressive rollout by shard
- Preserve backward-compatible RPC interfaces for 3 minor releases for pinned customer model variants
- Avoid co-locating canary control-plane changes with mass compute upgrades

Safe upgrade checklist (example procedure):
1) Preflight (automated)
   - Validate package signatures (cosign) for container images.
   - Run smoke-runner against the canary pool: generate 100 synthetic inference requests, assert latency and output hash within tolerance.
2) Canary deploy (1% of capacity) for 30–60 minutes
   - Monitor: latency P95, tail token generation time, error rate, output-quality hash diffs.
3) Progressive ramp (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 15–30 minute soak windows. Abort on threshold breach.
4) Post-upgrade KV reconciliation: run incremental sync and verify KV checksum equality across replica sets.

Rollback on upgrade failure:
- Immediate rollback trigger conditions: new error-rate increase > 2x baseline for 10m or a production-quality regression detected by evaluation hooks.
- Rollback steps (fast path):
  1) operator rollback --release last_good_release --target all
  2) Restore route pinning for affected tenants if migration was performed.
  3) Open incident, notify support and customer success for impacted accounts.

Customer requirements checklist (minimum, short-form)

- Network: BGP/VPN or Direct Connect for VPCs with mutual ASN, minimum 100Mbps burst for small deployments, 10Gbps+ recommended for production.
- IP addressing: Customer provides CIDR pool >= /20 for medium deployments; support for custom ENI ranges.
- KMS: Customer must provide KMS endpoint or accept Redwood-managed KMS with compliant key policies.
- Identity: OIDC with group-claim mapping or mTLS certificates.
- Compliance: Host firmware inventory and image signing policies required for air-gapped installations.

Acceptance tests (example):
1) Connectivity smoke: edge GW -> control-plane API (TLS) succeed, signed cert chain verified.
2) Performance smoke: synthetic inference P95 under SLA (per-tenant) with cold-cache and warm-cache baselines.
3) Failover smoke: simulate node outage and verify new sessions routed to failover pool within 20s.
4) KV integrity: run KV checksum and ensure reconciliation completes within configured window.

Owners and escalation

- Primary owner: Private Deployments SRE (oncall-private-deployments@redwood.ai)
- Secondary owner: Runtime team (runtime-oncall@redwood.ai)
- Escalation: See oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process for pager path.

Appendix: CLI examples and snippets

- Drain host:
  curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer ${OPERATOR_TOKEN}" https://operator.internal/v1/hosts/host-123/drain

- Create KV snapshot (high priority):
  curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer ${OPERATOR_TOKEN}" https://operator.internal/v1/kv/snapshot -d '{"tenant":"tenant-abc","priority":"high"}'

- Revert routing table to snapshot:
  operatorctl routing import --file /opt/operator/last_good_routing.json

Related reading and links:
- Deployment playbooks: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deliverables-and-runbook-templates (operator delivery)
- KV migration and state: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/kv-cache-migrations-and-runtime-state-migration-playbook-2025

Change log:
- 2025-11-10: Initial draft (M. Chen)
- 2026-01-15: Added KV snapshot retention guidance and hardware notes (review: L. O'Connor)
- 2026-02-08: Tuned failover thresholds and added rollback fast-path steps (review: P. Raman)

Notes and open questions:
- Option: support per-tenant configurable KV snapshot retention beyond default (requires billing delta).
- Work item: Automate cross-zone KV incremental sync instrumentation; tracked in runtime roadmap.

payload.page_title: Chronological operator escape-hatch topologies and customer notification protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines operator-visible escape-hatch topologies for private (VPC and on-prem) deployments and prescribes a chronological, time-boxed protocol for invoking them. It covers operator actions, automated triggers, SLO-preserving thresholds, and a customer communication protocol. The goal is to ensure predictable, auditable, and reversible degraded-mode behavior when the normal control plane or runtime cannot meet SLA targets.

Intended audience

- Field operators and SREs responsible for private deployments
- Solutions engineers coordinating with customers during incidents
- Engineering managers who approve escape-hatch playbooks

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: tenant-facing runtime escapes (routing changes, admission control, model fallback), operator APIs for manual intervention, and customer notification templates.
- Non-goal: detailed per-customer billing reconciliation or legal escalation templates (handled by finance-legal and customer-success).

Requirements and goals

- Preserve P95 latency SLO where possible, minimize customer-visible errors, and ensure forensic evidence is preserved for audits.
- Actions must be reversible and logged with operator identity and runbook step IDs.
- Automated triggers should handle immediate mitigations; operator interventions handle staged escalations.

Owners and escalation

- Primary owner: Private Deployments SRE (team: eng-private-deployments)
- Secondary owner: Field Operations (team: customer-success)
- Oncall escalation: Platform SRE -> Runtime lead -> Head of Private Deployments

Topologies (summary table)

Topology | When to use | SLO impact | Operator action (quick)
---|---:|---:|---
Local degraded-mode (node-level) | Single-node GPU thermal or kernel issues | Increases latency ~10-30% for affected tenants | Evict pods, enable degraded runtime kernel, notify customers if >15m
Regional redirect (regional proxy) | Regional control plane/MX backend fault | May add 50–200ms RTT, potential cost increase due to cross-region | Flip regional routing, enable cross-region kv-cache warmup
Model-fallback variant | Incompatible accelerator / quantization failure | Potential quality regression; latency similar | Swap to smaller quantized model, enable quality-monitor gating
Admission-control (rate-limiting) | Sustained overload or noisy tenant | Increased 429 rate; preserves core SLOs | Apply per-tenant throttles and quota enforcement
Operator-evacuation (tenant-level) | Tenant-specific state corruption or forensic need | May cause transient errors during state handoff | Quiesce tenant, snapshot state, evacuate to standby topology

Escape-hatch characteristics

- Time-boxed: each hatch has recommended check-points (T0, T+5m, T+15m, T+1h) and automatic rollback windows.
- Observable: instrumentation must emit events: hatch.triggered, hatch.action, hatch.operator, hatch.resolved.
- Reversible: every change includes a documented reversal path and sanity checks.

Chronological protocol (decision tree)

1) Detection (T0 — automated):
   - Trigger conditions: sustained P95 > configured threshold for 3 consecutive sampling windows (default: 1m windows, 3x) OR critical healthcheck failure on >2 nodes in region.
   - Automated mitigations attempted immediately: local admission-control increment, priority queueing, prefix-KV reuse.
   - Emit event: hatch.triggered with reason.

2) Initial operator checklist (T0 to T+5m):
   - Operator picks runbook ID and documents initial observations.
   - Run automated diagnostic commands:
     - kubectl get pods -n redwood-runtime --selector=tenant=affected -o wide
     - curl -sS http://controlplane.internal/health | jq '.'
   - If automated mitigations show improvement (latency back within 10% of SLO), continue monitoring for 30 minutes.

3) Escalation (T+5m to T+15m):
   - If degradation persists, choose topology from Topologies table. Prefer minimal-scope options first: admission-control -> model-fallback -> regional redirect -> operator-evacuation.
   - Execute the change using the operator API with an audit message. Example:

   curl -X POST https://operator-api.internal/v1/escape-hatch \
     -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"tenant":"tenant-123","action":"model-fallback","variant":"gptq-4-8x32-compact","runbook_id":"RH-ESC-2026-042","operator":"ava.martinez"}'

   - Verify effect: trace a sample request end-to-end and confirm new model variant served.

4) Customer notification (T+15m):
   - If customer-visible errors or quality regressions occur, notify customers according to the Customer Notification Protocol below.

5) Containment and stabilization (T+15m to T+1h):
   - Continue telemetry collection at increased resolution (15s).
   - If mitigations stabilize SLOs, start a 1-hour stabilization timer. If SLOs hold for 1 hour, begin post-incident actions.

6) Rollback and audit (after stabilization or negative outcome):
   - If hatch removed, run automated reconciliation: reconcile-kv-cache, refresh routing config, and validate state signatures.
   - Persist a forensic bundle: collection of operator logs, event IDs, snapshots (S3 path), and timeline.

Operator API and automation examples

- Trigger a limited admission-control (JSON payload example):
  {"scope": "tenant-123",
    "action": "admission_control",
    "limits": {"rps": 50, "burst": 25},
    "duration": "PT30M",
    "runbook_id": "RH-ESC-2026-042"
  }

- Example CLI to flip a regional proxy (operator tool example):
  redwood-ctl proxy-router promote --from=us-west-2 --to=eu-west-1 --tenants=customer-a,customer-b --reason="regional-controlplane-failure" --runbook RH-ESC-2026-042

Customer notification protocol (templates & thresholds)

Notification categories
- Advisory: SLOs impacted but no customer-facing errors. Threshold: mitigation invoked and expected stabilization within 2h.
- Alert: Visible errors, quality regressions, or >5% request error rate. Threshold: any 5m window matching condition.
- Critical: Data integrity, tenant state corruption, or SLA breach. Immediate outreach.

Customer message templates (short form)
- Advisory: "We observed elevated latency affecting inference for your tenant. We've applied automated mitigations and are monitoring. No action required from your side. Expected resolution within 2 hours. Runbook: RH-ESC-2026-042."
- Alert: "You may see increased errors or lower-quality outputs. We have applied an emergency mitigation and are actively investigating. We will provide updates every 30 minutes. Contact: field-ops@example.redwood.ai."
- Critical: "We have detected tenant state impact and are working on a safe remediation path. We will be in direct contact through your designated technical contact and provide hourly updates."

Notification channels and cadence

- Initial notification: 30 minutes after hatch reaches Alert category (email + webhook + PagerDuty if configured).
- Updates: every 30 minutes until escalation cleared; hourly during stabilization.
- Postmortem delivery: within 72 hours for all Alert/Critical events.

Testing and drill playbook

- Quarterly automated drills: simulate admission-control triggers and model-fallback swaps in a staging region.
- Annual end-to-end evacuation drill: coordinate with 2 customers (consent required) for a scheduled safe failover.
- Test checklist (sample):
  1. Validate operator API tokens and RBAC for emergency actions.
  2. Run a model-fallback swap on a canary tenant and validate quality gates.
  3. Run a routing flip between regions and verify cache warmup times.

Metrics, dashboards and alerts

- Dashboards should include: P50/P95/P99 latency, error rate (5m), successful model swaps (count), hatch-triggered events, and forensic bundle creation status.
- Alert thresholds (recommendations):
  - P95 > SLO * 1.5 for 3 consecutive windows -> Severity P2
  - Error rate > 5% for 5 minutes -> Severity P1
  - Forensic evidence missing 15m after hatch -> Severity P2

Appendix A: Safe rollback commands (examples)

- Revert model-fallback:
  curl -X POST https://operator-api.internal/v1/escape-hatch/revert \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN' \
    -d '{"tenant":"tenant-123","action":"revert","runbook_id":"RH-ESC-2026-042"}'

- Re-enable standard routing after regional redirect sanity checks:
  redwood-ctl proxy-router promote --from=eu-west-1 --to=us-west-2 --reverse --runbook RH-ESC-2026-042

Appendix B: Contact matrix

- Platform SRE: oncall-platform@redwood.ai (PagerDuty alias: platform-oncall)
- Field Ops: field-ops@redwood.ai
- Security/Compliance (for forensic preservation): security-incident@redwood.ai

Related documents

- See the private-deploy-onboarding-and-failover-runbook for tenant handoff checklists.
- See runtime-telemetry-and-kv-cache-playbook for cache reconciliation steps.

Change log

- 2026-02-12: Initial draft by Ava Martinez.
- 2026-04-08: Added operator API examples and customer templates (reviewers: Ethan Park).
- 2026-08-03: Finalized stabilization timers and added forensic bundle requirements.

payload.page_title: Asynchronous model fanout and incremental refresh reference

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines a reference architecture and operational playbook for deploying Redwood inference model artifacts to private (VPC or on-prem) edge sites where connectivity is constrained or intermittent. The strategy is an asynchronous model fanout with signed manifests and incremental (delta) refreshes so that local runtime instances can serve requests with predictable latency while minimizing bandwidth and preserving auditability.

Scope

- Applies to private deployments that operate in low-bandwidth, high-latency, or scheduled-connectivity environments (examples: retail kiosks, branch offices, manufacturing sites, regulated air-gapped facilities with nightly sync windows).
- Covers control-plane manifests, artifact packaging, delta computation, local runtime behavior, rollout/upgrade procedures, and day-2 operational checks.
- Does not replace normal hot-swap model-rollout flows used by always-on data center deployments; this is a specialization for constrained environments.

Goals and design constraints

1. Serve local inference requests with P95 tail latency <= 300ms for token generation for short sequences (<= 256 tokens) under typical hardware profiles.
2. Limit peak bandwidth consumption for model refreshes to configurable budget (default 500 MB/hour per site).
3. Ensure safe upgrades: ability to rollback to last known-good artifact within 10 minutes (operator-mediated) or automatically revert on health regressions.
4. Preserve cryptographic provenance for all model artifacts and delta updates (signed manifests + detached signatures).

High-level architecture
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Central Deployment Orchestrator (control plane): produces signed manifest files describing model bundles, versioned artifacts, and delta patches. Runs in Redwood control plane or customer-managed private control plane.
- Delta Generator service: computes compact binary diffs between consecutive model artifact tarballs and emits patch packages. Integrates with model registry.
- Edge Sync Agent: lightweight process on the private deployment that pulls manifests, validates signatures, applies delta patches to local artifact store, and signals runtime to atomically swap model artifact directories.
- Local Serving Runtime: Redwood inference runtime configured for local artifact directories, KV cache preservation, and structured fallback to regional service when configured.
- Audit & Telemetry Gateway: batched telemetry shuttle and signed evidence collector that aggregates sync/upgrade events and ships evidence to the control plane when connectivity allows.
sections.heading: Components

sections.body:
- Central Orchestrator --> publishes signed-manifest.json --> Edge Sync Agent
- Central Orchestrator --> Delta Generator --> delta-<vN>-<vN+1>.patch --> Edge Sync Agent
- Edge Sync Agent --(local apply)--> Local Artifact Store + runtime swap
- Local Serving Runtime --> Telemetry Gateway (batched) --> Central audit store

Key dataflows (numbered)

1. Manifest publish: Orchestrator composes manifest with metadata (model id, base artifact checksum, patch list, minimum-available-ram, hardware profile tag, rollout windows) and signs it using platform signing key.
2. Edge poll: Edge Sync Agent polls control plane for new manifests on configurable cadence (default: 30 minutes) or listens for push via an authenticated webhook when available.
3. Validation: Agent verifies manifest signature, checks local preconditions (disk free space, CPU/GPU idle threshold), and computes expected delta chain.
4. Fetch & apply: Agent downloads delta patches (or full artifact if delta chain broken), verifies detached signatures, applies patch into a new artifact directory, validates artifact (checksum + sample inference smoke test), then performs atomic symlink swap.
5. Evidence and telemetry: Agent records signed evidence of successful apply and local smoke-test output, pushes batched evidence when connectivity permits. If apply fails, the agent reverts to the previous artifact and raises an alert.

Manifest example (JSON snippet) - sample manifest should be treated as pseudocode when used in automation:

{
  "model_id": "redwood-2b-mix-quant",
  "version": "2026-02-05-3",
  "base_checksum": "sha256:abcdef...",
  "patches": ["delta-2026-01-27-to-2026-02-05.patch"],
  "min_free_disk_mb": 10240,
  "recommended_hw_tag": "t4-small|a10-large",
  "rollout_window": {"start_utc": "02:00","end_utc": "06:00"},
  "signature": "base64sig..."
}

Operational policies and rollout pattern

A. Canary phase (automated):
1. Publish manifest with rollout_window and target site list = small canary cohort (1–3 sites).
2. Edge Agents in cohort apply delta and run 10-minute smoke tests (API health, example prompts, model quality quick-check using curated seed prompts).
3. If telemetry indicates no CPU/GPU OOMs, P95 latency regressions, or quality regressions (see quality thresholds below) for 30 minutes, promote to progressive rollout.

B. Progressive rollout (time-based + health-gated):
1. Expand target cohort by percentage (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) every rollout window cycle, monitor metrics for each expansion for a full window.
2. If any cohort emits critical failures (defined below), automatically pause rollout and notify oncall.

C. Emergency rollback:
- Edge Agent always keeps last known-good artifact locally. The agent can revert by atomic symlink back to previous artifact and restart runtime within 2 minutes. If automatic revert fails, operator-run rollback steps (see runbook) apply.

Quality and safety thresholds (monitored during rollout)

- Latency: P95 token latency increase <= 20% vs baseline.
- Error rate: 500-level error rate < 0.1% over 10 minute windows.
- Smoke-quality: Failure rate on curated prompts (semantic score) <= 3% relative degradation.

Upgrade and rollback procedure (detailed)
sections.heading: Architecture diagram (textual)

sections.body:
- Verify site has min_free_disk_mb from manifest + 20% buffer.
- Confirm no active high-priority operator tasks or live cutovers scheduled.
- Check telemetry shuttle backlog < 1000 events.
- Ensure operator has current artifact checksums and rollback artifact id.
sections.heading: Pre-upgrade checks

sections.body:
1. Agent receives signed manifest.
2. Agent validates and downloads delta(s).
3. Agent applies patch into new directory /var/lib/redwood/artifacts/<model>-<version>.<timestamp>.
4. Agent runs smoke tests (pass/fail). Smoke tests include: start inference daemon in isolated mode, run 5 seed prompts, validate output tokens and latency thresholds.
5. On success, Agent performs atomic swap and gracefully drains in-flight requests (config: drain_timeout = 30s).
6. Agent records signed apply-evidence and schedules telemetry upload.
sections.heading: Automated upgrade steps (agent-driven)

sections.body:
1. If post-swap health checks fail, Agent swaps back to previous artifact and restarts runtime.
2. Agent marks manifest as failed and attaches error_clues (failed smoke tests, checksum mismatch, insufficient disk).
3. Control plane creates incident with attached evidence bundle.
sections.heading: Rollback (automated on health regression)

sections.body:
1. SSH to operator bastion or use operator console.
2. Verify evidence bundle and determine root cause (failed patch, corrupted delta, quality regression).
3. Trigger remote rollback API: POST /operator/v1/sites/<site_id>/rollback with payload {"artifact_id": "..."}.
4. Validate site returns to previous SLOs and mark incident resolved.

Day-2 operations and runbook (troubleshooting checklist)
sections.heading: Manual rollback (operator)

sections.body:
- Delta apply failure (checksum mismatch):
  1. Agent automatically attempts full artifact fetch.
  2. If full artifact fetch fails, agent halts and retains previous artifact, then raises CRITICAL alert to oncall.
- Disk pressure during apply:
  1. Agent aborts apply and cleans temporary files.
  2. Alert: "artifact.apply.disk_low". Operator must reclaim disk or expand ephemeral volume.
- Smoke-test degradation (semantic checks failing):
  1. Agent reverts immediately. 2. Oncall runs quality triage using sample inference traces, forwards artifacts to Applied ML for postmortem.
- Partial connectivity (patch download stalls):
  1. Agent resumes partial downloads with range requests and resumes after connectivity recovery; if unable within rollout_window, it aborts and schedules next attempt.
sections.heading: Common failure modes and recovery steps

sections.body:
- Force full artifact fetch: redwood-edge-agent fetch --site <id> --artifact <artifact_id> --force-full
- Query agent status: redwood-edge-agent status --site <id>
- Roll back to artifact: redwood-edge-agent rollback --artifact <artifact_id>

Hardware, network and customer requirements (table format described)

Table: Minimum site profile requirements
- CPU: 8 vCPU or equivalent (x86)
- RAM: 32 GB system RAM (64 GB recommended for model variants > 4B parameters)
- GPU: optional, recommended when model > 7B parameters. Supported tags in manifest must match actual installed GPU type.
- Disk: 25 GB free for runtime + model artifact working space (base artifact size + delta); ensure snapshot/backup partition available.
- Network: egress bandwidth >= 5 Mbps sustained for manifest sync windows; ability to make TLS connections to control-plane endpoints.
sections.heading: Runbook quick commands (agent-side)

sections.body:
- Allowlist control-plane FQDNs in egress policy.
- Provide KMS/HSM integration info if customer-managed signatures required.
- Agree to rollout windows (local quiet hours) and provide operator contacts for emergency interventions.

Security and compliance considerations

- All manifests and artifacts must be signed with a platform-approved key; edge agent enforces signature verification.
- Evidence bundles contain minimal telemetry and MUST be redacted for PII by default before transit.
- For highly regulated customers, evidence bundles can be stored in-customer-premise and uploaded via an agreed transfer process.

Telemetry, logging and alerts

Critical metrics to emit from each site (batch/shuttle semantics):
- artifact.sync.success_rate (1m/5m windows)
- artifact.apply.duration.p95
- runtime.inference.p95_latency
- runtime.inference.error_rate
- disk.free_mb
- telemetry.upload.backlog_count
sections.heading: Customer operational commitments (minimum)

sections.body:
- artifact.apply.failed (SEV2)
- runtime.inference.error_rate > 0.5% sustained (SEV1 for enterprise SLA customers)
- disk.free_mb < manifest.min_free_disk_mb + 1000MB (SEV2)

Acceptance tests and smoke checks (pre-flight)

- Deterministic smoke prompts: run canonical prompt set (5 prompts) verifying outputs match baseline signatures (semantic similarity > 0.92) and latencies within threshold.
- Artifact integrity: verify sha256 checksum and detached signature returned by control plane.
- End-to-end dry-run: simulate manifest application in staging agent and validate telemetry evidence creation.

Owners and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments - model-distribution squad (oncall roster: PD-ModelDist).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre - edge-ops squad.
- Escalation path: oncall -> PD-ModelDist senior -> Edge-ops staff engineer -> Applied ML lead.

Related pages and references

- Edge gateway and airgapped bridge architecture (see network bridging assumptions).
- Private deploy operator handbook (for operator commands and ACLs).

Change log

- 2026-01-20: Initial published draft.
- 2026-02-10: Clarified rollback timing and added smoke-test acceptance criteria.

Appendix: Sample delta download retry policy (pseudocode)

- retries = 8, backoff = exponential(base=5s, max=300s), use HTTP range requests, verify checksum after complete stream.

Contact

- Document author: Ava Martinez (ava@redwood.example.com).
- For urgent operational issues: PD-ModelDist oncall via the standard paging channel."

payload.page_title: Regional proxy fabric and data-path segmentation reference

sections.body:
Overview

This page describes the Regional Proxy Fabric and Data-Path Segmentation reference architecture for Redwood Private deployments. It is intended for operators, platform engineers, and customer field teams who are implementing VPC or on-prem private installs that require strong tenant isolation, controlled egress, and resilient fallbacks to hosted services.

Goals

- Provide a network and service topology that isolates tenant data flows while minimizing blast radius for failures.
- Support controlled egress and 'data ejection' patterns for model refreshes, telemetry, and optional hosted fallbacks.
- Enable safe upgrades and quick rollback with minimal customer impact.
- Define measurable SLOs, observability signals, and day-2 operational runbooks.

Scope and applicability
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Private VPC deployments (cloud-hosted customer VPC peering / transit scenarios).
- On-premise/private datacenter installs where a local control plane or sidecar control connectivity is used.
It does NOT attempt to replace tenant-level RBAC or customer-specific compliance rules; rather, it prescribes a network and service pattern that integrates with customer controls.

Terminology

- rwdn-proxy-fabric: Ensemble of proxy nodes (L7) that route inference requests to local runtime clusters or to hosted fallbacks.
- rwdn-edge-agent: Lightweight operator-managed agent on tenant subnets responsible for KV cache invalidation, telemetry batching, and health checks.
- data-ejection: The controlled transfer of specific telemetry or model artifacts to Redwood-hosted sinks under customer-approved contracts.
- surgical-fallback: Traffic-level switch to a hosted model variant when local resources are degraded.

High-level architecture (text diagram)

Customer VPC / On-prem Network --> [rwdn-edge-agent] --> [rwdn-proxy-fabric (regional)] --> {Local runtime cluster | Hosted fallback} --> Observability & KMS

Key components and responsibilities

1) rwdn-proxy-fabric (regional)
- Stateful L7 proxies (recommended: 3+ nodes per AZ/zone) that perform:
  - Tenant-aware routing (based on tenant-id header / mTLS SAN).
  - Per-tenant rate limiting and fairness policies.
  - Local prefix/KV cache routing decisions (TTL: configurable).
  - Egress gating: policy engine decides whether to allow data-ejection or to block external sinks.
- Failure modes: when a proxy loses connectivity to runtime, it signals a degraded state and applies surgical-fallback rules.

2) rwdn-edge-agent
- Deploy as a DaemonSet (Kubernetes) or systemd-managed service (bare metal).
- Responsibilities: health heartbeat to regional control plane, local sampling for telemetry, ephemeral credential management for KMS-bound operations.
- Security: enforce kernel-level network policies (iptables/update) to prevent direct egress from tenant subnets unless approved.

3) Control Plane (regional/tenant-aware)
- Policy service holds per-tenant routing rules, fallback thresholds, and egress allow-lists.
- KMS broker handles ephemeral session keys for model artifact access and data-ejection.

Security and compliance controls

- Mutual TLS (mTLS) for all inter-service traffic. Certificate issuance via customer PKI (recommended) or Redwood-managed short-lived certs per deployment.
- KMS integration: support for AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, GCP KMS, and on-prem HSM. Documented key rotation cadence: rotate master wrapping keys every 90 days, session keys every 24 hours.
- Egress allow-listing and ejection approval: any data-ejection flow requires an on-file approval form (see related_pages).

SLOs and thresholds (recommended defaults)

| Metric | Target | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Regional rwdn-proxy p95 latency | < 120 ms | measured at ingress-to-forwarding decision |
| Successful tenant requests (availability) | >= 99.95% | counted over 30d windows |
| Time-to-surgical-fallback | < 10 s | time from degraded signal to traffic steering |
| KV cache hit-rate (inference prefix) | >= 70% | workload dependent |

Operational patterns: surgical-fallback and ejection

Surgical-fallback intent: when local runtime cluster capacity or health drops below configurable thresholds, the proxy fabric will shift a tenant’s traffic to a hosted-compatible model variant that respects privacy constraints. Fallback must:
- Preserve tenant headers and do not forward any raw customer-provided PII to unapproved external sinks.
- Use model variants that have been vetted for token-level privacy equivalence (customer agreement required).
sections.heading: This architecture applies to

sections.body:
- Allowed only if customer has signed ejection agreement.
- Ejection flows are routed through a dedicated egress node that applies DLP-style filters, scrubbers, and audit stamping.
- All ejection transfers logged and provenanced to support compliance audits.

Configuration / example snippets

1) Example proxy routing rule (YAML-style snippet)
proxyRules:
  - tenantId: "acme-corp"
    routePriority: 10
    runtimeCandidates: ["local-cluster-01","local-cluster-02"]
    fallback: {type: "hosted-compat", modelTag: "redwood-compat-v2", allowedEgress: false}
    rateLimit: {requestsPerSecond: 50}

2) Edge agent systemd unit (excerpt)
[Unit]
Description=Redwood Edge Agent
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/rwdn-edge-agent --control-plane=cp.region.example.internal --agent-id=%H
Restart=on-failure

Testing, validation and acceptance criteria
sections.heading: Data-ejection policy pattern

sections.body:
1) Network path verification: verify that the customer VPC routing maps tenant subnets to the edge agent subnets and that egress is gated by proxy IPs. Use: `curl -sS --resolve proxy.region.customer:443:10.0.1.5 https://proxy.region.customer/health`
2) KMS handshake: confirm that the control plane can decrypt a test-wrapped token.
3) Cert provisioning: ensure mTLS certs are present and that SAN / tenant mapping is correct.
sections.heading: Pre-installation checks (operator-run)

sections.body:
1) Deploy synthetic workload (per-tenant): 10 TPS for 10 minutes, validate 2xx success >= 99% and p95 latency < 150ms.
2) Validate surgical-fallback: deliberately saturate local runtime to trigger fallback and measure time-to-fallback < target.
3) Ejection test (if enabled): attempt small telemetry ejection and confirm audit log entry and checksum match.

Upgrade and rollback guidance
sections.heading: Smoke validation (post-install)

sections.body:
- Prefer blue/green or canary operator model for rwdn-proxy-fabric and rwdn-edge-agent.
- Always capture snapshots of policy state and KV-cache manifests before changes.
- Maintain a validated fallback path so rollback can be executed without requiring code reversion of hosted components.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1) Create a policy snapshot: `rwdnctl policy snapshot --out policies-YYYYMMDD.json`
2) Deploy canary proxies to a single AZ (10% of traffic weight) and run synthetic workload for 20 minutes.
3) Monitor SLOs and error budgets; if errors exceed threshold (>= 1% elevated 5xx), abort and rollback.
4) If canary is healthy, ramp to 50% and then to 100% over 2h with health gates at each step.
sections.heading: Standard upgrade procedure (summary)

sections.body:
1) Run `rwdnctl routes promote --from previous-proxies --to all-zones` to rebind traffic immediately.
2) If control plane state is inconsistent, restore policy snapshot: `rwdnctl policy restore --from policies-YYYYMMDD.json`.
3) Open an emergency incident (see escalation below) if KV-cache mismatches or tenant-level errors persist for > 15m.

Day-2 operations checklist

Daily
- Verify proxy health: all proxies with lastHeartbeat < 60s flagged.
- Check ejection audit log for any unapproved transfers.

Weekly
- Rotate ephemeral session keys (automated) and verify KMS rotation logs.
- Review policy drift: diff control-plane snapshot with live rules.

On-call runbook (short)

1) Symptom: elevated p99 latency for a tenant.
  - Step 1: check rwdn-proxy-fabric metrics for 5xx spikes and CPU/connection queue length.
  - Step 2: if proxies healthy, inspect local runtime node health; scale up runtime replicas or evict problematic models.
  - Step 3: if runtime is degraded and cannot recover in 5 minutes, trigger surgical-fallback for affected tenant: `rwdnctl fallback trigger --tenant acme-corp --mode hosted-compat`.

2) Symptom: accidental egress to disallowed host.
  - Step 1: disable egress node via control-plane console.
  - Step 2: capture packet-level evidence (pcap) and forward to security with audit id.
  - Step 3: notify customer and follow restricted-incident-response checklist.

Acceptance checklist for customer handoff (table)

| Item | Operator verification | Customer sign-off required? |
|---|---|---:|
| mTLS certs issued and verified | `openssl s_client -connect proxy:443` returns valid SAN | Yes |
| Egress allow-list configured | Control-plane policy shows egress entries | Yes |
| KMS integration tested | Roundtrip encrypt/decrypt test passed | Yes |
| Surgical-fallback validated | Measured fallback time < 10s | No (operator provides evidence) |

Related pages and artifacts

- /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deliverables-and-day2-operational-contracts-2026 (hand-off template)
- /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/private-deploy-acceptance-and-smoke-validation-2026 (acceptance tests)
- /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/airgap-packaging-and-day2-hardening-2026 (packaging considerations)

Ownership and escalation

- Architecture owner: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
- Field operations lead: Rahul Singh (eng-private-deployments)
- Security escalation: Lena Ortiz (security)

Appendix: quick-check automation scripts

1) Canary health check example (bash)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for i in {1..20}; do
  status=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://proxy.region.customer/readiness)
  if [[ "$status" == "200" ]]; then
    echo "proxy ready"; exit 0
  fi
  sleep 6
done
echo "proxy not ready"; exit 1

2) Policy snapshot command examples
- `rwdnctl policy snapshot --out /tmp/policies-$(date +%F).json`
- `rwdnctl policy diff --since /tmp/policies-YYYYMMDD.json`

Document change log

- 2025-10-12: Created by Maya Chen (initial architecture and tests).
- 2026-02-15: Added upgrade/rollback fast-path and expanded day-2 checklist (reviewers: Arjun Patel, Lena Ortiz, Rahul Singh).

End of document

payload.page_title: Immutable quantized fanout & operator evacuation architecture

sections.body:
Summary:
This document describes an immutable, operator-driven reference architecture for private (VPC/on-prem) deployments that: (1) hosts quantized model variants, (2) performs controlled fanout to heterogenous GPU pools, and (3) includes an operator evacuation/escape-hatch pattern for rapid rollback or tenant quarantine. The pattern prioritizes reproducible artifacts, minimal runtime drift, and forensic-friendly rollback for regulated customers.

Goals and scope:
- Provide a repeatable topology for customers that need low-latency fanout across heterogeneous accelerators while preserving the ability to safely evacuate traffic and forensically preserve evidence.
- Include deployment packaging constraints, day-2 operator runbook items, upgrade & rollback steps, and a customer readiness checklist.
- Target platforms: VPC-hosted private control plane and fully air-gapped on-prem installs. This reference covers operator-driven, Kubernetes-based deployments with optional lightweight edge gateways.

High-level architecture overview:
- Immutable operator: an operator (redwood-operator) reconciles desired state from signed artifacts. Operators do not modify in-place model binaries — they reference immutable model artifact tags (SHA256) and image digests.
- Quantized model bundles: model artifact bundle contains model weights (quantized formats: int8/4bit) + metadata manifest (architecture version, quantization profile, compatible kernel list).
- Fanout fabric: request routing uses a local routing fabric that supports tiered fallback: local GPU pool -> regional GPU pool -> CPU-safe quantized variant. Routing decisions are policy-driven and annotated in the operator custom resource (CR).
- Evacuation/escape hatch: an operator-run evacuation job that: (a) atomically flips routing policy to safe-mode, (b) snapshots KV cache and in-flight sessions, (c) seals artifacts for forensic export.

Components and ownership:
- redwood-operator (owner: ops/runtime) — reconciles tenants, model bundles, routing CRs, and evacuation jobs.
- runtime-pool (owner: infra/serving-runtime) — per-pool daemonset/statefulset serving quantized bundles.
- routing-proxy (owner: infra/networking) — local gRPC/HTTP proxy that implements policy routing & backpressure.
- telemetry-gateway (owner: observability) — aggregates traces, token-level cost, and sampling for forensic snapshots.

SLOs and operational targets (recommended):
- Availability: 99.95% per-tenant for dedicated pools (business SLA maps to this).
- Latency SLOs: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 250ms for typical 128-token responses on A100/RTX models with quantization profile Q4.
- Evacuation window: operator can place tenant into safe-mode within 30s of triggering evacuation job; full KV snapshot completed within 5 minutes for typical tenant sizes.

Hardware and network requirements (table):
| Component | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---:|---:|
| GPU type | 1x A10 / T4 equivalent per 4 vcores | A100 / H100 families for high throughput |
| GPU memory | 24 GB | 40+ GB per GPU for large models |
| Node CPU | 8 vCPU | 32 vCPU |
| Node disk | 100GB | 500GB NVMe local cache |
| NIC | 1 Gbps | 25 Gbps RDMA for cross-rack fanout |
| Control plane bandwidth | N/A | 100 Mbps stable to customer control plane 

Packaging & artifact requirements (on-prem constraints):
- All images and model bundles must be signed (cosign) and versioned by digest. Operator requires a signed bundle manifest: {artifact_sha256, quant_profile, compat_kernels}.
- Offline airgap: provide an artifact bundle tarball with: OCI images (gzipped tar), model bundles, operator helm chart, and a verification manifest.
- Image layout: use immutable tags (digest-only in CRs). No floating tags permitted for production private-deploys.

Routing & fanout policy examples (CR snippets expressed as text):
1) Priority-based fanout:
- primary_pool: local-gpu-pool
- fallback_pools: [regional-gpu-pool, cpu-quant-safe]
- latency_target_ms: 200

2) Cost-aware fanout (billing-tier annotation):
- prefer_pool_when: {unit_cost_per_token < 0.0008}
- throttle_on_cost_delta: 2x expected

Day-2 operator runbook (quick actions):
1) Verify operator health:
- kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=redwood-operator
- Expected: 1/1 READY, restart_count < 3 in 24h

2) Trigger evacuation (safe-mode) for tenant "acme-tenant":
1. redwoodctl tenant safe-mode --tenant acme-tenant --reason "suspected data leak"
2. Operator flips routing CR to safe-mode and returns a job id: evac-20260118-42
3. Monitor snapshot progress: redwoodctl evac status --id evac-20260118-42
4. If snapshot fails, run diagnostic dump: redwoodctl evac dump --id evac-20260118-42 --include-kv --timeout 600

3) Rapid rollback of a model bundle (operator recommended):
1. Pin the previous model digest: kubectl patch modelbundle model-xyz --patch '{"spec":{"artifactDigest":"sha256:old"}}' --type=merge
2. Wait for operator to reconcile and for all runtime-pool replicas to report modelVersion=old in /metrics
3. Run health checks: curl -f http://{proxy}/health/tenant/acme-tenant/ready || rollback-operator-alert

Upgrade procedure (immutable-operator approach):
- Principle: staged artifact promotion using immutable digests, canary traffic split, and operator-ensured rollback.
- Pre-upgrade checks:
  - Ensure signed manifest present for new artifacts and documented kernel compatibility in the CR.
  - Run offline validation suite against synthetic load for cold-starts and KV cache seeding.
- Canary rollout steps:
  1. Create a modelbundle CR referencing new artifact digest and set trafficSplit: 5% to canary_pool.
  2. Monitor p50/p95 latency, error-rate, and token-accuracy regression alerts for 2h.
  3. If stable, increase to 25% for 1h, then 50%, then full promotion.
- Failure/rollback criteria:
  - Error-rate > 1% over baseline 15m window
  - Token-level quality regression > configured threshold (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE fall beyond pre-approved delta)
  - Operator automatically flips canary to safe-mode and reverts trafficSplit to previous digest.

Forensic-friendly rollback & evidence preservation:
- On any operator-triggered rollback, operator will: (a) create an evidence bundle (compressed, signed) containing: routing CR snapshot, modelbundle manifests, KV cache snapshot metadata (and optionally sampled keys), and request traces for the prior 30 minutes.
- Evidence retention: default 90 days for regulated tenants; configurable via tenant manifest.

Customer readiness checklist (pre-install to signoff):
1) Network: required outbound control-plane connectivity for signed manifest verification (unless airgapped).
2) Hardware: node + GPU minimums satisfied and local NVMe cache present.
3) Security: KMS integration for image signing; HSM recommended for private-managed customers.
4) Observability: telemetry-gateway endpoints reachable and sampling set to >= 10% request traces for first 72h after onboarding.
5) Runbook acceptance: customer has validated operator evacuation playbook in a rehearsal drill (see "Evacuation rehearsal template" below).

Evacuation rehearsal template (operator exercise):
1. Schedule a 90-minute game day off-peak.
2. Trigger a tenant-safe-mode for a non-production tenant. Verify routing flips within 30s.
3. Validate KV snapshot completes and is exported to a secure bucket.
4. Reconstitute the tenant into a test cluster from the evidence bundle and compare outputs to pre-evacuation baseline.

Monitoring & telemetry policy recommendations:
- Token-level metrics: collect tokens/second, median token latency, and per-route cost.
- Trace sampling: 10% baseline, 100% for canary periods and evacuation windows.
- Alerting thresholds (examples):
  - p95 latency > 2x baseline for 10 minutes -> P1 alert to oncall
  - model mismatch/regression alert (eval harness) -> P1 and automated canary rollback

Known failure modes and mitigations:
- Cold-start latency spikes: mitigate with warmstart pre-warming jobs controlled by operator, and with local NVMe warm caches.
- Incompatible quantization kernels: operator rejects modelbundle if kernel list mismatch; fallback to CPU-safe quantized variant is enabled by default.
- Snapshot failure during evacuation: operator attempts three retries with exponential backoff; if still failing, escalate to field operator for manual snapshot via kubectl exec into runtime-pod.

Operational runbook appendix (commands & examples):
- Inspect modelbundle: kubectl describe modelbundle model-xyz -n redwood
- Force reconcile: kubectl annotate modelbundle model-xyz redwood/reconcile-now=true
- Evacuation status: redwoodctl evac status --id evac-20260118-42 --json

Related pages:
- eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/private-deploy-livetail-and-debugging-runbook-2026
- eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-operator-handshake-and-runtime-guardrails-2026

Ownership & maintenance:
- Doc owner: Aisha Patel (ENG-Platform)
- Operational owner: infra/serving-runtime oncall rotation
- Review cadence: annual or after any breaking operator/runtime change

Appendix: artifact manifest example (text):
{
  "modelName": "redwood-transformer-xl",
  "artifactDigest": "sha256:...",
  "quantProfile": "Q4_ish",
  "compatibleKernels": ["cuda12_cublasLt_v1","trt-optimized-v2"],
  "signedBy": "redwood-signer@redwood.ai",
  "created": "2026-01-12T09:14:00Z"
}

Feedback and improvements:
- Send suggestions or requests for additional playbooks to infra-docs@redwood.ai.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Workplace Ops and Career Entry Toolkit

sections.body:
Summary:

This document is a consolidated toolkit for workplace operations that ties together role entry checklists, tooling access patterns, benefits orientation pointers, and the first-90-day career activation plan for new contributors at Redwood. The goal is to reduce time-to-productivity, codify predictable access provisioning, and provide a single reference for managers and new hires to run onboarding and early-career development in a consistent way.

Scope:
- Applies to all full-time employees, contractors with >3-month engagements, and interns who require system access.
- Excludes short-term vendors on a per-project basis (see vendor-engagement playbook).

Owner and expectations:
- Document owner: Riley Chen (people-ops)
- Operational owners: IT provisioning (eng-infra), Security (security-and-compliance), Hiring panel leads (hiring teams)
- SLA target for access: 95% of standard access bundles provisioned within 2 business days of start_date.

Quick start for managers (1-line action items):
1. Submit New Joiner form (People Portal) 10 business days before start.
2. Accept role-specific orientation packet and assign buddy.
3. Verify access bundle within 24 hours of orientation start.

Detailed sections

1) Onboarding flow (high level)

1. Pre-boarding (T-10 to T-1 days)
   - Manager completes New Joiner form and selects: role_band, team_template, hardware_pref (laptop/desktop), and remote_onboarding flag.
   - People-ops schedules orientation, issues welcome email and benefits primer.
   - IT kickstarts provisioning for standard bundles (see Access Matrix).

2. Day 0–7 (orientation and access verification)
   - Welcome session (People Ops): company values, benefits overview, org map.
   - Role-specific kickoff: product/engineering deep-dive, immediate deliverables.
   - Verify tool access and MFA. Run confirmation script in Section 5.

3. Weeks 2–4 (ramp and feedback)
   - Assign 30-day success goals.
   - Weekly 1:1 cadence established; first 30-day mentor check.
   - Run initial learning path modules in LMS (learning-management system).

4. Months 2–3 (career activation)
   - Establish measurable milestones for 60/90 days.
   - Perform 60-day manager check and 90-day review calibration.

2) Standard access bundles and SLA table

Bundle name | Typical recipients | Included systems | SLA (target provisioning)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Core Contributor | All employees and long-term contractors | SSO, email, VPN, Slack, HR portal | 2 business days
Engineering Starter | Engineers (ICs) | GitHub org, CI pipeline read, dev cluster access (staging) | 3 business days
Product & Design Starter | PMs, Designers | Product boards, analytics read, Figma org | 3 business days
Customer-Facing Bundle | CS & Sales | CRM, Zendesk, customer logs (redacted) | 2 business days
Privileged Admin | Named ops/security admins | KMS consoles, audit logs, production runbooks | 5 business days + approval

Notes:
- SLA clock starts when People-ops submits provisioning request to IT through the People Portal.
- Privileged Admin requires manager and security approval; expect manual review.

3) Access matrix (guideline table)

Role | Minimum bundle | Optional additions | Typical approver
--------------------------------------------------------------
New Engineer (IC L1-L3) | Core Contributor + Engineering Starter | Dedicated GPU lab access (if chosen), dedicated Slack channel | Team Lead
Senior Engineer (L4+) | Core Contributor + Engineering Starter + CI write | Prod monitoring access (read), release rotator role | Engineering Manager
Product Manager | Core Contributor + Product & Design Starter | Feature-flag dashboard write | Product Director
Customer Success Rep | Core Contributor + Customer-Facing Bundle | Customer production logs (read) | CS Manager
Security/IR | Privileged Admin | SIEM, KMS view | Security Lead

How to request changes:
- Use People Portal -> Access Requests -> Select bundle and justify. For bundle customizations add a short justification and list of owners.

4) Role and career ladder primer (summary)

This section provides orientation-level clarity for new joiners on how role progression is structured across engineering and product. The full competency maps live in the roles directory (linked in Related Pages).

- Bands: IC1–IC5 for engineers; PM1–PM4 for product; IC bands align to expectation matrices around: scope, technical/business impact, mentorship, and autonomy.
- Promotion cadence: Typical window is 12–18 months between-level, dependent on demonstrated impact and competency evidence.
- Promotion materials: manager-written promotion packet (impact write-up, peer feedback, selected work samples), competency matrix filled out, and calibration meeting.

5) Verification checklist and quick CLI sanity commands

Run this checklist with the new hire during Day 1 access verification:
- Can login via SSO and read onboarding intranet page.
- MFA enabled and confirmed.
- Slack access to team channels and #announcements.
- GitHub login, ability to view assigned repos.
- Access to CI pipeline read (if applicable).

Sample SSH/CLI checks (run from a terminal):
- Check VPN connectivity: curl -I https://intranet.redwood.internal/health || report to infra-support@redwood.ai
- GitHub check: gh auth status && gh repo view redwood/core || open a ticket
- CI view test: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" https://ci.redwood.ai/api/v1/projects | jq '.projects[0].name'

6) First-90 roadmap template (for managers to assign)

Week 1–2: Orientation and low-risk tasks
- Accept reading list: architecture overview, security basics, console tour.
- Deliverable: merge small docs or a noop PR to learn the workflow.

Week 3–6: Deeper integration and ownership
- Pair on a feature, own a small bugfix or internal improvement.
- Deliverable: own a ticket end-to-end and demo outcome.

Week 7–12: Impact and calibration
- Drive a measurable improvement (latency, cost, or a user metric) or ship a minor feature.
- 90-day review: manager collects feedback from peers and measures against initial goals.

7) Hiring & interview panel operational checklist

Before interviews:
1. Recruiter confirms job spec and hiring rubric with hiring manager.
2. Schedule panel with cross-functional representation (engineer, product, hiring manager).
3. Panel members accept rubric and scoring guidelines.

During interviews:
1. Use standard rubric and timebox each section.
2. Collect scorecards in the candidate folder.
3. Panel convenes within 48 hours to make decision and agree on feedback.

After offer:
1. People-ops issues offer and coordinates start date.
2. Manager initiates New Joiner form and hardware provisioning.

8) Benefits orientation highlights (concise)

- Enrollment window: first 30 days for base medical, dental, vision selections.
- Time off: flexible PTO policy; manager-approved leaves in HR portal.
- Parental leave: standard policy + phased return options (see detailed policy page).

9) Escalations and critical contacts

- People-ops escalation: people-ops@redwood.ai (primary), escalation channel #people-ops-urgent
- IT provisioning: infra-provisioning@redwood.ai (SLA tracked), oncall infra phone 1-800-555-IRUN
- Security approvals: sec-approvals@redwood.ai (manual review for privileged access)

10) Maintenance and change control

- Owners must review this doc every 6 months.
- For changes that affect SLAs or security posture, notify security and eng-infra and allow 7 days for stakeholder review.

Appendix A — Example access request justification (template)
- Requestor: [Name]
- Justification: Access needed to debug customer-reported issue #1234; needs read access to production logs for triage.
- Duration: 14 days (auto-expire)
- Approver: [Manager name]

Appendix B — FAQ
Q: Who assigns a buddy?
A: The hiring manager assigns the buddy before Day 1; people-ops can assist if not assigned.

Q: What if hardware is delayed?
A: Open a ticket with infra-provisioning and request a temporary loaner device; remote reimbursement options are available.

Change log:
- 2026-03-01: Initial published version.
- 2026-10-12: Updated SLA and added verification CLI snippets.
- 2027-01-15: Reformatted access bundles and clarified promotion packet requirements.

Related links:
- Roles directory: /confluence/company-handbook/02_roles-and-career/
- Benefits policies: /confluence/company-handbook/03_benefits-and-perks/
- IT runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/

Contact for feedback: riley.chen@redwood.ai
