payload.page_title: Service Telemetry & Supply-chain Compatibility Matrix for Private Deploys

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines a combined telemetry contract and hardware/software compatibility matrix that field engineers, SREs, and customer integration teams use to validate private (VPC and on-prem) Redwood deployments. The goal is to unify observability acceptance criteria, supply-chain hardware compatibility, and operational guardrails so private deploys meet product SLAs and regulatory requirements while minimizing day-2 surprises.

Scope

- Applies to: Redwood Private control-plane + runtime, customer-managed VPC branches, and on-prem appliance installs.
- Includes: telemetry schemas, retention and sampling contracts; required agent/collector versions; supported NICs, GPUs, firmware baselines; upgrade/rollback safety gates; post-install verification steps.
- Excludes: application-level prompts and customer data policies (see compliance-evidence pages).

Why this matters

- Inconsistent telemetry and unexpected firmware on GPUs or NICs are root causes for 45% of private-deploy incident escalations in 2025.
- A single compatibility matrix reduces ambiguous requirements during procurement and shortens field lead time by ~30%.

Telemetry contract (service-level)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Mandatory metrics (all must be emitted to the local collector within 60s of boot): runtime.request.latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), runtime.request.errors.count, runtime.kvcache.hits, runtime.kvcache.misses, gpu.utilization_pct, host.cpu_load_1m.
- Minimum span traces: request.received -> model.load -> token.stream -> response.sent. Span duration must include attributes: tenant_id, model_version, shard_id.
- Log levels: service logs must support structured JSON logs with keys: ts, level, svc, msg, trace_id, request_id.
- Sampling & retention: default trace sampling 5%; high-error routes sample 100% for up to 24 hours. Metric retention: 90 days at 1m resolution, 400 days at 1h resolution for customer-managed long-term retention packages.

Collector/agent versions and configuration

- Required collector: redwood-agent >= 2.4.0 (bundled with private-runtime image 2026.01+).
- Supported exporters: OTLP (gRPC), Prometheus remote_write (optionally to customer-prometheus).
- Example OTLP config snippet (YAML):

```yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
      http: {}
processors:
  batch: {}
exporters:
  otlp/remote:
    endpoint: "collector.redwood.local:4317"
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [otlp/remote]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [prometheus, otlp/remote]
```

Compatibility matrix (hardware, firmware, drivers)

This simplified table is the canonical acceptance matrix. Customers must provide inventory with exact SKUs and firmware versions. Any deviation must be flagged to Redwood Professional Services prior to cutover.

| Component | Supported SKU / family | Min firmware / driver | Notes / known issues |
|---|---|---:|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA A100 (PCIe) | GPU firmware 55.XX, NVIDIA driver 525.85+ | PCIe variants require IOMMU workarounds if host BIOS < 2022.6 |
| GPU | NVIDIA H100 SXM | GPU firmware 65.XX, NVIDIA driver 530.30+ | H100 requires UEFI secure boot off for current image (planner: 2026.2 runtime patch) |
| NIC | Mellanox ConnectX-6 | FW 18.30+, OFED 5.6+ | RoCE requires DSCP/Priority map on branch switch |
| Disk | NVMe Samsung PM1733 | FW 3B2QCX0 | Ensure SMART TL margin set to 5% for endurance class C |
| BMC/UEFI | Supermicro X12 series | UEFI 4.1+, BMC 3.2+ | BMC must have remote syslog enabled for warranty telemetry capture |

Acceptance thresholds and tests

Field acceptance consists of the following checks (performed after base install and before tenant handover):
1) Inventory verification: checksum manifest comparing reported device-ids/firmware vs. inventory CSV.
2) Telemetry smoke: emit a full request trace across 1, 10, 100 token loads; verify p95 < 200ms for local L2 model variants and p95 < 400ms for pinned remote variants.
3) KV cache validation: synthetic workload generates 10k prefix requests, expected cache hit ratio >= 0.72.
4) Telemetry completeness: 100% of requests produce a trace_id and logs within 60s; metrics visible in Prometheus and retained for 1 minute at 10s scrape interval.
5) Stress burn-in: 4-hour soak at 60% of projected steady-state QPS with incremental GPU temperature and telemetry sampling checks.

Automated acceptance playbook (CLI)

Run the built-in acceptance script (operator privileges required):

```bash
sections.heading: Summary requirements

sections.body: ./tools/acceptance/run-field-acceptance.sh \--inventory inventory.csv \--collector-endpoint 10.0.1.5:4317 \--soak-duration 14400
sections.heading: from operator host with SSH access to primary controller

sections.body:
```

Acceptance report schema (flattened JSON fields in output file)
- report_id (string)
- cluster_id (string)
- operator (string)
- pass_fail (string: pass|fail)
- p95_latency_ms (string)
- kvcache_hit_ratio (string)
- missing_telemetry_keys (string, comma-separated)
- incompatible_hardware (string, comma-separated SKUs)
- remediation_action (string)

Day-2 operations: telemetry-first runbook

This runbook complements existing day-2 ops docs by focusing on telemetry-driven troubleshooting.
sections.heading: output: acceptance-report-<date>.json

sections.body:
- runtime.request.errors.rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> P1 alert to oncall.
- gpu.utilization_pct > 98% for > 10m and queue-size growth -> action: scale-burst policy.
- telemetry.ingest.lag > 120s -> investigate network egress to collector.
sections.heading: Alerting thresholds (recommended)

sections.body:
1) Confirm agent health: `systemctl status redwood-agent` and `redwood-agentctl status`.
2) Check local metrics: `curl localhost:9100/metrics | grep runtime_request` for recent values.
3) Trace fetch: `otel-cli fetch --trace_id <id> --endpoint http://localhost:4318/v1/traces` to retrieve span chain.
4) If missing traces, check firewall rules (TCP 4317 and 4318) and MTU mismatch with NIC vendor drivers.

Upgrade & rollback safety gates for private deployments

Upgrade preflight checks (must pass before any coordinated upgrade):
- Inventory parity check (as above)
- Telemetry integrity: no missing mandatory keys in last 24 hours.
- Sufficient capacity: free GPU headroom >= 20% or validated burst policy.
- Upgrade window: customer-approved maintenance window and snapshot backup (if required by customer A/R policy).
sections.heading: Investigation steps (short)

sections.body:
1) Canary subset: 5% of tenants routed to new runtime image and collector config.
2) 60-minute monitoring window: key metrics (p95 latency, error rate, kvcache hit ratio) compared to baseline using rolling 10m windows.
3) Automatic rollback triggers: p95 increases > 20% OR error rate increase > 0.3% sustained for 5 minutes OR consumer error types matching model-compatibility signature.
sections.heading: Automated canary flow (recommended)

sections.body:
1) Trigger: Canary failed OR manual decision.
2) Execute: `k8s-rollback --deployment runtime --image <previous> --tenants all` (or use operator handoff for on-prem appliances).
3) Post-rollback verification: run telemetry smoke test and assert previous baselines restored.
4) Incident postmortem: attach acceptance-report and telemetry snapshots to the ticket.

Customer requirements library excerpts (inventory template)

Provide customers with the following CSV columns in advance of any private deployment engagement. Operators should reject manifests missing required fields.
sections.heading: Rollback procedure (operator steps)

sections.body:
- host_id
- mac_address
- sku
- serial_number
- gpu_type
- gpu_fw_version
- nic_model
- nic_fw_version
- bmc_fw_version
- uefi_version
- nvme_fw
- os_image_tag
sections.heading: Required CSV columns

sections.body:
- rack_position
- switch_port
- oncall_contact
sections.heading: Optional but recommended columns

sections.body:
host_id,mac_address,sku,serial_number,gpu_type,gpu_fw_version,nic_model,nic_fw_version,bmc_fw_version,uefi_version,nvme_fw,os_image_tag
redwood-node-001,00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e,SM-X12-2xA100,SN1234,H100,65.12,ConnectX-6,18.40,3.2,4.2,3B2QCX0,private-2026.01

Compliance & supply-chain notes

- Procurement: prefer vendors that provide signed firmware images and reproducible checksums. Record vendor-signed manifests in the deployment ticket.
- Evidence preservation: when a hardware incompatibility is detected during acceptance, capture a signed evidence blob (base64 of dmi + fw versions) and attach to the ticket for audit.

Appendix: troubleshooting matrix (common failure modes)

- Symptom: Missing traces only for large requests (> 10k tokens)
  - Likely cause: collector OOM or trace export batching misconfiguration
  - Action: increase collector memory to +2GB, lower batch export size to 200 events, re-run acceptance smoke.

- Symptom: High GPU temperatures during soak
  - Likely cause: incorrect thermal profile or chassis intake flow reversed
  - Action: confirm chassis airflow, apply OEM thermal firmware patch, re-run soak.

Ownership and contacts

- Document owner: Priya Nambiar (eng-private-deployments)
- Oncall for telemetry engineering: telemetry-sre@redwood.ai
- Professional Services pre-sales: ps-deploys@redwood.ai

Related pages and artifacts

- Field acceptance tool: repo `infra/field-ops/acceptance`
- Post-install telemetry checklist: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/post-installation-telemetry-and-acceptance-checklist-2026
- Hardware compatibility canonical list (internal): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/private-deploy-field-compatibility-matrix-2026

Change log

- 2025-11-04: Created initial draft for internal review (Priya N.).
- 2026-02-18: Updated GPU/NIC driver minimums and added automated acceptance CLI.

If you have questions or need a tailored compatibility review for an upcoming procurement, tag the page and request a field review with `@ps-deploys`.

payload.page_title: Tenant Telemetry Consent and Redaction Playbook for Private Deploys

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook defines the consent model, telemetry categories, mandatory redaction/minimization pipeline, and operator runbooks for tenant telemetry in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on‑prem variants). It is intended for field operators, customer success, and security stakeholders responsible for evidence artifacts required by regulated customers.

Applicability

- Applies to all private deployments managed by Redwood (VPC-private and on‑prem packages).
- Scope: runtime telemetry (service metrics, request traces, model metadata), operational telemetry (container metrics, host telemetry), and optional diagnostic dumps (heap, core, model weights metadata).
- Does NOT apply to customer application payloads that are explicitly forwarded through service proxies; those are covered by the customer data contract and separate redaction templates.

Telemetry Categories and Examples

1) Essential operational telemetry (always-on, low-cardinality)
   - Examples: instance_cpu_pct, gpu_util_pct, disk_iops_95, process_up
   - Purpose: SLO monitoring, alerting, capacity planning

2) Request-level telemetry (controlled sample rate / hashed identifiers)
   - Examples: request_latency_ms, tokens_generated, model_variant, route_name
   - Note: fields that could be PII/PHI must be redacted or hashed.

3) Diagnostic payloads (customer opt-in)
   - Examples: full request/response payloads, model KV cache snapshots, internal debug stacks
   - Must be opt-in and time-limited; stored in restricted buckets with customer approval.

Consent Model and Customer Controls

- Default mode: minimal telemetry (category 1 + aggregated request-level metrics with strict hashing and no payloads).
- Optional modes (customer selects during onboarding):
  1) "diagnostic-opt-in" (retains full request/response for T days)
  2) "enhanced-sampling" (higher sample rate for request-level metrics only)
  3) "no-external-telemetry" (local-only telemetry; no telemetry leaves VPC except for aggregated SLO telemetry if contract allows)

- Consent artifacts: a customer must sign the Telemetry Consent Form (template in Appendix) and specify: retention_days, sample_rate, redaction_profile_id. This metadata is stored in the deployment manifest under /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json and is surfaced in the control-plane UI.

Data Redaction & Minimization Pipeline

Overview:
1) Ingest filter (node-level): rejects known high-sensitivity fields before serialization.
2) Redaction transform (service-level): applies JSON path redactors, regex scrubbers, and structured PII detectors.
3) Hashing/Tokenization (metric-level): deterministic hashing of tenant identifiers using HMAC-SHA256 with tenant-specific key (rotated per policy).
4) Sink selector: routes telemetry to correct storage class (aggregated metrics store, restricted object store, local-only storage).

Redaction Profiles:
- profile-basic: remove keys named ["password", "ssn", "credit_card", "medical_record"], mask 80% of long strings, remove attachments > 128KB
- profile-strict: profile-basic + remove any field matching regex patterns for emails, phone numbers, and base64 blobs
- profile-none (diagnostic-opt-in only): no redaction beyond size caps

Sample redaction table (in prose):
- Field: request.user.name -> Action: drop
- Field: request.user.email -> Action: redact local-part, keep domain (e.g., xxxxx@company.com)
- Field: request.prompt -> Action: truncate to first 512 characters, then apply NER PII scrubber

Operator Runbook: Toggle, Audit, and Emergency Redaction

1) Verify consent manifest
   - Command: sudo cat /etc/redwood/telemetry/consent.json\   - Expected: valid JSON with keys: tenant_id, profile_id, retention_days, sample_rate, approved_by
\2) Switch deployment to 'local-only' for a tenant (example, safe mode for regulatory hold)\   - Steps:
     a) In the control plane: open tenant config -> Telemetry -> select 'no-external-telemetry' -> apply
     b) CLI fallback: redwoodctl tenant update --id <TENANT> --telemetry-mode local-only
     c) Validate: curl -sS http://localhost:9100/telemetry/status?tenant=<TENANT> | jq '.mode' should return "local-only"

3) Enforce emergency redaction for a window
   - Purpose: immediate purge or redaction when a customer requests removal for an incident
   - Steps (operator):
     1) Create a redaction job: redwoodctl telemetry redact --tenant <TENANT> --pattern "/request/payload" --mode truncate --reason "DSAR" --until 2026-07-01
     2) Monitor job: redwoodctl telemetry jobs get --id <JOB_ID>
     3) Generate evidence bundle: redwoodctl telemetry jobs export --id <JOB_ID> --output /tmp/evidence-<TENANT>.tar.gz

4) Audit logs and evidence retention
   - All toggle and redaction operations must be logged to the restricted audit log (immutable) with fields: operator_id, action, tenant_id, timestamp, justification_id.

Acceptance Tests & Evidence Requirements

Before handoff to customer, run the following checks and attach evidence to the onboarding package:

- Acceptance checklist (automated):
  1) consent.json present and schema-valid
  2) sample_rate applied (verify by synthetic trace generator with 1K requests)
  3) redaction profile enforced (submit synthetic PII and assert it is removed)
  4) local-only mode test (if requested)

- Evidence bundle contents:
  - consent.json (signed copy)
  - telemetry-config.yaml at deploy time
  - sample sanitized trace (redacted)
  - audit log entries showing operator approval

Upgrade & Rollback Considerations

- Upgrades that change redaction behavior must be treated as a migration: any profile changes require (A) migration script that reprocesses retained diagnostic payloads or (B) documented customer opt-in to reprocessing.
- Backward compatibility: new profiles must include a compatibility mapping and a migration tool: redwoodctl telemetry migrate-profiles --from old-id --to new-id --dry-run
- Rollback CPs: If a control-plane upgrade introduces a bug that lifts redaction rules, initiate emergency rollback and run the emergency redaction steps above. Preserve an evidence bundle that shows the rollback window and actions taken.

SLOs and Monitoring

- Telemetry integrity SLO: 99.9% of agent heartbeats per minute.
- Redaction correctness target: 100% synthetic-PII detection in test harness within 24 hours of deployment.
- Audit latency: toggles and redaction jobs appear in immutable audit log within 10s.

Operator Playbook Examples (Appendix)

Example consent.json (stored on node):
{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
  "profile_id": "profile-strict",
  "retention_days": 30,
  "sample_rate": 0.01,
  "approved_by": "legal@customer.com"
}

Sample CLI snippets:
- Switch to diagnostic opt-in for troubleshooting:
  redwoodctl tenant update --id tenant-1234 --telemetry-mode diagnostic-opt-in --retention 7 --profile profile-none

- Start a redaction job and monitor:
  JOB=$(redwoodctl telemetry redact --tenant tenant-1234 --pattern '/request/payload' --mode truncate --reason 'DSAR')
  redwoodctl telemetry jobs get --id $JOB

- Validate redaction locally (operator):
  curl -sS http://localhost:9101/debug/last-redacted?tenant=tenant-1234 | jq '.'

Owner & Contacts

- Document owner: Security (Asha Patel) – ascs@redwood.ai
- Oncall (telemetry-sre): pager: #telemetry-oncall (Slack) and schedule in the SRE rota
- Legal and Compliance: Maya Chen (reviewer)

Change History

- 2026-01-12: Created (Asha Patel)
- 2026-03-02: Added emergency redaction procedure (Ethan Brooks)
- 2026-06-15: Clarified profile mapping and added CLI validation steps (Maya Chen)

Appendix: Templates and Quick Reference

- Telemetry Consent Template (to be attached to onboarding package)
- Redaction profile mapping matrix (CSV)
- Synthetic PII test harness: runs 10K synthetic requests to validate redaction profile at sandbox rate

If you need an executable checklist or migration scripts, open a ticket to infra-sre with the tag "telemetry-redaction" and include tenant_id and deployment_id.

payload.page_title: Field Deployment: Capacity, Security and Hardware Readiness Profile

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a field-ready deployment readiness profile for Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) customers. It collects concrete, testable "minimum" and "recommended" requirements across compute, storage, network, security integrations (KMS, HSM), and telemetry so field engineers, SREs, and customer success can validate a site prior to handoff. The checklist is intended for pre-installation validation, acceptance tests during initial install, and as a reference for upgrades and hardware replacements.

Goals

- Provide a single checklist that is actionable for on-site engineers and customer IT teams.
- Reduce rework during field installs by surfacing incompatibilities early (firmware, drivers, MTU, BGP templates).
- Define measurable acceptance tests (commands, thresholds, and telemetry signals).

Scope
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Bare metal and VM hosts used for Redwood inference nodes (CUDA/GPU and CPU-only pools).
- Network topology and vendor-neutral routing and firewall expectations.
- Storage sizing and performance targets for model artifacts, KV- and prefix-caching, and local scratch.
- Key management and certificate/profile expectations for KMS integration, certificate rotation, and HSM requirements.
- Telemetry, logging and alert endpoints required for post-install monitoring and capacity planning.

Not in scope: detailed playbooks for product-specific upgrades (those live in upgrade-and-rollback).

Minimum hardware profile (pass/fail for initial acceptance)

| Component | Minimum | Recommended | Acceptance Criteria | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| GPU node SKU | 1 x A10 / A16 or equivalent (16GB) | 2 x A100 40GB (recommended for production inference) | GPUs visible via nvidia-smi, driver satsified (see driver section) | For small test clusters only; production should use >= 2x A100 or equivalent NVML capacity |
| CPU-only node | 16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM | 48 vCPU, 256 GB RAM | lscpu shows cores, top/htop stable under load | CPU nodes used for control plane, queuing, metrics ingestion |
| Local storage | 500 GB NVMe (persistent) | 2 TB NVMe (RAID1 if necessary) | fio random-read 128k: p95 latency <= 2 ms at sustained 300 MB/s | Fast local NVMe for model weights and KV cache |
| Network | 1 Gbps management + 10 Gbps service NICs | Dual 25 Gbps with SR-IOV | iperf3 throughput within 10% advertised; MTU 9000 when using jumbo frames | Ensure low jitter for p95 token latency |
| Control-plane nodes | 3 nodes, 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM | 3 nodes, 8 vCPU, 64 GB RAM | API handshake success <100ms on internal network | HA quorum required |
| KMS/HSM | Accessible KMS endpoint over TLS; service account with encrypt/decrypt keys | HSM or cloud KMS with dedicated HSM slot | Key wrap/unwrap tested; certificate chain validates | See KMS section for policies |

Driver, kernel and OS expectations

- Supported OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (preferred), RHEL 8.6+ (supported).
- Kernel: 5.15+ for Ubuntu 22.04; RHEL with tuned kernel errata applied.
- NVIDIA driver: 535.x or later for Ampere support. Verify with: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,name --format=csv
- CUDA: 11.8+ where GPU nodes are required.
- Container runtime: containerd 1.6+ or Docker 20.10+ (containerd preferred).
- Recommended sysctl adjustments:
  - net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1
  - vm.swappiness=10
  - fs.file-max >= 524288
- Hugepages: not strictly required, but document whether enabled; if enabled, confirm setup with: cat /proc/meminfo | grep HugePages

Network architecture and configuration patterns

- Topology: Separate networks for management, data plane (inference), and telemetry. Where possible, dedicate a NIC per plane.
- MTU: Preferred 9000 for data plane. Validate: ip link set dev <iface> mtu 9000; ip link show <iface> | grep mtu
- Routing: BGP is preferred for multi-rack failover. Provide the BGP template we use (example below).
- Firewall: Allow ports: 443 (control plane), 9090 (metrics pipeline), 50051 (gRPC between runtime nodes), 6379 (redis if deployed), 22 (SSH for field eng). Restrict to known management CIDRs.

Example BGP config template (customer to fill local-AS / neighbor):

router bgp CUSTOMER_AS
  neighbor REDWOOD_PEER remote-as 65021
  neighbor REDWOOD_PEER description "Redwood control plane"
  network 10.0.0.0/24

Storage topology and tuning

- Local NVMe used for model artifacts and KV cache; networked object store (S3 compatible) required for long-term model storage.
- Recommended filesystem: ext4 with noatime for local NVMe; mount options: noatime,nodiratime,barrier=1.
- Example fio workload for acceptance: fio --name=nvme-read --rw=randread --bs=128k --size=10G --numjobs=4 --runtime=60 --time_based --group_reporting
- Acceptance thresholds: p95 read latency <= 2ms; sustained throughput >= 300 MB/s per NVMe under load.

KMS and secrets integration

- Redwood requires an endpoint for envelope encryption. Supported KMS: AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS, or on-prem HSM with PKCS#11.
- Policy: Redwood will perform envelope encryption; customer must provide a key with encrypt/decrypt and generateDataKey permissions.
- Acceptance steps:
  1) Confirm network egress and TLS to KMS endpoint: curl -v https://kms.example.com/health
  2) Key wrap test: use provided test harness to perform GenerateDataKey / Encrypt / Decrypt cycle.
  3) Observe key rotation window and provide rotation schedule to Redwood.

Telemetry and observability requirements

- Required endpoints:
  - Metrics (Prometheus pull) on port 9090 (internal and optionally scraped by Redwood aggregator).
  - Traces (OTLP/OTel) via HTTP/GRPC to configured collector.
  - Logs: central logging (syslog/rsyslog -> collector) or Filebeat shipping to aggregator.
- Sampling and retention: initial pilot should send 1x traffic at full QPS to validate volume.
- Minimum labels and tags required on metrics: cluster_id, rack_id, node_role, gpu_model, tenant_id.
- Example prometheus scrape config snippet:
  - job_name: 'redwood-nodes'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['10.1.2.3:9090']

Operational acceptance tests (run during handoff)

1. Node inventory verification (pass/fail)
   - Run: inventory.sh --summary (provided in field-tools). Expected: GPUs, NICs, NVMe devices listed match customer manifest.
2. Network baseline test
   - Run iperf3 between two service NICs for 60s at expected MTU. Pass if throughput >=90% of link rate and packet loss <0.1%.
3. Storage performance test
   - Run fio workload above. Pass if p95 latency and throughput meet thresholds.
4. KMS handshake and key wrap test
   - Run sample key operations. Pass if round-trip completes and wrapped keys decrypt.
5. Control plane API validation
   - curl --cacert <ca.pem> https://control-plane.internal/v1/health -> expect 200 OK and JSON {"status":"ok"} within 500ms.
6. Inference smoke test
   - Deploy a canary model and send 100 concurrent small requests (<=64 tokens). Pass if p95 token latency < 250ms, error rate < 1%.

Procedures for common field issues

- Driver mismatch (GPU nodes fail to register):
  1) Collect: dmesg, nvidia-smi, kubectl describe node (if k8s).
  2) Action: Reinstall driver matching supported list; reboot host.
  3) If persistent, revert to known-good driver image provided in releases archive.
- High storage latency discovered after install:
  1) Confirm thermal throttling on NVMe (smartctl).
  2) Check IO scheduler and filesystem mount options.
  3) If hardware faulty, replace NVMe and rehydrate from object store.
- KMS connectivity intermittent:
  1) Validate TLS chain and proxy settings.
  2) Temporarily switch to offline key (pre-wrapped key in secure vault) per emergency policy. Notify security owner.

Ownership and contact matrix

- Field install lead: Customer Escalations (owner: customer-success).
- SRE escalation: eng-sre@redwood.example.com.
- KMS/security: security@redwood.example.com.
- Telecom/networking questions: infra-networking@redwood.example.com.

Rollout constraints and capacity planning guidance

- Minimum cluster size for production inference (p95 token latency SLAs): 4 GPU nodes with autoscale headroom of 50% for bursty traffic.
- Recommended headroom policy: configure autoscaler to maintain 20% idle GPU capacity for cold-start sensitive workloads.
- If using mixed-GPU types, validate model quantization fallback is enabled to allow CPU fallback for critical traffic.

Acceptance signoff artifact checklist

- Completed inventory sheet (CSV) with serial numbers and firmware versions.
- FIO and iperf3 run logs attached.
- KMS test logs and key IDs used for envelope test.
- Canary inference run logs (latency and error rates).
- Prometheus target list and sample metrics (30 minutes of data).
- Handoff email with runbook and emergency contact list.

Appendix: quick commands and scripts

- Verify GPUs: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,driver_version --format=csv
- Basic NVMe check: lsblk -d -o name,rota,model,size; smartctl -a /dev/nvme0n1
- Iperf3 example: iperf3 -c 10.1.2.4 -t 60 -P 8 -f m
- Fio example: fio --name=nvme-read --rw=randread --bs=128k --size=10G --numjobs=4 --runtime=60 --time_based

Revision history

- 2026-01-12: Draft created by Ava Martinez.
- 2026-02-10: Reviewed and validated with field team; added KMS acceptance steps and updated GPU driver version.

If you find discrepancies between this profile and customer manifest, escalate to eng-private-deployments triage with full inventory and test logs attached.

payload.page_title: Third-Party KMS & HSM Integration Requirements for Private Deployments

sections.body: This document defines Redwood Inference's minimum integration requirements, validation checklist, operational controls, and rollback procedures for third-party Key Management Systems (KMS) and Hardware Security Modules (HSM) used with Private deployments (VPC and on‑prem). It is intended for field engineers, SREs, and customers planning to bring their own key infrastructure or integrate a cloud KMS/HSM service.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Purpose: Ensure secure, auditable, and supportable key material management across private deployments while meeting regulatory constraints.
- Scope: Applies to any private deployment (VPC-hosted or on‑prem appliance) where customer-managed encryption keys are used for model artifacts, persistent KV caches, telemetry encryption, or secrets in the control plane. Excludes transient in-memory keys used only within process lifetimes.
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
- Protect customer keys with FIPS 140-2/3 validated HSM or cloud KMS equivalents.
- Provide deterministic, testable integration steps that SRE and field teams can execute during onboarding.
- Define day‑2 operational guardrails (rotation, revocation, incident response) and safe rollback paths.
sections.heading: Key objectives

sections.body:
| Area | Minimum requirement | Rationale | Evidence for acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|
| KMS/HSM validation | FIPS 140-2 Level 2+ or cloud-managed equivalent (Azure Key Vault, AWS KMS, GCP KMS with CMEK) | Regulatory and integrity assurances | Certificate or attestation document; test provenance file |
| Key wrapping and envelope encryption | Support AES-256-GCM or AES-256-GCM-SIV with asymmetric key wrapping (RSA-OAEP or ECDH) | Prevent plaintext key leakage in storage and backups | Sample wrap/unwrap logs and successful cryptographic unit test |
| Remote attestation | Support for remote attestation (where available) for on‑prem HSMs | Ensure firmware/trustworthiness of HSMs | Attestation report and verification steps |
| API compatibility | REST/gRPC with documented auth (mTLS or signed requests) and idempotent key operations | Operational reliability and automatable flows | Completed API smoke tests and example clients |
| Key lifecycle controls | Programmatic rotate, revoke, disable, and staged rollout with rollback window | Reduce blast radius and enable safe rotation | Rotation playbook runbook and automated test artifacts |
| Audit logging | Immutable audit trail exportable to SIEM with timestamps, actor, and operation | For compliance and incident forensics | Exported log sample and retention config |
| Latency and availability | 99.95% availability for KMS path and <50 ms median wrap/unwrap in region (hosted) | Prevents inference latency regressions | Synthetic latency tests and SLA statement |
| Network and trust boundary | TLS 1.3, mTLS for HSM control channel, IP allowlist for management plane | Network-level defense in depth | Network policy manifests and firewall rules |
sections.heading: Requirements matrix (summary)

sections.body:
1) Cloud KMS as CMEK (preferred for cloud VPC private deploys)
   - Use KMS to protect a locally generated data encryption key (DEK). Store the wrapped DEK in the deployment secret store.
   - Example: Generate DEK on the host, call KMS: Encrypt(DEK) -> store wrapped key.

2) HSM-backed key store (preferred for high compliance or on‑prem air‑gapped sites)
   - Keys never leave the HSM. Perform wrap/unwrap and asymmetric ops inside the HSM.
   - Use an HSM client that supports local caching of public material but not private key export.

3) Hybrid (HSM for master key, soft-DEKs for operational performance)
   - Master keys in HSM; DEKs generated locally and wrapped by HSM. Use a cache TTL and enable secure rotation.
sections.heading: Integration patterns (recommended)

sections.body:
- Management plane (control signals for wrap/unwrap/rotate): must be restricted to operator CIDR ranges and require mTLS client certs.
- Runtime nodes performing wrapping should authenticate with per-node mTLS certs or short-lived workload tokens (OIDC-based).
- Minimum IAM roles and privileges principle-of-least-privilege: separate roles for encryption, decryption, and key administration.
sections.heading: Network and IAM constraints

sections.body:
- Rotation frequency: default 90 days for DEKs; 1–3 years for master keys depending on compliance requirements.
- Staged rotation steps:
  1. Create new key version in KMS/HSM (do not enable immediately).
  2. Deploy runtime code supporting dual-key unwrap for a transition window.
  3. Generate new DEKs and rewrap artifacts incrementally.
  4. Monitor error rates and rollback if >1% increase in crypto errors across nodes within 30 minutes.
  5. Enable new key as primary, deprecate old key after retention window and proof of rewrap completion.
- Emergency revocation: Revoke master key -> system should immediately fail closed for any operations requiring the master key; field engineers to follow the Emergency Key Revocation runbook (Steps below).

Validation and onboarding checklist (pre-install, install, post-install):
sections.heading: Key rotation and emergency revocation policy

sections.body:
- Confirm KMS/HSM certification level and provide attestation.
- Exchange mTLS client certs and bootstrap root CA fingerprints.
- Agree on network ACLs, IP allowlists, and ports (TLS 1.3 only).
- Verify key naming conventions and rotation windows.
sections.heading: Pre-install (customer and field)

sections.body:
1. Confirm connectivity: curl -v --cert client.pem --key client.key https://kms.example.internal/healthz
2. Perform wrap/unwrap smoke test: generate local DEK, call Encrypt/Decrypt, verify plaintext equals original.
3. Check audit flush: request last 200 audit events and validate operation fields.
4. Run synthetic latency test (1000 ops) and assert median <50ms.
sections.heading: Install (operator)

sections.body:
- Run resilience tests: simulate KMS outage and confirm application fallback policy (cache usage) keeps critical operations for configured TTL, then observe graceful degradation.
- Confirm rotation process using canary tenants: rotate keys for a small tenant and validate end-to-end decryption.
- Provide onboarding report with evidence artifacts to security and customer success.
sections.heading: Post-install (validation)

sections.body:
- Monitoring: track wrap/unwrap rate, error rate, median latency, and audit log export success. Alerts:
  - P1: unwrap error rate >0.5% sustained 5 min -> Pager to oncall (SRE and field lead)
  - P1: Audit log export failure for 10 min -> Pager
  - P2: median unwrap latency >150ms for 5 min -> Slack alert to infra channel
- Capacity planning: for high-throughput inference workloads, use DEK caching with strict TTL and an LRU cache size tuned to node memory. Document recommended defaults in runtime config: cache_ttl=300s, cache_max_items=1000.
- Regular exercises: quarterly rotation drills and annual attestation re‑validation.
sections.heading: Day-2 operations and monitoring guidance

sections.body:
1. If a new key introduces unrecoverable errors, immediately mark the new key version as disabled in KMS/HSM.
2. Force all nodes to use previous wrapped DEKs from backup manifest.
3. If key compromise suspected: rotate master key in HSM, run full rewrap for persisted artifacts, and notify legal/compliance per incident policy.
4. Record and export full audit trail before any destructive actions; preserve evidence for forensic analysis.
sections.heading: Rollback and emergency procedures (short checklist)

sections.body:
- Wrap/unwrap with AWS KMS (example using AWS CLI):
  - Encrypt (wrap DEK): aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/redwood-master --plaintext fileb://dek.bin --output text --query CiphertextBlob > dek.wrapped
  - Decrypt (unwrap): aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://dek.wrapped --output text --query Plaintext | base64 --decode > dek.bin
- HSM client sample (pseudo):
  - hsm-client gen-key --label=\"rdw-master-v1\" --usage=wrap
  - hsm-client wrap --key=rdw-master-v1 --in=dek.bin --out=dek.wrapped
sections.heading: Example operational commands and snippets

sections.body:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments (field engineering) team — contact: field-eng-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Secondary owner: Security Engineering — contact: security-oncall@redwood.example.com
- SLA: KMS control-plane availability 99.95%; customer-specific SLAs to be reflected in the deployment contract addendum.
sections.heading: Operational ownership and SLAs

sections.body:
- KMS/HSM attestation and certs (PDF)
- API smoke test logs and latency reports
- Audit export sample covering onboarding actions
- Rotation acceptance test runbook outputs and canary results
sections.heading: Documentation and evidence to collect for sign-off

sections.body:
- Recommended configuration snippet (runtime config YAML example):
  runtime_crypto:
    key_provider: \"kms\"
    provider_endpoint: \"https://kms.example.internal\"
    mTLS_client_cert: \"/etc/redwood/client.pem\"
    wrap_algorithm: \"AES-256-GCM\"
    cache_ttl_seconds: \"300\"

- Related internal pages: see Related Pages metadata at top.
sections.heading: References and appendices

sections.body:
- Field engineering lead: Diego Ramos (diego@redwood.example.com)
- Security oncall: security-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Cust Success onboarding: onboarding@redwood.example.com
sections.heading: Contacts and escalation ladder

sections.body:
- 2025-11-15: Created (Aisha Moore)
- 2026-02-10: Expanded validation checklist and added latency SLO guidance (Aisha Moore)
sections.heading: Revision history

sections.body:
- Customers must provide required attestation documents and accept a short maintenance window for initial full rewrap if migrating legacy encrypted assets.
- Where customers cannot provide HSM attestation, field engineering may accept compensating controls (e.g., tamper-evident enclosures and enhanced logging) on a case-by-case basis with Security approval.

payload.page_title: Customer peer networking failover & RTT requirements (edge-to-control)

sections.body:
Summary:

This document defines minimal and recommended peer-networking and failover requirements for Redwood private deployments (VPC-connected and on-prem edge sites) with a focus on round-trip time (RTT), failover behavior, and measurable telemetry needed for acceptance and ongoing SLA compliance. It is intended for operators, field engineers, and customer networking teams responsible for connecting customer networks to Redwood control planes and runtime endpoints.

Scope and audience:

- Scope: connectivity between customer tenant endpoints (edge or on-prem runtime) and Redwood control plane / model-serving endpoints used for model routing, telemetry ingestion, and control messages.
- Audience: field ops, SRE, onboarding engineers, customer network architects, solutions engineers.

Goals:

1. Provide deterministic thresholds for RTT, jitter, and packet loss for different workload classes (latency-sensitive, throughput-oriented, telemetry).
2. Define failover behavior and expected time-to-recover (TTR) for common failure modes (link, BGP flap, VPN tunnel outage, regional control-plane failover).
3. Specify test and acceptance procedures (commands, expected outputs) used during onboarding and periodic validation.
4. List telemetry signals and alerting thresholds needed by Redwood to detect customer-visible regressions.

Definitions and workload classes:

- Latency-sensitive: interactive chat/assistant inference where tail token latency impacts UX. Typical traffic: small requests, streaming responses.
- Throughput-oriented: batch embeddings / reranking jobs tolerant of higher per-request latency but sensitive to sustained bandwidth.
- Control/telemetry: heartbeat, KV state replication, health-check streams; low bandwidth but strict delivery expectations for correctness.

Minimal baseline network requirements (acceptance):

| Metric                   | Latency-sensitive SLA | Throughput SLA       | Notes |
|-------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------|-------|
| RTT (p95)               | <= 45 ms              | <= 150 ms            | Measured edge -> control-plane region; p99 targets in notes. |
| Packet loss (1m avg)    | < 0.5%                | < 1.0%               | Loss above triggers immediate investigation. |
| Inter-packet jitter (p95)| < 8 ms               | < 20 ms              | Burst jitter tolerated for short windows. |
| Bandwidth (sustained)   | 50 Mbps per 1000 concurrent users | 1 Gbps for heavy batch nodes | Size to be adjusted by customer scale. |
| MTU                     | >= 1400 bytes         | >= 1400 bytes        | Path MTU discovery must succeed. |
| Symmetric NAT           | Unsupported for certain control-plane auth modes | See VPN note | Use NAT traversal only for non-privileged setups. |
| BGP/Route convergence   | < 60 seconds (planned maintenance) | < 120 seconds | Route flaps degrade token streaming; limits enforced. |

Recommended / aspirational targets (for premium customers):

- RTT p99 <= 80 ms for latency-sensitive workloads.
- Packet loss (5m moving average) < 0.2%.
- Jitter p99 < 12 ms.
- Redundant control-plane paths with < 3s failover for TCP-based streaming (when using dedicated interconnect + BFD).

Failover modes and expected behavior:

1) VPN tunnel outage (customer-managed IPSec):
   - Expected detection: Redwood control plane sees TCP connection reset and missing keepalives within 30s.
   - Customer expectation: re-establish or switch to backup tunnel within 60s for degraded but functional service; full restore within 180s.
   - Operator steps: (a) Verify tunnels via "show crypto ipsec sa" (vendor CLI) or equivalent; (b) verify BGP adjacency; (c) switch traffic via secondary route if primary fails.

2) BGP route flap or next-hop loss:
   - Expected detection: control-plane routing table changes observed; traffic shifts to secondary path. Redwood tolerates transient flaps < 30s.
   - TTR expectation: under normal config with BFD enabled, < 3s; without BFD, < 60s.

3) Regional control-plane failover (Redwood side):
   - Behavior: automatic routing to next-closest verified region/model variant. Customers should expect temporary increases in RTT consistent with regional hop differences and potential model variant fallbacks as per agreement.
   - Communication: automatic incident note + email and console banner.

Acceptance test checklist (onboarding):

1. Baseline measurements (edge host placed in scheduled test harness):
   - Run: ping -i 0.2 -c 100 <control-plane-ip> and record p50/p95/p99.
   - Run: iperf3 -c <control-plane> -t 60 -P 10 to validate sustained throughput.
   - Run: mtr -z --report <control-plane> for 120 probes to capture hop jitter patterns.

2. Packet loss simulation: use tc/netem on edge host to inject 1% loss for 60s and verify degraded connection detection and failover. Expected: control plane flags loss and opens fallback route.

3. BGP failover exercise: withdraw primary route from customer router; measure convergence and route re-announce time. Expected: BFD-enabled convergence < 3s; otherwise < 60s.

4. VPN failover test: bring down primary tunnel and validate traffic flow through secondary. Expected: application-level streaming resumes within 60-180s depending on tunnel ramp.

Operator runbook (quick steps):

1. Verify reachability:
   - ping -c 10 <control-plane>
   - tcpdump -i <iface> host <control-plane> and verify SYN/ACK flows
2. Check BGP state:
   - show ip bgp summary | grep <peer>
3. Check tunnel state (IPSec example):
   - show crypto isakmp sa
   - show crypto ipsec sa | include <peer-ip>
4. If failover not automatic: manually update route to point to backup next-hop and notify Redwood success channel.

Config example (YAML config fragment used by field agent to declare network requirements to Redwood):

---
agent_network_profile:
  name: "customer-edge-nyc-01"
  expected_rtt_ms_p95: 45
  expected_packet_loss_pct: 0.5
  preferred_transport: "ipsec" # alternatives: "bgp-direct", "aws-interconnect"
  bfd_enabled: true
  mtu: 1500
  redundancy:
    vpn_peers: ["10.10.0.1","10.10.0.2"]
    bgp_primary: "10.0.0.1"
---

(This fragment is used by the onboarding operator to generate the expected acceptance checks and to configure telemetry collection fields on Redwood side.)

Telemetry signals and alerting thresholds (what Redwood needs from customer or must be observable):

- RTT histogram (1s buckets) edge -> control-plane; alert if p95 > configured threshold for 5m.
- Packet loss percentage per 1m; alert if > configured threshold for 3m.
- TCP retransmits and zero-window events; alert if spikes > baseline by 3x for 2m.
- BGP adjacency flaps and number of route withdrawals; alert if > 3 withdraws in 10 minutes.
- Tunnel uptime percentage (daily); alert if < 99.5% for production-class tenants.

Acceptance gate PvRs (pre-deployment acceptance):

- Gate A (connectivity baseline): All baseline tests pass and agent_network_profile fields are populated.
- Gate B (failover validation): VPN and BGP failover scenarios executed and documented in on-call runbook.
- Gate C (telemetry): Continuous telemetry stream validated for 24 hours with no critical alerts.

Escalation and rollback guidance:

- If a failover test causes application regressions that cannot be mitigated via route failover, rollback to staged maintenance window: disable new routes and revert to known-good topology.
- Communication templates (short):
  - Subject: [ACTION REQUIRED] Network failover caused degraded inference latency for tenant <TENANT>.
  - Body: Summary of timeline, measured p95/p99 before and after, current mitigation, next steps.

Ownership and contacts:

- Onboarding owner: Field Onboarding Team (owner: Diego Morales)
- Network escalation: SRE-Networking (oncall)
- Customer contact: Solutions Engineer assigned during onboarding

Appendix A — Measurements & sample command outputs:

- Sample ping output snippet (p95 ~ 32ms):

64 bytes from 34.120.10.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=44 time=31.7 ms
--- 34.120.10.8 ping statistics ---
100 packets transmitted, 100 received, 0% packet loss, time 99123ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 31.569/33.102/45.786/2.311 ms

- Sample iperf3:

[SUM]   0.00-60.00 sec  1.02 GBytes   146 Mbits/sec  sender

Appendix B — Frequently encountered pitfalls and mitigations:

- Asymmetric routing: Causes failed TLS handshakes and unexpected packet loss. Mitigate by ensuring symmetric routing for control-plane subnets or by enabling TCP MTU blackhole detection and path MTU discovery.
- Deep packet inspection (DPI) appliances: May drop long-lived TLS streams; recommend bypass or apply permissive policies for control-plane IPs.
- Misconfigured NAT timeouts: Long-lived streaming sessions may be reset; set NAT keepalive intervals < 60s or use BFD and TCP keepalives.

References:

- Private deploy onboarding checklist (internal): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/customer-onboarding-deployment-readiness-and-risk-checklist-2026
- BFD for fast failover (vendor docs): https://example.vendor/bfd-guide

Change log:

- 2026-01-12 — Created by Aisha Patel (initial baseline and acceptance tests).
- 2026-03-05 — Added BFD guidance and tightened RTT targets for premium class.
- 2026-06-07 — Updated runbook commands and clarified telemetry thresholds.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Deployment Conformance Crosswalk and Checklist

sections.body:
Overview

This document provides a cross-functional conformance crosswalk and operational checklist for Redwood Private Deployments that maps common regulatory and customer data-classification requirements to specific deployment controls, packaging expectations, VPC design constraints, day-2 operational practices, and upgrade/rollback guardrails. Use this page during pre-sales technical validation, onboarding acceptance tests, and quarterly compliance reviews.

Scope

- Applies to: VPC-based private deployments, air-gapped on-prem packages, and hybrid control-plane deployments delivered to customers.
- Not covered: hosted API tenant operations, internal SRE-only playbooks (see eng-sre runbooks).

Audience

- Solutions Engineers, Field Engineering, Private Deployments PMs, Security & Compliance, Customer Ops.

How to use this doc

1. Select the customer's regulatory/data profile from the left column of the Conformance Matrix.
2. Apply the mapped controls and validate with the acceptance checklist at the end of this doc.
3. Capture evidence artifacts (audit logs, signed image digests, KMS policy snippets) and link into the customer folder.

Conformance Matrix (high level)

| Requirement / Profile | Network & VPC Controls | Data-at-rest | KMS & Key Management | Runtime Packaging | Day-2 Ops & Telemetry | Upgrade/Rollback Constraint | Acceptance Artifact Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low-sensitivity (internal dev) | Isolated VPC, optional public egress | AES-256 on disk | Redwood-managed key optional | Standard container image | Default telemetry on | Rolling upgrade allowed | Image digest, smoke test logs |
| Regulated PII (EU) | Private subnets, no public egress, egress via customer proxy | Encryption with customer-managed keys | Customer KMS recommended (Cloud KMS/HSM) | Signed images, attestation required | Telemetry sampling limit; PII redaction | Canary first; manual approval for global rollout | KMS policy, attestation report, telemetry config |
| HIPAA / PHI | VPC with strict ACLs, no third-party egress, dedicated subnet for inference | Customer KMS + HSM-backed keys | HSM-backed keys, rotation cadence defined | Air-gapped packaging option | Minimal telemetry; S3-level access logs only | Blue/green with automatic data-plane rollback | Signed SBOM, attestation, access logs |
| Classified / Highly Restricted | On-prem with FIPS-validated components, isolated build & deploy pipeline | FIPS-validated encryption, no external key exchange | HSM + internal KMS with strict split access | Ephemeral boot images, measured boot, attestation | No telemetry off-box; local observability only | Manual, documented upgrade window; rollback appendix required | Firmware attestation, measured boot report |
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- The rows map common profiles to minimal controls; customer-specific contracts may impose stronger controls.
- For hybrid control-plane deployments, apply control-plane telemetry except where restricted by contract.

Detailed Controls (selected fields)

1) Network & VPC controls

- VPC design must include: dedicated management subnet, tenant inference subnet, and optional shared services subnet.
- Mandatory NSG / ACLs: allow only ports 443 (control plane TLS), 2202 (optional SSH bastion restricted by allowlist), 50051 (gRPC internal), and custom health ports described in service manifest.
- Egress: either blocked or routed through customer-managed proxy/inspection appliance. No direct internet egress for regulated workloads.
- BGP / Cross-region failover: maintain pairwise BGP sessions with route targets documented in network runbook.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
control_plane_sg:
  - proto: tcp
    port: 443
    src: customer_mgmt_cidr
bastion_sg:
  - proto: tcp
    port: 2202
    src: operator_allowlist
inference_sg:
  - proto: tcp
    port: 50051
    src: control_plane_sg
```

2) Data-at-rest and Key Management

- Storage must be encrypted with AES-256 at minimum. For regulated profiles use customer-managed keys (CMKs) in cloud KMS or HSM.
- Key rotation cadence: default 90 days; for PHI/HIPAA recommend 30–60 days depending on contract.
- KMS access control: require separation of duties — CI/CD service accounts must not have unilateral key create/delete permissions.
sections.heading: Minimal security group rules (YAML snippet)

sections.body:
- CMK present and validated
- Key rotation policy documented
- Key usage logging enabled and exported to customer audit store

3) Packaging & Image Signing

- All images shipped for private deployments must be signed with our supply-chain signing keys and produce an SBOM. For air-gapped environments produce an offline signed bundle and provide verification steps.
- Image digest must be provided to customer in onboarding artifact.
- Reproducible builds: include exact build recipe and OS package list.
sections.heading: KMS policy checklist

sections.body:
- [ ] Image signed by Redwood CI signature
- [ ] SBOM included (CycloneDX or SPDX)
- [ ] Offline bundle includes signed tarball + verification script

4) Telemetry and Observability

- Default telemetry includes: health pings, model inference latency histograms, error rates, and token counts. For restricted deployments, provide a minimal local-only observability bundle.
- Telemetry must support filtering/sampling at customer request and remove PII at source.
sections.heading: Packaging checklist

sections.body:
- Full (hosted): metrics + traces + logs to Redwood observability (default)
- Filtered (private): metrics to customer endpoint only; traces retained locally
- Local-only (restricted): file-based logs and on-host metrics; periodic collection by ops under customer agreement

5) Day-2 Operations (operational runbook highlights)

- Routine checks (daily): pod health, KV cache hit-rate, GPU utilization, node disk pressure.
- Weekly: snapshot KV caches, verify KMS access logs, run full smoke test via customer API gateway.
- Incident escalation path: SRE on-call -> Private Deployments on-call -> Customer NOC; include runbook link and escalation matrix.
sections.heading: Telemetry options matrix

sections.body:
1. Capacity pressure (GPU contention):
   a. Evaluate batch targets and throttle non-critical routes
   b. Temporarily scale dedicated pool if autoscale enabled
   c. If scale fails, enact model-fallback policy (route to quantized variant)
2. KV cache corruption detected:
   a. Drain traffic from affected replicas
   b. Restore latest consistent snapshot from object store
   c. Reprime caches with warmup traffic using safe prompts
3. Telemetry spike with error rates >5% sustained for 10 minutes:
   a. Switch to degraded model variant
   b. Open incident and run guided debug checklist

Upgrade & Rollback Guidance
sections.heading: Key day-2 playbook entries

sections.body:
- Minimize data-plane exposure during upgrades. Prefer canary or blue/green when stateful components are involved.
- Automate preflight checks; require manual approval for production if new packaging changes (e.g., kernel, firmware, FIPS components) are included.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1. Preflight (automated):
   - Validate image signature and SBOM
   - Run integration smoke tests in staging that mirror customer routing (rate-limited)
   - Run KV cache migration dry-run (no write)
2. Canary deployment (1–5% traffic):
   - Monitor latency and error SLO (latency P99 <= baseline + 15% and error rate < 1%) for minimum 30 minutes
3. Gradual rollout (25%, 50%, 100%) with automated health gates
sections.heading: Recommended workflow

sections.body:
- P99 latency degradation > 50% for 10m AND CPU/GPU saturating beyond expected profile
- Error rate > 5% sustained for 10m on canary group
- Data plane inconsistency (KV mismatch, stateful restore failures)
sections.heading: Rollback triggers (examples)

sections.body:
1. Pause traffic to rolling set
2. Re-deploy previous signed image(s) and rehydrate caches from last successful snapshot
3. Run acceptance smoke tests tied to customer API (see Acceptance Checklist)
4. If rollback fails, escalate to engineering incident + customer war room and enact warm standby (route to hosted/dedicated fallback)

Acceptance Checklist (pre-delivery & post-upgrade)

- Identity & Access
  - [ ] Admin user provisioning completed and tested
  - [ ] Operator allowlist configured for SSH/bastion
- Network & Egress
  - [ ] Private subnets created and verified
  - [ ] Egress path validated (proxy inspection / no direct internet)
- Cryptography & Keys
  - [ ] CMK present (or HSM) and policy attached
  - [ ] Key rotation schedule agreed and documented
- Packaging & Supply Chain
  - [ ] Image digest provided & signature validated by customer
  - [ ] SBOM and build recipe delivered
- Observability
  - [ ] Telemetry mode and sampling configured per contract
  - [ ] Audit logging exported and verified
- Functional Acceptance
  - [ ] Latency P95/P99 and error SLOs validated under capped load (see Test Plan below)
  - [ ] KV cache priming validated and persistence verified

Test Plan (minimal smoke load)

- Run 10-minute capped load at 10 RPS with mixed prompt sizes (short/medium/long). Validate:
  - P95 latency within contract SLA (document SLA value in delivery notes)
  - Error rate < 0.5%
  - Token accounting matches expected limits

Evidence artifacts to collect and hand to customer

- Signed image digest and SBOM (file, path)
- KMS policy snippet and rotation proof (screenshot or policy JSON)
- Attestation report for offline bundle (if applicable)
- Telemetry config manifest showing sampling/filters
- Smoke test logs and SLO graphs

Owner and escalation

- Document owner: eng-private-deployments (Priya Shah)
- Delivery owner: Field Engineering lead (assigned per customer)
- On-call: Private Deployments SRE rotation (see eng-sre oncall roster)

Appendices

A. Minimal SLO examples (for acceptance tests)

- Availability: 99.9% (monthly) for dedicated pools; aim for 99.5% for small private installs
- Latency: baseline P95 as observed in staging + 20% allowed during first 24h after rollout
- Error budget: 0.5% monthly for non-critical routes

B. Example rollout command snippets

```
sections.heading: Rollback procedure (stateful focus)

sections.body:
redwoodctl deploy --image=redwood/private-runtime@sha256:<digest> --canary-percent=5 --health-check=/healthz
```

C. Common customer questions (FAQ)

Q: Can we disable all telemetry?
A: Yes, for the most restricted profiles we provide a local-only observability bundle and a documented process for on-site collection under customer control.

Q: Do you provide HSM integrations?
A: Yes; we support Cloud HSM offerings and on-prem HSMs for classified workloads. Integration verification and acceptance tests are part of onboarding.

D. Change log

- 2026-01-10: Created by Priya Shah (initial crosswalk)
- 2026-02-05: Added FIPS and measured boot notes per security review (Lena Fischer)
- 2026-03-02: Expanded acceptance checklist and telemetry matrix (Miguel Ortega)

If you have questions or need this crosswalk adapted to a specific regulation or customer contract, contact eng-private-deployments@redwood.com or open a request in the Private Deployments backlog.

payload.page_title: Concurrent Tenant Quota and Fairness Playbook for Private Deployments

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook describes Redwood's recommended policies, configuration patterns, and operational procedures for enforcing concurrent-tenant quotas and fairness in private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. It focuses on multi-customer sharing of GPU pools, predictable latency for tenant SLAs, cost transparency, and safe escalation paths for quota-related incidents. The guidance applies to both hosted control-plane-managed private deployments and fully air-gapped on-prem bundles.

Scope and intent:
- Prevent noisy-neighbor effects in shared inference pools while preserving utilization.
- Provide a clear mapping from business-level entitlements (committed vCPU/GPU units, burst windows, priority tiers) to runtime enforcement knobs.
- Offer deterministic operational procedures for emergency throttling, quota adjustments, and fairness audits during incidents and capacity changes.

When to use this playbook:
1) Customer requests: shared-GPU private deployment where multiple internal teams or customer tenants run inference workloads on the same cluster.
2) Observed tail latency or token throughput variance correlated with tenant workload spikes.
3) Pre-launch capacity validation for new tenant onboarding to identify fairness violations.

Definitions:
- Tenant: A logical customer (could be an internal business unit or external customer) with an isolated API key and billing account.
- Entitlement: Contractual or configured resource allocation (e.g., 2 reserved GPUs, 10 max concurrent generation requests).
- Soft quota: Dynamic throttling thresholds that can be exceeded briefly by burst policy.
- Hard quota: Enforced reject/fail path when exceeded.
- Fairshare window: Time window used to calculate proportional resource distribution (default: 5 minutes).

Design principles:
- Favor proportional fairshare over strict absolute caps to maximize utilization while bounding worst-case interference.
- Expose transparent metrics and quota usage per tenant to customers where allowed by confidentiality agreements.
- Provide graceful degradation: fall back to lower-cost model variant or lower max tokens before rejecting.
- Separate priority (SLA) from entitlement; priority affects preemption/reservation, entitlement is billing/accounting.

Configuration reference (example YAML snippet for quota controller):

quotaController:
  fairshare_window_seconds: 300  # 5 minutes
  per_tenant:
    default:
      max_concurrent_requests: 8
      max_total_tokens_per_minute: 20000
      soft_burst_multiplier: 2
      hard_reject: true
    enterprise-tier:
      max_concurrent_requests: 32
      max_total_tokens_per_minute: 200000
      soft_burst_multiplier: 3
      hard_reject: false
  eviction_policy:
    - name: low_priority_preempt
      priority_threshold: 20
      actions:
        - reduce_batch_size: 0.5
        - lower_model_variant: amd/quantized-8bit

Notes on fields:
- max_concurrent_requests: concurrency at the inference request level (requests that are currently holding KV-cache slots).
- soft_burst_multiplier: allows short bursts; quota controller will apply backpressure via 429 + Retry-After when sustained.

Monitoring & observability:
Essential metrics (Prometheus names given):
- tenant_quota_utilization{tenant_id} = gauge of usage / entitlement
- tenant_concurrency_active{tenant_id} = number of in-flight requests
- tenant_token_rate{tenant_id} = tokens/sec rolling mean
- quota_controller_rejections_total{tenant_id,reason}
- fairshare_score{tenant_id} = internal calculated fairness factor

Example PromQL alerts:
- High sustained concurrency for tenant:
  sum by (tenant_id) (tenant_concurrency_active) > 0 and avg_over_time(tenant_concurrency_active[10m]) > 0.9 * on(tenant_id) group_left() tenant_entitlement_concurrency
- Quota rejections spike (indicative of misconfigured entitlements):
  increase(quota_controller_rejections_total[5m]) > 10

Operational procedures (step-by-step):
1) Detection: automated alert triggers on quota rejections spike or sustained tail-latency across tenants.
2) Triage: on-call reviews Grafana dashboard: per-tenant concurrency, fairshare_score, model_variant distribution, node GPU load.
3) Fast mitigation (first 15 minutes):
   a) Enable global soft-throttling (reduce default soft_burst_multiplier to 1).
   b) If a single tenant is responsible, apply per-tenant temporary hard cap (e.g., set max_concurrent_requests=2) with a TTL of 30 minutes. Record change in incident channel.
   c) If cluster-wide contention, trigger autoscale (if allowed) or move low-priority pods to reserve pool.
4) Customer communication: Send templated status update to affected tenants with observed metrics, mitigation steps, and ETA for resolution.
5) Root cause & remediation (post-30 minutes):
   a) If a tenant is misbehaving repeatedly, schedule a billing/entitlement review.
   b) Adjust fairshare_window_seconds or reserve capacity for enterprise-tier tenants.
   c) Update runbook with any new thresholds discovered.

Safe rollback and escalation:
- Immediate rollback of quota controller changes: use the controller's versioned configstore. Command example:
  # rollback to previous config version
  rcli quota-config rollback --to-version=v21 --env=prod
- If config rollback fails or controller is unreachable:
  1) Flip global feature-flag to bypass fairshare controller and fall back to absolute per-tenant hard-caps (emergency limit).
  2) If the API gateway shows overload, enable 503-fastfail for non-enterprise tiers for 3 minutes while mitigation runs.

Sample CLI snippets for on-prem appliance (control-plane managed):
- Inspect current per-tenant usage:
  rcli tenant list-usage --format=table --filter="tenant:acme-corp"
- Apply a temporary hard cap:
  rcli quota set --tenant acme-corp --max-concurrent-requests 4 --ttl 30m --reason "Emergency mitigation"

Fairness audit and monthly reconciliation:
- Run monthly audit job to detect persistent unfairness (script runs nightly and emits a report):
  1) Compute 95th-percentile fairshare_score per tenant for the month.
  2) Flag tenants with score < 0.6 and > 3 incidents for manual review.
  3) Generate CSV for billing and product ops to reconcile entitlements vs usage.

Capacity planning knobs (recommendations):
- Reserve 10% of physical GPU capacity as "headroom" for eviction/burst handling.
- For mixed workloads (short chat vs long-completion), isolate long-token workloads into a dedicated node-pool labeled "long-running" and enforce stricter per-tenant token-rate caps.
- Use multi-queue scheduling: separate small-batch low-latency queue vs large-batch high-throughput queue, and map tenants based on SLAs.

Security, privacy, and compliance considerations:
- Do not expose per-tenant payloads in shared dashboards; only surface aggregated quota and latency metrics unless customer consent exists.
- Store quota change audit logs in the control plane KMS-encrypted audit store (retention 13 months for enterprise customers).

Ownership and escalation matrix:
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments Day-2-ops (owner: Asha Patel)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre on-call (pager rotation)
- Product/billing reviews: customer-success and finance-legal for entitlement disputes

Post-incident analysis checklist:
- Time-series graphs: fairshare_score, per-tenant concurrency, node_gpu_utilization for the incident window.
- Configuration diffs: compare quota controller versions and list any manual per-tenant overrides.
- Customer impact: enumerated tenants affected, duration, tokens lost or rejected.
- Action items: carry-forward changes, timeline for reserved capacity purchase, API changes if necessary.

Appendix A — Example fairshare calculation (simplified):
- For N tenants, each tenant i has entitlement E_i. Compute weight w_i = E_i / sum(E). Over fairshare_window_seconds, allocate capacity proportionally by w_i. If tenant exceeds 2x w_i in any sub-window, apply soft throttle.

Appendix B — Emergency contact templates:
- Slack: "@channel Incident: quota rejections spike. Mitigation: per-tenant caps applied to tenant=acme-corp. Owner: Asha Patel. ETA 30m. See dashboard: <grafana-link>"
- Email: short templated incident summary to customer-facing leads for affected tenants.

Appendix C — Related configuration files and locations:
- /etc/redwood/quota-controller/config.yaml (cluster-local copy)
- s3://redwood-controlplane/backups/quota-configs/ (retention 90 days)

Revision history:
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft and trial runbook (Asha Patel).
- 2025-11-03: Added PromQL alert examples and soft_burst semantics (Liam Chen).
- 2026-02-08: Hardened rollback steps and added per-tenant TTL policy for overrides (Sofia Martinez).

End of document.
```
