payload.page_title: Delegated Access, Change-Gates, and Travel Claims Playbook

sections.body:
Purpose:
This playbook defines the combined end-to-end processes for delegated access requests, change-management gates when requests affect permissions or spend, and the procedure for travel claim submission and adjudication. It is intended to reduce approval latency, maintain strong auditability, and ensure consistent financial controls across regions.

Audience and scope:
- Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and approved vendors.
- Covers role-based access requests, temporary and emergency exceptions, vendor service account provisioning, change reviews with cost impact, and corporate travel & expense claims.

Principles:
- Least privilege: default deny and time-bound privileges.
- Traceable delegation: all approver delegations must be recorded and rotated annually.
- Cost-aware changes: Finance reviews any change that increases monthly committed spend by >=10%.
- Consistent receipts: receipts required for line items > $25 USD; exceptions require manager attestation.

Quick glossary:
- Request Center: internal portal for submitting access, vendor, and expense requests.
- Delegation Registry: canonical list of approver delegations and expiry dates.
- CAB: Change Advisory Board for cross-domain or high-risk changes.

Access request categories and SLAs:
1) Tier A  (Non-sensitive, read-only data): Manager approval -> Automated provisioning. SLA: 48 business hours.
2) Tier B (Production deploy, write, or infra access): Manager + Security review -> Provisioning with audit log. SLA: 5 business days.
3) Tier C (Privileged admin, KMS or crypto operations): Manager + Security + Head of Service -> Multi-factor enrollment and just-in-time (JIT) where possible. SLA: 10 business days.
4) Emergency access for incident response: On-call manager approve -> Security on-call notified -> Grant with strict 8-hour expiry -> Post-incident review within 72 hours.

Delegation and rotation rules:
- Approver delegation may be granted to an explicit alternate (name and email) for up to 12 months. Delegations must be recorded in the Delegation Registry and include a rotation date.
- Delegations older than 12 months automatically expire and generate a renewal reminder to the owner.
- Delegated approvals inherit the same risk posture as primary approver and must complete any required training (security, procurement, or travel policy) prior to approval.

Exception lifecycle:
- Create an Exception Record via the Request Center with: justification, risk assessment summary, compensating controls, owner, expiry date, and link to affected assets.
- Security classifies the exception as low/medium/high risk. High-risk exceptions require weekly review and a mitigation plan.
- Renewal requires original approver chain sign-off. Exceptions longer than 90 days escalate to the Risk Committee.

Change-management gates when requests affect permissions or spend:
- Any request that touches IAM, network ACLs, KMS, or billing/configurable infra must include a Change Statement: scope, rollback plan, expected cost delta, and test/runbook references.
- Automated triage flags changes where estimated monthly spend delta >=10% for Finance review and where more than two services are touched for CAB scheduling.
- CAB review is required for policy-level changes (default session duration, cross-region access policies) and multi-team rollouts.

Vendor onboarding tied to access provisioning:
Required attachments for vendor requests that will receive service accounts: signed contract or SOW, vendor security attestation (SOC2 or equivalent), IP allowlist (if relevant), and a named vendor owner within Redwood. Finance must approve when expected vendor spend > $5,000/month. Default vendor service accounts are created with minimal privileges and require an owner to rotate credentials quarterly.

Travel & expense process (summary):
- Pre-trip approval: International trips require manager pre-approval; estimated total > $7,000 require VP sign-off.
- Allowed classes: Economy preferred; premium/elevated travel allowed only with prior approval for trips >6 hours flight time or Executive-level roles.
- Meals and per-diems: Region-specific caps published monthly in the policy portal. Attach receipts for any single item > $25 USD.
- Lost receipts: submit the Receipt Exception Form with manager attestation; Finance may approve up to $75 per item without a receipt when pre-authorized.
- Submission window: expenses must be filed within 30 days of trip end; late submissions require manager+finance sign-off.

Expense approval tiers:
- Tier 1: < $500 — Manager approval.
- Tier 2: $500$5,000 — Manager + Finance reviewer.
- Tier 3: > $5,000 — Manager + Finance + Director.

Retention and audit evidence:
- Access request records, approvals, and audit logs: retain 7 years.
- Exception records: retain 7 years for regulated accounts; otherwise retain 3 years.
- Vendor onboarding artifacts and contracts: retain 10 years post-termination.
- Travel receipts and T&E records: retain 6 years to satisfy cross-jurisdictional tax requirements.

Operational runbook (step-by-step):
1) Submit the request in Request Center using the appropriate form (Access Request / Vendor Onboard / Travel & Expense). Include justification, estimated cost, assets impacted, and requested expiry.
2) Auto-triage: system assigns reviewers based on request type and flags CAB/Finance/Security as needed.
3) Approver notifications: approvers receive an in-portal task and an email. Approvers are expected to action within the SLA or reassign via the Delegation Registry.
4) Fulfillment: engineering or IAM tooling performs provisioning and records the request_id in audit-index.
5) Close and tag: the Request Center applies retention tags and closes the request. Any deviations should create a post-fulfillment incident for follow-up.

Common scenarios (short guidance):
- Incident remediation: use the Emergency Exception path, include incident ID, and do the post-incident privilege review.
- Vendor needs a service account: attach vendor checklist and security attestation; limit privileges and set credential rotation.
- International travel with missing receipt: attach Receipt Exception Form and manager attestation; expect Finance review.

Controls and metrics (governance):
- SLA targets: Tier A 90% within 48 business hours; Tier B 95% within 5 business days.
- Exception maturity: 95% of exceptions reviewed before expiry.
- Financial gate effectiveness: 100% of changes with estimated spend delta >=10% routed to Finance for review.

Where to find templates and forms:
- Request Center forms: /internal/request-center/forms
- Delegation Registry: /internal/registries/delegations
- Vendor onboarding checklist: /internal/templates/vendor-onboard-checklist.docx
- Receipt Exception Form: /internal/forms/receipt-exception.pdf
- Travel expense workbook: /internal/templates/travel-expense-template.xlsx

Contacts and escalation points:
- T&E processing: finance-te@redwood.ai
- Security exceptions: sec-exceptions@redwood.ai
- Request Center support: request-support@redwood.ai

Review cadence and ownership:
- Annual policy owner: Finance-Legal (policy review each January).
- Quarterly risk & exception review: Security + Compliance.
- Delegation registry audit: People Ops + Security annually.

Change log:
- 2026-01-05: Playbook authored by Miguel Torres; initial publication.
- 2026-02-10: Clarified vendor onboarding attachments and credential rotation. Reviewer: Priya Shah.
- 2026-03-01: Updated SLA targets and added Delegation Registry link. Reviewer: Owen Brooks.

Related references:
- Redwood Security & Data Classification policy (internal).
- Request Center user guide (internal).

payload.page_title: Access & Ops Playbook for Remote-First, Procurement, and Contract Approvals

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines evergreen practices and step-by-step procedures covering five cross-cutting areas used by all Redwood teams: access & permissions lifecycle, approved change management pathways, data stewardship minimums, procurement & expense approvals, and vendor/travel intake templates. The goal is to reduce friction for remote-first teams while preserving least-privilege, auditability, and financial controls.

Scope
Applies to: all Redwoood employees, contractors, and vendors who request system access, submit procurement/expense requests, or manage changes impacting production systems. Exceptions must be requested via the Risk & Exceptions process (see "Requesting an Exception" below).

Key principles
- Least privilege: grant minimal access required for a task and enforce time-bounded entitlements.
- Separation of duties: approvals are split across requestor, technical owner, and finance/legal as appropriate.
- Remote-first friendliness: friction-reduced templates, automated approvals for low-risk requests, and synchronous approval SLAs for high-risk items.
- Auditability: every access and procurement action must link to a ticket (Jira ID) and include approval metadata for audits.

1) Roles and ownership
- Requestor: individual initiating access, change, or procurement. Responsible for describing business justification and SLA.
- Technical Owner: owner of the resource/service (e.g., runtime-team@redwood.com). Confirms technical validity and risk impact.
- Approver-Finance: finance-legal representative for spend > $5k.
- Approver-Security: security team member for high-scope access (data classified as PII or regulated).
- Access Steward: team responsible for periodic entitlement reviews (quarterly).

Contact matrix (examples)
- infra-prod: infra-oncall@redwood.com (Technical Owner)
- runtime-api: runtime-team@redwood.com
- procurement: procurement@redwood.com (Approver-Finance)
- security: security-ops@redwood.com (Approver-Security)

2) Access & permissions lifecycle
Minimum required fields for an access request (Jira template: ACCESS-REQ):
- Requestor name / email
- Justification & expiration date (required for contractors)
- Resource identifier (ARN, service name, dashboard link)
- Least-privilege role requested and list of actions
- Technical owner approval (required)
- Security sensitivity level: public | internal | restricted | regulated

Standard approval pathways
- Low-risk (read-only to internal services, spend < $1k): auto-approve within 8 hours if technical owner signs off via Slack/Confluence link.
- Medium-risk (write access to internal infra, non-production credentials): Technical Owner + Access Steward approval within 24 hours.
- High-risk (production write, PII access, KMS/HSM keys): Technical Owner + Security + Finance approval; must complete expansion checklist and security review; SLA 48 hours.

Entitlement management
- Time-bound access: default max duration 90 days for contractors and 365 days for employees; extensions require reapproval.
- Quarterly entitlement review: Access Stewards run reports (IAM tool: AegisIAM) and reconcile stale privileges.
- Emergency break-glass: requests via the oncall channel with post-facto Jira ticket and 24-hour incident debrief.

Example IAM policy snippet (provide in request as needed)
{\
  \"Version\": \"2023-10-01\",\
  \"Statement\": [\
    {\
      \"Effect\": \"Allow\",\
      \"Action\": [\
        \"s3:GetObject\"\
      ],\
      \"Resource\": [\"arn:aws:s3:::redwood-artifacts/*\"]\
    }\
  ]\
}

3) Change management (for infra, runtime, and customer-impacting changes)
Change classes and required artifacts
- Class A (Standard): routine config changes with a playbook, pre-approved rollback, no customer-facing impact. Requires Change Request ticket, automated CI test, and scheduled maintenance window.
- Class B (Significant): deployments that modify runtimes, stateful DB schema changes, or cross-cluster network changes. Requires Design Review (ADR link), runbook, canary plan, and request for change (RFC) with 48-hour review.
- Class C (High-risk / Emergency): production outages, security patches affecting secrets/KMS. Requires immediate oncall coordination, postmortem, and retrospective review.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. Summary and Jira ID
2. Owner and approver list
3. Risk classification and rollback plan
4. Pre-deploy validation steps and test commands
5. Canary rollout plan (traffic percentages and metrics)
6. Post-deploy validation metrics and SLO targets (latency, error rate)

SLOs and guardrails for deployed changes
- Production latency: no increase > 5% for 30m post-deploy relative to baseline.
- Error rate: no sustained > 2x spike in 15m window.
- If SLO breached, execute automatic rollback policy.

Automated gating examples (CI snippet)
- Run: make infra-plan && terraform apply -target=module.safe_changes --auto-approve
- Safety check: ./scripts/check-deploy-guardrails --canary 10 --observe 15m

4) Data management requirements
Classification levels
- Public: allowed to be shared externally.
- Internal: business data not intended for public release.
- Restricted: sensitive business or employee data; access limited to named roles.
- Regulated: PII/PHI/financial data subject to compliance controls (GDPR/PCI/ISO27001).

Minimum controls by classification
- Encryption at rest + in-transit: required for Restricted and Regulated.
- Audit logging: capture user ID, source IP, action, timestamp. Retain audit logs for 2 years for Regulated, 1 year for Restricted.
- Data residency: regulated datasets must be pinned to approved regions; list available in Data Residency matrix (appendix link).

Data handling checklist for projects
- Data minimization statement: why this dataset is necessary.
- Retention policy assigned & expiration date.
- Access matrix: list of users with access and justification.
- Masking/encryption strategy for non-production copies.

5) Procurement & expenses workflow
Spend thresholds and approval steps
- Under $200: manager-level approval via Expense form (automated).
- $200–$5,000: manager + finance designated approver.
- $5,000–$50,000: manager + procurement + finance.
- > $50,000: manager + procurement + finance + VP level sign-off and legal review for contract terms.
sections.heading: Change request checklist (RFC template)

sections.body:
- Business justification & Jira link
- Cost center and budget owner
- Preferred vendor, SOW/quote attachment, contract term length
- Security and data handling classification (is vendor processing regulated data?)
- Requested date and desired delivery/activation date

Vendor selection and negotiation guidance
- Standard vendors (SaaS infra, cloud providers) are pre-approved; use vendor-approved templates. Non-standard vendors require RFP and vendor risk assessment.
- For any vendor with access to Regulated data: require SOC 2 Type II report (or equivalent), encryption attestation, and a Data Processing Agreement (DPA).

Payment & billing
- Finance issues purchase orders (POs) for contractual spend > $5k.
- Contractors and small one-off purchases should use the corporate card with receipts uploaded to Expensify within 7 days.

6) Vendor management and contracts
Onboarding checklist for vendors with system access
- Completed vendor intake form + Jira ticket
- Security questionnaire (provided by security-ops) and evidence (SOC reports, pen test summaries)
- Contractual terms: NDAs, DPA, liability limits, termination clauses, and IP assignments as applicable
- Technical onboarding: least-privilege credentials, IP allowlists, and documented support contacts

Periodic review cadence
- Annual risk review for vendors handling Restricted/Regulated data.
- Quarterly performance review for strategic vendors (uptime SLAs, support metrics).

7) Corporate travel and remote work expense policy highlights
- Per diem and lodging caps defined by region (full matrix in appendix). Use company travel portal (TravelPortal) and preferred booking partners.
- Approval: manager pre-approval required for out-of-country travel; for trips > 5 days require People Ops sign-off.
- Expense submission timeline: receipts uploaded within 14 days of trip end. Card reconciliations within 30 days.
- Safety: employees traveling to Medium/High risk countries must register trip via TravelSafety and enroll in emergency assistance.

8) Templates and quick-start checklists (links and examples)
- ACCESS-REQ (Jira template id: ACCESS-REQ): minimal fields + IAM snippet inclusion.
- PRQ (Procurement Request): includes vendor risk section and budget owner approval.
- RFC-CHANGE: change request with canary rollout plan and rollback steps.
- VENDOR-ONBOARD: vendor intake form checklist.
sections.heading: Procurement request fields (PRQ template)

sections.body:
---
vendor: \"Acme Observability\"
quote_amount: 18000
contract_term_months: 12
dpa_required: true
cost_center: \"ENG-PLATFORM\"
justification: |\
  Replace legacy tracing system with vendor-managed SaaS to reduce MTTR and support distributed tracing for Redwood services.
---

9) Requesting an exception
- Exceptions go through the Risk & Exceptions board: file EXC-{team}-{YYYY}{NN} with rationale, compensating controls, and timebox. Exceptions are time-boxed (max 90 days) and require sponsor from the owner_team.

10) Enforcement, monitoring, and continuous improvement
- Monthly dashboards: top 10 stale entitlements, open procurement requests older than SLA, vendors with expiring evidence.
- Quarterly tabletop exercises covering break-glass and vendor incident response.
- Annual policy review owned by finance-legal; suggested updates accepted via PR on the policy repo and reviewed by the board.

Appendix (links and resources)
- Standard Jira templates: /confluence/templates/access-req | /confluence/templates/prq | /confluence/templates/rfc-change
- Data residency matrix: /confluence/security/data-residency-2027
- IAM tooling: AegisIAM runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/i-am-aegis-runbook
- Contact list: procurement@redwood.com, security-ops@redwood.com, infra-oncall@redwood.com

Revision history
- 2026-07-12: Initial draft authored by Maya Chen.
- 2027-03-02: Added remote-first accelerated approval paths and IAM automation guidance.
- 2028-02-14: Published: clarified approval thresholds and vendor evidence requirements (SOC 2/DPA).

End of document

payload.page_title: Cross-layer fidelity regression investigation guide

sections.body: This document is a cross-functional playbook for investigating fidelity regressions that surface as quality drops, hallucination spikes, or metric divergence between shadow and production models. It covers signal prioritization, cross-layer telemetry queries, step-by-step triage, and recommended mitigations. The playbook is intentionally prescriptive to reduce mean-time-to-diagnosis and standardize handoffs between runtime, model-onboarding, and product-quality teams.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Automated quality monitors (e.g., prompt-set drift alerts, eval regression alerts) detect a >2% drop on a key metric (BLEU/ROUGE/EMBED similarity/QA accuracy)
- Customer-reported quality regression with reproducible examples
- Canary mismatch: canary cohort shows degradation vs baseline
- Correlated changes to runtime (kernel/quantization rollouts), infra (GPU firmware, NUMA), or model variants (new weights/merges)
sections.heading: When to use this playbook

sections.body:
1) Decide whether the regression is model, serving, or data-related within 4 business hours for P1/P0 incidents.
2) Produce a reproducible minimal failing input and an action plan (rollback, model-safeguard, patch).
3) Capture investigation artifacts and link to a post-incident evaluation for continuous improvement.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
Order signals by fidelity of attribution (higher first). For each signal we include the typical query surface and primary owner.

1) Prompt-set evals (golden-suite)
- What: automated evaluation on a curated prompt set (deterministic or near-deterministic prompts).
- Query pattern: run nightly eval pipeline or local runner: `python eval_runner.py --suite golden-suite --model A --seed 42`
- Owner: applied-ml-and-evals / product-quality
- Why first: isolates model quality independent of client-side stochasticity and runtime batching effects.

2) Model variant diffs and weights metadata
- What: model artifact comparison (commit hash, tokenizer changes, quantization profile used).
- Query pattern: `redwood-metadata inspect --model model:v2.3 --fields commit,quant_profile,tokenizer_hash`
- Owner: model-onboarding / runtime-team
- Why: a model artifact change is a high-likelihood cause; checksum mismatches are decisive.

3) Execution-time fidelity signals (sampling config, temperature, stop tokens)
- What: request-level deltas between expected sampling params vs observed.
- Query pattern: logs: `SELECT * FROM request_logs WHERE trace_id IN (<samples>) AND timestamp > X`
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / eng-developer-experience

4) Kernel & quantization traces
- What: kernel selection, quantization pathway, per-layer quant-scheme (int8/4-bit), and dequant errors.
- Query pattern: `kernel_trace --trace-id=<trace> --dump-layer-errors` and kernel logs at /var/log/runtime/kernel-hint.log
- Owner: kernel-and-scheduling / runtime-architecture

5) KV-cache and prefix-mismatch anomalies
- What: stale or mismatched KV cache entries that alter context.
- Query pattern: KV cache checksum comparison for session: `kvtool inspect --session <sid> --compare baseline`
- Owner: runtime-team / eng-sre

6) Networking and compression artifacts
- What: payload truncation, UTF-8 corruption, or L7 proxy transformations.
- Query pattern: tcpdump of client-request vs ingress-raw payload, or request size histograms
- Owner: infra / cloud-accounts-and-networking

7) Post-processing and tool-calling schisms
- What: tool invocation ordering, function-calling hooks, or custom post-processors that alter output.
- Query pattern: trace function-call logs and post-processor exit codes
- Owner: eng-developer-experience / product
sections.heading: Signal catalog and priority ordering

sections.body:
1) Confirm and reproduce
  1.1. Collect 3 representative failing examples (customer-provided or automated).
  1.2. Run each example against the last known-good model and the current model in an isolated runtime (no batching, deterministic seed, single-thread):
       - `redwood-cli generate --model <model-id> --input-file examples.txt --seed 0 --deterministic --no-batching`
  1.3. If outputs diverge, label as model vs runtime regression candidate.

2) Quick artifact check (10–30 minutes)
  - Confirm model artifact checksums and quantization profile. If changed recently, escalate to model-onboarding.
  - Verify runtime rollout events (kernel plugin update, scheduler policy changes, autoscaler behavior). Check `/internal/deployments/rollout-log` for entries in the past 24–72 hours.

3) Isolate serving effects (30–90 minutes)
  - Re-run failing inputs on the same model under:
    a) Host-local developer runtime (CPU-only or dev-GPU)
    b) Production-like runtime with previous kernel mapping (if snapshots exist)
    c) Canary/Canary-rollback variant if applicable
  - Compare outputs and collect kernel traces for each. Use the `trace-collector` with `--annotation fidelity_regress_YYYYMMDD` to keep runs discoverable.

4) Telemetry deep-dive (1–3 hours)
  - Pull request-level metadata: sampling params, tokenization deltas, sequence lengths, and observed temperature sampling distributions.
  - Pull kernel-level metrics: per-layer quantization error metric (mean absolute error), kernel path (optimized vs fallback), kernel latency and SM occupancy.
  - Correlate by trace_id and request_hash. Prioritize traces where kernel path diverged between good and bad runs.

5) Hypothesis formation and narrow test (1–4 hours)
  - Form 1–3 hypotheses ranked by likelihood and effort-to-test. Example hypotheses: quantization profile introduced layerwise bias; tokenizer merged merges changed special tokens; kernel fallback path introduces subtle rounding.
  - Design a minimal reproducible test for each hypothesis (unit test or small benchmarking script).

6) Action and mitigation (depends on root cause)
  - Model artifact confirmed: roll back to prior model, pin model version, trigger model evaluation pipeline.
  - Runtime confirmed (kernel/quant): rollback kernel plugin or toggle legacy quant-path; if not available, use runtime-level heuristic: force higher precision exec for affected layers via `runtime-config set --model <id> --layer-precision "layer:fp16"`
  - Network/ingress confirmed: apply payload sanitization, reject malformed requests at the edge, inform infra to patch proxies.
  - Post-processing confirmed: disable post-processor and re-validate with golden suite.

7) Post-incident validation (24–72 hours)
  - Run the golden-suite eval and 3rd-party prompt-sets used by product teams.
  - Monitor rolling-window quality metrics and schedule a follow-up retrospective if regression was P1/P0.

Required data artifacts to attach to an investigation ticket:
- 3 failing inputs + outputs (good vs bad)
- Trace IDs and a link to raw trace artifacts (kernel traces, request logs, kv snapshots)
- Model artifact metadata (commit, size, tokenizer hash, quant profile)
- Runtime config snapshot (scheduler policy, kernel version, admission matrix)
- Minimal reproduction script used during triage
sections.heading: Triage checklist (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Fetch traces for a timeframe: `traces fetch --start 2025-11-01T00:00Z --end 2025-11-07T00:00Z --filter "label:fidelity_regress"`
- Dump kernel decision path: `kernel_inspector dump --trace <trace_id> --format yaml`
- Compare model artifacts: `model-registry diff --a model:v2.2 --b model:v2.3 --fields tokenizer,commit,quant_profile`
- Re-run deterministic generation: `redwood-cli generate --model model:v2.2 --input "<prompt>" --deterministic --seed 0 --no-batching`
sections.heading: Query recipes and useful CLI snippets

sections.body:

- If kernel/quantization suspected -> Page kernel-and-scheduling on-call; open a high-priority issue and attach kernel traces.
- If infra/networking -> On-call infra team and open cloud-accounts incident.
- If ambiguous after 8 hours -> Declare cross-functional War Room: runtime eng lead (owner), product-quality, SRE, and model lead. Capture decisions in the ticket.
sections.heading: Escalation matrix and ownership guide

sections.body:
- Require golden-suite pass for any model or quantization profile rollout (threshold: no >0.5% regression on core metrics).
- Kernel plugin rollouts must include a shadow traffic run for 72 hours and an automated comparison against baseline.
- Add a pre-deploy check that compares tokenizer hashes and token mapping diffs; fail pipeline if special-token mapping changed unexpectedly.

sections.body:
- Incident summary (what, impact, timeline)
- Root cause with supporting evidence (traces, diffs, metrics)
- Actions taken and verification steps
- Preventative measures and owners

payload.page_title: Experiment Service Overview (Control Plane) — Route-level Experiments

sections.body: The **Experiment Service** (internal name: `experiment-svc`) is the control-plane component that stores and validates route-level experiment configuration and publishes a fast, deterministic representation to the policy/routing layer.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- What `experiment-svc` owns vs. what the policy engine/router owns
- API surface (Console + internal)
- Storage model and versioning
- Validation rules and safety guardrails
- Interaction with the policy engine (config propagation)
- Caching strategy (server-side and data-plane)
- Failure modes and degraded behaviors
sections.heading: This document covers

sections.body: Route-level A/B testing requires customers to define experiments at the **route** boundary (endpoint + traffic policy), assign requests deterministically to a **variant**, and then attribute telemetry by `{route, experiment_id, variant}`.
sections.heading: Background and goals

sections.body:
- Single source of truth for experiment definitions and lifecycle state
- Strong validation to prevent unsafe/ambiguous routing behavior
- Auditable change history (enterprise requirement)
- Predictable propagation of config to routers (staleness bounds)
sections.heading: Control-plane requirements

sections.body:
- Statistical significance engine
- Customer-defined custom metrics ingestion
sections.heading: Non-goals (for GA)

sections.body:
**Experiment Service owns**:
- Canonical experiment spec + lifecycle state machine
- Validation and invariants (splits, eligibility rules, overlap constraints)
- Versioning, change diffs, and audit events
- Publishing compiled config to the policy config channel
- Read APIs for Console (list/detail, status, audit trail)

**Policy engine / routing layer owns**:
- Deterministic bucketing implementation and precedence rules (see ADR-047)
- Evaluating eligibility rules at request time
- Applying experiments in the request path with low latency
- Emitting attribution fields to request context and telemetry (see ADR-048)

**Telemetry/Analytics owns**:
- Aggregations and results datasets consumed by Console
sections.heading: Ownership and boundaries

sections.body:
- `console-api` (Console backend): calls `experiment-svc` for experiment CRUD/start/stop and reads status/results.
- `experiment-svc`: validates and persists experiment config; publishes compiled config snapshots.
- `policy-engine`: consumes published experiment config and evaluates experiments during routing decisions.
- `router` / `gateway`: calls policy engine and applies the chosen variant (model/route policy) before fallback.
- `audit-log-svc`: receives structured audit events for compliance retention/export.
- `metrics-pipeline`: consumes request spans/events with experiment dimensions.
sections.heading: Components

sections.body:
1) User creates/updates experiment in Console.
2) `console-api` performs RBAC checks and calls `experiment-svc`.
3) `experiment-svc` validates the spec, persists changes, writes audit events.
4) `experiment-svc` compiles an “evaluation-ready” config and publishes it (with a monotonic `config_version`).
5) `policy-engine` subscribes/pulls config updates and updates its in-memory store.
6) Routers use the policy engine evaluation result and attach `experiment_id`/`variant_id` to request context.
sections.heading: Data flow (control plane → data plane)

sections.body:
- Requests originate from `console-api` with a service-to-service identity.
- End-user permissions are evaluated in `console-api` and forwarded as signed principal context.
- `experiment-svc` enforces an additional “defense in depth” check on:
  - organization/account scope
  - environment scope (prod/staging)
  - mutation operations (create/update/start/stop/delete)
sections.heading: Authentication and authorization

sections.body:
Base path: `/v1/experiments`

**Write APIs (mutations)**
- `POST /v1/experiments` — create draft experiment
- `PUT /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}` — update draft (or update running if allowed by policy)
- `POST /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}:start` — transition to RUNNING
- `POST /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}:stop` — transition to STOPPED (optionally with drain)
- `DELETE /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}` — delete (restricted; typically only if never RUNNING)

**Read APIs**
- `GET /v1/experiments` — list experiments (filters: route_id, status, created_by, updated_since)
- `GET /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}` — detail view (spec + status + guardrails)
- `GET /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}/audit-events` — audit trail (paginated)
- `GET /v1/experiments/{experiment_id}/status` — runtime status + last publish + propagation health
sections.heading: Public (Console) APIs

sections.body: - Results metrics are served by the results API/analytics layer; `experiment-svc` only returns identifiers needed for attribution and links.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- `GET /internal/v1/experiments/{experiment_id}/compiled` — compiled evaluation config (for debugging/tools)
- `POST /internal/v1/assignment:explain` — explain assignment decision given inputs (gated; see debug endpoint guidance)
sections.heading: Internal APIs

sections.body: The canonical spec is stored as JSON but compiled into a restricted schema for the data plane.
sections.heading: Experiment spec model (conceptual)

sections.body:
- `experiment_id` (UUID)
- `account_id` / `org_id`
- `env` (prod/staging)
- `route_id` (normalized route identifier; see route normalization guidance)
- `status` (DRAFT, RUNNING, STOPPING, STOPPED, ARCHIVED)
- `eligibility_rules` (header presence, customer tier, region allowlist, etc.)
- `stickiness` (key precedence; hashing namespace)
- `variants[]` (variant_id, target policy/model reference)
- `allocation[]` (variant_id → weight)
- `guardrails` (thresholds and actions)
- `created_by`, `updated_by`
sections.heading: Key fields

sections.body:
- normalized route match key(s)
- pre-validated weight ranges and cumulative bucket boundaries
- allowed regions
- compatible model set (if constrained)
sections.heading: Compilation output includes

sections.body:
Primary store: Postgres (`controlplane-pg`) with logical tables:

| Table | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `experiments` | Current canonical spec and status | Includes `spec_json`, `status`, `account_id`, `route_id`, `config_version` |
| `experiment_versions` | Immutable history of spec revisions | Used for diff/audit, rollback to previous config |
| `experiment_audit_events` | Denormalized audit event store | Also forwarded to `audit-log-svc` for long-term retention/export |
| `experiment_publish_log` | Publish attempts and outcomes | Includes timestamps, target channel, error, propagation hints |
sections.heading: Storage model

sections.body:
- `spec_version` increments on every accepted mutation.
- `config_version` increments on every successful publish. `config_version` is the reference used by the policy engine and routers.
- Console displays both versions to help correlate “saved vs. deployed” state.
sections.heading: Versioning

sections.body:
- `experiment_versions` retained for 90 days by default (subject to enterprise overrides).
- Audit events follow security/compliance retention rules (see audit logging page).
sections.heading: Retention

sections.body: Validation happens synchronously on create/update/start.
sections.heading: Validation and guardrails

sections.body:
- Allocation weights sum to 1.0 (±0.0001) and each weight is within [0,1].
- Minimum allocation per non-control variant (default: >= 1%) when RUNNING (configurable; prevents “variant 0 traffic”).
- Variant count <= 5 (GA default) to reduce operational complexity and metrics cardinality.
- Each variant references a valid target (model_id / rollout policy / routing policy reference) in the same account/environment.
- Model compatibility checks when the experiment is scoped to a route with fixed request/response schema.
- Eligibility rules must be evaluable in the data plane (no arbitrary expressions).
- Overlap constraints:
  - By default, only one RUNNING experiment per `{account_id, env, route_id}`.
  - Additional experiments require explicit priority and must be non-overlapping by eligibility rules (restricted feature).
sections.heading: Hard validation (request rejected)

sections.body:
- Stickiness key missing or low entropy risk (e.g., defaulting to IP alone).
- Narrow region allowlist that may cause small sample sizes.
- Guardrail thresholds that are unusually strict vs. baseline noise.
sections.heading: Warnings (accepted but flagged)

sections.body:
- **Start**: DRAFT → RUNNING. Publishes compiled config and returns `publish_id`.
- **Stop**:
  - STOPPING is used when a drain period is requested (to reduce abrupt changes for long-lived streams).
  - STOPPED removes the experiment from the published config.
sections.heading: Start/stop semantics

sections.body: - Soft-stop only (mark degraded + notify). Hard-stop is available behind a kill-switch and requires explicit enablement.
sections.heading: Guardrail behavior (GA default)

sections.body:
`experiment-svc` publishes the compiled experiment config to the policy config distribution system (internally: `policy-config-store`).

The published payload is keyed by `{account_id, env}` and contains:
- all RUNNING experiments for that scope
- per-experiment `config_version`
- a compact representation optimized for fast evaluation
sections.heading: Compiled config channel

sections.body:
- Target p95 propagation time (publish → policy engine updated): defined in the control-plane SLO document.
- Routers consume policy engine decisions; they do not pull config directly from `experiment-svc`.
sections.heading: Propagation expectations

sections.body:
- Compiled schema is versioned (`compiled_schema_version`).
- Policy engine supports N and N-1 compiled schema versions during rollout windows.
- Migrations:
  - `experiment-svc` can recompile specs into both schemas during transitions.
sections.heading: Backward/forward compatibility

sections.body:
Goals: reduce DB load for list/detail views and avoid repeated compilation work.

- Read-through cache for `GET /v1/experiments/{id}` and list queries by account/env.
- Cache TTL: 10–30s (tunable); cache invalidated on mutation.
- Compiled config cache keyed by `{account_id, env, config_version}`.
sections.heading: Server-side caching (`experiment-svc`)

sections.body:
- In-memory map keyed by `{account_id, env, route_id}` for fast lookup.
- Periodic refresh + event-driven updates from the config channel.
- Safe defaults on cache miss:
  - If config unavailable, policy engine returns “no experiment” and routing proceeds with baseline rollout/fallback policies.
sections.heading: Data-plane caching (policy engine)

sections.body:
1) **DB unavailable / high latency**
- Impact: experiment mutations fail; reads may serve stale cache.
- Mitigation: serve cached read responses where possible; retryable errors on mutation.

2) **Publish channel degraded**
- Impact: saved spec may not reach data plane; Console shows “Not yet propagated”.
- Mitigation: publish retries with exponential backoff; emit propagation lag metrics and alerts.

3) **Audit log sink unavailable**
- Impact: audit export incomplete if not buffered.
- Mitigation: `experiment-svc` persists audit events locally first, then forwards asynchronously; if forwarding fails, alert but do not block the mutation (unless required by specific enterprise policy).
sections.heading: Control-plane failures

sections.body:
1) **Policy engine cannot load config**
- Behavior: no experiment applied; baseline routing continues.
- Risk: experiment traffic may drop to 0%. Console indicates “data plane not applying” via propagation health.

2) **Deterministic bucketing mismatch across regions**
- Behavior: inconsistent assignment.
- Mitigation: hashing namespace + stickiness precedence standardized (ADR-047); debug endpoint provides explain output.

3) **Metrics attribution drop / missing dimensions**
- Impact: results dashboards appear inconsistent.
- Mitigation: attribution drop rate alerting; known streaming retry edge cases documented in runbook.
sections.heading: Data-plane failures

sections.body:
- API availability and latency per endpoint
- Validation failures by category
- Publish success rate, retry count
- Propagation lag (publish timestamp → first observed policy engine config version)
- Cache hit ratio
sections.heading: Key metrics (emitted by `experiment-svc`)

sections.body:
- Structured logs include `experiment_id`, `account_id`, `env`, `route_id`, `spec_version`, `config_version`.
- Sensitive fields are redacted (eligibility rules that include customer identifiers, etc.).
sections.heading: Logging

sections.body:
- All mutation endpoints create a span with:
  - validation sub-spans
  - DB write
  - audit emit
  - publish attempt
sections.heading: Tracing

sections.body:
- For split anomalies, skew, or stickiness issues: see *Experiment assignment debugging runbook*.
- For propagation lag alerts: see *Experiment health dashboards spec* and linked runbooks.
sections.heading: Operational playbooks

sections.body:
- Cardinality control: `experiment_id` and `variant_id` are allowed on spans and selected metrics; high-cardinality expansions are sampled (see metrics attribution ADR and observability PRs).
- Multi-tenant isolation: all queries and publishes are scoped to `{account_id, env}` with explicit enforcement.
- Schema evolution: compiled output is the stability boundary for the data plane; canonical spec can evolve with migrations as long as it compiles to supported schema versions.
sections.heading: Implementation notes and constraints

sections.body: - DRAFT → RUNNING → STOPPING → STOPPED → ARCHIVED
sections.heading: Appendix: Status state machine

sections.body:
- Updates are unrestricted in DRAFT.
- Updates in RUNNING are restricted to safe fields (e.g., allocation ramp within bounds, guardrail threshold changes) unless explicitly forced by admin.
- STOPPED experiments cannot be restarted without creating a new experiment (default) to preserve interpretability; exceptions may be granted for internal testing.
sections.heading: Constraints

payload.page_title: Remote-first pilot: office supplies ordering & ergonomic chair reimbursement

sections.body:
This page documents the updated, standardized process for handling one-off office supply needs and ergonomic chair reimbursements for employees participating in the Remote-first Pilot program (including on-site pilot week preparation and new-hire onboarding bundles).

This guidance replaces ad-hoc handling captured in internal tickets (e.g., INT-324) and clarifies what is ordered centrally vs. what is reimbursed.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Pilot participants (Engineering, GTM, and other teams explicitly enrolled in the Remote-first Pilot)
- Hiring managers and People Ops supporting pilot new hires
- Office Ops / Procurement and Finance processing pilot-related purchases and reimbursements
sections.heading: Applies to

sections.body:
- Standard corporate office refresh projects
- Non-pilot remote-work stipends (see related pages)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
The following items are commonly requested for pilot week readiness and onboarding:
- Standing desk converters (temporary loaners) for on-site pilot week
- Assorted cables/adapters kits (USB-C, HDMI, ethernet) to restock shared drawers
- Ergonomic office chair reimbursement (employee-provided receipt) for remote onboarding ergonomics
sections.heading: Summary of common pilot requests

sections.body:
- Chair reimbursement cap increased from $350 to $400 for approved pilot new hires (effective 2026-04-01).
- Pre-approval is now required for chair reimbursements (exception: replacement due to documented damage during shipping).
- Reimbursements must be submitted through Expensify (paper forms are no longer accepted).
- Procurement now maintains a preferred vendor list for standing desk converter loaners; direct employee purchase of converters is not reimbursable.
sections.heading: What changed since the earlier pilot tickets

sections.body: The following caps apply per employee unless otherwise approved in writing by Finance-legal.
sections.heading: Policy: allowable items and caps

sections.body:
- Standing desk converters: Office Ops orders only; treated as loaner inventory. Not reimbursable.
- Cables/adapters kits: Office Ops orders only; treated as shared office supplies.
- Ergonomic chair: Reimbursable with pre-approval and receipt.
sections.heading: Allowable items (pilot program)

sections.body:
- Ergonomic chair reimbursement cap: $400 (USD) including taxes and shipping.
- Purchase window: within 30 days of employee start date for pilot new hires, unless an exception is approved.
- Receipt must show: vendor name, item description, purchase date, total paid, and payment method.
- Used items are not reimbursable.
sections.heading: Caps and requirements

sections.body:
- Hiring manager: confirms employee eligibility for Remote-first Pilot; initiates chair pre-approval.
- People Ops: confirms the pilot budget allocation and provides the correct budget code.
- Office Ops / Procurement: places orders for converters and shared cables kits; manages loaner inventory and lead times.
- Finance: validates reimbursement submissions, confirms cap compliance, and approves payment timing.
sections.heading: Roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
1. Hiring manager or pilot coordinator files a request with Office Ops including:
   - Quantity needed
   - Dates needed (pilot week start/end)
   - Delivery location (office or employee shipping address)
2. Office Ops checks existing loaner inventory (see INT-301 reference) and confirms whether additional units are required.
3. If procurement is needed, Office Ops purchases through preferred vendors only.
4. Office Ops tracks assignment and return date. Loaners must be returned within 10 business days after pilot week ends unless extended by Office Ops.
sections.heading: Procedure A: Ordering standing desk converters (loaner inventory)

sections.body: - Typical lead time is 3–5 business days. During peak onboarding periods, plan for 7 business days.
sections.heading: Lead time guidance

sections.body:
1. Office Ops maintains a standard kit with:
   - USB-C to HDMI
   - USB-C to USB-A
   - HDMI cable
   - Ethernet cable
   - USB-C multiport adapter
2. Requests should specify desired restock quantity (default: 5 kits).
3. Office Ops orders via preferred vendors and stocks the front desk drawer.
sections.heading: Procedure B: Ordering cables/adapters kits (shared supplies)

sections.body:
1. Hiring manager submits a pre-approval request to Finance with:
   - Employee name and start date
   - Confirmation the employee is in the Remote-first Pilot
   - Estimated chair cost (must be <= $400)
   - Rationale (ergonomics / onboarding need)
2. Finance responds in writing (email or ticket comment) with approval and the correct expense category/budget code.
sections.heading: Step 1 — Pre-approval (required)

sections.body:
- Employee purchases the chair after receiving pre-approval.
- The chair must be new and purchased from a reputable retailer.
sections.heading: Step 2 — Purchase

sections.body:
1. Employee submits the expense in Expensify under category: "Remote-first Pilot > Ergonomic Equipment".
2. Attach the itemized receipt.
3. Enter the pre-approval reference (email thread link or ticket key).
sections.heading: Step 3 — Submission in Expensify

sections.body:
- Finance verifies cap compliance and receipt validity.
- Processing target: within 5 business days.
- Cutoff for same-pay-cycle reimbursement: submit by end of day Friday before payroll processing week.
sections.heading: Step 4 — Finance review and payment timing

sections.body: Exceptions require written approval from Finance-legal and must include rationale and total cost.
sections.heading: Exceptions

sections.body:
- Medical accommodation requiring a specific chair model above the cap (must go through the accommodations process; do not process as a standard pilot exception).

sections.body:
Before marking a request "complete":
- Budget owner approval recorded (People Ops + Finance budget code confirmed)

sections.body:
- Direct platform impact is low; however, failure to fulfill these requests creates avoidable friction during pilot week (seat setup delays, onboarding disruptions).

payload.page_title: Change Management Policy for Model-Version and Runtime Changes

sections.body:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines the minimum change-management requirements for production changes that affect model versions, routing policies, serving runtime configuration, or customer-facing inference behavior.

h1. Scope
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Hosted API
* Dedicated capacity
* Private deployments (VPC and on-prem)
sections.heading: This applies to all production environments across

sections.body:
* Introducing a new model version behind an existing model alias
* Changing default routing/fallback policy
* Changing runtime settings that alter batching/caching/quantization
* Adjusting context-length limits or tool-calling behavior

Out of scope (but still recommended): documentation-only updates and non-production experiments in isolated sandboxes.

h1. Change classes
* Class 0 (Low risk): no customer traffic, no routing changes, no behavioral change (e.g., internal benchmarking).
* Class 1 (Moderate risk): canary to <= 5% traffic with immediate rollback.
* Class 2 (High risk): > 5% traffic impact, new default version, or changes to safety/tool calling/formatting behavior.
* Class 3 (Critical): global default changes, broad customer impact, or changes that can violate contracts/compliance commitments.

h1. Required artifacts (all classes 1–3)
A production rollout plan MUST include the following sections (link to template is mandatory):
1. Summary (what is changing, why now, customer impact)
2. Scope (which environments, regions, and customer tiers are included)
3. Success criteria and guardrails (explicit thresholds)
4. Monitoring plan (dashboards, alerts, owners)
5. Rollout steps (canary, ramp schedule, decision points)
6. Rollback and fallback rules (what happens automatically vs manually)
7. Customer communications plan (who, when, channels)
8. Approvals and change window

h1. Approvals

sections.heading: Examples in-scope

payload.page_title: Production Change Management Standard (v2)

sections.body:
h1. Purpose
This policy defines what constitutes a production change at Redwood Inference and the minimum requirements to plan, approve, execute, and validate the change. The goal is to minimize customer impact while maintaining developer velocity.

h1. Scope
Applies to all production environments for the Hosted API and Console, including:
* Hosted API control plane and data plane services
* Console UI and backend
* Shared platform dependencies (routing, auth, billing metering, observability agents)

Out of scope: customer-managed environments for *Private deployments* (see the Private Deployment Change Policy), and vendor-managed changes outside Redwood’s control (cloud provider maintenance).

h1. Definitions
* *Production:* Any environment serving external customer traffic (including canary and regional production).
* *Production change:* Any change that can affect confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness for customer-facing workloads.
* *Change owner:* The person accountable for end-to-end execution and follow-through.
* *Approver:* A designated peer/manager/SRE/security reviewer depending on risk tier.
* *Change record:* A durable record (ticket + links) capturing intent, risk, approvals, execution, and validation results.

h1. Change types
|| Change type || When used || Required approvals || Notes ||
| Standard | Low risk, pre-approved pattern (e.g., doc-only, internal dashboard query fixes, non-prod config) | 1 peer approval | Must match an approved standard template |
| Normal | Most code/config deploys to production | 1 peer approval + (1) service owner approval | Requires pre-deploy verification, canary, and comms assessment |
| Emergency | Active incident mitigation or preventing imminent customer impact | On-call incident commander (IC) + service owner approval (as available) | Retrospective change record required within 24 hours |

h1. What counts as a production change (non-exhaustive)
* Any deployment to production clusters (including canary regions)
* Any change to routing policies, fallback policies, or model selection rules
* Any change to auth, RBAC, API keys, rate limits, quotas, or billing meters
* Any schema migration, backfill, or data retention configuration change
* Any infrastructure change that affects capacity, autoscaling, or failover
* Any change to observability pipelines that could reduce visibility (logs, metrics, tracing)

h1. Minimum required artifacts
For every production change, the change owner must create a change record that includes:
* Summary of change and customer impact assessment
* Rollback plan (explicitly stated, even if “re-deploy previous build”)
* Verification plan (how we will know it worked)
* Links to: PR(s), build(s), dashboards, runbook used, and any migration plan
* Approvals (captured in the change record)

h1. Risk assessment checklist
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. Could this change affect auth, data paths, encryption, logging, or retention?
2. Could this change change request routing, batching, caching, or model version selection?
3. Could this change materially change token accounting/billing?
4. Is there any data migration/backfill involved?
5. Is rollback fast and safe (< 10 minutes) and does it revert the customer experience?

If “yes” to any of 1–4, the change is *Normal* at minimum and may require Security Review (see Secure SDLC requirements).

h1. Approvals
* *Peer approval:* A reviewer from the same engineering org who is familiar with the subsystem.
* *Service owner approval:* The tech lead or on-call owner for the service being changed.
* *SRE gate:* Required when the change affects capacity, SLO-sensitive paths, traffic routing, or any failover config.
* *Security gate:* Required when the change touches auth, secrets, encryption, audit logging, PII, or data retention.

h1. Change windows and freezes
* Default window: weekdays 09:00–16:00 local time for the primary owning team.
* Changes are prohibited during declared change freezes.
* Additional restrictions apply when error budgets are low (see “Change Freeze and Risk Assessment”).

h1. Execution requirements
sections.heading: Answer these before requesting approval

sections.body:
1. Use the documented runbook for the target system (Hosted API or Console).
2. Perform a canary rollout for traffic-bearing services unless explicitly exempted in the change record.
3. Confirm observability before and after (golden signals and specific dashboards).
4. Have a clearly defined rollback trigger and a “stop the line” principle.

h1. Communications requirements
Change owner must determine if customer communications are required:
* *Planned maintenance:* Status page notice and direct customer comms if any material impact is expected.
* *No expected customer impact:* Internal announcement in #eng-releases and on-call awareness if during core hours.
See “Planned Maintenance and Change Communications” for templates and required lead time.

h1. Post-change validation and closure
Within 60 minutes after completion, the change owner must:
* Validate key SLO metrics and error rates are within normal bounds
* Confirm canary is healthy before full rollout
* Update the change record with results and attach screenshots/links
* File follow-ups for any issues discovered

h1. References
* Prod Deployment Gates (Hosted API + Console)
* Hosted API Deploy Runbook
* Console Deploy Runbook
* Rollback and Post-change Validation
* Change Freeze and Risk Assessment
* Secure SDLC: Security Review Requirements for Prod Changes
* Planned Maintenance and Change Communications
sections.heading: All production changes must

payload.page_title: Production rollout approvals (change management)

sections.body: All production changes that can affect customer traffic must follow this approval policy. Model rollouts for the Hosted API qualify as production changes.
sections.heading: Policy summary

sections.body:
- new model version rollouts
- changing routing policies (including enabling or tuning automatic fallback)
- changing serving configuration that affects output, latency, or cost (e.g., quantization profile)
sections.heading: A change record is required for

sections.body:
- Change title and description
- Impact radius (routes, regions, customer pins)
- Rollout plan and rollback plan
- Owner/DRI and on-call coverage during execution
- Links to relevant runbooks and dashboards
- Evidence of readiness (eval report or reference to Applied ML gates)
sections.heading: Required information in the change record

sections.body:
- **Low risk** (default canary, no new regions, no new API features):
  - Platform Eng DRI approval
- **Medium risk** (fast canary, change to fallback triggers, large traffic share shift):
  - Platform Eng DRI approval
  - SRE approval
- **High risk** (new model family, tokenizer change for default route, major behavior change):
  - Platform Eng DRI approval
  - SRE approval
  - Applied ML approval
  - Product approval
sections.heading: Approvals required before execution

sections.body:
- Changes should be executed during defined business-hours windows for the owning region unless there is an incident response need.
- Avoid executing at the same time as known fleet maintenance events.
sections.heading: Timing

sections.body:
- Monitor for at least 60 minutes after reaching 100% traffic.
- Record outcome (success, partial rollback, full rollback) and attach dashboard screenshots or links.
- File follow-ups for any anomalies observed, even if rollback was not required.

payload.page_title: Emergency Change Policy (Production) — v3

sections.body:
h2. Purpose
This policy defines minimum requirements for *Emergency Changes* to Redwood production systems. Emergency changes are allowed to restore service or mitigate critical customer impact, but they must remain safe, auditable, and reversible.

h2. Scope
Applies to Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, control plane, serving runtime, routing, and any customer-impacting production service or configuration change.

h2. Definitions
*Emergency Change* = a change needed immediately to address: (a) Sev-1 incident, (b) active security exploit, (c) data loss/corruption risk, or (d) widespread outage/severe degradation.
*Hotfix* = emergency patch to a released component intended for expedited rollout.

h2. Required approvals (cannot be skipped)
All emergency changes must have *two-person approval* before production impact:
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Security-related or suspected exploit: *Security on-call*
* Customer-visible behavior change (responses/routing/model selection): *Product on-call* or responsible PM
* Any change requiring customer maintenance coordination (Dedicated/Private): *Customer Success escalation manager*

h2. Minimum checklist
sections.heading: Additional approvals based on scenario

sections.body:
* Hypothesis for the fix
* Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/customers; model families)
* Rollback plan with explicit trigger (metric or customer symptom)
* Risk assessment: data integrity, security, performance
* What is changing (code vs config vs infra)
* Owner for post-change monitoring

h2. Documentation and audit requirements
* Create/link a ticket (Linear preferred; Jira acceptable).
* Open a GitHub PR (even if fast-tracked) OR link to an existing PR and commit SHA.
* Record approvals in PR review, incident thread, or change record comment.
* Update incident timeline with: start time, change time, outcome.

h2. Rollout constraints
* Use a canary wherever possible (one Hosted region or a single Dedicated cluster) before broad rollout.
* If canary is not possible, document why and get IC sign-off.
* Do not deploy unrelated changes under one emergency change record.

h2. Post-change requirements
sections.heading: Record in ticket/PR/incident timeline

sections.body:
* Create follow-up in incident review (root cause, change made, why it worked).
* Document any deviations from normal release procedures and corrective actions.
* Remove any temporary flags/throttles (owner + deadline).

h2. Related pages
* /oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/sev1-communication-requirements
* /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/serving-runtime-hotfix-runbook
* /eng-platform/runbooks/hosted-rollout-and-rollback-procedure
* /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/hotfix-build-and-signing
