payload.page_title: Enterprise Operations Playbook: Access, Change, Data & Procurement

sections.body:
Overview
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s company-wide operational policies and reusable templates for: access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor management, travel, and internal templates. It is intended for people managers, engineers proposing changes, procurement requesters, security reviewers, and finance approvers. Use the checklists and templates in the final section when beginning a request.

Principles and governance
- Principle: Least privilege by default. Access is granted at the minimum level required and reviewed quarterly.
- Principle: Segregation of duties for procurement and change approvals where feasible.
- Principle: Data classification drives retention, access controls, and encryption requirements.
- Principle: Risk-based change management — low-risk operational changes may be expedited; high-risk, customer-impacting changes require formal approvals and rollback plans.

1) Access & permissions (high level)
Purpose: Define how to request, approve, and revoke access to internal services, cloud accounts, and sensitive datasets.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Requester: Employee submitting the access request.
- Manager: Verifies business justification and endorses.
- Owner (service/data owner): Grants final approval for resources they manage.
- IAM Team: Executes the access change and records the ticket.
- Security: Periodic auditor for privileged roles.
sections.heading: Key roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
- Tier 0 — Privileged administrative: root cloud accounts, KMS/HSM admin, production database admin. Approval: Director+ and Security. Review cadence: monthly.
- Tier 1 — Production service operators: deployment writers, runtime admins. Approval: Service owner + Engineering Manager. Review cadence: quarterly.
- Tier 2 — Internal tooling and analytics: dashboards, non-sensitive logs. Approval: Team manager. Review cadence: semi-annually.
- Tier 3 — Public/non-sensitive access: marketing tools, public docs. Approval: Team manager. Review cadence: annually.
sections.heading: Access tiers and examples

sections.body:
1. Requester files an access request via /tools/iam-requests (use template below). Include justification, duration (if temporary), and resources.
2. Manager endorses within 48 business hours.
3. Service/data owner reviews and approves or rejects within 3 business days.
4. IAM team implements and posts the ticket update with artifact of permission change (IAM policy diff, Terraform plan snippet).
5. For temporary access, IAM sets an expiration. Expired grants are auto-revoked and generate a compliance log.
sections.heading: Standard request process (numbered)

sections.body:
- Process: Pager duty to on-call identity engineer + security notify channel. Emergency grants must be requested with a post-facto justification and will be audited. Any break-glass grant must be short-lived (max 24 hours) and converted to a controlled access path if needed longer.

2) Change management (standardized flow)
Scope: Applies to infra, runtime, networking, and customer-impacting application changes. Software-only feature flags that do not change infra are exempt if covered by automated test gates and SLO guardrails.
sections.heading: Emergency access (break-glass)

sections.body:
- Standard change: Pre-approved routine changes with documented playbooks (e.g., routine config tweak). Approval: No additional approvals required; must follow runbook.
- Minor change: Low-risk code or infra change. Approval: Team lead + automated CI green. Implementation window: standard maintenance hours.
- Major change: Any change affecting production latency, availability, or data model. Approval: Service owner + SRE + Product manager + go/no-go meeting. Requires written rollback plan and canary plan.
- Emergency change: Pushed outside formal schedule for incident mitigation. Retrospective required within 72 hours and RCA if customer impact.

Change request (CR) template (fields to include in the ticket):
- Title, owner, change type, business justification, impact analysis, roll-forward steps, rollback steps, test plan, monitoring/alerting adjustments, scheduled window, approvers, related incidents, preconditions.

Pre-deployment checklist (must be completed for Major changes):
- Unit + integration tests green.
- Load and perf tests run against representative data (target latencies within 10% of baseline).
- Monitoring dashboards prepared (new panels if needed).
- Alert thresholds defined and tested.
- Canary plan: traffic percentage, duration, metrics to evaluate, abort criteria.
sections.heading: Change categories and approval matrix

sections.body:
- Canary for 5–10% for at least 30 minutes under normal load before increasing.
- Abort criteria: error rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes above baseline, p95 latency increase > 30% for 5 minutes, or any customer-visible failures.
- Rollback action: execute documented rollback steps and open an incident.

3) Data management (classification, retention, and handling)
sections.heading: Rollout and rollback guidance

sections.body:
- Confidential — customer PII, secrets, audit logs with identifiers. Controls: encryption at rest and in transit (AES-256 + TLS1.3), strict RBAC, additional DLP scans, retention policy 1–7 years depending on contract. Access requires Tier 0/1 approvals.
- Internal — internal telemetry, non-identifying logs, internal docs. Controls: RBAC, encrypted at rest, retention 1 year default.
- Public — marketing assets, public docs, open-source artifacts. Controls: public by default.

Retention and deletion policy (summary table described in text):
- Core customer records: retention 7 years unless contract specifies otherwise. Deletion requires data owner sign-off and a documented deletion runbook.
- Audit logs: retention 3 years for security logs, 90 days for operational logs unless investigation ongoing.
- Temp artifacts (scratch buckets): auto-delete after 30 days.
sections.heading: Data classification (three tiers)

sections.body:
- All Confidential data must never be stored in personal devices or unapproved cloud storage.
- Use approved ETL pipelines for moving data; ad-hoc exports require manager + security approval and must be tracked in the Data Export Registry.
- For datasets used in evals or research, apply anonymization steps (hashing, token removal) and document transformation steps in the dataset manifest.
sections.heading: Data handling requirements

sections.body:
1. Immediate containment: remove access to affected systems, rotate related credentials.
2. Notify Security immediately and open a breach incident (critical).
3. Begin forensic capture following Security runbook; notify Legal and Customer Success as required by contracts.
4. Communicate to impacted customers per contract SLAs and regulatory obligations.

4) Procurement & expenses (practical thresholds and templates)
sections.heading: Breach and suspected exposure process (high level)

sections.body:
- Micro purchases (< $1,000): Team manager approval. Use corporate card or expense tool.
- Standard purchases ($1,000–$25,000): Department head + Finance approval. Requires vendor record creation if new.
- Capital / Contracted services (> $25,000): Procurement + Legal + Finance + Director-level sign-off; requires vendor SLA and security questionnaire.
sections.heading: Procurement approval levels

sections.body:
1. Requester fills the Purchase Request form (template below) with justification, cost center, and preferred vendor.
2. Procurement validates vendor (existing vendor? security & compliance questionnaire).
3. Finance reserves budget and issues PO if required.
4. Legal reviews contract terms if > $25k or if vendor handles confidential data.
5. Procurement completes purchase and records vendor in Vendor Registry.
6. Post-purchase: submit receipts/ invoices to expenses@redwood.com and mark invoice against PO.
sections.heading: Vendor onboarding and expense flow (numbered)

sections.body:
- Booking: Use company travel tool; all international travel must be pre-approved by manager + People Ops for visa/insurance coordination.
- Class: Domestic economy for flights under 4 hours; premium economy or business only with Director approval for flights > 8 hours or medical/crew exceptions.
- Per diem and accommodation: Follow rate card in Travel Template. Higher-cost options require justification and manager approval.
- Expenses: Submit receipts within 10 business days. Unreported expenses after 60 days may be rejected.
- Safety: Employees traveling to high-risk regions require manager and Security sign-off and must register itineraries with People Ops.
sections.heading: Travel policy highlights (for traveler convenience)

sections.body:
- Manager approves up to $1,000/month per employee.
- Dept head approves $1,000–$5,000.
- Finance approves $5,000–$25,000.
- Director-level and Procurement for > $25,000.

5) Vendor management and security integration
sections.heading: Expense approval matrix (in text)

sections.body:
- Tier A — Highly sensitive (handles Confidential data or infra access). Requirements: full security questionnaire, penetration test results or SOC2 Type II, encryption controls, contractual SLAs, and periodic reviews every 6 months.
- Tier B — Moderate risk (SaaS with no customer-identifiable data). Requirements: standard security questionnaire and annual review.
- Tier C — Low risk (marketing, office supplies vendors). Requirements: minimal record in Vendor Registry.
sections.heading: Vendor risk tiers

sections.body:
- Initial intake: business case, procurement form, vendor questionnaire.
- Security assessment: Security + Product review for data handling capability.
- Contract negotiation: Legal + Finance. Include termination rights and data return/destruction clauses.
- Onboarding: Enter vendor into Vendor Registry and configure payments.
- Quarterly/annual review: performance, SLA compliance, security posture.

6) Internal templates and artifacts (copy & use)
sections.heading: Vendor lifecycle checklist (short)

sections.body:
- Access Request Template (fields: requester, resources, justification, duration, manager)
- Change Request Template (fields: title, owner, type, rollback steps, canary plan)
- Purchase Request Template (fields: budget code, vendor, line items, approvers)
- Travel Request Template (fields: trip reason, dates, approver, estimated cost)
- Vendor Onboarding Checklist (fields: risk tier, questionnaire link, contract ID)

Sample: Access Request Template (single-line JSON for programmatic use)
{ "requester": "<name>", "email": "<name@redwood.com>", "resource": "<service-or-bucket>", "level": "Tier 1", "justification": "<business-need>", "duration_days": "30", "manager": "<manager-name>" }

Sample: Change Request Checklist (copy into CR ticket)
- CR title:
- Owner and contact:
- Impacted services and paths:
- Canary metrics and thresholds:
- Rollback steps (explicit commands or runbook references):
- Post-deploy validation steps:

Operational runbooks and useful commands (examples)
- Deploy rollback (example for service-x):
  - kubectl -n prod set image deploy/service-x service-x=<previous-image>
  - kubectl rollout status deploy/service-x -n prod
- Revoke temporary AWS key (IAM):
  - aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id <KEYID> --status Inactive --user-name <user>
- Generate minimal Terraform plan snippet to show permission diffs:
  - terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan && terraform show -json plan.tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[] | {address, change: .change}'

Compliance, audit, and reporting
- Quarterly access certification: managers receive an automated list of direct reports’ privileged access and must certify or revoke.
- Procurement spend reporting: Finance publishes monthly departmental spend summaries and flags any single-vendor concentration > 30% of category spend.
- Change audits: All Major changes must attach a CR and monitoring snapshots; SRE will randomly audit 10% of Major changes each quarter.

Escalation and exception process
- To request an exception to any policy, open an Exceptions ticket in /tools/policy-exceptions with: policy referenced, duration requested, compensating controls, and approver signatures. Exceptions longer than 90 days require Director-level approval and a sunset plan.

Appendix: Contacts and owners
- People Ops (policy owner): people-ops@redwood.com (owner: Aisha Kapoor)
- IAM & Identity team: iam@redwood.com (lead: Daniel Hsu)
- Security (policy advisory): security@redwood.com (lead: Marta Lopez)
- Procurement & Finance: procurement@redwood.com (lead: Ethan Park)
- On-call SRE: see internal rota linked in monitoring console.

How to use this playbook
- For any request, start by selecting the relevant template above and attach it to the ticket.
- If in doubt about classification or approvals, tag Security and People Ops in your ticket for a rapid consult.
- This playbook will be reviewed annually; suggested edits may be submitted via a PR to the Policies repo or by emailing people-ops@redwood.com.

Document history
- 2024-10-15: Created by Aisha Kapoor.
- 2024-12-10: Procurement thresholds updated; added vendor risk tiers.
- 2025-02-12: Added canary guidance and change abort thresholds.

Attachments and templates (links)
- Access Request form: /confluence/templates/access-request-form
- Change Request form: /confluence/templates/change-request-form
- Purchase Request form: /confluence/templates/purchase-request-form
- Vendor questionnaire: /confluence/templates/vendor-security-questionnaire

End of document

payload.page_title: Incident Prioritization and Capacity Evidence Manifest

sections.body:
Summary
======

This page defines the Incident Prioritization and Capacity Evidence Manifest: a concise, reproducible rubric that engineers, oncall responders, and SRE tooling use to (1) score incidents for prioritization, (2) determine pre-approved capacity actions, and (3) produce a complete evidence bundle for post-incident review. The goal is to reduce subjective decisions during high-pressure incidents and to accelerate capacity-safe remediation.

When to use this manifest
------------------------
- Any multi-tenant or service-impacting event where SLO burn exceeds 3% in a 15-minute window.
- Any sustained latency tail (p95 -> p99.9 delta > 2x expected range for 30+ minutes).
- Any unexpected backend OOMs, queue growth, or cold-start cascades affecting routing/throughput.

Primary outcomes
----------------
1. A numeric incident priority (P0, P1, P2, P3) computed via evidence scoring.
2. A capacity action recommendation: NO_ACTION / SOFT_SCALE / HARD_SCALE / THROTTLE / EVICT.
3. A structured evidence bundle (telemetry, traces, sample requests, config snapshot) saved to the incident record.

Evidence types and weights (manifest table)
-------------------------------------------
The manifest uses a weighted scoring system. Evidence items are collected automatically where possible and manually validated by the responder. Scores are additive; thresholds map to a priority and to allowed capacity actions.

| Evidence type | Short id | Weight | Required for P0? | Notes |
|---------------|---------:|-------:|:----------------:|-------|
| SLO burn rate (15m) | slo15 | 40 | Yes | Measured as percentage points above baseline; baseline=expected 15m burn.
| Error surge (5m) | err5 | 25 | Yes | Rate of 5xx per 1k requests vs baseline.
| Tail latency delta | tail | 20 | Yes | p99.9 - p95 relative delta, normalized to expected tail.
| Queue length growth | qlen | 10 | No | Percent growth in service incoming queue over 10m.
| OOM or resource faults | oom | 30 | Yes | Boolean; if true, treat as hard signal.
| Traffic imbalance (region) | region | 8 | No | Delta of traffic routed to region vs median.
| Config change in last 30m | cfg | 15 | No | Link to change-id and diff.
| Canary evaluation failures | can | 20 | No | Failing canary checks for model or infra rollouts.
| Customer-impact reports | cust | 12 | No | Verified customer complaint count in last 30m.
| Synthetic canary failures | synth | 12 | No | From synthetic probes; include run id.

Scoring algorithm
-----------------
1. Gather available evidence and compute a total score = sum(weight * normalized_value). For boolean signals (OOM, config change) normalized_value is 1 if true, 0 otherwise. For proportion signals (slo15, err5, tail) normalized_value is a capped ratio: min(1, observed / threshold).
2. Normalize total_score to a 0-100 scale for mapping. Example mapping (tunable):
   - 75+ -> P0 (Immediate incident; pre-approved hard-capacity + mitigation).
   - 50-74 -> P1 (High; soft-scale + targeted throttles).
   - 30-49 -> P2 (Medium; routing adjustments + cache priming).
   - <30 -> P3 (Investigate; no aggressive capacity changes).

Capacity action mapping (policy)
-------------------------------
- P0: HARD_SCALE allowed (provision reserved nodes or burst capacity), EVICT allowed (tenant eviction on authorization), immediate rollback of recent config/rollout if cfg or can are true. Throttle policies may be applied only after scaling if scaling fails.
- P1: SOFT_SCALE recommended (warm pool expansion, increase concurrent slots by up to 30%), targeted THROTTLE for heavy tenants, enable additional batching or KV-prefetch caches.
- P2: NO_ACTION / ROUTE_ADJUST recommended (shift traffic within region), enable non-disruptive cache refresh.
- P3: INVESTIGATE; capture evidence and follow up.

Pre-approval matrix and guardrails
---------------------------------
- Engineering managers for affected services pre-authorize per-service burst limits and eviction tolerance in the service manifest. See service manifest key fields: "burst_limit_nodes", "eviction_allowed", "priority_tenants".
- Hard_scale actions must be invoked by a responder with role: "sre-lead" or via automation if score >= 85. Manual hard scale requires an entry in the incident comments with change-id and expected rollback window.
- Eviction for multi-tenant isolation requires sign-off from product on call or SRE director unless eviction is for a single tenant producing >50% of SLO burn.

Example CLI snippets and API calls
---------------------------------
- Retrieve 15m SLO burn: curl -sS \"https://telemetry.internal/api/v1/slo/burn?srv=MODEL-SERVING&window=15m\" | jq '.burn'
- Request soft-scale: rscale --service MODEL-SERVING --type soft --percent 25 --reason "P1 soft-scale auto-recommendation"
- Trigger eviction (automated, limited): evict-tenant --service MODEL-SERVING --tenant-id tenant-42 --grace 120 --auth-token $SRE_TOKEN
- Capture evidence bundle: incident-cli evidence capture --incident $INC_ID --include traces,metrics,config --output s3://inc-bundles/$INC_ID.tar.gz

Evidence bundle contents (required)
-----------------------------------
Every incident record where score >= 30 must have an evidence bundle attached with the following files/links:
- metrics.json (15m and 5m aggregations for latency, errors, qlen)
- top-traces.json (top 50 traces by duration and error)
- sample-requests.log (up to 200 anonymized requests with headers and latencies)
- config-diff.patch (git diff for services changed in last 30m) or "no-conf-changes" marker
- autoscale-actions.log (any autoscaling or scale requests made during the incident)
- routing-snapshot.json (live routing table and policies)

Incident playbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1. Detection & initial score (first 5 minutes):
   a. Pager fires or synthetic indicates failure. Open incident with template "capacity-evidence-manifest".
   b. Run automated evidence-collector (incident-cli evidence capture --quick). Collector fills initial values for slo15, err5, tail, qlen, region.
   c. Compute initial score and annotate incident: /incident annotate --score 72 --reason "slo15=0.8, err5=0.6, oom=0".
2. Triage (5-20 minutes):
   a. Identify owner service and run runbook: runbook exec service-owner-checklist.
   b. If score >= 75, escalate to SRE lead and consider HARD_SCALE via automation if pre-approval exists.
   c. If OOM detected (oom=1), prioritize memory stabilization: reduce concurrency, disable largest batchers, apply config rollback if recent change present.
3. Containment & mitigation (20-60 minutes):
   a. Apply recommended capacity action. Document commands and expected effect.
   b. Apply targeted throttles for heavy tenants: throttle --tenant tenant-42 --rate 0.2 --duration 30m.
   c. If scaling is constrained, apply graceful degradation routes (modes: short-responses, stubbed embeddings, reduced beam width).
4. Recovery verification (60+ minutes):
   a. Confirm SLO burn rate is decreasing over three consecutive 5m windows.
   b. Roll back temporary throttles and verify stability for 30 minutes before full rollback of scaling.
5. Evidence finalization & severity confirmation:
   a. Ensure evidence bundle is attached.
   b. Confirm final priority and enter remediation tasks (owner, ETA, MTTD, MTR).

Post-incident review requirements
--------------------------------
- If final priority was P0 or P1, convene a 1-hour postmortem within 5 business days. Required deliverables: timeline, evidence bundle link, root cause hypothesis, mitigation plan, owners, and scheduled follow-up (calendar invite).
- Postmortem must score the original incident scoring accuracy (was the computed score predictive of severity?). Include a short retro on thresholds and weight tuning.

Operational tooling integration points
-------------------------------------
- Telemetry pipeline: evidence-collector plugin must be wired into the SLO pipeline (namespace: slo.compute.v1). It provides slo15 and err5 signals.
- Incident CLI: incident-cli must implement automatic capture hooks for traces and metrics and produce the evidence bundle described above.
- Autoscale API: rscale service must accept signed requests from incident automation with a TTL and rollback hint. Every scale request must be logged to autoscale-actions.log and surfaced in the incident UI.
- Eviction service: evict-tenant must implement a dry-run mode and an audit webhook to record approvals.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Service owners (on-call rotation): ensure service manifest contains burst limits and eviction policy.
- SRE tooling team: maintain incident-cli, evidence-collector, and rscale integrations.
- SRE leads: authority to approve hard scale and eviction during P0 events per the pre-approval matrix.

Tuning playbook and cadence
---------------------------
- Quarterly review: the weights in the manifest and the score->priority mapping are reviewed end of quarter by SRE tooling + service leads. Adjust thresholds based on incident history and cost/availability tradeoffs.
- After a P0 incident: immediately convene a calibration session to test the score against the incident timeline and update weights if false positives/negatives occurred.

Appendices
---------
A. Example metrics.json snippet
{
  "service": "MODEL-SERVING",
  "window": "15m",
  "slo_burn_pct": 7.3,
  "error_rate_per_k": 4.2,
  "p95": 210,
  "p99_9": 980
}

B. Change approval template (for manual hard scale)
- Incident ID: {INC_ID}
- Requested action: HARD_SCALE + burst 20 nodes
- Justification: sudden p99.9 tail and OOMs in worker pool
- Expected rollback window: 120 minutes
- Approver: {SRE_LEAD}

C. Quick checklist for post-incident evidence verification
- [ ] metrics.json attached and matches incident timeline
- [ ] top-traces.json includes representative errors
- [ ] config diff attached or explicit marker present
- [ ] autoscale-actions.log present and annotated
- [ ] routing-snapshot captures the time-of-incident routes

If anything on this page conflicts with a service manifest (stored in service-configs repo), the service manifest takes precedence for burst limits and eviction policies.

For questions or tooling requests, contact the SRE tooling team (sre-tooling@redwood.ai) or open a ticket in the SRE queue.

payload.page_title: Edge prefetch topology and decision tree for latency-sensitive tenants

sections.body:
Summary

This document describes the recommended edge prefetch topology and an operational decision tree used to configure and troubleshoot prefetch behavior for latency-sensitive tenants. It defines the components, deployment topology, policy model, SLO targets and thresholds, monitoring dashboards, and a step-by-step rollout and incident playbook. The guidance is intended for platform operators, runtime engineers, and on-call operators.

Scope and intent

- Scope: Prefetching of model input prefixes, KV-cache priming, and small-response artifacts at the edge and regional ingress points for Redwood Inference hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Intent: Reduce foreground token latency for low-latency tenants without exceeding tail-cost or destabilizing shared GPU pools.
- Not covered: Long-term offline caching strategies (see cache-prefetch-prioritization-for-llm-workloads), on-prem customer-specific KMS details.

Key components and service names

- edge-router: L7 routing layer in regional PoPs. Responsible for request classification and hint propagation.
- prefetch-agent: Lightweight service colocated in edge PoPs that issues pre-warm/kv-priming requests to regional serving pools.
- kv-prefix-cache: Persistent prefix cache (namespace per-tenant) backed by Redis-cluster and sharded by tenant-score.
- request-classifier: gRPC microservice that applies tenant policy and assigns a prefetch score (0-100).
- prefix-cache-rebalancer: Offline/cron service that rebalances hot prefixes across Redis shards.
- traffic-telemetry: Metrics ingestion pipeline (Prometheus -> Cortex) and event bus for prefetch outcomes.

Topological overview (text diagram)

edge-router -> request-classifier -> if score >= threshold -> prefetch-agent -> regional-serving (warm path) -> kv-prefix-cache

If score < threshold -> direct-pass-through -> regional-serving (cold path)

prefetch-agent also emits telemetry to traffic-telemetry and writes prefetch attempts to a local short-lived LRU store for quick re-checks.

Decision tree and scoring heuristic

The decision tree converts signals into an integer score used by prefetch-agent. Signals (weighted):
- tenant-priority: numeric (0-100), owner_configured weight 0.4
- recent-hit-rate: rolling 5m % hit on prefix-cache weight 0.2
- request-size-category: categorical (short|medium|long) (short favors prefetch) weight 0.15
- latency-sensitivity-flag: boolean (from tenant profile) weight 0.15
- burst-counter: decaying counter to avoid over-prefetch weight -0.1 (penalty)

score = round(tenant-priority*0.4 + recent-hit-rate*0.2 + request_size_factor*0.15 + latency_flag*0.15 - burst_penalty*0.1)

Thresholds

- prefetch_score >= 65: trigger prefetch-agent (strong prefetch)
- 50 <= prefetch_score < 65: opportunistic prefetch if prefetch budget available
- prefetch_score < 50: no prefetch; request goes cold

Policy configuration table

| key | default | description |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| tenant_priority | 50 | Numeric tenant importance used in score calculation (0-100). Platform-managed for enterprise tiers. |
| prefetch_budget_tokens_per_min | 5000 | Soft budget of tokens usable for prefetch per tenant per minute. |
| burst_penalty_decay_minutes | 10 | Decay window for burst penalty counter. |
| edge_prefetch_timeout_ms | 120 | How long prefetch-agent waits for a warm response before aborting prefetch. |
| max_concurrent_prefetches | 20 | Max parallel prefetch RPCs initiated by prefetch-agent per PoP. |

YAML example (policy snippet)

policy: |
  tenant_id: tenant-42
  tenant_priority: 80
  prefetch_budget_tokens_per_min: 10000
  rules:
    - name: short-convo-fast-path
      match: request_size == 'short' and latency_flag == true
      action: prefetch
      max_parallel: 8

CLI and debug commands

- View runtime score and last decisions for a request-id:
  curl -s http://edge-router.internal/debug/decision?request_id=<REQUEST_ID> | jq
- Stream prefetch-agent logs (PoP eu-west-1):
  kubectl -n infra logs -l app=prefetch-agent -l region=eu-west-1 -f
- Inspect tenant prefetch budget usage (Prometheus):
  sum by (tenant_id) (rate(prefetch_tokens_consumed_total[1m]))

Operational SLOs and thresholds

- Foreground P95 token generation latency (tenant-tagged) target: <= 120ms for tenants with latency_flag=true (SLO enforcement on-service).
- Prefetch hit-rate SLI: >= 65% (measured as prefetch_probe_hits / prefetch_probes over 5m). Alert if < 55% for 10m.
- Prefetch cost budget burn rate: platform warns at 70% of monthly token budget, auto-throttles at 90%.
- Max prefetch-induced tail latency: 99th-percentile additional CPU/GPU scheduling delay <= 80ms.

Dashboards and alerting
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Prefetch success rate (5m, 1m): prefetch_probe_hits / prefetch_probes by region and tenant_tier.
- Token budget consumption: prefetch_tokens_consumed_total by tenant.
- Prefetch latency distribution: histogram of prefetch round-trip times.
- Decision tree breakdown: proportion of requests in each score bucket.
- Hot-prefix churn: top-100 prefixes by cache-write-rate.
sections.heading: Recommended dashboard panels (traffic-telemetry / Grafana)

sections.body:
1) prefetch_hit_rate_low
   - expr: (sum(prefetch_probe_hits[10m]) / sum(prefetch_probes[10m])) < 0.55
   - for: 10m
   - severity: major
   - runbook: see Incident playbook section below
2) prefetch_budget_burn_high
   - expr: sum(prefetch_tokens_consumed_total{window="30d"}) / tenant_prefetch_quota > 0.9
   - for: 5m
   - severity: critical
   - action: throttle tenant prefetch and page owner_team oncall

Rollout and change management

1. Canary (dev-pop): enable for 5 developer tenants with tenant_priority >= 70. Monitor prefetch_hit_rate and budget burn for 48h.
2. Regional pilot (single region, small set of enterprise tenants): expand to 10 tenants, 72h monitoring window.
3. Staged ramp: increase by 2x tenants/day for 7 days if metrics stable.
4. Global enable: gradual 10% tenant cohort expansion per day with automated rollback trigger if prefetch_hit_rate < 55% or budget burn > 90%.
sections.heading: Alerting rules (Prometheus)

sections.body:
- sustained prefetch_hit_rate < 50% for 15 minutes
- prefetch_budget_burn rate > 95% for 5 minutes
- 99th percentile scheduling delay increase > 150ms associated with prefetch-agent calls

Incident playbook (on-call operator)

1) Triage: Confirm alert and scope (single-tenant vs multi-tenant vs regional). Use dashboard: Decision tree breakdown, Prefetch success rate, Token budget consumption.
2) Short-term mitigation (0-15min):
   - If single tenant: set tenant_policy.prefetch_enabled = false for the tenant via admin CLI and notify CSE/SRE.
   - If multi-tenant regional regression: reduce max_concurrent_prefetches to 4 in affected PoP: kubectl patch deployment/prefetch-agent -n infra --patch '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"prefetch-agent","env":[{"name":"MAX_CONCURRENT_PREFETCHES","value":"4"}]}]}}}}'
3) Root cause analysis (15m-3h):
   - Check recent prefix churn and prefix-cache evictions: redis_exporter metrics and prefix-cache-rebalancer logs.
   - Verify regional network egress errors between PoP and regional-serving.
   - Correlate with recent model rollouts or kernel changes (see runtime release notes).
4) Permanent remediation (3h+):
   - Tune scoring weights or raise tenant_priority for valid enterprise requirements.
   - Add or resize Redis shards if eviction rate sustained > 5%.
   - Adjust prefetch budget policy or move heavy tenants to dedicated pools.

Owner and responsibilities

- Runtime Platform (owner): implement and maintain prefetch-agent and request-classifier. Primary contact: @maya.chen
- Edge Infra: operate edge-router and PoP-level health. Primary contact: @liam.oconnor
- Observability: own dashboards and Prometheus rules. Primary contact: @anika.rao

Postmortem and retrospective guidance

- When an incident involves prefetch: produce a focused retrospective that includes the decision-tree trace for sampled requests, prefetch budget timelines, and a prefix churn analysis.
- Suggested retrospective template: summary, timeline, impact matrix (tenants affected + SLOs missed), root cause, corrective actions (with owners), and a verification plan.

Appendix: quick reference commands and queries

- Query per-tenant prefetch hit rate in Prometheus:
  sum by (tenant_id) (increase(prefetch_probe_hits[5m])) / sum by (tenant_id) (increase(prefetch_probes[5m]))
- Disable prefetch for tenant (admin API):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' -d '{"tenant_id":"tenant-42","prefetch_enabled":false}' https://admin.internal/api/v1/tenant/policies

References and related reading

- cache-prefetch-prioritization-for-llm-workloads (internal)
- tenant-isolation-economics-playbook-2026 (internal)
- runtime-architecture/prefix-cache-and-kv-sharding (internal)

Document maintenance

- Owner: Runtime Platform (engineering). Review cadence: quarterly or after any incident that involves prefetch.
- Last reviewed: 2026-02-14 by Liam O'Connor and Anika Rao.

payload.page_title: Standby Augmentation Playbook — Holiday & Critical Capacity

sections.body: This playbook defines the process for activating, operating, and retiring a temporary standby augmentation cohort when Redwood faces predictable holiday staffing gaps or unexpected critical capacity stress (GPU exhaustion, region-wide quota loss, or sudden tenancy storms). It describes activation criteria, roles, communication templates for status pages and customer notices, runbook actions during augmentation, and post-incident handoff and compensation steps.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Purpose: Ensure safe, auditable, and fast onboarding of extra responders (internal volunteers, contractors, or cross-functional engineers) to maintain SLOs and customer trust during periods when primary on-call capacity is reduced or overwhelmed.
- Scope: Applies to all Redwood-hosted inference production environments (hosted API, Dedicated control plane endpoints, Private ops where Redwood provides operational support). Does NOT replace normal incident command; it augments responder capacity and bridge coverage.
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
1) Scheduled staffing shortfall: 40%+ of scheduled primary responders unavailable for a contiguous 8-hour period (e.g., major US/EMEA holiday windows).
2) Capacity emergency: Sustained GPU utilization > 92% across > 2 availability zones for 10+ minutes with queued requests growing by > 25% vs baseline.
3) SLO at-risk: Token-latency P95 > 3x baseline or error-rate (5xx) increase > 3x for 5+ minutes and automated mitigation has not stabilized.
sections.heading: Primary activation triggers (any of the following)

sections.body:
- Confirm incident classification in PagerDuty and link to the incident ID.
- Verify that primary on-call leads have attempted first-line mitigations: autoscale triggers, traffic shape, fallback routing.
- Obtain approval from the Contingency Coordinator (role defined below) if activation is out-of-band.
sections.heading: Pre-checks before activation

sections.body:
- Contingency Coordinator (CC): Senior SRE or SRE Manager who authorizes augmentation, assigns bridge, and approves customer notices. Ownership: eng-sre.
- Bridge Operator (BO): Person running the incident bridge and status page. Primary BO remains the incident commander or an assigned bridge operator.
- Standby Cohort Lead (SCL): Triage lead for the augmentation cohort — responsible for onboarding volunteers, distributing runbook tasks, and tracking action items.
- Standby Responder (SR): Volunteer or contracted engineer who executes focused runbook tasks (cache eviction, traffic routing, autoscaler tuning).
- Customer Comms Liaison (CCL): Owns external-facing messages and coordinates with account teams for enterprise customers. Typically from customer-success/eng-ops.
sections.heading: Roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
- Minimum cohort size: 3 responders per affected region for low-severity augmentations; 5+ for capacity-critical events.
- Max cohort tenure without rotation: 6 hours continuous work followed by mandatory 6-hour cool-down or handoff.
- Authorization: All SRs must have completed the Standby Safety Checklist (see below) and be on the valid escalation roster.

Standby Safety Checklist (must be completed before SR is placed on bridge):
1) Verified PagerDuty access and silence/ack privileges.
2) Confirmed read access to incident dashboards and traces.
3) Completed required runbook digest (15-minute read).
4) Communication channel test (bridge + slack + paging).
5) Agreed to cohort code of conduct and action logging.
sections.heading: Standby cohort composition and rules

sections.body:
1) CC confirms trigger and announces intent to activate standby in the incident channel.
2) BO creates a new cohort channel: #incident-<id>-standby and invites SCL and SRs.
3) SCL runs onboarding checklist with each SR (5–10 minutes per person).
4) BO updates the incident bridge header and status page with: "Standby augmentation active — additional responder cohort mobilized."
5) CCL drafts customer-facing short notice for status page (see templates).
6) SCL assigns clear tickets/tasks from the augmentation runbook and tracks in the incident board (Jira/linear).
7) Measure and report: SCL reports cohort headcount, primary tasks, and time on cohort start in the bridge cadence every 15 minutes.

Augmentation runbook (common tasks — assign by SCL):
- Traffic triage and routing:
  - Promote fallback model variants for best-effort customers.
  - Throttle/shape new sessions for non-paying tiers.
  - CLI: curl -X POST https://infra-api.redwood.internal/v1/traffic/route -d '{"route":"fallback","percent":30}' (example).
- Autoscaler and capacity tuning:
  - Validate autoscaler health: kubectl -n inference get hpa; check CPU/GPU metrics /cloud-metrics/hpa.
  - Temporarily bump minimum pool size according to policy (requires CC approval for >20% change).
- KV/prefix cache operations:
  - Trigger selective cache eviction for noisy tenants. Cache eviction script: /ops/scripts/evict-noisy-tenants.sh tenant-list.txt
- Burst offloading to Dedicated or alternate region:
  - Initiate cross-region failover runbook: see section "cross-region failover".
- Logging and artifact capture:
  - Ensure all SR actions are timestamped and posted to incident log: /incident/logs/<id>. Keep short notes with command outputs.
sections.heading: Activation procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
Status page short (100–180 chars):
- "Active mitigation: additional responder cohort mobilized to stabilize inference capacity in region <region>. We are managing traffic and expect improved response within 30-60 minutes. — Redwood Ops"
Status page long (for severity > P2):
- "Impact: customers in <region> may experience elevated latency or delayed responses. Action: a standby responder cohort has been activated and we are routing traffic to fallback model variants and scaling pools. ETA for stabilization: 30–60 minutes. Next update: in 15 minutes. Contact: support@redwood.ai for urgent account-specific questions."
sections.heading: Communication templates (status page & customer-facing)

sections.body:
Subject: "Service notice — temporary capacity mitigation in <region>"
Body: "Hi <Name>,
We’re reaching out to let you know Redwood Ops has activated a temporary responder cohort to mitigate elevated inference latency observed in <region>. Actions in flight: fallback routing, autoscaler adjustments, and targeted cache eviction to reduce queuing. We do not anticipate data exposure; this is an operational mitigation. ETA for improvement: 30–90 minutes. If you have mission-critical requirements, reply and we’ll prioritize routing for your account.
Regards,
<CCL name> — Redwood Support"
sections.heading: Customer email (enterprise)

sections.body:
- Cadence: 00, 15, 30, 45 minute updates. SCL provides: active SR headcount, top-3 tasks, observed metrics (P95 latency, queued requests), and blockers.
- Evidence: Snap a 5-min metrics window and attach to the incident board. Use timestamped screenshots or query outputs.
sections.heading: Bridge cadence and operational reporting

sections.body:
- Sustained stabilization: token-latency P95 back within 1.2x baseline for 15 consecutive minutes and queued requests reduced to <10% above baseline.
- Capacity reclaimed: GPU utilization < 85% for 15 minutes with autoscaler settled.
- CC or incident commander signs off.
sections.heading: Deactivation triggers (choose earliest of)

sections.body:
1) SCL completes outstanding task list and updates incident board.
2) BO announces planned retirement on bridge and schedules final status page update.
3) SRs complete evidence capture and sign out in cohort channel.
4) CC authorizes cohort disband and documents duration and headcount.
5) CCL publishes deactivation note to status page and sends enterprise close note if required.

Post-incident: handoff, review, and compensation:
- Post-incident survey: All SRs must complete a 10-question quick survey describing blockers, suggested runbook changes, and readiness feedback within 48 hours.
- Postmortem owner: Assigned to the SCL within 24 hours. Postmortem must include augmentation timeline, headcount, actions performed, customer impact, and cost estimate for any burst capacity billed.
- Compensation: Volunteers receive standby credit (4 hours of paid time-off equivalent for each 6-hour augmentation shift), unless otherwise covered by contractor terms. Team leads must approve time-off credits.
sections.heading: Deactivation steps

sections.body:
1) Schedule a 60-minute drill each quarter that includes standby cohort activation.
2) Validate cohort channel creation and onboarding flows.
3) Test status page templates and external email pipeline.
4) Run a simulated cache eviction and autoscaler bump (no-op mode for safety) and collect diagnostic outputs.
5) Scorecard: onboarding < 10 minutes per SR, first task assignment < 5 minutes after cohort creation, status page update within 10 minutes.

Operational metrics and KPIs to track for continuous improvement:
- Mean time to cohort activation (goal: < 12 minutes from CC authorization).
- Mean task assignment time (goal: < 10 minutes).
- Cohort effectiveness: % reduction in queued requests within 30 minutes of activation (goal: 50%+).
- Volunteer health: % of SRs reporting fatigue or inability to continue post-shift (goal: < 10%).

Governance, training, and documentation maintenance:
- Review cadence: This playbook is reviewed quarterly by eng-sre and customer-success.
- Training: All potential SRs complete a 30-minute mandatory Lightweight Incident Onboarding course and pass a short quiz.
- Documentation: SCLs and CCs are responsible for incorporating lessons into the master augmentation runbook in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library.

Appendix A — Cross-region failover quick reference:
- Preconditions: legal/data residency check, capacity in target region > 20% free, and routing policy allows cross-region failover for impacted tenants.
- Steps (high level):
  1) Authorize CC and update bridge.
  2) Add temporary routing policy via infra API: POST /v1/routing/override {"from":"us-east-1","to":"us-west-2","tenants":[...]}
  3) Monitor SLOs in target region closely for hot spots.
  4) Rollback policy within 1 hour if adverse effects observed.

Appendix B — Quick templates and commands:
- Create cohort channel: /ops/scripts/create-cohort-channel.sh <incident-id>
- Evict-noisy-tenants example: /ops/scripts/evict-noisy-tenants.sh --threshold 0.7 --region us-east-1
- Sample metrics query (PromQL): rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (le)
sections.heading: Game-day checklist (pre-run rehearsal)

sections.body:
- Owner: eng-sre
- Document steward: Priya N. Sharma (author)
- Last review: 2026-03-02
- Next scheduled review: 2026-06-01
sections.heading: Document history and ownership

sections.body:
- Incident board template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-board-template
- Runbook library: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library
- PagerDuty escalation roster: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/escalation-roster
sections.heading: Related resources

sections.body: Standby augmentation is intentionally lightweight: the goal is rapid, auditable expansion of human capacity paired with narrowly scoped runbook tasks. This reduces blast radius compared to wholesale incident role changes while preserving accountability and evidence for post-incident review.

payload.page_title: Responder rotation synthesis and deferred postmortem protocol

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's responder rotation synthesis process and a lightweight Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol for incidents that meet defined criteria. It combines on-call scheduling practices, a structured bridge handoff procedure, and customer-facing messaging templates designed for speed and clarity. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during high-impact events and to ensure timely learning when full postmortems are not immediately practical.

Scope:
- Applies to: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, and Incident Response stakeholders.
- Excludes: low-priority alerts that resolve without human intervention (see 'Auto-resolved alerts' below).

Definitions:
- Responder rotation synthesis: periodic review and rebalancing of on-call shifts, handoffs, and escalation ladders to maintain equitable load and coverage.
- Deferred Postmortem (DPM): a time-boxed post-incident review that defers non-critical analysis until stakeholders are available, while still capturing root evidence and action items immediately.

Key principles:
1) Fast stabilization first: prioritize containment and customer impact minimization.
2) Minimal friction handoffs: standardized bridge transfer reduces repeated context overhead.
3) Continuous learning: short DPMs for low-severity incidents; full postmortems for Sev1/Sev2.
4) Equity in rotations: no responder assigned >36 hours continuous duty without relief.

On-call rotation design (synthesis process):
1. Quarterly synthesis review (owner: SRE lead):
   - Pull the last quarter's on-call logs and pager counts.
   - Calculate median and 95th percentile pager counts per responder.
   - Identify top-10% busiest windows and common root causes.
2. Rebalance rules:
   - Move noisy services to a dedicated micro-rotation if they account for >25% of pages.
   - Limit night-weekend primary duty to volunteers in the rotation unless emergency staffing required.
3. Local fairness check (monthly):
   - Team leads run a 15-minute review in the first week of each month to confirm schedule fairness and swap if needed.

Rotation constraints (config):
| Constraint | Value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Max continuous on-call | 36h | Prevent fatigue and degraded decision-making |
| Minimum handoff overlap | 15m | Time to summarize bridge state and outstanding actions |
| Max weekly duty | 56h | Prevent single-responder overload across teams |
| Handoff notes retention | 90d | Auditability and incident reconstruction |

Bridge handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1) Pre-handoff checklist (outgoing):
   - Summarize incident timeline, current hypotheses, mitigation steps in progress, and customer impact.
   - Confirm runbook page(s) in Bridge tab are current and link to traces/log queries.
2) Live handoff (over bridge):
   - 5–15 minute verbal summary; ensure incoming acknowledges critical mitigations.
   - If unresolved customer-impacting work remains, assign an owner and ETA.
3) Post-handoff (incoming):
   - Record a 1-line status in the incident timeline and attach a minimum evidence set (logs, traces, alert IDs).

Incident lifecycle and DPM decision matrix:
- If incident is Sev1 or multi-tenant Sev2 -> full postmortem required within 72 hours of remediation.
- If incident meets ALL of the following, use DPM: single-tenant, <30 minutes customer-visible impact, known cause, effective mitigation applied at resolution.
- Otherwise triage for full postmortem.

Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol (when to use and how):
Purpose: capture essential facts and actions quickly when resource constraints or ongoing high operational tempo would make a full postmortem impractical in 72 hours.
DPM steps (owner: incident lead):
1) Within 8 hours of incident resolution: populate DPM template with
   - 1-line summary, impact window (start/end), services affected, severity, and customer impact.
   - Evidence snapshot (link to logs, runbook used, mitigation commands).
2) Create action items with clear owners and SLAs (default: 14-day action SLA).
3) Flag DPM for follow-up in the next synthesis meeting.
4) If DPM reveals systemic risk or unresolved unknowns, escalate to full postmortem.

DPM template (minimum fields):
- Title (1 line)
- Date/time window
- Affected services and teams (comma-separated)
- Immediate mitigations executed
- Evidence links (logs, traces, alert IDs)
- Action items (owner | due date | description)
- Decision to close DPM or escalate (yes/no)

Escalation and timeline expectations:
- Immediate: severity declaration and customer status update within 30 minutes of detection for Sev1/Sev2.
- Short window: initial triage and bridge stand-up within 60 minutes.
- DPM creation: within 8 hours.
- Full postmortem: published within 72 hours for Sev1/Sev2.

Customer communications templates (for bridge operator use):
- Initial status (first 30m):
  "We have identified an issue affecting [feature/service]. Our team has engaged and is investigating. We will provide an update within 30 minutes."

- Follow-up status (post-triage):
  "Update: The issue is caused by [brief cause]. Mitigations underway include [actions]. Current impact: [scope]. Next update scheduled at [time/ETA]."

- Resolution notice:
  "Resolved: The issue affecting [service] has been mitigated at [time]. Root cause and next steps will be published in a follow-up note or postmortem."

- SLA-credit preliminary message (if applicable):
  "We are assessing impact against our SLA commitments. If you are eligible, we will follow up with credit details once our postmortem is complete."

Game day design and schedule (90-minute template):
- Goal: validate handoff, DPM creation, and customer comms speed.
- Attendees: 1 bridge operator, 2 responders, 1 product EM, 1 customer success observer.
- Timeline:
  00:00 — Inject alert and distribute pager
  00:05 — Bridge up and first customer status sent
  00:20 — Handoff simulation between responders
  00:45 — DPM skeleton completed and action items assigned
  01:05 — Demo of status page update flow and mock SLA notice
  01:20 — 15-minute retro and lessons logged

Runbook snippets (examples):
- Quick KV-cache eviction (serving-runtime):
  "# Commands
  kubectl exec -n runtime svc/cache-operator -- cache evict --pattern=*
  # Verify: tail logs for 200 responses to health endpoint for 5m"

- Throttle mitigation (traffic spike):
  "1) Move non-critical traffic to burst_throttle=true route.
   2) Increase instance headroom by policy 'scale-now' for model-serving service.
   3) Notify customers via status page if >5% error rate persists after 5m."

Ownership and metrics (who owns what):
- On-call synthesis owner: SRE manager (quarterly cadence).
- DPM governance: Incident review council (product + SRE rep)
- Bridge operator: maintains status templates and runbook links.
- Metrics to track: mean time to ack (MTTA), mean time to remediate (MTTR), percentage of incidents resolved with DPM, action-item closure rate within 14 days.

Audit and retention:
- DPMs and postmortems retained for 2 years in the incident archive.
- Handoff notes retained for 90 days.

Related pages and references:
- Link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-collection-standard (internal)
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/kv-cache-eviction (internal)

Appendix: triage decision quick chart:
- High latency + multi-tenant -> Sev1 -> full postmortem
- Short outage <30m + single-tenant + known fix -> DPM
- Repeated flapping events -> escalate to hypothesis-driven postmortem

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12 — created by Priya Shah
- 2026-02-02 — added DPM SLA guidance (review: Miguel Alvarez)
- 2026-03-01 — formalized rotation constraints and game day template (review: Sara Kim)

payload.page_title: Responder orchestration and service degradation guidelines

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a responder-centric orchestration pattern for incidents that cause partial service degradation or feature-level customer impact. It complements generic incident runbooks by focusing on choreography: how roles hand off, what system-level thresholds trigger automated mitigation, and standard status-page/customer communication templates tailored for degradations (not full outages).

Scope

- Applies to Redwood-hosted API endpoints, Dedicated pools, and customer-facing Console services.
- Focuses on incidents where availability is nominal but user-facing latency, error rates, or correctness regressions produce degraded experience.
- Not a substitute for full incident postmortems or for security incident handling (see security-and-compliance pages).

Key goals

1. Restore acceptable customer experience (meet SLOs or provide timely mitigation).
2. Maintain clear, time-boxed communications with customers and internal stakeholders.
3. Ensure predictable handoffs and escalation with minimal cognitive load for responders.

Incident severity classification (degradation-focused)

- Sev-2 (Degraded): Multiple customers report slow or flaky responses; error rate for a critical route > 2% for 5m; P99 latency > 2x target for 10m.
- Sev-3 (Minor Degradation): Single-customer impact or single-route increase in latency/error; transient and recoverable within 30 minutes.

SLO reference table

- API text-generation availability: 99.95% monthly.
- Per-route P99 latency target: 250ms for short-completion routes; alert at 500ms sustained over 10m.
- Embeddings throughput SLO: 95% of requests complete within 1s; alert at 1.5s sustained over 5m.

Ownership and roles

- Primary Responder (on-call engineer): Triage, initial mitigation, own incident until handoff.
- Secondary Responder: Assist with runbook steps and deeper debugging.
- Incident Commander (IC): Engages for Sev-2 or above; owns external communication cadence and escalation.
- Customer Success Liaison: Drafts customer-facing notes when customers are impacted.
- SRE Runbook Maintainer: Keeps runbook up to date; runs post-incident validation.

Response choreography (high level)

1. Detection: Alert or customer report. Primary responder acknowledges within 5 minutes.
2. Quick assessment (10 minutes): Determine scope (routes, regions, model variants, caching).
3. Immediate mitigation (time-boxed to first 30 minutes): Apply one of the standard mitigations below.
4. Escalation / IC: If not resolved after 30 minutes or if mitigation has customer-visible cost, escalate to IC.
5. Communication cadence: Status page + internal Slack thread within 15 minutes of acknowledging.
6. Post-incident: Postmortem within 72 hours, runbook updates in 1 week.

Standard mitigations (partial-degradation focus)

- Toggle degrade-to-compact-mode: Switch non-essential features to reduced model size or quantized variants. Example CLI:
  redwood-ops-cli service set-variant --service api-text --variant small-quant --reason "auto-degrade-latency"

- Route-level rate-limiting and quota bump: Reduce client-level burst windows temporarily.

- KV/prefix cache warm and rollback: If a KV cache miss storm is suspected, rehydrate popular prefixes from snapshot:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-cache-snapshots/prefix-hot-20260201 /tmp/prefixes && redwood-cache-load /tmp/prefixes

- Bypass expensive post-processing: Disable optional reranking or expensive decoding passes for affected routes.

- Model variant fallback: Route to a lower-latency variant in the same family. Ensure semantic compatibility.

Runbook: Partial-degradation — step-by-step (for Primary Responder)

1. Acknowledge alert and post initial note to #incident-redwood with incident summary template (see Communications templates).
2. Identify impacted routes and regions using:
   - Metrics: Grafana dashboard "API route health" (panel ids: api-route-errors, api-route-p99)
   - Traces: Jaeger service="api-gateway"
   - Logs: elasticsearch query: service:api AND level:error AND timestamp:>now-30m
3. Check model-serving pool health: redwood-ops-cli pool status --region us-west-2 --model-family gpt-xx
4. Attempt a low-risk mitigation (choose one):
   - Switch to fallback variant for affected route
   - Enable prefix cache from snapshot
   - Apply temporary circuit-breaker thresholds (example below)
5. Verify customer-visible metrics improve within 10 minutes. If not, escalate to IC.
6. Document all actions in incident tracker ticket and tag with labels: degradation, route:<route>, region:<region>.

Circuit-breaker thresholds (recommended starting points)

- If error-rate > 5% for 5m: trip circuit for non-critical endpoints (return 503 + Retry-After).
- If P99 latency > 1s for 10m: enable degraded-variant routing for read-only flows.

Handoff checklist (end of shift or escalation)

- Summary of what happened and current mitigation in place.
- Known diagnostics and next steps.
- Links to dashboards, logs, and active runbook commands.
- Escalation contacts and times (who to page next).

On-call rotation guidance and best practices

- 24/7 primary on-call per region with a 1:6 rotation. Secondary is scheduled for overlap during business hours.
- Weekly swap deadlines are Monday 09:00 UTC.
- The outgoing on-call must complete the handoff checklist in the incident ticket and post to #oncall-handoffs.
- Use the oncall-roster tool to update your availability: oncall-roster set-unavailable --from 2026-03-10 --to 2026-03-17 --reason "vacation"

Game day (simulation) plan focused on degradations

Purpose: Validate partial-degradation mitigation choreography and customer comm flow.
Frequency: Quarterly.
Participants: 1 IC, 2 primary responders, 1 customer success liaison, 1 observability engineer.
Runbook for game day

1. Inject synthetic load to a single route (tool: redwood-loadgen) to create P99 latency spike.
2. Confirm alerts fire and primary responder acknowledges within 5m.
3. Follow mitigation steps — prefer automated variant fallback first.
4. Customer Success drafts an initial status page and internal comm.
5. Simulate spinning new model pool from snapshot (test automation) and measure recovery time.
6. Debrief and update the runbook within 3 business days.

Incident postmortem template (use in conjunction with incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework)

- Title
- Incident ID / ticket
- Severity
- Timeline (UTC) — bullet list of time-stamped actions
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence
- Mitigations applied (what worked / didn’t work)
- Customer impact summary (routes impacted, customers and regions, duration)
- Action items (owner, deadline)
- Runbook updates required

Status page and customer communication templates

Initial public status (short form) — post within 15 minutes

- Title: Degraded performance for text-generation in US-West
- Status: Investigating
- Impact: Some requests may experience higher latency or transient errors. Customers using large-context generation may be most affected.
- Next update: 30 minutes

Customer-facing email / support template (initial)

Subject: Incident affecting text-generation latency — we're investigating

Hello <CustomerName>,

We are investigating an issue affecting text-generation latency in the US-West region. Some requests may take longer than usual or see transient errors. Our on-call team is actively working to restore normal performance and we will provide an update within 30 minutes.

If you have a mission-critical workload, reply to this message and we will prioritize mitigation for your traffic.

Sincerely,
Redwood Incident Response Team

Update template (follow-ups)

- T+30: What we have observed, mitigations attempted, and immediate next steps.
- T+60: If resolved, include recovery details and whether customers need to take any action. If unresolved, indicate escalation and expected timeline.

Resolution template (final)

- Title: Resolved — text-generation latency incident in US-West
- Status: Resolved
- Impact: <summary of affected routes, customers, total duration>
- Root cause: <concise cause statement>
- What we changed: <list of config/deployment changes>
- Postmortem: Link to detailed postmortem

Automation and tooling notes

- Use redwood-ops-cli for safe, auditable mitigations; every CLI action will create an audit entry.
- Integration with PagerDuty: Sev-2 pages escalate to SRE lead after 20 minutes without acknowledgment.
- Status page publishing is handled by status-publisher service: status-publisher post --component api-text --status investigating --message "Investigating elevated latency"

Maintenance and runbook ownership

- SRE Runbook Maintainer (rotating): updates runbooks after each postmortem.
- IC rotation: weekly; nominated IC details stored in the oncall-roster.

Appendix: Example incident Slack checklist (to paste into channel)

1. Incident title and ticket link
2. One-line impact summary
3. Primary responder name + pager link
4. Current mitigation (if any) and who applied it
5. Next steps and owner
6. T+30 update ETA

Appendix: Common diagnostics commands

- Check API route metrics: curl https://metrics-api.internal/query?panel=api-route-p99&from=-15m
- Pool status: redwood-ops-cli pool status --model-family gpt-xx
- Force variant fallback (dry-run): redwood-ops-cli route set-variant --route /v1/generate --variant small-quant --dry-run

Related pages and references

- Incident comm and postmortem framework (link above)
- SRE runbook repo: gitlab.com/redwood/sre-runbooks

Owner: SRE team.

Document change log

- 2025-11-12: Created by Samira Patel.
- 2026-01-08: Added circuit-breaker thresholds (Ethan Zhao).
- 2026-02-01: Clarified game-day steps and sample CLI snippets (Miguel Alvarez).

payload.page_title: Incident scripting and stakeholder briefs: responder patterns, templates, and game-day scripts

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document provides canonical incident "scripting" — short, repeatable sequences for responders to follow during common incident classes — and stakeholder brief templates used for status pages, customer notices, and internal escalation. It is intended for oncall engineers, SRE responders, support, and product incident leads.

Scope: covers classification and initial triage, responder roles and play scripts for three priority incident classes (latency spike, model quality regression, capacity exhaustion), status page and customer notice templates, handoff checklists, and a game-day syllabus to validate scripts.

Guiding principles
- Keep early communications precise, time-bounded, and action-oriented.
- Use templated language to avoid confusion and legal exposure.
- Work in 15-minute cycles for high-severity incidents: detect -> assess -> mitigate -> communicate.
- Prefer graceful degradation (fallback models, reduced throughput) over hard failovers where possible.

Incident classification and thresholds
- P0 (Sev1): Global or multi-region outage affecting >25% of active requests or an SLO breach >5% sustained for 5m.
- P1 (Sev2): Significant latency or error spike affecting a major route (>10% requests) or single-customer degrading impact.
- P2 (Sev3): Isolated errors, degraded accuracy for small prompt sets, or minor infra alerts.

SLOs and detection signals (examples)
- Token latency p99: 500ms target; alert at p99 > 800ms for 5m.
- Request error rate: alert when 5xx > 0.5% sustained for 5m.
- Model-quality regression (production eval set): A/B delta with control >3% for two consecutive evaluation runs.

Responder roles and contact matrix
- Incident Lead (IL): coordinates the overall response, runs bridge, owns external comms. Primary: oncall-eng; Escalation: Eng SRE Lead.
- Mitigation Engineer (ME): implements technical mitigations (scaling, rollback, cache flush).
- Model Owner (MO): responsible for model-level rollbacks, quality mitigations.
- Communications Lead (CL): drafts and posts status page updates and customer notices.
- Support Liaison (SL): summarizes customer-facing impact and routes tickets to IL.

Contact table (text)
- IL: #oncall-bridge (pager) -> oncall rotation -> eng-sre@redwood.com
- ME: runtime-team rotation -> slack @runtime-oncall
- MO: model-onboarding team -> slack @model-owner-oncall
- CL: comms rotation -> slack @ops-comms

Play scripts (short, repeatable sequences)
1) Latency spike (Sev2 -> potential Sev1)
- Trigger: p99 latency exceeds alert threshold or regional p95 degrades by 2x.
- 0–5m (Assess): Incident Lead opens bridge, posts initial note: "Investigating increased token latency in <region>. Initial triage underway. Updates every 15 minutes." Assign Mitigation Engineer and check autoscaling events, queue lengths, GPU saturation.
- 5–15m (Mitigate): If autoscaling lag: temporarily increase replica weight or add burst instances for affected group. If one model variant shows heavy tail: route traffic to alternative compatible model (see routing policy).
- 15–30m (Stabilize): Validate p99 return to within 20% of baseline. If not, prepare rollback to prior model version or reduce concurrency. CL posts customer-facing status: see template A.
- Post-incident: IL runs short postmortem using template in "Postmortem skeleton" section.

2) Model quality regression (Sev2)
- Trigger: production eval detects regression or customers report consistent incorrect outputs.
- 0–5m (Assess): MO pulls latest diffs, checks rollout logs, and inspects prompting changes. Open bridge and tag product and support.
- 5–20m (Mitigate): If recent model rollout: immediately pin traffic to previous model version and suspend the current rollout. If model drift due to prompt ecosystem: enable prompt sanitizer or apply guardrail reranking.
- 20–60m (Correct): Run a targeted evaluation on the failing prompt set and triage whether quantization/profile change caused regression. If code/config related, revert commit. CL issues customer guidance: see template B.
- Post-incident: MO publishes a model root-cause note and follow-up quality tests to our eval harness.

3) Capacity exhaustion (Sev1 if sustained)
- Trigger: GPU pool saturation, autoscaler unable to provision within SLA windows, or complete region capacity loss.
- 0–3m (Immediate containment): IL enables degraded routing: shift non-critical traffic to backup region, enable rate-limit backpressure for lower-tier plans using token-bucket policies. Post initial public notice.
- 3–30m (Recovery): ME requests burst capacity via Dedicated pool or triggers reserved burst in config. If capacity cannot be procured, enforce firm throttles per plan until capacity returns.
- Post-incident: Full capacity review and committed capacity procurement policy update.

Runbook snippets (commands and checks)
- Check p99 latency: curl -s "https://metrics-api.internal/api/queries/p99?service=runtime&window=5m" | jq .value
- Inspect GPU utilization: kubectl top pods -l app=runtime --namespace=prod | sort -k3 -r
- Trigger rollback (example CLI): rwctl rollout rollback --service runtime --model-id rdm-20250115-v2 --reason "quality_regression"

Status page and customer notice templates
Template A (Initial short public status)
- Title: Service degradation - increased response latency (region)
- Time: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
- Summary: We are investigating increased response times for API requests in <region>. Some customers may experience slower responses or timeouts.
- Impact: Intermittent latency increases and request timeouts affecting <X>% of requests.
- Mitigation in progress: Diverting traffic and scaling additional capacity; engineers are actively investigating root cause.
- Next update: in 15 minutes or sooner.

Template B (Customer-facing follow-up with guidance)
- Subject: Update: Ongoing quality regression impacting responses for <model-name>
- Greeting: Hello,
- Body: We've identified an issue affecting output quality for requests routed to <model-name> starting at <time>. We have rolled back to the previous stable version while the team completes a thorough root cause analysis. If you rely on specific prompt patterns, please reach out to support with examples so we can prioritize remediation.
- ETA: Estimated resolution time: <window> or "under investigation".
- Contacts: support@redwood.com (for account-specific impact).

Template C (Detailed customer post-incident report)
- Title: Post-incident report: <incident-short-id>
- Impact window: start -> end (UTC)
- Summary: High-level chronology and impact table by region and plan.
- Root cause: short summary.
- Mitigation steps taken: list.
- Action items and owner: 1) Improve autoscaler metrics - owner: infra-team - ETA: 30d; 2) Add preflight model evaluation to rollout pipeline - owner: applied-ml - ETA: 14d.

Internal bridge posting checklist (first 10 minutes)
1. Bridge opened by IL; record start time and incident short-id.
2. Post initial one-line and severity.
3. Assign ME/MO/CL and confirm on-bridge presence.
4. Capture top-3 hypotheses.
5. Confirm monitoring dashboards and log links.
6. Publish initial public status using Template A.

Handoff and next-shift script
- Handoff timebox: 10 minutes.
- Outgoing oncall must provide:
  - incident short-id and start time
  - current status and last mitigation action
  - immediate next steps and blockers
  - contact list for escalation
- Incoming oncall confirms receipt by reading back the two most important open action items.

Postmortem skeleton (to be used within 72 hours)
- Title: Postmortem: <incident-short-id>
- Summary: 2–3 sentence impact plus customer count.
- Timeline: table of events (time, actor, event).
- Root cause analysis: technical cause and contributing factors.
- Corrective actions: Owner, severity, ETA.
- Learnings and follow-ups: process or monitoring changes.

Game-day syllabus (validates scripts and team readiness)
- Frequency: quarterly (core infra), biannual (model rollouts)
- Duration: 2–3 hours, with a 30-minute hot-debrief.
- Scenarios (pick 2 per run):
  - Fast p99 latency regression in one region with capacity replenishment delay.
  - Silent model-quality drift that affects only a high-value enterprise customer.
  - Autoscaler misconfiguration causing noisy neighbor CPU starvation.
- Success criteria: scripts completed in target timeboxes; public status drafted and approved within 15 minutes; handoff executed without dropped context.

Templates and implementation notes
- Save all comm drafts in #incident-drafts channel and tag @ops-comms for approval.
- Store pinned evidence (metric snapshots, sample traces) in the incident workspace with clear filenames: <incident-id>_p99.png, <incident-id>_trace.json.
- All rollbacks require a ticket in the change system (change-id) and must be referenced in the postmortem.

Appendix: quick reference checklist (single-page)
- If p99 > alert threshold -> open bridge -> post Template A.
- If model rollout in last 60 min -> pin previous version.
- If GPU pool >90% -> enable reserved burst or route traffic out of region.
- If customer-facing errors reported by Support -> tag SL and escalate to IL.

Example Slack status post (copy/paste)
- "[INC-<id>] Investigating increased latency in us-west-2. IL: @oncall-eng. Mitigation: scaling additional replicas. Next update in 15m."

Ownership and governance
- Document owner: Engineering SRE (oncall-and-incident-response). Review cadence: annually or after any Sev1.
- Training: New oncall rotates must complete an incident walkthrough with a senior responder and pass one mock game-day.

Related resources
- Link to monitoring dashboards: https://dashboards.internal/runtime
- Runbook index: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks
- Model rollout checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/rollout-checklist

Document change log
- 2025-03-10: Initial draft (Daniela Ruiz).
- 2025-06-02: Added model regression play script and customer templates (reviewers: Alex Chen).
- 2026-01-15: Updated thresholds and game-day syllabus (Daniela Ruiz).
