payload.page_title: Shift handoff, runbook retirement, and status automation bundle

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document codifies a compact, repeatable on-call handoff sequence, a lightweight runbook retirement lifecycle, and an opinionated set of templates and automation snippets for keeping the status page and customer communications accurate during incidents. It is intended for first responders, on-call leads, incident commanders, and the SRE engineers who maintain runbooks.

Scope: Applies to Redwood-hosted services, Dedicated control plane components, and customer-facing public APIs. Private deployments should mirror the same approach unless constrained by customer confidentiality agreements.

Quick reference (single-page)

- Primary SLOs: 99.95% p99 availability monthly for API gateway; latency SLO: 95% < 200ms for metadata endpoints.
- Alert thresholds: Error rate > 0.5% for 5m (P1 candidate); p95 latency increase > 3x baseline for 5m (P2 candidate).
- Escalation: Pager -> Team on-call -> On-call lead -> Incident commander.

Incident severity definitions

1) P0 - System outage: >30% customer impact or global API failure. Requires immediate full-bridge and exec notification.
2) P1 - Major degradation: Significant subset of customers affected, degraded core functionality, remediate within 2 hours.
3) P2 - Partial impact: Regional or non-critical feature regression, target TTR within 24 hours.
4) P3 - Cosmetic or low-priority: Minor bugs, documentation, or background jobs.

Handoff checklist (30–60s read for incoming on-call)

1. Confirm status page: verify there is a current incident or none. Command: curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $STATUS_API_KEY\" https://status.redwoood.example/api/v1/incidents | jq .active
2. Read the top pager alert: check alert source, service name, and immediate mitigation notes on the alert (pager message).
3. Verify recent playbook steps: open the active runbook URL indicated in the pager (if none, create an incident and attach a new runbook).
4. Confirm slack/bridge and add yourself: #incident-<service> and /join bridge.
5. Update the shift log: add your name, local timezone, and planned check-in cadence.
6. If any escalation has been triggered (escalation level >= 2), meet the on-call lead within 10 minutes.

Minimal triage flow (first 15 minutes)

1) Triage intent: Is this customer-visible?
  - Yes -> proceed to containment (identify proxy, throttle, or rollback).
  - No -> create follow-up ticket and classify as P2/P3.

2) Data collection checklist (commands you will run):
  - kubectl -n <svc> get pods -o wide --selector=app=<svc>
  - curl -v https://<svc>/.health || echo \"health-check-failed\"
  - ./infra/observability/query_histogram.sh --service <svc> --metric requests_latency_p95 --window 10m
  - aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace Redwood/Infer --metric-name ErrorCount --start-time $(date -u -d '10 minutes ago' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --period 60 --statistics Sum

3) Containment patterns (common fast mitigations):
  - Route around unhealthy AZs using traffic-split: edit TrafficSplit weight for region-b;
  - Temporary scale up replica count for autoscaled pools;
  - Use immediate config toggle (feature-flag rollback) to disable failing integration;
  - Revert recent deployment if the release is implicated.

Incident communication bundle

- Status page: Use the provided API snippet to open/update incidents. Keep updates every 15–30 minutes for P0/P1 until mitigation is in place.

API sample (curl)

curl -X POST https://status.redwoood.example/api/v1/incidents \
  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $STATUS_API_KEY\" \
  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
  -d '{"service":"api-gateway","severity":"major","title":"API error surge affecting requests","impact":"Customers may see increased 5xx errors","status":"investigating","visibility":"public"}'

Patch/update example

curl -X PATCH https://status.redwoood.example/api/v1/incidents/<incident-id> \
  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $STATUS_API_KEY\" \
  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
  -d '{"status":"monitoring","update":"Mitigation in place: traffic shifted to region-b. Error rate falling."}'

Customer-facing message templates

- Initial public message (short):
\"We are investigating an increase in error rates affecting requests to the Redwood API. Some customers may experience failed requests or timeouts. We will provide updates every 15 minutes.\"

- Messaging when mitigation is in place:
\"Mitigation is in place: traffic has been shifted and error rates are declining. We continue to monitor closely and will provide a post-incident summary.\"

- Private customer outreach (for affected high-tier customers):
\"Hi <Customer Name> — we detected a surge of 5xx responses impacting your requests. We’ve shifted traffic and applied a mitigation; the issue is being monitored. Your CS lead (<cs-lead@redwood.com>) will follow up with a detailed timeline and technical RCA.\"

Runbook retirement lifecycle (why this exists)

Runbooks degrade over time: steps become stale, owners change, and commands rot. This section defines how a runbook is retired, archived, or refreshed so the on-call corpus remains trustworthy.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- No runs in the last 12 months and the service is inactive or deprecated.
- > 3 broken/obsolete commands detected during annual review.
- Ownership undefined for > 60 days after team restructuring.

Runbook retirement process (4-step)

1) Identify candidate: automated scan or manual nomination (tag runbook with "candidate-for-retire").
2) Owner review: current runbook owner must respond within 14 days with either a refresh or agree to retirement.
3) Archive window: if no response, move runbook to Archived space with a notice and TTL 90 days where it is recoverable.
4) Final purge or convert to KB article: after TTL, archived runbooks are deleted from the active corpus and a short KB note is created summarizing the reason and replacement if any.

Runbook review cadence and responsibilities (table)

| Role | Cadence | Responsibility |
| On-call lead | Quarterly | Validate 3 selected high-importance runbooks end-to-end |
| Service owner | Annual | Complete full runbook verification and update |
| Documentation team | Annual | Run cross-service linting and command validation |

Post-incident micro-postmortem template (deliver within 72 hours for P0/P1)

1) Title: <Service> — <Date> — P1/P0
2) Summary (2–3 sentences): one-paragraph customer-facing summary.
3) Timeline: bullets (UTC timestamps) for discovery, mitigation, root cause, and resolution.
4) Impact: quantifiable metrics (requests affected, regional impact, error volume).
5) Root cause & contributing factors: concise bullets.
6) Actions: short-term (today), medium-term (30d), long-term (90d) with owners and target dates.
7) Postmortem review: date/time for cross-team alignment and verify actions closed.

Game day micro-syllabus (2-hour practical run)

Objective: validate handoff, status update cadence, and runbook accuracy.
sections.heading: Criteria to consider a runbook for retirement or refresh

sections.body:
- 0:00–0:15: Quick brief and roles assigned (IC, comms, responder, observer).
- 0:15–0:45: Inject failure A (latency spike) — run triage, identify mitigation.
- 0:45–1:05: Update status page and issue customer message; observers score clarity.
- 1:05–1:35: Inject failure B (partial outage due to deployment) — perform rollback.
- 1:35–1:55: Run a postmortem mini-write (15m) and present findings.
- 1:55–2:00: Retrospective: 3 takeaways and 2 action items.

payload.page_title: Operator action grid and staged customer notification scripts

sections.body: This document defines an operator action grid that maps common detection signals to immediate runbook steps, time-to-recovery (TTR) targets, and a staged customer notification strategy. It includes ready-to-use status-page JSON, Tiered customer notice scripts, and short game-day exercises to validate operator speed and communication clarity. Use this as the canonical reference for model-serving degradations and silent/slow degradations where user-visible quality or latency regresses without an obvious outage.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: Redwood inference runtime components (request routing, KV cache, batching layer, model variants), API gateway, and customer-facing rate limiting and quota subsystems.
- Intent: accelerate containment, reduce confusion during multi-service incidents, and provide clear, tiered customer communications that scale from internal note to external status page updates.
sections.heading: Scope and intent

sections.body:
| Signal (example) | Severity | Immediate operator actions (first 10 minutes) | TTR target | Notification tier |
|------------------|----------|---------------------------------------------|------------|------------------|
| 5x 5xx spike from model-workers (>=5% of requests) | Sev-2 | 1) Open bridge; 2) Identify failing worker pool (gpu-worker-*); 3) Toggle fallback policy to degrade to lower-cost variant; 4) Add traffic-steering rule | 15–30m | Tier A: internal + affected enterprise customers |
| Sustained 200–500ms p50 latency increase for embedding endpoints | Sev-3 | 1) Check batching backlog and queue length; 2) Inspect KV cache hit ratio; 3) Recycle batcher pods if backlog > 3000; 4) Escalate to serving-runtime team if kernel OOMs | 30–90m | Tier B: internal + status page note + customer success outreach for high-touch customers |
| Silent quality drift detected by evals (BLEU/ROUGE drop, or hallucination rate > threshold) | Sev-2 | 1) Run diagnostic prompt-set evals against pinned model version; 2) Pin to previous model variant if quality delta > configured threshold; 3) Create regression ticket in Tracker with reproduction artifacts | 60m | Tier A + targeted CS outreach to customers with regression-sensitive SLAs |
| KV cache thrash with increased miss rate and cache eviction | Sev-3 | 1) Increase cache retention to temporary mode; 2) Purge known bad prefixes; 3) Restart cache nodes sequentially | 45–120m | Tier B |
| Rate-limit cascade from a noisy tenant (burst > 20x baseline) | Sev-2 | 1) Isolate tenant via tenant-rate-limiter; 2) Notify sales/CS; 3) If abuse, apply temporary quota throttle | 20–60m | Tier A + direct customer notice |

Primary runbook template (use for all Sev-2/Sev-3 incidents):

1) Acknowledge and open bridge (first 2 minutes)
   - Bridge tool: #ops-bridge (Slack) and Zoom link generated via /bridge create
   - Primary on-call: (name) — announce role and read the initial evidence from monitoring (metrics, recent deploys, alerts).
2) Rapid evidence collection (2–8 minutes)
   - Paste: relevant Grafana panels (request rate, p50/p95 latency, error rate), last 3 deploys, and tail of worker logs for implicated services.
   - Commands:
     - kubectl -n runtime logs -l app=gpu-worker --since=15m | grep -i error
     - curl -sS https://internal-metrics/api/now?service=model-serving | jq '.metrics'
3) Containment actions (8–20 minutes)
   - Route traffic to compatible variant: /admin/traffic-shift --service model-serving --from=variant-v2 --to=variant-v1 --percent=100
   - Scale up a healthy worker-pool: kubectl scale deploy gpu-worker-spot --replicas=8 -n runtime
   - If memory pressure: restart the busiest pod with kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -n runtime
4) Communication and customer notice (10–40 minutes, depending on tier)
   - Use the templates in the next section. Update status page payload (example below) and post to #status-updates Slack channel.
5) Root-cause analysis and rollback (40–120 minutes)
   - If deploy is implicated, perform an automated rollback via deployment pipeline and verify metrics for 15 minutes.
   - Create post-incident ticket and assign owners for follow-up actions.
sections.heading: Operator Action Grid (quick reference)

sections.body:
- Tier A — High impact / high-touch customers (SLAs, enterprise contracts)
  - Trigger when: any Sev-1/Sev-2 incident that affects >1% of requests for enterprise customers or quality regressions impacting SLO-sensitive features.
  - Channels: direct email + CS phone call + dedicated Slack channel for customer.
  - Script (short form): "We are investigating an issue impacting model responses for your account. We have applied a temporary traffic reroute and expect stability within 30 minutes. You will receive updates every 20 minutes or on state changes. If this impacts production traffic, please reply to this thread and your CS contact will escalate."

- Tier B — Broad-but-non-critical incidents
  - Trigger when: latency/throughput regressions visible on status page but mitigated with routing or scaling.
  - Channels: public status page, scheduled emails to subscribed customers, and a short CS summary.
  - Script (short form): "We've detected elevated latencies on embedding endpoints and implemented traffic mitigation. We're continuing work to restore normal latencies. Next update in 30 minutes."

- Tier C — Internal-only incidents / low impact
  - Trigger when: local experimental clusters or developer-facing tools with minimal customer impact.
  - Channels: internal bridge, internal status notes only.

Status page payload examples (copy+paste):

- Minimal public update (Tier B):

{
  "component": "Embedding service",
  "status": "degraded_performance",
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-0456",
  "short_description": "Elevated latency on embedding endpoints",
  "updates": [
    {"time": "2026-03-02T10:15:00Z", "body": "Mitigation in progress: traffic routed to standby pool and batchers scaled."}
  ]
}

- Full customer notice (Tier A) — email template (subject + body):

Subject: Ongoing issue: model responses impacted for [customer-name] — update #1
sections.heading: Staged customer notification strategy

sections.body:
Hello [Customer First Name],

We are investigating an incident impacting model responses for your account that began at 10:03 UTC. Our engineers have temporarily routed traffic to a compatible model variant and scaled worker capacity. We expect a mitigation window of ~30 minutes to fully stabilize.
sections.heading: Body

sections.body:
- Rerouting traffic to compatible model variant
- Scaling worker pools and increasing KV cache retention
- Running targeted evals to ensure quality parity

Next update: in 20 minutes or on change.

If this incident affects features critical to your users, reply and we will prioritize a dedicated mitigation path.

Regards,
Redwood Systems Operations
sections.heading: What we are doing now

sections.body:
1) Confirm metrics returned to baseline for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows (p50/p95 latency and error rate)
2) Remove temporary traffic rules and re-enable automated fallback policies
3) Document the incident timeline with exact commands used and owners assigned
4) Open a postmortem issue with the following required artifacts:
   - Timeline (ISO timestamps), affected services, root cause hypothesis, RCA owner, mitigation commands, and a list of follow-up actions with owners and target dates
sections.heading: Operator checklist (post-mitigation)

sections.body:
- Summary (2–3 sentences): what happened and customer impact
- Timeline: minute-level events (first alert, detection method, containment steps, mitigation complete)
- Root cause analysis: evidence, why checks failed, and technical causes
- Contributing factors: tooling gaps, on-call fatigue, rollout policy mismatches
- Action items: prioritized, owner-assigned, and target date
- Validation plan: how to verify a fix (synthetic tests, gating in CI, runbook changes)

Game-day exercises (30–90 minute scenarios):

1) 30-minute silent-drift drill
   - Goal: detect quality drift from eval metrics, confirm alerting works end-to-end, and execute targeted rollback
   - Steps:
     a) Inject a synthetic increase in hallucination score into the eval harness (QA team creates simulated regression)
     b) Observe alert in the metrics channel
     c) Execute the runbook: pin to previous model, update status page, and contact affected CS leads
   - Scoring: detection (10 pts), containment (20 pts), customer comms (10 pts)

2) 60-minute multi-region throttle cascade
   - Goal: exercise rate-limiter isolation, status page updates, and cross-team coordination
   - Steps include: simulate noisy tenant, apply tenant-throttle, redirect traffic, escalate to SRE lead, and coordinate rollback of a bad config.
sections.heading: Postmortem rubric (minimum required sections)

sections.body:
- Owners: "serving-runtime" team owns the action grid and runbook lines for batcher, kernel, and model variant operations. On-call SRE owns the notification cadence and status page payloads.
- Review cadence: quarterly review and after each Sev-2 incident. All runbook changes must be reviewed by at least one serving-runtime engineer and one SRE.
sections.heading: Runbook governance and ownership

sections.body:
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) target: < 90 seconds for Sev-2 incidents.
- Mean time to mitigation (first stabilization action): < 20 minutes for Sev-2.
- Customer communication latency: initial Tier A customer notice within 10 minutes of bridge open.
- Postmortem completion: action items assigned within 72 hours; postmortem published within 7 days.

Appendix A — Quick command cheatsheet:

- Open bridge: /bridge create "model-serving incident" --severity Sev-2
- Scale worker pool: kubectl scale deploy gpu-worker-spot --replicas=8 -n runtime
- Pin model: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://internal-api/serve/pin?service=model-serving&variant=variant-v1"
- Update status page (curl example):
  curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '@status-payload.json' https://status.internal/update -H "Authorization: Bearer $STATUS_TOKEN"

Appendix B — Example evidence collection template (to paste into bridge):

- Alerts triggered: [list alert ids]
- Grafana links: [insert links]
- Recent deploys: [commit ids + author]
- Top error snippets (last 15m): [logs]
- Immediate mitigation actions taken: [traffic-shift, scale, restart]

Appendix C — Common templates (copy and paste):

- Internal Slack update (first message):
  :rotating_light: Incident INC-2026-0456: Elevated 5xx rate on model-serving. Bridge: <link>. Primary: @oncall. Mitigation: routing to variant-v1 and scaling gpu-worker-spot.

- Customer SMS (short, Tier A):
  Redwood: We are investigating an issue affecting model responses. We've applied a temporary mitigation and will update within 20 minutes. Reply for high-priority assistance.
sections.heading: Metrics and success criteria

sections.body:
- Incident lifecycle orchestration templates (link): /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-lifecycle-orchestration-templates-2025
- Triage for degraded latency and SLO regression (link): /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/triage-for-degraded-latency-and-slo-regression-2024

payload.page_title: Operator Shift Orchestra playbook and branded status bundles

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook — the Operator Shift Orchestra — defines standardized shift choreography, quick-run runbooks for common LLM-serving issues, a compact postmortem scaffold, game-day exercises, and a set of 'branded' status bundles for customer-facing communication. It is intended for primary/secondary on-call operators, duty engineers, SREs, and customer success liaisons.

Goals
- Reduce time-to-stable for incidents affecting Redwood inference endpoints.
- Provide easy-to-graft customer status messages that are brand-safe and accurate.
- Standardize handoffs and retros to preserve institutional knowledge.
- Exercise shift teams with game-day scenarios that reflect production failure modes (latency spikes, KV cache corruption, quiet degradations).

Ownership and scope
- Owners: Eng SRE (primary), Serving Runtime (secondary), Customer Success (customer notices).
- Scope: All public inference endpoints, Dedicated pools, and Private control-plane integrations.
- Author: Elena Park (Runtime Ops).

Shift choreography (how an on-call shift should flow)
1) Pre-shift (30 minutes before start)
   - Read the daily shift brief (Slack #ops-brief). Check the overnight incident digest and any active P0/P1s.
   - Verify heartbeating dashboards are green: API success rate >= 99.5%, 95th percentile latency within SLO, queue depths stable.
2) Handover (first 10 minutes)
   - Run automated handoff checklist: list active incidents, outstanding runbook actions, recent escalations, ongoing game-day exercises.
   - Acknowledge handover in the shift log with a timestamp and short summary.
3) During shift
   - Monitor: Alerts, Service Health dashboard, and status-page watch.
   - Respond: Follow runbook containment steps for alerts. Escalate per matrix.
   - Triage windows: perform a short triage on high-noise alerts every 4 hours.
4) Handoff-out (end of shift)
   - Complete runbook actions or add clear next steps.
   - Write a 5-line summary and outstanding items; post to the shift log and mention the next on-call.

Shift rules and roles
- Primary: owns customer impact, initial mitigation, and RCA kickoff.
- Secondary: supports debugging, deep-dive tasks, and can act as bridge lead if Primary is out.
- Escalation lead: Engineering manager on-call for P0s (paged at 30 minutes without containment).
- Shift length: 8–12 hours depending on rota (team-specific). No more than 2 consecutive long shifts without rest.

Escalation matrix (quick view)
- P0 (global outage): Page Primary -> Secondary -> Escalation lead -> Exec oncall (if > 60m unresolved).
- P1 (regional service degradation): Page Primary -> Secondary -> Team SME.
- P2/P3: Slack alert to team channel; create ticket as needed.

Runbook templates (copyable, short)
1) API surge / sustained latency
   - Detect: 95th percentile latency > SLO for 5 minutes AND error rate increase > 0.5%.
   - Contain: 1) Enable throttling rule for non-synthetic traffic; 2) Ramp down batch sizes for background clients; 3) Fail over routing policy to cheaper region-variant if configured.
   - Validate: Confirm 95th percentile latency returns within SLO for 10 minutes.
   - Restore: Gradually remove throttles, monitor metrics for 30 minutes.
2) KV cache eviction / cold-cache storm
   - Detect: Sudden increase in model token processing time; cache hit-rate drops > 30%.
   - Contain: 1) Switch to pre-warmed model variant (if available); 2) Increase cache persistence retention on affected nodes; 3) Temporarily increase autoscaling target for runtime pool.
   - Validate: Cache hit-rate trends up and tail latency reduces.
   - Restore: Rollback autoscaling and persistence changes after 60–90 minutes of stable metrics.
3) Silent quality degradation (model output regressions)
   - Detect: Eval alert triggered for production prompt set OR customer report with clear regression signature.
   - Contain: 1) Route traffic to previous pinned model version; 2) Reduce sampling temperature for generation endpoints; 3) Engage model-onboarding lead.
   - Validate: Quality telemetry and sample prompts match expected guardrails.
   - Post-incident: Create a model regression postmortem and tagging.

Runbook checklist (short form)
- Triage: summary, severity, customer impact, affected region, model/version, endpoints.
- Containment steps taken (with timestamps).
- Evidence snapshot (metrics, request IDs, representative logs).
- Communications sent (internal and external).

Status page and customer-facing bundles
We use 'bundles' to ensure brand-safe, consistent language. Choose the smallest bundle appropriate for impact (A, B, C).
- Bundle A (Major outage, customer impact across regions)
  - Title: 'Service disruption: Redwood inference API'
  - Body: 'We are aware of elevated errors and sustained latency for Redwood inference endpoints. Our engineers are actively investigating and we will provide updates every 30 minutes. Customers may experience failures or timeouts during this period.'
  - Actions: update status every 30 minutes, post to support portal, and notify enterprise POCs via email.
  - Suggested severity badge: Major
- Bundle B (Partial regional degradation)
  - Title: 'Partial service degradation in <region>'
  - Body: 'We are experiencing increased latency for a subset of requests originating from <region>. We have applied mitigations and are monitoring. If your service is impacted, please open a support ticket and reference incident ID {INC_ID}.'
  - Actions: update every 60 minutes, targeted emails to affected customers.
- Bundle C (Informational / scheduled maintenance)
  - Title: 'Planned maintenance: <component>'
  - Body: 'We will perform scheduled maintenance affecting <component> on <date/time>. No action is required unless you rely on pinned private deployments; contact support for accommodation.'
  - Actions: pre-notice 72h and 24h, and post-completion note.

Customer message templates (email + status snippet)
- Short status snippet (for status.redwood.com): 'We are investigating increased latency impacting inference calls in <region>. Our team has applied mitigations. Next update: <ETA>.'
- Enterprise email (first notification)
  Subject: 'Redwood Incident {INC_ID}: Service impact affecting inference requests'
  Body: 'Hello — We are currently investigating elevated error rates and latency affecting inference requests. Impacted customers may see failures or delays. Our team has applied initial mitigations and is working on full restoration. We will send an update in 30 minutes or sooner. If you have high-priority workloads, please reply and include your region and sample request IDs.'

Postmortem scaffold (compact)
- Title/Incident ID
- Timeline (UTC) — include detection, mitigation, and resolution timestamps
- Impact summary — customers, services, data-plane / control-plane effects
- Root cause (summary)
- Contributing factors
- Corrective actions (owners and due dates)
- Learnings and follow-up (A/B test or rollout policy changes)

Game-day exercises (90 minute template)
1) Objective: Practice coordinated triage for a silent degradation that requires model rollback.
2) Roles: Bridge lead, Primary on-call, Secondary, Customer liaison, Observability SME.
3) Scenario: Synthetic evals flag a 5% regression for a high-traffic prompt set; customers start reporting quality issues.
4) Tasks and scoring: 1) Detection within 10 minutes (3 pts). 2) Containment (model rollback) within 25 minutes (5 pts). 3) Brand-safe customer update posted within 30 minutes (2 pts). 4) Post-exercise quick retro completed within 24 hours (1 pt).
5) Debrief: run through what went well, what blocked, and actions assigned.

Shift log template (example entry)
- Timestamp: 2025-06-14T08:04Z
- Operator: @elena.park
- Active incidents: INC-2025-1123 (P1) — API latency in eu-west1
- Actions this shift: toggled throttling for background clients 08:15Z; engaged serving-runtime team 08:30Z
- Outstanding items for next shift: follow up on autoscaling tuning; validate canary traffic profile.

Evidence capture requirements (for P0/P1)
- Minimum evidence bundle: 1) Grafana snapshot for 1h pre/post; 2) 10 representative request IDs; 3) Bridge transcript or log excerpt; 4) Any customer reports or support tickets.

Retention and governance
- Runbooks: review cadence 6 months.
- Shift logs: retained for 2 years.
- Postmortems: retained permanently; action items tracked in Jira and closed with evidence.

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets and debug hints
- Export sample request IDs (example): curl -X POST https://internal-api/services/requests/query -d '{"filter":"status:\"error\"","limit":10}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
- Quick model rollback (internal CLI): rwoodctl deploy rollback --service inference --to-version v2025-03-01 --region eu-west1

Frequently asked questions
Q: When should Customer Success draft an email vs. posting to the status page?
A: Use status page for broad incidents. Draft an email when the incident affects enterprise customers or when follow-up actions are required (credits, post-incident briefings).

Related documents and links
- Incident comm & postmortem framework (link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework-2026)
- Oncall handoff and simulation scenarios (link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-playbook-rotation-handoff-and-simulation-scenarios-2026)
- Runtime runbooks index (link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks)

Revision history
- 2025-03-10 — initial draft by Elena Park
- 2025-04-22 — incorporated Customer Success messaging templates (review: Marcus Liu)
- 2025-06-15 — updated bundles and game-day scoring (review: Priya Nair)

payload.page_title: operational-signal-workflow-and-comm-templates-2026

sections.body:
Overview:

This document defines the Operational Signal Workflow used at Redwood Inference for turning monitoring signals into coordinated responder actions and customer communications. It includes a signal taxonomy, a step-by-step incident activation manual, an escalation matrix, a canonical runbook example, post-incident responsibilities, an on-call handoff template, a lightweight game-day scenario, and several pre-approved customer communication templates.

Audience:
- SREs, on-call engineers, incident commanders, support leads, and product owners.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted API surface, Dedicated serving pools, and the control plane. Not intended for HR or purely policy escalations.

Key principles:
- Single source of truth: alerts -> incident channel -> incident doc.
- Fast acknowledgement, slow noisy escalation: set thresholds to minimize unnecessary human interrupts.
- Customer-facing clarity: status page updates within 30 minutes of incident classification.

1) Signal taxonomy (how we classify incoming events)
- SEV0: Complete service unavailability for >5 minutes impacting >50% of requests (requires incident bridge).
- SEV1: Severe degradation (e.g., p95 latency >2x SLO or error rate >5%) affecting a large subset of customers.
- SEV2: Partial degradation or one-region issue with mitigations available.
- SEV3: Minor degradation, non-urgent operational tasks, or individual customer issues.

2) Signal flow (from monitor to resolution)
1. Detection: Metric/alert systems (Prometheus alertmanager, Datadog monitors, and synthetic checks) emit a signal.
2. Alert enrichment: Alertmanager attaches runbook link, recent deployments, and relevant traces (link to x-trace).
3. Alert routing: PagerDuty receives routed alert by service tag (example: service:text-gen-api-prod).
4. Initial paging: On-call engineer receives page according to the rotation policy.
5. Acknowledge within 5 minutes: On-call acknowledges in PagerDuty and posts a one-line status in Slack incident channel #inc-text-gen-prod.
6. Triage: Run basic checks (step 4 runbook).
7. Incident classification: If SEV1/0, incident commander (IC) is designated and an incident bridge is opened, incident doc created in confluence and a status page entry draft started.
8. Recovery & mitigation: Apply rollbacks, routing changes, capacity scale-up, or circuit breakers.
9. Postmortem: Within 72 hours, responsible engineer writes a blameless postmortem; within 10 business days, it must be reviewed by the reviewers list.

3) Escalation matrix (quick reference)
| Role | Responsibility | Escalation channel | Backup |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Primary on-call (text-gen) | Triage, quick mitigation, communicate | PagerDuty -> Slack #inc-text-gen-prod | Secondary on-call
| Secondary on-call | Take over if primary is unreachable or incident complexity grows | Slack mention, escalate in PagerDuty | Duty lead
| Incident Commander (IC) | Coordinate responders, prioritize customer comms, declare severity | Incident bridge (Zoom/Jitsi), #inc-ops | SRE manager
| Duty lead / Engineering manager | Make product/rollback decisions, approve customer messaging | Phone / Slack DM | Eng director
| Customer Success Lead | Customer-facing comms & coordinate escalations with customers | Email + SalesForce case | CTO on-call

Notes: phone numbers and individual contact lines are kept in the secure oncall vault (secrets manager).

4) Canonical runbook example: "High error rate - text-generation-hosting-api"
Purpose: Steps to bring error rate back under SLO and determine root cause.
Pre-conditions: Ensure you have PagerDuty, AWS/GCP console access, and sla-role access (see infra-standards).

Immediate steps (first 15 minutes):
1. Confirm alert: open Datadog monitor, check time series, and confirm increase in 5xx or gRPC failures.
2. Check recent deploys: 
   - CLI: git log -1 --pretty=oneline origin/main
   - Deploy dashboard: go to Deployments -> service=text-gen-api and note PRs rolled out in last 30m.
3. Identify scope: run synthetic-curl against a set of golden prompts (script: scripts/check_endpoints.sh) and record response codes.
4. Check downstream dependencies: embedding-store, kv-cache, model-serving pool health. Run: ./tools/health-check --service model-pool-prod
5. If p95 latency is high, check GPU utilization: kubectl top pods -n serving | grep text-gen; if nodes at >85% GPU, proceed to scale.

Mitigation options (ordered):
- Roll back the last deployment (if matching time window) using the control-plane rollback action and mark as rollback-in-progress in the incident doc.
- Increase serving capacity: trigger autoscale policy for dedicated pools (see eng-sre/runbooks/autoscale-ops).
- Enable degraded mode: route requests to model-variant:fast-quant where acceptable (only after product owner sign-off for quality tradeoffs).
- Short-term rate limits: apply per-tenant soft quotas to reduce error amplification.

When to declare IC and bridge:
- Declare IC if the incident meets SEV1/0 or persists for >20 minutes after first mitigation attempt.

Containment checklist (for stabilization):
- [ ] Acknowledge the page in PagerDuty
- [ ] Create incident confluence doc and link in channel
- [ ] Assign roles: IC, Scribe, Tech Lead, Comms
- [ ] Publish initial status page draft (see templates below)

Recovery steps and verification:
- Confirm latency and error rates trending to baseline for at least 15 continuous minutes before declaring recovery.
- Run synthetic success jobs and validate end-to-end requests.

5) Runbook-level quick commands (examples)
- Check pods: kubectl get pods -n serving -l app=text-gen-api -o wide
- Tail logs: stern text-gen-api --namespace serving --since 20m\-g "ERROR|WARN"
- Check rolling deploys: curl -s https://deploy.internal/api/status?service=text-gen-api | jq

6) SLOs and error budget policy (quick reference)
- Service: text-generation-hosting-api (prod)
  - Availability SLO: 99.9% monthly
  - Latency SLOs: p50 < 80ms, p95 < 250ms (in-region)
  - Error budget: 0.1% per month

Error budget burn thresholds & actions:
- 5% burn in 24h: Incident retrospective required, alert to platform reliability channel.
- 25% burn in 24h: Halt risky rollouts for the service, schedule immediate postmortem.
- 50% burn: Priority exec briefing + allocation of dedicated troubleshooting resources.

7) Status page & customer communications (automation rules)
- When to publish: A draft status message must be created within 30 minutes of IC declaration for SEV1/0; published within 60 minutes if public-impacting.
- Minimum status page fields: summary, impact, affected services, current actions, ETA for next update, link to incident doc.
- Automations: statusbot will post initial draft when incident tag is set to public-impact. Sample webhook payload (JSON):

POST /statusbot/webhook
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-0001",
  "severity": "SEV1",
  "summary": "Increased 5xx for text-generation-hosting-api",
  "affected": ["text-generation-hosting-api"],
  "created_at": "2026-02-14T14:12:00Z"
}

8) Customer comms templates (copy-paste placeholders)
Initial acknowledgement (public status):
Subject: Redwood Inference - Partial service degradation impacting text generation\nHello,

We are investigating elevated error rates impacting the text generation API. Our engineers have acknowledged the issue and are working on restoring normal service. We will post updates on this status page and in the incident doc: <CONFLUENCE-INCIDENT-URL>.

Next update by: <ETA 30m>

— Redwood Inference Trust & Ops

Status update (follow-up):
Subject: Update: text-generation API - mitigation in progress

Summary: We have identified increased load on the model-serving pool caused by a recent deploy. We are rolling back the deploy and scaling additional capacity. Error rates have decreased from 12% to 4%. Recovery ETA: ~25 minutes.

Customer-facing resolution (final):
Subject: Resolved: text-generation service restored

Summary: The service has recovered after rollback to commit <SHA> and scaling serving capacity. No data loss was observed. If you experienced errors during the incident, please open a support case referencing INC-<ID>.

9) Post-incident & learning loop
- Within 24 hours: IC posts initial incident timeline and provisional causes in confluence doc.
- Within 72 hours: Primary author drafts the postmortem using the template below.
- Within 10 business days: Review meeting with SRE, product, and customer success to validate remediation actions and owner assignment.

Postmortem minimum template (copy into confluence)
- Title: [SEV] Short title - YYYY-MM-DD
- Summary: 2–3 sentence blameless summary
- Impact: services/customers affected, times, measurable impact
- Timeline: minute-level timeline with commands & links
- Root cause analysis: evidence-backed cause(s)
- Action items: owner, ETA, verification steps
- Follow-ups: customer outreach tasks, docs to update

10) On-call handoff & rotation notes
Handoff checklist:
- Declare handoff in Slack with day-summary and known issues
- Share current incidents and link to the confluence incident doc
- Confirm runbook bookmarks and credentials (use secrets manager)
- Confirm primary backup contact for the rotation day

Rotation guidance:
- Rotation cadence: 1-week primary rotation for SRE on-call. Secondary is 2-week shift.
- Shift swaps: require owner manager approval and update to PagerDuty schedule.

Handoff template (Slack message):
Good morning, team — handoff to @oncall-text-gen for week of YYYY-MM-DD. No active SEV incidents. Active items: 1) rollout <PR#> paused; 2) spike in synthetic errors on us-east-1 (see inc doc). Primary backup: @secondary-text-gen.

11) Game-day exercise (lightweight scenario, 90 minutes)
Objective: Validate detection, automated mitigations, IC appointment, and status page publication.
Participants: 1 IC, 2 responders, 1 scribe, 1 comms owner.
Scenario: Synthetic monitor simulates a 6-minute SEV1 for text-generation-hosting-api caused by a model-serving OOM after a canary rollout.
Schedule:
- 0–10m: Detection & page
- 10–25m: Triage & initial mitigation (rollback)
- 25–45m: Bridge established & customer comm draft published
- 45–75m: Root cause discovery & implement longer-term fix (reproduce locally)
- 75–90m: Recovery confirmation & retrospective notes written
Success criteria:
- Acknowledge and start bridge within 10 minutes
- Status page update published within 45 minutes
- Post-exercise retro notes created within 24 hours

12) Metrics & tooling recommendations
- Monitors should include: high-cardinality error rates, synthetic end-to-end tests, model pool GPU saturation, and KV cache miss rate.
- Use the incident SDK to create incident docs automatically (inc-sdk create --service text-gen --severity SEV1).

13) Security & sensitive data handling during incidents
- Never paste full access tokens, private keys, or customer PII into incident Slack channels or confluence incident logs. Use references to secrets manager entries and redact values.

14) Appendix: quick pagerduty routing YAML sample
---
service: text-generation-hosting-api
escalation_policy: text-gen-escalation
routing_rules:
  - condition: "env == prod and severity >= SEV1"
    target: pagerduty_oncall_team_textgen
  - condition: "region == us-east-1 and severity >= SEV2"
    target: pagerduty_oncall_team_textgen_us_east
---

15) Appendix: related pages and references
- Internal deploy dashboard: https://deploy.internal/services/text-gen-api
- Incident SDK: confluence/eng-sre/incident-sdk-reference
- Autoscale ops runbook: confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/autoscale-ops

If you have suggestions for updates to this workflow or additional templates, contact the owner team: engineering@redwood-inference.internal

payload.page_title: Oncall Playbook for Throttle and Backpressure Events

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook defines the operational procedures for diagnosing, containing, and restoring services experiencing request throttling and internal backpressure. It covers first-responder actions, automated mitigations, escalation paths, customer-facing messaging templates, post-incident requirements, and recommended game-day exercises. The goal is to restore normal throughput while preserving data integrity and minimizing customer impact.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to service degradations where requests are being rejected, queued, or experiencing sustained elevated queue latency due to resource saturation or upstream/downstream throttles.
- Typical signals: elevated 5xx rates, rising queue length, worker OOMs, kernel-level I/O saturation, Redis/DB connection pooling exhaustion, or explicit 429 responses emitted by Redwood gateway or a dependency.
- Out-of-scope: routine rate limiting intentionally configured per-customer unless behavior is anomalous for that customer tier.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge pager and set a temporary incident channel (Slack): #incident-<service>-throttle-<YYYYMMDD>.
2) Identify scope: Which regions, zones, clusters, and customer segments are affected? Use the dashboard filter: Service=/service-name, Region, Model, Route.
3) Confirm pager validity: Check alert triggers (thresholds breached and previous alert history).
4) Apply read-only guardrail: If possible, flip to circuit-breaker mode for the affected route to stop accepting new long-running requests while preserving short calls.
5) Capture timeline: note first observed metric, alert name, runbooks invoked, and the oncall(s) assigned.

Immediate containment options (choose applicable):
- Degrade non-critical features: disable batch-heavy endpoints, async background processes, and non-essential telemetry ingestion.
- Scale horizontally: increase worker replicas for stateless request processors if autoscaling is healthy and there's capacity. Command: kubectl -n prod scale deployment/<service> --replicas=<n> (verify capacity with capacity-dashboard first).
- Apply temporary global rate limit / token bucket: route-level config can be tightened for bursty clients. Example CLI: rdlctl routes update --route-id <id> --rate-limit 100rps.
- Drop low-priority queue consumers to free up connections to the database/cache.
- Fallback to a downstream-compatible model variant with lower memory/latency if model serving is the bottleneck.

Diagnostic queries and telemetry (examples to run immediately):
- Redis/Cache:
  * redis-cli -h <host> info stats; check instantaneous_ops_per_sec, blocked_clients, used_memory.
  * Monitor slowlog: redis-cli --latency-history 1000
- DB/Connection pool:
  * SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';
  * Check max_connections and peak usage in last 5m from pg-monitor.
- Kernel/IO:
  * iostat -x 1 5; look for %util > 80.
  * dstat or vmstat to check for swapping.
- Service-level metrics (PromQL examples):
  * Increase in 429s: sum(rate(http_responses_total{code="429",service="<svc>"}[1m])) by (route)
  * Queue latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_queue_duration_seconds_bucket{service="<svc>"}[5m])) by (le))
  * Worker OOMs: increase in kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}

Escalation matrix (time-based):
1) 0-10 minutes: Primary oncall (service owner).
2) 10-25 minutes: Secondary oncall / team SRE.
3) 25-45 minutes: Platform oncall + runtime performance lead.
4) 45+ minutes or customer-impacting outage: Pager duty escalation to ENG_MANAGER_ONCALL and notify Customer Success + Legal (if SLA breach likely).
Add names/roles in incident channel pinned message.

Decision tree: when to declare Severity 2 vs Severity 1
- Severity 2: Significant fraction of customers (>= 10%) experience degraded throughput but essential functionality remains. Latency SLO violation > 5 minutes and sustained 5xx/429 increases.
- Severity 1: Widespread outage where >50% requests failing for >2 minutes, or key customers are blocked and revenue-impacting SLAs are at risk.

Customer communications (templates)
- Short urgent status (use within first 30 minutes; aimed at CS and impacted customers):
Subject: [Redwood] Service disruption affecting request processing (short update)
Body: Hello — we are investigating an incident impacting request processing for some customers in <region>. We have activated our responders and are applying mitigations to restore throughput. We will provide another update within 30 minutes. Impact: increased request rejects (429) and elevated queue latency. No indication of data loss.
- Detailed status (post containment or 60-minute update):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident update — mitigation in place for request throttling
Body: Team — we identified elevated backpressure originating from <root cause summary>. We scaled workers and applied temporary rate limiting for non-critical routes. Impact: partial restoration for most customers; some batch routes remain degraded. Next update at <time>. If you are impacted, contact <support-contact> with your request IDs.
- Post-incident customer summary (after RCA):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident resolved — summary and follow-up actions
Body: The incident that impacted request processing between <start> and <end> has been resolved. Root cause: <one-line root cause>. Actions taken: scaled compute, adjusted pool sizes, and deployed patch to mitigate retry storm. Next steps: permanent config change planned for <date>. Compensation: customers affected for >X hours will receive credit per SLA terms.

Automated mitigations & quick remediations (runbook commands):
- Toggle circuit-breaker (API):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane/api/v1/routes/<route>/circuit-breaker -d '{"state":"open","reason":"incident-throttle"}'
- Increase replica count with safety:
  ./infra-tools scale-safe --service <svc> --target-replicas 12 --check-capacity true
- Temporarily disable heavy telemetry ingestion:
  kubectl -n obs patch deploy telemetry-ingestor --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":1}]'

Post-incident requirements (must be completed within 72 hours):
- Postmortem created in Confluence following the standard template (title: PM: <service> throttle <YYYY-MM-DD>) and linked to incident ticket.
- Action items assigned with owners and ETA.
- Telemetry retention extended for 7 days for all relevant metrics and traces.
- If SLO breached, prepare customer notice and propose credit as per finance policy.

Game-day and simulation guidance (recommended exercises):
- Quarterly tabletop: simulate a downstream DB connection pool exhaustion and walk through containment options. Duration: 90 minutes. Objectives: runbook familiarity, communications, and scaling checks.
- Live drill: in a staging environment, inject 20k concurrent synthetic requests to replicate queue growth and validate circuit-breaker behavior. Validate rollback procedures.
- Oncall rotation training: new oncall shadow for two weeks during which they run at least one simulated throttle incident under supervision.

Oncall ownership and runbook hygiene:
- Service owner: responsible for maintaining this playbook, verifying commands/monthly, and confirming reviewer list.
- SRE team: responsible for platform-level mitigations (scaling automation, cluster capacity dashboard).
- Documentation checklist (every 6 months): verify telemetry queries, update escalation contacts, and test CLI commands in staging.

SLOs and thresholds (summary table):
| Metric | Warning threshold | Alert threshold | Owner |
| HTTP 429 rate (svc-wide) | 0.5% of requests over 5m | 2% of requests over 1m | Service owner |
| Request queue 95th pctl | > 500ms for 10m | > 2s for 5m | Service owner |
| Worker OOM rate | 1 per hour | 3 per 10 minutes | Infra team |
| DB connection usage | > 70% capacity | > 90% capacity | DB team |

Postmortem template (minimum fields to include):
- Title
- Incident timeline (1-minute resolution)
- Scope & impact (customers, features, SLAs)
- Root cause analysis (evidence-backed)
- Immediate mitigations and why they worked/didn't
- Corrective actions (owners, ETA)
- Follow-up verification plan

Appendix A — common root cause patterns and recommended fixes:
- Retry storm: implement jittered exponential backoff and client-side capped concurrency. Review client SDK for aggressive retries.
- Connection pool exhaustion: increase pool size with connection multiplexing or move to connection pooling proxy.
- Memory leak in model-serving worker: roll back to previous model variant and run perf test; schedule a GC-profiler run.
- Disk IO saturation: offload logs/telemetry or increase IOPS/throughput on affected volumes.

Appendix B — links and references:
- Incident ticket template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-ticket-template
- Runbook automation tools: /confluence/eng-platform/automation-scripts
- Pager rotations: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations-directory

If you update this document: add a changelog entry at the top of the body with date, author, and brief change note.

Contact: Anika Rao (service lead), eng-oncall@redwood.example.com

payload.page_title: Weekend and Holiday Rapid Restoration Blueprint

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This blueprint codifies a predictable, low-friction incident process for weekends, public holidays, and short-staff windows. It prioritizes rapid restoration, clear ownership handoffs, and timely customer status updates while minimizing cognitive load for responders. Use this runbook when service availability or latency SLOs are at risk outside core weekday coverage.

Audience: Oncall engineers (primary), SRE leads (secondary), CS/Support on-call (notification consumers).

Goals and constraints
- Restore customer-visible functionality within the target recovery window: P0 full restore goal = 60 minutes; P1 partial restore goal = 180 minutes.
- Maintain clear single-threaded ownership for the incident commander during the weekend window.
- Use automated tooling (status page, incident tags) to reduce manual communications.
- Minimize handoffs: if incident spans multiple days/rotations, favor overnight keepers rather than full re-briefs.

SLOs and alert thresholds (weekend/holiday specifics)
| Class | Symptom examples | Pager threshold | Target restoration | Customer comm cadence |
|-------|------------------|-----------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| P0 | Total serving outage for hosted API in a region; failed auth across fleet | Pager immediately (phone + slack) | 60 minutes | 0/15/30/60 min updates (status page) |
| P1 | Severe SLO degradation (p99 latency > 2x SLO) or batch job failures affecting background indexing | Pager + slack | 180 minutes | 0/30/90 min updates |
| P2 | Partial feature regressions, non-blocking errors | Slack-only | Next-business-day resolution | 1x status page update at incident start (if customer-visible) |

Ownership and roles (weekend adapted)
- Incident Commander (IC) — single oncall engineer assigned via pager. Responsible for decisions, customer-facing status updates, and declaring severity.
- Recovery Lead — optional; takes tactical restoration tasks (kernel restarts, capacity scaling).
- Communications Liaison — SRE or CS oncall who owns status page text and customer notices. May be the IC if small incident.
- Escalation Board — senior oncall engineers reachable by phone; default escalation window = 20 minutes if IC cannot make progress.

Pre-incident preparations (what to do before extended coverage windows)
1. Run the Holiday Healthcheck (48 hours before): automated script checks KV caches, queue depth, regional load balancing health, and model-serving capacity. Run locally:

$ ./tools/holiday_healthcheck.sh --regions us-east-1,eu-west-1 --full

2. Pre-warm capacity: run the auto-scale pre-warm playbook for the expected traffic delta. Example command:

$ ./infra/scale.sh --pool model-serving --target 1500

3. Create a weekend focused runbook index in Slack channel #ops-weekend with pinned runbooks and owner roster.

Activation procedure (0–5 min)
1. Pager fires. IC acknowledges via phone within 2 minutes.
2. IC posts initial message in #ops-weekend channel with incident-tag, severity, and quick context:

Incident: <short-identifier> | Severity: P0 | Region: us-east-1 | Impact: Host API 503s

3. Communications Liaison starts a status page incident in the StatusPage system (see templates below) and toggles maintenance mode if appropriate.

Triage and immediate containment (5–20 min)
1. Quick triage checklist (one-pass):
   a. Check control plane health: api-gateway, auth, config-service.
   b. Validate whether rollout, infra job, or third-party dependency changed in the last 30 min (gitops, deploy pipeline).
   c. Confirm scope: single-customer vs multi-tenant vs global.
2. Containment options (pick the lowest-impact action that reduces customer-visible errors):
   - Route traffic away from problematic AZ/region via traffic-control playbook (CLI steps below).
   - Fail open to a compatible model variant or cached responses (policy: only for non-sensitive endpoints).
   - Scale up dedicated pools (for Dedicated customers) per escalation rules in the dedicated-capacity runbook.

$ rwr --action drain --target az-us-east-1a --service host-api --by 10
(Wait 60s, validate 5xx graph and p99 latency)

Containment validation checklist: monitor 5xx rate, p99 latency, queue sizes. If containment reduces impact, keep IC in-loop and schedule follow-up fix.

Mitigation and recovery (20–60+ min)
- Rapid rollback: if the incident coincided with a deployment in the last hour, prefer rollback to last green revision after safety check. Use:

$ deploy rollback --service host-api --to-revision <sha> --force-if-empty

- Kernel/driver remediation: for GPU-fleet related incidents, follow the GPU fleet micro-runbook (GPUs should not be power-cycled without SRE approval during holiday windows unless explicitly required).

- Cache priming: after cache flushes, run priming job (CLI example):
$ jobs/prime_cache --model fastgen --top-n 500 --regions us-east-1

- If third-party dependency is failing (CDN, IAM provider), switch to retry policy and circuit-breaker settings for weekend: 3 retries with exponential backoff starting at 100ms.

Escalation matrix (weekend adjustments)
- IC -> Escalation Board member 1 (20 min) -> Escalation Board member 2 (40 min) -> CTO on-call (90 min)
- For customer-impacting P0s, automatically page the SRE Manager and CS Director after 30 minutes if not resolved.

Status page and customer communications (templates and cadence)
- Initial status page post (within 5 min):
Title: Service degradation in us-east-1
Details: We are investigating increased 5xx rates for the Redwood hosted API in us-east-1. Our on-call team is actively investigating and working to restore normal service. We will update at 15 minutes.
- Follow-up template (15/30/60 min)
Details template: Current impact: X%; Actions taken: traffic drain to healthy AZ, rollback of recent deploy, cache priming job launched. Next update in 30 minutes.
- Resolution message
Title: Service restored in us-east-1
Details: We have restored normal service and are monitoring. Root cause: incorrect rollout of a config change to the rate limiter. Post-incident report scheduled. Customer action: none required.

Customer email/snippet for enterprise tenants (CS liaison)
Subject: Incident update — Redwood API (us-east-1)
Body: Hello — We're writing to notify you of a service degradation affecting API calls to us-east-1 on <date>. We restored service at <time>. Our team is preparing a post-incident summary for any customers who require evidence for compliance. For immediate questions, reply to this email or contact your account manager.

Post-incident actions and short postmortem cadence
1. Evidence capture: collect timelines, logs, graphs, and deploy metadata within 2 business days. Keep original incident page pin in #ops-weekend.
2. Short postmortem (48–72 hours): IC produces a concise incident brief including timeline, root cause hypothesis, mitigation, and action items. Use the one-page template (appendix).
3. Full RCA (if P0 or if SLA credits are requested): assign an RCA owner and due date within 5 business days.

Game day and practice guidance for weekend incidents
- Quarterly weekend game day: simulate a P0 on a Saturday. Objectives: validate capacity pre-warm procedures, status page automation, and escalation tree. Record scores on the incident readiness dashboard.
- Roles to practice: IC handoff, Communications Liaison rapid post creation, automated rollback verification.
- Failure injection checklist: traffic-shift to a bad AZ, simulate model-serving OOMs, and flip a canary config. Use the staging chaos harness:

$ chaosctl inject --scenario weekend-route-failure --target us-east-1

Handoff and long-duration incidents (overnight policies)
- If incident remains active across a scheduled rotation, the incoming oncall must be briefed via a 5-minute handoff call with the current IC. If the incident is >4 hours and unresolved, escalate to the Escalation Board before handoff.
- Create a concise Handoff note in the incident Slack thread: progress to date, next steps, blockers, and outstanding action items.

Runbook index and quick reference (pinned)
- Traffic control playbook (commands and quick checks)
- Deployment rollback checklist
- GPU fleet micro-runbook
- Status page templates and automation scripts
- Enterprise customer email templates

Appendix A — One-page postmortem template
- Title: <Short incident title>
- Dates/times: Start, containment, restore, close
- Severity: P0/P1...
- Summary (1 paragraph)
- Timeline (bullet list, timestamped)
- Root cause (short)
- Immediate mitigation and long-term remediation actions (with owners & due dates)
- Monitoring and SLO changes (if any)

Appendix B — Status page automation snippets
- CLI to create an incident (internal status tool):
$ statusctl create --service host-api --region us-east-1 --impact major --visible true --summary "Investigating 5xxs"
- Script to auto-post first update if IC hasn't posted in 5 min (cron):
*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/status_autopost.sh --incident <id> --msg "We are investigating — will update in 15 minutes"

Appendix C — Weekend-specific safety guardrails
- Do not perform cross-region DB schema changes during weekend windows.
- Do not power-cycle GPU hosts unless authorized by SRE Manager.
- For rollback: prefer config rollbacks over code rollbacks when possible; code rollbacks require CI health verification.

Ownership and maintenance
- Document owner: SRE (oncall-and-incident-response) team — maintain cadence: review this blueprint 30 days before major US public holidays.
- Game day owner: Oncall ops lead (Marta Rios).
- Audit trail: update the last_reviewed tag and attach game-day scorecards after each practice.

Where to find related runbooks
- See pinned index in Slack #ops-weekend and the Runbook library: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/

Feedback and iteration
If this blueprint produces friction during an active holiday, file a feedback ticket in the internal tracker with label "ops-weekend-feedback". The oncall-and-incident-response team will triage and iterate.

payload.page_title: Silent Failure Detection and Mitigation Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines detection signals, automated mitigations, escalation flows, and communication templates for "silent" failures — incidents where service behavior degrades without clear error spikes (e.g., high-ratio malformed responses, sudden drop in success-rate, semantic regressions in outputs). Silent failures are high-impact because customers may not receive explicit errors, and traditional alerting can miss them.

Scope: gateway-api, inference-runtime, request-router, kv-cache, and the metrics/observability pipelines that report on them.

Summary of approach:
- Detect: Combine synthetic traffic, user-signal telemetry, anomaly detection (statistical and ML), and health sampling.
- Mitigate: Engage fast failover to cached variants, route to fallback models, or enable degraded mode with explicit customer messaging.
- Restore & Learn: Triage root cause, run postmortem, update detection rules, and schedule a targeted game day.

1) Key signals and detection recipes

1.1 Synthetic checks (primary early-warning)
- Every region runs three synthetic scenarios per minute: short prompt, long prompt, and streaming response test.
- Failure conditions (trigger): response latency > 1.5x baseline OR response token count < 60% of expected OR diffs in structured fields (JSON output mismatch).
- Synthetic check implementation: kubectl exec into synthetic-runner or run via k8s CronJob -> POST to /v1/generate with test prompts and validate schema.

1.2 Customer-facing signal telemetry
- Successful-response-rate (SRR): percent of requests that meet schema and pass quick content checks. Alert if SRR drops by >4 percentage points vs 1h rolling baseline AND absolute SRR < 98%.
- Model-quality edge-case: measured by sample-entropy and hallucination heuristics (semantic-checker). Alert if entropy distribution shifts > 2 standard deviations.

1.3 Infrastructure & proxy indicators
- Unexpected 200-with-empty-body: detect >0.1% of traffic in 5 minutes.
- KV-cache miss spike: cache hit-rate drop >25% in 10 minutes for a customer namespace.
- Router-tail-latency spike without CPU/GPU pressure suggests upstream silent fail.

Prometheus examples (copy-paste)
- SRR anomaly (example):
  sum(rate(inference_response_valid_total[5m])) / sum(rate(inference_requests_total[5m]))
- 200-empty-body detection (example):
  increase(http_requests_total{status="200",response_length="0"}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.001

2) Automated mitigations (fast actions)

2.1 Immediate automated responses (0 - 3 minutes)
- If synthetic check fails in >=2 regions OR SRR drop alert fires: automatically enable edge cache-only mode for the affected route for 2 minutes while the alert is routed to on-call. This is implemented by toggling the feature-flag: ffctl set route.<route>.degraded_mode=true.
- Circuit breaker: If router sees 200-empty-body ratio > 0.5% for >1 minute, trip circuit to fallback model (model-fallback:v2) and scale fallback pool by x2. CLI: rctl fallback enable --route <route> --model model-fallback:v2.

2.2 Safe degraded behavior (operator decision)
- Degraded mode behavior summary (recommended): return a 503 with friendly message for non-essential requests; for essential customers, route to cached-response + post-metadata that indicates potential degradation.
- Owner to evaluate: allowlist of customers to receive degraded responses vs. explicit failure.

3) Escalation matrix and on-call responsibilities

3.1 Triage ownership (first 10 minutes)
- Pager: primary SRE oncall (team: eng-sre) receives immediate alert.
- First action (within 5 minutes): acknowledge alert, confirm signal (synthetic logs, SRR graph), and execute automated mitigations if not already in flight.
- If automated mitigation applied, primary documents steps in incident channel and tags owners.

3.2 Next-phase escalation (10 - 60 minutes)
- If issue persists >10 minutes after mitigation: escalate to runtime-owner (serving-runtime) and network-owner (infra).
- Engage product on-call if customer-facing quality implications (samples failing structured output or hallucination).
- Standup a 15-minute bridge if customer-impacting and >30 minutes unresolved. Bridge owner: primary SRE.

3.3 Leadership & customer escalation (>60 minutes)
- Director on-call notified at 60 minutes for any active degradation impacting >2 customers or SRR < 95% company-wide.

4) Communication templates

4.1 Internal Slack (incident channel) — short template:
- [INCIDENT START] silent-failure detected: route=<route> regions=<regions> signal=SRR drop/synthetic fail. Actions: enabled degraded_mode, fallback model routed. Next: triage by @triage_owner.

4.2 Customer-facing status message (Status page snippet)
- Title: Degraded responses for generation API (investigating)
- Body: We are investigating reports of degraded responses from our generation API affecting a subset of requests. Some customers may see shorter-than-expected outputs or missing structured fields. Our team has enabled a temporary degraded mode to reduce incorrect outputs while we investigate. We will provide updates by 30 minutes and again hourly.
- Severity and ETA guidance: If you rely on structured outputs for critical workflows, contact support@redwood.ai with your account id and affected request ids.

4.3 Email template for high-touch customers
- Subject: Incident: temporary degradation of generation outputs (Investigation in progress)
- Body: short summary, mitigation steps taken, expected next update window, support contact, suggested temporary mitigations (e.g., pin to fallback model, increase prompt length).

5) Incident runbook checklist (post-detection to postmortem)
- Immediately: capture event id, affected routes, synthetic-runner output, sample failing payloads, and timestamps.
- Within 1 hour: collect core dumps, gpu metrics, router logs (indexed by trace_id), and sampling of returned outputs (store in secure S3 folder: s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/<incident-id>/samples).
- Within 24 hours: assign postmortem owner and file a postmortem draft.
- Within 72 hours: complete corrective actions list (with owners and due dates) and schedule a follow-up game day to validate fixes.

6) Postmortem framing and corrective action examples
- Statement of impact: customers affected, features impacted, SLO deviations (e.g., SRR fell from 99.98% to 94.2% between 02:12–02:44 UTC).
- Root cause hypothesis: model-quantization path selected new kernel that truncates streaming tokens under certain sequence lengths.
- Corrective actions: pin rollout, add unit test for kernel token preservation, update synthetic tests to include failing sequence shapes.
- Verification: create canary group (5% of traffic) with new test harness for two weeks, monitor SRR and entropy metrics.

7) Game day exercises (validation plan)
- Exercise A — Silent-degradation injection: intentionally introduce a semantic checker that mutates a small percentage of outputs without failing responses; confirm detection rules trigger and degraded-mode switches on within 3 minutes. Run quarterly.
- Exercise B — Observability blackout: simulate missing telemetry to verify fallback detection (synthetic checks + sampling).
- Exercise C — Customer escalation simulation: practice high-touch email + status page cadence for 60-minute scenario. Include runbook rehearsal.

8) Ownership and maintenance
- Runbook owner: eng-sre (primary: @oncall-runbook-owner).
- Detection rules maintenance: observability team owns Prometheus/Grafana rules.
- Synthetic scenarios: eng-dx (developer experience) maintains prompt sets.
- Review cadence: review this playbook quarterly and after any silent-failure incident.

Appendices
A) Example logs and traces to collect
- http_access.log sample entry to grep: route=<route> trace_id=<id> status=200 resp_len=0 tokens=0 body_checksum=abc123
- Synthetic-runner output: {"scenario":"long-prompt","latency_ms":342,"valid":false,"diff":"missing_structured_field"}

B) Quick commands
- Toggle degraded mode: ffctl set route.<route>.degraded_mode=true --reason "auto-detected-silent-failure"
- Enable fallback: rctl fallback enable --route <route> --model model-fallback:v2
- Download samples: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/<incident-id>/samples ./samples --recursive

C) Links and references
- Related runbooks: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework-2026
- Synthetic runner code repo: gitlab.internal/redwood/synthetic-runner

End of playbook
