payload.page_title: Duty roster synthesis and incident handback protocol

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document standardizes how we build duty rosters (rotas), synthesize overlapping coverage windows, and perform incident handbacks between responders. The goal is to reduce knowledge loss during shift transitions, ensure timely customer communication, and preserve investigational evidence for post-incident analysis.

Scope: Applies to all on-call engineers, SREs, and incident bridge operators responsible for Redwood Inference production services (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane). Does not replace service-specific runbooks — it augments them with handoff and roster-level rules.

Intended audience: on-call engineers, incident leads, SRE managers, customer-success on-call liaisons.

Key definitions
- Shift: a contiguous on-call assignment (typical length 8 or 12 hours).
- Handback window: the 20-minute overlap period reserved for warm transfer between outgoing and incoming responders.
- Evidence package: structured set of logs, traces, and artifacts captured for postmortem and regulatory evidence.
- Bridge Operator: primary coordinator for the incident bridge and external comms.

Principles
- Prioritize clarity: every handoff must include a short status summary, current mitigation state, and next action list (top 3).
- Make evidence immutable: when feasible snapshot traces and logs before changing system state.
- Prefer short, consistent templates for customer comms and status page updates.
- Automate where possible: roster publishes to Slack, calendar invites include handback reminders, handoff checklist persisted to incident ticket.

Duty roster synthesis (how we design rotas)
1) Shift cadence and lengths
   - Default: 12-hour shifts for primary responders; 8-hour shifts permitted for trainees and cross-team coverage.
   - Night coverage: when region has full-coverage teams, prefer 12-hour with 24-hour overlap on rotation change days (major releases).
2) Predictable overlaps
   - Reserve 20 minutes overlap at each shift boundary as a handback window. This is mandatory and cannot be used for pager swaps.
   - For critical services (SLO: 99.95% availability), add an additional 10-minute escalation buffer during high-traffic windows.
3) Shadow and backup assignments
   - Each primary shift has an assigned shadow (buddy) for the first two weeks after onboarding. Shadow shifts are half-duration and scheduled mid-shift for knowledge sharing.
4) Roster artifacts and automation
   - Roster publishes as a CSV and auto-posts to #oncall-status daily at 06:00 UTC.
   - Calendar invites include: shift owner, shadow, on-call playbook link, pager escalation matrix, and handback checklist link.

Handback protocol (step-by-step)
Pre-handback: (Outgoing)
1) Prepare your evidence package:
   - Snapshot the incident ticket with current timeline (timestamps ISO 8601).
   - Attach top-5 relevant logs (service, ingress, egress, kgv-cache stats, scheduler events) limited to 30MB total.
   - Export a 15-minute trace span surrounding the root-causing request (if available).
2) Draft the 3-line status summary (SMS format):
   - Line 1: Current impact and customer-facing symptom.
   - Line 2: Active mitigations and owners of each mitigation.
   - Line 3: Immediate next actions and risk level (low/medium/high).
3) Notify: post the status summary in the incident bridge and mark your calendar for the handback window.

During handback: (Overlap window)
1) Live voice/video: prefer a 5–10 minute live sync in the bridge channel. If voice unavailable, use the bridge chat and a short Loom or transcript.
2) Walkthrough agenda (5 bullets):
   - One-sentence incident summary.
   - Evidence artifacts and where to find them.
   - Active mitigations and their health checks.
   - Outstanding actions (owner and ETA).
   - Escalation triggers (explicit threshold values) and next-level contacts.
3) Incoming confirms: the incoming responder repeats back the top 3 next actions and acknowledges evidence locations.

Post-handback: (Outgoing)
1) Set the incident ticket field "handoff_complete" to true and add a 1-paragraph handover note.
2) Outgoing stays available for 15 minutes post-handoff for clarifying questions unless otherwise agreed.

Emergency hot-handover (when overlap cannot occur)
- Execute a cold handover: outgoing posts a preformatted incident stub and the evidence package, then immediately notifies the incoming responder via SMS/phone. The incoming responder must acknowledge within 5 minutes or escalate to L2 on-call.

Incident evidence package (required elements)
- Ticket timeline (ordered list of events with UTC timestamps).
- Key metric slices: request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, queue depth, GPU utilization (select 1–6 metrics relevant to service). Include pre-incident baseline and current window.
- Traces: root spans + top 3 child spans for the top failing path.
- Config snapshot: model-serving config (model version, quantization profile, batching settings), routing policy, and traffic split.
- Any recent deploy IDs (commit hashes) with timestamps.
- Links to long-term storage (S3/GCS) for large artifacts and a checksum (sha256) in the ticket.

Evidence retention policy for postmortem
- Keep short-term (attached to the incident ticket) for 180 days.
- Move curated artifacts (de-duplicated logs, trimmed traces, and config snapshots) to the postmortem folder in the evidence bucket for 7 years if incident meets "regulatory" criteria (customer SLA breach > 99.9% threshold or enterprise contract clause).

Customer communications templates (use and adapt)
- Immediate acknowledgement (within 15 minutes):
  "We’ve detected elevated error rates affecting the Redwood API in region <region>. Our engineers are investigating; we will provide an update within 60 minutes. Impact: <symptom>."

- Status update (1 hour):
  "Update: Root cause is under investigation; mitigation X has been applied (rate-limiter rollback / routing fallback). Customers may see reduced capacity but successful requests continue for most tenants. Next update at <time> or sooner if status changes."

- Post-incident summary (published with postmortem):
  "Summary: On <date> at <time> UTC, a codepath change caused increased latency and 5xx errors for the Hosted API in <region>. Impacted customers: <summary>. Mitigations: <actions>. Root cause: <concise root cause>. Remediation and follow-ups: <bullet list>."

Status page update snippets
- Short status (for banner): "Investigating: elevated 5xx in <region>."
- Medium status (detail):
  Title: Degraded: API error rate increased in <region>
  Body: We are actively investigating an increase in server errors impacting a subset of requests. Partial mitigations in place; monitoring.

Game day and handoff drills
- Objective: validate warm handoff under pressure and evidence preservation.
- Scenario examples:
  1) KV-cache eviction storm causing transient timeouts.
  2) Autoscaler misconfiguration leading to cold-start surge.
  3) Model-loading contention causing elevated latency on long sequences.
- Game-day schedule (90 min):
  - 00–10 min: pre-brief and objectives
  - 10–30 min: inject incident (simulated alerts)
  - 30–60 min: active mitigation; perform at least one handback across a shift boundary
  - 60–80 min: evidence snapshot and ticket finalization
  - 80–90 min: retro and action assignment
- Scoring: measure handback completeness (did incoming confirm: status, mitigation, evidence location). Pass threshold: 90% of handoffs include complete evidence package.

Runbook example: handoff checklist (pasteable)
- Handoff checklist (must complete before marking handoff_complete):
  * [ ] 3-line status summary posted to bridge
  * [ ] Evidence package uploaded and links present in ticket
  * [ ] Active mitigations and monitoring queries shared
  * [ ] Next 3 actions assigned with ETA
  * [ ] Incoming ack recorded in ticket
  * [ ] Outgoing set availability window (15 minutes)

Escalation matrix (short form)
- Pager L1 (primary responder) — 10 minutes to acknowledge
- Pager L2 (service on-call) — escalate if unresolved after 30 minutes or if SLO breach imminent
- Engineering oncall lead — engage if multiple services are impacted or if mitigation requires deploy rollback
- Customer-success escalation — notify when incident impacts >5% of enterprise customers or SLA credit may be required

SLO triggers and automated actions
- If p99 latency > 3x baseline for 5 minutes: auto-open incident ticket and notify L1 via paging system.
- If error rate > 2% (absolute) for 15 minutes: trigger automatic routing fallback to model-variant B and notify bridge operator.

Handoff quality metrics (tracked monthly)
- Handoff completeness rate (target >= 95%).
- Average handback overlap observed (target >= 18 minutes).
- Evidence capture rate (tickets with full evidence package) target >= 98%.

Operational ownership and review cadence
- Roster owner: SRE Ops (primary) — responsible for publishing and automation.
- Handoff protocol owner: Incident Response guild (rotating steward every quarter).
- Review cadence: quarterly review of handback failures and postmortem evidence quality; annual roster redesign aligned with team growth.

Templates & quick commands
- Incident ticket stub (copy into ticket):
  "Short summary: <one line>
  Impact window: <start time>
  3-line status: <status>
  Evidence locations: <links>
  Next actions: <bullets>"
- Helpful CLI snippets:
  - Export recent logs:
    rinfctl logs export --service api-gateway --since 30m --out /tmp/api-logs.tar.gz
  - Snapshot tracing window:
    rinfctl trace snapshot --service model-serving --span 00:15 --out /tmp/trace.zip
  - Publish to ticket:
    hub ticket comment --id 1234 --body "Evidence uploaded: s3://evidence/incident-1234/"

Appendix: examples of a strong handback note (templates)
- Example short handback note: "Handoff at 2026-03-02T07:40Z. Impact: elevated 5xx for tokenization service in us-west-2. Mitigation: routing fallback to variant-v2 applied (owner: Marcus). Evidence: s3://evidence/incident-5678/ (sha256: abc...). Next actions: 1) Confirm backpressure drains (Owen, 10m), 2) Validate quantization profile (Marcus, 60m). Outgoing available until 08:00Z."

- Example cold handover (emergency): "Cold handover — outgoing cut at 2026-02-11T23:50Z. Posted full evidence package and invited incoming via SMS. Incoming acknowledged at 2026-02-11T23:54Z and confirmed next actions."

Related resources
- Service runbook library (link in console)
- Incident postmortem template (postmortem-runbook)
- Roster automation repo: git://redwood/rerota

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Leah Martinez (initial draft)
- 2026-02-10: Added emergency cold-handover steps and evidence retention rules (review: Aisha Patel)
- 2026-03-02: Published with game-day schedule and metrics (review: Marcus Li)

payload.page_title: Status Cadence, Triage-to-Restoration Runbook and Responder Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This page defines a single runbook that covers the full incident lifecycle from first signal through triage, containment, restoration, and customer-facing status cadence. It combines responder playbook rules, sample status messages, postmortem requirements, and a game-day syllabus so teams can practice end-to-end incident handling with consistent customer communications.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood API, Redwood Dedicated, and Redwood Private control-plane incidents where customer-visible degradation (latency, errors, or availability) or data-plane anomalies occur.
- Excludes internal build failures that do not affect customer traffic (see eng-infra runbooks).

Key definitions
- P0: Total outage or sustained >50% customer requests failing for 5+ minutes.
- P1: Major degradation causing elevated errors/latency across multiple customers or routes for 10+ minutes.
- SLO breach: Any single route where 99th-percentile latency > 2x target or error rate > 5% over 10 minutes.

Roles & responsibilities
1) Incident Commander (IC) - owns coordination, stakeholder updates, and prioritization.
   - Primary: oncall-engineer for service owner.
   - Secondary: team lead or senior SRE if IC unavailable.
2) Lead Responder - technical triage and remediation (may be multiple).
3) Communications Owner - drafts status updates and customer-facing messages.
4) Postmortem Author - documents root cause, timeline, impact, and action items.
5) Oncall Backup - takes over after 2-hour shift or at IC request.

Incident lifecycle (high level)
1) Signal & Acknowledge
   - Alerts from Prometheus/Alertmanager, Observability Console, automated SLO-detector, or customer report.
   - IC acknowledges within 2 minutes for P0, 10 minutes for P1.
2) Initial Triage (0–10 minutes)
   - Verify scope and blast radius (routes, regions, customers).
   - Collect quick evidence: recent deploys, infra changes, autoscaler events, kernel OOMs, GPU failures.
   - Determine P-level and declare incident.
3) Containment (10–30 minutes)
   - Apply immediate mitigations: circuit-breaker, route remap, rollback, scale-up, static-capacity warmup.
   - Preserve forensic data (profiles, KV caches, coredumps) and tag logs.
4) Restoration (30–180 minutes)
   - Implement root fix or safe fallback. Validate with smoke tests and canary traffic.
5) Recovery & Close (>180 minutes)
   - Confirm stability for two consecutive 15-min windows, then move to closure.
6) Postmortem (within 72 hours)
   - Publish timeline, root cause, impact, corrective actions, and owners.

Triage checklist (quick reference)
- Is the issue global or region-specific?
- Which models/routes are impacted? (chat/generation/embeddings/rerank)
- Recent deploys or config changes in last 60 minutes?
- Error-class fingerprints (500s, 429s, timeout, model OOM).
- Resource signals: GPU mem err, node reboots, AZ network flaps.
- Is the Canary or Dedicated pool showing degraded metrics?

Escalation matrix
- P0: Notify IC -> Pager (all-hands for service) -> Exec on-call if >30 minutes unresolved.
- P1: Notify IC -> Pager -> Senior SRE on backup list if >60 minutes.
- If customer data exposure suspected: immediate Security/Privacy page and Legal notification (see security-and-compliance/audit-logging).

SLOs and thresholds (operational targets)
- API availability: 99.95% monthly. Critical route availability target: 99.9%.
- Error rate: <0.5% 5xx on aggregate; SLO trigger when route 5xx > 1% over 10 minutes.
- Latency: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 450ms. Alert when p99 > 2x target for 10 minutes.
- Customer impact window: track number of customers and percent of routed tokens affected.

Status cadence (customer-facing)
- Initial acknowledgement: within 15 minutes for P0/P1. Short single-sentence summary + next update ETA.
- Regular updates: every 30 minutes for P0 until stabilization, every 60 minutes for P1.
- Resolution notice: include root cause summary, restoration steps, and any mitigations for customers.
- Postmortem link: published within 72 hours with technical details and customer impact summary.

Customer status templates
- Initial (P0)
  Subject: Redwood status: Major service disruption affecting [service/region]
  Body: We are investigating elevated errors affecting [service/routes/region]. Customers may experience increased latency and request failures. Our oncall team is actively triaging. Next update: [ETA]. For urgent questions contact support@redwood.com with incident ID: [INC-ID].

- Update (mid-incident)
  Subject: Redwood status update: [short summary] — [INC-ID]
  Body: What changed: [brief note]. Current status: [mitigation in place / traffic partially restored / routing fallback active]. Impacted customers: [list or "broadly"]. Next update: [ETA].

- Resolution
  Subject: Redwood incident resolved: [service/region] — [INC-ID]
  Body: Summary: the incident that caused [symptoms] has been resolved at [time UTC]. Root cause: [concise root cause statement]. Customer impact: [affected routes/customers/time window]. Remediation and next steps: [rollout, hardening, follow-up]. Postmortem: [link].

Runbook snippets (common scenarios)
1) Model inference latency spike (generation APIs)\   - Verify whether problem is model-specific: check model variant metrics and KV cache hit-rate.\   - If a single model variant causing spike, shift traffic to verified fallback (model: redwood-lite-v1 -> redwood-stable-v1) and enable quantized profile.\   - If kernel-level GPU stalls detected: drain affected GPU, re-schedule workloads, and open a GPU-fleet ticket.\2) Backend datastore timeouts (config store or user metadata)\   - Check DB connection pools and read replicas.\   - Apply circuit-breaker at API layer, use cached responses for read-only endpoints.\   - Rollback recent schema migrations if correlated to deploy timestamp.\3) Region network degradation\   - Reroute traffic to healthy region per smart-routing policy.\   - Notify cloud provider and set support ticket.\   - If cross-region state sync affected: disable cross-region writes and operate read-only for affected region.

Forensic preservation steps
1) Preserve logs and tracing window: tag and extend retention for implicated hosts/services.
2) Snapshot KV cache and upload to incident storage with access logs.
3) If coredump created, store with obfuscated customer identifiers and notify Security.

On-call rotation & handoff guidance
- Rotation length: 7 days for primary oncall engineers. Secondary SRE rotates monthly.
- Handoff checklist (before leaving shift):
  - Confirm incident list and active mitigations.
  - Update bridge and status page.
  - Verify runbook references and open tickets assigned.
  - Confirm oncall backup acknowledged handoff.
- Incident fatigue policy: no engineer should serve more than two high-severity (P0/P1) incidents in a single rotation without cadence-adjusted break. Notify manager for relief.

Game day syllabus (quarterly)
- Objective: validate end-to-end triage, customer comms, and cross-team escalation for a region-level outage and a model regression scenario.
- Participants: service owners, SRE, Support, Product, Security representative.
- Exercises:\  1) Simulated region network partition at T0: validate routing failover and customer status cadence.\  2) Silent model quality regression at T30: detect via eval pipeline and trigger rollback + customer notice.
- Success criteria: mean time-to-detect < 10 minutes, mean time-to-restore < 45 minutes for simulated P1, customer comms delivered within 15 minutes.

Postmortem template & timeline
- Publishable within 72 hours. Required sections (publish to confluence page and link in status):\  - Title: concise summary and incident ID\  - Severity: P0/P1/P2\  - Timeline: minute-granular events from first signal to recovery\  - Impact: affected customers, % of requests, duration\  - Root cause analysis: technical cause + contributing factors\  - Corrective actions: short-term and long-term with owners and due dates\  - Detection & mitigation metrics: detection time, restore time, and verification plan\  - Follow-ups: verification tests and scheduled review (owner + date)

Post-incident follow-up cadence
- 24 hours: internal hotwash meeting to capture missing facts.
- 72 hours: publish postmortem draft and share with reviewers.\- 2 weeks: closure meeting for action items and verification of mitigations.

Instrumentation & telemetry requirements for incidents
- Mandatory signals to attach to incident: p95/p99 latency, 5xx error rate, request volume by route, model-KV cache hit-rate, GPU error counters, autoscaler events.\- Ensure all incidents are tagged with incident ID in log traces and alert annotations.

Document maintenance and ownership
- Owner: eng-sre team.
- Review cadence: annual review and after any P0.
- Game days: scheduled quarterly; rotation owners must run at least one per year.

Appendix: example internal incident status message (IC -> Execs)\- Subject: [INC-ID] P0 - Service degradation affecting Redwood API (summary)\- Body: Time: [T0 UTC] | Current status: partial traffic restored to 63% | Impact: 45% of customers saw errors on /v1/generate | Action taken: traffic staged to fallback model, GPU nodes drained in eu-west-1 | Next ETA: 30m | IC: @aisha.patel

Contact and references
- Support: support@redwood.com\- Security incident contact: security-ops@redwood.com\- Related runbooks: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture, eng-sre/capacity-planning

Change log
- 2026-11-02 created by Aisha Patel\- 2027-02-10 updated: added SLO thresholds and game-day syllabus

payload.page_title: SRE On-Call Guidelines and Game-Day Curriculum

sections.body:
This document codifies Redwood's SRE on-call expectations, a standard incident lifecycle, runbook patterns, rotation guidance, and a reproducible game-day curriculum for operational readiness. It also includes customer-facing and status-page templates for consistent communications.

Scope: eng-facing operational guidance for production incidents impacting hosted and dedicated inference services (redwood-api, inference-router, kv-cache, batch-scheduler). Not a replacement for service-specific runbooks, which should be linked below.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Sev 1 (P0): Customer-facing outage impacting >= 10% of requests or regional full-service outage. Response target: page within 5 minutes; reduce blast radius within 30 minutes.
- Sev 2 (P1): Partial degradation (latency/throughput degradation or errors affecting a subset of customers). Response target: acknowledge within 15 minutes; mitigation in 2 hours.
- Sev 3 (P2): Minor functional impact, non-urgent bug, or scheduled maintenance. Response target: triage within 24 hours.
sections.heading: Quick reference: severity definitions and thresholds

sections.body:
- redwood-api: error-rate > 1.5% sustained for 1 minute -> Sev2; > 5% for 1 minute -> Sev1.
- inference-router p95 latency: > 750ms for 2 minutes -> Sev2; > 1500ms for 1 minute -> Sev1.
- kv-cache miss ratio: > 40% for 5 minutes when baseline < 10% -> Sev2.
- batch-scheduler backlog: queue length > 3x provisioned capacity for 10 minutes -> Sev2.

SLOs and error budgets are authoritative for routing incident prioritization; always consult the SLO dashboard before declaring a Sev.

---
sections.heading: Alert thresholds (examples)

sections.body:
1. Detect/Alert: Monitoring or external report triggers an alert.
2. Triage & Severity: On-call accepts page, performs fast triage, and sets severity.
3. Mobilize Incident Commander (IC) and communicate initial status.
4. Contain & Mitigate: Apply short-term mitigation (traffic-shift, scale-up, fallback model variant).
5. Investigate Root Cause: parallel workstreams for mitigation and RCA.
6. Restore: Return system to normal service (SLOs met).
7. Postmortem: Blameless write-up within 72 hours of restore with action items.
8. Close: Verify actions and track to completion; update runbooks.
sections.heading: Incident lifecycle (standard procedure)

sections.body:
- Primary on-call: acknowledge, initial triage, own first-15-minute message.
- Incident Commander (IC): owns coordination, updates, and run of the incident; rotates every 60–90 minutes.
- Secondary on-call: backs up primary, owned service SME.
- Communications lead: posts to status page and customer comms when required.
- Engineers in the hot seat: follow IC direction and update the shared incident channel.

---
sections.heading: Responsibilities during an incident

sections.body:
Service owners maintain a local phone/cell list; below is the canonical escalation ladder for on-call responders:

| Level | Role | How to engage | SLA to respond |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | Primary on-call | Pager -> Slack DM -> phone | 5 minutes |
| 2 | Secondary / Team lead | Escalate via Slack @team-oncall -> phone | 10 minutes |
| 3 | SRE Manager / Service Owner | Phone -> pager | 20 minutes |
| 4 | Engineering Director / Incident Executive | Phone + email | 30 minutes |

Note: when a customer contractual SLA is implicated, escalate directly to Director and Customer Success.

---
sections.heading: Escalation matrix (reference)

sections.body:
Use this as the base structure for all service-level runbooks:
- Title & scope
- Owner & rotation contact
- Symptoms that should trigger the runbook
- Quick checks (0–5 minutes)
- Containment steps (5–30 minutes)
- Recovery & verification (30–120 minutes)
- Deep diagnostics (RCA) commands and logs
- Post-incident steps and follow-ups

Example: inference-router-p95-surge-runbook (abbreviated)
sections.heading: Runbook pattern (template and example)

sections.body:
1) Check routing health: curl -s https://internal-monitoring/api/v1/services/inference-router/health | jq .status
2) Check pods: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=inference-router -o wide
3) Check queue/backpressure: curl http://metrics:9090/api/v1/query?query=queue_length_inference_router
sections.heading: Quick checks

sections.body:
1) Scale replica sets: kubectl -n inference scale deploy/inference-router --replicas=6
2) Traffic shift: runbook-scripts/shift-traffic --from=inference-router --to=inference-router-hotfix
3) Apply temporary rate-limiter/short-circuit for heavy clients: rlimitctl set --service inference-router --max-rps 10000
sections.heading: Containment steps

sections.body:
- Monitor p95 and error rate for 15-minute rolling window.
- Run synthetic request checks: for endpoint X -> curl -sS https://redwood-api.internal/v1/health-check | grep OK
sections.heading: Recovery & verification

sections.body:
- kubectl logs -n inference -l app=inference-router --tail=1000 | grep -i error
- strace/heap profile collection: collect-profiles.sh --service inference-router --duration 60s

---
sections.heading: Diagnostics (RCA) commands

sections.body:
- Timeline: publish a draft within 72 hours of service restore.
- Required sections: summary, impact (customers/regions/tokens), timeline, root cause analysis, contributing factors, corrective actions (owner + ETA), detection & alert improvements, follow-up verification plan.
- Severity adjustments: postmortem author proposes final Sev and provides SLO impact calculation.
sections.heading: Postmortem expectations and template

sections.body:
1) Link to incident channel and runbook versions used.
2) Attach logs and key metrics snapshots.
3) Create Jira tasks for corrective actions with owners and dates.
4) Schedule a 30–60 minute blameless review within one week.

---
sections.heading: Postmortem checklist

sections.body:
- Primary rotations: 1-week primary on-call per engineer (typical for platform teams).
- Secondary rotations: 4-week secondary cycle (senior engineers).
- On-call shift handoff template (to use in Slack):
  - Current status: services passing/known issues
  - Active incidents: link + brief status
  - Nighttime guardrails: escalation contacts if auto-alerts trigger
  - Local maintenance windows scheduled

Handoff acceptance requires explicit acknowledgement ("I accept" in channel). If no acknowledgement in 10 minutes, escalate to Secondary.
sections.heading: On-call rotations: recommended patterns and handoffs

sections.body:
- Time-off: individuals with >3 on-call weeks in a 12-week window should rotate off for a recovery week.
- Pager load balancing: use schedule rules to avoid >2 consecutive critical incidents for same engineer when possible.

---
sections.heading: Compensation & fatigue management

sections.body: Purpose: validate runbooks, handoffs, communication templates, and escalation under realistic stress with a mix of planned failures.
sections.heading: Game-day curriculum (quarterly runbook)

sections.body:
- Week -2: Planning — scenario owners, objectives, and success criteria defined.
- Week -1: Participant notification and pre-reads distributed.
- Day 0 (game day): 4-hour exercise
  - 00:00–00:15: Inject incident, page primary.
  - 00:15–00:45: Triage & IC selection.
  - 00:45–01:30: Containment actions and communication to status page.
  - 01:30–02:30: Root cause investigation and mitigation.
  - 02:30–03:00: Restore and service verification.
  - 03:00–04:00: Hot debrief and action item capture.
- Week +1: Postmortem draft and follow-ups.
sections.heading: Quarterly schedule (example)

sections.body:
- Regional network partition affecting managed storage.
- Model-serving memory leak leading to OOMs under steady load.
- Credential rotation failure for a downstream dependency.
sections.heading: Common injection scenarios

sections.body:
- IC assigned within 10 minutes.
- Status page updated within 30 minutes of injection.
- Containment achieved within 90 minutes for Sev-equivalent scenarios.

---
sections.heading: Success criteria

sections.body: - "Partial service degradation in us-east affecting model inference latency. Investigating (last updated: {time})."
sections.heading: Status page brief (one-line)

sections.body:
- Impact: "Customers in us-east may experience elevated latency for inference requests. Error rates are not elevated across all customers."
- Scope: "Approx. 14% of requests routed through inference-router-us-east are impacted; other regions nominal."
- Mitigation: "We have shifted 30% of traffic away from affected hosts and are scaling warm pools. No data loss observed."
- ETA/Next update: "Targeting mitigation within 60 minutes; next update at {time}."
sections.heading: Status page detailed update (example)

sections.body:
Subject: "Redwood: Partial inference latency degradation in us-east — update"
Body: "Hi {CustomerName},
We are investigating an issue causing increased inference latency for a subset of requests in the us-east region. Our SRE team is actively mitigating and has shifted traffic to healthy hosts. We do not believe there is any data loss. We will follow up with another update within 60 minutes or when the issue is resolved.
Regards,
Redwood SRE"

Communication ownership: the IC assigns a communications lead within the first 15 minutes who is responsible for public-facing and customer comms. All outgoing messages must be approved by IC.

---
sections.heading: Customer email template (short)

sections.body:
- Create Jira tasks for immediate fixes (priority P1), medium-term improvements (P2), and long-term projects (P3).
- Ensure at least one automation item (alert, runbook step, or monitoring dashboard) is created per incident to reduce recurrence.
- Validate corrective actions within 30 days and mark completion in the postmortem.

---
sections.heading: Post-incident actions & tracking

sections.body:
- On-call schedule manager: SRE tooling team (sre-schedules@redwood.internal).
- Incident commander escalation: SRE Manager (pager: +1-555-0199).
- Status page publishing: comms-bot account (automated) and Communications lead for manual updates.

sections.body:

- SLO & Error Budgets dashboard: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets-2025.
- Incident channel naming convention: #inc-<YYYYMMDD>-<service>-<sevtier>

For immediate feedback or required amendments, ping the SRE team in #sre-process or contact the author.

payload.page_title: Synthetic Game Day Schedule and Status Automation Templates

sections.body: This page defines a reusable, low-friction playbook for running synthetic game days focused on multi-region degradations, KV-cache eviction events, and rate-limited bursts. The document bundles: (1) three compact schedule templates for 30/60/180-minute drills, (2) automated status-page payload templates for each stage of an exercise, and (3) a responder timeline for technical triage plus customer comm choreography.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- SRE and serving-runtime engineers running simulations
- Incident commanders and bridge operators
- Customer-facing teams (CS/Support) who exercise status communications
sections.heading: Intended audience

sections.body:
- Scope: synthetic exercises that emulate production signals but use isolated test tenants or canary regions (never customer-facing live traffic).
- Constraint: all synthetic traffic must use the test-keyspace and go through the canary routing policy.
- Safety check: confirm circuit-breaker and quota overrides are set to test-mode before starting.

Why synthetic game days?
- Exercises discover gaps in automation (status page wiring, alert deduping, runbook readability).
- Short, repeatable drills (<60m) keep oncall readiness high without heavy operational cost.
sections.heading: Scope and constraints

sections.body:
1) Organizer (Games Owner): schedules the exercise, publishes pre-brief and runbook link.
2) Bridge Operator: creates and manages the conference bridge, posts status page updates.
3) First Responder: follows the triage timeline, executes containment steps in the runbook.
4) Synthesis Lead: captures evidence, writes the one-sheet retrospective.
5) Customer Comms Liaison (optional): approves public-facing language and posts external notices if the exercise is run in a customer-visible channel.
sections.heading: Roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
- [ ] Test tenant and API keys validated (test-keyspace).
- [ ] Canary region isolated and traffic routing in test mode.
- [ ] Status page staging token available and webhook tested (curl ping).
- [ ] Shadow oncall informed and not paging customer-facing channels.
- [ ] Runbook link published and accessible to attendees.
sections.heading: Pre-run checklist (must pass before start)

sections.body:
- Type A — Fast Stabilization Drill (30 minutes): focus on quick detection and containment; limited scope (single availability zone).
- Type B — Multi-Region Degradation (60 minutes): simulate regional latency increase with KV-cache thrash and progressive throttling.
- Type C — Sustained Load Failure (180 minutes): longer scenario to exercise escalation, capacity burn, and delegation to product/infra teams.
sections.heading: Synthetic Game Day Types (pick the closest)

sections.body:
- 30-minute template (Type A):
  0:00 — Organizer opens bridge, posts pre-brief and objectives.
  0:03 — Inject synthetic error (canary traffic injection).
  0:05 — Pager alerts fire to responder; First Responder acknowledges within 2 minutes.
  0:08 — Containment step: toggle canary routing to divert test traffic.
  0:12 — Verify mitigation and close the bridge with short notes.
  0:15 — Synthesis lead publishes 1-page learning and action items.

- 60-minute template (Type B):
  0:00 — Pre-brief and safety gate.
  0:05 — Start injection: increase tail latency in Region-A, indirect KV cache misses.
  0:12 — Alerts fan out: bridge formed; roles assigned.
  0:20 — Escalate to platform owner; evaluate fallback model variants.
  0:35 — Post-incident customer-staged message (see templates below).
  0:50 — Runbook read-through and identify gaps.
  0:60 — Retrospective scheduling and evidence captured.

- 180-minute template (Type C):
  0:00 — Full org notice and executive brief channel created.
  0:10 — Inject load; simulate cross-region failover sequence.
  0:30 — Manual capacity increase and autoscaler validation.
  1:15 — Invoke reserved-capacity fallback and observe SLA impact.
  1:45 — Customer visible status update (if exercise is visible to customer test tenants).
  2:50 — Deep-dive teardown and lessons prepared for QBR.

Responder timeline (what responders should do, minute-by-minute for a 60m drill):
1) 0–5m: Acknowledge, gather initial signals (alerts, traces, SLO dashboards).
2) 5–15m: Validate whether it's synthetic injection (check test-keyspace, injection traces).
3) 15–30m: Execute containment (canary routing switch, KV cache warm-up, temporary throttles).
4) 30–45m: Coordinate rollouts/fallbacks with deployment owner; plan rollback if necessary.
5) 45–60m: Confirm stability, run a verification sweep, and document evidence (logs + traces).

Automated status page payload templates
- Principles: short, factual, timestamped, and clearly tagged with "(exercise)" for any synthetic run. Use templated JSON webhooks to post to the staging status page.

Template: status-open (POST payload example)
{
  "status": "investigating",
  "summary": "Synthetic: Elevated latency observed in us-west-2 canary region (exercise).",
  "start_time": "{{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}",
  "components": ["Serving Runtime: us-west-2", "KV Cache: canary"],
  "communication": "Teams are investigating. No customer tenant traffic is affected. This is an exercise."
}

Template: status-update (PATCH payload example)
{
  "status": "identified",
  "summary": "Mitigation in progress: diverting canary traffic and warming secondary cache (exercise).",
  "update_time": "{{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}",
  "actions": ["diverted canary routing", "scaling secondary pool"]
}

Template: status-resolved (PATCH payload example)
{
  "status": "resolved",
  "summary": "Synthetic exercise complete: monitoring shows latency back to baseline.",
  "end_time": "{{ISO_TIMESTAMP}}",
  "notes": "This was a planned exercise using test-keyspace. Retrospective will be published."
}

Automation examples (CLI snippets)
- Ping status page webhook (staging):
  curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"status":"investigating","summary":"Synthetic test ping"}' https://status-staging.redwood.example/hooks/abc123

- Toggle canary routing (kctl example):
  ./kctl routing set --canary false --region us-west-2 --token $TEST_ROUTER_TOKEN

- Inject synthetic load (locust wrapper):
  python tools/locust_run.py --profile synthetic-latency --target canary-usw2 --duration 300
sections.heading: Schedule templates (three reproducible scrims)

sections.body:
- Any unexpected pager to production customer-facing channel must trigger immediate abort and manual rollback.
- Error rates on the control plane exceeding 0.2% for production tenants -> abort.
- Any KMS/HSM or secret access error -> abort and escalate to Security.

Evidence collection checklist (automated + manual):
- export: traces (Jaeger) from 10m before injection to 20m after resolution.
- logs: aggregated request/response logs for canary-keyspace.
- metrics: SLO, p99 latency, error budget rate.
- artifacts: all status page payloads, bridge recording link, and the final synthesis note.
sections.heading: Safety and abort conditions (hard stops)

sections.body:
1) Synthesis lead runs 10-minute recap in bridge.
2) Capture three things: what worked, what failed, one immediate fix.
3) Create action ticket(s) with priority and owner; link back to the runbook section.
4) Publish 1-page synthesis note and tag relevant oncall rotation calendars.
sections.heading: Post-exercise synthesis (30-minute lightweight retro)

sections.body:
- After each synthetic exercise, update the related runbook with discovered friction points and a short snippet for automation recipes.
- Runbook owners must confirm remediation tickets or provide a justification why a ticket is deferred.
sections.heading: Runbook additions and governance

sections.body:
- Drill frequency by team (target: 1 drill/month per critical service).
- Mean time to acknowledge in drills (target < 2 minutes).
- Runbook friction score (post-drill survey, target average >= 4/5).
- Percentage of drills that generate at least one remediation ticket (target >= 40%).

Templates: brief message examples (copy/paste)
- Pre-brief (internal):
  Subject: [Game Day] Synthetic Multi-region Degradation — us-west-2 — 2025-08-05 09:00 UTC
  Body: We will run a synthetic game day in the us-west-2 canary region at 09:00 UTC. Test-keyspace only. Bridge: <link>. Objectives: validate staged status automation, KV-cache warm-up behavior, and canary routing fallback. Organizer: Miguel Santos.

- Bridge open (short post):
  "Bridge opened. Action: injection started. This is an exercise — no production tenant impact."

- Public (staged) status snippet (exercise):
  "We are running a planned exercise to validate detection and routing for a regional latency event. No customer traffic is impacted. We'll update at regular intervals (exercise)."

- Closure note (internal):
  "Synthetic exercise completed. Monitoring stable. One action created: SRE-4212 (increase cache warm-up threshold). Synthesis note: <link>."

Appendix A — Common failure patterns observed in prior drills:
- Delayed webhook auth failures when status page token rotates. Mitigation: add token expiry pre-check to pre-run checklist.
- Oncall confusion about the difference between test-keyspace and prod-keyspace; mitigation: add explicit keys in bridge pinned message.

Appendix B — Quick reference table for safe configuration parameters:
- Table (described):
  * parameter: test_traffic_ratio | recommended: 0.05 | note: fraction of normal traffic routed to canary.
  * parameter: canary_timeout_seconds | recommended: 30 | note: timeout faster than prod for quicker fail detection.
  * parameter: status_webhook_endpoint | recommended: status-staging.redwood.example/hooks/<token> | note: use staging endpoint for exercises.
sections.heading: Metrics to track for program health

sections.body:
- Runbook templates: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-curation-and-incident-ownership-guidelines-2025
- Incident evidence standard: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-chain-and-forensic-runbook-2025
sections.heading: Related documents and references

sections.body:
- For questions about scheduling: Miguel Santos (miguel@redwood.example).
- For status automation issues: Priya Natarajan (priya@redwood.example).
- Security abort escalation: Security oncall (sec-oncall@redwood.example).
sections.heading: Contact and escalation matrix

sections.body:
- Games Owner: SRE Operations (owner must review this document bi-annually).
- Reviewer cadence: reviewers listed above will be re-notified two weeks prior to the review window.

End of document.
sections.heading: Document owners and review cadence

payload.page_title: Proactive Stabilization and Warm-Handoff Playbook

sections.body: This playbook documents the proactive incident-avoidance workflow and a standardized warm-handoff procedure for operators managing Redwood Inference serving services. It covers monitoring triggers, pre-incident mitigation steps, automated remediation, manual escalation paths, warm-handoff checklist, customer-signal templates for status pages and CSRs, and a post-event debrief template. The goal is to detect and stabilize degradations before they become customer-impacting incidents and to ensure handoffs are smooth and information-rich when escalation is required.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to: inference fronting proxies, routing layer, runtime pods, KV cache, batching controller, model-serving workers, and serving control plane.
- Not covered: billing pipelines, onboarding identity flows (see separate billing and identity runbooks).
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- Detect 80% of actionable regressions inside the detection window (3min for latency spikes, 10min for throughput anomalies).
- Keep customer-visible error rate < 0.1% and P95 latency under SLO during transient degradations via automatic fallback.
- Average handoff documentation time < 5 minutes for operator->oncall.
sections.heading: Goals and success metrics

sections.body:
- Severity A (sev-1): Service outage, >50% tenant errors, or SLO breach with >5min customer-visible disruption.
- Severity B (sev-2): Significant degradation (P95 > 2x baseline or sustained token throughput reduction >30%) with limited customer impact.
- Severity C (sev-3): Internal-only regressions, alerting noise, or emerging anomalies requiring investigation.
sections.heading: Definitions and severity mapping

sections.body:
- Latency:P95 > 2x baseline for >2 consecutive minutes across >=2 regions.
- Errors: 5xx rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes and increase >300% vs rolling 24h baseline.
- Throughput: sustained backlog > 150% capacity of active GPU pool for 10 minutes.
- Cache: KV cache eviction rate > 10% per minute or miss-rate jump >50%.
- Autoscaler signals: repeated scale-up failures or OOM kill frequency > 3/hour.
sections.heading: Monitoring triggers (examples)

sections.body:
1) Circuit breaker: automatically route new requests to fallback model variant when error rate threshold hit.
2) Short-term autoscale: burst up to 30% extra capacity for 10 minutes if queue growth detected.
3) Prefix/KV cache warm-up: replay hot prefixes from recent traces to rebuild caches.
4) Rate-limit soft-fallthrough: reduce per-tenant token limits by 20% to protect global SLOs.
sections.heading: Automated (pre-manual) remediation chain

sections.body:
1) Any Sev-A trigger fires.
2) If automated remediation does not reduce customer-visible error rate below 0.1% within 5 minutes.
3) Repeated autoscaler failures or infrastructure health signals (OOM on >2 nodes) persist for >10 minutes.

Operator first-response checklist (10-minute stabilization script):
1) Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and create/attach timeline in the incident tracker.
2) Identify impacted service(s) and region(s).
3) Run quick health queries:
   - curl -s "https://ops-api.internal/health?service=serving" | jq .status
   - redis-cli INFO | grep evicted_keys
   - kubectl -n serving get pods -o wide | grep CrashLoopBackOff
4) If cache miss/eviction spike: invoke cache-warm command: opsctl cache warm --service serving --window 15m
5) If backlog spike: trigger short-term autoscale: opsctl autoscale request --service serving --scale-by 30 --duration 10m
6) Apply temporary routing fallback: opsctl route set --service serving --variant fallback-small --percent 100 --until now+15m
7) Notify stakeholders using the Incident Bridge template (see Customer & Exec comms).
8) Start evidence collection: collect traces (last 30m), pprof, kernel logs, and heap dumps where relevant.

Warm-handoff protocol (operator -> oncall or cross-team):
sections.heading: When to invoke a manual incident

sections.body:
- Operator has attempted automated remediation steps (above) and impact remains or further investigation is required.
- Handoff should occur within the same PagerDuty incident number; do not open separate incidents for the same problem.
sections.heading: Required conditions to perform a warm-handoff

sections.body:
1) Situation summary (2 sentences): what, where, when started, current impact.
2) Actions taken: list commands run and automated steps invoked, with timestamps.
3) Evidence links: traces, logs, dashboards, and key alerts with direct URLs.
4) Hypotheses: short bullet list of current working theories.
5) Next recommended action(s) and owner(s) with estimated time to complete.
6) Known constraints: deploy freeze windows, maintenance events, or cross-team dependencies.
7) Contact info: primary operator, backup, and escalation owner (Slack handles).
sections.heading: Warm-handoff steps (fill and paste into the bridge chat)

sections.body:
---
Situation: P95 latency in us-west-2 increased from 120ms to 520ms starting 2026-02-02T09:12Z; approx 12% of requests returned 502.
Actions: Applied fallback routing to fallback-small at 09:18Z; autoscale request +30% at 09:19Z; cache warm-up at 09:21Z.
Evidence: dashboards/redwood/serving/us-west-2?from=09:00Z, traces/redwood/serving/trace-id=abc123, logs: s3://ops-evidence/serving/2026-02-02/us-west-2.zip
Hypotheses: 1) new kernel version on gpu nodes introduced driver regression; 2) batch scheduler mis-calculated sequence lengths causing OOM.
Next steps: (1) Oncall: validate node driver health (owner: @sofia) within 10m; (2) Platform: roll back kernel on suspected node group if confirmed (owner: @marcus).
Constraints: Can only rollback nodegroup-2 between 09:30-09:45Z due to maintenance window.
Contact: @aisha (operator), @sofia (oncall), PagerDuty#12345.
---
sections.heading: Example warm-handoff script (copy/paste)

sections.body:
- Internal bridge join message (short):
   "Joining incident PD#12345 — service=serving, region=us-west-2, impact=latency/p95 520ms, operator=aisha, current actions: fallback routing, autoscale. Evidence: <link>"
- Customer-facing status page template (short window):
   Title: "Partial service degradation in US-West (latency) — investigating"
   Body: "We are currently investigating increased latency for inference requests in our US-West region. Some requests may experience delays or transient errors. Our engineers have applied a temporary routing fallback and are actively stabilizing the service. We will post an update within 30 minutes or sooner. Customer impact: intermittent increased latency and occasional 502 responses."
- Customer-facing status page template (extended incident):
   Title: "Service disruption affecting inference requests — US and APAC"
   Body: "We are experiencing a broader disruption affecting inference request latency and errors across multiple regions. Our on-call and platform engineers are engaged and performing targeted mitigations including autoscaling, cache warm-up, and controlled rollbacks where required. We will update every 60 minutes until service is restored. If you are experiencing critical production impact, please open a support ticket referencing incident PD#12345."
sections.heading: Incident bridge and communication templates

sections.body:
- Operator -> Oncall (SRE): immediate (PagerDuty)
- Oncall -> Platform GPU team: if infrastructure signal present or OOMs detected
- Oncall -> Eng serving-runtime: if kernel/scheduler or model-serving worker behavior suspected
- Oncall -> Customer Success: if customer-facing credit/communication required
sections.heading: Escalation matrix (condensed)

sections.body:
- Incident Commander (IC): owns coordination, public comms, and bridge timeline. Default is the oncall SRE for Sev-A/B incidents.
- Technical Lead: owns triage of technical hypotheses and directs rollbacks/config changes.
- Evidence Engineer: collects and stores forensic artifacts and ensures regulatory retention for enterprise customers.
sections.heading: Roles & ownership conventions

sections.body:
- Bi-weekly simulation: dedicated 90-minute sessions focusing on cache-eviction and batching failures.
- Scenario example: simulate a KV cache loss in one region; expected outcome: automatic fallback routes, cache warm replay, and recovery in <12 minutes.
- Scoring rubric: time to first mitigation <5m (10 pts), time to stable <12m (20 pts), handoff clarity score by reviewer >8/10 (10 pts).
sections.heading: Game day & proactive simulation guidance

sections.body:
- opsctl service status --service serving --region us-west-2
- opsctl logs tail --service serving --since 15m --filter "error OR OOM"
- opsctl route set --service serving --variant fallback-small --percent 100 --until now+15m
- opsctl cache warm --service serving --window 15m
- opsctl evidence collect --incident PD12345 --output s3://ops-evidence/serving/PD12345.zip
sections.heading: Runbook primitives (commands & endpoints)

sections.body:
- Critical incidents (Sev-A): retain full forensic bundle for 2 years.
- Non-critical incidents (Sev-B/C): retain artifacts for 90 days.
sections.heading: Evidence retention policy (short)

sections.body:
1) Incident summary (what happened and timeline).
2) Root cause(s) (confirmed and unconfirmed hypotheses).
3) Workarounds and mitigations applied.
4) Actions taken and owners (include PR/CL links).
5) Action items with due dates and measured risk reduction.
6) Postmortem severity and customer impact assessment.
7) Lessons learned and monitoring improvements.
sections.heading: Post-incident debrief template (to be filled within 72h)

sections.body:
- Playbook owner: Eng SRE (primary: Marcus Lee).
- Quarterly review: playbook and thresholds reviewed by SRE and Serving Runtime teams.
- Game day owner: Eng SRE rotations coordinator (Sofia Martinez).

Appendix A — Example packet of evidence to collect:
- kube events and pod manifests (kubectl -n serving get events --all-namespaces)
- pprof CPU/mem profiles for worker processes
- last 1 hour application traces (jaeger or opentelemetry) filtered by trace sampling ids
- exact CLI command history from remediation steps (opsctl logs)
- node-level dmesg and driver logs for GPU nodes

Appendix B — Template for customer support reply (short):
"Thanks for the report — we are aware of elevated latency in <region>. Our engineers are actively mitigating; we have applied temporary routing fallbacks and expect reduced impact within 30–60 minutes. We will follow up when service is fully restored. Incident reference: PD#12345."

Appendix C — Runbook change log:
- 2026-01-15: initial published playbook (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-02: clarified warm-handoff template and added cache-warm primitive (reviewers: Marcus Lee, Sofia Martinez).

For questions or to propose edits, ping #eng-sre-playbooks on Slack or email playbooks@redwood.example.com.
sections.heading: Operational run cadence & ownership for the playbook

payload.page_title: Responder Preparedness Simulator and Rotation Playbook

sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This document defines a compact, operationally focused playbook for responder preparedness: how we run on-call rotations, maintain high-quality runbooks, and validate readiness via a simulation (game-day) matrix. It is intended for SREs, platform engineers, and incident commanders who own model-serving, routing, and cache systems across Redwood Inference.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to all production incidents impacting Redwood-hosted inference services (hosted API, Dedicated runtime pools, and Private control plane).
- Includes on-call rotation design, handover expectations, runbook hygiene, game-day exercises, status-page templates, and postmortem requirements.

Definitions
- Responder: the engineer assigned primary for a given service on a rotation.
- Bridge: a communication channel (Zoom/Google Meet + Slack) used for incident coordination.
- Severity levels: Sev1 (major outage), Sev2 (degradation with customer impact), Sev3 (minor impact / ticketable).

Key Principles
- SLO-first triage: incidents are prioritized by customer-facing SLO impact, not by metric noise.
- Fail-fast containment: aim to isolate faulty components quickly and restore partial service where possible.
- Evidence-driven postmortem: every Sev1/Sev2 requires a postmortem capturing root cause, timeline, and measurable action items.

Roles & Responsibilities
- Primary Responder: initial triage, bridge operator, first customer-facing status update (15–30 min).
- Secondary Responder: supports mitigation steps, runs verification, escalates to on-call lead if needed.
- On-call Lead (SRE staff): owns escalation decisions, exec comms, and long-running mitigation coordination.
- Pager / Customer Liaison (Customer Success): translates engineering status into customer-friendly updates.

Rotation Patterns and Rationale
1) Rotation structure: 1-week primary shifts with 48-hour secondary coverage for follow-up and weekend continuity.
2) Rationale: Longer weekly shifts reduce context switch overhead for constant systems work, while secondary coverage prevents knowledge gaps during handovers.
3) Follow-the-sun addendum: For regions with active customer bases in APAC, maintain a 2-person regional rotation to meet latency-sensitive support.

payload.page_title: PagerFlow: responder orchestration guidelines and customer notice templates

sections.body: This page defines the PagerFlow model — a lightweight orchestration layer for responder handoffs, escalation routing, and customer-facing status updates across Redwood Inference. PagerFlow is meant to standardize triage decisions, accelerate containment, and ensure consistent, timely communication to stakeholders and customers.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to all service-impacting events that affect customer-facing inference (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Includes operational steps for triage, escalation, customer notice templates, on-call rotation fairness rules, and a game-day exercise plan for the next 12 months.
- Not intended for routine maintenance notices (see maintenance-notices policy).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
PagerFlow organizes incident response into three phases: Detect -> Route -> Restore. The goal is to automate decision points where safe, and provide clear human-readable steps where automation cannot cover context-sensitive choices.

1) Detect:
- Signals: SLO alerts (latency/availability), rate limit saturation, KV cache thrashing, elevated 5xx ratios, internal health-checks, and external customer reports.
- Evidence capture: always attach the following to a new PagerFlow incident: timestamped alert IDs, first 10 request traces, example failing request id, affected regions, and model(s) implicated.

2) Route:
- Automated routing: PagerFlow uses the signal type and impacted product tier to pick an initial responder (see Escalation matrix). For example, a Host API latency SLO breach triggers the Serving runtime on-call; an auth failure triggers infra/security triage.
- Manual reassignment: bridge operator or lead responder can re-route if evidence points to cross-team ownership. Include reason in the incident timeline.

3) Restore:
- Focus on quick, safe mitigations (prefix cache evict, temporary routing to fallback model, scale-up reserved capacity) before longer-term fixes.
- Use feature flags and canary rollbacks where applicable.
sections.heading: PagerFlow overview

sections.body:
- Bridge Operator (first 15 minutes): owns the incident page, status cadence, and escalation to L1/L2.
- L1 On-call (team-specific): executes containment steps, gathers metrics, and proposes a mitigation.
- L2 / Subject Matter Expert: performs deeper diagnostics, code-level rollbacks, or model variant routing.
- Incident Commander (IC): appointed for Sev1/Sev2 and owns stakeholder comms and postmortem initiation.
- Customer Success Liaison: drafts customer notices for anything customer-impacting beyond 30 minutes.
sections.heading: Roles & responsibilities

sections.body:
| Severity | Example symptoms | Initial responder | Escalation after | IC assignment |
| Severity-1 (Sev1) | Cross-region outage, sustained >30% 5xx, total traffic loss | Serving runtime on-call + Bridge | 10 minutes | Platform SRE lead |
| Severity-2 (Sev2) | High error rate for a major model or region, major degradation >20% | L1 Product infra on-call | 30 minutes | Team lead on rotation |
| Severity-3 (Sev3) | Single-region reduced throughput, rate limit hotspots | Service owner on-call | 2 hours | N/A |
| Severity-4 (Sev4) | Degraded internal tooling, minor customer impact | Ticket created, owner triages in working hours | N/A | N/A |
sections.heading: Escalation matrix (compact table)

sections.body:
1. Acknowledge & capture (Bridge Operator): confirm alert, open incident page, add links to dashboards and traces.
2. Initial classification: pick severity using the matrix above. Document rationale in the incident timeline.
3. Contain (L1): apply non-invasive mitigations first (traffic re-routing, throttling noisy tenants, apply temporary model fallback).
4. If containment fails within escalation window, escalate to L2 and request IC appointment.
5. IC coordinates cross-team work, authorizes any rollbacks, and sets customer notice cadence.
6. Stabilize, then run verification suite for affected paths, and proceed to post-incident review.
sections.heading: Triage & containment procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:

sections.body:

- Equity rules: maximum 48 hours back-to-back shift coverage; extra burn hours accrue compensatory time or on-call stipend adjustment.

sections.body:

sections.heading: Handover checklist (end of shift)

sections.body:

  2) Model archive corruption that requires automated fallback and manual model re-ingest.

- Degradation type: High 5xx after deploy. Action: rollback to previous deploy, isolate commit, run verification.
