payload.page_title: Postmortem: Latency regression after tokenizer update (2026-01-27)

sections.body: On 2026-01-27 we observed a significant p95 latency increase for chat completions on several popular models. The regression began shortly after a tokenizer library update was rolled out to the hosted fleet.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Symptoms: p95 end-to-end latency +38% for affected routes; some customers hit client-side timeouts
- Scope: Hosted API traffic in us-east-1 and eu-west-1
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- Alert: route latency SLO burn for /v1/chat/completions
- Perf dashboards showed elevated CPU in prefill pipeline
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 19:11: SLO burn alert fired
- 19:18: On-call correlates onset with tokenizer update rollout
- 19:30: Mitigation: rollback tokenizer update
- 20:09: Latency returns to baseline
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: A tokenizer update changed default normalization behavior, increasing average token counts and causing additional CPU overhead in request preprocessing. The change was not detected in canary because the canary prompt set did not include multi-language and emoji-heavy inputs that are common in production.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- Canary prompt set coverage gap
- Lack of automated guardrail on average tokens/request
- Rollout checklist did not include a CPU budget validation
sections.heading: Contributing factors

sections.body:
1. Expand canary prompt sets to include multilingual and special-character heavy inputs representative of production. Owner team: Applied ML. Priority: P0.
2. Add automated guardrail: alert when avg input tokens per request changes by >10% for a route/model over 15 minutes. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
3. Add perf CI check for tokenizer updates (CPU per 1k chars, tokens per 1k chars) and require approval on regressions. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
4. Update rollout checklist to include "tokenization cost" section and explicit rollback criteria. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P2.
5. Add a dashboard panel tracking avg tokens/request by top 20 customers (anonymized) to catch distribution shifts. Owner team: Observability. Priority: P1.
sections.heading: Follow-up action items

sections.body: Seemingly minor preprocessing changes can have first-order latency impact. Production-like prompt sets and token-count guardrails are necessary for safe rollouts."

payload.page_title: Postmortem: EU API latency and elevated 5xx (edge routing cache)

sections.body:
h1. Summary
On 2026-01-19 we experienced elevated p95 latency and intermittent HTTP 5xx for a subset of EU-hosted API traffic. The incident lasted 47 minutes end-to-end. Customer impact was concentrated in the eu-west region and primarily affected chat completions with streaming enabled.

*Customer impact:* Yes (degraded performance + partial errors)
*Severity:* SEV-2
*Owning engineering team:* Platform Engineering (Traffic & Edge)
*Primary services:* edge-router, request-gateway, redis-edge-cache

h1. Impact
* ~12% of EU requests exceeded the latency SLO (p95 > 3.5s)
* ~1.8% request failure rate (HTTP 502/503) for EU traffic
* No data loss; retries succeeded after mitigation

h1. Timeline (UTC)
* 10:12 - Alert fired: eu-west request-gateway 5xx > 1%
* 10:15 - On-call acknowledged; triage indicates edge-router cache churn
* 10:21 - Mitigation 1: disabled new cache key format via feature flag
* 10:28 - 5xx decreases but latency still elevated
* 10:35 - Mitigation 2: increased redis-edge-cache memory limit + restarted one shard
* 10:45 - Latency returns to baseline
* 10:59 - Incident resolved; monitoring for recurrence

h1. Root cause
A configuration rollout introduced a new cache-key schema for routing policy evaluation. In eu-west the cache key cardinality was higher than expected due to a region-specific header normalization discrepancy, causing excessive churn and evictions in redis-edge-cache. Evictions increased cache miss rate, pushing more requests into the slower policy evaluation path and increasing load on request-gateway. Under load, request-gateway emitted intermittent 502/503.

h1. Detection
Detected via automated alerting on request-gateway 5xx and latency SLO burn for eu-west.

h1. What went well
* Alerts triggered quickly and were actionable.
* Feature flag allowed fast rollback of the risky cache-key change.

h1. What went poorly

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Streaming stalls during peak traffic (2026-01-12)

sections.body: On 2026-01-12, streaming responses intermittently stalled for a subset of chat completion requests. Affected clients observed streams that paused mid-response for 10–45 seconds, then resumed or timed out. The incident correlated with a traffic surge and increased concurrent connections on the edge streaming gateway.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 41 minutes (peak impact window)
- Symptoms: stalled Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams; elevated client timeouts
- Scope: ~9% of streaming requests in us-east-1
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- Alert: "stream-gateway open connections" exceeded threshold
- Secondary signals: increased 499/504 rates at the edge; elevated p95 time-to-first-token
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 16:02: First alerts triggered (p95 TTFT + edge 5xx)
- 16:07: On-call confirms stalled streams in synthetic checks
- 16:15: Mitigation: reduce max concurrent streams per gateway pod; scale gateway
- 16:29: Runtime team rolls back a connection reuse optimization
- 16:43: Metrics return to baseline
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: A recently enabled connection reuse optimization increased head-of-line blocking within the streaming gateway under high concurrency. Combined with an overly permissive keepalive and a missing backpressure guard, the gateway accumulated slow clients and delayed flushes to the network.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- SRE alerting did not include a direct SLO for "stream stall duration"
- The runtime canary did not cover high-concurrency streaming workloads
- Gateway autoscaling policy used CPU only; connection count was the real driver
sections.heading: Contributing factors

sections.body:
- Synthetic streaming checks helped confirm impact quickly
- Scaling the gateway immediately reduced new stalls
sections.heading: What went well

sections.body:
- Rollback decision took longer than expected due to unclear ownership between gateway vs runtime
- Lack of a dedicated runbook step for diagnosing SSE buffering
sections.heading: What didn’t go well

sections.body:
(Each item counts toward the owning team’s total.)
1. Add an SLO/alert for "stream stall duration" derived from periodic flush timestamps. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P0.
2. Add connection-count based autoscaling to stream-gateway (HPA on open_conns). Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
3. Implement explicit backpressure guard in stream-gateway to drop/slow overly slow consumers. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
4. Add load-test scenario for 20k concurrent streaming connections to perf-canary suite. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
5. Update runbook: "Streaming issues" to include tcpdump/flush tracing steps and known failure modes. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
6. Document gateway/runtime responsibility boundaries and escalation path. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P2.
sections.heading: Follow-up action items

sections.body: Streaming incidents are often connection-management incidents. We need first-class metrics for stream health (stall duration, flush frequency) and scaling signals tied to open connections.
sections.heading: Lessons learned

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Autoscaler capacity thrash led to queue saturation (2026-01-09)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2026-01-09, multiple dedicated pools experienced oscillating capacity (rapid scale up/down) which caused intermittent queue saturation and long wait times for inference requests.

h2. Customer impact
* Time window: 07:4108:33 PT
* Symptoms: throughput drops, queue wait time spikes, intermittent timeouts
* Affected: Dedicated customers in us-west using autoscaling policy "balanced"

h2. Detection
* Alert: "dedicated_pool_queue_wait_p95 > 6s"
* CS escalation referencing "autoscaler flapping"

h2. Root cause
A change to the autoscaler cooldown logic reduced the minimum stabilization window from 10 minutes to 2 minutes. Under bursty load, this caused frequent downscales that immediately re-triggered scale-ups, creating a thrash loop and periods of insufficient GPU capacity.

h2. Resolution
* Restored cooldown to 10 minutes
* Temporarily pinned affected pools to a fixed minimum GPU floor

h2. Action items
1) Add canary tests for autoscaler stability under bursty workloads (Owner: Eng Platform)
2) Add guardrail: do not downscale if queue wait time > 1s (Owner: SRE)

h2. References

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Streaming responses stalling on long contexts (continuous batching regression)

sections.body:
h1. Summary
On 2026-02-07 a subset of streaming chat completions stalled (no tokens emitted for >30s) for requests with long input contexts. The incident was triggered by a serving-runtime change to continuous batching fairness that interacted poorly with high-concurrency workloads.

*Customer impact:* Yes (timeouts and degraded UX for streaming)
*Severity:* SEV-1
*Owning engineering team:* Serving Runtime
*Primary components:* runtime-scheduler, stream-forwarder, kv-cache-manager

h1. Impact
* ~4.5% of streaming requests in us-east stalled; clients timed out after 60s
* Elevated support tickets from 6 customers (Enterprise + PLG)
* No data integrity issues

h1. Timeline (UTC)
* 18:04 - Alert: streaming token rate anomaly
* 18:07 - On-call confirms stalled streams in traces
* 18:12 - Identified correlation with long-context prompts and high queue depth
* 18:18 - Rolled back runtime-scheduler build rwr-1.12.3 to rwr-1.12.2
* 18:29 - Streaming stabilized; backlog drained
* 18:45 - Incident resolved

h1. Root cause
A fairness tweak to continuous batching prioritized newly-arrived short requests too aggressively. Under high concurrency, long-context requests repeatedly yielded before first token emission, effectively starving the stream-forwarder. This increased time-to-first-token beyond client timeouts for the affected requests.

h1. Detection
Detected by automated metric: stream_forwarder_tokens_per_second drop combined with p99 time_to_first_token increase.

h1. Corrective actions
1) Add starvation protection for long-context streams in runtime-scheduler (Owner: Serving Runtime; Due: 2026-02-20)
2) Add canary workload that includes long-context + high concurrency to perf-canary (Owner: Applied ML; Due: 2026-03-01)
3) Update release checklist to require time_to_first_token regression gate (Owner: Release Eng; Due: 2026-02-22)

h1. Notes
This postmortem is scoped to customer-impacting streaming stalls. We excluded internal-only benchmark anomalies.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Hosted API latency spike and model fallback activation (2025-02-11)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-02-11, the Hosted API experienced elevated p95 latency on /v1/chat/completions for ~23 minutes. Mitigation included activating an automatic model fallback policy to keep requests flowing while we reduced load on the primary model pool.

h2. Impact
* Customer-facing: increased latency, intermittent timeouts, elevated 5xx for some bursts.
* Affected product: Redwood API (Hosted).
* Affected tiers: primarily Free and Growth tiers on the default route.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 17:06: Alert fired: Chat latency p95 > 4.0s (threshold 2.0s) for 5 min.
* 17:11: On-call confirmed queueing on primary model pool (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct).
* 17:14: Mitigation: enabled *automatic model fallback* on the router policy for the default route.
* 17:16: Router began automatically rerouting overflow traffic to rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct (fallback target) when saturation exceeded 85%.
* 17:22: Latency recovered; errors returned to baseline.
* 17:29: Fallback policy left on for 30 additional minutes to protect SLO.

h2. What we changed (Mitigation)
We activated a policy-based *auto-fallback* on the router:
* Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
* Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
* Trigger: saturation > 85% OR queue wait > 250ms
* Scope: /v1/chat/completions, tier in {free, growth}

h2. Root cause
A mis-sized continuous batching configuration on the primary pool caused queueing to grow quickly under a bursty prompt distribution (longer-than-expected context lengths).

h2. Detection
Automated latency and queue-wait alerts fired correctly, but we lacked a dedicated alert for “fallback activated” to help confirm mitigation status.

h2. Action items
1) Add a first-class router metric + alert: fallback_activated_count by route/model. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Update the on-call runbook to include the fallback policy toggle and rollback conditions. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Re-tune batching defaults for rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct on A100 pool. Owner: Serving Runtime.

h2. References
* Related page: Router policies and safe-mode toggles (internal)
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0211

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Perf Canary False-Positive Alert Storm (baseline drift + cardinality)

sections.body:
On 2026-02-12, the production performance canary generated a burst of false-positive alerts across multiple models and regions shortly after enabling warning + paging rules in the first expansion beyond the initial 2-model rollout. Alerts were high volume (warning + paging) and repeatedly reopened due to dedupe failures, resulting in on-call interruption and a temporary release freeze request.

There was **no confirmed customer-facing latency regression** attributable to this incident. The event was an alerting/observability failure caused primarily by (1) **baseline drift + baseline key mismatch** and (2) **metric label cardinality inflation** that fragmented the canary’s time series, defeating min-sample gating and dedupe.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body: - **None confirmed.** Runtime and customer SLO dashboards did not show correlated sustained p95 latency increases for customer traffic.
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- **Paging noise:** 19 paging alerts over ~38 minutes (with multiple re-pages due to missing dedupe keys).
- **Warning noise:** 60+ warning alerts over ~75 minutes.
- **Operational disruption:** SRE on-call and runtime on-call diverted to triage; release engineering requested a short freeze while signals stabilized.
- **Confidence impact:** Reduced trust in the perf canary as a rollout gate until remediations were in place.
sections.heading: Internal impact

sections.body:
- perf-canary service (prod)
- observability-pack alert rules + Grafana dashboards
- baseline store + baseline fetch client
- telemetry pipeline (metrics ingestion + aggregation)
- incident-bot alert handler
sections.heading: Services/systems involved

sections.body:
- Detected via automated paging to the on-call channel and incident-bot threads.
- Secondary signal: Grafana dashboard showed many “regression detected” annotations without corresponding customer latency change.
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- **2026-02-12 16:05** – Expanded canary coverage from 3 → 8 models in us-east; enabled paging rule for “top models”.
- **16:12** – First warning alerts fire for 3 models (p95 latency regression > threshold). Incident-bot starts threads.
- **16:16** – Paging alerts begin for a top model; on-call acknowledges.
- **16:18** – Additional paging alerts fire for multiple models; dedupe fails and creates multiple parallel threads.
- **16:23** – Runtime on-call compares canary runtime-only latency vs customer e2e; no matching regression observed.
- **16:28** – Telemetry team notices time series fragmentation: unexpected label combinations, very low samples per series.
- **16:34** – SRE disables paging rules (keeps warnings) and increases dampening window.
- **16:41** – Baseline store reads show frequent “baseline not found” with fallback to default thresholds.
- **16:46** – Canary config rolled back to previous 3-model set; alert volume drops.
- **17:02** – Incident declared resolved; follow-up investigation assigned.
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body:
The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:
- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set).
- Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried.
- Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds.
- incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.
sections.heading: What happened (symptoms)

sections.body: Baselines were stored per (model, runtime_version, hardware_sku, region) in the baseline store, but the canary emitted/evaluated metrics with an expanded set of labels including transient fields and “bucketed” dimensions that were not part of the baseline artifact key.
sections.heading: RC1: Baseline drift + key mismatch (primary)

sections.body:
- The canary evaluation path constructed a baseline key using **(model, model_version, runtime_build, region, hardware_sku, prompt_shape_bucket)**.
- Baseline artifacts were generated for **(model, model_version, runtime_build, region, hardware_sku)** only (no prompt bucket), and in some cases had **region omitted** (older artifacts) because early staging used a simplified schema.
- When the lookup did not match, the evaluator fell back to default thresholds, which are intentionally conservative and therefore easier to breach.

Additionally, baseline updates were set to a rolling policy during the first expansion.
- A rolling baseline can be valid, but in this case it introduced “baseline drift” during a period of changing model coverage and metric schema. Drift made alerts oscillate because the baseline distribution was not stable across the same label set.
sections.heading: Specifically

sections.body:
- `prompt_template_id` (seeded but still high cardinality across the prompt set)
- `workload_run_id` (unique per canary run)
- `route` (included full internal route string with version suffix)
sections.heading: Several labels unintentionally increased cardinality

sections.body:
- Fragmentation of histograms/counters into many short-lived series.
- “Min samples” checks passing on one series while the alert query aggregated differently.
- Increased ingestion lag and higher query variance due to sparse buckets.
sections.heading: This caused

sections.body:
The alert rules aggregated time series on a different dimension set than the evaluator used for baseline comparison.
- The evaluator grouped by (model, model_version, region, hardware_sku, runtime_build).
- Warning alert queries grouped by (model, region) for readability.
- Paging rules grouped by (model) only for top-model simplicity.

This mismatch made it possible for a small, noisy slice (e.g., one SKU) to trigger evaluator regressions while alerts appeared “global”, causing confusion in triage.
sections.heading: RC3: Alert policy mismatch with evaluator grouping (contributing)

sections.body:
incident-bot dedupe was based on (alert_name, model) only.
- As a result, changes in alert labels and repeated firing produced new threads/pages.
- With many models firing simultaneously, this amplified perceived severity and burden.
sections.heading: RC4: Incident-bot dedupe gaps (contributing)

sections.body:
- **Schema change during rollout:** Metric label set changed between the initial 3-model rollout and expansion.
- **Baseline artifact heterogeneity:** Some baseline artifacts were generated in a prod-like shadow environment with a different region/SKU mapping.
- **Telemetry ingestion delay:** During the event, ingestion lag fluctuated (minutes), causing “sawtooth” alert evaluation.
- **Runbook ambiguity:** The runbook guided “compare to baseline” but didn’t explicitly call out “baseline not found → fallback thresholds” as a first-class failure mode.
sections.heading: Contributing factors

sections.body:
1. **Disabled paging rules** for perf-canary regressions (kept warning-level visibility). (Owner: SRE on-call)
2. **Rolled back canary model coverage** to the previously stable 3-model configuration. (Owner: Runtime on-call)
3. **Pinned evaluator to fixed baseline artifacts** (no rolling updates) until schema/keys were corrected. (Owner: Nadia Rahman)
4. **Hotfix to drop high-cardinality labels** from canary metrics (`workload_run_id`, `prompt_template_id`, full `route`). (Owner: Logan Wright)
sections.heading: Actions taken during the incident

sections.body:
- **Baseline key normalization:** Baseline lookup now uses a canonical key:
  - `model_id` (canonical registry ID)
  - `model_version` (registry version)
  - `runtime_build_id`
  - `hardware_sku`
  - `region`
  - (explicitly does *not* include prompt bucket or run IDs)
- **Metric label contract:** Reduced emitted labels to an approved set; added a CI check that fails if new labels are added without review.
- **Evaluator “baseline missing” behavior:** Baseline missing is now treated as **“canary unhealthy”** (warn once) rather than “assume default regression thresholds”.
- **Min-sample + dampening alignment:** Alert rules now match the evaluator grouping and require:
  - minimum N requests per grouping
  - sustained breach across multiple evaluation intervals
- **Incident-bot dedupe key update:** Dedupe keys now include (model_id, model_version, region, hardware_sku, runtime_build_id, alert_type).
sections.heading: Implemented (completed)

sections.body:
- **Region/SKU-aware thresholds:** Allow thresholds that differ by SKU/region where variance is known to differ (documented + versioned).
- **Baseline drift guardrails:** Rolling baselines require an explicit “baseline update window” and block updates during rollout expansion or telemetry schema changes.
- **Canary alert gating:** Rollout gates will consume only “high-confidence” regression signals (enforced min samples + stable baseline + low ingestion lag).
sections.heading: Planned (in progress)

sections.body:
| ID | Action | Owner | Due date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ENG-4882 | Noise reduction: add smoothing (EWMA) + sustained-breach logic + ingestion-lag guard | Allison Grant | 2026-03-08 | In progress |
| ENG-4874 | Baseline store versioning: pin artifact schema + backfill missing region/SKU fields | Nadia Rahman | 2026-03-01 | In progress |
| ENG-4873 | Publish metric contract: required labels, forbidden labels, query examples | Logan Wright | 2026-02-28 | Complete |
| ENG-4878 | Update alert rules to align grouping with evaluator + enforce min samples | Aisha Bello | 2026-02-26 | Complete |
| ENG-4883 | Update runbook: add baseline-missing play + dedupe verification steps | Rafael Mendes | 2026-02-27 | In progress |
| ENG-4884 | CI perf smoke: verify metrics emission + no-cardinality regression + dashboards load | Caleb Johnson | 2026-03-15 | Not started |
| PM-642 | Rollout gates integration: define “auto-pause” policy + UX for confidence level | Paula Mendes | 2026-03-22 | Not started |
sections.heading: Action items

sections.body:
- On-call validated against independent customer-traffic dashboards quickly and avoided an unnecessary rollback of the runtime.
- Teams (Runtime/SRE/Telemetry) coordinated rapidly; paging rules were disabled within ~20 minutes.
- The canary’s strict “no customer prompts” policy kept investigation clean (no privacy concerns during deep dive).
sections.heading: What went well

sections.body:
- Baseline missing → fallback thresholds created a failure mode where instrumentation/config drift looked like performance regressions.
- Cardinality review was incomplete; labels that seemed “harmless” for logs caused large fragmentation for metrics.
- Alert grouping mismatch created confusion (alerts appeared “global” while underlying series were per-SKU/per-region slices).
- Dedupe failures amplified the incident by creating parallel incident-bot threads and repeated pages.
sections.heading: What didn’t go well

sections.body: - The storm happened during an expansion window and not during a high-risk runtime rollout; impact was primarily internal.
sections.heading: Where we got lucky

sections.body:
Before re-enabling paging and using signals as rollout gates, we will:
1. Run a **7-day warning-only bake** with expanded coverage and confirm:
   - baseline hit-rate > 99.5%
   - no unexpected label growth (cardinality budget)
   - alert volume within noise budget
2. Re-enable paging for **one top model** in one region with clear success criteria.
3. Only after stable paging, enable rollout gate consumption in “advisory” mode for 2 weeks, then move to “blocking” mode.
sections.heading: Follow-up validation plan

sections.body:
- “baseline missing → compare against default thresholds (often too strict)”

to:
- “baseline missing → emit canary health warning + stop regression evaluation for that grouping until baseline exists”.

Rationale: baseline absence is an operational/config issue. Treating it as a performance regression creates noisy pages and reduces trust.
sections.heading: We changed behavior from

sections.body:
- ADR: Baseline computation + thresholds: sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-perf-canary-baseline-and-thresholds.json
- Runbook: Responding to perf canary regression alerts: sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert.json
- Dashboard spec: sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/perf-canary-dashboards-spec.json

payload.page_title: Postmortem: SEV-2 Dedicated autoscaler stuck at min capacity (2026-02-09)

sections.body:
The Dedicated autoscaler stopped scaling above min due to a metrics query change that returned empty series for a subset of clusters.
Two Dedicated customers in us-west experienced sustained queueing and timeouts. p99 latency exceeded 6s for ~70 minutes; timeout rate peaked at 3.2%.
13:22 UTC: Support escalated customer reports of timeouts on Dedicated pools (us-west).
13:28 UTC: SRE on-call confirmed queue depth rising and no scale-out events.

14:05 UTC: Hotfix applied to autoscaler query; scale-out resumed.
14:20 UTC: Queue depth normalized; timeouts subsided.
14:47 UTC: Incident resolved.
A refactor in the autoscalerPromQL query switched label matching from cluster_id to cluster. Some clusters emitted cluster_id only, causing the query to return no data and preventing scale decisions.
Primary detection was via customer escalation; internal alerting on scale-out suppression was missing.
Rolled forward a hotfix restoring label compatibility and added a fallback query when no series are returned.
Once identified, the fix was small and low risk. Capacity was available to scale immediately.
Insufficient alerting on autoscaler making no decisions; canary did not include clusters with legacy labels.
Add alert: autoscaler decision loop sees empty metrics for >5 minutes (SRE; due 2026-02-25).

payload.page_title: INC-2025-0112 Postmortem: Hosted API us-east GPU pool capacity exhaustion

sections.body:

**Incident ID:** INC-2025-0112
**Customer impact:** Broad (self_serve + enterprise workloads routed to us-east)
**Owning engineering team:** Eng Infra (GPU fleet & capacity)
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body: A sustained burst in long-context chat workloads coincided with a delayed capacity scale-up. The scheduler began queuing requests beyond safe limits. Backpressure increased, and the API gateway started returning 429s. When queue timeouts were exceeded, the runtime returned 503s.
sections.heading: What happened

sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body:
**Primary:** Insufficient headroom in the us-east A100 pool during a burst; autoscaling lagged due to conservative safety thresholds and a pending cloud quota cap.
**Contributing factors:**
- Capacity forecast underweighted long-context workload mix shift

payload.page_title: Postmortem: 2025-11-03 Sev1 — Fleet-wide latency cascade triggered by hot /v1/chat/completions route

sections.body:
On 2025-11-03, the Hosted API experienced a Sev1 incident where a bursty, high-token-length workload on the `/v1/chat/completions` route caused a fleet-wide latency cascade across shared GPU pools. The event began as localized p99 latency elevation in `us-east` and progressed to elevated tail latency and increased 5xx rates across multiple routes (chat, embeddings, rerank) due to shared capacity and lack of effective tier-aware admission control.

The primary trigger was a single enterprise tenant workload (large prompts + high concurrency + streaming) that behaved like a noisy neighbor. Our control plane and routing stack at the time did not:
- enforce tier-aware budgets per route,
- gate best-effort traffic early when capacity is constrained,
- export/consume reliable queue depth signals to drive admission decisions,
- provide consistent overload semantics (429s) to shed load predictably.

We restored stability by applying manual throttles and re-routing traffic, but the incident highlighted systemic gaps that directly motivated the **Hot-route capacity protection** initiative.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
**Customer impact (external):**
- Hosted API: intermittent elevated latency and increased errors.
- Dedicated tier: minimal direct error impact, but some elevated tail latency observed in shared services (control plane / policy evaluation) due to knock-on effects.

**What customers experienced:**
- Increased response latency on `/v1/chat/completions` (notably for streaming clients where time-to-first-token degraded).
- Increased 5xx rates (primarily 503/504) for a subset of requests when upstream queues exceeded timeouts.
- Retries amplified load due to lack of consistent backpressure guidance and inconsistent 429 behavior.

**SLO/SLA impact (Hosted API):**
- A subset of enterprise accounts breached their route-level p99 latency objective for `/v1/chat/completions` during the peak window.
- Best-effort traffic experienced the largest latency variance and error spikes.

**Blast radius:**
- Primary: `us-east` hosted GPU pools (`hosted-gpu-a100-us-east-*`).
- Secondary: global impact via cross-region spillover as clients retried and traffic shifted.
sections.heading: Impact

sections.body:
**How we detected:**
- First alert was the standard Hosted API p99 latency alert (regional) and elevated 5xx rate alert.
- On-call noticed concurrent increases in GPU saturation and request queueing, but we lacked a single “overload protection active” signal.

**Detection gaps:**
- No tier/route-specific overload dashboards existed; we only had aggregate route latency and overall 5xx.
- Queue depth and scheduler lag signals were either unavailable or not normalized enough to be actionable.
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
> Note: Times are approximate; see incident channel transcript for raw timestamps.

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---:|---|
| 14:07 | First elevation in `/v1/chat/completions` p99 latency in `us-east` detected (latency alert fired). |
| 14:10 | 5xx begins rising on chat route; embeddings begins showing elevated p95 due to shared pools. |
| 14:13 | On-call (SRE) joins; initial hypothesis: regional capacity shortfall / GPU pool saturation. |
| 14:18 | GPU saturation at/near 100% for `us-east` shared pool; request queue depth increases rapidly. |
| 14:23 | Router continues admitting best-effort traffic; tail latency increases fleet-wide (clients retry and shift load). |
| 14:29 | Manual action: increase existing global throttle on Hosted API for best-effort tier (coarse limit). |
| 14:33 | Partial stabilization; chat route still elevated; 5xx plateaus but remains above baseline. |
| 14:41 | Identified dominant tenant/workload shape: long prompts + high concurrency + streaming on `/v1/chat/completions`. |
| 14:45 | Manual mitigation: apply temporary tenant-level rate limit at gateway (custom rule) and reduce burst. |
| 14:52 | Latency begins to recover; queue depth decreases; 5xx drops. |
| 15:06 | Traffic normalized; monitoring returns to near-baseline; incident downgraded from active mitigation to monitoring. |
| 15:35 | Incident resolved; begin drafting postmortem and follow-up items. |
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: A single high-traffic, high-token-length chat workload saturated the shared GPU pool serving `/v1/chat/completions` in `us-east`. Continuous batching and KV cache pressure amplified the effect: long sequences reduced effective throughput, increased queueing, and caused timeouts.
sections.heading: Immediate cause

sections.body:
1) **No tier-aware admission control tied to route budgets**
- We did not have explicit per-route/per-tier budgets aligned to enterprise vs best-effort SLOs.
- Under pressure, the router treated traffic more uniformly than intended, allowing best-effort to compete with enterprise traffic for the same constrained resources.

2) **Lack of reliable capacity signals in routing decisions**
- Routing did not consume normalized queue depth / scheduler lag signals to gate new requests.
- The system reacted only after latency and error rates rose, which is too late for overload management.

3) **Inconsistent overload shedding semantics**
- Many clients saw 5xx/timeout behavior rather than consistent 429s with actionable retry guidance.
- This increased retry storms and elevated load during recovery.

4) **Shared pool coupling across “hot routes”**
- Chat traffic saturation degraded other routes in the same shared pools (embeddings/rerank) via resource contention and control plane hot paths.
sections.heading: Systemic causes

sections.body:
- **Workload shape:** long prompts, high output token targets, and streaming increased GPU occupancy time per request.
- **Burst behavior:** rapid ramp-up exceeded what autoscaling could absorb in minutes.
- **Noisy neighbor isolation:** the tenant was in a shared hosted pool without strict per-tenant burst controls.
- **Observability gaps:** limited visibility into “why” requests were slow (queue depth, scheduler lag, shed reasons).
sections.heading: Contributing factors

sections.body:
- On-call triage was fast; we identified the dominant workload within ~35 minutes.
- Manual gateway throttles reduced load and helped restore stability without needing a full regional shutdown.
- Cross-team coordination (SRE + Routing + Gateway + Infra) was effective during mitigation.
sections.heading: What went well

sections.body:
- We relied on coarse throttles and manual tenant-specific rules; decisions were not deterministic or easily auditable.
- Lack of tier-aware protections meant enterprise and best-effort behaviors were not predictably separated under load.
- Customer-visible errors skewed toward 5xx/timeouts rather than 429 with clear retry semantics.
- Limited runbook coverage for overload: no standardized “overload mode” actions or dashboards existed.
sections.heading: What went poorly

sections.body:
- The trigger tenant’s burst tapered rather than sustaining for hours.
- `eu-west` had spare capacity, which reduced the duration of global spillover effects.
sections.heading: Where we got lucky

sections.body:
- Support sent targeted updates to affected enterprise accounts during/after the incident, but messaging was reactive.
- We did not have a pre-approved explanation for overload behavior or recommended client-side backoff.

Follow-up: create standardized customer-facing guidance for 429s/reason codes and predictable overload handling (see Action Items).
sections.heading: Customer communications

sections.body:
1) **Implement tier-aware rate limiting at the API gateway**
- Owner: Amara Diallo (API Gateway)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4922`
- Due: 2025-12-05
- Notes: Standardize 429 payload + headers; differentiate quota vs overload.

2) **Add priority classes + deterministic evaluation in policy engine**
- Owner: Jordan Lee (Policy Engine)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4923`
- Due: 2025-12-12
- Notes: Decisions must be explainable for enterprise escalations.

3) **Integrate capacity signals into routing for admission control**
- Owner: Elena Popov (Routing)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4924`
- Due: 2025-12-19
- Notes: Gate best-effort earlier; preserve enterprise route budgets.

4) **Export runtime queue depth and scheduler lag metrics (low cardinality)**
- Owner: Julian Moore (Runtime) / Logan Wright (Telemetry)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4925`
- Due: 2025-12-02
- Notes: Must be cheap on data plane; usable for dashboards and automated triggers.
sections.heading: P0 (committed / already in flight)

sections.body:
5) **Create SRE dashboards + paging rules for protected routes**
- Owner: Sergio Costa (Observability)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4926`
- Due: 2025-12-20

6) **Incident-bot notifications for overload protection triggers**
- Owner: Peter Holtz (Embedded SRE)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4927`
- Due: 2026-01-10

7) **Runbook: overload protection + admission control**
- Owner: Aisha Bello (SRE)
- Tracking: Confluence page `runbook-overload-protection-and-admission-control`
- Due: 2025-12-23

8) **Support playbook + customer docs for new 429 semantics**
- Owner: Dev Patel (Support) / Wei Chen (Docs)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4930`
- Due: 2026-01-15
sections.heading: P1 (operational readiness)

sections.body:
9) **Fallback policy guardrails for enterprise routes**
- Owner: Ravi Menon (Architecture) / Mina Haddad (Routing)
- Tracking: GitHub `pr-27460` + follow-ups
- Due: 2026-01-30
- Notes: Avoid silent quality changes; only allow fallback where explicitly permitted.

10) **Game day: simulate hot-route overload + validate enterprise SLO stability**
- Owner: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Tracking: Linear `ENG-4929`
- Due: 2026-02-07
sections.heading: P2 (hardening / longer-term)

sections.body:
This incident directly motivated the **Hot-route capacity protection** program with the following principles:
- **Protect the fleet:** overload in one hot route must not cause fleet-wide degradation.
- **Guarantee enterprise behavior:** explicit priority classes and per-route/per-tier budgets tied to SLOs.
- **Make overload behavior predictable:** consistent 429 semantics + reason codes; deterministic and auditable decisions.
- **Keep data-plane overhead low:** avoid high-cardinality checks and expensive policy evaluation on critical paths.
sections.heading: Prevention / design changes (high level)

sections.body:
- `/v1/chat/completions` p99 latency (us-east): elevated multiple times above baseline during 14:10–14:50 UTC.
- GPU saturation: effectively pinned at 95–100% for the affected shared pool.
- Queue depth: increased rapidly and remained elevated until tenant throttling was applied.
- Error profile: mix of 503/504 and client timeouts; 429 usage was inconsistent and not a reliable load-shed mechanism.
sections.heading: Key metrics observed (peak window)

sections.body:
- Severity: Sev1 due to broad customer impact and fleet-wide degradation risk.
- Duration: ~1h 30m from first alert to stable recovery.
sections.heading: Notes on incident classification

sections.body:
- Linear epic: `ENG-4921 Hot-route capacity protection`
- Design/ADR: see related pages above
- Support follow-ups: see Known Issues page `enterprise-priority-429-and-quota-behavior` (created later as part of program)

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Elevated KV cache evictions increased costs and latency (2026-03-02)

sections.body: On 2026-03-02 we observed a rise in KV cache evictions across the hosted fleet, leading to higher prefill compute, increased per-request latency, and higher unit cost.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 2 hours 12 minutes
- Symptoms: p95 latency +18% on long-context workloads; cost per 1k tokens +9%
- Scope: Hosted API, primarily long-context chat routes
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- Alert: cache eviction rate exceeded 5% on multiple clusters
- Cost dashboard: sudden increase in prefill FLOPs per token
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 13:06: Eviction alert triggers
- 13:20: Runtime on-call confirms elevated evictions on A100 clusters
- 13:38: Mitigation: reduce max batch size for affected models; increase cache reservation
- 15:18: Evictions return to baseline
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: A batching policy change increased concurrent sequence lengths beyond the KV cache reservation assumptions for long-context workloads. The policy improved throughput on short prompts but caused memory pressure on mixed workloads.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- Mixed workload distribution not represented in canary
- Insufficient observability for "cache headroom" at the model instance level
sections.heading: Contributing factors

sections.body:
1. Add model-instance metric for KV cache headroom (reserved vs used) and alert on sustained <10% headroom. Owner team: Observability. Priority: P0.
2. Update batching policy to be workload-aware (cap concurrency when long-context requests dominate). Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
3. Add perf-canary scenario for mixed short/long workloads and verify eviction rate <1%. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
4. Add cost guardrail: alert when prefill FLOPs/token increases >7% week-over-week for a model route. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
5. Document safe batching configuration defaults by model family and GPU type in the serving runtime standards. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P2.
sections.heading: Follow-up action items

sections.body: Throughput optimizations must be evaluated against mixed production distributions, not single-mode benchmarks. Cache headroom should be a first-class SLO for long-context serving.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Private VPC egress disruption and region fallback (2025-07-22)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-07-22, a networking change in a customer-controlled VPC (Private deployment) disrupted outbound connectivity to one of the inference subnets. As a mitigation, the customer and Redwood jointly activated *automatic region fallback* to a secondary region for non-residency-bound traffic until routing was corrected.

h2. Impact
* Customer: 1 Private deployment (customer-sensitive).
* Symptoms: intermittent timeouts and 502/504 on a subset of inference nodes.
* Duration: ~2 hours of partial impairment; user-visible errors concentrated in the first 35 minutes.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 16:20: Customer reports timeouts on chat endpoints.
* 16:27: Redwood on-call engaged; traces show failed egress from subnet private-inf-az2.
* 16:41: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for allowed routes to shift traffic from us-east-1 (primary) to us-west-2 (secondary).
* 17:05: Error rate reduced; customer confirms improvement.
* 18:02: Customer reverted the VPC route table change; primary region stabilized.
* 18:15: Disabled region fallback after validation.

h2. Mitigation details
* Primary region: us-east-1
* Fallback region: us-west-2
* Eligibility: routes not marked data_residency_strict and with customer approval
* Trigger: upstream timeout rate > 0.8% OR node connectivity check failures

h2. Root cause
A VPC route table update inadvertently removed a NAT gateway route for one availability zone, breaking outbound calls required for tokenization and telemetry sinks.

h2. Action items
1) Add a Private deployment pre-change checklist emphasizing NAT/egress requirements. Owner: Eng Private Deployments.
2) Improve health checks to distinguish ingress vs egress failures. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add documentation for region fallback prerequisites in Private reference architecture. Owner: Eng Private Deployments.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0722

payload.page_title: Incident Review: Fallback routing to legacy quantized variant during traffic surge (BrightHealthAI, 2026-03-12)

sections.body:
h1. Overview
On 2026-03-12, a customer traffic surge for BrightHealthAI (dedicated tier) caused elevated p95/p99 latency and request timeouts. A subset of requests were routed away from the pinned primary model variant to a legacy quantized compatible variant (redwood/quant-13b-q4). The quantized variant incurred repeated cold starts and had lower throughput, amplifying tail latency under load.

This document summarizes impact, timeline, contributing factors, root cause, and the remediation shipped after the event.

h2. Customer / Environment
* Customer: BrightHealthAI (dedicated)
* Environment: prod-us-east primary (spillover observed in us-west)
* Components: serving-runtime, smart-routing, api-gateway, scheduler/autoscaler
* Primary pinned model: redwood/rlhf-vicuna-13b (deployed train v2026-02-08; serving config hash updated 2026-03-05)
* Fallback variant observed: redwood/quant-13b-q4 (legacy quantized variant; no pre-warm pool at the time)

h2. Impact Summary (updated)
* Duration: 2026-03-12T18:33Z to ~19:00Z (most severe); residual elevated p99 until ~19:07Z due to client retries and draining queues.
* Error rate: ~7% of requests returned 504s at peak (previously estimated 10–20% during initial triage).
* Latency: p95 increased from ~0.9s baseline to ~3.8s; p99 peaked >10s for a subset of routed-to-quant traffic.
* Scope: BrightHealthAI dedicated pool traffic in us-east; limited spillover in us-west due to global routing retries.
* Secondary impact: increased billing risk due to client retry behavior (2 retries with short backoff), and increased load on router/serving queues.

h2. Detection
* Customer-reported: BrightHealthAI reported 504s starting ~18:45Z, noting a scheduled batch unexpectedly spiked traffic.
* Internal signals: router logs showed fallback routing reasons shifting to "capacity_unavailable" and then "compatible_variant"; serving-runtime showed cold-start spikes and queue growth (>250 pending on some workers).

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 18:32: Traffic spike begins (customer scheduled batch misconfiguration).
* 18:33–18:35: Smart-routing begins returning x-redwood-routing-reason: capacity_unavailable for the pinned pool; some requests routed to compatible legacy quant variant.
* 18:45: Customer reports 504s and asks whether requests were routed away from pinned model.
* 18:52: Support opens P1 and begins collecting request IDs/trace samples.
* 19:01: SRE confirms fallback routing to redwood/quant-13b-q4 and cold-start/queue pressure in serving-runtime.
* 19:02: Temporary mitigation applied: per-customer routing override to enforce strict pinning (no fallback to legacy quant).
* 19:07: Customer confirms immediate improvement; errors drop near-zero.
* 19:20: Customer acknowledges; agrees to update retry/backoff behavior.
* 2026-03-13: Engineering creates ENG-3124 (routing logic) and ENG-3140 (telemetry).
* 2026-03-18: ENG-3124 merged and rolled out to prod-us-east, then prod-us-west.
* 2026-03-20: ENG-3140 merged and rolled out; new headers/metrics available.

h2. Technical Details
h3. What happened (routing + serving)
During the surge, the dedicated pool for the pinned model temporarily exhausted warm capacity. Smart-routing interpreted this as "capacity_unavailable" and selected a compatible alternative variant (legacy quant). The legacy quantized variant:
* Lacked a warm pool at the time.
* Had higher cold-start time (observed ~3.2s average cold start during the incident window).
* Had lower effective throughput, causing queue growth and timeouts.

Client retry behavior (short 200–500ms backoff) amplified the pressure and increased tail latency.

h3. Observations / Signals
* Response headers observed by the customer: x-redwood-variant and x-redwood-routing-reason.
* Router logs: fallback routing reason "capacity_unavailable" then "compatible_variant" between ~18:33Z and ~19:00Z.
* Serving runtime: repeated cold starts for quant workers; queue depth spikes >250; workers timing out under load.

h2. Root Cause (final)
Smart-routing permitted fallback from a strictly pinned dedicated deployment to a "compatible" variant when the pinned pool reported transient capacity exhaustion. The selection algorithm did not sufficiently weight (or explicitly gate on) warm-pool capability and cold-start risk for candidate variants. Under high QPS, routing to a non-warmable legacy variant converted a short-lived capacity dip into sustained tail-latency and timeouts.

h2. Contributing Factors
* Autoscaler warmup policy did not pre-load or pre-warm the legacy quant variant; newly created workers entered service without mitigating cold-start penalties.
* Variant metadata did not explicitly expose warm-pool capability to routing decisions (prior to ENG-3140).
* Client retries used short backoff, effectively multiplying load during the period of degraded service.
* Dedicated pool had insufficient surge headroom for the customer’s unexpected batch.

h2. Mitigation (during incident)
* Applied per-customer routing override to enforce strict pinning for BrightHealthAI (blocked fallback to redwood/quant-13b-q4).
* Recommended customer retry change: exponential backoff with jitter and longer initial delay.

h2. Remediation (post-incident)
h3. Shipped changes
* ENG-3124 (Routing guardrails):
  * Added routing constraints so that for dedicated + pinned configurations, fallback to legacy quant variants is disabled unless explicitly allowed by policy.
  * Updated candidate scoring to prefer warm-pool-capable variants under capacity pressure; non-warmable variants are deprioritized and can be excluded when latency SLO risk is high.
* ENG-3140 (Telemetry):
  * Added router telemetry fields/metrics to record (a) warm-pool capability, (b) variant selection score breakdown, and (c) whether a fallback was blocked by policy.
  * Exposed additional debugging headers for internal use (restricted to trusted callers): x-redwood-warm-pool-capable and x-redwood-variant-score.

h3. Operational changes
* Updated fallback routing runbook to include a "Dedicated + pinned" decision tree and explicit instructions for applying per-customer strict pinning overrides.
* Added an on-call checklist item to capture: routed variant, routing reason, warm-pool capability, and queue depth.

h2. Customer Communication
* 2026-03-12 19:20Z: Customer informed of routing override + retry guidance.
* 2026-03-15: Post-incident review scheduled and completed with CS + Eng; customer provided root cause details (batch misconfiguration).
* 2026-03-21: Customer notified that routing guardrails + telemetry have been rolled out.

h2. Action Items
* [Done] Block fallback from pinned dedicated pools to legacy quant variants by default (ENG-3124).
* [Done] Add warm-pool capability telemetry and expose in router debug headers (ENG-3140).
* [Planned] Evaluate autoscaler pre-warm hook for quantized variants where allowed, or enforce "no-serve-until-warm" semantics for high-QPS pools (Owner: serving-runtime; Target: 2026-04).
* [Planned] Dedicated pool surge-capacity guidance for CS onboarding and periodic checks (Owner: Customer Success + SRE; Target: 2026-04).
* [Planned] Document recommended client retry policy and provide SDK defaults aligned with inference SLOs (Owner: Product + SDK; Target: 2026-05).

h2. Appendix: Original Incident Ticket References
* Support ticket: SUP-18501 ("Unplanned routing to degraded inference variant during traffic surge causing elevated p95/p99 and request timeouts")
* Incident ID: INC-20260312-01

Appendix notes: During live triage, the initial estimated timeout rate (10–20%) was refined after log sampling and aggregation to ~7% at peak. The mitigation time (routing override at 19:02Z) remains accurate and correlates with an immediate drop in error rate.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Scheduler queue backlog impacted streaming starts (2025-12-03)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-12-03, streaming requests experienced delayed first-token times due to a scheduler queue backlog. The backlog was amplified by a retry storm from a subset of SDK clients and insufficient backpressure when the GPU queue was saturated.

h2. Customer impact
* Time window: 14:0315:01 PT
* Symptoms: streaming first token delayed (queue wait time), elevated 429s and 5xx from gateway timeouts
* Affected: hosted traffic in us-west; some dedicated pools saw secondary impact due to shared scheduler control-plane load

h2. Detection
* Alert: "scheduler_queue_depth > 1500" and "first_token_p95 > 8s"
* Support tickets referencing "stream never starts"

h2. Root cause
A regression in the scheduler admission controller made it too permissive under high concurrency, allowing queue depth to grow faster than workers could drain.

h2. Resolution
* Rolled back scheduler admission controller to previous build
* Applied temporary rate limit tightening for affected endpoints

h2. Action items
1) Add load-shedding guardrail for queue wait time (Owner: Serving Runtime)
2) SDK guidance update on retry/backoff (Owner: DevEx)
3) Add synthetic streaming canary that triggers on first-token delay (Owner: SRE)

h2. References
* Related Jira: INT-1855
* Related GitHub: redwood/PR-8921 (rollback)

payload.page_title: Postmortem: RBAC policy deployment caused authorization failures (2026-03-18)

sections.body: On 2026-03-18, a production RBAC policy deployment caused increased authorization failures for Console and API key management operations. The issue was triggered by a deny rule that unintentionally matched a broad set of service principals.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 29 minutes
- Symptoms: users unable to rotate API keys; some Console pages failed to load; elevated 403s
- Scope: Primarily enterprise orgs using fine-grained role assignments
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- Alert: authz-service 403 anomaly
- Support escalation: enterprise admins unable to manage keys
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 09:14: 403 anomaly alert fired
- 09:18: Security on-call begins investigation
- 09:27: Mitigation: rollback RBAC bundle to previous version
- 09:43: Error rates return to baseline
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: A deny rule intended to restrict a deprecated permission used a wildcard principal selector. During compilation, the selector expanded to include internal service principals used by Console and key management workflows. The policy review process did not include a compilation preview step.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:
- Lack of policy compilation preview in CI
- Incomplete test coverage for key management operations under enterprise RBAC configurations
sections.heading: Contributing factors

payload.page_title: Experimental Metric Injection Campaign — Retrospective

sections.body:
Summary
=======

This document is a postmortem-style retrospective of the experimental metric injection campaign we ran from 2025-11-10 to 2025-12-05. The experiment intentionally injected synthetic telemetry into the platform metrics pipeline to validate: (1) alert sensitivity tuning for LLM prefix/KV cache degradation, (2) downstream dashboard behavior, and (3) costing and storage impact of higher cardinality metrics.

This retrospective records the experiment design, outcomes, operational impacts, lessons learned, and recommended next steps. It is intended for platform operators, SRE, observability engineers, and product owners evaluating telemetry tradeoffs.

Background and goals
--------------------

Context: The platform telemetry backlog showed repeated false-positive alerts during short-lived cache thrash events. To evaluate whether our alert rules, aggregation windows, and cardinality controls were balanced, the Observability team proposed a safe, time-limited metric injection campaign that simulates realistic degradation signals without impacting production services.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Validate alerting SLOs and silence durations for cache/serving regressions.
- Measure cost and cardinality impact when emitting per-tenant cache-hit partitions vs. aggregated metrics.
- Verify dashboard and runbook actions (including automated ticket creation) under noisy conditions.

Experiment design (high level)
----------------------------

1. Scope and windows:
   - Active window: 2025-11-10 08:00 UTC to 2025-12-05 20:00 UTC.
   - Test tenants: synthetic-tenant-001 .. synthetic-tenant-050 (no real customer traffic).
   - Injected services: kv-prefix-cache-service, serving-router, request-queue-proxy.

2. Injection mechanics:
   - A dedicated job (metric-injector v0.3.1) published synthetic Prometheus-compatible metrics into the metrics-ingest pipeline via the internal metrics-writer queue.
   - Mutation pattern: ramp-up (5m), steady-state (30m), burst (3m) — repeated every 2 hours.

3. Safety controls (must pass preconditions):
   - Injector uses a low-priority tag and sits behind a feature-flag (ff.metrics_injection).
   - AuthZ: only operator role obs-inject allowed to start/stop jobs.
   - Rate limit: 1500 metrics/sec throttle at the ingestion gateway.
   - Circuit breaker: ingestion spike > 10x baseline triggers automatic halt and alert to obs-ops.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: kv_prefix_cache_hit{tenant="synthetic-tenant-001",prefix_shard="shard-12",pool="fast",experiment="metric-injection-2025"} 1
sections.heading: TYPE kv_prefix_cache_hit counter

sections.body:
- 1m rate of synthetic hits (all tenants): sum(rate(kv_prefix_cache_hit[1m]))
- Per-tenant anomaly detection: increase(kv_prefix_cache_miss[5m]) / (increase(kv_prefix_cache_hit[5m]) + 1) > 0.25

Alerting rules exercised
-----------------------

We deliberately exercised three rule families to observe operator signal-to-noise and automated mitigations.

1) cache-degradation-severe
   - Expr: job:kv_cache_miss_ratio:5m > 0.25 AND sum(rate(kv_prefix_cache_miss[1m])) > 100
   - Severity: critical
   - Pager: obs-oncall -> eng-platform-sme (P1)
   - Runbook excerpt: see section "Runbook actions for severity-critical alerts" below.

2) cache-latency-elevated
   - Expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kv_cache_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 0.2
   - Severity: warning
   - Pager: obs-oncall (P2)

3) high-cardinality-telemetry-cost
   - Expr: increase(metric_series_count_total[1d]) > 10000
   - Severity: info (but channels to cost-engineering slack)

Runbook actions for severity-critical alerts
-------------------------------------------

1. Triage (minutes 0–5)
   - Confirm alert origin using the alert details page and run the Playbook Debug CLI:
     $ ./obsctl alert inspect cache-degradation-severe --start="-10m"
   - If source contains experiment tag experiment=metric-injection-2025, mark as "experimental" and follow experimental isolation path.

2. Isolation (minutes 5–20)
   - Use the operator UI to throttle metric-injector job:
     $ ffcli set metrics_injection off --env=prod
   - If throttling fails, disable ingestion at the gateway:
     $ kubectl scale deployment metrics-ingest-gateway --replicas=0 -n observability

3. Remediation (minutes 20–60)
   - If cache miss ratio reduces after halting injector, file a short incident note and run a post-incident checklist.
   - If not reduced, escalate to eng-serving-runtime and perform controlled model-swap fallback.

Observations and outcomes
-------------------------
sections.heading: PromQL queries used during the campaign

sections.body:
| experiment_id | start | end | peak_cardinality | peak_series_rate | downstream_slo_burn | operator_actions | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| MI-2025-11-A | 2025-11-12T08:00Z | 2025-11-12T20:00Z | 24,600 | 1,350/s | serving-router 95th latency +0.9% | throttled injector, no service restart | small, transient dashboard churn |
| MI-2025-11-B | 2025-11-18T02:00Z | 2025-11-18T06:00Z | 42,100 | 2,200/s | cache-service SLO burn 0.4% | ingestion gateway scaled down | required manual backfill of metrics |
| MI-2025-11-C | 2025-11-28T14:00Z | 2025-11-28T18:00Z | 9,800 | 720/s | no measurable SLO burn | no operator action | safe, within forecasted costs |
sections.heading: Summary of collected artifacts (table)

sections.body:
- Alert fidelity: The critical cache-degradation-severe rule fired 18 times; 11 were attributable to the experiment. After tuning the rule's population threshold (sum(rate(...)) > 250), false positives from the injection decreased by 72%.
- Dashboard behavior: High-cardinality injection increased dashboard load times for 30–45s during peaks. We found one Grafana dashboard panel using unbounded label expansion (tenant label) causing heavy rendering cost; we updated panel to use topk(10, ...) aggregation.
- Cost impact: Metric series cardinality increased ingestion storage costs by ~9% in the experiment window. Extrapolating to sustained per-tenant telemetry (not recommended) would add ~1.2% to monthly telemetry bill per 10k tenants.
- Operator cognitive load: During the first two weeks, oncall time to diagnose experimental alerts averaged 28 minutes per incident. After adding an explicit experiment tag and a fast-path in the alert details UI, triage time dropped to 9 minutes.

Lessons learned
-------------

1. Experiment tagging is critical. Without experiment=... in the injected metrics and the alert payload, engineers could not quickly differentiate synthetic vs real incidents. Add tag by default for future tests.

2. Cardinality control must be enforced in the ingestion layer. The experiment highlighted that per-tenant per-prefix labels explode series count; we should enforce a policy of max 3 dynamic labels for production metrics and apply sampler/rollup for ephemeral tenants.

3. Dashboard templates must use bounded aggregations. Panels that iterate across unbounded label sets are fragile under injection. Use topk(), group_left, or explicit tenant lists in dashboards that power runbooks.

4. Alert rules need two-dimensional thresholds: both ratio and absolute volume guards prevented noisy firing in high-cardinality situations.

Decisions and follow-ups (action items)
-------------------------------------

1) Enforce ingestion label policy (owner: eng-platform telemetry) — due 2026-02-15
   - Implement ingestion-side label whitelist and hard caps in metrics-ingest-gateway.
   - Metric filters to reject metrics with >3 dynamic labels or value cardinality > 100k/day.

2) Alert rule change (owner: obs-slo-team) — due 2026-01-31
   - Update cache-degradation-severe to require sum(rate(...)) > 250 OR increase(metric_series_count_total[1h]) < 5000 to fire.

3) Dashboard hardening (owner: observability-frontend) — due 2026-01-20
   - Audit top-30 dashboards for unbounded label expansions; apply topk(10) or explicit tenant scoping.

4) Experiment framework improvements (owner: platform-experiments) — due 2026-03-01
   - Add an "experiment registry" page that automatically annotates alerts and dashboards when a live experiment is active.
   - Provide a one-click ff toggle for emergency stop and escalation metadata populated in PagerDuty incidents.

Appendix A — Useful commands and snippets
----------------------------------------

- Inspect alert context:
  $ ./obsctl alert inspect cache-degradation-severe --start="-30m" --format=json | jq .context.tags

- Throttle injector (k8s job):
  $ kubectl patch cronjob metric-injector -n observability --patch '{"spec": {"suspend": true}}'

- Example Grafana panel safe query for cache misses:
  topk(10, sum by (tenant) (rate(kv_prefix_cache_miss[5m])))

Appendix B — Glossary and ownership
-----------------------------------

- metric-injector: internal test harness that emits synthetic metrics (repo: infra/metric-injector). Owner: platform-experiments.
- metrics-ingest-gateway: Kafka-ingest + transform service for Prom-compatible metrics. Owner: observability-infra.
- obsctl: command-line tooling for observability runbook actions. Owner: observability-tools.

Contact and follow-up meeting
----------------------------

We will host a 45-minute retro working session to review the findings and approve action items on 2026-01-19 16:00 UTC in #obs-retros and the Confluence meeting page (link below).

Meeting page: /confluence/eng-platform/retrospectives/experimental-metric-injection-campaign-retrospective-2025/meeting-notes

Document owner: Aisha Kapoor (aisha@redwood-inference.com).

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-12-07: initial draft
- 2026-01-12: updated with final measurements, action items, and dates

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Dedicated cluster degradation and fallback to Hosted pool (2025-06-08)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-06-08, a Dedicated GPU pool for a single-tenant customer experienced repeated node flaps and elevated error rates. To maintain availability, we activated an *automatic fallback* to a compatible Hosted pool (same model family) for the affected customer routes until the Dedicated pool stabilized.

h2. Impact
* Customer: 1 Dedicated tenant (customer-approved fallback to Hosted).
* Symptoms: 503 spikes and p95 latency > 6s on tenant routes.
* Duration: ~1 hour degraded performance; ~14 minutes of elevated 503.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 14:02: Dedicated pool alert: node health flapping on rw-ded-a100-tenant-17.
* 14:11: Error rate exceeded 2%; on-call paged.
* 14:18: Mitigation: enabled *auto-fallback to Hosted* for tenant routes "chat" and "embeddings".
* 14:23: Errors dropped; latency improved.
* 14:37: Infra drained unstable nodes and replaced 2 GPUs.
* 15:08: Dedicated pool stable; disabled fallback after validation tests.

h2. Mitigation details
* Primary: Dedicated pool rw-ded-a100-tenant-17
* Fallback: Hosted pool rw-a100-us-east-01
* Trigger: 503 rate > 1% OR unhealthy_nodes >= 2
* Guardrail: only for this tenant and only for model-compatible requests

h2. Root cause
A firmware/driver mismatch on two nodes caused intermittent GPU resets under high utilization.

h2. Action items
1) Add preflight validation to block driver rollouts that violate the Dedicated pool baseline. Owner: Eng Infra.
2) Add tenant-specific dashboard widget showing when fallback is active. Owner: Eng Platform.
3) Update customer-facing incident comms template for Dedicated-to-Hosted fallback. Owner: Customer Success.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0608

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Regional failover routed to incompatible model variants (2026-02-03)

sections.body: On 2026-02-03 a transient network event degraded availability in eu-west-1. Automated failover shifted a portion of traffic to us-east-1, but the routing policy selected model variants that were API-compatible yet behaviorally incompatible for a subset of customers who had pinned specific model families.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 33 minutes
- Symptoms: elevated 4xx due to validation mismatches, and quality complaints due to unexpected model behavior

sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body: The failover routing policy used a broad compatibility set ("same interface") rather than the intended constraint ("same model family"). The policy definition was duplicated across regions, and eu-west-1 had drifted from the hardened baseline.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: EU-West capacity shortage and region fallback (2025-03-03)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-03-03, a GPU capacity shortfall in eu-west-1 impacted a subset of Hosted and Dedicated traffic pinned to that region. Mitigation required activating *automatic region fallback* (eu-west-1 -> us-east-1) for eligible routes until additional capacity was brought online.

h2. Impact
* Elevated p95 latency and increased 429/503 responses for region-pinned routes in eu-west-1.
* Customers: 7 Hosted orgs and 1 Dedicated tenant with optional cross-region allowance enabled.
* Duration: ~41 minutes of degraded performance; ~18 minutes of hard errors for the most constrained pool.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 09:42: Capacity alert: available_gpu_count < 5 in eu-west-1 pool rw-a100-eu-01.
* 09:48: Saturation exceeded 95% and queue wait climbed > 400ms.
* 09:51: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for "chat-default" and "embeddings-default" where customer policy allows cross-region.
* 09:54: Router began directing overflow to us-east-1 for eligible traffic.
* 10:03: Error rate dropped; latency partially recovered.
* 10:23: Added 8 GPUs to eu-west-1 pool; disabled region fallback after stabilization.

h2. Mitigation details
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Primary region: eu-west-1
* Fallback region: us-east-1
* Triggers: saturation > 90% OR 503 rate > 0.5%
* Eligibility: routes not marked "data_residency_strict"

h2. Root cause
A delayed GPU delivery + slow provisioning left the eu-west-1 pool below the forecasted headroom for a scheduled customer load test.

h2. What went well
* Region fallback prevented a full outage for eligible traffic.
* On-call followed the capacity runbook and coordinated with Infra quickly.

h2. What went poorly
* We lacked a clear customer-facing flag indicating whether cross-region fallback was enabled for a tenant.

h2. Action items
1) Add tenant-level UI indicator and API field for cross-region fallback eligibility. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Improve capacity forecasting for scheduled load tests and Dedicated bursts. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add automated comms template for region fallback events. Owner: Incident Response.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: SEV-2 Console rollout UI bug triggered rollback loop (2026-02-22)

sections.body:
A Console UI change caused repeated client-side retries on a non-idempotent rollback endpoint, putting rollouts-service into a rollback loop for a subset of deployments.
Operators could not reliably pause or promote canary rollouts via Console. Some actions displayed as successful but were not applied, leading to confusion and delayed mitigations for unrelated rollouts.
19:05 UTC: Internal user reported Console rollout controls unresponsive.
19:10 UTC: Eng on-call saw elevated 5xx and increased write QPS to rollouts-service.
19:20 UTC: Isolated to Console release 2026.02.22.2 with a new retry wrapper.
19:28 UTC: Disabled feature flag for retry wrapper in prod.
19:40 UTC: Rollouts-service write QPS returned to normal; rollback loops stopped.
19:58 UTC: Incident resolved.
The Console’s new retry wrapper treated 409 conflict responses as retryable and retried POST /rollback automatically. The endpoint was not idempotent and could re-trigger rollback actions.
Internal report and rollouts-service error/QPS alerts.
Disabled the retry wrapper via feature flag and added a server-side idempotency key requirement for rollback actions.
Feature flag allowed immediate mitigation. Service-level alerts were actionable.
The UI change was not tested against the real rollouts-service conflict behavior; endpoint idempotency was assumed but not documented.
Document idempotency requirements for rollouts-service endpoints (Platform Engineering; due 2026-03-10).
Add integration tests in Console CI that simulate 409 and ensure no retries on non-idempotent endpoints (Console & Tooling; due 2026-03-15).
Introduce a standard client retry policy library with an allowlist of safe endpoints (DevEx; due 2026-04-01).

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Dedicated capacity starvation on gpu-pool-delta (2026-03-10)

sections.body: On 2026-03-10, several Dedicated customers experienced elevated queueing delays and request timeouts due to capacity starvation in gpu-pool-delta. The pool had sufficient total GPUs, but an imbalance in GPU fragmentation and incorrect priority weights prevented timely scheduling of certain large-model replicas.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Duration: 1 hour 26 minutes
- Symptoms: increased queue depth; p95 latency +55%; intermittent 504s
- Scope: Dedicated customers mapped to gpu-pool-delta in us-east-1
sections.heading: Customer impact

sections.body:
- Alert: dedicated queue depth > threshold
- Customer Success escalation: "timeouts on pinned dedicated endpoint"
sections.heading: Detection

sections.body:
- 17:42: Queue depth alerts fire
- 17:55: Infra on-call identifies fragmentation + weight misconfig
- 18:10: Mitigation: move two tenants to gpu-pool-echo; restart scheduler with corrected weights
- 19:08: Queue depth returns to normal
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body: The dedicated scheduler's priority weights were updated without considering large-model GPU packing constraints. The resulting placement favored smaller replicas, fragmenting GPU availability and starving large replicas that required contiguous resources.
sections.heading: Root cause

sections.body:

- Capacity dashboards did not show fragmentation metrics

1. Add fragmentation metric to capacity dashboards ("largest contiguous block" and "packing efficiency"). Owner team: Infrastructure. Priority: P0.
2. Implement CI simulation for scheduler weight changes using representative tenant/model mixes. Owner team: Infrastructure. Priority: P1.
3. Add SLO alert for dedicated queueing time (not just depth) and tie to paging policy. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P0.
4. Document dedicated pool rebalancing runbook including safe tenant move procedures and communication template. Owner team: Customer Success. Priority: P2.
5. Add safeguard: prevent weight rollout if predicted starvation risk exceeds threshold. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P1.

sections.body: Dedicated reliability depends on scheduler correctness and visibility into fragmentation. Simulations and better metrics are needed to prevent subtle capacity starvation failures.
