payload.page_title: Black Friday 2025 — Regional Model Failover and Emergency Model-Swap Retrospective

sections.body: This retrospective summarizes the November 27, 2025 Black Friday incident in which a cascading regional capacity degradation in us-west-2 coincided with an emergency model-swap that caused elevated tail latency and a ~41% drop in successful hosted generation requests for ~112 minutes. The actions taken kept customer-facing downtime under 1.5 hours at the global level, but exposed operational gaps in our model-swap fencing, circuit-breaker defaults, and synthetic canary sensitivity thresholds.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Affected surface: Redwood Hosted API (text generation endpoints) and a subset of Dedicated tenants using us-west-2 regional pools.
- User-visible incidents: increased 5xx rates and token timeouts for 6% of active tenants in the window; highest impact to tenants with latency SLOs <= 200ms.
- Quantitative metrics (peak):
  - 5xx rate (us-west-2 region): 3.8% (baseline 0.05%)
  - Median generation latency (global): +270ms vs baseline
  - Tail (99.9th) latency spikes in affected region: from 2.1s to 9.6s
  - Extra tokens billed (failed retries & fallbacks): ~1.9M tokens (~$650 net cost)
sections.heading: Scope and impact

sections.body:
1) 2025-11-27 14:02 — Synthetic canary for model-variant /redwood-002 failed health check in us-west-2; on-call SRE notified via pager. Canary mismatch: the canary synthetic used a short prompt set (~12 tokens) not representative of tenant median length (140 tokens).
2) 2025-11-27 14:10 — Operator triggered emergency model-swap to the CPU-quantized fallback across affected pool; rollout used the standard rollout DSL with 10% initial traffic.
3) 14:11–14:28 — Unexpected KV-cache warming pattern + aggressive autoscaler thrash led to extended request queuing; the 10% model-variant had a higher CPU path for large-sequence workloads which increased per-request service time.
4) 14:30 — Automated routing fallback attempted to route excess traffic to other regions; regional capacity was soft-capped by quota manager and rejected bursts leading to retries and tokenized backpressure.
5) 15:40 — On-call enacted manual prioritized-tenant steering and increased canary threshold; traffic normalized by 16:54 after staged rollback and progressive cache rehydration.
sections.heading: Timeline (UTC)

sections.body:
- Primary cause: Model-variant selection during emergency swap introduced a runtime path that deoptimized for long-sequence requests (KV-cache miss amplification + slower kernel path). This path was not exercised by our short synthetic canaries.
- Secondary causes:
  - Canary design mismatch: synthetic prompts not representative of production length distribution.
  - Rollout safety parameters: default 10% fanout allowed the slower path to amplify queuing when autoscaler thrash occurred. No per-variant CPU headroom check executed prior to swap.
  - Quota & burst caps in adjacent regions prevented clean cross-region shedding; fallback retries amplified load.
sections.heading: Root cause analysis (summary)

sections.body:
1) Immediate containment: temporarily freeze auto-rollout for model-variants and engage manual routing lock to limit swap fanout to 0%. Owner: Runtime Ops (Alex Huang).
2) Prioritized tenant steering: applied tenant-level sticky routing to known enterprise customers to minimize exposure. Owner: Customer Reliability (Nina Patel).
3) Rolling rollback: reverted to the previous model-variant incrementally, with additional warmup requests generated by the operator to rehydrate prefix and KV caches. Owner: Serving Runtime Team (Tobias Reed).
4) Cost containment: applied short-term token caps on automated retry logic to limit billing blowout. Owner: Billing Ops (Samir Gupta).
sections.heading: Detection and mitigation (what we did)

sections.body:
- Cache rehydration was manual and slow because our automated prefix rehydration service uses TTL windows that assume standard rollouts (not emergency swaps).
- The autoscaler thrash was caused by request latency feedback loops to the CPU scheduler; we lacked a short-circuit that recognized model-variant CPU path elevation.

Action items (owner + ETA + verification):
1) Canary redesign: expand synthetic canary corpus to include representative length and token distribution (short, median, long).
   - Owner: QA & Evals (Priya Nair)
   - ETA: 2026-02-12
   - Verification: Canary pass/fail correlated with a 14-day rolling sample of production traffic.
2) Variant preflight CPU headroom check: enforce a pre-swap probe that runs a standardized 128/512/1024 token microbenchmark against the candidate model-variant and asserts latency and CPU utilization bounds.
   - Owner: Serving Runtime (Tobias Reed)
   - ETA: 2026-03-01
   - Verification: All scheduled swaps require probe success; probes logged centrally.
3) Rollout safety tightening: change emergency-swap default fanout to 2% with dependent auto-escalation only after headroom validation.
   - Owner: Platform Orchestration (Carla Mendes)
   - ETA: 2026-01-31
   - Verification: New default applied in staging and validated during next canary.
4) Automated progressive KV-prefix rehydration: implement a background operator that issues warmup requests following a geometric distribution across shard key prefixes to restore effective cache hit ratio within 10–20 minutes.
   - Owner: Cache & Runtime (Alex Huang)
   - ETA: 2026-04-15
   - Verification: Hit ratio and tail latency return-to-baseline within target window in staging failure simulations.
5) Cross-region burst policy refinement: add a soft-burst escrow that allows temporary spillover for up to 2 minutes with cost caps and backpressure signals propagated to origin.
   - Owner: SRE Capacity (Diego Martinez)
   - ETA: 2026-02-28
   - Verification: Fault injection test with synthetic regional failure.
6) Incident automation cookbook: create an operator-runbook snippet that performs a rapid model-swap abort and a safe-rollforward path with metrics checklist and CLI commands.
   - Owner: Oncall Documentation (Maya Thompson)
   - ETA: 2026-01-31
   - Verification: Playbook exercised in next game day.
sections.heading: Why the mitigations initially underperformed

sections.body:
1) Abort rollout: redwoodctl rollout abort --variant <variant-id> --region us-west-2
2) Lock routing: redwoodctl routing lock --region us-west-2 --reason "emergency-model-path"
3) Issue progressive rehydration wave (operator): redwoodctl cache warmup --variant <variant-id> --wave 0.05 --sequences "128,512,1024"
4) Checklist before re-enable:
   - Confirm preflight probe success (3/3 sizes)
   - Verify KV hit ratio improved >= 70% vs pre-incident baseline
   - Validate region-level CPU headroom >= 18% for the variant
   - Confirm cross-region spill escrow available
sections.heading: Runbook snippet (CLI examples and safe checklist)

sections.body:
- New policy: Emergency model-swap must pass automatic preflight or be restricted to a 2% fanout and an operator-confirmed warmup plan.
- New automation: Canary corpus expansion + automatic variant preflight job + progressive KV rehydration operator + regional spill escrow.
sections.heading: Operational changes (policy and automation)

sections.body:
- Synthetic canaries must mirror production token length distributions; short prompt canaries provide false confidence for long-sequence workloads.
- Emergency rollouts are high-risk; instrument preflight checks that exercise multiple resource dimensions (CPU, memory, KV cache behavior).
- Fallback logic must consider cross-region quota and provide cost-aware short-term spill allowances to prevent retry storms.
- Invest in automated prefix rehydration to reduce manual toil and shorten recovery windows.

Appendix A — Incident timeline table (key events):
| Time (UTC) | Event | Immediate effect | Owner/action |
|------------|-------|------------------|--------------|
| 14:02 | Canary fail detected | Pager fired | QA/Evals review |
| 14:10 | Emergency model-swap initiated (10% fanout) | Small increase in median latency | Runtime Ops |
| 14:15 | Autoscaler thrash observed | Queueing and longer tails | SRE intervene |
| 15:40 | Manual tiered steering & rollback begin | Traffic stabilization begins | Serving Runtime |
| 16:54 | Service normalized | Post-incident checks start | Cross-team handoff |

Appendix B — Verification scenarios added to the resilience lab:
- Scenario 1: Emergency-swap with long-sequence workload (1–2M requests simulated) — verify progressive rehydration achieves 75% hit ratio within 20 minutes.
- Scenario 2: Cross-region spill under quota saturation — verify spill escrow allows controlled traffic absorption without retries.
- Scenario 3: Autoscaler thrash with variant CPU path elevation — verify short-circuit local-shed prevents tail amplification.
sections.heading: Lessons learned and recommendations

sections.body:
- Canary redesign: Priya Nair (QA & Evals)
- Preflight CPU probe: Tobias Reed (Serving Runtime)
- Rollout defaults: Carla Mendes (Platform Orchestration)
- KV rehydration operator: Alex Huang (Cache & Runtime)
- Cross-region escrow: Diego Martinez (SRE Capacity)
- Playbook and docs: Maya Thompson (Oncall Documentation)

Follow-up review: scheduled cross-team tabletop and game-day for 2026-02-18 to validate the automation and runbook changes.

End of retrospective. For questions or objections to action assignments, ping the owner_team channel: #platform-ops-retrospectives.

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Router policy regression triggered unintended model fallback (2025-04-19)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-04-19, a router policy change caused the system to activate *automatic model fallback* more aggressively than intended for several chat routes. While this reduced errors, it also introduced a quality regression for some customers because the fallback target had different instruction-following behavior.

h2. Impact
* Increased fallback usage on chat routes (primary -> smaller model) for ~52 minutes.
* Some customers reported degraded response quality and formatting differences.
* No prolonged outage; error rate remained below 1.0% due to fallback.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 20:05: Router policy v2025.04.19-1 deployed.
* 20:12: Metrics show a spike in fallback_activated_count on chat-default.
* 20:17: Support ticket indicates response quality changes.
* 20:26: On-call reverted router policy to previous version.
* 20:31: Fallback usage returns to baseline.
* 20:57: Follow-up: validate that quality guardrails did not alert because the canary prompts did not cover the affected format.

h2. Root cause
A boolean default in the policy compiler changed from "fail-open" to "fail-closed" for an optional constraint, causing the router to deem the primary model "ineligible" and immediately trigger fallback for certain request shapes.

h2. Mitigation
* Reverted policy deployment.
* Temporarily disabled auto-fallback for enterprise routes with strict quality requirements while we validated the policy fix.

h2. Action items
1) Add a routing policy unit test suite covering eligibility constraints and fallback triggers. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Expand eval harness prompts to include structured output format checks for top customers. Owner: Applied ML.
3) Add a canary alert when fallback usage deviates > 3x baseline for any route. Owner: Eng SRE.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0419
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: Postmortem: Hosted API latency spike due to GPU fleet saturation (2025-11-07)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
On 2025-11-07, the Hosted API experienced elevated p95 latency and intermittent 503s. The primary driver was GPU fleet saturation in us-east caused by a bursty customer workload combined with delayed scale-out of the shared A100 pool.

h2. Customer impact
* Time window: 09:12–10:26 PT
* Symptoms: long queue wait time, slow streaming starts, occasional 503 "no capacity" responses
* Affected: hosted API traffic in us-east (spillover increased load in us-west)

h2. Detection
* #incidents page triggered from alert: "gpu_pool_free_slots < 1 for 10m"
* Support received multiple reports of slow responses on /v1/chat/completions

h2. Root cause
Capacity allocator throttled scale-out due to a stale regional quota cache. Autoscaler continued to request nodes, but provisioning was rate-limited and the allocator did not reroute early enough.

h2. Contributing factors
* Regional A100 quota headroom was lower than forecasted for November peak
* Routing policy did not shift traffic until queue depth exceeded 500
* Runbook step to validate quota cache freshness was missing

h2. Resolution
* Forced refresh of quota cache and increased target capacity
* Temporarily lowered routing threshold to shift excess traffic to us-west
* Enabled burst pool for high-priority hosted tier

h2. Action items
1) Add quota-cache freshness checks to fleet runbook (Owner: Eng Infra)
2) Lower initial queue-depth threshold for cross-region spillover (Owner: Eng Platform)
3) Add dashboard panel: queue wait time vs. free slots (Owner: SRE)

h2. References
* Related Jira: INT-1842
* Related Confluence runbook: oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/gpu-capacity-triage

payload.page_title: Emergency secret rotation during an incident

sections.body: Provide a coordinated process for rotating secrets quickly during an active incident (suspected compromise or immediate containment need).
sections.heading: Goal

sections.body:
- credible evidence of secret exposure
- abnormal access patterns consistent with key misuse
- vendor reports compromised credentials
- attacker has access to systems that can read secrets

If impact is purely availability (no compromise signal), prefer standard mitigation first; emergency rotation adds risk.
sections.heading: Rotate immediately if any of the following are true

sections.body:
- Incident Commander (IC): authorizes emergency rotation and prioritizes which secrets first
- Ops/SRE: executes changes and monitors service health
- Security: advises on scope and evidence capture
- Service owners: update consumers and validate functionality
sections.heading: Roles

sections.body:
1. Declare in incident channel: 'Emergency secret rotation in progress' and list candidate secrets (names/paths only).
2. Link the break-glass event (if used) and ensure audit logging is on.
3. Identify rotation order:
   - Tier 0 first (signing keys, privileged service tokens)
   - Tier 1 next (DB creds, message bus creds, third-party keys with broad scopes)
4. For each secret:
   - confirm consumers from the Credential Dependencies inventory
   - choose rotation pattern (dual-valid if available; cutover otherwise)
   - rotate issuer-side credential
   - update Vault/secret store
   - restart/redeploy consumers as required
   - validate per-service health (auth failures, latency, error rate)
5. If failures persist beyond 10 minutes and customer impact is increasing, pause and reassess: rollback vs continue rotation.
6. Record exact timestamps for issuer-side change and consumer rollouts.
sections.heading: Procedure

sections.body:
- Do not paste secret values in Slack, tickets, or docs.
- If customer impact is expected, coordinate with Support for messaging.
sections.heading: Communications

sections.body:
- Ensure break-glass access is revoked.
- File a post-incident review item that lists rotated secrets, impacted services, and any follow-up rotations needed (derived tokens, cached credentials).
sections.heading: After-action requirements

payload.page_title: Service safeguards and dependency fallback playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines service-level safeguards and concrete dependency-fallback strategies for Redwood Inference runtime components. It codifies how the platform should behave when downstream dependencies (GPU fleet, KV caches, model stores, telemetry, or networking) degrade or fail, and prescribes deterministic fallback actions that protect user-facing SLOs, preserve cost constraints, and enable safe rollbacks.

Goals
-----
- Maintain 99th percentile end-to-end latency SLOs where possible by using tiered degradation rather than an all-or-nothing outage.
- Ensure correctness and reproducibility for degraded-mode responses (clear schema for partial results, explicit reason codes).
- Limit cost growth during incidents by bounding retry/hedge behavior and throttling expensive fallbacks.
- Make runbook actions simple and auditable for oncall and post-incident analysis.

Scope and applicability
-----------------------
Applies to the following runtime components and their immediate dependencies: inference-router, runtime-coordinator, model-worker, kv-cache, model-artifact-store, edge-proxy, and telemetry-pipeline. This playbook does NOT prescribe cluster-level recovery procedures (GPU hardware repair) but references those in eng-infra runbooks.

Key definitions
---------------
- Degraded mode: Any operational state where a dependency fails to meet its SLO for 3 consecutive minutes and the runtime initiates automatic mitigation.
- Fallback: A deterministic change in request handling that reduces resource usage or latency at the cost of fidelity. Examples: smaller model variant, quantized model, cached prefix, or truncated response.
- Safeguard: Non-fallback controls that limit blast radius (rate limits, per-tenant quotas, admission control).

SLO mapping and decision matrix (summary)
----------------------------------------
| Target SLI | Acceptable action within 30s | Allowed fallback | Cost impact | Rollback signal |
|------------|-----------------------------|------------------|-------------|----------------|
| 95p latency | Keep streaming; increase batching up to 10ms | None | low | client errors > 2x |
| 99p latency | Defer heavy synth requests to background; enable model-variant fallback | smaller-variant | medium | error-rate > 3% or hallucination metric spike |
| Availability | Serve partial/structured response with reason code | prefix-cache or local-sim | low | request failures > 1% absolute |

Playbook: pre-deployment hardening (checklist)
----------------------------------------------
1. Ensure model-variant compatibility manifest exists for each new model: supported-sequence-lengths, quantization-safe flag, graceful-shutdown-hook.
2. Validate runtime feature flags: fallback-enabled=true, hedging-window-ms=100, cache-read-through=true.
3. Run synthetic fault-injection test (see tests/fault-injection matrix) covering: cache miss storm, one-worker OOM, kv-store latency 2000ms, telemetry downstream outage.
4. Confirm alerting and dashboards include the following panels: per-route 95/99/999 latency, model-variant switch count, prefix-cache hit ratio, hedging rate, and fallback-reasons breakdown.

Runtime safeguards (automated)
-----------------------------
- Admission control: inference-router will enforce per-tenant concurrent request caps (default 100) and queue depth limits (default 500). Requests beyond caps receive HTTP 429 with retry-after and a structured body describing degraded options.
- Dynamic batching cap: runtime-coordinator increases batching window by up to 10ms under sustained throughput drops, bounded by per-route latency budget.
- Cost fence: If downstream cost estimator projects >120% budget for a tenant in a 5m window, enable tenant-specific model-variant downgrade and throttle synthesis endpoints.

Fallback strategies (ordered list)
--------------------------------
1. Local-prefetch/prefix-cache: for requests with known prompt prefixes, serve cached continuation for up to N tokens with reason_code=PREFIX_CACHE and cache_hit=true.
2. Variant-swap: switch to an explicitly registered smaller or quantized variant with same output schema. Reason_code=VARIANT_SWAP, include variant_id in response metadata.
3. Synchronous truncation + structured tail: return the first M tokens synchronously and enqueue background completion (user-optional webhook). Reason_code=TRUNCATED_WITH_BACKGROUND.
4. Safe-summarization: when both model-store and heavy compute are constrained, synthesize a concise summary via light-weight summarization model; mark as ESTIMATED_SUMMARY.
5. Fail closed: if integrity checks fail (signature mismatch, model trust failure), reject with 424 (Failed Dependency) and audit.

Example fallback policy (YAML config snippet)
--------------------------------------------
fallback_policy: |
  default:
    - condition: gpu_pool_unavailable
      action: variant_swap
      variant: small-v2-quant
      max_activation_minute: 5
    - condition: cache_miss_storm
      action: prefix_cache_fallback
      max_tokens: 64
    - condition: telemetry_outage
      action: synchronous_truncate
      truncate_to_tokens: 256
  tenant_overrides:
    enterprise-corp:
      allow_variant_swap: false
      max_concurrent_fallbacks: 10

Degradation semantics and response contract
------------------------------------------
- All degraded responses MUST include a top-level field 'redwood_degradation' with keys: reason_code, active_fallbacks (list), variant_id (if applicable), and confidence_estimate (if provided).
- Streaming responses that transition into degraded-mode must emit an explicit control frame: {"type":"degradation","reason":"VARIANT_SWAP","variant":"small-v2-quant"}.
- Clients must be able to opt-in to background completion via request metadata: {"completion_callback_url":"https://..."}.

Observability and telemetry requirements
--------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- request.count
- request.success.count
- request.error.count
- request.latency.p50/p95/p99/p999
- fallback.activation.count (tagged by type)
- cache.hit_ratio
- hedging.count and hedging.latency_delta
- model.quality_regressions (eval harness delta)
sections.heading: Essential metrics (per-route and per-tenant)

sections.body:
- P99 latency > 1.5x target for 5m -> PAGER (SRE)
- fallback.activation.rate > 5% of requests for 10m -> PAGER (oncall)
- cache.hit_ratio drop > 30% absolute for 10m -> PAGED to runtime-owner
- hedging.count spike with no latency benefit -> WARNING (investigate config)
sections.heading: Alert thresholds (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- All fallback events must emit a structured log with keys: request_id, tenant_id, fallback_type, decision_path, and trace_id.
- Set trace sampling to 100% for requests that trigger any fallback during an incident window of 30m.

Oncall runbook: immediate actions (high level)
------------------------------------------------
1. Identify scope: query fallback.activation.count by route and tenant for the last 5m.
2. If fallback is tenant-wide, run `rbac disable-tenant-hedging --tenant <id>` to disable hedging for affected tenant and observe.
3. If cache_miss_storm is detected, scale up local-prefetch proxy replicas: `kubectl scale deployment/prefix-cache --replicas=3 -n runtime`.
4. To forcibly disable variant-swap: flip runtime feature flag `fallback-enabled=false` for the staging subset of runtime-coordinator and monitor user-facing errors for 5m.
5. If cost fence triggered accidentally, revert `cost-fence-threshold` by 10% and notify billing.
6. Document all changes in incident ticket and set labels: fallback-activated, mitigation-applied, postmortem-required.

Post-incident: forensic checklist
--------------------------------
- Export traces for 30 minutes before and after peak fallback activation.
- Run the model-regression suite against the variant used in fallback (compare outputs on 100 representative prompts).
- Compute the cost delta for the incident window and attribute to tenant / route.
- Review whether fallback decision thresholds should be tightened/loosened and create a follow-up RFC if needed.

Testing matrix and automated validation
-------------------------------------
- Unit tests: ensure all fallback decision predicates (cache_miss_storm, gpu_pool_unavailable, telemetry_outage) have deterministic outputs with mocked metrics.
- Integration tests: fault-injection scenarios using chaosmonkey that validate: request contract including 'redwood_degradation' field, streaming control frames, and that hedging does not increase total cost by >10%.
- Load tests: simulate degraded cloud-network to verify admission control responds with HTTP 429 within 5s for bursty clients.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Runtime-safety guild (primary) owns the playbook and policy defaults.
- eng-sre owns alerting and oncall rotations triggered by this playbook.
- Product must sign off on any change that modifies client-visible response contracts (reason codes).

Open decisions (ADR references)
-----------------------------
- Decision: require explicit registration of replacement variants for each primary model (see ADR: variant-compatibility-contract, decision id pending).
- Decision: hedging defaults should be tenant-configurable with safe maximum windows to prevent cost spiral (see ADR under review).

Appendix: sample CLI snippets and quick references
--------------------------------------------------
- Check fallback activations by tenant: `redwoodctl metrics query "fallback.activation.count{tenant=\"enterprise-corp\"}" --range 5m`
- Toggle fallback for a single runtime shard: `redwoodctl runtime flag set --shard=us-west-2a fallback-enabled=false`
- Force variant swap on a test route: `redwoodctl route override set --route my-synth-route --variant small-v2-quant --until 2027-03-25T00:00:00Z`

Related links and references
----------------------------
- runtime-cache-invalidation-and-staleness-mitigation-playbook (model-serving-standards)
- adr-graceful-degradation-and-cost-surge-protection (decision-records)
- slo-driven-runtime-contracts-and-rollback-playbook (eng-serving-runtime)
Document history
----------------
- 2027-01-12 Created by Maya Chen
- 2027-02-02 Added tenant override examples and cost-fence semantics (reviewers: Diego Ramos)
- 2027-03-18 Expanded observability requirements and updated alert thresholds (reviewers: Priya Nair, Evan Park)
sections.heading: Tracing and logs

payload.page_title: Quickstart Templates: Release Process (Versioning, Changelog, Deprecations)

sections.body:
This page defines how Redwood Inference ships and maintains Quickstart Templates (RAG + Agents, etc.) across languages, including:
- Versioning policy (templates + scaffolding CLI)
- Changelog expectations
- Deprecation strategy
- Step-by-step instructions for cutting a release
- How docs link to “latest” vs “pinned” template versions
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Safe by default (security + privacy)
- Stable for production use (repeatable scaffolds, predictable upgrades)
- Easy to maintain (CI gates, reproducible builds)
sections.heading: The goal is to keep templates

sections.body:
**In scope:**
- Template repositories under the Redwood org (e.g., `redwood-quickstarts`)
- The scaffolding CLI used to initialize templates (e.g., `redwood-templates`)
- Docs-site integration (how we link templates and recommend versions)

**Out of scope:**
- SDK release processes (tracked in SDK repos)
- Observability Pack release process (separate repo cadence)
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- **Release owner:** Connor O'Brien (Release/versioning)
- **DevEx engineering lead:** Monica Patel (release readiness, cross-repo alignment)
- **Docs owner:** Elliot Price (docs linking, launch notes, changelog surfacing)
- **CI owner:** Sahana Iyer (release gates, smoke tests, vulnerability scanning)
- **Security reviewer:** Marcus Lin (secure defaults, supply chain policy compliance)
- **Observability reviewer:** Allison Grant (OTel conventions + cardinality review)
sections.heading: Ownership and roles

sections.body:
1) **Git tags + GitHub Releases** in the template repo.
2) **CLI-distributed scaffolds** that stamp an app with a template version.
3) **Docs pages** that reference a specific template version (pinned) or the current recommended version (latest).
sections.heading: Templates are shipped as

sections.body:
Every generated project must contain a machine-readable version stamp so Support and DevEx can quickly identify what a user is running.

**Required file:** `.redwood/template-version`
- Value: the template tag (e.g., `quickstarts/v1.4.2`) or a semver string (e.g., `1.4.2`) depending on the template family.
- Also include build metadata in logs (see Observability Standard) but do not include secrets.
sections.heading: Required version stamp in generated projects

sections.body:
We use **SemVer (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH)** for:
- Template families (e.g., `rag-agent-python`, `rag-agent-typescript`)
- The scaffolding CLI
sections.heading: Versioning policy

sections.body:
**MAJOR (X.0.0)**
- Breaking config changes (required env vars renamed/removed)
- Changes that break runtime behavior or API compatibility (e.g., tool schema format changes)
- Removal of an adapter/vector store option
- Breaking observability schema changes (span/metric renames) that would break dashboards/alerts

**MINOR (0.Y.0)**
- Add new optional features (new tool, optional adapter, new deployment recipe)
- New metrics/spans/attributes that do not break existing dashboards
- New docs and troubleshooting guidance paired with small code improvements

**PATCH (0.0.Z)**
- Bug fixes (streaming stability, retry correctness)
- Security fixes (dependency patch bumps, log redaction fixes)
- Documentation corrections
sections.heading: What constitutes a MAJOR vs MINOR vs PATCH

sections.body:
We tag releases at the repo level, and the release notes must enumerate which template families changed.

**Tag format (repo-level):** `quickstarts/vX.Y.Z`
- Example: `quickstarts/v1.3.0`

**Within the release notes**, call out which templates changed:
- `rag-agent-python`
- `rag-agent-typescript`
- (future) `rag-api-only-python`, etc.
sections.heading: Template families and tags

sections.body:
The CLI is versioned independently, but it must remain compatible with:
- The most recent MINOR of the latest MAJOR template series
- At least the previous MINOR (N-1) for upgrade safety

**Compatibility rule:** A CLI release may not require a template MAJOR bump unless explicitly planned and approved by DevEx lead + Docs lead.
sections.heading: CLI versioning

sections.body:
1) A **GitHub Release** with human-readable notes.
2) A **CHANGELOG.md** update in the repo.
3) A **docs note** (if the release changes user-facing behavior or upgrade guidance).
sections.heading: Every release must have

sections.body:
Add entries under a section for the new version.

**Template:**
- Summary (2–4 bullets)
- Added
- Changed
- Fixed
- Security
- Deprecations
- Upgrade notes (required when breaking or behavior-changing)
sections.heading: CHANGELOG format

sections.body:
- Template families impacted
- Any breaking changes and exact migration steps
- Any new/changed env vars (with defaults)
- Any observability schema changes (new metrics/spans; confirm no renames unless major)
- Any dependency upgrades with security implications (CVEs fixed)
sections.heading: Include

sections.body:
If the change affects a running deployment, include an explicit section:
- “Who is affected?”
- “What will break?”
- “What to change” (copy/paste-ready)
- “How to validate” (commands + expected output)
sections.heading: “Upgrade notes” bar for user-impacting changes

sections.body: We deprecate features/configs intentionally, with predictable timelines.
sections.heading: Deprecation strategy

sections.body:
- **MINOR release**: may introduce deprecations (warnings), must not remove behavior.
- **Next MAJOR**: may remove deprecated behavior.
sections.heading: Deprecation policy

sections.body:
- Default window: **90 days** from first deprecation notice to removal eligibility.
- For enterprise-facing items (common deployment recipes, major retriever adapter): **180 days**, unless a security incident requires faster action.
sections.heading: Deprecation windows

sections.body:
- CHANGELOG + GitHub Release
- A runtime warning (where applicable) that is:
  - visible in logs
  - non-spammy (rate-limited)
  - includes a link to migration docs
sections.heading: Deprecations must be communicated via

sections.body:
- Deprecated item name
- Removal target version
- Migration link
sections.heading: Message must include

sections.body: `DEPRECATION: VECTOR_STORE=faiss-legacy will be removed in v2.0.0. Migrate to VECTOR_STORE=local. Docs: https://docs.redwoodinference.com/quickstarts/templates/rag-agent#vector-store`
sections.heading: Example

sections.body:
- Target cadence: **biweekly** patch/minor releases while templates are in active launch iteration.
- Major releases: **as-needed**, explicitly planned (requires PM + Security + Docs alignment).
sections.heading: Release cadence

sections.body:
- security fixes
- broken onboarding paths
- severe reliability regressions (streaming disconnects, retry storms)
sections.heading: We may cut out-of-band PATCH releases for

sections.body:
A release cannot be cut unless the following are green on the release candidate commit:

1) **Unit + integration tests** (language-specific)
2) **Streaming stability smoke tests**
3) **Tool-calling schema validation tests**
4) **Eval harness hooks**: golden prompt set runs (baseline regression check)
5) **Security checks**:
   - dependency pinning is intact
   - vulnerability scan passes or has explicitly approved exceptions
   - secrets scanning passes
6) **Observability checks**:
   - spans/metrics emitted match the Observability Standard
   - no high-cardinality attributes added (or explicitly approved)
7) **Docs check** (if required): docs PR ready/merged per below
sections.heading: Release gates (must-pass checks)

sections.body:
- Patch: bug/security fix only
- Minor: new optional capabilities, new adapters/recipes, non-breaking improvements
- Major: breaking changes; requires explicit sign-off (DevEx lead + Docs lead + Security)
sections.heading: 0) Decide release type and scope

sections.body:
- Branch name: `release/quickstarts-vX.Y.Z`
- Branch from `main`.
sections.heading: 1) Create a release branch

sections.body:
- Update `CHANGELOG.md`
- Ensure generated project stamp logic writes `.redwood/template-version`
- If CLI is involved, ensure CLI metadata references the target template tag (or compatibility logic is updated)
sections.heading: 2) Update versions and stamps

sections.body:
- Run template generation once per language and confirm:
  - `init` succeeds
  - `doctor` passes with a local OTel collector
  - a basic run produces traces/metrics/logs
sections.heading: At minimum (release owner responsibility)

sections.body:
- Security: Marcus Lin must approve if dependencies changed, logging changed, or secrets-handling changed.
- Observability: Allison Grant must approve if metrics/spans changed.
sections.heading: 4) Security and observability review checkpoints

sections.body:
- Any env var schema changes
- Any troubleshooting changes needed
- Any user-facing behavior change
- Any deprecation introduced
sections.heading: Docs are required if

sections.body:
- reference the template tag
- include “Pinned version” links (see below)
- update troubleshooting entries if needed
sections.heading: Docs PR should

sections.body:
- Create tag: `quickstarts/vX.Y.Z`
- Push tag to origin
sections.heading: On the release branch tip commit

sections.body:
- `git tag quickstarts/v1.4.2`
- `git push origin quickstarts/v1.4.2`
sections.heading: Example

sections.body:
- Summary + Added/Changed/Fixed/Security/Deprecations
- Upgrade notes (if applicable)
- Link to docs
- Known issues (if any) and workarounds
sections.heading: The GitHub Release must include

sections.body:
- cut CLI release after the template tag is live
- verify CLI can target:
  - `--template-version quickstarts/vX.Y.Z`
  - default “recommended” version points to a stable pinned tag (not an untagged commit)
sections.heading: If the CLI needs an update

sections.body:
- Post in internal #announcements and #devex with:
  - version
  - highlights
  - any known issues
  - support notes
- Monitor:
  - template-tagged traffic (Console filter)
  - error rate changes (network/auth/quota/tool)
  - streaming disconnect patterns
sections.heading: 9) Announce and monitor

sections.body: Use a hotfix when an already-released tag is causing widespread breakage.
sections.heading: Hotfix process

sections.body:
- Do not rewrite existing tags.
- Cut a new PATCH release (e.g., `v1.4.2` → `v1.4.3`).
sections.heading: Policy

sections.body:
- Branch from the tag: `hotfix/quickstarts-vX.Y.(Z+1)`
- Minimal changes only
- Repeat release gates
- Publish new tag + Release notes clearly labeled “Hotfix”
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- **Latest recommended**: most users should follow this.
- **Pinned version**: platform teams and regulated customers need repeatability.
sections.heading: Docs must support two user modes

sections.body:
- **Latest recommended:** A docs page that points to the current recommended stable tag (updated as we release).
- **Pinned:** A versioned docs reference that points to a specific template tag.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) Docs must always show the recommended pinned tag near the top of the page.
2) The default docs flow should not require users to choose a version, but must expose an explicit pin option.
3) “Copy/paste” commands must include pinned versions when feasible.
sections.heading: Linking rules

sections.body:
- Recommended: `quickstarts/v1.4.2`
- Pinned init command: `redwood-templates init rag-agent-python --template-version quickstarts/v1.4.2`
- Latest init command: `redwood-templates init rag-agent-python` (with a note that it will resolve to the current recommended stable version)
sections.heading: Include a short block like

sections.body:
- Security/compliance guidance: always reference a pinned version (so instructions match behavior).
- Troubleshooting pages: can reference latest but must mention that symptoms may vary by version and how to check `.redwood/template-version`.
sections.heading: When docs must be pinned vs latest

sections.body:
- The latest release (N)
- The previous MINOR (N-1) within the same MAJOR

Example: if latest is `1.4.2`, we support `1.4.x` and `1.3.x`.
sections.heading: Support and DevEx will treat the following as supported

sections.body:
- announce in release notes
- add a docs note on the template page
- ensure the CLI defaults no longer resolve to an unsupported series
sections.heading: If we drop support for a MINOR train

sections.body:
- [ ] CHANGELOG updated
- [ ] Version stamp `.redwood/template-version` verified
- [ ] CI gates green
- [ ] Security scan passed / exceptions documented
- [ ] Observability review complete
- [ ] Docs PR merged (if required)
- [ ] Release notes drafted
sections.heading: Before tagging

sections.body:
- [ ] GitHub Release published
- [ ] CLI compatibility verified
- [ ] Announcement posted
- [ ] Post-release monitoring started (first 24 hours)
sections.heading: After tagging

sections.body:
- Cutting a release before docs land (leads to drift and support load)
- Adding new metric dimensions that explode cardinality (breaks dashboards and increases cost)
- Shipping “helpful” logs that accidentally include prompts/PII (violates safe defaults)
- Failing to stamp the template version in generated apps (blocks debugging)
sections.heading: Appendix: Common pitfalls

sections.body:
- 2025-03-18: Clarified docs “latest vs pinned” rules; added supported versions policy.
- 2025-02-21: Added release gates for streaming/tool-calling smoke tests and security scanning.
- 2025-01-29: Initial publication.

payload.page_title: Sev-1 Communication Requirements (Status Page + Customer Notifications)

sections.body:
h2. Goal
Ensure consistent, timely communication during Sev-1 incidents across Hosted and Dedicated customers. This page defines *what must be communicated*, *who does it*, and *when*.

h2. Scope
Applies when incident severity is Sev-1 (customer-visible outage or severe degradation) or when IC declares 'comms mode'.

h2. Roles and responsibilities
* Incident Commander (IC): owns message accuracy and cadence; delegates drafting if needed.
* Customer Success Escalation Manager (CSEM): owns direct enterprise outreach and coordination for Dedicated customers.
* Support On-call: monitors inbound tickets, ensures macros match the current incident status.
* SRE On-call: provides technical status, mitigation progress, and ETA confidence level.

h2. Required channels
* Status page: public (when impact is broad or uncertain).
* Email: targeted to affected enterprise contacts when impact is Dedicated-only or customer-specific.
* Slack internal: #incidents plus the incident channel created by incident-bot.

h2. Cadence
* Initial acknowledgement: within 10 minutes of Sev-1 declaration.
* Updates: every 30 minutes while customer impact is ongoing.
* Resolution message: within 15 minutes of mitigation being confirmed.
* Post-incident summary: within 1 business day (public-facing is optional; customer-facing for enterprise is required).

h2. Content requirements (status page + email)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* What customers are seeing (symptoms)
* Affected surfaces (Hosted API regions, Dedicated clusters, specific model families)
* Current mitigation steps
* ETA statement with confidence level (high/medium/low)
* Workarounds (if any)
sections.heading: Each update must include

sections.body:
* Overly specific internal details (hostnames, precise exploit details)
* Blaming language

h2. Dedicated-specific communication
sections.heading: Avoid

sections.body:
* CSEM must notify impacted customers directly (email + optional call).
* Include: whether a maintenance action is required (e.g., rolling runtime restart), expected duration, and whether customer traffic will fail over.
* If a hotfix rollout is planned, provide the rollout window and the rollback criteria in customer-friendly terms.

h2. Templates (copy/paste)
*Initial status page message*

We are investigating reports of elevated errors and latency affecting Redwood Inference. We will provide updates every 30 minutes until resolved.

*Update message*

We have identified the issue and are applying mitigation steps. Some requests may continue to see errors or increased latency. Next update in 30 minutes.

*Resolution message*

The issue has been mitigated and service is returning to normal. We are continuing to monitor closely.

* /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* /status-page-and-comms/status-page-update-runbook

payload.page_title: Onramp friction & usage-credit experiments roadmap

sections.body: This roadmap describes a structured program of product experiments aimed at reducing developer onramp friction and improving trial-to-paid conversion through targeted usage-credit policies and UI/UX changes. The scope covers self-serve signups, initial API usage flows (first 3 days), and the credit redemption experience in Console and SDKs. The goal is to increase meaningful activation (defined below) while minimizing wasted credits and preserving unit economics for hosted inference.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- New developer accounts often churn before generating production traffic because early evaluation is hampered by: unclear cost expectations, slow feedback loops, and lack of guided sample workloads.
- Broad unconditional credit grants improve vanity metrics (accounts created, tokens consumed) but do not reliably increase 30/90-day retained paid usage and can be exploited by synthetic traffic.
- We need a set of constrained, measurable experiments that balance low-friction evaluation with incentives to convert.
sections.heading: Problem statement

sections.body:
1. Increase 30-day active paid accounts by 18% for cohorts entering via product-led channels.
2. Improve ‘meaningful activation’ rate within 7 days from 12% -> 22%. Meaningful activation = at least one routed production-like request (>= 128 tokens input and model selection not dev-only) and one supervised eval run (developer-run prompt set).
3. Maintain or improve hosted per-token revenue by avoiding credit abuse (target <5% anomalous credit usage across cohorts).
sections.heading: Objectives (north star metrics)

sections.body:
- In scope: hosted API crediting flows, Console onboarding UX, quickstart templates, SDK sample apps, telemetry instrumentation, guardrail rules for credit redemption.
- Out of scope: Dedicated capacity commercial contracts, Private on-prem onboarding flows, enterprise sales-assisted migration paths (these will be referenced but not changed).
sections.heading: Scope & constraints

sections.body:
1) Guided credits (tiered, conditional)
   - Hypothesis: Small, targeted credits tied to completing a guided quickstart will increase meaningful activation without increasing abuse compared to blanket credits.
   - Treatment: 500 token credit + a required quickstart completion event (eg. run create-chat with supplied prompt) valid for 14 days.
   - Success metric: +6pp activation lift; <3% fraud signal.

2) Time-decayed trial buckets
   - Hypothesis: Front-loading tokens with an explicit decay curve nudges developers to evaluate quickly and reduces long-tail idle consumption.
   - Treatment: 1,500 tokens delivered as 900 immediate + 600 unlocked after completing an eval within 3 days.
   - Success metric: increased 7-day conversion, reduced idle-credit carryover by 40%.

3) Workload-aligned sample bundles
   - Hypothesis: Bundles that mirror common workloads (chat, summarization, embeddings) will produce higher meaningful evals than unrestricted credit.
   - Treatment: Offer three labelled bundles (Chat: 2k, Embed: 1k, Rerank: 800) with quickstart templates and sample prompt-sets.
   - Success metric: higher per-bundle activation and longer session lengths.

4) Microbilling preview and cost-guardrails in Console
   - Hypothesis: Transparent cost previews reduce surprise and increase retention.
   - Treatment: Inline estimator showing projected cost for a sample prompt + toggle to simulate quantization/warm-cache savings.
   - Success metric: decreased support tickets about billing and higher preference for paid upgrade.
sections.heading: Experiment themes and hypothesis matrix

sections.body:
- Required signals (priority order):
  1. Account_id, cohort, credit_type, grant_timestamp, redemption_timestamp
  2. First meaningful activation event (event_type, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out)
  3. Quickstart completion flags and sample prompt-set run ids
  4. Cost estimator interactions (toggle events) and upgrade clicks
  5. Fraud signals (high throughput from single IP, repeated credit re-creation, synthetic traffic heuristics)

- Dashboards: Product will own an experiment dashboard showing cohort performance, time-to-activate distribution, redemption decay curves, and cost delta vs control. SRE/Finance will have a subset view for abuse and cost anomalies.
sections.heading: Telemetry & measurement plan

sections.body:
Phase 0 — Prep (4 weeks):
1. Finalize experiment designs and commit to metric definitions.
2. Instrument Console events, SDK quickstart hooks, and server-side credit redemption logs.
3. Define fraud detection rules and cost-exposure caps per cohort.
Ownership: Product + Eng-DevEx + Telemetry.

Phase 1 — Guided credits A/B (6 weeks):
1. Launch A/B test with 25% treatment, 75% control for new signups via the webflow.
2. Monitor activation, fraud signals, and early feedback.
3. Stop / iterate after 6 weeks based on success criteria.
Ownership: Product (lead), Growth, Eng-DevEx.

Phase 2 — Bundles & time-decay experiments (8 weeks):
1. Sequential launch of workload bundles and time-decay experiment (split traffic).
2. Coordinate with docs to publish bundle quickstarts and sample prompt sets.
3. Tighten guardrails if abuse rate > 5% in any cohort.
Ownership: Product, DX, Security.

Phase 3 — Console estimator and commercialization pilot (ongoing):
1. Pilot cost-estimator in Console for treatment cohort.
2. Couple conversion nudges (upgrade CTA with one-click billing).
3. Prepare for commercial packaging changes if conversion and unit economics are favourable.
Ownership: Product, UX, Finance.
sections.heading: Rollout plan and timeline (quarterly roadmap)

sections.body:
- Per-cohort caps: Max 10k tokens exposure per account from experimental credits until fraud checks pass.
- Abuse response: Automatic freeze + manual review for accounts flagged by fraud heuristics.
- Observability: Real-time alert when credit redemption spike exceeds 3x baseline or when cost deviation > 30% projected.
sections.heading: Safety & guardrails

sections.body:
- If experiments succeed (target uplift and acceptable unit economics), recommend the following commercialization path:
  1. Convert guided credit into a permanent onboarding bundle (low-dollar, high-guidance) and expose as the default new account experience.
  2. Offer workload bundles as an upsell during sign-up with clear usage-to-cost mapping; bill leftover credits at standard hosted rates.
  3. For enterprise leads, map onboarding credit usage to sales-assigned demo credits (separate ledger) to avoid double-counting.

- Pricing risk mitigations: Run an offline cost-sensitivity simulator (Finance + Eng-Platform) on sampled cohorts before a full commercial rollout. Define a minimum acceptable gross margin contribution per converted account.
sections.heading: Commercial implications and pricing notes

sections.body:
- Gate 1 (go/no-go): After Phase 1, if meaningful activation lift < 3pp or fraud > 5% -> stop and iterate.
- Gate 2 (scale): After Phase 2, if 30-day paid conversion lifts by at least 10% and unit economics (LTV/CAC proxy) within acceptable band -> scale to 50% of self-serve traffic.
- Gate 3 (commercialize): After pilot of Console estimator and upgrade flow, if conversion and margin targets met -> productize bundles and update pricing docs and onboarding flows.
sections.heading: Success criteria and decision gates

sections.body:
1. Monitoring: Daily check on cohort dashboards for first 2 weeks of each launch. Pager if fraud/anomaly thresholds breached.
2. Support flow: Dedicated triage tag for onboarding-credit complaints; escalate to Product on pattern detection.
3. Rollback: Disable new cohort grants immediately and revoke unredeemed credits via ledger batch if abuse seen > 10% of treated cohort.
sections.heading: Operational runbook highlights (brief)

sections.body:
- Do we need new legal wording for trial credit expiry and conversion handling? (Legal + Finance decision)
- Telemetry dependency: require additional token-level attributes to be added to the event schema (ETA: 2 weeks).
- Cross-functional resourcing: need 0.5 FTE from Security for fraud rules during the pilot and 0.8 FTE from Telemetry for dashboarding.

Appendix — Experiment matrix (snapshot):

| Experiment | Treatment size | Duration | Primary metric | Owner |
|------------|----------------|----------|----------------|-------|
| Guided credits | 25% of new signups | 6 weeks | 7-day meaningful activation | Product |
| Time-decay trial | 20% of new signups | 8 weeks | 7-day conversion | Growth |
| Workload bundles | 20% split across bundles | 8 weeks | Bundle-specific activation | DX/Product |
| Cost-estimator UI | 10% of Console users | pilot 6 weeks | Upgrade CTR & support tickets | UX/Product |
sections.heading: Open questions & dependencies

sections.body:
- Quickstart templates and prompt-sets: /repos/onboarding/quickstarts (internal repo)
- Experiment tracking tickets: EXP-1201, EXP-1204, EXP-1210 (Jira)
- Fraud heuristics runbook: sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/fraud-detection-crediting-guidelines.json

payload.page_title: Multi‑Currency Procurement and Revenue Recognition Guidance for Contract Triggers

sections.body:
Summary:

This guidance establishes standard handling for procurement and B2B contract scenarios where (a) customer pricing, billing or acceptance is denominated in a foreign currency, and (b) contract terms create non-standard revenue recognition triggers (e.g., milestone-based billing, usage thresholds invoiced retrospectively, or capacity commitments with true-ups). The goal is to reduce month-end reconciliation risk, ensure consistent accounting treatment, and provide procurement and legal teams with boilerplate clauses and an approval checklist.

Scope:
- Applies to all commercial contracts that include: multi-currency settlements, milestone/thresholded billing, capacity commits with true-ups, or deferred invoicing longer than 30 days.
- Does NOT replace detailed ASC 606 or IFRS 15 assessments for complex, bespoke contracts; it provides operational standards and routing for accounting review.

Key definitions:
- Transaction Currency: currency in which the contract states prices and invoices are issued.
- Functional Currency: Redwood's reporting currency (USD).
- FX Revaluation Date: the date we remeasure contract assets/liabilities per accounting policy (monthly close).
- Recognition Trigger: a contractual event that creates the right to consideration or the satisfied performance obligation (e.g., delivery, acceptance, usage threshold reached).

Policy overview:
1) Price and Invoice Currency:
- Wherever possible, contracts should price and invoice in USD. If customer insists on local currency, Legal must include an explicit FX clause (see Clauses to Include section).
- Procurement must capture the Transaction Currency in the procurement system (Coupa/NetSuite field: transaction_currency).

2) Contract-level Accounting Assessment:
- All multi-currency or milestone contracts are routed to Accounting (revrec@redwood.com) during contracting. Accounting will confirm: allocation of transaction price, identification of performance obligations, and expected timing of recognition.

3) FX treatment and monthly close:
- Monetary items (receivables/payables) are remeasured at the FX spot rate on the balance sheet date.
- Non-monetary contract balances (unearned revenue measured on a unit-of-account basis) are translated at the rate at inception unless the contract requires later adjustment.

Procedures (contract drafting and pre-execution):
1) Procurement checklist before signature (must be attached to Procurement ticket):
   1.1 Confirm Transaction Currency field populated and indicate if hedging is requested.
   1.2 Confirm billing cadence (monthly/quarterly/milestone/usage-based) and define how usage is measured.
   1.3 If milestones or acceptance events are present, add clear, objective acceptance criteria and date-based fallback.
   1.4 For multi-currency deals, include FX clause template (below) and indicate whether customer or Redwood bears FX variance.
   1.5 Attach expected schedule of recognition and draft journal entry examples for Accounting review.
   1.6 Obtain Sign‑off: Legal, Sales Finance, and Accounting (email or e-signature).

2) Live contract amendments and true-ups:
- If a customer executes a true-up (e.g., exceeded committed tokens/GPU hours), the invoice currency and recognition follow the original contract unless an amendment states otherwise. Record true-up as additional consideration; allocate to existing performance obligations per ASC 606 rules.

Accounting treatment — common scenarios and sample entries (USD functional currency):

Scenario A: Customer billed in EUR for monthly subscription, billed in arrears on the 5th of each month.
- Recognition: revenue recognized ratably over the month as performance obligation is satisfied.
- Close treatment (example for a January invoice of EUR 50,000, FX spot on Jan 31 = 1.10 USD/EUR):
  - When invoice issued on Feb 05 (EUR 50,000): 
    - Accounts Receivable (EUR 50,000) recorded at the invoice date spot if using transactional approach.
    - For month-end Jan 31, if services performed in January but invoice not yet issued, record contract asset (unbilled receivable) in USD using average or spot guidance per accounting policy.
  - Sample closing journal (simplified):
    - Jan 31 (to accrue earned revenue): Dr Contract Asset (USD) 55,000; Cr Revenue 55,000.
    - Feb 05 (when invoice issued): Dr Accounts Receivable (EUR 50,000) / Cr Contract Asset (USD 55,000) and recognize FX difference in Other Income/FX Loss.

Scenario B: Milestone payment in JPY with acceptance clause and 30-day invoice terms.
- Ensure acceptance criteria include a fallback acceptance-by-date clause to avoid recognition delay.
- Sample clause (legal template below).

Journal entry examples (illustrative):
- When milestone achieved but invoice in foreign currency and not yet billed (accrual):
  - Dr Contract Asset (USD) X; Cr Revenue (USD) X
- When invoice issued in foreign currency and recorded:
  - Dr Accounts Receivable (JPY Y); Cr Contract Asset (USD X)
  - On settlement: Dr Cash (USD) Z; Cr Accounts Receivable (JPY Y) and record FX remeasurement to clear AR.

Contract clauses to include (templates):
1) FX clause — two options (select one):
- Option A (customer bears FX risk): "All prices and invoices denominated in [Transaction Currency]. Customer is responsible for any FX differences arising between invoice date and payment date; Redwood will invoice in [Transaction Currency]."
- Option B (Redwood bears FX risk): "All prices are set in USD and amounts billed in [Local Currency] are for convenience only. Payments received in Local Currency will be converted to USD at Redwood's spot rate on the date of receipt for accounting purposes."

2) Acceptance fallback clause (to avoid open-ended recognition delays):
"If the Customer does not provide written acceptance or documented rejection within 15 business days following delivery, the deliverable shall be deemed accepted on the 16th business day and any related milestone shall be deemed satisfied for invoicing and revenue recognition purposes."

3) Billing & True-up clause:
"Usage true-ups will be invoiced monthly in arrears. The Parties agree that invoices are due within 30 days. Any disputes to amounts must be raised within 30 days of invoice receipt; undisputed amounts remain due and payable."

Approval matrix (thresholds are USD equivalent):
| Contract Value | Required Approvals | Additional Steps |
|---------------:|-------------------|------------------|
| < 50,000       | Procurement Owner; Line Manager | Standard procurement review |
| 50,000 - 500,000 | Procurement Owner; Sales Finance; Legal | Accounting pre-signoff required |
| > 500,000      | Head of Finance; Legal; CRO | RevRec detailed assessment; Board notification for multi-year >2yr |

Escalation flow for close exceptions (month-end differences >USD 10k):
1) Finance Ops raises an exception ticket and routes to Sales Finance and Procurement.
2) If unresolved in 48 hours, alert Head of Revenue Operations and schedule an ad-hoc reconciliation call.
3) If legal interpretation needed (e.g., disputed acceptance), tag Legal and schedule decision within 5 business days.

Operational considerations and system fields (minimum required):
- Procurement system: transaction_currency, fx_hedge_requested (Y/N), billing_cadence, revenue_account_code, revrec_trigger (deliverable/milestone/usage), base_price_local and base_price_usd_estimate.
- Accounting system (NetSuite): contract_reference, deferred_revenue_schedule_id, realized_fx_gain_loss_account.

Reporting and dashboards:
- Monthly: a multi-currency close dashboard showing open AR by currency, unbilled contract assets, FX unrealized gain/loss, and invoices >60 days overdue. Owner: Finance Ops.
- Quarterly: summary of revenue recognized in non-USD currencies and P&L FX impact. Owner: FP&A.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ):
Q: Who chooses whether to hedge currency exposure?
A: Treasury/FP&A evaluates hedging for exposures >USD 250k expected over the next 90 days. Procurement indicates hedge request on the procurement ticket.

Q: If a contract is amended to change currency mid-term, what happens?
A: Amendments that change Transaction Currency require Accounting reassessment. Prior balances remain in original currency; future invoicing follows the amended currency.

Appendix — FX example table (simplified):
| Date | EUR Amount | USD Spot | USD Translated | Notes |
|------|-----------:|--------:|---------------:|-------|
| 2027-01-31 | 50,000 | 1.10 | 55,000 | Accrual for Jan services
| 2027-02-05 | 50,000 | 1.08 | 54,000 | Invoice date translation (AR)

Owner and contact points:
- Document owner: Finance Ops (Elena Martinez) — elena.martinez@redwood.com
- Accounting revrec mailbox: revrec@redwood.com
- Procurement triage: procurement@redwood.com

Change log:
- 2026-09-15: Created initial guidance and templates.
- 2027-02-10: Updated approval thresholds, added FX example and acceptance fallback language.

Notes and references:
- This operational guidance is intended to be used alongside Redwood's formal accounting policies (ASC 606/IFRS 15). For complex contracts (multi-element arrangements, significant financing components, or bespoke acceptance processes) Accounting must produce a formal memo prior to signature.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Hybrid Capacity Accounting and Billing — Ops Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook defines the end-to-end operational rules, accounting treatments, billing flows, and procurement handoffs for hybrid capacity agreements at Redwood Inference. 'Hybrid capacity' refers to any customer arrangement that mixes reserved (dedicated) capacity, committed spend, and on-demand hosted usage under a single commercial contract. The goal is consistent revenue recognition, timely invoicing, clear procurement linkage, and predictable customer experience across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to multi-product customer commitments that combine Dedicated pools, hosted API call volumes, and optional burst credits.
- Covers contracts signed from 2028-11-01 onward (legacy agreements are handled under migration procedure, see section "Migration & Reconciliation").
- Intended audience: Finance (RevRec), Billing Ops, Procurement, Legal, Sales Ops, and Customer Success.

Principles:
1. Economic substance over form: revenue recognition follows delivered capacity and consumption, not just invoice timing.
2. Single source of truth: UsageCollector -> UsageWarehouse -> RevenueEngine is canonical pipeline for meter data.
3. Separation of concerns: Procurement owns POs and vendor-like commitments; Finance owns GL mapping and rev rec.
4. Timely customer transparency: Draft invoices available within 48 hours of monthly cutoff; disputes acknowledged within 5 business days.

Key terms and definitions:
- Committed Credit: dollar commitment purchased for a period (monthly/annual) redeemable against usage or Dedicated reservation.
- Reserved (Dedicated) Unit: GPU capacity reserved and billed per the capacity contract; invoiced monthly or upfront depending on contract.
- Burst Credit: short-lived, non-recurring credits for on-demand spikes; expiration rules in section "Credit Lifecycle".

Roles & ownership:
- BillingService: Invoice generation, dunning, payments. Owner: Finance-Billing.
- UsageCollector: Collects per-request telemetry across Hosted and Dedicated routers. Owner: Eng-Platform.
- CommitmentOrchestrator: Matches customer POs to contract terms and issues commitment IDs. Owner: Sales-ops.
- RevenueEngine: Applies rev-rec rules and emits journal entries to LedgerAPI. Owner: Finance-RevRec.
- Customer Success: manages communication for monthly true-ups and usage anomalies.

Accounting & Revenue Recognition Rules (summary table):

| Scenario | Recognition trigger | Timing | GL account | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Upfront prepay for Dedicated (term) | Service delivery over time measured as capacity availability | Straight-line over term or practical performance measure if usage materially differs | Deferred revenue -> Revenue | If customer can use across months, straight-line unless usage-based consumption meets criteria for variable consideration.
| Monthly committed credit (redeemable) | When customer redeems credit (consumption) | At point of consumption | Revenue | Unredeemed credits recognized as deferred revenue and recognized on expiration per contract.
| On-demand hosted usage | Metered at request level | At point of usage (month-end) | Revenue | UsageCollector must reconcile to invoice within 48h of cutoff.
| Cross-product conversion (credit applied to Dedicated) | When system applies credit to invoice | When credit applied against invoice | Revenue/Contra-revenue mapping | Maintain audit trail: CommitmentID + ApplicationEventID.

Billing flow and timing:
1. Daily aggregation: UsageCollector batches per-customer telemetry into UsageWarehouse every 6 hours.
2. Invoice draft window: Monthly cutoff is the 1st of the month 00:00 UTC for prior-month usage; draft invoices produced within 48 hours by BillingService.
3. Approval & finalization: Finance-Billing has 3 business days to approve automated drafts. If manual review required, add 5 business days SLA.
4. Distribution: Final invoices published to Customer Portal (S3 link) and emailed. Payment terms default 30 days net unless contract specifies otherwise.

Procurement handoff & PO mapping:
- All POs must include: Customer legal name, Redwood customer ID, CommitmentID (if exists), PO amount, currency, billing cadence, and any invoice delivery exceptions.
- CommitmentOrchestrator creates a CommitmentID that links the signed contract to all billing events.
- If procurement issues a single PO that covers both Dedicated hardware reservations and variable usage, Sales-Ops must create line-item mapping so statements in BillingService show dedicated vs usage amounts.

Credit lifecycle and expiration rules:
- Standard committed credits expire 12 months from purchase unless otherwise specified in contract.
- Burst credits expire 30 days from issuance.
- Expired credits are moved from deferred liability to breakage revenue per ASC guidance after legal review.

True-up and credit allocation procedure (operational steps):
1. Trigger: At month end, UsageWarehouse emits a Redline Report where actual usage differs from committed levels by >10%.
2. CS notifies customer and opens a True-up ticket in Jira (project: FIN-BILL).
3. Billing Ops runs CommitmentOrchestrator transform to allocate committed credits against usage events.
4. If consumption > commitment: charge usage at overage rates; produce a supplemental invoice for the overage with 15-day payment term.
5. If consumption < commitment: calculate unused committed credit; propose one of: (a) apply credit forward (if contract allows), (b) issue a refund (rare; needs CFO approval), or (c) convert to breakage per contract.
6. Document outcome in the True-up ticket and tag with CommitmentID and InvoiceIDs.

Journal entries & GL mapping (examples):
| Action | Debit | Credit | Comment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Customer prepays annual Dedicated $120k | Cash | Deferred Revenue | Recognize deferred revenue on receipt; revenue recognized monthly at $10k unless practical performance indicates otherwise |
| Redeem committed credits $5k | Deferred Revenue | Revenue | When customer redeems credits against usage |
| Breakage recognition of expired credits $2k | Deferred Revenue | Misc Revenue (breakage) | Requires legal sign-off and disclosure in denial of refund clause |

Reporting, dashboards and thresholds:
- Daily metrics published to Finance Dashboard (Looker): committed_use_rate, month_to_date_invoice_delta, unredeemed_credit_balance.
- Alert: committed_use_rate < 60% for 14 consecutive days -> triggers CS review.
- Invoice generation SLA: 95% of draft invoices produced within 48 hours of cutoff.
- Billing latency tolerance: invoices finalized <= 10 business days after cutoff for complex contracts; otherwise <= 5 business days.

Example scenarios (worked):
1) Annual Dedicated + usage burst: Customer prepays $360k for 36 GPU-months plus 50k burst credits. RevenueEngine straight-lines the $360k. Burst credits consumed month-of are recognized as usage revenue at consumption.
2) Enterprise commitment with cross-product conversion: Customer buys $200k committed credit. 60% redeemed against Hosted API, 40% applied against Dedicated palette. CommitmentOrchestrator records application events and RevenueEngine recognizes revenue at time of redemption with reference to CommitmentID.
3) Under-consumption true-up: Customer contracted for 100 GPU-hours/month committed; actual average 60 GPU-hours. CS initiates True-up; Finance recommends apply-forward if contract allows; otherwise breakage recognition upon expiration.

Migration & reconciliation (legacy agreements):
- Legacy contracts with inconsistent credit expiry: create migration plan and normalized CommitmentID.
- Run a historical reconciliation job (script: scripts/recon/legacy_to_hybrid.py) to map prior invoices to current GL mapping. Finance-RevRec to approve mapping and communicate to auditors.

Escalation, approvals and exceptions:
- Refunds above $10k require CFO and Legal approval.
- Manual invoice adjustments must include memo with approver and Jira ticket link.
- Exceptions to expiration policy require Legal review and documented business rationale.

Implementation checklist for Billing and Finance teams (technical tasks):
- [ ] UsageCollector: ensure redelivery for missing telemetry >0.1% rate.
- [ ] BillingService: implement CommitmentID column in invoice line items.
- [ ] RevenueEngine: support breakage recognition flag and audit export.
- [ ] CommitmentOrchestrator: add API endpoint POST /commitments/{id}/apply-credit for CS workflows.
- [ ] Finance Dashboard: add committed_use_rate and unredeemed_credit_balance tiles.

Appendix A — Contract language snippets (recommended clauses):
- "Committed Credits: Credits are redeemable for services provided by Redwood Inference during the term and expire twelve (12) months after purchase unless otherwise stated."
- "Breakage: Except as otherwise agreed, unused committed credits at expiration shall be recognized by Redwood Inference as non-refundable breakage and recorded as revenue under applicable accounting standards."

Appendix B — Frequently asked questions:
Q: When do we treat committed credits as variable consideration?
A: If the customer has significant discretion in redemption that creates variability, revenue should be deferred until redemption (point of consumption). For predefined, non-refundable reservations that guarantee availability, consider performance over time. Work with Finance-RevRec.

References & links:
- Commitment accounting decision record: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/contract-decision-commitment-accounting-2027
- BillingService API docs: internal docs (BillingService swagger)
- Reconciliation scripts: git.redwood.com/infra/billing/scripts/recon

Owner and review cadence:
- Owner: Finance-RevRec (policy steward).
- Review cadence: Annual review in Q4 or sooner when accounting standards or product pricing changes.
- Contact: revenue-engineering@redwood.example for technical integration questions.

Change log:
- 2028-11-15: Initial draft (A. Kapoor).
- 2029-01-12: Added True-up procedure and example scenarios (D. Morales review).
- 2029-02-03: Finalized migration & GL mapping table; published.

payload.page_title: Enterprise deal forecast signoff and revenue trigger guide

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the operational workflow and decision criteria that link enterprise deal signoff, quarterly forecasts, contract milestones, and the revenue recognition / billing trigger events used by Finance, Sales Operations, Legal, and Revenue Engineering. It is intended for the teams listed in Scope and should be used whenever a deal meets the Enterprise Deal definition (see Scope).

Scope

- Applies to: all enterprise contracts (annual committed revenue >= $250k or complex procurement/legal terms such as escrow, data residency, or customer-hosted deployment).
- Excludes: self-serve and SMB deals (handled via standard billing platform workflows).

Definitions

- Forecast Signoff: formal acceptance by Finance and Revenue Operations that a committed opportunity is eligible to be included in the quarterly revenue forecast.
- Rev Trigger: the contractual or operational event that initiates revenue recognition and/or first invoicing (e.g., service acceptance, delivery milestone, go-live date, or effective date).

Roles & responsibilities

- Finance (Revenue Accounting): owns revenue recognition policy interpretation, approves rev trigger class, and creates recognition schedules in ERP.
- Sales Operations: ensures CRM/opportunity metadata is accurate (contract type, billing cadence, rev trigger candidate, legal approval status).
- Legal: approves contractual language and confirms binding effective date and any conditions precedent.
- Sales (AE/AM): obtains customer signoff, finalizes SOW/MSA countersignature, and submits procurement artifacts.
- RevOps / Billing: configures billing schedules and test invoices; coordinates billing cutover.

Quarterly forecast signoff workflow (numbered checklist)

1) Opportunity gating (Sales Ops)
   1.1 Confirm opportunity stage is "Contracting" or "Closed - Pending" and total contract value (TCV) >= $250k.
   1.2 Attach final contract, SOW, and procurement PO (if available) into the CRM record.

2) Legal review (Legal)
   2.1 Confirm MSA/SOW executed by authorized signatories; note any outstanding conditions precedent.
   2.2 If escrow/kms/data-residency clauses present, attach legal exception ticket and ETA for remediation.

3) Rev trigger classification (Finance + Legal + Sales Ops)
   3.1 Evaluate which of the standard rev triggers applies: Effective date, Delivery milestone acceptance, Customer go-live, or Usage-based threshold.
   3.2 If non-standard rev trigger is proposed, document risk and obtain Revenue Accounting signoff.

4) Forecast inclusion (Finance)
   4.1 Finance validates recognition schedule and confirms inclusion for the quarter when the rev trigger is expected to occur.
   4.2 Signoff captured via the Forecast Signoff spreadsheet and a stamped CRM field: "ForecastApprovedByFinance = true".

5) Billing readiness (RevOps)
   5.1 Ensure billing account exists, billing contact and tax details are captured, and payment terms are setup.
   5.2 Create test invoice and validate numeric mapping to contract line items.

Contract-to-Rev trigger matrix (use as a decision table)

| Contract pattern | Typical rev trigger | Required artifacts for signoff | Standard accounting treatment |
|------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| MSA + SOW (no delivery dependencies) | Effective date (signed) | Fully executed MSA + SOW | Recognize over subscription term (ratable) |
| SOW with delivery milestone(s) | Customer acceptance of milestone | Acceptance certificate, milestone report | Recognize on acceptance (milestone accounting) |
| On-prem / private deployment | Go-live / handover to customer | Deployment checklist, handover signoff | May require deferred revenue until acceptance |
| Usage-based pricing | Threshold met / first billable usage | Usage report, billing extract | Recognize as billed (variable consideration rules) |
| Trials / Pilot -> Enterprise | Conversion acceptance | Signed conversion amendment | Recognize from conversion effective date |

Billing cutover and invoicing checklist (operational playbook)

- 7 business days before expected rev trigger:
  - Confirm CRM > Billing alignment and contract mapping.
  - Create draft invoice in staging billing environment.
  - Confirm taxation and VAT handling with Tax Ops.
- 3 business days before expected rev trigger:
  - Legal to confirm no outstanding signature or CPs.
  - Finance to confirm recognition schedule entry created.
- Day 0 (rev trigger day):
  - Execute invoice run (RevOps), validate amounts, and send invoice to customer.
  - Upload invoice copy and recognition schedule into the contract folder.
- 3 business days after Day 0:
  - Revenue Accounting reconcilies invoice to recognition schedule and confirms posting.

Escalation & exception handling

- If Legal has open exceptions that change the rev trigger, Sales Ops must open a Forecast Exception ticket in JIRA (label: rev-trigger-exception) with owner and ETA.
- For disputes that block invoicing >10 business days past rev trigger, trigger the Revenue Hold escalation: notify VP Finance, General Counsel, and CRO.
- All exceptions must be reviewed in the monthly Revenue Governance meeting.

Artifacts & templates (links and code snippets)

- Forecast signoff template (use this as the canonical sheet):
  - Columns: OpportunityID, Account, TCV, ContractType, RevTrigger, ExpectedTriggerDate, ForecastQuarter, FinanceSignoff, LegalSignoff, BillingReady.

- Contract metadata JSON (to be attached to CRM record):

  {
    "opportunity_id": "OPP-12345",
    "contract_type": "MSA+SOW",
    "tcv": "550000",
    "currency": "USD",
    "rev_trigger": "effective_date",
    "trigger_date": "2026-02-01",
    "billing_cadence": "annual",
    "billing_contact": "finance@customer.com"
  }

Operational controls and thresholds

- Material contract threshold (requires senior finance review): TCV >= $1.5M or multi-year > 36 months.
- Revenue recognition policy exceptions: any clause that defers recognition beyond 90 days from effective date must be routed to Revenue Accounting for policy review.
- Billing hold threshold: disputes > $50k trigger immediate VP-level notification.

Monitoring and monthly governance

- Revenue Governance meeting cadence: monthly, chaired by Director of Revenue Accounting. Agenda includes: forecast accuracy review, open rev-trigger exceptions, and high-risk deals.
- Key metrics monitored:
  - Forecast accuracy (actual vs. forecasted recognized revenue) by deal cohort.
  - Time-to-invoice (days between rev trigger and first invoice).
  - Exception aging (days open).

Related pages and references

- Forecast sensitivity and contract alignment playbook (see related_pages).
- Contract clause library: data residency / escrow guidance.
- ERP recognition schedule template (internal link in ERP documentation).

Revision history

- 2026-01-12: Draft created by Eleanor Zhao.
- 2026-01-28: Reviewed by Jonah Meyer and updated with billing cutover checklist.
- 2026-02-08: Final review and published.

Contact

For questions about this guide, contact Revenue Accounting (revacct@redwood.ai) or the document owner, Eleanor Zhao.
