payload.page_title: API key lifecycle (Hosted): creation, rotation, and revocation

sections.body: This policy defines Redwood Inference requirements for **Hosted API key** lifecycle management, including creation, storage, rotation, and revocation.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to: Hosted API customers and internal staff with access to customer orgs/projects.
- Does not cover: Dedicated/Private customer-managed identity providers (SSO/IAM) beyond the Hosted API key surface.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Keys must be created per environment (prod vs non-prod) and per application/service when feasible.
- Keys must be named using the convention: `{env}-{service}-{owner}-{YYYYMM}` (example: `prod-billing-worker-cs-202504`).
sections.heading: 1. Creation

sections.body:
- Keys are secrets and must not be shared over Slack or pasted in Jira tickets.
- Keys must be stored in a secrets manager (1Password, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault) and injected via CI/CD.
sections.heading: 2. Storage

sections.body:
- Recommended rotation frequency: every 90 days for enterprise customers; every 180 days otherwise.
- Rotation must follow a **two-key overlap** approach when possible:
  1) Create new key
  2) Deploy new key
  3) Confirm success
  4) Revoke old key
sections.heading: 3. Rotation

sections.body:
- Revocation is the correct action if compromise is suspected.
- Revocation must be treated as a customer-impacting change because it can immediately break production traffic.
- Support/Security may revoke keys on behalf of the customer if the customer cannot access Console (e.g., RBAC lockout) and explicit authorization is documented in the support ticket.
sections.heading: 4. Revocation (emergency)

sections.body:
- For enterprise plans, key lifecycle events (create/regenerate/revoke) are recorded in Audit Logs.
- Support must link the relevant ticket key (SUP-*) when a manual revocation occurs.
sections.heading: 5. Audit and evidence

sections.body: - Confluence page: "Hosted API key rotation & revocation (customer guide)"
sections.heading: The customer-facing steps are documented in

sections.body:
- Open a Sev2+ security incident
- Revoke the impacted key(s)
- Assist customer in rotating keys across services
- Validate no further unauthorized usage
sections.heading: If an exposed key is confirmed or likely

payload.page_title: Scoped Service Token Issuance and Audit Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
========

Purpose
-------
This playbook defines how Redwood issues, manages, audits, and evidences scoped short-lived service tokens (SSTs) used for service-to-service authentication across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. It focuses on minimizing blast radius, ensuring audit fidelity, supporting regulatory evidence collection, and integrating with incident response and exception workflows.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all machine-to-machine credentials issued by Redwood central token service (token-redwood-svc) and by sanctioned customer-controlled token brokers used in Private deployments.
- Covers issuance, signing, rotation, revocation, audit instrumentation, log retention/residency requirements, compliance packaging, and risk exception handling.
- Excludes long lived human API keys; those are handled by the developer-keys policy.

Definitions
-----------
- Scoped Service Token (SST): A short-lived JWT or opaque token limited to an explicit set of capabilities (scopes).
- Token Broker: Component that mints SSTs on behalf of a workload after authenticating the requestor. Examples: token-redwood-svc, vpc-broker.
- Evidence Bundle: Structured archive (JSON + signed manifest) used to satisfy audit requests.

Ownership and Roles
-------------------
- Security team: policy owner, audit schema definition, compliance packaging.
- Identity & Access (I&A) infra: implements token brokers, signing key rotation automation, and audit enrichment hooks.
- SRE / Platform: ensures audit log ingestion SLOs and alerting on token anomalies.
- App owners: declare required scopes, TTL tolerances, and emergency contacts.

High-level Principles
---------------------
1. Least privilege by default: tokens must express minimum scopes and shortest practical TTL.
2. Strong auditability: every issuance and revocation event must emit a canonical audit event with correlation metadata.
3. Tamper-evident evidence: retention-ready manifests and signed digests allow reconstruction for regulatory requests.
4. Automated rotation and emergency revoke: no manual key-handling for standard flows.

Token Configuration Standard (example table)
-------------------------------------------
| Field | Requirement | Default / Allowed | Owner |
|-------|-------------|-------------------|-------|
| token_type | jwt | jwt | I&A infra |
| signing_alg | RS256 or PS256 | RS256 | I&A infra |
| scope | explicit resource:action strings | no wildcard allowed | App owner |
| ttl | seconds | 300–86400 (5m to 24h) default 3600 | App owner + Security approval for >24h |
| audience | service_id | must match target svc | App owner |
| issued_by | token broker id | token-redwood-svc | I&A infra |
| rotate_window | seconds before expiry to refresh | 0.5 * ttl recommended | I&A infra |
| key_id | signing key id | rotated daily for KMS keys | I&A infra |

Issuance Flow (step-by-step)
----------------------------
1. Requesting workload authenticates to the Token Broker using mTLS or platform identity (OIDC assertion) and presents the intended scope request.
2. Broker validates caller identity, enrollment status, and policy (including deny-lists and region residency constraints).
3. Broker performs policy evaluation and logs a pre-issue event containing request_id, caller_id, requested_scopes, policy_decision, and region_hint.
4. If approved, broker mints SST, attaches metadata header (key_id, issued_at, ttl, correlation_id), and returns token. The mint event is logged as an issuance event.
5. Client must persist correlation_id for future revoke/forensics workflows.

Audit Event Schema (canonical fields, JSON example)
--------------------------------------------------
- event_type: issuance | pre-issue | revoke | auto-rotate | validation-failure
- event_time: RFC3339 timestamp
- event_id: UUID
- actor: service or principal id
- target: token (kid / token hash partial), audience, scope list
- request_id: correlation id generated by broker
- decision: allow | deny | escalate
- region_hint: region code
- evidence_refs: list of evidence manifest ids

JSON example (shortened)
```
{\n  "event_type": "issuance",\n  "event_time": "2026-01-12T14:22:10Z",\n  "event_id": "9f14a3f2-2b6d-4c3a-b2e3-0a8f7d2c1e4a",\n  "actor": "svc-frontdoor-1.prod",\n  "target": {"kid": "key-20260112-12", "aud": "svc-backend-42"},\n  "request_id": "req-6f9b3a",\n  "decision": "allow",\n  "region_hint": "us-west-2",\n  "evidence_refs": ["evidence-20260112-req6f9b3a"]\n}\n```

Audit Logging Requirements
--------------------------
- All issuance/revoke/validation-failure events MUST be emitted to the central audit log stream.
- SLO: ingest to central system within 3 minutes for 99.9% of events; alert if pipeline lag > 5 minutes for >= 5 minutes.
- Logs must include partial token digests (first and last 8 hex chars) rather than full token values to avoid unnecessary exposure while enabling forensic correlation.
- Logs must include tenant_id, region, broker_id, and correlation_id.
- For Private deployments with customer-managed residency constraints, an event mirror must be maintained locally and a digest-only stub sent to central system if cross-border transfer is restricted.

Retention and Data Residency Guidance
------------------------------------
- Retention baseline: issuance/revoke events retained for 7 years for accounts with enterprise contracts; default retention 1 year for standard accounts.
- Sensitive tenants (regulated): evidence bundles preserved for contractual term + 3 years.
- When cross-border restrictions apply: keep full events in-region and publish signed digests to central compliance index. The digest must be sufficient to prove event existence and order but not contain PII.
- Archive format: gzipped JSONL + signed manifest (SHA256) stored in immutable object storage with WORM capability.

Evidence Bundle Contents (minimum)
---------------------------------
- manifest.json (signed by security-signing key)
- issuance-events.jsonl (canonical events for the period)
- broker-config.yaml (token policy snapshot)
- key-rotation-log.csv (keys used and time ranges)
- policy-decision-exports.json
- chain-of-custody.txt (who packaged, timestamp, package checksum)

Compliance Packaging: steps to produce an Evidence Bundle
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Query central audit store for all events matching correlation_id(s) and time window.
2. Include broker config snapshot as-of issuance time.
3. Export signing key metadata (key ids, rotation timestamps) — do not include private key material.
4. Produce manifest.json listing file names, sizes, and SHA256 digests.
5. Security signs the manifest using the security-signing key and uploads bundle to the compliance S3 bucket.
6. Register evidence id in evidence registry with retention policy and linked legal hold flags if required.

Runbook: Emergency Revoke (fast path)
------------------------------------
Purpose: immediate containment for suspected compromise.
Trigger: detection of anomalous token use, key compromise, or confirmed breach.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. SRE or Security runbook owner opens incident and adds legal/PR contacts.
2. Use the token-redwood-svc revoke API with correlation_id or token_digest as primary identifiers:
   - CLI example: token-redwoodctl revoke --digest "aa11ff...cc22" --reason "suspected-exfil"
3. Broker emits revoke event (must include incident_id).
4. Propagate revoke to edge caches and API gateways: force cache-bust and reject previously accepted tokens based on token digest or revocation list.
5. Produce evidence bundle for window T0-48h->T0+48h and mark as high-priority in evidence registry.
6. If signing key suspected, rotate signing key immediately using automated KMS flow and produce key-rotation log entry.
7. Post-mortem: collect issuance/revoke/validation logs, validate detection rules, and update deny-lists and policies.

Exception and Risk Acceptance Process
------------------------------------
- Request for non-standard token TTL or wildcard scope must be submitted via the Access Exception workflow with the following fields: owner, justification, risk-mitigation, compensating controls, expiry date.
- Security reviews exceptions, assigns a risk tier and mitigation steps, and issues a timebound approval if accepted.
- All exceptions are recorded in the exception register with evidence items attached. Exceptions for service tokens beyond 90 days require VP-level signoff.

Monitoring, Detection, and Alerting
----------------------------------
- Key signals to monitor:
  - Unusual issuance volume by principal or IP
  - High revoke frequency for a principal
  - Validation failures across regions
  - Issuance requests from unmanaged brokers
- Alerts: critical for cross-tenant anomalous issuance and for KMS key rotation failures.
- Weekly dashboard: top 10 callers by issuance count, top 10 scopes by volume, 90th/95th/99th percentile TTLs requested.

Developer & Operator Guidance
----------------------------
- App owners should declare required scopes in service manifests (service.yaml) and request longer TTLs only after load testing.
- Use SDK helper functions to obtain and cache SSTs with early-refresh: refresh at 50% ttl or on 401/invalid token.
- Avoid embedding tokens in logs. If unavoidable, redact and emit token digest only.

Examples and CLI snippets
------------------------
Minting request (curl)
```
curl -X POST https://token-broker.redwood.internal/v1/mint \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <platform-assertion>" \
  -d '{"aud":"svc-backend-42", "scope":["write:orders"], "ttl":3600}'
```
Revoke example (CLI)
```
token-redwoodctl revoke --digest "a1b2c3...f9e8" --incident "INC-20260112-45"
```

Compliance QA Checklist (pre-release)
-------------------------------------
- [ ] Policy rules for requested scopes exist and have test coverage.
- [ ] Audit events emitted for pre-issue, issuance, validation-failure, revoke.
- [ ] Evidence bundle generation validated end-to-end in staging.
- [ ] Retention and residency knobs configured for tenant.
- [ ] Automated key rotation timing tested with no more than 30s signing gap in rolling rotation.

Related Artifacts and Links
---------------------------
- Token broker design doc (I&A infra)
- Audit schema registry
- Evidence registry UI and API
- Access exception request form

Change Log
----------
- 2025-04-10: Initial draft created by Maya Alvarez.
- 2025-09-03: Added evidence bundle manifest and cross-border digest policy (reviewed by Luis Chen).
- 2026-01-15: Hardened emergency revoke runbook and tightened audit ingestion SLOs after SOC tabletop (reviewed by Amrita Kapoor).

Contact
-------
- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Token broker owners: token-infra@redwood.ai

Appendix: Token Broker Policy Decision Matrix (condensed)
-------------------------------------------------------
- If caller is platform-enrolled AND scope is read-only AND ttl <= 1h -> allow automated issuance.
- If caller is non-enrolled OR requested wildcard scope -> deny and escalate to manual approval.
- If caller requests cross-region audience where tenant residency disallows -> deny and produce digest-only event.

End of document

payload.page_title: Edge Authorization Evidence Orchestration Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the operational and compliance controls for collecting, packaging, and routing authorization and audit evidence from edge deployments (customer VPCs, on-premises gateways, and regional outposts). It explains RBAC constraints, minimal telemetry requirements, data residency considerations, secure SDLC hooks for evidence collection, incident response integration, and an exceptions workflow for proofs that cannot meet standard guarantees.

Audience: Security engineers, SREs supporting edge/private deployments, deployment leads, compliance officers, and support engineers involved in evidence collection and audit preparation.

Scope

- Applies to Redwood Private and dedicated edge connectors that run outside hosted control plane (VPC connectors, on-prem inference pods, and localized gateways).
- Covers authorization events, entitlement changes, service-to-service identity assertions, deployment rollouts that affect entitlements, and associated provenance metadata.
- Does NOT replace core enterprise audit pipeline; it augments the pipeline with edge-specific evidence packaging and proofchains.

Definitions

1) Authorization Evidence: the combined set of logs, policy snapshots, identity assertions, and manifests required to demonstrate who had what permission, when, and why.
2) Proof Bundle: signed, time-bounded archive of evidence prepared for audits or incident triage.
3) Edge Connector: software component deployed in a customer-managed environment to route inference requests and enforce tenancy controls.

Ownership and Roles

- Security (owner): policy definition, evidence schema, signing keys for Proof Bundles, and audit acceptance criteria.
- Edge Platform (owner): implement local collectors, ensure secure transport to Redwood evidence ingestion endpoints, and provide health/trust indicators.
- Customer Success: coordinate evidence handoffs with customers and legal for jurisdictional requests.

Policy Requirements (high-level)

- Minimum event set (must be captured at connector): authorization decisions (allow/deny), token issuance/rotation, role bindings, policy evaluation context (policy id + version), request context (route, model, tenant id), and deployment manifests (versioned).
- Cryptographic signing: Proof Bundles generated by the connector must be signed by a per-deployment key (customer-managed or Redwood-managed HSM). Signing metadata must reference the key rotation log.
- Immutability guarantees: local evidence must be append-only while retained locally; integrity proofs (merkle root or signatures) must be produced before local rotation or expiry.

Audit Logging and Retention

- Local retention baseline: 90 days of full fidelity logs within customer-managed storage for edge connectors.
- Central ingestion retention (Redwood): for ingested Proof Bundles, retain immutable copies for 7 years for enterprise customers requiring long-term retention, default retention 2 years for standard commercial customers.
- Redaction rules: PII must be redacted before central ingestion unless the customer contract and legal approvals permit transfer. A named redaction mapping must be included in the Proof Bundle manifest.

Secure SDLC Integration

- Build-time instrumentation: connectors must include a non-optional compile-time flag to enable evidence hooks. CI pipelines must run static analysis to ensure no evidence paths are disabled.
- Release gating: new connector releases require a policy-evidence conformance test in the release pipeline. Conformance artifacts (test vectors + results) are archived and referenced in the Proof Bundle when deployed.

Evidence Packaging: Proof Bundle Format (text table)

| Field | Description | Required |
| ----- | ----------- | -------- |
| bundle_id | UUID v4 | yes |
| signed_manifest.json | JSON manifest with schema_version, retention_policy, provenance | yes |
| auth_decisions.log | newline-delimited JSON, RFC 3339 timestamps | yes |
| policy_snapshot.tar.gz | tarball of active policy/role files (versioned) | yes |
| key_rotation.log | chronological list of key ids and thumbprints | conditional |
| redaction_map.json | keys that were removed/redacted | conditional |
| provenance.sig | detached signature over signed_manifest.json | yes |

Operational Playbook — Normal evidence collection

1) On connector start: generate ephemeral evidence-session-id and include in all auth decision logs.
2) Continuous: write auth_decisions.log locally; once per 6h generate signed_manifest.json and append provenance.sig.
3) Weekly: rotate local digest anchor (Merkle root) and push incremental Proof Bundle to Redwood ingestion endpoint over TLS 1.3 with mutual auth.
4) On deployment/role-change: produce on-demand Proof Bundle that includes the pre-change and post-change policy_snapshot. Mark this bundle asPriority=high.

Operational Playbook — Incident-triggered evidence flow

1) Triage kickoff: incident commander decides whether edge evidence should be exported immediately.
2) If yes: run the emergency evidence workflow (CLI or API) that instructs connector to compile a time-bounded Proof Bundle covering T0-6h to T0+6h.
3) Connector generates Proof Bundle, signs with the current key, and streams to a quarantined Redwood evidence ingestion endpoint.
4) Security team verifies bundle signature and performs integrity checks (signature validation, manifest schema).
4a) If signature verification fails: escalate to oncall (security) and preserve local artifacts per legal hold.

Exception and Approval Process

- Exception reasons: no outbound connectivity, local storage constraints, legal prohibition on cross-border transfer, or HSM unavailability.
- Approval flow: deployment owner opens an exception request ticket with an evidence fallback plan. Security and Compliance must jointly approve and attach compensating controls (e.g., on-demand remote joint-collection sessions with customer-located auditors, air-gapped USB-copy manifests held by legal).

Compensating Controls (examples)

- Where cross-border transfer is prohibited: retain full-fidelity logs in local jurisdiction and provide time-stamped digest + witness-signed manifest to Redwood.
- Where outbound connectivity is absent: enable offline Proof Bundle export (signed, physically transferred) with chain-of-custody checklist.

Operational Requirements and SLOs

- Evidence ingestion success: 99.9% of scheduled Proof Bundles must arrive at central ingestion within 24 hours under normal connectivity.
- Emergency export: connectors must be capable of generating an emergency Proof Bundle in <= 10 minutes.

Telemetry and Monitoring

- Health signals: last_successful_bundle_ts, last_signature_validation_ok, pending_bundle_size_bytes, error_rate_push_attempts.
- Alerts: page SRE on evidence_ingest_failure > 3 consecutive attempts or pending_bundle_size_bytes > 500MB for > 12h.

Integration with Incident Response

- Evidence preservation is a top-level priority in incidents affecting authorization. Incident commander should reference this playbook in the first 15 minutes of triage if authorization, entitlements, or access anomalies are suspected.
- For legal hold: compliance will issue a preservation order which freezes local deletion and marks bundles with hold=true. Connectors must honor hold flag and surface evidence export-only mode.

Compliance Acceptance Criteria

- A Proof Bundle is considered audit-ready when: signature verification succeeds, manifest schema_version is current (v2.1 as of this doc), redaction_map present if PII removed, and policy_snapshot includes a checksum that matches the deployment manifest.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: redwood-edgectl evidence create --window "2026-06-01T08:00Z/2026-06-01T20:00Z" --priority high --output /var/tmp/pb-20260601.tar
sections.heading: generate on-demand bundle

sections.body:
redwood-edgectl evidence push --file /var/tmp/pb-20260601.tar --endpoint ingress-evidence.redwood.internal --cert /etc/redwood/edge-cert.pem

Appendix B — Quick checklist for auditors

- Verify bundle_id is present and unique.
- Confirm provenance.sig verifies against known key thumbprint.
- Ensure policy_snapshot contains matching deployment hashes referenced in release pipeline artifacts.
- Check redaction_map for PII removal and legal basis for transfer.

References and Related Policies

- Authorization logging and deprovisioning guidance (rbac-and-auth).
- Audit schema and evidence tagging standard (audit-logging).
- Geo-smart retention policy and cross-border evidence playbook (data-residency-and-retention).

Change log

- 2026-02-18: created (A. Martinez) — initial draft and implementation checklist.
- 2026-04-12: updated emergency export SLA and added Merkle-root anchoring (reviewers: N. Patel).
- 2026-06-03: finalized signing guidance and added offline chain-of-custody template (E. Brooks).

payload.page_title: Hybrid deployment evidence retention and access reconstruction standard

sections.body:
Summary
This document defines the standard evidence retention, packaging, and access-reconstruction procedures for incidents that span hybrid deployments (hosted, dedicated, and private/VPC). It reconciles RBAC snapshots, audit logging, and data residency constraints with forensic requirements and compliance evidence workflows.

Scope
- Applies to all incident classifications that require forensic reconstruction or regulatory evidence where services or data cross deployment boundaries.
- Covers audit logs, entitlement snapshots, endpoint-level telemetry, model artifacts, persistent storage, configuration state, and chain-of-custody artifacts.
- Excludes ephemeral in-memory traces unless explicitly requested by the incident commander and approved by Legal.

Definitions
- Hybrid deployment: any customer or internal workload that is served across more than one deployment mode (hosted + dedicated, hosted + private, or dedicated + private).
- Evidence bundle: a timeboxed collection of logs, snapshots, and metadata prepared for audit or legal review.
- Access reconstruction: the steps required to map a user/service action to artifacts (logs, entitlements, and network flows) to prove who/what performed an action.

Roles and ownership
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates evidence collection, approves legal holds, ensures chain-of-custody continuity.
- Forensics Lead (Security): owns evidence bundle composition and integrity checks.
- Platform Owner (Infra/Eng): provides access to snapshots, storage, and retention policy enforcement.
- Customer Success / Account Security: flags customer-sensitive residency constraints.
- Legal / Compliance: approves retention beyond baseline and adjudicates cross-border transfer requests.

Retention matrix (baseline)
- Audit logs (ingestion-level): 365 days (hosted), 180 days (dedicated customer-managed), 90 days (edge/private default).
- RBAC snapshots (full entitlement graphs): 3 years for compliance-impacting incidents; otherwise 365 days.
- KV/cache access index (prefix/kv keys for reconstructions): 90 days.
- Model artifacts & provenance (manifest, hash, quantization profile): 5 years for production models used in regulated customers.
- Forensic disk images / VM snapshots: retained until case closure + 180 days (minimum 1 year if litigation expected).
- Legal hold: override baseline—retained until release by Legal.

Note: Retention windows are the minimum default. For hybrid deployments, retention is the intersection of the most restrictive jurisdictional residency and the technical mode (hosted vs customer-managed). Platform Owner must classify storage locations and mark evidence bundles with residency tags (e.g., eu, us, apac).

Evidence collection checklist (ordered)
1) Immediately create an incident evidence folder in the secure evidence store with a UUID and IC-assigned case ID.
2) Snapshot RBAC state at T0+0–5 minutes: identity provider claims, role bindings, service tokens, and temporary entitlements. Generate a signed digest (SHA256) and attach IC metadata.
3) Export ingestion and API gateway logs across all affected regions for T0-72h to T0+24h (default window).
4) Pull per-node/local runtime logs (stderr/stdout), model runtime traces, and cache eviction traces for affected nodes.
5) If private/dedicated, request customer-managed logs and attestations per the customer onboarding contract.
6) Preserve any ephemeral evidence (in-memory dump) only after Legal approval and using an approved preservation host.
7) Record transfer proof (S3 object hashes, transfer timestamps, TLS fingerprint) for every artifact moved across residency boundaries.

Chain-of-custody procedure
- Every evidence artifact MUST be recorded in the evidence ledger with: artifact ID, origin host/service, hash (SHA256), timestamp, collector identity, and transfer events.
- All collectors must sign the artifact metadata via platform signing key (automated where possible).
- When transferring across teams or exporting for legal/audit review, the Forensics Lead must generate a signed transfer manifest and obtain recipient acknowledgement.

Access reconstruction steps (technical runbook)
1) Correlate RBAC snapshot with authentication logs: map JWT/SAML/OIDC assertions to token exchange events.
2) Trace request path using API gateway trace IDs and service-level trace IDs; expand to host-level logs.
3) If KV/cache hits are relevant, consult prefix/KV access index to determine cache-primed prefixes and associated session IDs.
4) Reconstruct session timelines: sequence events, annotate with TTLs and observed latencies.
5) If model responses are in scope, include prompt inputs, model versioned manifest, and any reranking/reroute decisions.
6) Produce a narrative reconstruction document with supporting artifacts and a minimal reproducible timeline.

Technical configuration requirements (table)
- Audit log schema version: v3.2 (fields required: timestamp, trace_id, request_id, user_id, service, resource, action, result_code, client_ip, region, residency_tag).
- RBAC snapshot format: JSONL compressed + signed manifest.
- Evidence bundle packaging: tar.gz with manifest.json (signed), checksums, and chain-of-custody.csv.
- Storage encryption: AES-256 at rest, TLS1.3 in transit.
- Signature algorithm: rsa-4096 or ed25519 (preferred).

Exception and escalation (risk & exceptions)
- If retention or transfer conflicts with customer residency, initiate "Residency Exception" flow: submit an exception request including legal rationale, minimal artifact set, and proposed mitigations.
- Exception owners: Security + Legal + Product. Decisions must be recorded in the exception register and linked to the evidence bundle.
- Timebox for exception approval: 48 business hours for operational incidents; 7 business days for policy-level exceptions.

Automation & integrations
- SIEM ingestion: evidence bundles publish metadata to the SIEM; raw artifacts remain in secure evidence store with access gating.
- Orchestration: a set of Lambda/Cloud Functions to auto-snapshot RBAC, collect API gateway slices, and compute checksums. These tasks must be idempotent and reversible.
- Retention enforcement: lifecycle policies on evidence buckets enforce delete dates unless Legal hold flag exists. Audit retention TTL must be immutable for the period recorded in the manifest.

Verification and auditability
- Monthly integrity sweep: Forensics engineers run a checksum verification across a randomized 10% of evidence bundles older than 90 days. Failures trigger an incident for corruption investigation.
- Quarterly policy review: Security and Legal review retention matrix and residency tags.

Templates and artifacts (links)
- Evidence bundle manifest template (JSON) — /confluence/templates/evidence-manifest.json
- RBAC snapshot collector script — /confluence/eng-infra/automation/rbac-snapshot-collector.sh
- Chain-of-custody CSV template — /confluence/templates/chain-of-custody.csv

FAQ
- Q: Can customer-managed dedicated logs be forcibly ingested into hosted evidence store?
  A: No. We require customer approval or contractual entitlement. If unavailable, collect attestations and metadata from the customer and include in the bundle.
- Q: Who can release a Legal hold?
  A: Only Legal can release a hold; Forensics Lead may request release after closing activities.

Revision history
- 2026-03-15: Created by Maya Singh.
- 2026-07-01: Added automated RBAC snapshot guidance and SIEM integration notes.
- 2026-10-02: Aligned retention matrix with new data-sovereignty baseline and added verification sweep.

Appendix: quick checklists
- Incident start (first 30 minutes): create evidence folder, RBAC snapshot, ingest gateway logs, tag residency.
- 24-hour checklist: collect node-level logs, model manifests, customer attestations, and compute bundle checksums.
- Closure checklist: Legal hold review, manifest signoff, retention policy assignment, archive scheduling.

Contacts
- Security on-call: sec-oncall@redwood.ai
- Forensics engineering: forensics@redwood.ai
- Legal: legal-incident@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: Model artifact & audit chain-of-custody playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines an operational, auditable chain-of-custody (CoC) process for model artifacts (weights, tokenizers, compiled binaries, quantized blobs, and provenance manifests) and associated audit logs. It explains how to capture RBAC state, collect and package audit telemetry, preserve regionally constrained evidence, and hand off artifacts for legal/forensic review. The procedures apply to hosted, dedicated, and private deploys.

Scope
-----
- Incident types: suspected model exfiltration, unauthorized model modifications, data leakage via inference, and model-serving escalation requests from customers.
- Artifacts: model weights (.pt/.bin), tokenizer files, model config (json/yaml), KV cache snapshots, compiled runtime binaries, quantization metadata, provenance manifests, and request/response audit logs.
- Environments: Redwood-hosted, Dedicated pools, and Private (VPC/on-prem).

Key definitions
---------------
- Evidence bundle: timeboxed archive containing model artifact(s), audit log slice, RBAC snapshot, and an evidence manifest (see manifest example below).
- RBAC snapshot: a point-in-time export of entitlements, role bindings, service identities and active sessions relevant to the incident scope.
- Chain-of-custody stamp: signed metadata block appended to an evidence bundle describing collector, timestamp, checksum, location, and KMS key-id used for sealing.

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Incident Lead (security oncall): overall approval and legal interface.
- Forensics Collector (SRE / Infra): executes collection commands, packages evidence, and uploads to evidence store.
- RBAC Owner (IAM team): verifies snapshots and provides supplemental entitlement logs.
- Custodian (Legal/Compliance): requests evidence retention extension and triggers formal legal hold.

Preconditions and constraints
----------------------------
1) Always confirm the incident classification with the Incident Lead before collecting artifacts that contain customer data. 2) Respect data residency requirements — evidence for a region-bound tenant must remain in that region’s evidence store unless legal has approved cross-border transfer. 3) When collecting private deploy artifacts, coordinate with the Private Deploys team and the customer contact for on-prem packaging procedures.

High-level process (summary)
---------------------------
1. Triage and scope: identify affected model(s), time range, and impacted tenants.
2. Snapshot RBAC and active sessions.
3. Extract audit log slice and correlated API/infra traces.
4. Freeze model-serving nodes (as needed) and export model artifacts and runtime caches.
5. Create evidence manifest, compute checksums, and sign (KMS).
6. Ingest bundle into regional evidence store with access controls and retention policy applied.
7. Notify Legal/Compliance and attach bundle to incident record.

Detailed runbook (step-by-step)
-------------------------------
1) Triage & Authorization
   - Incident Lead confirms evidence collection scope and legal constraints.
   - If customer tenant is regulated (HIPAA, GDPR), set confidentiality=restricted and route approval to Legal.

2) Capture RBAC state (mandatory before artifact collection)
   - Purpose: record who could access the model and which service accounts were active at T0.
   - Commands (examples):
     - Service identity list (kubernetes + internal IAM):
       curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://iam.redwood.internal/api/v1/roles | jq '.' > /tmp/rbac-snapshot-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).json
     - Active sessions export (Auth service):
       rcli sessions export --since 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z --until 2025-01-01T03:00:00Z --out /tmp/sessions.json
   - Save RBAC snapshot to evidence staging area and record checksum (sha256).

3) Audit log extraction and correlation
   - Pull logs from the audit pipeline using log-store queries. Include request IDs, model IDs, and user/service identities.
   - Example KQL-like query (log-store):
     source:audit AND model_id:"model-abc" AND timestamp:[2025-01-01T00:00:00 TO 2025-01-01T03:00:00] | project timestamp, request_id, user_id, action, resource, outcome
   - Export logs in NDJSON; compute sha256 and include in manifest.

4) Model artifact preservation
   - If preservation will affect production SLAs, consult Incident Lead for canary freeze vs full node freeze.
   - Commands (examples):
     - Snapshot running container and copy model files:
       kubectl exec -n runtime svc/model-host-0 -- tar czf - /srv/models/model-abc | pv | gpg --encrypt --recipient "evidence@redwood" > /tmp/model-abc.tar.gz.gpg
     - Export KV cache (if applicable):
       redis-dump --host runtime-cache-0 --db 0 --keys "kv:cache:model-abc:*" > /tmp/kv-cache.json
   - Collect additional runtime metadata: GPU driver versions, runtime binary version, compilation flags, and quantization profile.

5) Evidence manifest (required)
   - A single top-level file named evidence-manifest.json describing all items in the bundle. Include these fields: id, collected_by, collection_time_utc, items:[{path, type, checksum, size_bytes, location, retention_policy_id}], rbacsnapshot_version, signed_by_kms_key.
   - Example manifest snippet (text example):
     {
       "id": "evidence-20250101-0001",
       "collected_by": "forensics-collector-1",
       "collection_time_utc": "2025-01-01T01:23:45Z",
       "items": [
         {"path":"model-abc.pt","type":"model-weights","checksum":"sha256:...","size_bytes":"123456789"},
         {"path":"audit-slice-20250101.ndjson","type":"audit-log-slice","checksum":"sha256:..."}
       ]
     }

6) Sealing, signing, and storage
   - Compute and record SHA256 checksums for each file.
   - Seal with KMS: use company evidence-seal key (kms://evidence/seal-key-prod). Example:
     aws kms encrypt --key-id arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111:alias/evidence-seal-key --plaintext fileb://evidence-manifest.json --output text --query CiphertextBlob | base64 --decode > evidence-manifest.json.enc
   - Attach a chain-of-custody stamp (signed blob) with collector id and certificate thumbprint.
   - Upload to the regional evidence store (S3 bucket or on-prem vault) and mark retention.

Retention and residency matrix
------------------------------
| Evidence type | Default retention | Regional constraint | Encryption | Owner |
|---------------|-------------------|---------------------|------------|-------|
| Model weights | 7 years (archival) | Must remain in tenant-region if tenant-regulated | AES-256 + KMS-seal | Security |
| Audit log slice | 10 years (per compliance) | Kept in region-bound audit-store; cross-border only via Legal | AES-256 | Observability |
| RBAC snapshot | 3 years | Internal only (no export) | AES-256 | IAM |
| KV cache snapshots | 90 days by default | Treated as PII if user data present; consult Privacy | AES-256 | Infra |

Access controls and proof-of-access
----------------------------------
- Only members of the approved forensics group may read sealed evidence buckets. Access is granted via timebound entitlement and JIT approval.
- Every access to evidence must generate an audit entry in the evidence-access ledger with fields: accessor_id, purpose, timestamp, justification, and link to incident id.

Forensics packaging checklist (must verify before handoff)
----------------------------------------------------------
1) RBAC snapshot present and checksumed.
2) Audit log slice in NDJSON and checksumed.
3) Model artifacts archived and sealed (GPG/KMS).
4) Evidence manifest created and KMS-signed.
5) Chain-of-custody stamp appended and logged in evidence ledger.
6) Evidence uploaded to regional store and retention policy attached.
7) Incident ticket updated with bundle location (internal id), legal hold flags, and custodian assigned.

Common queries and diagnostics (examples)
----------------------------------------
- Find requests that used model-abc with a high token count in the last 72 hours:
  SELECT timestamp, request_id, user_id, tokens_requested FROM audit WHERE model_id='model-abc' AND tokens_requested > 2000 AND timestamp > now() - interval '72 hours';
- Map role bindings for service accounts touching the runtime namespace:
  curl -sS https://iam.redwood.internal/api/v1/rolebindings?namespace=runtime | jq '.bindings[] | {role,subjects}'

Legal hold and retention extension process
------------------------------------------
- Custodian (Legal) files a retention extension request in the incident ticket. Include reason, extended retention window, and affected bundles.
- Security approves if the extension is consistent with internal policy and regional law.
- For cross-border transfer requests, Legal must complete a Data Transfer Impact Assessment and obtain Exec approval.

Post-collection: verification and cleanup
----------------------------------------
- Within 72 hours, the RBAC Owner must validate the snapshot for completeness and sign the verification record.
- If nodes were frozen for collection, SRE must implement scheduled rollout or rollback plan to resume normal service with minimal downtime (documented steps and release owner).

Appendices
---------
A. Evidence manifest fields (reference)
- id, version, collected_by, collection_time_utc, items[], retention_policy_id, sealed_by_kms_key, chain_of_custody_stamp

B. Example minimal evidence manifest (text)
- See step 5 example above; include full JSON file in the incident ticket when uploading.

C. Related runbooks and pages
- Incident evidence orchestration for multi-tenant model failures (link in related_pages).
- Audit schema contract and retention runbook.

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Primary: security-oncall@redwood.ai (pager)
- Forensics lead: Marek Novak (pager)
- IAM escalation: iam-ops@redwood.ai

Notes and rationale
-------------------
This playbook centralizes model-specific forensic handling because model artifacts present unique provenance requirements (weights can be forked, quantized artifacts change signatures). We treat model weights and audit slices as first-class evidence and apply stricter retention and sealing than generic logs to maintain legal defensibility.

Change history
--------------
- 2024-08-20: Initial draft (Arjun Patel)
- 2024-11-02: Add KV cache guidance and packaging checklist (Leah Morales)
- 2025-01-18: Update sealing commands and retention matrix; set confidentiality to restricted (Marek Novak)

payload.page_title: Evaluation Asset Registry and Evaluator Service Contract

sections.body: This document defines the Evaluation Asset Registry (EAR) — a canonical catalog and lifecycle for evaluation artifacts — and the Evaluator Service Contract (ESC) that runtime and eval components must implement to consume, produce, and promote assets safely across shadow, canary, and production stages. The EAR + ESC are intended to reduce duplicated probe creation, improve reproducibility, and provide clear operational guarantees for model onboarding, quantization, and regression triage workflows.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Goals:
  - Provide a single, queryable registry of evaluation assets (probe sets, slice tags, sample annotations, golden outputs, evaluator configs, telemetry fingerprints, quant-compatibility reports).
  - Standardize metadata such that evaluators, CI, and the serving runtime can make deterministic promotion/rollback decisions.
  - Define SLOs and behavioral expectations (the ESC) for asset producers and consumers (latency, freshness, compatibility checks).
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a replacement for the model artifact repository (weights). EAR references model snapshots but does not store binaries.
  - EAR is not itself an annotation UI — it references annotator outputs hosted in the annotation store.
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body: Each asset in the registry must include the following canonical metadata fields. Below we provide the minimal schema and rationale. Implementations should store metadata as JSON-LD-style flat maps; consumer code must treat unknown extra fields as opaque strings.
sections.heading: Asset types and minimal metadata contract

sections.body:
- asset_id: stable short id (e.g., ea-2026-000142)
- asset_type: one of [probe_set, slice_definition, golden_reference, eval_config, quant_report, telemetry_fingerprint, sample_bundle]
- title: human-friendly short title
- description: 2–6 sentence summary describing provenance and intended use
- author: full name of producer
- owner_team: team responsible for upkeep (applied-ml, runtime, platform, etc.)
- created_at: YYYY-MM-DD
- last_updated: YYYY-MM-DD
- stage: one of [draft, shadow, canary, production, deprecated]
- tags: comma-separated short tags (e.g., longcontext, finance, multilingual)
- privacy_level: one of [public, internal, restricted] — governs who can mount the asset in private deployments
- checksum: SHA256 over the canonical artifact bundle URI (not the metadata)
- canonical_uri: resolvable URI to download or mount the artifact (s3://, gs://, or internal artifact-store path)
sections.heading: Required fields (string values)

sections.body:
- seed_samples_count: integer as string (e.g., "128")
- languages: comma-separated ISO codes
- quant_compatibility: [none|soft|verified] — indicates if quant-eval has run against this asset
- evaluation_goals: short enum list (e.g., coherence, safety, latency-sensitivity)
- linked_model_snapshot: model-snap-id(s) that the asset was created against (comma-separated)
- expiration_date: YYYY-MM-DD (if temporary)

Example metadata JSON (stored as a flat string blob in the registry):
{
  "asset_id": "ea-2026-000142",
  "asset_type": "probe_set",
  "title": "longcontext-fewshot-coverage-v2",
  "description": "Stratified few-shot prompt families targeting long-context degradation across English/ES/FR tenants.",
  "author": "Priya Natarajan",
  "owner_team": "applied-ml",
  "created_at": "2026-01-10",
  "last_updated": "2026-01-30",
  "stage": "shadow",
  "tags": "longcontext,fewshot,multilingual",
  "privacy_level": "internal",
  "checksum": "sha256:3a1f...",
  "canonical_uri": "s3://redwood-eval-assets/ea-2026-000142/bundle-v2.tar.gz",
  "seed_samples_count": "512",
  "languages": "en,es,fr",
  "quant_compatibility": "soft",
  "linked_model_snapshot": "snap-ml-2026-0154"
}

Evaluator Service Contract (ESC): runtime and eval components that read or write assets must meet these expectations. The contract is intentionally small and actionable.
sections.heading: Optional but strongly recommended fields

sections.body:
1) Metadata completeness: before promoting an asset to shadow/canary, the producer must supply all required fields and run the automated metadata linter (lint-eval-asset CLI).
2) Compatibility verification: for assets labeled with quant_compatibility != "none", run the QuantCompatibilityRunner (see example CLI) and attach the quant_report asset_id as a linked artifact.
3) Privacy gating: assets with privacy_level == "restricted" must be hashed/DP-redacted upstream; the producer must include a redaction_manifest URI in the metadata.
4) Promotion tests: an automated smoke eval (10k token budget) must complete with success criteria (no runtime exceptions, coverage >= 75% of declared slices) before stage transitions.
sections.heading: Producer obligations (asset writers)

sections.body:
1) Freshness check: consumers must verify last_updated >= policy_age for the execution context. Default policy_age:
   - production: 30 days
   - canary: 14 days
   - shadow: 90 days
2) Checksum validation: consumer must verify the bundle checksum prior to use and abort on mismatch.
3) Quant fallback behavior: if quant_compatibility == "none" and consumer workload is quantized, the ESC requires either (a) skip asset with a logged skip reason, or (b) run a temporary quant-sim replay and annotate results with uncertainty tags.
4) Observability hooks: consumers must emit the following events to eval-metrics: asset.mount.start, asset.mount.complete, asset.evaluate.start, asset.evaluate.complete, asset.evaluate.failure. Each event MUST include asset_id and stage tags.
sections.heading: Consumer obligations (asset readers)

sections.body:
- Asset catalog query latency: p95 < 120ms
- Asset bundle download success rate: >= 99.5% over 24h window
- Smoke eval completion time (10k token test): p95 < 3 minutes in shadow environments
- Checksum validation failure rate: < 0.01% (incidents flagged if > 0.1%)
- Promotion pipeline mean time to promote (draft -> production when automated gates pass): target <= 48 hours (manual review adds headroom)
sections.heading: Operational SLOs and thresholds (for evaluator infra)

sections.body:
1) Create asset in draft stage. Run lint-eval-asset and attach quant_report if available.
2) Run automated smoke eval in shadow against linked_model_snapshot. Address any failing slices. Update metadata and increment version in canonical_uri.
3) Promote to canary and schedule a small canary eval (budgeted per-model token cap). Monitor eval-metrics for fidelity deltas and failure modes for 72 hours.
4) If canary passes (no critical fidelity regressions, checksum stable, quant fallback behavior acceptable), update stage=production and notify owner_team. Create a promotion audit record in the registry (promotion_event_id).
sections.heading: Promotion workflow (recommended steps)

sections.body:
- Immediate rollback to previous asset version if any of the following happen in production within a 24h window:
  - fidelity delta > 12% on top-priority slices
  - golden-reference mismatch rate > 5% for safety-critical slices
  - sustained asset bundle download failures > 0.5%
Remediation: demote offending asset to deprecated, instruct serving to remount previous production asset, open a regression triage ticket with tags: regression, eval-asset, urgent.
sections.heading: Rollback criteria and quick remediation steps

sections.body:
- Register an asset (example):
  $ lint-eval-asset validate --path bundle-v1/manifest.json
  $ ear-cli register --metadata bundle-v1/manifest.json --uri s3://redwood-eval-assets/ea-2026-000142/bundle-v1.tar.gz

- Querying by tag and stage (example):
  $ ear-cli search --tag longcontext --stage shadow --owner_team applied-ml --format=json | jq '.[] | {asset_id, title, canonical_uri}'

- Minimal quant compatibility check (example output):
  {"asset_id":"ea-2026-000142","quant_compatibility":"soft","quant_report":"ea-qr-2026-0099","notes":"KV-cache replay shows 2.3% coherence loss at q4; acceptable under soft policy"}
sections.heading: Integration examples and CLI snippets

sections.body:
- Registry owner: evaluated by applied-ml infra; operational stewardship lives with the platform team for availability SLOs and applied-ml for content quality.
- Promotion approvers: a promotion to production requires one applied-ml reviewer and one runtime reviewer (can be automated if smoke eval metrics and quant_report pass all gates).

Privacy, compliance, and access controls:
- Assets marked restricted are only mountable in private deployment targets after an access approval workflow. Access must be recorded in the registry audit log with approver and justification.
- Redaction manifests must include hashing/scrubbing algorithms and (if applicable) DP epsilon used.

Onboarding checklist for teams producing assets (quick start):
1) Read the EAR metadata spec and install ear-cli + lint-eval-asset.
2) Prepare canonical bundle with README, manifest.json, and sample index.
3) Run quant runner if the asset targets quantized deployments; attach quant_report.
4) Register artifact in EAR as draft, run shadow smoke eval, iterate until coverage & fidelity targets are met.
5) Promote to canary and observe for 72 hours.

Appendix: compatibility matrix (excerpt described in text)
- When to require quant_report: any asset intended for quantized serving or labeled tags containing any of [kv-cache, longcontext, streaming-functioncall].
- DP/redaction required: assets containing user-generated text, PII, or financial transaction samples.
- Storage lifecycle: production assets are retained for 2 years; shadow assets are retained for 180 days unless explicitly extended.
sections.heading: Governance and ownership

sections.body:
Q: Can an asset reference multiple model snapshots?
A: Yes — list them in linked_model_snapshot. Consumers should prefer the snapshot matching their runtime.

Q: What if a probe set grows after registration?
A: Create a new version (increment the asset_id version suffix) and register a new canonical_uri. Do not mutate production bundles in-place.
sections.heading: Frequently asked questions (short)

sections.body:
- Principal owner: Priya Natarajan (applied-ml) — priya@redwood.ai
- Platform SRE: Jin Park — jin.park@redwood.ai
- For immediate operational issues open an incident via PagerDuty with service id: eval-asset-registry

This document is intended to be referenced by the eval harness, model onboarding playbooks, quality guardrails, and regression triage runbooks. Implementers should link back to this page when creating or updating assets so that automated pipelines can discover expected lifecycle signals.

payload.page_title: Forensic Telemetry Mapping and Evidence Retention Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook establishes a single-source mapping for forensic telemetry across Redwood Inference services, defines retention windows and custody procedures for evidence, and documents the incident response handoff between Product/Platform, SRE, Security, and Legal. It is intended for incident responders, SREs, security engineers, and compliance reviewers who will prepare or respond to security incidents requiring forensic evidence collection and compliance reporting.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where Redwood controls telemetry collection.
- Covers: authentication/authorization events, audit logs, model inference telemetry, kernel/runtime traces, network flows, KMS access logs, and storage access events.
- Excludes transient developer IDE logs and ephemeral debug traces that are never persisted.

Key objectives:
1) Provide deterministic mapping from incident type to the minimal telemetry set required for investigation and compliance.
2) Standardize retention, immutability, and chain-of-custody controls across regions and residency requirements.
3) Define actionable runbook steps for evidence collection, preservation, and transfer to Legal/Compliance.

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Security (Arielle Chen)
- Secondary owners: Eng-SRE (Samuel Green), Eng-Serving-Runtime (Diego Morales)
- Oncall escalation: security-oncall@redwood-inference.com

Telemetry taxonomy (canonical event types):
1) AUTHZ events: login.success, login.failure, token.issue, token.revoke, role.change, role.provisioning
2) AUTHN events: mfa.challenge, mfa.success, service-identity-auth, service-identity-fail
3) AUDIT events: api.request, api.response, api.error, admin.change, policy.update
4) RUNTIME traces: model.start_inference, model.kv_cache_hit, model.kv_cache_miss, model.quantize_path, kernel.error
5) INFRA/NW: instance.spawn, instance.terminate, ip.conn.open, ip.conn.close, nat.gateway-fail
6) STORAGE/KMS: s3.get_object, s3.put_object, kms.encrypt, kms.decrypt, kms.key_rotate

Telemetry mapping matrix (what to collect per incident class):
- Incident class: Unauthorized console access
  - Required telemetry: AUTHZ (role.change, login.*), API audit (admin.change), SSO provider logs, session tokens, console command traces, S3 access where artifacts were accessed.
- Incident class: Model exfiltration suspicion
  - Required telemetry: model.start_inference, model.kv_cache_hit/miss, api.request/response payload meta, network flows to external IPs, storage GET/PRESIGNED URLs, private deployment egress logs.
- Incident class: Privilege escalation via svc account
  - Required telemetry: service-identity-auth, role.provisioning, KMS decrypt ops, admin.change events.

Retention and residency rules (summary table):
| Data class | Default retention | Immutability | Regional residency rule | Minimum indexing tier |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------|-------------------------|----------------------|
| AUTHZ / Audit | 7 years | Write-once S3 + object lock | Region-of-origin for tenant data | hot (30d) then warm |
| Runtime traces | 90 days | Append-only in logging cluster | Global except private deployments where local only | hot (14d) |
| Network flows | 365 days (summary), 90 days (pcap) | Encrypted archival S3 | Must follow customer residency for private deployments | warm |
| KMS access logs | 7 years | Immutable audit store | Tenant-region KMS logging | cold archival |

Notes: retention values above reflect Redwood baseline for enterprise customers. Individual contracts may override values; any exception must follow the Risk & Exceptions flow (see section).

Evidence packaging and chain of custody checklist:
- When evidence is identified, create an Evidence Ticket (EVID-<INCIDENT_ID>-<YYYYMMDD>) in the incident tracker and tag with confidentiality level.
- Freeze the relevant storage paths (S3 prefixes, logging streams) using object-lock or equivalent.
- Record the following metadata for each artifact: artifact_id, collector (team-oncall), collection_time (UTC), hash (sha256), storage_path, kms_key_id, retention_policy_reference.
- Transfer artifacts to the Evidence Bucket (s3://redwood-evidence/<incident-id>/) using server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) and enable MFA-delete on the bucket.
- Capture a signed custody receipt: template provided below.

Custody receipt (template):
- Incident ID: <id>
- Artifact ID: <id>
- Collected by: <name + team>
- Collected at (UTC): <timestamp>
- SHA256: <hex>
- Storage location: <s3 path or archive id>
- Notes: <short justification>
- Signature (collector) and Signature (security reviewer): <name + timestamp>

Runbook: Initial evidence collection for a verified security incident
1) Triage and classify incident (Security triage) — determine incident class per taxonomy.
2) Open Evidence Ticket and assign collector: security or SRE engineer.
3) Execute containment if required (isolate affected instances, revoke tokens).
4) Snapshot all relevant boxes: live memory snapshot (if approved by Legal and if necessary), core dumps, and runtime KV caches when supported.
5) Export logs: use logging-service export CLI and include time-window +/- 2 hours around first known anomalous event. Example commands:
   - logging-cli export --service inference-api --start 2027-07-01T09:12:00Z --end 2027-07-01T11:12:00Z --output s3://redwood-evidence/<incident-id>/logs/
   - audit-query "event.type:api.request AND request.path:\"/v1/generate\"" --from -2h --to +2h --out s3://redwood-evidence/<incident-id>/api-requests.ndjson
6) Apply immutability: aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket redwood-evidence-<id> --object-lock-configuration ... (security to assist).
7) Compute and log artifact hashes and upload custody receipt to ticket.
8) Notify Legal/Compliance for regulatory holds before any deletion or cross-border transfer.

Special handling: private deployments and customer-managed k8s
- For private deployments where customer controls persistence, Redwood will ship a forensics collection package (collector container + manifest) executed under customer operations supervision. The package produces the same artifact metadata schema and signs outputs with Redwood-provisioned signing keys.
- For air-gapped customers, follow the Offline Evidence Transfer (OET) flow: physical media are inventoried, hashed, and transported under signed chain-of-custody.

RBAC & Evidence access controls:
- Evidence buckets and artifact indices are restricted to the evidence_readers and evidence_admins roles.
- Just-in-time access (JIT) is supported for auditors: request via access-portal with automatic short-lived credential issuance (max 8 hours). Requests are logged in AUTHZ events and require approval by Security + Legal for Confidential artifacts.
- Privileged sessions to view raw artifacts must be done through a session-proxy that records video and keystroke metadata and deposits a session-audit event.

Audit logging and query patterns for investigators:
- Canonical index fields: timestamp, event_type, service, tenant_id, user_id, ip, request_id, parent_request_id, correlation_id, sha256_artifact.
- Example investigative queries:
  - Find all admin changes for user alice@example.com in 24h window: index:audit AND event_type:admin.change AND target.user:alice@example.com AND @timestamp:[now-24h TO now]
  - Trace inference requests that produced large responses: index:api AND event_type:api.response AND body_length:>1000000 | stats count by user_id

Secure SDLC touchpoints (what dev teams must do to support forensics):
- Instrumentation: all new services must emit the canonical index fields and include request_id propagation.
- Error classification: runtime errors that may be security-relevant must map to one of the runtime trace event types.
- Testing: every release must include an observability smoke test that verifies retention and exportability of 7 sample events.
- PR requirement: changes to telemetry schema or retention policies must include an ADR and a compliance review tag.

Risk & Exceptions workflow (short):
1) Submit a Risk Exception Request (RER) in the Risk Registry with justification, compensating controls, and TTL.
2) Security + Compliance review within 5 business days.
3) If approved, implement compensating controls (e.g., additional network egress restrictions, higher-frequency snapshots) and record automatic reminders for expiry.
4) All exceptions affecting retention must be escalated to Legal for customer notification if required by contract.

SLAs and operational targets:
- Evidence readiness SLA: initial evidence snapshot (logs + primary artifacts) available within 4 hours for hosted incidents during business hours; 8 hours for off-hours.
- Artifact hash verification: 100% of collected artifacts must have a recorded checksum within 1 hour of ingestion.
- Immutability enforcement: object-lock applied within 30 minutes of artifact upload.

Compliance checklist (pre-audit):
- Confirm evidence ticket exists and custody receipts are signed.
- Validate retention policy references and regional placement for each artifact.
- Verify KMS key IDs and key rotation status (last rotation within 365 days unless justified).
- Ensure difference between raw and redacted artifacts is documented and that redactions preserve original object hashes in metadata.

Appendices:
A. Artifact metadata JSON schema (single-line example):
{"artifact_id":"EVID-12345-20270701","collector":"samuel.green","collected_at":"2027-07-01T11:02:00Z","sha256":"<hex>","storage_path":"s3://redwood-evidence/EVID-12345/...","kms_key_id":"arn:aws:kms:...","retention_policy":"audit-7y"}

B. Quick reference commands:
- Export logs: logging-cli export --service <svc> --start <ts> --end <ts> --output s3://redwood-evidence/<incident-id>/
- Lock object: aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket <bucket> --object-lock-configuration Config=...
- Compute hash: sha256sum <file>

C. Frequently asked questions:
- Q: Who approves cross-border transfer of forensic artifacts?
  A: Security + Legal must approve. If customer residency constraints exist, follow private deployment OET flow.
- Q: Can developers access raw evidence?
  A: No. Developers require a JIT approval with explicit business justification; all access is logged and time-limited.

Revision history:
- 2027-03-15: Initial draft by Arielle Chen.
- 2027-05-10: Added private deployment OET flow (reviewers: Diego Morales).
- 2027-07-02: Published with updated SLA targets and retention matrix adjustments.

End of playbook.

payload.page_title: Incident scope decision tree and evidence collection playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines a deterministic decision tree to scope security incidents and a prioritized, evidence-first collection process that spans RBAC/auth artifacts, audit logs, model-serving telemetry, data residency concerns, and secure-SDLC triggers. It is intended for the Security Incident Lead (SIL), oncall SREs, and the forensic engineers who will assemble compliance evidence for audits and legal review.

Goals
- Determine incident scope within 30 minutes of triage start.
- Collect preserved evidence within 2 hours for high-severity incidents (P0/P1).
- Produce a compliance evidence bundle within 48 hours when required by legal or regional data-residency constraints.

Audience and ownership
- Primary owner: security (Incident Response).
- Secondary owners: eng-sre (log access), eng-serving-runtime (model telemetry), eng-private-deployments (data residency triggers).
- SIL responsibilities: run the decision tree, authorize containment actions, sign off on evidence handoff.

Decision tree (high-level)
1) Confirm detection source
   - Is the alert from an internal monitoring system (tracing/alerts/console) or an external report (customer/legal/regulator)?
   - If external, mark as candidate for restricted evidence packaging and notify Legal.
2) Rapid impact assessment (R0 - R3)
   - R0: Confirmed data exfiltration of customer PII or model weights.
   - R1: Suspicious authentication events or privilege escalations.
   - R2: System instability or degraded components without evidence of compromise.
   - R3: Informational or false-positive.
3) Residency and compliance flags
   - Does affected data fall under geo-residency or contractual restrictions? (EU/UK/CAN/Customer VPC).
   - If yes, escalate to Data Residency Owner and restrict exportable artifacts.
4) Evidence tiering decision
   - If R0 or R1 -> Tier A evidence collection (full forensic capture).
   - If R2 -> Tier B evidence (targeted logs + configuration snapshots).
   - If R3 -> Tier C (summary + monitoring retention).

Prioritized evidence collection checklist (Tier A / high-severity)
1) Snapshot and isolate:
   - Create immutable VM/container snapshots of affected hosts (note storage location and hash).
   - For managed GPU inference pods, snapshot the model-serving node and preserve KV-cache dumps where possible.
2) Access & RBAC artifacts (Collect first)
   - Identity events: authentication logs, MFA failures, JIT privilege activations, and service account tokens issued (last 7 days).
   - Group and role changes: audit entries showing role bindings, entitlement grants, and approval artifacts.
   - Active sessions: list of current sessions, open sockets, and process owners.
3) Audit logging (Collect second, but preserve early)
   - Ingestion: preserve raw audit streams for the incident window (+30 minutes before detection).
   - Relevant tables/indices: index names, schema versions, retention policies.\   - Query examples (CLI):
     # preserve index snapshot (Elasticsearch example)
     curl -XPOST "https://es.local/_snapshot/forensic_repo/snap1/_create?wait_for_completion=true" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"indices":"audit-*,auth-*,serving-*","ignore_unavailable":true}'
4) Telemetry and model-serving traces (Collect third)
   - Per-request traces for model endpoints: request id, model variant, sequence length, token counts.
   - Cache/KV artifacts and batching metadata.
5) Data residency-sensitive artifacts
   - If data is geo-fenced, collect metadata only and escalate for legal approval before exporting full payloads.
   - Maintain a redaction manifest for PII before any cross-region transfer.
6) Build and SDLC artifacts (Collect last)
   - Recent CI/CD pipeline runs, release tags, deployment approvals, and dependency manifests that could have introduced the change.

Roles and responsibilities matrix
| Role | Immediate action | Evidence ownership | Escalation |
| SIL (Security Incident Lead) | Run tree, set severity, approve Tier | Approves evidence package | Legal, CTO, Customer-commit owner |
| Forensic Engineer | Execute collection checklists, hash manifests | Stores immutable artifacts in forensic store | SIL |
| Oncall SRE | Provide snapshots, network captures, and shift logs | Live system telemetry collection | Forensic Engineer |
| Data Residency Owner | Approve cross-border exports, advise redaction | Manages residency flags and manifests | Legal |

Minimum artifact manifest (required for Tier A)
- incident-id: string (human and UUID)
- collection-time-window: string (UTC start/end)
- collectors: list of names and emails
- artifact-list: list of artifact identifiers and SHA256 hashes
- redaction-manifest: list of fields redacted and reason
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-0458",
  "window": "2026-02-28T16:12:00Z/2026-02-28T18:30:00Z",
  "collectors": ["lena.ortiz@redwood.ai", "marcos.lee@redwood.ai"],
  "artifacts": [
    {"id":"auth-events-20260228-1","sha256":"e3b0c442..."},
    {"id":"es-snapshot-20260228-1","sha256":"af12b9..."}
  ]
}

Evidence packaging SLOs and retention guidance
- Tier A: package produced within 48 hours; forensic retention 7 years (or contract-specified).
- Tier B: package produced within 7 days; retention 2 years.
- Tier C: incident summary in the incident log within 48 hours; follow standard retention.

Chain-of-custody and attestations
1) Every collector signs the manifest with an HMAC using their SSO private key and stores the signature in the evidence store.
2) For restricted/data residency incidents, Legal must sign the export authorization before any artifact leaves the region.
3) All handoffs must be recorded in the incident timeline (UTC timestamped) with actor and reason.

Special procedures by subsystem
- RBAC & Auth: preserve identity provider logs (OIDC provider audit, SCIM provisioning, IAM change approvals). If service accounts are implicated, rotate keys after snapshotting and log the rotation event as part of the manifest.
- Audit logging: do not reindex or transform raw logs prior to snapshot. If redaction is required, keep original checksums and store redacted copies separately.
- Data residency: if affected tenant data is located in a customer-managed VPC or a jurisdiction with legal hold, follow the Private Deployments evidence export checklist before any cross-boundary transfer.
- Secure SDLC: snapshot the exact CI artifact (container digest, commit SHA, build metadata). If a deployment approval bypass is suspected, include the pipeline run and approval token history.

Communication and escalation steps
1) SIL sets an internal comms channel (private incident room) with a documented retention and membership.
2) Notify Legal and Privacy for Tier A incidents and request export authorization early.
3) If a customer is affected, follow the Customer Communication SOP (product-docs) and obtain Legal/CS approval before external disclosure.

Query recipes and utilities (examples)
- Find all auth failures for a user in the window (Clickhouse example):
  SELECT * FROM auth_events WHERE user_id = 'alice@example.com' AND event_time BETWEEN toDateTime('2026-02-28 16:00:00') AND toDateTime('2026-02-28 18:30:00') AND result = 'FAIL'
- Capture open network connections on a host (linux):
  sudo ss -tupan > /forensic/INC-2026-XXXX/ss-connections.txt

Table: Recommended artifact retention by category
| Artifact category | Recommended retention | Export constraints |
| audit logs (raw) | 3 years (min); 7 years preferred for regulated customers | Export only after Legal approval for cross-border |
| RBAC change history | 7 years | Redaction allowed for PII identifiers in some regions |
| Model-serving traces | 1 year default; extend to 3 years for regulated customers | Sensitive request payloads require redaction |
| Build and CI artifacts | 2 years | No export constraints unless containing customer secrets |

Post-incident review and evidence disposition
- Within 10 business days, Security and Forensics produce an Evidence Disposition memo listing what was archived, what was returned to live systems, and any data destroyed per legal direction.
- Retention exceptions must be filed in the Risk Exceptions tracker with owner, justification, and expiration date.

Appendix A — Quick checklist (first 2 hours)
1) SIL: classify severity and set incident id.
2) Forensic Engineer: start VM/container snapshots and collect RBAC artifacts.
3) Oncall SRE: preserve audit index snapshot and provide query endpoints.
4) Data Residency Owner: flag any geo-sensitive payloads and approve manifest redaction plan.
5) Legal: if notified, confirm whether export is permitted and request embargo if required.

Appendix B — Contacts (roles only)
- Security Incident Lead: security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Forensics: forensics-team@redwood.ai
- Data Residency Owner: data-residency@redwood.ai
- Legal (incidents): legal-incidents@redwood.ai

Related documents
- Forensic log preservation and legal-hold playbook (link in related_pages)
- RBAC entitlement provenance and retention framework (link in related_pages)

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Created by Lena Ortiz (initial draft).
- 2026-03-01: Updated collection SLOs and added Clickhouse query example.

End of document
