payload.page_title: Pre-deployment Authorization Failure Modes and Forensic Checklist

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents anticipated authorization (RBAC/authz) failure modes that can occur during or immediately after pre-deployment and provides a forensic preservation and evidence-collection checklist to meet regulatory and internal compliance expectations. It is intended for security engineers, SREs, release approvers, and incident responders who must preserve evidentiary artifacts for audits, legal holds, or cross-region incident investigations.

Scope

- Applicable to: all model-serving, control-plane, and customer-metadata services that are staged or deployed through Redwood CI/CD pipelines.
- NOT applicable to purely client-side UI features (see UI release checklist).
- Regions: global; data-residency notes are included per-customer region.

Owner and escalation

- Primary owner: Security Response (security oncall rota).
- Secondary owner: Platform SRE oncall.
- Pager duties: security@redwood (primary), platform-oncall@redwood (secondary).

Summary of common pre-deployment authorization failure modes

1) Policy Drift at Compile-time
- Cause: Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego) changes not included in the same PR as code requiring new entitlements.
- Symptom: Deployment passes CI but runtime denies new API verbs for service identity -> 403s in smoke tests.

2) Attribute Broker Mapping Mismatch
- Cause: Identity provider (IDP) attribute changes (groups/claims) vs. attribute-to-role mapping in attribute broker.
- Symptom: Users with expected roles lose access; automated canary requests show permission errors.

3) JIT Provisioning Race
- Cause: Just-in-time entitlement activation (JIT) race between provisioning pipeline and service startup.
- Symptom: Temporary 401/403 windows for new instances during scale-up.

4) Service Identity Rotation/Key Mismatch
- Cause: Missing secret rotation step or stale service account token in image.
- Symptom: Mutual TLS/Tokens rejected; inter-service auth fails during deployment.

5) Environment-scoped Policy Leak
- Cause: Dev policy accidentally applied in stage/prod through IaC misconfig.
- Symptom: Over-permissive access in target environment or missing constraints.

Audit and logging prerequisites (what to capture and where)

- Minimum required event set (all services):
  - authn:login_attempt, authn:token_issue, authn:token_refresh
  - authz:policy_evaluation (include decision, policy_id, input_hash)
  - authz:decision_denied (include resource, principal, action, reason_id)
  - identity:attribute_change (old_claims, new_claims, actor, source_commit)
  - service:identity_rotation (service_id, old_key_id, new_key_id, rotate_actor)
  - pipeline:deploy_action (ci_job_id, commit_sha, artifact_id, target_namespace)

- Schema fields (required per event): timestamp, event_id, service, environment, region, request_id/correlation_id, principal_id, resource, action, outcome, policy_version, raw_payload_link.

- Retention and SLOs:
  - Ingest SLO: 99.9% of auth events available in audit index within 60 seconds of occurrence.
  - Retention baseline: 365 days hot; 5 years cold (for enterprise customers with contract).
  - Evidence hold policy: When a legal hold is opened, retention escalates to immutable 7-year hold for related objects.

Pre-deployment gating and SDLC checks (automated and manual)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Policy-as-code test suite (unit + integration): no new deny decisions for baseline smoke requests.
   - Command example:
     opa test -v policy/
2) Attribute mapping CI: compare IDP claim fixture to mapping table; fail on unmapped required attributes.
3) Authz simulation: run canary simulator against staging with new policy bundle.
   - Example: ./tools/authz-sim --bundle build/policy.tar.gz --test-suite smoke.json
4) Secret scaffolding validation: verify rotated credentials baked into image manifest.
   - Terraform plan checks and baked-in envscan: tfsec + internal secret-scanner.

Manual gates (required if any automated gate fails or high blast radius):
- Security review signoff in PR (security reviewer must check RBAC diffs).
- Scoped deployment windows for cross-region changes.

Detection and immediate containment steps (runbook)

1) Detect
- Alert triggers: sudden spike in authz:decision_denied for a service (>500/min for 5m) or failed smoke test post-deploy.
- Query example: authz_decisions | where service=="model-router" and outcome=="deny" | count_over_time(5m).

2) Contain
- If high-volume denies causing outage: roll back the deployment to previous artifact_id with known-good policy bindings.
- If isolated to single namespace, temporarily disable new policy bundle (use emergency-allow only with strict audit).

3) Preserve Evidence (first 2 hours are critical)
- Snapshot audit index segment containing relevant request_ids.
- Collect the following artifacts (minimum):
  - CI artifact manifest (ci_job_id, commit_sha)
  - Policy bundle (policy tarball) and policy bundle hash
  - Attribute broker mapping file at deployment time
  - IDP audit for attribute changes (export for time window +/- 1 hour)
  - Service logs (stdout/stderr), structured auth logs, and runtime metrics for the affected instances
  - Kubernetes API server audit logs for the target namespace (if applicable)
  - Machine images/tarball or container image digest for deployed artifacts
  - KMS key rotation logs and secret manager access logs for rotation window
  - Network flow logs (VPC flow / equivalent) if lateral movement suspected

- For each artifact include: collector name, start/end time, and storage location (immutable).
- Use evidence packaging tool: ./bin/evidence-collector --case-id <INCID> --artifact <type> --out s3://evidence-bucket/<INCID>/

Preservation commands / examples

- Elastic snapshot: curl -XPUT "${ES_HOST}/_snapshot/evidence_repo/snap-<INCID>?wait_for_completion=true" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"indices":"auth-*", "ignore_unavailable":true}'
- Kubernetes API audit slice: kubectl logs -n kube-system audit-logger --since=2h | gzip > /tmp/<INCID>-k8s-audit.gz
- IDP export (example for Okta via API): curl -s -H "Authorization: SSWS $OKTA_TOKEN" "https://api.okta.com/v1/logs?since=2026-01-12T00:00:00Z" > /tmp/<INCID>-okta-logs.json

Data residency and retention considerations

- If the incident involves customer data from region-bound customers (EU, UK, APAC), evidence copies must be stored in the same geo-fence for the duration of legal/local privacy holds. See: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/geo-smart-retention-and-audit-evidence-playbook-2027 for mapping rules.
- When transferring evidence for cross-border legal requests, consult Legal and Data Privacy before moving copies across regions.

Evidentiary packaging and chain-of-custody

- Evidence package metadata (required fields): case_id, collected_by, collected_at (UTC), artifact_type, original_location, integrity_hash (SHA256), storage_location, custody_chain (list of principal_ids), legal_hold_flag.
- Signing: all packaged artifacts must be signed by collector via internal signing service (signer-service).
- Maintain immutable audit trail for all access to evidence bucket; access requires two-person approval for restricted cases.

Compliance evidence workflow (timeline and responsibilities)

- T+0–2h: detection, containment, and initial evidence snapshot (security & platform).
- T+2–24h: complete evidence collection and package creation (assigned forensics engineer).
- T+24–72h: preliminary incident brief and evidence submission to Legal & Compliance (security).
- T+72h+: deep investigation, timeline reconstruction, and executive summary (security + SRE + Product).

Requesting and approving risk exceptions (pre-deploy)

- If a deployment requires an authorization exception (e.g., temporary broad role for migration), submit an authorization-exception request via the risk registry with the following:
  - business rationale, duration, compensating controls (audit sampling cadence, additional monitoring), rollback plan, and list of impacted principals.
- Approval requires: Security lead + Platform lead signoff. Exceptions >72h require Legal review.

Post-incident controls and SDLC hardening recommendations

- Enforce policy-as-code bundles are always reviewed in the same PR as application changes.
- Expand authz simulation coverage to include negative and race-condition scenarios.
- Add CI check: alert on any PR that modifies attribute mapping files without Security reviewer.
- Automate evidence packaging for any pre-deploy smoke test failure to reduce time-to-preservation.

Diagnostics and useful queries (examples)

- Find all denies for a principal in a time window:
  authz_decisions | where principal_id==":principal" and outcome=="deny" | sort timestamp desc
- Link CI job to deny events: join authz_decisions on correlation_id == ci.correlation_id where ci.commit_sha=="<sha>"

Appendix: quick checklist (for responders)

1) Identify scope (services, namespaces, customers)
2) Trigger containment (rollback or disable new policy bundle)
3) Snapshot audit index and export IDP logs
4) Collect policy bundle, attribute mapping, and CI artifact manifests
5) Package artifacts, compute SHA256, sign package, and place in evidence-bucket
6) Notify Legal if customer data or cross-border flows are involved
7) Open risk-exception entry if temporary mitigations are applied

References and related pages

- /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/authorization-logging-and-deprovisioning-guidance-2026
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/secure-sdlc/sdlc-security-gates-rbac-audit-residency-checklist-2026
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/geo-smart-retention-and-audit-evidence-playbook-2027

Revision history

- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Aisha Chen.
- 2026-02-04: Added evidence packaging commands and data-residency notes (reviewers: Marcus Diaz).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized retention SLOs and legal-hold procedures; published.

payload.page_title: Failover and Security Boundaries (Data Residency, Audit Logging, and Cross-Region Routing)

sections.body:
This document defines **security boundaries that must be preserved during regional failover** for Redwood Inference (Hosted API and Dedicated). It specifies:
- How **data residency constraints** restrict routing/failover.
- **Audit logging** requirements for automated and manual failover actions.
- Guardrails for **cross-region routing** by customer tier (especially Enterprise and regulated workloads).
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Smart routing and policy engine changes that can influence region selection.
- Failover automation controller behavior (including dry-run and simulation modes).
- On-call execution and controlled failover tests ("game days").
sections.heading: This guidance is mandatory for

sections.body:
**In scope**
- Hosted API and Dedicated failover behavior across Redwood-managed regions.
- Data residency enforcement at routing and control-plane policy layers.
- Audit events, retention, and access control for failover decisioning.

**Out of scope**
- Customer-specific Private deployment automation (see Private guidance). This doc provides patterns only.
- Changes to customer contracts/SLA language (handled separately).
sections.heading: Scope / Non-scope

sections.body:
- **Region**: A cloud provider region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- **Residency boundary**: The allowed set of regions in which a tenant’s **inference data plane** traffic may be processed.
- **Data plane**: Prompts, model inputs, outputs, embeddings, and tool/function payloads processed by inference.
- **Control plane**: Tenant metadata, config, quotas, routing policy config, and operational telemetry.
- **Failover**: Automatic or operator-approved routing change that shifts traffic from a primary region to another region.
- **Enterprise tier**: Contracted customers with security requirements (auditability, residency, notification expectations).
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) **Residency first**: If a tenant has a residency constraint, failover MUST stay within that boundary. Availability must be achieved *within* the allowed set; otherwise we prefer **graceful degradation** (e.g., 503 + Retry-After) over violating residency.
2) **Explicit allow-listing**: Cross-region routing must be controlled by explicit configuration per tenant (or per org) and audited.
3) **Least privilege and separation of duties**: Only designated on-call/SRE roles may initiate or approve production failover actions. Changes to residency boundaries require Security approval.
4) **Audit everything**: Every recommendation, execution, rollback, and override must emit a structured audit event with enough evidence to reconstruct “who/what/why/when/impact.”
5) **Deterministic policy evaluation**: Given the same inputs, routing policy evaluation must produce the same output (to enable security review, auditability, and predictable enforcement).
sections.heading: Security principles (must-haves)

sections.body:
Redwood supports the following residency categories for the **inference data plane** (prompts/outputs/embeddings):

| Category | Description | Example allowed regions | Example prohibited regions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global (no residency) | Tenant allows processing in any supported region | us-east, us-west, eu-west, ap-southeast | none |
| US-only | Processing restricted to US regions | us-east, us-west | eu-west |
| EU-only | Processing restricted to EU regions | eu-west, eu-central | us-east |
| Region-pinned | Processing restricted to a single region | eu-west only | all others |
| Custom boundary | Contract-defined set | (explicit per tenant) | all non-listed |
sections.heading: Residency categories

sections.body:
- Residency applies to **data plane processing**. Control-plane metadata may be replicated as needed for availability, but must follow the data classification and storage policies in Security standards.
- Region naming above is conceptual; the authoritative list is in routing config.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- **Self-serve / Standard Hosted**: Default category is **Global**, unless the tenant explicitly configures otherwise.
- **Enterprise Hosted**: Default category is **Global**, but residency constraints may be contractually required (EU-only, US-only, or Custom boundary). These constraints MUST be encoded as enforceable routing policies.
- **Dedicated**: Default category follows the contracted deployment footprint. Failover is restricted to the customer’s approved Dedicated regions.
- **Private**: Residency enforcement is the customer’s responsibility, but Redwood-provided guidance should mirror the principles in this document.
sections.heading: Default behavior by tier

sections.body:
1) **Do not route data plane traffic outside the tenant’s residency boundary.**
2) **Do not “temporarily” violate residency to restore availability.** If no in-boundary failover target is healthy, degrade service within the boundary.
3) **Do not change residency boundaries during an incident** to work around a capacity/regional outage unless:
   - Approved by Security (delegate on-call) AND
   - Approved by the customer (if Enterprise/regulated) AND
   - Documented in an incident timeline with explicit timestamps and scope.
sections.heading: Hard rules (never violate)

sections.body:
- **Within-boundary failover** (preferred):
  - EU-only: eu-west → eu-central
  - US-only: us-east → us-west
  - Custom: primary → secondary (both explicitly allow-listed)
- **Region-pinned tenants**:
  - No cross-region failover. Use load shedding and communicate impairment.
sections.heading: Allowed failover patterns

sections.body:
Routing may decide to fail over due to reachability, 5xx burn, tail latency burn, or capacity exhaustion; however:
- The policy engine MUST apply **residency gating as an absolute precondition** before evaluating “best” region.
- If the “best available” region is outside boundary, the decision must become **DEGRADE** (or keep traffic in-region with protective measures), not “fail over.”
sections.heading: Decision hierarchy interaction (security perspective)

sections.body:
The policy engine must support a first-class predicate (conceptual):
- `allowed_regions(tenant_id)` returns a stable allow-list.
- Region selection must be `candidate_regions = healthy_regions ∩ allowed_regions`.
- If `candidate_regions` is empty, policy result must be one of:
  - `DEGRADE_WITHIN_BOUNDARY` (e.g., return 503/429 with Retry-After, reduce max tokens, disable optional features), or
  - `STAY_PUT_WITH_PROTECTION` (tight circuit breakers and load shedding), depending on product behavior.

Security requirement: the code path must be **provably non-bypassable** (no “emergency override” without producing an audit event and requiring explicit approvals).
sections.heading: Residency gating in the policy engine

sections.body:
- Residency boundary configuration must be stored in a **controlled configuration system** with:
  - Change review (required reviewers include Security for any boundary-tightening/loosening).
  - Immutable change history.
  - Rollback support.
sections.heading: For Hosted and Dedicated

sections.body:
- Hard region allow-lists bound to capacity pools.
- Explicit “no failover without approval” requirements.
sections.heading: Dedicated customers may have

sections.body:
- Respect pool-level constraints (do not shift load to a pool not designated for that tenant).
- Coordinate with drain/evacuation procedures without exposing cross-tenant data.
sections.heading: Failover automation for Dedicated must

sections.body:
All systems participating in failover must emit structured events for:
- Recommendation (dry-run computation)
- Execution (policy flip applied)
- Rollback (automated or manual)
- Override (operator forcing a decision)
- Blocked action (attempted failover rejected due to residency boundary)
sections.heading: What must be logged

sections.body:
- **event_type**: recommend | execute | rollback | override | blocked
- **timestamp_utc**
- **tenant_id / org_id** (or an internal stable identifier)
- **tenant_tier**: self_serve | enterprise | dedicated
- **residency_category**: global | us_only | eu_only | region_pinned | custom
- **primary_region**, **target_region** (target may be empty for blocked/degrade)
- **decision**: failover | degrade | stay_put
- **reason_code**: reachability | error_burn | latency_burn | capacity | manual
- **evidence_refs**: links/IDs to region health snapshots, burn-rate alert IDs, probe runs
- **actor**: automation_controller | user:<id>
- **approval_state**: not_required | pending | approved | denied
- **change_id**: routing policy config revision / feature flag revision
- **correlation_ids**: incident_id (if any), request_id samples (optional), dashboard annotation ID
sections.heading: Each audit event must include (as applicable)

sections.body:
- Default retention (internal): **180 days** for audit events.
- Enterprise add-on / compliance packages: **≥ 400 days** retention, unless otherwise specified.
- Access must be restricted to:
  - SRE on-call and routing/control-plane engineers with an operational need
  - Security & compliance for audits and investigations
  - Customer Success only via approved exports/redactions (no raw prompt data)
sections.heading: Retention and access

sections.body:
- Prompt text, model outputs, embeddings, or customer payloads.
- Customer secrets (API keys, tokens).

If request samples are needed for investigation, use approved secure logging mechanisms and follow incident response data handling procedures.
sections.heading: Audit events must not include

sections.body:
Example: EU-only customer and eu-west is impaired.
- If eu-central is healthy and has capacity: **fail over to eu-central**.
- If no EU region is healthy/capable: **degrade within EU**.
  - Return 503 + Retry-After (preferred for overload)
  - Enforce stricter rate limits / max tokens for fairness
  - Disable non-essential optional features if supported by product policy
sections.heading: If a region impairment occurs within a constrained boundary

sections.body:
- During a real incident: follow the Regional Failover Communication Playbook.
- For planned tests: notify only customers whose traffic might be impacted, and explicitly state that residency boundaries will not be violated.
- If any customer perceives cross-region behavior, immediately:
  - Pull audit events for the tenant
  - Validate residency gating decisions
  - Engage Security and Support escalation
sections.heading: Communication expectations (Enterprise)

sections.body:
1) Confirm residency gating is active and validated in staging.
2) Explicitly exclude region-pinned and regulated tenants unless written approval is obtained.
3) Ensure audit events and dashboard annotations are functioning.
4) Validate that “blocked due to residency” is observable (metric + audit event).
sections.heading: Prior to production tests

sections.body: - Any attempted out-of-boundary action must be treated as a **SEV-2 security incident** if it results in data plane processing outside the boundary.
sections.heading: During the test

sections.body: - Export the audit event summary for the test window and attach it to the game day results doc.
sections.heading: After the test

sections.body:
1) Identify tenant tier and residency category.
2) Confirm proposed target region is in allow-list.
3) Confirm automation approval requirements (some Enterprise/Dedicated tenants require ack).
4) Verify audit event emission is healthy (controller + policy engine).
5) Execute or approve.
6) If boundary prevents failover, choose degrade/stay-put path and update incident comms accordingly.
sections.heading: When failover automation suggests a policy change

sections.body:
- Primary region: us-east (should not happen for EU-only; indicates misconfiguration)
- Required action:
  - Immediately block and correct routing policy (within incident change management)
  - File Security follow-up for residency misconfiguration
  - Confirm no data plane processing occurred outside EU via audit/telemetry
sections.heading: Example A: Enterprise EU-only tenant during us-east incident

sections.body:
- Primary: eu-west
- Allowed: any region
- Action: fail over to us-east (or nearest healthy region by policy), emit audit events for recommend + execute + any rollback.
sections.heading: Example B: Global tenant during eu-west reachability failure

sections.body:
- Primary: eu-west
- Allowed: eu-west only
- Action: do not fail over. Enable protective controls (circuit breakers, load shedding), return Retry-After, and communicate impact.
sections.heading: Example C: Region-pinned tenant when region is impaired

sections.body:
- Count of `failover_blocked_due_to_residency` by tier
- Audit event delivery health (ingest lag, drop rate)
- Unauthorized/rare overrides (manual force actions)
- Drift detection: tenants with residency=EU-only receiving any non-EU routing decisions (should be zero)
sections.heading: Minimum dashboards/alerts needed

sections.body:
- Owner: **Security & Compliance** (in partnership with SRE Reliability)
- Routing enforcement: **Smart Routing** team (Mina Haddad) + Policy engine owner (Jordan Lee)
- Audit event pipeline: **SRE / Observability** (Allison Grant)
sections.heading: Ownership and change control

sections.body:
- Security & Compliance
- SRE Reliability lead (Sean Gallagher or delegate)
- Routing policy tech lead (Ravi Menon)
sections.heading: Changes to this document require review from

sections.body:
- Define a standard “custom boundary” representation shared between Hosted and Dedicated policy configs.
- Confirm enterprise retention defaults for audit logs align with compliance add-ons.
- Add automated drift checks that continuously validate residency enforcement using synthetic tenant policies (no customer data).
sections.heading: Open questions / follow-ups

payload.page_title: Compliance Orbit: Access Procedures and Evidence Orchestration (Incident → SDLC)

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook defines the unified access containment, audit evidence orchestration, and downstream SDLC handoff processes we use when an incident impacts authorization, audit logging, or data residency guarantees. It bridges RBAC/auth, audit-collection, evidence packaging, and the secure-SDLC change loop so that post-incident remediation becomes measurable and auditable.

Scope
- Applies to incidents that: authz failures (mis-scoped roles, privilege escalation), suspicious access patterns, audit-log gaps, cross-region data residency concerns, or suspected exfiltration involving inference request payloads.
- Environments: hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private/VPC deployments.
- Systems in scope: authz-service, identity-broker, audit-collector, forwarder (kinesis/audit-stream), evidence-bundler, redwood-console, kms/hsm.

Owners and roles
- Incident Commander (IC): Security On-Call (primary).
- Auth Lead: Identity team (owns authz-service).
- Audit Lead: Observability team (owns audit-collector and retention pipelines).
- Privacy / Residency Lead: Compliance team.
- Evidence Custodian: SRE assigned to evidence-bundler.
- SDLC Handoff Owner: Product Engineering Manager.

When to apply this playbook
1) Unauthorized access confirmed or suspected.
2) Audit logs show missing segments or inconsistent indexing.
3) Data residency policy may have been violated by a failover or cross-region re-route.

Immediate containment (0–2 hours) — tactical steps
1. Triage & scope: IC declares Incident and tags severity with classification (see Severity table).
2. Freeze-delegate: For severe authz compromise, put target roles into quarantine by toggling role-activation flag (authz-service):
   - CLI: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" https://authz.redwood.internal/roles/quarantine -d '{"role_ids": ["data-processor","dedicated-admin"]}'
3. Session invalidation: Trigger short-lived-token revocation for affected clients:
   - CLI: /usr/local/bin/authctl revoke-sessions --filter "role:data-processor OR user:service-account-123" --reason "Incident containment"
4. Short-term routing: If cross-region routing caused residency violation, flip routing policy to region-only fallback:
   - redwood-console → Routing → Policy: set incident_residency_mode = strict
5. Preserve memory state: If model-serving nodes are implicated, snapshot KV caches and model metadata to evidence-bundler.

Evidence collection & packaging (2–24 hours)
Goal: produce a minimally sufficient, tamper-evident evidence bundle for auditors and legal.
Checklist (Evidence Custodian)
- Collect authz logs: token issuance, role evaluation traces, JIT activations.
- Collect session artifacts: revocation commands, session IDs, JWTs (where allowed).
- Gather audit-collector export: raw events for time window T0-6h → T1+6h.
- Capture routing and deployment events: cloud provider API logs, autoscaler events, traffic policies.
- Preserve config snapshots: /etc/authz/config, policy repo commit hash, infra IaC diff.
- Hashing & signing: sha256 of bundle and sign with evidence key in HSM (command below).

Evidence packaging commands (example)
- Export raw events (BigQuery): bq query --nouse_legacy_sql '\n  SELECT * FROM audit_events WHERE timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(TIMESTAMP("T0"), INTERVAL 6 HOUR) AND TIMESTAMP_ADD(TIMESTAMP("T1"), INTERVAL 6 HOUR);' > /tmp/audit_events.json
- Hash & sign:
  sha256sum /tmp/audit_events.json > /tmp/audit_events.json.sha256
  hsm-sign --key evidence-signing --input /tmp/audit_events.json --output /tmp/audit_events.json.sig
- Create bundle:
  tar czf /evidence/incident-${INC_ID}.tgz /tmp/audit_events.json /var/log/authz/* /etc/authz/config
  sha256sum /evidence/incident-${INC_ID}.tgz > /evidence/incident-${INC_ID}.tgz.sha256

Audit queries & artifacts (examples)
- Authz policy evaluation (Elasticsearch):
  GET /authz-eval/_search?q=request_id:${REQUEST_ID}&sort=timestamp:asc
- Token issuance timeline (SQL):
  SELECT issued_at, user_id, client_id, scopes FROM tokens WHERE user_id='service-account-123' ORDER BY issued_at DESC LIMIT 100;
- Suspicious pattern matcher (pseudo):
  COUNT(requests) GROUP BY user_id, region HAVING COUNT(requests) > 10 * median_weekly_requests

Decision matrix: Residency vs. Action (table)
| Residency impact | Immediate action | Retention & evidence target | Compliance owner |
|------------------|------------------|----------------------------|------------------|
| Potential cross-region exposure | Set incident_residency_mode = strict; snapshot routing; notify legal | Retain raw events 7 years (if PII) or 2 years otherwise; collect consent artifacts | Privacy / Residency Lead |
| Confirmed cross-border data movement | Pause cross-region sync; initiate cross-border notification workflow | Retain all packet captures and forwarder logs; notify regulators as required | Privacy / Legal |
| No residency impact | Normal containment; document rationale | Standard retention per policy | Audit Lead |

Severity classification (quick reference)
1. Sev-1 (Critical): Active privilege escalation affecting >1 production cluster or confirmed exfiltration of customer data.
2. Sev-2 (High): Scoped privilege misuse or audit gaps covering a single customer or legal region.
3. Sev-3 (Medium): Misconfiguration with no evidence of misuse; local containment possible.

Risk & exception handling
- If a required evidence artifact cannot be produced (e.g., rotated logs, truncated stream), create an Exception Record in the Risk Registry and escalate to Risk Board within 48 hours. The Exception Record must include: missing artifact, reason, compensating controls, estimated time to availability.
- For short-lived infra changes required to contain incident (e.g., emergency role quarantine), open a post-incident change in the SDLC backlog tagged emergency-access and include a reviewer from Privacy and SRE.

Post-incident SDLC handoff (24 hours → 6 weeks)
1. RCA & evidence package: Evidence Custodian uploads signed bundle to secure evidence storage and links it to the incident ticket.
2. Security remediation PR: Auth Lead creates a code/config PR with tests, a migration plan, and a rollback. PR template must include an evidence link and a compliance checklist.
3. Release gating: Any change that touches authz/service-identity, audit pipeline, or region-routing MUST pass the security gate: unit tests, integration tests (with replay of previously captured audit events), and an IR regression test.
4. Audit review & sign-off: Compliance team performs sign-off and records decision in the Compliance Ledger.

SDLC review checklist (PR requirements)
- Commit message references: Incident ID.
- Test matrix: replay of audit events, role-eval unit tests, scoped canary in Dedicated region.
- Evidence attachment: signed bundle hash and HSM signature.
- Rollback plan: explicit steps, opt-out routing toggles.

Monitoring & regression detection (ongoing)
- Post-fix, create an automated regression job that replays a subset of traffic and verifies: role evaluations unchanged, no new cross-region route, audit events present for every request.
- SLOs: authz-service must answer role evals in < 30ms P95; audit-collector ingestion latency < 60s P95. Degrade alerts if thresholds are missed during rollout.

Retention and legal notes
- Baseline retention: audit events = 13 months; privileged auth traces = 3 years; signed evidence bundles = 7 years.
- For regulated customers with different contracts, the Privacy / Legal lead will create a per-customer retention override and document in the Compliance Ledger.

Templates and artifacts (links)
- Incident evidence manifest template: evidence-bundler/templates/manifest.yaml
- SDLC emergency-PR template: engineering/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/emergency_authz_fix.md
- Risk exception form: /tools/risk-registry/new_exception_form

Appendix: Example incident timeline (illustrative)
- T0 (00:00): Alert from anomaly detector: high rate of role elevation events for service-account-123.
- T0+8m: IC declared; mapped affected systems; quarantine roles.
- T0+30m: Sessions revoked for affected tokens; snapshot audit window started.
- T0+3h: Evidence bundle created and signed; Exception Record opened (missing packet capture).
- T0+48h: Auth Lead opened remediation PR with tests; Security gate scheduled for T0+7 days.

Contact matrix
- Security On-Call: pager pagerduty://redwood-security-oncall
- Identity team Slack: #team-identity
- Observability: #team-observability
- Compliance / Legal: compliance@redwood.com

Notes and references
- This playbook ties into the evidence standards in /confluence/security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence/evidence-provenance-proofing-cross-domain-playbook-2026.
- For audit log schema, see audit-collector/README.md and schema_v2 in the observability repo.

Revision history
- 2024-11-08: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-02-12: Added SDLC gating requirements and extended retention guidance (reviewed by Arjun Patel, Sofia Martinez, Evan Brooks).

payload.page_title: Privileged Session Proxy — Evidence Orchestration & Retention Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the operational pattern we use to proxy, capture, and package privileged interactive sessions across Redwood-managed control planes and customer-managed Private deployments. It ties together RBAC controls, immutable audit logging, data-residency constraints, secure SDLC instrumentation, and incident-response evidence workflows so that privileged activity is recorded, searchable, and admissible for compliance audits.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all privileged access paths: admin console, host jumpboxes, Kubernetes API (kubectl-as-admin), database management consoles, and RPC shells used by oncall engineers and SREs.
- Covers both Hosted and Private (VPC / on-prem) deployments, including cross-region evidence packaging.
- Does NOT cover non-interactive service-to-service keys (those are addressed by key-life-cycle playbooks).

Objectives
----------
1. Ensure every privileged interactive session is proxied through a session broker that provides: strong authentication, session recording (keystrokes + terminal output), and tamper-evident audit records.
2. Provide an evidence orchestration pipeline that: collects session artifacts, enriches them with RBAC context, applies residency-aware packaging, and stores proofs in the immutable audit store.
3. Define retention, TTL, and legal-hold handling consistent with data residency policies.
4. Ensure incident responders can generate a cryptographically verifiable evidence bundle within SLO.

High-level architecture (text diagram)
-----------------------------------
- Identity Provider (IdP) -> Session Broker (proxy) -> Target (k8s/node/db/console)
- Session Broker writes: session-chunks -> Audit Ingest API -> Immutable Audit Store (WORM object store with manifest)
- Evidence Orchestrator retrieves manifests, builds evidence bundles, notarizes with HSM/KMS, and stores indexes in Evidence Catalog.

Key components and responsibilities
----------------------------------
- Session Broker (service: session-proxy): performs MFA enforcement, session recording, and live session tagging. Owned by eng-sre.
- Audit Ingest API (service: audit-ingest): receives gzipped session chunks + metadata. Owned by eng-platform.
- Immutable Audit Store (s3-worm): immutable object store with append-only manifests, retention enforcement and legal-hold support. Owned by eng-infra/security.
- Evidence Orchestrator (service: evidence-orch): automates bundle creation, notarization, and cross-region packaging. Owned by security & eng-infra.
- Evidence Catalog (indexed DB): searchable index of bundles with RBAC & residency metadata. Owned by security.

Operational SLOs and thresholds
------------------------------
- Session chunk ingestion latency: 95th percentile < 5s from time-of-write.
- Evidence bundle generation (critical incident): < 2 hours from request to notarized bundle.
- Search index propagation: < 15 minutes from bundle creation to index visibility.
- Tamper-detection alerting: immediate (max 1 minute) to pager if manifest hash mismatch detected.

RBAC & Auth Integration
-----------------------
- All session requests must carry an authorization token minted by the IdP and contain the following claims: subject (sub), roles, session_id, request_origin_region.
- The Session Broker will call the RBAC service at session start and every 30 minutes for long-lived sessions. If roles change to remove privilege mid-session, the Broker: 1) marks the session as suspended, 2) notifies the user and oncall, 3) records the event in the session transcript.
- Privileged roles require just-in-time (JIT) elevation with attestation (reason + approver) recorded. JIT events are stored in the evidence manifest.

Audit Logging & Tamper Evidence
-------------------------------
- Session chunks are written as sequential objects: <session_id>/chunk-0001.gz, chunk-0002.gz, ... Each chunk includes SHA256 and a monotonic sequence number in headers.
- Ingest API computes an object hash and appends a signed manifest entry using the platform KMS key. Example manifest entry (pseudo):

  {
    "session_id": "s-0a1b2c",
    "chunk": "chunk-0002.gz",
    "seq": 2,
    "sha256": "b1946ac92492d2347c6235b4d2611184",
    "signed_by": "platform-kms:ek-001",
    "timestamp": "2026-09-01T14:12:10Z"
  }

- Any mismatch between stored SHA256 and recomputed SHA256 triggers an automated integrity-alert and creates an Investigation Case ID.

Data residency & retention rules
--------------------------------
- Default retention policy (Hosted): session recordings retained for 365 days.
- High-sensitivity customers (contracted): configurable retention 30-3650 days and legal-hold overrides.
- For Private deployments: recordings remain in-customer-region by default. Evidence Orchestrator will only cross-package data for egress when a legal subpoena or customer-approved export is in place. All cross-region exports must be recorded with export reason, approver, and signed consent.
- Table: retention by classification

  Classification | Default retention | Region constraints
  ---------------|-------------------|------------------
  Standard ops   | 365 days          | same-region
  Security incident | 7 years (legal-hold possible) | same-region unless export approved
  PII access     | 3 years           | residency as customer contract

Evidence bundle format and manifest (example)
--------------------------------------------
- Each bundle is a signed tar.gz containing: session-chunks/, manifests/, rbactx.json, notarization.sig
- rbactx.json fields (example in-lined):
  - session_id: string
  - principal: email
  - roles: [list]
  - start_ts, end_ts: ISO8601
  - target: hostname/cluster
  - approver: email (if JIT)
  - residency_region: eu-west-1
  - evidence_id: bund-20260912-0001

- Notarization: evidence-orch computes bundle hash, requests a KMS HSM asymmetric-sign operation (key id: evidence-signing-01) and stores signature as notarization.sig. The signature envelope includes signer key metadata and chain-of-custody fields.

Evidence creation CLI (example)
------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwood-evidence create --session s-0a1b2c --reason "incident-INV-2026-233" --approver security@redwood.ai --output inv-INV-2026-233.tar.gz

- The CLI calls evidence-orch, which validates residency constraints, creates the bundle, notarizes it, and returns a signed manifest URL.

Incident responders playbook (summary)
-------------------------------------
1. Triage: confirm session_id(s) involved from alert or forensic query.
2. Freeze & Preserve: attach a legal-hold to identified bundles in the Immutable Audit Store (owner: security).
3. Create evidence bundle: use redwood-evidence CLI or UI request. Emergency mode sets retention to infinite and notifies legal.
4. Forensic review: responders use the Session Replay UI (read-only) or download the bundle for offline analysis.
5. Escalate & Notify: if evidence indicates exfiltration or tampering, follow Incident Response severity escalation and notify CISO and legal.

Step-by-step: urgent evidence generation (detailed)
-------------------------------------------------
1) Identify sessions: run Kibana query filtering by event_type:session_start and principal and time-range. Example query:
   event_type:session_chunk AND session_id:"s-0a1b2c"
2) Mark legal hold: POST /api/audit-store/v1/holds {"evidence_id": "bund-20260912-0001", "hold_reason": "incident-INV-2026-233", "owner": "security@redwood.ai"}
3) Initiate bundle: redwood-evidence create --session s-0a1b2c --mode urgent --approver security@redwood.ai
4) Validate notarization: evidence-orch returns notarization URL; verify signature with platform public key:
   openssl dgst -sha256 -verify platform_pub.pem -signature notarization.sig inv-INV-2026-233.tar.gz
5) Record chain-of-custody in the Incident Tracker (ticket link) and attach the signed manifest URL.

SDLC integration requirements
----------------------------
- All code that touches session-chunk generation must include: automated unit tests for chunk integrity, CI integration that runs manifest sign/verify emulation, and a code review checklist item: "produces signed manifests and validates on read".
- Release gating: any change to session-proxy or audit-ingest must pass an automated fuzz test that injects chunk-order gaps and validates the ingest pipeline detects gaps with alerts.

Forensics & analysis guidance
-----------------------------
- Use the Evidence Catalog to map sessions to principals and role-at-time-of-session. The catalog stores a timestamped RBAC snapshot.
- Terminal replay correlation: correlate session transcript timestamps with system-level telemetry (e.g., k8s audit logs, host syslogs) using the common timebase (UTC, NTP-synced).
- When reconstructing activity, responders should look for: unexpected binary transfers, privilege escalation commands, and outbound connections in the target's network logs.

Legal holds and export controls
------------------------------
- Legal-hold API must be used to prevent garbage-collection/retention lifecycle from deleting bundles. Holds are recorded in the manifest and visible in Evidence Catalog.
- Export outside customer region requires: documented export reason, named approver (legal-counsel or customer), and a signed export consent. EvidenceOrch will stamp export metadata into the bundle and create an audit trail.

Audit queries and examples
-------------------------
- Fast check: number of privileged sessions in last 24h per region:
  Kibana query: event_type:session_start AND roles:"admin" AND timestamp:[now-24h TO now] | stats count by request_origin_region
- Integrity verification CLI (example):
  redwood-evidence verify --bundle inv-2026-233.tar.gz
  Outputs: OK|MISMATCH with details about which chunk failed.

Ownership, escalation & contact matrix
------------------------------------
- Session Broker: eng-sre (oncall: s-sre-rotation@redwood.ai)
- Audit Ingest: eng-platform (oncall: platform-oncall@redwood.ai)
- Evidence Orchestrator & Catalog: security (pager: +1-555-0100)
- Legal/Compliance liaison: legal@redwood.ai

Metrics to monitor
------------------
- percent_of_sessions_proxied (target 100% for privileged roles)
- ingest_latency_p95
- notarization_success_rate
- evidence_bundle_creation_time_p95
- number_of_integrity_alerts

Appendix A — Example rbactx.json (raw)
-------------------------------------
{
  "session_id": "s-0a1b2c",
  "principal": "alice@redwood.ai",
  "roles": ["admin", "k8s-cluster-admin"],
  "start_ts": "2026-09-12T14:10:05Z",
  "end_ts": "2026-09-12T14:42:10Z",
  "target": "cluster-prod-03",
  "approver": "bob@redwood.ai",
  "residency_region": "us-west-2",
  "evidence_id": "bund-20260912-0001"
}

Appendix B — Common failure modes and mitigations
--------------------------------------------------
- Missing chunk sequences: ingest pipeline raises "chunk-gaps" alert and EvidenceOrch marks session as incomplete. Mitigation: re-request chunks from session-proxy temporarily held buffer and reconcile.
- KMS signing failures: fail-fast evidence creation and create an incident ticket; fall back to time-stamped hash (with increased scrutiny).
- Residency mismatch (bundle cannot be exported): provide a sealed, region-limited viewer link that allows legal/approved reviewers to view contents without export.

Change log
----------
- 2026-03-15 (Asha Patel): initial published playbook.
- 2026-05-02 (Marcos Alvarez): added notarization HSM key reference and CLI examples.
- 2026-09-12 (Priya Nair): clarified cross-region export rules and updated SLOs.

Related reading
---------------
- RBAC provisioning guide (rbac provisioning)
- Immutable audit store design (audit-logging)
- Incident response escalation playbook (incident-response-security)

End of document

payload.page_title: Evidence & Incident Integration Standard: packaging, access, and retention

sections.body:
Overview

This standard defines how evidence required for security incidents, compliance audits, and regulatory requests is collected, packaged, accessed, and retained across Redwood Inference. It unifies RBAC and audit-logging requirements with data residency and secure SDLC hooks so that incident responders, forensics teams, and compliance owners can produce verifiable evidence bundles within SLA windows.

Goals

- Ensure evidence is tamper-evident, auditable, and reproducible.
- Define minimum artifact sets for common incident classes (authz failures, exfiltration, misconfiguration, model-serving incidents).
- Control access to evidence using least-privilege RBAC and just-in-time escalation.
- Reconcile retention requirements across jurisdictions and customer commitments.
- Embed evidence generation points into the SDLC so artifacts are available for automated post-deploy audits.

Scope

Applies to: hosted, dedicated, and private deployments and the control plane components that manage deployments, telemetry, and audit logs. Excluded: third-party SaaS vendor operational logs unless explicitly integrated by contract.

Ownership and Roles

- Security (Evidence Owner): Lina Zhang — final signoff for evidence release.
- Incident Response (IR Lead): owns on-call evidence collection and packaging during incidents.
- Engineering SRE: provides access to runtime logs, snapshots, and rollback artifacts.
- Privacy & Legal: provides jurisdictional retention guidance and approves disclosure.
- Platform Engineering: implements secure hooks (see SDLC Integration) and storage backends.

Artifact taxonomy (minimum set)

For any classified incident, collect the following core artifacts unless explicitly waived by Security/Legal:

1) Authentication and authorization logs:
   - Token issuance logs, token revocation events, OAuth/JWT validation traces, and policy-evaluation decisions (WAF/authorization broker).
2) API request traces:
   - Request/response headers (redact PII), route, model name/version, latency, and error codes.
3) Model-serving runtime telemetry:
   - Sequence length distribution, KV cache hits/misses, quantization profile used, and GPU allocation events.
4) Audit-log bundle snapshot:
   - Immutable audit stream segment (timebox) covering the incident window.
5) Configuration snapshot:
   - Deployed config (feature flags, rollout policy, routing policy) and hash-signed manifest.
6) Evidence manifest (see example): a plain-text manifest listing each artifact path, SHA-256, storage location, and access policy.
7) Chain-of-custody log:
   - Who accessed/packaged the evidence and why (linked to a ticket/incident ID).

RBAC and Access Controls

Principles

- Use role-scoped access with narrow privileges (e.g., ir-lead.read:logs, sre.snapshot:write).
- Default deny for all evidence buckets; access granted by short-lived tokens (JIT) and recorded in audit logs.
- Separation of duties between evidence producers (SRE) and evidence approvers (Security).
- Multi-person approval for cross-border evidence exports (> 1GB or containing regulated PII).

RBAC mapping examples

- role:ir-first-responder -> permissions: incident:read, evidence:collect, evidence:ticket-link
- role:sre-oncall -> permissions: runtime:read, snapshot:create, evidence:upload
- role:legal-analyst -> permissions: evidence:read-redacted
- role:security-auditor -> permissions: evidence:read, chain-of-custody:verify

Just-in-time access flow

1. IR Lead opens evidence request via Incident ticket with justification.
2. System issues a scoped access grant (15 min default, configurable up to 2 hours).
3. All access is logged to the immutable audit stream and correlated with the incident ID.
4. Access extension requires escalation and multi-person approval if outside normal SLOs.

Audit Logging Requirements
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- event_id, timestamp (ISO8601), actor_id, actor_role, resource_id, action, outcome, request_id, correlation_id, region, shard_id.
- For authorization decisions include: policy_version, decision_path, policy_evaluation_time_ms.

Retention and partitioning

- Hot store (queryable): 90 days for operational troubleshooting.
- Warm store (indexable, lower-cost): 2 years for internal compliance reviews.
- Cold archive (immutable): per-jurisdiction minimums (see Retention Matrix).

Tamper-evidence

- All audit events are appended to an immutable store (WORM) with periodic Merkle-tree snapshots signed by the KMS key 'audit-root-redwood-v1'.

Data Residency & Retention Matrix
sections.heading: Minimum fields for each audit event (schema contract)

sections.body:
- US: Hot 90 days, Warm 24 months, Cold 7 years — follows internal baseline.
- EU: Hot 90 days, Warm 24 months, Cold 7 years — GDPR: identify PII and retain only if justified.
- APAC: Hot 90 days, Warm 12 months, Cold 5 years — local law may require longer for specific countries.
- Customer-specific: follow contracted retention.

Note: All archives must be tagged with residency attributes and stored in region-specific buckets when the incident involves that residency.

Secure SDLC integration points

1. Build time: produce signed artifact manifest including codehash, dependency SBOM, and build env.
2. Deployment pipeline: snapshot deployed configuration and route it to evidence staging unless flag skip_evidence_snapshot=true.
3. Post-deploy smoke: automatically capture a 24-hour rolling telemetry snapshot for new model variants for first 72 hours.
4. Pre-release security gating: ensure evidence export paths are registered and tested as part of the release checklist.

Incident evidence collection workflow (standard)

1. Triage (0-15 min): classify incident (authz, data-exfil, model-degradation), assign incident ID, and apply evidence-preservation hold.
2. Preserve (15-60 min): take immutable snapshots of audit log windows, lock affected config, and take a runtime memory snapshot if required.
3. Collect (1-4 hours): collect artifacts (see taxonomy), compute SHA-256 hashes, and write the evidence manifest.
4. Package (4-8 hours): encrypt the bundle with envelope encryption using KMS key evidence-enc-redwood-v2, and upload to the restricted evidence bucket (s3://evidence-restricted/{incident-id}/).
5. Verify (8-12 hours): Security reviews package, verifies hashes and chain-of-custody, and records approval in the incident timeline.
6. Release / Legal Review (as needed): Legal may request redaction or region-specific handling before external disclosure.

SLA targets for evidence delivery

- Internal evidence-ready for forensic review: within 12 hours for critical incidents, 48 hours for high, 7 days for medium/low.
- Immutable audit segment snapshot availability: within 30 minutes of preservation hold.

Packaging & Encryption rules

- All evidence bundles MUST be envelope-encrypted with a KMS key scoped to the owning team.
- For cross-border transfers a separate export KMS key is used and multi-sign approvals required.
- Use AES-256-GCM for symmetric wrapping and store ephemeral wrapping keys in the KMS.

Evidence release and exception handling

- Routine internal reviews: Security may release evidence to Legal and Product for investigation. Externally facing disclosures require Legal signoff and redaction.
- Exceptions (e.g., customer-specific data retention or third-party constraints): raise an evidence-exception via the Governance board; record in the Authorization Exceptions register using the company template.

Forensic tooling and CLI examples

- Pull an audit segment (30-min window):
  rwd-audit fetch --start 2026-11-10T14:00:00Z --end 2026-11-10T14:30:00Z --incident INC-2026-2143 --out ./audit-segment.ndjson
- Create a runtime snapshot (GPU state + container snapshot):
  rwd-runtime snapshot create --cluster cluster-prod-1 --selector "app=model-serving" --incident INC-2026-2143 --out s3://evidence-restricted/INC-2026-2143/runtime-snapshot.tgz

Verification and auditability

- Each evidence bundle must include: artifact checksums, manifest, and a signed approval record.
- Security rotates KMS keys per the Key Management Standard and publishes rotation events to the audit stream.
- Periodic table-top exercises (quarterly) require that the Evidence Owner can reconstruct any archived bundle within 72 hours.

Training and exercises

- IR runs quarterly evidence-packaging drills: produce a full package for a simulated model-exfiltration incident.
- Platform teams are required to complete an annual module on SDLC evidence hooks.

Appendix: Quick checklist (incident start to package)

- Assign incident ID and apply evidence hold
- Create scoped JIT access for collectors
- Snapshot audit logs and runtime state
- Collect config, policy, and deployment artifacts
- Upload to restricted bucket and compute SHA-256
- Encrypt with evidence KMS and publish manifest
- Security verifies hashes and signs chain-of-custody
- Legal reviews if external disclosure required

References and links

- Event schema contract: /confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025
- Incident triage playbook: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/incident-scope-decision-tree-and-evidence-collection-playbook-2026
- KMS key policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions/key-management-policy-2025

Revision history

- 2026-02-03: Draft created by Lina Zhang.
- 2026-06-15: Added secure SDLC hooks and CLI examples (reviewer: Priya Kapoor).
- 2026-11-12: Updated retention matrix and JIT access window defaults (finalized).

payload.page_title: Evidence Assembly Matrix for Regulatory Audits

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This page defines the Evidence Assembly Matrix (EAM): a concise, repeatable format for collecting, validating, and packaging technical evidence for regulatory audits (SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) and customer compliance requests. The EAM prioritizes reproducibility, minimal manual steps, and verifiable provenance for each artifact.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Redwood Inference platform components that generate or control security-relevant artifacts: API control plane, serving runtime, infra provisioning, audit pipelines, RBAC systems, and private deployment connectors.
- Audience: Security Engineers, Compliance Engineers, SREs, Incident Response, Legal/Security review, and Customer Trust teams.

Why we use an Evidence Assembly Matrix
-------------------------------------
- Single canonical source mapping regulations to artifacts and concrete collection steps.
- Reduces ad-hoc evidence requests during audits.
- Provides verifiable provenance and chain-of-custody metadata for each item.
- Enables automation where possible and clearly documents manual steps where automation is not feasible.

How to read the matrix
----------------------
Each row in the EAM corresponds to a single piece of evidence. Columns are: Regulation, Evidence ID, Artifact Type, Source Service, Collection Method, Retention Window, Custodian, Verification Procedure, Storage Location, Proof-of-Presence artefacts (hashes/logs). Example matrix rows are below. Use the "Evidence Collection CLI" (see section) to automate fetching when supported.

Evidence Matrix (examples)
--------------------------
| Regulation | Evidence ID | Artifact Type | Source Service | Collection Method | Retention Window | Custodian | Verification Procedure | Storage Location | PoP (proof-of-presence) |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|----------------|-------------------|------------------|-----------|------------------------|------------------|-------------------------|
| SOC2 | EAM-API-01 | Authz policy snapshot | IAM / RBAC service | automated: iam-export --date=YYYY-MM-DD | 3 years | security-team | verify sha256, diff against last snapshot | s3://redwood-compliance/soc2/api-polices/ | sha256:abc123, manifest.log |
| GDPR | EAM-DR-04 | Data residency map | Config DB (vault). | manual: export via admin UI & validate | 7 years | data-privacy | cross-check with infra tags and region ACLs | s3://redwood-compliance/gdpr/data-residency/ | manifest.log, signed-metadata.txt |
| PCI-DSS | EAM-LOG-12 | Immutable audit stream | Audit-logging pipeline (kinesis -> long-term) | automated: aws-kinesis-dump --range | 6 years | eng-sre | run query to ensure event types present; validate retention confirmation | gs://redwood-logs/pci/ | event-hashes.json |

Note: The above table is illustrative. The canonical EAM is maintained as a CSV in the compliance repo and exported to this page via automation.

Evidence collection procedures
-------------------------------
1) Identify audit scope and required regulations. Confirm with Legal/Compliance what evidence IDs are required.
2) Retrieve EAM rows relevant to the scope. Filter by Regulation and Source Service.
3) For each Evidence ID:
   a) Attempt automated retrieval using Evidence Collection CLI.
   b) If automation is unavailable, follow the explicit manual steps recorded in the EAM row. Document the operator and timestamp.
   c) Compute and record cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of each artifact.
   d) Generate a manifest entry containing: Evidence ID, artifact filename, sha256, collected_by, collected_at (UTC), collection_method.
   e) Upload the artifact and manifest to the ephemeral evidence bucket for audit assembly.

Evidence Collection CLI (examples)
----------------------------------
- Purpose: standardize automated retrieval for supported sources (IAM, audit pipeline, config DB exports, console logs).
- Location: git@redwood:infra/compliance/evidence-cli.git
- Quick example:
  # export RBAC snapshot for a given date
  ./evidence-cli iam-export --date 2026-02-15 --output /tmp/eam-iam-20260215.json

  # pull audit logs for a 1-hour window (UTC)
  ./evidence-cli logs-dump --service api-gateway --start 2026-02-14T10:00:00Z --end 2026-02-14T11:00:00Z --out /tmp/gateway-logs-1000-1100.jsonl

Manual collection guidance
-------------------------
- Always use a separate workstation with MFA and compliance-approved device posture.
- For UI exports: capture a video (screen recording) of the export operation if the service does not provide an automated export; attach the recording to the manifest.
- Do not sanitize logs unless explicitly instructed by Legal; instead, request a filtered export with the Compliance Engineer present.

Manifest format (plain text)
---------------------------
- Example manifest line (one-per-artifact) – store in UTF-8 text:
  EvidenceID: EAM-API-01 | Filename: iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json | SHA256: <sha256sum> | CollectedBy: a.patel | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T18:05:12Z | Method: automation | Location: s3://redwood-compliance/tmp/eam-20260215/iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json

Verification and signing
------------------------
1) After artifacts are uploaded, run the verify-manifest tool: ./evidence-cli verify-manifest --manifest /path/to/manifest.txt
2) Verify-manifest performs: sha256 validation, schema sanity checks, and cross-checks expected artifact counts for the audit scope.
3) The Security Custodian signs the manifest with a GPG key and stores the signed manifest alongside artifacts. Example: gpg --sign --armor --output manifest.txt.asc manifest.txt

Chain-of-custody and immutable storage
-------------------------------------
- All artifacts intended for long-term retention must be copied into the immutable evidence bucket: s3://redwood-evidence-immutable/<regulation>/<year>/
- Immutable bucket has MFA-delete enabled and lifecycle rules to transition to cold storage after 180 days.
- Each copy operation must be recorded in the chain-of-custody log (COC), which is an append-only audit stream (Kafka topic: coc-evidence-events). The Evidence CLI automatically emits COC events on successful uploads.

Retention and purge controls
----------------------------
- Default retention per regulation: SOC2=3 years, PCI-DSS=6 years, HIPAA=6 years, GDPR=7 years for residency-related artifacts. See the EAM retention column for exceptions.
- Purge requests must follow the Data Retention Exception process: file a request in the Risk and Exceptions portal with explicit business justification and legal approval. Purge actions are recorded and require a two-person approval from Security + Legal.

Audit-ready packaging checklist
------------------------------
Before handing artifacts to auditors or legal, confirm:
- [ ] Manifest present and signed
- [ ] sha256 hashes verified
- [ ] Chain-of-custody entries present for each upload
- [ ] Access control on the package limited to the audit team and Security Custodian
- [ ] Any redaction or PII handling steps documented and approved by Legal

Escalation and SLAs
-------------------
- Evidence retrieval SLA for external audits: 72 business hours for standard requests, 24 business hours for executive-critical escalations (requires Legal approval).
- If evidence collection cannot meet SLA due to technical gaps, notify Compliance@redwood.com with a remediation plan within 8 business hours.
- Owner escalation chain: Security Custodian -> Head of Security (Lena Ortiz) -> Chief Security Officer (Rahul Sharma).

Periodic maintenance and audits of the EAM
-----------------------------------------
- The EAM CSV and automation scripts are reviewed quarterly by Security and Compliance.
- Run an internal mini-audit every six months: select a random subset of 10 Evidence IDs and validate collection, verification, and archival end-to-end. Failures must be remediated within 30 days with a postmortem.

Change history and approvals
----------------------------
- 2026-01-18: Initial published by Aisha Patel (Security). Reviewed by Marco Nguyen and Lena Ortiz.
- 2026-03-02: Clarified immutable bucket lifecycle and added Evidence CLI examples (updated by Aisha Patel).

Related resources
-----------------
- Compliance repository: git@redwood:infra/compliance
- Evidence CLI project: git@redwood:infra/compliance/evidence-cli.git
- Chain-of-custody topic: kafka://coc-evidence-events
- Contact: compliance@redwood.com (for process questions), security-oncall@redwood.com (for urgent evidence preservation during incidents)

Appendix A: Example queries for audit-logging verification
---------------------------------------------------------
- Verify presence of service restart events:
  Elastic search query: service:runtime AND event:restart AND @timestamp:[2026-02-01 TO 2026-02-28]
- Verify RBAC change events (sample KQL):
  event.type: "rbac.change" AND user.role: ("admin","infra-admin") AND timestamp >= "2026-02-01"

Appendix B: Example minimal manifest snippet
------------------------------------------
- manifest.txt content (3 lines):
  EvidenceID: EAM-API-01 | Filename: iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: a.patel | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T18:05:12Z
  EvidenceID: EAM-LOG-07 | Filename: gateway-logs-2026-02-14.jsonl | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: s.sre | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T20:12:55Z
  EvidenceID: EAM-DR-04 | Filename: data-residency-map-2026-02-14.csv | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: d.privacy | CollectedAt: 2026-02-16T09:30:01Z

End of document

payload.page_title: Compartmentalized Authorization Forensics & Provenance Playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook defines a practical, end-to-end approach for performing forensic investigations and building provable authorization provenance in a compartmentalized inference platform. It is targeted at incidents that impact model-serving access paths (identities, service tokens, feature flags, and routing decisions) and where evidence must be collected, packaged, and retained across RBAC, audit logs, and data residency boundaries.

Goals:
- Ensure forensic evidence for authorization decisions is collected with minimal blast radius and meets audit retention and cross-border constraints.
- Provide a repeatable incident workflow for authentication/authorization failures and suspicious privilege escalations in model-serving/runtime components.
- Standardize evidence packaging so compliance teams can accept and reproduce authorization timelines.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private Redwood deployments.
- Covers service-to-service authn/authz, user sessions (console/API), and short-lived inferencing tokens.
- Assumes centralized audit stream (kafka -> audit-store) and per-region immutable archive.

Owner and stakeholders:
- Primary owner: security (authoritative custodian for evidence handling).
- Secondary owners: eng-serving-runtime (evidence producers), eng-sre (archival & retention), legal/compliance (evidence acceptance).

Key definitions:
- Provenance record: structured bundle that ties an authorization decision (who/what/why) to corresponding audit events, token metadata, and residency tags.
- Compartment: logical isolation boundary (customer tenancy, region, environment) used to minimize evidence exposure.

Evidence requirements (summary table):

| Evidence type                | Minimum fields (required)                                  | Retention SLA           | Residency constraints       |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------|----------------------------|
| Authorization decision      | timestamp, principal_id, resource, action, policy_id, result| 365 days (default)      | Same region as resource    |
| Token provenance            | token_id, issuer, expiry, scopes, parent_token_id          | 90 days (short-lived)   | Region-specific            |
| Audit log entry             | event_id, ts, svc, msg, trace_id, severity, tenant_id      | 3 years (audit)         | As contracted (may be geo) |
| Model request trace (KV)    | trace_id, seq_len, model_version, input_hash, user_id      | 180 days (ops)          | Redacted if PII present    |

Note: retention SLAs are baseline; adjust per customer contract and legal guidance.

Compartmentalization rules (high-level):
1) Evidence should be stored in the smallest compartment that satisfies the investigation and legal needs.
2) Use ephemeral evidence windows for cross-tenant correlation — do not copy tenant-scoped logs into global buckets without justification and approval.
3) All cross-compartment transfers must be recorded as an authorization decision and emitted to the audit stream.

Incident triage and evidence-collection workflow (step-by-step):
1. Detection & Triage
   - Alert sources: anomalous authz failures, privilege escalation alarms, abnormal token minting rates, policy-signer rotation alerts.
   - Initial owner: oncall SRE/security engineer.
   - Triage checklist: confirm scope (tenant(s), region(s), services), severity (impact to SLO/data residency), and containment requirements.

2. Freeze and Flag
   - If evidence spans multiple compartments, mark each compartment as "forensic-locked" in the evidence control ledger (see ledger CLI below).
   - Do not perform ad-hoc queries that copy raw log blobs across regions. Use stored queries that return references only.

3. Canonical evidence extraction (ordered):
   a) Authorization decisions from the authz service for the time window [+/- 5m].
   b) Token minting events and correlated KMS/HSM signing metadata.
   c) Audit log slices for services involved (trace_id correlation).
   d) Service configuration snapshots (policy_id -> policy rule text, role bindings).

4. Provenance assembly
   - Build a provenance record that links the above items. Each provenance record must include a content-hash (SHA256) and a signed manifest produced by the evidence-custodian service.

5. Packaging and retention tagging
   - Apply retention tag (baseline or contract override) and residency tag. If packaging for cross-border handoff, include minimal redaction map and justification.

6. Handoff to compliance/legal
   - Use the evidence packaging API to create a sealed bundle and notify legal via the incident ticket with a signed manifest reference.

Technical artifacts and commands:

Evidence control ledger (example CLI pattern):

```
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: evidence-ledger lock --compartment=tenant-123 --region=us-west-2 --reason="authz escalation" --owned-by=security
sections.heading: mark a compartment as locked for forensics

sections.body:
evidence-ledger register --manifest ./manifests/tenant-123-authz-20260215.json --signed-by=svc-evidence-01
```

Canonical query examples:
- Authorization decisions (SQL against authz-store):

```
SELECT decision_id, ts, principal_id, resource, action, policy_id, result
FROM authz_decisions
WHERE ts BETWEEN '2026-02-15T09:40:00Z' AND '2026-02-15T09:50:00Z'
AND principal_id IN ('svc-a','user:alice@example.com');
```

- Audit log slice (kql-like):

```
service:"authz" OR trace_id:"f24a3b..."
| where tenant_id=="tenant-123" and ts >= ago(1h)
| project ts, event_id, trace_id, severity, message
```

Provenance manifest schema (human-readable YAML example):

```
manifest_version: 1
provenance_id: prov-20260215-001
compartment: tenant-123
region: us-west-2
time_window:
  start: 2026-02-15T09:40:00Z
  end: 2026-02-15T09:50:00Z
items:
  - type: authz_decision
    ref: authz://authz-store/decision_id/dec-12345
    hash: sha256:...
  - type: audit_log_slice
    ref: audit://kafka/partition-22/offset-...
    hash: sha256:...
signed_by: svc-evidence-01
signature: <base64-signature>
retention_tag: contract-std-365d
residency_tag: us-west-2-only
```

Redaction & minimization guidance:
- Prefer referencing logs (IDs/hashes) instead of copying raw blobs across borders.
- When PII is present, follow the legal redaction checklist and replace values with deterministic redaction tokens in the package. Record mapping in a protected vault.

Evidence access controls and RBAC mappings:
- Role: evidence_custodian (security) -> full access to provenance manifests; ability to create sealed bundles.
- Role: incident_reviewer (legal/compliance) -> read-only access to sealed bundles after request approval.
- Role: svc-ops-oncall (eng-sre) -> permission to extract operational slices within local compartment only.

Minimum SLOs and thresholds for the evidence pipeline:
- Evidence ingestion from producers into audit-stream: 99.9% within 2 minutes (P95 latency).
- Manifest registration in ledger: 99% success under 30s during normal load.
- Cross-region sealed-bundle transfer (when authorized): <= 4 hours for emergency transfers (must include retention justification).

Integration checklist (prior to enabling compartmental forensics):
- [ ] Confirm authz decisions are emitted with trace_id and tenant_id.
- [ ] Ensure KMS signing metadata is included with token events.
- [ ] Configure evidence-ledger service account in each region.
- [ ] Enable immutable audit archives and verify retention tags.
- [ ] Validate all producers sign payloads with service identity.

Decision matrix: when to escalate to legal/compliance:
1) Evidence crosses jurisdictional boundaries OR includes PII -> escalate immediately.
2) Evidence indicates a signed KMS key compromise -> escalate + trigger key-rotation playbook.
3) Multi-tenant exposure (more than 1 tenant affected) -> treat as high-severity, follow cross-tenant containment flow.

Post-incident actions and hygiene:
- Run an evidence maturity review within 7 days: verify manifests, validate hashes, and check ledger immutability.
- Update policies and role bindings that contributed to the incident; create a targeted rollout with canary and monitoring.
- If evidence packaging required redaction, verify the redaction vault and access logs.

Templates and artifacts (links and samples):
- Minimal provenance manifest (YAML) — included above.
- Evidence packaging API example: POST /api/v1/evidence/package {manifest_ref: "prov-..."} -> returns sealed_bundle_id.
- Sample retention policy table (for inclusion in customer contracts):

| Retention profile | Audit logs | Authz decisions | Sealed bundles |
|------------------|-----------:|---------------:|---------------:|
| standard-365d     | 3 years    | 365 days       | 5 years        |
| short-90d         | 180 days   | 90 days        | 1 year         |

Risks and exceptions handling:
- Risk: Overexposure of tenant logs during cross-compartment analysis.
  Mitigation: Use reference-based queries and sealed bundle requests; require dual-approval for any raw log transfer.
- Risk: Key compromise undermines provenance signatures.
  Mitigation: KMS rotation, signed key-rotation manifests, and emergency revocation processes integrated with evidence-ledger.
- Exception flow: For time-sensitive law enforcement requests that conflict with residency rules, follow legal escalation policy and log every decision into the evidence ledger with justification.

Metrics to track (dashboards):
- Provenance manifests created per week, broken down by region and compartment.
- Average time-to-freeze (detection -> compartment lock).
- Percentage of sealed-bundle transfers that require redaction.

Appendix A: Role-to-permission mapping (summary):
- security:evidence_custodian = [manifest:write, manifest:sign, ledger:lock]
- legal:incident_reviewer = [manifest:read, bundle:request]
- eng-sre:svc-ops-oncall = [slice:extract_local, ledger:annotate]

Appendix B: Minimal incident ticket template (to create in incident system):
- Title: [INCIDENT][authz] short description
- Impacted compartments: list
- Time window: start/end
- Evidence manifest ref: prov-... (if registered)
- Actions taken: freeze, register_manifest, legal_notified (Y/N)
- Owner: team/person

If you have questions about implementing the ledger APIs or evidence packaging for a specific region or contract, contact security-evidence@redwood (primary contact) or open a runbook request in the security team workspace.
