payload.page_title: Customer-managed audit log export: security controls and approval gates

sections.body:
This page defines the **mandatory security controls** and **approval gates** for enabling **customer-managed audit log export** from Redwood Inference to customer-controlled cloud storage (e.g., S3/GCS/Azure Blob) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

This is a control surface that touches: customer data boundaries, identity and access, encryption, and retention. **Do not enable export** without satisfying the requirements below.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Export of **platform audit logs** (auth events, RBAC changes, API key lifecycle, console/admin actions, private control-plane actions).
- Delivery to a **customer-owned destination**.
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body: - Model inference payload logging (prompt/completion content). That remains disabled by default and requires a separate data logging exception.
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Audit log**: event records emitted by Redwood control plane and selected data-plane components.
- **Customer-managed export**: Redwood pushes logs to an endpoint owned/controlled by the customer; the customer sets retention and access.
- **Export Connector**: Redwood-managed service that ships logs (see architecture page for details).
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- Audit logs are classified as **Customer-Sensitive Metadata**.
- Audit logs may include: user identifiers, IPs, org IDs, resource IDs, timestamps, and administrative actions.
- Audit logs must **not** include request bodies or model outputs.
sections.heading: 1) Data classification

sections.body:
- In transit: TLS 1.2+ is required for any HTTPS endpoints.
- At rest: the customer destination must be configured with server-side encryption.
  - S3: SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS (customer preference).
  - GCS: Google-managed keys or CMEK.
  - Azure: Microsoft-managed keys or CMK.
- Redwood-side staging (if used by the connector) must be encrypted at rest using Redwood-managed KMS.
sections.heading: 2) Encryption

sections.body:
- Hosted and Dedicated exports must use **assume-role / workload identity** patterns; no long-lived customer keys stored in Redwood.
- The role/policy must only permit:
  - write/put to a specific bucket/container prefix
  - list only if required by the connector health checks
- Policies must be reviewed by Security for correctness.
sections.heading: 3) Least privilege access

sections.body:
- The destination must be customer-owned and reside in an allowed provider account/subscription/project per the contract.
- For Private deployments, outbound egress must be constrained by the customer (preferred) or by Redwood (if Redwood-managed networking is in scope).
- Public endpoints are allowed only if authenticated and protected with least-privilege credentials; **PrivateLink / private endpoints are preferred** when available.
sections.heading: 4) Network & destination allowlisting

sections.body:
- Default recommended destination retention: **90 days** (unless the customer requires more).
- If the customer requests retention < 30 days, note it in the request but it is allowed.
- If the customer requests retention > 1 year, Customer Success must confirm contract language supports it and that the customer understands storage cost/ownership.
sections.heading: 5) Retention and deletion

sections.body:
- The platform must emit events for:
  - export enabled/disabled
  - destination changes (bucket/container/prefix)
  - auth/role changes used by the connector
  - delivery failures and retries
- These events must be visible in Redwood internal dashboards and retrievable for incident response.
sections.heading: 6) Logging about logging (auditability of export)

sections.body:
- customer company + deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- target cloud + region
- desired log categories (standard only unless exception)
- retention intent
- contact for incident notifications
sections.heading: Required before Security review

sections.body:
- destination configuration meets encryption and least privilege requirements
- no inference payload logging is included
- any cross-region delivery is evaluated (see Cross-region constraints)
sections.heading: Security must approve before any production enablement

sections.body: - Jira internal-support ticket must include a Security comment: **“Approved for enablement”** with reviewer name + date.
sections.heading: Approval artifact

sections.body:
- customer requests cross-region export that changes data residency guarantees
- customer requests inclusion of user email addresses or other PII fields beyond standard audit schema
- customer contract includes bespoke audit log clauses
sections.heading: Required if any of the following are true

sections.body:
- Default rule: **export must stay within the customer’s chosen region** that matches the deployment region.
- Cross-region export is allowed only when:
  1) Legal confirms it does not violate contractual residency terms
  2) Security confirms threat model is acceptable
  3) Customer acknowledges increased failure modes and latency
sections.heading: Cross-region constraints

sections.body: If the customer cannot satisfy the above controls (e.g., insists on long-lived keys), file a Security exception under `security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions` and link it in the enablement ticket.
sections.heading: Security exception process

sections.body:
- Destination policy snippet (IAM policy / role trust policy / workload identity binding)
- Confirmation of encryption at rest on destination
- Proof of ownership (account/subscription/project identifiers)
- For Private: network diagram or egress policy statement
sections.heading: Required evidence (attach/link in the Jira ticket)

sections.body:
- Audit log export architecture (Observability Standards)
- Hosted enablement runbook (Eng Platform)
- Dedicated customer setup runbook (Eng Infra)
- Private configuration guide (Eng Private Deployments)
- Support intake process (Customer Success & Support)
sections.heading: Related pages

payload.page_title: Sovereignty impact assessment and evidence patterns for cross-border model deployments

sections.body: This page defines the 'Sovereignty Impact Assessment' (SIA) used to evaluate model-serving changes that may introduce new cross-border data flows, residency obligations, or different evidence requirements. It provides a reproducible assessment procedure, an evidence-pattern catalogue (what artifacts to collect), a retention/packaging schedule, and a decision matrix for risk acceptance and escalation. The guidance applies to hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) deployments.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to any model version, routing policy, or infra change that could alter the physical or logical location of inference inputs/outputs, logs, or derived artifacts.
- Includes model updates, new model variants (quantized or distilled), routing changes that move requests across regions, and export/replication workflows.
- Excludes purely local developer experiments that do not touch production capacity or customer data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1) New model onboarding that includes non-U.S. training data or PII-labeled datasets.
2) Enabling a region (e.g., EU, APAC) for a model previously served only from US regions.
3) Changes to the audit/audit-log pipeline (new exporters, retention changes, redaction rules).
4) Introducing third-party plugins or connectors that persist inference outputs.
5) Any customer request for contractual residency guarantees or legal-hold support.
sections.heading: When to run an SIA (short checklist)

sections.body:
- Requestor (Product/Platform owner): open an SIA request and provide deployment diagram, model artifact hash, and expected traffic profile.
- Security (policy and evidence lead): run the assessment, define the evidence bundle, and sign the acceptance.
- Infra/Networking: confirm network boundaries, egress points, and routing fallback behavior.
- Legal/Privacy: evaluate legal/regulatory acceptability and required contractual language.
- SRE/Oncall: validate runbook changes and rollback criteria for the deployment.
sections.heading: Responsibilities (owners)

sections.body:
1) Intake & triage:
   - Create an SIA ticket in the compliance tracker with model_id, proposed regions, expected data class (PD0/PD1/PD2), and deployment timeline.
   - Attach high-level diagram (png/svg) showing ingress, serving tier, cache layers, and logging collectors.
2) Technical mapping:
   - Identify all persistent and ephemeral data objects for this deployment: inference inputs, outputs, KV cache, intermediate traces, aggregated metrics, and debug snapshots.
   - List their storage locations (region, bucket id, DB cluster id) and retention defaults.
3) Evidence pattern selection:
   - Use the catalogue below to select evidence artifacts required for regulatory proof and audits.
   - Mark any artifacts that need stronger protection (signed attestations, notarized manifests, HSM-backed keys).
4) Risk evaluation and decision matrix (see section below).
5) Packaging & automation:
   - Create an evidence bundle generation job (CI step) that produces the artifacts described and deposits them to the compliance evidence store.
   - If packaging is manual, schedule the packaging owner and runbook steps.
6) Approval & rollout:
   - Security and Legal approve the SIA; SRE runs a staged rollout with pre-defined monitoring thresholds.
7) Post-rollout verification:
   - Run evidence collection for the first 7 days and verify artifact completeness.

Evidence-pattern catalogue (artifact -> purpose -> minimum retention):
- Serving manifest (YAML): records model_id, model_hash (sha256), container image tag, commit id, compiled-kernel version. Purpose: provenance. Retain: 7 years.
- Deployment topology diagram (png/svg + MD5): shows region-to-region routes and egress points. Purpose: residency mapping. Retain: 3 years.
- Authorization logs (append-only audit stream): token_ids, policy decisions, subject attributes, resource. Purpose: proof-of-access decisions. Retain: 7 years (searchable index); raw stream retained 90 days.
- Network egress snapshots (netflow export): sample of flow logs for rollout window (first 72 hours). Purpose: demonstrate no unexpected cross-border egress. Retain: 1 year.
- Storage location attestations (signed): bucket/DB residency declaration including encryption-at-rest keys. Purpose: legal proof. Retain: 7 years.
- KMS usage ledger (HSM-backed): envelope key ids and key usage events for the model artifact. Purpose: key provenance. Retain: 10 years.
- Model artifact signing record (sigstore or internal equivalent): signature, signer identity, timestamp. Purpose: artifact integrity. Retain: 10 years.
- Redaction & de-identification checklist (md): shows fields removed/hashed before downstream storage. Purpose: PII control evidence. Retain: 3 years.
- Access-control snapshot (RBAC export): role bindings and attribute-based policies effective during deployment. Purpose: authorization evidence. Retain: 3 years.
- Sampling of inference payloads (sanitized): examples demonstrating classification/PII handling. Purpose: quality and privacy verification. Retain: 1 year (sanitized); raw never stored unless customer explicitly consents.
- Audit packaging manifest (JSON): list of all artifacts included in bundle with checksums and packaging timestamp. Purpose: reproducible audit. Retain: 7 years.
sections.heading: Procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- If any persistent artifact is stored in a region outside the contractually-required residency zone -> action: block rollout, require data relocation or encryption+key-escrow with customer control.
- If audit logs show non-trivial policy-deny events during staged rollout (>1% of requests with unexpected denies) -> action: immediate rollback and root cause triage.
- If network egress samples show unexplained cross-border flows -> action: quarantine, capture full pcaps for 24 hours, engage Legal.
- If model artifact provenance cannot be cryptographically proven -> action: rebuild pipeline with signed artifacts before deployment.
sections.heading: Decision matrix (high level)

sections.body:
- Pre-rollout artifacts: serving manifest, topology diagram, RBAC export -> included in the initial evidence bundle and retained 7/3/3 years respectively.
- Rollout-window artifacts: netflow snapshots, authorization logs, KMS usage -> collected daily for 7 days, then aggregated indices retained 1 year / 7 years / 10 years as above.
- Post-rollout: audit packaging manifest and sanitized payload samples -> retain 7 years / 1 year.
sections.heading: Retention and packaging schedule (textual table)

sections.body:
- CI job to generate a serving manifest:
  - Example (bash pseudo):
    echo '{"model_id":"${MODEL_ID}","sha256":"$(sha256sum model.tar.gz | cut -d' ' -f1)","kernel":"${KERNEL_VERSION}" }' > serving-manifest.json
    sign-tool sign --input serving-manifest.json --key $CI_SIGNING_KEY --out serving-manifest.signed
- Residency assessment CLI (internal):
  - redwoodctl residency assess --model-id MODEL-123 --target-region eu-west-1 --output s ia-report.json
  - The command produces a recommended evidence pattern and a pre-filled packaging manifest.
sections.heading: Automation recipes (examples)

sections.body:
- Low risk (automated evidence available, all artifacts in-residency): Security approves; product may proceed.
- Medium risk (some artifacts require manual attestations or transient cross-border caching): Legal must sign a residual risk acceptance and SRE must add monitoring and an automatic rollback trigger.
- High risk (persistent storage outside allowed zones, inability to produce signed artifact provenance): Deployment is blocked until mitigations are in place; Executive Security must approve any exception.
sections.heading: Escalation and risk acceptance

sections.body:
- Short-lived exceptions (<=72 hours): require an exception ticket with owner, compensating controls (encryption + key control), and an evidence sweep at exception close.
- Longer exceptions (>72 hours): require formal risk acceptance, documented residual risk, and scheduled audits every 30 days.
sections.heading: Exception handling (ad-hoc evidence and timebox)

sections.body:
- Missing RBAC export: mitigate by running automated RBAC snapshot and validating role-to-subject bindings before packaging.
- Unsigned model artifact: mitigate with immediate CI rebuild and automatic signing enforced by gating policy.
- Unexpected egress because of third-party telemetry: mitigate by blackholing telemetry endpoints in staging and ensuring telemetry uses regional collectors.
sections.heading: Common failure modes and mitigations

sections.body:
- [ ] Serving manifest signed and checksummed.
- [ ] Topology diagram uploaded and MD5 recorded.
- [ ] RBAC export created and verified.
- [ ] KMS policy reviewed; key-escrow documented if required.
- [ ] Audit packaging job created and smoke-tested.
- [ ] Legal sign-off present for any cross-border storage.

Appendix A: example audit packaging manifest (JSON snippet described):
- The manifest must include: bundle_id, packaging_timestamp, artifacts: list of {name, path, checksum, signer}. Store manifest as text/json and preserve signed manifest in the evidence store.

Appendix B: retention FAQ:
Q: Can we reduce retention for low-risk models?
A: Any change to default retention must be approved by Security + Legal and recorded in the SIA ticket with business justification.

Appendix C: related artifacts and where to find them:
- Compliance evidence store: s3://redwood-compliance-evidence/<project>/<bundle_id>/
- RBAC export service: https://internal-console/audit/rbac-export
- KMS usage ledger: query via KMS-ops team (ticket required)
sections.heading: Checklist for evidence-ready deployment (pre-rollout)

sections.body:
- 2026-01-12: Created by Priya Malhotra.
- 2026-03-04: Clarified retention periods and added KMS ledger retention guidance (reviewed by Derek Wu).

payload.page_title: Crypto-audit tokenization and cross-tenant redaction policy

sections.body:
Summary
This document describes Redwoods standard for cryptographic audit tokenization, multi-tenant redaction, and how tokenized audit streams are retained and packaged as compliance evidence. It defines architecture, event schema extensions, key management requirements, verification procedures for auditors and incident responders, and a risk/exception handling process.

Purpose and scope
- Purpose: Reduce exposure of tenant-sensitive identifiers and PII in our long-term audit archive while preserving cryptographic proof-of-origin and the ability to rehydrate evidence for authorized investigation and audits.
- Scope: Applies to all production services that emit audit events into Redwoods centralized audit pipeline (audit-edge, ingestion, streaming, and cold-tier storage). Covers events for authentication/authorization (RBAC), model-serving inference logs, billing-relevant metadata, and administrative actions.
- Exclusions: Ephemeral debug logs (non-audit debug) and internal engineering sandboxes that do not feed the centralized audit pipeline.

Guiding principles
1) Minimally sufficient fidelity: Audit events retain schema fields required for reconstruction of a sequence-of-actions (timestamps, action type, resource type, outcome) while sensitive identifiers are replaced by verifiable tokens.
2) Verifiability: Tokens are cryptographically bound to the original identifier and to an event digest so investigators can cryptographically prove lineage without exposing the identifier in normal query flows.
3) Tenant separation and least privilege: Cross-tenant queries and support access must never return raw tenant identifiers unless an access workflow with attestation and approval is followed.
4) Retention and rehydration controls: Rehydration (revealing original identifiers) requires multi-party approval, timeboxed keys, and an audited packaging step that generates evidence bundles.

Architecture overview
- Producers: Application services produce canonical audit events (JSON) with a clear audit schema (see section Event schema). Producers call the Tokenization Service before emitting to the centralized stream.
- Tokenization Service (stateless API + HSM-backed signing): Replaces sensitive fields with a token and returns a signed token object containing a token_id, token_type, signer_id, and a signature over (tenant_id || original_value_hash || event_digest || timestamp).
- Audit Stream (Kafka): Tokenized events flow to the streaming tier. Consumers (alerting, SLO calculators, forensic indexing) operate on tokenized values.
- Key Management: Signing keys are held in KMS/HSM and rotated per policy. A separate rehydration keyset (limited-wrapping-keys) is required to unwrap confidential values and is controlled by the Evidence Service.
- Evidence Service: Orchestrates rehydration requests, approval workflows, transient key material creation, evidence packaging (signed bundle + index), and audit trail recording.

Event schema (required fields and tokenized patterns)
- Common top-level fields: event_id, timestamp, service, environment, severity, action, status, context
- Sensitive fields that must be tokenized at ingestion: user_id, account_id, api_key_id, session_id, model_input/embedding_id when it maps to PII, storage_object_path when it references customer-provided data
- Token object (example inserted in event):
  "tokenized_fields": [{
    "field_path": "context.user_id",
    "token": "TKN_7b3f...",
    "token_type": "sha256-hmac+sign",
    "signer": "token-svc-v2",
    "signature": "base64(sig)",
    "hash_alg": "sha256"
  }]
- The original hashed value is never stored in plain text in the stream. Instead, the token payload contains a hash of the original value (salted with tenant_id) that is part of the signature input so verification is possible without revealing the original.

Tokenization workflow (producer perspective)
1) Producer computes value_hash = HMAC(salt = tenant_id, value = original_identifier) using local service salt (rotated weekly).
2) Producer calls Tokenization Service: POST /tokenize { "tenant_id", "field_path", "value_hash", "event_digest" }
3) Tokenization Service issues token_id and signs (tenant_id || value_hash || event_digest || issued_at) with the HSM private key.
4) Producer writes the event replacing original_identifier with token_id and attaching the token metadata.
5) Central consumers treat token_id as opaque; only Evidence Service can request rehydration.

Key management and rotation
- Signing keys: Stored in KMS with HSM wrapping. Keys are rotated every 365 days, with an overlap window of 7 days for verification compatibility.
- Salt material: Service-level salts used to compute value_hash are rotated weekly. Salt rotations are logged and recorded in the salt registry.
- Rehydration keys: Strictly restricted. Rehydration requires a tombstone key that is created transiently, wrapped to the Evidence Service, and destroyed after bundle generation.
- Compromise procedure: If a signing key is suspected compromised, immediately stop acceptance of token signatures, issue a token revocation snapshot, and consult the Evidence and Legal teams for containment.

Rehydration and evidence packaging process
- Authorization gates: Rehydration requires: (a) at least two approvers from distinct teams (security and legal or security and customer-success), (b) a documented justification, (c) an expiration time for the rehydration session, and (d) an integrity check via event_digest verification.
- Packaging steps (automated by Evidence Service):
  1) Validate approvals and attestations.
  2) Create transient rehydration key bound to the request (TTL configurable, default 4 hours).
  3) Recompute value_hash for candidate tokens and attempt one-way mapping to original values stored in the Protected Mapping Store (PMS) accessible only to Evidence Service.
  4) Generate evidence bundle: zipped directory containing (i) tokenized event slice, (ii) rehydrated field mapping, (iii) signature chain and timestamp, (iv) approver audit trail, (v) integrity manifest (SHA256 checksums).
  5) Digitally sign the evidence bundle with Evidence Service signing key and store the bundle in restricted cold storage with a recorded access policy.
- Evidence delivery: Bundles for external auditors are delivered via an encrypted transfer channel (SFTP over VPN or customer-managed bucket with pre-signed URL + IP restrictions) and logged.

Operational runbook: investigating an RBAC anomaly with tokenized logs
1) Trigger: Alert from SSO or abnormal access pattern with referenced token IDs.
2) Triage: Determine tenant_id and affected token_ids from tokenized events.
3) Request rehydration: Open Evidence Service request (link generated automatically), include justification, and tag legal/security approvers.
4) Approvers review: Approvals must include an explicit timebox and expected recipients of the bundle.
5) Evidence Service packages bundle and posts an immutable record to the incident ticket.
6) Investigator receives bundle and performs correlation; any further rehydration requests for the same incident require a new approval.
7) Post-incident: Evidence expiration and deletion policy enforced; a retention snapshot is recorded for compliance tracing.

Retention, archival tiers, and deletion
- Hot tier (90 days): searchable tokenized stream stored in primary cluster.
- Warm tier (1 year): compacted tokenized events with indexed metadata.
- Cold tier (7 years default for regulated customers): tokenized events and signed evidence bundles (not plain identifiers).
- Rehydrated bundles persisted only if explicitly required by legal/regulatory hold; otherwise bundles are deleted after TTL and deletion is recorded and attested.

Audit and monitoring requirements
- SLOs: Tokenization latency must be < 20 ms p95 for 99% of requests; tokenization service errors must be < 0.1% monthly.
- Telemetry: Token issuance (count, latency), token verification attempts, rehydration requests (approvals, denials), key rotation events, and evidence bundle generation are emitted to security telemetry.
- Alerts: Tokenization service error spike, Evidence Service approval delays > 8 hours for high-severity incidents, key rotation failure.

Verification for auditors (ad-hoc)
- Auditor verification flow (read-only):
  1) Auditor receives signed evidence bundle and the Evidence Service public verification key.
  2) Auditor validates the evidence bundle signature and checks the manifest checksums.
  3) Auditor verifies token signatures against the token-svc public key and validates that token hashes correspond to tenant-provided sample identifiers (if permitted by NDA).
  4) For deeper verification, Redwood can perform a controlled rehydration in the presence of auditors following the standard approval gates.

Risk and exception handling
- Acceptable risks: Tokenization may reduce immediate readability for on-call engineers; mitigated by fast rehydration workflows and a rich token-to-metadata index for common diagnostics.
- Exceptions: Short-lived exceptions (e.g., emergency platform-wide debugging) may allow temporarily retaining un-tokenized fields, but must be recorded in the Exception Register with: owner, justification, TTL, and compensating controls (access logging, IP restrictions).
- Exception approval flow: Team Lead -> Security -> Legal (for cross-border data). Exceptions are timeboxed and audited.

Ownership and roles
- Tokenization Service: eng-infra (owner), oncall: infra-audits@redwood.com
- Evidence Service: security (owner), oncall: sec-evidence@redwood.com
- Key management & rotation: cloud-security team (owner), oncall: kms-ops@redwood.com
- Compliance packaging & external delivery: customer-success + security (shared)

Appendix A: Example tokenization request (producer)
POST /tokenize HTTP/1.1
Host: token-svc.internal.redwood.com
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-corp-123",
  "field_path": "context.user_id",
  "value_hash": "hmac-sha256:4f2b...",
  "event_digest": "sha256:ab12..."
}
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "token_id": "TKN_7b3f4c8a",
  "signer": "token-svc-v2",
  "signature": "base64(...)",
  "issued_at": "2026-03-15T18:22:31Z",
  "token_type": "sha256-hmac+sign",
  "hash_alg": "sha256"
}

Appendix B: Evidence bundle manifest (excerpt)
- bundle_id: EVID_20260315_0009
- requestor: sec-ops
- approvers: [security@redwood.com, legal@redwood.com]
- token_count: 42
- signed_by: evidence-svc-key-v1
- checksums: { "events.json": "sha256:...", "mapping.csv": "sha256:..." }

Policy change log
- 2026-03-15: Initial published policy and architecture (Maya Chen).
- 2026-06-02: Clarified rehydration TTLs and added SLOs for tokenization service (Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-09-02: Added cross-tenant redaction clarifications and tightened rehydration approval requirements (Priya Nair).

Contacts and escalation
- Security policy questions: security-policy@redwood.com
- Emergency rehydration approvals (oncall): sec-evidence@redwood.com
- KMS incidents: kms-ops@redwood.com

Related references
- Audit schema versioning and evidence tagging (internal)
- RBAC provenance and retention runbook
- Evidence packaging and transfer SOP

End of document

payload.page_title: Audit events for Dedicated rollout actions (staged rollouts)

sections.body:
This document defines the audit logging requirements and event schema for **Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools**. It covers:
- Event types and semantics for actions: **create/update/promote/abort/hold/force overrides**
- Required fields for compliance, forensic review, and customer change management
- RBAC requirements (who can do what, and what must be logged)
- Retention and export (internal UI + customer export + SIEM)
- Example event payloads

This spec applies to all deployment modes of Dedicated pools (single-region and multi-region), and to all rollout targets (model version, runtime build, routing policy, config changes).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. **Deterministic & auditable change history**: A human reviewer can reconstruct what changed, who initiated it, when it took effect, what gates were evaluated, and why the system promoted/aborted.
2. **Tamper-evident audit trail** suitable for regulated customers’ change-management expectations.
3. **Low risk of sensitive data leakage** (no prompts, user content, or secrets).
4. **Consistent eventing across entry points** (Console, API, automated policy engine actions).
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Provide a general-purpose eventing framework for all Redwood features.
- Store raw metrics time series in audit logs (we link to evidence queries and dashboards instead).
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- **Dedicated pool**: Reserved GPU capacity pool associated with a customer account.
- **Rollout plan**: A staged plan applied to a Dedicated pool.
- **Stage**: A defined traffic/replica partition in the rollout.
- **Gate**: A set of criteria that must pass to promote a stage.
- **Actor**: The entity that initiated the action (human user, service principal, or system automation).
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
Events MUST be emitted server-side by the system of record for the action:
- Control plane service: **dedicated-pool-rollouts-service**
  - Creates/updates rollout plans
  - Processes promote/abort/hold/override requests
  - Emits canonical audit events
- Policy engine (if it triggers automated transitions)
  - MUST call control plane transition APIs; the control plane emits the audit event with actor_type=system and actor_service=policy-engine
- Console
  - MUST NOT emit audit events directly; it calls control plane APIs with end-user identity and request context
sections.heading: 1) Where events are emitted

sections.body:
- All mutating endpoints MUST support an **Idempotency-Key** (header) and return the same result for a retry.
- Audit events MUST include:
  - `request_id` (unique per request attempt)
  - `idempotency_key` (dedupe across retries)
  - `event_id` (globally unique)
- The audit pipeline MUST de-duplicate on `(event_id)`; consumers should use `(event_id)` as primary key.
sections.heading: 2) Idempotency and deduplication

sections.body:
- `schema_name`: `redwood.audit.dedicated_rollouts`
- `schema_version`: `1.0`

Backward-compatible changes (additive fields) keep the same version. Breaking changes require a version bump and coordinated export updates.
sections.heading: All events include

sections.body:
- Prompts, completions, embeddings, customer payloads
- Secrets (API keys, tokens), KMS material
- Raw request/response bodies
sections.heading: Audit events MUST NOT include

sections.body:
- Resource identifiers, stage indices, stage configs at a high level
- Threshold configuration (numbers/percentages) and summarized observed values
- Links to internal dashboards / evidence queries
sections.heading: Allowable data includes

sections.body: All timestamps MUST be RFC3339 UTC (e.g., `2025-03-12T21:14:33Z`).
sections.heading: 5) Time

sections.body:
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.created`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.updated`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.promotion_requested`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.promoted`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.aborted`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.held`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.resumed`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.force_promoted`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.force_aborted`
- `dedicated.rollout_plan.gate_evaluation_recorded`
sections.heading: All event types share a prefix and use dotted naming

sections.body:
- We separate `promotion_requested` from `promoted` to capture async workflows.
- `gate_evaluation_recorded` is emitted when the system evaluates gates and persists a result that affected promotion/abort/hold decisions.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
Each event MUST contain the following fields (names are stable; values vary by event type):

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| event_id | string | yes | UUIDv7 recommended |
| event_type | string | yes | One of taxonomy values |
| occurred_at | string | yes | RFC3339 UTC |
| schema_name | string | yes | `redwood.audit.dedicated_rollouts` |
| schema_version | string | yes | `1.0` |
| environment | string | yes | `prod`, `staging`, etc. |
| region | string | yes | Control plane region emitting the event |
| actor_type | string | yes | `human` \| `service` \| `system` |
| actor_id | string | yes | User ID or service principal ID |
| actor_email | string | no | For humans when available |
| actor_service | string | no | e.g., `console-backend`, `policy-engine` |
| actor_ip | string | no | If sourced from user action |
| authn_method | string | no | e.g., `sso`, `api_key`, `service_token` |
| request_id | string | yes | Trace/request correlation ID |
| idempotency_key | string | no | If supplied |
| account_id | string | yes | Customer account ID owning the pool |
| org_id | string | no | Internal org mapping if applicable |
| dedicated_pool_id | string | yes | The Dedicated pool |
| rollout_plan_id | string | yes | Stable rollout plan identifier |
| rollout_plan_version | string | yes | Optimistic concurrency version (integer serialized as string) |
| console_session_id | string | no | If triggered via Console |
| change_reason | string | no | Required for overrides; recommended otherwise |
| ticket_ref | string | no | e.g., `INC-...`, `SUP-...`, `JIRA-...`, `LINEAR-...` |
| severity | string | no | `info` \| `warning` \| `critical` (for override/abort) |
| outcome | string | yes | `success` \| `failure` |
| error_code | string | no | If failure |
| error_message | string | no | Sanitized; no secrets |
sections.heading: Common event envelope (required fields)

sections.body:
- `account_id`, `dedicated_pool_id`, `rollout_plan_id` MUST be globally unique identifiers.
- For multi-region pools, the event should still reference the single pool; region-specific details belong in the per-event payload (see below).
sections.heading: Resource identity conventions

sections.body:
Event-specific fields MUST be included in the same JSON object as the envelope (no nested objects required by this spec), but nested structures are allowed in storage/export. When constrained to flat export (e.g., some SIEM sinks), use `payload_json` as a string.

For internal storage (Audit Log Store), nested JSON is allowed; for this Confluence spec, examples show nested JSON for readability.
sections.heading: Event-specific payload requirements

sections.body: Emitted when a rollout plan is created.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.created

sections.body:
- `rollout_target_type`: `model_version` \| `runtime_build` \| `routing_policy` \| `config_bundle`
- `rollout_target_ref`: stable reference (e.g., model id + version)
- `stages_count`
- `stage_spec_summary`: short string summary (e.g., `1%/10%/50%/100%` or `replicas: 1/2/5/all`)
- `initial_state`: expected `draft` or `running`
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when the plan definition is modified (before running) or when allowed editable fields are changed.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.updated

sections.body:
- `updated_fields`: list of field paths (stringified)
- `before_hash`, `after_hash`: stable hashes of canonicalized plan spec for tamper-evidence and quick diffing
- `edit_policy`: `allowed` \| `restricted` (indicates whether edit was permitted during running state)
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when a promotion is requested (human or system). This is important even if later denied.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.promotion_requested

sections.body:
- `from_stage_id`
- `to_stage_id`
- `requested_by`: `human` \| `system`
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when promotion completes and routing/pool partitioning is updated.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.promoted

sections.body:
- `from_stage_id`
- `to_stage_id`
- `promotion_mode`: `standard` \| `force`
- `gate_summary`: `passed` \| `skipped` \| `failed` \| `unknown`
- `routing_commit_id`: identifier of the routing config snapshot applied
- `effective_at`: RFC3339 timestamp when the new stage became effective
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when the rollout is aborted.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.aborted

sections.body:
- `abort_reason`: `gate_failure` \| `operator_action` \| `system_safety` \| `capacity_safety` \| `telemetry_missing` \| `other`
- `rollback_to_stage_id`: typically previous stable stage, often `0` (baseline)
- `in_flight_policy`: `pinned` \| `drain_then_reroute` (per streaming semantics)
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when the rollout enters/exits hold state.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.held / resumed

sections.body:
- `hold_reason` (for held)
- `hold_timeout_seconds` (if applicable)
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body: Emitted when an admin override is used.
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.force_promoted / force_aborted

sections.body:
- `override_type`: `force_promote` \| `force_abort`
- `override_scope`: `single_stage` \| `entire_rollout`
- `override_approver_id` (if dual-approval is enabled; optional in v1)
- `override_guardrails`: string summary of guardrails presented to actor (e.g., “requires dedicated_rollouts.admin; reason required; customer-visible”)
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body:
- `change_reason` MUST be provided.
- `severity` MUST be `warning` or `critical`.
sections.heading: Policy

sections.body: Emitted when gate evaluation is computed and persisted (including missing-data outcomes).
sections.heading: dedicated.rollout_plan.gate_evaluation_recorded

sections.body:
- `stage_id`
- `evaluation_window_seconds`
- `evaluation_start_at`, `evaluation_end_at`
- `gate_outcome`: `passed` \| `failed` \| `unknown`
- `missing_data_policy`: `fail_closed` \| `fail_open` \| `manual`
- `gate_evidence_uri`: link to Console evidence view (stable, permission-checked)
- `gate_evidence_summary`: short human-readable string

Recommended additional fields (when safe and not too high-cardinality):
- `observed_error_rate`, `threshold_error_rate`
- `observed_p95_ms`, `threshold_p95_ms`
- `observed_saturation`, `threshold_saturation`
- `observed_oom_rate`, `threshold_oom_rate`
sections.heading: Required additional fields

sections.body:
This spec assumes the following RBAC concepts (names are representative; implementation may map to Redwood’s authz system):
- `dedicated_rollouts.viewer`: read-only access to rollout plans and audit trail
- `dedicated_rollouts.operator`: can create plans, request promotion/abort/hold for eligible pools
- `dedicated_rollouts.admin`: can force overrides; can operate across accounts where allowed
- `customer_admin`: customer-side admin (Dedicated customer) with limited rollout controls if enabled
sections.heading: Roles

sections.body:
- The server MUST enforce RBAC.
- If RBAC denies, emit an audit event with:
  - `event_type`: same action family (e.g., `dedicated.rollout_plan.promotion_requested`)
  - `outcome`: `failure`
  - `error_code`: `forbidden`
  - `actor_id`, `account_id`, `dedicated_pool_id` populated

This creates a record of attempted access (important for regulated environments).
sections.heading: For any request that results in an audit event

sections.body:
- Create plan: operator/admin (and optionally customer_admin on allowlisted accounts)
- Update plan:
  - In `draft`: operator/admin
  - In `running`: restricted to admin-only fields (e.g., gate thresholds if allowed) — emit `edit_policy=restricted`
- Promote stage:
  - Standard: operator/admin
  - Force: admin only (always requires `change_reason`)
- Abort rollout:
  - Standard: operator/admin
  - Force abort: admin only
- Hold/resume:
  - Operator/admin; holds over N hours may require admin (configurable)
sections.heading: Actions matrix (v1)

sections.body:
- Audit Log Store (internal): **400 days** hot retention.

payload.page_title: Observable authorization log curation and evidence playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook prescribes a repeatable, audit-ready workflow for curating authorization (authz) and authentication (authn) logs into compliance evidence bundles. It covers log schemas, residency-aware retention, secure SDLC touchpoints, incident-response collection, and exception handling for risk-team approvals. The goal is to ensure every access decision that matters for compliance is observable, tamper-resistant, and packaged for audits within defined SLOs.

Scope
- Systems: API gateway, edge auth proxy, identity provider (IdP) assertions, service mesh, RBAC enforcement point, policy-evaluation service, admin consoles.
- Evidence types: authz decisions, token issuance/refresh, entitlement changes, role bindings, privileged session start/stop, delegation events.
- Audiences: security ops, compliance, SRE, product infra teams, legal.

Key definitions
- Decision Log: canonical record for an access decision (allow/deny) with context.
- Proof Bundle: cryptographically verifiable archive containing log slice, policy snapshot, role-mapping, and ingestion metadata for a given incident or audit window.
- Residency Boundary: geographic / legal boundary determining where PII or customer data can be stored.

Principles
- Always-on observability: authz telemetry must be emitted synchronously at enforcement points.
- Minimal latency impact: logs may be buffered, but not dropped; buffer thresholds ensure SLOs for request latency are met.
- Immutable tagging: each decision log gets an immutable trace_id, signing_key_id, and ingestion_timestamp.
- Residency-aware packaging: proof bundles must only include data allowed by the residency boundary of the tenant/customer.

Roles and responsibilities
- Security (owner): defines evidence format, signing policy, retention class, and approves exceptions.
- SRE/Platform: implements collectors, retention enforcement, and backup.
- Product Infra: maintains policy snapshot tooling and rollout linkage.
- Compliance: accepts proof bundles and performs audit completeness checks.

Logging requirements (schema and constraints)
Provide the canonical event schema for any enforcement point. All fields are required unless marked optional.

| field_name | type | required | example | notes |
|------------|------|----------|---------|-------|
| trace_id | string | required | tx-4f9b3c | UUID or span-id tying request traces to logs |
| timestamp_iso8601 | string | required | 2026-01-30T14:23:02Z | ingest client must use UTC |
| decision | string | required | allow/deny | canonical boolean as string |
| principal_id | string | required | user:alice@example.com | subject that requested access |
| principal_type | string | required | user/service | helps filter PII for residency |
| resource | string | required | model-serving:inference:request | resource identifier |
| action | string | required | generate/rollback/read | action attempted |
| policy_version | string | required | policy:v2026-01-28-4 | snapshot id of policy used |
| reason | string | optional | rate_limit_disabled | policy decision explanation |
| token_hash | string | optional | sha256(...) | hashed token id (masked in some regions) |
| enforcement_point | string | required | edge-auth-proxy | hostname/service |
| signing_key_id | string | required | sig-2026-01 | key used to sign this record |

Retention and residency model
- Retention classes: short-term (30 days), medium (1 year), long-term (7 years). Mapping to class is defined by classification rules in the retention registry.
- Residency constraints: tenant residency label appended to each decision log. Bundles for cross-border incidents must follow the cross-region-review procedure prior to movement.
- Automatic purging: SRE runs a monthly enforcement job that verifies retention policy and triggers secure deletion flows.

Secure SDLC integration
- Policy snapshotting: every policy change merges into a policy repository (git) and uses a deterministic snapshot id. The deploy pipeline records the policy_version tag and embeds it into the policy_version field in decision logs.
- Pre-merge checks: changes to RBAC or policy evaluation code require: unit tests, policy-consistency lint, static analysis for PII exfil patterns, and a security review label.
- Release gate: production rollout requires evidence bundle generation tests in staging that demonstrate log emission and proof-bundle creation for a sample workload.

Incident response collection procedure (quick play)
1) Triage and scope: incident lead identifies affected residency and initiates an evidence-capture ticket.
2) Freeze window: if live systems may overwrite logs, apply a short-term snapshot retention extension for impacted services (actioned by SRE on approval).
3) Collect proof bundle: follow the Proof Bundle checklist (below).
4) Verify integrity: check bundle manifests and signature verification using the signing_key_id key.
5) Handoff and storage: upload to the evidence vault (region-bound) and notify Compliance and Legal.

Proof Bundle checklist (must be included)
- Decision log slice (ndjson) covering the incident period.
- Policy snapshot (policy repo commit + human-readable rendered policy).
- Role mapping snapshot (current RBAC bindings).
- Service deployment manifest (image tags, config hash).
- Signing manifest: signatures of the decision log slice and manifest.json, with signing_key_id metadata.
- Chain-of-custody record: who requested/assembled the bundle, timestamps, and approvals.

Evidence packaging rules by residency
- For tenants in EU residency, PII fields (principal_id) are pseudonymized in shared audit extracts; full principal_id included only in proof bundles stored in EU vault.
- For US tenants, include masked token identifiers in audit extracts; full token_hash allowed in proof bundle when stored in US vault.
- For cross-border lawful requests, follow legal & compliance approval workflow (see "Risk exceptions and cross-border flow" below).

Risk exceptions and approval process
- Exceptions may be requested when operational constraints prevent meeting the logging or residency requirements (e.g., 3rd-party SaaS forwarder without regional storage).
- Exception request must include: impact statement, proposed compensating controls, TTL (max 90 days), and rollback plan.
- Approvers: Security (primary), Legal (if cross-border), Compliance (if audit scope affected).
- Exception automation: approved exceptions are recorded in the exception registry with a scheduled automated expiration and reminder to reviewers.

Operational playbook: daily and monthly tasks
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Verify collector health dashboards: ingestion lag < 30s across 99th percentile.
- Random bundle smoke-test: assemble a 1-hour proof bundle from staging and verify signatures.
sections.heading: Daily

sections.body:
- Retention enforcement run and deletion audit report.
- Key rotation check: verify signing_key_id rotation has been reflected in manifests.
- Cross-team tabletop: run a 30-min evidence handoff drill with Compliance and SRE.

Sample CLI snippets
- Assemble a proof bundle (example):
  redwood-evidence assemble --service edge-auth-proxy --start 2026-01-30T14:00:00Z --end 2026-01-30T15:00:00Z --output /tmp/bundle-20260130.tar.gz

- Verify signatures:
  redwood-evidence verify /tmp/bundle-20260130.tar.gz --keystore /var/keys/signing-pubring.json

Audit readiness SLOs and metrics
- Time-to-bundle: 95% of incident proof bundles assembled and uploaded within 4 hours of request.
- Completeness: 99.9% of enforcement points include required fields in logs across the rolling 30-day window.
- Integrity: 100% of stored proof bundles pass signature verification during random sampling.

Appendix: common failure modes and mitigations
- Missing policy_version: detect in CI via policy-injection linter; block merges that would remove policy snapshoting.
- Clock skew: enforce NTP and validate timestamp drift during daily collector health checks.
- Over-redaction: compliance complaints from audit; provide a reversible pseudonymization service that keeps a sealed mapping inside the regional vault.

Related artifacts and links
- Policy repo: git+ssh://git.redwood.internal/policy-eval
- Evidence vault runbook: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/forensic-log-preservation-and-legal-hold-playbook-2025
- Exception registry UI: https://internal.redwood/exceptions

Contact
For questions or to request an exception, contact security@redwood.com or use the internal Slack #sec-evidence channel.

sections.body: This page defines how long Redwood retains audit logs and who can access them. Audit logs cover security-relevant events across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Redwood-managed control plane components that support Private deployments.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Hosted API: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Dedicated: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Private: 365 days retention for Redwood control-plane audit logs (actions taken in Redwood-managed components).
- Customer-owned Private audit logs: customer-configured; Redwood does not set or enforce retention for customer-side logging systems.
sections.heading: Retention

sections.body:
- Audit logs are accessible only to Security and SRE on a need-to-know basis via the Audit Explorer tool.
- Access is governed by least-privilege RBAC and requires SSO + MFA.
- Any export of audit logs for a customer request must be approved by Security and tracked via a support ticket.
sections.heading: Access controls

sections.body:
- Standard turnaround: 5 business days for audit log exports (unless contractually obligated otherwise).
- Deletion: audit logs are not deleted early except where required by law or contract; exceptions require Legal + Security approval and are documented in a support ticket.

payload.page_title: Incident Bot v2 — Access Audit Logging (Config Diff + Privileged Telemetry)

sections.body:
h1. Purpose
This page defines the *audit logging requirements, event taxonomy, retention, and compliance review procedures* for Incident Bot v2 access to:
- Tenant-aware configuration diffs (feature flags, routing policy, quotas, model pins) via the config service diff endpoint.
- Privileged telemetry query primitives used to render saturation signals and diagnostic links.

This is a *restricted* document because it describes internal security controls, audit event fields, and review cadence.

h2. Scope
*In scope*
- Incident Bot v2 (Slack app + backend) access to privileged endpoints.
- Read access to tenant-aware config diff API (redacted output) and privileged telemetry query service.
- Break-glass elevation flows for Sev0/Sev1 incidents.
- Audit pipeline reliability requirements and escalation.

*Out of scope*
- General audit logging for non-incident tooling.
- Full incident management process (see on-call playbook).

h2. Systems / data flows (high level)
1) A responder invokes Incident Bot v2 in Slack (#incidents, #eng-oncall).
2) Bot backend calls one or more internal services:
   - *config-service* (tenant-aware diff endpoint)
   - *telemetry-query-service* (bounded, tenant-safe query primitives)
   - *deploy-metadata-service* (not privileged; included here only for correlation)
3) Each privileged call emits an *immutable audit event* to the central audit pipeline.
4) Audit events are streamed to the SIEM and stored in an immutable archive.

h2. Guiding principles
- *Least privilege:* bot uses a dedicated service identity with scoped permissions.
- *Auditability:* every privileged read includes actor + purpose + tenant context + incident context.
- *Data minimization:* audit payloads must not include secrets, raw configs, or query results.
- *Deterministic correlation:* events must include identifiers to correlate across Slack thread, incident ID, and backend request.
- *Operational usability:* security and SRE must be able to answer “who accessed what, when, why” within minutes.

h1. Roles and identities
h2. Service identities
- *incident-bot-prod* (service identity)
- *incident-bot-staging* (service identity)

h2. Actors (human)
When the bot performs an action triggered by an interactive Slack action (e.g., “Expand diff”, “Show tenant-level saturation”), the audit event must record:
- Slack user ID (stable) and, where available, Redwood employee identity (SSO subject)
- Whether the user is the currently paged on-call (best-effort)

h2. Break-glass
Break-glass access is allowed only for Sev0/Sev1 and requires additional audit events (see Event taxonomy).

h1. Event taxonomy
All events are emitted in the *Audit Event v3* format (central audit schema). Event *names* below are canonical.

h2. Required events
|| Event name || Trigger || Notes ||
| incident_bot.config_diff.read | Bot requests a config diff for a tenant/workspace/environment. | Emitted even when diff is empty (to show access). |
| incident_bot.config_diff.denied | Bot request is denied by authz policy. | Must include policy decision reason code. |
| incident_bot.telemetry.query | Bot issues a privileged telemetry query (GPU/queue/KV cache/etc.) for incident context. | Must include query class + boundedness metadata (not raw query). |
| incident_bot.telemetry.denied | Telemetry query denied by policy. | Include reason code + required scope. |
| incident_bot.break_glass.activate | Break-glass flow is initiated and granted. | Must include approver mechanism (policy rule) and expiration. |
| incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate | Break-glass expires or is revoked. | Include reason (expired/manual revoke). |

h2. Optional / recommended events
|| Event name || Trigger || Notes ||
| incident_bot.slack_action.invoke | A user clicks a bot action that can trigger privileged calls. | Provides correlation even if downstream fails. |
| incident_bot.privileged_call.failed | Downstream privileged call failed due to timeout/5xx. | Useful for detecting audit gaps vs upstream failures. |

h1. Required audit fields
All audit events MUST include the following fields (names shown as logical fields; actual field mapping is handled by the audit SDK).

h2. Core fields (required)
- *event_name* (see taxonomy)
- *event_time* (RFC3339)
- *environment* (prod/staging/dev)
- *service* (e.g., incident-bot, config-service, telemetry-query-service)
- *actor_type* (service | user)
- *actor_id*
  - For service actor: service identity name
  - For user actor: SSO subject (if available) and Slack user ID
- *request_id* (unique per backend request)
- *correlation_id* (stable across fan-out calls within a single bot invocation)
- *purpose* (incident_response | debugging | support_escalation)
- *permission_scope* used (e.g., config:diff.read_redacted; telemetry:query.tenant_safe)
- *authz_decision* (allow | deny)

h2. Tenant + incident context (required when applicable)
- *tenant_ref* (internal tenant/workspace identifier; do not log customer name)
- *tenant_ref_type* (tenant_id | workspace_id | org_id)
- *tenant_region* (if provided/known)
- *incident_ref* (Sev incident ID if available; otherwise Slack thread timestamp)
- *slack_channel_id* and *slack_thread_ts* (where action was invoked)

h2. Privacy & data handling constraints (hard requirements)
- DO NOT include:
  - Raw config values
  - Diff content
  - Secrets, tokens, API keys
  - Raw telemetry query strings
  - Query results
- OK to include:
  - Counts (e.g., “diff_keys_changed=12”)
  - Classifications (e.g., “query_class=gpu_utilization”, “time_range=15m”)
  - Hashes of stable identifiers when necessary for minimization

h1. Event payload guidance (by source)
h2. Config diff access (config-service)
When emitting incident_bot.config_diff.read:
- Include *diff_type* (feature_flags | routing_policy | quota_rate_limit | model_pins | other)
- Include *diff_window* (e.g., last 2h, since deploy X)
- Include *redaction_mode* (always “customer_safe_redacted” for bot output)
- Include *diff_summary_counts* (number of keys added/removed/changed) as a single string field

*Important:* redaction is enforced in the config-service response. Audit logs must still record the access event even if the response is fully redacted.

h2. Telemetry query access (telemetry-query-service)
When emitting incident_bot.telemetry.query:
- Include *query_class* (gpu_utilization | queue_depth | kv_cache_pressure | scheduler_backpressure | error_budget_burn | other)
- Include *aggregation_level* (service/route/region) and whether tenant-specific filters were applied
- Include *time_range* (e.g., 5m/15m/1h)
- Include *query_budget* metadata (e.g., “max_series=200; max_points=600; timeout_ms=2500”)

h1. Example events (sanitized)
These examples are representative. Exact field names may differ based on the audit SDK mapping.

h1. Retention and storage
h2. Primary retention policy
- *SIEM (searchable):* 400 days retention for all incident-bot privileged access events.
- *Immutable archive:* 7 years retention in WORM/immutable storage (for compliance evidence and customer contractual obligations).

h2. Storage locations and residency
- Audit events are stored in region-aligned buckets/indices.
- EU-scoped tenant events must remain within EU data residency boundaries for the archive (SIEM replication policy must preserve residency constraints).

h2. Access controls for audit logs
- Default access: Security Engineering and Compliance (named groups).
- SRE read-only access: limited to incident-related lookups (time-bounded, incident_ref required).
- All access to the SIEM indices containing these events is itself audited (SIEM native audit).

h1. Review procedure (compliance + operational)
h2. Ongoing monitoring
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Audit pipeline health (ingestion lag, drop rate, schema validation failures)
- Unexpected spikes in privileged access
- Break-glass activations outside Sev0/Sev1

h2. Monthly control check (owner: Security Engineering)
Performed by: *Kevin Osei* (primary) or delegate.
sections.heading: Security Engineering monitors

sections.body:
1) Pull last 30 days of incident_bot.config_diff.read and incident_bot.telemetry.query.
2) Verify:
   - Events include incident_ref + tenant_ref when applicable
   - actor_id is present for interactive actions
   - deny events are present for expected negative tests
3) Sample 10 incidents (or 10% of incidents, whichever is larger):
   - Confirm bot actions in Slack correlate to audit events (by slack_thread_ts/correlation_id)
4) File findings in the Security Controls tracker and assign remediation owners.

h2. Quarterly access review (owner: Security + Compliance)
Performed by: *Marcus Lin* and Compliance partner.
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
1) Review group membership for:
   - Audit log read access
   - Break-glass privilege approval roles
2) Validate least-privilege alignment with current on-call rotations.
3) Confirm break-glass activation counts and verify associated incidents were Sev0/Sev1.
4) Record evidence snapshot (export of membership + sample events) in the compliance evidence repository.

h2. Annual audit evidence package (SOC 2 / customer audits)
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- Current event taxonomy and required fields (this page)
- Retention configuration evidence (SIEM + archive)
- Proof of monthly and quarterly reviews (tickets + exports)
- Break-glass policy + sample activations with incident_refs

h1. Break-glass requirements (Sev0/Sev1 only)
- Break-glass is time-boxed (default 60 minutes; max 4 hours).
- Activation requires:
  - Incident severity (Sev0/Sev1)
  - Incident_ref
  - Requester identity (user)
- Events required:
  - incident_bot.break_glass.activate
  - incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate
- All privileged calls made under break-glass must include *break_glass=true* and *break_glass_session_id*.

h1. Failure modes and required behavior
h2. If audit pipeline is degraded
- Privileged endpoints must *fail closed* if audit emission cannot be confirmed within the configured window, *except* for explicitly approved emergency policy (Security + SRE).
- When fail-closed triggers, the bot should degrade gracefully in Slack:
  - Post a message indicating diagnostics are limited
  - Provide deep links to Console dashboards
  - Provide manual fallback commands (non-privileged)
- Emit incident_bot.privileged_call.failed with reason “audit_unavailable” where possible.

h2. If Slack identity mapping is unavailable
- Continue service-level audit logging.
- Populate actor_id with Slack user ID only, and mark identity_resolution=partial.

h1. Operational contacts
- Primary owner (audit logging / SIEM): *Kevin Osei*
- Security Engineering lead: *Marcus Lin*
- Authn/Authz and tenant isolation: *Kaitlyn Nguyen*

payload.page_title: Audit log export: role-aware filtered dump (2026)

sections.body:
This document specifies the Console and API capability to export filtered slices of tenant audit logs as a bulk dump while enforcing RBAC v2, retention limits, and SSO-backed administrative permissions.

The primary use cases are compliance reporting, e-discovery preparation, and offline analytics. The design explicitly prevents disclosure of sensitive fields to users without the appropriate allow-list role.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Role-aware bulk export for audit logs, initiated from Console (Admin) and backed by a server-side export worker.
- Query-scoped exports: time window, actor, resource, action, outcome.
- Field-level masking and omission using RBAC v2 policy evaluation.
- Export bundles include a manifest describing query, filters, snapshot time, and schema version.
- Support for multi-GB exports using cursor-based pagination and resumable multipart downloads.
- Export request auditing to an immutable audit stream separate from the exported data.
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- Real-time streaming feeds for customer SIEMs (handled by the Audit Streaming project).
- Interactive “preview rows” in Console (removed; see decision ADR-EXPORT-004 below).
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
1. Admin navigates to: Console → Security → Audit Logs → Export.
2. Admin configures filters (time range required; other filters optional).
3. Console shows:
   - Estimated record count and approximate size (best-effort)
   - Retention cutoff date for the tenant
   - Whether any sensitive fields may be included (based on role)
4. Admin submits export request.
5. Console shows export status: queued → running → completed/failed.
6. On completion, Console provides a time-limited download link and checksum.
sections.heading: User experience (Console)

sections.body:
- Requester identity is derived from SSO/SAML session (Console) or service token (API).
- The exported bundle records requester identity in the immutable audit stream (not inside the bundle manifest).
sections.heading: Authentication and identity

sections.body: RBAC v2 is enforced server-side for every exported row.
sections.heading: Authorization model

sections.body:
- audit.export.create: can initiate exports
- audit.export.read: can view export status and download links for exports they initiated
- audit.export.read_all: can view exports initiated by other admins within the same tenant
- audit.export.sensitive_fields: can receive fields classified as Sensitive (PII / payload bodies / tokens)
sections.heading: Permissions

sections.body:
- Default: sensitive fields are omitted entirely (not present) rather than present-but-null.
- If audit.export.sensitive_fields is present, sensitive fields are included, subject to any additional policy constraints.
sections.heading: Field handling rules

sections.body:
- Exports cannot retrieve records older than the tenant retention cutoff.
- The previous “super-admin retention override” is deprecated.
- New approach (2026-03 update): retrieval beyond standard retention requires an explicit Legal Hold, represented by a legal_hold_id, and is only allowed for tenants with Legal Hold enabled.
- All uses of legal_hold_id are logged to the immutable audit stream with ticket reference.
sections.heading: Retention and legal holds

sections.body:
- NDJSON (recommended/default): line-delimited JSON objects
- CSV: RFC 4180-ish with quoted fields and stable column order
sections.heading: Supported formats (2026-03 update)

sections.body: - “Pretty JSON array” export (removed due to memory pressure and poor incremental handling).
sections.heading: Not supported

sections.body:
- data.ndjson OR data.csv (may be split into multiple parts)
- manifest.json
- checksums.txt
sections.heading: Each export produces a bundle containing

sections.body:
- Exports larger than 1.0 GB are produced as multiple numbered parts (part-0001, part-0002, ...).
- Download is resumable using HTTP range requests.
sections.heading: Multipart behavior

sections.body: The manifest is designed to support downstream compliance workflows without leaking sensitive data.
sections.heading: Manifest contents (manifest.json)

sections.body:
- schema_version: string (e.g., "2026-03-18")
- snapshot_time: RFC3339 timestamp when the export job started reading
- tenant_id: internal tenant identifier
- requested_by: NOT included (identity is captured in immutable audit log)
- query: normalized filters (time window, actor/resource/action/outcome)
- applied_rbac_policy_hash: hash of effective RBAC v2 policy used for evaluation
- retention_cutoff: timestamp
- output_format: "ndjson" | "csv"
- part_count: integer
- total_records: integer (best-effort)
- warnings: array of strings (e.g., "Some fields omitted due to RBAC")
sections.heading: Fields (conceptual)

sections.body:
1. Console calls Export API to create an export job.
2. API validates permissions, normalizes query, enforces retention/hold rules.
3. API writes an export job record and enqueues work.
4. Export worker reads audit events in deterministic order, applies RBAC masking/omission, and streams output to object storage.
5. Worker writes manifest + checksums and marks job complete.
6. API returns a presigned download URL (time-limited) when requested.
sections.heading: High-level flow

sections.body:
- Data is streamed directly to object storage using multipart upload to avoid memory pressure.
- Encryption:
  - In transit: TLS
  - At rest: object storage server-side encryption (SSE) plus KMS key per environment
- Presigned download link TTL (2026-03 update): 4 hours default; configurable per plan tier (max 24 hours).
sections.heading: Storage and encryption

sections.body:
- Use cursor-based incremental listing to avoid deep OFFSET scans.
- Cursor format: <event_ts_ms>|<event_id>
- Ordering: (event_ts asc, event_id asc) to ensure deterministic traversal during concurrent writes.
sections.heading: Query and pagination

sections.body:
- RBAC v2 policy evaluation happens before serialization.
- Sensitive fields are dropped unless audit.export.sensitive_fields is granted.
- Additional gating (separate allow-list) applies to:
  - request_payload
  - response_content
  - ip_address (masked by default; last octet removed unless sensitive_fields granted)
sections.heading: Masking and serialization

sections.body:
| Limit | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Max concurrent exports per org | 1 | 2026-03 update (was 2) to reduce peak load |
| Max export lookback | Retention cutoff | Extended lookback requires legal_hold_id |
| Max parts per export | 2,000 | Prevent runaway multipart bundles |
| Rate limit: create export | 5 / hour / org | Burst allowed up to 2 within 5 minutes |
sections.heading: Limits and quotas

sections.body:
- audit_export_created
- audit_export_started
- audit_export_completed
- audit_export_failed
sections.heading: Telemetry events

sections.body:
- Telemetry includes tokenized requester ID (for correlation) and tenant ID.
- A separate immutable audit stream records:
  - requester identity (SSO subject or service token)
  - export job id
  - query summary (redacted)
  - whether sensitive fields were included
  - whether legal_hold_id was used and associated ticket reference
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- Object storage multipart upload failures: retry with exponential backoff; ensure worker has sufficient egress.
- Policy evaluation timeouts: reduce batch size and ensure policy cache is warm.
- Retention violations: confirm tenant retention and whether Legal Hold is enabled.
sections.heading: Common failures

sections.body:
- Dashboard: audit-export-metrics (queue depth, completion latency, failures)
- Verify KMS permissions for export worker identity
- Confirm org-level concurrency gate is functioning
sections.heading: On-call checks

sections.body:
- Synthetic large dataset test: 50M rows for cursor stability and throughput.
- RBAC masking matrix: org-admin, security-reader, billing-admin, auditor_role.
- Resumable download test: interrupt mid-download and resume via range requests.
- Security review: ensure no indirect disclosure via manifest, filenames, or error messages.
sections.heading: Testing and QA

sections.body:
- ADR-EXPORT-001: Background worker + presigned link chosen over synchronous generation.
- ADR-EXPORT-002: Cursor (time+id) chosen over offset-based pagination.
- ADR-EXPORT-003: NDJSON recommended for JSON-like exports to support streaming parsers.
- ADR-EXPORT-004 (2026-03 update): Removed “preview first 500 rows” from Console due to data leakage risk and inconsistent RBAC UX; replaced with size estimate + schema description.
- ADR-EXPORT-005 (2026-03 update): Deprecated super-admin retention override; replaced with Legal Hold workflow using legal_hold_id and mandatory audit trail.
sections.heading: Key decisions and changes

sections.body:
Primary owner team: Security (Audit & Compliance).
Implementation team: Engineering (Security-Logging-Initiative).
sections.heading: Ownership

sections.body:

- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4321
- Privacy matrix: https://drive.redwood.ai/attachments/audit-privacy-matrix.xlsx
