sections.body:
Purpose
-------
This playbook documents a canonical fallback matrix for Redwood embedded SDKs and a reproducible triage + remediation workflow for the most frequent customer-visible failure modes. It is intended for developer-experience engineers, support engineers, and SREs who need a deterministic path from alert -> mitigation -> long-term fix.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Embedded and local SDK integrations (JS/TS, Python, and light-weight mobile wrappers) that call Redwood hosted or dedicated endpoints.
- Excludes: Private on-prem runtime packaging steps for air-gapped installs (see eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging).

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Primary owner: devx-observability (team lead: Asha Patel)
- Secondary: eng-sre on-call for platform impacts
- Support escalation: follow the normal support-handoff runbook; for P1s notify SRE within 15 minutes.

How to use this document
------------------------
1. Use the matrix below to map symptoms to a recommended immediate fallback.
2. Execute the short remediation steps in the Incident TL;DR section.
3. Run the reproducible test in the Repro and Golden Trace section.
4. Patch, validate in canary, and schedule a follow-up RCA + regression test.

Fallback decision matrix (quick reference)
-----------------------------------------
Symptom | Probable cause | Immediate fallback | Severity | Owner
--------|----------------|--------------------|----------|------
Partial tokens / truncated streams | Client-side network stalls or stream abort | Switch to polling mode; increase client-side stream timeout to 60s | Medium | devx-support
Very high latency (end-to-end > 2x SLO) | Runtime hot-node or queueing | Route to cheaper warm replica model (fallback model ID: rdm-lite-1) and enable prefix-caching | High | eng-sre
Incorrect structured output (schema violations) | Prompt/SDK serializer mismatch | Switch to stable schema mode (v2025-schema) and enable strict validation flag | Medium | devx
Authentication errors (401/403) | Key rotation or KMS policy change | Temporarily allow tenant-scoped read-only API keys and trigger credential re-issue flow | High | security
Token cost spike without corresponding traffic | Client inadvertently enabling full context retention | Force local context-prune and enable sampling-based prompt bundling | Medium | product-eng
Model fallback produced degraded content quality | Fallback model quantization mismatch | Use model-agnostic postfilter (quality-gate v1) and route small fraction to golden model for diffing | Medium | applied-ml

Incident TL;DR (actions for first 15/60/240 minutes)
---------------------------------------------------
- First 15 minutes (Detect & Stabilize):
  1. Acknowledge the incident in PagerDuty and tag with product:embedded-sdk.
  2. Confirm scope: sample 5 traces across different tenants.
  3. If customers are impacted, switch affected SDKs to the recommended immediate fallback listed in the matrix.
  4. Capture a golden trace (see Repro section).
- First 60 minutes (Mitigate & Communicate):
  1. Open a dedicated Slack incident channel and post status every 15 minutes.
  2. Apply a short-lived hotfix (roll forward) to the SDK or routing rules as required.
  3. If routing change, validate error rate and latency for 5–10 minutes before notifying customers.
- First 4 hours (Restore & Begin RCA):
  1. Confirm functional restore across all affected tenants.
  2. Begin root cause collection (logs, heap/CPU profiles, kernel traces if runtime).
  3. Create follow-up Jira with mitigation, owners, and ETA for permanent fix.

Repro and Golden Trace instructions
----------------------------------
- Goal: produce a deterministic trace that demonstrates the failure across client + network + runtime.
- Steps to reproduce locally:
  1. Acquire an impacted API key (test tenant or redwood-internal sandbox).
  2. Set SDK env var REDWOOD_SDK_LOG_LEVEL=debug and REDWOOD_CLIENT_TIMEOUT=30s.
  3. Capture a streaming session with curl or local harness:
     - Example (curl streaming):
       curl -N -H \"Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY\" -H \"Accept: text/event-stream\" -d '{\"prompt\":\"<problematic input>\",\"max_tokens\":512}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embedded/generate
  4. Save client-side network dump (Wireshark/tcpdump), SDK debug logs, and the server trace id returned in headers (x-rw-trace-id).
- Golden trace: tag the trace with label \"golden:embedded:failure\" in the tracing system and upload artifacts to the incident Jira.

Canonical fixes (ranked by breadth & permanence)
------------------------------------------------
- Fix A: SDK serializer/validator patch (low-risk)
  - When to use: schema and serialization mismatches.
  - Steps: update SDK to use Schema v2025, add strict-mode opt-in, publish patch release with changelog.
  - Validation: run schema-golden-suite across 1000 prompts.
- Fix B: Routing policy temporary pin (medium-risk)
  - When to use: runtime node pressure or model-quality regressions.
  - Steps: pin traffic to warm pool, reduce batch size from 16 -> 8 for 30 minutes, enable model-agnostic postfilter.
  - Validation: compare token latency and cost delta pre/post.
- Fix C: Runtime kernel micro-patch (high-risk)
  - When to use: deterministic kernel crash or memory leak.
  - Steps: prepare canary image, run smoke bench for 1 hour, then deploy to 10% traffic with auto-rollback.
  - Validation: heap + GPU memory stable for 2 hours and no regressions in tail latency.

Telemetry checklist (what to check first)
--------------------------------------
- SDK metrics: call rate, stream aborts, local queue size, client-side timeouts.
- Platform metrics: per-model latency P50/P95/P99, queue length, GPU memory utilization per node.
- Trace sampling: confirm x-rw-trace-id exists and maps across client -> edge -> runtime.
- Cost signals: token count per user-session and token cost deltas.

Rollback and canary guidance
---------------------------
- Canary policy for SDK patches: 0% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 15-minute observation windows.
- Rollback triggers: P95 latency increase > 30% OR error rate increase > 2% over baseline.
- When routing changes, always enable traffic mirror to old path for 10 minutes for offline comparison.

Post-incident actions and tests to add to CI
-------------------------------------------
- Add a golden-trace regression test: replay captured golden traces against the new SDK release in CI.
- Add an integration test that toggles fallback policies and asserts no correctness regressions under 3 simulated network profiles.
- Schedule an applied-ml QA run for model fallback quality when new quantized variants are onboarded.

Frequently seen root causes and canonical remediation mapping
-----------------------------------------------------------
1. Client-side timeouts and stream buffering -> Increase client timeouts, switch to polling, and publish SDK guidance.
2. Model variant mismatch after rollout -> Immediate routing pin to previous model, diff-runner, and notify model-onboarding.
3. Key/credential rotation mismatch -> Short-lived allowlist and force re-issue; add SDK-friendly key refresh helpers.
4. Unexpected token inflation from prompt accumulation -> Enforce per-session token budget and add client TTL-based context pruning.

Appendix A: Example SDK patch commands
-------------------------------------
- Patch, build, and publish (JS/TS):
  1. git checkout -b fix/serializer-strict
  2. npm run test:unit && npm run build && npm run test:integration
  3. npm version patch && npm publish --tag canary
  4. Update docs site with migration note and sample diff.
- Patch, build, and publish (Python):
  1. git checkout -b fix/serializer-strict
  2. tox -e py && pytest tests/integration
  3. python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel && twine upload --repository-url testpypi dist/*

Appendix B: Quick reference config table
---------------------------------------
| Setting | Default | Recommended for failure | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------------------------|-------|
| REDWOOD_CLIENT_TIMEOUT | 20s | 60s | Prevents early client aborts |
| REDWOOD_SDK_VALIDATE_SCHEMA | false | true (strict) | Use when schema mismatches observed |
| FALLBACK_MODEL_ID | rdm-default | rdm-lite-1 | rdm-lite-1 is lower-cost and more robust under pressure |
| PREFIX_CACHE_ENABLED | true | true | Ensure prefix cache size >= 128k entries for embedded workloads |

Related links
-------------
- SDK release checklist: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-patch-release-playbook-and-compat-rules-2025
- Local sandbox repro: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/local-debug-sandbox-sdk-quickstart-2025
- Model onboarding expectations: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/

Contact and follow-up
---------------------
For questions or to propose a change to this playbook, open a PR against this page and ping @Evelyn Chen and the devx-observability squad.

sections.body:
Overview

This document describes the design, operational guidance, and diagnostic playbooks for request multiplexing and backpressure controls in the Redwood serving runtime. It explains how multiplexing interacts with kernel scheduling, KV cache behavior, and autoscaling; defines telemetry to collect for profiling; and includes runbook procedures and benchmarking guidance for validating changes.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals:
  - Improve GPU utilization via request multiplexing without violating latency SLOs.
  - Provide stable, predictable backpressure behavior across mixed-priority workloads (hosted + dedicated + private).
  - Expose observability and debugging surfaces so regressions are rapidly triaged.
- Non-goals:
  - Replace per-tenant rate limiting or high-level routing policies.
  - Eliminate all tail latency; aim is to bound and make it observable.

Design overview

1) Architectural components

- Multiplexer (MUX): in-memory request coalescer that forms micro-batches from ray/connection-level requests before kernel enqueue. Resides inside the runtime worker process.
- Scheduler: decides which micro-batch enters the device queue next. Implements priority buckets, aging, and SLO-aware admission.
- Admission & Backpressure Controller: converts runtime queue pressure signals into API-level backpressure (HTTP 429 / 202 or connection-level signals for streaming).
- Kernel Mapper: maps micro-batches to specific kernel paths (FP16/INT8/sharded attention). Provides cost estimates used by Scheduler.
- KV Cache Coordinator: manages per-shard KV cache occupancy and preferential eviction for multiplexed requests.

2) Throughput vs. latency tradeoffs

- The MUX increases throughput by aggregating prefix tokens across concurrent requests; however, large, heterogeneous micro-batches can amplify worst-case token latency for high-priority requests. The Scheduler therefore enforces a max-aggregate-seqlen bound per-priority bucket and a preemption threshold.

3) Priority model

- Requests carry a priority header (P0..P3). Typical mapping: P0 = system critical (control plane), P1 = enterprise SLAs, P2 = standard hosted, P3 = best-effort/batch.
- Scheduler uses a weighted deficit round robin with aging to prevent starvation. Weights configurable per deployment (defaults shown in table below).

Config (recommended defaults)

| Key | Default | Notes |
|-----|---------|-------|
| mux.min-batch-ms | 3ms | Minimum time window to collect requests before forcing dispatch |
| mux.max-batch-tokens | 4096 | Hard cap on total tokens in a micro-batch |
| scheduler.preempt-pct | 25% | If a high-priority request waits > preempt-pct of its SLO, it preempts the current kernel slot |
| admission.queue-high-water | 4000 | Number of pending tokens across worker before backpressure triggers |
| admission.queue-critical | 8000 | Hard limit that causes immediate 429s on P2/P3 |
| kvcache.prefetch-window | 8 | Number of next-token steps to prefetch into cache on micro-batch commit |
| kernel.estimate-latency-ms | 1.8 | Baseline single-token kernel latency estimate used for admission heuristics |

Operational sequences (runbooks)

1) Normal request path (submit -> serve)

1. API layer annotates request with priority, customer-tier, and model-variant tags.
2. Runtime worker accepts request and appends to MUX holding queue.
3. MUX groups requests by model-variant and priority, respecting mux.min-batch-ms.
4. Scheduler selects next micro-batch based on weighted DRR and kernel cost estimates.
5. KV Cache Coordinator reserves prefetched segments for chosen micro-batch.
6. Micro-batch dispatched to kernel; kernel emits per-token traces and completion.
7. Admission Controller updates backlog telemetry and may throttle by returning API-level backpressure signals if thresholds crossed.

2) Backpressure escalation (runbook, incident quick steps)

- Trigger: sustained worker backlog > admission.queue-high-water for > 30s or a GPU queue depth > 90% for > 60s on more than 2 nodes in the pool.
- Immediate mitigation steps:
  1. Remove P3 (best-effort) traffic from this pool via routing rule (Console -> Routing -> Pool Overrides).
  2. Lower mux.min-batch-ms by 50% on affected workers to favor latency.
  3. If backlog persists, enable conservative admission (admission.queue-high-water = 2000) and return 429s for P2/P3.
  4. Notify SRE on-call and document node IDs and pool label in incident ticket.
- Postmortem actions: adjust weight/aging parameters, run benchmark (see Benchmarking guidance) against a mixed-priority workload.

Profiling guidance (how to profile multiplexed workloads)

- Required traces/metrics to enable for experiments:
  - mux.hold_time_ms (histogram by priority)
  - mux.batch_token_count (gauge)
  - scheduler.select_latency_ms (percentiles)
  - kernel.exec_time_ms (per-kernel, per-seqlen)
  - kvcache.hit_ratio (per-shard, per-tenant)
  - admission.backlog_tokens and admission.drop_rate (by priority)
  - per-request tail token latency (p50/p95/p99)

- Profiling recipe (local reproducer):
  1. Recreate the production request mix using the perf-replay tool with --priority-dist and --seq-dist knobs.
  2. Enable verbose mux and scheduler traces (runtime flag: --trace-mux --trace-sched).
  3. Capture kernel timeline with nvprof/rocprof or the lightweight kernel-timeline agent (-k).
  4. Run for a minimum of 5 minutes at target QPS or until steady-state backlog appears.
  5. Post-process traces with tools/trace-aggregator --mux-view to visualize per-batch composition.

Benchmarking guidance

- Workloads to include in the standard suite:
  - Homogeneous short sequences (64 tokens) at high QPS (tests batching efficiency).
  - Mixed-priority realistic traffic: 10% P1, 60% P2, 30% P3 with sequence-length distribution sampled from production traces.
  - Long-prefix streaming scenario (512 prefix tokens then incremental).

- Validation metrics and thresholds for passing:
  - p50 token latency <= baseline * 1.15 for P1 requests
  - p95 end-to-end latency <= 1.8x baseline for P2 under multiplexing
  - throughput uplift >= 1.25x vs. no-mux baseline at same hardware cost
  - KV cache hit ratio >= 70% on mixed workloads

Release notes snippet (v1.0 multiplexing rollout)

- Added MUX v1.0: configurable request multiplexing with priority buckets and scheduler-aware preemption.
- New runtime flags: --mux.min-batch-ms, --mux.max-batch-tokens, --scheduler.preempt-pct.
- Observability: mux.* and scheduler.* metrics, traceable batch composition in trace-aggregator v0.9.

Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: Priority inversion under heterogeneous micro-batches.
  - Symptom: P1 requests see elevated p99 when coalesced into large batches dominated by P2 text.
  - Mitigation: Enforce per-priority max-aggregate-seqlen and lower mux.min-batch-ms for affected pools.

- Issue: KV cache thrash when working set overlaps heavily across tenants.
  - Symptom: Increased kernel latency due to repeated prefetch and eviction churn.
  - Mitigation: Enable tenant-aware cache windows (kvcache.tenant-isolation = true) for dedicated pools; tune kvcache.prefetch-window and kvcache.eviction-sensitivity.

- Issue: Unexpected 429 bursts after autoscaler events.
  - Symptom: When nodes are removed, admission controller returns 429s in waves instead of smoothing.
  - Mitigation: Add a 30s graceful-drain window with backlog redistribution; ensure autoscaler uses drain annotation (autoscaler.drain-window=30s).

Operational checklist for releases

1. Canary rollout: enable mux on 1–2 small canary pools with mixed-priority traffic for 72 hours.
2. Run the benchmarking suite and confirm thresholds.
3. Run chaos scenarios: node drain, kernel stalls, KV cache pressure.
4. If regressions observed, rollback by setting --mux.enabled=false and revert routing overrides.

Diagnostic examples (CLI snippets)

- Query backlog and batch composition (metrics API):
  curl -s "http://metrics:9200/query?m=mux.hold_time_ms,p90&pool=pool-1" | jq .

- Trigger a controlled eviction-friendly test:
  perf-replay --config tests/multiplex-eviction.yaml --qps 1200 --priority-dist 10,60,30

Team wiki and further reading

- See the runtime team wiki page for live dashboards: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2025
- See kernel mapper design notes for cost model details: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/sharded-attention-execution-guidelines-2026

Appendix: tuning knobs quick reference

- Latency-sensitive pools: mux.min-batch-ms = 1ms; mux.max-batch-tokens = 2048; scheduler.preempt-pct = 15%
- Throughput-optimized pools: mux.min-batch-ms = 5–8ms; mux.max-batch-tokens = 8192; scheduler.preempt-pct = 40%
- Mixed SLA pools (default): see Config table above.

Owners and escalation

- Component owners:
  - Multiplexer & Scheduler: Marco Ruiz (runtime-serving)
  - KV Cache Coordinator: Priya Desai (runtime-storage)
  - Admission Controller: Evan Thompson (sre-runtime)
- On-call escalation: runtime-sre -> infra-sre -> eng-serving-runtime leads.

Change log

- 2025-09-15: v0.1 initial draft (A. Patel)
- 2025-11-02: Added profiling recipe and CLI snippets (M. Ruiz)
- 2026-02-10: Finalized operational checklist and released default conservative configs (A. Patel)

sections.body:
Summary

Purpose: This playbook consolidates pragmatic, field-proven fixes and a prescriptive checklist for SDK integrations that cause the majority of support cases. It is intended for SDK maintainers, integration engineers, and support engineers who triage canonical failure modes.

Scope: Covers HTTP/streaming generation clients, embeddings/encode flows, adapter-layer failures, client-side batching/backoff, telemetry alignment (schema + cardinality), and the docs-site publishing steps for canonical fixkits. Does not replace product-level release notes or security incident response procedures.

Owner and contact
- Owner: SDK Platform (eng-devx)
- Primary contact: maya.patel@redwood.com
- Pager (support triage escalation): #sdk-support (Slack)

Quick reference: 3-minute triage
1) Identify symptom signature (error strings, status codes, stream abort reason).
2) Check last-deployed SDK version and release notes (git tag).
3) Query telemetry for corresponding trace_id / request_id to validate upstream timing and retries.
4) Apply canonical fix from table below; if no match, escalate to L2.

Canonical failure matrix (symptom -> root cause -> recommended fix)
| Symptom | Probable root cause | Recommended quick fix | Owner | Rollout urgency |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| Repeated 502s during burst test | Upstream gateway timeout + synchronous client retries | Switch client to non-blocking streaming path; enable jittered exponential backoff and reduce retry count to 2 | SDK Platform | high |
| Partial streaming output then stream stops with ECONNRESET | Incompatible keepalive/TCP idle settings on customer infra | Add client-side resume token support + instruct ops to increase TCP keepalive to 30s | Integrations | medium |
| High token cost from duplicated generation calls | Misconfigured callback / webhook causing duplicate call path | Add idempotency-key header and dedupe in server-side middleware; add test in sample-app | SDK Samples | high |
| Telemetry missing request_id or has multiple request_ids per operation | SDK emits telemetry before request-id binding or uses transient IDs | Align SDK telemetry schema to include request_id and parent_id; add schema validation in CI | Observability | high |
| Latency spikes for batched requests | Batch sizing mismatch and variable model seq length | Enable adaptive batch sizing and configure max_batch_tokens=4096; add per-tenant batch metrics | Serving Runtime | medium |

Detailed triage playbook (step-by-step)
1) Collect artefacts
   - Logs: full client log, server trace id, timestamp, and network layer logs.
   - Telemetry: trace_id, span ids, sampling rate, batch size metric.
   - Repro harness snippet: minimal request that reproduces the error.

2) Reproduce in isolation
   - Use the local-sdks-sandbox to replay the exact request with captured headers.
   - If streaming: run --stream-debug to emit low-level frames. Example:

   ```bash
   ./sdk-replay --source capture.json --stream-debug --region=us-west1
   ```

3) Apply targeted fixes (examples)
   - Retry/backoff tuning (recommended default):

     ```json
     {"retry": {"max_attempts": 2, "backoff_base_ms": 200, "backoff_multiplier": 2.2, "jitter": "full"}}
     ```

   - Idempotency headers (HTTP sample):

     curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate \\
       -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \\
       -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \\
       -d '{"prompt":"hi"}'

   - Streaming resume token pattern (pseudo):

     ```js
     // client keeps last-good-offset and sends on reconnect
     const resume = { resume_token: lastGoodOffset }
     ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: 'resume', metadata: resume }))
     ```

4) Validate metrics post-fix
   - Check 5xx rate, mean latency (p50/p95), and token-per-request for the affected route.
   - Use redwood-console query: route="/v1/generate" and tag customer_id=<id> for 72h window.

Telemetry alignment checklist (why this matters)
- Goal: ensure every user-visible operation is correlated with a single request_id and a trace that spans SDK -> Gateway -> Serving runtime.
- Minimum viable telemetry fields (schema):
  - request_id (string)
  - client_sdk.name (string)
  - client_sdk.version (string)
  - route (string)
  - model (string)
  - tokens_requested (int)
  - tokens_returned (int)
  - error.code (string)
  - upstream_latency_ms (int)

Telemetry enforcement steps
1) SDK CI should validate that emitted telemetry contains the minimum fields. Add a Pytest assertion that loads a local telemetry sample.
2) Docs-site: publish the telemetry contract page and version it at v1.2.
3) Sampling: ensure span sampling for retries is sampled at 100% for first 30s after a release that touches SDKs.

SDK-specific defensive patterns (templates)
- Connection handling
  - Exponential backoff with bounded maximum delay (no more than 10s).
  - Active ping/keepalive with configurable interval (default 20s).
- Batching
  - Expose max_batch_tokens and per-request token ceiling.
  - Provide a `batch_estimator` hook for clients to provide sequence-length distributions.
- Streaming
  - Provide resume tokens and ack windows.
  - Avoid re-emitting events on reconnect without dedupe tokens.

Canonical fixes and test cases (developer checklist)
1) Add a unit test that simulates gateway 502 and asserts the client backoff reduces retries and surfaces a clear error to the caller.
2) Add an integration test for the streaming resume flow that replays a disconnect in the middle of a response and validates the resume token path.
3) Add a golden telemetry sample to the repo under `tests/telemetry/golden` and fail CI on schema drift.

Publishing a canonical-fix kit to docs-site (ops steps)
1) Draft the docs page under docs-site/content/sdk-canonical-fixes/<issue-shortname>.md using the canonical template.
2) Attach minimal repro code and a mini-release patch (cherry-pick) to the SDK repo.
3) Run the docs-site preflight: `make docs-lint && make snippet-check`
4) Open PR against docs-site with the label `doc:fixkit` and request reviewers: @dx-docs, @sdk-owner.
5) After merge, trigger docs-site canary publish and smoke test the example.
6) Communicate on #sdk-releases and include a short blurb for release notes.

Ops runbook for high-severity customer cases (SLA influence)
1) Immediate steps (0-30m): gather trace IDs, reproduce, and apply a temporary client-side mitigation (reduce concurrency or force single-threaded path).
2) Short-term (30m-4h): ship a hotfix to SDK branch with a flag-based mitigation and provide a patched wheel/npm tarball to customer.
3) Medium-term (4h-72h): complete the full fix, add tests, merge release, and update release notes and docs.
4) Postmortem: publish a blameless incident review within 7 days, include root cause, telemetry gaps, and corrective actions.

Example incident timeline (realistic)
- 09:03: spike observed in 5xx. Automatic alert created.
- 09:09: triage: found matching telemetry; cause: a new gateway deployment changed header forwarding.
- 09:18: mitigation: released SDK v2.14.1 with header-stable fallback and published docs-site fixkit.
- 14:00: incident declared resolved. Postmortem drafted.

Appendix: common error patterns and fix snippets
- Error: "stream aborted: 1006" -> fix: enable resume tokens and increase ws keepalive; add server-side graceful-shutdown hook.
- Error: "duplicate webhook delivery" -> fix: require X-Redwood-Delivery-Id and dedupe in the webhook handler.
- Error: "missing request_id" -> fix: inject request_id at SDK boundary before any telemetry emission.

Maintenance and cadence
- Quarterly review of canonical-fixes matrix by SDK Platform and Observability teams.
- Telemetry contract bump policy: minor bumps for additional optional fields; major bump requires SDK client upgrades (announce 8 weeks in advance).

Feedback and improvement
- To propose additions, open an issue in the eng-developer-experience repo with label `canonical-fix-request`.
- For urgent gaps, ping @maya.patel or file a support ticket with priority P0.

Related resources
- SDK CI telemetry validator: /internal/repos/sdk-ci/actions/telemetry-validate
- Repro harness: /internal/tools/sdk-replay
- Docs-site canonical templates: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/canonical-templates

Document history
- 2026-11-15: Created by Maya Patel.
- 2026-12-03: Added streaming resume template and retry defaults (Liam Chen).
- 2027-01-18: Expanded telemetry contract and publishing workflow (Sofia Alvarez).

sections.body:
Summary
=======

This playbook defines the DevX 'Golden Trace' and Execution Replay workflows used by Redwood support, SDK, and runtime teams to reproduce intermittent, customer-facing failures deterministically. It codifies what to capture, how to store a gold trace, and a step-by-step replay and remediation loop that maps traces to canonical fixes.

Why we need a Golden Trace
-------------------------
- Intermittent production bugs (tokenization regressions, streaming discontinuities, racey cache state) are hard to reproduce locally.
- Golden traces are time-bounded, end-to-end recordings of a problematic request path that contain the minimal information needed to deterministically replay behavior against the runtime and SDK layers.
- A good golden trace reduces time-to-resolution from hours/days to typically under 90 minutes for known classes of issues.

Scope and definitions
---------------------
- Golden trace: an immutable artifact capturing input, SDK-side context, request metadata, and session-scoped runtime artifacts (KV-cache keys, model selection decisions) sufficient to re-run the request.
- Execution replay: the process and tooling that consumes a golden trace and replays it deterministically against a selected target (local shim, staging runtime, dedicated replay cluster).
- Canonical fix: a documented code/config change with a small runnable reproducer and owner.

Capture checklist (what to include)
----------------------------------
1) Customer-visible inputs (obligatory):
   - Original HTTP request payload as sent by customer (body)
   - SDK version and commit hash
   - Client configuration flags (timeout, retry/backoff policy, streaming enabled, prefetch/bundling params)
2) Runtime routing/selection metadata:
   - Model id and pinned version
   - Route id, datacenter/region, and pool id (if Dedicated)
   - Fallback decisions (if any) with timestamps
3) Telemetry and trace ids:
   - Request id, trace id, span ids (if present)
   - SDK correlation id and token-level sequence markers
4) Streaming artifacts (if applicable):
   - Ordered stream fragments, with sequence numbers and byte offsets
   - Partial content markers and end-of-stream flag
5) Deterministic seeds and KV cache snapshot (when available):
   - RNG/temperature seeds used by model sampling (if set)
   - KV cache keys relevant to the request and per-key sizes (not full token content unless requested)
6) System-level context:
   - Server-side execution timeline (timestamps of major phases: routing, queueing, start-of-inference, emit-token ranges)
   - Observability logs (error/warning lines) clipped to +/- 30s around the request
7) Customer consent flag and redaction plan:
   - Indicate whether customer approved full payload capture or requires redaction

Storage and retention policy
---------------------------
- Golden traces are stored in the DevX replay bucket (s3://redwood-devx-golden-traces) with ACLs restricted to support, runtime, and security.
- Naming convention: yyyyMMdd-<request-id>-<short-reason>-<env>.tgz
- Retention: default 90 days; extendable to 365 days with security approval for regulatory investigations.
- Labels and indexing: attach metadata (customer_id, region, SDK-version, model-id, issue-tag) for quick search.

Replay targets and tooling
-------------------------
- Local shim (recommended first step): developer uses devx-replay-cli to replay a trace against a local runtime container. Good for rapid iteration.
- Staging runtime: for environment parity, replay against the latest staging model bundle. Useful when the issue depends on infra config.
- Dedicated replay cluster: for high-fidelity replays that require GPU-level determinism (quantization/backing kernels). Only used for P0/P1 bugs.

Commands and examples
---------------------
- Capture helper (run inside SDK):
  curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
    -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/_internal/captureTrace
    -d '{"request_id":"req_12345","capture_level":"full"}'

- devx-replay-cli (replay locally):
  # download trace artifact then:
  devx-replay --trace /tmp/20270210-req_12345-stream-abort-prod.tgz --target local --runtime-image redwood/runtime:dev-20270201 \
    --env-vars 'SDK_DEBUG=1' --mount-keys /tmp/kv-snapshot.json

- replay to staging with model pinning:
  devx-replay --trace /tmp/trace.tgz --target staging --model sha256:abcdef --capture-logs --output /tmp/replay-output

Deterministic replay tips
------------------------
- Ensure the runtime image matches the kernel / quantization build used in production. Check the runtime build-id in the trace metadata.
- When sampling differences appear, confirm seed propagation: many SDKs default to non-deterministic seeding; customers who want deterministic replays should enable 'seed' in client-side config.
- For streaming mismatches: replay with identical chunk sizes and network pacing. devx-replay has a --pacing-ms option to emulate network behavior.

Triage workflow (step-by-step)
-----------------------------
1) Customer submits ticket with request id or SDK trace id.
2) Support captures a golden trace (use Capture checklist) or requests customer's artifact upload to the DevX bucket.
3) Support performs a local quick-replay. If the issue reproduces, attach logs and escalate to SDK/runtime owner.
4) If not reproducible locally, replay to staging. Record diff between production trace and staging replay (token diffs, timing diffs).
5) If staging reproduces, create a bug and mark P1/P2 depending on impact. Add the golden trace link to the ticket.
6) Create an executable reproducer (smallest possible shim) and a PR template that includes: steps to run the repro, expected vs actual, and telemetry pointers.
7) Owner lands fix and attaches a post-rollback golden trace showing resolution.

Mapping traces to canonical fixes (patterns)
-------------------------------------------
- Tokenization drift: compare tokenizer versions recorded in the trace header. Canonical fix: lock tokenizer version in SDK and add a compatibility test.
- Streaming gap at chunk boundary: often a client-side buffering change. Canonical fix: update SDK stream-assembler to use boundary-aware flush.
- Model-quality regressions: tie to model-version in trace. Canonical fix: update model rollout policy and create a prompt-based eval that catches the regression.
- Latency spike / queueing anomaly: identify queue wait timestamps; canonical fix: autoscale policy tuning or circuit-breaker configuration.

Security, PII, and redaction
---------------------------
- Default policy: redact customer PII from stored traces. Allowed fields: request id, model id, SDK version, timing metadata. Customer consent required to store full prompt content.
- Redaction checklist: run the redaction tool as part of capture pipeline; generate a redaction-report and store it alongside the trace.
- Access controls: trace artifacts are tagged as 'restricted' when full payload retained. Security approval required to share externally.

SLOs and operational metrics for the Playbook
--------------------------------------------
- Mean time to first-replay (MTFR): target <= 60 minutes for tickets marked "debuggable".
- Fraction of tickets with usable golden trace at intake: target >= 75%.
- Replay reproducibility rate (local + staging): target >= 80% for issues classified as deterministic.
- Owner assignment within 4 hours for P1 reproductions.

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Support: capture initial trace, perform first-replay, file ticket with trace link.
- DevX Tools (team): maintain devx-replay-cli, stub containers, and replay infra.
- Runtime owners: investigate runtime-level failures and own fixes that touch kernels/quantization.
- SDK owners: investigate client-side bugs and maintain SDK-level determinism flags.

Onboarding checklist for new engineers
------------------------------------
1) Read this playbook and the devx-replay-cli README.
2) Run the local replay example against the included sample trace (sample_trace.tgz) and verify output.
3) Pair with Support on a real ticket capture and walk through end-to-end replay.

Common pitfalls and mitigation
-----------------------------
- Pitfall: Capturing oversized traces that include entire datasets.
  Mitigation: Enforce size limits on capture; request targeted snapshots instead.
- Pitfall: Missing runtime build-id in trace metadata -> non-reproducible.
  Mitigation: Required schema field; capture pipeline rejects traces without build-id.
- Pitfall: Developers assuming replays are always byte-for-byte identical.
  Mitigation: Educate on non-determinism sources (sampling, kernel order) and provide diff tooling that focuses on clinically relevant differences.

Appendix A — Minimal trace JSON header example
----------------------------------------------
{
  "request_id": "req_12345",
  "sdk_version": "js-2.4.1",
  "runtime_build": "runtime-20270201-gpu-v2",
  "model_id": "open-llm-x:20270120",
  "timestamp": "2027-02-10T15:23:42Z",
  "capture_level": "partial",
  "consent_flag": "redacted"
}

Appendix B — Related pages and tools
-----------------------------------
- devx-replay-cli README: internal link (DevX Tools repo)
- Local reproducibility quickstart: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/local-repro-harness-2026
- SDK diagnostics and telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-telemetry-schema-2026

Change log
----------
- 2027-02-10 — v1.0 initial published by Aisha Patel.
- 2027-03-01 — v1.1 clarifications on retention and redaction added (reviewers: Liam Chen).

payload.page_title: SDK call tracing and root-cause playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes a standardized approach for instrumenting Redwood SDKs, propagating trace/correlation identifiers, and performing fast root-cause analysis when customer requests fail or show degraded latency. It consolidates client-side examples, server-side expectations, console lookup patterns, and a prioritized troubleshooting checklist.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- SDK engineers (Python, TypeScript/Node, Java)
- Backend engineers integrating Redwood APIs
- SREs and support engineers performing customer triage
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Ensure every SDK call can be correlated to a single trace or a small set of related traces in Redwood Console.
- Define minimal headers and span attributes to set in SDKs so SREs can diagnose errors without asking customers for payloads.
- Provide a compact runbook for reproducing, isolating, and escalating issues within 30 minutes.

Quick summary (one-line): Include an idempotent correlation_id on every user request, propagate trace/span headers, sample 1% of requests with full debug traces, and attach trace IDs to errors and telemetry emitted by the SDK.

Minimum tracing contract (what SDKs must implement)
1) Correlation headers: every outgoing HTTP request from SDK must set:
   - X-Request-Id: a UUID v4 (string) representing the client request lifecycle.
   - X-Traceparent: W3C Trace Context header (if available) for interoperability.
   - X-Sdk-Client: <sdk-name>/<version> (e.g. redwood-js/1.3.0)

2) Error enrichment: when an error is raised from the SDK to the customer app, the SDK should include the X-Request-Id value and the Redwood-side trace id (if received) in the error metadata.

3) Sampling and debug payloads:
   - Default sampling: 0.01 (1% full traces) for hosted customers to control cost.
   - Force-sampled flag: SDKs expose a debug override (environment variable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true) that forces full capture and returns a debug_trace_id in responses for triage.
sections.heading: Scope and goals

sections.body:
X-Request-Id: 8a7dd3e2-6f8b-4ea9-9f0b-2a9c3e5b9f0d
X-Traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
X-Sdk-Client: redwood-py/2.0.0

Recommended SDK implementation patterns
- Generate X-Request-Id at the top-level SDK API entry (e.g., client.generate_request_id()). Reuse it across retries and sub-requests spawned by the same logical call.
- If the host application provides a trace context (OpenTelemetry or W3C), prefer propagating that traceparent header instead of generating a new trace. Always attach X-Request-Id regardless.
- Avoid including user PII in correlation IDs or trace attributes. Use non-sensitive labels (e.g., user_hash, project_id).

Client examples
sections.heading: Header example (HTTP)

sections.body:
```python
import uuid
import requests

def call_redwood(payload, api_key, force_debug=False):
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "X-Request-Id": rid,
        "X-Sdk-Client": "redwood-py/2.0.0"
    }
    if force_debug:
        headers["X-Redwood-Trace-Debug"] = "1"
    r = requests.post("https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate", json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=30)
    # Attach request id to exceptions for faster triage
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Redwood server error ({r.status_code}), request_id={rid}")
    return r.json(), rid
```
sections.heading: Python (requests)

sections.body:
```ts
import {v4 as uuidv4} from 'uuid';

async function callRedwood(payload: object, apiKey: string, forceDebug = false) {
  const rid = uuidv4();
  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${apiKey}` ,
    'X-Request-Id': rid,
    'X-Sdk-Client': 'redwood-js/1.4.1'
  }
  if (forceDebug) headers['X-Redwood-Trace-Debug'] = '1'
  const resp = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    headers,
    // keep a short timeout at the application layer to avoid stuck clients
  })
  if (!resp.ok && resp.status >= 500) {
    throw new Error(`Redwood server error (${resp.status}), request_id=${rid}`)
  }
  const body = await resp.json();
  return {body, request_id: rid};
}
```

Server-side expectations (Redwood runtime)
- If incoming request includes X-Request-Id, the runtime must use it as the root-correlation-id for logs, traces, and KV-caches for that request.
- The runtime will return the header X-Redwood-Trace-Id when a full trace was captured for the request. SDKs should surface that id in error payloads.
- Runtime will also echo back X-Request-Id when present to verify propagation.

Common triage flow (30-minute runbook)
1) Gather artifacts: customer request time, X-Request-Id (or approximate timestamp), sample customer payload (if allowed), SDK name/version, region.
2) Search Console: filter by X-Request-Id or time window (+/- 2 minutes). If present, open the trace. Check service span latencies, kernel queue time, and tail token generation time.
3) If no trace found: verify if customer had client-side sampling or wrong header (common root cause). Ask customer to resend with REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true to force a debug trace.
4) If trace found and error is 5xx: inspect backend service spans in trace for exceptions and logs. Correlate with runtime logs (owner: serving-runtime team).
5) If high latency but no 5xx: check batching layer span and KV cache hit rate; correlate with GPU utilization from gpu-fleet-and-capacity dashboard.
6) Escalate: if issue is reproducible and affects Dedicated/Private customers or violates SLOs, open an Incident and notify eng-sre and serving-runtime on-call. Attach trace ids and representative payload.

Priority lookup table
| Artifact | Where to look | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| X-Request-Id | Redwood Console / request traces | SRE / support | Best single key for cross-system lookup |
| X-Redwood-Trace-Id | Trace view | Serving runtime | Indicates full capture; include in bug reports |
| SDK logs | Customer app logs | Customer / SDK-team | Ask for SDK debug logs with correlation id |
| GPU metrics | Grafana (gpu-fleet) | Infra / capacity | Helps diagnose batching/backpressure |

Canonical fixes and known patterns
- Symptom: No trace in Console but customer reports error. Cause: client stripped headers (proxies or CORS) or client used custom HTTP client without propagation. Fix: document header requirements in integration guide and add SDK instrumentation tests that assert header presence.
- Symptom: High 95th token latency. Cause: large request sequences hitting longer attention kernels or cache misses. Fix: include request size metrics and advise quantized model variants or lower max_tokens.
- Symptom: Intermittent 502/503. Cause: transient scaling/queue drains. Fix: implement exponential backoff with full jitter in SDKs (recommended default: initial=50ms, max=2s, max_retries=5).

Telemetry and logs to collect when filing a support ticket
- Timestamp (UTC), X-Request-Id, SDK name/version, region, sample payload (if customer consents), client-side logs (including stack traces), any returned X-Redwood-Trace-Id.

Debugging checklist for SDK authors (pre-release)
1) Unit tests assert X-Request-Id exists and is stable across retries.
2) Integration tests using a local proxy record all outgoing headers.
3) Optional e2e test that flips REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG=true and asserts the runtime returns X-Redwood-Trace-Id.
4) Add metrics emitted by the SDK for: requests_total, requests_errors_total (label: status_code), request_latency_seconds (histogram).

Escalation and ownership
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (SDK telemetry workstream)
- On-call for runtime tracing: eng-serving-runtime on-call (see runbooks/trace-oncall).
- Severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: Reproducible data-loss or SLO breach for Dedicated customer — immediate incident.
  - Sev-2: Widespread >=10% error rate increase for hosted customers — paged to eng-sre.
  - Sev-3: Single-customer sporadic errors — support ticket and scheduled follow-up.

Appendix A: Example support ticket template (copy/paste)
Subject: [Support] Request tracing artifacts for customer <customer-name> – request_id=<X-Request-Id>
sections.heading: Node/TypeScript (fetch)

sections.body:
- Time (UTC):
- Region:
- SDK: (name/version)
- X-Request-Id:
- X-Redwood-Trace-Id (if present):
- Sample payload (redacted if necessary):
- Customer logs attached: yes/no
- Screenshots of Console trace: yes/no

Appendix B: Reference commands
- curl example to include headers:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "X-Request-Id: $(uuidgen)" -H "X-Redwood-Trace-Debug: 1" -d '{"prompt":"hi"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

- Small grep to find request_id in logs (SRE):
  rg "8a7dd3e2-6f8b" /var/log/redwood/ -n || true

Appendix C: FAQ
Q: What if a customer cannot share payloads?
A: Request only the minimal redacted payload necessary to reproduce (e.g., token counts, sequence length, prompt shape). Ask them to enable REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG for a time window; debug traces are sampled and limited to triage windows.

Q: Is X-Request-Id globally unique across retries?
A: Yes — keep the same id for retries of the same logical call to simplify dedup and tracing.

Contacts and links
- SDK telemetry epic: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-telemetry-roadmap-2026
- Runtime tracing runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/trace-oncall
- Support triage playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/triage-playbook

Change log
- 2025-11-12: created by Sofia Lin (initial draft)
- 2026-01-15: added REDWOOD_TRACE_DEBUG guidance and Node example (reviewers: Arjun, Lena)
- 2026-02-01: updated sampling defaults and escalation mapping

payload.page_title: Console UX Spec: Route-level Experiments (A/B Testing) in Rollouts

sections.body:
This document specifies the Redwood Console UX for creating, operating, and reviewing **route-level experiments** (A/B/n tests) in the Rollouts surface area. The experience is designed to be safe-by-default (guardrails + clear blast radius), RBAC-aware, and metrics-forward.

Route-level experiments let users split traffic for a specific **route/endpoint** across multiple **variants** (typically model versions or compatible model IDs), deterministically assign requests to variants, and review results (latency, cost, errors, throughput, and optional quality/eval signals).
sections.heading: 1. Summary

sections.body:
- Experiments list + entry points
- Experiment creation wizard
  - Variant configuration
  - Deterministic assignment / stickiness key selection
  - Traffic split controls (A/B/n)
  - Guardrails configuration (latency/cost/error + optional quality)
  - Review + launch
- Experiment detail view
  - Status + guardrail state
  - Live metrics panels
  - Results (basic deltas; no formal stat-sig)
  - Stop / ramp controls
  - Audit/change history
- Empty states + error states
- RBAC-aware affordances
sections.heading: In scope (this UX spec)

sections.body:
- Statistical significance engine and powered recommendations (beyond basic deltas)
- Custom customer metrics ingestion
- Multi-region “population rebalancing” beyond deterministic bucketing
sections.heading: Out of scope (explicit)

sections.body:
1) **Platform Engineer / Infra Owner**
- Wants safe operations, controlled blast radius, and predictable rollback.
- Needs audit trails for who changed what and when.

2) **ML Engineer / Applied ML**
- Wants to compare model variants by latency/cost and quality signals.
- Needs a consistent way to interpret eval scores in the same view as performance.

3) **Engineering Manager / Product Owner**
- Wants quick answers: “Is variant B better?” and “Is the experiment safe?”
sections.heading: Personas

sections.body:
- Create a route experiment safely with deterministic assignment.
- Ramp traffic in stages and stop quickly if guardrails trip.
- Understand results and share a linkable view with stakeholders.
- Prove compliance readiness via audit log exports.
sections.heading: Primary jobs-to-be-done

sections.body:
- Console → **Rollouts** → **Experiments** (new top-level tab within Rollouts)
  - Sub-tabs:
    - **All Experiments** (list)
    - **Templates** (future; placeholder hidden)
sections.heading: Navigation & placement

sections.body:
- Route (existing) → may have:
  - Rollout policy (canary/fallback)
  - Zero or one active Experiment (GA default), with ability to view historical experiments

> UX note: to reduce operator confusion, the creation wizard blocks overlapping active experiments on the same route (see §9 Validation & errors).
sections.heading: Entity relationships (as users perceive them)

sections.body:
- Entire UX behind flag: `console.route_experiments_enabled`
- If disabled, user sees an informational empty state with a request-to-enable CTA (permission-gated).
sections.heading: Feature flag

sections.body:
We align to existing Redwood Console roles; exact role names may vary by tenant.

**Permission matrix (summary)**
| Action | Viewer | Operator | Admin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| View experiments list/details/results | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Create experiment (draft) |  | ✓ | ✓ |
| Start/stop experiment |  | ✓ | ✓ |
| Edit config while running (traffic split/guardrails) |  | ✓ (with confirmation) | ✓ |
| Delete experiment |  |  | ✓ |
| View audit history | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Export audit events |  |  | ✓ |
| Use internal assignment debug tools |  |  | ✓ (restricted) |
sections.heading: Roles & permissions (UX semantics)

sections.body:
- Hide actions the user cannot take; replace with “Read only” indicators in header.
- For disabled actions, show tooltip: “You don’t have permission to perform this action. Contact an admin.”
- Audit export and debug endpoints are marked **Restricted** and only shown to Admins.
sections.heading: UX affordances

sections.body:
- Rollouts → Experiments
- Route Details page (existing) shows an “Experiments” card:
  - If none: “Run an experiment on this route” (CTA)
  - If active: status + guardrail badge + “View”
sections.heading: Entry points

sections.body:
- Experiment name
- Route
- Status (Draft / Running / Degraded / Stopped / Completed)
- Traffic allocation summary (e.g., “A: 90% / B: 10%”)
- Primary metric delta (optional, if enough data; e.g., “p95 latency: -8%”)
- Created by
- Last updated
sections.heading: Columns

sections.body:
- Status (multi-select)
- Route
- Time range (Created date)
- Owner (actor)
sections.heading: Filters

sections.body:
- **No experiments yet**: explanation + “Create experiment” CTA (if permitted)
- **No matching filters**: “Clear filters” CTA
sections.heading: Empty states

sections.body:
- Safe-by-default: prevent invalid configs; encourage staged ramps.
- Make determinism explicit: assignment keys + expected stickiness behavior.
- Keep “launch risk” visible at every step (guardrails, blast radius, overlap).
sections.heading: Design principles

sections.body:
1) **Basics**
2) **Variants**
3) **Traffic split**
4) **Guardrails**
5) **Review & launch**

A persistent right-side panel (or top summary on smaller screens) shows:
- Route
- Current rollout/fallback policy on route (read-only)
- Assignment key selection
- Total traffic allocated (must equal 100%)
- Guardrail summary
sections.heading: Wizard steps

sections.body:
- **Experiment name** (required)
  - Helper: “Shown in dashboards and audit logs.”
- **Route** (required)
  - Route picker (searchable). Shows:
    - Route template (normalized) and environment (prod/staging)
    - Current active experiment status (if any)
    - Current rollout policy (canary/fallback) summary
- **Description** (optional)
- **Duration** (optional)
  - “No end date” default
  - If set, can schedule automatic stop (soft-stop) at end time
sections.heading: Fields

sections.body:
- **Stickiness key source** (required)
  - Options (ordered; UX labels map to backend precedence):
    1. “Explicit Experiment Key” (recommended) — provided via SDK/header
    2. “Customer ID” — if present
    3. “End-user ID” — if present
    4. “Session ID” — if present
    5. “Random (non-sticky)” — not recommended; requires confirmation
  - Helper text (important):
    - “Stable keys keep users in the same variant across requests and regions. Missing keys can cause skew and noisy results.”

Copy block: “What happens if the key is missing?”
- Explain fallback order and that Console will display an “Attribution & Assignment Health” panel.
sections.heading: Deterministic assignment / stickiness keys

sections.body: Variants are the set of targets the router can select for the experiment.
sections.heading: Step 2 — Variants

sections.body:
- Table with rows for each variant
  - Variant name (required)
  - Target model (required) — model selector
  - Optional: “Notes”
  - Read-only “Compatibility” indicator (based on route’s expected API shape/features)
sections.heading: Variant list UI

sections.body:
- Variant A pre-filled as “Control” pointing to the route’s current default target (snapshot).
- Variant B added empty.

Constraints (enforced via validation + UX):
- Minimum 2 variants, maximum 5 (GA default).
- Variant names must be unique.
- Model compatibility must match route capabilities (e.g., tool-calling enabled, context window requirements). If incompatible:
  - Block next step and show error with remediation.
sections.heading: Default variants

sections.body:
- “Pin model revision” (if model supports version pinning)
- “Allow fallback to route default if variant unavailable” (default ON, with info that this can dilute results)
sections.heading: Advanced toggle (collapsed)

sections.body:
Traffic split editor supports A/B/n allocation.

Primary control: **Split slider + table**
- For 2 variants: slider (e.g., 90/10)
- For 3+ variants: table with inline percent fields + “Normalize” button
sections.heading: Step 3 — Traffic split

sections.body:
- Total must equal 100%
- Minimum per-variant default: 1% (warning if below 5%)
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
- 99/1 (smoke)
- 95/5
- 90/10
- 50/50

Ramp plan helper (optional, not enforced):
- “Suggested staged ramp” widget based on guardrails enabled:
  - 1% for 15 min → 5% for 30 min → 10% for 2 hr → …
- CTA: “Save as ramp steps” (adds a plan to the Review screen; execution remains manual in GA)
sections.heading: Recommended presets

sections.body: - “This experiment affects traffic for route: {route}. It does not affect other routes.”
sections.heading: Blast radius callout

sections.body: Guardrails are monitored thresholds that drive banners, notifications, and optional auto-stop (depending on org policy).
sections.heading: Step 4 — Guardrails

sections.body:
- Latency: p95, p99
- Errors: 5xx rate, timeouts
- Cost: cost / 1K tokens, tokens / request (if available)
- Throughput: requests/min (informational by default)
- Quality (optional): eval score delta (if configured)
sections.heading: Guardrail categories

sections.body:
- Top: “Guardrails mode”
  - **Soft-stop (default)**: “Marks experiment as Degraded and notifies operators.”
  - **Hard-stop (optional)**: “Automatically stops the experiment when severe thresholds trip.”
    - Only shown if tenant policy allows + user has permission.
    - Requires explicit confirmation (“I understand this may stop healthy experiments due to noisy metrics.”)
sections.heading: UI structure

sections.body:
- Each guardrail row:
  - Toggle (on/off)
  - Metric selector (if multiple)
  - Threshold input (absolute or % regression vs control)
  - Evaluation window (e.g., last 10 min / 30 min)
  - “Applies to variants” (default: all non-control variants)

Defaults (initial GA recommendation; can be updated by SRE standards):
- p99 latency regression: +20% vs Control over 10 min (warning) / +35% (critical)
- error rate: +0.5% absolute over 10 min (warning) / +1.0% (critical)
- cost/1K tokens: +15% vs Control over 30 min (warning)
sections.heading: Guardrail editor patterns

sections.body:
- “Eval score delta” threshold
- Sampling note: “Quality signals may be delayed; do not use as the sole stop condition.”
sections.heading: Quality guardrails (if enabled)

sections.body: - Shows how banners will appear in the detail view.
sections.heading: Guardrails preview panel

sections.body:
- Route and environment
- Variants (model IDs, pinned revs)
- Traffic split
- Stickiness key and fallback behavior
- Guardrails summary + soft/hard stop mode
- Audit note: “Starting this experiment creates an audit event.”
sections.heading: Shows a read-only summary with explicit risk checks

sections.body:
- No other active experiment on route
- Split sums to 100%
- Variant compatibility valid
- Stickiness selection not “Random (non-sticky)” unless confirmed
sections.heading: Pre-flight validations (must pass)

sections.body:
- **Save as Draft**
- **Start Experiment**
  - Modal confirmation includes:
    - “Starting will apply immediately after config propagation (typically < X min).”
    - Checkbox: “Notify on-call channel/email list” (optional; tenant setting)
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- Name + status pill
- Route + environment
- Guardrail badge: Healthy / Warning / Degraded
- Time range selector (affects charts)
sections.heading: Page header

sections.body:
- Start (if Draft)
- Stop (if Running/Degraded)
- Edit (traffic split/guardrails) (if permitted)
- More: Delete (Admin), Export audit (Admin)
sections.heading: Primary actions (right side)

sections.body:
- **Draft**: not routing traffic
- **Starting**: start requested; propagation pending
- **Running**
- **Degraded**: guardrail(s) triggered
- **Stopping**: stop requested; propagation pending
- **Stopped/Completed**
sections.heading: Status states

sections.body: - If propagation lag detected: “Configuration is still propagating to data plane in some regions.” Link: “View propagation details.”
sections.heading: Propagation banner

sections.body:
1) **Overview** (default)
2) **Results**
3) **Guardrails**
4) **Audit & changes**
sections.heading: Tabs

sections.body:
- **Configuration summary** (route, stickiness, variants, split)
- **Assignment & attribution health**
  - Attribution drop rate (trend)
  - “Missing stickiness key rate” (trend)
  - Skew detector (e.g., “Variant B receiving 2.3x expected traffic”)
  - CTA (Admin/restricted): “Open assignment debug tool”

payload.page_title: Docs site change propagation & developer onramp playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines how content changes (snippets, SDK quickstarts, API examples, runbooks) move from authoring to published docs on the public developer docs site and how the developer onramp is kept in sync with canonical fixes and top support issue updates. It codifies roles, automation, verification checks, rollback criteria, and telemetry to ensure we ship accurate, timely developer-facing content.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: content owned by eng-developer-experience (quickstarts, API examples, docs-site pages, canonical fixes). Does NOT replace product PRDs or private customer runbooks living under eng-private-deployments.
- Audience: docs authors, SDK owners, DX PMs, Developer Support, and Docs site SRE.
sections.heading: Scope & audience

sections.body:
- Snippet: small code or config fragment included in multiple pages (examples, quickstarts).
- Golden trace: authoritative set of inputs and outputs used to validate an API example or sample app.
- Canonical fix: a vetted correction applied to docs after a support pattern is identified.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- Author: writes content and tests locally. Primary responsibility for correctness.
- Snippet owner: maintains a snippet library file; responds to breakages within 72 hours.
- Docs CI owner (team: eng-developer-experience/site): maintains docs pipeline and runbooks.
- Support liaison: triages incoming issue, recommends canonical fix, and opens PRs when urgent.
sections.heading: Roles & ownership (high level)

sections.body:
- Service: snippet registry | Owner: SDK team | SLA: 72h for critical bugs
- Service: docs-pipeline CI | Owner: site SRE | SLA: 24h for CI outages
- Service: published docs | Owner: docs product manager | SLA: 5 business days for content updates in non-critical path
sections.heading: Ownership quick table (described)

sections.body:
1. Authoring:
   - Create or update page in local markdown/snippet file. Use snippet IDs that match the registry (format: sdk-{lang}-{id}, e.g. sdk-py-auth-02).
   - Pre-commit hook runs: lint-md, snippet-validate, golden-trace-check.
2. Preview & review:
   - Push branch and open PR against docs-repo. CI generates a preview build and a preview URL. Command: `docs-pipeline preview --branch ${BRANCH}`
   - Add reviewers: at least one snippet owner and one domain SDK owner. Use the PR template which includes checklist (see Verification checklist).
3. Merge gating:
   - Passing CI and 2 approvals required. If change touches snippets used in published quickstarts, add `@site-sre` review.
4. Publish:
   - Merge triggers `docs-pipeline apply`. By default changes land in staging and are promoted to prod on a scheduled window (see Release windows).
   - For hotfixes (security, API-breaking), use `docs-pipeline apply --env=prod --hotfix --owner=${TEAM}`. Hotfixes bypass the scheduled promotion but require post-merge audit.
sections.heading: Publishing flow (end-to-end)

sections.body:
- Single source-of-truth: store snippets in `docs/snippets/` in canonical format (header with metadata).
- Metadata required per snippet (describe in text): snippet_id, owner, languages, last_tested, golden_trace_id.
- Naming convention: `{component}-{lang}-{short}` (lowercase, dashes).
- Test coverage: snippets must be covered by at least one unit/integration golden trace or CI smoke test.

Example snippet header (YAML in file top; shown here as plain):
```yaml
sections.heading: Snippet lifecycle & best practices

sections.body:
- Preview: `docs-pipeline preview --branch ${BRANCH}` generates a unique preview URL and lazy-evaluates large snippets.
- Validate: `docs-pipeline validate --path docs/snippets --schema snippet-schema.yaml` runs snippet schema checks.
- Apply (staging): `docs-pipeline apply --env=staging --owner=${TEAM}`
- Promote (staging -> prod): automatic nightly promotion at 02:00 UTC unless hold label is present. For emergency promotion use `--manual` flag.
sections.heading: Docs CI / automation (commands & policies)

sections.body:
- Job: snippet-validate
  - Runs: python scripts/snippet_validator.py --root docs/snippets
  - Produces: artifact list of changed snippet_ids and failing golden traces.
sections.heading: Sample CI job snippet (described)

sections.body:
1. Detect: Support files an issue or automated telemetry detects mismatch (e.g., example output drift).
2. Triage: Support liaison opens tracking issue and marks `impact:developer-experience`.
3. Reproduce: Author or on-call reproduces locally against golden-trace inputs.
4. Fix PR: Create PR that updates snippet/golden trace and includes test updates. Mark PR with `canonical-fix`.
5. Verification and merge: run CI, get approvals from snippet owner and Support liaison. For fixes that affect multiple quickstarts run `docs-pipeline preview --smoke` and validate sample matrix.
6. Postmortem: If the issue impacted >10 customers or was live >72 hours, create a short postmortem and link to PR.
sections.heading: Golden trace & canonical fixes workflow

sections.body:
- Pattern: Expired auth token in SDK quickstart causing 401s
  - Canonical fix: update example to show short-lived token exchange + note about token TTL. Add golden trace to assert new behavior.
- Pattern: Streaming API sample uses legacy param `stream_mode`
  - Canonical fix: update snippet to the current streaming API and add deprecation note with migration steps.
- Pattern: Embeddings dimensionality mismatch in example datasets
  - Canonical fix: add explicit schema validation in quickstart and provide a compatibility adapter snippet.
sections.heading: Top support patterns and canonical fixes (examples)

sections.body:
1. If a production page introduces a functional error and a hotfix PR is not ready, immediately revert the merge via `docs-pipeline revert --commit ${SHA}`.
2. Notify: post in #docs-pipeline Slack channel with incident tag and link to revert.
3. Create emergency PR that includes corrected snippet + tests. Mark as `emergency-hotpatch` and request expedited approvals.
4. After merge, run post-deploy checks (see Verification checklist) and close incident with owner notes.
sections.heading: Rollback & hotpatch playbook (numbered)

sections.body:
- [ ] Preview build URL accessible and renders without JS console errors.
- [ ] All snippet IDs referenced exist in `docs/snippets/` and validate against schema.
- [ ] Golden trace tests pass locally and in CI.
- [ ] If change touches quickstarts: run smoke integration (`docs-pipeline preview --smoke`) and confirm example app starts within 60s.
- [ ] PR includes update to changelog or release notes when removing/deprecating examples.
sections.heading: Verification checklist (before merging)

sections.body:
- Normal content: automated nightly promotion to prod (02:00 UTC).
- Low-risk updates: minor content updates may be scheduled weekly.
- Hotfix SLA: docs-pipeline CI owner will respond within 24h to CI outages; snippet owners have 72h for critical fixes.
sections.heading: Release windows & SLAs (short)

sections.body:
- Preview build success rate (target > 98% monthly).
- `snippet-validate` failure rate and top offending snippet IDs.
- Time-to-merge for canonical fixes (median target <= 4 business days).
- Support ticket count tagged `docs-issue` (reduce by 30% YoY).
sections.heading: Telemetry & monitoring (what to track)

sections.body:
1. Support opens an internal issue with labels `impact:developer-experience` + `severity`.
2. Support liaison assigns to snippet owner and adds a suggested canonical fix draft (if known).
3. If not resolved in SLA, escalate to Docs Product Manager and schedule a triage sync.
sections.heading: Support escalation paths (how Support interacts with docs)

sections.body:
Q: Who can mark a change as a hotfix?
A: The snippet owner or Docs Product Manager. Hotfixes require `site-sre` notification post-deploy.

Q: What counts as a canonical fix that needs postmortem?
A: Any change that: a) affected >10 paying customers, or b) caused a documented outage of a sample app for >72 hours.

sections.body:
- Docs pipeline README: `/confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/docs-pipeline-readme`
- Snippet schema: `/confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/snippet-schema`
- Support triage runbook: `/confluence/eng-developer-experience/support-top-issues/support-triage-runbook`

Appendix: Quick commands reference (one-liners):
- Preview a branch: `docs-pipeline preview --branch feature/x-example`
- Validate snippets: `docs-pipeline validate --path docs/snippets`
- Apply staging: `docs-pipeline apply --env=staging --owner=sdk-python`
- Emergency revert: `docs-pipeline revert --commit ${SHA}`

Document versioning: major edits should increment the header version and add a short summary line in the top of the page.

payload.page_title: Docs Site: SDK sample rotation and issue synthesis playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes the end-to-end process for maintaining a curated matrix of SDK examples (the "Sample Catalog"), rotating and retiring samples regularly, and creating an issue-synthesis pipeline that turns recurring support incidents and telemetry signals into updated, canonical example code and docs edits. The goal is to keep examples accurate, minimal, secure, and aligned with runtime and API changes while reducing support toil.

Scope: Applies to all SDK sample code and small reference applications hosted in the docs site and the SDK repositories (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java). It covers: authoring standards, review cadence, automated validation, rotation schedule, mapping to product priorities, and the remediation path for support-derived fixes.

Owner and stakeholders
- Document owner: Engineering Developer Experience (DevX) team (owner: Aisha Patel)
- Primary stakeholders: SDK teams (Python/JS/Go/Java), Runtime product, DX Docs, Support & Customer Success
- Secondary stakeholders: Security, Observability, Solutions Engineering

Goals and success metrics
- Accuracy: 0 known example regressions in production-facing docs for 30 days after release.
- Freshness: rotate at least 30% of the Sample Catalog each quarter for major API surface changes.
- Support reduction: 25% fewer "example bug" tickets year-over-year attributed to our documented samples.
- CI health: All sample validation jobs green before docs publish.

High-level lifecycle (concise)
1) Catalog: maintain a living YAML/JSON manifest (sample-catalog.yaml) listing each sample, SDK language, primary intent, owner, last-updated, stability tag (stable/experimental/retired).
2) Validation: run language-specific linters, unit smoke tests, runtime contract tests, and snippet extraction validation on every PR.
3) Rotation: scheduled quarterly review + on-demand churn for breaking platform changes.
4) Issue synthesis: automated aggregation of support tickets, telemetry alerts, and crash logs mapped to catalog entries; create remediation work items and track via the "sample-fixes" board.
5) Release: publish updates with release notes and tagging; notify downstream repos and customers as needed.

Authoring standards (applies to all samples)
- Small is better: prefer 10–30 lines for inline page snippets. Full examples may be larger but should live in the samples repo.
- Copy/paste-safe: no production secrets, no hard-coded tenant IDs. Use environment variables and small bootstrap instructions.
- Deterministic outputs: where possible, use fixed seeds or deterministic model prompts in examples, and show sample input/output in comments only.
- Minimal dependencies: prefer only official SDKs and widely adopted libs; document required versions.
- Multi-language parity: every canonical sample must have parity mappings for supported SDK languages where feasible.
- Licensing: include license header in sample repo files matching Redwood standard (Apache-2.0).

Snippet extraction and docs pipeline
- Snippet format: use the standard snippet markers used by the docs site generator: // BEGIN_SNIPPET <id> and // END_SNIPPET <id> (or block-style for markdown fenced snippets).
- Extraction CI: incremental snippet extraction on PRs produces a "snippet diff" that is validated against the sample-catalog manifest (ensures snippet id, language, and page mapping exist).
- Validation steps (CI):
  1. Lint (language specific)
  2. Build/Install deps (isolated env)
  3. Smoke run (execute main path or unit test)
  4. Output assertions (for deterministic snippets)
  5. Size check (inline snippets < 200 lines)
- Failure handling: failing jobs should add a descriptive artifact to the PR with stdout/stderr, failing test file, and suggested remedial steps.

Sample Catalog (manifest) - example YAML schema (as a single-line table for docs)
- Path: /repos/docs/samples/sample-catalog.yaml
- Required fields per entry: id, title, language(s), page, owner, stability, last_updated, test_job_id

Example manifest table (rendered as text table)
| id | title | languages | page | owner | stability | last_updated |
| sample.chat.basic | Basic chat loop | python,ts | /docs/sdk/chat | eng-dx | stable | 2027-01-10 |
| sample.embed.search | Embeddings search | python,ts,go | /docs/sdk/embeddings | eng-dx | experimental | 2026-09-08 |

Rotation cadence and criteria
- Quarterly scheduled pass (default): review samples with last_updated > 90 days and stability=experimental first.
- Triggered rotation (on-demand): API contract changes, runtime behavior shifts, security advisories, or when a support cluster shows >5 related tickets in 14 days.
- Retirement criteria: low usage (<5 page hits/month), unmaintainable dependency, or duplicated capability covered by newer sample. Retired samples move to a /retired folder and maintain an archive entry in the catalog.

Automated issue synthesis pipeline (implementation summary)
- Inputs: support ticket labels (example-bug, sample-mismatch), stack traces, telemetry alerts (snippet failures, example runtime exceptions), periodic fuzz tests against samples.
- Mapping: use a deterministic mapping table that correlates error signatures to sample IDs. When a match probability > 80% we auto-create a remediation ticket in the sample-fixes board; when 30–80% we create a flagged suggestion for a human reviewer.
- Ticket template fields: sample_id, observed_symptom, telemetry_links, reproducer-snippet, priority (P1–P4), owner, proposed-fix-surface (docs, sample code, CI).
- Escalation: P1 or high volume items are auto-notified to the SDK owner, Support TL, and DevX lead.

Release checklist for sample updates
1) Update sample file and manifest entry.
2) Ensure CI validation green across all languages listed.
3) Update page with snippet ids; run docs-site preview tests.
4) Bump sample-catalog.yaml last_updated and add short changelog in manifest.
5) Create release PR with the tag "sample-release" and link runtime/product change if applicable.
6) Post release note in #devx-docs Slack and the monthly sample digest channel.

Rollback and emergency hotfix process
- If a sample update breaks CI or causes incorrect guidance in the docs, create a hotfix branch named hotfix/sample/<sample-id>/<short-reason>.
- Revert path for docs-site: revert the snippet PR, re-run snippet extraction, and republish docs via the emergency docs pipeline (see docs-site emergency-patch playbook).
- For customer-impacting sample regressions (support escalations pointing to production code failures), fast-track a patch release and coordinate with Support and Customer Success for guidance and mitigations.

Top support issue categories and canonical fixes (examples)
1) Example fails due to auth change (most common): Fix = update sample to use new header format, add a pre-run check that validates token env var and provide helpful error text.
2) Dependency breaking change: Fix = pin supported dependency version in sample manifest and add a compatibility note.
3) Runtime mismatch (generation parameters changed): Fix = update snippet default params and add comment block that explains tradeoffs for latency vs cost.
4) Multi-language parity gap: Fix = add a minimal TS/Go mapping and mark as "work-in-progress" in manifest.

Canonical fix template (to include in remediation PR)
- Problem statement (1–2 lines)
- Root cause analysis (2–4 lines) with links to telemetry or ticket ids
- Change summary (what changed in sample or docs)
- Validation steps (how we validated)
- Rollout plan (tags, publish, notify)

Observability signals for sample health
- Docs page hits (pageviews per sample page)
- Snippet CI pass rate (percent of PRs with snippet validation passing)
- CR (customer reports) rate with label example-bug/sample- mismatch
- Execution failure rate from fuzz tests and nightly sample runs
- Time-to-fix for sample-related tickets

Roles & Responsibilities (concise)
- DevX (owner): sample catalog, snippet CI, coordination with SDK owners, run quarterly reviews.
- SDK owners: update language parity, validate runtime compatibility, respond to P1/P2 sample fixes.
- Support: apply labels and sanity-check mapping when filing tickets.
- Docs engineering: snippet extraction tooling, preview pipeline, and emergency publish path.

Quickstart: adding a new canonical sample (step-by-step)
1) Create sample in /repos/docs/samples/<language>/<sample-id>/ with README.md and tests.
2) Add entry to sample-catalog.yaml with required metadata.
3) Add snippet markers and reference IDs in the target docs page.
4) Open PR to samples repo and docs repo simultaneously (link PRs).
5) Wait for CI: fix lint/build/test failures.
6) Request review from SDK owner and DevX reviewer.
7) Merge after approvals; CI will publish preview and then the live page in the next docs deployment window.

Example API snippet (Python)
