payload.page_title: Public Docs Plan: Workload-Aware Batching Defaults (Fast / Standard / Cost-Efficient)

sections.body: This document is the execution plan for updating Redwood’s external documentation to support “workload-aware batching defaults”: three customer-facing latency SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient) that map to recommended batching profiles.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Explain tier meanings clearly without over-promising.
- Document default behavior (what happens if a customer does nothing).
- Show how to select a tier and how to override/opt out safely.
- Provide examples (REST + SDKs) and troubleshooting guidance.
- Provide an FAQ that sets expectations for latency vs cost trade-offs and streaming.
sections.heading: The public docs must

sections.body:
1) Reduce configuration confusion and support load during rollout.
- Customers can answer: “Which tier should I use?” and “How do I set it?” within 2 minutes.

2) Avoid customer foot-guns.
- Clear warnings around per-request overrides, Dedicated precedence, and overload/backpressure behavior.

3) Align messaging across product surfaces.
- Terminology and claims match Console copy and runtime behavior.

4) Support staged launch.
- Docs support: internal canary → Hosted subset → Dedicated opt-in → broad default.
- Clearly indicate availability by deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private).
sections.heading: Goals (docs outcomes)

sections.body:
- Publishing internal knob values (e.g., exact max_wait_ms) or hardware-specific tuning tables beyond what Product approves.
- Promising fixed latency numbers for every workload; we will point to published tier targets and caveats.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Application engineers integrating Redwood API (Hosted).
- Platform engineers operating Dedicated clusters.
- SRE/ops teams troubleshooting latency/cost regressions.
sections.heading: Primary audience

sections.body:
- Choose a tier for a new route.
- Change tier for an existing route after observing p95/p99 or cost.
- Force fast tier for streaming endpoints.
- Verify which tier is currently effective (and why) in Console.
- Troubleshoot “why did my effective profile change?” (reason codes / overload mode).
sections.heading: Key use cases

sections.body:
- “Tiers are a high-level intent (latency vs cost). Redwood picks safe batching defaults consistent with that intent.”

sections.body:
Page: “Batching defaults & latency SLO tiers”

1) What batching is (1–2 paragraphs)
- How batching improves throughput and cost.
- Why batching can affect tail latency (waiting to form batches).

2) What changed (workload-aware defaults)
- Redwood uses runtime heuristics and workload signals to pick safe batching behavior.

3) Tier definitions (high-level)
- **Fast:** prioritizes tail latency stability and streaming responsiveness.
- **Standard:** balanced default for most production workloads.
- **Cost-efficient:** prioritizes throughput / $/token; higher tolerance for queuing.

4) Decision table (choose a tier)
- If you stream user-facing chat: start with fast.
- If you run mixed workloads or general API: standard.
- If you run async/batch summarization or offline processing: cost-efficient.

5) Default behavior
- If a customer does not select a tier: explain which tier is applied by default per product policy (Hosted default) and how that may evolve during rollout.
- Provide a “How to pin your tier” callout.

6) Overload behavior (public-safe)
- Explain backpressure/load shedding at a high level.
- Clarify that cost-efficient may accept higher queueing than fast.

7) Observability
- Where to see effective tier in Console.
- “Why this profile?” explanation and reason codes (public-friendly phrasing).

- Opt-out: document the supported mechanism (e.g., pin legacy behavior or disable tiered defaults) only if Product approves exposing it publicly. If opt-out is intended to be support-assisted, say so explicitly.

sections.body:
- Don’t set per-request tier dynamically based on user identity (can increase variance and complicate debugging).
- If you change tier, observe p95/p99 and error rates for at least one peak window.
sections.heading: Warnings to include

sections.body:
We will publish answers aligned to policy and avoid internal implementation details.

1) “What happens if I don’t pick a tier?”
- Explain default tier behavior and how to pin it.

2) “Does fast mean real-time?”
- Clarify expected use (interactive) and that latency still depends on model size, output length, and region.

3) “Will cost-efficient increase latency?”

4) “Does tier selection affect output quality?”
- State: batching should not change model outputs; mention rare edge cases we monitor (e.g., truncation/limits) and recommend contacting support if quality regressions are suspected.

5) “Does tier selection change logging/retention or data handling?”
- State explicitly: no; tier only affects runtime scheduling and batching.

6) “Can I use fast tier for streaming only and standard for non-streaming?”
- Yes; recommend per-route configuration.

7) “How do Dedicated overrides work?”

8) “How can I tell which tier is in effect and why?”

payload.page_title: Docs Site: Localization, Release Branching, and Emergency Rollback Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook defines how the Redwood docs site handles localization (i18n), release branching, staged rollouts, and emergency rollback. It documents responsibilities, CI/CD expectations, branching patterns, localization handoff templates, and canonical fixes for top support scenarios related to localized content. The guidance applies to all markdown-based content in the docs repository (repo: docs-site) and automated site builds that publish to docs.redwood.ai.

Goals:
- Ensure localized sites are consistently updated without blocking fast English-first releases.
- Keep full-site build times predictable: full build < 12 minutes (median), incremental builds < 3 minutes.
- Maintain publish pipeline success >= 98% across regions.
- Provide a clear rollback path that restores a previously validated site within 15 minutes.

Scope:
- Applies to content under /docs, /reference, /sdk-guides, /quickstarts in docs-site repository.
- Includes automated translations (translate-api), human-reviewed translations, UI strings, and localized code samples.
- Excludes marketing site and blog pipelines (handled by growth team).

Ownership and Roles:
- Docs Platform (owner): eng-developer-experience/docs-platform (primary on-call rotation: docs-oncall@redwood.ai).
- Localization Owners: product-i18n (coordinates translation vendors and review).
- Release Manager (weekly releases): product-platform PMs.
- CI/CD Owner: eng-infra (maintains docs-builder and docs-pipeline).

Branching and Release Strategy:
1. Branch types
   - main: English canonical content. Always deployable to production (docs.redwood.ai/en).
   - release/*: short-lived release branches for coordinated releases (e.g., release/2026-02-10).
   - hotfix/*: emergency patches that should be cherry-picked into main and also merged into relevant release/* branches.
   - i18n/*: language-specific branches used for bulk localization work (e.g., i18n/ja-2026-q1).

2. Merge rules
   - All PRs to main require: 1 tech reviewer, 1 localization reviewer (if UI or UX strings), and passing CI (lint, link-check, content-tests).
   - Release branches are created from main at the release cut. Only PRs with the label `release-allowed` may merge into release/*.

3. Tagging
   - Use semantic docs tags: vYYYY.MM.DD (e.g., v2026.02.10). Tags map to stable snapshots exposed in the Docs Console.

Localization Workflow:
- Modes supported:
  1) Auto-translated + human post-edit: For high-velocity pages (API reference, SDK snippets).
  2) Human-first translation: For product marketing, legal, and compliance-sensitive pages.

- Hand-off template for translation teams (use in PR description):
  - source_path: /docs/guides/sdk-auth.md
  - locale: ja-JP
  - context_notes: "CLI examples assume linux/bash"
  - expected_tat: 5 business days

- i18n CI checks (run in docs-pipeline):
  - verify-language-tags: ensures locale codes exist and content falls back to en when missing.
  - localized-link-check: validates internal links are present in target locale or have fallback.
  - sample-run: executes code snippets in a sandbox for supported SDKs (node, python) in a localized locale where variable names may differ.

Templates and Quickstarts for Localizers:
- Localization PR template (docs/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/i18n.md) includes required checklist: glossary entries, date/time formatting, number formatting, code sample verification steps.
- Quickstart: "Produce a reviewed localized patch" - a 6-step quickstart that includes running `make i18n-check` and `yarn docs:preview --locale=ja` locally.

CI/CD and Build Expectations:
- Pipeline stages: checkout -> lint -> build-incremental -> run-tests -> deploy-staging -> run-smoke-tests -> promote-to-prod (manual for release/*).
- Performance SLOs:
  - Full build median < 12m; 95th percentile < 20m.
  - Incremental build median < 3m; 95th percentile < 8m.
  - Publish success rate >= 98% per week.
- Key services and owners:
  - docs-builder (eng-infra) — builds static site.
  - content-sync (docs-platform) — syncs translated content from translation service workspace to repo.
  - translate-api (product-i18n) — vendor integration layer.

Staged Rollout Pattern:
1. Canary (10%): deploy to staging subdomain (staging.docs.redwood.ai/<locale>) and run localized smoke suite.
2. Regional rollout (50%): push to CDN edge nodes in a single region.
3. Global rollout (100%): full CDN invalidation and production route switch.

Promote conditions:
- Canary smoke tests green for 30m.
- No critical page regressions (broken links, missing code blocks) reported by content-tests.
- Rollout approval by Release Manager or on-call engineer.

Rollback and Hotfix Procedures:
- Soft rollback (preferred): promote last successful tag (vYYYY.MM.DD) through docs-pipeline. Expected restoration time: < 15 minutes after roll command.
- Hard rollback: if tag promotion fails, revert merge commit on release/* and trigger hotfix/hard-redeploy.
- Hotfix flow:
  1) Create hotfix/<ticket-id> branch from main or from release/* (depending on scope).
  2) Patch the content and add CHANGELOG entry.
  3) Tests: run lint, link-check, localized sample-run.
  4) Merge to main and into active release/* branches.
  5) Trigger docs-pipeline: deploy-hotfix job.
- Communication: Page status at status.redwood.ai and #docs-status Slack channel. Use the incident template under confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems for post-release follow-up.

Top Support Issues (localized content) and Canonical Fixes:
- Issue: localized code samples fail due to locale-specific characters or missing escaping.
  - Fix: enforce UTF-8 in pipeline, run `sample-run --locale` during PR, add unit test that executes samples in a containerized environment.
- Issue: broken links in localized pages because translated page path mismatches.
  - Fix: enable localized-link-check, require `localized-path` field in i18n frontmatter.
- Issue: terminology mismatch (e.g., "Dedicated" translated inconsistently).
  - Fix: central glossary enforced via docs-glossary.yml and pre-commit hook.

Monitoring and Alerts:
- Metrics emitted to observability stack (prometheus -> grafana): build_duration_seconds, publish_success_rate, i18n_plugin_errors_total, localized_link_errors_total.
- Alert rules (examples):
  - ALRT_DOCS_PIPELINE_FAILURE: publish_success_rate < 95% over 15m -> Pager to docs-oncall.
  - ALRT_LOCALIZED_LINK_ERRORS: localized_link_errors_total > 10 in 30m -> Slack @docs-team, Email product-i18n.

Quality Gates and Acceptance Criteria:
- Every PR that adds or changes localized content must satisfy:
  - link-check: pass
  - glossary-check: no new undefined terms
  - sample-run: all runnable samples pass in sandbox
  - translations: vendor status either `human-reviewed` or `auto+postedit` with translation_changelog in PR body.

Operational Playbook Snippets (commands):
- Build and preview a locale locally:
  - `yarn install && yarn build && yarn preview --locale=fr-FR`
- Run i18n checks locally:
  - `make i18n-check` (runs verify-language-tags and localized-link-check)
- Promote a tag to production (soft rollback):
  - `./scripts/promote-tag.sh v2026.02.10`

Appendix: Example frontmatter for localized page (YAML):
```
---
title: "Getting started with the SDK"
locale: ja-JP
i18n_source: /docs/getting-started-sdk.md
localized_path: /docs/ja/getting-started-sdk.md
translation_status: human-reviewed
glossary_terms: ["Dedicated", "Private deployment"]
---
```

Review cadence and improvements:
- Annual localization strategy review (owner: product-i18n) scheduled in Q1.
- Post-release retrospective after every major release (owner: Release Manager).

Related docs and references:
- docs-site content lifecycle and preview (link in related_pages).
- Quickstarts for localizers and sample-run CLI (see related quickstart page).

Contact and escalation:
- Primary on-call: docs-oncall@redwood.ai
- Escalation: contact eng-platform lead (pager: Evan Chen) if rollback does not complete within 30 minutes.

This playbook is normative — deviations must be approved by release manager and documented on the PR. For questions or suggested edits, open a PR against docs-site or ping the docs-platform channel.

payload.page_title: Deterministic Replay & Auth Testkit for SDKs — Golden Trace Library

sections.body: This document defines the deterministic replay and authentication injection testkit for Redwood SDKs (the "Replay & Auth Testkit"). The goal is to make integration tests for client SDKs and platform integrations reproducible across developers, CI, and release gates, while exercising auth flows, token rotation, and golden-trace comparison of outputs.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- SDK engineers building language client libraries
- DevX reliability engineers integrating tests into CI
- QA engineers responsible for output quality regressions
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Goals:
  - Provide a single, language-agnostic format for recording API interactions (requests, upstream model id, tokenization metadata, response chunks).
  - Allow deterministic replay with optional auth injection (simulate expiring tokens, 401 flows, refresh token rotations).
  - Provide golden-trace diff tooling for token-level and semantic differences to catch quality regressions.
  - Fit into CI: record on master, run replay in PRs and fail on regressions above thresholds.
- Non-goals:
  - Not intended to replace e2e UX testing that requires full UI and network stacks.
  - Not a load-testing tool (use benchmark suites under eng-serving-runtime).
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body:
1) Recorder: lightweight HTTP/SDK interceptor that captures requests and structured responses into a single Replay Manifest (.rdm).
2) Replay Server: deterministic backend that serves recorded responses to the SDK under test and simulates auth behavior based on an Auth Scenario file.
3) Golden-trace comparator: CLI tool that compares replayed outputs against a golden trace and reports token-level diffs, ROUGE-like summary metrics, and semantic embedding drift.
sections.heading: The testkit has three components

sections.body:
- Replay Manifest (.rdm) — JSON lines file with records: request, response, tokenization, model_meta, timestamps. All examples below use a compact spec (see example).
- Auth Scenario (.auth.json) — small JSON describing token lifetime, rotation cadence, and injected errors.
- Golden Trace (.golden.json) — canonical outputs with canonical prompts and acceptance thresholds.
sections.heading: Key files and formats

sections.body:
- Node >= 18 or Python 3.10 for testkit runners (both supported).
- Access to the local Replay Server (docker-compose provided) or a CI-hosted instance.
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.body:
1) Install the recorder shim in your local test environment: npm install @redwood/replay-recorder or pip install redwood-replay-recorder.
2) Run your unit/integration test with RECORDER=on and RECORD_OUTPUT=./replays/my-feature.rdm.
3) Validate the manifest with: rdm-validate ./replays/my-feature.rdm.
4) Submit the .rdm and a matching .golden.json when opening a PR (see CI gating below).

Recording checklist: (table)
| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| request.path | yes | Path + method, must be stable (no timestamps in path) |
| request.prompt_hash | yes | Deterministic hash of preprocessed prompt |
| response.tokens | yes | Token list with token ids and strings |
| model_meta | yes | Model id, quantization profile |
| sdk_version | yes | SDK semver that produced the capture |

Example Replay Manifest record (single-line for .rdm):
{"record_id":"abc123","request":{"path":"/v1/generate","method":"POST","body_hash":"h1"},"model_meta":{"id":"redwood/fast-7b","max_tokens":512},"response":{"status":200,"tokens":[{"id":50256,"text":"Hello"},{"id":11,"text":", world"}],"streaming":false},"tokenizer":{"vocab":"gpt2-tokenizer-v1","normalized_prompt":"Hello, world"},"ts_recorded":"2026-11-02T17:03:21Z","sdk_version":"1.4.0"}

Auth Scenario example (.auth.json):
{
  "scenario_name": "refresh-rotation-10s",
  "initial_ttl_s": 5,
  "rotation_every_s": 10,
  "inject_errors": [
    {"after_request": 2, "status": 401, "retryable": true}
  ]
}
sections.heading: Recording workflow (developer)

sections.body:
- Modes:
  - strict: only serve exact matching (request.body_hash + model_meta) records; mismatch => 409 (CI failure expected).
  - tolerant: fallback to best-match by prompt_hash (useful for dev iteration).
- Auth injection: load .auth.json, trigger 401s and token expirations per scenario.
- Latency simulation: per-record latency override to reproduce network jitter.
sections.heading: Replay Server behavior and flags

sections.body:
1) git clone git@github.com:redwood/replay-testkit.git
2) cd replay-testkit && docker compose up --build -d
3) export REPLAY_SERVER=http://localhost:8080
4) python -m pytest tests/ --replay-server=$REPLAY_SERVER --replay-manifest=./replays/my-feature.rdm --auth-scenario=./replays/rotation.auth.json
sections.heading: How to run locally (example with Docker)

sections.body:
1) Recording: Record manifests on merged main periodically and store in artifacts bucket (s3://redwood-ci/replays/<branch>/).
2) PR runs: Pull down golden traces and run replay in "strict" mode. Fail PR if:
   - token-level divergence count > 2% of tokens OR
   - semantic embedding cosine similarity < 0.985 OR
   - more than 1 unmatched request (409)
3) Flaky handling: CI will re-run the replay once; if failure repeats, tag as a potential regression and open a triage issue with trace attached.
sections.heading: CI integration (recommended)

sections.body:
- Summary: 120 tokens compared, 3 token mismatches (2.5%), semantic similarity 0.992 (pass)
- Token diff sample:
  - expected: "the AI will respond with a greeting"
  - actual:   "the assistant replies with a salutation"
- Retain raw token ids in output to disambiguate tokenizer drift.
sections.heading: Golden-trace comparator output (example)

sections.body:
- token_mismatch_pct: 1.5% for generation models; 0.5% for deterministic outputs (embeddings, classification).
- semantic_similarity: 0.99 for headline-level, 0.985 for long-form.
- unmatched_request_count: 0 for strict mode.
(Teams may tighten thresholds per product surface.)
sections.heading: Acceptable thresholds (team defaults)

sections.body:
- expired_token_immediate_401: simulate immediate 401 for unauthenticated request; ensure SDK retries once with refresh token.
- rotation_under_load: rotation every 10s while serving 50 recorded interactions in quick succession.
- refresh_failure_then_recovery: simulate intermittent 500 from auth endpoint and eventual success.
sections.heading: Auth test scenarios to include in CI matrix

sections.body:
1) Provide .rdm (recording) file and .golden.json metadata describing acceptance thresholds.
2) Include rationale in PR description: why the golden is correct and how it was validated.
3) Add unit tests that assert the comparator passes locally.
4) Request reviewer from teams: devx + product owner.
sections.heading: Adding a new golden trace (PR checklist)

sections.body:
- Tokenization drift: differening tokenizer versions will change token ids. Fix: update tokenizer field in .rdm and run tokenizer-rewrite tool to map ids, or pin tokenizer versions in the SDK test runner.
- Environmental timestamps in prompt: prompts that include dynamic timestamps will produce non-deterministic body_hash. Fix: sanitize dynamic fields via recorder preprocessor.
- Model variant mismatch: recorded model id differs from allowed model in CI. Fix: add model mapping entry in replay server config (model_aliases).
sections.heading: Troubleshooting common failure patterns

sections.body:
- Testkit maintainer: Priya Kannan (platform-testkits@redwood.com)
- DevX reliability lead: Luca Moretti (luca@redwood.com)
- SDK owners: see per-language OWNERS file in each SDK repo
sections.heading: Owners and contacts

sections.body:
- Q1 2027: add per-token probability traces to manifest to enable ranking/regression detection.
- Q2 2027: integrate with Redwood Console for trace exploration and diff visualization.
- Long term: reduce friction for recording in serverless environments and add built-in model-compatibility suggestions.

Appendix A: Minimal Python example to replay a single manifest:
```python
import requests, json
REPLAY_SERVER = "http://localhost:8080"
with open("./replays/sample.rdm") as fh:
    for line in fh:
        rec = json.loads(line)
        r = requests.post(REPLAY_SERVER + rec['request']['path'], json={'__replay_id': rec['record_id']})
        print(r.status_code, r.text[:120])
```

Appendix B: Example comparator CLI usage:
$ rdm-compare --golden=./goldens/my-feature.golden.json --replay=./replays/my-feature.rdm --thresholds=./configs/default-thresholds.json

Appendix C: FAQ:
- Q: Can I use the replay testkit against hosted Redwood endpoints?
  - A: Yes, but only in controlled environments. Hosted endpoints may change; prefer private replay server for deterministic checks.

- Q: What about PII in recordings?
  - A: Recordings must be scrubbed before upload. Use rdm-scrub scrubber to remove emails, phone numbers, and customer data. See security-and-compliance/data-management for scrubber configuration.
sections.heading: Roadmap and next steps

sections.body:
- SDK recorder repo: git@github.com:redwood/replay-recorder.git
- Replay server repo: git@github.com:redwood/replay-server.git
- Golden-trace comparator: git@github.com:redwood/golden-compare.git
sections.heading: Related links

sections.body:
- 2026-11-02: Initial published draft (Priya Kannan)
- 2026-12-15: Clarified CI thresholds and added auth-scenario examples (Priya Kannan)
sections.heading: Revision history

payload.page_title: Request sampler and golden-trace validation playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes the Request Sampler and Golden-Trace Validation workflow used by Developer Experience (DX) to: 1) capture representative SDK/API requests with low overhead, 2) produce golden traces for deterministic integration tests and quality checks, and 3) validate telemetry stability across SDK and runtime releases. The goals are reproducible samples for regression detection, minimal perf impact (<0.5% p50 latency change), and a well-defined triage path for telemetry drift.

When to use this playbook

- Onboarding: collect starter traces for new SDK integrations.
- Release gating: validate that SDK vX and runtime vY produce matching golden traces for canonical prompts.
- Incident analysis: replay sampled traces when investigating errors or regressions.

High-level architecture

- Request Sampler (client-side): lightweight component embedded in SDKs that probabilistically captures request metadata and optionally full payloads when consented.
- Sample Collector (ingest): a Redwood internal service (service name: dx-sampler-ingest) that receives sampled envelopes over HTTPS and writes to a partitioned S3 bucket and an internal RocksDB index for quick lookup.
- Golden-Trace Builder: offline job (dx-golden-builder) that normalizes payloads, redacts PII, and computes canonical outputs against target models for golden traces.
- Validator: CI job and on-demand service (dx-trace-validate) which compares new traces against goldens and emits metrics/alerts.

Ownership and SLAs

- Request Sampler library: eng-developer-experience team. Primary owner: Maya Rivera.
- dx-sampler-ingest and dx-golden-builder: eng-platform. Primary owner: Liam Chen.
- Validation CI and dashboards: eng-sre. Primary owner: Asha Patel.
- Support response time: P1 triage within 2 business hours, P2 within 24 hours.

Sampling policy and config

Default policy (applies to SDKs unless overridden by tenant config):

1) Low-volume tenants (<1000 requests/day): deterministic capture of first 50 requests/day, then 1% random sampling.
2) Mid-volume tenants (1k-100k/day): Poisson sampling at 0.5% with deterministic capture for error responses (HTTP >= 500) and slow responses (>99th latency pct).
3) High-volume tenants (>100k/day): reservoir sampling capped to 10k samples/day with priority for error/slow traces and explicit developer flags.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- sampler.enabled: true|false
- sampler.rate_pct: "0.5"
- sampler.max_daily: "10000"
- sampler.capture_response: true|false
- sampler.capture_headers: ["x-request-id","x-redwood-route"]
- sampler.redact_fields: ["user.email","user.phone"]

Example SDK snippet (JavaScript)

const redwood = new RedwoodClient({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY,
  sampler: { enabled: true, rate_pct: 0.5, capture_response: false }
});

// Attach an explicit sample request when you need a guaranteed capture
redwood.sampler.markForCapture({ reason: 'onboarding:sample-1' });

Collector contract and envelope schema (example JSON)

{
  "envelope_id": "uuid-v4",
  "sdk_name": "js-client",
  "sdk_version": "1.12.0",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-08T10:12:34Z",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "metadata": { "tenant_id": "acct-123", "region": "us-west-2" },
  "payload_redacted": true,
  "response_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "latency_ms": 128
}

(Collector stores redacted payloads by default; full payloads require customer consent and a signed ACL)

Golden-trace generation and normalization rules

1) Redact: PII fields defined by sampler.redact_fields must be removed or replaced with stable placeholders (user.email -> <REDACTED_EMAIL>).
2) Determinize: random seeds, timestamps, and ephemeral IDs must be normalized. Examples: unify date formats to YYYY-MM-DD, inject stable pseudo-random seed from envelope_id.
3) Tokenization consistency: use dx-golden-builder's tokenization v2 (tokenizer version baked into golden metadata).
4) Output canonicalization: strip whitespace-only differences and apply language-specific normalization (Unicode NFKC).

Validator checks (ordered)

1) Hash match: compare response_hash to golden. If identical -> PASS.
2) Fuzzy-match: if hash differs, compute token-level diff and score. Thresholds: fuzzy_score >= 0.98 -> WARNING, 0.9-0.98 -> INVESTIGATE, <0.9 -> FAIL.
3) Latency delta: if median latency for this trace class increases >20% in canary -> PERFORMANCE ALERT.

CI gating and rollout integration

- Pre-merge: run dx-trace-validate on a curated set of 100 golden traces. Failures block merges for runtime or SDK changes that touch tokenization, serialization, or sampling logic.
- Post-deploy canary: run validation against a live golden cohort for first 1% of traffic. If FAIL or >20% WARNINGs, automatic rollback to previous runtime version.

Dashboards and metrics to monitor

- trace.validation.pass_rate (per sdk_name, per model)
- trace.validation.fuzzy_score_p50/p90
- sampler.ingest.latency_ms (SLO: p95 < 200 ms)
- sampler.ingest.error_count (SLO: <0.1% errors/day)
- validation.ci_blocked_count

Operational playbook: triage path

1) Alert triggers: validation FAIL or validation.pass_rate < 99% for 10 minutes.
2) On-call (eng-sre) creates incident and assigns to dx-telemetry rotation.
3) Initial checks (10 minutes): verify dx-sampler-ingest health, storage quotas, and collector error logs (/var/log/dx-sampler/*.log).
4) Reproduce locally: use dx-replay tool to replay the offending envelope against current runtime and golden runtime. Command example:
sections.heading: Config table (example values to include in SDK config)

sections.body:
dx-replay --env-id uuid-v4 --target runtime://staging-us-west-2

5) If mismatch is reproducible: collect a golden-diff artifact and escalate to eng-developer-experience and eng-serving-runtime for root cause. Attach artifacts: envelope.json, golden.json, diff.patch.
6) If mismatch is non-reproducible or intermittent: increase sampling rate for the tenant to 5% and enable full payload capture for 24 hours (requires customer notification if not internal).

Compliance and privacy notes

- Default behavior is to redact PII. Full payload capture requires explicit customer consent and a signed Data Collection Addendum (DCA).
- Stored samples are retained 90 days in S3 partitioned by tenant and then moved to cold archive for 1 year. Retention overrides for security incidents must be approved by Security.

Examples and troubleshooting

Q: I’m seeing validation WARNINGS on benign formatting changes.
A: Use dx-golden-builder normalization rules to re-run the golden build with updated normalization for this language. Document the normalization change and add the new golden to the curated cohort.

Q: Sampling rate seems to reduce SDK performance.
A: Validate with feature flag: disable capture_response or reduce rate_pct. Expected p50 latency delta with sampler.enabled:true is <5ms for typical requests.

Appendix: rollout checklist for enabling sampler in a new SDK

1) Add sampler config defaults to SDK config schema and unit tests for rate boundary conditions.
2) Integrate SDK telemetry with dx-sampler-ingest using the envelope contract.
3) Add golden traces for 10 representative prompts to the curated cohort (include at least 3 edge-case prompts).
4) Run dx-trace-validate locally and in CI.
5) Deploy to canary population (1% traffic) and monitor trace.validation.pass_rate for 24 hours.
6) Ramp to 10% then 100% by manual approval once pass_rate >= 99.5% for 24 hours.

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-bootcamp-labs-and-observability-sprints-2024
- /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-telemetry-telemetry-snapshotter-and-bootstrapping-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Created initial draft (Maya Rivera)
- 2026-01-15: Added fuzzy-match thresholds and CI gating rules (Liam Chen)
- 2026-02-08: Finalized retention policy and rollout checklist (Asha Patel)

payload.page_title: blackbox-api-mirroring-workflow-and-debug-playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes a safe, repeatable workflow for creating blackbox mirrors of production API traffic, sanitizing the captured payloads, and replaying requests against local SDKs, staging stacks, or canary model variants. The goal is to reproduce real-world failure patterns, measure regression risk for SDK/serving changes, and accelerate bug triage without exposing customer PII or impacting production.

When to use

- Reproducing a hard-to-trigger error that only appears under production traffic mixes (multi-route, multi-tenant, variable prompt sizes).
- Verifying that an SDK or runtime change preserves downstream observability (trace IDs, latency distributions, token counts).
- Running end-to-end golden checks against a candidate model or quantization profile.

Prerequisites

1. Ownership and approvals: security and product sign-off for capturing traffic (see Security & Compliance for approvals).
2. A dedicated capture window or sampling rate that keeps production impact negligible. Typical default: 1% request sampling for high-volume tenants; full-capture only with explicit approval.
3. Access to the capture bucket (S3-compatible) and a staging cluster or local harness with the same API surface.

High-level approach

1. Capture: sample and persist a representative request set.
2. Sanitize: remove or obfuscate PII and customer identifiers.
3. Enrich: add metadata needed for deterministic replay (headers, seed RNG hints, model pinning).
4. Replay: run the harness against the target (local SDK, staging endpoint, or canary model).
5. Observe: compare telemetry (latency histograms, error rates, token counts, outputs).

Traffic capture & sanitization

Capture locations and mechanisms (choose one):

- Edge proxy (Envoy / NGiNX filter): captures request/response envelopes and headers. Pros: earliest point-of-ingress, consistent headers.
- Platform gateway (API router): captures enriched metadata (customer_id, route, feature flags).
- SDK-side logging (developer box): for telemetry cases where full body capture is not allowed.

Capturing example (Envoy Lua filter snippet):

# lua snippet (Envoy) - capture headers and body to stdout for an external collector\local function capture(request)
  local h = request:headers()
  local body = request:body():getBytes(0, request:body():length())
  -- emit to a logging pipeline, not stdout in prod\end

Sanitization rules (enforce with automated pipeline):

- Remove fields: user_email, full_name, ssn, credit_card, device_id when present.
- Hash or salt identifiers: customer_id -> sha256(customer_id + capture_salt). Store salt in KMS.
- Prompt shortening: truncate prompts > 10k chars to first/last 1k with a hash placeholder for the middle.
- Skip binary attachments entirely (log metadata only).

Example sanitization command (jq + openssl):

cat raw_capture.jsonl | jq '.request.body |= (.prompt |= (if length > 10000 then (.[0:1000] + "\n...<TRUNCATED>...\n" + .[-1000:]) else . end) | del(.user_email, .ssn))' \
  | openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pass pass:$SANITIZE_KEY > sanitized.jsonl.enc

Metadata enrichment

Before replay, add fields that help determinism and observability:

- replay_id: uuid4
- original_timestamp_utc
- route_hint (e.g., text-generation v.s. embeddings)
- model_pin (if the capture included a model alias)
- intended_sampling_mode (sync|stream|function_call)

Replay harness patterns

Supported harness targets: local SDK (Python/TS), staging HTTP endpoint, canary-serving runtime.

Core replay modes:

1. Synchronous request-by-request: replay each captured request and persist the result. Useful for correctness and output diffs.
2. Concurrency-preserving replay: preserve timestamps and inter-request arrival spacing to exercise batching and runtime scheduling. Use for performance regressions.
3. Batched trace replay: replay only requests that hit specific code paths (e.g., long-prompt cache misses).

Python replay harness (simplified):

# replay_harness.py (pseudocode)
import json, requests, time, uuid
with open('sanitized.jsonl') as f:
    for line in f:
        rec = json.loads(line)
        rec['replay_id'] = str(uuid.uuid4())
        headers = { 'X-Replay-ID': rec['replay_id'], 'X-Original-Ts': rec['original_timestamp_utc'] }
        resp = requests.post(STAGING_URL + rec['route'], json=rec['request'], headers=headers, timeout=30)
        save_result(rec['replay_id'], resp.status_code, resp.text)
        time.sleep(adjust_interarrival(rec))

SDK integration patterns

- Hook points: provide an X-Replay-ID header and ensure SDKs propagate this to tracing and metrics.
- Deterministic seeds: when the SDK exposes sampling or soft-rng features, allow setting a replay seed from replay_id to reduce nondeterminism in comparisons.
- Output normalization: SDKs should offer a normalize_output() helper to remove metadata such as timestamps, non-deterministic ids, and token boundary differences prior to diffing.

Observability and diffs

Compare the following telemetry between original-capture-derived expectations and replay outputs:

- Latency P50/P95/P99 (ms)
- Token usage distribution (input_tokens, output_tokens)
- Error taxonomy (HTTP 4xx, 5xx, SDK exceptions, model-timeouts)
- Output similarity score (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-cosine) where applicable

Example diff command (jq + python):

python tools/diff_outputs.py --expected expected_results.jsonl --actual replay_results.jsonl --metrics latency,token_counts,similarity --out diffs/summary.json

Safety, rollout and data governance

- Captured datasets are to be stored in a restricted bucket with lifecycle 90 days then auto-delete unless flagged for retention.
- All datasets must be tracked in the internal capture registry (include name, sample rate, captain, purpose, retention).
- For customer-sensitive captures require explicit legal approval; label those captures in the registry and limit replay to isolated air-gapped environments.

Operational checklist (before you start)

1. Confirm approvals and sampling rate recorded in capture registry.
2. Verify KMS key for salt hashing is accessible and audited.
3. Reserve replay environment with sufficient tokens/quota and model pins.
4. Run a small sanity replay (10 requests) to validate harness and normalize functions.

Post-replay triage workflow

1. Open an investigation ticket with replay_id, sample inputs, and failing response slices.
2. Attach diffs and telemetry reports.
3. If regressions are observed, run targeted replays focusing on affected route/model pins.
4. For SDK regressions: bisect across SDK versions with the same corpus.

Appendix: example capture record (sanitized, single-line JSONL)

{"replay_id": "<filled-at-enrich>", "original_timestamp_utc": "2025-03-05T14:22:11Z", "route": "/v1/generate", "request": {"prompt": "The quick brown fox...<TRUNCATED>", "max_tokens": 256}, "customer_hash": "sha256:abcd..." }

Appendix: portability matrix (recommended replay target by investigation goal)

| Goal | Target | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| Output correctness | Local SDK (pinned) | Fast iteration, low cost |
| Performance regression | Staging runtime with same hardware profile | Preserve batching and kernels |
| Production-only scheduling bugs | Canary-serving pool | Must be isolated and monitored |

Ownership and contacts

- Playbook author: Evan Morales (engineering)
- Runbook owner: Observability team (platform.eng@redwood.example.com)
- Security contact: Rina Kapoor (security@redwood.example.com)

Change log

- 2025-03-12: Created initial draft.
- 2025-06-18: Added deterministic seed guidance and replay_id standardization.
- 2025-09-01: Hardened sanitization rules and added lifecycle/retention guidance.

Links and references

- See Security & Compliance: capture-approval-process for approval workflow.
- See eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/replay-harnesses for sample harnesses and perf tooling.
- Tools: tools/diff_outputs.py, tools/normalize_output.py (internal repo)

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes recommended patterns for local SDK caching, lightweight stub servers, and graceful degradation when the Redwood runtime or network is unavailable. It covers: developer-local workflows, SDK configuration recipes, canonical API examples, telemetry expectations, and a short incident / support playbook for common failures. The goal is to make offline development reliable, make error modes deterministic for QA, and reduce support churn from transient runtime outages.

When to use this playbook

- Building local prototyping sandboxes where calling hosted inference is slow or costly.
- Enabling reliable CI for prompt-driven tests without hitting production endpoints.
- Implementing client-side fallbacks for consumer apps that must remain partially functional during runtime incidents.

Motivation and constraints

- Developer velocity: enable fast local iteration without paying tokens or waiting on remote cold-starts.
- Determinism for tests: replayable responses and deterministic stubs improve eval reliability.
- Safety: cached responses should be labeled and quality-monitored to avoid leaking stale outputs in production.

Service names and components referenced

- redwood-sdk: the official client library (node/py/go)
- runtime-proxy: the local dev proxy used to route requests to stubs or the real API
- dev-sandbox: internal template repo for running the local stack (docker-compose/k8s manifests)
- telemetry-orch: ingestion pipeline for SDK telemetry including cache-hit metrics and stub usage

High-level patterns

1) Local-Cache-as-Primary (for dev)
- SDK consults a local cache first (LRU/TTL-based).
- If cache miss, SDK records the request to a local "capture log" and then either: (a) forward to runtime in debug mode, or (b) return a synthetic placeholder.
- Use for: rapid iteration, offline demos.

2) Stub-Server with Replay Mode (for CI)
- A small HTTP stub implements the Redwood API surface required by the app.
- Stub seeded with golden responses (JSON) and a deterministic matching algorithm (exact prompt key + normalized params).
- Use for: CI acceptance tests, performance smoke tests without production cost.

3) Graceful-degradation policy (for production clients)
- Control via SDK config: on_failure = [retry, use_cache, degrade_to_default] with per-endpoint policy.
- Fallback tiers: local-cache -> lightweight-model-variant -> default-static-message.
- Use for: user-facing features that must never block user flows.

Configuration reference (SDK examples)

NodeJS sample (redwood-sdk config snippet)

```js
const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk');
const client = new Redwood({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY,
  dev: {
    localCache: { path: './.redwood/cache.json', ttlSeconds: 3600 },
    stubServer: { url: 'http://localhost:19527' },
    gracefulDegrade: {
      defaultAction: 'use_cache',
      retry: { attempts: 2, backoffMs: 200 },
    }
  }
});

await client.generate({ model: 'rw-medium-v1', prompt: 'Summarize the doc' });
```

Python sample (redwood_sdk config)

```py
from redwood_sdk import Redwood
client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), dev={
    'local_cache': {'path': '.redwood/cache.json', 'ttl_seconds': 600},
    'stub_server': {'url': 'http://localhost:19527'},
    'graceful_degrade': {'default_action': 'use_cache', 'retry': {'attempts': 1, 'backoff_ms': 300}}
})
response = client.chat.create(model='rw-medium-v1', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'Hello'}])
```

Canonical stub-server behavior

- API: Accepts the same REST endpoints as hosted API (POST /v1/generate, /v1/chat, /v1/embeddings).
- Response matching: normalizes inputs (strip timestamps, normalize whitespace, canonicalize numeric seeds) then performs exact or prefix matching.
- Fallthrough: if no match, stub returns HTTP 404 with a clear body showing the captured request id and a CLI hint to seed the data.

Seeding stubs for CI

1) Capture mode: run the app against production or dev runtime with SDK dev.capture = true to record request/response pairs to ./test-fixtures/seed.json.
2) Review and redact sensitive fields (PII, private data) using the seed-redact utility: `dev-sandbox/bin/seed-redact ./test-fixtures/seed.json`
3) Commit fixtures to repo and use the stub image that mounts fixtures at /app/fixtures.json.

Example captured entry (fixture)

```json
{
  "id": "fixture-20260111-001",
  "endpoint": "/v1/chat",
  "request": {"messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Explain event sourcing"}], "max_tokens": 200},
  "response": {"choices": [{"message": {"role":"assistant","content":"Event sourcing stores state changes as a sequence of events..."}}], "meta": {"model":"rw-medium-v1","latency_ms":123}}
}
```

Operational guidance and SLOs

- dev-sandbox templates: owner eng-developer-experience team (team wiki link in references).
- Cache TTL recommendation: 600s for interactive dev, 3600s for offline demos.
- Production-only: SDK must never return cached model outputs to end-users unless the app explicitly allows it and audit-flagging is enabled. Default: cache-only-for-local.
- Telemetry metrics to emit: sdk.cache.hit, sdk.cache.miss, sdk.stub.request, sdk.stub.miss, sdk.degrade.invocations.
- Alerting thresholds (telemetry-orch): raise when sdk.degrade.invocations > 5% of requests over 10m or stub.miss > 1% of CI runs.

Runbook: common support issues and canonical fixes

1) Symptom: local cache never hits
- Check: correct cache file path and permissions; ensure request normalization key matches (strip session IDs).
- Fix: run `node tools/debug-cache-key.js --sample` to inspect key extraction. Regenerate cache with `REDWOOD_DEV_CAPTURE=1 node ./scripts/capture.js`.

2) Symptom: stub server returns 404 on CI
- Check: fixtures bundle was mounted and the fixture keys match the normalized request. Verify CI uses the correct stub image tag.
- Fix: re-seed fixtures from a reproducible run, run `./dev-sandbox/bin/seed-validate /app/fixtures.json`.

3) Symptom: app shows stale cached outputs in production
- Check: ensure SDK is not running in dev mode (REDWOOD_ENV must be 'prod'), verify cache policy.
- Fix: rotate cache storage, invalidate entries with `redwood-cli cache invalidate --all` and ensure telemetry flagged the incident.

Testing guidance

- Unit tests: mock the SDK transport layer and verify fallback order (retry -> cache -> stub -> default).
- Integration tests: run against stubbed dev-sandbox using `make ci-stub` to ensure deterministic runs.
- Golden regression: include a small set of prompt-based golden responses in PRs; run `tools/compare-golden --update` for intentional updates.

Docs site and snippet hygiene

- Snippets: always use `<!--redwood-snippet:example-id-->` in docs to enable automated snippet validation. The docs-site will run the snippet through the local stub server in the preview pipeline.
- Canonical fixes: when a snippet fails due to API drift, update the fixture then triage under `devx/snippet-failures` with a tag `snippet-fix`.

Telemetry and privacy notes

- Captured fixtures must be reviewed and redacted before committing: remove PII, customer IDs, and long personal text. Use `dev-sandbox/bin/seed-redact` which applies a standard redaction policy.
- Telemetry events that include sampled prompt hashes (sha256) are acceptable for diagnostics, but never store raw prompt text in centralized logs by default.

Rollout and ownership

- Owner: eng-developer-experience (primary), eng-sre (secondary for telemetry/alerting).
- Rollout steps: 1) publish dev-sandbox templates and sample app; 2) add snippet validation to docs-site preview; 3) enable telemetry metrics for cache/stub usage; 4) run team-wide training and update runbooks.

FAQ

Q: Can cached outputs be used in user-facing production flows?
A: No — not by default. The SDK config explicitly separates dev cache from production cache and requires an explicit opt-in flag plus audit-trace to allow any cached outputs to be surfaced to users.

Q: How do we keep fixtures small and maintainable?
A: Seed minimal representative responses, prefer short completions, and compress fixtures with `tools/fixture-compress` in CI.

References and related pages

- dev-sandbox repo: (internal link) /repos/dev-sandbox
- SDK config reference: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides/client-resilience-and-zero-touch-sdk-onboarding-2026
- Snippet validation pipeline: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/docs-site-content-staging-and-canary-publishing-2026

Change log

- 2025-11-05: Initial draft (Claire Mendoza)
- 2026-01-09: Added telemetry thresholds and CI seeding flow (Aisha Khan)
- 2026-02-14: Finalized runbook and redaction instructions (Miguel Santos)

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines recommended SDK design patterns for tenant-scoped authentication and robust local fallbacks. Its goal is to reduce support incidents and production outages in multi-tenant applications that call Redwood inference endpoints. The guidance is written for SDK implementers (client libraries and server-side helper libs) and for developer-facing code patterns used by product teams.

Intended audience:
- SDK engineers implementing Redwood client libraries
- Platform engineers integrating tenant-aware routing
- Support engineers troubleshooting tenant-impacted incidents

Why this matters
- Multi-tenant workloads commonly fail in two categories: auth/identity mispropagation and global rate-limit storms.
- Proper tenant-scoped tokens, local caches, and graceful fallbacks prevent noisy neighbor effects and provide predictable user experience when upstream capacity is constrained.

Key responsibilities
- SDK: perform tenant identity propagation, token refresh, bounded local caching, and deterministic fallback behavior.
- App: supply tenant context and define fallback UX.
- Platform: expose per-tenant rate quota headers and circuit-breaker metadata.

Recommended patterns (summary)
1) Tenant context must be explicit and immutable per request
- Each API call requires either a tenant_id header or a tenant-scoped API key. Do not rely on global process state.
2) Token lifecycle and refresh
- SDKs should implement background refresh with jittered scheduling and a single-flight refresh per tenant.
3) Local prefix caching for short prompts and embeddings
- Cache recent request/response pairs keyed by (tenant_id, prompt_hash, model, max_tokens). Keep TTL <= 5 minutes by default.
4) Rate-limit and quota-aware backoff
- Honor 429s + Retry-After header and implement exponential backoff with capped jitter.
5) Graceful degradation modes
- Define fast-fail, cached-response, degrade-to-embedding, and queued-retry strategies.

Detailed patterns and examples

1) Explicit tenant propagation
- Enforcement: SDK constructors should require a tenant context provider or explicit tenant_id for each call. Example signatures:
  - Node: client.generate({ tenantId, input, model })
  - Python: client.generate(tenant_id=..., prompt=..., model=...)

- Rationale: implicit global state leads to cross-tenant leaks and hard-to-reproduce bugs.

2) Single-flight token refresh (pseudo-code)
- Behaviour: when access token is expired or near expiry (<30s), allow only one inflight refresh operation per tenant to avoid stampeding.

Pseudo-code (Python style):
```
# per-tenant cached state
if token.near_expiry():
    await tenant_refresh_lock.wait_or_run(refresh_function)
# proceed with the fresh token
```

3) Local prefix / KV caching (config table)
- Default config values to start with (tunable):
| Key | Default | Notes |
| cache_ttl_seconds | 300 | Keep short to reduce staleness for dynamic prompts |
| cache_max_entries_per_tenant | 200 | Prevent unbounded memory growth |
| cache_key_components | tenant_id,prompt_hash,model,max_tokens | Ensures tenant isolation |

Example Node snippet (pseudo):
```
const key = `${tenantId}:${hash(prompt)}:${model}:${maxTokens}`;
const cached = cache.get(key);
if (cached) return cached;
const res = await client.call({tenantId, prompt, model});
cache.set(key, res, {ttl: config.cache_ttl_seconds});
return res;
```

4) Rate-limit handling and backoff strategy
- Behavior table:
| Response | SDK action | User-visible outcome |
| 429 + Retry-After | Respect header, jittered sleep, retry up to 3 times | May delay completion; falls back to cached response if available |
| 503 / 504 | Apply exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 3 retries | Consider degrade-to-embedding strategy |
| Network error | Circuit-breaker increment and local short-circuit if threshold exceeded | Fast-fail mode after repeated failures |

Backoff algorithm (recommended parameters):
- base_delay_ms = 200
- max_delay_ms = 5000
- factor = 2.0
- jitter_fraction = 0.2
- max_retries = 3

5) Degradation strategies (choose one per codepath)
- Fast-fail: return a deterministic error to the caller immediately (use for synchronous user-facing flows).
- Cached-response: return last-known-good response if cached and TTL valid.
- Degrade-to-embedding: for long-form generation failures, fallback to shorter embedding-based retrieval + template reply.
- Queue-and-retry: push to durable work queue for eventual processing (async jobs).

Operational observability (what SDKs MUST emit)
- Telemetry events (logged + metric tags):
  - request.start (tags: tenant_id, model, route)
  - request.retry (tags: reason=rate_limit|network|gateway)
  - request.cached_hit (tags: tenant_id, cache_key)
  - token.refresh (tags: tenant_id, result=success|failure)
  - circuit.opened / circuit.closed (tags: tenant_id, route)
- Metrics to expose (per-tenant rollup):
  - requests_total, requests_success, requests_429, requests_503, cached_hits, token_refresh_failures, circuit_breaker_open_count
- Log context: always include tenant_id, request_id, and trace_id.

Support runbook - triage steps (for SRE / support)
1) Identify impacted tenants via logs and metrics (dashboard: SDK -> requests_429 by tenant).
2) Gather single example request: tenant_id, request_id, timestamp, model, SDK version.
3) Check token status: was a refresh attempted? (token.refresh events).
4) Check upstream headers: Retry-After, x-redwood-quota-remaining, x-redwood-tenant-quota.
5) If a tenant shows persistent 429s and no quota header: escalate to Platform with tenant config snapshot.
6) If circuit-breaker open: check SDK local metrics to confirm per-tenant threshold.

Example diagnostic CLI snippets
- Query logs (internal ELK):
```
# find all 429s for tenant abc-123 in last hour
kql: tenant_id:"abc-123" and http_status:429 and @timestamp:[now-1h TO now]
```
- Inspect SDK debug output (recommended env var):
  - REDWOOD_SDK_LOG=debug
  - REDWOOD_SDK_CACHE_DUMP=true

Compatibility and versioning notes
- New SDKs must be backward compatible for token metadata headers: the platform will accept both legacy header X-Redwood-Tenant and new header X-RW-TenantId for a transition period of 12 months.
- Feature gates: local-cache and degrade-to-embedding are opt-in per-major SDK (default off for 1.0.0 releases).

Example policy for product teams (short checklist)
1) Confirm tenant identity is explicit at call site.
2) Choose a degradation strategy appropriate for the UX (fast-fail for transactional, queue for background jobs).
3) Ensure SDK telemetry is enabled in staging and production.
4) Validate with synthetic load test: run 1k QPS multi-tenant traffic and observe per-tenant quota isolation.

Appendix A: Sample SDK config YAML
```
sdk:
  cache_ttl_seconds: 300
  cache_entries_per_tenant: 200
  backoff:
    base_delay_ms: 200
    max_delay_ms: 5000
    factor: 2.0
    jitter_fraction: 0.2
    max_retries: 3
  token:
    refresh_margin_seconds: 30
    single_flight: true
  telemetry:
    enabled: true
    log_level: INFO
```

Appendix B: Common support tickets and canonical fixes
- Symptom: Sporadic 401s for one tenant only
  - Cause: token refresh race, stale tenant-scoped API key in app config
  - Fix: Validate the app rotates tenant-scoped keys on deploy; enable single-flight refresh in SDK.
- Symptom: Sudden increase in 429s across tenants
  - Cause: platform-wide quota misconfiguration or routing degradation
  - Fix: Open platform incident, switch affected customers to reduced throughput plan, enable queued processing.

References and related docs
- SDK telemetry contract: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/sdk-telemetry-contract-stability-playbook-2026
- Rate-limit etiquette and headers: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/rate-limit-and-quota-spec
- Multi-tenant security checklist: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/multi-tenant-auth-checklist

Owner and maintenance
- Doc owner: Priya Natarajan (sdk-platform team)
- Review cadence: yearly or when SDK major version changes
- Contributors: Marco Silva (devx), Aisha Thompson (platform)

Feedback and changes
- To propose changes, create a PR against the docs repo and add reviewers listed above. For urgent corrections (bug in recommended behavior) tag @oncall-sdks in Slack and file a short changelog entry in the SDK release notes."

payload.page_title: Streaming event model conventions (canonical for SDK + docs examples)

sections.body:
This page defines the canonical *example-level* streaming event model used across Redwood docs, quickstarts, and SDK READMEs.

**Goals**
- Provide a single mental model for streaming across Python/TypeScript/Go.
- Make copy/paste examples robust to real-world issues (partial deltas, tool-call argument fragmentation, disconnects).
- Standardize naming and logging so support and Solutions Engineering can quickly interpret customer logs.

**Non-goals**
- This is not a product-level protocol redesign.
- This does not introduce new SDK APIs; it documents how examples should consume the events that already exist.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- **Stream**: A sequence of events emitted by the server for a single request.
- **Event**: A typed envelope with metadata plus a payload (delta/final/error).
- **Delta**: Partial data emitted incrementally (e.g., assistant text tokens, partial tool args).
- **Final**: A terminal representation for a logical unit (e.g., a completed message, completed tool call), or the end-of-stream marker.
- **Transcript**: The assembled conversation messages (user, assistant, tool, etc.) that the client maintains.

---
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body: Examples must treat events as an envelope with at least: `type`, `request_id`, and a type-specific payload.
sections.heading: Canonical event types (examples MUST use these names)

sections.body:
| Event type | When it appears | What examples do | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `response.started` | First event for a stream | Initialize per-request state, record start time | Always expected for healthy streams |
| `message.delta` | Assistant is producing text (or other message content) | Append delta to the current assistant message buffer | Deltas may be empty or may arrive in bursts |
| `tool_call.delta` | Model is emitting tool call(s) with partial arguments | Accumulate tool call args as raw text; do not parse until final | Partial args are expected; must handle fragmentation |
| `tool_call.final` | A tool call is complete (name + args complete) | Validate + parse arguments; enqueue tool execution | Parsing should happen here, not on delta |
| `message.final` | Assistant message is complete | Freeze the assistant message, add to transcript | May arrive with or without prior `message.delta` |
| `response.completed` | Normal end-of-stream | Emit final assembled result; stop loop | The only “success terminal” event |
| `response.error` | Non-retryable failure (request rejected, validation error, etc.) | Surface error, stop loop, log structured error details | May appear after `response.started` |
| `response.interrupted` | Stream ended prematurely (disconnect, timeout, cancellation) | Trigger retry policy (if applicable) or fail with guidance | Examples should distinguish this from `response.error` |

**Important:** SDKs may internally expose slightly different shapes, but examples and docs must map to these canonical types for explanation, comments, and logging.

---
sections.heading: Event type table

sections.body: Examples should assume the following fields are available (or can be derived).
sections.heading: Envelope and required fields (for examples + logging)

sections.body:
- `type`: canonical event type string
- `request_id`: stable identifier for the request (used for support correlation)
- `event_id`: monotonically increasing per stream if provided; otherwise maintain a local counter
- `model`: the model identifier used for the request (when available)
- `created_at`: server timestamp if available; otherwise local receive time
sections.heading: Required fields to log

sections.body:
- `attempt`: retry attempt number (client-side)
- `stream_id`: if the backend provides a stream-level id distinct from request id
- `usage`: token usage summaries (often only present on final/completed)
- `warnings`: server-provided warnings (e.g., degraded mode, fallback model)

---
sections.heading: Optional (recommended) fields

sections.body: Examples MUST assemble assistant content in a predictable way.
sections.heading: Message assembly rules (assistant text)

sections.body:
- `current_assistant_text` (string builder)
- `current_tool_calls` (map keyed by `tool_call_id` to a tool-call accumulator)
- `transcript_messages` (list of messages to show in examples)
sections.heading: Maintain these per-request variables

sections.body:
1) On `response.started`:
   - Reset all per-request accumulators.
   - Log: `stream_start` with `request_id`, `model`, `attempt=0`.

2) On `message.delta`:
   - Append `delta.text` to `current_assistant_text`.
   - Print streaming output in examples only if it improves clarity (see “Logging guidance”).

3) On `message.final`:
   - If `final.text` exists, set `current_assistant_text = final.text` (final wins over delta accumulation).
   - Append an assistant message to `transcript_messages`:
     - `role = "assistant"`
     - `content = current_assistant_text`
     - If tool calls exist, attach them as part of the assistant message context as appropriate for the SDK.
   - Clear `current_assistant_text` (so a subsequent assistant message starts fresh).

4) On `response.completed`:
   - Stop consumption.
   - Return the finalized transcript and any usage details.
sections.heading: Assembly algorithm

sections.body:
- **Always prefer the final** as the canonical message content.
- Deltas are for streaming UX and intermediate logging only.
sections.heading: If both deltas and a final are present

sections.body:
Some models/configurations may produce only `message.final` without deltas. Examples must still work.

---
sections.heading: Handling “no delta” streams

sections.body: Tool call arguments may be streamed as fragments; examples must handle **partial JSON** safely.
sections.heading: Tool calling assembly rules (partial args + finalization)

sections.body:
Track per `tool_call_id`:
- `name` (string, may arrive early or late)
- `args_text` (string builder of raw argument text)
- `is_final` (bool)
sections.heading: Tool call accumulator

sections.body:
1) On `tool_call.delta`:
   - Identify `tool_call_id`.
   - If `name` is present, set it.
   - Append `delta.args_fragment` to `args_text`.
   - **Do not parse JSON here.**

2) On `tool_call.final`:
   - Mark the tool call `is_final=true`.
   - Parse `args_text` as JSON.
   - Validate against the tool’s argument schema (or minimal required fields if no schema is available in the snippet).
   - If parsing/validation fails:
     - Log `tool_args_invalid` (include `tool_call_id`, tool name, and a truncated args preview).
     - Follow the example’s documented fallback (see “Error handling and fallbacks”).
sections.heading: Assembly algorithm

sections.body:
- Partial tool args are normal; they may be split across many events.
- Never assume a delta ends on a JSON boundary.
- Never run a tool until `tool_call.final` is received.
sections.heading: Partial-arguments guidance (must be explicitly called out in examples)

sections.body:
- Accumulate each tool call independently.
- On each `tool_call.final`, enqueue tool execution.
- Examples may run tools in parallel *only if the language supports it ergonomically*; otherwise run sequentially but preserve ordering in logs.
sections.heading: When multiple tools are requested

sections.body:
After a tool is executed, examples should add a tool-result message into the transcript before requesting the model to continue:
- `role = "tool"`
- `tool_call_id = <id>`
- `name = <tool name>` (if required by the SDK)
- `content = <string result>` (JSON-stringified if structured)

---
sections.heading: Tool result messages

sections.body: Structured output is frequently requested alongside streaming, but incremental JSON is fragile.
sections.heading: Structured output / JSON schema notes (streaming-safe)

sections.body:
- If you need reliable JSON validation: **prefer non-streaming** for the structured-output request, or stream but only parse at `message.final`.
- If streaming UI is required: stream deltas to the console, but validate only once the final message is received.
sections.heading: Canonical guidance for examples

sections.body:
At `message.final`:
1) Extract the candidate JSON string.
2) Parse JSON with a strict parser.
3) Validate against the schema.
4) If invalid: apply the fallback (see below).

---
sections.heading: Minimal safe parsing approach (examples)

sections.body: Examples must distinguish between **terminal errors** and **interruptions** that may be retried.
sections.heading: Error events, interruption, and retry conventions

sections.body:
- Request validation error (bad tool schema, invalid parameters)
- Authentication/authorization failure
- Model not available / unsupported features for that model
sections.heading: Typical causes

sections.body:
- Stop the stream consumer.
- Raise/return a clear error.
- Log `request_failed` with:
  - `request_id`, `type=response.error`, `status_code` (if present), `error_code`, `message`.
sections.heading: Example behavior

sections.body:
- Client network disconnect
- Idle timeout
- Server-side transient disconnect
sections.heading: Typical causes

sections.body:
- Stop the stream consumer.
- If safe to retry, retry with backoff.
sections.heading: Example behavior

sections.body:
Examples should implement a small, deterministic policy:
- Max attempts: **2 retries** (total attempts = 3)
- Backoff: exponential with jitter (e.g., 250ms, 500ms)
- Retry only if:
  - The request is idempotent for the given example, AND
  - The failure is an interruption/transient network error, AND
  - The tool side effects are safe (see below)
sections.heading: Retry rules used in examples

sections.body:
If the example executes tools with side effects (e.g., “send_email”, “create_ticket”):
- The example MUST either:
  - Use an idempotency key passed into the tool, OR
  - Disable auto-retry after tool execution begins, OR
  - Use a “dry_run” tool variant in the example.
sections.heading: Idempotency + side effects

sections.body:
- Before running any side-effecting tool, generate `idempotency_key = <request_id>:<tool_call_id>`.

---
sections.heading: Recommended convention for examples

sections.body: Examples should print enough to be educational *without* dumping sensitive payloads by default.
sections.heading: Logging guidance (examples and supportability)

sections.body:
Examples (and golden tests) should log the following events in a consistent shape:
- `stream_start`: `{request_id, model, attempt}`
- `stream_event`: `{request_id, attempt, type, event_id}` (only when running in debug)
- `tool_call_started`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name}`
- `tool_call_finalized`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name, args_bytes}`
- `tool_result_ready`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name, result_bytes}`
- `stream_completed`: `{request_id, attempt, duration_ms}`
- `stream_interrupted`: `{request_id, attempt, reason}`
- `request_failed`: `{request_id, attempt, error_code, status_code}`
sections.heading: Required log points (canonical keys)

sections.body:
- Never log raw authorization headers or API keys.
- Tool arguments: log a **truncated preview** (e.g., first 200 chars) only in debug mode.
- Structured output: log validation failures with a short reason + pointer to schema, not the full payload.
sections.heading: Redaction rules

sections.body:
- `REDWOOD_DEBUG_STREAM=1` enables per-event logs.

---
sections.heading: Examples should accept an env var or flag

sections.body:
When examples are backed by “golden transcript” fixtures, they must:
- Assert a stable sequence of canonical event types (not raw provider-specific fields).
- Verify the **final assembled assistant message** text and tool-call arguments after `tool_call.final`.
- Include at least one fixture with:
  - fragmented tool args across multiple `tool_call.delta` events
  - an interruption and a successful retry
sections.heading: Golden test / fixture conventions (cross-language parity)

sections.body:
- `streaming_text_only.<lang>.jsonl`
- `streaming_tool_call_fragmented_args.<lang>.jsonl`
- `streaming_interrupted_then_retry.<lang>.jsonl`

---
sections.heading: Recommended fixture naming

sections.body: These are not copy/paste SDK code; they represent the required control flow.
sections.heading: Example snippets: reference pseudocode

sections.body:
1. `start = now()`
2. `attempt = 0`
3. `while attempt <= 2:`
   - create stream
   - for each event:
     - switch on `event.type`
     - apply assembly rules
     - on `response.completed`: return
     - on `response.error`: raise
     - on `response.interrupted`: break and retry
   - `attempt += 1`
   - sleep(backoff(attempt))
4. raise “stream interrupted after retries”
sections.heading: Streaming consumer loop (canonical)

sections.body:
- Consume stream until you have one or more `tool_call.final`.
- Execute tools.
- Append tool-result messages.
- Send a follow-up request (may be streaming) to allow the model to incorporate tool results.

---
sections.heading: Tool calling loop (canonical)

sections.body:
**Pitfall: Tool-call args look truncated mid-stream.**
- Expected behavior: args are fragmented across deltas.
- Fix: accumulate raw args text; parse only at `tool_call.final`.

**Pitfall: JSON parsing fails during streaming.**
- Expected behavior: incremental JSON is often invalid until complete.
- Fix: parse only at `message.final`; validate; retry with a stricter instruction if needed.

**Pitfall: Customers retry and accidentally double-execute a tool.**
- Fix: idempotency keys or disable retries after side-effecting tool execution begins.

**Pitfall: Mixing provider-specific event names in docs.**
- Fix: always present the canonical event types on this page; add a brief mapping note elsewhere if needed.

---
sections.heading: FAQ / common pitfalls (what examples must proactively address)

sections.body:
- Owner: DevEx (SDK parity)
- Any change to canonical event names must be reviewed by:
  - SDK parity tech lead (Ibrahim Khan)
  - API/SDK semantics reviewer (Brian Murphy)
  - Docs owner for Hosted API (Wei Chen)
- If a change impacts fixture formats, update all language fixtures in the same PR set.
