payload.page_title: SDK developer sandbox isolation and tenant patterns

sections.body:
Overview

This guide documents recommended patterns for creating developer sandboxes and local test environments for Redwood SDK consumers who need multi-tenant isolation, reproducible telemetry, and lightweight cost controls. It targets SDK engineers, platform integrators, and developer advocates who maintain example apps, starter repos, and internal sandbox fleet.

Goals

- Provide clear levels of isolation (read-only fixtures, per-developer API keys, ephemeral tenant sandboxes).
- Ensure telemetry continuity: consistent tags, sampling rules, and synthetic workloads so local dev activity maps to product analytics without inflating production metrics.
- Minimize cost and capacity impact by enforcing quotas, request shaping, and local mocking.
- Offer downloadable templates and scripts for ephemeral sandboxes (Docker, docker-compose, k3d) and examples for CI usage.

Isolation levels (recommended matrix)

1) Fixture Mode (low isolation)
- Purpose: fastest onboarding for new developers and demos. Uses shared demo tenant and sanitized datasets.
- Characteristics: single read-only API key, no persistent writes, limited rate (10 r/s).
- Use when: onboarding workshops, docs examples, quickstarts.

2) Scoped Dev Key (medium isolation)
- Purpose: per-developer API keys scoped to a sandbox tenant. Supports read/write, but live writes are proxied to ephemeral datasets.
- Characteristics: keys expire (7–30 days), quota 1000 requests/day, telemetry includes developer_id tag.
- Use when: feature development and local validation against the real routing/serving stack.

3) Ephemeral Tenant (high isolation)
- Purpose: fully isolated tenant with dedicated mini-resources, used for integration testing and pre-prod validation.
- Characteristics: tenant provisioned on demand (k8s namespace or dedicated VPC subnet), KV cache cleared between runs, quotas enforced at infra layer, budget guardrails.
- Use when: integration tests, customer demo environments, A/B testing validation.

Quickstart: Scoped Dev Key sandbox (CLI + docker-compose)\nPrereqs:
- Docker and docker-compose installed
- Redwood CLI (rwd) v0.9+ configured with org-level credentials
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Create ephemeral API key (scoped):
- Command: rwd keys create --scope sandbox --expires 14d --tags "dev-sandbox"
- Save the returned key to ~/.rwd/sandbox-keys/<your-name>.json

2) Clone the starter repo and start the local proxy:
- git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/dev-sandboxes.git
- cd dev-sandboxes/scoped-dev-key
- docker-compose up --build -d

3) Configure local SDK to use the key and proxy:
- Export env vars: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=$(jq -r .key ~/.rwd/sandbox-keys/<your-name>.json)
- Point SDK to local proxy: export REDWOOD_API_BASE=http://localhost:8080/v1

4) Run a smoke test (example cURL):
- curl -X POST $REDWOOD_API_BASE/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -d '{"model":"redwood-small-2025","prompt":"Hello sandbox"}'

Telemetry and tagging conventions

Consistent telemetry is essential so that local sandbox traffic can be filtered or aggregated without affecting production. Use the following required tags for all sandbox traffic:
- env:sandbox
- sandbox.owner:<username>
- sandbox.mode:fixture|scoped|ephemeral
- repo:dev-sandboxes
- ci_job_id (when running from CI)
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- Apply a default sampling rate of 5% for sandbox generation calls longer than 1s.
- Always forward error traces at 100% for triage.
- Route sandbox traces and logs to a separate index in observability to avoid ingestion cost mixing.

Template snippets

Example docker-compose snippet (as plain-text example to paste into repo):
- version: '3.8'
  services:
    rwd-proxy:
      image: redwood/rwd-proxy:stable
      ports:
        - "8080:8080"
      environment:
        - REDWOOD_API_KEY_FILE=/secrets/sandbox-key.json
      volumes:
        - ./secrets:/secrets:ro

Example small script to provision ephemeral tenant (pseudocode CLI):
- #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -e
  TENANT_NAME=dev-$USER-$(date +%s)
  rwd tenants create --name $TENANT_NAME --quota "monthly_tokens=50000" --labels "sandbox.owner=$USER"
  rwd keys create --tenant $TENANT_NAME --expires 3d --output ./secrets/sandbox-key.json
  echo "Provisioned $TENANT_NAME and key at ./secrets/sandbox-key.json"

Cost controls and guardrails

- Default quotas for sandboxes: 50k tokens/month per ephemeral tenant, 5k tokens/day per scoped key.
- Budget webhook: if a tenant spends >80% of token budget in a 24h window, send notification to #sandbox-costs and auto-suspend generation for that tenant until reviewed.
- Chargeback: for long-lived demo tenants or customer-facing sandboxes, require explicit approval from product finance to exceed baseline quotas.

Operating runbook (for platform engineers)

1) Detect noisy sandbox behavior:
- Query observability index for env:sandbox and tokens_per_minute > 500 for any sandbox.owner.
- If noisy, throttle at the ingress proxy and notify owner via email and Slack.

2) Recover an ephemeral tenant after a failing test:
- rwd tenants snapshot --tenant <tenant> --since -1h --output /tmp/last-snapshot.json
- rwd tenants restore --tenant <tenant> --from /tmp/last-snapshot.json
- If snapshot not available, reprovision tenant and replay CI fixtures.

3) Rotate stale keys automatically:
- Keys older than 30 days: mark for rotation and notify owner.
- Automatic rotation pipeline will create new key, update secrets in the sandbox repo (if CI-backed), and revoke the old key after owner ack.

Security considerations

- Never use production admin keys in sandbox repos. Gate the rwd CLI production config behind MFA and team-specific RBAC.
- Encrypt sandbox secrets at rest (KMS) and avoid committing keys in git. Use ephemeral secrets in CI (e.g., HashiCorp Vault or cloud secret manager).

Troubleshooting checklist (common issues)

- Error: 401 Unauthorized from proxy
  - Verify REDWOOD_API_KEY file exists and is valid.
  - Confirm token hasn’t expired (rwd keys list --filter owner:$USER).

- Symptom: Local runs are invisibly inflating product metrics
  - Check telemetry tags; ensure env:sandbox is present. Verify sampling policy.

- Symptom: High latency in sandbox but not in staging
  - Confirm proxy is in pass-through mode vs. local mock. Check local CPU/GPU availability (docker stats).

Ownership and contacts

- Owner: Developer Experience (internal team alias: devx@redwood.ai)
- Oncall for sandbox infra: eng-platform oncall (rotation schedule in /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks)
- Billing escalation: finance-legal@sales.redwood.ai

Examples and templates repo

All starter repositories, scripts, and CI workflows are stored in the internal org repo: github.com/redwood-inference/internal-samples/dev-sandboxes. The repo contains:
- scoped-dev-key starter (docker-compose)
- ephemeral-tenant provisioner (k3d + helm chart)
- CI job examples to run ephemeral tenants in ephemeral clusters

Change log

- 2025-11-03: Initial draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-12-14: Added telemetry sampling guidance and cost webhooks.
- 2026-02-10: Hardened security section and added runbook recovery steps.

Related reading

- See: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/local-emulation-stub-harness-and-telemetry-2026 for local mock best-practices.
- See: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks for oncall and tenant provisioning runbooks.

Appendix: small diagnostics commands

- rwd keys list --owner $USER --format table
- rwd tenants usage --tenant <tenant> --last 24h
- curl -v $REDWOOD_API_BASE/health (proxy health endpoint)

End of document
sections.heading: Sampling and ingestion rules (ops note)

payload.page_title: SDK compact builds and runtime-stub playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook documents the standard approach for producing compact SDK builds and lightweight runtime stubs used by Redwood customer integrations and internal sample apps. It targets two immediate goals: minimize client-side artifact size for web and edge consumers, and provide deterministic runtime stubs for local development and CI that reproduce production behavior without requiring a full runtime backend.

Audience

- SDK engineers responsible for packaging and releases
- Developer advocates creating sample apps and quickstarts
- Support engineers shipping canonical fixes for client-side issues

When to use this playbook

- New SDK languages or client bindings are being introduced
- Bundle size regressions are detected in CI (>20% increase)
- Customers report long cold-load times for browser-based SDKs
- Local developer loops require deterministic handing of streaming/fallback behavior

What you will find in this document

1) Build targets and thresholds
2) Recommended toolchain configurations (Rollup / esbuild / swc)
3) Minimal runtime stub reference and behaviour matrix
4) CI release checks and gating rules
5) Troubleshooting and canonical fixes for top support issues
6) Ownership and rollout steps

1) Build targets and thresholds

- Primary artifact goals (web/browser bundles):
  - Max gzipped bundle size (core SDK + runtime adapter): 200KB for core build, 300KB including optional adapters
  - Tree-shaken ESM output and a single UMD for legacy consumers
  - API surface exported by package must not increase major version without a migration document

- Edge/Serverless adapters:
  - Unminified dev build for source maps is allowed up to 1.2MB; production artifact max 450KB gzipped

- Telemetry and stability SLOs for SDK releases:
  - CI package integrity checks: 100% pass for lint/build/test gates
  - Post-release client error rate (first 48 hours): <= 0.5% increase in observed API errors from SDK-tagged requests

2) Recommended toolchain configs (examples)

- Default choices (recommended order): esbuild -> Rollup (with terser) -> swc (for advanced transforms). Pick one primary tool per repo and standardize on config presets below.

- Minimal Rollup config (text example):
  // rollup.config.js
  export default {
    input: 'src/index.ts',
    output: [
      {file: 'dist/index.esm.js', format: 'esm', sourcemap: true},
      {file: 'dist/index.umd.js', format: 'umd', name: 'RedwoodSDK', sourcemap: false}
    ],
    external: ['events','buffer'],
    plugins: [require('@rollup/plugin-node-resolve')(), require('@rollup/plugin-commonjs')(), require('rollup-plugin-terser').terser()]
  }

- Example esbuild command (CI friendly):
  esbuild src/index.ts --bundle --minify --target=es2019 --format=esm --outfile=dist/index.esm.js --sourcemap=external

- Package.json snippet for publishing (small):
  {
    "name": "@redwood/sdk-client",
    "version": "1.6.2",
    "main": "dist/index.umd.js",
    "module": "dist/index.esm.js",
    "types": "dist/index.d.ts",
    "files": ["dist/*"]
  }

3) Runtime stub reference

Purpose: provide a tiny deterministic implementation of network and streaming semantics so that developer local loops and CI tests can exercise retry, backpressure and fallback logic without contacting Redwood runtime. Stubs live under /dev-stubs in the SDK repo and are shipped as a separate dev-only package @redwood/sdk-stubs.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
| Feature | Prod runtime behavior | Stub behavior | Config knobs |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Streaming tokens | Chunked HTTP/2 or server-sent events with resume tokens | Emit pre-recorded chunks at configurable intervals | REDWOOD_STUB_LATENCY_MS (default 40) |
| Retry/backoff | Exponential backoff with jitter, secondary model fallback | Deterministic fixed backoff for fast CI | REDWOOD_STUB_FAIL_AFTER_N (default 0 for success) |
| KV cache hits | Backend-driven cache hits based on prefix | Local in-memory prefix cache with transparent hits/misses | REDWOOD_STUB_CACHE_HIT_RATE (0.3) |
| Auth errors | 401/403 from KMS/OIDC gates | Optionally inject 401 for testing via env var | REDWOOD_STUB_INJECT_AUTH_ERROR=true |

Stub usage examples

- Start local dev server using stubs (node):
  REDWOOD_USE_STUBS=1 REDWOOD_STUB_LATENCY_MS=30 node examples/playground.js

- Jest unit test example using stubbed fetch:
  import {setupStub} from '@redwood/sdk-stubs'
  beforeAll(() => setupStub({latencyMs: 10, failAfter: 0}))

4) CI release checks and gating rules
sections.heading: Behavior matrix (summary)

sections.body:
1. typecheck (tsc)
2. lint (eslint + custom rules in devx/eslint-plugin)
3. unit tests + coverage (threshold 90%)
4. bundle analysis job (generates size report and fails if thresholds exceeded)
5. runtime-stub integration smoke tests (fast, < 30s)
6. telemetry contract test (validate event names and schema)

Failing a gate: branch must be fixed, and the author opens a PR with either the fix or a documented exception with a reviewer from the release leads team. Exceptions are temporary and expire after 7 days.
sections.heading: Required CI pipeline steps (order matters)

sections.body:
- CI job runs 'node tools/bundle-check.js' which computes gzipped sizes and compares to baseline artifact in artifacts/baseline.json.
- Baseline update requires a documented release note and approval from the SDK release lead.

5) Troubleshooting and canonical fixes for top support issues

Canonical Issue 1: Browser bundle causes main thread jank on page load
- Symptom: first paint delayed, SDK initialization synchronous for >100ms on slow CPUs
- Fix: convert heavy synchronous initialization (telemetry reporter construction and config fetch) into async background init. Provide a lazy init API: await Redwood.init({lazy:true}) or Redwood.getClient() triggers real init.

Canonical Issue 2: Streaming responses truncated in browser builds
- Symptom: client receives only the first chunk when using fetch polyfills or service workers
- Fix: Ensure the SDK uses native ReadableStream when available and falls back to a stream adapter that preserves backpressure. Add tests that run in headless Chromium in CI.

Canonical Issue 3: Local dev tests flake because of non-deterministic retry timing
- Symptom: CI tests intermittently fail on timeout due to jittered backoff in production retry logic
- Fix: Use the runtime stub with deterministic backoff in test environments (REDWOOD_USE_STUBS=1). Add environment gating so tests never hit production retry timers.

Canonical Issue 4: Bundle size regressed after adding a third-party adapter
- Symptom: PR passes tests but bundle-check fails with +120KB gzipped
- Fix: Move adapter to optional peer dependency and expose a lazy-loading factory: importAdapter('speech') which dynamic-imports the adapter only when used. Update docs and migration notes.

6) Ownership and rollout steps

- Owners:
  - SDK packaging & CI: @sdk-release-team (team lead: Mateo Alvarez)
  - Runtime stubs: @runtime-tools (owner: Priya Shah)
  - Telemetry contract: @observability (owner: Jordan Li)
sections.heading: Bundle analysis (implementation)

sections.body:
1. Branch off main and implement changes.
2. Run local bundle-check and stub smoke tests.
3. Open PR and add 'sdk-bundle-check' label.
4. Reviewers: one SDK packaging reviewer + one runtime-tools reviewer.
5. Merge when CI green. The merge trigger publishes a canary alpha to npm with tag next.
6. Canary verification: automated smoke runs against sample-apps playground for 24 hours.
7. Promote to stable after no regressions for 48 hours.

Rollback plan

- If post-release error rate > 0.5% above baseline or bundle-size increase is detected in downstream apps:
  1. Immediately unpublish newest package (mark deprecated) and repoint sample apps to previous tag.
  2. Postmortem: 72-hour incident review with owners, include root cause, rollout telemetry, and mitigation steps.

Appendix A: Small scripts and helpers

- bundle-check.js (concept):
  - Computes sums of gzipped sizes for dist/*.js
  - Reads artifacts/baseline.json and compares; exits 1 on threshold breach

- telemetry-schema.json example fields to assert in CI:
  ["sdk.init","sdk.request","sdk.error","sdk.streaming.chunk"]

Appendix B: Frequently asked questions

Q: Can stubs be used in staging environments?
A: Yes, but only for dev-mode smoke tests. Staging should validate production integration against the runtime unless connector costs or data residency prevents it.

Q: Who approves bundle baseline updates?
A: SDK release lead (Mateo Alvarez) plus one reviewer from devx or observability. Document reasons in the release notes.

Contact and feedback

- Primary author: Elena Rivera (elena@redwood.ai)
- SDK packaging Slack channel: #sdk-release

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Drafted initial thresholds and stub design (Elena Rivera)
- 2025-12-18: Added CI gating rules and bundle-check script template (Mateo Alvarez)
- 2026-02-03: Finalized SLOs and promoted to published (Priya Shah, Jordan Li)
sections.heading: Release checklist (minor patch)

payload.page_title: Quickstarts Update Spec: Agentic Workflows (Streaming + Tool Calling + Structured Output)

sections.body:
This document specifies the refresh to Redwood Inference quickstarts/templates to ensure every “agentic workflow” starter demonstrates the current best-practice interface for:
- Streaming responses (consistent event model + delta assembly)
- Function/tool calling (single + parallel tool calls + tool-result messages)
- Structured output (JSON schema-constrained output + validation + safe retry)
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Copy/paste runnable end-to-end
- Consistent across Python/TypeScript/Go
- Explicit about environment variables, model selection, and failure handling
sections.heading: The deliverable is a set of quickstarts that are

sections.body:
- Introducing new API semantics beyond existing streaming/tool calling/structured output behavior
- Building a full agent framework or long-lived state store
- Adding complex hosting/deploy infrastructure (these remain local-first quickstarts)
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Repo: `redwood-quickstarts`
  - `templates/agentic-workflows/node/`
  - `templates/agentic-workflows/python/`
  - `templates/agentic-workflows/go/`
- Repo: `redwood-docs` (links and “Next steps” blocks only; canonical docs live there)
sections.heading: Repositories and target locations

sections.body: Templates MUST follow the event conventions described in `streaming-event-model-conventions`.
sections.heading: 1) Streaming (event model)

sections.body:
- Maintain an accumulator for assistant text deltas.
- Treat tool-call arguments as potentially partial during streaming.
- Only parse/validate tool arguments and structured JSON when the SDK signals the tool call / message is complete.
- Handle and log disconnects with a single retry strategy that is safe by default.
sections.heading: Implementation requirements

sections.body:
- Request ID (if available from SDK)
- Model name
- Stream lifecycle: start → tool_call (if any) → tool_result → final_message
- Any retry occurrence including the reason (disconnect vs validation failure)
sections.heading: Minimum logging (stdout)

sections.body:
- Defining tools with names + JSON schema for arguments
- Handling one tool call and one parallel tool call
- Sending tool results back as tool-result messages
- A bounded loop (max tool turns) to avoid infinite cycles
sections.heading: Templates MUST demonstrate

sections.body:
- Validate tool arguments against schema before executing.
- Time-bound tool execution with a per-tool timeout.
- Never execute unknown tools (explicit allow-list).
sections.heading: Required guardrails

sections.body:
- Providing a JSON schema for the model output
- Validating the final JSON against the schema (after the model completes)
- A safe fallback when validation fails:
  - 1 automatic retry with a “repair” instruction OR
  - degrade to non-structured output and display raw text with an explicit warning

Important: streaming + structured output should not rely on incremental JSON parsing. Validation should happen on the final assembled message.
sections.heading: Templates MUST demonstrate

sections.body: The following templates will be updated/added under `templates/agentic-workflows/*`.
sections.heading: Template inventory and what changes

sections.body:
Goal: Demonstrate a realistic multi-step agent loop that uses tools and produces schema-constrained output.

**Languages:** Node (TypeScript), Python, Go

**Tools demonstrated (minimum):**
- `search_knowledge_base(query: string) -> { results: [{ title, url, snippet }] }`
- `create_ticket(subject: string, description: string, severity: "low"|"medium"|"high") -> { ticket_id: string }`

**Structured output schema:**
- Final output must be a JSON object containing:
  - `summary` (string)
  - `customer_impact` (string)
  - `probable_root_causes` (array of strings)
  - `recommended_next_steps` (array of strings)
  - `ticket_to_create` (object with `subject`, `description`, `severity`) OR `null`

**Parallel tool calling requirement:**
- The agent should be able to call `search_knowledge_base` twice in parallel with two different queries (e.g., error message + product area).
sections.heading: A) Template: “Support Triage Agent” (primary agentic workflow)

sections.body:
Goal: Show the simplest tool-call → tool-result → schema-constrained summary flow.

**Languages:** Node (TypeScript), Python

**Tools demonstrated (minimum):**
- `lookup_company(domain: string) -> { name, industry, size, notes }`

**Structured output schema:**
- `company_brief` (string)
- `risk_flags` (array of strings)
- `follow_up_questions` (array of strings)

**Streaming requirement:**
- Streaming is enabled and displayed, but the template keeps the UI minimal (console-only). This template is explicitly positioned as the “hello world” for tools + schema.
sections.heading: B) Template: “Data Enrichment Agent” (tool calling + structured output, minimal streaming)

sections.body:
Goal: Show robust schema validation, failure modes, and repair retry.

**Languages:** Node (TypeScript), Python, Go

**Tools demonstrated:**
- None required (this template is structured-output-only), but SHOULD include a commented “optional tool calling extension” block.

**Structured output schema:**
- `title` (string)
- `attendees` (array of strings)
- `decisions` (array of strings)
- `action_items` (array of objects: `owner`, `task`, `due_date` (ISO date string or ""))

**Validation behavior:**
- If JSON is invalid or fails schema: print a clear error, run one repair retry, then exit non-zero if still invalid.
sections.heading: C) Template: “Meeting Notes to Action Items” (structured output focus)

sections.body: All templates MUST document environment variables in the template README and provide `.env.example`.
sections.heading: Required environment variables and configuration

sections.body:
| Variable | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `REDWOOD_API_KEY` | Yes | (none) | API key with Hosted API access. |
| `REDWOOD_BASE_URL` | No | `https://api.redwoodinference.com` | Support staging via alternate URL. |
| `REDWOOD_MODEL` | No | language-specific default (see below) | Used for chat/generation + tool calling. |
| `REDWOOD_TIMEOUT_MS` | No | `60000` | Overall request timeout. |
| `REDWOOD_MAX_TOOL_TURNS` | No | `4` | Hard cap to prevent infinite tool loops. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | No | `info` | `debug` enables event-level logging. |
sections.heading: Common environment variables (all templates)

sections.body:
**Support Triage Agent**
| Variable | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `KB_SOURCE` | No | `local` | `local` uses bundled fixtures; `remote` calls a sample endpoint. |

payload.page_title: Client SDKs: Error Hunting Blueprint and Integration Checklist

sections.body:
Overview

This document is a practical blueprint for engineering teams integrating Redwood client SDKs (Node, Python, and REST) into production services. It collects an integration checklist, common error patterns and canonical fixes, diagnostic commands, telemetry thresholds to watch, and an escalation path. The intent is operational clarity: fast onboarding and reliable debugging when issues crop up.

Audience
- SDK integrators (frontend/back-end engineers)
- Developer experience (DX) engineers and on-call SREs
- Solutions engineers assisting customers

Quick summary checklist (pre-integration)
1) Confirm API key provisioning and least-privilege scopes (test key vs production key).
2) Choose SDK and pin to a specific minor version (e.g., node-client@1.14.x).
3) Validate network routing to: api.redwood.ai, telemetry.redwood.ai, and any dedicated endpoints per contract.
4) Run the smoke test suite (examples below).
5) Configure client-side retry and timeout policy consistent with service SLOs.

Integration checklist (detailed)
- Credentials and security
  - Ensure keys are stored in the secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Vault).
  - Rotate test keys on a 90-day cadence and production keys per customer policy.
- SDK configuration
  - Pin SDK: avoid floating major versions. Example package.json entry:

  {
    "dependencies": {
      "@redwood/inference": "^1.14.3"
    }
  }

- Timeouts and retries (recommended)
  - Client default request timeout: 10s (adjust for large-generation workflows).
  - Per-request retry: exponential backoff, 3 attempts, jitter.
  - Circuit breaker: open after 5 errors in 60s, reset 30s.

- Telemetry and logging
  - Log request_id / trace_id on all SDK calls.
  - Capture model_name, model_version, token_count, latency_ms at p50/p95/p99.
  - Send a periodic heartbeat event to telemetry.redwood.ai with SDK version and region.

Smoke test examples
- Curl (REST)
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY"
    -H "Content-Type: application/json"
    -d '{"model":"redwood-13b","input":"Say hello in 3 languages."}'

- Node (minimal)
  // JavaScript example (Node 18+)
  import Redwood from '@redwood/inference';
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
  const r = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-13b', input: 'Health check' });
  console.log(r.output);

- Python (minimal)
  from redwood import RedwoodClient
  client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_KEY'))
  resp = client.generate(model='redwood-13b', input='Health check')
  print(resp.output)

Common error patterns and canonical fixes
1) 401 / invalid_auth: "Authentication failed"
   - Cause: wrong key, key expired, using test key against dedicated/private endpoint.
   - Fixes: verify header Authorization Bearer, confirm key scope and environment. Run:
     curl -I -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health

2) 429 / rate_limited: "Rate limit exceeded"
   - Cause: burst traffic or missing client-side rate limiting.
   - Fixes: implement token bucket at client; honor Retry-After header. For Dedicated customers, check reserved capacity metric (dashboard -> Dedicated -> capacity-utilization).

3) 504 / gateway_timeout or long tail latency
   - Cause: oversized batch, model cold start, backend queueing under pressure.
   - Fixes: reduce request size, use streaming endpoints for long outputs, add per-call timeout and graceful fallback to smaller model. Check p95 latency and recent deployment rollouts.

4) 422 / invalid_request: "Prompt invalid or exceeds token limit"
   - Cause: prompt length > model limit, malformed JSON for structured outputs.
   - Fixes: run tokenizer count locally (sample tokenizer commands below); enforce client-side truncation + summary.

5) SDK serialization errors (language-specific)
   - Node: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split') when passing non-string input.
   - Python: TypeError: 'dict' object is not JSON serializable when passing nested dicts to a simple text endpoint.
   - Fixes: validate types before send, use SDK helpers (client.prepare_input) where provided.

Diagnostic commands and how to gather a reproducible report
1) Collect client environment: OS, SDK version, node/python version, region, network egress IP.
2) Reproduce with curl against api.redwood.ai/v1/health and /v1/generate with minimal payload. Include request_id header in logs.
3) If using Dedicated or Private: capture the endpoint used and the dedicated_pool_id or vpc_id.
4) Export SDK logs with DEBUG verbosity for the failing window (example env var: REDWOOD_LOG_LEVEL=debug).
5) Gather traces: attach trace_id to ticket and link to Redwood Console request trace.

Telemetry thresholds and SLOs to watch (recommended)
| Metric | Threshold | Action |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| client_error_rate (4xx) | < 0.5% | Investigate prompt validation issues |
| server_error_rate (5xx) | < 0.2% | Escalate to eng-serving-runtime on-call |
| p95 latency | < 250ms (short ops) / < 2s (standard) | If rising >20% week-over-week, trigger perf review |
| retry_count per request | < 0.15 | Reduce client retries or check downstream flakiness |

Examples: tokenizer check (Python)
  from redwood.tokenizer import count_tokens
  n = count_tokens(model='redwood-13b', text=my_prompt)
  if n > 4096:
      # truncate or summarize

Canonical fixes (snippet library)
- Truncation helper (Node):
  export function truncatePrompt(prompt, maxTokens) {
    // naive: cut characters; replace with tokenizer-based approach in prod
    return prompt.slice(0, Math.floor(maxTokens * 4));
  }

- Retry wrapper (Python):
  import backoff

  @backoff.on_exception(backoff.expo, (TimeoutError, ConnectionError), max_tries=3, jitter=True)
  def call_generate(client, **kwargs):
      return client.generate(**kwargs)

Escalation and ownership
- Triage (first 15 minutes): integrator or on-call SRE performs the smoke tests and collects logs.
- Level 2: DX engineering reviews SDK-related bugs and provides reproduction.
- Level 3: eng-serving-runtime owns backend issues (latency regressions, kernel-level faults).
- Contact channels: #devx-sdk (Slack), pager for eng-serving-runtime on-call, platform-support@redwood.ai.

Runbook: reproducible-error -> triage -> mitigate -> followup
1) Repro (0–15m): reproduce with minimal payload. Capture request_id.
2) Mitigate (15–60m): apply client-side guardrail (shorter timeout, smaller model) or toggle fallback route.
3) Fix (1–72h): if bug in SDK, open PR against sdk repo, include unit tests and changelog entry. If backend, open incident and link to postmortem.
4) Postmortem (by owner): write blameless postmortem for any outage > 5min or > 0.5% error spike impacting customers.

Developer guidance: versioning, changelogs, and deprecation
- Follow semver for SDKs. Deprecation policy: 90 days notice for breaking changes.
- DX publishes a short migration guide for every breaking release.
- Changelog must include sample code diffs and a test-plan for customers to validate.

Appendix: useful snippets and references
- SDK debug env vars:
  - REDWOOD_LOG_LEVEL=debug
  - REDWOOD_SDK_PROFILE=true

- Useful API endpoints:
  - https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health (GET)
  - https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate (POST)
  - https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings (POST)

Related pages and owners
- DX SDK team owner: devx-sdks@redwood.ai (primary)
- Eng-serving-runtime on-call: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/index

Change history
- 2025-09-12: created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2025-11-05: added tokenizer and tracer guidance (review: Miguel Santos).
- 2026-01-15: expanded telemetry thresholds and canned fixes; prepared for DX internal review (review: Lena Fischer).

If you find a missing canonical fix or recurring error pattern, add it to this page and notify devx-sdks@redwood.ai so we can include a small reproducer and a unit test in the SDK repo.

payload.page_title: Embeddings index consistency and rollback workarounds

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page documents common failure modes we see for customer-managed or Redwood-managed embeddings indexes, recommended short-term workarounds to restore service, and longer-term fixes to prevent recurrence. It is intended for Customer Success, Support Engineers, and the Embeddings SRE/Infra teams.

Scope
-----
- Applies to vector indexes used with Redwood's embeddings API, including: local index servers (faiss/hnsw), managed index service, and third-party vector DB connectors (Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate).
- Addresses consistency problems (missing vectors, partial queries, index drift), indexing failures during bulk ingest, and rollback/restore guidance.

Impact and priority guidance
---------------------------
- P0: Index returns wrong vectors for >20% of queries, or customer-facing search/generation failures. Immediate page + incident.
- P1: Partial degradation (increased latency, missing results <20%). Open escalation ticket and apply quick fix within 4 business hours.
- P2: Non-critical background failures (reindex jobs failing but fallbacks exist). Track in backlog.

Owners and escalation contacts
----------------------------
- Customer Success (first responder): #cust-success, oncall cs lead (cs-lead@example.com).
- Embeddings Infra / SRE: #infra-embeddings, oncall (infra-emb-oncall@example.com).
- Integrations / Connectors: #platform-connectors.

Detection checklist (signals to watch)
------------------------------------
1) Telemetry / Alerts
- Index error rate > 0.5% for 5m (alert).
- Query hit-rate drop > 30% vs baseline (30d rolling).
- Unexpected reindex job failures with non-zero exit code.

2) Customer-reported symptoms
- Identical queries return different top results across time windows.
- Recently-ingested documents do not appear in search results.
- High latency on embedding-lookup calls.

Symptoms -> Likely causes -> Immediate action (table)
---------------------------------------------------
| Symptom | Likely cause | Immediate action |
|---|---|---|
| Missing recent documents | Partial ingest failure (batch abort) | Re-run incremental ingest for affected batches; verify via sample queries |
| Query returns stale vectors | KV cache serving old embeddings | Invalidate prefix cache for impacted keyspace; force cold read |
| Higher-than-expected false positives | Wrong vector dimension / model mismatch | Validate embedding model version; temporarily route queries to compatible model variant |
| Index returning 500 errors | Index process crash / OOM | Restart index pod; inspect OOM logs; scale up memory if reproduces |
| Inconsistent shard responses | Corrupt shard or split-brain | Quiesce writes, trigger shard re-sync, or restore last known-good snapshot |

Quick fixes (playbook)
----------------------
These are ordered from least intrusive to most. Prefer non-destructive options first.

1) Verification and scoped rollback
- Step 1: Ask customer for a minimal failing query set (3–10 examples) and time window.
- Step 2: Re-run queries against the same index with a strict timestamp filter to reproduce.
- Step 3: If problem is limited to a single ingest batch, re-run the ingest for that batch. Use the ingest job ID and the incremental ingest API:

  curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.com/v1/ingest/retry" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"ingest_job_id":"INGEST_JOB_ID"}'

- Step 4: Verify results by running the customer's example queries and checking top-5 similarity scores differ from baseline by > 0.

2) Cache invalidation
- When stale vectors are suspected, invalidate prefix/KV cache for the index keyspace:

  curl -X POST "https://internal-admin.redwood.local/v1/cache/invalidate" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"namespace":"indexes","key_prefix":"index-<INDEX_ID>-kv"}'

- Confirm by comparing timestamps on vectors returned and re-running queries.

3) Snapshot rollback (managed indexes only)
- Preconditions: We have a validated automatic snapshot policy and a snapshot taken prior to the incident.
- Steps:
  1. Put index into read-only mode (no writes).
  2. Create an incident branch and notify customer of potential write loss after snapshot rollback.
  3. Restore snapshot to a new index instance using the internal restore tool:

    redwood index restore --snapshot-id SNAPSHOT_ID --target-index restored-index-<INCIDENT_ID> --region us-west-2

  4. Run a smoke test using customer query set. If restored index meets quality checks, perform cutover routing.

- Cutover rollback considerations: keep original index for 72 hours to allow delta reconciliation.

4) Rebuild strategy (when snapshot not available or corrupt)
- Run parallel rebuild to a new index instance. Use staged rollback:
  - Start incremental rebuild with throttling: redwood index rebuild --source-batch-list BATCH_IDs --throttle 250/s
  - Monitor build success rate and sample top-n results.
  - Once parity reached on verification queries, switch traffic.

Operational validation criteria (minimum before cutover)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Sample accuracy: For customer-provided verification set, top-5 recall >= 95% of baseline or pre-incident run.
- Latency: P95 lookup latency <= 1.5x baseline and absolute P95 < 300ms for managed indexes in production tiers.
- Error rate: < 0.1% 5m rolling.

Permanent mitigations and engineering requests
-------------------------------------------
1) Preflight schema validation in ingest pipeline (reject mismatched dimension vectors).
2) Improve snapshot frequency for high-change customers (default 4h -> 1h for enterprise).
3) Add a lightweight background parity checker that compares recent ingest batches against the index every 30 minutes and alerts on divergence > 5%.
4) Improve connector backpressure behavior to avoid partially applied batches when downstream errors occur.

Monitoring and alerting recommendations for CS/SRE
-------------------------------------------------
- Metrics to surface to customer and internal dashboards: ingest_success_rate, index_build_progress, top_k_recall_on_verification_set, prefix_cache_hit_rate.
- Recommended alert thresholds:
  - ingest_success_rate < 98% for 30m -> P1
  - top_k_recall_on_verification_set < 90% -> P0
  - index_build_progress stalls for > 15m without progress -> P1

Customer communication template (short)
-------------------------------------
Subject: Incident update — embeddings index for <customer-name>

We detected inconsistent search results impacting a subset of queries. We have isolated the affected index and are running an incremental rebuild. Expected recovery window: 2–6 hours. There is no evidence of data exfiltration. We will notify you after verification tests complete or sooner if the window changes.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Re-run failed ingest batches and validate results
- Restore from snapshot if incremental rebuild fails
- Provide post-incident summary and plan to prevent recurrence

How CS should engage engineering
--------------------------------
1) Open a Priority ticket with embedding-infra and include: customer name, index ID, ingest job IDs, sample failing queries, and timestamps.
2) Ask Infra to create a temporary read-only replica for forensic analysis before any destructive operation.
3) Coordinate customer-facing communications; avoid promising specific cutover times until validation criteria are met.

Post-incident checklist (RCA & follow-up)
----------------------------------------
- Collect: ingest logs, index build logs, snapshot logs, telemetry around cache invalidation, and thread dumps if crashes occurred.
- Determine root cause classification (ingest, cache, index binary, connector).
- Create engineering ticket for permanent fix with owner and target milestone.
- Offer customer a mitigation plan (snapshot frequency change, managed rebuild voucher) depending on severity.

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets and queries
----------------------------------------
- List recent snapshots for index:
  redwood index snapshots --index-id <INDEX_ID> --limit 10 --format json

- Trigger a controlled rebuild for specific batches:
  redwood index rebuild --index-id <INDEX_ID> --batches "batch1,batch2" --concurrency 16

- Sample verification query (embedding + similarity):
  curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.com/v1/embeddings/query" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"index_id":"<INDEX_ID>","query_embedding": [0.123, ...], "top_k": 5 }'

References
----------
- SDK Embedding Integration Playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/integration-guides/sdk-embedding-integration-and-operational-playbook-2026
- Index snapshot and restore internal runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/index-snapshot-restore-2025

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-10: Created by Elena Morales (published)
- 2026-03-01: Added snapshot rollback procedure and updated validation criteria (reviewed by James Li, Nora Patel)

payload.page_title: runtime-integration-blueprint-2026

sections.body:
Overview

This page is a step-by-step blueprint for integrating Redwood client SDKs (HTTP/JS/Python) with production runtime patterns. It focuses on safe, observable, and cost-conscious runtimes: prefix caching, batching, retry/backoff policies, telemetry hooks, and graceful fallbacks to cheaper model variants. The goal is a repeatable template engineering teams can copy into new services.

Audience

- Software engineers building product features that call Redwood inference.
- Platform engineers embedding SDKs into microservices and serverless functions.

Prerequisites

1) Redwood API key and team permissions.
2) Runtime variant choices defined (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
3) CI pipeline with canary deploy capability.
4) Access to the service observability workspace (Datadog / Honeycomb / internal).

Quickstart summary (5-minute checklist)

1. Install SDK: `pip install redwood-sdk` or `npm install @redwood/inference`
2. Configure client with env var: `REDWOOD_API_KEY` and `REDWOOD_REGION`
3. Enable prefix caching and batching in client config (example below)
4. Add telemetry hooks to platform tracing span
5. Add unit tests for model-level regressions (small eval prompt set)
6. Deploy as canary (10%) with automatic rollback on latency/cost SLO violation

Detailed integration steps

1) Initialize client with runtime profile

- Rationale: explicitly binding to a runtime profile (latency-optimized vs cost-optimized) prevents accidental cost spikes during rollout. Profiles are mapped to model variants and batching configs server-side.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```python
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"), profile="latency-optimized", region="us-west-2")
```

2) Enable prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts

- When user sessions include stable system prompts or shared context, enable prefix caching at the SDK layer to reduce tokens and latency.
- Cache invalidation: tie cache keys to model_version + prompt_hash + user_ttl. Default TTL: 1 hour for conversational prefixes.
sections.heading: Example (Python)

sections.body:
| setting | recommended default | rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| batching.max_batch_size | "16" | safe throughput on T4/RTX fleets |
| batching.max_wait_ms | "20" | micro-batching latency tradeoff |
| cache.prefix_ttl_seconds | "3600" | balance freshness and hit-rate |
| fallback.order | "gpt-equivalent -> quantized-econ -> small-econ" | keep UX while saving cost |
| telemetry.sample_rate | "0.05" | 5% traces for full payloads |

3) Adopt a deterministic retry and idempotency scheme

- Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent generation requests. Keys should be `sha256(user_id + prompt_id + model_version)`. Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 attempts. Retries for 5xx and connection errors only; do not retry 4xx.
sections.heading: Config table (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
1. generate_idemp_key(request)
2. try request with timeout 6s
3. on 5xx: backoff 200ms -> 600ms -> 1800ms
4. record metrics: request_attempts, final_status, latency_ms

4) Streaming and early-commit patterns

- For chat UIs, enable token streaming. If the client can accept partial outputs, early-commit the first coherent chunk to UX and continue streaming remaining tokens. This reduces perceived latency.
- When streaming to mobile clients, include a lightweight summary chunk within the first 300ms of generation (use short-form mode).
sections.heading: Retry pseudocode
Example (JS streaming snippet)

sections.body:
- redwood.request.count (tags: model, profile, region, route)
- redwood.request.latency_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- redwood.request.tokens_in / tokens_out
- redwood.cache.hit_rate (per prefix scope)
- redwood.fallback.count (tags: from_model,to_model,reason)
- redwood.retry.attempts (histogram)
sections.heading: Emit the following at request boundaries

sections.body:
- Start a platform span named `redwood.call` with attributes: model, profile, idempotency_key, tokens_requested.
- Attach the Redwood request id to the top-level trace as `redwood.request_id` to ease server-side lookup.

6) Cost-control and fallback policies

- Configure client-side hints: `max_model_cost_usd_per_request` and `model_preference_order`. These are advisory and may be enforced by server-side routing policies during load.
- Example fallback policy: if p95 latency > 800ms or error rate > 1% for 5 minutes, automatically route 25% of traffic to a quantized-econ variant, and keep 5% to high-quality for verification.

Deployment checklist and rollout steps

1. Create feature branch and update service config with runtime profile and telemetry.
2. Add unit/integration test that asserts the model response shape on a fixed prompt set (use small eval harness).
3. Deploy canary at 1% for 30 minutes; monitor latency, error-rate, token-cost; abort on SLO breach.
4. Increase to 10% for 1 hour; run automated smoke tests.
5. Gradual ramp to 100% with staged verification (24h windows between ramps).

Common failure modes and canonical fixes

- Symptom: sudden spike in tokens_out and cost.
  - Fix: inspect `redwood.request_id` traces; check for malformed prompts causing repetition loops. Add prompt-length cap and guard rails to UI input.

- Symptom: high p95 latency after deploy.
  - Fix: check batching.max_wait_ms and model routing changes; temporarily pin profile to latency-optimized and rollback if needed.

- Symptom: cache misses are near 0% (no benefit).
  - Fix: validate cache key composition and TTL. Confirm prefix hashing includes model_version. Run a small synthetic workload to verify hits.

Support & escalation playbook

1. Triage in Slack channel #runtime-support: include request_id, model, profile, region, and a minimal reproduction.
2. If incident is P1 (production-wide latency or >5% error for 10m): page oncall SRE and eng-serving-runtime lead.
3. For suspected model quality regressions (NLP hallucination or incorrect formatting): open a ticket in the eval-harness board and tag Applied ML.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (Maya Chen)
- Runtime owners: eng-serving-runtime (Diego Alvarez)
- Observability owner: eng-platform (Priya Nambiar)

Appendix: reproducible example & CI test

- Minimal integration test (pytest) sketch:

```python
def test_generative_smoke(client):
    prompt = "Summarize: Redwood provides inference platform for developers."
    resp = client.generate(prompt, model='redwood-512-lite', timeout=4)
    assert resp.text.startswith('Redwood')
    assert resp.token_count < 2000
```

- CI should run this test against a sandbox API key and fail the build when latency > 1s or token_cost_usd > 0.003 for the smoke prompt.

payload.page_title: Developer Token Economics Simulator — Local Quickstart and Templates

sections.body:
Overview

This page describes the Developer Token Economics Simulator — a lightweight toolkit and set of templates that lets engineers model per-request and per-feature token costs for Redwood API calls in a local developer sandbox. The simulator helps teams estimate unit economics prior to production rollout, validate cost-related changes to prompts or batching strategies, and exercise quota/fallback policies in isolated environments.

When to use

- Planning: estimate monthly spend for feature launches based on expected request volumes and prompt length distributions.
- CI checks: add cost regressions to pre-merge checks to prevent accidental token regressions.
- Debugging: reproduce customer-reported high-cost patterns by replaying requests and inspecting token breakdowns.
- SDK tuning: test client-side bundling, prompt truncation, and streaming-to-batch tradeoffs.

Key features

- Pluggable price profiles (hosted, dedicated, committed-tier).
- Simulated batching and streaming models with configurable latency tradeoffs.
- Token attribution per request: system/instruction/user/content/embedding.
- Canary scenario runner for rollout experiments (A/B cost comparison).

Quickstart — run locally (10 minutes)

Prerequisites

1. Node 18+ or Python 3.10+.
2. Docker (optional, for reproducible runs).
3. Local copy of your reference prompt sets (see Files and templates).

Step 1 — clone the simulator templates

1. git clone git.example.com/internal/dev-token-econ-sim.git
2. cd dev-token-econ-sim/templates/basic-quickstart

Step 2 — configure a price profile

Create config/prices.yaml with a profile for your intended deployment. Example:

prices.yaml (example):

```
profiles:
  hosted_small:
    prompt_per_token_usd: 0.000004
    completion_per_token_usd: 0.000012
    embeddings_per_unit_usd: 0.0002
  dedicated_committed:
    prompt_per_token_usd: 0.0000025
    completion_per_token_usd: 0.0000075
    embeddings_per_unit_usd: 0.00015
```

Step 3 — provide a request sample set

Place a JSONL file at data/requests.jsonl where each line is a simple JSON object with keys: route, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, embeddings_count, and tags. Example line:

```
{"route":"/v1/chat/completions","model":"redwood-large-1","prompt_tokens":320,"completion_tokens":120,"embeddings_count":0,"tags":["checkout","english"]}
```

Step 4 — run the simulator

- Node: npm run simulate -- --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --output reports/hosted_small_report.csv
- Python: python simulate.py --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --output reports/hosted_small_report.csv

The simulator will produce: a CSV with per-request token breakdown, aggregate cost summary, and a small JSON with percentile distributions (p50/p90/p99 prompt/completion tokens).

Files and templates included

- templates/basic-quickstart/
  - prices.yaml.example (price profile templates)
  - data/requests-sample.jsonl (sample requests for ecommerce and search features)
  - bin/run-local.sh (wrapper for common runs)
- templates/ci-check/
  - GitHub Actions workflow template for adding a cost gate in PRs (checks cost delta <= configured threshold)
- templates/canary/
  - ab-config.yaml (A/B test config: traffic split, profiles to compare)

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| key | type | recommended example | notes |
|-----|------|---------------------|-------|
| profile | string | hosted_small | logical name used in CLI |
| prompt_per_token_usd | float | 0.000004 | vendor-specific published price |
| completion_per_token_usd | float | 0.000012 | often higher than prompt price |
| embeddings_per_unit_usd | float | 0.0002 | per embedding vector unit |
| batch_window_ms | int | 10 | simulates client batching window |
| streaming_penalty_ms | int | 20 | additional latency for streaming-to-batch conversion |

Example outputs

- reports/hosted_small_report.csv (columns: request_id, route, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, cost_usd, tags)
- reports/hosted_small_summary.json (p50/p90/p99 token stats and total cost)

Common support issues & canonical fixes

1) Discrepancy between local simulation and production billing
   - Symptom: simulated cost is significantly lower than billing.
   - Cause: production uses larger context windows or reference prompts not included in the simulation.
   - Fix: ensure request sample set includes pre-pended system instructions and real user context lengths. Update data/requests.jsonl to mirror production request envelope. See checklist below.

2) CI cost gate causing false positives on low-volume spikes
   - Symptom: PR blocked because cost delta > threshold from small sample noise.
   - Cause: PR sample set too small or not representative.
   - Fix: enlarge sample set to at least 500 requests or use percentile-based comparison (use p90 cost instead of mean). Update workflow to use templates/ci-check/github-actions-cost-gate.yaml.

3) Unexpectedly high embedding cost on hybrid features
   - Symptom: embedding spend dominates estimates for search-as-you-type features.
   - Cause: counting every preview query as full embedding.
   - Fix: instrument client to delay embeddings until a debounce window (example client change included in templates). Use embeddings_per_unit_usd from dedicated_committed profile to estimate committed-tier savings.

Checklist for accurate reproduction

- [ ] Include system prompts and metadata token counts in the sample lines.
- [ ] Mirror client-side bundling window and batch sizes.
- [ ] Represent expected user locale/tokenization differences (non-ASCII can change token counts).
- [ ] Verify price profile matches billing contract for the environment being simulated.

Adding a CI cost gate (example)

1. Copy templates/ci-check/github-actions-cost-gate.yaml to .github/workflows/
2. Update inputs: sample_path, baseline_report_artifact, cost_threshold_usd
3. The workflow will: run the simulator, upload the report, compare to baseline, and fail if delta > threshold.

Troubleshooting commands

- Run a single-sample run and view verbose token breakdown:
  - python simulate.py --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --single 42 --verbose
- Re-run with adjusted tokenization model:
  - NODE_TOKENIZER_MODEL=gpt-tokenizer-v2 npm run simulate -- --profile hosted_small

Ownership and maintenance

- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (Priya Menon)
- Secondary: eng-platform (Marco Liu)
- Suggested review cadence: quarterly or whenever pricing contract changes.

Change log

- 2025-11-10: Initial draft and template import.
- 2025-12-18: Added CI workflow templates and embedding debounce example.
- 2026-02-01: Clarified reproduction checklist and added p90-based gate recommendation.

Related links

- Cost telemetry guide: /confluence/eng-platform/observability-and-costing/cost-metrics-telemetry-2025
- SDK profiling and cost debugging quickstart: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-profiling-cost-debugging-quickstart-2026.json

If you have questions or want a pairing session to model a specific customer workload, file a ticket in #devx-sim or ping Priya.

payload.page_title: DevX Embedded Sandbox: Chaos & Metrics Lab Runbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This runbook describes the DevX Embedded Sandbox Chaos & Metrics Lab: a reproducible environment and process for exercising SDK + client integration failure modes, measuring telemetry signal quality, and producing canonical fixes for top support issues. The Lab is intended for developer-experience engineers, on-call support, and SDK maintainers.

Goals
- Provide a low-friction sandbox that mirrors production request/response shapes and token budgets.
- Enable controlled failure injection (network/TLS/latency/partial responses) and workload perturbation (concurrency spikes, bursty prompts).
- Validate telemetry cohorts, golden traces, and alert thresholds before shipping SDK changes.
- Produce actionable canonical fixes and reproducible tickets for product/support teams.

Scope and Non-Scope
- Included: JS/TS and Python SDKs, local telemetry agent, replay harness, failure-injector, cost/latency profiling hooks.
- Excluded: full GPU runtime performance testing (use eng-serving-runtime benchmarking suites), customer-specific private deployment configurations unless a dedicated private-lab exists.

Architecture (high level)
- Sandbox controller: CLI + lightweight web UI that orchestrates runs and retains artifacts.
- Local telemetry agent: captures in-process SDK events, token counts, latencies, and sampling flags; exposes a replayable trace archive (.trace.json).
- Failure-injector: configurable middleware that can simulate: timeouts, truncated streams, 502/503 responses, slow TLS handshakes, and intermittent connection drops.
- Golden runner: a scenario harness that executes prompt bundles and compares outputs/metrics against goldens.

Key components and ownership
- devx-sandbox (service template): Owner: DevX SDK team (Maya Chen). Contains docker-compose for the sandbox stack.
- telemetry-agent (library): Owner: Observability team (Carlos Ruiz). Emits schema v2 events and provides trace archival.
- injector (module): Owner: Reliability & Platform (Anita Patel). Implements failure primitives and blast-radius controls.

SLOs and success criteria for lab runs
- Turnaround: sandbox should be deployable locally in < 5 minutes (cold start).
- Trace quality: >95% of SDK calls include correlation_id and token_count fields.
- Determinism: golden-run comparisons should be reproducible in 9/10 consecutive runs; tolerances configured per scenario.
- Triage signal: failing scenario must produce at least one of the following: error-level trace, latency spike > 2x baseline, or token-count deviation > 10%.

Quickstart: Local sandbox (3-minute developer path)
1) Prereqs: Docker (20.10+), Node 18+/Python 3.10+, git.
2) Clone repo and bring up stack:
   git clone git@repo.redwood.ai:devx/devx-sandbox.git
   cd devx-sandbox
   ./bin/start-local.sh --profile default
3) Run a smoke scenario against the bundled SDK sample (Node):
   cd examples/node-streaming
   npm install
   SDK_SANDBOX_URL=http://localhost:8080 node run-smoke.js
4) Capture a trace and export golden:
   ./bin/collect-trace.sh --scenario=smoke --out=goldens/smoke.trace.json

Failure-injection matrix (example)
| Scenario | Failure type | Expected metric change | Blast radius | Runbook step on failure |
| Network flaps during streaming | intermittent connection reset | stream-error rate +50% | low (1 container) | increase retry-backoff and verify stream-idempotency |
| Truncated response mid-stream | server closes connection after N tokens | partial-response traces, user-visible truncation | medium | enable fallback-to-sync and replay last-segment |
| Elevated latency for model init | 5–10s slow path on cold start | startup p95 > SLA (2s) | high | enable prewarm policy and adjust client connect timeout |

Experiment templates and YAML examples
- Scenario definition (yaml):
  name: streaming-truncate-check
  description: Validate client handles truncated streams and replays last 2KB of prompt
  failure_injection:
    - type: truncate_stream
      after_tokens: 128
      probability: 0.5
  metrics_expectation:
    latency_p95_ms: 1200
    stream_error_rate_percent: 10

- Local CLI run (example):
  ./bin/run-scenario --scenario=streaming-truncate-check --iterations=50 --telemetry=sampled

Telemetry: sampling, cohorts, golden traces
- Sampling policy: default sample-rate = 1/10 for non-failing runs; sample all failing runs and any run marked smoke.
- Cohorts: SDK-language (js/python), runtime-mode (streaming/sync), route (generation/embeddings). Label traces with these fields for cohort-based alerting.
- Golden traces: store in /goldens with CI gating. Golden artifacts include: request bundle (.jsonl), trace (.trace.json), response-checksum (.sha256).

CI integration and gating
- Add a CI job "devx/telemetry-golden-check" that:
  1) Boots a headless sandbox via docker-compose with deterministic fixtures.
  2) Runs golden scenarios and compares trace diffs with tolerant thresholds.
  3) Fails the pipeline if regressions exceed configured thresholds (latency, token_count, error_rate).

Canonical fix playbook (when a lab run surfaces a reproducible issue)
1) Triage: assign to SDK owner and attach the trace artifact + failing request bundle.
2) Root cause hypotheses (2h): run targeted experiments (increase sampling, run with debug logs, compare code branches).
3) Patch + unit tests: add behavioral unit test in sdk-integration-suite that replicates the trimming/retry case.
4) CI goldens: update golden only if behavior change is intentional; otherwise produce a rollback patch for the SDK change that introduced the regression.
5) Postmortem artifact: short-form writeup (owner, cause, fix, release version, rollback window) and link to the ticket.

Top support issues mapped to lab scenarios
- "Client sees truncated streamed reply" -> scenario: streaming-truncate-check -> fix: strengthen streaming checksum and idempotent resume.
- "High token counts on short prompts" -> scenario: tokenizer-leak-sim -> fix: isolate and patch double-encode path.
- "Unexpected 502s during bursts" -> scenario: concurrency-burst-502 -> fix: client-side concurrency slotting and exponential jitter.

Safety and blast-radius controls
- All failure injections default to "local" network namespace.
- When running in shared CI pool, set BLAST_RADIUS=ci-small and require two approvers before enabling medium/high blast radius.
- Audit: injector logs are archived alongside trace artifacts for 30 days (configurable).

Operational checklist (pre-run)
- Verify telemetry-agent version matches the golden schema v2.
- Confirm golden artifacts checksum and CI env variables.
- Notify on-call Slack channel #devx-labs with run id and expected duration.

How to onboard a new SDK or scenario
1) Create scenario bundle in devx-scenarios/ with request samples, expected checksums, and a scenario.yaml.
2) Add a runner in examples/ that demonstrates minimal usage pattern and exposes a smoke endpoint.
3) Request reviewer from Observability and Reliability via the "lab-onboard" GitHub action.

Troubleshooting tips
- If sandbox fails to start: run ./bin/start-local.sh --debug and inspect logs in ./logs. Typical causes: port conflicts, old docker images, or Compose version mismatch.
- If traces lack correlation_id: bump telemetry-agent to >= v2.1.0 and re-run with --full-trace.

Appendix: Example Node snippet (stream resume)
const client = new RedwoodSDK({ baseUrl: process.env.SDK_SANDBOX_URL, timeoutMs: 120000 });
async function resumeStream(sessionId) {
  try {
    const res = await client.streamResume({ sessionId });
    res.on('data', (chunk) => console.log(chunk.text));
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('resume failed', err);
    // canonical fallback: sync fetch last chunk then restart streaming
  }
}

Contact and escalation
- Lab owner: Maya Chen (devx@redwood.ai)
- Observability contact: Carlos Ruiz (obs@redwood.ai)
- Reliability contact: Anita Patel (reliability@redwood.ai)

Change log
- 2027-02-15: created by Maya Chen.
- 2027-02-20: content additions (CI gating, sample YAML) by Carlos Ruiz.

References
- SDK golden-runner README: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-debugging-labs-and-support-playbook-2026
- Telemetry schema v2: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/sdk-telemetry-schema-evolution-migration-playbook-2027

payload.page_title: sdk-playground-labs-and-error-injection-recipes-2026

sections.body:
Title: SDK Playground Labs and Error Injection Recipes
Space: eng-developer-experience
Author: Aditi Rao
Owner team: engineering
Status: published
Last updated: 2026-10-12
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This document provides a compact, hands-on set of playground labs, SDK integration templates, API examples, and canonical error-injection recipes intended for developer onboarding, SDK maintainers, and support engineers. It is optimized for fast experimentation in a local sandbox and for producing reproducible support bundles when escalating issues to runtime or infra teams.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Give engineers a low-friction sandbox to validate common SDK integration patterns (auth, streaming, batching, local cache).
- Provide reproducible error-injection recipes to surface failure modes seen in customer support cases.
- Capture canonical fixes and triage checklists so support and SDK teams respond consistently.
- Define docs-site ownership and release steps for snippets and quickstarts.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Developer experience engineers (SDK owners)
- Support engineers and solutions engineers
- New platform integrators and developer advocates
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) Quickstart labs (local)
2) API examples (curl, Python, Node)
3) SDK template layout and recommended config table
4) Docs site operating procedure for snippet updates and release gating
5) Top support issues and canonical fixes (triage + commands)
6) Ownership, metrics, and lifecycle

1) Quickstart labs (local)
Overview: Each lab is runnable in under 10 minutes on a developer workstation. The labs assume a Redwood API key available in REDWOOD_API_KEY and Docker (for the local proxy) if you want to simulate network faults. Use the sandbox token (org-sandbox) for functional testing only.

Lab A: Auth + Simple Generation
- Objective: Validate SDK credential handling and error semantics.
- Steps:
  1. Install: pip install redwood-sdk==0.6.0 (or npm i @redwood/sdk@0.6.0)
  2. Set credentials: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk-sandbox-xxxx"
  3. Run example: python examples/auth_gen.py
- Expected output: JSON with tokens_used, model_name, and a 200-level response.
- Failure injection: run with REDWOOD_API_KEY="" to verify 401 handling and telemetry breadcrumbs.

Lab B: Streaming and Resume Simulation
- Objective: Validate partial responses and resume semantics used by front-end clients.
- Steps:
  1. Start local stub: docker run -p 8080:8080 redwood/local-runtime-stub:0.4
  2. Run node streaming example: node examples/stream_resume.js --url http://localhost:8080
  3. Kill the process at token 60 and run again to validate idempotent resume.
- Failure injection: use tc/netem to add 200ms packet loss on loopback.

Lab C: Batching + Local Prefetch Cache
- Objective: Measure latency and unit cost impact of local prefetch + batcher.
- Steps:
  1. Start the batcher: ./bin/local-batcher --config examples/batcher.yaml
  2. Run the load script: python examples/batch_load.py --qps 20 --dur 60
  3. Inspect metrics: curl http://localhost:9100/metrics | grep redwood_batch_latency
- Expected thresholds: p95 < 120ms with batch size <= 8; cost/token reduced by ~18% when cache hit ratio >= 0.6

2) API examples (copiable)
Curl: single-shot generation
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-small-2026","input":"Summarize the following..."}'
```
Python (requests): streaming w/ reconnect logic
```
import requests
from requests.exceptions import RequestException

URL = "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']}"}
try:
  r = requests.post(URL, json={"model":"redwood-small-2026","input":"..."}, stream=True, timeout=30)
  for line in r.iter_lines():
    if line:
      print(line.decode())
except RequestException as e:
  # canonical retry backoff for SDKs: 100ms, 500ms, 1s
  print("retrying", e)
```
Node (sdk snippet): resumable stream + telemetry event
```
const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk')
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const stream = client.stream({ model: 'redwood-small-2026', input: '...' })
stream.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk))
stream.on('closed', () => client.telemetry.event('stream.closed'))
```

3) SDK template layout and recommended config
Purpose: A baseline SDK layout that reduces onboarding time for new language SDKs.
sections.heading: Contents

sections.body:
- /src/index.js or /src/__init__.py (public entrypoint)
- /examples/* (playground snippets)
- /test/golden/* (integration goldens e2e-lite)
- /docs/snippets/* (extracted snippets for docs site)
- /scripts/ci/* (smoke harness)
sections.heading: Recommended file layout

sections.body:
| setting | description | recommended default | owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| batcher.max_size | max queued requests per batch | 8 | sdk-team |
| retry.backoff_initial_ms | initial backoff on 5xx/timeout | 100 | sdk-team |
| telemetry.level | snapshot vs full | snapshot | devx-team |
| local_cache.ttl_seconds | ephemeral prefetch TTL | 30 | devx-team |
| snippet.auto_sync | copy examples into docs site on release | true | docs-engineering |

4) Docs site operating procedure (snippets and releases)
This section defines how snippet changes are validated and released to the docs site to avoid regressions.
sections.heading: Minimum config table

sections.body:
1. Update snippet in /docs/snippets with a runnable marker and include a smoke test under /test/golden that completes inside CI (30s wall).
2. Open PR with label docs:snippet and request reviewers from devx and sdk teams.
3. CI must pass both unit + golden smoke. Golden run must post a synthetic telemetry event to the staging snippet-harness.
4. Docs release steps (owner: docs-engineering):
   a. Merge PR after approvals.
   b. Run docs-site preview pipeline and verify snippet rendering at https://docs-staging.redwood.ai/snippets/<slug>
   c. Create release note in product-docs/release-notes referencing snippet id.
   d. If change modifies API surface, a feature flag must be set and a 2-week deprecation notice posted on SDK CHANGELOG.
sections.heading: Checklist for snippet or quickstart updates

sections.body:
1. Revert merge in the docs repo.
2. Create a Patch release for the SDK with the old snippet embedded as a fallback comment.
3. Notify support and post incident note in #devx-snippet-incidents.

5) Top support issues and canonical fixes
A compact list of recurring issues observed in support tickets, with triage steps and canonical fixes. Use these as the first-pass checklist when assembling a support bundle.

Issue: Authentication failures (403/401)
- Symptom: sudden spike of 401s from a single tenant after a regional failover.
- Quick triage:
  1. Verify token expiry: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 --decode || (note: some tokens are opaque)
  2. Check request timestamps vs server logs: curl "https://logs.redwood.ai/query?tenant=...&from=now-15m" -H "Authorization: Bearer $AUDIT_TOKEN"
- Canonical fix: Confirm token rotation window was applied; if rotated mid-deploy, advise client to use retry with 429/401 handshake: 1) fetch new token, 2) replay idempotent requests.

Issue: Streaming partial payload stops mid-response
- Symptom: Front-end sees stream close at ~50–80 tokens with no finalization event.
- Quick triage:
  1. Collect client side socket logs and server stream-ids: identify last sequence id.
  2. Correlate with runtime instance (X-Instance-ID header) and check instance health (systemd logs, OOM).
- Canonical fix: In SDKs implement resumable sequence-id resume: send last_ack and resume_token; if resume fails, fall back to retriable deterministic regeneration with a note in telemetry.

Issue: Batcher latency spikes at p95
- Symptom: p95 latency for generation increases by >200ms after traffic shift.
- Quick triage:
  1. Inspect batch size distribution: curl http://batcher-host:9000/debug/batches
  2. Check cache hit ratio: curl http://local-cache:9119/metrics | grep cache_hit_ratio
- Canonical fix: Reduce max window to 50ms for latency-sensitive routes and promote local cache prefetch for the affected route. Add an autoscaling policy for batcher pool if sustained QPS over commit.

6) Metrics, ownership, and lifecycle
- Runtime for docs updates: docs snippets should be validated weekly in a Golden CI job. Failing snippets generate a pager during business hours only.
- Owners:
  - SDK snippets: devx-sdks (primary), sdk-team (secondary)
  - Streaming examples: eng-serving-runtime (primary), devx-sdks (secondary)
  - Docs publishing pipeline: docs-engineering (primary)
- KPIs to track:
  - snippet_runnable_rate (goal 98%)
  - mean_time_to_fix_snippet_broken (target < 48 hours)
  - support_escalation_rate_due_to_snippets (target < 2%)

Appendix: Useful commands and debugging snippets
- Collect support bundle (local):
  tar czf support-bundle-$(date +%s).tgz logs/*.log metrics/*.prom diagnostics/*.json
- Simulate 10% packet loss locally (Linux):
  sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 10%
- Canonical script to replay a failed request with idempotency key (bash):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/replay -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -d '{"idempotency_key":"<key>","original_request":{...}}'
sections.heading: Emergency rollback (if snippet causes production SDK break)

sections.body:
- See also: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/multi-model-orchestration-sdk-samples-and-exchange-format-2025
- See also: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook
sections.heading: Cross references

sections.body:
- Reviewed quarterly by devx owners. Major SDK version bumps require snippet smoke revalidation and a docs freeze window of 72 hours prior to release.

If you have questions or want a live walkthrough of the labs, ping #devx-playgrounds or assign to the author.
