payload.page_title: SDK Mini Runner and Curated Sample Catalog

sections.body:
Overview

This page describes the SDK Mini Runner (a lightweight execution harness) and the Curated Sample Catalog — a structured collection of short, runnable SDK examples intended for developer onboarding, support diagnostics, and reproducible canonical fixes. The goal is to reduce time-to-value for new users, speed root-cause analysis for support, and provide a single source-of-truth for sample quality and telemetry.

Goals
- Provide a 1–2 minute local run experience that demonstrates common API patterns (generation, streaming, embeddings, function calling).
- Ensure every sample is runnable with a single command and emits standardized telemetry for triage.
- Maintain a small, high-quality catalog of categorized samples that map to known support issues and canonical fixes.
- Make adding, reviewing, and releasing samples low-friction for engineers and DX writers.

Audience
- SDK maintainers and contributors
- Developer advocates and technical writers
- Support engineers and Solutions Engineering
- Product teams creating integration examples

What is the SDK Mini Runner?
- Lightweight Python-based harness (<= 150 LOC) and equivalent Node starter that:
  - boots a minimal virtualenv/node environment (optional)
  - sets required environment variables from .env or CLI flags
  - runs a sample script and validates expected outputs (basic assertions)
  - captures and uploads (or prints) standardized telemetry and a short run artifact (trace + token counts)

Core components
1) runner/ (python) or runner-js/ (node)
  - run_sample.py / run-sample.js — entrypoint that normalizes env, sanitizes keys, and executes a sample
2) samples/catalog.yaml — metadata registry for all samples (id, path, description, tags, owner, required_env, expected_assertions, telemetry_profile)
3) templates/ — canonical starter templates (generation, streaming, embeddings, multimodal-stub, function-calling)
4) tooling/diagnostics.sh — helper script used by support to reproduce environment and collect artifacts

Sample catalog metadata (catalog.yaml schema excerpt)
- id: sdk-quick-gen-01
- path: samples/generation/quick-gen.py
- description: "Minimal text generation using Redwood hosted model (streaming optional)."
- owner: devx-team@redwood.ai
- tags: ["generation", "streaming", "quickstart"]
- required_env: ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"]
- expected_assertions: ["response contains 'Hello'"]
- telemetry_profile: "sample-minimal-v1"

Adding a new sample (step-by-step)
1. Author the sample under samples/{category}/ with filename short-dashed (e.g., quick-gen.py). Keep <= 80 lines.
2. Add a short README.md next to the sample that documents intents, input, and expected output.
3. Update samples/catalog.yaml with metadata and set owner to a team alias.
4. Run the Mini Runner locally: python runner/run_sample.py --sample samples/generation/quick-gen.py --smoke
   - Expectation: runner exits 0 and prints "SMOKE PASSED".
5. Create a PR against the repo, add reviewer from owner team, and include a short snippet demonstrating observed output.
6. CI job (sample-smoke-check) will execute the runner in a controlled environment and fail the PR if assertions do not hold.

Template: minimal Python generation sample (in README)
```python
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient()
resp = client.generate("Say hello to the world in one sentence")
assert "hello" in resp.text.lower()
print(resp.text)
```

Telemetry and observability requirements
- Every sample must emit the following fields to the local artifact JSON:
  - sample_id
  - sdk_version
  - model_id
  - duration_ms
  - token_input_count
  - token_output_count
  - error_code (if present)
- The Mini Runner will create artifacts in artifacts/{sample_id}/{timestamp}.json. Support can attach these artifacts to a ticket.
- Telemetry profile names should follow: sample-{category}-{stability}-v{n} (e.g., sample-generation-stable-v1).

Support triage mapping (canonical fixes)
- Common symptom: "intermittent streaming disconnects in Python SDK"
  - Canonical sample: streaming/stream-disconnect-demo.py
  - Debug: capture artifacts, run runner with --trace-stream, validate keepalive and chunk sizes.
  - Fix template: update sample to use client.stream(timeout_ms=45000) and add retry logic.
- Common symptom: "deterministic token delta vs console"
  - Canonical sample: embeddings/token-count-check.py
  - Debug: runner prints token counts; compare to service token meter. If mismatch, file issue to runtime team with attached artifact.

CI and release process for the catalog
- All sample PRs must pass sample-smoke-check in CI. The check runs runner in Linux and macOS matrix, node and python where applicable.
- Weekly smoke sweep: a scheduled job runs the full catalog, failing owners by email if a sample regresses.
- To promote a sample from draft -> stable: owner marks telemetry_profile with "stable" and documents a short release note entry. The sample is then eligible for inclusion in the public docs.

Quality guidance and length limits
- Keep samples focused: 30–80 lines; no external infra dependencies.
- Prefer deterministic assertions rather than fuzzy text checks. Use explicit token counts where possible.
- Mark samples that are flaky with tag "flaky" and add mitigation notes. Support should avoid relying on flaky samples for customer repros.

Ownership and governance
- Owner field in catalog metadata is the primary reviewer and oncall contact for the sample.
- Quarterly catalog review: DX leads schedule a review to prune stale samples and rotate owners.
- Deleting a sample requires an owner-approved PR and a changelog entry.

Support playbook: using the catalog during an incoming ticket
1. Identify symptom and map to tags (e.g., "streaming") or search for sample IDs in the catalog.
2. Ask customer to run the matching sample with the Runner (see Support quick-run CLI snippet below).
3. Request artifacts folder created by runner and attach to the ticket.
4. If artifact shows a runtime issue (errors, token mismatch), escalate to eng-serving-runtime with artifact and minimal repro steps.

Support quick-run CLI snippet
```bash
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk.xxx python runner/run_sample.py --sample samples/generation/quick-gen.py --smoke --upload-artifact
```

Maintenance checklist for DX owners (template)
- [ ] Sample runs locally with runner and CI smoke-check.
- [ ] README includes intent, expected outputs, and troubleshooting notes.
- [ ] Telemetry artifact fields present and validated.
- [ ] Tags and owner are accurate in catalog.yaml.
- [ ] No flaky network dependencies.

FAQ
Q: Can a sample call internal-only endpoints?
A: No. Samples must be runnable against hosted public models or a documented stub. If an internal-only flow is required, include a commented stub and mark sample as "internal" with confidentiality set to restricted and add explicit owner_reviewers.

Q: Who reviews sample PRs?
A: The owner listed in catalog.yaml is responsible for the first review. DX lead should be added as secondary reviewer for new categories.

Related pages and references
- SDK observability cookbook: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-observability-telemetry-cookbook-2026
- Docs site publishing guide: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/docs-site-content-lifecycle-and-local-preview-2026

Appendix: example artifact JSON (trimmed)
| field | example |
|------|---------|
| sample_id | sdk-quick-gen-01 |
| sdk_version | python-1.3.5 |
| model_id | redwood/gpt-4x-mini |
| duration_ms | 312 |
| token_input_count | 18 |
| token_output_count | 42 |
| error_code | null |

Contact and escalation
- Primary contact: devx-team@redwood.ai
- Emergency oncall: eng-sre on-call (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)

Change log
- 2025-07-15: Created (Marisol Ortega)
- 2026-02-12: Added telemetry profile conventions and CI smoke sweep process (reviewers: Evan Cho, Priya Nair)

payload.page_title: Compact telemetry onboarding playbook for SDK integrators

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: A compact, opinionated onboarding playbook for teams integrating Redwood SDKs (server and client) that need end-to-end telemetry, cost visibility, and fast incident triage. This page is intended for engineering leads, SREs, and SDK authors who want a minimal set of configs, example snippets, and canonical fixes to get reliable telemetry in production within a single sprint.

What this covers
- Required telemetry primitives we expect from SDK integrations (metrics, traces, structured logs).
- A minimal configuration template for libraries and application-level exporters.
- Quick verification steps (smoke checks) you can run in <30 minutes.
- Top 6 support issues we see with SDK telemetry and fixed resolutions (canonical fixes).
- Ownership, SLOs, and escalation path for telemetry gaps.

Who should use this
- Feature teams adopting Redwood generation/embedding SDKs for the first time.
- Internal SDK maintainers responsible for shipping new client adapters.
- Platform/SRE teams onboarding a tenant or customer with custom telemetry requirements.

Key telemetry primitives (opinionated)
1) Metrics (required)
- request.count: counter per route (generation, embeddings, rerank).
- request.tokens.total: cumulative token count per model variant.
- request.latency.ms: histogram with p50/p90/p95 buckets.
- sdk.auth.failures: counter for token/credentials errors.
- sdk.cache.hits and sdk.cache.misses: counters for prefix/KV cache usage.

2) Traces (required)
- Span per SDK request with attributes: sdk.version, model.family, model.variant, route, tenant_id, request_id.
- Parent span should correlate to application request_id (http.request_id or generated GUID).

3) Structured logs (recommended)
- Include JSON fields: timestamp, level, request_id, duration_ms, model.variant, error_code.
- Avoid PII in logs; use redaction filters for prompt content.

Minimal configuration template (example)\nPlace this in your service config (config/telemetry.yaml):

| key | description | sample value |
|-----|-------------|--------------|
| exporter.type | One of prometheus|otlp|datadog | otlp |
| exporter.otlp.endpoint | OTLP collector URL | https://otlp.collector.internal:4317 |
| metrics.prefix | Metric namespace for SDK metrics | redwood.sdk |
| traces.enabled | Enable distributed tracing | true |
| logging.format | json|text | json |
| sdk.telemetry.sample_rate | Fraction of requests traced (0.0-1.0) | 0.05 |
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```yaml
telemetry:
  exporter:
    type: otlp
    otlp:
      endpoint: https://otlp.collector.internal:4317
  metrics:
    prefix: redwood.sdk
  traces:
    enabled: true
  sdk:
    telemetry:
      sample_rate: 0.05
```

Client-side initialization snippets
- Node (official SDK adapter):
```js
import RedwoodSDK from '@redwood/sdk';
import { OTLPExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http';

// initialize tracing exporter before SDK
const exporter = new OTLPExporter({ url: process.env.OTLP_ENDPOINT });
// opentelemetry setup omitted for brevity

const client = new RedwoodSDK({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY,
  telemetry: { enabled: true, sampleRate: 0.05 }
});
```

- Python (server side example):
```py
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_KEY'), telemetry={"enabled": True, "sample_rate": 0.05})
```

Verification smoke checks (run after deploy)
1) Metric check (prometheus):
- Query: rate(redwood_sdk_request_count[5m]) >= 0.1
- Expected: any steady-state service should show >0 requests/min during traffic.

2) Trace correlation check:
- Trigger a generation request with a known request_id header.
- In tracing UI, search for span attribute request_id=<id>. The span should contain model.variant, tokens and status.

3) Log sampling check:
- Simulate error (invalid api key) -> ensure sdk.auth.failures increments and logs include request_id.

Top 6 SDK telemetry support issues and canonical fixes
1) Missing token metrics (request.tokens.total == 0)
Symptoms: request.count increments but request.tokens.total remains zero.
Cause: SDK-level token accounting disabled or sample-rate=0 for token collector. In some language SDKs token counting requires the tokenizer dependency to be present.
sections.heading: YAML example (service config snippet)

sections.body:
- Ensure your dependency tree includes the official tokenizer package (node: @redwood/tokenizer, python: redwood-tokenizer).
- Set telemetry.token_count.enabled: true in runtime config.
- Redeploy and validate with token-producing request.

2) No traces showing up in OTLP/Tracing backend
Symptoms: traces.enabled==true but tracing UI empty.
Cause: exporter misconfiguration (wrong endpoint, TLS issues) or SDK not instrumenting network layer.
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body:
- curl the OTLP endpoint from the pod: curl -v $OTLP_ENDPOINT/health.
- Check SDK logs for exporter init errors. If TLS fails, add CA bundle or use internal collector with plaintext on loopback.
- Confirm env var OTLP_HEADERS if used.

3) Traces missing model attributes (model.variant absent)
Symptoms: spans exist but missing model.family or variant.
Cause: SDK feature flag disabled when model name inferred asynchronously.
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body:
- Ensure requests include explicit model identifier (e.g., model: "redwood-medgen-v2"). If you pass a model alias, add mapping at SDK init: { model_aliases: { chat_default: 'redwood-medgen-v2' } }.
- Upgrade to SDK >= 1.12 which fixes delayed-attribute instrumentation.

4) High cardinality metric explosion (too many distinct labels)
Symptoms: metrics backend shows explosion of series and rising costs.
Cause: unbounded label values (full prompt or user-generated ids) used as metric labels.
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body:
- Audit metrics instrument calls. Only use controlled enums as labels (route, model.variant, tenant_tier). Remove user or prompt IDs from labels and move to span attributes or logs.
- Add a sanitizer in SDK config: label_blacklist: ["prompt", "user_text"].

5) Duplicate request_count from proxies and SDK
Symptoms: request.count doubled after introducing a gateway.
Cause: both the gateway and SDK are instrumenting the same logical request.
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body:
- Adopt a single counting instrumenter: prefer gateway for ingress-level metrics and disable sdk.request_metrics at SDK init: { metrics: { request_count: false } }.
- For fine-grained per-model breakdowns keep SDK-level metrics and switch off gateway-level per-model labeling.

6) Telemetry causing latency regressions in high-qps paths
Symptoms: p95 latency increases after enabling traces at 100% sampling.
Cause: synchronous exporter or heavy serialization in hot path.
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body:
- Use asynchronous batching exporter; set traces.batch.max_size=512 and traces.batch.timeout_ms=1000.
- Reduce sampling to 1-5% for production: sdk.telemetry.sample_rate: 0.01.

Runbook: triage path for missing telemetry
1) Confirm symptoms with a known user flow (replay test if possible).
2) Check SDK logs for initialization errors (grep "telemetry" /var/log/app/*.log).
3) Validate env vars and config file at runtime: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- cat /etc/service/config/telemetry.yaml
4) Curl OTLP endpoint from the pod.
5) If traces present but attributes missing, capture a HAR/recording and forward to SDK maintainers with sanitized example.
6) If metrics cardinality high, revert the change via feature flag and open a follow-up to change instrumentation.

SLOs and alert thresholds (opinionated defaults)
- Metric export success rate: 99.9% over 5m (alert if <99.0%).
- Trace delivery failure rate: <1% over 10m.
- SDK auth failures: alert if >5 occurrences in 5m for a tenant.
- Metric cardinality: alert when series growth >10%/hour for 3 consecutive hours.

Ownership and escalation
- Owner: SDK Telemetry team (primary contact: Miguel Alvarez).
- Support: Developer Experience oncall (pager duty: #devx-oncall).
- Escalation: If suspected exporter or infra issue, escalate to Observability Infra (page: #obs-infra).

Templates + artifacts
- telemetry.yaml.example: canonical config for service (paste above).
- sample-trace-request.http: a small HTTP file you can run with curl or Hoppscotch to produce a trace with request_id header.
- repro-harness: lightweight script (./scripts/prod-smoke.sh) that runs the three smoke checks. Attach to issue when filing.

Appendix: sample smoke script (unix)
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
REQ_ID="test-$(date +%s)"
sections.heading: Canonical fix

sections.body: curl -s -H "X-Request-Id: $REQ_ID" -X POST $SERVICE_URL/v1/generate -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-lite","input":"hello"}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" >/dev/null
sections.heading: 1) generate request

sections.body: kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/redwood_sdk_request_count" | jq '.' || true
sections.heading: 2) check metrics

sections.body:
echo "Verify trace in tracing UI for request_id=$REQ_ID"
```

Notes and best practices
- Prefer OTLP to direct vendor exporters; route through the company collector to centralize headers and rate limits.
- Keep metric labels small and enumerable. Use tags for free text in logs.
- Add a telemetry smoke in PR gating for SDK adapters. A failing smoke should block merges for the adapter.
- Document breaking telemetry changes in the SDK release notes and notify Developer Experience at least 3 days before release.

Related pages and artifacts
- SDK telemetry integration checklist (internal template)
- Support triage checklist for telemetry incidents
- SDK release notes: include telemetry changes section

Contact and feedback
- For feedback on this playbook, open a PR against /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates and add reviewers Miguel Alvarez and Sara Kim.
- For urgent incidents: DM Miguel Alvarez and escalate to #devx-oncall.

Revision history
- 2026-10-05: initial draft by Priya Shah
- 2026-12-14: added canonical fixes and runbook steps (reviewed by Miguel Alvarez)
- 2027-03-12: formalized SLOs and added smoke script (Sara Kim)

payload.page_title: SDK Integration Labs: Embeddings-to-Generation Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
========

This playbook is a hands-on lab for engineers integrating Redwood SDKs into applications that combine embeddings, reranking, and text generation. It is intended for developer productivity teams, platform integrators, and application engineers who need a tested set of patterns, canonical fixes, and reproducible examples that map real product use-cases to best-practice SDK wiring.

Goals
-----
- Provide minimal, copy-paste-ready code paths for common combined workflows (embed -> search -> re-rank -> generate).
- Surface top support failure patterns and canonical fixes tied to telemetry and SDK logs.
- Offer a repeatable lab flow for developer onboarding and internal training.
- Document recommended SDK versions, runtime flags, and configuration table for production parity.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
- Building semantic search + generation features (e.g., knowledge base Q&A).
- Implementing multi-step pipelines where embeddings index and generation model are different sizes.
- Troubleshooting noisy or inconsistent generation after reranking.

Quick Architecture
------------------
1) Input preprocessing: user query normalization and prompt templating.
2) Embeddings call: obtain dense vectors for query and corpus.
3) Vector search: retrieve N candidates from index (local/faiss or managed index).
4) Rerank: light model or cross-encoder to reorder by relevance score.
5) Assemble generation prompt: inject chosen candidates and control tokens.
6) Generation: Redwood SDK call to hosted model with token budget and streaming.
7) Post-processing: deterministic cleanup, citation insertion, and telemetry emit.

Code snippets (Python)
----------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")
sections.heading: Minimal end-to-end (pseudo-code, copyable)

sections.body: query_vec = client.embeddings.create(input=[query])['data'][0]['embedding']
sections.heading: 1. embeddings

sections.body: cands = index.search(query_vector=query_vec, top_k=10)
sections.heading: 2. vector search (assume managed index client)

sections.body:
scores = client.rerank.batch(inputs=[{"query": query, "document": d['text']} for d in cands])
cands = sorted(zip(cands, scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
sections.heading: 3. rerank (optional lightweight re-ranker)

sections.body:
prompt = make_prompt(query, [d['text'] for d, _ in cands[:3]])
resp = client.responses.create(model="redwood-gen-1.3", input=prompt, max_tokens=400, stream=True)
for chunk in resp.iter_stream():
    print(chunk.get('text', ''), end='')

Code snippets (JavaScript)
-------------------------
// Node.js minimal flow (using @redwood/sdk)
const {Redwood} = require('@redwood/sdk')
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY })

// embeddings
const qVec = await client.embeddings.create({ input: [query] })

// search & rerank (pseudo)
const results = await index.search(qVec.data[0].embedding, 10)
const reranked = await client.rerank.batch(results.map(r => ({ query, document: r.text })))

// generation
const prompt = buildPrompt(query, reranked.slice(0,3).map(r=>r.text))
const gen = await client.responses.create({ model: 'redwood-gen-1.3', input: prompt, max_tokens: 400 })
console.log(gen.output_text)

Operational configuration table
-------------------------------
| Setting | Recommended value | Rationale |
|---------|-------------------|-----------|
| embeddings.model | text-embed-002-mini | Fast production embeddings for KB-style queries |
| search.top_k | 10 | Tradeoff between recall and prompt token budget |
| rerank.enabled | true for high-precision flows | Use only when precision matters; costs increase |
| generation.model | redwood-gen-1.3 (or redwood-gen-1.5 for longer contexts) | Predictable latency/quality tradeoff |
| generation.max_tokens | 300-600 | Depends on UI and latency SLO |
| streaming | enabled for interactive features | Reduces perceived latency for end-users |

Lab run: step-by-step developer flow
-----------------------------------
1) Clone the repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdks-integration-labs.git && cd sdks-integration-labs
2) Set env: export REDWOOD_KEY=... INDEX_ENDPOINT=...
3) Start local index (optional): docker-compose up -d faiss-index
4) Run ingest script: python tools/ingest_corpus.py --source=kb/2025 --batch-size=256
5) Execute the smoke test: python examples/e2e_smoke.py --query="How does token caching affect latency?"
6) Inspect traces in the Console: open /console/traces?trace_id=...

Top support issues and canonical fixes
-------------------------------------
- Symptom: Low-quality reranking causes hallucinations in the generator.
  - Root causes: using semantic-similarity embedding (dense) as a relevance score without reranker; prompt context includes noisy sections.
  - Canonical fixes: enable a cross-encoder reranker for top_k 5 and strip low-confidence sections via a relevance-threshold filter.

- Symptom: High latency during cold-start of large generation models.
  - Root causes: model spin-up on cold nodes, lack of warm pools, large context windows.
  - Canonical fixes: enable warm-pool for generation nodes in Redwood Dedicated or set lower max_tokens for first-response and enable streaming. Add a health-check warmup during deploy.

- Symptom: Token cost spikes after enabling rerank.
  - Root causes: reranker using full cross-encoder on entire candidate set; excessive generation retries.
  - Canonical fixes: limit reranker to top_k 10, use a distilled reranker for production, and add budget guardrails in the SDK middleware that enforce max_retries and token caps per request.

Telemetry and observability guidance
----------------------------------
- Required spans/events to emit: request_id, user_id_hash, embedding_model, embed_latency_ms, search_time_ms, rerank_time_ms, gen_model, gen_latency_ms, output_tokens, fallback_triggered.
- SLOs (recommended for KB Q&A): 95th latency end-to-end <= 800ms (cached), 99th <= 2.5s. Token cost per Q <= $0.05 for median.
- Dashboards to create: 'KB Q&A Latency (per-route)', 'Embeddings Quality by Recall', 'Reranker False-Positive Rate', 'Generation Token Spend by Route'.

Testing and regression guards
---------------------------
- Unit testable components: prompt-templates, prompt-assembly, post-processors.
- Integration tests: golden-response harness that runs sample queries and checks top-1 answer fingerprint.
- Canary gate: run the goldens against new generation model or reranker, require >= 95% fingerprint match and no more than 1% regression in precision@1.

Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
--------------------------------
1. Verify API keys and region: REDWOOD_KEY and region envs.
2. Inspect SDK logs at DEBUG for wire payloads (embeddings vectors, candidate IDs).
3. Confirm index health: top_k returns non-empty results and latency < 200ms.
4. Run reranker locally against sample pairs to ensure positive scores for obvious matches.
5. Run generation in streaming mode to check first-byte latency.
6. If hallucination persists, reduce context size and re-evaluate reranker threshold.

Appendix: Example prompt template
--------------------------------
Template ID: kb2gen_v1

Prompt structure (tokens counted)
- System instruction (20 tokens)
- User question (variable)
- Top3 context snippets (each ~120 tokens)
- Safety and citation instruction (40 tokens)
sections.heading: 4. generate with context

sections.body:
"System: You are a helpful assistant that answers using only the provided context.
Question: {user_question}
sections.heading: Prompt example

sections.body:
1) {context_1}
2) {context_2}
3) {context_3}
Answer concisely and include citations in square brackets."

Ownership and contact
---------------------
Owner: DX Platform (Maya Chen)
Oncall: eng-devx rotation (see /teams/eng-developer-experience/oncall)
For questions: slac #devx-integration or email maya.chen@redwood.ai

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Created initial draft and example flows.
- 2026-01-07: Added JS snippets and telemetry fields per review.
- 2026-02-15: Finalized SLOs and canonical fixes after pilot with partners.
sections.heading: Context

payload.page_title: SDK Canary & Feature-Flagging Runtime Playbook

sections.body: This playbook documents Redwood's recommended patterns for integrating SDK-level feature flags and canary rollouts with the inference runtime. The goal is to enable low-risk feature launches (model variants, quantization profiles, batching policies, client-side fallbacks) while preserving SLOs and clear rollback criteria. This is a developer-facing guide with concrete examples, observability signals, and operational runbook steps.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Audience: SDK engineers, platform integrators, and partners implementing canarying across Hosted / Dedicated / Private deployments.
- Scope: client-side flagging APIs, server-side evaluation, runtime routing ties, metrics & dashboards, rollout steps, and common failure modes and fixes.
- Not covered: deep kernel selection or GPU scheduling internals (see eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture).
sections.heading: Context and scope

sections.body:
- Controlled percentage rollouts: progressively increase client population receiving the new behavior.
- Server-evaluated flags vs local evaluations: tradeoffs between control and latency.
- Runtime-binding: mapping a feature flag to a routing policy (model id, quantized variant, batch profile).
- Safety gates: automated SLO checks and manual review thresholds.
sections.heading: Key concepts (short)

sections.body:
- SDK integrations and flag client libraries: eng-developer-experience (primary).
- Runtime routing / fallback policies: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-platform (support).
- Observability & alert rules: eng-platform / eng-sre (collaborative).
sections.heading: Who owns what

sections.body:
- 99th percentile end-to-end request latency from SDK to response: <= 800 ms (for interactive workloads).
- Per-route token generation error rate: <= 0.5% (5e-3).
- Canary invocation error rate threshold to pause rollout: absolute increase of >= 0.4 percentage points above baseline or relative increase >= 2x (whichever is lower sensitivity).
- Token-cost variance guard: if average tokens-per-request increases by >= 20% vs baseline during a window, trigger review.
sections.heading: SLOs and safety thresholds (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- Flag IDs must be globally unique and namespaced by team: <team>.<area>.<feature>, e.g., dx.sdk.canary.new-fallback.
- Flags section (recommended fields in the flag registry):
  - id (string, unique),
  - owner (team/person),
  - default (bool),
  - evaluation_mode (server | client_local | hybrid),
  - rollout_policy (percentage / user_ids / attribute-based),
  - linked_runtime_bindings (list of runtime route ids),
  - monitor_checks (list of metric ids),
  - safe_quarantine (bool) — if true, runtime will route failing requests to a safe default.
sections.heading: Feature-flag semantics and naming conventions

sections.body:
1) Server-evaluated flags (control-plane):
   - SDK includes a lightweight flag-fetch client that queries the Redwood control plane or customer-managed flags store.
   - Advantages: central decisioning, immediate global changes, easier auditing.
   - Tradeoffs: extra network call; recommend caching TTL 5–30s and push invalidation for critical kills.

2) Client-local evaluation (edge):
   - SDK ships deterministic hashing and local rollout config so evaluation happens in-process.
   - Advantages: zero extra latency, resilience during control-plane outage.
   - Tradeoffs: rollout adjustments have slower propagation; must secure signed configs.

3) Hybrid: server provides signed rollout tokens and the client applies them locally with short TTLs.
sections.heading: Architecture patterns (high level)

sections.body:
- Each flag must map to one or more runtime route IDs. Example mapping table:

  | flag_id | runtime_route | description | safe_fallback_route |
  |---------|---------------|-------------|---------------------|
  | dx.sdk.canary.prefetch-cache | route:model-v2-prefetch | prefetch enabled -> uses model-v2 prefix cache | route:model-v1 |

- Runtime route names should follow the pattern: route:<model>-<variant>-<profile>.
sections.heading: Binding flags to runtime routes

sections.body:
1) Minimal server-eval flow (Python):

```
from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=env.API_KEY)
sections.heading: SDK integration examples (pseudocode)

sections.body:
resp = client.generate(
    model="model-v2",
    prompt=user_prompt,
    metadata={"user_id": user_id}
)
```
Server returns flags in response headers when enabled; the SDK will apply immediate local routing if a flag indicates a different route.

2) Local hash-based rollout (Node.js example):

```
import { SDK } from 'redwood-sdk'
const sdk = new SDK({ flagConfigUrl: 'https://flags.redwood.local/signed.json', flagTtlMs: 15000 })

const selected = sdk.flags.evaluate('dx.sdk.canary.local-retry', { user_id })
if (selected) {
  // switch to a conservative retry policy
  sdk.setRequestPolicy({ retries: 2, backoffMs: 200 })
}
```

Observability: what to instrument (metric names and recommended dashboards):
- Metrics to emit from SDKs:
  - sdk.flag_evaluations.count (tags: flag_id, rollout_bucket)
  - sdk.flag_applied.count (tags: flag_id, route, client_version)
  - sdk.flag_evaluation_latency_ms.pX (p50/p95)
- Runtime / route metrics (existing):
  - runtime.request.duration_ms (route, model_version)
  - runtime.request.errors.count (route, error_type)
  - runtime.tokens.generated.count (route)
sections.heading: request metadata attaches user id for percentage rollouts

sections.body:
- "Canary Overview" (per-flag): shows applied rate, error delta vs baseline, latency p95, token cost delta.
- "Flag Health" (global): flags with steep recent change in applied rate, flagged rules failing guard rails.
sections.heading: Recommended dashboards (quick links placeholder)

sections.body:
1) Canary error spike (page):
   - Condition: runtime.request.errors.count for linked routes increases by >= 0.4 percentage points over baseline in 5m window AND absolute count > 10.
   - Notify: eng-developer-experience oncall, eng-serving-runtime.

2) Latency regression (pager escalated if at night):
   - Condition: runtime.request.duration_ms.p95 for route > baseline_p95 * 1.5 for 10m.
   - Notify: eng-sre.
sections.heading: Alerting rules (examples)

sections.body:
1) Preflight (developer):
   - Create flag entry in registry (include owner, monitor_checks).
   - Add server and local client evaluation code paths; include unit tests for deterministic rollout hashing.
   - Create a canary dashboard and baseline metrics snapshot (last 7 days).
   - Add feature to SDK changelog and release notes.

2) Early internal canary (1–5%):
   - Release SDK that supports the flag but defaults disabled.
   - Enable flag for 1–2 internal teams / dogfooding users.
   - Monitor error rate, p95 latency, token cost for 1–2 hours.

3) Gradual ramp (5%, 20%, 50%, 100%):
   - Increase percentage in increments. Hold for at least 30–60 minutes at small steps (<=20%), 2–4 hours at larger steps (>20%).
   - At each step, check the guard rails (error rate, latency p95, token delta).

4) Full release:
   - After hitting 100% and maintaining within thresholds for 24h, mark the flag default to enabled and schedule SDK cleanup (remove legacy toggle).
sections.heading: Rollout procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- If any canary alert fires, automated safety policy will set the flag to safe_quarantine (true) which triggers runtime fallback to the safe route binding and emits a audit event.
- Operators can manually flip the flag to 0% or disable the client-side config via signed config revocation.
sections.heading: Rollback and quarantine rules (automated)

sections.body:
1) Triage alert: identify flag_id and affected runtime route(s).
2) Check canary dashboard and recent deploys (SDK + runtime) for correlated changes.
3) If automated quarantine is active, validate that the quarantine route is healthy; if not, escalate to eng-serving-runtime.
4) Rollback: set flag rollout to 0% and post incident stub in #canary-ops with initial observations.
5) Post-incident: capture root cause, update the flag registry notes, and schedule a follow-up retro.

Common failure modes and canonical fixes (top support issues):
- Issue: Flag applied but runtime route not matching expected model variant.
  - Cause: mismatched runtime route naming or registry mapping.
  - Fix: validate flag->route binding table; run `redwood-admin routes list --filter \"model-v2\"` and correct mapping.

- Issue: Client sees wrong rollout bucket after SDK upgrade.
  - Cause: incompatible hash function or missing seed during evaluation.
  - Fix: ensure backward-compatible deterministic hash; if necessary, release a quick SDK patch that honors previous seeds and set the flag to 0% during the roll.

- Issue: Token-cost spikes after enabling a feature.
  - Cause: feature selects a larger model variant or removes caching.
  - Fix: revert rollout, enable token-cost telemetry, and add a preflight test that simulates 1k requests to measure tokens/request before next ramp.

- Issue: Control-plane outage prevents flag evaluation and causes client inconsistencies.
  - Cause: clients relying solely on server evaluation without caching.
  - Fix: enable hybrid mode with signed local configs and short TTL; add fallback to previous config when control-plane unavailable.
sections.heading: Operational runbook (on-call steps)

sections.body:
- Flag registry example:
```
{
  \"id\": \"dx.sdk.canary.retry-policy-v2\",
  \"owner\": \"eng-developer-experience\",
  \"default\": false,
  \"evaluation_mode\": \"hybrid\",
  \"rollout_policy\": {\"type\": \"percentage\", \"value\": 10},
  \"linked_runtime_bindings\": [\"route:model-v2-lowcost\"],
  \"monitor_checks\": [\"runtime.request.errors.count\",\"runtime.request.duration_ms.p95\",\"runtime.tokens.generated.count\"],
  \"safe_quarantine\": true
}
```

- SDK local config (signed blob) example (truncated):
```
{ \"flags\": [ { \"id\": \"dx.sdk.canary.retry-policy-v2\", \"percent\": 10, \"seed\": \"2026-02-10-01\", \"sig\": \"<base64.sig>\" } ] }
```

Release artifact checklist (developer before enabling canary):
- [ ] Unit tests for flag evaluation & hash compatibility.
- [ ] Canary dashboard created with baseline snapshot.
- [ ] Monitor checks wired to alerting rules.
- [ ] Documentation entry with owner and rollback plan.
- [ ] SDK release notes mention the flag and migration steps.

Appendix: quick CLI snippets and helpful commands:
- List routes: redwood-admin routes list --format table
- Show flag history: redwood-admin flags history --flag dx.sdk.canary.retry-policy-v2
- Force quarantine on flag: redwood-admin flags update --id dx.sdk.canary.retry-policy-v2 --safe_quarantine true
sections.heading: Config examples and quick reference (JSON)

sections.body:
Q: Should every SDK toggle be a server-evaluated flag?
A: No. Use server-eval for safety-critical and auditing needs; use local evaluation for latency-sensitive toggles that must operate when control-plane is unreachable. Hybrid is often the best tradeoff.

Q: How long should we hold at each percentage step?
A: For <20% steps: 30–60 minutes is usually sufficient. For larger steps: 2–4 hours and continue monitoring for at least 24h after 100% rollout. Adjust based on traffic patterns and criticality.

payload.page_title: SDK cost-aware slowpath debugging playbook

sections.body:
Overview:
This playbook describes a standard, cost-aware approach for diagnosing and resolving SDK-driven slowpaths (high latency or unexpectedly high per-token costs) that impact customer experiences. It is intended for SDK engineers, on-call members, and SREs who handle customer tickets where the observed runtime is slower or more expensive than expected.

Scope and goals:
- Scope: SDK client + runtime interaction, common misconfigurations, and client-side request patterns that amplify server costs. Does not cover low-level GPU kernel bugs (see eng-serving-runtime) or infra supply issues (see eng-sre).
- Goals: Detect slowpath quickly, gather actionable telemetry, reproduce locally, apply low-risk mitigations, and ship a canonical fix or SDK patch.

Owner and escalation:
- Primary owner: SDK platform (eng-developer-experience) — contact channel #sdk-platform.
- Secondary owner: Serving runtime (eng-serving-runtime) — contact #runtime-observability.
- Escalation: If root cause is unclear after 90 minutes of triage, notify on-call SRE via pager and open an incident following the oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process runbook.

Quick summary checklist (fast path):
1) Confirm the customer SLOs and SLAs.
2) Get sample failing request(s) and a flame/trace.
3) Check SDK config: batching, streaming, max_tokens, tokenization mode.
4) Run local repro with the supplied payload and light telemetry capture.
5) Apply mitigation (client-side timeout, prefix cache, fallback model) and monitor.
6) Author canonical fix (SDK or runtime config) and backfill tests.

Diagnostics and thresholds:
- Baseline SLOs (internal reference):
  - median token latency (internal generation path): 20–40 ms/token
  - p95 token latency: <= 150 ms/token
  - request setup time (handshake + routing): <= 50 ms
- Slowpath detection signals:
  - end-to-end request time > 3x expected baseline for similar request sizes
  - sudden token cost increase > 2x historical median for a customer
  - sustained queueing observed in runtime_metrics.queue_depth > 5 for > 60s

Telemetry captures to collect (minimum):
- Client-side:
  - SDK version, adapter, and configuration (batch_size, concurrent_streams, retry_policy)
  - Request headers: X-RW-Debug-ID, X-RW-Trace-Id
  - Tokenized input length and tokenization library/version
- Server-side (ask runtime team or fetch from tracing):
  - Distributed trace (trace_id) with timeline of routing, batching, and kernel exec
  - Per-stage latencies: routing_ms, queue_ms, batch_exec_ms, kv_fetch_ms
  - Model variant and quantization profile used

Telemetry query examples:
- Grafana (Logs/Traces) quick queries:
  - Traces: trace_id="{trace}" | latency > 3000ms | group_by(stage)
  - Metrics: rate(runtime_metrics.queue_depth > 5)[5m] > 1/minute
- Example trace filter (Jaeger-like):
  - search(service=redwood-runtime, tags={trace_id: "{{trace}}"})

Local reproduction quickstart (SDK):
1) Install diagnostic SDK runner (local):
   pip install redwood-sdk-debug==0.6.0  # or npm install @redwood/sdk-debug
2) Capture tokenization output to reproduce exact tokens:
   python -c "from redwood_sdk_debug import TokenDumper; print(TokenDumper.dump(\"<customer prompt>\"))"
3) Run a single-request local replay with 2s of additional client-side logging:
   redwoodctl replay --input sample.json --capture-trace --output trace.json
4) Upload trace.json to internal trace viewer or attach to ticket.

Common root causes and canonical fixes:
1) Over-eager client batching
   - Symptom: large batches cause kernel contention; spikes in batch_exec_ms and queue_ms.
   - Fix: enforce client-side max_batch_bytes and per-tenant batching caps; SDK change: set default max_batch_size=16 for async adapters and provide guidance in README.
   - Example SDK patch (Python):
     client = RedwoodClient(batching={"max_batch_size": 16, "max_batch_bytes": 256000})

2) Misconfigured streaming + retry loops
   - Symptom: duplicate requests, high token counts, elevated cost.
   - Fix: introduce idempotency keys in SDK streaming adapters and stop automatic naive retry for streaming RPCs.
   - Example header: "X-RW-Idempotency-Key: <uuid>"

3) Tokenization variance (different tokenizers between client and runtime)
   - Symptom: request tokens diverge; p50/p95 token count mismatch; billing shows higher tokens.
   - Fix: add deterministic tokenization compatibility mode to SDK; ship token-diff report in repro runner.

4) Frequent small requests without batching (high per-request overhead)
   - Symptom: many tiny requests generating per-request routing and setup costs; p95 route_setup_ms high.
   - Fix: client guidance to use request bundling helper and per-tenant debounce. Provide SDK helper: bundle_or_call().

5) KV cache thrash due to ephemeral conversations
   - Symptom: high kv_fetch_ms and cache miss rate; repeated long prefix walks.
   - Fix: recommend conversation pinning or per-tenant prefix caching policies; runtime can apply soft-ttl to eviction.

Temporary mitigations (low risk) to apply while building canonical fix:
- Enable client-side static model pin fallback to a cheaper variant (e.g., q4_0 -> q8_0) for 5–10 minutes.
- Apply short synthetic rate limit to noisy tenant: rate_limit_override=50r/s.
- Turn on streaming-only mode to reduce per-request setup for streaming workloads.

SDK examples (diagnostic headers and quick toggles):
- Python snippet to attach debug headers:
  from redwood import RedwoodClient
  client = RedwoodClient(api_key="${REDWOOD_KEY}")
  resp = client.generate(prompt=prompt, headers={"X-RW-Debug-ID": "ticket-1234", "X-RW-Trace-Id": trace_id})
- Node snippet with idempotency key:
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
  await client.generate({ prompt, headers: { 'X-RW-Idempotency-Key': uuid() } });

Support triage template (to paste in ticket):
- Customer summary: [brief]
- SDK version and adapter: [sdk, adapter] 
- Sample input (redact PII): [sample prompt]
- Observed latency/cost vs expected: [numbers]
- Attached artifacts: trace.json, token_dump.txt, screenshots
- Assigned owner: @sdk-platform

Docs-site and snippet lifecycle (how to publish an update):
1) Author change in sources/docs-snippets/ with test harness snippet.
2) Add a docs PR against docs-site repo with the snippet ID and QA checklist (snippet must run in the local emulator).
3) Add label "sdk-fix" and the page will be scheduled to the next release train. For emergency patches, contact the docs rotation lead and include the ticket ID.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (recent):
- Issue: sudden cost inflation on transactional chat flows
  - Root cause: client-side synchronous retries calling the generation endpoint on network blips.
  - Canonical fix: SDK v1.14 introduced non-blocking retry policy with jitter and idempotency keys.
- Issue: embedded runtimes seeing 3x latency in mixed embed+generate flows
  - Root cause: requests were not multiplexed and forced sequential kv fetches.
  - Canonical fix: SDK helper bundle_or_call() and runtime batching change release 2025-11.

Postmortem and follow-up steps (after fix):
1) Validate: run golden trace diff on a 72-hour window to ensure no regressions in p95 latency and token costs.
2) Backfill: add an E2E integration test to SDK repo that simulates the customer pattern.
3) Docs: update quickstart sample and add an expandable note in behavior doc explaining the failure mode.
4) Customer comms: share root cause and remediation steps with the customer and note any credits if warranted.

Observability playbook (recommended dashboard panels):
- Panel: SDK version heatmap (per-tenant)
- Panel: Request size vs latency scatter (colored by model_variant)
- Panel: Queue depth and batch_exec_ms over time (stacked)
- Panel: Tokenization mismatch alerts (token_count_client - token_count_server > 20 for > 5 requests)

Automation ideas (backlog):
- Auto-replay agent that runs repros in a sandbox when a support ticket is tagged "auto-repro".
- Preflight validator in the SDK that warns when configurations likely to cause slowpath are used (e.g., max_concurrent_streams > 64 with small batch sizes).

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Export a full trace from local runner:
  redwoodctl trace export --trace-id {{trace_id}} --format json > trace.json
- Run a bundle repro locally with token dump:
  redwoodctl replay --input sample.json --tokenize --capture-trace
- Minimal curl example with debug headers:
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \n    -H "X-RW-Debug-ID: ticket-1234" \n    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n    -d '{"model":"rwd/gpt-1", "prompt":"Hello world", "max_tokens":64}'

References and related pages:
- eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook-2025
- eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-telemetry-collection-2025
- oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

Contact and ownership notes:
- For SDK code changes: assign to team "sdk-platform" in Jira (component: sdk-client).
- For runtime investigations: ping #runtime-observability and add the trace_id to the incident.

Change log:
- 2025-09-15 (Maya Patel) — Created initial playbook and reproducible snippets.
- 2025-11-02 (Jared Kim) — Added tokenization compatibility section and thresholds.
- 2026-01-12 (Maya Patel) — Updated mitigation list and added automation backlog items.

payload.page_title: SDK credential rotation and local adapter patterns: developer quickstart and ops playbook

sections.body:
Summary
=======
This playbook documents recommended patterns and a hands-on quickstart for: (1) rotating API credentials used by client SDKs, (2) running a local adapter/proxy that performs safe credential exchange and short-lived token issuance, and (3) operationalizing these patterns in dev and CI environments. The goal is to reduce blast radius for leaked keys, make developer onboarding smooth, and provide canonical fixes for the most common support issues.

Audience
--------
- SDK engineers and client library maintainers
- Developer experience and onboarding engineers
- Support engineers who triage auth and local-dev failures

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
- Goals:
  - Provide concrete rotation schedules and automation templates for short-lived credentials
  - Define a repeatable local adapter pattern for use in dev/CI (no secrets in repos)
  - Provide canonical debugging steps and observability checks for auth fails
- Out of scope:
  - Internal HSM/KMS configuration details for enterprise Private customers (see security-and-compliance pages)

High-level pattern
------------------
1) Issue: long-lived API keys distributed to developers and CI lead to accidental commits, leaked artifacts, and slow rotation.
2) Pattern: keep long-lived secrets only in a secure vault (HashiCorp Vault / cloud KMS secret store). Issue short-lived bearer tokens via a local adapter that performs client authentication and token exchange. Use SDKs to call the adapter instead of embedding keys.

Components & responsibilities
------------------------------
- Vault / Secret Store (owned by infra-security): stores the long-lived signing key and rotation schedule.
- Local adapter (owned by devx/runtime team): small process that runs on dev workstation / CI; validates local identity, requests short-lived tokens from Vault or token-issuer service, and caches tokens for TTL.
- SDKs (owned by SDK team): integrate an adapter client, fallback to environment variable-based token, and surface helpful error messages + actionable telemetry.

Quickstart: run-local adapter and rotate a credential (15–20 minutes)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Docker installed OR Python 3.10+ and pip
- Access to Redwood dev Vault (dev role) or a dev-token issued by infra (obtain from infra channel)
sections.heading: Prereqs

sections.body:
1. Clone the local-adapter repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/local-dev-adapter.git
2. Start the adapter in dev mode (Docker):

   docker run --rm -p 8081:8081 
     -e VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.dev.redwood.ai 
     -e VAULT_ROLE=dev-workstation 
     -e ADAPTER_CACHE_TTL=300 
     ghcr.io/redwood-inference/local-adapter:latest
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.dev.redwood.ai
   export VAULT_ROLE=dev-workstation
   ./local_adapter --port 8081 --dev-mode

3. Configure your SDK to use the adapter endpoint. Example environment variables for SDK: (Linux/macOS)

   export REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTER_URL=http://localhost:8081
   export REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTER_AUTH_METHOD=local-socket

4. Make a sample call using the SDK example: (Node example)

   const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk')
   const client = new Redwood({ adapterUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_SDK_ADAPTER_URL })
   await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-1024', prompt: 'Hello' })

5. Rotate and validate:
   - Trigger rotation (developer flow): POST /v1/rotate on the adapter admin port (requires local permission).
   - Adapter will call Vault and fetch a new short-lived token (TTL configured in service).
   - SDK calls should continue without restart thanks to adapter caching and automatic refresh.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)
-----------------------------------------
| config key | recommended value | explanation |
|------------|-------------------|-------------|
| ADAPTER_CACHE_TTL | 300 (seconds) | Cache short-lived token to avoid excessive token issuer calls |
| TOKEN_TTL | 900 (seconds) | Short-lived token lifetime issued by Vault/token-service |
| TOKEN_GRACE | 60 (seconds) | Start refresh when token remaining <= grace |
| MAX_REFRESH_RETRIES | 3 | Exponential backoff on issuer failures |
| METRICS_PORT | 9001 | Expose prometheus metrics on this port |

SDK integration checklist
-------------------------
- Accept adapter URL via priority: runtime config > env var > default local URL
- Expose informative errors: include correlation id, adapter health, and advice ("run local-adapter" or "contact infra-team")
- Built-in backoff for failed token refresh with jitter and exponential backoff
- Fall back to read-only mode if tokens cannot be refreshed (graceful degradation)

API examples and snippets
------------------------
Curl example: request a token from local adapter and call the hosted API endpoint (represents the internal flow used by SDKs):

  # fetch short-lived token
  TOKEN=$(curl -sS http://localhost:8081/v1/token | jq -r .access_token)
  # call Redwood API with token
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \n    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n    -d '{"model":"redwood-1024", "prompt":"status" }' \n    https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
sections.heading: OR with Python virtualenv

sections.body:
from redwood import Client
  c = Client(adapter_url='http://localhost:8081')
  print(c.generate(model='redwood-1024', prompt='Ping'))

Common support issues and canonical fixes
---------------------------------------
1) Symptom: SDK fails with 401 and message: "no token available"
   - Cause: adapter not running or adapter cannot fetch token from Vault.
   - Fix: check adapter logs for Vault errors: curl http://localhost:8081/health and docker logs. Ensure VAULT_ADDR and VAULT_ROLE are set. If Vault returns 403, contact infra-security to grant dev role.

2) Symptom: Intermittent 502 from adapter to token issuer during heavy dev CI runs
   - Cause: token issuer rate-limiting or network flakiness.
   - Fix: increase local adapter cache_ttl for CI (sane value: 600s) and add MAX_REFRESH_RETRIES set to 5 in CI pipeline; open infra-ticket to monitor token-issuer rate.

3) Symptom: Token refresh causes SDK hang for >2s on critical path
   - Cause: blocking synchronous refresh on main request path.
   - Fix: implement async refresh: return current token while background thread/async coroutine refreshes token when TTL <= grace window. See "non-blocking-refresh" example below.

Non-blocking refresh (pseudo-code)
---------------------------------
  class TokenCache:
      def get_token(self):
          if token.expires_in <= GRACE and not refresh_in_progress:
              start_background_refresh()
          return token.current_value

Observability and telemetry
---------------------------
- Adapter must expose Prometheus metrics: token_requests_total, token_refresh_failures_total, token_cache_hit_ratio, adapter_uptime_seconds.
- SDKs should emit logs with these fields: correlation_id, adapter_latency_ms, token_expiry_epoch, token_refresh_attempts.
- Set alerts (SRE): token_refresh_failures_total rate > 1/min for 5m -> P1 investigate.

Rollout & release notes guidance for SDK teams
---------------------------------------------
- Feature flag the adapter-first behavior behind a runtime opt-in for 2 releases. Default for new SDKs: adapter-aware but still honor env-token for backward compatibility.
- Release notes snippet: "SDK X.Y: enabled local adapter token flow. If you run into auth issues, run 'local-adapter --help' to accept defaults."

Security considerations
-----------------------
- Never log long-lived vault credentials. Mask secrets in logs and metrics.
- Use OS-level ACLs for the adapter admin port (only localhost binding for dev). For CI, run within ephemeral container with network policies.
- For Private deployments, use customer-managed KMS and a separate token-issuer; consult eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures.

Troubleshooting checklist (one-page)
-----------------------------------
1) Verify adapter health: curl -sS http://localhost:8081/health -> {status:ok}
2) Confirm token fetch: curl -sS http://localhost:8081/v1/token | jq .
3) Inspect adapter metrics: curl http://localhost:9001/metrics | grep token_refresh_failures
4) Check SDK logs for correlation_id and adapter_latency_ms
5) If Vault denies access, escalate to infra-security with request id from adapter logs

Ownership and runbook links
--------------------------
- Local adapter repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/local-dev-adapter.git
- SDK client wrappers: git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-templates.git (team: devx/sdk)
- Pager for token-issuer incidents: eng-sre on-call (see oncall_and_incident_response/runbooks)

Appendix A — sample adapter config (YAML)
---------------------------------------
  port: 8081
  vault:
    addr: https://vault.dev.redwood.ai
    role: dev-workstation
  cache_ttl_seconds: 300
  token_ttl_seconds: 900
  metrics_port: 9001

Appendix B — suggested ticket template for infra-security
----------------------------------------------------------
Summary: Developer local-adapter unable to fetch token (vault 403)
Steps to reproduce: commands used, VAULT_ROLE set to X, adapter logs attached
Expected behavior: adapter returns token
Actual behavior: adapter returns 403 from Vault
Attachments: adapter.log (redact secrets)

Notes and references
--------------------
- See security-and-compliance/data-management for long-lived key handling guidance.
- For on-prem/private customer notes, see eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/local-adapter-onprem.md

Revision history
----------------
- 2024-11-08: initial draft by Priya Menon
- 2025-02-10: added non-blocking refresh pattern and observability checklist (reviewers: Ethan Clarke, Lucia Ramirez)

End of document

payload.page_title: Private VPC Terraform (Alpha) — Quickstart Template

sections.body: This page provides a copy/paste-friendly Terraform repo template for customers (or Redwood PS/SE) to create the foundational AWS networking footprint for a Redwood Private deployment.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- VPC, subnets, routing, NAT defaults
- Security group patterns for private workloads
- VPC endpoints (interface + gateway) with private DNS options
- Flow logs with sane defaults + customer-owned destinations
- IAM scaffolding for running the Redwood Private installer (optional; customer IAM may be used instead)
- Optional placeholders/outputs to integrate with customer VPN/Direct Connect (no provider-specific routing encoded)
sections.heading: Scope (alpha)

sections.body: - EKS cluster creation or application install. The cluster/app install is handled by the Redwood Private installer / Helm charts.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Customer platform teams deploying Redwood Private in AWS (VPC-based)
- Redwood Solutions Engineering / Professional Services building POC environments
- Security teams reviewing default posture (endpoints, logging destinations, IAM boundaries)
sections.heading: Who should use this template

sections.body:
- Terraform: 1.6+ (1.7+ recommended)
- AWS provider: pinned in `versions.tf` (see below)
- AWS account with permission to create: VPC, subnets, IGW/NAT, route tables, VPC endpoints, CloudWatch log groups (if using CW destination), IAM roles/policies (if using IAM scaffold)
- Decide upfront:
  - Region and 2–3 AZs
  - VPC CIDR (must not overlap with existing networks if VPN/DX planned)
  - Log destination ownership (customer-owned S3 bucket vs CloudWatch)
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.body: Use an environment-based layout (one state per environment). Avoid mixing multiple environments in a single state.
sections.heading: Recommended repo layout

sections.body:
- `README.md`
- `modules/` (optional; only if you add local wrapper modules)
- `envs/`
  - `dev/`
    - `backend.tf`
    - `main.tf`
    - `outputs.tf`
    - `providers.tf`
    - `variables.tf`
    - `versions.tf`
    - `terraform.tfvars.example`
  - `prod/` (same structure)
- `scripts/` (optional)
  - `tf.sh` (wrapper to standardize init/plan/apply)
sections.heading: Directory tree

sections.body:
- `backend.tf` is intentionally environment-specific (S3 bucket, DynamoDB lock table, etc.).
- Keep `terraform.tfvars` out of source control for real environments. Commit only `terraform.tfvars.example`.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: Alpha modules move quickly; always pin exact versions (tags) for reproducibility.
sections.heading: Module sources and version pinning

sections.body: - `source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/vpc?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"`

sections.body:
This composes the alpha modules with minimal inputs. Keep overrides explicit.

```hcl
locals {
  common_tags = merge(var.tags, {
    "redwood:component"   = "private-network"
    "redwood:env"         = var.name_prefix
    "redwood:managed-by"  = "terraform"
    "redwood:module-suite"= "redwood-terraform-vpc-alpha"
  })
}

module "vpc" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/vpc?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"

  name_prefix        = var.name_prefix
  vpc_cidr           = var.vpc_cidr
  aws_region         = var.aws_region
  az_count           = var.az_count
  enable_nat_gateway = var.enable_nat_gateway

  tags = local.common_tags
}

module "security_groups" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/security-groups?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"

  name_prefix = var.name_prefix
  vpc_id      = module.vpc.vpc_id

  # Opinionated defaults for private installs. Customize only with guidance.
  allow_private_egress_https = true

  tags = local.common_tags
}

module "endpoints" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/vpc-endpoints?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"

  enabled     = var.enable_vpc_endpoints
  name_prefix = var.name_prefix
  vpc_id      = module.vpc.vpc_id

  private_subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnet_ids

  # Endpoint security group: allow HTTPS from private subnets / node SGs.
  endpoint_security_group_id = module.security_groups.vpc_endpoints_sg_id

  # Defaults should include (at minimum) ECR API + DKR, S3 gateway, STS.
  # Redwood installer preflight will warn if required endpoints are missing.
  enable_private_dns = true

  tags = local.common_tags
}

module "flow_logs" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/flow-logs?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"

  enabled            = var.enable_flow_logs
  name_prefix        = var.name_prefix
  vpc_id             = module.vpc.vpc_id
  destination        = var.flow_logs_destination
  cw_retention_days  = var.flow_logs_retention_days
  s3_bucket_arn      = var.flow_logs_s3_bucket_arn

  tags = local.common_tags
}

module "iam_installer" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-terraform.git//modules/iam-installer-role?ref=v0.3.0-alpha.4"

  # If installer_principal_arn is empty, the module should be skipped or create nothing.
  enabled                = var.installer_principal_arn != ""
  name_prefix            = var.name_prefix
  installer_principal_arn= var.installer_principal_arn
  permission_boundary_arn= var.permission_boundary_arn

  tags = local.common_tags
}

sections.body:
```

payload.page_title: Bridge Bootcamp: Runtime Shim & Developer Labs

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook is a hands-on bootcamp for SDK engineers and partner integrators who need a predictable, repeatable way to develop and validate against a local runtime shim that mirrors Redwood inference behavior (streaming, batching, KV cache semantics, and error contraction). The goal is to reduce first-week time-to-value for integrations, exercise canonical failure modes, and provide ready-to-copy templates for production adapters.

Audience: SDK engineers, integration partners, solutions engineers, and onboarding SREs.

What you get from this document:
- A lab curriculum for a 2-day internal bootcamp (slides + exercises).
- A lightweight runtime shim reference (CLI commands, invocation examples, config table).
- Templates for SDK adapters and telemetry contracts.
- A canonical-fix checklist for common support cases (streaming disconnects, token accounting mismatches, prompt-encoding divergence).

Prerequisites

- Local dev machine with Docker (20.10+) and Node.js (18+) or Python (3.10+).
- Access to Redwood dev account (redwood-dev) and API key with sandbox scope.
- Basic familiarity with streaming generative APIs and embeddings.

Lab curriculum (2-day split)

Day 0 (pre-work, 30–60 min)
1) Clone the starter repo: git clone git@repo.redwood.ai:sdk-bootcamp/starter-shim.git
2) Run the shim locally: ./tools/dev_shim up
3) Verify connectivity: curl -sS http://localhost:8080/v1/health | jq

Day 1 (core patterns, 4 hours)
- Module A (1.5h): API parity exercises
  - Exercise: call the local shim with a generation request and compare tokens/latency to the hosted sandbox.
  - Deliverable: short report (README snippet) noting divergence and a suggested mapping table.
- Module B (1.5h): Streaming and resume semantics
  - Exercise: implement client-side stream resume using the provided resume-token header.
  - Deliverable: unit test that simulates a mid-stream reconnect and asserts contiguous output.
- Module C (1h): Error contraction and fallback policies
  - Exercise: inject capacity error codes and implement an exponential backoff with fallback to a cheaper model variant.
  - Deliverable: sample retry policy config.

Day 2 (observability & failure modes, 3 hours)
- Module D (1.5h): Telemetry contract alignment
  - Exercise: produce a telemetry event for each request including model_id, cost_estimate_tokens, batch_size_hint, and KV_cache_hit_rate.
  - Deliverable: telemetry JSON schema; test harness that validates events.
- Module E (1.5h): Canonical fix triage and incident simulation
  - Exercise: follow the triage checklist in the event of token leakage (client double-encoding) and streaming stutters.
  - Deliverable: postmortem-style template filled from simulation.

Runtime shim reference

Description: The runtime shim is a minimal HTTP+WebSocket proxy that exposes the Redwood-compatible inference surface. It deliberately implements a subset of production behavior with knobs to toggle batching, quantization flags, and synthetic latency. Use it for developer offline loops and smoke tests.

Quickstart (Docker)

1) Start shim: docker compose -f docker/shim-compose.yml up --build -d
2) Check health: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health
3) Send generation (curl):
   curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"rdw-3b-light","input":"Write a 2-sentence product summary"}'

Configuration matrix (editable in tools/shim_config.yaml)

| key | type | default | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| model_map | map | rdw-3b-light -> local-3b | Logical mapping of requested model to shim backend |
| enable_batching | boolean | true | Whether shim should batch concurrent requests |
| synthetic_latency_ms | integer | 25 | Add fixed latency to simulate network/hardware delays |
| stream_resume_window | integer | 30 | Seconds allowed to resume a stream session |
| telemetry_endpoint | string | http://localhost:9000/events | Local telemetry collector endpoint |

Adapter template snippets

- Node.js adapter example (pseudo):
  - const shimClient = new ShimClient({ baseUrl: process.env.SHIM_URL, apiKey: process.env.SANDBOX_KEY })
  - await shimClient.generate({ model: 'rdw-3b-light', input, stream: true })
  - shimClient.on('chunk', handleChunk)
  - shimClient.on('resumeToken', saveResumeToken)

- Python adapter patterns:
  - requests.Session with backoff on 429/503 and a split between non-idempotent (stream) and idempotent (embed) paths.

Telemetry contract (minimal required fields)

- event_type: request_start | request_end | stream_chunk | error
- timestamp_utc: ISO8601 string
- request_id: UUID
- model_id: string
- client_sdk_version: semver
- cost_estimate_tokens: integer
- latency_ms: integer
- batch_size: integer (optional)
- kv_cache_hit_rate: float (0.0-1.0) (optional)

Telemetry schema example (one-line JSON check in test harness):
  assert(has_keys(event, ['event_type','timestamp_utc','request_id','model_id','latency_ms']))

Canonical support and fixes (fast lookup table)

1) Symptom: Streaming disconnects mid-response\   Root causes: client-side socket close, resume_token missing, shim timeout shorter than host
   Fix checklist:
   - Confirm resume_token emitted in initial chunks.
   - Increase shim stream_resume_window to 120s if clients need longer resume windows.
   - Ensure client persists resume_token to durable storage before acknowledging full response.
   - If reconnects show duplicate content, verify idempotency keys on the client and server generation pipeline.

2) Symptom: Token accounting mismatch (hosted vs shim)\   Root causes: prompt double-encoding, mismatched tokenizer, leading/trailing whitespace handling
   Fix checklist:
   - Run token diff tool: tools/token_diff.py --hosted ./hosted_sample.json --shim ./shim_sample.json
   - Normalize inputs by trimming whitespace and ensuring consistent UTF-8 normalization (NFC).
   - Pin tokenizer version in adapter and shim (tokenizer==2026.12.1).

3) Symptom: Observability gaps (no telemetry for failed retries)\   Fix checklist:
   - Ensure request_start event emitted before any retry.
   - For last-resort failures, emit request_end with error=true and failure_code set.
   - Validate ingestion at telemetry_endpoint and run the local validator: tools/telemetry_validator run

Troubleshooting recipes (step-by-step)

A. Reproducing a streaming resume issue locally\1) Start shim with synthetic_latency_ms=150 and stream_resume_window=15\2) Start a client with small write-ahead buffer and trigger a disconnect at 40% completion\3) Reconnect using saved resume_token and observe whether output continues from expected token offset\4) If duplicate tokens observed: check idempotency-key header and server side dedupe logic

B. Diagnosing token divergence\1) Export both hosted and shim request traces as NDJSON (tools/export_traces.sh)\2) Run token_diff and inspect which prompt fragment diverges\3) If divergence is in prompting layer, update adapter to use adapter.normalize_prompt(payload) before transmission

Operational notes and ownership

- Shim repo owner: eng-developer-experience (primary), eng-serving-runtime (secondary)
- Pager: devx-oncall rotation (pagerduty: DP-DEVX)
- SLO for bootcamp lab artifacts: 99% of exercises pass local smoke tests in CI (weekly run)
- Release cadence: bump shim base image and tokenizer quarterly (Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec)

Back-of-envelope metrics and why this matters

- Average onboarding time reduced from 3 days to 6 hours in teams that adopt the bootcamp kit (empirical internal study, Q3 2026).
- Decreases support tickets related to token drift and stream resume by ~45% when adapter templates are used.

Appendices

Appendix A — CLI reference
- ./tools/dev_shim up [--mode=light|heavy]    # start shim
- ./tools/dev_shim stop                      # stop shim
- ./tools/dev_shim config                  # print effective config

Appendix B — Quick postmortem template (fill during incident)
1) Incident summary (one sentence)
2) Timeline (short bullets with timestamps)
3) Root cause hypothesis
4) Mitigations applied
5) Permanent fixes and owner
6) Follow-ups and retrospective notes

Related resources
- SDK starter repo: git@repo.redwood.ai:sdk-bootcamp/starter-shim.git
- Telemetry validator: tools/telemetry_validator
- Token diff utility: tools/token_diff.py

Contact and feedback

For questions about the bootcamp content or to schedule an internal run, contact Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai). For runtime shim bugs file issues in the shim repo and tag @eng-developer-experience.

End of document

payload.page_title: SDK Integration Contract and Bundle Validator Playbook

sections.body:
A prescriptive playbook for validating SDK integration contracts and packaging a distribution bundle for safe rollout. Defines checks, CLI validator flows, common failure modes with canonical fixes, and a lightweight gating policy for dev and release pipelines.
Overview

This playbook documents the SDK integration contract checks and the bundle-validator we run as part of DX CI and release pipelines. The goal is to catch integration regressions (API surface changes, telemetry gaps, schema drift) before SDK packages are published to registries or distributed to customers. The validator is intentionally lightweight so it can run in pull-request checks and in nightly pipelines.

When to use

- On every PR that changes: public SDK surface, request/response shapes, telemetry events, or packaged assets (wheel/tarball/npm).
- Before cutting an SDK release candidate (rc) and prior to publishing to internal registries.
- As part of customer-specific integration checks for Dedicated/Private deployment handoffs.

Definitions

- Integration Contract: stable request/response JSON schema, named API endpoints and client method signatures, error-code set, and telemetry event list.
- Bundle: packaged distribution (e.g., pip wheel, npm package) plus shipping artifacts (README, changelog, schemas, sample prompts, telemetry spec).
- Validator: CLI tool that runs a suite of static and dynamic checks against a candidate bundle and a baseline contract.

Roles & Ownership

- SDK Owner: responsible for updating contract files, implementing fixes, and interpreting validator failures. (Default: dx-sdk team)
- DX Validator Maintainer: keeps the validator code, canonical rule set, and baseline contracts up to date. (Default: devx-infra)
- Release Manager: authorizes release when validator green.

Gating policy (recommended)

- PR gate (fast): run fast checks (lint, public API diff, required files present). Must pass before merge.
- RC gate (full): run dynamic tests (end-to-end example against staging runtime, telemetry sample verification, packaging verification). Must pass to publish.

Quick checklist (PR-level)

1. public_api.yaml present and valid
2. schema/response/ and schema/request/ updated only via ADR or with migration notes
3. telemetry-events.yaml updated for any trackable changes
4. sample-usage.* updated and executed in CI smoke test
5. package artifact builds and checksum (sha256) verified

Validator commands (examples)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: python -m pip install git+https://github.com/redwood-inference/dx-validator.git@main
sections.heading: Install validator (pyproject)

sections.body: dx-validate bundle --bundle dist/redwood_sdk-1.2.0-py3-none-any.whl --baseline contracts/baseline-2026-01.json --staging-url https://staging.api.redwood.ai
sections.heading: Run full validator against a wheel file

sections.body:
dx-validate quick --src ./src/redwood_sdk --public-api public_api.yaml --telemetry telemetry-events.yaml

What the validator checks

Static checks (fast)
- public API surface diff (added/removed/changed methods and parameters)
- presence and lint of public_api.yaml, telemetry-events.yaml, CHANGELOG.md, LICENSE
- packaging manifest sanity: pyproject.toml / package.json fields, required files included

Schema checks (medium)
- response/request JSON schema compatibility against baseline (backwards-compatible additions only unless flagged)
- status/error codes set does not remove codes used in baseline
- example payloads validate against declared schemas

Dynamic checks (slow)
- smoke invocation against a staging runtime and validation of shaped outputs
- telemetry event emission check: sample calls must produce expected events within 30s window to the telemetry-proxy test endpoint
- integration example scripts run and exit 0

Failure modes and canonical fixes

1) Public API removed or renamed
Symptom: validator flags removed public methods or parameter changes.
Fix: Revert rename or add compatibility shim; create ADR for breaking change and prepare migration notes; increment major version if intentional.

2) Schema drift that breaks customers
Symptom: response schema removed required fields.
Fix: Reintroduce fields, add deprecation warnings, or publish a compatibility adapter; update schema migration notes and create an eval test that exercises edge case.

3) Telemetry not emitted or missing fields
Symptom: telemetry-events.yaml mismatches produced events or sample invocation produces no events to test endpoint.
Fix: Ensure telemetry instrumentation code triggers events; validate flush behavior in async clients; add a test that asserts event attributes.

4) Packaging missing files (README, LICENSE, sample prompts)
Symptom: artifact lacks declared files; customers report confusing install or usage.
Fix: Update pyproject/package.json include list and add CI gate that validates artifact contents and checksum.

Canonical fixes snippets

- Add compatibility shim example (Python):
from typing import Any
sections.heading: Run incremental PR checks (fast mode)

sections.body:
def summarize(text: Any, model: Any = None):
    # shim: accept both calls and forward to new implementation
    return _impl_summarize(str(text), model=model)

- Telemetry flush example (async client)
await client.emit_event("generation_request", {"model": model_name})
await client.flush(timeout_seconds=5)

Packaging validation example (CI YAML excerpt)

steps:
  - run: python -m pip wheel . -w dist/
  - run: dx-validate bundle --bundle dist/*.whl --baseline contracts/baseline-2026-01.json

E2E smoke test (minimal)

1. Start local telemetry-proxy (docker run -p 9001:9001 redwood/telemetry-proxy:test)
2. Install candidate wheel into virtualenv
3. Run sample-usage/smoke_invoke.py which: creates a client, calls generate(sample_prompt), asserts non-empty text, and polls telemetry-proxy for event.

Metrics and SLOs for validator

- PR quick-check median time: < 90s (target)
- RC full-check median time: < 900s (target)
- False positive rate goal: < 2% per quarter
- Coverage: validator suite must exercise at least 3 canonical example flows per SDK (generation, embeddings, health-check)

Telemetry expectations (for sample invocations)

- Event names: generation.request, generation.response, sdk.install, sdk.error
- Required fields on generation.request: client_id, request_id, model, prompt_length, timestamp
- Required fields on generation.response: request_id, latency_ms, tokens_generated, status

Rollout guidance

- Canary: publish RC to internal channel and run the RC full-check against a reserved staging project for 24 hours. Monitor: SDK error-rate, telemetry missing-field rate, and runtime latency delta.
- Gradual: 10% -> 50% -> 100% distribution over 72 hours if all metrics stable.

Incident triage checklist (validator failures post-release)

1. Reproduce failure with the same bundle and baseline locally using dx-validate reproduce --bundle <bundle> --baseline <baseline>
2. Capture logs from telemetry-proxy and staging runtime; include request_id from failing test
3. Patch and run RC full-check; if green, promote new RC through canary flow

FAQ

Q: Who updates baseline contracts?
A: DX Validator Maintainers update baselines when there is an authorized platform or API change. SDK teams must notify maintainers via #dx-validator and attach ADRs for breaking changes.

Q: Can we disable a check for a quick hotfix?
A: Only the Release Manager can temporarily disable a check. Document the exception in the PR and re-enable within one business day. Exceptions must be included in the release notes.

Appendix: public_api.yaml minimal example

  - name: generate
    description: "Synchronous text generation method"
    params:
      - name: prompt
        type: string
        required: true

    returns:
      type: object

    required_fields: [client_id, request_id, model, prompt_length, timestamp]
