    required_fields: [request_id, latency_ms, tokens_generated, status]

Related artifacts (repo & CLI)

- dx-validator repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/dx-validator
- sample bundles: s3://redwood-devx/sdks/candidates/
- staging runtime: https://staging.api.redwood.ai

Contact

payload.page_title: Quickstart Templates Observability Hooks Standard (OTel + Redwood Conventions)

sections.body:
This document defines the **required observability hooks** for Redwood Inference Quickstart Templates (RAG + agents, Python + TypeScript). Templates must emit consistent **metrics, traces, and logs** so that:
- Users can validate correct behavior (streaming, retrieval, tool-calling) quickly.
- Redwood Support/SRE can debug issues with minimal back-and-forth.
- Product/Analytics can segment template-originated traffic (where allowed) without collecting sensitive payloads.

This standard is implemented via the **Template Observability Pack** (OTel collector config + dashboards + alert recommendations) and lightweight template libraries/wrappers.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- RAG API template
- RAG UI template (if applicable)
- Agent loop with tool calling
- Batch embeddings / ingestion jobs (where present)
sections.heading: Applies to all template apps shipped by DevEx

sections.body:
- Defining full org-wide OTel conventions (see related pages).
- Collecting prompt/content payloads (explicitly disallowed by default).

---
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
1. **Debuggable by default**: a user should be able to answer “why is this slow / failing?” from a single trace + logs.
2. **Low cardinality**: metrics must avoid unbounded labels (no user prompts, doc IDs, URLs with IDs, raw tool args).
3. **Safe by default**: logs/traces redact secrets and likely-PII; payload logging is opt-in and documented.
4. **Correlatable**: every log line related to a request must include a correlation ID and trace context.
5. **Comparable across languages**: Python and TypeScript templates must use the same span names/attributes and metric names.

---
sections.heading: Guiding principles

sections.body:
Templates must propagate and surface the following identifiers:
- **`redwood.request_id`**: request ID returned by Redwood gateway (from response header). This is the primary support/debug handle.
- **`trace_id` / `span_id`**: OpenTelemetry trace context IDs.
- **`client.request_id`** (optional): an application-generated request ID for inbound HTTP requests (e.g., from `X-Request-Id`).
sections.heading: Correlation IDs

sections.body:
- **Logs**: include `redwood.request_id` when available; always include `trace_id`.
- **Spans**: include `redwood.request_id` on the top-level LLM span once known.
- **User-facing errors**: include `redwood.request_id` in error responses and README troubleshooting guidance.
sections.heading: Where identifiers must appear

sections.body:
- Inbound API requests: accept `X-Request-Id` (do not generate if present; generate if absent).
- Outbound calls to Redwood: pass through trace context (W3C Trace Context) and any Redwood-supported request ID headers via SDK helpers.

---
sections.heading: Header propagation requirements

sections.body: Templates must create a trace for every inbound request (or job run) and include a consistent span hierarchy.
sections.heading: Tracing standard

sections.body:
**HTTP API template (server):**
1. `http.server` (framework auto-instrumentation OK)
2. `redwood.quickstart.request` (root logical span; child of `http.server`)
3. `redwood.llm.request` (one per LLM call; includes streaming metrics)
4. Optional child spans (as applicable):
   - `redwood.rag.retrieve`
   - `redwood.rag.rerank`
   - `redwood.rag.build_context`
   - `redwood.agent.loop`
   - `redwood.tool.call` (one per tool invocation)
   - `redwood.cache.lookup` / `redwood.cache.write` (template-level caches only)

**Batch ingestion job:**
1. `redwood.quickstart.job`
2. `redwood.embeddings.embed_batch`
3. `redwood.vectorstore.upsert`
sections.heading: Span hierarchy (minimum viable)

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.request`
- `redwood.llm.request`
- `redwood.rag.retrieve`
- `redwood.rag.rerank` (if reranking is enabled)
- `redwood.agent.loop`
- `redwood.tool.call`
- `redwood.embeddings.embed_batch` (if embeddings used)
- `redwood.vectorstore.query` / `redwood.vectorstore.upsert` (if vector DB used)
sections.heading: Required span names (exact)

sections.body:
Add these attributes to the relevant spans. Attribute keys are standardized for dashboards and support tooling.

**On `redwood.quickstart.request`**
- `template.name`: e.g., `rag-agent-python`
- `template.version`: semver or git tag embedded at scaffold time
- `app.route`: stable route name (avoid raw URL with IDs)
- `deployment.mode`: `hosted` | `dedicated` | `private` | `unknown`
- `deployment.environment`: `local` | `dev` | `staging` | `prod` (map from env var)

**On `redwood.llm.request`**
- `llm.provider`: `redwood`
- `llm.operation`: `chat.completions` | `responses` | `embeddings` | `rerank`
- `llm.model`: pinned model identifier configured in template
- `llm.streaming`: `true` | `false`
- `redwood.request_id`: set once response received
- `llm.max_output_tokens`: configured limit (integer as string accepted by exporters)

**Token & cost attributes (set on `redwood.llm.request` when known)**
- `llm.usage.prompt_tokens`
- `llm.usage.completion_tokens`
- `llm.usage.total_tokens`
- `redwood.cache.prefix_hit`: `true` | `false` (only if reliably detectable; otherwise omit)

**On `redwood.rag.retrieve`**
- `rag.top_k`: configured k
- `rag.vectorstore`: `local` | `<vendor>` | `unknown`
- `rag.query_length_chars`: integer (length only; do NOT store query)
- `rag.results_count`: integer

**On `redwood.tool.call`**
- `tool.name`: stable tool name (e.g., `web_search`, `get_user_profile`)
- `tool.status`: `ok` | `error` | `timeout`
- `tool.output_size_bytes`: integer (size only; do NOT store output)

**Errors (all spans)**
- Use OTel span status + exception events.
- Add `error.category` and `error.code` (see Error taxonomy below).
sections.heading: Required span attributes

sections.body:
- **TTFT (time to first token)**: captured as an event on `redwood.llm.request`:
  - Event name: `llm.first_token`
  - Attribute: `llm.ttft_ms`
- **Streaming disconnects**: if a stream terminates unexpectedly, record:
  - `error.category=streaming`
  - `error.code=stream_disconnected`
  - `retry.attempt` if a reconnect was attempted
sections.heading: Templates must measure and emit these timings for streaming

sections.body:
- Do not attach prompt text, retrieved document text, tool args, tool outputs, or raw user identifiers to span attributes.
- Allowed: lengths, counts, booleans, stable names, and configured limits.

---
sections.heading: Redaction requirements (tracing)

sections.body: Metrics are emitted via OpenTelemetry Metrics (preferred). If a template uses framework-native metrics, it must export to OTel with equivalent names.
sections.heading: Metrics standard

sections.body:
- Prefix all template metrics with: `redwood.quickstart.`
- Use dot-separated names.
- Units should be explicit where supported (ms, bytes).
sections.heading: Metric naming

sections.body: Below is the minimum metric set required for all templates.
sections.heading: Required metrics (must emit)

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.request.duration_ms` (Histogram)
  - Description: end-to-end app request duration.
  - Dimensions (low-cardinality): `template.name`, `app.route`, `deployment.environment`.

- `redwood.quickstart.llm.duration_ms` (Histogram)
  - Description: time spent in the Redwood LLM call (including streaming until completion).
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `llm.model`, `llm.operation`, `llm.streaming`.

- `redwood.quickstart.llm.ttft_ms` (Histogram)
  - Description: time to first token for streaming calls.
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `llm.model`.
sections.heading: Request and LLM latency

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.llm.tokens.prompt` (Counter)
- `redwood.quickstart.llm.tokens.completion` (Counter)
- `redwood.quickstart.llm.tokens.total` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `llm.model`, `deployment.environment`.
sections.heading: Tokens and throughput signals

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.rag.retrieve.duration_ms` (Histogram)
- `redwood.quickstart.rag.retrieve.results_count` (Histogram)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `rag.vectorstore`.

- `redwood.quickstart.rag.retrieve.empty_results` (Counter)
  - Increment when `results_count=0`.
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `rag.vectorstore`.
sections.heading: Retrieval (RAG)

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.tool.call.duration_ms` (Histogram)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `tool.name`.

- `redwood.quickstart.tool.call.errors` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `tool.name`, `error.code`.

- `redwood.quickstart.tool.call.timeouts` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `tool.name`.
sections.heading: Tools (agents)

sections.body:
Note: platform-level caching may not be observable in all SDKs; emit these only for caches the template controls.
- `redwood.quickstart.cache.lookup` (Counter)
- `redwood.quickstart.cache.hit` (Counter)
- `redwood.quickstart.cache.miss` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `cache.name`.
sections.heading: Cache signals (template-level only)

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.http.client.retries` (Counter)
  - Description: retries performed by the client wrapper for outbound calls (Redwood or tool HTTP).
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `retry.reason` (bounded enum).

- `redwood.quickstart.streaming.disconnects` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `llm.model`.
sections.heading: Reliability / retries

sections.body:
- `redwood.quickstart.errors` (Counter)
  - Dimensions: `template.name`, `error.category`, `error.code`.
sections.heading: Error rate

sections.body:
- `template.name`, `template.version`
- `deployment.environment`
- `app.route`
- `llm.model`, `llm.operation`, `llm.streaming`
- `rag.vectorstore`
- `tool.name`
- `error.category`, `error.code`
- `cache.name`
- `retry.reason`
sections.heading: Allowed dimensions MUST be from a bounded set

sections.body:
- Prompt text, tool args, tool output, document IDs, raw URLs, user IDs/emails, session IDs, IPs, arbitrary error messages.

---
sections.heading: Prohibited dimensions

sections.body: Templates must use **structured JSON logs** by default.
sections.heading: Logging standard

sections.body:
- `timestamp` (RFC3339)
- `severity` (`DEBUG` | `INFO` | `WARN` | `ERROR`)
- `message`
- `service.name` (e.g., `redwood-quickstart-rag-agent`)
- `template.name`
- `template.version`
- `deployment.environment`
- `trace_id` and `span_id` (when in request scope)

Request-scoped logs (within handling of a request/job) must also include:
- `client.request_id` (if available)
- `redwood.request_id` (if available)
- `app.route`
sections.heading: All log lines must include

sections.body:
- `llm.model`
- `llm.operation`
- `llm.streaming`
- `llm.usage.prompt_tokens`, `llm.usage.completion_tokens`, `llm.usage.total_tokens`
sections.heading: LLM-related logs should additionally include (when known)

sections.body:
- Authorization headers, API keys, cookies
- Prompt text and retrieved doc text
- Tool arguments and tool outputs
- Any detected emails, phone numbers, SSNs, or high-entropy secrets (best-effort)

If a template provides an opt-in `LOG_PAYLOADS=true`, it must:
- Be OFF by default
- Include clear README warnings
- Apply allowlisting (log only specific fields) rather than dumping raw requests
sections.heading: Default behavior must redact

sections.body:
**Error log example (shape only; values illustrative):**
- `message`: "tool call failed"
- `error.category`: `tool`
- `error.code`: `tool_timeout`
- `tool.name`: `web_search`
- `duration_ms`: `3000`
- `redwood.request_id`: `<from gateway>`

---
sections.heading: Logging examples

sections.body: Templates must map common failures into a stable taxonomy.
sections.heading: Error taxonomy (for logs + metrics + traces)

sections.body:
- `auth`
- `network`
- `quota`
- `rate_limit`
- `timeout`
- `streaming`
- `tool`
- `retrieval`
- `validation`
- `server`
- `unknown`
sections.heading: Categories (bounded)

sections.body:
- Auth: `missing_api_key`, `invalid_api_key`, `unauthorized`
- Quota/limits: `insufficient_quota`, `limit_exceeded`
- Rate limit: `http_429`, `backoff_exhausted`
- Network: `dns_failure`, `connection_refused`, `tls_error`, `proxy_rejected_header`
- Timeout: `request_timeout`, `tool_timeout`
- Streaming: `stream_disconnected`, `stream_parse_error`
- Tool: `tool_schema_invalid`, `tool_execution_error`
- Retrieval: `vectorstore_unreachable`, `empty_results`, `index_not_ready`
- Validation: `invalid_env`, `invalid_config`, `structured_output_parse_error`
- Server: `http_5xx`, `gateway_error`
sections.heading: Common `error.code` values (bounded; extend only with review)

sections.body:
- Always emit a taxonomy code even if an exception includes a message.
- Store the raw exception message only in logs (redacted) and never as a metric label.

---
sections.heading: Mapping rules

sections.body:
Templates may optionally tag outbound requests for adoption metrics ONLY if:
- The tag contains no user or payload data.
- It is safe with common proxies (headers must be allowlisted and opt-in where required).
sections.heading: Template telemetry tagging (adoption metrics) — constraints

sections.body:
- `template.name`
- `template.version`
sections.heading: Standard fields (recommended)

sections.body:
- Prefer a single, short header (e.g., `X-Redwood-Template: <name>@<version>`) if supported by gateway allowlist.
- Provide a config toggle to disable tagging (`TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY_OPT_IN=false` by default where proxy issues are likely).

---
sections.heading: Implementation guidance

sections.body:
These dashboards are included in the Observability Pack and referenced from template READMEs.

1) **Quickstart: RAG & Agents — Overview**
- Request rate, error rate, p50/p95 request latency
- LLM call latency + TTFT
- Tokens over time (prompt/completion/total)

2) **Quickstart: RAG — Retrieval Health**
- Retrieval latency
- Empty results rate
- Results count distribution
- Vectorstore error rate

3) **Quickstart: Agents — Tooling Health**
- Tool call rate, latency
- Tool error + timeout rates by tool.name
- Top error codes (taxonomy)

4) **Quickstart: Streaming Reliability**
- Streaming disconnect rate
- TTFT distribution by model
- Retry counts (bounded reasons)

5) **Quickstart: Cost & Token Economics**
- Tokens/request and tokens/minute
- Completion/prompt ratio
- Top routes by token usage

---
sections.heading: Example dashboards to ship with templates

sections.body:
To avoid noisy defaults, templates ship alert recommendations as disabled-by-default examples.

- High error rate: `redwood.quickstart.errors` / request count > 2% for 10m
- Streaming instability: `redwood.quickstart.streaming.disconnects` > threshold for 10m
- Retrieval failing: `vectorstore_unreachable` errors > 0 for 5m OR empty_results rate > X% for 15m
- Tool timeouts: `redwood.quickstart.tool.call.timeouts` spikes above baseline

---
sections.heading: Recommended alert rules (ship as examples; not enabled by default)

sections.body:
- Use OTel SDK + auto-instrumentation for HTTP server where possible.
- Wrap Redwood SDK calls to create `redwood.llm.request` spans and set token attributes when responses return.
- Ensure logs include trace context (logging formatter/enricher).
sections.heading: Python

sections.body:
- Use OTel Node SDK and context propagation (async context manager).
- Ensure streaming uses a wrapper that records TTFT and disconnects.
- Use structured logging (pino or equivalent) with redaction.

---
sections.heading: TypeScript

sections.body:
1. Running locally with the provided collector config shows:
   - A trace for each request
   - `redwood.llm.request` spans with model + operation
   - TTFT recorded for streaming
2. Dashboards populate with the required metrics names.
3. Logs are JSON and include `trace_id` and `template.version`.
4. No payload fields appear in logs/traces by default (spot-check with a test prompt that includes an email and a fake key).
5. Metric dimensions are bounded (confirm no raw URL/user IDs).

---
sections.heading: Verification checklist (must pass before release)

sections.body:
- Owner: **Observability/SRE** (Allison Grant) + **DevEx** (Monica Patel)
- Changes to required metric names, span names, or attribute keys require:
  - Review by Observability Standards owner
  - Confirmation from DevEx leads (Python + TS)
  - Update to dashboards in Observability Pack
  - Template changelog entry and migration note if breaking
sections.heading: Ownership and change process

payload.page_title: SDK Observability Onboarding Playbook — Integration Orchard

sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```python
from redwood import Client
from redwood.telemetry import wrap_client, emit_error, emit_metric

client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
telemetry_client = wrap_client(client, service='customer-portal', sdk='redwood-python')

def generate_sync(prompt):
    import time
    start = time.time()
    try:
        resp = telemetry_client.generate(model='redwood-beta-1', prompt=prompt)
        return resp
    except Exception as e:
        emit_error(e, { 'route': 'generate' })
        raise
    finally:
        emit_metric('request.latency_ms', int((time.time() - start) * 1000))
```

Config templates (example env vars and runtime flags)

| Name | Purpose | Recommended default | Notes |
|------|---------|--------------------|-------|
| REDWOOD_API_KEY | API key for calls | n/a | Must be kept secret |
| REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_KEY | Ingest key for telemetry | generated-per-customer | Should be rotated quarterly |
| REDWOOD_SDK_ENV | runtime tag (dev/staging/prod) | prod | used to split metrics |
| REDWOOD_SDK_BATCHING | toggles client-side prompt batching | true | set to false for low-volume interactive apps |

Smoke tests and sample prompts

- Smoke prompts set (run 5 requests):
  1) Short generate: 'Summarize: Redwood Inference in one sentence.'
  2) Long-context generate (>=512 tokens): a 700-token lorem input to exercise KV cache behavior.
  3) Embeddings call for a short string: 'redwood inference'
  4) Streaming response session: follow-up question to streaming-enabled route
  5) Failure injection: toggle network to simulate 503 and confirm retry behavior

Runbook: triage steps when metrics are abnormal

1. Validate client health
   - Confirm SDK version and environment variables.
   - Check client-side logs for repeated retry patterns or immediate 401/403.
2. Check telemetry pipeline
   - Confirm events flowing into the telemetry backend (Datadog/Loki/CloudWatch).
   - If missing: verify REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_KEY and network egress.
3. Backend API health
   - Query /healthz for the Redwood route the customer uses (internal URL pattern: https://s-api.redwood-inference.internal/healthz).
   - Review per-route latency and error trends in last 15m and 1h.
4. Model saturation and capacity
   - Check GPU pool saturation metrics: dedicated_pool.utilization > 85% indicates contention.
   - For hosted customers, confirm fallback policy triggered? If so, identify variant used.
5. Mitigation steps
   - If retries spike: advise client-side jittered exponential backoff and temporary rate limit on client.
   - If 5xx rates high and capacity saturation is visible: escalate to Serving Runtime oncall.

Common patterns & canonical fixes (support playbook)

- Symptom: Sudden increase in token mismatch between telemetry and billing
  Fix: Run token accounting audit: sample 100 requests and compare tokens_out between telemetry and billing logs. If discrepancy > 5%, enable SDK token-echo debug (REDWOOD_SDK_TOKEN_ECHO=true) and collect a trace.

- Symptom: P95 latency has increased by >40% after deploy
  Fix: Revert client-side batching config to previous value; check model rollout history for a new model variant; roll back canary.

- Symptom: Missing traces but metrics present
  Fix: Ensure tracing backend endpoint and SDK trace sampler are configured; check for dropped spans due to size (very long streaming sessions).

Escalation matrix

- Level 1 (Support): response target 15m — first contact, capture logs, confirm telemetry presence. Owned by Customer Support.
- Level 2 (Integrations): response target 60m — reproduce, collect SDK logs, run smoke tests. Owned by Integrations team (eng-developer-experience).
- Level 3 (Serving Runtime / SRE): response target 2h — investigate fleet, model variants, capacity. Owned by eng-serving-runtime and eng-sre.

Diagnostic commands and snippets

- Check logs (example):

```bash
sections.heading: Python example (fast path)

sections.body: kubectl logs -l app=customer-portal --tail=200 | grep redwood
sections.heading: tail last 200 lines of SDK logs

sections.body:
dd logs 'trace.id:TRACE_ID' --from 15m
```

- Local replay test (developer):

```bash
REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-test REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_KEY=tk-test node scripts/smoke-runner.js
```

Safety & privacy guidance

- Never include customer PII in telemetry payloads. The SDK includes a scrubber that redacts high-entropy tokens; for regulated customers set REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_PII_FILTER=strong.
- For restricted customers use the private telemetry gateway option; contact Solutions Engineering to provision.

Appendix A — diagnostic checklist (one-page)

- Confirm: SDK pinned to supported minor
- Confirm: REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_KEY present and accepted by backend
- Confirm: 5 smoke prompts returned expected shapes
- Confirm: Token accounting sample within ±3%
- Confirm: No sustained P99 > 2s or errors > 0.5%

Appendix B — ownership and contacts

- SDK Observability lead: Ava Martinez (eng-developer-experience) — ava@redwood.example.com
- Integrations oncall: see /confluence/eng-developer-experience/runbooks/oncall-rotations
- Serving runtime oncall: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/oncall-rotations

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Created (A. Martinez)
- 2026-02-08: Added Python examples, refined SLOs, and added telemetry token audit step (L. O'Neill review)

payload.page_title: Quickstart Templates (RAG + Agents) — Project Brief

sections.body:
h1. Summary
Redwood Inference’s Developer Experience (DevEx) org is building *production-minded Quickstart Templates* for *RAG + agents*.

These templates are opinionated scaffolds that help developers go from *sign-up → running locally → deployed app → observable in production* with safe defaults. The goal is to reduce onboarding friction while ensuring templates are reliable, secure, and maintainable.

This brief defines goals, non-goals, target personas, initial template lineup, and the definition of success (including time-to-first-success, template retention, and support deflection).

h1. Problem Statement
Developers evaluating Redwood often ask for “a working, production-ready RAG app” rather than isolated SDK snippets. Current gaps:
* Too many choices early (models, frameworks, infra) without guardrails.
* Lack of consistent instrumentation makes debugging and cost attribution hard.
* Examples are not always resilient to real-world failure modes (streaming disconnects, proxy behavior, rate limits).
* Support tickets repeat the same setup issues (401s, 429s, OTel exporter configuration).

h1. Goals
h2. Primary goals (v1)
1) *Fast activation:* Provide a guided path to a first successful, observable request.
2) *Production-minded by default:* Safe timeouts/retries, sensible token/cost limits, guardrails for agent loops and tool calls.
3) *Operational hooks:* Standard metrics, traces, and logs that align with Redwood Observability/SRE standards.
4) *Maintainability:* Versioned releases, CI smoke tests (streaming/tool-calling), dependency pinning, and a consistent template structure across languages.

h2. Secondary goals
* Keep *vendor lock-in minimal* via provider abstraction and “drop-in” replacement patterns.
* Provide deployment recipes covering common paths for Hosted API users and a clear bridge to Dedicated/Private guidance.

h1. Non-Goals
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Building a full-featured end-user product UI (templates may include a minimal web endpoint or simple UI, but not a complete app).
* Supporting every vector database and every framework (we will start small with one local default and optional adapters).
* Shipping a fully managed ingestion service; templates will include basic ingestion/indexing and clear extension points.
* Creating a new Redwood product feature branded as “Agents.” Templates demonstrate agent loops using existing API/SDK primitives.
* Supporting in-place auto-upgrades of existing apps. We will support “generate a new version” + documented migration steps.

h1. Target Personas
h2. Persona A: PLG engineer (self-serve)
*Profile:* Full-stack or backend engineer evaluating Redwood for a new feature.
*Needs:*
* Get running quickly with minimal setup.
* Clear defaults and guardrails that avoid footguns.
* Troubleshooting guidance that maps to common errors.
* Observability they can verify locally.
*Success looks like:* “I can answer questions over my docs in <1 hour, and I can see latency/token metrics and traces.”

h2. Persona B: ML/Platform engineer (enterprise)
*Profile:* Platform team standardizing inference; cares about reliability, compliance posture, and operability.
*Needs:*
* OTel-compatible telemetry with clear naming conventions.
* Secure patterns for secrets handling, logging redaction, and PII safety.
* Deployment options (Docker/k8s) and compatibility with Dedicated/Private.
* Model pinning and rollout-safe configs.
*Success looks like:* “This template is a credible starting point for a production service and aligns with our standards.”

h2. Persona C: Solutions/Support engineer (internal)
*Profile:* Helps customers adopt Redwood and needs reproducible reference implementations.
*Needs:*
* Predictable template behavior.
* Standardized error taxonomy and logs.
* A ‘doctor’ workflow for environment validation.
*Success looks like:* “I can diagnose issues quickly using the same signals across customers.”

h1. Scope and Deliverables
h2. What we are shipping (v1)
1) *Template repositories*
   * Python: RAG + agent quickstart (default)
   * TypeScript: RAG + agent quickstart (parity-focused)

2) *Core template capabilities*
   * Retrieval pipeline: ingestion → chunking defaults → indexing → retrieval interface
   * Agent loop with tool calling:
     * Tool schema validation
     * Max-iterations guard
     * Tool output size limits
     * Clear tool error handling
   * Streaming robustness:
     * Safe timeouts
     * Retry/backoff (including guidance for streaming reconnect)
     * Circuit breaker behavior for repeated failures
   * Config via environment variables (documented schema + validation on startup)
   * Example “golden prompts” and eval hook points for regression testing

3) *Observability instrumentation (standardized)*
   * OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and structured logs
   * Required attributes/fields and redaction rules
   * Correlation IDs and Redwood request ID propagation
   * Prebuilt dashboards and recommended alert rules (via Observability Pack)

4) *Template CLI / scaffolder*
   * `init`: create a new project from a chosen template + write a version stamp
   * `doctor`: validate env vars, API connectivity, and local collector health with actionable remediation

5) *Documentation integration*
   * Docs IA updates: Quickstart Templates section + navigation
   * Walkthrough: RAG + agents template
   * Troubleshooting: common errors and how to interpret signals
   * Instrumentation guidance (language-specific patterns)

h2. Initial template lineup
We will launch with a deliberately narrow set to reduce maintenance risk:
* *RAG + Agents (Python)* — reference implementation and first-class support.
* *RAG + Agents (TypeScript)* — parity implementation with streaming and middleware patterns.

Planned follow-ons (post-v1, not launch blockers):
* “Batch embeddings” template (cost-focused ingestion)
* “RAG API only” minimal backend template
* Optional hosted vector DB adapter (one selection based on partner/customer demand)

h1. Design Principles (v1)
* *Secure by default:* no secrets in repo, no keys in logs, redaction enabled.
* *Resilient by default:* safe timeouts/retries; explicit backpressure and concurrency guidance.
* *Observable by default:* OTel-first with stable naming conventions and low-cardinality dimensions.
* *Opinionated but extensible:* clear interfaces and “replace this module” extension points.
* *Minimal vendor lock-in:* provider abstraction, model pinning configuration, and portability across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

h1. Definition of Success (Metrics)
We will measure success using a mix of product analytics, operational signals, and support outcomes.

h2. KPI 1: Time-to-first-success (TTFS)
*Definition:* elapsed time from template start (CLI init or repo clone) to first successful, tagged Redwood response from a template run.

*Measurement approach:*
* Funnel events (opt-in telemetry):
  * `template_init` → `template_config_valid` → `template_first_request_started` → `template_first_request_succeeded`
* Use a template tag/header convention that does not include user content (privacy-safe).

*Targets (v1, 30 days post-launch):*
* Median TTFS: *≤ 20 minutes* (Python), *≤ 25 minutes* (TypeScript)
* 75th percentile TTFS: *≤ 45 minutes*

h2. KPI 2: Template retention (developer re-use)
*Definition:* the percentage of template-initialized projects that generate traffic again after initial day.

*Measurement approach:*
* `template_first_request_succeeded` followed by any `template_request_succeeded` in subsequent windows.

*Targets (v1, 60 days post-launch):*
* D7 retention: *≥ 25%*
* D30 retention: *≥ 10%*

h2. KPI 3: Support deflection
*Definition:* reduction in repetitive onboarding tickets attributable to improved templates + docs.

*Measurement approach:*
* Track volume and resolution time for top issues:
  * Auth misconfig (401)
  * Rate limits (429)
  * Streaming disconnects
  * OTel exporter misconfiguration
  * Tool schema/structured output parse errors
* Compare against a pre-launch baseline and monitor with Support Ops.

*Targets (v1, 60 days post-launch):*
* 15–25% reduction in tickets for the top 3 template-related categories
* ≥ 20% reduction in median time-to-resolution for template-tagged tickets

h2. Engineering quality gates (must-have)
* CI smoke tests for:
  * streaming stability
  * tool-call parsing + schema validation
  * basic retrieval correctness
* Dependency pinning + vulnerability scanning workflow
* Docs completeness checklist met for each template release

h1. Milestones and Timeline
Dates are targets and may shift with SDK dependencies.

*Phase 1 — Discovery & requirements (Feb 2025)*
* Finalize v1 requirements, safe defaults, and observability standard.
* Confirm model targets and pinning guidance.

*Phase 2 — Core templates + baseline RAG/agent loop (late Feb – early Mar 2025)*
* Python template scaffold + RAG baseline + agent/tool loop.
* TypeScript scaffold with streaming.
* Evals hook + golden prompts.

*Phase 3 — Observability pack integration (Mar 2025)*
* OTel conventions implemented.
* Dashboards and recommended alert rules published.

*Phase 4 — Docs integration + launch readiness (Mar – Apr 2025)*
* Docs IA updates.
* Walkthrough + troubleshooting.
* Release process + support playbooks.

*Phase 5 — Iterate from beta feedback (Apr 2025+)*
* Fix top friction points, reduce CI flakiness, refine defaults.

h1. Dependencies
* SDK changes (blocking or high leverage):
  * TypeScript: streaming reconnect behavior and improved error types
  * Python: trace context propagation helpers, standardized timeouts/retry policy
* Gateway support for a small, validated set of telemetry headers/tags (opt-in, privacy-safe)
* Observability Pack: dashboards/alerts and collector config examples
* Docs team bandwidth for IA and new content

h1. Risks and Mitigations
| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|--------|------------|
| Streaming instability across proxies | Poor UX, support load | Conservative defaults; reconnect guidance; CI smoke tests; documented proxy considerations |
| High-cardinality telemetry dimensions | Cost/perf issues in metrics backend | Enforce naming/dimension allowlist; review by Observability; default to low-cardinality attributes |
| Telemetry headers blocked by corporate proxies | Requests fail; adoption metrics incomplete | Make telemetry opt-in; fall back to query param or SDK tag where possible; document workaround |
| Template maintenance burden grows | Slow releases; quality regressions | Narrow v1 scope; shared utilities; versioned releases; CI gates; standard README structure |
| Security regressions (secrets/PII) | Compliance risk | Redaction by default; secure SDLC checks; dependency scanning; explicit logging guidance |
| Confusion around “agents” terminology | Misaligned expectations | Clear glossary and positioning (“agent loop example,” not a Redwood product feature) |

h1. Ownership and Working Model

*Program management:* Talia Benson
*Engineering lead:* Monica Patel
*Docs lead:* Elliot Price
*Observability standards owner:* Allison Grant
*Hosted API PM stakeholders:* Nikhil Sharma, Henry Cho
*Security reviewers:* Kaitlyn Nguyen, Marcus Lin

payload.page_title: Developer Onramp: Localization, Docs-site Ops, and Canonical Fixes Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook bundles three tightly related areas that frequently cause onboarding friction for new integrations: SDK localization (i18n) readiness, docs-site operational procedures (staging/canary/translation pipelines), and a compact set of canonical fixes for the top support issues we see from developer onramps. The goal is a one-page operational reference that engineering, Docs, and Support can use during new SDK ship weeks and customer trials.

Goals
- Reduce mean-time-to-first-success (MTTFS) for new SDK adopters by 30% through localized examples and a repeatable docs deploy pipeline.
- Provide concise canonical fixes for the top 8 devx support issues so Support can resolve 60% of triageable tickets without engineering intervention.
- Maintain a low-friction docs release process (canary -> staged -> prod) with clear rollback semantics and telemetry hooks.

Audience
- Developer Experience engineers and tech writers shipping SDK examples and docs.
- Support engineers handling integration issues and reproductions.
- Product engineers owning SDKs or client libraries.

Scope and non-goals
- Included: JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Go SDK snippets; docs-site content lifecycle; translation handoff and CI checks; canonical fixes for common API/SDK errors.
- Excluded: full localization of legal or marketing copy; mobile SDKs beyond sample snippets.

Prerequisites
1) Repo layout: all SDK examples live under repo: redwood/devx-examples (branch: main).
2) Docs-site: hosted via docs.redwood-inference.internal, uses static site generator with i18n plugin (locales in /i18n/*.json).
3) CI: GitHub Actions with workflows: docs-canary.yml, docs-staged.yml, docs-prod.yml.
4) Telemetry: snippet telemetry.events.example_load, telemetry.tags.locale, and telemetry.context.sdk_version must be emitted by sample harness.

Quickstart: Localized SDK Example Bundle (developer flow)
1. Clone examples: git clone git@github.com:redwood/devx-examples.git && cd devx-examples
2. Install toolchain (node/pip/go): ./scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh
3. Generate locale-specific examples: ./scripts/generate-localized-examples --locales=en,es,fr --sdk=python
4. Run local docs server including translations: npm run docs:local -- --locale=fr
5. Verify telemetry events appear in staging stream (kinesis-devx-staging):
   - Expected event: {"event":"example_load","locale":"fr","sdk":"python","version":"0.12.0"}
6. Submit PR to docs-examples with i18n diffs and request docs-site canary deploy via label: docs-canary-request

SDK Localization Checklist (per release)
- [ ] Confirm sample text keys are externalized (no hard-coded English strings in code examples).
- [ ] Provide translation-ready README and example captions in /i18n/{locale}.json.
- [ ] Localized code comments: keep English primary, add short localized caption lines under // LOCAL: ... to avoid syntax churn.
- [ ] Add locale-specific smoke tests: tests/smoke/{locale}/example_test.py (asserts example runs and emits telemetry).
- [ ] Bump telemetry schema version if adding fields: TELEMETRY_SCHEMA: v2 -> notify analytics@redwood.com.

Table: Supported Example Locales and Priority
Locale | Priority | Owner | Notes
------ | -------- | ----- | -----
en (English) | high | devx-eng | baseline; all CI gates run against en
es (Spanish) | medium | intl-ops | customer-facing regions: LATAM, EU-ES
fr (French) | medium | intl-ops | EU-FR customers
de (German) | low | intl-ops | add on request
ja (Japanese) | low | intl-ops | APAC pilot only

Docs-site Operating Procedure (canary -> staged -> prod)
1) Authoring and PRs
   - Create content branch in docs-content repo and include locale JSONs under /i18n.
   - Attach smoke test run output to PR (artifact: smoke-{sha}.zip).
   - Tag PR with labels: [docs-canary-request] or [docs-staged-request] as appropriate.
2) Canary deploy (automatic with label docs-canary-request)
   - Action: GitHub Action docs-canary.yml runs build and deploys to docs-canary.redwood-inference.internal.
   - Checks (must pass): build (exit 0), i18n-linter (no missing keys), smoke-tests (artifacts present), telemetry sanity (at least one example_load event during smoke test).
   - Rollback: manual; revert PR or trigger docs-canary-rollback workflow.
3) Staged deploy (after 48h of Canary uptime and signoff)
   - Add label docs-staged-request. Ops lead runs gated promote: ./tools/promote_docs.sh --from=canary --to=staged --approve="<approver>"
   - Staged URL: docs-staged.redwood-inference.internal. Run translation QA with translator team.
4) Prod promote
   - Window: M-F 9:00-17:00 PT. Approvals: 2 reviewers (author + docs eng). Run promote script with --to=prod and monitor SLOs for 30min.

Operational SLOs for Docs-site during promote windows
- Build success rate >= 99% (30-day rolling).
- Canary smoke-tests pass within 15 minutes after deploy.
- No production downtime > 1 minute caused by new docs push.

Canonical Support Issues and Fixes (top issues during onramp)
Issue A: SDK example fails to authenticate (401)
- Detection: error pattern in logs: "error=unauthorized, code=401, hint=apiKey"; Support: run reproduction script with -v flag.
- Root cause: sample uses environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY unset or using expired demo key.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm env var exists: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY
  2. If missing, instruct customer to create API key via console (link: internal:product-docs/create-api-key).
  3. For expired keys, rotate and confirm permission scopes: scopes must include: [inference:invoke, metrics:read].
  4. Add small code snippet to sample that fails fast with helpful error message (example below).
- Owner: Support -> escalate to SDK owner if repro fails.

Code snippet: fail-fast auth check (Python)
```python
import os
api_key = os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError('Missing REDWOOD_API_KEY environment variable. Create one at https://console.redwood-inference.internal/settings/api-keys')
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```

Issue B: Streaming responses stall mid-stream
- Detection: client receives first tokens then stalls; metrics show open connection but no bytes.
- Root cause: client-level keepalive mismatch or proxy buffering (common with corporate proxies).
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Ask customer to test with curl -N to confirm raw stream:
     curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -N \"https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/stream?...\"
  2. If curl works, recommend SDK change: prefer chunked transfer decoding and set socket keepalive: true.
  3. Provide fallback example using poll-based generation with polling timeout 5s.
- Owner: SDK eng + DevX docs for the streaming troubleshooting page.

Issue C: Localized examples missing strings or have placeholders ("__MISSING__")
- Detection: i18n-linter failure in CI; smoke test asserts replaceable keys remain.
- Root cause: upstream translations not merged to branch or translation key mismatch after refactor.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Run i18n-linter locally: npm run i18n-lint -- --locale=es
  2. Check missing keys report: ./tools/i18n-report --sha <pr-sha>
  3. If keys changed upstream, rebase PR and run ./scripts/merge-i18n.sh
  4. If translation missing, create placeholder and flag translator for fast-turn merge.
- Owner: Docs + Intl-ops.

Issue D: SDK telemetry not appearing in staging (no example_load events)
- Detection: telemetry dashboard shows zero events for smoke-run timeframe.
- Root cause: SDK example uses wrong telemetry endpoint, or telemetry schema mismatch.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm telemetry endpoint env var: TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT points to staging ingestion.
  2. Run smoke tests locally with verbose flag and inspect emitted payloads: ./scripts/run-smoke --verbose | jq .
  3. If schema mismatch, check TELEMETRY_SCHEMA in repo and bump analytics contract.
- Owner: DevX instrumentation owner.

Emergency rollback recipe (docs-site)
- Trigger: Canary or staged build causes widespread example breakage or production regressions.
- Steps:
  1. Revert offending PR or tag immediately. Use GitHub UI or: git revert --no-edit <merge-commit> && push.
  2. Run docs-canary-rollback action: ./tools/docs_rollback --env=canary --commit=<last-good-commit>
  3. Notify #devx and #sre-channels with incident summary template (include commit, author, time).
  4. Run postmortem within 72 hours if > 15 developer-impacting incidents occurred.

Telemetry and Monitoring (what to watch)
- Telemetry events: example_load, example_error, docs_build_status
- Dashboards: DevX -> Examples Overview, Docs -> Build Health, Support -> Top SDK Errors
- Alerts: Build failure rate > 5% in 1h (PagerDuty to Docs oncall), Missing telemetry events for a deployed smoke run (Slack alert to #devx-monitor).

Owner matrix and contact points
- DevX Docs (authoring + i18n): Marisol Vega (owner)
- Intl-ops (translation & QA): Sana Ribeiro
- SDK engineering (runtime fixes): Evan Park
- Support triage lead: Luis Moreno

Appendix: Example file layout (minimal)
- /devx-examples/
  - /python/
    - example_quickstart.py
    - README.md
    - /i18n/en.json
    - /i18n/es.json
  - /js/
    - example_quickstart.js
    - /i18n/en.json

Contact and escalation
- For blocked promotes contact: #devx-ops on Slack and add pager: docs-oncall@redwood-inference.internal
- For telemetry contract questions: analytics@redwood-inference.internal

Revision history
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft by Marisol Vega
- 2025-11-03: Added streaming troubleshooting and telemetry checks (review: Evan Park)
- 2026-02-20: Finalized canary/staged procedure and rollback script path updates

Related artifacts and snippets
- Scripts referenced live in repo: https://github.com/redwood/devx-examples/tree/main/scripts
- Translation handoff template: /templates/translation-handoff.md

End of playbook

payload.page_title: SDK sample codegen and API stub runbook

sections.body:
Overview

This runbook describes the automated generation of SDK sample code, in-repo API stubs, and the pipeline that publishes those artifacts to the docs site. It combines the codegen tooling (openapi-codegen + internal templates), a lightweight stub generator used by support and DX engineers, and the recommended CI integration and canonical fixes for the top operational issues we encounter.

Goals
- Keep SDK sample snippets in docs consistent with product API surface and runtime examples.
- Provide a reproducible, auditable codegen pipeline that runs on pull request and release builds.
- Ship small, targeted API stubs for customer repros and support playbooks.
- Reduce drift between SDKs and API reference by running nightly validation and example smoke tests.

Scope and non-goals
- Included: TypeScript/Python/Go samples, OpenAPI-driven method stubs, example prompts for generation endpoints, CI validation harness, and docs site publishing.
- Excluded: Full SDK compilation pipeline (this runbook ties into SDK pipelines but does not replace them).

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (Aisha Patel)
- Secondary owners: eng-serving-runtime (Marco Reyes) for API shape changes, eng-platform (Emily Chen) for CI integration.
- Pager: devx-oncall (see /confluence/eng-developer-experience/support-top-issues/devx-oncall-roster)

Prerequisites
- Repo layout: examples/ templates/ openapi/ scripts/codegen/
- Tooling: Node 18+, Python 3.10+, openapi-generator-cli v6+, internal template repo at git@redwood:devx/codegen-templates.git
- Secrets: DOCS_SITE_API_KEY (encrypted in CI), SAMPLE_RUNNER_KMS (for signing examples)

Architecture summary
- Source of truth: openapi/ openapi.yaml (maintained by runtime & API owners)
- Generator: scripts/codegen/generate-samples.js (wraps openapi-generator with internal templates)
- Stub generator: scripts/stubgen/create_stub.py — creates small JSON + server shim for local repros
- Validation: scripts/validate/run_examples.py — starts sample runner and asserts expected tokens and status codes
- Docs pipeline: docs-site build step consumes examples/dist/ and publishes code blocks via docs site content-plugin

How it works (high level)
1. On PR to openapi/ or templates/, CI triggers codegen job.
2. Generator emits language-specific examples to examples/generated/{lang}/.
3. Validation jobs run smoke tests (unit + sample runner).
4. If green, examples are committed to the examples/ branch and a docs site preview build is published.
5. Nightly job compares examples against running runtime (canary) to detect drift.

Developer quickstart: generate a single endpoint sample locally
1. Ensure prereqs installed:
   - nvm use 18 && npm ci
   - pyenv local 3.10.8 && pip install -r scripts/requirements.txt
2. Pull the openapi file: cp openapi/openapi.yaml /tmp/openapi.yaml (or pull latest via git).
3. Run generator for TypeScript snippet:
   - node scripts/codegen/generate-samples.js --lang typescript --openapi /tmp/openapi.yaml --operation listModels --out examples/generated/typescript/
4. Inspect snippet: examples/generated/typescript/listModels.sample.ts
5. Run the sample against local dev runtime: NODE_ENV=local node examples/generated/typescript/listModels.sample.ts

Generator CLI reference (common flags)
- --lang {typescript,python,go}  # language target
- --openapi <path|url>
- --operation <operationId|all>
- --out <dir>
- --template-repo <git-url>
- --force (overwrite existing examples)

Example: full run for Python + smoke test
- python3 scripts/codegen/generate-samples.py --lang python --openapi openapi/openapi.yaml --out examples/generated/python/ && python3 scripts/validate/run_examples.py --dir examples/generated/python/ --runner-url http://localhost:8080

API stub generator (support playbook)
- Purpose: produce a minimal, reproducible server shim and JSON fixture for fast problem reproduction and for attaching to support tickets.
- Invocation: python3 scripts/stubgen/create_stub.py --operation chatCreate --status 200 --body fixtures/chat-create-ok.json --out stubs/chat-create/
- Output: stubs/chat-create/{server.sh, fixture.json, README.md}
- The server shim is a tiny Flask or FastAPI app that returns the fixture payload; it includes a small README with curl examples for reproducing the exact request/response pair.

Docs site integration
- Plugin: docs-site consumes examples/dist/ and inlines code blocks through frontmatter reference: example:
  - frontmatter: example: examples/dist/typescript/listModels.sample.ts
- Build: docs-site CI step 'generate-examples' should run after openapi and before site build.
- Preview: Pull requests that change examples/ will create a preview deploy to staging-docs.redwood.internal for QA.

CI job templates (GitHub Actions sample)
- name: Generate API examples
  uses: actions/checkout@v4
  steps:
    - run: setup-node-and-python.sh
    - run: node scripts/codegen/generate-samples.js --openapi openapi/openapi.yaml --lang all --out examples/generated/
    - run: python3 scripts/validate/run_examples.py --dir examples/generated/
    - name: Upload examples artifact
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: generated-examples
        path: examples/generated/

Release checklist (for codegen and docs publishing)
1. Verify openapi.yaml has been approved by API owners.
2. Run codegen locally and run full smoke tests.
3. Create PR; include generated artifacts if change is to templates or canonical examples.
4. Wait for CI: generation + validation + docs preview.
5. Reviewer checklist: sample output runs, no secrets in generated files, samples follow style guide (see examples/style-guide.md).
6. Merge and monitor the staging-docs preview for regressions.

Monitoring and SLOs for examples pipeline
- Nightly drift detection run (cron @ 02:30 UTC) — target: run within 15 minutes window.
- Validation pass rate target: 99.5% over 30 days.
- Alert: Generate-examples job failure fires P0 to devx-oncall if > 5 consecutive nightly failures.

Common problems and canonical fixes (top support issues)
1. Generated examples use old auth header schema
   - Symptom: examples fail with 401 and stack trace indicates 'invalid_token'
   - Root cause: openapi.yaml credential scheme name changed from 'bearerAuth' to 'redwoodAuth' but templates still reference bearerAuth.
   - Fix: Update templates in codegen-templates repo to map securitySchemes.redwoodAuth -> Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}. Run codegen and regenerate examples.
2. Docs inlined examples render with wrong language fence
   - Symptom: Syntax highlighting is incorrect on site and code blocks marked as 'text'
   - Fix: Ensure frontmatter contains language key (exampleLang: typescript). Validate frontmatter -> examples/dist/manifest.json in preview build.
3. Smoke tests intermittently fail due to rate-limiting in shared dev runtime
   - Symptom: 429 returned from example runner in CI flakily
   - Fix: Add retry/backoff to run_examples.py and enable ephemeral per-job API key generated by CI. For immediate mitigation, re-run job after 60s. Long term, use local stub runner for stable CI results.
4. Example output contains real customer data
   - Symptom: generated fixture includes PII values observed in openapi example payloads
   - Fix: Run scripts/sanitize/sanitize_fixtures.py across examples/ and add check to validate no email/phone patterns. Block merge if detected. Rotate and remove any published artifacts containing sensitive data.

Troubleshooting checklist (steps to remediate quickly)
1. Recreate locally: clone repo, run codegen with --operation <id> and point openapi to the PR branch.
2. Validate: run_examples.py --verbose and collect logs to attach to ticket.
3. If CI shows 429s or auth failures, try stubgen to reproduce without sharing dev runtime.
4. If highlights or inlining fail on staging-docs, check examples/dist/manifest.json and ensure hashes match artifact in CI.

Operational runbooks and playbooks
- Emergency rollback: if docs site publishes broken examples, revert examples/ commit and trigger docs rebuild. Notify support and post an incident update with impacted pages.
- Canary release: for major template changes, push templates to a canary branch and run full validation against canary runtime and internal SDK CI.

Appendix: sample template mapping table
| Template variable | Description | Example |
|------------------|-------------|---------|
| {{OPERATION_ID}} | OpenAPI operationId | chatCreate |
| {{LANG}} | Target language | typescript |
| {{AUTH_HEADER}} | Resolved auth header snippet | Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_TOKEN} |

Change log
- 2026-11-02: Created initial runbook (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-12-10: Added stub generator playbook and CI action (Marco Reyes).
- 2027-02-15: Added drift detection SLOs and sanitization step (Emily Chen).

Related resources
- examples/style-guide.md
- scripts/validate/run_examples.py
- git@redwood:devx/codegen-templates.git
- /confluence/eng-developer-experience/support-top-issues/sdk-call-tracing-root-cause-playbook-2026

Contact and escalation
- Primary: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Secondary: eng-devx Slack channel #devx-support

End of document

payload.page_title: SDK Experimentation Labs and Issue Resolver Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page describes the SDK Experimentation Labs program and the associated Issue Resolver Playbook used by Developer Experience (DevX) to onboard new SDK patterns, validate API examples, and reduce repetitive support escalations. The goal is to make safe, fast iteration on SDK features while producing reproducible canonical fixes for the support team and docs site.

Audience
--------
- SDK engineers and maintainers
- Developer advocates and technical writers
- Support engineers and on-call devx leads

What the labs deliver
---------------------
- Reproducible quickstarts and minimal sample apps for each SDK surface (generation, streaming, embeddings, batching).
- A canonical-fixes catalog: triaged patterns + root cause + validated patch.
- A docs-site lifecycle that ensures snippet parity between README, quickstart, and docs rendering.
- A short feedback loop from support issues to SDK tests and docs changes.

Program structure
-----------------
1. Lab intake: maintainers file a lab request when a new API surface or model variant is introduced. Include: rationale, target customers, API contract, and telemetry flags to collect.
2. Authoring: SDK author pairs with a tech writer to produce: minimal quickstart, two API examples, and an integration test harness.
3. Validation: run the examples across local emulation and a CI lab against the runtime staging cluster and with a small set of live model variants.
4. Publish: merge artifacts into the docs site and the SDK repo. Tag the quickstart with a canonical-fix id if it closed a support pattern.

Quickstarts and templates catalog (summary table)
------------------------------------------------
Name | Purpose | Minimum deliverables | Owner
-----|---------|----------------------|------
sdk-experimentation-template | Fast scaffold for new SDK features | README, quickstart app, CI job, telemetry knobs | SDK author team
sample-embed-to-gen | Show embedding-driven retrieval + generation | sample app, test dataset, golden traces | Integrations team

(Avoid copy/paste: actual catalog is a living Confluence table; link in related_pages above.)

Authoring guidelines (checklist)
--------------------------------
- Keep quickstarts under 200 lines of code.
- Include a network/emulation mode for offline devs (see example below).
- Provide an explicit "expected output" golden trace for every example.
- Add a short troubleshooting section with at least one likely symptom and a reproducible command.

Example: minimal streaming quickstart (pseudo-code)
--------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
from redwood_sdk import Client
client = Client(api_key="${REDWOOD_API_KEY}")
with client.stream("gpt-4o-mini") as stream:
    stream.send({"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about compilers"})
    for chunk in stream.recv_chunks():
        print(chunk.text, end="")

Dev note: Add a test that asserts concatenated chunks == golden_output.

Docs site operating procedures
------------------------------
- Branching: all quickstarts live in docs-source/quickstarts. Changes must include a generated snippet diff via the docs CI preview job.
- Canary publishing: new quickstarts are published to the staging docs site under /labs/ for 72 hours. During canary window, telemetry is collected (snippet usage, example run failures, runtime error rates).
- Ownership: each quickstart must include a two-line metadata header: maintainer, last-verified-date, and supported SDK versions.
- Snippet canonicalization: snippets in SDK READMEs are the canonical source. Docs site build pulls snippets from those files rather than inlining long copy. This reduces drift.

CI and test requirements for lab merges
--------------------------------------
- Unit tests covering API contract surface (>= 90% contract assertions).
- Integration harness that runs the quickstart end-to-end in emulation and reports a golden-trace hash.
- Telemetry smoke: example should emit at least these telemetry events: example.start, example.success/failure, example.latency_ms.
- Docs preview: docs CI must show snippet diffs and render warnings if a code block exceeds 200 lines.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (summary)
------------------------------------------------
1) Symptom: streaming partials drop order in some consumers.
   - Root cause: client code concatenates chunks without respecting 'sequence_id' emitted by runtime when multiplexing multiple streams on the same connection.
   - Canonical fix: use stream.recv_chunks(order_by='sequence_id') helper or enable "ordered_streaming": true in client config.
   - Playbook steps:
     1. Reproduce with the failing snippet in the lab emulation mode (run reproduce_stream_drop.sh).
     2. Patch the example to use ordered recv helper.
     3. Add regression test that interleaves 5 concurrent streams and asserts ordering.
     4. Publish fix and cross-link support ticket with canonical-fix id CF-2027-014.

2) Symptom: embedding indexes return inconsistent distances after SDK update.
   - Root cause: SDK float32->float16 conversion was applied at client-side before normalization step, causing small numerical drift for low-norm vectors.
   - Canonical fix: move quantization to server-side and document the versioned vector schema in quickstart.
   - Playbook steps: see repository patch in sample-embed-to-gen quickstart; add an end-to-end golden trace to catch drift.

3) Symptom: elevated error-rate for ephemeral tokens in CI.
   - Root cause: token provider rotated keys mid-run without propagating the new token to ephemeral test runners.
   - Canonical fix: add a token refresh hook to the test harness and a CI gating step that ensures all ephemeral runners have token_version == latest.

Triage runbook (short)
----------------------
1. Capture: request telemetry id from support ticket and copy the golden-trace id.
2. Reproduce: clone the associated quickstart and run in emulation mode: ./dev/run_emulation.sh --trace ${ID}
3. Isolate: toggle SDK feature flags to find the minimal repro.
4. Patch: create minimal PR in sdk/ with test and example fix.
5. Verify: run canary docs preview + CI lab.
6. Ship: merge, publish docs, add note to the support ticket, and mark canonical-fix label.

Metrics and success signals
--------------------------
- Reduction in "same root cause" tickets for SDK surfaces by 60% within 90 days of lab adoption.
- Mean time to publish a canonical fix: target <= 7 days from first support ticket.
- Snippet drift: target < 2% of quickstarts per quarter requiring emergency patch.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Emulation local run:
  export REDWOOD_EMULATE=1
  ./dev/run_example.sh --example quickstarts/sample-embed-to-gen

- Golden trace check (CI):
  python tools/compare_traces.py --expected traces/golden.hash --actual traces/latest.hash

- Create a canonical-fix PR template (example title):
  [CF-<id>] fix: streaming-order-preservation in python-sdk quickstart

Ownership and escalation contacts
--------------------------------
- DevX on-call: devx-oncall@redwood.ai
- SDK authors: see quickstart metadata header (maintainer)
- Docs site owner: Marco Chen (docs-infra)

Notes and future work
---------------------
- Plan to add a lightweight sandbox runner that spins up a tenant-scoped runtime for higher-fidelity validation.
- Investigate automated snippet linting that validates both syntax and golden-trace equivalence during PR reviews.

If you are proposing a new lab, copy the SDK Experimentation template and complete the intake form attached to this page, then tag @devx-oncall for review.

sections.body:
Summary
This page is a compact reference for engineers integrating Redwood SDKs who want an opinionated, low-friction pattern for local testing (stubbed runtime), client-side prefetch/prediction batching, and cost-sensitive request shaping. It combines a short quickstart, recommended configuration table, canonical fixes for common support issues, and an on-call checklist for shipping safely.

When to use this cheatsheet
- Building or iterating an LLM-backed feature locally where full runtime access is slow or costly.
- Prototyping client-side batching or prefetch strategies before server rollout.
- Validating cost vs. latency tradeoffs with offline traces.

Goals
- Provide a reproducible local stub pattern that mirrors Redwood routing semantics.
- Offer a narrow set of batching/prefetch defaults with clear cost and latency tradeoffs.
- List deterministic troubleshooting steps (canonical fixes) for the top 6 support patterns we see.

Quickstart: local stub + prefetch loop (5 steps)
1) Install local stub CLI and runtime shim
   - Linux/macOS: pip install redwood-runtime-stub==0.2.1 or use the prebuilt docker image redwood/stub:0.2.1
   - Start a stub that accepts the same HTTP/JSON surface as hosted API for generation + embeddings:

     ```bash
     # Docker (recommended):
     docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e REDWOOD_STUB_MODE=prefetch redwood/stub:0.2.1

     # Python CLI (dev):
     redwood-stub serve --port 8080 --mode prefetch --cache-size 500
     ```

2) Wire SDK to local endpoint (example Node.js)
   - Set endpoint override in environment for local dev only:

     ```js
     // process.env.REDWOOD_API_URL = 'http://localhost:8080/v1'
     import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference-js';
     const client = new RedwoodClient({ baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_API_URL });
     ```

3) Add a simple prefetch + bundling layer in the client
   - Strategy: collect similar prompts for 50ms window, then issue a batched request. Keep max bundle size = 8 unless latency SLO allows higher.

     ```js
     // pseudo-code: bundler.js
     const queue = [];
     function request(modelInput) {
       return new Promise((resolve) => {
         queue.push({ modelInput, resolve });
       });
     }
     setInterval(async () => {
       if (!queue.length) return;
       const batch = queue.splice(0, 8);
       const response = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-alpha', inputs: batch.map(b=>b.modelInput) });
       response.forEach((r,i)=> batch[i].resolve(r));
     }, 50);
     ```

4) Enable cache hints and KV prefixing on the stub for realistic behavior
   - The stub includes a switch that simulates prefix/KV cache hits. Turn on using REDWOOD_STUB_CACHE_HINTS=1. This will let you test eviction behavior locally.

5) Run trace-driven cost sensitivity tests
   - Replay a 10k request trace against the stub, measure tokens and latency, and tune bundle window and max size until you hit target token/unit cost or latency. Use the provided trace-replayer: redwood-stub replay --trace example-trace.json --metrics out.csv

Recommended parameter table (opinionated defaults)
| Parameter | Default | When to increase | Expected cost impact | Expected latency impact | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| bundle_window_ms | 50 | When requests are bursty and SLO allows +20ms | lowers per-token cost via batching | +10–+60ms tail latency | Good starting point for web UX features |
| max_bundle_size | 8 | For high-throughput background jobs | reduces calls & per-call overhead | may increase median latency if window grows | Keep <= 32 for general purpose |
| prefetch_lookahead_tokens | 64 | For completion-heavy prompts where next-token distribution is predictable | modest increase if predictions wrong | reduces latency on hit | Use in product flows with strong user-action priors |
| cache_ttl_seconds | 300 | When results are stable (e.g., embeddings) | large savings for repeated queries | none on hit; misses cost same | Use longer TTLs for idempotent outputs |
| kv_cache_max_entries | 5_000 | Large conversational workloads | big savings for repeated prefixes | small memory cost | Evaluate on representative trace |

Cost/latency tradeoff guidance
- If 95th pct latency increases > 150ms after raising bundle_window_ms, reduce window or lower max_bundle_size.
- If per-request cost (tokens billed) exceeds projection by >10%, enable prefix hashing to increase cache hit rates.
- For interactive UIs, prefer bundle_window_ms <= 50 and max_bundle_size <= 8. For batch jobs, you can push both higher.

Canonical fixes for top support patterns
1) Symptom: Local responses are faster than hosted but production shows high variance
   - Fix: Confirm production routing policy is routing to the same model family and not falling back. Check /api/v1/routing/debug for active policies. Add a traffic mirror to the stub to compare payloads.
2) Symptom: Stubbing shows consistent cache hits, but production misses frequently
   - Fix: Ensure request fingerprinting (prompt normalization + tenant-scoped key) matches production. Production includes tenant_id and model_version in the cache key; stub uses a simplified key unless REDWOOD_STUB_FULL_KEY=1. Turn it on to replicate misses.
3) Symptom: Batches sometimes split identical prompts into different calls
   - Fix: Confirm bundler groups by fingerprint canonicalization (strip timestamps, IDs). Add a deterministic sort step before batching.
4) Symptom: Observed token usage > expected after enabling prefetch
   - Fix: Reduce prefetch_lookahead_tokens, and use conservative prefetching profiles per model. Run A/B test with sampled traffic to measure delta.
5) Symptom: Intermittent 429s from stub during replay tests
   - Fix: Increase stub's simulated capacity (REDWOOD_STUB_SIMULATED_TPS) or reduce bundle concurrency. For production 429s, check rate-limit headers from Redwood API and back off exponentially.
6) Symptom: Local trace replay mismatches production outputs
   - Fix: Ensure model_version pins are identical and that quantization profiles are compatible; the stub defaults to the float32 path unless REDWOOD_STUB_QUANTIZED=1 is set.

Observability checklist (for SDK integrations)
- Instrument: request_id, tenant_id, model_version, prompt_fingerprint, bundle_size, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, cache_hit (bool).
- Dashboards: per-route token cost, bundle_size distribution, cache hit rate, and 95/99 latency.
- Alerts: cache_hit_rate < 5% for 1h; median bundle_size < 1 for feature routes; 95 latency degradation >20% week-over-week.

Rollout checklist (safe progression)
1) Smoke in sandbox with stub: run 10k synthetic requests, validate outputs and metrics.
2) Canary 1% on hosted: enable canary routing to dedicated canary pool, collect 24h of telemetry.
3) Canary 10%: expand if metrics within thresholds. 48h telemetry.
4) Gradual ramp to 100% with monitoring playbook active and an automatic fallback to single-request, low-batch mode.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary author: Maya Chen (DevX)
- Runbook owner: Ravi Patel (Developer Platform)
- On-call contact: eng-sre rotation - see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations

Related resources and commands
- Stub repo and image: git@internal:redwood/runtime-stub.git
- Trace replayer: redwood-stub replay --help
- Helpful query (routing debug): curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://runtime-api.internal/v1/routing/debug

Appendix: small sample trace JSON (3 entries)
```json
[
  {"tenant_id":"team-123","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Summarize: The Q4 roadmap includes...","timestamp":1650000000},
  {"tenant_id":"team-123","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Summarize: The Q4 roadmap includes...","timestamp":1650000001},
  {"tenant_id":"team-456","model":"redwood-alpha","input":"Extract keywords: machine learning, inference","timestamp":1650000003}
]
```

Notes and rationale
- The bundling defaults balance web UX latency against unit-cost reduction and were calibrated against production traces from marketing site search and in-product suggestions.
- The stub intentionally offers toggles (full key mode, quantized path, simulated TPS) so teams can reproduce a range of production phenomena without full infra access.

If you have questions or want a pairing session to run your trace against the stub, open a ticket with tag "devx-stub-support" and reach out to any reviewer.

sections.body:
- Primary monorepo: git@internal:redwood/sdk-sample-bundles (canonical master)
- Short-lived forks for demos: git@internal:redwood/dx-demo-<bundle>

Quickstart — clone and run (common steps)
1) Clone the canonical monorepo and change into the example directory:
   git clone git@internal:redwood/sdk-sample-bundles.git
   cd sdk-sample-bundles/bundles/support-chat-v2
2) Create a .env (example below) and export locally: see .env.example
3) Install dependencies and run the dev server (example shown for Python):
   python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-test-xxxx
   export REDWOOD_API_URL=https://api.redwood-inference.internal
   ./dev_server.sh

Example .env.example (do not commit secrets)
REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-<REDACTED>
REDWOOD_API_URL=https://api.redwood-inference.internal
REDWOOD_PROJECT=demo-support-chat
LOG_LEVEL=debug
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel-ingest.internal:4317

API usage snippets (Python)
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), base_url=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_URL'))

with client.chat_stream(model="rwd-small-1", messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Help me find invoice 4823"}]) as stream:

        print(chunk.text, end='')

Adapter example (Node) — local sidecar pattern
// HTTP adapter that translates app payload to Redwood API calls
const express = require('express')
const app = express()
app.post('/local-chat', async (req, res) => {
  // translate and forward to Redwood through local credentials or direct fallback
})

Telemetry and observability guidance
- Each sample includes an OpenTelemetry scaffold. Configure OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in .env for dev/staging.
- Recommended spans: request.receive, redwood.call, redwood.stream, downstream.db.lookup.
- Attach these tags to all Redwood client calls: service.redwood.bundle, bundle.version, env.
- Suggested error rate alert during demo runs: >1% 5m window (reduce noisy alerts by excluding synthetic test tokens).

SLOs and performance notes for sample apps
- Demo latency targets (for dev/staging): P50 < 120ms for non-streaming embed calls; P95 < 600ms for chat with streaming off.
- Cost guidance: use quantized model variants in demos for cost-limited environments; see quantization_guidelines.md in repo.

Canonical fixes and common support patterns included in the bundles
- Retry with idempotency token pattern: examples include retry middleware for transient 5xx and 429 with exponential backoff.
- Circuit breaker wrapper: demonstrates graceful fallback to secondary model or cached response after N consecutive failures.
- Telemetry mismatch debugging: sample script that replays a failing trace and compares token-level timing to local simulated server.

Contribution and release process for the sample bundles
1) Branch off 'main' with prefix bundle/<bundle-name>/feature
2) Implement code and add a smoke test script under ./smoke-tests/<bundle>
3) Update the bundle manifest file bundles/manifest.yml with new version and changelog line
4) Open a PR, assign reviewers listed in this doc, and attach a short GIF demonstrating the app running
5) CI will run linters, unit tests, and a containerized smoke test. After merge, the package is tagged as: bundle-<bundle>-vX.Y.Z and published to our internal artifact index.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-dx (SDK examples) — eng-dx@redwood.internal
- Maintainer for support-chat-v2: Marcus Hill (marcus.hill@redwood.internal)
- Maintainer for embeddings-search-demo: Lina Chen (lina.chen@redwood.internal)

Onboarding notes for non-engineers
- Solutions engineers: there is a workspace with pre-provisioned API keys and a step-by-step slide deck in the /sales folder of the repo. Follow the "Slides -> Run demo" section.
- Developer advocates: use modal-llm-playground for tutorial videos — it includes a built-in recording toggle and synthetic data mode.

Operational runbook snippets (for demos in staging)
- If a demo experiences persistent 503s:
  1. Check REDWOOD_API_URL and DNS resolution
  2. Confirm API key validity: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" $REDWOOD_API_URL/v1/health
  3. Inspect application logs and traces in the OTEL backend for redwood.call errors
  4. If rate-limited, rotate to the low-traffic demo key and add a note to the bundle's README

FAQs
Q: Can I use these bundles with the Hosted offering?
A: Yes — update REDWOOD_API_URL to the hosted endpoint and set a hosted API key. Some demo configurations assume lower quotas; change model to a hosted-compatible SKU.

Q: Are the bundles production-ready?
A: They are reference-quality prototypes intentionally configured for clarity and educational value, not hardened production services. Use the design notes in each bundle (design.md) before productionizing.
