payload.page_title: SDK multimodal sample app blueprint and UX guidelines

sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This page provides a compact, production-minded blueprint for a multimodal sample application built with Redwood SDKs (client + server patterns). The goal is to give developers a ready-to-run reference that demonstrates: image + text prompts, streaming responses, result enrichment with embeddings, cost-aware batching, and UX patterns for predictable latency and graceful degradation.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- SDK users building multimodal front-ends
- Developer advocates creating example apps
- Support engineers diagnosing common integration issues
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
Provide a small end-to-end example demonstrating: 1) a browser or mobile client sending text+image prompts to Redwood API via the SDK; 2) server-side orchestration that routes to appropriate model variants, caches image embeddings, and streams token-level updates to the client.

Design principles
- Predictable latency: surface an upper-bound latency to the user and enable progressive partial results (streaming).
- Cost transparency: log per-request token & image embedding cost to telemetry for optimization experiments.
- Resilience-first: local fallback (reduced-quality model) on timeouts, with clear UX affordances.
- Minimal friction: single-file example for quickstarts, with optional feature toggles for advanced behavior.

Architecture overview
- Client (browser/mobile): captures text and image(s), displays a progressive response UI, and shows quality/cost indicators.
- Backend proxy (Node/Go/Python): validates requests, applies tenant quotas, invokes Redwood SDK, manages caching and batching, and emits telemetry.
- Redwood inference: model catalog selection (image-capable model, text-only fallback), streaming responses, embeddings endpoint.
- Cache store: Redis for prefix/KV and image embedding cache.

Key flows
1) Image+text prompt flow:
   - Client: captures image (base64 or multipart) and text; sends to backend with small metadata (image_size, intent).
   - Backend: check image_embedding_cache; if miss, call /embeddings endpoint (batched) and store embedding with TTL 7d.
   - Backend: call /generate with model variant selection (see routing policy table). Use streaming for first N tokens then aggregate.
   - Client: render streaming tokens and a placeholder for final structured output.

2) Embeddings-only flow (search/enrichment):
   - Client or batch job maps images and candidate text to embeddings, then sends a nearest-neighbors query to rank candidates server-side before final generation.

Routing policy (example table)
- Purpose: decide model variant by desired latency, cost tier, and input size.

Model purpose | Latency target | Model variant | Fallback
Short chat | <200ms first-byte | small-quantized-2x | small-quantized-cpu
Image caption | <500ms per-step | image-capable-8k | text-only+ocr-fallback
Long-form generation | burst-tolerant | large-32k-fp16 | large-16k-quant

SDK patterns and code samples
- Note: snippets below use the official Redwood JavaScript SDK pattern. Replace with Python/Go equivalents in the repo samples.

1) Client: streaming handler (browser)
```js
const ws = new WebSocket('/sse-proxy');
ws.onmessage = (ev) => {
  const payload = JSON.parse(ev.data);
  if (payload.type === 'token') appendTokenToUI(payload.text);
  if (payload.type === 'done') showFinalCard(payload.result);
};
// send image as multipart to backend
```

2) Server: batched embedding call and generate orchestration (Node/Express pseudocode)\```js
// batcher: groups embedding requests for 50ms then sends a single /embeddings call
batcher.add(request, (embedding) => {
  // attach embedding to request and continue orchestration
});

// orchestration: pick model and call Redwood SDK
const model = pickModelByPolicy({inputTokens, clientTier});
const stream = redwood.generate({model, prompt: promptWithEmbedding, stream: true});
stream.on('data', (chunk) => proxyToClient(chunk));
stream.on('end', () => finalizeResponse());
```

3) Client fallback flow (pseudocode)\```js
const response = await fetch('/api/generate', {timeout: 2500});
if (!response.ok || response.timedOut) {
  // show degraded UI and optionally re-issue with lower-cost model
  showErrorOverlay('Response delayed. Showing cached result or quick summary.');
}
```

Telemetry and observability
- Events to emit per request:
  - request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, input_tokens, output_tokens, image_size_bytes, embedding_cache_hit (bool), duration_ms, cost_estimate_cents
- SLOs to track:
  - P95 end-to-end latency by route (chat, caption, embed) < configured target
  - Embedding cache hit rate > 70% for repeated assets
  - Streaming first-byte latency P50 < 150ms for chat flows
- Dashboards suggested:
  - 'Multimodal API': throughput, errors, avg token cost, cache hit heatmap by tenant
  - 'Sample app health': per-example telemetry, user-visible degraded-flow count

Feature toggles and runtime config (table)
- toggle_name | description | default
- enable_embedding_cache | Use Redis to cache image embeddings | true
- streaming_enabled | Send token-level updates to clients | true
- model_routing_mode | auto|manual|canary | auto
- low_latency_fallback_ms | threshold to trigger fallback | 1200

UX patterns and copy guidance
- Progressive rendering: show partial text as tokens arrive; avoid flicker by reserving space for long-form answers.
- Latency affordance: display a subtle ETA bar at request start (calculated from historical medians).
- Cost transparency: optional developer toggle in the sample app to annotate responses with approximate token cost. Useful for demos.
- Fallback messaging: Be explicit — "Using a low-latency fallback; quality may be lower." Avoid technical jargon for end-users.

Common integration pitfalls and canonical fixes
1) Large image uploads cause timeouts:
   - Fix: upload to a presigned object store and send reference; calculate embedding server-side. Ensure backend accepts small metadata only.
2) Missing or inconsistent streaming boundaries:
   - Fix: standardize chunk envelope (type, seq, timestamp) and use a reconnect+resume token.
3) Embedding TTLs too short, causing repeated cost spikes:
   - Fix: extend TTL for stable assets to 7–30 days depending on size and privacy. Add eviction TTL for ephemeral uploads.
4) Telemetry mismatch between client/server:
   - Fix: generate a single request_id at the edge and propagate through headers. Instrument at three points (edge, backend, redwood).

Operational runbook (quick checklist)
- Symptoms: cascading slow responses for image prompts, high embedding costs, or spike in streaming disconnects.
- Immediate steps:
  1) Check embedding queue depth and Redis latency.
  2) Inspect per-tenant model routing decisions and fallback counts in the last 10m.
  3) Verify CDN/presigned upload success rate and median upload times.
  4) If streaming disconnect rate > 2%, enable the non-streaming fallback for new requests and investigate network errors.

Rollout guide for example app
1) Ship as an opt-in sample (feature-flagged) for internal users.
2) Run a 2-week pilot with the telemetry toggles enabled to collect: embedding cache hit, avg per-request cost, fallback frequency.
3) Iterate UX copy and token cost estimator based on pilot data.
4) Open-source the sample with a trimmed config file and 'safe defaults' (no retention beyond 7d, obfuscate tenant ids).

Files included in repo (suggested)
- README.md (quickstart + security notes)
- server/ (backend orchestrator and batcher)
- client/ (production example and a minimal dev-only preset)
- infra/ (redis, presigned-upload sample, feature flag config)
- telemetry/ (dashboard JSONs and example export pipeline)

Security and privacy notes
- Images may contain PII; default to opt-in storage and do not persist raw images unless customer explicitly enables storage.
- Encrypt embedding payloads at rest if retention > 24h.
- Provide a debug-mode that strips tenant ids for public example runs.

Appendix A — small checklist for SDK authors adding multimodal helpers
- Provide a single-call integration that accepts file references (presigned URL) and handles embedding cache + generation orchestration internally.
- Expose streaming and non-streaming variants with identical response shapes.
- Include idiomatic samples: React hook, Flutter handler, and a small CLI for batch conversion.

Appendix B — sample API schema (simplified)
- Request:
  {
    "type": "multimodal.generate",
    "image_refs": ["s3://..."],
    "prompt": "Summarize this image for a shopping app",
    "options": {"max_tokens": 256, "stream": true}
  }
- Streaming chunk:
  {"type":"token","seq":45,"text":"..."}
- Final event:
  {"type":"done","structured": {"caption":"...","tags":["shoe","men"]}}

Contact and ownership
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience (Aisha Rao)
- Secondary reviewers: Platform SDK and SDK docs team
- For urgent production issues, escalate to eng-sre with the request_id and tenant_id.

CHANGELOG (high-level)
- 2024-09-12: Initial draft and internal validation build.
- 2024-12-15: Added embedding cache guidelines and telemetry schema.
- 2025-02-14: Polished UX copy guidance and expanded rollout guide.

sections.body: Title: Client integration fastpath and canonical workarounds
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This page is a compact, production-ready playbook for product and platform engineers integrating Redwood's API/SDKs into customer-facing services. It focuses on a small set of starter templates, recommended runtime configuration, observability mappings, and the canonical fixes we repeatedly apply during support escalations. Use this as the 30–90 minute integration roadmap and the first-stop triage playbook for common runtime problems.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Audience: backend engineers, platform engineers, SREs, and SDK maintainers.
- Scope: SDK initialization, request patterns (sync/streaming/batching), canary checklist, standard metrics/logs, and top 6 canonical fixes.

Quickstart: minimal server-side integration (Python)
1) Install SDK
   pip install redwood-sdk-client==1.4.0  # recommended stable release for 2026

2) Minimal example (thread-safe client, connection pooling):
```python
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY", max_connections=50, timeout_ms=7000)

response = client.generate(model="redwood-medium-v1", prompt="Summarize user message:\n\n" + user_message, max_tokens=150)
print(response.text)
```
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body:
- Use environment variables for keys and rotate with your secret manager.
- max_connections controls local connection pool; tune to your worker concurrency.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
```bash
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-small-v1","prompt":"Extract action items:\n- "}'
```

Starter adapter template (generic microservice pattern)
- Purpose: uniform wrapper to centralize retries, cost guards, and telemetry.
- Responsibilities:
  - Token budgeting (max_tokens per request)
  - Function-call routing for tools
  - Backoff & retry policy centralized
  - Metrics tags: model, route, customer_tier, prompt_template
sections.heading: Node/HTTP curl example (quick sanity)

sections.body:
| key | example | description |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| model | redwood-medium-v1 | Default model for route |
| max_prompt_tokens | 1024 | Trim user input beyond this threshold |
| retry_policy | exponential: base=200ms, max=5 | Retries on 429 & 5xx except 501/502 special-cases |
| stream_timeout_ms | 20000 | Per-request streaming idle timeout |

Observability mapping (minimal required metrics & logs)
sections.heading: Adapter config example (YAML)
Required metrics (emit as Prometheus or StatsD)

sections.body:
- request_id, session_id, model, model_version, route, tokens_prompt, tokens_completion, status_code, latency_ms, retry_count

Canary checklist (pre-rollout, applies to SDK upgrades, model swaps, or config changes)
1) Unit + integration tests: include snapshot tests for prompt templates.
2) Traffic split: route 98% stable, 2% canary for 30 minutes.
3) Alert hooks: create an ephemeral alert for p95 latency > 2x baseline or error rate > 0.5%.
4) Manual quality gate: run a small eval prompt set (20 inputs) measuring semantic similarity > 0.9 against baseline embeddings.
5) Observability smoke: verify token usage metric and trace context propagation.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (empirically most common)
1) Symptom: intermittent 429s during traffic bursts
sections.heading: Structured log fields (append in JSON logs)

sections.body:
- Implement exponential backoff + jitter (base 200ms, max 6s, attempt cap 6).
   - Add local admission control: circuit-breaker that rejects low-priority background requests when inflight > X (X = concurrency * 4).
   - For user-visible requests, queue briefly (25–100 ms) to allow the serving runtime to batch efficiently.
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- if status == 429 or 5xx:
       sleep(backoff_with_jitter())
       retry up to N

2) Symptom: streaming responses terminate mid-token or client sees EOF
sections.heading: Example retry snippet (pseudocode)

sections.body:
- Ensure SDK/HTTP client supports keep-alives and per-chunk timeouts.
   - Increase stream_idle_timeout to 20s for mobile networks and 5s for LAN.
   - Server-side: verify you are using the streaming endpoint ("/v1/stream") and not an SDK wrapper that buffers.
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- curl with --no-buffer and watch chunk boundaries; capture TCP level resets with ss/netstat.

3) Symptom: embedding vectors drift or mismatch across calls
sections.heading: Diagnostic commands

sections.body:
- Explicitly pin model version in production (model: text-embedding-2025-10).
   - Add a compatibility test in CI that compares embeddings for a fixed prompt set within cosine similarity thresholds.

4) Symptom: unexpectedly high token usage/cost
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- Enforce input pruning rules and token-aware truncation: keep last N tokens of conversation when summarizing.
   - Use streaming completion with max_tokens set conservatively.
   - Employ instruction templates that request concise output (e.g., "Respond in <= 40 words").

5) Symptom: auth failures after a secret rotation
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- Validate clock drift (some internal short-lived tokens require < 30s drift).
   - Add a readiness probe post-rotation that attempts a lightweight /v1/health call and falls back to cached credentials for 30s.

6) Symptom: high p99 latency when batching-enabled
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- Check batching window config: lower it for latency-sensitive routes (20ms) or increase for throughput routes (100–250ms).
   - Add priority routing: small requests routed to low-batch fast-path, large batched payloads to throughput path.

Triage runbook (first 10 minutes)
1) Reproduce: run the failing request locally against the same model version using the exact prompt.
2) Gather: request_id, model, route, timestamps, client logs, SDK version, and last config change.
3) Check metrics: increase in redwood_request_count and redwood_request_latency_ms; check for correlated infra alerts.
4) Quick mitigations: reduce traffic to the affected route, increase capacity if Dedicated, or enable automatic fallback to a cheaper model for non-critical requests.
5) Escalate: if error rate > 5% for 10m or p99 latency > 3s for user-critical routes, page oncall SRE and attach trace and a reproducible curl snippet.

Template: reproducible curl snippet to include in tickets
```bash
curl -v -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-medium-v1","prompt":"<paste prompt here>","max_tokens":150,"stream":false}'
```

Testing and CI recommendations
- Add a lightweight integration stage that runs once per PR with a small set of canary prompts (10–20). Fail if embedding drift or generation regression exceeds thresholds.
- Run nightly stability tests under synthetic burst traffic to surface 429 patterns.

Rollout notes for SDK upgrades
- Follow semantic versioning; prefer non-breaking patches for security fixes.
- When rolling an SDK with changed defaults (timeouts, retries), use the canary checklist above and include a migration doc in the release notes.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-developer-experience. For escalations: oncall-eng-sre@redwood.ai.
- SDK maintainers: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel.

Appendix A — Useful command snippets
- Check health endpoint:
  curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health | jq
- Trace sampling quick check (look for trace_id in response headers):
  curl -I https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY"

Appendix B — Sample evaluation prompts for canary quality gate
1) Summarization: "Summarize the following thread into 3 bullets"
2) Extraction: "List all named entities and roles"
3) Instruction following: "Convert this prose into a terse checklist"
sections.heading: Canonical fixes

sections.body:
- 2026-01-15: Created initial fastpath playbook.
- 2026-02-02: Added triage runbook and expanded canonical fixes list.
sections.heading: Change log

sections.body:
- Developer SDK best practices (internal): /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/developer-integration-checklist-and-examples-2026
- Streaming and batching patterns: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/sdk-batching-streaming-playbook-and-canonical-fixes-2026

End of document.

payload.page_title: Developer Shield: SDK Chaos & Recovery Lab

sections.body: This lab is a hands-on developer-ready guide for intentionally breaking SDK integrations, observing telemetry "golden traces", and validating recovery strategies against Redwood inference endpoints. The goal is to provide a repeatable workshop that SDK authors, platform engineers, and support oncall can run in ~90 minutes to verify resilience SLA behaviors and canonical fixes.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Create deterministic fault patterns targeting SDK -> runtime interactions (timeouts, partial responses, truncated streams).
- Validate observability: traces, spans, logs, and token-level cost telemetry for each failure mode.
- Exercise client-side fallbacks (retry jitter, streaming resume, local cache) and server-side graceful degradation (model variant fallback, rate-aware routing).
- Produce documented artifacts: golden-trace examples, regression tests, and a triage checklist for support.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
1) Developer machine with Python 3.10+ and Node.js 18+.
2) Access to a Redwood dev tenant (api key with dev-level quota).
3) Local test harness repo cloned: git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git (or use the starter scaffold below).
4) Docker (for running a local network proxy/fault injector) and curl.

Quickstart scaffold (clone + bootstrap):
1. git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git && cd sdk-chaos-lab
2. cp .env.example .env && edit REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_BASE_URL if needed
3. make deps  # installs node_modules and pip env
4. ./scripts/start-proxy.sh  # starts the fault-injection proxy on localhost:8080
sections.heading: Prerequisites
High-level lab exercises (90 minutes)

sections.body:
- The lab standard for a golden trace is a JSON file with a top-level array of spans. Each span in the array must contain the following string fields:
  - trace_id
  - span_id
  - parent_id (nullable string allowed; include as empty string if none)
  - name (e.g., http.request, sdk.serialize, runtime.infer)
  - start_ts (ISO 8601)
  - end_ts (ISO 8601)
  - attributes (a flattened comma-separated key=value list including model_variant, token_count, route_key, billing_unit)

Example attributes string: "model_variant=m-latest,token_count=42,route_key=us-east-1,billing_unit=gen_token"
sections.heading: Golden trace format and required fields (table)

sections.body:
1) Reproduce the failure with the lab harness using the same API key and region.
2) Capture and attach the golden trace and failing trace.
3) Check telemetry for double-billing: token_cost spikes immediately after retries.
4) If truncated stream: confirm resume id exists in traces (span name runtime.stream.resume).
5) If fallback occurred: compare model_variant attributes between baseline and failing trace.
6) File a regression ticket including: failing_trace.json, command run, SDK version, and proxy logs.
sections.heading: Triage checklist (support-friendly)

sections.body:
"scenario,proxy_fault,client_timeout_ms,expected_behavior,primary_validation"
"baseline,none,1500,success,golden_trace match"
"delay-first-post,delay(1200ms),1000,retry-with-backoff,no double-billing"
"truncate-stream,truncate-after-3-chunks,2000,resume-able stream,resume span present"
"model-oom,503-on-cold-start,800,auto-fallback,latency<800ms"
sections.heading: Config matrix (copyable CSV row for quick reference)

sections.body:
- Lab owner: eng-developer-experience (primary: Maya Chen).
- Oncall escalation: if the lab reproduces a production bug, open an incident in PagerDuty and tag "runtime-serving" and "sdk".
- Persist golden traces under s3://redwood-dev-golden-traces/sdk-chaos-lab/ with role-based ACLs.

Rollout and integration guidance (how teams should use this lab):
- SDK authors: integrate one golden-trace capture into CI for each major release (post-merge job). If a change causes a >5% regression vs the golden baseline, block the release.
- Platform: run the full lab in the dedicated staging cluster before deploying model-serving kernel changes or routing logic changes.
- Support: use the triage checklist when customers report truncated streams or unexpected token billing.
sections.heading: Operational notes and ownership

sections.body:
- traces/golden_baseline.json (golden)
- traces/failure_mode_<name>.json (failing traces)
- coverage/regression_<sdk-version>.md (short summary)
- ticket templates/auto-fill for support with fields pre-populated from the harness run
sections.heading: Artifacts to produce after running the lab

sections.body:
- eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-resiliency-orchestrator-and-ops-playbook-2026
- eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-streaming-troubleshooting-2025
- security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/streaming-data-retention-policy

Appendix: common canonical fixes (short list)
- Ensure idempotency tokens are attached to generation requests; server will dedupe within 30s window.
- Surface resume IDs for streaming RPCs and persist a short-lived local buffer to permit dedupe.
- Add token-cost snapshot before and after retries in telemetry to detect billing anomalies.
- If model fallback is frequent, add a cold-start pre-warm task for high-SLA tenants and/or enable burst-capacity for the dedicated pool.
sections.heading: References and related docs

sections.body:
- Maya Chen (owner, eng-developer-experience) - maya@redwood.ai
- Support escalation alias: support-oncall@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: Route Experiments (A/B testing) – SDK integration notes (stickiness keys, headers, docs plan)

sections.body:
These notes describe how Redwood SDKs and examples should integrate with **Route Experiments** (route-level A/B/n testing in Console Rollouts), with specific focus on:
- How customers provide **deterministic stickiness keys** (so a user consistently receives the same variant)
- How SDKs should expose and document **experiment/variant response headers**
- A documentation + examples plan for beta → GA

This page is DX-facing (SDKs, docs, examples). It is not the source of truth for routing semantics; see ADR-047 / ADR-048.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
1. An experiment is attached to a **route** (endpoint / routing policy).
2. Each request is assigned to a **variant** based on a stable **stickiness key**.
3. Redwood returns optional **debug headers** so customers can tell which variant they hit.
4. Console shows per-variant metrics (latency/cost/error/quality) using experiment attribution emitted by the platform.

In docs and SDKs, we should present experiments as “**routing-layer experiments**” (not application-layer experiments). Customers do not need to run their own bucketing logic.

---
sections.heading: Customer-facing mental model (what we want users to understand)

sections.body:
Deterministic assignment requires a key with adequate entropy and stability. If customers omit a stable key, they can observe:
- Variant skew (one variant accidentally getting most traffic)
- Assignment churn (same end-user bouncing between variants)
- Harder-to-interpret metrics and regressions
sections.heading: Why stickiness keys matter

sections.body:
SDK docs should recommend one of the following, in this order:
1. **A customer-defined stable end-user identifier** (e.g., internal user UUID)
2. **Account/tenant identifier** (B2B SaaS) if experiments are intended to be “per-tenant”
3. **Session identifier** (only if the experiment is short-lived and per-session consistency is acceptable)
sections.heading: Recommended key choices (in priority order)

sections.body:
- Random UUID generated per request
- Raw IP address as the only identifier (low quality, NAT/shared IP issues, privacy concerns)
- Email address in plaintext (PII). If email is the only available stable identifier, recommend hashing on the client side before sending.
sections.heading: Avoid

sections.body:
We should support a first-class, consistently named option in SDKs.

**Canonical name (docs):** `experiment_sticky_key`
sections.heading: SDK parameter and header names

sections.body:
- If the API supports explicit fields on the request body, pass it as a request field.
- Otherwise (or additionally), pass as a header.

**Request header:** `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key`
sections.heading: Transport

sections.body:
- The stickiness key is used only for experiment bucketing. It is not a security boundary.
- SDKs should treat the stickiness key as **potentially sensitive**, and should not log it at INFO by default.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
Platform-side precedence (high level, aligned with ADR-047):
1. `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key` (explicit)
2. Authenticated `customer_id` / `tenant_id` if available
3. End-user identifier passed via customer application (if explicitly mapped by the customer)
4. Fallback: request-derived identifiers (discouraged; may be disabled or changed)

Docs should emphasize: **If you care about determinism, set the explicit sticky key.**

---
sections.heading: Precedence rules (what SDKs should document)

sections.body:
When a request is eligible for a route experiment, the gateway/router may attach:
- `x-redwood-experiment-id`: Stable experiment identifier
- `x-redwood-variant-id`: Assigned variant identifier (e.g., `control`, `v1-quantized`, `new-model`)
sections.heading: Required-to-document headers

sections.body:
- `x-redwood-experiment-config-version`: Helps support debug config propagation issues
- `x-redwood-route-id`: Normalized route identifier (template form; may differ from raw URL path)

When no experiment applies, headers may be omitted. SDKs should expose a convenient way to read these headers without forcing customers to parse low-level HTTP objects.
sections.heading: Recommended additional headers (where available)

sections.body:
For each SDK, support:
- Access to raw headers (existing behavior)
- A small helper to parse experiment info into a typed structure
sections.heading: SDK ergonomics goal

sections.body:
- `experimentId: string | null`
- `variantId: string | null`
- `configVersion: string | null`
sections.heading: Example structure to document

sections.body:
If a customer reports “my experiment isn’t splitting traffic” or “variant is always control”, ask them to capture:
- Their configured `experiment_sticky_key` logic (is it stable? is it always present?)
- One request/response showing returned `x-redwood-experiment-id` and `x-redwood-variant-id`
- Region and route name
- Whether they are using streaming + retries (older SDKs may drop headers if they only surface the streaming iterator)

---
sections.heading: Troubleshooting guidance to include in docs
TypeScript SDK (redwood-sdk-typescript)

sections.body:
**Add to request options:**
- `experiment_sticky_key: Optional[str] = None`

**Behavior:**
- If set, add header `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key`
- Expose parsed headers:
  - `response.experiment_id`
  - `response.variant_id`
  - (optional) `response.experiment_config_version`

**Example (Python):**
```py
from redwood import Redwood

client = Redwood(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"])

user_id = "user_2f3a9c1b"  # must be stable

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="redwood/llama-3.1-70b-instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this article..."}],
    experiment_sticky_key=user_id,
)

print(resp.experiment_id, resp.variant_id)
```
sections.heading: Python SDK (redwood-sdk-python)

sections.body:
- Adding the request option is backward compatible.
- Adding response fields is backward compatible if we avoid breaking existing response types and keep raw header access unchanged.
sections.heading: Backwards compatibility

sections.body:
- Do not log the sticky key at INFO.
- If customers enable debug logging, redact or hash the sticky key in logs.
- It is OK to log `experiment_id` and `variant_id` (not typically PII), but treat them as customer-sensitive in shared logs.

---
sections.heading: SDK defaults

sections.body:
1. **Customer Guide:** “Route experiments (A/B testing) in Console”
   - What it is, when to use it
   - Creating an experiment (Console workflow)
   - Choosing stickiness keys (with examples)
   - Reading variant headers / debugging
   - Guardrails + stopping semantics (soft-stop vs optional hard-stop)

2. **SDK reference additions:**
   - `experiment_sticky_key` / `experimentStickyKey` option in the API reference
   - Response header fields / helper structure

3. **Example app updates (redwood-examples):**
   - A minimal route experiments demo showing:
     - Passing a stable stickiness key
     - Printing assigned variant
     - A note on stable routing keys in multi-tenant apps

4. **Troubleshooting page / section:**
   - “Variant skew / always control”
   - “Headers missing”
   - “Streaming retries missing attribution”
   - “Results in Console not updating (propagation lag / aggregation delay)”
sections.heading: Docs artifacts to ship

sections.body:
- Avoid promising advanced statistics/significance analysis in GA (out of scope).
- Be explicit that metrics may take time to appear due to aggregation windows.
sections.heading: Beta documentation constraints

sections.body:
- SDKs released with stickiness key option in TS + Python
- Example app merged and referenced from docs
- Customer guide includes a “How to pick a stickiness key” section with at least 3 concrete patterns
- Docs reviewed by:
  - Policy Engine (assignment semantics)
  - Telemetry (header naming + attribution correctness)
  - Security (PII guidance / redaction)

---
sections.heading: GA readiness checklist (DX-owned)

sections.body: No. Bucketing is performed by Redwood’s routing layer.
sections.heading: Do customers need to implement their own bucketing?

sections.body: Recommend tenant-level stickiness or session-level stickiness depending on product needs. Explicitly warn about churn/skew if they cannot provide any stable key.
sections.heading: What if the customer cannot provide a stable user identifier?

sections.body: Only when a request is eligible for an experiment and the request path surfaces headers. Some intermediaries can drop headers; if customers are behind proxies, advise them to allowlist the Redwood headers.
sections.heading: Are headers always present?

sections.body:
Not in GA docs. Any internal override mechanism should be treated as restricted/internal-only and gated by RBAC/feature flags.

---
sections.heading: Can customers force a variant?

sections.body:
- Confirm final header names with Observability + Policy Engine owners (align with OTel tag naming conventions).
- Finalize copy for Console tooltips explaining headers and stickiness.
- Add a short section in docs on hashing PII identifiers before using them as sticky keys.
- Ensure streaming clients surface response headers consistently (prior issues observed with retries).
sections.heading: Open items / follow-ups

payload.page_title: SDK Parity Matrix: Auth, Retries, Timeouts, Streaming, and Error Taxonomy (Python / TypeScript / Go)

sections.body:
This page is the working parity matrix for the cross-language SDK parity initiative. It documents **current behavior** and **target behavior** across:
- **redwood-sdk-python**
- **redwood-sdk-typescript**
- **redwood-sdk-go**
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
1) the source-of-truth for what “parity” means for auth/retry/timeout/streaming/error behavior,
2) the checklist for code changes and docs updates, and
3) the basis for the cross-language conformance test suite.
sections.heading: The matrix is used as

sections.body:
- API key / bearer token auth resolution order, env var naming, headers
- Retry policy: retryable status codes, network errors, backoff/jitter, respect Retry-After
- Timeout model: connect/read/overall semantics and defaults
- Streaming behavior: disconnects, partial output, cancellation, retry guidance
- Error taxonomy: typed errors + standardized fields (request_id, retry_count, timeout_ms, etc.)
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- New auth mechanisms (e.g., OAuth flows)
- Major API surface redesign
- Streaming “exactly once” semantics (SDKs remain conservative; idempotency guidance is documented)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body: This is the parity target (see linked standards/ADRs for the full rationale):
sections.heading: Target Standard (summary)

sections.body:
1. **Explicit client configuration** (e.g., constructor `api_key` / `token`)
2. **Environment variables** (preferred names)
3. Optional: shared config file is **not** supported in v1 parity scope
sections.heading: Auth resolution order (all SDKs)

sections.body:
- `REDWOOD_API_KEY` (primary)
- `REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN` (if using bearer tokens)
- `REDWOOD_BASE_URL` (optional; defaults to hosted API)
sections.heading: Preferred env vars

sections.body:
- API key: `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (consistent across SDKs)
- Never log secrets; error messages must be redaction-safe
sections.heading: Header rules

sections.body:
- Max attempts: **4 total** (1 initial + up to 3 retries)
- Retryable HTTP status codes:
  - **429** (rate limited) — must respect `Retry-After`
  - **408** (request timeout)
  - **409** (conflict) only when `code` indicates transient (see error taxonomy below)
  - **5xx** (500, 502, 503, 504)
- Retryable network errors:
  - DNS errors, connection refused/reset, TLS handshake errors, socket timeouts, unexpected EOF
- Non-retryable:
  - **4xx** by default (400, 401, 403, 404, 422) unless explicitly documented and flagged retryable by server error `code`
- Backoff:
  - Exponential backoff with jitter
  - Base delay: **250ms**
  - Max delay: **8s**
  - Jitter: full jitter (random in [0, delay])
- Retry-After:
  - Parse `Retry-After` as either seconds or HTTP date
  - When present and valid, it overrides backoff for the next sleep (bounded by a max of 60s)
sections.heading: Retry policy defaults (all SDKs)

sections.body:
Timeouts are expressed as **overall** plus optional granular timeouts.
- Default connect timeout: **10s**
- Default read timeout (non-streaming): **60s**
- Default overall timeout (non-streaming): **90s**
- Streaming:
  - Overall timeout applies to request setup (connect + first byte)
  - Streaming read is governed by an **idle timeout** (no bytes received) default **30s** (configurable)
  - Streaming must support user cancellation (AbortController/context/cancel token) and must terminate promptly
sections.heading: Timeout model defaults (all SDKs)

sections.body:
- **No automatic retry after partial streaming output** (to avoid duplicate side effects / duplicated tokens)
- If the connection fails **before first content event**, SDK may retry (subject to retry policy) when safe
- If failure happens **after partial output**, SDK raises a typed streaming interruption error containing:
  - request_id (if known)
  - bytes/events received count (best effort)
  - partial text (if buffering is enabled) or the last event seen
- Docs recommend:
  - use request_id for support
  - use idempotency keys for non-streaming or “safe-to-retry” flows
sections.heading: Streaming retry guidance (all SDKs)

sections.body:
- `message` (string; redaction-safe)
- `request_id` (string; from response headers/body when available)
- `status_code` (int; if HTTP response exists)
- `code` (string; Redwood error code enum)
- `retryable` (bool)
- `retry_after_ms` (int; when available)
- `attempt` / `retries` (int; how many retries already performed)
- `timeout_ms` (int; the configured timeout that triggered the failure, when applicable)
- `cause` / `wrapped_error` (language-native error, if exposed)


---
sections.heading: All SDKs should expose typed errors with consistent fields

sections.body:
- ✅ = matches target
- ⚠️ = partially matches / edge cases
- ❌ = mismatch
sections.heading: Legend

sections.body:
| Behavior | Python (current) | TypeScript (current) | Go (current) | Target (desired) | Gap / Notes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Env var names recognized | ⚠️ `REDWOOD_API_KEY` plus legacy `RW_API_KEY` in some examples | ⚠️ `REDWOOD_API_KEY` + `REDWOOD_TOKEN` in older versions | ⚠️ `REDWOOD_API_KEY` + `REDWOOD_BEARER` in older builds | `REDWOOD_API_KEY`, `REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN`, `REDWOOD_BASE_URL` only (legacy allowed with deprecation warnings) | Align naming; add migration messaging | Sabrina / Dana / Mateusz |
| Resolution order | ⚠️ explicit param wins; env fallback; but error text differs by path | ✅ explicit param wins; env fallback | ⚠️ env sometimes overrides when both set due to init helper | Explicit > env > error | Fix Go init helper precedence; standardize error text | Mateusz |
| Header format | ✅ `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | ⚠️ some endpoints set `X-Api-Key` in older compatibility layer | ✅ Bearer | Bearer everywhere | TS must stop emitting `X-Api-Key` unless explicitly configured (compat) | Dana |
| Missing auth error | ⚠️ raises generic ValueError with setup message | ⚠️ throws Error without remediation guidance | ⚠️ returns error without indicating env var names | Typed AuthError with message listing supported env vars (no secret echo) | Standardize message template | Ibrahim |
| Secret redaction in logs | ⚠️ redacts in most paths, but debug mode can leak headers in Python | ✅ redacts | ⚠️ Go debug logs included full headers in one helper | Never log `Authorization`; redact known token patterns | Security signoff required; add tests | Marcus + language owners |
sections.heading: A) Authentication

sections.body:
| Behavior | Python (current) | TypeScript (current) | Go (current) | Target (desired) | Gap / Notes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Default max attempts | ⚠️ 3 total in some clients; 4 in others | ✅ 4 total | ⚠️ 5 total (historical) | 4 total | Align defaults + docs | Ibrahim |
| Retryable status codes | ⚠️ retries 429 + 5xx; 408 inconsistent | ⚠️ one bug: retried 400 in middleware edge case | ⚠️ retries 429 + 5xx but missed 408 | Retry 429/408/5xx; 409 only when transient | Fix TS 400 retry; include 408 across all | Dana / Sabrina / Mateusz |
| Network error retries | ✅ connection errors retried | ⚠️ fetch abort handling categorized incorrectly | ✅ net/http errors retried | Retry network errors; do not retry user cancellations | TS must differentiate AbortController cancel vs network failure | Dana |
| Backoff + jitter | ⚠️ exponential but jitter differs; base delay not consistent | ⚠️ jitter added but not full-jitter | ✅ close to target | Base 250ms; max 8s; full jitter | Normalize algorithms; align test fixtures | Ibrahim |
| Retry-After parsing | ✅ parses seconds; date format missing | ✅ parses seconds + date | ❌ ignores Retry-After | Parse seconds/date; override backoff; max 60s | Go must implement; Python add date parsing | Mateusz / Sabrina |
| Retry instrumentation fields | ⚠️ logs attempt count but not standardized keys | ⚠️ request_id missing on some retry errors | ❌ no consistent fields | Standard fields: request_id, retry_count, retry_reason, retry_after_ms | Align logging schema; docs | Logan Wright + Nadia Rahman |
sections.heading: B) Retry Policy / Backoff / Retry-After

sections.body:
| Behavior | Python (current) | TypeScript (current) | Go (current) | Target (desired) | Gap / Notes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Timeout configuration surface | ⚠️ `timeout` overloaded; connect/read not consistently exposed | ⚠️ per-request abort only; defaults not obvious | ✅ context + client timeout exists, but mapping inconsistent | Provide overall + connect/read/idle (stream) where supported; map consistently | Align naming + docs snippets across languages | Ibrahim + language owners |
| Default connect timeout | ⚠️ 5s in one client | ✅ 10s | ⚠️ OS default (unbounded) when context missing | 10s | Ensure Go always sets connect timeout when using default client | Mateusz |
| Default overall timeout (non-stream) | ⚠️ 60s | ✅ 90s | ⚠️ 120s | 90s | Normalize; include migration notes | Henry + DevEx |
| Streaming timeout semantics | ❌ streaming ignored `timeout` in iterator path (support driver SUP-29410) | ⚠️ abort cancels fetch, but idle timeout not implemented | ⚠️ context cancel works, but idle timeout not consistent | Streaming: connect/first-byte uses overall; read idle timeout default 30s | Implement idle timeout for TS/Go; fix Python honoring timeouts in stream | Sabrina / Dana / Mateusz |
| User cancellation | ✅ `KeyboardInterrupt`/cancel bubbles; explicit cancel supported | ✅ AbortController supported | ✅ context cancellation supported | All must stop promptly and surface as CancelledError (not retryable) | Ensure cancellation is never retried; consistent error type | Ibrahim |
sections.heading: C) Timeouts

sections.body:
| Behavior | Python (current) | TypeScript (current) | Go (current) | Target (desired) | Gap / Notes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Event model | ⚠️ yields raw chunks in some examples; structured events elsewhere | ✅ structured events (`message.delta`, `message.completed`, etc.) | ⚠️ mixed: some helpers emit raw lines | Standardize event names + payload fields in docs; keep language-idiomatic wrappers | Docs + examples must match; conformance fixtures for event ordering | Wei Chen + language owners |
| Partial output on disconnect | ⚠️ partial text lost if exception thrown mid-chunk | ✅ surfaces partial text in most cases | ⚠️ surfaces last event only | Typed StreamingInterruptedError includes partial output when available | Decide buffering policy (memory tradeoff) and document it | Ibrahim + Henry |
| Disconnect classification | ⚠️ raised as generic connection error | ⚠️ sometimes treated as retryable network error even after content | ⚠️ ambiguous EOF vs server close | If disconnect after content: not auto-retry; raise streaming interruption (retryable=false) | Fix classification and retry suppression | Dana / Mateusz |
| Retry behavior for streaming | ⚠️ may retry pre-first-event; inconsistent | ⚠️ retried after some events in one path | ✅ generally no retry after events | Only retry if no content delivered yet; never after partial | Conformance test should simulate “first token then FIN” | Ibrahim |
| Proxy buffering / keep-alives | ⚠️ no documented guidance | ⚠️ no documented guidance | ⚠️ some guidance in README only | Document recommended keep-alive/idle timeout settings and proxy caveats | Capture in streaming guide + quickstarts | Wei Chen |
sections.heading: D) Streaming Semantics / Edge Cases

sections.body:
| Behavior | Python (current) | TypeScript (current) | Go (current) | Target (desired) | Gap / Notes | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base error type | ⚠️ multiple base classes across modules | ⚠️ Error subclasses exist but missing consistent fields | ⚠️ errors wrap net/http without stable fields | Single family: RedwoodError + typed subclasses | Align naming; publish mapping table | Ibrahim |
| request_id propagation | ⚠️ missing on some streaming exceptions | ✅ present for most HTTP errors | ❌ missing in some cases | request_id always present when server emitted it; best effort on network failures | Requires gateway + SDK work; ensure header parsing in all clients | Ethan Park + language owners |
| retryable flag | ⚠️ computed ad-hoc | ⚠️ present but not always accurate | ❌ absent | Always compute using standard classifier; included on error | Shared classifier behavior via fixtures | Ibrahim |
| Error `code` field | ⚠️ present only when JSON body parses | ✅ present | ⚠️ present but naming differs | Use Redwood error code enum; consistent string values | Ensure OpenAI-compat surfaces same fields | Ibrahim |
| Safe error messages (no secrets) | ⚠️ some include base URL with query params | ✅ safe | ✅ safe | No tokens/headers; sanitize URLs; include remediation | Add lint/tests for common secret patterns | Marcus Lin |


---
sections.heading: E) Error Taxonomy (Typed Errors + Fields)

sections.body:
1) **Legacy env vars support window**: Do we allow `RW_API_KEY` / `REDWOOD_TOKEN` / `REDWOOD_BEARER` for one minor release with deprecation warnings, or do we drop immediately?
   - Proposed: support for **2 minor releases**, with warnings and migration guide.

2) **Streaming buffering policy** for partial output: Should SDKs buffer full generated text by default to include it in StreamingInterruptedError?
   - Proposed: default **no full buffering** (stream-first), but include:
     - `last_event` (always)
     - optional `partial_text` when the SDK already has it (e.g., user concatenates deltas)
     - optional `buffer_output=true` option (document memory risk)

3) **409 retry semantics**: Which error codes should be considered transient (retryable) under 409?
   - Proposed: retry 409 only when server error `code` in allowlist (to be defined in error code enum docs).

4) **Timeout defaults for enterprise**: Some customers want stricter defaults (e.g., overall 30s). Do we provide a named preset (e.g., `timeouts="interactive"`) or keep only numeric config?
   - Proposed: numeric config only for v1 parity; presets can be introduced later.

5) **Telemetry/analytics**: For environments where telemetry is not permitted, do we require standardized structured logs only?
   - Proposed: minimum requirement is standardized logger/hook fields; telemetry remains opt-in per SDK policy.
sections.heading: Open Questions / Decisions Needed

sections.body: Parity is “done” when all conditions below are met:
sections.heading: Acceptance Criteria (Parity Definition)

sections.body:
- Auth:
  - Explicit credentials always override env vars
  - Env var names and missing-auth errors are consistent (including remediation text)
  - Secrets are never logged in any mode
- Retries:
  - Same retryable status codes and network errors
  - Same defaults: max_attempts=4, base=250ms, max=8s, full jitter
  - All SDKs respect Retry-After (seconds + HTTP date)
  - Cancellation is never retried
- Timeouts:
  - Defaults match (connect=10s, read=60s, overall=90s)
  - Streaming honors connect/first-byte timeouts and idle timeout (30s default)
- Streaming:
  - No automatic retries after partial output
  - Typed streaming interruption errors contain request_id when available and a stable reason
- Errors:
  - Typed errors across SDKs expose: message, request_id, status_code, code, retryable, retry_after_ms, attempt/retries
sections.heading: Functional parity

sections.body:
- Conformance suite passes for all SDKs:
  - 429 + Retry-After seconds
  - 429 + Retry-After HTTP date
  - 5xx retry with jitter bounds
  - network reset mid-request
  - streaming disconnect before first event (may retry)
  - streaming disconnect after N events (must not auto-retry)
- Docs pages and quickstarts show the same option names and recommended defaults across languages.
sections.heading: Test and docs parity

sections.body:
- Standardized log/hook fields available:
  - `request_id`, `retry_count`, `retry_reason`, `retry_after_ms`, `timeout_ms`, `streaming_disconnect_reason`
- Rollout dashboard includes dimensions by SDK + version (where available).
sections.heading: Operational readiness

sections.body:
- Streaming timeouts not honored in Python streaming iterator path (repro’d; aligns with SUP-29410)
- TS retry bug retried non-retryable 400 in one middleware edge case (billing concern; SUP-29438)
- Go ignored Retry-After on 429 (burst retries; SUP-29477)
- Enterprise proxy environments cause streaming disconnects; need consistent error surfaces + guidance (SUP-29505)
sections.heading: Notes on Top Support Drivers (why we’re doing this)

sections.body:
- Each row should be updated when:
  - a parity PR merges, or
  - conformance tests uncover a mismatch
- When updating, include:
  - “current” column changes (what is now true)
  - “gap/notes” updates (what remains)
  - link to the PR/ticket in the appropriate repo (via the parity epic)

payload.page_title: Structured logging and privacy-aware context guidelines

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This page defines the corporate standard for structured application logging and the rules for including request context while protecting customer and user privacy. Goals: standardize searchable fields, make logs machine-consumable for alerting and cost analysis, and reduce accidental PII/secret leakage. This standard applies to all services and SDKs that emit production logs (hosted, dedicated, and private deployments).

Why this matters
----------------
- Inconsistent log schemas slow incident response and make automated analysis brittle.
- Unchecked inclusion of request context increases risk of PII or secrets in telemetry.
- Structured logs enable downstream consumers (alerts, cost attribution, ML ops) to reliably parse and correlate events.

Scope and ownership
-------------------
- Applies to all backend services, edge proxies, workers, and ingestion pipelines. UI/browser logs are out-of-scope for this doc (see frontend logging guidance).
- Owner: Observability Platform (engineering). Primary steward: Priya Desai.
- Enforced by: CI lint rules, pre-merge checks, and runtime sanitizers.

Quick reference: required fields (JSON log object)
------------------------------------------------
Every production JSON-structured log entry MUST contain the following top-level fields:
- timestamp (ISO-8601 UTC)
- service (string): service short name, e.g. "api-gateway"
- env (string): one of [prod, staging, canary, integration]
- level (string): one of [DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL]
- trace_id (string | null): distributed trace id when available
- request_id (string | null): per-request opaque id for correlation
- tenant_id (string | null): customer id for multi-tenant attribution (see tenant redaction rules)
- msg (string): human-friendly short message
- event (string): machine-friendly event code, e.g. "model.infer.start"
- attrs (object): libre key/value bag for non-sensitive dimensions (see attrs policy)

Example (single-line JSON)
-------------------------
{"timestamp":"2026-01-18T15:22:43.123Z","service":"embedder","env":"prod","level":"INFO","trace_id":"4a1f...","request_id":"r-3b9c","tenant_id":"acct-123","msg":"inference_start","event":"model.infer.start","attrs":{"model":"gptx-8b-q4","seq_len":128,"gpu":"p3.8xlarge"}}

Field guidance and allowed values
--------------------------------
- timestamp: RFC3339 / ISO-8601 in UTC (no epoch-only logs).
- service: use service registry short names (see appendix A). Avoid environment or role suffixes.
- env: controls downstream retention and alerting tiers.
- level: follow semantic logging levels and avoid encoding state in level (e.g., don’t use WARN for throttled INFO flows).
- trace_id/request_id: prefer OpenTelemetry trace IDs where present. If absent, set to null. DO NOT synthesize ids that include PII.
- tenant_id: use internal stable identifier; map external account IDs to internal opaque ids in the ingest pipeline.
- attrs: strictly non-sensitive dimensions (see allowed/forbidden list below).

Allowed attributes (attrs) examples
----------------------------------
- model: model short name (no path or key)
- model_variant
- shard
- sequence_length (integer)
- prompt_tokens, output_tokens (integers)
- gpu_type
- request_cost_microcents (integer)
- rollout_phase (string: canary|gradual|stable)

Forbidden attributes (must never appear in logs)
------------------------------------------------
- Raw user prompts or responses (full text)
- API keys, secrets, and credentials
- Full email addresses, phone numbers, SSNs, or unredacted identifiers
- File contents, attachments, or binary blobs
- Raw system-environment variables that include secrets

PII/Secrets handling and redaction rules
----------------------------------------
1) Prevention-first: instrumentations MUST avoid placing raw text fields that could contain PII into attrs or top-level fields.
2) Tokenization: where textual context is required for debugging, services should emit a hashed token (sha256 hex, prefixed with "h:") and store the raw payload only in a secured, audited data store (not logs).
3) Masking: for structured fields that may contain partial PII (for example, username), emit a redacted version and a fingerprint: e.g. "user.name_redacted":"j****n","user.name_fp":"h:5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99"
4) Sampling controls: if textual context must be logged for a subset of requests (e.g., failing cases), use explicit sampling—only 0.1% by default in prod, configurable per service and subject to review.
5) Secrets detection: pre-commit linters and a runtime filter must check new log keys and values for regex patterns matching known secret shapes (AWS keys, JWTs). Any detection causes surfaced test failures.

Structured vs. unstructured fields
----------------------------------
- Prefer typed attributes inside attrs for all dimensions consumed by downstream systems. Avoid free-form "details" strings for machine logic.
- Human narratives or stack traces may appear in a separate field called "debug" but MUST be escaped and sampled; debug is excluded from high-retention indexes.

Sampling and retention policy
----------------------------
- Default prod sampling: INFO and below: 1% indexed, 100% stored for 7 days in low-cost blob store; ERROR and above: 100% indexed and retained per SLO (default 90 days).
- Retention tiers are managed by env and service: heavy-volume infra services (e.g., ingress proxies) should apply higher sampling.
- Cost allocation: include a per-log token request_cost_microcents when emitting long-running batch jobs to attribute cost to teams.

Enforcement: linters, CI checks, and runtime guards
--------------------------------------------------
- Lint rules (pre-commit): enforce presence of required fields, banned keys, and allowed attrs types.
- CI contract tests: each service must provide a minimal JSON schema file (example: schema/log-schema.json) and a test that validates emitted logs against the schema.
- Runtime sanitizer: a library used in prod ingestion that enforces max-key-length (256 chars), strips values matching PII patterns when sampling is off, and rates-limits very large log objects.

Schema example (log-schema.json excerpt)
--------------------------------------
{"type":"object","required":["timestamp","service","env","level","msg","event","attrs"],"properties":{"timestamp":{"type":"string"},"service":{"type":"string"},"env":{"enum":["prod","staging","canary","integration"]},"level":{"enum":["DEBUG","INFO","WARN","ERROR","FATAL"]},"attrs":{"type":"object"}}}

Library and language recommendations
-----------------------------------
- Use the company-maintained logging SDK (github.com/redwood-inference/logging-sdk) which provides:
  - JSON formatter with required field injection
  - PII-safe helpers (hashing, redaction utilities)
  - Sampling decorator and integration with OpenTelemetry tracing
- Python example:
  from rdl.logging import get_logger
  logger = get_logger(service="embedder", env="prod")
  logger.info(event="model.infer.start", attrs={"model":"gptx-8b-q4","seq_len":128})
- Go example:
  logger := rdl.NewLogger("api-gateway", "prod")
  logger.Info("model.infer.start", rdl.Attrs{"model":"gptx-8b","seq_len":64})

Operational playbook: incident debug workflow
-------------------------------------------
1) Pager triggers a trace id. On-call engineer retrieves traces and then runs a log query across service and time window using trace_id and request_id.
2) If textual context is missing due to sampling, escalate to Debug Sampling: toggle a temporary 10x increase in debug sampling for the affected service (requires approver and audit log).
3) If PII is suspected in logs, follow incident-secured procedure (see security-and-compliance/incident-response-security).

Rollout and migration plan for legacy services
----------------------------------------------
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): adopt SDK wrapper and add required fields to emitted events. No removal of legacy keys.
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): start CI schema tests; run in dry-mode for two weeks to surface mismatches.
- Phase 3 (2 weeks): enable linter enforcement in main branch and require schema test green for merges.
- Phase 4 (ongoing): runtime sanitizer enforced at ingestion; remove legacy unstructured fields after 60 days.

Compliance and audits
---------------------
- Log storage and access follow data-residency and retention policies (see security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention).
- Access to raw logs with potentially sampled-textual context requires an audit approval.

Appendix A: service registry excerpt
------------------------------------
| service | short-name | owner |
|---------|------------|-------|
| API Gateway | api-gateway | infra-team |
| Embedding worker | embedder | ml-serving |
| Model router | model-router | runtime-core |

Appendix B: common failures and remediation
-------------------------------------------
- Missing request_id in a high-throughput path: add request-id middleware at the earliest ingress layer.
- Excessive log size: blocklist large keys at the serialization layer and emit a small fingerprint instead.
- Secret leakage detection in CI: open a ticket with Security and rotate affected keys immediately.

FAQ
---
Q: Why not log raw prompts for failed requests?
A: Raw prompts are high-risk PII and may contain customer secrets. Use hashed tokens and secure payload stores for debug-only retrieval.

Q: Who approves increased sampling for debugging?
A: On-call + service owner (or their delegate). All sampling increases are audited.

Change log
----------
- 2025-10-12: created (initial draft).
- 2025-11-05: added CI schema requirement and runtime sanitizer details (reviewers: Michael Carter).
- 2026-01-18: formalized sampling defaults and example schemas; promoted to published.

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Observability Platform Slack: #obs-platform
- Pager: oncall-observability
- Owner: priya.desai@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: Typed Service-Stub Orchestration and Test Factory Guidelines

sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: Provide a concrete, opinionated pattern for creating, versioning, and orchestrating typed service stubs and an accompanying test-factory used across Redwood Inference CI, SDK tests, and local developer workflows. This document defines surface-level contracts, lifecycle states, orchestration rules for multi-variant APIs, and a portable test-factory that can run compatibility suites against live and simulated backends.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to all public-facing inference API surfaces (generation, embeddings, streaming) and internal service mesh contracts used in the serving runtime layers.
- Intended for SDKs (Python, Go, JS), integration tests, and can be adopted by enterprise/private deployment test harnesses.
- Does not prescribe a single mocking library; focuses on contract and orchestration patterns so teams can use native frameworks.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: - Contract drift between clients and runtime variants causes production incidents and subtle regressions. Typed stubs with an orchestrated test factory reduce divergence by providing reproducible, automated compatibility checks and developer-first local simulation.
sections.heading: Why this matters

sections.body:
1) Strong typing at the contract boundary: every stub manifest MUST declare typed request/response shapes and error variants.
2) Single source of truth for behavioral sampling: a stub manifest includes examples and traffic-weighted scenarios used by tests and synthetic telemetry.
3) Deterministic replay: test factory must be able to replay recorded inputs (seeded RNGs and fixed timestamps) to reproduce flaky cases.
4) Lightweight orchestration: orchestration should be filesystem-first and CI-friendly (no heavy distributed dependency to run local test factories).
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
- Stub manifest: declarative YAML that describes endpoint name, typed schema (JSON Schema reference), variants, and scenario seeds.
- Variant: named runtime behavior (e.g., v1-exact, v1-approx-quantized, degraded-fallback).
- Test factory: a CLI/worker that loads manifests and executes scenarios against a target (stub or live service) while producing structured evidence.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
---
endpoint: /v1/generate
component: synthesis
version: 2026-01-01
variants:
  - id: baseline
    description: Reference deterministic generator for integration tests
    schema: ./schemas/generation-response-v1.json
    scenarios:
      - id: short_prompt
        weight: 70
        request: {
          "prompt": "Translate to French: Hello",
          "max_tokens": 16
        }
        response_seed: 12345
      - id: long_prompt
        weight: 30
        request: {
          "prompt": "Summarize the following document...",
          "max_tokens": 512
        }
        response_seed: 98765
metadata:
  author: teams/synthesis
  compatible_clients: ["python-sdk>=1.4.0", "go-sdk>=0.9.2"]
  telemetry_tags: ["synthetic", "ci"]
---
sections.heading: Example (yaml-like)

sections.body:
- Schemas should be JSON Schema v2020-12. Prefer typed enums for status/error codes.
- Include examples in the schema (under x-examples) that the test factory can import.
sections.heading: Typed schema guidance

sections.body:
- Every change that modifies a schema or removes a field MUST be accompanied by a compatibility test that runs the consumer SDK matrix and verifies graceful degradation or explicit migration pathways.
- New optional fields: allowed under minor bumps; tests must assert clients ignoring unknown fields still function.
- Field renames / semantic changes: requires staged rollout and ADR (see Decision Log below).

Test factory: responsibilities and outputs
- Responsibilities:
  - Load one or more stub manifests.
  - Spin up the stub server in-process or call remote stub runner.
  - Execute scenarios deterministically; for streaming endpoints, assert chunk ordering and boundary markers.
  - Produce evidence bundles: structured traces, response diffs, and a compatibility verdict per variant-client pair.
- Outputs (artifact file names):
  - evidence-<endpoint>-<variant>-<timestamp>.ndjson (per-scenario events)
  - verdict-<matrix-hash>.json (pass/fail and failure reasons)
  - recorded-seed-<id>.tar.gz (replayable payloads)
sections.heading: Variant compatibility rules

sections.body:
1) Local developer mode: test-factory run --manifest ./stubs/generate.yaml --mode local --port 5050
   - Starts ephemeral stub, blocks until Ctrl-C. Fast feedback for SDK devs.
2) CI integration mode: test-factory run --manifest ci-manifest.yaml --matrix python:3.11-js:node18 --reporter s3://ci-artifacts/
   - Runs matrix across SDK versions and uploads verdicts.
3) Canary / release gating: registry of manifest hashes recorded in release metadata. Gate: all matrix combinations must pass for canary rollout to proceed.
sections.heading: Orchestration patterns (recommended)

sections.body:
- Each manifest MUST include scenario weights and a synthetic-telemetry mapping so CI can generate realistic distribution of cases.
- When running against live services for regression checks, the test factory MUST throttle to <= 0.5% production equivalent traffic per test run and add noise-trace headers to clearly label the run.
sections.heading: Behavioral sampling and telemetry integration

sections.body:
- Classification:
  - Type A: Schema mismatch (syntactic) — immediate blocker.
  - Type B: Semantic drift (e.g., changed default behavior) — degrade-to-warning, requires triage.
  - Type C: Non-deterministic failure (timing/ordering) — flaky test; capture full event stream and seed for replay.
- Triage steps (numbered):
  1) Reproduce locally with the recorded-seed artifact.
  2) Run targeted SDK matrix to confirm consumer impact.
  3) If schema-related, open an ADR referencing the manifest and tag release notes.
  4) If semantic, propose migration plan: compatibility shim, deprecation notice, or staggered rollout.
sections.heading: Failure classification and remediation playbook

sections.body:
State | Meaning | Required actions
----- | ------- | ----------------
draft | Under team iteration | tests <- local only; no CI gates
registered | Ready for CI | manifests stored in registry; CI runs matrix on PRs
pinned | Part of release baseline | manifest hash recorded in release metadata; used for canary gating
deprecated | Scheduled removal | Add deprecation_notice, set sunset_date, run compatibility tests for dependent clients
sections.heading: Lifecycle states for stub manifests (table)

sections.body:
- [ ] Add stub manifest file under /stubs/<component>/<endpoint>-manifest.yaml
- [ ] Include JSON schemas and example payloads under /stubs/<component>/schemas/
- [ ] Add test-factory job to PR CI: .github/workflows/stub-compat.yml
- [ ] Update component README with manifest hash and matrix results link
sections.heading: Implementation checklist (PR template snippet)

sections.body:
1) pip install redwood-test-factory  # or refer to internal package
2) git clone <repo> && cd stubs/synthesis
3) redwood-test-factory run --manifest ./generate.yaml --mode local --port 5050
4) In another shell: python -c "from redwood_sdk import Client; c=Client(base_url='http://localhost:5050'); print(c.generate('Hello'))"
sections.heading: Quick start (developer)

sections.body:
- Ownership: teams/<component> maintain manifests and scenario definitions. Test-factory runner is owned by infra/ci-team (on-call: infra).
- SLA for CI verdict upload: 95% of matrix runs should produce verdict artifacts within 30 minutes. Failures to produce artifacts must notify the owning component Slack channel and attach raw logs.
sections.heading: Operational ownership and SLAs

sections.body:
- ADR-2025: contract-driven-client-simulator (recommends a test harness approach; this doc operationalizes that idea with typed manifests).
- ADR-2026: versioned-schema-fencing (guides schema bump semantics referenced earlier).
sections.heading: Decision log (summaries of related ADRs)

sections.body:
- Minimal stub runner (pseudo-Python):
  from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
  import json

  class StubHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_POST(self):
          body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers['Content-Length'])))
          # lookup scenario by prompt length, seed RNG, return precomputed tokens
          self.send_response(200)
          self.end_headers()
          self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"id":"synth-1","text":"Bonjour"}).encode())

- CI job (YAML fragment):
  jobs:
    stub-compat:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Run test factory
          run: redwood-test-factory run --manifest stubs/generate.yaml --matrix python:3.11 --reporter s3://ci-artifacts/
sections.heading: Non-normative implementation examples (snippets)

sections.body:
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/coding-standards/contract-driven-client-simulator-and-compat-test-spec-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026

Appendix A — Manifest example checklist:
- endpoint, component, version present
- At least two variants (baseline, degraded)
- Schemas present and referenced
- Scenario weights defined and sum > 0
- telemetry_tags populated
- compatible_clients listed

Appendix B — FAQ (short)
Q: Can teams use their own mock servers instead of the test-factory-run stub?
A: Yes. The manifest is the contract; any runner that implements the manifest contract is acceptable. However CI gating must use the canonical redwood-test-factory or an approved wrapper.
sections.heading: References and related pages

sections.body:
- Primary author: Marina Kwon (marina@redwood.ai)
- Infra/CI on-call: infra-team@redwood.ai
- For ADRs and schema disputes open a PR against /specs/manifests and add the 'schema-discussion' label.
sections.heading: Contact and escalation

sections.body:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft and local developer workflow
- 2026-02-18: Added lifecycle states and CI outputs
- 2026-03-02: Finalized telemetry and SLA sections

payload.page_title: Staged payload evolution and client feature negotiation playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook specifies an operational pattern for evolving request/response payloads and shipping server-side changes while preserving safe client compatibility. It pairs staged payload extensions with an explicit client negotiation header and client-side feature flags. The goal is to make schema evolution predictable, measurable, and reversible for both hosted and private deployments.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
- Backwards-compatible and additive schema changes (new optional fields, extended enums).
- Introduction of experimental fields that should be opt-in per client.
- Rolling out server-side behavior changes that require explicit client opt-in.
- Coordinating cross-service payload migrations where clients are deployed at varying cadences.

Key concepts and guarantees
---------------------------
- Compatibility tiers (server promises):
  - stable: field is safe for all clients; server must handle absence and presence consistently.
  - opt_in: server will treat the field as no-op unless client explicitly declares support.
  - experimental: short-lived, may be removed; enabled only via canary client population.

- Client capability negotiation: clients announce supported features via a single header X-Client-Capabilities containing a compact JSON map (base64 or URL-safe encoding allowed). Example header: X-Client-Capabilities: eyJ2IjoiMSIsImZlYXR1cmVzIjp7ImJhdGNoX3mdIjoiMSJ9fQ== (decoded -> {"v":"1","features":{"batch_v2":"1","safe_tags":"opt_in"}})

- Server adaptation layer: servers must contain a small, tested adaptors registry that maps capability sets -> effective response shape. Adaptors are feature-gated and exercised by contract tests.

Compatibility matrix (behavioral guarantees)
-------------------------------------------
| Change type             | Guarantee to older clients                   | Recommended strategy             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Add optional field      | Ignore/strip for older clients                | Add as "stable" with default    |
| Add enum variant        | Map unknown enum to legacy fallback value     | Introduce with opt_in then stable|
| Change semantics        | Not allowed without opt_in and canary         | Use experimental then opt_in      |
| Remove field            | Deprecate for 6 months, then remove with warning | Deprecate -> remove              |

Client negotiation protocol
---------------------------
- Header name: X-Client-Capabilities
- Payload: JSON object with keys: version, features, client_id (optional), timestamp
- Encoding: RFC-safe base64 or URL-encoded JSON; servers must accept either.
- Server behavior: build an "effective policy" by merging default server flags with client-declared features.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "version": "1",
  "client_id": "web-frontend-12",
  "features": {
    "batch_v2": "opt_in",
    "precise_tokens": "stable"
  },
  "timestamp": "2026-03-10T14:22:00Z"
}

Migration rollout procedure (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------------
1. Design: publish a short design note listing new fields, semantics, opt_in vs stable decision, and tests. Owner: product/engineering.
2. Contract tests: author a contract test suite that validates both old and new capability permutations. Add tests to CI.
3. Server implementation: add adaptor logic behind feature flags and a runtime toggle. Deploy to staging.
4. Canary: enable experimental fields for 1% of traffic from clients that advertise experimental capability. Monitor metrics for 72 hours.
5. Incremental opt-in: invite client teams to opt-in by setting X-Client-Capabilities or via client-side feature flag rollout.
6. Observability gate: require 0.1% error impact, <3% latency increase, no regression in quality metrics for canary to proceed.
7. Scale: increase traffic % in geometric steps (1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%).
8. Stabilize: after 14 days at >=50% with no regressions, promote the field from opt_in to stable.
9. Deprecation (when removing): publish 6-month deprecation schedule and include server-side warning header X-Deprecated-Fields.

Rollout checklist (short)
-------------------------
- [ ] Design doc published and linked.
- [ ] Contract test coverage added (positive and negative cases).
- [ ] Staging deployment with flags.
- [ ] Canary launch and metrics monitored.
- [ ] Client opt-in instructions published.
- [ ] Post-mortem template ready for any regression.

Monitoring and SLOs
-------------------
- Essential metrics to collect per rollout:
  - feature_error_rate: errors on requests with feature enabled (SLO: <= 0.1% above baseline)
  - feature_latency_p50/p95: latency with feature (SLO: < 10% above baseline p95)
  - feature_quality_delta: if applicable, quality regression metric (custom per eval)
  - adoption_rate: number of distinct clients that advertise a capability

- Traces: add a tag feature.vector to spans to make it filterable in flame/trace views.
- Dashboards: create a short-lived rollout dashboard for each migration showing the above metrics vs baseline. Keep dashboards linked in the design doc.

Contract testing and CI requirements
----------------------------------
- Contract tests must run on:
  - server default (no capabilities)
  - explicit opt_in capability set
  - experimental capability set (if applicable)
  - mixed-client scenarios (requests from both old and new clients)
- Add a synthetic traffic job that periodically exercises edge cases (unknown enum values, missing optional fields).

Emergency rollback and mitigation
--------------------------------
1. Immediate toggle: flip runtime flag to ignore the experimental/opt_in fields and return legacy shape.
2. Rate-limit: if feature is resource-heavy, apply per-client rate limits and sticky routing away from overloaded shards.
3. Communication: page involved on-call list, update the rollout dashboard with red status, and create an incident ticket with the migration id.
4. Post-incident actions: root cause analysis, publish postmortem, revise playbook if needed.

Operational ownership and responsibilities
-----------------------------------------
- Feature owner: product or feature engineering team — responsible for design doc, adoption plan, and client communications.
- Runtime owner: serving/runtime team — responsible for adaptor code, flags, observability hooks, and rollback toggles.
- Quality owner: Applied ML / Evals (when change affects model outputs) — provides quality evaluation and acceptance criteria.

Examples and snippets
---------------------
- Sample server-side adaptor pseudocode:

// adaptor registration snippet (pseudo)
registerAdaptor("batch_v2", (req, capabilities) => {
  if (!capabilities.features.batch_v2) {
    return transformToLegacy(req);
  }
  return req; // support batch_v2 shape
});

- Sample curl using base64-encoded capability header:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Client-Capabilities: eyJ2IjoiMSIsImZlYXR1cmVzIjp7ImJhdGNoX3YyIjoib3B0X2luIn19" -d '@payload.json' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
sections.heading: Client capability JSON example (before encoding)

sections.body:
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "prompt": {"type": "string"},
    "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "x-compatibility": "stable"},
    "priority": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low","medium","high"], "x-compatibility": "opt_in"}
  },
  "required": ["prompt"]
}

Related pages and references
----------------------------
- Link to schema-fencing playbook (referenced for deprecations and fence periods).
- Runtime feature-flagging standards page.

Appendix: Quick decision rubric for opt_in vs stable
---------------------------------------------------
- Opt_in when any of the following are true:
  - Behavioral semantics change (not just additional data).
  - Server will incur >5% CPU or memory increase for enabled requests.
  - Changes affect billing/chargeable token accounting.
- Promote to stable when:
  - 90% of active client surface supports the capability for 14 days, and
  - No increase in error rate beyond 0.1% and latency within SLOs.

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-03-15: created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-06-02: added monitoring thresholds and sample header encoding guidance (reviewers: Daniel Kim).
- 2026-09-12: clarified adaptor testing requirements and rollback steps (reviewer: Priya Singh).

Owners and contacts
-------------------
- Feature owner: product/eng (see design doc)
- Runtime owner: runtime-team@redwood.internal
- On-call: serving-sre oncall rotation
