payload.page_title: SDK Retry & Timeout Standard (v1)

sections.body: This document defines Redwood Inference’s company-wide standard for **SDK retry/backoff** and **timeout behavior** across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Predictable behavior across languages (“same input, same failure semantics”).
- Avoid retry storms while still handling transient failures safely.
- Respect platform signals (e.g., **Retry-After**, request IDs) and preserve debuggability.
- Provide consistent configuration knobs and typed errors.
sections.heading: The goals are

sections.body:
- Redefining Redwood API error shapes beyond what the gateway already emits.
- Adding new auth mechanisms.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- **Attempt**: a single HTTP request execution.
- **Retry**: re-issuing an attempt after a failure and delay.
- **Retry budget**: the maximum number of attempts and/or maximum total elapsed time spent retrying.
- **Overall timeout**: the maximum time allowed for the full request lifecycle (including retries and backoff).
- **Connect timeout**: time allowed to establish TCP/TLS connection.
- **Read/response timeout**: time allowed while waiting for response bytes after a request is sent.
- **Streaming**: server-sent incremental response body where partial output may be delivered.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body: The defaults below MUST be the same across SDKs unless explicitly noted.
sections.heading: Standard behavior summary (defaults)

sections.body:
| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| max_attempts | 4 | 1 initial + up to 3 retries |
| retry_on_status_codes | 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 | See “Retryable errors” |
| retry_on_network_errors | true | See “Retryable network errors” |
| respect_retry_after | true | For 429 and 503 when present |
| backoff_strategy | exponential + jitter | Full jitter; see algorithm |
| initial_backoff_ms | 250 | First retry delay baseline |
| max_backoff_ms | 8000 | Caps per-delay |
| max_total_retry_time_ms | 20000 | Budget excluding the first attempt wall time; see guidance |
sections.heading: Default retry policy (non-streaming)

sections.body:
| Timeout | Default | Applies to |
|---|---:|---|
| connect_timeout_ms | 5000 | All requests |
| read_timeout_ms | 60000 | Non-streaming requests |
| overall_timeout_ms | 90000 | All requests (includes retries/backoff) |
| stream_idle_timeout_ms | 30000 | Streaming: max idle time between bytes/events |
sections.heading: Default timeout model

sections.body:
- If an SDK cannot express all timeouts natively, it MUST approximate the semantics and document the mapping (see “Language mapping requirements”).
- overall_timeout_ms MUST cap the request, even if connect/read timeouts are higher or “infinite” under a language’s HTTP client.
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: SDKs MUST retry only on the conditions below (subject to the retry budget).
sections.heading: Retryable errors

sections.body:
- **408 Request Timeout**
- **429 Too Many Requests** (rate limit or quota)
- **500 Internal Server Error**
- **502 Bad Gateway**
- **503 Service Unavailable**
- **504 Gateway Timeout**
sections.heading: SDKs MUST treat these as retryable by default

sections.body: - Other **4xx** (e.g., 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422) because these are typically caller errors and retries can create duplicate side effects or unnecessary load.
sections.heading: SDKs MUST NOT retry by default on

sections.body: - If the platform introduces a specific error code that is explicitly marked retryable (via a stable field, e.g., error.code + error.retryable), SDKs MAY extend retryability for that case, but ONLY via a reviewed change and conformance tests.
sections.heading: Exception policy

sections.body:
SDKs MUST retry by default on transient network/transport failures where the request likely did not reach Redwood or the response could not be received reliably, including:
- Connection failures (ECONNREFUSED, ENETUNREACH, EHOSTUNREACH)
- DNS lookup failures (temporary) / resolver timeouts
- TLS handshake failures that are not clearly configuration errors (treat as retryable once; see “Max attempts”)
- Connection resets (ECONNRESET), broken pipe (EPIPE)
- Read timeouts waiting for the first byte (non-streaming) when no response has been received
sections.heading: Retryable network / transport errors

sections.body:
- Certificate validation failures / invalid CA / hostname mismatch (likely misconfiguration)
- Explicit client cancellation (user abort / context canceled)
- Non-idempotent retry scenarios for streaming after partial output (see “Streaming rules”)
sections.heading: SDKs MUST NOT retry by default on

sections.body: - Because HTTP client error taxonomies differ, SDKs MUST implement a conservative mapping and include conformance tests for representative cases.
sections.heading: Implementation note

sections.body: When a response includes **Retry-After**, SDKs MUST respect it as follows:
sections.heading: Retry-After handling

sections.body:
- Honor Retry-After on **429** always.
- Honor Retry-After on **503** when present.
- Ignore Retry-After on other statuses unless explicitly introduced by platform contract.
sections.heading: When to honor

sections.body:
1) **delta-seconds** (e.g., "Retry-After: 2")
2) **HTTP-date** (e.g., "Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT")
sections.heading: SDKs MUST support both Retry-After formats

sections.body:
- Clamp computed Retry-After delay to: **[0ms, 60000ms]**.
- If Retry-After is invalid/unparseable/negative: ignore it and fall back to exponential backoff.
sections.heading: To prevent pathological delays and improve predictability

sections.body:
- If Retry-After is present and valid, it overrides the computed exponential backoff for that retry.
- Jitter MUST NOT be applied on top of Retry-After (to preserve the server’s intended pacing). If load-shaping is desired, the platform should randomize Retry-After values upstream.
sections.heading: Interaction with backoff

sections.body: SDKs MUST implement “exponential backoff with full jitter” for retries that do not have a valid Retry-After.
sections.heading: Backoff algorithm (exponential + jitter)

sections.body:
- base = initial_backoff_ms (default 250ms)
- cap = max_backoff_ms (default 8000ms)
- attempt_number starts at 1 for the first retry (i.e., after the initial failed attempt)
sections.heading: Parameters

sections.body:
- exp = min(cap, base * 2^(attempt_number - 1))
- sleep_ms = random_uniform(0, exp)
sections.heading: Compute

sections.body: - Full jitter reduces synchronization and thundering herd risk more effectively than fixed jitter.
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body:
- max_attempts default is **4**.
- max_total_retry_time_ms default is **20000ms**.
sections.heading: Defaults

sections.body:
- The next attempt would exceed max_attempts.
- The accumulated time spent in backoff delays would exceed max_total_retry_time_ms.
- The overall_timeout_ms would be exceeded.
sections.heading: SDKs MUST stop retrying when either is exceeded

sections.body:
- SDKs SHOULD prioritize overall_timeout_ms as the “hard stop” for user expectations.
- SDKs SHOULD include the final error as the surfaced exception (not a generic “retry exhausted”), but MUST attach retry metadata (attempt count, last delay, whether Retry-After was used).
sections.heading: Guidance

sections.body: SDKs MUST expose and implement the following timeout concepts:
sections.heading: Timeouts

sections.body:
- connect_timeout_ms: max time to establish the connection.
- Default: 5000ms.
sections.heading: Connect timeout

sections.body:
- read_timeout_ms: max time waiting for the response after the request is sent.
- Default: 60000ms.
sections.heading: Read/response timeout (non-streaming)

sections.body:
- overall_timeout_ms: max wall-clock time for the full operation (including retries and backoff).
- Default: 90000ms.
sections.heading: Overall timeout (hard cap)

sections.body:
- overall_timeout_ms MUST apply even if the underlying client does not support a true overall timeout. Implement via an outer timer/abort mechanism.
- If overall_timeout_ms < connect_timeout_ms or read_timeout_ms, overall_timeout_ms wins.
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
Streaming requests have different expectations and failure modes.
- stream_idle_timeout_ms: max time with no bytes/events received before considering the stream stalled.
- Default: 30000ms.
sections.heading: Streaming idle timeout

sections.body:
- stream_idle_timeout_ms resets each time a valid stream chunk/event is received.
- overall_timeout_ms MUST still apply to the streaming request.
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
SDKs MUST follow these rules to avoid duplicate outputs and confusing customer semantics:

1) **No automatic retry after partial output**
   - If any portion of the streaming response body has been delivered to the caller, the SDK MUST NOT automatically retry.
   - The SDK MUST raise a typed streaming disconnect error that includes:
     - request_id (if known)
     - bytes/events received
     - whether partial output was delivered
     - attempt count

2) **Allowed automatic retry before first byte**
   - If the stream fails before any bytes/events are received (e.g., connect failure, TLS handshake error, 503 before body), the SDK MAY retry using the standard retry policy.

3) **Documented manual retry guidance**
   - SDK docs MUST recommend:
     - using idempotency keys for operations where duplication is harmful
     - logging request_id and retry_count
     - treating streaming retries as app-level decisions
sections.heading: Streaming retry rules (safety-first)

sections.body:
Each SDK MUST expose configuration knobs with consistent naming (language-idiomatic casing is allowed) and consistent semantics:
- max_attempts
- initial_backoff_ms
- max_backoff_ms
- max_total_retry_time_ms
- connect_timeout_ms
- read_timeout_ms
- overall_timeout_ms
- stream_idle_timeout_ms
- retry_on_status_codes (advanced)
- retry_on_network_errors (advanced)
sections.heading: Configuration requirements (SDK surface)

sections.body:
1) Per-request options override client defaults.
2) Client defaults override environment configuration.
3) Environment configuration overrides hardcoded defaults.
sections.heading: Precedence

sections.body:
On any error surfaced after retries, SDKs MUST include:
- request_id (if present in response headers/body)
- status_code (if applicable)
- code (Redwood error code when available)
- retryable (boolean)
- attempt (current attempt number)
- max_attempts
- elapsed_ms (best-effort)

SDKs SHOULD additionally expose (via hooks/logging callbacks):
- retry_count
- last_backoff_ms
- used_retry_after (boolean)
- timeout_type (connect/read/overall/stream_idle)
sections.heading: Error reporting & observability (minimum contract)

sections.body: - SDKs MUST NOT log or include secrets in error messages. Any debug logging MUST redact Authorization headers and API keys (see security guidance page).
sections.heading: Security note

sections.body: SDKs MUST document (in their README or reference docs) how this standard maps to the underlying HTTP client.
sections.heading: Language mapping requirements (implementation notes)

sections.body:
- Python: must clarify mapping to httpx/requests semantics for connect/read/write/pool timeouts, and how overall_timeout_ms is enforced.
- TypeScript: must clarify AbortController usage for overall timeout and streaming cancellation, plus behavior in Node vs browser fetch.
- Go: must clarify mapping to net/http Transport timeouts and context cancellation; overall_timeout_ms enforced via context.WithTimeout.
sections.heading: Minimum requirements

sections.body:
A shared conformance suite MUST validate, at minimum:
- 429 with Retry-After (seconds) is honored and clamped correctly.
- 429 with Retry-After (HTTP-date) is parsed correctly.
- 500/502/503/504 trigger retries up to max_attempts.
- 400/401/403/404 do NOT trigger retries.
- Network error triggers retry with exponential full jitter (validated by bounds, not exact values).
- Streaming disconnect after partial output does NOT auto-retry and surfaces partial output metadata.
- overall_timeout_ms caps the request even when per-attempt timeouts are higher.
sections.heading: Conformance testing (required)

sections.body:
- Any changes to defaults (max_attempts, timeouts, retryable codes) require:
  1) SRE review (load impact / thundering herd risk)
  2) Security review if error/logging behavior is affected
  3) Updated conformance tests and migration notes
sections.heading: Rollout and change control

sections.body: We avoid broad retries on 4xx because they are often caller errors and can cause repeated failures and amplified load. If the platform introduces a stable, explicit “retryable” signal for specific cases, we can expand safely with conformance coverage.
sections.heading: Why not retry 409 or 425 by default?

sections.body: This caps client-side amplification during incidents and keeps tail latency predictable. Customers can opt in to higher budgets explicitly if their workload prefers eventual success over latency.
sections.heading: Why cap max_total_retry_time_ms at 20s?

sections.body:
Once partial output is delivered, automatic retry risks duplicating content and confusing application state. Retrying streaming is an app-level decision and should be tied to idempotency strategy.

---
**DRI / owner:** DevEx + SRE (Allison Grant, Sean Gallagher)

**Last reviewed:** 2026-02-18

**Next review window:** 2026-05 (or earlier if gateway error semantics change)
sections.heading: Why does streaming have stricter retry rules?

payload.page_title: Capability Signal Profiles and Client Negotiation Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines a compact, observable protocol for advertising runtime capabilities and negotiating effective behavior between clients and Redwood inference endpoints. The protocol reduces brittle client checks, enables safe feature rollouts, and provides structured signals for debugging and cost accounting.

Scope: Applies to HTTP and gRPC endpoints that expose evolving inference features (streaming modes, structured outputs, function/tool calling semantics, fidelity/quantization hints, early-exit heuristics). Exempt: purely documentation-only changes and telemetry-only fields.

Background and motivation
- Frequent client breakages occurred when runtime features changed without an explicit compatibility surface.
- Feature guards and ad-hoc query params proved inadequate for multi-variant deployments and private/legacy tenants.
- A negotiation layer allows clients to express intent and ordered fallbacks to avoid failures and provide higher-quality telemetry.

Key concepts and definitions
- Capability profile: a short, self-describing descriptor naming a capability and enumerating minimal contract points (semantic id, implied failure modes, preferred fallback).
- Client intent: the set of capabilities the client wishes to use for a request, with a priority order and whether each is required.
- Negotiation handshake: single-round exchange encoded at the request/response header level (no extra RTT).

Design principles
- Explicit, machine-readable: use compact JSON in headers (base64-encoded where needed) rather than free-form flags. Keep header payloads < 1KB.
- Backwards compatible: servers that ignore the header must return conservative behavior and emit a missing-header metric.
- Observability-first: every negotiation must emit a span event and metrics with standardized tags for aggregation.
- Low latency: negotiation piggybacks on the initial request. No additional handshake RTTs.
- Fail-safe: if a required capability is unavailable, servers should fail fast with a clear status and negotiation explanation.

Wire representation (example patterns)
- Request header name: X-RW-Capability-Intent
- Response header name: X-RW-Capability-Profile

Request header (JSON, recommended base64-encoded for transport):
{
  "intentVersion": "1",
  "capabilities": [
    {"id": "structured-output.v2", "required": false, "fallback": "text-only"},
    {"id": "early-exit.v2", "required": true}
  ],
  "costSensitivity": "low"
}
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "agreedVersion": "1",
  "applied": ["structured-output.v2"],
  "unavailable": [{"id":"early-exit.v2","reason":"model-incompatible","fallback":"none"}],
  "notes": "Quantized variant chosen (q4)"
}

Negotiation semantics and server behavior
- Unknown header: server treats as no intent and records metric rw.negotiation.missing_header.
- Best-effort application: server should attempt to apply requested optional capabilities and list applied/unavailable in the response header.
- Required capability failure: if a capability is marked required and cannot be provided, server returns 412 Precondition Failed with X-RW-Capability-Profile describing the mismatch and an explicit \"fallback\" field (\"none\" indicates hard failure).
- Fallback execution: when server applies a fallback, it must include \"fallback_applied\" semantics in traces and provide a human-readable note in response headers for quick diagnosis.

Observability and telemetry
- Mandatory metrics:
  - rw.negotiation.requests: counter (labels: endpoint, intentVersion)
  - rw.negotiation.applied_count: counter (labels: capability, endpoint)
  - rw.negotiation.unavailable_count: counter (labels: capability, reason)
  - rw.negotiation.required_failures: counter (labels: endpoint)
- Tracing tags (span attributes): negotiation.client_intent_version, negotiation.applied_list (comma-separated), negotiation.unavailable_reasons.
- Logs: negotiation decisions must be recorded at INFO level with correlation_id and minimal profile content.

Compatibility, schema evolution, and versioning
- intentVersion bumps: non-breaking additions (new optional capabilities) may be added without a version bump. Removing or reinterpreting a capability requires a new intentVersion and documented migration steps.
- Deprecation window: when deprecating a capability, announce in release notes and emit rw.negotiation.deprecation_warning when clients request a deprecated id. Keep behavior stable for a minimum of 90 days.

Security and privacy considerations
- Capability headers may contain sensitive hints (e.g., private feature flags). Mark headers as non-cacheable and avoid echoing sensitive details into high-cardinality logs.
- For private deployments, negotiation may surface tenant-specific variant IDs; redact tenant identifiers in aggregated metrics.

Rollout and testing guidance
1) Add capability: author schema, document behavior, and add unit/integration tests that simulate degraded runtimes.
2) Canary: enable support on a canary region with augmented sampling of negotiation traces.
3) Metrics gating: require zero required_failures and <0.1% required failure rate in canary before wider rollout.
4) Partner testing: notify SDK teams to exercise new optional capabilities and update client-side hinting helpers.

Operational playbook and runbook entries
- Diagnostic checklist when clients report failures:
  1. Inspect X-RW-Capability-Intent in client request and X-RW-Capability-Profile in response.
  2. Check rw.negotiation.required_failures for spike correlated to deploys.
  3. Look for \"model-incompatible\" or \"resource-constrained\" reasons in unavailable list.
  4. If fallback_applied, verify downstream processing and cost accounting.

Examples
- curl example (CLI, unencoded for readability):
  curl -H 'X-RW-Capability-Intent: {"intentVersion":"1","capabilities":[{"id":"structured-output.v2","required":false}]}' \\  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
- Server response header example:
  X-RW-Capability-Profile: {"agreedVersion":"1","applied":["structured-output.v2"],"notes":"applied q4 quantized path"}

Troubleshooting examples
- Symptom: Client got a 412 when requesting early-exit.v2.
  Action: Verify server reported \"reason\":\"model-incompatible\"; if so, check model variant mapping and quantization policy for the tenant.
- Symptom: High rate of fallback_applied.
  Action: Correlate with rw.capacity.preemption and resource metrics; consider enabling fallback caching or adjusting batching profiles.

Ownership and next steps
- Primary owner: eng-platform / runtime-protocols (reach out via #eng-runtime-protocols).
- Implementation trackers: create a feature branch for the header parsing library in sdk-shared/protocols.
- Suggested rollout: start with internal endpoints and SDK test harness before externalizing to hosted API.

References and related documents
- See related standards: service-contract-change-signal, wire-format-negotiation, and runtime-sidecar-contract for private deployments.
- ADRs to consult during design: progressive-degradation-and-quality-fallback-playbook, model-annotation-format, and runtime-cache-invalidation.

Revision history
- 2026-02-10: initial draft by Ava Chen.
- 2026-03-01: added observability metric labels and rollout guidance (reviewers: Marcus, Priya, Ethan).

payload.page_title: typed-error-model-and-client-contract-recommendations-2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the canonical, typed error model and client contract recommendations for Redwood public and internal inference APIs. It standardizes machine-friendly error schema, HTTP status mappings, retry semantics, SDK behavior, observability signals, and a migration/playbook for rolling these changes out with minimal customer impact. The recommendations apply to text generation, chat, embeddings, and management endpoints.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single parsable error schema usable by SDKs and monitoring systems.
- Make retry logic deterministic (retryable vs non-retryable).
- Ensure backward-compatible enrichment path: servers may add fields but not change semantics.
- Tie error types to SLO and alerting rules so failures surface consistently.
- Document deprecation/compatibility rules for future error code changes.

Error model overview
--------------------
All endpoints MUST return an error payload with HTTP status and the following JSON envelope when an application-level error occurs (200 responses for success remain unchanged):
sections.heading: Overview
Example error envelope (minimally required fields)

sections.body:
- error.code (string): machine-readable, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE token. See taxonomy below.
- error.message (string): human-readable description for logs and developer UX. Should not be relied on for parsing.
- error.status (integer): canonical HTTP status matching the envelope. MUST match the HTTP status header.
- error.retryable (boolean): explicit recommendation whether client should attempt an automated retry.
- error.request_id (string): unique request id for support and tracing.
sections.heading: Field definitions (required)

sections.body:
- error.meta (object encoded as string if SDKs can't handle raw objects): free-form key/value pairs for debugging (model_id, node_pool, shard).
- error.hint (string): short remediation hint for users.
- error.documentation_url (string): link to an internal/external page with more context.

Error taxonomy and HTTP mapping
------------------------------
We mandate a bounded set of canonical error codes. Each code maps to HTTP status and expected retry behavior. SDKs MUST map HTTP and transport-level failures into these codes where possible.

Table: canonical codes
- INVALID_INPUT => 400, retryable: false. Use when request payload fails schema/validation. Include field-level errors in error.meta.validation.
- AUTHENTICATION_FAILED => 401, retryable: false. Token invalid/expired.
- PERMISSION_DENIED => 403, retryable: false. RBAC/ACL error.
- NOT_FOUND => 404, retryable: false. Unknown model/resource.
- RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED => 429, retryable: true (with backoff). Provide error.meta.retry_after_seconds when available.
- QUOTA_EXCEEDED => 402 or 429 (team may choose), retryable: false. Indicates customer's billing/commit limits.
- MODEL_UNAVAILABLE => 503, retryable: true. Model runtime not available in chosen tier/region. Suggest fallback model in error.meta.fallback_model when present.
- INTERNAL_ERROR => 500, retryable: true (with capped attempts). Use for transient infra problems.
- TIMEOUT => 504, retryable: true. Long-running inference timeout.
- PARTIAL_RESPONSE => 206, retryable: false. Generation produced partial output; include meta.partial=true and best-effort continuing instructions.
- DATA_POLICY_VIOLATION => 403, retryable: false. Request triggers policy blocking; include documentation_url and policy_id.
- DEPRECATED => 299 (or 200 with warning header), retryable: false. Use to indicate deprecated parameter/route was used; include error.meta.migration_guide.

Retry semantics and idempotency
------------------------------
- Use explicit retryable boolean rather than inferring from status alone. This prevents ambiguous behavior in SDKs.
- Clients SHOULD implement exponential backoff with jitter for retryable errors. Default: initial backoff 200ms, multiplier 2, max attempts 5 for typical hosted endpoints.
- For non-idempotent operations (e.g., model fine-tuning jobs), servers MUST require an idempotency key; if provided, server must make retries safe. Document idempotency in individual route specs.

SDK requirements and behavior
---------------------------
- Language SDKs MUST expose: parsed error.code, message, status, retryable, request_id, and any meta fields.
- SDKs SHOULD surface a typed exception hierarchy (e.g., RedwoodApiError -> RateLimitError/AuthenticationError).
- SDKs MUST not make automatic retries for errors with retryable=false. For retryable=true, retries must be configurable and disabled by default in critical interactive paths.
- SDKs SHOULD provide helpers: isRetryable(err), getRetryAfter(err), getRequestId(err).

Observability and alerting
-------------------------
- All error responses MUST be instrumented with the following tags/labels: endpoint, model, deployment_tier (hosted/dedicated/private), region, customer_id (if applicable), error.code.
- Metric: inference.errors.count{code,endpoint,model} incremented for every non-2xx/non-206 response.
- SLI: 99.9% success rate (2xx) over 5m sliding window for hosted API endpoints (see performance-standards for per-route SLOs).
- Pager thresholds: sustained error rate > 0.1% for control plane endpoints or >1.0% for tenant-level endpoints over 5m should create an alert. High-severity alerts should use request samples with request_id for postmortem.

Logging and support data
-----------------------
- Error logs MUST include request_id, error.code, upstream node id (if applicable), and logged stacktrace only for internal errors. Do not log sensitive customer payloads; apply redaction rules in data-management policies.

Compatibility and evolution rules
--------------------------------
- Servers may add new fields to the error envelope at any time.
- Servers MUST NOT change meaning of existing error.code tokens. To change semantics, create a new error code and deprecate the old one via public deprecation schedule (see deprecation policy).
- New error codes MUST be introduced behind feature flags for 4 weeks with monitoring of client failures and SDK adoption.

Migration and rollout playbook
-----------------------------
1) Implement server-side error envelope in a layered rollout: production -> canary -> beta tenants. 2) Monitor client parsing failures via a synthetic test suite that validates each SDK correctly interprets the envelope. 3) Gradually enable additional metadata fields (meta, hint, documentation_url) ensuring SDKs tolerate unknown fields. 4) Announce breaking changes (if unavoidable) with 90 days notice and provide a compatibility shim for the prior behavior.

Example: client handling pseudocode
----------------------------------
try {
  const resp = await client.generate(...);
} catch (err) {
  if (sdk.isRetryable(err) && attempts < cfg.maxAttempts) {
    await backoff.wait(attempts);
    retry();
  } else if (err.code === 'DEPRECATED') {
    console.warn('Deprecated param used', err.meta.migration_guide);
    // still return the response if present, or surface as warning
  } else {
    throw err; // propagate to caller
  }
}
Appendix: JSON Schema (human-readable)
-------------------------------------
- error: object (required)
  - code: string (required)
  - message: string (required)
  - status: integer (required)
  - retryable: boolean (required)
  - request_id: string (required)
  - meta: object (optional)
  - documentation_url: string (optional)

Decision links and references
-----------------------------
- See ADRs on API evolution and fallback policies for related decisions.
- Aligns with observability SLI guidance for error tagging and tracing.

Ownership and next steps
------------------------
- Owner: API Platform (engineering).
- Action items: SDK maintainers to add typed exceptions (deadline 2025-05-15), infra team to emit new error envelope (canary by 2025-04-01), product to publish migration docs and examples.

Notes and rationale
-------------------
Typed error envelopes reduce fragmentation in client logic, make retry behavior explicit, and improve signal quality for SLOs and incident response. They intentionally separate human-facing messages from machine tokens to prevent brittle parsing.

Document history
----------------
- 2024-10-12: initial draft by Aisha Kapoor.
- 2024-12-03: added PARTIAL_RESPONSE handling and observability tags (reviewers: Michael Chen).
- 2025-03-05: published after cross-SDK compatibility validation.
sections.heading: Optional fields (allowed but not required)

payload.page_title: request-semantics-and-cost-aware-payload-guidelines

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook specifies a cross-cutting standard for request semantics and payload design that makes API contracts explicit about cost impact, caching affordances, and degradation behavior. The goal is to give clients clear, machine-parseable signals they can use to choose request shapes (stream vs. unary, chunking, brevity vs. verbosity) and to enable the platform to account for cost deterministically and enforce predictable SLOs.

Scope
-----
Applies to all public and private inference endpoints (hosted Redwood API, Dedicated, and Private runtime sidecars). It covers:
- Request headers and annotations that convey cost-relevant intent.
- Payload size and composition limits tied to cost accounting.
- Preferred patterns for streaming and chunked requests.
- Server-side optimization hints (caching keys, bloom filters, idempotency).
- Operational metrics and SLI mappings required on all services that implement inference endpoints.

Design principles
-----------------
1) Explicit cost semantics: every request MUST either provide or inherit a cost-class annotation (see section "Cost class header"). This prevents surprises from opaque payloads and lets routing/quotas make informed choices.
2) Graceful degradation by intention: clients declare how much quality they will trade for reduced cost/latency (e.g., prefer-quantized, max-latency-ms, quality-floor).
3) Minimal server-side inference for uncacheable requests: servers should avoid speculative heavy work for requests marked cacheable=false.
4) Observability-first: request annotations flow through traces and are present in aggregated SLI dimensions.

API semantics and headers (required)
-----------------------------------
The following headers are required on all inference requests unless a client is explicitly pinned to an internal nonstandard contract:
- X-RW-Cost-Class: one of [free, standard, priority, enterprise] (string). Determines billing tier routing and latency SLO bucketing.
- X-RW-Quality-Hint: one of [max_quality, balanced, low_cost] (string). Informs fallback quantization/beam-size policies.
- X-RW-Cache-Key: opaque string (optional). When present, used as a cache key for prefix/response caching. Services MUST document the canonical construction for the key.
- X-RW-Idempotency-Key: opaque string (optional). Required for non-idempotent payloads that may be retried by clients.
- X-RW-Max-Latency-MS: integer (optional). Client's preferred upper latency bound; used by smart routing for selecting fastest replica or smaller model.

Behavioral contract (server obligations)
--------------------------------------
- Cost-class routing: servers must map X-RW-Cost-Class to internal routing pools and SLOs. Default mapping: free -> best-effort, standard -> 99th percentile latency target 800ms, priority -> 99th percentile target 200ms, enterprise -> customer SLA mapping.
- Quality fallback: when system load or capacity forces a fallback, server may pick a lower-quality model variant but MUST annotate responses with X-RW-Fallback-Variant and X-RW-Quality-Used.
- Rejection and backlog signals: if request cannot be accepted within X-RW-Max-Latency-MS, server SHOULD return 429 with Retry-After and Rw-Degrade-Info header explaining options.

Payload-size and composition rules
---------------------------------
1) Token accounting: request size is measured in input tokens according to the model tokenization. Client libraries should provide a preflight token-count API to estimate cost.
2) Max payloads by tier (enforced by gateway):
   - free: max 2K tokens (input+expected output), 1 request/sec
   - standard: max 8K tokens, 20 requests/min
   - priority: max 32K tokens, 200 requests/min
   - enterprise: negotiable via contract; defaults to 64K tokens
3) Composite payload guidance: when sending structured contexts (logs, documents, tables), prefer a content-addressed document store (provide doc IDs via X-RW-Cache-Key) instead of embedding raw text.

Streaming vs Unary rules
------------------------
- Streaming should be used when client expects progressive partial results or when long-running decoding would degrade head latency.
- For streaming endpoints: the initial request MUST include X-RW-Cost-Class and X-RW-Quality-Hint. Streaming session metrics (tokens_streamed, session_duration_ms) MUST be emitted as system metrics.
- Unary endpoints are preferred for short, single-shot completions where batching is more effective.

Caching contract
----------------
- Cache key canonicalization: callers should combine stable context identifiers (document_id, user_id, prompt_template_id) hashed with a stable salt. Eg: sha256(user_id + '::' + document_id + '::' + prompt_template_id) placed in X-RW-Cache-Key.
- Cache TTL defaults: 24h for document-level keys, 5m for user-session keys. Services MUST support TTL override via server-side policy.

Coding standards (client and server expectations)
------------------------------------------------
- Input validation: servers MUST perform strict schema validation with clear 4xx error messages (use typed error codes defined in API catalog).
- Defensive deserialization: never dynamically evaluate client content. Use validated parsing.
- Backpressure handling: clients must respect 429+Retry-After and implement exponential backoff with jitter for transient errors.
- SDK helpers: official SDKs MUST expose token-preflight, automatic idempotency key generation, and a 'cost_estimate' helper that returns per-tier cost estimates.

Infrastructure requirements
---------------------------
- Gateway enforcement layer: an edge service must enforce header presence, token limits, and rate quotas per cost-class.
- Routing policy: the router must map X-RW-Cost-Class -> routing pool and preserve X-RW-Cache-Key forwarding.
- Quota accounting: billing records must include cost-class, token counts, and a hashed payload signature for auditing.
- Prewarming: routers may prewarm model shards for priority/enterprise pools when X-RW-Max-Latency-MS < 300ms.

Model-serving expectations
-------------------------
- Variant contract: model artifacts served in the same logical endpoint must implement a deterministic version tag and provide a quick metadata route (/v1/meta) returning: model_name, variant_id, quantization, expected_max_tokens, sample_token_cost_ms.
- KV cache rules: when X-RW-Cache-Key is present, runtime should attempt prefix/KV cache lookup before any compute-heavy steps. Cache miss counters must be emitted.
- Quantization hinting: X-RW-Quality-Hint maps to quantization suggestions (max_quality -> fp16 or higher, low_cost -> 8-bit quant). These are hints; runtime may override depending on capacity.

Observability and SLI mapping
----------------------------
Required telemetry (all services exposing inference endpoints must emit):
- Metrics (counter/gauge/histogram names):
  - rw.infer.requests_total{cost_class,quality_hint} (counter)
  - rw.infer.tokens_processed{model,variant,cost_class} (counter)
  - rw.infer.latency_ms_p99{cost_class} (histogram)
  - rw.infer.cache_hit_ratio (gauge)
  - rw.infer.fallback_rate (counter)
- Traces: every request must include trace/span tags: cost_class, cache_key (redacted), model_variant, quality_hint, idempotency_key (redacted).
- Logs: structured JSON lines should include request_id, user_id (hashed), cost_class, effective_latency_ms and error_code.

SLOs (recommended baseline)
---------------------------
- Standard tier: 95th <= 300ms, 99th <= 800ms for single-shot < 2K tokens.
- Priority tier: 95th <= 120ms, 99th <= 200ms for single-shot < 2K tokens.
- Streaming SLOs measured in first-byte latency and time-to-nth-token. Define customer-facing SLAs for enterprise in contracts.

Operational runbook (acceptance, fallback, and escalation)
----------------------------------------------------------
1) Acceptance plan for new endpoint:
   - Review header schema with API-gate team (ownership: api-gateway).
   - Add token-preflight and cost estimation tests to CI.
   - Verify observability tags are emitted by automated trace-linting job.
   - Canary rollout: start with standard cost-class and verify p50/p95/p99 across traffic.

2) Fallback behavior (service overloaded):
   - Step 1: Router applies queue shedding for "free" and "standard" classes while preserving "priority/enterprise".
   - Step 2: If degradation persists, pick lower-quality variant and annotate X-RW-Fallback-Variant.
   - Step 3: If model memory pressure persists, reject new sessions with Rw-Degrade-Info and provide a recommended payload (e.g., shorter context or doc-id path).

3) Escalation: If fallback rate > 1% for 15m in priority tier, page ML Serve on-call. If p99 latency > SLA for 30m, page infra-sre.

Implementation checklist (for product and infra teams)
----------------------------------------------------
- [ ] Update API gateway to validate and forward required headers.
- [ ] Add cost-class mapping to billing pipeline.
- [ ] Implement token-preflight API in SDKs.
- [ ] Add trace-linting rule to CI to assert required tags.
- [ ] Add canary job that simulates cross-tier load and validates fallback annotations.

Appendix: Example client usage
-----------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/completions 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
  -H "X-RW-Cost-Class: standard" 
  -H "X-RW-Quality-Hint: balanced" 
  -d '{"prompt": "Summarize the following doc...", "max_tokens": 256}'
sections.heading: Curl (unary)

sections.body:
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=TOKEN)
session = client.stream("/v1/chat/stream", headers={"X-RW-Cost-Class":"priority","X-RW-Quality-Hint":"max_quality"})
for partial in session:
    print(partial.text)

Decision record (ADR)
--------------------
Title: Standardize explicit cost-class and quality hint headers
ADR ID: 2026-API-014
Status: accepted
Date: 2026-02-18
Authors: Elena García
Context: Many services previously inferred cost intent from opaque client behavior and token usage. That led to surprising bill spikes and poor routing decisions during mixed workloads.
Decision: We require X-RW-Cost-Class and X-RW-Quality-Hint headers on all public inference requests and map them to routing/billing pipelines.
sections.heading: Python (streaming)

sections.body:
- Pro: deterministic billing and better routing hygiene; enables eager prewarming and quota isolation.
- Con: client migration cost; potential for clients to misclassify and underpay (mitigated by server-side overrides and audits).
sections.heading: Consequences

sections.body:
- Implicit inference (status quo): rejected due to opacity.
- Per-request cost budget token field: considered but rejected because it made routing brittle and prone to gaming.
sections.heading: Alternatives considered

sections.body:
- Gateway will accept both header-based and legacy flows for 6 months while emitting a deprecation warning header. After 6 months, legacy flows will be rejected for new tenants.
Owners: API Gateway team, Billing, ML Serve

Related decisions and references
-------------------------------
- See API contract versioning playbook for migration cadence.
- See model-slicing guidelines for variant selection rules.

Notes and next steps
--------------------
- Product should add a migration guide for common OSS SDKs and recommended header builders.
- Observability should add a dashboard for cross-cost-class usage, token-cost heatmap, and fallback-rate alerting.

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-03: Draft created (Elena García)
- 2025-12-18: Internal review with Gateway and Billing (Marcus Lee, Priya Sharma)
- 2026-02-18: Published; ADR accepted and checkpointed for enforcement

payload.page_title: Streaming Fidelity Handshake and Progressive Degradation Protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the Streaming Fidelity Handshake and Progressive Degradation Protocol (SF-Handshake). SF-Handshake is an API-level contract between clients, edge proxies, and the streaming runtime that enables: negotiation of output fidelity and cost/latency tradeoffs, progressive degradation when capacity or latency constraints are hit, and traceable fallbacks with deterministic observability hooks.

Motivation

As Redwood serves a spectrum of applications (interactive chat, embedders, high-volume summaries), we need a common, lightweight mechanism for clients to express fidelity preferences and for the runtime to respond with deterministic degradation steps rather than opaque failures. Existing streaming contracts either assume fixed fidelity or rely on ad-hoc headers. SF-Handshake standardizes the capabilities, signals, and telemetry so downstream systems (billing, routing, caching) can make consistent decisions.

Scope

- Applies to: hosted API streaming endpoints (edge-proxy -> stream-gateway -> runtime).
- Not in scope: non-streaming batch RPCs, internal-only debug hooks (these remain separate).
- Backwards compatibility: servers must accept requests without SF-Handshake fields and use safe defaults.

Owner and Contacts

- Document owner: eng/runtime-platform
- Primary implementation owners: service-edge team (edge-proxy), stream-runtime team (stream-gateway).
- Pager: eng-sre rotation (see runbook link in related pages).

Protocol overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Client sends an initial negotiation envelope as the first message or as request headers.
2) Edge validates the envelope, applies client-tier policies (quota, tenant SLOs), and forwards a server decision object.
3) Runtime executes generation respecting the decision and emits streaming tokens with fidelity annotations.
4) If the runtime must degrade, it emits a deterministic degradation event and updates the decision path; clients can optionally request a retry or accept degraded output.

Core concepts

- Fidelity Vector: A small typed set of dimensions describing desired result quality and cost: {accuracy, verbosity, creativity, safety_strictness, latency_priority}. Each dimension is an integer 0..100.
- Decision Envelope: Server-side response containing: selected fidelity vector, reason_code, allowed_cost_multiplier, degradation_plan (if applicable), observable_keys.
- Degradation Plan: Ordered instructions the runtime may apply in sequence (e.g., reduce creativity -> truncate output -> switch to cached summary).
- Observable Keys: Set of short opaque strings used to link tokens/events to telemetry traces and billing entries.

Negotiation surface (HTTP + streaming)

- Endpoint: POST /v1/stream/generate (existing streaming endpoint). SF-Handshake may be provided either as headers or as a JSON negotiation preamble.
- Headers (optional, lightweight):
  - X-RW-Fidelity: base64url(JSON) — compact fidelity vector when using headers.
  - X-RW-Client-Tier: free | standard | enterprise
  - X-RW-Negotiate-Mode: prefer | require | best-effort

- JSON preamble (recommended for full expressivity). Example:
sections.heading: High-level flow

sections.body:
{
  "handshake_version": "1.0",
  "fidelity_vector": {"accuracy": 80, "verbosity": 60, "creativity": 40, "safety_strictness": 90, "latency_priority": 70},
  "budget_usd": 0.02,
  "client_tier": "standard",
  "request_id": "cli-1234-ctx-7890",
  "negotiate_mode": "prefer"
}

Server Decision object (example returned synchronously or as the first streamed control event):
{
  "decision_version": "1.0",
  "selected_fidelity": {"accuracy": 75, "verbosity": 55, "creativity": 35, "safety_strictness": 90, "latency_priority": 80},
  "allowed_cost_multiplier": 1.2,
  "reason_code": "latency_slo_adjustment",
  "degradation_plan": ["prune_long_form_summaries","early_token_exit","quantize_hidden_states"],
  "observable_keys": ["ok_47f3","path_99b1"]
}

Client behavior and expectations

- Conservative clients: set negotiate_mode=require. If the server cannot honor the request, the request should fail with 422 /error {"reason":"UNABLE_TO_SATISFY_FIDELITY"}.
- Opportunistic clients: set negotiate_mode=prefer or best-effort. They should accept decision objects with lower fidelity.
- Clients should always correlate server observable_keys to local telemetry and include request_id in logs.

Server behavior and enforcement rules

- Edge-proxy must validate handshake_version and apply tenant policy (quota, minimum fidelity floor for enterprise tier).
- If negotiate_mode=require and constraints cannot be met, reject early with detailed reason_code and allow clients to retry with altered fidelity/budget.
- When allowed_cost_multiplier > 1.0, billing signals must be emitted to the cost pipeline; stream-gateway must annotate tokens with the chosen multiplier.

Degradation semantic primitives (order matters)

1) Soft downgrades (non-destructive): reduce creativity, shorten verbosity, increase repetition penalty.
2) Structural downgrades: switch to a lighter head model (same family), reduce sequence rematerialization.
3) Performance tradeoffs: enable aggressive KV-cache eviction policies or turn on quantized kernels.
4) Fallbacks (last resort): return cached or synthetic summary, mark response as degraded=true, attach degradation_plan_trace.

Concrete headers and token annotations (stream payload)

- Control event structure (first stream event):
  - type: "decision"
  - payload: <Decision object JSON above>

- Token annotation envelope (attached to token frames):
  - token_text: "..."
  - fidelity_annotation: "f:75,v:55,c:35,l:80,s:90"
  - trace_key: "ok_47f3"

Observability and SLOs

Minimum telemetry required for each SF-Handshake request (emitted as structured events):
- handshake.received (tags: request_id, client_tier, hashing of fidelity_vector)
- decision.emitted (tags: decision_version, reason_code, allowed_cost_multiplier)
- degradation.event (tags: plan_step, runtime_node, latency_ms)
- token.emitted (tags: trace_key, fidelity_annotation)
sections.heading: Preamble JSON example

sections.body:
- handshake latency (time to first decision event): p95 <= 30ms for edge-proxy local decisions; p99 <= 120ms globally.
- faithful-degradation response time (time between decision to degrade and first degraded token): p95 <= 40ms.
- correctness alerting: if more than 2% of standard-tier requests receive a degradation_plan with step "fallback_cached" for 12h window, create an incident.

Billing and cost signals

- If allowed_cost_multiplier != 1.0, stream must emit cost.multiplier events to the billing pipeline.
- Offline aggregator will compute unit-cost adjustments; design of the billing pipeline is outside this doc but streams must contain observable_keys for correlation.

Testing, rollout, and compatibility

- Feature gate: SF-Handshake is gated via feature-flag edge.synthetic.sf_handshake. Default off for free-tier.
- Canary plan: enable for 5% of traffic with negotiate_mode=prefer, collect metrics for handshake.latency, degradation.rate, billing.adjustments.
- Backwards compatibility: if client sends no handshake, runtime must behave as if fidelity_vector={accuracy:70,verbosity:60,creativity:50,safety_strictness:80,latency_priority:50}.

Operational runbook (high-level)

1) Detect spike in degradation.event rate (dashboard alert).
2) Validate whether increased degradation correlates with capacity events, policy changes, or a new model rollout.
3) If caused by model rollout, trigger automatic rollback to previous variant and alert product/ML.
4) If caused by tenant quota misconfiguration, apply tenant-specific temporary uplift and notify billing.

Security and privacy considerations

- Fidelity Vector values are not PII but may correlate with business-critical usage. Mark handshake events as internal.
- Observable_keys must be short opaque tokens; do not encode tenant or user IDs directly.

Compatibility matrix and decision rationale

- Rationale: We prefer an explicit JSON preamble to allow extensibility; header form remains for low-bandwidth clients.
- Compatibility: Servers will maintain a mapping layer to translate legacy headers into the fidelity_vector shape for at least 12 months.

Open questions and follow-ups

- Should we define a canonical set of degradation_plan steps and identifiers across runtime teams? (Action: convene engineering standards working group Q1 2026).
- How granular should cost multipliers be (per-token vs per-request)? Current recommendation: per-request multiplier with downstream prorated attribution.

Appendices

A. Example client curl (preamble body approach)

curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"handshake":{ "handshake_version":"1.0", "fidelity_vector":{"accuracy":85,"verbosity":50,"creativity":30,"safety_strictness":95,"latency_priority":40}, "negotiate_mode":"prefer" }, "prompt":"Summarize the following..." }' \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream/generate

B. Short glossary

- handshke_version: version string for ability to evolve envelope schema.
- negotiate_mode: how strict the client is about fidelity.
- observable_keys: short opaque tokens for telemetry/billing correlation.

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft authored.
- 2026-02-03: Added SLOs and example decision object; reviewer feedback incorporated.

Related references

- See related cost-aware streaming payload schema guideline for details on token framing and billing annotations.
- See runtime observability contract for event naming and ingestion paths.
sections.heading: SLOs (service-level guidance)

payload.page_title: Polyglot Contracts and Adaptive Client-Shielding Standards

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the standard patterns, manifests, and runbook for supporting polyglot service contracts (multiple protocol bindings and schema variants) while providing an adaptive client-shielding layer (runtime adapters/shims) that keeps consumers stable during iterative API evolution and operational incidents. The goal is predictable compatibility, measurable risk, and fast safe rollouts for multi-protocol endpoints (HTTP/JSON, gRPC, streaming RPCs, and binary bindings).

Context and motivation:
- Redwood services increasingly present multiple bindings and client surfaces for the same logical capability (public REST, internal gRPC, streaming websockets, SDKs). Without disciplined approach this leads to schema drift, client breakage, and operational cost from firefighting.
- We adopt a deliberate, auditable pattern: a machine-readable "contract manifest" published with each service + a small runtime adapter layer (shield) that performs schema negotiation, lightweight transforms, defaulting, and graceful degradation.

Principles:
1) Contracts are the source of truth: every service exposes a versioned contract manifest (see manifest schema below).
2) Single logical shape, many bindings: the logical API (operations, semantics) is primary; protocol bindings are adapters, not separate feature sets.
3) Fail-safe by default: adapters must prefer conservative compatibility (drop new optional fields, provide defaults) and emit telemetry for mismatches.
4) Measurable risk: every adapter change is gated by SLOs and telemetry thresholds (see rollout policy).
5) Minimal-latency adapters: runtime shielding must add minimal latency (adapter budgets) and be independently scalable.

Contract manifest (required fields):
- service_name: unique service identifier (e.g., "synthesis-api")
- logical_version: semver (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for behavior semantics
- bindings: list of {protocol, schema_ref, compatibility_level} where protocol in [http-json, grpc, websocket-stream, binary] and compatibility_level in [backward, forward, symmetric]
- transforms: optional list of canonical->binding transforms (if nontrivial)
- adapter_policy: id referencing the runtime adapter config to use
- steward: team@redwood.com (oncall PagerDuty)

Example contract manifest (YAML snippet):
---
service_name: synthesis-api
logical_version: 2.1.0
bindings:
  - protocol: http-json
    schema_ref: s3://contracts/synthesis-api/2.1.0/http.json
    compatibility_level: backward
  - protocol: grpc
    schema_ref: s3://contracts/synthesis-api/2.1.0/synthesis.proto
    compatibility_level: symmetric
adapter_policy: adapters/passthrough-limited.json
steward: service-synthesis@redwood.com
---

Adapter contract and runtime expectations:
- Adapter latency budget: p95 < 12ms, p99 < 40ms for simple transform adapters. Complex shims (aggregation/extra calls) require explicit SLO waivers.
- CPU and memory: adapter container must be tagged and autoscalable independently of core serving runtime. Use resource class: adapter.small / adapter.medium / adapter.large.
- Observability: adapters must emit the following metrics (names are canonical):
  - adapter.latency_ms{protocol,adapter_version}
  - adapter.transform_errors_total{error_type}
  - contract.mismatch_count{direction}
  - adapter.degraded_responses_total
- Traces must preserve trace_id and annotate spans: adapter.transform, adapter.negotiate, adapter.fallback.

Compatibility rules (how to interpret semver + manifest):
- MAJOR bump: breaking behavioral changes. Consumers must be migrated or adapter must implement behavior shim.
- MINOR bump: additive, allowed without adapter changes if binding compatibility declared backward/forward.
- PATCH: non-functional fixes; adapters should pass through.
- Binding-level compatibility annotations tell adapters allowed evolution (e.g., a "backward" binding may drop newly-added optional fields for older clients).

Adapter types and responsibilities:
1) Protocol adapters: translate between transport/protocol frames (e.g., websocket -> internal streaming RPC).
2) Schema adapters: inline transforms to map field names, types, and defaulting rules.
3) Aggregation adapters: make additional service calls to fill missing fields (expensive; declare cost).
4) Degradation adapters: respond with structured fallback payloads when core runtime is unavailable (must use standard fallback schema).

Adapter manifest example (JSON allowed):
{
  "adapter_name": "http-json-defaulting-v1",
  "version": "2026-10-18",
  "type": "schema",
  "resource_class": "adapter.small",
  "latency_budget_ms": "12",
  "transform_rules": ["rename: body->content", "default: priority=low"],
  "telemetry_endpoint": "telemetry/adapters/synthesis-api"
}

Testing and verification matrix:
- Contract unit tests: every manifest must include a test vector suite (producer and consumer fixtures) executed in CI.
- Integration grid: for each binding, CI must run a 3x matrix: (current producer, previous producer MAJOR-1, consumer-stub-old). The grid must pass with <=0.1% semantic mismatches.
- Synthetic load tests: adapters run a short synthetic workload (5m) verifying latency and error ratios before rollout.

Rollout and rollback playbook (step-by-step):
1) Design review & manifest PR: include test vectors and adapter manifest. Reviewer: API steward + eng-platform.
2) CI checks: contract tests, adapter unit tests, integration grid.
3) Canary stage: deploy adapter to 1% of traffic with canary tag. Monitor for 30 minutes.
   - Key signals: contract.mismatch_count per 10k requests < 1, adapter.transform_errors_total == 0, consumer-error-delta < 0.5%
4) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 30–90m observation windows.
5) Full rollout: update contract registry and service docs.
6) Rollback: immediate rollback if any of the following sustained for 10 minutes: adapter.transform_errors_total rate > 1 per 1k, consumer-error-delta > 5%, adapter.p99 latency > 2x baseline.

Operational thresholds and SLOs (service-level):
- Adapter availability: 99.95% monthly for adapter.small/medium, 99.9% for adapter.large (due to complexity).
- Contract fidelity: contract.mismatch_count per 10k requests <= 2 (target)
- Consumer impact guardrail: change must not increase consumer-side error rate by more than 1% absolute in first 24h.

Telemetry-driven alarms and automated mitigations:
- Alarm: contract.mismatch_rate > 5 per 10k for 5m -> auto-scale adapter pool x2 and open incident ticket.
- Alarm: consumer-error-delta > 2% for 5m -> automatic traffic pinning to previous adapter version (if available) and notify oncall.
- mitigation: adapter can return standardized degraded payload with header X-Redwood-Degraded: true and diagnostics link.

Config table (recommended default adapter classes):
- adapter.small: 0.5 vCPU, 512Mi memory, target p95 latency <= 12ms
- adapter.medium: 1 vCPU, 1Gi memory, target p95 latency <= 20ms
- adapter.large: 4 vCPU, 4Gi memory, target p95 latency <= 50ms

Ownership and responsibilities:
- API steward (primary): review and publish contract manifests, own test vectors.
- Eng-platform: provide adapter runtime platform, autoscaling policies, and adapter resource classes.
- Eng-runtime: ensure adapters have safe headers for routing and tracing and maintain the adapter SDKs.
- Security: review adapter transforms for sensitive-field exposure.

Oncall playbook (short):
1) Detect: PagerDuty alert from telemetry (see alarms above).
2) Triage: Identify adapter version, recent manifest change (PR link), and traffic percentage.
3) Quick mitigation: pin traffic away from failing adapter (automated OR via console), scale replica set, or enable degraded responses.
4) Postmortem: owner team to publish postmortem within 3 business days if incident > 1h or > 0.1% customer errors.

Examples and common migrations:
- Adding an optional field: increment MINOR; update schema_ref and test vectors; adapters for older bindings must default new field or drop silently.
- Renaming a field: prefer aliasing transform in adapter for one release cycle, mark as DEPRECATION in manifest, then MAJOR change to remove.

Related artifacts and references:
- Contract manifest schema (link): s3://contracts/schema/contract-manifest-v1.json
- Adapter SDK and examples: internal-repo/adapters/sdk/README.md
- Compatibility test harness: ci/tools/contract-grid/README.md

Appendix A: Checklist for service owners before publishing a change:
1) Update contract manifest and increment logical_version where appropriate.
2) Add/extend test vectors and run CI grid.
3) Prepare adapter manifest and perform local adapter synthetic run.
4) Schedule canary and include rollback playbook in PR description.
5) Notify oncall and stakeholders (slack channel).

Appendix B: CLI commands and quick snippets:
- Validate manifest: rdx-contract validate --manifest synthesis-api.yaml
- Run local adapter smoke: rdx-adapter run --manifest adapters/http-json-defaulting-v1.json --smoke-test
- Promote adapter in console: rdx-control promote adapter/http-json-defaulting-v1 --to=canary --traffic=1%

Questions and escalation contacts:
- API steward: service-synthesis@redwood.com
- Eng-platform triage: platform-oncall@redwood.com
- Security review: security-platform@redwood.com

Document change history:
- 2026-11-10: Draft created by Maya Chen (initial principles, manifest schema)
- 2026-12-08: Added adapter manifests and CI grid requirements (reviewers: Arjun Patel)
- 2027-01-18: Finalized rollout windows and SLO thresholds; published.

payload.page_title: Parameterized Endpoint Hinting and Fidelity Bridging Guidelines

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a lightweight, consistent standard for parameterized endpoint hinting (client-supplied signals) and the server-side fidelity-bridging behavior that uses those hints to balance latency, cost, and output quality. The goal is to provide a predictable, testable contract that SDKs and platform components can implement to enable graceful degradation, cost-aware routing, and safe rollouts of new fidelity tiers.

Scope and motivation

- Applies to public and private Redwood inference endpoints that accept narrative/text generation, chat, or structured-response requests.
- Covers: request surface (headers/query/payload hints), server routing decisions, recording telemetry, contract tests, deprecation semantics, and rollout / rollback procedures.
- Motivation: customers and internal services need explicit controls to trade fidelity for latency/cost without opaque behavior or hard failures. This reduces emergent faults where mixed client expectations and runtime capacity produce surprising outputs.

Terminology

- Fidelity hint: optional client-provided signal that expresses a preference for latency/cost vs. quality (e.g., high, balanced, low).
- Bridge variant: a runtime-selected model or config that provides a fidelity tier (for example, quantized small-model, full-precision large-model, cached-prefix-boost).
- Degradation plan: the observable path the service takes when capacity or SLO pressure requires lowering fidelity.

Surface contract (required fields)

All endpoints must accept fidelity hints and a stability header. The server MUST treat the absence of a hint as "balanced" and continue to serve. The canonical names and allowed values are:

| Field | Location | Allowed values | Default | Description |
|-------|----------|----------------|---------|-------------|
| X-Redwood-Fidelity | request header | low, balanced, high | balanced | Client preference for latency vs. output fidelity |
| fidelity_hint | JSON body / top-level | "low"/"balanced"/"high" | balanced | Mirrors header for clients that cannot set headers |
| X-Redwood-Stability | request header | experimental, stable, pinned | stable | Signals client expectation about API/format stability |
| X-Redwood-Return-Variant | request header | variant-id (string) | unset | If provided, server should attempt to route to exact variant or return 412 if incompatible |

(Represented here as a plain-text table; servers should include these names verbatim.)

Behavior rules (server-side)

1. Respect hints: The server SHOULD attempt to honor X-Redwood-Fidelity when selecting a bridge variant. Hints are advisory, not authoritative; servers may choose a higher fidelity than requested but must never silently drop from high to low without telemetry and a routed reason code.
2. Capability negotiation: If a requested fidelity or variant is impossible for the tenant (e.g., regulatory pinning, private deployment constraints), the server must return 412 Precondition Failed with a machine-parsable JSON explaining the allowed options and the owner link. Example:

```json
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "error": "fidelity_not_available",
  "allowed": ["balanced"],
  "message": "Tenant policy pins model to balanced. Contact infra@redwood.example.com for exceptions.",
  "owner": "/teams/eng-serving-runtime"
}
```

3. Deterministic bridging: When routing to a bridge variant because of capacity or cost policies, routing must use deterministic keys (tenant id, request hash, or session id) to avoid flapping across sequential requests in a session.
4. Circuit transparency: If the runtime degrades fidelity due to SLO pressure, the response MUST include the applied_variant and fidelity_reason fields in the response metadata. Example response snippet:

```json
{
  "output": "...",
  "meta": {
    "applied_variant": "gptx-lite-q4_5",
    "fidelity_reason": "slo_pressure::cpu_90pct"
  }
}
```

Telemetry and SLI obligations

- Every request must emit telemetry with dimensions: tenant_id, fidelity_hint, applied_variant, latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, tokens_generated, and fidelity_reason (when applicable).
- SLOs tied to fidelity tiers: each fidelity tier must declare a latency SLO and a quality SLI (see Quality monitoring section). Example: balanced: p95 < 450ms, quality_score >= 0.92 on canonical tests.
- Sampling guidance: For 'low' hints, record 100% of telemetry for the first 72 hours after a new bridge variant is introduced, then reduce to 10% unless anomalies are detected.

Contract testing and SDK expectations

- SDKs must expose an enum for Fidelity {LOW, BALANCED, HIGH} mapped to the header/value strings. SDKs should provide a default of BALANCED.
- Contract tests (run in CI) must include:
  1) Round-trip test asserting that sending fidelity_hint results in either the same applied_variant or a deterministic and documented alternate.
  2) Compatibility test asserting 412 behavior when tenant policy forbids a fidelity.
  3) Telemetry hook test verifying presence of applied_variant and fidelity_reason in response metadata for degraded paths.

Quality monitoring and regression gating

- Each bridge variant must have an associated prompt-suite (subset of the canonical eval harness) and a quality baseline.
- Changes to bridge variants must pass: automated regression checks (no >2% drop in baseline metric) and a manual signoff from the model steward.
- Degradation alerts: if the quality metric for any fidelity tier drops below its baseline by threshold (configurable; default 3%) for a 1-hour window, trigger P1 alert and automatically mark the variant as quarantined for rollback.

Rollout and rollback playbook (high level)

1. Preflight (local + staging): run full contract tests and the variant-specific prompt-suite.
2. Canary release: route 1–5% of traffic using deterministic bucketing tied to tenant or API-key. Monitor fidelity-specific SLIs for 24 hours.
3. Incremental ramp: increase to 20% and then 50% only if no quality/latency regressions.
4. Full release: after 72 hours with stable telemetry, mark variant as default for the target fidelity hint.
5. Hot rollback: on P1 or automated quarantine, switch deterministic routing to previous stable variant and open an incident with the serving-runtime on-call.

Each rollout step must annotate the release with: owner, targeted tenants (if any), monitoring playbook link, and a revert tag. Use the release metadata schema:

```yaml
release_id: r-2026-xxxx
owner: eng-serving-runtime
canary_fraction: 0.01
start_time: 2026-02-01T15:00:00Z
revert_to: gptx-lite-q4_4
notes: "introduce q4_5 for low fidelity to reduce cost for short conversations"
```

Runtime and infra safeguards

- Cost cap: bridge variants labeled "low" must have a budget tag and be subject to daily spend caps enforced by the quota controller.
- Preemption policy: instances running high-fidelity variants must register preemption handlers; during forced preemption the service should attempt to complete in-flight tokens up to a safety cutoff (e.g., 50 tokens) and emit fidelity_reason = "preempt_shutdown".
- Cache-awareness: when applying a cached-prefix-boost as a bridge variant, ensure the cache TTL respects data retention policies and is tagged with the tenant id and prompt-suite hash.

Security and privacy considerations

- Any bridge variant that uses external retrieval or tool-calling must verify tenant authorization for external calls and redact telemetry fields that may contain PII before export.
- For Private deployments, the runtime MUST honor tenant-configured accepted_fidelities and may reject hints that would route traffic outside approved artifact manifests.

Observability: dashboards and alerts (example)

- Dashboard: Fidelity Overview (filters: tenant, variant, hint) showing applied_variant distribution, p95 latency per variant, tokens per request, and quality_metric trendlines.
- Alert examples:
  - fidelity_quarantine_trigger (P1): quality_metric_deviation > 3% for 1h on any fidelity tier.
  - fidelity_unexpected_variant (P2): >0.5% of 'high' hint requests served by 'low' variants without explicit fidelity_reason tag.

Appendices

A. Example request/response (full)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```http
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Content-Type: application/json
X-Redwood-Fidelity: low
X-Redwood-Stability: stable

{
  "model": "text-creative-v2",
  "prompt": "Summarize the release notes in 3 bullet points.",
  "fidelity_hint": "low"
}
```
sections.heading: Request

sections.body:
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "output": "- Released performance improvements.
- Fixed bug in telemetry.
- Improved deployment safety.",
  "meta": {
    "applied_variant": "text-creative-v2-q4_5",
    "fidelity_reason": "slo_pressure::gpu_85pct",
    "latency_ms": 312
  }
}
```

B. Quick CLI checks for on-call
sections.heading: Response (degraded path)

sections.body: ```bash
sections.heading: Run a fidelity-bridge health check against a tenant

sections.body:
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "X-Redwood-Fidelity: low" \
  -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/debug/bridge-health \
  -d '{"tenant_id":"t-1234"}' | jq
```

Interpret output: presence of "quarantined": true indicates the variant is currently blocked.

C. Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: runtime@sre.redwood.example.com)
- Quality steward: applied-ml-and-evals (evals@redwood.example.com)
- Infra quotas: eng-infra (quota-owners@redwood.example.com)

D. Migration notes for clients

- SDKs: add Fidelity enum and expose a client flag `auto_fidelity_fallback` (default true). If set to false, client must handle 412 responses.
- Backwards compatibility: servers must accept legacy header X-RW-F (values numeric 0/1/2) mapping to low/balanced/high for at least 18 months and emit a deprecation header: X-Deprecation-Notice: "X-RW-F is deprecated; use X-Redwood-Fidelity".

E. Open questions (to be reviewed quarterly)

- Should fidelity hints be weighted by account spend tier? (Pros: better UX for premium customers. Cons: coupling billing to model quality.)
- How to standardize quality_score computation across very different prompt suites?

Related pages and references

- See also: contract-driven-client-simulator-and-compat-test-spec (integration with contract tests)
- See also: model-invocation-stability-and-tooling-contract (runtime variant stewardship)

Conformance checklist (copy this into PRs that add a bridge variant)

- [ ] Variant has a prompt-suite and baseline quality metrics
- [ ] Contract tests included in CI
- [ ] Telemetry dims emitted and validated
- [ ] Cost cap and quota tags set
- [ ] Rollout metadata created and linked

Contact and feedback

For feedback or proposed changes, open an issue in the architecture repo and tag @eng-serving-runtime.
