payload.page_title: Contract Oracle and Synthetic Harness Specification

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document specifies the Contract Oracle and Synthetic Harness (COSH) used to validate API and runtime behavior across model rollouts, runtime kernel changes, and client SDK updates. COSH is a lightweight, opinionated test harness that generates deterministic synthetic traffic, exercises contract boundaries, and evaluates observable side effects (metrics, traces, logs) against a versioned oracle.

Scope
-----
- Applies to public API surface area used by customer-facing SDKs (text-generation, chat, embeddings, streaming).
- Includes REST and streaming endpoints, request/response schemas, error and retry semantics, and runtime degradation/fallback behavior.
- Excludes internal infra-only endpoints (admin, billing).

Motivation
----------
We run frequent changes to model variants, quantized kernels, and routing policies. Traditional schema-only contract tests miss behavioral regressions introduced by runtime fallback, early-exit streaming, and probabilistic model outputs. COSH provides:
- An executable oracle that encodes expected behaviour for a set of representative prompts and request patterns.
- Synthetic traffic with controlled randomness and determinism seeds so results are reproducible across CI runs.
- Observability assertions that verify telemetry emission and stability during rollouts.

Definitions
-----------
- Oracle: A versioned artifact (JSON) that contains canonical expectations for a request set: normalized tokens, expected status classes, allowed ranges for numeric scores, and required telemetry labels.
- Harness: The executable runner that replays synthetic workloads against a target environment and evaluates results against an oracle.
- Deterministic seed: A PRNG seed stored with the oracle to reproduce the same tokenization/beam-selection traces for non-deterministic model outputs.

Design Principles
-----------------
- Determinism where possible: use seeds, fixed model weights (when benchmarking), and deterministic tokenizers for oracle generation.
- Lightweight and hermetic: COSH should run in CI as a job that completes in < 20 minutes for core suites and < 90 minutes for extended suites.
- Observability-first: tests assert telemetry (metrics/traces) in addition to payload correctness.
- Progressive coverage: core, extended, and stress tiers to balance CI time and signal quality.

Specification
-------------
1. Oracle format (JSON)
   - metadata: id (sha256), created_at, author, target_api_version, oracle_version
   - tests: list of test cases; each test case is a flat-record with fields: id, description, endpoint, method, request_payload (string), expected_status (one of: success, client_error, server_error, degraded), allowed_response_schema_hashes (list of hashes), numeric_assertions (list of `{metric_name, min, max}`), telemetry_expectations (list of `{span_name, min_count}`), seed (integer)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
     "id": "core-001",
     "description": "short-chat-completion-stable",
     "endpoint": "/v1/chat/completions",
     "method": "POST",
     "request_payload": "{\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Summarize the policy in one sentence.\"}], \"max_tokens\":60}",
     "expected_status": "success",
     "allowed_response_schema_hashes": ["sha256:..."],
     "numeric_assertions": [{"metric_name":"token_count","min":"10","max":"70"}],
     "telemetry_expectations": [{"span_name":"runtime.infer","min_count":"1"}],
     "seed": "42"
   }

2. Harness modes
   - dry-run: validate oracle JSON syntax and schema only.
   - local: run harness against a developer-local environment with mocking options.
   - ci-core: run core test set in CI for each PR touching API surface or runtime.
   - ci-extended: nightly job against canary and staging clusters to catch low-frequency regressions.

3. Test tiers and budget
   - Core tier: 120–200 test cases, CI runtime target < 20m. Failure blocks PR if related files change.
   - Extended tier: 800–2,000 cases, nightly only. Used for regression detection.
   - Stress tier: 10k+ synthetic events, used in dedicated performance pipelines.

4. Assertions and tolerances
   - Exact match assertions allowed for deterministic fields (status codes, JSON schema hashes, top-k token IDs when seeded).
   - Range assertions for numeric metrics (latency_ms, token_count) with annotated SLAs.
   - Telemetry assertions: require presence of critical spans (runtime.dispatch, runtime.infer, api.auth) and dimension labels (model_variant, shard_id, request_class). Missing critical spans marks the test as failed.

Observability contract
----------------------
- Each test run must emit a test-run trace with tag: test.run_id and test.oracle_id. Traces should link to per-request runtime traces via parent/child relationships.
- Metrics to assert in core suite:
  - cosh.test.success_rate (goal >= 99% for core suite in staging)
  - cosh.runtime.infer.latency.p50/p95/p99 (values depend on test profile; see appendix)
  - cosh.telemetry.span_presence (boolean per required span)

CI integration
--------------
1. PR validation:
   - If a change touches any of: api schema, client SDKs, runtime kernel, routing, or model manifests, run ci-core.
   - ci-core failures for changed areas block merge; failures unrelated to changed files produce non-blocking warnings and create a ticket.

2. Nightly pipeline:
   - Run ci-extended against staging and canary. If core success_rate drops by > 2 percentage points vs. previous successful run, auto-open an incident for investigation.

3. Artifact storage:
   - Oracles are stored in the contract-oracle S3 bucket with key pattern: oracles/{target_api_version}/{oracle_id}.json and signed by the author using repo GPG.

Rollout and Canary guidance
---------------------------
1. Canary policy: when rolling a model or runtime change, run the core harness against the canary cluster before traffic ramp. If any core test fails with expected_status != success or missing telemetry spans, abort rollout and trigger rollback.
2. Progressive enablement: if canary passes, run a 2-hour extended run with sampling at 10% traffic in production (metric-driven ramp). Monitor cosh.test.success_rate and cosh.runtime.infer.latency.p95.

Runbook: failed core suite
-------------------------
1. Triage owner: oncall-runtime (pager duty).
2. Immediate steps:
   a. Retrieve last successful oracle id and recent run artifacts from S3.
   b. Compare failed test IDs and diffs in response schema hashes.
   c. If telemetry spans are missing, check tracer agent versions and environment variable injection in deployment.
   d. If numeric assertions violated (latency/token_count), check recent infra events (GPU preemption, autoscale) and routing logs.
3. Escalation:
   - If > 20% core tests failing or success_rate < 90%, page oncall-sre and oncall-infra; treat as Sev2.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- COSH steward: Priya Ramanathan (eng-infrastructure).
- Owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-infra (support for CI and artifacts), eng-dx (SDK integrations).
- Review cadence: core suite and oracle format reviewed quarterly; oracle artifact rotation annually.

Appendix A — Example CLI usage
-----------------------------
sections.heading: Example (excerpt)

sections.body: redwood-cosh validate --oracle s3://oracles/v1/core-2026-01-20.json
sections.heading: validate oracle

sections.body:
redwood-cosh run --oracle s3://oracles/v1/core-2026-01-20.json --target staging --mode ci-core --output results/core-staging-2026-03-08.json

Appendix B — Core test matrix (excerpt)
--------------------------------------
| test_id | endpoint                 | intent                  | key_assertions                  | latency_budget_ms |
|---------|--------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------|
| core-001| /v1/chat/completions     | short summarization     | status=success, span=infer      | 250               |
| core-012| /v1/completions          | streaming long-form     | partial_chunk_count>=3, span=stream.write | 1200         |
| core-024| /v1/embeddings           | vector stability        | vector_dim=1536, cosine_stable >0.95 | 100           |

Notes and limitations
---------------------
- COSH does not attempt to prove semantic equivalence for open-ended generation — we use token-level or schema-level checks with human-in-the-loop for extended validation.
- Oracle maintenance is an operational cost: owners must keep gold samples up-to-date when intentional behavioral changes are introduced.

Change history
--------------
- 2026-01-20: Initial draft by Priya Ramanathan.
- 2026-03-08: Published after review; added CI integration details and failure runbook.

payload.page_title: Sandboxed-extension-and-observability-adaptor-contract

sections.body:
Summary:
This page defines the contract and safe-implementation playbook for third-party or internal runtime extensions that attach to Redwood inference services via a lightweight adaptor (sidecar or plugin). The goal is to allow extensibility (custom routing, enrichers, feature flags, policy checks, and observability hooks) while preserving SLOs, tenant isolation, resource safety, and privacy requirements. This is a cross-cutting standard: it applies to API gateways, runtime sidecars, private deployments, and Hosted API integrations.

Why we need it:
- Demand for custom behavior (enterprise filtering, telemetry enrichment, domain-specific prompt transforms) is increasing.
- Unconstrained extensions risk latency SLOs, telemetry noise, PII leakage, and resource exhaustion.
- We need a repeatable, auditable path that enables safe extension with clear operational controls.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to any component that attaches runtime code to request/response paths in inference services: sidecars, dynamic adapters, SDK-provided middleware, and runtime plugins for Dedicated/Private.
- Excludes build-time model changes and offline data processors (those follow separate artifact provenance and model-onboarding processes).

Principles:
1) Fail-safe: extensions must be isolatable and must never break the base runtime.
2) Resource bounded: CPU, memory, network, and I/O must be capped and observable.
3) Non-blocking: code in extensions cannot block token-generation critical paths beyond a strict tail latency budget.
4) Privacy-aware: default deny for data export; explicit allow-list flows required for PII-sensitive telemetry.
5) Observable and auditable: every extension action must emit typed telemetry and be linkable to a release/owner.

Contract: surface and behavioral guarantees
- API surface: each adaptor exposes a single typed RPC (gRPC/HTTP) entrypoint per request that accepts the canonical request envelope and returns a canonical response envelope. The envelopes are defined as:
  - Request envelope fields (string list): ["request_id", "tenant_id", "model_id", "input_digest", "partial_prompt_hash", "route_metadata"]
  - Response envelope fields (string list): ["decision", "mutations", "annotations", "latency_ms", "extension_trace_id"]
- Latency budget: maximum added tail latency per-adaptor: 15ms p95, 60ms p99. If an adaptor exceeds these by policy it will be hedged/short-circuited.
- Retries/hedging: adaptors must be idempotent for safe retries. Sidecar contract includes an idempotency token.
- Concurrency model: adaptors must support a non-blocking async call pattern. Blocking sync calls are prohibited on token-critical threads.
- Error contract: adaptor errors must map to typed error codes (E_ADAPTOR_TIMEOUT, E_ADAPTOR_MALFORMED, E_ADAPTOR_POLICY_VIOLATION). Error codes are logged and surfaced to tracing with recommended remediation steps.

Safety controls and enforcement layers:
1) Build-time: static linting for prohibited syscall usage, banned dependencies, and license checks.
2) CI gate: integration tests against a synthetic latency harness and privacy regression tests (prompt-scrubbing oracle).
3) Runtime sandboxing: seccomp+namespaces for Linux sidecars, or language-level sandbox (WASM) for plugin runtimes in Hosted offerings.
4) Quotas and throttles: per-tenant adaptor request rate and CPU shares. Default: 50 qps per adaptor per tenant and 5% CPU share on the serving container unless explicitly increased by dedicated contract.
5) Telemetry budget: adaptors may emit a maximum of 10 telemetry events per request path by default; overage is sampled and flagged for review.
6) Egress governance: all external calls from an adaptor must go through the egress proxy and be declared in the adaptor manifest.

Operational requirements (runbook-style):
1) Onboarding steps for a new extension:
   1.1) Submit extension manifest (schema below) to the Extensions Registry.
   1.2) Run local integration against the Synthetic Token Load harness (see CLI commands).
   1.3) Pass CI static analysis and privacy lint.
   1.4) Security review (automated + manual) and test deployment to canary namespace.
   1.5) 72-hour canary with telemetry and SLO gates.
2) Incident flow when an adaptor violates SLOs:
   2.1) Automated detection triggers hedging: runtime replaces adaptor call with cached default or bypass.
   2.2) Pager duty: alert to owning team and runtime-sre.
   2.3) Immediate mitigation: throttle adaptor traffic to 0% for the offending tenant or globally, based on severity.
   2.4) Post-incident: forensic trace review, root cause, and mandatory fix window (7 days for critical violations).

Extension manifest (example YAML):
| field | meaning | required | example |
|------|---------:|:-------:|--------:|
| name | unique adaptor id | yes | domain-filter-v2 |
| owner | owning team | yes | customer-solutions |
| runtime | sandbox runtime target (wasm|container) | yes | wasm |
| exposures | allowed external hosts | conditional | [api.example.com] |
| telemetry_budget | max events/request | no (default 10) | 8 |
| resource_limits | cpu,memory | yes | cpu:0.05,memory:128Mi |

Example manifest (YAML snippet):
---
name: domain-filter-v2
owner: customer-solutions
runtime: wasm
exposures: ["s3.amazonaws.com"]
telemetry_budget: 8
resource_limits: "cpu:0.05,memory:128Mi"
---

CLI quickcheck harness (examples):
- Run the synthetic latency harness against local adaptor:
  ./dev/tools/adaptor-harness --manifest=./manifests/domain-filter-v2.yaml --rps=100 --duration=60s
- Check audit and trace consistency:
  ./dev/tools/trace-assert --trace-prefix=adaptor:domain-filter-v2 --max-tail=60ms

Telemetry and observability:
- Required traces: each adaptor-augmented request must include extension_trace_id and adaptor.version tag.
- Metrics to emit (per adaptor): adaptor.latency_ms.p95, adaptor.latency_ms.p99, adaptor.error_rate, adaptor.telemetry_events_per_request.
- Dashboards: standard adaptor overview dashboard (per-tenant filter) and global adaptor-safety heatmap.
- SLOs: adaptors are covered by the parent service SLO. We maintain an adaptor-specific SLA for Dedicated/Private customers where adaptors recommended latency allocation is configurable.

Security review checklist (summary):
- No outbound IPs that aren’t declared in manifest and allowed via egress proxy.
- No write access to persistent model KV unless explicitly requested and approved.
- Secrets: adaptor must not include embedded secrets; use service-managed provisioning.
- Signed artifact: manifest must reference a signed bundle (SHA256) and a verifiable release tag.

Compatibility and versioning:
- Adaptor API versioning: major.minor semantic versioning required. Major version changes require explicit contract compatibility tests and staged rollout.
- Downgrade policy: runtime prevents automatic rollbacks to older adaptor majors without an owner-approved migration plan.

Metrics and acceptance gates for rollout:
- p95 tail added latency <= 12ms for target traffic mix.
- error_rate <= 0.1% for adaptor returns.
- telemetry_events_per_request <= declared budget.
- no PII-exfiltration alerts in the privacy oracle run.

Related pages and references:
- link: architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/egress-proxy-and-tenant-egress-policy (see egress governance)
- link: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/adaptive-kv-coordinator-and-eviction-contract-2026 (for KV access patterns)

Appendix: enforcement matrix (policy -> enforcement):
- Unauthorized external call -> egress proxy block + alert -> runtime eviction if repeated
- Latency breach -> hedging + telemetry create incident -> owner throttle -> rollback
- Excess telemetry -> sampling applied + owner notified -> manual quota increase request

Ownership and stewardship:
- Primary owner: runtime-platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.example.com)
- Security reviewer: infra-security team
- Extensions registry: platform-tools team

Open questions (to be decided in follow-up ADR):
- Default telemetry sampling strategies per-tenant versus global.
- Fine-grained budget negotiation API for enterprise tenants in Dedicated offering.

Change history:
- 2025-11-12: initial draft by Priya Desai.
- 2026-01-15: added WASM runtime guidance (reviewers: Ethan Park).
- 2026-03-02: tightened latency budgets and egress governance notes (published).

Please review this contract for inclusion in the runtime onboarding checklist and extension registry automation. For questions, contact the runtime-platform owners or add to the next architecture SIG meeting agenda.

payload.page_title: Streaming Error Taxonomy and Retry Contract

sections.body:
Overview:
This page defines a company-wide error taxonomy and client-facing retry contract specifically for streaming endpoints (server-sent events, HTTP/2/gRPC streaming, and chunked streaming). It supplements existing API compatibility and typed-error guidelines by focusing on streaming-specific failure modes, resume semantics, and SLO-safe retry behavior. The goal is to make client behaviour predictable, reduce unnecessary load from aggressive retries, and provide observability hooks that map streaming errors to operational responses and SLIs.

Audience:
- API owners and backend engineers implementing streaming endpoints
- Client SDK authors and integrators
- SRE and monitoring owners responsible for SLIs/alerting

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all external-facing streaming endpoints and internal long-lived RPC streams used for inference (chat, generation streams, long-poll embeddings).
- Does NOT replace general HTTP status conventions; it augments them with stream-level semantics, resume tokens, and partial-result handling.

Key principles:
1) Explicit classification: every stream-termination event must be classified using a canonical "stream_error_type" (see table below) and include a machine-readable error payload in the final frame or trailing metadata.
2) Idempotency + resume: where feasible, streams must support resume tokens or sequence checkpoints that allow clients to retry without reprocessing already-delivered tokens.
3) Backpressure-aware retries: retry guidance must be safe for SLOs—clients should use exponential backoff with jitter and obey service-supplied Retry-After or Rate-Hint headers when present.
4) Observability linkage: every error must correlate to a set of telemetry fields (trace id, stream id, shard, kernel-version, model-variant) to enable triage and automated alerts.

Canonical stream error taxonomy (summary table):
| stream_error_type | HTTP/gRPC mapping | Meaning | Client action (default) | SRE severity |
|-------------------|-------------------|---------|-------------------------|--------------|
| TRANSIENT_NETWORK | 502/503/gRPC UNAVAILABLE | Network hiccup; partial frames may be lost | Retry with resume token if present, otherwise backoff & restart | P2 |
| RATE_LIMITED | 429/gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED | Service is overloaded or rate quota exceeded | Honor Retry-After/Rate-Hint; exponential backoff; consider degrading quality | P2 |
| PARTIAL_RESULT_CANCELLED | 499/gRPC CANCELLED | Client or network closed mid-stream; server stopped delivery | Do not retry automatically; client may resume if token available | P3 |
| MODEL_DEGRADATION | 200 + application error / gRPC OK + payload error | Server returned lower-quality output or switched to a degraded variant | Best-effort retry to higher-quality variant (respecting cost), or surface to user | P3 |
| CHECKPOINT_MISMATCH | 400/gRPC INVALID_ARGUMENT | Resume token invalid or sequence gap detected | Full restart from start; surface error to client | P1 |
| INTERNAL_FT | 500/gRPC INTERNAL | Server runtime failure (kernel crash, OOM) | Retry with exponential backoff; if repeated, fail and surface | P1 |
| AUTHZ_DENIED | 401/403/gRPC PERMISSION_DENIED | Authentication/authorization failure | Do not retry; require token refresh or user action | P1 |
| STREAM_TIMEOUT | 504/gRPC DEADLINE_EXCEEDED | Stream exceeded server-imposed idle or total time | Restart with shorter client-side timeout; do not infinite-repeat | P2 |

Detailed contract for clients:
1) Error payload shape
- All streaming close frames or trailing metadata MUST include a JSON object under the key "x-stream-error" (or gRPC trailing metadata key "x-stream-error-bin" for binary) with this flat schema: {
  "stream_error_type": "<one of canonical types>",
  "message": "human-friendly explanation",
  "resume_token": "<opaque-token>" (optional),
  "retry_after_seconds": "<int>" (optional),
  "request_id": "<internal-request-id>"
}
- Example (HTTP chunked):
  {"x-stream-error": "{\"stream_error_type\": \"TRANSIENT_NETWORK\", \"message\": \"connection reset by peer\", \"resume_token\": \"rt:abc123\", \"request_id\": \"req-2026-01-17-42\"}"}

2) Resume semantics
- Resume token semantics: a resume token encodes the last-delivered sequence position for the stream and is opaque to the client. It MUST be safe to replay the request from that point without duplication of side-effects on the backend (idempotency).
- Server obligations when providing a resume_token:
  a) retain the minimal replay window for at least 2 minutes past token issuance by default (configurable per service)
  b) include in telemetry: resume_token, retention-window, and token-ttl at issuance time
- Client obligations:
  a) if resume_token present, attempt at most 3 resume attempts with exponential backoff (base 200ms, max 5s), unless server sends explicit retry_after_seconds > 0.
  b) if resume fails due to CHECKPOINT_MISMATCH, perform a full restart and surface to user.

3) Retry budget and SLO safety
- Clients must incorporate a retry budget to avoid cascading retries: no more than 5% extra requests per-minute per-caller beyond normal traffic for automated retries. This is a soft limit; platform may return RATE_LIMITED to enforce.
- Internal SRE rule: automated client retries that cause 10% increase in tail latency or 3x increase in queue depth trigger alert and automatic throttling of resume responses.

4) Idempotency and side-effects
- Streaming endpoints that can trigger server-side side-effects must publish whether the stream is "idempotent" in the initial handshake (response header "X-Stream-Idempotent: true/false").
- If not idempotent, clients must avoid blind retries and require explicit user confirmation or server-provided safe-retry markers.

5) Backoff algorithm (recommended)
- Use decorrelated jittered exponential backoff:
  wait = min(max_backoff, base * 2^attempt) * random(0.5, 1.5)
  where base = 200ms, max_backoff = 5000ms, attempts <= 5.
- If server includes retry_after_seconds, add that to the computed wait and respect it as a floor.

6) Quality fallback strategies
- If MODEL_DEGRADATION is signaled, server MAY include the active variant and a suggested lower-cost variant in the error payload. Client options:
  a) surface degraded output with UI hint; do not retry automatically;
  b) call an explicit "regenerate" with higher quality variant if user requests and the client can pay.

Observability and telemetry requirements:
- Every terminal event for a stream must emit metrics and traces with these fields: stream_id, request_id, user_id (if available), model_variant, kernel_build, node_shard, stream_error_type, resume_token_present (bool), duration_ms, bytes_sent, bytes_received.
- SLIs to track (per-service and per-model-variant):
  - streaming_success_rate (target: 99.5% p99 over 1h)
  - resume_success_rate (target: 99% p95 over 24h)
  - incremental_retries_due_to_network (target: <0.5% of requests)
  - tail_stream_latency_p99 (service-specific budgets; default 2.5s for single-response-turn streams)

Testing, verification, and rollout checklist:
1) Unit tests: error payload is emitted and parsable for all close paths.
2) Integration tests: simulate network drop, partial frames, and CHECKPOINT_MISMATCH to verify client behavior in SDK tests.
3) Load tests: measure impact of retries under 2x, 5x failure scenarios and assert tail latency remains within budget when retries occur.
4) Canary rollout: enable streaming error payloads on a narrow user segment (5% traffic) for 72h, monitor resume_success_rate and streaming_success_rate.
5) Gradual expansion: 5% -> 25% -> 75% -> 100% with 24h observation windows and automated rollback on SLO degradation.

Runbook excerpts (for SRE):
- Symptom: large spike in TRANSIENT_NETWORK closures
  1) Query traces for stream_error_type = TRANSIENT_NETWORK and filter by node_shard.
  2) If >5% of streams in last 5m originate from a single shard, evacuate shard and check recent kernel_release changes.
  3) If resume tokens are present but resume_success_rate < 90%, extend token retention window temporarily and eject suspect kernel build.

- Symptom: elevated CHECKPOINT_MISMATCH errors
  1) Identify latest schema or checkpoint encoding changes via artifact release logs.
  2) If change is recent, roll back the release to previous artifact and escalate to runtime team.

Implementation recipes and examples:
- Example streaming close header (HTTP chunked):
  Trailer: x-stream-error
  x-stream-error: {"stream_error_type":"RATE_LIMITED","message":"burst quota exceeded","retry_after_seconds":30,"request_id":"req-2026-01-21-11"}

- Example gRPC trailing metadata (pseudo):
  grpc-status: 8
  x-stream-error-bin: <base64(json-payload)>

- Example client pseudo-code for resume attempt:
  1) onStreamClose(meta):
     if meta.x-stream-error.resume_token:
       for attempt in 1..3:
         wait(randomized_backoff(attempt))
         resp = openStream({resumeToken: meta.resume_token})
         if resp.ok: attach and continue
       surface "Resume failed" and fall back to full restart
     else: full restart or surface to user

Enforcement and governance:
- API gate: all streaming endpoints must implement the x-stream-error payload by Q3 2026. Non-compliant services will be flagged by the nightly API conformance job.
- SDKs: official Redwood SDKs will implement default retry logic conforming to this contract; third-party clients are encouraged but not forced to use SDKs.
- Auditing: Weekly reports will summarize top stream_error_types by service and client platform; Product and SRE will review during the reliability sync.

Ownership and contacts:
- Specification owner: Priya Natarajan (eng/platform)
- Runtime/implementation owner: Runtime Team (eng-serving-runtime) – primary contact: Ethan Park
- Observability owner: Platform SRE – primary contact: Marta Silva
- Rollout coordinator: Product Infrastructure – Samira Ahmed

Appendix: change log
- 2025-09-17: Drafted initial taxonomy and payload schema (Priya).
- 2025-11-10: Added resume token retention and TTL guidance (Ethan).
- 2026-02-08: Finalized SLI targets and rollout checklist; changed base backoff to 200ms (Marta).

References:
- API compatibility and deprecation policy (see related_pages)
- Partial result checkpointing and client resume playbook (see related_pages)

Feedback and revision process:
- Send suggested edits as PRs to the spec repo and include a short impact note. Major changes (affecting client retry behavior or resume semantics) require reviewers from Runtime, SRE, and SDK teams and a two-week review period.

payload.page_title: Client Backpressure, Hedging, and Timeout Standards

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines Redwood's cross-cutting standards for client-side backpressure, request hedging (duplicate/backup requests), timeouts, and related retry/circuit-breaker behaviour. The goal is to ensure predictable latency, protect model-serving capacity, avoid cascading failures across services, and provide consistent telemetry for SLOs and incident response. These standards apply to: Redwood public-facing APIs, internal microservices, Redwood Dedicated control planes, and any Private deployment agent code maintained by Redwood.

Motivation and scope
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Spikes in upstream latency causing large retry storms and cascading capacity exhaustion.
- Client libraries with inconsistent default timeouts/hedging leading to unpredictable tail latency.
- Lack of uniform metrics makes it hard to distinguish client-side timeouts from server-side throttling in alerts.
sections.heading: Observed issues (motivation)

sections.body:
- All HTTP/gRPC clients in Redwood-managed services and official SDKs.
- Edge proxies and API gateways (as the first line of defense).
- Model-serving request paths where per-token latency can amplify resource impact.

Definitions

- Backpressure: Mechanisms by which a client (or proxy) limits the rate at which it sends requests to a downstream service.
- Hedging (backup requests): Sending a duplicate request to an alternate replica/region after a short delay to reduce tail latency.
- Timeout: Maximum wall-clock time a caller waits for a response before giving up.
- Retry: Resending a request after a failure; distinct from hedging because retry is triggered after failure, hedging proactively sends duplicates.
- Circuit breaker: State machine that stops attempts to a target when error rates/timeouts exceed thresholds.

Standards (overview)

1) Default timeout and deadline policy
- Public SDKs and internal clients MUST set a default per-request deadline for user-facing generation endpoints: 15 seconds for short completions (<=512 tokens), 45 seconds for long completions (>512 tokens). These defaults can be overridden by developer intent via explicit call parameters.
- Internal control/management plane APIs (e.g., model upload, rollout control) MAY use longer defaults (120s) but should document the reason.

Rationale: Model generation has high variance; explicit defaults prevent indefinite waits and make downstream capacity planning tractable.

2) Hedging policy (when to use backup requests)
- Hedging SHOULD only be enabled in high-SLA, read-heavy, stateless query paths where duplicate execution is cheap (e.g., embedding, retrieval, short-chat queries).
- Hedging SHALL NOT be enabled for any state-changing endpoints (e.g., billing operations, provisioning, annotation ingestion) unless idempotency guarantees and duplicate-suppression are implemented.
- Hedge delay default: 50th percentile p50_latency * 0.6, bounded to [25ms, 200ms]. Example: if p50=200ms, hedge delay=120ms.
- Max outstanding hedged duplicates per client: 1 (i.e., one backup request only).

3) Retry policy (after explicit failure)
- Favor exponential backoff with jitter. Default retry window: up to 3 attempts (initial + 2 retries). Backoff base: 100ms, multiplier: 2x, max backoff: 1.6s. Add randomized jitter of +/-20%.
- Retries are only allowed for idempotent or safe-to-retry endpoints (GET/embeddings status checks). For non-idempotent endpoints, return the original error to caller and surface guidance.

4) Circuit breakers and failure-domain mapping
- Each downstream dependency MUST have a circuit-breaker configuration in the client wrapper with the following default thresholds:
  - Rolling window: 60s
  - Request volume threshold: 50
  - Error ratio trip threshold: 25%
  - Reset timeout (half-open check): 30s
- Circuit breakers must be tagged with service and failure-domain (region, availability-zone, model-variant) for observability.

5) Backpressure signals and client-side queuing
- Clients MUST expose an admission control limit (max_in_flight) to avoid unbounded request spikes. Defaults: 200 concurrent short requests per client process; 50 concurrent long-generation requests per client process.
- When admission limit is reached, clients MUST return 429 to local callers with Retry-After header, rather than queuing indefinitely. Internal SDKs should provide a configurable in-process queue with a bounded TTL (default 2s) that returns 429 if full.

6) API contract and headers
- To aid observability and coordinated throttling, clients MUST propagate these headers on every request:
  - X-Request-Deadline: absolute RFC3339 timestamp of deadline
  - X-Client-Max-In-Flight: configured max_in_flight value
  - X-Hedge-Attempt: 0/1 (0 for primary, 1 for hedged replica)
  - X-Caller-Id: internal caller/team id
- Servers SHOULD honor X-Request-Deadline for graceful cancellation and should return X-Observed-Processing-Time in the response for debugging.

Telemetry and SLO integration
sections.heading: Scope (applies to)

sections.body:
- client.requests_total{outcome=success|timeout|error|hedged_success} (counter)
- client.latency_ms{quantile} (histogram/summary)
- client.in_flight (gauge)
- client.hedge_attempts_total (counter)
- client.retry_attempts_total (counter)
- client.circuit_open{target} (gauge boolean)
sections.heading: Metrics (per client and per upstream target)

sections.body:
- P95 latency increase > 2x baseline for 10m -> P1 alert to owning service.
- Circuit breaker opens for more than 3 consecutive reset windows -> P1.
- Ratio of hedged_success / success > 0.2 sustained for 30m -> investigate upstream tail latency.

Tracing and logs

- Every request SHOULD include a trace span with tags: service.target, model.variant, hedge=0/1, request.deadline. Hedged requests must share a parent trace id with the primary and set the attribute hedged=true for the backup attempt.
- Logs should record per-request decision points: admission drop, hedge launched, retry attempted, circuit breaker state change. Include request id and caller id.

Configuration examples
sections.heading: Standard alerting thresholds (examples)

sections.body:
---
client:
  max_in_flight:
    short: 200
    long: 50
  timeouts:
    short_default_ms: 15000
    long_default_ms: 45000
  hedging:
    enabled: true
    enabled_for: ["embedding", "query"]
    max_duplicates: 1
    hedge_delay_strategy: "p50*0.6"
  retries:
    max_attempts: 3
    base_backoff_ms: 100
    multiplier: 2
    max_backoff_ms: 1600
  circuit_breaker:
    window_s: 60
    volume_threshold: 50
    error_ratio: 0.25
    reset_s: 30
---
sections.heading: Example client YAML configuration (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
// JavaScript pseudo-code using Redwood SDK
const resp = await redwood.client.generate({
  model: 'openlm/c30-xxl',
  prompt: 'Summarize quarterly revenue',
  timeoutMs: 20000, // overrides default for this call
  hedging: { enabled: true }
});

Edge / API gateway rules

- API gateways (Envoy/Traefik) MUST enforce a hard request timeout no greater than the client's deadline + 1s to avoid proxy-induced indefinite waits.
- Gateways SHOULD emit a standardized client timeout response body with fields: request_id, original_deadline, observed_processing_time_ms, and recommended_retry_after_seconds.

Testing and rollout guidelines

1) Unit and integration tests
- Client libraries MUST include unit tests that validate header propagation, deadline cancellation, and hedging metrics.
- Integration test harnesses should include a fault-injection mode (inject artificial 95th-percentile latency at upstream) and validate: hedging launches, duplicate suppression for stateful endpoints, and circuit-breaker behavior.

2) Canary rollout checklist for enabling hedging in a service
- Start with hedging disabled.
- Canary 1: 1% traffic, observability only (do not hedge; emit metric as if hedging occurred). Duration: 24 hours.
- Canary 2: 5% traffic, hedging enabled against cold standby replica; run 48 hours. Monitor hedged_success ratio, error rates, and downstream CPU/GPU utilization.
- Canary 3: 25% traffic, full observability and throttling. Duration: 72 hours. If hedged_success>0.2 or downstream utilization increases >15% without latency improvement, rollback.

Operational playbook (runbook excerpt)
sections.heading: SDK usage example (pseudo-code)

sections.body:
1) Identify top clients by client.caller_id and top targets by service.target.
2) Check admission drops (client.in_flight at limit). If admission triggered: scale clients horizontally OR adjust max_in_flight short-term with caution.
3) If hedged_success ratio is high and circuits are opening upstream, reduce hedging traffic by toggling hedging.enabled_for to a smaller subset.
4) If circuit-breakers remain open after multiple reset windows, escalate to owning service and consider temporary capacity boost for critical model variants.

Ownership and exceptions

- Owning teams: client-side library owners (SDK team) are primary for defaults. Each service owns its local configuration and must declare deviations in service README.
- Exceptions: Any deviation from defaults (timeouts, hedge enabled for non-stateless endpoints) requires an ADR filed in architecture-and-standards/decision-records and approval from the Observability and Serving Runtime owners. Submit exceptions via PR to this directory with the same metadata envelope.

Security and privacy considerations

- Hedging duplicates must not leak ephemeral credentials or secrets to additional targets. All credentials must be fetched from safe stores per request, and hedged requests must use the same credential context as the primary.

Decision log (summary of why this policy exists)

- 2025-09: Postmortem for incident INF-2025-09 identified retries and missing client deadlines as primary contributors to cascading GPU exhaustion.
- 2025-10: Experimentation showed hedging reduces P99 by up to 30% in queries but increases total token compute by 8% when broadly enabled. Therefore hedging is limited to stateless read paths and bounded duplicates.

Appendix: Quick reference table

| Area | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Short request timeout | 15s | <=512 tokens, SDK default |
| Long request timeout | 45s | >512 tokens |
| Hedge delay | p50*0.6 (min 25ms, max 200ms) | 1 backup max |
| Max in-flight short | 200 | per client process |
| Circuit breaker window | 60s | volume threshold 50, error ratio 25% |

Related reading

- RFC: Hedging and backup requests in high-scale RPC systems (internal link)
- Load-shedding and graceful degradation patterns (internal playbook)
- Observability SLI catalog (for metric names and dashboards)

Contact and ownership

For questions or to propose changes: contact Maya Patel (owner) or the SDK team slack channel (#sdk-developers).

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: Created by Maya Patel (initial draft).
- 2025-12-08: Updated hedging bounds after experiments (reviewers: Ethan Zhao).
- 2026-02-18: Clarified header contract and added API gateway guidance (reviewers: Rashmi Verma, Luis Ortega).

payload.page_title: Cross-service contract and schema evolution playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines a pragmatic, enforceable process for defining, validating, evolving, and retiring cross-service JSON/HTTP contracts used across Redwood inference stacks (API gateways, routing proxies, runtime sidecars, and model-serving endpoints). It consolidates requirements from API standards, model-serving stability, and infra rollout constraints into a single reference engineers can follow to avoid breaking production dependencies.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Multiple services (frontend SDKs, edge proxies, routing layers, runtime backends) share contract expectations. Uncoordinated schema changes cause silent regressions, billing anomalies, and latency regressions.
- Model-serving contracts are particularly brittle: small output-schema changes can break downstream batching, caching, and metric extraction.
- A clear, automated evolution path reduces outage risk and speeds feature delivery.
sections.heading: Why this matters

sections.body:
- Scope: JSON-based request/response schemas, streaming payload envelopes, header-level contract metadata, and client-server compatibility semantics.
- Applies to: all services under the Redwood inference surface (hosted API, Dedicated, Private runtime sidecars, and console integrations).
- Excludes: internal-only feature flags not exposed via APIs, and binary model artifact formats (handled by model-artifact-provenance).
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- Contract: signed expectation describing request/response shapes and semantics.
- Producer: service that emits the schema (e.g., model-serving runtime).
- Consumer: service that depends on the schema (e.g., aggregator, billing).
- Minor-compatible change: additive, non-breaking (new optional property).
- Major-incompatible change: removes/renames/changes semantics of fields.
sections.heading: Key terminology

sections.body:
- id: stable contract identifier (reverse-dns style), e.g. com.redwood.model.response.v1
- version: semver-like token: MAJOR.MINOR (we disallow patch-level; patch used for implementation only)
- description: single-sentence intent
- producer: service owner team
- schema: JSON Schema draft-07 compatible object (stringified in the contract manifest)
- compatibility: "backward" | "forward" | "none"
- lifecycle: draft | published | deprecated | retired

Example contract manifest (contract.json):
{
  "id": "com.redwood.runtime.model-output",
  "version": "1.2",
  "description": "Structured generation output for text-completion endpoints",
  "producer": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "compatibility": "backward",
  "lifecycle": "published",
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "request_id": {"type": "string"},
      "tokens": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
      "score": {"type": "number"},
      "metadata": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}
    },
    "required": ["request_id", "tokens"]
  }
}
sections.heading: Contract format (required fields)

sections.body:
1) Schema linting: all contract manifests must pass the contract-lint ruleset (see repo: infra/contract-lint).
   - Command (CI): ./tools/contract-lint --path contracts/ --require-ids
2) Consumer-driven tests: every consumer must publish a minimal fixture and acceptance test referencing contract id+version.
   - Example (pytest): tests/test_contract_compat.py asserts runtime output validates against contract schema.
3) Contract signing: when publishing MAJOR version bumps, producer must create a signed change note and an ADR referencing impact assessment. CI will block merging until signoff.
4) Canary validation: new MAJOR versions require a 7-day canary with traffic-scoped routes (see rollout steps).
sections.heading: Validation and CI gates

sections.body:
- Additive fields: allowed if marked optional in schema and documented.
- Field renames: forbidden without a MAJOR bump and migration plan.
- Type changes: forbidden (MAJOR required).
- Moving nested fields: requires compatibility proof and consumer test adjustments.
- Header-level contract hints (x-contract-version) must be included on cross-cluster calls.
sections.heading: Backward/forward compatibility rules (short checklist)

sections.body:
1) Design: Producer drafts new contract manifest and a brief compatibility assessment (1–2 pages). Attach to PR.
2) Consumer discovery: run static graph analysis to list consumers (command: ./tools/contract-graph --id com.redwood.runtime.model-output).
3) Consumer opt-in tests: each consumer adds an opt-in test fixture for new version and runs smoke tests in staging.
4) Canary publish: producer publishes new version to canary deployment namespace. Expose via a canary header: "x-contract-canary: <version>".
5) Monitoring window (7 days): monitor SLI deltas (errors, invalid-schema, p50/p95 latency) and business metrics (cost per token, billing noise). Use Redwood Console prehook dashboard: /dashboards/contract-canary.
6) Gradual ramp: if no regressions, increase traffic 5x per day until 100%. If regressions are detected, automatically revert with the canary rollback job.
7) Publish: mark lifecycle=published and update contract index. Notify consumer teams via email/Slack with migration checklist.
sections.heading: Rollout and migration procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Contract validation failures: target < 0.01% of requests after 24h of GA.
- Schema-invalid responses (downstream): alert if > 0.05% sustained for 30m.
- Latency delta attributable to contract change: p95 increase <= 15% or require rollback.
sections.heading: SLOs and telemetry (what to monitor)

sections.body:
- contract.id, contract.version, validation.status (ok|invalid), validation.reason, request_id, route
- consumer-side metric: contract.validate.success ratio and consumer.fallback.count

Ownership, exceptions, and decision gates:
- Contract steward: the producer service owner is the primary steward and approver for minor changes.
- Cross-team major changes require: (a) owner-team signoff; (b) consumer-team acknowledgement; (c) infra SRE review; (d) product-impact assessment.
- Exceptions: short-lived experimental fields are allowed under lifecycle=draft and must include an explicit TTL and owner. Experimental contracts must not be used by production consumers without a feature-flagged opt-in.
sections.heading: Telemetry to emit (producer)

sections.body:
| Contract id | Current version | Consumers (team) | Allowed change class | Notes |
| com.redwood.runtime.model-output | 1.2 | console-ingest (eng-platform), billing (finance), deduper (eng-serving-runtime) | minor-additions | avoid adding top-level new property named "tokens" |

Operational playbook for incident response to contract breakages:
1) Pager alert triggers: "contract.validation.rate" fires.
2) Run: ./tools/contract-inspect --id <contract> --since 10m to enumerate failing payloads.
3) If root cause is producer: rollback to previous contract implementation and/or toggle compatibility shim in gateway.
4) If root cause is consumer: implement graceful fallback, update consumer parsing, and request staged deploy.
5) Postmortem: update contract manifest with discovered gaps and record remediation steps in regression-triage.

Appendix A — Minimal CI YAML (example):
name: Contract CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: ./tools/contract-lint --path contracts/
  consumer-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: pytest tests/ --contract-id ${{ inputs.contract_id }}

Appendix B — Small compatibility checklist for reviewers:
- Is the change additive? If yes, mark minor.
- Are all consumers discovered and fixture-tested?
- Are telemetry keys present?
- Is there a fallback path for invalid payloads?
- Is the rollout plan and SLA window specified?
sections.heading: Compatibility matrix (example)

sections.body:
- canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025 (schema linting rules)
- runtime-cache-invalidation-and-staleness-mitigation-playbook-2026 (cache implications)
- regression-triage/runbook (post-incident workflow)
sections.heading: Related pages and references

sections.body:
- Primary steward: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com)
- Playbook author: Ethan Liu (ethan.liu@redwood.example.com)
- Questions and change requests: open PRs against infra/contracts/ with reviewer tag @api-standards.
sections.heading: Contact & ownership

sections.body:
- 2024-11-05: initial draft authored.
- 2025-03-18: added canary traffic ramp and telemetry keys after incident review.
- 2025-07-12: clarified lifecycle states and enabled signed-major-change gate.

payload.page_title: Service Interoperability Accord and Runtime Handshake

sections.body: This document defines the Service Interoperability Accord (SIA) — a cross-cutting API and runtime standard for how Redwood services (API gateway, routing plane, model proxies, and downstream composition services) negotiate request semantics, exchange capability metadata, and execute graceful fallbacks. The goal is predictable composability of inference and post-processing pipelines while keeping latency and cost within budgeted SLOs.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Scope: API-level headers, request/response envelope, schema negotiation, runtime handshake sequence, observability annotations, cost attribution fields, and fallback/degeneration policies.
- Audience: API authors, runtime engineers, infra architects, SRE, and platform/SDK teams implementing clients or service adapters.
sections.heading: Scope and audience

sections.body: As Redwood grows the number of interdependent services that perform inference, transformation, and enrichment, inconsistent assumptions about schemas, retry semantics, and capability signals have led to: increased tail latency, poor cost attribution, silent degradation of output quality, and brittle rollouts. SIA provides a single-mode-of-behavior for cross-service interactions to avoid these issues.
sections.heading: Motivation and problem statement

sections.body:
1) Explicit capability discovery: every service exposing model-backed behavior advertises a capability manifest (schema, max_tokens, supports_streaming, quality_tier).
2) Minimal handshake latency: negotiation must complete within a bounded add-on (default 5ms) to request path.
3) Cost-aware routing: routing decisions must consider estimated token cost and configured budget tags.
4) Observable causality: every request carries a lineage envelope for cross-stack correlation and billing.
5) Deterministic fallback paths: fallback rules are declared and versioned with the service contract.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1) Client -> Edge/Gateway: Submit request with preliminary intent envelope and headers (see "Headers and envelope" below). Gateway performs quick capability match against model catalog and assigns request route.
2) Gateway -> Runtime Mediator: Runtime Mediator performs a capability handshake (capability-query) with candidate model proxies that returns explicit runtime attributes and an acceptance token.
3) Gateway -> Selected Proxy: Final request forwarded with acceptance token and immutable route context. If acceptance token is rejected or times out, a deterministic fallback route is used.
sections.heading: Handshake sequence (3-step canonical path)

sections.body:
Use HTTP/REST examples. All headers prefixed with X-RW- unless otherwise noted.
- X-RW-Request-Id: (required) UUID, top-level request ID propagated across services.
- X-RW-Trace: (required) W3C traceparent.
- X-RW-Capability-Intent: (required) short token key representing desired capability set (e.g., "chat:structured-output:v2").
- X-RW-Region-Hint: (optional) region preference for routing (e.g., "us-west-2").
- X-RW-Cost-Budget-Tag: (optional) budget key for cost attribution (e.g., "marketing-bot:low").
- X-RW-Acceptance-Token: (set by mediator) cryptographic token proving capability match.
- Content-Type: application/redwood+json; version=2026-01 (required for schema negotiation).

Capability manifest (example JSON snippet—must be published in service registry):
{
  "capability_id": "chat-structured-output:v2",
  "max_input_tokens": "8192",
  "supports_streaming": "true",
  "quality_tier": "standard",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "response_schema": "https://internal.schema.redwood.com/chat/structured-output-v2"
}
sections.heading: Headers and envelope (required/optional)

sections.body:
- Clients must specify desired response schema version via Content-Type parameter or the X-RW-Requested-Schema header.
- Runtime must validate incoming request against the declared input schema. Invalid requests return 422 with error details and schema diff id header (X-RW-Schema-Diff).
- Schema evolution rules: additive changes are allowed across minor versions; breaking changes require a major version bump and coordination via the registry and a 30-day deprecation window.
sections.heading: Schema negotiation and versioning

sections.body:
All model-backed endpoints must publish a fallback graph that describes prioritized fallback nodes and degradation semantics. The runtime implements the graph as a deterministic state machine.
- Fallback levels (examples):
  - level_0: primary model (low latency, high cost)
  - level_1: reduced-context variant (quantized, fewer tokens)
  - level_2: cached prefix response (if applicable)
  - level_3: rule-based template response (last resort)
sections.heading: Fallback and degradation contract

sections.body:
1) If acceptance token not returned within handshake_deadline (default 50ms), attempt level_1.
2) If runtime returns 5xx or OOM, initiate level_2 where applicable.
3) If fallback step cannot satisfy output schema, emit structured degraded response with "degradation_reason" field and an SLO-impact tag.
sections.heading: Failure rules (ordered)

sections.body:
- Metric names (standardized):
  - rw.requests.total (counter, tags: service, capability_id, budget_tag)
  - rw.requests.latency_ms (histogram, tags: service, capability_id)
  - rw.fallbacks.count (counter, tags: service, fallback_level, reason)
  - rw.cost.estimated_tokens (gauge, tags: service, model_variant)
- Traces must include span attributes: rw.capability_id, rw.fallback_level, rw.estimated_token_count, rw.cost_budget_tag.
- Logs: structured JSON with request_id and a field "decision_path" showing handshake/matching/fallback steps.
sections.heading: Observability requirements (what to emit)

sections.body:
- 95th pctl end-to-end latency (gateway -> final response): <= 250ms for interactive capabilities (quality_tier==standard)
- Handshake additional latency (mediator): <= 5ms p95; handshake_deadline default 50ms
- Fallback rate: intended <2% for primary traffic; >5% triggers alert.
sections.heading: SLOs and thresholds (defaults to be negotiated by teams)
Testing and validation

sections.body:
1) Register capability manifest in service registry and add feature flag (sia-enabled) default false.
2) Canary: enable sia-enabled for 0.5% of traffic with strict telemetry.
3) Expand: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% while monitoring fallback_rate and p95 latency.
4) If fallback_rate > 5% or p95 increases > 30% from baseline, rollback to previous stage and open an incident.
sections.heading: Rollout and migration playbook (high-level)

sections.body:
- Runtime/Serving team: implement mediator, acceptance token semantics, and fallback execution engine.
- API/Gateway team: enforce envelope headers and preliminary capability matching.
- Model-onboarding: publish capability manifests and maintain schema endpoints.
- SRE: define SLOs, alerts, and synthetic checks for capabilities.
sections.heading: Ownership and responsibilities

sections.body:
- Acceptance tokens must be signed (ed25519) by the mediator and validated by proxies to prevent unauthorized rerouting.
- Sensitive budget tags or customer ids must be hashed (salted) before being propagated to downstream logs.
sections.heading: Security and integrity considerations

sections.body:
1) Detecting an elevated fallback rate: alert rw.fallbacks.count with threshold > 5% in 5m window.
2) Quick triage: check recent decision_path logs for the most common fallback_level and reason.
3) If handshake failures are root cause: verify mediator healthy endpoints, check certificate rotation, and validate signature verification logs.
4) Mitigation: temporarily route traffic to a hardened model-variant pool or enable cached-prefix responses.

Appendix: example request/response (simplified)
sections.heading: Operational runbook (quick steps)

sections.body:
- Content-Type: application/redwood+json; version=2026-01
- X-RW-Request-Id: 7a9f4c2e-1b2a-4cbe-ae55-d4f2e0c299ff
- X-RW-Capability-Intent: chat-structured-output:v2
- X-RW-Cost-Budget-Tag: marketing-bot:low
sections.heading: Request headers
Response (success)

sections.body:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/redwood+json; version=2026-01
{
  "response": {"blocks": [...]},
  "meta": {"capability_id": "chat-structured-output:v2", "fallback_level": "level_2", "degradation_reason": "handshake_timeout"},
  "slo_impact": "minor"

payload.page_title: Partial-result Checkpointing and Client Resume Contract

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines a cross-service contract and operational playbook for partial-result checkpointing and client-driven resume for streaming inference calls. It provides a deterministic HTTP/WebSocket/HTTP/2 streaming contract that enables clients to tolerate transient connection failures, resume long-running generation requests, and reconcile partial outputs without risking duplicate side-effects or quality regressions. The contract balances developer ergonomics, predictable economics, and production safety for Redwood’s hosted and dedicated offerings.

Scope
-----
Applies to API surfaces that provide: text generation streaming, structured output streaming (tables/records), long-running embeddings/rerank jobs with incremental progress, and any route that supports server-sent partial outputs (examples: /v1/generate.stream, /v1/chat.stream, /v1/rerank.stream).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Wire-level semantics for checkpoints and resume tokens.
- Idempotency requirements and server-side deduplication semantics.
- Storage, retention, and encryption requirements for checkpoint artifacts.
- Operational SLOs and alerting thresholds.
- Client and server rollout and compatibility strategy.

Motivation
----------
We observe that long-running streams (interactive assistants, long-form generation, batched rerank) are sensitive to transient network glitches and HTTP connection limits, which cause poor user experience or expensive restarts. Implementing a lightweight checkpoint/resume mechanism: reduces perceived latency, lowers token cost by avoiding full re-generation, and improves reliability for customers on poor networks or intermediate proxies.

Goals (non-exhaustive)
- Allow clients to resume a previously-started stream from the last acknowledged checkpoint.
- Guarantee exactly-once external side-effect semantics for requests that produce side-effects (webhooks, downstream writes) via server-side gating.
- Keep checkpoint storage small and short-lived by checkpointing only the minimal resume state (KV cache ID, consumed token count, model variant id, deterministic RNG seed if applicable).
- Make the contract backward-compatible with clients that do not implement resume.

Contract: Wire semantics and payloads
----------------------------------
1) Checkpoint messages
- Servers MUST emit a stable checkpoint envelope at configurable intervals (default every 512 tokens or 10s, whichever comes first).
- Checkpoint envelope fields (JSON):
  - type: "checkpoint"
  - checkpoint_id: string (UUIDv4)
  - request_id: string (Redwood request id)
  - model_variant: string
  - token_offset: integer (number of tokens produced so far)
  - kv_cache_ref: string (opaque id for server-side cache)
  - truncated_output_hash: string (SHA256 of last emitted chunk to enable client reconciliation)
  - expires_at: ISO8601 timestamp (checkpoint TTL)
  - signature: string (HMAC-SHA256 of envelope using per-tenant key)

Example checkpoint envelope (server -> client):
{
  "type": "checkpoint",
  "checkpoint_id": "b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb",
  "request_id": "r-2026-00012345",
  "model_variant": "redwood-large-v2-quant",
  "token_offset": 1536,
  "kv_cache_ref": "cache://tenant-42/shard-17/ckpt-42",
  "truncated_output_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "expires_at": "2026-03-12T18:42:00Z",
  "signature": "sig:..."
}

2) Resume requests
- Client may initiate a resume by sending a ResumeRequest to the same endpoint (prefer HTTP/2 or WebSocket), passing the checkpoint_id and an optional client_ack_hash to indicate the last received chunk.
- ResumeRequest fields (JSON):
  - type: "resume_request"
  - checkpoint_id: string
  - client_ack_hash: string (optional)
  - client_id: string
  - request_metadata: map (opaque string kvs)
  - desired_resume_window: integer (tokens; server may honor subset)

Example ResumeRequest (client -> server):
{
  "type": "resume_request",
  "checkpoint_id": "b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb",
  "client_ack_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "client_id": "web-6d2a",
  "request_metadata": {"ui_session":"sess-123"},
  "desired_resume_window": 1024
}

3) Server resume response
- Server verifies signature and TTL. If valid, server responds with either:
  - resume_accepted: provides a new stream that resumes generation from token_offset, or
  - resume_denied: provides reason (expired, checkpoint-not-found, variant-mismatch) and optional best-effort fallback (restart token and cost estimate).
- Servers must not resume across incompatible model variants; resume across quantization variants is allowed only if deterministic equivalence is guaranteed (see model-compatibility ledger).

4) Idempotency and side-effect handling
- For requests that may trigger external side-effects, servers MUST not replay side-effects on resume. Implement one of two modes chosen per-route:
  - server-gated side-effects: the first successful finalization of the request generates an immutable side-effect token; clients must present this token when invoking any follow-up action.
  - client-ack-guarded mode: side-effects are only emitted after explicit client acknowledgement of final chunk.

5) Failure modes and reconciliation
- If the client’s client_ack_hash does not match the server’s truncated_output_hash, server SHOULD emit a ‘divergence’ event containing the minimal suffix the client is missing and a suggested merge strategy.

Operational requirements and configuration table
------------------------------------------------
| Key | Default | Unit | Description | Owner |
|-----|---------|------|-------------|-------|
| checkpoint.interval_tokens | 512 | tokens | Default token cadence for emitting checkpoints | inference-runtime |
| checkpoint.interval_seconds | 10 | seconds | Time-based cadence upper bound | inference-runtime |
| checkpoint.ttl_seconds | 86400 | seconds | Default checkpoint retention (24h) | storage-team |
| checkpoint.max_size_bytes | 16384 | bytes | Max size of serialized checkpoint metadata | storage-team |
| resume.auth_window_seconds | 300 | seconds | Time window after checkpoint creation where resume is allowed without re-authorization | identity |
| resume.p95_restart_latency | 150 | ms | SLO for resuming and starting token emission after a resume request | eng-sre |
| resume.max_parallel_resumes_per_tenant | 5 | count | Rate-limit per tenant to prevent abuse | quota-service |

Storage and encryption
- Checkpoints are stored in the checkpoint-store service (S3-compatible). All checkpoint metadata must be encrypted at rest with customer KMS, and signed with a per-tenant resume key. Checkpoint payloads must avoid storing user PII or full prompts unless configured by customer (private deployments).

SLOs and alerts
---------------
- Resume success rate (per-tenant) >= 99.5% over 24h.
- Resume p95 latency <= resume.p95_restart_latency (150ms default).
- Checkpoint persistence latency (write to checkpoint-store) p99 < 200ms.
- Alert if > 1% of resumed streams require full restart due to divergence in a 24h window.
- Alert on checkpoint-store error rate > 0.5% sustained for 5 minutes.

Observability and telemetry
-------------------------
- Emit events with standardized tags: checkpoint.emitted, checkpoint.persisted, resume.requested, resume.accepted, resume.denied, resume.divergence.
- Each event must include: request_id, checkpoint_id, tenant_id, model_variant, route, token_offset, and p99 latency metric dimensions.
- Trace spans: stream-gateway -> checkpoint-service -> inference-runtime -> checkpoint-store must be stitched with the same trace id for end-to-end debugging.

Rollout and compatibility
-------------------------
1) Backwards compatibility
- If an older client does not implement resume, server continues to emit checkpoints but ignores resume requests. The server must support default behavior of restarting from scratch with a clear restart-cost estimate.
2) Canary rollout steps (recommended):
  a) Implement server-side checkpoint emission behind a runtime flag (flag: checkpointing.enabled).
  b) Enable for internal tenants only and run synthetic failover tests for 72h.
  c) Gradually enable for 5% of external tenants, monitor resume success metrics and downstream cost delta.
  d) Increase to 25% then 100% if thresholds met.
3) Rollback plan: TTL reduction + immediate disable of checkpointing flag. Documented incident playbook in eng-platform/runbooks.

Testing and validation checklist
-------------------------------
- Unit tests for checkpoint envelope creation and signature verification.
- Integration tests: simulate connection interruption at token boundaries and mid-chunk; validate client resume produces the same final payload within tolerance threshold for structured outputs.
- Chaos tests: drop TCP connections, simulate transparent proxies, and ensure resume success > 99.5%.
- Cost regression: ensure average token cost delta after enabling resume < 3% (positive or negative).

Security considerations
----------------------
- Ensure checkpoint signatures use per-tenant HMAC keys stored in KMS. Rotate keys with zero-downtime using dual-signature validation during rotation window.
- Checkpoints must not expose raw secret keys, or PII unless explicitly enabled by customer and documented in private deployment configs.

Appendix: example CLI flows and cURL
-----------------------------------
sections.heading: This specifically covers

sections.body: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -d '{"prompt":"Write a long analysis...","stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate.stream
sections.heading: Emit stream (client)

sections.body:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type":"resume_request","checkpoint_id":"b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb","client_id":"web-6d2a","client_ack_hash":"sha256:abcd..."}' \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate.resume

Operational owners and contact
----------------------------
- inference-runtime: @inference-runtime-team (primary implementer)
- checkpoint-store/storage-team: @storage-team (persistence, encryption)
- stream-gateway: @edge-team (protocol / rate-limiting)
- eng-sre: oncall for SLO violations and rollback.

Related reading
---------------
- Model variant compatibility ledger (model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026)
- Cost-aware streaming payload schema guideline
- Runbook: stream-resume-incident-playbook (eng-platform/runbooks/stream-resume-incident-playbook)

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-05: Added SLO thresholds and storage encryption detail (reviewers: Rohit, Liam).
- 2026-03-05: Final edits and publication, clarified divergence reconciliation logic.

payload.page_title: Stitching and composition spec for multi-variant API responses

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines a company-wide standard for server-side response stitching and composition when serving multi-variant inference results (for example: base model output + reranker segment + tool-augmented content). The goal is to provide deterministic client-visible contracts, backward-compatible extension techniques, and runtime guidance for gateway and edge components that assemble partial results from multiple internal services.

Motivation

As Redwood exposes model families, variant fallbacks, and tool-calling, downstream clients expect a stable JSON contract. Untyped and ad-hoc composition has caused:
- Client-side parsing errors during rollouts
- Hard-to-debug semantic drift when a secondary service changes schema
- Increased latency due to synchronous composition loops

This spec reduces those risks by standardizing envelope shapes, merging rules, and compatibility testing requirements.

Scope
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- All public and private API endpoints that return composed/aggregated inference payloads (hosted API, dedicated, and private control plane)
- Gateway/edge services that stitch responses across internal services (e.g., generation runtime, reranker, post-processor, plugin/tool adapters)

Not in scope: low-level model artifact formats and internal-only telemetry shapes.

Definitions

- response fragment: a JSON object produced by a single internal service (e.g., {"generation": {...}}).
- composition layer: component responsible for merging fragments into a final client payload. Typical components: edge-stitcher, runtime-aggregator, fallback-composer.
- stable field: a top-level field marked in the contract as guaranteed by semantic compatibility rules.

High-level contract

1) Top-level envelope
- Every composed response MUST use a consistent envelope with these top-level keys:
  - id (string): server-assigned inference transaction id.
  - status (string): one of "ok", "degraded", "partial", "error".
  - variants (array): ordered list of variant descriptors used to produce fragments.
  - payload (object): merged fragments (see merging rules).
  - meta (object): composition metadata (timestamps, sources, cost-estimates).
sections.heading: Applies to

sections.body:
```json
{
  "id": "rwd-req-20260302-7f4d",
  "status": "ok",
  "variants": ["gptx-42b-q4f", "reranker-v2"],
  "payload": { /* merged content */ },
  "meta": {
    "composition_ms": 42,
    "sources": ["runtime/generation-1","ranking/alpha-2"],
    "billing_tokens": 312
  }
}
```

2) Fragment shape guidance
- Each fragment MUST be namespaced under a single key inside payload (see examples below). No fragment may write to another fragment's namespace.
- Namespaces should be short, lowercase, hyphen-delimited, and stable (e.g., "generation", "reranker", "tool-wolfram").
- Fragments MUST include a version marker: "_schema_version": "v1" (string).

3) Merging and conflict resolution rules
- Shallow-merge only: the composition layer performs a deterministic, shallow merge of top-level namespaced entries in payload.
- For fields that are arrays and explicitly annotated as "appendable": composition appends in deterministic order (see ordering rules).
- If two fragments attempt to expose the same namespaced field, composition MUST fail with status "degraded" and include a compatibility hint in meta (see Error handling).

4) Optional augmentation keys
- Each fragment MAY set "_confidence" (number 0..1) and "_trace_id" (string) on its namespace. Those keys are reserved and must be preserved by the composition layer.

Ordering and determinism
sections.heading: Example envelope

sections.body:
- The composition layer MUST order appended array elements by source priority then by fragment timestamp. Source priority is determined by variants[] index and then by service-defined priority.
- When performing asynchronous composition (streaming partials), the composer must expose incremental tokens via an explicit streaming envelope (see Streaming/partial responses).

Streaming / partial responses

1) Streaming envelope (for chunked generation + late-arriving reranker):
- Streamed chunks use the same top-level envelope, with an additional key "streaming": true and "stream_sequence" (integer).
- The final chunk must set "streaming": false and include the final "status" and a final snapshot of payload.
sections.heading: To prevent client-facing nondeterminism

sections.body:
```json
{
  "id": "rwd-req-20260302-7f4d",
  "status": "partial",
  "variants": ["gptx-42b-q4f"],
  "payload": {"generation": {"tokens": ["Hello"," "]}},
  "streaming": true,
  "stream_sequence": 1,
  "meta": {"composition_ms": 12}
}
```

Compatibility and versioning rules

- Schema versioning: Every namespace MUST increment _schema_version for incompatible changes. Backwards-compatible additive changes should use version-preserving migration strategies (see Compatibility checklist).
- Consumers MUST rely only on stable top-level keys documented in the public contract. Fields inside fragment namespaces are considered semantically subordinate and may change when schema version increments.
sections.heading: Example first chunk

sections.body:
- New fields are additive and optional.
- Enum expansions documented and feature-flagged for clients that depend on exact enum sets.
- Field renames must use a 2-release deprecation: 1) introduce new field, 2) remove old field after consumers signal migration.

Error handling and graceful degradation

- If a fragment fails or is incompatible during composition:
  1) Composer records the fragment id in meta.failed_fragments.
  2) If the fragment was non-critical (policy-driven), composer sets status="degraded" and includes partial payload from remaining fragments.
  3) If the fragment was required by the public contract, composer must fail the overall response with status="error" and return an error object in payload.error.
sections.heading: Compatibility checklist (must be validated before rollout)

sections.body:
```json
"meta": {
  "failed_fragments": ["reranker-v2"],
  "compatibility_hint": "reranker-v2: schema mismatch _schema_version expected v1, got v2"
}
```

Operational requirements

- Automated contract tests: Every service that emits a fragment MUST publish a contract test (JSON schema + example fragments) to the central contract repo. The composition layer runs these tests in CI.
- Runtime validation: Composer should run a lightweight schema check in production (fail closed vs fail open controlled by config). Default behavior: fail open for non-critical fragments, fail closed for critical fragments.
- Telemetry: Emit per-transaction metrics: composition_ms, fragments_count, failed_fragments_count, merge_conflicts_total. These metrics must be tagged by tenant, route, and primary_variant.

Security and privacy considerations

- No PII should be introduced by auxiliary fragments unless the fragment explicitly declares a privacy label and the tenant allows it. Composer must respect per-tenant privacy policies in meta.
- Cost/billing-sensitive fields (e.g., billing_tokens) MUST be present only in meta and filtered for customer-facing logs based on confidentiality level.

Examples

1) Typical generation + reranker composition:

payload example:

```json
{
  "generation": {
    "_schema_version": "v1",
    "text": "The quick brown fox",
    "tokens": ["The", " quick", " brown", " fox"],
    "_confidence": 0.92
  },
  "reranker": {
    "_schema_version": "v1",
    "top_scores": [{"span": "The quick", "score": 0.97}]
  }
}
```

2) Tool-augmented composition with appends (deterministic ordering):

```json
{
  "tool-search": { "_schema_version": "v1", "results": [ {"title":"A"}, {"title":"B"}], "_confidence": 0.9 },
  "generation": { "_schema_version": "v1", "tokens": ["Answer part A"], "_confidence": 0.85 }
}
```

Rollout checklist and testing playbook

1) Pre-merge CI gates for fragment publishers:
   - JSON schema test passes against canonical example set.
   - Contract regression test runs against composition layer's golden fixtures.
2) Canary rollout steps for composer changes:
   1. Deploy composer change to canary region (10% traffic).
   2. Run synthetic workloads that exercise composition edge-cases (conflicting namespaces, streaming interleaving).
   3. Monitor merge_conflicts_total, failed_fragments_count, and SLOs for 72 hours.
   4. If metrics exceed thresholds, rollback and open an incident.
3) Consumer signalling: require at least one downstream SDK to pass compatibility tests before full rollout.

Ownership and contact

- Composer service steward: eng/platform team (on-call: @platform-composer).
- Contract repository owner: eng/developer-experience.
- For compatibility disputes or schema deprecation requests, open a PR against the central contracts repo and tag reviewers: @applied-ml, @runtime-kernel.

Appendix: quick checklist for fragment authors

- Use a stable short namespace (e.g., "myservice").
- Include "_schema_version" and keep versions semver-like (v1, v2).
- Mark arrays that should be appended with "_appendable": true.
- Avoid top-level keys outside your namespace.
- Publish example fixtures to the central contracts repo and include a README with migration notes.

Revision history

- 2026-01-20: Initial draft by Maya Patel.
- 2026-02-10: Added streaming envelope semantics (reviewer feedback Arjun Rao).
- 2026-03-02: Clarified error handling and operational telemetry (Becca Lin).
