payload.page_title: Client Embargo and Call Shaping Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines the Client Embargo protocol and recommended client-side call shaping patterns to protect runtime SLOs and reduce cascading overloads. It is designed for external and internal SDKs that call Redwood inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, and private), and for intermediate proxies and edge adaptors.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a deterministic, low-latency friendly approach for clients to react to transient backpressure and service-driven embargo signals.
- Minimize wasted retries and noisy fanout during partial outages or capacity constraints.
- Preserve compatibility across client versions and server-side rollout stages with minimal coupling.
- Offer observability hooks and testing guidance so teams can validate behavior during rollouts.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body: When runtime capacity is constrained, naive client retry/backoff patterns often amplify load (retry storms), increase tail latency, and undermine SLOs for foreground traffic. Existing guidance covers hedging and timeouts, but lacks a concise, implementable handshake that: (a) communicates temporary embargo windows from server to client, (b) permits clients to shape traffic predictably, and (c) degrades safely when either side is upgraded independently.
sections.heading: Problem statement

sections.body:
- Applies to all text generation, chat, and embeddings REST endpoints exposed by Redwood API and to on-prem sidecar runtimes that implement the Embargo Header contract.
- Not intended for long-running batch jobs (use dedicated bulk endpoints and the Batch Escrow pattern).
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- Server signals short-term “embargo windows” via standard response header: X-Redwood-Embargo: <until-timestamp-ms>.<priority-hint>
- Header semantics:
  - until-timestamp-ms: absolute epoch ms when embargo ends (clients may apply jitter/holdoff to resume).
  - priority-hint: optional token (low|normal|high) that suggests preferred routing or client-level throttling.
- When present with a future timestamp, clients must treat the endpoint as "embargoed" for the given resource, and follow client-side shaping rules below.
sections.heading: Embargo protocol overview

sections.body:
1. Client issues request -> runtime responds 503 with X-Redwood-Embargo: 1700000000000.low
2. Client marks resource embargoed until timestamp and records embargo-origin and reason (if returned in body).
3. Client enters shaped holdoff path for that resource: apply local embargo policy (see policy matrix).
4. Client either (A) route to fallback compatible model/region or (B) queue with exponential-jittered resume windows under a cap.
5. When local embargo expires, client issues a single probe request (fast-path) to validate service health. If probe is successful, resume; otherwise re-enter embargo with exponential backoff up to max-holdoff.
sections.heading: Handshake and call shaping sequence (text diagram)

sections.body:
| Client tier | Action on "low" hint | Action on "normal" hint | Probe cadence after expiry | Max holdoff |
|-------------|-----------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------:|-----------:|
| SDK (PLG)   | Route to fallback model; queue small UI-friendly retry | Queue with capped jitter (base 150ms) | single probe after expiry | 30s |
| Server-to-server (high throughput) | Queue and downgrade weight to 10% of baseline; stream-level pause | Throttle to 50% of baseline | probe every 500ms up to 5 probes | 120s |
| Edge proxy | Route to alternate region; if none, return controlled 503 with embargo header | Prioritize high-fidelity traffic, degrade others | 1 probe after expiry | 60s |
(Notes: teams may tighten defaults per product risk profile. See "SLOs and metrics" below.)
sections.heading: Client policy matrix (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
- Single header, low priority: X-Redwood-Embargo: 1710000000000.low
- With server reason in body (JSON):

```json
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
X-Redwood-Embargo: 1710000000000.normal
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "capacity_exhausted",
  "embargo_reason": "zone_bursting",
  "recommended_fallback": "gptl-quantized-v2"
}
```
sections.heading: Embargo header examples (HTTP)

sections.body:
- Embargo header is additive and optional for older clients. Older clients that do not recognize the header must fall back to existing 5xx retry/backoff behavior.
- Server-side must not rely on client support during migration: always provide a standard 5xx response body and a machine-readable embargo header.
- When adding new priority hints, servers must ensure: default behavior for unknown hints is the same as "normal".
sections.heading: Compatibility and versioning rules

sections.body:
- Primary choices for fallback: cheaper quantized variant (same schema), lower-fidelity model with same output envelope, or regional reroute.
- Maintain model-compatibility manifest for each public model describing safe downgrade models (see Related Pages).

Configuration and sample settings (example YAML style shown as table of safe defaults):

| config_key | default | description |
|------------|---------|-------------|
| embargo.enabled | true | enable client embargo handling in SDKs/proxies |
| embargo.jitter_ms | 120 | additional random holdoff to avoid synchronized resume |
| embargo.probe_retries | 3 | probes after embargo expiry before backoff escalation |
| embargo.max_holdoff_ms | 120000 | upper bound of holdoff for S2S clients |
| embargo.fallback_preference | [quantized,region,model] | ordered fallback choices |
sections.heading: Fallback routing guidance

sections.body:
- SDK pseudocode (recommended):

```python
def handle_response(resp, resource_key):
    embargo_hdr = resp.headers.get("X-Redwood-Embargo")
    if embargo_hdr and resp.status_code >= 500:
        until_ms, hint = parse_embargo(embargo_hdr)
        if until_ms > now_ms():
            record_embargo(resource_key, until_ms, hint)
            apply_local_shaping(resource_key, hint)
            return EMBARGOED_RESPONSE
    return resp
```

- Probe example (curl):

curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \\  \
  -H "X-Redwood-Embargo-Probe: 1" \\  \
  "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models/gpt-infer/probe"
sections.heading: Implementation snippets

sections.body:
- Runtime must emit embargo events to telemetry pipeline with these fields: service, resource_key, embargo_until_ms, hint, origin_zone, backing_model.
- Client-side metrics to capture in SDKs/proxies: embargo_received_count, embargo_duration_histogram, probe_success_rate, fallback_routed_count, embargo_abort_count.
- Alerting thresholds (suggested):
  - If embargo_received_count increases by >200% over 15m and probe_success_rate < 10% -> paging to runtime oncall.
  - If fallback_routed_count > 5% of requests for 30m -> product/infra review for capacity or model degradations.
sections.heading: Operational SLOs and metrics to publish

sections.body:
1. Unit tests: ensure SDK parses header variants and honours unknown hints.
2. Integration test: simulate server returning embargo header with different timestamps and measure client holdoff and probe behavior.
3. Chaos/Sim lab: inject embargo signals across regions to verify routing and telemetry. Include synthetic workloads that simulate 10% of clients resuming simultaneously to validate jitter strategies.
sections.heading: Testing and verification

sections.body:
1. Implement client handling behind feature flag and enable for internal sandbox customers.
2. Enable embargo header emission in runtime for a small percentage (canary) of requests with low priority hints.
3. Monitor embargo metrics and iterate defaults for jitter and max holdoff.
4. Expand client SDK rollout to default-on once 72h canary shows stable probe_success_rate > 95% and no spike in tail latency.
sections.heading: Rollout and migration plan (recommended)

sections.body:
- Runtime teams: emit embargo header consistently and publish recommended fallback in response body.
- SDK teams: implement shaping, metrics, and probe behavior; expose configuration knobs to integrators.
- Observability: create dashboard named "Embargo Signals & Client Behavior" and maintain alert rules described above.
sections.heading: Ownership and responsibilities

sections.body:
- Embargo headers and reasons are operational metadata and must not contain PII. Avoid including tenant-identifying strings in embargo_reason.
- Telemetry containing embargo events should follow existing retention and redaction policies.
sections.heading: Security and privacy considerations

sections.body:
- Should embargo originate only from edge proxies or also from runtime backends? (Consequence: wider surface area vs earlier signaling).
- Standardize a machine-readable reason code set (e.g., zone_bursting, model_transient, maintenance_window) and publish mapping.
sections.heading: Open decisions (ADR candidates)

sections.body:
- See client-backpressure-hedging-and-timeouts-standards for baseline retry patterns.
- See runtime-workload-signatures-and-slo-derivation-playbook for SLO alignment.

Appendix A: Quick checklist for oncall when embargo signals surface:

- Confirm embargo origin and scope (zone, model, global).
- Check capacity spikes, recent rollouts, and preemption events.
- Validate fallback models are healthy and that probe endpoints respond.
- If embargo persists beyond configured max_holdoff for core customers, trigger capacity escalation and provide recommended communication script to affected teams.

This playbook should be treated as the canonical engineering guidance for client-side embargo behavior. Teams that change defaults must document differences and add them to the Related Pages list.
sections.heading: References and related pages

payload.page_title: service-contract-change-signal-and-safe-fallback-playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines a cross-cutting standard for signaling intentional API contract changes and executing safe fallback behavior across the Redwood inference stack. It ties together API surface design, runtime coding patterns, infra controls, model-serving expectations, observability gates, and performance verification steps. The objective is to allow evolution of request/response contracts while guaranteeing predictable degradation behavior, traceability, and rapid rollback when quality or SLO regressions are detected.

Why this exists

- Contract changes are inevitable: model capabilities, streaming semantics, and cost-tiered payloads will evolve.
- Poorly signaled changes cause silent client failures, high-error rates, and costly rollbacks.
- Cross-layer coordination is required: routing, cache affinity, runtime kernels, and telemetry must cooperate during change windows.

Scope

Applies to: public and internal REST/gRPC/streaming endpoints that carry model invocation payloads, especially generation, chat, embeddings, and reranking APIs. Not intended for front-end-only UI changes.

Owners and Contacts

- Primary owner: API Platform (engineering) — contact: amina.duarte@redwood.ai
- Runtime fallback steward: Serving Runtime team — contact: marco.li@redwood.ai
- Observability owner: Eng Platform — contact: sofia.patel@redwood.ai

Key Principles

1) Explicit capability negotiation: clients must express a minimal capability header for optional features. Backends may return a compatible response and a summary of accepted capabilities.
2) Non-breaking defaults: server-side additions must preserve existing fields unless an explicit opt-in signal is present.
3) Fail-safe fallbacks: when a new field or variant is not understood by downstream components, the request must either (a) fall back to a conservative variant, or (b) return a clear 4xx/422 with guidance.
4) Observable contract transitions: every change window must emit structured telemetry: change_id, gating_metric, rollforward/rollback decisions.

Contract Signaling Specification

Headers and Metadata

- X-Redwood-Contract: semantic token representing contract version (e.g., contract.v2.render-hints)
- X-Redwood-Contract-Intent: comma-separated capabilities the client is requesting (e.g., structured-output,stream-multiplex)
- X-Redwood-Client-Approx: optional perf hint (fast|balanced|high-fidelity) used by routing and kernel selectors

Request Body Schema Rules

1. Additive-only for opt-in fields: new optional fields must be namespaced under 'opt' or 'features'.
2. Required fields may only be added after a staged rollout and with explicit deprecation windows.

Sample header example

curl -X POST \ \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Contract: contract.v2.render-hints' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Contract-Intent: structured-output,function-calls' \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

Fallback Patterns (ranked by recommendation)

1) Variant Downgrade (preferred): map the request to a previous model variant or quantization profile that maintains semantics.
2) Partial Response + Hints: return a partial structured response with a top-level 'incomplete: true' flag and diagnostic suggestion.
3) Reject-with-guidance: return 422 with a structured error pointing to required contract capabilities and a suggested client fix.

Implementation Checklist (developer-facing)

- API: validate X-Redwood-Contract and X-Redwood-Contract-Intent; log mismatches at info level with change_id.
- Runtime: expose a fast-path for variant downgrade that preserves tokenization and KV cache compatibility.
- Cache: ensure prefix cache keys include contract.version to avoid poisoning.
- Router: make traffic-splitting rules aware of contract token and use weighted fallbacks.
- SDKs: expose helper to query supported capabilities and to opt-in safely.

Observability and Telemetry Gates

Mandatory telemetry emitted for a contract transition window:

- contract.change_id (tag)
- contract.request_count (counter)
- contract.error_rate (p50/p95/p99) per route and per variant
- contract.latency_ms.p95
- contract.fidelity_regressions (derived from eval harness)
- contract.rollback_reason (event)

Alerting thresholds (default)

- Error rate > 2% absolute increase over baseline in first 30 minutes -> P1 alert to oncall.
- 95th latency increase > 50% vs baseline -> P1.
- Fidelity regression (eval set delta) > configured threshold -> block rollout.

Testing and Performance Verification
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Unit + contract tests: validate new optional fields deserialize in both new and old code paths.
2) Integration: run canary traffic at 0.5% for 30 minutes with synthetic load.
3) Perf: run 5-minute stress with representative sequence length histogram; capture kernel selection variance.
4) Eval: run a small eval set (100 prompts) comparing outputs against quality gates; track semantic drift via automatic scoring.

Rollout Procedure (numbered)

1. Open a Change Window: register change_id and high-level plan in the rollout registry.
2. Run preflight: run CI checks, integration smoke, and perf profile.
3. Canary 0.5% for 30m: monitor contract metrics and fidelity evals.
4. Gradual expand: 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation at each step.
5. Automatic halt: gate expansion on telemetry; halt if any P1 threshold triggers.
6. Rollback: if halted, execute variant-downgrade path and open incident ticket; capture diagnostics and run postmortem.

Coding and Infra Standards (practical rules)

- Backwards compatibility suites must be part of the pre-merge CI for any API surface change.
- Use feature flags for server-side opt-ins; flags must include owner, expiry date, and test coverage.
- Prefix cache key and KV layout with contract.version and variant.id.
- Runtime sidecar must support a /compat endpoint that returns current supported contract tokens and capability matrix.

Model-serving expectations

- Model artifacts must include a capability manifest (manifest.json) listing supported contract tokens, max_sequence, quantization profile, and deterministic_hash.
- When serving multiple variants, maintain a compatibility ledger that maps variant->compatible-seed-versions for KV cache reuse.

Decision Record (ADR) — summary of tradeoffs

Decision ID: ADR-2027-04-contract-signal
Date: 2026-11-14
Decision: Require explicit contract headers and conservative fallback by default.
Reasoning: Implicit changes were causing silent client breakages and made incident triage slow. Explicit headers improve observability and allow deterministic routing to compatible variants.
Consequences: Slightly larger request surface (extra headers), additional runtime checks, more complex cache keying. Long-term benefit: faster rollouts, fewer P1 incidents.

Appendix: Quick reference table

| Field | Purpose | Required during rollout? | Default behavior |
|-------|---------|--------------------------|------------------|
| X-Redwood-Contract | Contract token | Yes | When missing, server treats as contract.v1 (legacy) |
| X-Redwood-Contract-Intent | Opt-in capabilities | No | Missing intent => conservative processing |
| contract.change_id (telemetry) | Traceable rollout id | Yes | Populated by router during change window |

Sample compatibility policy (YAML)

---
fallback_policies:
  - name: variant-downgrade
    match_order: [structured-output,stream-multiplex,function-calls]
    fallback_to: previous_stable_variant

Related reading

- See runtime /compat endpoint design in: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/slo-driven-runtime-contracts-and-rollback-playbook-2026
- See canary and telemetry gates in: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts (internal dashboard playbook)

Questions and escalation

- For rollout help, open an issue in #api-rollouts Slack channel and tag @api-platform.
- If a P1 triggers during a change window, follow the Incident Playbook and notify the oncall SRE.

Document history

- 2026-11-15: Drafted by Amina Duarte
- 2026-12-04: Review iteration with Serving Runtime (Marco Li) and Observability (Sofia Patel)
- 2027-02-10: Published after adding perf verification steps and ADR summary

payload.page_title: Client Contracts for Structured Tool Calls and Retry Semantics

sections.body: Guidelines and decision rationale for the client-side contract used when making structured tool calls (function/tool invocation) to Redwood inference endpoints, including envelope format, idempotency semantics, retry windows, and telemetry signals required for safe and cost-predictable retries.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This document specifies a cross-cutting client-side contract for making structured tool calls (a.k.a. function or tool invocation) via Redwood inference APIs. It describes: the JSON/YAML envelope, required fields, idempotency and retry semantics, backoff guidance, failure modes and mitigation, observability signals clients must emit, and recommended server-side acceptance tests. The intent is to reduce incorrect duplicate tool executions, limit surprise billing, and make retries diagnosable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Tool calls can trigger side effects (webhooks, DB writes, external API calls). Poorly specified retries lead to duplicated side effects or inconsistent state.
- LLM tool-calling increases per-request token usage (function args, structured outputs). Clients should be able to reason about safe retry windows and idempotency.
- Observability and request metadata are required for post-incident triage and cost allocation.
sections.heading: Why this exists

sections.body:
- Scope: client contract and minimal server acceptance expectations for structured tool calls on Redwood inference endpoints. Includes offline SDK behavior and recommended tests for SDKs.
- Non-goal: a full two-phase commit protocol or distributed transactions for customer tool endpoints. We assume many destination tools are external and uncontrolled.

Contract: request envelope (JSON)
- Required top-level fields (example):
  {
    "request_id": "uuid-v4",
    "client_id": "string (project or org id)",
    "model": "string",
    "prompt": "string",
    "tool_call": {
      "tool_name": "string",
      "inputs": { /* arbitrary JSON */ },
      "expected_response_schema": "json-schema-v4-string (optional)"
    },
    "idempotency_key": "optional-string",
    "created_at": "RFC3339 timestamp",
    "safety_hints": ["no-exec", "dry-run"]
  }

- Semantics: request_id is our canonical correlation id that must be unique per logical client request. idempotency_key is a client-chosen stable key that indicates the same logical operation (e.g., create-invoice-123). If idempotency_key is present, Redwood must make best-effort deduplication within the configured idempotency window (see below).
sections.heading: Scope and non-goals

sections.body:
- Default idempotency window: 5 minutes for hosted endpoints (configurable per-customer for Dedicated/Private).
- Guarantee: If two requests arrive with the same idempotency_key within the idempotency window, Redwood will return the cached response (or the same success/failure disposition) for non-streaming tool-calls. This is an at-most-once best-effort guarantee for side-effecting tool-calls; clients should not rely on absolute deduplication for longer-lived operations.
- Stronger options: customers can request extended deduplication (up to 7 days) for Dedicated/Private via per-account config with associated storage and billing implications.
sections.heading: Idempotency window and guarantees

sections.body:
1) Safe to retry immediately (no idempotency concerns): idempotent read-only tool calls (e.g., lookup-by-id), or calls marked with safety_hints: ["dry-run", "no-exec"].
2) Retry with deduplication: calls with idempotency_key present. Client may retry with exponential backoff but must preserve idempotency_key.
3) Unsafe to retry automatically: tool calls that mutate external systems without idempotency support. Clients must use human confirmation, manual dedup keys, or server-side orchestration to avoid duplication.
sections.heading: Retry classification (client guidance)

sections.body:
- Immediate: 200ms jittered initial delay for transient network failures (TCP connection reset, short timeout).
- Exponential backoff: factor 2, max backoff 30s for single request. Give up after 5 attempts unless idempotency_key is present and client has explicit reason to continue.
- Token-cost-aware retry: SDKs MUST avoid unbounded rapid retries for streaming responses — track tokens consumed on partial responses and surface partial tokens to clients before retrying.
sections.heading: Backoff and retry windows (recommended)

sections.body:
1) Idempotency key echo: server must return an idempotency_status field indicating: ["accepted", "duplicate", "expired", "unsupported"].
2) Request correlation headers: server returns request_id, server_received_at, and a dedup_cache_hit boolean.
3) Safety hint enforcement: if client sets safety_hints: ["dry-run"], server must not perform external side effects and should label outputs with dry_run: true.
sections.heading: Server-side acceptance tests (minimum)

sections.body:
- Clients must attach these fields to telemetry events: client_id, sdk_version, idempotency_key (if set), request_id, tool_name, estimated_token_budget.
- Servers must record: received_at, processing_latency_ms, idempotency_status, output_token_count, external_tool_invocations (count), and a trace_id mapping to distributed traces.
- Labeling convention: all telemetry fields MUST use snake_case keys.
sections.heading: Telemetry and logging requirements (client and server)

sections.body:
- Duplicate execution: encourage use of idempotency_key. For legacy clients, server-side replay-detection heuristics may be applied (best-effort).
- Partial streaming / truncated outputs: SDKs should expose truncated = true and partial_token_count to the caller. Automatic retries are allowed only if client confirms they accept truncated results; otherwise surface an error with code PARTIAL_OUTPUT.
- Billing surprises: server must report output_token_count and bill only for tokens accepted by the client at acknowledgement time (see billing policy linked below).

Client SDK checklist (minimum implementation for Redwood official SDKs):
1) Provide automatic idempotency_key generation for common operations and allow client override.
2) Expose telemetry hooks allowing customers to forward native telemetry to their systems.
3) Surface partial-stream events with token counts and a simple API to either commit, retry, or discard.
4) Implement retry backoff policy above and make it configurable.
sections.heading: Failure modes and recommended mitigations

sections.body:
- Phase 0 (internal testing): SDK + server implement idempotency_status echo and minimal telemetry. Run against integration testbed.
- Phase 1 (opt-in beta): Add idempotency_key support to hosted endpoints behind a feature flag. Invite 10 trust accounts.
- Phase 2 (default): Gradual ramp to 100% of new endpoints over 4 weeks. Deprecate previous ambiguous retry semantics.
sections.heading: Compatibility and rollout plan

sections.body:
- Trigger: sharp increase in external_tool_invocations combined with dedup_cache_hit rate < 1% for requests with idempotency_key.
  - Action: verify idempotency store health, check storage latency, rollback recent change to dedup index writes, notify integrators.
- Trigger: increase in PARTIAL_OUTPUT errors > 0.5% of requests over 1h.
  - Action: examine streaming backend latency, verify kernel memory pressure, check client SDK releases for changed read buffer sizes.

Acceptance tests (CI) for SDKs and server: (table)
- Test name | Purpose | Expected result
- idempotency-duplicate | ensure same idempotency_key returns duplicate status | duplicate returned, no second external invocation
- dry-run-safety | ensure dry-run prevents side effects | external_tool_invocations == 0, dry_run == true in response
- streaming-truncation | simulate partial chunk then abort | SDK surfaces truncated=true and partial_token_count > 0
sections.heading: Operational runbook snippets (on-call triggers)

sections.body:
- Idempotency keys must not contain PII. SDKs must sanitize common inputs before using them as idempotency keys.
- Telemetry fields that may contain user content must be hashed before transmission per privacy policy.
sections.heading: Security and privacy notes

sections.body:
- ADR 1: long-term storage duration for deduplication keys for Dedicated/Private (trade-offs: cost vs. customer safety).
- ADR 2: canonical token accounting for partially streamed responses (how many tokens billed on retry).
sections.heading: Open decisions (ADRs to follow)

sections.body:
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/request-semantics-and-cost-aware-payload-guidelines-2026
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/structured-response-contract-testing-guidelines-2026
- Billing policy (internal link): /confluence/finance-and-legal/revrec-and-billing/token-billing-and-partial-response-policy-2025

Appendix: example server response (minimal):
{
  "request_id": "uuid-v4",
  "status": "ok",
  "idempotency_status": "accepted|duplicate|expired|unsupported",
  "server_received_at": "2026-02-08T18:42:00Z",
  "dedup_cache_hit": false,
  "output_token_count": "42",
  "external_tool_invocations": 1,
  "dry_run": false
}

payload.page_title: Inference request idempotency and deduplication standard

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a company-wide standard for request idempotency and deduplication for inference APIs. The goal is to ensure predictable semantics for duplicate or retried requests, reduce wasted GPU work, and provide clear observability and controls for customers and platform services. This standard covers request fingerprinting, idempotency-key semantics, server-side deduplication windows, storage of deduplication metadata, and required metrics and alerting.

Scope

- Applies to all public and private inference endpoints that accept generation, chat, or embedding requests.
- Includes hosted API, Dedicated endpoints, and Private (VPC/on-prem) runtimes where the Redwood control plane or runtime implements request deduplication.
- Does NOT apply to streaming partial-response retries at the transport layer (those are handled by streaming protocol rules).

Motivation

Retries and client-side duplicates are frequent in distributed systems (network glitches, SDK retries, user code bugs). Left unchecked, duplicates cause:

- wasted GPU cycles and higher unit cost
- inconsistent billing/usage attribution
- ambiguous conversational state when repeated requests mutate external state or trigger side effects

The standard reduces ambiguity by providing deterministic server behavior for duplicates and clear guidance for client SDKs.

Definitions

- Idempotency-Key: an optional client-supplied opaque string that the server will use as a primary deduplication hint.
- Request Fingerprint: canonicalized hash computed by the server from the request payload when idempotency-key is not provided.
- Deduplication Window: configurable time window during which two requests with the same idempotency-key or fingerprint are considered duplicates.
- Outcome Record: stored result metadata (status, model version, output hash, cost) used to answer duplicate requests without re-executing inference.

Principles

1. Deterministic answer: If a request is considered a duplicate, the server should return the earlier outcome when available rather than re-executing inference.
2. Bounded state: Deduplication metadata must be bounded by time and size to avoid unbounded storage growth.
3. Transparent observability: Metrics and traces must indicate deduplication behavior to owners and customers.
4. Configurable scope: Customers and internal services can opt-in/out of deduplication semantics for sensitive workloads.

API Contract and Headers

- Idempotency-Key header: X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key
  - Optional string up to 128 characters (client-generated UUIDv4 recommended).
  - Semantics: If present, server uses this key as the primary deduplication identifier.
  - Use case: clients that replay requests on failure and want strong retry semantics.

- Request fingerprinting: When Idempotency-Key is absent, server computes a fingerprint over canonicalized payload fields described below.

Canonicalization rules for fingerprinting (applied in this order):
1. Normalize JSON: sort object keys, remove insignificant whitespace.
2. Strip transient metadata fields: request.timestamp, client_trace_id, ephemeral SDK fields (configurable list).
3. For chat generation requests, normalize message array by preserving role and content but removing per-message client-provided IDs.
4. For prompt templates, replace resolved parameter placeholders with their canonical values before hashing.

Algorithm: SHA-256(hex) on the canonicalized UTF-8 bytes. Result is fingerprint string: fp_sha256:<hex>

Server Behavior on Duplicate Detection

1. On receive, server evaluates: presence of X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key -> use as primary key; else compute request fingerprint.
2. Look up deduplication index (in-memory + persisted fast store).
3. If an Outcome Record exists and is within the Deduplication Window, return cached outcome with HTTP 200 (or the same status the original returned) and include header X-Redwood-Duplicate: true and X-Redwood-Original-Timestamp.
4. If no outcome is stored but an identical request is currently executing, attach the caller to a joiner channel: the joiner will receive the execution result when ready (no duplicate execution). Include header X-Redwood-Joiner-Attached: true.
5. If no outcome and not executing, proceed to execute, store Outcome Record atomically when complete.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- request_id (server-generated)
- idempotency_key or fingerprint
- status (succeeded/failed/cancelled)
- model_version
- truncated output hash (sha1:8)
- token_cost (tokens_in + tokens_out)
- timestamp_completed

Storage and retention

- Default Deduplication Window: 5 minutes. Rationale: balances transient network retries versus storage costs and typical client retry backoffs.
- Maximum configurable window: 24 hours (customer-controlled on private deployments with storage/backing-store implications).
- Storage tiers: In-memory LRU cache for sub-60s entries, fast KV store (Redis Cluster or Cockroach cache layer) for full window. Outcome Records must expire via TTL.

Configuration table

| config_key | default | allowed_range | recommended_owner | note |
|-----------|---------|---------------|-------------------|------|
| dedupe.window.default | 300s | 30s — 24h | serving-runtime | default for hosted API |
| dedupe.in_memory_ttl | 60s | 10s — 1800s | serving-runtime | fast path to avoid KV hops |
| dedupe.max_record_size | 4096 | 1024 — 65536 | serving-runtime | prevents storing full outputs |
| dedupe.enabled_by_default | true | boolean | product | opt-out for sensitive endpoints |

Observability requirements

- Metrics (per service):
  - redwood.dedupe.requests_total (labels: outcome={hit,miss,joiner,expired}, endpoint, model)
  - redwood.dedupe.saved_tokens_total (counter; tokens saved by not executing duplicates)
  - redwood.dedupe.outcome_store_errors_total

- Tracing: Every request should include trace/span tags: dedupe.key, dedupe.result, dedupe.latency_ms. For duplicates, include original_request_id tag.

- Logs: Emit structured event when an Outcome Record is served for a duplicate: {event: "dedupe.serve", key: "...", original_request_id: "...", latency_ms: 12, saved_tokens: 42}

Billing and Usage semantics

- For duplicates that are served from an Outcome Record, bill using the earlier execution’s token cost; do not bill again.
- For joiner-attached requests that avoid a second execution, mark in billing ledger as dedupe_joiner to allow transparency in billing exports.

Edge cases and security considerations

- Sensitive-output endpoints: For endpoints that can return PII or one-time tokens, deduplication is disabled by default unless customer explicitly enables it and accepts shared outcome semantics.
- Replay attacks: Idempotency-Key should not be relied on as an authorization token. Servers must validate request auth scopes independently. Outcome Records should not be accessible from other tenants.
- Key exhaustion: Large numbers of unique idempotency keys from malicious clients must be mitigated. Rate-limit idempotency-key creation per tenant and evict using LRU + bounded TTL.

Compatibility and migration guidelines

- Backwards compatible behavior: New servers implementing this standard must accept requests without Idempotency-Key. Existing clients continue to work.
- SDK changes: Official Redwood SDKs (Python/JS/Go) will add a high-level retry helper that generates UUID idempotency keys by default for safe retries. Docs and migration examples included in SDK release notes.

Testing checklist (pre-merge for runtime changes)

1. Unit tests for canonicalization rules and fingerprint collisions (include fuzz tests).
2. Integration test: concurrent duplicate requests should result in single execution and joiner attachments.
3. End-to-end test: verify billing ledger marks joiners and duplicates correctly.
4. Load test: simulate high rate of unique idempotency-keys to validate eviction policy.
5. Security review: ensure Outcome Records cannot be returned cross-tenant.

Rollout plan

1. Canary: Enable dedupe on 5% of server pools behind a feature flag with dedupe.window.default=60s. Monitor saved_tokens_total and redwood.dedupe.requests_total.
2. Gradual ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over 2 weeks with rollback triggers: out_of_memory on cache nodes, >1% dedupe.outcome_store_errors_total, unexpected customer errors.
3. SDK release: publish retry helper in the same week as full rollout.

Ownership and contact

- Standard owner: Serving Runtime team (primary: @marcus-alvarez).
- Product owner for customer toggles: API Product team.
- Security reviewer: Security & Compliance.

Appendix: Examples

1) Client request with idempotency key (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -H 'X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key: 3f2b7b8a-...-f9ee' -d '{"model":"redwood-mini-1","input":"Translate to French: hello"}'
sections.heading: Outcome Record contents (minimal)

sections.body:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Redwood-Duplicate: true
X-Redwood-Original-Timestamp: 2026-02-18T14:12:03Z
X-Redwood-Original-Request-Id: req_01GZ...

2) Fingerprint computation (pseudocode)
sections.heading: Possible server response headers on duplicate

sections.body:
canonical = canonicalize_json(request.payload, strip_fields=["timestamp","client_trace_id"])
fingerprint = sha256_hex(canonical)
return f"fp_sha256:{fingerprint}"

Rationale summary

Deterministic deduplication improves cost predictability and customer experience while remaining opt-in/configurable for privacy-sensitive workloads. The combination of client-supplied idempotency keys and server-side fingerprinting covers common retry models without requiring clients to change behavior immediately.

Related documents

- API compatibility and deprecation policy (see related_pages)
- Runtime kernel selection and sequence handling (see related_pages)

Document history

- 2025-11-12: Draft created by Marcus Alvarez
- 2025-12-15: Engineering review additions (Anita Chen)
- 2026-01-09: Security review (Sofia Park)
- 2026-02-18: Published with rollout plan and SDK notes

payload.page_title: Typed Extension Discovery and Backward Shimming Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines a pragmatic, engineering-friendly approach for discovering typed API extensions and serving backward-compatible responses via shims. It focuses on model-serving and edge APIs where schema changes, optional extensions, and hosted client diversity create compatibility risk. The guidance balances strict typing for server-side validation with flexible runtime shimming to preserve client behavior and avoid mass client updates.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Provide a predictable discovery protocol so clients and services can negotiate optional extensions without full deployment coordination.
- Define a small set of supported extension patterns and canonical shims that maintain observable semantics for downstream consumers.
- Establish rollout, testing, telemetry, and alerting practices to detect compatibility regressions early.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to Redwood public inference APIs, internal service-to-service RPCs that return structured outputs (JSON or protobuf), and streaming session responses.
- Not intended for: complete breaking schema redesigns, contract-first public SDKs without a migration window, or binary wire-format incompatibilities.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Base Contract: the canonical response schema version that clients are guaranteed to understand (e.g., v1.2.0).
- Extension Field: a non-required field added to the schema with clearly documented type and semantics.
- Discovery Header/Frame: a metadata mechanism (HTTP header or initial streaming frame) that advertises supported extensions and server capabilities.
- Shim: server-side transformation that produces a response compatible with older clients by removing/transforming new fields or mapping new enums to legacy values.
sections.heading: Key Definitions

sections.body:
1) Discovery header (HTTP): services must advertise supported schema features in a single header named X-RW-API-Features. Format: comma-separated tokens with optional versioned suffixes. Example: X-RW-API-Features: structured-embeddings:v2,role-metadata:v1.
2) Streaming: the initial control frame must include a features list and a shard of the chosen model variant. Example JSON control frame: {"features": ["role-metadata:v1"], "variant": "redwood-base-1"}.
3) Client hints: clients may include Accept-Extensions header to request opt-in fields. Servers must respect client hints for opt-in extensions but may still send non-critical fields when safe.
sections.heading: Discovery and Negotiation

sections.body:
- Optional scalar fields: must be nullable or absent when unknown.
- Namespaced extension objects: fields grouped under an extensions map (recommended key: "x_rw_extensions"). Example: "x_rw_extensions": { "safety_flags": {...} }
- Enum additive expansion: new enum values must include a legacy fallback mapping in the contract manifest.
- Versioned sub-schemas: complex extensions with their own schema version (e.g., "summarization:v2").
sections.heading: Extension Pattern Catalog (supported)

sections.body:
1) Remove-for-legacy: strip unknown optional fields before sending to clients that don’t advertise the extension. Use when the field is purely additive and no behavior changes are required.
2) Fallback-mapping: convert new enum values or structured objects into legacy representations using declared mapping rules. Maintain mapping table in service config.
3) Simulated-synthesis: if an extension provides higher-fidelity output, produce a synthesized legacy surrogate when possible (e.g., reduce structured answer to plain text summary). Only use when synthesis is deterministic and well-tested.
4) Dual-response (conditional): for a small set of high-value clients, send both new-typed payload and a legacy wrapper under a single response envelope where bandwidth and client parsing permit.

Compatibility Manifest (service config) — required fields and example:
- service: inference-gateway
- base_contract: v1.3.0
- supported_extensions: ["role-metadata:v1", "structured-embeddings:v2"]
- default_shim_policy: remove-for-legacy
- enum_mappings: [{"field": "sentiment", "mapping": {"very_positive": "positive", "very_negative": "negative"}}]
sections.heading: Shim Strategies (server-side)

sections.body:
- Unit tests: every new extension must ship with unit tests for shim logic and mapping tables.
- Contract tests: add a contract suite run in CI that exercises:
  1) feature discovery header permutations
  2) Accept-Extensions variations
  3) shim policy correctness (strip/map/synthesize)
- Synthetic production canary: deploy a canary that mirrors traffic to a shadow instance where new extensions are enabled and verify parity metrics (error rate, token delta, latency) over 24–72 hours.
sections.heading: Testing and Validation

sections.body:
Essential metrics (per-route, per-model):
- shim_rate: percentage of responses altered by a shim (SLO target: < 2% for stable releases).
- extension_usage: count of requests that accepted or requested each extension.
- mapping_failures: count of enum mapping anomalies (alert if > 0.1% over 1h).
- client_parse_errors: 4xx/5xx originating from downstream client integrations (alert threshold depends on client tier).
- response_size_delta: average bytes added/removed by shims (monitor for unexpected growth).
sections.heading: Observable Signals and Alerts

sections.body:
- P1: mapping_failures rate > 0.1% sustained for 15m -> Pager (team: runtime).
- P2: shim_rate > 10% with extension_usage < 1% -> Slack alert to owners (indicates misconfiguration).
- P3: client_parse_errors spike correlated with a recent extension rollout -> Notify owners and pause rollout.
sections.heading: Alerting rules (examples)

sections.body:
1) Feature flag gating: every extension must be behind a rollout flag. Feature flag should control: discovery header advertisement, field emission, and shim policy.
2) Phased rollout:
  a) Internal-only (10% traffic; engineering org)
  b) Beta customers (+ selected enterprise customers)
  c) Gradual ramp to 100% with automated health checks at 5/25/50/100%
3) Rollback criteria: any of the following observed within the rollout window -> automatic rollback: mapping_failures > threshold, client_parse_errors up > 30%, error rate increase > 0.5%.
sections.heading: Rollout and Canary Guidance

sections.body:
1) If an alert fires for mapping_failures:
  a) Identify the mapping table and recent commits via service config history.
  b) Run the contract test locally against the canary binary.
  c) If mapping is incorrect, update mapping in config and deploy hotfix to canary; if unsure, pause advertisement by toggling discovery header.
2) If client_parse_errors spike:
  a) Correlate client user agents and ingress tokens.
  b) Revert extension advertisement for affected routes and roll back at traffic layer.
  c) Engage customer success for impacted customers.
sections.heading: Operational Runbook (quick)

sections.body:
- Service owner: runtime-api-team (primary), with policy stewardship by API standards working group.
- Extensions registry steward: model-onboarding (maintains canonical list of extension tokens and schema links).
- Quarterly review: Every extension must be reviewed by API standards working group for lifecycle (deprecation, promotion to base contract).

Migration Checklist for Promoting an Extension to Base Contract:
1) At least 90 days of stable usage and < 0.05% mapping_failures.
2) Client adoption > 80% for internally vetted clients or a signed delivery plan for external SDKs.
3) All shims and mappings audited and checked into the config repo.
4) Update public API docs, SDK changelogs, and release notes.
sections.heading: Ownership and Governance

sections.body:
- Discovery header example:
  curl -v -H "X-RW-API-Features: role-metadata:v1,structured-embeddings:v2" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate"

- Shim mapping example (YAML):
  enum_mappings:
    sentiment:
      very_positive: positive
      very_negative: negative
sections.heading: Example snippets

sections.body:
- [ ] Add extension token and schema doc to extensions registry (model-onboarding).
- [ ] Draft mapping rules and shim policy in service config.
- [ ] Add unit and contract tests.
- [ ] Instrument shim_rate, mapping_failures, extension_usage.
- [ ] Run synthetic canary for 72 hours.
- [ ] Schedule API standards review within 2 weeks of initial canary.

Appendix: Related pages and references:

- Variant compatibility ledger (xref).
- Contract test harness README (internal repo link).

payload.page_title: Per-tenant Request Transform and Augmentation Standard

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This standard defines how Redwood Inference performs per-tenant request transformation and augmentation at the API gateway and edge layers. It establishes the allowed transformations, runtime semantics, safety checks, observability requirements, performance budgets, rollout procedures, and ownership model. The goal is to enable tenant-specific routing, enrichment, and cost/quality controls without compromising compatibility, latency SLOs, or security.

Motivation
----------
Teams have repeatedly requested tenant-scoped policy hooks for: prefix normalization, quota-aware request shaping, automatic prompt enrichment (e.g., adding tenant metadata), and lightweight per-tenant feature flags (e.g., enabling alternative model variants). Left unregulated, ad-hoc transforms cause drift between client expectations and server contracts, create security exposures (sensitive data injection), and increase tail latency. This standard provides a guarded, observable, and testable way to implement those transforms.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all HTTP/HTTP2 and streaming endpoints that pass through Redwood edge/gateway components.
- Covers transformations executed in: edge proxies, API gateway request processors, and the request-enrichment sidecar in private deployments.
- Excludes: deep model input rewriting performed inside model runtime (those should follow model-serving transform guidelines).

Definitions
-----------
- Transform: deterministic modification of a request payload or headers (e.g., normalization, trimming).
- Augmentation: insertion of derived data into requests (e.g., tenant profile embeddings, prompt templates).
- Tenant Policy: a configuration object (JSON) that enumerates allowed transforms and associated limits.
- Safe Zone: transformations that are guaranteed to preserve request semantics and schema.

Design Principles
-----------------
1. Fail closed: any transform failure must not corrupt client request; default behavior is to pass the original request or fail with a deterministic 4xx/5xx depending on policy.
2. Minimal surface: transforms are limited to a well-defined set of primitives (see below).
3. Observable: every transform execution must emit telemetry (success/failure, latency, reason code, tenant_id).
4. Budget-aware: transforms that increase compute/latency (e.g., on-the-fly embedding generation) must declare cost and fit within per-tenant performance budgets.
5. Configured, not coded: all tenant-specific transforms should be expressed as declarative Tenant Policy objects stored in configuration service; no ad-hoc code forks.

Allowed Transform Primitives
----------------------------
- Header add/remove/normalize (safe)
- JSON field add/remove/rename (schema-validated)
- Prompt prefix/suffix injection (template-based, length-limited)
- Token trimming and max-length enforcement (with deterministic truncation strategy)
- Rate-aware payload shaping (rewrite to lower-fidelity prompt or downgraded model hint)
- Redirect or rewrite of model selection routing hint (only to compatible variants)
- Annotate with tenant metadata (non-sensitive)

Disallowed Operations
---------------------
- Arbitrary code execution in transform layer
- Injection of secrets or private customer data pulled from unrelated tenants
- Modifications that change canonical API schema without versioned contract change

Tenant Policy Schema (example)
-----------------------------
| Field | Type | Description | Default |
| tenant_id | string | ID of tenant | required |
| transforms | list<transform> | Ordered list of transform primitives | [] |
| cost_budget_ms | integer | Max additional median latency allowed (ms) | 50 |
| max_added_tokens | integer | Max tokens allowed to be injected to prompt | 32 |
| allowed_model_hints | list<string> | Allowed model variants for rewrite | [] |

Transform primitive example (declarative JSON fragment)
------------------------------------------------------
{
  "type": "prompt_prefix",
  "template_id": "tenant-presets/welcome-v2",
  "max_tokens_added": 16,
  "apply_when": {"header_exists": "X-Tenant-Feature-Enable"}
}

Runtime Semantics
-----------------
1. Execution order: transforms apply in the sequence specified by Tenant Policy. Each primitive is transactional: failures roll back to pre-transform state for that request.
2. Safety validation: before any mutation is committed, the transform engine runs schema validation against the API contract. If validation fails, action depends on "enforce_mode":
   - strict: return 422 with error payload and log.
   - permissive: skip upgrade and emit warning telemetry.
3. Latency accounting: all transforms must annotate request trace with transform.duration_ms. Transform total must not exceed tenant.cost_budget_ms. If it does, subsequent transforms are skipped and a telemetry marker "transform_budget_exceeded" is emitted.
4. Streaming behavior: for streaming endpoints transforms that would change initial handshake (e.g., prompt prefix) must be applied before the stream is accepted. Mid-stream dynamic augmentation is only allowed for metadata (not model input tokens).

Compatibility and Contract Guarantees
------------------------------------
- Transforms residing at edge must preserve response determinism: the same input + tenant policy must produce the same transformed output.
- Any transform that changes request schema must be accompanied by an API contract version bump and client-adaptor mapping declared in the tenant policy.

Observability Requirements
-------------------------
Every transform execution must emit the following telemetry fields as structured logs and spans:
- transform.name
- tenant_id
- transform.duration_ms
- transform.result (ok|skipped|failed|budget_exceeded)
- reason_code (when not ok)
- pre_transform_payload_hash and post_transform_payload_hash (safe, salted HMAC for privacy)

Metrics and SLOs
----------------
- transform_success_rate (per-tenant, 7d rolling) target >= 99.5%
- transform_p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms per transform type
- budget_exceeded_rate (per-tenant) target < 0.5% over 30d
- impact on downstream request latency must be accounted under the API endpoint SLOs. Any tenant that causes >5% global SLO regression will be subject to throttling and remediation.

Security and Privacy Controls
----------------------------
- No transform primitive may inject raw tenant secrets. Any sensitive enrichment must be performed by an authenticated KMS-backed sidecar that returns a short-lived artifact reference.
- Tenant Policy store must be ACL-protected and audited. All policy changes require two reviewers for production scopes.
- Payload hashes must be salted with shard-specific key and stored in telemetry vault for 30 days.

Performance and Load Considerations
----------------------------------
- At scale, tenant transforms are a source of tail latency. To mitigate:
  1. Transform execution threads are isolated from request-acceptor threads using an internal worker pool per-edge-shard.
  2. CPU-bound augmentations (e.g., on-the-fly embeddings) must be offloaded to specialized ML worker pools and declared with cost estimates.
  3. A synthetic test harness must run per-tenant policy at acceptance time to validate median latency impact.

Rollout and Change Management
----------------------------
1. Policy authoring: developers create Tenant Policy in staging namespace and run unit + integration tests using the transform emulator.
2. Staged rollout:
   a. Canary: apply policy to a small percentage (1%) of traffic via runtime flag. Monitor transform_success_rate and latency metrics for 24h.
   b. Ramp: increase to 10% for 24–72h if canary is healthy.
   c. Full: apply to 100% after passing guardrails.
3. Automated rollback: if transform_success_rate drops below 98% or budget_exceeded_rate rises above 2% in any 10m window, policy is automatically rolled back and an alert triggers.

Operational Playbook (on-call steps)
-----------------------------------
1. Identify: alert receives "transform_budget_exceeded" or sudden jump in transform p99.
2. Triage: query tenant_id, transform.name, and inspect last 1h trace samples.
3. Mitigate: toggle tenant policy enforcement to permissive mode or disable the policy for the tenant.
4. Fix: escalate to owning team to optimize transform or increase budget.
5. Postmortem: if incident impacted SLOs, run a 72h postmortem with root cause and remediation actions.

Migration Guidance
------------------
- For teams with existing edge-layer scripts: migrate logic into Tenant Policy primitives. Maintain a compatibility shim during rollout for 30 days.
- For clients relying on implicit transform behavior, provide a migration window and a compatibility endpoint that preserves legacy behavior for signed tenants.

Example: API request before/after transform
------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
POST /v1/generate
{
  "prompt": "Summarize: \n- input: ..."
}

After (with prompt_prefix transform):
POST /v1/generate
{
  "prompt": "[Tenant: AcmeCorp | tone: concise]\nSummarize: \n- input: ..."
}

Testing and Acceptance Criteria
-------------------------------
- Unit tests for each transform primitive with schema validation cases.
- Integration tests exercising policy store + edge emulator.
- Performance gate: median added latency across a representative sample of requests must be <= tenant.cost_budget_ms.

Ownership and Contacts
----------------------
- Transform Engine: eng-serving-runtime (primary owner: Marco Ruiz)
- API Gateway Integration: eng-platform (primary owner: Priya Raman)
- Security Review: security-and-compliance (primary owner: Liang Zhao)

FAQ
---
Q: Can tenants define arbitrary templating for prompt injection?
A: Only the approved template library is allowed; custom templates require security and perf review.

Q: Are transforms versioned?
A: Yes — Tenant Policy references template and transform versions. Rollbacks must target the policy revision.

References
----------
- API Context Enrichment and Observability Contract (internal)
- Runtime-sidecar contract for private deployments (internal)
- Transform emulator test harness docs (eng-serving-runtime/test-harness/v1)

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft (Aisha Menon)
- 2025-11-03: Added streaming semantics and budget rules (Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-02-18: Finalized rollout automation and telemetry schema (Priya Raman)

payload.page_title: backward-compatibility-strategies-for-streaming-endpoints-2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This guideline defines our company-standard approach to backward compatibility for streaming inference endpoints (gRPC/HTTP2 server-sent events/HTTP chunked streaming). Streaming endpoints have different compatibility constraints than request/response APIs: long-lived connections, stateful per-request lifecycles (KV cache, partial outputs), and client SDK expectations for chunk framing. The goal is to provide concrete practices that minimize customer disruption while allowing the runtime and model-serving stack to evolve.

Applicability
-----------
- Applies to all public and internal Redwood inference streaming endpoints (hosted API streaming, Dedicated streaming, Private deployments) and any SDKs that surface streaming primitives.
- Applies to protocol-level changes, envelope/metadata changes, chunk framing, and semantic changes to streaming messages.
- Does NOT replace per-model quality change policies (use Optimize & evals to manage generation/regression risks).

Principles
---------
1. Principle of least surprise: preserve existing client parsing semantics for active minor versions.
2. Safe evolution: prefer additive changes; avoid breaking clients during long-lived connections.
3. Observable rollouts: all streaming changes require observability gates (SLOs, error metrics) before serving to >=10% of traffic.
4. SDK-first compatibility: SDKs are the reference implementation of client-side expectations — changes must ship SDK updates and server fallbacks.

Versioning model
---------------
- Major.Minor.Patch for API contracts. Major changes = incompatible protocol or message framing changes. Minor = additive fields, new optional events. Patch = server bugfixes and non-behavior changes.
- Streaming endpoints MUST include an explicit "stream_api_version" string in initial connection metadata/headers and first control message. Example header: "X-Redwood-Stream-Version: 1.4.0".
- Server behavior: if a client presents an unsupported major version, reject the connection with a typed error (see Error model).

Streaming-specific compatibility rules
----------------------------------
1. Framing and chunk semantics:
   - Never change chunk separator characters or byte-encoding without a major version bump.
   - For text-based streams (SSE/HTTP chunking), continue supporting CRLF and LF as delimiters for two minor releases.
2. Envelope and metadata additions:
   - Add fields only under an explicit envelope extension object: "extensions": {"field_name": value}. Clients that ignore unknown keys must continue to operate.
   - If adding required metadata for downstream routing (e.g., tenant-mapping), include it on a separate control event rather than embedding in every chunk.
3. Control events and lifecycle messages:
   - Control events (start, heartbeat, partial-complete, final-complete, error) are part of the stable contract. Add new control event types as optional until a major bump.
4. Binary payloads and serialization:
   - When introducing new serialization (protobuf v2 schema changes, compressed frames), the server must advertise supported encodings in initial handshake and accept negotiated encodings.
5. Behavioral changes (generation semantics):
   - Any change that could alter tokenization, KV cache semantics, or partial completion timing must be accompanied by a compatibility report and a canary plan (see Rollout steps).

Error model for streaming endpoints
--------------------------------
- Use typed control errors encoded as JSON in a control-event envelope: {"type":"stream.error","code":"UNSUPPORTED_VERSION","message":"...","retry_after_secs":30}.
- Map streaming control errors to standard HTTP/gRPC codes when the underlying connection is terminated (e.g., UNSUPPORTED -> 400/INVALID_ARGUMENT or gRPC INVALID_ARGUMENT).

Observability and gating
-----------------------
All streaming contract changes require telemetry to be added to the platform dashboards prior to broad rollout. Minimum telemetry set:
- Connection acceptance rate (per version)
- Control-error-rate (per code)
- Partial-output-latency P50/P95/P99 (ms)
- Token-throughput and per-token CPU/GPU utilization
- Client disconnects and reconnection rates within 60s of control events
- Data-plane cost delta (tokens * cost-per-token delta)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Connection success rate: >= 99.5% for non-heavy workloads
- Partial-output latency (P95) must not regress more than 20% relative to baseline for the first 24h of canary
- Control error rate < 0.1% for the affected traffic slice

Testing and CI gates (mandatory)
-------------------------------
1. Contract tests:
   - Unit and integration contract tests using the server and SDK mocks that validate behavior across advertised versions.
   - Golden-frames test: capture representative long-lived session traces and diff chunk sequences after changes.
2. Load and stability tests:
   - Simulate sustained 10k concurrent long-lived streams for Dedicated and Private serving variants.
   - Measure resource usage and KV cache growth (memory-pressure indicators).
3. Regression evals:
   - If streaming behavior affects generation output, run an automated eval against a blocklist of critical prompt-sets used by customers.
4. Chaos tests:
   - Connection flapping, mid-stream server restarts, and abrupt event drops. Ensure graceful reconnection semantics in >=90% of simulated sessions.

Deployment and rollout checklist
-----------------------------
1. ADR and design sign-off: create or update an ADR for major changes. Minor changes should reference existing ADRs when applicable.
2. SDK release: new SDK must be published with clear migration notes and deprecation warnings 2 weeks before server-enforced changes.
3. Observability: dashboards and alerting added to staging and prod.
4. Canary: start at 1% traffic for 6 hours -> 10% for 24 hours -> 30% for 24 hours -> 100%. Advance only if SLO gates are met.
5. Rollback plan: automated traffic routing rollback and feature flags to disable new control event types.
6. Customer communication: for changes that require client action, send targeted notices at 30/14/3 days before rollout with migration examples.

Performance budgets and infra considerations
----------------------------------------
- Target per-stream memory usage: < 200MB peak for 90% of streams on Dedicated instance classes (r5-gpu-48).
- KV cache growth threshold: if average per-stream KV cache grows > 2x baseline under canary, abort rollout and investigate.
- Burst capacity: streaming endpoints should permit 3x ephemeral bursting for 60s during client reconnection storms; autoscaling must honor burst limits configured in Dedicated.
- Quantization/Kernel changes: changes to runtime kernels that affect per-token latency must be tested with long-lived streaming workloads; measure tail-latency P99 and 99.9.

Developer and SDK guidance (examples)
---------------------------------
- Handshake header example (HTTP2):
  curl -v -H "X-Redwood-Stream-Version: 1.4.0" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
    https://inference.redwood.ai/v1/stream/generate

- Client expectation checklist:
  1) Treat unknown control events as ignorable for two minor versions.
  2) Implement idempotent reconnection: include last-acknowledged-token index in reconnection handshake.
  3) Respect backpressure signals from server control events (e.g., "throttle_hint_ms").

Decision records & history
------------------------
- ADR: stream-versioning-and-handshake-2025 (major model informing header usage).
- ADR: control-event-typing-2024 (defines control event envelope and error model).
- This document supersedes ad-hoc streaming notes and centralizes rollout/gating flow.

Appendix: sample control-event envelope (JSON)
-------------------------------------------
{"event":"control","name":"partial_complete","seq":12,"meta":{"token_index":256}}

Migration examples
-----------------
- Adding an optional confidence field in partial outputs:
  - Server adds: "extensions":{"confidence":0.94}
  - SDKs ignore unknown extension keys; server servers should not make client behavior rely on presence of extensions for two minor versions.

Ownership and contacts
---------------------
- API contract owner: Maya Chen (api-contracts@redwood.ai)
- Runtime lead (canary infra): Rajesh Nair (serving-runtime@redwood.ai)
- SDK owners: client-eng@redwood.ai

Notes and follow-ups
------------------
- Follow-up action: create an automated contract-diff job in CI that flags framing changes. Owner: api-contracts team.
- Quarterly review: this guideline will be revisited Q1 2027 or after two major streaming changes, whichever is earlier.

References
---------
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/api-compatibility-and-deprecation-policy-2026.json
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/streaming-protocols-and-kv-cache-2025
- ADR: control-event-typing-2024
