payload.page_title: Hardware Telemetry: Annotated Billing & Usage Schema

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the canonical telemetry envelope, field-level annotations, and aggregation rules used for hardware-level billing and usage accounting across Redwood Inference GPU and accelerator fleets. It describes the required schema for per-request and per-batch telemetry, encryption and redaction rules, sampling/aggregation guidance, SLOs for ingestion and billing pipelines, and a migration plan for rolling the schema to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals
- Produce a single, auditable canonical record that maps runtime signals to billable units (GPU-seconds, memory-hours, energy-kWh).
- Avoid leakage of customer PII or sensitive prompt content into billing datasets.
- Ensure forward/backwards compatibility for model and hardware changes.
- Provide clear owner and rollout steps to minimize chargeback disruption.

Scope
Applies to: runtime serving-side telemetry emitted by the serving runtime (service name: runtime-proxy), the node agent (service: hw-telemetry-agent), and the billing ingestion service (service: billing-ingest). Excludes: SDK-side client telemetry, customer application logs, and offline benchmarking harnesses (refer to related pages for those standards).

Key Definitions
- billable_unit: The atomic unit used for charging (e.g., gpu_core_second, mem_gb_hour, energy_kwh).
- telemetry_envelope: Top-level JSON object emitted per logical request/batch with metadata, cost attribution, and measurement array.
- annotated_field: A telemetry attribute that includes an annotation tag describing sensitivity, retention, and aggregation policy.

Telemetry envelope (required top-level fields)
The runtime MUST emit a single telemetry_envelope for every completed inference transaction (logical request) or for periodic batch windows (when batching/coalescing occurs). Fields below are required unless noted optional. Table described as bullet list:
- envelope_id (string, required): UUIDv4, unique per envelope.
- emitted_at (ISO8601 timestamp, required): time the envelope was emitted by runtime-proxy.
- source_service (string, required): one of [runtime-proxy, hw-telemetry-agent, model-runner].
- tenant_id (string, required): opaque tenant identifier (no customer names or emails).
- billing_keys (array of strings, required): list of billing tags that map to pricing tiers (e.g., ["dedicated:large-gpu", "region:us-west-2"]).
- measurements (array of measurement objects, required): see Measurement object schema below.
- annotations (object, optional): free-form annotation map; keys MUST follow dotted-naming and values MUST be strings. Annotations are intended for internal tooling only and are not persisted in raw billing export unless explicitly flagged.

Measurement object (fields)
Each measurement represents a time-windowed metric sample tied to the envelope. Measurements MUST include:
- metric_name (string, required): one of ["gpu_core_seconds", "gpu_memory_gb_seconds", "energy_kwh", "kv_cache_mb_seconds", "io_bytes"].
- value (decimal as string, required): numeric value represented as string to avoid float rounding in transit (e.g., "0.125").
- window_start (ISO8601, required) and window_end (ISO8601, required): inclusive start/exclusive end.
- aggregation (string, required): one of ["sum", "max", "p95"]. For billing, preferred aggregation is "sum".
- provenance (string, optional): low-cardinality tag indicating source e.g., "node-agent", "runtime-sampler", "scheduler-estimate".
- annotations (array of strings, optional): standardized annotation tokens (see annotation catalog).

Annotation catalog (selected tokens)
- sensitive:retain_short — data may contain short-lived sensitive metadata; retention 7 days.
- sensitive:redact_hash — raw content must be hashed with SHA256 and stored only as hash.
- retention:30d — retain raw metric for 30 days then roll up.
- public_aggregate — safe to include in public dashboards.

PII and Prompt Redaction Rules
- The telemetry envelope MUST NOT contain raw prompts, prompt fragments, or customer content. If the serving runtime currently attaches context for debugging, that payload MUST be replaced by a redaction marker and optionally a SHA256 hash (annotation token: sensitive:redact_hash).
- Tenant identifiers must be opaque numeric/hex tokens. No email addresses, organization names, or API keys in telemetry fields.

Encryption and Transport
- All envelopes sent from runtime-proxy or hw-telemetry-agent to intermediate collectors MUST be transmitted over mTLS with at least TLS 1.3.
- Fields annotated with sensitive:* MUST be encrypted at rest with a per-space envelope key managed by KMS. The billing-ingest pipeline will have a KMS consumer role (billing-ingest-kms) and must request decryption only for reconciliations under a compliant audit trail.

Sampling and Aggregation Guidance
- Production high-volume tenants: Runtime may sample telemetry at 10% by default for full-resolution measurements when emissions exceed 10k envelopes/min. Sampling MUST be deterministic by tenant_id and time-slice to allow unbiased extrapolation.
- For sampled envelopes, add annotation sampling:rate=0.1 and include an extrapolation_factor decimal as string ("10.0" for 10% sampling). Billing pipelines MUST multiply sampled measurements by extrapolation_factor during raw-to-billable transforms.
- Aggregation windows MUST align to 1s multiples; billing-ingest will convert to billing_unit rounding up to 10ms resolution.

Billing transformation rules (example)
1) Convert gpu_core_seconds to billable gpu_core_second unit (1 gpu_core_second = 1.0 core * 1 second).
2) If envelope contains sampling.extrapolation_factor, multiply summed metric by that factor.
3) Apply tenant pricing lookup using billing_keys and price_table version header (pricing_version in envelope annotations).
4) Round resulting cost to 4 decimal places for ledger entries.

SLOs and Monitoring
- Telemetry ingestion availability: 99.95% monthly for billing-ingest (tracked by uptime and queue latency).
- Bill latency: 95% of envelopes transformed and written to billing-staging within 1 minute of emitted_at; 99th percentile within 5 minutes.
- Data correctness: nightly reconciliation job between billing_ledger and raw_metrics must produce missing-rate < 0.01% and cost-delta < 0.1% across top-10 tenants.

Ownership and Roles
- Owner: infra-costing team (primary contact: Sanjay Patel).
- Runtime emission owner: serving-runtime team (on-call: runtime-squad).
- Billing ingestion owner: platform-billing team (contact: Marina Alvarez).
- Security reviewer: security-compliance team (contact: Priya Nair).

Versioning and Compatibility
- Schema uses semantic schema_version field (major.minor). Major bump indicates incompatible changes (required code changes in ingesters). Minor/patch bumps are additive and implementers must tolerate unknown fields.
- Backward compatibility rules: consumers MUST ignore unknown measurement.metric_name values but MUST log and alert if unknown metric_name persists for >6 hours to avoid silent billing gaps.

Implementation checklist for runtime teams
1. Implement envelope_id and basic fields.
2. Ensure tenant_id obfuscation logic (no email/name).
3. Add annotations for any sensitive content and implement redaction per rules.
4. Integrate mTLS client certs and KMS encryption for sensitive fields.
5. Emit sampling metadata when sampling is active.
6. Run local validation tool (telemetry-validator CLI) against schema.
7. Coordinate rollout with platform-billing for a staged ingestion: shadow -> partial pay -> full billing.

Example telemetry envelope (JSON for illustration)
{
  "envelope_id": "a3f4e2d0-6f12-4b9a-8c1f-9ef2b0b9a1c2",
  "emitted_at": "2026-02-28T17:23:54.123Z",
  "source_service": "runtime-proxy",
  "tenant_id": "t-8f7a6c4b",
  "billing_keys": ["dedicated:dgx-a10x","region:eu-central-1"],
  "measurements": [
    {"metric_name":"gpu_core_seconds","value":"0.450","window_start":"2026-02-28T17:23:54Z","window_end":"2026-02-28T17:23:55Z","aggregation":"sum","provenance":"model-runner"},
    {"metric_name":"gpu_memory_gb_seconds","value":"4.500","window_start":"2026-02-28T17:23:54Z","window_end":"2026-02-28T17:23:55Z","aggregation":"sum","provenance":"node-agent"}
  ],
  "annotations": {"schema_version":"1.0","sampling.rate":"0.1","sampling.extrapolation_factor":"10.0"}
}

Testing and validation
- Run telemetry-validator against 1000 synthetic envelopes; ensure schema errors < 0.1%.
- Use billing-staging to replay sampled data; verify cost extrapolation correctness with simulated price_table changes.
- Chaos test: run node-agent disconnect scenario for 30m and ensure billing-ingest fills gap with scheduler-estimate provenance and reconciliation rate remains within SLO.

Rollout plan (staged)
1. Week 0: announce change and provide client library and telemetry-validator tool.
2. Week 1-2: runtime-proxy emits new envelope with `schema_version=1.0` in shadow mode (no billing applied).
3. Week 3: platform-billing enables partial cost attribution for small tenant subset (5% traffic).
4. Week 5: full migration if nightly reconciliation metrics are within thresholds.
5. Rollback criteria: cost-delta > 1% for top 10 tenants OR missing-rate > 0.05% over 24h.

Appendix: CLI snippets and helpers
- telemetry-validator: `telemetry-validator --input sample.json --schema version=1.0`
- local-run replay: `replayer --env-file sample.json --dest billing-staging --replay-rate 100/s`

Related pages and references
- GPU maintenance and tenant fairness policy (link in related_pages).
- Service energy and cost accounting metadata standard (link in related_pages).

Questions and feedback
Send comments to infra-costing@redwood.com or open a PR in the infra-standards repo.

payload.page_title: Cold Start & Warmup Sequence Specification for Inference Nodes

sections.body:
Purpose
This page defines the standardized cold start and warmup sequence for Redwood inference nodes (hosted / dedicated / private) to ensure predictable latency, controlled cost, and reproducible behavior across deployments. It describes the desired state transitions, required telemetry, configuration knobs, and an executable warmup recipe for common model classes.

Scope
- Applies to all GPU-backed inference nodes managed by node-provisioner and serve-runtime across Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private runtime-sidecars.
- Covers node lifecycle states: PROVISIONING -> BOOTSTRAPPING -> MODEL_PREFETCH -> KV_CACHE_WARM -> READY -> DEGRADED.
- Excludes application-level client warmup (client libraries should implement separate jitter/backoff).

Goals and SLOs
- Node readiness p95 <= 30s for warm reboots (same model pinned)
- Cold provisioning p95 <= 120s for full model load (large foundation models up to 70B in sharded mode)
- Model load time per-shard p95 <= 20s (target for shard sizes <= 8GB)
- KV cache priming success rate >= 99% within warmup window
- No more than 0.5% additional request error budget consumed by cold-starts in Normal load profiles

Key Concepts and Components
- node-provisioner: allocates VM/GPU nodes and performs OS-level bootstrapping (networks, mounts). Responsible for PROVISIONING -> BOOTSTRAPPING.
- runtime-agent (on-node): lightweight agent that coordinates model fetch, integrity verification, and exposes readiness via /internal/health/node-ready.
- model-cache: local disk/LV store where model shards are persisted and validated; sealed artifacts are signed and verified against artifact-provenance metadata.
- model-loader (integration in serve-runtime): loads model into GPU memory, shards KV cache if applicable, and reports model_load_time metric.
- kv-cache-service: optional prefilling of KV cache from persisted previous sessions or precomputed prefixes.

Acceptable Degradation Modes
1) Fallback to quantized variant (Q4_K_M) when model load time > configured threshold (see Config table).
2) Serve from smaller context window with early-exit policy for streaming requests until KV cache is warm.
3) Route low-priority requests to Best-Effort pool until node reaches READY.

Warmup Sequence (detailed)
1) PROVISIONING (node-provisioner)
   - Allocate requested GPU type and attach model-store volume
   - Emit metric: node_provision_requested{gpu_type} and node_provision_duration_seconds
2) BOOTSTRAPPING (runtime-agent)
   - Start runtime-agent, mount model-store, apply node-level flags from config service
   - Verify connectivity to model-catalog and key-management service (KMS)
   - Health probe: runtime-agent exposes /internal/health/agent-ready
3) MODEL_PREFETCH (model-loader)
   - Validate model artifact signature and compare checksum
   - Stream shards from model-store to local cache in parallel (default parallelism = min(4, vCPU_count))
   - Metric to emit: model_shard_stream_time_seconds and model_shards_failed
4) MODEL_LOAD (serve-runtime)
   - Load shards into device memory; allocate KV cache buffers according to flavor profile
   - Emit model_loaded{model,variant,shard_count} and model_load_time_seconds
5) KV_CACHE_WARM (kv-cache-service + serve-runtime)
   - Execute a configurable set of synthetic prompts to prime common attention patterns and populate KV entries
   - Default warmup prompt set: 10 prompts per shard tuned for tokens distribution representative of production workload
   - Metric: kv_cache_fill_ratio and kv_cache_priming_success
6) READY
   - runtime-agent sets /internal/health/node-ready = 200 once model_loaded and kv_cache_fill_ratio >= configured threshold (default 0.6)
   - Emit node_ready_time_seconds (from provision request to READY)

Configuration Table (required fields and suggested defaults)
| key | service | default | description |
| node.warmup.parallel_shard_streams | node-provisioner | 4 | Parallel streams used when fetching shards from model-store |
| node.warmup.kv_prompt_set | serve-runtime | /etc/warmup/default_prompts.txt | Path to warmup prompts used to seed KV cache |
| node.warmup.kv_threshold | serve-runtime | 0.6 | Fraction of expected KV entries that must be present before READY |
| node.warmup.model_load_timeout_s | runtime-agent | 120 | Max time to attempt model load before falling back to quantized variant |
| node.warmup.allow_quant_fallback | serve-runtime | true | Enable automatic fallback to quantized variant on load/timeouts |
| node.warmup.prefetch_retries | node-provisioner | 2 | Number of retries for shard streaming before failing node provisioning |

Warmup Prompt Example (default_prompts.txt)
- "Translate the following sentence to French: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.'"
- "Summarize the key points: (a) product launch (b) target audience (c) go-to-market channels."
- "Classify the sentiment for: 'This update significantly improved our onboarding flow.'"

YAML Recipe: prefetch-and-prime (runtime-agent CLI)
---
steps:
  - name: prefetch-shards
    command: "/usr/local/bin/runtime-agent prefetch --model-id {{MODEL_ID}} --parallel 4 --dest /var/lib/model-cache"
    timeout: 90
  - name: load-model
    command: "/usr/local/bin/model-loader load --path /var/lib/model-cache/{{MODEL_ID}} --variant auto"
    timeout: 120
  - name: prime-kv
    command: "/usr/local/bin/kv-primer --prompts /etc/warmup/default_prompts.txt --concurrency 8 --budget-ms 5000"
    timeout: 30
---

Telemetry and Metrics (required)
- node_ready_time_seconds (histogram) - labels: region, gpu_type, pool_id, model_family
- model_load_time_seconds (histogram) - labels: model_id, variant, shard_index
- model_shard_stream_time_seconds (histogram) - labels: model_id, src_bucket
- kv_cache_fill_ratio (gauge) - labels: model_id, shard_group
- cold_request_latency_inflation_percent (gauge) - measure of latency delta for initial requests vs steady-state

Alerting and Runbook Integrations
- Alert: NodeWarmupFailure (SEV3) when node_ready_time_seconds.p95 > configured cold threshold (default 180s) or model_shards_failed > 0 for > 3 nodes in 15m
- Alert: KVPrimingLag (SEV4) when kv_cache_fill_ratio < node.warmup.kv_threshold for > 10m after model_loaded
- Runbook: See /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/node-warmup-and-prewarm-troubleshooting (includes commands: runtime-agent logs, model-loader --debug, re-trigger prefetch)

Fallback and Safety Policies
- If model_load_time > node.warmup.model_load_timeout_s and allow_quant_fallback = true, automatically switch to quantized variant and mark node with label fallback_quant=true. Teams must record quality impact in rollout notes.
- Respect cost-control flag node.warmup.disable_prefetch in burst mode to avoid cross-tenant egress spikes.

Rollout and Adoption Guidance
1) Canary: enable warmup recipe for 1% of newly provisioned nodes in a single region for 48 hours and track node_ready_time_seconds and cold_request_latency_inflation_percent.
2) Gradual ramp: increase to 10% for 72 hours, then 50% for 7 days, validating no more than 2x baseline egress cost and no SLA regressions.
3) Full rollout: enable by default once metrics and cost are within acceptable ranges.

Ownership and Responsibilities
- eng-infra: node-provisioner and model-store maintenance, capacity accounting, and billing impact evaluation.
- eng-serving-runtime: runtime-agent, model-loader, KV primer, and readiness contract.
- product: communicate behavioral changes for Dedicated/Private customers and provide migration notes.

Open Questions and Future Work
- Adaptive warmup: investigate ML-driven prompt selection for KV priming to minimize tokens while maximizing hit-rate.
- Cross-tenant warmup sharing for identical model variants on the same node while preserving tenancy isolation and accounting.
- Persistence optimizations for incremental shard diffs to reduce prefetch bandwidth for minor patch releases.

References
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/model-artifact-provenance-and-signing-standard-2026
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026

Appendix: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
1) Verify runtime-agent logs: sudo journalctl -u runtime-agent -n 500
2) Check model-store connectivity: curl -sSf https://model-catalog.internal/v1/models/{{MODEL_ID}}/manifest
3) Re-run prefetch: /usr/local/bin/runtime-agent prefetch --model-id {{MODEL_ID}} --parallel 2 --dest /var/lib/model-cache
4) If quant-fallback triggered, compare sample outputs against golden set and file a regression ticket with eng-serving-runtime

Document history
- 2024-11-15: Draft created by Priya Rao
- 2024-12-02: Added YAML recipe and updated metrics (review by Diego Martin)
- 2025-02-10: Finalized SLOs and rollout plan, published

payload.page_title: elastic-tenant-quarantine-and-throttle-procedure

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook defines detection, containment, and remediation steps for noisy or misbehaving tenants that threaten cluster stability or SLOs. The procedure covers automatic and manual quarantine flows, throttling profiles, verification steps, and postmortem expectations. It is intended for Eng-SRE on-call and platform engineers who operate the runtime-router, edge-proxy, and autoscaling controllers.

Why this exists

As Redwood scales, a single tenant (customer, internal team, or integration test harness) can cause disproportionate resource consumption (GPU saturation, massive KV cache pressure, or telemetry storms). The goal is to contain impact quickly, restore service-level SLOs for other tenants, and provide reproducible remediation and follow-up.

Scope and applicability

- Applies to Hosted API and Dedicated pools where multi-tenant eviction/soft-quota is enabled.
- Not intended for air-gapped Private deployments — see eng-private-deployments runbooks for localized controls.
- Covers both burst and steady-state noisy neighbors.

Detection signals (primary)

1. p95 inference latency for runtime-router > configured latency budget AND error rate spike for a tenant (>= 5x baseline in 5m).
2. GPU util (per-pool) > 85% sustained for 10m with a single tenant accounting for >50% of requests.
3. KV cache churn > 1.5x normal eviction rate OR prefix miss ratio > 30% for a tenant's keys.
4. Edge-proxy 5xx rate >= 0.5% absolute or 5x baseline for 3m.
5. Telemetry ingestion backlog increases > 2x for tenant metrics or trace volume (indicates noisy sampling).

Detection signals (secondary)

- Rate limiter tripping frequently for a client token.
- Excessive streaming open connections per tenant (> 200).

Thresholds and containment decision matrix

| Signal | Alert threshold | Initial action | Escalation threshold |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| p95 latency (runtime-router) | > 400ms for 5m | soft-throttle 50% | > 800ms or sustained 15m -> quarantine |
| GPU pool util (per-GPU) | > 85% sustained 10m | shed low-priority queues | > 95% sustained 5m -> quarantine |
| KV cache eviction rate | > 1.5x baseline | increase cache-ttl weighting for high-hits | > 3x -> quarantine |
| 5xx rate (edge-proxy) | >= 0.5% for 3m | apply 429-based backpressure | >= 2% or >10m -> quarantine |

Definitions

- Soft-throttle: a per-tenant token-based rate limit and early drop that reduces throughput but allows best-effort traffic through. Implemented via edge-proxy token-bucket adjustments.
- Quarantine: a higher-confidence containment that moves tenant to a restricted policy (aggressive rate limits, disallow long-running streams, route to lower-fidelity model variants). Quarantine can be automatic or manual.

Automated flow (recommended)

1. Alert fires on the detection rule in PagerDuty (SRE-runbook alert). The alert page includes tenant-id, top endpoints, example requests, and recent telemetry link.
2. Automated controller evaluates runbook rules (runtime-guardian) and computes containment action: either apply soft-throttle profile or quarantine profile.
3. If soft-throttle selected: runtime-guardian issues config to edge-proxy with a JSON patch to tenant-rate-limits. Sample CLI:

rctl tenant throttle --tenant-id tenant_1234 --mode soft --ingress-rps 120 --burst 200

4. If quarantine selected: runtime-guardian triggers a higher-priority policy and notifies on-call with pre-populated remediation checklist. Quarantine command (manual approval required for non-critical tenants):

rctl tenant quarantine --tenant-id tenant_1234 --apply-policy quarantine-2026-01 --reason "gpu-saturation"

Manual flow (when automation is disabled or ambiguous)

1. Triage the alert: confirm tenant, inspect traces, check recent deploys, load tests, and internal jobs. Primary dashboards: runtime-router/top-tenants, gpu-fleet/pool-util, kv-cache/tenant-breakdown.
2. If tenant is internal or test harness, contact owning team and apply temporary shutdown via service token rotation or disable client key.
3. For production tenants, engage account exec only after containment — do not delay containment for notification.

Containment profiles (examples)

- soft-throttle-profile-v1: ingress-rps = tenant_baseline * 1.2, burst = 200, priority = normal, stream-max-duration = 60s.
- restricted-quarantine-v1: ingress-rps = 50, burst = 20, priority = low, stream-max-duration = 10s, route-model = small-fallback-v1, disallow tools/function-calls.
- critical-cold-cut: immediate connection drain + 0 rps (use only for proven hostile or runaway billing risk).

Configuration table

| Config key | Location | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| tenant-rate-limit.rps | edge-proxy config | 100 | Per-tenant default; adjusted by runtime-guardian |
| tenant-burst | edge-proxy config | 300 | Applied as token-bucket capacity |
| quarantine-policy | runtime-config-store (/configs/quarantine) | n/a | JSON policy documents referenced by runtime-guardian |
| telemetry-snapshot-window | telemetry-pipeline | 5m | Window used for moving averages in alerts |

Step-by-step containment procedure (on-call)

1. Acknowledge PagerDuty alert and open the SRE incident channel.
2. Verify the tenant-id and the signal(s). Capture the last 10 requests (request-ids) and attach to the incident.
3. Try soft-throttle first unless GPU util > 95% or 5xx >2% (see matrix). Apply:

rctl tenant throttle --tenant-id <id> --mode soft --ingress-rps <calc> --burst <calc>

4. Monitor for 5 minutes. Verify p95 latency improvement and drop in cross-tenant impact. If no improvement or tenant is bypassing throttles, escalate to quarantine.

5. Quarantine steps (manual approval required unless automated rule matched):
  a. Apply quarantine policy: rctl tenant quarantine --tenant-id <id> --apply-policy restricted-quarantine-v1 --ticket <pd-incident-id>
  b. Rotate tenant token if abuse suspected: rctl tenant rotate-token --tenant-id <id> --force
  c. If streams persist, forcibly close long connections via edge-proxy: kubectl exec -n edge-proxy edge-proxy-0 -- /bin/close-conns --tenant <id>

6. Notify account and product teams after containment. Provide observed metrics and applied policy.

Rollback and recovery

- Recovery criteria: p95 latency < baseline + 20% for 15m AND GPU pool util < 70% for 15m AND 5xx < 0.2% for 15m.
- To rollback: incrementally restore rate limits over a 30 minute window:

rctl tenant throttle --tenant-id <id> --mode blended --ingress-rps <50% of previous> --burst <half>
(wait 10m) then increase to 75%, etc.

- Document applied changes in the incident ticket and schedule a post-incident review if quarantine lasted > 10m or if billing exposure occurred.

Testing and validation

- Canary tests: apply quarantine policy to a synthetic tenant in staging and validate that the policy limits remove load from pool without affecting other tenants.
- Chaos test: run a scheduled SRE game-day that simulates a tenant with high streaming connections and verify monitoring/automations.

Metrics and SLOs to observe

- Cross-tenant p95 latency (runtime-router): target < 250ms; alert if > 400ms.
- GPU pool saturation: alert if per-GPU util > 85% for 10m.
- Telemetry backlog: no more than 2x baseline for more than 10m.
- Quarantine false-positive rate: target < 1% of quarantines per quarter (measured by post-incident rollbacks where tenant had no abnormal behavior).

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: Eng-SRE (sre-team@redwood.com).
- Secondary owner: Platform (platform-ops@redwood.com).
- On-call escalation: PagerDuty -> Platform lead -> VP Eng (if customer-impacting and > 60m unresolved).

Communication templates

- Customer notification (template):

"Redwood Inference has detected abnormal traffic from your integration (tenant-id: <id>) and has applied temporary rate limits to protect service stability. We are investigating and will restore normal traffic when safe. Contact: support@redwood.com."

Post-incident review requirements

- Owners must create a short incident summary within 48 hours with: timeline of actions, telemetry snapshots, root cause (if identified), remediation plan, and any billing adjustments.
- If removal of a customer key or token rotation occurred, include audit log references.

Security and compliance notes

- Quarantine/rotation actions are audited in audit-logging/tenants with correlated request IDs and actor.
- For regulated customers, coordinate with Security prior to any token rotation that may cause data deletion or loss of audit continuity.

References and links

- Runtime guardian controller design: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/adaptive-kv-coordinator-and-eviction-contract-2026
- Tenant rate-limiter implementation (edge-proxy): /confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/edge-proxy-request-mux-and-tenant-routing-standard-2026
- SLOs and escalation matrix: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/cascading-slo-failure-mitigation-and-federated-budget-playbook-2024

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: created by Aisha Patel (initial draft)
- 2026-01-20: added automated runtime-guardian flow, reviewer feedback incorporated (Marcus Chen)
- 2026-02-15: tightened thresholds for GPU util and added recovery criteria (approved)

Appendix: example quarantine policy (JSON)

{
  "policy_name": "restricted-quarantine-v1",
  "ingress_rps": 50,
  "burst": 20,
  "stream_max_seconds": 10,
  "route_model": "small-fallback-v1",
  "disallowed_features": ["function-calls", "long-streams"]
}

(Insert this JSON into /configs/quarantine via the runtime-config-store CLI.)

End of document

payload.page_title: Artifact Signing Standard (Company-wide)

sections.body:
This standard defines Redwood Inference’s minimum requirements for cryptographic signing of release artifacts. The goal is to reduce supply-chain risk by ensuring integrity and provenance of artifacts delivered to customers or used to run customer workloads.

This document is company-wide and applies to all product lines and deployment modes (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Additional requirements may be layered on by product-specific docs, but may not weaken the controls here.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- What artifacts must be signed and verified
- Minimum metadata and canonicalization requirements
- Key custody and access controls
- Verification requirements (including “fail-closed” expectations)
- Audit logging and evidence expectations
- Exception / break-glass process
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- Full customer-managed signing root delegation (tracked as a future capability for some Private deployments)
- Detailed per-repo CI/CD implementation steps (see Release Engineering pipeline docs)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Artifact**: Any file, bundle, image, or manifest used to deploy, operate, or upgrade Redwood software.
- **Signature**: Cryptographic signature over an artifact (or over a canonical manifest describing a set of artifacts).
- **Trust root / trusted key**: Public keys distributed with Redwood verification tooling or configured in customer environments.
- **Fail-closed**: Verification failures prevent install/upgrade/runtime use unless an approved break-glass path is invoked.
- **SBOM**: Software Bill of Materials for an artifact or bundle.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
- **Installers and on-prem tooling**: CLI installers, bootstrap binaries, upgrade utilities.
- **Offline bundles** (Redwood Private VPC/on-prem): bundle manifest + signature; SBOM pointer + hash; any deterministic bundle metadata.
- **Helm chart artifacts**: chart tarballs and/or a signed chart manifest that includes chart checksums.
- **Runtime binaries**: Redwood runtime components shipped to customers (agents, controllers, node daemons).
- **Configuration schemas and policy bundles** that affect runtime security posture (e.g., RBAC/policy bundles).
sections.heading: The following MUST be signed for any customer distribution

sections.body:
- **Container images** for Redwood services and dependencies distributed to customers (Private / Dedicated images distributed via registry export or offline mirror).
- **Model/runtime artifacts** delivered for Private deployments (e.g., quantized weights, tokenizer assets, engine-specific compiled artifacts).

Requirement note: Where signing a “set” of artifacts is more practical (e.g., an offline bundle), Redwood MUST sign a canonical manifest that includes hashes for each artifact and MUST verify those hashes during installation.
sections.heading: 2) Customer-impacting machine artifacts (strongly recommended; required when feasible)

sections.body:
Artifacts used solely in internal environments SHOULD be signed where possible, and MUST be signed if:
- They are promoted across environments (dev → staging → prod) and are executable or deployable; or
- They are referenced as part of customer evidence (e.g., provenance attestations used in audits).
sections.heading: 3) Internal-only artifacts

sections.body:
- Approved signature algorithms: **Ed25519** or **ECDSA P-256**.
- Approved digests for artifact hashing: **SHA-256**.
- Hashes MUST be computed over the exact bytes delivered to the customer (post-packaging). If compression is used, the signed data MUST be clearly defined (e.g., the compressed tarball bytes, or an inner manifest listing uncompressed file hashes).
sections.heading: Algorithms

sections.body:
1) **Direct signing**: signature is over a single artifact (e.g., installer binary).
2) **Manifest signing** (preferred for bundles): signature is over a canonical manifest that lists all artifacts and their hashes.

For Redwood Private offline bundles, manifest signing is REQUIRED.
sections.heading: One of the following patterns MUST be used

sections.body:
If the signed object is structured data (JSON/YAML), the signing pipeline MUST use a deterministic canonicalization scheme.
- The canonicalization method MUST be explicitly documented in the owning design/ADR.
- Canonicalization MUST not depend on tool versions that can reorder fields nondeterministically.
- The verifier MUST reproduce the canonical form (or verify a canonical-by-construction encoding).
sections.heading: Canonicalization

sections.body:
- Signatures MUST be distributed alongside artifacts in a predictable location.
- Signature metadata MUST allow identifying the signing key (Key ID / fingerprint).
- For offline/air-gapped scenarios, verification MUST work with no network access.
sections.heading: Signature storage and distribution

sections.body:
For each signed artifact OR each entry in a signed manifest, Redwood MUST record and expose (to verifiers and for auditability):
- Artifact name
- Artifact type (e.g., installer, chart, image, model asset, manifest)
- Version (semantic version or release identifier)
- Build identifier (bundle build ID / pipeline run ID)
- Source revision (git commit SHA) and repo name (or monorepo path)
- SHA-256 digest
- Size (bytes) where applicable
sections.heading: Artifact metadata (minimum)

sections.body:
For each signature, Redwood MUST record and expose:
- Signature algorithm
- Signing key identifier (Key ID / fingerprint)
- Signing timestamp (UTC)
- Signing service identity (e.g., “Release Signing Service”)
- Optional validity window info (when applicable)
sections.heading: Signature metadata (minimum)

sections.body:
- An SBOM MUST be produced and referenced (either embedded or via pointer) for offline bundles and installers.
- The signed manifest MUST include the SBOM filename/pointer and SHA-256 of the SBOM artifact.
- Where supported by the build system, provenance attestations SHOULD be generated (e.g., build provenance describing builder identity, inputs, and outputs).
sections.heading: For customer-delivered artifacts

sections.body:
- Release signing private keys MUST be stored in a managed key system with strong access controls (HSM or cloud KMS with HSM-backed keys where feasible).
- Private keys MUST NOT be exportable to developer laptops.
- Private keys MUST NOT be stored as plaintext in CI variables.
sections.heading: Key storage

sections.body:
- Access to use signing keys MUST be limited to a designated **Signing Operator** role and an automated signing service identity.
- Separation of duties:
  - Individuals who approve a release SHOULD NOT be the only individuals who can perform signing.
  - Signing operations MUST be auditable and attributable.
sections.heading: Access control

sections.body:
- New signing keys MUST be created via a documented key ceremony.
- The ceremony MUST capture evidence artifacts sufficient for customer security reviews (attendees, approvals, key IDs/fingerprints, system of record).
- Trust root distribution changes (e.g., adding a new public key to verifiers) MUST follow a controlled release process and be communicated for air-gapped customers.
sections.heading: Key ceremony and onboarding

sections.body:
- Keys MUST have an established rotation cadence (at least annually) and an emergency rotation process.
- Verifiers MUST support multiple trusted public keys to allow safe rotation.
- A compromised key MUST be treated as a security incident and follow the Security incident response process, including:
  - Revocation/disable of signing operations
  - Distribution of updated trust stores
  - Customer communication plan (for Private/Dedicated)
sections.heading: Rotation and revocation

sections.body:
Any system that consumes signed artifacts MUST verify signatures and MUST fail closed by default.
- Install/upgrade operations MUST block when signature verification fails.
- Verifiers MUST validate:
  - The signature cryptographically matches the signed content
  - The signing key is trusted
  - The artifact hashes match the manifest entries (if manifest-based)
sections.heading: Fail-closed behavior

sections.body:
- Verification MUST require no network calls.
- Any time-based checks MUST document how time is obtained/validated in offline environments and MUST provide clear remediation when time is invalid (e.g., skew). Diagnostic overrides may be permitted only via break-glass.
sections.heading: For air-gapped environments

sections.body:
- The verifier SHOULD enforce anti-downgrade using signed version metadata plus a local install state record.
- Replayed bundles MUST be detectable where it materially impacts security posture (e.g., reintroducing known-vulnerable components).
sections.heading: Where artifacts are used for upgrades

sections.body:
- Provide a stable error code taxonomy and human-readable message
- Log the failing key ID, artifact name, and which check failed (unknown key, signature invalid, hash mismatch, manifest parse error, etc.)
- Provide remediation steps (update trust store, re-transfer bundle, obtain correct bundle version, check time source)
sections.heading: Verification failures MUST be actionable

sections.body:
For customer-facing releases, CI/CD MUST enforce:
- Artifacts cannot be promoted to “release” state without successful signing
- Verification tests run against produced artifacts (including negative tests: tampered manifest, swapped artifact, truncated bundle)
- Signed artifacts are immutable once published (or publication creates a new version/build ID)
sections.heading: Release pipeline gates

sections.body: - Build outputs referenced by signed manifests SHOULD be deterministic (same inputs produce identical outputs). Where full determinism is not feasible, the manifest MUST capture the exact output digests and build identifiers.
sections.heading: Reproducibility and determinism

sections.body:
Systems performing verification MUST emit audit events (locally for Private; centrally where applicable) for:
- Verification success
- Verification failure (with reason category)
- Break-glass override used
- Trust store updates (addition/removal of keys)
sections.heading: Minimum audit events

sections.body:
- Avoid logging sensitive customer payload data
- Prefer hashed identifiers and explicit redaction rules
sections.heading: Audit events MUST

sections.body:
- Events MUST be retained locally according to the Private audit logging guidance.
- Where a customer has SIEM export enabled, events SHOULD be mappable to common schemas.
sections.heading: For Private deployments

sections.body: Unsigned artifacts are a last resort. Exceptions are permitted only to restore availability in time-critical incidents and MUST be timeboxed, risk-accepted, and auditable.
sections.heading: Principle

sections.body:
- Emergency hotfix where the signing service is unavailable and customer impact is severe
- Verified internal-only artifact for a short-lived dev environment (never customer-distributed)
sections.heading: Allowed exceptions (examples)

sections.body:
1) Be approved by:
   - Release Engineering Lead (or delegate)
   - Security Engineering Lead
   - Security executive sponsor for high-risk customer distributions
2) Include documented risk acknowledgment and customer communication plan (if customer-facing)
3) Produce an auditable record (ticket + approvals + artifacts shipped)
4) Include a remediation plan to return to signed distribution and prevent recurrence
sections.heading: Any exception to this standard MUST

sections.body:
If a product includes a break-glass flag to bypass verification, the following MUST be true:
- Default behavior is still fail-closed
- Break-glass is explicitly labeled, requires an intentional flag, and prints warnings
- Break-glass usage emits an audit event and is included in support bundles
- Documentation clearly states that break-glass is for diagnostic/emergency use only and should be reversed as soon as possible
sections.heading: Break-glass verification override (customer environments)

sections.body:
- **Owner (policy)**: Security Engineering
- **Owner (implementation)**: Release Engineering for signing; individual product teams for verification in their installers/runtimes
- **Compliance mapping**: GRC owns evidence mapping to customer/security questionnaires and frameworks
sections.heading: Roles and ownership

sections.body:
- New systems that ship artifacts to customers MUST implement signing/verification before GA.
- Existing systems MUST align to this standard per the roadmap defined by Release Engineering and Security; exceptions must be documented and timeboxed.
- Security reviews for Private/Dedicated deployments MUST include validation that this standard is met (signing, trust store, verification tests, audit events).
sections.heading: Compliance and enforcement

sections.body:
- 2026-01-30: Clarified offline/air-gapped requirements (no network verification), added minimum audit event list, and aligned exception language with break-glass policy.
- 2025-11-12: Initial publication of company-wide artifact signing requirements.

payload.page_title: Dynamic Priority Sharding and Tenant Fairness Policy

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document specifies a cross-cutting policy and implementation guidance for dynamic priority sharding in Redwood’s inference runtime. The policy defines how inference traffic is partitioned across GPU shards by tenant priority while enforcing tenant fairness, cost allocation transparency, and SLO preservation. It includes an ADR-style decision rationale, infra and API contract changes, code-level best practices, monitoring queries, alert thresholds, and a staged rollout plan.

Motivation
----------
- We repeatedly observe two correlated problems in multi-tenant clusters: (1) high-priority tenants can monopolize shared resources in bursty scenarios causing lower-priority tenants to miss latency SLOs, and (2) static shard assignment or naive priority queuing leads to poor cost allocation and degraded overall throughput.
- Goals: preserve per-tenant latency SLOs where committed, avoid starvation, make cost attribution deterministic, and enable rapid graceful degradation of low-priority workloads under contention.

Decision (what we are adopting)
--------------------------------
1. Implement a dynamic priority sharding layer in the request router that assigns incoming requests to logical shards based on a time-windowed token budget computed per-tenant and per-priority class.
2. Enforce tenant fairness via two complementary mechanisms: weighted share guarantees and periodic rebalancing (every 60s) based on observed consumption and a configurable fairness floor.
3. Expose a tenant_priority_level and tenant_budget token on the Redwood API request envelope; clients can request a priority but allocation is controlled server-side.
4. Provide an opt-in "priority isolation" mode for Dedicated customers who purchase guaranteed capacity (B2B contract).

Tradeoffs considered
-------------------
- Static partitioning: simpler but underutilizes GPUs during uneven load. Rejected.
- Pure queuing with head-of-line preemption: low implementation complexity but risk of long tail latency for lower-priority tenants. Rejected.
- Dynamic sharding + fairness floor: more complex but balances utilization, SLOs, and cost attribution. Accepted.

Implementation overview
-----------------------
- Components touched:
  - Edge router (request classification and token accounting)
  - Shard scheduler (per-GPU logical queues and admission controller)
  - Token-accounting service (lightweight in-memory service with persistence to etcd for durable counters)
  - Billing pipeline (consumption tags for cost attribution)
  - Observability instrumentation (metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts)

- High-level flow:
  1. Incoming request arrives with tenant_id and optional requested_priority."server assigns effective_priority" based on tenant config and recent consumption.
  2. Token-accounting service computes current budget for that (tenant_id, priority) pair using exponential moving average (EMA) of consumption and the contract-specified baseline.
  3. Router maps request to a logical shard bucket using consistent hashing augmented with a spare-capacity bias.
  4. Admission controller decides immediate dispatch, delayed enqueue, or reject-with-fallback depending on budget, shard headroom, and SLO projections.

API and contract changes
------------------------
- New response header: X-Redwood-Effective-Priority: <level>
- New request metadata (optional): tenant_priority_hint (string: low|normal|high)
- Server-side enforced fields remain authoritative; clients should not assume grant of higher priority.
- Example request snippet (JSON metadata passed in SDK):

```json
{"metadata": {"tenant_priority_hint": "high", "trace_id": "abc-123"}}
```

Configuration: parameters and defaults
-------------------------------------
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| fairness_floor_percent | 10 | Minimum guaranteed fraction of shard tokens per tenant during contention |
| rebalancing_interval_s | 60 | Seconds between rebalancing evaluations |
| max_priority_levels | 3 | Number of discrete priority buckets (0=low,1=normal,2=high) |
| token_bucket_alpha | 0.2 | EMA alpha used for smoothing consumption estimates |
| admission_latency_headroom_ms | 25 | Latency headroom used when predicting whether to admit a request |

Coding standards and patterns
-----------------------------
- Keep token-accounting logic thread-safe and lock-free where possible: use per-core ring buffers and epoch-based reconciliation to limit contention.
- Strong separation of concerns: router must not perform token accounting; it should call the token-accounting RPC and act on the deterministic response.
- Input validation: always validate tenant_id and priority_hint at the API edge; reject malformed hints with 400 and a header X-Redwood-Reason explaining the issue.
- Idempotency: admission decisions must include an idempotency token: admit_id, passed through traces to make replay analysis deterministic.

Observability and SLOs
----------------------
- Required metrics (per-tenant, per-priority, exported with tenant tag):
  - requests_total (counter)
  - tokens_consumed (counter)
  - admitted_count (counter)
  - rejected_count (counter)
  - queue_latency_ms (histogram)
  - service_latency_ms (histogram)
  - shard_utilization_percent (gauge)

- Derived SLOs / fairness indicators:
  - Per-tenant P95 service_latency_ms <= configured SLO (e.g., 150ms for committed tenants)
  - Per-tenant share_gap_percent = 100 * (allocated_share - observed_share) / allocated_share; target <= 20%

- Example Prometheus alerts (names and thresholds):
  - Alert: TenantLatencyBreach
    - Condition: tenant:P95_service_latency_ms:avg_by_tenant > tenant_slo_ms for 3m
    - Severity: page
  - Alert: FairnessViolation
    - Condition: tenant:share_gap_percent:avg_by_tenant > 20 for 5m
    - Severity: ticket
  - Alert: ShardOvercommit
    - Condition: shard_utilization_percent > 95 for 2m and queue_latency_ms.p95 > 200ms
    - Severity: page

Monitoring queries (PromQL examples)
-----------------------------------
- Per-tenant P95:
  - quantile_over_time(0.95, service_latency_ms_bucket{tenant=~"$tenant"}[5m])
- Share gap:
  - 100 * (allocated_tokens_total - tokens_consumed_total) / allocated_tokens_total

Graceful degradation and fallback behavior
-----------------------------------------
1. If tenant_budget is exhausted and the tenant is non-committed (not in Dedicated priority isolation), router should:
   a. Attempt delayed enqueue with jitter up to 200ms if SLO projection still acceptable.
   b. If projection fails, return 429 with X-Redwood-Fallback: true and payload: {"reason":"budget_exhausted","suggested_alts":["lower_temperature","shorter_max_tokens"]}.
2. For committed tenants in priority_isolation mode, requests are admitted up to contract limits; if overcommit risk detected, borrow from global spare pool or trigger autoscale.

Cost attribution and billing implications
---------------------------------------
- All consumed tokens must be emitted to the billing pipeline with tags: tenant_id, effective_priority, shard_id, model_id, quantization_profile.
- Consumption emitted as structured events to Kafka topic redwood.billing.consumption_v2 for downstream aggregation and per-contract chargeback.

Testing and validation
----------------------
- Unit tests around token refill, EMA calculations, and edge cases for concurrent admits.
- Integration test harness (in eng-serving-runtime/testing) to run workload simulations: 200 tenants, Zipf distribution of QPS, variable priority mixes. Baseline expectations:
  - committed tenants: P95 latency within 150ms 99% of simulation runs.
  - non-committed tenants: share_gap_percent <= 25 after warmup period.

Rollout plan (staged)
---------------------
1. Canary (week 0–1): internal traffic only, 1 region, 2 shards. Observe metrics for 48h.
2. Beta (week 2–4): opt-in for selected low-impact customers. Add billing tag validation.
3. Gradual ramp (week 5–8): enable auto-join for remaining customers with conservative fairness_floor_percent=20.
4. Full production (week 9): default fairness_floor_percent=10, monitoring runbook in place.

Runbook excerpt: incident triage steps
------------------------------------
1. If ShardOvercommit alert pages:
   - Pager oncall: check per-shard queue_latency and admitted_count.
   - If utilization > 95% and queue p95 > 300ms: scale up shard count (manual or trigger autoscaler), temporarily raise fairness_floor by 10% to reduce headroom contention.
   - If degraded due to single tenant: identify tenant via topk(tokens_consumed_total, 5) and open customer success ticket.
2. If FairnessViolation ticket:
   - Validate token-accounting logs for 5-minute window. If bug found in EMA or reconciliation, roll back to static partitioning flag via feature toggle.

Ownership and open questions
----------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-architecture team). Secondary owners: eng-sre (alerts and runbook), finance (billing tags).
- Open questions:
  - Should we expose an admin API to temporarily bump a tenant’s budget during live incidents? (proposal: yes, gated by RBAC and audit logs)
  - What is the long-term plan for fairness across heterogeneous hardware (A100 vs H100)? We will add hardware weighting to the token model in Q2 2026.

Appendix: example YAML config for a tenant
-----------------------------------------
```yaml
tenant_id: "acme-corp-123"
priority_config:
  default_priority: normal
  priority_overrides:
    - key: "workflow:realtime-search"
      priority: high
  isolation: false
  budget_policy:
    fairness_floor_percent: 12
    burst_multiplier: 2.0
    token_bucket_alpha: 0.15
```

Notes and related design artifacts
---------------------------------
- See supplementary simulation notebooks in eng-serving-runtime/testing/simulations/priority-sharding.ipynb for reproduction steps and datasets.
- This policy complements (but does not replace) Dedicated capacity contractual guarantees.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-01-15: Draft created by Arjun Patel.
- 2026-01-28: Reviewed by Leah Martinez and Sofia Chen; updated fairness floor defaults.
- 2026-02-20: Added runbook actions and PromQL alert examples per eng-sre feedback.

payload.page_title: Graceful GPU Preemption and Prewarming Guidelines

sections.body:
Overview:

This document defines the recommended runtime and infrastructure standards for handling GPU preemption (spot/interruptible instances, cloud maintenance) and for prewarming execution slots in Redwood inference pools. Goal: minimize user-visible errors and latency regressions while preserving cost efficiency. Applies to: hosted and dedicated GPU pools, Dedicated autoscalers, and Private deployment automation where interruptible GPUs may be used.

Why this matters:
- GPU preemption is a common cost optimization (spot/interruptible). If handled poorly, preemption causes request errors, cold-start latency, and state loss (KV cache, model warmup).
- Prewarming warm pools reduces cold-start amplification on traffic spikes and supports SLO stability.

Principles:
1) Fast, observable handoff: preemption should trigger deterministic graceful-shutdown windows and observable signals.
2) Preserve model working set: persist or checkpoint KV cache and other ephemeral state as required by model SLAs.
3) Asymmetric cost model: prioritize critical low-latency routes for reserved (non-interruptible) capacity and permit batch/elastic workloads to use interruptible nodes.
4) Automated recovery and admission control: autoscaler and scheduler must consider warm pool size, in-flight request draining, and admission thresholds.

SLO and thresholds (example targets - tune per-customer):
- Target availability for production routes: 99.95% monthly (exclude scheduled maintenance).
- Latency SLO for interactive routes: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 250ms; cold-start allowance: additional 1500ms for <1% of tokens.
- Preemption drain window requirement: min 45s SIGTERM window (60s recommended) before instance termination.
- Warm pool min sizing heuristic: max(2, floor(0.05 * replica_count)) with a floor of 2 GPUs per pool.

Signals and integration points:
- Cloud provider signals: GCP Preemptible 'TERMINATE' notice, AWS Spot interruption notice (two-minute warning), Azure Spot/maintenance notifications. Map each cloud signal to the same local lifecycle path.
- Cluster orchestrator: for k8s-based Dedicated/Private clusters, rely on preStop hooks and Pod lifecycle events to drain. For non-k8s orchestration, ensure a comparable lifecycle API exists.
- Redwood control plane: control-plane should expose a preemption event webhook that downstream components (autoscaler, router, cache manager) subscribe to.

Graceful shutdown sequence (ordered):
1) Receive preemption signal.
2) Mark node "draining" in scheduler and remove from routing pools for new requests.
3) Immediately capture KV cache snapshot to durable store if model state lifetime > 30s. Use asynchronous flush with confirmation (see persistence policy).
4) Finish in-flight requests within a hard deadline (default 45s). Long-running requests beyond deadline should be cut over to fallback routing: retry to compatible variant (smaller/quantized model) or queue for retry.
5) Evict ephemeral processes and run final health/metrics flush.
6) Release node.

KV cache and working set persistence:
- Persist only when necessary: large context models (context > 8k tokens) and long-running chat sessions require KV checkpointing.
- Snapshot policy: incremental append to object store (S3/GCS) using per-shard checkpointing. Each snapshot must complete within 20s to be effective for preemption windows. If snapshot cannot be completed, fallback to non-persistent strategy and mark traced requests as potentially "cold" in analytics.
- Retention and hygiene: keep last 3 snapshots per model-shard, TTL 1 hour by default.

Prewarming strategies:
A) Warm pool (preferred for low-latency routes): maintain a small number of pre-initialized VM/GPU instances with model artifacts loaded and an empty KV cache. Warm pool sizing: see heuristic above. Warm pools are paid capacity and should be reserved only for routes with strict latency SLOs.
B) Lazy-warm with fast-preload: maintain pre-pulled model artifacts and quantized weights on local disk cache. Boot workflow: launch container -> mount artifact -> start runtime -> accept traffic. Target bootstrap time: < 20s for 7B-class models on NVidia H100-like hardware.
C) Shared warm containers: run multiple lightweight worker processes per GPU to amortize warmup cost for small models.

Admission control and routing policies:
- Tag routes by latency-critical vs elastic. Latency-critical routes must be routed to reserved or warm nodes only. Elastic routes may be routed to interruptible instances with best-effort latency.
- Router should implement immediate fallback: if selected node is draining or preempted, route to next compatible node and, if not available, fallback to smaller model variant or enqueue request with a bounded retry.
- Throttling thresholds: if warm pool saturation > 85% and queue > 100 requests, trigger auto-increment policy to create additional warm instances (see autoscaler section).

Autoscaler integration (recommended config fields):
- warmPool.minSize: integer
- warmPool.scaleFactor: float (0.0-1.0, fraction of steady-state replicas to keep warm)
- preemptionDrainWindowSec: integer (default 60)
- snapshot.timeoutSec: integer (default 20)
- fallbackModelOrder: list (ordered model ids to try when primary unavailable)

Example autoscaler YAML (conceptual):

warmPool:
  minSize: 3
  scaleFactor: 0.05
  maxBurst: 10
preemption:
  drainWindowSec: 60
  snapshotTimeoutSec: 20
fallbackModelOrder: ["redwood-small-quant", "redwood-medium-quant", "redwood-legacy-small"]

Commands and operational recipes:
- Force warm pool resize (example CLI):
  rctl warmpool set --pool inference-nyc-a --min 4
- Trigger manual snapshot flush for model shard: 
  rctl model snapshot flush --model-id redwood-34b --shard 2 --timeout 30s
- Observe draining nodes: 
  rctl nodes list --filter state=draining --output table

Testing and validation checklist (pre-merge for changes):
1) Unit tests for lifecycle handlers and snapshot logic.
2) Staging preemption simulation: inject synthetic preemption signals and assert that no more than 0.5% of requests fail for interactive routes and that cold-start percentiles are within tolerance.
3) Load test with warm pool at target sizing: validate p95 latency and error budget.
4) Chaos test: randomly terminate 5% of warm nodes and verify fallback routing and autoscaler ramp.

Rollout plan for changes to these guidelines/software: 
1) Draft changes in feature branch; unit + integration tests passing.
2) Canary deploy to low-traffic region (Region: us-west-2 / pool: canary-warm-1) for 48 hours.
3) Monitor metrics: preemption-induced 5xx rate, cold start percentiles, warm pool utilization.
4) Gradual 20/40/100% rollout to remaining pools with 24-hour observation windows.

Operational runbook (immediate actions on preemption spikes):
1) Check control-plane alerts: preemption events per-minute > X (threshold).
2) If warmPool utilization > 90%: increase warmpool.minSize by +2 and scale up reserved instances.
3) If snapshot timeouts occur: disable persistence for affected model shards and escalate to runtime team.
4) If p95 latency > SLO for > 10 minutes: enable emergency routing to lower-cost quantized model variant and notify product owners.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Runtime team: implement graceful shutdown hooks, snapshot API, and KV flush logic.
- Infra autoscaler team: expose warmPool config and implement scale policies.
- Router/service-mesh team: implement drain-aware routing and fallback logic.
- Observability team: provide dashboards and alerts (see Observability section).

Observability and alerts (minimum set):
- preemption.events.rate (per-pool) -> alert when > 5/min for 15m
- warmpool.utilization (per-pool) -> warn at > 85% for 10m, critical at > 95%
- snapshot.failure.rate (per-model-shard) -> alert at > 1%
- runtime.shutdown.durations -> SLO: 95% < drainWindowSec

Metrics dashboards (recommended panels):
- Warm pool capacity vs active queries
- Cold-start percentile heatmap by model family and region
- Snapshot latency histogram and failure counts
- Routing fallback counts and fallback model latency

Security and cost notes:
- Warm pools increase baseline cost. Use route tagging and cost allocation to bill back customers.
- Snapshot data must be stored encrypted-at-rest using customer or Redwood-managed KMS depending on privacy/confidentiality.

Appendix A — Example k8s preStop snippet (for k8s-based deployments):

# preStop: give the process time to drain and snapshot
preStop:
  exec:
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/opt/redwood/bin/drain-and-snapshot --timeout=45"]

Appendix B — Small model boot sequence (timings observed in staging):
- Container start: 1.2s
- Artifact mount and checksum: 1.0s
- Runtime warm init (weights mmap / cuda init): 6.8s
- Accept traffic: ~9.0s total

Related documents and references:
- GPU failure mitigation playbook: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-failure-mitigation-2024
- KV cache persistence runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/kv-cache-persistence-2025

Document history and changelog:
- 2025-11-12: created by Priya Shah (initial draft)
- 2025-12-18: added autoscaler fields and k8s preStop guidance (review: Ethan Morales)
- 2026-02-03: tightened snapshot timeouts and added runbook actions (review: Claire Johnson)

Contact: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai for runtime incidents and infra-autoscaler@redwood.ai for scaling requests.

payload.page_title: GPU Fleet Health: Annotated Vitals, Telemetry Mapping, and Alerting Matrix

sections.body:
Summary
This document defines a standard mapping from raw GPU telemetry and host signals to a small set of annotated "vitals" used for health judgement, alerting, dashboarding, and automated operational actions for the Redwood GPU fleet. The goal is to make GPU health signals consistent across providers and machine types, enable deterministic runbooks, and provide clear ownership boundaries for SRE and infra teams.

Why this exists
- GPU telemetry is noisy and vendor-specific; teams spend too much time translating signals during incidents.
- Consistent health annotations let higher layers (schedulers, autoscalers, runtime) make safe decisions: drain, prewarm, fall back to CPU, or route to alternate regions.
- This doc standardizes derived metric names, severity thresholds, sampling/aggregation windows, and the associated automatic remediation ladder.

Scope and applicability
- Applies to all GPU nodes in Redwood-managed fleets (hosted and Dedicated).
- Covers device-level telemetry (temperature, power, ECC), host-level signals (OOM kills, cgroup throttles, kernel messages), and derived invariants (thermal climb rate, error-rate-per-hour).
- Not a replacement for vendor firmware guides; ties those signals to our operational model.

Definitions (canonical terms)
- GPU_VITAL_THERMAL: derived single-value state representing thermal safety. One of: normal | warm | hot | critical. Computed from temperature and climb-rate.
- GPU_VITAL_ECC: ECC error classification: none | transient | persistent | fatal. Uses ECC counters and DDR parity logs.
- GPU_VITAL_POWER: power headroom state: normal | capped | unstable. Based on power draw and power-limit throttles.
- GPU_VITAL_MEM_PRESSURE: memory contention state: normal | fragmentation | OOM-risk. From free VRAM, allocation failure events, and fragmentation heuristics.
- GPU_VITAL_PREEMPT_SCORE: a 0..100 score indicating preemption risk (higher = more likely to preempt). Derived from preempt events, priority shares, and soft-quota usage.

Telemetry fields and mapping table
Use the following canonical metric names in Prometheus and the telemetry envelope. Vendors may export different field names; collectors must map vendor IDs to these canonical names at ingestion.

| Canonical metric | Typical sources | Aggregation window | Notes / derived use |
|------------------|-----------------|--------------------|---------------------|
| gpu.temp_celsius | nvidia_smi.temperature.gpu, amd_gpu.temp | 30s -> 1m | Use instantaneous and 1m rolling mean for climb-rate calculation. |
| gpu.temp_climb_c_per_min | derived | 60s -> 5m | 1m delta extrapolated to per-minute rate; important for hot transitions. |
| gpu.ecc.corrected_count | nvidia_smi.ecc.corrected | 5m | Convert to errors/hour metric; transient vs persistent rule below. |
| gpu.ecc.uncorrectable_count | vendor | 5m | Immediate critical if >0 AND not from NVLink retry storms. |
| gpu.power_w | nvml.power | 30s | Track against configured TDP and observed power cap throttles. |
| gpu.power_limit_throttle | nvml.power.limit_throttled | 1m | Binary flag used in GPU_VITAL_POWER. |
| gpu.vram_free_mb | nvml.memory.free | 30s -> 1m | Use percentile (p5, p50) over 5m for OOM risk. |
| node.oom_kills | kernel.oom | 1m | If OOM occurs on a node with active GPU workloads, escalate to persistent memory issues. |
| node.cgroup_throttle_count | cgroup.v2.io.throttled | 1m | Correlate with preempt_score and slow-path fallbacks. |
| pci.link_errors | kernel.pci.link_errors | 5m | High-rate link errors influence ECC and fatal classifications. |
| gpu.utilization_pct | nvml.utilization.gpu | 30s | Used for autoscaler and scheduling heuristics. |
| gpu.driver_recoveries | vendor | 1m | Count of recoveries / GPU resets; 3 in 10m -> persistent fault. |

Severity thresholds and derived rules
The following table is the canonical severity matrix used by alerting rules. Rules should use the aggregation windows above and apply deduplication across sources for the same host.

| Vital | Transition condition | Alert severity | Automated action |
|-------|---------------------|----------------|------------------|
| GPU_VITAL_THERMAL: warm -> normal | temp_celsius between 70-80C and climb_rate < 5 C/min | info | log to fleet metrics, no remediation |
| warm -> hot | temp >= 80C OR climb_rate >= 5 C/min | warning | reduce tenant concurrency on node; notify owner_team |
| hot -> critical | temp >= 90C OR sustained climb_rate >= 10 C/min | critical | initiate graceful drain with 10s token window, trigger preemptible fallback routing |
| GPU_VITAL_ECC: transient | corrected_count spikes > 100/hour but no driver_recoveries | warning | increase ECC sampling, tag node for observation for 6h |
| ECC persistent | corrected_count persists > 10/hour for 24h OR 1 uncorrectable_count | critical | schedule urgent maintenance, remove node from allocator until sign-off |
| GPU_VITAL_POWER: capped | power_limit_throttle observed 3x in 5m | warning | reduce batch sizes for new sessions, notify infra team |
| GPU_VITAL_MEM_PRESSURE: OOM-risk | vram_free_mb p5 < 200MB OR node.oom_kills > 0 | critical | prevent new allocations, drain long-running low-priority sessions |

Behavioral guidelines for derived states
- Do not take the node off rotation for a single transient metric spike; require 3 observations across 2 minutes unless the metric is explicitly fatal (e.g. uncorrectable ECC).
- Combine signals: an isolated temperature spike with no climb-rate and no driver_recoveries = informational. Temperature + climb + driver_recovery = critical.
- Prefers graceful draining over immediate VM termination. Draining: mark as DRAINING, allow up to X=10s for active generation tokens to finish; after that attempt cancellation and eviction.

Alerting and runbook mapping
- Alerts are categorized and routed using the canonical vital name in the alert label (alert:gpu_vital_thermal, gpu_vital_ecc, etc.).
- Each alert must include: node_id, instance_type, model_variants_active (top-3 by qps), recent_driver_recoveries, and last_3_temp_samples.

Minimal runbook (summary)
1) Acknowledge within SLO: 5 minutes for warning, 2 minutes for critical.
2) Quickly determine if the node is in a multi-node tenant pool or dedicated to a single tenant.
3) For thermal warning: reduce concurrency -> monitor temperature; if climbs continue escalate to critical.
4) For ECC persistent or driver_recovery storms: cordon node from scheduler immediately and schedule maintenance ticket (priority P1 for critical).
5) For OOM-risk: set node-prevent-new-allocations flag and migrate priority sessions.
6) Include a short post-incident run listing: timestamps of first detection, remediation start, drain completion, follow-up maintenance ticket id.

Sample PromQL rules (examples)
- Thermal critical alert (pseudo):
  max_over_time(gpu.temp_celsius[2m]) > 90 and increase(gpu.temp_climb_c_per_min[5m]) > 20
- ECC persistent:
  increase(gpu.ecc.corrected_count[24h]) > 240
- Driver recovery storm:
  increase(gpu.driver_recoveries[10m]) > 3

Telemetry ingestion and mapping responsibilities
- Collector teams must publish vendor-to-canonical mappings in a small config file (YAML) kept in the infra telemetry repo. Example mapping: vendor.nvml.temperature.gpu -> gpu.temp_celsius.
- Sampling: device-level metrics at 30s; host-level at 15s if the host is in a degraded state. Retention: raw samples 90d; rolled-up 1m aggregates for 1y.

Dashboard and SLOs
- Dashboards must expose the 90-day incidence rate of each critical vital per pool. Target: <0.5 critical thermal events per 100 nodes per 90 days for stable pools.
- SLOs for remediation: 95% of warning-class events should be acknowledged in 5 minutes and have an automated mitigation (concurrency reduction or drain) applied within 10 minutes.

Automated remediation ladder (preferred order)
1) Soft remediation: reduce tenant concurrency, lower batch sizes, and increase per-request CPU fallback ratio.
2) Scheduler-level: stop placing new jobs, mark node as_low_priority.
3) Drain: graceful drain window (10s) then force-evict if necessary.
4) Cordon and maintenance: mark node as out-of-service, create maintenance ticket tied to the telemetry snapshots.

Ownership and escalation
- First-line responder: infra-gpu-oncall (team: eng-infra SRE rotation).
- Secondary: hardware-ops (for hardware-level ECC/unrecoverable errors).
- If maintenance involves vendor intervention, escalate to Vendor Partnerships (cc: infra-ops-lead).

Acceptance criteria for node re-introduction
- Node must show: no uncorrectable ECC events for 72 hours, driver_recovery_count < 1 in last 24h, and temps stable below 75C for 24 hours under 50th percentile load.
- A human sign-off by infra SRE is required for nodes that had ECC persistent or critical thermal events.

Migration notes and integration guidance
- When adding a new GPU type, the collector must ship a mapping and small calibration dataset that defines safe thresholds specific to the SKU. Calibration steps: run the canonical GPU stress harness for 4 hours at 70%-100% utilization and produce the p25/p50/p75 temp distribution. Attach mapping PR to telemetry repo.

Appendix A: Example mapping YAML snippet

- See eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/adaptive-kv-coordinator-and-eviction-contract-2026 for scheduler interaction patterns.

payload.page_title: Service configuration convergence and safe defaults playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents the recommended architecture, standards, and operational procedures for ensuring service configuration convergence and safe defaulting across Redwood Inference deployments (hosted, dedicated, private). It codifies validation, rollout, detection, and automated-repair patterns so teams can change configuration with predictable safety and low operational overhead.

Motivation

Configuration drift and incorrect defaults are a recurrent root cause of reliability incidents and customer-facing regressions. We need a standard, automated approach that: 1) prevents unsafe defaults from reaching production, 2) guarantees high probability of convergence to the intended state within defined windows, and 3) provides clear rollback and remediation steps.

Scope

- Applies to runtime configuration that affects inference behavior, routing, billing metadata, and security-sensitive toggles (e.g., model-variant routing weights, batching policies, KV-cache TTLs, telemetry sampling rates).
- Excludes per-request payloads and ephemeral runtime state (cache contents, in-memory metrics).

Principles

1. Declarative intent: all production-facing configuration should be represented as declarative artifacts (YAML/JSON) stored in the config control plane and versioned in the Config Git repository.
2. Safe defaults: each configurable field must have a documented safe default that limits cost, exposure, and tail-risk.
3. Convergence SLOs: the platform commits to measurable convergence SLIs and alerts when the SLO is violated.
4. Canary-first: multi-stage rollouts with automated checks reduce blast radius.
5. Observability-first: configuration changes are always accompanied by telemetry, traceable via change ids.

Key definitions

- Convergence: a service is converged when the live effective config observed by runtime agents matches the declared artifact (within tolerances).
- Drift: mismatch between declared config and observed effective config.
- Safe default: a conservative value that keeps the service within latency/cost/security bounds unless explicitly overridden.

Config precedence model (ordered, highest first)

1. Per-request override (explicit request-level hint)
2. User/tenant-scoped override (per-customer pin)
3. Service-level declared config (Git + control plane)
4. Global platform defaults (safe defaults)

Design and runtime behavior

- Control plane publishes a monotonic change-id for every config commit. Agents subscribe to change events and pull the manifest version referenced by the change-id.
- Each runtime agent exposes a /health/config endpoint returning {"change_id": "abc123", "applied_at": "2025-11-02T14:12:07Z", "diff": "..."}. This is sampled by the convergence aggregator.
- Agents should attempt at least 3 retries over progressive backoff windows before reporting a hard failure to the control plane.

Convergence SLIs and SLOs

- Primary SLI: config.convergence.success_rate (percentage of services reaching target change_id within window)
- SLO target: 99.9% of non-degraded services converge within 120 seconds of change publication
- Alert threshold: config.convergence.success_rate < 99.0% for 5 minutes -> P1 page to oncall
- Secondary SLI: config.convergence.median_latency_ms (median time to converge) target < 45,000 ms

Metrics and telemetry (recommended labels)

- metric: config.sync_latency_ms (per-service, histogram)
- metric: config.sync_retries_total (counter)
- span tag: change_id, author, git_commit, environment, service_name
- log lines: structured JSON with fields {"change_id","service","agent_version","status","error_code"}

Validation and preflight checks (CI gating)

1. Schema validation (required): every declarative artifact must pass the JSON Schema/Protobuf schema.
2. Static linting (policy): cost-guardrail lints, security lints (no open endpoints, no disabled auth).
3. Local simulation: run `redwoodctl config simulate --manifest=path --sim-targets=staging` and require zero regressions in golden prompt set.
4. Behavioral smoke test: run end-to-end inference smoke with a 95th percentile latency baseline check against staging.

YAML example (service-level manifest)

```yaml
service: text-generation-worker
version: v2.7.1
change_id: cfg-2025-11-02-ashaiyer-17
defaults:
  batching:
    max_tokens: 2048
    max_batch_size: 16
    max_latency_ms: 50
  kv_cache_ttl_seconds: 300
  telemetry_sampling: 0.05
overrides:
  tenant_overrides: []
rollout_policy:
  strategy: progressive_canary
  canary_steps:
    - pct: 5
      min_duration: 10m
    - pct: 25
      min_duration: 30m
    - pct: 100
      min_duration: 10m
checks:
  - type: latency_regression
    threshold_p95_ms: 1.25x
  - type: cost_delta
    threshold_percent: 7
```

API and CLI examples

- Publish: `redwoodctl config publish --manifest ./manifests/text-gen.yaml --author asha.iyer@redwood.ai`
- Inspect live: `redwoodctl config status --service text-generation-worker --env prod`
- Rollback: `redwoodctl config rollback --service text-generation-worker --to-change cfg-2025-10-30-bkup`

Rollout and verification playbook (operational steps)

1. Prepare: author creates manifest in config repo, opens PR with rationale and rollout_policy. Add related evals and latency baselines.
2. CI gates: on PR merge CI runs schema lint, simulation, and smoke. If any check fails, block merge.
3. Canary stage: control plane publishes change id and routes 5% traffic to canary agents. Automatic verifiers run for min_duration.
4. Automated analysis: compare canary vs baseline on p95 latency, token cost delta, error-rate. Use statistical tests (two-sided equivalence with alpha=0.05).
5. If checks pass, promote to next step; if checks fail, automatic immediate rollback to previous change-id and create incident for owner.
6. Post-rollout: run a 24h regression scan and publish summary in the change PR.

Failure modes and mitigations

- Slow convergence due to agent GC pauses: detect via agent metrics; mitigation: stagger rollout and increase retry window.
- Partial apply (some agents show older change id): remediation: force sync via `redwoodctl config sync --service X --force`, escalate if not resolved in 10 minutes.
- Unsafe default uncovered post-deploy: immediate protective rollback, mark config as restricted, and require a hotfix PR with additional evals.

Automated repair and self-heal policy

- For transient failures (network blips, short outages) the system will self-heal with exponential backoff up to 15 minutes.
- For persistent divergence beyond 15 minutes or detected policy violation (e.g., disabled auth), control plane must automatically set service to last-known-good change_id and notify owners.

Testing and continuous validation

- Nightly canary: randomly select low-risk services and reapply latest change_id to validate long-term convergence health.
- Chaos injection: monthly game-day that simulates control plane partition and measures median convergence and failure modes.

Ownership and runbook links

- Primary owner: Config Platform (eng-infra/config-platform)
- Secondary owner: SRE teams per product line
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/config-sync-incident, /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/agent-debugging

Audit and compliance

- Every change_id must be recorded in the audit log with author, PR link, and checksum. Audit retention policy: 3 years.
- For Private deployments, a signed manifest copy must be retained in customer tenant storage and key-hashed in the central audit pipeline.

Appendix: sample alerts and escalation

- Alert: CONFIG_CONVERGENCE_PCT_DROP -> fires when primary SLO < 99.0% for 5m. Escalation: oncall -> config-platform -> engineering manager -> SOC if security-related.
- Pager runbook: 1) confirm alert via `redwoodctl config status --all --since 1h`, 2) check control plane event stream, 3) identify services failing and their owners, 4) execute rollback or force-sync.

Questions and future work

- Integrate canary verification with the Optimize evaluation service to automatically tune rollout step sizes based on historical traffic volatility.
- Evaluate hierarchical backoff for multi-tenant customers with strict isolation (different SLOs for high-priority tenants).

Related artifacts

- Schema repo: git@internal:redwood/config-schemas.git
- CLI: docs at /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/redwoodctl

Contact

For questions or feedback on this playbook, contact Asha Iyer (asha.iyer@redwood.ai) or the Config Platform Slack channel (#cfg-platform).
