payload.page_title: ADR: Synthetic-Traffic Privacy and Safe Injection Policy

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This ADR establishes a company-wide policy for generating, routing, and observing synthetic traffic (synthetic requests, test prompts, replayed user traces) injected into Redwood inference stacks. The decision balances the operational need for realistic, continuous testing and monitoring with user privacy, cost containment, and production stability.

Decision
--------
We adopt a conservative, opt-in safe-injection model for synthetic traffic with strong tagging, privacy-preserving data transformations, strict rate & cost budgets, and dedicated isolation lanes where appropriate. Synthetic traffic that includes or is derived from customer data requires explicit approval and additional safeguards (anonymization, differential-privacy transformations, and customer consent).

Motivation and context
----------------------
- Synthetic traffic helps detect regressions, validate rollouts (canaries), exercise fallback paths, and calibrate SLOs and cost models.
- Prior internal incidents: noisy synthetic workloads causing cache pollution and unexpected billing spikes; unclear telemetry attribution between real and synthetic requests; accidental exposure of customer prompt material in debug logs.
- Requirements: preserve ability to run realistic tests; keep production SLAs unaffected; enforce privacy & compliance; make observability and billing clearly attributable.

Scope
-----
Applies to all Redwood runtime modes: hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Affects teams producing synthetic traffic (QA, SRE, Perf, Product), ingestion/edge proxies, serving runtime, telemetry pipelines, billing, and model evaluation tooling.

Policy details
--------------
1) Tagging and provenance
   - All synthetic requests must include a top-level header/field: X-Redwood-Synthetic: "true" and a synthetic-origin tag with one of the allowed values: {"canary", "perf", "integration-test", "eval-harness", "chaos"}.
   - Telemetry must propagate these tags in traces, metrics (as a cardinality-limited dimension), and logs (redacted).

2) Privacy-preserving transformations
   - If synthetic traffic is derived from customer prompts or logs, it must be transformed by one of the approved methods before injection: token-level anonymization, entity redaction, or differential-privacy noise (per the Privacy Toolkit). Raw customer data is not permitted in synthetic feeds without an approved exception.

3) Isolation and soft lanes
   - Runtime will enforce soft lanes for synthetic traffic: "preferred" (same pools but lower priority) and "isolated" (dedicated worker pools) for heavy perf injection. Routing default: small-volume synthetic -> preferred; large-scale perf/chaos -> isolated.
   - Lanes are implemented via request metadata: synthetic-priority: low|isolated and corresponding queue configurations (see infra changes table).

4) Rate, budget, and cost control
   - Per-team daily budget (tokens and calls) for synthetic traffic. Default soft budget: 1% of team’s peak production tokens or an absolute floor of 50k tokens/day, whichever is smaller.
   - Exceeding budget triggers throttling and an automated escalation to the owning team and SRE. Production customer traffic never yields to synthetic requests when capacity is constrained.

5) Observability and metrics
   - Synthetic-aware SLIs: we add parallel SLIs measuring synthetic success, synthetic-induced error rate, and synthetic latency. Synthetic requests are excluded from customer-facing SLO calculations by default, but we maintain a derived SLO that measures runtime correctness under synthetic load.
   - Tagging keys: synthetic=true, synthetic.origin, synthetic.run_id, synthetic_owner_team.

6) Logging and data retention
   - Logs containing synthetic request content must be redacted of any customer-identifying tokens. Retention for synthetic payloads is limited to 7 days by default and stored in a synthetic-only retention tier.

7) Admission for sensitive synthetic content
   - Any synthetic feed that attempts to include PII, customer prompts, or other sensitive content must gain approval from Security and Privacy (formal ticket), include a transformation proof, and be labeled confidentiality=restricted.

Tradeoffs considered
--------------------
- Pros: preserves ability to run realistic tests in production; improves early detection of regressions; clearer telemetry; controlled cost.
- Cons: added complexity in routing and budget enforcement; risk of synthetic-only blind spots if synthetic lanes diverge from production; small cost overhead for maintaining isolated lanes.

Alternatives evaluated
----------------------
1) No synthetic traffic in production: rejected. Reduced fidelity for rollout and monitor tests deemed unacceptable.
2) Unrestricted synthetic injection: rejected. Real incidents have shown this causes cost spikes and telemetry noise.
3) Total isolation to separate clusters only: rejected for small-scale tests due to increased latency/fidelity loss; accepted for large perf tests.

Implementation plan and rollout steps
-----------------------------------
1) Phase 1 (30 days):
   - Implement tagging enforcement at edge proxies (API gateway) and client SDKs. Add validation: requests missing X-Redwood-Synthetic when flagged by internal tooling are rejected with 400.
   - Add synthetic flags to telemetry pipeline and ensure synthetic dimension cardinality is capped.
   - Owners: Edge (Asha Patel), Telemetry (Liam Chen), SDKs (Priya Nair).

2) Phase 2 (60 days):
   - Implement soft-lane queueing and throttles in runtime. Add budget check in request admission layer with per-team quotas.
   - Owners: Runtime (Maya Rodriguez), SRE (Omar Castillo).

3) Phase 3 (90 days):
   - Add UI in Redwood Console for teams to view synthetic budgets, current consumption, and submit approval requests for sensitive synthetic feeds.
   - Provide SDK helpers for privacy transformations and a CLI utility to generate proof artifacts.
   - Owners: Console (Jin Park), Security/Privacy (Priya Nair).

Infra and config table (high level)
----------------------------------
| Component | Change | Default |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Edge/API Gateway | Validate X-Redwood-Synthetic header + origin | Reject invalid with 400 |
| Runtime admission | Per-team synthetic token quota + lane hint | 50k tokens/day default |
| Queues | priority queue for synthetic.low and isolated queue | soft-limit 10% of worker capacity |
| Telemetry pipeline | tag propagation + cardinality cap 100 | retention 90 days for metrics |
| Logs | redact synthetic payloads by default | retention 7 days |

API and SDK guidance
--------------------
- SDKs will expose a typed SyntheticRequest builder which sets recommended headers and run_id, and attaches a local annotation proving transformations applied when deriving from customer data.
- Example header: { "X-Redwood-Synthetic": "true", "X-Redwood-Synthetic-Origin": "perf", "X-Redwood-Synthetic-RunId": "perf-20260203-87a2" }
- Clients must not attempt to bypass header validation. Attempts to circumvent will be rate-limited and flagged.

Observability and runbook changes
---------------------------------
- SRE will add synthetic-focused dashboards: synthetic-concurrency, synthetic-error-rate, synthetic-token-consumption-by-team.
- Runbook excerpt: if synthetic traffic causes production error surge, the admission layer will automatically triage and shed synthetic lanes; SRE oncall must: 1) confirm shed; 2) notify affected teams; 3) enable temporary stricter throttles until next business hour.

Testing and evaluation
----------------------
- Unit tests: header validation, budget enforcer.
- Integration tests: end-to-end synthetic run with telemetry propagation.
- Performance tests: validate that small-scale synthetic injection (<0.1% traffic) does not affect p95 latency by more than 1%.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Policy owner: Engineering Standards (Maya Rodriguez).
- Runtime & Telemetry implementers: Runtime team and Telemetry team.
- Approval for exceptions: Security & Privacy (Priya Nair) + SRE lead.

Monitoring & SLO impact
----------------------
- Customer-facing SLOs remain computed over non-synthetic traffic.
- New derived SLO: Runtime-availability-under-synthetic (target 99.9% monthly) measured by success rate of canary runs.

Consequences and follow-ups
--------------------------
- Short term: improved detection capabilities and clearer billing attribution.
- Medium term: potential need to tune synthetic generation to stay representative without being costly.
- Follow-ups: add automated differential-privacy transformation library to the SDKs; schedule quarterly review of synthetic budgets.

Related pages
-------------
- /architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/telemetry-ingestion-and-retention-guidelines-2025
- /eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/adaptive-kv-coordinator-and-eviction-contract-2026
- /security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/pseudonymization-guidelines-2025

Decision date: 2026-01-12

- Reviewed: Liam Chen, Priya Nair, Omar Castillo

payload.page_title: ADR: Shadow Traffic Routing Architecture (Inline Mirroring, Bucketing, Fail-Open)

sections.body: Published (approved for Phase 1 MVP). Any material changes to timeouts, bucketing inputs, or request capture fields require a follow-up ADR.
sections.heading: Status

sections.body: We will implement shadow traffic by **inline mirroring** a sampled subset of production requests in the **data plane routing path**, sending a best-effort duplicate request to one or more shadow targets while returning the **control** response to the user.
sections.heading: Summary of decision

sections.body:
- **Fail-open**: shadowing must never block or degrade the user path. Shadow execution is best-effort with strict timeouts and circuit breaking.
- **Deterministic bucketing**: a stable request fingerprint drives sampling and variant assignment for consistent comparisons.
- **Minimal capture**: shadow request/response artifacts are redacted and retained briefly; scoring happens asynchronously.
sections.heading: Key properties

sections.body:
Redwood’s Rollouts framework supports canaries and A/B testing for latency/cost, but customers and internal teams need a safe way to measure **quality regressions** (format adherence, refusal/safety, instruction following, etc.) for model/version/quantization/prompt changes without impacting user-visible responses.

Shadow traffic duplicates a subset of real production requests to candidate variants and scores outputs asynchronously. This ADR focuses on **where** shadow duplication happens (data plane vs offline replay), **how** requests are sampled/assigned, and **what** fail-open means operationally.
sections.heading: Context

sections.body:
1) Produces comparable control vs shadow outputs using real production prompts/contexts.
2) Keeps user-path latency and reliability unchanged (or within a tightly bounded overhead budget).
3) Works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with consistent semantics.
4) Minimizes data retention and reduces exposure of sensitive prompt/response data.
5) Integrates cleanly with existing routing and rollouts primitives (variants, policies, guardrails).
sections.heading: We need a routing architecture that

sections.body:
**Description:** After request admission and route selection, the router mirrors the request to shadow target(s) asynchronously, while processing the control request normally.

**Pros**
- Highest fidelity: shadow sees the same request payload, same headers/metadata policy, and same timing window.
- Enables deterministic bucketing keyed on request fingerprint at the moment of routing.
- Works for “online-only” traffic (no dependence on log availability).
- Natural integration point with routing policies and rollouts objects.

**Cons / risks**
- Any synchronous work on the user path risks tail latency impact if not carefully bounded.
- Requires robust guardrails (timeouts, backpressure, circuit breakers) to avoid resource contention.
- Streaming requests need special semantics to avoid mirroring an unbounded stream.
sections.heading: Option A — Inline mirroring in the data plane (chosen)

sections.body:
**Description:** Capture production requests into a log/queue and replay them later to candidate variants.

**Pros**
- No data plane mirroring overhead if capture is lightweight.
- Replays can be scheduled/regulated to fit scoring capacity.
- Easier to “pause and resume” experiments without touching the router.

**Cons / risks**
- Lower fidelity for requests with ephemeral context (tool results, auth-derived features, time-sensitive prompts, retried requests with altered metadata).
- Adds pressure to retention/storage; higher compliance complexity (more prompt storage by default).
- Harder to guarantee that replay payload matches what the model actually saw (normalization/versioning drift).
- Delayed feedback; less usable for real-time canary decisions.
sections.heading: Option B — Async replay from captured traffic/logs

sections.body:
**Description:** Capture a canonical, normalized request envelope inline, then replay later.

**Pros**
- Can reduce immediate shadow target load.
- Preserves a “canonical input” concept.

**Cons / risks**
- Combines the main risks of A (data plane work) and B (retention/compliance).
- Still requires careful decisions on what to capture; mismatches remain likely.
sections.heading: Option C — Hybrid: inline capture + later replay

sections.body:
Adopt **Option A: Inline mirroring in the data plane** with the following constraints:
- Mirroring is **asynchronous** relative to the user-path response.
- The router enforces **strict resource isolation** for shadow (separate connection pools/queues; bounded concurrency).
- Shadowing is **fail-open** with circuit breaking and backpressure.
- Sampling and assignment use a **deterministic request fingerprint** and consistent bucketing.
- For streaming requests, mirror only a bounded, well-defined portion (see “Streaming semantics”).
sections.heading: Decision

sections.body:
1) Request arrives at Router.
2) Admission checks (auth, quotas, basic validation).
3) Determine control target using existing routing policy.
4) Compute request fingerprint and evaluate shadow policy:
   - sampling decision
   - shadow target set (one or more variants)
   - metadata/header handling rules
5) Execute control request normally.
6) If sampled, enqueue shadow work item (non-blocking):
   - fire-and-forget dispatch to shadow target(s)
   - record telemetry links between control and shadow
7) Return control response to user.
sections.heading: Data plane flow (conceptual)

sections.body:
- Shadow dispatch uses a dedicated internal “shadow egress” queue and concurrency limiter.
- Shadow requests are executed with:
  - lower priority
  - strict timeouts
  - capped retries (default: none; see below)
- Shadow failures are logged as telemetry but never surface to the user.
sections.heading: Shadow path isolation

sections.body:
- Stable assignment for a given “logical request” to reduce variance when comparing control vs shadow.
- Privacy-preserving: avoid storing raw prompt text or high-risk identifiers in telemetry.
- Works across regions and deployment modes.
- Avoids high-cardinality explosion.
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
We define a **normalized fingerprint input string** composed of:
- `tenant_id` (internal UUID)
- `route_id` (stable route identifier)
- `request_type` (chat.completions | responses | embeddings | rerank)
- `canonical_messages_hash` OR `canonical_input_hash` (see below)
- `tooling_mode` (none | tool_calling_enabled) when applicable
sections.heading: Fingerprint inputs (v1)

sections.body:
- Chat/messages: normalize to a stable JSON representation (ordering, whitespace) before hashing.
- Remove/zero fields known to be unstable across retries (timestamps, request_id, tracing ids).
- Truncate inputs before hashing at a configured limit (default 8KB of canonicalized text) to bound CPU.
sections.heading: Canonicalization rules

sections.body:
- Compute `fingerprint = HMAC-SHA256(tenant_fingerprint_key, normalized_input)`.
- Use the first 64 bits as `fingerprint64` for bucketing.
sections.heading: Hash function

sections.body:
- HMAC prevents cross-tenant correlation and reduces risk if fingerprints leak.
- Per-tenant key rotation is supported (see consequences).
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body:
- Use consistent bucketing over `[0, 9,999]`:
  - `bucket = fingerprint64 mod 10,000`
  - sampled if `bucket < (sampling_rate_bps)` where bps is basis points (0–10,000).
- For multi-shadow-target experiments, assign targets deterministically:
  - `target_index = (fingerprint64 / 10,000) mod N`
  - For “mirror to all” experiments, dispatch to all targets but still use a single sampling gate.
sections.heading: Sampling and assignment

sections.body: - This is not a user-level sticky assignment; it is request-level stability. If customers want session-level stickiness, they should pass a stable user/session key (future enhancement, explicitly not required for v1).
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- Collisions are expected to be extremely rare and acceptable at our sampling rates.
- No special collision detection in v1; metrics are computed in aggregate.
sections.heading: Collision handling

sections.body: Shadow traffic must be invisible to end users and must not affect control-path SLOs.
sections.heading: Fail-open behavior (hard requirements)

sections.body:
- If shadow dispatch fails (queue full, timeout, shadow target errors), the control request proceeds normally.
- The router must never wait on shadow completion to respond to the user.
- Shadowing must not consume unbounded resources (CPU, memory, connections).
sections.heading: What “fail-open” means

sections.body:
Defaults (v1; may be tuned under SRE guardrails):
- Shadow dispatch enqueue: **<= 1ms** budget on the user path.
- Shadow target request timeout: **2s** absolute (configurable per request type).
- Shadow overall work item TTL: **10m** (after which it is dropped and recorded as expired).
sections.heading: Timeouts

sections.body:
- Shadow path retries are **disabled by default** to prevent amplification.
- Exception: idempotent request types may allow **1 retry** behind a feature flag, only when SRE confirms no correlated incident risk.
sections.heading: Retries

sections.body:
- If shadow queue utilization exceeds threshold (e.g., 80% for 5 minutes) OR scoring/telemetry lag exceeds SLO, automatically:
  - reduce effective sampling (e.g., clamp to 10% of configured rate)
  - then disable shadowing for the route if the condition persists
- If shadow target error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., >5% 5xx over 5 minutes), open circuit for that target.

Operational note: exact thresholds are specified in the SLO/guardrails doc; this ADR establishes the principle and required mechanisms.
sections.heading: Backpressure and circuit breakers

sections.body: Streaming requests require bounded behavior to avoid mirroring indefinite token streams and to control egress cost.
sections.heading: Streaming semantics

sections.body:
- Mirror the **initial request** payload (messages/instructions/tools) and request parameters.
- Shadow requests may be executed in non-streaming mode, capturing only the **final completion** (or up to a configured max tokens) for scoring.
- If the control request is cancelled by the client, shadow continues best-effort up to a cap, then is cancelled.
sections.heading: Decision (v1)

sections.body:
- Quality metrics generally evaluate final output structure/content; streaming chunk-by-chunk parity is not required for v1.
- Non-streaming shadow reduces complexity and cardinality of partial-chunk telemetry.
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body:
- Fingerprints are HMAC’d and non-reversible without tenant keys.
- Telemetry must not include raw prompts by default. Shadow artifacts are referenced via redacted storage pointers with strict retention.
- Header/metadata mirroring is policy-controlled (default denylist for sensitive headers).
sections.heading: Security and privacy considerations

sections.body:
- High-fidelity comparisons: control and shadow are derived from the same live request.
- Fast feedback: supports near-real-time monitoring during canaries.
- Clean integration with routing policies and rollouts (single place to enforce sampling, guardrails, and audit logs).
sections.heading: Positive

sections.body:
- Router complexity increases (must maintain shadow queue, isolation, and circuit breakers).
- Adds bounded CPU overhead (fingerprinting + enqueue) on the user path.
- Requires careful tuning to avoid egress pressure and connection pool contention.
- Per-tenant HMAC key rotation can shift sampling assignments over time; comparisons across rotation windows must be treated carefully.
sections.heading: Negative / trade-offs

sections.body:
- Deterministic sampling can under-sample rare but critical request classes. This is mitigated via segmentation and manual overrides (future: stratified sampling; not in v1).
- If the request includes tool calling with non-deterministic tool outputs, shadow results may diverge due to tool side effects. For v1, shadowing should disable external side-effecting tools or mirror in “read-only” tool mode where supported.
sections.heading: Non-obvious implications

sections.body:
1) Internal-only feature flag: `shadow_traffic_enabled` (off by default).
2) Enable for a single internal tenant + single route at <=0.1% sampling.
3) Verify:
   - p99 control latency delta within budget
   - shadow queue health, circuit breakers, and telemetry correctness
4) Expand to limited beta (Dedicated) behind allowlist.
sections.heading: Rollout plan (routing component)

sections.body:
- Stratified sampling support (by route segment, request type, or customer-provided key).
- Session-level deterministic assignment (customer-provided stable key) vs request-level only.
- Shadowing for multi-modal inputs (images/audio) and canonicalization rules.
sections.heading: Open questions (tracked outside ADR)

sections.body:
- SLOs/Guardrails: shadow traffic SLOs and guardrails
- Data model/cardinality ADR: telemetry schema constraints and required dimensions
- Data retention/redaction policy: prompt/response handling rules
- Control plane policy service: shadow policy schema and validation rules
sections.heading: References

payload.page_title: ADR: Rollout policy evaluation order and precedence (Hosted canary rollouts)

sections.body: Published.
sections.heading: Status

sections.body:
This ADR defines how **rollout policies** (guardrails, approvals, stop/rollback) compose with existing **routing policies** (fallback chains, region routing / data residency, quotas/rate limits) for **Hosted canary rollouts**. It also defines precedence and deny semantics so the Console, control plane, and data plane behave consistently.

Key decision: we treat policies as a layered system with **hard denies first**, then **routing constraints**, then **rollout split selection**, then **runtime fallback execution**. Explicit deny always wins.

---
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Route-level model selection and fallback chains (e.g., Model A → Model B)
- Region routing and data residency constraints
- Quotas / rate limits and tenant suspension mechanisms
- Reliability behaviors (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers)
sections.heading: Redwood Hosted routing already supports

sections.body:
- A rollout object that selects a **baseline** and **canary** target (usually model version/config variants)
- Percentage-based traffic splitting with deterministic cohorting
- Guardrails (max step size, min soak time, approvals) and stop conditions (auto-pause/rollback)

We need a single, predictable evaluation order for:
1) **Write-time actions** (create/start/advance/pause/rollback), evaluated in Console/backend/control plane
2) **Request-time routing** (which model/variant actually serves a given request), evaluated in Smart Routing/data plane

We also need to avoid ambiguous behavior when multiple policies apply (e.g., canary says “send 10% to canary” but region routing or quota rules force otherwise).

---
sections.heading: Hosted canary rollouts introduce

sections.body:
Policies are evaluated under three domains with distinct execution points:

**A. Authorization policies (who can do what)**
- Evaluated at request time for Console/API actions.
- Driven by RBAC permissions (e.g., rollout:create, rollout:start, rollout:approve, rollout:rollback).

**B. Control-plane validation policies (is the config/action allowed)**
- Evaluated at write time by the policy engine and orchestrator.
- Includes guardrails (max jump %, min soak) and approval gates.

**C. Data-plane runtime policies (how requests are served safely)**
- Evaluated per inference request.
- Includes quotas/rate limits, region constraints, traffic splitting enforcement, fallback execution.

These domains are intentionally separated: control-plane policies prevent invalid rollout plans from being stored; data-plane policies ensure safety and correctness under partial failure or inconsistent state.

---
sections.heading: 1) Policy composition model

sections.body:
**Explicit deny wins.**
- If any applicable policy yields a deny for an action or request, evaluation stops and the deny is returned.
- When multiple policies can deny, we return the most actionable error (see “Reason codes”).

**Most restrictive constraint wins** for constraints (not denials), e.g.:
- Region allowlist intersection
- Capacity tier constraints
- Max-concurrency restrictions

**Rollout policy may not override hard safety/availability controls**, including:
- Tenant suspension
- Route disabled
- Quota/rate limit exceeded
- Data residency/region constraints

Rollout policy is a *traffic selection mechanism*, not an entitlement bypass.

---
sections.heading: 2) Precedence and deny semantics

sections.body: This is the normative order for Smart Routing when a Hosted route has an active rollout.
sections.heading: Request-time routing evaluation order (Hosted data plane)

sections.body:
- tenant_id, project_id
- route_id
- request_id
- end_user_id (optional)
- selected region (if client pinned) / inferred region
- headers affecting routing (e.g., debug, internal override; subject to allowlist)
sections.heading: Inputs

sections.body:
- effective_route_config (resolved)
- effective_rollout (if active)

Note: Deterministic cohorting inputs are governed by ADR “Cohorting and traffic splitting”. This ADR assumes we can compute `cohort = baseline|canary` deterministically when rollout is active.
sections.heading: Outputs

sections.body:
Evaluate and enforce, in order:
1. Tenant/project suspended or billing lock → DENY
2. Route disabled / route deleted → DENY
3. Authentication invalid → DENY
4. Quota/rate limit exceeded (tenant, project, route) → DENY
5. Regional hard deny (data residency / region disallow) → DENY

Rationale: these are correctness and compliance requirements; any attempt to “route around” them violates guarantees.
sections.heading: Step 1 — Hard denies (fail closed)

sections.body:
- If route has region pinning or residency constraint, restrict eligible regions.
- If client requested a region, enforce allowlist; otherwise choose per existing region policy (latency/cost/capacity).
sections.heading: Apply region routing policy

sections.body:
- selected_region
- selected_capacity_tier (if applicable)

Important: rollout splitting is applied **within** the selected region/tier. We do not “count” traffic percentage globally across regions because it makes percentages unpredictable under region failover. (Metrics are still aggregated cross-region, but the selection decision is region-scoped.)
sections.heading: Output

sections.body:
- Primary target(s): baseline target and canary target as defined by rollout (often same model family, different version/config)
- Route fallback chain: existing fallback targets for that route (if configured)

We do not allow a rollout to define a target that violates route-level allow/deny lists (e.g., blocked models).
sections.heading: Construct an ordered candidate set

sections.body:
If rollout is active and in a “serving” state:
1. Compute cohort assignment (baseline vs canary) deterministically.
2. Select the cohort’s primary target.
sections.heading: Step 4 — Apply rollout split selection (if rollout active)

sections.body:
- Paused: cohort selection freezes; continue serving last stable configuration (see “Paused behavior”)
- Rolled back: serve baseline
- Completed: serve promoted target (implementation defined; typically the canary target becomes baseline)

**Paused behavior (normative):**
- When a rollout is paused, new requests are served by the baseline target by default unless the rollout is explicitly configured with “freeze cohorts on pause”. For GA we default to **baseline-on-pause** because it is safer and simpler to reason about for customers.
sections.heading: If rollout is paused/rolled back/completed

sections.body:
Dispatch to the selected primary target.

On failure, apply fallbacks in the following order:
1) **Intra-rollout fallback:**
   - If canary primary fails due to capacity/5xx/timeout, fallback to baseline primary **within the same route/region**, unless explicitly disabled by policy.
   - If baseline primary fails, do not “fallback up” to canary. Continue to route fallback chain.

2) **Route fallback chain:**
   - Apply existing fallback chain for the route (Model A → Model B → …).

3) If no fallbacks succeed → return error.
sections.heading: Step 5 — Dispatch and apply runtime fallback (cohort-aware)

sections.body:
- Canary should never reduce availability when baseline is healthy.
- Fallback to baseline from canary reduces blast radius and makes stop conditions more meaningful.
- Allowing baseline → canary fallback creates confusing “hidden canary traffic” during incidents and distorts cohort comparisons.
sections.heading: Rationale

sections.body:
For every request, emit:
- rollout_id (nullable)
- cohort (baseline|canary|none)
- selected_target (logical target id)
- fallback_used (true/false)
- decision_reason_code (see below)

---
sections.heading: Step 6 — Emit reason codes + telemetry tags

sections.body: This defines how we evaluate actions like create/start/advance/pause/rollback.
sections.heading: Control-plane action evaluation order (Console/API)

sections.body:
For any action, evaluate in order:
1) **RBAC authorization** (Marcus/Kaitlyn ownership; enforced at API gateway and/or Console backend)
2) **Entitlements** (is tenant allowed to use canary rollouts / approvals / auto-rollback)
3) **Guardrails validation** (max step size, min soak time, required approvals)
4) **State machine validity** (orchestrator: can this transition occur from current state)
5) **Write config + emit events** (audit + telemetry)

If any layer denies, stop and return the error.
sections.heading: Actions and evaluation layers

sections.body:
Guardrails are evaluated **before** state transitions to provide clearer errors. Example:
- If a user attempts to jump from 5% → 50% and max step size is 20%, return a guardrail error rather than “invalid transition”.

---
sections.heading: Precedence between guardrails and state machine

sections.body: To avoid inconsistent UX, we standardize a small set of reason codes surfaced in Console and logs.
sections.heading: Reason codes (standardized)

sections.body:
- DENY_TENANT_SUSPENDED
- DENY_ROUTE_DISABLED
- DENY_QUOTA_EXCEEDED
- DENY_REGION_NOT_ALLOWED
- DENY_MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED
- ROLLOUT_INACTIVE
- ROLLOUT_PAUSED_BASELINE_FORCED
- ROLLOUT_COHORT_SELECTED
- ROLLOUT_CANARY_FAILED_FALLBACK_TO_BASELINE
- ROUTE_FALLBACK_APPLIED
sections.heading: Recommended set (initial)

sections.body:
- Reason codes must be stable across minor releases; add new codes without changing semantics.

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
- Tenant exceeds route QPS limit.
- Result: DENY_QUOTA_EXCEEDED.
- No cohort selection occurs; no routing attempts occur.
sections.heading: Example 1 — Quota exceeded should not “spill” to baseline/canary

sections.body:
- Rollout configured on route, 10% canary.
- Request arrives pinned to a region not in allowlist.
- Result: DENY_REGION_NOT_ALLOWED.
sections.heading: Example 2 — Region residency constraint overrides rollout split

sections.body:
- Request assigned to canary cohort.
- Canary target returns 5xx.
- Data plane falls back to baseline target.
- Telemetry:
  - cohort=canary
  - fallback_used=true
  - decision_reason_code=ROLLOUT_CANARY_FAILED_FALLBACK_TO_BASELINE

Rationale: for canary analysis, we want visibility into canary-induced failures even if baseline served the final response.

---
sections.heading: Example 3 — Canary fails; fallback to baseline; cohort attribution remains canary

sections.body:
Rejected.
- Would make cohort assignment inconsistent under region failover.
- Causes unpredictable canary percentage per region and increases debugging complexity.
sections.heading: A) Apply rollout split before region selection

sections.body:
Rejected.
- Canary is explicitly the “riskier” target; using it as an availability fallback contradicts expectations and distorts cohort comparisons.
sections.heading: B) Allow baseline to fall back to canary to preserve availability

sections.body:
Rejected.
- Violates fairness and safety properties.
- Increases attack surface (users could create rollouts to bypass enforcement).

---
sections.heading: C) Treat rollouts as an overlay that can override quotas/limits

sections.body:
- Predictable precedence: hard denies and compliance constraints always win.
- Canary blast radius is reduced: canary failures degrade to baseline without requiring customer action.
- Metrics remain interpretable: canary cohort includes fallback events.
sections.heading: Positive

sections.body:
- Percentages are effectively **region-scoped**. Cross-region aggregate traffic may not match exact configured percentage during capacity shifts.
- Baseline-on-pause may surprise customers who expected cohorts to freeze. We mitigate with explicit UI copy and an advanced setting later.

---
sections.heading: Negative / tradeoffs

sections.body:
- Smart Routing must have a single “effective routing plan” structure that includes:
  - selected_region/tier
  - cohort selection result
  - target list with fallback ordering
  - reason codes

- Control plane should persist:
  - rollout state
  - step schedule
  - policy evaluation results at time of change (for auditability)

- Orchestrator emits audit events for:
  - create/start/advance/pause/resume/rollback
  - approval granted/denied
  - auto-pause/auto-rollback triggers

- Telemetry cardinality control:
  - rollout_id tagging is required but must be capped by retention and sampling strategies as per Observability guidance.

---
sections.heading: Implementation notes

sections.body:
1) Add an optional tenant setting for “freeze cohorts on pause” for advanced users.
2) Define how retries interact with cohort selection for streaming requests (see cohorting ADR; ensure stickiness across retries).
3) Extend reason codes to cover policy-denied rollout actions with user-friendly remediation hints.

---
sections.heading: Open questions / follow-ups (non-blocking for GA)

sections.body:
- Policy engine semantics: Jordan Lee / Benji Okafor
- Control plane/orchestrator: Ethan Park
- Smart Routing/data plane: Mina Haddad / Ravi Menon
- SRE signals/stop conditions: Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes
- Audit/RBAC: Marcus Lin / Kaitlyn Nguyen

payload.page_title: Quantized pipeline latency budgets and evaluation gates

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the latency budgeting, evaluation gates, and rollout guardrails for introducing quantized model artifacts into Redwood’s production inference pipelines. It covers expected operator metrics, benchmark procedures, mandatory quality gates (functional + human), and safe rollback paths. The goal is to make quantization a production-grade lever that reduces cost without unexpected latency regressions or quality drops.

Why this matters

- Quantized artifacts reduce GPU memory footprint and per-token compute cost but can change kernel selection, batching behavior, and KV cache pressure.
- Minor instruction-level changes can create outlier tail latency events, or spuriously increase token generation time at certain sequence lengths.
- We need a reproducible, automated gate that ensures any quantized model meets both latency and quality budgets before traffic migration.

Scope

Applies to: hosted API model catalog, Dedicated model pools, and Private runtime-sidecar deployments.
Out of scope: offline embeddings vector-store-only quantization done solely for storage reduction (still recommended to follow quality gating but not latency buckets here).

Definitions

- P50/P95/P99: standard latency percentiles for end-to-end request duration (edge ingress -> final token emitted).
- Token latency: per-token generation time measured inside runtime from next-token request to token output.
- Cold-start: first request cost when GPU cache and compiled kernels are not warmed.
- Quantized artifact: model weights converted to int8/4/llm-int* using Redwood-approved toolchain and a documented quantization profile.

Latency budgets (end-to-end)

Budgets are expressed as percentage deltas relative to the floating-point (FP16/FP32) baseline for the same model and traffic profile. Baseline measurements must be from the same commit of the serving runtime and same hardware SKU.

| Traffic class | P50 delta (vs FP) | P95 delta | P99 delta | Acceptable? | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Interactive (SLO: 100ms P95) | <= +10% | <= +15% | <= +25% | Yes if pass all gates | measured at seq=128, batch=1 typical client pattern |
| Conversational (SLO: 250ms P95) | <= +12% | <= +18% | <= +30% | Yes if pass all gates | seq distribution: 32/128/512 mix per profile |
| Background (SLO: 1s P95) | <= +20% | <= +30% | <= +40% | Conditional | acceptable for batch workloads only |

Hard rejection: if token latency increases more than 50% at any tested sequence length or P99 regression > +40% for Interactive class, the artifact fails the gate and must be re-tuned.

Measurement methodology

1) Use the canonical benchmarking harness (eng-serving-runtime/benchmark-suite) pinned to the runtime commit used in CI.
2) Run load-controlled experiments on the target hardware SKU with identical pod/worker counts between FP and quantized runs. Disable autoscaling and non-deterministic background jobs.
3) Collect: end-to-end latency percentiles, per-token latencies, CUDA kernel time breakdown, KV cache hit ratios, and memory headroom.
4) Use the following CLI (example):

```bash
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: ./bench/runner.sh --model=redwood-7b-fp16 --profile=conv-128-32-512 --hardware=A100-80GB --reps=5 --out=baseline_fp.json
sections.heading: run baseline (FP)

sections.body:
./bench/runner.sh --model=redwood-7b-q8_0 --profile=conv-128-32-512 --hardware=A100-80GB --reps=5 --out=quant_q8.json
```

5) Normalize results by taking the median across reps and compute percent deltas for the target traffic class. Attach raw artifacts to the PR.

Quality gates (automated + manual)
sections.heading: run quantized

sections.body:
- Unit/regression tests: exact-match and JSON-schema validation for structured responses.
- Perf gate: must meet the latency budgets above for the designated traffic class.
- Determinism gate: for deterministic prompts (seeded), output top-1 token sequences must match FP baseline for > 95% of cases (exceptions allowed when quantization intentionally trades determinism for size; must be declared).
- Token-safety gate: prompt telemetry must not show a >2x increase in rejected tokens or malicious content scoring in automated safety model.
sections.heading: Automated checks (must all pass)

sections.body:
- Any P95 regression > +12% for Interactive.
- Any change that causes >5% divergence in top-3 responses for the canonical prompt-set.
- New quantization profile (not previously used in production).
sections.heading: Human review (required when any of below triggers true)

sections.body:
- Product owner confirms user-visible quality is acceptable for canary traffic.
- Applied ML verifies decoding characteristics and failure modes.
- SRE confirms rollout plan and rollback hooks.

Rollout & traffic migration plan

1) Canary (0 -> 1%): route 1% traffic using traffic-shaping router with header flag test-quantized-artifact. Monitor the Canary dashboard for 60 minutes.
2) Ramp (1% -> 10%): if canary is green, step to 10% for 2 hours.
3) Broaden (10% -> 50%): gradual doubles with 4-hour watch windows and gating.
4) Full (50% -> 100%): trust but verify sampling for 24 hours.
sections.heading: Human review checklist

sections.body:
- P95 for Interactive exceeds SLO + 10% absolute within watch window.
- Error rates increase > 1% absolute or request timeouts spike > 3x.
- Human-reported severe quality regressions.

Safe defaults and configuration knobs

- Default deployment policy for any new quantized artifact: canary_only=true, max_ramp_rate=2x/hour, rollback_on_p95_breach=true.
- Runtime flag: enable_quant_cache_prefetch=true for quantized artifacts; default unchanged until artifact has passed canary.
- Fallback variant: each catalog entry must include a float (FP16) fallback variant in same model family to fail open.

Observability and dashboards

Must produce the following telemetry from the serving runtime during gate tests and canaries:
- quant.artifact.id, quant.profile.name, runtime.commit, hardware.sku, batch_size, seq_len
- latency.percentiles (P50,P95,P99) per seq_len bucket
- token.latency.histogram
- kernel.time.breakdown (matmul, softmax, gelu, other)
- kv.cache.hit_rate and memory_headroom_gb
- error_rate_4xx, error_rate_5xx, timeout_count

Dashboards: Create an artifact-specific dashboard with a 24h rolling window that highlights percentile deltas vs baseline and a signal bar for gate failure. Canary runbooks must be linked in the dashboard.

Developer checklist (pre-PR)

- [ ] Attach FP baseline artifacts and raw bench outputs.
- [ ] Attach quantization recipe (tool version, calibration dataset, per-layer min/max if applicable).
- [ ] Include deterministic test manifests and a human evaluation sample set (10–30 prompts).
- [ ] Add rollout config to manifest.yaml with canary policy and fallback variant.
sections.heading: Abort and rollback conditions (immediate rollback)

sections.body:
```yaml
artifact:
  id: redwood-7b-q8_2026_01
  profile: q8_0
  baseline: redwood-7b-fp16_2025_12
  rollout:
    canary: 1%
    ramp_policy: doubling
    fallback: redwood-7b-fp16_2025_12
```

Operational runbook (short)

- If canary shows latency breach: immediately flip traffic routing to fallback using router flag: `traffic-router set priority artifact_id --fallback=artifact_fp`. Notify SRE team and open an incident if customer-facing errors are observed.
- If kernel breakdown shows disproportionate softmax or matmul time increase: open a profiling ticket to runtime-kernel team and mark artifact as blocked for production.

Ownership and contacts

- Performance and benchmarking owner: eng/perf (Marcus Green)
- Applied ML quantization owner: applied-ml (Lina Sørensen)
- Serving runtime owner: eng-serving-runtime (Diego Alvarez)

References and artifacts

- Quantization toolchain repo: git.redwood.ai/infra/quantize-tooling (pin tag in PR)
- Benchmark runner: eng-serving-runtime/benchmark-suite
- Canary router docs: eng-infra/edge-proxy-request-mux-and-tenant-routing-standard-2026

Open questions and future work

- Define automated perceptual quality delta metric for large open-ended generation beyond top-k overlap. A research spike is scheduled Q2 2026.
- Expand sequence-length-aware budgets to include streaming partial-token latency for streaming endpoints.

Change log

- 2026-01-10: Created (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-20: Added human review checklist and clarified canary rollback thresholds (reviewers: Marcus Green, Lina Sørensen).

payload.page_title: Service profiling experiment matrix and SLO extrapolation playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a standardized experiment matrix, data schema, measurement methodology, and extrapolation techniques for predicting service-level objective (SLO) behavior at scale. It is intended to help engineering teams validate capacity changes, quantify expected P50/P95/P99 latency shifts when scaling QPS or changing kernel/quantization profiles, and produce evidence for release decisions.

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
- Goals:
  - Provide a repeatable set of profiling experiments for inference services (inference-proxy, runtime-batcher, variant-router).
  - Define minimum data quality and sample sizes for reliable quantile estimates.
  - Offer an extrapolation method to estimate SLOs at higher QPS and alternate batch/sequence distributions.
  - Produce a clear runbook for diagnosing and mitigating regressions discovered by experiments.
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a full capacity planner for fleet-level autoscaling (see eng-sre capacity-planning).
  - It does not replace real production chaos testing; it's a controlled profiling toolset.

Scope and applicable services
----------------------------
This playbook applies to services that are on the inference request path:
- inference-proxy (edge -> ingress point, request enrichment)
- runtime-batcher (continuous batching layer that aggregates requests to model shards)
- model-executor (per-GPU inference process; capture as aggregate metrics where direct instrumentation is unavailable)

Key SLOs targeted
----------------
- Request latency (P50, P95, P99) measured at the API boundary (inference-proxy) with tokenized request/response timestamps.
- Token throughput (tokens/sec) and model-level throughput (inferences/sec) as secondary metrics.
- Error rate (5xx) and circuit-breaker invocations.

Experiment matrix (canonical)
----------------------------
Run experiments across a Cartesian product of the following dimensions. Each cell is a single experiment run (30–60 minutes steady state recommended).
1) QPS target: [10, 50, 200, 500, 1000]
2) Sequence length buckets: [short (<=64), mid (65-512), long (>512)]
3) Batch size behavior: [no-batching, observed-batching, forced-batch=16, forced-batch=32]
4) Model runtime profile: [fp32, int8-quant, kernel-optimized]
5) Hardware class: [A100, H100, T4] (if available)
6) KV/prefix cache hit-rate: [0%, 50%, 90%]

Minimum experiment duration and sample sizes
-----------------------------------------
- Warmup: 5 minutes to allow KV caches and batchers to stabilize.
- Steady-state collection: 30 minutes per cell.
- Minimum successful requests per cell: 50,000 or 30 minutes whichever yields more samples.
- For quantile stability, target at least 1,000 samples in the P99 tail bucket.

Data schema and required telemetry
--------------------------------
Collect both aggregated time-series and per-request traces/samples. Required fields for per-request samples (CSV/JSON):
- timestamp_utc
- request_id
- service (inference-proxy | runtime-batcher | model-executor)
- request_qps_target
- sequence_length_tokens
- batch_size
- kernel_profile (string)
- hardware_type
- kv_cache_hit (true|false)
- latency_ms_total
- latency_ms_ingress
- latency_ms_batching
- latency_ms_inference
- success (true|false)
- error_code (if any)
- sample_tags (comma-separated labels)

Example CLI commands
--------------------
- Start a canonical profile collection (example):
  rinfer profile collect --service inference-proxy --duration 45m --qps 200 --seq-dist mid --batch-policy observed --out /tmp/profiles/ip-qps200-mid.json
- Convert profile to aggregated metrics:
  rinfer profile summarize --input /tmp/profiles/ip-qps200-mid.json --out /tmp/summary/ip-qps200-mid.summary.json

Extrapolation methodology
-------------------------
We provide a pragmatic, defensible extrapolation approach rather than a single black-box model. Two levels of extrapolation are supported:
A) Dimension-preserving interpolation/extrapolation (statistical):
  - For each metric (P50/P95/P99), fit a smooth monotonic function over QPS (use log(QPS) as independent variable).
  - Use quantile regression (e.g., linear quantile regression on log-QPS) to estimate the quantile at an unseen QPS.
  - Provide bootstrap confidence intervals (95%) using sampled experiment runs.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Model runtime-batcher as M/G/1 queue with service time distribution derived from sampled latency_ms_inference.
  - For each QPS target, compute expected queueing delay and add to measured inference latency to estimate end-to-end latency.
  - Apply correction factor for batching nonlinearities observed in profiling (empirically derived multiplier).

Operational pseudocode (high-level)
-----------------------------------
```
sections.heading: B) Queueing-informed extrapolation (system-aware)

sections.body: models = fit_quantile_regression(M, quantiles=[0.5,0.95,0.99])
sections.heading: step 1: fit quantile_regression models on log(qps) -> quantile

sections.body:
service_time_dist = estimate_service_time_distribution(latency_samples)
queue_delay(qps) = mg1_expected_wait(service_time_dist, qps)
predicted_p95 = models['p95'](log(qps)) + queue_delay(qps) * correction_factor
sections.heading: step 2: if queueing extrapolation requested:

sections.body:
```

Quality gates and acceptance criteria
------------------------------------
- Calibration check: when extrapolating to a QPS for which an experiment exists, predicted P95 must be within ±12% of measured P95 for the same cell. If not, rerun experiments and review data collection fidelity.
- Minimum CI width: if 95% bootstrap CI for P95 is wider than ±25% relative, mark the cell as low-confidence and increase sample duration or repeat runs.
- Regression triage: any predicted increase in P95 > 20% compared to baseline must open a triage ticket (label: perf-regression) and follow the runbook below.

Regression runbook (for predicted or observed regressions)
--------------------------------------------------------
1) Verify instrumentation and data integrity: check timestamps, clock skew, and sampling consistency across services.
2) Reproduce minimal failing experiment: isolate single dimension (e.g., keep QPS and seq-length constant) and run targeted 15m test.
3) Compare span-level breakdown: ingress vs batching vs inference.
4) If batching contribution > 40% of delta: inspect runtime-batcher logs for scheduling delays and nonideal batch composition.
5) If inference contribution dominant: capture model-executor telemetry and check kernel selection, quantization toggles, GPU utilization, and memory pressure.
6) Temporary mitigations: reduce max batch size, enable forced prefix caching, degrade to lower model variant, or redirect traffic to dedicated capacity pool.
7) Permanent fixes: raise follow-up engineering story with root cause and rollout plan.

Owner and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Experiment design and execution: Performance Platform (perf-platform) team (primary).
- Data ingestion and summary tooling: Observability Platform team (metrics and traces).
- Runtime-level changes (batcher/kernel): Eng Serving Runtime (owners: runtime-batcher, kernel-and-scheduling).
- Decision to change customer-facing SLOs: Product and SRE leadership.

Templates and artifacts to attach
--------------------------------
- experiment-matrix.csv (columns: qps, seq_bucket, batch_policy, kernel, hw, cache_hit_rate, run_id)
- sample-schema.json (per-request sample definition)
- example-summary.json (expected aggregator output)
- artifact naming convention: svc-experiment-<service>-<qps>-<seq>-<batch>-<kernel>-<hw>-<timestamp>.json

Example aggregated table (one line per experiment)
-------------------------------------------------
| run_id | qps | seq_bucket | batch_policy | kernel | hw | p50_ms | p95_ms | p99_ms | err_rate | comments |
| r-20260203-01 | 200 | mid | observed | int8 | H100 | 34 | 112 | 240 | 0.02% | steady-state 40m |

Testing checklist before release
-------------------------------
- All target cells in experiment matrix executed at least once.
- Calibration checks passed for holdout QPS points.
- Extrapolation notebook and bootstrap artifacts attached to the run ticket.
- Runbook and mitigation steps documented on the ticket.

References and related docs
---------------------------
- Eng Serving Runtime: sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026
- Performance: predictable-cost-latency-simulator-specification-2026
- Observability: telemetry-ingestion-and-retention-guidelines-2025

Appendix A — Quick checklist for engineers
-----------------------------------------
1) Pick canonical experiment cell and run warmup + 30m steady window.
2) Ensure rinfer profile collect uses the --trace-sample-rate 0.01 for per-request traces.
3) Upload artifact to perf-bucket with metadata tag run-owner.<owner> and link in ticket.
4) Run extrapolation script and attach results: scripts/extrapolate_qps.py --input /tmp/summaries/*.json --target-qps 1000 --out /tmp/predictions.json

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Perf-platform oncall: perf-platform-oncall@redwood.com
- Observability infra: observability-team@redwood.com

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Draft created (Asha Kapoor)
- 2026-02-15: Added queueing-informed extrapolation and calibration gates (review feedback)
sections.heading: output: predicted quantiles + 95% bootstrap CI

payload.page_title: SLO Heatmap Entropy and Traffic Reshuffle Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook explains how Redwood Inference generates SLO heatmaps, computes an entropy-based prioritization score, and executes a traffic reshuffle to protect high-impact SLOs during capacity pressure or degradation events. It is intended for SRE, eng-platform, and runtime owners responsible for service-level guarantees and operational resilience.

Goals

- Provide an automated, explainable mechanism to prioritize traffic to instances/variants that preserve critical SLOs.
- Reduce customer-visible latency/regression by steering lower-priority requests to degraded/cheaper variants while preserving higher-priority traffic.
- Create observable, reversible traffic reshuffles with clear rollback criteria.

Scope and applicability

- Applies to production inference endpoints and internal control-plane services wired into the runtime routing mesh.
- Not intended for offline batch workloads.
- Works with Redwood’s multi-variant model serving (e.g., fp32/quantized/ distilled variants) and regional routing policies.

Key definitions

- SLO heatmap: A time-windowed matrix of SLO attainment across dimensions (route, model-variant, region, customer-tier).
- Entropy score: A scalar derived from the heatmap distribution that quantifies dispersion of failures across dimensions. High entropy indicates widespread degradation; low entropy indicates concentrated degradation.
- Traffic reshuffle: Policy-driven rerouting that shifts fractional traffic among variants/regions to maximize preserved SLO attainment.

Heatmap construction (data sources)

1. Dimensions: route_id, model_variant, region, customer_tier, latency_class (p95/p99 buckets), window (5m).
2. Signals: success_rate (>= configured threshold), p95_latency_ms, token_cost, error_rate, kv-cache_hit_rate.
3. Aggregation: per-dimension sliding window (default 5m with 1m step) producing:
   - heatmap_cell = {requests, good_requests, total_latency_ms_sum, cost_sum}.
4. Export: heatmap is exported every 1m to the telemetry index with TTL = 30d.

Entropy metric and prioritization formula

- For each SLO class (e.g., Latency SLO for interactive endpoints), compute distribution p_i = failures_i / total_failures across the chosen dimension (example: model_variant).
- Entropy H = - sum_i p_i * log2(p_i) (treat p_i=0 as 0).
- Prioritization score for a cell combines:
  - criticality_weight (derived from customer_tier and route importance),
  - cell_failure_rate (failures / requests),
  - inverse_entropy_boost = (1 / (1 + H)) to prefer concentrated failure repair.

CombinedScore = criticality_weight * cell_failure_rate * inverse_entropy_boost

Interpretation: higher CombinedScore => candidate for traffic-preserving action (either move high-priority traffic away from this cell or move low-priority traffic into it depending on policy).

Policy taxonomy

1. ProtectHighPriority: move customer_tier=enterprise and route=payment-checkout to low-latency variants/regions first.
2. CostDegrade: route best-effort trials to quantized/cheap variants under sustained load.
3. RegionalIsolation: when a region shows low entropy (failures concentrated in region), failover cross-region before variant-level reshuffle.

Runbook: automated reshuffle flow (high level)

1. Detection
   - Alert fires when route-level p99 latency > SLO threshold for 3 consecutive windows (default 3*5m).
   - Heatmap shows cell_failure_rate > 3x baseline for a cell contributing >= 10% of route failures.
2. Scoring and decision
   - Compute CombinedScore for affected cells.
   - If the top N cells (configurable by route) account for >= 60% of failures and entropy H < H_threshold (default 1.2), mark as concentrated failure.
3. Action selection (automated policy engine)
   - If ProtectHighPriority: attach a temporary priority route to affected enterprise tokens redirecting to preserved-variant (fractional 100% enterprise traffic).
   - Otherwise apply graduated reshuffle: reduce traffic fraction to hit cell by delta = min(0.25, observed_failure_fraction).
   - Apply traffic changes via control-plane patch API in two waves: immediate partial steering (10%) then ramp after 60s when probes confirm.
4. Validation
   - Post-action check: 2 consecutive windows with p99 latency improvement >= 15% for protected traffic or total error reductions for route >= 20%.
5. Rollback/Manual intervention
   - If metrics worsen or new cells degrade (entropy increases > +0.5), revert changes and trigger escalation.

Operational configuration (table)

| key | default | purpose |
|-----|---------|---------|
| detection.window | 5m | sliding window for heatmap aggregation |
| detection.threshold_multiplier | 3.0 | multiplier of baseline failure rate to trigger cell alert |
| entropy.h_threshold | 1.2 | below this value treat failures as concentrated |
| reshuffle.max_fraction_delta | 0.25 | max per-step traffic fraction change |
| reshuffle.ramp_delay_s | 60 | time between partial and full ramp steps |
| validation.windows_required | 2 | consecutive windows for post-action validation |
| preserve.customer_tiers | [enterprise, paid] | tiers treated as high criticality |

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-sre (team: runtime-slo-ops).
- Secondary owner: eng-platform (team: routing-and-mesh).
- On-call: runtime-slo-ops rotation. Page slack channel: #slo-ops.
- Escalation matrix: first 10m -> on-call, 30m -> runtime lead, 2h -> eng manager and product.

Monitoring and alerting (rules)

- Alert A1: Route p99 exceedance (severity P1) when > SLO*1.1 for 3 windows. Notify #oncall, create incident.
- Alert A2: Heatmap concentration (P2) when top cell contributes >= 40% of route failures. Annotate with cell id, entropy, CombinedScore.
- Synthetic probes: per-variant probes at 10s cadence; missing probe data for 3 probes triggers degraded telemetry fallback.

Safe rollout practices and preflight checks

1. Canary validation: always run traffic reshuffle on 1–2 non-production shadow accounts to validate pathing and observability.
2. Safety gates: reshuffle control-plane API requires dual approval if intended fraction delta > 0.15 for production routes.
3. Simulation: before global reshuffle, run simulator with historical heatmap (90th percentile worst-case window) to ensure > 95% probability of SLO preservation for protected tiers.

Manual playbook (when automation disabled)

1. Identify affected route and top failing cells using heatmap UI or telemetry query.
2. Evaluate entropy H; if H < 1.2 follow concentrated-failure path; else follow dispersed-failure path.
3. For concentrated-failure path: perform targeted route override for customer_tier=enterprise to preserved_variant with a 10% partial ramp.
4. Validate with live queries and tracing; if green, continue ramp to required fraction.

Example CLI snippets
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: redwood-slo-tool heatmap fetch --route checkout --window 5m | redwood-slo-tool score --entropy-threshold 1.2 --output json
sections.heading: compute CombinedScore for route "checkout" (pseudo)

sections.body:
redwood-control patch-traffic --route checkout --from variant:q123 --to variant:q456 --fraction 0.10 --reason "reshuffle: protect enterprise" --author a.patel

Testing and retrospective requirements

- Any automated reshuffle that ran on production must have a post-incident note in the incident tracker within 24h with: inputs (heatmap snapshot), decision rationale, validation windows, and a playback of the traffic-change timeline.
- Quarterly simulation exercises to validate entropy thresholds and weighting parameters against synthetic failure modes.

Audit and compliance

- All traffic patches are auditable: control-plane writes event with user, timestamp, before/after fractions, and heatmap snapshot id. Retention = 1y.

FAQ and rationale highlights

Q: Why entropy instead of raw failure counts?
A: Entropy helps detect whether failures are concentrated (safe to surgically reroute) or widespread (requires capacity/proactive remediation). It reduces oscillation and wrong corrective actions.

Q: Won't reshuffles cause customer impact?
A: The policies prioritize protecting high-criticality tiers and use gradual ramps with validation windows. Every production reshuffle requires post-run documentation.

Related pages and references

- See SLO derivation playbook for baseline SLOs and p99 targets (linked above).
- See queue smoothing runbook for interplay between reshuffle and queue backpressure.

Appendix: example heatmap JSON schema

{
  "route_id": "checkout",
  "window_start": "2026-10-02T15:40:00Z",
  "cells": [
    {"model_variant": "fp32-x", "region": "us-west-2", "customer_tier": "enterprise", "requests": 12000, "good_requests": 11880, "p95_ms": 180},
    {"model_variant": "quant-y", "region": "us-west-2", "customer_tier": "trial", "requests": 4300, "good_requests": 3800, "p95_ms": 420}
  ]
}

Contact

For questions or to propose changes: contact runtime-slo-ops@redwood.ai or open a PR against this page.
