payload.page_title: Performance Regression Policy & Thresholds (Company Standard)

sections.body:
This page defines Redwood Inference’s company-wide standard for:
- What counts as a performance regression vs. measurement noise.
- Minimum sample sizes and repeatability requirements.
- Pass/fail thresholds used by automated perf gating (PR checks, nightly canaries, and release-branch gates).
- Required artifacts and triage expectations when a regression is detected.

This policy is designed to support the “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” program and applies broadly to the serving runtime, kernels, scheduler/batching, and benchmark harness changes.

**Owner:** Observability (Engineering) in partnership with Serving Runtime and SRE.

---
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
This policy applies to any change that can affect latency/throughput/cost-relevant behavior for production inference:
- Serving runtime changes (prefill/decode scheduling, KV cache management, batching/backpressure, memory behavior).
- Kernel changes and kernel auto-selection changes.
- Model serving configuration defaults that affect runtime behavior (e.g., quantization profile defaults, attention/kernels toggles).
- Infrastructure and deployment changes that impact perf measurement (driver/CUDA/runtime/container base images, node configuration).
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- Application-level changes outside Redwood control (customer client code).
- One-off research experiments without a run manifest and reproducible harness.

---
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body: Metrics and definitions are standardized per **ADR-0172**. Any new metric must be proposed via an ADR update.
sections.heading: Canonical metrics and measurement boundaries

sections.body:
1) **TTFT (Time To First Token)**
- Definition: time from server request acceptance (server-side) to first token emitted by the server streamer.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.
- Notes: TTFT explicitly excludes client receive/render overhead. Client-side measurements must be labeled as such and cannot be used for gating.

2) **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**
- Definition: average per-token time during decode, measured server-side from first token emission to last token emission.
- Report: p50, p95, p99.

3) **Throughput**
- For generation/chat: tokens/s (server-side) and optionally req/s (if output length is fixed/controlled).
- For embeddings: req/s and embeddings/s (if batch mode is used).
- Report: mean and p95 where applicable.
sections.heading: Primary metrics (must-report)

sections.body:
- **Queue wait time** (scheduler): p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch assembly time**: p50/p95/p99.
- **Batch size distribution**: histogram summary (p50/p95 max).
- **GPU memory peak**: max (MiB) per run.
- **Error rate**: fraction of requests failing (timeout, OOM, internal errors).
sections.heading: Secondary metrics (required when available)

sections.body:
Because caching materially affects cost/latency and is production-relevant, results must be reported as:
- **Cold**: prefix/KV caches cleared for the workload cohort.
- **Warm**: a defined warmup phase and cache retention enabled.
sections.heading: Cold vs warm cache requirements

sections.body:
- Default gating uses **Cold** unless a workload is explicitly designated “cache-dependent” in the representative suite spec.
- Warm results are recorded and monitored; large cold↔warm deltas are treated as a diagnostic signal (not a failure by default).

---
sections.heading: For gating decisions

sections.body: Performance data has unavoidable variability (GPU clocks, placement, thermal behavior, background IO, kernel selection changes, cache state). This policy uses a two-level model:
sections.heading: Noise model (how we distinguish regression vs. variance)

sections.body:
A “run” is a single harness execution with a pinned workload definition + seed + manifest.
- Each gated comparison must include **multiple independent runs** (see minimum sample sizes below).
- Runs must include a standardized warmup period and must capture environment details in the run manifest (driver/CUDA/runtime build, kernel selection mode, scheduler policy, node type, region).
sections.heading: Level 1: Run-level repeatability

sections.body:
We compare a candidate (PR branch / release build) against a baseline (golden build tag for a given suite version).

**Default test statistic:** percent change of the run-median metric across repeats.
- For each metric M, compute the median value per run.
- Across runs, compute the median-of-medians for baseline and candidate.
- Compute %Δ = (candidate - baseline) / baseline.

**Confidence / robustness:**
- Use bootstrap resampling across runs to estimate a 95% confidence interval (CI) on %Δ.
- A change is considered “actionable” only if it clears the **noise floor** and breaches warning/fail thresholds with CI support.

**Noise floor (ignore region):**
- If |%Δ| < **2%** for a metric, treat as noise by default (unless the absolute delta is operationally meaningful; see “absolute thresholds”).

**Absolute thresholds (override noise floor):**
- TTFT: **+20 ms** at any percentile is considered actionable even if <2%.
- TPOT: **+0.20 ms/token** actionable.
- Error rate: **+0.10% absolute** actionable.

**Known high-variance environments:**
- If a particular SKU/region cohort is flagged as high-variance (SRE-owned designation), gating requires either (a) more repeats or (b) an isolated fleet window. High-variance designations must be documented and time-bounded.

---
sections.heading: Level 2: Statistical comparison across runs

sections.body: Minimums are chosen to balance cost with statistical power for typical Redwood workloads.
sections.heading: Minimum sample sizes (gating requirements)

sections.body:
- **PR gating (fast path):** 2 runs (same environment), only for “tier-1 smoke” workloads.
- **Nightly canary:** 3 runs.
- **Release branch gate:** 5 runs (or 3 runs across 2 separate fleet windows).
sections.heading: A. Minimum repeats (independent runs)

sections.body:
The representative suite defines workload cohorts; use the cohort type to select minimums:

| Workload cohort | Example | Minimum requests/run | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Chat streaming (short prompts, variable decode) | interactive chat | 10,000 | Must include concurrency ramp and steady-state window. |
| Tool/function calling (bursty multi-turn) | burst + idle cycles | 6,000 | Must include burst period long enough to show queueing dynamics. |
| Long-context prefill stress (large prefill, modest decode) | summarization | 1,200 | Prefill dominates; ensure long-context bin coverage. |
| Embeddings high-QPS (small payloads) | embeddings API | 50,000 | Prefer fixed-size payload bins to reduce confounding. |
sections.heading: B. Minimum requests per run (by workload type)

sections.body:
- Warmup is completed (standard warmup defined by the suite).
- At least **10 minutes** of steady-state measurements are collected (embeddings may use 5 minutes if QPS is high and variance is stable).
- Error rate is below the maximum allowed (see thresholds). If errors exceed allowed rate, the run is invalid unless the error itself is the regression under investigation.

---
sections.heading: A run only counts if

sections.body: Thresholds are expressed as % change vs. baseline (negative throughput change is regression). Unless otherwise noted, thresholds apply to **cold-cache** results.
sections.heading: Pass / warn / fail thresholds

sections.body:
**Latency metrics (TTFT, TPOT):**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| TTFT p50 | +5% | +8% |
| TTFT p95 | +8% | +12% |
| TTFT p99 | +10% | +15% |
| TPOT p50 | +4% | +7% |
| TPOT p95 | +6% | +10% |
| TPOT p99 | +8% | +12% |

**Throughput metrics:**

| Metric | Warn if regression ≥ | Fail if regression ≥ |
|---|---:|---:|
| tokens/s (generation) | -5% | -8% |
| req/s (embeddings) | -6% | -10% |

**Reliability guardrails (hard fail):**
- Error rate increase of **+0.10% absolute** or more (e.g., 0.05% → 0.15%) is a **Fail**.
- Any new OOM pattern that did not occur in baseline is a **Fail** (even if latency improves).
sections.heading: A. Default thresholds (company-wide)

sections.body:
A candidate fails gating when **both** are true:
1) The bootstrap 95% CI of %Δ overlaps the fail region (i.e., regression is statistically supported), and
2) The regression clears the noise floor (or crosses an absolute threshold).

If the point estimate is in fail but CI is wide (insufficient power), the result is “Inconclusive” and must be retried with additional repeats or an isolated fleet window.
sections.heading: B. CI-aware gating interpretation

sections.body:
The representative suite may specify tighter or looser thresholds per cohort if justified by:
- Customer impact (SLO sensitivity of that cohort).
- Historical variance characteristics.
- Known scheduling/kernels sensitivity.

Overrides must be documented in the suite definition and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE + Observability.

---
sections.heading: C. Workload-specific overrides

sections.body:
- Purpose: quick iteration.
- Not authoritative; no formal pass/fail.
- Must still emit a run manifest when shared.
sections.heading: Tier 0: Developer local (non-gated)

sections.body:
- Runs a reduced workload subset (“tier-1 smoke”), typically on one region + one SKU.
- Goal: catch large regressions quickly.
- Thresholds: use **Fail** thresholds only (warnings are surfaced but do not block merges unless configured by the owning team).
- If PR gating is flaky, SRE/CI may temporarily disable with an incident/issue and an ETA to restore.
sections.heading: Tier 1: PR perf checks (gated when enabled)

sections.body:
- Runs the representative suite nightly for supported baselines.
- Produces trend charts and variance panels.
- Failures page the owning triage rotation only if configured as “page-worthy” (see Alerting section).
sections.heading: Tier 2: Nightly perf-canary (always-on)

sections.body:
- Representative suite green under this policy for the release candidate.
- Runs must include the release’s target regions (minimum: us-east, eu-west) and key SKUs for that release.
- Any waiver must follow the exception process below.

---
sections.heading: Required before a serving runtime release is approved

sections.body:
- **Run manifest** (per ADR-0172) including:
  - Runtime build identifiers (git SHA, build ID), container image digest.
  - Region/SKU/node type, driver/CUDA, and relevant runtime flags.
  - Scheduler policy name + config hash.
  - Kernel selection mode + any pinned kernels.
  - Workload suite version + cohort ID + seed.
- **Results export** containing:
  - Metric definitions, aggregation method, percentile calculation method.
  - Raw summary stats per run (not only deltas).
- **Links** to dashboards/traces:
  - Dashboard panel link (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) for the run.
  - Trace/profiling artifacts when a regression is flagged (see profiling playbook).

Any result without a manifest is not eligible for gating decisions.

---
sections.heading: All gated perf results must include

sections.body:
- **Page (on-call):** release-branch gate failures for tier-1 models/workloads; error-rate/OOM regressions.
- **Triage channel only:** warning-level regressions, inconclusive results, or failures in non-tier-1 cohorts.

Routing is managed by SRE in collaboration with runtime owners.
sections.heading: What pages vs. what posts to triage

sections.body:
- If the regression is clearly attributable to a PR: the PR author/owning team is responsible for first response.
- If attribution is unclear: Serving Runtime on-call (or designated triage rotation) coordinates bisect.

---
sections.heading: Ownership on regression

sections.body: Waivers exist to unblock releases when the business impact of delaying exceeds the perf risk, but they must be rare and time-bounded.
sections.heading: Exception (waiver) process

sections.body:
1) A written justification including affected cohorts/metrics, expected customer impact, and mitigation.
2) A link to the failing run(s) and manifests.
3) Approval from:
   - Serving Runtime Engineering Lead (or delegate), and
   - SRE Integration Lead (or delegate).
sections.heading: A waiver requires

sections.body:
- Expiration date (default: 14 days).
- A follow-up issue/ticket to remove the waiver.

---
sections.heading: Waivers must include

sections.body:
1) **Validate reproducibility**
   - Rerun with the same manifest (same suite version, seed, and environment) if possible.
   - Confirm warmup was applied and steady-state criteria were met.

2) **Check environment drift**
   - Driver/CUDA/runtime container changes.
   - Node type differences, GPU clock/power settings.
   - Placement/isolation differences.

3) **Attribute to scheduler vs. kernels vs. workload**
   - Inspect queue wait time and batch assembly metrics.
   - Compare batch size distributions.
   - Check kernel selection debug dumps (selected kernel, fallback reasons).

4) **Inspect tail behavior**
   - Identify whether regression is p99-only (queueing contention, cache thrash) vs. broad (kernel/runtime change).
   - Use profiling playbook to collect traces for a small reproduction.

5) **Decide action**
   - Fix forward (preferred) or revert.
   - If neither is immediately possible, pursue a temporary mitigation (pin kernel, adjust backpressure guardrails) with an explicit rollback plan.

---
sections.heading: When a regression is detected

sections.body:
- Proposed changes to thresholds, sample sizes, or metric definitions require review by Observability + SRE + Serving Runtime.
- Any change must document:
  - Rationale (variance data, customer/SLO sensitivity).
  - Expected impact on flake rate and compute cost.
  - Backwards compatibility for dashboard queries and historical comparisons.

---
sections.heading: Change management

sections.body:
- TTFT p99 regressions often indicate scheduler backpressure, queue discipline changes, or prefill/decode overlap issues.
- TPOT regressions often indicate kernel selection changes, KV cache behavior changes, or decode batch inefficiencies.
- Throughput regressions without latency regressions can indicate conservative batching caps or increased per-request overhead.
sections.heading: Recommended interpretation

sections.body:
- #eng-runtime (coordination)
- #eng-sre (fleet stability, variance)
- #eng-platform (dashboards)

(If these channel names change, update this page; do not create duplicate policy pages.)
sections.heading: Contact / channels

payload.page_title: Economizer Serving Recommendations Standard (Batching, Prefix Cache, Quantization)

sections.body:
This standard defines how Redwood Inference uses Economizer to generate, review, and safely apply automated serving recommendations for batching, prefix caching, and quantization on a per-route and per-model basis. It establishes required guardrails (SLO impact thresholds, rollback, audit logging), telemetry requirements, and the operator workflow in Console/CLI.
h1. Overview
Economizer is Redwood Inference’s recommendation engine for serving configuration changes. It analyzes historical request traces plus live telemetry summaries to propose per-route and per-model adjustments that reduce token spend while keeping latency and error-rate within policy.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* *Batching* (e.g., target batch size range, max queue delay)
* *Prefix caching* (e.g., enablement, TTL and admission thresholds)
* *Quantization profiles* (e.g., FP16 baseline to INT8/FP8 where validated)

This page is the canonical standard for how recommendations are generated, surfaced, validated, and applied.

h1. Scope
sections.heading: Economizer produces three classes of recommendations

sections.body:
* All production serving routes in Redwood Inference clusters
* Console-based recommendation preview and canary application flows
* CLI export used for audit/on-prem workflows
sections.heading: This standard applies to

sections.body:
* Model quality evaluation methodology beyond the defined quantization gates (see related pages)
* Customer-facing product messaging and pricing (handled in product docs)

h1. Principles
1. *Advisory by default.* Recommendations are read-only until explicit org-level opt-in is enabled.
2. *Safety over savings.* Any change must pass canary guardrails with automatic rollback.
3. *Explainability.* Each recommendation must include a rationale, expected savings range, and primary risk.
4. *Least-privilege & auditability.* Applying recommendations requires permissions and produces audit logs.

h1. Inputs & Telemetry Requirements
Economizer relies on aggregated telemetry, not raw prompts.

h2. Required telemetry signals (aggregated)
* Request rate, concurrency, and queueing delay
* Token counts (prompt/completion), distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99)
* Prefix recurrence and estimated cache hit opportunity
* Model identifier, route identifier, and hardware class
* Latency (p50/p95/p99) and error rate

h2. PII and retention requirements
* PII scrubbing is mandatory at collection time (no raw user text in Economizer pipelines).
* Aggregation windows:
  * Online summaries: 5-minute rollups
  * Offline scoring windows: 7 days by default
* Retention:
  * Aggregated Economizer summaries retained for *14 days* (updated from earlier 30-day guidance)
  * Audit logs retained per platform audit policy (see related pages)

h2. Cardinality limits (required)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
* Route-level keys must be normalized (no user IDs, no per-session keys).
* Prefix signatures use hashed buckets with a fixed cap per route per window.
* Any new telemetry dimension added to Economizer must include an explicit cardinality budget and a test demonstrating bounded growth.

h1. Recommendation Types and Constraints
h2. Batching recommendations
sections.heading: To prevent high-cardinality explosions

sections.body:
* Target batch size range (min/target/max)
* Max queue delay (ms)
* Per-route concurrency caps where required to protect tail latency
sections.heading: Economizer may propose

sections.body:
* Recommendations must not increase p95 latency beyond the policy threshold in canary (see Guardrails).
* Routes marked as "latency-critical" (SLO tier 0) must use the stricter latency threshold.

h2. Prefix cache recommendations
sections.heading: Hard constraints

sections.body:
* Enable/disable prefix cache per route
* TTL range for cached prefixes
* Admission threshold based on observed recurrence (e.g., only cache prefixes above a recurrence score)
sections.heading: Economizer may propose

sections.body:
* Cache memory headroom must remain above the service minimum (see Guardrails).
* Any recommendation that increases cache footprint must include an eviction-risk note.

h2. Quantization recommendations
sections.heading: Hard constraints

sections.body:
* FP16 (baseline)
* INT8 (validated models only)
* FP8 (validated models and hardware only; added in 2026-05 standard update)
sections.heading: Economizer may propose

sections.body:
* Quantization recommendations are only surfaced if the Model Registry indicates the (model, quantization, hardware) combination is "validated".
* For models without validation, Economizer may suggest "candidate" quantization but it must be labeled *Requires QA* and cannot be auto-applied.
* A fallback profile must always be included (typically FP16) to enable safe rollback.

h1. Scoring Policy (Cost vs Latency)
Economizer ranks candidates using a utility score balancing cost savings and latency risk.

h2. Default policy weights (2026-05)
* Cost savings weight: 1.0
* Latency penalty weight: 1.3 (increased from 1.0 to reduce tail-latency regressions observed in early beta)
* Error-rate penalty: hard fail if error-rate increases above guardrails
sections.heading: Constraints and gates

sections.body:
* The policy uses p99 latency as a primary risk signal for SLO tier 0 routes; p95 is the primary signal for other routes.
* Operators may tune sensitivity via approved configuration only. Any non-default weight set must be documented in the change ticket.

h1. Guardrails and SLO Thresholds
These guardrails are mandatory for any recommendation application.

h2. Canary eligibility checks (pre-flight)
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
* It has at least 72 hours of stable telemetry in the last 7 days
* Baseline error rate is below 0.5% over the last 24 hours
* The route is not under active incident mitigation

h2. Canary rollout guardrails (must pass)
Guardrails are evaluated against baseline for the same route.

Table: Default guardrails
* SLO tier 0 routes:
  * p99 latency change: <= +2%
  * p95 latency change: <= +1%
  * error rate change: <= +0.1% absolute
* SLO tier 1+ routes:
  * p95 latency change: <= +3%
  * p99 latency change: <= +5%
  * error rate change: <= +0.2% absolute
sections.heading: A route is eligible for canary if

sections.body: * Cache memory headroom must remain >= 15% during canary (updated from 10% to reduce eviction storms)
sections.heading: Cache safety

sections.body:
* Any guardrail breach sustained for >= 10 minutes
* Any sudden error spike > 2x baseline for >= 5 minutes

h2. Rollout stages (standard)
1. 1% traffic for 30–60 minutes
2. 5% traffic for 60 minutes
3. 25% traffic for 2 hours
4. 100% if stable

Operators may extend stages for high-risk changes (quantization, large cache expansions).

h1. Operator Workflow (Console)
h2. Preview
1. Open *Console → Economizer → Recommendations*.
2. Filter by route, model, and time window.
3. Inspect each recommendation’s:
   * Expected savings range
   * Expected latency delta range
   * Primary risk factors
   * Compatibility notes (especially for quantization)

h2. Simulation (required for quantization; recommended otherwise)
The simulator replays anonymized trace summaries to estimate deltas.
sections.heading: Auto-rollback conditions

sections.body:
* Simulations must reference the same scoring window as the recommendation.
* If the simulator output diverges materially from the recommendation rationale, do not proceed; investigate telemetry quality.

h2. Apply via canary
1. Select recommendation → *Create Canary*.
2. Confirm rollback target (fallback profile must be set).
3. Start canary with default stages unless an exception is approved.
4. Monitor guardrails in the Rollouts dashboard.
5. Promote to 100% only after all stages pass.

h2. Audit logging (required)
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
* Actor (user/service)
* Route and model
* Before/after configuration
* Canary stage timestamps
* Rollback events (if any)

h1. Operator Workflow (CLI Export)
CLI export is supported for audit and on-prem workflows.
sections.heading: Every applied recommendation must record

sections.body: redwood-cli economizer export --route <route-id> --window 7d --format json --out recommendations.json
sections.heading: Example

sections.body:
* Exported artifacts must be stored in an approved audit location.
* Any manual application of exported recommendations must still follow the canary standard.

h1. Expected Impact (Updated Guidance)
Based on internal benchmarks and production-like traces, typical savings are:
* 10–30% token spend reduction for chat-heavy workloads when combining batching + prefix caching
* Additional savings from quantization vary widely and are gated by validation status
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
* With default policy weights, expected p95 impact is usually within +0% to +3% for eligible routes.

This guidance updates earlier internal claims of 15–35% typical savings; the current range better reflects mixed workloads and stricter latency weights.

h1. Known Limitations
* Cold-start routes with limited telemetry can receive noisy recommendations.
* Some proprietary or newly onboarded models may lack quantization validation metadata.
* Prefix cache recommendations are sensitive to prompt normalization; changes in templating can invalidate recurrence estimates.

h1. Responsibilities
* Serving Runtime team: owns Economizer engine, scoring policy defaults, and rollout integration.
* SRE: owns telemetry retention, PII scrubbing enforcement, and observability requirements.
* Service owners: review recommendations, run canaries, and approve promotion to 100%.

h1. Change Management
sections.heading: Latency impact

sections.body:
* Default policy weights
* Guardrail thresholds
* Telemetry retention or aggregation windows

must be documented as a standards update and reviewed by Serving Runtime + SRE.

h1. References
* Economizer engine implementation: internal/economizer (repo: redwood)
* Rollout mechanism: standard canary rollout APIs and Console Rollouts dashboard
* Model Registry validation: Quantization compatibility matrix (see related pages)

2026-05-12: Updated retention to 14 days for aggregated summaries; raised cache headroom requirement to 15%; introduced FP8 as a gated/validated quantization option; increased default latency penalty weight to 1.3; updated expected savings guidance to 10–30% typical.
2026-03-10: Initial published standard aligned with Economizer v1 rollout (batching, prefix cache, INT8 where validated), advisory-by-default posture, canary guardrails, and audit requirements.

payload.page_title: Request fanout attenuation and resilience guardrails

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines Redwood's standards and recommended patterns for controlling request fanout, attenuating amplification effects, and providing resilient graceful degradation across API, infra, and model-serving layers. It unifies API semantics, infra-level controls, and observability signals so teams can safely expose multi-target requests (fanout) without risking cascading failures or large cost spikes.

Goals

- Limit unbounded amplification from single client requests (e.g., one client -> many model/auxiliary calls).
- Ensure predictable cost/latency profiles under bursty or adversarial traffic.
- Provide standard, interoperable controls for graceful degradation: partial responses, early-exit, and failure domains.
- Tie telemetry and SLOs to attenuation behavior so automated policies can act safely.

Scope

Applies to: API gateway, edge & ingress proxies, orchestration layer that fans out to model variants or auxiliary services (search, rerank, tool calls), and model-serving runtime. Not covered: client SDK behavior beyond suggested headers.

Design principles

1. Fail fast where impact is unbounded: Prefer rejecting or attenuating requests early when amplification risk cannot be bounded.
2. Explicit budget per request: Every request carries a request budget (tokens, RPCs, compute-units) conveyed through headers and enforced through gateways and router tiers.
3. Observables-first: Each attenuation point must emit an event with reason, decision (attenuate/allow), and the budget delta.
4. Composability: Attenuation controls are layered and orthogonal (client hints, gateway caps, model runtime early-exit).

API-level contract

- Request budget header: X-RW-Req-Budget (integer, compute-units). Default if absent: 100 compute-units.
- Max-fanout header: X-RW-Max-Fanout (integer). Gateway will reject requests that request fanout beyond allowed per-plan limits.
- Partial-response mode: X-RW-Partial-Mode (values: none|partial-keys|summary). If partial allowed, backends may return summarized or partial content.
- Failure-hint header: X-RW-Failure-Mode (values: retryable|fail-fast|fallback-preferred). This is advisory; enforcement is infra-driven.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
curl -i -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  -H 'X-RW-Req-Budget: 150' \
  -H 'X-RW-Max-Fanout: 10' \
  -H 'X-RW-Partial-Mode: summary' \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/compose

Infra controls and runtime enforcement

Table: key attenuation controls and recommended defaults

| Control | Enforcement point | Default / recommended value | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Per-request compute budget | Edge gateway + router | 100 compute-units (soft), 300 (hard for enterprise) | Edge team |
| Fanout cap | Gateway + router | 12 parallel targets per request | Router team |
| Staggered fanout window | Router | 200ms jitter spread for parallel calls >4 | Runtime team |
| Early-exit threshold | Model-serving runtime | Stop at 0.6 quality score drop or 80% token budget | Runtime team |
| Cumulative cost guard | Billing-middleware | Reject if projected spend > monthly quota slice | Finance/Quota service |

Notes: compute-units are an internal abstraction that combines expected token cost, KV cache usage, and auxiliary RPC counts. Each service publishes a compute-unit price in the service catalog.

Attenuation strategies (patterns)

1) Fanout cap and tiering
- Gate maximum parallel targets at edge based on plan (free/dev/prod) and request budget.
- Tiered behavior: below 25% budget use full parallelism; 25–75% use staggered; above 75% reject or require partial mode.

2) Staggered concurrency (jittered waterfall)
- When making many parallel backend calls (search + rerank + tool call), the router adds jitter and progressive concurrency windows to smooth spikes.
- Example: 8 targets -> start 2, after 50ms start 3 more, remaining after next 150ms.

3) Early-exit and progressive refinement
- Model-serving runtime supports returning intermediate summaries or truncated outputs with confidence signals.
- Clients are encouraged to accept X-RW-Partial-Mode to enable progressive refinement.

4) Aggregation and sampling as amplification antidotes
- For duplicate or similar fanout targets, combine queries server-side (e.g., batch or multi-query).
- When cost risk is high, sample 50% of non-critical targets and mark response with attenuation.reason = sampled.

Observability and SLOs

Every attenuation decision must emit the following telemetry fields (minimum):
- request_id, route, attenuation_point (edge|router|runtime), decision (allow|attenuate|reject), budget_before, budget_after, reason_code, downstream_targets, latency_ms.
sections.heading: Example request headers

sections.body:
- Attenuation rate: <= 2% of production requests should be attenuated for cost reasons under baseline traffic. Alert if > 5% sustained over 15m.
- Amplification spikes: Alert when median downstream_targets per request > baseline+3*stdev for 5m.
- Partial-response quality regression: If average downstream eval score for partial responses falls below baseline by 10%, trigger regression alert tied to quality-monitoring.

Operational playbook (incident triage)

1) Detection: Alert fires for amplification spike or high attenuation rate.
2) Initial triage (5 min): Identify impacted routes and top client tokens. Escalate to Router and Edge on-call.
3) Containment (10 min): Apply emergency fanout cap through router feature-flag (binary knob), or engage plan-level hard caps.
4) Mitigation (30 min): Enable partial-response mode for affected routes; activate cached-response fallback; enable sample-only mode (reduce noncritical fanout).
5) Root-cause (2–8 hours): Run request sampling and golden-trace correlation to find bad clients or regression in model cost-profile.
6) Remediation: Deploy model artifact rollback, adjust compute-unit pricing, or issue client rate-limits.

Rollout checklist for new fanout-enabled API

1. Define compute-unit cost for every backend target and publish in service catalog.
2. Add budget headers and client SDK support for X-RW-Req-Budget and X-RW-Partial-Mode.
3. Implement edge-level soft caps with clear rejection reasons (429 + X-RW-Attenuation-Reason).
4. Emit attenuation telemetry events and validate in staging ingestion.
5. Run chaos tests simulating client bursts and confirm SLOs (latency, cost, error budget) remain within thresholds.
6. Documentation and customer communication (if plan limits change).

Configuration example (router agent YAML snippet)

agent:
  name: router-attenuation-agent
  fanout:
    default_max_parallel: 12
    stagger_windows_ms: [50,150]
    soft_budget_threshold: 0.75
    enforce_partial_header: true
  telemetry:
    emit_attenuation_events: true
    sample_rate: 1.0

Ownership and governance

- Edge team: validate and enforce plan-level caps; return standard attenuation response codes.
- Router team: implement staggered fanout, budget enforcement, and per-route policies.
- Runtime team: expose early-exit APIs and confidence signals; expose cost telemetry.
- Observability: define attenuation event schema, maintain dashboards and alerting runbooks.
- Product/Finance: set default compute-unit pricing per model/service and define plan caps.

Compatibility notes and backwards-compatibility

- Clients that do not supply X-RW-Req-Budget will use the default. A migration window of 90 days is required before changing defaults.
- If X-RW-Partial-Mode is absent, systems assume partial-mode=none and will apply stricter caps.

Security and privacy considerations

- Attenuation telemetry must avoid logging prompt text; include only hashed prompt fingerprints where needed.
- When sampling requests for RCA, ensure PII redaction and adherence to retention policies.

Appendix: standard attenuation reason codes

- ATTN_OVER_FANOUT_CAP: request exceeds allowed parallel targets
- ATTN_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED: request compute budget would be exceeded
- ATTN_SAMPLING: non-critical targets sampled down to reduce cost
- ATTN_PARTIAL_OK: request accepted but returned partial response per client preference
- ATTN_REJECT_PLAN: request exceeds plan-level contractual limits

Related artifacts and references

- See /confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/queue-smoothing-and-throttling-safeguards-2026 for queueing interactions.
- Runtime early-exit contract: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/deterministic-inference-and-reproducibility-standards-2026

Questions and feedback

For design questions or to request a non-default plan cap, contact the Edge team or open a PR on the attenuation-agent repo.

payload.page_title: Hosted model performance bar (catalog launch requirements)

sections.body: This standard defines the minimum performance and reliability bar a model must meet before it can be launched in the Hosted API catalog.
sections.heading: Summary

- Context sizes: 2k, 8k, 16k

- TTFT p95 <= 2.5s (2k context)

payload.page_title: Predictable Cost & Latency Simulator: Specification and Validation Checklist

sections.body: Overview
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This document specifies the Predictable Cost & Latency Simulator (PCLS): a company-standard lightweight simulator and validation checklist teams must use to estimate per-request latency distributions and token-unit costs for proposed runtime changes (model upgrades, quantization, batching, kernel selection, memory layouts, and routing policy changes) before any staged rollout. The simulator is intended to be conservative, reproducible, and fast enough to run in CI and preflight pipelines.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to: model serving changes (new model versions, precision changes, KV-cache behavior), routing/policy changes that alter execution path (fallback variants, cross-region routing), and infra changes that affect scheduling or preemption behavior.
- Out of scope: long-running load testing at fleet scale (use the perf-lab harness for full-scale testing). PCLS is for per-config, workload-local predictions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- p95-latency: 95th percentile end-to-end response time measured from request arrival at rwd-router to final token emission.
- unit-cost: blended per-token cost estimate including GPU execution token cost, memory/DRAM charge, and amortized network overhead for streaming tokens.
- sample-workload: an anonymized, non-PII prompt trace representing the target application workload.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) Predictability: simulator inputs are explicit and versioned (model artifact id, kernel profile, sequence-length histogram, batch-policy).
2) Conservatism: when uncertain, prefer pessimistic estimates (higher latency, higher cost) with documented uncertainty bounds.
3) Reproducibility: run deterministically in CI with recorded seeds and explainable approximations.
4) Lightweight: complete in under 90 seconds for a typical sample-workload (1000 requests) on a single CI worker.

Architecture (textual diagram)
- Input layer: sample-workload plus config file containing model_variant, quantization_profile, batch_policy, routing_policy.
- Execution model: microkernel-profile lookup leads to a per-token execution estimate, which is fed into a batching simulator, a KV-cache hit/miss model, and then a network/serialize latency layer.
- Cost model: per-kernel token-cost plus amortized pre/post processing costs and memory delta charge.
- Output: latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99), cost per request, hotspot breakdown (GPU, batching delay, serialization, network), and CI-friendly artifacts (JSON report and CSV traces).

Required Inputs
- model_id: immutable artifact id used by rwd-runtime (string).
- kernel_profile: kernel timing table name and version (string).
- seq_length_histogram: sequence length distribution as list of length:frequency pairs (CSV or JSONL serialized as string).
- batch_policy: policy name and parameters (e.g., continuous, fixed-N, adaptive).
- kv_cache_profile: hit_rate estimate (0.0-1.0) and avg_kv_latency_ms.
- concurrency_pattern: arrival process (poisson|bursty|steady) and mean_rate.
- quantization: profile id (none|int8|nf4|mixed).

Validation Checklist (must-pass to proceed to canary)
1) Completeness: Simulator run completed and produced a JSON report in the expected schema.
2) SLO delta check: predicted p95 must not exceed baseline p95 by more than the allowed delta in the change request (default +15%).
3) Cost delta check: predicted unit-cost must not exceed baseline by more than the allowed delta (default +30% unless product approval is provided).
4) Regression hotspots: any component contributing 20% or more of the delta must have an owner and an action plan attached to the change ticket.
5) Uncertainty bounds: bootstrap on trace samples to produce 90% confidence intervals; if interval width exceeds 12% relative, annotate the run as 'high-variance' and require manual review.
6) Sensitivity scan: run three additional simulations with arrival rate +/-10% and kv_cache hit rate +/-0.1; differences should be within tolerances or explicitly documented.
7) Artifact storage: upload simulator JSON report to the perf-artifacts bucket path perf/pcls/{change_id}/{run_id}.json.

Example config (YAML-like sample)
change_id: R-2026-1130-batcher-tuning
model_id: redwood-3b-v2:2026-01-15
kernel_profile: amx-ops-v3
quantization: nf4-compact
batch_policy:
  name: adaptive
  max_batch_size: 64
  latency_target_ms: 35
kv_cache_profile:
  hit_rate: 0.78
  avg_kv_ms: 1.2
seq_length_histogram: |
  16, 0.55
  32, 0.30
  128, 0.10
  512, 0.05
concurrency_pattern:
  type: poisson
  mean_qps: 12

CLI and CI integration
- Local run example: pcls run --config config.yaml --workload traces/sample-app-1.json --output ./reports/report.json
- CI job snippet (GitHub Actions): check out repo, run tools/pcls/bin/pcls run with config and upload resulting report as an artifact.

Metrics and Reporting Format
Required fields in the JSON report (keys must exist; use empty arrays if no data):
- change_id, run_id, timestamp, model_id, kernel_profile, quantization, batch_policy.
- latencies: p50, p90, p95, p99 in milliseconds.
- unit_cost_usd (per request).
- breakdown: list of component delta strings (e.g., 'gpu: +6.1ms', 'batching-delay: +12.4ms').
- uncertainty: p95_ci_lower and p95_ci_upper recorded as numeric strings.
- artifacts: raw_trace_csv path and histogram_png path as strings.

Hotspot categories and remedial actions
- GPU-kernel: re-evaluate kernel selection or request investigation from kernel-ops.
- Batcher: tune adaptive settings, reduce max_batch_size, or change latency_target_ms.
- KV-cache: investigate eviction patterns, warmup strategies, or increase cache sizing.
- Serializer/network: consider switching to gRPC streaming, adjust chunk sizes, or tune serialization buffers.

Acceptance gates and rollouts
- Must pass simulator validations and be approved by the owning service SRE and the model owner.
- If SLO delta is between +10% and +15%, require a staged canary at 5% then 20% traffic with automatic rollback if observed p95 exceeds predicted by more than +5%.
- If cost delta is >= +20%, product finance must approve or provide an offset plan.

Ownership and responsibilities
- Document owner: engineering service owner (must be set in the change ticket).
- Simulation tool maintainer: perf-infra team (on-call contact: perfinfra@redwood.com).
- Kernel profile sources: kernel-ops team.
- Cost model steward: finance-engineering.

Appendix: example report snippet (flat representation)
- change_id: R-2026-1130-batcher-tuning
- run_id: pcls-20260203-001
- model_id: redwood-3b-v2:2026-01-15
- p50_ms: 18.2
- p90_ms: 31.7
- p95_ms: 39.8
- p99_ms: 62.1
- unit_cost_usd: 0.0034
- breakdown_items: ["gpu: +6.1ms", "batching-delay: +12.4ms", "serialize: +1.3ms"]

Related artifacts and references
- perf-lab/harness README (full-scale load testing).
- kernel-ops/profile-catalog (kernel_profile naming and versions).
- docs/routing-policies (fallback and variant routing definitions).

Frequently asked questions (short)
Q: When should I prefer perf-lab over PCLS?
A: Use perf-lab for cluster-level behaviors (preemption across tenants, multi-node sharding) or to validate autoscaling and prewarming policies at scale. PCLS is for fast, per-change estimates.

Q: How does PCLS treat streaming token emission?
A: Streaming is modeled as incremental serialization plus network overhead per token and amortized GPU kernel time. Teams should include realistic chunk sizes in seq_length_histogram.

Change log
- 2025-11-12 (Maya Chen): initial spec and checklist.
- 2026-02-03 (Maya Chen): added uncertainty bootstrap, updated cost thresholds, added CI snippet.

Contact
For questions or tool access, ping #perf-infra on Slack or email perfinfra@redwood.com.

payload.page_title: Forensic-Friendly Rollback Protocol and Telemetry Preservation — Operator Guide

sections.body: This runbook describes a forensic-friendly rollback protocol for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It prioritizes safe service recovery, preservation of diagnostic telemetry and evidence, and minimal customer impact while keeping a clear chain-of-custody for postmortem analysis. Use this guide when a production rollout or upgrade causes: total or partial service regressions, data-integrity concerns, or regulatory-impacting failures.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to: Private (VPC) control-plane coordinated upgrades, on-prem appliance upgrades, model artifact swaps, KV cache schema or migration rollouts.
- Not intended for: transient infra flakiness that can be resolved by autoscaler/tuner. Use the incident triage playbooks in day-2-ops for those cases.
sections.heading: Scope and applicability

sections.body:
- RTO target: 15 minutes for partial rollbacks, 60 minutes for complex stateful rollbacks across regions.
- Preserve at least 99% of request-level telemetry for the incident window (see Telemetry Preservation below).
- Maintain auditable evidence for all changed artifacts and operator actions.
- Avoid customer data loss; if unavoidable, follow the evidence and notification procedures in Customer Impact and Legal Notification.
sections.heading: Goals and acceptance criteria

sections.body:
- Primary on-call: Private Deployments SRE (team: eng-private-deployments).
- Escalation: Platform Reliability -> Security Incident Response (if evidence tampering or exfiltration suspected) -> Legal & Compliance.
- Communications: use #private-deploy-ops and the customer-facing incident template to coordinate external communications.
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:
1) Confirm problem scope: model-only (inference quality), runtime-only (latency/CPU/GPU), or data plane (egress/ingest).
2) Confirm reproducible signal: elevated 5xx rate, token-level latency regression >2x baseline, or model-output quality regressions on canary prompt set.
3) Snapshot metadata and top-level state: control-plane revision, model artifact versions, KV-cache epoch IDs, node inventory.
sections.heading: Prerequisites and pre-rollback checks

sections.body:
- Sampling: switch to full-sampling for the incident window for these streams: request traces, model-input snapshots (redact PII), kernel-level GPU telemetry, and operator CLI actions.
- Buffering: for on-prem/airgapped sites, enable the local telemetry buffer retention (config: telemetry.buffer.enabled=true, telemetry.buffer.size=10GB) and do not rotate buffers until evidence preserved.
- Export: immediately trigger an export job to the secure evidence S3 bucket (or customer-specified bucket for VPC) with prefix: evidence/rollback/{customer}/{YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS}.
- Hashing: compute SHA256 of exported archives and record in the evidence ledger.

Decision matrix: rollback vs degrade vs fix-forward
- Rollback if any of:
  - Model artifact causes a quality regression >10% on production prompt set AND cannot be mitigated by config knobs in 10 minutes.
  - New runtime binary causes persistent 5xx >0.5% for 30 minutes.
  - Migration causes KV-cache inconsistency across >5% of tenants.
- Degrade (gradual feature toggle) if the failure is localized and rollback would cause broader disruption (use canary-unwind pattern).
- Fix-forward if the change is non-stateful and small patch can be validated within the SLO windows.

Pre-rollback checklist (operator must complete this before initiating rollback):
- [ ] Document incident id and reason in ticketing system.
- [ ] Record control-plane revision, model and artifact checksums.
- [ ] Trigger telemetry full-sample and evidence export.
- [ ] Validate backups for KV-store and model artifact repository exist (timestamped).
- [ ] Notify impacted customers per SLA template if customer-facing.

Rollback procedure (high-level, numbered steps):
1) Enter safe-mode for the affected tenants: restrict new model swaps and disable autoscale-driven node churn.
2) If a model artifact is the rollback target: mark model variant as deprecated and pin to previous stable artifact; run model-swap API with --force=false to ensure an orchestrated swap.
3) For runtime binary rollbacks: initiate orchestrated canary rollback through the control-plane with the stable image tag. Use the operator CLI:
   - rwdctl rollout rollback --service serving-runtime --to-tag v2026.01.10-stable --max-in-flight 2
4) If stateful (KV) migration was applied, follow the stateful rollback cookbook: pause writes, run the reversible migration revert script, and coordinate epoch rollback across shards.
5) During rollback, keep telemetry full-sampling active and stream a copy of logs to the evidence bucket.
6) After each chunk of traffic is moved back, run verification tests (see Verification below).
7) When green, slowly re-enable autoscaling and unpin services; leave monitoring elevated for three full SLO windows.
sections.heading: Telemetry preservation strategy

sections.body:
- Smoke tests: /health, per-tenant routing checks, and tokenized latency suite (p95 and p99 targets).
- Functional: run canary prompt set against model (if model swap) and compare quality metrics to baseline.
- Consistency: KV checksum and sample query validations for 1000 random keys.
- Telemetry: confirm export archive integrity and SHA256 matches evidence ledger.
sections.heading: Verification and acceptance tests (run after each step)

sections.body:
1) Evidence artifacts to preserve: control-plane snapshots, model artifact checksums, operator CLI history, telemetry export, node-level system profiles (journalctl /var/log/syslog), and storage backend snapshots.
2) Evidence packaging: package artifacts into a single signed archive, compute SHA256 and sign with operator key (KMS/HSM).
3) Ledger entry: add an immutable ledger record with fields: incident_id, archive_path, sha256, signer, timestamp. Use the ledger CLI: ledger add --incident $ID --path s3://evidence/... --sha256 $HASH --signer priyam
4) Secure storage: move the archive to the restricted evidence S3 with bucket-policy: deny-delete-unless-role:legal_audit.
sections.heading: Evidence collection and chain-of-custody

sections.body:
- VPC (customer-attached bucket):
  - Ensure export job uses the customer-approved encryption key.
  - Confirm network egress rule allows telemetry export to the bucket; if not, use the edge-proxy relay pattern.
  - Coordinate with customer security contact before moving evidence off-network where required by contract.
- On-prem / Airgapped:
  - Use local-attested USB transfer procedure only after signing and storing checksums in the control-plane ledger.
  - Maintain chain-of-custody paper or digitally-signed receipts for physical transfers.
sections.heading: Special considerations by deployment type

sections.body:
- Rolling back a model that requires a changed KV cache schema requires a two-phase approach: first, restore service to stable model and keep both schema-compatibility adapters active; second, run adapter-based reconciliation across tenants for 48–72 hours before deprecating the old adapter.
- Avoid purging KV epochs until reconciliation is complete. If storage pressure requires pruning, take snapshots and store in the evidence bucket with explicit ledger references.
sections.heading: KV cache and model artifact specifics

sections.body:
- If rollback affects committed SLA windows, follow the customer compensation matrix and notify Customer Success.
- For regulated customers (finance/healthcare), follow the additional evidence preservation checklist in the Customer Requirements Library (see Related pages).
sections.heading: Interaction with customer requirements and SLAs

sections.body:
- Trigger full telemetry sample: rwdctl telemetry sample --scope incident --enable true --duration 2h
- Export evidence: rwdctl evidence export --prefix evidence/rollback/${CUSTOMER}/${ID} --include logs,traces,artifacts --encrypt-kms arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:1234:key/abcd
- Roll back runtime image (canary-aware): rwdctl rollout rollback --service serving-runtime --to-tag v2026.01.10-stable --max-in-flight 2
sections.heading: Runbook snippets and CLI examples

sections.body:
1) Keep monitoring elevated for 72 hours; collect SLO/quality metrics and compare to pre-incident baseline.
2) Populate postmortem with: timeline, root-cause hypothesis, decision justification for rollback, evidence ledger entries, and remediation action items.
3) If rollback should be automated for similar failures, open a design ticket for a safe-automation RFC and schedule a canary test.

Appendix A — Minimal evidence metadata table:
| artifact | required fields | retention (default) | notes |
| control-plane-snapshot | revision, timestamp, operator | 2 years | include config and feature flags |
| model-artifact | checksum, manifest, provenance | 3 years | include model-card with eval snapshot |
| telemetry-archive | sha256, start/end, redact-policy | 2 years | store redaction policy reference |
| kv-snapshot | shard-id, epoch, checksum | 3 years | required for regulated tenants |
sections.heading: Post-rollback steps and postmortem

sections.body:
- See: customer-requirements-library/private-deploy-acceptance-and-smoke-validation-2026 (telemetry and evidence contracts)
- See: upgrade-and-rollback/private-deploy-evidence-preservation-and-forensic-playbook-2026 (detailed forensic scripts)
- See: day-2-ops/private-deploy-livetail-and-debugging-runbook-2026 (live debugging and elevated telemetry patterns)
sections.heading: Related pages and references

sections.body:
- Document owner: eng-private-deployments (oncall@redwood.com).
- For legal/evidence escalation: legal-evidence@redwood.com.
sections.heading: Contact and ownership

sections.body:

- 2026-03-01: updated verification checklist and VPC evidence notes (reviewers: David Chen, Aisha Gomez)

payload.page_title: SLO Composition for Multi‑Tenant Model Serving

sections.body:
Purpose

This page defines Redwood's standard approach for composing, allocating, and monitoring Service Level Objectives (SLOs) across multi-tenant model-serving surfaces (hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private runtime sidecars). The goal is predictable customer experience, fair resource isolation, and measurable unit economics that feed billing and capacity planning.

Scope

- Applies to: text generation, chat streaming, embeddings and reranking endpoints that are served from a shared runtime (multi-tenant GPU pools and multi-variant model deployments).
- Excludes: one-off batch-only offline workloads and single-tenant appliance deployments with explicit per-customer SLA contracts.

Key principles

1) Tenant-first SLOs: SLOs are expressed from the consumer's perspective (e.g., 95th percentile request latency for a customer route), not only internal pod metrics.
2) Composability: Service-level SLOs are built from per-route, per-variant, and infra SLO primitives using explicit weighting and error budgets.
3) Isolation and fairness: Composition must support throttling and fallback policies that avoid noisy-neighbor effects.
4) Cost-awareness: SLO formulas must account for cost amplification (model size, quantization, batch size) so capacity planning and billing reflect true unit economics.

Definitions and primitives

- route: the API surface configured by a customer (e.g., /v1/generate with model=redwood-alpha).
- variant: an individual model binary/configuration (fp16, q4_0, q8_0) served behind a route.
- infra_slo: cluster-level SLOs (e.g., GPU prewarm availability, queue latency).
- tenant_slo: per-tenant observable (latency_p95_ms, error_rate_5m, token_throughput_rps).

SLO composition model (formula)

We define a deterministic composition function that aggregates variant-level observations into route-level SLOs and then into service-level commitments. The canonical form:

route_slo = sum_i(weight_i * variant_slo_i) + infra_risk_margin
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- weight_i is the traffic-weight fraction for variant i over a sliding window (default 1-minute).
- variant_slo_i is the measured objective (e.g., p95 latency) for that variant.
- infra_risk_margin is a fixed offset derived from infra_slo violations (see infra interaction).

Example: p95 latency composition

If variant A (weight 0.7) has p95=120ms and variant B (weight 0.3) has p95=260ms, route_p95 = 0.7*120 + 0.3*260 = 162ms.

Per-tenant SLO tiers

We standardize on three tenant tiers for hosted and dedicated customers. Private deployments may map these to contract terms.

| Tier | Commitments (example) | Error budget
|------|-----------------------|----------------|
| Standard | p95 <= 250ms, available 99.9% (monthly), error_rate < 0.5% | 0.1% monthly
| Premium  | p95 <= 150ms, available 99.95% (monthly), error_rate < 0.2% | 0.05% monthly
| Latency-Optimized | p95 <= 80ms, available 99.99% (monthly), error_rate < 0.1% | 0.01% monthly

Note: These are customer-facing commitments. Internally we map them to route and variant objectives with explicit headroom and safety margins.

Infra interaction and risk margins

Infra SLOs (GPU prewarm time, queueing time, streaming packet loss) feed a risk score R in [0,1] every minute. We add an infra_risk_margin_ms = baseline_margin_ms * R to composed latency SLOs. Baseline_margin_ms = 40ms by default for shared pools, 10ms for Dedicated.

Monitoring and queries

Instrumentation must expose the following time series per (tenant, route, variant):
- redwood.requests.latency_ms.p95
- redwood.requests.errors.count (HTTP 5xx, model-runtime-failure)
- redwood.tokens.generated.total
- redwood.queue.wait_ms.p50/p95

sections.body:
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (tenant, le) (rate(redwood_requests_latency_bucket[1m])))

Alerting thresholds (recommended)

- Alert: tenant_p95_exceeded
  - Condition: tenant_p95 > committed_p95 for 3 consecutive 1m windows
  - Severity: P2 for Standard, P1 for Premium / Latency-Optimized
  - Runbook: see runbook id: eng-sre/runbooks/tenant-slo-breach

- Alert: infra_risk_degraded
  - Condition: infra_risk_score > 0.6 for 5m
  - Severity: P1

Operational behaviors on SLO pressure

1) Reactive traffic shaping (automated): when a tenant exceeds error budget and infra risk > 0.5, system applies soft-throttles (rate limit 10% reductions, per-tenant) and moves lower-priority traffic to fallback variants.
2) Canary-aware rollbacks: deployment changes that increase variant tail latency by > 15% must be automatically rolled back (see ADR: canary-mesh-guidelines).
3) Billing impact: sustained tier violations >72h triggers account review and cost-corrective actions (credits, prioritized capacity purchase offers).

SLO spec (YAML example)

  kind: SLO
  tenant: example-corp
  route: /v1/generate
  metric: latency_p95_ms
  objective: 150
  window: 30d
  weights:
    variants:
      - name: redwood-alpha-fp16
        weight: 0.8
      - name: redwood-alpha-q4_0
        weight: 0.2

CLI integration
sections.heading: Example PromQL for tenant p95 latency (1m lookback)

sections.body:
# redwoodctl is the internal control-plane CLI
  redwoodctl slo apply -f tenant-slos/example-corp-slo.yaml --env=prod

Rollout and validation checklist (owners must complete before going GA)

1) Define per-variant telemetry exports (owner: runtime-team).
2) Configure composition weights and initial infra_margin (owner: eng-sre).
3) Smoke tests: synthetic traffic that exercises 99th percentile flows for 24h (owner: perf-team).
4) Observability validation: dashboards, alerts, and sampled traces available for tenant (owner: eng-platform).
5) Assume-failure drills: simulate node preemption and verify fallback routing (owner: eng-serving-runtime).

Ownership and governance

- Runtime: implementation of variant-level metrics and weight reporting — eng-serving-runtime team.
- SLO system & alerts: eng-sre.
- Billing & cost mapping: finance-legal + product (billing-data-pipeline).
- Policy & tier definitions: product team (final approval).

Runbooks and links

- eng-sre/runbooks/tenant-slo-breach (detailed triage steps)
- eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/fallback-orchestration
- perf-team/simulations/multi-tenant-loadbook-2025

Appendix: Examples and edge cases

1) Cold-start amplification: for routes with >25% cold starts in a 5m window apply an extra cold_start_penalty_ms of 200ms to the composed SLO and escalate to eng-sre.
2) Skewed variant traffic: If any variant weight < 0.05 but variance in p95 > 3x other variants, ignore that variant's p95 and use cluster-median instead (to avoid noisy short-lived canaries impacting route commitments).
3) Private deployments: customers may opt-in to "contractual isolation" where infra_risk_margin is negotiated and removed from public commitments; documentation lives in eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops.

Change log

- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Maya Patel)
- 2025-06-10: Added infra risk margin and monitoring queries (Ethan Wong)
- 2025-09-01: Finalized rollout checklist and tier definitions (published)

If you have questions or need a tailored SLO mapping for a specific customer, open a ticket with the runtime or eng-sre team and include the tenant_id and intended traffic profile.

payload.page_title: Degradation Simulation Lab and Benchmarking Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook defines the Degradation Simulation Lab (DegradLab): an automated, repeatable harness for injecting controlled resource and behavioral degradation into Redwood Inference stack components to validate SLO resilience, fallback correctness, and cost/quality tradeoffs before deployments. It codifies scenarios, instrumentation requirements, pass/fail criteria, and an owner-run checklist for both feature rollouts and model/quantization changes.

Goals:
- Provide reproducible degradation scenarios that exercise latency, throughput, cache-staleness, and model-fidelity fallbacks.
- Surface regressions in end-to-end latency SLOs and quality regressions tied to degraded paths (quantization, fallback variants).
- Standardize acceptance criteria for production rollouts and model promotions.

Scope and non-goals:
- In-scope: API gateway, edge routing, runtime serving tier (GPU pools), KV/prefix cache, model variant fallback, telemetry pipeline.
- Out-of-scope: third-party infra outside Redwood control (cloud provider control plane).

Key concepts:
1) Degradation modes:
  - Resource contention (CPU/GPU throttling, memory pressure)
  - Network degradation (increased egress latency, packet loss emulation)
  - Service slow-downs (artificial request processing delay)
  - Cache staleness (prefix/KV cache eviction and cold-hit ratios)
  - Model fidelity shift (downgrading from full-precision to quantized variant)
2) Fidelity tiers and fallbacks:
  - Tier 0: Default model (highest-quality)
  - Tier 1: Quantized/fast variant with verified quality budget
  - Tier 2: Small-context or summary fallback (reduced cost/latency)

DegradLab architecture (logical):
- Experiment controller (k8s job with declarative JSON experiment manifests)
- Synthetic traffic generator (workload profiles: chat-heavy, short-gen, embedding-batch)
- Failure injectors (chaos proxy for network, cgroups-based CPU/GPU throttler, cache warm/cold driver)
- Telemetry collector (aggregates traces, histograms, error rates to the observability cluster)
- Analysis engine (computes SLO deltas, regression alerts, and artifact storage)

Standard scenarios (examples):
1) Cold-cache burst: 5-minute warmdown; then ramp 200 rps for 10 minutes with cache disabled. Pass if p95 latency <= 2x baseline and error rate < 0.2%.
2) Quantization fallback under GPU pressure: throttle 40% GPU cycles on 20% of shards and observe automatic quantized variant routing. Pass if output-churn is within 1% of baseline accuracy for labeled prompt set and tail latency SLOs hold.
3) Out-of-region failover: simulate region 1 routing drop; verify routing to nearest region, tokens-per-second degradation <= 30% and no more than 1% client-facing errors.
4) Streaming slow-path: inject 500ms additional per-chunk processing for streaming endpoints; pass if partial-result checkpoints resume without user-visible corruption and retry logic recovers within configured window.

Metric mapping and thresholds (excerpt):
| Metric | SLO | Alert threshold | Analysis window |
| p50 latency (ms) | baseline+10% | >= baseline+40% | 5m |
| p95 latency (ms) | baseline+50% | >= baseline+100% | 5m |
| request_error_rate | <= 0.5% | >= 1% | 5m |
| model-quality-regression | delta F1 <= 0.01 | delta F1 >= 0.03 | experiment run |

Experiment manifest (short example):
{
  "name": "quant-fallback-under-gpu-pressure-2026-06",
  "duration": "15m",
  "traffic_profile": "chat-heavy-200rps",
  "injectors": ["gpu-throttle:40%:shard=odd", "cache-evict:100%:namespace=prefix-store"],
  "quality_checks": ["evalset:release-candidate-prompts", "threshold:delta-f1<=0.01"]
}

How to run (operator steps):
1) Create experiment manifest in /infra/experiments/ and open PR referencing the target rollout.
2) Start a dry-run in staging: kubectl apply -f degradlab/experiment-job.yaml --namespace=staging. Monitor logs: kubectl logs -f job/degradlab-controller.
3) Verify baseline collection and artifact upload to s3://redwood-degradlab-results/<run-id>.
4) If artifacts pass local quality gates, schedule a controlled run in canary environment with traffic mirroring.
5) Report: attach autogenerated PDF summary to the rollout ticket and notify owners.

Acceptance checklist for releases (must be completed before gated rollout):
- [ ] Relevant scenarios executed for the change type (code, model, infra).
- [ ] No metric exceeded alert threshold for >5m during run, or documented mitigation.
- [ ] Model-quality regression within defined budget on the canonical evalset.
- [ ] Artifacts stored and linked on the release PR.
- [ ] Rollback plan documented with exact version IDs.

Dashboards and alerts required (minimum):
- DegradLab overview (run state, pass/fail, run-id)
- Latency heatmap per service over the experiment window
- Model-quality delta panel with prompt-level breakout
- Experiment-run SLO delta and incident indicator (auto-open if alert threshold crossed)

Ownership and cadence:
- Owner: runtime-performance team (primary), eng-sre (on-call escalation).
- Monthly automated regression runs against the default model catalog.
- Ad-hoc runs required for any quantization change, runtime kernel update, or routing policy change.

Decision record summary (ADR required):
- This playbook implements ADR-PRE-23: experiments are mandatory for any production change that could alter per-token latency or model fidelity beyond defined budgets. The ADR mandates storing run artifacts for 90 days and attaching the run-id to the release.

Appendix: common CLI snippets
# launch local experiment against staging cluster
make degradlab-run EXPERIMENT=./manifests/quant-fallback.json TARGET=staging

# download run artifacts
aws s3 cp s3://redwood-degradlab-results/<run-id>/summary.json ./ --profile redwood-admin

Contacts:
- runtime-performance owner: @arjun.patel (Slack: #runtime-performance)
- eng-sre on-call: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations

Notes and follow-ups:
- Add a dedicated synthetic embedding workload to the catalog (action: runtime-performance, due 2026-07-01).
- Integrate artifact provenance signature to meet compliance for Private deployments (action: security-and-compliance).

Related artifacts:
- example results: s3://redwood-degradlab-results/sample-run-2026-05
- canonical evalset: evalsets/release-candidate-2026.json

If you are implementing a new quantization or routing policy and have questions about which scenarios to run, ping the reviewers listed on this page before starting the experiment.

payload.page_title: Synthetic workload orchestration and stressor manifest specification

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the synthetic workload orchestration framework and the canonical "stressor manifest" schema used for performance testing of Redwood Inference services. It standardizes how we declare, schedule, and validate stress tests that exercise multi-tenant scenarios, quantized model variants, streaming responses, and cache-locality behavior. The goal is repeatable, auditable perf experiments that map to production SLOs and cost models.

Scope

- Applies to: inference-runtime, edge-proxy, request-router, kv-cache, and perf-orch service.
- Targets: load generation for unit, integration, and system-level performance validation across Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Excludes: data labeling pipelines and offline batch-only workloads.

Motivation

Teams producing inference-focused changes (kernel swaps, batching logic, routing policies, quantization pipelines) need a shared way to describe realistic stress scenarios and a single orchestration layer to run them at scale. Current ad-hoc scripts produce non-reproducible results and divergent artifact formats. This spec reduces friction, improves traceability, and ties back to SLO/acceptance criteria.

Terminology

1. Stressor: the injected synthetic load (e.g., conversation-stream, embedding-bulk, rerank-burst).
2. Stressor manifest: declarative YAML that describes a test scenario.
3. Perf-orch: the orchestration service that schedules manifests, collects telemetry, and stores artifacts in perflab.
4. Workload fingerprint: compact identifier derived from a manifest used for artifact deduplication and result lineage.

Design principles

- Declarative: manifests are YAML-first and environment-agnostic.
- Idempotent: running the same manifest twice produces the same artifact names and metrics keys.
- Observable: perf-orch must attach run metadata to telemetry and snapshots.
- Tenant-aware: manifests may declare multi-tenant mixes and fairness expectations.
- Safety: default run mode is dry-run; destructive options require an explicit allowlist and operator confirmation.

Stressor manifest schema (canonical fields)

Provide manifests as UTF-8 YAML files named using the convention: <fingerprint>-<short-desc>.stressor.yaml
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
---
version: "1.0"
name: "conv-burst-embed-hybrid"
description: "Mixed conversation + embedding spike to exercise KV-locality and model-fallbacks"
owner: "platform-loadlab@redwood.com"
profiles:
  - id: "primary-conv"
    traffic_shape: "burst" # options: steady, burst, poisson, sine
    rps: 1200
    concurrency: 320
    sequence_length_p95: 512
    variant_policy:
      prefer: ["r-instruct-32q", "r-instruct-16q"]
      degrade_to: ["r-instruct-cpu-8bit"]
    headers:
      client-tier: "gold"
  - id: "background-embed"
    traffic_shape: "steady"
    rps: 400
    batch_size: 128
    variant_policy:
      prefer: ["embed-xf-8q"]
    isolation: "no-cache"
multi_tenant_mix:
  tenants:
    - name: "tenant-a"
      share: 0.6
    - name: "tenant-b"
      share: 0.4
observability:
  trace_sampling: 1.0
  metrics_labels: ["stressor:fingerprint", "test-run:ci-2026-11"]
  artifact_retention_days: 90
runtime_constraints:
  max_wall_time: 1800 # seconds
  max_requests: 500000
  node_affinity: ["gpu-large"]
safety:
  allowlist: ["perf-stage", "perf-canary"]
  dry_run: false
---

Key fields explained

- version: schema version for backward compatibility.
- profiles: one or more driving traffic shapes. Each profile maps to a generator instance in perf-orch.
- variant_policy: ordered list of preferred model variants and safe fallbacks used to validate runtime fallback behavior.
- multi_tenant_mix: optional; models realistic tenant mixes and enables fairness checks.
- observability: controls trace sampling and artifact tagging; perf-orch will inject run_id and fingerprint.
- runtime_constraints: caps to protect clusters from runaway tests.
- safety: gate for destructive or production-adjacent tests.

Workload profiles (recommended presets)

We maintain a set of recommended presets under /perf-presets in the repo. Use these as the basis for realistic tests:

- conversational-latency-sensitive: rps=200, concurrency=16, seq_p95=256, prefer low-latency kernels.
- embedding-bulk: rps=1000, batch_size=256, isolation="cache-friendly".
- rerank-late-binding: rps=300, long-tail latency, high memory KV pressure.
- hybrid-burst: mixes conversational + embedding to test contention.

Orchestration lifecycle (how perf-orch executes a manifest)

1. Validate: perf-orch validates manifest schema and owner allowlist.
2. Plan: compute candidate target pools using node_affinity and budget constraints.
3. Dry-run (unless dry_run: false): emit a run plan and estimate token cost.
4. Acquire: reserve ephemeral capacity via capacity-manager with request tags (run_id, fingerprint).
5. Execute: launch generators, apply tenant routing mix, and stream telemetry to perflab.
6. Collect: aggregate metrics, traces, and sample transcripts; store snapshots and artifacts.
7. Analyze: perf-orch runs baseline comparisons and generates a summary artifact (JSON + HTML).
8. Release: free reserved capacity and publish run result to the artifacts bucket.

Operational runbook (quick steps to run a sanctioned stress test)

1. Author or pick a preset manifest under repo perf/manifests/. Ensure owner is set.
2. Run local validation:
   - cli: perf-orch validate --manifest ./my-test.stressor.yaml
3. Request quota for test window via perf-ops: /jira/REQ-Perf-xxxx with run fingerprint.
4. Execute in perf-stage: perf-orch run --manifest ./my-test.stressor.yaml --env perf-stage --notify # attaches traces
5. Monitor dashboards: perf/runtime/last-run and tenant-fairness/heatmap during the test.
6. Postmortem: attach artifacts to run ticket, include fingerprint and diff vs baseline.
sections.heading: Example (annotated)

sections.body:
$ perf-orch run --manifest conv-burst.stressor.yaml --env perf-stage
Plan: reserve 12 gpu-large nodes (estimated 4h, est_cost $420)
Run id: run-20260122-7a4c
Artifacts: s3://perflab/artifacts/run-20260122-7a4c/summary.json

Acceptance criteria and gating rules

- For pull requests touching runtime kernel selection, perf sanity must pass: P99 latency not increase by >5% and mean tokens/sec degrade <= 7% vs baseline.
- For multi-tenant fairness: 95th-percentile per-tenant performance must not regress >10% for tenants with share >=5%.
- For fallback policy changes: no more than 0.1% of requests may hit a CPU-only fallback under steady-state tests.
- All runs must produce a summary artifact with fields: run_id, fingerprint, manifest_sha, baseline_diff, key_metrics.

Artifact naming and fingerprinting

- Fingerprint = sha1(manifest_yaml + preset_tag + env) truncated to 10 chars.
- Artifacts path: s3://perflab/artifacts/<fingerprint>/runs/<run_id>/
- Summary file: summary.json (schema v1).

Telemetry and labels (required)

Inject the following labels on all metric series created by perf-orch:
- service: <service-name>
- stressor:fingerprint=<fingerprint>
- test.run_id=<run_id>
- manifest.name=<name>

These allow downstream SLO dashboards and historical comparison tools to attribute runs safely and avoid mixing production telemetry with synthetic data.

Safety and production isolation

- Default test environment is isolated perf-stage with separate tenant prefixes (perm: perf-ops).
- Any manifest that targets production must have a security review and an explicit production approval token stored in vault. The review must include a run blast-radius analysis and cost estimate.

Acceptance tests (automated checks perf-orch runs post-execution)

1. Schema validation: manifest and resulting summary.json conform to canonical schemas.
2. Baseline comparison: compute relative diffs for key metrics (latency percentiles, tokens/sec, GPU utilization).
3. Regression alerting: if diffs exceed gating thresholds, mark run failed and create an incident with attached trace links.

Ownership and maintenance

- Owner: Platform Loadlab (team alias: platform-loadlab@redwood.com).
- Backing repo: git@repo:redwood/perf-orch-manifests.git (presets in /perf-presets).
- Perf-orch service responsible engineers: Samira Holt, Kevin Du.
- Review cadence: quarterly review of presets and gating thresholds aligned to SLO changes.

Migration plan for legacy scripts

1. Inventory all existing load scripts under infra/perf and categorize by workload type.
2. Convert highest-priority scripts to stressor manifests and add tests in a migration PR.
3. Deprecate legacy scripts with a two-release notice and update runbooks.

Appendix: example summary.json schema (flattened keys)

{
  "run_id": "string",
  "fingerprint": "string",
  "manifest_name": "string",
  "start_time": "iso8601",
  "end_time": "iso8601",
  "metrics": ["p50_ms","p95_ms","p99_ms","tokens_per_sec","gpu_util_pct"],
  "baseline_diff": {"p95_ms":"-3%","tokens_per_sec":"+6%"}
}

Related documents and references

- perf-presets README: git@repo:redwood/perf-presets/README.md
- artifact retention policy: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/telemetry-ingestion-and-retention-guidelines-2025
- SLO composition playbook: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/slo-composition-multi-tenant-models-2025

Revision history

- 2025-10-12: Draft created by Daniela Park.
- 2025-12-02: Added multi-tenant mix and variant_policy fields (reviewers: Sanjay V., Maya O.).
- 2026-01-22: Published with gating thresholds and operational runbook.
