payload.page_title: Kernel Selection Determinism and Telemetry Standards

sections.body: h1. Standard: Kernel Selection Determinism and Telemetry (PERF-STD-014)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Determinism and replayability requirements for *kernel selection* decisions in the Serving Runtime.
* Required telemetry fields to make selection decisions explainable and debuggable at scale.
* Performance regression gating requirements for selector changes and new kernel mappings.

These requirements apply to the kernel auto-selection module (v1, v2, and future versions) and any control-plane policy/gate that influences which kernel is chosen.

h2. Scope
sections.heading: This standard defines

sections.body:
* Selector decision logic (candidate generation + scoring/rules + tie-breaking)
* Feature extraction used by the selector (model family/arch tags, sequence length regime, GPU SKU, driver/CUDA, quantization profile, etc.)
* Fallback logic and denylist/allowlist evaluation
* Runtime configuration that changes selector behavior (feature gates, overrides, per-model policy)
* Telemetry emitted for per-request selection decisions
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
* General request tracing standards not specific to kernel selection
* Model quality/eval telemetry (covered by separate eval standards)

h2. Definitions

* *Kernel selection*: choosing an execution kernel implementation/config for an inference request (e.g., attention kernel variant, fused kernels, prefill vs decode tuned paths).
* *Determinism*: given an identical set of inputs, the selector produces the same decision.
* *Replayability*: the selection decision can be reproduced offline (or in a debug environment) using the recorded inputs and selector version.
* *Selection event*: telemetry emitted when a selection decision is made, containing fields defined below.
* *Gate*: runtime or control-plane condition that enables/disables selector versions or specific kernels (e.g., v2 enablement, driver guardrails, denylist rules).

h2. Determinism requirements

h3. D1. Inputs must be explicit and complete
The selector MUST depend only on an explicit input set ("selection context") and MUST NOT consult implicit process-local state that changes nondeterministically.

The selection context MUST include, at minimum:
* Model identity and serving variant (model_id, model_version, quantization profile)
* Workload regime signals (prompt/prefill length bucket, decode length bucket or target, and whether the request is prefill-only vs streaming decode)
* Hardware identity (GPU SKU normalized), plus driver/CUDA/runtime build identifiers
* Selector configuration (selector version, config hash, enabled flags, and applicable allowlist/denylist ruleset version)

h3. D2. Stable ordering and tie-breaking
If multiple candidates are equivalent by score/rules, the selector MUST choose deterministically by a documented tie-break order.
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
* Candidate lists MUST be sorted deterministically (e.g., by kernel_id then config_id) before evaluation.
* Tie-breaks MUST be stable across runs and machines (no iteration over hash maps without sorting).
* If randomness is required for experimentation, it MUST be:
  * Disabled by default for production.
  * Controlled by an explicit seed in the selection context.
  * Logged in telemetry (seed + experiment_id).

h3. D3. No time-based or load-based branching
Selection MUST NOT branch on wall-clock time, system load, or other ephemeral signals unless:
* The signal is explicitly part of the selection context AND
* The behavior is documented AND
* Replay tooling can supply the same value.

(Note: scheduler-provided *workload hints* are allowed if they are explicitly passed in the context and logged.)

h3. D4. Versioning and compatibility
The selector MUST expose a *selector_version* and a *schema_version* for its telemetry payload.
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
* Increment selector_version (semantic versioning recommended: major.minor.patch).
* If telemetry semantics change, increment schema_version.
* Maintain backward compatibility for offline replay for at least 2 minor versions, or provide a documented migration tool.

h3. D5. Deterministic replay tests (CI)
Every selector change MUST include deterministic replay tests that assert:
* Given identical selection contexts, the chosen kernel_id/config_id is identical.
* Candidate sets (post-filtering) are identical.
* The decision path (rule hits / score components) is identical.
sections.heading: When selector logic changes

sections.body:
* A fixed suite of replay fixtures covering: 2+ model families, 3+ seq buckets (short/medium/long context), and 2+ GPU SKUs.

h2. Replayability requirements

h3. R1. Minimum data for offline reproduction
To reproduce a decision, the recorded event MUST be sufficient to reconstruct:
* The selection context
* The set of candidates considered (or a reproducible method to generate it)
* The final chosen kernel and the reason

At minimum, record:
* selector_version, schema_version
* features (model_family, seq buckets, gpu_sku_norm, driver/cuda, quantization profile)
* candidate list (or candidate_set_hash + a registry_version that can regenerate it)
* chosen kernel_id/config_id
* filters/fallbacks applied (denylist hit, missing kernel, unstable SKU guardrail, etc.)
* configuration provenance (gate state + config hash)

h3. R2. Trace correlation
Selection events MUST be correlatable to request traces and aggregated metrics.
sections.heading: Minimum requirement

sections.body:
* Include trace_id and span_id when available.
* Include a stable request_id (internal) for joining with runtime logs.
* Include model_route and region/cluster identifiers for fleet-level analysis.

h3. R3. PII and prompt safety
Selection telemetry MUST NOT include raw prompts or user content.
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body: * Token counts, sequence buckets, and coarse distribution stats.
sections.heading: Allowed

sections.body:
* Prompt text, tool arguments containing user content, user identifiers beyond a pseudonymous internal customer_id.

h2. Required telemetry fields (per-request selection event)

All fields below are REQUIRED unless marked OPTIONAL. Fields may be emitted as structured logs and/or spans/events in tracing.

h3. Event naming
* Event name: kernel_selection.decision
* Category: runtime.performance

h3. Field requirements

|| Field || Required? || Type/Format || Description ||
| event_timestamp | REQUIRED | RFC3339 | Time selection was made (for ordering/triage; not used for decision-making). |
| schema_version | REQUIRED | string | Telemetry schema version (e.g., "2"). |
| selector_version | REQUIRED | string | Selector implementation version (e.g., "2.1.0"). |
| runtime_build_id | REQUIRED | string | Runtime build or git SHA. |
| environment | REQUIRED | enum | hosted | dedicated | private. |
| region | REQUIRED | string | Cloud region or site (e.g., us-east-1). |
| cluster | REQUIRED | string | Cluster/pool identifier (cardinality-controlled). |
| request_id | REQUIRED | string | Internal request id. |
| trace_id | REQUIRED | string | Distributed trace id ("" if unavailable). |
| span_id | OPTIONAL | string | Span id ("" if unavailable). |
| customer_id | REQUIRED | string | Internal customer/account identifier (no end-user identifiers). |
| model_id | REQUIRED | string | Canonical model name (e.g., llama-3.1-70b). |
| model_version | REQUIRED | string | Pinned serving version/hash. |
| model_family | REQUIRED | string | Family tag used by selector (llama/mistral/qwen/gemma/other). |
| quantization_profile | REQUIRED | string | fp16/bf16/int8/int4, etc. |
| gpu_sku_norm | REQUIRED | string | Normalized SKU (e.g., "nvidia-h100-sxm", "nvidia-a100-80gb"). |
| gpu_count | REQUIRED | int | GPUs per replica for this request context (if applicable). |
| cuda_version | REQUIRED | string | CUDA runtime version. |
| driver_version | REQUIRED | string | NVIDIA driver version. |
| seq_bucket_prefill | REQUIRED | enum | prefill length bucket: short/med/long/xlong (definitions below). |
| seq_bucket_decode | REQUIRED | enum | decode length bucket or target token bucket. |
| is_streaming | REQUIRED | bool | Whether request includes streaming decode. |
| workload_hint_source | OPTIONAL | enum | none/scheduler/static-config. |
| workload_hint_summary | OPTIONAL | string | Coarse, cardinality-safe summary (e.g., "mixed-short+long"). |
| candidate_kernels | REQUIRED | string | Comma-separated kernel_id list OR compact-encoded list (size-limited). |
| candidate_count | REQUIRED | int | Number of candidates considered after filtering. |
| chosen_kernel_id | REQUIRED | string | Kernel identifier chosen. |
| chosen_kernel_config_id | REQUIRED | string | Specific config variant (tile sizes, fused path, etc.). |
| decision_reason | REQUIRED | string | Human-readable short reason (e.g., "rule:long-context->flashattn_v3" or "fallback:denylist-hit"). |
| decision_path | REQUIRED | string | Compact encoding of rules/score components hit (bounded length). |
| fallback_level | REQUIRED | enum | none/soft/hard/emergency. |
| denylist_rule_id | OPTIONAL | string | Denylist rule identifier if applied. |
| allowlist_rule_id | OPTIONAL | string | Allowlist rule identifier if applied. |
| gate_v2_enabled | REQUIRED | bool | Whether v2 was enabled for this request context. |
| gate_guardrail_reason | OPTIONAL | string | If v2 disabled due to guardrail (e.g., driver/CUDA), record reason code. |
| override_type | OPTIONAL | enum | none/manual-pin/model-policy/oncall-mitigation. |
| override_id | OPTIONAL | string | Identifier of override policy if used. |
| selector_eval_us | REQUIRED | int | Selector evaluation time in microseconds. |
| kernel_switch_overhead_us | OPTIONAL | int | If measured, overhead attributable to switching/initialization. |
| sampling_rate | REQUIRED | float | Effective sampling rate for this event (e.g., 0.01). |

h3. Sequence bucket definitions (standard)
Buckets MUST be consistent across runtime and perf tooling. Unless explicitly overridden for a model family, use:
* prefill short: 0–512 input tokens
* prefill med: 513–2,048 input tokens
* prefill long: 2,049–8,192 input tokens
* prefill xlong: 8,193+ input tokens
sections.heading: Disallowed

sections.body:
* decode short: 0–128
* decode med: 129–512
* decode long: 513+

If a model uses different context window semantics, map into these buckets and record the raw counts only as integers (no text).

h2. Telemetry overhead and cardinality controls

h3. Sampling
Because per-request decision telemetry can be high volume, sampling is REQUIRED.
sections.heading: Decode buckets (target/new tokens) recommended

sections.body:
* Hosted: 1% sampled globally, with burst to 10% during active canaries.
* Dedicated: 5% sampled for allowlisted pools during rollout, 1% after GA.
* Private: default off unless customer enables; if enabled, 1% with local retention.

Sampling policy MUST be recorded in sampling_rate.

h3. Field length limits
sections.heading: Default policy (can be tightened for incidents)

sections.body:
* decision_path MUST be <= 512 bytes.
* candidate_kernels MUST be <= 1,024 bytes (use compact encoding or hash if needed).
* workload_hint_summary MUST be <= 128 bytes.

If truncation occurs, set decision_reason to include "truncated" and include candidate_count.

h3. Cardinality rules
sections.heading: To protect logging pipelines

sections.body:
* cluster MUST be from a controlled vocabulary (pool ids), not pod names.
* model_version should be a stable serving version, not a per-build artifact id.
* denylist_rule_id/allowlist_rule_id MUST be stable identifiers, not free-form text.

h2. Performance regression gating requirements
sections.heading: To avoid high-cardinality explosions

sections.body:
* Any selector logic change
* Any new kernel mapping by GPU SKU
* Any change to fallback precedence or denylist defaults

h3. G1. Required benchmark coverage
Before enabling a selector change beyond internal dev environments, teams MUST run the perf suite across:
* At least 3 model families relevant to production traffic (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Qwen/Gemma)
* At least 3 seq regimes (short, med, long/xlong)
* At least 2 GPU SKUs (one data-center, one cost-optimized SKU if applicable)

h3. G2. Pass/fail thresholds (default)
Unless an exception is granted by Runtime Architecture + SRE, the following thresholds apply.

Metrics are compared v2 vs v1 (or change vs baseline) per {model_family, model_id, gpu_sku_norm, seq_bucket_prefill, seq_bucket_decode}:

* p95 latency: must not regress by > 3% for any bucket
* p99 latency: must not regress by > 5% for any bucket
* Throughput (tokens/sec at steady state): must not regress by > 2% for any bucket
* Error rate attributable to kernel execution: must not increase by > 0.05% absolute
sections.heading: These gates apply to

sections.body:
* The bucket is explicitly excluded in the rollout allowlist, AND
* An issue is filed with owner and mitigation plan, AND
* Dedicated/Private guidance is updated to avoid the bucket/SKU combo.

h3. G3. Canary requirements
sections.heading: Any single bucket breach is a FAIL unless

sections.body:
* Run v1 and v2 in parallel cohorts where possible.
* Monitor for at least one full traffic cycle (minimum 24 hours) OR 2x the longest expected workload cycle for dedicated customers.
sections.heading: For canary rollout

sections.body:
* No sustained p99 regression > 3% at the fleet level for any top-10 model routes
* No increase in kernel-related error rate beyond error budget policy
* Selection distribution stable (no unexplained drift in chosen_kernel_id shares > 10% day-over-day, excluding planned policy changes)
sections.heading: Canary success criteria

sections.body:
* p99 latency regression >= 8% for 15 minutes on any top-5 model route within a region
* Kernel error spike >= 0.2% absolute for 5 minutes
* Widespread denylist/fallback activation (fallback_level=hard/emergency) >= 1% of sampled events

h3. G4. SLO/error budget coordination
Selector rollouts are considered *performance-impacting changes*.
sections.heading: Rollback triggers (recommended defaults)

sections.body:
* SRE MUST approve alert threshold changes prior to canary.
* Error budget burn MUST be monitored for the canary cohort separately when possible.
* If rollback is initiated, retain selection telemetry at elevated sampling for 2 hours post-rollback to confirm recovery and diagnose.

h2. Operational requirements for overrides
sections.heading: Requirements

sections.body:
* Manual pinning of kernel choice MUST be possible at least by model_id + gpu_sku_norm + region/cluster.
* Overrides MUST be auditable and show up in telemetry (override_type, override_id).
* Overrides MUST have safe defaults and an expiration mechanism (time-based or explicit removal procedure).

h2. Exceptions

Any exception to this standard (telemetry omissions, determinism relaxation, threshold changes) requires:
* Documented rationale
* Risk assessment (tail latency + correctness)
* Explicit owner and expiration date
* Approval from Runtime Architecture (Noah Patel or delegate) and SRE (Aisha Bello or delegate)

h2. Ownership and maintenance

Owner: Observability Standards (Allison Grant) in partnership with Runtime Architecture (Noah Patel).
sections.heading: To support oncall and customer escalations

sections.body:
* Quarterly review or after any major selector version rollout.

h2. Changelog

* 2026-01-22: Initial publication aligned to kernel auto-selection v2 rollout needs.
* 2026-02-14: Added driver/CUDA guardrail fields, clarified bucket definitions, and tightened rollback triggers for tail-latency regressions.
sections.heading: Review cadence

payload.page_title: ADR: Prompt-splitting and Response-reassembly Contract for Multi-Model Fanout

sections.body:
Summary
This ADR defines a service-level contract for deterministic prompt-splitting and response-reassembly when a single logical request is fanned out to multiple model variants or shards. The goal is to guarantee item-level ordering, completeness, and bounded reassembly latency while allowing the runtime to schedule heterogeneous backends (e.g., embeddings shards, retrieval-augmented text models, and different precision variants).

Problem statement
As Redwood supports multi-variant serving and compositional prompts (example: long-context summarization that is split across segmenting, retrieval, and synthesis steps), we observed three classes of production problems:
- Missing or duplicated token blocks when responses from parallel model shards overlap or timeout.
- Non-deterministic ordering between parts that break downstream structured parsers and evals.
- Unbounded reassembly latency when slow variants stall final response assembly, causing client timeouts and SLO violations.

This ADR prescribes a minimal contract that all model-serving components and the request router must satisfy to eliminate these failure modes and enable safe progressive rollouts and fallbacks.

Decision
We adopt a deterministic prompt-splitting and response-reassembly contract with the following guarantees:
1) Idempotent fragment identifiers: every split fragment carries a globally unique id composed of request_id:fragment_index:split_hash. Fragments must be safe to resend and replay without causing duplicate logical output.
2) Causal ordering vector: each fragment includes a small integer sequence number and an optional dependency vector (comma-separated fragment ids) for non-linear assembly. The reassembler must honor ordering constraints before emitting a contiguous response.
3) Completeness window and partial-accept policy: the reassembler waits for either all required fragments or until the completeness window expires (default 300ms). Partial assemblies must be marked with metadata field \"partial=true\" and an explict missing_fragments list.
4) Slow-variant hedging and graceful degradation: the router may issue hedging requests to faster compatible variants after a hedging threshold (default 120ms). Hedged responses are only accepted if they provide equal-or-better \"fidelity_score\" metadata (see Fidelity scoring below).
5) Deterministic merge strategy: reassembly uses fragment.sequence_number to place fragments; in case of overlapping token ranges, the merge precedence is: (1) full-fidelity variant, (2) higher fidelity_score, (3) earlier finish time. Overlap resolution must be documented in the response metadata.
6) Observability markers: fragments and final assemblies must emit correlation fields: request_id, fragment_id, variant_id, node_id, start_ts, finish_ts, fidelity_score, and reassembly_reason.

Alternatives considered
- Option A: Best-effort merge with no completeness window — rejected because it caused silent data loss and nondeterministic behavior for structured outputs.
- Option B: Strict-all-or-nothing assembly — rejected because it increased tail latency and degraded availability for customers with large multi-shard requests.
- Option C: Client-side reassembly API — rejected to keep consistent service guarantees and avoid reimplementing complex logic across SDKs.

Implementation details
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Router (edge/ingress): performs prompt-splitting, assigns fragment IDs, annotates fragment metadata, enforces hedging threshold, and routes to candidate variants.
- Model backend: returns fragment payload with required metadata fields; treats duplicate fragment_ids as idempotent requests.
- Reassembler service (stateless or lightweight stateful): collects fragments, applies deterministic merge, enforces completeness window, emits final response to client or marks partial.
- Telemetry pipeline: consumes fragment and reassembly markers for SLO and incident analysis.
sections.heading: Roles and responsibilities

sections.body:
- fragment_id (string)
- request_id (string)
- fragment_index (int as string)
- sequence_number (int as string)
- split_hash (string)
- token_range (string, e.g. \"0-511\")
- variant_id (string)
- start_ts (ISO8601)
- finish_ts (ISO8601)
- fidelity_score (float as string: 0.0-1.0)
- required_for_completion (\"true\"|\"false\")
- payload (string or base64)
sections.heading: Required fragment metadata (JSON fields)

sections.body:
1) At assembly start, record earliest fragment start_ts and set reassembly_deadline = max(earliest_start_ts + completeness_window, now + minimal_wait).
2) Continuously accept fragments until either all required fragments arrive or reassembly_deadline is reached.
3) If all required fragments present: deterministic-merge -> emit final response with reassembly_reason=\"complete\".
4) If deadline reached and some required fragments missing: perform best-effort merge, flag response as partial, list missing_fragments, set reassembly_reason=\"deadline_partial\".
5) Emit observability events for each path (complete, deadline_partial, conflict_resolved).

Fidelity scoring (optional variant contract)
The runtime exposes a simple fidelity_score in responses to aid hedging and merge precedence. Score should be normalized across variants and is intended to reflect subjective quality for the request category (e.g., summarization fidelity, embedding precision). Guidelines:
- Score 0.0-0.4: low-fidelity (e.g., quantized >8-bit, short-context coarse embeddings)
- Score 0.4-0.75: medium-fidelity (standard quantized kernels, chunked context)
- Score 0.75-1.0: high-fidelity (fp16/full-precision, long-context)
Hedging only substitutes a missing fragment if hedged_variant.fidelity_score >= original_variant.fidelity_score - 0.1 (configurable).

Configuration knobs (defaults)
- completeness_window: 300ms
- hedging_threshold: 120ms
- maximal_reassembly_delay: 1000ms
- overlap_resolution_precedence: [\"full_fidelity\",\"fidelity_score\",\"finish_time\"]
- partial_flag_field: \"partial\"

SLOs and metrics to track
- Correct reassembly rate (goal >= 99.9%)
- Partial assembly rate (target <= 0.5% for host-tier customers)
- Average reassembly latency (95th <= completeness_window + 50ms)
- Hedged substitution rate and post-hedge quality regression (no more than 0.1% increase in semantic regression score)
- Fragment duplication/replay rate (tooling should detect and alert >0.1%)

Testing and validation
- Unit tests for split/merge deterministic properties with randomized fragment arrival orders.
- Integration tests: inject delays, simulate missing fragments, overlapping token ranges, and hedged responses.
- Canary: deploy reassembler behind a feature flag and run traffic split 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with continuous evaluation on a golden prompt set.
- Evals: add evaluation prompts that detect order-sensitivity and structured parsing mismatches.

Rollout and migration plan
1) Implement router and backend metadata fields in a backward-compatible manner (optional fields are ignored by older components).
2) Launch reassembler as an opt-in runtime flag; observe telemetry for 2 weeks on non-critical customer buckets.
3) Enable hedging only in non-blocking mode (hedges do not replace primary fragments unless reassembler marks them missing).
4) After metric thresholds are satisfied for 4 weeks, flip \"strict-merge\" for all internal traffic and roll to customers with canary cohorts.
5) Document client-visible behavior changes in the API changelog and SDK release notes.

Operational runbook (short)
- Symptom: increased partial assembly rate.
  1) Check fragment ingestion logs for missing fragment_ids and high duplication rates.
  2) Validate reassembly_deadline and completeness_window configuration drift.
  3) Identify slow variants via fidelity_score decay and finish_ts tail.
  4) Temporarily increase completeness_window or enable hedging on affected routes.

Ownership and follow-ups
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture team (primary), eng-platform (router/edge), eng-infra (capacity/latency tooling).
- Follow-up ADRs suggested:
  - Formal fidelity_score calibration protocol
  - Fragment storage/retention policy for debug traces
  - SDK-level partial-response handling guidelines

Consequences and risks
- Positive: deterministic behavior for complex multi-variant pipelines, fewer silent failures, and safer rollouts.
- Negative: increased complexity in router and reassembler, potential additional latency for strict completeness on large-fanout requests, risk of miscalibrated fidelity scores causing lower-quality hedges.

Appendices
A. Example fragment JSON (snip)
{\n  \"fragment_id\": \"req-123:0:a1b2c3\",\n  \"request_id\": \"req-123\",\n  \"fragment_index\": \"0\",\n  \"sequence_number\": \"0\",\n  \"token_range\": \"0-511\",\n  \"variant_id\": \"rwd/summarize-v2-fp16\",\n  \"start_ts\": \"2026-01-15T12:01:02.123Z\",\n  \"finish_ts\": \"2026-01-15T12:01:02.321Z\",\n  \"fidelity_score\": \"0.83\",\n  \"required_for_completion\": \"true\",\n  \"payload\": \"...base64...\"\n}

B. Example reassembly result metadata fields
- partial: \"false\"
- missing_fragments: []
- reassembly_reason: \"complete\"
- merged_token_ranges: [\"0-1023\"]
- conflict_resolutions: []

C. Related guidelines and pages
See: model-slicing-and-fallback-routing-guidelines, prompt-telemetry-response-lineage-spec, and rollout-safety-and-telemetry-driven-rollback-playbook for intersecting policies.

Document history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Asha Patel
- 2026-02-12: Updated hedging thresholds and fidelity guidance after integration tests by Miguel Ortega

payload.page_title: request-fidelity-declaration-and-compatibility-protocol-2028

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the Request Fidelity Declaration (RFD) and the Compatibility Protocol that together standardize how clients declare quality/latency/cost expectations to Redwood Inference model-serving endpoints and how the runtime negotiates, routes, and reports on those declarations. The goal is to make tradeoffs explicit at the API boundary so that: (1) clients can express precise fidelity requirements; (2) the runtime can perform deterministic routing to appropriate model variants, quantization levels, or fallback policies; and (3) observability and billing are correlated to declared fidelity.

Why this matter now

- Increasingly we serve multiple model variants (full-precision, quantized, distilled, cached-prefill) behind a single API surface.
- Customers need predictable tail latency and cost for business-critical flows while still using lower-cost variants for non-critical traffic.
- Without a standard, clients embed fidelity hints in ad-hoc headers or in prompt content, which hinders routing, testing, and SLO enforcement.

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: API-level request metadata, runtime negotiation handshake, billing and telemetry labels, rollout strategy, test cases and compatibility guidance. Intended primarily for hosted and dedicated runtimes; private deployments may adopt the same protocol.
- Non-goals: model-internal loss functions, training-time labels, or prompt-level semantic transformations (these remain in model/MDL docs).

Decision summary (ADR-style)

We adopt a lightweight request metadata envelope named Request Fidelity Declaration (RFD) and a deterministic Compatibility Protocol:

- RFD is an explicit JSON object passed in the request metadata (or a compact header) that declares fidelity tier, max-cost, latency-class, required-output-schema, and optional fallback policies.
- The runtime exposes a capability manifest per endpoint that enumerates supported fidelity tiers and variant mappings.
- On mismatch, the runtime applies a deterministic compatibility strategy (best-effort mapping -> canary-warn -> reject) based on endpoint policy and client permissions.
- Observability attaches declared fidelity and resolved variant tags to traces, metrics, and billing events.

Detailed specification

1) Request Fidelity Declaration (RFD) schema (transport-agnostic)

- rfd_version: string (current: "1.0")
- fidelity_tier: string (one of: "ultra", "standard", "economy", "best-effort")
- max_cost_nanos: integer-string (optional) — micro/billing cap in nanodollars to allow deterministic routing to cheaper variants
- latency_budget_ms: integer-string (optional) — soft target for tail P99; runtime will prefer low-latency variants when provided
- required_schema: string (optional) — canonical response schema id (e.g. "structured:receipt-v2")
- allow_fallbacks: list-of-strings (optional) — ordered fallback tier names the client will accept
- require_strict: boolean-string (optional) — if "true", reject if runtime cannot meet declared tier instead of downgrading
- client_tag: string (optional) — customer-side tag to correlate requests

Encoding and transport

- Primary transport: HTTP header X-RFD with compacted base64(JSON) for production; SDKs should expose a typed object.
- Alternative transport: metadata field in streaming gRPC call (key: rfd-bin) using protobuf wrapper.
- Backwards compatibility: servers must accept unknown fields and the absence of RFD; absence maps to fidelity_tier="standard".

2) Endpoint Capability Manifest

Each runtime endpoint publishes a capability manifest accessible via a lightweight introspection endpoint: /internal/manifest or via runtime discovery API. Manifest fields (summary):

- endpoint_id: string
- supported_tiers: list-of-strings (runtime-defined names mapped to canonical tiers)
- tier_to_variant_map: simple mapping (tier -> preferred variant ids)
- enforcement_policy: string ("soft", "strict", "warn-and-downgrade")
- max_latency_by_tier_ms: list (for planning)
sections.heading: Overview
Example (pseudo)

sections.body:
1. Parse RFD (or default).
2. Fetch endpoint manifest cached locally (stale tolerance 10s).
3. If declared fidelity_tier available -> route to mapped variant and tag span with resolved_variant.
4. If not available and allow_fallbacks provided -> try first available fallback in order.
5. If not available and require_strict=="true" or manifest.enforcement_policy=="strict" -> return 422 + structured error with reason and suggested alternatives.
6. Else if not available -> apply policy: downgrade to next-best variant and include negotiated_fidelity header in response.
7. Add telemetry tags: rfd.fidelity_tier, resolved_variant, negotiation_path, cost_estimate_nanos, latency_hint_ms.

Observability and billing integration

- Traces: annotate root span with rfd.fidelity_tier and resolved_variant. Use trace attributes rfd.* and runtime.variant.
- Metrics: produce a dimensioned counter fidelity.request.count{tier,variant,tenant} and histogram fidelity.latency_ms{tier,variant}.
- Logs: structured log entry per request that includes negotiation_path and decision_code (OK, FALLBACK, REJECT).
- Billing: attach declared max_cost_nanos and resolved_variant to billing event. If runtime had to downgrade and cost_estimate exceeds declared max_cost, runtime returns a warning and records discrepancy in a dedicated metric fidelity.cost_violation.count.

Security and abuse considerations

- Clients may declare unrealistically low latency or cost to force cheap variants; abuse is mitigated by tenant quotas and enforcement_policy.
- RFD values are part of request metadata and should be recorded in audit logs; avoid storing PII in client_tag.

Compatibility and migration strategy

- Phase 0 (Q1): SDKs add explicit RFD support and default to no header (server maps to "standard"). Instrumentation is added to record prevalence.
- Phase 1 (Q2): Enable manifest discovery and routing for internal endpoints with enforcement_policy="soft" and emit negotiation telemetry. No rejections.
- Phase 2 (Q3): Opt-in customers can set require_strict for critical routes. Runtime will reject non-matching requests for those endpoints.
- Phase 3 (Q4): Toggle manifest enforcement to "warn-and-downgrade" org-wide and start billing correlation to declared tier.

Testing and verification

- Unit tests: RFD parser fuzzing and header encoding/decoding.
- Integration tests: synthetic manifests and simulated unavailability to verify negotiation_path semantics.
- E2E: Canary rollout that asserts telemetry tags are present and cost_violation metrics do not spike.
- Compliance: add sample prompt-suite tests to the prompt-telemetry CI gate to validate required_schema enforcement.

Operational runbook (short)

- Symptom: Unexpectedly high fidelity.downgrade.rate for an endpoint.
  1. Check endpoint manifest /internal/manifest for supported_tiers changes.
  2. Inspect fidelity.request.count and negotiation_path histogram for recent shifts.
  3. If rollout caused variant unavailability, roll back variant deployment or update manifest mapping.

- Symptom: spike in fidelity.cost_violation.count
  1. Identify tenants with the highest volume of violations via billing events.
  2. Notify customer and recommend raising max_cost_nanos or pinning to a specific variant.

Adoption guidance for client teams

- Start by adding RFD through SDK helpers (set fidelity_tier and latency_budget_ms).
- Add integration tests that assert negotiated_fidelity header and track negotiation_path metric.
- For critical flows, use require_strict only after running canaries to ensure variant availability.

Ownership and contact

- Spec owner: Aisha Patel (Serving Runtime team)
- Runtime implementation owners: Runtime Core (team: runtime-serving)
- Observability owner: Platform Monitoring (team: eng-platform)

Future work and open questions

- Add formal cost-sla contract mapping between resolved_variant and expected cost range.
- Explore machine-readable fidelity profiles for automatic client SDK optimization.
- Investigate cross-tenant fairness when multiple tenants declare "ultra" during burst windows.

Appendix: example request/response
sections.heading: On request arrival

sections.body:
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Authorization: Bearer ...
X-RFD: eyJ... (base64 of {\"rfd_version\":\"1.0\",\"fidelity_tier\":\"ultra\",\"latency_budget_ms\":200})
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "prompt": "Summarize the following..."
}
sections.heading: HTTP request (pseudo)

sections.body:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Negotiated-Fidelity: standard
X-Runtime-Resolved-Variant: m8-q4
X-Runtime-Negotiation-Path: requested=ultra->downgraded=standard(reason=variant-unavailable)

{
  "content": "... summary ..."
}

Impact and consequences

- Positive: Enables explicit, auditable routing decisions and ties billing/observability to declared requirements. Improves predictability for critical customers.
- Negative: Adds complexity to request surface and requires careful SDK adoption and runtime manifest hygiene. Misconfigured manifests can lead to regressions; mitigated by staged rollout and telemetry.

Document change log

- 2027-11-02: Draft created by Aisha Patel.
- 2027-12-12: Added manifest fields and negotiation details (reviewer: Daniel Kim).
- 2028-01-18: Finalized telemetry naming and rollout phases; published.

References

- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/model-capability-manifest-runtime-discovery-2026
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/request-provenance-and-enrichment-standard-2025
- Internal SDK proposal: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides/rfd-sdk-proposal-2027

payload.page_title: Output Schema Versioning and Walkback Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook defines Redwood's recommended approach for evolving model output schemas, negotiating versions between clients and runtime, and performing an automated "walkback" (safe rollback with stateful validation and postmortem hooks) when schema incompatibilities cause customer-impacting failures. It applies to hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes and complements the API compatibility and deprecation policy.

Goals

- Limit visible breaking changes in outputs to <0.01% of active tokens served per month.
- Detect and contain schema regressions within 15 minutes of rollout, with automated rollback for severe regressions.
- Provide clear remediation paths and observability (telemetry, traces, and example-request capture) for customers and SRE.

Scope

Applies to: model-serving responses (text generation JSON envelope, structured-tool outputs, embeddings/metadata payloads) produced by services: runtime-router, model-loader, generation-worker, and response-formatter. Does NOT change input prompt semantics or API routing rules (see API-deprecation doc).

Compatibility model (summary)

1) Semantic minor versions (vMAJOR.MINOR):
   - MAJOR change: incompatible removal or rename of top-level fields (requires documented migration & canary).
   - MINOR change: additive, non-breaking fields or explicit opt-in flags.
2) Backwards-compatibility rules: clients must tolerate unknown top-level fields and must read using declared output type fields rather than position-dependent arrays.

Version negotiation rules (runtime-router)

- Default behavior: runtime advertises the active schema version in response metadata header X-Redwood-Output-Schema: v1.3.
- Clients may send Accept-Output-Schema: v1.2,v1.3 to indicate preference list. The runtime will select the highest compatible version that satisfies both sides.
- If no overlap, runtime returns HTTP 406 with a structured error and a brief example of available schema fields.

Observability and SLOs

- Schema mismatch rate (SLO): <= 0.1% requests/hour for stable models; alert when > 0.05% sustained for 10 minutes to paging channel SRE-Model-Alerts.
- Example-capture retention: store one failing request per unique client API key per hour (rotate after 30 days).
- Traces: ensure generation-worker spans include schema_validation:{result: pass|fail, details: short-string}.

Deployment and rollout checklist

1. Authoring and Validation (developer):
   - Update schema definition in /repo/serving/schemas/<model-name>/schema-v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.json (JSON-Schema Draft 2020-12).
   - Run local compatibility check: tools/schema-compat check --from v<prev> --to v<new>. This verifies additive-only fields for MINOR bumps or reports diffs for MAJOR bumps.
   - Add unit tests that deserialize representative request corpus (see tests/schema-corpus).

2. Preflight (CI):
   - CI runs batch of representative prompts (real anonymized sample or synthetic seed set) with schema validation enabled.
   - Gate: 0 failing schema validations allowed for a MINOR; for MAJOR, require manual approval by API-standards owner.

3. Canary (runtime-router + canary group):
   - Deploy model with schema vX.Y to canary pool (1–2% traffic) for 2 hours.
   - Monitor: schema_mismatch_rate, token_latency_95, example_capture_failures.
   - If schema_mismatch_rate > 0.01% or a customer-facing error >= P1 appears, trigger automated rollback.

4. Progressive rollout:
   - 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% with metric checks at each step (10 minute steady-state window).

Walkback (automated rollback and containment)

Definition: walkback is the coordinated sequence that returns traffic away from a problematic model schema while preserving trace and sample evidence for analysis.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- schema_mismatch_rate > 0.1% for 5 minutes.
- API error rate from response-formatter >= 0.5% (client-visible errors).
- Manual SRE/PM request labeled urgent.
sections.heading: Trigger conditions (any of)

sections.body:
1) runtime-router marks the offending model-version:status=draining and reroutes new requests to fallback-compatible variant (same family) or fallback model alias configured in model_catalog.
2) generation-worker emits finalization span and persists last-K KV cache snapshots for repro (K = 3 per shard).
3) telemetry-ingest creates a high-priority incident with attached example captures and trace URLs.
4) Automated rollback job (walkback-runner) flips active alias to last-known-good model-version and validates 1,000 synthetic requests before confirming success.
5) If rollback validation fails, escalate to SRE on-call and hold route at 0% to problematic variant.
sections.heading: Walkback steps (automated)

sections.body:
- Run compatibility-diff to produce human-readable delta and attach to incident.
- Notify customers affected via customer-success runbook and share remediation timeline.

Schema validation configuration (table)

| Setting | Default | Description | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| schema.validation.enabled | true | Turn on validator in response-formatter | runtime-team |
| schema.validation.mode | strict | strict |runtime-team |
| schema.validation.sample_rate | 0.005 | Fraction of successful responses to validate for statistical coverage (0–1) | runtime-team |
| schema.mismatch.alert_threshold | 0.0005 | Fraction of requests triggering an alert (per minute) | SRE |
| schema.mismatch.auto_rollback | true | Allow automated walkback when thresholds breached | platform-ops |

Error types and client guidance

- 422 SchemaMismatch: the payload structure does not match requested schema. Clients should fallback to a compatible schema from Accept-Output-Schema or refresh their client library.
- 406 NotAcceptable: no compatible schema available; clients must request a supported schema list.
- 500 OutputGenerationError: generation failed before schema validation. Retry semantics: exponential backoff with jitter; max 3 retries.

sections.body:
```json
{
  "error": "SchemaMismatch",
  "message": "Missing field: generation.metadata.language",
  "expected_schema": "v1.2",
  "available_schemas": ["v1.0", "v1.1", "v1.2"],
  "example_snippet": {"generation": {"text":"Example"}}
}
```

Client migration guidance

- For MINOR additions: use tolerant parsers and ignore unknown fields. Add explicit unit tests that parse the live API payloads periodically (weekly).
- For MAJOR renames/removals: opt-in migration mode via query param ?output_schema=v<MAJOR>.<MINOR> and schedule coordinated cutover windows. Notify customers two weeks in advance for enterprise tenants.

Telemetry and diagnostics checklist

- Ensure spans and logs include: schema.version, schema.validation.result, client.api_key_hash, model.version_alias.
- Export a daily compatibility report to /dashboards/schema-evolution with a 90-day rolling window.
- Retain one example capture per unique failing client per hour for 30 days (configurable).

Roles and responsibilities

- Runtime-team: implement header negotiation, validation hooks, and rollout tooling.
- Model-onboarding: author and publish schema definitions; tag model_catalog entries with supported_schemas metadata.
- SRE: define alert thresholds and own pager rotation for schema regressions.
- Customer-success: coordinate communication with customers impacted by MAJOR changes.

Decision log (when to do MAJOR vs MINOR)

- If the change alters field names or removes required fields -> MAJOR. Requires ADR + cross-team sign-off.
- If change is purely additive and consumers are expected to ignore unknown fields -> MINOR. Can be shipped with canary and automated gates.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Validate new schema against previous:
  tools/schema-compat check --old schema-v1.2.json --new schema-v1.3.json

- Run canary batch locally (example):
  ./scripts/run_canary.sh --model alias:stable-v1 --schema v1.3 --sample prompts/canary-seed.csv

- Manual walkback trigger (admin CLI):
  rwctl model walkback --model-id model-abc --version v1.3 --reason "schema-mismatch-spike"

References

- API Compatibility and Deprecation Policy: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/api-compatibility-and-deprecation-policy-2026
- Model Artifact Provenance and Signing Standard: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/model-artifact-provenance-and-signing-standard-2026

- 2025-11-03: added automated rollback flow and example error payloads (Marco Rivera)
- 2026-01-18: tightened SLOs and added telemetry checklist (Aisha Raman)

payload.page_title: Input Normalization and Tokenization Guardrails — Model Serving Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook defines Redwood's standards for input normalization and tokenization compatibility across the inference stack. It prescribes deterministic normalization rules, a tokenization compatibility matrix, regression detection tests, and rollout guidelines for changes that affect user-visible tokenization or input canonicalization. The goal is to avoid subtle output regressions, cost changes, and security inconsistencies that can arise when the pre-processing pipeline, tokenizer, or model variant drift across environments.

Motivation

Tokenization and input normalization are a frequent source of reproducibility and cost issues in production inference: the same logical prompt can map to different token sequences depending on unicode normalization, whitespace handling, or model-specific tokenizers. That produces token-count variability (affecting billing), unpredictable semantic differences, and can break structured prompts and tool-calling. This playbook reduces blast radius by setting deterministic defaults, compatibility requirements, and observable tests.

Scope

- Applies to: Redwood API (hosted), Dedicated and Private runtimes, edge-proxy, ingest-normalizer, runtime-bridge, and client SDKs.
- Not in scope: model training tokenization choices (except insofar as serving must preserve a documented mapping) and third-party adapter behavior outside Redwood's runtime.

Definitions

- Normalization: deterministic conversion of bytes/characters before tokenization (unicode normalization, trailing whitespace, line endings).
- Tokenizer: the byte/wordpiece/merge-based algorithm used by a specific model artifact.
- Tokenization drift: measured difference in token sequences for the same input between two versions of a preprocessor/tokenizer serving a route.

Principles

1. Determinism: normalizer behavior must be deterministic and idempotent; given identical bytes the same canonicalized string is produced.
2. Transparency: every runtime must expose the normalization configuration used for a response in telemetry (normalized_preview field).
3. Minimal exposure: prefer server-side canonicalization to avoid client mistakes; however client SDKs must document and optionally expose the same canonicalization logic for offline reasoning.
4. Low-latency: normalization should add no more than 10ms median added latency in the ingress path for typical short prompts.

Mandatory Normalization Rules (default canonicalizer)

All services must implement the following as the default 'canonicalizer:v1' unless a route explicitly pins a variant:

- Unicode: apply NFC normalization to all input text.
- Line endings: normalize CR, LF, CRLF to LF.
- Whitespace: collapse sequences of zero-width spaces (U+200B) and normalize consecutive whitespace to single space except inside code-block markers (```).
- Directionality: preserve character directionality but strip explicit bidi controls (U+202A..U+202E).
- Tabs: replace tabs with single space.
- Trailing/leading: trim trailing and leading ASCII whitespace.
- Control characters: drop non-printable control characters except TAB and LF which are normalized above.
- Byte-preserving flag: for routes that require exact binary passthrough (e.g., bytes-based embeddings), canonicalizer must support a passthrough mode that only enforces line ending normalization.

Tokenization Compatibility Matrix

A text table below must be published alongside each model variant and consumed by the route config. Example (displayed as plain text in the model manifest):

| Model family | Tokenizer family | canonicalizer:v1 compatible | notes |
|--------------|------------------|----------------------------:|-------|
| redwood-7B   | bpe-v2           | true                       | uses unicode NFC in training |
| open-ggml-13B| byte-level       | false                      | requires preserving raw bytes for historical artifacts |

Service Requirements

- Edge-proxy: perform canonicalizer:v1 by default. Add header X-Redwood-Normalized-Preview (first 256 chars) and X-Redwood-Token-Preview (first 64 tokens as hex hash) to responses for internal customers.
- Ingest-normalizer: central library (go/text/canonicalizer) used by all Go services; Python runtimes must vendor a behaviorally-equivalent implementation and include a CI compatibility test.
- Runtime-bridge (gRPC frontend to serving): must accept pre-tokenized payloads and verify token counts against server-side tokenizer for billing; mismatches trigger a 409 with detailed diagnostic in internal-only responses.

Change and Migration Process (when updating canonicalizer or tokenizer mapping)

1. Prepare a compatibility test matrix and run across a standardized prompt corpus (prompt-set-serving-normalization) that includes: short prompts, code blocks, whitespace-heavy inputs, emoji, non-latin scripts, and boundary-case unicode.
2. Measure: token-count delta distribution, semantic fuzz-rate (see regression tests below), and cost delta impact (projected monthly cost change at 95th percentile load).
3. If token-count delta > 0.5% for top-tier customers' routes or median added latency > 10ms, the change requires staged canary rollout and an ADR signoff.
4. Canary: deploy to 1% of traffic with traffic shadowing enabled for the remainder; collect telemetry for 72 hours or 5M requests (whichever comes first).
5. If regressions exceed thresholds, abort and roll back. Document outcome and artifact in an ADR linked from the model manifest.

Regression Detection and Tests

- Tokenization drift test (unit): deterministic check comparing token sequences before/after change for a curated set of 5k prompts. Allowed failure rate: 0.1% without ADR.
- Semantic fuzz test (eval): random perturbations of whitespace/punctuation should not change top-1 intent classification for 99.5% of prompts in the intent-suite.
- Billing delta monitor (SLO): monthly token-count change for a model-route baseline must remain within +/-2% or trigger cost review.

Observability and Telemetry

Every inference response (internal telemetry) must include the following metadata fields:

- normalization_version: e.g., canonicalizer:v1
- tokenizer_id: e.g., redwood-bpe-v2-2026-01
- normalized_preview: first 256 characters after normalization (internal only)
- token_count: integer used for billing computation
- tokenization_hash: SHA256 of token sequence (for drift detection)

Alerting

- Alert: tokenization-drift-high when >0.5% of requests over a rolling 1h window have tokenization_hash mismatches against the golden service. Pager: oncall-runtime.
- Alert: normalization-latency when p99 added latency > 50ms for canonicalizer operation on edge-proxy. Pager: eng-infra.

SDK and Client Guidance

- SDKs must expose a helper normalize_input(text) that uses the same canonicalization rules and produce an RFC describing equivalence with server canonicalizer.
- Clients may submit pre-tokenized payloads; when they do, they must set pretokenized=true and include tokenizer_id. The runtime will verify token counts and fail if inconsistent.

Security and Prompt Injection Considerations

Normalization can be used adversarially to hide injection patterns (e.g., manipulative unicode combining marks). Mitigations:

- Reject inputs containing combining sequences larger than 128 codepoints.
- Enforce a max normalized length that maps to a safe token upper bound; if an input expands under normalization by >2x, reject with 413.

Operational Runbook (high level)

1. On tokenization-drift-high alert: open incident, capture sample of raw_inputs and normalized_preview, run token-diff tool (scripts/token_compare.sh) and assess customer impact.
2. If customer-impacting, engage product & CS to coordinate mitigation (temporary per-customer canonicalizer pinning).
3. Post-incident: capture root cause, add test to compatibility suite, and file ADR if the fix changes default behavior.

Examples

- CLI to run local compat test suite against a candidate canonicalizer:

  ./tools/normalize_compat_test --manifest candidate_manifest.json --bucket prompt-set-serving-normalization --output report.json

- Sample canonicalizer config (YAML):

  canonicalizer:
    version: v1
    unicode: NFC
    trim_whitespace: true
    collapse_zero_width: true
    passthrough_mode_for_routes: ["embeddings_binary", "file_uploads"]

Ownership and Governance

- Owner: Model Serving Standards group (eng-serving-runtime). Primary contact: Aisha Patel.
- Review cadence: quarterly review of canonicalizer behavior and annual review before large model-family imports.
- ADR requirement: any change that affects token-count distribution by >0.5% for production traffic requires an ADR filed under architecture-and-standards/decision-records with measurable compatibility results.

Appendix: Example token-diff output (text)

- input_id: 2026-02-01-abc123
- raw_input: "Hello\u00A0World"
- normalized: "Hello World"
- tokens_before: [34, 102, 11]
- tokens_after: [34, 102, 11]
- token_delta: 0

References and related pages

- See model manifest tokenization matrix for each variant.
- Related: prompt-suite-ci-contract-testing-guidelines (for test corpus composition).

Change log

- 2025-11-12: v0.1 initial draft (A. Patel).
- 2026-01-05: added passthrough-mode exceptions and canary thresholds (reviewers: D. Ramirez).
- 2026-02-08: published version with rollout playbook and alerts (A. Patel).

payload.page_title: Adaptive Session Compression: Product Brief and Roadmap

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This brief describes the product concept, technical approach, rollout plan, and commercial considerations for "Adaptive Session Compression" — a Redwood Optimize adjunct designed to reduce per-session token cost and memory pressure while preserving conversational fidelity for production deployments.

Scope: This document covers customer-facing behavior, high-level runtime design, telemetry and success metrics, staged rollout plan, and pricing/packaging options. Implementation-level kernel selection and per-hardware optimizations are covered in a separate runtime design spec (see related pages).

Problem statement

Redwood customers running long conversational sessions (median history > 2k tokens) experience two correlated pain points:

- Rising per-request token cost as sessions grow without bound.
- Latency and memory pressure on inference nodes caused by large KV caches and repeated re-encoding of semantically redundant context.

Existing mitigations (static retention windows, manual summary prompts, or aggressive eviction) either risk dropping crucial context or require significant engineering effort from customers.

Goals and success metrics
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1. Reduce aggregate token consumption for long-running sessions by 25% (median) without measurable regression in task-level fidelity for targeted workloads (conversational QA, customer support threads, agent workflows).
2. Lower average inference memory footprint (KV cache + prompt residency) by 30% on affected routes, enabling higher packing density on Dedicated pods.
3. Provide deterministic controls and observable impact so customers can opt in, tune, and rollback.
sections.heading: Primary goals

sections.body:
- Token delta: median and 90th percentile reduction in tokens emitted to model per session.
- Fidelity delta: automatic evaluation using prompt-set folds — allowable drop <= 2% absolute on target evals.
- Latency delta: average p95 token latency change <= +10ms (targeting neutral or improved latencies).
- Resource delta: reduction in average GPU memory used per session and increased sessions per pod.

Non-goals

- Not a replacement for high-level summarization features that change user-visible semantics.
- Not supporting arbitrary third-party model integrations at GA; we will support Redwood-verified variants and an adapter API for partner models in a later phase.

Customer scenarios and personas

- SaaS support bots with multi-turn troubleshooting sessions (median length 3k–8k tokens) that want lower per-ticket cost.
- Embedded assistants inside productivity apps where users keep long context windows across days.
- Platform teams migrating hosted to Dedicated who want higher packing density and predictable tail latencies.

Design principles

- Fidelity-first: Compression must preserve task-relevant tokens and metadata; heuristics are secondary to evaluation-driven thresholds.
- Observable and reversible: Operators must be able to see what was compressed, why, and restore original context when needed.
- Progressive & opt-in: Default off for existing customers; provide automatic suggestions via Redwood Optimize.

High-level approach

1. Multi-pass session summarization pipeline (runtime-adaptive):
   - Lightweight semantic clustering: identify contiguous and non-contiguous blocks of redundant context (messages, system instructions, long code blocks).
   - Localized compression strategies: per-cluster choose between pruning, extractive summary, or template-based replacement.
   - Fidelity budget enforcement: adaptive quality floor determined by route-level fidelity SLA and historical evals.

2. Runtime artifacts and contracts:
   - Compression metadata envelope: small JSON blob attached to each request describing applied transformations (cluster ids, removed token ranges, summary hash).
   - Rehydration hooks: for debugging or emergency rollback, the runtime can fetch compressed fragments from a short-term cache (configurable retention) to reconstruct original context.

3. Integration points:
   - Redwood API: new optional parameter session_compression: {mode, fidelity_budget, retention_ttl}.
   - Console: per-route toggle, per-tenant suggestions, and a compression insights dashboard.

API surface (proposal)

POST /v1/chat/completions or /v1/generate\Request body additions:
- session_compression (object) – optional
  - mode: "off" | "suggested" | "enforced"
  - fidelity_budget: "high" | "medium" | "low" (maps to internal loss budgets)
  - retention_ttl: ISO8601 duration (how long rehydration fragments are kept)

Console controls

- Per-route default mode and fidelity budget
- Per-tenant opt-in experiments with rollback button
- Insights: token savings, fidelity regressions, examples of transformations (approved sampling only)

Telemetry and observability requirements

Minimum telemetry to emit for every compressed request (all values emitted as tags/fields):

- compression_applied: true/false
- mode, fidelity_budget, retention_ttl
- tokens_before, tokens_after, tokens_saved
- cluster_count, compression_strategy_breakdown (prune/summary/template)
- fidelity_eval_id (if automated eval captured)
- rehydration_requested: true/false

Dashboards and alerts

- Savings dashboard: cumulative tokens_saved per route and per-tenant; trendlines (7d/30d).
- Fidelity alerts: when route-level automated evals exceed threshold regressions (default 2% absolute).
- Rehydration spike alert: sudden increase in rehydration_requested (>5x baseline) -> investigate false positives.

Rollout plan and milestones

Phase 0 (Lab, Q3 2029):
- Build evaluation harness with representative prompt sets for target workloads.
- Implement semantic clustering prototypes in a sandboxed runtime.

Phase 1 (Alpha, Q4 2029):
- Internal alpha on Redwood-owned routes; telemetry and rehydration hooks enabled.
- End-to-end fidelity evaluation automated.

Phase 2 (Beta, Q1 2030):
- Early access customers (up to 10 tenants) by invitation; per-route console controls live.
- Pricing experiments begin (see pricing section).

Phase 3 (GA, Q2 2030):
- Public GA; console self-serve onboarding and SDK docs.
- SLA: compression feature will be covered under existing route SLOs; we will provide a fidelity guarantee (monitoring-backed).

Pricing and packaging considerations
sections.heading: Success metrics (measured per-route and per-tenant)

sections.body:
- Compression is a value-add that reduces overall consumption; pricing should not be purely additive.
- Provide both free-tier suggestions and a paid managed compression offering with stronger fidelity SLAs and longer rehydration retention.
sections.heading: Principles

sections.body:
1. Opt-in free feature: customers benefit from token reduction at no charge; Redwood applies limits on retention_ttl and access to rehydration.
2. Managed compression subscription (monthly): includes extended retention (30d), audit logs of transformations, and fidelity insurance (automated rollback assistance).
3. Credits-based rehydration: rehydration calls charge a small token or credit-based fee to account for extra storage/IO.
sections.heading: Proposed models to evaluate in Beta

sections.body:
| Tier | Retention | Fidelity SLA | Monthly Price | Notes |
| Free | 6 hours | No guarantee | $0 | basic savings, console insights |
| Managed | 30 days | 99% fidelity floor (per route) | $500 / route | 24/7 support, extended retention |
| Enterprise | custom | Contracted fidelity | custom | integration, on-prem packaging |

Risks and mitigations

- False positives where critical context is removed -> mitigation: conservative default budgets, automatic fidelity evals, immediate rollback hooks.
- Customer trust/visibility concerns -> mitigation: transparency in console, example diffs, opt-in by default.
- Increased control-plane storage load for rehydration -> mitigation: tiered retention, archival to cold storage after TTL.

Open questions

- Should Redwood expose a "compression preview" API for customer-side verification before committing changes?
- What is the right fidelity budget mapping to internal loss budgets for specialized LLMs (code vs. conversational vs. summarization)?
- Appropriate pricing elasticity: how to share savings with customers while monetizing premium retention and fidelity guarantees?

Ownership and next steps

- Product owner: Priya Nair (Product)
- Runtime engineering lead: Ethan Park (Eng - Serving Runtime)
- Observability lead: Lina Morales (Eng - Platform)
sections.heading: Short example pricing table (illustrative)

sections.body:
1. Finalize evaluation datasets (responsible: Product, due: 2029-07-22).
2. Prototype compression metadata envelope and rehydration cache (responsible: Runtime, due: 2029-07-29).
3. Wire telemetry events into lab dashboard (responsible: Observability, due: 2029-07-29).

Appendix

- Example compression metadata envelope (stringified JSON stored in request header X-RW-Compress-Meta):
  \{"compressed\":true, \"clusters\":[\{"id\":\"c1\",\"strategy\":\"summary\",\"removed_tokens\":120\}], \"summary_hash\":\"sha256:abc123\"\}

- Evaluation rubric: each candidate compression must pass a run of 1000 synthetic sessions per route with fidelity checks (thresholds configured per route).

Related docs

- Conversational compression product brief (2026) — background research and initial user interviews.
- Degradation lattice design spec (2028) — approach for graceful fidelity fallbacks.

This document is intended as the canonical product brief for Adaptive Session Compression during scoping and go/no-go decisions. Feedback and review comments should be added to the reviewers list and the related issues in the Product board.

payload.page_title: Continuous Fallback Orchestration for Multi-Variant Serving Standards

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines standards and an operational playbook for continuous fallback orchestration across multi-variant model serving at Redwood Inference. It codifies the contract between routing, runtime, and control-plane services to ensure predictable quality degradation, fast recovery, and cost-aware decisioning when primary model variants are unavailable or underperforming.

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
- Goals:
  - Provide a deterministic, observable orchestration model that selects fallback variants based on SLOs, cost budgets, and quality constraints.
  - Define API-level contracts and telemetry to enable automated failover while preserving user experience.
  - Standardize rollout and canary patterns for introducing fallback variants.
- Non-goals:
  - This doc does not prescribe specific model architectures or quantization strategies; it focuses on orchestration and contracts.

Scope
-----
Applies to: Redwood hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments where multiple model variants (e.g., full-precision, quantized, distillations, smaller context-length variants) are available for a single route. The standards cover:
- Control-plane fallback policies (routing decisions, priorities, cost caps)
- Runtime handoff semantics (session/kv-cache compatibility, deterministic tokenization mapping)
- Observability contract (events, metrics, traces)
- Operational playbook for incidents and rollouts

Principles
----------
1. Predictable user-facing behavior: clients should see gradual, measurable changes in latency/quality, not abrupt failures.
2. Idempotent routing and safe retries: fallback actions must be idempotent and traceable.
3. Cost-awareness: fallback selection may prefer cheaper variants if quality impact is within allowed thresholds.
4. Test-first rollout: fallback variants require a validated prompt-set and regression thresholds before becoming eligible.

Definitions
-----------
- Primary Variant: default model variant for a route (e.g., model-a-v3-16k-fp16).
- Fallback Variant: any compatible variant that the control-plane can route to (quantized, small-LLM, different region).
- Fallback Policy: machine-readable policy that expresses ordering, triggers, and constraints.
- Compatibility Profile: metadata describing session semantics: tokenizer id, kv-cache schema, response schema version.

Policy schema (JSON-LD, simplified)
----------------------------------
The control plane expects a minimal, forward-compatible policy envelope attached to routing configs. Example snippet (human-readable):

```json
{
  "policy_id": "pfallback-2026-001",
  "route": "/v1/generate/chat",
  "ordered_variants": ["model-a-v3-16k-fp16", "model-a-v3-8k-qat8", "model-a-slim-4k"],
  "triggers": {
    "error_rate_gt": 0.05,
    "p50_latency_ms_gt": 300,
    "cpu_util_pct_gt": 85
  },
  "constraints": {
    "max_quality_regression_pct": 3,
    "cost_delta_pct_limit": 50
  },
  "rollout_canary": {"pct": 5, "duration_minutes": 30},
  "compatibility_profiles": ["tokenizer:v2","kv_schema:2"]
}
```

Design: orchestration choreography
----------------------------------
1. Detection layer (Telemetry):
   - Aggregates per-variant SLI intake (error rate, tail latencies, util, memory pressure).
   - Emits a canonical FallbackSignal when thresholds are hit.
2. Decision layer (Control plane):
   - Ingests FallbackSignal and applies the policy envelope for the route.
   - Produces a FallbackDecision with chosen target variant, action type (soft-route, hard-route, shed), and backoff window.
3. Enforcement layer (Edge/Router):
   - Applies the decision using sticky headers and request attributes. For streaming endpoints, the router may convert a streaming session to the selected variant using compatibility checks.
4. Graceful-degradation adapter (Runtime):
   - If a runtime detects incompatibility at handoff (tokenizer mismatch, kv cache format), it returns a deterministic HANDOFF_INCOMPATIBLE event to the control plane, which triggers the next variant in-ordered_variants.

Routing policy table (reference)
--------------------------------
- Action: soft-route -> Description: route a percentage of new requests to fallback variant while primary remains available. Use for low-severity regressions.
- Action: hard-route -> Description: route all traffic to fallback variant. Use for sustained outages or safety violations.
- Action: shed -> Description: reject or degrade request (e.g., return cached answer). Use as last resort with clear user messaging.

API contract between components
-------------------------------
- FallbackSignal (Telemetry -> Control plane):
  - Fields: route_id, variant_id, time_window_sec, error_rate, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, util_pct, host_count
- FallbackDecision (Control plane -> Edge):
  - Fields: decision_id, route_id, selected_variant_id, action, start_time, end_time, reason_codes, decision_provenance
- Handshake headers (Edge -> Runtime):
  - X-Redwood-Fallback-Decision: <decision_id>
  - X-Redwood-Compat-Profile: <compatibility_profile_id>

Telemetry, traces, and observability contract
---------------------------------------------
All fallback events must be recorded with the following labels/dimensions: route, request_id, decision_id, original_variant, selected_variant, trigger, owner_team. Minimum metrics:
- fallback_decisions.count (by action, route, variant)
- fallback_failures.count (handoff incompatibility, runtime rejects)
- fallback_latency_delta.p50/p95 (selected vs original)
- fallback_quality_regression_pct (from eval harness)

SLOs and thresholds (recommended defaults)
-----------------------------------------
- Detection threshold: error_rate > 5% sustained for 3m OR p95 latency > 750ms for 3m -> create FallbackSignal.
- Soft-route promotion: initial canary 5% for 15–60m, promoted if no regression > configured limit.
- Hard-route: after 30m of sustained violation or critical safety event.
- Recovery target: restore primary variant within 60m or escalate.

Quality and cost guardrails
--------------------------
- A fallback variant must supply a signed evaluation artifact: prompt-set regression report with metrics (EM, BLEU-like if applicable, and Redwood semantic-score) and a declared max_quality_regression_pct.
- If cost_delta_pct_limit is exceeded, control plane must annotate decision with "cost_preference" that can bias towards cheaper variants or request shedding.

Validation and deployment requirements
------------------------------------
1. All fallback variants must pass an on-call validation suite including:
   - Compatibility smoke tests (tokenization, schema, kv-cache)
   - Latency and tail tests under synthetic traffic at target QPS
   - 1000 example prompts from route-specific regression set; acceptable regression <= configured constraint
2. Canary process: attach a canary policy to any new fallback candidate with canary_pct and canary_duration. Use telemetry-based gates for promotion.

Testing matrix (example)
-----------------------
- Unit: policy parser, decision encoder/decoder
- Integration: decision flows (Telemetry -> Control -> Edge -> Runtime) with simulated signals
- Load: verify promotion behavior at 10k RPS with mixed contexts
- Chaos: simulate runtime incompatibility and verify deterministic fallthrough behavior

Operational runbook (incident response)
-------------------------------------
1. Detection:
   - Pager triggered by fallback_failures.count > 10 in 5m OR fallback_decisions.hard-route.count > 0 for a high-value route.
2. Triage:
   - Owner: runtime-orchestration-svc oncall.
   - Actions: check decision_id in request traces, examine Telemetry->Control latencies, examine runtime logs for HANDOFF_INCOMPATIBLE.
3. Mitigation steps (priority):
   a. If handoff incompatibility: fail open to next compatible variant in policy and mark incompatible variant as quarantined.
   b. If high error rate on primary with no compatibility issues: trigger automated soft-route to next variant (5% -> 25% -> 100% per policy).
   c. If cost runaway: apply temporary cost cap rule that prefers cheaper variant or reduction in batch size.
4. Post-incident:
   - Create an incident summary with decision_id timeline, root cause, and remediation checklist.

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Primary owner: Model Serving Orchestration team (oncall: #ms-orch-pager)
- Secondary owner: Runtime Platform SRE (oncall: #runtime-sre)
- For customer-impacting incidents: notify CS and Account Lead within 30 minutes.

Appendix: Practical examples
---------------------------
1) Canary-to-hard-route example (CLI):
```bash
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwoodctl routes update \
  --route /v1/chat --policy-file fallback-policy.json
sections.heading: create a fallback policy for route

sections.body:
redwoodctl policy promote --policy pfallback-2026-001 --target 100
```
2) Handoff incompatibility flow (trace example):
- trace: req-42 -> decision d-123 -> router returns HANDOFF_INCOMPATIBLE -> control plane issues d-124 -> router routes to model-a-slim-4k

Appendix B: Compatibility checklist (runtime)
- Tokenizer ID matches route's expected tokenizer
- Output schema version equality or compatible mapper present
- KV cache format header present and compatible

Related work and references
---------------------------
- See: runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026 (performance interplay)
- See: decision-records/adr-request-segmentation-cost-priority-routing-2026 for cost-prioritization rationale

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-01-12: initial draft (Elena Ramos)
