payload.page_title: Pitch playbook: compact economics & risk scripts

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook gives field teams a compact, repeatable set of messaging scripts, competitive talking points, pricing heuristics, and a short customer case study to accelerate technical discovery conversations with platform and engineering buyers. It is optimized for 10–25 minute technical deep dives and CISO/Finance readiness checks.

Who this is for
- Sales Engineers: concise scripts for demos and risk conversations.
- Account Executives: framing snippets for exec/C-level briefs.
- Solution Architects: competitive countermeasures and deployment notes.

Positioning pillars (30-second soundbites)
1) Predictable inference economics: "Redwood converts model choices into predictable per-token costs via quantization profiles, smart batching, and autoscaling policies—so you can forecast ML spend like any other infra line item."
2) Production-grade reliability: "We provide SLAs, fallbacks, and dedicated capacity options so user-facing LLM features stay online even under load or model regressions."
3) Deployment flexibility and security: "Host with Redwood, or deploy Redwood Private into your VPC / on-prem—with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs for regulated workloads."
4) Developer-first operations: "Same API, tooling, and rollouts across hosted, dedicated, and private—reduces cognitive load for platform teams."

Competitive brief (quick reference)
- OpenAI / Anthropic (hosted LLM APIs)
  - Strengths: largest model ecosystem, simple API, fast time-to-prototype.
  - Redwood response: Emphasize SLO-backed dedicated capacity, cost controls (batching/quant), and enterprise security for regulated customers. Highlight predictable unit economics and rollout controls.
- Cloud-managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex)
  - Strengths: deep cloud integration, billing consolidation.
  - Redwood response: Stress inference-optimized runtime (KV cache, continuous batching) that typically reduces per-token runtime by 20–40% vs generic endpoint configurations; point to dedicated GPU pool options and multi-cloud routing.
- Self-hosted runtime vendors (open-source runtimes/orchestration)
  - Strengths: control, no vendor lock.
  - Redwood response: Call out the operational burden, ongoing kernel selection, and performance tuning required. Position Redwood as a managed alternative that preserves control (Private deployment) while removing engineering debt.

Quick battlecards (friction points + counters)
- "We can just run this ourselves on EC2/GKE."
  - Counter: For sustained user-facing latency SLOs, the engineering cost of kernel tuning, KV cache correctness, and autoscaling policy development is non-trivial. Offer a 6–8 week pilot that shows unit-cost delta and time-to-market delta.
- "OpenAI has better models / quality."
  - Counter: Redwood supports model rollouts and automatic fallback to tuned variants; for many production workloads model parity is not the primary constraint—latency, cost, and observability are. Offer a side-by-side eval with traffic replay.

Demo scripts: 12-minute technical deep dive (structure)
1) 0:00–1:30 — 30-second product framing & value props (use positioning pillars).
2) 1:30–4:00 — Live trace: show Console call graph, per-token cost breakdown, and latency SLOs for a sample chat workload.
3) 4:00–7:00 — Deployment options: toggle to Dedicated and simulated failover to Private mock (show routing policy UI + audit logs).
4) 7:00–10:00 — Economics toggle: show autoscaling, batching, and quantization profiles and an on-screen estimator for per-10k tokens cost.
5) 10:00–12:00 — Security & compliance quick tour: KMS key rotation demo, RBAC role preview, and a link to compliance evidence pack.

Concise SE scripts (one-liners and short paragraphs)
- For platform engineers: "You can pin model versions and route traffic by latency or cost tiers so your product teams get consistent latency while finance keeps predictable billing."
- For CISO/InfoSec: "We integrate with customer KMS and provide immutable audit logs per request; Private installs run entirely in your VPC and optionally air-gapped environments."
- For Finance: "Our optimizer provides cost-sensitivity controls—scale down quantization for low-risk workloads and reserve Dedicated capacity for high-throughput endpoints to cap spend."

Pricing guidance (heuristic framework)
- Pricing levers to discuss: model class, dedicated capacity vs hosted, latency SLO, caching hit rate, and quantization profile.
- Sample scenarios (illustrative; use the pricing calculator for final quotes):

| Scenario | Model class | Traffic pattern | Key levers | Expected per-10k token cost (est) |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Small chatbot MVP | Llama2-13B quantized | 10 reqs/s bursts | aggressive batching, prefix caching | $1.20 |
| Customer support scale | Llama2-70B trimmed | 50 reqs/s sustained | Dedicated pool, conservative quant | $5.60 |
| Document embeddings | Efficient embed model | batch offline | batch-only, high throughput | $0.08 |

- Pricing talking tips: always include three levers customers can act on immediately (batching, cache, quantization) and show dollarized impact in the demo. Use committed Dedicated capacity to cap unit costs for high-throughput endpoints.

Security FAQ for prospects (top 8 questions)
1) Where are request logs stored and who can access them?
   - Answer: Request logs are stored in the customer’s control plane for Private deployments or in a tenant-isolated storage layer for Hosted; access is RBAC-controlled and recorded in audit logs.
2) How do you handle encryption and key management?
   - Answer: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM; keys are never exported to third parties in Private deployments.
3) Can we run Redwood in a fully air-gapped environment?
   - Answer: Yes — an on-prem package is available with an install guide and cross-checklist.
4) How do you support data residency and retention policies?
   - Answer: Per-route retention settings and legal hold controls are available; we provide exportable evidence for audits.
5) What is your incident notification and SLA for security incidents?
   - Answer: We follow our security incident playbook; affected customers receive email + console notifications within 2 hours and a root-cause summary within 72 hours for P1 security incidents.
6) How are model weights/vulnerable artifacts controlled in Private installs?
   - Answer: Model artifacts are stored in customer-managed artifact stores with provenance metadata; automated checks prevent execution of unsigned artifacts.
7) Do you provide penetration test reports and SOC/compliance evidence?
   - Answer: Yes — we supply SOC2 Type II reports and pen test summaries in the compliance evidence pack; for dedicated/Private customers we provide redacted reports as appropriate.
8) How do you prevent model extraction or prompt-injection leakage?
   - Answer: We recommend a layered approach: response filtering, graduation of quantization for sensitive models, request size and rate limits, and application-layer input validation; we also provide monitoring that detects anomalous query patterns.

Short customer case study (anonymized)
- Customer: "FinScale" (financial SaaS platform, mid-market)
- Problem: Unpredictable inference costs and frequent user-visible latency spikes as demand scaled from 5k to 50k daily queries.
- Solution: Migrated 3 high-volume customer-facing endpoints to Redwood Dedicated, applied prefix caching and conservative quantization profile, and set autoscaling policies with burst capacity.
- Outcome (90 days):
  - 38% reduction in per-token runtime latency (median p50)-> from 230ms to 143ms.
  - 27% reduction in unit inference spend vs their prior cloud endpoint configuration.
  - Zero production incidents during Black Friday-like traffic test.

Objection handling cheat sheet
- "We need to keep everything in-house for compliance." => Offer Private deployment checklist and propose a technical pilot in their lab environment with our SRE support.
- "This is a pricing/ROI conversation." => Use the per-10k demo estimator and propose a 30-day traffic replay pilot to measure delta.
- "Model quality concerns." => Offer traffic-split rollouts and A/B evaluation harness; commit to quality regression alerts tied to their prompt set.

Next steps & pilot template (3-step rapid pilot)
1) Align scope (week 0): Confirm 2 endpoints, traffic replay dataset, and success metrics (latency p50/p95, cost per 10k tokens).
2) Pilot (weeks 1–3): Deploy Redwood in org trial mode or light Private deployment, run traffic replay, and tune batching/cache/quant profiles. Provide daily checkpoint notes.
3) Wrap & decision (week 4): Deliver ROI report, long-term capacity recommendation, and a production rollout checklist.

Owner & contacts
- Playbook owner: Aisha Patel (Go-to-Market)
- Escalation for security questions: Priya Nair (Security & Compliance)

sections.body:
Overview

This sales kit is designed for sellers and solutions engineers working outbound or responding to RFPs in Retail & Commerce. It combines crisp positioning, a competitive brief, a pitch-deck outline, price/TCO guidance, a one-page case study, a demo recipe, and a short Security FAQ tailored for procurement and technical evaluation.

Audience and target personas

- Head of Product / Director of Search: cares about relevance, conversion lift, latency and cost per query.
- Engineering Manager (ML/Infra): needs predictable inference runtimes, versioned rollouts, and observability.
- Platform/Cloud Architect: evaluates network, VPC, and deployment models (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- Procurement / Legal: looks for pricing predictability, SLAs, and security/compliance evidence.

Key positioning and messaging (Retail-focused)

Elevator pitch (15s): Redwood Inference gives retail teams enterprise-grade LLM serving that improves search relevance and personalization while keeping latency low and operating costs predictable — across hosted, reserved, or private deployments.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Conversion-first inference: optimized runtimes and caching reduce median query latency to 50–120ms at scale, improving add-to-cart and checkout conversion.
- Cost predictability: reserved/Dedicated GPU pools and unit economics tooling reduce per-query cost up to 6x vs naïve cloud-hosted endpoints for high QPS workloads.
- Safe rollouts and regressions guardrails: canary rollouts, eval integration, and quality monitoring prevent relevance regressions in production.
- Hybrid deployment flexibility: self-hosted/private options for PII-sensitive catalogs and hosted API for rapid POC.

Use cases and value metrics (quick bullets for discovery)

1) Query rewriting & relevance tuning
- Outcome: 8–20% improvement in click-through and add-to-cart for long-tail queries.
- Metrics to ask for: daily search QPS, current median latency, % long-tail queries, baseline conversion rate.

2) Conversational shopping / chat assistants
- Outcome: reduced contact center volume, increased AOV via guided upsell flows.
- Ask for: monthly conversations, average session turns, SLA for response latency.

3) Product summarization & auto-descriptions (catalog enrichment)
- Outcome: faster catalog onboarding, consistent description quality, better SEO.
- Ask for: catalog size, ingestion frequency, human review ratio.

4) Personalization & ranking re-rank
- Outcome: lift in basket size and time-on-site; reranking latency budgets.
- Ask for: rerank QPS, batch vs online constraints, click-through baselines.

Competitive brief (battlecard)

- Major cloud LLM endpoints (AWS/Azure/GCP managed LLM services):
  - Strengths: easy integration, broad platform services, enterprise contracts.
  - Weaknesses / friction: limited fine-grained performance tuning for inference, less control over GPU stack, and fewer integrated caching/batching optimizations that matter at high QPS.
  - Redwood counter: Our runtime selects kernels, manages KV cache and continuous batching automatically and exposes predictable unit economics for production retail workloads.

- Open-source self-hosted stacks + internal infra teams:
  - Strengths: full control, potential low model licensing costs.
  - Weaknesses: high operational burden, variance in latency, ongoing engineering cost for GPU ops and rollout tooling.
  - Redwood counter: Offers the same deployment flexibility with turnkey tooling (rollouts, metrics, SLOs) and a productized private option to reduce ops lift.

- Specialized inference vendors (inference runtimes / orchestration startups):
  - Strengths: high-performance primitives, tight optimization claims.
  - Weaknesses: narrow scope; may lack product integrations (console, evals, pricing tooling, enterprise SLAs).
  - Redwood counter: Combines a production-first platform (console, observability, rollouts) with kernel and runtime optimizations—bridging engineering and product needs.

Win themes to emphasize during discovery

- Measureable conversion impact (show a short case-driven ROI)
- Predictable unit economics at scale (dedicated capacity + Optimize recommendations)
- Low-friction deployment path: POC on hosted API -> reserved Dedicated pool -> private deployment if needed
- Enterprise controls: VPC, KMS integration, audit logs, role-based access

Pricing guidance and sample TCOs (retail scenarios)

High-level guidance: Redwood offers three pricing levers: hosted-per-use (best for POC & low-volume), Dedicated reserved capacity (best for steady high-QPS workloads), and Private (enterprise licensing for regulated deployments). Use these worked examples in commercial conversations.

Scenario A: Mid-market retailer running search + personalization (steady 200 QPS, ~30M tokens/day)
- Recommended plan: Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit) with 2x burst capacity
- Expected benefits: 3–5x cost reduction vs unmanaged hosted endpoints at this scale; stable latency SLOs for search.

Scenario B: Enterprise omnichannel retailer (peak 2000 QPS during promotions, heavy rerank workloads)
- Recommended plan: Hybrid approach — hosted API for low-priority workloads, Dedicated pools for search/rerank, optional Private for PII-sensitive catalog processing.
- Commercial terms to pursue: 6–12 month commit with burst engineering support, SLA add-on for promotional periods.

Pricing examples (do not treat as final — use for guidance in deals):

- Hosted: $0.0008–$0.003 per token-equivalent depending on model class and throughput.
- Dedicated base: monthly capacity payment + reduced per-token compute for steady-state throughput. Typical committed monthly price starts in low five-figures for a production small retailer up to mid-six-figures for enterprise.

Use these numbers only as directional; always route to pricing@redwood or solutions-engineering for formal quotes.

Pitch deck outline (10 slides recommended)

1. Title + one-line value prop
2. Retail challenges: conversion, latency, cost, quality regressions
3. Redwood solution overview (hosted/dedicated/private)
4. How it works: runtime + caching + routing + rollouts (1-slide architecture)
5. Case study / customer outcomes (numbers)
6. Demo: search rerank + conversational quick flow (link to demo recipe)
7. Pricing approach & deployment path
8. Security & compliance (VPC, KMS, audit logs)
9. Implementation plan & timeline (POC -> pilot -> production)
10. Ask and next steps

Demo recipe (solutions engineer playbook)

Objective: Show a live search rerank POC that reduces latency and increases relevance for business-critical queries in 45 minutes.

Prep steps (30–60 minutes prior):
1. Ask customer to provide a small catalog CSV (<= 2k SKUs) and a sample of 200 real search queries with click labels.
2. Preload catalog into a demo index and enable a small hosted model instance.
3. Prepare two routes: baseline (current ranking) and Redwood model + rerank.

During demo (20–25 minutes):
1. Quick context (2m): what we measure and success metric (e.g., position-weighted CTR).
2. Live queries (10m): run sample queries side-by-side and show latency, token usage and result changes.
3. Observability (5m): show per-route token cost, latency percentiles and error rates in Console.
4. Next steps (3m): touch on Dedicated option and timelines.

Objection handling (short scripts)

- "We can self-host and save money."
  - Reply: Self-hosting can save model licensing but operational and engineering costs for GPU ops, kernel tuning, and building rollouts usually exceed savings for production-grade throughput. We offer private deployments and transfer operational knowledge during onboarding.

- "Latency during peak sales is non-negotiable."
  - Reply: We support SLO-driven routing and Dedicated capacity with burst policies; for major promotional events we can pre-stage capacity and provide SLA add-ons.

Customer case snapshot (one-pager you can hand to prospects)

Title: "How Northside Apparel cut search latency by 55% and lifted add-to-cart by 12%"
- Customer: Northside Apparel (hypothetical profile: omnichannel retailer, 12M annual sessions)
- Problem: outdated search infra with high tail latency and poor mobile conversion
- Solution: POC using Redwood hosted API for rerank + Dedicated pool for production; KV prefix caching for common queries and a canary rollout.
- Outcomes (90-day): median search latency from 410ms -> 180ms, add-to-cart +12%, cost per search down 35% vs previous managed endpoint.

Security FAQ for prospect evaluations (concise answers)

Q: Can Redwood run inside our VPC / on-prem?
A: Yes. Redwood Private provides a customer-managed control plane with optional on-prem packaging for air-gapped environments. Many enterprise retail customers run catalog ingestion and PII-sensitive transforms in private deployments.

Q: What encryption & key management options exist?
A: All data at rest and in transit is encrypted. We integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private deployments and support customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private offerings.

Q: How do you handle access controls and auditing?
A: Role-based access control (RBAC) at the Console level, API keys with scoped privileges, and audit logs that capture request metadata, model versions, and operator actions — exportable to SIEM.

Q: Do you persist user prompts or customer PII?
A: For hosted API, data persistence policies are configurable per contract; we provide options for non-retention for PII and can route sensitive processing to Private deployments. See evidence pack for specific retention policies.

Q: What certifications and compliance evidence do you provide?
A: We publish SOC2 Type II and maintain a compliance evidence portal for enterprise procurement. For sector-specific requirements we work with customers on addendum contracts and data residency commitments.

Q: Can Redwood prove no model regression after updates?
A: Yes. Our rollout system integrates with evals and regression monitoring; canary rollouts and automatic rollback rules are available to prevent quality regressions.

Sales motion and recommended next steps (seller checklist)

1. Discovery: collect QPS, latency targets, catalog size, and sample queries.
2. Business case framing: show conversion-impact scenarios and TCO examples tailored to their metrics.
3. POC offer: 2–4 week hosted POC with provided sample prompt sets and eval harness.
4. Pilot: Dedicated reserved pool for production pilot with SLA and support.
5. Enterprise conversion: negotiate private deployment or 12-month dedicated commit, finalize security addenda.

Appendix and links (internal)

- Security evidence portal: /confluence/security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence

Contact

sections.body:
Summary:

This companion document is a compact, engineer-facing toolkit for sales engineers and platform owners evaluating Redwood Inference. It bundles: concise positioning and messaging for technical audiences; a competitive snapshot focused on operational trade-offs; a recommended three-stage pilot-to-scale plan with telemetry thresholds and rollout steps; code snippets and integration examples (hosted + private); a pricing guidance cheat sheet for pilots and committed capacity; a short customer case study; and a CISO-friendly security FAQ with concrete evidence artifacts and owner contacts.

Audience and intent:
- Primary: Platform engineers, SREs, security reviewers, and sales engineers running technical evaluations.
- Secondary: Solution architects, procurement leads, and technical product managers.

1) Engineer-focused positioning (elevator + technical themes)

Elevator (for engineers):
Redwood Inference provides a single runtime that makes production LLM inference predictable and economical across hosted, reserved (Dedicated), and private deployments. It reduces per-token cost through automatic batching/caching, improves latency via hardware-aware kernel selection, and preserves safety with audit logs and deterministic fallbacks.

Key technical themes to lead with:
- Unified API and SDKs: same request semantics for hosted, dedicated, and private (minimizes integration surface).
- Deterministic performance controls: configurable batching/caching, quantization profiles, and autoscaling policies with observable unit economics.
- Graceful degradation: policy-driven routing and automatic fallback to lower-capacity model variants by latency/cost tiers.
- Security-by-design: VPC-private control plane, KMS integrations, and end-to-end audit logging for compliance checks.

2) Quick competitive snapshot (operational lens)

Competitors considered: major managed LLM APIs, generic cloud-managed endpoints, and self-hosted inference runtimes.

Differentiation matrix (operational priorities):
- Latency predictability: Redwood (high) | Generic APIs (variable) | Self-hosted (depends)
- Cost control per token: Redwood (high, explicit controls) | Generic APIs (moderate) | Self-hosted (high ops cost)
- Deployment flexibility: Redwood (hosted/dedicated/private) | Generic APIs (hosted) | Self-hosted (on-prem only)
- Enterprise evidence (SOCs, KMS): Redwood (SOC2 + KMS patterns) | Generic APIs (varies) | Self-hosted (customer-owned)

Operational trade-offs to call out:
- Self-hosted wins for absolute data control, but requires significant SRE investment for batching/kv/cache optimizations.
- Generic managed APIs are easiest to start with but can expose cost/latency unpredictability at scale.
- Redwood aims to reduce that operational burden while offering enterprise controls.

3) Three-stage pilot-to-scale playbook (engineer-friendly)

Goal: deliver a production-quality route from PoC to serving 10M tokens/day with <75ms P50 generation latency for short prompts (<=128 tokens) by the end of Stage 3.

Stage A — Rapid proof-of-concept (1–2 weeks)
- Scope: implement a single endpoint call (chat or generation) in a sandbox account with sample prompts.
- Success criteria: end-to-end request <200ms P50 (hosted), valid example responses for 95% of test prompts, and a basic security checklist signed off by security engineer.
- Deliverables: integration demo app, sample prompt set (50 prompts), cost estimate for expected per-token usage.
- Owner: Sales Engineer + Customer Platform Engineer.

Stage B — Pilot with observability (3–6 weeks)
- Scope: integrate Redwood Console observability hooks, enable token-level cost reporting, configure a canary route (5% traffic).
- Success criteria: cost per 1k tokens within target (example: <= $1.20 / 1k tokens for medium prompt lengths when using curated model X-q4), latency SLO met (P95 < 350ms), and end-to-end tracing present for 100% of errors.
- Ramp steps: 1) shift 5% traffic, 2) validate logs & metrics for 7 days, 3) run adversarial prompt set and evaluate responses vs baseline.
- Deliverables: tracing dashboard, regression report, cost/billing export, rollback runbook.
- Owner: Customer Platform Engineering & Redwood Customer Success.

Stage C — Production rollout (4–12 weeks)
- Scope: Dedicated capacity or Private deployment as required; configure autoscale and fallback policies; run a 30-day burn demonstrating SLO attainment.
- Success criteria: sustained throughput matches SLAs (e.g., 100 qps sustained on a 4-GPU Dedicated pool), error budget <1% monthly, and documented security evidence for procurement.
- Deliverables: Dedicated pool sizing spec, autoscaling policy YAML, quantization profile recommendation, post-mortem on pilot anomalies.
- Owner: Customer SRE + Redwood Dedicated Ops.

4) Observability & telemetry checklist (required for pilot acceptance)
- Token-level cost reporting enabled (Console export + S3 export).
- Latency by route: P50, P95, P99 for generation and streaming.
- Error class breakdown: rate-limited, model-unavailable, decode errors, network errors.
- Trace IDs correlated with platform logs for triage (linkable to request_id).
- Drift monitoring: weekly prompt set pass/fail and MRR for quality regressions.

5) Pricing guidance cheat sheet (pilot vs committed)

Pilot (recommended):
- Free trial credits + usage-based billing: estimate pilot cost with formula: expected_tokens_per_day * days * pilot_unit_cost
- Example: 500k tokens/day * 14 days * $0.0007/token = $4,900 (one-time pilot consumption)

Committed / Dedicated guidance (example ranges):
- Small reserved pool (2 x A100 equivalent): $30k–$50k/month, target throughput ~150–300 qps depending on model and sequence length.
- Medium reserved pool (4 x A100 equivalent): $55k–$95k/month, target throughput ~300–700 qps.
- Private on-prem licensing: one-time platform fee + support contract; licensing varies by customer scale — typical starting TCV for midmarket $250k/year.

Negotiation levers for deals:
- Burst capacity add-on: available for Dedicated to handle 30–50% peak spikes for a premium.
- Longer-term commits reduce unit cost and improve model variant availability.
- Observability & retention add-ons for enterprise compliance (longer log retention, full trace retention).

6) Integration examples (copy-paste friendly)

Hosted API: simple streaming generation (curl)

curl -s -N https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"rwd-neo-medium-2027","input":"Summarize the following conversation...","max_tokens":128,"stream":true}'

Hosted SDK (python, minimal):

from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'])
resp = client.generate(model='rwd-neo-medium-2027', input='Hello world', max_tokens=64)
print(resp.text)

Private deployment sample (k8s values snippet):

# values.yaml (snippet)
replicaCount: 3
nodeSelector:
  kubernetes.io/instance-type: gpu-rtx8000
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
modelCache:
  enabled: true
  sizeGb: 64
quantizationProfile: q4_0
networking:
  controlPlaneCIDR: 10.0.0.0/24
  allowedEgress: ["s3://redwood-artifacts", "api.redwood.ai"]

Config-as-code example (autoscale policy YAML):

policyName: latency-aware-autoscale
minReplicas: 2
maxReplicas: 12
targetP95LatencyMs: 300
scaleUpStep: 1
scaleDownCooldownSec: 600

7) Sample acceptance checklist for procurement & security
- SOC2 Type II report available (attach latest artifact).
- Penetration test summary and remediation log (last 12 months).
- KMS integration guide and key rotation cadence.
- Data flow diagram showing PII ingress, processing, and retention points.
- Audit log retention options and export mechanism (S3 / SIEM).
- SLAs and outage RTO commitments for Dedicated.

8) Customer case vignette (BrightCart e-commerce)

Context: BrightCart is a mid-market e-commerce platform that deployed Redwood Dedicated to replace a mixture of host-model endpoints and in-house inference.
Outcome summary (90-day):
- 60% reduction in per-conversation inference cost after moving to batching + q4 quantized model for short queries.
- Average latency P95 reduced from 520ms to 260ms on product search reranking.
- One-month pilot led to a committed 6-month Dedicated contract.

Key instrumentation used: token-level billing exports, canary route (10% traffic), and week-over-week quality regressions reported to product via the Console.

9) Security FAQ for prospects (CISO-friendly answers)

Q: Where is my data stored and is data retained?
A: For hosted API, customer request payloads are stored for up to 30 days for quality/regression monitoring by default and can be configured per-account. For Dedicated and Private, customers control retention policy; retention can be set to 0 days and logs exported to customer S3/KMS.

Q: What controls exist for encryption and key management?
A: We support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS or HSM-backed key stores for Dedicated and Private control planes. TLS 1.3 enforced for in-transit; AES-256 for at-rest.

Q: Can Redwood operate in an air-gapped environment?
A: Yes — our Private on-prem package includes an installer and attestable binary set. We run an airgap validation checklist and work with the customer's security team for attestation and smoke tests.

Q: What compliance evidence is available?
A: SOC2 Type II report, ISO 27001 scope summary (select customers), vulnerability management policies, and supply-chain security statement. Specific artifacts are shared under NDA.

Q: How do you handle model hallucinations and guardrails?
A: We provide structured output schemas, response filters, and reranking integrations. Customers can attach deterministic filters and fallback handlers in the platform routing policies. We surface quality regressions via the Console and support custom eval sets.

Q: What is the incident response and notification policy?
A: Critical incidents (P1: platform-wide outage) trigger immediate pager notifications to customers with subscription to status updates. Post-incident reports are shared within 72 hours and include root cause, impact, and remediation steps. Dedicated customers may opt into a 24/7 escalation channel.

Q: Who owns security support during pilot?
A: Primary contact is Redwood Customer Security Liaison (security-liaison@redwood.ai). For Dedicated/Private projects, a named Solutions Security Engineer is assigned during Stage B.

10) Appendix: copyable artifact links and owner contacts
- Example prompt set (50 prompts): /internal-assets/prompt-sets/quickship-50.json (sales access only)
- SOC2 report (redacted): /legal-artifacts/soc2/redwood-soc2-2026-redacted.pdf (NDA required)
- Contact roster: Maya Chen (SE lead) maya.chen@redwood.ai; Diego Alvarez (Solutions Engineering) diego.alvarez@redwood.ai; Security liaison: security-liaison@redwood.ai

How to use this file in customer conversations:
1) Start with the elevator and the three technical themes to align with platform engineers.
2) Run the Stage A PoC with the hosted curl example and capture baseline cost/latency.
3) If pilot criteria are met, promote to Stage B and enable Console telemetry; provide the procurement checklist to legal/security.
4) Use the pricing guidance to provide a near-term conservative quote and table the dedicated capacity options for engineering review.

Change history:
- 2026-11-07: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2027-02-10: Added Dedicated sizing guidance and new Hosted API curl example.

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: Maya Chen (Sales Engineering).
- Security reviewer and escalation: Priya Natarajan (Security & Compliance).
- Legal/procurement escalation: procurement@redwood.ai

End of document.

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This single-page deliverable is a compact, ready-to-present kit for Sales Architects and Solutions Engineers to use in discovery, technical demos, and negotiation calls. It bundles concise positioning, battle-tested win themes, a short competitive brief, three pricing scenarios with math, a one-paragraph customer case study, a pilot-to-production checklist, and a security FAQ tailored for prospect technical reviewers. Use this when you have 30–60 minutes with an engineer, platform lead, or security reviewer.

How to use this pack

1) Start with the 2-slide narrative (covered in "Deck outline"). 2) Run a 10-minute demo focusing on the model routing and cost controls. 3) Present the pricing scenarios and recommend a pilot path. 4) Close technical questions with the Security FAQ and the Pilot Checklist.

Core positioning and win themes

- Developer-first inference platform that prioritizes predictable economics and production reliability.
- Unified runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — same API and observability regardless of where models run.
- Cost controls: intelligent batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization recommendations that reduce per-token costs while preserving quality.
- Reliability: automated fallbacks (model variants, regions, capacity tiers) and SLA-backed Dedicated options for enterprise needs.
- Operational visibility: token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, and rollout controls for safe rollouts and fast triage.

Value statements for buyers

- For Platform Engineers: "Ship consistent inference with a single API and then tune economics centrally."
- For ML Engineers: "Keep model evaluation and rollout safe — Redwood handles serving performance and KV cache reuse so you can iterate models faster."
- For Security/Compliance: "Private deployments with customer-controlled networking and KMS/HSM integrations — audit logs are first-class."

Competitive brief (3-minute view)

Summary: Competitors range from public LLM APIs to self-hosted runtimes. Redwood wins when customers need production-grade SLAs, predictable unit economics, and a unified operational model across hybrid deployments.

Key competitive differentiators

- vs. general cloud-managed endpoints: Faster TTV and model catalog tuned for inference + prebuilt fallback policies.
- vs. single-vendor LLM APIs: Transparent performance profiles and better cost controls via batching/caching.
- vs. self-hosted runtimes: We provide orchestration, routing policies, and SRE-grade telemetry out-of-the-box.

Typical competitive objections and counter-frames

1) "We can host cheaper ourselves." → Counter: Provide 3-scenario economic model (below) showing total cost of ownership including SRE time, forecasting error, wasted capacity, and regression risk.
2) "Vendor lock-in risk." → Counter: Highlight unified API, ability to pin model versions, and exportable rollout configs; private deployments remove shared control plane concerns.
3) "Quality/regression safety." → Counter: Redwood Optimize + evals + per-prompt quality monitoring with regression alerts.

Pricing guidance & scenarios (example math)

Assumptions: 1M generated tokens/month; 200k embedding units/month; latency SLO <= 300 ms p50 for interactive routes.

Scenario A — Proof-of-concept (Pilot)
- Hosted API, Pay-as-you-go.
- @ 1M tokens: $0.25 / 1K tokens = $250. Embeddings: $0.03 / unit => $6k? (see math correction below)
- Recommended: 6-week pilot, $5k credit + technical onboarding.

Scenario B — Mid-market committed (Predictable)
- Dedicated small pool (reserved): baseline Uptime SLA + burst policy.
- Commit: $6k / month for reserved capacity that covers 1M tokens/month typical; effective blended token cost = $0.12 / 1K tokens.
- Add-ons: observability retention + dedicated support = $1k / month.

Scenario C — Enterprise Private (Compliance-focused)
- On-prem/VPC private deployment with platform license and support. Typical contract: $80k annual platform fee + $X infra costs (customer).
- Includes deployment packaging, HSM/KMS integration, audit log retention config, and on-site enablement.

Note on math: These scenarios are templates — always run the deal economics calculator in the Deal Engineer toolkit and replace placeholder unit prices with current rate card. Use the token breakdown from the demo to size the dedicated pool.

Pilot-to-production checklist (technical and commercial)

1) Discovery: Confirm throughput needs (rps and tokens/session distribution), compliance requirements, and third-party network constraints.
2) Pilot design: Select a single route + two model variants; enable KV caching and streaming.
3) Bench: Run synthetic load at 2x expected peak for 24 hours; capture p50/p90 latencies and cost per 10k tokens.
4) Instrument: Hook Redwood Console dashboards, add tracing hooks, and upload a set of guardrail prompts for quality monitoring.
5) Commercial: Align billing model (PayG vs reserved), SLA expectations, and draft renewal/scale triggers.

One-paragraph customer case study (condensed)

Acme Retail (mid-market, multi-region): Replaced an ad-hoc mixture of cloud endpoints and home-grown inference serving. Outcome after 90 days: 35% lower per-token cost via caching and batching, 40% reduction in tail latency for shopping assistant flows (p95 from 850ms to 520ms), and an operationally simpler deployment with a single dashboard for model rollouts. Contract expanded to Dedicated within 6 months.

Security FAQ for technical reviewers (top 10 quick answers)

Q1. Can we deploy Redwood in our VPC or on-prem?
A1. Yes — Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages with a customer-controlled control plane and optional air-gapped deployment.

Q2. How are encryption keys managed?
A2. Integrations: cloud KMS (AWS/GCP/Azure) and HSM options supported. Keys can be customer-managed; we do not persist plaintext keys.

Q3. Is customer data logged?
A3. Audit logging is configurable. By default, core operational metadata is logged; payload logging is off for Private deployments unless explicitly enabled for troubleshooting under an NDA.

Q4. What compliance evidence do you provide?
A4. SOC2 Type II report, penetration test summary, and architecture diagrams for private deployments. For customers with HIPAA needs we provide a BAA template and deployment checklist.

Q5. How do you protect model outputs against data leakage?
A5. We provide model variant pinning, strict rollout controls, prompt/eval-based regression alerts, and input/output redaction options.

Q6. What's your incident response posture?
A6. Eng-SRE maintains an incident runbook with 24/7 paging for high-sev production incidents. Customers on enterprise SLAs receive a designated TAM and post-incident RCA within 3 business days.

Q7. Are there VPC peering or private link options?
A7. Yes — VPC peering, PrivateLink (AWS), and private interconnects (GCP/Azure) are supported for low-latency, secure traffic.

Q8. How is customer isolation guaranteed on Dedicated?
A8. Dedicated capacity provides isolated GPU pools, tenant-level quotas, and network segmentation. Control plane metadata can be restricted per-customer.

Q9. Can we bring our own model weights?
A9. In most cases yes: Redwood supports customer-supplied models with a model onboarding process and verification runbook (performance and security checks). Private deployments are preferred for sensitive IP.

Q10. What are typical breach response commitments?
A10. For enterprise contracts we include notification timelines, RMS contact list, and collaboration commitments for remediation and forensics.

Appendix: 12-slide deck outline (two-slide quick start)

- Slide 1: Hook — "Make LLMs predictable: cost, latency, and reliability across any deployment." (1–2 bullets + logo)
- Slide 2: Architecture sketch — unified API + routing + caching + hosting modes (visual).

payload.page_title: Platform Operator Conversion Playbook — Integrations & Risk Reduction

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook is designed for platform and infrastructure engineers evaluating Redwood Inference for platform-wide adoption. It synthesizes positioning, concise messaging, competitive differentiators for technical buyers, a deployable pitch-deck outline, pricing scenarios tailored to platform teams, a sample conversion script for pilot-to-production, and a short anonymized case study focused on integration and risk reduction.

Use: Sales engineers, solution architects, and GTM leads should use this document during discovery calls, pilot proposals, and executive briefings.

1) One-line and three-line value props

One-line: Redwood Inference gives platform teams a predictable, cost-aware inference runtime that standardizes LLM serving across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Unifies a single API and deployment model so your platform can standardize operators across teams.
- Optimizes for production economics with intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and deployment-aware routing to lower per-token costs without sacrificing latency SLOs.
- Ships with operational tooling (per-token traces, per-model dashboards, rollouts, and automatic fallbacks) to reduce incident surface area and migration risk.

2) Target audience and buyer personas

- Platform Engineer (primary): cares about standardization, SRE tooling, capacity planning, and predictable SLAs.
- ML Infrastructure Lead: cares about kernel selection, quantization profiles, and model lifecycle integration.
- Security/Compliance Engineer: cares about private control plane, KMS integrations, and audit logs.
- Product/Feature Owner: cares about unit economics, time-to-market, and quality regression protections.

3) Competitive brief (concise, technical)

Competitors considered: public LLM APIs, cloud-managed endpoints, and self-hosted inference runtimes.

- Public LLM APIs (ease vs control):
  - Strengths: fast time-to-value, simple API.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: opaque performance economics, limited private deployment options, and fewer operational controls for rollout and tracing.

- Cloud model endpoints / managed EC2-style services (scale vs ops):
  - Strengths: integration with cloud accounts, familiar billing.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: more custom glue required for batching/caching, inconsistent latency across model variants, and limited model-catalog performance tuning.

- Self-hosted inference runtimes (control vs maintenance):
  - Strengths: maximum control, potential lower cost at large scale.
  - Weaknesses vs Redwood: heavy ops burden, long iteration cycles for kernel/quantization tuning, and missing unified product/observability layer.
sections.heading: Three-line technical lead pitch

sections.body:
- Single operational plane: standard API + rollout controls across hosted/dedicated/private reduces long-term platform fragmentation.
- Cost-aware controls: automated batching + prefix/KV cache policies with dashboard-level unit economics.
- Production tooling: token-level traces, per-model SLIs, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to compatible model variants.
- Private deployment parity: same feature set and telemetry whether running hosted or on-prem.

4) Battlecard — objection/response quick hits

Objection: "We can self-host and save money."
Response: "At small-to-medium scale, self-hosted options incur hidden costs (engineering headcount, maintenance, kernel tuning). Redwood reduces total cost of ownership by combining runtime optimizations with a product surface for rollouts, tracing, and caching — accelerating time-to-value and reducing ops overhead. We provide transparent per-token reports so you can validate unit economics during pilot.

Objection: "We are concerned about data residency and compliance."
Response: "Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging. The private control plane mirrors the hosted feature set, so you do not trade observability for isolation.

Objection: "What if latency matters for small LLMs at high QPS?"
Response: "Redwood's runtime selects optimized kernels based on model shape and sequence distribution and offers dedicated GPU pools for predictable latency. We maintain latency SLOs and provide per-route latency breakdowns so you can tune batching vs SLO trade-offs.

5) Pitch deck outline (recommended 8 slides for technical buyer)

Slide 0: Title + Summarized Ask (pilot success criteria, target SLA, duration, sample QPS)
Slide 1: Problem statement for platform — fragmentation, cost unpredictability, and operational risk
Slide 2: Redwood solution overview — unified API + runtime + controls (diagram of hosted/dedicated/private parity)
Slide 3: Technical architecture (routing, batching, caching, KV store, model variants)
Slide 4: Operational story (dashboards, token-level traces, rollouts, SLI examples)
Slide 5: Pilot plan & success metrics (latency SLO, cost per 1M tokens, error rate, rollback criteria)
Slide 6: Pricing scenarios & sample math (see Pricing Scenarios section below)
Slide 7: Security & compliance checklist (network boundaries, KMS, auditability, certification status)
Slide 8: Next steps & integration asks (engineering contact, artifact list, timeline)

6) Pricing guidance + sample scenarios
sections.heading: Redwood differentiators to emphasize to platform buyers

sections.body:
- Redwood pricing components: hosted token usage (generation + embedding), dedicated monthly reserved capacity (per GPU cluster), and private deployment license + support.
- Typical levers: batching configuration, sequence-length budgets, quantization profile, and cache hit rate.

Sample scenario A — Proof-of-Concept (3 months)
- Target: 250 RPS peak, 20 tokens avg per request, expect 20M tokens/month
- Offer: Hosted pilot with usage cap + 2-week committed dedicated capacity trial
- Estimated bill (hosted): 20M tokens * $0.0008/token = $16,000/month (example illustrative rates)
- Support: onboarding + 8h/week SRE engagement included in pilot package

Sample scenario B — Platform pilot to Dedicated migration
- Projection: 1B tokens/month at 30 tokens/request, 400 RPS peak
- Options: Reserved Dedicated cluster (monthly commit) vs continued hosted at volume discounts
- Break-even: Model savings from batching/quantization typically pay for a medium dedicated cluster at ~500M–800M tokens/month depending on model family and quantization.
sections.heading: Pricing considerations for platform decision-makers

sections.body:
- Ask for your expected token mix (generation vs embedding) and sequence length distribution early.
- Validate cache-hit assumptions; a 20–40% prefix cache hit can materially reduce egress token costs.
- Discuss SLOs and required burst capacity. Dedicated clusters support burst policies to avoid overprovisioning.

7) Pilot-to-production conversion script (30-day cadence recommended)

Week 0: Kickoff & discovery
- Deliverables from prospect: sample workload traces, authentication plan, regulatory constraints, network topology diagram.
- Redwood deliverables: pilot environment, initial model catalog matching expected workloads, integration checklist.

Week 1: Integration & smoke tests
- Integrate auth (API keys or token exchange).
- Validate network connectivity for private/dedicated deployments.
- Smoke test with representative prompts and measure latency/throughput baselines.

Week 2: Tuning and observability setup
- Tune batching/windowing and prefix cache policies.
- Instrument token-level traces and SLI dashboards.
- Run quality checks vs golden prompt-sets to detect regressions.

Week 3: Load ramp & canary rollouts
- Gradually shift a small % of production traffic (5–10%) via canary.
- Monitor error budget, latency SLO, and cost per 1M tokens.

Week 4: Production cutover
- Execute full rollout or multi-stage expansion.
- Enable final redundancy/fallback policies and hand off runbooks to platform SRE.

8) Short anonymized case study — Acme Retail (platform integration)

Context: Acme Retail runs a centralized developer platform that exposes recommendation and search microservices. They needed unified inference across cloud regions and improved unit economics for recommendations.
sections.heading: Pricing nuance checklist to discuss during negotiations

sections.body:
- Pilot: 6-week pilot focused on recommendations reranker and contextual embeddings.
- Cost: realized a 28% reduction in per-token spend after enabling prefix caching and optimized batching.
- Reliability: platform reduced inference-related incidents by 60% in the first 90 days due to canary rollouts and automatic fallback to smaller model variants.
- Time-to-value: integration took 2 engineers ~3 weeks to reach production canary.
sections.heading: Outcome highlights

sections.body:
- Deployed Redwood Dedicated cluster in us-west-2, with private control plane for audit logging.
- Integrated KMS for model-encryption-at-rest and forwarded token-level traces into Acme’s centralized observability stack (Datadog).

9) Security FAQ for prospects (short, technical)

Q: Can Redwood run inside our VPC?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane that runs in your VPC or on-prem. Network egress is under your control, and private peering is supported for dedicated clusters.

Q: How is customer data encrypted?
A: Data is encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest. For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM for root keys. Access to logs and traces is role-based and can be shipped to your SIEM.

Q: Do you store prompt transcripts?
A: By default hosted telemetry stores anonymized traces for operational debugging. For customers requiring no telemetry persistence, Redwood offers telemetry exclusion options in Private deployments and controlled log retention policies.

Q: What compliance evidence is available?
A: Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II evidence and provides configuration checklists for customers to complete audits in Private deployments. Specific evidence bundles are shared under NDA.

Q: How do rollbacks and fallbacks work?
A: Rollouts are canary-based with automatic fallback policies. If a canary crosses configured SLO thresholds (latency/error), traffic is redirected to the previous model variant or a lower-cost compatible variant. Rollbacks are logged and auditable.

10) Integration checklist (developer-ready artifacts)

- Network diagram with allowed ranges
- Auth model selected (API key, OIDC integration, mTLS)
- Sample workload traces (.json) with timestamps and token counts
- Golden prompt set for quality/regression testing
- Compliance requirements (retention windows, audit frequencies)
- Target SLOs and error budgets

11) Appendix — sample CLI/test commands

payload.page_title: Security FAQ & RFP Guidance: What We Do (and Don’t) Say

sections.body:
This page is the canonical “guardrails” reference for Security FAQ and RFP responses. It exists to prevent over-commitment, inconsistent wording, and accidental promises (especially around compliance certifications, data residency, retention, and testing).

**Use this page when:**
- You are answering a security questionnaire or RFP.
- A prospect asks for a “simple yes/no” on a nuanced topic.
- You need approved phrasing that is accurate across **Hosted**, **Dedicated**, and **Private** deployments.

**Do not improvise** security/legal claims. If a question goes beyond the approved language below, use the escalation guidance at the end.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
1) **Describe what exists today; never promise roadmap.** If the customer asks “when,” reply with: “We can’t make commitments outside our product and contract. We can share current capabilities and discuss requirements with our team.”
2) **Be deployment-mode specific.** Many controls differ between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem). If you’re unsure which mode applies, ask.
3) **Avoid absolute statements** unless Legal/Security has approved them in the RFP library (e.g., “never,” “always,” “guarantee,” “fully compliant”).
4) **Evidence is gated.** SOC 2 reports, detailed pen test letters, and sensitive architecture details are shared via the evidence request process (typically under NDA).
5) **If the questionnaire is trying to force a “yes,” provide an accurate “alternate control” statement** and reference the exception policy.

---
sections.heading: Golden rules (read first)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood Inference maintains a SOC 2 Type II report. We can share the report under NDA via our evidence request process.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We can send it right now.” (Don’t bypass NDA / process.)
- “We are SOC 2 certified.” (SOC 2 is an attestation/report, not a certification.)
sections.heading: 1) “Can you share your SOC 2 report?”

sections.body:
**Do say (standard):**
- “By default, Redwood does not use customer prompts, completions, files, or embeddings to train or fine-tune foundation models.”
- “Customer content is processed to provide the service and may be handled by authorized personnel only as needed for security, abuse prevention, support, and reliability, subject to access controls and contractual commitments.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We never access customer data.” (Support/security access may occur under controls.)
- “We don’t store any data.” (Retention varies by configuration and telemetry/logging.)
sections.heading: 2) “Do you train models on customer data?”

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood is not currently ISO/IEC 27001 certified. We align our security program to widely adopted security best practices and have controls that map to ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A domains. We can discuss our control set and provide SOC 2 evidence under NDA.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We are ISO compliant.”
- “We meet ISO 27001 requirements.” (Unless certified; avoid implying certification.)

---
sections.heading: 3) “Are you ISO 27001 certified?”

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood maintains a SOC 2 Type II report covering relevant Trust Services Criteria (Security; additional criteria as scoped in the report).”
- “SOC 2 evidence is available under NDA; request via the SOC 2 evidence playbook.”

**Don’t say:**
- “SOC 2 certified.”
- “Covers all products and all regions.” (Scope is defined in the report; do not generalize.)

**Notes:**
- If the customer requests control-by-control mappings, route to GRC. Provide only approved mapping excerpts from the RFP library/claims matrix.

---
sections.heading: A) SOC 2 (Type II)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Not currently ISO 27001 certified; we can share how our controls map to key ISO domains (access control, cryptography, operations security, supplier relationships, incident management).”

**Don’t say:**
- “ISO compliant / certified / audited.”
- “In progress to certify by <date>.” (No timelines; no roadmap commitments.)

**Notes:**
- If a questionnaire requires a “Yes” for ISO certification, use the exception policy: provide an alternate statement + SOC 2 evidence path.

---
sections.heading: B) ISO/IEC 27001 (alignment vs certification)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Data residency depends on the selected deployment mode and region. We support region selection for applicable workloads and can discuss options for EU/US constraints.”
- “Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) provide the strongest residency control because the customer controls the network boundary and hosting environment (subject to the chosen architecture).”

**Don’t say:**
- “We guarantee all data stays in-country.” (Too absolute; depends on region, telemetry, and integrations.)
- “No data ever leaves the EU.” (Avoid absolutes; confirm actual data flows.)

**Notes / nuance to preserve:**
- Clarify *what* data the question refers to: customer content vs metadata/telemetry vs billing/support artifacts.
- If the prospect requests “EU-only support access,” escalate to Security/GRC and Legal (access controls + contractual terms).

---
sections.heading: C) Data residency (where data is processed/stored)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Retention depends on deployment mode and configuration. We provide documented retention and deletion behavior and, for enterprise plans, configurable retention options for certain logs.”
- “Upon contract termination or upon request (subject to contractual terms), Redwood supports deletion workflows and provides confirmation according to policy.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We retain nothing / zero retention.”
- “We delete immediately everywhere.” (Deletion can be asynchronous across systems/backups; keep wording accurate.)

**Notes:**
- Always reference the customer-facing retention overview for the latest approved specifics.
- If asked about backup retention and purge timelines, do not invent numbers. Escalate to GRC.

---
sections.heading: D) Data retention & deletion

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood encrypts data in transit using TLS and encrypts data at rest using industry-standard mechanisms.”
- “Key management approach depends on deployment mode; enterprise customers may have options for customer-managed keys (CMK) or KMS integrations in certain deployments.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We support HSM everywhere.”
- “Customers always hold the keys.” (Shared responsibility varies; only claim where explicitly supported/contracted.)

**Notes:**
- If the customer asks for “BYOK/HYOK” specifics, route to Solutions Engineering + Security for the correct deployment-mode answer.

---
sections.heading: E) Encryption (in transit / at rest) and keys (KMS/HSM)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood conducts regular security testing, including vulnerability scanning and penetration testing, and remediates findings according to risk-based SLAs.”
- “Pen test summaries/attestations can be shared under NDA where available.”

**Don’t say:**
- “Pen tests happen quarterly.” (Don’t state frequency unless approved and current.)
- “We can share the full pen test report.” (Often restricted; share via evidence process if approved.)

**Notes:**
- If a questionnaire asks for specific scanning tools or exact remediation timelines, use approved ranges from the RFP library or escalate.

---
sections.heading: F) Penetration testing & vulnerability management

sections.body:
**Use these definitions to avoid accidental misrepresentation:**
- **Customer content**: prompts, completions, uploaded files/attachments, embeddings, and customer-provided evaluation datasets.
- **Service data/telemetry**: metrics, logs, traces, and operational metadata (may include identifiers; avoid claiming it never exists).

**Do say:**
- “By default, Redwood does not use customer content to train or fine-tune foundation models.”
- “We may process customer content to provide the service and to maintain safety, reliability, and security, under access controls.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We don’t store prompts.” (Not universally true across modes/configs; refer to retention doc.)
- “We never look at prompts.” (Support/security exceptions may apply.)

**If asked about ‘model improvement’:**
- Approved response: “We may use aggregated and de-identified service metrics to improve performance and reliability. We do not use customer content to train foundation models by default.”

---
sections.heading: G) “No customer data used for training” (definitions and traps)

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood maintains a subprocessor list and will provide it through the standard procurement path.”
- “Subprocessors are assessed as part of our vendor risk management program.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We have no subprocessors.”
- “We can add your required vendor terms automatically.” (Legal review required.)

**Notes:**
- Any request for special subprocessor notice periods or custom audit rights should go to Legal (Finance & Legal process).

---
sections.heading: H) Subprocessors / vendors

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood supports regulated workloads through deployment and contractual controls; eligibility depends on the deployment model, scope, and the specific regulatory requirements.”
- “We can discuss requirements (including a BAA request) with our Security and Legal teams.”

**Don’t say:**
- “HIPAA compliant out of the box.”
- “We will sign a BAA for any product/use case.”

**Notes:**
- Treat BAA language as Legal-owned. Do not commit on calls or in writing without Legal approval.

---
sections.heading: I) HIPAA / BAA / regulated workloads

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood Private includes private deployment options; some customers deploy in isolated environments depending on architecture and requirements.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We support fully air-gapped deployments as a standard offering.” (Only state if explicitly validated for the specific deal.)
- “No external connectivity is required.” (Often untrue for updates, licensing, monitoring, support workflows.)

**Notes:**
- If a customer requires true air-gap, immediately escalate to Solutions Engineering + Product Security PM.

---
sections.heading: J) “Air-gapped” / on-prem claims

sections.body:
**Do say:**
- “Redwood provides audit logs for key administrative and access events. Export options (e.g., to customer SIEM/storage) depend on deployment and configuration.”
- “Retention options are available on enterprise plans; details are documented in the audit logging overview.”

**Don’t say:**
- “We log everything.”
- “All events are available via API in real time.” (Only claim features that exist.)

**Notes:**
- If a customer provides a required event list, validate against the audit log taxonomy and escalate gaps.

---
sections.heading: K) Audit logs, SIEM export, and retention

sections.body:
- “Certified” (unless referring to an actual current certification and within scope)
- “Compliant” (as a blanket statement)
- “Guarantee” / “always” / “never”
- “Meets all requirements of <framework>”
- “Air-gapped” / “zero trust” as marketing shorthand without specifics
- “No data stored” / “no logs” / “no access ever”

Use: “supports,” “provides,” “can be configured,” “subject to contract,” “within scope,” “depending on deployment mode,” “under NDA.”

---
sections.heading: Words/phrases to avoid (unless explicitly approved for that deal)

sections.body:
Escalate to the listed owner(s) if any of the following occur:
- The customer requests **SOC 2 report**, pen test letters, or other restricted evidence → **GRC (Olga Petrov / Daniel Carter)** via evidence request playbook.
- The customer asks for **contractual security commitments** (BAA, breach notification timelines, audit rights, indemnities) → **Legal (Michael Grant) + GRC**.
- The customer requires **country-specific residency guarantees** or “EU-only admin access” → **GRC + Security** (and EMEA reviewer for wording).
- The questionnaire forces a “Yes” that is not accurate → use the **questionnaire exceptions policy** and route to **GRC**.
- The question touches **roadmap / not-yet-shipped features** → **Product Security PM (Naomi Feldman)**.

**Fast path for Sales/SE:** If the deal is time-sensitive, tag the Security review escalation page owners and include (a) exact question, (b) customer-required wording, (c) deployment mode, (d) due date/time zone.

---
sections.heading: Escalation: when to stop and ask for review

sections.body:
- In RFP responses, cite the specific artifact version/date when referencing a Redwood security statement (example: “Redwood Enterprise Security FAQ (Last reviewed: 2026-02-10)”).
- Do not quote Slack messages or “tribal knowledge.” Use the Security FAQ, one-pagers, or RFP library as the source of truth.
- If you must deviate from standard language, follow the RFP approvals SOP and capture the deviation so it can be upstreamed to the claims matrix.

---
sections.heading: Versioning and citation guidance

sections.body:
**2026-02-14:** Refreshed ISO language to avoid implied certification; tightened data residency “no data leaves region” anti-claim; added standard phrasing for “no training on customer data” with support/security access nuance; aligned pen test wording to avoid fixed frequency claims.

---
sections.heading: Change log (summary)

sections.body:
- **Primary owner:** Product Marketing (Camila Reyes)
- **Security accuracy:** Security Engineering (Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei)
- **Compliance language & evidence:** GRC (Olga Petrov, Daniel Carter)
- **Contractual language:** Legal (Michael Grant)

If you see language in the field that conflicts with this page, file a request against the RFP library process and link the customer prompt/questionnaire item.

payload.page_title: SIEM-Ready Audit Export (Beta) — Security & Compliance FAQ (Sales Enablement)

sections.body:
This FAQ equips Sales, SE, and Security reviewers with consistent language for customer conversations about Redwood Inference’s **SIEM-ready audit export (Beta)**.

**What it is:** A feature-flagged capability that exports Redwood audit events to customer-controlled destinations for security monitoring, compliance evidence, and incident response.

**Beta integrations (initial):**
- **Splunk HEC** (HTTP Event Collector)
- **Datadog Logs intake**
- **Amazon S3 delivery** (object storage delivery for downstream ingest)

**Important:** This is a **beta** feature. See “Beta limitations and disclaimers” below for required customer-facing caveats.

---
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
Redwood can export audit events to a customer’s SIEM/log platform (Splunk, Datadog, or S3) with **at-least-once delivery**. Events include a stable **event_id** to support downstream deduplication. Exports support **configurable filtering**, secure secret handling, and operational visibility (export lag/health). Redwood retains audit logs for a limited period; customers should rely on their SIEM for long-term retention.

---
sections.heading: Summary you can use in customer-facing language (approved)

sections.body: The export includes **Redwood audit events** emitted by the Redwood control plane and supporting systems (e.g., authentication, RBAC policy changes, configuration changes, key administrative actions).
sections.heading: 1) What events are included in the audit export?

sections.body:
- **Authentication & session events** (e.g., login, SSO/SAML config changes)
- **Authorization / RBAC changes** (role assignments, permission changes)
- **Administrative configuration** (API keys, service accounts, workspace settings)
- **Security and compliance controls** (audit export configuration changes, credential rotations)
- **Platform operations** that are relevant for customer security monitoring (where applicable and policy-approved)

**Not included (explicit):**
- Customer prompt content, model inputs/outputs, or embeddings payloads
- Any customer-provided secrets
- Free-form request/response bodies that could introduce PII leakage

For the canonical field list and examples, reference: **Audit Event Schema v2 & SIEM Mapping**.
sections.heading: Typical categories include

sections.body: Audit Event Schema v2 is a canonical JSON structure with stable identifiers and consistent timestamps.
sections.heading: 2) What does a single audit event look like?

sections.body:
- **event_id** (stable unique identifier)
- **occurred_at** (event timestamp)
- **received_at / exported_at** (pipeline timing metadata)
- **tenant_id / workspace_id** (customer scoping)
- **actor** (user/service principal where applicable)
- **action** (what happened)
- **resource** (what the action was performed on)
- **result** (success/failure + reason when available)
- **source_ip / user_agent** (where applicable; may be absent for service-to-service events)

**PII minimization:** Fields are curated and redacted according to Redwood’s audit logging policy. If a customer requests additional fields, that request must go through Security review.
sections.heading: Common fields (high level)

sections.body: **At-least-once delivery.**
sections.heading: 3) Does Redwood support at-least-once, exactly-once, or at-most-once delivery?

sections.body:
- During downstream errors (timeouts, 4xx/5xx responses, throttling), Redwood will retry delivery with backoff.
- An event (or batch) may be delivered **more than once**.

**Customer guidance:** Deduplicate using **event_id** in the SIEM/indexing pipeline.

What we do **not** claim in beta:
- Exactly-once delivery
- Strict ordering across all events (ordering is best-effort; customers should use timestamps and event_id)
sections.heading: What that means

sections.body:
- The exporter checkpoints progress and retries transient failures.
- If delivery repeatedly fails beyond policy thresholds, batches may be moved to a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)** for operator attention and controlled replay.
sections.heading: At a high level

sections.body:
- A downstream outage may increase **export lag**.
- Once the downstream destination recovers, the exporter will catch up; customers may observe bursty delivery during recovery.
sections.heading: Operational behaviors customers should understand

sections.body:
In beta, Redwood’s goal is **durable export with at-least-once semantics**, with operational visibility into lag and failures.

However, customers must understand that:
- Export relies on Redwood’s audit log retention window for backfill/retry boundaries.
- For long-term retention and compliance archiving, customers should store events in their SIEM/object store.
sections.heading: 5) How does Redwood prevent data loss?

sections.body:
Customers can configure export filters to control which audit events are delivered. Filters are intended to support:
- Reducing noise
- Separating security-relevant events into a dedicated index/pipeline
- Meeting internal data minimization policies
sections.heading: 6) What filtering is supported?

sections.body:
- **Category allowlist/denylist**
- **Action allowlist/denylist**
- **Resource-type predicates** (where applicable)
- **Actor-type predicates** (e.g., user vs service)

**Important:** Redwood may enforce “safe defaults” and validation to prevent invalid/overly broad filters that could destabilize export performance.
sections.heading: Supported filter dimensions (beta)

sections.body: **Principle:** Redwood retains audit logs for a limited window to support operations and customer access; customers are responsible for long-term retention in their SIEM.
sections.heading: 7) What is Redwood’s retention policy for audit logs vs. the customer’s SIEM retention?

sections.body:
- Redwood provides audit log retention in-product for a defined period (contract/plan dependent).
- **Audit export is the mechanism for customers to store and retain audit events in their own systems** for longer durations, immutability, and internal policy compliance.
sections.heading: Customer-facing language (use this framing)

sections.body:
- Provide the contracted retention if known.
- If unknown, state: “Retention is plan/contract dependent; we can confirm in writing for your account.”

Do not guess retention durations in a security review unless confirmed for that specific account.
sections.heading: If a customer asks for exact numbers

sections.body: Yes—exports support a **backfill window** to replay recent historical audit events into a new destination or after filter changes.
sections.heading: 8) Does the export support backfill? What are the limits?

sections.body:
- Backfill is intended for **short, operational recovery windows**, not for rebuilding an entire year of history.
- Backfill limits are enforced to protect platform stability.

If a customer requires large historical backfills (e.g., multiple months), treat as **GA requirement** and route to Product (Naomi Feldman) and Security (Marcus Lin/Kevin Osei).
sections.heading: Beta guidance

sections.body: **Secrets are handled as sensitive and stored encrypted at rest.**
sections.heading: 9) How are audit export credentials handled (Splunk token, Datadog API key, AWS role/KMS)?

sections.body:
- Encryption at rest using Redwood-managed KMS controls for secret storage
- Strict RBAC for viewing/managing export configurations
- Redaction in logs (we do not log customer tokens/keys)
sections.heading: Controls (beta)

sections.body:
- **Splunk HEC:** customer provides HEC endpoint + token; Redwood uses TLS.
- **Datadog:** customer provides API key; Redwood uses TLS.
- **S3:** supports customer buckets with SSE (including SSE-KMS where configured). Cross-account delivery is supported via assume-role patterns where enabled.
sections.heading: Destination-specific notes

sections.body:
**In transit:** Yes. Audit export connections use HTTPS/TLS to destination endpoints.

**At rest:**
- Redwood stores audit events and export configuration data encrypted at rest per Redwood platform standards.
- For S3 delivery, customers can enforce bucket encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) according to their requirements.
sections.heading: 10) Is data encrypted in transit and at rest?

sections.body: Audit export is protected by least-privilege RBAC.
sections.heading: 11) What permissions/RBAC are required to configure or view audit exports?

sections.body:
- **Manage audit exports** (create/update/delete destinations, rotate credentials, change filters): restricted to **Org/Workspace Admin** or a dedicated **Security Admin** role.
- **View audit export status/health** (lag, last success, last error): allowed for **Admin** and optionally **Auditor/Read-only security roles**.

**Note:** Changes to audit export configuration are themselves audit-logged.
sections.heading: Typical model (may vary by tenant RBAC configuration)

sections.body:
- Export enablement status
- Per-destination health
- Export lag indicators
- Recent delivery errors (sanitized)

Internally, Redwood SRE/Telemetry also monitors:
- Lag metrics
- Retry/DLQ rates
- Adapter error rates
- Downstream throttling patterns
sections.heading: Customers can view

sections.body: Beta support is targeted at **Hosted + Dedicated** deployments.
sections.heading: 13) Which regions are supported? Does this help with data residency?

sections.body:
- Audit events are generated and exported from the customer’s Redwood tenant region (where applicable).
- Data residency ultimately depends on the customer’s chosen destination endpoints and bucket locations.
sections.heading: Region behavior (customer-facing framing)

sections.body:
- If a customer configures a destination endpoint in another geography (e.g., a global Splunk endpoint or cross-region S3 bucket), audit export will deliver there by customer choice.
- If strict residency requirements exist (e.g., EU-only), confirm destination endpoints and storage regions align to those constraints.
sections.heading: Important clarifications

sections.body:
**Not in beta.**

For Private/on-prem, export patterns may require:
- Customer-managed sinks and networking
- Restricted egress and allowlists
- Different secret management integrations

We can document likely approaches and roadmap, but we should not commit beta support.
sections.heading: 14) Is Redwood Private / on-prem supported?

sections.body:
Required disclaimers for customer conversations and written follow-ups:
- **Beta feature**: functionality and limits may change prior to GA.
- **At-least-once delivery**: duplicates possible; customer should dedup using **event_id**.
- **Best-effort ordering**: do not assume strict ordering; use timestamps and event_id.
- **Backfill is limited**: intended for operational recovery; not a bulk historical reconstruction tool.
- **Not for Private/on-prem in beta**.
- **Integration scope is limited**: Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs, and S3 only in beta.
- **No GA-grade SLA** for exports in beta; support is best-effort with defined on-call and escalation paths.
sections.heading: 15) What are the main beta limitations and disclaimers we must communicate?

sections.body:
- Redwood provides audit logging and export capabilities that support common evidence and monitoring controls.
- Customers are responsible for configuring their SIEM, retention, alerts, and review workflows to meet their internal control requirements.
- For formal assurance questions, route to Compliance (Olga Petrov) with the customer’s specific control language.
sections.heading: Recommended response

sections.body:
- Claiming audit export alone “ensures compliance”
- Committing to retention periods or event coverage beyond what is documented and contractually agreed
sections.heading: Avoid

sections.body:
Where applicable and policy-approved, audit events may include:
- **source_ip** and **user_agent** for user-initiated events (Console/API)
sections.heading: 17) What does Redwood log about end users (IP address, user agent)?

sections.body:
- Some events may not include IP/UA (e.g., internal service actors, proxying, or where upstream context is unavailable).
- Redwood follows PII minimization and redaction rules; we do not include payloads that are not required for audit/security purposes.
sections.heading: Caveats

sections.body: Yes. Export configuration and export pipelines are scoped to the customer’s tenant/workspace boundaries. RBAC and control-plane validation prevent one tenant’s configuration from affecting another tenant’s exports.
sections.heading: 18) Are audit exports tenant-isolated?

sections.body:
Yes. The Console supports a “test connection” style workflow (destination-dependent) and provides initial health/validation errors.

For Splunk and Datadog, common misconfigurations include:
- Wrong endpoint URL
- Invalid/expired token/API key
- Destination-side allowlists/firewalls
- Throttling/rate limits
sections.heading: 19) Can a customer “test” their destination before turning exports on?

sections.body:
- Additional SIEM destinations (e.g., syslog-style, other commercial SIEMs)
- Expanded filtering and routing options
- Enhanced residency controls and more explicit regional guarantees
- Private/on-prem support patterns
- More granular admin/auditor views and audit export reporting

Use: “We’re actively collecting requirements during beta to prioritize GA scope.”

---
sections.heading: Non-binding roadmap themes (do not promise dates)

sections.body:
- **Delivery guarantee:** “At-least-once; duplicates possible; use event_id to deduplicate.”
- **What is logged:** “Security-relevant control-plane actions and administrative events; not prompts/model payloads.”
- **Retention:** “Redwood retains logs for a limited period; your SIEM is the system of record for long-term retention.”
- **Encryption:** “TLS in transit; encryption at rest; secure secret storage; S3 supports SSE-KMS.”
- **Permissions:** “Only admins/security admins can manage export configs; changes are audit-logged.”
- **Regions:** “Export runs with your tenant; residency depends on destination endpoints/bucket region.”
- **Beta scope:** “Hosted/Dedicated only; Splunk/Datadog/S3; no Private/on-prem in beta.”

---
sections.heading: Talk tracks (quick answers)

sections.body:
- **Product scope / roadmap / beta cohort:** Naomi Feldman
- **Security semantics / PII / threat review:** Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei
- **Compliance language / questionnaires / evidence:** Olga Petrov
- **SLOs / incidents / operational readiness:** Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
