payload.page_title: Temporal Anomaly Hypothesis Framework and Dashboard Kit

sections.body:
Overview:

This page defines the Temporal Anomaly Hypothesis Framework (TAHF) and provides a reusable dashboard + alerting kit for investigating short- and medium-duration anomalies in platform telemetry (tokens/sec, tail latency, cache miss ratio, model swap rate, cost-per-token). The goal is to move operator investigation from ad-hoc firefighting to hypothesis-driven triage: formulate a small number of falsifiable hypotheses, run fast experiments/queries, and converge to mitigation actions within the first 30 minutes of an incident.

Motivation:

- Platform signals are high-cardinality and noisy; naive alerting produces noisy pages and long mean-time-to-detect/repair.
- Operators need a concise, repeatable workflow when faced with temporal anomalies (spikes, regressions, step-changes, slow-drifts).
- Provide a dashboard and query kit that supports quick A/B-style hypothesis checks and produces machine-readable evidence for postmortems.

Definitions and scope:

- Temporal anomaly: any unexpected deviation from baseline across a time window (seconds to hours). Examples: token request bursts, sudden tail-latency regressions, cache contention events.
- Baseline: rolling 7-day median + IQR by tenant-class (free/paid/enterprise) or by model-shard for internal services.
- Hypothesis: short declarative statement of a potential root/cause and a measurable prediction (e.g., "Spike is due to tenant X sending batched prefix requests; we expect per-tenant token rate to explain >60% of total delta").

High-level workflow (operator-facing):

1) Ingest alert and open the TAHF dashboard for the impacted region.
2) Immediately capture the top 3 candidate hypotheses using the template below.
3) Run the baseline checks (quick queries, widget correlation) to falsify at least one hypothesis within 10 minutes.
4) If none falsified, escalate to secondary investigator and enable targeted mitigations (rate-limits, temporary routing to variant model) within 20 minutes.
5) Log the final hypothesis and actions to the incident ticket and mark for postmortem input.

Hypothesis template (use in initial triage):

- Hypothesis ID: H1
- Statement: one-sentence cause hypothesis.
- Prediction: measurable numeric expectation and window (e.g., tenant X increase explains >= 60% of token delta in last 5m).
- Required queries/widgets: list of 2-4 metrics/queries to confirm/falsify.
- Confidence & next action: low/medium/high and immediate mitigation plan if confirmed.

Dashboard kit (widgets and recommended layout):

Top row - Incident snapshot (single-row summary widgets):
- Global delta sparkline (tokens/sec) vs 7d median (1m, 5m, 15m windows).
- Tail latency 99.9th percentile (ms) and delta percentage.
- Active model swaps/min and model-variant bleeding rate.
- Incidence score: weighted sum of token surge + latency surge + error rate (configurable weight table below).

Second row - Cardinated breakdowns (drill-down panels):
- By tenant class: tokens/sec and delta, top 10 tenants contributing to delta.
- By model-shard: requests/sec, cache-miss-rate, avg-kv-cache-evictions/min.
- By region/edge node: tail latency heatmap (per-az breakdown).

Third row - Hypothesis probes (quick queries to run):
- Tenants: per-tenant contribution query (example PromQL below).
- Prefetch/KV cache: eviction rate and prefix-cache-hit-rate.
- Batching: average batch size distribution and sudden shifts.
- Downstream services: third-party model-host latency and drop rates.

Operator alert rules (recommended starting set):

Rule 1: Temporal surge alert (short-window)
- Trigger: tokens/sec > baseline + 5 * IQR for 3 consecutive 1m buckets
- Severity: P2
- Operator action: open TAHF dashboard, capture hypotheses H1-H3, run per-tenant contribution query

Rule 2: Tail latency burst
- Trigger: p99.9 latency > 2x baseline for 3m and error-rate increase > 0.5%
- Severity: P1
- Operator action: verify model swaps, check CPU/GPU utilization on target pool, consider model-variant fallback

Rule 3: KV cache thundering
- Trigger: prefix-cache-eviction-rate > 250 evictions/min and cache-hit-rate drop > 20%
- Severity: P2
- Operator action: confirm eviction storms, enable per-tenant kv-cache backoff, assess prefix hotness

Example queries (Prometheus/Traces/SQL snippets):

- Per-tenant token contribution (PromQL):
  sum(rate(redwood_requests_tokens_total{job="runtime",region="us-west-2"}[1m])) by (tenant_id)
  --> sort_desc and show top 20, compare to global delta

- Cache miss ratio (PromQL):
  sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total[1m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_lookup_total[1m])) by (model_shard)

- Average batch size distribution (SQL over telemetry store):
  SELECT bin_size, count(*) AS requests FROM batch_events WHERE ts > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY bin_size ORDER BY bin_size DESC LIMIT 50;

Dashboard widget spec (text table):

- Widget: "Top contributing tenants" | Type: table | Query: per-tenant token contribution | Columns: rank, tenant_id, tokens_1m, delta_vs_baseline | Refresh: 30s | Owner: platform-telemetry
- Widget: "Model shard heatmap" | Type: heatmap | Query: p99 latency by shard, region | Color scale: linear | Owner: serving-runtime
- Widget: "Hypothesis checklist" | Type: text/checkbox | Content: three hypothesis entries with links to quick queries | Owner: platform-oncall

Config and thresholds (operator-tunable):

- Baseline window: 7 days (default)
- Short-window anomaly sensitivity: IQR multiplier (default 5)
- Hypothesis check deadline: 10 minutes from alert open
- Escalation deadline: 20 minutes

Ownership and contacts:

- Dashboard owner: platform-observability (pager: #oncall-platform-observability)
- Primary incident owner for temporal anomalies: platform-operator-runbook (oncall rotation)
- Model-fallback owner: eng-serving-runtime (separate escalation)

Operator runbook (triage checklist) - execute in order:

1) Confirm alert validity:
   - Check for recent configuration changes (deploys, kernel switches) in the last 30 minutes. Query: deploy_events{service=~"runtime|allocator"} and correlate.
2) Snapshot evidence (first 5 minutes):
   - Save top-20 per-tenant token list, p99.9 latencies by shard, and active model swap count. Attach to ticket.
3) Run hypothesis probes (10 minutes):
   - H1: Tenant-driven surge? Run per-tenant token contribution and look for a top tenant explaining >60% delta. If yes, apply tenant soft-rate-limit and monitor.
   - H2: Model-variant regression? Verify model-variant BLEED and run comparison queries across variants. If confirmed, route to fallback variant.
   - H3: Cache storm / prefetch hotness? Inspect prefix-cache-eviction-rate and batch-size distribution. If confirmed, enable conservative prefetch backoff.
4) Apply minimal blast-radius mitigation first (15 minutes):
   - Prefer targeted tenant limits, model-variant routing, or temporary regional throttling over global changes.
5) Escalate to SRE/Serving Runtime if mitigation not effective within 20 minutes.

Post-incident artifacts (what to attach to ticket):

- Hypotheses tried and outcomes (use the template).
- Saved dashboard snapshot urls and raw query outputs.
- Operator play-by-play timestamps (actions taken and times).
- Suggested follow-ups for retrofit automation or alert tuning.

Retrospective guidance (to be included in postmortem):

- Label incident with dominant signal (tokens/latency/cache/other).
- Evaluate whether the IQR multiplier or baseline window needs tuning for this tenant-class.
- Capture additional instrumentation gaps and add instrumentation tickets (examples: per-prefix hotness metric, per-batch-id trace).
- If human mitigation was required repeatedly (>2 incidents in 30 days), create a small engineering project for automated mitigation.

Roadmap and next steps (quarterly):

- Q2 2026: Add per-prefix clustering on dashboard and automated candidate-tenant-suggestion for triage.
- Q3 2026: Integrate TAHF checklist into incident response UI and allow one-click mitigations (soft-rate-limit, variant-route).
- Q4 2026: Build a supervised classifier for anomaly type (tenant vs. model vs. cache) to reduce manual hypothesis count.

Appendix - Quick links and snippets:

- Runbook template (copy): /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/operator-scenario-playbooks-template
- Telemetry queries: saved query set "TAHF - quick probes" in Grafana (folder id: platform-tahf)
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: Dedicated Throughput SLO Dashboards (Tier-aware) — Specification

sections.body:
This page specifies the dashboards and supporting instrumentation needed to monitor the Dedicated Throughput SLO. The dashboards are tier-aware (Standard / Plus / Premium) and designed to:
- Track per-customer throughput floor adherence over the SLO measurement window.
- Surface saturation and overload signals early (before SLO impact).
- Provide fast drilldowns from “SLO at risk” → “why” → “what to do next” (links to runbooks).

Primary audience: SRE oncall, Observability, Infra/Fleet, and Product Dedicated.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Provide a single “Dedicated Throughput SLO Overview” dashboard that answers:
   - Which Dedicated deployments are currently below their committed throughput floor?
   - Which are trending toward an SLO miss (burning error budget fast)?
   - Are issues isolated (one customer/region) or systemic (shape/cluster/pool)?

2) Provide a per-customer / per-deployment dashboard that answers:
   - What is the committed throughput floor and how is it measured?
   - Is the miss due to Redwood capacity/runtime (queueing, GPU saturation, admission control) vs customer-side exclusions (throttling, invalid usage patterns, unsupported model/version)?

3) Make tier posture visible:
   - Premium expected to have stronger headroom + failover posture; dashboards must make that observable (warm pool status, spare capacity, failover events).
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Replacing customer-facing reporting in Console (Console will consume a subset of these signals with additional filtering/aggregation).
- Building a full capacity planning UI (see capacity model and Fleet tooling).
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Primary: `tokens_per_second` attributed to `deployment_id`.
- Measurement uses generated tokens for text/chat routes, counted consistently for streaming and non-streaming.
- Aggregate throughput is computed from monotonic counters (preferred) to avoid sampling artifacts.

**Important:** Streaming token accounting must use “token emitted” counters, not “chunk count”. (See bug history: double-counting in early streaming instrumentation.)
sections.heading: Canonical throughput metric

sections.body:
- SLI: `actual_tps / committed_tps` over defined windows.
- Primary compliance window for operational tracking: 5m and 30m (fast detection) plus 7d/28d for reporting.
- Dashboard panels should expose both:
  - “point-in-time floor adherence” (last 5m)
  - “error budget burn indicators” (multi-window burn rate)
sections.heading: SLO signal used in dashboards

sections.body:
Dashboards assume the following metric labels exist (or will be added as part of ENG-19244/ENG-19302):
- `deployment_id` (Dedicated deployment identifier; stable)
- `customer_id` and `customer_name` (internal only; avoid exposing in any public dashboards)
- `tier` (standard|plus|premium)
- `region` (e.g., us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-central-1)

- `route` (chat.completions, responses, embeddings, rerank, etc.)

sections.body:

- Exported as time series or queryable lookup:

sections.body:

**Runbook links (top nav):**

sections.body:
**Purpose:** Account-focused view used by SRE, CS escalation support, and Solutions (internal).

**Inputs:** customer_id/customer_name (required); optional region, deployment_id.

**Panels:**
1. **Committed vs Actual Throughput (timeseries)**

3. **SLO Exclusion Signals (diagnostic)**

4. **Latency and Queueing**

5. **Admission Control / Overload**

6. **Fleet/Infra signals**

**Action section:**

sections.heading: Burn rate (multi-window)

sections.body:
These panels exist to identify risk before throughput floor violation.

**Primary early signals (most actionable):**
- `queue_time_p95` rising while GPU util near ceiling → capacity contention.
- `shed_rate` > 0 → admission control engaged; floor at risk for lower tiers first.
- `gpu_mem_util_p95` near 95% + higher context lengths → risk of OOM/fragmentation; watch for fallbacks.
- `avg_batch_size` falling while request rate steady → runtime inefficiency/regression.

**Secondary signals (diagnostic):**
- Increased `tokens/request` (prompt length changes) can reduce TPS; highlight changes.
- Model version changes (rollout annotations) correlated with efficiency drop.

payload.page_title: SLO variance stabilization and dashboard primer

sections.body:
Overview

This primer describes a repeatable approach for identifying, stabilizing, and visualizing SLO variance across the LLM inference platform. It covers: how variance arises, investigative workflows, dashboard patterns for rapid operator triage, and a lightweight stabilization playbook for short-to-medium term remediation. The goal is to reduce noisy SLO flips, shorten oncall burn, and produce clear operator signals for capacity and quality workstreams.

Key definitions

- SLI: observed measurement (latency, availability, correctness).
- SLO: target for an SLI (example: 99th percentile latency <= 250ms).
- Variance: sustained or transient movement in an SLI distribution that increases SLO burn without actionable root cause.
- Noise: high-frequency small changes that falsely trigger alerts.

Why SLO variance matters for LLM inference

- Tokenized workloads produce heavy outliers (longer sequences, multi-turn chat) which inflate tail latencies.
- Auto-scaling and burst routing introduce non-stationary capacity.
- Model swaps/rollouts change compute characteristics; small changes in prompt distributions can change token counts and decoding costs.
- Instrumentation sampling and aggregation windows can mask bursts or amplify noise.

Detecting variance early: signals to watch

1) Burst patterns in SLO burn curve that do not line up with other system-level metrics (GPU utilization, queue depth).
2) Discrepancies between tokenized cost metrics and raw request counts.
3) Cross-region divergence: same tenant has different SLI behavior in another region.
4) Increased correlation of tail latency with specific model variants or with prefix-cache misses.

Dashboard patterns (recommended panels)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- SLO burn timeline (1h/6h/24h windows) with annotation band for rolling deploys.
- Token-rate vs request-rate heatmap to reveal shifting token distribution.
- 99th/95th/50th latency series per model-variant (stacked small multiples).
- Prefetch/KV-cache hit ratio and average KV lookup time.
- Queue depth and per-tenant priority-slice occupancy.
- Operator action timeline (manual evictions, model swaps, scale events).
sections.heading: Top-level dashboard (single-screen for paging)

sections.body:
- Sampled request trace table (columns: timestamp, tenant, model, seq_len, prefix_hit, decoding_ms, serving_node).
- Cold-start/warm-start marker overlay.
- Correlation matrix: SLO burn vs GPU throttling, host OOMs, network errors.
- Histogram: sequence length distribution comparing current window vs baseline.
sections.heading: Investigation view (linked from top-level)

sections.body:
- Quick filter for affected tenants.
- Toggle to switch between token-normalized and request-normalized views.
- Runbook link and one-click PagerDuty escalation button.

Recommended telemetry and query examples
sections.heading: Operator-friendly widgets (search/filterable)

sections.body:
- request.count (tags: tenant, model_variant, region, priority)
- request.tokens.total and request.tokens.prompt/completion
- serve.latency.decode_ms (percentiles + exemplar traces)
- kv_cache.hit and kv_cache.miss (per-tenant)
- queue.depth and queue.wait_ms
- gpu.utilization and gpu.sched_delay_ms
- deploy.rollout_id and operator.eviction_event (annotation metrics)
sections.heading: Metrics to collect (minimally)

sections.body:
- 99th latency per model:
  quantile_over_time(0.99, serve_latency_decode_ms_bucket{job=\"runtime\", model_variant=~\".*\"}[1h])
- Token-normalized 99th:
  (quantile_over_time(0.99, serve_latency_decode_ms_bucket[1h]) / avg_over_time(request_tokens_total[1h])) * 1000
- SLO burn (5m sliding):
  sum(rate(serve_latency_slo_violation[5m])) / sum(rate(request_count[5m]))

Alert design guidance

- Use multi-signal rules: require both SLO burn rate > threshold AND one secondary signal (queue depth > X OR token-rate spike > Y) to reduce noise.
- Use graded notifications: page on sustained burn (>= 15m) or large single-interval burn spike (> 3x baseline).
- Suppress alerts during scheduled rollouts using rollout_id annotation windows.
- Provide actionable alert text with immediate triage steps and links to the investigation view.

Stabilization playbook (15–90 day cadence)

Short-term (minutes–hours):
1) Throttle noisy tenants using soft-priority reduce (operator tool).
2) Route affected requests to a compatible lower-cost model variant (fallback policy) to buy time.
3) Increase sampling rate for traces for the affected window.
4) Open a P0 incident if burn persists beyond 30 minutes with growing SLO debt.

Medium-term (days–weeks):
1) Reconcile token accounting: ensure token-normalized SLO panels are visible to product and platform.
2) Adjust autoscaler warmup parameters to reduce oscillation (min replicas, startup_probe tuning).
3) Run A/B on compiler/kernel switch if runtime patching is suspected.
4) Add targeted prefetch cohorts for high-variance tenants.

Long-term (weeks–quarters):
1) Model onboarding checklist: require per-sequence-length perf profile and SLO impact test.
2) Kernel and quantization profiles gated by SLO sensitivity matrix.
3) Tenant-level budgeting and higher-fidelity throttles tied to billing signals.

Runbook: immediate triage steps (operator-facing)

1) Confirm: check SLO burn dashboard and cross-check region and model-variant panels.
2) Fetch exemplar traces for top 10 violating requests (use trace-explorer or trace_id list).
3) Check for recent deploys (deploy.rollout_id) and operator actions.
4) If token spike: switch dashboard to token-normalized view; share findings on incident channel.
5) If queueing: check per-node eviction logs and reassign tenant to alternate pool if available.
6) Apply soft-priority throttle for the tenant for 5–30 minutes and observe burn response.
7) If mitigated, file a stabilization ticket with owners (platform infra + tenant product team).

Post-incident retrospective template (to be filed after stabilization)

- Incident summary (1 paragraph).
- Timeline (5m resolution for first 60 minutes, 15m thereafter).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
- Short-term mitigations applied and effectiveness.
- Medium/long-term actions and owners with due dates.
- Learnings for model onboarding and SLO definitions.

Dashboard maintenance and ownership

- Dashboard steward: platform-observability (primary) and runtime-team (secondary).
- Monthly checklist:
  - Validate exemplar traces sampling rate.
  - Verify alert thresholds against rolling 90-day baseline.
  - Confirm annotation pipeline is capturing deploys and operator events.
  - Run synthetic scenarios (prefetch miss, token spike) quarterly.
sections.heading: PromQL examples (Grafana/Prometheus)

sections.body:
| panel_id | title | refresh | primary_owner | query_hint |
| P1 | SLO burn (1h/6h/24h) | 15s | platform-observability | slo_burn_rate() with rollout annotations |
| P2 | Token-rate vs request-rate heatmap | 30s | runtime-team | rate(request_tokens_total[1m]) / rate(request_count[1m]) |
| P3 | 99/95/50 latencies by model-variant | 15s | runtime-team | quantile_over_time(...) |
| P4 | KV-cache hit ratio by tenant | 30s | cache-service | sum(kv_cache_hit) / sum(kv_cache_hit + kv_cache_miss) |
| P5 | Queue depth and eviction events | 15s | platform-allocator | rate(queue_depth[1m]) and operator.eviction_event |

(Panel table above should be copied into the dashboard metadata when creating the Grafana dashboard.)

Acceptance criteria for stabilization work items

- Reduce false pages by >= 60% for the affected alert channel over a 30-day window.
- Maintain SLO compliance within 1.5x of baseline tail for 90 days post-change.
- Ensure token-normalized and request-normalized SLO views are reconciled in the next oncall rotation.

Appendix: useful CLI and queries

- Fetch top traces (pseudo-CLI):
  rtxctl traces query --start=now-1h --end=now --filter=\"slo_violation:true\" --group-by=model_variant --limit=50

- Soft-priority throttle example (operator API):
  curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN\" https://api.internal.redwood/v1/tenants/THX-123/actions \\
    -d '{"action":"set_priority", "priority":"soft_reduced", "duration_minutes":30 }'

- Example alert text (template):
  [PAGING] SLO burn exceeded for runtime service in region {{region}}
  Symptoms: 99th latency spike, queue depth rising, token-rate above baseline
  Immediate actions: 1) Check traces dashboard 2) Apply soft-priority throttle 3) Verify recent rollouts
  Links: {{dashboard_url}} | {{runbook_link}}

Notes and known caveats

- Token-normalized views require correct instrumentation upstream; partial coverage will produce misleading normalization.
- Some model variants have non-linear decoding characteristics (e.g., sampling-based decoding) which appear as high variance—treat these specially in onboarding.
- Avoid aggressive autoscaler reaction to short token bursts; prefer smoothing windows aligned to SLO windows.

Contacts and escalation path

- Primary: platform-observability (pager: #platform-oncall)
- Secondary: runtime-team (pager: #runtime-oncall)
- Escalation: SRE manager on-call if incident remains P0 after 60 minutes.

Related artifacts

- Model onboarding performance checklist (link to models page).
- KV-cache consistency playbook.
- Token-cost attribution spec.

This document should be used as the baseline for any new dashboard or alert related to SLO variance. If you make changes to panels or thresholds, add an entry to the dashboard changelog and notify the platform-observability mailing list.

payload.page_title: Asynchronous Telemetry Gating and Traffic-Shed Strategy for Platform Observability

sections.body: This document defines Redwood’s standard for adaptive telemetry gating and traffic-shed behavior for the platform control plane and inference runtime. The goal is to preserve actionable observability while bounding ingest cost and avoiding monitoring-induced cascades during high-load or failure modes. It applies to all platform telemetry producers: runtime agents, API gateways, dedicated pool controllers, and customer-facing routers.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Telemetry itself can become a source of load (high-cardinality traces, heavy span emission, verbose debug logs).
- During incidents, uncontrolled telemetry growth increases downstream latency, bloats storage, and can worsen customer-facing SLOs.
- We need a deterministic, reversible way to reduce telemetry volume while retaining critical signals for remediation and postmortem.
sections.heading: Why this matters

sections.body:
- Gate: a configurable, runtime-enabled rule that reduces or transforms telemetry emitted by a service (example: drop non-error traces, reduce sampling rate, redact high-cardinality fields).
- Shed: temporary, automatic reduction of inbound request traffic to downstream consumers (eg. metrics pipeline, trace collector) under overload conditions.
- Tiered signal categories:
  - Critical signals: errors with customer impact, core SLO breaches, control-plane state changes (must be preserved).
  - Operational signals: high-resolution latency histograms, traces used for triage (preferred to preserve but can be throttled).
  - Diagnostic signals: debug logs, verbose span details, high-cardinality fields (can be gated aggressively).
sections.heading: Scope and definitions

sections.body:
- Owner: eng-platform (primary), eng-sre (secondary) — responsible for global gating policies and tooling.
- Service owners: each service must implement the standard client libraries and honor gating decisions (see rollout checklist).
- Observability infra: observability team operates the ingest-side policies (collector, samplers, retention) and provides dashboards to track gating impact.
sections.heading: Ownership and teams

sections.body:
- Control-plane API p95 latency: target <= 120ms, SLO 99.5%/30d
- Inference routing 99th percentile token latency: target <= 400ms, SLO 99%/30d (customer-facing)
- Telemetry pipeline ingestion lag: target <= 30s, alert if > 60s for 5m
The gating system must reduce telemetry ingest to keep pipeline ingestion lag under alert threshold.
sections.heading: SLOs and thresholds we protect

sections.body:
- Instrumented service -> local SDK (adaptive sampler + gate client) -> agent/collector -> central router -> storage/analysis systems
- Central control plane exposes runtime gate decisions via: 1) feature flag push (repos: ff-proxy), 2) pub/sub control topic (kafka/arn), 3) HTTP pull endpoint for low-latency overrides.
sections.heading: High-level architecture (text diagram)

sections.body:
1. Circuit-grade safety: if the collector reports ingestion-backpressure or high-lag, central controller triggers a conservative shed across all agents (global "emergency-shed" policy).
2. Priority preserving: always preserve Critical signals even during emergency-shed.
3. Graceful degradation: drop Diagnostic signals first, then progressively reduce Operational signals (e.g., reduce trace sampling from 10%->1%->0.1%).
4. Scoped application: policies can be applied by namespace, service, environment (prod/stage), or by tenant (priority tenant slicing).

Policy examples (JSON examples shown as pseudo-config in docs):
- Global emergency-shed policy (applied when pipeline_lag > 60s for 2m):
  - preserve: ["error_events", "control_plane_state_change"]
  - traces_sample_rate: 0.001
  - log_level_min: "WARN"
  - redact_fields: ["user_input.text", "request.headers.x-session-id"]

- Cost-conservative day policy (non-incident):
  - preserve: ["error_events"]
  - traces_sample_rate: 0.02
  - log_level_min: "INFO"
sections.heading: Runtime behaviors and priorities (ordered)

sections.body:
- Ingestion lag alert:
  - promql: |
     max_over_time(collector_ingestion_lag_seconds[5m]) > 60
  - alert: CollectorIngestLagHigh (SEV-3)

- High-cardinality trace volume (example query):
  - promql: |
     sum(rate(trace_spans_emitted_total[1m])) by (service) > 1000
  - action: consider reducing per-service sample rate
sections.heading: Collector-side thresholds (PromQL examples)

sections.body:
- SDK reads latest gate config from local cache; fallback to last-known-good config if controller is unreachable.
- When gate indicates reduced sampling, SDK must apply deterministic sampling (hash-based) for traces and metrics to preserve reproducibility in rollouts and debugging.
- SDK provides a local override API for operator e2e tests (disabled by default in prod).

Operational runbook: when alerts indicate telemetry/backpressure issues:
1. Pager: CollectorIngestLagHigh -> notify oncall observability and eng-platform on same page.
2. Triage: observe pipeline lag, check broker (kafka) lag, and verify collector CPU/IO.
3. If lag persists > 5m, engage global emergency-shed:
   a. Open Gate Console (internal: /gate-console) and enable emergency-shed (automated button).
   b. Confirm preserve list contains "error_events" and "control_plane_state_change".
   c. Apply redaction rules for any PII fields discovered in active logs.
4. Route: notify service owners of each top contributor (via top_n by emitted_spans metric).
5. After stabilization (lag < 30s for 10m), progressively relax gates in reverse order and monitor for recurrence.
sections.heading: Local SDK behavior (must be implemented by service owners)

sections.body:
- Collector ingestion lag (time series, 1h/6h/24h) with alert band overlay.
- Emitted spans by service (top 20) with per-service sample rate.
- Storage ingress bytes per hour and projected 30d burn-rate estimate.
- Emergency-shed state timeline (annotation stream).
- Critical-signal delivery rate (sanity check that critical signals are still flowing).
sections.heading: Dashboard panels and queries to include (minimum)

sections.body:
- SEV-1 (system-wide pipeline outage): page oncall (paging window per incident policy), eng-platform lead, SRE director.
- SEV-2 (sustained ingestion lag > 60s): page observability oncall + service owners for top contributors.
- SEV-3 (spike in trace emission from a single tenant): notify affected service owner and customer success if customer impact suspected.

Rollout checklist for services (must be completed before a service goes to prod):
1. Integrate Redwood telemetry SDK and feature-flag client (library: telemetry-client v2.4+).
2. Add unit tests for deterministic sampling behavior.
3. Add config UI hints in service manifest (annotations: telemetry.policy).
4. Run staged canary for 72 hours in staging env with sample_rate=0.02 and verify dataset quality.
5. Sign-off from eng-sre and observability.
sections.heading: Alert routing and escalation

sections.body:
- Scenario A: burst of 10x trace volume from a non-critical background job. Verify emergency-shed triggers and critical signals persist.
- Scenario B: persistent moderate increase in cardinality. Measure cost delta and tune day-policy sampling.

Post-incident analysis and metrics to capture in retrospectives:
- Time to detect: time from first lag metric > 60s to emergency-shed activation.
- Time to stabilize: time from shed activation to ingestion lag < 30s.
- Lost signal analysis: number of traces/logs dropped per category; note any missing critical signals and root cause.
sections.heading: Testing and verification exercises (gamedays)

sections.body:
- Deterministic hashing for sampling must use stable seed per deploy to avoid churn across restarts.
- Redaction must be applied before any externally-shared telemetry to guard PII.
- Producers must not embed unbounded high-cardinality fields in span attributes; these should be mapped to tags with cardinality guards.

Appendix: quick CLI and API examples
- Check current global gate state (curl):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATE_TOKEN" https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/gates/global/state

- Force enable emergency-shed (for runbook use only):

payload.page_title: Regional failure-mode mapping and observability patterns

sections.body: This document catalogs observed failure modes by region, prescribes a set of reusable observability patterns and dashboard templates, and defines alerting and escalation defaults to keep cross-region inference availability within SLOs. It is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and oncall responders operating Redwood’s hosted and dedicated regions.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
This page defines a structured approach to mapping regional failure modes (network, capacity, dependency, and control-plane regressions) to specific observability patterns, dashboard templates, and alerting thresholds. It captures:

- canonical metric sets for LLM inference services (runtime, queueing, cache hit-rate)
- dashboard views for triage (region health, tenant impact, degradations)
- per-failure-mode alert rules with severity and oncall routing
- remediation runbook pointers and rollout guidance for dashboards/alerts
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: Regional incidents are often similar on surface (elevated latency) but have different root causes and therefore require different mitigations. Standardizing how we observe, alert, and route reduces mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to repair (MTTR) and makes cross-region failover decisions more reliable.
sections.heading: Why this matters

sections.body:
- Scope: Hosted API regions, Dedicated region routing tiers, cross-region control plane. This document does NOT cover customer-local Private deployments (see eng-private-deployments).
- Document owner: eng-platform (platform-observability team).
- Oncall owners: eng-sre for region-level escalation; serving-runtime for kernel/interference issues.
sections.heading: Scope and ownership

sections.body:
1) Network fabric degradation
   - Symptoms: increasing p95/p99 egress RTT, packet drops on node-level NICs, increased retry rates in edge proxies
   - Typical root causes: provider network congestion, BGP flaps, vSwitch driver regression, peering misconfiguration

2) Local GPU saturation or interference
   - Symptoms: rising per-GPU utilization, kernel retries, higher generation tail-latency only for long-context requests
   - Root causes: noisy neighbor jobs, kernel scheduling bug, degraded cooling causing thermal throttling

3) KV/prefix cache collapse
   - Symptoms: drop in cache hit-rate, sudden increase in model re-computation token/sec, correlated cost-per-token spike
   - Root causes: cache TTL misconfiguration, eviction storms after cache rebuild, rollout that changes key format

4) Load-balancer / routing misconfiguration
   - Symptoms: skewed request distribution across nodes, hotspots, some tenants seeing 502/504 while overall cluster throughput is nominal
   - Root causes: lb hash change, routing policy update, service mesh sidecar failure

5) Control plane or autoscaling failure
   - Symptoms: inability to scale up worker pools, queued requests backpressure, scaling requests stuck in provisioning state
   - Root causes: quota exhaustion, provisioning API errors, image registry latency

Canonical metric sets (recommended for all region dashboards):

- Frontend/edge: requests/sec, 5xx rate, p50/p95/p99 latency (in ms), connection error rate, retries/sec
- Router/LB: per-node qps, route skew (% of traffic per instance), active connections, time-to-first-byte
- Serving runtime: tokens/sec, token-latency p50/p95/p99, batch-size distribution, kv-cache-hit-rate, kv-cache-latency
- GPU & host: GPU_utilization, GPU_memory_free_bytes, kernel-oa-errors, host_cpu_iowait, host_net_dropped_packets
- Queues & throttles: queue_length_by_priority, head_request_age_seconds, backpressure_events
- Cost signals: estimated_token_cost_per_minute, cache-miss_token_count
sections.heading: Failure-mode taxonomy (high level)

sections.body:
1) Region Overview (one-line health):
   - Top row: SLO health (availability %, error budget burn), region capacity utilization (GPU pools used / total), request qps
   - Middle: latency heatmap (per-model and per-route), cache hit-rate trend, queue depth by tenant tier
   - Bottom: dependency sprocket - external registry / KMS / storage latency and error rates

2) Degradation Triage (for oncall):
   - Focused drill-down for a single symptom (e.g., p99 tail latency increase) with correlated graphs: GPU temp/thermal events, kv-cache hit-rate, router skew, infra network RTT
   - Prebuilt LogQL and trace queries for quick filters (examples below)

3) Tenant Impact Lens:
   - Table of top-25 impacted tenants by error rate, latency regression, and cost impact (estimated tokens lost). Allows quick decision to apply tenant QoS or reroute.
sections.heading: Dashboard templates (to be installed per-region)

sections.body:
- Correlation-first rows: graphs should be paired with correlated dependency signals (e.g., pair p99 latency with kv-cache-hit-rate and gpu_utilization).
- Percentile deltas: show delta from 1h and 24h baseline for p95/p99 to highlight sudden regressions.
- Token-normalized cost: include cost-per-token post-cache to detect hidden cost spikes when cache collapses.
- Error bloom detectors: run a service-level Bloom filter that counts distinct error signatures over 15m to avoid alert storms from identical underlying root-causes.
sections.heading: Reusable observability patterns (implementation notes)

sections.body:
Table: (as text)

- Sev P0 (SLO at risk or customer-facing outage):
  - Trigger examples: availability below 99.5% for 5m (region-wide), total token throughput drop >30% with error rate >2%
  - Pager: eng-sre primary + serving-runtime secondary
  - Runbook: region outage runbook

- Sev P1 (Degradation that affects SLOs soon):
  - Trigger examples: p99 latency > configured threshold for 10m AND cache-hit-rate drop >20%
  - Pager: oncall platform engineer
  - Runbook: degradation triage runbook

- Sev P2 (Operational anomaly / noise):
  - Trigger examples: single-node GPU thermal events, LB 5xx increase confined to <5% instances
  - Pager: slack alert to #platform-ops, only escalate if persists >30m
sections.heading: Alerting defaults and severity mapping

sections.body:
1) Region-wide cache collapse (example):
expr: (sum by(region)(llm_kv_cache_hit_total{job=\"runtime\"}) / sum by(region)(llm_kv_cache_requests_total{job=\"runtime\"})) < 0.60
for: 10m
labels: severity = \"P1\", team = \"platform-observability\"
annotations: summary = \"{{ $labels.region }} KV cache hit-rate below 60% for 10m\"

2) Tail latency escalation (example):
expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by(instance, le)(rate(llm_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 2.0
for: 5m
labels: severity = \"P1\"
annotations: summary = \"99th percentile request latency > 2s on {{ $labels.instance }}\"
sections.heading: Alert rule examples (Prometheus/SigV4 style)

sections.body:
- Region outage runbook: steps to suspend non-critical tenants, enable burst capacity, and trigger cross-region failover. Key checks: control-plane API health, autoscaler event log, image-pull errors.
- Cache collapse triage: verify key namespace format, TTLs, recent deployment events; look for coordinated cache warmup traffic causing eviction storms; consider controlled cache-priming sequence.
- GPU interference mitigation: identify noisy tenants via per-tenant batch-size distribution, evict suspect jobs to isolated maintenance pool, and if necessary migrate to dedicated-capacity pool.
sections.heading: Runbook pointers (quick links and steps)

sections.body:
- Logs (LogQL):
  {app=\"runtime\", region=\"us-west-2\"} | json | status_code >= 500 | count_over_time(5m)

- Traces (example):
  Service: runtime.v2 -> shows spans for request.router -> scheduler -> kernel.exec -> kv.lookup. Look at kv.lookup latency distribution to rule out cache impact.
sections.heading: Quick diagnostic queries (examples)

sections.body:
1) Authoring: create local dashboard in grafana/editor using the Region Overview template. Add instance selectors and permission groups.
2) Staging: add to the staging region and run through a synthetic traffic scenario (see runbooks/gameday tests). Confirm queries are performant (panel query run-time < 2s).
3) Review: request review from platform-observability and eng-sre (two reviewers).
4) Publish: promote dashboard to production region and register under dashboards catalog with ownership metadata and maintenance window.
sections.heading: Dashboard rollout and change process (how-tos)

sections.body:
- Dashboards must include an explicit owner (team and person) and a maintenance cadence. Dashboards without owner or updates for > 12 months will be flagged for archival.
- Alert rules must have a documented runbook link and a severity rationale. Unjustified P0/P1 rules will be downgraded after review.
sections.heading: Governance and deprecation rules

sections.body:
1) High p99 latency but normal cache hit-rate
   - Check GPU utilization and kernel error counters
   - If single-node: cordon node and drain; move traffic via lb -> notify infra to investigate noisy neighbor

2) High latency with low cache hit-rate
   - Check recent deployments that touch cache key formats
   - If eviction storm: temporarily increase cache size or add controlled priming job

3) Region 5xx spike with router skew
   - Verify lb config change (last 30m) and routing policies; rollback if necessary
   - Apply targeted tenant QoS to protect SLOs

Post-incident analysis checklist (to include in retrospectives):

- Record timeline of metric inflection points (p95/p99, cache hit-rate, queue depth)
- Map to recent changes (deployments, infra updates, policy changes)
- Identify missing signals that would have reduced MTTD (add instrumentation)
- Update dashboard templates and add new alert rules if needed

Appendix: sample Grafana dashboard JSON snippet (minified example)

{\n  \"meta\": {\"name\": \"region-overview-template\", \"owner\": \"platform-observability\"},\n  \"panels\": [\n    {\"title\": \"Region SLO Health\", \"type\": \"stat\", \"targets\": [\"sum(slo_availability{region=\\\"$region\\\"})\"]},\n    {\"title\": \"KV Cache Hit Rate\", \"type\": \"timeseries\", \"targets\": [\"sum(rate(llm_kv_cache_hit_total[5m])) / sum(rate(llm_kv_cache_requests_total[5m]))\"]}\n  ]\n}
sections.heading: Oncall play actions by symptom (cheat-sheet)

sections.body:
- Platform-observability (primary): #platform-ops, oncall rotation via PagerDuty (team handle: PD:platform-observability)
- Eng-SRE (escalation): #eng-sre-oncall, PD:eng-sre
- Serving-runtime (secondary): #serving-runtime, PD:serving-runtime
sections.heading: Contacts and escalation matrix

sections.body:
Q: How do we pick p99 thresholds per region?
A: Start with historical 99th percentile baseline over last 90 days and add 25–40% headroom depending on tenant mix. Revisit quarterly and after major model upgrades.

Q: When should we opt for cross-region failover versus burst-capacity?
A: Prefer burst-capacity if the root cause is transient (e.g., capacity pressure) and latency remains within degraded SLO. Failover is preferred for persistent control-plane outages or when data residency and tenant isolation allow it.

payload.page_title: platform-telemetry-cost-playbook-for-product-engineering-2026

sections.body:
Title: Platform telemetry & cost playbook for product engineering

Summary
This playbook is for product engineering teams building user-facing features on top of Redwood’s inference platform. It defines a shared vocabulary, dashboard and alert patterns, cost-attribution signals, and a step-by-step investigation and action workflow that balances product quality, latency SLOs, and operational cost. The goal is to give product teams a practical, repeatable route to evaluate cost impact, iterate safely, and engage platform/ops when needed.

Who should use this doc
- Product engineers and PMs shipping LLM-backed features
- Engineering managers reviewing rollout economics
- Platform operators who will be contacted for escalations

When to use it
- Pre-launch: establish telemetry baselines and cost budgets
- During rollout: monitor early token/latency anomalies and cost spikes
- Post-rollout: reconcile actual spend, tagging, and retention windows

Key principles
- Measure close to the cost surface: attribute at the token, route, and model-variant level where possible.
- Prioritize product-level KPIs first (perceived latency, error rate), then cost as a secondary constraint with explicit budgets.
- Safety-first alerts: alert on potential customer impact, not raw dollar movement. Use cost alerts for ops and cadence reviews.
- Make tradeoffs auditable: keep canonical query definitions and dashboards in the platform repo.

Required ownership and contacts
- Product engineering: owns feature instrumentation, route labels, and baseline queries.
- Platform Observability: maintains the canonical cost dashboards and sampling manifests.
- Finance/Cost Ops: provides monthly reconciliation and tagging rules.
- Oncall: SRE/Platform oncall is the escalation target for automated cost controls.

Definitions and canonical signals
- token_count: total generated tokens per request (server-side counter).
- token_cost_estimate: derived metric = token_count * model_unit_cost + runtime_overhead.
- route_id: logical API route or product feature label.
- model_variant: the exact model/version / quantization profile used for inference.
- latency_p50/p95/p99: standard latency quantiles measured at front-door and runtime.
- error_rate: HTTP 5xx + model mis-invocation rate.

Dashboards to create (minimum viable set)
1) Product cost rollup (per-week, per-route)
   - Key panels: total token_count, token_cost_estimate, top-10 routes by spend, spend trend vs. budget.
   - Filters: route_id, team, region, model_variant.
2) Quality vs cost scatter (per-route)
   - X axis: token_cost_estimate per request, Y axis: perceived latency (front-door p95), point size = request volume.
   - Purpose: find high-cost low-value outliers.
3) Real-time token surge watch
   - Stream panel: 1m token_count, 5m rolling token_cost_estimate, anomaly band (expected ±2σ).
4) Model-variant economics matrix
   - Table: model_variant | avg token_count | avg token_cost_estimate | p95 latency | error_rate | last_deployed_by

Dashboard implementation notes
- All dashboard panels must reference canonical PromQL/SQL named queries (store queries in telemetry/query-definitions repo).
- Use consistent timezones (UTC) and sample windows: 1m for real-time, 1h/24h for trends.
- Provide drilldowns to raw traces and a canonical Kibana/Trace link.

Alerting patterns and thresholds
- Product-impact alerts (paged to product + oncall):
  1) p95 front-door latency increases > 40% vs baseline AND error_rate > 0.5% sustained 5m.
  2) Route-level request drop > 20% with no upstream deployment in last 10m.
- Cost-awareness alerts (email/Slack to product + cost-ops):
  1) 24h spend for route > 2x expected daily budget AND token_cost_estimate growth rate > 50% 12h.
  2) Sustained model_variant cost per request > baseline + 30% for 6h.
- Automated mitigation actions (must be gated by an `operator_reauth` flag and runbook):
  - soft-throttle route to 80% traffic to force degrade safely
  - route fallback to cheaper model_variant (see safe-fallback checklist below)

Investigation and response workflow (step-by-step)
1) Triage (product engineer) — 0-15m
   - Validate alert: check dashboard, compare against baseline windows (previous 7 days).
   - Correlate with deploys: query CI/CD tag and model release events.
   - Run a quick per-user sampling query to determine per-customer impact.
2) Contain (product engineer + platform oncall) — 15-45m
   - If cost spike is due to runaway requests: apply a rate limit or quota at the ingress.
   - If due to model degradation producing longer token outputs: apply a soft-model swap to the cheaper variant (see safe-fallback checklist).
   - Document commands and actions in the incident channel.
3) Stabilize (platform) — 45m-3h
   - Execute a controlled canary swap on a small shard of traffic. Monitor quality regressions using predefined eval prompt set.
   - If stable, scale the fallback; if not, revert and open an investigation.
4) Reconcile (product + finance) — 1-7 days
   - Run full cost attribution, update budget estimates, and identify long-term mitigations (prompt engineering, batching, cache).

Safe-fallback checklist (must be completed before automated fallback)
- Confirm model_variant compatibility: identical tokenizer and prompt contract.
- Verify evaluation set: run 50 synthetic prompts and validate BLEU/ROUGE or product MP metrics.
- Confirm no new PII/data-routing constraints for fallback variant.
- Notify stakeholders (product, security, customer-success) via preconfigured channel.
- Record fallback as a short-lived feature flag with owner and rollback window.

Sample runbook commands (examples only)
- Inspect top spenders:
  SQL: SELECT route_id, SUM(token_count) as tokens, SUM(token_cost_estimate) as cost FROM telemetry.requests WHERE ts > now() - interval '24 hours' GROUP BY route_id ORDER BY cost DESC LIMIT 25;
- Trigger soft throttle (CLI):
  ./platform-ctl routes throttle --route=my-feature --limit=80% --reason="cost-spike-2026-02-03" --owner=product-oncall
- Canary swap (CLI):
  ./platform-ctl rollout model-swap --route=my-feature --from=redwood/gptx-quant-8bit --to=redwood/gptx-fp16 --canary=5% --monitor=/dashboards/model-variant-eval

Telemetry and tagging checklist (pre-launch)
| Field | Required | Purpose | Owner |
|-------|----------|---------|-------|
| route_id | yes | logical product surface | product eng |
| team | yes | cost rollups | product eng |
| customer_id | recommended | top-customer attribution | product eng |
| model_variant | yes | accurate unit economics | infra/platform |
| experiment_id | recommended | A/B cost impact | product eng |
| retention_tier | yes | trace/log retention policy | platform |

Common root causes and mitigations
- Root cause: prompt changes causing longer generations
  - Mitigations: add max_tokens cap, introduce model-side length heuristics, evaluate prompt templating.
- Root cause: traffic shift from a partner causing burst of requests
  - Mitigations: add per-tenant soft quotas, burst credits, and route-level throttles.
- Root cause: abrupt model-version change with higher token churn
  - Mitigations: require pre-deploy economic smoke tests and a canary stage with cost hooks.

SLOs and budgets (recommended defaults)
- Product-level latency: p95 front-door <= 600ms for interactive features; stricter targets for sync UIs.
- Incident escalation budget: product owners must be notified for any >25% daily budget overshoot.
- Monthly experiment cost budget: any A/B experiment must have an upfront cost cap and an automatic kill threshold.

Playbook for product onboarding (2-week checklist)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Define expected routes and assign route_id.
2) Draft provisional cost budget and add to project PR.
sections.heading: Week 0 (planning)

sections.body:
1) Instrument route_id and model_variant tagging in requests.
2) Add sample queries for dashboard panels to telemetry/query-definitions.
3) Run a 24h smoke test with synthetic traffic to record baselines.
sections.heading: Week 1 (integration)

sections.body:
1) Configure alerts for product-impact and cost-awareness thresholds.
2) Add runbook stub and assign a named oncall owner for first 72h post-launch.
3) Schedule a postmortem + budget reconciliation meeting at day 7.

Appendix: example Slack escalation template
Channel: #prod-my-feature-ops
sections.heading: Week 2 (go-live and guardrails)

sections.body:
"ALERT: Route my-feature exceeding 2x daily budget. p95 latency = $LATENCY, token_rate = $TOKEN_RATE, top-customer = $TOP_CUSTOMER. Actions taken: soft-throttle applied (80%), canary fallback initiated. Paging: @platform-oncall @product-owner. Runbook: <link>."

References and links
- Canonical queries repo: git.company.internal/telemetry/query-definitions
- Cost dashboard template: /dashboards/product-cost-rollup-template
- Safe-fallback operator runbook: /runbooks/safe-model-fallback

Change log
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft and product sync (Priya Nanduri).
- 2026-01-18: Added safe-fallback checklist and alert thresholds (Marcus Lee).
- 2026-02-03: Published with onboarding checklist and runbook examples (Alyssa Chen).

Contact
For questions or to request a dashboard template, contact: priya@redwood.ai or open a ticket in #observability-requests.

payload.page_title: Technical Health Sentinel: Enterprise Post-Provision Monitoring & QBR Feed Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
=======
This playbook defines the Technical Health Sentinel (THS): a prescriptive set of telemetry monitors, smoke checks, and QBR signal extractions that Customer Success (CS) uses for enterprise post-provision monitoring (first 90 days + quarterly health reviews). THS is intended to catch operational, performance, and quality regressions before they impact the customer and to provide a repeatable set of artifacts and dashboards for QBRs.

Goals
-----
- Detect regressions in availability, latency, correctness, and cost within 1 business hour of occurrence.
- Provide a structured triage path to resolve common classes of customer-impacting issues within SLOs.
- Standardize QBR inputs so CS and Product can make data-driven decisions.

When to use this playbook
------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- All enterprise customers during the 90-day post-provision window.
- Any Dedicated or Private deployment cutoff (when handing over to customer ops).
- Ongoing QBR preparation for customers with >$5k/month spend or latencies close to SLO.

Definitions and ownership
-------------------------
- THS Owner: Customer Success (Primary) — Maya Chen (authored).
- Technical Escalation: Eng-SRE (secondary) — Pager rotations in #oncall-redwood.
- Model/Quality Escalation: Applied ML & Evals team.
- Observability & Dashboards: Eng-Platform owns instrumentation.
- Data retention for QBR artifacts: Finance/Legal policy defines how long telemetries can be stored, default 18 months.

High-level workflow
-------------------
1. Post-provision (days 0–14): enable THS baseline monitors and run onboarding smoke tests.
2. Stabilization (days 15–90): monitor trends, perform weekly health reviews, fix configuration/backfills.
3. Handover / QBR (day 90 and quarterly): produce QBR packet with THS extracts and recommendations.

Automated sentinel monitors (recommended list)
----------------------------------------------
We recommend creating these monitors in the customer’s telemetry workspace (or forward via telemetry-gatekeeper):
- Availability check (heartbeat) — frequency: 30s; threshold: missing 3 samples -> P1 alarm.
- Request error rate — window: 5m; P99 target: < 0.5% (critical if > 1.5% for 5m).
- Tail latency (95th/99th) — window: 5m; thresholds: 95p > 350ms for hosted small models or > 700ms for long-context models -> P2.
- Token-level throughput / saturation — window: 1m; alert when GPU utilization > 88% and queue length grows > 12 requests.
- Model quality delta (eval set drift) — daily job comparing baseline eval set (seeded prompts) -> trigger when BLEU/ROUGE/metric drops > 4 points or human-quality score drops >10%.
- Cost per 1k tokens anomaly — daily; notify on >30% variance vs baseline 7-day median.
- KV cache hit rate — window: 15m; target: depends on workload, recommend > 60% for chat-heavy prefixes; alert if < 40% and latency increases.
- Telemetry forwarding lag — window: 5m; alert if event lag > 2m (indicates tracing / ingestion problem).

Alert severity mapping
----------------------
- P1 (customer-visible outage): availability fail, persistent error rate >5% for 15m, or model-serving API returning 5xx for >10% of requests. Assign to Eng-SRE tower.
- P2 (degradation): tail latency exceeded, cost spike, or quality regression in golden set; owner: Customer Success + Eng Platform.
- P3 (informational): telemetry lag, non-impacting config drift. Owner: Customer Success.

Pre-go-live health gates (checklist)
-----------------------------------
Run these before the customer is marked "go-live" in the billing system:
1) Smoke traffic test — ramp to 2x expected peak for 10m with synthetic prompts (document payloads).
2) Model correctness gate — run golden prompt set (example: 100 prompts) and compare aggregated pass rate vs baseline (>92%).
3) Latency SLO verification — 95p latency under target for 30m sustained.
4) Telemetry sanity — traces, logs, and metrics flowing; sample trace includes request id, model version, node id.
5) Failover drill — force a single-node outage and validate automatic fallback to warm pool within 60s.
6) Billing & quotas check — verify token accounting matches expected.

Playbook: Common scenarios and triage steps
-----------------------------------------
Scenario A: Latency spike on customer route
1. Confirm alert and scope: check route_id, model_version, region.
2. Validate ingestion: Confirm no ingestion lag (telemetry lag monitor).
3. Check GPU & host metrics: utilization, memory errors, host load. Command examples:
   - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l route=<route_id>
   - query: sum(rate(gpu_utilization[1m])) by (instance)
4. Verify KV cache hit rate and batching behavior; if hit rate drops, identify cache-miss prefix regression.
5. If hosts saturated and autoscale not triggering, run: rwdctl scale --route <route_id> --delta 2 (Eng-Platform only).
6. If root cause is model variant change, rollback to previous pinned model_version via console or API.
7. Communicate to customer: status update within 15 minutes for P1/P2.

Scenario B: Quality regression detected by eval harness
1. Confirm regression on seeded prompts and a random sample of live requests (sanitized).
2. If reproducible, pin traffic to previous model variant immediately and open a ticket to Applied ML.
3. Run localized A/B (5% traffic) comparing outputs and log label for failed prompts.
4. Produce QBR-quality artifact: sampling of 30 representative failures + 5 human annotations.

Scenario C: Unexpected cost anomaly
1. Validate anomaly: cross-check billing pipeline and usage catalyst (7-day median).
2. Check client-side changes: prompt length, new embeddings/long-context usage, and new batch jobs.
3. If runaway jobs present, temporarily apply quota hold at route level and notify customer.
4. Reconfigure batching or suggest quantization profile (Eng-Platform assisted).

Escalation & communication templates
----------------------------------
sections.heading: Use THS for

sections.body:
- T+0–15m: Acknowledge to customer via designated channel (Slack/email) with immediate mitigation steps.
- T+15–60m: Cause analysis summary and expected ETA.
- T+60m+: Regular updates every 30–60m until resolved.
- Post-mortem: deliver within 3 business days for P1; 7 business days for P2.

Template: initial customer message (P1)
"We’ve detected an availability issue impacting your inference route <route_id>. Our mitigation team is engaged; we’ve rerouted traffic and are working on a fix. We will follow up within 15 minutes with an ETA. Contact: Maya Chen (CS), Eng-SRE oncall."

Observability artifacts & queries (examples)
-------------------------------------------
Prometheus/Datadog example queries you should include in the shared dashboard:
- 95th latency: p95(api_request_duration_ms{route_id=\"<route_id>\"})
- Error rate over 5m: increase(error_count{route_id=\"<route_id>\"}[5m]) / increase(request_count{route_id=\"<route_id>\"}[5m])
- Token cost: sum(rate(token_emitted_total{route_id=\"<route_id>\"}[1m])) * cost_per_token
- KV cache hit rate: sum(kv_cache_hits{route_id=\"<route_id>\"}) / sum(kv_cache_lookups{route_id=\"<route_id>\"})

Example alert JSON (ingestable by gatekeeper)
---------------------------------------------
{
  "name": "THS - High 95p latency - <route_id>",
  "expr": "p95(api_request_duration_ms{route_id=\\\"<route_id>\\\"}) > 350",
  "for": "5m",
  "severity": "P2",
  "owners": ["customer-success:maya.chen", "eng-platform:oncall"]
}

QBR feed and required metrics
----------------------------
sections.heading: Use the following cadence and channels

sections.body:
- Executive summary (1 page): availability, cost delta, net customer impact.
- Key metrics (30/90/365 day views):
  - Availability (percent uptime), target: 99.95% for hosted; 99.9% for Dedicated.
  - 95p / 99p latency by route and model.
  - Error rate (5m and 30d rolling).
  - Cost per 1k tokens and trend delta vs prior quarter.
  - Quality regressions count and triaged outcomes.
- Recent incidents and status of action items.
- Recommendations: batching, cache tuning, suggested model quantization, or Dedicated capacity increase.

Dashboard export checklist (what to attach)
- Time-range: include 30-, 90-, and 365-day graphs.
- Raw samples: 200 sample request/response pairs with PII removed (sanitization script included below).
- Alert history: print last 90 days of alerts with state changes.

Sanitization script (python snippet)
-----------------------------------
sections.heading: Prepare the following artifacts for every QBR packet

sections.body:
import json, re
PII_KEYS = ["email", "ssn", "phone", "credit_card"]
pat = re.compile(r'\\b\\w+@\\w+\\.\\w+\\b')

def sanitize(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: ("<REDACTED>" if k in PII_KEYS else sanitize(v)) for k,v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [sanitize(x) for x in obj]
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        return pat.sub('<REDACTED_EMAIL>', obj)
    return obj

Operational handoff & runbooks
------------------------------
- Day-90 handoff package must include: route configuration export, pinned model_version, telemetry dashboard links, escalation contacts, and artifact bundle (sanitized samples + eval results).
- Handoff checklist: owner signs off that remaining action items have owners and due dates.

Template: Day-90 Handover checklist (table)
- Route config export: yes/no
- Golden set baseline: attached
- Alerts enabled: list
- SLOs documented: yes/no and values
- Cost controls: quotas set (amount)

Known limitations & caveats
--------------------------
- Quality regression detection relies on seeded prompt sets — novel prompts from end-users may still cause silent regressions.
- Telemetry sampling rates may omit cold-start anomalies; we recommend 100% sampling for first 24 hours post-go-live.
- Private deployments with restricted networking may delay telemetry; adjust lag thresholds accordingly.

Appendix: Quick links & contacts
--------------------------------
- Oncall channel: #oncall-redwood (Slack)
- Incident creation: /inc create (internal CLI)
- Telemetry gatekeeper doc: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts
- CS leads: maya.chen@redwood.com, diego.alvarez@redwood.com

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-10: Initial draft (Maya Chen).
- 2026-01-22: Added KV cache guidance and cost anomaly playbook (review: Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-02-15: Finalized QBR feed list and added templated alert JSON (published).

Acknowledgements
----------------
Thanks to Eng-SRE (Jordan Blake) and Eng-Platform (Priya Nair) for monitoring requirements and thresholds.

payload.page_title: Alert Context Enrichment and Priority Scorer Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook describes the priority scoring algorithm and enrichment pipeline used by platform on-call operators to triage, classify, and act on cross-service degradation alerts. It covers the data inputs to the scorer, the threshold matrix for severity buckets, recommended operator actions for each bucket, dashboard queries, and automated remediation policies.

Intended audience:
- Platform operators
- Observability engineers
- SREs on-call for inference-router, batcher, and cache services
- Product owners responsible for SLOs

Goals and scope:
- Make alert severity predictable and repeatable across regions and tenants.
- Surface business impact (cost, affected customers, token loss) alongside technical signals.
- Provide deterministic operator steps for each priority to reduce cognitive load.
- Apply only to alerts that originate in the platform telemetry pipeline: inference-router, kv-prefix-cache, batcher, model-variant-router, and platform-sidecar.

Key concepts:
- Priority score: numeric 0-100 computed per alert. Higher == greater urgency.
- Impact signals: token-rate-loss, success-rate-drop, latency-tail-95 delta, tenant-count-affected, estimated-dollar-loss-per-hour.
- Confidence signal: corroboration across telemetry sources (traces, logs, metrics).
- Priority buckets: P1 (>=85), P2 (65-84), P3 (40-64), P4 (<40).

Priority scorer inputs (enrichment pipeline):
1) Raw alert payload: alert_name, service, region, metric, observed_value, threshold, query_id.
2) Correlated traces: sampling of trace IDs tagged by alert query.
3) Recent incident history: incidents for same service in last 72h.
4) Tenant impact lookup: mapping of active tenants and their SLA tier (free/standard/premium).
5) Cost model estimator: converts token loss or extra compute to USD/hr.
6) User-facing feature map: list of product features tied to the impacted route (ex: streaming-chat, embeddings).

Scoring heuristic (human readable):
- Base = normalize(metric_delta) * 40
- Tenancy multiplier = min(1 + 0.15 * premium_tenants_impacted, 1.6) * 25
- Cost signal = sigmoid(estimated_usd_loss_hour / 100) * 15
- Confidence bonus = (corroborated_sources / 3) * 10
- Recurrence penalty = +10 if incident_count_last_72h >= 2
- Final = clamp(Base + Tenancy + Cost + Confidence + Recurrence, 0, 100)

Severity buckets and immediate operator actions:
- P1 (>=85) — Immediate paging, run emergency playbook:
  1) Page on-call (pager duty): platform-core-P1
  2) Attach top 5 traces to incident, run "model-swap-preflight" if model-serving variant is failing
  3) Trigger auto-fallback to compatible model-variant if configured (see automatic-fallback policy table below)
  4) If latency tail-95 > SLO by >300ms, enable fast-path routing (route small requests to regional-cache)
  5) Create incident in incident tracker, tag with tenants impacted and estimated cost.
- P2 (65-84) — Operator attention during shift, potential canary rollback:
  1) Create a channel and add service owner, SRE and product owner
  2) Run diagnostic queries (examples below) and collect full stack traces
  3) If token loss estimate > $200/hr or >50 premium tenants, escalate to on-call lead
  4) Prepare canary rollback or model variant swap, but do not execute without approval
- P3 (40-64) — Investigate during normal rota, file RCA if unresolved after 24h:
  1) Validate signal (ensure not synthetic or scheduled maintenance)
  2) Run correlation notebook and check KV cache hit-rate, prefix-cache pressure, and scheduling queue depth
  3) If verified, open a maintenance ticket for dev-owner to address
- P4 (<40) — Informational, no immediate action required:
  1) Attach to weekly dashboard for trend analysis
  2) Auto-close alert after 4h if no escalation

Example diagnostic queries (Grafana / PromQL):
- Latency tail-95 delta for inference-router (5m):
  sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/generate|/v1/chat"}[5m])) by (le)
- Token throughput loss (per cluster):
  sum(rate(tokens_produced_total[1m])) by (cluster)
- KV prefix cache miss storm indicator:
  increase(kv_prefix_cache_evictions_total[5m]) > 100

Automatic remediation policies (safe-by-default):
- model-fallback-policy (table):
  | condition | action | safety | owner |
  |-----------|--------|--------|-------|
  | model-ooms >= 3 in 10m | swap to quantized-variant | automated | eng-serving-runtime |
  | tail-latency > 2x SLO and confirmed cache-miss | enable regional-cache-prefetch | automated, rate-limited | eng-platform |
  | token-loss > 100k tokens/min and premium-tenants>10 | throttle non-premium traffic 20% | automated with cooldown 10m | eng-platform |

Dashboard and alert templates to inspect (links):
- Platform impact dashboard: grafana/platform/impact-summary
- Tenant exposure heatmap: grafana/platform/tenant-exposure
- Cost drift dashboard: grafana/platform/cost-drift
- On-call context snapshot (generated per alert): /dashboards/alert-context/{{alert_id}}

Alert payload example (JSON forwarded to scorer):
{
  "alert_id": "a1b2c3",
  "service": "inference-router",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "metric": "request_duration_ms_p95",
  "observed": "1250",
  "threshold": "700",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-03T02:14:00Z"
}

Operator checklist for P1 (step-by-step):
1) Acknowledge the page in PagerDuty and set the incident priority to SEV1.
2) Grab the auto-generated context URL and verify impacted tenants and estimated cost.
3) Attach top-5 traces (click "collect traces") to the incident.
4) If model-ooms or GPU errors appear in logs, run: 
   $ rwdctl model swap --from current --to fallback-quantized --region us-west-2 --dry-run && rwdctl model swap --from current --to fallback-quantized --region us-west-2 --confirm
5) If high tail-latency with cache misses: enable cache-prefetch for the affected prefix:
   $ rwdctl cache prefetch --prefix /v1/chat --region us-west-2 --rate-limit 500
6) Notify CS if >50 premium-tenants impacted and create a customer comms stub.
7) Keep incident channel open and post updates every 15 minutes until mitigated.

Post-incident duties and retrospective triggers:
- Create an RCA within 48 hours if incident classified P1 or P2.
- Run the priority-scorer sensitivity test: replay the alert through historical telemetry for last 90 days and confirm bucket assignment.
- If false-positive or noisy P3/P4, add suppression rule to the alert-router with expiration.

Operational metrics for the scorer itself (SLOs for observability):
- False escalation rate <= 5% (monthly)
- Mean enrichment latency <= 8s (95th <= 12s) from alert ingestion to score published
- Corroboration coverage >= 70% for P1 alerts

Maintenance and tuning playbook:
1) Monthly: review tenant weightings and cost model coefficients with product and finance.
2) Quarterly: run a sensitivity analysis and publish suggested coefficient edits.
3) After every on-call rotation: operator should flag misclassifications in the shared spreadsheet: /team-wiki/alert-classification-feedback

Ownership and escalation contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-platform-observability (on-call alias)
- Secondary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager alias)
- On-call lead: Priya Nair (pager)
- Incident commander rotation: see /team-schedule/oncall-rotation

Open questions and known limitations:
- Current cost estimator is calibrated for CPU/GPU price points from 2025; large hardware price changes need coefficient updates.
- Cross-region tenant deduplication can inflate tenant counts when traffic bursts replicate across regions; there's an open ticket ENG-PLATFORM-847 to address it.

Appendix: quick tuning knobs (operators only):
- config/env PRIORITY_BASE_SCALE (default 40)
- config/env TENANCY_MULTIPLIER_CAP (default 1.6)
- config/feature auto_fallback_enabled (true/false), cooldowns are enforced at API-gateway layer

Related docs and templates:
- See: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/platform-operator-snapshot-and-rollback-patterns-2026 for snapshot patterns
- Alert template: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/incident-signal-playbook-dashboard-library-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Ava Chen
- 2026-01-25: Incorporated feedback from Diego and Samir; added example rwdctl commands
- 2026-02-03: Finalized scoring coefficients and published as canonical playbook

payload.page_title: Token Cost Attribution and Explainable Trace Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:

This playbook documents the platform approach for token-level cost attribution and explainable traces through the inference stack. It defines dashboards, alerts, queries, and a step-by-step investigation and mitigation runbook for token-cost anomalies and regressions. The goal is to provide deterministic, auditable explanations for cost changes down to request and model-variant level so product teams and SREs can act quickly.

Why this matters:
- Token costs are the dominant operational variable for LLM inference. Small per-token regressions compound quickly.
- Root causes often cross layers: prompt changes, model variant selection, batching configuration, KV cache misses, or routing fallbacks.
- Observability that ties tokens -> request metadata -> model variant -> runtime path is required for targeted remediation and accurate customer billing.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: Platform SREs, Runtime Engineers, Cost Ops, Product owners for high-volume endpoints.
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated inference paths; Private deployments should mirror instrumentation via the same schema. Does NOT include offline training costs.

Definitions:
- token_event: single emitted token record including model_variant, request_id, client_key, latency_bucket, cost_unit.
- explain_trace_id: deterministic id connecting an HTTP request through routing, batching, and GPU execution shards.
- effective_cost_per_token (ECPT): normalized cost metric after batching and amortized KV cache credit.

High-level design:
1) Instrumentation: insert token_event emitters at two points: (a) post-generation in the runtime (per-token metadata), (b) router/gateway that records request metadata and selected model_variant. Both share explain_trace_id.
2) Aggregation pipeline: events flow to Kafka -> materialized into a short-term OLAP (ClickHouse) and long-term cube (Druid/BigQuery) for cost analytics.
3) Dashboards: a set of Grafana panels that join request metadata and token_event aggregates to produce explainable cost breakdowns.
4) Alerting: SLO-driven alerts for delta in ECPT and token-volume-weighted model fallback rates.

Dashboards and panels (owner: platform-observability):
| Panel | Primary metric | Target | Notes |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
| ECPT overview | 24h rolling ECPT | < baseline +5% | Spotlight by model_family |
| Explainable trace explorer | sample traces by explain_trace_id | interactive | linkable from incidents |
| Model-variant fallback heatmap | fallback_rate per region | <1% | per-hour granularity |
| KV cache hit-rate vs ECPT | hit_rate | >90% | stratified by prefix |

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- ecpt_delta_1h: trigger when ECPT increases >7% vs 7-day baseline and token_volume_1h > 10k.
- fallback_surge: trigger when model_variant_fallback_rate_10m > 2% AND affected_routes > 3.
- cache-degradation: KV cache hit_rate_15m drops >15% AND corresponding ECPT increases.

Investigation runbook (on-call SRE):
1) Triage from PagerDuty alert: record alert id and time.
2) Open Explainable Trace Explorer and select top-10 traces by ECPT delta.
3) Identify common attributes: request route, model_variant, region, client_key, sequence_length_bucket.
4) Correlate with deploys: check deployments in the last 60 minutes (CI/CD pipeline).
5) Check runtime metrics: batch_size distribution, GPU utilization, KV cache hit/miss heatmap.
6) If fallback_surge: inspect routing logs for capacity errors or API quota nodes. Rollback routing rule if necessary.
7) If cache-degradation: trigger cache warmup and re-evaluate batch policies.
8) Communicate: post status in incident channel with a one-line cause hypothesis and mitigation steps.

Mitigation play actions (ordered by impact and reversibility):
1) Apply tiered throttling to low-priority tenants to restore ECPT for critical routes.
2) Switch high-latency routes to a lower-cost cached model_variant for a rolling 5-minute window.
3) Reconfigure batch_max_latency to avoid pathological micro-batches (runtime flag: --batch-max-ms).
4) Evict stale KV prefixes if hit_rates show long-tail pollution.

Ownership and escalation:
- First responder: platform-oncall (SRE).
- Secondary: runtime-team (kernel/scheduler owner).
- Escalation: head of platform within 60 minutes if user-impacting costs persist or SLAs are breached.

Implementation notes: sample instrumentation and queries
- Example ClickHouse insert (simplified):
INSERT INTO token_events (ts, explain_trace_id, request_id, client_key, model_variant, token_count, token_cost, kv_hit) VALUES (...);

- Sample ClickHouse aggregation query for ECPT by model_variant:
SELECT model_variant, sum(token_cost) / sum(token_count) AS ecpt, countDistinct(request_id) AS requests
FROM token_events
WHERE ts BETWEEN subtractHours(now(), 1) AND now()
GROUP BY model_variant
ORDER BY ecpt DESC
LIMIT 20;

- Prometheus / Alertmanager (conceptual) PromQL examples:
ecpt_delta = (sum(rate(token_cost_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(token_count_sum[5m])))
alert: ECPTIncrease
expr: ecpt_delta / (avg_over_time(ecpt_delta[7d])) > 1.07 and sum(rate(token_count_sum[1h])) > 10000
for: 10m

Runbook play examples for automation (playbook scripts):
- automated-mitigation: on ECPTIncrease, run a canary re-route for 5% of traffic to stable-model-001, notify on call and open MR to revert if stable.

Rollout and guardrails:
1) Feature-flag dashboard rollout: start with platform-internal only for 72 hours.
2) Telemetry completeness gate: require >=99% of explain_trace_id presence across router + runtime for a 48h window.
3) Read-only export: provide product teams a daily CSV of ECPT by route for billing reconciliation.

Post-incident retrospective checklist:
- Timestamped timeline of signals and actions (10-minute resolution).
- Root cause summary with evidence (traces, queries, deploy diff).
- Cost impact estimate (USD/day) and affected customers list.
- Action items with owners and due dates (e.g., instrumentation gaps, 1-week follow-up).

Appendix: quick debugging commands and common failure patterns
- Common patterns and likely causes:
  * Single route spike with stable fallback rate -> suspect prompt/usage change from a customer.
  * Global ECPT increase + batch size drop -> suspect upstream throttling or backend cold starts.
  * ECPT increase with KV miss spike -> model or prefix mis-routing or cache eviction policy change.

- Useful queries and flags:
  * Get recent traces for a request_id: SELECT * FROM token_events WHERE request_id = '<id>' ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 500;
  * Dump a sample explainable trace: platform-cli trace get --id <explain_trace_id> --format json
  * Runtime flags to inspect: --batch-max-ms, --kv-cache-window-seconds, --quantize-profile-id

Related work and next steps:
- Integrate explainable traces with alert annotations to automatically attach root-cause candidates.
- Add model-variant cost-simulations to the Console so product owners can forecast ECPT before rollouts.
- Expand long-term retention of per-request traces for monthly billing audits (cost/space tradeoff).

Contacts and ownership:
- Document owner: platform-observability@redwood.com
- On-call rotation: see /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/platform-regional-capacity-matrix-and-shifthandoff-handbook-2024 for current oncall roster.

This playbook is intended to be updated iteratively. If you find gaps in instrumentation or analysis, add a follow-up action to the retrospective section and assign it to the runtime or platform-observability team.
