payload.page_title: Token Reclamation and Cold-Cache Resuscitation: Operator Playbook

sections.body:
A pragmatic operator playbook to reclaim leaked/stranded request tokens, repair and warm LLM KV/prefix caches after extended cold periods, and restore service SLOs while minimizing cost impact. Includes monitoring checks, fast remediation steps, safe rollbacks, and post-run analysis templates.
Summary

This playbook provides step-by-step guidance for platform operators to: (1) identify and reclaim token leaks or stranded compute attributed to stalled/gone-away clients, (2) resuscitate model prefix/KV caches after prolonged cold periods (e.g., single-tenant idleness, regional failovers), and (3) safely ramp the cache warm-up to meet latency SLOs without unbounded cost.

Context and motivation

- Problem space: long-lived KV/prefix caches and batching/queueing optimizations significantly reduce per-token cost and latency, but they can be underutilized after long idle windows, or corrupted/fragmented due to partial failures. Token accounting mismatches (leaked tokens) can also cause billing anomalies and resource exhaustion.
- Impact: tail latency SLO breaches (P99 > 500ms), elevated GPU time with low throughput, unexpected overprovisioning/evictions, and customer billing disputes.
- Goal: restore functional caches and correct token accounting within 30–90 minutes while limiting incremental GPU spend to a configurable budget.

When to run this playbook

- Alerts firing: "kv-cache-hit-rate < 20% for 10m", "P99 inference latency > target for 15m", "token-burst-forensics suspicious-token-duration > 5m"
- Symptoms: surge of cold-starts on specific model shards/regions, rising unit-cost per token, repeated cache rehydration failures, or tenant complaints about sluggish responses after failover.
- Preconditions: ensure no active global deploy/rollout that would confound the runbook. If a rollout is in progress, coordinate with the deployment owner.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: Platform Operator on shift (eng-platform).
- Secondary escalation: Serving Runtime on-call (eng-serving-runtime) if kernel-level or GPU errors observed.
- Time-to-escalate: escalate to secondary if remediation steps 1–3 completed with no improvement after 30 minutes.

SLOs and run acceptance criteria

- Target for remediation window: reduce P99 latency back to baseline within 60 minutes for affected route(s).
- Cost cap: incremental GPU spend for warmup must not exceed configured burst budget (default: $500 per region for emergency warmups) unless approved by capacity owner.
- Post-fix: no residual token accounting anomalies older than 10 minutes.

Monitoring and dashboards to consult

1) Primary dashboards (operator console):
- Model shard heatmap (qps, prefix-cache hit-rate, kv-cache size)
- Token-forensics timeline (per-tenant token durations, open token sessions)
- Cost burn and GPU utilization per region
- Tail-latency waterfall (queueing vs kernel time)

2) Alerts and thresholds to watch:
- kv-cache-hit-rate < 20% for 10m (severity P1)
- p99-latency-route > 2x target for 15m (severity P1)
- token-session-duration > 5m for sessions > 100k tokens (severity P2)

Immediate remediation checklist (fast path)

IMPORTANT: Run through steps sequentially unless you identify a clear single root cause. Note commands are examples — use the operator CLI with your region and cluster flags.

1) Verify scope and list affected shards/tenants

- Action: Open Model Shard Heatmap, filter for low cache-hit-rate and high P99.
- Command (example): redwood operator shards list --region us-west-2 --filter "cache_hit_rate<0.2"

2) Isolate suspected leaked token sessions

- Action: Query token-forensics for long-lived sessions on the affected shard.
- Command (example): redwood telemetry token-sessions query --since 30m --region us-west-2 --min-duration 300s --output table
- If sessions are "stuck" (clients disconnected but server retains session): mark for reclamation.

3) Reclaim tokens (safe reclamation)

- Goal: free stranded KV references and close dangling streams without impacting healthy sessions.
- Command (example): redwood operator tokens reclaim --shard <shard-id> --dry-run
- Inspect dry-run output. If safe, run: redwood operator tokens reclaim --shard <shard-id> --force --reason "operator-reclaim-<INC_ID>"
- Consequence: reclaimed tokens will be reported as reclaimed in token-forensics and should reduce reported in-use GPU time.

4) Trigger targeted cache compaction and integrity check

- Action: Run a cache integrity job to remove orphaned KV entries and compact prefix indexes.
- Command (example): redwood runtime cache-integrity run --shard <shard-id> --level compact --max-io 50MB/s
- Expected outcome: immediate reclaim of memory and improved hit-rate on subsequent requests.

5) Controlled warm-up (gradual traffic replay pattern)

- Rationale: Full fan-out warmups are expensive and can overshoot burst budget. Use staged synthetic or low-priority replay.
- Steps:
  a) Schedule a low-QPS synthetic replay: redwood replay start --shard <shard-id> --template warmup-small --qps 2 --duration 10m --tag operator-warmup-<INC_ID>
  b) After 10m, measure cache-hit-rate and latency. If hit-rate improves >= 15 percentage points and P99 improves, increase to qps 8 for 15m.
  c) Continue incremental increases until baseline reached or budget exhausted.
- Safety: replay traffic must be tagged and rate-limited. Reject or pause replay if GPU utilization climbs > 85% or cost burn nears cap.

6) Post-warmup verification

- Verify: cache-hit-rate at pre-incident baseline, P50/P95/P99 latencies back to expected ranges, token-session counts normalized.
- Commands: redwood telemetry metrics get --metric kv_cache_hit_rate --shard <shard-id> --window 5m

Safe fallback and rollback procedures

- If synthetic warmup causes degradation or cost runaway: immediately stop all replay jobs: redwood replay stop --tag operator-warmup-<INC_ID>
- If reclamation caused client disruption (rare): restore token state via token-snapshot rollback if snapshot exists: redwood operator tokens rollback --snapshot <snapshot-id> --shard <shard-id>. Contact serving-runtime on-call before running rollback.

Longer-term remediation (after immediate fix)

- Run an automated job to pre-warm cache for low-traffic tenants during predictable windows (off-peak).
- Add hysteresis to token lifetime detection to avoid premature reclamation.
- Update routing policy to prefer warm shards for high-latency-sensitive routes for the first 30 mins after regional failover.

Operator checklist (to paste in incident ticket)

- [ ] Confirm affected shard IDs and tenants
- [ ] Retrieve token-session snapshot (pre-action)
- [ ] Run token reclaim dry-run and capture output
- [ ] Execute reclaim (if safe) and note command/flags
- [ ] Start controlled warmup (tag with incident number)
- [ ] Monitor key metrics for 60 minutes post-reclaim
- [ ] Stop warmup and record cost delta
- [ ] Create postmortem ticket if root cause unknown or if SLOs not restored within 90 minutes

Templates and example incident annotations

- Incident note (one-line): "Token reclamation + targeted warmup for shard s-0452 — reclaimed 1.1m stranded tokens; cache hit-rate recovered from 12% -> 71% in 42m; P99 returned to 240ms"
- Ticket snippet: "Commands executed: tokens reclaim --shard s-0452 --force --reason operator-reclaim-INC-2027-012; replay start --shard s-0452 --template warmup-small --qps 2 --duration 10m --tag operator-warmup-INC-2027-012"

Post-run analysis and retro triggers

- Metrics to capture: pre/post kv_cache_hit_rate, P50/P95/P99 latency deltas, GPU-hours consumed, cost delta, number of reclaimed tokens, list of affected tenants.
- Retro triggers (create a retrospective if any of the following):
  - SLO not restored within 90 minutes
  - Cost delta > configured budget without prior approval
  - Repeated occurrence for same shard or tenant within 30 days

Appendix A — recommended dashboard queries

- KV cache hit-rate (per-shard):
  query: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_lookups[5m])) by (shard)
- Token session duration distribution:
  query: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_session_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant))
- Synthetic warmup job CPU/GPU throttle check:
  query: max_over_time(gpu_utilization[5m]) by (shard)

Appendix B — safe-parameter reference

| Parameter | Default | Rationale |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| warmup_qps_initial | 2 | conservative start to avoid sudden load spikes |
| warmup_step_qps | 4 | incremental increase per stage |
| warmup_max_gpu_util | 85% | throttling threshold to avoid contention |
| reclaim_dry_run | true | always validate results before forcing |
| burst_cost_cap | $500 | emergency budget per region (configurable) |

Related improvements backlog (examples)

- Automate token leak detection to create auto-PRs for suspected client SDKs with long-lived sessions.
- Add safe, cluster-level pre-warm schedules for low-traffic shards.
- Expose per-tenant warmup budgets and automated approval flows.

Contacts and escalation directory

- Platform Operator lead: priya@redwood.ai (primary contact)
- Serving Runtime on-call: see rotation page /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/oncall-rotation.json
- Billing dispute contact: billing@redwood.ai

Document history

- 2026-12-15: Draft authored by Priya Nambiar
- 2027-01-12: Reviewed by Liam O'Connor and Sana Patel; added controlled-warmup/playback guidance
- 2027-02-10: Published after small clarifications to rollback guidance

End of playbook

payload.page_title: Platform traffic decision notebook: tiering, cost-sensitivity, and operator heuristics

sections.body:
Overview

This notebook captures a compact, operator-friendly decision model for routing, tiering and emergency actioning of LLM inference traffic. It combines an explicit traffic-tier matrix, a numeric Cost-Sensitivity Index (CSI) for tenants/routes, and clear operator heuristics for common platform incidents (token surges, model variant misfires, regional capacity loss). The goal is to provide a single-page reference that on-call operators and product engineers can use to: 1) decide routing adjustments, 2) enact graceful degradation, and 3) quantify expected cost/latency tradeoffs for choices.

Why this exists

- Platform traffic is multi-dimensional: latency SLOs, cost budget, tenant priority, model quality. Operators need a crisp decision surface that maps observability signals to safe actions.
- Many incidents are about tradeoffs (lower cost vs higher latency or slightly reduced quality). This doc standardizes vocabulary and numeric scoring so different operators make consistent choices.

Scope

- Applies to hosted and dedicated runtime pools (all regions).
- Assumes route-level metadata: tenant_id, route_tier, max_token_budget, model_variant, sla_tier.
- Does NOT replace tenant billing policy or contractual SLAs; use this notebook for operational actions when immediate mitigation is needed.

Definitions

- Route: API route /customer/{tenant}/generate or embedding route.
- Route tier: a discrete label {platinum, gold, standard, free}.
- CSI (Cost-Sensitivity Index): 0.0–1.0 numeric score indicating how sensitive a tenant/route is to cost increases (1.0 = very cost-sensitive).
- Latency criticality: {high, medium, low} per route definition.
- Model variant fallback: pre-approved model replacement candidates for quality/cost/latency tradeoffs.

Decision primitives

1) Compute route impact score (RIS): numeric composite used to prioritize actions.

RIS = (SLA_weight * SLA_factor) + (CSI_weight * CSI_factor) + (Burst_weight * Burst_factor) + (Quality_regress_weight * Quality_factor)

- SLA_factor = 1.0 for platinum, 0.7 for gold, 0.4 for standard, 0.1 for free.
- CSI_factor = CSI (0.0–1.0).
- Burst_factor = normalized token surge (0–1) over baseline for route in last 5m.
- Quality_factor = 1 if recent quality alerts triggered for route, else 0.
- Weights (default): SLA_weight=0.4, CSI_weight=0.25, Burst_weight=0.25, Quality_regress_weight=0.1.

Interpretation: RIS in [0,1.0+]; higher RIS -> higher operational priority (prefer fast recovery over cost-saving action).

Traffic tier matrix (operator reference)

| Action category | Preconditions (observability) | Typical operator action | Expected immediate impact | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emergency failover | Regional capacity loss OR sustained latency p95 > 2*SLO for 5m | Route-level failover to alternate region or standby model pool; enable short-lived bilateral burst credits | Latency drop to within SLO for routes with standby capacity; cost may increase by 10–40% temporarily | Platform Ops |
| Cost-damp mitigation | Token cost spikes across multi-tenant pool, cost burn > 120% of forecasted for hour | Apply per-tenant soft rate-limit; reduce batching window; switch high-CSI tenants to cheaper quantized variant for non-critical routes | Immediate cost reduction; latency +5–15ms | Platform Operators |
| Quality-first rollback | Quality regression alerts triggered for model variant with correlated increased hallucinations | Roll back to previous verified variant; mark suspected model variant restricted for canary traffic | Quality restored; token cost unchanged | Model Onboarding + Platform |
| Graceful degradation | Sustained high queue lengths and rising p99 > 1.5*SLO | Temporarily reduce max allowed sequence length per route; enable prefix-KV cache hints; demote free/standard tier traffic to background queue | Lower p99 tail; higher rejected long-sequence requests for low-tier | Platform Ops |

Operational playbook (step-by-step)

1. Detect: Confirm incident by cross-checking metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, queue length, token burn rate, model error rate) and alert context. Use the Incident Triage Dashboard (see Dashboards).
2. Score: Compute RIS for top 10 impacted routes. Sort descending.
3. Choose action category using matrix above and context: if regional capacity loss -> Emergency failover; if platform token burn -> Cost-damp mitigation; if model-specific quality alerts -> Quality-first rollback; if tail latency -> Graceful degradation.
4. Execute: Follow runbook snippet below for the chosen action. Document the change in incident ticket with tags: action:, rationale:, expected_impact:, rollback_plan:.
5. Monitor: Watch SLO dashboards and cost delta for 10m, then 30m. If change not improving RIS top 3 routes, escalate to SRE lead.
6. Remediate permanently: If temporary action stayed > 2 hours, schedule follow-up with owning teams and add a task to the platform backlog.

Runbook snippets (CLI and safe checks)

- Emergency region failover (safe mode):

1) Mark affected region read-only in control-plane: `redwoodctl region set-mode --region eu-west-2 --mode read-only --ticket $INC_ID`
2) Move traffic: `redwoodctl route reroute --from-region eu-west-2 --to-region eu-central-1 --match 'tenant in ($IMPACTED)' --max-in-flight 50`
3) Toggle auto-burst to standby: `redwoodctl pool set-burst --pool standby-eu --enabled true --burst-multiplier 2`
4) Validate: check p95 and queue_length for top 5 routes. If p95 still > SLO*1.5, step back and notify SRE lead.

- Cost-damp soft rate-limit (per-route):

1) Identify top 5 cost contributors: query `billing.query.top_token_burn(3600)`
2) For each route where CSI > 0.7 and tier != platinum, apply soft throttling: `redwoodctl route set-rate-limit --route-id $ROUTE --qps 0.8 * current_qps --grace 10s`
3) Notify tenant owner via tenant-notify pipeline: `notify tenant $TENANT --subject "Temporary rate-limits due to platform capacity" --runbook $INC_ID`

SLO / alert mapping (concise)

| Metric | SLO | Alert threshold | Suggested default action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| p95 latency (model gen) | 150ms global hosted gold | p95 > 300ms for 5m | Graceful degradation or failover |
| Queue length (per-pool) | 500 | > 1000 for 3m | Burst credits, prefetch hints, reduce concurrency |
| Token burn rate (global) | forecasted +10% | > forecast*1.2 for 10m | Cost-damp mitigation |
| Model quality regression (eval) | 95% pass on critical eval set | regression > 5% vs baseline | Quality-first rollback |

Dashboards (what to open first)

- Incident Triage Dashboard (operators): single view with top routes by RIS, p95/p99, queue depth, token burn delta.
- Regional Capacity Heatmap: node-level free/used GPU, preemptible share, thermal headroom.
- Token burn leaderboards: rolling 1h/6h/24h with tenant CSI and quotas.
- Model variant canary traces: error rate, divergence, hallucination scoring.

Incident retrospective template (fill after remediation)

1) Summary (1–2 lines)
2) Timeline (epoched events, actions, durations)
3) Root cause (short)
4) What worked well (bulleted)
5) Gaps / surprises (bulleted)
6) Follow-ups (owner, priority, due date)
7) Cost impact estimate (USD, approx)

Example retrospective action items (from a recent dry run)

- Automate RIS computation in triage dashboard (owner: telemetry, P2, due 2026-03-15)
- Add per-tenant soft rate-limit playbook to customer success templates (owner: customer-success, P3)
- Expand standby model pool in eu-central-1 by 20% before Q2 (owner: infra, P1)

Platform roadmap tie-ins (next 12 months)

- Q2 2026: RIS engine GA (server-side scoring + webhook to incident system).
- Q3 2026: Per-route automated soft-mitigations (rate-limit and variant-swap) with audit trails.
- Q4 2026: Cost-aware routing policy (runtime will pick cheaper compatible variant when CSI > 0.8 and latency slack >= 30ms).

Ownership and escalation matrix

- First responder: Platform operator on regional on-call.
- Escalation: SRE lead (after 30m of unsuccessful mitigation) -> Head of Serving Runtime (after 2h) -> Incident commander for customer-impacting outages.

Quick FAQs

Q: When do we prefer model variant fallback vs reducing sequence length?
A: Fallback to a cheaper/quantized variant if quality is acceptable for route (CSI >= 0.6) and latency slack < 30ms. Reduce sequence length if requests are long-tail and route cannot tolerate reduced quality.

Q: How long can temporary measures remain active?
A: Temporary mitigations should be logged and reviewed; if active > 2 hours, file a follow-up action and create a rollback criterion.

Appendix: Example CSI assignment guideline

- Platinum enterprise customer with explicit cost-escalation clause: CSI = 0.2
- Startup on free plan with strict credit limit: CSI = 0.95
- Internal testing tenants: CSI = 0.8

Table: quick numeric reference

| Route tier | SLA_factor | Default CSI | Priority rank baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| platinum | 1.0 | 0.2 | 1 |
| gold | 0.7 | 0.4 | 2 |
| standard | 0.4 | 0.7 | 3 |
| free | 0.1 | 0.95 | 4 |

Related links and artifacts

- Playbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026
- Telemetry: instrumentation spec (telemetry repo link)
- Billing: cost-attribution contract and token-leaderboard queries

Contact and feedback

If this notebook is unclear or you observe repeated manual work that could be automated, add an issue to the Platform backlog and tag `triage:operator-notebook`. For urgent changes propose edits directly on this page and ping @Asha.

payload.page_title: Oncall Psychological Safety & Handoff Checklist

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This checklist captures behavioral guardrails, concrete handoff steps, and tooling guidance for platform operators to preserve psychological safety during oncall shifts and incident handoffs. The goal is to reduce cognitive load, prevent blame, and ensure reliable context transfer so teams can make correct decisions under stress.

Audience
--------
- Platform operators (first- and second-line)
- Platform oncall leads
- Engineering managers and team leads who run rotations

Why this matters
----------------
- Oncall is high-cognitive-load work; poor handoffs increase time-to-restore and escalate stress.
- Psychological safety reduces fear of speaking up, which improves post-incident learning and reduces repeat errors.
- A short standardized handoff plus behavioral expectations prevents context loss during busy windows (deploys, high traffic) and multi-team incidents.

Principles (short)
------------------
- People > Pager: prioritize health and respectful communication over triaging every non-critical alert.
- Assume good intent: treat missing details as coordination gaps, not blame.
- Make implicit knowledge explicit: write what you would have wanted to know when you were in the middle of an incident.

Pre-shift checklist (what the incoming operator should do before taking the pager)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Review your upcoming 2-hour window on the platform-operator-dashboard; note any active experiments, deploy windows, or maintenance tasks.
2. Read the last 24h Handoff Note (see Handoff template below). If the outgoing operator attached a runbook ticket or incident ID, open it now.
3. Confirm PagerDuty assignment and communication channels (Slack: #platform-oncall, Incident Bridge URL).
4. Ensure you have access to the three quick tools: telemetry query UI, service-graph, and incident-tracker (local aliases: p-telemetry, p-graph, p-inc).
5. State a definite time to the outgoing operator for the swap (do not do asynchronous handoffs during active mitigation unless required).

During-shift behavioral expectations
-----------------------------------
- Communicate status concisely: short updates in #platform-oncall reduce redundancy (format: [SYSTEM] short-status — next-step — ETA).
- Use clarifying questions rather than assumptions. If you don’t understand a decision, ask in-bridge: "Can you confirm why we chose X vs fallback Y?"
- Declare escalation early: if an incident looks broad or crosses teams, tag sev2/3 and call the SRE lead.
- Pause and rest: if you’re fatigued, notify the outgoing or escalation contact and request a swap. Safety > completion.

Handoff pattern (structured template)
-------------------------------------
Always use the template below. If the handoff is verbal, paste this into the incident-tracker and Slack immediately after.

Handoff Title: [service-name] — brief status (e.g., "kv-prefix-cache: degraded, 15% error rate")
- Incident/Runbook ID: <ID or none>
- Current impact: (user-visible effects, customers affected)
- Last action taken: (what I did and when)
- Next required step (explicit, single-owner recommended): (e.g., "force-restart shard 4 via pctl; rollback prefetch experiment if errors persist")
- Open hypotheses (bullet list): (e.g., "1) prefetched KV writeback saturation; 2) kernel-level GPU memory fragmentation")
- Known mitigations and outcomes to date: (what worked/didn't)
- Data to watch (links): (telemetry query, dashboard panels, span IDs)
- Escalation contacts: (name + preferred channel)
- Confidences / TODOs: (explicit unknowns and blockers)

Example (one-line brief)
------------------------
kv-prefix-cache — degraded reads across us-west; rollback of prefetch-2 experiment pending; see runbook: p-inc-4912

Emergency swap criteria (when the incoming operator may request immediate takeover)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Outgoing operator is actively in another oncall-critical incident and cannot provide a coherent handoff.
- The outgoing operator reports fatigue, unclear mental state, or requests swap.
- There is new, high-severity customer impact that requires fresh context.
If criteria are met, perform an emergency swap and create an Incident Swap note in the incident-tracker with timestamp and reasons.

Communication language guide (phrases to use)
--------------------------------------------
- Use: "I’m unsure — can we slow down and confirm the last action?"
- Use: "I’m going to take a minute to reproduce this locally before escalating."
- Avoid: "That was dumb/obvious"; instead say: "We didn’t factor X into the experiment; let’s record it."

Post-handoff housekeeping (outgoing operator responsibilities)
-------------------------------------------------------------
- Attach telemetry snapshots and any terminal logs to the incident-tracker.
- Mark unresolved follow-ups in the incident-tracker and assign owners.
- Add a single-line summary to #platform-oncall and tag the next oncall.
- If you were the owner of a mitigation, note whether it should be rolled forward or reversed at next engineer availability.

Runbook integration points (where to link things)
------------------------------------------------
- platform-operator-dashboard: provide panel links for the impacted service, latency and error-rate panels, and the last deploy marker.
- incident-tracker: always create or append to an incident ID for anything outside routine thresholds (error-rate > 1% for 10m or latency P95 > 3x baseline).
- PagerDuty: update the incident with handoff notes and any temporary suppressions.

Operator fatigue & swap protocol (practical)
------------------------------------------
1. If you feel cognitive decline, signal in the bridge: "Swap requested — tired".
2. A backup operator or escalation contact should accept and perform a 5-minute sync.
3. If no backup is available within 10 minutes, mark the incident as "operator-swap-pending" and escalate to oncall lead.
4. Documentation after swap: both operators must write a 3-sentence context summary within 30 minutes.

Metrics and signals we track for continuous improvement
-----------------------------------------------------
- Handoff completeness score (manual audit metric): % of handoffs that include all template fields. Target: 95%.
- Swap frequency per operator per quarter: target < 2 emergency swaps per operator per quarter.
- Post-incident stress survey (anonymous): median score baseline and target improvement.

How managers and leads should use this playbook
----------------------------------------------
- Review a sample of handoff notes during oncall retro cycles (weekly).
- Monitor swap frequency and investigate operational causes (chronic midnight deploys, understaffing).
- Run a quarterly 1-hour "handoff role-play" gameday for new rotations.

Runbook examples and templates (text table)
------------------------------------------
The table below is a short reference you can paste into runbook templates.
Fields | Purpose | Example
-------|---------|-------
Handoff Title | Short one-line summary | kv-prefix-cache — degraded reads
Impact | Who/what is affected | internal tenants; us-west traffic 40% of requests
Immediate Action | Next step to carry forward | rollback prefetch-2 experiment
Signal Links | Dashboards & queries | panel:platform-operator-dashboard?k=kv-cache
Escalation | Who to page next | SRE Lead (Ethan Li) — Slack @ethan

Retrospectives and continuous improvement
----------------------------------------
- Capture learning: each oncall team should nominate two handoffs per month for anonymized review.
- Feed learnings into the operator-playbook repo as examples (create PRs with redacted content).
- Track whether handoff completeness correlates with time-to-restore and adjust training content.

Ownership and contact list
--------------------------
- Playbook owner: Maya Patel (eng-platform) — contact: maya@redwood.example.com
- Oncall lead: Ethan Li — contact: ethan@redwood.example.com
- Psychological safety liaison: Nadia Gomez (People Ops) — contact: nadia@redwood.example.com

Appendix A: Quick handoff script (30 seconds)
--------------------------------------------
1. State the one-line brief.
2. Say the current impact and last action.
3. State the one next step and the confidence level (high/medium/low).
4. Confirm the outgoing operator’s swap criteria and fatigue level.

Appendix B: Example Slack snippet to use after handoff
------------------------------------------------------
"Handoff: kv-prefix-cache — degraded reads; rollback prefetch-2 pending. Incident p-inc-4912. Next: rollback (manual) at 14:17 UTC if errors persist. Contact: @ethan for escalation. Full handoff note attached to p-inc-4912."

Related pages
-------------
- Platform runbooks and operator tools (link in Related Pages)
- Incident retro templates (search: oncall-retro-template)

Revision history
----------------
- 2024-11-10: Initial draft by Maya Patel.
- 2025-03-15: Incorporated reviewer feedback; added fatigue swap protocol (Ethan Li, Priya Rao).

Acknowledgements
----------------
Thanks to the eng-platform oncall cohort for role-play feedback and People Ops for psychological-safety guidance.

payload.page_title: Platform degradation simulation training curriculum

sections.body: This curriculum defines a repeatable lab series and assessment for platform operators to learn how to detect, simulate, and remediate realistic degradation modes in the Redwood inference stack. The focus is on inference-specific failure classes (latency tail, KV cache thrash, model-variant fallout, and eviction storms) and on exercising cross-team runbooks (platform, serving-runtime, SRE).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Teach operators to map observability signals to root causes for LLM inference disruptions.
- Practice coordinated remediation (traffic steering, model swap, cache rebuild, tenant throttling).
- Validate dashboards, synthetic tests, and escalation paths used during incidents.
- Produce measurable improvement in mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to mitigate (MTTM) for platform degradation incidents.
sections.heading: Goals and learning objectives

sections.body:
- Platform operators, SREs, and on-call engineers who operate inference endpoints and GPU pools.
- Product/platform engineers who own rollout or model-variant fallback logic.
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) Access: operators need "platform-operator" role and read/write to the synthetic-lab project namespace.
2) Environments: a dedicated lab region (eu-lab-1) with scaled-down GPU pool and an isolated tenant for load generation.
3) Baseline artifacts: a baseline dashboard (link below), traffic-replay assets, and a pre-seeded KV prefix cache snapshot.
sections.heading: Prerequisites and setup summary

sections.body:
- Lab SLO dashboard (latency percentiles, token-cost, error-rate, model-variant-fallbacks).
- Cost & token breakdown per-request traces viewer.
- Incident runbook checklist (playback-able via the operator CLI).
- Synthetic load harness: lab-loader (Git repo: git://redwood/lab-loader).

Curriculum modules (4 weeks recommended, modular delivery):
Week 1 — Foundations and Signals
- Lecture: LLM-specific telemetry (prefix cache hit/miss, batch sizes, KV latency, model-switch counters).
- Workshop: interpret lab dashboard panels and map signals to the incident taxonomy.
- Assessment: identify root cause given 3 recorded incidents.

Week 2 — Cache & Batching Failure Modes
- Scenario lab: deliberate cache-shard desync and prefix eviction storm.
- Operator tasks: detect eviction spike, apply cache-prefetch policy toggle, and initiate cached-prefix reseed.
- Key checks: cache hit ratio improvement, token-cost delta, service CPU on inference hosts.

Week 3 — Model Variant and Fallbacks
- Scenario lab: deploy a model variant with increased generation latencies that triggers fallback flow.
- Operator tasks: observe fallback percentages, adjust routing policy, perform controlled model rollback.
- Validation: confirm fallback counts drop and p95 latency returns below SLO.

Week 4 — Multi-tenant Throttling and Degradation Containment
- Scenario lab: tenant spike that saturates GPU pools and causes soft-degradations for other tenants.
- Operator tasks: exercise tenant soft-quota enforcement, apply prioritized-tenant burst credits, and test eviction policy.
- Outcome: isolation preserves SLO for priority tenants while back-pressure is applied to lower tiers.
sections.heading: Required dashboards and tools

sections.body:
Scenario | Trigger | Primary SLO impacted | Operator action | Expected measurable result
---------|--------:|---------------------:|-----------------|--------------------------
KV eviction storm | Simulated cache corruption | p99 latency | Toggle cache-prefetch, reseed prefixes, monitor cache hit ratio | p99 latency reduces >30% within 10m
Model-variant latency | New model build with regressed kernels | p95 latency and error rate | Route traffic to stable variant, rollback model, open model-onboarding ticket | Fallback rate drops to <1% and p95 recovers
Tenant surge | Synthetic tenant traffic spike | availability and tail-latency for platform | Apply tenant throttling, activate burst-credit reconciliation | Priority tenant SLO preserved; overall throughput reduced
Routing split misconfig | Incorrect weight in feature flag | correctness and latency | Reconcile feature flags, run canary rollback, reweight traffic | Errors in canary drop, p95 stable
sections.heading: Lab scenarios and exercise matrix (table)

sections.body:
1) Triage: confirm alert on Lab SLO dashboard and annotate suspected failure class.
2) Contain: apply conserved traffic steering (mute non-critical regions / enable degraded routes).
3) Remediate: follow scenario play instructions (cache reseed, model rollback, tenant throttle).
4) Stabilize: observe 2x SLO window; if not recovered, escalate to Serving Runtime on-call.
5) Postmortem: create incident with evidence (traces, before/after metrics) and link to lab exercise ID.
sections.heading: Runbook excerpt (operator checklist)

sections.body:
- Generate synthetic tenant spike:
```
lab-loader --tenant lab-tenant-42 --rps 1200 --pattern spike --duration 15m --seed 2026
```
- Toggle cache-prefetch feature flag for lab region (OPA CLI):
```
opa-cli set-flag --env eu-lab-1 --flag cache-prefetch-enabled --value false
```
- Rollback model variant via operator CLI:
```
redwoodctl models rollback --region eu-lab-1 --service inference-prod --target-variant stable-v1
```

Observability acceptance criteria (what to validate after each exercise):
- Alert reduction: active incident alerts should go from >1 to 0 within 15 minutes for contained scenarios.
- Latency improvement: p95/p99 reduce by target thresholds defined per scenario table.
- Token-cost: documented token-cost delta must be within allowed guardrail (no more than +10% for remediation actions).
- Audit trail: runbook steps and CLI commands used must be committed to incident timeline.
sections.heading: Commands and snippets (lab tooling)

sections.body:
- Each operator must complete three graded labs: one cache incident, one model-fallback incident, one multi-tenant containment.
- Passing criteria: successful remediation in under 25 minutes on average across the three labs, full runbook documentation, and verbal debrief.
- Certification: operators who pass receive the "Platform Degradation Responder (PDR)" badge in the internal learning system.

Post-lab retrospective template (to be completed after each game):
1) Summary of what happened and timeline.
2) What signals were most/least useful?
3) Runbook steps that worked / failed.
4) Dashboard gaps and instrumentation requests.
5) Follow-ups and owners (with target dates).
sections.heading: Assessment and certification

sections.body:
- Mean time to detect (MTTD) for lab incidents.
- Mean time to mitigate (MTTM) for each incident class.
- Percentage of labs that required escalation to serving-runtime team.
- Operator confidence score (post-lab survey).

Appendix A — Dashboard links and queries:
- Lab SLO dashboard: /dashboards/lab-slo-platform-2026
- Trace query example (token-cost attribution):
```
trace.query("service:inference AND tag:lab-tenant-42") | group_by(model_variant) | top(10, p95_latency)
```

Appendix B — Lab environment teardown checklist:
- Stop lab-loaders and verify zero synthetic sessions.
- Re-enable any disabled feature flags.
- Clear lab-only KV prefixes: `redis-cli --scan --pattern lab:* | xargs redis-cli del`.
- Ensure model traffic weights returned to production values.
sections.heading: Metrics to track across training cohort (quarterly)

sections.body:
- Curriculum owner: Platform Training Squad (owner: Asha Kapoor).
- Quarterly gamedays scheduled: first Monday of each quarter.
- Curriculum review: semi-annual or after any production incident that reveals gaps.
sections.heading: Ownership and cadence

sections.body:
- Incident runbook library: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks
- Operator onboarding pathway: /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/operator-onboarding-certification-pathway-2026
- Lab tooling repo: git://redwood/lab-loader
sections.heading: Related resources

sections.body:
- Pilot: run a pilot gameday with 6 operators in March 2026 and collect MTTD/MTTM baselines.
- Integrations: explore adding synthetic golden-metrics to the CI pipelines to detect subtle regressions earlier.
sections.heading: Notes and next steps

sections.body: - Curriculum authored by Asha Kapoor. Reviewed by Jonah Li, Priya Menon, and Derek Hale.

payload.page_title: Operator Sandbox: Synthetic Scenarios & Verification Catalog

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page is a curated catalog of synthetic, reproducible platform scenarios for the operator sandbox environment (sandbox.redwood.internal). The goal is to provide a single, searchable library of tests that operators and SREs can run to validate runtime behavior, fallback logic, and observability plumbing before changes reach staging or production.

Short intro: each entry is a self-contained scenario with intent, preconditions, steps to execute, expected signals, verification checks, and teardown instructions. Scenarios are designed to be idempotent and safe to run in the operator sandbox; some are safe to run in regional staging with approval.

Goals
-----
- Provide reproducible test cases for common and high-risk operational behaviors (eviction, batching regression, fallback misfire, cold-cache storms).
- Surface gaps in dashboards, alerting, and tracing by driving deterministic failure modes.
- Create a lightweight verification workflow to gate merges that change routing, batching logic, kernel selection, or cache sharding.
- Maintain scenario metadata and example observability queries that map to SLOs.

Audience
--------
- Platform operators, oncall SREs, runtime engineers, release engineers, applied ML infra teams.

Scope and Safety
----------------
- Runs are permitted only in operator sandbox unless a scenario explicitly marks regional staging as allowed.
- All scenarios include a rate/impact cap. Do not exceed those caps without senior operator approval.
- Scenarios that touch customer tenants or production data are explicitly forbidden.

Catalog: high-level scenario index
--------------------------------
(Use the scenario ID to reference in runbooks and PR checks)

| Scenario ID | Title | Primary intent | Safe in staging? | Estimated duration |
| SCN-001 | KV-prefix-cold-cache-spike | Validate prefix/KV cache miss storm handling and warmup behavior | no | 12m |
| SCN-002 | Batch-size-regression-inject | Confirm batcher caps and slow-path fallback when batch sizes exceed threshold | yes (staging) | 8m |
| SCN-003 | Model-variant-fallback-loop | Verify model variant fallback policy does not enter retry loops under transient errors | yes (staging) | 10m |
| SCN-004 | Tenant-throttle-and-credit-surge | Simulate tenant sudden delta in token usage and validate soft-quota enforcement | no | 15m |
| SCN-005 | Kernel-switch-latency-impact | Force JIT kernel switch on live small-batch workload and capture tail latency regressions | yes (staging) | 20m |
| SCN-006 | Graceful-degrade-region-split | Simulate partial region partition and validate zero-trust fallback routing | no | 25m |

Detailed scenario example: SCN-001 (KV-prefix-cold-cache-spike)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Summary: Drive a controlled burst of requests that hit a previously-evicted KV prefix to validate warmup throughput, operator backpressure signals, and cache warmup dashboards.

Preconditions
1) Sandbox cluster has small test cache pool named sandbox-kv-01.
2) Test model "tiny-verify-v1" pinned for the tenant used by the scenario (tenant-id: sandbox-verify-001).
3) Operator must create an ephemeral prefix set using the helper:
   rctl sandbox create-prefix --pool sandbox-kv-01 --size 128 --output prefix-list.txt

Execution steps (operator)
1) Evict target prefixes to ensure cold cache:
   - CLI: rctl sandbox evict-prefix --pool sandbox-kv-01 --file prefix-list.txt
2) Fire synthetic load with rate limits (cap: 500 concurrent tokens/s total, 50 requests/s):
   - Test harness script (bash):
     ./sandbox-loadgen --tenant sandbox-verify-001 --model tiny-verify-v1 --prefix-file prefix-list.txt --rate 50 --concurrency 8 --duration 600s
3) Monitor dashboards (see Observability section) and watch for backpressure signals.
4) Stop load after 10 minutes and run verification queries.

Expected signals and tolerances
- Cache hit ratio for target prefix should rise from ~0% to >60% within 5 minutes.
- Per-request tail latency (p95) should not exceed 600ms for more than 2 minutes during warmup.
- Batch rejection rate should remain <1% during the run.
- Operator backpressure metric sandbox.kvpool.backpressure_events should not exceed 3 events for the pool.

Verification checks (automated where possible)
1) Cache warmup: run query against metrics store: "sum(rate(kv_cache_hits{pool='sandbox-kv-01',prefix=~'scn1-.*'}[1m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests{pool='sandbox-kv-01',prefix=~'scn1-.*'}[1m]))" and assert > 0.6 at minute 5.
2) Latency: p95 tail from APM: "trace_latency_p95{service='runtime-proxy',route='generate'}" - assert <= 600ms except for allowed window.
3) Batch rejection: alert metric "batcher.rejection_rate{pool='sandbox-kv-01'}" - assert < 0.01.
4) Backpressure events: check logs and metric sandbox.kvpool.backpressure_events <= 3.

Observability & dashboards
-------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Sandbox KV Warmup (dashboards/platform/sandbox-kv-warmup)
- Operator Backpressure Summary (dashboards/platform/operator-backpressure-summary)
- Batch Rejections & Queue Depth (dashboards/platform/batcher-health)
sections.heading: Required dashboards (links are internal)

sections.body:
- Cache hit ratio (per-prefix):
  promql: |
    sum(rate(kv_cache_hits{pool="sandbox-kv-01"}[1m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests{pool="sandbox-kv-01"}[1m]))
- Tail latency (p95):
  promql: |
    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="generate"}[1m])) by (le))
- Operator backpressure events (counter):
  promql: |
    increase(sandbox_kvpool_backpressure_events_total{pool="sandbox-kv-01"}[10m])

Alerting & gating rules (for sandbox verification only)
-------------------------------------------------------
These are soft gates used by verification CI runs. They do not auto-incident in production.
- ALRT-SCN-001-LATENCY: p95(generate) > 1000ms for 5m -> mark scenario failed.
- ALRT-SCN-001-BATCH-REJ: batcher.rejection_rate > 0.02 for 3m -> fail.
- ALRT-SCN-001-BP: increase(sandbox_kvpool_backpressure_events_total[10m]) > 5 -> fail.

Runbook excerpt: operator actions on failure
------------------------------------------
1) Immediately stop the load generator: ./sandbox-loadgen --stop --run-id <run-id>
2) If p95 remains > 1000ms after 2 minutes, scale sandbox-kv-01 pool by +1 instance: rctl pool scale --pool sandbox-kv-01 --delta 1
3) If backpressure persists, enable temporary routing to fallback-variant: rctl routing set-policy --tenant sandbox-verify-001 --policy fallback-variant
4) Capture a sampling trace set: curl -s "http://apm.internal/trace/sample?service=runtime-proxy&tag=scn=SCN-001" -o scn001-traces.json

Post-run checklist and reporting
--------------------------------
1) Attach run metadata to the scenario ticket (SCN-001-<YYYYMMDD>-<operator>): run-id, start/end timestamps, run artifacts (traces, metric screenshots).
2) Run automated verification script: ./sandbox-verify --run-id <run-id> --scenario SCN-001 --output verification.json
3) If verification fails, open a platform-ops ticket with severity "verification-fail" and tag the owning teams.
4) Add a short blameless note to the scenario log explaining the root cause if understood.

Adding new scenarios: process and metadata
-----------------------------------------
1) Create a new markdown file under the operator-sandbox repository at docs/scenarios/SCN-XXX-<short-name>.md using the template below.
2) PR must include: intent, preconditions, exact execution commands, monitoring panels to check, exact verification queries, owner, and safety caps.
3) Required metadata fields (front-matter):
   - scenario_id: SCN-
   - title:
   - owner_team:
   - safe_in_staging: yes/no
   - estimated_duration_minutes:
   - rate_cap_description:

Naming convention
-----------------
- SCN-<NNN>-<short-keyword> (e.g., SCN-042-evict-warmup). Keep NNN zero-padded 3 digits. Use short-keyword for readability.

Scenario metadata template (example)
----------------------------------
---
scenario_id: SCN-XXX
title: Short descriptive title
owner_team: eng-platform
safe_in_staging: no
estimated_duration_minutes: 10
rate_cap_description: "max 100 reqs/s, max 500 tokens/s"
---

Ownership and cadence
---------------------
- Maintainers: eng-platform/operators (primary), eng-serving-runtime (secondary).
- Scenario review cadence: quarterly review of top 20 scenarios; new scenarios require at least two approvers (one from ops, one from runtime).
- Scenario retirement: mark with status "deprecated" and add migration notes if replaced.

Appendix: CLI snippets and example payloads
------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Recommended dashboard panels and example PromQL snippets

sections.body: - CLI: rctl sandbox evict-prefix --pool sandbox-kv-01 --file prefix-list.txt
sections.heading: Evicting prefixes (example)

sections.body: - ./sandbox-loadgen --tenant sandbox-verify-001 --model tiny-verify-v1 --prefix-file prefix-list.txt --rate 50 --concurrency 8 --duration 600s
sections.heading: Load generator (example invocation)

sections.body: - curl -s "http://apm.internal/trace/sample?service=runtime-proxy&tag=scn=SCN-001" -o scn001-traces.json
sections.heading: APM sampling (curl)

sections.body:
{
  "scenario_id": "SCN-001",
  "run_id": "scn001-20260202-01",
  "operator": "maya.chen",
  "start_ts": "2026-02-02T15:04:05Z",
  "end_ts": "2026-02-02T15:14:05Z",
  "notes": "Warmup behavior within expected bounds"
}

Contacts and escalation
----------------------
- Primary owner: eng-platform/operators (oncall roster)
- Secondary: eng-serving-runtime oncall
- For CI gating failures escalate to release-engineering lead.

Change history
--------------
- 2025-03-12: Initial catalog and SCN-001..SCN-003 entries (Maya Chen).
- 2025-09-18: Added SCN-004 tenant throttle scenario and gating rules (Rafael Ortiz).
- 2026-02-02: Added kernel-switch example and clarified verification PromQLs (Sabrina Li).

Related runbooks and docs
------------------------

payload.page_title: Runbook Writing and Telemetry Bootcamp Curriculum — Operator Training

sections.body:
Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router).

Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

1. Produce a runbook that contains a clear escalation path, data-driven detection predicates, and an operator checklist.
2. Write two telemetry queries (one metric-based, one log-based) that reliably surface the condition the runbook describes.
3. Create a synthetic verification (unit) that validates the runbook’s detection predicates against a small replay dataset.
4. Implement a post-incident update cycle and link to the action in the runbook so it can be closed by the owner.

Curriculum overview (3-day instructor-led)

Day 0 — Prework (self-paced)
- Read: "Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines" (required).
- Complete a short quiz on SLO definitions and common platform failure modes.
- Setup: access to Grafana/Tempo, Kibana, and a sandbox tenant. Confirm permissions with infra-oncall.

Day 1 — Foundations and detection
- Morning: Lecture (1.5 hr) — Runbook structure and the telemetry-first principle.
  - Sections: Summary, Impact, Detection (metric + log predicates), Immediate actions, Escalation, Rollback, Postmortem link.
  - Example services: kv-prefix-cache, dynamic-allocator, model-variant-router.
- Lab (2.5 hr): Write detection predicates for a synthetic latency spike:
  1) Metric predicate: p95 latency > 300ms for 5m AND error rate > 1% for 2m.
  2) Log predicate: queries that include "kv-cache:miss" and "eviction-reason=reshuffle" for >50 events in 10m.
- Homework: Author a first draft runbook for a provided scenario.

Day 2 — Triage, actions, and testability
- Morning: Workshop (2 hr) — Mapping telemetry to operator actions.
  - Instrumentation checklist: SLI names, tag conventions (region, tenant_id, model_variant), and minimum retention expectations (30 days for alerts, 90 days for postmortem traces).
  - Ownership patterns: primary, secondary, oncall-runbook-maintainer.
- Lab (3 hr): Implement a synthetic verification for the runbook detection predicates using the synthetic-replay harness.
  - Deliverable: three test cases (baseline, transient spike, persistent degradation).
- Evening: Peer review session — teams exchange runbooks and provide 3 actionable comments.

Day 3 — Escalation, de-escalation, and lifecycle
- Morning: Tabletop simulation (2 hr) — live incident with operator rotation. Measured outcomes: time to detection, time to mitigate, number of escalations, checklist completeness.
- Afternoon: Retrospective (1.5 hr) — calibrate SLOs and adjust detection thresholds.
- Closing: Runbook merge checklist and post-incident update procedure.

Assessment and certification

- Pass criteria: runbook accepted in repo (PR merged), synthetic verification green, and at least one successful tabletop participation.
- Certificate: "Telemetry-Driven Runbook Author (Redwood)" valid for 18 months. Re-certification: 2-hour refresher + one tabletop.

Delivery model and resourcing

- Instructor: Platform training lead (approx. 1 dedicated trainer per cohort of 12).
- Duration: 3 days (24 total hours including pre/post work).
- Environment: sandbox cluster with one copy of kv-prefix-cache and dynamic-allocator seeded with synthetic load.
- Tools: Grafana (dashboards pre-built), Loki/Kibana, Tempo (trace slices), synthetic-replay harness (repo: infra/synthetic-replay).

Runbook template (required fields)

1) Title (single line)
2) Summary (1–2 sentences) — short impact statement
3) Owner (primary, secondary) — team and pager alias
4) Impact and user-visible symptoms — list
5) Detection
   - Metric predicate (exact expression)
   - Log predicate (example query)
   - Trace pattern (optional)
6) Immediate mitigation steps (numbered)
7) Escalation path (names/roles and contact method)
8) Safe rollback / service-level de-escalation (how to revert changes)
9) Diagnostics checklist (commands, queries, dashboard links)
10) Post-incident required actions (TTR SLA for update: 7 days)
11) Verification tests (links to synthetic tests)
12) Related runbooks and runbook-ids

Required telemetry examples (copyable)

- Metric predicate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job="kv-prefix-cache",le="0.3"}[5m])) by (region) / sum(rate(request_duration_ms_count{job="kv-prefix-cache"}[5m])) by (region) > 0.95
- Log predicate (Loki):
  {app="kv-prefix-cache",env="prod"} |= "kv-cache:miss" | json | tenant_id!="" | count_over_time(10m) > 50
- Trace predicate (Tempo/trace): search for spans with operation.name =~ "kv-prefix-cache.*evict" and duration > 100ms, aggregated by tenant_id.

Synthetic verification example (bash)

- Reproduce a persistent-degradation case with synthetic-replay:
  1) ./synthetic-replay --scenario=kv-cache-eviction-heavy --duration=15m --tenants=10
  2) Wait for PromQL predicate to evaluate true in the sandbox (check metrics-exporter).
  3) Run owner diagnostics script: tools/diagnostics/kv-cache-inspect.sh --tenant <id>

Tabletop scenarios (catalog)

- KV cache shard reshuffle during black-box warmup
- Region-specific allocator starvation (spot preemption cascade)
- Model-variant fallback thrash causing token-cost spikes
- Multi-tenant cold-cache cold-start causing onboarding failures

Retention and SLO guidance for runbooks

- Telemetry retention required for runbook validation: metrics 30d, logs 90d, traces 90d.
- Alert SLO: detection-to-acknowledge median <= 3m for SEV2, median <= 1m for SEV1 during business hours.
- Escalation target: oncall primary owns initial mitigation within 15m of alert for SEV1.

Merge checklist (PR to runbook repo)

1) Runbook filled using template and linked to service metadata (service ID, repo).
2) At least one synthetic verification included and green in CI.
3) Two reviewers from different teams approved (one operator, one service owner).
4) Dashboard links present and dashboards annotated with threshold panels.

Ownership and follow-up

- Course owner: Priya Kapoor (eng-platform training). Contact: priya@redwood.ai (internal).
- Curriculum reviewers: see metadata above.
- Quarterly review: curriculum and scenario catalog reviewed each quarter; runbook templates updated at least annually.

Appendix A — Example telemetry queries and dashboard panels

- Grafana panel: "kv-prefix-cache p95 by region"
  - PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- Alert rule: "kv-cache-p95-region-high"
  - Expression: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region)) > 0.3
  - For: 5m, Labels: severity=SEV2, owner=kv-cache-team

- Example debug command (operator):
  - kubectl -n platform logs -l app=kv-prefix-cache --since=15m | jq -r '.message' | grep eviction

Related pages and templates

- Runbook authoring guidelines (required pre-read) — /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/runbook-authoring-and-maintenance-guidelines-2025
- Synthetic-replay repository — infra/synthetic-replay (internal git)

Revision history

- 2025-09-10: Created by Priya Kapoor (initial curriculum draft).
- 2025-11-02: Added PromQL examples and tabletop scenarios (reviewers: Ethan, Marta).
- 2026-02-15: Adjusted assessment criteria and certification validity (finalized).

payload.page_title: Observability Playground & Simulation Lab — Setup Guide

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the recommended procedure to provision, configure, and operate an Observability Playground: a repeatable, low-cost sandbox that platform operators and SREs use to run controlled degradation, telemetry injection, and tenant-safety simulation experiments. The Playground is intended for operator training, dashboard verification, alert tuning, and pre-rollout validation of runtime changes.

Goals

- Provide a safe, reproducible environment to validate dashboards, alerting rules, and degradation playbooks.
- Enable deterministic injection of degradation signals (latency, error rates, token-cost spikes) tied to synthetic tenants.
- Offer easy cleanup and cost controls so experiments do not affect production billing or shared capacity.

Audience

Platform oncall, SREs, platform operators, operator-training team, and product reliability engineers.

Prerequisites

1. Access: member of the `platform-operators` and `sandbox-admins` groups.
2. Cloud project: a dedicated Playground cloud project with isolated VPC and limited GPU quota.
3. Redis or KV: a local-backed test KV instance (we recommend a small-memory redis-playground cluster).
4. Helm + kubectl: client at platform standard versions (kubectl 1.26, helm 3.9).
5. Workspace: short-lived credentials via vault path `secret/playground/operators`.

Architecture (text diagram)

- Synthetic traffic generator (k8s job) -> Playground ingress (ingress-nginx) -> API route layer (service-mock) -> runtime-mock (prefetcher, kv-cache) -> metrics exporter (statsd/prometheus)
- Telemetry path: metrics -> Prometheus (playground) -> Tempo (traces) -> Loki (logs) -> Grafana (dashboards)

Quick provision checklist

1) Bootstrap cloud project
   - Create project: `rcli projects create --name=observability-playground-<team>-<date>`
   - Apply budget alert: cloud console -> budgets -> threshold 10% of monthly dev budget
2) Create k8s namespace
   - `kubectl create ns observability-playground`
3) Install playground chart
   - `helm repo add rwood-playground https://charts.redwood-inference.net/playground`
   - `helm install playground rwood-playground/playground --namespace observability-playground -f playground-values.yaml`

Recommended playground-values.yaml (example)

apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
metadata:
  name: playground-values
spec:
  ingester:
    replicaCount: 1
  simGenerator:
    cpuRequest: "200m"
    memoryRequest: "256Mi"
    qps: 50
  telemetry:
    prometheus:
      retention: 72h
    loki:
      retention: 72h
  costGuard:
    enabled: true
    monthlyBudgetUsd: 50

(Use the above as a template; keep quotas deliberately small to prevent runaway costs.)

Experiment primitives

- Fault injection: add HTTP latency (ms), 5xx error rate (%), or simulated token surges (tokens/sec) at service-mock.
- Traffic shaping: workloads with different sequence length distributions (short, medium, long) and chat-pattern distributions.
- Prefetch/kv-cache toggles: enable/disable caching to validate fallback and cold-start dashboards.
- Multi-variant routing: route a percentage of requests to a "slow" model variant to test degradation dashboards.

Dashboard and alert onboarding

1. Import dashboard JSON: Grafana -> + -> Import -> `playground-degradation-lab.json` (attached to this page in attachments).
2. Critical panels to verify:
   - Token per request distribution
   - 95th/99th tail latency by tenant
   - KV cache hit-rate by prefix
   - In-flight batches and batch size histogram
3. Alert rules to test:
   - token_cost_spike_playground: trigger when tokens/sec > 3x baseline for > 2m
   - playground_tail_latency_slo: trigger when p99 latency > 1200ms for 5m
4. Verification steps:
   - Start baseline generator: `kubectl apply -f syn-gen-baseline.yaml`
   - Run spike job: `kubectl apply -f syn-gen-token-spike.yaml`
   - Confirm Grafana panels display corresponding signal within 60-90s (Prometheus scrape + Grafana refresh)

Operator runbook (for a standard degradation experiment)

1. Create experiment ticket in the Operator Playground board, fill experiments template (see table below).
2. Provision the lab (Bootstrap checklist).
3. Start baseline traffic and capture baseline metrics (export to /tmp/playground-baseline-<ts>.json).
4. Announce experiment window in #platform-ops (duration and rollback triggers).
5. Run injection with a single toggle (latency OR error OR token spike); do not combine primitives on first run.
6. Observe dashboards for 10 minutes; if alerts fire, follow the Alert Triage Checklist.
7. Tear down injection and run cooldown for 15 minutes.
8. Archive artifacts and retrospective notes to the ticket.

Experiment template (copy into ticket)

- Title: <short description>
- Owner: <operator name>
- Window: <UTC start/end>
- Primitive: latency | error | token_spike | cache_toggle | routing_variant
- Expected impact: <p50/p95/p99 changes, tokens/sec change>
- Safety gates: list of alerts/thresholds that will cause immediate abort
- Cleanup steps: k8s job deletion, costGuard reset, KV flush

Safety & cost controls

Table: Minimum enforced guardrails

| Guardrail                     | Value / Command                                   |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Monthly budget (USD)         | 50 (playground-values.yaml -> costGuard.monthlyBudgetUsd) |
| Max GPU count                | 0 (CPU-only by default)                            |
| Max QPS per tenant           | 200                                               |
| Alert auto-abort             | If token_cost_spike_playground fires twice in 24h |

Cleanup and post-experiment

- Run `kubectl delete -f syn-gen-*.yaml` to stop generators.
- Remove any persisted KV state: `redis-cli -h $REDIS_HOST FLUSHALL` (playground-only cluster).
- Reset Prometheus retention if exceeded and rotate test indices in Loki.
- Attach artifacts (dashboards snapshot, traces, metrics export) to the experiment ticket.

Practical examples and CLI snippets

- Start single tenant latency inject (example):
  curl -X POST http://service-mock.playground.svc.cluster.local/inject -d '{"type":"latency","ms":350,"tenant":"sim-0"}'

- Run token surge generator (k8s job YAML snippet):
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: token-surge-2024-11
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: surge
          image: rwood/playground-sim:latest
          args: ["--mode=token-surge","--qps=450","--tenant=sim-burst"]
        restartPolicy: Never

Oncall verification checklist (fast triage)

1. Confirm whether alerts are Playground-labeled; if so, follow Playground runbook rather than production runbook.
2. Check costGuard dashboard for unexpected spend.
3. If tenant-affecting alert occurs in production, escalate to production runbook immediately.
4. Document time-to-detect and time-to-mitigate in the ticket.

Responsibilities & ownership

- Owner team: engineering
- Primary owner: Avery Chen (Platform Reliability) — avery.chen@redwood.ai
- Secondary owners: Platform Ops Training (rotation), SRE triage oncall

Reviewers

- Miguel Ortega
- Priya Patel
- Elena Smirnova

Labels

- observability
- playground
- operator-training
- synthetic-testing
- dashboards

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/preemptible-workload-graceful-handback-and-notification-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/prefetch-experiment-validation-cookbook-2025

Retrospective & continuous improvement

- After each experiment add a short retro: what telemetry missed the signal, what panels were noisy, what alert thresholds were too sensitive.
- Weekly practice: run one 30-minute desktop exercise in the Playground and record time-to-detect metrics

Roadmap (next 12 months)

- Q1 2025: Add automated experiment runner with parametrized scenarios and reproducible seeds.
- Q2 2025: Integrate small synthetic model variants (quantized) to test end-to-end model swap fallbacks.
- Q3 2025: Cost-aware experiment scheduler that enforces daily budget and operator quotas.

Attachments

- playground-degradation-lab.json (Grafana dashboard)
- syn-gen-baseline.yaml, syn-gen-token-spike.yaml (k8s job templates)

Confidentiality

internal

Last notes

This guide is intentionally pragmatic: keep experiments small, iterate, and record each result. The Observability Playground is a critical training surface to avoid surprises when similar signals appear in production.

payload.page_title: Infrastructure Telemetry Consumer Registry & Ownership Matrix

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the canonical registry for consumers of infrastructure telemetry at Redwood Inference, the ownership matrix for telemetry producers and consumers, and the processes to register, change, or retire telemetry contracts. The goal is to reduce alert fatigue, prevent duplicate dashboards, and ensure clear oncall responsibilities for metrics, logs, and traces.

Scope
- Applies to all infrastructure and platform teams that produce or consume platform-level telemetry (metrics, logs, traces, events).
- Consumer types covered: dashboards, alerting rules, SLO reports, cost dashboards, and ML service profiling jobs.
- Out of scope: application-specific business metrics owned by product teams (see related product metrics governance).

Why this matters
- Prevents drift: multiple teams building different dashboards for the same signal without shared context.
- Ensures ownership: clear pager/responsibility for alerts tied to infra signals.
- Improves signal hygiene: standard labels and contracts reduce false positives.

Registry design & schema
The registry is a lightweight catalog stored in Git (infra/telemetry-registry/) and mirrored to the internal Confluence index. Each entry follows the schema below. Entries are YAML files; the registry index in Confluence is a human-readable view of that catalog.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
---
name: gpu-pool-utilization
signal_type: metric
producer_service: gpu-pool-manager
primary_owner: infra-gpu-team
secondary_owner: serving-runtime
consumer_examples: [cost-dashboard, autoscaler, oncall-alert]
label_contract: ['env', 'region', 'pool_id', 'job_type']
ingestion_tier: core
alertable: true
alert_owners: [infra-gpu-oncall]
retention_policy: 90d
change_window: business-hours
notes: "Primary metric for capacity and autoscaling decisions."
---
sections.heading: Registry entry (YAML) example (for reference)

sections.body:
- name: short identifier for the signal (snake_case).
- signal_type: metric | log | trace | event.
- producer_service: canonical service name that emits the signal.
- primary_owner / secondary_owner: team names for operational ownership.
- consumer_examples: common consumers to aid impact analysis.
- label_contract: required labels/tags and their semantics.
- ingestion_tier: core | recommended | experimental (impacts retention & SLA).
- alertable: whether alerts should be permitted directly against this signal.
- alert_owners: oncall group(s) to page; must match SRE oncall rosters.
- retention_policy: default retention.
- change_window: preferred times for breaking changes.
- notes: free-form guidance.

Consumer tiers and guidance
- Tier 0 (core): signals required for cluster health, capacity, billing accuracy. Producers must maintain labeling and a 90-day retention. Alertable by default; any alert must be routed to primary owner.
- Tier 1 (recommended): useful operational signals; 30–90 day retention; preferred to be consumed via shared dashboards rather than custom copies.
- Tier 2 (experimental): short-term signals for feature work; 7–30 day retention; no alerts without explicit approval from producer.

Onboarding process (step-by-step)
1. Developer creates a registry YAML in infra/telemetry-registry/{signal-name}.yaml with required fields.
2. Open a Git PR: include sample queries (PromQL/SQL) and an example dashboard panel.
3. Change owner(s) add reviewer(s) from producer and consumer teams.
4. CI checks run: label contract verification, required retention and tier rules.
5. After approvals, merge; the Confluence index auto-updates within 10 minutes.
6. Notify on Slack channel #telemetry-registry with a link to the PR and the dashboard example.

CLI shortcuts (examples)
- Create stub entry: infra-tool telemetry init --name gpu-pool-utilization --type metric --producer gpu-pool-manager
- Validate entry: infra-tool telemetry validate path/to/file.yaml
- List conflicts: infra-tool telemetry conflicts --signal gpu-pool-utilization

Telemetry contracts and backward-compatibility rules
- Producers must not remove required labels without a deprecation notice in the registry and a 2-week migration window.
- Remove or rename metrics only after: (a) registry update, (b) consumers notified, (c) migration runbook published, (d) 2-week wait period unless emergency.
- If a metric changes type (gauge -> counter) the producer must create a new metric name and mark the old one deprecated.

Alerting and dashboard standards
- Naming convention for alerts: svc.signal.short_description (e.g., gpu-pool-manager.utilization.high).
- Alert severity mapping: Sev1 (page) = P99 latency > 2x target OR sustained GPU pool failure of >2 regions; Sev2 (email + Slack) = transient capacity degradation; Sev3 (ticket) = minor deviation with auto-retry.
- Dashboard panel conventions: title = "{service} — {signal} — {operation}", panel description includes link to registry entry, producer owner, and example query.
- Rate limit alerts per signal: maximum of 3 unique pager rules per core signal. If more are needed, consolidate.

Ownership matrix (human-readable table)
| Signal / Service | Primary team | Secondary team | Pager group | Notes |
|------------------|--------------|----------------|-------------|-------|
| gpu-pool-utilization | infra-gpu-team | serving-runtime | infra-gpu-oncall | affects autoscaler and cost dashboards |
| runtime.latency.p99 | serving-runtime | infra-sre | runtime-oncall | High business impact; linked to SLA dashboards |
| storage.iops.threshold | infra-storage | data-platform | infra-storage-oncall | Pager only for sustained degradation > 5m |

Runbook for breaking changes (producer responsibilities)
- Prepare a migration playbook: include queries for identifying consumers, recommended client changes, and rollback steps.
- Coordinate: schedule change during the registry change_window and post to #deployments and #telemetry-registry.
- Run synthetic checks: after change, run 15-minute synthetic checks for core signals to verify no regressions.
- Rollback plan: documented command(s) and expected RTO.

Incident playbook (consumer-facing guidance)
1. Verify the signal: validate queries and labels match registry contract.
2. Escalate: if the pager group matches the registry, follow their oncall steps; otherwise, notify producer primary and open an incident.
3. Short-term mitigations: add temporary dedup or mute rules (documented and timeboxed).
4. Post-incident: add lessons to the registry notes and, if needed, propose schema/label changes via a PR.

Enforcement and CI checks
- The telemetry CI validates: label_contract present, ingestion_tier used correctly, retention defined, and alertable flag consistency.
- PRs that change label_contract require signoff from both primary and secondary owners.

Dashboards & alert hygiene library
- We maintain a panel library (grafana/panels/shared) with vetted visualizations for common signal types. Consumers should prefer building dashboards from library panels rather than ad-hoc panels.
- Shared dashboard ownership: dashboards derived from core signals should include the producer team as watcher and have a documented owner in the dashboard metadata.

Migration & roadmap (next 12 months)
- Q1 2025: complete registry seeding for all core infra signals and run a cross-team audit.
- Q3 2025: enforce CI gate preventing alerts on unregistered signals.
- Q4 2025: build a lightweight UI for telemetry dependency graphs (visualize producers -> consumers).
- 2026: integrate registry with incident automation to auto-open tickets for unregistered consumers.

Operational ownership & contacts
- Registry maintainer: infra-tooling (oncall rota) — infra-tooling@redwood.example.com
- Governance board: Platform Observability Guild: Aisha Kapoor, Miguel Santos, Claire Bennett (rotating chair).

Appendices
A. Example PromQL snippets used in PRs:
- GPU utilization (99th percentile over 5m):
  max_over_time(gpu_utilization_percent[5m])
- Node CPU saturation (per region):
  sum(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!='idle'}[5m])) by (region) / sum(machine_cpu_cores) by (region)

B. Dashboard metadata template (JSON) to include in PR:
{
  "title": "{service} - {signal} - example panel",
  "query": "<insert PromQL>",
  "registry_link": "<link>",
  "owner": "team-name"
}

C. Frequently asked questions
- Q: Who can create registry entries?
  A: Any engineer; entries require at least the producer team member as reviewer before merge.
- Q: What if a consumer needs a modified label?
  A: File a PR to adjust the label_contract. Producers must approve; changes follow the standard window.

D. Related policies and runbooks
- Metric deprecation policy (link in repo).
- Oncall escalation playbook (see eng-platform/oncall-and-incident-response).

E. Change log (summary)
- 2024-09-15: Initial draft and registry schema published.
- 2025-06-03: Added ingestion_tier and experimental retention guidance.
- 2026-01-10: Introduced CLI examples and enforcement roadmap.

If you have questions or want to propose a bulk migration of signals, please open a PR against infra/telemetry-registry and ping #telemetry-registry.

payload.page_title: Operational Scenarios Run Matrix — Platform Team Playbook

sections.body: This page provides a prescriptive, scenario-driven run matrix for platform engineers and on-call responders. It consolidates detection signals, immediate mitigation steps, service owners, dashboard panels to inspect, and escalation criteria for the most frequent operational scenarios we observe across Redwood’s serving runtime and platform stack.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Purpose: Reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) by giving responders a short, prioritized checklist tailored to each scenario.
- Scope: Platform control plane, serving runtime (GPU pools, batching layer, KV/prefix cache), routing and queuing, observability and billing pipelines. Does NOT cover application-level business logic outages (see customer-facing product runbooks).
- Audience: Platform SREs, runtime engineers, on-call rotations, incident commanders.
sections.heading: Purpose and scope

sections.body:
- Platform SRE (pager): oncall-platform@redwood.com
- Serving Runtime (pager): oncall-runtime@redwood.com
- Capacity/Autoscale: capacity-ops@redwood.com
- Escalation chain: oncall -> senior oncall -> runtime lead -> engineering manager -> incident commander (IC)
sections.heading: Owners and contact matrix

sections.body:
1) Identify the scenario by matching the top-level trigger (alerts or user reports).
2) Follow the Immediate Triage checklist for the scenario verbatim where possible.
3) Run the short investigation queries listed. If the problem is not resolved within the Fast Mitigation Window, escalate per escalation thresholds.
4) For any mitigation that alters routing, capacity, or model variants, record the change in the incident timeline and notify product stakeholders.
sections.heading: How to use this matrix

sections.body:
| Scenario ID | Trigger (typical alert) | Primary owner | Fast mitigation (first 10 min) | Escalation threshold | Dashboard panels to inspect |
| S-01 | Tenant foreground tail latency > 2x SLO for > 3m | Platform SRE | 1) Check per-tenant SLI panels 2) Validate batching queue length 3) Failover to lower-latency model variant for impacted tenant | If latency > 2x SLO for 15m or > 5% request error rate -> escalate to runtime lead | latency-by-tenant, batching-queue-depth, model-variant-calls |
| S-02 | GPU pool eviction or preemption rate > 1% /min | GPU Fleet Team | 1) Pause new allocations to affected pool 2) Drain and reprovision nodes from burst pool 3) Switch high-priority tenants to reserved pools | If preemptions continue after 10m or capacity drop > 10% -> escalate to capacity-ops | gpu-pool-health, eviction-events, tenant-placement |
| S-03 | KV/prefix cache miss ratio spike (cache hit rate drop > 20%) | Serving Runtime | 1) Inspect cache hit heatmap 2) Temporarily increase cache memory for hot-shard 3) Enable prefix-caching fallback for prioritized routes | If hit-rate recovers < 10% within 5m -> escalate to runtime lead | kv-cache-hitrate, prefix-cache-errors, request-latency-by-route |
| S-04 | Routing controller error budget burn (excess 5xx count) | Platform SRE | 1) Validate routing policy logs 2) Toggle safe-mode routing (prefer fallback variants) 3) Throttle non-critical background workloads | If 5xx persists > 10m or error budget > 40% -> escalate to oncall-runtime | routing-controller-errors, 5xx-rate-by-route, traffic-split-overview |
| S-05 | Cost anomaly: token spend spike > 3x baseline for a tenant | Finance + Platform | 1) Freeze high-cost tenant routes (soft block) 2) Switch tenant to cheaper model-quantization profile 3) Notify customer-success for billing hold | If unusual spend continues > 30min or affects multiple tenants -> notify finance and escalate to manager | token-cost-by-tenant, model-profile-usage, billing-alerts |

Detailed scenario playbook: S-03 KV/prefix cache miss spike
- Detection signals:
  - Grafana alert: kv_prefix_cache_hitrate_drop (threshold: 20% relative drop sustained > 2m)
  - An uptick in per-request end-to-end latency for short prompts (P95 increase)

- Fast triage (0–10 minutes):
  1) Open dashboards: kv-cache-hitrate (panel), prefix-cache-errors (panel), request-latency-by-route (panel).
  2) Run the query (PromQL):
     sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total[1m])) / (sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total[1m])) + sum(rate(kv_cache_misses_total[1m])))
  3) Identify hot shards: top 5 shard IDs by miss rate.
  4) Apply temporary cache increase for shard X (example CLI):
     rctl cache set --shard X --memory 12GB --ttl 600s
  5) If memory change not available, enable prefix fallbacks for critical routes:
     rctl routing set --route <route-id> --prefix-cache-fallback enabled

- Fast mitigation window (10–30 minutes):
  - Monitor for hit-rate recovery to within 5% of baseline. If recovered, keep changes and create a short follow-up ticket to analyze root cause.
  - If not recovered, snapshot cache eviction metrics and escalate.

- Post-incident remediation checklist:
1) Revert temporary cache allocations if they cause cross-tenant memory pressure.
