payload.page_title: SLO-driven session slicing and cost localization playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: Provide an operator- and product-friendly playbook for slicing long LLM sessions (chat or multi-turn inference) into runtime-aligned chunks that preserve user-perceived quality while minimizing cross-tenant cost leakage. This doc ties SLOs to concrete slicing heuristics, telemetry dashboards, alert thresholds, and an incident runbook for mis-slicing-induced regressions.

Scope
- Applies to: Redwood hosted API and Dedicated routing layers that perform server-side batching, KV/prefix caching, and warmset affinity.
- Excludes: client-side truncation policies (client SDKs own that) and model-training pipelines.

Definitions
- Session slice: a contiguous sequence of tokens within a user session that is treated as a single inference request by the serving runtime (including batching and KV cache semantics).
- Cost localization: the process of ensuring token/compute costs are attributed and limited to the session/tenant that generated them (queued prefetches, cache warming, and auxiliary reranks included).
- Quality SLO: percent of requests where first-token latency < 150ms and final-response perplexity delta vs baseline model < 5% on canonical prompt set.

Why slicing matters
- Large sessions produce hot KV traces that force long-lived warmsets and biased batch shapes -> increased tail latency and per-token cost.
- Naive slicing (fixed token windows) can break coherence for system prompts, tool calling contexts, and tool state.
- Good slicing reduces redundant compute, improves batch packing, and makes cost attribution tractable across multi-tenant pools.

High-level design principles
1) SLO-first: choose slice boundaries so that the 95th/99th tail of latency stays within SLO while keeping quality regression < step budget.
2) Semantic-aware boundaries: prefer semantic cut points (turn boundaries, tool-call boundaries) over fixed token counts.
3) Conservative cache semantics: maintain a compact prefix copy for short-range coherence and a looser long-term reference for conversational context.
4) Localize prefetches and warmups with tenant credits to avoid cross-tenant cost bleeding.

Heuristics and operator knobs (recommended defaults)
- Default max-slice-tokens: 1024 for chat sessions with existing context < 3k tokens; reduce to 512 for cross-tenant-mixed pools.
- Soft boundary detection: apply sentence/turn break heuristic (stop-token + punctuation) with minimum lookback 32 tokens.
- Tool-call pinning: when a tool call is present in the last 128 tokens, extend slice to include tool output framing to preserve continuity.
- KV cache lifespan: short-lived slices -> kv-prefix-ttl = 15s; for heavyweight sessions with streaming > set to 120s + operator approval.
- Prefetch budget per-tenant: 5 warmset prefetches / minute by default; can be increased for Dedicated customers under committed capacity.

Telemetry and dashboards (recommended metrics)
- Slice metrics (per-slice): slice_tokens, slice_duration_ms, batch_size_at_slice, kv_hits_at_slice, prefetch_count, tenant_credit_used.
- Quality signals (per-session): user_prompt_loss_delta, next_token_accuracy_sample, tool-call-success-rate.
- Cost signals: tokens_charged_per_slice, gpu_ms_per_slice, prefetch_gpu_ms.
- SLOs and thresholds (dashboard rows):

Table: recommended alert thresholds
| metric | scope | warning | critical | rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| first_token_latency_p95 | global | 120ms | 150ms | Catch tail growth early |
| slice_kv_hit_rate | tenant | 65% | 45% | Low hit rate -> wasted compute |
| prefetch_gpu_ms/tenant_min | tenant | 300ms/min | 800ms/min | Indicates cost leakage |
| session_quality_regression | cohort | 2% | 5% | Protect user experience |

Dashboard layout guidance
- Cluster-level overview: SLO burn rate, aggregate slice tokens, median batch size, cross-tenant prefetch heatmap.
- Tenant drilldown: per-tenant slice histogram, recent regression examples with prompts, tenant credit balance.
- Investigation panes: trace links to span-level batch composition, KV-shard map, and kernel switch events.

Runbook: investigating a slicing-induced regression (step-by-step)
1) Triage the alert: identify which signal tripped (latency vs quality vs cost).
2) Capture a reproducible session: use synthetic-replay harness to re-run the last 15 slices with the exact model variant and routing policy. CLI: rw-replay --session-id <id> --model <variant> --limit 15
3) Inspect traces: open the batch composition view; look for high variance in batch_size_at_slice or frequent kernel-switch spans.
4) KV analysis: check kv_reads vs kv_misses for that tenant; if kv_misses > 40% investigate prefix TTL and shard locality.
5) If user-quality is degraded: compare user_prompt_loss_delta across slices. If > 3%, mark rollback flag and open model-variant fallback.
6) Mitigation options (ordered):
   a) Fast rollback of slice-policy: set default max-slice-tokens -> 256 for the tenant (operator CLI).
   b) Temporarily disable prefetch for tenant: tenant-config set --no-prefetch <tenant-id>.
   c) Increase kv-prefix-ttl for session affinity windows in the region while adding guard rails to tenant credits.
7) Post-mitigation monitoring: monitor the SLO burn and run synthetic replay for 30 minutes.
8) Postmortem: assign action items and update the slice heuristic parameters if a regression is confirmed.

Operator CLI examples
- Toggle conservative slicing for a tenant:
  rw-tenant-config update <tenant-id> --max-slice-tokens 256 --kv-prefix-ttl 60
- Pause prefetching for a region:
  rw-runtime set-prefetch --region eu-west-1 --enabled false --reason "investigating slice regression"
- Run a session replay (developer sandbox):
  rw-replay --session-id s_92b3 --model rdx-v1.3-quant --trace > replay.log

Evaluation and regression guardrails
- Every change to slice heuristics must go through: unit tests (synthetic workload), canary (1% traffic for 24h), and an automated regression-check job against the canonical prompt set.
- Regression signal gating: do not roll a slicing parameter change to >10% traffic unless session_quality_regression < 1% over canary window and first_token_latency_p95 improvement > 10ms.

Post-incident retrospective checklist
- What happened: timeline of slice-policy changes, rollout windows, and affected tenants.
- Why: root cause (heuristic drift, model change, unexpected long-turn patterns).
- Detection: which dashboard/alert first surfaced issue and time-to-detect.
- Mitigation effectiveness: which operator action (CLI rollback, prefetch pause) produced most improvement and time-to-stabilize.
- Action items: code owner, ETA, priority, verification steps.

Roadmap items (next 12 months)
- Q1: launch semantic-turn-boundary detector (ML small model within gateway) to reduce unnecessary slice extensions.
- Q2: tenant-prefetch-crediting feature + UI in Console for Dedicated customers.
- Q3: integrate slice-cost-attribution into billing pipeline for per-slice tagging.
- Q4: automated slice-safety guard implemented in runtime to prevent slice heuristics from producing > 2x cost variance vs baseline.

Ownership and contacts
- Product owner: Priya Rao (eng-platform - runtime economics).
- Tech lead: Maya Chen (runtime heuristics).
- Oncall rotation: platform-operator oncall (pager duty: #platform-ops).

Related files and references
- See predictive-batching-routing-roadmap for planned scheduler hooks.
- See token-cost-attribution-and-explainable-trace-playbook for cost instrumentation primitives.

Appendix: example JSON slice-policy config
{
  "slice_policy_name": "semantic-default",
  "max_slice_tokens": "1024",
  "min_sentence_lookback": "32",
  "tool_call_extension_tokens": "128",
  "kv_prefix_ttl_seconds": "15",
  "prefetch_budget_per_minute": "5",
  "tenant_override_allowed": "true"
}

Notes and changelog
- 2026-03-02: initial draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-06-10: added CLI mitigation steps after Q2 incident.
- 2026-11-15: published after review; added roadmap Q4 safety guard and conservative defaults.

payload.page_title: Resilience Responsibility Canvas and Rollback Primer

sections.body:
Purpose:

This page provides a compact, actionable canvas teams must complete for any platform service before major rollouts. It unifies ownership declarations, bounded-context mappings, mandatory dashboard artifacts, and a short, operator-focused rollback primer. The intent is to reduce ambiguity during incidents and accelerate safe remediation without prescribing a single tooling path.

Scope:
- Applies to services in eng-platform: control plane components, runtime subsystems, and cross-cutting platform helpers (prefetch, cache coordinator, allocator).
- Not for one-off developer experiments; those must use a disposable canary environment.

High-level checklist (fill before production change):
1) Service identity and impact
- Service id: e.g., allocator-cohort-manager
- Customer-visible symptoms when degraded: increased p95, 5xx, slow-start failures, token cost surge
- Blast radius estimate: single-region / single-tenant cohort / all-tenants

2) Clear ownership (must be named)
- Engineering owner (code + rollout): full name and team handle
- Platform oncall owner: rotation alias or person
- Capacity owner: team owning GPU/quota reservations
- Escalation contact (secondary): email or slack alias

3) Bounded contexts and rollback scope (map explicitly)
- Code-level rollback: revert git ref or model variant tag? (yes/no)
- Config-level rollback: feature-flag toggle, routing table change, or infra config? (specify)
- Data-level rollback: is there a schema or downstream state that would prevent simple revert? (yes/no)

4) Minimum observability surface (non-negotiable)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, requests/sec, error_rate_by_code (4xx/5xx), token/sec, cache_hit_ratio
- Traces: distributed traces with deploy_id, model_variant, tenant_id
- Synthetic probes: minute-level probe per-region and per-priority cohort (canary + user-facing)
- Log fields: request_id, deploy_id, model_version, routing_decision, error_context

Dashboard requirements (template to copy):
- Summary row: current SLOs and a 24h sparkline (p95, error_rate)
- Deploy & flags: active deploy id and feature flags with timestamps
- Traffic breakdown: tenants, regions, model variants
- Operator tools: one-click links to toggle feature-flag, start rollback job, and run prefetch script

Alerting expectations (naming and gating):
- Use pattern: platform.<service>.<signal>.<severity>
- Each alert must include: Pager policy, runbook link, diagnostic queries, and mitigation hints
- Example thresholds (adjust per-service):
  - platform.allocator.p95.p0 -> p95 > 200ms for 5m with > 10rps
  - platform.cache.hitratio.p1 -> avg(kv_cache_hit_ratio[10m]) < 0.70
  - platform.runtime.error_rate.p0 -> increase(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.005

Canary gating minimum flow (automatable):
1. Deploy to canary cohort (1% or defined tenants) behind feature flag.
2. Run warmup job for cache and any prepopulation tasks.
3. Monitor two gating signals for 15 minutes: p95 within 20% of baseline AND error_rate <= 2x baseline.
4. If gating fails, automated rollback to previous variant and create incident ticket.

Rollback primer (operator quick guide):
- When to rollback (require two corroborating signals):
  1) P0 alert (user-facing latency or errors) AND trace evidence tying deploy_id to errors
  2) Unexpected cost surge (token/sec increase) without proportional traffic increase
  3) Downstream integration failures (schema or contract breaks)

Fast rollback steps (concise):
1. Confirm scope: identify deploy_id and affected tenants. Take a dashboard screenshot.
2. Open incident channel and tag oncall and engineering owner.
3. Execute safest revert: toggle feature flag or repoint traffic to previous deploy. Prefer config toggle over infra rebuild.
4. Validate: run synthetic probes for 5–10 minutes and watch SLOs for 30 minutes.
5. If rollback cannot be applied: throttle traffic, engage capacity owner, and escalate to secondary oncall.
6. Record artifact links in incident ticket (deploy id, trace ids, dashboard snapshot).

Compact runbook template (copy into alert action):
- Name: platform.<service>.fast-revert
- Intent: immediate revert for customer-impacting deploys
- Preconditions: operator has feature-flag write and deploy rollback permission
- Commands: (examples)
  - Rollback variant (flag): curl -X POST https://flags.internal/toggle -d '{"flag":"<flag>","value":false}'
  - Rollback deploy: deployctl rollback --service <svc> --to-ref <git-sha>
  - Prefetch warmup: infra/scripts/prefetch-warmup --service <svc> --region <r>

Post-rollback actions and retro triggers:
- Required: open a retrospective ticket when any rollback occurs or any single-day SLO burn > 20%
- Postmortem must include: timeline, root-cause analysis, corrective actions, verification plan, and sign-off from engineering owner

Operational ownership matrix (copy to team pages):
- Primary oncall: first responder, executes rollback, initial comms
- Engineering owner: code fixes, roll-forward plan, postmortem author
- Capacity/infra: investigate preemptions, reallocate quotas
- Product/CS: customer impact assessment and blocking communication

Roadmap guidance (how to include in planning):
- Any planned change that touches the runtime kernel, quantization, or model-routing must include: expected latency/cost delta, fallbacks, dashboard updates, and a filled canvas before merge to main.
- Track temporary mitigations (hotfixes) in the technical debt log; each hotfix needs a scheduled durable fix within two sprints.

Retrospective template (short):
- Title: <service> rollback <date>
- Summary: what happened, impact, time to recovery
- Hypothesis: probable root cause with evidence
- Actions: owner / due date / verification steps

Appendix A — Example diagnostic queries (PromQL-like):
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- error rate: increase(http_requests_total{job=~"<service>",code=~"5.."}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total{job=~"<service>"}[5m])
- cache hit ratio: sum(kv_cache_hits[10m]) / sum(kv_cache_requests[10m])

Appendix B — Common immediate mitigations (short list):
- High latency + 5xx: rollback deploy -> increase burst pool -> enable degraded-mode routing
- Token cost spike: rollback heavy model -> throttle non-critical tenants -> enable low-cost routing
- Cache collapse: run prefetch, rebuild warmset, throttle cache-populators

Maintenance and governance:
- Document owner: Ravi Patel (platform resilience)
- Review cadence: every quarter or after any service-level rollback
- When to escalate doc-level changes to leadership: if the same service class triggers >2 rollbacks in a quarter or if mean time to recover increases across platform by >25%

How to adopt this canvas:
- Copy this page into your release ticket, complete the fields, attach intended deploy ids and feature-flag names.
- Link the completed canvas to your PR and to any alert rules created for the rollout.
- Use the runbook snippets as the first lines of your alert actions so responders can act without hunting for documentation.

payload.page_title: Workload behavior heatmap spec and query cookbook

sections.body:
Summary

This doc defines a standardized heatmap visualization and a small cookbook of queries to surface workload behavior across Redwood’s inference platform. The heatmap is intended to be a first-response surface for operators and platform engineers to quickly identify: regional hotspots, tenant-induced degradation, unusual batching profiles, and memory / KV cache pressure correlated with latency regressions.

Scope

- Systems: inference-router, request-batcher, kv-cache, model-worker, autoscaler
- Data sources: Prometheus (service metrics), ClickHouse (request traces/aggregates), logs (ELK)
- Consumers: oncall, platform SRE, runtime product managers

Motivation

Operators were repeatedly spending time building ad-hoc dashboards during incidents. A single, well-documented heatmap and query cookbook reduces cognitive load, supports consistent RCA, and enables automated alert enrichment.

Definitions and conventions

- Foreground requests: requests with priority=foreground (low-latency user-facing). SLO: p95 < 300ms, p99 < 600ms for small tokens (<=512).
- Background/batch: priority=batch. Throughput-focused; tail latencies are expected to be higher.
- Heatmap cell: intersection of (time bucket) x (dimension bucket).
- Dimensions used: service, region, model_variant, tenant_tier.

Heatmap visualization spec

1) Layout and axes
- X axis: time, rolling window default = 2h, resolution 1m (120 columns).
- Y axis: primary dimension default = service; secondary drilldown = model_variant or tenant_tier.
- Color intensity: primary metric = p95 latency (ms) for foreground requests. Alternate metric toggle = request_rate (req/s) or token_cost/s.

2) Bucketing rules
- Time bucket: 1m for 2h window, 5m for 24h overview.
- Dimension bucket: group low-cardinality values explicitly; all others collapsed into "other" after top-15.
- Missing data: render as light-grey (no telemetry).

3) Color scale (hex stops)
- 0-50ms: #00b37e (green)
- 50-150ms: #ffd166 (amber-low)
- 150-300ms: #ff8a00 (amber-high)
- 300-600ms: #ff3b30 (red)
- >600ms: #7c0a02 (dark-red)

4) Panels to include (single dashboard)
- Heatmap (primary) with service verticals
- Top 10 tenants by p95 in last 5m (table)
- Latency distribution sparkline (p50/p95/p99) per selected row
- KV cache hitrate and mem usage small time-series
- Correlated model-worker OOM and eviction events (log count)

Table: recommended thresholds and alert mapping

| Name | Heatmap threshold | Alert rule | Pager severity |
|------|-------------------|------------|----------------|
| Foreground p95 degraded | cell > 300ms for 2 consecutive minutes | metric-based alert: p95_foreground > 300ms (2m) | P1 |
| Tenant spike | tenant p95 > 600ms and token-rate increased 5x | anomaly-detection (ClickHouse) | P1 |
| Batch backlog | queue depth > 10x baseline for 5m | synthetic SLI breach | P2 |
| KV-cache eviction rate | evictions/s > 100 | metric alert | P2 |

Query cookbook (examples)

1) Prometheus: p95 foreground latency per service (PromQL)
- Query (5m lookback, use histograms):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{env=\"prod\",priority=\"foreground\"}[5m])) by (le, service))

2) Prometheus: service x region heatmap matrix (timeseries list)
- Query (timeseries per (service,region)):
  sum(rate(request_count_total{env=\"prod\"}[1m])) by (service, region)
- The dashboard engine should pivot those series into heatmap cells via the bucketing rules above.

3) ClickHouse: detect tenant p95 spike compared to baseline (SQL)
- Example:
  SELECT tenant_id,
         quantile(0.95)(latency_ms) AS p95_now,
         quantile(0.95)(latency_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_id ORDER BY event_time RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 1 HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS p95_baseline
  FROM requests
  WHERE event_time >= now() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
    AND env = 'prod'
  GROUP BY tenant_id
  HAVING p95_now > 3 * p95_baseline
  ORDER BY p95_now DESC

  Note: ClickHouse syntax varies by deployment; the intent is to compare recent p95 with 1h baseline.

4) ELK (KQL) example: find OOM or eviction log spikes correlated with model-worker
- KQL:
  service:\"model-worker\" AND (level:\"error\" OR message:/OOM|evict/i) AND @timestamp >= now-15m

5) Token-cost heatmap (aggregate tokens/s by service)
- PromQL:
  sum(rate(tokens_processed_total{env=\"prod\"}[1m])) by (service)

Operational runbook: investigating a red heatmap cell

1) Identify scope
  1. Click the cell to reveal service, time window, and top-k tenant models.
  2. If tenant list shows a single tenant responsible for >50% of requests, tag as tenant-local.

2) Quick triage (5–15 minutes)
  1. Check p99 latency for the same bucket. If p99 >> p95, suspect head-of-line or queueing.
  2. Verify model-worker CPU/GPU utilization and OOMs (metrics: model_worker_gpu_util, model_worker_oom_count).
  3. Check KV-cache hitrate; eviction spikes often correlate with latency regressions.

3) Containment steps
  1. For tenant-local spikes: apply soft throttle (tenant burst-limit) via router: POST /admin/tenants/{id}/throttle with body {\"limit_rps\": 5} (operator API).
  2. For region-wide overload: trigger autoscaler manual burst (see autoscaler runbook).

4) Remediation and postmortem
  1. Rollback any recent model or config rollout that coincides with incident.
  2. Capture queries from the heatmap and link them to a postmortem ticket and dashboard snapshot.

Visualization implementation notes (Grafana/Chronograf/Custom console)

- Data ingestion: Prometheus scrape interval 15s for router/batcher; exporters must include service, region, model_variant, tenant_tier labels.
- Pre-aggregation: we recommend a ClickHouse hourly rollup for high-cardinality tenant-level quantiles to support drift detection queries.
- Dashboard-level caching: heatmap panels should use a 20s cache to avoid overload when many operators open the dashboard.

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: Platform Observability (team: eng-platform). Primary contact: Priya Narayanan.
- Instrumentation owners per service: inference-router (team: runtime-routing), request-batcher (team: batching), kv-cache (team: cache), model-worker (team: model-runtime).
- Rollout steps:
  1. Instrument missing labels and validate via unit test (2 weeks)
  2. Deploy heatmap panel in staging and collect operator feedback (1 week)
  3. Lock thresholds and deploy to prod with 2-week monitoring window (1 week)
  4. Add automated alert enrichment (post-deploy)

Telemetry & dashboard QA checklist (table)

| Item | Check |
|------|-------|
| Label completeness | service, region, model_variant, tenant_tier present on router and batcher metrics |
| Quantile sanity | p50/p95/p99 within expected ranges for smoke tests |
| Sparsity handling | heatmap cell fallback to \"no telemetry\" tested |
| Scaling | dashboard panel load tested with 200 concurrent viewers |

Appendix: sample panel JSON (abbreviated)

- The appendix contains a small pseudo-JSON block to show mapping of series -> heatmap cells. This should be adapted to your dashboard platform.

  "time_bucket": "1m",
  "color_scale": [0,50,150,300,600]
}

Frequently asked questions

Q: Why use p95 instead of p99 for the heatmap intensity?
A: p95 provides a more stable, lower-noise signal for visual correlation across many services; once a hotspot is detected the panel shows p99/p50 sparklines for deeper investigation.

Q: How do we prevent tenant IDs from leaking to dashboards?
A: Dashboard templates should mask tenant_id or only show hashed/shortened IDs unless viewer has need-to-know and the dashboard context is restricted by RBAC.

Contact

For questions or help creating a team-specific heatmap view, contact Priya Narayanan (obs owner) or open an issue on the eng-platform board.

payload.page_title: Hot-route capacity protection — Technical Design (Hosted API + Dedicated)

sections.body:
This document describes the end-to-end design for **hot-route capacity protection** across Redwood Inference’s **Hosted API** and **Dedicated** tiers.

The objective is to prevent a small set of high-volume, high-SLA routes (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`) from causing **fleet-wide tail latency and 5xx cascades**. The system introduces:

- **Tier-aware rate limits and quotas** at the API gateway with consistent 429 semantics.
- **Priority classes** evaluated in a deterministic policy engine.
- **Admission control / controlled shedding** in routing based on real-time capacity signals.
- **Per-route budgets** that reserve capacity for enterprise traffic under pressure.
- **Observability and operational readiness** (metrics, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, incident-bot notifications).

This design is intentionally incremental: it does **not** replace the serving runtime scheduler; it adds explicit controls and signals so that the scheduler is not forced into unstable regimes.

---
sections.heading: 1. Summary

sections.body:
Historically, overload on a single hot route has caused:

- Queue buildup in shared GPU pools → **p99 latency spikes** → client retries amplify load.
- Increased timeouts → upstream cancellations → wasted compute.
- Saturation of routing and gateway resources → elevated 5xx → cascading failures.
sections.heading: 2.1 The incident pattern

sections.body:
1) No deterministic admission control to protect enterprise traffic during overload.
2) Inconsistent throttling semantics (mixed 429 payloads, unclear reason codes), making Support/SRE response slow and customers surprised.
sections.heading: The 2025-11-03 Sev1 postmortem identified two primary gaps

sections.body:
When overloaded, the system must behave like a controlled valve:

- **Enterprise**: preserve SLOs with explicit reserved budgets and predictable outcomes.
- **Best-effort/self-serve**: throttle earlier and more predictably (with clear 429s and retry guidance).
- **Fleet**: surface clear capacity signals and prevent unstable queue growth.

---
sections.heading: 2.2 Design principle

sections.body:
- Protect fleet health by preventing overload on one hot route/customer/workload shape from degrading shared pools.
- Guarantee enterprise behavior via explicit priority classes and per-route/per-tier budgets tied to SLOs.
- Deterministic, auditable policy evaluation with explainable decisions.
- Low overhead on the request path (bounded latency and cardinality).
- Observability and operational supportability (dashboards, alerts, runbooks, incident-bot).
- Progressive rollout with safe defaults and reversible flags.
sections.heading: 3.1 Goals

sections.body:
- Billing/pricing changes (only hooks/metadata are added).
- A full fairness scheduler rewrite.
- Per-token dynamic congestion pricing.

---
sections.heading: 3.2 Non-goals (for this phase)

sections.body:
- **Route**: API endpoint and method, e.g. `POST /v1/chat/completions`.
- **Route group**: a policy-level grouping for limits/budgets, e.g. `chat`, `embeddings`, `rerank`.
- **Tier**: customer entitlement tier, e.g. `enterprise`, `pro`, `starter`.
- **Priority class**: execution priority derived from tier + overrides, e.g. `P0_ENTERPRISE`, `P2_BEST_EFFORT`.
- **Budget**: a per-route-group capacity reservation/limit (requests/s, tokens/s, and/or concurrency).
- **Overload**: routing/runtime capacity signals indicate elevated risk of SLO burn (queue depth/scheduler lag/timeout rate).
- **Admission control**: routing-level decision to accept, delay, or shed requests.
- **Shedding**: deliberate rejection with a controlled 429 response and reason code.

---
sections.heading: 4. Terminology

sections.body:
- Enforce tier-aware **rate limits and quotas** with consistent 429 payloads and headers.
- Evaluate policy (priority class + budgets + allowed fallbacks) deterministically.
- Under overload:
  - Prefer admitting higher priority traffic.
  - Shed best-effort traffic first.
  - Optionally apply controlled fallback policies where explicitly allowed.
sections.heading: 5.1 Functional

sections.body:
- P50 overhead added to request path by policy evaluation: **< 2ms** in-region.
- No unbounded tag cardinality in metrics (explicit constraints in §11).
- Policy decisions must be explainable for escalations (decision log + debug endpoint).
- Rollout must be reversible per region and per account.

---
sections.heading: 5.2 Non-functional

sections.body:
1) **API Gateway** (edge)
- Authn/authz
- Rate limit + quota enforcement
- Standardized 429 response semantics
- Injects policy context (tenant/tier/route group) into downstream request headers

2) **Policy Engine** (control plane read, data plane evaluate)
- Evaluates priority class, budgets, fallback guardrails
- Produces deterministic decision object
- Logs decisions with stable identifiers (low-cardinality)

3) **Smart Routing Service**
- Applies admission control under pressure based on capacity signals
- Routes to appropriate model pool / region / variant
- Enforces “protect enterprise budget” behavior

4) **Serving Runtime + Scheduler**
- Executes inference
- Exports capacity signals (queue depth, scheduler lag, saturation signals)

5) **Telemetry pipeline + SRE dashboards**
- Aggregates per-route-group and per-tier outcomes
- Alerting tied to enterprise SLO burn and overload activation
sections.heading: 6.1 Components

sections.body:
- Control plane defines **policies** (route groups, budgets, tier mappings, overrides).
- Data plane performs **evaluation** with caching and bounded latency.

---
sections.heading: 6.2 Control plane vs data plane

sections.body:
| Tier | Priority class | Notes |
|------|----------------|------|
| enterprise | P0_ENTERPRISE | Protected under overload; reserved budgets apply |
| dedicated (contracted) | P0_ENTERPRISE | Treated as enterprise for routing admission decisions |
| pro | P1_STANDARD | Not protected by reserved budgets during severe overload |
| starter/free | P2_BEST_EFFORT | Shed early under pressure |
| internal | P0_ENTERPRISE | Guarded by allowlist + separate budgets; not a bypass |
sections.heading: 7.1 Default mapping

sections.body:
- Temporary burst exceptions (time-boxed)
- Route-specific entitlements
- “No fallback” or “Fallback allowed” constraints
sections.heading: We support explicit overrides for specific tenants

sections.body:
- `requestor` (human owner)
- `ticket_ref` (Jira/Linear)
- `expires_at`

---
sections.heading: Overrides are stored in policy config and must include

sections.body:
- `chat`: `POST /v1/chat/completions` (streaming + non-stream)
- `embeddings`: `POST /v1/embeddings`
- `rerank`: `POST /v1/rerank`
sections.heading: 8.1 Initial protected route groups (MVP)

sections.body:
Gateway derives a stable **route_id**:
- Format: `method + canonical_path`
- Canonicalization removes version noise only when explicitly configured (avoid accidental grouping).

Routing and telemetry use **route_group** as the primary dimension to avoid high cardinality.

---
sections.heading: 8.2 Route identification

sections.body:
Budgets are represented across three dimensions to match real overload patterns:

1) **Requests per second** (RPS): protects gateway/routing overhead and avoids spiky thundering herds.
2) **Estimated tokens per second** (TPS): approximates GPU compute demand.
3) **Concurrency**: caps in-flight requests to prevent runaway queues.

> Note: We use *estimated* tokens at admission time based on request fields (e.g., `max_tokens`) and conservative heuristics. Exact billing tokens are not required for admission decisions.
sections.heading: 9.1 Budget dimensions

sections.body:
Budgets are defined at the following levels (highest precedence first):

1) Tenant + route group override
2) Tenant override (applies to all route groups)
3) Tier + route group default
4) Tier default
5) Global safety caps (hard ceilings)
sections.heading: 9.2 Budget hierarchy

sections.body:
- **Reserved enterprise budget**: only P0 traffic can consume during overload.
- **Shared budget**: all tiers can consume when the system is healthy.

When healthy, P0 traffic may consume shared budget as needed. Under pressure, P0 is preferentially admitted and best-effort is constrained to protect reserved budget headroom.
sections.heading: Each route group maintains two logical partitions

sections.body:
These are examples to illustrate structure; actual values are set per region based on capacity planning.

| Route group | Tier | RPS limit | TPS limit (estimated) | Concurrency limit | Reserved? |
|------------|------|----------:|-----------------------:|------------------:|----------|
| chat | enterprise | 250 | 1.2M | 3,000 | Yes |
| chat | starter | 30 | 80k | 250 | No |
| embeddings | enterprise | 400 | 900k | 2,000 | Yes |
| embeddings | starter | 60 | 120k | 400 | No |
| rerank | enterprise | 300 | 600k | 1,500 | Yes |

---
sections.heading: 9.4 Example budget defaults (illustrative)

sections.body:
1) **Gateway** authenticates, resolves `tenant_id`, determines `tier`, determines `route_group`.
2) Gateway enforces:
   - Token-bucket rate limit (short window)
   - Quota (longer window) where applicable
3) Gateway calls **Policy Engine** (or uses cached decision) to compute:
   - priority class
   - budget keys
   - fallback guardrails
4) Gateway forwards request to **Routing** with policy context headers.
5) **Routing** evaluates real-time capacity signals + budgets and decides:
   - admit to preferred pool
   - admit with fallback (if allowed)
   - shed with 429 (overload)
6) **Runtime** processes admitted requests and emits capacity signals.
sections.heading: 10.1 High-level flow

sections.body:
- Client → Gateway: request
- Gateway → Quota service: evaluate window (cached)
- Gateway → Policy Engine: evaluate priority + budgets (cached)
- Gateway → Routing: forward with `x-rw-priority`, `x-rw-route-group`, `x-rw-budget-keys`
- Routing → Capacity signals store: read current region/pool signals
- Routing → Runtime pool: dispatch if admitted
- Routing → Gateway: 429 if shed
sections.heading: 10.2 Sequence diagram (text)

sections.body:
- `x-rw-tenant-id: tnt_...` (internal only; not forwarded beyond routing)
- `x-rw-tier: enterprise|pro|starter|internal`
- `x-rw-priority: P0_ENTERPRISE|P1_STANDARD|P2_BEST_EFFORT`
- `x-rw-route-group: chat|embeddings|rerank|other`
- `x-rw-policy-version: <hash>`
- `x-rw-budget-key: rg:<route_group>;tier:<tier>;region:<region>` (stable, low cardinality)

Security note: headers are injected server-side; external clients cannot set/override.

---
sections.heading: Gateway attaches stable headers

sections.body:
Routing uses a small set of signals designed to be reliable and low-latency:

- **Queue depth** per pool/route group (aggregated): `rw_runtime_queue_depth{pool,route_group}`
- **Scheduler lag** (ms) per pool: `rw_runtime_scheduler_lag_ms{pool}`
- **GPU saturation** (smoothed) per pool: `rw_pool_gpu_utilization{pool}`
- **Timeout / cancel rate** per route group: `rw_requests_canceled_rate{route_group,tier}`

Signals are aggregated by pool and route_group; we do not alert on per-tenant metrics.
sections.heading: 11.1 Capacity signals

sections.body:
Routing computes an overload state per (region, pool, route_group):

- **GREEN**: normal operations
- **YELLOW**: early pressure; begin throttling P2 (best-effort) to prevent queue growth
- **RED**: sustained overload; enforce enterprise reserved budgets and shed aggressively
sections.heading: 11.2 Overload states

sections.body:
- Enter YELLOW if threshold exceeded for > 30s
- Enter RED if exceeded for > 60s or if 5xx/timeouts spike
- Exit requires 2–3 minutes below thresholds to avoid flapping
sections.heading: Hysteresis

sections.body:
**GREEN**
- Admit all tiers subject to gateway rate limits/quotas.

**YELLOW**
- P0: admit; may consume reserved + shared budgets.
- P1: admit with tighter concurrency caps.
- P2: shed once route-group shared budget hits threshold (protect headroom).

**RED**
- P0: admit up to reserved budget; if reserved is exhausted, return 429 with enterprise-specific message.
- P1/P2: shed early with overload reason; no retries without backoff.
sections.heading: 11.3 Admission rules

sections.body:
We shed at routing before dispatch to runtime to avoid wasted queueing.

We only implement “delay/queue” at the gateway for short, bounded durations (future enhancement). Today, we prefer immediate 429 with explicit retry-after.

---
sections.heading: 11.4 Shedding granularity

sections.body:
- **Rate limit**: short window (e.g., per-second), token bucket; prevents microbursts.
- **Quota**: longer window (e.g., per-minute/hour/day); protects cost and broad entitlement.
sections.heading: 12.1 Rate limits vs quotas

sections.body:
1) Authn/authz
2) Route group mapping
3) Rate limit
4) Quota
5) Policy context injection
sections.heading: Order of evaluation (gateway)

sections.body:
- HTTP status: `429`
- A stable `error.code`
- A stable reason header
- A `Retry-After` or `retry_after_ms`

**Reason taxonomy**
- `quota_exceeded`: quota window exhausted
- `rate_limited`: short-window limit hit
- `overload_shed`: routing admission control shed due to overload
- `enterprise_budget_exhausted`: P0 request could not be admitted within reserved budget
- `policy_denied`: explicit policy disallow (e.g., route not allowed on tier)

**Headers**
- `x-rw-throttle-reason: <reason>`
- `x-rw-policy-version: <hash>`
- `retry-after: <seconds>` (where applicable)
sections.heading: All throttling and shedding must return
12.3 Error payload (example)

sections.body:
- `priority_class`
- `budget_keys` (stable)
- `fallback_allowed: true|false`
- `decision_tags` (bounded list)
sections.heading: Policy Engine returns a compact decision

sections.body:
- overload state
- capacity signal snapshot (coarsened)
- admit/shed decision
sections.heading: Routing logs

sections.body:
An internal admin endpoint provides “why was this request throttled?” output for on-call:
- Input: request_id / trace_id
- Output: policy decision, route group, tier, overload state, reason code
sections.heading: 13.2 Debug endpoint (internal)

sections.body:
- Restricted to on-call roles via SSO + audit logs
- No tenant data payloads returned

---
sections.heading: Access control

sections.body: Fallback is powerful but risky (quality drift, compliance constraints). For protected routes, fallback is disabled by default unless explicitly allowed.
sections.heading: 14. Fallback policy guardrails

sections.body:
- Enterprise routes default to **strict admission** (no silent model changes).
- Allow fallback only when:
  - Model family is declared compatible
  - Customer contract allows it
  - The route group is tagged `fallback_safe`
sections.heading: Rules

sections.body:
- Model variant (e.g., quantization profile)
- Pool within region
- Region fallback (only where data residency permits)

When fallback is used, we annotate responses with internal metadata and emit a metric event for audit.

---
sections.heading: Fallback dimensions

sections.body:
- Adds tier-aware limiter modules
- Standardizes 429 payloads/headers
- Emits request outcome metrics with `route_group` and `tier`
sections.heading: 15.1 Gateway

sections.body:
- Reads capacity signals at fixed cadence (e.g., 1s) from local cache
- Computes overload state with hysteresis
- Applies admission rules and budgets
- Emits overload activation annotations (for dashboards)
sections.heading: 15.2 Routing

sections.body:
- Exports queue depth and scheduler lag
- Ensures streaming termination semantics are consistent during shedding/cancellations
sections.heading: 15.3 Runtime

sections.body:
- Policy engine calls must be cacheable; routing must not block on remote calls on the hot path.
- All high-cardinality identifiers (tenant_id, request_id) must be excluded from metrics tags.

---
sections.heading: 15.4 Performance constraints

sections.body:
- `rw_requests_total{route_group,tier,outcome}` where `outcome ∈ {ok,429,5xx,timeout,canceled}`
- `rw_throttles_total{route_group,tier,reason}` where `reason` is from §12.2
- `rw_overload_state{route_group,pool}` as a gauge (0/1/2 for GREEN/YELLOW/RED)
- `rw_runtime_queue_depth{route_group,pool}`
- `rw_runtime_scheduler_lag_ms{pool}`
- `rw_admission_decisions_total{route_group,tier,decision}` where `decision ∈ {admit,shed,fallback}`
sections.heading: 16.1 Required metrics (core)

sections.body:
Allowed tags: `route_group`, `tier`, `region`, `pool`, `reason`, `decision`.

Not allowed in tags: `tenant_id`, `model`, `request_id`, `prompt_hash`, `account_name`.
sections.heading: 16.2 Cardinality guidance

sections.body:
- Enterprise p95/p99 latency vs SLO (per route_group)
- 429 rate by reason (per tier)
- Overload state timeline with annotations
- Queue depth and scheduler lag correlations
sections.heading: Dashboards must support

sections.body:
- Enterprise SLO burn-rate alerts (multi-window)
- Overload RED sustained > N minutes with enterprise latency degradation
- Shedding anomaly (e.g., P0 shedding > threshold)

---
sections.heading: Alerts

sections.body:
- `route_groups`: mapping of route_id → route_group
- `tier_mapping`: tenant_id → tier
- `priority_mapping`: tier → priority_class
- `budgets`: (tier, route_group, region) → limits
- `overrides`: tenant-specific policies with expiry
- `fallback_matrix`: allowed fallback modes per route_group and tier
sections.heading: 17.1 Policy config entities

sections.body:
```yaml
route_groups:
  "POST /v1/chat/completions": chat
  "POST /v1/embeddings": embeddings

priority_mapping:
  enterprise: P0_ENTERPRISE
  starter: P2_BEST_EFFORT

budgets:
  - tier: enterprise
    route_group: chat
    region: us-east
    rps: 250
    tps_est: 1200000
    concurrency: 3000
    reserved: true

fallback_matrix:
  chat:
    enterprise: strict
    starter: allowed_in_yellow
```

---
sections.heading: 17.2 Example (conceptual)

sections.body:
- `hot_route_protection.enabled` (global master)
- `hot_route_protection.region_enabled[us-east|eu-west|...]`
- `hot_route_protection.account_allowlist`
- `hot_route_protection.enforce_gateway_limits`
- `hot_route_protection.enforce_routing_admission`
- `hot_route_protection.enable_overload_metrics`

We also support a “shadow mode”:
- Evaluate policy + compute overload state
- Emit metrics and decision logs
- Do not shed traffic (except existing baseline limits)
sections.heading: We gate by region and allowlist

sections.body:
1) Shadow mode in one region (us-east) for all traffic
2) Enforce on allowlisted enterprise accounts for protected route groups
3) Expand to all enterprise accounts in us-east
4) Multi-region rollout (eu-west next)
5) Enable best-effort shedding policies after alert tuning
sections.heading: 18.2 Rollout phases

sections.body:
- Enterprise 429 (non-quota) > threshold
- Enterprise p99 latency regression beyond SLO guardrail
- Unexpected 5xx increase correlated with protection
sections.heading: Rollback triggers

sections.body:
1) Disable `hot_route_protection.enforce_routing_admission`
2) If needed, disable `hot_route_protection.enforce_gateway_limits` and revert to legacy limiter
3) Keep metrics enabled if safe to preserve debugging context
sections.heading: Rollback actions

sections.body:
- Confirm overload state returns GREEN (or at least shedding stops)
- Confirm enterprise p95/p99 recovers
- Confirm 429 reason distribution returns to baseline

---
sections.heading: Rollback verification

sections.body:
- Unit tests: policy evaluation determinism, budget precedence, override expiry.
- Integration tests: concurrent load with mixed tiers; verify P0 admitted while P2 sheds in YELLOW/RED.
- Load tests: simulate burst on chat; validate enterprise SLO protection and stable fleet health.
- Game day: coordinated overload injection with SRE observing dashboards and verifying alert behavior.

---
sections.heading: 19. Testing plan

sections.body:
- **Policy engine unavailable**: use cached last-known-good policy; fail closed only for explicit denies (configurable). Emit `policy_stale` metric.
- **Capacity signals stale**: degrade to conservative YELLOW behavior for best-effort; never bypass hard safety caps.
- **Metric cardinality regression**: automatic CI check + runtime guardrails; hotfix playbook.
- **Misconfigured budgets**: validation on publish; canary rollout; require SRE sign-off for enterprise changes.

---
sections.heading: 20. Failure modes and mitigations

sections.body:
- Do we need limited “bounded delay queueing” at gateway (e.g., 50–100ms) to reduce retries, or is immediate 429 preferred universally?
- Should P1 traffic ever borrow from reserved enterprise budget in GREEN? (Currently: no; reserved is logical only used under pressure.)
- Standardizing token estimation heuristics across chat/embeddings/rerank to better approximate GPU cost.

---
sections.heading: 21. Open questions

sections.body:
- Platform (gateway + policy evaluation): Ethan Park, Amara Diallo, Jordan Lee
- Routing admission control: Mina Haddad, Elena Popov
- Runtime signals: Sofia Ivanova, Julian Moore
- Observability and SLO alignment: Allison Grant, Sergio Costa, Rafael Mendes
- Support readiness and customer guidance: Dev Patel, Wei Chen

For operational procedures and incident response, see:
- Runbook: `runbook-overload-protection-and-admission-control`
- Support doc: `enterprise-priority-429-and-quota-behavior`
sections.heading: 22. Ownership

payload.page_title: Service fallback catalog and decision matrix

sections.body:
Summary

This document catalogs approved service fallback policies, the decision matrix used to choose a fallback, and operational runbook steps for applying fallbacks during production degradation. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and runtime engineers who own traffic steering, model routing, or tenant isolation.

Scope

- Applies to request routing inside Redwood Inference serving and routing layers (hosted, dedicated, and private control planes).
- Covers model/service fallbacks (model variant substitution, degraded feature mode, degraded QoS class) and not data migration or schema changes.
- Includes observability signals, alerting thresholds, ownership, and rollback criteria.

Goals

- Ensure graceful degradation with bounded user impact.
- Keep decision logic auditable and reversible.
- Minimize USD cost and token waste during fallbacks.

Terminology

- Primary: the default model or service variant receiving traffic.
- Fallback: an alternative variant or policy used when Primary fails to meet SLOs.
- Degraded Mode: feature-limited responses (no streaming, shorter max tokens).

Decision matrix (summary)

| Triggering signal | Primary degradation symptom | Preferred fallback type | Quick selector criteria | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Latency p95 > 3x SLO for 3m | Severe tail latency | Lower-cost/quantized model variant | Compatible tokenizer + same response shape | Use when latency is dominating but correctness must be preserved |
| Error rate > 1% (5m) or spike > 3x baseline | Elevated 5xx/timeout | A/B split to older stable model or degraded mode | Same auth/response contract | Prefer model variant if available; otherwise enable degraded mode |
| KV cache miss storm + backend saturation | Increased cold-starts and rate limiter hits | Enable prefix-caching bypass + reduce max_tokens | Local cache priming + warmup | Short-lived; requires operator rewarm step |
| Cost over-budget (billing policy) | Sustained cost > budget window | Route non-critical tenants to cheaper variants | Tenant tag based (non-enterprise) | Requires billing approval for cross-tenant moves |
| GPU OOM or node preemption | Resource failures | Pause large-batch workloads; route to smaller-batch pool | Batch-size threshold + worker-tag | Maintain throughput-sensitive paths on separate pools |

Fallback catalog (approved entries)

- rwd-instruct-13b-int8 -> rwd-instruct-7b-quant (response parity: high for short-form; degrade for long-form)
- rwd-chat-16k -> rwd-chat-8k (truncate context and provide context-summary header)
- rwd-embed-enc1 -> rwd-embed-lite (lower dimension, faster)

Operational SLOs and fallback thresholds

- Primary SLOs (example): 99.9% success rate; p95 latency < 400ms for short gen endpoints; p99 < 1.2s.
- Fallback activation rules (automated):
  1) Latency p95 > 3x target for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows.
  2) Error rate (HTTP 5xx + timeouts) > 1% sustained over 5 minutes.
  3) FallbackRate (ratio of requests routed to fallback) > 5% sustained for > 10m triggers on-call review.

Alerting and dashboarding (panels to include)

- Fallback rate by service/model (graph, 1m and 5m).
- P95, P99 latency heatmap by model and tenant.
- 5xx rate and timeout breakdown grouped by routing hop.
- Capacity pressure: GPU utilization, queue length, and avg batch size.

Alert rule examples (Prometheus/Alertmanager friendly)

- Alert: HighFallbackRate
  - expr: sum(rate(fallback_routed_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) > 0.05
  - for: 10m
  - severity: P2
  - runbook: runbook link + initiate on-call review

- Alert: SustainedModelLatency
  - expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(model_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model)) > (3 * model_target_p95_seconds)
  - for: 3m
  - severity: P1 if also paired with increased error rate

Ownership and escalation

- Ownership matrix:
  - Platform routing & policies: team-platform-routing@redwood (primary owner)
  - Serving runtime (model runtime issues): team-serving-runtime@redwood (secondary)
  - Tenant-impact & billing moves: customer-success (notify before persistent moves)

Runbook: automated fallback activation (operator path)

1. On P1 or P2 alert, open the cluster incident channel and paste alert JSON.
2. Verify the signal using dashboard: check p95, error breakdown, and fallback_routed_total.
3. If automated fallback triggered: inspect rollout window and rate. If fallback_rate > 10% and user-facing errors > 0.5%, run emergency rollback: disable fallback via routing toggle.
4. If manual fallback required:
   a. Identify candidate fallback from catalog.
   b. Apply routing rule in the runtime control plane (CLI snippet below).
   c. Monitor p95 and error rate for 5 minutes; if metrics improve to within 1.5x SLO, proceed to staged rollout (10% -> 30% -> 100% over 15m windows).

CLI examples

- Apply a 10% fallback split to rwd-instruct-7b-quant for service "text-generate":
  rwdctl route update --service text-generate --add-split "model=rwd-instruct-7b-quant,percent=10" --reason "emergency latency mitigation"

- Rollback fallback split:
  rwdctl route update --service text-generate --remove-split "model=rwd-instruct-7b-quant" --reason "rollback: increased errors"

Configuration table (safe defaults)

| Config key | Default value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| fallback_max_initial_pct | 10 | Prevents large instantaneous user impact |
| fallback_auto_cooldown_min | 10 | Minutes to wait before auto-incrementing fallback pct |
| fallback_max_pct | 100 | Full failover allowed if approved |
| fallback_watchdog_threshold | 5 | Percent fallback rate that requires on-call review |

Testing and rollout guidance

- Canary runs: always canary fallback changes in a staging environment with traffic-replay and the same tokenizer/model binary.
- A/B evaluate quality drift using the prompt-set  critical-path-evals in applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.
- Maintain a prompt corpus for regression tests (stored in eval-harness) with acceptance thresholds: embedding cosine > 0.86 for embed fallbacks; ROUGE-l drop < 0.08 for gen fallbacks.

Retrospective template (for each fallback event)

1. Incident summary (short description, start/end time).
2. Triggering metrics and root cause hypothesis.
3. Why selected fallback was chosen (decision matrix entry).
4. What worked / did not work (lists).
5. Follow-up actions (owner and due date).

Planned roadmap items (Q2 2026 and beyond)

- Fallback simulation lab: automated chaos experiments to validate fallbacks for 50 representative prompt flows.
- Dynamic cost-aware routing: integrate cost signals into fallback selection to reduce per-token spend without human approval.
- Fallback auditing: persistent audit log with diffs and approvals for enterprise customers.

Appendices

A. Compatibility checklist before approving a new fallback candidate
- Tokenizer match (yes/no)
- Max tokens behavior (same/less)
- Streaming support (yes/no)
- Output schema compatibility (e.g., JSON output keys)

B. Short checklist for private deployments
- Confirm local quantized binary is present on private control plane nodes.
- Validate KMS access if key-wrapped model artifacts are required.
- Coordinate with customer on planned degrade windows if fallback will surface observable differences.

C. Example YAML (circuit-breaker style)

circuit_breaker:
  name: model_latency_cb
  window_seconds: 60
  p95_mult_threshold: 3.0
  min_samples: 50
  action:
    type: fallback
    candidate_model: rwd-instruct-7b-quant
    initial_pct: 10

Related reference links

- Platform routing policies (internal): /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/service-traffic-topology-and-adaptive-shaping-guide-2026
- Observability SLI onboarding: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/platform-observability-sli-onboarding-playbook-2026

Document history

- 2025-11-05: Created by Anjali Mehta.
- 2026-01-12: Added capacity pressure row to decision matrix (Ravi Patel).
- 2026-02-10: Published and approved by reviewers.

payload.page_title: shadow-traffic-fidelity-and-load-profile-tracing-2026

sections.body:
Title: Shadow Traffic Fidelity and Load Profile Tracing

Overview
-------
This document describes the design, implementation, dashboards, alerting, and operational runbook for our Shadow Traffic Fidelity service and Load Profile Tracing pipeline. The goal is to safely inject realistic shadow traffic and capture high-fidelity traces and load profiles so platform teams can:

- Validate routing and fallback policies under realistic shapes
- Measure SLO impact of traffic mixes before production rollouts
- Calibrate autoscalers, batching, and KV-cache heuristics with representative workloads
- Reproduce production anomalies in a safe, reproducible sandbox environment

Scope
-----
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Shadow traffic generation architecture and fidelity controls
- Load profile extraction and canonicalization format
- Dashboards (Prometheus+Grafana) and example panels
- Alerting and SLO-aware degradation signals for shadow experiments
- Operator runbook for enabling/disabling experiments and investigating anomalies
sections.heading: Included

sections.body:
- Customer-specific private deployment steps (see eng-private-deployments)
System goals and success criteria
--------------------------------
1) Non-impacting: Shadow traffic must never affect customer-visible capacity or billing.
2) High fidelity: Request shape (seq length distribution, prompt templates, function calls) should match sampled production percentiles within configurable deltas.
3) Trace completeness: KV cache hits, batch sizes, kernel selection, and fallback decisions must be captured for each shadow request.
4) Reproducibility: Captured load profiles can be replayed in the synthetic shadowing lab with seedable RNG.

Architecture and components
---------------------------
- Shadow Proxy (svc-shadow-proxy): receives mirrored copies of live requests, applies sampling and transformation rules, forwards to shadow runner.
- Shadow Runner (svc-shadow-runner): stateless workers that execute requests against model variants in a sandbox VPC with isolated GPU pools.
- Tracing Aggregator (shadow-trace-collector): consumes opentracing-compatible spans and enriches with runtime decisions (kernel, quantization, cache tags).
- Load Profiler Service (load-profiler): normalizes request metrics to the canonical Load Profile Format (LPF) and stores artifacts in object storage (s3://redwood-shadow-profiles/).
- Dashboard + Alerting (Grafana + Prometheus rules + Alertmanager): visualizes fidelity metrics and surfaces regressions.

Data flow (high level)
1. Production ingress copies request -> Shadow Proxy (sampling rule applies).
2. Shadow Proxy mutates sensitive fields (PII redaction) and rewrites routing metadata.
3. Shadow Runner executes request in isolated environment with experimental model variants.
4. Each shadow execution emits spans and a Load Profile artifact saved to LPF bucket.
5. Tracing Aggregator correlates traces and metrics, exposing Prometheus metrics and logs to the observability stack.

Security and privacy rules
- All payloads must be sanitized via the redaction pipeline (see redaction policy v2).
- Shadow VPCs are isolated and have egress disabled by default.
- LPF artifacts are encrypted at rest (KMS key: projects/redwood/shadow-lpf) and ACLed to eng-platform and applied-ml-and-evals teams.

Load Profile Format (LPF) - canonical fields
------------------------------------------
| field                 | type   | description                         | example |
|-----------------------|--------|-------------------------------------|---------|
| request_id            | string | sampled production request id       | r-20260101-0001 |
| timestamp             | string | ISO-8601                            | 2026-01-12T12:02:34Z |
| seq_len               | int    | token count                          | 432 |
| prompt_template_hash  | string | fingerprint of prompt template      | pth-abc123 |
| model_variant         | string | variant run in shadow               | gptx-q8b |
| kv_cache_hits         | int    | prefix/KV cache hits served         | 3 |
| batch_size            | int    | runtime batch size observed         | 8 |
| runtime_ms            | int    | total execution wall time           | 254 |
| kernel_path           | string | selected kernel identifier          | fmha-opt-v2 |
| trace_span_ids        | string | comma-separated span ids            | s1,s2,s3 |

Prometheus metrics emitted by shadow pipeline
------------------------------------------------
- shadow_requests_total{experiment="canary-2026-01"}  (counter)
- shadow_requests_sampled_ratio{policy="prod-1p"}  (gauge)
- shadow_runtime_ms{model_variant,region}  (histogram)
- shadow_kv_cache_hits_total{model_variant}  (counter)
- shadow_batch_size_summary{}  (histogram)
- shadow_fidelity_score{dimension="prompt_shape|seq_len|kernel_match"}  (gauge, 0..1)

Example Grafana panels (PromQL examples)
----------------------------------------
1) Shadow fidelity time series (panel):
   PromQL: avg_over_time(shadow_fidelity_score{dimension="prompt_shape"}[5m])
   Note: display with 95th/50th percentiles and annotate experiment windows.

2) Production vs Shadow latency comparison:
   PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(shadow_runtime_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))
   + overlay on prod runtime histogram (prod_runtime_ms_bucket).

3) KV cache hit rate by model variant:
   PromQL: rate(shadow_kv_cache_hits_total[10m]) / ignoring(job) group_left() rate(shadow_requests_total[10m])

Alerting rules (examples)
------------------------
- Name: Shadow fidelity drop (High)
  Expr: avg_over_time(shadow_fidelity_score{dimension="prompt_shape"}[10m]) < 0.85
  For: 15m
  Labels: severity=page, team=eng-platform
  Annotations: runbook_url=/eng-platform/runbooks/shadow-experiment-failure-2026

- Name: Shadow to prod latency divergence (Medium)
  Expr: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(shadow_runtime_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le)) / histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(prod_runtime_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))) > 1.25
  For: 30m
  Labels: severity=critical, owner=serving-runtime

Operational runbook: enabling an experiment
-----------------------------------------
1. Create experiment manifest in experiments-db:
   - fields: name, sampling_policy, target_model_variants, sandbox_gpu_pool, redaction_profile, start_time, end_time, owner.
sections.heading: Not included

sections.body:
$ rdx experiments create --name canary-shadow-2026-01 --sampling-policy prod-1p --variants gptx-q8b --gpu-pool sandbox-gpu-a --start 2026-02-15T10:00Z --end 2026-02-15T16:00Z
2. Dry-run locally with the shadow-runner smoke test:
   $ kubectl exec -n eng-platform $(kubectl get pods -l app=svc-shadow-runner -o name | head -1) -- /bin/sh -c 'python3 /opt/shadow/tests/smoke.py --profile samples/lpf-sample.json'
3. Schedule the experiment during low-risk window and notify oncall channel #platform-shadow with experiment manifest and link to dashboard.
4. Monitor fidelity panels and the shadow_fidelity_score for first 30 minutes. If score < 0.9 immediately abort (see abort steps).

Abort and mitigation steps
-------------------------
1. Quick abort (operator): toggle experiments-db entry state -> aborted. CLI: $ rdx experiments abort <experiment-id>
2. If abort toggle fails: scale down shadow-proxy replicas to 0 in the control namespace: $ kubectl scale deployment svc-shadow-proxy -n control --replicas=0
3. Verify no further shadow traffic: promql: rate(shadow_requests_total[1m]) == 0
4. If residual traffic persists, revoke mirror rule in ingress controller (owner: infra-net team).

Investigation checklist (post-abort)
-----------------------------------
- Extract LPF artifacts from s3 for the experiment window.
- Correlate trace ids with production traces (noting redacted fields).
- Check kernel selection distribution for anomalies: query: topk(5, sum by (kernel_path) (rate(shadow_runtime_ms_count[10m])))
- Re-run failing LPF artifacts in isolated replay lab with seed from artifact (document seed in artifact metadata).

Dashboard ownership and maintenance
----------------------------------
- Dashboard: Shadow Traffic Fidelity (grafana slug: shadow-fidelity)
  - Owner: observability squad (eng-platform)
  - Review cadence: quarterly with applied-ml-and-evals for fidelity thresholds
  - Dashboard test: automated synthetic query that validates panel thresholds nightly

Rollout and testing plan
------------------------
1. Internal dogfood: run short 1h experiments targeting dev-only traffic to validate the full pipeline (week 1).
2. Canary with 0.1% production sampling against non-critical routes (week 2).
3. Gradually increase sampling while verifying fidelity score and GPU utilization (target <=5% of prod equivalent).
4. Post rollout retrospective and KPI report (SLOs: fidelity_score >=0.9, shadow-induced resource consumption <5% prod baseline).

Cost and capacity guardrails
--------------------------
- Default sandbox_gpu_pool size: 8 GPUs (n1-standard equivalent).
- Soft quota per experiment: 40 GPU-hours. Exceeded -> auto-abort with label quota-exceeded.
- Billing flag: experiments are tagged with project=shadow and are excluded from customer billing; finance alert on unexpected cost tags.

SLOs and acceptance criteria
---------------------------
- Fidelity SLO: 95% of experiments must maintain shadow_fidelity_score >= 0.9 (weekly window).
- Non-impact SLO: No customer request's p99 latency increase attributable to shadowing > 1% (continuous monitoring).

Appendix A - sample LPF artifact (JSON snippet)
------------------------------------------------
{
  \"request_id\": \"r-20260112-0003\",
  \"timestamp\": \"2026-01-12T12:02:34Z\",
  \"seq_len\": \"432\",
  \"prompt_template_hash\": \"pth-abc123\",
  \"model_variant\": \"gptx-q8b\",
  \"kv_cache_hits\": \"3\",
  \"batch_size\": \"8\",
  \"runtime_ms\": \"254\",
  \"kernel_path\": \"fmha-opt-v2\",
  \"trace_span_ids\": \"s1,s2,s3\"
}

Appendix B - example alertmanager route snippet
------------------------------------------------
routes:
- match:
    severity: page
  receiver: oncall-page
  continue: false

Related documents and links
--------------------------
- Redaction policy v2: /security-and-compliance/data-management/redaction-policy-v2
- Shadow experiment runbook: /eng-platform/runbooks/shadow-experiment-failure-2026
- LPF schema definition (proto): /eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/lpf-schema-v1

Author and owners
------------------
Author: Aisha Patel (Platform Observability)
Primary owner: eng-platform / observability squad
Secondary owner: applied-ml-and-evals (model-fidelity)

Change log
----------
- 2026-01-15: created (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-02-10: clarified fidelity scoring and added abort CLI steps (Marco Chen)

Review checklist before changes
------------------------------
- Confirm experiments are gated behind feature flag and can be globally disabled.
- Ensure redaction is verified by security (reviewers listed).
- Run synthetic replay lab on every major change to the shadow-runner or load-profiler components.

payload.page_title: Feature Flag Governance and Rollout Playbook

sections.body: This playbook defines Redwood Inference's conventions, ownership, and operational procedures for feature flags used across the platform (hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane and Console). It focuses on safety, auditability, and fast recovery to keep customer-facing services within SLOs during rollouts.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to all runtime, API, console, and infra-facing feature flags (server-side toggles and rollout configuration stored in the feature-flag service).
- Does NOT cover client-side feature flags embedded in browser SDKs (see frontend-flagging-guide).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Ensure consistent naming, lifecycle, testing, monitoring, and rollback mechanics for every flag.
- Provide clear ownership and decision gates for risky or customer-impacting flags.
- Minimize blast radius with progressive rollouts and automatic safety gates.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Flag owner: individual responsible for the flag while active (creates the flag, writes tests, monitors rollout).
- Flag steward: platform team member responsible for flag lifecycle policies and audits.
- Canary: small percentage rollout to verify basic behavior.
sections.heading: Key definitions

sections.body:
- Feature flag creator (engineering/product): proposes, implements flag, writes unit/integration tests, and owns initial rollout.
- Flag reviewer (peer): approves naming, safety gates, and test coverage in PR.
- Release manager (platform ops): approves production rollout windows and coordinates with SRE if required.
- Flag steward (platform): runs monthly audits and maintains flag registry.
sections.heading: Roles & Ownership

sections.body:
| Prefix | Description | Examples |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| ff.feature. | Behavioral or UX feature flags | ff.feature.persist-kv-cache |
| ff.experiment. | A/B experiments and user-variant flags | ff.experiment.rank-v2 |
| ff.unsafe. | High-risk flags that require SRE approval | ff.unsafe.kv-shard-remap |
| ff.rollout. | Rollout strategy definitions (percent, cohorts) | ff.rollout.prompt-prefetch |
sections.heading: Use this ASCII table for quick reference

sections.body:
- description: short intent and expected behavior (1–2 sentences).
- owner: GitHub handle and pager.
- risk_level: low|medium|high. High must include SRE approver.
- rollout_plan: percentages, target cohorts, burn-in window.
- kill_switch: documented immediate revert path.
sections.heading: Flag metadata requirements (in flag registry entry)

sections.body:
- All flags default to "off" unless explicitly scoped to a safe experiment cohort.
- High-risk flags must require a secondary approval in PRs and a scheduled rollout window.
sections.heading: Safe default policy

sections.body:
1) Code-level: unit tests, integration tests exercising both on/off paths, lint pass.
2) CI smoke: e2e smoke with default off and a test cohort on.
3) Canary plan: define metrics and acceptance criteria (latency, error-rate, CPU).
4) Rollout approval: release manager sign-off for high-risk.
sections.heading: Pre-rollout checks (automated & manual)

sections.body:
1. Create flag in the feature-flag service using the standard CLI or API. Record metadata in the registry.
   - Example CLI: redwood-ff create --name ff.feature.new-cache --owner maya.liang --desc "Enable KV prefetch for L1 cache" --risk low
2. Deploy code behind flag to staging with default OFF. Run integration tests.
3. Canary: target 1% of internal traffic (team cohort) for 1 hour. Observe metrics.
4. Progressive ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%. Each step requires a minimum observation period: low risk 15m, medium 30m, high 60m.
5. If any safety gate trips, execute rollback procedure (see "Kill switch and rollback").
sections.heading: Rollout procedure (step-by-step)

sections.body:
- Service error rate (5xx) increase <= +0.05% absolute and <= 10% relative vs baseline.
- Median p95 latency change <= +25ms.
- CPU/GPU utilization increase <= +8% sustained per node.
sections.heading: Acceptance criteria (examples)

sections.body:
1) Use the feature-flag control plane UI or API to immediately set flag to OFF for all cohorts.
   - API example: curl -X POST https://ff-api.redwood.internal/v1/flags/ff.feature.new-cache/toggle -d '{"state":"off"}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $FF_TOKEN"
2) If flag toggle fails or downstream state persists, scale affected service replica count to 0/replace pods as a last resort, following SRE coordination.
3) Open an incident channel (#platform-incident) and tag SRE and the original owner. Document time, actions, and telemetry snapshot.
sections.heading: Kill switch and rollback (fast-path)

sections.body:
- Flag-specific dashboard card: rollout percentage, user-cohort counts, success_ratio, errors/sec, p50/p95 latency, CPU/GPU per-pod.
- Cross-service SLO delta panel: compare baseline SLO windows to current.
- Alerting: create short-lived rollout alerts for the duration of the ramp. Example thresholds (temporary alerts):
  - ff.rollout.error-rate-high: error_rate_change > 0.1% for 3m -> Pager to SRE and owner.
  - ff.rollout.latency-regression: p95_increase > 50ms for 5m -> page owner only.
sections.heading: Monitoring and dashboards (what to watch)

sections.body:
- error rate delta: (sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"api-server\", code=~\"5..\", flag=~\"ff.feature.new-cache\"}[1m])) by (instance)) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"api-server\", flag!~\"ff.feature.new-cache\"}[1m])) by (instance)

Audit, retention & cleanup:
- Flags older than 90 days in ON state must have an audit entry explaining ongoing need.
- Stale flags (not toggled or referenced for 180 days) will be listed for deletion in the monthly steward review.
- Flag registry keeps a change log with actor and timestamp for 365 days.
sections.heading: Example dashboard query snippets (PromQL)

sections.body:
- Any rollout that causes a P1 incident or SLO breach requires a postmortem with RCA and follow-ups.
- Minor incidents (brief rollbacks with no customer impact) should be recorded in the monthly platform retrospective.
sections.heading: Postmortem and retrospective triggers

sections.body:
- Toggle flag (CLI): redwood-ff toggle ff.feature.<name> --state off --reason "rollout regression"
- Check cohorts: redwood-ff inspect ff.feature.<name> --format json | jq '.cohorts'
- List recent changes: redwood-ff history --name ff.feature.<name> --limit 25
sections.heading: Runbook snippets (quick commands)

sections.body:
- 0-5 minutes: Flag owner attempts immediate toggle. Notify #platform-incident.
- 5-20 minutes: Platform on-call (pager) engages, SRE joins if there are signs of cluster-level impact.
- >20 minutes: Declare incident P1, invoke incident response runbook, consider rollback and rollback mitigation plans (DB migrations, long-running jobs).
sections.heading: Escalation matrix (summary)

sections.body: - Flag control plane schema changes must be backwards compatible. Any migration requires a migration plan and a canary.
sections.heading: Versioning & deployments to control plane

sections.body:
- Q1 2026: Implement automated canary analysis (auto-rollback if metric divergence exceeds threshold).
- Q2 2026: Add cohort-aware distributed tracing to tie user cohorts to request traces.
- Ongoing: tighter CI hooks to require registry metadata in PRs for any code that introduces flags.

Appendix: Example flag registry JSON template (stored in the registry UI):
{
  "name": "ff.feature.new-cache",
  "description": "Enable L1 KV prefetch for short-lived tokens",
  "owner": "maya.liang@redwood.ai",
  "risk_level": "low",
  "rollout_plan": "1% internal -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%",
  "kill_switch": "redwood-ff toggle ff.feature.new-cache --state off"
}
sections.heading: Operational improvements & roadmap items

sections.body:
- Service lifecycle orchestration guidelines
- Platform incident runbook
- Frontend feature flag guidance (frontend-flagging-guide)
sections.heading: Related pages and references

sections.body:
- 2025-04-10: Draft created by Maya Liang.
- 2025-06-12: Added automatic audit policy for stale flags (reviewer: Diego Marquez).
- 2025-11-01: Published with rollout timing and dashboard examples (reviewers: Priya Patel, Omar Haddad).
