payload.page_title: Capacity decomposition and SLI ownership matrix

sections.body:
Summary
This document defines a reproducible decomposition of platform capacity into orthogonal buckets (critical-path, best-effort, cacheable, ephemeral) and provides an SLI/SLO ownership matrix to map each bucket to teams, dashboards, alerting thresholds, and operational runbooks. The goal is to make capacity reasoning explicit for product and operator teams, enable cost-aware routing, and reduce cross-team incident ambiguity.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood Inference runtime components and platform control plane services that affect inference availability and throughput: router, request-router, kv-prefix-cache, batch-worker, model-proxy, autoscaler-controller, tenant-allocator.
- Covers hosted and dedicated fleets; private deployments are guidance-only (network/topology differences require local adaptation).

Why this matters
- Recent incidents highlighted unclear ownership when tail latency rose during tenant bursts. A shared decomposition reduces firefighting time.
- Capacity-driven decisions (eviction, throttling, model swap) require consistent SLI definitions to ensure safe automation.

High-level decomposition
1) Critical-path (CP) capacity
- Definition: CPU/GPU cycles and networking that directly contribute to foreground, interactive generation requests for SLO-backed tenants (e.g., enterprise customers with low-latency guarantees).
- Examples: small-batch infer on dedicated GPUs pinned to tenant, router control-plane connections for model version pinning.
- Typical SLO: p95 latency < 150ms; availability 99.95%.

2) Best-effort (BE) capacity
- Definition: Background or non-SLA workloads that may be throttled during contention (free-tier, async batch jobs, low-priority pipelines).
- Examples: non-interactive batch embeddings, scheduled offline reranks.
- Typical SLO: p95 latency < 1s (soft); availability 99.5% (degradation acceptable).

3) Cacheable/Prefetch (CPF) capacity
- Definition: Memory and KV prefix cache resources that reduce upstream compute by serving repeated prefixes. Errors here manifest as increased upstream token cost and latency.
- Examples: kv-prefix-cache shards, pre-warm workers, local LRU caches.
- Typical SLO: cache hit ratio >= 60% on tail-tenants; eviction rate < 0.5% per minute in steady state.

4) Ephemeral/Startup (EP) capacity
- Definition: Transient resources used for cold starts, model warmups, and autoscaler ramping. High variance and typically backed by warm pools.
- Examples: warmup workers, container boot sequences, JIT kernel compilation windows.
- Typical SLO: cold-start time < 750ms for warm-pool-backed requests; < 5s for cold-only paths.

SLI/SLO Ownership Matrix
| Capacity bucket | Primary SLI | SLO (target) | Alert threshold | Primary owner | Primary dashboard |
|-----------------|------------:|--------------|----------------:|---------------|------------------|
| Critical-path | p95 request latency on production router (ms) | < 150ms | p95 > 200ms for 10m | runtime-team | runtime/critical-path-latency |
| Best-effort | tail job completion time (99th percentile) | < 1s (soft) | 99th > 2s for 30m | batch-team | batch/job-latency |
| Cacheable | kv-prefix-cache hit ratio (5m rolling) | >= 60% | < 45% for 5m | platform-cache | cache/prefix-hitratio |
| Ephemeral | cold-start time (p95) | < 750ms | p95 > 1500ms for 10m | autoscaler | autoscaler/cold-starts |

Notes on the table: The dashboard names above are internal grafana panels (e.g., grafana/redwood/runtime/critical-path-latency). Alert thresholds are intentionally conservative as a starting point — teams should tune after one quarter of SLI-driven incident reviews.

Ownership details and responsibilities
- runtime-team (primary): maintain router, model-proxy, and request-router. Responsible for: low-latency optimizations, kernel selection telemetry, and p95 latency SLOs for CP. Runbooks: emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation.
- platform-cache: owns kv-prefix-cache deployment, shard rebalancer, and caching heuristics. Responsible for hit-ratio telemetry and cache-eviction alarms. Runbooks: platform-operator-snapshot-and-rollback-patterns.
- autoscaler: owns warm pools, cold-start metrics, and safe-autoscaling policies. Responsible for warm-pool sizing and ramp policy config. Runbooks: predictive-scale-and-eviction-playbook.
- batch-team: owns scheduled jobs, embedding workers, and best-effort quotas. Responsible for job queuing, backfill mechanisms, and soft-SLO communications.

Dashboards and telemetry guidelines
- Each SLI must have: primary timeseries, derived rolling window (5m, 1h), error budget burn-rate, and per-tenant split for the top 20 tenants by traffic. Use tokenized SLI approach where applicable to correlate cost.
- Standard dashboard panels (recommended IDs):
  - runtime/critical-path-latency (p95, p99, traces link)
  - cache/prefix-hitratio (global + per-shard)
  - autoscaler/cold-starts (p50/p95/p99 + warm-pool occupancy)
  - tenant/impact-scatter (top 50 tenants by latency+/cost)

Alerting policy (templates)
1) Severity-1 (S1) — Immediate operator paging
   - Trigger: p95 latency for CP > 300ms sustained for 5 minutes AND error rate increased by > 2x baseline.
   - Actions: page runtime oncall, follow emergency model swap runbook (section below).
2) Severity-2 (S2) — Team email + rotation watch
   - Trigger: cache hit ratio < 40% for 10 minutes OR cold-start p95 > 2s for 15 minutes.
   - Actions: page platform-cache/autoscaler teams, investigate recent config rollouts.
3) Severity-3 (S3) — Inbox (triage within 24h)
   - Trigger: BE job p99 > 5s for 1 hour.

Emergency model swap and token surge (abridged runbook)
1) Detect — Confirm p95/p99 increase via runtime/critical-path-latency and recent kernel-selection failures in logs.
2) Isolate — Mark suspect model variant as degraded in model-catalog (CLI):
   - rh model mark --model-id m-rlhf-2026-v2 --state degraded --reason "p99 token latency spike"
3) Swap — Use canary route to redirect 20% traffic to fallback variant:
   - rh routes update --route-id rt-234 --weight {"m-rlhf-2026-v2": 80, "m-rlhf-2026-v2-quant": 20}
4) Evict — If eviction required, execute tenant-priority shedding: set tenant priority to best-effort for the impacted bucket and enable soft-eviction window:
   - rh tenant update --tenant t-123 --priority best-effort --eviction-window 5m
5) Observe — Monitor error budget burn on runtime/critical-path-latency for 30m; rollback if SLO improves.

Configuration examples
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
----
service: request-router
profiles:
  - name: critical-path
    min_replicas: 8
    max_replicas: 200
    warm_pool: 2
    prefetch: true
    eviction_policy: "never"
  - name: best-effort
    min_replicas: 1
    max_replicas: 50
    warm_pool: 0
    prefetch: false
    eviction_policy: "lowest-cost-first"
----

Operational cadence and review
- Quarterly SLI review: owners reconvene to: validate SLI collection, adjust thresholds, and publish a 1-page change summary.
- Post-incident: map root cause to capacity bucket and update the decomposition if failures expose a new cross-cutting resource.
- Roadmap tie-in: capacity decomposition outcomes feed into the Capacity Synchronization roadmap (owners: eng-platform/roadmap).

Onboarding checklist for new platform engineers
1) Read this doc and the related runbooks (links above).
2) Complete the operator sandbox certification (team-wiki/operator-sandbox-synthetic-scenarios-and-verification-catalog).
3) Verify access to dashboards and alerting channels; run the local SLI query against dev stack. Example query (PromQL):
   - histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
4) Shadow the runtime oncall for two weeks and run at least one capacity-driven fire drill.

Appendix: example PromQL & alert rule
- PromQL (p95 request latency over 5m):
  > hist_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service))
- Alert rule (YAML Prometheus):
----
alert: CriticalPathLatencyHigh
expr: >
  hist_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) > 0.2
for: 10m
labels: {severity: "page"}
annotations: {summary: "CP p95 latency > 200ms"}
----

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Created by Evan Ramirez (initial decomposition and draft SLIs)
- 2026-01-09: Reviewer feedback incorporated (Priya Natarajan) — tightened cache hit target and added runbook snippet
- 2026-02-15: Published after trialing thresholds in staging (Liam Chen)

Related reading
- capacity-synchronization-cost-attenuation-roadmap-2026
- predictive-scale-and-eviction-playbook-2026
- runtime/critical-path-latency dashboard

Questions / feedback
For questions or suggested edits, open a PR on the confluence page or ping @Evan Ramirez on the platform Slack channel.

payload.page_title: PRD: Fallback Confidence Service and Migration Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This PRD describes the Fallback Confidence Service (FCS): a lightweight, low-latency classifier and scoring service that predicts the expected quality delta and operational risk of routing a request to a cheaper or higher‑latency model variant. The FCS is intended to power automated fallback decisions in the runtime, provide explainability signals to the Console, and enable a safe migration playbook for customers moving between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals
-----
- Provide a real-time confidence score (0.0–1.0) per request that estimates whether a fallback variant will meet tenant-defined quality bounds.
- Surface per-route and per-tenant historical fallback outcomes to Console and telemetry for auditing and billing.
- Enable an automated, reversible migration playbook for customers transitioning between model variants or deployment types with minimal regression risk.
- Keep inference latency impact <= 5 ms p50 when integrated into the fast path.

Non-goals
---------
- Replacing full model evaluation (shadowing/evals) for every regression check. FCS augments, not substitutes, robust offline evals.
- Supporting arbitrary third-party models in the initial rollout; launch supports Redwood-verified variants and marketplace-adapted adapters.

Product requirements (high level)
--------------------------------
| ID | Requirement | Rationale | Priority | Acceptance criteria |
|----|-------------|-----------|----------|---------------------|
| R-1 | Per-request confidence score API (float) | Drive routing decisions and analytics | P0 | API returns score within 0–1 and 95th percentile latency < 8ms under production load |
| R-2 | Per-route historic outcome stream (success/fallback/regression) | Auditable rollback and billing adjustments | P0 | Console shows aggregated fallback accuracy and daily regression counts |
| R-3 | Tenant policy DSL for fallbacks | Customers set allowable quality deltas and SLOs | P1 | Policies editable in Console; policy evaluation tests pass in sandbox |
| R-4 | Migration playbook templates (hosted↔dedicated↔private) | Reduce operational risk during migration | P1 | Step-by-step runbook with automated canary steps and rollback triggers |
| R-5 | Shadow mode and backtesting harness | Validate FCS decisions against offline evals | P0 | Shadow runs produce matching metrics with live traffic within tolerance |

API contract (example)
----------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```yaml
model_variant: "redwood-llm-ggml-compact-v1"
input_hash: "sha256:..."
prompt_features:
  - token_count: 38
  - contains_code: false
  - avg_sentence_length: 12.3
  - domain: "support-ticket"
tenant_id: "tenant-123"
route: "/chat/complete"
```
sections.heading: Request (POST /v1/fcs/score)

sections.body:
```json
{
  "score": 0.87,             // higher => safe to fallback
  "explanation": "prefix-match to high-confidence prompts; few OOV tokens",
  "model_compat": ["compact-v1", "compact-v1-quant"],
  "evaluation_ts": "2026-10-20T16:02:30Z"
}
```
Note: score interpretation is tenant-configurable (example: score>=0.8 allowed).

Policy DSL (concise)
--------------------
- allow_fallback_when: score >= 0.8
- max_quality_delta: 0.03 (relative likelihood of answer match)
- min_success_rate_last_24h: 0.985
- rollback_on: regression_count >= 3 in 1h

Telemetry and observability requirements
--------------------------------------
- Emit metrics per request: fcs.score (gauge), fcs.decision (enum: allow/deny), fcs.latency_ms (histogram).
- SLOs: FCS availability 99.99% monthly; false-allow rate <= 0.5% for P0 routes; processing p95 latency < 12ms.
- Traces: attach FCS decision as tag to request traces for per-request debug.
- Console: new FCS dashboard with per-tenant heatmaps (score distribution), rollback events, and a migration timeline view.

Migration playbook (high level)
------------------------------
1. Pre-migration validation (3–14 days):
   - Run FCS in shadow mode against intended fallback variant.
   - Collect shadow_metrics: "predicted_safe_rate", "observed_success_rate".
   - Required threshold: predicted_safe_rate >= 99% and observed_success_rate >= tenant_policy.min_success_rate_last_24h.
2. Canary (0.5–2% traffic):
   - Enable automated canary routing where FCS decides; monitor replay validation and user-facing errors.
   - Run for 4–24 hours depending on traffic volume.
3. Gradual ramp (2%→25%→50%→100%):
   - Ramp steps tied to time and explicit success gates (no regressions for 4 hours).
   - Automated rollback triggers on regression_count or drop in NPS for tenant.
4. Post-migration audit (7 days):
   - Run a full drift report comparing pre/post lexicon coverage, latency, and cost delta.
   - Create a migration summary for the customer and for internal SRE review.

Operational runbook (excerpt)
----------------------------
- P0: FCS returns malformed responses or causes routing errors:
  1. Switch runtime routing to "deny-by-default" (block fallback) using the feature toggle.
  2. Promote last known good FCS model via the model-store API.
  3. Notify oncall: eng-serving-runtime and product oncall.
- P1: Elevated false-allow rate (>0.5%):
  1. Throttle fallback decisions to shadow mode for affected route.
  2. Start capture: save last 10k affected request payloads for offline analysis.
  3. Trigger targeted retrain/eval in the lab.

Security and data handling
-------------------------
- Inputs to FCS must honor tenant privacy: no PII retention beyond 7 days in hot storage; all persisted features are hashed or token-count-only when possible.
- FCS runs in a tenant-scoped namespace; access controlled via RBAC and audit-logged.
- Any explainability artifacts stored with request traces are redacted for PII.

Acceptance criteria (detailed)
-----------------------------
- Functional: Per-request score available and evaluated by runtime for 99% of supported routes.
- Performance: End-to-end fallback decision adds <5ms p50 latency and <12ms p95 latency.
- Quality: False-allow rate <= 0.5% on P0 routes during 30-day canary window.
- Observability: Console displays historical accuracy and has filters by tenant/route/variant.

Rollout timeline (tentative)
---------------------------
- Q4 2026 (alpha): internal Redwood services and 3 pilot customers; shadow-only mode.
- Q1 2027 (beta): graduated pilot customers on hosted; Console integration for policies and dashboards.
- Q2 2027 (GA): Dedicated and Private onramp; migration playbook published and SRE playbooks finalized.

Ownership and stakeholders
------------------------
- Product lead: Aisha Khan (product)
- Engineering lead: Marcelo Ruiz (serving-runtime)
- SRE owner: Jade Park (eng-sre)
- Developer experience: Priya Patel (eng-devex)
- Customer success: Marco Nguyen (customer-success)

Risks and mitigations
---------------------
- Risk: FCS makes conservative decisions that reduce cost-savings.
  - Mitigation: Allow tenant-tunable sensitivity and post-migration cost-reconciliation credits.
- Risk: Latency regression on high-throughput routes.
  - Mitigation: Local caching and a lightweight feature extractor; fallback to precomputed scores for common prefixes.
- Risk: Explainability reveals sensitive prompts.
  - Mitigation: Redaction and hashed feature storage; privacy review for any explainability UI.

Related artifacts and references
-------------------------------
- Design: latency-aware-cost-fallback-protocol-spec (see related_pages).
- Telemetry: consumption-telemetry-provenance-and-crediting-spec.
- Migration patterns: hosted-to-dedicated-transition-playbook.

Appendix: sample backtesting query
--------------------------------
- Query: compare FCS predicted_allow at T0 to observed success at T+24h for N=100k requests; compute confusion matrix and expected cost delta.
- Example SQL pseudocode:
  SELECT predicted_allow, observed_success, COUNT(*) FROM shadow_runs
  WHERE route = '/chat/complete' AND date BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30'
  GROUP BY predicted_allow, observed_success;

Next steps
----------
- Align product and serving-runtime on feature set and API latency budget (by 2026-10-27).
- Kickoff alpha integration with two internal services and identify 3 external pilot customers (by 2026-11-10).
- Draft Console policy editor mockups and telemetry dashboard wireframes (by 2026-11-03).

payload.page_title: Operator fallback experiment matrix and cost penalty catalog

sections.body:
Overview
========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies.

Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks are a major lever for preserving SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they have measurable cost and quality impacts.
- Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies.
- This doc standardizes experiment telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks.

Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Provide a repeatable experiment matrix that yields quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evaluations), and operator intervention effort.
- Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), and routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling).
- Out of scope: Model training/data pipelines, legal/customer contract negotiation.

Definitions and abbreviations
---------------------------
- Fallback variant: Any alternative response path (e.g., model C => model B, or cached response) used when the primary path is unavailable or overloaded.
- Cost penalty: Unit cost increase or revenue impact metric associated with using a fallback (e.g., tokens * $/token diff, or additional infra cost).
- SLO preservation: Fraction of requests meeting 95th percentile latency target and error-rate SLO.

Experiment matrix (canonical)
---------------------------
Columns: experiment_id | description | fallback_type | trigger | primary-metric | cost-metric | quality-metric | run-length | owner
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) EXP-001 | Model-variant degrade (Llama-70B -> Llama-13B-int8) | model_variant | queue-depth > 100 OR p95 latency > 600ms | p95 latency, error-rate | token-cost-delta-per-hour | eval-regression@20 prompts | 2h | operator-team
2) EXP-002 | Regional drain to peer region (eu-west -> us-east) | regional-routing | region capacity throttle 80% | p99 tail latency cross-region | egress-cost-delta | user-visible-quality (latency jump) | 4h | platform-network
3) EXP-003 | Prefetch cache fallback (serve from prefix cache) | cache_prefetch | cold-start rate > 30 req/min | mean latency | compute-cost-savings | correctness mismatch ratio | 3h | runtime-team
4) EXP-004 | Token-budgeted throttling for low-priority tenants | quota_throttle | burst credits exhausted | 95th latency of high-priority | revenue-at-risk | customer-error-annotations | 6h | platform-ops

Telemetry and dashboarding recipe
--------------------------------
Create a dedicated experimental dashboard with following panels per experiment run:
- SLO heatmap: p50/p95/p99 latency over time (per region, per tenant priority). Query examples:
  - latency_p95{experiment_id="EXP-001"} (PromQL)
  - request_duration_bucket_sum by (le, region)
- Cost delta stream: rolling token-cost-per-minute and infra-cost-surge.
  - token_cost_rate{fallback_variant!=""}
- Quality regression signal: evaluation pass-rate across a held promptset (20-50 prompts) run every 15 minutes.
  - eval_pass_rate{promptset="fallback-20"}
- Operator interventions: number and duration of manual rollbacks, with links to runbook tickets.
  - operator_rollbacks_total{experiment_id="EXP-001"}
- Composite KPI panel: cost-penalty vs. SLO-preservation scatter plot for each variant.

Minimum instrumentation checklist
--------------------------------
1) Annotate requests with experiment_id and fallback_variant in trace metadata.
2) Emit fallback_reason counter in request pipeline.
3) Record per-request token accounting and model_version label.
4) Attach prompt-set id for synthetic eval traffic.
5) Ensure operator actions log into the incident system with experiment_id tag.

Cost penalty catalog (examples and formulae)
-------------------------------------------
Catalog rows: fallback_variant | per-token-diff | expected-throughput | hourly-cost-delta | rollback-cost-estimate | notes
sections.heading: Example rows (use these as templates)

sections.body:
- L70B -> L13B-int8 | +0.002 $/token (lower cost) | 2k tokens/s | -$14.4 / hour per 1000 rps | negligible | reduced quality on long-form completion
- cross-region-eu->us | +$0.05 / 1k tokens (egress) | 1k tokens/s | +$180 / hour at 1000 rps | potential SLA credits | watch cold-start p95
- cached_prefix_response | -$0.001 $/token (savings) | N/A | -$3.6 / hour per 1000 rps | risk of stale content | requires invalidation policy
- quota-throttle-low | revenue-at-risk estimate (see calc) | depends on tenant mix | - | revenue-impact = average-MRR-per-req * blocked-reqs | requires customer comms plan

Cost calculations (short formulas)
- token_cost_delta_hourly = sum_over_requests(token_count * (cost_primary - cost_fallback)) per hour
- egress_delta_hourly = egress_bytes * egress_rate
- revenue_at_risk = blocked_requests * avg_revenue_per_request
Include these calculations in the dashboard as derived timeseries.

Experiment run playbook (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------
1) Planning (2–4 days)
   a) Define hypotheses: e.g., "model-variant fallback preserves p95 latency with <5% quality regression and cost delta < $200/hr"
   b) Pick held promptset (20–50 prompts) and synthetic traffic profile matching customer mix.
   c) Create experiment_id, add telemetry tags and dashboard.
2) Preflight (1 day)
   a) Run synthetic traffic against fallback in staging and collect baseline metrics.
   b) Validate eval pass-rate and trace annotation.
   c) Pre-commit rollback playbook and test it in canary.
3) Execution (2–6 hours normally, up to 24 hours for long-run metrics)
   a) Apply experiment on a small cohort (1% of traffic or single region).
   b) Monitor SLO panels and operator intervention panel.
   c) Escalate to oncall if p99 > target * 2 or error-rate increases > 2x baseline.
4) Ramp or rollback (decision gates)
   a) If cost-savings or SLO-preservation meet hypothesis -> ramp to 10% then 50% using pre-defined step intervals.
   b) If quality regression > threshold or operator rollbacks > 1 -> rollback immediately, file incident.
5) Post-run analysis (within 48 hours)
   a) Populate experiment report template (see artifacts).
   b) Archive synthetic trace samples and evaluation results.

Rollback quick commands (examples)
--------------------------------
- Immediate global rollback: CLI helper
  - redwoodctl rollout cancel --experiment EXP-001 --force
- Regional undo (eu-west):
  - redwoodctl routing set-region-weight --region eu-west --weight 1.0 --experiment EXP-001
- Re-enable primary model:
  - redwoodctl model set-default --model redwood/llama-70b --variant baseline --experiment EXP-001
Include these command snippets in runbook templates and verify operator RBAC before using.

Decision criteria matrix (accept/ramp/abandon)
--------------------------------------------
- Accept: p95 latency maintained within 10% of baseline AND eval regression <= 3% AND hourly cost delta within budgeted threshold.
- Ramp: p95 within 20% and eval regression <= 7% with operator acceptance.
- Abandon: p95 > 20% degradation OR eval regression > 10% OR unexpected customer errors in the error-tracking system.
Document reasons in experiment report.

Artifacts to capture and store
----------------------------
- Experiment report (.md) with: hypothesis, traffic profile, duration, metrics before/after, cost calculations, operator notes.
- Trace bundle (link to S3) and synthetic eval outputs (json).
- Dashboard snapshot and Prometheus queries used.
- Postmortem if rollback occurred.

Operational responsibilities and ownership
----------------------------------------
- Owner: platform-ops (primary contact: oncall@platform) for run coordination.
- Instrumentation: runtime-team for trace and metric changes.
- Cost modeling: finance-eng liaison for hourly cost validation.
- Security review: security-team if any customer data is used in synthetic prompts.

Safety and customer communication
--------------------------------
- For tenant-facing throttles or degradations that materially impact customer SLAs, coordinate with Customer Success for banner messaging and QBR notes.
- For enterprise customers with Dedicated/Private deployments, require explicit sign-off per the customer SLAs before ramping.

Retrospective template (post-experiment)
--------------------------------------
1) Summary: one-paragraph outcome
2) Metrics: baseline vs. experiment (latency, error-rate, cost, eval pass-rate)
3) What went well
4) What failed / surprises
5) Action items (owner + due date)
6) Decision: accept/ramp/abandon

Appendices
----------
A. Sample PromQL snippets
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference",experiment_id=~"EXP-.*"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- fallback rate: sum(rate(fallback_reason_total[1m])) by (fallback_variant)

B. Template experiment report checklist (copy into new experiment ticket)
- Experiment ID:
- Owner:
- Hypothesis:
- Synthetic promptset id:
- Baseline run links:
- Dashboard link:
- Rollback commands verified: Y/N
- Customer communication required: Y/N

C. Related runbooks and pages
- emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation (runbook)
- platform-operator-handbook-degraded-kv-prefix-cache (operator runbook)

D. Change log
- 2025-11-12: Document created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-08: Added cost-penalty formulas and cross-region egress example (review: Miguel Torres).
- 2026-01-18: Finalized decision criteria and PromQL snippets (review: Dana Li).

Contact and follow-up
--------------------
For questions or to schedule a live walk-through of the experiment templates, ping #platform-ops or email aisha.patel@redwood.ai.

payload.page_title: ADR: Optimization Config Versioning Model (Immutable Versions + Scoped Pointers)

sections.body: Published (approved in Architecture Review on 2025-10-21).
sections.heading: Status

sections.body:
Redwood Optimize supports a set of operational inference optimizations (batching heuristics, caching toggles/parameters, and quantization profiles). Historically, optimization changes have been applied as mutable configuration updates. This has caused:
- Limited traceability (difficult to answer “what changed, by whom, and where is it active?”).
- Higher change-failure risk (hard to stage safely across tenant/model/region).
- Incomplete rollback semantics (partial worker apply, race conditions, and unclear “current” config).

This ADR defines the **versioning model** for Optimization Configs in the control plane, including:
- Immutable version objects vs mutable config objects.
- How “active config” is represented (pointers/bindings).
- Promotion semantics and environment scoping.

The model must support Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments while keeping behavior consistent across runtime/apply pipelines.
sections.heading: Context

sections.body:
1. **Auditability**: every change must be attributable (who/what/when) and reconstructable.
2. **Safe apply**: staged rollout must reference a stable, immutable configuration.
3. **Rollback correctness**: one-click rollback should be implemented as repointing to a known-good version, not editing values.
4. **Scoping and blast radius control**: apply at tenant/model/region (and optionally deployment) granularity.
5. **Operational simplicity**: easy to reason about “what is active” and “what will change if I click rollback”.
6. **Compatibility with runtime idempotency**: runtime should treat config apply as a transaction keyed by version ID.
7. **Private deployments**: must work with pinned versions and operator workflows (Helm/Terraform/installer).
sections.heading: Decision drivers

sections.body:
- **Optimization Config**: the logical configuration content used by the serving runtime (batching/caching/quantization settings).
- **Version**: an immutable snapshot of an Optimization Config plus metadata.
- **Binding/Pointer**: a mutable record defining which version is active for a scope.
- **Scope**: the set of dimensions that determine where a config is active (tenant/model/region/deployment mode/environment).
- **Promotion**: moving a version from one environment/scope to another via an explicit operation.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
**Description**: Store one OptimizationConfig per scope and mutate it on update.

**Pros**
- Simple storage model.
- Fewer records.

**Cons**
- Poor auditability: diffs require reconstructing prior state from logs (often incomplete).
- Rollback becomes “write old values back” (error-prone and not atomic with distributed runtime).
- Difficult to stage: canary would require temporary values or shadow copies.
- Race-prone when multiple operators/tools update the same object.

**Decision**: Rejected.

---
sections.heading: Option A — Mutable config objects (single record updated in place)

sections.body:
**Description**: Store immutable versions and define the “active” version as the most recently created version for a scope.

**Pros**
- Great auditability.
- Easy rollback by “creating a new version identical to old one.”

**Cons**
- “Latest” is not a controlled concept; applies become implicit and can happen accidentally.
- Promotions across environments become ambiguous (creating a new prod version vs reusing a staging version).
- Canaries are awkward: “latest” changes while a canary is running.
- Hard to implement cooldowns/approvals because activation is coupled to creation.

**Decision**: Rejected.

---
sections.heading: Option B — Immutable versions only (no pointers; each worker queries “latest”)

sections.body:
**Description**: Store immutable versions and separately store mutable pointers per scope that declare the active version. Apply/promote/rollback are pointer operations (with gates).

**Pros**
- Strong audit trail: versions are immutable; pointer changes are explicit events.
- Safe apply: canary references a fixed version ID.
- Rollback is repointing a pointer to a prior known-good version.
- Clean promotion semantics: “promote version X to environment/scope Y” means updating the binding in Y to X.
- Works well with runtime idempotency (apply keyed by version ID).
- Compatible with Private pinning (operator pins version ID).

**Cons**
- More entities to manage (versions + bindings + rollout state).
- Must design around pointer races (apply vs rollback).

**Decision**: Accepted.
sections.heading: Option C — Immutable versions + mutable scoped pointers (bindings)

sections.body: We will implement **Optimization Config Versioning as immutable version objects plus mutable scoped bindings**.
sections.heading: Decision

sections.body:
1. **Version objects are immutable**: content and key metadata do not change after creation.
2. **Activation is explicit**: a version is not active until a binding is updated via an apply/promote/rollback operation.
3. **Bindings are per-scope**: “active config” is always evaluated by finding the best matching binding for the request’s scope.
4. **Promotion is a binding update with rules**: promoting to broader blast radius requires gates, RBAC permissions, and audit events.
sections.heading: Core principles

sections.body: This ADR is normative for the model; exact field names may differ slightly in implementation.
sections.heading: Data model (conceptual)

sections.body:
- `version_id` (UUID)
- `config_type` (e.g., `batching`, `caching`, `quant_profile`, `composite`)
- `payload` (canonical JSON; schema validated)
- `created_at`, `created_by`
- `source` (console | api | automation)
- `parent_version_id` (optional; for lineage)
- `change_summary` (human readable)
- `risk_level` (low | medium | high; derived from diff heuristics)
- `validation_status` (valid | invalid) and `validation_report_ref` (immutable artifact reference)

**Immutability rule**: payload and these metadata fields do not change post-create. Any modification produces a new version.
sections.heading: Entity 1: OptimizationConfigVersion (immutable)

sections.body:
- `binding_id` (UUID)
- `scope` fields:
  - `environment` (prod | staging | dev)
  - `deployment_mode` (hosted | dedicated | private)
  - `tenant_id` (nullable)
  - `model_id` (nullable)
  - `region` (nullable)
- `active_version_id`
- `updated_at`, `updated_by`
- `rollout_state_ref` (optional; points to rollout controller state)

**Scope matching rule**: resolution prefers most-specific binding.
Order (most to least specific): tenant+model+region+mode+env → tenant+model+mode+env → tenant+mode+env → model+mode+env → mode+env → env default.

**Constraint**: for any exact scope tuple, at most one binding exists.
sections.heading: Entity 2: OptimizationConfigBinding (mutable pointer)

sections.body:
We will persist rollout state separately from bindings so that:
- binding changes are auditable events
- rollouts can pause/resume independently
sections.heading: Entity 3: OptimizationConfigRollout (mutable state machine)

sections.body:
- target binding scope
- target version ID
- strategy (canary % or shard-based)
- checkpoints and gate evaluations
- timestamps and operator actions
sections.heading: Rollout state includes

sections.body: Promotion is defined as updating a binding in a different environment and/or a broader scope to point at an existing immutable version.
sections.heading: Promotion semantics

sections.body:
- **staging → prod** for the same scope dimensions (common for Dedicated and Hosted internal testing).
- **narrow → broad** (e.g., `tenant_id=acme` to `tenant_id=null` within same env/mode/model/region), subject to policy.
sections.heading: Allowed promotions

sections.body:
- Promotions never mutate a version.
- Promotions do not “copy” versions by default; the same version ID can be referenced by multiple bindings.
- Promotion is blocked unless:
  - version has `validation_status=valid`
  - operator has RBAC permission for target scope
  - rollout gates are satisfied (or explicitly overridden with justification)
sections.heading: Promotion invariants

sections.body:
- “Apply” means: start rollout that will eventually update the binding’s `active_version_id` to target version.
- “Promote” means: create or update a binding at a different scope/environment to reference a chosen version, typically after a successful rollout elsewhere.
sections.heading: Console/API semantics

sections.body: We will model environment explicitly in the binding scope.
sections.heading: Environment scoping

sections.body:
- The same version can be evaluated in staging and later activated in prod without duplication.
- Audit events can clearly distinguish “created version” vs “activated in prod”.
sections.heading: Why environment is in the binding (not the version)

sections.body:
- `dev`: internal testing; relaxed gating.
- `staging`: pre-prod; gating enabled with lower blast radius.
- `prod`: customer impact; strict policy and gating.
sections.heading: Supported environments (control plane)

sections.body: Private deployments may not run Redwood-managed staging/prod environments in the same way. We still model `environment` for parity, but Private operators may choose to only use `prod`.
sections.heading: Private deployments

sections.body: Rollback is defined as a binding update that repoints `active_version_id` to a prior version.
sections.heading: Rollback semantics

sections.body:
- **One-click** in Console calls Rollback API, which:
  1) selects a rollback target version (explicit choice or “previous known-good”)
  2) starts a rollback rollout (fast path; higher priority)
  3) updates binding when rollback rollout reaches checkpoints
- **Idempotent**: repeated rollback to the same version results in no-op once binding already points to that version.
- **Race-safe**: binding updates use optimistic concurrency (e.g., compare-and-swap on `updated_at`/`etag`) to prevent apply and rollback from interleaving silently.
sections.heading: Properties

sections.body: A version is eligible as known-good if it was previously active for the same binding scope and did not trigger an auto-pause/failed gate within a defined window (initial default: 60 minutes). The service will still allow manual selection of any valid version with appropriate permissions.
sections.heading: “Known-good” definition

sections.body:
- change management policy enforcement
- RBAC at a clear target (scope)
- audit logging of activation
- rollback behavior that does not require creating new versions or rewriting payloads
sections.heading: Bindings provide a stable unit for

sections.body:
- Create initial `OptimizationConfigVersion` records by snapshotting current effective configs.
- Create `OptimizationConfigBinding` per existing scope currently supported (initially: tenant/model/region for Hosted/Dedicated; Private as `deployment_id`/operator-managed binding).
- For a transition period, runtime will accept both legacy config fetch and versioned fetch, with versioned taking precedence when binding exists.
sections.heading: Migration plan (from existing mutable configs)

sections.body:
- Version creation and binding updates emit audit events defined in `optimization-config-audit-events`.
- RBAC enforcement is done on binding operations (apply/promote/rollback), not on version read.
- Sensitive payload fields (if any appear in future) must be either prohibited in Optimization Config payloads or redacted in audit exports; current schemas do not include secrets.
sections.heading: Security / compliance considerations

sections.body:
- Clear traceability: “what is active” is always the binding’s active version.
- Safer operations: canary and rollback are pointer-based with explicit rollout state.
- Easier support: operators can cite version IDs and diff between versions.
sections.heading: Positive

sections.body:
- Requires careful implementation to avoid mixed states during rollout/rollback.
- More storage records (acceptable; versions are small JSON payloads).
sections.heading: Negative / trade-offs

sections.body:
1. Should we allow multiple bindings to compose (e.g., separate bindings for caching and batching) or enforce a single composite config binding per scope? (Current direction in design spec: composite config with typed sections, but staged rollout may still operate per-section.)
2. How long should the system retain versions and rollout artifacts by default (Hosted/Dedicated vs Private)?
3. What is the minimum viable “blast radius summary” computed from bindings for the Console confirmation modal?
sections.heading: Open questions / follow-ups

sections.body:
- Design spec: Optimization Config Versioning (data model, APIs, Console flows)
- ADR: Safe apply gating signals (SLO + eval gates)
- Optimization Config Service doc (endpoints and consistency guarantees)
- Production optimization change policy (required canary by blast radius)
sections.heading: References

payload.page_title: service-call-graphs-and-cascading-failure-mitigation-playbook-2026

sections.body: Title: Service Call Graphs and Cascading Failure Mitigation — Platform Playbook
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: This playbook documents how Redwood’s platform teams should model service call graphs, detect emerging cascading failures, and apply mitigation patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, adaptive throttling) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. It combines design guidelines, concrete dashboard and alert recommendations, incident runbooks, retrospective checklists, and a short roadmap for incremental improvements.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Applies to platform-facing services in the eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime domains (routing, model-proxy, cache-service, quota-service, autoscaler, sidecars).
- Not intended for application-level business logic (product teams should have their own fallbacks per SLAs).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1. Reduce blast radius of failures that originate from downstream services by 80% for common dependency classes within 6 months.
2. Detect cascading patterns earlier using call-graph-derived composite SLOs and anomaly detection.
3. Provide a repeatable incident response runbook to restore service with minimal human coordination.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Call graph: Directed graph where nodes are services and edges are RPC/HTTP/call relationships with associated P95/P99 latency and error rate meta.
- Cascading failure: When degradation in a downstream node increases load or errors upstream, triggering a chain reaction.
- Circuit breaker: Logical switch to fail-fast or route around a failing dependency.
- Bulkhead: Resource partitioning technique (threadpools/connection pools/GPU pools) to limit cross-service interference.
sections.heading: Definitions and Concepts

sections.body:
- Platform Core (team lead: Miguel Torres) owns the canonical call-graph generation pipeline and visualization components.
- Observability (team lead: Priya Reddy) owns the alerting library and composite SLO definitions.
- Runtime (team lead: Sam Bennett) owns sidecar-level resilience primitives and rollout controls.
sections.heading: Ownership

sections.body:
- Per-edge metrics: request_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, error_rate (4xx/5xx split), retry_rate, queue_depth.
- Per-node metrics: concurrent_requests, cpu_util, mem_rss, thread_pool_busy_pct, inbound_rate, outbound_rate.
- Traces: sampled distributed traces with service and edge annotations (call_site, retry_type, circuit_state).
- Composite indicators: normalized downstream_health_score (0-1), cascading_index (0-100) derived by call-graph propagation.
sections.heading: Observability (what to collect)

sections.body:
- "Service Heatmap": grid of downstream_health_score for top 50 dependencies.
- "Call Graph Live Topology": interactive view with edge thickness = request_rate and color = cascading_index.
- "Upstream Impact Table": top upstream services sorted by delta(error_rate) attributable to a single downstream failure.
- "Retry Storm Detector": retry_rate spike charts + source of retries (client vs internal).
sections.heading: Suggested dashboard panels (standardized across regions)

sections.body:
1) Overview: availability, composite SLOs, top anomalous edges
2) Topology: interactive call graph + node detail selector
3) Latency & Errors: P95/P99 by edge, error types, recent changes
4) Resource Pressure: queue_depth, thread pool saturation, connection pool exhaustion
5) Incident Signals: unusual fan-in/out, synchronized latency spikes across edges

Alerting: rules and thresholds
- Important: Avoid identical thresholds across different services — use risk tiers (Tier 0 critical infra, Tier 1 high-volume platform services, Tier 2 low-volume utilities).
- Basic edge alerts (Tier 1 example):
  * edge_error_rate > 4% for 3m (alert: paging)
  * p99_latency_increase >= 2x baseline for 2m AND request_rate_drop > 20% (alert: paging)
  * retry_rate_spike > 5x baseline for 1m (alert: on-call)
- Composite alerts (derived):
  * cascading_index > 30 for 5m => escalate to platform SRE lead
  * cross-service error correlation (>=3 upstreams show error_rate delta > 2%) => trigger incident bridge
- Alert routing: paging should go to the owning service on-call first. If cascading_index > 50 or multiple teams implicated, escalate to platform triage channel and platform core on-call.
sections.heading: Example dashboard layout (panel rows)

sections.body:
- Maintain per-service request_success SLO (e.g., 99.9% success over 30d) and downstream_dependency_availability SLO (95% for best-effort dependencies).
- Define composite SLOs that represent user-facing flows (e.g., "Model inference end-to-end"), computable by expanding call graphs and weighting edge SLOs by traffic contribution.
- Use composite SLO degradations as a primary signal to trigger rollback of recent platform changes or to activate graceful degradation.
sections.heading: SLO mapping and composite SLOs

sections.body:
1. Circuit Breaker (recommended primitives):
   - Failure threshold: sliding window 60s, if error_rate > 5% and p99 > 2x baseline then open.
   - Half-open policy: allow 5% of requests through for 30s probe.
   - Fallback strategy: cached response or 503 with user-facing retry-after header where safe.
2. Bulkhead: partition pool by upstream caller type (control plane vs data plane). Default pool sizes defined per instance class in config table below.
3. Adaptive Backpressure: when downstream queue_depth > 75% of configured max, start shedding or downgrade non-essential requests (e.g., telemetry writes).
4. Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter; max attempts: 3 for idempotent calls, 0 for non-idempotent. Do not retry on 4xx errors except 429.

Config table (defaults — tune per service):
| config_key | default_value | notes |
|-----------|---------------|-------|
| thread_pool_size | 128 | medium instance; reduce for small utility services |
| connection_pool_max | 64 | per-upstream pool |
| queue_max_items | 10000 | used by adaptive backpressure |
| circuit_failure_threshold_pct | 5 | percent errors in sliding window to open |
| circuit_window_seconds | 60 | size of sliding window |
| bulkhead_partitions | 3 | reservations for control/data/unknown traffic |

Incident Runbook: Cascading Failure (quick restore)
1. Triage (0-5 min):
   a. Open incident bridge and post incident header with initial hypothesis.
   b. Identify the high cascading_index node(s) via the topology panel.
   c. If cascading_index < 20, monitor and rate-limit alerts; if >=20, proceed to mitigation.
2. Containment (5-15 min):
   a. For each implicated downstream node, toggle circuit breaker to "open" (fail fast) for non-essential call paths using rollout flag.
   b. Apply temporary routing rule to route critical traffic to a known-good region or model variant if available.
   c. Reduce global client concurrency for affected upstreams via per-route quotas (throttle by 30%).
3. Mitigation (15-60 min):
   a. If a specific service shows resource exhaustion, increase pool limits or restart worker pool if safe (use canary restart first).
   b. If error cause is degeneration (e.g., bad cache corruption), perform targeted cache invalidation.
   c. If root cause unknown, enable extended tracing for affected edges (increase sampling to 100% for 10 minutes).
4. Recovery (60-180 min):
   a. Gradually close circuit breakers and ramp concurrency with canary checks and health probes.
   b. Monitor composite SLO and cascading_index for regression.
   c. Once stable for 2x SLO window, close incident and begin retrospective.
sections.heading: Design Patterns and Libraries (how-to)

sections.body:
- Toggle circuit via admin CLI: redwood-circuitctl set --service model-proxy --dependency quota-service --state open --reason "cascade-mitigation"
- Increase thread pool (safe restart): kubectl -n platform scale deployment model-proxy --replicas=3 && apply configmap threadpool=192
- Increase tracing sampling (temporarily): curl -X POST http://obs-controlplane/api/sampling -d '{"service":"model-proxy","rate":1.0}'
sections.heading: Runbook commands and quick snippets

sections.body:
- Capture timeline with signal timestamps (alerts, mitigations applied, service changes).
- Identify earliest signal: was this an edge anomaly, resource exhaustion, configuration change, or external dependency?
- Quantify blast radius: affected services, customer impact, error budget burn.
- Action items: assign owners, set due dates, and prioritize in platform roadmap. Typical action examples:
  * Add top-10 dependency heatmap to weekly on-call dashboard (owner: Observability).
  * Harden circuit-breaker tuning for the quota-service (owner: Runtime).
  * Add regression test for the failing call pattern in CI (owner: Eng-Devex).
- Retro: schedule 60-min cross-team review with platform, runtime, and observability within 3 business days.
sections.heading: Postmortem & Retrospective Checklist

sections.body:
- Chaos test: simulate downstream latency and saturated queues for 30s and validate that the upstream service’s retries, circuit-breakers, and bulkheads behave within thresholds.
- Synthetic flows: run black-box synthetic composite SLO checks (end-to-end) against canary cluster prior to major rollout.
- Load tests: include fan-in scenarios that replicate typical production call graph degrees (e.g., 1:50).
sections.heading: Testing & Pre-deployment Validation

sections.body:
- Q2 2026: Canonical call-graph ingest pipeline (owner: Platform Core) — export per-deployment graphs to the topology service and persist weekly snapshots.
- Q3 2026: Composite SLO engine GA (owner: Observability) — define user flows and automated rollback triggers.
- Q4 2026: Automated circuit tuning (owner: Runtime) — leverage reinforcement signals to recommend/roll optimal circuit thresholds.
- Ongoing: Add regional policies for private deployments (on-prem) to respect customer network constraints.
sections.heading: Roadmap (next 6 months)

sections.body:
- Nightly job: snapshot call graph and run heuristics to precompute top-25 dangerous dependency pairs; email to platform lead.
- Weekly runbook drill: 30-min tabletop on cascading scenario with at least one cross-team participant.
- Documentation: keep service-level fallback contracts published in each service repo README and link from the call-graph node metadata.

Appendix A: Incident examples (anonymized)
- Case 1: Quota-service connection pool leak (Jan 2026) — symptoms: upstream p99 climb and synchronized retries. Mitigation: opened circuit breakers, drained stale connections, rollout of connection pool fix.
- Case 2: Cache corruption (Nov 2025) — symptoms: mass 500s with low downstream cpu but high queue_depth. Mitigation: cache invalidation + gradual restart.

Appendix B: Quick links and resources
- Call-graph topology UI: https://internal-console/redwood/topology
- On-call rota: https://internal-console/redwood/oncall
- Composite SLO docs: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/platform-observability-sli-onboarding-playbook-2026
sections.heading: Operational Playbook Notes (team wiki items)

sections.body:
- 2026-02-15: Draft created by Aisha Kumar.
- 2026-03-01: Reviewed and published; added incident examples and CLI snippets (reviewers: Miguel, Priya, Sam).

Contact: Platform Core Slack #platform-core and platform-triage@redwood.example.com

payload.page_title: Micro-SLO Composition and Platform Consolidation Patterns

sections.body:
Summary:
This document describes a practical set of patterns for composing micro‑SLOs across platform services and consolidating platform responsibilities to improve operational clarity, reduce alert noise, and align operator actions with tenant economic signals. It combines architectural guidance, dashboard and alert recommendations, operational runbooks, a short retrospective of a pilot, and next‑step roadmap items.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to platform services owned by the eng-platform team (allocators, prefetch coordinator, runtime routing, telemetry pipeline).
- Goal: give operators deterministic decision surfaces during degradation and make cost/latency tradeoffs explicit to product owners.
- Not in scope: customer application SLOs or model quality SLOs (handled by product/Applied ML).

Primary outcomes:
- A composable micro‑SLO taxonomy and examples
- Dashboard primitives and alert thresholds tuned for consolidation operational flows
- A runbook for graceful consolidation and operator playbooks for safe rollback
- Retrospective lessons from a Q4 2025 pilot and a prioritized roadmap for adoption

Owner and contributors:
- Owner: Evan Brooks (eng-platform)
- Contributors: Priya Nandakumar (SRE), Marco Li (runtime), Ana Gomez (observability)

Micro‑SLO taxonomy and composition rules:
1) Unit micro‑SLOs (low-level):
   - e.g., allocator.cpu_saturation_p50 < 65% (30s window), connection_pool.utilization_p95 < 80%
   - Action: local throttling or transient evictions; no global customer notifications.
2) Composite micro‑SLOs (service-level):
   - Example: tenant_token_latency_p95_across_runtime <= 250ms AND tenant_throughput_success_rate >= 99.5%
   - Action: trigger consolidation workflow (see runbook).
3) Business impact SLOs (customer-facing):
   - e.g., api_text_generation_p99_latency < 1s or api_error_rate < 0.5%
   - Action: customer incident, public comms, and dedicated rollback.

Composition rules (operationally enforced):
- Prefer conjunctive composition for safety (A AND B) except when cost control requires disjunctions for graceful degradation.
- Tag each micro‑SLO with: service, steward, default remediation action, and cost impact estimate (tokens/sec-equivalent).
- Maintain a "composability matrix" (see table below) to enumerate safe and unsafe combinations.

Config table: micro‑SLO metadata (example rows)
| key | steward | window | threshold | remediation | cost_impact_estimate |
| allocator.cpu_saturation_p50 | eng-platform/allocator | 30s | 65% | soft_eviction | 8 tokens/sec |
| runtime.kv_cache_miss_p95 | eng-serving-runtime | 60s | 12% | increase_prefetch | 14 tokens/sec |
| telemetry.ingest_lag_p90 | eng-platform/telemetry | 2m | 90s | backpressure_routing | 2 tokens/sec |

Dashboards and visual primitives:
- Canonical dashboard layout (one per composed SLO):
  1) Top row: composed SLO status (red/yellow/green), current burn rate, and owner card.
  2) Middle row: contributing micro‑SLO panels with heatmap (trend over 6h, 24h, 7d).
  3) Bottom row: economic signal — token cost delta, estimated spend impact, and active consolidation credits.
- Visual primitives to create: sparkline + current_value + slow_change_indicator (small delta arrow).
- Shared short query snippets (to be copied into dashboards):
  - "composed_slo_status(service, window)" -> boolean rollup of tagged micro‑SLOs
  - "economic_delta(tenant, interval)" -> token-equivalent cost delta estimator

Alert design and thresholds (examples):
- Severity: P0 (immediate ops interrupt), P1 (operator action within 15m), P2 (investigate in next oncall shift).
- Sample rules:
  - P1: composed_slo_burn_rate >= 1.2 for 5m AND composite_error_rate > 0.3% -> page on‑call SRE.
  - P2: single micro_slo breach lasting 15m but composite still green -> ticket for steward, no page.
- Noise reduction strategies:
  - Only page when composed SLO trips or when two or more independent micro‑SLOs breach within a 10m window.
  - Suppress lower severity alerts when platform consolidation workflow is actively running.

Consolidation workflow (operator runbook) — rapid reference:
1) Detection:
   - Observe composed SLO flagged on dashboard or receive P1 page.
2) Triage (first 5 minutes):
   - Identify which micro‑SLOs are breached and their stewards.
   - Run the diagnostic script: /ops/bin/compose-diagnose --slo <id> --since 10m (returns ranked causes).
   - Check economic delta panel and active burst credits.
3) Immediate mitigations (5–20 minutes):
   - If allocator.cpu_saturation_p50 high: enable soft_eviction for non-critical tenants (soft_eviction policy id: se-policy-3).
   - If runtime.kv_cache_miss spikes: enable cohort_prefetch for high-hit cohorts for 10 minutes.
   - If telemetry.ingest_lag high: switch to reduced-sampling ingest mode and route backpressure to low-cost region.
4) Consolidation decision (20–40 minutes):
   - If mitigations recover composed SLO to green: schedule followup postmortem and mark actions in ticket.
   - If not recovered: escalate to consolidation plan B (regional burst shift with explicit tenant credits) and notify product owners.
5) Rollback and monitoring (40+ minutes):
   - Roll back experimental mitigations in reverse order if they cause regressions.
   - Keep composite dashboard pinned for 2h and monitor economic delta for cost spikes.

Runbook checklist (operator copyable):
1) Page received: confirm paging context.
2) Attach composed SLO link to incident ticket.
3) Run compose-diagnose and capture top 3 suggested causes.
4) Execute immediate mitigation(s) with rollback plan.
5) Update ticket with times and actions, set follow-up postmortem.

Safe consolidation patterns (architectural guidance):
- Consolidate routing and prefetch decisions under a single coordinator service to avoid split-brain in mitigation.
- Maintain an immutable mapping of "consolidation credits" per tenant to authorize temporary resource moves.
- Implement feature toggles for consolidation mitigations with built-in guard rails (max-duration, cost-threshold).

Pilot retrospective (Q4 2025):
What we did:
- Ran a two-week pilot consolidating three micro‑SLOs (allocator CPU, runtime cache miss, telemetry ingest lag) into a single composed SLO for a low-latency tenant cohort.
Outcomes:
- Alert volume for the cohort dropped 43% (fewer transient pages).
- Mean time to mitigation decreased by 26% because operators had a single decision surface.
- However, cost spikes occurred during an automated cohort-prefetch mitigation on two occasions (root cause: missing cost_impact_estimate tagging).
Action items from pilot:
- Require cost_impact_estimate for every micro‑SLO (blocked mitigations with unknown cost).
- Add a cost-safety limiter to prefetch mitigations (max token-equivalent per minute).
- Expand composed SLO dashboards and default suppressions to reduce page storms.

Metrics we measured:
- Alert volume, MTTR, cost delta, composed_slo_recovery_rate, false_positive_pages.
- Baseline -> pilot improvements available in the attached experiment sheet (see related_pages).

Roadmap (next 6 months):
- M1 (30 days): Publish composability matrix and annotate existing micro‑SLOs with cost_impact_estimate.
- M2 (60 days): Implement compose-diagnose CLI and two canonical composed SLO dashboards.
- M3 (90 days): Add cost-safety limiter to prefetch and soft_eviction mitigations.
- M4 (120+ days): Expand to regional consolidation patterns and run a second pilot across multiple regions.

Operational responsibilities and RACI (short):
- R: eng-platform (compose orchestration, dashboards), eng-serving-runtime (runtime micro‑SLOs), eng-sre (oncall/runbooks).
- A: eng-platform lead.
- C: product owners for affected tenants.
- I: finance and customer success for cost/customer-impact communication.

Templates and links (copy to incident ticket):
- Composed SLO ticket stub: [Composed SLO incident template]
- Dashboard links: [Composed SLO dashboard template 1], [Economic delta panel template]
- Diagnostic CLI: /ops/bin/compose-diagnose (internal tool)

Follow‑ups and governance:
- Quarterly audit: each composed SLO must have a documented steward, cost estimate, and a signed acceptance from product owner.
- Monthly retros: eng-platform runs a 30-minute retrospective on consolidation incidents and updates playbooks.

Related pages:
- /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/composed-slo-dashboard-library-2026
- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/rapid-consolidation-operator-runbook-2025
- /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/economic-signal-and-tenant-crediting-2025

Appendix: quick CLI cookbook
- Diagnose composed SLO: /ops/bin/compose-diagnose --slo composed_slo_id --since 15m --format short
- Toggle soft_eviction: /ops/bin/evict-toggle --policy se-policy-3 --enable --duration 10m --reason "composed_slo_mitigation"

Document history:
- 2026-02-10: Created by Evan Brooks
- 2026-02-24: Pilot retrospective added (Priya Nandakumar)
- 2026-03-01: Roadmap and governance items finalized (Marco Li)
