payload.page_title: Component Deprecation and Dependency Matrix Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the process, artifacts, and operational steps for deprecating platform components (services, libraries, sidecars) while managing dependency impact across Redwood Inference. It includes a recommended dependency matrix format, deprecation lifecycle phases, monitoring and dashboard requirements, alert thresholds, migration patterns, and retrospective templates.

Intended audience
-----------------
- Platform engineers (owners and consumers)
- SRE and oncall teams
- Product managers coordinating cross-team migrations
- Release engineers and change control

Why this matters
-----------------
Deprecations without a controlled process create outages, regressions in latency or correctness, and hidden technical debt. The goal is to make deprecations predictable, observable, and reversible with a clear owner and migration path.

Scope and definitions
---------------------
- Component: any deployable or package (service, library, sidecar, infra template) that other services depend on.
- Deprecation lifecycle: the stages from announcement through removal.
- Matrix: a single-table source of truth tracking consumers, owners, SLO impact, and migration status.

Quick reference: when to use this playbook
----------------------------------------
1. Owner decides a component is end-of-life (EOL) or harmful (security/bug/perf)
2. A breaking change to a central library or sidecar is required
3. Infrastructure consolidation that removes platform primitives (e.g., legacy cache layer)

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Component Owner: primary engineer responsible for the deprecation (name and pager).
- Platform PM: coordinates stakeholder communication and migration incentives.
- Consumer Leads: engineers owning services that depend on the component.
- SRE: verifies monitoring, alerting, and rollback capability before removal.
- Release Manager / Change Control: schedules canary windows, maintenance windows.

Required artifacts
------------------
1. Deprecation Notice (public Confluence page + internal changelog entry)
2. Dependency Matrix (canonical CSV/Confluence table)
3. Migration Plan per consumer (owner, ETA, blocker list)
4. Dashboard + Alerts (SLO to detect regressions)
5. Feature flag or compatibility shim where applicable
6. Post-deprecation retrospective template

Canonical dependency matrix (recommended columns)
------------------------------------------------
Use a single table for the component that is easy to query and export. Minimal recommended columns:
- Component
- Component Owner (email)
- Component Type (service/library/sidecar/infra)
- Current Version(s) in use
- Consumers (service names)
- Consumer Owner(s)
- Migration ETA (YYYY-MM-DD)
- Compatibility Risk (low/medium/high)
- SLOs impacted (route or service-level)
- Blockers (short text)
- Status (notified/in-progress/migrated/blocked/removed)

Sample ASCII table (for quick copy to Confluence)
------------------------------------------------
| Component | Owner | Type | Consumers | Migration ETA | Risk | SLOs impacted | Status |
| cache-legacy | priya@redwood.ai | sidecar | api-gateway, embeddings-worker | 2026-04-01 | high | api-gateway: p99 latency < 200ms | in-progress |

Deprecation lifecycle and timeline (recommended minimum windows)
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Announcement phase (>= 60 days)
   - Publish Deprecation Notice to Confluence and platform-team email list.
   - Create dependency matrix and assign consumer leads.
   - Begin automated discovery: run dependency scanner to list indirect dependencies.
2. Migration support phase (>= 30 days)
   - Provide migration guides, sample code, and compatibility shim (if feasible).
   - Schedule weekly migration syncs with major consumers.
   - Instrument tracing and add dashboards defined below.
3. Restriction phase (>= 14 days)
   - Apply linting or CI warnings for new usages.
   - Feature flags default to warn/deny for new deploys if migration is urgent.
4. Removal window (>= 7 days notice)
   - Announce final removal date, schedule canary cutover.
   - Oncall standby during initial removal and 72-hour high-frequency checks.
5. Post-removal review (<= 14 days after removal)
   - Collect metrics, incidents, and run retrospective template.

Migration patterns (examples)
----------------------------
- Service -> Library migration: publish compatibility adapter and deprecate API surface in two phases.
- Sidecar removal: provide a replacement host-level library + configuration migration guide; recommend rolling restart strategy.
- Central infra elimination (e.g., shared cache): provide fallback configuration, throttling rules, and capacity plan for consumers.

Required monitoring, dashboards, and alerting
--------------------------------------------
Before restriction phase the owner must create or update dashboards and alerts:
- Migration dashboard: consumer migration statuses, per-consumer error/latency deltas vs baseline (7d).
- Dependency heatmap: counts of services by dependency version.
- Canary health dashboard: real-time error rate, latency histograms, saturation metrics for services in the canary cohort.

Minimum alerts to create
- Migration regression alert: service X error rate increase > 50% over baseline (5m), or p95 latency increase > 30% (5m) — severity P1.
- Unmigrated consumer near removal date: consumer remaining > 5 days before removal — severity P2.
- Unexpected traffic to removed endpoint: any 5xx > 0.5% post-removal (1m) — severity P1.

Sample alert rule (Prometheus-ish pseudo YAML)
------------------------------------------------
alert: MigrationLatencySpike
expr: increases(p95(latency_seconds{service=~"api-gateway|embeddings-worker"}[5m])) > 0.30
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: P1
annotations:
  summary: "Migration latency spike for {{ $labels.service }}"
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/service-dependency-fault-isolation-and-fallback-runbook-2025"

Feature flags and compatibility shims
------------------------------------
- Use redwood-feature-flags to gate removal behavior. Flag naming convention: deprecate.<component>.<YYYYMMDD>.
- If a compatibility shim is provided, ensure it is behind a flag and namespaced to the owning repo.

Example deprecation flag naming and rollout plan
- Flag: deprecate.cache-legacy.20260401
- Rollout: off (default) -> enable warnings to 10% of consumers -> 100% warnings -> deny new allocations -> removal window

CI and linting changes
----------------------
- Add a linter rule that fails builds when new code imports the deprecated package after the restriction phase.
- Track linter exceptions in the dependency matrix under Blockers.

Canary / rollback procedure (high-level)
----------------------------------------
1. Prepare canary cohort: 2–3 low-risk services representing 5–10% traffic.
2. Run canary for 24–72 hours with SRE monitoring.
3. If P1 alert triggers: rollback immediately by re-enabling compatibility shim or reinstating the component.
4. After successful canary, progressively widen cohort in 3 stages (25%, 50%, 100%).

Operational checklist before removal
-----------------------------------
- [ ] Deprecation notice published and communicated (>= 60d)
- [ ] Dependency matrix complete and consumer leads assigned
- [ ] Dashboards and alerts created and tested
- [ ] Migration plans exist for all high-risk consumers
- [ ] Canary plan and rollback steps documented
- [ ] Change-control slot reserved and SRE pager coverage assigned

Post-deprecation retrospective template
---------------------------------------
1. Summary: component removed, removal date, owner.
2. Metrics: traffic, error rates, latency before/after (7d)
3. Incidents: list with severity and remediation steps
4. What went well
5. What didn’t go well
6. Action items and owners (with due dates)

Sample metrics to collect
- Total dependent callers (count)
- Number of callers migrated successfully
- Delta in platform costs (if component removal affects infra billing)
- Customer/consumer reported issues

Common anti-patterns and mitigations
-----------------------------------
- Anti-pattern: Quiet removal without broad communication.
  Mitigation: Mandatory 60+ day public notice and weekly migration syncs.
- Anti-pattern: Skipping dashboard instrumentation.
  Mitigation: SRE gate — no restriction unless dashboards exist.
- Anti-pattern: Single-person ownership for complex removals.
  Mitigation: Assign a cross-functional triage lead (owner + SRE + PM).

Appendix A: Example migration guide snippet (cache-legacy -> cache-v2)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. High-level change: cache-legacy sidecar removed; cache-v2 is a host library exposing identical API.
2. Steps for consumers:
   a. Update build dependency to cache-v2:
      - Gradle: implementation 'com.redwood:cache-v2:2.1.0'
      - Maven: <dependency>com.redwood:cache-v2:2.1.0</dependency>
   b. Replace sidecar client instantiation:
      - Old: SidecarClient.connect("cache-legacy:1234")
      - New: CacheClient.newInstance(Config.fromEnv())
   c. Run integration tests locally and in CI.
   d. Deploy to staging; monitor p95 latency and success rate.

3. Compatibility shim: small adapter package available at github.com/redwood/cache-legacy-adapter (feature-flagged).

Appendix B: Suggested SLOs impacted and thresholds to monitor
------------------------------------------------------------
- API Gateway (route /v1/generate): p95 latency baseline threshold 300ms; alert if +30% sustained for 10m.
- Embeddings Worker: error rate baseline 0.2%; alert if > 1% for 5m.
- Model-serving pods: CPU saturation > 85% after migration — investigate.

Communications and timeline template (email + Slack cadence)
-----------------------------------------------------------
- Day 0 (announcement): Confluence page + #platform-announcements + email to stakeholders.
- Weekly: migration progress summary in Confluence + short sync for blocked consumers.
- Day -14: Reminder to consumer leads and change-control approvers.
- Day -7: Final readiness runbook and oncall roster.
- Day 0: Removal notice + live updates in #platform-ops during removal.

Related templates and links
-------------------------
- Service dependency runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/service-dependency-fault-isolation-and-fallback-runbook-2025
- Service lifecycle guidelines: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/service-lifecycle-orchestration-guidelines-2026

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-09-15: Initial draft by Priya Patel
- 2025-12-10: Added alerting rules and matrix template (review by Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-02-10: Incorporated SRE feedback and canary/rollback clarification (Alice Chen)

Contact
-------
For questions or to request exception, contact Priya Patel (pri@redwood.ai) or the Platform PM channel (#platform-pm).

payload.page_title: Cost Model Service (cost-model-api) — Service Overview

sections.body: Cost Model Service (service name: **cost-model-api**) provides a single, versioned implementation for inference cost estimation and cost breakdowns across Redwood products.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- **Per-request cost estimates** and standardized breakdown taxonomy (prefill/decode, cache, batch efficiency, overhead allocation, quantization deltas)
- **Aggregated cost breakdowns** for Console dashboards (bounded-cardinality responses)
- **What-if projections** used by Optimize to quantify ROI from configuration changes (batching/caching/quantization)

This document describes architecture, dependencies, SLOs, ownership/on-call, and rollout strategy.

---
sections.heading: It is the canonical source for

sections.body:
**Primary owner team:** Platform Control Plane
- Service/API lead: Ethan Park
- Control plane integration: Benji Okafor, Cole Summers
- Auth/tenancy: Kaitlyn Nguyen

**Reliability partner:** SRE
- Reliability lead: Rafael Mendes

**Key dependencies owners:**
- Telemetry & Analytics: Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman
- Runtime metrics/instrumentation: Sofia Ivanova, Omar El-Sayed, Grace Kim
- Finance alignment: Laura Bennett, Rishi Malhotra

---
sections.heading: Service owners

sections.body: The Cost Model Service is an internal service + shared library that standardizes cost calculations. It is intentionally *not* the billing system of record.
sections.heading: Where this service sits

sections.body:
- **Redwood Console backend** (hot path for cost breakdown pages; calls are cacheable)
- **Redwood Optimize backend** (what-if projections; heavier compute but guarded and bounded)
- **Finance/analytics pipelines** (offline reconciliations and reporting windows; typically via batch exports or aggregated endpoints)

---
sections.heading: Primary callers

sections.body:
```
            +-----------------------+
            |  Redwood Console BE   |
            |  (dashboards, APIs)   |
            +-----------+-----------+
                        |
                        | (internal, mTLS)
                        v
+-----------------------+-----------------------+
|                cost-model-api                 |
|----------------------------------------------|
|  1) Request validation + tenancy/authz        |
|  2) Version negotiation (schema + semantics)  |
|  3) Cost computation engine                   |
|     - cost breakdown taxonomy                 |
|     - overhead allocation policy              |
|     - quantization profile deltas             |
|  4) Response bounding + aggregation guards    |
|  5) Cache (read-through) for hot keys         |
+-----------+-------------------+---------------+
            |                   |
            |                   |
            v                   v
  +------------------+   +---------------------+
  | Telemetry Store  |   | Model Catalog       |
  | (token + runtime |   | (model + quant      |
  |  metrics, lag)   |   |  profile metadata)  |
  +------------------+   +---------------------+
            |
            v
  +------------------+
  | Drift Monitor Job|
  | (scheduled; SLI) |
  +------------------+
            |
            v
  +------------------+
  | Observed Spend / |
  | Billing Primitives|
  +------------------+

            +-----------------------+
            |   Redwood Optimize    |
            | (recommendations/ROI) |
            +-----------+-----------+
                        |
                        v
                 (what-if endpoints)
```
sections.heading: High-level architecture (text diagram)

sections.body:
- **Console** calls are latency-sensitive; the service is designed to be cache-friendly and returns bounded responses.
- **Optimize** calls can be more compute-heavy, but are constrained by request guardrails (limits on parameter ranges, cardinality, and time horizon).
- A **drift monitoring job** compares predicted vs observed spend to produce a correctness/drift SLI.

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body:
1) **Telemetry Store** (authoritative inputs for per-request and aggregated cost)
- Token accounting: prompt/prefill tokens, decode tokens, output tokens
- Cache metrics: KV cache hit/miss rates and bytes (when available), cache eligibility flags
- Scheduling metrics: effective batch size, queue time, batching window outcomes
- Runtime stage breakdown: prefill vs decode wall time and/or token accounting split

Owners: Telemetry & Analytics (Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman)

2) **Model Catalog**
- Model identifiers, versions, architecture class
- Hardware compatibility metadata
- **Quantization profile IDs** and relevant metadata used by the cost model

Owner: Platform / Model Catalog maintainers (in coordination with Applied ML)

3) **Overhead allocation policy**
- Finance-approved policy to allocate shared costs to request-attributable vs overhead buckets
- Reporting windows and reconciliation rules

Owners: Finance/FP&A (Laura Bennett, Rishi Malhotra) + Platform
sections.heading: Required upstream data

sections.body:
- Console cost breakdown views (feature flag gated)
- Optimize ROI estimates and recommendation guardrails
- Billing hooks alignment (shared primitives; may intentionally differ for invoicing semantics; see ADRs)

---
sections.heading: Downstream integrations

sections.body:
- **Estimate**: Per-request estimated cost + breakdown (for request detail / tracing contexts)
- **Breakdown**: Aggregated cost breakdown over a bounded query window (for dashboards)
- **What-if**: Projected deltas based on configuration changes (for Optimize)
sections.heading: Request types supported (v1)

sections.body:
To prevent cardinality and latency blowups, the service enforces:
- Maximum time window per request (e.g., dashboard query windows must be bounded; long-range queries require pre-aggregation)
- Maximum number of group-by dimensions
- Maximum response size (rows and bytes)
- Allowed parameter ranges for what-if (e.g., batch size multipliers, cache warm-rate assumptions, quantization profile sets)

The exact limits are maintained in the API standards addendum and service config.

---
sections.heading: Query bounding (hard requirements)

sections.body:
1) **Standard Cost Spec (schema + semantics)**
- Versioned schemas for inputs/outputs (e.g., cost_model_spec v1)
- Explicit semantics for:
  - Prefill vs decode attribution
  - Cache hits vs misses vs ineligible requests
  - Batch efficiency and queue-time effects
  - Quantization profile deltas (throughput/memory impacts; quality guardrails)
  - Overhead allocation buckets

2) **Deterministic computation engine**
- Pure functions over canonical inputs where possible
- Stable rounding rules and currency/unit conventions
- Explicit “unknown/unavailable” handling for missing telemetry fields (no silent backfill that changes semantics)

3) **Confidence/uncertainty for projections (What-if only)**
- What-if returns a point estimate plus a confidence indicator when driven by empirically learned parameters
- Guardrails prevent projections when input uncertainty is too high or when inputs are out of policy bounds

---
sections.heading: The cost-model-api combines three layers

sections.body: Detailed SLO definitions live in the SLO page (see related pages). This section summarizes the operational targets used by Platform + SRE.
sections.heading: SLAs / SLOs (service-level)

sections.body:
- **99.9%** monthly availability for core endpoints used by Console
- Degraded-mode behavior is allowed (see “Fallbacks”)
sections.heading: Availability SLO

sections.body:
- Estimate/Breakdown endpoints (Console path): **p95 < 250ms** for cache-hit and **p95 < 600ms** for cache-miss under typical dashboard query bounds
- What-if endpoint (Optimize path): **p95 < 2.0s** for bounded scenarios
sections.heading: Latency SLO (p95)

sections.body:
- A scheduled drift job compares predicted costs (from cost-model primitives) to observed spend attribution over an agreed reporting window.
- Alerting is based on drift thresholds that account for telemetry lag and overhead allocation windows.
sections.heading: Correctness / Drift SLI

sections.body:
- If latency or errors threaten Console UX, the Console integration must automatically fall back to the legacy breakdown path (flag-controlled), and SRE may request a rollout pause.

---
sections.heading: Error budget policy

sections.body:
- Console must implement:
  - Timeouts (short)
  - Retries (bounded)
  - Fallback behavior (legacy cost breakdown implementation) behind a feature flag

- Optimize must implement:
  - Timeouts (longer)
  - No unbounded retries
  - Safe default behavior (suppress recommendation / show “insufficient confidence”) when the what-if endpoint is unavailable
sections.heading: Client fallbacks (required)

sections.body:
- **Telemetry lag / partial ingestion** → drift alerts, missing fields, inconsistent breakdowns
- **Schema mismatch / version negotiation errors** → 4xx from service; clients should downgrade gracefully
- **Cardinality explosion** from overly broad group-bys → request rejected with explicit error code
- **Cache stampede** on common dashboard keys → mitigated via request coalescing + short TTL caching

---
sections.heading: Common failure modes

sections.body:
- Environments: dev, staging, prod
- Deployed as a standard internal control-plane service with:
  - mTLS service-to-service auth
  - Tenant-aware authorization checks
  - Per-route rate limits (stricter for what-if)
sections.heading: Deployment & environments

sections.body:
- Cache TTLs are endpoint-specific
- Feature flags control:
  - Console adoption percentage
  - Optimize what-if enablement
  - Strictness of schema enforcement (e.g., rejecting vs warning on unknown fields)

---
sections.heading: Config highlights

sections.body:
- **Primary:** Platform Control Plane on-call (cost-model-api)
- **Secondary:** SRE on-call (platform services)
sections.heading: On-call rotation

sections.body:
- Telemetry ingestion incidents: page Telemetry & Analytics on-call
- Runtime instrumentation regressions: page Runtime Scheduling/Kernels on-call
- Finance reconciliation concerns (non-urgent): route to FP&A partner (Rishi Malhotra) via ticket
sections.heading: Escalation

sections.body:
- Dashboards exist for latency, error rates, request volume, version distribution, and drift
- Runbook is current and linked in service alerts
- Client fallback is verified in staging with forced fault injection

---
sections.heading: Before enabling Console in production beyond initial canary

sections.body:
- Request volume by endpoint + tenant tier (bounded cardinality)
- Latency (p50/p95/p99) by endpoint
- Error rates by error class (validation, auth, upstream dependency, compute timeout)
- Cache hit ratio (endpoint-level)
- Schema version distribution (requested vs served)
- Drift metrics (from scheduled job) and telemetry lag indicators
sections.heading: Metrics emitted by cost-model-api

sections.body:
- Trace IDs propagated from Console/Optimize
- Logs must not include raw prompts or customer content; only derived counts and stable identifiers

---
sections.heading: Logging/tracing

sections.body:
- Ship service skeleton, auth/tenancy, and schema package
- Implement bounded endpoints with deterministic behavior
sections.heading: Phase 0 — Service bootstrap (completed)

sections.body:
- Console integration behind flag with fallback enabled
- Optimize integration behind flag for internal tenants only
- Validate schema version negotiation behavior
sections.heading: Phase 1 — Staging integrations

sections.body:
- Enable for a small set of internal tenants and low-risk customers
- Monitor: latency, errors, schema version distribution, and drift SLI
- Compare Console breakdowns vs legacy for a sample of dashboard queries
sections.heading: Phase 2 — Production canary

sections.body:
- Increase Console coverage gradually (e.g., 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%)
- Expand Optimize what-if access with strict guardrails
- Align billing hooks to consume the same primitives (document intentional differences)
sections.heading: Phase 3 — Expand adoption

sections.body:
- Immediate rollback via feature flag to legacy breakdowns (Console)
- Disable what-if endpoint exposure (Optimize) and freeze new recommendation rollouts
- If drift alerts are driven by telemetry lag: widen lag tolerance window temporarily and open follow-up work with Telemetry

---
sections.heading: Rollback plan

sections.body:
- Finalize drift thresholds by deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
- Reduce dependency on high-cardinality telemetry dimensions for dashboard queries (prefer pre-aggregations)
- Document a clear customer-support explanation template for “Console vs invoice differences” rooted in the standard taxonomy and reporting windows

---
sections.heading: Open items / follow-ups

sections.body:
- [ ] Pager routes to Platform Control Plane on-call
- [ ] Dashboards present in Grafana (latency/errors/version/drift)
- [ ] Alerts link to runbook
- [ ] Client timeouts + fallback verified
- [ ] Request bounds tested (reject oversized queries)
- [ ] Schema version negotiation tested across Console/Optimize client library versions
sections.heading: Appendix: operational checklist (quick)

payload.page_title: Predictive Cost & Latency Surface Matrix — Operator Guidance

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the predictive cost/latency surface matrix for platform LLM inference traffic and provides a concrete operator guidance playbook for calibrating dashboards, tuning alert thresholds, and running controlled experiments that impact prefetch/caching, eviction and model-variant routing. The goal is to make threshold decisions explainable, reversible, and aligned to tenant SLAs and cost budgets.

Audience:
- Platform operators
- Observability engineers
- Oncall and SRE
- Product managers owning tenant SLAs and pricing signals

Scope:
Covers: per-tenant and cluster-level cost vs. latency tradeoffs for common request categories (foreground low-context, foreground long-context, batch embeddings), required dashboard panels, recommended alerting rules and escalation workflow, calibration procedure and a short experiment template. Does NOT replace individual service runbooks for model-swap emergencies — see related runbooks.

Definitions and key signals:
- surface point: (q, s, m) tuple where q=request category, s=sequence-length bucket, m=model-variant.
- Q categories: foreground-latency (interactive), foreground-throughput (long sequence), batch-embedding (async), rerank (short cached).
- Core signals: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens-per-request (avg), tokens-per-second (cluster), avg-gpu-util, prefix-kv-hit-rate, token-cost-per-request (USD), request-success-rate (200s / total).

Recommended SLOs (examples — translate per-customer):
| Category | p50 | p95 | p99 | success-rate SLO | cost-sensitivity |
|----------|-----|-----|-----|------------------|------------------|
| foreground-latency | 40ms | 120ms | 250ms | 99.9% | high |
| foreground-long | 120ms | 400ms | 1,200ms | 99.5% | medium |
| batch-embedding | n/a | n/a | n/a (throughput SLO) | 99.0% | very-high |

Surface matrix template (operator view):
For each (q, s, m) surface point capture these baseline columns as dashboard filters:
- baseline p50/p95/p99 (rolling 30d)
- burst multiplier (current window / baseline 5m)
- prefetch KV hit-rate (0–100%)
- avg tokens/request and tokens/sec
- estimated token USD cost (model + infra) per request
- failure mode tag (OOM, eviction, timeouts)

Dashboards (panel library):
Create an "Inference Surface" Grafana board composed of:
1) Surface heatmap: rows=model-variants, cols=sequence-length buckets; color = p99 latency normalized by SLO (value >1 = violation).
2) Cost-sensitivity strip: per-tenant cost delta if moving to next-cheaper variant (estimate formula displayed).
3) Prefetch KV hit-rate trend + operator-annotated maintenance windows.
4) Eviction events timeline (annotated by model version rollouts).
5) Composite alert scoreboard (active alerts, SLO burn rate per tenant).
6) Synthetic lab panel: run controlled synthetic workloads and show baseline vs experiment.

Example PromQL alert recipes (tune thresholds to environment):
- Alert: surface-p99-violation-high
  Expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket{le, model_variant, job="inference"}[5m])) by (le, model_variant)) > 1.0
  For: 5m
  Labels: severity=page, owner=platform-operators
  Annotation: "p99 exceeding configured SLO for model_variant={{ $labels.model_variant }}; check prefetch hit-rate and eviction logs."

- Alert: kv-hit-rate-drop
  Expr: avg_over_time(kv_hit_rate{service="prefetch"}[10m]) < 0.6
  For: 10m
  Labels: severity=sev2
  Annotation: "Probable cache degradation; review prefetcher and Redis/metadata latency."

Alert tuning guidance:
- Use burn-rate derived SLOs for noisy signals (p95/p99): e.g., configure SLO burn alerts when 14-day burn-rate > 1.0 and 30-min burn-rate > 3.0.
- Add a recovery condition: cancel page if p99 returns under 80% of SLO for 15m.
- Correlate p99 alerts with token-cost deltas: If p99 violation coincides with >20% cost increase, consider temporary model-rollforward to a cheaper stable variant with documented quality delta.

Operator runbook: threshold calibration workshop (90 minutes)
1) Prep (15m): pick 3 representative tenants (one small, one mid, one large) and load 30d baseline metrics into the synthetic lab panel.
2) Discovery (20m): for each tenant, map top 10 request prefixes by token consumption and annotate current model_variant mapping.
3) Hypothesis (15m): propose one change per tenant (e.g., lower prefetched KV retention from 10s to 2s; try quantized model_variant for batch embeddings). Write down expected cost delta and latency risk.
4) Controlled test (25m): execute experiment against 1% of traffic or in synthetic lab. Observe 30m rolling metrics.
5) Decision & roll plan (15m): if cost drops >=10% and p99 increases <10% and success-rate unaffected, schedule gradual rollout with canary and automatic rollback conditions.

Operator runbook: emergency mitigation (short form)
1) If p99 > 2x SLO and request-success-rate < 95% for >10m:
  a) Check prefetcher KV hit-rate and recent eviction spikes.
  b) If eviction spike present: throttle batch and long-foreground queues by 30% using runtime quota escape hatch.
  c) If KV hit-rate low: temporarily expand prefix cache TTLs or fallback to model-variant pinned in cold cache.
  d) If model OOM observed: immediately switch traffic to next-compatible model-variant with known quality delta; create incident and page ML-developer oncall.
2) Post-stabilize: collect traces, annotate incident timeline, and file a short retro entry in the retrospective board (tag: incident-llm-surface).

Experimentation recipes (examples):
- Quantization A/B for embeddings: route 10% of embedding load to q8_variant, measure retrieval AUC on a fixed eval set, cost delta, and latency p95.
- Prefetch TTL sweep: run five TTL values [0.5s, 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s] on synthetic replay and compute cost/latency per TTL.
- Model-compression fallback: test a smaller model_variant for high-length tails and compute quality delta vs user-facing metrics.

Quality and rollback criteria (must be explicit in every experiment):
- Quality gate: downstream eval metric (rerank accuracy or embedding cosine recall) cannot degrade by >2% absolute for broadly impacting customers unless pre-approved.
- Latency gate: p99 must not increase by more than 15% for foreground-latency category.
- Cost gate: expected cost reduction must be >=8% to justify potential small quality hits.
- Automatic rollback: any sustained success-rate drop >1% for 10m triggers immediate rollback.

Operational telemetry checklist (must be onboarded to the board):
- request_duration_p50/p95/p99 by model_variant and tenant
- kv_hit_rate, kv_miss_latency_ms by cache-shard
- eviction_count and eviction_reason by node and tenant
- model_gpu_mem_pressure_pct and OOM events
- token_cost_estimate_per_request (running estimate)
- synthetic load experiment results and annotated diff from baseline

Maintenance and accountability:
- Quarterly calibration: SRE + Observability + Applied ML run the calibration workshop; notes stored under team-wiki/calibration-workshops.
- Ownership: Observability owns dashboards; Platform SRE owns alert rules; Applied ML owns model-variant quality gates.
- Audit: every threshold change must include: author, justification, experiment id, and rollback plan.

Roadmap items (next 12 months):
- H1 2026: Add model-quality metadata to surface matrix (per-variant eval curves) and auto-suggest cheaper variants with estimated quality delta.
- H2 2026: Rollout per-tenant simulated cost impact preview in the dashboard (what-if for 30d baseline).
- H2 2026: Integrate runbook automation: one-click canary creation and auto-rollback via orchestration service.

Appendix: sample PromQL snippets and synthetic load command
- Sample token-cost estimate (pseudo):
  token_cost_per_request = model_token_price * avg_tokens + gpu_infra_cost_per_token_estimate

- Synthetic load example (CLI):
  echo '{"prompt":"<sample>", "n":1}' | loadgen --target=https://inference-internal.svc.local --rps=20 --concurrency=50 --model=mistral-small --duration=300s

- PromQL for eviction spikes:
  increase(eviction_count{job="inference"}[5m]) > 0

Document maintenance:
- This doc is reviewed quarterly; next scheduled review 2026-05-01.
- Keep experiment artifacts under /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/calibration-workshops/ with experiment IDs referenced from here.

Contact and escalation list:
- Platform SRE oncall: #platform-sre-oncall (Slack)
- Observability owners: Diego Martinez (diego@redwood.ai)
- Applied ML model oncall: ml-oncall@redwood.ai

payload.page_title: Regional Fallback Zero-Trust Routing Playbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents the decision flow, operator procedures, configuration artifacts, and dashboard checks for performing region-level fallback routing under a zero-trust posture. It is intended for platform operators and SREs who must preserve application SLAs while maintaining cryptographic and policy boundaries during regional failover.

Scope: Applies to L7 request routing for inference endpoints, internal control-plane traffic (controlplane.redwood-inference), and telemetry egress. Does NOT modify tenant data at rest or change model weights.

Goals and constraints
- Preserve p99 latency SLOs for interactive tenants where possible. Target: p99 < 450ms after failover for priority-tenants.
- Maintain zero-trust authentication for cross-region routing (mTLS + OIDC token exchange).
- Avoid mass-credential exfiltration: do not embed long-lived credentials in routing configuration.
- Prefer model-variant fallback (smaller/quantized variant) before re-routing traffic across jurisdictions.

Owner and escalation
- Primary oncall: Platform Operators (platform-oncall rotation).
- Secondary: Runtime Reliability (runtime-rel team).
- Pager escalation: use the oncall rota in PagerDuty, tag incidents with component:regional-routing.

Preconditions (automated checks to run before executing manual steps)
1) Confirm region health summary dashboard: all dataplane pods reporting Ready > 95% and GPU utilization < 92%. Query: sum(kube_pod_status_ready{region=~"us-.*"}) / count(kube_pod_status_ready{region=~"us-.*"})
2) Verify SLO burn: tokenized_sli_burn{route=~"/v1/generate|/v1/chat"} < 0.25 in last 5m.
3) Ensure KMS cross-region key policy allows transient-wrap for fallback exchange.
4) Validate OPA policy test-suite passes locally (opa test ./policies)

Decision matrix (high-level)
- Severity: Control plane outage (no) | Dataplane partial outage (yes) | Dataplane full outage (yes)
- If partial outage and prioritization score > 0.7 => route priority-tenants only to adjacent region with model-variant fallback enabled.
- If full outage in region and adjacent region capacity < 25% spare => enable degraded-mode local queue + burst-credit gate.

Runbook: step-by-step procedure
1) Initial triage (0-5m)
   a) Open incident channel and paste region health snapshot.
   b) Run 'region-health-check --region=eu-west-1 --include=dataplane,controlplane' (internal CLI).
   c) If controlplane healthy and dataplane degraded, proceed to step 2.
2) Preflight policy & auth checks (5-10m)
   a) Confirm cross-region mTLS trust chain: `openssl s_client -connect gateway-eu-west-1:8443 -servername controlplane` (expect cert CN includes region-allow-list).
   b) Run OIDC token exchange smoke using ephemeral service account: `rcli oidc:exchange --aud=regional-fallback --expiry=5m` (expect token returned).
   c) Verify KMS wrapping permitted for target region: `kms-validate-wrap --key=arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:...`
3) Canary routing (10-25m)
   a) Create a canary route that matches 2% traffic from the failing region for high-priority tenants. Example Routing YAML (apply via platform-router):

```
apiVersion: routing.platform.redwood/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: regional-fallback-canary-eu-to-us
spec:
  match:
    - prefix: "/v1/generate"
      tenant_priority: "priority"
  filters:
    - name: auth-mtls-bridge
  destination:
    host: router-us-east-1.internal
    weight: 2
    headers:
      x-fallback: "eu->us-canary"
```

   b) Observe metrics for 5 full p99 windows (typical 5m each). Key queries listed in Observability section.
4) Incremental ramp (25-60m)
   a) If canary p99 < target and error-rate delta < 0.5%, increase weight in controlled steps: 2% -> 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%. Each step: wait for 2 p99 aggregation windows, validate tracing spans for auth latency below 60ms.
   b) If auth failures occur (5xx auth errors), rollback to previous weight and open follow-up task to fix policy.
5) Full cutover (60-90m)
   a) After 100% validation, convert temporary route to permanent fallback with explicit auditing metadata and automated TTL for reversal.
   b) Create incident annotation linking to route change and KMS wrap operation id.
6) Post-cutover cleanup (90-180m)
   a) Validate billing/telemetry tags for cross-region egress.
   b) Run regression tests on a representative prompt set (see 'Validation suites' below).

Rollback criteria and emergency rollback steps
- Rollback immediately if: error rate increases > 1% absolute, p99 > 2x target, auth errors > 0.2% of requests, or downstream model responses indicate corruption (LLM quality regression alert).
- Emergency rollback CLI: `platform-router rollback --route=regional-fallback-canary-eu-to-us --to-weight=0` and `platform-router remove --route=regional-fallback-canary-eu-to-us --grace=5m`
- If rollback fails: disable routing rules and enable local degraded queue: `platform-queue enable-degraded --region=eu-west-1 --duration=2h` and page runtime-reliability.

Observability and dashboards
- Add/verify the following panels on regional-fallback dashboard:
  - Per-region p50/p95/p99 latency for /v1/generate and /v1/chat (group by tenant_priority).
  - Auth handshake latency (mTLS) and OIDC token exchange success rate.
  - Cross-region egress bytes and billing tags.
  - Route weight vs error-rate heatmap (1m resolution).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- p99 latency: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/.*",region="eu-west-1"}[5m])) by (le))`
- mTLS handshake failures: `sum(rate(tls_handshake_errors_total{peer_region!=""}[1m]))`
- OIDC failures: `sum(rate(oidc_exchange_error_total[5m])) by (error_type)`

Configuration artifacts and policy examples
- OPA policy snippet (guarding cross-region):
```
package routing.zero_trust

allow {
  input.destination_region == "us-east-1"
  input.tenant_priority == "priority"
  valid_token(input.oidc)
}

valid_token(t) {
  t.iss == "https://auth.redwood-inference"
  t.exp > time.now_ns() / 1000000000
}
```

- Route manifest fields (table):
| Field | Description | Example |
|-------|-------------|---------|
| match.prefix | Request path prefix | /v1/generate |
| match.tenant_priority | Priority bucket label | priority |
| destination.host | Upstream routing host | router-us-east-1.internal |
| destination.weight | Traffic percent weight (0-100) | 2 |
| filters | Chain of policy bridges (auth, audit) | [auth-mtls-bridge, audit-proxy] |
| metadata.audit_tag | Freeform audit tag for change logs | eu->us-jan-18-cutover |

Access control and auditing
- All route changes must be applied via the platform-router CLI or the UI with RBAC role: routing.operator. Manual etcd edits are forbidden.
- Each routing change must include `metadata.audit_tag` and reference the incident id. Automated commit hooks validate presence.
- Audit logs for cross-region KMS wrap operations must be captured and stored in the secure audit bucket with 365-day retention.

Validation suites (post-cutover)
- Latency smoke: synthetic runner (srunner) executes 2000 representative prompts (mix of short/long) and produces metrics. Pass threshold: p99 < target and error-rate < 0.5%.
- Quality smoke: run eval subset (eval-suite/regional-fallback/quality-100) and compare BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity delta < 1.5% vs baseline.
- Security smoke: run penetration-tokenization test to verify no header leakage across tenant boundaries.

Runbook example checklist (single-page)
1) [ ] Incident channel created and health snapshot posted
2) [ ] OIDC + mTLS verification passed
3) [ ] Canary route applied (2%)
4) [ ] Canary p99 & error rates within thresholds
5) [ ] Incremental ramp steps completed with checks
6) [ ] Final route hardened with audit metadata
7) [ ] Post-cutover validation suites passed

Known limitations and follow-ups
- Cross-region egress cost spike risk: ensure finance has been notified via the cost-ops flow if predicted egress > $5k/hr.
- Some on-prem private deployments may require manual KMS bridge installation; see eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging for instructions.
- Future work: automate canary ramp using adaptive ramp heuristics tied to SLI burn. See roadmap ticket ROAD-1824.

Appendices
A) Quick reference CLI commands
- region-health-check --region=<r> --include=dataplane,controlplane
- rcli oidc:exchange --aud=regional-fallback --expiry=5m
- platform-router apply --file=canary.yaml --dry-run=false
- platform-router rollback --route=<name> --to-weight=<n>
- platform-queue enable-degraded --region=<r> --duration=2h

B) Rollout example timeline (operator estimate)
- T0 (0m): incident declared
- T+10m: preflight checks complete
- T+25m: canary applied and first evaluation window
- T+90m: full cutover if all validations pass
- T+180m: post-cutover validations complete and incident closed

C) Contacts and ownership
- Platform Operators: platform-oncall@redwood.ai
- Runtime Reliability: runtime-reliability@redwood.ai
- Security (KMS/OIDC): security-crypto@redwood.ai
- Cost ops: cost-ops@redwood.ai

Document history
- 2024-11-12: Created by Priya Singh (draft)
- 2025-06-03: Reviewed by Marcus Lee; added OIDC exchange step
- 2026-01-18: Published after tabletop exercise and game day validation

payload.page_title: Operator feedback playback and cost-debt reconciliation

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines the operator feedback-playback process and the linked cost-debt reconciliation workflow for platform services. The goal is to create a reproducible cadence that converts operator observations and incident playback notes into prioritized, tracked work to reduce recurring cost and reliability debt. This doc covers signals, dashboard ownership, alert thresholds, an operator runbook for playback, the cost-debt triage process, metrics used for prioritization, and a 6-month roadmap for adoption.

Goals
- Close the loop between operations (oncall/platform-ops) and engineering teams so runbook learnings produce measurable debt reduction.
- Track and reduce recurring token/cost debt and wasteful patterns by 30% for target services within 6 months.
- Standardize playback artifacts so retrospective insights are actionable and schedulable.

Scope
- Applies to platform-managed LLM inference services, caching layers (KV prefix cache), batching subsystems, and tenant-routing controllers.
- Not in scope: customer-managed private deployments (those follow customer-specific SOWs) and billing/legal reconciliation.

Background and Rationale
Operators frequently observe recurring cost spikes, repeated fallbacks, and cache-miss storms that indicate systemic design debt rather than isolated incidents. Historically, playback notes lived in ad-hoc folders or Slack threads, delaying remediation. This process aims to formalize "operator playback" (a short, structured debrief) and create a connected cost-debt ticket lifecycle from observation -> triage -> fix -> validation.

Key Definitions
- Operator Playback: a 30–60 minute structured debrief performed by the operator team after a noteworthy event or synthesis of recurring alerts.
- Cost debt: any measurable recurring or avoidable expense driven by platform behavior (e.g., excessive cold starts, token leaks, inefficient model routing, misconfigured batching).
- Reconciliation ticket: an engineering task with a defined acceptance test and metric target aimed at eliminating the root cause of cost debt.

Ownership and Roles
- Platform Oncall (primary): capture playback, raise triage tickets, and assign preliminary impact estimates.
- Service Owner (secondary/assignee): engineers responsible for the affected service; own implementation and verification.
- Cost Steward (finance-eng): validates cost-savings estimates and provides historical cost data for prioritization.
- Platform Program Manager: runs the quarterly review and ensures SLAs for reconciliation.

Signals and Dashboards
The operator playback must reference a standard dashboard snapshot. Below are required widgets and who owns them.

Required dashboard widgets (table)
| Widget | Description | Owner | Notes |
| Runtime token cost by tenant | 7d and 30d rolling token spend, P50/P95 cost-per-request | cost-steering | Show top 20 tenants and trailing 7d spike annotations |
| KV cache hit/miss by prefix | Per-prefix hit-rate, eviction rate, and TTL distribution | caching-team | Correlate with request sequence-lengths |
| Model-routing fallbacks | Count of requests routed to fallback variants per region | routing-service | Include last 24h timeline and per-region heatmap |
| Cold-start latency vs warm | Warm-up success ratio and average cold start penalty (ms) | runtime-team | 1h & 24h views, grouped by instance flavor |
| Batching efficiency | Effective batching window utilization and average tokens per batch | batching-team | Include coalescing latency percentiles |
| Synthetic cost regressions | Synthetic job that runs the canonical prompt suite and reports delta cost/latency | eval-infra | Synthetic baseline and rolling regression line |

Alert thresholds and routing
- Token-cost anomaly alert: trig when top-3 tenants combined 24h spend increases > 40% vs baseline and absolute spend > $X/day for that tenant class. Route to oncall and Cost Steward.
- Cache-eviction storm: trig when global eviction rate > 0.5% of cache size per hour for 30 minutes. Route to caching-team and oncall.
- Fallback surge: >10x increase in fallback routing rate for region-tier and >1000 events in 10 minutes. Route to routing-service and platform oncall.
- Cold-start epidemic: 20% of warmup attempts failing across pool for >15 minutes. Route to runtime-team and SRE.

Operator playback runbook (30–60m)
1. Gather artifacts (5m): take the dashboard snapshot links (use the "Playback snapshot" button), collect relevant alert IDs, and attach the synthetic regression run.
2. Quick impact estimate (5m): estimate customer-facing impact (users affected, latency degradation, cost delta). Use the impact checklist below.
3. Root-cause hypothesis (10–15m): walk through recent deploys, config changes, model swaps, and any capacity events. Add a hypothesis with supporting evidence.
4. Temporary mitigations (5–10m): if a mitigation exists (traffic steering, throttles, emergency model swap), note it and owner.
5. Create a reconciliation ticket (10m): the ticket must include: summary, hypothesis, dashboard links, proposed acceptance criteria (metric and time-based), estimated cost impact, and preliminary priority tag. Assign to service owner.
6. Post-playback notification (1–2m): post a short summary in #platform-playback with ticket link and runbook snapshot.

Impact checklist (used during quick estimate)
- Visibility: whether customers will notice latency or cost changes.
- SLA exposure: any SLOs affected (percent error or latency).
- Revenue risk: potential churn or big-tenant exposure.
- Reproducibility: can we reproduce in canary or synthetic job?

Cost-debt triage lifecycle
1. Intake: Platform oncall files a reconciliation ticket tagged "cost-debt". Must include estimated $/day waste and concrete metric to be fixed.
2. Triage (weekly): Platform Program Manager and Cost Steward run through new tickets in a 1-hour triage meeting. Tickets are scored on impact, effort, and confidence.
3. Prioritization matrix: use the following scoring (each 1–5): impact (cost reduction), effort (engineering hours), confidence (likelihood of root cause). Compute a priority score = (impact * confidence) / effort.
4. Scheduling: high-priority tickets are slotted into the next sprint or into a 2-week cost-debt blitz; medium go to backlog with monthly review.
5. Implementation and verification: Service Owner implements fix and provides a validation job (synthetic + 7d retrospective).
6. Close and retro: after validation, ticket moves to "verified savings" and is discussed in the monthly cost-debt bulletin.

Acceptance criteria examples (must be included in every reconciliation ticket)
- Reduce average token cost per request by >= 18% for the target workload over 14 days.
- Improve KV prefix hit-rate from 78% to >= 92% for at least 7 consecutive days.
- Eliminate fallback events for the top-2 tenants for 30 days.

Metrics and SLOs used for prioritization
- Cost-per-inference (P50/P95) – baseline & target
- Cache hit-rate by prefix – baseline & improvement target
- Fallback rate per 10k requests – baseline & target
- Mean time to mitigation (MTTM) – operator efficiency metric to track process health

Example reconciliation ticket template (short)
- Title: "Reduce token cost for PDF embedding flow (tenant: acme-inc)"
- Summary: one-paragraph with link to playback snapshot
- Hypothesis: misconfigured batching window + oversized model variant -> high tokens per call
- Acceptance: P50 token cost down 25% over 14d synthetic run
- Estimated effort: 3 engineering days
- Owner: embeddings-service team

Implementation checklist for Service Owners
- [ ] Clone playback snapshot dashboard and add the fix validation widgets
- [ ] Add synthetic job and ensure it is running daily with a regression alert
- [ ] Implement change behind a feature flag or canary rollout where possible
- [ ] Run 14-day validation window, attach results to ticket
- [ ] Close ticket or escalate if criteria not met

Retrospective cadence and artifacts
- Short playback (for single incidents) -> immediate triage ticket + weekly triage meeting.
- Monthly cost-debt bulletin -> summary of closed tickets, estimated savings, and outstanding blockers. Published by Platform Program Manager.
- Quarterly 2-hour retrospective -> cross-team deep-dive into recurring patterns and roadmap adjustments. Outcomes are added to the 6-month roadmap.

Roadmap (next 6 months)
- Month 0–1: adopt standard playback snapshot button and ensure all oncall have write access to triage board.
- Month 1–2: roll out synthetic-regression standard job across 8 critical services.
- Month 2–4: pilot cost-debt blitz with 3 targeted services; aim for ~20% aggregate cost reduction in pilot group.
- Month 4–6: integrate cost-steward approvals into triage flow and automate close-on-validated-savings.

Retrospective insights (initial pilot notes)
- Common root causes found so far: batching window misconfiguration, oversized model selection by fallback policy, and stale cache TTLs after model swaps.
- Operator friction: missing snapshot links and inconsistent evidence lengthened triage. Fix: standardized snapshot export and a 6-field minimal evidence requirement.
- Cultural insight: giving small, measurable wins (e.g., one tenant 12% savings) drives adoption faster than large multi-team projects.

Open risks and mitigations
- Risk: engineering prioritization fatigue. Mitigation: timebox blitzes and require service owners to commit a level of effort in advance.
- Risk: noisy synthetic regressions producing false positives. Mitigation: tune baselines and require confirmation by manual replay before scheduling fixes.

Appendix
- Playback snapshot CLI (example):
  # take a snapshot of current playback dashboard
  rdx dashboards snapshot --dashboard platform-cost-debt --output-url

- Example alert rule (YAML snippet):
  alerts:
    - name: token_cost_anomaly
      expr: |
        increase(token_cost_total[24h]) / max(1, avg_over_time(token_cost_total[28d])) > 0.4
      for: 10m
      labels:
        severity: major
      annotations:
        runbook: "/eng-platform/systems-and-services/operator-feedback-playback-and-cost-debt-reconciliation-2026"

Related pages
- See also: /eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/runtime-cost-instrumentation-and-alerting-2026 (dashboard templates)
- See also: /eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026 (mitigation primitives)

Contact and next steps
- Primary contact: Aisha Patel (platform-ops lead)
- Program owner: Priya Nair (Platform Program Manager)
- Next step: platform-ops to run a pilot playback for three services during week of 2026-02-15 and report results in the monthly bulletin.

payload.page_title: Operator Collaboration & Shared-State Contract (runtime operators)

sections.body: This document defines the collaboration contract between platform operators who manage the LLM runtime (prefetch, KV cache, batching, allocator) and platform services that depend on shared in-memory or metastore state. The goal is to reduce oncall churn, make handoffs deterministic, and provide a single source of truth for operator actions that affect runtime health and tenant isolation.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Platform operators (primary)
- Service owners and oncall engineers (secondary)
- SRE and infra ops (tertiary)
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
- Define a compact, unambiguous shared-state schema and ownership model.
- Provide standard preflight checks and safe mutation patterns for operators.
- Describe handoff and takeover procedures for rapid incident response.
- Standardize instrumented signals and dashboards to detect contract violations.

Scope and non‑goals:
- Scope: coordination patterns around KV prefix caches, tenant warmsets, allocator credits, and model-variant routing metadata.
- Non-goal: replacing higher-level orchestration policies (e.g., scheduler decisions) — this contract complements them.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Shared state is a small set of canonical keys in the runtime metastore. Services may read keys freely. Any operator or automated process that mutates keys must:
  1) Record intent via the operator-ledger entry (see "Operator Ledger" below),
  2) Run the preflight checks (Section: Preflight),
  3) Execute the mutation via the approved CLI or orchestration endpoint, and
  4) Post a postcondition note and alert the owning service channel if the change is nontrivial.

Operator Ledger (audit + intent registration):
- The ledger is a single append-only stream stored in the internal metadata service. For ad-hoc operational changes, write a ledger record before mutating shared state. Each ledger record must include: author, timestamp, target_key(s), intended_mutation, expected_impact, rollback_plan, and a correlation_id.
sections.heading: Contract overview (plain language)

sections.body:
{
  "author": "avery.li@redwood.ai",
  "timestamp": "2025-03-12T09:42:00Z",
  "target_keys": ["kv-prefix/tenant-123/warmset"],
  "intended_mutation": "evict-prefix",
  "expected_impact": "approx 20% increase in token-latency P95 for tenant-123 for up to 60s",
  "rollback_plan": "re-add prefix from snapshot: snapshot://prefetch/2025-03-12/tenant-123",
  "correlation_id": "op-20250312-0942-tenant123-evict"
}
sections.heading: Ledger record example (JSON)

sections.body:
1) Confirm ledger entry is present and visible in the operator dashboard.
2) Validate the change against the service compatibility matrix: ensure tenant-123 is allowed to be evicted during the current maintenance window.
3) Check token budget and allocator credits: operation must not cause allocator to drop below the safety floor (see thresholds).
4) Synthetic load simulation (where applicable): run a 30s synthetic prefix-read trace in the staging overlay.
5) Stakeholder notification: add an @mention to the service Slack channel and wait the configured quiet-period (default 90s) unless an emergency takeover is declared.
sections.heading: Preflight checklist (must pass before manual/CLI mutation)

sections.body:
- Evicting a KV prefix:
  - Use: rld-cli runtime evict --target-prefix tenant-123/warmset --ledger-cid op-...
  - Steps: preflight, dry-run (no-op), execute, monitor P95 token-latency for 5 minutes, rollback if >2x baseline for >2 consecutive minutes.
- Warmset reseed:

payload.page_title: Operational Economics: Prefetch & Cache Investment Framework

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines a decision framework for when and how the platform should invest in prefetch and KV-prefix cache population for multi-tenant LLM inference workloads. It combines economics (tokens saved vs. GPU-time cost), SLO surface impacts, operator runbooks, observable signals, and a lightweight experimentation roadmap. The goal is to give operators and product engineers a repeatable playbook for deciding which prefixes, cohorts, or tenants merit prefetch investment.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Redwood Inference platform-level prefetch/priming systems (edge-prefetch, regional warmsets, and in-memory KV prefix caches used by the serving runtime).
- Targets multi-tenant hosted and Dedicated offerings. Private deployments may reuse the framework for knob selection but must follow customer constraints.
- Not intended for application-layer, customer-managed caches.

Motivation
----------
Prefetching reduces per-request token generation by avoiding repeated decoding/encoding costs and by priming model KV caches. However, prefetch itself consumes GPU cycles (batching + warmup) and operator effort. Without a robust decision framework, prefetch policies drift toward over-provisioning (wasted cost) or under-provisioning (avoidable latency and quality regressions). This doc balances:
1) expected token-cost savings (both direct and downstream),
2) the marginal GPU and operator cost to prefetch, and
3) SLO risk (latency/quality) if prefetch is absent.

Decision Framework (high level)
--------------------------------
1) Identify candidates: prefixes, prompt-sets, tenants, and model-variant combos with a consistent warmset hit-rate > H_min (default 5%).
2) Estimate benefit: calculate expected token-savings per hour (tokens_saved/hr) and convert to $/hr using current token unit price.
3) Estimate cost: measure prefetch GPU-time per hour including batching inefficiency and warmup overhead; convert to $/hr. Include operator+telemetry amortized cost (default 5% of infra cost).
4) Compute ROI: ROI = (benefit - cost) / cost. Treat ROI > 1.25 as high-priority, ROI between 0.4–1.25 as experimental, ROI < 0.4 normally not worth investing.
5) Safety gate: ensure that SLO risk index (latency_p50_increase * quality_regression_score) does not exceed defined safety thresholds before enabling automatic prefetch. If it does, require manual canary and QA.

Concrete signals and formulas
-----------------------------
- tokens_saved/hr = observed_request_rate * avg_tokens_saved_per_request * observed_prefix_hit_rate
- prefetch_cost_gpu_hr = measured_prefetch_gpu_seconds_per_hour / 3600 * unit_gpu_hour_cost
- operator_overhead = prefetch_cost_gpu_hr * 0.05 (configurable)
- benefit_usd_hr = tokens_saved/hr * token_unit_price_usd
- ROI = (benefit_usd_hr - (prefetch_cost_gpu_hr + operator_overhead)) / (prefetch_cost_gpu_hr + operator_overhead)

Example threshold table
-----------------------
| Metric | Default threshold | Rationale | Action when exceeded |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|----------------------|
| observed_prefix_hit_rate | 0.05 | below this hit-rate prefetch rarely amortizes | reject candidate |
| tokens_saved/hr | 50,000 tokens | small hourly benefit | mark as low-priority |
| prefetch_cost_gpu_hr | $0.80 | platform average for short warmups | requires optimization |
| ROI | > 1.25 | strong case for automated prefetch | enable auto-prefetch |
| SLO risk index | < 0.02 | small combined latency/quality risk | pass safety gate |

Operator procedures (runbook)
-----------------------------
1) Candidate review (manual or via automation):
   a) Run `prefetch-candidate-scan --window=1h --min-hit=0.05` to produce a candidate CSV.
   b) Inspect the top 15 by tokens_saved/hr.
2) Local canary:
   a) Create canary cohort: tag 5% of requests (cohort canary) or a single tenant if available.
   b) Enable prefetch with `admin-cli prefetch enable --cohort canary --ttl=30m --batch-target=16`.
   c) Monitor the canary for 30-90 minutes.
3) Validation checklist (during canary):
   - p50 and p95 latency for the cohort (should not increase >10% over baseline)
   - quality regression QA run (prompt set of 50 golden prompts) -> regression score < 0.03
   - token-savings and cost measurement recorded in the preftech-dashboard
4) Rollout
   - If canary passes, staged rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 100% over at least 24 hours with automated SLO checks.
   - If regression observed, run rollback: `admin-cli prefetch disable --cohort <id>` and open a postmortem.

Dashboard & Alert design
------------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Prefetch Economics Overview: ROI heatmap by tenant/model/region, tokens_saved_hr, prefetch_cost_gpu_hr, active_prefetch_count.
- Canary Health: per-canary p50/p95 latency, quality_regression_score, error-rate.
- Warmset Efficiency: batch fill rates, avg KV hits per decoded token, waste ratio (prefetch cycles with zero hits).

Suggested alert rules (name, trigger, owner):
1) alert/prefetch-roi-degrading -> trigger when ROI for top-10 candidates falls below 0.8 for 3 consecutive 10m windows -> owner: platform-operator
2) alert/prefetch-canary-latency-regression -> trigger when canary p95 increases > 15% vs baseline and sustained for 10m -> owner: oncall
3) alert/prefetch-waste-ratio-high -> trigger when >40% prefetch cycles have zero post-warm hits in a 1h window -> owner: platform-costing
4) alert/prefetch-telemetry-gap -> missing telemetry (tokens_saved or gpu_seconds) for 2m -> owner: observability

Example alert rule (Prometheus-ish pseudo-YAML)
------------------------------------------------
- alert: PrefetchCanaryLatencyRegression
  expr: (prefetch_canary_p95{cohort="canary"} / baseline_p95{cohort="canary"}) > 1.15
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Canary p95 latency regression for prefetch cohort"

Runbook snippet: escalation steps
--------------------------------
1) Respond to page within 15 minutes.
2) Identify affected cohort and prefetch bucket: `prefetch-cli list --cohort <id>`
3) If p95 regression confirmed, immediately disable prefetch for cohort: `admin-cli prefetch disable --cohort <id>`
4) Capture a trace bundle and token cost samples: `observability-cli capture --trace prefetch --duration 10m`
5) Triage: open incident in Jira component PLATFORM-PREFETCH; assign to owner oncall and platform-costing.

Retrospective & success metrics
-------------------------------
Every enabled prefetch feature must have a 30-day retrospective scoped to:
- realized token-savings vs predicted (target within +/- 20%)
- total infra spend change (GPU-hours)
- SLO impacts (customer-facing latency and quality metrics)
- operator toil (human-hours to maintain)
sections.heading: Essential dashboards (templates provided in the appendix)

sections.body:
1) Did the ROI model over/under estimate benefit? Why?
2) Which telemetry signals were most/least predictive?
3) Were the canary validation windows sufficient?
4) What automation could reduce operator toil?

Roadmap & next steps (quarterly cadence)
---------------------------------------
- Q1 2026: Deploy preftech-dashboard, integrate token-costing pipeline, implement automated candidate scanning.
- Q2 2026: Add model-variant-aware prefetch strategies (per-quantization-class knobs).
- Q3 2026: Experiment with adaptive prefetch windows driven by upstream feature flags and customer-tier economics.
- Q4 2026: Expand framework to Private edition with customer-level opt-out and policy bindings.

Appendix: Telemetry schema & sample queries
------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Template retrospective questions

sections.body:
- prefetch_candidate_id (string)
- cohort_id (string)
- model_name (string)
- region (string)
- tokens_saved (int)
- prefetch_gpu_seconds (float)
- requests_observed (int)
- prefix_hit_rate (float)
- quality_regression_score (float, 0-1)
sections.heading: Telemetry fields (required)

sections.body:
SELECT tenant_id, sum(tokens_saved) as tokens_saved_24h, sum(prefetch_gpu_seconds)/3600 as gpu_hours FROM prefetch_telemetry WHERE ts >= now() - interval '24 hours' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY tokens_saved_24h DESC LIMIT 50;

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------
- Product: define acceptable quality/regression thresholds and token-unit pricing for ROI calculations.
- Platform Engineering (eng-platform): implement candidate-scan automation, dashboards, and runbook automation.
- Observability: ensure telemetry schema and alerting plumbing are available and maintained.
- Platform Costing: validate unit cost numbers and reconcile monthly.

Appendix B: Lightweight experiments checklist (1-page)
-----------------------------------------------------
1) Hypothesis statement.
2) Expected token/hr savings and expected prefetch GPU/hr cost.
3) Canary cohort definition and length.
4) Acceptance criteria (SLO + ROI).
5) Rollout and rollback plan.
6) Postmortem and 30-day retrospective owner.

Related artifacts & links
------------------------
- Prefetch dashboard template: /dashboards/prefetch-economics-template
- Candidate scan job: infra repo /ops/prefetch/scanner
- Canary validation notebook: /notebooks/prefetch-canary-validation.ipynb

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Created initial draft (Emily Chen).
- 2026-01-07: Added ROI thresholds and safety gate (Ravi Singh review).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized dashboards and alert set (Marco Alvarez review).

payload.page_title: Capacity Crediting and Deficit Reconciliation Framework

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the standardized framework for: capacity crediting (assigning burst/flat credits to tenants), forecasting credit consumption, and reconciling credit deficits across multi-region Redwood platform deployments. It consolidates the financial and operational rules that platform operators and the billing team use to keep tenant economics predictable during capacity shortfalls and burst events.

Goals
-----
- Provide a deterministic algorithm for credit accrual and burn that is simple to audit.
- Provide clear operator workflows for detecting, reconciling, and communicating deficits.
- Define dashboard metrics and alert thresholds for early detection of credit exhaustion.
- Supply SQL/CLI snippets for automated reconciliation jobs and manual investigations.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Hosted API and Dedicated (reserved) capacity crediting rules.
- Cross-region deficit propagation and reconciliation.
- Dashboards and alerts for operator/finance teams.
sections.heading: In scope

sections.body:
- Customer contract negotiation guidance (handled by Legal/Sales).
- Upstream cloud provider billing reconciliation (handled in finance receipts pipeline).

Key definitions
---------------
- Tenant: billing entity (customer account) consuming API tokens and embeddings.
- Credit: a unit representing entitlement to consume capacity beyond baseline (expressed in token-seconds-equivalent, TSE).
- Baseline allocation: monthly TSE reserved for a tenant via subscription or Dedicated commitment.
- Burst allowance: temporary credits automatically granted under policy during short-term spikes.
- Deficit: negative credit balance at reconciliation time.

Data sources and inputs
-----------------------
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
1. token_worklog (time-series of per-tenant token counts, sequence_length histogram).
2. allocation_catalog (tenant_id -> baseline_tse, reserved_pool_id, region).
3. burst_policy_events (policy_id, start_ts, end_ts, reason, operator_id).
4. region_capacity_signals (pool_utilization_pct, congested_tier_flags).
5. invoice_ledger (monthly billed credits, adjustments).

Calculation primitives
----------------------
All math uses integers where possible. Time is aligned to 5-minute windows (epoch aligned).

- TSE calculation: TSE = tokens * (sequence_length / 512) rounded up.
- Burn rate per window: burn = max(TSE - baseline_window_allocation, 0).
- Burst credit grant: grant = min(burst_policy.window_limit, deficit_tolerance * baseline_window_allocation)

Example table: crediting formulas
| Name | Formula | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Window baseline (WB) | WB = monthly_baseline_tse / (30*24*12) | 5-minute windows assumption |
| Window TSE | WT = sum(tokens_i * max(1, ceil(len_i/512))) | per-request sequence lengths |
| Burn | B = max(WT - WB, 0) | added to tenant_credit_balance |

Policy rules (priority order)
1. If region_capacity_signals.congested_tier_flags contains tenant's pool, do NOT auto-grant burst; instead mark as soft-throttle candidate.
2. If tenant_credit_balance > 0, consume from balance.
3. If balance == 0 and tenant is in managed-burst-tier, attempt grant per burst_policy_events constraints.
4. Persistent burn over 72 hours triggers operator review and potential temporary quota reduction.

Operator workflows
------------------
1) Daily reconciliation job (automated, runs 02:00 UTC)
   - Run query:
     SELECT tenant_id, SUM(burn) AS monthly_burn, credit_balance FROM tenant_credit_rollup WHERE month = '{{prev_month}}';
   - Generate report: tenants with monthly_burn > baseline*1.25 OR credit_balance < -10% baseline -> tag for manual review.

2) Manual deficit reconciliation (steps for oncall/operator)
   1. Triage alert in PagerDuty / issue tracker with tenant_id, deficit amount, and region.
   2. Run quick audit:
      - Check burst_policy_events for the tenant: SELECT * FROM burst_policy_events WHERE tenant_id = 'X' ORDER BY start_ts DESC LIMIT 20;
      - Inspect region capacity during deficit window: SELECT timestamp, pool_utilization_pct FROM region_capacity_signals WHERE region='R' AND timestamp BETWEEN A AND B;
   3. Categorize deficit root cause: policy-granted, unmanaged-surge, or telemetry-loss.
   4. If policy-granted and within finance threshold (<= $5000 equivalent), create adjustment request to invoice_ledger and set reconciliation_status=auto_adjusted.
   5. If > threshold or contractual sensitivity, escalate to BillingOps and Customer Success following the Escalation matrix (see related_pages).

3) Emergency temporary credit grant (operator fast path)
   - Criteria: customer-facing outage, revenue-impacting, region healthy (no global congestion).
   - Command (CLI):
     rctl credits grant --tenant-id T123 --amount 50000 --reason "emergency-burst" --expires-at 2026-03-15T08:00:00Z --owner {{operator_id}}
   - Follow-up: Open internal ticket with reconciliation checklist and require a postmortem within 7 days.

Dashboard and alert spec
------------------------
Primary dashboard: Tenant Credit Health (operator view)
- KPIs (5-min refresh):
  - Credit balance (TSE) trend over 30 days
  - 5-min burn rate percentile (p50, p95, p99)
  - Baseline vs Actual utilization ratio
  - Active burst grants (count) and pending reconciliations

Alert rules (PagerDuty + Slack channel #platform-credits):
1. Alert: Tenant credit balance < -5% baseline for > 3 windows (15 minutes)
   - Severity: P2
   - Actions: auto-ticket + DM oncall + post message to #platform-credits with link to tenant dashboard
2. Alert: Tenant monthly_burn > baseline * 2 before day 8 of billing cycle
   - Severity: P1 (billing ops review)
   - Actions: create BillingOps task and notify AE/CS owner
3. Alert: Region-backed pool utilization > 92% AND cumulative pending bursts > 15% pool capacity
   - Severity: P1 (platform ops)
sections.heading: Primary inputs

sections.body:
{
  "tenant_id": "T123",
  "balance_tse": -12450,
  "window": "2026-02-19T16:25:00Z",
  "reason": "rapid_burst",
  "link": "https://confluence.redwood.internal/dash/tenant-credit/T123"
}

Runbook: deficit reconciliation (condensed)
-----------------------------------------
- Trigger: P1/P2 alert from above.
- Oncall steps (first 30 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge alert.
  2. Check tenant dashboard + allocation_catalog.
  3. If region congested -> follow the Platform Region Congestion Runbook (related).
  4. If tenant caused by telemetry anomaly, mark as telemetry-incident and file ticket to infra-telemetry.
  5. For verified policy grants, schedule invoice adjustment job: POST /internal/billing/adjustments {tenant_id, amount_tse, reason, operator_id}.

CLI/SQL snippets for auditors
----------------------------
- Monthly burn rollup:
  -- SQL (run in analytics db)
  SELECT tenant_id, SUM(burn) AS monthly_burn_tse, SUM(grants) AS monthly_grants_tse, SUM(adjustments) AS monthly_adjustments_tse, AVG(pool_utilization_pct) AS avg_pool_util FROM tenant_credit_rollup WHERE month = '2026-02' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY monthly_burn_tse DESC LIMIT 200;

- Reconciliation job pseudo-command (k8s CronJob):
  kubectl -n platform jobs run credit-reconciler --image=gcr.io/redwood/credit-reconciler:stable -- "--month=2026-02" --output=/tmp/recon-2026-02.csv

Retrospective and measurement cadence
------------------------------------
We will review reconciliation outcomes in the Monthly Platform Finance Retro (first Tuesday of each month). Focus items for the retro:
- Top 10 tenants by unexpected burn and root cause classification.
- False-positive/false-negative alert rates and operator response times (target: mean time to reconcile < 48 hours).
- Adjust burst policy parameters if >30% of grants require manual adjustment in a month.

Success metrics
- Reconciliation accuracy (post-adjustment delta) > 99.5%
- Operator manual adjustments < 5% of monthly grants
- Mean time to remediate deficit alerts < 48 hours

Roadmap (next 12 months)
----------------------
- Q2 2026: Implement ML-based burst prediction model (feature: sequence-length-aware forecasting).
- Q3 2026: Add per-tenant cost-estimate column to dashboards (USD-equivalent) using exchange-rate and GPU-cost mapping.
- Q4 2026: Expose self-service tenant reconciliation tickets to AEs (with templated justification).
- Q1 2027: Integrate crediting engine into Dedicated capacity autoscaler to proactively reserve warm capacity for large tenants.

Ownership and contact matrix
---------------------------
- Credit engine and rolling logic: eng-platform/allocator (primary)
- Dashboards & alerts: eng-platform/observability (primary)
- Billing adjustments & finance reconciliation: finance-and-legal/billing-ops (primary)
- Escalations to customers: customer-success/team (primary)

Related pages
-------------
- /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/tenant-fairness-auditing-framework-2026
- /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/billing-adjustment-process-2025
- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/region-capacity-failover-playbook-2026

Appendix A: example reconciliation record (CSV)
tenant_id,month,monthly_burn_tse,monthly_grants_tse,monthly_adjustments_tse,final_balance_tse,notes
T123,2026-02,124500,50000,2000,-7200,"auto_adjusted: within threshold"

Appendix B: glossary & audit tips
- Always reference event_ids when making manual adjustments.
- When in doubt, prefer temporary quota reduction over large emergency grants; temporary quota is reversible without invoices.

Document maintenance
--------------------
- Owners must review and sign off on this document quarterly or after any major billing policy change.
- To propose edits, create a PR against this page and request reviewers listed above.
