payload.page_title: Workload Rehearsal and Deterministic Replay Framework

sections.body:
Summary:

This page documents the Workload Rehearsal and Deterministic Replay Framework (WRDR). WRDR provides a safe, repeatable way to replay historical production traffic—or synthesized equivalents—against staging or canary environments to validate changes to batching, kernel selection, routing policies, and cache/quantization profiles. The framework emphasizes deterministic input replay, observability parity, safety fences, and measurable pass/fail criteria tied to token cost, tail latency, and quality regressions.

Why this exists:
- Changes to the serving runtime (batching, KV cache sharding, kernel switching) can have non-linear effects on tail latency and cost.
- Unit tests and microbenchmarks miss emergent behavior from real multi-tenant traffic and inter-service dependencies.
- WRDR lets platform and runtime engineers validate regressions before large-scale rollouts and provides a forensics tool for incident reconstruction.

When to use WRDR:
- Before merging runtime patches that touch the batching layer, scheduler, or kernel selection heuristics.
- Prior to toggling global rollout flags (e.g., JIT kernel switching).
- For incident reenactments where traffic pattern needs reconstruction.
- As part of quarterly operator-run rehearsals and postmortem verification.

High-level design:
1) Input capture: ORION collector ingests representative traces with deterministic request payloads and anonymized context (no PII). Capture includes: request id, model id, sequence length, client hints, token counts, KV-prefix keys, and timestamp series.
2) Normalization: A replay manifest normalizes variable fields (timestamps, ephemeral IDs) and optionally synthesizes client-hint variations for edge-case coverage.
3) Deterministic driver: The WRDR driver replays requests with preserved inter-arrival timing (or accelerated modes) and enforces ordering where required (e.g., prefix cache priming sequences).
4) Isolation harness: Replays run in a constrained canary/staging tenancy with traffic throttles, quota knobs, and network egress controls.
5) Observability parity: During replays we materialize the same metrics, distributed traces, and cost-attribution signals into the platform observability stack.
6) Analysis engine: Post-run diffs compute delta on SLIs/SLOs, token-cost distribution, latency CDFs, and quality deltas (if reference evaluator is attached).

Safety & compliance:
- All captures must be scrubbed of customer PII at capture-time. See Security-and-Compliance checklist (link internal).
- Replays that contain production-sensitive prompts require explicit approval by the Security team; annotate manifest with "confidential=true".
- Throttle policy: default max QPS during rehearsal = 5% of observed peak for the tenant or a hard 500 RPS cap, whichever is lower.

Gameplan: Typical rehearsal run (operator checklist)
1. Select capture manifest and target environment.
2. Dry-run manifest validation (local driver, no network).
3. Provision isolated canary namespace: 2-3 nodes, same flavor as target, KVM/GPU configuration matching the change under test.
4. Start telemetry mirroring (prometheus federation job + trace sampler at 10%).
5. Run deterministic replay in three phases:
   a. Priming: replay 2 minutes of prefix/cache priming traffic at 10% speed to populate KV caches.
   b. Ramp: replay 10 minutes at 25% speed with controlled concurrency to surface queuing/backpressure.
   c. Stress validation: replay production timing for 10 minutes or until agreed inspection points.
6. Collect artifacts and run automated diff tasks.
7. If regression observed, abort and escalate; otherwise proceed to step rollouts.

Operational runbook: Step-by-step commands
- Environment prep (example):
  # create isolated namespace
  rdxctl cluster namespace create replay-canary-{{run-id}} --region us-west-2 --gpuflavor a100-80g --nodes 3

- Mirror telemetry:
  # start prom federator job (example)
  rdx-observability federate --source prometheus-prod --target prometheus-staging --labels replay_run={{run-id}}

- Start deterministic driver (YAML manifest example):
  ---
  replay_run_id: "replay-2027-01-18-42"
  source_capture: "s3://orion-captures/2027/01/09/edge-peak-1.jsonl"
  anonymize: true
  max_qps: 300
  interarrival_mode: preserved   # preserved | scaled | burst-emulate
  priming_window_seconds: 120
  phases:
    - name: priming
      scale: 0.10
      duration_seconds: 120
    - name: ramp
      scale: 0.25
      duration_seconds: 600
    - name: nominal
      scale: 1.00
      duration_seconds: 600

  # run
  rdx-replay run --manifest replay-manifest.yaml --target cluster:replay-canary-{{run-id}}

Verifications and pass/fail criteria:
- Latency: 99th percentile token response latency must not increase by > 15% vs baseline (baseline from same manifest replay against golden runtime).
- Cost: per-token compute cost must not increase by > 8% for 95% of requests.
- Error budget impact: aggregate 5xx rate must be < 0.05% during replay.
- Quality: if evaluator attached, aggregated BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity must be within configured regression tolerance (label in manifest).
- Resource utilization: GPU mem fragmentation and SM occupancy should not exceed historical peaks by > 20% without operator sign-off.

Analysis artifacts produced:
- latency-cdf.png, cost-distribution.csv, trace-diff-report.html, kv-prefix-heatmap.png, kernel-selection-log.json, batch-size-timeline.csv

Example analysis command (one-liner):
  rdx-replay analyze --run-id replay-2027-01-18-42 --baseline replay-golden-2026-11-01-08 --output /tmp/replay-analysis-42

Table: Minimum compute & storage requirements for rehearsal types
| Rehearsal type | Target parity | Min nodes | Prometheus retention | S3 capture size | Notes |
|---------------|---------------:|---------:|--------------------:|---------------:|-------|
| Quick smoke | functional | 1 | 1d | <1GB | fast checks, low fidelity |
| Canary-level | config parity | 3 | 7d | 1-10GB | matches runtime sizing for config under test |
| Full replay | production parity | N (match prod slice) | 30d | >10GB | used for incident reenactment or major infra changes |

Rollout and safety fences:
- If quick-smoke passes, schedule a canary replay with the same manifest in the target staging region.
- Automate a rollback trigger: CI/CD job creates a rollback tag and sends a Slack signal to #platform-ops if any pass/fail metric breaches.
- Gate canary-to-prod rollout on three successful WRDR runs by different engineers within 7 days.

Owner and contacts:
- Runbook owner: Sofia Alvarez (platform runtime team) 
- Primary on-call: platform-operators rotation (see team wiki).
- Security contact: Priya Menon.

Key dashboards and alerts to enable during a run:
- replay/{{run-id}}/latency/p99 (alert if > baseline * 1.15 for 3m)
- replay/{{run-id}}/token-cost/perc95 (alert if > baseline * 1.08 for 10m)
- replay/{{run-id}}/errors/5xx-rate (alert if > 0.05%)
- replay/{{run-id}}/kernel-switch/count (informational)

Post-run retrospective template (fill-in):
1. Run-id:
2. Purpose (patch verification / incident reenactment / routine rehearsal):
3. Owners and participants:
4. Key diffs observed (latency/cost/quality):
5. Root cause hypothesis (if regression):
6. Immediate mitigations taken:
7. Follow-up actions (owners + due dates):
8. Learnings for capture design (e.g., need more long tail sequences, increase trace sampling rate):

Roadmap and open work (next 12 months):
- Integrate reference-quality evaluator to attach automated quality diffs on replay.
- Add differential tracing that stitches per-request kernel selection decisions to downstream latency.
- Support cross-region preserved-replay to validate multi-region routing policies.
- Build UI in Console for one-click replays with pre-checks and approval flow.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: replay accidentally exercises a destructive API. Mitigation: manifest validation rejects any request that targets admin endpoints and enforces a read-only overlay.
- Risk: noisy telemetry impacts production observability. Mitigation: mirror to staging observability tenants and limit federation sampling to avoid ingestion spikes.

Appendix: capture manifest best practices
- Capture window: prefer 30–90 minutes around representative peak and tail windows.
- Sampling: use deterministic sampling seeds for reproducibility.
- Anonymization rules: drop fields user.email, user_id, ip_address; hash customer_id with stable salt stored in KMS.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting
- Replay driver stalls at "priming" stage: check S3 read throughput limits, increase IAM read concurrency for replay role.
- Traces missing during run: confirm federator job is running and trace-sampler percentage > 0.
- Observability discounting: confirm labels replay_run and run_id are present so dashboards can segregate replay metrics.

References and links:
- Platform operator sandbox: eng-platform/team-wiki/operator-sandbox-synthetic-scenarios-and-verification-catalog-2025
- Observability onboarding: eng-platform/team-wiki/observability-contracts-and-dependency-slo-onboarding-handbook-2025
- Security capture checklist: security-and-compliance/data-management/capture-and-scrub-guidelines (internal link)

Last updated 2027-01-18 by Sofia Alvarez. For questions or to book a rehearsal slot, ping #platform-replay in Slack.

payload.page_title: Operator prefetch validation lab playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook describes the Operator Prefetch Validation Lab: a practical, repeatable process for validating prefetch heuristics, cohort configurations, and their operator automation at scale. It is intended for platform operators and SREs running experiments against the prefetch stack (prefetch-service, kv-prefix-cache, prefetch-allocator, runtime-router) and for product/ML partners who own workload definitions.

Goals:
- Verify that a prefetch change (heuristic, TTL, cohort weighting) improves tail latency and token-cost per request without increasing error rate or violating SLOs.
- Provide safe operator tooling to run staged rollouts, limit blast radius, and automatically revert on regression.
- Produce reproducible artifacts: dashboards, alert rules, experiment results, and a short retrospective.

When to use this playbook:
- Introducing a new prefetch heuristic or cache key transformation.
- Changing cohort selection or burst-credit policy.
- Updating allocator capacity scoring or eviction policy.

Key metrics (table):

Metric | PromQL / source | Alert threshold (operator)
-------|-----------------|-------------------------
P50 generation latency (ms) | histogram_quantile(0.50, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket[2m])) by (le)) | see SLOs
P95 generation latency (ms) | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket[2m])) by (le)) | warning: > 450ms, critical: > 700ms
P99 generation latency (ms) | histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket[2m])) by (le)) | warning: > 900ms, critical: > 1500ms
Token cost per request (mean) | sum(rate(token_cost_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) | > 1.3x baseline -> investigate
Request error rate | sum(rate(request_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) | warning: > 0.5%, critical: > 1.5%
Prefetch hit ratio | sum(prefetch_hits[5m]) / sum(prefetch_lookups[5m]) | regression: drop > 5%
KV prefix cache evictions | rate(kv_evictions_total[1m]) | spike above baseline by > 10x
Allocator steal/rebalance events | rate(allocator_rebalances[1m]) | investigate if sustained for > 10m

Preflight checklist (operator):
1) Confirm the experiment ticket (RFC/PRD) is labeled with the prefetch experiment tag and has owner and rollback plan.
2) Ensure a canary cohort with <1% traffic is available and isolated by tenant and region.
3) Verify baseline telemetry for the last 7 days is captured and bookmarked (save dashboard snapshot ID).
4) Build a synthetic load profile that matches the real request size/sequence distribution for the target tenants.
5) Prepare dashboards, Grafana panels, and PromQL alerts listed below.
6) Create a feature-flag with percentage rollout and ability to pin by tenant ID.
7) Verify operator runbook and automated rollback policy are staged in the orchestrator (canary: auto-revert after N violations).

Experiment design and sizing:
- Minimum detectable effect (MDE): define target reduction in P95 latency or token cost (e.g., 8–12%). Use historical variance to estimate sample size.
- Duration: minimum 3 full days for steady-state workloads; extend to 7–14 days if weekly patterns exist.
- Cohorts: Canary (0.5–1%), Ramp (1–25%), Full (gradual to 100%). Always keep a control group pinned to baseline.
- Statistical test: use non-parametric tests on latency distributions (Mann-Whitney U) and bootstrap for token-cost means. Capture p-values and confidence intervals in the experiment report.

Operator run steps (ordered):
1. Create an experiment change in the experiments repo with: description, feature flag key, cohorts, expected impact, rollback criteria, monitoring links.
2. Dry-run config validation: `./tools/experiment-validate --file exp.yaml --env staging`.
3. Deploy to staging cohort and run synthetic load for 2 hours, confirm no regressions.
4. Snapshot dashboards: `curl -X POST "https://grafana.internal/api/dashboards/db" -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d @dashboard-snapshot.json` (store snapshot id).
5. Release to canary cohort (0.5–1%) and monitor for 30–60 minutes.
6. If all checks pass, ramp to 5% and wait one hour per step; run the full validation battery at 25% for 24–72 hours depending on workload.
7. Final decision meeting: capture metrics, statistical tests, and operational notes.
8. Promote to production with a staged rollout and 24/7 pager coverage for the first 48 hours.

Automated guardrails (recommended alert rules):
- Alert: prefetch-regression-critical
  - Expr (PromQL): `increase(request_errors_total{job="runtime-router",experiment="$experiment"}[5m]) / increase(requests_total{job="runtime-router",experiment="$experiment"}[5m]) > 0.015`
  - For: 5m
  - Severity: critical
  - Action: immediate rollback of experiment flag, notify oncall, open Ops incident.

- Alert: prefetch-latency-p95-degradation
  - Expr: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket{experiment="$experiment"}[2m])) by (le)) > scalar(0.9 * baseline_p95)`
  - For: 10m
  - Severity: warning
  - Action: throttle rollout to previous safe percentage and escalate if persists.

- Alert: prefetch-cache-eviction-spike
  - Expr: `rate(kv_evictions_total{region="$region"}[1m]) > 10 * avg_over_time(rate(kv_evictions_total{region="$region"}[1m])[1h:1m])`
  - For: 5m
  - Action: notify operator and reduce prefetch footprint.

Suggested Grafana panels (copyable notes):
- P95 / P99 latency split by cohort and control (stacked line).
- Prefetch hit ratio heatmap by tenant and model family.
- Token cost per request (rolling 1h) with baseline overlay.
- KV prefix cache occupancy and eviction rate.
- Allocator rebalance events and prefetch queue depth.

Quick CLI snippets:
- Enable feature flag for tenant: `rctl feature-flag set --key prefetch_new_heuristic --tenant TENANT_ID --percent 1`
- Revert feature flag: `rctl feature-flag set --key prefetch_new_heuristic --tenant TENANT_ID --percent 0`
- Fetch last dashboard snapshot: `graf-snap fetch --id $SNAP_ID --out report.html`

Rollback decision matrix (simple):
- Immediate rollback: any critical alert fires (error rate > 1.5%, P99 > 1500ms sustained > 5m).
- Throttle and observe: warning-level latency or hit-ratio drop between 3–10%.
- Continue and monitor: positive token-cost improvement with stable latency and error rates.

Post-experiment reporting (template):
- Title, experiment ID, owner, start/end times, cohorts and traffic percentages.
- Baseline metrics snapshot (P50/P95/P99 latencies, token cost, hit ratio).
- Observed delta and statistical significance.
- Operator notes: anomalies, infra events, transient external factors.
- Actions: promote, iterate, rollback, or close.
- Retrospective: 3 bullets for what went well, 3 bullets for what to change, owners for next steps.

Retrospective checklist (team):
1) Within 3 business days, owners submit the experiment report to the experiments tracker.
2) Host a 30-minute sync with platform, product, and ml-eval teams to review results.
3) Update dashboards/alerts if new signals are needed.
4) Schedule follow-up experiments if marginal gains require iteration.

Roadmap and follow-ups (recommended):
- Q2: integrate automatic statistical-significance checks into the experiment pipeline (block merge if p>0.05). Owner: experimentation infra.
- Q3: add cohort-slicing by model family and prompt-shape to reduce noise. Owner: prefetch product.
- Q4: surface prefetch economics per-tenant in the Console (billing + per-tenant ROI). Owner: console and billing teams.

Owner ship and escalation:
- Primary owner: Platform Operators (eng-platform/operators).
- Secondary owners: Serving runtime (eng-serving-runtime) and Applied ML (applied-ml-and-evals) for workload definitions.
- Escalation path: oncall -> platform lead -> eng-sre -> CTO if customer impact > P1 and > 60 minutes.

Appendix A — Example experiment config (YAML):

```yaml
experiment_id: pf-2025-042
description: test new prefetch heuristic that biases by prompt-prefix similarity
cohorts:
  - name: control
    percent: 50
    config: baseline
  - name: heuristic_v1
    percent: 1
    config: prefetch_heuristic_v1.yaml
  - name: ramp
    percent: 49
    config: rolling
rollback_criteria:
  - name: error_rate
    expr: 'increase(request_errors_total{job="runtime-router",experiment="pf-2025-042"}[5m]) / increase(requests_total{job="runtime-router",experiment="pf-2025-042"}[5m]) > 0.015'
  - name: p99_latency
    expr: 'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket{experiment="pf-2025-042"}[2m])) by (le)) > 1500'
```

Appendix B — Common troubleshooting scenarios:
- Symptom: P95 increases, but hit ratio rises and token cost decreases.
  - Likely cause: prefetch is increasing the amount of prefetched context but inducing longer serialization or KV pressure.
  - Action: throttle prefetch footprint, increase prefetch priority for small sequence-length requests, schedule a follow-up experiment tuning TTL.

- Symptom: Eviction spike after rollout.
  - Cause: prefetch key growth or bad key entropy.
  - Action: revert, run key-cardinality audit (`kv-audit key-cardinality --prefix prefetch/`) and prune noisy prefixes.

- Symptom: Allocator rebalances increase and tenant requests see transient 429s.
  - Cause: aggressive allocator scoring change.
  - Action: roll back allocator change, increase reserved capacity for critical tenants, and run controlled rebalancing with drain windows.

Concluding notes:
This playbook is designed to be prescriptive and repeatable. Keep experiment artifacts (dashboards, snapshots, experiment YAMLs) attached to the experiment ticket. If you identify missing telemetry or false positives in alerts, update the experiment template and notify the telemetry engineering group.

Document history and references:
- Template inspired by platform experimentation best practices and prior regional-prefetch cohort experiments.
- Related pages: see related_pages list above for operator guides and earlier runbooks.
- Contact: maya.chen@redwood-inference.internal for clarifying questions or to request tooling enhancements.

payload.page_title: Service Dependency Fault Isolation and Fallback Runbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This runbook describes deterministic steps to detect, isolate, and apply safe fallbacks for production service failures that are caused by downstream dependencies (internal microservices, third-party APIs, or data stores). The goal is to protect user-facing SLOs while minimizing blast radius and preserving customer data integrity.

Scope and when to use this document:
- Applies to all Redwood platform services that depend on other services via HTTP/gRPC/RPC, shared caches, or queues.
- Use when alerts indicate dependency degradation (increased error rate, latency, or timeouts) or when degradation is observed in dashboards.
- Not for full-site outages caused by control-plane failures; see the platform incident runbook for those scenarios.

Key contacts and ownership:
- Primary oncall: service owner team (listed in service metadata).
- Platform SRE escalation: eng-sre@redwood.com, PagerDuty: Redwood-SRE-oncall.
- Runbook steward: Maya Chen (eng-platform).

SLOs and detection thresholds (concrete):
- User-facing P95 latency target: 200ms. Alert if P95 > 500ms for 5m.
- Error rate threshold: >3% 5xx rate across 5m relative to baseline (or 2x baseline sustained).
- Dependency timeout threshold: >200ms 95th for downstream RPC, or >1s for third-party API (5m window).
- Queue backlog: >1000 unprocessed messages for more than 10m.

Alert mapping (example):
- ALERT_DEPENDENCY_SPIKE_HIGH_ERRORS: triggered when dependency 5xx% >3% for 5m.
- ALERT_DEPENDENCY_P95_LATENCY: triggered when dependency P95 > configured threshold.
- ALERT_CACHE_MISS_STORM: Redis/Memcached miss rate spike >5x baseline.

Initial verification and scope isolation (15 minutes):
1) Confirm the alert: check the dashboard (Platform Services -> <service-name> -> Dependencies pane). Capture timestamp, graphs, and initial hypothesis.
2) Identify the failing dependency: use traces in Jaeger/Tempo and the dependency heatmap to confirm which host or external endpoint is causing errors/latency.
3) Confirm blast radius: list callers of dependency using service registry (ServiceGraph). If caller list >10 services, escalate to SRE lead.
4) Check rollout/changes: confirm whether a deployment or configuration change preceded the incident (CI/CD deployments, canary rollouts, config flags). Query gitops history: git log --since="1 hour" --pretty=oneline for the service and immediate dependencies.

Fast containment options (choose one based on severity):
- Local Retry Backoff Increase: flip config_rapid_retries=false to avoid retry storms.
  CLI example (kubectl patch): kubectl -n <ns> patch deploy/<svc> -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"<svc>","env":[{"name":"RAPID_RETRY_ENABLED","value":"false"}]}}]}}}}'
- Circuit Breaker Engage (recommended): set circuit_breaker threshold to 50 failures/min. Service mesh command example (consul/istio): istioctl replace -f circuit-breaker-fallback.yaml
- Traffic Shift to Degraded Mode: route 90% of traffic to a path that uses cached data or a read-only backend. Example: /v1/feature?mode=readonly
- Flow Control via Rate Limits: apply per-user rate limit of 10rps to reduce load and protect downstream stores.

Fallback strategies (ordered by safety):
1) Read-from-cache: if the dependency is primarily used for enrichment (non-authoritative), switch to cache-only responses with TTL-based staleness header.
2) Read-only degraded mode: block write operations and return 503 for write requests that require the failing dependency, but continue read paths.
3) Graceful degradation: return a placeholder response with a clear client-visible flag (e.g., "field_unavailable": true) and log metrics for evaluation.
4) Alternate service routing: if replica or warm-standby exists, switch dependency DNS or mesh routing to replica cluster.

Detailed run steps (escalation ladder):
Triage (0–15 minutes)
1. Acknowledge the alert in PagerDuty and post to #platform-incidents with "ACK - <service> dependency spike". Include initial graph screenshot and current hypothesis.
2. Open a mitigation channel and invite SRE and service owner.
3. Run quick diagnostics: curl -v --max-time 5 https://dependency.internal/health and compare 200 vs 5xx.

Containment (15–45 minutes)
4. If error rate >5% or P95 > 1s, engage circuit breaker or increase retry backoff immediately. Document config change in the incident channel.
5. If replica available, shift 30% traffic to replica and monitor. Use the routing CLI: rctl route set --from <svc> --to <replica> --weight 30
6. If third-party provider is failing and SLA allows, switch to degraded cached content: set DEPENDENCY_CACHE_ONLY=true via feature flag system (LaunchDarkly or FFClient).

Recovery (45–120 minutes)
7. Monitor key metrics: P95 latency, 5xx rate, request throughput, queue backlog. Use dashboard time windows 1m/5m/30m.
8. Once metrics return below thresholds for 15 continuous minutes, slowly revert changes: reduce circuit breaker threshold, re-enable retries, or shift traffic back in 10% increments every 5 minutes.
9. If recovery stalls, schedule owner-led rollback to last stable deployment and coordinate with SRE for DB/queue restorative tasks.

Post-incident actions and checks (owner must complete within 48 hours):
- Create postmortem with timeline, root cause, and follow-ups in the incident tracker. Link to this runbook.
- Add an automated synthetic check for the dependency if none exists.
- Evaluate and implement one long-term fix from the mitigation list (e.g., improve circuit-breaker thresholds, add cache fallbacks, or provision warm-standby).

Suggested metrics and dashboards to add (table-style list described):
- Dependency health: 1) 5xx rate (5m), 2) P95 latency, 3) Success rate by upstream caller.
- Traffic shaping: % traffic to fallback paths, cache hit ratio, retry counts.
- Backpressure: queue length, consumer lag per topic.
- Cost/usage: requests served by fallback vs normal path.

Configuration examples:
- Circuit breaker (YAML) snippet for Istio-style policies (example to store in /ops/istio/):
  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
  kind: DestinationRule
  metadata:
    name: dependency-cb
  spec:
    host: dependency.internal.svc.cluster.local
    trafficPolicy:
      outlierDetection:
        consecutive5xxErrors: 5
        interval: 10s
        baseEjectionTime: 30s
        maxEjectionPercent: 50

- Fallback response pattern (JSON example returned to clients):
  {
    "status": "partial",
    "fields_unavailable": ["profile_picture","recent_activity"],
    "stale": true,
    "served_from": "cache-v2"
  }

Runbook decision matrix (short):
- If dependency is internal and < 30 callers: consider direct restart of dependency and immediate circuit breaker.
- If dependency is external or >100 callers: prefer traffic shaping, cache, or contacting vendor support before restarts.
- If writes are failing and data loss risk is high: disable writes and enable queuing with durable storage.

Common CLI snippets and observability checks:
- kubectl -n <ns> get pods -l app=<dependency> -o wide
- kubectl -n <ns> logs -f deploy/<dependency> --since=10m | jq -R 'select(.|test("ERROR|WARN"))'
- curl -sS -D - https://<dependency>/health | sed -n '1,20p'
- jaeger UI: search traces by operation name or http.status_code>=500
- prometheus query examples: sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{job=~".*dependency.*",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (instance)

Risk controls and safety notes:
- All immediate config changes must be recorded in the incident channel and committed to the ops repo within 24 hours.
- Avoid mass restarts of dependent services unless you have an explicit rollback plan; rolling restarts with 10% concurrency are preferred.
- Any fallback that changes client-visible behavior must increment a metric named fallback.feature_name.invoked and include a Feature Flag to disable if unintended consequences occur.

Postmortem checklist (owner):
1. Write timeline and impact statement.
2. Identify root cause and contributing factors.
3. Assign action items with owners and due dates.
4. Add or update dependency health checks.
5. Add test cases to the eval harness to simulate dependency failures.
6. Review incident with product/solutions if customer-facing impact occurred.

Retrospective prompts (for the postmortem):
- What early signal did we miss and how can we detect it automatically?
- Which fallback choices minimized customer impact and which caused regressions?
- Were runbook steps clear and followed? If not, what changes are needed?
- Are threshold values in the alert mapping still appropriate?

Appendix: useful links and templates
- Incident postmortem template: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/postmortem-template-2024
- Service registry and caller graph: /internal/service-registry
- Feature flag control panel: https://flags.redwood.com
- Playbook artifact folder: /ops/playbooks/dependency-fallbacks

Document history and notes:
- Created by Maya Chen 2024-11-03.
- Reviewed by Ellen Park and Diego Morales 2025-01-15.
- Updated with Istio circuit-breaker snippet and traffic-shift CLI examples 2025-02-14.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Operator knowledge decay and handbook grooming retrospective

sections.body:
Overview:

This retrospective summarizes a six-month program (May–Oct 2025) that targeted operator knowledge decay across platform operator teams and the associated handbook/runbook drift we observed. The goal was to (1) measure how rapidly critical operational knowledge diverged from canonical runbooks, (2) trial lightweight grooming processes to keep runbooks accurate, and (3) define a repeatable cadence and ownership model for ongoing maintenance.

Background and scope:

- Scope: all production-facing runbooks and operator-facing handbooks in the eng-platform space (runbooks, playbooks, troubleshooting guides, preflight checklists).
- Motivation: repeated incidents in Q1–Q2 2025 where on-call operators performed non-standard remediation because runbooks were out of date (example incident IDs: INC-2025-412, INC-2025-589).
- Participants: Platform Operators, Observability, Runtime teams, and Documentation Guild.

Key timeline:

1. 2025-05-01: Baseline measurement (doc freshness audit + operator quiz).
2. 2025-06 to 2025-09: Pilot grooming squads (rotating 2-week sprints) and automated stale doc alerts.
3. 2025-10-15: Mid-pilot checkpoint and operator feedback synthesis.
4. 2025-11-01: Consolidation of changes and initial productionization of grooming workflow.

Observations & evidence:

- Quantitative metrics collected at baseline (2025-05):
  - Runbook freshness: 38% of runbooks had last_updated > 180 days.
  - Accuracy score (operator quiz vs runbook answers): average 68% across sampled operators.
  - Time-to-first-action (TTFA) during simulated incident: median 9.8 minutes with docs; 6.2 minutes when operator had recent tabletop training.
  - Post-incident runbook edits occurred in only 23% of incidents where runbooks were referenced.

- Qualitative findings from interviews and postmortems:
  - Operators reported uncertainty about which runbook version was canonical for multi-region failovers.
  - Smaller, tactical fixes (CLI flag changes, new diagnostic endpoints) were rarely captured because they happened during on-call rush and were deferred.
  - Ownership ambiguity: many runbooks lacked a named owner or had owners that moved teams.

Root causes identified:

- No enforced update SLA for runbooks when code/config changes; engineering changes often outpaced documentation updates.
- Low cognitive overhead on on-call to file a small post-incident doc edit; not incentivized or observed.
- Lack of clear owner and lifecycle state for each doc (draft, verified, deprecated).
- A proliferation of near-duplicate playbooks across teams with small divergent edits.

Decisions from the retrospective (summary):

1. Establish a lightweight, enforced runbook lifecycle with a 30/90/180 day freshness policy and automation for reminders.
2. Create a rotating "Grooming Squad" (2 engineers from Platform + 1 Documentation Guild member) for each quarter to perform targeted updates.
3. Introduce a post-incident documentation blotter: mandatory one-line postmortem action to be filed in the incident ticket within 3 business days; documentation edits tied to the ticket are required before the incident is marked resolved for knowledge-related incidents.
4. Add explicit owner, secondary owner, and verification date metadata fields to the Confluence runbook templates.
5. Start a quarterly handbook grooming sprint tied to on-call schedules and conduct an annual doc audit.

Action plan and owners (table):

| Action | Owner | Due | Success criteria |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add owner/secondary/verification fields to runbook template | Documentation Guild (lead: Sofia Guerrero) | 2025-12-01 | New template enforced on page creation; 100% of new pages include metadata |
| Implement automated stale-doc alert pipeline (Slack + dashboard) | Observability (lead: Marcus Lee) | 2026-01-10 | Alerts show docs with last_updated > threshold; daily digest for Grooming Squad |
| Runbook linter for missing commands/outputs (CI check) | Eng-Platform Tools (lead: Daniel Park) | 2026-02-01 | Linter added to runbook PR checks; blocked merges when template fields missing |
| Pilot quarterly Grooming Squads and measure coverage | Platform Managers (lead: Aisha Patel) | 2026-03-30 | Coverage >= 80% of production runbooks in pilot cohort |
| Post-incident documentation requirement added to incident playbook | Eng-SRE (lead: Priya Nair) | 2025-12-15 | Incident workflow enforces doc edit checkbox before incident closure for knowledge gaps |

Grooming workflow (step-by-step):

1. Triage: Automated stale-doc alert selects 30 candidate runbooks by SLO impact and incident reference count.
2. Assign: Grooming Squad assigns owners and secondary reviewers for each candidate.
3. Vet: Runbook owner runs the documented steps in a sandbox or simulation (if safe) and notes mismatches.
4. Edit: Owner updates commands, outputs, prerequisite lists, and adds "last_verified_by" and "verification_notes" sections.
5. Review: Secondary reviewer validates changes; Documentation Guild runs linter and style check.
6. Publish: Update last_verified_date and close the grooming task; changes are summarized in a release note in the team channel.

Runbook template checklist (must be present for every production runbook):

- Title and short description (1–2 lines)
- Owner and secondary owner (with team)
- Last updated and last verified dates
- Severity and SLO impact tags (e.g., P0, P1, latency-sli)
- Preconditions and required tooling (CLI, service account scopes)
- Step-by-step remediation with expected outputs and verification steps
- Rollback and escalation paths (who to call, Slack channels, pager rotations)
- Post-incident edit section with change summary and ticket reference
- Related artifacts (dashboards, playbooks, runbook id)

Ownership matrix (string table):

| Runbook category | Primary owner team | Secondary owner | Review cadence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global failover & routing | Eng-Platform Routing | Eng-SRE | 90 days |
| Runtime quantization rollout | Serving Runtime | Observability | 180 days |
| GPU pool maintenance | Eng-Infrastructure | Platform Operators | 90 days |
| Cost and billing alerts | Finance-Eng | Eng-Platform Tools | 180 days |

Measurement and CI gates (how we'll know this is working):

- Freshness rate target: >= 75% of production runbooks last_verified within 90 days by end of Q2 2026.
- Post-incident edit rate target: >= 70% of incidents that reference a runbook must result in a documented edit or verification within 3 business days.
- On-call quiz retention: baseline 68% -> target 82% average correct on sampled quarterly quizzes.
- TTFA improvement: median TTFA during synthetic incidents reduced from 9.8 minutes to <= 6 minutes in one year for covered runbooks.

Risks and mitigations:

- Risk: Grooming becomes a checkbox exercise with superficial edits.
  - Mitigation: Require verification evidence (logs/screenshots) and secondary reviewer sign-off; random audits by Documentation Guild.
- Risk: Added overhead for small teams causing backlog.
  - Mitigation: Automate obvious edits (metadata fill, link corrections) and provide a lightweight CLI for quick edits during hotfixes.
- Risk: Runbook duplication across teams persists.
  - Mitigation: Canonicalization initiative: identify duplicates quarterly and fold them into cross-team canonical pages; deprecate duplicates with redirect notes.

Retrospective takeaways (short):

- Small, regular investments in runbook hygiene yield measurable reductions in confusion during incidents.
- Tying documentation updates to incident closure and making owner fields explicit materially improved edit rates during the pilot.
- Automation is required to keep human overhead reasonable; human review remains necessary for verification.

Next steps (90-day plan):

- 2026-01-10 to 2026-01-30: Deploy stale-doc alerting pipeline and enforce new template on all new pages. (Owner: Observability + Documentation Guild)
- 2026-02-01 to 2026-02-28: Runbook linter in PR checks + training session for grooming best practices. (Owner: Eng-Platform Tools)
- 2026-03-01 to 2026-03-31: First full quarter of Grooming Squads; collect metrics and present at Platform Quarterly Review. (Owner: Platform Managers)

Appendix and artifacts:

- Baseline metrics spreadsheet: /docs/ops-metrics/runbook-freshness-2025-q2.csv
- Pilot grooming example edit: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/region-failover-runbook (revision 14)
- Incident references: INC-2025-412, INC-2025-589, INC-2025-602
- Grooming squad retrospective notes (internal board): /boards/grooming-squad/retro-2025-10

Document history:

- Author: Aisha Patel (Platform Manager)
- Reviewers: Marcus Lee (Observability), Sofia Guerrero (Documentation Guild), Daniel Park (Platform Tools)
- Status: published 2026-01-12

If you are an operator or runbook owner: please add missing metadata to any runbook you are responsible for by 2026-02-01. Questions or pushback: ping #platform-docs or contact the Documentation Guild.

payload.page_title: Gameday 2024: Chaos Injection Case Study — Prefix Cache Starvation

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This case study documents the Nov 2024 gameday in us-west-2 where a planned chaos injection (simulated node OOM + high churn) exposed a latent failure mode that caused prefix-cache starvation and tenant-priority inversion. The incident produced a 95th percentile generation latency SLO breach (target 120ms, observed spike to ~420ms for 28 minutes) for a tranche of production customers.

Context and goals
-----------------
- Exercise regional degradations and validate automated fallback policies, cache coherence, and operator runbooks.
- Validate SRE/operator response time and remedial actions for resource-starvation scenarios on the serving runtime.
- Evaluate observability coverage: can we detect cache-quality regressions early and attribute to tenant slices?

Planned experiment
------------------
1) Inject simulated OOM on 3/12 nodes in the us-west-2 GPU pool (controlled, orchestrated via chaos harness).
2) Induce synthetic tenant traffic burst skewed to long-sequence requests for a set of low-priority tenants.
3) Enable a short-lived configuration toggle (test) to reduce global prefix-cache capacity by 40% to simulate metadata pressure.
4) Observe routing, latency, eviction rates, and cost attributions.

Timeline (high level)
---------------------
- 2024-11-12 09:00 UTC — Gameday kickoff; baseline dashboards validated.
- 09:15 UTC — Node OOM injections start; cluster autoscaler triggers but with 3–4 min delay.
- 09:22 UTC — Synthetic tenant burst begins (long context, frequent new prefixes).
- 09:27 UTC — Cache capacity toggle flipped (40% reduction).
- 09:30 UTC — Platform synthetic SLI probe alerts: "prefix_cache_hit_rate_usw2 < 0.6 for 10m" fires.
- 09:40–09:58 UTC — 95p latency breach for tiered tenants; increased cost token usage observed.
- 09:58 UTC — Operators apply emergency mitigations (see below).
- 10:05 UTC — Latency returns to within SLO for most tenants; follow-up cleanup completed by 11:00 UTC.

Impact summary
--------------
- Customer-facing: 28 minutes of elevated latency for ~7% of production requests routed to us-west-2. Surface errors were low (error rate stayed <0.5%), impact primarily latency.
- Economic: transient increase in per-token cost from repeated re-generation and backend retries, estimated additional cost ~$1.8k for the window.
- Operational: identified ambiguous alerting coverage and a missing fast path to bump priority weights for critical tenants during cache degeneration.

Observations and signals
------------------------
- Telemetry: rapid increase in prefix_cache_eviction_rate_usw2 and per-tenant eviction skew. Prometheus query we used:
  - prefix_cache_hit_rate = sum by (tenant) (cache_hits_total{region="us-west-2"}) / sum by (tenant) (cache_requests_total{region="us-west-2"})
  - eviction_rate = increase(cache_evictions_total{region="us-west-2"}[5m])
- Tracing: KV cache miss traces showed repeated long-tail lookups hitting remote blobstore (200–400ms additional latency per miss).
- Router behavior: Smart routing attempted cross-region failover but constrained by regional deployment pins for dedicated tenants, leading to uneven load distribution.
- Tenant priority inversion: the eviction policy used a global LRU with tenant-weighted tokens, but under metadata pressure the implementation favored recency over configured tenant weight, causing high-priority tenants to lose cached prefixes.

Root cause analysis
-------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
1) Cache eviction algorithm gap: an implementation detail in the weighted-LRU fast path ignored per-tenant weight during accelerated eviction windows. This was triggered by reduced cache capacity combined with high churn.
2) Insufficient TTL isolation: shared prefix cache for variable-length contexts allowed long-context synthetic workloads to occupy the same cache region as short-context, high-throughput tenants.
3) Alerting gaps: existing alert "prefix_cache_hit_rate" was aggregated across the region and did not include per-tenant or per-slice triggers; by the time the regional alert fired, high-priority tenants were already degraded.
4) Runbook friction: the operator runbook required manual escalation to change tenant weights (config change propagated via the control plane), a path that took ~7 minutes to execute and validate.

Mitigations and follow-ups (short/medium/long-term)
---------------------------------------------------
Short-term (emergency during gameday) — completed:
- Emergency bypass: toggled per-tenant cache isolation flag for two high-priority tenants to allocate dedicated prefix-sets (runtime config via control plane):
  - curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/runtime-config
    -d '{"region":"us-west-2","tenant":"TENANT-CRITICAL-1","prefix_cache.isolated":true}'
- Temporarily increased tenant weight for critical tenants to 3x via the control plane to prevent eviction.
- Rebalanced synthetic traffic to limit new-prefix churn while cluster recovered.

Medium-term (2–6 weeks) — in progress / scheduled:
- Implement correctness fix for weighted-LRU fast path to respect tenant weights even during accelerated eviction. (owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel_team; due: 2025-03-01)
- Add per-tenant prefix-cache SLI rollups and dashboards, with alert rules:
  - Alert: PrefixCacheDegradationPerTenant
    - Trigger when: prefix_cache_hit_rate{tenant="$TENANT"} < 0.7 for 5m
    - Pager: oncall-platform
- Add TTL bucketing in the cache allocator so long-context prefixes cannot evict short-context hot prefixes. (owner: eng-serving-runtime/cache_team; due: 2025-02-15)
- Automate a rapid operator action: a new CLI helper and Control Plane API to set temporary tenant priority weights with a 1-click Console button and rollback. (owner: eng-platform/tools; due: 2025-02-28)

Long-term (quarterly roadmap) — planned:
- Regional redundancy improvements: reduce failover friction for dedicated tenants by allowing controlled cross-region evictions or warm-standby routing when local cache degraded. (product + eng; Q2 2025)
- E2E canary that exercises cache eviction paths under simulated prefix churn monthly.
- Cost-sensitive heuristics to detect repeated regeneration loops and auto-throttle offending clients.

Runbook snippet: immediate operator steps for prefix-cache degradation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm alert and scope: check dashboard "Prefix Cache Health — REGION" and run:
   - promql: topk(20, (sum by (tenant) (cache_hits_total{region="us-west-2"}) / sum by (tenant) (cache_requests_total{region="us-west-2"})))
2) If high-priority tenant hit-rate < 0.7: set isolation flag for tenant via control plane (example above).
3) If overall eviction_rate > 200/min: reduce incoming new-prefix churn by applying soft-rate-limiting on synthetic/integration tenants:
   - curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/traffic-controls -d '{"region":"us-west-2","selector":"tags:integration","qps":10}'
4) To temporarily bump tenant weight:
   - rtictl set-weight --region=us-west-2 --tenant=TENANT-CRITICAL-1 --weight=3 --expires=10m
5) Monitor: cache_hit_rate, eviction_rate, downstream 95p latency, and token_cost_rate.
6) When stable for 15 minutes, roll back control-plane temporary flags and open follow-up ticket.

Observability: dashboards and alerts added as part of postmortem
----------------------------------------------------------------
- New dashboards created:
  - Prefix Cache Health — Region (per-tenant panes)
  - Tenant Priority Exposure (histogram of eviction events by weight)
  - Cache Miss Trace Correlation (percent of misses that hit remote blobstore)
- New alert rules:
  - PrefixCacheDegradationPerTenant (threshold: <0.7 for 5m, severity: P1)
  - CacheEvictionStorm (evictions/min > 250 for 5m, severity: P2)
  - TenantRegenLoopDetected (if a single client triggers >10 headroom retries in 5m)

Action items (owners and due dates)
----------------------------------
- Fix weighted-LRU correctness in fast path — eng-serving-runtime/kernel_team — due 2025-03-01 — owner: Diego Morales
- TTL bucketing and allocator change — eng-serving-runtime/cache_team — due 2025-02-15 — owner: Priya Shah
- One-click tenant-priority toggle in Console + CLI helper — eng-platform/tools — due 2025-02-28 — owner: Leah Morgan
- Add per-tenant SLI/alerting and dashboard templates — observability-team — due 2025-01-31 — owner: Lena Kovacs
- Monthly gameday canary for cache eviction paths — runbooks-team + platform-eng — due Q1 2025 — owner: Aisha Patel

Metrics captured (key numbers during incident window)
--------------------------------------------------
- Max prefix_cache_eviction_rate_usw2: 382 evictions/min
- Lowest median per-tenant cache_hit_rate (critical tenant): 0.42
- 95th request latency (affected tenants): 420ms (SLO target: 120ms)
- Estimated incremental cost: ~$1.8k

Lessons learned and recommendations
----------------------------------
- Surface per-tenant cache SLIs by default for multi-tenant components; region-level aggregates hide targeted degradations.
- Implement isolation primitives earlier in the caching stack (TTL buckets, reserved slots for critical tenants).
- Reduce operator friction: add validated fast paths for emergency weight changes; document rollback safeguards.
- Include synthetic churn scenarios in routine canaries; ensure canaries exercise eviction and rehydration cycles.
- Improve alert signal fidelity to reduce mean time to detect and mean time to mitigate.

Appendix: useful queries, commands, and links
--------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Primary causes (ordered)

sections.body:
- Regional 95p latency for generation route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(gen_request_duration_seconds_bucket{region="us-west-2"}[5m])) by (le))
- Per-tenant cache hit rate: sum by (tenant) (increase(cache_hits_total{region="us-west-2"}[5m])) / sum by (tenant) (increase(cache_requests_total{region="us-west-2"}[5m]))
- Eviction storm detector: increase(cache_evictions_total{region="us-west-2"}[5m]) > 250
sections.heading: PromQL examples

sections.body:
- Set tenant isolation:
  curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/runtime-config -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"region":"us-west-2","tenant":"TENANT-CRITICAL-1","prefix_cache.isolated":true}'
- Set tenant weight CLI (example uses rtictl):
  rtictl set-weight --region=us-west-2 --tenant=TENANT-CRITICAL-1 --weight=3 --expires=10m

Retention and follow-up cadence
--------------------------------
- Engineering owners to provide weekly status updates in the platform-runbook channel until all medium-term items are closed.
- Re-run a scoped gameday within 6 weeks to validate the correctness fix and TTL bucketing.

Acknowledgements
----------------
Thanks to the gameday participants and responders: eng-serving-runtime teams, observability, eng-platform/tools, and oncall SREs. Special thanks to Diego Morales and Priya Shah for leading the realtime mitigation and to the control plane team for fast rollback support.

payload.page_title: Operator knowledge synthesis and runbook creation playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook codifies the process for converting incident investigations and retrospectives into operational runbooks and structured knowledge artifacts. It is intended for Platform Operators, Incident Leads, and Engineering managers who are responsible for ensuring that knowledge produced by post-incident analysis becomes runnable, testable, and discoverable runbooks.

Goals

- Ensure every Sev2+ incident has an associated runbook or a clearly scoped action item to produce one within the follow-up window.
- Reduce mean time to first action (MTTFA) for recurring failure modes by providing validated operator procedures.
- Maintain a living library of runbooks with versioning, ownership, test records, and a quarterly verification cadence.

Scope

Applies to platform services owned by the eng-platform org including but not limited to: routing-service, batching-engine, kv-prefix-cache, runtime-gateway, and region-failover. Does not replace product-facing runbooks maintained by individual product teams (those live in their team spaces but should follow the same templates).

When to run this playbook

- After every incident with severity >= Sev2.
- When a change introduces a new operational surface (new autoscaler, new cache sharding scheme, new quantized runtime).
- During scheduled knowledge-transfer sprints (quarterly).

Stakeholders and responsibilities

- Incident Lead: Owns the conversion of the retrospective findings into a draft runbook within 5 business days.
- Service Owner: Validates technical accuracy and assigns an owner for ongoing maintenance.
- Platform Operator (Operator Author): Formalizes steps, produces test scripts, and executes dry-runs.
- Oncall Manager: Schedules tabletop/test windows and ensures runbook is included in oncall playbooks.
- Documentation Reviewer(s): Approve content for publication in the runbook library.

Key Definitions

- Runbook: A step-by-step operational document that an operator can follow to mitigate or recover from a known failure mode.
- Testable Runbook: A runbook with automated or manual verification steps that can be executed in a failure-injection or replay environment.
- Coverage: Percentage of Sev2+ incidents that have an associated runbook or active-creation ticket.

Procedure (ordered)

1) Incident classification and triage (Day 0–1)
   - Incident Lead tags the postmortem with label: postmortem/runbook-required if the issue is repeatable, not previously documented, or requires multi-step operator action.
   - Create a parent JIRA ticket in project PLAT-OPS: type=Documentation, priority=Highest, summary="Runbook: <service> — <short-title>". Link to the incident and retrospective artifacts.

2) Drafting the runbook (Day 1–5)
   - Use the official runbook template (see Appendix) and store in Confluence path runbooks/<service>/<major-version>/<slug>. Example slug: runbook/routing-service/v3/prefix-cache-warmup.
   - Include: problem statement, symptoms, pre-req checks, impact scope, mitigation steps (with safety checks), rollback steps, post-restore verification, and owner contact information.
   - Add explicit SLO context: e.g., "service P99 latency target: <120ms; error rate target: <0.05%". If the incident consumed >20% error budget, mark runbook as high-priority.

3) Operator validation and tabletop (Day 3–10)
   - Operator Author performs a dry-run in staging or in a controlled chaos workspace. Attach test logs to the runbook page.
   - Run a 30-minute tabletop with the oncall rotation for the affected region: agenda in Appendix. Record minutes and update the runbook.
   - If a step requires privileged access (KMS/HSM or node-level), document exact RBAC roles and the least-privilege escalation path.

4) Publication and assignment (Day 5–14)
   - Documentation Reviewer(s) check for clarity, safety, and completeness. Approved runbooks are moved from draft -> published and tagged runbook:published.
   - Assign a recurring quarterly owner check (Confluence task with assignee = Service Owner).

5) Procedural automation and integration (Day 7–30)
   - Create automation where possible (CLI snippets, runbooks-as-code modules, or a small Playbook script). Host artifacts in platform-ops/runbook-scripts repo.
   - Add link to PagerDuty escalation PD-Platform-Primary and Slack incident channel #platform-ops. Add a Notify step that includes the JIRA parent ticket ID.

6) Ongoing maintenance and verification (Quarterly)
   - Owners must re-run testable steps at least once per quarter or after any major service release. Maintain a verification log on the runbook page.
   - If a runbook fails a verification run, create a remediation ticket and mark runbook:stale until fixed.

Templates and conventions

- File and page naming: runbook/{service}/{major-version}/{short-title}; example: runbook/kv-prefix-cache/v2/eviction-rebalance.
- Minimum content sections (must be present): Summary, Symptoms, Preconditions, Mitigation Steps, Verification, Rollback, Owner and Contact, Change Log, Test Log, Related Incidents.
- Tone and voice: imperative, concise, and free of speculative debugging notes. Keep heuristics in an appendix, not in the main mitigation steps.

Runbook Skeleton (copy into new runbook)

---- START RUNBOOK TEMPLATE ----
Title: <service> — <short-title>
Summary: One-sentence description of the failure mode and impact.
Symptoms: Bullet list of observable indicators (metrics, logs, error messages).
Preconditions: Checks to run before taking action (region, credentials, current load).
Mitigation steps: Numbered, safety-claused commands and expected observables after each step.
Verification: Exact metrics/log queries and thresholds to confirm service health.
Rollback: Reverse steps with precise condition checks.
Owner: Name, pager (PD escalation), Slack handle.
Test log: Date, executor, environment, result, artifacts (links).
Change log: Date, author, summary of changes.
Related incidents: List of retrospective links.
---- END RUNBOOK TEMPLATE ----

Operational quality gates and acceptance criteria

- Runbook created within 7 business days for Sev2+ incidents (measured by PLAT-OPS ticket creation timestamp).
- At least one successful dry-run or automated test recorded before publication.
- Oncall MTTFA for matching incidents decreases by 20% within two quarters of runbook publication (if runbook addresses the dominant fault class).
- Quarterly verification pass rate >= 90% across published runbooks.

Metrics and KPIs to track (dashboard suggestions)

- runbook.coverage.percent: (Sev2+ incidents with runbooks / total Sev2+ incidents) * 100. Target: >= 95%.
- runbook.test.pass_rate: Ratio of verification runs passing to total verification attempts. Target: >= 90%.
- oncall.mttfa: Median time between pager trigger and first mitigation action by oncall. Target: reduce by 20% after runbook publication.
- runbook.age: Time since last verification. Alert when > 90 days.

Suggested dashboard widgets (Grafana)

- Single line: runbook.coverage.percent (30-day)
- Heatmap: runbook.age by service
- Bar: runbook.test.pass_rate by owner_team
- Table: Open PLAT-OPS runbook tickets with due dates and owners

Owner ship and lifecycle

- Creation: Incident Lead -> creates draft and JIRA ticket.
- Primary owner: Service Owner (responsible for content accuracy).
- Operational author: Platform Operator (maintains step-level accuracy and test logs).
- Reviewer: Documentation Reviewer (publishes and validates readability).
- Archivist: Oncall Manager (marks runbook stale/archived after two consecutive failed verifications or after service deprecation).

Oncall and tabletop agenda (30 minutes)

- 0–5m: Context and symptoms recap (Incident Lead)
- 5–10m: Walkthrough of the runbook mitigation steps (Operator Author)
- 10–20m: Simulated execution and decision points discussion (all attendees)
- 20–25m: Ownership, permissions, and automation gaps
- 25–30m: Action items, ticketing, and verification assignment

Change control, versioning and auditing

- Each published runbook page must include a Change Log table at the top with entries: date, author, change-summary, and a link to the PLAT-OPS ticket that triggered the change.
- Maintain a runbook:git-ref property with the SHA of any scripts or playbooks used during mitigation.
- Periodic audit: Oncall Manager will run an automated query for runbook.age > 90d and produce a weekly remediation queue.

Failure modes and special cases

- If a failure mode is only reproducible under high regional load, add explicit throttling thresholds and a step to coordinate cross-region traffic shaping.
- For incidents caused by model swaps or quantization regressions, include a tie-in to model-release notes and evasion criteria (link to eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding pages).

Appendix: Examples and snippets

- Example CLI snippet to add a Confluence skeleton (runbooks-as-code):

  git clone git@github.com:redwood/platform-ops.git
  cd platform-ops/runbook-templates
  ./create_runbook.sh --service routing-service --version v3 --slug prefix-cache-warmup

- Example verification query (PromQL):

  # Verify P99 latency under 120ms for the last 5m
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(routing_service_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) < 0.12

- Table: runbook lifecycle states (described):

  - draft: Created, not yet validated
  - published: Validated and approved
  - stale: Failed verification or pending update after a release
  - archived: Service decommissioned or runbook superseded

Related pages and links

- Platform operator handbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/platform-operator-handbook-degraded-kv-prefix-cache-2026
- Model onboarding guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding/standards
- PLAT-OPS JIRA project: PLAT-OPS (use component=runbook)
- PagerDuty escalation: PD-Platform-Primary
- Slack channel: #platform-ops

Appendix: Quick checklist for Incident Leads

- [ ] Tag retrospective "postmortem/runbook-required" when applicable
- [ ] Create PLAT-OPS ticket linking to retrospective and assign priority
- [ ] Ensure Operator Author is identified and booked for a tabletop
- [ ] Verify a dry-run is scheduled before publication
- [ ] Confirm owner and quarterly verification date are set

Revision history

- 2024-11-12 — Priya Raman — Initial draft and publication.
- 2025-05-03 — Alex Kim — Added PromQL example and clarified quarterly cadence.
- 2026-02-15 — Maya Patel — Expanded failure-mode guidance and added git-ref requirement.

payload.page_title: sli-cost-latency-ablation-retrospective-2026

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This retrospective documents the ablation study we ran across Q4 2025 and early Q1 2026 that intentionally removed or degraded telemetry signals used in the token-latency and cost SLI system to understand sensitivity, false-positive rates, and operator cognitive load. The goal was to produce concrete runbook changes, dashboard improvements, and rollout guidance to reduce SLI churn during regional blips and model-variant rollouts.

Background
----------
- Context: Several oncall incidents in Oct–Nov 2025 showed oscillating SLI alerts tied to noisy cost-signal spikes (billing anomalies) and intermittent token-latency reports stemming from partial KV cache failures. We wanted to quantify which signals were essential and which amplified noise.
- Hypothesis: Some telemetry variants (per-tenant token-cost per-minute, short-window p50/p95 token latency computed at the ingress proxy) amplify transient noise. Ablating secondary signals and relying on orthogonal indicators (GPU-queue length, model-variant error-rate, KV-hit ratio) will reduce alert fatigue without increasing time-to-detect real regressions.

Study design
------------
1. Scope and targets
   - Services: routing-proxy, inference-runtime, kv-prefix-cache, cost-aggregator
   - SLIs evaluated: token-latency (user-facing tail), token-cost (per-tenant cost rate), request-error-rate, model-variant-fallback-rate
2. Ablation matrix
   - Full signal set (baseline)
   - Remove short-window p50/p95 at ingress (30s windows)
   - Remove per-tenant minute-level cost derivative alert (keep hourly)
   - Replace synthetic-sla synthetic checks with synthetic-sla-lite (less frequent)
   - Silence KV-hit ratio-derived micro-alerts (promote to advisory)
3. Duration and rollout
   - Canary region: us-west-2 (2 weeks)
   - Staged rollouts: canary -> 3 regions -> global (each stage 72h observation)
   - Automated rollback if combined SRE detection score > 0.7 (see detection scoring below)

Timeline and data collected
-------------------------
- Nov 20–Dec 04, 2025: Baseline observability capture (pre-ablation)
- Dec 06–Dec 20, 2025: Canary ablation in us-west-2
- Jan 05–Jan 19, 2026: Regional expansion and stress-testing during model-variant rollout
- Jan 20–Feb 10, 2026: Post-rollout monitoring and manual incident injections
- Data sources: Prometheus (metrics), ClickHouse traces, billing-tables (hourly), incident tickets, oncall annotations

Key findings
------------
- Removing short-window ingress p95 reduced alert volume by ~43% without increasing median time-to-detect for verified incidents (median time-to-detect increased from 3.8m to 4.2m).
- Silencing minute-level per-tenant cost derivative alerts cut false positives from noisy metering by 78% but allowed two low-impact cost leaks to persist 6–12 hours longer; both were detected by hourly summaries and manual audits.
- Promoting KV-hit micro-alerts to advisory reduced operator context-switching; when KV-hit advisory crossed 5% degradation coincident with GPU-queue growth > 12, it reliably predicted tail-latency regressions within 18 minutes.
- Synthetic-sla-lite (less frequent synthetic checks) caught only 60% of degradation events that affected <5% of traffic; use synthetic-sla-lite only when paired with additional internal-sided health checks.

Root cause and analysis
-----------------------
- Many false-positives originated from noise in short aggregation windows at the proxy (burst traffic patterns, backoff storms). The ingestion pipeline's downsampling amplified micro-bursts into perceived p95 regressions.
- Billing-metering noise was caused by short-lived quantization in our cost-aggregator and delayed reconciliation between per-token meter and hourly summary tables.
- The observability deck lacked cross-signal correlation at alert time; operators had to manually stitch the timeline across cost, latency, and queue metrics.

Decisions made
--------------
- Keep tail-latency SLI (token-latency p99/p95) but remove 30s short-window p95 from primary alerting rules. Short-window p95 will appear on a "fast-sight" dashboard only.
- De-prioritize per-tenant minute-level cost derivative alerts: move to advisory channel and require corroborating signals (e.g., billing reconciliation anomaly OR persistent token-inflation for 2 consecutive windows) before paging.
- Add a combined-rule: page only when (tail-latency SLI breach AND (gpu-queue > 10 OR model-variant-fallback-rate > 0.5%)). This reduces noise while preserving detection power.

Runbook changes (short list)
--------------------------
- New play: "Cost-Derivative Advisory Investigation" (see steps below). Owner: Platform Observability (pager duty: platform-observability rota).
- Update: "Tail-Latency Pager" flow now includes immediate checklist to check KV-hit advisory and GPU-queue before escalation to runtime owners.
- Add guidance for oncall: use the "fast-sight" dashboard when investigating sub-5min blips; do not escalate immediately unless corroborating signals exist.

Cost-Derivative Advisory Investigation (new play)
--------------------------------------------------
1. Observe advisory channel for per-tenant cost spikes.
2. Check hourly summary table: `SELECT tenant_id, sum(tokens) as tokens_hour FROM billing.hourly WHERE ts >= now() - interval 2 hour GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY tokens_hour DESC LIMIT 10;`
3. Cross-check model-variant fallback rate and token-latency p99 for the same tenant and time window.
4. If both token-latency p99 and cost derivative are elevated for >2 windows, open an incident and follow standard cost-incident runbook.

Detection scoring and rollback guard
----------------------------------
- Each stage of rollout computed an SRE detection score (0–1) aggregated from: SLI-breach-rate (0.5), new incident count (0.2), manual operator escalation (0.2), noise ratio (false-alerts / total-alerts) penalty (0.1).
- If detection score > 0.7 within 72h, automatic rollback to previous alerting config triggered. We used this to protect regional rollout.

Dashboard and alerting changes (implementation plan)
---------------------------------------------------
- Dashboards
  - Create "fast-sight" dashboard (ingress-short-window-metrics, kv-hit-ratio, gpu-queue, model-variant-fallback) for first responders. Embed a small timeline correlator widget.
  - Add a cost-reconciliation panel showing hourly vs per-minute aggregates and a reconciliation delta heatmap.
  - Tag all relevant panels with "advisory" or "primary" to guide oncall focus.
- Alerts
  - Primary alerts updated in Prometheus rules: remove 30s p95-based alert rules; add combined-rule described above.
  - Advisory alerts routed to a different channel (platform-advisory) with a lighter notification policy (email + slack thread, no paging).

Operational impact and metrics
-----------------------------
- Alert volume (pager count) reduced 32% across platform owners during rollout windows.
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for genuine incidents remained stable (median 3.9m pre, 4.1m post).
- Operator-reported cognitive load (post-deployment survey, n=34) improved: 67% reported fewer unnecessary escalations; 12% reported slower initial detection on low-impact cost leaks.

Follow-up actions (owners and deadlines)
---------------------------------------
- Platform Observability: implement fast-sight dashboard (due 2026-03-15). Owner: Marcus Green.
- Runtime: add a lightweight internal health-check endpoint in inference-runtime to supplement synthetic-sla-lite by 2026-04-01. Owner: Daniela Park.
- Billing: add a reconciliation job that writes a "reconciliation_delta" metric hourly to Prometheus by 2026-03-31. Owner: Diego Alvarez.
- SRE: codify detection scoring and automated rollback in rollout tooling by 2026-03-10. Owner: Priya Nair.

Guidelines for future experiments
--------------------------------
- Always pair ablation of a signal with at least one orthogonal guardrail (queue length, error-rate, or reconciliation delta).
- Use a detection score with at least four independent components (SLI, incidents, operator escalation, noise penalty).
- Reserve "advisory" channel for signals that historically cause >60% false positives and are actionable only with corroboration.

Appendix: queries and snippets
-----------------------------
- Ingress short-window p95 query (Prometheus example):
```
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(proxy_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30s])) by (le, region))
```
- GPU-queue alert snippet (Prometheus rule example):
```
- alert: GPUQueueHigh
  expr: sum(queue_length) by (region) > 10
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "GPU queue length > 10 (region={{ $labels.region }})"
```
- Reconciliation delta SQL (ClickHouse example):
```
SELECT toHour(ts) as hour, tenant_id, sum(per_minute_tokens) as minute_tokens, sum(hourly_tokens) as hourly_tokens, (hourly_tokens - minute_tokens) as reconciliation_delta
FROM billing.per_minute JOIN billing.hourly USING (tenant_id, hour)
WHERE ts >= now() - interval 24 hour
GROUP BY hour, tenant_id
ORDER BY reconciliation_delta DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

Related artifacts and links
---------------------------
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026
- Dashboard template: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/token-cost-attribution-and-explainable-trace-playbook-2026
- SLI economics guidance: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/sli-economics-mapping-and-runtime-decision-guide-2026

Conclusion
----------
The ablation experiment validated that careful de-emphasis of short-window ingress and minute-level per-tenant cost signals materially reduces operator noise while preserving detection of genuine regressions when combined with orthogonal guardrails. The changes above balance reduced pager fatigue with a modest increase in time-to-detect low-impact cost leaks. We recommend the configuration changes be rolled out broadly after the planned runbook and dashboard work is completed.

payload.page_title: Postmortem-to-Automated-Playbook Conversion Retrospective

sections.body:
Overview

This retrospective summarizes the 6-month program to convert high-fidelity postmortems into automated, operator-facing runbooks ("playbooks"). The goal was to reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) for LLM inference incidents by replacing ad hoc operator procedures with deterministic, tested automation and decision artifacts.

Summary and outcome

- Program start: 2025-11-01 (pilot).
- Scope: 28 postmortems identified as repeatable incident classes across platform, runtime, and capacity layers.
- Outcome: 22 automated playbooks shipped to production, 4 operator-runbooks (manual steps retained), 2 deferred for further instrumentation.
- Measured impact (first 3 months): Median MTTM for converted incident classes dropped from 38 minutes to 11 minutes. Operator handoff error rate reduced by 63%.

Why we ran the program

- Repeated manual steps across incidents (cache rebuilds, warmset rehydration, tiered-fallback wiring) increased cognitive load and variability.
- The operator runbook library was fragmented: inconsistent format, missing predicates, and untested commands.
- We wanted automated guardrails that are reversible and safety-checked by operators.

What we converted (example incident classes)

1) Degraded KV-prefix cache (partial corruption)
2) Model variant fallback misfire (incompatible variant served)
3) Token surge leading to quota exhaustion and throttling fallback
4) Regional capacity imbalance causing latency SLO violations

Conversion approach (high level)

1. Triage and repeatability assessment
   - For each postmortem: identify repeatable decision points, operator commands, and safety preconditions.
   - Label incident clusters with severity, frequency, and SLO impact.
2. Playbook design (template-driven)
   - Convert narrative steps into a deterministic decision DAG with: preconditions, idempotent commands, verification checks, rollout windows, and rollback criteria.
3. Automation engineering
   - Implement operator CLI wrappers + orchestration jobs (Argo Workflows or internal operator CLI) and test harnesses that simulate degraded signals.
4. Safety & review
   - Multi-team review (SRE, runtime, product) and a staged rollout (canary → limited-operator group → org-wide).
5. Metrics & telemetry integration
   - Attach SLO burn rate, Stage acceptance criteria, and post-execution telemetry to each playbook run.

Playbook template (canonical fields)

- id: short unique id (e.g. playbook.kvcache.partial-corrupt.v1)
- title: human readable title
- owner: team + pager (e.g. eng-serving-runtime, #oncall)
- severity: Sev1 | Sev2 | Sev3
- detectors: list of telemetry predicates that trigger recommendation
- preconditions: safety checks that must be true before executing an automated step
- steps: numbered steps with explicit verification checks and expected signals
- rollback: explicit rollback actions and verification
- audit: required tags, change-id, and run-notes fields
- testcases: path to synthetic scenario and acceptance criteria

Example playbook excerpt (kv-prefix cache rehydrate)

- id: playbook.kvcache.rehydrate.v1
- title: 'KV prefix cache rehydrate — partial shard corruption'
- owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #runtime-oncall)
- severity: Sev2
- detectors:
  - metric: runtime.kv_cache.error_rate.prefix_shard > 0.8% for 3m
  - trace sig: broken-rcu in 5% of ops across two hosts
- preconditions:
  - >= 72h since last full-shard-reshuffle (safety window)
  - no ongoing maintenance windows in target region
- steps:
  1) Run 'operator kv inspect --prefix P --shard S' to confirm bad shard nodes.
  2) If shard nodes are still alive, schedule 'operator kv partial-copy --from NODE_X --to NODE_Y --prefix P --shard S' (dry-run flag first).
  3) Verify success with 'operator kv verify --prefix P --shard S' (expect <0.1% miss rate).
  4) If verification fails, run 'operator kv rollback-copy --id ID' and notify runtime pager.
- rollback:
  - full-shard-reshuffle with live eviction safeguard; see rollback playbook id 'playbook.kvcache.full-reshuffle.v1'
- testcases:
  - synthetic scenario path: ops/synthetic/kv-rehydrate-cases/partial-corrupt-2026
  - acceptance: verification step returns <0.1% miss rate in 95% of runs

Implementation patterns and lessons learned

- Start with small, autop-run-safe steps. The biggest wins were read-only and verification automation (inspect, verify) before any mutation.
- Idempotency is mandatory. All automated mutations must include an idempotency token and an operator-observable run id. Example CLI pattern: 'operator kv partial-copy --run-id {{timestamp}} --idempotency-token {{uuid}}'.
- Safety windows and cooldowns reduced accidental double-actions. We standardized a 15-minute minimum cooldown between successive mutation steps for the same resource.
- Feature flags for automation: Each automated playbook is behind a feature flag scoped to operator groups. Rollout used a three-stage progression: off → pilot (3 operators) → team-wide → org-wide.
- Testing: For each playbook we implemented a synthetic scenario that runs nightly in the platform lab. Playbooks must pass 5 deterministic synthetic runs before licensed automation is allowed.

Key metrics we tracked

| Metric | Baseline | Post-conversion | Target |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Median MTTM (converted classes) | 38m | 11m | <=10m |
| Operator error incidence (per 100 runs) | 9.4 | 3.5 | <=2.5 |
| Playbook execution success rate | 72% | 93% | >=95% |
| Time-to-rollout (pilot → org-wide) | N/A (manual) | 18 days | <=10 days |

Operational changes we introduced

- Runbook registry: added metadata fields into service-catalog and exposed via operator CLI 'operator playbook list --service runtime'.
- Runbook schema v1.2 enforced via CI: linting, testcases, and runbook acceptance hooks in PRs.
- Playbook audit trail: every automated run emits 'playbook.run' telemetry with run_id, operator_id, and step-level timestamps. These events feed the incident-analysis pipeline.

Failures and what didn't work

- Over-automation for low-confidence decisions: Two playbooks were reverted because their detectors lacked precision, causing unnecessary evictions. Lesson: prefer recommendation-first where detectors <95% precision.
- Tooling mismatch: Early Argo-based flows required flakier network dependencies; we migrated mutation steps to the internal operator service with a lightweight task queue.
- Documentation gaps: Some playbooks assumed undocumented operational knowledge (exact CLI flags). We required embedded command examples and a short 'cheat-sheet' per playbook.

Action items (owners and timeline)

1) Incident detectors refinement: data team to add new signals for model-variant compatibility (owner: Applied ML; due: 2026-08-01).
2) Runbook schema -> v1.3: add 'confidence' field to detectors (owner: eng-platform; due: 2026-07-30).
3) Operator CLI ergonomics: reduce noisy flags and add '--dry-run --run-id' standard (owner: eng-developer-experience; due: 2026-09-15).
4) Playbook testing expansion: schedule nightly synthetic runs across 50% of playbooks (owner: platform-lab; due: 2026-08-15).
5) Rollout playbook for playbooks: create a meta-playbook that automates canary rollout steps (owner: eng-sre; due: 2026-08-05).

Decision log (selected decisions)

- D1: Prefer 'recommendation-first' for detectors with precision < 95% — approved 2026-01-10.
- D2: All mutation steps must have idempotency and run-id — approved 2025-12-20.
- D3: Nightly synthetic acceptance required before org-wide automation — approved 2026-02-04.

Runbook rollout checklist (operator playbook adopters)

1. Review detector precision (>95%) OR mark as recommendation-only.
2. Confirm preconditions (safety windows, maintenance).
3. Verify testcases have passed 5/5 synthetic runs.
4. Enable feature flag for pilot group (3 operators).
5. Run 3 supervised live runs during low-traffic window.
6. If stable, move through team-wide and org-wide stages with telemetry review after each stage.

CLI and example automation snippet
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
operator playbook run --id playbook.kvcache.rehydrate.v1 --dry-run --run-id "rehydrate-2026-07-12T08:10Z"
operator playbook run --id playbook.kvcache.rehydrate.v1 --run-id "rehydrate-2026-07-12T08:10Z" --confirm

Example automation YAML (Argo-style for reference)

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  generateName: playbook-kv-rehydrate-
spec:
  entrypoint: rehydrate
  templates:
  - name: rehydrate
    steps:
    - - name: inspect
        template: inspect-task
    - - name: partial-copy
        template: partial-copy-task

(We migrated away from a heavy Argo footprint for mutation steps but keep this as a reference pattern.)

Appendix: templates and examples location

- Playbook templates repo: git+ssh://git.internal/redwood/platform/playbooks-templates (path: /templates/v1.2)
- Synthetic labs: ops-lab.redwood.internal/synthetic-playbooks/kvcache
- Acceptance dashboard: internal-grafana/d/Playbook-Acceptance/playbooks?orgId=1

Concluding notes

Converting postmortems into automated playbooks delivered measurable operational improvements and reduced cognitive load for our operators. The program highlighted the importance of detector quality, rigorous synthetic testing, and staged rollouts. The remaining work focuses on instrumentation, detector refinement, and broader operator ergonomics to ensure playbooks remain safe, reversible, and well-observed.
