payload.page_title: Runbook Publishing Pipeline — retrospective and remediation plan

sections.body:
Summary:

This retrospective analyzes the Runbook Publishing Pipeline (RPP) project (Q3–Q4 2025). The pipeline was introduced to make runbook creation, validation, and rollout faster and safer by automating linting, schema checks, ownership tracking and staged publication to the Confluence corpus. After six months of production use we observed improved publication velocity but also several regressions in discoverability and operator trust. This doc summarizes outcomes, root causes, measured impact, and an actionable remediation roadmap.

Background and scope:

- RPP goals: reduce friction for engineers to publish operable runbooks; ensure runbook syntactic/semantic consistency; wire ownership and alerting into runbook lifecycle.
- Scope for retrospective: pipeline components (CI validators, doc linter, meta-schema, staged review queue, automatic metadata tagging, and publish/rollback automation). Excludes runbook content quality (play-by-play procedures) except where pipeline changes affected it.

Key metrics (pre/post deploy):

- Median time from draft to published: 12d -> 4d (improvement).
- % of runbooks passing automated checks on first push: 42% -> 81% (improvement).
- Search click-through rate (CTRs) for runbooks: 8.1% -> 6.3% (regression).
- Average operator satisfaction score (internal survey): 4.1/5 -> 3.6/5 (regression).
- Incidents where runbook step mismatch contributed to longer MTTR: 5 (pre) -> 9 (post), across 6 months.

What went well:

1) Faster authoring and release loop:
   - Developers reported the linting + schema check feedback cycle cut iteration time in half.
   - Ownership metadata and reviewer assignment eliminated ambiguous ownership for 78% of new runbooks.

2) Increased safety for formatting and basic completeness:
   - The validator rejected runbooks that omitted required SLO/SLO-owner sections, reducing incomplete runbooks in the published corpus.

3) Reduced editorial variance:
   - Automatic tagging and templating brought greater consistency for headings, step numbering, and runbook metadata.

What didn't go well / observed regressions:

1) Discoverability and search regression:
   - Template-heavy pages and automated boilerplate increased keyword dilution. Operators reported difficulty finding the "right" runbook in incidents (search CTR down 22%).

2) Over-automation of procedural content:
   - The linter enforced structural constraints that encouraged authors to hide contextual guidance in attachments or external docs (breaking the single-source-of-truth pattern).

3) Staged publish queue latency and manual backlog:
   - The staged review queue (for automated approvals and canary publish) accumulated a backlog. Small teams without dedicated reviewers experienced delays; some team members circumvented the pipeline by publishing direct edits, creating partial duplication.

4) Operator trust erosion in runbook fidelity:
   - Several incidents cited stale or truncated steps that passed checks but omitted critical operator-side hints (timing, mitigation thresholds). The automated checks did not validate those implicit details.

Root cause analysis (top contributors):

- Rule-scope mismatch: validation rules focused on formal structure and metadata but not semantic completeness (e.g., explicit remediation thresholds, alternative paths).
- Template verbosity: autogenerated sections (eg. large boilerplate SLO blocks) pushed essential procedural text below the fold and reduced signal in search indexes.
- Reviewer coverage gap: ownership tagging improved assigned owners but did not ensure reviewer availability; teams lacked SLAs for review cycles.
- Feedback loop missing for operators: no lightweight mechanism for operators to flag minor but urgent corrections and have them prioritized in the pipeline.

Concrete examples (anonymized):

1) Cache shard reconstitution runbook: auto-template added an extensive SLO table, pushing the quick recovery checklist below the fold; during an incident the operator opened the page but missed the checklist and followed a slower path.

2) Regional model fallback runbook: linter accepted a runbook missing service-specific circuit-breaker values because the schema accepted a free-text field; incident required on-the-fly tuning and manual coordination.

Action items (owners, due dates, success criteria):

1) Introduce a semantic completeness check (Pilot) — owner: Priya Nair — due: 2026-03-15
   - Add a lightweight NLP-based heuristic that flags missing explicit remediation thresholds, rollback steps, and operator hints.
   - Success: reduce MTTR incidents attributable to semantic omissions by 60% in 3 months.

2) Revise templates to prioritize operator quick paths — owner: Diego Alvarez — due: 2026-02-28
   - Move the "Quick recovery checklist" and "Immediate actions (0-10 min)" to the top of the rendered page and set them as searchable anchors.
   - Success: improve runbook search CTR by 15% in the next 90 days.

3) Review SLA and reviewer on-call rota for staged queue — owner: Oncall Platform Leads (Ethan Brooks) — due: 2026-02-20
   - Define a 48-hour review SLA for small teams (<6) with fallback reviewers. Add metrics to dashboard that surface queue age.
   - Success: 95% of staged runbooks reviewed within SLA.

4) Lightweight "Quick Edit" emergency channel — owner: Maya Chen — due: 2026-03-05
   - Implement a CLI action that allows an operator to propose an inline critical correction flagged for expedited review with a one-click revert path.
   - Success: operators can push critical corrections with audit trail and revert; measured operator satisfaction rises 0.3 points in next survey.

5) Search index tuning for templated sections — owner: Search Infra (TBD) — due: 2026-03-01
   - Teach the search index to downweight boilerplate sections and upweight the first two headings and the recovery checklist anchor.
   - Success: search CTR returns to or exceeds baseline.

Proposed pipeline changes (high-level):

1) Validation layering model:
   - Fast syntactic checks (current linter) -> semantic heuristics (NLP flags) -> human review (staged queue).

2) Publish UX changes:
   - Rendered pages must surface condensed "Immediate actions" at top and expose a TTL for the last verified operator review.

3) Observability and dashboards:
   - Add dashboard tiles: staged-queue age, % runbooks with semantic flags, search CTR by anchor, recent critical quick edits, and runbook-linked incident count.

4) Runbook lifecycle SLA and audit policy:
   - Add policy: runbook must have active owner with review SLA (48 hrs default). Auto-escalate if owner unresponsive for 72 hrs.

Implementation timeline (90-day plan):

- Weeks 1–2: finalize rule updates and prototype semantic heuristic (small sample corpus).
- Weeks 3–6: build quick-edit workflow and top-of-page rendering change; parallel search index tuning.
- Weeks 7–10: run pilot with two platform teams; monitor dashboards and iterate.
- Weeks 11–12: roll out org-wide; publish updated authoring guidance and mandatory reviewer SLA.

Risks and mitigations:

- Risk: NLP semantic checks generate false positives creating reviewer noise.
  - Mitigation: apply conservative thresholds initially and expose "dismiss" reasons to improve model.
- Risk: Quick-edit path abused to bypass proper review.
  - Mitigation: require audit metadata, automatic revert button, and limit use to incidents with documented ticket references.

Follow-up and ownership matrix:

- Roadmap lead: Maya Chen (eng-platform) — owner for coordination and status reports.
- Engineering delivery: Priya Nair & Search Infra squads — implement validators and index changes.
- Oncall ops & policy: Ethan Brooks — steward reviewer rotas and SLA enforcement.
- Product/documentation: Diego Alvarez — update templates and authoring docs.

Appendix A — Quick reference: new publish flow (draft):

1) Author submits runbook draft to repo.
2) CI syntactic lint runs; failures returned to author immediately.
3) Semantic sanity heuristic runs; non-blocking flags are surfaced as QC comments.
4) Staged review queue: assigned reviewer has 48 hours to approve or comment.
5) On approve: pipeline publishes to Confluence with "last verified by" header and anchor for Quick Actions.

Appendix B — Example metadata table (new required fields):

| field | type | example | notes |
|-------|------|---------|-------|
| owner_email | string | platform-ops@redwood.ai | primary owner (required) |
| reviewer_rota | string | region-a-oncall | rota id for 48h SLA |
| quick_actions_anchor | string | quick-actions | anchor used by search (auto-generated) |
| semantic_flag_score | number | 0.27 | heuristic score (0-1); >0.6 escalates mandatory review |

Appendix C — Survey snapshot (operator feedback highlights):

- "Love the faster publishing but I miss the old page structure where the checklist was obvious."
- "Linter is great but it never tells you what to include for our service - that's still on subject matter experts."

Conclusion:

RPP delivered clear engineering wins for speed and structural consistency, but over-automation exposed gaps in semantic validation, discoverability, and reviewer coverage. The proposed remediation balances automation with operator-first presentation changes, lightweight semantic checks, and concrete SLA/ownership commitments. We will track the impact via the dashboards above and reconvene for a follow-up retrospective in 90 days.

Document history:

- 2026-01-15 Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-01-28 Revised with reviewer feedback (Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-02-10 Published after adding implementation owners and dates

payload.page_title: Operator Autoscaler Feedback Loop Retrospective

sections.body:
Summary
-------

This retrospective documents a series of incidents in Q4 2025 and early Q1 2026 where the operator-tier autoscaler introduced a feedback loop that caused repeated token-surge-induced scaling oscillations for several multitenant GPU pools. The oscillations increased p99 latencies, caused SLA burn, and generated significant operational toil. This doc explains timeline, root causes, mitigations performed, permanent fixes, monitoring changes, and a rollout checklist to avoid recurrence.

Impact and metrics
------------------

- Affected services: runtime-serving-llm, tenant-scheduler, operator-autoscaler
- Customer-visible impact window: 2025-11-03 03:12 UTC — 2026-01-18 21:40 UTC (intermittent spikes)
- Measured effects (example aggregate across 3 impacted GPU pools):
  - p95 request latency: +18% average during surge events
  - p99 request latency: +42% (worst week)
  - Token throughput variance: +/- 38% minute-to-minute
  - Autoscaler churn: average 4 scale actions/hour during bursts (desired <= 0.5/hr)
  - Operator on-call interrupts: 38 pages over 10 incidents

Timeline (high level)
--------------------

1. Nov 3 2025: First operator pages from regional oncall for pool-3 showing rapid scale-outs followed by immediate scale-ins.
2. Nov 4-10: Initial mitigations applied: increased stabilization window, raised min-replicas. Churn slowed but returned.
3. Dec 12: Canary rollout of autoscaler v1.5 introduced a heuristic that aggressively scales based on short-term token rate forecasts.
4. Dec 18–Jan 12: Multiple rolling oscillations coincident with tenant token surges (marketing-driven user spikes); autoscaler reacted too quickly, then evicted workloads, which triggered retries and more surges.
5. Jan 13: Emergency manual override to pin scale to safe capacity for impacted pools.
6. Jan 18: Root cause analysis complete, permanent mitigations scheduled.

Root causes
-----------

- Short-term forecasting heuristic in autoscaler v1.5 used a rolling 15s window and a naive extrapolation factor (x2) without dampening, making the control loop underdamped for bursty LLM workloads.
- Eviction policy triggered on scale-in when memory footprint briefly exceeded the target; evictions caused request retries which amplified token-rate transiently.
- Metrics used by the autoscaler (tokens/sec) were sampled at coarse Prometheus scrape intervals (15s) with aggregation that lost burst peak shape; combined with the heuristic this produced overconfidence in forecasted demand.
- Lack of a stabilization policy scoped to tenant categories (i.e., bursty marketing tenants vs stable API tenants).
- Insufficient alerting for oscillatory behavior (we alerted on scale actions but not on action-rate per time window or on upstream retries triggered by evictions).

Immediate mitigations applied
---------------------------

1. Reverted autoscaler to v1.4 on 2025-12-20 for all production pools to remove aggressive forecasting heuristic. (Owner: infra-autoscale team)
2. Applied a temporary global stabilization window: require 90s sustained change before scale-in; scale-out kept at 30s guard.
3. Pinned eviction policy to favor soft-eviction (throttling) for 72 hours after scale events.
4. Increased min-replicas for high-variability pools (pool-2, pool-3).
5. Added an ad-hoc dashboard and runbook for operators to observe: scale-action-rate, eviction-rate, retry-rate, tokens/sec 5s/30s.

Why the initial mitigation was insufficient
-----------------------------------------

- Reverts reduced immediate oscillation but did not give a durable design change: the underlying telemetry and policy mismatch remained.
- Existing dashboards surfaced per-action counts but did not visualize the control loop phase/lag, which made tuning blind.

Permanent remediation work (accepted design)
------------------------------------------

Design summary (approved Feb 2026): replace the naive short-window forecast with a multi-timescale controller and tenant-aware stabilization rules. High-level components:

- Multi-timescale demand estimator: compute tokens/sec at 5s, 30s, and 5min windows; use a conservative compose function: demand = max(smoothed(5s) * 1.15, smoothed(30s)*1.05, smoothed(5m)).
- Dampened control law: introduce PI-like term with capped derivative contribution to eliminate overshoot for short bursts.
- Tenant profiles: label tenants as BURSTY, STEADY, or LATENT in tenant-metadata service; different stabilization windows and min-replicas per profile.
- Eviction policy change: soft-eviction-first, prefer request-level shedding and token-throttling over immediate pod eviction; escalate to hard-eviction only if memory pressure persists > 60s after shedding.
- Observability: new control-loop health SLI and dashboard, plus synthetic canary workload to exercise the loop.

Ownership and timeline
----------------------

- Design owner: infra-autoscale team (lead: Diego Alvarez)
- Runtime changes: eng-serving-runtime (kernel) and infra-autoscale (controller) — coordinated rollout.
- Observability: eng-platform/dashboards (owner: Priya Nair)
- Tenant profiling and metadata service: product-platform (owner: Evan Brooks)

sections.body:
1) Mar 2026: Implement multi-timescale estimator behind feature flag; unit and integration tests.
2) Apr 2026: Deploy to staging and run 2-week synthetic canary; collect metrics.
3) May 2026: Gradual rollout to non-critical pools with A/B monitoring.
4) Jun 2026: Full rollout and deprecation of feature flag.

Dashboard and alerting changes (concrete)
---------------------------------------

New dashboards (owner: eng-platform/dashboards):
- Autoscaler-control-loop-overview: shows tokens/sec 5s/30s/5m, estimator output, desired_replicas, actual_replicas, derivative_term, and active_feature_flags.
- Oscillation-forensics: scale-action-rate (per-minute), eviction-rate, retry-rate, average backoff time, tenant-token-variance heatmap.
sections.heading: Planned rollout milestones

sections.body:
1. Alert: autoscaler_oscillation_rate_high
   - Expr: rate(autoscaler_scale_actions_total[5m]) > 2
   - For: 3m
   - Severity: page
   - Runbook: confirm whether evictions correlate with scale-ins; if yes, pin scale and notify infra-autoscale.
2. Alert: eviction_retry_amplification
   - Expr: increase(evictions_total[5m]) > 10 and rate(retries_total[5m]) > 50
   - For: 1m
   - Severity: page
   - Runbook: temporarily set soft-eviction-only and increase min-replicas; open incident if sustained.
3. Alert: control_loop_derivative_spike
   - Expr: autoscaler_derivative_term > 0.2 * autoscaler_baseline (unitless)
   - For: 1m
   - Severity: ticket
   - Runbook: investigate recent policy changes or tenant labeling mismatches.

Query examples (PromQL)
----------------------

- 5s vs 30s token rate:
  - tokens_5s = increase(tokens_total[5s]) / 5
  - tokens_30s = increase(tokens_total[30s]) / 30
- Oscillation rate: rate(autoscaler_scale_actions_total[5m])
- Eviction versus retry correlation: correlation_over_time(evictions_total, retries_total, 5m) (pseudo-query; implement with recording rules and join in Grafana).

Runbook snippet (operator steps on page)
---------------------------------------

1. Pager: receive page for autoscaler_oscillation_rate_high.
2. On-call: open Autoscaler-control-loop-overview dashboard.
3. Check scale-action-rate and eviction-rate graphs for the past 15 minutes.
4. If scale-ins were immediately followed by evictions and a retry spike, run:
   - kubectl annotate pool/<pool-id> autoscaler.scale=paused --overwrite
   - curl -X POST https://internal-api/ops/pools/<pool-id>/min-replicas -d '{"min": <safe-count>}'
5. Notify infra-autoscale and assign owner.
6. If manual pin applied, continue to monitor for 1 hour; if behavior stabilizes, migrate to scheduled remediation.

Checklist for future autoscaler rollouts
---------------------------------------

- Telemetry readiness: ensure tokens/sec recorded at 5s and 30s windows with dedicated recording rules.
- Canary readiness: synthetic canary capable of producing 1.5x mean load for 10s bursts.
- Control-loop simulation: local sims demonstrating damping across tenant profiles.
- Dashboard and alert coverage validated before feature flag flip.
- Rollout gating: success criteria defined (oscillation_rate < 0.3 actions/min and p99 latency within 5% of baseline).

Lessons learned
-------------

- LLM workloads are inherently bursty; control systems designed for web-traffic patterns (smooth, predictable) need re-evaluation.
- Observability should be designed around the control loop — not just per-metric. Visualizing estimator inputs, derivative terms, and action rates is critical.
- Tenant semantics matter: a one-size-fits-all stabilization window will fail.
- Small changes to forecasting heuristics can cascade when combined with eviction/retry behaviors.

Open action items (owner and due dates)
--------------------------------------

- Implement multi-timescale estimator and damped control law (owner: infra-autoscale — Diego Alvarez, due 2026-03-31).
- Add control-loop dashboards and recording rules (owner: eng-platform/dashboards — Priya Nair, due 2026-03-15).
- Add tenant profiling attributes and retroactive labeling for top 100 tenants (owner: product-platform — Evan Brooks, due 2026-04-15).
- Update operator runbooks with new CLI snippets and emergency pin procedure (owner: eng-platform/runbooks — Maya Chen, due 2026-03-10).
- Post-rollout gdoc checklist and handoff for SREs and Solutions Engineers (owner: eng-sre, due 2026-06-01).

Appendix: useful commands and test scripts
-----------------------------------------

- Pin autoscaler: kubectl annotate pool/<pool-id> autoscaler.scale=paused --overwrite
- Increase min replicas (internal API):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN' https://internal-api/ops/pools/<pool-id>/min-replicas -d '{"min": 4}'
- Synthetic canary runner (example):
  python tools/canary_runner.py --target https://staging-runtime.example --rps 50 --burst 10 --duration 900

Acknowledgements
----------------

Thanks to: infra-autoscale (Diego Alvarez), eng-platform dashboards (Priya Nair), eng-serving-runtime (Anika Patel), product-platform (Evan Brooks), and oncall volunteers who triaged pages during the outage windows.

Document history
----------------

- 2026-02-10: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-28: Added mitigation timeline and immediate mitigations.
- 2026-03-15: Finalized acceptance design and action items after cross-team review.

payload.page_title: Platform technical debt heatmap and remediation journey

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines a repeatable heatmap-based approach for identifying, prioritizing, and remediating platform technical debt across the Redwood Inference runtime, operator surfaces, and observability pipelines. It combines quantitative signals (SLO breaches, incident frequency, cost exposure) with qualitative risk (regulatory/customer impact, security) to produce a prioritized remediation backlog and a quarterly remediation journey with ownership and validation steps.

Scope:
- Applies to eng-platform owned systems and services: serving runtime helpers, telemetry and dashboards, allocators, tenant-slicing, and operator automation.
- Excludes product-level model code maintained by Research/Applied ML unless the debt materially impacts serving economics or SLOs.

Why this matters:
- Unremediated debt increases incident MTTR, raises unit cost, and reduces the velocity of safe rollouts (model variants, quantization).
- A targeted program reduces mean time to safe-deploy, stabilizes cost per token, and lowers SLO breach frequency for top 10 tenants.

Heatmap methodology (overview):
1) Signal collection (automated):
   - SLO breach history (90d): count and severity per component.
   - Incident tags: recovery_time_mins, customer_impact (binary), ticket_count.
   - Cost exposure: token/CPU/GPU cost delta attributable to the component (monthly).
   - Change velocity: number of safe-rollout rollbacks or incidents tied to recent deploys (30d).
2) Manual review: engineering leads add qualitative attributes: security_exposure, regulatory_exposure, and customer_visible.
3) Scoring: each candidate gets numeric scores 0-5 for the following axes: impact, likelihood of recurrence, cost_exposure, and remediation_complexity.
   - Impact = weighted average of customer_exposure (0-5) and SLO severity (0-5).
   - PriorityScore = (Impact * 0.45) + (Likelihood * 0.25) + (CostExposure * 0.20) - (RemediationComplexity * 0.10).
   - PriorityScore normalized to 0-5. Items with PriorityScore >= 3.5 are P1 remediation candidates.

Heatmap (text table):
Rows = Impact (High / Medium / Low), Columns = Likelihood (High / Medium / Low) 
Legend: H=High, M=Medium, L=Low; examples and current backlog items: 
| Impact \ Likelihood | High                              | Medium                            | Low                               |
|--------------------|------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| High               | H/H -> "prefix-cache-coherence" (P1, owner: infra-warmset) | H/M -> "tenant-eviction-simulator" (P1, owner: platform-slicer) | H/L -> "legacy-model-variant-fallback" (P2, owner: runtime) |
| Medium             | M/H -> "observability-telemetry-sampling" (P1, owner: telemetry) | M/M -> "operator-automation-race" (P2, owner: platform-ops) | M/L -> "deprecated-schema-cleanup" (P3, owner: storage) |
| Low                | L/H -> "edge-prefetch-tuning" (P2, owner: edge) | L/M -> "docs-and-oncall-playbooks" (P3, owner: eng-platform) | L/L -> "minor-ci-legacy-scripts" (P3, owner: infra) |

Prioritization rules (operationalized):
- Anything with PriorityScore >= 3.5 => tag as remediation:P1 and schedule in the next quarter roadmap sprint.
- PriorityScore 2.5-3.49 => remediation:P2 candidate to be batched with P1 items if owner bandwidth permits.
- PriorityScore < 2.5 => remediation:P3, eligible for deferred cleanup windows (maintenance weeks).
- Exceptions: any item with security_exposure >=4 must be escalated to SecOps immediately regardless of PriorityScore.

Owner matrix (described):
- Each remediation ticket must include the following fields in the issue tracker (Jira/Backstage): component, owner_team, primary_owner (GitHub handle), estimated_story_points, rollback_plan_reference, canary-tests (link), validation_prompt_set (if LLM-facing).
- Example mapping (text form):
  - Observability pipeline: owner_team=engineering/telemetry, primary_owner=@mayachen, SLA for fix=45 days for P1.
  - Runtime cache subsystem: owner_team=engineering/serving-runtime, primary_owner=@ravisingh, SLA=30 days for P1.
  - Platform operator scripts: owner_team=eng-platform, primary_owner=@cejorg, SLA=60 days for P1.

Remediation workflow (step-by-step):
1) Triage & tag (2 business days): add labels (remediation:P1/P2/P3, risk:security/regulatory/cost).
2) Scoping (3 business days): owner drafts technical design with: rollback plan, canary criteria, and automated validation checklist.
3) Implementation sprint(s): breaking into <=2-week work items; align with oncall-free windows for high-risk changes (see Runbook 7.2).
4) Canary + validation (minimum 48h active canary): run synthetic scenario suite that includes: tail-latency lab, token-cost regression test, and failure-injection of dependent caches.
5) Post-deploy verification (72h): SLOs monitored; flag auto-close only if no regressions and cost delta within forecast.
6) Incident retro (if any) and knowledge transfer: add final notes to the team-wiki and attach runbook snippets.

Validation artifacts (required for closure):
- Canary dashboard link and synthetic-sla run id.
- Diff of telemetry (pre/post) showing SLO trend lines for 30d window.
- Cost delta estimation and real usage confirmation.
- Updated runbook section and search tags.

Quarterly remediation journey (Q1–Q3 2026 example plan):
- Q1 2026 (Audit & Quick Wins):
  - Run full heatmap collection and dry-run scoring. Owners assigned and 6 P1 tickets created.
  - Quick-win sprint: reduce telemetry fanout in two consumers (expected 12% infra cost reduction).
  - Owner: telemetry team (primary: Maya Chen).
- Q2 2026 (High-impact remediations):
  - Execute runtime prefix-cache coherence refactor (owner: serving-runtime, primary: Ravi Singh). Expected outcomes: 30% lower tail-latency incidents for prefix-heavy workloads and 8% token-cost reduction for top 5 tenants.
  - Rework canary gating to include cost-based abort (owner: eng-platform).
- Q3 2026 (Platform hardening & automation):
  - Automate remediation ticket generation from the heatmap report for items with PriorityScore >= 3.8.
  - Deliver runbook templates and training (operator sandbox labs).

KPIs and success metrics (tracked monthly):
- Reduction in P1 tech-debt item count (target: -40% by end of Q3 2026).
- Mean incident MTTR attributable to platform debt (target: -25% by Q3).
- Cost per million tokens for top 10 tenants (target: -6% by Q3 after Q2 remediations).
- Percentage of remediations with canary validation artifacts (target: 100% for P1).

Risk & mitigations:
- Risk: Remediations cause regressions in downstream model behavior.
  - Mitigation: require model-facing validation prompt sets and shadow traffic run for 72h.
- Risk: Owner bandwidth and context switching.
  - Mitigation: dedicate a 30% remediation rotation for each owner team for the quarter (tracked in capacity planning).

Governance and review cadence:
- Monthly heatmap review (first Monday of every month): Product + Eng leads review new candidates and agree on escalations.
- Quarterly remediation retrospective: review successes, missed SLAs, and adjust scoring weights.
- Annual policy review: security_exposure thresholds and SLA targets to be updated by Security by Jan each year.

Runbook and tooling references (inline):
- Runbook: "operator-automation-rollout" (link placeholder) for change freeze windows.
- Dashboard templates: "heatmap-priority-dashboard" (Grafana) and "remediation-sprint-tracker" (Looker).
- Scripts: telemetry-heatmap-collector (repo: infra/telemetry/tools/heatmap-collector).

Action items (next 30 days):
1) Q1 heatmap collection run: telemetry to produce CSV export and scoring snapshot (owner: telemetry team, due: 2026-03-10).
2) Create Jira template with required closure artifacts (owner: eng-platform, due: 2026-03-20).
3) Schedule first cross-team heatmap review (calendar invite by Eleanor Park, due: 2026-03-05).

Appendix (scoring cheat-sheet):
- Impact weight breakdown: customer_exposure=0.6, slo_severity=0.4 (scale 0-5).
- Likelihood mapping: historical incidents in 90d -> {0:0, 1-2:2, 3-5:3.5, >5:5}.
- CostExposure: monthly cost delta normalized to team cost buckets (0-5).
- RemediationComplexity: engineer-days estimate mapped to 0-5 with 0 being trivial (<1 day) and 5 being >60 engineer-days.

Document owner and contact:
- Author: Eleanor Park (epark@redwood.com).
- Operational owner for program: Ravi Singh (ravi@redwood.com).

Change log:
- 2025-11-02: Created initial template and method (Eleanor Park).
- 2026-01-18: Added scoring weights and examples after pilot (Ravi Singh).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized Q1 action items and added closure artifact checklist (Eleanor Park).

References and related templates:
- heatmap-collector README (repo link placeholder).
- remediation-jira-template (backstage ticket id placeholder).

If you are an owner preparing a remediation ticket, use the checklist above and attach the canary dashboard and synthetic run id to the ticket before requesting scheduling with platform-ops.

payload.page_title: Regional On-call Rotation Simplification — Retrospective

sections.body:
Summary:

Background: In H2 2025 the platform team expanded regional coverage to three additional cloud regions (eu-west-3, ap-southeast-2, and us-west-3). The on-call rotation grew organically: separate regional rotations, multiple overlap windows, and bespoke escalation rules for legacy services. By late 2025 we observed higher page fatigue, increased cross-region handoffs, and slower mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for multi-region incidents.

This retrospective reviews the simplification project (Project ROTA-SIMP) that ran from 2025-11-02 to 2026-01-28 with the goal to reduce operational cognitive load while preserving SLOs and regional ownership.

Scope and goals:
- Reduce the number of distinct rotations covering core platform services from 6 to 3.
- Reduce cross-region handoffs during incidents by 50% within 2 months of rollout.
- Maintain or improve 99th percentile page-to-acknowledge (P2A) latency.
- Document and publish updated runbooks and dashboard views.

Timeline and milestones:
1. 2025-11-02: Project kickoff; stakeholders: Eng-Platform, Eng-SRE, Eng-Infra, Product.
2. 2025-11-16: Audit of existing rotations and escalation graphs completed.
3. 2025-12-01: Prototype unified regional rotation design approved by oncall leads.
4. 2025-12-15: Small internal pilot with us-central and eu-west on core infra services.
5. 2026-01-05: Gradual rollout to remaining teams and regions.
6. 2026-01-28: Formal project close and start of monitoring phase.

Data and key metrics (pre vs post, baseline window: 2025-09-01 — 2025-11-01; post window: 2026-01-01 — 2026-02-15):
- Number of distinct rotations covering core services: 6 -> 3
- Average page-to-acknowledge (median): 2.4 min -> 2.1 min
- 99th percentile page-to-acknowledge: 18.2 min -> 12.7 min
- Cross-region handoff rate (incidents requiring >1 region team): 34% -> 14%
- Paging noise (pages per oncaller per week): 18 -> 13

Root causes identified:
- Over-specialization: Many rotations were scoped to single-region operational tasks; as services became globally routed, incidents crossed boundaries and required multiple teams.
- Divergent escalation trees: Small, ad-hoc differences in escalation (who to call at 15 vs 20 minutes) created inconsistent behavior.
- Tooling configuration sprawl: Pager and roster configurations lived in multiple spreadsheets and two different PagerDuty teams.
- Insufficient runbook normalization: Runbooks used different naming conventions and inconsistent troubleshooting steps, increasing cognitive load during high-pressure incidents.

What worked well:
- Cross-team working group: Weekly cross-functional syncs (Platform, SRE, Infra) accelerated decisions and surfaced edge cases early.
- Pilot-first rollout: A conservative pilot reduced blast radius and produced real production data.
- Observability changes paired with rota changes: Updating SLO dashboards and adding region labels to alerts made responsibilities clearer.

What didn't work / surprises:
- Short-term increase in duplicate notification noise during reconfiguration windows due to overlapping schedules in PagerDuty. Mitigation required three emergency rollbacks and a follow-up cleanup job.
- Underestimated training time: New oncall run-throughs and handover docs took two additional weeks of SMEs' time.
- A handful of legacy services required custom escalation rules which complicated consolidation.

Decisions made:
- Consolidation model: Adopt a hybrid regional-owner model — three rotations (Americas, EMEA, APAC). Each rotation owns initial triage for services routed to that region; for cross-region stateful failures the owning region coordinates fixes with a designated global follow-up (Global-Fix rotation).
- Standard escalation windows: 0/5/15/30/60 minutes for first/second/tech-lead/engineering-manager/exec escalation respectively for critical SLO breaches.
- Centralized roster storage: Single source of truth in the platform team repo: infra/oncall/roster.yml with automated PagerDuty sync.
- Runbook normalization: All core runbooks must conform to the runbook template (section table below) and include explicit 'handoff' steps.

Runbook template (mandatory fields):
- Service name
- Region labels (Americas/EMEA/APAC/global)
- Owner (primary, secondary)
- Symptoms and first checks (bullet list)
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered)
- Escalation path with contact links and time windows
- Post-incident checklist and RCA pointer

Operational changes to deploy (action items):
- A1: Implement roster.yml and PagerDuty sync automation (owner: Infra-Automation, due 2026-02-15).
- A2: Migrate 42 runbooks to normalized template; prioritize core services (owner: Platform-Docs, due 2026-03-01).
- A3: Update SLO dashboards: add rotation-aware widgets and handoff metrics (owner: Observability, due 2026-02-10).
- A4: Add a dedicated 'Global-Fix' weekly rotation (owner: Eng-SRE, due 2026-02-01).
- A5: Run four 60-minute playbook drills (regional and cross-region scenarios) across Q1 2026 (owner: Eng-Platform, due 2026-04-30).

Risk assessment and mitigations:
- Risk: Single roster source is a single point of configuration failure.
  - Mitigation: GitOps workflow with required PR approvals from two distinct oncall leads and automated unit tests for roster sanity (e.g., coverage by role, no overlapping primary slots).
- Risk: New rotation boundaries might reduce local oncall domain knowledge in small regional teams.
  - Mitigation: Pairing windows and weekly 'regional clinic' office hours during the first 8 weeks after rollout.

Dashboard and alert changes (examples):
- New dashboard panels: 'Active incident by rotation', 'Handoff count (last 24h)', 'Pages per oncaller (7d rolling)'.
- Alert label changes: add label rotation=americas|emea|apac. Use this label in the Alertmanager routing tree to control deduplication and notification channels.
- SLO watchlist: For the first 60 days after rollout, add SLOs for page-to-acknowledge 99th percentile to the daily ops digest.

Communication and rollout plan summary:
- Week 0 (pre-rollout): Publish runbook guidelines and hold two 1-hour training sessions.
- Week 1 (pilot): Enable merged rotations in PagerDuty for two non-critical services. Monitor for 7 days.
- Week 2–3: Iterate on config and runbooks based on pilot findings.
- Week 4 (full rollout): Switch remaining eligible services during low-traffic window and trigger verification playbooks.
- Week 5–12: Monitoring phase and weekly status updates to platform leadership.

Follow-ups and measurement plan:
- Weekly post-rollout review for first 8 weeks focusing on: handoff rate, paging noise, MTTA percentiles, pager overlap incidents.
- After 8 weeks produce an outcome memo with updated metrics and recommended further changes.

Owners and stakeholders:
- Project lead: Asha Patel (Eng-Platform)
- Infra-Automation: Ethan Morales
- Observability: Sofia Chen
- Eng-SRE liaison: Priya Nair
- Platform docs: Liam O'Connor
- Product stakeholder: Maya Rodriguez

Participants in retrospective workshop:
- 14 total: representatives from Platform (6), SRE (3), Infra (2), Product (2), Support (1).

Appendix — sample roster.yml schema (example snippet):

# roster.yml (example)
# Note: actual file is in infra/oncall/roster.yml in the platform repo
- rotation: americas-core
  primary: ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"]
  secondary: ["carol@example.com"]
  regions: ["us-central", "us-west"]

- rotation: emea-core
  primary: ["dan@example.com"]
  secondary: ["eve@example.com"]
  regions: ["eu-west-3", "eu-central-1"]

(Operational team: Do not edit roster.yml directly in PagerDuty. All changes must be PR -> CI -> PD-sync.)

Lessons learned (top three):
1. Simplify first, automate second: consolidations without automated, testable configuration caused the largest operational headaches.
2. Pilot in production at small scale is invaluable — it uncovered unexpected notification duplication caused by historic PD integrations.
3. Documentation and runbook normalization are as important as technical changes; consistent language reduced cognitive load during incidents.

Open questions / parking lot:
- Should the Global-Fix rotation be staffed by a smaller, dedicated cross-functional team or a larger on-call pool? (Decision required by 2026-03-15).
- How should we handle customer-facing incident comms when multiple regions are involved? Propose a templated comms flow tied to rotation ownership.

Tags and archival notes:
- Retrospective created as part of continuous reliability improvements; archive after 18 months unless requirements change.

If you have updates to the action items or metrics, add a comment on this page and tag the owner.

payload.page_title: Multi‑Horizon Warmup and Capacity Orchestration Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes a repeatable, operational pattern we call 'multi-horizon warmup' for Redwood's inference platform. It covers goals, telemetry and dashboard panels to create, automated and manual orchestration steps, SLOs and alerting thresholds, rollback criteria, and a short roadmap for improving warmup fidelity. Use this when launching new tenants, onboarding models or rolling out regionwide capacity changes.

Why multi-horizon warmup?

- Inference workloads have distinct 'horizons' where different preparatory actions reduce tail latency or token cost:
  - Seconds-to-minutes: connection pools, kernel JIT, process hot paths.
  - Minutes-to-hours: KV cache warm (prefixes), batching affinity, model shard residency.
  - Hours-to-days: thermal/availability stabilization, learned cache cohorts for tenants, offline optimizer replays.
- Treating warmup as a single step causes either over-provisioning (cost) or under-preparedness (latency/regressions). Multi-horizon warmup stages let us apply different controls and measurement hooks at each timescale.

Scope and applicability

- Applies to: hosted and dedicated pools, regional capacity expansions, tenant onboarding (>1000 monthly tokens), large model swaps, prefetch cohort rollouts.
- Not intended for: trivial config-only deploys (<5% expected traffic), or single-VM testbeds.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner_team: eng-platform (capacity and operator automation).
- Secondary owners: eng-serving-runtime (kernel/JIT), eng-sre (SLO monitoring), customer-success (tenant verification).
- On-call escalation chain: platform-oncall -> runtime-engineering -> eng-sre (see runbook links).

Goals and acceptance criteria

1) Within the short-horizon window (0–10 minutes after activation):
   - 95th token latency for cold-primed requests must be <= 1.5x steady-state 95p baseline.
   - Connection pool utilisation > 60% for tenant traffic.
2) Within the medium-horizon window (10 minutes–4 hours):
   - KV cache hit rate for pinned prefixes >= 85% (for workloads that expose prefixes).
   - Batch formation latency <= 50ms for batchable routes.
3) Within the long-horizon window (4 hours–72 hours):
   - Sustained throughput reaches expected capacity curve within 24 hours with no >5% tail-latency regressions.

Instrumentation and dashboard panels (minimum required)

Create a dashboard named: "Warmup: <cluster/tenant/model> — Multi‑Horizon View" with these panels:

- Live token latency heatmap (per-region, per-model).
- Connection pool state (idle/active/queued).
- KV cache hit-rate (prefix-level if available).
- Batch size distribution and batch latency percentiles.
- Warmup progress KPI: staged completion (short/medium/long).
- Cost delta estimator: predicted vs measured token cost during warmup.

Suggested alert rules (examples)

1) Short-horizon alert: "warmup-short-latency-regression"
   - Trigger when 95p token latency > 1.8x baseline for > 3 minutes AND connection pool utilisation < 40%.
   - Priority: P2; Notify: platform-oncall.
2) Medium-horizon alert: "warmup-cache-not-warming"
   - Trigger when KV cache hit rate < 50% after 30 minutes for known-prefix workloads.
   - Priority: P3; Notify: owner_team + customer-success if affected tenant.
3) Long-horizon alert: "warmup-sla-slope-miss"
   - Trigger when steady-state throughput plateau after 24 hours is < 90% of expected commit for > 2 hours.
   - Priority: P1; page eng-sre and runtime-engineering.

Operator workflows (playbook)

Pre-step: create the warmup ticket in the platform tracker with: target cluster, tenant(s), model(s), horizon timelines, expected traffic profile and rollback trigger thresholds. Attach a baseline snapshot.

Short-horizon (0–10 minutes) — automated first pass
1) Activate routing with gradual ramp flag (weight=0.1 -> 1.0 over 10 minutes) using the routing API:

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/routing/gradual -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLATFORM_TOKEN" -d '{"target": "cluster-nyc-1", "traffic_weight": 0.1, "ramp_minutes": 10, "validation": "latency"}'

2) Trigger kernel/JIT prime job if model variant supports it:
   - /srv/tools/runtime-prime --model model-id --p90-seqs 4
3) Verify connection pool and worker spin-up panels; if pools not healthy after 6 minutes, escalate to runtime-engineering.

Medium-horizon (10 minutes–4 hours) — prefetch and affinity
1) Start prefix prefetch jobs for top N prefixes derived from tenant's historical promptsets (N default 50). Example config:

{
  "job": "prefix-prefetch",
  "tenant": "acme-corp",
  "target_prefixes": ["home_page_summary_v1", "search_prompt_v2"],
  "concurrency": 8,
  "rate_limit": "200r/s"
}

2) Monitor KV cache hit-rate; if below target, increase concurrency by +2 and re-evaluate after 20 minutes.
3) Enable batch affinity (sticky-binning heuristics) with conservative thresholds: prefer max_latency 30ms and min_batch_size 8.

Long-horizon (4 hours–72 hours) — cohort and thermal stabilization
1) Run cohort-learning job to create tenant warmset fingerprints for automated future onboarding. Persist as a "warmset-vX" artifact.
2) For dedicated pools, check GPU thermal telemetry and pre-warm NVMe-backed model shards to reduce I/O stalls.
3) Validate cost delta estimator; ensure unit cost for warmup period remains within 15% of normal unit economics unless approved.

Rollback and safety gates

- Immediate rollback triggers (perform automatic rollback and page on-call):
  - P95 tail latency > 3x baseline for > 5 minutes.
  - Error rate increase > 500 rps above baseline or > 2% absolute increase.
- Manual rollback triggers (operator decision):
  - KV cache not improving after two scaled prefetch attempts.
  - Cost delta estimator projecting > 30% incremental spend vs projected.

Operator checklists (condensed)

- Pre-rollout checklist:
  1) Attach baseline snapshot and expected traffic profile.
  2) Confirm prefetch job seed prefixes are sourced and validated.
  3) Schedule communications with affected on-call windows.
- During rollout checklist:
  1) Watch short-horizon panels; confirm kernel prime succeeded.
  2) Confirm batch formation and pool utilisation targets.
  3) Track cost delta and update ticket notes every hour.
- Post-rollout checklist:
  1) Confirm warmset artifact created and stored.
  2) Run a short regression: compare sample prompts vs pre-rollout answers for quality drift.
  3) Close warmup ticket and annotate lessons-learned.

Concrete runbook commands and snippets

- View warmup dashboard (Grafana):
  - Open: https://grafana.internal.redwood/warmup-dashboard?cluster=cluster-nyc-1&tenant=acme-corp
- Trigger a targeted rollback via CLI:
  - redwoodctl routing rollback --ticket 12345 --reason "latency spike"
- Sample prefetch orchestration (Kubernetes CronJob snippet):
  apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: prefix-prefetch-acme
  spec:
    schedule: "*/15 * * * *"
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
            - name: prefetch
              image: redwood/prefetch:stable
              args: ["--tenant", "acme-corp", "--concurrency", "8"]
            restartPolicy: OnFailure

Telemetry queries (examples)

- KV cache hit-rate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{cluster="cluster-nyc-1", tenant="acme-corp"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{cluster="cluster-nyc-1", tenant="acme-corp"}[5m]))
- Batch latency p95 (PromQL):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(batch_latency_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate",cluster="cluster-nyc-1"}[5m])) by (le))

Postmortem and retrospective guidance (how to capture learning)

- Template to capture: timeline of actions (with exact timestamps), top 3 metrics that failed/succeeded, operator decisions, and suggested configuration deltas.
- Run a 2-week rolling retrospective after first 50 warmups to tune heuristics and thresholds. Capture retrospective in the platform retrospective board and tag with label "warmup-learning".

Roadmap (next 12 months)

- Q2 2026: automated warmset synthesis — automatically derive top prefixes from anonymized prompt telemetry and auto-seed prefetch jobs.
- Q3 2026: warmup cost forecasting model — attach confidence bands and estimated spend.
- Q4 2026: warmup-as-a-service API — tenant self-service warmups with opt-in safety gates.

Appendices

A) Minimal SLO/threshold table

| Horizon | Key metric | Acceptance threshold | Escalation window | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Short | p95 token latency | <= 1.5x baseline | 10m | platform-oncall |
| Medium | KV cache hit-rate | >= 85% | 2h | runtime-engineering |
| Long | Throughput curve | >= 90% expected | 24h | eng-platform |

B) Example ticket template fields

- ticket_id, cluster, tenant, model, expected_traffic_profile (CSV), warmup_horizons (short/medium/long), rollback_triggers, dashboards_link, owners, communication_plan, estimated_cost_budget.

C) Links and references

- Runtime prime tool: /internal/tools/runtime-prime
- Prefetch service spec: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/prefetch-spec-2025

If you are executing a warmup for an enterprise customer, attach the customer-approved spend budget and notify Customer Success before starting medium-horizon prefetches. payload.page_title: OPA policy examples for tenant quota and eviction

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This document provides concrete Open Policy Agent (OPA/Rego) policy examples for encoding tenant quota enforcement and staged eviction decisions inside Redwood's runtime control plane. The intent is to provide safe, testable, auditable policy snippets that operators and platform engineers can adapt to: token quotas, cost budget windows, SLO-driven soft-eviction, and emergency hard-eviction.

Why OPA here?
- OPA enables a declarative, versionable policy surface separate from runtime code.
- Policies can be unit-tested, linted, and evaluated in CI before being deployed to the policy decision point (PDP).
- Clear policy semantics reduce operator cognitive load during incidents and make rollback trivial.

When to use these examples
- Enforcing per-tenant token or request quotas (daily/hourly windows).
- Implementing eviction heuristics when capacity pressure or SLO risk exceeds thresholds.
- Configuring short-circuit operator overrides (emergency pause, global protect).

High-level design constraints
1) Safety-first: default effect must be "allow" for non-critical paths; for eviction decisions default to "no-evict" unless explicit conditions are met.
2) Idempotence: policies must evaluate deterministically given the same input.
3) Auditability: every decision must include evidence fields (reason, metric snapshot, rule id).
4) Performance: policy evaluation should be O(1) per decision or cached for short time windows.

Input schema (expected by PDP)
- input.tenant_id: string
- input.window: {"start": string (RFC3339), "end": string (RFC3339)}
- input.metrics: {"tokens_used": number, "requests": number, "slo_violations_1h": number, "cost_usd_24h": number, "queue_time_ms": number}
- input.config: {"quota_tokens": number, "quota_requests": number, "cost_budget_usd": number, "slo_violation_threshold": number}
- input.runtime: {"capacity_pressure": "low"|"moderate"|"high", "region": string}
- input.operator_override: {"action": "none"|"evict"|"protect", "reason": string, "expires_at": RFC3339}

Policy example 1 — soft quota enforcement (hourly tokens)
- Objective: mark tenants as "throttable" when they exceed 90% of hourly token quota.
- Action: return decision {allow: boolean, mode: "normal"|"throttle", evidence: {rule: string, tokens_used: number, quota: number}}

Rego snippet (copy/paste)
```
package redwood.tenant.quota

default decision = {"allow": true, "mode": "normal", "evidence": {"rule": "none"}}
sections.heading: Overview
Condition: tokens exceed 90% of configured hourly quota

sections.body:
- Throttling versus outright eviction: this snippet triggers a throttle mode; downstream controllers should map throttle -> token rate-limit or 429 behavior.
- Tune the threshold (0.9) per tenant-class; consider using input.config.per_tier_thresholds for fine-grained control.

Policy example 2 — cost-budget-driven graceful eviction
- Objective: initiate a staged eviction plan if a tenant exceeds cost budget and region capacity is under high pressure.
- Action: return decision {evict: boolean, stage: "warn"|"soft_eviction"|"hard_eviction", evidence: {...}}

Rego snippet (copy/paste)
```
package redwood.tenant.eviction

default decision = {"evict": false, "stage": "none", "evidence": {"rule": "none"}}
sections.heading: Notes
Helper: cost over budget
Rule: soft eviction (warn) if cost over budget and moderate pressure
Rule: soft eviction if cost over budget and high pressure or SLO violations rising
Rule: hard eviction if cost massively exceeds budget (e.g., > 200%) and region is at critical pressure

sections.body:
- Stages map to operator actions in the orchestration layer:
  - warn: send billing notice + reduce burst credits
  - soft_eviction: reduce priority, evict from best-effort pools to reserved or blocked queues
  - hard_eviction: terminate or suspend non-essential sessions and refuse new requests
- Ensure billing team is notified on "warn" decisions.

Policy example 3 — SLO-driven preemptive protection (protect tenants with paid SLA)
- Objective: protect tenants with enterprise SLA from being evicted unless operator_override is explicit.

Rego snippet (copy/paste)
```
package redwood.tenant.protection

default decision = {"protected": false, "reason": "none"}
sections.heading: Notes
Protect if tenant has enterprise_sla flag attached in config

sections.body:
decision = {"protected": false, "reason": "operator_forced"} {
  input.operator_override.action == "evict"
  time.now_ns() < time.parse_rfc3339_ns(input.operator_override.expires_at)
}
```

Testing and CI patterns
- Unit tests: write rego tests alongside policy file and run `opa test ./` in CI. Example test case names should cover boundary conditions (e.g., 89%, 90%, 91% of quota).
- Fuzz inputs: run a small fuzzer for metrics ranges to catch non-determinism.
- Linting: run `opa fmt` and `opa check` as part of pre-commit.
- Data-driven policy variation: use input.config.per_tier_thresholds to avoid hardcoding numeric thresholds.

Operational rollout checklist
1) Stage policy in the policy staging PDP with read-only mode for 24 hours (evaluate decisions but do not enforce).
2) Compare decisions vs actual runtime actions using a decision-sampling pipeline (capture decisions into telemetry).
3) Gradually enable enforcement for a small percentage (5%) of tenants using a rollout flag.
4) Expand by doubling percentage every 6 hours while monitoring SLOs and cost signals.
5) After 72 hours without regressions, promote to stable.

Rollout metrics to monitor (minimum)
- decision_mismatch_rate: fraction of sampled decisions that would have differed from previous rule baseline (>1% triggers pause).
- evictions_per_hour: baseline must be stable; >3x baseline triggers immediate rollback.
- downstream_429_rate_by_tenant: spikes indicate throttle mapping regressions.
- billing_alerts_sent: ensure notify pipeline fires for warn-stage decisions.

Dashboard and alerting guidance
- Create a dashboard with: capacity_pressure_by_region, top-20 tenants by cost_usd_24h, evictions_by_stage, decision_mismatch_rate, and operator_override_activity.
- Alerts:
  - decision_mismatch_rate > 1% for 30m => P2 to eng-platform
  - evictions_per_hour increases >3x baseline for 15m => P1 oncall page
  - operator_override with action=evict without expires_at => compliance alert (security team)

Operator runbook (short)
1) When an alert fires (evictions spike or mismatch): collect last 30m of decisions and metric snapshots.
2) If evictions are accidental, flip enforcement flag to "read-only" and scale down enforcement percentage to 0% immediately.
3) Notify affected tenants via preconfigured messaging channels; enable billing hold if necessary.
4) Re-run policy tests locally with captured input examples to reproduce the trigger.
5) Roll back policy commit and open a post-incident ticket including decision evidence.

Compliance & audit notes
- All policy changes must be committed to the policy repo and require two reviewers for production promotion.
- Decision sampling logs must be stored for 90 days to support billing and compliance disputes.
- Operator overrides are immutable records: require operator id, reason, and expires_at; store in audit log.

Examples of CLI commands and tests
- Evaluate a single decision locally:
  opa eval -i input.json -d tenant_quota.rego "data.redwood.tenant.quota.decision" --format pretty
- Run unit tests in repo:
  opa test ./policies -v
- Format and lint:
  opa fmt ./policies && opa check ./policies

Migration notes (from legacy heuristics)
- Legacy eviction code used heuristic thresholds embedded in runtime (hardcode). Migration steps: 1) port heuristic to rego with equivalent semantics, 2) run staging for 48 hours, 3) compare outputs, 4) flip enforcement.
- Where a historical exception list exists, import it into a policy data file (data/legacy_exceptions.json) and reference via input.data.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-platform (policy-pdp team).
- Pager: eng-platform oncall rotation.
- Policy review cadence: quarterly or upon major pricing/model changes.

Related artefacts and next steps
- Add a scheduled synthetic job that generates representative tenant inputs nightly and asserts no-rule regressions.
- Integrate the decision-sampling telemetry with the billing pipeline to validate financial impact.

Appendix: sample input.json for local testing
{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
  "window": {"start": "2026-02-14T10:00:00Z", "end": "2026-02-14T11:00:00Z"},
  "metrics": {"tokens_used": 910000, "requests": 12000, "slo_violations_1h": 2, "cost_usd_24h": 450.25, "queue_time_ms": 15},
  "config": {"quota_tokens": 1000000, "quota_requests": 20000, "cost_budget_usd": 200, "slo_violation_threshold": 5, "enterprise_sla": false},
  "runtime": {"capacity_pressure": "high", "region": "us-west-2"},
  "operator_override": {"action": "none", "reason": "", "expires_at": ""}
}

Document history
- 2025-11-12: Created by Priya Nair (initial draft).
- 2026-01-18: Added cost-driven eviction stages and operator override guidance (reviewers: Evan Chen).
- 2026-02-15: Finalized rollout checklist, dashboards and alerts; promoted to published.

END OF DOCUMENT

payload.page_title: Operator Script DSL and CLI Runtime: design & roadmap

sections.body:
Summary
This document specifies the design, safety constraints, telemetry contract, and a two-quarter roadmap for a small, opinionated Operator Script DSL and accompanying CLI runtime. The goal is to enable platform operators and SREs to author compact, auditable, and executable operational playbooks (runbooks) that can be validated, simulated, and executed against the platform with minimal risk.

Context and motivation
- Current pain: engineers author free-form runbooks (markdown + ad-hoc scripts). Operators copy/paste and run commands manually; this is error-prone, hard to test, and hard to attribute.
- Desired: a constrained, declarative script model for common operator actions (drain, rebalance, prefetch cohort, model swap, promote-canary, manual-evict, snapshot) plus a CLI that validates, simulates, and executes with RBAC, dry-run, and observability hooks.
- Non-goal: replace full orchestration systems (k8s operators) or business logic embedded in services. This is for human-operated, low-latency corrective actions and routine maintenance.

Principles
1. Safety-first: all scripts are validated against a safety policy before execution. Defaults are pessimistic (fail closed).
2. Idempotency: operations should be re-runnable where possible; DSL encourages idempotent primitives.
3. Auditable: every execution is logged, versioned, and tied to a ticket/incident and an operator identity.
4. Testable & simulatable: a local "simulator" mode mirrors platform state for offline testing.
5. Minimal surface area: DSL primitives are intentionally small and vetted. Extend via approved extension points only.

DSL overview (human-friendly description)
- Format: YAML-first, 1–2 screens per script.
- Top-level fields: metadata, preconditions, steps, postchecks, rollbacks, telemetry.
- Primitives (examples):
  - api_call: call an internal platform API with typed input and explicit timeout
  - shell_safe: run a restricted shell command in a sandboxed operator container
  - schedule_prefetch: request prefetch cohort for model X with cohort_id
  - model_swap: swap runtime model variant on a host/pool with validation window
  - drain_node / undrain_node: soft drain with annotated reason and ETA
  - wait_for_sli: await an SLI condition using timeframe and threshold
  - notify: send structured notification to ops channels (Slack, PagerDuty)
  - approve_gate: require an interactive approve step tied to a ticket id

Example script (YAML)
---
metadata:
  name: "rebalance-small-prefetch-cohort"
  owner: "platform-operator-team"
  ticket: "INC-4321"
preconditions:
  - cluster-health: "green"
  - s3-access: "has_key"
steps:
  - schedule_prefetch:
      model: "redwood/llama-13b-q8"
      cohort_id: "cohort-202611"
      expected_size: 40
  - wait_for_sli:
      sli: "prefetch-complete"
      window: "10m"
postchecks:
  - query-prefetch-status: "cohort-202611"
  - assert: "complete == true"
rollback:
  - api_call:
      endpoint: "/prefetch/cancel"
      body: {cohort_id: "cohort-202611"}
telemetry:
  runbook_id: "prf-2026-11"
  emit: ["prefetch.requested", "prefetch.completed"]
---

Execution model and CLI behaviors
- validate: runbook-cli validate <file> -> schema check + static analysis + safety policy check
- simulate: runbook-cli simulate <file> --state snapshot.json -> executes in simulator, emits synthetic telemetry and cost estimates
- dry-run: runbook-cli execute <file> --dry-run -> runs prechecks and prints planned API calls without changes
- execute: runbook-cli execute <file> --ticket INC-4321 -> runs with RBAC, interactive approve gates prompt, logs to operator-audit
- guardrails: operations are rate-limited, concurrency-limited, and may require multi-approver for high-impact changes

Safety policy (summary)
- Thresholds requiring multi-approver:
  - any operation affecting > 20% of a tenant's capacity
  - model-swap to a non-verified variant
  - cluster-wide drains
- Time windows: destructive operations are not allowed during blackout windows (nightly commit window 02:00–05:00 UTC unless emergency)
- Immutable audit fields: metadata.owner, metadata.ticket enforced at validation time

Telemetry contract (what the runtime emits)
- runbook.execution.start {runbook_id, operator_id, ticket, mode}
- runbook.step.start {runbook_id, step_index, primitive, inputs}
- runbook.step.end {runbook_id, step_index, status, duration_ms, result_codes}
- runbook.execution.end {runbook_id, status, duration_ms, total_cost_estimate}
- runbook.simulation.report {runbook_id, checks, estimated_telemetry}
- Error taxonomy: validation_error, safety_block, runtime_error, external_api_error

Observability & dashboarding requirements (minimum)
- Build a "Runbook Execution" dashboard with the following panels:
  - Recent executions table (last 7d) with runbook_id, operator, ticket, status, duration
  - Failure heatmap by primitive type (api_call, model_swap, drain_node)
  - Average time-to-complete for common runbooks (prefetch, rebalance)
  - Safety policy blocks over time (count and top blocking rules)
- Alerts:
  - runbook.execution.failure.rate > 5% for a given runbook in 1h -> pager to platform-operator oncall
  - simulation vs execution divergence > 20% (estimated vs actual cost/time) -> create investigation ticket

Operator UX and CLI ergonomics
- Default to interactive mode with compact progress spinner and context lines for failures
- Provide auto-generated human-readable changelog for each runbook execution
- Support auto-complete for primitives and recommended argument values via CLI plugin (bash/zsh/fish)
- CLI must include a "why-blocked" explainer that surfaces the safety rule and suggested remediation

Rollout plan (milestones)
Quarter A (Q1 2027) - prototype & internal pilot
  - implement YAML schema, validator, and simulator (local-only)
  - implement 6 vetted primitives: api_call, wait_for_sli, schedule_prefetch, model_swap, drain_node, notify
  - integrate audit logging to operator-audit service
  - internal pilot with one operator pod group (platform-core)
Quarter B (Q2 2027) - hardened runtime & observability
  - RBAC enforcement and multi-approver flows
  - telemetry contract implemented and dashboard panels created
  - cost-estimation module and simulation divergence alert
  - operator training + playbook migration clinic

Migration & backward-compatibility strategy
- Provide a migration helper that converts canonical markdown runbooks to the DSL where possible.
- Maintain a compatibility shim for legacy scripts executed via a sandboxed runner; mark those runs with label legacy_runner.

Testing & verification matrix
- Unit: schema and primitive unit tests (owner: eng-platform-infra)
- Integration: simulator vs staging platform (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
- Chaos tests: intentionally fail API endpoints during simulate to validate rollbacks (owner: eng-sre)
- Safety fuzzing: randomized scripts run against simulator with safety policy enforced (owner: reliability lab)

Open risks & mitigations
- Risk: operators over-rely on simulation and skip live safety checks -> Mitigation: enforce safety checks at runtime and add a mandatory post-execution verification step tied to ticket closure.
- Risk: misplaced trust in cost estimates -> Mitigation: conservative defaults, require opt-in for any runbook that estimates > $500 estimated cost.
- Risk: DSL proliferation/duplication -> Mitigation: runbook registry + required review for new runbook entries; quarterly registry pruning.

Ownership & contacts
- Product owner: Priya Raman (platform-product)
- Engineering lead: Maya Chen (eng-platform)
- Observability: Diego Alvarez (eng-platform-observability)
- SRE safety review: Ethan Cole (eng-sre)

Appendix: sample validator CLI output (stylized)
$ runbook-cli validate rebalance.yaml
✔ schema: OK
✖ safety: BLOCKED -> rule: "cluster-wide drains require 2 approvers"
  reason: affects 32% of tenant capacity
  suggestion: reduce target scope or request multi-approver flag (--approvers 2)

Appendix: minimal YAML schema excerpt
- metadata.name: string (required)
- metadata.owner: string (required)
- preconditions: list of precondition objects
- steps: ordered list of primitives (mapping of primitive name -> args)
- rollback: ordered list
- telemetry: runbook_id, emit list

Next steps (immediate)
- Approve the safety policy draft (owners: eng-sre, security)
- Allocate 3 FTEs (1 infra, 1 observability, 1 SRE) to Q1 prototype
- Schedule pilot week with platform-core operators (target date: 2027-02-14)

This document should be treated as a living specification. Feedback and suggested changes should be submitted as PRs against the runbook-dsl repo and new reviewers added to the reviewers list above.

payload.page_title: Deferred prefetch rollforward and catchup: operator playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes operator steps, decision thresholds, tooling snippets, and post-recovery checks for handling deferred prefetch windows that require rollforward and catchup processing of KV/prefix caches in the runtime. It is intended for platform operators and oncall engineers running the Redwood inference control plane and platform operator surface.

Problem statement
-----------------
When the runtime defers prefetch work (due to resource constraints, backpressure, or safety cages), cached state (KV/prefix) for models and tenants can lag behind live traffic. If deferred windows grow, operators must reconcile degraded inference quality / higher token cost against capacity and thermal constraints. This playbook provides a safe rollforward/catchup procedure to catch caches up while preserving SLOs and avoiding cascading evictions.

Scope and applicability
----------------------
- Applies to multitenant prefix/KV caches and cross-region prefetch coordinators.
- Intended for cases where deferred prefetch backlog > 5% of steady-state rate OR when tail-latency SLOs show progressive degradation.
- Not intended for full rebuilds after data corruption; see Recovery from corrupt KV index runbook.

Definitions
-----------
- deferred window: period where prefetch worker(s) paused or intentionally delayed work.
- rollforward: operator-driven controlled processing of deferred queue with throttles.
- catchup: continuous incremental rebuild until backlog below target threshold.
- catchup rate: configured fraction of peak prefetch throughput used during catchup.

Prerequisites and safety checks
-------------------------------
1) Confirm data integrity: run kv-checksum --model <model> --shard <id>.
2) Verify operator runway: ensure oncall capacity and cross-team pager coverage for 2 hours.
3) Ensure snapshot retention present for rollback: s3://redwood-prefetch-snapshots/<date>.
4) Confirm capacity cushion: free GPU headroom >= 12% on target pools or have burst credits enabled.

Observability to inspect before starting
--------------------------------------
- SLOs and current burn: dashboards/runtime/slo-summary (look for token latency p95/p99).
- Prefetch backlog: metric prefetch.backlog.count (alert level: > 2000).
- Catchup consumer lag: prefetch.consumer.lag_seconds.
- Token cost delta: cost.tokens.delta_last_1h.
- Thermal and GPU interference: gpu.thermal.high and gpu.interference.score.

Decision matrix (quick)
-----------------------
1) If backlog < 1,000 and p99 latency stable -> schedule low-priority background catchup (dry run).
2) If backlog 1,000–5,000 with p95 rising -> soft rollforward at 10% catchup rate with verification windows.
3) If backlog > 5,000 or p99 > SLO threshold -> escalate and run controlled rollforward with tight throttles and tenant prioritization.
4) If GPU thermal alarms active -> abort rollforward and escalate to infra runbook.

Operator runbook: step-by-step
-----------------------------
1) Notification and coordination
   - Notify impacted owners via #platform-operators and create an incident channel (if not already).
   - Post short summary to status page draft: "Prefetch deferred backlog detected; running controlled catchup".

2) Lock-in safety config
   - Set cluster flag to safe-mode=true: curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/flags/safe-mode -d '{"value":true}'.
   - Annotate deployment with tag rollback-safe:true.

3) Select catchup plan
   - Tiered tenant prioritization table (example):
     | priority | criteria | catchup rate | notes |
     | P0 | enterprise SLA customers | 20% | prefer local shard catchup |
     | P1 | high-value active tenants | 10% | stagger across regions |
     | P2 | best-effort tenants | 5% | throttle aggressively |

4) Execute staged rollforward
   - Start with a canary shard:
     a) Run: prefetchctl start-catchup --shard shard-12 --rate 0.1 --dry-run=false
     b) Watch metrics for 10 minutes: prefetch.backlog.count, latency p95/p99, token cost.
   - If stable, expand to contiguous shards in batches of 4 every 15 minutes.
   - Commands:
     - prefetchctl inspect-backlog --model <model> --shard <shard>
     - prefetchctl start-catchup --shard <shard> --rate <decimal> --owner <team>

5) Adaptive throttling rules
   - If p95 latency increases by > 12% over baseline -> reduce catchup rate by 50% and wait 5 minutes.
   - If GPU utilization > 88% or thermal alarm -> pause catchup immediately and rollback that batch.
   - If token cost delta > 30% and business owner requests -> degrade to P0-only catchup.

6) Monitoring windows and verification
   - Run automated verification suite after each batch:
     - Sample requests for top-10 P0 tenants and run evals against golden prompt set.
     - Verify output similarity score >= acceptance threshold (0.92).
   - Commands:
     - ./tools/eval-sample --tenant <tenant> --prompt-set p0-smoke --expected-score 0.92

7) Completion and cleanup
   - When backlog < 5% of baseline, gradually restore safe-mode=false.
   - Record catchup run in incident log with timestamps, shards acted on, and final metrics.

Rollback playbook (if degradation observed)
-----------------------------------------
1) Pause current batch: prefetchctl pause-catchup --batch <id>.
2) Rollback to last stable snapshot: prefetchctl rollback --shard <shard> --snapshot s3://...
3) Re-open operator channel; call for cross-team mitigation and thermal remediation.

Preflight checklist (operator)
-----------------------------
- [ ] KV checksum passed for targeted shards.
- [ ] Snapshot verified and accessible.
- [ ] Backup plan created with exact rollback commands.
- [ ] Owners and SRE notified and oncall assigned.
- [ ] Observability panels open and annotated.

YAML example: catchup schedule config
-----------------------------------
```yaml
catchup_plan:
  name: staged-rollforward-2026-07
  global_rate_limit: 0.2
  batches:
    - id: batch-1
      shards: [12,13,14,15]
      default_rate: 0.10
      priority_overrides: {p0: 0.20}
    - id: batch-2
      shards: [16,17,18,19]
      default_rate: 0.08
      priority_overrides: {p0: 0.18}
  telemetry_verification:
    sampling_prompts: p0-smoke
    acceptance_score: 0.92
```

Post-recovery metrics to capture
--------------------------------
- backlog reduction curve (minutes vs backlog count).
- token cost delta and chargeback per tenant.
- latency histogram pre/during/post for top 3 models.
- number of rollbacks and snapshots used.

Automation and tooling notes
--------------------------
- The prefetchctl CLI is the canonical operator surface. For one-off operations use the CLI; for scheduled orchestration use the catchup-controller service which consumes YAML plans.
- Alerts tuned for this procedure:
  - prefetch.catchup.progress.stalled -> alert if no progress for 20 minutes.
  - prefetch.rollforward.error -> immediate P0 notify.

Postmortem template (to fill after run)
-------------------------------------
1) Summary of event and root cause.
2) Timelines: detection, run start, batches, completion.
3) Metrics and impact table.
4) What went well and action items (owner + due date).

Open risks and follow-ups
------------------------
- Need stronger GPU thermal prediction for rollforward windows (action: infra to run thermal forecasting POC).
- Improve tenant scoring to automatically prioritize by latency sensitivity rather than static labels.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary owner: Platform Operators team (pager: platform-operators).
- Secondary: Serving Runtime SRE.
- Escalation: follow the oncall SLO escalation ladder documented in /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/oncall-lagging-telemetry-reconstitution-and-synthetic-backfill-guide-2025.

References and links
-------------------
- Cache prefetch prioritization guide: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/cache-prefetch-prioritization-for-llm-workloads-2026
- Emergency model swap runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026

Contact and feedback
--------------------
If this playbook missed a case or you ran an incident with different outcomes, email the author or open a doc edit proposal in the page comments.
