payload.page_title: How-to: Integrate Redwood Console with the Cost Model API (v1)

sections.body: This page documents the recommended integration pattern for **Redwood Console** backend services calling the **Cost Model API (v1)**.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Cost breakdown tables (prefill vs decode, cache hit attribution, overhead)
- Time-series dashboards (bounded, aggregated breakdowns)
- Drill-down views for a request or small cohort

The intent is that Console uses a **single canonical source** of cost semantics and breakdown taxonomy, rather than duplicating logic.
sections.heading: Console uses the Cost Model API to power

sections.body:
- Console backend engineers and dashboard engineers
- On-call engineers debugging cost discrepancies in Console
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) Use the shared client library (preferred) with **schema version negotiation enabled**.
2) Use **bounded queries** (time windows, group-by dimensions, and result limits).
3) Add **multi-layer caching** in Console for hot dashboard paths (60s default TTL).
4) When the Cost Model API is degraded, **fall back** to existing Console aggregates (feature-flagged) and surface a UI banner.
5) Validate changes against **staging fixtures** and golden datasets before rollout.

---
sections.heading: Quick start (TL;DR)

sections.body:
- Console services must authenticate to Cost Model API using standard service-to-service auth (mTLS / workload identity as configured by Platform).
- Ensure the calling service has the IAM permission:
  - `costmodel.estimates.read` (for request-level estimate/breakdown)
  - `costmodel.aggregates.read` (for time-window aggregates)

If you get `403` errors in staging, file an access request with Platform Control Plane (tag Kaitlyn Nguyen).
sections.heading: Access + service identity

sections.body: All calls must include tenant context. In Console, this should come from the authenticated user/session and be forwarded to the backend service.
sections.heading: Required context

sections.body:
- `org_id` (required)
- `project_id` (required)
- `environment` (required; `prod|staging|dev`)

Do not infer tenant context from URL parameters without auth validation.

---
sections.heading: Console must supply

sections.body: Console should not hand-roll HTTP calls except in emergency debugging tools.
sections.heading: Use the shared client library

sections.body:
- **Go** (Console aggregator services): `go.redwood.ai/costmodel/client`
- **TypeScript/Node** (if applicable): `@redwood-inference/cost-model-client`
sections.heading: Supported clients

sections.body:
- Timeouts + retries (idempotent requests only)
- Version negotiation (`schema_version` pinning + fallback)
- Standard error mapping (4xx vs 5xx vs policy guardrails)
- Request bounding helpers (max ranges, max group-by)

---
sections.heading: Client features you should rely on

sections.body: Console primarily uses aggregated breakdown endpoints for dashboards, plus request-level breakdown for drill-down.
sections.heading: Endpoints Console typically uses

sections.body:
Use this for time-series charts and tables.

Conceptual operation: “Give me cost breakdown for org/project over a bounded time window, optionally grouped by a small set of dimensions.”
sections.heading: 1) Aggregate breakdown (dashboards)

sections.body:
- `model_id`
- `route`
- `deployment_mode` (hosted/dedicated/private)
- `region`
sections.heading: Common groupings

sections.body:
- Prefer **one aggregate request** per widget rather than N small requests.
- Keep `group_by` small (0–2 dimensions). More than that will amplify cardinality.
sections.heading: Hard rules for Console

sections.body: Use this for request detail pages (or small cohorts).
sections.heading: 2) Request breakdown (drill-down)

sections.body:
- Batch request IDs (if the API supports it) rather than calling per-request in a loop.
- Avoid powering infinite-scroll UIs by repeatedly calling request-level endpoints. Prefer aggregate endpoints and sampled drill-down.

---
sections.heading: Hard rules for Console
Example usage (Go)

sections.body:
- Console should treat the Cost Model API as an internal dependency with strict timeouts. Do not allow slow cost computation to cascade into overall page latency.
- Prefer `Granularity=5m` for most dashboard widgets; use `1m` only for short windows.

---
sections.heading: Notes

sections.body: Cost Model API is designed to be fast, but dashboard workloads are spiky and repetitive. Console should cache aggressively.
sections.heading: Caching guidance (Console)

sections.body: Cache the **entire Cost Model API response** for a given query.
sections.heading: What to cache

sections.body:
- `org_id`, `project_id`, `environment`
- endpoint name + normalized query params
- `schema_version` actually used (after negotiation)
- time range + granularity
- `group_by` and `filters`
sections.heading: Cache key should include (at minimum)

sections.body:
- Dashboard aggregate breakdown: **60 seconds** default TTL
- High-traffic landing pages: **30 seconds** if freshness concerns
- Drill-down by request_id: **5 minutes** (request costs don’t change unless backfilled; see caveat below)
sections.heading: Recommended TTLs

sections.body:
- L1: in-process LRU (fast path; helps thundering herd within a single pod)
- L2: shared Redis cache for Console backend (recommended for dashboards)
sections.heading: Cache layers

sections.body:
Some cost inputs can be corrected by backfills (e.g., telemetry lag, late-arriving KV cache stats). For Console UI correctness:
- Prefer a small “data freshness” indicator on cost widgets.
- Do not cache aggregate responses longer than 5 minutes.
- If a user requests “Last 24h”, compute from **rolling cached chunks** (e.g., 5m buckets), not a single massive response.
sections.heading: Backfill / late telemetry caveat

sections.body:
Use singleflight / request coalescing keyed by the cache key to ensure only one in-flight request per unique query.

---
sections.heading: Thundering herd prevention

sections.body: Cost queries are naturally high-cardinality. The API enforces policy guardrails; Console should stay well within them.
sections.heading: Bounds, pagination, and cardinality rules

sections.body:
- Default: max window **24 hours** per widget
- Deep history: use pre-aggregated pipelines (Analytics) or request coarser granularity (1h)

If you need >24h at 5m granularity, discuss with Telemetry & Analytics (Logan Wright / Mei Lin) because this is usually a product/design smell.
sections.heading: Guidelines for dashboards

sections.body:
- Recommended: 0–2 group-by dimensions
- Avoid: `group_by=[route, model_id, region]` unless strictly bounded with strong filters
sections.heading: Group-by limits

sections.body:
- `max_groups` (e.g., 200)
- `max_series` (e.g., 1000)
- Prefer “Top N by total_cost_usd” semantics when available
sections.heading: Set explicit bounds on response sizes

sections.body:
If an endpoint returns `next_page_token`:
- Always implement pagination loops with a hard cap (e.g., max 5 pages)
- Surface partial results and a warning rather than looping unbounded
sections.heading: Pagination

sections.body:
1) Request page 1
2) While token != empty AND pages < maxPages: request next page
3) If maxPages hit: stop and log `costmodel.pagination_truncated=1`

---
sections.heading: Pseudo-pattern

sections.body: Console must not become unavailable if Cost Model API is degraded.
sections.heading: Error handling + fallback behavior

sections.body:
- Timeout: 500–750ms for dashboard paths; 1–2s for drill-down
- Retries: at most 1–2 retries for safe/idempotent reads
- Use jittered exponential backoff; do not retry `4xx`
sections.heading: Recommended timeout/retry policy

sections.body:
- `400/422` Invalid request bounds or unsupported fields: fix Console query construction; do not retry.
- `429` Rate limited: rely on caching; reduce widget fanout; consider adding server-side batching.
- `503/504` Temporary outage/overload: fail fast and use fallback.
sections.heading: Common error classes

sections.body:
- Feature flag: `console.cost_model_api.enabled` (per environment)
- Feature flag: `console.cost_model_api.fallback_to_legacy` (default ON during rollout)
sections.heading: All Console surfaces using cost-model must support

sections.body:
- Use legacy Console aggregation logic (existing pipeline) for that widget/page
- Emit metrics:
  - `console.costmodel.fallback.count`
  - `console.costmodel.fallback.reason` (timeout|5xx|rate_limit|schema)
- UI: show a non-blocking banner “Cost breakdown temporarily using legacy estimator; values may differ from invoice.”

---
sections.heading: When fallback triggers

sections.body: Console changes must be validated against known-good datasets before production rollout.
sections.heading: Testing against staging fixtures

sections.body:
1) **Contract tests (schema + semantics)**
- Ensure Console can parse responses for `cost-model/v1`
- Ensure unknown fields are ignored safely

2) **Golden fixtures (deterministic outputs)**
- Use fixture datasets produced by the validation harness
- Snapshot a small set of queries that match Console widgets

3) **Backtesting (drift checks)**
- Compare aggregate outputs vs observed spend attribution (within defined thresholds)
sections.heading: Recommended test types

sections.body:
Set env vars (names may vary; follow monorepo conventions):
- `COST_MODEL_BASE_URL=https://cost-model-api.staging.redwood.internal`
- `COST_MODEL_SCHEMA_VERSION=cost-model/v1`
- `COST_MODEL_TIMEOUT_MS=750`
sections.heading: How to run locally (typical)

sections.body: ```bash
sections.heading: Run Console backend tests with recorded fixtures

sections.body: rw costmodel fixtures pull --dataset console_breakdown_v1 --out ./testdata/costmodel
sections.heading: Pull latest staging fixtures used by validation harness

sections.body:
go test ./... -run TestCostModel -update-golden=false
```
sections.heading: Run Console contract + golden tests

sections.body:
- Load time window: Last 1h, 24h
- Group-by: route, model_id
- Validate that:
  - totals are non-negative
  - prefill + decode + overhead == total (within rounding tolerance)
  - cache attribution fields are present when cache is enabled
  - p95 API latency stays within budget during normal load

---
sections.heading: For each of the main Console cost views

sections.body: When calling Cost Model API, emit client-side metrics to correlate widget regressions with API behavior.
sections.heading: Observability (what Console should emit)

sections.body:
- `console.costmodel.client.latency_ms` (p50/p95)
- `console.costmodel.client.status_code`
- `console.costmodel.client.endpoint` (aggregate|request)
- `console.costmodel.client.schema_version_used`
- `console.costmodel.client.cache_hit` (l1|l2|miss)
- `console.costmodel.client.query_cardinality_estimate` (best-effort)
sections.heading: Required metrics/tags

sections.body:
- Log full request bounds (time window, group_by, limits), but **do not** log customer prompts or raw request payloads that may contain sensitive text.

---
sections.heading: Logging

sections.body:
- Console is still using legacy fallback for part of traffic
- Telemetry lag/backfills changed cost attribution after the fact
- Invoice includes intentional billing-specific adjustments (taxes, credits, rounding rules) that are out of scope for cost model primitives
sections.heading: This is expected during rollout windows if

sections.body:
1) Check if fallback is active (`console.costmodel.fallback.count`)
2) Check Cost Model API drift dashboard (SRE-owned)
3) Confirm the widget is using the correct time window + granularity
4) If mismatch persists, open a thread with Finance (Laura Bennett / Rishi Malhotra) and include:
   - org_id/project_id
   - time range
   - schema version used
   - breakdown totals
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- Confirm Console timeouts are enforced (do not wait >750ms on dashboard paths)
- Verify caching is functioning (L2 hit rate)
- Reduce fanout: consolidate multiple widget queries into one aggregate query where possible
- If persistent, file an incident and include:
  - endpoint, group_by, time range, max_groups/max_series
  - request volume and concurrency

---
sections.heading: Actions

sections.body:
- Cost Model API service owner: Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park)
- Telemetry inputs/data quality: Telemetry & Analytics (Logan Wright)
- Console integration owner: Console Backend (Chloe Martin / Jada Williams)
- SLO/on-call: SRE (Rafael Mendes)

For changes to required fields, open a PR against the versioned schema package and tag:
- `@platform-control-plane`
- `@console-backend`
- `@telemetry-analytics`

---
sections.heading: Ownership + support

sections.body:
- One aggregate query
- `group_by=[route]`
- `max_groups=50`
- `granularity=1h`
- Cache TTL: 60s
sections.heading: Pattern A: Top routes by cost (Last 24h)

sections.body:
- One aggregate query
- `group_by=[model_id]`
- `granularity=5m`
- Cache TTL: 30–60s
sections.heading: Pattern B: Model cost split (Last 1h)

sections.body:
- One request breakdown query
- Cache TTL: 5m
- UI: show schema version + “data freshness” timestamp
sections.heading: Pattern C: Drill-down (single request)

payload.page_title: Adaptive Tenant Scorecard and Auto-Buydown for Throttling

sections.body:
Overview
========
This document describes the Adaptive Tenant Scorecard (ATS) — a lightweight, realtime heuristic that ranks tenants by operational risk — and the Auto-Buydown (AB) action that temporarily reduces a tenant's burst/priority during system stress. The goal is to protect platform SLOs while minimizing manual intervention and preserving customer experience for high-value tenants.

Scope
-----
- Applies to multi-tenant inference pools managed by platform scheduler: service name: "redwood-infer-pool-v2".
- Covers transient throttling (soft buydown) actions and automatic recovery.
- Does NOT replace contractual hard throttles (billing/commit enforcement) or Dedicated/Private tenant controls.

Motivation & goals
------------------
1. Avoid system-wide SLO degradation (target: 99.9% request success and p95 latency <= 450ms across public pools).
2. Provide predictable, auditable decisions during surge events so SRE and Platform Ops can explain impact to customers.
3. Minimize revenue impact by choosing poor-behavior tenants (high-cost, low-value, high-error) as candidates for buydown.
4. Ensure safety: human-in-the-loop override, cooldown windows, and conservative thresholds.

Ownership
---------
- Product owner: Priya Shah (Platform Reliability).
- Engineering owner: Miguel Alvarez (Scheduler & Autoscaling team).
- Oncall responder: platform-oncall rotation (see /confluence/eng-platform/oncall-rotation).

Design summary
--------------
Adaptive Tenant Score (ATS) = weighted sum of normalized signals. When ATS > BUYDOWN_TRIGGER and system stress is detected, the Auto-Buydown controller will apply a temporary policy change to the tenant's queue slice.

Signals and normalization
-------------------------
Each signal is normalized to a 0..1 range where 1 is worst. We compute a rolling 5m and 30m view — both are retained and combined for smoothing.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- sustained_token_rate_per_second (w=0.28): normalized by 99th-percentile historical peak for tenant class.
- error_rate_5m (w=0.20): failed requests / total requests (5m).
- tail_latency_score (w=0.18): p99 latency relative to target (p99 / 2000ms clipped).
- cache_miss_ratio (w=0.12): KV prefix cache miss fraction for tenant.
- SLO_violation_delta (w=0.12): percent points of SLO burn above baseline in last 5m.
- recent_manual_flags (w=0.10): operator-supplied flag (0 or 1) multiplied by 1.0 (instant full weight).
sections.heading: Signals (weights shown are defaults)

sections.body:
ATS = sum(weights_i * normalized_signal_i) / sum(weights)

Scoring thresholds (defaults)
---------------------------
- ATS < 0.25: green — no action.
- 0.25 <= ATS < 0.45: watch — notify tenant owner, prepare mitigation.
- 0.45 <= ATS < 0.70: soft-buydown candidate — throttle best-effort capacity by 20-40%.
- ATS >= 0.70: hard-buydown candidate — apply aggressive limits, route to low-priority queue, or temporarily evict non-critical background work.

Safety and eligibility filters
----------------------------
Do not consider a tenant for Auto-Buydown unless all of the following are true:
- tenant not in Dedicated or Private mode.
- no active enterprise SLA exception for platform-degraded events.
- tenant has not been manually flagged with "protected_until" metadata.
- tenant historical_commit_level == "low" OR (billing_tier == "free" and recent_support_tickets == 0).

Operational actions (Auto-Buydown controller)
--------------------------------------------
When controller decides to act, it runs a deterministic action plan:
1) Mark candidate in audit_log with reason, ATS value, and selected policy.
2) If ATS in soft range: reduce burst tokens by 25% and decrease priority score by 0.15 for 10 minutes.
3) If ATS in hard range: move to low-priority queue, cap token rate to historical 10th percentile for 15 minutes, and enable prefix-caching overrides.
4) Notify tenant owners and SRE oncall via Slack channel #platform-throttles and create incident draft (auto-populated template).
5) Start cooldown window: controller prohibits further buydown to same tenant for 30 minutes after action ends.

Configuration table (operator-editable values)
----------------------------------------------
| parameter_key | default_value | description | owner |
| ATS_WEIGHTS | "token:0.28,error:0.20,tail:0.18,cache:0.12,slo:0.12,manual:0.10" | weights for each signal | Scheduler team |
| BUYDOWN_TRIGGER | "0.45" | ATS threshold to consider buydown | Platform Reliability |
| SOFT_BUYDOWN_DECAY_MIN | "10m" | duration of soft action | Scheduler team |
| HARD_BUYDOWN_DECAY_MIN | "15m" | duration of hard action | Scheduler team |
| COOLDOWN_WINDOW | "30m" | cooldown for same tenant | Platform Ops |
| MAX_CONCURRENT_BUYDOWNS | "25" | max number of simultaneous buydowns per region | SRE |

Decision workflow (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1. Detection: telemetry pipeline emits region_stress signal when platform p95 > 600ms OR token_concurrency > 95th configured capacity.
2. Candidate ranking: compute ATS for tenants in affected pools, sort descending.
3. Pre-filter: apply safety and eligibility filters.
4. Simulate impact: controller runs a fast simulation using historical 1h workload to estimate SLO lift. If estimated lift < 0.5% SLO improvement, skip action.
5. Execute: apply action and create audit entries.
6. Observe & iterate: monitor impact for 5m; if platform SLO improves, keep until decay window. Otherwise rollback immediately.

Monitoring and dashboards
-------------------------
sections.heading: ATS formula (textual)

sections.body:
- "ATS Leaderboard" — per-region table of top 200 ATS tenants with trend sparkline. (Metric: platform.tenant.ATS)
- "Buydown Events" — timeline of recent buydown actions with before/after SLO deltas. (Metric: platform.buydown.events)
- "Region Stress Monitor" — p50/p95/p99 and token concurrency. (Metric: platform.region.latency.*)

Suggested alert rules
---------------------
- region-stress-warning: when region_p95_latency > 600ms for 3m -> notify #platform-ops (severity: P2).
- buydown-activation-fail: when buydown_action_count increases but platform p95 does not decrease by at least 0.5% in 10m -> P1 paging to oncall.
- buydown-surge: if > MAX_CONCURRENT_BUYDOWNS triggered in 5m -> P1 (possible controller misconfiguration).

Runbook: If you are paged for a failed buydown or unexpected side-effects
---------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge page and pull the last buydown event from audit_log (query: SELECT * FROM platform_audit WHERE op = 'buydown' ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1).
2. Inspect ATS components for the tenant: check token_rate, error_rate, tail_latency, cache_miss.
3. If action caused regression for other tenants: rollback immediately via controller API: POST /admin/v1/buydown/rollback {tenant_id, event_id}.
4. If platform SLO unaffected: escalate to Scheduler team, open a debugging playbook, and consider manual transient increases in capacity (regional spillover) as short-term measure.
5. Document post-action analysis in incident tracker and tag related pages.

Metrics to capture for each buydown event
-----------------------------------------
- event_id, tenant_id, ats_before, ats_after, action_type, start_ts, end_ts, rollback_flag, estimated_slo_improvement, actual_slo_delta_5m.

Testing and rollout plan
-----------------------
Phase 0 (lab): implement controller in canary region, run synthetic surges via chaos harness for 2 weeks.
Phase 1 (limited): enable ATS computation in US-west for low-commit tenants only, no automatic actions (alerts only) for 4 weeks.
Phase 2 (soft): enable soft-buydown (no more than 5 concurrent) with extended observability for 6 weeks.
Phase 3 (global): enable full policy with MAX_CONCURRENT_BUYDOWNS=25 and automated notifications.

Retrospective cadence and KPIs
------------------------------
- Weekly review during rollout: count of buydown events, false positives, SLO improvement per event, customer escalations.
- 90-day retrospective: analyze revenue impact vs SLO recovery, tune weights and thresholds.

Operational considerations and known limitations
----------------------------------------------
- ATS relies on accurate tenant metadata; stale billing or "protected_until" flags may cause poor decisions. Ensure metadata sync job runs every 5 minutes.
- Simulation uses historical data and may mispredict when tenant workload changes shape rapidly (e.g., model updates).
- Avoid irreversible actions: Auto-Buydown never changes billing state or model versions.

Appendix A: Example audit entry (JSON)
-------------------------------------
{  "event_id": "bd-20260211-9f3a",  "tenant_id": "tenant-8342",  "ats": "0.69",  "action": "soft-buydown",  "policy": "burst_reduction_25pct_priority_decrease_0.15",  "start_ts": "2026-02-11T14:23:10Z",  "end_ts": "2026-02-11T14:33:10Z",  "initiated_by": "auto-controller-v1",  "reason": "region_p95 720ms + ATS 0.69"}

Appendix B: Frequently asked questions
-------------------------------------
Q: Will buydown affect dedicated tenants?
A: No. Dedicated and Private tenants are excluded by eligibility filters.

Q: Can sales request exceptions?
A: Yes — add an SLA exception artifact to tenant metadata with expiration. This will mark tenant as "protected" until expiration.

Related docs
------------

payload.page_title: Regional Model Gatekeeper & Rolling Eviction Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes the Regional Model Gatekeeper pattern and an operator-friendly rolling-eviction workflow to perform model version rollouts, regional capacity rebalancing, and emergency model swaps with minimal customer-visible impact. It applies to Redwood hosted & dedicated regions and private deployments where a central decision plane coordinates model placement and eviction heuristics.

Goals and constraints

- Zero (or near-zero) request error rate during model rollout and eviction events for high-tier customers. Target: error-rate increase < 0.2% for a 1-hour window.
- Maintain tail latency SLOs: 95th percentile request latency <= 120ms for generate/chat, 99th percentile <= 350ms.
- Graceful fallback to compatible variants (quantized / smaller architecture) if primary model capacity unavailable.
- Avoid wholesale restart of serving nodes; prefer warm model swap and KV-cache transfer where possible.

Key components

1) Regional Model Gatekeeper (service name: gatekeeper-service)
   - Responsible for decisioning: which model variant to serve per region and tenant slice.
   - Inputs: capacity signals (gpu_mem_util, gpus_free), telemetry (tail_latency_ms, error_rate), cost signals, customer tier policies.
   - Outputs: routing rules pushed to runtime-proxy, eviction decisions pushed to allocator, model swap jobs to runtime-operator.

2) Runtime Operator (service name: runtime-operator)
   - Executes safe rolling eviction jobs, coordinates warm loads, monitors cache rehydration.

3) Runtime Proxy / Router (service name: serving-router)
   - Enforces routing rules and fallbacks; emits per-route token and latency telemetry.

SLOs and thresholds (defaults)

- Region availability SLO: 99.95% per region (monthly).
- Eviction gating thresholds (trigger candidate when both conditions hold for 2m):
  - GPU memory utilization > 90% on >= 3 nodes in the region OR
  - Tail latency (99th) > 400ms for model X across the region AND error rate > 0.75%
- Immediate hard eviction criteria: GPU OOM observed, node memory corruption, or sustained node crash loop > 3 restarts in 10m.

Runbook: Rolling eviction (operator procedure)

Pre-flight checks (operator)
1) Verify running capacity and traffic profile: check dashboard panel "Gateway - Region Capacity".
2) Confirm active rollouts / canaries: run `rk rollout list --region=us-west-2` and verify no overlapping rollouts.
3) Ensure backup fallback variants available for affected model family (e.g., bert-base-q4, gpt2-small-fp16).
4) Confirm runbook owner & pager: add `@oncall-platform` to the ticket.

Execution steps
1) Create a Gatekeeper job: `rk gatekeeper create-eviction-job --model model-X:v3 --region us-west-2 --reason "hotspot eviction" --dry-run`
   - Dry-run mode simulates decisions and lists affected tenants; review for unexpected impact.
2) Approve and promote to plan: `rk gatekeeper approve-job <job-id> --approve-by <operator>`
3) Runtime-operator will generate a rolling plan grouped by shard/affinity. Default cadence: 10% of shards every 90s.
4) For each shard group:
   a) Quiesce new long-running requests (soft drain) with serving-router header injection.
   b) Warm-start target model variant on target node: `runtime-operator warm-start --node <id> --model model-X:v3`
   c) Verify model health (kernel init complete, KV cache warm percent > 40%).
   d) Switch routing atomically for the shard to the new node.
   e) Monitor metrics for 5 minutes: tail latency, error-rate, token-per-second.
   f) If metrics breach rollback thresholds (see below), abort and trigger rollback for the group.
5) After completing all shard groups, mark job complete and run post-deploy validation.

Rollback and abort criteria (per shard group)
- If 95th latency increases by > 30% vs baseline for 5 minutes.
- If error-rate for the group increases > 0.5 percentage points.
- If model crash/reload observed > 2 times in the 10m window.
- If synthetic QA prompts (canary set) fail > 2/5 checks.

Rollback steps
1) Pause the job: `rk gatekeeper pause-job <job-id>`
2) Re-route shards to previous variant: `runtime-operator route-back --group <id>`
3) Trigger an incident and assign SRE + model-release owner.
4) Capture telemetry snapshot and KV cache heatmap for postmortem.

Eviction safety knobs and operator overrides

- Speed caps: max_shards_per_minute (default 10 shards/min).
- Conservative mode: require 2 independent metrics (latency + error) to pass before eviction.
- Tenant protection list: tenants with platinum tier are excluded unless explicitly allowed.
- Force-evict token: `--force` only allowed if approval from oncall lead and customer-impacting condition.

Dashboards and alerts (what to watch)

Recommended dashboard panels to include in the "Regional Gatekeeper" view:
- Model capacity heatmap: nodes x memory_reserved, memory_used, gpu_utilization.
- Shard progress timeline: percent shards migrated, groups completed.
- Per-tenant token rate & tail latency.
- Canary prompt success rate (synthetic): rolling 5-min window.
- KV-cache warm percent per node.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- gatekeeper.eviction.job-failure: fires if a job group fails > 2 groups (severity P1).
- serving-router.tail-latency.spike: 99th latency > 450ms sustained 2m (P1).
- runtime-operator.model-crash: model process crash > 3 events in 10m on same node (P0).
- kvcache.rehydration.slow: median rehydration time > 5m (P2).

Operator checklist after a rolling eviction

- Verify all shards show healthy traffic with pre-rollout baselines.
- Confirm KV cache hit-rate is within 5% of baseline or explain delta.
- Run canary prompt suite and record results (attach to ticket).
- Communicate completion: update status page for impacted tenants if customer-visible.
- Create a short post-action note with metrics snapshot.

Automation & CI guardrails

- All gatekeeper jobs must pass CI validation which runs a smoke traffic replay in a sandbox region.
- Integration test: `tests/gatekeeper/smoke_replay.py` runs synthetic traffic with canary prompts; must succeed before production-promote.
- Feature flag: `gatekeeper.enable-automated-eviction` default off for new regions.

Retrospective template (to be filled after significant events)

- Event summary: short description and timeline.
- What went well: e.g., warm-start reduced cold token surge by X%.
- What failed or surprised us: e.g., KV cache warming slower than predicted for model-Y.
- Action items (owner + due date): discrete experiments, monitoring improvements, dashboard additions.

Common gotchas and mitigation tips

- KV cache transfer may not be possible across different kernel/quantization runtime variants; plan fallbacks accordingly.
- Synthetic canaries should represent both short interactions (chat) and long generations (streaming) to catch tail effects.
- Be mindful of tenant-affinity: moving a shard can concentrate heavy tenants on the same node if not balanced.

Roadmap & improvements (21-month horizon)

- Q2 2026: Implement model-level graceful degradation scoring to prefer lighter variants automatically under load.
- Q4 2026: Gatekeeper ML heuristic: predictive eviction scheduling using 30m lookback time-series and anomaly detection.
- H1 2027: Cross-region KV cache tiering: coordinate warm replicas ahead of large migrations.
- H2 2027: Self-healing rollouts: automated rollback + automated sandboxed remediation + postmortem draft generator.

Ownership

- Gatekeeper service: eng-platform (primary: Maya Patel)
- Runtime-operator: eng-serving-runtime (primary: Javier Morales)
- Dashboards & alerts: observability core (primary: Priya Nair)

References

- See runtime-operator runbook for warm-start CLI reference: ../runbooks/runtime-quantization-rollout-operator-playbook-2026.json
- Use the operator-sandbox and replay lab for dry runs: ../team-wiki/operator-sandbox-synthetic-scenarios-and-verification-catalog-2025.json

Appendix: Example CLI snippets

- Create dry-run job:
  rk gatekeeper create-eviction-job --model model-X:v3 --region eu-central-1 --dry-run --reason "capacity reclaim"

- Approve and start (operator):
  rk gatekeeper approve-job j-42 --approve-by maya.patel@redwood.ai

- Pause/Abort a running job:
  rk gatekeeper pause-job j-42 --reason "latency spike"

- Inspect job details:
  rk gatekeeper describe-job j-42 --output yaml

This document should be kept in sync with the gatekeeper-service API spec and the runtime-operator CLI docs. For questions or suggested improvements, ping @maya.patel on the eng-platform Slack channel.

payload.page_title: Instrumentation Sunset and Cleanup Playbook

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This playbook describes the approved, low-risk process to retire (sunset) unused or harmful instrumentation signals, remove stale dashboards/alerts, and reclaim telemetry budget. It's intended for platform engineers, telemetry owners, and oncall operators. Follow the steps below to minimize alert churn, SLO regressions, and data-loss surprises.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
- A metric or log signal has no active consumer for >= 90 days.
- An alert fires repeatedly but has no owner or actionability (signal noise).
- A dashboard is irrelevant after a major architecture change (service split, deprecation).
- Telemetry cost budget is exhausted by high-cardinality data that provides low value.

Goals and constraints
---------------------
- Ensure no customer-facing SLOs are degraded by telemetry removal.
- Maintain auditability: every sunset must have an associated ticket and rollback plan.
- Prefer retirement to deletion where possible (reduce retention, disable ingestion, keep archived raw data for 90 days).

Prerequisites and ownership
---------------------------
- Signal owner: The team or person who created/consumes the signal. If unknown, platform team will take temporary ownership and run a discovery window.
- Ticket: Create a tracking ticket in the platform backlog with links to dashboards, alerts, and PRs.
- Canary window: Minimum 14-day discovery/notice window before irreversible deletion.

Key roles and contacts
- Signal owner (required): Accepts responsibility for validation and rollout steps.
- Platform telemetry lead: Coordinates cross-team impact and capacity planning (pager: @oncall_platform).
- Oncall operator: Executes rollback and monitors during the canary window.
- Observability SRE reviewer: Confirms metrics/alerts removal is safe.

Step-by-step process
--------------------
1) Discovery and annotation (days 0–3)
   - Run the telemetry ownership scan: query our metrics registry for signals with zero consumers in the last 90 days.
   - Add annotation in the metric registry: "sunset:proposed" with ticket ID.
   - Post a short note on the platform-team Slack channel with the signal list and the proposed sunset date (14 days out).

2) Impact assessment (days 1–5)
   - For each signal, fill the Impact Table (see template below). Include dashboard references and alerts.
   - Run a dependency trace (prometheus/rbac -> alertmanager routes -> alert pages) to ensure nothing unexpected will break.

3) Canary / Notice window (days 6–20)
   - Lower ingestion rate: if possible switch the signal to lowered sampling or 30-day retention to surface consumers that depend on long-tail data.
   - Convert alerts that use this signal to a non-firing mode: set severity to informational or add a temporary mute with an owner.
   - Monitor for unexpected consumer activity for at least 14 days.
   - If an owner claims the signal, cancel sunset and update docs.

4) Disable ingestion and retention step (days 21–28)
   - Disable producers at source by toggling feature flags or config (preferred). Example: toggle in config-service:
     - curl -X PATCH https://config.redwood.internal/api/flags/metrics-foo -d '{"enabled": false}'
   - If producers cannot be toggled, add a write-side filter in the ingest pipeline to discard or sample events.
   - Reduce retention in the storage policy to 7 days for archived signals.

5) Dashboard and alert cleanup (days 28–35)
   - Mark dashboards as "deprecated" (add banner and owner field) for 7 more days.
   - Remove alerts using the signal after re-verifying related SLOs; create PRs and reference the ticket.
   - Update dashboard catalogs and alert directories to remove entries.

6) Final deletion or archive (day 36+)
   - If no dependency surfaced, perform final deletion of the timeseries and dashboard objects. Prefer archive-first where the storage system supports it.
   - Record the deletion PR, archive link, and snapshot in the ticket.

Impact Table (template)
-----------------------
| Signal name | Owner | Dashboard refs | Alerts affected | Consumer teams | Risk level | Rollback action |
|-------------|-------|----------------|-----------------|----------------|------------|-----------------|
| metrics/foo_latency | payments-team | payments/latency-dashboard | alert:payments-high-latency | payments, billing | Medium | Re-enable producer flag + backfill |

Risk categories and mitigations
- High: Potential to affect public SLOs. Require manual signoff from SRE and product.
- Medium: Internal tooling or non-critical dashboards. Canary as normal.
- Low: Developer debug-only signals. Remodel to archive after 7 days.

Alert migration checklist (text)
-------------------------------
- Identify alert rules referencing the signal: prometheus rule groups, alertmanager receivers.
- For each alert: change severity to info and add annotation "sunset in progress" for the canary window.
- Create an alternative alert where necessary using fallback signals (document fallback math).
- Add noise suppression policy: not more than 1 alertdedup per hour during migration.

Example Prometheus rule change (before -> canary):
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- alert: FooLatencyHigh
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(foo_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, job)) > 1.2
  for: 5m
sections.heading: BEFORE

sections.body:
- alert: FooLatencyHigh_Canary
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(foo_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, job)) > 1.2
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: info
  annotations:
    note: "Sunset candidate: watch-only; will be removed if no owner claims it during 14d window"

Rollback playbook (if consumer appears)
-------------------------------------
1) Identify which consumer surfaced and confirm the dependency.
2) Re-enable ingestion at source: flip feature flag or remove filter.
3) Backfill critical data where needed using archived exports (S3 path documented in ticket).
4) Re-enable alerts and dashboards.
5) Update the metric registry to set owner and increase retention.

Backfill and data export guidance
--------------------------------
- Preferred: ask the producer team to replay events from local logs or job archives.
- Platform-level export example (Prometheus snapshot):
  - curl -sS -XPOST "http://prometheus.redwood.internal/api/v1/admin/tsdb/snapshot"
  - Copy snapshot from /var/lib/prometheus/snapshots/<id> to s3://observability-archive/<ticket-id>/

Telemetry cost-saving targets and KPIs
------------------------------------
- Target: reclaim 15% platform telemetry cost each quarter via sunsetting and sampling.
- KPIs to track: ingestion volume (GB/day), number of signals retired, dashboards archived, alert noise reduction (alerts/day).

Post-cleanup retrospective and documentation
------------------------------------------
- Within 21 days of final deletion, the signal owner or platform lead must run a short retrospective covering: what claimed the signal, any rollback steps, time saved, and lessons learned.
- Update the telemetry catalog with the final status and link to archives.

Appendix: Automation recipes and scripts
--------------------------------------
- Ownership scan (example query):
  - TSDB: select distinct(metric_name) from metrics where last_consumer_ts < now() - interval '90 days';
  - PromQL: count_over_time(alerts{alertname!~""}[90d]) == 0 // combined with consumer registry
- Example CI PR template snippet for alert removal:
  - Title: remove alert FooLatencyHigh (sunset ticket #12345)
  - Body: rationale, canary dates, rollback steps, owner signoff, snapshot link.

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Platform telemetry channel: #platform-telemetry (primary)
- Pager: @oncall_platform (for production-impact concerns)
- Escalation to Observability SRE: @sre-observability on Slack and email sle@redwood.internal

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-12: created by Priya Natarajan
- 2025-11-20: added alert migration checklist (reviewed by Alex Rivera)
- 2026-02-10: clarified rollback/backfill guidance and added KPIs (Maya Chen)

payload.page_title: Operator synthetic-burst scenario authoring and validator

sections.body:
Overview

This guide describes a repeatable authoring and validation workflow for operator-facing synthetic burst scenarios. The goal is to let platform operators and SREs define, validate, and certify synthetic bursts that exercise tenant slicing, prefetch, KV cache, and model-variant fallback behaviors without risking production customer impact. This doc complements the Synthetic Scenario Orchestrator Runbook by focusing on scenario design, validation heuristics, and dashboard/alert templates used during experiments.

Why this exists

- Avoid accidental regressions from new allocator, prefetch, or routing changes.
- Provide a shared format and validator so scenarios are reviewable and automatable.
- Make synthetic bursts safe: scoped traffic, blast-radius controls, and automatic rollback triggers.

Scope

- Audience: platform operators, platform engineering, and observability engineers.
- Workflows covered: scenario authoring, local dry-run validation, controlled regional execution, dashboard/alert binding, and post-experiment retrospective.
- Not covered: full orchestration (see the orchestrator runbook), tenant-sensitive production load injection (requires customer opt-in).

Ownership and roles

- Scenario author: platform operator or SRE who writes the scenario JSON and test hypothesis.
- Reviewer: at least one senior operator + an observability engineer.
- Executor: platform operator with runbook approval.
- Validator: observability engineer who certifies metrics and dashboards.

Scenario format (JSON template)

Each scenario is a single-line JSON file (UTF-8). Below is the canonical template and field descriptions. Save variants under /synthetic-scenarios/ in the experiments repo.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "name": "burst-affinity-rebalance-30s",
  "description": "Short prefix-burst targeting tenant slice A to validate eviction heuristics",
  "target_region": "us-west-2",
  "start_delay_s": 60,
  "duration_s": 30,
  "qps_profile": {"type": "step", "steps": [{"qps": 800, "duration_s": 30}]},
  "tenant_affinity": {"target_tenants": ["tenant-A"], "share": "isolated"},
  "signature": {"model": "redwood-turbo-v1", "seq_len": 256},
  "blast_radius_controls": {"max_nodes": 5, "allow_preemptible": false},
  "rollback_triggers": [{"metric": "p50_token_latency_ms", "threshold": 1200, "window_s": 60}, {"metric": "error_rate", "threshold": 0.02, "window_s": 60}],
  "observability_bindings": {"dashboards": ["platform/burst-lab"], "alerts": ["burst-regional-latency"]}
}
sections.heading: Example template

sections.body:
- qps_profile.type: step | ramp | poisson. Use poisson for realistic burstiness.
- tenant_affinity.share: isolated | shared | mixed. Isolated runs should use dedicated tenant-slice tokens.
- rollback_triggers must include both latency and error-rate checks.
- signature.model must map to a runtime model alias recognizable by the orchestrator.

Scenario authoring checklist

1. Hypothesis: write a 1–2 sentence hypothesis (what you expect and what will prove/regress).
2. Blast radius controls: set max_nodes, tenant whitelist, and execution window.
3. Observability: list dashboards and the panels you will inspect.
4. Recovery steps: explicit rollback policy and manual cutover steps.
5. Preflight: run local validator (see below).
6. Reviewer approval: attach PR and get at least two reviewers.

Local validator (synthetic-validator CLI)

Run the synthetic-validator before any orchestrated execution. The validator performs schema checks, resource-estimate sanity checks, metric-to-alert mapping validation, and dry-run tokenization checks.
sections.heading: Field notes

sections.body: $ synth-validate --file experiments/synthetic-scenarios/burst-affinity-rebalance-30s.json
sections.heading: lint + schema validation

sections.body: $ synth-validate --file ... --dry-run --estimate-nodes
sections.heading: dry-run with demand estimate (no traffic injected)

sections.body:
- PASS / FAIL
- estimated_nodes_needed: 3
- estimated_token_rate_per_node: 1200/s
- mapped_alerts_ok: ["burst-regional-latency"]
- recommended_batching_profile: small_seq_conservative

Validation heuristics (key rules)

- If qps > 500 and duration < 60s, require explicit allow_preemptible: false.
- If target_region is multi-az, set max_nodes <= 50% of region pool by default.
- If seq_len > 1024, multiply estimated nodes by 1.5.
- For tenant-affinity.isolated, require preflight tokens and owner_team signoff.

Execution runbook (controlled regional execution)

Prereqs: scenario PR merged, validators PASS, runbook approval ticket, pre-allocated experiment namespace.
sections.heading: Validator outputs

sections.body:
1. Reserve experiment namespace: platform-experiments/<scenario-name>.
2. Schedule in off-peak window and notify on-call two hours in advance.
3. Run committed scenario in canary region first (non-production AZ).
   - Command: synth-orchestrate --scenario <file> --mode canary --notify slack:#platform-experiments
4. Monitor critical dashboards for first 60s. Abort if any rollback trigger fires.
5. If canary passes, roll to target_region using controlled ramp (50% nodes for first 120s).
6. On completion, wait stabilization window (2x duration).
7. Collect artifacts: flamegraphs, allocator-metrics, tenant-fallback-logs, orchestrator-traces.
8. Create a ticket and attach artifacts for the retrospective.

Dashboard and alert binding examples
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- alert: BurstRegionalLatency
  expr: avg_over_time(platform_request_latency_ms{region=~"us-.*"}[60s]) > 1000
  for: 30s
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Regional burst latency above 1s during synthetic run"
sections.heading: Prometheus alert rule (example)

sections.body: - Panel: Burst QPS and node utilization
sections.heading: Grafana panel recipe (short)

sections.body:
- sum(rate(inference_tokens_total[10s])) by (node)
    - node_cpu_percent, node_gpu_utilization_percent
sections.heading: Metrics

sections.body:
- yellow: 60% GPU util, red: 90% util

Safe alerting profile for experiments

- Alerts triggered by experiments should map to an "experiment" routing key so ops are aware events are experiment-driven.
- Silence noise-based alerts by binding a temporary suppression window in AlertManager, but do NOT silence SRE-page alerts for fatal error rates.

Artifacts to collect (minimum)

- Orchestrator trace (trace_id)
- Allocator decision log (allocator-<timestamp>.log)
- Per-node perf counters (GPU SM, memory, kernel-latency histogram)
- Synthetic client request log (sampled tokens)
- Snapshot of dashboards (PNG) and raw metrics export (Prometheus snapshot)

Acceptance criteria (pass/fail)

- Pass if: no rollback triggers fired, p99 latency <= baseline*1.35, error_rate <= baseline + 0.5 percentage points, no tenant unintended-fallbacks.
- Fail if: rollback triggers fired, sustained p50 > 2x baseline, any customer-visible errors detected.

Post-run retrospective template

1. Hypothesis and result (pass/fail and short rationale).
2. Metrics (time series snippets and summary table).
3. Artifacts attached.
4. Root cause analysis for any failures.
5. Action items with owners and due dates.
sections.heading: Thresholds

sections.body:
| metric | baseline | observed peak | decision |
| p50 latency (ms) | 120 | 430 | accept |
| p99 latency (ms) | 900 | 1400 | investigate |
| error_rate | 0.3% | 0.9% | fail |

Roadmap and continuous improvement backlog

- 2026-Q2: Integrate synthetic-validator with CI so scenario PRs auto-run dry-runs.
- 2026-Q3: Add adaptive blast-radius control (auto-throttle based on allocator signals).
- 2026-Q4: Publish a cross-team catalog of certified scenarios for common regressions.

Appendix A: Safe knobs for experiment owners

- max_nodes: hard upper bound on number of worker nodes the orchestrator may schedule.
- allow_preemptible: boolean to permit scheduling on cheaper preemptible pools.
- enforcement_window: UTC window where traffic may be injected.

Appendix B: Quick troubleshooting checklist (operator)

1. If latency spikes immediately: abort, check node thermal throttling, inspect kernel-switch logs.
2. If errors increase: collect sample requests and compare model variant mapping.
3. If allocator fails to schedule: increase max_nodes temporarily and re-run small step.

References

- Synthetic Scenario Orchestrator Runbook (link internal)
- Operator Simulation Syllabus and Certification Pathway
- Observability Dashboard: platform/burst-lab

Related pages: see related_pages metadata for quick links.

Contact

For questions or to propose a certified scenario, open a PR in the experiments repo and ping #platform-experiments.

payload.page_title: Tenant-aware feature switch integration cookbook

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This cookbook documents recommended integration patterns for tenant-scoped feature switches across Redwood's platform. It combines design patterns, schema examples, telemetry and dashboard recipes, runbook steps for safe rollouts, automated rollback criteria, and a short retrospective template for post-rollout review. This is intended for platform engineers, operator teams, and product owners coordinating multi-tenant rollouts.

When to use this guide
- New features that may impact latency, token cost, or model quality per tenant.
- Behavioural changes (prompt templates, reranking heuristics) that must be gated by tenant.
- Experiments requiring controlled exposure, KPI gating, or immediate rollback capability.

Key goals
- Minimize blast radius per-tenant.
- Provide clear observability and automated safety gates.
- Make rollouts repeatable and auditable.

Design patterns and tradeoffs
1) Scope choices
   - Global switch (global): Fast and simple, but high blast radius. Use only for non-risky UX flags.
   - Tenant-scoped switch (tenant): Defaults to off. Stores per-tenant metadata and rollout percent. Good for production experiments.
   - Cohort-based switch (cohort): Group tenants by risk profile (e.g., dev, low-volume, enterprise) and apply policies.

2) Rollout strategies
   - Fixed-percent progressive rollout: Increase percent of tenant traffic in steps (1%, 5%, 20%, 100%) with evaluation windows.
   - Tenant whitelist: Start with specific tenant IDs (customer X, internal staging) before percent ramp.
   - Metric-gated rollout (KPI gating): Only advance when SLOs/quality metrics meet thresholds.

3) Safety primitives (must-haves)
   - Kill switch: Immediate global-off with a single API call.
   - Tenant-level emergency off: Operators can flip off a single tenant.
   - Automatic rollback: Triggered by guardrail alerts (see telemetry section).
   - Audit log + change id: All changes include author, change_id, and reason.

Feature switch schema (recommended canonical fields)
- The service storing switches should use the following JSON schema (example):
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
{
  "id": "string (unique)",
  "name": "human-readable string",
  "scope": "global | tenant | cohort",
  "default": "on | off",
  "tenant_overrides": [{"tenant_id": "string", "state": "on | off", "note": "string"}],
  "rollout": {"strategy": "percent | whitelist | gradual", "percent": "0-100", "whitelist": ["tenant_id"], "step_seconds": 3600},
  "metrics": ["list of telemetry keys to evaluate"],
  "auto_rollback": {"enabled": true, "conditions": ["expression strings"]},
  "owner": "team/email",
  "created_by": "user",
  "change_id": "uuid",
  "last_modified": "ISO8601"
}

Integration examples
1) API (control plane)\- Endpoint: POST /api/v1/feature-switches/{id}/apply
   - Example curl to enable for tenant t-123:
     curl -X POST https://feature-switch.redwood.internal/api/v1/feature-switches/llm-prefetch/apply \
       -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN' \
       -d '{"tenant_id":"t-123","state":"on","note":"canary for tenant t-123"}'

2) SDK snippet (Node.js)
   - Purpose: Local evaluation to short-circuit expensive controls at request time.
   const flags = await flagsClient.getForTenant(tenantId, ['llm-prefetch']);
   if (flags['llm-prefetch'] === 'on') {
     // call new path
   }

3) Gate at the routing layer (example architecture)
   - Client -> Edge -> Router -> Inference-runtime
   - Router performs a lightweight feature-check (cache first, then control-plane fallback) and attaches X-Feature-Flags header for downstream deterministic behavior.

Caching and TTLs
- Cache tenant flags at edge with a short TTL (default 30s).
- Control-plane changes propagate via event bus (kafka) for near realtime invalidation.
- Use ETag/Version headers in responses from the flags service.

Telemetry and dashboards (concrete recipes)
- Emit these per-tenant metrics from the serving runtime and router:
  - platform.feature_flags.active{feature="llm-prefetch", tenant_id="t-123"} = 1/0
  - platform.requests.count{tenant_id="t-123", route="chat"}
  - platform.latency.p50_ms{tenant_id="t-123"}
  - platform.latency.p95_ms{tenant_id="t-123"}
  - platform.cost.per_token{tenant_id="t-123"}
  - llm.quality.eval_score{tenant_id="t-123", eval_set="smoke"}

Dashboard panels to create (Prometheus + Grafana)
- Per-feature overview: total tenants with feature on, rollouts in progress, last change_id, owner.
- Risk heatmap: top 20 tenants by request volume with feature on + delta in p95 latency vs baseline.
- KPI gate panels: SLO burn rate, error rate, and quality delta for the last 30m/1h windows.

Alert recipes (Prometheus alert expressions)
- Urgent: Feature-induced latency SLO breach (10m window)
  - alert: FeatureRolloutLatencyBurn
    expr: increase(platform.slo_burn[10m]) > 0.05 and sum by (feature) (increase(platform.requests[10m])) > 100
    for: 5m
    labels: {severity: "critical", team: "platform"}
    annotations: {runbook: "/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026"}

- Quality regression: Eval score drop greater than 5% for the feature cohort versus baseline
  - alert: FeatureQualityRegression
    expr: (avg(llm.quality.eval_score{feature_on="true", window="1h"}) / avg(llm.quality.eval_score{feature_on="false", window="1h"})) < 0.95
    for: 30m
    labels: {severity: "high"}

Automatic rollback criteria (policy examples)
- If p95 latency increases by >30% for >= 5% of requests over a 20-minute window AND absolute SLO burn > 5% in 15m, then: trigger auto_rollback.
- If eval_score drops > 7% on the smoke eval set for >= 2 consecutive evaluation runs, trigger auto_rollback.

Rollback orchestration (operator-safe sequence)
1) Detection: Alert fires or metric threshold crossed.
2) Pause rollout: Feature control-plane action: set rollout.percent = current_percent and freeze.
3) Notify stakeholders via slack channel #platform-rollouts and create incident with change_id.
4) Execute tenant-level rollback for impacted tenants (script example below).

Rollback script (example CLI)
- A: Global kill (fastest):
  curl -X POST https://feature-switch.redwood.internal/api/v1/feature-switches/llm-prefetch/kill \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN' \
    -d '{"reason":"auto rollback triggered - latency burn"}'

- B: Per-tenant rollback (selective):
  curl -X POST https://feature-switch.redwood.internal/api/v1/feature-switches/llm-prefetch/apply \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN' \
    -d '{"tenant_id":"t-123","state":"off","note":"rollback: latency spike"}'

Runbook: Operator steps (short version)
1) Triage: Check dashboards — feature panels, heatmap, and per-tenant p95 deltas.
2) Scope: Run the SQL to list top impacted tenants:
   SELECT tenant_id, count(*) as requests, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_ms
   FROM request_events
   WHERE timestamp >= now() - interval '20 minutes' AND feature_flags->>'llm-prefetch' = 'on'
   GROUP BY tenant_id
   ORDER BY requests DESC
   LIMIT 50;
3) If >= 3 high-volume tenants show p95 delta > 30%: pause rollout and issue global kill.
4) For single-tenant regressions: flip per-tenant flag to off and monitor for 30 minutes.
5) After rollback: tag change_id with incident id and complete postmortem template.

Post-rollout retrospective checklist (to be completed within 72h)
- Summary: owner, change_id, start/end times, tenant list impacted.
- Metrics: aggregate p95 delta, SLO burn percent, cost delta.
- Root cause hypothesis: configuration error / runtime regression / model variant mismatch / infra degradation.
- Action items: short-term (fix/rollback), medium-term (add telemetry or gate), long-term (automation).
- Acceptance criteria for re-rollout: explicit KPI gates and a re-run of smoke evals.

Access control and governance
- Only platform ops + product owners may set global-level kill switches.
- Tenant-level overrides allowed for SRE and assigned customer success engineers via scoped RBAC.
- All changes to feature switches must create an audit record retained for 1 year.

Security and secrets
- Control-plane API tokens for programmatic rollouts live in the ops vault.
- Use short-lived tokens for CI-driven rollouts and require MFA for manual global kills.

Operational telemetry retention and cost considerations
- High-cardinality per-tenant metrics are expensive: sample heavy tenants (top 10% by traffic) at full granularity; aggregate lower-volume tenants daily.
- Store daily rollup metrics for 90 days and high-resolution (1m) for 30 days.

Testing and preflight guidance
1) Unit test: flagsClient behavior for on/off/partial percent.
2) Integration test: router and edge cache invalidation with control-plane change propagation tests.
3) Synthetic canary traffic: run 10k synthetic requests per minute for 30 minutes under the feature flag in a staging environment.
4) Degradation simulation: use the platform synthetic-degradation-lab (link below) to validate rollback triggers.

Roadmap and next improvements (owner: eng-platform)
- Q2 2026: Automated KPI gating engine (alpha) that advances rollouts on SLOs.
- Q3 2026: Tenant risk scoring and automated whitelist suggestions.
- Q4 2026: Self-service UI for product teams with RBAC and audit-first workflows.
- 2027: ML-assisted rollback predictor (predicts likely regressions before ramp).

Owners and contacts
- Platform feature-flags service: team-platform-flags@redwood.com (owner: Marcus Huang)
- Platform observability: team-platform-observability@redwood.com (owner: Priya Nair)
- Oncall escalation: #platform-oncall in Slack.

Appendix: Useful queries and commands
- List tenants with feature on and recent p95 delta > 20% (Postgres example):
  WITH recent AS (
    SELECT tenant_id, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_ms
    FROM request_events
    WHERE timestamp >= now() - interval '30 minutes' AND feature_flags->>'llm-prefetch' = 'on'
    GROUP BY tenant_id
  ), baseline AS (
    SELECT tenant_id, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_base
    FROM request_events
    WHERE timestamp >= now() - interval '7 days' AND feature_flags->>'llm-prefetch' = 'off'
    GROUP BY tenant_id
  )
  SELECT r.tenant_id, r.p95_ms, b.p95_base, (r.p95_ms / nullif(b.p95_base,0)) - 1 as p95_delta
  FROM recent r JOIN baseline b USING (tenant_id)
  WHERE (r.p95_ms / nullif(b.p95_base,0)) - 1 > 0.20
  ORDER BY p95_delta DESC
  LIMIT 50;

- Quick kill (CLI):
  ./ops-cli feature kill --id llm-prefetch --reason "auto-rollback - latency burn"

References
- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026
- /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/llm-quality-regression-alerting-and-dashboard-guidelines-2026

Document maintenance
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major incident involving feature flags.
- Owner for reviews: team-platform-flags@redwood.com

payload.page_title: operator-entropy-control-and-telemetry-debias-playbook-2026

sections.body:
SUMMARY

This playbook defines a repeatable program — Operator Entropy Control (OEC) — to reduce misleading signal, sampling bias, and alert noise in LLM-serving telemetry that operators depend on for oncall and capacity decisions. It documents goals, SLOs, detection heuristics, dashboard patterns, sampling and debiasing procedures, runbook actions, rollout safeties, ownership, and retrospective triggers.

WHY THIS MATTERS

Problem statement: operator decisions (evictions, tenant throttling, model fallbacks, prefetched cache policies) are increasingly driven by telemetry slices that can be biased by sampling, cohort skews, and aggregation semantics. This leads to:
- False-positive degradation incidents caused by sampling spikes (short-lived bursts treated as systemic).
- Hidden tail-latency regressions masked by mean/median-only dashboards.
- Costly operator actions triggered by telemetry artifacts (e.g., bursty telemetry from canaries).
- Regressions in fairness when tenant-level sampling is nonuniform.

Goal: ensure the telemetry surface used for operational decisioning is:
1) low-entropy (stable and explainable),
2) debiased across tenants and routes, and
3) actionable (high precision for true degradation).

SCOPE AND AUDIENCE

Scope: platform control plane + runtime operator dashboards, tenant chargeback telemetry, and regional prefetched cache health panels. This playbook does not replace per-service SLI design but provides platform-level controls and templates.
Audience: platform operators, oncall SREs, platform product, telemetry engineers, and observability SMEs.

MEASURABLE SUCCESS CRITERIA

- Reduction of paging noise: 40% drop in P1/P0 pages attributed to telemetry sampling artifacts over 90 days.
- Increase in alert precision: operator-confirmed false-positive rate ≤ 12% for major degradation alerts.
- Fairness lift: variance of token-per-tenant sample weights reduced by ≥ 50% across top-200 tenants in monthly audits.

DESIGN PRINCIPLES

- Prefer deterministic heuristics over opaque ML for oncall gating.
- Make sampling explicit and versioned; never rely on opaque “adaptive sampling” without a flag and rollout plan.
- Surface uncertainty intervals (90% conf) on cost and latency widgets.
- Provide both cohorted and global views side-by-side for context.

SLOS, ALERT CONTRACTS, AND ESCALATION FLOW
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Prefix-cache-hit-rate (p95): 98%
- Token-latency (p99): ≤ 600ms (regional)
- Token-cost-variance-index: <= 0.15 (monthly)
sections.heading: Primary SLOs (platform-facing)

sections.body:
1) Telemetry-entropy-warning (warning):
- Expr: increase in telemetry sampling variance by > 3x vs 1h baseline AND sample-count < 500 in last 10m
- Action: annotate dashboards, do not page.
2) Telemetry-entropy-degradation (page):
- Expr: p95 token-latency breach AND sample-count >= 1000 AND cohort-skew-score < 0.25
- Action: page oncall and attach debug bundle.
sections.heading: Alert categories and sample rules (examples)

sections.body:
alert: TelemetryEntropyWarning
expr: (stddev_over_time(metric_sample_count[10m]) / avg_over_time(metric_sample_count[1h])) > 3 and avg_over_time(metric_sample_count[10m]) < 500
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: warning
annotations:
  summary: "Telemetry sampling variance spike on {{ $labels.route }}"

TELEMETRY DESIGN PATTERNS (OPERATOR-FACING)

1) Dual-pane dashboards: every operator dashboard MUST show a cohorted pane (tenant/route/region) and an ensemble pane (global + weighted CI).
2) Sample-weighted aggregations: compute weighted means where each tenant contribution is capped to an upper bound (configurable; default 5% of total tokens) to avoid tail-dominance.
3) Explicit sample-count heatmap: include sample-count-by-minute with drift shading to indicate low-confidence periods.
4) Versioned samplers: any sampling config change must be tagged (sampler_v=N) and visible in panel headers.

SAMPLING & DEBIASING PROCEDURE (STEP-BY-STEP)

1) Baseline audit (weekly automated job):
   a) Compute token-per-tenant distribution for last 7d.
   b) Compute coefficient of variation (CV) and identify top-200 tenants by tokens.
   c) Report a sample-weight map that normalizes to target percentiles.
2) Apply capping and reweighting:
   - Cap method: clip tenant-token-contribution to max_cap = 0.05 * total_tokens_by_window.
   - Reweight method: redistribute excess mass proportionally to remaining tenants.
3) Inject synthetic control stream for small tenants: to avoid losing signal, inject a low-rate, deterministic probe request per tenant every 6 hours for health checks.
4) Adaptive sampling guardrails: if sample_count < 200 in window, suspend automated scaling decisions and mark charts as low confidence.

TELEMETRY DEBIASING ALGO (PSEUDO)
sections.heading: Prometheus example (conceptual)

sections.body:
1. total = sum(tenant_token_counts.values())
2. cap = target_cap_fraction * total
3. adjusted = empty map
4. spare = 0
5. for tenant, count in tenant_token_counts:
     if count > cap:
         adjusted[tenant] = cap
         spare += (count - cap)
     else:
         adjusted[tenant] = count
6. redistribute = spare / sum(adjusted[tenant] < cap)  # proportional
7. for tenant where adjusted[tenant] < cap:
     adjusted[tenant] += adjusted[tenant] / sum_remaining * redistribute
8. normalize weights = adjusted[tenant] / sum(adjusted.values())

DASHBOARD TEMPLATES AND TABLE (EXAMPLE)

| Panel | Purpose | Minimum Metrics | Confidence Indicator | Owner |
|------|---------|-----------------|----------------------|-------|
| Prefix cache health (cohort) | detect tenant-specific cache thrash | cache_hit_p95, sample_count | heatmap sample_count | cache-ops |
| Token latency ensemble | global latency trends with CI | token_latency_p50/p95/p99, sample_count | shaded CI | platform-observability |
| Sample-weight map | show per-tenant weights used for aggregates | token_count, adjusted_weight | numeric badge | telemetry-eng |

OPERATOR RUNBOOK: RESPONDING TO ENTROPY-RELATED PAGES

Priority: follow standard incident handling but add entropy-specific checks early to avoid wrong remediation.

1) Triage (0-5m):
   - Confirm the alert: check sample_count and telemetry-entropy-warning flags.
   - If sample_count < 200 or sample-count heatmap shows a gap, annotate and mark low-confidence. De-escalate automated eviction runbooks until sample_count recovers.
2) Context (5-15m):
   - Open tenant cohort vs ensemble panes side-by-side.
   - Run quick cohort-sanity query: compare recent 1m/5m windows against 1h baseline.
   - Check recent sampler_version and any recent sampler config rollouts.
3) Action (15-45m):
   - If signal is high-confidence: follow mitigation paths (evict tenant, bump priority, fallback model).
   - If low-confidence but operator sees sustained trend: increase sampling rate for affected cohorts (flip sampler_v) and schedule synthetic probe injection.
4) Communication (15-60m):
   - Annotate dashboards, add incident id to panels, notify tenant-facing CS if customer impact likely.
5) Post-incident (within 24h):
   - Run full sampling audit job, capture pre/post adjusted weights, and record in incident notes.

ROLLBACKS, SAFETIES, AND FLAGGING

- Any sampler config change requires: feature flag, Canary (5% traffic), automatic rollback threshold (increase in false-positive pages > 20% vs baseline), and runbook link.
- Default behavior on low-sample windows: suspend automated tenant-eviction and autoscale down decisions.
- CI for sampler changes: unit tests covering reweighting math + end-to-end synthetic probe integration.

ROLLOUT PLAN (QUARTERLY CADENCE)

1) Week 0: baseline audit and dashboard rollout (read-only).
2) Week 1–2: Canary sampler_v rollout to low-risk cohort (5% traffic).
3) Week 3: expand to 25% if false-positive pages unchanged; run targeted operator drills.
4) Week 4: platform-wide rollout with 24/7 operator shadowing for first 72 hours.

OWNER ROLES AND CONTACTS

- Platform Observability (owner): telemetry-eng@redwood.com (primary contact for dashboards and CI).
- Operator Liaisons: platform-ops@redwood.com (runbook execution).
- Product / Cost: cost-analytics@redwood.com (chargeback and fairness audits).

RETRO TRIGGERS AND LEARNING LOOPS

Open a retrospective when any of the following occur within a 30d window:
- ≥ 3 entropy-related pages for the same root cause,
- False-positive page rate > 12% for major alerts, or
- Rollback triggered during sampler rollout.
sections.heading: output: adjusted_weights map

sections.body:
- Timeline and actions
- Telemetry evidence (pre/post sampling maps)
- Root-cause hypothesis and validation queries
- Remediation plan and owner assignment

APPENDIX A: EXAMPLE QUERIES (BIGQUERY/SQL STYLE)

-- compute tenant token distribution over 7d
SELECT tenant_id, SUM(tokens) AS token_sum
FROM llm_token_events
WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY token_sum DESC
LIMIT 500

-- compute sample-weighted token latency p95
SELECT approx_percentile(latency_ms, 0.95, adjusted_weight) AS p95_latency
FROM telemetry_aggregates
WHERE window = '5m'

APPENDIX B: SAMPLE ALERT RULE (YAML FOR ALERTMGR)

- alert: TelemetryEntropyDegradation
  expr: |
    (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > 0.6)
    and (avg_over_time(sample_count[10m]) > 1000)
    and (cohort_skew_score < 0.25)
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "High-confidence token latency degradation with low cohort skew on {{ $labels.route }}"

APPENDIX C: QUICK CHECKLIST FOR OPERATORS (SHRINKED)

- Check sample_count and sampler_v on alert panes.
- Confirm cohort vs ensemble divergence.
- If low-sample, increase sampling or defer automated eviction.
- If canary sampler recently rolled, mark it and consider quick rollback.
- Run post-incident sampling audit job and attach results to incident.

DOCUMENT MAINTENANCE

- Owner (telemetry-eng) reviews this playbook quarterly and after any sampler rollouts.
- Change log:
  - 2025-09-15: Initial draft (Marcus Chen)
  - 2025-11-05: Added synthetic probe pattern (Aisha Patel)
  - 2026-01-22: Formalized alert contracts and rollout cadence (Leah O'Connor)

END OF DOCUMENT

payload.page_title: Capacity Drift Detection & Correction Playbook

sections.body:
Overview:

This playbook describes how the platform team detects, triages, and corrects capacity drift across Redwood’s serving fleets (hosted, dedicated, and private). Capacity drift is any slow-moving divergence between provisioned capacity and actual workload demand that leads to elevated tail latency, reduced throughput, or unexpected cost. The procedures below assume the platform observability stack (Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager), the capacity datastore (capacity-store), and the autoscaler/fleet manager (fleetmgr) are available.

Why this matters:

- Prevents user-facing latency degradations by keeping headroom aligned with request distributions.
- Controls cost by avoiding overprovisioning driven by stale sizing heuristics.
- Ensures predictable rollouts of new models and kernel changes by limiting surprise capacity shortages.

Scope and ownership:

- Services covered: platform-scheduler, request-router, model-proxy, inference-pool (GPU), batch-encoder, kvcache-store.
- Primary owner: eng-platform (capacity reliability pod).
- Secondary owners: eng-sre (monitoring+alerts) and eng-serving-runtime (runtime regressions).

Detection signals (ranked):

1) Tail latency divergence
- Signal: 95th/99th percentile token-generation latency increases relative to rolling baseline (>20% over 6 hours).
- Query example (PromQL):
  increase(token_generation_latency_seconds_bucket{quantile="0.99"}[6h]) / ignoring(quantile) group_left() token_generation_latency_seconds_count > 0

2) Average queue depth per replica
- Signal: sustained queue depth > configured headroom threshold (default 2.0 requests per replica) for >15 minutes.

3) Autoscaler scaling failures or backoff events
- Signal: fleetmgr scaling_backoff_total > 0 within last 10 minutes.

4) Capacity-store consistency alerts
- Signal: desired_capacity != reported_capacity for >10m for any pool.

5) Cost-to-throughput ratio shift
- Signal: tokens/instance-hour drops by >25% relative to rolling 7d baseline.

Alerting and dashboards:

- Golden dashboard: "Capacity Drift — Platform" (Grafana panel set) with:
  - 95/99 latency heatmap by pool,
  - desired vs actual capacity timeseries,
  - queue depth histogram,
  - autoscaler activity timeline,
  - cost per token and tokens per instance-hour.

- Alert rules (Alertmanager):
  - capacity_drift_latency_high: fires when p99_latency > p99_baseline * 1.25 for 15m. Severity: P2.
  - capacity_store_mismatch: fires when sum(desired_capacity - actual_capacity) != 0 for 10m. Severity: P1.
  - autoscaler_backoff_rate: fires when rate(fleetmgr_scaling_backoff_total[5m]) > 0. Severity: P1.

Triage checklist (first 10 minutes):

1) Confirm alert and scope
- Identify affected pools and models from alert metadata.
- Check whether incident correlates with a deployment, config change, or scheduled maintenance (look at runbook events dashboard and changelog).

2) Check autoscaler status
- Run: fleetmgr describe-pool <pool-name> --output=json\- Review recent scaling events: fleetmgr events --since 1h --pool <pool-name>

3) Verify capacity-store consistency
- Query: curl -s https://capacity-store.internal/api/v1/pools/<pool-name> | jq .desired_replicas,.reported_replicas

4) Validate resource constraints
- Check cloud quotas and node health: kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=<pool-name>
- If using bare-metal racks, check rack-healthboard and rack p95 power draw.

Automated correction actions (safe-by-default):

- If desired_capacity > actual_capacity and cloud quota is available -> automated replenishment job: capacity-replenish --pool <pool> --reason "capacity-drift-auto"
- If queue depth is high and autoscaler healthy -> temporary burst scaling: fleetmgr scale --pool <pool> --replicas +20% --ttl 10m (must include cust tag and queue drain hook)
- If autoscaler is failing due to config -> fallback to emergency static scaling: fleetmgr set-static --pool <pool> --replicas <safe-min>

Manual remediation runbook (for P1 incidents):

Step 0: Pager and comms
- Notify: #platform-incident Slack channel, @oncall-eng-platform.

Step 1: Isolate cause (10–25m)
- Check correlation with recent change: query deploy-history --since=1h --service=<service>
- Check model onboarding jobs: rocket-queue inspect --tag model-onboard
- Check kernel/driver updates that could reduce scheduling density: list latest node-agent versions.

Step 2: Capacity correction (25–45m)
- If quota-limited in cloud: open support ticket using cloud-cli support create --title "quota bump for <pool>" and attach reproducible load snapshot (grafana link + promql snapshot).
- If node health issues: cordon unhealthy nodes: kubectl cordon <node>; provision replacement nodes: cloud-cli node create --type <instance-type> --tags pool=<pool>.
- If autoscaler misconfiguration: revert autoscaler config to last-known-good: git checkout refs/heads/ops/autoscaler-config@{2025-01-10} && apply.

Step 3: Validate and de-escalate (45–90m)
- Watch key signals for improvement for 10–15 minutes.
- If corrected, close alert and file an incident with root-cause hypothesis. If not, escalate to eng-sre and eng-serving-runtime.

Post-incident retrospective template (to be completed within 3 business days):

- Summary: one-paragraph timeline and impact metrics (requests affected, p99 uplift, cost delta).
- Root cause: (human + technical).
- What went well: automated mitigations, alert fidelity, comms.
- Action items (owner + due date): e.g., update autoscaler config, add quota preflight job, improve alert threshold.
- Validation plan: how we will confirm the action reduced recurrence risk.

Runbook automation snippets (examples):

- Prometheus query for p99 baseline comparison:
  baseline_p99 = avg_over_time(p99_latency_seconds[7d:1h])
  alert_expr = (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_generation_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool)) / baseline_p99) > 1.25

- Fleetmgr CLI burst scale example:
  fleetmgr scale --pool inference-gpu-us-east-1 --replicas +200 --ttl 600 --reason "burst-autoscale"

- Capacity-store reconciliation cron (k8s CronJob):
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: capacity-reconcile
  spec:
    schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
            - name: reconcile
              image: redwood/capacity-tool:stable
              args: ["reconcile", "--dry-run=false"]

Metrics to add to dashboards (short list):

- desired_capacity / reported_capacity (per pool)
- p50/p95/p99 latency ratio to 7d baseline
- queue depth per replica across pools
- tokens generated per instance-hour
- fleetmgr scaling backoff rate and reasons

Roadmap items (next 6 months):

1) Preflight capacity check for canary rollouts (Q2 2025): integrate canary with capacity-store to ensure new model does not cause >10% headroom consumption.
2) Predictive scaling prototype (Q3 2025): use short-term demand forecasting to pre-warm pools before peak windows.
3) Cost-signal integration (Q3 2025): surface cost-per-token in autoscaler decisions to trade cost vs latency.

Appendix: links & contacts

- Runbook owners: eng-platform_capacity@redwood.com
- On-call rotations: /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/platform-regional-capacity-matrix-and-shifthandoff-handbook-2024
- Relevant dashboards: Grafana > Capacity Drift — Platform

Change history:

- 2024-11-15: Created by Maya Chen (v1).
- 2025-02-10: Updated automation snippets and added predictive scaling roadmap item (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Priya Nair).
