payload.page_title: gpu-traffic-synthesis-and-tenant-fingerprint-library

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the GPU Traffic Synthesis and Tenant Fingerprint Library: a canonical set of synthetic tenant profiles, traffic scenario definitions, and CI/CD integration guidance used to exercise the fleet, account egress paths, and quota/egress throttles in preflight and continuous validation. The library enables repeatable capacity tests, regression detection, kernel-mix experiments, and telemetry-map validation without using customer data.

Goals
- Provide a concise, extensible fingerprint schema that describes tenant workload characteristics (token distribution, sequence length, KV cache reuse, model family, quantization profile).
- Offer a curated scenario catalog (bursting, long-seq tails, chat-like small messages, eval-eval concurrent workloads) that maps to operational risk categories.
- Define how to run the harness locally, in CI, and at scale against shadow endpoints (capacity-sentry / shadow-cluster).
- Ensure telemetry emitted during runs maps back to SLO signal names (p99_latency_ms, token_cost_usd, kv_cache_hit_rate).

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: infra testing that exercises serving runtime, egress fabric, allocator, and rate-limit controllers. Includes Terraform module shapes for synthetic-tenant provisioning and CI pipelines for nightly and PR checks.
- Non-goal: Final production load-testing of customer traffic — do not reuse production credentials or customer prompts.

Fingerprint schema (v1)
Each fingerprint is a small JSON document that describes a simulated tenant. Fields shown below are required unless noted. Keep entries under 2 KB.
- tenant_id: string (human-readable id used in metrics tags)
- model: string (e.g., gptj-6b-qlora, rwx-13b-8bit)
- seq_length_p50: integer (median sequence length)
- seq_length_p95: integer
- tokens_per_minute: integer (steady-state tokens/min)
- burst_profile: enum [none, short, medium, long] (describes burst duration patterns)
- kv_reuse_rate: float (0.0-1.0 fraction of requests that can reuse KV cache)
- concurrency: integer (parallel in-flight requests)
- call_type: enum [text_generate, chat_stream, embedding, rerank]
- quant_profile: string (e.g., q4_0, q8_0, fp16)
- egress_pattern: enum [low, balanced, egress_spike] (used to route synthetic egress)
- labels: list of strings (optional tagging)

Example fingerprint (JSON)
{
  "tenant_id": "search-svc-sim-01",
  "model": "rwx-13b-8bit",
  "seq_length_p50": 32,
  "seq_length_p95": 127,
  "tokens_per_minute": 15000,
  "burst_profile": "short",
  "kv_reuse_rate": 0.8,
  "concurrency": 4,
  "call_type": "chat_stream",
  "quant_profile": "q8_0",
  "egress_pattern": "balanced",
  "labels": ["indexing","search"]
}

Scenario catalog (select)
We keep a small, well-defined catalog that maps to operationally meaningful tests. Use the scenario id when scheduling runs.

| scenario_id | description | primary_risk | expected_metric_priority | run_target |
|-------------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------|-----------|
| sustained-burst-60m | Steady tokens/min with periodic short bursts, 60 minutes | throughput / allocator pressure | p95_latency, queue_length, token_cost_usd | shadow-cluster |
| long-seq-tail | Small number of tenants issuing sequences > 1k tokens intermittently | memory / KV cache fragmentation | kv_cache_miss_rate, memory_pressure, p99_latency | capacity-sentry |
| embed-blast | High-concurrency small embedding requests | egress cost and network throughput | egress_bytes/s, embedding_unit_cost | shadow-proxy |
| mixed-precision-roll | Mixed q4/q8/fp16 allocation churn | kernel degradation and flakiness | kernel_error_rate, quant_fallbacks | kernel-lab |

(ASCII table above intended for copy/paste; internal tooling will translate into Confluence table automatically.)

How to run the harness
1) Local quick check
- Prereqs: python3.11, virtualenv, docker (for local shadow proxy).
- Checkout repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/gpu-sim-harness.git
- Setup: make venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
- Run: python run_harness.py --fingerprint samples/search-svc-sim-01.json --scenario sustained-burst-60m --target shadow-local

2) PR-level smoke (CI)
- CI job name: ci/gpu-sim/pr-smoke. Minimal run: 5 minutes against mini-shadow deployed in the PR sandbox.
- Pass criteria: no kernel_error_rate > 0.5% and p95_latency within baseline +/- 30%.
- Failure action: raise the PR check and attach a telemetry dump at /artifacts/sim/{run-id}.tgz

3) Nightly full sweep
- Job: ci/gpu-sim/nightly-catalog. Runs full catalog across two regions (us-west-2 shadow, eu-west-1 shadow).
- Observability: automated diffs for these telemetry signals: p99_latency_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, egress_bytes_per_min, token_cost_usd. Alerts created when any signal drifts > 10% vs 28-day baseline.

CI/CD integration details
- The harness lives in infra/ci/gpu-sim. A GitHub Actions workflow templates/gpu-sim.yml is used across repos to invoke the harness.
- The Terraform module for provisioning synthetic tenants is tfmodule/gpu-sim-tenant. Module inputs: tenant_count, allowed_egress_buckets, target_region, sandbox_account_id. Example snippet:
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
module "sim_tenant" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/tfmodules.git//gpu-sim-tenant?ref=stable"
  tenant_count = 3
  allowed_egress_buckets = ["sg-analytics-sim"]
  target_region = "us-west-2"
  sandbox_account_id = "111222333444"
}

Telemetry mapping and dashboards
- Metric tag conventions: sim.tenant_id, sim.scenario, sim.run_id. Use these tags for querying in Grafana/Influx.
- Canonical metrics emitted by harness: tokens/min, p50/p95/p99 latency_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, kernel_error_rate, egress_bytes, cpu/gpu_util_pct.
- Dashboards: dashboards/gpu-sim/overview and dashboards/gpu-sim/{scenario}-breakdown. Each dashboard includes a baseline overlay (28-day rolling median).

Ownership and SLAs
- Owner: infra/gpu-team (primary), eng-platform (secondary).
- On-call: gpu-team oncall handles synthetic-run alerts during nightly windows (00:00-04:00 UTC).
- SLAs for the harness itself: nightly run must complete within 3 hours; if it fails 2 nights in a row, SEV-3 ticket with ops team.

Runbook: triage checklist when a simulation indicates regression
1) Validate run integrity: confirm run_id completed and that synthetic tenants were actually provisioned (check tfstate/artifact manifest).
2) Check kernel_error_rate and collect last 2 minutes of kernel logs from kernel-lab nodes:
- CLI: ./infra_tools/collect_kernel_logs.sh --run ${RUN_ID} --out /tmp/kernel-${RUN_ID}.tgz
3) Verify allocator saturation: query allocator-operator:
- kubectl -n allocator get pods -l app=allocator-operator -o wide
- curl -sS http://allocator-operator.internal/debug/metrics | grep queue_length
4) If egress_bytes spike is primary signal, check VPC egress proxy and NAT gateway metrics and correlate to tenant labels.
5) Open a postmortem if regression persists for > 6 hours or customer-facing traffic impacted. Include telemetry diff screenshot and run fingerprint JSON.

Extensibility patterns
- Add a fingerprint by creating a JSON under samples/fingerprints and incrementing catalog.json. Keep new fingerprints small and add reviewer.
- For new scenarios, add an entry to scenarios/catalog.yaml and include expected signal priority and baseline. New scenarios must be reviewed by GPU-runtime and Observability teams.

Security and safety constraints
- Do not store PII or customer prompts. All synthetic input content must be generated from the licensed synthetic corpus (repo: datasets/synthetic/README.md).
- Synthetic tenants must be isolated to sandbox accounts and use dedicated service accounts with limited iam:PassRole rights.

Appendix: Quick example of a CI job step (GitHub Actions)
- name: Run GPU sim smoke
  uses: redwood-inference/infra-actions/run-sim@v1
  with:
    fingerprint: samples/search-svc-sim-01.json
    scenario: sustained-burst-60m
    target: shadow-pr

Related pages
- /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-demand-forecasting-and-ml-backed-scaling-playbook
- /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook

Maintainer notes
- Keep baseline windows at 28 days. If we change the baseline window, record the change in the page history and notify the Observability team.
- Periodically (quarterly) run a cross-team rehearsal with product/eval teams to ensure the synthetic corpus reflects realistic prompt mixes.

Document history
- 2024-02-15: initial sketch (Priya Singh)
- 2024-05-02: added long-seq-tail scenario and TF module example (Jason Liu)
- 2025-07-10: updated CI pass criteria and nightly window (Maya Chen)

payload.page_title: GPU runtime compatibility matrix and rollout playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the compatibility matrix for GPU runtimes we operate at Redwood and provides a step-by-step rollout playbook for introducing new runtime versions or kernel stacks to the fleet. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform release owners.

Goals
- Reduce model regressions introduced by runtime/kernel changes.
- Provide a repeatable, low-risk rollout path for runtime upgrades across regions and tenant classes.
- Capture compatibility constraints (CUDA/cuDNN/NCCL/kernel combos) so IaC and scheduler can make safe placement decisions.

Scope
- Applies to on-host GPU runtimes used by the serving runtime (service name: gpu-orchestrator) and the batch/eval fleet (service name: gpu-eval-worker).
- Covers Linux AMI bundles, CUDA/cuDNN/NCCL versions, GPU driver ABI compatibility, and kernel-level optimizations used by our inference kernels (kernel-hint v2).
- Does NOT cover hardware-level procurement or firmware upgrade procedures (see gpu-fleet-scaling-metrics-and-oncall-runbook).

Compatibility matrix (reference)

Note: This table is authoritative for the scheduler and Terraform placement modules. When adding a new runtime, update the Terraform module variable supported_runtimes and the placement constraints in module.gpu-node.

| Runtime name | Host driver (NVIDIA) | CUDA | cuDNN | NCCL | Models verified | Max seq len | Notes |
|--------------|---------------------:|-----:|------:|----:|----------------|-----------:|-------|
| runtime-2024-10 (stable) | 535.86 | 12.1 | 9.3 | 2.16 | Llama2-13B, Mistral-7B, Bloom | 4096 | Default for hosted-prod; supports tensor-core int8 kernels. |
| runtime-2025-01 (canary) | 545.23 | 13.0 | 9.5 | 2.18 | Llama2-13B (quantized), RedModel-Base | 8192 | New kernel-hint v3 enabled; improved KV-cache layout. Canary only. |
| runtime-arm64-2024-12 | 520.61 | 11.8 | 8.2 | 2.10 | Mistral-7B (arm build) | 2048 | For edge/arm pools; limited NCCL rings. |
| runtime-legacy-12x | 470.42 | 11.4 | 8.0 | 2.8 (legacy) | Legacy models for Dedicated customers | 1024 | Keep on a small pool for customers that pinned legacy stack. |

Compatibility guidance
- Scheduler should match model profile to runtime: e.g., models requiring kernel-hint v3 must be placed on runtime-2025-01 or higher.
- If driver bump > major (e.g., 535 -> 545), create a canary pool with isolated VPC/subnet and enrollment tag gpu:canary=true.
- Maintain at least one node pool with 'legacy' runtime for customer pinning; enforce capacity quotas to prevent accidental eviction.

Terraform / IaC changes required when adding a runtime
1) Module changes (recommended pattern):
   - Filename: modules/gpu-runtime/README.md and variables.tf
   - New variable: supported_runtimes = ["runtime-2024-10", "runtime-2025-01"]
   - Add data source to map AMI -> runtime tag: data.aws_ami.gpu_runtime_lookup
2) Example snippet to pin a pool to a runtime (HCL):

   module "gpu_pool_canary" {
     source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu-pool"
     name   = "gpu-pool-canary-us-west-2"
     node_count = 8
     runtime_tag = "runtime-2025-01"
     tenancy = "dedicated"
     labels = { "gpu:canary" = "true", "tier" = "canary" }
   }

3) Apply pattern: use -target for initial provisioning and avoid full plan apply when seeding canaries. Example CLI:
   terraform apply -target=module.gpu_pool_canary -var='region=us-west-2' -var='runtime=runtime-2025-01'

Rollout playbook (high-level)
Prerequisites
- CI/CD artifact: runtime AMI baked and signed, image tag uploaded to image registry (ami://redwood/gpu/runtime-2025-01).
- Benchmarks: perf run artifacts uploaded to S3 (s3://redwood-benchmarks/runtime-2025-01/).
- Owner assigned (release owner): infrastructure release lead (see Ownership).

Step 0 — Create canary pools (isolated)\1. Provision 2 canary pools: one for hosted-prod traffic (8 nodes), one for eval/batch (4 nodes).
2. Tag pools with gpu:canary=true and runtime_tag=runtime-2025-01.
3. Update scheduler placement rules to consider runtime_tag label for canary traffic only.

Step 1 — Validation smoke tests (automated, 4h window)\1. Run model seeding smoke: 1000 short inference requests across canary pools.
2. Verify functional correctness: token outputs must match golden references within tolerance thresholds for 95% of requests.
3. Run perf regression check: p50, p95, p99 token latency and token/s throughput compared to baseline.
   - Pass if p95 latency delta <= +10% and p50 delta <= +5% and token/s delta <= -10%.
4. Run memory and OOM soak: 72h soak with a mix of sequences up to declared max seq len; monitor gpu.memory.used.

Step 2 — Canary traffic ramp (gradual)\1. Open routing for <1% of production traffic to runtime canary. Hold 2 hours.
2. If no alerts and metric deltas within thresholds, increase to 5% for 4 hours.
3. Then 10% for 12 hours.
4. Evaluate logs for tail errors, e.g., NCCL errors, driver warnings.

Step 3 — Regional expansion\1. After successful canary in primary region (us-west-2), provision canary pools in eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1.
2. Repeat Steps 1–2 in each region.

Step 4 — Fleet-wide roll\1. Convert canary pools into standard pools by scaling node counts and flipping labels, or provision new pools and repoint routing.
2. Rollout in waves by tenant class: non-SLA dev -> hosted standard -> dedicated reserved -> high-priority tenants.
3. Use cluster autoscaler safeguards: set max surge of +20% and drain strategy = safest.

Rollback / emergency procedure
- Trigger conditions: sustained p99 token latency > 2x baseline, spike in kernel OOMs > 0.5% of requests, or NCCL driver errors with severity >= WARN.
- Immediate actions:
  1) Remove runtime_tag from scheduler rotation to stop new placements onto runtime-2025-01 (CLI: curl -XPOST https://gpu-scheduler.internal/api/v1/placement/disable?tag=runtime-2025-01).
  2) Start a controlled drain of pods on runtime-2025-01 nodes: kubectl cordon/evict with drain-grace-period=120s and retry backoff.
  3) Repoint affected tenant routes to compatible runtime pools using fallback policy (fallback runtime: runtime-2024-10).
  4) Open incident in PagerDuty and page infra-oncall and runtime-release-owner.

Monitoring and SLOs (examples)
- Latency SLOs to watch during rollout: p95 token latency < 120ms (small models), p99 < 350ms for long-seq workloads.
- Availability SLO: < 0.1% error rate increase from baseline during rollout windows.
- PromQL examples:
  - p95 token latency (hosted): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(token_generation_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  - GPU memory OOMs: sum(rate(gpu_memory_oom_total[5m])) by (region)
  - NCCL warnings: sum(rate(nccl_warning_total[5m])) by (driver_version)

Ownership and contacts\- Release owner (runtime upgrades): Aisha Patel (infra-release@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler owner: Diego Martinez
- GPU fleet lead: Sofia Nguyen
- Oncall rota: infra-oncall@redwood.ai (see oncall-and-incident-response team wiki for current schedule)

Instrumenting the scheduler and placement module\- Add runtime_tag as a first-class constraint: placement must consider {runtime_tag, driver_version, arch}.
- Example placement JSON label used by scheduler:
  {"labels": {"runtime_tag": "runtime-2025-01", "gpu_driver": "545.23", "arch": "x86_64"}}
- Terraform variable to expose in module.gpu-pool: allowed_runtime_tags = ["runtime-2024-10", "runtime-2025-01"]

Testing checklist (pre-roll)
- Unit: module/gpu-runtime unit tests and AMI validation script pass.
- Integration: allocator + scheduler + ci-eval workflows green in staging.
- Perf: perf artifacts within thresholds and comparison report uploaded.
- Canary: automated rollback script validated in integration.

Post-roll validation (48–72h)
- Verify per-tenant cost delta (tokens/s) and GPU utilization trend.
- Run synthetic evaluation against golden prompt set and validate output-quality metrics (exact-match, BLEU-like metrics for structured outputs).
- Capture and file any regressions as regression tickets with tags: regression/runtime/<runtime-name>.

Appendices\A. Example AMI tagging policy (bash snippet)\\n#!/bin/bash
AMI_ID=$1
RUNTIME_TAG=$2
aws ec2 create-tags --resources ${AMI_ID} --tags Key=Runtime,Value=${RUNTIME_TAG} Key=Owner,Value=infra-team Key=Signed,Value=true

B. Minimum CI perf suite (high level)\- microbench: 1000 generations of short (<128 tokens) requests\- kv-cache test: open-loop 1M tokens across sequences\- memory-soak: allocate up to declared max seq len for 24h

C. Short glossary\- runtime_tag: logical label used to represent a specific runtime/driver/kernel stack.
- canary pool: an isolated node pool used for initial validation.
- kernel-hint: our inference runtime configuration that toggles optimized kernels.

Change log\- 2024-11-05: Created initial doc (Aisha Patel).
- 2024-12-16: Added PromQL examples and terraform snippets (reviewer: Diego Martinez).
- 2025-01-18: Clarified rollback thresholds and added regional expansion guidance (Sofia Nguyen).

Related pages and references\- Runtime versioning and deprecation policy: /confluence/eng-infra/runtime-architecture/runtime-versioning-guidelines
- Terraform runtime module: git@repo.redwood.ai:infra-modules/modules/gpu-runtime

End of document

payload.page_title: hetero-burst-simulation-and-ci-safety-catalog

sections.body:
Overview:
This runbook-and-catalog collates operational patterns, Terraform validation checks, CI/CD safety heuristics, and a small batch of deterministic simulation tests for heterogeneous (CPU/GPU/TPU) burst scenarios. It is intended for infra engineers who operate Redwood's tenant-facing GPU pools, platform SREs who run capacity simulations, and the CI/CD team that gates GPU node and runtime changes.

Goals:
- Provide a reproducible simulation harness and dataset for modeling short-duration bursts (1–30 minutes) across heterogeneous pools.
- Define a set of CI safety checks that prevent disruptive kernel/runtime/driver changes from reaching prod GPU pools.
- Offer Terraform/IaC validators and example module contracts for tenant network/e­gress and quota behavior during bursts.
- Capture oncall runbook steps for degradation, tenant backpressure, and graceful spillover to reserve pools.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated GPU pools (warm-pool and spot-fallback configurations).
- Covers egress-sensitive workloads (large embeddings and eval jobs) and short-lived interactive inference bursts.
- Not a replacement for full-scale capacity procurement planning—this focuses on operational safety, simulation, and CI gating.

Key Concepts and Definitions:
- Burst window: A contiguous period of high request rate for a tenant (default 1–30 minutes).
- Hetero pool: A logical GPU pool that mixes instance types (A100, H100, fractional GPUs) and CPU types.
- Tenant reservation: Dedicated allocation or soft quota assigned via Terraform module.
- Reserve hot-pool: Standby pre-warmed nodes used for immediate spillover (SLO-backed).
- Cost-smoothing multiplier: Policy parameter used by scheduler to prefer fractional multiplexing during bursts.

SLOs and Targets (applies during bursts):
- 95th pct latency for short text completion requests: <= 200 ms on dedicated path, <= 350 ms on hosted fallback path.
- Burst success rate (requests served without fallback to cold-start): >= 98% for tenants with active warm allocations.
- Tenant isolation (no noisy neighbor > 10% increase in latency for adjacent tenants) during controlled tests.

Simulation Harness (quickstart):
1) Repository and entrypoint:
- repo: github.com/redwood-inference/infra-sim/hb-sim
- command: ./simulate-burst --config configs/hetero-10k-1m.yaml

2) Example config (YAML fragment):

# configs/hetero-10k-1m.yaml
pool_profile: hetero-mixed
node_counts: [8, 4, 2] # A100, H100, fractional pools
tenants:
  - id: tenant-redwood-eval
    rps: 10000
    tail_percentiles: [95,99]
burst_window_seconds: 60
retries: 2
network_latency_ms: {p50:2, p95:8}

3) Outputs:
- time-series of per-tenant latency (p50/p95/p99), queue depth, node-utilization, and KV-cache hit-rate
- allocation trace that shows where scheduler routed requests and whether spillover occurred

CI/CD Safety Heuristics (gates and checks):
- Pre-merge: Linting and unit tests for Terraform modules; static analysis for changes to iac-module manifests.
- Merge-blocking: If a PR touches GPU runtime or kernel packaging, require successful CI simulation that runs at least two deterministic scenarios (a short burst and a cold-start scale-up).
- Canary gating: Changes that adjust scheduler heuristics or Cost-smoothing multiplier must run a gated canary that:
  1) Deploys to a staging hetero pool (min 3 nodes)
  2) Runs burst sim job with tenant traffic mix (configs/staging-hetero.yaml)
  3) Validates SLOs above; otherwise automatically rollback.

Terraform/IaC Module Contracts and Validators:
- Module contract example for tenant reservation (short form):
  - variables: tenant_id (string), min_gpu (number), max_gpu (number), reserved_egress_mbps (number), region (string)
  - outputs: reservation_id (string), route_table_id (string)

- Policy as Code checks (pre-apply):
  - Ensure reserved_egress_mbps <= account_quota_egress_mbps
  - Validate that min_gpu <= max_gpu and min_gpu <= 128
  - Confirm that network CIDR does not overlap shared-management subnets

Example Terraform validation command (CI step):
- terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform validate && ./policy-checks.sh --module path/to/tenant-reservation

Network and Egress Considerations During Bursts:
- Egress shapers: Use per-tenant token bucket policer on egress sidecar, set burst_bucket_ms to 50 ms and max_burst_bytes to reserved_egress_mbps * 1000 / 8 * 5 (5s of burst).
- NAT pool sizing: For short high-RPS bursts, ensure NAT ephemeral ports per account are provisioned to handle peak connections; NAT shortage leads to TCP stalls and amplified latency.
- Cross-account peering: Prefer privatelink-style peering with enforced MTU 8900 to reduce serialization for large embedding payloads.

Runbook: Burst detection and mitigation (oncall steps)
1) Detection:
  - Alert: A composite alert fires when tenant_p95_latency >= threshold AND tenant_queue_depth > 50 for > 30s.
  - Dashboard: Open the hetero-burst dashboard and inspect allocation trace.
2) Triage:
  - Identify affected tenant_id and trace route (scheduler -> pool -> node).
  - Check node-level metrics: GPU util, process OOMs, kernel restarts, NVLink errors.
3) Immediate mitigations (in order):
  a) Activate reserve hot-pool spillover (runbook command: infractl pool spillover --tenant <id> --target reserve-hot-pool)
  b) Apply per-tenant throttling: infractl tenant throttle --tenant <id> --qps 0.8*current
  c) If egress saturation observed, apply egress-policing override to prioritize control-plane traffic.
4) If mitigations fail within 3 minutes:
  - Escalate to Senior SRE oncall and run kernel-driver rollback (only in emergency).
  - Notify customer-success for tenants in dedicated agreements.
5) Post-incident:
  - Collect sim traces and run the same simulation config with increased fidelity (network & serialization flags enabled).
  - Create an incident postmortem with root cause, timeline, and remediation checklist.

Safety Catalogue (short rules):
- Never merge driver updates without a green canary simulation and one successful canary on staging hetero pool.
- IaC changes that increase tenant max_gpu require an approvals label from finance for cost exposure > $5k/month.
- Any change to default per-tenant egress_shaper must include a migration plan and a monitored rollout window (48 hours).

Telemetry and Dashboarding:
- Required metrics (instrumentation keys): tenant_p50_latency_ms, tenant_p95_latency_ms, tenant_queue_depth, node_gpu_util_pct, node_kernel_errors_total, nat_ephemeral_ports_in_use, egress_bytes_per_min
- Dashboards: hetero-burst-live, tenant-spillover-history, nat-port-heatmap
- Synthetic probes: Schedule a 1-min burst probe per region every 2 hours to detect regressions early.

Examples and Snippets:
- infractl CLI spillover example:
  # spillover to reserve pool
  infractl pool spillover --tenant redwood-eval --target reserve-hot-pool --duration 300

- Minimal policy-checks.sh (bash):
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  module=$1
  terraform validate "$module" || exit 1
  # run OPA policies
  opa test policies/ -b "$module" || exit 1
  echo "policy checks passed"

Ownership and Responsibilities:
- Primary owner: GPU Fleet and Capacity team (eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity)
- CI gating & simulation harness: CI/CD and Build team (eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build)
- Network and egress policies: Cloud Accounts and Networking (eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking)
- Oncall escalation target: Platform SRE (eng-sre)

Roadmap and Next Steps:
- Q4 2025: Add multi-region correlated burst simulations (simulate cross-region failover cases).
- Q1 2026: Integrate sim harness outputs with Optimize to generate automated batch recommendations for cost-smoothing multipliers.
- Short-term: Add a canary pipeline that mirrors real tenant traffic patterns for high-fidelity validation.

Appendix: Useful links and references
- IaC module templates: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/module-stability-testing-and-rollback-catalog
- CI sim harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/infra-sim/hb-sim
- Incident postmortem template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

If you plan to run the simulation locally or add new scenarios, file a short RFC in the team wiki and tag the CI team for a new job slot.

payload.page_title: Heterogeneous GPU Fleet Shaping — Lab Notebook

sections.body:
Overview

This lab notebook documents reproducible experiments and operational recipes for shaping a heterogeneous GPU fleet to optimize inference cost, latency, and reliability. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and performance-focused platform owners who run experiments to inform pool sizing, placement policies, and IaC configurations.

Goals

- Produce repeatable experiments that compare mixed-GPU pools (e.g., A100, H100, L4, T4) across representative inference workloads.
- Measure economics (per-token CPU/GPU cost), tail latency (p95/p99 for token generation), throughput, and preemption impact.
- Generate Terraform variants and CI artifacts that can be promoted into staging for safety testing.
- Deliver recommendations (pool mixes, instance families, spot vs on-demand ratios) and a data capture template for decision records.

Scope and assumptions

- Focus on inference-serving workloads (short to long context LLM token streaming and batch embedding jobs).
- Experiments run in a dedicated sandbox AWS account with service quotas isolated from prod.
- The notebook emphasizes metrics capture over model selection — model variants are instrumented separately in the eval harness.

Prerequisites

1) Sandbox AWS account with permissions: terraform, EC2/GPU quota, CloudWatch, S3.
2) CI runner with GPU access (Buildkite/Runner images as provisioned by ci-cd team).
3) Runner image containing: nvidia drivers, CUDA, docker, runc, and the inference harness container.
4) Terraform module catalog referenced: sources/confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/* (use the fleet-allocator module in staging).

Experiment matrix (example)

Columns: experiment_id | pool_mix | spot_pct | region | workload_profile | target_qps
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- E1 | 1x A100 + 4x L4 | 10% | us-west-2 | streaming-short (context=1024) | 500 qps
- E2 | 2x H100 + 2x A100 | 0% | us-east-1 | batch-embeddings (batch=512) | 200 qps
- E3 | 6x L4 | 40% | us-west-2 | low-latency-chat (context=256) | 800 qps
- E4 | mixed (A100/H100/L4) with node-affinity tiling | 25% | eu-west-1 | mixed (100ms/500ms tail targets) | 600 qps

Workload profiles (definitions)

- streaming-short: synthetic prompt stream that produces 50–300 tokens per request, 10–40 ms token inter-arrival for burst simulation.
- batch-embeddings: CPU-heavy batching workload; high memory usage per request; measures per-item latency and tokenized overhead.
- low-latency-chat: small contexts (<=256), high QPS, sensitive to p95/p99 tail.

Data capture schema (CSV/JSON keys)

- experiment_id, timestamp, region, instance_type, pool_mix, spot_pct, qps_target, measured_qps, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, avg_gpu_util_pct, avg_gpu_mem_pct, cost_per_hour_usd, tokens_generated, failure_count, preemptions_count

Operational runbook (high-level steps)

1) Create a new experiment branch and Terraform workspace:

   $ git checkout -b exper/hetero-shape-E1
   # update variables in examples/hetero/vars.tfvars
   $ terraform workspace new lab-E1 || terraform workspace select lab-E1

2) Apply IaC with a canary: deploy a minimal canary allocation (10% of target traffic) using the fleet-allocator module.

   $ terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=examples/hetero/vars.tfvars -target=module.fleet_allocator.canary

3) Validate node boot and agent health: verify node labels, kubelet registration (if using k8s), or placement service logs.

   - Check cloud console for driver installation status.
   - Validate node exporter and nvidia-smi metrics streaming to CloudWatch.

4) Kick off synthetic load generator (inference-harness container) with experiment metadata tag to S3:

   $ docker run --rm \
     -e EXPERIMENT_ID=E1 \
     -e S3_BUCKET=redwood-lab-artifacts \
     redwood/inference-load-generator:latest \
     --profile streaming-short --target-qps 500 --duration 30m --sink s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/E1/

5) Monitor telemetry for SLOs and abort conditions (these are automated in the CI runner):
sections.heading: Rows

sections.body:
- p99 latency increases > 2x baseline for 10m
   - GPU OOMs > 0.5% of requests
   - Preemptions increase by > 3x baseline

6) After run completion, collect artifacts, attach to experiment branch and register on the lab index.

Terraform variants and recommended flags

- Suggested variables (examples/hetero/vars.tfvars):

  instance_families = ["a100", "l4", "h100"]
  pool_tiles = { a100 = 1, h100 = 1, l4 = 4 }
  spot_ratio = 0.25
  preemptive_safe_margin_pct = 30
  node_taints = ["gpu:reserved"]

- Module usage example (snippet):

  module "hetero_fleet" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.internal/infra/fleet-allocator.git//modules/hetero"
    region = var.region
    pool_tiles = var.pool_tiles
    spot_ratio = var.spot_ratio
    user_tags = { team = "infra-labs", experiment = var.experiment_id }
  }

CI/CD integration (promote -> staging -> canary)

- Pipeline stages: plan -> apply-canary -> run-smoke -> run-lab -> collect-and-archive -> promote.
- Buildkite job names (recommended): gpu-lab/plan, gpu-lab/apply-canary, gpu-lab/launch-loadgen, gpu-lab/collect.
- Safety gates: plan must be signed; apply-canary requires manual approval by infra-sre on-call.

Telemetry and dashboards

- Core metrics to stream to CloudWatch/Prometheus: gpu_util_pct, gpu_mem_pct, gpu_power_w, nvidia_gpu_temp_c, inference_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), request_rate, tokens_per_second, preemption_events, node_boot_duration_sec.
- Dashboard template: heterogeneous-fleet/lab-experiment-template (save as JSON in Grafana dashboard repo).

Decision criteria (how we decide winners)

- Winner is a pool_mix that: meets p99 latency target <= baseline_target AND reduces per-token cost >= 10% over reference mix, with preemption risk acceptable (<2% additional failures).
- Secondary filters: operational complexity (number of distinct instance families), observable variance across regions, and Terraform churn risk (module changes required).

Example findings summary (fictional example)

- E1 (A100 + L4) reduced cost per token by 18% vs A100-only baseline, p99 increased by 8ms (within SLO). Preemptions were stable at 0.7%.
- E3 (L4 heavy, 40% spot) showed best cost but p99 spikes at high burst windows; recommend hybrid with reserve on-demand buffer for peak windows.

Artifacts and deliverables

- Experiment CSV/JSON results (S3 path): s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/{experiment_id}/results.json
- Terraform varfiles for each variant in git: infra-labs/experiments/{experiment_id}/vars.tfvars
- Grafana dashboard snapshot link: grafana/internal/dashboards/hetero-lab/{experiment_id}
- Post-run decision note (short ADR): register in confluence under eng-infra/decision-records with link to artifacts.

Safety considerations and rollback

- Never promote lab module changes directly to prod without a staged rollout and automated SLO fuzz tests.
- Rollback path: terraform workspace select <prod> && terraform apply -var-file=prod/vars.tfvars -refresh-only to remove lab tags; then run fleet rebalancer with target pools pinned to prod mix.

Appendix A — Synthetic load generator CLI example

  redwood-loadgen --profile streaming-short --model gptx-mini --target-qps 500 --concurrency 200 --duration 1800 --report s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/E1/reports/

Appendix B — Minimal Terraform vars file (examples/hetero/vars.tfvars)

  region = "us-west-2"
  experiment_id = "E1"
  pool_tiles = { a100 = 1, l4 = 4 }
  spot_ratio = 0.1
  qps_target = 500
  canary_percentage = 10

Appendix C — Postmortem checklist (if experiment triggers incident)

1) Capture CloudWatch exports to S3 within 30 minutes.
2) Revert Terraform apply if unintended drift applied to prod workspace.
3) Notify infra-oncall and attach experiment artifacts.
4) Open a P0 if customer-facing SLAs were impacted.

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/fleet-allocator-module-design (reference)
- /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/gpu-ci-release-safety-lab-and-slo-simulator (CI harness)

Contact

- Lab owner: Maya Chen (infra-labs@redwood.ai)
- SRE reviewer: Liam O'Connor

Notes

This page is intended to be a living notebook. Add new experiments as child pages (convention: lab-{experiment_id}-notes) and attach raw telemetry. When an experiment leads to a permanent policy change, convert findings into a short ADR and move operational configs under terraform-and-iac for proper lifecycle management.

payload.page_title: GPU runtime debugging and tenant triage checklist

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook is a concise, ordered checklist for on-call engineers and infra SREs to triage GPU runtime incidents that impact tenant throughput, tail latency, or availability. It covers quick health checks, tenant isolation checks, CI/IaC failure modes, and safe remediation steps. Use this document when a tenant or pool reports increased errors, slow tokens, or abnormal GPU behavior.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood hosted GPU pools and edge clusters managed by eng-infra.
- Includes multi-tenant and fractional-GPU scenarios, dedicated pools, and spot-backed fallback tiers.
- Does NOT replace the full incident runbook (see related_pages) — this is the operational triage checklist to get from alert to stable.

Ownership
- Primary owner: eng-infra GPU reliability squad.
- Escalation: eng-sre for cross-region network issues, eng-serving-runtime for kernel-level regression, eng-platform for CI/IaC gating regressions.

How to use this doc
1) Run the Preflight checks in order.
2) If root cause is identified, apply the targeted remediation.
3) If issue spans multiple tenants or regions, follow the Incident Response doc and notify Product/Security as required.

Preflight checks (0–5 minutes)
- Confirm the alert: check PagerDuty incident and correlate with Grafana dashboards (gpu-utilization, per-tenant-p99-latency, scheduler-errors).
- Confirm blast radius: identify affected tenants and regions via the request router logs and token-level traces.
- Preserve state: do NOT recycle pods unless instructed; take a heap/profile snapshot for runtime teams.

Quick visibility matrix (what to check first)
- Metrics: GPU utilization, GPU memory pressure, host OOMs, scheduler reject rate, pod restart count, k8s node conditions.
- Logs: kubelet, runtime pod logs, containerd, dmesg, nvidia-smi (on-host), nv-host-engine logs if present.
- IaC/CI: check recent Terraform deploys, pipeline runs, and canary-promote events in the last 30 minutes.

Runtime triage steps (ordered)
1) Node health (cluster-level)
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady or Kubelet-related taints.
   - Check node memory pressure: kubectl describe node <node> and dmesg /var/log/messages for OOM killers.
   - Run on-host: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.total,memory.free --format=csv -l 1 (if available).
2) Pod and container checks
   - kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
   - kubectl logs pod -c runtime --since=15m to spot repeated errors (e.g., KV cache misses, backend timeouts).
3) Scheduler and queueing
   - Inspect router tracing for request queuing and prefix-cache misses.
   - Check batch queue length and worker saturation metrics (auto-batcher backlog).
4) Memory/KV cache consistency
   - Look for sudden increases in KV eviction or cache miss rates. Suggest rolling a cache warm-up if eviction rate is >10% sustained for 5m.
5) Network and egress
   - Confirm node egress connectivity (curl to health-check endpoints across AZs), check VPC flow logs for DENY entries.
   - For cross-account or peered VPCs, validate that the peering route tables have not been modified in the last deploy window.

CI/IaC checks (5–15 minutes)
- Terraform: terraform state list | grep redwood_gpu; check recent runs in the last 2 hours for changes to nodePools, subnet-route tables, or egress firewall rules.
- CI: Inspect the last green canary pipeline for the GPU runtime bundle promotion. If a signed runtime was promoted in the last hour, consider rolling back to previous signed bundle.
- Image artifacts: validate image digest match: docker inspect --format='{{.Id}}' registry.redwood.com/gpu-runtime:<tag> and compare with canary manifest.

Common root causes and targeted remediations
- Cause: Sudden node OOMs or host-level memory pressure.
  Fix: Migrate affected tenants off the node (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data) and scale up a healthy pool. File infra ticket to investigate host kernel OOM logs.
- Cause: Kernel/runtime regression after canary promotion.
  Fix: Revert runtime image to previous digest via CI rollback and re-run canary tests. Notify eng-serving-runtime and attach trace and profile.
- Cause: Network egress rule change prevents access to S3/kms or shared prefix-caches.
  Fix: Reapply last-known-good terraform plan and run smoke tests; if blocked, open change window with netops.
- Cause: Spot preemption cascade.
  Fix: Trigger burst to pre-warmed reserved capacity pool, enable autoscaler fallback policy for affected tenant(s) and notify billing/CS of potential cost impact.

Safe remediation/rollbacks (ordered)
1) If a single runtime image is implicated: revert image tag in the image promotion pipeline (CI) and let the automated canary rollout handle replacement.
2) If nodes are unhealthy: cordon > drain > replace via autoscaling group or Terraform replace for immutable nodes.
3) If network rules are the problem: revert Terraform change or attach emergency egress rule with minimal scope (IP and port) and document the temporary change for audit.

Runbook commands (copyable)
- Confirm GPU hardware state on node: sudo nvidia-smi -q | egrep -A2 "GPU Current Temp"
- Check container GPU usage: docker stats --no-stream --format "{{.Name}}: {{.CPUPerc}} {{.MemUsage}}" | grep runtime
- List recent terraform runs: aws s3 ls s3://terraform-state-redwood/gpu/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize | tail -n 20
- Drain a node safely: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m

Alert thresholds (recommended)
- GPU memory pressure: warning 70% | critical 90%
- per-tenant-p99 latency: warning 300ms | critical 700ms
- scheduler-reject-rate: warning 1% | critical 5%
- pod restart rate: warning 0.2/min | critical 1/min

Post-incident checklist
- Attach traced requests and representative flame graphs to the incident ticket.
- Run a targeted eval against a small prompt suite to validate quality/regression after any runtime rollback.
- Update the IaC changelog and add a remediation note if a Terraform plan caused the incident.
- Run a capacity analysis: were autoscaler thresholds adequate? If not, propose new thresholds.

Playbook notes and escalation
- If the issue cannot be stabilized within 30 minutes and affects >2 regions or >10 tenants, escalate to the on-call engineering manager and open an incident bridge.
- For suspected hardware faults (ECC errors, repeated PCI bus errors), involve metal-ops and schedule node quarantine.

payload.page_title: Signal-driven GPU eviction wake patterns and mitigations

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes the observed "wake" patterns that precede GPU evictions in our multi-tenant fleet and prescribes signal-driven mitigations and IaC toggles to stabilize warm-pools. The intent is to give oncall and infra owners concrete detection thresholds, a prioritized mitigation ladder, and safe test steps to validate changes without broad impact.

Who should use this
- Oncall engineers in the GPU and capacity teams
- SREs responsible for deployment rollouts that affect burst/spot pools
- Infra engineers evolving Terraform modules for warm-pools and preemptible capacity

When this runbook applies
1. Spike in preemption_count or instance-termination events for a specific AZ or pool.
2. Warm-pool refill rate fails to meet baseline for 5 consecutive 1-minute windows.
3. Application latency degradation correlated with GPU reallocation events.
4. Scheduled cloud provider maintenance windows that historically cause cascading evictions.

Signals and thresholds to detect the "wake"
- telemetry/gpu/preemption_rate (1m avg) >= 0.05 for pool X for 3+ minutes.
- telemetry/warm_pool/refill_latency_p99 > 30s for 3 consecutive minutes.
- infra/instance/terminated_by_cloud_reason contains "preemptible" and count > 8 in 1m for an AZ.
- api/tenant/error_rate increase > 2x coincident with the above signals.

Recommended monitoring queries (PromQL examples)
- preemption rate:
  increase(cloud_instance_terminated_total{reason="preemptible"}[1m]) / 1m
- warm-pool refill latency p99:
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(warm_pool_refill_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool))

Diagnosis checklist (quick triage)
1. Confirm scope: which pools/pod labels/regions are affected.
2. Check cloud provider incident feed for the region.
3. Verify recent IaC changes affecting auto-scaling, eviction-protection tags, or warm-pool size.
4. Correlate tenant traffic spikes; tag tenant IDs for remediation if necessary.

Mitigation ladder (ordered, lowest-risk first)
1) Soft throttles and redirecting traffic
- Reduce best-effort load to bursty tenants by applying rate-limit rules for 10 minutes.
- Route new requests to lower-cost model variants if latency-sensitive requests are impacted.

2) Increase warm-pool warmup parallelism (safe config flip)
- Toggle warm_pool.refill_parallelism from 2 -> 6 for the affected pool.
- Expected effect: faster instance bring-up; risk: short-term API saturation to provisioning service.

3) Temporarily mark critical instances as protected (non-preemptible)
- Use the cloud API to add protection tag to 2-4 nodes in the affected AZ.
- Policy: only apply for < 6 hours and document the owner + reason.

4) Move noisy tenants to isolated pools
- Apply tenant affinity label and shift pod scheduling to an isolated burst pool.
- Requires coordination with the tenant-owner and may need an IaC promote.

5) Scale up on-demand capacity and drain spot pools gracefully
- Provision additional on-demand nodes into the target VPC subnet via Terraform variable override (see examples).
- Drain and cordon nodes in spot pools to reduce churn.

Operational steps (runbook)
1. Acknowledge incident and create an incident channel with the following subject line: "GPU Eviction Wake - <region> - <pool>".
2. Run detection queries (see Monitoring queries) and paste outputs to the channel.
3. Apply the lowest-risk mitigation in the ladder and wait 3 minutes for telemetry to stabilize.
4. If non-responsive, escalate through ladder items 2–5.
5. When resolved, run postmortem checklist and attach graphs for preemption_rate, refill_latency_p99, oncall actions, and IaC changes.

Terraform / IaC toggles (examples)
- Example: increase warm-pool parallelism via module variable override (HCL snippet):

resource "redwood_compute_warm_pool" "gpu_pool" {
  name                     = var.pool_name
  target_size              = var.target_size
  refill_parallelism       = var.refill_parallelism # default 2
  preemptible_preference   = var.preemptible_preference
  provider_zone            = var.zone
}

sections.body:
Testing changes safely
- Use the sandbox pool (pool label: "env:sandbox-warm") to test parallelism changes.
- Run a synthetic warmup job: curl -X POST https://warmup.internal.redwood/v1/seed -d '{"pool":"sandbox-warm","count":6}'
- Validate there is no cross-pool bleed: confirm metrics for non-sandbox pools unchanged (within ±5%).

Rollback guidance
- Always prepare a tfvars file containing previous values. Example rollback command:
  terraform apply -var-file=rollback-20250120.tfvars
- If cloud tags were added (protection tags), schedule automated removal via a ticket if not removed during the incident.

Automations and safe-guards to implement (recommended follow-ups)
- Auto-scale dampening: add a 1–2 minute cooldown for auto-scaler decisions affecting spot-to-on-demand transitions.
- Eviction circuit-breaker: a service that temporarily disables warm-pool refill_parallelism changes if preemption_rate spikes while provisioning.
- Tenant impact labels: automatically tag tenant traffic that experienced reallocation so CS can notify customers.

Ownership, SLAs and run frequency
- Primary owner: gpu-capacity team (oncall rotation)
- Secondary owner: infra-platform (Terraform changes and approvals)
- Runbook review cadence: quarterly or after any major provider incident
- Resolution SLO: for signals matching the thresholds above, the target time-to-stabilize is 20 minutes (measured as refill_latency_p99 returning to baseline).

Post-incident checklist
1. Record exact IaC changes and approvals.
2. Attach time-series graphs for preemption_rate, refill_latency_p99, instance_provisioning_error_count.
3. Create a follow-up ticket for automations with an owner and due date.
4. If tenant-impacting, coordinate a customer-facing summary with CSM and Legal (template below).

Customer communication template (short)
- Subject: Brief outage impact for <tenant-name> on <date>
- Body: We observed increased GPU preemptions in <region> causing elevated request latency between HH:MM and HH:MM UTC. We applied targeted mitigations and implemented a follow-up action to prevent recurrence. Contact <oncall-email> for details.

Appendix: Suggested dashboards and panels

| Preemption heatmap | increase(cloud_instance_terminated_total[5m]) by (zone,pool) | Identify where evictions are concentrated |
| Tenant error tag counts | sum(rate(api_errors_total{tenant!=""}[5m])) by (tenant) | Rapidly surface impacted tenants |

payload.page_title: GPU telemetry schema evolution and backcompat playbook

sections.body:
Purpose:
This playbook documents the schema evolution policy, CI validations, ingestion rollout steps, and rollback/runbook for GPU inference telemetry used by Redwood Inference. It is intended for infra engineers, telemetry owners, data-platform, and anyone proposing a change to telemetry events (schema migrations, new fields, renamed fields, or removals).

Scope:
- Applies to all GPU runtime telemetry emitted from the serving runtime, warm pools, batching sequencers, and edge proxies.
- Includes event formats sent into the primary telemetry Kafka topics (raw-gpu-events), the schema registry entry, and downstream transformation layers (ingest->warehouse).
- Excludes UI-only metrics (console dashboards) and ephemeral debug logs that are not persisted to the schema registry.

Why this matters:
- Removing or renaming fields without a managed migration has caused loss of tenant attribution, broken cost allocation pipelines, and production tracing gaps in prior incidents.
- Telemetry is used for billing, SLOs, autoscaling heuristics, and regression detection; breaking changes must be planned and observable.

High-level policy:
1) Semantic versioning for telemetry schemas: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
   - MAJOR: incompatible changes (field removal, type change incompatible with previous parsers).
   - MINOR: additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, additional enums that consumers can ignore).
   - PATCH: documentation/description updates and metadata only.
2) Backward compatibility requirement: Consumers must be able to parse events stamped with any MINOR within the current MAJOR for 6 months after a new MAJOR is published.
3) Deprecation window: Fields targeted for removal must be marked deprecated for at least two release cycles (>= 90 days) and instrumented with a vanity metric that counts emitted deprecated-field usage.

Minimum schema contract (required fields):
- event_type (string) — e.g., "inference.request", "inference.latency", "kv.cache.eviction"
- schema_version (string) — e.g., "1.0.0"
- tenant_id (string) — Redwood tenant GUID
- trace_id (string) — distributed trace id (if present)
- model_id (string) — serving model identifier (catalog: model:q1/2025:llama-3-8b)
- timestamp_iso (string, RFC3339)
- ingestion_host (string) — host/pod id that produced event

Optional but recommended fields:
- kernel_version (string)
- quant_profile (string)
- seq_len (integer)
- token_count (integer)
- latency_ms (number)
- shard_id (string)
- region (string)
- billing_unit (string) — host/allocator billing tag

Note: All numeric fields must be nullable rather than omitted to avoid downstream type fluctuation in strongly typed ETL stages.

Adding a new field (approved path):
1) Design PR: Open an RFC-style design doc in the infra team repo referencing this playbook. Include sample events and a rationale for consumer updates.
2) Schema registry change: Create a JSON Schema draft and increment MINOR (e.g., 1.3.0 -> 1.4.0) with new optional fields.
3) Consumer readiness: Notify downstream consumers via #infra-telemetry and add a one-week heads-up to the weekly telemetry sync. Consumers are expected to ignore unknown fields for MINOR bumps.
4) CI validation: Add schema tests (see CI steps below) and a canary dataset for the new fields.
5) Canary rollout: Emit the new field from 1% of production traffic for 48 hours and monitor the ingest errors and consumer processing lag.
6) Full rollout: If no regressions, increase to 100% and update the docs and schema registry.

Removing or renaming a field (incompatible change):
1) Mark field deprecated: Add deprecation metadata to schema and emit a "telemetry.deprecation.warning" event whenever the deprecated field is set.
2) Monitor usage: Maintain a dashboard (telemetry.deprecation.<field_name>.usage) and require usage to be <1% of events for 14 consecutive days before proceeding.
3) Announce removal: 90-day announcement notice across Slack, weekly sync, and the README for the telemetry repo.
4) Create MAJOR schema bump: Update JSON Schema and increment MAJOR (e.g., 1.4.0 -> 2.0.0).
5) Migration window: For 90 days after MAJOR publish, support compatibility via proxy shim or producer fallback (see Rollout shims below).
6) Final removal: After the window, remove the field from all producers and mark documentation accordingly.

CI validation and pre-merge checklist (must be present in telemetry-related PRs):
- [ ] Add/modify JSON Schema file under infra/telemetry/schemas/<topic>.json and update schema_version in the producer config.
- [ ] Unit tests validating example payloads against the schema (go/pytest/heavyweight optional).
- [ ] Integration test: run local schema-registry validator against a simulated Kafka topic. Example GH action job:
  name: telemetry-schema-check
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Setup node/python
      run: make telemetry-env
    - name: Validate sample events
      run: ./bin/telemetry-validator --schema infra/telemetry/schemas/gpu-events.json --samples infra/telemetry/samples/new-field-sample.json
- [ ] Add schema migration notes to CHANGELOG and a short runbook stub if the change is MAJOR.

Schema registry and ingestion details (implementation notes):
- Registry: Confluent Schema Registry is used for Kafka topics (topic raw-gpu-events). JSON Schema format is the canonical source.
- Topic partitioning: preserve partitioning key = tenant_id to maintain ordering for per-tenant pipelines.
- Avro/Parquet transforms: Ingest workers convert JSON Schema validated events into columnar Parquet for the warehouse; ensure nullable types map to nullable Parquet types.
- Producer config: Producers must send schema_registry_id and schema_version in the event envelope header. Example envelope: {
  "schema_version": "1.4.0",
  "payload": { ... }
}

Rollout shims and proxy compatibility patterns:
- Producer fallback: When a MAJOR change is required but consumers cannot be updated, use a producer-side translation shim that emits both old and new field names (old_field and new_field) for 90 days.
- Ingest proxy: A lightweight ingest proxy (ingest-shim) deployed in the same cluster can translate new-major payloads back to old-major format for old consumers while allowing new consumers to read the native event.
- Translation table: Store a translation map in Git (infra/telemetry/translation-maps/<major>-<major-1>.yaml) used by shims.

Monitoring and SLOs for schema migrations:
- Ingest error rate (schema validation fail) target: < 0.01% sustained during rollout windows.
- Consumer side errors (deserialization) target: 0 during canary; alert threshold 0.1% over 15m.
- Freshness SLO: 95th percentile processing lag for canary traffic < 30s.
- Deprecation metric: telemetry.deprecated_field.<field>.count must be visible in the telemetry-owner dashboard.

Runbook: schema migration failure during canary (pager steps):
1) Pager: alert to #oncall-telemetry. Oncall reviews the schema-validation logs (kibana index telemetry-schema-errors) and canary metrics dashboard.
2) Rollback producers to previous schema_version by flipping the feature flag: infra/flags/telemetry_schema_version -> previous. Command: toggle-flag infra telemetry_schema_version --value=1.4.0
3) If producers cannot be toggled, deploy ingest-shim to translate failing payloads to the old shape.
4) If the issue persists, pause production emission for the affected producer group via the producer circuit-breaker endpoint: POST /api/v1/producers/<producer>/pause with body {"reason": "schema-failure"}.
5) Postmortem: within 72 hours, owner must publish a short incident summary that includes root cause, mitigation, and proposed changes to the rollout process.

Terraform / IaC considerations:
- Schema changes that require infra updates (e.g., new Kafka topic, new consumer cluster, or a shim service) need a TF plan that includes a non-destructive migration path.
- Example variables to include in topology module: | variable | purpose | default |
  | telemetry_schema_version | version exposed to producers | "1.4.0" |
  | ingest_shim_enabled | toggle to deploy translation proxy | "false" |
- Apply pattern: terraform plan -> terraform apply in a shadow account first (telemetry-canary) and run the canary dataset before global apply.

Checklist: PR template for telemetry schema changes (required fields)
1) Link to this playbook and the RFC.
2) List of producers modifying schema (service names and owners).
3) Downstream consumers and owners.
4) Canary fraction and duration.
5) Monitoring dashboards + alert thresholds added.
6) Rollback plan and contact list.

Examples: sample JSON schema snippet (abbreviated)
{
  "\$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "gpu-inference-event",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["event_type","schema_version","tenant_id","timestamp_iso","ingestion_host"],
  "properties": {
    "event_type": {"type":"string"},
    "schema_version": {"type":"string"},
    "tenant_id": {"type":"string"},
    "model_id": {"type":"string"},
    "latency_ms": {"type":["number","null"]},
    "token_count": {"type":["integer","null"]},
    "kernel_version": {"type":["string","null"]}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Sample local validation command (developer laptop):
- Install: pip install -r infra/telemetry/requirements.txt
- Validate: ./bin/telemetry-validator --schema infra/telemetry/schemas/gpu-inference-event.json --samples infra/telemetry/samples/patch-sample.json

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Priya Kannan (@priya) — infra telemetry & ingestion
- Secondary: Lillian Chen (@lchen) — data platform
- Slack channels: #infra-telemetry (announce changes), #oncall-telemetry (alerts)
- Pager escalation: oncall-telemetry -> oncall-sre -> eng-infra manager (escalation matrix in Oncall handbook).

Housekeeping and documentation:
- Maintain CHANGELOG.md in infra/telemetry with schema_version, author, date, and short rationale.
- Keep a translation map for MAJOR bumps and link it from the schema entry in the registry.
- Add a short note to product docs if a removed field affects billing or customer-visible metrics.

Appendix: quick migration example (1.4.0 -> 2.0.0 rename kernel_version -> runtime_kernel):
1) Day 0: open RFC, publish translation map, add deprecation flag in schema 1.4.0 that still accepts kernel_version.
2) Day 7: producers start emitting both kernel_version and runtime_kernel behind flag. Canary 1% traffic.
3) Day 30: confirm consumers are ignoring kernel_version or have migrated. usage <0.5%.
4) Day 90: publish MAJOR 2.0.0, deploy ingest-shim for remaining legacy consumers.
5) Day 180: remove kernel_version from producers and update schema docs.

Related resources:
- infra/telemetry/schemas/README.md
- infra/telemetry/bin/telemetry-validator
- dashboards/telemetry/schema-migration-health
- Oncall handbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems

If you are planning a change and are unsure about MAJOR vs MINOR impact or need help scaffolding the canary, ping @priya in #infra-telemetry or open a ticket in the infra backlog with label: telemetry-schema.

payload.page_title: GPU allocator safety checklist and IaC adapter guide

sections.body:
Overview:

This page is a combined safety checklist and Terraform/adapter guide for the GPU allocator components that schedule, reserve, and reclaim fractional and whole GPU capacity across production pools. It is written for infra engineers and SREs who own allocator logic, IaC modules, and the preflight gates used by CI/CD. The objective is to reduce production regressions from allocator changes and provide a deterministic rollback surface.

Scope:
- GPU allocator service (allocatord) and sidecars
- Warm-pool manager and preemptive seeding logic
- Tenant egress segmentation policies related to allocator decisions
- Terraform modules and the IaC adapter that exposes allocator knobs to teams

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-infra - Allocator squad
- Secondary owner: eng-sre - Capacity squad
- Pager: allocator-oncall (rotation)
- Escalation path: oncall -> allocator tech lead -> infra manager -> platform engineer

Safety checklist (pre-merge):
1) Unit & integration tests:
   - All allocator code must have unit tests covering allocation heuristics for at least 95% of branches.
   - Integration tests must run against a small simulated pool (N=3) in CI that validates: placement, eviction, warm-pool seeding, and metric emissions.
2) IaC contract validation:
   - Terraform plans must be run with the IaC adapter in dry-run mode and diff reviewed.
   - Module interface cannot remove or rename stateful attributes without a compatibility shim.
3) Canaries and traffic shaping:
   - New allocator rollouts must use a 5% canary window for 24 hours before 25% rollout.
   - Canary nodes must be tagged with allocator-canary=true and isolated via egress fence.
4) Rollback rehearsals:
   - For any allocator binary change, run the rollback script against the staging warm-pool and validate state reconciliation within 10 minutes.
5) Observability and alarms:
   - Ensure the following metrics are present and green in Grafana before approval: allocator.success_rate, allocator.latency_p95, warmpool.fill_ratio, tenant_eviction_count.
   - Alert thresholds: allocator.success_rate < 99.5% over 5m; warmpool.fill_ratio < 30% for 10m; tenant_eviction_count > baseline + 50% in 15m.

Configuration table (minimum fields required in module):
| field | type | description | default |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| allocator.enabled | bool | Enable allocatord scheduling | true |
| warmpool.target_percent | number | Target warm-pool fill as percent of capacity | 20 |
| eviction.backoff_seconds | number | Backoff applied after eviction to same tenant | 300 |
| network.egress_segment | string | Egress segment id used by canaries | "egress-fence-main" |

Terraform adapter pattern (example):
- Design principle: modules must be additive and expose a single small map of knobs. Avoid exposing allocator internals.

Example module usage snippet (terraform):
```
module "allocator_profile" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.com/infra/terraform//modules/allocator-profile"
  name   = "slo-balanced"
  knobs = {
    warmpool_target_percent = 25
    eviction_backoff        = 600
    preempt_mode            = "soft"
  }
  tags = ["team:search", "env:prod"]
}
```

CI/CD gates and checks:
1. Preflight: run tf plan with the "allocator-diff-checker" CI job which validates there are no unsupported state changes.
2. Integration: run e2e allocator simulation job (containerized) with test harness (see /infra/test-harnesss/allocator-sim).
3. Canary deploy: automated canary via deployment job that annotates canary nodes and waits for metric stabilization (p95 latency <= 120ms and eviction delta <= 10%).

Incident runbook (allocator regressions):
1) Detect: Pager triggers on allocator.success_rate or warmpool.fill_ratio.
2) Triage: Check recent deploys (gitops commit history) and Terraform plan diffs.
3) Immediate mitigation steps (ordered):
   a) Pause gitops reconciliation for allocator modules.
   b) Disable new allocation decisions by toggling allocator.enabled=false via feature flag (fast path).
   c) Scale the warm-pool by +30% using the warmpool_scaler endpoint: POST /api/v1/warmpool/scale {"delta_percent":30} (auth: allocator-admin).
   d) If tenant evictions spike, run redispatch: POST /api/v1/allocator/redispatch?mode=gentle and monitor for 5m.
4) Post-incident: create postmortem with timeline and include: commit hashes, tfplan artifacts, canary logs, metric graphs.

Testing matrix (minimal):
- Unit tests: fast, run on PR with every commit.
- Integration (sim): nightly and PR on large changes.
- Chaos run: weekly chaos job that simulates preemption and verifies allocator recovers within 3x baseline latency.
- Performance: monthly perf suite with N=100 nodes and mixed tenants.

Metrics and dashboards to maintain:
- allocator.success_rate (percentage)
- allocator.allocations_per_minute
- allocator.latency_p50/95/99
- warmpool.fill_ratio
- tenant_eviction_count (per-tenant)
- net.egress_bytes_by_segment

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Validate Terraform plan with adapter: 
  ./infra-tools/allocator-iac-adapter validate --plan=plan.tfout --profile=slo-balanced
- Rehearse rollback (staging): 
  ./scripts/allocator-rollback.sh --cluster=staging --timeout=600
- Quick metric check (prod): 
  curl -s "https://metrics-api.redwood.internal/series?name=allocator.success_rate&window=5m" | jq .

Related documents and background reading:
- Placement SLO-driven provisioning playbook (see related pages)
- Warm-pool sizing heuristics (arch notes)

Notes and rationale:
- We intentionally keep the IaC adapter surface minimal to avoid teams coupling to internal allocator heuristics. The warm-pool is the primary safety valve for short-term capacity perturbations, and the checklist emphasizes fast toggles and scale-up paths before aggressive evictions.

If you update this page, append a one-line summary, the date, and your name to the change log at the bottom of this page.

payload.page_title: GPU tenant degradation simulator and IaC contracts cheat sheet

sections.body:
Overview:

This cheat sheet documents the GPU tenant degradation simulator (GTDS) — a lightweight, reproducible test harness used by infra engineers to model and validate how tenant-facing inference services degrade under constrained capacity, networking stress, and Terraform/IaC policy changes. The goal is to provide a single-page reference with runnable steps, CI gating patterns, IaC contract checks, telemetry assertions, and operational playbook snippets.

Scope:
- Simulate tenant-level capacity pressure (warm-pool exhaustion, preemption, burst-to-spot fallback).
- Model network degradations (egress shaping, NAT exhaustion, packet loss).
- Validate Terraform/IaC changes that affect GPU pools, NAT gateways, and burst orchestrator policies.
- Verify CI/CD gating rules and telemetry-based alerts that should prevent dangerous rollouts.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
- Reproducible scenario container images + Terraform workspace per test.
- Coverage: cold-start latency increases, kv-cache miss-rate, token throughput loss, and tail-latency regressions.
- CI policy: any IaC change that increases 95th-latency by > 20% in the simulator must block merge.
- Telemetry contract: simulator emits the same metric names as production (inference.tokens_generated_total, runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio, network.egress_errors_total).

Key components (short):
1) GTDS harness (service: infra/gtds) — Go binary + k6 traffic profiles that drive realistic inference patterns (mix of short-chat, long-context, streaming).
2) Injector VM set — small fleet of emulated tenants that hold ephemeral KV state and open long-lived connections to the runtime under test.
3) Network shim — eBPF-based traffic shaper for per-tenant egress shaping and synthetic packet loss.
4) IaC workspaces — per-test Terraform directory that can apply/destroy a sealed, isolated GPU-capacity topology (uses tfcloud-ephemeral-account pattern).
5) CI adapter — Jenkins/GHA job templates that run the harness and compare results to golden thresholds.

Run instructions (quick start):
1) Prepare environment:
   - git clone git@github.com:redwood-infra/gtds.git
   - export GTDS_ENV=staging-sim-<your initials>-$(date +%s)
   - ensure you have Terraform service account with ephemeral creds: run scripts/get-ephemeral-creds.sh
2) Start a baseline topology (30m warm pool, 4 regional NATs):
   - cd infra/tf/workspaces/gtds-baseline
   - terraform init && terraform apply -var="warm_pool_size=30" -var="nat_count=4" -auto-approve
3) Launch the harness (30m test):
   - make build && ./bin/gtds run --topology ./topologies/baseline.yaml --duration 30m --metrics-prefix gtds.baseline
   - tail logs: kubectl -n gtds logs -f deploy/gtds-runner
4) Apply stress variant (warm-pool drain + egress noise):
   - terraform apply -var="warm_pool_size=8" -var="egress_shaper_profile=loss-5pct" -auto-approve
   - ./bin/gtds run --topology ./topologies/drain-then-burst.yaml --duration 30m --metrics-prefix gtds.drain
5) Gather results and compare (local CLI):
   - ./bin/gtds compare --baseline gtds.baseline --variant gtds.drain --asserts asserts/ci-block.yaml

Assertions and thresholds (suggested):
| metric | block threshold | warn threshold | note |
| inference.95_latency_ms | > +20% | > +10% | 95p tail latency is primary SLO for interactive tenants |
| runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio | < -15% absolute | < -7% | decline indicates bad prefix caching or incorrect cache seeding |
| network.egress_errors_total | > 100 / minute | > 20 / minute | NAT or proxy exhaustion flag |
| inference.tokens_per_second | < -25% | < -10% | protects throughput-sensitive batch pipelines |

Example asserts/ci-block.yaml (YAML shown inline):
```
# asserts/ci-block.yaml
asserts:
  - metric: inference.95_latency_ms
    comparator: relative_increase
    threshold_pct: 20
  - metric: runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio
    comparator: absolute_decrease
    threshold_pct: 15
```

CI/CD integration (recommended pattern):
1) PR workflow (GHA):
   - Step A: Run unit IaC checks (tf fmt, terraform validate, tflint).
   - Step B: Spin ephemeral TF workspace (ephemeral creds), run terraform plan; capture plan delta against current baseline.
   - Step C: Kick GTDS in ephemeral overlay mode (10–30m); run short smoke + tail-latency probe.
   - Step D: Run comparators using asserts/ci-block.yaml. If any assert fails, post failure and block merging.
2) Promotion gates: successful PR must be promoted to a longer nightly run (2–4h) for changes touching burst or scaling modules.
3) Canary rollout (post-merge): patch releases require a staged rollout with automatic rollback if production telemetry mirrors simulator regressions.

Terraform / IaC contracts and checks (patterns):
- Contract A: warm_pool_size must have a minimum value set in module defaults (no implicit null). Example: var "warm_pool_size" { default = 10 }
- Contract B: nat_gateway_count must be >= 2 for any public egress topology.
- Contract C: any change to module gpu_pool.* must include a tfplan annotation explaining risk and expected impact on inference.
- Contract D: module outputs must expose telemetry hooks: metrics_exporter_endpoint and otel_resource_name.

Example Terraform snippet (module wrapper):
```
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu-pool?ref=main"
  warm_pool_size = var.warm_pool_size
  tenant_tag = var.tenant_tag
  metrics_exporter_endpoint = format("https://metrics.%s.internal", var.region)
}
```

Network considerations (operational):
- Per-tenant NAT allocation: prefer per-tenant SNAT pools for high-throughput tenants. Default: 64 ephemeral ports per tenant NAT.
- Egress shaping: use the network shim to simulate 99th percentile ingress-to-egress RTT increases of up to +200ms to model multi-region failover.
- BGP / Transit: tests should include a transit-flip scenario where a region’s egress path is rerouted for 5 minutes to detect session churn.

Telemetry and dashboards (what to compare):
- Primary: inference.95_latency_ms, inference.error_rate, inference.tokens_per_second
- Secondary: runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio, cache.evictions_total, network.egress_errors_total
- Supporting: infra.tf_apply_duration_seconds, ci.gtds_run_time_seconds, tfplan.change_count

Runbook snippets (when simulator shows regression):
1) Triage (5m): compare variant metrics to baseline; tag failing asserts and owners.
2) Short-term mitigation (15m): if latency spike correlates with warm_pool decline, increase warm_pool_size + scale replica count by 20% via emergency tf apply (use emergency service account).
3) Network mitigation (30m): if NAT exhaustion seen, route affected tenants to a fallback NAT pool (tf variable nat_pool_fallback = true) and enable egress proxy scaling.
4) Rollback (TBD): revert IaC change and re-run GTDS to validate restoration.

Owner and escalation matrix:
- Primary owner: gpu-fleet-team@redwood.internal (oncall: gpu-fleet-rotation)
- Network lead: netops@redwood.internal
- IaC policy owner: infra-iac-team@redwood.internal
- Escalation: if incident extends > 60 minutes with customer impact, notify SRE Pager and Customer Success.

Best practices and tips:
- Keep topologies small and declarative: prefer small ephemeral accounts over modifying prod-like tenants.
- Use deterministic seeds in traffic workloads to make runs comparable. Add `--seed` flag to gtds run.
- Record full tfplan JSON: attach to PR for reviewers to quickly determine proposed resource delta.
- Maintain a golden artifacts bucket with baseline metrics for each major release (path: s3://redwood-gtds/goldens/<release>).

CI templates (copy-paste):
- .github/workflows/gtds-smoke.yaml: runs on changes to terraform modules/** and modules/gpu-pool/**. Uses action redwood/ephemeral-terraform to create a workspace, then runs `gtds run --duration 15m --topology smoke`. Compare with asserts and post status.

Appendix A — common failure patterns and quick remediations:
- Symptom: sudden kv_cache_hit_ratio drop with steady token generation. Cause: cache seeding disabled in module change. Remediation: revert seeding-related tf var, reapply, and run gtds seed-only mode.
- Symptom: bursted tenants hit 429s and network.egress_errors_total spikes. Cause: NAT port exhaustion. Remediation: allocate per-tenant SNAT, increase NAT gateway count, and deploy egress proxy autoscaling.
- Symptom: 95p latency regresses only under long-context tests. Cause: batching parameter change or kv-cache eviction tuning. Remediation: review runtime config (batch.max_tokens, kv_cache.max_entries) and roll forward a kernel tweak in a canary.

References and related artifacts:
- repo: git@github.com:redwood-infra/gtds.git
- tf modules: git@github.com:redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu-pool
- dashboard: infra -> GTDS Simulator (grafana link internal)
- contact: #infra-gtds on Slack

Notes: keep this cheat sheet focused on reproducibility and gating; longer design docs belong in eng-infra/runbooks or terraform-and-iac folders. If you extend GTDS harness, add an entry to the runbook index and include a small tutorial for new engineers.
