payload.page_title: GPU Oscillation Detection and Auto‑Stabilizer — Cheat Sheet

sections.body:
Overview

This cheat sheet describes a repeatable pattern for detecting GPU allocation oscillation (rapid scale up/down or frequent preemptions/evictions) and an opinionated Auto‑Stabilizer that can be deployed as a lightweight control loop in the fleet controller. It is intended for clusters running Redwood serving workloads (service names: rwd-infer-scaler, rwd-batcher, rwd-shipper).

Why this matters

- Oscillation symptoms: sudden spikes in allocation followed by large evictions (within 1–5 minutes), high job churn, elevated tail latency, and inefficient GPU utilization.
- Business impact: increased cost (extra launches), latency SLO violations, and customer-facing errors during rollouts.

Detection signals and concrete queries

Monitor the following signals (examples use Prometheus/Thanos):

1) Allocation churn rate (per pool):
   - PromQL: increase(gpu_alloc_events_total{pool=\"$POOL\"}[5m]) / 5m
   - Alert if > 0.8 allocations/min for > 10m and stable backlog > 20% of warm_pool_size

2) Eviction spike:
   - PromQL: increase(gpu_evictions_total{pool=\"$POOL\"}[5m])
   - Alert if evictions > 4 in 5m or eviction_rate > 2% of running tasks in 5m

3) Thundering backfill (queue growth + launch spike):
   - Queue: rwd_job_queue_length{pool=\"$POOL\"}
   - Launch rate: increase(gpu_launch_total{pool=\"$POOL\"}[1m])
   - Alert when queue_length increases > 30% and launch_rate > 50 launches/min simultaneously

4) 99p latency AND jitter:
   - PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(rwd_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
   - Alert when 99p increases > 2x baseline for 15m

Oscillation score (heuristic)

We use a lightweight score (0–100) that sums normalized signals. Tuning knobs live in config: /etc/rwd/auto_stabilizer/config.yaml

- allocation_churn_score = min(40, 20 * allocation_churn_per_min)
- eviction_score = min(30, 10 * evictions_per_5m)
- queue_launch_mismatch_score = min(30, 15 * (queue_increase_pct + launch_spike_pct))
- total_score = allocation_churn_score + eviction_score + queue_launch_mismatch_score
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- total_score < 30: healthy
- 30 <= total_score < 60: degraded — notify oncall, no auto action by default
- total_score >= 60: oscillating — auto stabilizer triggers mitigation

Auto‑Stabilizer mitigation actions (ordered, idempotent)

When total_score >= 60, Auto‑Stabilizer attempts mitigations in sequence. Each action is reversible and has a cooldown (default 10m). The controller records actions in a central audit log (service: rwd-autostab-audit).

Action 1 — Soft throttle launches (duration: 10m)
- Reduce new GPU launches by setting fleet-controller launch_rate_limit for affected pool to max(10, current_rate * 0.5).
- Command (kubectl to controller configmap):
  kubectl patch cm rwd-fleet-config -n rwd-system --type merge -p '{"data":{"launch_rate_limit":"{\"pool-123\":\"20\"}"}}'
- Rationale: gives warm pool and KV caches time to settle and avoids thundering herd.

Action 2 — Prefer warm nodes and backfill policies
- Enforce placement policy: prefer nodes with last_seen_ready < 30m and last_eviction_count == 0.
- Update placement priority via API: POST /internal/v1/pools/{pool}/placement with body {"prefer_warm":true,"min_warm_age":1800}

Action 3 — Increase eviction buffer (ephemeral)
- Temporarily increase per‑tenant eviction buffer to 10% (from default 2%) so the scheduler reduces preemptive evictions.
- Terraform variable path: module/fleet/variables.tf var eviction_buffer_percent
- Example terraform override: var.eviction_buffer_percent = 10

Action 4 — Gradual scale policy (hard rollback prevention)
- Switch pool from aggressive-reactive to smoothing policy (exponential backoff on scale down).
- Config snippet (YAML):
  scale_policy:
    mode: smoothing
    scale_down_cooldown_seconds: 900
    min_stable_time_seconds: 600

Action 5 — Canary route fallback
- If oscillation coincides with a recent model rollout, temporarily route a configurable percentage (default 20%) of traffic to a pinned model variant in a different pool/region. See service: rwd-router.

Operational run steps (when auto action fires)

1) Oncall receives alert or sees autostab audit event.
2) Triage: verify the total_score and examine the last 30m of metrics (allocation, evictions, queue length, 99p latency).
3) If an action is in progress, confirm the cooldown and outcome. If not, trigger manual mitigation (repeat Auto‑Stabilizer actions as needed).
3) If oscillation persists after Action 3 for > 30m, escalate to {owner_team: "eng-infra"} and open an incident. Include logs: rwd-autostab-audit, fleet-controller events, kube events for affected nodes.

Checklist for escalation

- Collect: last 60m Prometheus graphs for the four signals above.
- Collect: controller logs (rwd-infer-scaler, rwd-fleet-controller) from the 30m window beginning at first anomaly.
- Provide: last deployment IDs for model-serving images and any IaC changes in the last 24h (terraform plan/apply IDs).

Playbook knobs (config file example)

-- /etc/rwd/auto_stabilizer/config.yaml (YAML excerpt) --
pool_configs:
  pool-123:
    allocation_churn_threshold: 0.8 # allocs per min
    eviction_threshold_5m: 4
    queue_increase_pct_threshold: 0.3
    total_score_threshold: 60
    cooldown_seconds: 600
    action_sequence: [throttle_launches, prefer_warm, increase_eviction_buffer, smoothing_policy, canary_fallback]

Testing and local chaos experiments

Before enabling Auto‑Stabilizer in production pools, run the following:

1) Canary cluster: enable autostab in a non‑critical pool with 25% of production load for 48h.
2) Inject allocation churn using the test harness: rwd-loadgen --target-pool pool-canary --rate 200 --burst 500 --duration 20m
3) Validate that autostab reduces launches and that throughput degradation is < 15%.
sections.heading: Thresholds

sections.body:
- median latency change, 99p latency, total GPU-hours used, number of launches, number of evictions.

Operational cautions and known limitations

- Auto‑Stabilizer is a mitigation — it reduces thrash but does not replace capacity planning. If a pool is saturated for sustained periods (> 24h), file a capacity growth ticket.
- Interactions with tenant quotas: throttling launches may cause longer queues and impact customer SLAs; make conservative thresholds for production high‑priority tenants.
- Stateful jobs: the pattern assumes ephemeral stateless GPU tasks. For stateful streaming/offline jobs coordinate with owning teams before applying action 3 (increase eviction buffer).

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: eng-infra (primary), eng-serving-runtime (secondary for scheduler integration).
- Rolling enablement: staged by environment (dev -> staging -> prod-canary -> prod-global). Each stage requires 48h monitoring and sign‑off.

SLOs and success criteria for enabling Auto‑Stabilizer in a pool

- Post‑enablement targets (measured over 7 days):
  - allocation churn rate reduced by >= 60% during incidents
  - eviction rate reduced by >= 50%
  - 99p latency not degraded by more than 10% compared to baseline

Appendix: useful commands and artifacts

- View autostab audit log: kubectl -n rwd-system logs deploy/rwd-autostab-audit --tail 200
- Force a manual throttle: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/pools/pool-123/actions -d '{"action":"throttle_launches","params":{"rate":20}}'
- Promote smoothing policy via Terraform: cd infra/modules/fleet && terraform apply -var 'pool=pool-123' -var 'smoothing=true'

Contacts

- Primary owner: eng-infra oncall (pagerduty: eng-infra-pgd)
- Secondary: serving-runtime (Slack: #serving-runtime-ops)

Change log

- v1.0 (2025-11-02): initial draft and canary test plan.
- v1.1 (2025-12-15): added eviction buffer action and terraform override examples.
- v1.2 (2026-02-15): tightened scoring thresholds, added canary fallback step and PromQL examples.

Concise operational guide to detect oscillatory scheduling/scale behavior in GPU pools and a lightweight automatic stabilization pattern (Auto‑Stabilizer) that reduces thrash without compromising throughput.

payload.page_title: GPU workload classifier and SLA tagging guidelines

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: Provide a consistent classification and tagging scheme for GPU workloads across Redwood Inference so that scheduler, billing, and SRE tooling can make deterministic decisions about placement, preemption tolerance, and SLA enforcement. This document defines the taxonomy, tag conventions, enforcement patterns (Terraform + CI gates), and operational runbooks for common mis-tagging and quota scenarios.

Scope: Applies to all internal and customer-facing GPU workloads running on Hosted, Dedicated, and Private clusters. Excludes ephemeral CI CPU-only jobs (see CI/CD playground policies).

Goals
- Enable automated placement decisions (warm pool vs. spot vs. reserved) by exposing workload intent via tags.
- Make SLAs machine-readable for routing, preemptibility, and cost accounting.
- Reduce incidents caused by misconfiguration (e.g., production traffic scheduled on preemptible nodes).
- Provide a clear rollback and remediation runbook for tag-related incidents.

Tagging taxonomy
We standardize a set of tags attached to job/tenant metadata and Terraform resource labels. Tags must be present on cluster attachments, pod templates, and tenant manifests. All tags are lowercase, dash-separated.

Tag schema table
| tag | description | allowed values / format | owner |
|-----|-------------|------------------------:|-------|
| env | workload environment | prod | staging | dev | product (string) | SRE / platform |
| sla.priority | routing and placement priority | platinum | gold | silver | bronze | product / infra |
| sla.latency | expected 95th percentile token latency | <milliseconds, e.g. 150ms> | infra |
| preemptible | preemption tolerance | true | false | infra |
| workload.class | coarse workload class | realtime-inference | batch-eval | training | background | product |
| cost.center | billing cost center id | CC-xxxxx | finance |

Example tag set (string representation):
- env=prod
- sla.priority=gold
- sla.latency=120ms
- preemptible=false
- workload.class=realtime-inference
- cost.center=CC-02142

SLA mapping and enforced behaviors
- platinum: guaranteed capacity in Dedicated pools, sla.latency <= 50ms p95, preemptible=false, rollback to compatible low-memory variant if perf regression > 20% within 10m.
- gold: routed to warm pools or reserved burst; sla.latency <= 150ms p95; preemptible=false preferred but can be true with explicit approval.
- silver: allowed on heterogeneous or preemptible-backed pools; sla.latency <= 500ms p95; preemptible=true allowed.
- bronze: background and low-priority batch work, preemptible=true mandatory for cost control.

Enforcement patterns
1) Terraform module validation (pre-commit/CI):
   - A policy-as-code check that validates required tags exist for every gpu_node_group and tenant module. Missing tags fail plan stage.
   - Integrate with OPA/rego gate in the repo: repo: infra/tenant-modules -> pre-merge gate.

2) Admission webhook in clusters:
   - kube-metadata-admitter validates pod labels and rejects pods that run GPUs without env and sla.priority tags.

3) Runtime auditing:
   - nightly job (gpu-tag-auditor) that emits violations to metrics (counter: gpu_tag_violations_total) and opens tickets when high-cost mis-tagging detected.

Terraform snippet (example enforcement variable and tag usage)
```
module "tenant_gpu" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@redwood/repo.git//modules/tenant-gpu?ref=v1.4"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  tags = {
    env            = var.env
    sla_priority   = var.sla_priority
    workload_class = var.workload_class
    cost_center    = var.cost_center
  }
}
```

Admission policy example (Rego pseudo-rule)
```
package admission.gpu

deny[msg] {
  input.request.object.spec.gpu_count > 0
  not input.request.object.metadata.labels.env
  msg = "GPU pod missing env label"
}
```

Classifier rules (yaml example used by scheduler):
```
- match:
    labels:
      workload.class: realtime-inference
  route:
    pool: warm-reserved
    preemptible: false
- match:
    labels:
      workload.class: batch-eval
  route:
    pool: spot-burst
    preemptible: true
```

Operational runbooks
1) Incident: Production traffic scheduled on preemptible nodes
   Indicators:
   - Elevated p95 token latency for prod tenants
   - Alert: node_eviction_rate > 0.5% and pods with env=prod and preemptible=true present
   Triage steps:
   1. Oncall pulls last 30m of allocation events: `kubectl get pods -l env=prod -o wide` and cross references node labels.
   2. If pods are on preemptible nodes, check Terraform plan history: `git log -S"preemptible=true" infra/tenant-modules` to identify recent changes.
   3. Remediate: If mis-tagged, patch workload labels: `kubectl label pod <pod> preemptible=false --overwrite` and trigger a rolling restart of the deployment.
   4. If the issue is widespread, escalate to infra@redwood and trigger warm-pool scale-up policy: `./tools/warm-pool-scale --tenant $TENANT --factor 1.5`
   5. Open a post-incident ticket and set required fix: update the Terraform module to include explicit tag validation and add unit tests in the module's test harness (owner: tenant-iac-team).

2) Incident: Missing mandatory tags detected in nightly audit
   Triage steps:
   1. gpu-tag-auditor will create a jira with list of resources. The SRE triage lead assigns to tenant owner.
   2. If owner is unknown, use cost.center to map via finance ledger and notify cost center owner.
   3. Fix: apply tag patch through terraform import + `terraform apply` or for ephemeral CI jobs, update pipeline variables to append required tags.

Rollout plan for enforcement changes
- Week 0: Soft audit only – nightly auditor creates tickets but does not block deploys.
- Week 2: CI fails on missing tags for new merges (enables rewrite for contributors).
- Week 4: Admission webhook enabled in staging clusters.
- Week 6: Admission webhook enabled in prod for non-critical namespaces.
- Week 8: Full enforcement in prod namespaces; auto-remediation playbooks enabled.

Observability and metrics to monitor
- gpu_tag_violations_total (counter) – goal < 5/week
- gpu_pod_misplacement_ratio (gauge) – p95 < 0.5%
- sla_latency_p95_by_tenant (histogram) – alert when above mapped sla.latency for more than 5m
- cost_center_gpu_spend_by_sla (timeseries) – used for monthly chargeback and anomaly detection

Ownership and contacts
- Policy owner: Platform / infra (owner alias: infra-platform@redwood)
- Oncall: SRE rotation (see /eng-infra/eng-sre/oncall-rotations for roster)
- Terraform module owner: tenant-iac-team (leads: Maya Chen, Rafael Ortiz)
- CI gate maintainers: CI/CD team (lead: Priya Nair)

Testing guidance
- Unit tests: module-level unit tests for tag generation (use terratest) are required for all changes.
- Integration: run admission webhook against a local kind cluster in CI.
- Chaos: include one scheduled experiment per quarter where a small set of prod-like tenants are intentionally mis-tagged and the auditor/alerting paths are validated.

Frequently asked questions
- Q: What if a tenant needs low-latency but also wants to use spot instances?
  A: Use sla.priority=gold and set a preemptible flag with an approved exception. The scheduler will attempt warm-reserved and fallback to compatible quantized models if preemption occurs.

- Q: How do we onboard a new cost center?
  A: Create an entry in finance ledger, then update the tenant onboarding Terraform module with cost_center value. The onboarding runbook will validate tags as part of the CI pipeline.

Appendices
- Commonly referenced automation: `gpu-tag-auditor`, `gpu-classifier`, `warm-pool-scale` (internal tools in infra/tools).
- Related pages: see page links in metadata for quota and fair-share patterns.

Change log
- 2024-11-12: Created initial draft by Jordan Patel.
- 2024-12-18: Added enforcement rollout schedule and CI/OPA examples (reviewers: Maya Chen).
- 2025-02-14: Published with completed Terraform module snippets and expanded runbook for large-scale remediation.

payload.page_title: GPU CI dependency slimming and release stability playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes a pragmatic, operational pattern for slimming CI/CD dependency graphs for GPU workloads and improving release stability for inference runtime changes. It combines build-time techniques (dependency pruning, delta-builds, content-addressable caching) with runtime release controls (canaries, staged rollout windows, flaky-test quarantine) and terraform/IaC contract checks to reduce CI latency, lower cost, and reduce release-induced regressions.

Goals
- Reduce median CI runtime for GPU-eval and runtime-integration pipelines by 30–50% without losing test coverage.
- Limit blast radius of runtime/kernel/orchestrator changes by enforcing staged rollouts, improved gating, and automated rollback.
- Provide clear triage and remediation runbook for CI-induced production regressions and infra flakiness.

Scope
- Applies to: GPU build and eval CI pipelines, e2e inference integration jobs, image promotion pipelines, and terraform modules used to provision GPU testbeds.
- Excludes: user-facing SDK unit tests (non-inference), low-cost CPU-only CI lanes.

Ownership and Roles
- CI pipeline owner: eng-infra/ci-cd team (primary contact: Maya Chen).
- Runtime & kernels: eng-serving-runtime (reviewer on gating rules).
- GPU fleet provisioning / IaC: eng-infra/terraform (owner for TF contract checks).
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre oncall (see incident procedures).

High-level strategy
1) Dependency slimming: identify minimal graph of inputs required to validate a change and run only those shards.
   - Use change-file ownership mapping (CODEOWNERS-like) to map PRs to impacted integration shards (model, kernel, image, infra).
   - Build a fast static analyzer that inspects changed files and maps them to test shards via a YAML mapping table: {path_glob -> shards}.
2) Delta builds + content-addressable caches:
   - Use content-hash of source tree + toolchain -> cache key. Cache artifacts: wheel/tarball, container layers, kernel-build artifacts, quantized artifacts.
   - Promote cache hits to ephemeral registry/registry-snapshot for downstream jobs.
3) Parallel but prioritized scheduling:
   - Fast-preflight lane (unit tests, lint, small integration smoke) runs in <10m and gates PRs.
   - Full validation lanes (GPU-heavy) are scheduled with priority tokens and can be preempted for critical CI windows.
4) Release stability controls:
   - Canary windows: small percentage of traffic / small canary tenant pool hooked to new runtime image (config via rollout policy).
   - Canary SLOs: p99 latency, error-rate, per-tenant cost-per-token.

Pipeline config table (recommended defaults)
| config_key | recommended_value | rationale |
|---|---|---|
| fast_preflight_timeout | 12m | Keep preflight fast to unblock authors |
| gpu_validation_timeout | 180m | GPU runs may take long depending on evals |
| max_parallel_gpu_jobs | 6 | Prevent GPU starvation; adjust per region |
| cache_ttl | 72h | Balance storage vs cache-hit rate |
| canary_traffic_pct | 5% | Small canary to detect regressions without broad impact |

(Use simple markdown table above in Confluence; ingest into pipeline config as ENV_VAR defaults where possible.)

Detailed procedures
A. Author pre-merge flow (fast path)
1. Author opens PR. CI preflight triggers (unit tests, lint, build-sanity).
2. Static analyzer computes affected shards and annotates PR with expected CI lanes.
3. Fast-preflight lane must pass before any GPU job is scheduled.
4. If static analyzer or CODEOWNERS marks kernel/runtime changes, label PR with `runtime-impact`. This triggers additional IaC contract checks.

B. IaC contract checks (pre-merge)
- The TF contract test runs a dry-run plan against a synthetic sandbox account to verify network/egress changes do not violate tenant isolation policies.
- Contract failures must block the PR. The test emits: changed_resources.json (content-hash), impacted_subnets (list).

C. GPU-heavy validation lane (post-merge or gated pre-merge)
1. Use promoted cache snapshots for base images and kernel artifacts.
2. Run a minimal set of long-running tests first (smoke generation + kv-cache warmup) with strict timebox.
3. If minimal smoke fails, abort and notify author; do not proceed to full eval.
4. Full eval runs are queued; if queue time exceeds 30m, demote job priority and notify release manager.

D. Release gating and promotion
1. Image promotion flow: `build -> snapshot-registry -> staging -> canary -> production`. Each stage requires a sign-off from owner teams listed in `repository/MANIFEST/owners.yaml`.
2. Canary is automated: deploy to 5% of tenants or a dedicated canary tenancy. Monitor the canary for 24–48 hours before staged ramp.

Incident triage & rollback (oncall playbook)
1. Detection signals (any of): sudden p95/p99 latency jump >30%, 5xx increase >1% absolute, token-cost spike >20% vs baseline, or customer error reports.
2. Immediate mitigation steps:
   a. Pause rollout: flip rollout policy to route 100% traffic to previous image.
   b. If pause fails or cannot be toggled cleanly, fail open to a safe fallback model variant (lower-capacity but stable) using the smart routing fallback.
   c. If traffic is still degraded, trigger emergency image rollback to last known-good image (<2h target).
3. Post-rollback: collect artifacts (CI logs, kernel build logs, promoted-cache manifest, infra plan diff). Tag a postmortem ticket and attach artifacts.

Runbook checklist for CI flakiness (triage steps)
- Check the preflight static analyzer annotation for false-positives.
- Verify cache hit rate for recent builds (target: >60% for kernel artifacts).
- Inspect runner health: GPU driver version drift, CUDA mismatch, containerd or node disk pressure.
- If a pattern is detected across multiple PRs, open an RFC for changing static analyzer mapping.

Telemetry and alerting
- CI SLOs to track: median preflight runtime < 8m, 95th percentile GPU queue wait < 25m, cache hit-rate > 60% for kernel artifacts.
- Alerts:
  - CI: ci-preflight-latency-high (p95 > 12m) -> paged to ci-cd oncall.
  - GPU-queue-surge (95th > 45m) -> routed to eng-infra oncall.
  - Canary-regression-detected (error-rate delta > 0.5% absolute) -> paged to runtime owners + eng-sre.

Automated remediation playbooks (examples)
- Automated cache warming: when a promoted-cache snapshot is published, kick off warmers in each region to prime LRU caches for the next 1–2 hours.
- Job re-scheduler: if a GPU job fails due to transient infra (node reboot, preempt), automatically requeue once with backoff and annotate failure type.

CLI examples and snippets
- Query cache hit-rate (example):

Terraform/IAAC checks snippet (example)

Postmortem and continuous improvement
- Every CI incident that caused >30 minutes of release block or customer impact must have a postmortem with a timeline, RCA, and at least two corrective actions: one short-term (config change / hotfix) and one long-term (instrumentation / design change).

payload.page_title: Schema validation + release note build pipeline (Model Metadata v1)

sections.body: This document defines the required CI/CD checks and build steps used when changing Model Metadata Schema v1 or any model/version metadata records that feed customer-visible release notes.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Metadata is syntactically valid, semantically consistent, and compatible with serving/runtime constraints.
- Customer-visible release notes are always generated for promotions, consistently categorized, and appropriately redacted.
- There is a deterministic artifact trail from a specific metadata change to:
  - what was published publicly,
  - what was retained internally for audit/support,
  - and which model version was promoted.
sections.heading: The pipeline exists to ensure

sections.body:
Applies to repositories and paths that influence model metadata and release notes:
- `redwood-model-registry` (schema + model records; fixtures)
- `redwood` (control plane event emission; promotion flows)
- `redwood-docs` (public release notes site generation)
- SDK repos consuming the release note endpoints (non-blocking for promotion, but required for SDK release train)
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Customer notification subscriptions (email/webhook) beyond internal webhook plumbing
- Rewriting full historical release notes (we validate new and a small curated backfill only)
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body:
- **Metadata Schema v1**: The canonical structure defining required/optional fields for models/variants/quantization profiles.
- **Metadata record**: A single model version (or variant) entry stored in the model registry.
- **Change event**: Structured event emitted by the control plane on create/update/promote/deprecate actions.
- **Changelog artifact**: The generated release note payloads (public + internal) produced from events + metadata.
- **Promotion**: Marking a model version as eligible/active for a given deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and/or region.
sections.heading: Definitions

sections.body:
1) Engineer updates schema and/or metadata records via PR.
2) CI validates:
   - JSON Schema conformance and invariants
   - redaction rules for public fields
   - deterministic release note preview generated from the diff
3) On merge to `main`, a build publishes updated registry data.
4) On promotion (typically a control plane operation), the control plane emits a `model.version_promoted` event.
5) The changelog generator ingests events and produces:
   - public release note entries (Console + docs)
   - internal release note entries (support/admin)
   - audit events (security/compliance)
6) Docs builds pull the public artifacts and render versioned pages.
sections.heading: High-level flow (what happens on a metadata change)

sections.body: The following checks are required and are configured as branch protections for `main` in the model registry repository.
sections.heading: Required checks (PR gating)

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching schema files or any `models/**/*.json` metadata.

**What it does:**
- Validates JSON syntax.
- Validates against the published JSON Schema (Schema v1).
- Runs additional semantic validation rules not expressible in JSON Schema (see “Semantic validation”).

**Failure examples:**
- Missing required fields (e.g., `version`, `deployment_availability`, `public.summary`).
- Invalid semantic version (`version` must be SemVer, `X.Y.Z` or `X.Y.Z-suffix`).
- Unknown deployment mode or invalid region code.
sections.heading: 1) `metadata-schema-validate`

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching schema definition files.

**What it does:**
- Calculates a schema diff vs `main`.
- Enforces a compatibility policy:
  - Additive changes are allowed by default.
  - Removing or renaming fields requires explicit approval and a migration plan.
  - Tightening validation that breaks existing stored records requires a backfill job merged first (or same PR with backfill + verification).

**Policy outcomes:**
- PASS: additive / backward compatible.
- WARN: potentially breaking; requires `release-eng-approval` label.
- FAIL: breaking without an approved migration plan.
sections.heading: 2) `metadata-schema-diff-policy`

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching metadata records OR promotion-related templates.

**What it does:**
- Generates a release note preview artifact from the metadata diff using the standard templates and category mapping.
- Produces two outputs:
  - `public_preview.md` (customer-visible)
  - `internal_preview.md` (includes internal-only notes)
- Fails if required release note inputs are missing for changes that will be customer-visible.

**Required inputs for preview generation:**
- `public.summary` (1–3 sentences)
- `public.category` (one of: security | breaking | perf | quality | bugfix | deprecation)
- `public.customer_impact` (brief, plain-language)
- `public.rollback_guidance` (if category is breaking/security/deprecation)
sections.heading: 3) `release-note-preview`

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching templates, redaction rules, or any metadata fields flagged as internal.

**What it does:**
- Ensures fields classified as internal (e.g., internal incident links, vendor/hardware debug notes, customer-specific identifiers) cannot appear in public artifacts.
- Runs snapshot tests that render release notes under multiple roles:
  - `admin`
  - `support`
  - `standard_user`

**Hard rule:** public output must never contain:
- Internal-only fields (`internal.*`)
- Customer identifiers (account IDs, emails, contract names)
- Incident channel links or ticket IDs (unless explicitly approved in `public.references`)
sections.heading: 4) `redaction-and-rbac-tests`

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching schema files.

**What it does:**
- Verifies example payloads/fixtures still validate.
- Ensures at least one fixture exists for each supported model family and at least one quantization profile example.
sections.heading: 5) `fixtures-and-examples-check`

sections.body:
**Trigger:** PR touching event emission for model metadata changes.

**What it does:**
- Verifies event payloads adhere to the event contract (required fields, idempotency key presence).
- Ensures the event includes:
  - actor (service principal or human)
  - timestamp
  - affected model id + version
  - environment and deployment mode
  - schema hash
sections.heading: 6) `audit-event-contract-check` (control plane repo)

sections.body: CI runs a semantic validator (`metadata-lint`) to enforce cross-field invariants.
sections.heading: Semantic validation rules (beyond JSON Schema)

sections.body:
- `version` must be SemVer.
- `compatibility.min_runtime_version` must be set and must not regress for an existing major line unless the change is marked `public.category=breaking`.
- Tokenizer constraints:
  - `tokenizer.name` and `tokenizer.revision` must be set.
  - Tokenizer changes require `public.category` of `breaking` or `quality` (depending on impact), and must include `public.customer_impact` describing potential output drift.
sections.heading: Versioning and compatibility

sections.body:
- Each model version must declare availability by deployment mode:
  - Hosted: required regions list (even if single region)
  - Dedicated: eligibility policy reference (capacity tier constraints)
  - Private: packaging support (bundle name or “not supported”)
- If Hosted availability changes (region added/removed), release note preview is required.
sections.heading: Deployment availability

sections.body:
- Deprecations must include:
  - `deprecation.state` (announced | active | removed)
  - `deprecation.effective_date`
  - `deprecation.replacement` (if available)
  - public deprecation note with action required
sections.heading: Deprecations

sections.body:
- Public quality improvements/regressions must not include unqualified statistical claims.
- If `public.category=quality`, the metadata must include at least one quality signal reference:
  - eval run id(s)
  - baseline version id
  - guardrail outcomes summary (allowed values only)
sections.heading: Quality claims

sections.body: The changelog generator produces standardized artifacts consumed by Console and docs.
sections.heading: Release note artifact formats

sections.body:
- Public:
  - `release-notes/public/{model_id}/{version}.md`
  - `release-notes/public/feed.json`
- Internal:
  - `release-notes/internal/{model_id}/{version}.md`
  - `release-notes/internal/feed.json`
sections.heading: Artifact outputs

sections.body:
- Model name + version
- Category + severity language (per style guide)
- Summary (plain language)
- Customer impact
- Deployment availability notes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private where applicable)
- Rollback guidance when relevant
- References (docs links only; internal links are stripped)
sections.heading: Public artifacts must include

sections.body:
- All generated notes are keyed by `(model_id, version, change_event_id)`.
- Template rendering must be deterministic given the same inputs; timestamps are sourced from event time, not build time.
sections.heading: To prevent duplicate entries and drift

sections.body: Promotion is a control plane operation, but it is gated by the following checks.
sections.heading: Promotion gates (before a model version can be promoted)

sections.body:
- Metadata record validates.
- `public.summary` and `public.category` are present.
- Availability is declared for the target deployment mode.
sections.heading: A version cannot be promoted unless

sections.body:
- There must exist a generated public release note entry for the promotion event.
- If the changelog generator is degraded, promotion may proceed only under a break-glass procedure (see below) and must generate notes within the defined SLA.
sections.heading: For promotions in Hosted and Dedicated

sections.body:
Promotion cannot proceed unless audit event emission is healthy:
- Audit event must be emitted and acknowledged (async with retry; promotion call blocks until event is enqueued).
- If audit pipeline is down, promotion requires Security on-call approval.
sections.heading: Gate C: audit logging

sections.body:
- The version must declare rollout eligibility fields (e.g., allowlisted tiers/regions).
- Rollback policy must exist for breaking/security/deprecation categories.
sections.heading: If promotion is tied to canary/A-B rollout

sections.body:
- `metadata-schema-validate`: runs on PR and `main` pushes
- `metadata-schema-diff-policy`: runs on PR when schema changes
- `release-note-preview`: runs on PR when metadata changes
- `redaction-and-rbac-tests`: runs on PR when templates/redaction rules change
- `fixtures-and-examples-check`: runs on PR when schema changes
sections.heading: Standard jobs (model registry repo)

sections.body:
- `schema-diff.txt`
- `metadata-lint-report.json` (machine readable; used by bot comments)
- `release-note-preview-public.md`
- `release-note-preview-internal.md`
sections.heading: Artifacts uploaded by CI

sections.body:
- Validation status and errors
- A rendered release note preview snippet
- A checklist of missing required fields
sections.heading: CI posts a PR comment with

sections.body:
The following labels are used to route approvals and enforce additional checks:
- `model-metadata-change` (required for any metadata record change)
- `schema-change` (required for schema changes)
- `release-notes-reviewed` (required when `public.category` is breaking/security/deprecation)
- `security-review-required` (automatically applied when internal/public boundary rules are touched)
- `release-eng-approval` (required for schema diffs flagged WARN by policy)
sections.heading: Required PR labels and approvals

sections.body:
- Schema changes: must be approved by Model Catalog schema owner (Quentin Harris) and Release Eng (Connor O'Brien) when diff-policy is WARN/FAIL.
- Redaction rules or template changes: must be approved by Security (Naomi Feldman or delegate).
- Console/API contracts for release notes: must be approved by Console backend EM (Chloe Martin) if endpoints are impacted.
sections.heading: Approval requirements

sections.body:
If the changelog generator or docs publishing pipeline is down, promotion can proceed only if all conditions are met:
- Incident is declared (or tracked) and linked in the internal-only promotion ticket.
- Release Eng on-call approves.
- Security on-call approves if audit emission is impacted.
- A manual public release note stub is created (public-safe, minimal) and later reconciled with the generated canonical artifact.
sections.heading: Break-glass procedure (rare)

sections.body: - Within 24 hours, a backfill job must generate the canonical release note artifact and replace the stub.
sections.heading: Post-incident requirement

sections.body:
- Backfill jobs must run in staging first.
- CI must validate a representative sample of existing records (minimum 95% coverage by model family and deployment mode).
- A rollback plan is required, including:
  - revert commit instructions
  - DB migration rollback steps (if applicable)
  - monitoring dashboards to confirm health post-rollback
sections.heading: When migrating existing model records to Metadata Schema v1

sections.body:
- % of promotions with a public release note published within SLA
- Time from promotion event to release note availability in Console
- Redaction test failures and attempted leaks caught by CI
sections.heading: We monitor

sections.body:
- 99.5% of promotions produce a public release note artifact within 10 minutes.
- 99.9% of promotions emit an audit event within 1 minute.
sections.heading: Target SLOs

sections.body:
- Ensure the metadata change includes required `public.*` fields.
- If change is internal-only and should not produce public notes, mark the change accordingly in metadata (internal-only change classification) and re-run CI.
sections.heading: CI fails: "release note preview missing required fields"

sections.body:
- Search the template inputs for `internal.*` or restricted references.
- Ensure links in `public.references` point to docs-site URLs only.
sections.heading: CI fails: "public artifact contains internal-only content"

sections.body:
- Check audit pipeline status in observability dashboards.
- If confirmed outage, follow break-glass procedure and obtain approvals.
sections.heading: Promotion blocked: "audit enqueue failed"

sections.body:
Category: perf
Summary: Reduced time-to-first-token and improved throughput stability under bursty traffic.
Customer impact: Lower latency and fewer tail spikes during peak hours; no API changes.
Deployment availability: Hosted (us-east-1, eu-west-1); Dedicated (all tiers); Private (next bundle).
Rollback guidance: Pin to the previous patch version via Console or API if you observe regressions.
sections.heading: Appendix: example release note preview (public)

sections.body:
- 2025-12-03: Updated approval gates for audit enqueue failures; clarified artifact paths for public/internal feeds.
- 2025-11-11: Added role-based rendering snapshot tests following internal-notes leakage regression.
- 2025-10-09: Initial publication.
sections.heading: Change log

payload.page_title: GPU release staging and traffic shaping catalog

sections.body:
Overview

This catalog documents the canonical staging lanes, traffic shaping profiles, and Terraform operator contract that the GPU fleet and CI/CD teams use for safe runtime and kernel rollouts. It is intended for infra engineers responsible for GPU releases, release engineers running snack-sized fleet rollouts, and SREs on rotation. The guidance balances:
- predictable tenant impact (SLO-driven)
- burst/spot behavior across regions
- fast rollback when regressions are seen

Why this exists

We observed two common failure modes during model runtime/kernel rollouts: (1) sudden tenant throughput collapse caused by aggressive warm-pool rotation, and (2) egress/congestion spikes when multi-region burst orchestration lands capacity in a small set of AZs. This catalog standardizes staging lanes and CI contracts so changes are exercised against realistic traffic shaping before hitting prod.

Summary of artifacts in this page

1) Staging lanes and their acceptance criteria
2) Traffic shaping profiles and mappings to GPU pools
3) Terraform operator interface (contract) and sample module snippet
4) CI job templates (Buildkite and GitHub Actions) and synthetic workload generators
5) Release checklist and rollback playbook
6) Ownership and metrics to watch

1) Staging lanes and acceptance criteria

Each change (kernel, runtime, quantization profile, or Terraform operator) must pass one of the lanes below before gradual rollout to production:

- shadow-sim: unit + synthetic shadow traffic run (local CI). Acceptance: no kernel-level OOMs, KV cache miss rate < 2% on synthetic workload, unit tests pass.
- canary-1p (single-tenant canary): 1 production tenant routed to the new variant in single AZ. Acceptance: 24h latency P95 increase < 15% relative to baseline, error rate delta < 0.1% abs.
- canary-5p (multi-tenant micro-canary): 5 production tenants distributed across two AZs. Acceptance: throughput per-tenant variance < 20% and token-cost delta within budgeted window.
- staging-scale: scaled synthetic traffic across GPU pool slice (20% of warm pool capacity) for 6h. Acceptance: SLOs hold for 6h and memory pressure stable.
- preprod-mirror: mirrored traffic at full QPS (no user-visible fallthrough) for at least 2h. Acceptance: no regression alerts, telemetry matches baseline within 95% CI.

Acceptance metrics (table)

| Metric | Threshold (pass) | Notes |
|--------|------------------|-------|
| Latency P95 | < baseline * 1.15 | Measured per-route and aggregated |
| Error rate (5xx/timeout) | delta < 0.001 (absolute) | Compare to 24h baseline |
| KV cache miss rate | < 0.05 | Synthetic workloads should exercise caching |
| OOMs / GPU | 0 | Any OOM fails the lane |
| Token-cost delta | within budgeted profile | Provided by Optimize signals |

2) Traffic shaping profiles and mappings

Traffic shaping profiles are small JSON blobs used by the release orchestrator to inject controlled gradients of traffic:

- spike-buffered: fast ramp to 30% of target, hold 30m, then ramp to 100% over 2h. Use for low-risk micro-changes.
- conservative-step: 10% increments every 30m with health-check gate. Use for kernel changes.
- regional-fanout: sequential enrich of regions to avoid AZ-local egress spikes (region-by-region roll).
- burst-suffix: preserves a 15% reserved buffer for burst tenants and preempts canary traffic if burst > 60% pool usage.

Mapping guidance

- Kernel hotpatches -> conservative-step, canary-1p then canary-5p.
- Runtime config toggles -> spike-buffered on non-critical routes, conservative-step on critical routes.
- Quantization profile flips -> staging-scale first with representative synthetic workloads.

Example profile (canonical shape)

```
{
  "name": "conservative-step",
  "steps": [
    {"pct": 0.10, "duration_m": 30, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 0.20, "duration_m": 30, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 0.40, "duration_m": 60, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 1.00, "duration_m": 120, "gate": "manual-approval"}
  ],
  "safety": {"reserved_pct": 0.15, "abort_on": ["oom", "p95_increase>0.15"]}
}
```

3) Terraform operator interface and sample module snippet

Contract summary

The Terraform operator (the fleet-release-operator) receives a release plan resource which expresses: target_variant, traffic_profile, pool_selector, precondition_checks, and rollback_policy. The contract guarantees idempotency, plan validation, and status subresource updates. All changes must be applied via the operator in CI/CD pipelines (no human-crafted TF applies to fleet pools).

Required resource fields (brief)

- name (string)
- target_variant (string) — runtime/kernel image tag or operator version
- pool_selector (map) — labels: {region, pool_type, gpu_family}
- traffic_profile (string) — one of profiles defined above
- precondition_checks (list) — list of telemetry queries that must pass
- rollback_policy (map) — abort window, auto-rollback on X failures

Sample Terraform module usage

```
module "release_plan_example" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@our-repo/infrastructure/terraform-plugins//modules/release_plan?ref=v2026"

  name           = "runtime-2026-02-10-canary"
  target_variant = "runtime:v2.14.3-kernel-3b"
  pool_selector  = { region = "us-west-2", pool_type = "warm", gpu_family = "a100" }
  traffic_profile = "conservative-step"

  precondition_checks = [
    "metric(query: 'kv_cache_miss{env:prod} > 0.05', window: '10m', op: '<'),",
    "metric(query: 'oom_count{region:us-west-2} == 0', window: '10m', op: '==')"
  ]

  rollback_policy = { abort_window_m = 30, auto_rollback_on = ["oom", "p95_increase>0.15"] }
}
```

Operator behavior notes

- Validation: operator rejects plans that target > 50% of warm pool without preprod signoff.
- Idempotency: re-applying the same release_plan should be a no-op if status.phase in [succeeded, in_progress].
- Status updates: operator writes status {phase, applied_pct, active_step, last_health_eval} to the resource.

4) CI job templates and synthetic workload generators

Buildkite pipeline sample (simplified)

```
steps:
  - label: ":docker: build release artifact"
    command: 
      - ./scripts/build-runtime.sh --tag ${BUILDKITE_COMMIT}
  - wait
  - label: ":rocket: apply release plan (shadow-sim)"
    command: |
      ./ci/apply_release_plan.sh \n        --plan-file release_plan.json \n        --lane shadow-sim \n        --dry-run=false
  - label: ":test_tube: run synthetic stress"
    command: ./ci/run_synthetic_suite.sh --profile staging-scale
  - label: ":eyes: promote to canary"
    if: "branch = main"
    command: ./ci/promote_release.sh --lane canary-1p --require-approval
```

GitHub Actions snippet for preprod-mirror validation (simplified)

```
name: preprod-mirror-validate
on: [workflow_dispatch]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Apply release plan
        run: ./ci/apply_release_plan.sh --plan-file preprod.json --lane preprod-mirror
      - name: Invoke telemetry assertions
        run: ./ci/assert_telemetry.sh --checks preprod_checks.yaml
```

Synthetic workload generator guidance

- Use the GPU traffic emulator (repo: infra/gpu-traffic-emulator) which can reproduce token distribution, KV cache prefix skew, and tail-latency patterns.
- Seed the emulator with real traffic fingerprints (anonymized) from the traffic-fingerprint catalog.
- When running staging-scale, run for a minimum of 6h with periodic forced KV-cache invalidation to exercise cache warmup behavior.

5) Release checklist and rollback playbook

Pre-release checklist (must be green)

- [ ] Release plan resource created in staging environment and validated by operator.
- [ ] Synthetic workloads executed: shadow-sim and staging-scale with no critical failures.
- [ ] Observability: dashboards updated and alert thresholds temporarily lowered for the canary window.
- [ ] Pager rota notified and release channel created (#infra-release).
- [ ] Ownership: release owner and backout owner identified.

Promotion procedure (high-level)

1) Create release_plan Terraform module in feature branch.
2) Run shadow-sim via CI and collect telemetry.
3) Promote to canary-1p with conservative-step profile and monitor 2h.
4) If canary passes, promote to canary-5p and monitor 6h.
5) Execute staging-scale for 6h. If all gates pass, promote to preprod-mirror.
6) At preprod-mirror, validate billing/telemetry and then schedule gradual production roll with regional-fanout.

Abort & rollback policy (ordered steps)

1) Abort the current step via operator (operator API: POST /release_plans/{name}/abort).
2) If immediate rollback required, set release_plan.rollback_policy.auto_rollback_on and invoke auto-rollback.
3) If auto-rollback fails or the operator is unhealthy, manually scale down target_variant on fleet allocator:

kubectl -n fleet scale deployment runtime-v2 --replicas=0 --selector=release=unsafe

4) Notify #infra-incidents and create incident with preliminary impact assessment.

6) Ownership, run metrics, and dashboards

Owners and on-call

- Release owner: infra-release-engineering (primary contact: Priya Menon)
- Kernel/runtime owners: serving-runtime team (pager: @oncall-serving-runtime)
- Fleet allocator / operator owners: eng-infra (pager: @oncall-infra)

Telemetry to watch during windows (minimum)

- API latency by route (P50/P95/P99) — alert: P95 > baseline * 1.2 for 15m
- Error rate (5xx + timeouts) — alert: > 0.5% absolute increase for 10m
- GPU memory used / GPU (OOM alerts immediate)
- KV cache miss ratio by pool — alert: > 5% abs increase vs baseline for 10m
- Warm pool utilization and reserved buffer usage — alert: reserved_pct < 0.10
- Egress bytes per AZ — alert: top-az > baseline * 2.5

Dashboard & runbook links

- Release dashboard: /dashboards/release-orchestrator/active-release-plans
- Canary health: /dashboards/inference/canary-health
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-graded-degradation-and-tenant-fallback-playbook

Appendix: common troubleshooting scenarios

Scenario A: P95 spike in canary after a kernel rollout
1) Check operator status for last_health_eval and applied_pct.
2) Compare canary tenant tail-latency against baseline for same route fingerprints.
3) If p95 increase correlates with memory pressure, abort step and roll back kernel.
4) If p95 increase correlates with egress imbalance, trigger regional-fanout pause and rebalance traffic.

Scenario B: OOMs observed only in staging-scale
1) Halt progress and mark plan aborted.
2) Capture minidumps and GPU memory profiles from the affected nodes (run: ./scripts/collect_gpu_profiles.sh --since 30m).
3) Reproduce locally with emulator using the same prefix/key distribution.

FAQ (short)

Q: Can I manually apply Terraform to a fleet pool for emergency rollback?
A: No. All fleet-facing changes must go through the release operator. For emergencies, use the operator API which is faster and guarantees status propagation.

Q: What if synthetic workload cannot reproduce an expensive tail-case?
A: Work with the telemetry team to add a traffic fingerprint to the emulator catalog. Use a short targeted preprod mirror with the fingerprint before promoting.

Contributors

- Primary author: Priya Menon (infra-release-engineering)
- Reviewers: Ethan Kim, Lucas Ortega, Ritika Sharma

Revision history

- 2025-09-15: initial draft and staging lane definitions.
- 2025-11-02: added Terraform operator contract and sample module.
- 2026-02-10: updated acceptance thresholds and CI templates to include GitHub Actions snippet.

If you have questions or want to propose a new traffic profile, file an issue in infra/release-orchestrator and tag infra-release-engineering.

payload.page_title: GPU Eval Backpressure Simulator and Canary Playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This document describes the GPU Eval Backpressure Simulator (GEBS) and an associated canary gating playbook used by the CI/CD and GPU fleet teams to validate how model-eval workloads respond to resource contention, egress limits, and burst traffic. The simulator is intended to run as part of gated evaluation pipelines and to provide deterministic, repeatable stress checks before promotions to staging/production GPU pools.

Goals

- Provide a reproducible test harness that simulates: queueing/backpressure, preemption, bursty arrival patterns, and egress-constrained workloads.
- Integrate with CI/CD (Buildkite) so every eval job can opt into a backpressure check.
- Produce metric-driven canary gates (pass/fail) so model/infra changes cannot be promoted if they cause SLO regressions.
- Offer an oncall-friendly runbook for triage when a backpressure gate fails during rollout.

Scope and Non‑Goals

- In scope: developer-triggered eval pipelines, nightly batch evals, and canary promotions for Dedicated pools.
- Out of scope: host-level thermal or hardware failure simulation (handled by GPU-fleet chaos-day docs), and billing/cost chargeback automation.

Architecture overview

The simulator is implemented as a containerized service that can be executed inside Buildkite CI agents or ephemeral eval clusters. It has three components:

1) Workload generator: produces synthetic requests with configurable arrival distributions (Poisson, burst, ramp) and payload characteristics (seq length, kv cache size).
2) Resource stress controller: triggers artificial constraints (CPU steal, cgroup CPU quota reductions, network egress shaping, simulated preemption via SIGSTOP cycles) to model contention scenarios.
3) Metrics exporter and gate engine: gathers latency percentiles, queue length, token throughput, failure rates, and computes gate decisions against configured thresholds.

Design details

- Language/stack: Go service + Python client harness. We chose Go for the stress controller because of lightweight static binaries suitable for Buildkite agents.
- Container image: internal registry: redwood/gpu-gebs:stable (image must be signed and scanned by the CI pipeline).
- Config model: YAML file with sections for generator, stressors, and gate thresholds. Examples below.

Simulator configuration table

| parameter | example | description | recommended range |
|---|---:|---|---|
| arrival_distribution | burst | arrival pattern: poisson|burst|ramp | burst for smoke, poisson for steady-state |
| rps_target | 250 | target requests per second | 1 - 2000 |
| seq_length | 512 | tokens per request | 32 - 4096 |
| kv_cache_reuse_ratio | 0.6 | proportion of requests that reuse prefix cache | 0.0 - 1.0 |
| egress_limit_kbps | 10240 | network egress shaping in kbps | 256 - 65536 |
| preempt_cycle_s | 5 | seconds to SIGSTOP the model process per minute | 0 - 30 |
| gate_latency_p95_ms | 120 | p95 latency threshold used for canary gate | 50 - 500 |
| gate_error_rate_pct | 1 | percentage of requests allowed to fail | 0 - 5 |

CI/CD integration (Buildkite example)

- Trigger point: optionally run GEBS during the `eval` pipeline job, between model artifact validation and canary promotion steps.
- Job snippet (Buildkite YAML):

pipeline:
  steps:
    - label: "Eval: Backpressure Simulation"
      command:
        - \"docker run --rm -v $BUILDKITE_BUILD_PATH:/work -e CONFIG=/work/gebs-config.yaml redwood/gpu-gebs:stable \"
      agents:
        queue: gpu-eval
      env:
        GEBS_OUTPUT: /work/gebs-output.json
      timeout_in_minutes: 45

- Gate behavior: the job must exit non-zero if the gate engine computes a failure. The gate engine writes a human-readable summary to GEBS_OUTPUT and uploads artifacts to the Buildkite run.

Canary promotion procedure (automated + manual steps)

1) Automated pre-checks in CI (pass required): model artifact checksum, unit tests, smoke generation against a local CPU fallback, GEBS simulation with default config.
2) If GEBS passes, pipeline triggers a staged canary deploy to a small Dedicated pool segment (5–10% of canary capacity) with traffic ratio 10:1 to baseline.
3) Monitor the canary for 30 minutes against the SLOs below. If any gate fires, automatically rollback the canary and open an incident ticket assigned to the owning infra/product team.
4) If canary is healthy, expand to 50% for an additional 60 minutes; if healthy, promote to 100% and mark the pipeline step as completed.

Gate thresholds and SLOs

- p95 latency < gate_latency_p95_ms (configurable, default 120 ms)
- error_rate < gate_error_rate_pct (configurable, default 1%)
- queue_length < 250 requests (guardrail)
- token_throughput degradation < 15% vs baseline

Metrics collection and dashboards
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- gebs_request_latency_seconds{quantile=\"0.95\"}
- gebs_request_failure_total / gebs_request_total (error rate)
- gebs_queue_length
- gebs_token_throughput_tokens_total

Dashboards: a dedicated `GEBS / CI Gates` dashboard in Grafana (dashboards/gpu-gebs.json). Buildkite artifact uploads include the raw GEBS_OUTPUT JSON and a compact HTML summary.

Triage runbook (oncall + developer flow)

1) Alert created by CI: `gebs:ci:gate_failed` with step URL and GEBS_OUTPUT artifact.
2) Primary responder: owner of the pipeline (tagged in Buildkite job); secondary: eng-infra oncall.
3) Quick checklist:
   - Review GEBS_OUTPUT summary (p95, error samples, queue length spikes).
   - Re-run GEBS locally with the same config but reduced RPS to isolate whether the failure is linear (scale) or threshold-sensitive.
   - Check GPU pool metrics (utilization, preemption events, host OOMs).
   - If failure correlates to network egress shaping, inspect VPC egress ACLs and NAT gateway metrics.
4) Common resolutions:
   - If p95 regressed due to scheduling delays: increase warm pool size for canary or reduce batch size in runtime config.
   - If error rate is due to KV cache misses: pin model variant with smaller context or enable prefix caching for canary.
   - If caused by noisy neighbor: move canary to different physical host group or use stricter QoS tags.

Rollback steps (fast path)

1) Abort canary promotion in deployment system (console or CLI).
2) Trigger automatic revert to previous model version: `rwdctl infra canary rollback --deployment-id <id>`
3) Run a diagnostic GEBS with `--diagnose` flag to capture core traces and upload to S3: `docker run --rm -e CONFIG=/tmp/gebs.yaml redwood/gpu-gebs:stable --diagnose`
4) Create incident with runbook link and assign to the model owner and infrastructure owner.

Operational run modes and scheduling

- Per-PR gating: lightweight GEBS run with `rps_target=50` and `seq_length=256` (max 15 minutes).
- Nightly regression: full GEBS profile (RPS 500–1500, multiple egress/stop cycles) to detect non-linear issues.
- Pre-release dry-run: run in a private staging Dedicated pool with realistic traffic mix and enable end-to-end observability (A/B tracing).

Security and compliance notes

- GEBS containers must not ship customer data. Use synthetic payloads only.
- Image must be signed and scanned; CI rejects unsigned images.
- When running in customer-facing Dedicated pools (rare), run with read-only service accounts and egress policies that match customer constraints.

Ownership and maintenance

- Owners: eng-infra (primary), eng-serving-runtime (secondary for model runtime parameter coupling).
- Maintenance cadence: quarterly updates to keep arrival models in sync with production telemetry; monthly smoke-run in CI.

Appendix: example GEBS YAML config

```
generator:
  arrival_distribution: burst
  rps_target: 250
  seq_length: 512
  kv_cache_reuse_ratio: 0.6
stressors:
  egress_limit_kbps: 10240
  preempt_cycle_s: 5
gates:
  latency_p95_ms: 120
  error_rate_pct: 1.0
```

Appendix: quick CLI snippets

- Run locally with artifact output:
  docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -e CONFIG=/work/gebs.yaml redwood/gpu-gebs:stable --output /work/gebs-output.json
- Compute a CI-friendly artifact summary:
  python ci/parse_gebs_output.py --input ge bs-output.json --format html --out summary.html

Related pages

- eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-rolling-reboot-and-network-bridge-playbook (operational reboot guidance)
- eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-demand-forecasting-and-ml-backed-scaling-playbook (capacity forecasting)

Document history

- 2024-08-15: initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2024-10-01: added Buildkite snippets and gate thresholds (Diego Ramos)
- 2025-01-12: updated runbook and CI artifact flow to include HTML summaries (Lena Ho)

payload.page_title: mixed-precision-kernel-rollout-playbook

sections.body:
Summary
This playbook describes the end-to-end process for rolling out mixed-precision (FP16/INT8) inference kernels and quantization-enabled runtime changes across Redwood's hosted, dedicated and private GPU fleets. It covers CI/CD pipeline artifacts, Terraform/IaC touches, networking and cross-account rollout choreography, canary strategies, observability guardrails, and an operational runbook for rapid rollback or mitigation.

Scope
- Changes covered: kernel binaries, cuDNN/kernel-shim variants, quantization glue (runtime flags), and model-compatibility patches.
- Environments: staging-cpu, staging-gpu, canary-gpu (fractional tenants), production-hosted, production-dedicated, production-private (VPC).
- Exclusions: hardware firmware/driver upgrades (separate process).

Goals
- Deploy kernels with 95th-percentile latency regression < 5% for P50-target routes and error rate delta < 0.5% for generation failures.
- Ensure deterministic rollback within 15 minutes of a critical alert.
- Prevent noisy neighbor regressions by preserving per-tenant latency SLOs.

Prerequisites
1) Kernel binary artifacts published to our artifact registry: artifact path format artifacts.redwood/nn-kernels/{version}/{platform}/{sha}.so
2) Runtime image promotion pipeline green: image tag format rh-runtime:{version}-k{kernel_version}
3) Terraform module changes reviewed in modules/gpu-runtime-variants and a promoted plan in the module registry.
4) Smoke and perf suites present in CI: perf/kernels/smoke.yml and perf/kernels/regression.yml.

Ownership
- Release lead: eng-infra release engineer (Primary)
- Kernel maintainers: serving-runtime team (Secondary)
- Tenant communications: customer-success (Notify for Dedicated/Private customers)
- IaC changes: infra-terraform owners

Test Matrix (minimum)
- Functional: run model sanity (token-by-token equality for FP32 baseline) on a 50-case prompt-set.
- Perf: 1k sample streaming gen with representative prompt distribution; measure P50/P95 latency and throughput.
- Memory: max KV cache size verification with sequence length 4096.
- Quantization (INT8): quality regression A/B eval (BLEU/ROUGE or custom embed-sim) on 200 prompts.

CI/CD Pipeline (high level)
1) PR to runtime repo triggers: unit tests -> smoke perf (one small node) -> integration on staging-gpu.
2) If green, artifacts built and uploaded: kernels/{version}/{platform}.so and image rh-runtime:{ver}-k{kv}.
3) Promotion job: ci/promote-kernel -> creates PR to IaC repo with version bump in modules/gpu-runtime-variants.
4) IaC plan job: runs terraform plan with cloud-account matrix (hosted, dedicated, private) and posts plan output.
5) Manual approval gate for canary rollout with checklist items (see Canary Gate).

Canary Strategy
- Canary scope: route selection by tenant tag (canary=true) and 5% of host-routed requests for hosted. For dedicated/private, use single low-impact tenant or customer-provided staging VPC.
- Stages:
  1) Single pinned node (1 GPU) running new kernel under low load for 30m (sanity + smoke).
  2) 3-node warm pool at 10% of normal scale for 2 hours (stress + perf).
  3) 20% traffic split against a matched baseline model variant for 4 hours (A/B).
  4) Gradual ramp to 50% then 100% over 24 hours if metrics stable.
- Canary telemetry: P50/P95 latency, error_rate, OOM counts, kernel-crash-rate, GPU_utilization, queue-depth.

Canary Gate (manual approval)
- Required checks before moving to next stage:
  - No kernel crashes in last 30 minutes.
  - P95 latency change <= 7% relative to baseline.
  - Error rate delta <= 0.5% absolute.
  - GPU memory pressure <= 85% steady-state.
  - No regression alerts firing for quality-monitoring (embedding-sim drift).
- Approvers: release lead + serving-runtime tech lead + infra oncall. Document approval with PR comment and CI job signature.

Rollback Criteria and Immediate Mitigations
- Automatic immediate rollback triggers (CI/CD hooks or autoscaling):
  - kernel-crash-rate > 0.1% sustained for 5m.
  - P95 latency regression > 15% or P50 > 25% for 5m.
  - Error rate increase > 2% absolute.
  - OOMs observed on > 1% of requests in 10m window.
- Manual mitigations:
  1) Shift traffic to baseline variant via router flag (runtime route override).
  2) Evict canary nodes and mark image as quarantined in the artifact registry.
  3) Revert IaC change and run terraform apply to restore pinned node pools.

Operational Runbook (incident play)
1) Detection: Pager triggered for P95 latency or kernel_crash alerts.
2) Triage (5 minutes): assess scope (tenants impacted, fleet region, node image). Use query:
   - metrics: query(kernel_crash_count[10m]) by node_image
   - logs: grep for SIGSEGV or cuBLAS error signatures in /var/log/runtime/kernel.log
3) Containment (10 minutes): set routing override to baseline: curl -X POST https://admin.redwood/api/routes/override -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","variant":"baseline"}'
4) Remediation (15-45 minutes): rollback IaC if needed, drain affected nodes, redeploy baseline image.
5) RCA and corrective action (24-72 hours): create postmortem, add test case to perf/regression suite, or pin kernel variant compatibility in model onboarding.

Terraform / IaC Guidance
- Module: modules/gpu-runtime-variants should receive only: kernel_version (string), kernel_artifact_sha (string), runtime_image_tag (string), allowed_quant_modes (list-of-strings)
- Plan checks: use terraform plan with -out and record plan diff; require that any change which touches auto-scaling policies or network ACLs is escalated.
- Example (pseudo-terraform snippet inserted in PR body):
  resource "redwood_gpu_runtime_variant" "canary" {
    kernel_version = "k2026-02-mpk-1"
    kernel_artifact = "artifacts.redwood/nn-kernels/k2026-02-mpk-1/x86_64/sha256:abcd1234"
    runtime_image = "rh-runtime:2026.02-k2026-02-mpk-1"
    quant_modes = ["fp16"]
  }
- Promotion rule: do not modify production default variant in the same PR as a kernel bump. Use explicit canary-only variant until validated.

Networking and Cloud Accounts Considerations
- For private/VPC deployments ensure kernel artifacts are mirrored into the private registry or accessible via signed URL. Add a manifest entry in customer-managed artifact list.
- Cross-account role: IaC plan must verify that the ci-promote role has read-only access to target accounts for plan only; apply must be performed by the account owner account.
- Egress: artifact pulls during rollout may spike egress; schedule large mirror jobs in maintenance windows for Private customers.

Observability and Alerting (minimum rules)
- Alert: kernel_crash_rate > 0.05% for 3m -> PAGER oncall-runtime
- Alert: p95_latency_delta > 10% for 5m -> PAGER infra-oncall + release lead
- Alert: gpu_memory_pressure > 90% -> PAGER infra-oncall
- Dashboards: per-kernel-version heatmap for p95 and error_rate, per-tenant perf scatter.

Quality Monitoring
- Add a permanent A/B eval flag for canary traffic: sample 0.5% of requests to run both baseline and new kernel when feasible to measure output drift. Store results in quality-monitoring index for post-deploy analysis.

Post-release Verification Checklist (24/72hr)
- 24hr: no critical alerts, rolling 24h A/B drift within target thresholds.
- 72hr: perf stable and customer telemetry clear.
- If issues: open change to pin kernel version per model and include compatibility matrix entry.

Appendix: Useful Commands
- Promote artifact: ci-tools promote-artifact --artifact artifacts.redwood/... --to registry.private.redwood/customers/
- Apply IaC (account owner): terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve plan.tfplan
- Router override example: curl -u $ADMIN_USER -X POST "https://admin.redwood/api/routes/override" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","variant":"baseline"}'

Change log
- 2025-08-12: Created initial draft with stakeholders.
- 2025-11-05: Added Terraform promotion rule and private registry mirror guidance.
- 2026-02-03: Updated canary gates and automated rollback thresholds after field exercise.

References
- Serving runtime kernel compatibility matrix (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/serving-runtime/release-notes/kernel-compatibility-matrix
- CI jobs: ci/buildkite/pipelines/runtime-kernel.yml

Contact
- Release lead on-call: #infra-release (Slack)

payload.page_title: Ephemeral GPU Pools for CI and Short-lived Evaluation Runs

sections.body:
Overview:

This page documents the design, Terraform/IaC module interface, CI/CD integration, operational runbook, and monitoring requirements for "ephemeral" GPU pools: short-lived GPU capacity that is created on-demand for CI jobs, short evaluation (eval) runs, and developer experiments. The goal is to provide reliable isolated GPU capacity for transient workloads while minimizing cost and blast radius compared to long-lived nodepools.

Key goals:
- Start-up latency <= 120s for 90% of requests (soft SLO for CI speed).
- Average cost per ephemeral-hour kept below the configured budget (see Cost Controls).
- Clear lifecycle: create -> run -> destroy (no leftover instances).
- Safe defaults for tenant isolation, tagging, and IAM.

Use cases:
- CI jobs that run model validation or inference tests needing a GPU.
- Short evaluation harnesses (30s–30m) used by research or QA teams.
- Developer ad-hoc experiments that must not affect production capacity.

Design summary:
- Controller: gpu-ephemeral-manager (stateless service running in control plane) handles requests from CI and eval services, reconciles Terraform module executions, and emits events to the provisioning queue (SQS/Kafka).
- Provisioner: fleet-provisioner workers consume the queue and run Terraform apply/destroy for module.module_ephemeral_gpu_pool (see IaC section).
- Runtime: ephemeral pools are Kubernetes nodepools labelled "pool-type=ephemeral" and tainted to accept only workloads with tolerations set by approved CI pipelines.
- Lifecycle: pools default to TTL=30 minutes unless overridden. A heartbeat mechanism extends TTL if the job reports active usage.

Security and isolation:
- Ephemeral pools use dedicated IAM role templates (least privilege) and restricted service accounts.
- Network: pools are placed in tenant-dedicated subnets created from shared VPCs; egress is limited via egress policies; default firewall only allows control-plane to nodepool comms and CI runner IP ranges.
- Images: nodes use a signed runtime image (GCR/S3) that is promoted through the CI image pipeline.

Terraform / IaC module interface (module.ephemeral_gpu_pool):

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| name | string | (required) | Human readable pool name (e.g. "ci-ephemeral-nv16") |
| gpu_type | string | "a100-80gb" | GPU SKU variant (a100-80gb, a10, h100) |
| gpu_count | number | 1 | GPUs per node |
| node_count_min | number | 0 | Lower bound for autoscaling (usually 0) |
| node_count_max | number | 4 | Upper bound for pool size |
| ttl_minutes | number | 30 | Default TTL after creation |
| subnet_id | string | (required) | Subnet to attach nodes to |
| iam_role | string | (required) | IAM role for node instances |
| tags | map | {} | Resource tags for billing and ownership |

Recommended defaults (module input guidance):
- gpu_type: prefer cost-effective GPUs for CI (a10 or a100-40gb) unless the evaluation explicitly needs larger memory.
- node_count_max: 4 for multi-job runs; set to 1 for isolated single-job runs to limit cost.

CI/CD integration (Jenkins / Buildkite / GitHub Actions patterns):
1. CI job calls the gpu-ephemeral-manager API with: {pool_profile: "short-eval", gpu_type: "a10", max_nodes: 2, ttl_minutes: 45, job_id: <uuid>}
2. gpu-ephemeral-manager creates a request record and emits a provisioning event.
3. fleet-provisioner applies module.ephemeral_gpu_pool using a dedicated TF workspace per request. Workspace name: "ephemeral/<request-id>".
4. Once nodepool is Ready (k8s API condition sync), CI uses kubeconfig scoped to a temporary service account with granular RBAC to schedule pods.
5. Job posts heartbeat every 2 minutes; lack of heartbeat triggers TTL countdown.
6. On completion, CI calls Destroy endpoint; if absent, automated destroy runs at TTL expiry.

Example CI job YAML snippet (Buildkite):
```yaml
steps:
  - label: "run-eval"
    env:
      GPU_POOL_REQUEST: "{\"gpu_type\":\"a10\",\"max_nodes\":1}"
    command: |
      curl -X POST $EPHEMERAL_MANAGER/api/request -d "$GPU_POOL_REQUEST" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
      export KUBECONFIG=$(./scripts/wait-for-kubeconfig.sh $REQUEST_ID)
      ./run-eval.sh
      curl -X POST $EPHEMERAL_MANAGER/api/request/$REQUEST_ID/destroy -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

Operational runbook: provisioning failures and common remediation
1. Failure mode: Terraform apply times out or errors with OOM on remote state locking.
   - Action: Check `fleet-provisioner` logs in logging cluster (service=gpu-ephemeral-provisioner).
   - Command: kubectl -n infra logs deploy/fleet-provisioner --since=1h
   - Quick fix: If apply failed due to quota, mark request as "retry" and escalate to capacity team (see Contacts).
2. Failure mode: Nodes remain NotReady after creation
   - Action: Inspect node events and kubelet logs.
   - Command: kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A5 Events; journalctl -u kubelet -b
   - Common cause: custom image missing NVidia driver; roll forward to validated image via image promotion pipeline.
3. Failure mode: CI cannot authenticate to temporary kubeconfig
   - Action: Verify SA tokens and RBAC bindings. Recreate kubeconfig via `./scripts/recreate-kubeconfig.sh $REQUEST_ID` and notify job owner.

Monitoring, metrics and SLOs:
- Metrics to emit: request_latency_seconds, pool_provision_time_seconds, pool_destroy_time_seconds, cost_per_request_usd, active_requests_total, orphaned_pools_total.
- Alerting rules (examples):
  - High orphaned pools: orphaned_pools_total > 3 for 10m -> pager to infra-oncall.
  - Provision latency regression: p95(pool_provision_time_seconds) > 180s for 30m -> P1 incident.
  - Cost threshold breach: cost_per_request_usd averaged > $5 for last 24h -> page cost-ops (Slack #cost-ops).

Suggested dashboards:
- Ephemeral pool health: per-GPU-type provision time, success rate, active request heatmap.
- CI cost burn: cost per pipeline and tag-based breakdown.

Cost controls:
- Mandatory tags: owner, project, billing_code, env (ci/eval/dev). Enforcement: terraform pre-apply hook checks tags and rejects if missing.
- Budget enforcement: account-level budget alerts via cloud billing; ephemeral requests that would exceed daily budget are rejected and return 429 to the caller with a human-readable reason.
- Autoscaling caps: node_count_max enforced in module; fleet-provisioner refuses apply requests above allowed per-team quotas.

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: infra-team (oncall: infra-oncall rotation).
- Code owner of Terraform module: eng-infra/terraform -> @evan.park (Evan Park).
- Oncall escalation: 1) infra-oncall Slack, 2) PagerDuty infra escalation policy, 3) PM on-call for CI (if access/permission related).

Upgrade, rollback and maintenance windows:
- Module versioning: use semantic versions; breaking changes must have a migration guide and a 2-week deprecation window.
- Rolling upgrades: new nodepools are provisioned and workloads drained from old pools before destroy.
- Planned maintenance: notify teams via #infra-announce and set maintenance flag that prevents new ephemeral allocations during window.

FAQ / edge cases:
- Q: What if a pool is orphaned because the CI runner died?
  A: Orphaned pools are detected by a reconciler every 10m; if no active job and TTL expired, pool is destroyed. For manual cleanup: terraform workspace: `terraform workspace select ephemeral/<id>` then `terraform destroy -auto-approve`.
- Q: Can we run long-running experiments on ephemeral pools?
  A: No — TTL and autoscaling caps make ephemeral pools unsuitable for long experiments. Use Dedicated pools instead.

Appendix: example Terraform snippet
```hcl
module "ephemeral_gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal-modules.git//ephemeral_gpu_pool"
  name = "ci-ephemeral-${var.request_id}"
  gpu_type = "a10"
  gpu_count = 1
  node_count_min = 0
  node_count_max = 1
  ttl_minutes = 45
  subnet_id = var.subnet_id
  iam_role = var.ephemeral_node_role
  tags = { owner = var.requesting_team, project = var.project_code }
}
```

Related pages and references:
- /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/gpu-spot-fallback-autoscaler-module-and-runbook.json
- /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-demand-forecasting-and-ml-backed-scaling-playbook.json
- /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/gpu-image-promotion-canary-cd-playbook.json

Last reviewed: 2025-01-20 by Evan Park, Lina Rodriguez.
