payload.page_title: CI/CD for GPU-Optimized Images and IaC Modules

sections.body:
Overview

This document describes Redwood's standard CI/CD patterns for building, testing, scanning, and publishing GPU-optimized container images plus the companion Terraform / IaC modules that provision GPU capacity and networking for inference clusters. It covers pipeline topology, gating tests (functional, perf, quantization), image signing and SBOM generation, module publishing, rollback processes, and runbook steps for common failures.

Goals

- Ensure reproducible, auditable GPU images with verified runtime characteristics (CUDA/cuDNN, kernel compatibility, quantization variant artifacts).
- Keep build times and costs predictable: median pipeline time < 12 minutes for incremental builds; < 40 minutes for full image builds.
- Prevent regressions in latency/cost by running lightweight perf checks as part of CI.
- Automate safe rollout of new images to Hosted/Dedicated pools with canaries and automated fallback.

Scope

Included: Docker container images for inference runtime (Torch/Triton/TF), multi-variant artifacts (fp16, int8/quantized), Helm charts, Terraform modules for cluster/ASG, VPC and subnet modules, and pipeline templates.
Excluded: Model training pipelines, third-party marketplace build processes.

Pipeline architecture (recommended)

1) Source push / PR triggers pipeline in CI system (we use Buildkite for infra-sensitive pipelines).
2) Stages (parallel where safe):
   - Lint & static analysis (Dockerfile, IaC linting: tflint, checkov)
   - Unit tests (python unit tests, infra module unit tests via terratest)
   - Build image variants (cache layer: base-image digest + buildkit)
   - SBOM generation and image signing (syft + cosign)
   - Vulnerability scan (trivy)
   - Lightweight perf smoke against local emulation or small Dedicated dev pool (latency, memory, kv-cache warmup)
   - Publish to internal registry (artifact tag: semantic + commit + build id)
   - IaC module publish (registry and git tag)
   - Release gating: QA approval or automatic canary rollout to 5% traffic

Diagram (text)

[PR] -> [Buildkite pipeline] -> parallel: [Lint, Unit tests] -> [Image builds -> SBOM/Sign -> Scan] -> [Perf smoke] -> [Publish registry + Tag IaC] -> [Canary deploy]

Pipeline conventions and naming

- Image tag: redwood/<service>:v{major}.{minor}.{patch}-{commit_sha_short}-{variant} e.g. redwood/inference-runtime:v2.4.1-ab12f3-int8
- Terraform module versioning: semantic vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with module-test/CHANGELOG in module repo root.
- Buildkite pipeline naming: infra-ci/<service>/<variant>
- Secrets stored in Vault paths: secret/ci/buildkite/<service> and secret/ci/docker-creds/<registry>

Preconditions & permissions

- Service account for CI with minimal IAM: storage writer to registry bucket, ECR push (or GCR/ACR equivalent), KMS encrypt/decrypt only for signing keys, and Terraform state write access to the specific backend bucket.
- Vault policy: ci-build can read signing key path and docker credentials; rotate keys quarterly.

Example Buildkite YAML (snippet)

steps:
  - label: ":docker: build runtime int8"
    commands:
      - "./ci/build-image.sh --variant=int8 --tag=${BUILDKITE_COMMIT:0:7}"
    agents:
      - queue=ci-small
    env:
      - IMAGE_REGISTRY=registry.internal.redwood.com

ci/build-image.sh (excerpts)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
VARIANT=$1
TAG=$2
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  --build-arg VARIANT=${VARIANT} \
  --cache-from=type=registry,ref=${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/base:cache \
  --tag ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} \
  --push .

SBOM + Signing + Scan sample commands

syft ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} -o json > build/sbom.json
cosign sign --key k8s://projects/redwood/secrets/signing-key ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT}
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH ${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/${SERVICE}:${TAG}-${VARIANT} || echo 'VULNERABILITY_FAIL'

Gating tests (must pass before publish)

- Lint and unit tests: exit on any failure.
- Trivy vulnerability check: block if CRITICAL vulnerabilities found. For HIGH vulnerabilities, policy depends on whitelist and CVSS comments.
- Perf smoke: must meet baseline threshold calculated from last successful release. Baseline stored in /infra/perf-baselines (internal). Failure triggers automatic rollback of publish step and notifies owners.

Terraform / IaC module publishing flow

1. Module PR -> tests (tflint, terratest) -> merge to main.
2. CI runs module validation and increments module patch version (via semantic-release or manual tag).
3. Publish module artifact to module-registry (internal) and update module CHANGELOG.
4. Notify downstream stacks via automatic pull request with pinned version bump.

IaC module requirements table

| Field | Requirement | Rationale | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| module_name | prefix: rdw- | Identify Redwood modules in registry | infra-iac-team |
| inputs | explicit, no implicit region defaults | Avoid accidental cross-region deployments | infra-iac-team |
| outputs | standardized tagging outputs (service, env, owner) | For observability and cost allocation | platform-observability |
| tests | terratest + tfsec | Prevent regressions | infra-iac-team |

Canary rollout and rollback policy (images)

- Canary phases: 5% -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 10–30 minute observation windows depending on traffic.
- Automated health checks during canary: 200 OK rate, p95 latency within baseline +20%, error budget burn < 2% per window.
- If any check fails, the pipeline triggers an automated rollback to the previous image and opens an incident in PagerDuty (see Runbook: Canary Failure).

Runbooks (high-level)

1) Build fails on buildkite (common causes: cache miss, base image change, low disk)
   - Owner: infra-ci oncall
   - Steps:
     1. Inspect Buildkite logs and the buildkite-agent machine: tail /var/log/buildkite-agent.log
     2. Check cache hit rate: registry API for cache layer digest mismatch. If cache miss, rebuild base-image and re-run.
     3. If machine disk pressure: trigger ephemeral agent reprovisioning: aws ec2 reboot or delete instance in the ci-agent autoscaling group.
     4. If base-image change detected, validate base digest and coordinate with base-image owner to cut a compatible patch.

2) Image scan returns CRITICAL vulnerabilities
   - Owner: security-engineering & infra-ci
   - Steps:
     1. Gate publish: image is not pushed to prod registry (pipeline should prevent).
     2. Retrieve SBOM and vuln report: build/sbom.json and trivy output.
     3. Triage: if fixable by package upgrade, patch Dockerfile and re-run. If requires upstream OS rebuild, escalate to security for policy decision.
     4. Record incident and add CVE to vulnerability backlog with severity and ETA.

3) Canary health check failed after rollout
   - Owner: infra-sre + service owning the image
   - Steps:
     1. Abort further rollout. Trigger rollback to previous image tag via deployment controller.
     2. Attach perf traces and logs (tracing link) to incident.
     3. Run local repro steps against canary instances: reproduce request patterns used in health checks.
     4. If root cause is infra (node kernel, NV driver), follow GPU fleet runbook (see related page).

Operational metrics and SLOs for pipelines

- Build success rate: >= 98% (weekly rolling).
- Median incremental build time: <= 12 min.
- Median full build time: <= 40 min.
- Time-to-publish after merge (automated): <= 30 minutes for non-manual releases.
- Image scanning block on CRITICAL vulnerabilities: 100%

Secrets and signing keys management

- Cosign keys stored in KMS-backed Vault path: secret/signing/ci, rotated quarterly.
- SBOMs persisted alongside artifact metadata in the artifact registry for reproducibility.

Owner & contact matrix

- infra-ci team (primary): infra-ci@redwood.internal
- infra-iac-team (modules): infra-iac@redwood.internal
- security-engineering: security-eng@redwood.internal
- SRE oncall: see rota in PagerDuty

Onboarding checklist for a new service to adopt the pipeline

1. Create service repo with Dockerfile following runtime base-image guidelines.
2. Add pipeline.yaml using template (contrib/pipeline-templates/ci-image.yaml).
3. Add module.tf referencing rdw-gpu-cluster module with explicit inputs.
4. Run `./ci/local-smoke.sh` and push PR for infra review.

Troubleshooting tips and FAQs

Q: My perf smoke is flaky across runs.
A: Use a fixed random seed, control concurrency, and warm KV cache before measuring. Capture the full p95 distribution for 50 runs instead of a single run.

Q: How do I test int8/quantized runtime locally?
A: Use the small dedicated dev-pool (namespace: rdw-dev-gpu-small) and limit traffic via k8s patch to avoid consuming production capacity.

Appendix: Useful commands and links

- Publish a module locally: `make module-publish MODULE=rdw-gpu-cluster VERSION=0.3.1`
- Force-retry a failed Buildkite job: `buildkite-agent build retry <build-id>`
- View SBOM for image: `curl -s https://artifact-registry.internal.redwood.com/sbom/<image-tag>.json`
- Internal wiki links:
  - GPU node sizing: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-node-sizing-guidance
  - Module publishing standards: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/module-publishing-standards

Change log

- 2024-01-15: Initial draft and approvals (Ana Gomez).
- 2024-06-03: Added SBOM/signing flow and trivy policy (Marcus Lee).
- 2024-11-02: Updated canary observation windows and perf gating thresholds (Sasha Patel).
sections.heading: Use buildkit + cache-from to speed up repeated builds

payload.page_title: ci-gpu-lease-broker-and-self-serve-portal

sections.body:
Overview

This document describes the CI GPU Lease Broker and Self-Serve Portal: an internal service that mediates short-lived GPU allocations for CI/eval workloads, enforces tenant quotas and cost-centers, and integrates with our CI systems (Buildkite, GitLab Runner) and IaC pipeline (Terraform dynamic sandbox modules). It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and CI owners.

Goals
- Provide a low-latency API for CI jobs to request ephemeral GPU slots with predictable fairness.
- Account GPU usage to cost-centers and tag Cloud billing correctly.
- Minimize wasted warm-up time by reusing warm pools and seeding KV caches where appropriate.
- Offer strong guardrails to prevent budget overruns and noisy-neighbor issues.

Scope and non-goals
- In-scope: ephemeral GPU leasing for CI/eval (max lease 6 hours), integration with Buildkite and GitLab Runners, lease ledger, quota enforcement, preemption orchestration, warm-pool hints.
- Out-of-scope: long-running dedicated tenant workloads (use Redwood Dedicated) and private on-prem orchestration.

Actors and services
- Lease Broker API (internal service): issues JWT-backed lease tokens, writes ledger entries.
- Lease Ledger DB (Postgres): authoritative record of outstanding leases, owner, cost-center, tags, image fingerprint.
- Provisioner (controller): reconciles leases to GPU node attachments via Kubernetes CRDs + Terraform dynamic sandboxes.
- Warm-Pool Manager: maintains a small pool of pre-warmed nodes per region/flavor.
- CI Integrations: Buildkite plugin and GitLab Runner helper that call the broker and attach the token to job environment.
- Cost Allocator: periodic job that converts ledger rows to billing exports.

SLOs & monitoring (primary metrics)
- API latency: P50 < 60ms, P95 < 300ms (for token issuance).
- Queue wait: 95th percentile < 30s for small (<=4GB) requests during normal hours.
- Preemption spike: < 3% of active leases preempted per hour target.
- Lease leak rate: < 0.25% of leases remain after 2x TTL without reconciliation.
- Billing tag fidelity: 99.9% of consumed GPU-hours include a cost-center tag.

Instrumentation and dashboards
- Dashboards: Broker API latency, active leases by tenant, average lease duration, preemption events, warm-pool occupancy, billing tag compliance.
- Alerts (pager):
  - broker-api-5xx-rate > 1% sustained for 5m -> page oncall-infra.
  - queue-wait-95 > 120s for 5m -> page oncall-sre.
  - leak-detector-count > 5 in 1h -> page infra-leases.

Operational runbook: common incidents
1) Broker API returns 500s at scale
   1. Confirm via dashboard that error rate spike correlates with traffic.
   2. Increase provisioner replicas (k8s deployment: ingress-broker) by 2x using kubectl scale if CPU/latency metrics show saturation.
   3. If DB is the bottleneck (Postgres CPU or connection saturation), promote read replicas and temporarily disable non-essential background reconciliations (warm-pool refresh).
   4. Rollback recent deploy if metrics started after deployment; follow normal CD rollback.

2) Large preemption wave (many leases get preempted)
   1. Identify preemption cause: node preemption vs. provider reclaim. Check cloud events and node-level logs.
   2. If provider-driven (spot/interrupt), trigger immediate warm-pool refill in unaffected regions and route new leases away from affected capacity zones.
   3. If caused by overpacking policy change, revert policy and run a controlled drain in small batches.
   4. Communicate to CI teams via #infra-alerts channel and annotate affected ledger rows with "preemption:mass" tag for billing adjustments.

3) Stuck lease (job exited but lease remains active)
   1. Run lease-reconciler job to probe the attached node and job heartbeat.
   2. If job absent for > 10m and health-checks negative, mark lease for forced reclaim and attach reclaim_reason=orphan.
   3. Notify owner (email/Slack from ledger owner field) with a one-click reclaim link.

4) Warm-pool exhaustion leading to long cold-starts
   1. Increase warm-pool target for the affected region/flavor via the admin portal.
   2. As an immediate mitigation, mark small jobs as "best-effort" allowing fractional multiplexing on lightly loaded nodes.
   3. Post-incident: run a demand forecast job and update warm-pool sizing policy.

Lease lifecycle (how it works)
- Request: CI job POST /v1/leases {flavor, max_duration, cost_center, image_hash, tags} with bearer service token.
- Broker: evaluates quota, fairness score (sliding-window per-tenant consumption), warm-pool hints and returns lease token and node assignment (if immediate) or queue position.
- Provisioner: watches for new active leases and reconciles attachments (K8s PVC, node affinity, TF dynamic sandbox apply).
- Run: job uses lease token to mount GPU and begins work. Lease heartbeat every 30s optional.
- Expire/Reclaim: upon TTL or job completion, provisioner detaches resources and records final usage in ledger.

Fairness and quota model (short)
- Quotas: two-dimensional: concurrency slots and hourly GPU-hour cap per cost-center.
- Fairness score calculation:
  - score = alpha * recent_gpu_hours + beta * queued_jobs + gamma * priority_override
  - alpha/beta/gamma are tunable in config service (default alpha=1.0 beta=0.5 gamma=2.0).
- Scheduler favors lower-score tenants but provides occasional credit for bursty tenants (token-bucket).

CI integration examples
- Buildkite plugin (snippet)
  - CLI call for job:
    curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $BROKER_TOKEN\" -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
    -d '{"flavor":"a2-medium","max_duration_minutes":120,"cost_center":"ai-team","image_hash":"sha256:..."}' \
    https://broker.internal/v1/leases
  - Broker returns JSON:{"lease_token":"eyJ...","node":"gpu-a2-07","attach_cmd":"/opt/redeem --token=..."}

- GitLab Runner helper: the helper will call the API at runner startup and export GPU_DEVICE environment variables if lease granted. Failures fall back to cpu-only (configurable).

Terraform / IaC considerations
- Pattern: the Lease Broker does not run Terraform at request time for every lease. The Provisioner maintains a pool of pre-created dynamic sandboxes represented as K8s NodePools and NodeClaim CRs.
- Example snippet for terraform module usage (admin/operator):
  module "ci_gpu_sandbox" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@infra-repo//modules/ci-gpu-sandbox?ref=v0.4.0"
    region = "us-west-2"
    flavor = "a2-medium"
    min_prepared = 2
    warm_pool_size = 3
    tags = { team = "infra", purpose = "ci-broker" }
  }

- Module responsibilities: creation of node pools, IAM service account for the provisioner, Cloud NAT/epheremal EIP policy for egress, and a small image cache bucket. Ensure module creates billing-tags on node metadata for cost allocation.

Security and tokens
- Lease tokens are short-lived JWTs (default TTL 1h) signed by infra-kms and include claims: lease_id, owner, cost_center, allowed_mounts.
- CI tokens are scoped to project-level principal; cross-tenant requests must be approved via workspace policy.
- Admin role: admin-broker role can bypass certain quota checks for emergency flows. Use sparingly and audit via CloudTrail.

Upgrade and rollout steps (for changes to broker/provisioner)
1. Create canary deployment in staging with parity config and run at 5% of CI traffic using routing flag.
2. Run load test mimicking 10K small launches and validate SLOs for 1h.
3. Gradually increase traffic to 25% and monitor preemption and queue wait.
4. If regressions occur, revert canary and capture metrics for postmortem.
5. When promoting, use a blue/green deployment and a short feature-flag window to disable new fairness algorithm.

Cost controls and throttles
- Soft caps: warn tenant owners via Slack when 75% of hourly cap consumed.
- Hard caps: deny new leases after 100% cap unless emergency override used.
- Emergency override: admin token with reason tag recorded into ledger.

Post-incident checklist
- Timeline: reconstruct events from broker API logs and lease ledger.
- Usage reconciliation: run billing export and reconcile ledger->billing for the incident window.
- Blame and remediation: identify misbehaving jobs (large image pulls, leaking sessions), add guardrails (image size limits, session TTL), and deploy patch.

Appendix: troubleshooting commands
- Force reclaim a lease: curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN\" https://broker.internal/v1/leases/{lease_id}/reclaim
- Probe lease ledger for orphaned entries: psql -c \"SELECT lease_id, owner, created_at FROM leases WHERE status='active' AND created_at < now() - interval '2 hours';\"
- Refill warm-pool (operator CLI): infractl warm-pool refill --region us-west-2 --flavor a2-medium --count 2

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-ci ( rotation: @infra-oncall )
- Secondary owner: platform-ops@redwood.com
- Pager: #infra-pager (Slack) -> infra oncall escalation policy

FAQ and known limitations
- Q: Why not Terraform-per-lease?
  A: Terraform at request-time has high latency and Terraform state contention; we prefer pre-created sandboxes reconciled by a controller.
- Q: Can a CI job request >6 hours?
  A: Not via the broker. Long-running runs should request Dedicated capacity via the Dedicated onboarding flow.
- Q: How do we handle large image pulls causing network egress spikes?
  A: The module tags heavy-image jobs; the Cost Allocator can throttle or charge a differential egress surcharge to the cost-center.

Change log
- 2024-08-15: initial draft (Maya Patel).
- 2024-10-02: added warm-pool heuristics and fairness parameters (Diego Ramirez).
- 2025-01-20: expanded incident playbook and onboarding steps; added Terraform module snippet (Priya Shah).

References
- See also: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/ephemeral-gpu-pools-for-ci-and-eval-runs.json (operational patterns)
- See also: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/gpu-lease-ledger-and-claim-module.json (ledger schema and api)

payload.page_title: GPU IaC Guardrails and CI/CD Policy Kit

sections.body:
Overview
========
This document describes a reusable policy kit and CI/CD patterns for provisioning GPU pools, tenant network attachments, and GPU-enabled instances via Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform) with automated safety checks. The kit is intended for teams building self-service GPU environments (hosted, burst, or dedicated) and focuses on: cost guardrails, cross-account networking constraints, deployment safety, and testable pipelines.

Goals
-----
- Prevent accidental large-scale GPU spend from misconfigured IaC.
- Standardize tagging and cost attribution for tenant resources.
- Enforce network and security constraints for cross-account GPU attachments.
- Provide CI/CD templates that run policy-as-code checks and ephemeral integration tests before merge.
- Enable fast, safe promotion of GPU module changes across staging -> prod.

Scope
-----
Includes: Terraform modules that provision GPU pools, autoscaling groups (or node pools), VPC attachments, NAT/egress config, and IAM roles for GPU tenancy. Also includes GitHub Actions / Buildkite templates for linting, policy checks, plan review, and canary applies into a sandbox account.
Excludes: GPU runtime image build pipelines (see ci-cd/gpu-image-rotation-and-cve-response-runbook).

Ownership
---------
- Module owner (primary): infra-iac-team
- CI templates: platform-ci-team
- Cost attribution & billing tags: finance-legal (advisor) + infra-iac-team
- Security & network rules: security-and-compliance (review)

High-level architecture (text diagram)
------------------------------------
- Git repo (gpu-iac-modules) -> PR triggers CI checks (lint, fmt, tfsec, OPA)
- If checks pass -> plan in sandbox account via ephemeral creds -> run integration smoke tests against ephemeral GPU pool
- Manual review gate for production plans -> canary apply to a single region/zone -> monitor metrics -> promote via automated apply job

Module contract (required variables and outputs)
------------------------------------------------
| Variable | Type | Description | Constraint / Guardrail |
|----------|------|-------------|------------------------|
| cluster_name | string | Logical name of the GPU cluster | must match regex ^[a-z0-9-]{3,32}$ |
| tenant_id | string | Internal tenant identifier | required for billing tags |
| max_gpu_count | number | Maximum GPUs allowed for this cluster | <= account_quota AND <= 1024 by default |
| preemptible_policy | string | fallback behavior for spot/preemptible nodes | enum: [disabled, opportunistic, constrained] |
| network_attachment_mode | string | how to attach tenant traffic | enum: [isolated, shared-vpc, proxy] |
| billing_center | string | Finance cost center code | must be present |

Outputs (must include): cluster_id, pool_stack_version, last_apply_id

Example Terraform module usage (snippet)
--------------------------------------
```hcl
module "gpu_pool_tier_a" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/gpu-iac-modules.git//pool?ref=v1.12.0"

  cluster_name = "tenant-foo-gpu-a"
  tenant_id = "foo-prod"
  max_gpu_count = 64
  preemptible_policy = "opportunistic"
  network_attachment_mode = "isolated"
  billing_center = "FC-1234"
}
```

Policy-as-code checks (required in CI)
------------------------------------
1. Terraform fmt and validate
2. tfsec with company profile (block IAM wildcard, public S3, etc.)
3. OPA / Rego policies (examples below)
   - deny if max_gpu_count > account_quota_threshold
   - require billing_center tag with valid pattern (FC-\d{4})
   - deny public subnet for GPU nodes unless explicit allow flag set
4. Sentinel/Conftest for network_attachment_mode constraints

Example Rego rule (text)
-----------------------
```
package redwood.iac

deny[msg] {
  input.resource_changes[_].change.after.max_gpu_count > input.policy.max_allowed
  msg = sprintf("max_gpu_count exceeds allowed threshold: %v", [input.resource_changes[_].change.after.max_gpu_count])
}
```

CI/CD pipeline template (GitHub Actions example)
------------------------------------------------
name: GPU IaC CI

on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check -diff
      - name: Terraform init
        run: terraform init -backend=false
      - name: Run tfsec
        run: tfsec . || true
      - name: Run OPA policies
        run: |
          opa test ./policies || exit 1
      - name: Plan (sandbox account)
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.SANDBOX_AWS_KEY }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.SANDBOX_AWS_SECRET }}
        run: |
          terraform workspace select pr-${{ github.event.number }} || terraform workspace new pr-${{ github.event.number }}
          terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
          terraform show -json plan.tfplan > plan.json
          ./scripts/plan-analyzer.py plan.json || exit 1

Canary apply and promotion
--------------------------
- After merge to main, the pipeline automatically applies to the staging account (non-prod) using a queued runner.
- Production applies are gated: a canary apply job will apply in one region (region-priority list) limited to a single availability zone, and then wait for 30–60 minutes while metrics are evaluated.
- Metrics to evaluate during canary:
  - node-provision-latency (95th percentile) < 15 minutes
  - failed-instance-rate < 1% over the monitoring window
  - unexpected egress bytes increase > 20% triggers rollback

Ephemeral integration smoke tests (what we run against sandbox)
--------------------------------------------------------------
1. Node boot health check: SSH to one provisioned node, verify GPU driver present, run nvidia-smi, confirm expected CUDA major version.
2. Workload warmup: schedule a short eval run that generates 500 inference tokens spread across 5 models to verify scheduler and autoscaling.
3. Network validation: ensure tenant-specific egress path, IP addressing, and NAT gateway are reachable from a test harness.

Runbook: failed apply in sandbox (quick recovery steps)
-----------------------------------------------------
1. Abort apply job and capture logs: artifacts/plan.json and terraform logs.
2. If apply partially succeeded, run `terraform state list` to identify partially created resources.
3. If orphaned instances exist, tag them with `iac-orphan: true` and notify infra-oncall.
4. Re-run plan with `TF_LOG=TRACE` for debugging and attach to the PR.
5. If a resource exceeded max_gpu_count, update the PR to reduce requested capacity or open a request to infra-capacity-runbook for quota increase.

Cost and tagging policy (mandatory)
----------------------------------
All resources created by these modules must include the following tags:
- Name: cluster_name
- Tenant: tenant_id
- BillingCenter: billing_center
- Env: {dev,staging,prod}
- CostOwner: team-email (for chargeback)
- OwnerOncall: team-pager-duty

If any tag is missing OPA denies the plan. Finance will reconcile cost reports weekly and provide alerts for anomalous spend.

SLOs and operational metrics
---------------------------
- Provisioning SLO: 95% of sandbox applies complete within 20 minutes.
- Canary success SLO: 99% of canary applies complete without manual rollback within 1 hour.
- Cost guardrail: no single PR can increase committed GPU capacity by more than 10% for a tenant without explicit finance approval.

Monitoring & Alerts
-------------------
Emit the following metrics to telemetry: cluster.provision.duration_seconds, cluster.node.failures_total, cluster.egress.bytes, cluster.max_allocated_gpus.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- P1: cluster.node.failures_total > 5 in 10m after an apply -> paging oncall (pagerduty: infra-iac-pager).
- P2: cluster.egress.bytes increase > 200% vs baseline in 30m -> email + slack channel #infra-cost-alerts.

Promotion checklist (manual gate before prod apply)
--------------------------------------------------
1. CI checks green and all OPA rules passed.
2. Sandbox integration tests passed and artifacts uploaded.
3. Canary plan reviewed by two infra approvers.
4. Finance sign-off if requested capacity delta > 10%.
5. Runbook owner oncall acknowledged the window and rollback plan.

Security considerations
----------------------
- GPU admin roles must use least privilege; forbid broad IAM policies on instance roles.
- SSH bastion access only via ephemeral SSO session and short-lived certs.
- Kernel and GPU driver upgrades must be staged via image promotion pipeline and linked in the module's `image_id` variable.

Decommissioning and deprecation policy
-------------------------------------
- Modules have semantic versioning. Major version bump required for breaking changes (network mode, tag schema).
- A deprecation label must be added in code and docs 90 days before removal.

Troubleshooting tips
--------------------
- If OPA denies due to billing tag pattern, add `billing_center = \"FC-XXXX\"` and run `opa eval -i plan.json -d policies/ -f pretty` locally.
- For slow node provisioning, capture cloud provider events and compare with `cluster.provision.duration_seconds` to identify API throttling.

Appendix: Useful CLI commands
-----------------------------
- `terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan`
- `terraform show -json plan.tfplan > plan.json`
- `jq . < plan.json | less`
- `tfsec .`
- `opa test ./policies`

Appendix: Example plan-analyzer rules (short)
-------------------------------------------
- Reject plans that create more than 100 GPUs in a single apply unless `force_approval=true`.
- Translate plan.json into an HTML summary and post to PR as a comment for reviewers.

FAQ
---
Q: Can a tenant request >1024 GPUs?
A: Yes but must go through capacity request process and require finance + infra leadership approval.

Q: How do we handle spot preemption for long-running jobs?
A: Use `preemptible_policy = \"constrained\"` which pins a fraction of the pool to on-demand instances.

Related work
------------
- See `eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-ephemeral-sandbox-lifecycle-and-cost-reclamation-playbook` for sandbox lifecycle.
- Coordination with `security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth` for IAM baseline.

Document cadence
----------------
This doc is reviewed quarterly or on major infra module changes.

payload.page_title: Runtime release pipeline: rollback procedure

sections.body:
h1. Summary
This page documents the standard and emergency rollback procedure for Serving Runtime deployments to *Hosted* and *Dedicated* environments using Redwood release tooling.

h1. Definitions
* *Runtime release tag*: immutable identifier for a runtime build (example: runtime-release-2025.02.01)
* *Hosted*: multi-tenant regional fleets
* *Dedicated*: per-tenant or per-cluster fleets
* *Rollback*: re-pin the deployment to a previous runtime release tag

h1. Preconditions
* You have prod deploy permissions (see Access & Permissions).
* You know the rollback target tag and it is present in the artifact registry.
* For customer-impacting changes, an incident exists OR an emergency change is logged.

h1. Rollback workflow (high level)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: h1. Hosted rollback (regional fleets)
sections.heading: Document outcome in incident/change record

sections.body:
In #eng-releases, ask the release captain to pause the rollout, or do it directly:
* Command (example):
  `rw-release pause --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod`
sections.heading: Step 1: Pause any in-flight rollout

sections.body:
* Command (example):
  `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`
sections.heading: Step 2: Pin runtime release tag

sections.body:
* Command (example):
  `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --regions us-east-1,us-west-2,eu-central-1`
sections.heading: Step 3: Redeploy

sections.body:
* 5xx < 0.5% for 10 minutes
* ttft_p95_ms within 10% of 7-day baseline
* gpu_oom_count returns to baseline (or zero)
sections.heading: Minimum verification before declaring rollback complete

sections.body:
If the progressive delivery controller is configured to auto-advance, apply the lock:
* `rw-release lock --service serving-runtime --env hosted-prod --reason "Emergency rollback stability hold"`

h1. Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)
sections.heading: Step 5: Lock the tag (to prevent auto-advance)

sections.body: Use the Console dashboard "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" and confirm the cluster names (e.g., ded-use1-a, ded-euc1-b).
sections.heading: Step 1: Identify impacted clusters

sections.body: * `rw-release set-tag --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a --tag runtime-release-2025.01.17`
sections.heading: Step 2: Pin tag per cluster

sections.body: * `rw-release deploy --service serving-runtime --env dedicated-prod --cluster ded-use1-a`
sections.heading: Step 3: Redeploy per cluster

sections.body:
If a tenant has special comms requirements (regulated / premium SLA), coordinate with CS before or immediately after action depending on SEV level (see comms guide).

h1. Evidence to capture
Record these in the incident channel and/or emergency change ticket:
* Job URLs from CI/CD
* Regions/clusters affected
* Old tag and new tag
* Start/end times
* Verification results

h1. Common pitfalls
* Picking a rollback target that is not compatible with the current model set (check model registry notes).
* Forgetting to lock the tag, causing auto-advance to reintroduce the bad release.
* Rolling back only some regions, leaving cross-region routing sending traffic into degraded pools.

h1. Related
* Emergency rollback runbook (runtime-owned)
* Emergency change policy (approvals)

payload.page_title: Hotfix Build + Signing Procedure (Containers, SBOM, Provenance)

sections.body:
h2. Summary
This page defines how to build and sign production hotfix artifacts for Redwood services, with emphasis on the serving runtime. Hotfixes must meet supply-chain requirements even during incidents.

h2. Requirements
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
* Container image must be signed (cosign)
* SBOM must be generated and uploaded
* Provenance attestation must be generated (SLSA level target: L3)
* Artifacts must be stored in the production registry (no personal namespaces)

h2. Supported build pipelines
* GitHub Actions: 'release-hotfix.yml' in repo redwood
* Internal Buildkite: 'runtime-hotfix-build' (use only when GitHub Actions is degraded)

h2. Procedure (GitHub Actions)
1. Ensure PR is approved per emergency policy.
2. Add label: hotfix-ready
3. Trigger workflow: 'Release Runtime Hotfix'
4. Provide inputs:
   * base image tag (previous production runtime)
   * new tag suffix (e.g., hotfix-2026-02-02a)
sections.heading: For any production hotfix artifact

sections.body:
* ghcr.io/redwoodinference/runtime:<tag>
* SBOM: s3://redwood-release-artifacts/sbom/runtime/<tag>.json
* Provenance: s3://redwood-release-artifacts/provenance/runtime/<tag>.intoto

h2. Signing verification
Before rollout, verify signatures:
* cosign verify --key k8s://prod/signing/runtime ghcr.io/redwoodinference/runtime:<tag>
* cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance ghcr.io/redwoodinference/runtime:<tag>

h2. Emergency exception handling
Exceptions are rare and require Security on-call approval recorded in the incident channel. Acceptable exception: temporary delay in SBOM upload *only* if the SBOM is generated and attached to the incident within 4 hours. Image signing cannot be skipped.

h2. Related pages
* /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/serving-runtime-hotfix-runbook
* /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
sections.heading: Artifacts produced

payload.page_title: Emergency release checklist (runtime + platform)

sections.body: This checklist is used when a release must be cut quickly to mitigate an incident. It defines what can be expedited and what must not be skipped.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- You may reduce test scope to *targeted* suites for the impacted component.
- You may use an existing approved base image if rebuilding would delay mitigation.
- You may merge directly to a release branch if main is currently unstable (with approvals).
sections.heading: What you can expedite

sections.body:
1. Artifact provenance: build must be from a known branch and pinned commit SHA.
2. Unit tests relevant to the touched area must be run (or justified and approved).
3. Security scanning must run (SAST + dependency scan) unless Security Oncall explicitly approves bypass.
4. Rollback plan must be written before deploy.
sections.heading: What you must not skip

sections.body:
1. **Branching**
   - Create `hotfix/<short-desc>` from `release/runtime/<yyyy-mm-dd>` or from `main` if release branch is behind.
2. **Versioning**
   - Bump runtime version: `runtime-<semver>+hotfix.<n>`
3. **Build**
   - Run: `bazel test //runtime/...` (or equivalent targeted suite).
   - Build image: `//runtime:image`
4. **CI checks to capture in the PR**
   - build: pass
   - tests: pass (or enumerated failures + justification)
   - lint: pass
   - image scan: pass
5. **Approvals**
   - Minimum: Runtime Eng Oncall + SRE Oncall (or IC)
6. **Publish**
   - Push image tag to registry
   - Generate release notes snippet (one paragraph) for incident timeline
7. **Deploy**
   - Follow serving runtime hotfix runbook for canary + gates
sections.heading: Runtime emergency release steps

sections.body:
- Identify last known good tag
- Confirm it exists in the registry
- Confirm deploy tool supports selecting it
- Confirm the rollback does not require a DB migration reversal (runtime should not require DB migrations)
sections.heading: Rollback readiness checklist

sections.body:
- GitHub PR link
- Incident link (if applicable)
- EPC record link (Confluence)

payload.page_title: Self-Serve GPU Provisioning Gateway + CI/CD Rollback Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents the self-service GPU provisioning gateway and the associated CI/CD rollback procedures used by Redwood Inference engineering teams. It is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and infra owners who operate or maintain the self-service path for creating ephemeral and reserved GPU environments.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Enable safe, auditable, self-serve provisioning of GPU node pools and sandbox clusters.
- Enforce CI/CD safety gates (plan reviews, quota checks, tenant tagging).
- Provide deterministic rollback / evacuation steps for failed provision or degraded fleets.

Scope
-----
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Self-serve provisioning gateway (internal API + UI) that triggers Terraform modules to create GPU pools.
- Associated CI/CD pipelines (Buildkite) and Terraform state backends.
- Networks relying on shared VPC egress and cross-account routing.
sections.heading: Applies to

sections.body:
- Long-lived enterprise Dedicated contracts (handled by Reserved Capacity runbooks).
- On-prem appliance packaging which uses a separate release flow.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
1. A developer or tenant requests a new ephemeral GPU pool via the self-serve gateway.
2. A CI/CD run that provisions or updates GPU node images fails staging smoke tests.
3. Observability detects a rapid rise in GPU preemptions or eviction rates tied to a recent iac change.

Prerequisites / Ownership
------------------------
- Owners:
  - Self-Serve Gateway: eng-infra/platform (Primary: Aisha Patel)
  - Terraform modules: eng-infra/terraform (Primary: Miguel Santos)
  - CI/CD pipelines: eng-infra/ci-cd (Primary: Lena Fischer)
- Permissions: operator service account must have access to the appropriate Terraform remote state and the target cloud project.
- Tooling: terraform >= 1.4.0, tflint, buildkite-agent, kubectl >= 1.27.
- Monitoring dashboards: gpu-provisioning, gpu-evictions, warmpool-availability (linked in related pages).

Quick reference SLOs and thresholds
----------------------------------
- Warm pool availability: 95% of requested warm nodes ready within 10 minutes.
- Preemption spike: trigger if preemption rate > 5% of active nodes sustained for 2 minutes.
- CI/CD plan approval: no unreviewed plan > 1 hour in prod-like environment.

Runbook: Self-Serve Provision Flow (happy path)
---------------------------------------------
1. User submits request through gateway UI -> gateway enqueues request (request-id returned).
2. Gateway runs preflight checks: tenant quota, IAM tagging policy, VPC egress path, and image signing status.
3. Gateway creates a PR in the infra repo with terraform plan attached and pushes to the provisioning pipeline.
4. Buildkite pipeline performs: tflint -> terraform init -> terraform plan -> automated policy checks -> optional human approval for quota > threshold.
5. On successful apply, the node pool autoscaler is primed and warm-pool preallocation starts. Gateway marks request as provisioned and notifies tenant.

Commands and examples (snippet)
------------------------------
sections.heading: Exclusions

sections.body:
```bash
export TF_WORKSPACE=tenant-abc-prod
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-infra-state"
terraform plan -var-file=tenant-abc.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan
terraform apply plan.tfplan
```
sections.heading: Terraform apply (manual emergency apply)

sections.body:
```yaml
steps:
  - label: "tflint"
    command: "tflint ./modules/gpu_pool"
  - label: "terraform-plan"
    command: "terraform init && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan"
  - wait
  - block: "Manual approval (quota > 2 T4s)"
  - label: "terraform-apply"
    command: "terraform apply plan.tfplan"
```

Terraform variables (reference table)
------------------------------------
| variable | description | example | required |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| tenant_id | Unique tenant identifier used for tagging | tenant-abc | true |
| node_type | GPU SKU (e.g. nvidia-t4, a100-80gb) | nvidia-t4 | true |
| desired_count | Autoscaled desired node baseline | 4 | true |
| warm_pool_count | Number of preallocated nodes to keep ready | 2 | false |
| preemptible | Use preemptible/spot instances to save cost | true | false |

CI/CD Safety Gates and Policy Checks
------------------------------------
- Lint & Static Checks: tflint and tfsec must pass with zero high findings.
- Quota Policy: automated check against the tenant quota store; fail pipeline if exceed.
- Image Signing: image digest must match signed digest repository, otherwise block.
- Network Egress: the candidate pool must validate egress paths to required endpoints (artifact registries, telemetry).
- Canary Smoke: for any image or kernel upgrade, a canary pool of up to 2 nodes is provisioned and must pass smoke tests (startup, model load, inference latency) before full rollouts.

Rollback and Failure Procedures
-------------------------------
Use-case A: Terraform apply failed during provisioning
1. Abort buildkite job if still running (Buildkite UI or buildkite-agent cancel <build-id>).
2. Inspect terraform plan and error logs: check terraform state locking issues (S3/Dynamo or remote backend).
3. If partial resources were created (VPC subnets, instance profiles): run terraform destroy on the partial workspace with `-target` for the dangling resources.
4. Re-run gateway preflight after fixing the root cause.

Use-case B: Post-provisioning degraded fleet (high evictions / bad kernel image)
1. Mark cluster as degraded in gateway admin UI to prevent new allocations.
2. Scale down tenant traffic routing (feature-flag or API routing) and move active requests to fallback region/model variant.
3. Drain affected nodes gracefully:
```bash
sections.heading: Buildkite pipeline example (relevant steps)

sections.body:
kubectl cordon <node-name>
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
```
4. Roll back the node image by updating the Terraform variable `node_image_tag` to the previous known-good tag and trigger pipeline to apply canary first.
5. If rollback fails or many nodes are unhealthy, initiate emergency capacity bleed to a warm spare pool (see emergency capacity section).

Emergency capacity bleed (fast path)
1. Trigger `provision-emergency` job in Buildkite with `warm_pool_count=10` and `node_type=nvidia-t4` in a pre-approved emergency account.
2. Notify on-call SRE and tenant primary; post status to #gpu-ops channel.
3. Monitor warm pool readiness and route traffic slowly (max 10% ramp per minute).

Troubleshooting checklist & play-by-play notes
---------------------------------------------
- Terraform stuck on lock: check S3/Dynamo locks, run `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` if owner process dead.
- Plan fails with quota: verify tenant quota service (internal API) is healthy and reconcile counts.
- Image mismatch errors: check the signed-image index and the digest the pipeline references.
- Slow warm-pool fill: look at cloud provider placement failures and preemption history. If placement failures exceed 20% within 5 minutes, abort and request a different zone.

Monitoring and Alerts
---------------------
sections.heading: For Kubernetes-managed nodes

sections.body:
- warmpool-not-ready: triggered when >10% of requests pending provisioning > 5 minutes. Severity: P2.
- gpu-eviction-spike: preemption rate > 5% for 2 minutes. Severity: P1.
- terraform-apply-failure: Apply step fails 3 times in 1 hour for the same workspace. Severity: P2.
sections.heading: Essential alerts

sections.body:
- Warm pool fill time distribution (p50/p95/p99)
- Eviction count and rate by node_type and zone
- Pending-provision queue length and age
- Terraform plan vs apply delta (lines changed / resources added)

Post-incident run & RCA guidance
-------------------------------
1. Collect all pipeline logs, terraform state diffs, and gateway request audit for the incident window.
2. Reproduce the plan in a private sandbox workspace and run `terraform plan` with `-out` to capture the exact diff.
3. Create an incident timeline with: request-id, pipeline-id, critical error messages, human approvals, affected tenants, cost impact.
4. If the incident was caused by a Terraform module change, open an ADR referencing the module and propose a mitigation (e.g., stronger preflight checks or canary pool requirement).

Runbook maintenance
-------------------
- Owners must review this playbook every quarter or after any P1 GPU incident.
- Significant changes to terraform modules or gateway APIs must update this playbook prior to rollout.

Escalation contacts
-------------------
- Oncall SRE: #sre-oncall (page: eng-sre/oncall-rotations)
- Terraform module owner: Miguel Santos (miguel@redwood.ai)
- CI/CD owner: Lena Fischer (lena@redwood.ai)
- Platform lead: Rajiv Menon (rajiv@redwood.ai)

Appendices
----------
A. Example terraform variable file (tenant-abc.tfvars)
```hcl
tenant_id = "tenant-abc"
node_type = "nvidia-t4"
desired_count = 4
warm_pool_count = 2
preemptible = true
```

B. Common Buildkite debugging tips
- Re-run a single step with `--step <label>`
- Download artifacts for a failed plan: `buildkite-agent artifact download plan.tfplan --job <job-id>`

C. Change log (high level)
- 2025-09-12: Initial published playbook by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-08: Added canary smoke step and image signing gate (reviewers: Miguel, Lena).
- 2026-02-05: Clarified warm-pool SLOs and added emergency capacity fast path.

- eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/gpu-shared-vpc-egress-and-ip-management
- eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-warm-pool-replenishment-and-iac-sync

payload.page_title: Burst Fabric Simulation Lab Operator & IaC Conformance

sections.body:
Summary

This doc describes the design and operational runbook for the GPU Burst Fabric Simulation Lab (BurstLab) operator and the accompanying Terraform/IaC conformance checklist. BurstLab is a self-service sandbox for validating multi-region/burst workloads, preemption-fallback logic, and IaC safety gates before changes are promoted to production GPU pools. The goal is to reduce rollout risk for autoscalers, burst-orchestrators, and tenant-facing network egress policies.

Key outcomes
- Automated simulation of burst scenarios (sudden large allocations, spot preemption waves, egress saturation).
- IaC conformance checks that validate topology, routing, and egress-burst constraints.
- CI gating: safe promotion only when simulations and telemetry assertions pass.
- Clear incident playbook for common failure modes discovered by lab runs.

Scope and boundaries
- Scope: GPU allocation, warm-pool handoff, egress routing under burst, cross-region replica fallbacks, and Terraform module compatibility.
- Out of scope: customer-facing billing reconciliation (handled elsewhere), model-level token accounting instrumentation.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-infra: capacity-team (oncall: @capacity-oncall)
- Secondary owner: eng-infra: cloud-networking
- CI/CD owner: eng-infra: ci-team
- Emergency contact: Pager duty for infra SRE (page policy: Severity 1)

Architecture overview (text diagram)

BurstLab operator sits in a staging AWS/GCP account and orchestrates ephemeral multi-region test clusters. Text diagram:

[BurstLab controller] -> creates -> [test GPU pool A (us-west1)] -> attaches -> [burst-orchestrator]
                              \-> creates -> [test GPU pool B (europe-west1)] -> attaches -> [warm-pool replicator]

A traffic generator submits synthetic inference traffic via a tenant-proxy that exercises: batching, KV cache hit/miss patterns, long-tail sequence lengths. The operator can inject failures: simulated spot preemption, egress NAT exhaustion, and TC/iptables route blackhole.

Prerequisites
- Burstable staging accounts with isolated VPCs and ephemeral IAM roles (see Terraform module: burstlab/account-module).
- Access to test image registry: gcr/redwood-infra-burstlab and a signed image promotion flow.

Terraform/IaC conformance checklist (table-style bullets)
- Module version pinning: terraform >= 1.4, modules pinned to a release tag.
- Network CIDR safety: test-subnets must be /22 or larger and annotated with purpose=burstlab.
- Egress guardrail: nat-gateway count >= expected-burst-egress/64MBps.
- IAM least privilege: ephemeral role sasl/burstlab-runner limited to create:test-* prefixed resources.
- KMS & secrets: all test artifacts must use customer-managed test KMS key with key policy: allow principals from burstlab account.
- CI token scoping: GHA runner tokens expire in < 1h and are restricted to project:test only.

Terraform snippet (example)

```hcl
module "burstlab_account" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//burstlab-account?ref=v0.12.0"

  account_name = "burstlab-staging-usw1"
  region       = "us-west1"
  vpc_cidr     = "10.40.0.0/16"
  tags = {
    purpose = "burstlab"
  }
}
```

CI/CD gating and pipeline example (GitHub Actions snippet)

- Pipeline phases: plan -> apply-test -> simulate -> assert -> destroy
- Gate rule: PR cannot be merged unless simulation assertions pass in the last successful workflow run.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```yaml
name: BurstLab Conformance
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan

  apply-test:
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: terraform apply -auto-approve plan.tfplan
      - run: ./scripts/launch-burstlab.sh --profile ${{ secrets.BURSTLAB_ROLE }}

  simulate:
    needs: apply-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 120
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/run-burst-scenarios.sh --scenarios all

  assert:
    needs: simulate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/check-telemetry-assertions.sh --ci

  destroy:
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: terraform destroy -auto-approve
```

Simulation scenarios (examples)
1) Rapid tenant spike: 10k concurrent small inference requests over 30s to test autoscaler reaction and KV cache miss storm.
2) Spot wave: terminate 40% of nodes in us-west1 in a coordinated window to validate warm-pool seeding and cross-region fallback.
3) Egress saturation: flood NAT gateway to exceed allocated throughput to test egress-sharding logic and tenant backpressure.
4) Kernel update ripple: deploy quantized kernel change and assert latency regression < 5% p95.

Telemetry assertions (pass/fail criteria)
- Allocation success rate: >= 99.5% across the 5m window post-spike.
- Eviction cascade depth: <= 2 (no more than 2 handoff hops).
- Tenant request p95 latency regression: < 10% vs baseline.
- Token billing hook verified: synthetic tokens recorded in staging billing sink.

SLOs used by this lab (for gating)
- Simulation pass rate required: 100% of defined assertions for critical PRs.
- Allowed transient flakiness: no more than 1 non-critical assertion failure per week for the ci:burstlab job.

Runbook: failure modes & remediation

Mode A: Plan/apply fails due to module pin mismatch
- Symptom: terraform plan errors with provider version mismatch.
- Triage steps:
  1. Check workflow logs for exact provider requirement.
  2. Confirm tfenv/terraform setup in GHA matches pipeline version.
  3. If module requires provider bump, open a follow-up PR to update module references and add a changelog entry.

Mode B: Allocation success < SLO after spike
- Symptom: allocation success 93% in 5m window.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Page capacity-oncall.
  2. Run `./scripts/collect-cluster-state.sh --since 10m` and attach to the page.
  3. Check warm-pool sizes: `kubectl -n burstlab get hpa,warmpool` and confirm desired replicas.
  4. If warm-pool not seeding, manually increase warm-pool to target and re-run scenario.

Mode C: Egress NAT saturation causing cross-account fallout
- Symptom: persistent SNAT exhaustion, TCP resets for external storage replication.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Switch burstlab test VPC to backup egress (egress-fabric-fallback) via console toggle.
  2. Throttle synthetic traffic generator: `kill -SIGTERM $(cat /tmp/burstlab-gen.pid)` and backoff.
  3. Patch Terraform nat-gateway count and reapply with a canary target.

Investigation checklist
- Gather: terraform state, kube events, node-level dmesg, cloud provider event feed (preemptions), and NAT gateway metrics.
- Telemetry queries: preemption_count_by_zone, kv_cache_miss_rate, nat_snat_errors, allocation_failure_reasons.

Safety & cost controls
- Each run is limited by default budget tags and an automatic destroy step. Runs exceeding $2000 estimated cost abort and notify finance.
- Test accounts are flagged so billing export streams are separated from prod.

Promote-to-prod criteria
1. Module and network changes must pass BurstLab simulation with zero critical assertions failing in 3 consecutive runs.
2. A performance benchmark (p95 latency delta) must be within the accepted regression window (< 5% for non-quant kernel changes; < 10% for large kernel experiments).
3. Runbook steps documented and reviewed by at least two reviewers.

Operational play: how to run a manual ad-hoc simulation
1. Checkout repo: `git clone git@github.com:redwood-infra/burstlab-operator.git`
2. Create ephemeral workspace: `make workspace && export TF_WORKSPACE=pr-<id>`
3. Apply with test role: `terraform apply -var-file=tests/pr-<id>.tfvars -auto-approve`
4. Launch scenario: `./scripts/launch-scenario.sh spike --concurrency 10000 --duration 30s`
5. Record run id and attach logs to PR.

Postmortem requirements for failed gates
- If a PR fails the gate, author must: attach failing run id, telemetry dashboards, and a short failure summary in PR description.
- If failure causes production impact, open a full incident with Sev classification and link to burstlab run ids that reproduce the issue.

Appendix: diagnostic commands
- Collect node telemetry: `for n in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do kubectl logs -n kube-system $n || true; done`
- Check NAT metrics (GCP example): `gcloud compute routers get-status <router> --region=us-west1`
- Retrieve preemption feed: `aws ec2 describe-spot-instance-requests --filters Name=state,Values=active,closed`

References
- See Terraform module catalog: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/module-stability-testing-and-rollback-catalog.json
- Burst orchestrator design notes: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-burst-fairshare-lattice-allocator-playbook.json

Notes and future work
- Plan to integrate an experimental cost-simulator that estimates token-level chargebacks across burst scenarios.
- Add a synthetic tenant harness that mirrors top-10 customer traffic patterns for more realistic regressions.

Document history
- Created 2024-09-03 by Maya Patel
- Major update 2025-01-18: added CI gating snippet and stricter telemetry assertions

payload.page_title: Multi-Account GPU Change Orchestrator and CI Canary Handbook

sections.body:
Operational handbook describing the orchestration pattern used to roll platform-wide GPU infra changes across multiple cloud accounts and regions using a CI-driven canary pipeline and Terraform/IaC controllers. Focuses on automated safety gates, account-level throttling, telemetry-driven promotion, and post-deploy reconciliation.
Redwood runs a multi-account, multi-region GPU fleet with strict SLOs for latency and availability. Changes to GPU node profiles, network egress plans, or allocation operators can have cross-account impact (egress spikes, tenant evictions, thermal hotspots). We historically relied on manual change windows for large changes. This handbook defines the automated orchestrator and canary pattern to reduce human toil and risk while preserving predictable capacity behavior.
- Declarative, auditable change promotion across AWS/GCP accounts
- Fast rollback and safe halting on safety gate failures
- Minimal steady-state customer-visible disruption during rollouts
- Reusable IaC and CI patterns for new change types
Applies to: Terraform module updates affecting GPU pools, node-image rotations, driver/kernel rollouts, burst-broker operator changes, VPC egress routing policies, and admission-policy changes that affect pod scheduling. Excludes application-level model changes and customer-managed private deployments unless explicitly opted-in.
1) Author creates IaC change in feature branch with change-meta.yaml (targets, risk-level, estimated-duration).
2) CI runs static safety checks (policy-as-code, cost-estimate, tfplan diffs, image-signature verification).
3) Successful CI triggers a canary promotion to a synthetic 'canary account' with mirrored telemetry.
4) Observability agent evaluates canary for 30m–2h depending on risk level.
5) If all gates pass, orchestrator promotes change incrementally to account groups (low->medium->high).
6) Each account promotion includes preflight snapshot, staggered rollout, and post-promotion reconciliation.
7) Automatic rollback on gate failures and alert-driven manual review if repeated failures.
- TF plan contains only allowed resource types for the target risk-level.
- Image/container signatures validate against signing KMS/HSM.
- Cost delta estimate computed and within budget threshold.
- RBAC approval label present for high-risk changes.
- Smoke job definitions included for deployed components (eg: tiny inference traffic injectors).
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Critical SLOs: node_p95_latency < 120ms, tenant_throttle_rate < 0.5%
- Thermal spike threshold: GPU inlet delta > 8C within 15m triggers halt
- Egress spike threshold: Bps increase > 30% over baseline for account
- Preemptive eviction rate: > 2 evictions/min across pool halts rollout
- Max concurrent accounts promoted: configurable by risk-level (default low=6, medium=3, high=1)
sections.heading: Safety rules used by the orchestrator (examples)

sections.body:
name: gpu-change-canary
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  static-safety:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: ./ci/policy-check.sh $CHANGED_FILES
      - run: ./ci/cost-estimate.py --plan tfplan.out
  plan-and-sign:
    needs: static-safety
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform plan -out=tfplan.out
      - run: sigstore sign --input=tfplan.out --key-ref=projects/redwood/kms/keys/cicd
  trigger-orchestrator:
    needs: plan-and-sign
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: curl -X POST $ORCHESTRATOR_ENDPOINT -d @change-meta.yaml -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ORCHESTRATOR_TOKEN'
- Each change must include a change-meta.yaml with: targets (accounts/tags), risk_level (low|medium|high), rollback_strategy (auto|manual), and smoke_test job.
- Use module versions (semantic tags) and tfstate promotion: canary -> staging -> prod workspaces.
- Include 'preflight-and-snapshot' module that captures current allocation, warm pool sizes, and egress config into an S3/GCS snapshot before each account promotion.
- Avoid cross-account resource creation in a single plan; orchestrator splits plans per account and creates a promotion bundle.
sections.heading: Example GitHub Actions snippet (simplified)

sections.body:
- Minimum mirrored fleet size: 2% of production GPU capacity (or 4 nodes, whichever is larger)
- Synthetic tenants: pre-seeded tenants with deterministic traffic (qps, sequence lengths)
- Observability: full traces, per-tenant cost telemetry, thermal sensors exposed to control plane
- Network: egress path mirrors production (NAT or proxy) and pre-authorized peering to telemetry backends
sections.heading: Canary account requirements (text table)

sections.body:
- Latency gate: increase in model-serving tail latency p99 > 10% over baseline for 30m -> fail
- Eviction gate: sum(increase(gpu_preemptions[15m])) > account_threshold -> fail
- Egress gate: increase in outbound_bytes_account_rate > 25% for two consecutive 10m windows -> warn/hold
- Error budget gate: active_slo_error_budget(account) < 10% -> hold promotion
sections.heading: Representative gates (PromQL/SQL examples described)

sections.body:
- Group definitions by tenant criticality and cost center (eg: infra-dev, non-prod, core-prod, enterprise-prod).
- Default stagger: low risk: 6 accounts every 45m; medium: 3 accounts every 90m; high: 1 account every 4h.
- Orchestrator supports backoff and paused windows if external incidents are open (references incident tracker).
Rollback procedure (automated + manual):
1) Automated rollback triggers on gate failure: orchestrator applies stored 'preflight snapshot' and runs a reconciliation plan to restore previous node-pool sizes and routes.
2) If automated rollback fails or partial state remains, oncall performs described manual rollback steps (CLI snippets included).
3) After a rollback, create an incident and assign to area owner; run postmortem within 72 hours.

Post-deploy reconciliation: orchestrator runs a 24h reconciliation job to ensure tfstate consistency and repair drift (retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff).
Trigger point: CI notifies Orchestrator with change bundle (change-meta.yaml + signed tfplan).
Canary: Orchestrator deploys to canary account and starts synthetic traffic. Wait 30m–2h depending on risk. Monitor gates.
Evaluate gates: If any FAIL -> automated rollback and paged alert to oncall. If WARN -> hold and notify owners for manual approval.
Promotion: If canary PASS -> orchestrator promotes to next account group with configured concurrency and delay windows.
Stabilization: After each account, run smoke tests (predefined test jobs) and wait stabilization window before next promotion.
Post-promotion audit: Orchestrator emits audit event and snapshot for each account; record in deployment ledger.
Completion: After final group promoted, run 24h reconciliation and file a short deployment summary in the change ticket.
Examples (aws/gcloud + terraform):
sections.heading: Promotion groups and timing guidance

sections.body:
aws s3 cp s3://redwood-preflight-snapshots/account-123/snapshot.json ./snapshot.json
terraform apply -var-file=snapshot.json -auto-approve
sections.heading: fetch snapshot and apply rollback plan

sections.body:
TF_WORKSPACE=account-123 terraform plan -out=tfplan-account-123.out
terraform apply tfplan-account-123.out
- Dashboards: Canary Health (latency p50/p95/p99, eviction rate, egress delta, thermal delta).
- Alerts: configured as policy thresholds in Alertmanager; critical alerts page to oncall Slack + PagerDuty.
- Audit trail: Orchestrator posts signed events to internal eventbus and writes deployment ledger entries to DynamoDB/BigTable.
- Cost telemetry: each promotion logs cost delta per account and tags for billing reconciliation.
sections.heading: force plan split for single account

sections.body:
- Unit: policy-as-code rules, module contract tests.
- Integration: terraform plan apply in ephemeral test accounts.
- Canary simulation: run a synthetic canary in the staging canary account that intentionally exercises edge conditions (eg: small thermal spike).
- Chaos: optional chaos run to validate orchestrator's pause/rollback behavior under network partitions.
Owners: GPU Fleet (primary): @gpu-fleet-team; CI/IaC Orchestrator: @ci-platform; Observability SRE: @obs-sre.
Oncall rotation: gpu-fleet oncall (primary), infra-sre (secondary). PagerDuty escalation policy defined in team runbooks.
After every high-risk rollout or any rollback, complete the postmortem template: summary, timeline, root cause, action items (owner + ETA). Key KPIs tracked per rollout: mean time to rollback, % change promotions that required manual intervention, average eviction delta during promotion, cost delta vs baseline.

link: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook.json
link: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/gpu-ci-safety-orchestrator-and-cost-simulation-harness.json
link: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-tenant-eviction-predictor-and-provisioning-guidelines.json

payload.page_title: GPU build fan-out and stampede mitigation guide

sections.body:
Overview

Purpose: This guide describes patterns, Terraform/IaC examples, monitoring signals, and an operational runbook to prevent and mitigate GPU stampedes and uncontrolled fan-out from CI pipelines and evaluation jobs. It targets infra engineers, CI owners, and platform SREs who operate GPU pools used for builds, evaluations, and canary workloads.

Summary: When large CI/eval jobs scale concurrently (nightly evals, multi-PR dependency checks, or mass rollouts), we observe sudden demand spikes that cause long queue times, warm-pool depletion, preemptions, and downstream latency for customer-facing inference. The mitigation strategy here is multi-layered: admission control + backpressure at CI, rate-limited fan-out adapters, autoscaler safeguards, pre-warm and warm-pool budgeting, token-bucket throttles, and telemetry-driven emergency throttles.

Key goals
- Ensure 95th percentile CI queue time to acquire a GPU stays below 4 minutes for short jobs (<= 30m).
- Bound impact of bulk-eval windows to < 10% of production capacity at any time.
- Provide fast operational controls to throttle/unwind runaway fan-outs within 2 minutes.

Scope and audience
- CI pipelines (Buildkite, GitHub Actions runner fleet) that request GPU nodes via internal provisioner.
- Evaluation clusters (ephemeral vs reserved) and scheduled eval grids.
- Autoscaler and GPU pool managers implemented in terraform + operator.
- Platform SRE, Eng-Infra, and Evaluation owners.

Patterns and controls (high level)
1) Source-side admission control (preferred):
   - Gate large fan-outs in the pipeline DSL: add a controlled "fanout" step that calculates effective concurrency and respects a per-repo concurrency quota.
   - Example policy: max 8 concurrent GPU jobs per repo by default; increase via request.
2) Rate-limited fanout adapter (thin service):
   - Implement an adapter between CI and the provisioner which enforces a token-bucket per-tenant and per-repo. The adapter emits telemetry for queue depth and throttle events.
3) Warm-pool budgeting and reservation:
   - Reserve a small fraction of capacity for latency-sensitive workloads (e.g., 10% of steady-state production) and a separate warm-pool for CI burst absorbtion.
4) Autoscaler soft/hard limits and plateau detection:
   - Autoscaler must support: soft_scale_thresholds, hard_capacity_cap, plateau-detection (sustained increase > X mins), and cooldown windows.
5) Emergency throttles and circuit breakers:
   - Automated circuit breaker that reduces non-critical starter tokens (evals, scheduled CI) when the cluster cross-stage: GPU eviction rate > 2% OR avg token acquisition latency > 5m for 1 minute.

Operational metrics and dashboards
- Required metrics emitted by adapter and provisioner:
  - adapter.requests_total (counter)
  - adapter.tokens_acquired (counter)
  - adapter.tokens_throttled (counter)
  - provisioner.queue_depth (gauge)
  - provisioner.token_acquire_latency_seconds (histogram)
  - pool.warm_nodes (gauge)
  - pool.preemptions_per_minute (counter)
  - autoscaler.scale_events (counter)

SLOs and alerts (recommended thresholds)
- SLO: CI GPU token acquire P95 <= 4 minutes. Alert if P95 > 4m for 10m.
- Alert: queue_depth > 200 for any single cluster for 5m.
- Alert: preemption_rate > 2% sustained for 5m.
- Alert: tokens_throttled > 5% of requests for 1m (indicates adapter saturation).

Terraform / IaC patterns (examples)
- Purpose: keep module surface small and pluggable to both ephemeral eval and shared production pools. Use variables to express budgets and emergency throttle knobs.

Example terraform variables (text table)
- Variable: name | type | default | description
- max_concurrent_per_repo | number | 8 | Default admission concurrency per repo for CI tokens
- warm_pool_size | number | 20 | Number of pre-warmed GPU nodes reserved for CI/eval bursts
- emergency_throttle_pct | number | 15 | Percent of non-prod tokens to disable when circuit breaker trips

Example terraform snippet (pseudo-HCL)
-----BEGIN HCL-----
module "gpu_fanout_adapter" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/gpu-adapter.git//terraform/module"
  max_concurrent_per_repo = var.max_concurrent_per_repo
  warm_pool_size          = var.warm_pool_size
  emergency_throttle_pct  = var.emergency_throttle_pct
  monitoring_topic        = module.monitoring.topic
}
-----END HCL-----

CI pipeline changes (practical checklist)
- Replace raw parallel map steps with "fanout-step" that:
  1. requests N tokens from adapter APIs with a single bulk request,
  2. implements backoff (exponential with jitter) if tokens are denied,
  3. publishes telemetry labels (repo, pr, build_id).
- Example: Buildkite YAML patch (conceptual)
-----BEGIN YAML-----
steps:
  - label: "run-eval-grid"
    commands:
      - scripts/request-gpu-tokens --count 16 --timeout 30m --tags ${BUILDKITE_PIPELINE_SLUG}
      - if: "\"$TOKENS_GRANTED\" == \"true\""
        commands: ["./run-grid.sh"]
      - else:
        commands: ["./notify-throttled.sh"]
-----END YAML-----

Adapter implementation notes
- Keep adapter state small: token-bucket counters in redis (per-tenant, per-repo), with TTLs to avoid leaks.
- Emit metrics at token request and token release. Tag metrics with owner, repo, job-type, and build_id.
- Add a soft-deny reason string to event logs so CI owners can detect whether denial is due to 'per_repo_quota', 'global_capacity_safety', or 'circuit_breaker'.

Warm-pool sizing guidance
- Base warm_pool_size calculation:
  - warm_pool_size = max(ceil(steady_state_prod_gpus * 0.08), 8)
  - Example: if production steady state is 250 GPUs, warm_pool_size = max(ceil(250*0.08)=20, 8) = 20.
- Use scheduled warm-pool daily windows (nightly evals) but cap the fraction of production used for scheduled batches to 10%.

Scaling safety: plateau detection and gradual scale-up
- When demand spike occurs, require autoscaler to do:
  1. fast warmup + limited scale (scale up to 30% over current)
  2. plateau detection (if tokens_acq_latency keeps increasing or queue_depth keeps growing, pause further scale and evaluate)
- Rationale: prevents us from autoscaling into a runaway eviction loop or cold-start cost spiral.

Runbook: Mitigate an active stampede (priority playbook)
1) Triage (0-2 minutes)
   - Owner: oncall infra/ci-cd SRE.
   - Dashboard to open: CI Token Health, Cluster queue_depth, Preemptions, Warm-pool utilization.
   - Immediate check: is global preemption_rate > 2%? Is token_acquire_latency P95 > 5m? If yes, escalate.
2) Contain (2-8 minutes)
   - Flip adapter emergency_throttle to 100% for non-prod and scheduled-evals. CLI: curl -XPOST https://internal-adapter/controls/throttle
     Payload: {"scope":"non_prod","throttle_pct":100,"reason":"stampede-mitigation"}
   - If adapter not responsive: add iptables rate-limit on provisioner port for eval CI agents (last-resort).
3) Stabilize (8-30 minutes)
   - Reduce autoscaler max scale rate to 10% per 10m window.
   - Spin additional warm nodes only into a dedicated buffered pool; do not attach to production until preemption_rate < 1% for 10m.
4) Root-cause and fix (30m-4h)
   - Identify offending pipelines (use adapter logs -> tag build_id).
   - Reconfigure pipelines: reduce per-repo fanout, batch tests into chunked runs, or move large eval grids to off-peak windows with prebooked capacity.
   - If a buggy PR is identified that caused exponential fan-out, block that PR by pipeline gate and notify respective owners.

Post-incident actions
- Postmortem must include: timeline, top 5 callers, % capacity consumed by offender, advisory to CI owners, and proposed change to admission control.
- Consider introducing scheduled capacity reservations (paid reservations) for large eval jobs to reduce contention with on-demand usage.

Testing and rollout checklist
- Unit and integ tests for adapter token-bucket behavior (race conditions around concurrent release).
- Load test harness: simulate X=200 concurrent repo builds with variable job durations and preemption interactions.
- Canary rollout: deploy adapter to single region and enable per-repo quotas set at 50% of expected. Monitor metrics for 48hrs before global rollout.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-infra/ci-cd team (oncall alias: oncall-ci-cd@redwood.com)
- Secondary escalation: platform-sre@redwood.com
- Pager escalation policy: if token_acquire_latency P95 > 10m for 15m, page platform-sre.

Related resources and links
- Implementation repo: git@github.com:redwood/gpu-adapter (internal)
- Dashboard: Grafana -> CI GPU Token Health (link internal)
- IaC modules: internal terraform registry -> gpu_fanout_adapter module
- Follow-up docs: runbook for warm-pool orchestration, CI pipeline best-practices for fan-out

Appendix: example telemetry alert rule (pseudo PromQL)
- Alert: CI_GPU_Token_Acquire_P95_High
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(provisioner_token_acquire_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 240
  for: 10m
  labels: {severity: "page"}
  annotations: {summary: "CI GPU token acquire p95 > 4m"}

Notes and rationale
- We prioritize source-side admission control because it is the most deterministic and lowest-cost mitigation. Fallbacks (adapter throttles, warm pools) are safety nets.
- Warm pools reduce latency but cost money; budget decisions should be aligned with business priorities (e.g., scheduled evals contributing to core product quality may deserve higher reservations).

Document revision history
- 2024-05-10: Initial draft.
- 2024-09-03: Added terraform variables and adapter implementation notes.
- 2025-06-18: Updated warm-pool sizing heuristics and autoscaler plateau logic after incident IR-2025-06-gpu-spike.
- 2026-01-12: Finalized emergency throttle API and added rollout checklist.
