payload.page_title: GPU Day-2 Configuration Templates and Rollforward Strategy

sections.body:
Overview

This page gathers: a set of standardized Day‑2 configuration templates for GPU node pools and inference runtime parameters, an operational decision tree favoring controlled rollforward (fix-forward) when safe, and a canary + load simulation harness pattern for CI/CD. The goal is predictable, low‑risk changes to GPU fleet behavior after initial provisioning (Day‑0), especially in high‑throughput inference clusters.

When to use this document
- Post-provisioning configuration changes (scaling policies, kernel/driver flags, cgroup/oom tuning, NVLink topology hints)
- Node image / runtime library patching where rollback is expensive or slow
- Changing batching / KV cache parameters that affect latency tail
- Upgrading autoscaler or spot fallback logic in Terraform modules

Key principles
- Prefer rollforward when the change is small, has an automatic remediation, or requires a state migration that rollback cannot undo (e.g., checkpoint reformatting).
- Canary at the smallest logical surface area (single AZ warm pool) with production traffic replayed locally.
- Run a simulated production load before promoting changes beyond canary.
- Maintain clear owner, SLO, and cost thresholds tied to the change.

Ownership and SLOs
- Owner: infra-gpu-ops (primary) / runtime-team (secondary)
- SLO targets (must be validated for the canary window):
  - P95 latency for 512 token requests <= 220ms
  - Error rate (5xx + model-fallbacks) <= 0.2%
  - Allocation success (GPU scheduling) >= 99.5% over 30m
- Cost guardrail: incremental per-hour cost increase for the fleet under experiment <= +12% (auto-fail if exceeded)

Quick decision tree (summary)
1. Is change reversible without state loss? If yes, default to rollback path.
2. Is change small and idempotent (config toggles, knob changes)? If yes, prefer rollforward with canary and automated reversion.
3. Does change require persistent migration (checkpoint format, KV index change)? If yes, plan rollforward—prepare migration, snapshot current KV/metric state, and create rollback plan that includes forward-fix options.

Canary pattern and load simulation harness
1) Canary surface: single warm‑pool (1–3 nodes), single AZ, single tenant with synthetic traffic mirror.
2) Traffic: replay last 1 hour of production token-level traces (anonymized) via the replay harness.
3) Metrics to validate: latency (P50/P95/P99), error rate, GPU util, OOM events, GPU temperature, KV cache hit rate.
4) Monitoring window: minimum 20m steady state after warmup.
5) Auto‑abort if any metric breaches configured thresholds (see Threshold table).

Threshold table (example)
| Metric | Canary threshold | Auto-abort condition | Owner action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P95 latency (512 tokens) | 220ms | >220ms for 2 consecutive 10m windows | rollback or investigate kernel path |
| Error rate | 0.2% | >0.5% in 5m | abort canary, scale down canary nodes |
| GPU alloc success | >=99.5% | <98% | re-route traffic to fallback pool |
| KV cache hit rate | +/-5% relative | drop >10% | investigate mismatch in cache keys |
| Fleet cost delta | +12% | >12% increase sustained 30m | cancel promotion, evaluate batching change |

Day-2 Terraform module templates
The repo has three template variants: minimal, conservative, and performance‑first. Use the conservative template by default for live fleets. Below is a representative snippet for the autoscaler and warm pool definitions (HCL-style example):

```
module "gpu_warmpool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood/infrastructure/terraform-modules.git//gpu-warmpool?ref=v1.6"

  name               = "inference-warmpool-${var.cluster_suffix}"
  instance_type      = var.instance_type
  min_size           = 2
  max_size           = 16
  warm_pool_size     = 2
  preemptible_policy = "balanced"    # options: balanced | spot-first | reserved-first

  lifecycle = {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }

  extra_user_data = file("${path.module}/templates/day2-bootstraps/${var.template}.sh")
}
```

Note: day2-bootstraps include gpu-tuned sysctl, cgroup settings, and an init script that registers the node with the appropriate KV cache warmup service.

CI/CD flow (canary + promote)
1. Developer/infra engineer opens PR modifying module var or bootstrap script.
2. Pipeline runs: unit tests -> linter -> plan -> ephemeral apply to canary sandbox (namespace/canary cluster).
3. Integration step: traffic replay job executed against canary.
4. Prometheus checks run; if pass, human approval required (owner + oncall) for staged promote.
5. Promote executes staged Terraform apply that adds nodes in target region using rolling wave of NCC (node-change coordinator) to minimize evictions.

Example GitHub Actions stage (simplified YAML snippet):

```
jobs:
  canary-apply:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init -reconfigure
      - name: terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -out=tfplan
      - name: terraform apply to canary
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan -var='target=canary'
      - name: traffic replay
        run: |
          python infra/replay/replay.py --trace last-1h --target canary

  validate-canary:
    needs: canary-apply
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: wait and validate
        run: ./ci/validate_canary.sh --window 20m
```

Runbook: when canary fails (step by step)
1. CI auto-aborts and opens incident ticket tagged "canary-failed".
2. Oncall: examine canary metrics dashboard and logs.
3. If failure is resource transient (OOMs during warmup), scale canary up by X2 and re-run replay.
4. If deterministic (repro on second run), snapshot canary nodes (logs + nvprof traces) and escalate to runtime-team.
5. If migration-related (checkpoint version mismatch), run rollback if a safe snapshot exists; otherwise invoke rollforward: apply fix-forward migration job to canary and re-run validation.
6. Document RCA in the ticket and link to this page.

Rollforward recipe (when chosen)
- Preconditions: snapshot of KV and model checkpoints taken; automated drain/retry configured; rollback plan recorded but may be infeasible.
- Steps:
  1) Stage migration in canary only.
  2) Execute fix-forward automated script (example: checkpoint-rewrite --in-place --safe-backup=/snapshots/...)
  3) Run full traffic replay and cold-start tests.
  4) Monitor metrics for 2x canary window before expanding.
  5) Promote to a larger ring with pause points and human approvals.

Telemetry and observability checklist
- Dashboards: gpu-canary-overview (per-change), kv-cache-health, node-image-metrics, temperature-and-power
- Alerts (Prometheus): canary_failure_total > 0 OR p95_latency_increase_ratio > 1.15 for 10m -> pager (severity P1/P2 depending on impact)
- Logs: centralized nvprof/producer logs, system journal, k8s events, terraform apply audit

Operational templates (attachments)
- day2-templates/minimal.tf (example minimal knobs)
- day2-templates/conservative.tf (default for prod)
- ci/scripts/validate_canary.sh (validation helper)
- infra/replay/replay.py (trace anonymization + replay harness)

Appendix: safe-change checklist (must be completed and referenced in PR description)
1. Owner assigned and oncall notified.
2. Canary target and replay trace selected.
3. Backups & snapshots scheduled (KV, checkpoints).
4. Prometheus and Grafana panels linked in PR.
5. Rollback and rollforward scripts validated in staging.
6. Cost guardrails configured on the pipeline.

FAQ
Q: Why prefer rollforward vs rollback?
A: When changes mutate on-disk formats, caches, or checkpoint versions, rolling back can leave the fleet in a persistent incompatible state. A controlled fix-forward is safer in those cases.

Q: Who can approve a rollforward?
A: The change owner + runtime-team lead + infra oncall. If customer impact is high, include SRE manager.

Q: Are there automated safeties?
A: Yes — the CI pipeline enforces auto-abort thresholds and will revert Terraform state for canary applies if the auto‑abort condition triggers.

If you have additions to templates or new example scripts, please attach them to this page and add a reviewer tag.

Document history
- 2024-03-12: initial draft (Alejandra O.)
- 2024-05-07: added rollforward decision tree (Marcus Lin)
- 2024-09-08: updated thresholds and Prometheus alert names (Priya Desai)

payload.page_title: Terraform validation harness for GPU topology changes with simulated traffic

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents the recommended Terraform validation harness used to safely change GPU pool topology (instance types, AZ placement, placement groups, taints/tolerations) by running an automated, CI-driven simulation of representative inference traffic against a temporary environment. The goal is to detect capacity, latency, and egress regressions before Terraform changes reach production gates.

Scope

- Applies to Terraform changes that modify: GPU pool sizes, instance flavors, network egress routes, subnets, placement groups, or tenant QoS tags.
- Intended for use in the main infrastructure CI pipeline (Buildkite) and also as a manual preflight for large migration windows.

Why we run simulated traffic during TF validation

Terraform plan/validate and policy-as-code checks catch many problems (iam, security, drift). However, changes that affect topology can cause emergent behavior only visible under realistic load: KV cache warmup time, network egress hot spots, host-level forks, instance scheduling differences, or kernel-level performance regressions for quantized kernels. Running a short, deterministic traffic simulation in an isolated environment reduces risk and gives measurable pass/fail criteria tied to SLOs.

Ownership and roles

- Owner: infra/gpu-platform (pager: #infra-gpu on Slack)
- CI pipeline owner: infra-ci-team
- Reviewer(s): Perf team for benchmark definitions; Security for service identity changes.

Prerequisites

1) Feature branch containing Terraform changes targeting the gpu-allocator module.
2) CI credentials: a service account with limited create/delete rights in the sandbox AWS/GCP account. The account must be constrained to the sandbox project and tagged appropriately.
3) Canary image bundles must be published to the build artifact registry (image tag ref used by the simulation harness).
4) Telemetry exporters enabled in the test environment: metrics (Prometheus push/gateway), traces (Jaeger), and logs (ELK/Cloud Logging).

High-level flow

1. Developer opens PR with Terraform changes.
2. CI runs terraform fmt/validate, policy checks (OPA/Conftest).
3. CI creates a short-lived sandbox environment by applying a curated Terraform overlay (isolated VPC, dedicated subnets, ephemeral GPU nodes).
4. Once infra is healthy and node agents report ready, CI deploys the simulation harness and a minimal control plane (service discovery + routing).
5. CI kicks off a deterministic workload generator (see workload profiles below) for 6–20 minutes.
6. Telemetry is collected and evaluated against thresholds. If thresholds are exceeded, the run is marked failed and the TF change is blocked.

Workload profiles (examples)

- baseline-infer: 200 rps, short prompts (avg 48 tokens), 95th latency expected < 150ms, KV hit ratio 35%
- bursty-chat: 50 rps with Poisson bursts up to 400rps for 30s windows, avg seq length 256, tail P99 < 2.2s
- long-context-eval: 8 rps, sequence length 2048, measures KV growth and memory pressure

Configuration table (thresholds used by CI guard)

| metric | acceptable threshold | failure condition |
|---|---:|---|
| 95th response latency (baseline-infer) | < 150 ms | > 180 ms for 3+ sample windows |
| P99 latency (bursty-chat) | < 2.2 s | > 3.0 s for > 10% of samples |
| GPU util (avg across pool) | 25% - 85% | sustained > 95% for 2+ minutes or < 5% for 3+ mins |
| KV cache miss rate | < 20% | > 40% |
| Packet drops (instance NIC) | < 0.1% | > 1% |
| Egress errors (5xx from proxy) | < 0.5% | > 2% |

Note: CI evaluates both absolute thresholds and delta-from-baseline (the baseline is the last green canonical run for the same infra-module version). An increase > 20% relative to baseline triggers an investigator review even if absolute thresholds are still within limits.

Terraform overlay pattern

We use a small overlay module that reuses the same tf-modules as production but isolates resources: unique VPC, namespacing tags, and a shortened lifetime. Example usage within the pipeline:

```bash
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
export TF_VAR_prefix=ci-sim-${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER}
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=ci-terraform-state" \
  -backend-config="key=ci/${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER}/tfstate"
terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=overlays/sim.vars.tfvars
```

Policy gates (pre-apply and post-apply)

- Pre-apply: OPA checks for forbidden instance types, missing tenant tags, and network exposure.
- Post-apply: Smoke tests (SSH to nodes, kube node ready, NVidia driver loaded), and an automated kernel/cuda version detector that fails if the new image/container runtime loses required drivers.

Simulation harness implementation notes

- Harness is a containerized service (go/python) that drives traffic using a combination of k6 for synthetic HTTP loads and a lightweight client that exercises the actual inference path (auth, routing, streaming).
- Test orchestration is implemented as a Buildkite step that: deploys harness, configures the target load profile, and pulls telemetry snapshots into a verification step.
- Harness supports deterministic replay from a recorded trace to ensure reproducibility across runs.

CI pipeline example (Buildkite YAML excerpt)

```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":terraform: TF validate + OPA"
    command: scripts/tf-validate.sh
  - wait: ~
  - label: ":rocket: Create sandbox infra"
    command: scripts/tf-apply-sim.sh
    timeout_in_minutes: 30
  - label: ":zap: Run sim traffic"
    command: scripts/run-sim.sh --profile baseline-infer
    timeout_in_minutes: 20
  - label: ":mag: Verify telemetry & teardown"
    command: scripts/verify-and-destroy.sh
    timeout_in_minutes: 10
    parallelism: 1
```

Pass/fail decision logic

- If any absolute threshold fails => fail the CI job, keep state for investigation (do not automatically destroy until reviewed unless configured).
- If delta-from-baseline > 20% => mark job for manual review by perf/infra owner.
- If smoke checks fail => immediate fail, skip simulation, and tear down if teardown policy allows.

Failure investigation checklist (quick triage)

1. Capture CPU/GPU profiles from the nodes (nvidia-smi stats, pid memory).
2. Check kernel and driver versions: mismatch with expected (see /ops/gpu-driver-manifest) is common root cause.
3. Inspect network telemetry (observability dashboard: egress QPS heatmap, ENI metrics).
4. Validate Terraform diff: did the change reduce pool size or modify AZ distribution?
5. If a regression is reproducible locally, escalate to runtime/kernel team.

Rollback and state cleanup policy

- By default the sandbox environment is set to auto-destroy on success or failure after a configurable hold window (default 30 minutes).
- For failing runs flagged for investigation, terraform state is preserved under a build-specific key and the infra owner is paged.

Operational runbook snippets

- Manually re-run a simulation against a historical TF plan:
  1. Check out the PR branch and download the terraform state snapshot associated with the build.
  2. Recreate the sandbox (scripts/tf-apply-sim.sh --preserve-state).
  3. Run the harness with the recorded trace that previously failed: scripts/run-sim.sh --replay trace-id.

- If an infra change requires immediate production roll (emergency):
  1. Ensure runbook owner signoff.
  2. Apply change to a single small region using the same overlay but with production credentials.
  3. Run a scaled-down sim for 10 minutes and monitor.
  4. Roll forward only if no regression; otherwise revert using the last-known-good module version.

Telemetry and artifacts retained per run

- Prometheus snapshot (Promtool export) - retained 7 days
- Trace dump (Jaeger) - retained 14 days
- Terraform state snapshot - retained 30 days for failed runs; 7 days for successful runs
- Benchmark artifacts (raw k6 output, harness logs) - retained 14 days

Limitations and known caveats

- Sandbox infra cannot perfectly mimic multi-tenant noisy neighbor patterns present in production; use the multi-tenant stress harness in conjunction with the sim for large migrations.
- GPU kernel quantization regressions that only appear at very long context lengths (> 8k) may require specialized long-run tests outside the standard CI window.

Related resources

- gpu-driver-manifest (internal): canonical mapping of OS/kernel/CUDA/cuDNN combos
- infra-ci/scripts: repo housing tf-apply-sim.sh and run-sim.sh examples
- perf-team/benchmarks: canonical baseline traces and replay IDs

Appendix: sample verification script (pseudo)

```bash
sections.heading: pipeline step (pseudocode)

sections.body:
set -e
BUCKET=s3://ci-telemetry
build=$BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER
prom_snapshot=$(curl "http://prometheus/api/v1/snapshot?job=sim&build=${build}")
python tools/evaluate_thresholds.py --snapshot "$prom_snapshot" --baseline latest_green || {
  echo "Thresholds failed; preserving state for investigation"
  # keep state around and notify owners
  scripts/preserve-state.sh $build
  exit 1
}
sections.heading: verify-and-destroy.sh (high level)

sections.body:
scripts/tf-destroy.sh --state-key ci/${build}/tfstate
```

Contact and escalation

For questions about the harness, contact infra/gpu-platform. When a scaffolded run fails and the issue appears to be a runtime or kernel problem, include perf@redwood and runtime-eng in the Slack thread and create an investigation ticket with the build id, snapshot links, and trace ids.

Changelog

- 2024-11-05: Initial draft (Priya Natarajan)
- 2025-02-14: Added delta-from-baseline gating and retention policy updates (Marta Ruiz)
sections.heading: success path

payload.page_title: Terraform VPC Modules (Alpha): Upgrade and Rollback Procedure (Day-2 Runbook)

sections.body: This runbook defines the supported, low-risk procedure for upgrading the **Redwood Private VPC Terraform modules (alpha)** in customer or Redwood-managed AWS accounts, and how to rollback safely if an upgrade introduces networking regressions.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Applies to the `redwood-terraform` module suite used for **AWS VPC-based private deployments** (EKS assumed).
- Focuses on networking + foundational infra modules (VPC/subnets/routing/NAT, endpoints/DNS, security groups, flow logs/log sinks, IAM scaffolding).
- Applies to both **design partner pilots** and internal dogfood environments.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Full application/cluster rollback (handled by `redwood-private-installer` + Helm rollouts).
- Major topology migrations (e.g., CIDR changes, multi-VPC redesign). These require an engagement plan and change window.
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
- Infra (modules + CI): **Irene Choi**, **Victor Alvarez**
- SRE (runbook + operational readiness): **Sean Gallagher**, **Rafael Mendes**
- Security review (IAM/logging defaults): **Marcus Lin**
sections.heading: Primary owners

sections.body:
- Production-impacting traffic loss, DNS outage, or inability to pull images from ECR.
- Planned changes that require resource replacement for: subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, VPC endpoints, or security groups that gate cluster control-plane/node traffic.
sections.heading: Escalation triggers

sections.body:
1) **Version pinning is in place**
- Root module pins every Redwood module to an explicit version tag (no floating branches).
- Terraform and AWS provider versions match the compatibility matrix for the target module version.

2) **State is healthy and backend is stable**
- Remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock or equivalent) is reachable and locking works.
- No stuck locks; `terraform plan` completes without backend errors.

3) **Change window and access**
- A maintenance window is approved if the plan includes any “High Risk” items (see Risk Table below).
- Break-glass AWS access is confirmed (restricted, time-bound). Required for rollback if connectivity is impacted.

4) **Baseline snapshots are captured**
- Save outputs: `terraform output -json > outputs.pre.json` (store in ticket/attachment).
- Export current plan context:
  - `terraform version` and provider lock file checksum
  - module versions in use
  - AWS account/region, VPC ID, cluster name
sections.heading: Preconditions (must be true before upgrading)

sections.body:
- **Patch upgrade** (x.y.Z): bugfixes; normally safe, but still requires plan review.
- **Minor upgrade** (x.Y.z): may add resources/inputs; risk depends on module area.
- **Major upgrade** (X.y.z): treat as migration; requires explicit approval from Infra + Private Deployments.

For alpha design partners, prefer: patch/minor upgrades only unless explicitly coordinated.
sections.heading: Step 0 — Identify the upgrade type

sections.body:
- Review the relevant release notes page for:
  - breaking changes
  - new required variables
  - default changes (especially private DNS or flow logs)
  - deprecations
sections.heading: Step 1 — Read the release notes and known limitations

sections.body: Update module sources to the new version tag.
sections.heading: Step 2 — Update module versions in a branch

sections.body:
- Use a single PR per environment for traceability.
- Include a short upgrade summary (from version → to version) and risk classification.
sections.heading: Required conventions

sections.body:
1) `terraform fmt -recursive`
2) `terraform init -upgrade`
3) `terraform validate`
4) `tflint --recursive`
5) `checkov -d .` (or org-approved equivalent)
sections.heading: Minimum local checks (mirrors CI gates)

sections.body: - Do not bypass without owner approval. Open an issue and document mitigation.
sections.heading: If any new check fails

sections.body:
- Use the same `*.tfvars` used by the environment.
- Ensure the same workspace and backend.
- Save the plan artifact:
  - `terraform plan -out tfplan.upgrade`
  - `terraform show -no-color tfplan.upgrade > plan.upgrade.txt`
sections.heading: Generate plan with a stable input set

sections.body:
**A) Safety checks**
- [ ] Plan is produced from the correct workspace/account/region.
- [ ] No unexpected provider upgrades.
- [ ] No change to backend, state, or workspace naming.

**B) Resource replacement / destructive changes**
- [ ] No `-/+` (replace) actions for: `aws_vpc`, `aws_subnet`, `aws_route_table`, `aws_nat_gateway`, `aws_internet_gateway`.
- [ ] No deletion of VPC endpoints required for ECR/S3/STS/CloudWatch Logs.
- [ ] No security group changes that open public ingress, broaden egress unintentionally, or remove required intra-cluster rules.

**C) DNS and endpoint correctness**
- [ ] VPC endpoints with `private_dns_enabled` match intended behavior.
- [ ] Resolver/DNS prerequisites are unchanged or explicitly planned.
- [ ] If endpoints are added/changed: confirm required services for installer image pulls and logging.

**D) Logging and retention**
- [ ] Flow log destination is correct (CloudWatch Logs group or S3 bucket) and owned/approved.
- [ ] Retention settings align with security guidance.
- [ ] No accidental disabling of flow logs.

**E) IAM boundaries and least privilege**
- [ ] Permission boundaries remain attached where required.
- [ ] New IAM permissions are reviewed by Security when scope expands.

**F) Drift vs intended changes**
- [ ] Any drift is understood (see Drift Handling below) and not being “fixed” accidentally.
sections.heading: Plan review checklist (must be completed in the PR or change ticket)

sections.body:
- Low Risk: Private Deployments on-call (SRE) + Infra reviewer.
- Medium Risk: add Victor Alvarez.
- High Risk: add Irene Choi + Marcus Lin; schedule a change window.
sections.heading: Approval requirements

sections.body:
- Apply during low-traffic window for pilots; mandatory for High Risk.
- Use a single operator (one AWS identity) to avoid concurrent applies.
sections.heading: Preferred apply approach

sections.body: - `terraform apply tfplan.upgrade`
sections.heading: Commands

sections.body:
**A) Terraform state & outputs**
- `terraform output -json > outputs.post.json`
- Confirm key outputs are unchanged unless expected (e.g., endpoint IDs).

**B) Connectivity checks (minimum)**
- From private subnets / cluster nodes (or a test instance), verify:
  - ECR auth + image pull (common failure mode)
  - S3 endpoint access if used for artifacts/logs
  - STS calls for IAM role assumptions
  - CloudWatch Logs ingestion if enabled

**C) Installer preflight checks**
- Run the Redwood Private installer preflight (or equivalent) to confirm:
  - required endpoints exist
  - private DNS resolution is stable
  - egress policies match expectations

**D) Observability checks**
- Flow logs present and writing to expected destination.
- CloudWatch Logs groups exist with correct retention.

If any check fails, stop and proceed to “Rollback decision tree”.
sections.heading: Perform these checks immediately after apply

sections.body:
Drift is common in enterprise accounts (security tooling, centralized networking, or manual hotfixes). Handle drift explicitly:

1) Classify the drift
- **Allowed drift** (do not revert): changes performed by customer network/security baselines that Redwood supports (e.g., additional VPC endpoints, organization-level tags, extra route propagation for DX/VPN).
- **Risk drift** (must reconcile): changes that reduce isolation, disable logs, or break required egress/endpoint paths.
- **Unknown drift**: anything else; treat as Medium Risk.

2) Decide the remediation approach
- If drift is allowed, codify it (recommended) by adding configuration inputs/overrides in the customer root module, not by manual changes.
- If drift is risky, engage customer network/security owners and plan a controlled remediation.

3) Avoid “drift cleanup” during module upgrades
Upgrades should not be used as an opportunity to sweep unrelated drift unless explicitly approved. Keep the change set small.
sections.heading: Drift handling (how to treat differences between state and reality)

sections.body:
Use this table to classify the plan and choose the right execution/rollback approach.

| Area | Examples | Risk | Why it’s risky | Guidance |
|------|----------|------|----------------|----------|
| Subnets/CIDR | subnet recreation, CIDR change, AZ remap | High | breaks node networking, ENIs, route associations | Do not proceed in-place; design migration |
| NAT strategy | NAT gateway replacement, change per-AZ NAT assumptions | High | outbound connectivity loss, ECR pulls fail | Change window + rollback plan + validation instance |
| Route tables | default route changes, propagation toggles | High | can blackhole traffic | Require peer review + apply in window |
| VPC endpoints | delete/replace ECR/S3/STS endpoints, private DNS toggles | High | installer fails, control-plane/services fail | Validate endpoint/DNS preflight |
| Security groups | removing intra-cluster rules, tightening egress unexpectedly | Medium/High | outages look like “random timeouts” | Diff rules carefully; verify ports/cidrs |
| Flow logs | destination change, IAM role change | Medium | compliance/audit gaps | Coordinate with Security; ensure retention |
| IAM scaffolding | boundary removal, trust policy changes | Medium | breaks installer automation | Security approval required for scope changes |
sections.heading: Risk table (known risky changes)

sections.body: Rollback should be based on observable impact and the feasibility of reverting safely.
sections.heading: Rollback decision tree

sections.body:
- Cluster or installer cannot reach ECR / cannot pull images.
- DNS resolution failures in private subnets affecting core services.
- Control-plane or node-to-node traffic is disrupted.
- NAT/route changes cause widespread timeouts.
sections.heading: When to rollback immediately

sections.body:
- Only logging/retention settings are incorrect (can often be patched forward).
- Non-critical endpoint additions cause no connectivity impact.
- Cosmetic drift/tag changes.
sections.heading: When to NOT rollback immediately

sections.body:
- The apply succeeded but behavior regressed due to a default change.
- Resource replacements did not occur, or the previous version recreates the same resources.
sections.heading: Best when

sections.body:
1) Revert module version pins in git to the last known-good tag.
2) `terraform init -upgrade` (ensures lockfile consistency with the reverted versions).
3) `terraform plan -out tfplan.rollback`
4) Review rollback plan for replacements (do not “double-break” the environment).
5) `terraform apply tfplan.rollback`
sections.heading: Procedure

sections.body:
- Rollback would force replacements.
- The issue is addressable via explicit inputs/overrides (e.g., toggling a DNS flag, adding a missing endpoint, restoring a security group rule).
sections.heading: Best when

sections.body:
- Add minimal overrides in the root module.
- Create a hotfix PR with a narrow plan.
- Apply and re-run post-apply verification.
sections.heading: Procedure

sections.body:
- Terraform rollback/patch-forward cannot restore connectivity quickly.
- There is an active outage.
sections.heading: Only when

sections.body:
- Temporarily add a required route or security group rule.
- Re-enable `private_dns_enabled` on a critical endpoint.
sections.heading: Examples

sections.body:
- Manual changes must be recorded immediately (ticket + exact console/CLI steps).
- Follow-up action is mandatory to codify the fix in Terraform and remove snowflake state.
sections.heading: Important

sections.body:
- Target environment identifiers: account ID, region, VPC ID
- From/to versions for each Redwood module
- `plan.upgrade.txt`
- `outputs.pre.json` and `outputs.post.json`
- Risk classification + checklist completion
- Verification results (ECR pull, STS, logs)
- If rollback occurred: `plan.rollback.txt` and a short incident summary
sections.heading: Required artifacts for every upgrade (attach to ticket/PR)

sections.body:
- Notify the customer primary and Redwood SE lead at least 24 hours before any Medium/High risk change.
- Agree on a rollback decision point (e.g., “if ECR pulls fail for >10 minutes, rollback”).
- Keep a live channel during the apply.
sections.heading: For design partner pilots

sections.body:
1) Installer fails pulling images (ECR)
- Symptoms: image pull backoffs, auth errors, timeouts
- Checks:
  - ECR API/DKR endpoints exist in the VPC
  - private DNS enabled matches the environment expectations
  - route/NAT or endpoint security groups allow 443

2) Intermittent DNS resolution
- Symptoms: sporadic service failures, timeouts, resolver errors
- Checks:
  - VPC DNS settings (hostnames/support)
  - endpoint private DNS toggles
  - security tooling intercepting DNS

3) Logs missing after upgrade
- Symptoms: flow logs not delivered, CloudWatch group not receiving
- Checks:
  - IAM role/policy for flow logs
  - destination/retention configuration
  - KMS key permissions if encryption is enabled
sections.heading: Common failure modes and quick triage

sections.body:
- Plan shows no High Risk replacements OR change window is approved.
- ECR/S3/STS endpoints remain present and correctly configured.
- No unexpected widening of ingress.
- Flow logs remain enabled (or explicitly approved to disable).
sections.heading: Go if all are true

sections.body:
- Subnet CIDR or AZ mapping changes in-place.
- NAT gateways are replaced without a window.
- Endpoint deletions/replacements for ECR/S3/STS without a tested rollback plan.

---
Document owner: Sean Gallagher (SRE). For proposed changes to this procedure, open a PR against this page and request review from Infra + Security.
sections.heading: No-go if any are true

payload.page_title: Self‑Service GPU Enrollment and Egress Guard Terraform Contracts

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the Terraform contract and CI gating required to enable self-service GPU enrollment for tenant teams while enforcing per-tenant egress safety and cost accountability. The goal is to allow product and infra teams to provision accelerator capacity quickly without risking large cross-account egress spikes, runaway billing, or network saturation.

Scope
-----
- Declarative Terraform module contract for tenant GPU enrollment and egress policy attachment.
- CI contract tests that validate module outputs, IAM boundaries, and egress guard integration.
- Runtime telemetry and alert thresholds used by SRE to detect policy violations.
- Runbook for elevated egress events and remediation steps.

Goals and non‑goals
-------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Standardized Terraform contract that every tenant onboarding flow must satisfy.
- Enforce egress quotas and safe fallback routing for burst events.
- CI gating that prevents Terraform PRs from merging if contract checks fail.

Non‑goals:
- This doc does not prescribe hardware SKU procurement. See "gpu-provisioning-immutable-state-and-disaster-recovery" for capacity lifecycle.

Principles
----------
1. Safe defaults: newly enrolled tenants get conservative egress budgets and burst allowances.
2. Observable by design: Terraform modules must emit metadata that maps to billing and telemetry pipelines.
3. Contract-first: CI must assert the module API surface and policy hooks before deployment.
4. Least privilege networking and IAM for cross-account access.

Architecture & Flow
-------------------
1. Tenant creates a PR against the self-service inbox repository with a minimal enrollment HCL using the shared module.
2. CI runs contract tests (unit + integration) that validate the module outputs, checksums, and a dry-run against a sandbox account.
3. On successful CI, the Terraform apply is executed into a staging environment where a smoke test triggers a synthetic egress trace.
4. If smoke tests pass and egress telemetry is within budget, the change is promoted to production via the gated release pipeline.

Required outputs from the enrollment Terraform module
--------------------------------------------------
The shared module must expose these outputs (names and types are enforced by CI):
- tenant_id (string)
- billing_tag (string)
- gpu_pool_id (string)
- egress_policy_id (string)
- egress_budget_bytes_per_hour (number as string)
- egress_burst_window_seconds (number as string)
- owner_contact (string)
- monitoring_service_endpoint (string)

These outputs are consumed by the egress guard operator and the billing exporter. CI contract tests will fail if any output is missing or malformed.

Terraform contract rules (must pass CI checks)
---------------------------------------------
- Module must be pinned to a canonical version: module.source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-internal/tf-gpu-enroll.git?ref=v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>"
- No hardcoded credentials or long‑lived keys in module parameters.
- All networking attachments must use approved VPC connectors and NATs defined in org modules.
- Egress budget must be explicitly set; if omitted, CI will set it to the platform default and require an owner approval.
- Outputs mapping for telemetry must include billing_tag and monitoring_service_endpoint.

CI/CD contract tests (pipeline: enroll-contract-checks)
----------------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
1. fmt_check: terraform fmt and HCL lint; fail fast.
2. unit_validate: static schema validate of enrollment HCL/variables.
3. module_hash_check: ensure the module ref matches pinned SHA (prevent accidental float).
4. plan_and_diff_check: terraform plan against a sandbox account; parse plan for any disallowed resources (e.g., internet-exposed load balancer).
5. output_contract_asserts: run a small harness that executes terraform output and asserts presence + basic patterns of required outputs.
6. smoke_egress_simulation: run a synthetic workload in a staging account that emits traffic up to 10% of the configured egress_budget to verify telemetry plumbing.
7. cost_estimate_verify: run the cost estimator; if estimated monthly egress > $X (configurable, default $200), require manual approval.

The pipeline must return structured artifacts: plan.json, outputs.json, cost_estimate.json, smoke_result.json. These artifacts are archived and linked to the PR.

Example Terraform enrollment snippet
----------------------------------
(Example provided for onboarding teams; CI expects the exact output names)

```
module "tenant_gpu_enrollment" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-internal/tf-gpu-enroll.git?ref=v1.2"

  tenant_id                     = "acme-io"
  owner_contact                 = "oncall+acme@redwood.com"
  requested_gpu_count           = 4
  requested_machine_profile     = "a2-highmem"
  egress_budget_bytes_per_hour  = 1073741824 # 1 GiB/hour
  egress_burst_window_seconds   = 300
  billing_tag                   = "team:acme"
  vpc_connector                 = "org-vpc-connector-prod"
}
```

Example expected outputs.json (CI will validate keys exist)
---------------------------------------------------------
```
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-io",
  "billing_tag": "team:acme",
  "gpu_pool_id": "gpool-42",
  "egress_policy_id": "egp-9",
  "egress_budget_bytes_per_hour": "1073741824",
  "egress_burst_window_seconds": "300",
  "owner_contact": "oncall+acme@redwood.com",
  "monitoring_service_endpoint": "https://telemetry.prod.redwood/v1/streams/egp-9"
}
```

Telemetry and alerts (SRE integration)
-------------------------------------
sections.heading: The enrollment pipeline must run the following stages
Metric names (required)

sections.body:
| Alert name | Signal | Trigger | Severity | Owner |
|------------|--------|---------|----------|-------|
| EgressBudgetApproach | infra.egress.bytes per hour vs budget | >= 85% of budget sustained for 10m | P3 | tenant oncall |
| EgressBurstExceeded | infra.egress.burst_rate > budget/burst_window | single spike > 3x burst allowance | P2 | infra-networking oncall |
| EgressPolicyViolation | infra.egress.policy_violations > 0 | any violation | P1 | infra-security oncall |

When an alert fires, the following tags must be attached to the incident: tenant_id, gpu_pool_id, commit_sha (from enrollment), pipeline_run_id. Attach smoke_result.json and plan.json.

Runbook: Elevated egress event (summary)
--------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge the alert and attach artifacts from the enrollment pipeline.
2. Check infra.egress.policy_violations for explicit blocks (e.g., unapproved NATs). If present: immediately activate egress-policy circuit breaker (see step 5).
3. If violations absent, consult recent flows in the packet telemetry dashboard for signs of data exfil or runaway inference evals.
4. Contact tenant owner_contact; request immediate throttling of synthetic/traffic jobs.
5. Circuit breaker options (ordered):
   a. Apply egress-policy emergency patch that reduces egress_budget_bytes_per_hour by 80% (fast path for critical incidents).
   b. Reroute tenant public traffic through the egress-scrubber proxy to enforce rate limits and TLS termination.
   c. As last resort, detach the tenant from the shared GPU pool and move to a quarantined warm pool with no external egress.
6. After stabilization, run forensics, create post-incident report, and require the tenant to provide remediation and long-term plan.

Ownership and escalation
-----------------------
- Module ownership: infra/terraform-team (primary)
- Egress guard operator: infra/networking-team (primary)
- Billing tag and cost pipeline: finance-infra (secondary)
- Oncall routing: infra-sre (escalation for P1/P2)

Rollout plan for existing tenants
--------------------------------
1. Publish module v2.0 with backward-compatible outputs and deprecation notices.
2. Run a compatibility scanner across existing Terraform state to detect missing outputs.
3. Create a migration PR template that populates conservative egress budgets and adds owner_contact.
4. Run a phased enforcement: 30% tenants (canary) -> 50% -> 100% over 8 weeks.
5. Enforce strict CI contract checks at 100% enforcement.

Operational notes and caveats
---------------------------
- The cost estimator is intentionally conservative; tenants with high egress patterns should be counseled to use dedicated networking or compress payloads.
- The smoke_egress_simulation must not exceed 10% of the tenant egress budget; CI enforces this upper bound to avoid billing surprises.
- For air-gapped/private deployments, the monitoring_service_endpoint is a stub that the Private team wires to customer telemetry. CI still validates the URL format.

Appendix A: CI job definitions (high level)
-----------------------------------------
- enroll-contract-checks: runs on PR; required status check.
- enroll-staging-deploy: gated by enroll-contract-checks; runs terraform apply in staging and triggers smoke simulation.
- enroll-prod-promote: manual approval required if cost_estimate.json > $200; otherwise automatic after 24h successful smoke in staging.

Sample CI command snippets
-------------------------
- terraform init -backend-config="bucket=tf-state-sandbox"
- terraform plan -out=plan.binary | jq -r '.planned_values.root_module' > plan.json
- python tools/validate_outputs.py outputs.json --schema schemas/enrollment_outputs.json
- ./tools/smoke_simulator --endpoint $MON_ENDPOINT --bytes 10485760 --duration 60

Appendix B: Contact matrix
--------------------------
- infra/terraform-team: infra-terraform@redwood.com
- infra/networking-team: infra-networking@redwood.com
- infra-sre: infra-sre-oncall@redwood.com
- finance-infra: infra-billing@redwood.com

Revision history
---------------
- 2024-02-14: Initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2024-06-20: Added CI contract stages and cost gating (Ravi Patel)
- 2025-08-12: Finalized runbook and escalation paths, updated alert thresholds (Lena Ortiz)

References
---------
- See org modules: org-vpc-connector, nat-gateway-shared, tf-cost-estimator.
- Related runbooks: preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook.json, egress-fairness-request-shaper-and-proxy-patterns.json

Feedback and next steps
-----------------------
Open action: add an automated remediation playbook that can reduce egress_budget_bytes_per_hour automatically when the platform detects sustained elevated cost for 3 hours. Assign to infra/automation for Q4 2025.
sections.heading: Recommended alerting thresholds (defaults)

payload.page_title: GPU module compatibility and deprecation plan

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page documents the compatibility matrix for Redwood's GPU Terraform modules, the automated tests we run to validate upgrades, and a concrete deprecation plan for older module versions. It is intended for infra engineers, platform owners, and module maintainers who are planning module upgrades, breaking changes, or sunsetting older variants.

Goals
- Provide a single source of truth for which versions of modules, Terraform and cloud providers are supported.
- Define an automated validation pipeline that prevents accidental breaking changes from reaching production.
- Establish a predictable deprecation timeline and communication checklist for module consumers.

Scope
- Includes: terraform-modules/gpu-pool, terraform-modules/gpu-instance, terraform-modules/gpu-network, and common helpers (tagging, iam, monitoring).
- Excludes: customer-specific forks in private repos and one-off PoC modules.

Compatibility matrix (current snapshot)
| Module | Min Terraform | Max Terraform | AWS provider tested | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| gpu-pool | 1.4.0 | 1.8.x | 4.60.0 | Supports fractional GPU tiling when "fractional_enabled=true"; 1.9+ untested. |
| gpu-instance | 1.3.0 | 1.8.x | 4.58.0 | Provides node bootstrap user-data scripts; uses local-exec hooks. |
| gpu-network | 1.2.0 | 1.8.x | 4.60.0 | Contains egress fencing submodule; careful with route propagation changes. |
| gpu-tags | 1.0.0 | 1.8.x | 4.60.0 | Simple tagging helper; no state. |
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- "Max Terraform" reflects the latest version we run CI against; we keep this updated quarterly.
- AWS provider column is the pinned provider used in module CI tests. A mismatch at the customer level is supported but may require adaptation.

Automated validation pipeline (CI)
1) PR linting: validate TF fmt, tflint ruleset (redwood-tflint), and module docs.
2) Static checks: run terraform 0.15 upgrade checks (if PR contains upgrade), module input schema validation with custom scripts.
3) Unit plan tests: run terraform init/plan using terratest wrapper against a small sandbox account. Plan must be stable and show no unexpected replacements.
4) Integration smoke: apply to ephemeral account with minimal resources (1 node, small disk), run bootstrap smoke tests (SSH into instance or validate cloud-init finished), then terraform destroy.
5) Backwards-compatibility check: for any change that modifies state layout or resource addresses, run `terraform state pull` and a scripted diff to ensure state moves are explicit.

CI job names and targets (for repo: infra/terraform-modules)
- ci/lint-terraform (runs on every PR)
- ci/plan-unit-tests (matrix: [tf_version: 1.4.6, 1.5.7, 1.8.5])
- ci/integration-ephemeral (runs on merge to main for non-breaking changes)
- ci/compatibility-regression (runs nightly; compares latest main to last released tag)

Example compatibility test commands (developer run)
- terraform init -upgrade -backend-config=backends/ephemeral.tfvars\- TF_VAR_region=us-west-2
- TERRATEST_ACCOUNT=ephemeral make test-plan MODULE=gpu-pool TF_VERSIONS="1.4.6 1.8.5"
- ./scripts/state-diff-check.sh --old-tag v1.12.0 --new-branch main --module gpu-pool

State-migration checklist (for changes that rename/move resources)
1) Prepare migration plan and add to PR description with explicit `terraform state mv` commands.
2) Add automated `post_upgrade` plan that runs in CI and demonstrates state move in ephemeral account.
3) Provide rollback `state mv` commands and a tested sequence to revert if failure occurs.
4) Coordinate with consumers: identify workspaces that use the module (see Module-usage inventory) and notify owners with a migration window.

Deprecation policy and timetable (example for v1.x -> v2.0)
- Announcement phase (Day 0): publish deprecation notice in #infra-update and add banner to module README.
- Soft-deprecation (Day 30): CI will flag but not block usage of deprecated versions. Add warning to `terraform init` via README and example.
- Hard-deprecation (Day 90): Remove automatic updates/compatibility guarantees for deprecated branch. New changes merged to main may not backport fixes.
- Sunset (Day 180): Tag deprecated versions as EOL in registry, and optionally remove modules from default published mirror.

Communication checklist (who to notify and how)
- Module owners: create GitHub issue with migration checklist and link to state-migration PR.
- Platform teams (kubernetes, eval infra): direct Slack mentions + brief runbook for migration during low-traffic window.
- Security/Compliance: ensure new IAM changes are reviewed; attach policy diffs to the PR.
- Customers (internal product teams): send short email and calendar invite for migration help session (if larger than 2 workspaces).

Rollout / Canary strategy for breaking changes
1) Publish a v2.0-preview tag and run `ci/integration-ephemeral` across a set of tagged non-prod tenants (testing accounts A,B,C).
2) After 7 days of successful runs, promote the preview to `canary` and run weekly plan checks against low-risk production workspaces (read-only plan run).
3) Require a manual approval gate in CI before any `apply` in production workspaces when the module major version increments.

Operational runbook (if migration fails)
1) Immediately open a Priority-1 GitHub issue and notify on-call infra via #infra-oncall.
2) Revert the merge that introduced the breaking change (if applicable) and run the rollback `state mv` sequence documented in PR.
3) If revert is impossible, run the pre-tested rollback steps listed in the state-migration checklist.
4) Perform postmortem within 7 calendar days and update this document with root cause and improved checks.

Module-usage inventory (how to find consumers)
- Use `scripts/find-module-refs.sh modules/gpu-pool` to locate workspaces in our monorepo and external repos that reference the module.
- Maintain a living spreadsheet (stored at /ops/module-usage/gpu-pool-usage.csv) with owner, workspace path, cloud account, and last-updated.

Ownership and escalation
- Module owner: @marcus-chen (responsible for design, tests, and release notes).
- Release custodian: infra-release@redwood.com (tags releases, coordinates publish).
- Emergency escalation: on-call infra (see runbook for pager duty rotation) and Platform Eng manager for cross-team coordination.

Appendices
A) Example `state mv` snippet
- terraform state mv module.old_name.aws_instance.node module.new_name.aws_instance.node

B) Quick checklist for module authors (pre-merge)
- [ ] Add changelog entry with impact surface.
- [ ] Add compatibility matrix update.
- [ ] Add unit and integration tests for every supported TF/provider version.
- [ ] Run state-diff and verify no implicit replacements.

C) Contact list
- Module owner: Marcus Chen (marvin@redwood.com)
- CI owner: Leah Patel (leah.p@redwood.com)
- Security reviewer: Diego Alvarez (diego.a@redwood.com)

payload.page_title: Tenant GPU Quotas and Fair-Share Terraform Patterns

sections.body: This document defines a reproducible Terraform-based pattern for enforcing per-tenant GPU quotas and a fair-share scheduler policy across Redwood Inference reserved clusters and shared GPU pools. It combines IaC best practices, runtime enforcement mechanisms, CI/CD gating, and oncall runbook steps so teams can request capacity safely without destabilizing production.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide a standard Terraform module layout for tenant quota definitions that is auditable and testable.
- Enforce soft and hard GPU limits per tenant with automated reclamation and notifications.
- Ensure fair-share scheduling across interactive (dev/test) and production workloads.
- Integrate quota changes into pipelines with policy checks and canary rollout.
- Minimize blast radius for capacity requests and simplify chargeback labeling.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Applies to all AWS deployments using NVIDIA GPU instance families (G4/G5/A100-equivalent) and our on-prem clusters managed by the same orchestration layer.
- Covers Terraform modules, cloud IAM roles, controller automation, CI/CD gating, and SRE runbook for quota incidents.
- Does NOT cover low-level GPU driver installation or image build pipelines (see ci-cd/gpu-images).
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
- Terraform registry modules: tenant-gpu-quota (records desired quotas), shared-gpu-pool (defines pool metadata), fairshare-policy (scheduling weights).
- Central Quota Controller (k8s controller or managed service) watches a namespaced CRD mirrors Terraform-state outputs and enforces runtime limits via Kubernetes ResourceQuota / device-plugin annotations or cloud autoscaling group tagging for non-k8s clusters.
- Alerting and billing: Controller emits metrics to DataDog (metric names below) and writes quota events to audit-log S3 and to the Console entitlement API.
sections.heading: Architecture overview (textual diagram)

sections.body:
- tenant_id: canonical identifier for an internal product/team.
- requested_gpus: desired max GPUs for a tenant (soft limit).
- hard_limit_gpus: strict ceiling enforced by the controller (must be <= pool_capacity).
- fair_share_weight: integer weight used by the fair-share scheduler to proportionally allocate burst capacity.
sections.heading: Key Concepts and Definitions

sections.body:
- modules/tenant-gpu-quota/
  - main.tf (resource schema, state outputs, example CRD export)
  - variables.tf (tenant_id, requested_gpus, hard_limit_gpus, labels)
  - outputs.tf (quota_id, policy_arn)
  - examples/tenant-basic/
sections.heading: Recommended Terraform module layout (convention)
Example usage (snippet - terraform)

sections.body:
- quota_id: "quota-acme-marketing"
- controller_cr_manifest: serialized YAML to apply (for non-managed clusters)
sections.heading: Module outputs (example)

sections.body:
1) Terraform writes desired state to a central state bucket and triggers the Quota Controller via a gitops push (we prefer push to the controller's CRD API).
2) Controller compares requested_gpus to pool_capacity. If requested_gpus + sum(other_hard_limits) > pool_capacity: controller marks quota request as PENDING and emits a metric `infra.gpu.quota.request_denied`.
3) For allowed requests, controller creates/updates a runtime representation: k8s ResourceQuota, nodeselector labels, or cloud autoscaling tag depending on environment.
4) Soft-limit behavior: when tenant usage exceeds requested_gpus but is under hard_limit_gpus, controller triggers throttling annotations and sends warning notifications to tenant owners.
5) Hard-limit behavior: usage above hard_limit_gpus results in immediate pod eviction ordering based on QoS and eviction policy. Evicted jobs are requeued per tenant retry policy.
sections.heading: Policy enforcement and automation

sections.body:
- All changes to modules/* require: terraform fmt, terraform validate, unit tests (terratest), and a policy check step that enforces max hard_limit per module (policy as code using Sentinel or Open Policy Agent).
- PR workflow:
  1. Developer opens PR to modules repo.
  2. Pipeline runs lint/test/policy.
  3. If module changes affect outputs consumed by controller, CI triggers a staging apply (to a dedicated staging workspace) and runs end-to-end smoke tests that validate controller reconciliation.
  4. After 24h in staging with green health checks, a manual approver can promote to production via the module registry UI.
sections.heading: CI/CD and testing patterns for quota modules

sections.body:
- terraform plan shows only intended changes.
- terratest asserts that CRD manifest contains expected hard_limit and labels.
- Controller metrics in staging: infra.gpu.quota.reconcile_success == 1 after apply.

Runbook: quota exhaustion (pageable flow for SRE/Oncall)
- Symptoms: high infra.gpu.quota.denied rate, pending scheduling backlog, tenants hitting hard limit eviction.
- Immediate steps (TL;DR):
  1. Pager receives alert (alert name: GPU_QUOTA_EXHAUSTION_HIGH).
  2. Open the quota controller dashboard and filter by `pool_id` in incident.
  3. Identify offending tenants: query DataDog metric `infra.gpu.usage_by_tenant` and sort desc.
  4. If a tenant is misbehaving (runaway jobs), pause their job queue via Console API: POST /internal/admin/tenant/{tenant_id}/pause (requires admin role).
  5. If total hard_limits exceed pool_capacity, follow emergency mitigation: temporarily increase pool_capacity via autoscaling group override OR reduce per-tenant soft limits for non-critical tenants.
  6. Notify stakeholders (Slack channel #infra-gpu-capacity) with template: incident id, pool, top 5 tenants, mitigation action.
sections.heading: Testing checklist (automated where possible)

sections.body:
- Use CLI: `infractl pool update-capacity --pool-id <pool> --capacity <n>` (requires infra-admin).
- If infractl is unavailable, patch the controller CRD to set poolOverride=true and manualCapacity integer.
sections.heading: Detailed rollback mitigation (if autoscaler misbehaves)

sections.body:
- Requests <= 4 GPUs: auto-approve for teams with dev tag.
- Requests 5-16 GPUs: require approval from pool-owner and finance for chargeback assignment.
- Requests >16 GPUs or cumulative team commit >32 GPUs: require infra capacity planning review and lead sign-off.

Naming, labels and tagging conventions (enforced by module):
- tenant_id: lower-case hyphenated, e.g., acme-marketing
- labels: team, cost_center, environment (dev|staging|prod), business_unit
- Terraform tags map to cloud tags: Owner=team, CostCenter=cost_center, InfraProject=redwood-gpu
sections.heading: Governance and approval matrix

sections.body:
- infra.gpu.quota.request_denied > 5/min => Pager (P1) if sustained > 5m
- infra.gpu.usage_by_tenant{env=\"prod\"} > 95% of hard_limit for 3m => Alert to tenant owner + SRE channel (P2)
- infra.gpu.pool_utilization > 85% for 10m => Ops warning (P3)
sections.heading: Metrics and alert thresholds (recommended)

sections.body:
- Use semantic versioning for modules. Major bumps require migration notes and an automated migration plan that maps old outputs to new names.
- Backwards compatibility: keep old outputs for 2 releases before removal.
- Migration steps:
  1. Publish module vX.Y with compatibility shim outputs.
  2. Update consumer workspaces to reference new module version and run `terraform plan` in staging workspace.
  3. Validate controller metrics and reconnect hookpoints.
  4. After 1 week of green, remove legacy outputs in next major release.
sections.heading: Module versioning and migration guidance

sections.body:
- Tenant quota modules must set a principal that maps to a team-specific IAM role (arn:aws:iam::redwood:role/tenant-{tenant_id}-quota-admin).
- Controller service account requires a narrow policy that can only patch the controller CRD and update tags/labels on node pools, not full EC2 or IAM privileges.
- Audit logs: every quota change must be written to S3 with server-side encryption and a retention policy of 2 years for auditability.
sections.heading: Security and IAM considerations

sections.body:
- Module owner: infra/iac-team (primary: Maya Patel).
- Controller owner: eng-platform/scheduling (primary: Jon Rivera).
- Oncall rotation: see eng-infra/oncall rota page (linked in related pages).
sections.heading: Ownership and contacts

sections.body:
- 0-30 days: deploy module and controller in staging, migrate two pilot teams (internal platform & search).
- 30-60 days: enable auto-approval rules for <=4GPU requests and collect telemetry.
- 60-90 days: open self-serve request path for all teams, run a full capacity planning drill.

Appendix A — Example controller CRD (YAML excerpt):
```yaml
apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
kind: TenantGPUQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-acme-marketing
spec:
  tenantId: acme-marketing
  hardLimitGpus: 12
  requestedGpus: 8
  fairShareWeight: 20
  labels:
    team: marketing
    cost_center: cc-1234
```

Appendix B — Example IAM policy (abbreviated):
```json
{
  \"Version\": \"2012-10-17\",
  \"Statement\": [
    {
      \"Effect\": \"Allow\",
      \"Action\": [\"autoscaling:UpdateAutoScalingGroup\", \"ec2:DescribeInstances\"],
      \"Resource\": \"*\"
    },
    {
      \"Effect\": \"Allow\",
      \"Action\": [\"s3:PutObject\"],
      \"Resource\": [\"arn:aws:s3:::infra-audit-logs/*\"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Appendix C — Quick QA checklist for approvers:
- Does requested_gpus fit within pool capacity projections for the quarter?
- Are cost center and business case provided?
- Is tenant using fair-share weight appropriately (not >100)?
- Has the team provided a deprovision plan for idle GPUs?
sections.heading: Rollout plan (30/60/90)

sections.body:
- Next iteration will add a simulated capacity planning tool (what-if) into the Console using the modules' state outputs.
- Investigate integration with the billing pipeline to show predicted monthly spend by tenant for requested_gpus.
sections.heading: Notes and future work

sections.body:
- Module registry: https://registry.redwood.internal/modules/tenant-gpu-quota
- Quota controller dashboard: https://ops.redwood.internal/quota-controller
- Slack channel: #infra-gpu-capacity
