payload.page_title: GPU environment churn management and IaC strategy

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines recommended patterns, Terraform/IaC primitives, CI/CD controls, and operational runbooks for managing high-churn GPU environments used for short-lived workloads (experiments, evals, CI jobs, ephemeral dev sandboxes). The goal is to limit cost leakage, maintain predictable capacity for production tenants, and provide safe automated lifecycle operations that are auditable and reversible.

Scope

- Applies to all GPU pools that allow automated provisioning or destruction at runtime, including: ephemeral CI pools, eval clusters, developer sandboxes, and short-lived tenant environments.
- Does NOT replace long-lived Dedicated GPU reservations for production traffic; interactions with Dedicated are covered in a separate policy.

Motivation

High churn on GPU environments creates three recurring problems: unexpectedly high spend, fragmented topology leading to reduced packing efficiency, and cascading preemption events that impact production SLOs. This doc prescribes explicit IaC patterns and operational controls to mitigate those risks while preserving developer velocity.

Key principles

1. Declarative minimums: Environments should be provisioned using small, composable Terraform modules that expose a minimal surface area (size, ttl, labels, owner).
2. Short-lived by default: TTLs and automated teardown are enabled for non-production environments.
3. Observability-first: Every environment must register metrics and lifecycle events to the infra telemetry pipeline.
4. Safe defaults: Provisioning pipelines must require approvals beyond cost/size thresholds and support fast rollback.
5. Ownership & accountability: Each environment has a single responsible owner (user or service account) recorded in tags and audit logs.

Definitions

- Churned environment: any GPU instance/pool created and destroyed more than 4 times in a 24h window.
- Ephemeral pool: a logically grouped set of GPU nodes created for a single CI job, eval run, or ad-hoc developer session with expected life < 24h.
- Persistent pool: long-lived GPU pool used for production serving or reserved capacity.

Design patterns and IaC primitives

1) Module composition pattern
- core/gpu-node: defines node shape (gpu type, disk image, taints, kube labels)
- core/gpu-pool: orchestrates autoscaler, capacity provider, and placement strategy
- control/teardown: TTL controller, lifecycle hook, and notification sink
- governance/labels: standardized tags for owner, cost-center, stack-id, purpose

2) Single-responsibility variables
- variables exposed by modules must be small and typed: size, max_count, min_count, ttl_hours (default 6), tenant, owner_email, cost_center, provisioning_reason

3) Tagging and audit boundary (must):
- tag.owner = owner_email
- tag.stack_id = ${var.stack_id}
- tag.env_purpose = ephemeral|dev|ci|eval|prod
- tag.policy_profile = low-cost|high-availability|gpu-sensitive

Terraform interface matrix (example)

| Input name | Type | Default | Notes |
|------------|------|---------|-------|
| stack_id | string | (required) | Unique short id used for naming and deletion policy |
| owner_email | string | (required) | Primary contact for alerts and approvals |
| ttl_hours | number | 6 | TTL after which automated teardown runs |
| max_count | number | 4 | Upper bound to protect capacity |
| gpu_type | string | a100-80gb | Allow only approved gpu types via validator |

CI/CD pipeline patterns

- All environment creation is controlled via a single pipeline template: infra/ephemeral/gpu-create.yml. Pipelines must:
  1. Validate HCL with tflint/terraform validate
  2. Run module-level policy checks (policyengine/opa) enforcing tag and size constraints
  3. Simulate plan and generate a human-readable diff artifact
  4. Apply in a dedicated control account using an ephemeral service principal
  5. Emit lifecycle event to infra.telemetry.gpu.events
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- name: validate
  run: terraform validate && tflint
- name: policy-check
  run: opa test /policies/gpu-size.rego
- name: plan
  run: terraform plan -out plan.tfplan
- name: human-approval
  when: conditional(contains(var.owner_email, "@redwood.com") == false || var.max_count > 8)
- name: apply
  run: terraform apply plan.tfplan

Operational runbook: preflight checklist
sections.heading: pipeline: infra-gpu-create > steps

sections.body:
- Confirm owner_email, cost_center, and stack_id are set.
- Confirm ttl_hours <= 72 (enforced by policy).
- Confirm gpu_type is allowed for the region.
- Confirm max_count <= account_quota_limit (CI will query account quota API).
- Verify alert hook (pager/slack) configured for lifecycle failures.

On-provision steps (automated)

1) Create pool via CI/CD pipeline (outputs cluster_id, nodegroup_id).
2) Wait for cluster registration: monitor kube-system readiness (target 90% nodes Ready within 10 minutes).
3) Emit event: infra.telemetry.gpu.events -> {action: created, stack_id, owner, expires_at}

Scale-up procedure (manual/automated)

1) Automated autoscaler increments min_count up to max_count when pending pods > 2 for > 2 minutes.
2) If pending pods persist for > 5 minutes, alert ops (severity: P2).
3) If ops approve, pipeline will update Terraform variable max_count and reapply (procedure documented in change approval).

Scale-down and teardown (numbered procedure)

1. TTL controller triggers when expires_at <= now.
2. Controller annotates cluster with teardown_pending and notifies owner via email and slack (48h, 12h, 1h cadence).
3. If owner requests extension: owner updates stack_id.ttl_hours via self-service UI (if allowed) or raises a support ticket.
4. If no extension, controller drains nodes (kubectl cordon + drain with grace period 120s) and deletes node groups.
5. Terraform destroy is executed in the control account with confirmation token recorded in audit log.

Escalation and rollback steps

- If teardown collides with an active production pod (unexpected taint leak):
  1) Immediately halt destroy (cancel destroy job).
  2) Re-label affected pods and cordon affected nodes.
  3) Notify Platform SRE and product owner; create incident if production SLOs are impacted.
  4) Restore cluster from snapshoted node images if deletion partially completed.

Monitoring and alerts (recommended SLOs/thresholds)

- Metric: ephemeral_gpu.node_ready_ratio -> SLO: >= 0.9 within 10 minutes of creation. Alert P2 if below.
- Metric: ephemeral_gpu.creation_rate -> Alert if > 3x baseline for 30m (possible runaway provisioning).
- Metric: ephemeral_gpu.destroy_failures -> Alert P1 if > 3 failures in 1h.

Cost controls and billing integration

- Every ephemeral stack_id is billed to a cost_center string; infra billing pipeline charges back weekly.
- Auto-mitigation: if projected daily spend for ephemeral pools exceeds $X (configurable), new ephemeral create requests are blocked until quota uplift is approved.

Security and networking constraints

- Ephemeral pools are created in a shared tenant VPC namespace with restricted egress via NAT gateway.
- Default network ACL denies external SSH; all access mediated via jump-host bastions with session recording.
- Subnet selection is restricted by policy to avoid cross-account peering that bypasses egress control.

Terraform module example (excerpt)

module "ephemeral_gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/modules//gpu-pool?ref=stable"
  stack_id = var.stack_id
  owner_email = var.owner_email
  ttl_hours = var.ttl_hours
  max_count = var.max_count
  gpu_type = var.gpu_type
}

Policy enforcement (examples)

- OPA rego snippets enforce: ttl_hours <= 72, max_count <= 16 for non-prod accounts, required tags present, gpu_type in allowed list for region.
- Terraform Cloud runs use policy sets with blocking checks; self-hosted CI uses opa gate jobs.

Migration checklist (moving ad-hoc pools to controlled IaC)

1) Identify unmanaged GPU instances from cloud inventory (last updated > 24h).
2) Reach out to owners discovered via tags; offer migration plan and eviction timelines.
3) Create IaC stack_id that models current configuration and run a dry-run migrate (terraform import where feasible).
4) After validation, enable TTL and observe for one lifecycle before enforcing automated teardown.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary maintainer: infra/gpu-team (owners: ava@redwood.com, daniel@redwood.com)
- Oncall escalation: platform-sre-pager (see oncall rota page)
- Billing questions: finance-infra@redwood.com

Risks and trade-offs

- Strict TTLs reduce developer friction in the long run but can block long-running experiments; mitigations include controlled extension requests and temporary persistent staging pools.
- Aggressive automated teardown needs robust detection of production labeling mistakes to avoid accidental deletion.

Appendix

- Quicklinks:
  - Module repo: git@repo.redwood.ai:infra/modules/gpu-pool
  - Policy repo: git@repo.redwood.ai:policy/opa/gpu-policies
  - Telemetry channel: infra.telemetry.gpu.events

- Glossary of useful commands:
  - terraform plan -var='stack_id=ABC123'
  - aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:stack_id,Values=ABC123"
  - kubectl get nodes -l stack_id=ABC123 -o wide

Change history

- 2025-06-02: Initial draft (Ava Martinez)
- 2025-08-19: Added CI/CD pipeline template and OPA rules (Daniel Cho)
- 2026-02-14: Clarified escalation steps and added billing throttle policy (Priya Nair)
sections.heading: Before provisioning an ephemeral GPU pool

payload.page_title: Remote state segmentation and cross-account locking — primer

sections.body:
SUMMARY
-------
This document defines Redwood Inference's recommended approach for Terraform remote state segmentation across accounts and teams, and the cross-account locking model we use to prevent concurrent state mutations. It consolidates security constraints, migration steps, CI/CD integration, and an operational runbook for state-related incidents.

GOALS
-----
- Prevent accidental state corruption by enforcing strong locking for all remote backends.
- Limit blast radius by segmenting state into logical units (environment, team, application).
- Enable safe cross-account operations for customers and infra teams (e.g., dedicated GPU accounts, shared networking accounts).
- Provide a repeatable migration path from monolithic state to segmented backends.
- Integrate state operations into CI/CD with automated approvals and observability.

NON-GOALS / OUT OF SCOPE
------------------------
- Replacing Terraform Cloud/Enterprise — this doc covers S3/DynamoDB and GCS/Cloud KMS patterns used today.
- Detailed module design — see iac-module-lifecycle-and-migration-guidelines for module-level guidance.

BACKGROUND / RATIONALE
----------------------
Historically we've seen a handful of incidents caused by large, shared tfstate files: long plan/apply cycles, accidental resource deletion during state moves, and occasional lock contention. To improve safety and scalability as the infra footprint grows (multi-region GPU fleets, private deployments), we standardize on small, environment-scoped state files with strong server-side locking and cross-account IAM roles for authorized operators.

STATE SEGMENTATION PRINCIPLES
-----------------------------
- Ownership boundary: each state file should map to a clear ownership boundary (team or product), not to person-level ownership.
- Environment isolation: prod/staging/dev must never share a backend bucket prefix. Use separate state files and (preferably) separate buckets.
- Resource surface: group resources that are operated together (networking, core infra, gpu-fleet) so changes are small and reviewed.
- Naming: terraform/state/<account-alias>/<env>/<component>.tfstate
- Least privilege: IAM roles that access state backends should follow least privilege and be audited.

RECOMMENDED BACKEND PATTERN (AWS example)
-----------------------------------------
- Backend: S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) and versioning enabled.
- Locking: DynamoDB table with single-item locks using "LockID" key.
- Access model: S3 bucket owned by a central infra account; each consumer account assumes a "tf-state-access" role to read/write state for its assigned prefixes.
- Bucket policy: limit PutObject/DeleteObject to the infra role and prevent public access.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "redwood-tfstate-prod"
    key    = "terraform/state/account-gpu/prod/gpu-network.tfstate"
    region = "us-west-2"
    encrypt = true
    kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111122223333:key/abcd-1234-efgh"
    dynamodb_table = "redwood-tfstate-locks"
  }
}

SAMPLE S3 BUCKET POLICY SNIPPET
-------------------------------
- Allow only the central infra account and authorized roles from consumer accounts to Get/Put objects.
- Deny s3:DeleteObject unless requester matches an escalation role.

IAM CROSS-ACCOUNT ROLE (consumer account -> infra account)
----------------------------------------------------------
- Role name: InfraStateWriter
- Trust policy: allow consumer account's CI/CD execution role to assume
- Attached policy: limited to s3:PutObject/GetObject/ListBucket on the state prefix and dynamodb:PutItem/GetItem for the lock table.
sections.heading: Example backend block (terraform)
Example trust policy (conceptual)

sections.body:
1) Identify logical components and owners. Create a migration plan spreadsheet with old keys and target keys.
2) Ensure target S3 buckets and DynamoDB locks exist and are configured (encryption, versioning, lifecycle rules).
3) CI/CD pipelines must have access to assume the InfraStateWriter role for the target prefix.
sections.heading: Preconditions

sections.body:
1. Lock the source state by performing a no-op apply from a controlled operator machine (ensures the state is stable).
2. On a machine with the operator's AWS credentials, run:
   - terraform state pull > legacy.tfstate
   - terraform state list (inspect to confirm)
3. For each component to split:
   a) terraform state mv -state=legacy.tfstate -state-out=component.tfstate 'module.network.aws_vpc.vpc' 'aws_vpc.vpc'
   b) Upload component.tfstate to the new backend via `aws s3 cp` using the infra account role (or use `terraform init -migrate-state`).
4. Validate by initializing Terraform in the consumer workspace and running `terraform plan`.
5. Remove moved resources from legacy state once all components are verified.
6. Repeat until legacy state is empty; keep a read-only archived copy with strict retention.

NOTE: Prefer using `terraform init -migrate-state` with remote backends when possible — it performs a coordinated move with automatic locking. Manual state mv is the fallback for complex moves.

ROLLBACK AND EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
---------------------------------
- If an apply corrupts a resource, restore a previous state version from the S3 object version history to a new key suffixed with `.recovery` and re-run `terraform plan` against that file.
- If locks are stuck (e.g., DynamoDB item never cleared), follow the Lock Escalation Runbook (below) before manually deleting the lock item.

LOCK ESCALATION RUNBOOK
-----------------------
1) Verify there are no running Terraform processes in CI/CD (check recent pipeline history within last 30 minutes).
2) If none, inspect the DynamoDB lock table for the LockID entry for the key prefix.
3) Check the lock item's "Info" field to see owner identity and timestamps.
4) If owner is an active session, wait or coordinate. If the owner is stale (e.g., > 2 hours), escalate to infra-oncall.
5) Infra-oncall to annotate the lock item with a comment, and if approved, delete the item. Record the deletion in the incident tracker and notify affected teams.

CI/CD INTEGRATION
-----------------
- Pipeline practice: Do not allow direct human-initiated terraform apply in prod. All applies must flow through an approved pipeline with an approver gate.
- Plan step: terraform init; terraform plan -out=tfplan; upload plan artifact.
- Apply step: gated; performs assume-role (InfraStateWriter) and terraform apply tfplan.
- Secrets: Use KMS-wrapped Terraform variables in the pipeline. Do not store raw credentials in repo.
- Drift detection: run scheduled plan jobs nightly for prod prefixes and alert on non-empty diffs.

OBSERVABILITY AND ALERTING
--------------------------
- S3: enable object-level logging via CloudTrail and send write/delete events to an ElasticSearch index for quick auditing.
- DynamoDB: CloudWatch alarm for ConditionalCheckFailed events (indicating lock conflicts > threshold).
- CI: failed lock acquisition more than 5 times in 10 minutes triggers an oncall page.

ACCESS CONTROL AND AUDIT
------------------------
- All state write roles are required to be assumed via an OIDC-connected CI principal or a long-lived service principal with MFA enforced for human-driven actions.
- Periodic audit: quarterly review of who can assume InfraStateWriter roles; automate via IAM Access Analyzer reports.

SECURITY HARDENING CHECKLIST
----------------------------
- [x] S3 bucket encryption with KMS
- [x] Versioning enabled on buckets with MFA delete for critical prefixes
- [x] DynamoDB lock table SSE enabled
- [x] Bucket policies restricting access to infra account and named roles
- [x] CloudTrail logging of s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject
- [x] Automated retention policy for archived tfstates (7 years for compliance cases)

EXAMPLE CI PIPELINE (conceptual YAML)
-------------------------------------
- name: terraform-plan
  steps:
    - checkout
    - setup-terraform
    - assume-role: infra-state-writer
    - terraform init -backend-config=key=terraform/state/${ACCOUNT}/${ENV}/${COMPONENT}.tfstate
    - terraform plan -out=tfplan
    - upload-artifact: tfplan
- name: terraform-apply (manual approval required for prod)
  steps:
    - assume-role: infra-state-writer
    - terraform apply tfplan

OPERATIONAL OWNERSHIP
---------------------
- State namespace ownership is assigned to the team listed on the state file path. Example: terraform/state/account-gpu/prod/* -> GPU Platform team.
- Central Infra team owns the S3 bucket, DynamoDB table, and central IAM roles.
- Oncall escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-sre lead -> head of infra.

VALIDATION & TESTING
--------------------
- Test migration in a synthetic account before real move. Maintain a test harness that simulates concurrency.
- Run chaos tests that simulate lost locks and concurrent applies in staging.

FREQUENT PITFALLS AND MITIGATIONS
---------------------------------
- Problem: Long terraform plans due to large state files. Mitigation: split state and reduce resource counts per state.
- Problem: Stale locks due to CI crashes. Mitigation: implement ownership metadata and shorter TTLs with automatic alerting.
- Problem: Cross-account role assumptions failing due to trust policy drift. Mitigation: include automated integration tests that validate assume-role flows weekly.

APPENDIX
--------
sections.heading: Migration steps

sections.body:
- terraform init -reconfigure -backend-config="bucket=redwood-tfstate-prod" -backend-config="key=terraform/state/..."
- terraform state pull | jq '.' > snapshot.json
- terraform state mv -state=old.tfstate -state-out=new.tfstate "module.foo.aws_resource.bar" "aws_resource.bar"
- aws s3api get-object --bucket redwood-tfstate-prod --key terraform/state/... ./local.tfstate

CHANGELOG
---------
- 2023-08-15: Initial draft (Elena Park)
- 2024-01-10: Added CI pipeline excerpts and lock runbook (Marco Alvarez)
- 2024-10-12: Expanded migration playbook and security checklist; clarifications on assume-role flows (Sofie Nguyen)

payload.page_title: Soft Commitment Allocator and SLA Harmony — spec & runbook

sections.body:
Overview

This document defines the Soft Commitment Allocator (SCA): a control-plane component and accompanying Terraform/IaC contract that converts customer reserved commitments (monthly/annual) into operational tokenized allocations across heterogeneous GPU pools while preserving SLAs and preventing hard over-provisioning. The SCA exists to: balance cost-efficiency (oversubscription), maintain per-tenant latency SLOs, and provide a safe Terraform-based operator interface for reservations and rollback.

Background and motivation

Problem: reserved capacity contracts (Committed Capacity / Dedicated pools) are expensive to hold as hard-isolated allocations. Historically our stacks either: (a) over-provision by strictly dedicating GPUs per tenant, leading to low utilization; or (b) oversubscribe without formal bounds leading to periodic SLO violations during correlated spikes.

SCA goal: provide a repeatable, auditable mechanism to convert a financial commitment to a set of soft guarantees (min-available fraction, preemption budget, warm-pool weight) that are enforced by infrastructure controllers and reconciled in Terraform state.

High-level design

- Input: commitment record (customer_id, commitment_units/GPU-hours, region, SLA tier, start/end date, billing_bucket).
- Output: allocation profile (soft_fraction, reserved_bandwidth_egress_Gbps, preemptible_quota, warm_pool_target, tf_module_ref).
- Controllers: 1) SCA API (internal service) exposes commit -> profile conversion, 2) Allocation Operator (K8s operator) reconciles profiles to GPU pool labels and node taints, 3) Billing reconciler writes commitment consumption back into billing buckets and quota counters.

Key concepts and terms

- Soft fraction: the fraction of a GPU (or pool) that is effectively reserved for a tenant under normal operating conditions; values range (0.0, 1.0]. Example: 0.25 implies the tenant is treated as owning 25% of a node’s capacity for scheduling and warm-pool seeding purposes.
- Preemption budget: number of concurrent preemptions the tenant’s jobs are allowed per minute during global pressure before fallback to lower-tier model variants is triggered.
- Warm-pool target: number of pre-warmed sessions (kv-cache seeded or model instances loaded) to keep available in region for latency-sensitive traffic.
- Reconciliation window: periodicity at which SCA adjusts allocations (default: 5 minutes).

Operational SLOs (gold tier example)

- P99 tail latency for interactive requests: <= 220 ms (when within soft_fraction and warm_pool_target).
- Allocation reconciliation lag: 95% updates applied within 2 reconciliation windows (<= 10 minutes).
- Billing sync consistency: commitment consumption reconciled within 1 hour for invoicing accuracy (drifts > 1% trigger investigation).

Terraform / IaC contract

The SCA introduces a small Terraform module contract that customers of our infra team use to provision commitments. The module is intentionally declarative and idempotent. Example module usage: 

```hcl
module "customer_commitment_acme" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules//sca-commitment?ref=v1.2.0"

  customer_id            = "acme-corp"
  commitment_gpu_hours   = 100000
  region                 = "us-west-2"
  sla_tier               = "gold"  # bronze | silver | gold | platinum
  billing_bucket         = "enterprise-q3"
  warm_pool_target      = 8
  preemption_budget_per_min = 1
}
```

Module outputs (contract):

| name | type | description |
|------|------|-------------|
| sca_profile_id | string | internal profile id for the commitment |
| tf_commitment_ref | string | canonical ref for operator to reconcile |
| estimated_oversub_ratio | number | guidance for accounting and showback |

Terraform expectations and safety nets

1) The module must be applied in a workspace tied to a billing account. It writes a sealed commitment object to the SCA API (via the provider).
2) Applying the module without provider connectivity creates a local plan-only record and marks the commitment as "pending". The operator will not reconcile pending commitments.
3) Deletions are soft: removing the module sets an exit_date on the profile and reduces warm_pool_target over the configured ramp-down window (default: 72 hours).

Allocation algorithm (summary)

The conversion from commitment -> allocation is deterministic and parameterized per region and hardware family. In pseudocode: 

1. compute base_fraction = min(1.0, commitment_gpu_hours / region_fair_share_hours)
2. soft_fraction = clamp(base_fraction * quality_multiplier(sla_tier), min=0.05, max=0.95)
3. warm_pool_target = ceil(soft_fraction * regional_session_density * latency_weight(sla_tier))
4. preemption_budget = max(1, floor(soft_fraction * region_preempt_factor))

Quality multipliers and knobs are encoded as data in the SCA API and exposed in the Terraform module as "tuning_parameters" for platform operators.

Configuration table (defaults)

| key | default | description | owner |
|-----|---------|-------------|-------|
| reconciliation_window_minutes | 5 | How often operator reconciles active profiles | platform-allocator |
| ramp_down_hours | 72 | Warm-pool ramp-down window after a commitment is removed | platform-allocator |
| min_soft_fraction | 0.05 | Minimum soft reservation fraction | platform-allocator |
| max_soft_fraction | 0.95 | Maximum soft reservation fraction | platform-allocator |
| region_preempt_factor | 10 | Factor to compute preemption budget per region | platform-allocator |
| billing_sync_interval_minutes | 60 | Frequency of billing reconciler writes | billing |

Monitoring and signals

Primary metrics (exposed to Grafana/Prometheus):
- sca_profile_reconciliations_total (labels: region, sla_tier, status)
- sca_profile_reconciliation_duration_seconds (p95, p99)
- tenant_soft_fraction_utilization (gauge per tenant)
- warm_pool_availability_ratio (per tenant per region)
- sca_billing_drift_percentage (alert if > 1%)
- tenant_preemption_count_per_minute (alert if > preemption_budget * 2)

Alerting thresholds (initial):
- P0: sca_profile_reconciliation_duration_seconds (p99) > 180s for > 10m -> page on-call infra-scheduling
- P1: warm_pool_availability_ratio < 0.7 for gold/platinum tenants for > 5m -> notify infra-sre and tenant success
- P1: sca_billing_drift_percentage > 1.5% sustained for 2 runs -> create billing investigation ticket

Runbook: noisy-warmpool-and-preemption-spike (on-call)

1) Triage: check the SCA dashboard for region and tenant. Identify whether utility signals are elevated: (a) tenant_preemption_count_per_minute, (b) node_pressure_cpu/GPU, (c) warm_pool_restarts.
2) If warm_pool_availability_ratio < 0.6 for a gold tenant: escalate to oncall infra-scheduling, increase warm_pool_target by +2 via SCA UI (immediate) and open a fix PR to Terraform workspace to persist the change.
3) If sca_profile_reconciliations are failing: check operator logs (k8s namespace: infra-allocator). Restart operator pod(s) with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/allocator` and monitor `sca_profile_reconciliations_total` for recovery.
4) For billing drift > 1.5%: run the billing reconciler job manually: `make run-billing-reconciler PROFILE=<profile_id> --region=<region>` and inspect exported reconciliation artifact S3 path (documented in billing playbook).

CI/CD and release process for the module and operator

- Repo layout: `infra-modules/sca-commitment` (terraform module), `platform-allocator` (k8s operator + SCA API).
- Release pipeline: PR -> unit tests (go/py), terraform validate, module integration test (localkind or test-cluster), canary operator deployment to `staging` region, promote to `prod` with a controlled percent of profiles in canary mode.
- Feature flags: enable `sca_harmony_v2` via feature-flag service. All releases must include a migration plan for in-flight commitments.

Migration and backfill

When upgrading the operator or module, run the migration script to convert legacy hard reservations into soft profiles: `scripts/migrate-hard-to-soft --cutoff=2025-11-01`. Migration steps:

1) Dry-run: produce mapping of legacy reservations -> proposed soft profiles.
2) Review mapping with capacity and billing team (signoff required).
3) Run actual migration during a low-traffic window (region-specific), and monitor reconciliation and P99.

Risk analysis and mitigations

- Risk: correlated spikes may saturate soft pools leading to SLO breaches. Mitigation: pre-defined regional surge capacity buffer (10% of total pool) and automated cross-region fallback routing policy.
- Risk: misapplied Terraform changes could spike warm_pool targets. Mitigation: workspace-level policy to require `approve-by` and an automated safety check that warns when delta warm_pool_target > 50% in a single apply.
- Risk: billing drift due to short-lived test traffic. Mitigation: tag test profiles with `test:true` and exclude from billing counters; enforce by pre-apply checks.

Ownership and contacts

- Product owner: Priya Nair (serving-runtime/product)
- Platform owner: Aisha Meyer (eng-infra)
- Operator code owner: Liam Chen (runtime infra team)
- Billing reconciler owner: Marco Ruiz (finance-legal infra)

Rollout checklist (recommended phased approach)

1) Canary cohort: onboard 3 internal teams (billing, eval, docs) to SCA profiles and validate reconciliation & billing sync for 7 days.
2) Expand to 10% of committed enterprise tenants for 14 days; monitor P99 and billing drift.
3) Open enrollment for all new commitments; require signoff before migrating existing legacy reservations.
4) Full migration for old reservations after 30 days of stable metrics.

Appendix: troubleshooting snippets

- Inspect profile and recent reconciliations: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://sca.internal.redwood/api/v1/profiles/<profile_id>/reconciliations`
- Force reconciliation for a profile: `kubectl exec deploy/sca-operator -n infra-allocator -- /bin/scactl reconcile --profile <profile_id>`
- Terraform provider debug: `TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply -var-file=secrets.tfvars`

Related docs and references

- See `eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/gpu-node-lifecycle-orchestrator-and-ci-tf-pipeline.json` for node tainting patterns.
- See `eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-capacity-runway-and-auto-sinking-playbook.json` for runway calculations and safety budgets.

Change history

- 2024-08-01: initial spec drafted (Aisha Meyer)
- 2025-03-12: added Terraform module contract and reconciliation knobs (Liam Chen)
- 2025-09-15: updated rollout checklist and monitoring thresholds (Priya Nair)

End of document

payload.page_title: Declarative GPU feature flagging and IaC guardrails

sections.body:
A prescriptive pattern for managing GPU-related feature flags (scheduling toggles, kernel rollout, quantization profiles) as first-class Terraform artifacts with policy checks, CI gates, and runtime wiring. This doc defines modules, policies, rollout steps, and monitoring contracts to safely enable/disable inference features across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.
Purpose: reduce blast radius and operational toil when changing GPU runtime behavior by: (1) codifying flags in Terraform, (2) enforcing policy-as-code at merge time, (3) providing a repeatable canary + automated rollback flow, and (4) instrumenting observability for safety and cost impact.
GPU runtime changes (e.g., new kernels, mixed-precision switches, KV cache prefetch tweaks) frequently affect latency, cost, and correctness. Ad hoc toggles in code or ad hoc scripts lead to drift, lack of audit, and slow incident response. Treating flags as IaC gives us versioning, reviewability, and a single source of truth that the deployment control plane and SREs can rely on.
- Make GPU-related feature flags discoverable and auditable
- Prevent unsafe flag combinations via pre-merge policy checks
- Provide a low-friction canary rollout path with automated monitoring
- Ensure rollbacks are fast, measured, and reversible
- Keep runtime flag evaluation light-weight and decoupled from control plane

- This doc does not replace application-level feature flags (end-user UI toggles)
- Not a detailed kernel implementation guide — focus is operational control, not kernel dev

Applies to flags that change inference serving behavior or allocation semantics: kernel selection, mixed-precision enablement, prefix/KV caching modes, tenant preemption preferences, and autoscaling aggressiveness. Excludes per-request prompt-level flags and user-visible product feature flags.
High level: 1) Flags are defined in a central Terraform module (gpu_flag). 2) Each environment (prod/dedicated/staging/private) consumes the module and sets values in environment-specific tfvars tracked in Git. 3) A GitHub Actions pipeline runs policy-as-code (OPA checks) + integration canaries (lightweight smoke tests) on PRs. 4) Runtime path: serving control plane reads the consolidated flag state from an immutable configuration store (S3/GCS) generated by terraform apply and served by a read-optimized metadata service. 5) Telemetry tags on inference traces annotate which flags were active.
Recommended Terraform module layout and usage (example):

Module: modules/gpu_flag/main.tf

```hcl
variable "name" { type = string }
variable "enabled" { type = bool }
variable "rollout_percent" { type = number, default = 100 }
variable "owner" { type = string }
resource "redwood_infra_flag" "this" {
  name = var.name
  enabled = var.enabled
  rollout_percent = var.rollout_percent
  metadata = { owner = var.owner }
}
output "flag_id" { value = redwood_infra_flag.this.id }
```

Example usage in env overlay (env/prod/main.tf):

```hcl
module "kv_cache_prefetch_v2" {
  source = "../../modules/gpu_flag"
  name = "kv_cache_prefetch_v2"
  enabled = true
  rollout_percent = 10
  owner = "serving-runtime-team"
}
```

Notes: - All flag names are lower_snake_case and must include a component prefix (e.g., serving_kernel_*, cache_*). - Use rollout_percent to perform percentage canaries at the traffic router layer (see rollout procedure).
Pre-merge checks (run in CI):
- OPA/rego rules ensure: no conflicting flags enabled simultaneously (e.g., kernel_x_v2 + kernel_x_safe_mode), rollout_percent in [0,100], owner is non-empty, and any flag that reduces isolation requires an approved exception.
- tfsec/static analysis verifies there are no secrets in tfvars.
- Integration smoke: a lightweight canary job runs the serving smoke harness against a staging namespace with the new flags applied.

Example Rego rule (human readable):
- Deny if rollout_percent > 0 and enabled == false (misconfigured semantics).
- Deny if name contains "private_" and target environment != private.
1) Create feature-flag TF change in a branch targeting the appropriate env overlay (e.g., env/prod). 2) Open PR with 'flag: <name>' label. 3) CI runs OPA checks + staging smoke tests. 4) Once CI passes, merge to main. 5) Terraform apply runs in GitOps runner and writes a new flags manifest to stable bucket (s3://redwood-config/flags/<env>/<timestamp>.json). 6) Router reads manifest and begins rollout by evaluating 'rollout_percent' (deterministic hashing on tenant id) and activating the flag for the first X% of tenants. 7) Observe for 1h: latency P95, error rate, cost per request, and qualitative QA checks. 8) If metrics breach thresholds (see guardrail thresholds), automatically trigger rollback-conductor to revert the tf change or set rollout_percent back to previous value.

Guardrail thresholds (example):
- latency_p95 increase > 18% over baseline -> alert
- request_error_rate increase > 1.0 percentage point -> alert
- cost_per_token increase > 12% -> alert

Automated rollback policy: the monitoring job can open a hotfix PR that sets the flag back to the previous stable tag and auto-merge under an emergency policy if SRE approves.
- GitHub Actions pipeline jobs: validate, opa_check, smoke_canary, plan, apply (apply runs only in main branch via runner with least-privilege service account).
- Example job fragment:

```yaml
jobs:
  opa_check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: opa test ./policy -v
  smoke_canary:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./ci/smoke_canary.sh --env=staging --flag-manifest=./out/flags.json
```

- Secrets and cloud creds: restrict terraform apply runner to dedicated CI machine with ephemeral creds and narrow IAM role: flags:Write to config-bucket, read-only on infra-state, no admin on compute resources.
- The serving control plane uses a read-only manifest derived from Terraform outputs. Manifests are versioned and immutable (content-addressed).
- Runtime evaluation code is simple: lookup flag_name -> {enabled, rollout_percent, metadata}. Hash tenant_id % 100 < rollout_percent -> enabled for tenant.
- Flag evaluation must be non-blocking and default to safe state (disabled) if manifest is unreachable.
- Telemetry: attach flag_version and active_flag_list as tags to traces and span logs to enable post-hoc rollback/traffic-slicing analysis.
Required metrics and dashboards:
- Flag rollout dashboard: flag name, version, rollout_percent, active_tenants_count, applied_regions
- Safety signals: latency_p50/p95/p99 by flag_version, error_rate by flag_version, cost_per_token by flag_version
- Canary healthcheck SLO: smoke_canary must succeed at > 99% per 5m window during rollout

Alerting playbook:
- SEV1 if latency_p95 increase > 30% and > 5% tenants affected -> paging SRE and Serving Runtime owner
- SEV2 for cost regressions > 25% -> notify FinOps and runtime owner
- All alerts should include: flag name, manifest version, tf commit hash, link to PR and runbook.
Flag ownership matrix:
- Definition/Module ownership: eng-infra/Terraform team (primary)
- Runtime wiring and router gating: serving-runtime team (primary)
- CI & policy automation: eng-ci team (primary)
- Emergency rollback conductor: on-call SRE for serving-runtime (primary)

Contacts: aisha.patel@redwood.ai (module lead), ethanc@redwood.ai (OPA & CI), marta.r@redwood.ai (runtime), oncall-serving-runtime@pagerduty.com
For existing ad-hoc flags: 1) Inventory -- run a 2-week discovery job scanning repos and runtime manifests. 2) Create mapping PRs that produce equivalent Terraform gpu_flag resources with rollout_percent set to 0. 3) Run smoke tests and increment rollout_percent in small steps. 4) Deprecate inline toggles and add a blocking pre-merge OPA rule that denies direct changes to runtime flag endpoints without corresponding tf change.

Backfill schedule example: Week 1: inventory and mapping, Week 2: create tf modules and PRs (rollout_percent=0), Week 3-6: staged rollouts and deprecation of old toggles.
Quick rollback steps: 1) If a severe regression is detected, run: `terraform -chdir=env/prod plan -var 'kv_cache_prefetch_v2.rollout_percent=0' && terraform -chdir=env/prod apply -auto-approve` (GitOps runner will prefer hotfix PR flow). 2) If apply is blocked, run the emergency API: `curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/flags/<flag>/override -d '{"enabled":false}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'` (requires on-call SRE token). 3) After rollback, create a postmortem and tag the PR with 'incident:flag-rollout'.
- All flag changes must be auditable via Git history and bucket manifest versions. - Sensitive flags (those that affect tenant isolation or data residency) must be marked with metadata.sensitivity = "high" and require an approved security exception before enabled in non-private envs. - Terraform state for flag modules is stored in the same backend as infra state but with a separate key prefix and read ACL restricted to infra service accounts only.
Conflict detection Rego pseudo-rule: `deny[msg] { input.flag1.enabled == true; input.flag2.enabled == true; msg = sprintf("%v conflicts with %v", [input.flag1.name, input.flag2.name]) }`

Sample flags table (informal):
| flag_name | component | default | owner | sensitivity |
| serving_kernel_x_v2 | serving-runtime | false | serving-runtime | medium |
| kv_cache_prefetch_v2 | cache | false | storage-team | low |
| mixed_precision_global | runtime | true | serving-runtime | low |

- RFC: Flag-as-IaC proposal (internal RFC link)
- Serving Runtime rollout API docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-flag-eval.json
- CI templates: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/flag-ci-templates.json
- Pilot with two low-risk flags (kv_cache_prefetch_v2, serving_kernel_x_v2) in staging within 2 sprints.
- Add OPA policies to the central CI pipeline and enforce on all infra repos.
- Schedule a runbook game-day with SRE and serving-runtime to exercise automated rollback.
This pattern intentionally prioritizes auditability and small-step rollouts over speed. For emergency patches we keep an approved escape hatch documented in the runbook_snippets. Please send implementation questions to the owners listed above.

payload.page_title: Edge GPU Node IaC patterns and network security constraints

sections.body:
Summary:
This document captures recommended Terraform/IaC patterns and network-security constraints for deploying 'edge' GPU nodes (colocated, partner data centers, or cloud-based regional edge zones) that will join Redwood's inference fleet. It focuses on repeatable module patterns, secure network topology options, CI/CD validation steps, and a short runbook for emergency isolation and rollback. The guidance is aimed at infra engineers and platform owners who will provision, maintain, and operate GPU instances outside Redwood's primary cloud accounts.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: provide a canonical, auditable pattern so edge GPU deployments are consistent, secure, and compatible with Redwood serving runtime and autoscaling.
- Scope: Terraform modules, account-level guardrails, network ACLs and firewall recommendations, bootstrapping CI jobs, image signing checks, and emergency isolation steps.
- Out of scope: on-host model packaging and customer-specific application configuration (covered by eng-serving-runtime docs).

Goals and constraints:
1) Security-first: least privilege access, mandatory private connectivity back to control plane for telemetry, and strict egress controls.
2) Observability: node-level metrics, agent heartbeat, and log forwarding to central observability endpoints.
3) Deterministic bootstrapping: a single-API compatible node image (golden image) with signed artifacts and health checks.
4) Reproducible IaC: standard Terraform module inputs, versioned module registry, and test harness for plan/apply validation.
5) Network resilience: explicit fallback for cross-region outages and fast circuit-breaker isolation.

Ownership and contacts:
- Module owner: infra-iac team (primary: @Maya Patel)
- Networking reviewer: cloud-networking team (lead: @Ethan Ross)
- Security approver: security-and-compliance (lead: @Lina Gomez)
- Oncall for edge node incidents: eng-sre oncall rotation

High-level topology patterns (3 supported patterns)
1) Private-VPN Peered Edge (recommended)
- Edge node in partner datacenter or cloud edge zone connects via an IPSec VPN to a dedicated Redwood transit VPC.
- CIDR allocation: each customer edge site uses /26 for control plane endpoints and /24 for worker nodes.
- NAT: no public egress from worker subnet; egress proxied through a managed NAT/egress gateway for updates.
- Use-case: partners that cannot support AWS Direct Connect but allow VPNs.

2) Dedicated VPC with PrivateLink to Control Plane
- Edge resides in its own VPC with PrivateLink endpoints exposing control plane APIs and observability endpoints.
- Security: tighter, supports AWS PrivateLink-style setups where VPN is not allowed.
- Use-case: cloud-edge zones and strategic partner integrations.

3) Public-assist with Strict Egress and mTLS (least preferred)
- Minimal private networking; worker instances reach control plane APIs over the public internet using mTLS client certs and egress allowlist.
- Egress must be via a managed egress proxy with request-level auditing.
- Use-case: true edge locations that cannot support IPSec and where throughput/latency constraints are strict.

Terraform module interface (summary table)
- Module: redwood_edge_gpu_node
- Inputs (required): region, site_id, node_pool_id, instance_type, gpu_type, image_id, control_plane_endpoint, vpn_psk_secret_arn, allowed_egress_cidrs
- Inputs (optional): spot_preference, dedicated_host, ssm_enable, syslog_forwarder_endpoint
- Outputs: instance_ids, subnet_ids, vpn_connection_id, bootstrap_status_url

Example usage (Terraform snippet):
```
module "edge_gpu_pool_sfo1" {
  source = "git::https://git.redwood.internal/infra/modules.git//redwood_edge_gpu_node?ref=v1.3.0"

  region                 = "us-west-2"
  site_id                = "sfo1-colocat"
  node_pool_id           = "edge-gpu-pool-01"
  instance_type          = "g5.4xlarge"
  gpu_type               = "nvidia-a100" # canonical mapping in module
  image_id               = var.gpu_golden_image
  control_plane_endpoint = "vpn-control.redwood.internal"
  vpn_psk_secret_arn     = aws_secretsmanager_secret.edge_vpn.arn
  allowed_egress_cidrs   = ["10.0.0.0/16"]
}
```

Network security constraints (required guardrails)
- No direct inbound public SSH to worker nodes; all admin access via bastion with session recording.
- Control plane egress ports: 443, 8443 (API), 123 (NTP) only.
- Health check and metrics ports: 9100 (node exporter) and 9000 (agent) must be reachable from observability collectors only.
- Use mutual TLS for control-plane API; client certs rotated quarterly.
- Block outbound access to known malicious IP ranges and disable IPv6 where partner facilities do not support it.

Image and bootstrap hardening
- Golden image must be built via CI pipeline with reproducible Packer templates.
- Image artifacts signed using internal image-signing key; instance boot scripts verify signature before starting runtime processes.
- Mandatory host-level compliance checks during cloud-init: disk encryption policy, sysctl hardening, container runtime cgroup v2.

CI/CD pipeline checks (recommended steps)
1) terraform fmt/validate + tfsec and checkov static scans
2) terraform plan with remote state using a test account or terraform-spoke workspace
3) plan approval gate: automated policy checks (OPA/Rego) for allowed instance types, allowed regions, and egress rules
4) image artifact verification: assert image signature and image provenance metadata
5) staged apply: create a single node in 'test' site -> smoke test connecting to control plane -> collect metrics for 10 minutes -> continue rollout

CI snippet (example GitHub Actions matrix):
```
name: edge-iac-validation
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Run fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check
      - name: Tfsec
        run: tfsec .
      - name: Tf plan
        run: terraform plan -out plan.tfplan
```

Testing and preflight checklist
- Unit tests for Terraform modules (terratest) must pass.
- Network simulation: simulate control-plane latency and verify reconnection/backoff behavior.
- Bootstrapping test: a fully provisioned node must register to the fleet management API within 3 minutes.
- Telemetry test: metrics must be visible in the central Prometheus within 2 minutes of registration.

SLOs and operational thresholds (edge node)
- Node boot/register time: 95% under 3 minutes, 99% under 5 minutes.
- Heartbeat latency: 99% messages delivered to control plane within 15s.
- Node incident MTTR: 1 hour for circuit-breaker or isolation, 4 hours for full replacement.

Runbook: emergency isolation and rollback (short)
1) Detect: alert fires when node heartbeat missing for >2x expected interval.
2) Quarantine: use IaC to apply network ACL that denies all outbound except control-plane and observability collector. Command: `terraform apply -target=module.edge_gpu_pool_sfo1.aws_network_acl.quarantine`
3) If suspicious traffic is observed, execute temporary ACL: deny_all_egress for the node subnet.
4) Replace: if quarantine fails or node unresponsive, mark node out of rotation via fleet API and trigger replacement via `terraform apply` to recreate instance (module supports recreate_on_drift flag).
5) Postmortem: record findings in /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/edge-node-incident-postmortems and tag with incident id.

Drift detection and autoscaling considerations
- Enable periodic `terraform plan` run for each site (daily) to detect drift and notify module owner.
- Autoscaling: prefer horizontal autoscaler controllers invoked by the control plane. IaC should manage node pool target sizes but not rapid scale-to-zero operations.

Cost and rightsizing guidance
- Default instance families for edge: g5.x for low-latency workloads, g5.4xlarge for throughput-first.
- When using spot/interruptible instances, maintain a mixed-pool strategy with at least 20% on-demand to satisfy SLA.

Backwards compatibility and module versioning
- Modules must follow semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Breaking changes require a migration guide in the module README and an upgrade path branch in IaC repo.

Appendix A: Example Terraform variable table
- variable gpu_type: description "GPU SKU mapping string" - type string - default "nvidia-a100"
- variable image_id: description "Golden image AMI/ID" - type string - required
- variable control_plane_endpoint: description "FQDN of control plane" - type string
- variable vpn_psk_secret_arn: description "SecretsManager ARN for VPN PSK" - type string - sensitive

Appendix B: Frequently asked questions
Q: Can we use IPv6 for edge sites?
A: Only if the partner location advertises native IPv6 to Redwood transit and the module parameter `enable_ipv6` is set; otherwise IPv6 is disabled by default.

Q: Are GPUs allowed to pull arbitrary images from the internet?
A: No. Containers/images must be pulled from approved registries or mirrored to a private artifact registry that enforces scanning and signing.

Related documentation and links:
- IaC module lifecycle: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/iac-module-lifecycle-and-migration-guidelines.json
- Cross-account VPC runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/cross-account-gpu-vpc-modules-and-network-runbook.json
- Edge incident postmortem template: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/edge-node-incident-postmortems.json

Change log:
- 2024-09-15: Draft created by Maya Patel.
- 2024-11-05: Added CI/CD validation and example snippets (review by Ethan Ross).
- 2025-01-10: Security guardrails updated to require mTLS and image signing (review by Lina Gomez).

Action items and next steps:
- [ ] Module PR: implement `quarantine` network ACL resource and add plan-time OPA checks. Owner: Maya Patel. Target: 2025-01-31.
- [ ] Add terratest coverage for Golden image verification. Owner: eng-ci-cd. Target: 2025-02-14.

payload.page_title: GPU GitOps guardrails and network assertions

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook documents the GitOps-oriented guardrails and automated network assertions we use to safely provision and modify GPU fleet resources and related networking (VPCs, subnets, route tables, egress NAT, and security groups). The goal is to make each merge to infra repositories produce an auditable, testable plan that enforces tenant isolation, egress constraints, and preflight capacity checks before any cloud change is applied.

Why this exists

- GPU infrastructure changes are high-risk: machine types, quotas, and egress rules can cause region-wide outages or unexpected billing.
- GitOps provides a reliable single source of truth, but needs automated policy checks (assertions) to prevent unsafe merges.
- This doc binds together Terraform module conventions, CI test patterns, OPA/conftest policies, and runtime checks against Canary tenants.

Scope

Applies to changes in the following repositories and module namespaces:
- infra/gpu-* (terraform modules for pools, node groups, launch templates)
- infra/networking/* (VPC, subnet, NAT gateway, route options used by GPU clusters)
- infra/gitops-clusters (cluster manifests that reference GPU node pools)

Out of scope: single-tenant customer config stored in customer repos (customer-sensitive templates require the private deployment playbooks).

High-level guardrail patterns

1) Declarative assertions (pre-merge)
- Enforce minimal required labels on GPU pools: owner-team, cost-center, sla-tier.
- Prohibit wide-open security groups attached to GPU node pools.
- Require explicit egress policy for evaluation jobs (allowed egress CIDR list).

2) Capacity & quota checks (pre-apply and pre-merge)
- Require a "quota-budget" file for any pool increase > 20% of region capacity.
- Simulate spot/preemptible drain impact via the GPU capacity simulator test (see CI steps).

3) Network safety assertions
- Prevent changes that remove cross-account VPC peerings used for monitoring/backup.
- Disallow changes that expand public subnet allocation for GPU subnets without an approved security review.

Detailed CI pipeline pattern

This is the recommended GitHub Actions pipeline for infra modules touching GPU or network resources:

1) lint (fast)
- terraform fmt -check
- tflint --module
- check-docs-snapshot.sh

2) plan + snapshot
- terraform init -backend=false
- terraform plan -out=plan.binary
- terraform show -json plan.binary > plan.json

3) policy checks (conftest/OPA)
- conftest test plan.json --policy ./policies/gpu-network
- return non-zero on any policy violation

4) unit/simulation tests (terratest / in-memory simulator)
- go test ./test/sim -run TestGpuCapacitySimulator -v
- simulators validate eviction rate, warm-pool size impact, and preemption hedging

5) integration (optional gated)
- apply to sandbox account using a short-lived run (feature-branch environment)
- run smoke checks against Prometheus/alertmanager endpoints that assert new nodes join and health checks pass

6) human approval required for large changes
- If the diff increases target_pool_size by > 200 GPUs or egress CIDR widens, require the security-reviewers group approval.

Policy examples (human-readable)

- Block: any security_group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 tcp:22 attached to gpu_node_group resource.
- Block: subnet.az_count < 2 for a production GPU cluster.
- Allow only approved AMI IDs for GPU nodes (map maintained in modules/ami-allowlist.yaml).

Sample conftest policy (text description)

We use Rego policies with conftest. Example checks:
- rego/gpu/allowlist.rego: verifies instance types are in the supported list (A100, H100, etc.).
- rego/network/egress-CIDR.rego: enforces that any new egress CIDR intersects the allowed-egress list in org-config.

Preflight assertions run by the CI (commands)

- Generate plan JSON
  terraform init -backend=false && terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
- Run policies
  conftest test plan.json --policy ./policies || exit 1
- Run simulator tests (requires Go + docker)
  go test ./test/sim -run TestGpuCapacitySimulator -v || exit 1

Runtime assertions (post-apply)

After apply (automated via the CD process), a short-lived probe validates that the change behaves as expected. The CD job will:
- Wait for new nodes to register with the cluster for up to 15 minutes.
- Run the following checks (examples):
  - kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=<new-pool> --no-headers | wc -l >= expected_count
  - curl -fsS http://prometheus-api:9090/api/v1/query?query=up{job=\"gpu-exporter\",pool=\"<new-pool>\"} and ensure > 0 results
  - Check NAT gateway allocation: aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=tag:pool,Values=<new-pool>

Failure handling and automatic rollback

- If any runtime assertion fails, the CD job marks the deployment as failed and triggers an automated rollback to the previous terraform state using the saved state snapshot.
- Alerting: page oncall-sre and open an incident in PagerDuty with runbook link. The CD job should annotate the PR with failure reasons and links to logs.

SLOs and thresholds to enforce in assertions

| Assertion | Warning threshold | Failure threshold | Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Node join latency | 60s | 300s | mark rollback after 300s; create ticket on warning |
| Pod scheduling success rate (first 2m) | 95% | 80% | rollback and scale back pool |
| Egress connection success to monitoring endpoints | 98% | 90% | open incident and isolate network change |

Operational runbook (short)

1) On failed CI policy check:
   - Click the failed check and inspect conftest output.
   - If the violation is legitimate, revert the change and create an RFC describing the exception.

2) On apply failure / runtime assertion fail:
   - CD job will try to rollback automatically. Follow the CD job link and confirm rollback completed.
   - If rollback failed, escalate to infra-oncall and run the manual rollback procedure (apply previous state snapshot and force-replace nodes).

3) For suspected network regressions:
   - Run a targeted traceroute from the failing node to the monitoring endpoint.
   - Verify route tables and NACLs in the account: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=<vpc-name>

Developer guidance for creating safe module changes

- Small, isolated diffs are safer. Prefer adding a new module version that exercises the new behavior in a sandbox account rather than altering the production module directly.
- Add a unit test in test/sim for any capacity change logic. The GPU capacity simulator must exercise at least 3 preemption scenarios.
- Add a policy comment in policies/README.md if you need to request a policy exception. Track exceptions in the exceptions.csv with an owner and expiration.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owners: infra/gpu-team (oncall rotation: infra-gpu-oncall).
- Secondary owners: infra/networking-team.
- Security reviewers: security-cloud (required for egress widening or public subnet changes).

Related pages

- infra/terraform-and-iac/gpu-provisioning-immutable-state-and-disaster-recovery (for state snapshot procedures)
- eng-infra/runbooks/preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook (detailed step-by-step rollback)

Appendix: quick checklist for reviewers

- Does the plan avoid introducing permissive security groups?
- Does the plan include an explicit quota-budget entry for pool size increases?
- Are AMI and kernel versions in the allowlist?
- Has the change been exercised in a sandbox with the simulator tests passing?
- Is a security reviewer included if required?

If the answer to any checklist item is no, request changes and do not merge.

Document history

- 2024-04-12: created by Daniel Kim.
- 2024-07-09: added conftest policies and sample rego references (review by Aisha Patel).
- 2025-01-15: clarified runtime assertion thresholds and automated rollback behavior.

End of document.

payload.page_title: Fleet Canary Allocator Terraform Module and Runbook

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the design, Terraform module interface, CI/CD integration, and on-call runbook for the Fleet Canary Allocator: a small control-plane component that performs safe, SLO-driven gradual rollouts of allocation rules and GPU placement policies across heterogeneous GPU pools. The primary goal is to minimize blast radius for policy changes that affect tenant placement, preemption behavior, and burst capacity while keeping rollout automation auditable and reversible.

Why this exists

- We frequently change allocation policies (fair-share weights, priority buckets, spot fallback policy) and kernel/runtime flags that affect performance and preemption probability.
- A full fleet-wide change can cause regressions in latency/SLOs or tenant evictions if there is an unseen interaction with topology or the scheduler.
- Existing canary tooling targets provisioning; this module ties Terraform-driven policy changes to a staged placement rollout and provides an automated fallback and remediation path.

Scope and Goals

- Provide a Terraform module that deploys the Canary Allocator with opinionated defaults for Redwood GPU fleets.
- Expose variables for canary population sizing, ramp cadence, health checks, and failover targets.
- Integrate with the CI/CD canary pipeline so every policy change is gated by plan-time validation and short-circuitable rollout.
- Offer an on-call runbook covering detection, mitigation, and postmortem guidance for a failed canary.

Non-goals

- Replacing core scheduler logic: the allocator orchestrates placement policy application and traffic-shifting, but does not modify underlying scheduler algorithms.
- End-user tenant-level billing decisions.

High-level design

Components

1) Canary Allocator Controller (K8s Deployment)
   - Watches Policy CRDs and orchestrates staged application across target GPU pools.
   - Uses allocation tiers: canary, ramp, steady, reserve.
   - Exposes REST endpoints for manual pause/rollback and metrics (Prometheus).

2) Policy CRD (YAML)
   - Holds allocation policy payload (weights, priority buckets, preemption thresholds, KV cache affinity tags).

3) Terraform Module
   - Encapsulates K8s manifests, RBAC, service account IAM bindings, and optional external canary targets (CloudRun Lambda).

4) CI/CD Integration (Buildkite + TF Cloud workspace)
   - Plan + policy linting stage -> canary deployment stage -> automated health gate -> ramp stage -> steady stage.

Allocation tier semantics

- canary: 1–3 nodes or 0.5–2% of active capacity, whichever is larger. Short window (10–30 minutes) for quick validation.
- ramp: incremental increase to 10–25% over configurable period (1–24 hours) with continuous health checks.
- steady: remaining production capacity.
- reserve: preconfigured fallback capacity identified at plan time for immediate traffic shift on failure.

SLOs and health checks

- Primary SLOs to monitor during canary: 95th percentile token latency (SLO delta threshold +20%), error rate (>= 5xx) increase > 0.5% absolute, tenant eviction rate delta > 1 per hour, and queue-time percentiles.
- Checks performed every 60s. If any check crosses threshold for 3 consecutive samples, the health gate fails.

Terraform module interface (example)

Note: this is a high-level excerpt — full module lives in the terraform registry module path referenced below.

Required variables (Terraform var names)

- cluster_name (string) — k8s cluster to deploy into
- namespace (string) — namespace for controller and CRDs
- canary_capacity_pct (number) — target percent for initial canary population (default 1.0)
- ramp_duration_minutes (number) — time to reach ramp target (default 120)
- health_checks (list) — list of named health checks to run (default ["latency_p95", "error_rate"])
- reserve_target (string) — label selector for reserve pool nodes
- iam_bindings (map) — optional map of IAM roles to service-account emails

Outputs

- controller_service_endpoint (string)
- canary_policy_crd_id (string)

Sample terraform usage (snippet)

module "fleet_canary_allocator" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules.git//fleet-canary-allocator"
  cluster_name = var.k8s_cluster_name
  namespace = "fleet-allocator"
  canary_capacity_pct = 1.5
  ramp_duration_minutes = 180
  health_checks = ["latency_p95","error_rate","eviction_rate"]
  reserve_target = "gpu-pool:reserve-v2"
}

Policy CRD example (extracted)

apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
kind: AllocationPolicy
metadata:
  name: preempt-threshold-adjust-2026-02
spec:
  policyPayload:
    preemption_threshold: 0.65
    priority_weights:
      enterprise: 1.0
      standard: 0.7
    kv_cache_affinity: ["tenant-critical"]
  rolloutStrategy:
    tiers: ["canary", "ramp", "steady"]
    canaryTargetSelector: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone==us-west1-b"
    rampSteps: 4
    stepDurationMinutes: 45

CI/CD flow (Buildkite)

1) pre-commit: policy linting (policy-schema-validator).
2) plan: terraform plan in isolated workspace. Policy diff is recorded as structured JSON artifact.
3) canary-deploy job: applies the policy as a canary-only CRD.
4) canary-health-gate: queries Prometheus metrics + log-based signals for the canary window. If pass, continue; if fail, mark pipeline and trigger rollback job.
5) ramp-job: incrementally expands target selectors per rampSteps.
6) promote-job: marks policy as steady and writes rollout metadata to audit log (CloudSQL).

Observability and dashboards

- Prometheus metrics exposed by controller: allocator_canary_state{tier=}, allocator_health_check_failures_total, allocator_rollout_progress_percentage.
- Grafana dashboard panels: Canary Latency Delta, Canary Error Spike, Eviction Delta Heatmap (by tenant), Node-level GPU Utilization (canary vs baseline).
- Alert rules (examples):
  - ALERT CanaryLatencyRegression
    IF canary_latency_p95_delta > 0.20 FOR 2m
    LABELS {severity=\"critical\"}
    ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Canary latency P95 regression >20%\"}

Runbook: on-call steps for failed canary

1) Detect
   - Pager triggers via CanaryLatencyRegression or CanaryErrorSpike alerts.

2) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   - Identify policy CRD name and canary selector: kubectl -n fleet-allocator get allocationpolicy -o wide
   - Query controller logs: kubectl -n fleet-allocator logs deploy/fleet-canary-allocator --since=15m | tail -n 500
   - Check metrics: run promql queries for allocator_* metrics and tenant evictions.

3) Immediate mitigation (if health gate failed)
   - Pause rollout: curl -X POST $CONTROLLER_SERVICE_ENDPOINT/api/v1/rollouts/{policy}/pause
   - Shift traffic off canary: kubectl label nodes -l <canary-selector> canary.offload=true (label is interpreted by node router to deprioritize)
   - If pause attempt fails or errors persist, run emergency rollback:
     terraform workspace select <canary-workspace> && terraform apply -var 'force_revert=true' -auto-approve

4) Post-mortem and permanent fix
   - Open incident ticket with labels [canary, allocator, gpu-fleet] and assign to owner team.
   - Collect artifacts: terraform plan diff JSON, policy CRD YAML, controller logs (last 2h), kube events (kubectl get events --all-namespaces --since=2h).
   - Run regression test harness (see infra/eval-harness) against the exact canary node topology to reproduce.

Safety and guardrails

- All Terraform changes that create/modify AllocationPolicy CRDs must run in a dedicated TF Cloud workspace with run-time approval configured.
- The module enforces an explicit reserve_target parameter; disallow empty reserve targets in production environments.
- Canary window default is short and must be explicitly extended in PR body to be allowed beyond 4 hours.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-infra (allocator-service subteam) — oncall rotation: infra-allocator@redwood.com
- Secondary owner: eng-serving-runtime for interactions with scheduler and kernel flags

Migration plan for existing policies

1) Audit all current AllocationPolicy records (kubectl get allocationpolicies --all-namespaces -o yaml).
2) Create a TF import mapping file (tools/imports/canary-policy-imports.tf) to import existing policy state into TF state.
3) Run a dry-plan in the module workspace to validate no-op diffs.

Security and IAM

- Controller runs under a dedicated service account with least privilege. Module creates IAM binding only when iam_bindings variable is provided.
- All controller endpoints are behind mTLS and authenticated via K8s service account tokens issued from the cluster OIDC provider.

Operational playbook for upgrades

- Module semantic versioning: major bump required for any backward-incompatible CRD change.
- Canary for allocator controller itself: deploy controller change using the same module but use the allocator to rollout controller changes as well (self-hosted canary).

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets

- Pause rollout:
  curl -s -X POST $CONTROLLER_SERVICE_ENDPOINT/api/v1/rollouts/my-policy/pause \n    -H \"Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)\"

- Query canary health summary (PromQL):
  sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"inference\",outcome=\"error\"}[5m])) by (tenant) / sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_count{job=\"inference\"}[5m]))

- Force revert via TF (last resort):
  terraform workspace select canary-my-policy && terraform apply -var 'force_revert=true' -auto-approve

Where the module lives

- Repo: github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules (path: modules/fleet-canary-allocator)
- Design doc: linked internal design doc id: infra-allocator-design-2025-09 (refer to related_pages above)

Notes and open questions

- Should the allocator be able to operate across clusters (multi-cluster canary)? Current MVP is single-cluster.
- Does the allocator need to surface tenant-level rollback recommendations (per-tenant fallbacks)? Next-phase roadmap item.

If you are implementing or changing allocation policies, follow the CI/CD flow above and schedule a shadow run against a synthetic traffic profile before opening a production rollout.

-- Priya Natarajan, eng-infra (allocator-service)

payload.page_title: GPU rebalancer operator design and TF schema

sections.body: This document describes the design, Terraform schema, CI/CD gating, and operational runbook for the GPU Rebalancer Operator — a control-plane component that automatically rebalances heterogeneous GPU pools across regions, instance types, and tenant slices to preserve SLOs (latency, throughput, cost) while minimizing disruption.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Goals:
  - Maintain per-tenant placement SLOs (95th latency < 120ms for inference class A; token/sec floor for batch workloads).
  - Reduce hot/cold pool imbalances that cause tenant throttling or excessive preemptions.
  - Make rebalancing decisions auditable, reversible, and IaC-configurable via Terraform modules and Helm values.
  - Ensure operator changes can be safely rolled out through CI/CD canaries + perf validation.
- Non-goals:
  - Not intended to implement tenant-level billing changes (billing handled downstream).
  - Not a replacement for long-term capacity planning; it smooths short-to-medium-term skew only.
sections.heading: Goals and non-goals

sections.body:
- Control plane (k8s)
  - Rebalancer Controller (CRDs: PoolSlice, RebalancePlan, EvictionFence)
  - Decision Engine (policy engine + cost model)
  - Intent store (etcd via k8s CustomResources)
- Data plane
  - Node agents (lightweight daemon): collect utilization, drain hooks, safe-eviction handshake
  - Placement API sidecar: accepts safe-routing updates for the serving runtime
sections.heading: High-level architecture (text diagram)

sections.body:
1) Conservative, reversible actions: every move must be represented as a RebalancePlan with a TTL and explicit approve/rollback lifecycle.
2) Workload-aware moves: decisions weigh KV-cache reseeding cost, model checkpoint transfer size, and tenant prewarm state.
3) IaC-first configuration: operator policy primitives are configured and versioned in Terraform modules so infra owners can review changes via PRs.
4) Safety nets: circuit breakers (max concurrent live evictions per AZ), probe-based canaries, and automatic abort on SLO degradation.
sections.heading: Key design principles

sections.body:
- PoolSlice: logical grouping (region, instance family, runtime flavor, tenant tag).
- RebalancePlan: list of intended moves, priority, estimated disruption score, and dry-run flag.
- EvictionFence: temporary hold to prevent moves for a pool during maintenance.
sections.heading: CRD summary (conceptual)

sections.body:
| Field | Type | Description | Default | Validation |
| pool_rebalancer_enabled | bool | Enable operator for the account | true | - |
| default_concurrency | number | Max live node drains per AZ | 4 | >=1 and <= 50 |
| eviction_timeout_minutes | number | Grace period for a live eviction to finish | 30 | >=5 and <= 180 |
| probe_canary_thresholds | map | Performance checks to run post-move | see example | - |

Terraform usage snippet (example values shown as HCL; include in PRs to infra repo):
module "gpu_rebalancer" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules.git//gpu-rebalancer?ref=v0.6.0"
  pool_rebalancer_enabled     = true
  default_concurrency         = 3
  eviction_timeout_minutes    = 25
  probe_canary_thresholds = {
    inference_p95_ms = 120
    embedding_throughput = 1000
  }
  iam_sa = "infra-rebalancer-sa@redwood.iam"
}
sections.heading: Terraform module schema example (text table)

sections.body:
reconciler:
  concurrency: 3
  maxEvictionsPerAZ: 2
  dryRun: false
decisionEngine:
  costModelWeightings:
    kvCacheTransfer: 0.6
    prewarmPenalty: 1.2
    crossAzTransfer: 2.0
  moveApprovalMode: "manual" # manual | auto | staged

CI/CD gating and perf validation
- Pipeline goals:
  1) Every change to Terraform module or operator manifests must pass unit tests, integration tests against a local k8s testbed, and a perf canary stage that validates key thresholds.
- Pipeline stages (high level):
  1. Lint & static checks (terraform validate, tfsec, tflint).
  2. Unit tests for decision engine logic (python/Go).
  3. Integration: deploy operator to ephemeral cluster (KinD) and run end-to-end move simulations using synthetic tenant traces.
  4. Canary perf stage: deploy to a shadow AZ (or small percentage of traffic) and run the canonical workload suite (latency, throughput, KV-cache hit recovery).
  5. Promote: if canary passes SLOs and disruption score below threshold, allow module promotion.
