payload.page_title: Causal Observability Hypothesis Lab Guide

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines a repeatable lab process for designing, instrumenting, and validating causal hypotheses about runtime behavior. It is intended for engineers and SREs who need to move beyond correlation and produce defensible, actionable conclusions about how runtime subsystems (kernel scheduler, KV cache, request router, model variants) affect SLOs, cost, and fidelity.

Goals
- Provide a minimally invasive experiment framework for production-like workloads.
- Standardize telemetry, experiment matrices, and statistical thresholds.
- Produce runbooks and artifact templates (traces, dashboards, cohort exports) that can be handed to product/ops.

Scope
- Focus: serving runtime subsystems: kernel scheduler, KV cache, batching, model-variant routing, and prefix/sequence handling.
- Not in scope: model architecture changes, upstream customer prompts, and offline training pipelines.

Owners and Roles
1) Lab Owner: eng-serving-runtime / Profiling team (primary contact: Asha Kulkarni).
2) Experiment Lead: engineer running instrumentation and experiment orchestration.
3) Data Owner: Observability team (responsible for query access and retention).
4) Oncall / Escalation: runtime-oncall@redwood (see runbooks for pager steps).

When to use this guide
- Tail-latency spikes correlated with kernel scheduler changes.
- Cost-per-token regressions that coincide with quantization/kernel rollouts.
- Suspected causal link between caching behavior and degraded throughput for specific tenant shapes.

Required telemetry and data products
- High-cardinality traces (span-level): sampler rate >= 1/100 for public prod; full traces for canary.
- Per-request SLI metrics: request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, tokens_generated, kernel_ms, queue_ms, kvcache_hit(boolean).
- Kernel-level counters: kernel_invoke_ms, kernel_queue_length, occupancy_percent.
- Cost and billing signals: token_cost_estimate_per_request.

Minimal SLOs for experiments
- Baseline SLO: p95 <= 250ms for interactive routes; p99 <= 800ms.
- Canary gating: no >5% relative increase in p95 and no >2x increase in p99 for test groups.

Telemetry table (minimum dataset)
Metric | Source | Retention | SLI mapping
-------|--------|----------|------------
request_latency_ms_p95 | Prometheus + aggregated traces | 90d (raw histograms), 365d (rollup) | p95 latency SLI
tokens_generated | App logs / usage stream | 180d | cost per token derivation
kernel_invoke_ms | kernel telemetry agent | 30d (detailed) | kernel cost attribution
kvcache_hit | runtime logs (structured) | 90d | fidelity/cold-start analysis
trace_id | zipkin/jaeger | 30d | causal trace stitching

Hypothesis design template
1) Hypothesis statement (explicit): e.g., "Enabling cold-cache prefetch reduces p99 latency for short prefix requests by >= 20% for route=/chat-compact".
2) Expected causal mechanism: describe the chain (prefetch -> less KV cache miss -> fewer kernel cold-starts -> lower tail latency).
3) Observable signals: which metrics/spans will change and direction.
4) Minimum detectable effect (MDE): numeric threshold (e.g., 20% reduction at p99).
5) Failure modes and safety checks: e.g., overall throughput drop, token-cost increase > 5%.

Experiment design checklist
- Select cohorts: use tenant hashing or route-based split. Use 10% treatment size for initial runs; scale to 30–50% for power.
- Control for confounders: time-of-day, model-variant, request-size distribution.
- Instrument additional spans: add a short-lived span around kvcache.lookup and kernel.warmup to capture warm paths.
- Set sampling rules: increase trace sampling for affected tenants during experiment window.
- Run synthetic replays (shadow) if safe to reproduce traffic shape.

Statistical rules and significance
- Primary test: two-sample non-parametric test (Mann-Whitney U) on latency percentiles; bootstrap confidence intervals for p99.
- Significance threshold: alpha = 0.05; report two-sided p-values.
- Powering: aim for 80% power to detect the MDE; if not achievable, increase treatment size or test duration.
- Multiple comparisons: control family-wise error rate when testing multiple routes/percentiles using Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg as appropriate.

Instrumentation snippets and commands
- Start a focused trace capture (developer-friendly CLI):
  rwdctl trace start --service runtime-service --filter 'route=/chat-compact and model_variant in (v1,v1-quant)' --sampler 0.1 --output run-\"kv-prefetch-2025-03\"

- Prometheus example queries (copyable):
  p95 latency by route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime-service\"}[5m])) by (le, route))
  kv cache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total[5m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_lookups_total[5m]))

- Example structured trace span (JSON example, truncated):
  {
    "trace_id": "abcd1234ef",
    "spans": [
      {"name": "kvcache.lookup", "start_ms": 1690000000, "duration_ms": 2, "tags": {"hit": true}},
      {"name": "kernel.invoke", "start_ms": 1690000010, "duration_ms": 14, "tags": {"kernel_name": "cuda-attention-v2"}}
    ]
  }

Hypothesis example: KV-prefetch probe
- Context: a rollout of an adaptive prefetch feature showed mixed latency signals. We need a causal test to prove net tail-latency benefit without cost regressions.
- Hypothesis: adaptive prefetch reduces p99 by >= 15% on short-prefix chat requests while keeping token-cost delta <= +3%.
- Steps:
  1) Canary prefetch on 10% of tenants, instrument additional spans.
  2) Run 7-day experiment (to cover daily cycle) with baseline and treatment cohorts.
  3) Collect traces for treatment and control (increase sampling to 1/20).
  4) Compute bootstrap CI for p99 and test using Mann-Whitney U.
  5) If p-value < 0.05 and effect size >= 15% with cost delta <= 3%, promote to 30% and repeat.

Data artifacts to commit
- Experiment README (short): purpose, hypothesis, dataset keys, queries, dashboards used, failure criteria.
- Trace bundles: path to zipped traces and a small sample of full trace JSONs.
- Notebook: analysis notebook (BigQuery or pandas) with code to compute p95/p99, bootstrap CI, and cost apportionment.
- Dashboard snapshot: Grafana panel JSON or link.

Canary gating and rollout policy (recommended)
1) Preflight: unit tests, microbenchmarks, and synthetic replay on staging.
2) Canary 10% for 48–72 hours with elevated telemetry.
3) Safety checks: no >5% regression on p95 and p99, no >10% increase in kernel invocation rate, token-cost delta <= 3%.
4) If passed, expand to 30% for 3–7 days.
5) If passed, promote to 100% via staged waves with monitoring runbooks active.

Troubleshooting and common pitfalls
- Confounding rollout traffic: model variants or user-agent skews can mimic treatment effects. Always stratify by model_variant and request_size.
- Sampling bias: low sampling can hide tail effects; increase sampling or use targeted full-trace capture for affected tenants.
- Metric cardinality explosion: avoid instrumenting high-cardinality labels for long retention; use sharding keys and aggregate at ingestion.

Safety, privacy, and compliance notes
- Traces may contain prompt tokens; redact or pseudonymize before exporting to notebooks. Follow data-residency policy for customer-sensitive tenants.
- For private deployments, ensure KMS authorization for trace export.

Post-experiment checklist
1) Summarize results (1-page). Include effect sizes, p-values, CI, and cost impact.
2) Runbook update: if behavior changes runtime response patterns, add/update runbook steps.
3) Backfill monitoring: add long-term dashboards for any new spans/metrics.
4) Archive artifacts: notebook, trace bundle, dashboard, and README in the experiments bucket with tagging.

Appendices
A. Experiment matrix template (CSV columns)\- experiment_id, hypothesis_statement, treatment_percent, start_ts, end_ts, route, model_variant_filter, sampling_delta, primary_metric, mde, p_value, owner, artifacts_link
\B. Quick grep commands\- Find traces containing kernel name:
  rwdctl traces grep --contains \"cuda-attention-v2\" run-\"kv-prefetch-2025-03\"
\C. Related pages and references\- Runtime anomaly hypothesis playbook: /eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-anomaly-hypothesis-and-investigation-patterns-2026\- Telemetry rollup guide: /eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/telemetry-rollup-and-sample-strategies-2026

Contact and feedback
For questions or to propose additions to this lab guide, open a PR in the eng-serving-runtime docs repo and ping #runtime-profiling on Slack.

Document history
- 2025-03-12: created by Asha Kulkarni.
- 2025-06-02: added statistical powering guidance (reviewer: Marcus Li).
- 2025-09-30: clarified canary gating thresholds and privacy redaction note (reviewer: Ellen Park).

payload.page_title: GPU reservation signal protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the GPU Reservation Signal Protocol (GRSP) — a lightweight, idempotent reservation and release signaling layer used by tenant services, the capacity allocator, and the Terraform operator that manages warm pools and reserved slices. GRSP standardizes guardrails for short-lived soft reservations, long-term commitments, and operator-driven reclamation so infra teams can reason about fairness, billing, and rollout semantics across accounts and regions.

Why this exists

- Current ad-hoc reservation calls are a source of eviction cascades, billing surprises, and terraform drift.
- GRSP provides clear signal semantics so: allocation is reversible, metrics are auditable, and TF operator manifests express intent (not imperative state).

Scope

- Applies to Redwood-managed GPU fleets and warm pools across public cloud regions.
- Affects: tenant requesters (eval jobs, CI, hosted customers), the capacity allocator service (allocator-api), and the tf-gpu-operator.
- Out of scope: spot price selection logic, model-level scheduling decisions, and edge-local offload.

Terminology

- Reservation token: an opaque string returned by the allocator to the requester. Tokens are idempotent and short-lived by default (TTL).
- Soft reservation: short TTL (default 15m) with high likelihood of preemption. Used for interactive evals/CI.
- Hard reservation: longer TTL (hours/days) with billing lock and priority. Requires commit via long-reserve API.
- Slice: an operator-managed allocation unit (set of GPUs + network egress quota) that maps to a Terraform resource when pinned.

Protocol overview (high level)

1) Request path: requester -> allocator-api -> (optionally) tf-gpu-operator to pin slice
2) Response: {\n   status: granted|deferred|rejected,\n   token: <reservation-token> (when granted),\n   ttl: seconds,\n   pool_hint: pool-id,\n   preempt_score: 0.0-1.0\n}
3) Release path: requester releases token via /reservations/release or token expires.
4) Reclamation: operator may convert a soft reservation into a reclaimable lease if under pressure, emitting events and metrics.

Core invariants (must hold)

- Idempotency: calling the same reservation request (same request_id header) must return the same token or the same definitive failure.
- Time-bounded occupancy: every granted token has an associated TTL. Renewals require a separate renew call.
- Operator determinism: tf-gpu-operator only creates Terraform resources when a token is promoted to a pinned reservation and after passing admission checks.
- Auditability: all reservation events are logged to audit-log service and mapped to billing records.

API examples
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
curl -X POST https://allocator.redwood.internal/v1/reservations -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '
{
  "request_id": "ci-5678-20250201",
  "gpu_count": 1,
  "duration_hint_sec": 900,
  "priority": "interactive",
  "egress_bytes_hint": 200000000
}
'
sections.heading: Request (short interactive reservation)

sections.body:
{\n  "status": "granted",\n  "token": "rsv::us-west-2::abc123",\n  "ttl": 900,\n  "pool_hint": "warmpool-usw2-highmem-1",\n  "preempt_score": 0.12\n}

Promotion to pinned (tenant wants a stable slice that the operator will manage):

curl -X POST https://allocator.redwood.internal/v1/reservations/promote -d '{"token":"rsv::us-west-2::abc123","commit_hours":24}'

Terraform operator contract (spec + manifest example)

Design principles for the operator: the tf-gpu-operator must treat token promotion as the only signal that creates persistent TF-managed resources. It must be reconciler-safe and tolerate duplicate events.
sections.heading: Response (granted)

sections.body:
---
apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
kind: GPUReservationSlice
metadata:
  name: demo-tenant-slice-001
spec:
  reservationToken: "rsv::us-west-2::abc123"
  gpuCount: 1
  pinned: true
  egressQuotaBytes: 2147483648
  tenantAccount: "acct-demo-1234"
  lifecyclePolicy: "auto-release-on-ttl-expiry"
  tags:
    - team:platform
    - project:ci-sandbox

Operator responsibilities

- Validate token with allocator-api before creating TF resources. If token invalid/expired, mark status=Rejected and emit event.
- Create TF module with immutable name derived from token (so promotion is idempotent).
- Annotate created TF resources with reservation-token and request_id for billing mapping.
- Support a safe conversion path: when token is released, operator adds a grace window (default 5m) before triggering TF destroy.
- Expose status fields: Ready, PendingValidation, Draining, Releasing, Errored.

Terraform module conventions

- Module must be deterministic and reference variables only (no local imperative discovery).
- Resource names must include short token-hash to avoid collisions.
- Example published module: redwood/modules/gpu-slice/aws.

SLOs and thresholds (infra-level)

- Warm pool fill fraction (warm_pool_fill_fraction): target >= 0.90 (90%) measured at 5m intervals. Alert on < 0.75 for 15m.
- Reservation request success rate (redwood_gpu_reservation_success_ratio): target >= 99.5% over 1h window. Alert on < 98%.
- Promotion-to-pinned latency: median < 60s, p95 < 180s. Alert if p95 > 300s for 3 consecutive checks.
- Reclamation false-positive rate (reservations reclaimed but still active): target < 0.1% monthly.

Metrics (prometheus names)

- redwood_gpu_reservation_requests_total{result="granted|deferred|rejected"}
- redwood_gpu_reservation_promotions_total{policy="auto|manual"}
- redwood_gpu_reservation_ttl_seconds_summary
- warm_pool_fill_fraction
- redwood_tf_operator_reconcile_duration_seconds

Monitoring and dashboards

- Dashboard: "GPU Reservations - allocator" (panels: success ratio, qps by region, average ttl, pool fill).
- Dashboard: "TF GPU Operator" (panels: reconcile latencies, error rate, pending validations).
- Alerting: Pager duty integration for operator errors where > 5% of promotions fail in 10m.

Rollout plan (safest progression)

1) Canary allocator change: enable GRSP v1 for a single internal tenant namespace (ci-sandbox) for 48h.
2) Instrument metrics & audit logging; validate idempotency by replaying historical request_ids.
3) Deploy tf-gpu-operator v1 as canary in same namespace (annotation opt-in).
4) Expand to 10% of tenants and run chaos test (simulate preemption & token expiry).
5) Full rollout if no critical regressions for 7 days and metrics meet SLOs.

Runbook: common failure modes and remediation

- Symptom: Promotion stuck PendingValidation > 5m
sections.heading: Sample CRD / operator manifest fragment (yaml)

sections.body:
1) kubectl describe gpureservationslice demo-tenant-slice-001. Check status and events.
  2) curl allocator API /v1/reservations/validate?token=<token> to see TTL and preempt_score.
  3) If token expired, ask tenant to re-request or request a manual promotion with governance approval.
  4) If allocator healthy but operator failing, restart operator pod and inspect reconcile logs: kubectl logs -l app=tf-gpu-operator.

- Symptom: Warm pool fill drops below 60%
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
1) Trigger on-call playbook for capacity runway (see /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-capacity-runway-and-auto-sinking-playbook).
  2) Temporarily increase burstable preemption threshold or enable bursting to cloud-edge pools.
  3) Notify FinOps if burst will incur >$5k/day incremental cost.

- Symptom: TF resources orphaned after token release
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
1) Verify audit-log for release event matching token.
  2) Check operator status for grace-window. If grace window elapsed and TF destroy failed, run operator repair CLI: tf-gpu-operator repair --token <token>.
  3) If failing, manually run terraform destroy with locking comments and escalate to infra-eng.

Security and billing considerations

- Tokens are bearer tokens scoped to account and should never be logged in plaintext to general purpose logs. Audit log redaction is enforced in the allocator pipeline.
- Promotion to pinned reservation triggers billing ledger entry. The operator must annotate resources with billing tags: billing:reservation, reservation_id, tenant_account.
- Long-term reservations require finance approval if commit_hours * gpu_count cost > $50k.

Developer guidance and examples

- CI jobs should prefer soft reservations with request_id set to CI_JOB_ID to enable safe retries.
- Backoff strategy: on deferred responses, clients should implement jittered exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 30s, and give up after 6 attempts (for interactive workloads).

Troubleshooting checklist for operators

- Ensure allocator API version matches operator config (GRSP_V1 vs GRSP_V2).
- Confirm Terraform state backend credentials for the workspace the operator uses.
- Check for drift: resource name collisions usually indicate operator double-apply; ensure reconcile idempotency keys are used.

Open items and future work

- Support cross-region token reservation with transparent egress balancing.
- Formal rate-limiting policy per tenant and per-org to replace current global soft-limits.
- Integration with cost-forecasting to auto-deprioritize promotions that would blow monthly budget.

Ownership and contacts

- Protocol owner: Maya Patel (infra-capacity).
- TF operator owner: Connor Liu (infra-platform).
- On-call rota: see team wiki infra/oncall. For emergencies, page #infra-pager (PD).

References

- allocator-api swagger: https://internal-api-docs.redwood/allocator
- TF operator repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/tf-gpu-operator.git
- Audit log schema: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/gpu-egress-metering-and-tenant-cost-allocator-playbook

Appendix: token lifecycle diagram (text)

1. Request -> 2. Allocator grants token (soft) -> 3a. Use token and release before TTL OR -> 3b. Promote token -> operator validates -> operator creates TF resources -> token pinned -> billing entry created -> eventual release triggers TF destroy (with grace window).

payload.page_title: Edge GPU onboarding: zero-trust IaC patterns and CI/CD runbook

sections.body:
Summary

This document describes a standardized, zero-trust IaC pattern and associated CI/CD runbook for onboarding new edge GPU pools (on-prem or cloud-edge sites). It combines Terraform modules, network guardrails, CI jobs, preflight validation, and a short operational runbook for day-0/day-1 capacity and safety checks. The goal is to make onboarding reproducible, secure, and measurable with minimal ad-hoc manual steps.

Scope

- Target environments: edge-colocated racks, partner co-lo, AWS Outposts, GCP Anthos (edge).
- Components covered: GPU node provisioning, VPC & routing, egress fencing, identity & certs, warm-pool registration, and CI/CD promotion paths.
- Not covered: tenant application-level SLO tuning, model serving configuration.

Owner and contacts

- Document owner: Alex Chen (eng-infra)
- Primary contact team: GPU Fleet & Capacity (eng-infra)
- Oncall escalation: GPU-oncall (pager) -> infra-platform-engineer -> Network-SRE

High-level design principles

1) Zero-trust first: every node authenticates with mTLS before joining control plane; no long-lived SSH keys.
2) Immutable provisioning: nodes are created with signed images and attested via node attestation service (NTAS).
3) Network minimalism: default-deny egress and explicit egress-shield for allowed telemetry and registry endpoints.
4) Safe promotion: CI/CD pipeline gates for terraform plan/apply, automated preflight, postflight smoke tests, and quarantine rollback.

Required services and modules

- Terraform modules (canonical names used in examples): tf_gpu_node, tf_vpc_gateway, tf_egress_shield, tf_kms_integration, tf_warm_pool_registration.
- Runtime services: gpu-allocator, warm-pool-registry, kv-cache-rebuilder (runtime team).
- Network components: egress-shield-proxy (HTTP+TLS), nat-gateway with egress quotas, private endpoint for control-plane API.

Preflight checklist (automated and manual)

1) IaC lint and static checks (automated)
   - terraform fmt && terraform validate
   - tflint with our policy plugin (checks module inputs, IAM least-privilege)
2) Image provenance (automated)
   - Verify image signature against KMS/HSM: cosign verify --key kms://alias/redwood-edge <image>
3) Networking & DNS (automated)
   - Validate route table entries, private link endpoints, and that egress-shield is addressable from the new subnet.
4) Identity & attestation (manual automated)
   - Confirm NTAS policy exists for new site id (site-zone tag).
5) Capacity & thermal (manual)
   - Confirm on-site power/PDUs are in the expected list and rack-level heat budget <= 85% before onboarding.

Acceptance criteria (automated smoke tests)

- Node registers with warm-pool registry within 300s after bootstrap.
- Control-plane health check: /healthz returns 200 over mTLS (mutual TLS) using node cert.
- Tokenized egress: requests to package registry succeed via egress-shield proxy; all other egress flows are blocked.
- Warm-pool metrics: available_warm_nodes >= 2 for the first 10 minutes.

Terraform example (pattern)

```
module "gpu_node" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-infra/tf_gpu_node?ref=v1.4.0"
  site_id = var.site_id
  node_count = var.node_count
  instance_type = var.instance_type
  image_signed_digest = var.image_signed_digest
  kms_key = module.kms.edge_signing_key_id
  subnet_id = module.vpc.edge_subnet_id
  tags = {
    team = "gpu-fleet"
    environment = var.environment
    site = var.site_id
  }
}

module "egress_shield" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-infra/tf_egress_shield?ref=stable"
  allowed_endpoints = var.allowed_endpoints
  zone = var.region
}
```

Terraform variables table (reference)

- site_id: string – unique human-readable site code (e.g., nyc-edge-03)
- node_count: number – initial nodes to provision (start small, 1–8)
- instance_type: string – instance or board SKU (gpu.a100-40gb)
- image_signed_digest: string – cosign digest for signed image
- allowed_endpoints: list of strings – egress targets for shield (registry, metrics, ntas)

CI/CD pipeline (Buildkite example)

- Branching model: feature branch -> infra review -> merge to staging -> integration tests -> promote to production.
- Two-stage apply: staging apply (non-production site tag) then production apply gated by owner approval and preflight green.

Example job snippet:

```
steps:
  - label: "terraform: plan"
    command: "./scripts/ci/terraform-plan.sh $BUILDKITE_BRANCH"
    agents: { queue: "infra-ci" }
  - wait
  - block: "Approve staging apply"
  - label: "terraform: apply staging"
    command: "./scripts/ci/terraform-apply.sh staging"
  - label: "smoke: onboarding checks"
    command: "./scripts/ci/onboard-smoke.sh"
    retry: 2
  - block: "Approve production apply"
  - label: "terraform: apply prod"
    command: "./scripts/ci/terraform-apply.sh prod"
```

Promotion safety gates

1) PR must have owner_team and at least two reviewers from GPU fleet and Network-SRE.
2) tflint policy violations block merge.
3) Auto-created plan is posted to the PR with cost delta estimate. Any delta > $1,000/mo must have finance review.
4) Staging apply must pass smoke tests and sit for 30 minutes to allow telemetry sampling.

Runbook: day-0 onboarding (fast path)

1) Author PR with module inputs and signed image digest. Include runbook checklist in PR description.
2) CI runs plan -> address feedback -> merge to staging.
3) Approve staging apply (oncall or owner) -> terraform apply staging.
4) Wait for node bootstrap (watch warm-pool-registry).
5) Run smoke script: ./scripts/ci/onboard-smoke.sh --site $site_id.
6) If smoke passes, wait 30 minutes and review telemetry (cpu/thermal/egress errors).
7) Approve production apply -> terraform apply prod.

Rollback and quarantine

- If nodes fail to register or repeatedly crash within first 20 minutes, run: terraform destroy -target=module.gpu_node 
- Quarantine network: apply egress-shield rule that blackholes non-control-plane traffic for the site until remediation.
- For image failures, revert to last signed digest and trigger a redeploy.

Operational alerts and SLOs

- Alert: Node registration failure spike (>3 nodes failing in 15m) -> page GPU-oncall.
- Alert: Warm-pool undersupply (available_warm_nodes < 2) -> page GPU-oncall and scale policy.
- SLO: first-node-registration <= 300s (p95) after successful terraform apply.
- SLO: no unapproved egress flows observed in the first 30 minutes.

Testing matrix (minimum)

- Unit: tflint + terraform validate + module unit tests (mocks).
- Integration: apply to staging virtual site with synthetic registry and telemetry endpoints.
- Chaos: simulate egress failure and preemption in staging to validate fallback and warm-pool resilience.

Operational notes and tips

- Prefer small batches for first rollout (1–3 nodes) when onboarding new sites.
- Use cosign image digests to avoid drift and accidental image updates during rollout.
- Keep egress whitelist tight; any new registry must be added via PR and pass security review.
- Annotate PRs with capacity-impact: low|medium|high for finance visibility.

Related documents

- See egress-shielding playbook for implementation details and firewall rules.
- See warm-pool registration API spec for registration protocol and guaranteed response codes.

Appendix: quick commands

- Local plan: TF_LOG=info terraform plan -var="site_id=nyc-edge-03"
- Validate image signature: cosign verify --key kms://alias/redwood-edge ghcr.io/redwood/edge-image@sha256:deadbeef
- Run smoke locally: ./scripts/ci/onboard-smoke.sh --site nyc-edge-03

End of document

payload.page_title: Dedicated Fleet Provisioning: Terraform Conventions

sections.body:
This page defines the canonical Terraform conventions for provisioning **Dedicated GPU fleets** (and their supporting resources) in a way that is:
- Repeatable across regions and GPU SKUs
- Safe to roll out incrementally with hard guardrails
- Observable (clear outputs/tags for downstream provisioning automation)
- Drift-resistant with clear expectations for detection and remediation

These conventions are used by Infra/Fleet and Release Engineering and are prerequisites for the Provision-to-Ready automation workflow.
sections.heading: Purpose

sections.body:
- Dedicated GPU pools (node groups/instance groups, launch templates, autoscaling)
- Pool-level networking attachments (subnets, security groups) where owned by fleet modules
- IAM/service accounts needed for node bootstrap + validation agent
- Tags/outputs required by the provisioning orchestrator and readiness control plane integration
sections.heading: Applies to Terraform used to provision

sections.body:
- Kubernetes manifests (managed in Helm charts)
- Application-level serving configuration (managed in control plane)

---
sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.body: **Principle:** one environment entrypoint, composable modules, and zero “snowflake” region copies.
sections.heading: Repository + directory structure

sections.body:
- `environments/`
  - `prod/`
    - `dedicated/`
      - `main.tf` (composes modules)
      - `variables.tf` (minimal; pass-through only)
      - `outputs.tf`
      - `versions.tf` (provider + Terraform version)
      - `regions/` (thin region overlays)
        - `us-east-1.tfvars`
        - `eu-west-1.tfvars`
- `modules/`
  - `dedicated_pool/` (top-level pool module; composes other modules)
  - `gpu_node_group/` (node group primitives)
  - `fleet_tags/` (tag standardization + validation)
  - `rollout_guardrails/` (region/SKU gating logic)
sections.heading: Recommended layout

sections.body:
- `modules/dedicated_pool`: owned by **Infra/Fleet**
- `modules/rollout_guardrails`: owned by **Infra/Fleet** with **SRE** review for safety knobs
- Provider/backend/state: owned by **Release Engineering**

---
sections.heading: Module ownership boundaries

sections.body:
- Use predictable, queryable names; avoid random suffixes unless required.
- Format:
  - Dedicated pool name: `dedicated-${var.pool_id}`
  - Node group name: `dedicated-${var.pool_id}-${var.gpu_sku}`
  - Launch template name prefix: `ded-${var.pool_id}-${var.gpu_sku}`
- If the cloud provider has name length limits, apply a stable shortener (documented in module) rather than ad-hoc truncation.
sections.heading: Resources

sections.body:
- Use `snake_case`.
- Prefix booleans with `enable_`, `disable_`, or `use_`.
- Prefer enums (strings with validation) over multiple booleans.

**Examples**
- `pool_id` (string)
- `region` (string)
- `gpu_sku` (string; e.g., `a100-80gb`, `h100-80gb`)
- `capacity_mode` (string; e.g., `dedicated`, `burst`)
- `image_channel` (string; `candidate` | `stable`)
- `image_version` (string; explicit pin)
- `enable_provision_to_ready` (bool)
sections.heading: Variables

sections.body:
- Use `locals {}` for derived values only (names, labels, merged tags).
- Locals must not hide business logic (rollout gating stays in `rollout_guardrails`).

---
sections.heading: Locals

sections.body:
**Principle:** tags are not optional. They are the join key between cloud resources, fleet automation, dashboards, and audit trails.

All resources created by fleet modules **MUST** include these tags (or their cloud-native equivalents):

| Tag key | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `redwood:service` | `gpu-fleet` | Cross-system ownership + inventory |
| `redwood:env` | `prod` | Environment boundary |
| `redwood:pool_id` | `dp-01842` | Primary lookup key for Dedicated pools |
| `redwood:region` | `us-east-1` | Routing + rollout segmentation |
| `redwood:gpu_sku` | `a100-80gb` | Capacity planning + failure heatmaps |
| `redwood:image_channel` | `candidate` | Rollout + rollback workflows |
| `redwood:image_version` | `2025.10.12-1` | Pin + forensic attribution |
| `redwood:provisioning_mode` | `provision-to-ready-v1` | Gating/automation compatibility |
| `owner_team` | `eng-infra` | Human ownership |
| `cost_center` | `inference-platform` | Finance tracking |
| `data_classification` | `internal` | Compliance routing |
sections.heading: Required tags (cost, ownership, automation)

sections.body:
- Centralize tag generation in `modules/fleet_tags`.
- Always merge tags in a predictable order:
  1) required base tags from module
  2) environment tags (e.g., `redwood:env`)
  3) user-provided `additional_tags` (restricted to a safe allowlist)

**HCL pattern**
```
variable "additional_tags" {
  type    = map(string)
  default = {}
}

locals {
  required_tags = {
    "redwood:service"          = "gpu-fleet"
    "redwood:env"              = var.environment
    "redwood:pool_id"          = var.pool_id
    "redwood:region"           = var.region
    "redwood:gpu_sku"          = var.gpu_sku
    "redwood:image_channel"    = var.image_channel
    "redwood:image_version"    = var.image_version
    "redwood:provisioning_mode"= "provision-to-ready-v1"
    "owner_team"               = "eng-infra"
  }

  tags = merge(local.required_tags, var.additional_tags)
}
```
sections.heading: Tag implementation

sections.body:
- Enforce required tags via `validation` blocks and/or module-level checks.
- Do not allow overriding the `redwood:*` namespace via `additional_tags`.

---
sections.heading: Tag guardrails

sections.body: We gate provisioning automation and new pool creation by **region** and **GPU SKU** to support staged rollouts and fast rollback.
sections.heading: Region rollout toggles (staged enablement)

sections.body:
- `enable_staged_rollout` (bool)
- `rollout_allowlist_regions` (list(string))
- `rollout_allowlist_gpu_skus` (list(string))
- `enable_provision_to_ready` (bool) — toggles integration hooks for readiness gating
sections.heading: All Dedicated pool entrypoints must support these variables
Guardrail behavior

sections.body:
- `enable_staged_rollout = true`
- Allowlist only the first rollout slice (example):
  - `rollout_allowlist_regions = ["us-east-1"]`
  - `rollout_allowlist_gpu_skus = ["a100-80gb"]`

---
sections.heading: Recommended rollout defaults (early stages)

sections.body: Dedicated fleets must pin to a golden image **channel** and **version**.
sections.heading: Golden image pinning (channel + version)

sections.body:
- `image_channel` is an operational control: `candidate` or `stable`.
- `image_version` must be explicitly set (no implicit “latest”).
- Promotion from candidate → stable must be a deliberate change (PR) and must emit audit events in the control plane (handled outside Terraform, but Terraform must carry the tags/outputs).
sections.heading: Policy

sections.body:
- The module must expose outputs used by automation:
  - `image_channel`
  - `image_version`
  - `launch_template_id` (or equivalent)

---
sections.heading: Expectations

sections.body:
Terraform is the source of truth for identifiers needed by the provisioning orchestrator.

Every `dedicated_pool` must output:
- `pool_id`
- `region`
- `gpu_sku`
- `node_group_name` (or ASG/MIG name)
- `instance_profile_arn` (or equivalent)
- `security_group_ids`
- `subnet_ids`
- `image_channel`
- `image_version`

Outputs must be stable and not include per-apply randomness.

---
sections.heading: Outputs required by provisioning automation

sections.body: To reduce blast radius during staged rollout, apply conservative defaults when `enable_staged_rollout = true`.
sections.heading: Capacity safety defaults

sections.body:
- Start with `desired_capacity = 0` for new pools unless explicitly overridden in a rollout ticket.
- Set `max_unavailable` (if applicable) to 0 for disruptive operations.
- Prevent accidental scale-ups:
  - Add a max cap variable (e.g., `rollout_max_nodes`) and enforce `max_size <= rollout_max_nodes` during rollout.

---
sections.heading: Recommended

sections.body:
- Use remote state with locking (provider-native locking where supported).
- State must be encrypted at rest.
- No local state for `prod`.
sections.heading: Remote state

sections.body:
- PR-required changes only.
- CI must produce:
  - `terraform fmt` + `terraform validate`
  - `tflint` / static analysis
  - `terraform plan` artifact for reviewers
- Applies are executed via the standard automation runner (e.g., Atlantis/CI apply job) with explicit approvals.
sections.heading: Apply workflow

sections.body:
- Any change affecting:
  - `image_channel`, `image_version`
  - security groups / ingress/egress
  - instance profile / IAM
  - rollout allowlists or guardrails
  requires review from **Infra/Fleet** and **SRE**; security-related changes require **SecOps** consult.

---
sections.heading: Approval expectations (prod)

sections.body: **Principle:** drift is expected (cloud noise, emergency ops) but must be detected quickly and remediated safely.
sections.heading: Drift detection and remediation

sections.body:
- Nightly drift plan against `prod/dedicated` entrypoints.
- Alert on:
  - tag drift (missing required tags)
  - launch template / image version drift
  - security group rule drift
  - autoscaling min/max/desired drift beyond tolerated bounds
sections.heading: Drift detection expectations

sections.body:
- Provider-managed fields (timestamps, provider default descriptions)
- Autoscaling desired capacity changes made by the approved autoscaler (if explicitly documented and handled via `ignore_changes`)
sections.heading: What is considered acceptable drift

sections.body:
- `lifecycle.ignore_changes` must be rare, documented inline, and reviewed by SRE.
- Never ignore:
  - image pinning fields
  - security group rules
  - IAM policies/attachments
sections.heading: Avoiding misuse of `ignore_changes`

sections.body:
1) Confirm whether the drift came from:
   - Approved automation (autoscaler) OR
   - Manual console change OR
   - Provider-side reconciliation
2) If manual change:
   - Prefer reverting via Terraform (make Terraform match intended state).
   - If urgent, document the emergency change and file a follow-up to re-align IaC within 24 hours.
3) If drift indicates compromised/unsafe config (e.g., SG opened broadly):
   - Treat as a security incident per on-call policy and remediate immediately.

---
sections.heading: Remediation procedure

sections.body:
These variables must exist at the `dedicated_pool` boundary and must be passed explicitly from environment entrypoints:

| Variable | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `environment` | string | `prod`, `staging`, etc. |
| `pool_id` | string | Immutable identifier; do not reuse |
| `region` | string | Cloud region |
| `gpu_sku` | string | Standard SKU string (see allowlist) |
| `cluster_name` | string | Kubernetes cluster identifier |
| `subnet_ids` | list(string) | Must be private subnets |
| `security_group_ids` | list(string) | Must include baseline GPU worker SG |
| `image_channel` | string | `candidate`/`stable` |
| `image_version` | string | Explicit pin |
| `enable_provision_to_ready` | bool | Enables provisioning hooks/tags/outputs |
| `enable_staged_rollout` | bool | Hard gate for rollout |
| `rollout_allowlist_regions` | list(string) | Required when staged rollout enabled |
| `rollout_allowlist_gpu_skus` | list(string) | Required when staged rollout enabled |

---
sections.heading: Variable catalog (minimum required)

sections.body:
- Copy-pasting modules per region (creates inconsistent behavior and missed fixes)
- Using `latest` for image selection
- Introducing per-node identifiers in tags (high-cardinality cost/metrics explosion)
- Disabling guardrails to “get it working once” in prod
- Ignoring drift broadly with `ignore_changes = all`

---
sections.heading: Common anti-patterns (do not do these)

sections.body:
- 2025-10-18: Added explicit rollout allowlist guardrail examples and clarified drift detection expectations during staged rollout.
- 2025-10-06: Introduced required `redwood:image_version` tag and pinned image policy for Dedicated pools.
sections.heading: Change log

sections.body:
- Primary: **Sahana Iyer** (Release Engineering)
- Infra/Fleet: **Vanessa Ortiz**, **Keiko Yamamoto**
- SRE escalation: **Rafael Mendes**

payload.page_title: Self-serve GPU environments: IaC patterns and CI/CD pipeline

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the recommended infrastructure pattern and CI/CD pipeline for self-serve GPU environments (dev sandboxes, feature-branch testbeds, and ephemeral eval clusters). The goal is to provide engineers a predictable, low-friction way to provision short-lived GPU environments while enforcing cost, security, and network constraints via Terraform modules and automated pipelines.

Goals
- Provide a self-serve flow for creating ephemeral GPU namespaces with minimal manual approvals.
- Enforce cost/egress/networking constraints by default.
- Keep IaC modules composable, testable in CI, and safe to roll back.
- Ensure reclamation and chargeback automation for unused resources.

Scope
- Covers single-tenant ephemeral environments (one Kubernetes namespace + dedicated fractional GPU or whole GPU allocation on the Redwood cluster).
- Integrates with: fleet-provisioner service, gpu-tenant-operator, terraform-iac modules, and the infra-ci GitHub Actions pipelines.
- Does NOT cover Dedicated (reserved) or Private on-prem installs; those follow the Dedicated onboarding flow.

Architecture (text diagram)
- Developer Git branch -> PR triggers infra-ci pipeline -> terraform plan/app against ephemeral workspace -> fleet-provisioner creates pod/VM with GPU -> gpu-tenant-operator enforces RBAC, egress fencing, and PVCs.

Provisioning flow (high level)
1. Developer opens a PR to a repository that contains an infra/preview/terraform/ directory.
2. infra-ci (GitHub Actions) runs lint, module unit tests, and a terraform plan using an ephemeral workspace (named pr-<number>).
3. On approval, infra-ci runs terraform apply to a pre-authorized ephemeral workspace; this creates an entry in the provisioning service (fleet-provisioner) and triggers a tenancy allocation request.
4. gpu-tenant-operator validates the request, allocates fractional GPU via k8s-device-plugin or attaches a whole GPU node from the ephemeral-pool autoscaler.
5. Post-provision: tagging, cost-center label injection, and a 48-hour automatic reclamation timer are applied.

Terraform module contract (summary table)
| Input | Type | Description | Default |
|-------|------|-------------|---------|
| name | string | short environment id (alphanumeric) | required |
| owner_email | string | requestor contact for reclamation notices | required |
| gpu_fraction | number | fraction of GPU to allocate (0.25, 0.5, 1) | 0.25 |
| max_hours | number | lifetime in hours before auto-delete | 48 |
| egress_profile | string | network policy profile (restricted|dev|open) | restricted |
| cost_center | string | billing tag injected into resources | infra-sandbox |

Implementation notes
- Module must validate inputs and fail-fast on invalid names or unsupported GPU fractions.
- Use remote state per-workspace (S3/GCS) using a workspace name prism: con-redwood-ephemeral-pr-<number>. Remote state keys must be namespaced to the repo and PR.
- State locking must use DynamoDB/GCS locking table to avoid concurrent applies.

CI/CD pipeline details
- Pipeline name: infra-ci/ephemeral-provision. Implemented as GitHub Actions with the following stages:
  1) terraform-format & tfsec lint
  2) module-unit-tests (go test / terratest)
  3) terraform-plan (ephemeral workspace) -> uploads plan JSON as artifact
  4) human approval (protected by CODEOWNERS) OR automatic merge if PR label 'auto-provision' present and requester is in the list of trusted devs
  5) terraform-apply -> post-apply validation (k8s smoke tests)

Sample GitHub Actions snippet (plain text)
```
name: Ephemeral Provision
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v1
      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${{ secrets.TF_STATE_BUCKET }}" -backend-config="key=${{ github.repository }}-pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}.tfstate"
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
      - name: Upload Plan
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: plan
          path: plan.tfplan
```

Reclamation and quota enforcement
- Autosweep policy: environments are created with a 48-hour TTL. Two email notifications are sent: at 24 hours (reminder) and at 12 hours prior to deletion.
- Metrics: number_of_ephemeral_envs, avg_cost_per_env_hour, reclaimation_failed_count. Alert if reclaimation_failed_count > 3 in 1 hour.
- Quota check: infra-ci checks per-user and per-team active env count prior to apply. Defaults: 3 active envs per user, 10 per team. Requests over quota are denied and require ticket to infra.

Cost controls and tagging
- Every provisioned resource must have labels: owner_email, cost_center, terraform_workspace, provisioning_request_id.
- Fractional GPU chargeback measured by gpu_fraction * time_active. Billing export job runs hourly to attribute spend to cost_center tag.

Networking & security
- Egress fencing is applied by default using the egress_profile input. Policy mapping: restricted -> deny all egress except internal APIs; dev -> allow common dev endpoints (apt, dockerhub, internal staging); open -> unrestricted but only for specific trusted groups.
- All environments use a dedicated NetworkPolicy resource and shared NAT gateways per region to consolidate egress IPs.
- Secrets: no long-lived secrets are injected by default. KMS-wrapped secrets are requested via a short-lived token from secret-broker.

Observability and post-provision validation
- Smoke checks (run as post-apply job): sample inference call against a small local model, node GPU utilization > 5% within first 10 minutes, pod readiness > 95%.
- Dashboards: Ephemeral Provisioning (panels: active envs by owner, avg creation latency, reclaimation lag, per-environment cost).

Runbook (oncall steps for reclaimation failures)
1. Alert: reclaimation_failed_count > 3 -> page oncall (infra-onsite) with ticket id.
2. Check the provisioning service (fleet-provisioner) logs: `kubectl -n infra logs deploy/fleet-provisioner` and look for provisioning_request_id.
3. If terraform destroy failed due to lock, run: `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` in the corresponding workspace after verifying no active apply.
4. If deletion blocked by finalizers (PVCs), escalate to storage team; run `kubectl delete pvc --grace-period=0 --force` only after confirming data is not required.
5. Post-incident: add failing env id to the reclaimation_failed_count dashboard and kick off a cleanup job `infra-scripts/cleanup-ephemeral --request-id <id> --dry-run` then without --dry-run once validated.

Ownership and lifecycle
- Owner services: fleet-provisioner (svc-owner: infra-provisioning-team@redwood.com), gpu-tenant-operator (svc-owner: infra-gpu-team@redwood.com).
- Module maintainers: eng-infra/terraform-team. Changes to core module must include a migration section and a canary rollout plan.

Testing & migration guidelines
- Module changes must include terratest unit coverage and a staged rollout: canary apply to `ci-ephemeral` workspace, smoke validation, then roll to prod ephemeral workspace.
- For breaking input changes, provide a compatibility shim (deprecated inputs still supported for one quarterly release cycle).

Appendix: Example Terraform input snippet (plain text)
```
module "ephemeral_env" {
  source        = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//ephemeral-gpu?ref=v1.3.0"
  name          = "pr-432-feature-x"
  owner_email   = "dev@example.com"
  gpu_fraction  = 0.5
  max_hours     = 72
  egress_profile = "dev"
  cost_center   = "feature-x"
}
```

Related decisions
- Default TTL of 48 hours set (see migration notes) after an incident where lingering dev environments caused a 22% bump in spot usage costs.

Questions & future work
- Add per-environment GPU auto-scaling for multi-stage tests.
- Integrate sandbox cost estimation into the PR UI before apply.

Contact
- For infra module questions: infra-terraform@redwood.com
- Oncall for provisioning: infra-onsite@redwood.com

Revision history
- 2024-05-18: initial draft by Maya Chen
- 2024-07-09: added CI snippet and quota rules (Ravi Patel)
- 2025-02-20: updated reclamation runbook and increased max default TTL to 72 for long-running evals (Elena Garcia)
sections.heading: Overview

payload.page_title: burst-credit-settlement-terraform-adapter-and-ci-negotiation-playbook

sections.body:
Overview

This playbook describes the design, Terraform adapter contract, CI negotiation workflow, and runbook for settling burst-credit usage across accounts and teams. It applies to Burst-Orchestrator v2 and associated billing pipelines (Credit-Settler service). The goal is accurate cross-account settlement, safe Terraform changes to allocation rules, and automated negotiation when account owners disagree about credit transfers.

Why this exists
- Burst credits are used to permit short-term GPU capacity bursts across tenant accounts. Settlement must be: auditable, idempotent, and safe to apply via IaC.
- We need a Terraform adapter that can: declaratively bind credit budgets to accounts, emit intent-only plans for negotiation, and apply agreed transfers.
- CI must coordinate multi-team approvals (owner negotiation) before state-mutation applies.

Scope and definitions
- Burst credit: transient credit bucket consumed when a tenant bursts above committed capacity.
- Allocation rule: a declarative entry in Terraform defining budget, priority, recovery-window, and settlement-policy.
- Credit-Settler: internal microservice that reconciles usage events to transfers and posts accounting entries to Billing Pipeline (internal).
- Terraform adapter (terraform-burst-credit): a small provider module that talks to Credit-Settler service via signed API.

High-level design
1) Desired state expressed in terraform-burst-credit module.
2) CI (buildkite/github-actions) runs plan and a negotiation step that posts the plan to the Negotiation Queue.
3) The affected account owners receive a review request with a diff and proposed transfers. They can Accept / Propose Counteroffer / Reject.
4) Once consensus is reached, CI triggers apply that calls Credit-Settler apply API. The apply is idempotent and produces a settlement report.

Service-level constraints and SLOs
- Credit-Settler availability SLO: 99.95% (regional).
- Plan-to-applied latency target for small changes (<5 accounts): <= 10 minutes end-to-end (negotiation excluded).
- Audit retention: settlement reports retained for 7 years in audit-bucket (GCS).

Terraform Adapter: API and example usage
- Module name: redwood/terraform-burst-credit/aws
- Responsibilities: validate allocation rules, produce an "intent" document, sign requests with module-level service account keys, and submit to Negotiation Queue when plan contains transfers.
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
```hcl
module "tenant_burst_credit" {
  source = "redwood/terraform-burst-credit/aws"

  tenant_id          = "acct-1234"
  budget_tokens      = 25000
  priority           = "standard" # low|standard|high
  recovery_window    = "1h"
  settlement_policy  = "deferred" # immediate|deferred|manual
  notification_emails = ["infra-ops@redwood.ai", "team-owner@customer.com"]

  // Optional: a human-readable justification used in negotiation messages
  justification = "Q4 eval season expected burst for retraining and evals"
}
```

Module plan behavior
- On terraform plan, the module will:
  - Emit a plan artifact to the CI build (artifact/key: burst-credit-intent.json).
  - If the plan includes cross-account transfers or budget reductions, it will POST the intent to /negotiation/intents with an HMAC header.
  - Terraform apply is gated on a confirmed negotiation token.

Negotiation workflow (CI side)
1) CI detects burst-credit intents in plan artifacts.
2) CI uploads the intent to Negotiation UI (internal). The UI shows proposed transfers with estimated dollar impact and a 72-hour window to respond.
3) Notification delivered to owner emails + Slack channel (#burst-negotiations).
4) Owners can: Accept (single-click), Propose Counteroffer (adjust budget or time window), or Reject. Counteroffers produce a new intent revision and restart the 72-hour timer.
5) If an owner does not respond within 72 hours, a default escalation policy applies (Auto-approve if low-dollar impact < $50; otherwise escalate to infra-manager).

CI/Apply safety checks
- Apply requires:
  - Negotiation token (negotiation/confirmed/<token>)
  - Signed plan hash matches stored artifact
  - Proposal age <= 30 days
  - Billing account healthy (billing-service.health == OK)
- Apply command (example):

```bash
sections.heading: Example module usage (root module snippet)

sections.body:
terraform apply -auto-approve \
  -var=negotiation_token=$NEG_TOKEN
  -var=plan_hash=$ARTIFACT_PLAN_HASH
```

Credit-Settler service contract (summary)
- Endpoints:
  - POST /v1/intents -> validate and store intent (returns intent_id)
  - GET /v1/intents/{id}/status -> status (pending/accepted/applied/rejected)
  - POST /v1/apply -> apply an accepted intent (idempotent)
  - GET /v1/settlement-reports/{id} -> full report (CSV/JSON)
- Security: all calls require signed JWT from terraform-burst-credit provider principal.
- Response example (apply):

```json
{
  "settlement_id": "setl-20260111-abc123",
  "status": "applied",
  "transfers": [
    {"from": "acct-ops", "to": "acct-1234", "tokens": 1000, "units": "burst_tokens"}
  ],
  "audit_url": "gs://audit-bucket/settlements/setl-20260111-abc123.json"
}
```

Monitoring, metrics and alerts
- Metrics emitted by Credit-Settler: intents_received, intents_accepted, intents_rejected, applies_succeeded, applies_failed, reconciliation_lag_seconds.
- Dashboard (Burst Billing) should surface: 7-day rolling unsettled tokens, top 10 accounts by unsettled tokens, recent failed applies.
- Alerts:
  - P0: applies_failed > 5 in 5m -> paging to infra-oncall
  - P1: reconciliation_lag_seconds > 24h for > 1000 tokens -> slack alert to #billing-ops
  - P2: intents_rejected_rate > 10% for 24h -> email to product and infra teams

Testing and CI validation matrix
- Unit tests: module validation of inputs and HMAC signing.
- Integration tests (CI staging): a simulated Credit-Settler endpoint (test double) that validates idempotence and signed calls. These run in ephemeral envs and must pass before merge.
- E2E smoke test: create two test accounts, propose a 1k token transfer, accept via API, run terraform apply via CI runner, assert settlement report exists and tokens reflected in simulated billing.

Operational runbook: failed apply
1) Triage: Check CI job logs and settlement report retrieval.
2) If apply returned 409 conflict: check whether settlement_id already exists. If yes, fetch settlement report and correlate.
3) If apply returned 5xx or timeout: retry with exponential backoff (3 retries). If still failing, open incident and manually run apply via admin tool with a privileged key.
4) If settlement created but accounting not reflected in billing: run reconciliation job (billing-reconciler) with settlement_id and attach trace id.

Owner matrix and responsibilities
- infra-infra-team: Maintain terraform-burst-credit module and CI negotiation pipeline.
- billing-ops: Run Credit-Settler service and reconciliation pipeline.
- tenant-owners: Respond to negotiations and maintain justification fields.
- security: Approve the provider principal and JWT signing policy.

Rollout plan (3 phases)
- Phase 1 (canary): Single region, test tenants (5 internal teams). Monitor applies_succeeded and reconciliation_lag_seconds for 72h.
- Phase 2 (wider): Production accounts under $500 monthly burst budget. Add evaluation accounts and expand to 3 regions.
- Phase 3 (global): All accounts, enable auto-approve policy for low-impact transfers.

Backout and emergency manual settlement
- Backout: If a terraform apply accidentally transfers tokens incorrectly, use settlement reversal API: POST /v1/reversals with settlement_id + justification. Reversals are audited and require two infra-manager approvals.
- Emergency manual settlement: billing-ops can create a manual settlement via the admin UI; the action produces a reconciliation ticket that must be attached to the terraform change PR.

Auditing and compliance
- Every intent, acceptance, rejection, and apply produces an audit record with user, principal, plan hash, and IP.
- Audit records are immutable and stored in gs://audit-bucket/burst-settlements/<year>/<month>/. Access governed by IAM group: billing-audit-readonly.

Appendix A — Negotiation message template
Subject: [Burst Credit] Proposed transfer for acct-1234 (25000 tokens -> 24000 tokens)
sections.heading: within CI job after negotiation token received

sections.body:
- Proposed transfer: acct-ops -> acct-1234 1000 tokens
- Reason: short-term eval season
- Estimated cost impact: ~$32
- Owner action: Accept | Propose Counteroffer | Reject (links in UI)

Appendix B — Example Terraform plan artifact (trimmed)
```json
{
  "plan_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "changes": [
    {"tenant_id":"acct-1234","old_budget":25000,"new_budget":24000,"delta":-1000,"policy":"deferred"}
  ]
}
```

Appendix C — Contact and escalation
- Primary oncall: infra-oncall@redwood.ai (rotation: infra SRE)
- Billing ops PagerDuty: PD ID 2345
- Slack channels: #burst-negotiations (notifications), #billing-ops (incident triage)

Related docs
- See also: gpu-tenant-eviction-predictor-and-provisioning-guidelines.json for eviction implications when budgets change.

Revision history
- 2025-03-18: Initial draft (Anika Patel)
- 2025-10-22: Added negotiation window default and auto-approve rules (Miguel Santos)
- 2026-01-12: Finalized CI checks and security contract (Priya Kapoor)

payload.page_title: GPU Fleet Federated Slice Controller — Operator Design and CI Adapter

sections.body:
Overview

This page documents the design and operational integration of the GPU Fleet Federated Slice Controller (GFFSC): a cluster-native operator and accompanying Terraform/CI adapter that automates realistic, cost-aware slicing and rebalancing of GPU capacity across multiple cloud accounts and regions. The goal is to provide a single control surface for:

- Creating bounded GPU slices (fractional/whole) per tenant or workload class.
- Federated placement across accounts or zones to maximize utilization while meeting tenant SLOs.
- Controlled rebalancing and eviction windows that are IAC-driven and testable via CI.

The document covers: design, Terraform interface, Helm/values, CI adapter patterns, test harnesses, runbook for urgent re-slicing, metrics/SLOs, and ownership.

Context and motivation
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Inefficient static reservations that leave GPUs idle while other pools spike.
- Manual cross-account rebalancing that is slow and error-prone.
- Lack of automated, repeatable safety checks for migrations and drain operations.
- Difficulty exercising slice changes with the same pipelines used for IaC and runtime validation.

High-level constraints and principles

1) Safety-first: every re-slice operation must be reversible and guarded by automated canaries and rate limits.
2) Declarative intent: slices are expressed as Terraform resources and reconciled by the operator.
3) Federated awareness: the controller reasons about cross-account capacity and egress cost signals.
4) Observability & tests: every change triggers a CI validation job (synthetic traffic + telemetry assertions).

Architecture overview
sections.heading: Problems GFFSC addresses

sections.body:
Terraform (git ops) ---> GitHub Actions --> Terraform Cloud / Runner ---> GFFSC CRD apply ---> Operator (k8s) ---> Placement engine ---> GPU nodes / Pools (cloud accounts)
                                                         |
                                                         +--> Canary jobs / Eval pods (runtime test harness)

Components

- CRDs: SliceRequest, SliceBinding, RebalancePlan, EvictionWindow.
- Controller: written in Go using controller-runtime. Responsible for validating, planning, and executing re-slices.
- Placement engine: policy module (pluggable) that consumes capacity models and cost signals.
- Terraform adapter: small CLI that converts Terraform-managed intent into CR manifests and pushes to the Git repo consumed by the operator.
- CI adapter: GitHub Actions workflows that run planning, dry-run validations, and runtime canaries before approving the change.

CRD examples (YAML snippet)

apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
kind: SliceRequest
metadata:
  name: research-spot-slice-2026-02
spec:
  tenant: research
  gpuType: A100-80GB
  fraction: 0.25 # fractional slice per node
  poolAffinity:
    - account: research-payg
      region: us-west-2
  minThroughputTokensPerSec: 200
  evictionPolicy: graceful

Operator responsibilities

- Reconcile SliceRequest -> create SliceBinding when placement confirmed.
- Build RebalancePlan that sequences node drains to maintain warm-pool coverage.
- Apply rate limits to avoid >10% concurrent live-evictions per topology domain.
- Integrate with billing signals: prefer cheaper accounts if latency budget allows.
- Emit Events and structured telemetry for every step (plan.created, plan.started, step.succeeded, plan.failed).

Terraform module interface

We expose a Terraform module (registry/internal) that teams use to declare slices. The module performs a validation pass and then triggers the adapter to create the SliceRequest CR. Below is the public variable surface:

| variable | type | default | description |
|---|---|---:|---|
| tenant | string | n/a | Logical tenant id (used in naming + billing) |
| gpu_type | string | "A100-40GB" | Preferred instance/GPU family |
| capacity_fraction | number | 0.5 | Fraction of a node to allocate (0 < x <= 1) |
| regions | list(string) | ["us-west-2"] | Preferred regions in order of preference |
| min_tokens_per_sec | number | 100 | Minimum throughput tokens required by workload |
| max_eviction_rate_pct | number | 10 | Maximum percentage of pool that can be evicted during rebalance |
| sla_latency_ms | number | 200 | Target p95 latency for the target workload |
sections.heading: Textual diagram (ASCII)

sections.body:
module "research_slice" {
  source = "internal/modules/gpu-slice"
  tenant = "research"
  gpu_type = "A100-80GB"
  capacity_fraction = 0.25
  regions = ["us-west-2","us-east-1"]
  min_tokens_per_sec = 200
  max_eviction_rate_pct = 8
  sla_latency_ms = 180
}
sections.heading: Usage example (terraform snippet)

sections.body:
1) run local plan checks (node-level capacity simulation)
2) emit a dry-run RebalancePlan to the PR as a JSON artifact
3) create a SliceRequest CR when the PR is merged

Helm chart / operator deployment (values.yaml snippet)

controller:
  replicas: 3
  podSecurityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    limits:
      cpu: "1"
      memory: "1Gi"
placementEngine:
  mode: hedged # hedged | conservative | cost_aware
  cloudSignalEndpoint: https://signals.internal.redwood.ai
  requeueIntervalSeconds: 30

CI Integration (GitHub Actions)

We require the module to run the following pipeline on each PR:

1) terraform fmt & validate
2) terraform plan (with -out=plan.tfplan) and module static checks
3) adapter-dryrun: run the Terraform adapter in dry-run mode to generate a RebalancePlan JSON
4) runtime-canary: spin up 2 ephemeral canary pods that exercise the target endpoints at representative load for 3 minutes; collect latency and token cost metrics
5) telemetry-assertions: compare canary metrics against thresholds (p95 latency < sla_latency_ms, warm_pool_hit_rate > 0.85, eviction_rate < max_eviction_rate_pct)
6) merge gate requires approvals and successful runtime-canary + telemetry-assertions
sections.heading: On module apply the adapter will

sections.body:
- name: Adapter dry-run
  run: |
    ./terraform-gffsc-adapter --config ./module/adapter.yml --dry-run --output rebalancetest.json
    jq . rebalancetest.json > rebalancetest.pretty.json

Runbook: emergency re-slice (oncall steps)

Trigger: critical hotspot identified (more than 3 SLO violations in 10 minutes, or thermal/power emergency).

1) Page oncall and create incident ticket.
2) Identify offending tenant(s) via telemetry dashboard -> top-n token consumers.
3) Run immediate soft-reslice: mark RebalancePlan with evictionPolicy=expedite for <=5% of pool.
   - kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
     apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
     kind: RebalancePlan
     metadata:
       name: emergency-reslice-{{timestamp}}
     spec:
       targetTenants: ["<tenant-id>"]
       maxConcurrentEvictionsPct: 5
       expedite: true
     EOF
4) Execute: controller will create drain jobs and start rebalancing. Monitor step.* events.
5) If SLOs worsen after 3 concurrent steps, abort by setting plan.status.abort=true and trigger rollback: kubectl annotate slicebinding <name> gffsc/rollback=forced
6) Post-incident: raise PR with exact Terraform delta that caused change and include rebalancetest.json as artifact.

Observability and telemetry

- Required metrics emitted by controller: slice.requests.total, slice.bindings.active, rebalance.plans.created, rebalance.step.duration_seconds, eviction.count, warm_pool.hit_ratio, node.utilization.percent.
- Traces: each plan execution should be traced end-to-end (trace id annotated on emitted events).
- Dashboards: per-tenant SLO dashboard (p95 latency, token cost per 1k tokens, warm_pool_hit_rate).
- Alerts: fire when warm_pool_hit_rate < 0.6 for 5m OR eviction.count > configured threshold OR node.utilization > 95% for 2m.

SLOs and thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Provisioning latency (time from SliceRequest accepted -> binding): p95 < 8 minutes.
- Eviction concurrency cap: <=10% of pool topology domain.
- Warm pool coverage during rebalance: >=80% of pre-change capacity.
- Cost tradeoff ceiling: controller must not increase egress/cross-account cost by >15% without manual approval.

Testing strategy

- Unit tests for placement policies and cost arithmetic.
- Integration tests: mocked cloud accounts with synthetic capacity models (runs in CI).
- Synthetic chaos: weekly chaos job that replays a RebalancePlan with simulated node failures to validate safety circuits.
- End-to-end smoke: run terraform module apply against a sandbox cluster and execute runtime-canary.

Operational considerations and limitations

- The GFFSC is not a substitute for application-level autoscaling; it rebalances reserved capacity across pools.
- Cross-account changes that cross billing boundaries require finance approval flag in Terraform variables (force_approve_billing_change=true).
- The placement engine will be conservative in regions with low telemetry coverage; teams can opt into riskier modes via placementEngine.mode.

Ownership and run cadence

- Service owner: eng-infra/gpu-platform (primary: Priya Nair).
- Oncall: gpu-platform rotation (see team wiki for schedule).
- CI owner: eng-infra/ci (responsible for the adapter runner and GitHub Actions).
- Quarterly: capacity reconciliation and cost review with finance and capacity forecasting team.

Rollout plan and migration steps

1) v0: operator + CRDs in sandbox, Terraform adapter dry-run only (Q1 pilot).
2) v1: enable create-on-merge for non-prod accounts with canary enforcement (Q2).
3) v2: cross-account rebalancing in production with conservative mode + finance guardrails (Q3).
4) v3+: automated cost-aware policies and RBAC-based tenant self-serve (Q4).

Appendix: common CLI commands

- Run adapter locally in dry-run: ./terraform-gffsc-adapter --config ./module/adapter.yml --dry-run
- Inspect RebalancePlan: kubectl get rebalanceplan -o wide
- Force-annotate rollback: kubectl annotate slicebinding <name> gffsc/rollback=forced --overwrite
- Collect controller logs (last 1000 lines): kubectl logs deploy/gffsc-controller -n infra --tail=1000

References and links

- Placement policy spec (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/placement-policy-spec.json
- Capacity forecasting playbook: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-demand-forecasting-and-ml-backed-scaling-playbook.json

Notes and next steps

- Action item: engineering to implement adapter telemetry schema by 2026-03-01 (owner: Ben Chu).
- Action item: CI team to add telemetry-assertions library as an internal action (owner: Sofia Martinez).

payload.page_title: Terraform Module Publish Safety Harness & Contract Testing

sections.body: This document describes a prescriptive, repeatable safety harness for publishing Terraform modules used by Redwood’s GPU and network infrastructure. The harness combines automated contract tests, security and lint gating, an account-aware canary rollout, and a fast rollback path. Its goal is to reduce surprise changes to customer-facing infra, maintain statefile compatibility, and make module upgrades reversible at low operational cost.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Terraform modules that are published to our internal registry and consumed by tenant onboarding, GPU pool provisioning, VPC modules, and edge-burst orchestration.
- CI/CD pipelines and test harnesses executed in Buildkite (primary) and GitHub Actions (backup).
- Does NOT apply to ephemeral one-off scripts or local developer-only modules. Those must be promoted before being used in production.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body:
1. Prevent breaking API/behavior changes from reaching production accounts.
2. Ensure module publishes are accompanied by deterministic smoke tests.
3. Maintain semantic versioning and compatibility metadata.
4. Allow safe, automated rollouts with observability and fast rollback.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Contract test: automated test asserting the module’s public inputs, outputs, and remote-state-side effects match a consumer contract.
- Canary account: a low-risk internal account with synthetic tenants used for early validation.
- Consumer matrix: list of critical consumer stacks (e.g., gpu-pool-bootstrap, tenant-onboard) that must be exercised by the test suite.
sections.heading: Terminology

sections.body:
- Pre-publish gates (local CI): terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec, module unit tests (kitchen-terraform or terratest), contract tests against mocked providers.
- Integration smoke (integration CI): apply/destroy in a dedicated ephemeral workspace against the canary account. Validate outputs and run reconciliation checks.
- Semantic-versioning enforcement: major/minor/patch policy via git tags and semver verification job.
- Publishing pipeline: automated registry publish only after gates pass and a manual approval for major versions.
- Rollout orchestration: staged apply to consumer matrix with percent-based canary windows and automated monitoring checks.
- Rollback automation: previous module version promotion and automated terraform state drift check and revert playbook.

Pre-publish pipeline (local CI) — checklist:
1. Developer runs tflint and fmt locally: `tflint --error` and `terraform fmt -recursive`
2. Run static security scan: `tfsec .` and fail on critical findings.
3. Run unit contract tests (mocking IaaS APIs) using terratest: `go test ./test -run TestModuleContracts`
4. Bump semantic version candidate in CHANGELOG and add release tag in branch.

Buildkite pipeline: contract-and-publish (high-level)
- Steps:
  1. checkout -> cache modules
  2. static-lint: terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec (fail fast)
  3. unit-tests: terratest / kitchen integration against mocks
  4. integration-smoke: apply to canary account workspace (auto-destroy on failure)
  5. publish-stage: upload artifact + registry metadata (only when branch is tagged)
  6. canary-rollout: trigger staged applies to consumer matrix (see Rollout policy)
  7. notify: slack channel #infra-module-publishes with results and link to runbook
sections.heading: Safety harness components

sections.body:
```
steps:
  - label: "🧪 Static + Unit"
    command: "./ci/run-lint-and-unit.sh"
  - label: "🔬 Integration (canary)"
    command: "./ci/run-integration.sh --workspace=canary"
    agents:
      queue: gpu-ci
  - wait
  - label: "📦 Publish"
    command: "./ci/publish-module.sh --tag=${BUILDKITE_TAG}"
    if: "build.tag == true"
```
sections.heading: Example Buildkite step snippet (pipeline YAML)

sections.body:
- Every published module must include: semantic version, CHANGELOG entry, consumer-compatibility matrix, backward-compatibility notes, and a module-usage example showing default inputs used by GPU stacks.
- Modules must set a `compatibility` metadata field listing minimum required provider versions and known incompatibilities. Example JSON for registry metadata: `{"semver":"1.4.0","compatibility":"aws>=4.0","consumers":["gpu-pool","tenant-onboard"]}`
sections.heading: Publishing rules and metadata requirements

sections.body:
- Contract tests are authored by module owners and reviewed by consumer owners. Each contract test must:
  - Instantiate the module with representative inputs for at least 2 consumer patterns.
  - Assert outputs shape / naming (e.g., `subnet_ids`, `asg_name`) and resource tags used for billing.
  - Validate post-apply reconciliation: simulate a control-plane restart and re-run `terraform plan` to ensure idempotency.
- Contract tests run in two modes: mocked (fast, part of PR) and live (slower, integration smoke).

Integration smoke (canary) acceptance checks — automated:
- Health checks: expected number of resources (table below)
- Cost sanity: quick estimator to ensure changes don’t increase ephemeral GPU pre-warm size by >12% for canary stack
- Drift check: run `terraform plan` post-apply and assert no diffs
- Tagging and audit: ensure `owner`, `component`, and `publish_tag` tags present on all top-level resources
sections.heading: Contract testing strategy

sections.body:
| Check | Success criteria | Failure action |
|---|---|---|
| resource-count | >= 12 nodes provisioned in canary pool | abort publish and notify owners |
| drift | `terraform plan` == no changes | auto-destroy canary, open incident ticket |
| cost-delta | estimator delta <= 12% | abort and require cost review |
| tags | tags present on 100% of root resources | abort and block publish |

Rollout policy (consumer matrix + windows):
- Stage 0: Canary account (internal) — run 1 full integration smoke. (0% customer exposure)
- Stage 1: 5% accounts in staging fleet (non-critical tenants) over 4 hours; monitor error rate, provisioning latency, and cost delta.
- Stage 2: 25% accounts across 2 regions over 12 hours if metrics are green.
- Stage 3: Full release to all consumers.
- Each stage includes an automated hold step if any gating metric exceeds thresholds (see Monitoring section).
sections.heading: Acceptance table (example for gpu-pool-bootstrap canary)

sections.body:
- Provisioning error rate > 2% (relative to baseline) -> hold and revert
- Median provisioning latency increase > 30% -> hold
- Cost delta > 18% on rolling average -> hold and require manual review
sections.heading: Gating metric thresholds (initial)

sections.body:
1. Trigger rollback job in Buildkite (pipeline: module-rollback). This repromotes the last known good module semver and marks the problematic semver as deprecated in the registry.
2. For affected consumers, gated terraform runs will apply the previous module version by updating module source reference and running `terraform init -upgrade=false && terraform apply -lock=true`.
3. If state drift prevents a clean revert, escalate to oncall and run the manual rollback playbook (link below).
sections.heading: Rollback procedure (fast path)

sections.body:
1. Identify last good version: `registry get-module-versions --module mycompany/gpu-pool`
2. Update consumer repo: bump module source to `vX.Y.Z` (last good) and open a gated PR.
3. Approver: module owner + consumer owner are required for the PR.
4. CI will run smoke tests and apply to a small subset of accounts.
5. Monitor for 1 hour; if metrics stabilize, continue rollout. If not, open incident and run deeper remediation.
sections.heading: Rollback playbook (short)

sections.body:
- Never remove outputs used by active consumers without issuing a major version with explicit migration steps.
- Schema change steps: document a migration recipe and provide an automated script where feasible.
- For state move/rename operations, prefer `terraform state mv` helper scripts in the consumer repo with step-by-step instructions.
sections.heading: Statefile compatibility guidance

sections.body:
- Dashboards: infra-module-publishes (publish success rate, integration failure rate, canary metrics: provisioning-latency, error-rate, cost-delta).
- Alerting: PagerDuty on oncall when a canary-stage fails gating checks or when rollback automation fails.
- Slack: verbose, colored notifications in #infra-module-publishes and @channel for stage holds/rollbacks.
sections.heading: Monitoring and alerts

sections.body:
- Module owner: publishes module, maintains contract tests, triages publish failures. (Primary: infra-module-team)
- Consumer owners: maintain consumer matrix entries and review contracts. (Examples: gpu-team, private-deploys)
- CI owners: maintain Buildkite steps and runner pools (Primary: eng-infra-cicd)
- Oncall: respond to rollout holds and escalate per incident runbook.
sections.heading: Ownership and responsibilities

sections.body:
- [ ] Linting green and no tfsec criticals
- [ ] Contract tests written for all consumers in consumer matrix
- [ ] CHANGELOG entry and migration notes present
- [ ] Publish metadata (compatibility, consumers) populated
- [ ] Owner and reviewer set in registry metadata

Appendix A — Example minimal GH Actions job for mocked contract tests:
```
name: Contract Test
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  contract:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Go
        uses: actions/setup-go@v4
        with:
          go-version: '1.21'
      - name: Run terratest contracts
        run: go test ./test -run TestModuleContracts -v
```

Appendix B — Example terratest assertion (pseudo-code):
```
func TestModuleContracts(t *testing.T) {
  t.Parallel()
  options := &terraform.Options{...}
  defer terraform.Destroy(t, options)
  terraform.InitAndApply(t, options)
  subnetIds := terraform.OutputList(t, options, "subnet_ids")
  assert.GreaterOrEqual(t, len(subnetIds), 2)
}
```
sections.heading: Operational checklists (pre-publish quick checklist)

sections.body:
Q: Who approves major version publishes?
A: Module owner + two consumer owners + security reviewer. Major versions must include a migration guide.

Q: Can a module bypass canary steps?
A: Only in emergency with exec approval and a documented post-publish remediation plan; all bypasses are audited.
sections.heading: Frequently asked questions (FAQ)

sections.body:
- Module stability & rollback catalog (internal)
- CI gating patterns for GPU stacks (internal)
- Oncall runbook: module-publish-incident (internal)
sections.heading: Links and references

sections.body:
- 2024-09-12: Initial draft by Maya Lindstrom
- 2025-03-10: Added cost-delta threshold and automated rollback script
- 2026-02-14: Updated Buildkite pipeline snippet and canary windows
