payload.page_title: Tenant Egress Rate Limiter (RLS) — Policy & Terraform Spec

sections.body:
Overview:

This document defines the architecture, policy model, Terraform/IaC modules, operational runbook, testing and rollout plan for the Tenant Egress Rate Limiter (RLS). RLS provides enforceable, auditable egress rate and bandwidth controls per tenant (account) across our inference fleet and burst fabric. The target audience is infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who implement tenant isolation, cost controls, and egress SLA guarantees.

Goals:
- Provide per-tenant and per-route rate limits (tokens/sec, max burst bytes) that are enforceable at the network edge and/or NAT egress proxies.
- Integrate with Terraform and our tenant onboarding pipeline so policies can be declared as code.
- Emit metrics and logs for billing reconciliation, SLA reporting, and incident triage.
- Support tiered SLOs (free/dev/paid/enterprise) and emergency shielding for customer-sensitive incidents.

Definitions and Concepts:
- Tenant: Redwood customer account identifier (tenant_id) used across billing and routing.
- Egress policy: A named rate-policy attached to a tenant or tenant+route.
- Token bucket: Enforcement primitive used by the RLS (rate r tokens/sec, burst b tokens).
- Enforcement point: The process/location where an egress decision is applied (edge-proxy, NAT gateway, egress sidecar, or cloud load balancer WAF).
- Global circuit-breaker: Account-level emergency fallback which immediately caps a tenant to a minimal safe rate.

Architecture overview:
- Control plane: Policy API service (internal-only) where RBAC-bound users and CI apply declared policies. Stores policy objects in DynamoDB (or our ConfigStore) keyed by tenant_id and policy_name.
- Sync agent: Periodic pull/push that translates policies to enforcement configs and pushes to edge-proxies or cloud route objects.
- Enforcement plane: Nginx/Envoy egress proxies + iptables token-bucket shim on self-managed NAT pools. For cloud-managed egress we use provider rate-limit objects where supported.
- Observability: Prometheus metrics (ratelimit_allowed, ratelimit_denied, egress_bytes), audit logs (policy change events), and a billing reconciliation export.

Policy model (declarative example):
- Fields:
  - policy_id: string (human name)
  - tenant_id: string
  - scope: [global, region, route]
  - rate_rps: integer (requests per second)
  - bandwidth_bps: integer (bytes per second)
  - burst_bytes: integer
  - sku_tier: [free, dev, standard, enterprise]
  - effective_from / effective_to: ISO timestamps (optional)
  - enforcement_points: list of strings (edge-proxy, nat-pool-a, aws-tgw)
  - tags: list of strings

Sample Terraform YAML snippet (module usage):
```
module "rls_policy_myapp" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra/terraform-modules.git//rls-policy?ref=v1.2.0"

  tenant_id       = "tenant_1234"
  policy_id       = "standard-tenant-default"
  scope           = "global"
  rate_rps        = 200
  bandwidth_bps   = 5_000_000   # 5 MB/s
  burst_bytes     = 10_000_000  # 10 MB burst
  sku_tier        = "standard"
  enforcement_pts = ["edge-envoy-eu", "nat-pool-us-west-2"]
  tags            = ["gpu-inference", "slo:standard"]
}
```

Terraform module outputs (contract):
- policy_resource_id (string) — unique id used by sync agent
- last_apply_sha (string) — commit used for audit
- enforcement_targets (list) — list of endpoints that will receive the config

Enforcement semantics and algorithm:
- Primary primitive: hierarchical token buckets. Tenant-level bucket is checked first, then route-level buckets. If either bucket denies, request is rejected or queued depending on enforcement-point capability.
- Bandwidth accounting uses byte-level tokens for streaming responses; request-rate uses request tokens.
- Grace window: newly-created policies start with a 10-minute grace (soft enforcement) where violations are counted and emitted as metrics but not blocked. This avoids accidental customer impact from IaC mistakes.

SLOs & thresholds (suggested):
- Free tier: 20 rps, 500 KB/s, 2 MB burst (best-effort, excess requests are rejected)
- Dev: 100 rps, 2 MB/s, 8 MB burst (soft throttling preferred)
- Standard: 1000 rps, 10 MB/s, 40 MB burst (strong enforcement, low-latency SLO)
- Enterprise: custom per-contract (configurable via CLI/console and priority queueing)

Observability and metrics (Prometheus tags):
- rls_policy_applied_total{tenant_id, policy_id, enforcement_point}
- rls_rate_allowed_total{tenant_id, policy_id}
- rls_rate_rejected_total{tenant_id, policy_id, reason}
- rls_egress_bytes_total{tenant_id, policy_id, direction}
- rls_policy_sync_latency_seconds

Dashboards & Alerts (recommendations):
- Dashboard: Tenant Overview: per-tenant latency, egress bytes, rejects, and last policy_apply.
- Alert: PolicySyncFail if a policy hasn't been acknowledged by all enforcement_points for > 5m (P2).
- Alert: UnusualRejects if rejects for a tenant spike > 10x baseline in 5m (P1).
- Alert: BillingMismatch if daily egress bytes differ > 3% vs billing export (Finance triage).

Runbook: common incidents and playbook steps:
1) Symptom: Tenant traffic suddenly denied / 503 on inference routes.
   - Check dashboard for rls_rate_rejected_total and policy_sync status.
   - Confirm if a policy change was recently applied (check audit logs last 30m).
   - If within grace window: treat as policy misconfiguration and rollback the Terraform apply.
   - If not: escalate to RLS owners, run steps below.
2) Emergency shielding (fast mitigation):
   - Use rls emergency CLI: `rlsctl shield tenant_1234 --temporary-rate 10` to place tenant into a safe minimal rate. This bypasses per-route blocks and creates a short-lived override (15 minutes).
3) Rolling rollback:
   - Revert the last terraform apply that changed the policy and run `terraform apply -target=module.rls_policy_myapp` in staging, then canary to edge proxy.
4) Long-term fix:
   - Update policy tests, add additional explicit testcases to CI (see Testing section).

Testing strategy (CI/CD):
- Unit: Policy schema validation and invariants (no negative rates, burst limit capped at 10x rate*60s).
- Integration: A local envoy sandbox test that applies the policy via module and then drives synthetic traffic across different routes asserting allow/deny counts.
- Chaos: Periodically run a canary chaos test that injects 10% additional traffic to an internal tenant to verify graceful degradation and alerts.

Terraform/IaC module requirements and constraints (table):
| Input | Type | Required | Notes |
|------|------|----------|-------|
| tenant_id | string | yes | must match tenant registry ID |
| policy_id | string | yes | alphanumeric-dash-only |
| scope | string | yes | global | region | route |
| rate_rps | number | conditional | required for rate policies |
| bandwidth_bps | number | conditional | required for bandwidth policies |
| burst_bytes | number | optional | default = min(bandwidth_bps * 5s, 50 MiB) |
| enforcement_pts | list | yes | map to existing envoy/nat pools |

Operational notes & ownership:
- Team owners: networking-platform@redwood.com (primary), gpu-fleet@redwood.com (secondary).
- Audit and compliance: Every policy change writes an immutable audit event with user, commit sha, and diff. Finance receives a nightly export for billing reconciliation.
- IAM: Only the onboarding CI and designated SREs have write permission to the control plane apply endpoint. Use least-privilege TF service accounts.

Rollout plan (canary phases):
1) Internal-only: deploy RLS in us-west-2 test cluster and validate with synthetic tenants (2 weeks).
2) Beta tenants: opt-in list of internal customers and dev teams (4 weeks) — collect metrics and iterate policy defaults.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% of production egress traffic to enforcement points in us-west-2, 10% in eu-west-1 (4 weeks).
4) Wide rollout: make enforcement default, keep soft-grace for 24h for new policies.

CLI snippets and debug commands:
- Show active policy for tenant: `rlsctl show --tenant tenant_1234 --format json`
- Force re-sync policy to enforcement point: `rlsctl sync --tenant tenant_1234 --point edge-envoy-eu`
- Get recent rejects: `rd-prom-query "sum(rate(rls_rate_rejected_total{tenant_id=\"tenant_1234\"}[5m]))"`

Security and failure modes:
- Threat model: malicious tenant attempting exfiltration via high volume streaming. Mitigation: byte-level enforcement + per-connection caps and connection-level tracking.
- Failure modes: Sync agent crash (policy drift), enforcement point OOM (egress proxy misconfigured), Terraform apply with wrong variables.
- Safe defaults: if enforcement point becomes unreachable, the sync agent enters read-only (no deletes) and health-checks escalate to oncall.

Appendix A — Example incident timeline (realistic exercise):
- 10:03 UTC: Synthetic spike causes Tenant A rejects; dashboard alert fires.
- 10:05 UTC: SRE uses shield CLI to restore minimal operations.
- 10:10 UTC: Audit shows a recent policy apply by CI; rollback performed and new canary applied.
- 10:40 UTC: Metrics stabilize; ticket created for policy/test gaps.

Appendix B — Implementation checklist for module owners:
- [ ] Schema validation unit tests added to module repo.
- [ ] Sync agent acknowledgment handshake implemented (ACK/NAK).
- [ ] Prometheus metrics instrumented and dashboard templates committed.
- [ ] IAM roles and TF service account documented and reviewed.
- [ ] Emergency shield CLI tested and RBAC locked down.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary oncall: networking-platform rotation (see oncall schedule).
- Secondary: gpu-fleet team pager.
- For billing disputes: finance-billing@redwood.com.

Document history and notes:
- v0.1 (2024-03-12) initial draft
- v0.6 (2024-09-02) added enforcement semantics and grace window
- v1.0 (2025-09-18) expanded Terraform contract and finalized rollout plan

Related artifacts (repo links):
- Terraform module repo: git@github.com:redwood-infra/terraform-rls-modules.git (internal)
- Sync agent: git@github.com:redwood-infra/rls-sync-agent.git
- CLI: git@github.com:redwood-infra/rlsctl.git

If you have questions or need a workshop to map tenant policies to your product routes, ping networking-platform or request a design review via the infra lifecycle board.

payload.page_title: GPU Interconnect Profile Ledger and CI Validator

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the GPU Interconnect Profile Ledger: a canonical catalog of validated network/interconnect profiles used by GPU fleets at Redwood Inference, the Terraform module schema to provision those profiles, and a CI validator that gates changes. The ledger captures requirements for RDMA/RoCE, MTU, QoS policy, NIC placement, and cross-account gateway configuration so infra teams and tenant owners can select guarded profiles that align to SLOs and billing classes.

Why this exists:
- GPU workloads are sensitive to network characteristics (latency, jitter, packet loss) and to host topology (PCIe/NUMA/RDMA).
- Ad hoc network changes have caused silent regressions in throughput for high-concurrency inference and eval jobs.
- We need a single source of truth for profiles, automated validation in CI, and terraform primitives that enforce guardrails across accounts and regions.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: Infra engineers, platform SRE, private deploy engineering, infra CI owners, and tenant oncall engineers.
- Scope: Network/interconnect-level profiles for GPU pools (host and VPC-level), Terraform inputs and outputs, CI validation rules, and runbook for profile rollout and emergency rollback. Not included: per-application tuning of batching or model-level kernels.

Ownership:
- Ledger owner: infra-networking team (primary contact: Marcus Rivera).
- Terraform module maintainer: infra-iac team (reviewers: Ava Chen, Priya Singh).
- CI validator steward: infra-ci team.

Ledger format (human-readable):
Each profile in the ledger is an immutable entry with a numeric release tag (vX.Y), documented constraints, measured telemetry baselines, and a canonical terraform profile key. Example ledger entry (plain text):

Profile ID: rdmv2-highband-v1
Short desc: RDMA-enabled, 9k MTU, high-throughput RDMA fabric for inference-burst workloads.
Intended workloads: high-concurrency token-generation, long KV cache sessions, eval microbenchmarks.
Kernel/hardware requirements: Mellanox ConnectX-6 or equivalent, OFED 5.7+, host NUMA affinity pinning recommended.
Network constraints:
- MTU: 9000
- RDMA/RoCE: enabled
- Egress QoS class: gpu-high-bandwidth
- Expected p95 latency (intra-subnet): <= 80us (baseline), packet loss < 0.03%
Security/ACLs: only tenant subnets listed in profile may attach; SSH access limited to bastion-gallery; KMS access separate.
Terraform profile key: "profile_rdmv2_highband_v1"
Telemetry baseline id: telemetry/baselines/rdmv2-highband-2024-08
Release notes: Verified with integration-test-run: gpu-net-perf-2024-08-12, rollback if p95 > 120us for 1h.

Profile table (for quick reference):
| profile_key | mtu | rdma | qos_class | recommended_hardware | p95_latency_baseline | primary_region | notes |
| rdmv2_highband_v1 | 9000 | true | gpu-high-bandwidth | CX6+ | 70-80us | us-west-2 | uses dedicated fabric VLAN |
| standard-10gmtu | 1500 | false | gpu-standard | 10GbE | 300-600us | multi-region | general purpose |
| nearline-1g | 1500 | false | gpu-econ | 1GbE | 1-3ms | eu-west-1 | evaluation sandboxes only |

Terraform module schema (minimal working example):
The terraform module 'redwood_gpu_interconnect_profile' accepts a profile key and enforces network constructs across accounts. Lower snippet is illustrative HCL to pick a ledger profile.

Example variables.tf snippet:
```hcl
variable "profile_key" {
  type = string
  description = "Canonical ledger key (e.g. profile_rdmv2_highband_v1)"
}
variable "tenant_account_id" {
  type = string
}
variable "region" {
  type = string
  default = "us-west-2"
}
```

Example main.tf usage (simplified):
```hcl
module "interconnect_profile" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood/repo/terraform-modules.git//gpu-interconnect-profile?ref=main"
  profile_key = var.profile_key
  tenant_account_id = var.tenant_account_id
  region = var.region
  enforce_qos_classes = true
  attach_gateway = true
  allowed_subnets = var.allowed_subnets
}
```

Terraform inputs & guardrails table (documented expectations):
- enforce_qos_classes: boolean (default true). If true, module will create or attach to QoS policy with rate limits and tagging.
- attach_gateway: boolean, requires cross-account role if true.
- allowed_subnets: list of subnet ARNs. Module will fail plan if subnets outside tenant allowlist are supplied.
- mtu: optional override only allowed for sandbox profiles; production profiles reject custom mtu in the module.

CI Validator: Overview
We provide a validator that runs in PR pipelines whenever the ledger JSON, terraform module, or profile selection inputs change. The validator has three phases: static schema validation, simulation checks, and telemetry compatibility checks.

1) Static schema validation
- Validate ledger entries against JSON schema (fields required: profile_key, mtu, rdma, qos_class, hardware_tags, telemetry_baseline_id, terraform_key).
- Lint rules: no profile mutability (changes must create new vX.Y), naming convention enforcement, and allowed regions guardrails.

2) Simulation checks
- Run a lightweight VPC/profile simulation: the CI job uses a terraform plan with a mock tenant-account (test account) to ensure module can attach gateway and does not create cross-account roles outside policy.
- Run tflint and checkov with custom ruleset that prohibits direct internet-exposed fabric attachments.

3) Telemetry compatibility checks
- If a profile change references a telemetry baseline, CI will compare latest baseline percentile numbers with historical baselines stored in S3 (max drift allowed: p95 latency +30% or p99 +40%). If drift exceeds thresholds, CI flags the change for manual review.

CI job sample (GitHub Actions style, simplified):
```yaml
name: Ledger CI Validator
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install tools
        run: |
          pip install jsonschema yq
          curl -L -o tflint.zip https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint/releases/download/v0.34.0/tflint_linux_amd64.zip
          unzip tflint.zip && sudo mv tflint /usr/local/bin/
      - name: Schema validate ledger
        run: |
          jsonschema -i ledger/rdm_profiles.json ci/schemas/gpu_interconnect_ledger_schema.json
      - name: Terraform plan simulation
        run: |
          cd terraform/test-harness
          terraform init -backend=false
          terraform plan -var="profile_key=profile_rdmv2_highband_v1" -var="tenant_account_id=test-account"
      - name: Telemetry drift check
        run: |
          python ci/check_telemetry_drift.py --baseline-id telemetry/baselines/rdmv2-highband-2024-08 --s3-bucket telemetry-baselines --threshold-p95 0.3
```

Validator helper: check_telemetry_drift.py (behavioral contract)
- Accepts baseline id and compares JSON time-series with stored historical baseline.
- Emits non-zero exit code on failure.
- Outputs a short report with p50/p95/p99 comparisons and a suggested canary test plan (see rollout below).

Rollout and canary strategy (recommended):
1) Internal Canary (1% of GPU capacity): attach new profile to isolated canary pool in us-west-2 for 24h; collect p95 latency, packet loss, and error-rate on inference API.
2) Internal Ramp (10% capacity): 24–72h, monitor cost delta, egress QoS contention, and cross-region replication effects.
3) Gradual Enterprise rollout (per-customer gating): enable via feature-flag for dedicated pools tied to SLA tier.
4) Full rollout: after 7d of stable metrics and no regressions in telemetry thresholds.

Rollback triggers (automated):
- p95 latency increase > 25% vs baseline persisting for 1h
- sustained packet loss > 0.2% for 30m
- unexpected egress billing spike > 50% in a billing window for the affected pool
On trigger: automated jobs revoke new profile attachment and reattach previous profile, alert oncall and create an incident with prefilled template.

Runbook (incident response for profile regressions):
1) Triage: Confirm regression via Grafana dashboard 'gpu-interconnect/latency-by-profile' and Inspect recent changes in ledger/terraform.
2) Canary revert: Run terraform apply to reassign instance pool to previous profile_key (module supports immutable switch).
3) Telemetry collection: Collect pcaps (where permitted), RDMA counters, dmesg for NIC errors and kernel drops. Store artifacts in the incident bucket.
4) Postmortem: within 72h write a blameless incident review linking to ledger PR and CI run.

Testing matrix (minimum):
- Unit: ledger JSON schema tests, naming validation.
- Integration: terraform plan in test account, tflint and checkov passes.
- Perf: smoke netperf (iperf3 + rdma_test) for p95/p99 baseline reproduction in a sandbox-runner.
- Chaos: simulated packet-drop injection in staging to ensure rollback automation triggers.

Operational notes and constraints:
- Production profiles are immutable: any change must be a new profile_id (vX.Y). Reusing keys is disallowed by CI.
- Only infra-iac maintainers may update the terraform module; ledger entries can be proposed by platform teams but must include telemetry baseline evidence.
- Cross-account gateway attachments require an approver from security; CI will fail plans that create IAM roles without approval tags.

Appendix: Troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- If p95 increases: check NIC offload settings, ensure MTU set end-to-end, validate no fragmented MTU on transit gateways.
- If RDMA sessions fail to establish: verify OFED userspace modules, check roce enablement at switch level, confirm firmware compatibility.
- If egress QoS enforcement not observed: verify tc qdisc on hosts and that egress-proxy sidecar tags are present.

References and links:
- Terraform module repo: git::ssh://git.redwood/repo/terraform-modules.git//gpu-interconnect-profile
- Telemetry baselines S3 location: s3://redwood-telemetry/baselines/gpu-interconnect/
- CI schemas: ci/schemas/gpu_interconnect_ledger_schema.json
- Grafana dashboards: gpu-interconnect/latency-by-profile, gpu-interconnect/egress-qos-usage

Revision history:
- 2024-08-12: Initial draft and ledger template (Marcus Rivera)
- 2024-10-04: Added CI telemetry drift check and thresholds (Ava Chen)
- 2025-01-15: Published with rollout and automated rollback playbook (Priya Singh)

End of document.

payload.page_title: GPU Egress Proxy Heatmap and Fallback Routing Guide

sections.body:
Summary:

This page defines the GPU fleet egress proxy heatmap, the fallback routing policy for degraded egress paths, and the operational procedures for incident response and planned changes. It covers detection signals, the routing decision matrix, Terraform/IaC change patterns, CI/CD gating, and step-by-step runbooks for active incidents and maintenance windows.

Scope:

- Applies to GPU tenant traffic leaving Redwood-managed VPCs to public model registries, S3, container registries, and partner clouds.
- Focuses on the egress proxy layer (service mesh sidecars + egress proxies + NAT/egress gateways) used by inference and eval clusters.
- Excludes internal control-plane traffic and private VPC peering (those are documented in the VPC peer runbook).

Owners & Contacts:

- Primary owner: eng-infra / Network Reliability (oncall: net-oncall@redwood.internal)
- Secondary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-networking@redwood.internal)
- Pager: #infra-ops (urgent)
- Emergency Escalation: Diego Moreno (pager), Rina Shah (pager)

SLOs and Operational Thresholds:

- Egress success rate (TCP/443) from GPU clusters to registry endpoints: 99.95% monthly.
- Median egress latency to model-registry endpoints: < 60ms; P95 < 250ms.
- Failover initiation threshold: sustained >1.0% 5m error rate or >30% increase in latency over baseline for 5 consecutive minutes.

Detection and Heatmap Generation:

Purpose: produce an egress heatmap to visualize per-tenant, per-region egress health and historical fallbacks. This is used by oncall to decide whether to fail over traffic or to scale proxies.

Signals used to construct the heatmap:
- Proxy success_rate (per-proxy, per-tenant) - metric: infra.egress.proxy_success_rate{cluster,region,tenant} (Prometheus)
- Proxy latency histogram infra.egress.proxy_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le,cluster,region}
- TCP connection resets and TLS handshake failures infra.egress.tls_errors_total{cluster,region}
- NAT gateway metrics: aws_nat_gw_bytes/packets_dropped and GCP equivalent
- Route table error counters: infra.egress.route_rejects_total

Heatmap layout (rows = regions, cols = external destinations):
- Color scale: green (<0.1% errors), yellow (0.1-1%), orange (1-5%), red (>5% or >300ms p95)
- Granularity: 5-minute buckets, 12h rolling window shown by default

Operational use of heatmap:
- Oncall should open the heatmap on incident detection. Look for cluster/tenant columns in orange/red and identify whether multiple clusters hit the same external destination (indicates remote endpoint problem) or multiple destinations per cluster (indicates local egress).

Routing Decision Matrix (simplified):

1) Detect remote endpoint outage (many tenants/regions failing to same destination):
   - Priority: route to alternate mirror endpoint (if available) or fallback to cached model store.
   - Action: mark destination as degraded, update egress policy to route matching requests to fallback mirror.

2) Detect regional egress degradation (one region many destinations failing):
   - Priority: steer traffic to neighboring region pool if policy allows tenant-level cross-region failover.
   - Action: trigger cross-region routing via service-mesh egress policy and update DNS TTLs for internal mirrors.

3) Detect per-tenant saturation/local networking: (single tenant/cluster high errors):
   - Priority: isolate tenant, apply stricter rate limiting, and migrate workloads to alternative burst pool.
   - Action: notify product-owner, scale warm pool or provision on-demand nodes.

Runbook: Active Incident (egress rate/error spike)

1) Triage (first 5 minutes)
   - Open incident in StatusPage and notify #infra-ops.
   - Verify metrics: check infra.egress.proxy_success_rate (5m) and infra.egress.proxy_request_duration_seconds@p95.
   - Look at the heatmap: identify which regions/destinations are red/orange.

2) Narrow scope (5-10 minutes)
   - If many regions/destinations fail -> suspect remote endpoint. Verify with curl from a non-GPU bastion: curl -v https://<dest> --connect-timeout 5
   - If single region -> check NAT gateway metrics and VPC flow logs for dropped packets. CLI examples:
       - kubectl -n infra logs deployment/egress-proxy -l app=egress-proxy --since=10m | grep -i error
       - terraform state list | grep nat_gateway || aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc>" --query "NatGateways[*].{Id:NatGatewayId,State:State}"

3) Apply mitigations (10-30 minutes)
   - Remote endpoint problems: add a routing-rule to route-match requests to alternate mirror via service-mesh egress config. Example (istio-style pseudo):

# example: create DestinationRule to prefer mirror
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: model-registry-fallback
  namespace: infra
spec:
  host: registry.main.internal
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 1000
EOF
   - Regional network issues: shift tenant routing policy via feature-flagged routing in config-store. CLI to flip flag:
       curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CFG_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n         https://config-store.internal/api/v1/flags/egress_cross_region_failover -d '{"enabled":true, "target_regions":["us-west-2"]}'

   - Per-tenant saturation: enforce temporary per-tenant QPS cap using rate-limit policy and schedule migration to burst pool.

4) Validate (30-60 minutes)
   - Confirm heatmap moves from red/orange to yellow/green.
   - Run synthetic checks from canary pods: for i in {1..50}; do curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}\n" https://registry.mirror.internal; done
   - Measure success_rate > 99.9% for 10 minutes before declaring recovery.

5) Post-incident (90 minutes+)
   - Capture timeline, root-cause hypothesis, and mitigations in the incident doc.
   - If Terraform/IaC changes were applied, open a Terraform PR that documents the emergency change and schedule a follow-up to convert ad-hoc changes into tracked IaC.

Runbook: Planned Maintenance / Patch Window

1) Preflight (72-48 hours)
   - Update change ticket and run the heatmap to baseline current health.
   - Notify impacted tenants (email + in-console banner) if cross-region failover will be triggered.
   - Create Terraform plan and run in staging cluster: terraform plan -var-file=vars/stage.tfvars -out=tfplan

2) During maintenance (0-4 hours)
   - Enable failover flag in config-store and observe heatmap.
   - Run synthetic traffic tests as above and watch infra.egress.* metrics.
   - If errors > threshold, abort maintenance and revert flags.

3) Post-maintenance (4-24 hours)
   - Reconcile all temporary runtime flags back to false.
   - Create PR to commit intended IaC changes to main branch; ensure CI runs the e2e-network-tests.

Terraform/IaC patterns and CI/CD gating

Purpose: emergency fixes are sometimes applied via runtime changes. We require a discipline to convert these to IaC with tests and gated CI.

Required pattern for egress routing changes:
- All route changes must be represented as one of the following IaC artifacts:
  - Terraform module: modules/egress-routing (preferred for NAT/route-table/GW)
  - Helm chart values: charts/egress-proxy/values-*.yaml (preferred for sidecar and mesh configs)
  - Config-store JSON: config-store/egress-rules/<tenant>.json (runtime flags)

CI gating checklist (PR must pass before merge):
- unit tests for Terraform modules (tflint + terrascan)
- terraform plan must succeed in a disposable workspace and produce an intended diff (no unintended resource replacements)
- e2e-network-tests run in the GPU staging cluster (GitHub Actions workflow: .github/workflows/e2e-network.yml)
- Canary rollout policy: changes to egress proxy charts must include a canary config and the helm chart PR must include helm test results

Sample Terraform snippet (illustrative, keep in module):

resource "aws_route" "egress_to_mirror" {
  route_table_id = var.route_table_id
  destination_cidr_block = var.mirror_cidr
  gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.mirror.id
}

Important: never perform route table replacements without rolling updates and canary verification. Use the apply-time lock in CI (terraform apply -lock=true -auto-approve) only when PR has been signed off by network owners.

CI/CD rollback automation:

- Every Terraform PR that mutates egress routing must include a rollback plan (a terraform state snapshot and an approval path). The CI job produces a rollback artifact stored in GCS under gs://ci-rollback-artifacts/<pr-number>/snapshot.tfstate.
- Helm chart changes must support a --rollback flag via the deploy script: scripts/deploy-helm-egress.sh --namespace infra --chart charts/egress-proxy --rollback <release>

Testing Checklist (pre-merge and pre-deploy)

- Local linting: tflint, terraform fmt, helm lint
- Staging apply success and smoke tests: e2e-network-tests (100 synthetic requests across 3 regions).
- Heatmap sanity: run heatmap job for a 15m window and ensure no new orange/red artifacts introduced.
- Owner signoff: network-owner + runtime-owner reviewers must sign the PR.

Rollback Procedures (fast rollback):

1) Runtime flag revert: set config-store flag to previous state; observe heatmap for immediate improvement.
2) Helm rollback: scripts/deploy-helm-egress.sh --rollback <release> (monitor for crashloops).
3) Terraform rollback: restore snapshot state from gs://ci-rollback-artifacts and run terraform apply against snapshot plan.

Appendix: Example monitoring queries

- Proxy success rate (PromQL):
  1 - sum(rate(infra_egress_proxy_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(infra_egress_proxy_requests_total[5m]))

- Heatmap grouping query (PromQL example):
  sum by (region, destination) (rate(infra_egress_proxy_errors_total[5m])) / sum by (region,destination) (rate(infra_egress_proxy_requests_total[5m]))

Appendix: Config / Environment reference (table as plain text)

ENV VAR | DESCRIPTION | EXAMPLE
CFG_TOKEN | API token for config-store writes | redwood-config-abc123
MIRROR_CIDR | CIDR block for internal mirror gateway | 10.150.200.0/24
EGRESS_FAILOVER_FLAG | Feature flag key to enable failover routing | egress_cross_region_failover
PROXY_MAX_CONN | Sidecar connection cap per proxy | 1200

Appendix: Quick commands cheat-sheet

- Show proxy logs (last 20m): kubectl -n infra logs deploy/egress-proxy --tail=200 --since=20m
- Rotate egress proxy pods gracefully: kubectl -n infra rollout restart deployment/egress-proxy
- Check NAT gateway health (AWS): aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter "Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>" --query "NatGateways[*].{Id:NatGatewayId,State:State,Addresses:NatGatewayAddresses}"
- Trigger config-store flag: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CFG_TOKEN" -d '{"enabled":true}' https://config-store.internal/api/v1/flags/egress_cross_region_failover

Postmortem expectations and follow-up

- For every incident where runtime mitigations were used to restore service, open a follow-up ticket within 48 hours that:
  - Describes the short-term fix and the migration plan to IaC within 7 days.
  - Names a remediation owner and lists required work (example: convert runtime mirror routing to terraform module).

References and related docs

- GPU egress billing and tagging guide (billing owners)
- VPC peer runbook (private peering exceptions)
- CI e2e-network-tests workflow (.github/workflows/e2e-network.yml)

Change log

- 2024-09-05: Document created by Aisha Patel (draft).
- 2024-11-12: Added canary and CI gating checklist (reviewers: Diego).
- 2025-02-28: Expanded heatmap signals and added Terraform rollback artifact path (published).

payload.page_title: Global traffic routing controls (GSLB + DNS): Hosted API

sections.body:
h1. Purpose
This page documents the *authoritative* steps for steering production Hosted API traffic between regions using Redwood's Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) and DNS controls. This is used during outages, planned maintenance, and game days.

*Entry point:* api.redwoodinference.com
*Owned by:* Eng Infra

h1. Current routing architecture (summary)
- Clients resolve api.redwoodinference.com to a GSLB endpoint.
- GSLB distributes traffic to regional gateways using weighted targets.
- Each regional gateway forwards to the routing service (regional) which selects model backends (regional).

h1. Regions and default pairings
Default primary -> secondary pairings for failover:
- us-east-1 -> us-west-2
- eu-west-1 -> eu-central-1
- ap-southeast-1 -> ap-northeast-1

h1. Where to change weights
Weights are controlled in Terraform-backed config, but during incidents we use the "trafficctl" emergency tool to avoid slow IaC cycles.

*Tool:* trafficctl
*Auth:* requires oncall elevated role "infra-traffic-admin"

h2. Read current distribution
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- trafficctl gslb get --record api.redwoodinference.com

Expected output includes targets and weights, e.g.:
- us-east-1-gw weight=100
- us-west-2-gw weight=0

h2. Weighted failover procedure (preferred)
1) Set TTL to 60 seconds (temporary)
- trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 60
2) Shift to 10% secondary
- trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=90,us-west-2-gw=10
3) Validate metrics for 5-10 minutes
4) Shift to 50% secondary
- trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=50,us-west-2-gw=50
5) Validate metrics for 5-10 minutes
6) Shift to 100% secondary
- trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=0,us-west-2-gw=100
7) Keep TTL at 60 for the first hour after full cutover, then restore to 300
- trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 300

h2. Hard failover procedure (primary down)
If the primary region is hard down (no metrics, no gateway health):
- trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 60
- trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=0,us-west-2-gw=100

h1. Rollback procedure
Rollback is done by restoring the previous weights from the incident log. Default steady state is 100/0 to the designated primary.
sections.heading: Command

sections.body:
- trafficctl gslb set-weights --record api.redwoodinference.com --weights us-east-1-gw=100,us-west-2-gw=0
- trafficctl dns set-ttl --record api.redwoodinference.com --ttl 300

h1. Validation signals (regional)
sections.heading: Commands
Validate per-region while weights change

payload.page_title: Bandwidth-aware GPU placement and IaC lifecycle playbook

sections.body:
Overview:
This playbook codifies an egress/bandwidth-aware GPU placement strategy and the associated Terraform/IaC lifecycle for Redwood’s multi-tenant inference fleet. The goal is to reduce noisy-neighbor egress contention, improve tail latency for latency-sensitive tenants, and maintain clear operational procedures for rollout, monitoring, and rollback.

Scope:
- Applies to all GPU clusters managed by the gpu-allocator service in public cloud regions (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1).
- Covers node labeling, tenant egress tagging, scheduler policy, IaC module variables, CI/CD gating, and runbook actions for hotspots.
- Does NOT change model-level runtime parameters (those are handled by eng-serving-runtime docs).

Context and motivation:
- Observed incidents in 2024 where a small set of tenants with high-embedding workloads saturated node egress links, leading to 99.9th percentile generation latency spikes.
- Existing placement is GPU-count-first; we add a bandwidth signal to avoid co-locating heavy-egress workloads with latency-sensitive customers.

Key components (short):
- tenant-metadata-service: authoritative egress profile for a tenant (low/medium/high).
- gpu-allocator: placement controller that consumes tenant egress profile + node egress capacity annotations.
- egress-sharder: sidecar/proxy for shaping and tagging flows per-tenant for billing/telemetry.
- IaC modules: tf-module/gpu-node-profile and tf-module/egress-pool to manage node pools, tags, and autoscaling policies.

SLOs and thresholds:
- Per-tenant soft egress SLO: 250 Mbps sustained per GPU for "medium" profile, 50 Mbps for "low" profile.
- Node-level saturation alert: sustained >= 80% egress utilization for 60s => P3 alert (investigate).
- Tail-latency objective: 99th percentile generation latency < 450ms for latency-tier customers; placement policy aims to keep node egress headroom >= 30% for those tenants.

Node labeling and tagging conventions:
- node.kubernetes.io/gpu-type = a100|h100|t4
- node.redwood/egress-capacity-mbps = "4000" (example per-node uplink)
- node.redwood/egress-pool = "high-throughput" | "isolation" | "shared"
- Tenants are annotated via tenant-metadata-service with tenant.egress_profile = "low|medium|high". This drives placement decisions.

Placement policy rules (ordered):
1) If tenant.egress_profile == "isolation", place on nodes in egress-pool=isolation (single-tenant node pool).
2) Else prefer nodes where (node.egress_free_mbps - requested_estimated_mbps) >= 30% of node.egress_capacity.
3) When multiple candidates, prefer the node with lowest co-located "high" tenants count.
4) If no node satisfies headroom, route to dedicated burst pool (capacity permitting) or fall back to cross-region placement as configured by routing policy (costly; used as last resort).

Estimating requested_estimated_mbps (simple estimator):
- generate request: token-rate * avg-token-size-bytes * api-overhead-factor -> convert to Mbps.
- Embedding-heavy jobs include an override parameter in the request metadata to help allocator (recommended).

IaC module contract (variables and defaults):
| variable | type | default | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| egress_pool_name | string | "shared" | Name for the egress pool attached to node group |
| node_egress_capacity_mbps | number | "4000" | Advertised uplink capacity for node type |
| isolation_max_tenants | number | "1" | Max tenants for isolation pool nodes |
| enable_egress_shaper | bool | "true" | Inject egress sidecar configuration |
| autoscale_min | number | "1" | Min node count |
| autoscale_max | number | "50" | Max node count |

(Represented above as a preformatted table in Confluence - the IaC modules in the repo use these variables.)

CI/CD and gating for IaC changes:
- All changes to tf-module/gpu-node-profile or tf-module/egress-pool must have:
  - an accompanying plan that includes an estimated egress capacity delta and tenant-impact analysis.
  - at least two reviewers from eng-infra and eng-platform (automated reviewer assignment: CODEOWNERS).
  - Canary deployment: promote to a single region small pool (canary pool) behind feature-flag:placement.egress-aware=true.
- Automated tests in the CI pipeline (Buildkite):
  - terraform fmt & validate
  - unit tests for module input validation (go/py tests)
  - integration test: deploy a small cluster in ephemeral sandbox, simulate three tenant profiles and verify scheduler respects headroom constraints.

Rollout playbook (high-level):
1) Create IaC change with new variables set for isolation pools and node annotations.
2) Run CI, deploy to staging region, run integration test harness (see infra/ci-eval).
3) Enable canary pool in us-west1 with 3 nodes; route 5% of matching traffic via feature-flag routing.
4) Observe for 48 hours: target metrics (node egress utilization, 99p latency, tenant error rate).
5) Gradually ramp to 25% -> 50% -> 100% by region using rollout automation.
6) If any threshold breach occurs (see Rollback criteria), disable feature-flag and revert IaC changes.

Rollback criteria (automated):
- 99p latency for priority tenants increases > 20% over baseline for 30m.
- Node-level network saturation > 95% for 10m.
- Unbounded increase in network error rates (5xx) for any tenant > 1% of requests for 15m.

Operational runbook (responding to an egress hotspot):
1) Detect: Prometheus alert egress_node_sustained_high (>=80% for 5m).
2) Triage: identify top contributors using egress_sharder.flow_breakdown_by_tenant dashboard.
3) Immediate mitigation options (in order):
   a) Evict best-effort pods for non-isolated tenants from affected node: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 <node>
   b) Apply temporary per-tenant shaping via egress-sharder: redwoodctl egress-sharder throttle --tenant=<id> --mbps=100
   c) Scale up isolation/burst node pool (if autoscale_max allows): terraform apply -var="egress_pool_name=burst" -auto-approve
4) If eviction or shaping insufficient, enable cross-region fallback in gpu-allocator config for impacted tenant(s): update placement policy via config map and restart allocator (rolling): kubectl rollout restart deployment/gpu-allocator
5) Post-incident: run hotspot postmortem, capture tenant patterns, and consider promoting heavy tenants to scheduled isolation pools (owner: capacity team).

Monitoring and dashboards (recommended panels):
- Node egress utilization (per-node, 1m/5m/1h)
- Top-20 tenant egress by node
- 99p generation latency by tenant tier
- Egress sharder drop/shape rates and per-tenant throttles
- IaC drift: desired node annotations vs observed annotations

Prometheus alerts (examples):
- alert: NodeEgressSustainedHigh
  expr: node_network_transmit_bytes_rate{job="node-exporter"} / node.redwood_egress_capacity_mbps > 0.8
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: "warning" }
- alert: PriorityTenantLatencyRegression
  expr: increase(request_latency_count{priority="high",quantile="0.99"}[30m]) > scalar(0) and (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant)) > 450)
  for: 10m
  labels: { severity: "critical" }

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: capacity@redwood (capacity team)
- Service owner: eng-infra GPU team (oncall: infra-gpu@pagerduty)
- IaC module owner: infra-iac (codeowners: @infra-iac)

Post-incident actions and continuous improvement:
- Add failing tenant patterns to synthetic load tests and CI integration tests.
- Consider quota or surcharge for sustained high egress to encourage tenant migration to isolation pools. Finance and pricing should be consulted before enforcement.

Appendix A — Example terraform snippet (gpu node pool):
```hcl
module "egress_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/tf-module/egress-pool.git"
  name   = "isolation-eu-west1"
  node_egress_capacity_mbps = 10000
  isolation_max_tenants = 1
  autoscale_min = 1
  autoscale_max = 10
}
```

Appendix B — Quick CLI commands:
- throttle tenant: redwoodctl egress-sharder throttle --tenant=tenant_123 --mbps=150
- force drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- restart allocator: kubectl rollout restart deployment/gpu-allocator -n redwood-infra

Notes and references:
- For full billing/chargeback integration see cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-billing-clarity-and-multipath-metering-spec.json
- For scheduler internals see eng-infra/team-wiki/gpu-allocator-safety-checklist-and-iac-adapter-guide.json

Revision history:
- 2024-07-15: Drafted by Priya Patel (initial policy, metrics, and IaC contract).
- 2024-11-02: Updated SLOs and added egress-sharder integration (reviewers: Diego Morales).
- 2025-02-10: Finalized rollout playbook, CI gating steps, and example Terraform snippet.

payload.page_title: Egress temporal smoothing and burst fallback protocol

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines the egress temporal-smoothing strategy and the end-to-end burst-fallback protocol used by Redwood’s tenant egress pipeline. It covers the design, operational playbook, Terraform configuration snippets, alerting rules, and post-incident checks used when tenants hit short-lived egress spikes that could otherwise lead to cross-tenant impact or billing anomalies.

Goals

- Protect shared outbound bandwidth and NAT resources from short-lived tenant spikes.
- Provide graceful degradation and predictable latency for active inference requests.
- Ensure automated fallback to burst capacity with safe accounting and recoverable state.
- Make the mechanism auditable and reversible via IaC and telemetry.

Scope

Includes: tenant-level egress credit ledger, local smoothing (token bucket + leaky window), global burst pool, redispatching to alternate regions, and the operational runbook for incidents.
Excludes: long-lived tenant policy changes (handled by quota service), cross-region legal/GDPR routing.

Terminology

- egress-credit-balance: numeric accounting of a tenant’s remaining burstable bytes.
- smoothing-window: a short window (default 30s) that averages egress rate to avoid immediate drops.
- burst-orchestrator: service that provides temporary egress capacity from the global pool.
- tenant-sidecar-proxy: per-tenant proxy that applies token-bucket smoothing and reports telemetry.

High-level architecture (text diagram)

Client -> tenant-sidecar-proxy -> local egress-shaper -> egress-allocator -> (normal NAT path OR burst-orchestrator) -> internet

Key services and ownership

- tenant-sidecar-proxy (service-tenant-proxy) — owner: eng-infra/networking
- egress-allocator (service-egress-allocator) — owner: eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking
- burst-orchestrator (service-burst-orchestrator) — owner: eng-fleet/capacity
- billing-ledger (service-credit-ledger) — owner: finance-legal (integration maintained by eng-infra)

SLOs and thresholds

- Normal egress latency (measured at sidecar): p95 <= 120ms
- Degradation tolerance during burst fallback: p95 <= 500ms (target)
- Egress credit low watermark: 20% of tenant's configured burst allowance (alert)
- Global burst pool reserve: 10% of total pool must be reserved for emergency SLA-preserving operations

Config table (defaults)

| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| smoothing_window | 30s | Rolling window for leaky averaging |
| token_bucket_size | 10MB | Max instantaneous allowance before smoothing applies |
| token_fill_rate | 1MB/s | Sustained replenishment rate for standard tenants |
| burst_pool_size | 2TB | Global burst capacity available for all tenants |
| burst_max_per_tenant | 200MB | Max concurrent burst allocation per tenant |
| preemptive_reclaim_delay | 60s | Wait before reclaiming burst capacity from low-priority tenants |

Terraform / IaC snippet (usage pattern)

Below is an example Terraform variable block used by the burst-orchestrator module. It is intentionally simplified for clarity:

```
variable "egress_burst_profile" {
  description = "Per-tenant burst profile: size (bytes), refill_rate (bytes/s), priority"
  type = map(object({
    size        = number
    refill_rate = number
    priority    = string
  }))
  default = {
    "default-tenant" = { size = 209715200, refill_rate = 1048576, priority = "standard" }
  }
}

module "burst_orchestrator" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules//burst-orchestrator"
  global_pool_size = 2199023255552  # 2 TB in bytes
  profiles         = var.egress_burst_profile
}
```

Prometheus alert examples

- Alert: EgressCreditLow
  - expr: egress_credit_balance_bytes{job="service-credit-ledger"} < (tenant_burst_allowance_bytes * 0.2)
  - for: 5m
  - labels: severity=warning, team=infra-networking
  - annotations: runbook=/confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-temporal-smoothing-and-burst-fallback-protocol.json

- Alert: BurstPoolDepletion
  - expr: sum(burst_pool_free_bytes{job="service-burst-orchestrator"}) / sum(burst_pool_total_bytes{job="service-burst-orchestrator"}) < 0.10
  - for: 1m
  - labels: severity=critical, team=infra-sre
  - annotations: pagerduty=infra-oncall

Operational runbook: tenant spike detected

1) Detection (automated):
   - Pager triggers: EgressCreditLow OR tenant-sidecar-proxy reports sustained egress_bytes/s > (token_fill_rate * 3) for > 20s.
2) Automated smoothing:
   - tenant-sidecar-proxy engages smoothing-window and applies token-bucket enforcement. The client sees backpressure (HTTP 429 with Retry-After header) if immediate rate > token_bucket_size.
3) Automated fallback:
   - egress-allocator requests burst from burst-orchestrator (gRPC: AllocateBurst(tenant_id, requested_bytes)).
   - If allocation successful, apply NAT path binding to the tenant’s burst pool subnet and update billing-ledger via /api/v1/credits/alloc.
4) If allocation fails (insufficient pool):
   - Policy order: a) try alternate region with spare burst capacity (redispatch), b) gracefully queue requests locally for up to 10s, c) apply tenant-priority preemptive reclaim signals.
5) Human escalation (if automated measures fail):
   - Notify infra-oncall (pagerduty) with tag: "egress-burst-fallback-failed".
   - Runbook owner: eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking oncall.

Manual mitigation commands (kubectl / CLI)

- Force an allocation snapshot and inspect allocations:
  kubectl -n infra logs deploy/service-burst-orchestrator --tail=200 | grep "AllocationSnapshot"

- Revoke a tenant allocation (immediate reclaim):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://burst-orchestrator.internal/api/v1/revoke -d '{"tenant_id":"TENANT_ID","bytes":104857600}'

- Move a tenant to alternate egress pool (redispatch):
  terraform apply -var='tenant_egress_pool=eu-west-redispatch' -target=module.tenant_onboarding

Post-incident checklist

- Confirm billing-ledger allocations matched actual egress usage (finance reconciliation).
- Increase smoothing_window or token_fill_rate for tenants with repeated short spikes, or create a custom burst profile.
- Run a capacity simulation (see section "Simulation and testing") to validate pool sizing and preemptive reclaim tuning.
- Add retrospective notes with timeline and affected tenants.

Simulation and testing

- Use the egress-load-generator harness located in infra-eval repo: scripts/egress-flood-test.py.
- Test cases: short spike (60s), multi-tenant coordinated spike (10 tenants, 30s), region failover path (simulate eu->us redispatch).
- Success criteria: no tenant p95 > 2x normal latency after fallback, burst_pool_free_bytes never goes below reserve.

Telemetry and dashboards
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- global: burst_pool_total_bytes, burst_pool_free_bytes, burst_allocations_by_tenant (top 20)
- per-tenant: egress_credit_balance_bytes, egress_bytes_per_second, sidecar_backpressure_rate (429/s)
- system health: allocator_error_rate, orchestrator_alloc_latency_p95

Audit and compliance notes

- All allocations are recorded in the billing-ledger with a unique allocation_id and TTL. Retention: 1 year.
- For private deployments, the burst-orchestrator module ships a PII-safe mode that masks tenant identifiers in telemetry.

Risks and trade-offs

- Aggressive smoothing increases tail latency for short-running inference requests. Balance with business needs.
- Large global burst pools can mask tenant anti-patterns; use periodic reviews and quota guardrails.

Future improvements

- Adaptive smoothing windows driven by per-tenant workload classification.
- Machine-learned prefetching into burst pool based on historical spike likelihood.
- Expose a self-serve tenant UI in Redwood Console for temporary burst purchase with auto-reconcile.

Appendix: quick incident timeline template

1. Detected: <timestamp> — alert fired (EgressCreditLow/BurstPoolDepletion)
2. Automated actions: <timestamp> — smoothing applied, burst allocate attempted
3. Allocation result: <timestamp> — success/failure and allocation_id
4. Manual actions: <timestamp> — oncall actions and commands run
5. Resolved: <timestamp> — final state and SLA impact

Appendix: contact matrix

- infra-oncall: #pagerduty-infra (primary)
- network-eng: network-eng@redwood.com
- finance-ops: billing-ops@redwood.com

Document history

- 2024-11-12: Created by Maya Chen
- 2025-02-20: Tested and updated runbook steps; added Terraform examples (Priya Natarajan)

payload.page_title: Bastionless GPU Access and IaC Playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the recommended architecture, Terraform/IaC modules, and runbook for *bastionless* access to on-prem or VPC-isolated GPU nodes. The goal is to enable secure, auditable, ephemeral developer and operator access without a permanent bastion host, lowering attack surface while preserving fast interactive debugging.

Scope and applicability
-----------------------
- Applies to on-prem GPU clusters and private VPC deployments used for inference or evaluation where SSH/RDP-like access is required for debugging, profiling, or emergency remediation.
- Intended for GPU infra owners, SREs, and platform eng who manage node images, networking, and access tooling.
- Not a replacement for fully automated remediation; use for short-lived investigative sessions only.

Assumptions
-----------
- Central identity provider supports OIDC and short-lived certificates (e.g., Okta/GCP/Azure AD).
- Customers/operators can run a small control-plane service in the perimeter (K8s, VM) that acts as an access broker.
- Terraform module repository is available at git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//bastionless-tunnel

High-level architecture
-----------------------
1) Access broker (control-plane): mTLS-protected service in a public subnet that exchanges OIDC tokens for ephemeral SSH certs and injects ephemeral routes for a specific session.
2) Short-lived overlay tunnels: IPSec/WireGuard or TLS-based tunnels created per-session. Tunnels are timeboxed (default 15m) and automatically torn down.
3) Node-side agent: lightweight agent on GPU node (or sidecar) that accepts ephemeral certs and enforces ALLOW lists at process/user level.
4) Audit pipeline: all grants, cert issuance, and session metadata are written to the centralized audit log (immutable S3/GCS bucket + SIEM ingest).

Architecture diagram (text)
- User -> (OIDC) -> Access Broker -> (WireGuard mTLS tunnel) -> Node Agent -> GPU Node
- Audit -> S3 bucket + Dataflow -> Security team SIEM

Design goals and constraints
----------------------------
- No long-running bastion VMs or permanently open SSH ports.
- Least-privilege: every session scoped to a single node or node-set, single command scope optional.
- Short-lived credentials and network paths (default 15 minutes; min 5m, max 1h with approval).
- Full audit trail: who, when, command list (where legal), session duration, and outbound egress origin.

Terraform module & config table
-------------------------------
Below are the core variables and recommended defaults for the *bastionless-tunnel* module. Apply per-region.

| variable | type | default | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| region | string | us-west-2 | cloud region or datacenter identifier |
| onprem_subnet_cidr | string | 10.50.0.0/24 | CIDR for ephemeral tunnel endpoint on the customer side |
| broker_instance_count | number | 2 | HA pair recommended (keep odd for leader election) |
| oidc_provider_url | string | <required> | OIDC issuer used for short-lived cert exchange |
| max_session_ttl_minutes | number | 15 | enforcement ceiling for ephemeral tunnels |
| allowed_user_groups | list | ["infra-operators"] | IAM groups allowed to request sessions |
| audit_bucket | string | redwood-infra-audit | S3/GCS bucket for session logs |

Example Terraform snippet
-------------------------
```hcl
module "bastionless_tunnel" {
  source            = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//bastionless-tunnel?ref=v0.3.1"
  region            = "us-west-2"
  onprem_subnet_cidr = "10.50.0.0/24"
  broker_instance_count = 2
  oidc_provider_url  = "https://accounts.redwood.ai"
  max_session_ttl_minutes = 15
  allowed_user_groups = ["infra-operators", "oncall-gpu"]
  audit_bucket = "redwood-infra-gpu-audit"
}
```

Network firewall / NAT rules (minimum)
-------------------------------------
- Allow outbound 443 from broker to OIDC provider and SIEM endpoint.
- Allow broker -> node control port (WireGuard UDP 51820 or configured TLS port).
- Restrict management plane to known IP ranges and tenant tags.

Operational runbook: typical session flow
---------------------------------------
1) Request: Operator runs CLI/console to request a session. Example:
   - redwoodctl access request --node gpu-node-123 --ttl 15m --reason "perf-debug"
2) Broker validates OIDC token, group membership, and optional 2nd factor.
3) Broker provisions ephemeral WireGuard keypair and injects a temporary route via SDN controller (or BGP session) scoped to the node for the session TTL.
4) Node agent accepts the ephemeral key and starts a lightweight tunnel endpoint bound to localhost:2222.
5) Operator connects: ssh -i /tmp/session.key -p 2222 operator@gpu-node-123 (proxying through local tunnel).
6) On session expiry or manual termination, broker signals node agent to tear down tunnel and revokes certs; audit event recorded.

Emergency remediation (when ephemeral path fails)
------------------------------------------------
1) If automated tunnel creation fails:
   - Step 1: Re-run `redwoodctl access request` with `--debug` and capture broker logs.
   - Step 2: Verify SDN controller accepted the route (check BGP/route-update logs).
   - Step 3: If node-agent failed to bind, use the control-plane API to push the agent status patch or rebootstrap the agent via: `kubectl -n infra-tools rollout restart daemonset/gpu-node-agent`.
   - Step 4: If immediate access still required and security-approved, escalate to oncall and temporarily open port 22 from your IP with a short TTL rule in the perimeter firewall (manual exception tracked in ticket).

Canary rollout checklist (how we deploy this capability safely)
---------------------------------------------------------------
1) Deploy broker and Node Agent in non-prod region. Verify session lifecycle end-to-end.
2) Add telemetry: session_issued_total, session_failed_total, tunnel_create_latency_seconds.
3) Enable audit export to staging SIEM.
4) Run 50 low-risk sessions (15m each) and validate no data-plane leakage.
5) Gradually enable in prod for a subset of tenants (feature flag) with 24/7 oncall coverage for first 72 hours.

Monitoring, SLOs and alerting
-----------------------------
- SLOs (access flow):
  - Mean tunnel creation latency < 5s (95th percentile < 15s).
  - Cert issuance success rate >= 99.5%.
  - Unauthorized access attempts < 0.5% of total requests.
- Key alerts:
  - FIRING: session_failed_total > 5 in 5m (severity P2)
  - FIRING: cert_issue_latency_seconds:95th > 30s (P2)
  - FIRING: audit_sink_write_errors > 0 (P1)
- Suggested PromQL examples: `sum(rate(session_failed_total[5m])) by (region) > 5`

Security & compliance notes
--------------------------
- All session metadata must be retained for at least 365 days in the audit bucket.
- Node agents must run as unprivileged processes; do not give direct root shells by default. Use sudo policies limited to a pre-approved command list.
- Approvals for session TTL > 1h must be recorded with a time-stamped signature in the ticket system.
- Periodic automated penetration tests should validate that ephemeral tunnels cannot be extended past TTL.

Testing & CI/CD guidance
-----------------------
- Add unit tests for the Terraform module variables and a plan-stage check that denies if `max_session_ttl_minutes` > 60.
- Integration tests: a small VM-based harness that performs a full session lifecycle (request -> connect -> run command -> teardown) as part of the CI pipeline. Use ephemeral GPU testbeds in the CI environment.
- Release gating: require `tfsec` and `checkov` scans, plus e2e session probe success >= 95% before promote.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: infra-networking (team alias: infra-networking@redwood.ai)
- Secondary owner: gpu-runtime@redwood.ai
- Oncall rotation: infra-sre oncall; escalate per standard incident process.

References and related pages
---------------------------
- gpu-bastion-hardening-and-remote-debugging-runbook (existing)
- onprem-packaging/airgap-gpu-image-promotion-and-hsm-signing-pipeline (for image provenance)

Appendix: quick CLI examples
---------------------------
- Request session:
  `redwoodctl access request --node gpu-node-123 --ttl 15m --reason "OOM trace"`
- Revoke session (manual stop):
  `redwoodctl access revoke --session-id sess-20250214-84f`
- Debug broker logs:
  `kubectl -n infra-broker logs deployment/broker -f --since=1h`

Change log
----------
- 2024-11-05: Created (Aisha Patel).
- 2025-02-14: Added canary checklist and tightened SLOs (Marco Chen).

End of playbook.

payload.page_title: tenant-egress-burst-budgeting-and-cni-qos-playbook

sections.body:
Overview
This document defines the design and operational procedures for enforcing tenant-level egress burst budgets and applying CNI-based QoS shaping for inference (GPU-backed) pods. The goal is to provide predictable egress spend and stable network behavior for latency-sensitive inference while preserving the ability to burst for short windows.

This is targeted at platform infra engineers who own multi-tenant GPU clusters, networking and cost allocation (eng-infra + cloud accounts team).

Goals
- Prevent unbounded egress spikes that cause billing surprises and noisy-neighbor effects.
- Allow short burst windows (seconds-to-minutes) for model cold-start KV cache warmups and eval jobs.
- Provide clear observable signals and automated throttling fallback to protect SLOs.
- Integrate policy as code into Terraform/IaC and CI so changes are reviewable and testable.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: Kubernetes clusters running inference services (GKE/EKS/AKS), VPC egress path accounting, per-tenant billing tags, CNI tc-based shaping via node-init daemonset.
- Non-goal: Replacing L7 application rate-limiting (those remain in-app). This doc focuses on infra-level protection and cost control.

Terminology
- tenant: logical customer or product team mapped to cloud account or tenant label.
- egress-burst-credit: short-duration burst allowance measured in MiB/minute or tokenized credits.
- sustained-budget: steady-state egress rate in MiB/minute that a tenant can consume without throttling.

Design summary
- Each tenant has two policy primitives: sustained-budget and burst-credits.
- Budgets are enforced at two layers: (1) Kubernetes node-level CNI shaping applied to pod sets via tc/netem classes, (2) VPC egress policer for cross-account/cross-region enforcement (where supported).
- A controller (policy-operator) maps tenant labels to tc configs and reconciles kernel qdisc state on each node.
- Billing telemetry is tagged with tenant identifiers; an aggregator correlates egress bytes to budget consumption and emits events when thresholds are crossed.

Architecture (text diagram)
- tenant app pods (node) --> CNI tc qdisc (per-tenant classes) --> node egress interface --> VPC NAT / egress gateway --> cloud egress meter --> billing collector

Policy primitives and config table
| Field | Description | Example |
|---|---:|---|
| tenant_id | canonical tenant label | tenant:acme-prod |
| sustained_budget_mib_per_min | long-run rate without throttling | 50 |
| burst_credits_mib | one-time burst window allowance | 500 |
| burst_decay_seconds | linear decay window for credits | 300 |
| hard_throttle_after_mib | absolute ceiling per-minute | 2000 |

Implementation details
1) Terraform module interface (IAC): create a reusable module that publishes tenant budgets and IAM bindings. Example usage:

```
module "tenant_egress_budget_acme" {
  source = "git::ssh://github.com/redwood-infra/terraform//modules/tenant-egress-budget"
  tenant_id = "acme-prod"
  sustained_budget_mib_per_min = 50
  burst_credits_mib = 500
  burst_decay_seconds = 300
  quota_owner = "team-acme"
}
```

Module outputs should include a policy resource id and a K8s ConfigMap payload that the cluster policy-operator consumes.

2) Policy-operator contract
- A lightweight controller runs in each cluster with the following responsibilities:
  - Watch ConfigMaps in a control namespace for tenant budget records.
  - Reconcile node-level tc qdiscs into three classes per tenant: sustained, burst, and overflow (throttled).
  - Emit prometheus metrics: tenant_egress_bytes_total, tenant_egress_budget_remaining_mib, tenant_egress_throttle_events_total.

3) Node-level shaping (CNI integration)
We rely on CNI hooks (preStart or daemonset) to ensure qdisc and class setup per-tenant. Example tc commands that the operator applies:

```
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 30
sections.heading: create root qdisc

sections.body: tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:10 htb rate 50mbit ceil 50mbit
sections.heading: sustained class for tenant

sections.body: tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:20 htb rate 50mbit ceil 500mbit
sections.heading: burst class (higher ceil but token bucket enforced by operator)

sections.body:
tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:30 htb rate 10mbit ceil 10mbit
```

The operator programs filters to map pod IP CIDRs or cgroups to classes. Use cgroup v2 and net_cls where available for correctness.

4) VPC egress fallback
Where cloud provider allows (egress gateway or NAT gateway policies), the control plane also provisions IAM+route-based rules to apply a coarse-grained burst cap. This prevents a single noisy node from bypassing node-level shaping.

Observability and alerts
- Metrics (prometheus):
  - tenant_egress_bytes_total{tenant} (counter)
  - tenant_egress_budget_remaining_mib{tenant} (gauge)
  - tenant_egress_burst_consumed_mib{tenant} (counter)
  - tenant_egress_throttle_events_total{tenant} (counter)
  - node_qdisc_error_total (counter)

- Key alerts:
  1. Billing-early-warning: when tenant_egress_bytes_total in 24h > (sustained_budget_mib_per_min * 60 * 24 * 0.8) AND burst_consumed_mib > 0 -> paging to capacity-owner oncall if projected spend > $X/day.
  2. Throttle-surge: tenant_egress_throttle_events_total > 50 in 10m -> alert oncall and owners.
  3. Qdisc-desync: node_qdisc_error_total > 0 -> infra SRE investigation.

SLOs and thresholds
- Sustained egress budget usage must not exceed 110% of configured sustained_budget_mib_per_min for more than 10 minutes without triggering billing-early-warning.
- Node-level enforcement success rate (fraction of tenant classes reconciled without errors) > 99.5% per 24h.

CI/CD and test harness
- Terraform module acceptance tests (run in PR):
  - unit test verifies HCL plan contains expected resources and outputs.
  - integration test deploys module to a sandbox cloud account with mocked billing tags and verifies policy-operator picks up ConfigMap.
- Kubernetes e2e in CI: use KinD or a sandbox cluster to run the operator and a small synthetic tenant workload that produces controlled egress. Verify metrics and that tc classes are present on nodes.
- Chaotic test: inject packet-surge and verify fallback to VPC-level cap.

Deployment and rollout (safe path)
1. Create tenant budget in Terraform in a canary sandbox account.
2. Run CI integration test; validate operator metrics.
3. Apply to a single cluster and enable only monitoring mode (operator will not throttle, only emit events) for 48 hours.
4. Enable burst-region throttling (soft throttle) for a second cluster.
5. Full enablement: propagate configs to prod clusters.

Rollback and emergency steps
- If a tenant reports regressions (too aggressive throttling): set policy-operator into "monitor" mode for that tenant by annotating the ConfigMap (operator ignores qdisc changes). Rollback Terraform policy to previous stable version.
- If node-level qdisc corrupts many nodes: run automation to clear qdiscs and restart operator daemonset:

```
kubectl -n infra exec -it <node-debug-pod> -- bash -c 'tc qdisc del dev eth0 root || true'
kubectl -n infra rollout restart daemonset/policy-operator
```

Operational playbook (incident flow)
1. Receive alert: Throttle-surge.
2. Triage: check tenant_egress_budget_remaining_mib and burst_consumed_mib.
3. If consumption is expected (e.g., known eval run) notify tenant owner and ask to reduce concurrency; consider temporary increase of sustained_budget via emergency terraform change (MUST go through emergency change process).
4. If consumption is unexpected: run pod-level diagnosis (kubectl top pod, tcpdump on pod node) -> determine whether traffic is legitimate.
5. If malicious/bug: isolate tenant (set operator to monitor) and revoke external egress via cloud-level firewall + IAM to stop costs.
6. Post-incident: create incident note with root cause, explain remediation, and update regression tests.

Troubleshooting checklist
- No metrics for tenant: confirm ConfigMap present and operator logs show reconciled=true.
- Throttling but budget remains: verify tc filters map correct cgroup/pod ips. Check cgroup v2 mode.
- Billing mismatch: confirm cloud tags and billing collector's join keys match tenant_id. Re-run billing reconcile tool.

Security and least privilege
- Terraform module that provisions IAM roles for the operator must follow least-privilege: only allow reading ConfigMaps, writing to SSM/Parameter Store for policy metadata, and tagging resources. No broad ec2/nat gateway modify rights unless explicitly approved.

Change control and testing matrix
- Minor changes to sustained_budget: PR -> automated tests -> canary cluster monitor -> 24h -> gradual rollout.
- Changes to operator binary or qdisc templates: PR -> e2e + canary -> staged rollout across node pools.

Appendix A: Example ConfigMap payload (operator input)
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: tenant-egress-acme-prod
  namespace: infra-policy
data:
  tenant_id: "acme-prod"
  sustained_budget_mib_per_min: "50"
  burst_credits_mib: "500"
  burst_decay_seconds: "300"
  hard_throttle_after_mib: "2000"
```

Appendix B: Verification checklist (pre-merge)
- [ ] Terraform plan shows only expected additions.
- [ ] Module tests pass (unit + integration).
- [ ] Operator logs show no reconciliation errors in sandbox.
- [ ] Prometheus metrics for tenant appear within 5 minutes post-deploy.

Related pages
- See also: egress metering and billing spec; preflight GPU deployment validation runbook.

Owner and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-infra:networking (Aisha Patel)
- Oncall: cloud-accounts oncall rotation

Document history
- 2024-09-18: created (Aisha Patel)
- 2024-11-04: added node-level tc examples and prometheus metrics (Carlos Mendes)
- 2025-01-14: clarified CI harness steps and emergency rollback commands (Priya Rao)
