payload.page_title: Edge-to-Core GPU Offload: Network, Egress Controls, and IaC Patterns

sections.body: This doc describes a standardized, SLO-driven pattern for offloading inference work from edge-deployed GPU nodes to core/cloud GPU pools. It covers networking and egress controls, Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD promotion guidance, operational runbook steps for capacity and cost incidents, and the telemetry/alerting contract teams must implement. The goal is to enable predictable performance and cost visibility while preserving tenant isolation and safety for regulated workloads.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Edge device pools (on-prem, retail sites, customer-managed racks) occasionally need to offload heavy sequences or large-batch evals to core GPUs.
- Workloads that degrade tail latency on the edge when run locally (e.g., long-context generations, large batch retraining).
- Customers that require local inference for privacy-sensitive inputs but allow aggregated or redacted offload.
sections.heading: When to use this pattern

sections.body:
1) Decision boundary: a local router component (edge-router) applies policy rules to decide if a request stays local or is offloaded. Policies consider sequence length, model family, tenant egress budget, and KV cache hit.
2) Secure egress tunnel: offloads travel over a mutually authenticated tunnel (mTLS or AWS PrivateLink) with per-tenant service accounts and scoped IAM roles.
3) Cost-aware throttling: an egress controller evaluates daily/rolling credits and applies backpressure or degradation (model quantized variant) when budgets approach thresholds.
4) Fallback/hedging: always attempt local quick-pass; if local slow-path begins, start a hedged request to core and cancel the slower path when the first completes.
5) IaC modules: a composable Terraform module exposes variables for routing policies, egress budgets, IAM bindings, and network endpoints to be consumed by both edge and core stacks.
sections.heading: High-level design

sections.body:
- Successful offload completion (core) 99.95% per 7d window.
- Median offload latency (edge->core->resp) < 1200ms for short sequences, < 2000ms for long sequences.
- 99th percentile < 5s (non-real-time batch workloads excluded).
- Egress budget warning at 70% of daily/rolling budget; automatic soft-throttle at 90%; hard block at 100% unless override by oncall.
sections.heading: SLOs and thresholds (recommended)

sections.body:
- Metrics (per-tenant): offload_requests_total, offload_success_total, offload_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), egress_bytes, egress_cost_estimate_usd.
- Traces: distributed tracing across edge-router -> tunnel -> core-serving (span naming: edge.router.offload, network.tunnel.tx, core.inference.serve).
- Alert rules: offload_success_rate < 99.9% over 5m (sev2), egress_budget_usage >= 90% (cost-alert sev2), offload_latency_p95 >= 3s for >10% of tenants (perf-eng sev2).
sections.heading: Telemetry & dashboards (required)

sections.body:
- Module responsibilities:
  - networking: provision PrivateLink/NLB endpoints, VPC peering config, subnet routing assertions
  - security: create offload-specific IAM roles, STS trust policies, KMS keys for in-flight key wrapping
  - service: register edge-router service discovery entry and per-tenant egress quota object
sections.heading: Terraform / IaC patterns (example)

sections.body:
| variable | type | default | description |
|---------|------|---------|-------------|
| region | string | "us-west-2" | Core region for offload endpoints |
| offload_network_mode | string | "privatelink" | one of ["privatelink","mtls","vpn"] |
| daily_egress_budget_gb | number | "5" | per-tenant soft budget in GB/day |
| enable_burst | bool | "true" | allow short burst above budget with analytics capture |
sections.heading: Example module interface (variables and defaults table)

sections.body:
```
module "edge_to_core_offload" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.example.com/infra/terraform-modules.git//edge-offload?ref=v1.2.0"
  region = var.core_region
  offload_network_mode = "privatelink"
  daily_egress_budget_gb = lookup(var.tenant_defaults, "egress_budget_gb", 5)
  enable_burst = true
}
```
sections.heading: Terraform snippet (consuming module)

sections.body:
- Use regional PrivateLink or equivalent to avoid public egress where possible. If PrivateLink is unavailable, require mTLS over NAT egress with strict IP allowlists.
- Split control plane vs data plane: control plane (service discovery, policies) should use dedicated control subnets with least-privilege security groups. Data plane traffic flows over dedicated attachment subnets with high MTU and flow logs enabled.
- Egress cost accounting: tag offload flows with per-tenant identifiers at the NAT/proxy layer for billing. Enforce egress marking headers at the edge-router so core billing pipelines can attribute cost.
sections.heading: Network design patterns and constraints

sections.body:
1) Module versioning: follow semver for the edge-offload module. Breaking changes must have a migration guide file in the module repo.
2) Integration tests: provide a lightweight emulation harness that spins up a fake core endpoint and validates hedging, cancelation, and egress marking flows. Run in PRs and nightly canaries.
3) Canary rollout: deploy edge-router changes to a single tenant or 2% of edge nodes, monitor p99 latency and offload success rate for 24 hours before broader promotion.
4) Safety gates: terraform plan must include a diff check that ensures no new open egress rules are added without an explicit reviewer tag.

Operational runbook: Offload incident flow
- Trigger: alert for offload_success_rate < 99.9% or offload_latency_p95 spike.
- Owner: oncall-infra (primary) -> runtime-team (secondary).
sections.heading: CI/CD and promotion guidance

sections.body:
1) Triage: check dashboard for tenant impact, identify whether failures are network (tunnel) or core serving errors.
2) Confirm NAT/PrivateLink health: run quick checks from an affected edge node:
   - curl -v https://offload-core.example.internal/healthz (expect 200)
   - tcpdump -i <iface> 'tcp port 443' -w /tmp/offload.pcap (capture 30s)
3) If tunnel down: verify edge-router certificate validity, rotate cert if expired, and restart edge-router with zero-downtime rolling restart: kubectl rollout restart deploy/edge-router -n infra-edge.
4) If core saturated: validate core GPU pool metrics (utilization > 85%), check autoscaler and queued_requests_total. Scale path:
   - Increase reserved_capacity in the dedicated GPU autoscaler manifest (path: //deploy/core/autoscaler/overrides.yaml) and apply via the safe-promote pipeline (ci/cd).
5) If egress budget breach: notify tenant with pre-defined template, optionally flip tenant policy to local-only (toggle in tenant policy store) and credit-back actions.
6) Post-incident: open an incident ticket, attach traces, and run a short RCA focusing on whether router heuristics underpredicted sequence length or cache misses spiked.
sections.heading: Steps

sections.body:
- PII: only allow offload if inputs are marked offloadable by upstream PII classifier. Documented flag: input_metadata.offload_allowed = true.
- Audit logging: every offload decision must include a reason code (e.g., cache_miss, seq_len_gt_2048, model_not_supported) and recorded to a tamper-evident audit log persisted for 90 days.
- KMS: use envelope encryption with per-tenant KMS keys when moving sensitive payloads; module exposes a kms_key_id variable.
sections.heading: Safety and compliance notes

sections.body:
1) Revert to previous module tag via terraform workspace and apply.
2) If terraform revert fails due to drift, run the emergency manual remediation script located in //infra/tools/edge-offload/fix_drift.sh and notify oncall.
3) Ensure tenant egress policies are re-applied and validate with the integration harness.
sections.heading: Rollback checklist for a bad module deploy

sections.body:
- Runtime infra (owner): runtime-team@redwood.example.com (primary oncall)
- Network & Egress (owner): cloud-networking@redwood.example.com
- Module maintainer: infra-modules-team (github: infra/edge-offload)
- Escalation: Head of Infrastructure (Marco Ruiz)

Appendix A: Example k8s annotations (edge-router):
- annotations:
  - "offload.redwood.io/egress-budget-gb": "5"
  - "offload.redwood.io/priority": "standard"
  - "offload.redwood.io/policy-hash": "${policy_hash}"

Appendix B: Example audit entry (JSON line)
{"ts":"2025-02-06T15:04:05Z","tenant":"tenant-42","decision":"offload","reason":"seq_len_gt_2048","egress_bytes":1240000,"trace_id":"abcd-1234"}

Appendix C: Quick verification checklist (preflight before onboarding tenant):
- PrivateLink endpoint is reachable from sample edge node (curl to healthz).
- IAM role binding exists with only necessary STS AssumeRole permissions.
- Billing tagging header is applied and visible in core http logs.
- E2E test in CI passes (hedge/cancel, latencies under threshold).
sections.heading: Ownership and contacts

sections.body:
- Maintainer must update the runbook after any major change to the hedging algorithm or offload policy.
- Quarterly review with cloud-networking and runtime-team is required; schedule is maintained in the infra-team calendar.
sections.heading: Document maintenance

sections.body:
- github.com/redwood/infra/edge-offload-module (Terraform module and unit tests)
- github.com/redwood/runtime/edge-router (edge routing logic & canary harness)
- dashboards: /dashboards/edge-offload/overview (shared read-only)

End of document.

payload.page_title: Self-service tenant provisioning and KMS rotation patterns

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines a self-service tenant provisioning flow for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem variants) and prescribes KMS/HSM credential rotation patterns. It is intended for platform engineers operating Private control planes and field engineers responsible for customer onboards. The goals are: reduce time-to-tenant, maintain cryptographic hygiene, and provide safe emergency rotation and rollback procedures.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Redwood Private (VPC-hosted control plane) and on-prem packaged runtime installations.
- Covers tenant bootstrap (network + compute + storage), tenant API keys and TLS cert issuance, and cloud/customer KMS/HSM integration rotation patterns.
- Does NOT cover supply-chain signing of binary images (see onprem-packaging/hardware-root-of-trust playbook).

Actors and responsibilities
---------------------------
- Platform (owner): implement and maintain automation, RBAC templates, and audit hooks.
- Field Ops / Customer Success: validate provisioning results, perform acceptance testing with customers.
- Security: approve rotation schedule, emergency thresholds, and HSM usage patterns.
- Customer IAM Admin: grant network-level connectivity and KMS credentials for integration.

Design and architecture overview
------------------------------
High-level design: self-service provisioning is implemented as an API-backed orchestration service that drives Terraform modules and the control-plane onboarding API. The orchestration produces three canonical artifacts per tenant: network bundle, runtime tenant object, and credential bundle. KMS integrations are stored as references in the tenant object; actual DEK/KEK material remains in customer KMS/HSM where possible.

Diagram (text)
- User/Portal -> Provisioning API -> Orchestrator -> Terraform modules -> Customer VPC / On-prem installer
- Provisioning API -> Control Plane (tenant object) -> Key references -> KMS/HSM

Prerequisites
-------------
1. Platform automation account credentials with least privilege to create VPC subnets, route tables, and provision compute resources.
2. Terraform state backend configured (S3/GCS with encryption).
3. Control plane API endpoint reachable from orchestrator.
4. Customer KMS/HSM credentials (service account with crypto:Encrypt/Decrypt or HSM token).
5. Approved RBAC templates and a signing key for tenant API keys.

Provisioning flow (step-by-step)
-------------------------------
1. Customer or internal operator submits a tenant request via portal or CLI (fields: tenant-id, name, deployment-target, cidr, kms-integration, sla-tier).
2. Validation step: check CIDR availability, quota, and routeability. Return failure with remediation steps if validation fails.
3. Create network bundle using Terraform module: subnets, route tables, NAT/egress, security-groups.
4. Create runtime tenant object via control plane API including KMS reference, quota profile, and metadata.
5. Generate ephemeral bootstrap credential sealed by platform signing key. Store credential in tenant vault and return secure pointer to customer.
6. Kick off post-provision tests: TLS handshake test, KV cache warm-up, and sample inference request against canary model.
7. Mark tenant as Live and start meter/telemetry collection.

CLI example (provision)
-----------------------
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
redwoodctl tenant create --id acme-2027 --target vpc-us-west-2 --cidr 10.20.0.0/24 --kms customer-kms-ref --sla business

Terraform snippet (network module invocation)
-------------------------------------------
module "tenant_network" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.company/internal-modules//tenant-network?ref=v1.3.0"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  cidr = var.tenant_cidr
  region = var.region
  egress_nat = true
}

Required IAM / Permissions (table)
---------------------------------
| Actor | Minimum permissions | Purpose |
|-------|---------------------|---------|
| Orchestrator service account | ec2:CreateNetworkInterface, ec2:CreateRoute, iam:PassRole, kms:Encrypt (if storing sealed values) | Create cloud resources and store sealed secrets |
| Control Plane API service | dynamodb:PutItem, s3:PutObject, kms:Decrypt (to read customer references) | Persist tenant state and access metadata |
| Field operator | iam:ListRoles, iam:GetRole, ec2:Describe* | Troubleshooting and validation |

KMS / HSM integration patterns
------------------------------
sections.heading: example CLI invocation (simplified)

sections.body:
1) Customer-managed KMS/HSM (recommended): Customer keeps KEKs/DEKs; Redwood stores only references and uses the customer KMS via API.
2) Customer-managed KMS with platform proxy: Customer allows Redwood a dedicated service principal with narrowly scoped keys and rotation hooks.
3) Platform-managed envelope keys (fallback): Redwood manages a KEK in our KMS and encrypts tenant DEKs; used only when customers cannot provide KMS.

Rotation strategy and cadence
---------------------------
- Tenant DEKs (data encryption keys): rotate every 90 days by default.
- Tenant API signing keys: rotate every 180 days.
- TLS leaf certs: rotate per-certificate CA policy (default 365 days); wildcard certs 2x per year.
- Emergency rotation: trigger when a key compromise is suspected or when an HSM reports anomalous activity.

Automated rotation sequence (customer-managed KMS)
1. Orchestrator schedules rotation job in 7-day window.
2. Orchestrator requests new DEK from customer KMS using the existing KEK.
3. Orchestrator re-encrypts any stored tenant secrets with the new DEK locally (sealed envelope) and updates tenant object with new key reference.
4. Warmup: perform a smoke inference with KV cache to validate runtime accepts new key.
5. Commit: mark rotation complete and emit audit event.

Emergency rotation and rollback
------------------------------
sections.heading: We support three integration patterns (ordered by security)

sections.body:
- Thresholds: >3 failed KMS auth in 1 hour, HSM physical alert, or confirmed leaked API key.
- Steps:
  1) Pause all automated key fetches and set tenant-level circuit breaker.
  2) Create emergency DEK with platform HSM when customer-managed KMS is unavailable.
  3) Reconfigure runtime to accept the emergency DEK (maintain dual-key acceptance for 10 minutes).
  4) Revoke compromised credentials and issue new bootstrap credentials.
  5) Run acceptance smoke tests and reopen the tenant.
sections.heading: Emergency rotation checklist

sections.body:
- If rotation causes failures in >1% of sampled requests over 10 minutes, revert to previous DEK by re-inserting the prior key reference and restart services. Log the event and trigger a postmortem.

Testing and validation checklist
-------------------------------
- Preflight: CIDR conflict check, KMS permissions test, terraform plan success.
- Post-creation: TLS handshake test, tenant API authentication test, end-to-end sample inference (latency < SLA baseline).
- Rotation test: test rotation in staging with synthetic traffic and assert no more than 2% error increase and <5s median latency spike.

Monitoring and alerts
---------------------
- Alerts to create:
  - KMS auth failures > 5/min -> P1 paging to oncall.
  - Rotation job failures -> P2 ticketing and email.
  - Tenant acceptance test fail -> P2 page to Field Ops.
- Dashboards: Tenant provisioning success rate, avg time-to-live (TTL) from request to Live, rotation success rate, key age distribution.

SLOs and guardrails
-------------------
- Provisioning: 95% of tenants should be marked Live within 30 minutes of request for VPC workflows.
- Rotation: 99% of scheduled rotations must complete within their maintenance window.
- Safe rollback: Automated rollback must succeed within 10 minutes for regressions detected by canaries.

Operational runbook (quick commands)
-----------------------------------
sections.heading: Rollback guidance

sections.body: redwoodctl tenant describe --id acme-2027
sections.heading: Inspect a tenant

sections.body: redwoodctl tenant rotation trigger --id acme-2027 --type emergency --reason "suspected-leak"
sections.heading: Force a rotation (emergency)

sections.body:
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://provisioner.internal/api/v1/jobs/<job-id> | jq .

Data retention and audit
------------------------
- Rotation audit events are stored in an immutable audit bucket for 7 years (encrypt-at-rest).
- Access to rotation logs requires security group membership and must be requested via ticket for customer-sensitive entries.

Acceptance testing matrix (short)
--------------------------------
| Test | Purpose | Pass criteria |
|------|---------|---------------|
| TLS handshake | Validate network and certs | Successful handshake to control-plane API and tenant endpoint |
| KMS permission check | Validate user/service can request keys | KMS returns 200 and key wrap/unwarp succeeds |
| Sample inference | Validate runtime integration | Response within SLA and token usage accounted |

Rollout considerations
----------------------
- Canary: pilot the self-service flow with 5 internal tenants for 2 weeks.
- Gradual ramp: increase to 20% of new customer onboards for 1 month before full automatic opt-in.
- Fallback: if any provisioning component fails, revert to operator-assisted provisioning with a diagnostic packet.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Provisioning API: ownership: infra-provisioning team (oncall contact: #infra-provisioning-oncall).
- KMS/HSM integrations: ownership: security-crypto team.
- Field validation and customer acceptance: ownership: customer-success-engineering.

Related pages
-------------
- eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/ephemeral-boot-and-attestation-playbook-2026
- eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-operator-handshake-and-runtime-guardrails-2026

payload.page_title: GPU burst credit pooling and egress slicing playbook

sections.body:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the GPU burst credit pooling and egress-slicing pattern we use to provide predictable tenant-level throughput while minimizing egress cost surprises. It covers architecture, Terraform module usage, runtime configuration, CI/CD validation, monitoring, and incident response steps.

Scope
-----
Applies to: multi-tenant GPU clusters used for inference workloads across Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes when tenant traffic must be rate-controlled at the network egress boundary. It does NOT cover storage-tiering or application-level rate limits.

Goals and guarantees
--------------------
- Per-tenant egress fairness: tenants should not exceed their granted burst credits for outbound bandwidth.
- Predictable billing: cost attribution to tenant owners must align with observed egress volume within 5% monthly.
- Safety SLOs: system must prevent noisy neighbors from degrading cluster-level packet loss beyond 0.5% and tail latency beyond the defined thresholds for control-plane operations.

High-level architecture
-----------------------
- Credit Manager (control-plane service): centralizes tenant burst credit balances, issues refills, and exposes a consistent API for proxies to query allowances. Owned by infra-networking.
- Edge Egress Proxies (data-plane): per-node or per-subnet sidecar proxies enforce token-bucket shaping and apply per-tenant slices. Implemented as a fast userspace proxy (Envoy with custom filter or small Rust proxy).
- Accounting pipeline: streaming ingest into billing topics (Kafka) with per-flow annotations and sampled packet headers for verification.
- Terraform module: exposes variables for credit parameters, routing attachments, and IAM bindings for cross-account proxy roles.

Design details
--------------
1) Credit model
- Each tenant has a persistent monthly allocation (egress_bytes/month) and a burst_credit pool measured in bytes.
- Burst refill signals occur at configurable intervals (default 5m). Refill rate = base rate + carryover (up to max_pool).
- Credits consumed on egress; when depleted, requests are shaped to a default throttled rate or redirected to a lower-cost model tier.

2) Slicing enforcement
- Enforcement points live as a) per-node sidecar for low-latency enforcement and b) an aggregated per-subnet egress gateway for legacy workloads.
- Proxies implement the token-bucket algorithm with per-tenant state keyed by tenant-id header or IP/MAC mapping issued by the Credit Manager.
- Optional kernel offload (tc + fq_codel) is used for best-effort shaping; proxy remains authoritative for precise accounting.

Configuration reference (table)
-----------------------------
| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| burst_refill_interval | 300s | Control-plane refill cadence |
| base_rate_per_tenant | 128KiB/s | Sustained egress guaranteed per tenant |
| max_burst_pool | 10GiB | Max bytes a tenant may accumulate |
| shaping_strategy | token-bucket | Enforcement algorithm (token-bucket | leaky-bucket) |
| enforcement_mode | proxy-first | proxy-first | kernel-fallback |

Terraform module usage example
------------------------------
Use the module in the tenant account to create the necessary IAM role and attach proxy routing. Example snippet:

```hcl
module "egress_slicing" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.company/internal-terraform//egress-slicing-module?ref=v1.4.0"
  tenant_id = "acme-corp"
  base_rate_per_tenant = "128KiB"
  max_burst_pool = "10GiB"
  attach_vpc_subnet_ids = ["subnet-abc123", "subnet-def456"]
  enforcement_mode = "proxy-first"
}
```
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- proxy_role_arn (string)
- routing_attachment_id (string)
- accounting_topic (string)

Proxy bootstrap and config (example)
----------------------------------
- Proxies fetch per-tenant policy via: GET https://credit-manager.internal/v1/policies?tenant_id=<id>
- Example JSON policy (simplified):
```json
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-corp",
  "base_rate_bps": 1048576,
  "max_burst_bytes": 10737418240,
  "priority": "standard"
}
```
- Local kernel shaping fallback (example commands to apply on node):

sudo tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root tbf rate 128kbit burst 32k latency 50ms

CI/CD: validation and gating
---------------------------
- Terraform changes: PR must include a plan with diff checks that show no IAM role escalations and no subnet attachment removals. Add an automated policy test that runs "terraform validate" and checks module variable ranges.
- Proxy builds: unit tests for token-bucket invariants; integration test spins up a 3-node k8s cluster in ephemeral environment that runs a synthetic tenant with configurable burst pattern.
- Performance test: nightly benchmark that exercises 95th/99th percentile enforcement accuracy. Goodness criteria: accounting error <= 1% and enforcement latency < 2ms added at proxy.

Observability and metrics
------------------------
sections.heading: Important module outputs

sections.body:
- egress.bytes_total (counter)
- egress.burst_credits_remaining (gauge)
- egress.throttled_bytes (counter)
- egress.enforcement_latency_ms (histogram)
- egress.drop_rate (gauge)

Important dashboards and alerts
- Dashboard: Tenant Egress Overview (by tenant, last 30d)
- Alert: tenant_burst_credit_negative -> P3 to infra-networking if any tenant balance < 0 for > 10m
- Alert: accounting_lag_seconds > 120 -> P2 (investigate Kafka consumer backlog)
- Alert: cluster_wide_egress_drop_rate > 0.5% -> P1 (possible noisy neighbor)

Cost attribution and billing
---------------------------
- Accounting pipeline produces per-tenant hourly summaries landed in billing S3 bucket with schema: tenant_id, window_start, window_end, bytes_egressed, observed_cost_usd, verified_flag.
- Reconciliation job runs nightly to compare accounting-based charges with cloud egress metering. Tolerance target: 5% discrepancy.

Runbook: incident scenarios and steps
-----------------------------------
1) Noisy tenant (sustained high egress)
- Detect: alert cluster_wide_egress_drop_rate or tenant.throttled_bytes spike.
- Immediate: add emergency cap via Credit Manager API: POST /v1/admin/cap?tenant_id=<id>&cap_bytes=1GiB
- Mitigation: move tenant to isolated subnet and create a temporary per-tenant gateway. Notify customer success.
- Postmortem: include evidence from accounting topic and schedule tenant quota review.

2) Accounting consumer lag (billing pipeline)
- Detect: accounting_lag_seconds > 120
- Immediate: scale Kafka consumer group (infra-tools consumer-scale --group billing-consumers --replicas 4).
- If backlog persists, enable compute-only fallback where proxies write hourly manifest files to S3 for temporary billing ingestion.

3) Proxy crash loop or elevated enforcement latency
- Detect: pod restart count > 5 in 10m or enforcement_latency_ms 99th > 10ms
- Immediate: redirect traffic to kernel shaping fallback by toggling enforcement_mode in Credit Manager (fast-path toggle endpoint).
- Replace proxy build with last-known-good image; roll back PR if the change is recent.

Ownership and run cadence
------------------------
- Owner: infra-networking team (primary), billing-team (secondary).
- On-call: infra-networking oncall rotates weekly; paging rules configured for P1/P2 alerts.
- Review cadence: quarterly policy review to adjust base_rate and max_burst_pool based on usage trends.

Testing checklist before rollout
-------------------------------
- [ ] Terraform plan shows only additive changes to IAM and routing attachments
- [ ] Integration tests show accounting error <= 1% in staging
- [ ] Performance test shows enforcement latency < 2ms for 95th pct
- [ ] Billing reconciliation job passes on staging dataset

Appendix: example debug commands
--------------------------------
- Query tenant balance: curl -sS "https://credit-manager.internal/v1/balance?tenant_id=acme-corp"
- Force refill for tenant (admin only): curl -X POST "https://credit-manager.internal/v1/admin/refill" -d '{"tenant_id":"acme-corp","bytes":104857600}'
- Temporarily cap egress on a node: sudo tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root tbf rate 1mbit burst 64k latency 100ms

Related reading
---------------
- See also: gpu-tenant-credit-buckets-and-granular-throttling-policy (policy rationale)
- See also: gpu-shared-vpc-egress-and-ip-management (VPC attachment patterns and NAT considerations)

Notes and provenance
--------------------
- Design informed by 2024 noisy-neighbor incidents and the Multi-Tenant Egress WG recommendations.
- Implemented first in Dedicated clusters, later generalized to Hosted API in 2025-Q1.

payload.page_title: GPU Egress Sidecar and Proxy Mitigations for Multi-Account Burst

sections.body:
Summary:
This document defines the GPU egress sidecar + proxy pattern we use to protect tenant egress, provide accurate per-tenant accounting, and mitigate sudden burst traffic across cloud accounts. It includes design rationale, Terraform module interface, CI/CD image requirements, runtime configuration, SLOs and throttling rules, and an operational runbook for incidents and testing.

Context and motivation:
- Problem: GPU-backed inference pools occasionally generate large egress spikes (model downloads, large embedding uploads, telemetry, or customers issuing batch jobs). When pools are shared across multiple cloud accounts or projects, these spikes can saturate NAT gateways, exhaust egress quotas, or cause noisy-neighbor billing and throttling.
- Goals: provide predictable egress behavior, fine-grained per-tenant accounting, quick mitigation for bursts, and a secure, auditable proxy path that integrates with our IaC and CI/CD workflows.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: multi-account GPU pools, tenant-facing inference services, dedicated NAT/egress accounting, Terraform modules for sidecar deployment, CI pipelines for sidecar image promotion, and runbooks for surge events.
- Non-goals: egress encryption (handled by TLS end-to-end at application layer) and upstream provider-level quotas on partner clouds (we surface them but do not control provider limits).

Architecture overview:
1) Sidecar proxy (per-pod or per-vm lightweight process)
   - Runs alongside inference runtime container as an iptables redirector or transparent HTTP/HTTPS forward proxy.
   - Responsibilities: enforce per-tenant egress token, annotate flows for billing, perform simple rate limiting, short-circuit cache for common model artifacts, and emit metrics to our telemetry pipeline.
2) Account-level aggregator
   - A small fleet of regional egress-aggregator instances (managed by auto-scaling groups) that accept proxied traffic from sidecars and forward to internet with centralized NAT. Implements more advanced buffering, bucket-based throttling, and cross-account fair-share decisions.
3) NAT / Egress Gateway cluster
   - Manages cloud NATs (NAT Gateway / Cloud NAT) and handles failover across subnetworks. Exports per-ENI/elastic-IP usage to billing pipeline.
4) Control plane connectors
   - IAM service account rotation for sidecars, config distribution via SSM/Secrets Manager, and Terraform modules to declare account bindings and routing.

Key design decisions:
- Transparent redirect vs explicit proxy: we prefer explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy for TLS termination avoidance and simpler multi-protocol handling (TCP/UDP too). Transparent redirect is supported as fallback for legacy workloads.
- Per-tenant token in egress header: sidecar injects X-Redwood-Tenant and signed egress-token so downstream aggregators can attribute bytes reliably.
- Two-tier throttling: lightweight local token-bucket at sidecar (<100ms enforcement) plus global account buckets in aggregator for fairness across instances.
- Cache model artifacts close to runtime: sidecar local disk cache + regionally shared object cache to avoid repeated downloads to internet.

Terraform module: redwood/gpu-egress-sidecar (inputs/outputs)
- Module purpose: deploy sidecar DaemonSet or VM-agent with associated IAM roles, security groups, and routing rules.
- Inputs (table):
  name: module name identifier as string
  deployment_mode: [daemonset | vm-agent]
  sidecar_image: container image URI to use
  cache_size_gb: numeric (string) - disk cache size per node
  local_rate_limit_mbps: per-instance default rate limit (string, Mbps)
  aggregator_endpoint: URL for regional aggregator
  iam_role_arn: role used by sidecar for config fetch and token signing
  allowed_outbound_ports: CSV of ports
  nat_public_ip_pool: list of allowed elastic IPs for egress (stringified list)
- Outputs (table):
  sidecar_daemonset_name: name
  iam_role_binding: arn
  vpc_route_patch_id: id
  aggregator_security_group: id
- Example usage snippet (YAML-ish):
  module "gpu_egress_sidecar" {
    source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra-modules//gpu-egress-sidecar?ref=v1.2.0"
    name = "inference-egress-a"
    deployment_mode = "daemonset"
    sidecar_image = "ghcr.io/redwood/egress-sidecar:2025-02-08"
    cache_size_gb = "12"
    local_rate_limit_mbps = "400"
    aggregator_endpoint = "https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal"
    iam_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/egress-sidecar-role"
    allowed_outbound_ports = "80,443,853"
    nat_public_ip_pool = "[\"34.12.34.10\", \"34.12.34.11\"]"
  }

Sidecar runtime config (defaults)
- config file path: /etc/redwood/egress-sidecar/config.yaml
- default settings (key: value list):
  - local_token_bucket_capacity: "1000000"  # bytes
  - local_refill_rate_bps: "50000000"       # bytes/sec ~50Mbps
  - header_injection: "X-Redwood-Tenant"
  - cache_eviction_policy: "lru"
  - health_check_path: "/healthz"
  - telemetry_flush_interval_seconds: "10"

CI/CD and image promotion rules
1) Image build pipeline (Buildkite):
   - Trigger: changes to infra/egress-sidecar repository or security patches to base image.
   - Steps: unit tests -> static analysis (C/C++/Go or Python lint) -> container image build -> SBOM generation -> vulnerable dependency scan -> canary image push to ephemeral registry -> integration tests in ephemeral GPU sandbox -> promote to staging registry.
2) Promotion gating:
   - Staging -> production promotion requires: passing integration tests, review from networking owner, and signing by SREs.
   - Image tag pattern: yyyy-mm-dd-commitsha (promoted tags for production use "prod-YYYYMMDD-vN").
3) Terraform module release:
   - Module releases are semver. Any change affecting IAM, routing, or NAT must have a cross-team review and an ADR link in the module CHANGELOG.

Operational SLOs and metrics to monitor
- Availability: sidecar DaemonSet rollout success >= 99.9% per region per week.
- Latency: proxy-handshake added latency < 5ms p50 and < 20ms p99 under normal load.
- Egress accounting accuracy: attribution mismatch < 0.1% over 24h window.
- Throttling effectiveness: during simulated bursts, account-level drop rate <= 2% while maintaining aggregate fairness.
- Key metrics: sidecar.health, sidecar.cache_hit_ratio, sidecar.local_throttle_count, aggregator.bucket_balance, nat.ip_utilization, egress.bytes_by_tenant, egress.errors_5xx.

Runbook: Egress surge (priority P1)
1) Detection triggers:
   - NAT public IP 90% utilization sustained for 5m OR
   - sudden rise in egress.bytes_by_tenant > 3x baseline for > 2m OR
   - aggregate 5xx egress errors across aggregator > 1% for 5m.
2) Initial mitigation (0-5m):
   - Page oncall (eng-infra).
   - Enable soft-throttle mode via control plane (set aggregator_global_limit = 80% of baseline) to reduce outgoing rate.
   - Identify top-10 tenant contributors from egress.bytes_by_tenant.
3) Triage (5-15m):
   - For each top tenant, check recent config: job runs, model downloads, scheduled batch windows.
   - If a tenant has runaway traffic, apply tenant-specific token-bucket reduction in aggregator (example command):
     curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CTRL_API' -d '{"tenant":"t-123","limit_mbps":50}' https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal/api/token-buckets
   - If traffic is due to model downloads, enable cache prewarming for that model in the aggregator to reduce outbound bytes.
4) Recovery (15m-1h):
   - Gradually raise global limit while validating nat.ip_utilization and 5xx rates.
   - If NAT IP pool exhausted, coordinate with cloud-ops to allocate extra elastic IPs or failover to secondary region.
5) Post-incident (1h+):
   - Run automated attribution audit (compare egress.bytes_by_tenant to sidecar emitted events) and store report.
   - Create incident summary and attach to postmortem board.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-deploy)
- Unit and integration tests for sidecar (mock aggregator, simulate partial packet loss).
- Load test: 1.5x baseline sustained for 30 minutes with synthetic tenant distribution to validate throttling.
- Failure injection: simulate aggregator restart and ensure sidecars buffer or fallback to direct egress with alert.
- IaC static checks: terraform fmt, validate, and a policy-as-code scan (OPA) for IAM scope.
- Security review: SBOM inspection and image CVE threshold (no critical CVEs).

Security and compliance considerations
- Sidecars authenticate to aggregator using short-lived mTLS certificates provisioned via our internal PKI.
- Egress headers are signed; sensitive tenant identifiers are hashed in logs.
- Audit logs for token issuance and aggregator decisions retained for 90 days by default (configurable per-customer for Dedicated/Private).

Operational ownership and run cadence
- Service owner: eng-infra networking subteam (primary oncall rotation).
- Tier-2 support: infra SREs for escalation.
- Weekly reports: egress utilization digest every Monday to capacity-planning channel.

Appendix: related knobs and quick reference
- Quick CLI snippets:
  - Check aggregator bucket status: curl -s https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal/api/buckets | jq
  - Reduce tenant limit: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tenant":"t-456","limit_mbps":20}' $AGG_API/tokens
- Default cache paths: /var/lib/redwood/egress-cache, cache size per node defined in module param cache_size_gb.
- Ownership matrix:
  - sidecar code and CI: eng-developer-experience (codeowner: @lina-zhang)
  - aggregator ops and autoscaling: eng-sre (codeowner: @ethan-rivera)
  - IAM & accounts: eng-infra cloud-accounts team (owner: @marco-alvarez)

End of document.

payload.page_title: GPU NAT Fabric Orchestrator and Service-Account Routing Playbook

sections.body: This playbook describes the NAT Fabric Orchestrator (NFO) pattern we use to provide predictable, accountable egress from GPU tenant environments. It bundles: a Terraform module (nat_fabric) for per-account SNAT allocation, a control-plane service that maps service-accounts to NAT pools, CI/CD validation for network changes, and an on-call runbook for egress incidents. The goal is to ensure tenant isolation, avoid noisy-tenant egress storms, and enable safe burst routing into shared burst pools.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Past incidents showed that unmanaged SNAT exhaustion and hairpinning caused large customer-facing tail-latency spikes.
- The NFO enforces per-tenant quotas, predictable billing attribution, and safe fallback to burst NAT pools.
sections.heading: Why this exists

sections.body:
- nat_fabric Terraform module: creates NAT pools, route tables, allocation resources and IAM bindings.
- nfo-controller: Kubernetes control plane that watches ServiceAccount annotations and allocates an IP from the tenant pool.
- egress-metrics pipeline: Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, and billing tags exported to telemetry.
- e2e network test pipeline: runs in CI to validate SNAT allocation, NAT failover, and DNAT whitelist rules.
sections.heading: Key components

sections.body:
- Total egress connection setup failure rate: <= 0.2% (5m window)
- Redis-backed allocation latency (p99): <= 75ms
- SNAT exhaustion alerts: trigger when free IPs < 10% per pool
sections.heading: SLOs and thresholds

sections.body:
| Variable | Type | Default | Notes |
| nat_pool_size | number | 64 | Number of IPs in the pool (per-region) |
| pool_region | string | us-west-2 | Region for the NAT pool |
| tags | map | {} | Billing tags attached to NAT resources |

Example nat_fabric usage (terraform snippet):
```hcl
module "tenant_egress" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//nat_fabric?ref=v1.3.0"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  nat_pool_size = 32
  pool_region = var.region
  tags = { team = "gpu-platform", tenant = var.tenant_id }
}
```

nfo-controller annotations (Kubernetes):
- redwood.io/egress-pool: "tenant-123-usw2"
- redwood.io/egress-band: "standard|burst"
- redwood.io/egress-retries: "3"
sections.heading: Terraform module reference (summary table)

sections.body:
1) Terraform plan must include nat_fabric schema lint and an assertion that no public IPs are leaked.
2) Network emulator test: create ephemeral pod with annotated SA and assert outbound IP matches allocated pool.
3) Failover test: simulate pool drain and assert controller switches to burst pool within 30s.
4) Billing tag check: all created resources contain required billing tags.

Runbook: Egress exhaustion or unexpected NAT failures
1) Detection: Pager fires from "nat_pool_exhaustion" alert (prometheus rule).
2) Initial triage (5m): on-call runs `kubectl get ephemerals --selector=redwood.io/egress-pool=POOL` and `redis-cli -h redis-nfo-1 HGETALL allocations:POOL`.
3) If free IPs < 5%: an automated scale job (terraform apply via pipeline) will be triggered to add pools. If automation fails, follow manual scale (see section below).
4) If allocation latency high: check nfo-controller logs `kubectl logs -l app=nfo-controller -n platform` and `systemctl status nfo-allocator` on dedicated nodes. Restart nfo-controller if stuck: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/nfo-controller -n platform`.
5) Fallback to burst pool: annotate critical service-accounts with `redwood.io/egress-band: burst`. Use the helper script: `scripts/burst-fallback --tenant tenant-123 --region usw2` (stored in repo infra/tools).
6) Communication: update status page and slack channel #infra-egress with pool, impact, and mitigation steps.
sections.heading: CI/CD validation checks (Buildkite / GitHub Actions)

sections.body:
1) Checkout terraform branch `git checkout infra/nat-pool-scale` and update module nat_pool_size.
2) Run `mage tf:init && mage tf:plan` in the repo root.
3) Approve via terraform pipeline with required two reviewers.
4) After apply, validate with CI network emulator and confirm allocations.
sections.heading: Manual scale (when automation fails)

sections.body:
- Grafana dashboards: "NFO Overview", "Per-pool utilization", "Per-tenant egress latency".
- Prometheus alerts of interest: `nat_pool_exhaustion`, `nfo_alloc_latency_high`, `nfo_controller_restart_rate`
- Example PromQL: `sum by(pool) (nat_pool_ip_free{job="nfo-exporter"}) / sum by(pool) (nat_pool_ip_total{job="nfo-exporter"})`
sections.heading: Observability runbook (dashboards & queries)

sections.body:
- Primary owner: GPU Platform (oncall alias: oncall-gpu-platform@redwood.com)
- Secondary: Core Networking (oncall alias: oncall-core-network@redwood.com)
- Pager escalation: 15m to secondary, 60m to engineering manager on-call.

sections.body:

payload.page_title: GPU Egress Fencing and Service-Account Burst Control Playbook

sections.body:
Summary:
This playbook defines the design, IaC patterns, CI/CD requirements, alerting, and operational runbook for implementing egress fencing and service-account burst control for GPU tenant workloads. The goal is to prevent noisy-tenant egress spikes, reduce accidental cross-tenant DDoS risk, and provide predictable billing attribution while preserving controlled bursting behavior for latency-sensitive inference workloads.

Scope:
- Applies to all GPU tenant VPCs and shared-burst routing paths across cloud accounts where Redwood-managed inference services run.
- Includes Terraform modules, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy examples, NAT gateway/BGP patterns, CI/CD gates, monitoring dashboards, and incident runbook steps.
- Excludes edge/on-prem network appliances (see eng-private-deployments).

Objectives:
- Prevent >3x baseline egress spikes from a single tenant for more than 5 minutes without automated throttling/mitigation.
- Ensure egress-policy enforcement success >= 99.9% across all active GPU pools.
- Enable rapid isolation and rollback within 15 minutes for suspected egress leaks.
- Maintain billing accuracy for egress at per-tenant granularity.

Architecture Overview:
- Each tenant gets a per-tenant NAT pool/egress IP range (allocated via Terraform).
- Egress policy enforcement happens in three layers: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies + eBPF sidecars (per-node) for per-pod shaping + centralized egress-proxy cluster for policy-controlled burst gating.
- Smart burst tokens: short-lived service-account scoped tokens issued by the egress-proxy for controlled temporary increases above baseline. Tokens are rate-limited and audited.
- Fallback: If proxy is unavailable, flows are limited to baseline NAT throughput and flagged; critical inference routes can obtain emergency tokens via the canary fallback path (requires approval).

Key Components and Owners:
- infra-networking (owner): Terraform modules and BGP/NAT design.
- infra-runtime (owner): eBPF sidecar and egress-proxy code.
- eng-sre (oncall): Alerts, runbooks, and operational mitigation.
- cost-ops (billing): Billing tagging and export.

Terraform module example (minimal excerpt):
```
module "tenant_egress" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/infra/terraform//modules/tenant-egress"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  nat_ip_count = var.nat_ip_count
  egress_tag = "tenant:${var.tenant_id}:egress"
  enable_burst_proxy = true
}
```
Notes: module must be run with `terraform fmt` and `tflint` in CI. The module creates: per-tenant nat-gateway(s), tags, route-table associations, and a small proxy autoscaling group with IAM roles scoped to the tenant proxy.

Kubernetes network policy (example):
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-through-proxy
  namespace: tenant-<TENANT>
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inference-worker
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: <EGRESS_PROXY_CIDR>/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3128
```
Operational controls and CI/CD requirements:
- CI pipeline for terraform module changes must include: `terraform validate`, `terraform fmt -check`, `tflint`, `checkov` security scan, and a `terratest` integration test that contrives a minimal tenant environment and asserts NAT IP allocation and tag propagation.
- egress-proxy changes: unit tests, integration test against a local eBPF shim, and an end-to-end staging validation that issues burst tokens. Canary rollout required.
- Gate: Any change that increases default tenant NAT throughput or adds unbounded egress IP ranges requires eng-sre approval.

Monitoring, Metrics and Alerts (recommended):
- Metrics to emit: `tenant.egress_bytes_total`, `tenant.egress_packets_total`, `tenant.egress_burst_tokens_issued`, `tenant.egress_denied_flows`.
- Dashboards: per-tenant time series with 1m/5m/1h rollups; heatmap of tenants by 5m egress rate.
- Alerts (PagerDuty -> eng-sre):
  - EgressSpikeHigh: tenant.egress_bytes_total (5m rate) > 10x historical 95th percentile for tenant, sustained 5m. Severity: P1.
  - EgressLeakDetected: tenant.egress_denied_flows > 1000 in 1m (indicates policy drift). Severity: P2.
  - BurstProxyUnavailable: healthcheck fail > 2m and >50% of tenant tokens failing issuance. Severity: P1.

Billing and Tagging:
- All NAT gateways and proxy ASGs MUST include `billing_tag = tenant:<TENANT_ID>` and `cost_center` tags. Cost-ops will run daily exports to match egress_bytes_total to cloud egress billing file. Discrepancies > 5% trigger billing-review workflow.

Operational Runbook (incident steps):
1) Triage: Identify tenant and scope using dashboard and `tenant.egress_bytes_total`. Record tenant_id and peak rate.
2) Temporary throttle: Scale egress-proxy to 0 replicas for the tenant's proxy ASG to force baseline NAT-only behavior OR apply per-tenant tc-scripts via the eBPF control plane to cap to baseline Mbps.
3) Preserve evidence: Capture `tcpdump` on affected node(s) for 5 minutes, and export proxy logs (S3 path: s3://redwood-ops/egress-incidents/<INCIDENT_ID>/).
4) If traffic is legitimate burst for latency-sensitive inference, issue emergency token via `egressctl issue-token --tenant <ID> --expires 15m` (requires two approvers if production).
5) Root cause analysis: Check recent deploys (CI job IDs), new container images, and tenant configuration changes.
6) Rollback path: If a tenant config change caused leak, revert via `terraform apply -target=module.tenant_egress` to previous module inputs and redeploy k8s networkpolicy.
7) Post-incident: Create incident page, schedule follow-up with tenant owner and cost-ops; update playbook if automation gap found.

Verification checklist (pre-rollout):
- [ ] Terraform plan shows only expected NAT IPs and tags.
- [ ] `terratest` passed with tenant allocation assertions.
- [ ] Staging egress proxy issued burst tokens successfully and metrics emitted.
- [ ] Alert rules deployed and tested against synthetic traffic.
- [ ] Billing export mapped to tenant tags for 7 consecutive days in staging.

Rollback and emergency mitigation patterns:
- Revoke burst tokens globally: `egressctl revoke-all --tenant <ID>` (immediate).
- If NAT-level leak persists, detach route to NAT and attach to isolated sink VPC (blackhole) while preserving logs.
- If proxy change introduced regression, revert canary via CI/CD `promote` pipeline which re-deploys previous image tag.

Testing and chaos experiments:
- Quarterly chaos test: simulate noisy tenant issuing steady 20% above burst budget for 15 minutes and verify automatic throttling and alerting. Document results in eng-infra/team-wiki.

Notes and FAQs:
Q: Why per-tenant NAT IPs instead of shared NAT?
A: Per-tenant NAT IPs enable precise billing, easier reputation isolation, and faster forensic traceability. Shared NATs reduce allocation pressure but make attribution and mitigation harder.

Q: Can tenants reserve longer burst windows?
A: Yes — through the billing-controlled reservation flow: tenant requests reservation -> cost-ops approves -> module updated with `preapproved_burst_token` TTL. All reservations are visible in the billing dashboard.

References and related policies:
- See `gpu-network-topology-and-tenant-isolation-patterns.json` for topology diagrams.
- See `gpu-tenant-credit-buckets-and-granular-throttling-policy.json` for burst budget math.

Appendix: example `egressctl` commands
- Issue token (normal): `egressctl issue-token --tenant t-123 --quota 100MB --ttl 300s`
- Revoke tokens: `egressctl revoke --tenant t-123 --token-id <id>`
- Snapshot metrics: `prometheus-query 'sum(rate(tenant_egress_bytes_total[1m])) by (tenant)' > /tmp/egress-snapshot.json`

Owner contacts:
- infra-networking Slack: #infra-networking
- eng-sre oncall: pagerduty schedule 'eng-sre/gpu-oncall'

If you plan to modify the Terraform module or egress-proxy, coordinate with infra-networking and eng-sre at least 3 business days before the change window.

payload.page_title: Egress Lease Manager — spec and CI/CD adapter

sections.body:
Overview
========

This document specifies the Egress Lease Manager (ELM): a small control plane service + Terraform/CI-CD adapters that orchestrate short-lived "egress leases" to guarantee tenant egress capacity across multi-account GPU pools. The ELM prevents noisy-tenant egress storms, enables predictable cross-account bursting, and provides a simple CI/CD integration for automated allocation and failover during deploys.

Key goals
---------

- Provide per-tenant egress capacity reservations with timeboxed leases (default: 10m, configurable).
- Enable programmatic lease acquisition from CI/CD pipelines and runtime orchestrators (e.g., burst orchestrator, canary deploy pipelines).
- Integrate with Terraform modules to map leases to NAT gateways / egress proxies and enforce IAM/egress controls.
- Expose telemetry, SLOs, and alerts for egress exhaustion and lease contention.
- Offer safe fallback policies when leases cannot be granted (queueing, degrade-to-throttled-egress).

When to use ELM
----------------

- Tenant needs predictable large-volume egress (model downloads, checkpoint replication, dataset syncs).
- Canaries or mass rollout jobs that can overwhelm shared NATs or egress proxies.
- Private deployments where VPC egress capacity must be accounted against a budget or billing center.

System components
-----------------

1) Egress Lease Manager service (ELM-core)
   - REST API (JSON over HTTPS) and gRPC endpoints
   - Lease store: DynamoDB / Spanner (configurable) for single-source-of-truth
   - Leader election for multi-region HA
   - Plugin interface for enforcement (Terraform, cloud-provider quotas, egress-proxy API)

2) Terraform adapter (terraform-elm)
   - Terraform module + provider wrapper that reads lease assignments and binds NAT / proxy routes and tags
   - Generates IAM bindings for temporary service principals used during the lease

3) CI/CD integration (elm-ci-adapter)
   - CLI utility and Buildkite / GitHub Actions steps to request/renew/release leases
   - Idempotent behavior for retrying acquisitions during pipeline restarts

4) Observability layer
   - Prometheus metrics + Grafana dashboards
   - Audit logs streamed to centralized logging (Stackdriver/CloudWatch/ELK)

SLOs and limits
---------------

- Lease acquisition latency: 99th perc <= 150ms (regional LB + ELM-core)
- Lease decision accuracy: 100% (no overcommit) — leases are conservative by default
- Lease renewal jitter: <= 50ms
- Global concurrent leases per region: configurable (default 500)

API contract (summary)
----------------------

POST /v1/leases
sections.heading: Overview
Request body (JSON)

sections.body:
- 201 CREATED: {"lease_id":"...","granted_bandwidth_mbps":100,"expires_at":"2025-02-20T12:34:56Z"}
- 202 ACCEPTED: queued (with ETA)
- 409 CONFLICT: cannot satisfy (includes suggested fallback: throttle 10mbps)

PUT /v1/leases/:lease_id/renew
DELETE /v1/leases/:lease_id
GET /v1/leases?tenant_id=...

Terraform module design
-----------------------
sections.heading: Responses

sections.body:
- Materialize infrastructure attachments (NAT gateway route, egress-proxy config) for an acquired lease
- Create short-lived credentials (service account / role) scoped to the lease duration

Example usage (pseudo-Terraform)

module "elm_lease_attach" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-elm.git//modules/attach"

  lease_id                 = var.lease_id
  region                   = var.region
  nat_gateway_resource_id  = aws_nat_gateway.shared.id
  egress_proxy_endpoint    = module.egress_proxy.endpoint
  lease_tag_key            = "elm-lease"
}

Module variables table
| Name | Type | Description | Default |
|------|------|-------------|---------|
| lease_id | string | ELM lease UUID | (required) |
| region | string | Cloud region for attachment | (required) |
| nat_gateway_resource_id | string | NAT resource id to attach rule | (required) |
| egress_proxy_endpoint | string | Optional proxy control-plane endpoint | null |

CI/CD integration examples
--------------------------
sections.heading: The terraform-elm module has two responsibilities

sections.body:
- name: "Acquire Egress Lease"
  command: |
    elmctl acquire --tenant $TENANT --bandwidth 200 --duration 600 --purpose deploy > lease.json
    export LEASE_ID=$(jq -r .lease_id lease.json)
sections.heading: Buildkite pipeline step (shell)

sections.body:
1. Acquire lease with --duration 600
2. Run canary deploy traffic scoped to granted_bandwidth_mbps
3. Renew lease for another 600s if canary passes
4. Release lease after canary completes

CLI semantics
-------------

- elmctl acquire: idempotent, returns existing lease if same tenant/purpose is active
- elmctl renew: extends expiry; fails fast if allocation impossible
- elmctl release: returns resources; Terraform module observes release and tears down attachments

Enforcement patterns
--------------------
sections.heading: Canary rollout sequence (recommended)

sections.body:
A) Cloud-native NAT tagging
- Terraform writes a short-lived tag on NAT resources mapping to lease_id
- Egress dataplane periodically reads active tag list and enforces token bucket policing

B) Egress-proxy token-based routing
- Egress proxy (Envoy cluster with rate-limiter filter) accepts per-connection lease tokens
- Terraform registers token with proxy control-plane during attach

Fallback policies
-----------------
sections.heading: We support two enforcement backends (pluggable)

sections.body:
- If request has purpose=best-effort: return 202 with ETA in seconds
- If purpose=strict: return 409 with suggested alternate bandwidth
- For CI/CD jobs: the pipeline step should implement exponential backoff with max retries 5

Metrics and alerts
------------------
sections.heading: If a lease request cannot be satisfied immediately

sections.body:
- elm_lease_requests_total{status}
- elm_lease_granted_gbps
- elm_lease_denied_total
- elm_active_leases_gauge
- elm_lease_queue_length

Alerting rules (examples)
1) High denial rate: if rate(elm_lease_denied_total[5m]) > 5/min and elm_lease_requests_total[5m] > 20 -> Pager
2) Exhausted capacity: elm_active_leases_gauge == region_capacity -> Pager + auto-throttle mode
3) Long queue: elm_lease_queue_length > 50 -> Ops channel and QBR review

Runbook: Lease acquisition fails during deploy
--------------------------------------------

1) Check ELM-core health page: https://elm.redwood.internal/health
2) Inspect logs for 409 / 202 responses (trace_id header forwarded by pipeline)
3) If denial due to capacity, either:
   a) Wait until a running lease expires (default) or
   b) Escalate to SRE to increase region_capacity (see emergency scaling section below)
4) For CI/CD: mark pipeline step soft-fail vs hard-fail based on purpose tag
5) If ELM-core is unhealthy: fail open -> pipelines should fall back to throttled-egress profile
6) Post-incident: add tenant to backfill queue and run retrospective to tune defaults

Emergency scaling (SRE procedure)
---------------------------------

1) Validate increased capacity will not violate cross-tenant fairness.
2) Use the admin UI (ELM Admin) or the admin API to increase region_capacity by 10-20%.
   - POST /v1/admin/regions/:region/adjust_capacity {"delta":100} (requires admin-token)
3) Notify billing and security teams of transient capacity change.
4) Observe metrics for 10 minutes; roll back if contention appears.

Security and IAM notes
----------------------

- All acquisition/renewal API calls require mTLS + short-lived bearer tokens obtained via the internal STS.
- Terraform adapter creates and destroys a short-lived role binding for the lease; expiry aligns with lease expiry.
- Audit logs must include: actor, tenant_id, lease_id, requested_bandwidth_mbps, decision, trace_id.

Rollout plan
------------

Phase 0 — Canary (internal tenants only)
- Deploy ELM-core in us-west-2, enable terraform-elm in a single staging org.
- Run 20 synthetic lease acquisitions at 50/100/200mbps.

Phase 1 — Beta (select customers / infra teams)
- Onboard infra CI pipelines (canary/promote) to opt-in to ELM via elmctl.
- Validate Terraform attach/teardown across failovers.

Phase 2 — GA
- Open tenant enrollment, expose usage dashboard, add billing tags and cost attribution.

Testing matrix
--------------

- Unit tests for allocation algorithm (edge cases: rounding, time skew)
- Integration test: terraform-elm attaches NAT rules and performs e2e egress enforcement in dry-run
- Chaos test: simulate NAT failure and verify lease rebind to fallback proxy

Operational ownership
---------------------

- Primary owner: infra-networking team (oncall rotation)
- Backup owner: gpu-fleet-capacity team
- SLO/alert steward: eng-sre

Appendix A — Terraform example (provider shim)
----------------------------------------------
sections.heading: Recommended metrics (Prometheus names)

sections.body:
provider "elm" {
  endpoint = "https://elm-admin.redwood.internal"
  token    = data.aws_iam_role.terraform_session.credentials.token
}

resource "elm_lease_binding" "canary" {
  lease_id = var.lease_id
  nat_id   = aws_nat_gateway.shared.id
}

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist
--------------------------------------

- If lease shows granted but traffic isn't using bandwidth: check egress-proxy token binding and NAT route tags
- If multiple tenants starve: inspect tenant priorities and run the fairness audit script
- If renewals unexpectedly fail: verify clock skew on CI runners and the ELM-core cluster

Appendix C — Dashboards and links
---------------------------------

- Grafana: Cluster -> ELM Overview (internal link)
- Kibana: query: "source:elm AND level:ERROR"
- Admin UI: https://elm-admin.redwood.internal

Change log
----------
- 2024-09-15: Draft spec created
- 2024-11-02: Added Terraform adapter details and CI/CD examples
- 2025-02-20: Updated SLOs and emergency scaling procedure

Related decisions
-----------------
- Decision: conservative allocation to avoid cross-tenant overcommit (see: /confluence/eng-infra/decision-records/elm-conservative-allocation-2024)

Contact
-------

For questions or rollout requests, ping #infra-egress on Slack or contact the owner: evan.li@redwood.com

payload.page_title: GPU fleet network telemetry: sampling, tagging, and cost allocation

sections.body:
Overview:

This document defines the telemetry sampling strategy, mandatory network tagging, and cost-allocation mapping for the GPU fleet. It combines implementation guidance (Terraform and CI/CD validators), operational runbook steps for network-related billing incidents, and the rollout plan for sampling rate changes. The goal is to ensure accurate tenant-level egress/cost visibility with minimal telemetry volume impact on the logging pipeline.

Scope:
- Applies to all AWS-based GPU pools managed by the infra team (shared and tenant-dedicated).
- Covers ENI/instance tagging, VPC Flow Logs sampling, eBPF-based connection metadata, telemetry ingestion retention and dimensions used for chargeback.
- Not in scope: compute-side application-level tracing (see app observability docs).

Goals:
- Produce a reliable mapping from network activity to tenant (customer_id / team_id) for chargeback and anomaly detection.
- Keep telemetry ingestion costs < 3% of network egress spend by using targeted sampling and enrichment.
- Provide CI/CD guardrails so Terraform changes cannot remove required tags or sampling configs.

Non-goals:
- Full packet capture or deep packet inspection.
- End-to-end per-request cost attribution at the application layer.

Owner and contacts:
- Product owner: Elena Martinez (infra cost engineering)
- Implementation owner: Marcus Liu (networking)
Oncall and escalation:
- Primary oncall: infra-sre (rotation: #infra-sre-oncall)
- Escalation: pager -> infra oncall -> networking lead (Marcus) -> Eng Director
- Billing investigations: loop in finance-legal and customer-success when tenant charges > $5,000 unexpected in 24h

Design summary:
- Source events:
  - VPC Flow Logs (filtered, sampled) at sub-second ingestion for spikes
  - ENI metadata enriched with terraform-provided tags (tenant_id, billing_code, environment, pool_type)
  - eBPF agent on gateway nodes to capture NAT/gateway translations and associate ephemeral connections with ENIs
  - Periodic reconciliation job (hourly) to backfill missing tag mappings from instance metadata API and config DB

- Attribution model:
  - Primary join key: eni_id -> terraform tag tenant_id
  - Fallback: instance_id -> patch metadata mapping -> tenant_id
  - When tenant_id missing: mark as "unannotated" and surface for Terraform enforcement CI

Sampling strategy and thresholds:
| Area | Default sampling | Canary/cost mode | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| VPC Flow Logs (production) | 1% continuous | 10% for detected spike windows | Spike windows auto-enable increased sampling for 30m
| eBPF connection metadata | 5% consistent | 50% during incident investigations | eBPF events are enriched with ENI tags before export
| Gateway NAT logs | 0.5% | 5% for billing reconciliation | Rare but very high-cardinality; sample conservatively |

Sampling ramp & safety:
1. Canary: 1% of GPU fleet for 24h with full enrichment pipeline enabled.
2. Gradual ramp to target (5% eBPF, 1% flow logs) over 72h if ingestion and costs are within thresholds.
3. Automatic rollback if monthly forecast delta > 2% or pipeline error rate > 0.5%.

Terraform/IaC requirements:
- All GPU compute modules must set the following tags on created ENIs and instances (enforced by module outputs and unit tests):
  - tenant_id (string, required)
  - billing_code (string, optional but recommended)
  - pool_type ("shared" | "dedicated" | "burst")
  - owner (team alias)

Sample Terraform snippet (module input enforcement):

```hcl
module "gpu_node" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwoodinfra/terraform-modules//gpu-node"

  tenant_id   = var.tenant_id
  billing_code = var.billing_code
  pool_type    = var.pool_type
  owner        = var.owner
}

# module should attach tags to ENI resource with terraform provider
resource "aws_network_interface" "eni" {
  tags = merge(var.common_tags, {
    "tenant_id"   = var.tenant_id
    "billing_code" = var.billing_code
    "pool_type"    = var.pool_type
    "owner"        = var.owner
  })
}
```

CI/CD validators (pre-merge and plan-time):
- PR lint: tfsec + checkov rules to ensure required tag variables are present and not empty.
- Plan-time gating: a custom validator runs `terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan` and scans for any aws_network_interface or aws_instance resources without a tenant_id tag. The plan fails if missing tags for production workspaces.

Example GitHub Actions job (simplified):
```yaml
name: tf-validate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init
      - name: terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
      - name: check tags in plan
        run: python infra-tools/plan_tag_checker.py plan.tfplan --require tenant_id
```

Telemetry enrichment pipeline (brief):
- Collector: Fluent Bit (VPC flow logs) and custom eBPF forwarder (connection metadata) write to Kinesis Data Streams.
- Processor: Lambda/Glue job that enriches with tenant mapping from DynamoDB (hourly refreshed from config DB).
- Store: Flow logs -> S3 + Athena for ad-hoc queries; aggregated metrics -> Prometheus-compatible timeseries in Cortex; high-cardinality events -> Datadog log ingestion (sampled).

Cost and alerting thresholds:
- Metric: hourly_unannotated_bytes (bytes per hour with missing tenant_id) -> Alert at > 50GB/hr for > 30m
- Metric: pipeline_error_rate -> Alert at > 0.5% over 5m
- Metric: forecasted_monthly_telemetry_cost_delta -> Alert at > 2% of current month forecast

Dashboards and queries (examples):
- Dashboard: GPU Fleet Network Annotation Health
  - Panels: % annotated traffic (1h/24h), unannotated by AZ, top 10 untagged ENIs, telemetry ingestion lag (p90)
- Athena sample query to find top untagged ENIs:
```sql
SELECT eni_id, sum(bytes) as total_bytes
FROM vpc_flow_logs_parquet
WHERE tenant_id IS NULL
GROUP BY eni_id
ORDER BY total_bytes DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

Operational runbook: unexpected spike in network egress or cost attribution gaps
1. Triage: Check Dashboard -> % annotated traffic. If annotated < 90% in last hour, proceed to step 2.
2. Verify ingestion: check Kinesis consumer lag and Lambda processor error rate. If lag > 5m or errors > 0.5% escalate to infra-sre.
3. Reconciliation: run the Athena query above to list top unannotated ENIs. Cross-reference with instance inventory: `aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=network-interface.network-interface-id,Values=<eni>`
4. If missing tags found in infra (Terraform state), open a PR to the module that created them and apply a targeted tag patch via `terraform state` + `terraform apply` in a maintenance window.
5. For immediate billing mitigation, apply a temporary accounting_tag (billing_code=manual-mitigation) using `aws ec2 create-tags` and notify finance.
6. If pipeline errors are root cause, rollback the last collector-related deploy (see CI/CD rollback playbook) and scale collector fleet by +30% to catch up.
7. Post-incident: run backfill job (hourly_reconciliation) to enrich historical events and produce corrected chargeback reports. Document the incident and update related pages.

Backfill job sample command:
```bash
python tools/reconcile_tags.py --start 2025-01-10T00:00Z --end 2025-01-12T00:00Z --output s3://redwood-telemetry/backfill/2025-01-12/
```

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: terraform module unit tests assert that tags are present and not empty.
- Integration: synthetic workload that generates known egress pattern and asserts the telemetry enrichment maps 98% of bytes to tenant_id within 60 minutes.
- Load test: run 10x sampling at canary for 1h and verify pipeline scales and cost delta is within budget.

Rollout plan for sampling rate changes:
1. Proposal PR with expected cost delta and dashboard mockups.
2. Approvals: infra-sre, cost-eng, finance (if delta > 1% of monthly forecast).
3. Canary in single AZ for 24h.
4. Monitor: annotated %, pipeline errors, ingestion cost.
5. Ramp per schedule (24h -> 3 days -> full fleet).
6. Post-rollout review and SRE postmortem if any alerts were triggered.

Troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- If unannotated spikes: check module version and workspace used to provision nodes.
- If ingestion cost unexpectedly high: reduce sampling rate to last known-good, set circuit-breaker in Kinesis to drop non-critical events.
- If tags missing from new nodes: block PRs that change variables related to tagging via the CI blocker.

Appendix: quick references
- Terraform tag checker: infra-tools/plan_tag_checker.py (GH link)
- Reconciliation script: tools/reconcile_tags.py (GH link)
- Related runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook

Revision history:
- 2024-09-15: Document created by Marcus Liu (draft)

payload.page_title: Multi-cloud GPU bursting orchestration and egress-slicing pattern

sections.body:
Summary:

This document describes the pattern we use to orchestrate short-duration GPU bursting across multiple cloud providers while minimizing cross-cloud egress costs and preserving latency SLOs for inference jobs. It combines an orchestration policy, an "egress-slicing" traffic shaping model, and IaC modules to make bursts safe, auditable, and revertible.

Goals:
- Allow Redwood workloads to burst into alternate clouds or dedicated partner pools for 1–90 minute windows without losing request-level SLOs.
- Keep cross-account and cross-cloud egress costs predictable and bounded.
- Provide Terraform/IaC primitives and CI/CD hooks so teams can enable bursting safely in their service stacks.
- Provide a minimal on-call runbook for common failures during burst events.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: inference-serving traffic (text generation, embeddings, reranking) and offline eval batches that need GPU headroom.
- Non-goals: full multi-cloud data plane replication (we do not attempt to mirror large model checkpoints during a burst).

Key concepts:
- Burst window: a short, policy-defined interval where a service can consume capacity from an alternate provider (usually to avoid throttles or solve regional incidents). Typical window: 5–60 minutes.
- Egress slice: a rate-limited, labeled egress path reserved for burst traffic. Slices are tagged with cost-limits, TTL, and routing priority.
- Cost guardrail: a per-tenant and global budget that gates burst expansion.
- Warm-standby model variants: lightweight model variants (quantized/short-context) used during burst windows to reduce per-token cost and memory.

Architecture overview:
1) Control plane (Redwood scheduler service): evaluates policy and initiates bursts.
2) Routing layer (edge proxies + service mesh): applies egress slicing rules and enforces token-level shaping.
3) Data plane (GPU pools in primary and partner clouds): runs inference tasks; model artifacts are referenced read-only from an immutable object-store snapshot.

Operational pattern — Egress Slicing:
- Each burst-capable service is configured with 2 egress slices: "primary-egress" and "burst-egress".
- "Burst-egress" has an associated egress-budget, cost-tier (spot/commit), and max-pps (packets per second).
- Requests are labeled at the ingress with the workload and customer tags; routing policy uses these tags + cost-remaining to decide whether to forward to burst-egress.

Example policy (natural language):
1) If 95th-percentile latency of primary pool > 2x target for 2 consecutive minutes, attempt small-scale burst (10% of traffic) to partner pool A.
2) If error rate drops and latency improves, grow the burst by +20% every 30s until cost_guardrail or max-burst-percent hit.
3) If cross-cloud egress estimated cost > egress-budget or if error rate increases, immediately retract burst and fallback.

Terraform / IaC patterns:
- Provide a reusable module: redwood-cloud-bursting-slice. Inputs: provider, vpc-id, allowed-subnets, egress-bandwidth-shards, egress-budget-USD, slice-tags. Outputs: route-table attachments, egress-metering labels (via cloud provider tags), and a terraform state locker.

Example minimal module usage (HCL):

```
module "burst_slice_gcp" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules.git//cloud-bursting-slice?ref=v1.2.0"
  provider = "gcp"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
  allowed_subnets = ["subnet-analytics", "subnet-burst"]
  egress_bandwidth_shards = 3
  egress_budget_usd = 150.00
  slice_tags = { team = "search-infra", purpose = "bursting" }
}
```

Note: modules must emit named billing tags used by the cost reporting pipeline. CI/CD pipelines should run a dry-run plan and post the delta to the change approver channel.

CI/CD and image orchestration:
- Build: GPU-sidecar and runtime bundles are built in the same CI job as inference images. Tags: sha, model-shim-hash, kernel-flags.
- Promotion: images must pass the "burst-safety" canary (see test matrix below) before they are allowed onto partner pools.
- Release gate: a policy bot enforces that any change to redwood-cloud-bursting-slice module requires: Terraform plan approval, egress budget signoff by cost-ops, and security scanning for open egress ports.

Burst-safety test matrix (CI):
| Test | Purpose | Threshold |
|------|---------|-----------|
| Load-scaled inference smoke | Ensure model starts under reduced-precision variant | <2% error rate |
| Egress metering/unit test | Validate billing tags emitted | 100% tags present |
| Network failover test | Verify fallback to primary within 8s on simulated egress blackout | 100% success |

Runbook: initiating a controlled burst (procedural steps):
1) Triage root cause of primary-region pressure and confirm burst justification in incident channel.
2) Execute: `terraform apply -var 'enable_burst=true'` in the service's bursting module workspace.
3) Use the scheduler API to start a 10% trial window: `POST /api/v1/scheduler/burst` with body: `{ "service": "svc-name", "percent": 10, "duration": 600 }`.
4) Monitor the "burst-egress" dashboards: egress-cost, p50/p95 latency, packet-drop, and model-error-rate.
5) If metrics remain within thresholds after 5 minutes, expand per policy. Otherwise rollback: `POST /api/v1/scheduler/burst/retract` and set the module flag to `force_disable`.

Troubleshooting quick hits:
- Symptom: burst traffic not reaching partner pool.
  - Check: egress route tables for missing next-hop tags (run `gcloud compute routes list --filter="tags:(burst-ingress)"`).
  - Check: service-mesh egress policy logs for mismatched labels.
- Symptom: unexpected spike in egress estimated cost.
  - Check: cost-ops ledger for untagged flows, verify module emitted billing tags.
- Symptom: model mismatch errors in partner pool.
  - Check: model-shim-hash and runtime bundle tag alignment in the image registry.

SLOs and limits (examples):
- Inference latency SLO during burst: p95 < 250ms for short-context requests.
- Egress budget hard cap: $500/day per service unless explicit escalation.
- Burst growth rate: +20% per 30s; maximum 60% of original traffic.

Ownership and roles:
- Burst controller service: eng-infra/scheduler (primary owner).
- Terraform modules: infra-iac team (owner).
- Cost monitoring and reconciliation: finance-ops/cost-ops.
- Security review and egress policy: security-and-compliance/netsec.

Onboarding checklist for a service enabling bursting:
1) Complete burst-capable runbook template and attach to service page.
2) Add egress tags to CI pipeline and validate tags in dry-run.
3) Confirm warm-standby model variants available in the image registry.
4) Run the burst-safety CI matrix end-to-end.
5) Get egress-budget signoff from cost-ops.

Change log:
- 2024-11-03: Created — initial draft of bursting pattern and egress-slice concept.
- 2024-12-14: Added Terraform module contract and CI gate requirements.
- 2025-01-12: Expanded troubleshooting section and tightened burst growth rate.

References and links:
- See the infra-modules repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/infra-modules
- Billing tags convention: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-billing-clarity-and-multipath-metering-spec
- Scheduler API spec: /confluence/eng-infra/platform/scheduler-api-spec (internal)

Appendix — Example alert queries:
- PromQL: `sum by (service, slice) (rate(egress_bytes_total[1m])) > 1e8 and service =~ "svc-.*"` (alerts when burst egress exceeds 100MB/s).
- Pager duty rule: page on persistent egress_budget_spend > 90% for 5 minutes.

End of doc.
