payload.page_title: GPU tenant eviction predictor and provisioning guidelines

sections.body: This document describes a pragmatic system for predicting tenant GPU preemption/eviction risk and tying that prediction into provisioning, autoscaling, and tenant-level mitigation flows. It combines telemetry signals, a lightweight ML scoring pipeline, observability dashboards, Terraform/IaC tagging patterns, and CI/CD safety checks. The goal is to reduce application-visible disruptions and cost by proactively migrating or warming capacity for high-risk tenants while preserving fairness and SLOs.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Preemptible/spot/interruptible GPU instances improve economics but increase evictions that impact tail-latency SLOs.
- Current reactive approaches (post-eviction retry/backoff) let production customer requests surface incidents.
- A low-latency predictor + automated provisioning flow reduces p99 latency spikes, decreases expensive emergency burst allocations, and improves tenant experience.
sections.heading: Why this exists (Motivation)

sections.body:
- Applies to all multi-tenant hosted inference pools that use preemptible GPU instances or cloud shapes with eviction signals.
- Not intended for on-prem private deployments (separate guidance in eng-private-deployments).
- Predictor must be auditable, have a low query latency (<50ms), and be operated by infra SRE in partnership with runtime owners.
sections.heading: Scope and constraints

sections.body:
1) Telemetry ingestion: sample, store, and aggregate eviction-related signals per-host and per-tenant (see Telemetry section).
2) Feature extraction: streaming windowed features (5m, 30m) and historical baselines.
3) Scoring service: lightweight model (logistic-regression or small XGBoost) served as a single API that returns risk score [0.0-1.0].
4) Decision layer: configurable policies translate scores into actions (no-op, pre-warm, start-dedicated, throttle-burst).
5) Execution: IaC/Orchestrator triggers: Terraform run for reserved capacity, autoscaler signals, or request rerouting to resilient pools.
6) Observability & auditing: dashboards, SLO checks, and rollout gating.
sections.heading: Overview of the system

sections.body:
- Instance-level: cloud interrupt_notice_count, instance_uptime, instance_type, lifecycle_event (spot-interruption, maintenance).
- Kernel/driver: GPU_utilization_5s, mem_free_mb, cudnn_errors, nvlink_errors.
- Scheduler: queue_depth_per_tenant, pending_requests_1m, avg_inflight_per_tenant.
- Network/storage: egress_bandwidth_pct, disk_iops_burst, tail_retransmits.
- Historical: eviction_rate_24h, eviction_rate_7d, tenant_recent_evictions (count).
- External: provider_spot_capacity_index (region-level signal provided by cloud cost analytics).
sections.heading: Telemetry and signals (what we collect)

sections.body:
- Windowing: compute rate features at 5m and 30m windows + exponential decay for 24h baseline.
- Binarize categorical fields (instance_type family), normalize GPU_utilization by instance GPU count.
- Use missing-value sentinel (-1) and include a feature 'signal_completeness' (percent of signals present) to guard against blind spots.
sections.heading: Implementation notes (feature engineering)

sections.body:
- Model family: start with regularized logistic regression (interpretable) for first 30d; consider small tree ensembles if feature interactions justify it.
- Training cadence: daily retrain on rolling 14d window, validate on last 7d holdout.
- Metrics: ROC-AUC target >0.72, precision@0.1 recall >0.6 on labeled eviction events.
- Labeling: binary label when a tenant has a disruptive eviction requiring request-level retry within 30 minutes of interruption.
- Explainability: store top-3 contributing features per prediction for troubleshooting.

Decision policies (mapping score -> action):
- score < 0.05: no action (baseline).
- 0.05 <= score < 0.2: monitor & increase sampling frequency for tenant telemetry.
- 0.2 <= score < 0.5: pre-warm strategy — allocate a warm slot in a non-preemptible warm-pool (time-limited reservation: default 20m).
- 0.5 <= score < 0.8: proactive dedicated allocation or burst reserve, and notify runtime-owner channel.
- score >= 0.8: immediate protective action — move new requests to a resilient pool, fail fast for batch jobs with retry token, and trigger an on-call page if SLO impact is expected.

Operational runbook (when predictor raises a tenant to >=0.5):
1) Alerting: create an Ops alert with ticket auto-created in PagerDuty playbook. Relevant labels: tenant-id, predicted_score, region.
2) Triage (SRE on-call): check top-3 feature contributors and recent host eviction events in last 60m.
3) Mitigate: engage the decision policy — attempt pre-warm or provision dedicated capacity. If the provisioning API fails, run fallback route: redirect requests to fallback model variant (lower-cost) or to a multi-region fallback.
4) Post-mortem: if an actual eviction occurs that resulted in customer-visible errors, label the incident with model-prediction outcome and update training label store.
5) Feedback: incrementally adjust policy thresholds in the feature-flagged decision service after triage approval.
sections.heading: Eviction Risk Model (operational profile)

sections.body:
- Prediction latency: median <25ms, p95 <80ms.
- False positive mitigation budget: at most 2% of pre-warm actions per week may be false-positive without manual sign-off.
- Cost guardrail: monthly cost impact must be <5% of spot-savings; infra-finance pipeline will sample cost-impact reports every 7 days.
- Auditing: every prediction and action must be logged in the audit sink (request id, tenant id, features, score, chosen_action).
sections.heading: SLOs and guardrails for predictor-driven actions

sections.body:
- Tagging: all GPU hosts must include tags: {"gpu_pool":"<pool>", "preemptible":"true|false", "tenant_priority":"<tier>"}. Decision service reads these tags when choosing migration targets.
- Warm-pool resource module: introduce module 'infra-gpu-warm-reservations' with small ephemeral reservations (default 20m).
- Provider abstractions: create an interface module that can call cloud provider instance-creation steps via Terraform Cloud run tasks or an orchestrator operator.

Appendix: example Terraform variable table (as text):
- variable name: tenant_eviction_policy
  - type: map(string)
  - description: mapping of tenant-id -> policy tier (e.g., "gold", "silver", "bronze")
- variable name: warm_pool_default_ttl_minutes
  - type: number
  - default: 20
- variable name: eviction_predictor_endpoint
  - type: string
  - description: internal scoring API URL
sections.heading: Terraform / IaC changes required (patterns and examples)

sections.body:
```hcl
module "warm_reservation" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.company/infra/terraform-modules//gpu-warm-reservation"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  ttl_minutes = var.warm_pool_default_ttl_minutes
  pool_selector = "gpu-pool-spot-us-west2"
}
```
sections.heading: Example IaC snippet (pseudo-terraform)

sections.body:
- Unit tests: model scoring service must have a deterministic test harness that includes adversarial examples (missing signals).
- Integration tests: run a synthetic pipeline that injects a fake eviction spike and asserts that the decision layer triggers a pre-warm (observed via terraform plan/apply mocks).
- Canary: enable predictor for 1% of tenants initially (labelled test-tenants) with full logging. Gradually increase to 10% and then to 100% after cost and false-positive checks.
- Git reviewers: any change to action thresholds or IaC modules must be reviewed by infra-sre and runtime-team leads (use CODEOWNERS).

Dashboards and alerts to create (metric names are canonical):
- dashboard: tenant-eviction-risk-overview — top tenants by weekly avg_score, recent actions, and cost impact.
- panel: predictor-health — latency_histogram_ms, errors_per_min, model_drift_score.
- alert: predictor-latency-high — trigger when p95 latency >200ms for 5m. PagerDuty severity: P2.
- alert: prewarm-failure-rate — trigger when prewarm_apply_fail_rate >2% over 10m. Severity: P1 if >5%.
sections.heading: CI/CD and testing guidance (safety-first)

sections.body:
1) Dev sandbox: deploy scoring service to staging and wire to synthetic telemetry generator.
2) Safety canary: enable decisions in read-only mode (log-only) for 2 weeks.
3) Small active canary: 1% of tenants with prewarm enabled and a tight manual rollback path.
4) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%; perform cost & false-positive review at each step (2 business days).
5) Post-migration audit: after 100% rollout, run a 30-day cost & SLO review; if cost>target, revert policy changes behind feature flag.
sections.heading: Rollout plan and change control

sections.body:
- On-call owner (first responder): infra-sre team (pagerduty: infra-sre-eviction).
- Long-term owner: infra-platform (runtime & autoscaler) with weekly syncs with serving-runtime team.
- Data & model owner: applied-ml-and-evals.
- Finance contact for cost analysis: finance-infra-analytics.
sections.heading: Ownership and contacts

sections.body:
- Q1: Approve the initial action thresholds and cost guardrails with finance (owner: infra-platform, due: 2026-03-01).
- Q2: Implement feature-flag framework for policy tuning exposed in the Console (owner: eng-developer-experience, due: 2026-04-15).
- Q3: Evaluate moving from logistic regression to a calibrated ensemble if precision/recall plateau (owner: applied-ml-and-evals, due: 2026-06-01).

Appendix B: Example queries and CLI checks:
- List tenants with recent high risk (SQL pseudo-query):
```sql
SELECT tenant_id, avg(score) as avg_score, count(*) as samples
FROM eviction_predictions
WHERE ts > now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY avg_score DESC
LIMIT 50;
```
- CLI check for prewarm reservations (kubectl/infra-ctl):
```bash
infra-ctl warm-reservations list --region us-west2 --state active --json | jq '.[] | {tenant_id, ttl_remaining}'
```
sections.heading: Open questions and next steps (actions)

sections.body:
- See runbooks: kv-cache-consensus-and-warmup-coordination-runbook for KV cache thawing implications.
- See infra-iac module: infra-gpu-warm-reservations (module repo link in internal git).
sections.heading: References and related pages

sections.body:
- 2025-09-10 (Riley Chen) - initial draft created.
- 2025-11-02 (Riley Chen) - added terraform patterns and CI/CD gating section.
- 2026-02-12 (Maya Patel) - finalized thresholds and reviewer feedback incorporated.

End of document.

payload.page_title: GPU QoS Reservoir and Tenant Priority Allocator

sections.body: This document defines the GPU QoS Reservoir and Tenant Priority Allocator (QRTPA): a cross-region/multi-cloud allocation control plane that enforces per-tenant quality-of-service (QoS) targets while enabling economic burst capacity. QRTPA is intended for Redwood’s Dedicated and Private deployments and is optional for Hosted where isolation is less strict.
sections.heading: Summary

sections.body:
- Provide firm guarantees for on-contract tenants (reserved capacity) while allowing elastic burst usage for non-reserved workloads.
- Minimize application-visible latency regressions during capacity pressure via graceful preemption policies and fallbacks.
- Support multi-cloud placement decisions with affinity hints and failover.
- Expose a Terraform module and a small control-plane microservice to coordinate allocation decisions and audit logs.
sections.heading: Goals and scope

sections.body:
- Infra engineers operating GPU fleets
- Platform SREs and capacity planners
- Product and sales teams that manage tenant SLAs
sections.heading: Audience

sections.body:
1) Components:
- Reservoir Manager (service): tracks global burst tokens (reservoir) per cluster pool and per region.
- Tenant Profile Store (KVS): stores tenant SLAs, reserved units, priority, and preemption policy.
- Allocator API (gRPC + REST): decision interface used by the scheduling layer and autoscaler.
- Enforcement hooks (kube-scheduler plugin / VM agent): implements soft/hard preemption and transfer to fallback model variants.
- Auditor (job): writes allocation decisions and preemption events to audit-log S3/GCS and exposes query endpoints.

2) Key concepts and invariants:
- Reserved Capacity: guaranteed GPU units assigned to a tenant (monthly/annual purchase).
- Burst Reservoir: short-term pool of tokens representing GPU-seconds available for transient spike usage. Tokens replenish at a configured rate per cluster.
- Priority Levels: integer scale 0..10. Reserved customers default to >=6. Trial/free-tier is 0–2.
- Soft Preemption: lower-priority jobs are signaled to checkpoint / reduce concurrency; they have a configurable grace window (default 90s).
- Hard Preemption: immediate eviction; only applied for priority difference >=5 or when hard-safeguard thresholds reached.
sections.heading: High-level design

sections.body:
| setting | description | example |
|---|---|---|
| reservoir_replenish_rate | tokens/sec added to the pool per cluster | 20 |
| reservoir_max_tokens | maximum tokens storable | 86400 |
| hard_preempt_threshold_pct | cluster GPU utilization percent to trigger hard preemption | 95 |
| soft_preempt_grace_s | grace period before eviction during soft preemption | 90 |
| tenant_priority | tenant priority integer | 8 |
| reserved_gpu_units | units guaranteed for tenant | 64 |
sections.heading: Configuration table (example)

sections.body:
- The module deploys the Reservoir Manager CRD, configmap templates, and an IAM/service-account per-region.
- It is designed to integrate with existing gpu-node pools; it does not create compute nodes itself.
sections.heading: Usage notes

sections.body:
module "gpu_qos_reservoir" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal.redwood.ai/infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu/qos-reservoir"
  cluster_name = "gpu-prod-us-west-2"
  reservoir_replenish_rate = 20
  reservoir_max_tokens = 86400
  audit_log_bucket = "s3://redwood-gpu-audit-prod"
  default_soft_grace_s = 90
}
sections.heading: Example variables (YAML snippet)

sections.body:
- Allocation decision latency: 99th percentile < 45ms for Allocator API.
- Preemption success rate (after soft-grace): >= 99% within 2 minutes of decision.
- Audit-log lag: < 30s for write-through; batch export < 10m.
- Preemption churn: < 2% of running jobs per cluster per hour.
sections.heading: Operational SLOs and thresholds

sections.body:
- qr_reservoir_tokens_total{cluster,region} (gauge)
- qr_alloc_decision_latency_seconds (histogram)
- qr_preempt_events_total{outcome,reason,tenant} (counter)
- qr_soft_preempt_signals_total (counter)
- qr_hard_evictions_total (counter)
- qr_audit_export_lag_seconds (gauge)
sections.heading: Metrics to instrument (suggested Prometheus names)

sections.body:
- Cluster overview: reservoir tokens, GPU utilization, preemption rate, pending allocation queue length.
- Tenant QoS view: reserved vs used GPUs, burst consumption over time, preemption incidents.
sections.heading: Dashboard suggestions

sections.body:
- Each tenant profile includes affinity tags: [region_preference], [latency_budget_ms], [data_residency_constraint].
- The Allocator computes a placement score factoring: available tokens, reserved capacity, cross-region egress cost, and data residency.
- Placement fallback order: local reserved pool -> local reservoir -> peer-region reserved -> peer-region reservoir -> preemptible spot pools.
sections.heading: Multi-cloud placement and affinity rules

sections.body: 1) Symptom: Reservoir tokens rapidly deplete and preemption spikes increase.
sections.heading: Failure modes and mitigation (runbook excerpts)

sections.body:
1. Verify metrics: qr_reservoir_tokens_total and qr_preempt_events_total.
2. Temporarily raise soft_preempt_grace_s to 300s to reduce churn: kubectl patch configmap qr-config -n infra --type merge -p '{"data":{"soft_preempt_grace_s":"300"}}'
3. Trigger capacity burst: request emergency spot burst via cloud provisioning playbook (link referenced below).
4. Notify on-call: pg-infra-sre@groups.redwood.ai.
sections.heading: Immediate action

sections.body:
- Which tenants consumed >50% of reservoir in 10m windows?
- Were any misconfigured tenant priorities?

2) Symptom: Allocator API 99th latency spikes > 200ms.
sections.heading: Postmortem checks

sections.body:
1. Check service pods and threadpool contention. Scale controller replicas: kubectl scale deployment/qr-allocator -n infra --replicas=3
2. Fallback: enable local cache mode (config flag: allocator_cache_enabled=true) to serve decisions for 30s TTL.

3) Symptom: Auditor export failing, audit lag grows > 10m.
sections.heading: Immediate action

sections.body:
1. Identify S3/GCS permission errors in pod logs; rotate IAM keys if needed.
2. Switch to local durable queue: kubectl patch deployment/qr-auditor -n infra --type merge -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"qr-auditor","env":[{"name":"AUDIT_MODE","value":"local-queue"}]}]}}}}'
sections.heading: Immediate action

sections.body:
1. Developer/staging validation:
- Deploy module into a staging cluster with synthetic tenants.
- Run synthetic spike tests (see scripts/synthetic-burst-test.sh) verifying preemption behavior and audit logs.
2. Canary in a small production pool:
- Target one non-critical cluster.
- Monitor allocation latency and reservoir stability for 72 hours.
3. Gradual expansion:
- Increase rollout by doubling cluster count every 24h while watching preemption churn < 1.5%.
4. Full rollout and retrospective.
sections.heading: Rollout checklist (for module upgrade or policy change)

sections.body:
- The module uses a stateful CRD; upgrades must preserve existing CR objects. Always run terraform plan and inspect changes to aws_s3_bucket or IAM bindings.
- Back up the Tenant Profile Store before applying changes: kubectl get tenants -A -o yaml > backup/tenants-$(date +%F).yaml
sections.heading: Terraform migration notes

sections.body:
- Primary owner: infra-gpu@redwood.ai (team: infra engineering GPU-fleet)
- Secondary: platform-sre@redwood.ai
- Pager: infra-oncall rotation (see oncall-and-incident-response docs).
sections.heading: Ownership and escalation

sections.body:
- Allocate a transient burst token for tenant T123 from CLI (admin only):
redwoodctl qr grant-burst --tenant T123 --tokens 1200 --reason "test-burst"

- Revoke a granted burst token:
redwoodctl qr revoke-burst --grant-id abc123 --force

- Query allocation decisions for tenant over last 1h:
redwoodctl qr query-decisions --tenant T123 --window 1h --output json | jq '.'

payload.page_title: Cross-region spot diversity, placement, and rollback strategy

sections.body:
Summary

This page defines Redwood's recommended approach for running a cost-optimized, resilient GPU fleet using a mix of spot/preemptible and reserved instances across multiple regions and instance types. It describes placement strategies, Terraform/IaC patterns, CI/CD considerations for node image promotion, expected SLO impacts, monitoring metrics, and an explicit rollback/runbook for spot preemption storms. Use this as the canonical guidance for teams provisioning GPU capacity for inference, training experiments, and batch workloads.

Goals and constraints

- Primary goals:
  - Maintain production throughput SLOs (median token latency per request, and per-model QPS) while minimizing unit GPU cost.
  - Keep unplanned user-visible degradation below the reliability error budget (see SLOs section).
  - Provide deterministic rollback and failover steps when spot markets cause capacity loss.
- Constraints:
  - Some workloads (inference tail-latency-critical) must never run on preemptible instances; training and batch workloads can tolerate preemption.
  - Network egress/regional compliance restrictions may limit placement to specific regions for certain customers (see Private deployments).

Service-level objectives (SLOs) and thresholds

- Availability SLO for inference control-plane: 99.95% monthly.
- P99 generation latency SLO (hosted tier): < 550ms.
- Queue depth (pending model requests) must be < 75 requests per node-class during steady-state.
- Preemption rate alert thresholds:
  - info: 0.5% 1h rolling
  - warning: 2% 30m rolling
  - critical: 5% 15m rolling -> triggers runbook below

Placement strategy overview

1) Region diversity by workload class
   - Reserved/Guaranteed: Provision minimal reserved pools in 1 primary region per customer/tenant (for Dedicated). All latency-sensitive inference replicas must be pinned to reserved pools.
   - Spot/Preemptible pools: Maintain spot pools in at least 3 regions (primary, secondary, tertiary) with varied instance types to avoid correlated pre-emption.
   - Edge/nearby regions: For regional customers with residency constraints, run spot fallback only within allowed regions.

2) Instance type diversity
   - For each spot pool, configure 2–3 GPU instance families (e.g., A100-80GB, A10G, H100 where supported) prioritized by cost-performance profiles.
   - Use the autoscaler to prefer lower-cost types but allow substitutions up to +15% latency degradation (configurable per model).

3) Fractional capacity split (example)
   - Reserved/Guaranteed: 40% of steady-state capacity for production inference.
   - Spot: 50% (spread across regions/types).
   - Burst/on-demand: 10% for immediate scale-up while provisioning on-demand replacements.

Terraform / IaC patterns

- Use the gpu-spot-pool module pattern: a single module that exposes:
  - regions: list(string)
  - instance_families: list(string)
  - desired_capacity: number (per-region desired)
  - min_capacity, max_capacity
  - preemption_policy: {drain_timeout_seconds, fallback_priority} (string or map)

Example module invocation (pseudo-Terraform HCL inside YAML for readability):

module "gpu_spot_pool_us_east" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood/internal/infra-modules.git//gpu-spot-pool"
  regions = ["us-east-1", "us-east-2"]
  instance_families = ["a100-80gb","a10g","h100"]
  desired_capacity = 120
  min_capacity = 30
  max_capacity = 300
  preemption_policy = {drain_timeout_seconds = 45, fallback_priority = "region_first"}
}
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Keep each module idempotent and safe to run in CI pipelines.
- Use remote state keyed by region and environment.
- Tag instances with: service=gpu-inference, team=${var.team}, pool_type=spot, stack=${var.env}
- Don't hardcode quotas; surface quotas in outputs for quota checks in CI (see CI checks).

CI/CD and node image promotion

- Image pipeline: build -> unit tests -> GPU smoke tests -> canary bake -> promote to regional channels.
- Promotion channels: staging -> canary -> production. Each channel corresponds to a Terraform workspace and image channel tag.
- Canary policy: deploy new node-images to 2% of spot instances in secondary region and run the perf/compat test-suite for 2 hours before wider rollout.
- Blockers: kernel mismatches, CUDA/cuDNN version regressions, driver OOMs. If any are detected, block promotion and auto-open an incident.

Autoscaling and draining behavior

- Continuous batching and GPU-sharing require graceful node drains: set kubectl drain timeout to 90s and grace period to 120s on inference pods that support checkpointable KV caches.
- Drain policy for spot preemption: drain -> re-route traffic -> wait (drain_timeout) -> terminate. For non-drainable workloads (some training jobs), enable checkpointing or migrate to reserved nodes.

Monitoring, dashboards, and alerting
sections.heading: Module implementation notes

sections.body: - GPU utilization (avg, p95), GPU memory utilization, host CPU steal/time, node preemption_count, node_boot_time, pod_eviction_count, queue_depth, pending_pods
sections.heading: Key metrics (per region/pool/type)

sections.body:
- Pool health: desired vs available nodes, preemption rate heatmap across regions
- Latency impact: P50/P95 gen latency versus pool capacity
- Cost panel: $/GPU-hour by region and instance family
sections.heading: Suggested dashboard panels

sections.body:
- preemption_rate >= 5% over 15m -> PagerDuty SEV2 -> trigger runbook A (preemption storm)
- available_capacity < 60% of desired for > 10m -> PagerDuty on-call -> trigger scale-up to on-demand and start capacity-rebalance (see runbook)

Runbook A: Spot preemption storm (critical)

1) PagerDuty alert fires with tag : preemption-storm. On-call acknowledges within 5 minutes.
2) Triage (10 min): check preemption_rate by region, identify primary impacted pools using the spot preemption heatmap dashboard.
3) Immediate mitigations (automated where possible):
   - Increase fallback priority to prefer lower-cost on-demand types in secondary region.
   - Trigger terraform apply for on-demand fallback pools (pre-created IaC but scaled to 0) using the image channel currently marked 'production'.
   - Reduce scheduling of non-critical batch training: mark training queue to paused (CI/CD job label: resource:noncritical).
4) If latency SLOs are breached (p99 > SLO):
   - Move traffic to reserved pools and regional replicas via smart routing (console route override).
   - If reserved pools are insufficient, escalate to SEV1 and activate emergency capacity purchase (finance-approved commit).
5) Recovery: once preemption rate < 1% for 30m and queue depth back to < 50 per node-class, begin rebalancing spot pools back to target and restore batch schedules.
6) Post-incident: open a postmortem and update the tokenized cost registry with the additional on-demand spend.

Rollback playbook: image-related instability during wide spot rollout

- Trigger: canary-to-prod rollout causes driver OOMs on 3% of new nodes within 90 minutes.
- Steps:
  1) Promote previous stable image into the production image channel (CI rollback job).
  2) Terraform apply to update node pool launch template to stable image (use rolling_update_strategy: 5% parallel).
  3) Monitor: verify GPU smoke tests pass on new nodes, check p99 latency and pod restart counts.
  4) If errors persist, revert configuration changes and schedule an emergency freeze on image promotions.

Ownership and run cadence

- Ownership: infra capacity team (eng-infra/gpu-fleet) owns modules, dashboards, and runbooks. Service owners own model-level fallback settings.
- Weekly cadence: 30-minute architecture sync to review spot availability changes and cost targets. Monthly: revisit capacity split and reserved commitments against usage trends.

Operational checklist for new pool creation

1) Submit IaC change with module invocation and required tags.
2) Run terraform plan in CI and wait for quota-checks to pass.
3) Create image channel and run canary bake for 2 hours.
4) Scale pool to min_capacity and validate node registration and smoke tests.
5) Set alerts and dashboards for new pool (use templated dashboard JSON).
6) Announce in #infra-gpu with runbook link and owner.

Appendices

A. Example Terraform outputs table (rendered)
| output_name | description | sample_value |
| desired_capacity | Desired number of nodes across the module | 120 |
| quota_check_passed | CI gate result | true |

B. Common CLI snippets
- List spot instances by region: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:pool_type,Values=spot Name=instance-state-name,Values=running --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].[InstanceId,InstanceType,Placement.AvailabilityZone,Tags]' --output table
- Drain a node safely: kubectl cordon node/<node> && kubectl drain node/<node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=300s

C. Related policies
- Cost governance: reference internal chargeback policy (finance) for emergency on-demand purchases.
- Compliance: ensure region choices honor data-residency restrictions per-customer label.

Document change history

- 2024-04-22: created by Lena Thompson (initial draft).
- 2024-09-10: added CI image promotion canary policy (Aisha Patel).
- 2025-02-14: clarified preemption alert thresholds and added rollback playbook (Marcus Green).

References

- See: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/gpu-spot-fallback-autoscaler-module-and-runbook
- See: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-fleet-scaling-metrics-and-oncall-runbook

payload.page_title: Proactive GPU Warm-pool Federation and Cost Throttler

sections.body:
Summary:
This page describes the design, Terraform module usage, CI/CD rollout, operational runbook, and alerting for the Proactive GPU Warm-pool Federation and Cost Throttler (PGW-C). PGW-C is a multi-account, multi-region warm-pool coordination layer plus a cost-aware admission controller that: 
- Keeps preloaded model KV caches and warmed containers on a curated set of GPU nodes.
- Federates warm capacity across regional pools with fair-share and reclaim policies.
- Enforces cost throttling and burst protection to meet monthly committed capacity budgets.

Goals:
- Reduce cold-starts for inference by maintaining a warmed pool of model-serving sessions.
- Provide predictable unit economics by limiting uncontrolled burst usage and applying fair-share.
- Enable safe, incremental rollouts of warm-pool policies via CI/CD and Terraform.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated clusters managed by eng-infra (gpu clusters tagged: redwood:gpubackend).
- Covers on-demand, spot, and dedicated pre-warm nodes.
- Integrates with: gpu-warm-manager, pool-orchestrator, spot-fallback-allocator, warm-pool-metrics-exporter, account-billing-sidecar.

Architecture Overview:
- gpu-warm-manager (Kubernetes deployment per region): watches model manifests, reconciles warm sessions, and executes seeding jobs to load KV cache into serving runtime.
- pool-orchestrator (central control plane service): maintains global view of warm-pool capacity, enforces federation policies, computes cross-region rebalancing ops, signals terraform operator for provisioning.
- cost-throttler (admission controller): webhook that inspects incoming infer requests and applies throttles or fallback model variants when cost budgets are exceeded.
- metrics pipeline: warm-pool-metrics-exporter -> prometheus -> cortex long-term store.

Key Metrics and SLOs:
- Warm-hit-rate (fraction of requests served from warmed sessions): target >= 95% (prod); warning >= 92%.
- Cold-start-rate (requests that triggered a cold session): target <= 5% per hour window.
- Average rewarm latency (time to seed a KV cache on a node): target <= 18s (95th percentile).
- Budget overspend incidents (cost from burst above committed budget): target 0 per month; alert on > 1% over commitment for 24h.

Federation & Fair-share Policies (summary):
- Pools are grouped by tenant priority (tiers: enterprise, plat, self-serve).
- Each pool advertises: available-warm-sessions, preemptible-capacity, cost-rate-per-token.
- Orchestrator computes fair-share allocation every 60s and emits transfer proposals.
- Transfer proposals are gated by safety checks (latency impact, network egress threshold, cross-account policy).

Terraform modules and variables (example):
- Module path: terraform/modules/gpu-warm-pool
- Important variables:
  - name (string)
  - region (string)
  - account_id (string)
  - desired_warm_sessions (number)
  - spot_fallback_ratio (number, default 0.25)
  - budget_monthly_usd (string)

Terraform snippet (example usage):
```
module "eu-warmpool" {
  source = "../modules/gpu-warm-pool"
  name   = "eu-prod-warmpool"
  region = "eu-west-1"
  account_id = "123456789012"
  desired_warm_sessions = 120
  spot_fallback_ratio = 0.2
  budget_monthly_usd = "15000"
}
```

CI/CD and Rollout Strategy:
1) Feature branch: create terraform/pgw changes and a small canary for gpu-warm-manager (2 nodes) in staging.
2) Integration tests: automated smoke that verifies warm-hit-rate improves vs baseline and that cost-throttler correctly gates tokens.
3) Canary promotion: promote to 10% of traffic in prod region; observe for 72 hours.
4) Gradual ramp: expand to 30% then 60% over successive days if no regressions.
5) Full promotion: apply Terraform to all configured regions and mark the module as promoted in the iac registry.

Rollback criteria (automated gates):
- Warm-hit-rate drop > 2% from pre-rollout baseline for 30m.
- Error-rate increase > 1% (absolute) or latency P95 increase > 150ms.
- Cost anomalies: projected monthly overrun > 3% on daily extrapolation.

Operational Runbook (Incident Triage):
1) Detection:
  - Alerts: warm-hit-rate < 92% (critical), cold-start-rate > 8% (critical), cost-overspend-warning (high).
  - Dashboards: per-region warm session inventory, cross-account transfer queue, admission-blocked-requests.
2) Initial mitigation:
  - If warm-hit-rate low: execute `kubectl -n redwood scale deployment/gpu-warm-manager --replicas=3` to force additional seeding.
  - If cold-start storm: enable emergency soft-throttle: POST /v1/admin/throttle?policy=soft-burst to cost-throttler.
  - If cross-region egress threshold tripped: pause federation by toggling orchestrator flag: `kubectl set env deployment/pool-orchestrator ENABLE_FEDERATION=false`.
3) Reconciliation steps:
  - Run `pgwctl rebuild --region eu-west-1 --models popular-models` to re-seed top-20 models.
  - Inspect Prometheus query: `sum(rate(warm_pool_seed_errors_total[5m])) by (region)` and remediate pod logs.
4) Post-incident:
  - Create a postmortem within 48 hours. Record state changes and terraform diffs.
  - Adjust warm_session targets or bump budget; add preflight checks in CI if needed.

Prometheus Alerts (examples):
- Alert: PGW_WarmHitRateLow
  Expression: `warm_hit_rate{env="prod"} < 0.92`
  For: 10m
  Severity: critical
  Runbook: Follow Operational Runbook above.

- Alert: PGW_BudgetOverspendForecast
  Expression: `increase(cost_throttler_spend_usd_total[24h]) / (budget_monthly_usd / 30) > 1.01`
  For: 6h
  Severity: high
  Runbook: Throttle non-enterprise tiers and open a billing incident.

Cost Throttler Config (table):
| key | description | example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| global_burst_limit | Max sessions above target across all pools | 150 |
| tenant_min_reserve | Minimum sessions reserved per tier | enterprise: 30, plat: 10 |
| burst_window_seconds | Sliding window for burst accounting | 3600 |
| overspend_action | Action on projected overspend | soft_throttle | 

Admission Control behaviors:
- soft_throttle: queue requests up to 30s and return token cost hints to clients.
- hard_reject: immediate 429 with recommended fallback model id.
- fallback_model: map of compatible lower-cost model variants per tenant.

Safety and Security Considerations:
- Account boundaries: cross-account federation writes are implemented using provisioning roles with least privilege policies; terraform operator uses temporary STS tokens.
- KMS: all model seeds are performed with ephemeral keys; KMS key usage logged in audit-logging service.
- Data residency: federation respects region-specific residency flags; orchestrator rejects proposals that violate residency.

Operational Playbooks and Commands (cheat-sheet):
- Check warm inventory: `pgwctl inventory --region us-west-2`
- Force re-seed model list: `pgwctl rebuild --models "gpt-small,gpt-embed" --parallel 8`
- Pause federation: `kubectl set env deployment/pool-orchestrator ENABLE_FEDERATION=false -n redwood`
- Unblock cost-throttler: `curl -X POST https://admin.internal/cost-throttler/unblock --header "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"`

Testing Guidance for Eng Teams:
- Local run: run `make dev-warm-manager` to start a single-node warm-manager and exercise seeding flows against a local runtime.
- CI testcases to include: 
  - Warm session reconciliation under flapping node conditions.
  - Cross-account transfer approval/denial flows.
  - Cost-throttler behavior under synthetic overspend.

Ownership and Contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-infra/gpu-capacity team (oncall: gpu-capacity-oncall@redwood.internal)
- Pager: #infra-oncall (Slack)
- Escalation: Head of Eng Infra (Arjun Patel) -> CTO on-call if incident > 4h.

References and Links:
- terraform/modules/gpu-warm-pool (internal git)
- internal runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/kv-cache-consensus-and-warmup-coordination-runbook.json
- observability dashboards: grafana/redwood/pgw-overview

Change Log:
- 2024-11-05: Document created by Maya Chen.
- 2024-12-10: Added cost-throttler policies and Prometheus alerts (review by Arjun).
- 2025-01-18: Updated SLO targets and rollback criteria; added federation pause command.

Appendix: Sample alert playbook checklist (to attach to pager duty incidents)
1) Acknowledge incident in PagerDuty.
2) Run `pgwctl inventory` and capture top 5 models by cold-start count.
3) If warm-hit-rate trending down, scale warm-manager and trigger re-seed for top models.
4) If cost forecast > 2% overspend, enable tiered soft-throttle and notify billing.
5) Attach terraform plan and recent CI job ids to the incident ticket.

Note: This document is intended to be a living playbook. Engineers should update the Terraform module references and CI job names when promoting changes.

payload.page_title: GPU Capacity Reconciliation Audit and Credits Ledger

sections.body:
Overview
--------
This page defines the GPU Capacity Reconciliation Audit process and the canonical Credits Ledger used by Redwood Inference to reconcile physical/virtual GPU allocations, tenant consumption, and accounting credits across cloud accounts and on-prem pools. The goal is a repeatable, auditable monthly reconciliation that ties IaC state, telemetry, allocation decisions, and billing signals together for accuracy and dispute resolution.

Intended audience
- Infra oncall and SREs responsible for GPU fleet accounting
- FinOps and billing analysts performing chargeback reconciliations
- Platform engineers who own Terraform/IaC modules for GPU pools
- Engineering managers reviewing quota disputes

Scope
- Applies to all public cloud GPU pools (aws/gcp/azure) and managed on-prem clusters that are reconciled into Redwood’s capacity ledger.
- Includes reserved capacity, burst credits, spot fallback usage, and warm-pool reservations.
- Excludes ephemeral developer laptops and third-party managed services (unless explicitly integrated).

Key principles
- Single source of truth: Terraform state plus cloud metadata + runtime telemetry -> reconciliation pipeline -> Credits Ledger.
- Immutable audit trail: every reconciliation run produces an immutable snapshot and an exportable CSV/Parquet file stored for 12 months by default.
- Explainability: every ledger entry references the upstream evidence (Terraform resource id, VM instance id, Pod/node id, telemetry export path).
- Triage first, chargeback second: reconcile for correctness before making billing adjustments.

Terminology
- Allocation: A logical reservation of GPU capacity to a tenant or system (examples: reserved pool, dedicated reservation, ephemeral lease).
- Consumption: Observed usage derived from tokenized runtime telemetry (tokens/minute, GPU-hours, vram-second counters).
- Credit: Accounting unit used for chargeback. For Redwood we use GPU-credit where 1 GPU-credit == 1 GPU-hour at baseline SKU.
- Adjustment: Manual or automated change to the ledger to reflect contract terms, refunds, or errors.

Architecture and data flow
1. IaC source: Terraform state (S3/remote) + module metadata (module tags: team, environment, tier).
2. Cloud inventory: periodic cloud provider API snapshots (instance IDs, SKUs, zone, preemptible flag).
3. Runtime telemetry: serving-runtime exports per-node GPU-hours and system tags via metrics pipeline (Prometheus -> metrics-bridge -> bigquery).
4. Reconciliation service: batch job (airflow/kubernetes CronJob) that ingests the three sources and emits a Credits Ledger snapshot.
5. Ledger storage: canonical ledger stored in BigQuery (or internal RDS replica) and exported to S3/GS for archived snapshots.
6. Downstream: FinOps dashboards, billing exports, and dispute management UI.

Ledger schema (canonical columns)
| column | type (conceptual) | description |
|--------|-------------------|-------------|
| snapshot_id | string | reconciliation run UUID |
| run_date | date | reconciliation run date |
| resource_id | string | cloud instance / node / terraform id |
| resource_type | string | "instance" | "node" | "reservation" |
| sku | string | cloud GPU SKU (e.g., nvidia-a100-80gb) |
| allocated_to | string | tenant id or system tag |
| allocation_type | string | reserved | burst | spot | warm_pool |
| observed_gpu_hours | string | float stored as string for export compatibility |
| ledger_credits | string | computed credits assigned |
| evidence_refs | string | comma-separated list of evidence ids (terraform_state_key, metrics_blob) |
| adjustment_note | string | free text for manual adjustments |

Reconciliation cadence and windows
- Daily lightweight run: verifies inventory and emits alerts for drift > 5% between IaC and cloud snapshot. Produces diffs stored in /reconciliations/daily/.
- Weekly audit run: full ingest of metrics and IaC, writes ledger snapshot, runs automated validation checks.
- Monthly financial snapshot: authoritative export of the Credits Ledger used by billing exports. Locked for edits after 14 days unless a formal correction request is approved.

Automated validation checks (examples)
- IaC vs cloud count check: |expected_instances - cloud_instances| / expected_instances < 0.05 passes.
- Telemetry continuity: nodes must have >= 90% telemetry coverage in the window or be flagged as telemetry-missing.
- SKU mismatch: SKU in Terraform must match SKU reported by cloud API.
- Double allocation: Ensure resource_id assigned to at most one tenant allocation.
- Credits bounds: ledger_credits must be within +/-20% of observed_gpu_hours * SKU-factor unless an adjustment rule exists.

Alerting and SLOs
- SLO: Daily reconciliation job success 99.5% monthly.
- Alert: reconciliation-failure high priority -> page oncall SRE immediately.
- Alert: drift-detected (>=5% on daily run) -> slack channel #gpu-infra and create ticket in JIRA with priority P2.
- Alert: telemetry-missing for a reserved resource in monthly snapshot -> notify owner_team and create follow-up task.

Terraform / IaC integration patterns
- Canonical tags required on every GPU resource: terraform module should set tags {"gpu:allocation_owner": "<team>", "gpu:pool": "<pool-name>", "gpu:billing_tier": "<tier>"}. The reconciliation service relies on these tags to map instances to ledger allocations.
- IaC sentinel policy: run a pre-apply check that validates required tags and denies apply if missing. Example sentinel rule snippet: `deny unless has_tag("gpu:allocation_owner")`.
- Module outputs: every gpu pool module must export `pool_id`, `pool_tier`, and `default_billing_profile` to the Terraform state so the reconciliation job can link module-level reservations to instances.

CI/CD validations (merge-time checks)
1. Terraform plan Linting: PRs touching gpu modules trigger `tfsec` and `terraform plan` validations.
2. Reconciliation schema contract test: changes to module outputs must increment the reconciliation contract version (a small JSON file tracked in repo). This prevents silent schema drift.
3. Integration test: for major changes, create a canary pool in staging using the module and run a reconciliation dry-run that validates the mapping end-to-end (IaC -> cloud -> metrics).

Operational runbook: Monthly reconciliation failure -> triage and resolution (step-by-step)
1. On alert, open the reconciliation run details page (link in alert).
2. Check job logs: `kubectl logs -n infra reconciliation-job-<snapshot_id>`. Look for the first error block.
3. If IaC remote-state fetch failed: verify remote state S3 role access by running `aws s3api get-object --bucket terraform-state-prod --key <key>` from reconciliation pod credentials.
4. If cloud API rate limit: escalate to platform API quota owner, and retry with exponential backoff. Record rate-limit headers.
5. If telemetry ingestion missing: run manual metrics export from the metrics-bridge `python scripts/export_metrics.py --window 2026-02-01 --out /tmp/metrics.json` and validate with `jq`.
6. If ledger computation error: run the ledger verifier locally using `make ledger-verify SNAPSHOT=<snapshot_id>` which executes the same checks as the pipeline.
7. If manual adjustment required: add an adjustment row in the corrections UI and create a JIRA ticket with category `finops:ledger-correction`. Attach evidence refs.
8. After fix, re-run the reconciliation job with the same snapshot_id + `--force-apply` and verify the export matches expected.

Dispute and correction policy
- Corrections window: 14 days after MONTHLY snapshot lock for automated edits. After 14 days, corrections require approval from FinOps and Infra Director.
- Evidence required: Terraform state key, instance lifecycle event, and metrics blob covering the disputed period. Partial evidence may be accepted for developer errors but requires approver sign-off.
- Adjustment auditing: all manual adjustments create an immutable log entry that includes approver, reason, and evidence refs.

Retention and export
- Daily diffs: retained 30 days in S3.
- Monthly authoritative snapshots: retained 12 months in both BigQuery and an archived S3 path with access controls.
- Full export format: compressed Parquet with columns matching the ledger schema and a companion manifest.json listing evidence files.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: Infra Capacity Team (team slack: #infra-capacity).
- Document owner: Aisha Khan (aisha@redwood.ai).
- FinOps contact: Priya Natarajan (priya@redwood.ai).
- Oncall: rotation visible in /confluence/eng-infra/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations.

Appendix: SQL & CLI snippets
-- Example SQL to compute monthly credits per tenant (BigQuery-like syntax)
SELECT allocated_to AS tenant, SUM(CAST(ledger_credits AS FLOAT64)) AS gpu_credits
FROM `redwood-prod.ledger.credits_monthly`
WHERE run_date = DATE('2026-01-31')
GROUP BY tenant
ORDER BY gpu_credits DESC;

-- Query to find drifted instances
SELECT r.resource_id, r.allocated_to, r.sku, r.observed_gpu_hours, i.cloud_state
FROM `redwood-prod.ledger.credits_latest` r
LEFT JOIN `redwood-prod.inventory.cloud_instances` i USING(resource_id)
WHERE ABS(CAST(r.observed_gpu_hours AS FLOAT64) - i.reported_gpu_hours) / NULLIF(i.reported_gpu_hours,0) > 0.05;

-- Example kubectl command for logs
kubectl -n infra exec -it reconciliation-job-<snapshot_id> -- /bin/bash -c "cat /var/log/reconcile.log | sed -n '1,400p'"

Appendix: Terraform example (module contract)
```
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.git//modules/gpu-pool"
```

payload.page_title: GPU burst resiliency crediting model and IaC integration

sections.body:
Summary

This document defines a resilient GPU bursting and crediting model, the operational rules for applying it at tenant and fleet levels, and the recommended Terraform/IaC integration patterns and CI/CD gating to ensure safe rollouts. The design balances cost predictability, fairness across tenants, and SLO preservation during transient load spikes.

Purpose

- Provide a single canonical definition for GPU burst credits and the capacity floor used by Redwood’s multi-tenant GPU allocator.
- Describe how credits are earned, consumed, and reconciled across billing windows.
- Show concrete Terraform module changes and CI/CD checks required to deploy policy updates.
- Offer an on-call runbook for bursting incidents (exceeded credits, noisy tenant throttles, and preemption storms).

Scope

This applies to: hosted API tenants, Dedicated pools with shared bursting, and ephemeral test/eval pools. It does NOT change reserved capacity contracts or Dedicated strict isolation modes where bursting is disabled.

Background and motivation

We operate a heterogeneous GPU fleet with a mix of on-demand, reserved, and spot-backed capacity. To maximize utilization and reduce wasted reserved capacity, Redwood supports a burst mechanism that allows tenants to temporarily exceed their steady-state allocation. Without strict rules, bursting can cause noisy-neighbor issues, exceed provider quotas, and create unstable latency SLOs. The crediting model ensures bursts are constrained, auditable, and reversible.

Key concepts

- Capacity floor: guaranteed baseline vGPU/slice per tenant (steady-state allocation).
- Burst credit: a consumable budget (measured in GPU-credit-seconds) that lets a tenant exceed their floor for limited time.
- Replenishment window: rolling 24-hour window when credits regenerate.
- Throttle policy: ordered fallback actions when credits are exhausted (soft-degrade -> model fallback -> queuing -> hard-throttle).
- Fleet reservoir: an emergency global pool used for critical tenants or safety net during partial outages.

Design: credit accounting and formulas

1) Units: GPU-credit-seconds (GCS). 1 GCS = 1 GPU * 1 second at baseline utilization. We normalize multi-GPU instances and fractional multiplexing into equivalent GCS.

2) Baseline allocation: each tenant has an allocated baseline B (GCS/sec). Typical baseline examples: 0.05 GCS/s (light), 0.5 GCS/s (medium), 2.0 GCS/s (heavy).

3) Credit pool size (P) formula:

P = min(MAX_POOL, floor_multiplier * B * REPLENISH_WINDOW_SECONDS)
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- floor_multiplier = default 6 (configurable by tenant tier)
- REPLENISH_WINDOW_SECONDS = 24 * 3600 = 86_400
- MAX_POOL = 1_000_000 GCS (global per-tenant cap)

4) Consumption during burst:

consumed = sum_over_time((consumed_gpus(t) - B) * delta_t) for consumed_gpus > B

5) Soft recovery: if consumed < B, credits are replenished at a configurable reclaim rate (default 1.0x real-time up to the pool cap).

Policy tiers and knobs

- Free/Starter: floor_multiplier = 3; MAX_POOL = 50_000 GCS; soft-reclaim capped at 0.5x real-time.
- Professional: floor_multiplier = 6; MAX_POOL = 300_000 GCS; soft-reclaim 1.0x.
- Enterprise: floor_multiplier = 12; MAX_POOL = 1_000_000 GCS; soft-reclaim 2.0x; access to fleet reservoir subject to SLA.

Fleet reservoir behavior

- Reservoir is funded from idle capacity and admin allocations.
- Reservoir allocation is discretionary and requires an active ReservoirGrant policy binding (owner team: capacity-ops).
- Reservoir grants are time-limited (default 15 minutes) and require telemetry checks before and after grant (latency, GPU util, preemption rate).

Examples (calculation)

- Tenant A (Professional): B = 0.5 GCS/s => P = min(300_000, 6 * 0.5 * 86_400) = min(300_000, 259_200) => P = 259_200 GCS.
- If Tenant A runs 2.0 GCS/s for a sustained 30 minutes: consumed = (2.0 - 0.5) * 1_800 = 2_700 GCS => credits remaining = 256_500.

IaC / Terraform integration pattern

Guiding principles

- Policies are controlled through a dedicated Terraform module (module: gpu_burst_policy) and parameterized per-tenant via a tenant_env layer.
- Runtime decisions (enforcement) are made by allocator services reading the policy via the config store (e.g., Consul or SSM) that Terraform updates as part of deployments.
- All changes require automated policy-linting and a canary toggle for 1% of tenants before a fleet-wide rollout.

Recommended module (example)

Code: examples/terraform configuration

```
sections.heading: Where

sections.body:
module "tenant_gpu_burst_policy" {
  source        = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/tf-modules//gpu_burst_policy?ref=v2025.02"
  tenant_id     = var.tenant_id
  tier          = var.tenant_tier # starter | professional | enterprise
  floor_seconds = var.baseline_gcs_per_sec
  enabled       = true
  canary_pct    = 1
  labels        = var.labels
}
```
sections.heading: module usage for tenant policy

sections.body:
```
{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-123",
  "tier": "professional",
  "floor_gcs_per_sec": 0.5,
  "pool_gcs": 259200,
  "reclaim_rate": 1.0,
  "throttle_sequence": ["soft-degrade","model-fallback","queue","hard-throttle"],
  "canary_pct": 1
}
```

Terraform deployment checklist

1) Update module version and commit policy change in feature branch.
2) Run `terraform plan` and `policy-lint` (see policy-lint config below).
3) Create Dynamic Canaries: set `canary_pct=1` and route traffic via allocator canary flag.
4) Monitor canary for 30-60 minutes. If no regressions, gradually increase canary to 5% -> 20% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows.

policy-lint snippet (part of CI):

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
sections.heading: Policy manifest (JSON blob written to config store)

sections.body:
polylint --module module/tenant_gpu_burst_policy --rules ./ci/policy-rules.json
```

CI/CD gating and observability

- Every change to the module must pass unit tests (module-level), integration tests (using a local allocator mock), and canary smoke tests (in staging).
- Canary must exercise the throttle sequence: simulated spike causing soft-degrade, then model fallback and queue progression.
- Observability: dashboards should include per-tenant credit burn, credit remaining, throttle events, average latency P95/P99, and GPU preemption rate.

Required monitoring metrics and alerts

Table: key thresholds and alerts

| Metric | Normal / Threshold | Alert | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Credit burn rate (tenant) | > 80% of pool in 1h | Pager if > 90% remaining < 10% and latency > SLO | capacity-ops |
| Throttle event rate | > 5/min | Pager | oncall |
| Preemption rate (fleet) | > 3% / 10m | Pager + reservoir freeze | infra-sre |
| Canary regression count | any regression during canary | Block rollout | release-eng |

Operational runbook: bursting incident (short form)

1) Detection
   - Alert: tenant-credit-exhausted OR sustained throttle events.
   - Check dashboard: credit burn, credit remaining, throttle sequence, latency P95/P99.

2) Triage (5 minutes)
   - Identify tenant and tier.
   - Confirm burst source: production traffic, scheduled eval runs, CI jobs, or eval sandbox.
   - If caused by CI/eval: block job and reclaim credits.

3) Immediate mitigations (10–30 minutes)
   - Apply soft-degrade policy (reduce allowed concurrency / sample rate) via allocator admin API:
     curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://allocator.internal/api/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-123/actions -d '{"action":"force_soft_degrade"}'
   - If latency continues to spike and tenant is enterprise: request reservoir grant from capacity-ops.
   - If noisy neighbor and credits exhausted across tenants: toggle队列 (queue) + preemption shielding.

4) Recovery and reconciliation (30–120 minutes)
   - If credits used legitimately, check billing/export records and mark as chargeable overage.
   - If caused by runaway job, refund credits and add rate-limits to tenant CI config.

5) Post-incident
   - Create incident summary with root cause, changes to pool parameters, and recommended safeguards (guardrails, e.g., job-level GPU request limits).

Ownership and escalation

- capacity-ops: owns policy parameters, reservoir grants, and tier definitions.
- infra-sre: owns allocator service, preemption behavior, and fleet telemetry.
- release-eng: owns Terraform module and CI gating.
- customer-success/product: owns communication for any customer-visible overages.

Rollout plan for policy changes

1) Dev branch: update module and add unit tests.
2) Internal staging: deploy policy change with canary_pct=1 and steady-state synthetic load.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% with automated health checks.
4) Post-rollout audit: run credit-reconciliation for 48h and compare expected vs observed burn.

Backout/rollback guidance

- If canary fails or fleet-level regressions detected, revert Terraform to previous tagged module (git tag), set `canary_pct=0`, and run `terraform apply`.
- If rollback not possible quickly, apply runtime emergency knob: set global `bursting_enabled=false` via allocator admin API and notify affected tenants.

Safeguards and hard limits

- All tenant policies must have a MAX_POOL hard ceiling defined in the module (prevent runaway totals).
- CI pipelines that run evals must include a `gpu_quota` annotation; pipeline runners will be checked by admission webhook.
- Terraform module enforces ACLs: only release-eng and capacity-ops groups can change pool caps.

Appendix A: Example admin API snippets

```
sections.heading: policy-lint enforces numeric ceilings and required fields

sections.body:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"action":"force_soft_degrade","duration_seconds":600}' \
  https://allocator.internal/api/v1/admin/tenants/tenant-123/actions
sections.heading: force soft degrade

sections.body:
http POST https://capacity-ops.internal/grants Authorization:"Bearer $TOKEN" \
  tenant_id=tenant-123 duration=900 reason="emergency latency mitigation"
```

Appendix B: Minimal Terraform policy-lint rule example (ci/policy-rules.json)

```
{
  "rules": [
    {"id": "max_pool_ceiling", "type": "numeric_max", "field": "module.tenant_gpu_burst_policy.pool_gcs", "max": 1000000},
    {"id": "require_reclaim_rate", "type": "exists", "field": "module.tenant_gpu_burst_policy.reclaim_rate"}
  ]
}
```

Appendix C: Frequently asked questions

- Q: Can we disable bursting per-tenant?
  - A: Yes — set `enabled=false` in the tenant module. Reserved Dedicated tenants default to `enabled=false` to honor isolation contracts.

- Q: How do credits affect billing?
  - A: Credit usage is exported to billing every hour. Excess consumed by a tenant is either charged at the overage rate or reconciled per account agreement.

- Q: How are fractional GPUs accounted?
  - A: The allocator converts vCPU/slot multiplexing to equivalent GCS using a calibration table maintained by capacity-ops.

Related reading

- GPU demand forecasting and ML-backed scaling playbook (link in related_pages)
- Spot fallback autoscaler module and runbook (link in related_pages)

Contact and owners

- Primary owner: capacity-ops@redwood.internal (team lead: Marco Nguyen)
- Infra SRE on-call: see oncall rota in eng-sre team space
- Terraform module owner: release-eng@redwood.internal (Priya Desai)

Document history

- 2024-07-18: Initial draft by Asha Patel.
- 2024-09-03: Added reservoir grant flow and example API snippets (review: Marco Nguyen).
- 2025-02-12: Finalized Terraform canary rollout and CI policy-lint rules (review: Priya Desai).

payload.page_title: Capacity Sentry: SLA-driven GPU Rebalancer operator — design & deploy playbook

sections.body:
Summary

This playbook describes the Capacity Sentry operator: a lightweight, opinionated controller that monitors GPU pool health, enforces per-tenant SLOs, and triggers safe rebalancing actions across accounts/regions using Terraform-managed allocation primitives. It is meant to be a production-safe, auditable mechanism to reduce SLA incidents caused by capacity skew, noisy neighbors, and spot preemption waves.

Why we built Capacity Sentry

- Multiple customers experienced performance regressions during burst/spot events when capacity was unevenly distributed.
- Existing allocators are good at initial packing but lack continuous SLO-driven rebalancing and auditability for cross-account moves.
- We need an operator that integrates with our IaC modules and CI/CD guardrails so any reallocation is reversible and visible.

Goals and non-goals
sections.heading: Overview

sections.body:
- Detect capacity SLO drift per-tenant (latency P95, queue length, warm pool hit rate).
- Calculate safe rebalancing actions (move warm slots, drain/evict, increase burst budget).
- Apply changes via Terraform modules or orchestration APIs with a recorded change set.
- Provide playbooked runbook steps for oncall to verify and rollback.
sections.heading: Goals

sections.body:
- Not a replacement for long-term capacity planning/ordering.
- Not intended to perform mass node reclamations; actions are incremental and conservative.

High-level architecture
sections.heading: Non-goals

sections.body:
1) Capacity Sentry controller (K8s operator) — continuous loop reading telemetry, SLO engine, action planner.
2) Rebalancer action engine — uses our Terraform operator (tf-operator) to apply minimal terraform plans for allocation changes or calls the Burst Orchestrator service for runtime moves.
3) Audit store (S3 + event log) — records detected drifts, proposed plans, approvals, and applied changes.
4) Dashboard/alerting — Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager rules for SLO breaches and plan failures.
sections.heading: Components

sections.body:
- Telemetry -> SLO engine -> Action planner -> Plan preview -> (auto-apply / require-approval) -> Terraform or API call -> Audit log -> Telemetry verifies effect.

Service names and ownership

- capacity-sentry-controller (K8s deployment) — owner: eng-infra/gpu-fleet.
- tf-operator (existing) — owner: eng-infra/terraform-and-iac.
- burst-orchestrator (runtime move API) — owner: eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity.
- capacity-sentry-audit-bucket (s3) — owner: eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking.

SLOs and thresholds the operator enforces

- Per-tenant tail latency SLO: P95 <= 1200ms for interactive generation; alert at 1500ms.
- Queue length SLO: average queued requests <= 8 per minute; alert at 16.
- Warm pool hit rate SLO: >= 75% for reserved workloads; alert at 60%.
- Rebalancer action rate: <= 3 plan-applies per tenant per 24h (safety throttle).

Configuration (table)

- Pool selector labels: k8s labels used to identify candidate pools (e.g., node.kit=gpu, pool.tier=dedicated).
- Scoring weights: latency:0.5, queue:0.3, warm_hit:0.2.
- Max concurrent moves: 2 per region.
- Terraform plan approval mode: auto | manual | staged.

(Example configuration YAML)

apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1
kind: CapacitySentryConfig
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  poolSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node.kit: gpu
      pool.tier: dedicated
  sloTargets:
    latencyP95Ms: 1200
    queueMax: 8
    warmHitRatePercent: 75
  scoringWeights:
    latency: 0.5
    queue: 0.3
    warm_hit: 0.2
  maxConcurrentMoves: 2
  tfApplyMode: staged

Terraform / IaC integration patterns

- Use existing allocation modules: tenant-gpu-claim, warm-pool-provisioner. Capacity Sentry generates a minimal patch to the tenant-gpu-claim module (delta in vCPU/GPU units or burst budget) rather than replacing full state.
- Plan preview artifacts are stored in the audit S3 bucket with a digest and linked to the change request.
- Apply modes:
  - auto: controller performs terraform apply as long as plan has no breaking changes and action rate is below throttle.
  - staged: controller opens a PR to the tenant iac repository with the plan attached; CI runs tf-plan and policy checks; human approves to merge.
  - manual: controller only posts recommended plan to the dashboard for oncall to action.

CI/CD and release gating

- Operator image build pipeline: buildkite-gpu-pipeline -> image registry (signed).
- IaC PR gating: every staged change must pass terraform-policy (OPA) checks, unit tests in terra-test suite, and run tf plan in a sandbox account.
- Canary rollout: 5% of tenants (selector label canary=true) for 24h; monitor warm_hit_rate and P95 regressions.
- Rollback policy: automated rollback triggered if P95 increases by > 25% for canary or if warm_hit rate drops > 15%.

Runbook: common incident scenarios

1) SLO breach due to sudden preemption wave

- Symptoms: P95 spikes above 1500ms, queue grows > 16, warm hit rate drops below 60%.
- Immediate steps (oncall):
  1. Acknowledge alert and check capacity-sentry dashboard for active plans.
  2. If a plan is in-flight, check tf-operator logs: kubectl -n infra logs deploy/tf-operator | grep "capacity-sentry".
  3. If no plan, trigger emergency plan generation: POST /api/v1/sentry/plan?mode=auto&throttle_override=true (requires 2FA).
  4. Monitor plan apply: tail the audit log in S3 or use the dashboard link.
  5. If apply fails, revert using saved plan snapshot: tfcli apply --state-backup s3://capacity-sentry/backups/<plan-id>.
  6. Notify customers via status page if degradation > 30 minutes.

2) Failed Terraform apply in staged mode

- Symptoms: PR created but CI plan step fails OPA checks or sandbox plan shows drift.
- Steps:
  1. Inspect PR and policy failures.
  2. If policy failure is false positive, add an exception following the policy-exception process (see related page: terraform-policy-exceptions).
  3. If drift indicates a broader infra issue, pause further automated plans: kubectl annotate deployment capacity-sentry-controller infra.redwood.ai/paused=true.

3) Rebalancer oscillation (flip-flop moves)

- Symptoms: multiple opposite plans for same tenant within 4h.
- Steps:
  1. Increase action cooldown for the tenant: kubectl patch capacitysentryconfig default --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/maxConcurrentMoves","value":1}]'.
  2. Mark tenant as manual-mode until human review.
  3. Run forensic comparison of telemetry to detect noisy neighbor root cause.

Safety controls and rate limits

- Global action throttle: 10 plan-applies per hour across all tenants.
- Per-tenant cooldown: 24h by default after a plan is applied.
- Drift severity classification: informational / warning / critical determines auto-apply eligibility.
- Policy checks: every generated plan runs OPA policies and a terraform-diff validator to ensure no destructive node deletions unless explicitly required and approved.

Observability and telemetry
sections.heading: Data flows

sections.body:
- capacity-sentry: SLO heatmap, per-tenant scorecard, active plans list.
- rebalancer-playbook: recent plan outcomes, tf-operator success rate, apply latency distribution.
sections.heading: Dashboards to create

sections.body:
- capacity_sentry_tenant_score (tenant,score)
- capacity_sentry_active_plans_total
- tf_operator_plan_apply_success_total
- warm_pool_hit_rate{tenant}

Alerting rules (examples)
- alert:CapacitySentry_Tenant_SLO_Breach
  expr: capacity_sentry_tenant_score < 0.6 for 5m
  severity: page
- alert:TerraformPlanApply_Failure
  expr: increase(tf_operator_plan_apply_failures_total[10m]) > 0
  severity: ticket

Operational play: escalation matrix

- First responder (oncall infra): own the dashboard and initial mitigation.
- Secondary (gpu-fleet engineer): investigate tf-operator or runtime move failures.
- Tertiary (platform reliability): pause operator and coordinate cross-account interventions.

Ownership and rollout plan

Phase 0 (Q4 2025): prototype in staging with canary tenants; limited to non-critical accounts.
Phase 1 (Q1 2026): staged mode for all tenants with human approval via IaC PRs.
Phase 2 (Q2 2026): enable auto mode for low-risk tenants and burst budgets.

Checklist before production enablement

- [ ] OPA policies written and tested for tenant-claim module.
- [ ] Audit S3 bucket and lifecycle policy in place.
- [ ] CI gating for tf-plan sandbox runs.
- [ ] Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager rules added.
- [ ] Oncall runbook training and short game-day executed.

Appendix: example tf patch (pseudo)

module "tenant_claim" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-terraform//tenant-gpu-claim?ref=stable"
  tenant_id = "tenant-123"
  gpus_allocated = 12 // previous 8 -> delta +4
  burst_budget = 600 // seconds
}

Commands quick reference

- Check controller logs: kubectl -n infra logs deploy/capacity-sentry-controller -f
- List active plans: curl -sS https://sentry.internal/api/v1/plans | jq .
- Force a staged PR: curl -X POST https://sentry.internal/api/v1/plan -d '{"tenant":"tenant-foo","mode":"staged"}'

References and related pages

- terraform-and-iac/gpu-allocator-operator-terraform-primitive-spec (terraform primitives we patch)
- runbooks/gpu-provisioning-contracts-and-sla-alignment-playbook (SLA mappings)
- cloud-accounts-and-networking/gpu-mesh-egress-iac-and-cicd-gatekeeping (cross-account apply constraints)

Document maintenance

- Owner: eng-infra/gpu-fleet (Elliot Chen).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major preemption incident.
- When updating: bump last_updated and add changelog entry to audit S3 with plan-id.

Feedback

If you find false positives in the scoring, file an issue in the infra jira under component=capacity-sentry and add label triage-capacity.
